• fruitful; nor is it said what land it compasses, because it waters the land of promise nearby, and could easily be known by the people who would read these things
2.15:
**“And the Lord God took man,”** — he took flesh
**“and put him into the paradise of pleasure, to dress it,”**
• so that he might fill the Church from all nations
• man, paradise, for pleasure; or God, man, by making him just
**“and to keep it.”**
• man, paradise, so as not to lose it; whence: “Those whom thou gavest me have I kept”
• And the Lord God took, etc. AUGUSTINE. He has already said that man was placed in paradise. Now he sums up for what he was placed: “to dress it,” etc. For it is not believable that God condemned him to labour before sin; but we see some farming for pleasure, which was greater then, when nothing adverse befell from heaven or earth. But he had given man the means of working as much as would satisfy his will, not as much as need would force. For the working of providence is twofold: natural and voluntary. Natural, through God’s hidden governing; voluntary, through the working of angels or men. According to the first, shrubs and animals are conceived and born, heavenly and earthly things set in order; according to it come about the things done by an inward and natural movement. According to the other, men teach, learn, farm and the like. In the human body too a natural working goes on, by which the human body naturally comes to be, grows and ages; but by the voluntary it is cared for. The soul too naturally lives and feels; voluntarily it learns and consents. But God creates all creatures good and orders all wills justly. It is believable, then, that man was placed in paradise to work not laboriously but delightfully, and that great and useful things should put the mind of a prudent man in mind. “And to keep it”: that is, perhaps, so that what he did in the earth by farming he should keep in himself by discipline; that as the field obeyed the one who tilled it, so he should obey God commanding, namely that, having received the command, he should yield the fruit of obedience, not the thorns of disobedience. But because he would not, he was condemned and received a field like himself, which yielded thorns and thistles. Or “to keep” paradise, that he should not commit anything for which he ought to be expelled. Whence he received a command too, by keeping which, that is, by observing which, he would not lose it. For he is said not to have kept his property who acts so as to lose it, even if it is safe for others. But above all it is to be said that God should work and keep man himself. Man works the earth, not to make it be earth, but tilled and fruitful; and God works man, whom he created to be man, that he may be just, if he does not depart from him through pride. For “the beginning of the pride of man is to fall off from God.”
• And put him, etc. ISIDORE. MYSTICALLY. From what is added, “and to keep it,” it is hinted what kind of working it would be: because in the peace of the blessed life, where there is no death, all working is keeping what you hold. A command was given that they should take of every tree of paradise, but not of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; that is, he should not so enjoy it as to break the prohibition by claiming for himself the wholeness of his own nature.
*Gregory:* In the Morals, book 18. “And the Lord God took man and put him in paradise,” etc. It is to be weighed that good things cannot profit if the evils that creep in are not guarded against; for all that is done perishes unless it is carefully kept in humility. Whence: “to dress it and to keep it,” etc. For he dresses who does the good that is commanded; but he does not keep what he dresses when what is forbidden creeps in. So we must always do good things, and guard ourselves carefully in thought from those very good works, lest, if they lift up the mind, they be not good, since they fight not for their author but for pride. From books too that are not canonical, but put out for edification, we bring a witness: Eleazar, striking an elephant in battle, laid it low, but fell under it. For there are those who overcome vices but, being proud, sink under them.
*Jerome:* “And the Lord God took man and put,” etc. For “pleasure,” the Hebrew has Eden. So the Seventy here have now interpreted Eden as pleasure. But Symmachus, who had earlier translated it “a flowering paradise,” here put “delightfulness” or “delights.”
2.16:
**“And he commanded him, saying: Of every tree of paradise thou shalt eat:”**
• that is, use every virtue for living blessedly
• And he commanded him, etc. AUGUSTINE. He was forbidden a tree which was not evil, so that the very keeping of the command should be good for him, and transgression evil. Nor is it better seen how great an evil disobedience is than when man became guilty because, being forbidden, he touched a thing which, had he touched it unforbidden, he would not have sinned. For if, being forbidden, you touch a poisonous herb, punishment follows; and if no one had forbidden it, it would follow likewise. But if a thing is forbidden to be touched which harms not the one touching but the one forbidding, like another’s money, the forbidding is there because it is harmful to the one forbidding. But when a thing is touched which neither harms the one touching if it is not forbidden, nor anyone else if it is touched, why is it forbidden, unless that the good of obedience and the evil of disobedience may be shown by itself? The sinner sought only not to be under God’s lordship, when he committed that from which the command of the Lord alone ought to have dissuaded him, so that God’s will should be set before man’s. The Lord commands; let the servant do what he commands. It is a great profit to man that he serves God, who by commanding makes it profitable. One’s own will lies open to a great fall if, lifting itself up, it sets itself before God’s will. Having experienced this, man learned what lies between the good of obedience and the evil of disobedience.
*Augustine:* It is asked whether he commanded this to the man alone or to the woman too. It is written: “The Lord commanded Adam, saying.” It is not said “he commanded them.” And there is added: “Of every tree of paradise thou shalt eat,” not “ye shall eat”; “but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil thou shalt not eat”; he did not say “ye shall not eat.” Afterwards he speaks in the plural: “In what day soever thou shalt eat of it, thou shalt die the death.” Perhaps because he was going to make the woman, he so commanded that it should reach the woman through the man. Whence the Apostle: “If they would learn any thing, let them ask their husbands at home.”
**“And he commanded him, saying”** — “Of every,” etc. If it is asked how he spoke these things, it cannot properly be grasped by us. For it is certain that he speaks either through his own substance or through a creature subject to him. But through his own substance he speaks only for creating all creatures, and for enlightening spiritual ones when they can now grasp the speech which is in the Word of God. But to those who cannot grasp it he speaks through a creature: either a spiritual one, as in ecstasy or in dreams by a likeness of bodily things, or a bodily one too, when he appears to the bodily senses in some form or by a sounding voice. If, then, Adam could grasp the speech of God which he gives the angels through his own substance, he moved his mind for the moment in a wonderful and unspeakable way. But if there was still need of the authority of a holier creature by which he should know God’s command, as for us the prophets and angels, God spoke to him through some creature in words he would understand. And afterwards they heard the voice of God walking in paradise, not through his very substance but through a creature subject to him.
*Augustine:* It is asked how they could speak, or understand one speaking, who had not learned it by growing up among speakers or by teaching. But God had made them such that they could speak and learn from others.
*Augustine:* It is said of Christ: “Before he know, through good or evil, he shall refuse the evil and choose the good.” How does he either refuse or choose what he does not know? These two are known in one way through the prudence of good, in another through the experience of evil. Through the prudence of good, evil is known and not felt; for one holds to good so that evil is not felt. Through the experience of evil, good is known; for he who has fared badly when the good was lost feels what he has lost. So the child, before he knew by experience the good he would lack or the evil he would feel when the good was lost, refused the evil so as to love the good; that is, he would not lose what he had, so as not to feel, by losing it, what he ought not to lose.

**“But of the tree”** — as if: do not corrupt the middle place, by which you are under God and over the creature
**“of knowledge of good and evil,”** — of one’s own choice, which is set in the middle for knowing good and evil; whoever, leaving the grace of God, tastes of it shall die the death, deprived of the blessed life
**“thou shalt not eat. For in what day soever thou shalt eat of it, thou shalt die the death.”**
• Symmachus better: “thou shalt be mortal”
• deprived of the blessed life
• For in what day soever, etc. He does not say “if thou eat, thou shalt be mortal,” but “thou shalt die the death.” For man died in the soul when he sinned, because God, who is the life of the soul, departed from him; which the death of the body followed, the soul, which is the life of the body, departing from it; which happened to Adam when he ended the present life. It can be understood thus: that when they sinned, they were at once punished with that death of which it is said, “Unhappy man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” and elsewhere, “The body indeed is dead because of sin.” He does not say mortal but dead, though mortal because it would die. It is not to be believed that those bodies were so before sin; but though natural, not yet spiritual, yet not dead, that is, such that they must necessarily die, which came about on the day of the transgression.
**“But of the tree of knowledge of good and evil”** — AUGUSTINE. The tree took its name from what followed. For we would not feel evil except by experience, because there would be none had we not done it; for evil is not a nature, but the loss of good is so called. But if they had been obedient and had not sinned against the command, it would still have been called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, because this would happen if it were wrongly taken. But they say: how would man understand that the tree was of the knowledge of good and evil, who knew nothing at all of the use of evil? But contraries are known from contraries, as we judge emptiness from fullness and hearing from silence; so from the life that was in him the lack of life, which is now called death, could be known. And the life was sweet which they would avoid losing; nor would sin be urged on them unless it were first said that they would not die of it, that is, would not lose what they loved.
**“thou shalt die the death”** — A twofold death is signified: of the soul, God departing, who is its life; or of the body, which he received at the end of life. But at once he incurred the necessity of dying.
2.18:
**“And the Lord God said:”** — Augustine: perhaps by voices in time; or the very reason was recalled which was in the Word of God first of all
**“It is not good for man to be alone:”** — because in the man taken up the Church is joined to God
**“let us make him a help like unto himself.”**
• a woman, for bearing children
• And the Lord God said, etc. AUGUSTINE. Or perhaps he spoke in the mind of the man himself, as he speaks to certain saints within them, whence: “I will hear what the Lord God will speak in me”; or some revelation was made to the man himself by an angel, either in dreams or in ecstasy or otherwise, as to the prophets; or a voice sounded through a bodily creature, as from the cloud: “This is my beloved Son.” But if we do not know the manner, yet we do not doubt that God spoke. And if he spoke by a bodily voice, or by a likeness of a body expressed in time, he spoke not through his own substance but through a creature subject to him; as he was seen with a head white like wool, and below like fine brass. Let us understand, then, what he said: that eternal truth holds that a help like to man was to be made, and in it he hears who can know what was created and why. And the help was to be made for the begetting of children, as the earth is a help to seed, so that a plant may be born of both. Whence: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth,” etc. This reason for joining did not fail even after sin and punishment, by which the earth is full of men. Sent out of paradise, they came together and begot. But in paradise they could have had honourable marriage and an undefiled bed, without the heat of lust, without the labour of giving birth; not that sons should succeed fathers who were dying, but that, while these remained in some state of form and took vigour from the tree of life, the sons too should be brought to the same state, until, the number being filled, the natural bodies should pass without death into another quality, in which they would wholly serve the ruling spirit and live by the spirit alone giving life, without bodily food. Why then did they not come together in paradise? Because as soon as the woman was created the transgression took place and they were cast out of paradise. For how long a time there was between their being made and Cain’s being born Scripture does not say. Or because God had not yet commanded them to come together, and divine authority could be waited for where desire did not press. But God had not commanded it because he foreknew their fall, from which the mortal human race was to be propagated. But if parents had to give place to children so that a fixed number should be filled by successions, they could, when children were born and the justice of human duty was fulfilled, be carried over to better things not through death but through some change: either that highest one, by which, receiving their bodies, they would become holy like the angels in heaven, or some lower one, by which they would have a better state than this body has; or as the things made before: the man from the slime of the earth, the woman from the man’s flesh. For it is not to be thought that Elias is now as the saints will be when they have received their reward, nor as men who are still living. But if anyone thinks that Elias could not have deserved this if he had taken a wife and begotten children (for he is believed not to have had them, because Scripture did not say so, though it said nothing of celibacy either): Enoch, having begotten sons, pleasing God, did not die but was translated. In the same way Adam and Eve could have been translated. For if Enoch and Elias, dead in Adam and bearing in their flesh the offspring of death, from which they are believed about to return to this life so as to die, are yet now in another life where, before the resurrection of the flesh, before the natural body becomes spiritual, they fail neither by sickness nor by old age, how much more would it be given to the first men, if they had not sinned, that when children were born they should give way to a better state, whence, when the world was ended, they should be changed with all their posterity into the angelic form, not through death but through the power of God. So the woman was made for the sake of begetting, which is not to be taken away. For with God virginity excels, because, since a most plentiful supply is at hand for filling the number of the saints, lust does not claim for itself what the need of receiving offspring no longer requires. Weakness too, prone to a fall into shame, is caught by the honour of marriage; and what is a duty for the healthy is a remedy for the sick. Incontinence indeed is an evil; but marriage, by which the incontinent are joined, is not therefore not good; nor is this good blameworthy because of that evil, but that evil is pardonable because of this good. For the good of marriage cannot be sin, that is, faith, offspring, sacrament. Faith, that there be no coming together with another man or woman, because of the marriage bond; offspring, that it be lovingly received, fed, and brought up religiously; sacrament, that the marriage be not separated, and that the man or woman put away be not joined to another, not even for the sake of offspring. This is the rule of marriage, by which the fruitfulness of nature is adorned and the wickedness of incontinence ruled.
*Augustine:* Those who hold that it was not lawful in paradise to come together to beget children perhaps think that all marriage is sin. Those who do not do so, but hold that the fruitfulness of the flesh was given by God for the succession of mortality, do not agree that the first men could have lain together except after sin. But if successors can rightly be sought for those who will die, partners are more rightly sought for those who will live. And they were indeed natural, but would not die had they not sinned, and would receive the angelic form and heavenly quality; when they sinned, a deadly sickness was at once conceived in their members; for even if the body was not yet spiritual but natural, it was not yet of this death, of which and with which we are born. Why then should we not believe that before sin they could command their members of generation for begetting, as the others which the soul has in any work without any trouble or itch of pleasure? Why too should it seem unbelievable that God made such bodies that, had they not sinned, they would command those members as they do their feet, and neither sow with heat nor bring forth with pain? But after sin they deserved the motion of that law which fights against the law of the mind, which marriage orders and continence forbids; so that, as from sin came punishment, so from punishment may come merit. Whoever doubts, then, that the woman was made for the man, from the man, in that sex, in that form and with that distinction of members by which women are known, who bore Cain and Abel, is forced to change all that we believe. And what more just than this punishment: that the body should not serve the soul at its every nod like a servant, as the soul itself would not serve its Lord? Whether both come from the parents, body from body and soul from soul, or the soul is made in some other way.
2.19:
**“And the Lord God having formed out of the ground all the beasts of the earth, and all the fowls of the air, brought them to Adam to see what he would call them:”** — Augustine: by the nod by which he made them, or through angels, so that they should thus understand their lord
**“for whatsoever Adam called any living creature the same is its name.”** — Brought them, etc. Not as hunters or fowlers do; nor was a voice of command made from a cloud, which rational souls are wont to understand; for beasts and birds do not naturally understand this; but through the ministry of angels, who grasp in his Word what ought to be done and when. For every soul, even the irrational, is moved by commands; but the rational consents or not by the choice of its will; the irrational, which has not this, is driven according to its kind when touched by the command. And when commands are carried out by angels, God’s command reaches not only men, cattle and birds but fishes too, as the whale which swallowed Jonas; and not only these greater ones but even the little worm. It is not said of the fishes that Adam gave them names, but it is believable that, as they were gradually known, names were given according to the difference of nations. But it is to be noted that he did not say “the flying things being formed from the waters,” but from the earth, according to the general use of the word earth by which it is said, “God who made heaven and earth,” etc.; by which whatever was created, whether from the dry land or from the waters, is understood to have been created from the earth.
*Jerome:* It seems that the first language of the human race was Hebrew, because it is agreed that the names which we read in Genesis up to the dividing of tongues are of that language.
2.20:
**“And Adam called”** — in the Hebrew tongue, which alone existed before the confusion of the tower
**“all the beasts by their names, and all the fowls of the air, and all the cattle of the field: but for Adam there was not found”** — among all the living creatures brought to him
**“a helper like himself.”**
• the Apostle: “We are God’s helpers”; these were not found before Christ’s falling asleep
• And Adam called, etc. AUGUSTINE. MYSTICALLY. Signifying that the nations which would be saved in the Church through Christ would receive the name of Christ, which they had not before. Whence: “I will call my servants by another name.”
**“but for Adam there was not found a helper, etc.”** — AUGUSTINE. We must see how the forming of the woman, which is mystically called a building, was done. The angels can create no nature; so neither can they form the rib into a woman, nor the filling of flesh in the place of the rib; not that they do nothing for something to be created, but they are not therefore creators, as neither are farmers of crops or trees. For God alone, that is, the Trinity, is creator. So the woman was made by God, even if the rib was ministered by angels; as a man was made from a woman without any intercourse, when the seed of Abraham was ordained by angels in the hand of a mediator. But it is asked whether the reason which God created together with the first works held that according to it the woman must be made from the man’s side, or only that she could be. But that it should necessarily be done so was not already made there, but hidden in God. The most just course of all nature has natural laws, according to which both the spirit of life, which is created, has its desires bounded in a way which even an evil will cannot pass, and the elements of the bodily world have their fixed force and quality, what each can or cannot do, what can or cannot be made from what. Above this natural course the Creator has it in himself to make from all things something other than their natural reason holds: that a dry rod should suddenly flower and bear fruit, that a woman barren in youth should bear in old age, that an ass should speak, and the like. But God gave natures that these things too could be made from them, not that they should have them in their natural movement. And he has in himself the hidden causes of certain things to come or done, which he did not put into the things made; and he fulfils them not by the work of providence by which natures subsist so as to be, but by that by which he governs as he willed those which he made as he willed. So of all the things which were done to signify grace, not by the natural movement of things but wonderfully, the hidden causes were in God. One of which was that the woman was made from the side of the sleeping man; she was made strong through him, because from his bone; he weak for her sake, because not a rib but flesh was filled in. The first making of things, when it was said on the sixth day, “male and female he created them,” did not hold that the woman should be made so, but that she could be; so that he should not do anything with a changeable will against the causes which he willingly established. So the ecstasy is rightly understood to have been sent for this: that the mind of Adam, sharing in the angelic court and entering the sanctuary of God, should understand the last things. Whence, waking, he uttered with a prophetic spirit: “This now is bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh”; and though Scripture says these words were Adam’s, Christ in the gospel declares that God said them, so that we may understand that through that ecstasy Adam said these things by God’s power.
**“for Adam there was not found a helper”** — No faithful just man can be made equal to Christ. For he is “beautiful above the sons of men.” For no one could free the human race except himself. Whence: “No man was found worthy to open the book, and to loose the seals thereof,” etc.
*Mystically:* “But for Adam,” etc. The woman was made as a help to the man because there was still something to be done: that not only should the soul rule the body, but also the manly reason should bring under itself its natural part, through which help it commands the body. After the pattern of this the woman was made, whom reason subjected to the man; so that what appears more plainly in two, that is, in male and female, may be considered in one: that the mind should keep subject the desire of the soul through which we work by the bodily members, that is, rule its helper justly. It is shown to man too how far he is above the beasts, which, brought to him, he distinguishes by name and discerns by the judgment of reason. But this understanding is easy; that one harder, by which he understands that the rational which rules is one thing, the natural which is ruled another. In which it is given him to discern irrational movements and, with grace working with him, to bring them under the lordship of reason.
2.21:
**“Then the Lord God cast”** — the Father
**“a deep sleep”** — through the death of the cross
**“upon Adam:”** — namely Christ
**“and when he was fast asleep,”** — for the sake of a mystery the woman is not formed from the earth as the man was
**“he took one of his ribs,”** — the Church is strong in Christ
**“and filled up flesh for it.”**
• because Christ was weak for the Church
• others: he put flesh in its place, namely Christ dying for the Church
• Cast … God, etc. ISIDORE. MYSTICALLY. These things cannot be seen with bodily eyes; but the more anyone withdraws, as if falling asleep, from visible things to the secrets of the understanding, the better and more purely he sees. So the very knowledge by which it is known that reason, which commands, is one thing, and the natural part, which obeys, another, is as it were the making of the woman from the man’s rib, to signify their joining. That each may rule this part and become as it were married in himself needs perfect wisdom, whose contemplation is secret and removed from the sense of the body, which is understood by the deep sleep. For then the man is most rightly the head of the woman, when Christ is the head of the man. In the place of the rib he put flesh, not so that flesh should signify fleshly desire, but the affection of love with which each loves his own soul and is not hard so as to despise it; for each loves that over which he is set. So Adam called his wife as the stronger the lesser, and said: “This now is bone of my bones,” etc. Bone of bones because of fortitude, and flesh of flesh because of temperance. These two virtues belong to the lower part of the soul, which rational prudence rules. Whence this part of the soul is called virago, as derived from vir, man. But what follows, “Wherefore a man shall leave father and mother,” etc., is a prophecy to be referred to the sacrament of Christ and the Church.
*Augustine:* Those who think that soul comes from soul as flesh from flesh say that God made one soul by breathing into the face of the man, so that from it the others should be created, since Adam was formed first, then Eve. And it has been said whence he had body and soul; but it is not said of her that she was given a soul by God’s breath, as if both were drawn from the man, who already had a soul. But if they think the woman’s soul came from the man’s soul because it is not written that God gave her a soul by breathing, why do they believe she was given a soul from the man, when this too is not written? But if God made all souls as he made the first, Scripture was silent about the others because what was done in one could be understood of the rest. For if something else were done in the woman than in the man, so that the soul should be drawn from flesh that had a soul, and not, as in the man’s case, the body from one source and the soul from another, Scripture ought not to have been silent about what was done otherwise, lest we should think it done as we had already learned. So because it did not say the woman’s soul was made from the man’s soul, it hints that nothing else is to be thought than had been said of the man.
*Augustine:* If it is asked whence Christ received his soul, I would rather hear better and more learned men; yet according to my grasp I answer more willingly: not from Adam rather than from Adam. If we say that Levi was in Abraham not according to the soul but only according to the flesh, Christ was there, who according to the flesh is from Abraham, and so he too was tithed. What then is the difference between the priesthood of Christ and the Levitical? Because Levi was tithed by Melchisedech? Unless because it is necessary that in some way Christ was not there. For according to the flesh he was there, according to the soul he was not. So the soul of Christ is not from the stock of the transgression. But it is to be said: although no one’s soul is in his father’s loins according to the flesh, yet in Abraham’s loins Levi was tithed and Christ not tithed, because Levi was there according to the seminal reason, by which reason he would come into his mother through intercourse; according to which Christ’s flesh was not there, although Mary’s flesh was there according to it. For Levi is born of flesh by desire; Christ according to the bodily substance alone. In Abraham was tithed that which was being healed, not that from which it was healed. But if it is said that, as he could be there according to the flesh and not be tithed, so according to the soul: the answer is, if what was said of the flesh could be done with the soul, then the soul of Christ is from the stock in such a way that it did not contract the stain of the transgression. But if it could not be from there without guilt, it is not from there. But as to the other souls, whether they are from the parents or from above, let those prevail who can; I am still moved between the two, sometimes this way and sometimes that. And I would pronounce all the defences of reasons equal or nearly equal on both sides, did not the view of those who think souls are created from the fathers outweigh it on the baptism of little ones, about whom what could be answered has not yet occurred to me.
*Morally:* GREGORY. In the Morals, book 80. “The Lord God cast,” etc. We do not reach the summit of contemplation if we do not cease from the burden of outward care; nor do we gaze on ourselves so as to know that within us the rational which rules is one thing and the natural which is ruled another, unless, running back to the secret place of silence, we are lulled to sleep from outward disturbance. Which Adam sleeping well figured, from whose side the woman soon came forth. For he who is caught up to understand inward things closes his eyes to visible things, and then understands that in himself there is one thing which ought to rule, as the man, another which is to be ruled, as the woman.
2.22:
**“And the Lord God built”** — the Church is the temple of God, begotten through the sacraments coming out of his side
**“the rib which he took from Adam into a woman: and brought”** — through faith
**“her”** — the Church
**“to Adam.”** — Christ
2.23:
**“And Adam said: This now is bone of my bones,”**
• because among the rest he did not find a help like himself, and because he knew they were not from his own substance but from the waters and the earth
• because the Church is the body of Christ, according to the Apostle, made of his flesh, that is, of the weak, and of bones, that is, of strong members
**“and flesh of my flesh;”** — in ecstasy, by the spirit of prophecy, he understood that a rib had been taken from him and the woman formed
**“she shall be called woman,”** — it fits likewise in Hebrew, because from is, which is “man,” issa, that is, “woman,” is said. Theodotion supposed another derivation, saying: “and she shall be called taking,” because she was taken from the man; for issa, by a difference of accent, also sounds as “taking”
**“because she was taken out of man.”**
• from Christ’s side
• as from Christ the name Christian was given to the Church
2.24:
**“Wherefore a man shall leave father”**
• the Word was made flesh
• taking the form of a servant
• I came forth from the Father and am come into the world
**“and mother,”** — the observance of the synagogue, which is Christ’s mother according to the flesh
**“and shall cleave to his wife:”** — that is, the Church
**“and they shall be two”** — Christ and the Church
**“in one flesh.”**
• because Christ and the Church are one body
• And … built, etc. “Wherefore a man shall leave,” etc. ISIDORE. MYSTICALLY. What was fulfilled historically in Adam signifies by prophecy Christ, who left his Father, that is, did not appear to men as he is with the Father; and his mother, that is, the fleshly observance of the synagogue, of which he was born according to the flesh; and clove to his wife, that is, the Church, so that they are two in one flesh; for he is the head of the Church and she his body; who was lulled in the sleep of the passion so that his spouse, that is, the Church, might be formed. Whence: “I have slept and have taken my rest,” etc. So the Church was formed from his side, that is, by faith in the passion and by baptism, because from his side came out blood and water. And he was made of the seed of David according to the flesh, as from the slime of the earth, when there was not a man to till the earth, because no man worked in the virgin of whom Christ was born. A spring rose out of the earth and watered the face of the earth: the face, that is, the dignity of the earth, is the Lord’s mother, whom the Spirit watered so that from such slime that man should be made who was set in paradise, that is, in the will of the Father, to dress and keep it, namely to fulfil and preserve it. For we have received the command in him who said: “As long as you did it to one of these my least, you did it to me.” The tree of paradise signifies spiritual delights; the fruit of the Spirit is joy, peace and the like. We must not touch the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; that is, we must not grow proud of the nature which is a middle thing for us, lest, deceived, we experience the difference between good and evil, namely between the Catholic faith and the deceits of heretics. For so we come to the knowledge of good and evil. For “there must be also heresies, that they also who are approved may be made manifest.” For the serpent foreshadows the poisons of the heretics.
2.25:
**“And they were both naked:”** — of the veil of double-dealing
**“to wit, Adam and his wife: and were not ashamed.”**
• because they felt no movement of the flesh
• because without spot or wrinkle
**“And they were both naked”** — AUGUSTINE. If by the words of God or of any prophet something is said which seems absurd according to the letter, and is therefore said figuratively, yet it is not to be doubted that it was said for a meaning. But the bodies of the two people in paradise were naked and they were not ashamed, because they had felt no law in their members fighting against the law of the mind, which followed disobedience. They thought nothing needed covering, because they had felt nothing that needed reining in.
*Isidore:* MYSTICALLY. “And they were both naked,” etc. That they were naked and not ashamed signifies simplicity of soul and chastity. Whence: “For I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ. But I fear lest, as the serpent seduced Eve, so your minds should be corrupted,” etc. The serpent signifies the devil, who is not simple. Whence there follows: “Now the serpent was more subtle than any of the beasts,” in which his cunning is signified. Paradise is the blessed life, in which the serpent was not, because he was already the devil. That speech is hidden temptation, as he came to Judas persuading him to betray Jesus, since he entered into his heart. But the man who dwells in paradise drives him back; but he is deceived through the woman, because our reason is not led to consent unless delight has been stirred in some part of the soul which ought to obey reason as its ruling husband; nor does anyone slip into sin otherwise. In the serpent is the suggestion; in the woman, lust; the consent of reason, in the man. So desire was stirred; the woman was persuaded. If reason consents to persuading lust, man is driven out of the blessed life as out of paradise, and sin is imputed even if the deed does not follow, because in consenting the conscience is held guilty.

3.1:
**“Now the serpent”** — allegorically, the devil, or heretical error
**“was more subtle”**
• because full of the demon
• because the children of darkness are wiser in their generation than the children of light
• Jerome: in the Hebrew there is arom, which Theodotion and Aquila translated “wicked” or “shifty”
**“than any of the beasts of the earth which the Lord God had made. And he said to the woman:”** — the devil or the heretic deceives not Christ but the Christian
**“Why hath God commanded you, that you should not eat of every tree of paradise?”**
• ALCUIN. As if: why do you flee the hidden knowledge? Seek out new things, and pierce into the knowledge of evil and good; whence: “Stolen waters are sweeter.”
• Now the serpent was more subtle, etc. AUGUSTINE. Others have “most prudent,” said in a transferred sense. Some copies have “most wise,” not properly, as the wisdom of God or of the angels or of the rational soul is usually taken in a good sense, but as we call bees or ants wise because of works that imitate wisdom; though the serpent could be called most wise not by a rational soul but by the devil’s spirit, because the evil angels, cast down by pride, are by nature more excellent than all beasts because of the eminence of reason. So it is no wonder if the devil, filling the serpent with his spirit, as he used to fill soothsayers, had made it the wisest of all the beasts living by a living and irrational soul. Yet wisdom is said in an evil sense as astuteness is in a good one, since in Latin the wise are properly taken in a good sense, the astute as ill-minded. Nor is it to be thought that the devil chose the serpent through which to tempt; but when he wished to deceive, he could do so only through the animal through which he was allowed. For the will to harm is in each from himself, but the power from God.
• And he said to the woman, etc. AUGUSTINE. The woman’s transgression is without excuse, because she remembered God’s command. Yet forgetting one command, and so necessary a one, would be the fault of damnable negligence. But the transgression is greater from this, that she remembered the command, and God is despised in it as if present.
• They say: he should have made man such that he would not will to sin at all. We grant that a nature which would not will to sin at all is better. Let them grant that that nature is not evil which was so made that it could not sin if it willed, and was justly punished, since it sinned by will, not necessity. Since, then, this is good and that better, why should he not make both, so as to be praised more richly for both? For that one is in the holy angels, this in holy men.
• But what sane man would say: Better that he should not create one whom he foreknew would be corrected by another’s wickedness, than that he foreknew would be condemned for his own wickedness? That is to say: Better that one should not be who would be crowned by another’s evil being mercifully used for good, than that an evil one should be who would be justly punished for his own evil.
• They say: could he turn their will to good? Since he is almighty, he could. Why did he not do it? Because he would not. Why would he not? He knows. We ought not to be more wise than it behoveth. But I think it no small good that there should be a rational creature which, by comparison with the evil, guards against evil; which kind of good creature would not exist if God turned all wills to good and inflicted no punishment on any wickedness, and there were only the kind which would profit by no comparison of sin and punishment. He foresees that there will be good and evil, and creates them, giving himself to the good to enjoy, and bestowing much even on the evil.
• Why hath … commanded, etc. STRABO. The crafty enemy asks this, and recalls the command of God, so that when she has sinned she may have no excuse, as if she had forgotten.
• Some try to take the nature of the devil away from God’s creation and give it another principle against God, not understanding that all that is, is good, and cannot be from another; that the evil will is moved disorderly by putting lower goods before higher; by which power of the rational creature the spirit, delighted, swelled and fell, and wastes away with envy. Yet in him this is good: that he lives and quickens a body, whether airy, as the devil’s, or earthly, as man’s.
• This question about the blessed life, whether one has it when it is uncertain whether it will last or misery will follow, can be raised about the first man. For if he foreknew his sin and punishment, he could not be blessed; so he was not blessed in paradise. But if he did not foreknow it, how was he truly blessed, being through this ignorance uncertain of that blessedness? If he was certain by a false hope, how was he not foolish? But of a man set in a natural body, to whom, if obedient, the fellowship of the angels was to be given and the change of the body from natural to spiritual, we can in a way understand a blessed life even if he did not foreknow his future sin; as neither did those of whom it is said, “You, who are spiritual, instruct such a one in the spirit of meekness,” etc.; they were blessed because they were spiritual, not in body but by justice. How much more, then, was man blessed before sin, though uncertain of his fall, who rejoiced in the reward of the future change in such a way that there was no tribulation for patience to fight against. For though not certain of an uncertain thing by vain presumption, as a fool, but by a hope not faithless, he could be blessed, less than in the life of the holy angels.
• It can be thought, not in vain, that the devil fell from the beginning of time, and never lived at any time at peace and blessed with the holy angels, but soon fell away. Whence: “He was a murderer from the beginning, and he stood not in the truth,” so that we may understand that he did not stand in the truth from when he was created, who would have stood had he willed. For how was he blessed among the angels who did not foreknow his future sin and punishment? But it is asked why he did not. For the holy angels are not ignorant of their eternal blessedness, nor uncertain of eternal life. Perhaps God would not reveal to the devil what he would do or suffer, but willed to reveal it to the others, because they would remain in the truth. But he was not equally blessed, indeed not fully blessed, because the fully blessed are certain of their blessedness. But how was he set apart from the others, so that God would not reveal to him what concerned him, since he is not an avenger before one is a sinner? For he does not condemn the innocent. Or are they of another kind of angels, to whom God did not give foreknowledge about themselves? But how can they be blessed to whom their blessedness is uncertain? For some have held that the devil was not in that lofty nature of the angels which is above the heavens, but among those made lower in the world, distributed in offices; for perhaps something unlawful could delight such, which delight they would restrain by free choice if they would not sin; as man, above all the first, who did not yet have the penalty of sin in his members.
• But here it is to be asked whether, delighted by his own power, he departed from the beginning from that fellowship and charity of the good angels, or was at some time just and blessed in the holy company of angels. For he is said to have fallen because he envied man, made to the image of God; but envy follows pride. For the cause of envying is pride, which is the love of one’s own excellence; but envy is hatred of another’s happiness. For he who loves excellence envies either equals, because they are made equal, or superiors, because he is not made equal to them, or inferiors, lest they be made equal. But when pride cast the devil down, so that by a depraved will he perverted his nature, good in itself, Scripture does not say; but reason shows that from this he envied man.
• But to say of angels that in their own kind they could be blessed while uncertain of damnation or salvation, with no hope that they would at some time be certain in that change for the better, is too great presumption; unless perhaps it be said that they were so created, distributed in worldly ministries, that for things rightly done they should receive a blessed life of which they could be most certain, and be called blessed in hope of it; if the devil fell from among these, it is like men falling from the justice of faith by a like pride. But let those who can assert two kinds of angels: one of those above the heavens, in which he who fell never was; the other of the worldly ones, in which he was. But I do not see whence they assert it.
*Strabo:* Now the serpent, etc. The devil spoke through the serpent, which did not understand, as he does through the possessed or the frenzied; for whomever he seizes he takes away understanding and reason. But the good Spirit makes all whom he fills with grace seeing and understanding; whence: “The spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets.”
*Augustine:* Some are troubled that God allowed Adam to be tempted, as if they did not see that all are tempted daily by the snares of the devil, which God allows, perhaps because virtue is tried and exercised, and it is more glorious not to have consented than not to have been able to be tempted; since even those who consent give the just an example of avoiding desire and the swelling of pride. In vain then is it said: God should not create those whom he foreknew would be evil. For he knew they would profit the good and would be justly punished for their evil will. Someone says: if God willed, these too would be good. But he willed better, that they should be what they willed. But the good would not be without fruit, and the evil would not be unpunished, and by that very fact they would be useful. But he foreknew that their will would be evil; he foreknew it surely, because his foreknowledge cannot be deceived; it is not therefore his will but theirs. Why then did he create those whom he foreknew would be such? Because he foresaw what good he would make of their evils. For he so made them that he left them something to do; and if they did anything blameworthily, they would find him working praiseworthily concerning them. From themselves they have the evil will; from him a good nature and a just punishment and the place due to them; for others, a help of exercise and an example of fear.
*Gregory:* In the Morals, book 24. “Why hath … commanded,” etc. The enemy of the human race does the same daily: he strives to pluck the words of God out of men’s hearts and to lighten the threats, and invites them to believe what he falsely promises. For he invites them to temporal things, so as to lighten the eternal punishments which God threatens. Promising the glory of the present life, he says: Taste, and you shall be as gods; touch temporal desire, and appear lofty in this world; and when he tries to remove the fear of the divine sentence, he says in a way: “Why hath God commanded you?”
*Augustine:* It is asked why God allowed man to be tempted, whom he foreknew would be deceived. But it would not be praiseworthy for man if he could live well only because no one urged him to live badly, since he had it in his nature to be able, and in his power to will, not to consent, God helping. So he was rightly allowed to be tempted who was going to do something by his own will through fault and to be set in order by God’s equity through punishment; so as to show the proud soul, for the instruction of those to come, how rightly God would use the evil wills of souls, while they used good natures perversely.
*Augustine:* Nor is it to be thought that man would have been cast down unless there had gone before in him a certain lifting-up which had to be pressed down, so that through the humiliation of sin he should know what he had falsely presumed of himself, and that a nature does not fare well if it departs from its Maker. For it is made known what a good God is when it goes well with no one to depart from him.
*Augustine:* But it is to be thought, not in vain, that he fell from the very beginning of the creation, that is, from the beginning of time or of his making, and never stood in the truth. Whence some think he was not bent into this malice by free choice, but was created in it by God, according to the saying, “This is the beginning of the ways of God, which he made, that he may be mocked by his angels,” and elsewhere, “This dragon which thou hast formed to play with it”; as if he were made evil, envious and a devil from the first, not depraved by his will. But God made all things very good; though they try, not unlearnedly, to show that not only in the first making but even now, when so many wills have been depraved and turned away, all things created are, in sum, equally very good; not that the evil are good, but that by malice they do not bring it about that the order of the whole is broken in any way under God’s rule, since even evil wills have fixed limits of power and weights of merit. But because it is unjust that God should condemn in anyone, for no merit, what he created, it is to be believed that not the nature but the evil will is to be punished; nor is his nature signified when it is said, “This is the beginning of the ways of God,” etc., but the airy body which he fitted to such a will, or the very ordering by which he made him useful to the good even against his will; or that, foreknowing he would be evil by will, he yet made him, foreseeing how much he would make of him by his goodness. He is called the beginning of the ways not because he was made first or made evil in the beginning, but because, knowing he would be evil by will so as to harm the good, he created him so that from him he might profit the good. For thus he is mocked, when his temptation profits the saints. The beginning, for mocking, because evil men too, whom God foreknew or foresaw would be, he yet created for the profit of the saints. Likewise he is mocked when caution is given to the saints by comparison with them, and humility under God, and exercise in bearing with the evil, and trial in loving enemies. But he is the beginning because he goes before in age and in leadership of malice. And this God does through the holy angels, as he governs created natures, subjecting the evil angels to them, so that they can do not as much as they strive but as much as they are allowed, as also evil men. So what is thought, that the devil never stood in the truth, never led a blessed life, but fell from the beginning, is not to be taken so that he is thought to have been created evil by the good God; for then he would not be said to have fallen from the beginning. For he did not fall if he was made such; but, made, he at once turned himself away from the truth, delighted by his own power. So he did not taste the sweetness of the blessed life, because he did not disdain it after receiving it, but lost it by not willing to receive it. So he could not foreknow his fall, because wisdom is the fruit of godliness. And he fell at once, not from what he had received but from what he would have received had he been willing to be subject. But what Isaias says, “How art thou fallen, O Lucifer, who didst rise in the morning,” etc., and Ezechiel, “Thou wast the seal of resemblance,” etc., some fit him, more fit his body.
*Gregory:* The devil tempted our first parent in three ways: by gluttony, vainglory and avarice; and he overcame him. By gluttony, when he urged him to eat the forbidden food; by vainglory, when he said, “You shall be as gods”; by avarice, when he added, “knowing good and evil.” For there is an avarice of height too, when loftiness is sought beyond measure; whence: “He thought it not robbery to be equal with God.” But by the second Man he was overcome in the same ways by which he boasted he had overcome the first. For the rest see below: “The serpent deceived me.”
*Gregory:* Sin is committed in three ways: by suggestion, delight and consent; the first through the enemy, the second through the flesh, the third through the spirit. For the enemy suggests evil things, the flesh yields itself to delight, at last the spirit consents to the delight. Whence too the serpent suggested evil things; Eve, as the flesh, yielded herself to delight; but Adam, as the spirit, overcome by suggestion and delight, assented. So by suggestion we recognise sin, by delight we are overcome, by consent we are bound.
3.4: **“And the serpent said to the woman: No, you shall not die the death.”** — heretics promise immortality
3.5:
**“For God doth know”** — heretics profess the merit of godhead, and deceive by the promise of knowledge, and rebuke the simple
**“that in what day soever you shall eat thereof, your eyes shall be opened:”** — he wishes to close the eyes of the heart, so as to open the fleshly ones
**“and you shall be as Gods,”** — by the promise of height and knowledge he deceives the simple
**“knowing good and evil.”** — You shall be as gods, etc. STRABO. He puts the words together with artful guile, so that if he could not overthrow her by the contempt of disobedience, he might at least boast himself victor in this, that he had corrupted faith and urged her to idolatry; but if he led her astray by the contempt of disobedience, he might stand victor in both.
*Mystically:* The woman, being asked, answered what had been commanded. But he said: “No, you shall not die the death. For God doth know,” etc. It is plain from these words that the sin was urged through pride, because it was said, “You shall be as gods. For God doth know,” etc. Where it is noted that they were persuaded only so far as that they would not be under God, but in their own power, so as not to keep the law of him, by obeying, who envied them ruling themselves, not needing his inward light but using their own foresight, as their own eyes, to see the good and evil which he had forbidden. So they were persuaded to love their own power too much; and because they willed to be equal to God, using their middle place badly, by which, being subject to God, they had bodies subject to them, as the fruit of the tree set in the midst of paradise, they lost what they had received, because they seized what they had not received: namely to be blessed by their own power, God not ruling them. For God alone is blessed by his own power, with no one ruling him.
3.6:
**“And the woman saw”** — looking round to see if she could see anything harmful in it
**“that the tree was good”** — the woman, that is, our fleshliness, is deceived by the serpent’s words, and through her Adam, that is, the spirit
**“to eat, and fair to the eyes, and delightful to behold: and she took”** — the woman
**“of the fruit thereof, and did eat,”** — the fleshly are more easily led astray
**“and gave to her husband who did eat.”**
• because reason is led astray by the delights of fleshly desire
• And … saw, etc. ISIDORE. How did they see if their eyes were closed? But it was said so that we may understand that the eyes were opened after they ate of the fruit, by which they saw themselves naked and were displeased with it, that is, the eyes of cunning, to which simplicity is displeasing. For when anyone has fallen from the inmost light of truth, he has nothing by which he would please in his pride except deceitful pretences; for hence hypocrisy is born, in which those seem very clever who have been able to deceive whom they would.
*Gregory:* And the woman saw, etc. So as not to dwell in slippery thought, we ought not to look on what it is not lawful to desire. For that the mind may be kept clean in thought, the eyes, as it were robbers leading to fault, are to be kept and checked from wanton pleasure. Eve would not have touched the tree unless she had first looked carelessly. We must weigh, then, how much we who live mortally ought to restrain our sight from unlawful things, when even the mother of the living came to death through the eyes. Hence, in the voice of Judea (which, desiring outward things by seeing them, had lost the inward goods), the prophet says: “My eye hath wasted my soul.” For desiring visible things she lost invisible virtues, and through the eye of the body she suffered the plundering of the heart. So to guard the cleanness of the heart, the outward discipline of the senses too is to be kept.
3.7:
**“And the eyes of them both were opened:”**
• perverse, because simplicity seemed shameful
• to desire and to the knowledge of the beastly movement
**“and when”**
• feeling the beastly movement
• by making
• by feigning
**“they perceived themselves to be”** — heretics: that they were naked of the simplicity of faith
**“naked,”** — of the grace of God
**“they sewed together fig leaves,”** — coverings of lying, which signify the itch of the flesh and the heat of lust
**“and made themselves aprons.”**
• girdles or breeches
• with which they seek to gird, that is, to defend, themselves
*Isidore:* MYSTICALLY. “And gave to her husband who did eat, and the eyes of them both were opened,” etc., of which it has been spoken. Then they saw that they were naked, namely with perverse eyes, to which nakedness, that is, simplicity, seemed something to blush at. So, that they might not be simple, they made themselves girdles covering their shame, that is, hiding the simplicity at which cunning pride blushed. The fig leaves signify the itch which the mind suffers from the desire and delight of lying; whence those who love jesting are called false, because pretence rules in jests. So when the Lord walked in paradise, that is, when he came to judge them, before the punishment he walked, that is, the presence of God was moved in them, because they were not steadfast in the command. “At the afternoon air,” or according to others “toward evening,” namely when the sun set for them, and the inward light of truth. “They heard his voice and hid themselves.” He hides himself from the sight of the Lord who forsakes him and begins to love what is his own. They already had the coverings of lying; but he who speaks a lie speaks of his own. Therefore they are said to hide themselves at the tree which is in the midst of paradise, that is, at themselves, who had been set below God and above bodies. So they hid themselves at themselves, so as to be troubled by wretched errors, having left the light of truth, which they themselves were not. For the human soul can share in it, but the truth itself, God, is unchangeable, above it; whoever turns away from it and turns to himself is darkened by lying. For he who speaks a lie speaks of his own, and is troubled, according to the saying: “My soul is troubled within myself.”
*Augustine:* “Who did eat, and the eyes of them both were opened,” etc. Namely to desiring one another, to the penalty of sin, conceived by the death of the flesh, so that the body should be not only natural but also of death, in which the law of the members fights against the law of the mind. For they had not been made blind, nor had they plucked the forbidden fruit by groping; but as in the breaking of bread the disciples’ eyes were opened and they knew him whom they could not know, so their eyes were opened to what they had not been open to before, because the rational soul blushed at the beastly movement in its flesh and was ashamed, not only because it felt what it had not felt before, but also because that shameful movement came from the transgression. For there it felt, where grace was unknown, since in nakedness it suffered nothing unseemly. There was fulfilled: “O Lord, in thy favour, thou gavest strength to my beauty. Thou turnedst away thy face from me, and I became troubled.” For this trouble they ran to figs or fig-tree leaves and sewed themselves girdles, and those who had left glorious things covered shameful ones. Nor do I think they thought there was anything in the leaves fitting for covering the itching members; but by a hidden instinct they were driven to it by their trouble, so that such a signification of the penalty should be made by those who did not know it, which would convict the sinner by the deed and teach the reader by the writing.
**“they sewed together fig leaves”** — ALCUIN. Because they lost the glory of simple chastity, they fled to the double itch of lust; whence: “When thou wast under the fig tree, I saw thee,” and I came down (understand) to set thee free.
3.8:
**“And when they heard”** — through preachers
**“the voice of the Lord God”** — because they did not stand in his command
**“walking”**
• not standing or dwelling
• through a creature subject to him
**“in paradise”** — the Church
**“at the afternoon air,”** — charity growing cold, and the light declining, and their darkness drawing near
**“hid themselves”** — turning himself away from the truth
**“Adam”** — reason
**“and his wife”** — desire
**“from the face of the Lord God,”** — namely forsaking God and loving what is their own
**“amidst the trees of paradise.”**
• having left the middle place in which they had been made
• Amidst paradise he hides himself who, turned away from his Creator’s command, lives by the will of his own error and choice.
*Augustine:* And when they heard, etc. For it was fitting that such should be visited at that hour, because they had fallen away from the light of truth. For perhaps God spoke to them before inwardly, in ways that can or cannot be told, as to the angels, enlightening their minds with unchangeable truth, where there is the understanding to know together whatever things are not done together through times; perhaps, I say, he spoke to them so, and if not with as great a share of divine wisdom as the angels receive, yet less according to human measure; but perhaps also in that kind of speech which comes about through a creature, either in ecstasy of the spirit by bodily images, or to the very senses of the body, some form being presented to be seen or heard, as is wont to happen with angels, and to be heard in a cloud. But now that they heard the voice of God walking was done only through a creature, lest the invisible substance, wholly everywhere, which is of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, be believed to have appeared to the bodily senses by a movement in place and time.
*Augustine:* Hid … himself, etc. When God turns away his face inwardly and man is troubled, things like madness are done, from too great fear and shame, a hidden instinct too not resting, so that unknowing they should do things that would signify something to those after them, for whose sake these things were written.
**“at the afternoon air”** — Whence Christ, who was crucified at the sixth hour, gave up the spirit at the ninth hour, so that man should be restored at the same hour at which he was cast out of paradise.
3.9:
**“And the Lord God called Adam,”** — he calls him so that he may return by penance, because he desires not the death of the sinner
**“and said to him:”** — the words of one rebuking and driving to confession, not of one who does not know
**“Where art thou?”** — as if: in how great misery
*Augustine:* And the Lord God called Adam. Namely rebuking, not not knowing. And this belongs to the signification: that as the command was given to the man, through whom it should come to the woman, so the man is questioned first. For the command came from the Lord through the man to the woman, but sin from the devil through the woman to the man. And these things are full of significations, not by the doing of those in whom they were done, but by the wisdom of God doing it concerning them; but now we are not setting out the things signified but defending the things done.
3.10:
**“And he said: I heard thy voice in paradise; and I was afraid, because I was naked, and I hid myself.”**
• foolishly, as if he who had been made so were displeasing naked
• he does not hide so that the Lord should not see his crimes, but to show himself unworthy of his sight. For they were pressed by a double shame: because now for the first time they felt an obscene movement in their members, and because they felt this had happened because of the transgression
• I heard thy voice, etc. AUGUSTINE. HISTORICALLY. It is probable that a human form was wont to appear to the first men through a fitting creature; whom yet, lifting them to higher things, he did not let notice their nakedness, except after sin, when they had felt the shameful movement in their members by a law of punishment. So they were affected as men are wont to be under the eyes of men; which was the penalty of sin: to wish to hide from him from whom nothing can hide, and to conceal the flesh when he looks into hearts. But wishing to be as gods, they became vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened. And God turning away his face, they were made foolish; they blushed indeed at themselves and made girdles, but they feared still more to be seen even girded by him who, as by a familiar tempering, brought as it were human eyes to see, through a visible creature. For he appeared thus so as to speak to men as a man, as to Abraham at the oak of Mambre; by this friendship he burdened their shame after sin, which before had given them confidence. Nor did they dare to show to such eyes the nakedness which displeased even their own. So the Lord, unwilling to punish the sinners except with the penalty by which they were forced to blush, says: “Who told thee that thou wast naked, but that thou hast eaten,” etc. For from there death, conceived by the sentence of God who had so threatened, made them notice their members with desire, where their eyes are said to have been opened; and there followed what would shame them.
*Isidore:* MYSTICALLY. “I heard thy voice,” etc. He answers that, having heard his voice, he hid because he was naked. Now he answered foolishly, as if he were naked displeasing to God, who had made him naked. But what displeases each, he thinks displeases God. But what is said is to be understood loftily: “Who told thee,” etc. He was naked of pretence but clothed with divine light; turned away from which and turned to himself (which signifies having eaten of that tree), he saw his nakedness and was displeased, because he had nothing of his own. And in the manner of pride he does not accuse himself for having consented to the woman, but throws the blame back on her; and out of the cunning he had conceived he turns back on God what he had sinned; whence he added: “The woman, whom thou gavest me,” etc. It is proper to sinners to want to put on God what they are accused of; which comes from this, that man so sinned that he wished to be equal to God, namely free, like him, from all lordship. So since he could not be equal to him in majesty, he strives to make him equal to himself in sin; indeed he wants to show him guilty and himself innocent. But the woman puts the blame on the serpent, as if he had forced her to obey, or as if she could hear the serpent’s words and not obey the command.
*Gregory:* And God called Adam. Because he saw him fallen into fault, now under sin, as if hidden from the eyes of truth, because he does not approve the darkness of his error, as if he did not know where the sinner is, he calls him and seeks him, saying: “Adam, where art thou?” By calling he signifies that he calls him back to penance; by seeking he suggests that he does not know sinners rightly condemned.
3.11: **“And he said to him: And who hath told thee”** — that is, who brought you to this unshapeliness, except that you did not keep my command?
3.12:
**“And Adam said: The woman, whom thou gavest me to be my companion,”** — not humbly confessing but proudly excusing himself, and turning the blame back on the woman’s maker
**“gave me of the tree, and I did eat.”** — And Adam said: The woman, whom thou gavest, etc. AUGUSTINE. He does not say “I have sinned.” For pride has the ugliness of confusion, not the humility of confession. And this was written, and the questions were asked, so that they should be written truly and profitably, that we may know how the proud labour today, trying to put evil on their Creator and to take to themselves whatever good they do. “The woman, whom thou gavest me to be my companion,” etc.: as if she had been given for this, that she should not obey her husband, and both of them God.
*Gregory:* In the Morals, book 4. “The woman, whom thou gavest,” etc. Sin is committed in four ways in the heart, completed in four in deed. In the heart: by suggestion, delight, consent, and the boldness of defending. Suggestion comes through the adversary, delight through the flesh, consent through the spirit, the boldness of defending through pride. For the fault which ought to have frightened the mind lifts it up. Whence too the serpent urged, Eve delighted, Adam consented, who even when questioned would not, through boldness, confess his fault. So daily the hidden enemy suggests; Eve, that is, the fleshly sense, lays herself under delight; Adam, set over the woman, consents, because the spirit, that is, reason, weakened from uprightness, is bent down. Adam, questioned, would not confess his fault, because the spirit, by sinning separated from the truth, by that very fact sinks more wickedly into the boldness of its ruin. Adam had fled through fear to hide himself, yet in fearing he swelled. For when punishment is feared from sin and the lost face of God is not loved, the fear is from swelling, not from humility. For he is proud who does not forsake sin, if he could do it unpunished. In the same four ways sin is completed in deed: first the hidden fault is done; afterwards it is laid open even without shame; then it is drawn into habit; at last it is fed by the deceit of false hope or by the obstinacy of wretched despair.
3.13:
**“And the Lord God said to the woman: Why hast thou done this? And she answered:”** — likewise proudly excuses herself and throws the blame on the serpent’s maker
**“The serpent deceived me, and I did eat.”**
• AUGUSTINE. “And the Lord God said to the woman.” Nor does she confess sin, but puts it on another; in an unequal sex, with equal haughtiness. Yet David, born of these, says until the end of the world: “I said: O Lord, be thou merciful to me: heal my soul, for I have sinned against thee.” This should have been said by them; but the necks of sinners still remained unbroken: the labours and pains of death, and the crushing of the world, and the grace of God, which comes to help in its time, teaching the afflicted not to presume on themselves. “The serpent deceived me,” etc.: as if anyone’s persuasion should prevail over God’s command.
• But here it is to be asked whether, delighted by his own power, he departed from the beginning from that fellowship and charity of the good angels, or was at some time just and blessed in the holy company of angels. For he is said to have fallen because he envied man, made to the image of God; but envy follows pride. For the cause of envying is pride, which is the love of one’s own excellence; but envy is hatred of another’s happiness. For he who loves excellence envies either equals, because they are made equal, or superiors, because he is not made equal to them, or inferiors, lest they be made equal. But when pride cast the devil down, so that by a depraved will he perverted his nature, good in itself, Scripture does not say; but reason shows that from this he envied man.
*Augustine:* “The serpent deceived me.” How would she believe from these words, namely “For God doth know that in what day soever,” etc., that God had forbidden them a good and useful thing, unless there was in her mind that love of her own power and proud presumption about herself, which was to be shown up or destroyed by the temptation? Then, not content with the serpent’s persuasion, she looked at the tree, good to eat and fair to see; and not believing that she could die of it, she perhaps thought God had said for the sake of some meaning, “If you eat, you shall die the death.” So she ate, and gave to her husband, perhaps with some persuasion which Scripture has left to be understood. Or perhaps there was no need to persuade him, since he did not see that she had died from that food.
*Augustine:* It is to be noted that the devil was not allowed to tempt the woman except through the serpent, nor the man except through the woman. For he used the serpent as an instrument, moving its nature to utter the sounds of words and signs by which he would show his will. But in the woman, who was rational, it was not he who spoke but his persuasion, though by an instinct he helped inwardly what he was doing outwardly through the serpent. So the serpent neither understood the words nor was made rational. For that serpents are drawn from their lairs by the words of the Marsi is a power of the devil, which is allowed in memory of the first deed, so that it may be known that he has a familiarity with this kind. The serpent was called most subtle because of the devil’s cunning. And it spoke as Balaam’s ass did; but this was devilish, that angelic. For good and evil angels work in a like way, as did Moses and Pharao’s magicians.
*Alcuin:* The angel’s sin is passed over in silence, man’s laid open, because that one is incurable, this one has been cured.
*Strabo:* “And … saw,” etc. She is openly shown to be without excuse, who was free, with such deliberation, to notice the enemy’s wiles.
3.14:
**“And the Lord God said to the serpent:”** — the devil, who creeps secretly; for as he spoke through the serpent, so he is cursed in the serpent
**“Because thou hast done this thing, thou art cursed among all cattle, and beasts of the earth: upon thy breast”**
• pride, because in the breast the onrush of the mind rules
• in which are guile and snares
**“shalt thou go, and earth”**
• in the Hebrew it has asphar, that is, ashes or dust
• sinners
• earthly works
**“shalt thou eat all the days of thy life.”**
• while you have the power of deceiving
• And the Lord God said, etc. This whole sentence is figurative; where yet it is to be believed that all the things were said. The serpent is not asked why it did it, because it did not do it by its own will and nature, but the devil did it concerning it and through it and in it, who had already been destined to the eternal fire for his impiety and pride. So what is said to the serpent is referred to him, and it is shown what he will be to the human race.
• Upon thy breast shalt thou go, etc. JEROME. The Seventy added “belly,” but the Hebrew has only “breast,” to lay open the craftiness and cunning of his thoughts, that is, that his every step is of wickedness and fraud.
*Mystically:* “And the Lord God said to the serpent.” The serpent, not questioned, receives punishment first, who can neither confess nor has anything with which to excuse himself. “Upon thy breast shalt thou go,” etc.; according to another edition, “On breast and belly shalt thou creep,” which is noticed in the snake, and from it the speech is figured toward the invisible enemy. By the breast it signifies pride, in which the onrush of the mind rules; by the belly, fleshly desire, which is the softer part in the body; and because he creeps by these on those he wishes to deceive, it is said, “On breast and belly shalt thou creep, and earth shalt thou eat all the days of thy life,” that is, all those over which you have power before the last punishment of judgment; for he rejoices and glories in this life. And “earth shalt thou eat” is understood in two ways: either, those whom you deceive with earthly desire will belong to you; or a third kind of temptation is figured, which is curiosity. For he who eats earth goes into deep and dark things, and only temporal and earthly ones. Enmities are put not between the serpent and the man but the woman, because we are tempted by the devil only through the natural part, which in one man shows the image and pattern of the woman. Enmities are put between the seed of the devil and of the woman. The devil’s seed is evil suggestion; the woman’s, the fruit of good work, by which she resists suggestion. Therefore he watches the woman’s heel, so that if she slips into unlawful delight he may catch her; she watches his head, so as to shut out the very beginning of evil suggestion.
*Gregory:* In the Morals, book 20. “On breast and belly shalt thou creep.” The evil of lust is committed either in thought or in deed. For the enemy, when he is driven out of the doing of the deed, strives to defile the secret places of thought. He creeps on the belly when, slippery, he works lust in deed through the human members subject to him; he creeps on the breast when he defiles in thought. But because through thought one comes to deeds, he is described as creeping first on the breast and then on the belly.
3.15:
**“I will put enmities between thee and the woman,”**
• the natural part, by which he tempts
• the Church
• the human race
**“and thy seed”**
• evil suggestion and all wickedness
• original sin
**“and her seed:”**
• the fruit, which is Christ
• the fruit of good work
**“she”** — the Church
**“shall crush”** — when Christ rises again
**“thy head,”**
• which is death; whence: “Thou shalt walk upon the asp and the basilisk”
• the beginning of suggestion
**“and thou shalt lie in wait”**
• so as to catch her
• that is, you will trip Christ up so that he dies
**“for her heel.”**
• if she slips into unlawful things; or for the end, at which the devil lies in wait most of all
• I will put enmities between thee, etc. GREGORY. In the Morals. To crush the serpent’s head is to root out the beginnings of suggestion from the entrance of the heart with the hand of careful consideration; and when he is caught at the beginning, he strives to strike the heel, because whom he does not strike with the first temptation he aims to deceive at the end. But if the heart is corrupted in temptation, the middle and end of the following action are held by the enemy, because he sees the whole tree bearing fruit for him which he has spoiled at the root with the tooth of poison.
*Jerome:* “She shall watch thy heel, and thou shalt watch her heel.” The Hebrew has it better: “She shall crush thy head, and thou shalt crush her heel”; because our steps too are hindered by the snake, and the Lord shall crush Satan under his feet.
3.16:
**“To the woman”**
• the history is plain
• who signifies that part of the soul which rejoices in fleshliness
**“also he said: I will multiply thy sorrows, and thy conceptions: in sorrow shalt thou bring forth children,”** — by the difficulty of overcoming an evil habit
**“and thou shalt be under thy husband’s”** — of reason
**“power,”**
• through good habit
