• so that the spirit may rule the flesh
**“and he shall have dominion over thee.”**
• having overcome the evil habit, you will obey reason more carefully, lest you slip down into some ruinous habit
• To the woman also, etc. AUGUSTINE. HISTORICALLY. These things are better understood figuratively and prophetically. But because the pain and groaning of one in labour is from the body of death, which was conceived by the transgression, this punishment too is referred to the proper sense of the letter. But as for what is said, “Thou shalt be under thy husband’s power, and he shall have dominion over thee,” we must see how it can be taken properly. For even before sin she was so made that the man should rule her and she, turned to him, should serve. But it can be understood that this service is rather of condition than of love, so that even such service, by which men would afterwards serve men, is found to have arisen from the penalty of sin. So spouses can serve one another through charity; but the woman is not allowed to rule over the man; and unless this is guarded against, nature will be depraved and fault increased.
• I will multiply thy sorrows, etc. It is plain that the woman’s pains and sighs have been multiplied. But it is a great sacrament. For no one abstains from fleshly pleasure without suffering pains at the beginning, until habit is turned to better. But when he has come to this, a son as it were is born, that is, an affection ready for good through good habit; but first it struggled with pain against the evil habit. “Thou shalt be under thy husband’s power,” etc.: that is, when that part of the soul which rejoices in fleshly things, having suffered difficulty and pain, has willingly overcome the evil habit and brought forth a good one, it will obey the husband, that is, reason, more carefully, and serve him more gladly as he commands, lest it slip down into a ruinous habit. But the sentence given on Adam is plain, because no one escapes it. “Cursed is the earth in thy work.” For this very thing, that each one born on this earth suffers difficulty in finding the truth, he has from the corruptible body. For “the corruptible body is a load upon the soul”; hence pains and sorrows; these the earth brings forth for man. Thorns and thistles: the prickings of twisted questions and thoughts about providing for this life, which, unless they are rooted out and cast away, choke the word so that it does not bear fruit in man. He who tills his field suffers these until he returns to the earth from which he was taken, that is, until he ends this life.
3.17:
**“And to Adam he said: Because thou hast hearkened to the voice of thy wife, and hast eaten of the tree, whereof I commanded thee that thou shouldst not eat, cursed is the earth in thy work;”** — Jerome: not of tilling the country, but in sin, as the Hebrew has it
**“with labour and toil”** — of finding the truth
**“shalt thou eat thereof all the days of thy life.”**
• Cursed is the earth, etc. AUGUSTINE. HISTORICALLY. No one is unaware that these are the labours of the human race on earth; and it is agreed beyond doubt that they would not be if the happiness which was in paradise had been kept.
• With labour, etc. RABANUS. There were thorns before, but not so as to bring labour to man; for whom after sin they were for labour and affliction, as serpents too and whatever things are harmful were harmless before. And it is to be noted that an outward punishment is laid on Adam, “Cursed is the earth in thy work,” but an inward one on the woman, when it is said, “I will multiply thy sorrows,” etc., because, having been led astray, she led her husband astray.
*Strabo:* The earth is cursed, not Adam, so that all for whose sake these things were written should be frightened, lest doing the like they be struck with the like punishment. But Cain himself, because he added fratricide to the first transgression, is cursed, when it is said: “Now therefore cursed shalt thou be upon the earth,” etc.
*Alcuin:* He cursed the earth, not the waters, because man ate of the fruit of the earth against the prohibition, not drank of the waters; and in waters the sin contracted from the fruit of the earth was to be washed away. Land animals too have more of the curse than water ones, because they live more from the cursed earth. Hence Christ after the resurrection ate of a fish, not of a land animal.
*Gregory:* In the Morals. “Cursed is the earth in thy work.” God curses sinning man, and man is forbidden to curse. But cursing is spoken of in two ways: one is approved, the other disapproved; one comes from the judgment of justice, the other from the spite of revenge. The curse in the judgment of justice is “Cursed is the earth in thy work,” and what is said to Abraham, “I will curse them that curse thee.” But of that which comes from the spite of revenge it is said: “Curse not”; and elsewhere: “Railers shall not possess the kingdom of God.” Holy men too curse, not from desire of revenge but by the punishment of justice. For inwardly they gaze on the lofty judgment of God, and know with what curse the evils rising up outside ought to be struck; and they do not sin, because they do not disagree with the inward judgment of God. Hence Peter says: “Keep thy money to thyself, to perish with thee”; for by saying not “is” but “be,” he showed that he said it not in the indicative but in the optative mood. Hence Elias: “If I be a man of God, let fire come down from heaven and consume you”; yet the outcome showed that their sentence was spoken by reason of truth. For Simon perished in eternal damnation, and the flame burnt up the two captains of fifty.
3.18:
**“Thorns”** — of vices
**“and thistles shall it bring forth to thee;”** — the prickings of twisted questions and thoughts about providing for this life
3.19:
**“In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread till thou return to the earth,”** — that is, until you end this life
**“out of which thou wast taken: for dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return.”** — Dust thou art, etc. GREGORY. Man was so made that, while he remained, the times should pass away, and he should not pass with the times. So he stood amid the running moments, and did not tend toward the end of life by the adding of days, because he clung to him who always stands. When the forbidden thing was done and the Creator offended, he began to go with time. Whence: “Earth thou art, and to earth thou shalt go.” The state of immortality, namely, being lost, the course of mortality swallowed him; and passing toward death he learned, by standing, what he had been; the bitterness of whose root we hold as in the shoot, because by being born we take up his course, so that at the very moment in which we live we pass away from life, while infancy passes to childhood, childhood to adolescence, adolescence to youth, youth to old age, old age to death.
3.20:
**“And Adam called the name of his wife Eve:”** — that is, life
**“because she was the mother”**
• he gave the reason why he called her life
• the natural part, turned to reason, is the mother of the living, that is, of good works
**“of all the living.”**
• of things rightly done, to which sins are contrary, which are called dead
• And … called the name of his wife Eve, etc. AUGUSTINE. These were the words of the first man: “because this is the mother of all the living,” as if he gave the reason for the name he had given, namely why he called her Eve.
*Mystically:* After the sin and the judge’s sentence Adam called his wife Eve, because she is the mother of the living, though she had deserved to bear death and mortal offspring. But Scripture has in view those offspring which, when she has borne them in pain, she turns to her husband so that he may rule her. For so she is life and the mother of the living; life in sins is called death. So rightly the natural part, when through reason it has conceived from the word of life the affection of living rightly, is called life and the mother of the living, that is, of good things; although, resisting the evil habit with pain and groaning, it has brought forth a good habit for things rightly done, to which sins are contrary, which are wont to be called dead. But the death which is owed to nature after sin is figured in the garments of skins. And they were in paradise, though under the sentence of God condemning them, until it came to the garments of skins, namely the mortality of this life. And the death which we feel in the body is well expressed in skins, which are stripped from dead bodies.
3.21:
**“And the Lord God made”** — before he cast them out of paradise
**“for Adam and his wife, garments”** — by which is signified the death which was owed to nature after sin
**“of skins,”** — because mortal from mortals
**“and clothed them.”** — And the Lord God made, etc. AUGUSTINE. This too was done for the sake of a meaning; and in things done it is asked what was done and what it signifies, and in things said, what was said and what it signifies.
*Strabo:* They themselves made aprons to hide their sin; but God made garments of skins, with which he clothed their whole body, because he justly condemned them both in body and in soul. But it is a foolish question to ask how, or by whose working, the skins were drawn from the animals; for he who made all things from nothing made these how and in what way he willed.
3.22:
**“And he said: Behold”**
• these are not the words of God mocking but of God frightening others away from pride
• irony
• as if: he has neither gained what he wanted and has lost what he was made
**“Adam is become as one of us,”** — mention of the Trinity is pressed home
**“knowing good and evil: now, therefore,”**
• these are God’s words
• aposiopesis, which suits one angered and troubled
**“lest”** — that is, if
**“perhaps he put forth his hand,”** — when the number of the elect was filled, they were to taste of the tree of life and so pass to the blessed state; but a guard was set so that those who have been made unworthy should not touch it any further
**“and take also of the tree of life, and eat,”** — which was a sacrament for him
**“and live for ever.”**
• this is God’s action
• And he said: Behold Adam is become as, etc. AUGUSTINE. JEROME. The plural number is put because of the Trinity, as also there: “Let us make man,” etc. So it is turned back on the head of the proud man, to what end he had come, what was suggested by the serpent: “You shall be as gods.” Nor are they the words of God mocking, but frightening others away from pride, seeing that man was not made such as he wished, but lost what he was made. “Lest perhaps he take of the tree of life,” etc. The words before are God’s; but this was done, following upon God’s words: he was cut off from life, not only that which he would have received with the angels had he persevered, but from that which he had in paradise, as if excommunicated from the tree of life, which was a sacrament for him, as in the Church men are wont to be removed from the visible sacraments of the Church by discipline.
• Now, therefore, lest perhaps, etc. The Apostle says the like: “If peradventure God may give them repentance to know the truth.” But man seems to have been sent away into the labours of this life so that at some time he may stretch out his hand to the tree of life, that is, to the cross, through which eternal life is restored. The forbidding can also be understood as a just punishment, that after sin the way to wisdom is shut until, by the mercy of God, he who had been dead lives again.
*Augustine:* It is a wonder, if Adam was spiritual in mind though not in body, how he believed the serpent saying that God had forbidden the tree because he knew that if they ate they would become like gods by the knowledge of good and evil, as if the Creator grudged the creature this alone. But in no way is it to be believed that one endowed with a spiritual mind could believe this. Whence: “Adam was not seduced,” etc., so that the man transgressed through the woman, according to the saying, “after the similitude of the transgression of Adam.” Yet he was not seduced. Whence he does not say “the woman seduced me,” etc., but “she gave me, and I did eat.” But she says, “the serpent seduced me,” etc. So Solomon, a man of such great wisdom, did not believe there was any profit in the worship of idols, but could not resist the love of women, and did what he knew should not be done, so as not to sadden his deadly delights. So Adam would not sadden his wife, who, already seduced, had eaten, and whom he believed would pine away, estranged from him, and perish without comfort; not from the desire of the flesh, but from friendly goodwill, by which God is often offended lest a friend be offended. So he was deceived in another way than the woman, who thought the false true.
*Mystically:* “Behold Adam is become as one,” etc. It can be understood in two ways. “As one of us,” that is, God, which belongs to mockery, as it is said “one of the senators,” that is, a senator; or that he would be God not by nature but by the kindness of his Creator, had he been willing to remain under him. “Knowing good and evil”: as if he will learn by his punishment that the power of God is unavoidable, which he would not undergo while blessed and consenting; and he will have knowledge through punishment, which God has through wisdom.
3.23:
**“And the Lord God sent him out of the paradise”** — as if by excommunicating, as now the wicked are sent out of the Church
**“of pleasure, to till”** — so that he should labour in this body and lay up for himself the merit of returning
**“the earth from which he was taken.”** — Sent him out, etc. Into a place fitting for him; as for the most part an evil man, when he has begun to live among the good, if he will not be changed for the better, is driven from the gathering of the good by the weight of his evil habit.
3.24:
**“And he cast out Adam;”** — as if excommunicated
**“and placed before the paradise of pleasure”** — the fullness of knowledge, and charity
**“Cherubims,”** — angelic power
**“and a flaming sword,”** — temporal punishment, burning but passing
**“turning every way,”** — because it is to be removed at the coming of the Son
**“to keep the way of the tree of life.”** — because we cannot return except through these
**“And he cast out Adam”** — JEROME. The Seventy: “And he cast out, and made him dwell over against the paradise of pleasure, and set the Cherubim and a flaming sword which turns, to guard the way of the tree of life.” There is another sense in the Hebrew. For it says, “And the Lord cast out Adam, and made to dwell before the paradise of pleasure Cherubim and a flaming sword,” etc.; not that he made Adam dwell over against the paradise of pleasure, but that when he had been cast out he set the Cherubim and the flaming sword before the doors of paradise, so that no one could enter.
*Augustine:* HISTORICALLY. “And placed,” etc. It is to be believed that this was done through the heavenly powers in the visible paradise too, so that through the ministry of angels there should be a fiery guard there; yet not in vain, but because it signifies something of the spiritual paradise.
*Strabo:* “Placed,” etc. That is, through the ministry of angels he set up a fiery guard. The flaming sword is the tribulations and pains and labours of this life, by which we are exercised; or the sentence of just damnation which was given to man, who was so condemned that he could be redeemed by the passion of Christ. Whence the sword is called turning, because it can be removed. For it was removed for Enoch and Elias, and is removed daily for the faithful passing from this life to the blessedness above. Nor does he say “flame and sword,” but “flaming sword”; for those who return to paradise must burn up all the desires of this life with the fire of the Holy Spirit and cut off all harmful things with the sword of the Word of God.
*Isidore:* MYSTICALLY. “And placed,” etc. Cherubim is the fullness of knowledge; this is charity, which is the fullness of the divine law. The flaming sword is temporal punishments, which turn, since times roll round. So there is no return to the tree of life except through the Cherubim, that is, the fullness of knowledge, that is, charity, and through the turning sword, that is, temporal endurance.

4.1:
**“And Adam”** — now guilty
**“knew Eve his wife:”**
• not in paradise
• in paradise virginity; outside it, marriage
**“who conceived and brought forth”** — for that is first which is natural
**“Cain,”** — the Jewish people
**“saying: I have gotten a man through God.”**
• these are those who court earthly riches and possess them as far as they can; for Cain is interpreted “possession” or “acquiring”
• And Adam, etc. AUGUSTINE. In paradise there would have been virginity, outside it marriage; yet there would have been honourable wedlock in paradise, had not disobedience first earned exile before God brought in fleshly union. Therefore the whole posterity was condemned to death in the loins of Adam, because it was not separated from the mass in the place of life before the transgression, but was begotten after it in exile.
• Conceived and brought forth, etc. Cain and Abel, born of one mother, are signs of all men who are propagated into this life from the root of sin; some will love the earthly city and deadly delights and possess them by ambition as far as they can, whom Cain signifies, who is interpreted “possession”; others will seek the city to come and, mourning over the miseries of this dwelling, will pass with all their desire to the glory to come, whom Abel signifies, who is interpreted “mourning.” And he is later, because that is not first which is spiritual, but that which is natural. Hence Cain is called a husbandman, that is, given to earthly works; but Abel a shepherd of sheep, loving, namely, simplicity and innocence.
*Isidore:* ALLEGORICALLY. The two sons of Adam express two peoples: the Jewish, namely the elder by birth, and the Christian, the younger. The sacrifice of the elder, from earthly works, is rejected. For though the Jews rightly made fleshly sacrifices, yet they did not distinguish the time of the New Testament from the time of the Old. Whence, according to the Seventy: “If thou offer rightly but divide not rightly, thou hast sinned; be still.” He offered rightly, because to God; but he did not divide rightly, because he gave outward things and confirmed himself in wickedness. The sacrifice of the younger is approved, or, according to Theodotion, set on fire, because out of the love with which Christ loved us he offered to the Father not outward things but himself; whom, the head of the younger people, the elder by birth, that is, the Jewish, crucified in the place of Calvary, as Cain killed his younger brother in the field. In the falling of Cain’s countenance is marked the useless shame of the Jews, who still strive to set up the fleshly things rejected by God, and, blaspheming the Christian name, kill Christ as far as they can; yet if they come to their senses, rewards are promised; otherwise punishment is foretold. “If thou do well,” etc. But what strength reason ought to have against the first suggestion is signified when it is said, “The lust thereof shall be under thee”; as if reason should not let the evil movement come to effect, but strive to subdue it.
4.2:
**“And again she brought forth his brother Abel.”** — the Christian people
**“And Abel was a shepherd,”** — one who cultivates simplicity and innocence
**“and Cain a husbandman.”**
• given to earthly things
• And Abel was a shepherd, etc. In him are signified those who mourn over the earthly dwelling; for Abel is interpreted “mourning” or “vapour,” because he was a mourning to his parents, or because he soon vanished like a vapour.
4.3:
**“And it came to pass after many days, that Cain offered, of the fruits of the earth, gifts to the Lord.”**
• some, offending God in many things, think in this way that God is appeased by riches and offerings
• And it came to pass, etc. Cain offers a sacrifice from the fruits of the earth, because lovers of earthly things, when they offend God in many things, think he is appeased by a bounty of riches; against whom it is said: “If I should distribute all my goods to feed the poor, and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing.” For all that is given is weighed by the mind of the giver.
4.4:
**“Abel also”** — the faith of the New Testament, pleasing through innocence, praises God and is set before the earthly works of the Old Testament
**“offered of the firstlings of his flock,”** — by faith, by charity
**“and of their fat:”** — by charity, without which the soul is dry and faint
**“and”**
• first
• afterwards
**“the Lord had respect”**
• the Father
• who looks at the mind of the offerer, not at the offering, which pleases by the cleanness of the mind
**“to Abel”** — Christ, the head of the Christian people
**“to his offerings.”**
• the offering of the cross
• Abel also offered, etc. Because the just man strives to please God in all that he does through faith and charity (from which the other virtues spring, and without which they profit nothing); which is signified in the fat offered. Whence: “Let my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness.” Without charity the soul is lean and faint and will please God in nothing.
• And the Lord had respect to, etc. JEROME. How could Cain know this, unless Theodotion’s rendering were true: “And the Lord set fire upon Abel and upon his sacrifice; but upon Cain and his sacrifice he did not set fire”? We read that fire was wont to come from heaven to devour the sacrifice both at the dedication of the temple under Solomon and when Elias built an altar on Mount Carmel.
4.5:
**“But to Cain”**
• the Jewish people
• because the gift is received or refused according to the giver’s heart
**“and his offerings”**
• fleshly sacrifices
• the cleanness of the heart ought to have seasoned the gifts
**“he had no respect:”** — rejected for fleshly things
**“and Cain was exceedingly angry, and his countenance fell.”**
• from shame
• by useless confusion
4.6:
**“And the Lord said to him:”** — by rebuking
**“Why art thou angry?”**
• you are tormented by envy
• do not be angry without cause
**“and why is … fallen?”** — not a good shame
**“thy countenance”**
• the inner as much as the outer
• And the Lord said to him: Why is … fallen, etc. JEROME. “If thou offer rightly but divide not rightly, hast thou not sinned? Be still: to thee shall be his turning, and thou shalt rule over him.” In the Hebrew the sense is different: “Why art thou angry, why is thy countenance fallen? If thou do well, shall it not be forgiven thee? And if thou do ill, shall not thy sin sit before the doors? To thee is its fellowship, but do thou rather rule over it.” As if: Why are you angry, and, tormented by envy, cast your countenance to the ground? If you do well, will not every fault be forgiven you? Or, according to Theodotion, “it shall be acceptable,” that is, I will receive your gift as I received your brother’s gift. But if you do ill, at once your sin will sit before your entrance, and you will be accompanied by such a doorkeeper. But because you have free choice, I warn you that sin should not rule over you, but you over sin.
4.7:
**“If thou do well,”** — if you offer with a pure mind
**“do”** — by coming to your senses
**“shalt thou not receive?”**
• a reward
• God having respect to you and to your sacrifice
**“but if”** — punishment is foretold to the obstinate
**“ill, shall not sin forthwith”** — at the first entrance; as if: resist beginnings
**“be present at the door?”** — that is, it will lie open to all, and you will be accompanied by this doorkeeper
**“but … shall be under thee,”** — not over you, because you have free choice
**“the lust thereof … and thou shalt have dominion over it.”** — if, once the wickedness of the heart is seen, it is pressed down more quickly
**“If thou do well”** — GREGORY. In the Morals, book 32. “If thou offer rightly but divide not rightly, thou hast sinned.” One offers rightly when one acts with a right intention; but one does not divide rightly if what is done devoutly is not finely discerned. For to divide offerings rightly is to weigh good efforts by carefully discerning them; and he who neglects to do so sins even while offering rightly. For often what we do with good effort, while we neglect to discern it carefully, we do not know with what end it will be judged, and what is thought the cause of virtue becomes the guilt of crime.
*Isidore:* “If thou offer rightly and divide not rightly, thou hast sinned”; because even if the Jews offered those things rightly before, they are guilty in this, that they did not distinguish the New Testament from the Old.
**“be present at the door”** — ALCUIN. That is, sin will accompany you as you go in and go out, and the Lord will not keep your going in and your going out.
4.8:
**“And Cain said”** — the Jewish people
**“to Abel”** — Christ
**“his brother:”** — according to the flesh
**“Let us go forth abroad. And when they were in the field,”** — because the Jews think on rustic and earthly things
**“Cain rose up against his brother Abel, and slew him.”** — And Cain said, etc. JEROME. Understand: what the Lord had spoken. So what is found in the books of the Samaritans and in ours, “Let us go into the field,” is superfluous.
*Isidore:* “And Cain said,” etc. He does not heed the Lord saying “be still,” but hastens to fratricide. So the Jews, thinking on rustic and earthly things, if they had been still from disturbance and, knowing the time of grace, had heard, “If the Son shall make you free, you shall be free indeed,” and the like, would have turned their sin back to themselves in confession, saying to the Lord, “Heal my soul, for I have sinned against thee,” and so would have ruled over sin. But now, not knowing the justice of God and seeking to establish their own, not humbled for their sins but glorying in the works of the law, they stumbled at the stone of stumbling and killed their physician, whose works they saw pleasing to the Lord and grieved at with a blind mind. So Christ, the head of the younger people, is killed by the elder by birth.
4.9:
**“And the Lord said to Cain:”** — not as one ignorant, to learn, but to punish the guilty
**“Where is … Abel?”** — he reproaches him with fratricide
**“thy brother … And he answered, I know not:”** — today too the Jews answer that they do not know Christ
**“am I my brother’s keeper?”** — the Jews would in some way be the keepers of Christ if they believed and confessed
**“And the Lord said to Cain”** — ISIDORE. The Lord questions Cain, not as one ignorant, to learn, but as a judge, to punish. Until today, when we question the Jews about Christ through the Scriptures, they answer that they do not know what we are saying. The ignorance of the lying Cain is the false denial of the Jews; but they would be Christ’s keepers if they believed with the heart and confessed with the mouth.
4.10:
**“And he said to him: What hast thou done?”** — because he would not confess, he is charged with a just rebuke
**“the voice of thy brother’s blood”**
• which is uttered by the mouth of the faithful redeemed by that blood, namely, Amen
• the plainness of the crime committed needs no accuser’s outcry
**“crieth”** — by the mouth of the redeemed
**“to me from the earth.”**
• as if: the guilt of the murder is in my sight
• And he said to him, etc. ISIDORE. And so the Jews are rebuked in the Scriptures. The blood of Christ has a great voice on the earth, when, at its being received by all nations, Amen is answered. This the blood itself utters from the mouth of the faithful whom it redeemed.
• The voice of the blood, etc. “Now, therefore,” etc. Great is the power of justice, which seeks vengeance for the blood of the innocent.
4.11:
**“Now, therefore,”** — who, knowing the guilt of the first transgression, added fratricide
**“cursed shalt thou be upon the earth,”**
• the Church
• by those who are upon the earth
**“which hath opened her mouth”** — in the confession of sins
**“and received”**
• by believing
• that is, with a desire of great devotion it received the blood of Christ unto salvation
**“the blood”** — shed for remission
**“of thy brother at thy hand.”**
• of the persecutor, who wishes to be under the law so as to be cursed
• Now, therefore, cursed shalt thou be, etc. RABANUS. It is to be noted that in Adam’s sin the earth is cursed; [Cain himself is cursed] because, knowing the condemnation of the first transgression, he added fratricide.
*Isidore:* “Now, therefore, cursed shalt thou be,” etc. By the place, those who are in the place are signified; as if: you will be cursed by those who are upon the earth, who opened their mouth in the confession of sins to receive the blood which was shed for their remission from the hand of the persecutor, who would not be under grace but under the law, so that he should be cursed by the Church, which understands and shows that he is cursed. For “as many as are of the works of the law are under a curse.”
4.12:
**“When thou shalt till”** — the earthly working, or Christ’s incarnation, or Christ’s flesh
**“it, it shall not yield to thee its fruit:”** — spiritual understanding, or justification
**“a vagabond”** — among the nations
**“a fugitive … shalt thou be”** — from Jerusalem
**“upon the earth.”**
• When thou shalt till, etc. The reference is to the word, not to the sense, because earth is taken one way here and another above: there for the Church, here for the earthly working which the Jews still practise, that is, fleshly circumcision, the pasch, the sabbath and the like, which have a hidden power of understanding the grace of God, but give no fruit to the Jews, who will not pass over to Christ. By the earth Christ’s flesh can be understood, in which the Jews, by crucifying it, worked our salvation. For he “was delivered up for our sins, and rose again for our justification”; and because they denied him, they were not justified.
• A vagabond and a fugitive, etc. ISIDORE. Scattered among the nations, a fugitive from Jerusalem. The Seventy: “groaning and trembling”: groaning with grief for the lost kingdom; trembling under the multitude of the Christian people, lest he be killed. “My iniquity is greater,” etc.: he heaps up the fault, but confesses proudly and does not beg pardon.
4.13:
**“And Cain said to the Lord:”** — condemning himself
**“My iniquity is greater than that I may deserve pardon.”** — he heaps up the fault, confesses proudly, and does not ask pardon
**“My iniquity is greater”** — ISIDORE. Adding sins to sins, he despairs and does not believe that he can obtain pardon; which is the blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, which is not forgiven in this world nor in the world to come, because he thinks that God either will not forgive or cannot, as if he either could not do all things or grudged salvation.
4.14:
**“Behold thou dost cast me out this day”** — as unworthy of your sight
**“from the face of the earth, and I shall be hidden from thy face, and I shall be a vagabond and a fugitive on the earth: every one, therefore, that findeth me, shall kill me.”** — Every one, therefore, that, etc. STRABO. Because from the trembling of my body and the agitation of my maddened mind, whoever finds me will know me guilty of death.
4.15:
**“No, it shall not be so”** — You will not die soon, as you wish, as a remedy for your torment; but it will be punished, impersonally, that is, punishment will be taken of you sevenfold, because you will live in torment until the seventh generation, in which you will be killed by Lamech. So everyone who kills (understand) will free you from that torment of a bad conscience. This sense appears more plainly according to the Seventy: “Everyone who kills Cain will pay off seven vengeances,” that is, whoever kills you in the seventh generation will release you by death from the torment, you who are to be kept alive until that time only for punishment; which punishment would soon be ended if you were soon killed. So whoever punished the Jews with visible death would take away from them the seven vengeances to which they are bound for the guilt of killing Christ, because he would lighten their miseries and scatterings which they suffer.
**“whosoever shall kill Cain”** — The Seventy: “He will pay off seven vengeances.” Aquila: “sevenfold.” Symmachus: “seven times.” Theodotion renders it “by a week”; in which it is signified that he will be punished long and thoroughly, so that no one should dare to repeat murder.
*Jerome:* “He who kills Cain shall be punished sevenfold.” If anyone kills you, he shall be punished sevenfold, that is, he shall be punished with the heaviest vengeance; a man ought not to kill him whose life God kept, either for his punishment or for the correction of others.
*Isidore:* “But whosoever shall kill Cain.” It is to be read by ellipsis: “whosoever shall kill Cain,” a break here, then is to be joined: “it shall be punished sevenfold,” not Cain nor the killer, because it is put impersonally; so that we have the same sense as the words of the Seventy translators contain, namely, “he will pay off seven vengeances.” Historically, he was to live in scattering until seven generations; which punishment would at once have been paid off had he been killed then. So whoever punished the Jews with visible death would take away the seven vengeances to which they are bound for the death of Christ; for he would lighten their miseries and scattering, which they suffer in this time, which rolls on in sevens; and that is fulfilled: “Scatter them by thy power.”
*Jerome:* What Aquila put, “sevenfold,” and Symmachus, “a week,” or “the seventh shall avenge,” our elders so understood, that Cain was killed by Lamech in the seventh generation. Others, because seven is a full and perfect number, so say that whoever kills Cain will free him from great punishment and every passing torment. Others suppose various things about seven sins of Cain. The first sin, they say, is that he did not divide rightly; the second, that he envied his brother; the third, that he acted craftily, saying, “Let us go into the field”; the fourth, that he killed; the fifth, that he shamelessly denied it; the sixth, that he condemned himself: “My iniquity is greater than that I may deserve pardon”; the seventh, that even when condemned he did not do penance. Hence they say he was put off by God until the seventh generation, so that at least, driven by evils, he might do penance and deserve to be absolved.
**“And the Lord said to him: No, it shall not be so: but whosoever shall kill Cain, shall be punished sevenfold. And the Lord set a mark upon Cain, that whosoever found him should not kill him.”** — And the Lord set a mark, etc. ISIDORE. Though all the nations conquered by the Romans passed into their rites, the Jewish nation, whether under heathen or under Christian kings, has not given up the sign of circumcision and fleshly observance by which it is distinguished from the other nations; and whoever finds them in his kingdom with this sign does not kill them, that is, does not bring it about that they are not Jews, set apart from all by their own sign. But whoever of them has passed over to Christ is no longer found Cain, nor goes out from the face of the Lord, nor dwells in the land of Naid, which is interpreted “commotion,” or unstable and wavering and of uncertain seat; which all suffer who go out from the face of the Lord, that is, from the mercy of his love, and dwell in fleshly disturbance, over against Eden, which is interpreted “feasting,” where paradise was planted.
4.16: **“dwelt as a fugitive”** — JEROME. The Seventy: “He dwelt in the land of Naid.” In the Hebrew it is called Nod, that is, unstable and wavering and of uncertain seat. It is not a land of Naid, as our common people think; but the Lord’s sentence is fulfilled while he wanders here and there, a vagabond and fugitive.
4.17:
**“And Cain knew his wife, and she conceived, and brought forth Henoch: and he built a city, and called the name thereof”** — dedication
**“by the name of his son Henoch.”**
• because the wicked dedicate themselves to earthly life
• And Cain knew, etc. ISIDORE. Figuratively, the offspring of the wicked, seeking its foundation in the very beginning of the world, built a city in this life, which it called Henoch, which is interpreted “dedication,” because they dedicate themselves in the beginnings, while they plant the root of the heart in this life, which comes first, so as to flourish here as they wish and wither from the glory to come. But Abraham dwelt in huts, because the saints know themselves to be guests and pilgrims, looking for a city that hath foundations, whose builder is God.
• And he built, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is asked with what helpers he built it, if there were no more men than Scripture says. But it is to be known that there were many more then, because by living long they could beget more; nor is it a wonder, since the children of Israel are read to have so multiplied in four hundred years that their army could not be counted.
4.18:
**“And Henoch begot Irad, and Irad begot Maviael, and Maviael begot Mathusael, and Mathusael begot Lamech:”** — And Henoch, etc. JEROME. Not from all these are sure mysteries carved out; nor would they be found unless certain roots of history were first laid down; nor would you gather fruit from the branches of trees unless you had first planted the trunks.
*Isidore:* It is to be noted that the generations from Adam through Cain end in eleven, in which transgression is marked. For Lamech is the seventh, to whom three sons and one daughter are added so that eleven is filled, by which sin is signified; for the generation is closed by a woman too, who was the beginning of sin, through which the pleasure of the flesh, which resists the spirit. Whence she is called Noema, that is, pleasure. In this line Lamech first, against custom and against nature, committed adultery by bigamy.
4.19: **“Who took two wives:”** — first committing adultery against nature and custom
4.20:
**“And Ada brought forth Jabel: who was the father of such as dwell in tents, and of herdsmen.”**
• whose changeableness signifies those who are carried about with every wind of doctrine
• And Ada brought forth Jabel, etc. JEROME. From bigamy is born Jabel, dwelling in tents, which, being changeable, figure the instability of those who are carried about with every wind of doctrine. Jubal too is born, who was the inventor of music, of which it is said that through tuneful music it tempts the ears; which belongs to the pleasure of the ears. Tubalcain is born, who by works of brass invited the desire of the eyes, and by the smith’s art stirred up the cruelty of wars; by whose sister, who is called Noema, that is, pleasure, the desire of the flesh is marked. It is to be noted that these are understood, by figurative speech, partly through the meanings of the names, as Henoch and Noema; partly through the actions of men opposed to good ways, as Jabel, Jubal and Tubalcain.
4.21:
**“And his brother’s name was Jubal; he was the father of them that play upon the harp and the organs.”** — he was the inventor, namely of music, which belongs to the pleasure of the ears
**“And his brother’s name was Jubal”** — RABANUS. Josephus writes that he wrote music on two columns, one of stone, the other of brick, of which one would not be dissolved by the flood, the other would not be dissolved by fire; which two judgments Adam had foretold would come.
4.22:
**“Sella also brought forth Tubalcain, who was a hammerer”** — who, namely by works of brass, stirred up the desire of the eyes
**“and artificer in every work of brass and iron.”** — by the smith’s art he practised the cruelty of wars
**“And the sister of Tubalcain was Noema.”** — which is interpreted “pleasure,” in which the desire of the flesh is signified
**“Tubalcain”** — RABANUS. Who, according to Josephus, practised the arts of war and taught the smith’s art fittingly; he also invented certain things which belong to the desire of the eyes.
4.23:
**“And Lamech said to his wives Ada and Sella: Hear my voice, ye wives of Lamech, hearken to my speech: for I have slain a man”** — Cain, according to the Hebrews
**“to the wounding”** — which I inflicted
**“of myself,”** — as if: by this deed, my conscience biting me, I have grievously wounded myself
**“and a stripling”** — who guided the old man
**“to my own bruising.”** — in the zeal of my rage
**“Lamech said”** — RABANUS. The Hebrews say that Lamech, from living long, came into dimness of the eyes and had a young man as guide and director of his way. So, while hunting, he aimed an arrow where the young man showed him, and by chance killed Cain, hiding among the shrubs. And this is what he says: “I have slain a man to my wounding,” that is, by the wound which I inflicted I killed not a beast but a man. Whence, kindled with rage, I killed the young man too.
*Strabo:* “I have slain a man,” etc., that is, Cain, “to my wounding,” because for him I shall be wounded, that is, killed; “and a stripling to my bruising,” because for him too I shall be condemned.
4.24:
**“Sevenfold vengeance shall be taken for Cain: but for Lamech”**
• as sin grows, vengeance grows
• because he added murder to adultery, which sins are heavier among men
**“seventy times sevenfold.”**
• that is, after seventy-seven generations
• Sevenfold vengeance shall be taken, etc. ALLEGORICALLY. ALCUIN. The sin of Lamech (which is interpreted “humbled”) signifies the casting-down of the human race, which fell when Adam transgressed and could not rise by the law or circumcision or by its own justice, until after seventy-seven generations, according to Luke, Christ, coming into the world, blotted out sin by the shedding of his blood. Whence: “I say not to thee, till seven times; but till seventy times seven times”; that is, the Jew is to be received after seventy-seven vengeances, if he comes to his senses and seeks Christ’s pardon.
• Seven signifies the whole; by which, eleven being multiplied, seventy-seven is made, in which transgression of every kind is marked; which yet in the gospel is commanded to be forgiven the penitent.
*Jerome:* They say that from Adam to Christ there are seventy-seven generations, according to Luke. So as the sin of Cain was released in the seventh generation (for God will not judge twice for the same thing, and he who has received his punishment once in his life will not suffer in death the same torments he suffered in life), so too Lamech, that is, the sin of the whole world, will be released by the coming of Christ. A certain Hebrew told me that seventy-seven souls came forth from Lamech, all of whom perished in the flood.
4.25:
**“Adam also knew his wife again: and she brought forth a son, and called his name Seth,”** — “setting,” who rose up in the place of the one killed
**“saying: God hath given me another seed,”** — the joy of the resurrection
**“for Abel”** — by the mourning of death
**“whom Cain slew.”**
• the Jewish people
• Adam also knew … again, etc. By Seth, who is interpreted “resurrection,” is marked the life of Christ from the dead, which is signified in the mother’s words: “The Lord hath given me another seed”; as if the Church should say: I who bore mourning for the dead rejoice over the one raised up.
4.26:
**“But to Seth also was born a son, whom he called Enos;”** — man
**“this man”** — confessing God the Creator and the restorer of life
**“began to call upon the name of the Lord.”**
• to worship and to pray
• Whom he called, etc. Enos is interpreted “man,” who began to call upon the name of the Lord; because through the death of Christ, which Abel signified, and through the resurrection, which Seth signifies, man is made, confessing the Lord, the Creator and restorer of the life that was lost.
*Jerome:* “Whom he called Enos.” Enos is interpreted “man,” who began to call upon the name of the Lord. As Adam is interpreted “man,” so also Enos, according to the Hebrew truth, “man” or “husband”; and fittingly, because he had this name, it was said that the calling upon the name of the Lord began then; although very many of the Hebrews think that then for the first time idols were made in the name of the Lord and in his likeness.

5.1:
**“This is the book of the generation of Adam. In the day”** — in the time
**“that God created”** — because he was made in the brightness of contemplation
**“man, he made him to the likeness of God.”** — in understanding, will and memory
**“This is the book of the generation”** — Adam was made to the likeness of God, the others to the likeness of Adam; and it is as it were a conclusion from what goes before, with a summing-up: “In the day that God created man.” For he was created in the day, because he was set in the brightness of divine contemplation. “To the likeness of God,” because he gave him reason, by which, understanding, he should discern good and evil, love what he understood, and not hand over to forgetfulness what he loved; and in this he would keep the likeness of God. But after he blotted out this likeness by disobedience, made earthly, he begot earthly ones. Whence: “Such as is the earthly, such also are the earthly.”
5.2:
**“He created them male and female;”** — because this was done in both sexes
**“and blessed them: and called their name Adam,”** — that is, man, because he was taken from the ground
**“in the day when they were created.”** — he returns to the order of weaving the genealogy
5.3:
**“And Adam lived a hundred and thirty years,”** — And Adam lived, etc. JEROME. It is to be known that up to the flood, where in our copies someone is said to have begotten at two hundred and some years, the Hebrew has a hundred years and the rest that follow.
**“and begot a son”** — nor was this one excepted
**“to his own image and likeness, and called his name Seth.”** — And begot, etc. As if: this one too, who was put in place of the just Abel and by the meaning of his name signifies Christ, bore the image of the earthly. But all bear the image of the earthly man before the heavenly, although many before the coming of Christ had, through faith, the same grace by which Christians are saved.
5.5: **“And all the time that Adam lived”** — man, or red earth
5.6:
**“Seth also lived”** — resurrection, or setting
**“a hundred and five years, and begot Enos.”** — man
5.15:
**“And Malaleel lived”** — praising God
**“sixty-five years, and begot Jared.”** — strengthened
5.18: **“And Jared lived a hundred and sixty-two years, and begot Henoch.”** — dedication
5.22: **“And Henoch walked with God: and lived after he begot Mathusala,”** — the sending-forth of death
5.23:
*Strabo:* They say that after the death of Abel Adam vowed that he would no more know his wife nor beget a son. But at God’s command he broke the vow, so that the Son of God should be born of him and man be redeemed; for he ought not to be born from the stock of Cain. Whence no one is read to have been begotten before Seth; but after him it is said that he begot sons and daughters.
**“And all the days of Henoch were three hundred and sixty-five years.”**
• This reckoning of the genealogies spreads as it were branches of histories, from which in their own places the fruits of mysteries are gathered. And it is to be noted that in the generation of Seth no woman is set down by name, as in the generation of Cain. For it belongs to the just to do all things manfully, to take up nothing womanish, nothing frail. For this generation goes on by ten up to Noe, in whom the fulfilling of the commandments is marked, as by eleven in the generation of Cain, transgression.
• In the generation of the unjust Henoch is put first, which is interpreted “dedication,” because the reprobate fix the root of their hope in the present life and wither from love of the unfading inheritance; of whom it is said: “I have seen a fool with a strong root, and I cursed his beauty immediately.” In the generation of the just Henoch is put seventh from Adam, because these do not seek an abiding city here, but stretch their expectation to the end of time, which is closed by the sevenfold turning, when the eighth, eternity, shall have followed. Whence this Henoch, who is put seventh and was translated because he pleased God, signifies the seventh rest, to which whoever clings to God perseveringly is carried without delay after this life. The meaning of the names of this generation, too, marks the same thing. Adam is interpreted “man” or “red earth”; Seth, “setting” or “resurrection”; Enos, “man”; Cainan, “lamentation”; Malaleel, “praising God”; Jared, “strengthened”; Henoch, “dedication”; Mathusala, “the sending-forth of death”; Lamech, “humbled”; Noe, “rest.” So man, coming forth from the earth, rising again from sins, will be a man calling upon God and weeping for his former sins; and so, praising God, strengthened by the Spirit of God, he is dedicated to eternal life; and, victor over death, subject to God, he possesses everlasting rest, which Noe signifies, who is interpreted “rest” and is counted in the tenth place, because the kingdom of heaven is possessed through the fulfilling of the commandments.
5.24:
**“And he walked with God, and was seen no more: because God took him.”** — And he walked with God, etc. ISIDORE. Henoch, seventh from Adam, pleasing God, who was also translated, signifies the seventh rest, to which is carried he who is formed as on the sixth day, that is, in the sixth age of the world, through the coming of Christ; and when six thousand years are past, the judgment made, and heaven and earth renewed, the saints will be carried into eternal life. But that through Seth, from Adam to Noe, the number ten is suggested, the fulfilment of the commandments in the Church in works is figured; to which number, if the two sons of Noe are added, the middle one being rejected, twelve is completed, which is held notable in the number of the patriarchs and apostles because of the parts of seven multiplied one by the other; for three fours make it.
*Alcuin:* Henoch is kept from death for so long a time, in which it is shown that man would always have lived had he not sinned.
5.25:
**“And Mathusala lived a hundred and eighty-seven years, and begot Lamech.”**
• humbled
• And Mathusala lived, etc. It is asked how Mathusala, by the reckoning of the years, could live after the flood, since all perished except those who went into the ark. But the faultiness of the copies gave rise to this question; for not only is it found otherwise in the Hebrew, but also in the Seventy translation, in a few copies, Mathusala is found to have died seven years before the flood.
• That the years of Mathusala are counted beyond the flood according to the Seventy is because he signifies Christ, whose life feels no age; so that in the elders too he should seem not to have felt the flood.
5.27: **“And all the days of Mathusala were nine hundred and sixty-nine years, and he died.”** — And all the days … were, etc. JEROME. “And all the days of Mathusala which he lived were nine hundred and sixty-nine years, and he died.” By careful reckoning he is said to have lived fourteen years after the flood. For when he was a hundred and eighty-three years old he begot Lamech; again, Lamech, when he was a hundred and eighty-two years old, begot Noe; and there are three hundred and fifty-five years from Mathusala to the day of Noe’s birth. But the flood came in the six hundredth year of Noe’s life, that is, in the nine hundred and fifty-fifth year of Mathusala; and since he is said above to have lived nine hundred and sixty-nine years, it is plain that he lived fourteen years after the flood. But only eight souls were saved in the ark; so there is an error in the number, as in many places. For in the books of the Hebrews and the Samaritans I found it thus: “And Mathusala lived a hundred and eighty-seven years and begot Lamech; and Mathusala lived after he begot Lamech seven hundred and eighty-two years and begot sons and daughters; and all the days of Mathusala were nine hundred and sixty-nine years, and he died. And Lamech lived a hundred and eighty-two years and begot Noe.” That makes three hundred and sixty-nine years; add to these the six hundred years of Noe, because the flood came in the six hundredth year of his life; and so it comes about that Mathusala died in the nine hundred and sixty-ninth year of his life, namely in the year in which the flood began.
5.31: **“And all the days of Lamech came to seven hundred and seventy-seven years, and he died. And Noe”** — rest, that is, Christ, in whom we find rest
5.32: **“when he was five hundred years old, begot Sem, Cham, and Japheth.”** — And Noe, etc. JEROME. Noe is interpreted “rest,” because under him all the works of the past came to rest through the flood.

6.1: **“And after that men began to be multiplied upon the earth”** — JEROME. The Hebrew word Elohim is of both numbers, for it signifies God and gods. Therefore Aquila dared to say “sons of the gods,” understanding holy gods or angels; following whom Symmachus says: “the sons of the mighty, seeing the daughters of men.”
6.2:
**“The sons of God seeing”** — the godly sons of Seth
**“the daughters of men,”** — of the stock of Cain
**“that they were fair, took”** — overcome by desire
**“to themselves wives of all which they chose.”** — The sons of God seeing, etc. By the sons of God are understood the godly sons of Seth, who, overcome by desire, took wives from the daughters of men, that is, from the stock of Cain, and begot mighty men, namely huge in body, proud in strength, lawless in ways, who are called giants. It is not unbelievable that such men were begotten by men, not by angels or certain demons who are wanton toward women, because after the flood too the bodies not only of men but also of women were of unbelievable size.
6.3:
**“And God said: My spirit shall not remain”** — indignation
**“in man for ever, because he is flesh,”** — of a frail condition
**“and his days shall be a hundred and twenty years.”**
• until the flood, for doing penance; during which the ark was built
• before the ark began to be made
• My spirit shall not remain, etc. JEROME. The Hebrew: “My spirit shall not judge men for ever, because they are flesh”; that is, because the condition of men is frail, I will not keep them for eternal torment, but will pay them here what they deserve. So it is mercy, not severity, that the sinner is visited here for his crime. Whence God, angered, says: “I will not punish your daughters when they shall commit fornication.” And elsewhere: “I will visit their iniquities with a rod,” etc. But lest he seem cruel because he gave no room for penance, he adds: “But his days shall be a hundred and twenty years.” For these are not understood to be the years of human life foretold, since men are found afterwards to have lived longer; but it is understood that God said this to Noe twenty years before the ark began to be made, which is read to have been made in a hundred years, foretelling the flood; not prescribing the span of human life thereafter, but of those whom he was going to destroy by the flood.
• And his days shall be, etc. STRABO. Before the flood, namely for doing penance. But because they persevered in malice, they were destroyed before the fixed term, in the hundredth year.
6.4:
**“Now giants were upon the earth in those days.”**
• huge in body, proud in strength, lawless in ways; whence giants, that is, sons of the earth, are named
• in the Hebrew, “falling ones”
6.5: **“And God seeing that the wickedness of men was great on the earth, and that all the thought of their heart was bent upon evil at all times,”** — And God seeing, etc. Repentance or sorrow of heart does not befall God, whose judgment of all things is as fixed as his foreknowledge is sure; but Scripture uses everyday words, fitting itself to our littleness, so that from known things we may know the unknown. For the anger of God is not a disturbance of mind but the judgment that is brought on the sinner; and the thought of his heart is the unchangeable reason of things to be changed.
6.6:
**“It repented him”** — Scripture speaks to us in everyday words, so as to go on from the known to the unknown
**“that he had made man on the earth. And being touched inwardly with sorrow of heart,”** — lest something worse happen
**“It repented him that he had made man”** — GREGORY. In the Morals, book 5. Often in sacred speech the wise draw God’s counsel from the wise of the world. So now, for man’s profit, the very maker of men takes upon himself the voice of human feeling, since it is agreed that he who sees all things before they come made nothing which he should come to his senses about by repenting. So as it is no wonder if spiritual men often use the words of the fleshly, so neither is it to be wondered at if the Creator of all himself, to draw the flesh to understanding him, keeps or takes up in himself the speech of the flesh.
6.7: **“He said: I will destroy man, whom I have created, from the face of the earth, from man even to beasts, from the creeping thing even to the fowls of the air,”** — He seems to repent when he changes his work, while his will and disposing remain unmoved.
6.9:
**“These are the generations of Noe: Noe was a just and perfect man”**
• a traveller, not one who has arrived
• that is, according to the perfect justice of the present life, not of the life to come
**“in his generations, he walked with God.”**
• following his footsteps
• Noe was a just man, etc. If no one is without sin, how was he perfect? Some are called perfect, not as they are to be perfected when they will be made equal to the angels, but as they can be in pilgrimage. Whence he adds: “in his generations,” that is, as he could be perfect by God’s grace after his own measure, not as in the other life, in which he will neither will nor be able to sin. “He walked with God,” following his footsteps.
• “In his generations”: as if not of finished justice, but according to his generation.
**“Noe was a just … man”** — ALLEGORICALLY. This man by his deeds signifies Christ, who says: “Learn of me, because I am meek, and humble of heart.” He alone is found just, to whom for his justice seven persons are given; Christ too is just and perfect, to whom seven churches, enlightened by the sevenfold Spirit, are given in one Church. Noe is freed through water and wood, and his household; so the household of Christ through baptism and the cross.
6.10:
**“And he begot three sons, Sem,”** — name, or named
**“Cham,”** — crafty
**“and Japheth.”** — breadth
6.11: **“And the earth was corrupted before God, and was filled with iniquity.”** — man, for whose sake all things were created; when he sins, all things are said to be corrupted
6.12: **“And when God had seen that the earth was corrupted (for all flesh had corrupted its way upon the earth,)”** — life, actions
6.13:
**“He said to Noe: The end of all flesh is come”** — of all mortals, except those who were to be saved in the ark as the seed-bed of a second origin
**“before me,”** — by a judgment well pleasing to me
**“the earth is filled”** — that is, the dwellers on the earth
**“with iniquity through them,”** — presence
**“and I will destroy them with the earth.”** — so that it should not be fruitful in its own manner
**“I will destroy them with the earth”** — The doctors teach that the greenness and fruitfulness of the earth were far less after the flood, and that therefore the eating of flesh was granted to men, whereas before they lived only on the fruits of the earth.
6.14:
**“Make thee an ark”** — the Church
**“of timber planks:”**
• in the Hebrew, “pitched”
• others, “squared”
• smoothed, so that nothing harmful should cling to them
• because the life of the saints is firm and stable
**“little rooms”** — different orders of life
**“thou shalt make … in the ark, and thou shalt pitch it”**
• which is a most fiery glue; timbers smeared with it are loosened by no violence
• by the heat of love
**“within and without.”**
• so that it is not loosened by those who are within or by those who are without
• Make thee an ark of timber: namely strong and not to be loosened and well fitted together, which another translation calls “squared,” so that it should be loosened neither by the force of the winds nor by the flood.
• Little rooms, etc. STRABO. The SEVENTY: “Thou shalt make it with two storeys and three storeys in the ark”: two storeys in the lower parts, three storeys in the upper; so it was divided into five rooms. The first, that is, the lowest, was for dung, to which the dung flowed down, so that those who were in the ark should not be hurt by the stench. The second was the storeroom. The third, of the fierce animals and serpents. The fourth, of the tame. The fifth, that is, the highest, of men and birds; where the two-storeyed and three-storeyed parts were joined, that is, between the storeroom and the dwelling of the beasts.
• For pitch is a most fiery and most strong glue, and signifies the heat of love, bearing all things by the strength of its greatness to hold fellowship together. That the ark is six times as long as it is broad and ten times as long as it is high shows a likeness to the human body, in which Christ appeared. For the length of the body from the crown to the sole holds six times the breadth, which is from one side to the other, and ten times the height, which is from the back to the belly. That the breadth is spread out to fifty cubits signifies the breadth of the heart, which comes about by spiritual charity. Whence: “The charity of God is poured forth in our hearts by the Holy Ghost.” On the fiftieth day after the resurrection Christ sent the Spirit, by whom he enlarged the hearts of believers. And the length of three hundred cubits holds fifty six times, as all the time of the world stretches through six ages, in which Christ has not ceased to be preached: in five, prophesied; in the sixth, proclaimed in the gospel.
*Augustine:* In the first dwelling, in the lower parts, the ark had one storey; in the second, above the lower dwelling, two storeys; but in the third, above the second, three storeys.
*Augustine:* Others say that in the lower parts there were two little rooms, and so the ark was two-storeyed; of these the lower received the dung, the second the food, which was called the storeroom. In the upper parts it was three-storeyed, where men and animals were kept with fitting distinction.
*Isidore:* Noe built the ark of timbers that do not rot, and Christ the Church of men who will live for ever, which, like the ark, floats on the waves. The ark is of squared timbers, the Church of saints, whose stable life is ready for every good work, as a squared timber stands firm on every side. The timbers are glued together with pitch within and without, so that by the fitting-together of unity the patience of charity may be signified, lest the Church, shaken by those who are within or by those who are without, give way from brotherly joining.
6.15:
**“And thus shalt thou make it: … three hundred cubits:”** — geometrical cubits, each of which is made up of six cubits of a human hand
**“The length of the ark shall be …: the breadth of it fifty cubits, and the height of it thirty cubits.”**
• the ark at its foundation was four-sided, of unequal length and breadth, rising from the corners into an arch until the top was finished in one cubit of length and breadth
• Three hundred cubits, etc. ISIDORE. In the three hundred cubits the wood of the cross can be shown; for the letter tau, of this number, shows the sign of the cross, by which, made partners of the passion through baptism, we gain the length of eternal life. The height rises to thirty cubits, which number the length holds ten times in three hundred cubits, because Christ is our height, who hallowed the gospel at thirty years, bearing witness that he came not to destroy the law but to fulfil it; and since the law is known in ten commandments, the length of the ark is completed in ten times thirty cubits. Whence too Noe is reckoned tenth from Adam. A hundred, the solid square, made by multiplying ten by itself, signifies the elect who are to be glorified through the justification of the commandments. Whence the man who had a hundred sheep, when one was lost, left the ninety-nine and sought the one that had perished, and when he found it put it back, to make up the hundred; which, multiplied by three, receives the grace of immortality from the Father through the Son and the Holy Spirit, among those who are increased by the grace of the Trinity and who, fallen from the hundred, are made up again to it through knowledge of the Trinity. The breadth of fifty cubits signifies remission, because the fiftieth year, that is, the jubilee, freed slaves, restored possessions, gave pardon to debtors and their homeland to exiles. So Christ in his Church set the number fifty in the breadth; for had he not given the remission of sins, the Church would not have been spread through the world. The number thirty in the height holds a sacrament like that of three hundred. But the whole is brought back to one, because there is one God, of whom are all things, and one faith, and one baptism.
*Gregory:* The ark, which was commanded to be made three hundred cubits in length, fifty in breadth, thirty in height, was finished in one cubit. For it signifies the Church, which is broad below and narrow above; because, narrowed a little from the breadth which it still has in its weak members, and advancing on high, it tends to one. For reason requires that within the length of the ark all the beasts, four-footed and creeping things, should have been in the lower parts; man and the flying things in the upper. Near the upper part there was a window in the side, from which the man let out the dove or the raven. So man and the flying things were near the one cubit. For in her many fleshly ones the Church is broad, in her few spiritual ones narrow; and because she is gathered to the one Man who is without sin, she is as it were finished in one cubit. We see many in the Church who are proud, wanton, gaping after earthly things, angry and quarrelsome, and hurting their neighbours. But because the Church bears with them, that they may be converted, they are said, as it were, to have been beasts in the breadth of the ark. We see others who do not seize what belongs to others, bear injury done to them calmly, are content with their own things, and live humbly. But because these are now few, the ark is narrowed. We see others too leaving what they possess, giving no care to earthly things, loving their enemies, taming the flesh, pressing down all movements by reason, raised up on the wing of contemplation by heavenly desire. But because they are very rare, the ark is now drawn in near the cubit, where men and flying things are held. But because no one is without sin except him who was conceived without sin, the ark is finished in one cubit, because there is one author and redeemer of the Church without sin, to whom and through whom all advance who know themselves sinners.
6.16:
**“Thou shalt make a window in the ark,”**
• in the Hebrew: “Thou shalt make a noon for the ark.” Symmachus: “Thou shalt make a daylight for the ark,” that is, a window
• for sending out the raven or the dove
• the Jews hold that this was of crystal
**“in a cubit shalt thou finish the top of it”** — So the Church, gathered in unity, is raised up and advances. Whence: “He that gathereth not with me, scattereth.”
**“the door”** — the door in the side of the ark: the wound in the side of Christ
**“of the ark thou shalt set in the side: with lower, middle chambers, and third stories”** — the Seventy: “two-storeyed and three-storeyed”
**“shalt thou make it.”**
• And the door of the ark thou shalt set, etc. For no one enters the Church except through the sacrament of the remission of sins, which flowed from the opened side.
• Lower, middle chambers and third stories, etc. The Seventy: “two-storeyed and three-storeyed.” For from all nations the Church gathers either a twofold multitude, from the circumcision and the uncircumcision, or a threefold one, from the three sons of Noe, by whose offspring the world is filled. And the lower parts of the ark are divided, because in this earthly life there is a diversity of nations; but at the top all are finished in one, because Christ is all and in all.
*Alcuin:* Fittingly the ark came to a point at the top like a sort of narrow roof, so as to shed the threats of the rains; and standing below in the waters with four-square stability, it could be neither tipped over nor sunk by the push of the winds or the onrush of the waves or the restlessness of the animals within.
*Gregory:* The ark was broad in the lower parts, narrow in the upper, and at the top it rose to the measure of one cubit. For below it is believed to have held the four-footed beasts and creeping things; above, the birds and men. It is broad where the beasts are, narrow where the men are, because it is broad in the fleshly, narrow in the spiritual. For where it bears with the beastly, it loosens its bosom more widely; where it holds the rational, it is drawn to the top. “For wide is the way that leadeth to destruction, and many there are who go in thereat. Narrow is the gate that leadeth to life, and few there are that find it.” The ark narrows at the top to one cubit, because in the Church, the holier they are, the fewer they are, who are led at the top to him who alone was born a man holy beyond compare, as “a sparrow all alone on the housetop.” So the evil are to be borne with all the more as they are the more numerous; for in the threshing of the floor the grains that are kept in the barns are few, the heaps of chaff that are burnt in the fire great.
*Gregory:* Morally, he who turns himself from love of the world builds the ark of salvation in his heart, having in himself length, that is, faith in the Trinity and length of life and immortality; breadth, in charity, by which he can do good even to enemies; height, in hope, by which he lifts himself to heavenly things and refers the sum of his actions to one.
6.18: **“And I will establish my covenant with thee,”** — concerning you and your household, to be kept for the restoring of the human race
6.19: **“And of every living creature of all flesh, thou shalt bring two of a sort into the ark, that they may live with thee: of the male sex, and the female.”** — And of every living creature, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is asked about the tiniest animals, such as mice and lizards, and flies and beetles and fleas, whether the number was kept. But those which are not begotten by mating but are born from the moisture of the earth, or from the corruption of carcasses or other things, did not need to be in the ark; which is hinted when it is said of the birds “according to their kind” and of the beasts “in their kind.” Those too which live in houses, like fleas, mice and flies, did not need to be there by number, since they are understood to have been in the houses in greater numbers then. And those which are born from the mixing of different kinds, like mules, hinnies and the like, are not to be said to have been in the ark. But those which live both in the waters and on land, like otters and seals, had little places prepared outside the ark, in which they could take refuge as on dry land. The same is to be thought of sea and river birds. That all kinds of animals are shut in the ark signifies that the Church is gathered from all peoples and nations; as in Peter’s dish there are clean and unclean animals, so in the sacraments of the Church good and bad are found.
6.20:
**“Of fowls according to their kind, and of beasts in their kind, and of every thing that creepeth on the earth according to its kind; two of every sort shall go in with thee,”** — of their own accord; not by the act of man but at the nod of God
**“that they may live.”** — so that they should not perish by the flood
6.21:
**“Thou shalt take unto thee of all food”** — as if he were asking whence he should live
**“that may be eaten, and thou shalt lay it up with thee: and it shall be food for thee and them.”** — Thou shalt take, etc. It is often asked, about the animals which are thought to feed only on flesh, whether they were there beyond the number without breaking the command, because the need of feeding the others had forced them to be shut in; or, as is rather to be believed, whether there could have been foods besides flesh suitable for all. For many animals whose food is flesh feed on fruits and apples, above all the fig and chestnuts. So a just and wise man, warned by God, could find and store up food besides flesh suitable for each; and hunger forces all to eat; and there is nothing that God cannot make pleasant and wholesome, who could even grant by divine power that they should live without food.

7.2:
**“Of all clean beasts take seven and seven,”** — so that there should be more that would profit men than that would harm them
**“the male and the female. But of the beasts that are unclean two and two, the male and the female.”**
• all things are clean by nature, but some are called unclean by comparison with a better nature; as the ox is better than the lion, because more needful to man, for whose sake all things were created
• Of all clean beasts take, etc. RABANUS. We should take not seven doubled, that is, fourteen, but only seven. Likewise “two and two” is not four but only two, male and female. And it is to be noted that the clean animals are brought in by an odd number, that is, seven, the unclean by an even one; because an odd number holds out the look of virtue, an even one weakness. The clean are more, so that Noe, going out of the ark, should have something to sacrifice and to eat.
*Isidore:* “Of all clean beasts take,” etc. Not that the good are more than the evil, but because the good keep the unity of the spirit in the bond of peace, which is commended by a sevenfold working: of wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, godliness and the fear of the Lord. Whence the number fifty, which belongs to the coming of the Holy Spirit, is completed in seven sevens, which are forty-nine, one being added. Whence: “Careful to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.” But the evil are held in two, as being divisible and easy to schism. And Noe with his own is counted eighth, because in Christ the hope of resurrection appeared, who rose on the eighth day, that is, after the seventh of the sabbath; which day, the third from the passion, is both the first and the eighth in the number of the days that roll through all time.
*Augustine:* It is asked whether so great an ark could be built in a hundred years by four men, that is, Noe and his three sons. But if it could not, it was no great matter to bring in other craftsmen; who, having received the wages of their work, did not care whether Noe acted wisely or foolishly, and did not enter it, because they did not believe what he believed.
7.4:
**“For yet a while, and after seven days, I will rain upon the earth forty days and forty nights; and I will destroy every substance that I have made, from the face of the earth.”**
• he often repeats the wickedness of the evil by rebuking it, and announces evils to come, so as at least thus to move them to penance
• I will rain, etc. ISIDORE. Because all guilt is committed against the ten commandments throughout the whole world, which is divided into four parts; and four tens make forty: whether the guilt is contracted from prosperity, which belongs to the days, or from adversity, which belongs to the nights, it is washed away in baptism.
7.6: **“And he was six hundred years old, when the waters of the flood overflowed the earth.”** — And he was six hundred years old, etc. ISIDORE. Noe was five hundred years old when the Lord commanded him to make the ark, and six hundred when he had now gone in. From which it is gathered that the ark was built over a hundred years. And the hundreds of years signify the single ages of the world. Whence the sixth hundred, from the completion of five hundred to six hundred, signifies the Church being built in the making known of the gospel. So let him who wants life be a squared timber, ready for every good work, and enter the holy building. The second month of the six hundredth year, too, signifies the sixth age; for two months are closed in sixty days. And from six are named sixty, and six hundred, and six thousand, and six hundred thousand, and so on in greater sums, while the number rises by the same step. That the twenty-seventh day is recalled belongs to the squaring of which it was written above. But here it is to be said more openly that the Trinity makes us ready for every good work: by memory, with which we recall God; understanding, with which we know him; and love, with which we love him. For three times three, and these three times, make twenty-seven, which is three squared.
7.7:
**“And Noe went in and his sons,”** — the men apart
**“his wife and the wives of his sons”** — the women apart, because one must abstain in affliction
**“with him into the ark, because of the waters of the flood.”** — And Noe went in, etc. “And his wife,” etc. RABANUS. It is to be noted that Noe goes into the ark with his sons apart, and their wives apart. Therefore it is said separately, “Noe went in and his sons,” and there is added separately, “his wife and the wives of his sons.” But they came out men and women together; for so it is written: “Noe went out, and his wife.” For there is “a time to embrace, and a time to be far from embraces.”
7.9: **“Two and two went in”** — at the divine nod, as they were brought to Adam that he might name them
7.10:
**“And after the seven days were passed, the waters of the flood overflowed the earth.”**
• at the divine nod
• And after … were passed, etc. ISIDORE. Because we are baptized in the hope of the rest to come, which the seventh day signifies, all flesh outside the ark was consumed by the flood; because outside the Church the water of baptism, though it is the same, avails not for salvation but for ruin.
7.11:
**“In the six hundredth year of the life of Noe,”** — what was fixed beforehand above he carries out in order
**“in the second month,”** — Nisan, which the Latins call May
**“in the seventeenth day of the month, … were broken up”** — so that they should not flow gently, as usual, but cover the earth with a sudden flood
**“In the six hundredth year”** — ALLEGORICALLY. It is to be noted that the waters of the flood overflowed in the six hundredth year, because in the sixth age of the world the sacrament of baptism was first commended; and this on the seventeenth day of the second month, because ten signifies the ten commandments, and seven, because of the sabbath, signifies the seventh rest; and because in the ten commandments the renouncing of vices is seen, whoever is initiated in baptism professes, for the sake of eternal rest, that he renounces all things within himself.
**“the flood gates”** — The windows, namely the clouds, which were opened so that unusual and greater rains should pour from them. Cataracts are properly the mouths of the Nile, but are used loosely for all windows.
*Rabanus:* It is often asked about the ark whether, with so great a capacity as is described, it could bear all the animals that are said to have gone in, and their food.
