Origen solves this by the geometrical cubit, asserting that it was not said in vain that Moses was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, who loved geometry, and that the geometrical cubit holds as much as six of ours.
7.15: **“Went in to Noe into the ark, two and two of all flesh, wherein was the breath of life.”** — Two and two, etc. AUGUSTINE. He commanded above that seven and seven of the clean, two and two of the unclean should be taken. How then does he now say that two and two went in, whether of the clean or of the unclean? But this refers not to the number of the clean and unclean but to male and female. For in all there are two, male and female. But it is to be noted that what is said, “wherein was the breath of life,” is said not only of men but also of cattle; because some want what is written, “he breathed into his face the spirit of life,” to be understood of the Holy Spirit. But some copies have better “the breath of life.”
7.16: **“And they that went in, went in male and female of all flesh, as God had commanded him: and the Lord shut him in on the outside.”** — what man could not do: lest the waters should come in, God pitched it on the outside
7.17: **“And the flood was forty days upon the earth, and the waters increased, and lifted up the ark on high from the earth.”** — Forty days, etc. ALCUIN. The rain flooded by the number forty, which shows the tribulation of penance. After forty days Noe opened the window, signifying that heaven is opened to those who fast. Whence Moses, Elias and the Saviour himself hallowed fasts by the number forty, as needful in the three times: before the law, under the law, under grace.
7.20:
**“The water was fifteen cubits higher than the mountains which it covered.”** — The water was fifteen cubits higher, etc. If the earth of Mount Olympus (as history tells) could reach into the space of calm air, where it is said that neither clouds are seen nor wind felt, why not the waters too by rising? But the seventh rest is joined with the eighth resurrection. For when the body is given back, the rest of the saints, which is given after this life, does not end; but the whole man, no longer in hope but in reality, renewed in body and spirit with perfect and immortal salvation, is taken up into eternal life. So in the sacrament of our regeneration, that is, baptism, it is a deep mystery that the water rose fifteen cubits above all the height of the mountains. For seven and eight make fifteen. Seven signifies rest, eight resurrection. So this sacrament of resurrection and rest goes beyond all the wisdom of the proud, so that they cannot search out the rest of the resurrection by the height of their knowledge. And because seventy is named from seven and eighty from eight, the two numbers being joined, the water was lifted up for ninety days, commending and confirming the same height of baptism in hallowing the new man to hold rest and the faith of the resurrection.
**“fifteen cubits”** — There are those who think that neither the quality of the earth nor the height of the mountains was before the flood such and so great as it is today.
7.23: **“they were destroyed from the earth”** — ALCUIN. Therefore the land animals perished rather than the water ones, because they live from the cursed earth.

8.1:
**“And … remembered”** — after the flooding of forty days
**“God … Noe, and all the living creatures, and all the cattle which were with him in the ark, and brought a wind”** — the Holy Spirit, or a wind, by whose blasts the water should go back
**“upon the earth, and the waters were abated.”** — And brought, etc. ALCUIN. It can be understood of that Spirit of which it was said, “The Spirit of God moved over the waters”: then he moved so that, the waters being gathered into their place, the earth should appear; now he is brought so that, the waters of the flood being taken away, he should uncover the face of the earth. By the spirit a wind can be understood, according to that saying, “And the stormy wind stood,” namely by whose blasts the water should go back.
8.3:
**“And the waters returned from off the earth going and coming:”** — it seems that the courses of rivers and streams return through the veins of the earth to the mother deep
**“and they began to be abated after a hundred and fifty days.”** — And the waters returned, etc. ALCUIN. It seems that all the courses of rivers return through hidden passages to the deep, according to that saying: “Unto the place from whence the rivers come, they return.”
8.4:
**“And the ark rested in the seventh month, the seven and twentieth day of the month, upon the mountains of Armenia.”** — And the ark rested in the … month, etc. ISIDORE. It signifies the sevenfold rest; and because the perfect rest there, the number of the squaring spoken of above is repeated too. For on the twenty-seventh day of the second month the sacrament is commended, and again on the twenty-seventh day of the seventh month it is confirmed, when the ark rested; for what is promised in hope is shown in reality.
*Augustine:* Whether these things were done after the hundred and fifty days, or all are recalled by way of summing-up which began to be done after the forty days of rain? So that this alone belongs to the hundred and fifty days, that the water was raised up to the mountains themselves, either from the fountains of the deep when the rain had now stopped, or because it stayed at its height with no wind drying it. But the other things that have been said were not all done after the hundred and fifty days, but are recalled which began to be done from the end of the forty days.
8.5: **“for in the tenth month”** — It is to be noted that in the tenth month the tops of the mountains appeared, which the waters of the flood had passed by fifteen cubits; because the sacraments of eternal rest and the glory of the resurrection, which the wisdom of the proud did not know, the eminence of the saints understood through the fulfilling of the commandments. Whence: “By thy commandments I have had understanding.” And elsewhere: “Thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them to little ones.”
8.7:
**“Which went forth and did not return, till the waters were dried up upon the earth.”** — In the Hebrew: “It went forth going out and returning, until the waters were dried up.”
**“went forth and did not return”** — ISIDORE. That after forty days the raven did not come back, either cut off by the waters or lured by a floating carcass, figures those most foul with the uncleanness of desire, and therefore too intent on the things that are outside in the world, either to be rebaptized or to be led astray and held by those whom baptism, because of the ark, that is, the Church, kills.
*Augustine:* It is asked whether the raven died or could live in some way. For if there was land where it could rest, the dove likewise would have found rest. Whence it is guessed that the raven could settle on a carcass, which the dove naturally shuns.
8.8:
**“He sent forth also a dove”** — ISIDORE. The dove sent out, and returning when it found no rest, signifies that through the New Testament rest is not promised to the saints in this world; for it was sent out after forty days, by which number the life that is led in the world is marked.
*Strabo:* The ark holds the raven and the dove, and the Church the good and the evil. The raven sent out does not return, because the reprobate, clinging to the enticements of the world, perish. The dove came back carrying an olive branch with green leaves in her mouth, because the saints, rejoicing in simplicity, carry the gift of peace in their mouth, saying: “With them that hated peace I was peaceable: when I spoke to them,” etc.
8.9: **“returned to him”** — The question is how the dove did not find where to settle, when the tops of the mountains had already been laid bare, according to the order of the telling. Which can be solved by summing-up, so that the things told later are understood to have been done earlier; or rather, they had not yet dried.
8.10: **“And having waited yet seven other days, he again sent forth the dove out of the ark.”** — Having waited, etc. The dove, sent out after another seven days because of the sevenfold spiritual working, brought back a fruitful shoot of olive, signifying that many baptized outside the Church, if the richness of charity is not lacking, are brought back at a later time into the fellowship of unity in the mouth of the dove, as in the kiss of peace.
8.11: **“carrying a bough”** — ALCUIN. The dove, the foulest bird having been driven out, carries an olive branch to Noe after the flood, because the dove of the Holy Spirit, coming to Christ after baptism, announces peace with a branch of refreshment and light.
8.12: **“And he stayed yet other seven days: and he sent forth the dove, which returned not any more unto him.”** — And he stayed yet, etc. ISIDORE. The dove, sent out after another seven days and not returning, signifies the end of the world, when rest will be for the saints not in the sacrament of hope, by which the Church is now joined in fellowship as long as that is drunk which flowed from Christ’s side, but in the perfection of salvation, when the kingdom shall be delivered up to God and the Father, so that in that clear contemplation of the truth we may need no ministries.
8.13: **“in the six hundredth and first year”** — ISIDORE. “Of the life of Noe,” that is, when six hundred years are completed, the roof of the ark is opened, because when the sixth age of the world is finished the sacrament is revealed. On the twenty-seventh day of the second month the earth is said to be dried, as if the need of baptizing were ended.
8.14:
**“In the second month”** — STRABO. That is, May. Noe spent a year in the ark and went out on the very day on which he had gone in. For he went in on the seventeenth day of the second month; now it says that he went out on the twenty-seventh day of the same month. But it is to be known that if eleven are added to the present day, as the moon is today, so it will be a year later on that day. So when Noe went in, it was the seventeenth moon, or the seventeenth day of the second month. Therefore after a year, eleven being added, it was the twenty-seventh day and the twenty-seventh moon.
*Mystically:* “In the second month,” etc. As was said above, on the seventeenth day of the six hundredth year the earth was soaked by the waters of the flood, but on the twenty-seventh of the second month it was dried, when it was commanded that they should go out of the ark and receive a covenant, that they should no more perish by the waters of a flood. In which it can be understood that by seventeen, as above, the state of beginners can be signified, when vices are renounced; by twenty-seven the advancement of the perfect in the completion of virtues. For if you add ten to seventeen, it makes twenty-seven. For if to the ten commandments, by which sin is renounced, you add the perfection of the gospel, by which it is commanded not only not to be angry but even to love enemies and the like, you have come to that age of perfection in which you need not the sacraments spoken of; and going out of the ark, that is, coming from hope to hope, you will find the rest promised in the sacraments.
8.16:
**“Go out of the ark, thou and thy wife, thy sons, and the wives of thy sons with thee.”**
• the men and women go out together who went in apart
• Go out of the ark, etc. ISIDORE. They go out joined who went in apart, because now the flesh lusteth against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh; but in the resurrection of the just the body will cling to the spirit in perfect peace, with no need or desire of changeableness resisting.
8.17: **“All living things that are with thee of all flesh, as well in fowls as in beasts, and all creeping things that creep upon the earth, bring out with thee, and go ye upon the earth: increase and multiply upon it.”** — because the world was to be filled by these, the blessing of the first creation is given back
8.20: **“And Noe built an altar unto the Lord: and taking of all cattle and fowls that were clean, offered holocausts upon the altar.”** — And taking, etc. AUGUSTINE. Clean and unclean animals went into the ark, but after the going out only the clean are offered to God. But what he says, “I will not strike every living soul as I have done,” and what he adds, which goodness gives the unworthy by its bounty, perhaps figures the indulgence of the New Testament; so that the past vengeance belongs to the severity of the law, this to the goodness of grace.
8.21:
**“And the Lord smelled a sweet savour, and said: I will no more curse the earth for the sake of man: for the imagination and thought of man’s heart are prone to evil from his youth:”** — For the imagination, etc. GREGORY. In the Morals, book 38. Let no one ascribe it to himself if he has overcome his thoughts; because the evil of corruption which each has taken from the rise of fleshly desires works on as age advances, and unless the hand of divine strength quickly checks it, fault swallows up all the good of nature into the deep. “Neither he that planteth is any thing, nor he that watereth; but God that giveth the increase.”
**“therefore I will no more destroy”** — by a bodily judgment
8.22: **“All the days of the earth, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, night and day, shall not cease.”** — by serving man

9.1: **“Increase and multiply”** — Man is set over the other animals in the inner man, as a comfort after the vengeance that had been carried out, and lest a few men be overwhelmed by many beasts; and that they may know that they rule over the irrational, not over the rational.
9.2:
**“And let the fear and dread of you be upon all the beasts of the earth, and upon all the fowls of the air, and all that move upon the earth:”** — man is set over not men but the irrational
**“all the fishes of the sea are delivered into your hand.”** — into your power
**“And let the fear and dread”** — GREGORY. Man by nature was set over not the rational but the irrational. Therefore it is said to him that he should be feared by the animals, not by man; because it is against nature to be proud and to wish to be feared by an equal. Whence the ancient fathers are said to have been not kings of men but shepherds of flocks. So nature brought forth all men equal; but for various merits God’s just but hidden dispensing sets some over others, so that those who do not fear the divine judgments may be afraid to sin through fear of men. But let those set over others not be proud of this fear, in which they should seek not their own glory but the justice of those under them. For they rule not over men but over beasts, because in the part in which they are beastly they are subjected to fear. So the swelling of pride is to be pressed down by the hand of the humblest consideration. For if the mind comes down within itself from the summit of its height, it will find the plain of natural equality, so as to rejoice not in being over others but in doing them good.
9.4:
**“Saving that flesh with blood you shall not eat.”** — because the seat of the soul is in the blood
**“flesh with blood”** — ISIDORE. All animals are given them for food, because in the calling of the Gentiles to the faith there is no difference, which is figured in Peter’s dish. They are forbidden to eat blood, so that the former life should not be held in the conscience as if choked, but poured out through confession. The eating of flesh seems to have been granted after the flood because of the barrenness of the earth and the frailty of man.
9.5:
**“For I will require the blood of your lives at the hand of every beast,”** — of strong men
**“and at the hand of man, at the hand of every man, and of his brother, will I require the life of man.”** — he wants every man to be understood as the brother of every man, because all are from one
9.10: **“And with every living soul that is with you, as well in all birds as in cattle and beasts of the earth, that are come forth out of the ark, and in all the beasts of the earth.”** — Behold I will establish, etc. God set a testament between himself and men and every living soul, that he would not destroy it by a flood: namely the bow which appears in the clouds, which never shines except from the sun. For they do not perish by the flood, cut off from the Church, who in the prophets and in all the holy Scriptures, as in God’s clouds, recognise the glory of Christ and do not seek their own. But lest worshippers of this sun swell up, let them know that Christ is signified by the sun as by a lion, by a lamb, by a stone: for the sake of likeness, not by the property of substance.
9.13:
**“I will set my bow in the clouds, and it shall be the sign of a covenant between me, and between the earth.”** — I will set my bow, etc. ALCUIN. God gave the bow as a sign of safety, lest fearful men, often seeing floods of rain, should fear to be destroyed by another flood. It was set in heaven so that it could be seen by all, and that in any tribulation we should lift up the eyes of the heart to him who dwells in heaven. And because the bow does not come except from the rays of the sun and a moist cloud, it seems that there had been no rains before the flood; but the earth could be made fruitful by dew and the overflowing of springs.
*Strabo:* The bow has two colours, sky-blue and fiery, which express two judgments: one of water, which is past; the other of fire, which is believed to be coming at the end of the world. Whence the sky-blue colour is on the outside, the fiery on the inside.
9.16:
**“And the bow shall be in the clouds,”** — by the sky-blue colour marking the past flood, by the fiery the judgment to come
**“and I shall see it, and shall remember the everlasting covenant,”** — entered into, or held
9.18:
**“And the sons of Noe who came out of the ark, were Sem,”** — name, or named
**“Cham,”** — crafty
**“and Japheth.”** — breadth
**“And the sons … were”** — JEROME. Often the Seventy, not being able to turn into Greek the letter heth, which sounds a double aspiration, added the Greek chi, teaching that in such words there is to be aspiration. Whence they rendered Cham for what is Ham, from whom Egypt is called Ham in the Egyptians’ tongue to this day.
9.20:
**“And Noe, a husbandman, began”** — Christ made man
**“to till the ground, and planted a vineyard.”** — the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel
9.21:
**“And drinking of the wine was made drunk,”**
• with the cup of the passion
• he suffered
**“and was uncovered”** — he was crucified, where the weakness of mortality appeared
**“in his tent.”** — others: in his house, that is, in his own nation, namely the Jewish
**“drinking of the wine”** — Christ too was made drunk when he suffered, uncovered when he was crucified. “In his tent,” that is, among the household of his own blood; then the mortality of the flesh was laid bare: to the Jews a stumbling-block, to the Gentiles foolishness; but to them that are called, Jews and Gentiles, as Sem and Japheth, the power of God and the wisdom of God; because “the foolishness of God is wiser than men.”
*Alcuin:* After the flood Noe was made drunk, because perhaps he did not know that one could be made drunk by wine; for before the flood men are not read to have used wine. Therefore it is said of Noe specially that he planted a vineyard. The uncovering of the thigh follows drunkenness, as lust follows fullness.
9.22:
**“Which when Cham”**
• because he consented to the killing of Christ
• Israel according to the flesh
• the middle brother, that is, the people of the Jews, which neither held the first place of the apostles nor believed last among the Gentiles
**“the father of Chanaan had seen, to wit, that his father’s nakedness”** — the father’s mortality laid bare
**“was uncovered, he told it”** — through the letter of the law and of prophecy
**“to his two brethren without.”**
• Which when … had seen, etc. ISIDORE. The Jews, seeing the death of Christ, mocked it. But Sem and Japheth, the two peoples believing from the uncircumcision and the circumcision, covered it turned away and did not see. We cover the passion of Christ with a kind of veil, that is, we honour it by a sacrament, and, giving the reason of its mystery, we cover it from the detraction of the Jews. For the garment signifies the sacrament, the backs the memory of things past; for the passion is past, not looked for as to come. Cham saw, because he consented to the Lord’s death. He told it outside, because through him was made plain what was secret in the prophet. Therefore he is made a servant of the servants of his brethren, because that nation, as the Christians’ book-bearer, carries the law and the prophets in witness for the Church, so that we may honour by a sacrament what that letter announces.
• Which when, etc. Heretics are reckoned in the cursed middle, because they are recognised neither in the wall which believed from the circumcision, from which the apostles came, nor in that from the uncircumcision, from which the Gentiles run together into the unity of faith as into the peace of the corner.
9.23:
**“But Sem and Japheth”** — the two sons, the eldest and the youngest, are the two peoples
**“put a cloak upon their shoulders,”** — the sacrament of the passion that is past
**“and going backward, covered the nakedness of their father:”** — honouring with a veil that from which they know they were born
**“and their faces were turned away, and they saw not their father’s nakedness.”**
• because they did not consent to the killing of Christ
• But Sem, etc. GREGORY. In the Morals. We are said to turn away from what we disapprove. What then is it that the sons, coming turned away, covered their father’s nakedness with cloaks thrown over their backs, unless that the good under authority so dislike the evils of those set over them that they hide them from others? Turned away, they bring the covering, because, judging the deed and revering the master, they will not see what they cover.
9.24: **“And Noe awaking from the wine, when he had learned”** — by the prophetic spirit
9.25:
**“He said: Cursed be Chanaan,”** — the Jewish people, which, when it crucified Christ, passed the punishment on to its children, saying: “His blood be upon us and upon our children”
**“Cursed be Chanaan”** — GREGORY. In the Morals, book 26. God does not let many sins go before, but begins his judgment in our correction so that it may come to rest in the damnation of the reprobate. For “judgment begins at the house of God.” What then is the end of those who have not believed, who do not feel temporal scourges because they will perish for ever? Whose wickedness was figured in Cham’s sinning, to whom it is said: “Cursed be Chanaan the boy,” etc. When the father sinned, the son received the sentence, because the wickedness of the reprobate prospers long here but perishes afterwards.
9.26:
**“And he said: Blessed be the Lord God of Sem,”** — from whom are the Jews
**“Blessed be the Lord God of Sem”** — Though God is the God of all nations, as by a proper name he is called the God of Israel even among the nations themselves; which comes from the blessing of Japheth, because among the people of the Gentiles the Church has taken the whole world; which was foretold when it was said, “May God enlarge Japheth.”
**“Chanaan”** — STRABO. From whom the Chanaanites, who by this curse are foretold to be driven out of the place of their dwelling.
9.27:
**“May God enlarge Japheth,”** — from whom are the Gentiles
**“and may he dwell”** — the Jews and Gentiles coming together in the Church
**“in the tents of Sem,”** — in the Churches which the apostles, the sons of the prophets, built
**“and Chanaan be his servant.”**
• the keeper of the books of God
• May God enlarge Japheth, etc. JEROME. From Sem the Hebrews, from Japheth the Gentiles. So because the multitude of believers is broad, he is named from the breadth which is called Japheth. But what he says, “and may he dwell in the tents of Sem,” is prophesied of us, who, Israel being cast out, are busied in the learning and knowledge of the Scriptures.
• ISIDORE. “May God enlarge,” etc. Sem, the elder by birth, is the Jewish people, from whom are the patriarchs and prophets and apostles. Japheth is the father of the Gentiles, who is interpreted “breadth.” For the Gentile people has been spread wide, which receives the inheritance with the prophets and apostles. And the dwelling of Japheth passed into the tents of Sem, that is, the Church is justified in the house of the law and the prophets. For it is lesser in age of time, but greater by the law of grace. But Cham, which is interpreted “crafty,” is as it were the middle one, set apart from both, neither among the firstfruits of the Israelites nor in the fullness of the Gentiles. He signifies not only the Jews but also crafty heretics, not with the spirit of wisdom but of impatience, with which they are wont to burn first and to trouble the saints. He signifies also all false Christians, who proclaim the passion of Christ by professing it but dishonour it by living badly: “By their fruits you shall know them.” He is cursed not in himself but in his son, as in his fruit, that is, in his work; for Chanaan is interpreted “their movement,” that is, their work.

10.1:
**“These are the generations”** — The two sons of Noe having been blessed and the middle one cursed, their generations are woven together, from which seventy-two generations arose: fifteen from Japheth, thirty from Cham, twenty-seven from Sem. To these the Lord sent seventy-two disciples.
*Alcuin:* ALCUIN. Sem, as they reckon, received Asia by lot, Cham Africa, Japheth Europe.
**“Japheth”** — Of the younger son, from whom were born seven sons, who held the northern region from Taurus and Amanus, mountains of Cilicia and Syria, as far as the river Tanais; and in Europe as far as Gades, leaving their names to places and peoples, of which very many have been changed and the rest remain.
10.2:
**“The sons of Japheth: Gomer,”** — the Galatians
**“Gomer”** — These are the Galatians according to Josephus, who in Latin are called Gallo-Greeks.
**“and Magog,”** — the Scythians, who are also thought to be the Massagetae
**“and Madai,”** — the Medes
**“and Javan,”** — the Ionians, who are also the Greeks, from whom the Ionian Sea is named, and their fifth tongue is called Ionic
**“and Thubal,”** — the Iberians, or Spaniards
**“Thubal”** — The Iberians, who are also the Spaniards, from whom Celtiberia is named; though some suspect the Italians.
**“and Mosoch,”** — the Cappadocians, whose chief city is today called Mazaca
**“and Thiras.”** — from whom the Thracians
10.3:
**“And the sons of Gomer: Ascenez”** — whom the Greeks call Rhegini
**“and Riphath”** — the Paphlagonians
**“and Thogorma.”** — and the Phrygians
10.4:
**“And the sons of Javan: Elisa”** — from whom the Eliseans, that is, the Greeks, who are also the Aeolians
**“and Tharsis,”** — the Cilicians, whose city Tarsus is renowned for the apostle Paul
**“Cetthim”** — from whom the Citians, whose city today is called Citium
**“and Dodanim.”** — these are the Rhodians
10.5: **“By these were divided the islands of the Gentiles in their lands, every one according to his tongue and their families in their nations.”** — this is said by prolepsis, that is, by anticipation; for the tongues were not yet divided
10.6:
**“And the sons of Cham: Chus,”** — this is Ethiopia
**“and Mesram,”** — Egypt
**“and Phuth,”** — Libya; whence a river of Mauretania is called Phut, and all the region about it Phutensis
**“and Chanaan.”** — from whom the Chanaanites
**“Chanaan”** — He held the land which the Jews afterwards possessed when the Chanaanites had been cast out.
10.7:
**“And the sons of Chus: Saba,”** — from whom the Sabaeans
**“and Hevila,”**
• part of western Ethiopia
• the Gaetulians, in part of further Africa, bordering the desert
**“and Sabatha,”** — from whom the Sabatheni, who are now the Astabari, according to Jerome
**“and Regma, and Sabatacha. The sons of Regma: Saba”**
• Arabia
• SABA: another than the one above, and different in Scripture; for that one is written with samech, this one with shin. For where we say, “The kings of the Arabians and of Saba shall bring gifts,” in the Hebrew there is “Saba” and “Saba.”
**“and Dadan.”**
• the furthest region of Ethiopia
• Regma and Sabatacha, etc. JEROME. Little by little they lost their ancient names, and what they now have in place of the old is not known.
10.8:
**“Now Chus begot Nemrod:”** — who was the prince of the proud tower
**“he began”** — after the flood
**“to be mighty”** — or a giant
**“Nemrod”** — He who wished to pierce heaven beyond nature signifies the devil, who said: “I will ascend above the stars of heaven.”
**“on the earth.”** — Nemrod, according to Josephus, seized new kingdoms by greed and tyranny, and was the author of the building of the tower that should touch heaven. “He began to be mighty,” or “a giant,” according to others. But Scripture records giants born before. Perhaps, though, the newness of the human race being restored after the flood is recalled, because he began to be a giant upon the earth.
10.9:
**“And he was a stout hunter”** — a deceiver of souls, because he compelled men to worship fire
**“before the Lord.”** — that is, not without the Lord’s knowing, or against the Lord
**“a stout hunter”** — ALCUIN. That is, an oppressor and destroyer of men, whom he enticed to build a tower against God.
10.10:
**“And the beginning of his kingdom was Babylon,”** — confusion
**“and Arach,”** — Edessa, a city of Mesopotamia
**“and Achad,”** — Nisibis
**“and Chalanne”** — now called Seleucia, from Seleucus, king of Asia
**“in the land of Sennaar.”** — Babylonia, where there are pits of bitumen
**“Babylon”** — It is “confusion,” because there the division of tongues was made.
10.11:
**“Out of that land”** — Sennaar
**“came forth Assur, and built Ninive,”** — according to the Hebrews; although Ninus, son of Belus, built it and called it Ninive
**“and the streets of the city, and Chale.”** — which in Hebrew is Rehoboth
**“Assur”** — The empire of the Assyrians, which was the first, under Ninus, who built Ninive, which because of its penance is called beautiful.
10.13:
**“And Mesraim begot Ludim, and Anamim, and Laabim, Nepthuim,”**
• These are the Libyans, who before were Phut
• And Mesraim, etc. JEROME. Except for the Laabim, from whom the Libyans were afterwards named, who before were called Phutaeans, and the Casluim, who were afterwards called the Philistim, whom we corruptly call Palestinians, the other six nations are unknown to us, because they were overthrown in the Ethiopian war. And they possessed the land from Gaza to the furthest borders of Egypt.
10.14: **“Ludim, Anamim, Phetrusim, Capthorim”** — These names are unknown, either because the nations were destroyed in the Ethiopian war, or because it is not known what names they now have.
10.15:
**“And Chanaan”** — the son of Cham
**“begot Sidon,”** — from whom Sidon, a city of Phoenicia
10.16: **“And the Jebusite, and the Amorrhite, and the Gergesite,”** — these peoples Israel drove out of the land of promise
10.17:
**“The Hevite and the Aracite:”** — JEROME. He founded Arca, a town over against Tripolis at the foot of Libanus
**“the Sinite,”** — who built a city near the one just named, called Sin
10.18:
**“And the Aradian,”** — from whom the Aradians, who held the island of Aradus
**“the Samarite,”** — from whom Samaria
**“and the Hamathite:”** — by the Syrians or the Hebrews, Antioch, as among the ancients it is called Emath
10.19: **“And the limits of Chanaan were from Sidon as one comes to Gerara even to Gaza, until thou enter Sodom and Gomorrha, and Adama, and Seboim even to Lesa.”** — these cities are known for their overthrow
10.21:
**“Of Sem also, the father of all the children of Heber, the elder brother of Japheth, sons were born.”** — the younger brother
**“Of Sem”** — He speaks of him last because he follows out his generation and the line of his generation.
**“Heber”** — Who is yet the fifth from Noe’s son Sem. Whether the Hebrews are said to be named from him, or because through him the generation passes to Abraham? So it is rightly asked which is more likely: that the Hebrews are so called as being Heberites, or as being Abrahamites.
10.22:
**“The sons of Sem: Elam”** — from whom the Elamites, namely the princes of Persia
**“and Assur,”** — from whom the Assyrians
**“and Arphaxad,”** — from whom the Chaldeans
**“and Lud,”** — from whom the Lydians
**“and Aram.”** — the Syrians, whose chief city is Damascus
**“Assur”** — Who built Ninive.
10.23:
**“The sons of Aram: Us”** — from whom the land of Hus, which the Seventy call Ausitis, that is, the southern; whence “there was a man in the land of Hus whose name was Job.” He founded Trachonitis and Damascus
**“and Hull,”** — from whom the Armenians; they hold the part of Asia from the river Euphrates to the Indian Ocean
**“and Gether,”** — from whom the Acarnanians, or Carians
**“and Mess.”** — from whom are the Maeonians, whom the Seventy call Mosoch, that is, Maeonians
10.25:
**“And to Heber were born two sons: the name of the one was Phaleg,”** — division
**“because in his days”** — perhaps in his days the division of tongues was made, by which the nations too were divided
**“the earth was divided: and his brother’s name Jectan.”**
• And to Heber were born, etc. Heber is “one who passes over,” from whom the Hebrews, that is, those who pass over. They are true Hebrews who pass over from things present to things to come, from things that fall to things that endure.
• These nations possessed all the region from the river Cophen which is called Seria.

11.1: **“And the earth was”** — AUGUSTINE. It was said above that the sons of Noe, or of his sons, were distributed through the lands according to their tongues. But here by way of summing-up he recalls afterwards what was before. But it causes obscurity that he weaves it together in such a manner of speaking as if a telling of things that were done afterwards followed.
11.4:
**“Come”** — They feared a flood again; therefore, with Nemrod as author, they wished to build themselves a tower in which they should not fear a flood.
**“And they said: Come, let us make a city and a tower, the top whereof may reach to heaven: and let us make our name famous before we be scattered abroad into all lands.”** — A foolish and wicked boldness; whence followed vengeance and the division of tongues.
11.5:
**“And the Lord came down”** — When he fits himself to human senses or works. Whence: “I have seen the affliction of my people, and I am come down to deliver them.” And elsewhere: “I will go down and see whether they have done according to the cry.”
*Isidore:* Mystically. The tower is the pride of the world, or the teachings of heretics, who, moved from the east, that is, from the true light, and coming into Sennaar (which is “the shaking out of teeth”), raise up the pride of their teaching against God, wishing by unlawful curiosity to pierce the height of heaven; but, cut off from the unity of faith and the confession of faith, are they not separated from one another by the diversity of error, as by the discord of tongue? A ruinous agreement arms them against God; a sudden confusion of error divides them. The Trinity, against which they have offended, condemns and scatters them. Whence: “Come ye, therefore, let us go down, and there confound their tongue,” namely by the variety of errors or schisms, when the division of tongues was made. In the house of Heber alone the first tongue remained, as in the Church alone, which is the house of Christ, the unity of confession and faith.
11.7:
**“Come ye, therefore,”** — the Trinity in persons, as there: “Let us make man,” etc.
**“let us go down, and there confound their tongue, that they may not understand”** — understand
**“one another’s speech.”** — the accustomed
**“Come ye, therefore, let us go down”** — He is understood to have said it to the angels. Or according to that: “Let us make man to our image and likeness.” For in the singular number there is added, “and he scattered them,” etc., as there: “God made man to his image and likeness.”
*Gregory:* In the Morals, book 2. “Come ye,” etc., is said to those who cleave to God. “Come,” because never to decrease from divine contemplation but always to increase, and never to draw back in heart, is by a steady motion always to come. The angels go up by beholding the Creator; they come down by pressing down, with the scrutiny of strictness, the creature that raises itself unlawfully. So to say, “Let us go down and confound their tongue,” is to show in himself what is rightly done, and by the force of inner vision to breathe into their minds, by hidden movements, the judgments to be shown.
11.8: **“And so the Lord scattered them”** — the unity of the Godhead, as there: “God made man to his image,” etc.
11.9: **“scattered them”** — ALCUIN. In this division of tongues God made nothing new, but divided the manners of speaking and the forms of speech among the different nations. Whence we find the same syllables and letters of the same value joined otherwise in different tongues, and often the same nouns or verbs signifying something else. Where we say in the psalm, “with a rod of iron,” the Greek has en rhabdō sidēra; but sidera in Latin signifies not “of iron,” as in Greek, but stars.
11.10:
**“Sem was a hundred years old”** — BEDE. A great question arises for us according to the letter: how Sem is said to be a hundred years old two years after the flood, when above he is asserted to have been born in Noe’s five hundredth year, and the flood is read to have come in the six hundredth year of the same Noe? So that the number of the times may not fight against itself, it is to be understood either that Noe was two years more than five hundred when Sem was born, or two years less than six hundred when the flood came, or that Sem was a hundred and two years old when Arphaxad was born. For Scripture is sometimes wont so to speak that, even if a little is over or short, it gives a full and complete number in the reckoning. But it seems likely, as my guess goes, that when Sem was born Noe was two years over five hundred. Nor did Scripture speak falsely in saying that he was five hundred years old, even if he was five hundred and two, since of course the smaller number is contained within the greater. But perhaps the writer of the holy history took care to set it out more carefully in this place, saying that Sem was a hundred years old two years after the flood, because he remembered that he had noted the year of his birth somewhat loosely.
**“These are the generations of Sem: Sem was a hundred years old when he begot Arphaxad, two years after the flood.”** — Nowhere in this whole series of generations has he added “he died,” as in the age that went before the flood; because there was no one in all this line of those born of whom, as an exception from the others, it could be said, as there of Henoch: “And he walked with the Lord, and was seen no more: because God took him.”
11.27:
**“And these are the generations of Thare: Thare begot Abram, Nachor, and Aran. And Aran begot Lot.”** — JEROME. “These are the generations of Thare,” and the rest. For what we read according to the Seventy, “in the region of the Chaldeans,” the Hebrew has “in Ur Casdim,” that is, “in the fire of the Chaldeans.” And from this occasion the Hebrews hand down a story of this kind: that Abraham was thrown into the fire because he would not worship the fire which the Chaldeans worship, and, freed by God’s help, fled from the fire of idolatry. Where it is written in what follows that Thare went out with his offspring “from the region of the Chaldeans,” in the Hebrew there is “from the burning of the Chaldeans”; and this is what is now said: “And Aran died before Thare his father, in the land of his nativity, in the fire of the Chaldeans,” namely that, not wishing to worship the fire, he was consumed by fire. Afterwards the Lord says to Abram: “I am he who brought thee out of the fire of the Chaldeans.”
**“Thare begot Abram”** — AUGUSTINE. Not at once, but at their own times, from when he began to beget. Nor is the order of birth to be heeded here, but the signifying of the dignity to come, in which Abram excels.
11.28:
**“And Aran died”** — consumed by the fire, as the Hebrews say, which he would not worship
*Jerome:* In Ur of the Chaldees. In the Hebrew, “in Ur Casdim,” that is, “in the fire of the Chaldeans.” Here the Hebrews tell the story that Abram was thrown into the fire because he would not worship the fire which the Chaldeans worship, and, freed by God’s help, escaped from the fire of idolatry. Whence it is said to him: “I am he who brought thee out from Ur of the Chaldees.”
11.29: **“Aran, father of Melcha”** — JEROME. The same Aran, son of Thare, brother of Abraham and Nachor, was father of both: he begot two daughters, Melcha and Sarai, surnamed Jescha. Nachor married Melcha and Abram Sarai; for marriages between uncles and nieces had not yet been forbidden, which in the beginning were held even between brothers and sisters.
11.31:
**“And Thare took Abram, his son, and Lot the son of Aran, his son’s son, and Sarai his daughter in law, the wife of Abram his son, and brought them out of Ur of the Chaldees, to go into the land of Chanaan: and they came as far as Haran,”** — or Charran
**“and dwelt there.”** — And Thare took Abram his son, etc. AUGUSTINE. “And the days of Thare were two hundred and five years, and he died in Haran.” It is said first that when Thare was seventy years old he begot Abram, and afterwards he stayed with all his household in Charran and died. And it was said to Abram that he should go out of Charran, and he went out when he was seventy-five years old. But by summing-up it is shown that the Lord commanded it while the father was alive, and that Abram went out of Charran when he was seventy-five years old and his father a hundred and forty-five, if the days of his life were two hundred and five years; so that it is therefore written, “the years of the life of Thare were two hundred and five years in Charran,” because there he filled up the years of his whole life. So the question is solved by summing-up, which is unsolvable if we should say that the Lord told Abram to go out of the land after Thare’s death; because he was not seventy-five years old when his father was already dead, who begot him in the seventieth year of his age, so that after his father’s death he would be a hundred and thirty-five years old, if all the father’s years were two hundred and five. But because some wish Abram’s years to be counted from when he was freed from the fire of the Chaldeans, according to the tradition of the Hebrews, it can be said that the Scripture which says, “When Thare was seventy years old he begot Abram, and Nachor, and Aran,” did not mean that he begot the three in the seventieth year, but recalled when he began to beget. It may be that he begot Abram later, but he was named first by the privilege of dignity, as was done there: “I have loved Jacob, but have hated Esau”; and in Paralipomenon, Juda, fourth in order, was named first, from whom the Jews were named, because of the royal tribe.

12.1:
**“And … said”** — Augustine: while his father was living
**“the Lord”** — the Father
**“to Abram:”** — to Christ
**“Go forth out of thy country,”** — from the earthly man
**“and from thy kindred,”**
• the Jewish
• of vices
**“and out of thy father’s house,”**
• of the devil
• “forget thy people and thy father’s house”
**“and come into the land”** — of the Gentiles
**“which I shall shew thee.”**
• by giving knowledge of thee through the apostles
• Go forth out of thy country, etc. AUGUSTINE. The account of Stephen on this matter is to be considered, so that it may not be contradicted by any of these explanations. And indeed it happened that God did not speak to Abram, as it seems to be told in Genesis, after the death of Thare, that he should go out of his country and from his kindred; but when he was in Mesopotamia, before he dwelt in Charran, having already gone out of the land of the Chaldeans, so that God is understood to have spoken to him on that journey. But because Stephen afterwards tells it thus, “Then Abraham went out of the land of the Chaldeans and dwelt in Charan; and from thence, after his father was dead, he removed him into this land,” he brings no small difficulties to this explanation, which is made by summing-up. For he seems to have had the command of the Lord, who had spoken to him on the journey in Mesopotamia when he had gone out of the land of the Chaldeans and was going to Haran, and to have fulfilled it after the death of his father, when it is said, “He dwelt in Charan; and from thence, after his father was dead, he removed him into this land.” And by this the question remains, if he was seventy-five years old when he went out of Charran, how can this be true? Unless perhaps what Stephen says, “Then Abraham went out of the land of the Chaldeans and dwelt in Charan,” is taken thus: “then he went out” after the Lord had spoken; for he was already in Mesopotamia (as was said above) when he heard it from the Lord. But by the rule of summing-up Stephen wished to weave it together and say at once from where he went out and where he dwelt, when he says: “Then Abram went out of the land of the Chaldeans and dwelt in Charan.” But in between, that is, between the going out of the land of the Chaldeans and the dwelling in Charran, God spoke to him. And as to what Stephen adds, “and from thence, after his father was dead, God removed him into this land,” it is to be noted that he does not say, “and after his father was dead he went out of Charran,” but, “from thence God removed him into this land”; so that after the dwelling in Charran he was settled in the land of Chanaan: not that he went out after his father’s death, but that he was settled in the land of Chanaan. So that the order of the words is: he dwelt in Charran, and from thence he removed him into this land after his father was dead; namely, he was settled then when he received there the grandson whose whole seed was to reign, by God’s promise, the inheritance being given. For from Abraham himself was born Ismael of Agar, and others of Cetura, and of Isaac Esau, to whom the inheritance does not belong; but of Jacob, the son of Isaac, as many as were born, that is, his whole seed, belonged to that inheritance. So Abram was settled in that land in this way, when he lived there until the birth of Jacob.
*Strabo:* It is to be noted that he had already gone out of his country; but then he had gone out in body, not in mind and will, for he perhaps had a mind to return when it was said to him: “Go forth,” etc.
*Isidore:* He left the land, the time, the kindred of the Jews, and was magnified among the peoples of the Gentiles. We too must go out of our country, that is, from our earthly means and wealth; and from our kindred, that is, from the way of life of vices, which, clinging to us from birth, are joined to us as by the bond of blood; and from our father’s house, that is, from the memory of the world; so that, renouncing it, we may be spread abroad with the people of God and, when the time comes, be brought into the land of the heavenly promise.
12.2:
**“And I will make of thee”** — the first blessing, of temporal height
**“a great nation,”** — “a people which I knew not hath served me”
**“I will make of thee a … nation”** — ISIDORE. Two things are promised to Abram: namely, that his seed shall possess the land of Chanaan, when it is said, “and come into the land which I shall shew thee”; but the other, far more excellent, is not of the fleshly but of the spiritual seed, by which he is to be the father not only of the Jewish nation but of all nations that follow his faith; which is promised thus: “And in thee shall all the kindred of the earth be blessed.”
12.3:
**“I will bless them that bless thee, and curse them that curse thee, and in thee”** — in Christ, who is from thee
**“shall … be blessed:”** — the second blessing, of spiritual breadth
**“all the kindred of the earth”** — nations
12.4:
**“So Abram went out”** — STRABO. With a firm mind, never to return; for he had already gone out in body
**“as the Lord had commanded him, and Lot went with him: Abram was seventy-five years old when he went forth from Haran.”** — AUGUSTINE. While his father was living
**“seventy-five years old”** — JEROME. If Thare, Abraham’s father, begot Abram in the region of Chaldea at seventy years old, and died in Charran in his two hundred and fifth year, how is Abram recorded as going out of Charran after Thare’s death at seventy-five years old, when from his birth to his father’s death there are shown to have been a hundred and thirty-five years? So the tradition of the Hebrews is true, that Thare went out with his sons from the fire of the Chaldeans, and that Abram, hemmed in by the Babylonian fire because he would not worship it, was freed by God’s help, and that from that time the span of his age is reckoned to him, from when he confessed God, spurning the idols of the Chaldeans. But it may be, since Scripture has left it uncertain, that Thare, having set out from Chaldea, came into Haran a few years before he died, or straight after the persecution, and stayed there a long time.
12.6:
**“Abram passed through the country into the place of Sichem,”** — the city which is corruptly called Sychar, and is interpreted “shoulder”
**“as far as the noble vale:”** — which is now called the Salt Sea, or the Dead Sea, and the Lake of Asphalt, and the Valley of the Salt Pits
12.7:
**“And the Lord appeared to Abram,”** — who, renouncing idolatry, built an altar to the Lord
**“and said to him: To thy seed will I give this land. And he built there an altar to the Lord, who had appeared to him.”** — having despised the fire of the Chaldeans
12.8:
**“And passing on from thence to a mountain, that was on the east side of Bethel,”** — a city in the tribe of Benjamin which was before called Luza, that is, almond tree
**“he there pitched his tent, having Bethel on the west, and Hai on the east;”** — a city in the tribe of Juda
**“he built there also an altar to the Lord, and called upon his name.”** — because a worshipper of one God
**“Bethel”** — RABANUS. It is interpreted “house of God,” which was afterwards called Bethaven, that is, “house of an idol.”
**“Hai”** — It is interpreted “eye” or “fountain.” So the patriarch, making for the land of promise, pitched his tent between Bethel and Hai, because the saints, reborn in the fountain of baptism, are watchful in the course of this life and hasten to God’s tent, that is, to the heavenly city.
12.13:
**“Say, therefore, I pray thee,”** — he wished the truth to be hidden, not a lie to be told
**“that thou art my sister:”** — because the daughter of his brother
**“that I may be well used for thee, and that my soul may live for thy sake.”** — Say, therefore, I pray thee, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is asked why the patriarch wished to lie so as to call her his sister, and did not rather commit it to God, who, if he wished, could keep her chastity safe with Pharao. But he wished the truth to be hidden, yet not a lie to be told. For she is called a sister because she was a brother’s daughter. And in this it is shown that no one should tempt his God while he has something he can do by reasonable counsel. For he did for his life what he could; but what he could not, he committed to God, in whom he hoped, to whom he entrusted his wife’s chastity; nor did faith or hope deceive him. So let a man not dare to tempt God while he has a reasonable way to escape what he ought to beware of. Nor did Paul despair of God’s protection or lose faith when, let down in a basket, he escaped the hands of his enemies. But Abram himself, if when asked he had declared her his wife, would have committed two things to God: both his own life and his wife’s chastity.
12.15:
**“And the princes told Pharao, and praised her before him: and … was taken”** — against her will
**“the woman was taken”** — RABANUS. Sarai is excused, who is taken into the house of Pharao against her will, not only in this, that the body is not defiled, nor the soul, except by the mind’s consent, but also in this, that it was done with her husband’s agreement and permission.
*Augustine:* She could remain untouched so long with Pharao because it is read in Esther that the maidens were not brought in to the kings at once, but were kept for a year, and for six months were anointed with oil of myrrh, and for another six months were in various perfumes. So through this respite of time she could remain untouched, and meanwhile the Egyptians used Abram well, until Pharao, scourged by God and learning that she was his wife, gave her back untouched.
12.16: **“And they used Abram well”** — the Egyptians
12.17: **“But the Lord scourged Pharao and his house with most grievous stripes for Sarai, Abram’s wife.”** — whom he wished to keep untouched

13.1: **“And Abram went up out of Egypt, he and his wife, and all that he had, and Lot with him, into the south.”** — And Abram went up, etc. JEROME. Freed from Egypt, he is well read to have gone up. But how could he be very rich? But in the Hebrew truth there is “exceedingly heavy,” for he was weighed down by the weight of Egypt. And though they seem to be riches of gold and silver, yet if they are Egyptian they are heavy to a holy man. Nor is it, as is read in the Seventy, “he went whence he had come, into the desert, as far as Bethel,” but according to the Hebrew, “he went on his journey through the south as far as Bethel.” For he set out from Egypt not to make for the desert, which he had left in Egypt, but to come through the south, which is opposite the north, to the house of God, where his tent was, between Bethel and Hai.
13.3:
**“And he returned by the way that he came, from the south”** — though night presses upon the worshippers of God, and persecution, yet their zeal for divine worship does not grow cold
**“to Bethel, to the place where before he had pitched his tent between Bethel and Hai:”** — To Bethel, etc. Bethel is a small town at the twelfth milestone from Aelia, on the right as one goes to Neapolis, which was before called Luza, that is, almond tree, in the tribe of Benjamin. But Hai is in the tribe of Juda, set apart for the priests. Bethel is “house of God”; Hai, “eye” or “fountain.” So, pitching his tent between Bethel and Hai, he rightly built an altar to the Lord, because the saints, withdrawing from the prince of the world and the pleasures of the age, washed in the holy fountain of baptism, leading the course of the present life with care, and offering to God the sacrifice of praise and of good work upon the altar of faith, happily make for the house of God, that is, the heavenly Jerusalem.
13.7:
**“Whereupon also there arose a strife between the herdsmen”** — catholics and heretics
**“of the flocks”** — of those under them
**“of Abram”** — of the catholic prelates
**“and of Lot.”** — of the heresiarchs
13.8:
**“Abram therefore said to Lot: Let there be no quarrel, I beseech thee, between me and thee, and between my herdsmen and thy herdsmen:”** — to be noted, how great a care the holy man has to keep peace
**“for we are brethren.”**
• by kinship; for Lot was the son of Aran, Abraham’s brother
• Let there be no quarrel, I beseech thee, etc. Let us too put nothing before concord and charity, but through the right hand of prosperity or the left of adversity persevere in peace and love. The strife between Lot’s herdsmen and Abraham’s herdsmen signifies the controversy between catholic pastors and heretical subverters. Whence Lot, who is interpreted “turning aside,” signifies the heresiarchs, and he chose for himself the region about the Jordan, that is, “descent.” His herdsmen signify heretics and schismatics, who seek what is fair and sloping, and do not go up the mountain with Moses to the Lord; despising peace and unity, they take the choice of going where they will, and fleeing grace they commit themselves to free will. But Abraham’s herdsmen signify catholic teachers, who flee heretics even in place, according to that: “A man that is a heretic, after the first and second admonition, avoid.” And this in the land of the Chanaanite and the Pherezite, namely in the land of promise; because between catholics and heretics there is wont to be contention over whose is the kingdom of heaven.
• From here we learn that there is an earthly paradise, to which an earthly watering is compared. For this region was level and open and watered by the flowing Jordan, as Egypt by the Nile.
**“for we are brethren”** — In three ways men are called brethren in holy Scripture: by nature, as Jacob and Esau; by kinship, as Abram and Lot; by nation, as all the Jews. Whence: “If thy brother, constrained by poverty, sell himself to thee,” etc.
13.9:
**“Behold the whole land is before thee: depart from me I pray thee:”** — “if thy eye scandalize thee, pluck it out, and cast it from thee”
**“if thou wilt go to the left hand”** — that is, whether adversity befall thee and prosperity me, or prosperity thee and adversity me
13.10:
**“And Lot, lifting up his eyes,”** — having looked round the region
**“saw”** — it pleased him
**“all the country about the Jordan,”** — set, namely, on a descent
**“which was watered throughout,”** — by the Jordan
**“before the Lord destroyed Sodom and Gomorrha, as the paradise of the Lord,”** — a delightful and well-watered garden
13.11:
**“And Lot chose to himself the country about the Jordan,”** — not the steep but the sloping
**“and he departed from the east:”** — to fall into the west
**“and they were separated one brother from the other.”**
• otherwise: “and they were separated one from the other, from his brother”
• so heretics and catholics, as much in place as in manners
• “they went out from us, but they were not of us”
13.13: **“And the men of Sodom were very wicked, and sinners before the face of the Lord, beyond measure.”** — Before the Lord, to whom the crime is committed to be punished. For the crime was plain to men too, but not to be punished by them.
13.14:
**“And the Lord said to Abram, after Lot was separated from him:”** — the schism departing, a broad inheritance is promised, spread through all parts of the world by the merit of faith
**“Lift up thy eyes, and look from the place wherein thou now art, to the north and to the south, to the east and to the west.”** — Lift up thy eyes, etc. As if: look through the four quarters of the world. The possession of Palestine is promised to him and to his seed. That in some copies “the sea” is put for “the west” is because Palestine has the sea on the west.
13.15:
**“and to thy seed”** — that is, to Christ, who is of his seed
**“for ever.”** — All the land, etc. Not this alone was promised; for it is not said, “I will give thee as much land as thou seest,” but, “I will give thee the land which thou seest.” For though the further land on every side was given too, this which was seen was given especially. Whence he also added, “Arise and walk through the land,” etc., so that by walking through he might come to that which he could not see standing in one place. And that land is signified which Israel received, Abraham’s seed according to the flesh, not according to faith, which was to be as the sand of the sea, because it could not be numbered.
**“I will give to thee”** — To Christ is promised the inheritance of all nations, who has spread his Church through the whole world, to whom the Father says: “Ask of me, and I will give thee the Gentiles for thy inheritance.” And the Psalm: “And he shall rule from sea to sea.”
13.16: **“And I will make thy seed as the dust of the earth: if any man be able to number the dust of the earth, he shall be able to number thy seed also.”** — the seed of Israel according to the flesh
13.17:
**“Arise”** — lest it be thought that only that land is promised which could be seen by Abram standing in the same place
**“and walk through the land in the length, and in the breadth thereof: for I will give it to thee.”** — namely, to those who shall be born of thee
13.18:
**“So Abram removing his tent”** — because he had here no lasting city
**“came and dwelt by the vale of Mambre,”** — which is so called from Mambre, Abraham’s friend
**“in Hebron”** — It is a city in the tribe of Juda, which is also called Cariatharbe, that is, “city of four”; for in Hebrew cariath is “city,” arbe “four.” For there are laid Adam the greatest, and Abram, Isaac and Jacob.
**“and he built there an altar to the Lord.”** — so as to show worship to him to whom he owed faith

14.1:
**“And it came to pass at that time, that Amraphel”** — “he said that he might fall”: these are they who, speaking against the Lord, fall
**“king of Sennaar,”** — “the stench of their teeth,” namely of those who spread a stinking teaching
**“and Arioch”** — “drunken,” namely he who, forgetting the worship of God, worships the creature
**“king of Pontus,”** — of the nations surrounded by every error
**“and Chodorlahomor”** — “a comely sheaf”: these are the hypocrites, who wish to seem comely with virtues
**“king of the Elamites,”** — of worldly men
**“and Thadal king of nations,”**
• “knowing the yoke”: he signifies avarice, the mistress of the nations
• Amraphel is interpreted “he said that he might fall,” and he is king of Sennaar, which is interpreted “the shaking out of teeth,” or “their stench.” He signifies heretics, who make for a fall and with deceitful words vomit out a stinking meaning. Arioch is interpreted “drunken” or “drunkenness”; he signifies the folly of the Gentiles, who, drunk with wickedness, worship the creature instead of the Creator and roll in the enticements of the world. Chodorlahomor is interpreted “a comely sheaf”; he is king of Elam, that is, of this world, and signifies hypocrisy, which, though it is empty and ruinous, yet seems comely on the surface; but in the future what it was will appear. Thadal, “knowing the yoke” or “a spy,” who is king of nations, signifies avarice, which, shrewd and cunning, puts many under its yoke.
• Amraphel king of Sennaar, etc. These four kings figure the four chief vices contrary to the four chief virtues, which strive to subdue the five senses, signified by the five kings, through the concupiscence of the flesh, through the concupiscence of the eyes, through the ambition of the world.
14.2:
**“Made war against Bara”** — malice
**“king of Sodom,”** — “of the silent beast”
**“and against Bersa”** — “in straits”
**“king of Gomorrha,”** — “of the swelling people”
**“and against Sennaab”** — which is interpreted “shaking out” or “stench of teeth”
**“king of Adama,”** — of earthly men
**“and against Semeber”** — perdition
**“king of Seboim,”** — which is “a little village of death,” or “of mourning”
**“and against the king of Bala,”** — “devouring” or “casting headlong”
**“which is Segor.”** — “very little”
**“Bala”** — JEROME. In Hebrew it is called “devouring.” The Hebrews hand down that elsewhere it is called Salissa and “the heifer of three years,” because it was swallowed up by a third earthquake. After Sodom and Gomorrha, Adama and Seboim were overthrown by divine fire, it is called “the little one”; for Segor is rendered “little,” which in the Syrian tongue is called Zoara. But the vale of the salt pits, in which there were pits of bitumen, after God’s anger and the rain of sulphur, was turned into the Dead Sea, which is called by the Greeks the lake of asphalt, that is, of bitumen.
*Mystically:* Four kings overcome five, when the contrary powers ensnare and take captive by vices the five senses of the body, which misuse them.
*Allegorically:* Such kings overcome first Bara, who is interpreted “malice” or “creature,” and is king of Sodom, that is, of blindness or of the silent beast, when they persuade those who persist in their old malice to follow the blindness of lust after the manner of beasts. They overcome also Bersa, that is, one set in straits, king of Gomorrha, that is, of a swelling and seditious people, when they overwhelm and lay low those who are straitened by the cares of the world and do not fear to commit the wickedness of robbery. They overcome also Sennaab, king of Adama, that is, of the earthly, when they urge those who savour only earthly things to remain in luxury, so that they say: “Let us eat and drink, for to morrow we shall die.” They overcome Semeber, who is interpreted “there perdition,” and is king of Seboim, that is, of the girdle of mourning, when through anger and envy they deceive the unwary. Whence: “Anger killeth the foolish, and envy slayeth the little one.” They overcome the king of Bala too, when they send the faint-hearted into despair. For Bala is interpreted “casting headlong” or “swallowing up”: the devil strives most of all for this, that after the fall of sin he may send a man into despair.
14.3:
**“All these came together into the woodland vale,”** — or “noble”
**“which now is the salt sea.”** — after the overthrow of Sodom
14.4:
**“For … twelve years,”** — he sets out the cause of the war
**“they had served Chodorlahomor”** — “the generation of the sheaf,” or “having a comely sheaf”
**“and in the thirteenth year”** — an odd number signifies the concord of the Trinity
**“they revolted from him.”** — For … twelve years, etc. Twelve is a superfluous number, in which superfluity our five senses serve the vain superstition which Chodorlahomor signifies, and the four vices that lie beside it; and wishing to withdraw, they suffer heavy persecution and are often overcome.
14.5:
**“And in the fourteenth year”** — the frailty of the fourfold returning, they strive to overcome by turns
**“came Chodorlahomor, and the kings that were with him: and they smote the Raphaim in Astaroth”** — giants, that is, those who presume upon themselves
**“carnaim,”** — “horns” or “defences,” “cutting the wave,” or “the division of the stirring”
**“and the Zuzim”** — “terrible ones”
**“with them, and the Emim”** — “dreadful ones”
**“in Save of Cariathaim.”**
• “perfect fullness,” “calling seven times,” or “abounding”
• The Raphaim in Astaroth, etc. The names of the places and nations signify those living carnally, whom vices easily overcome.
**“and they smote”** — JEROME. Another edition has: “And the giants fell in Astaroth Carnaim, and strong nations together with them, and the men in the city of Save, before they came to Sodom.” The four kings, setting out from Babylon, killed the giants, that is, the Raphaim; also the strong men of Arabia, and the Zuzim and Emim in the city of Save, which is so called to this day. Zuzim and Emim are interpreted “terrible” and “dreadful,” for which the Seventy, following rather the sense, put “very strong nations.” And returning they came to the fountain of judgment, that is, Cades; it is said by anticipation, because it was afterwards so called. And it signifies the place by the rock which is named the fountain of judgment, because there God judged the people.
14.6:
**“And the Chorreans in the mountains of Seir,”** — “in their swelling,” of those who are rough in manners
**“even to the plains of Pharan,”** — “their fierceness”
14.7:
**“And they returned, and came to the fountain”**
• the rock from which Moses brought forth water
• the rush of the waters
**“of Misphat,”** — where afterwards the murmuring people was judged
**“the same is Cades:”** — “judgment”
**“and they smote all the country”** — it is also interpreted “holy,” by antiphrasis
**“of the Amalecites,”** — “of those who lick the earth”
**“and the Amorrhean”** — “embittering”
**“that dwelt in Asasonthamar.”** — that is, in the city of palms, where the proud kings won the victory; this is the town of Engaddi, fruitful in balsam and palms; for Asasonthamar is interpreted “city of palms”
14.8:
**“And the king of Sodom”** — of the silent beasts
**“and the king of Gomorrha,”** — of the swelling people
**“and the king of Adama,”** — of earthly men
**“and the king of Seboim,”** — of those who mourn
**“and the king of Bala,”** — of those devoured
**“which is Segor, went out: and they set themselves against them in battle array in the woodland vale:”** — in the baseness of rough manners
14.10:
**“Now the woodland vale”** — because rough manners drag the stubborn into the depth of evils
**“had many pits of slime. And the king of Sodom, and the king of Gomorrha”** — “dumb dogs, not able to bark”: and being lifted up they give way to vices
**“turned their backs and were overthrown there: and they that remained”** — not giving way to vices
**“fled to the mountain.”** — the eminence of the virtues
14.11:
**“And they took all the substance of the Sodomites, and Gomorrhites,”** — this happens when vices overcome reason and send a famine of the word, by which the soul should have been fed
**“and all their victuals, and went their way:”** — by hiding their snares
14.12: **“And Lot also … and his substance.”** — from the company of the wicked the just sometimes bear temporal punishments
14.13:
**“And behold one that had escaped told Abram the Hebrew,”** — in the Hebrew, “the one who passes over”
**“who dwelt in the vale of Mambre”** — a proper name
**“the Hebrew”** — The Seventy: “the one from beyond the river,” because, coming from Mesopotamia, having crossed the river Euphrates, he set his seat in the land of Chanaan. Whence Josue the son of Nun: “Will you serve the gods of your fathers, who are beyond the river?”
14.14:
**“Which when Abram had heard, to wit, that his brother Lot was taken, he numbered of the servants born in his house”** — not married men, of whom it is said in what follows, “Except such things as the young men have eaten”
**“three hundred and eighteen well appointed: and pursued them to Dan.”**
• where one of the springs of the Jordan rises, which is now called Dan
• Jerome: a town of Phoenicia which is now called Paneas
**“And when … had heard this”** — ISIDORE. In like manner our faith, when it has been strengthened by the principal spirit, subdues the five senses of the body as five kings, triumphing over the outward man by the word of God. He overcame his enemies with three hundred and eighteen, because we, in the sacrament of the cross, which the letter tau signifies, which stands for three hundred, overcome the five fleshly senses that before took us captive by various vices. Eighteen, multiplied from three and six, signifies faith in the Trinity and the perfection of work, by which the full victory of the virtues against the vices is accomplished.
*Strabo:* Allegorically. Abraham’s war with the four kings signifies the war of virtues and vices. So the father of faith and the first way of believing fought for his brother Lot and conquered, not in the multitude of an army but with three hundred and eighteen servants born in his house, well appointed. So let each wage war for his soul against the spirits of wickedness with three hundred and eighteen servants born in his house, that is, with the help of the holy cross. For the letter tau, which has the shape of a cross, expresses three hundred.
**“Dan”** — Dan is one of the springs of the Jordan; for the other is called Jor, which is interpreted “stream.” So from the two springs, which are not far from each other, joined into one stream, the Jordan is named.
14.15:
**“And dividing his company,”**
• the companions of Abram, that is, of faith, are charity and hope, which in their turns, as if separately, pour into minds full of vice by hidden inspiration
• faith with hope and charity pursues the vices
**“he rushed upon them in the night: and defeated them, and pursued them as far as Hoba, which is on the left hand of Damascus.”** — that is, as far as the adversity of shedding blood; for Damascus is interpreted “a drink of blood”
14.16:
**“And he brought back”** — faith frees from the captivity of the vices reason and understanding, as a brother, and the brother’s substance, with the virtues of the cleansed mind
**“all the substance, and Lot his brother, with his substance, the women also”** — the civic virtues
**“and the people.”** — the kinds of all the virtues
14.17: **“And the king of Sodom went out”** — when the vices are overcome, they plot other snares, above all lust, which rules over the Sodomites
14.18:
**“But Melchisedech the king of Salem, bringing forth bread and wine,”** — these sacraments were a figure of our sacraments
**“for he was the priest of the”** — signifying the High Priest
**“most high God,”**
• or “highest”
• But Melchisedech, etc. JEROME. The Hebrews say that this is Sem, the son of Noe, and show by the reckoning of years that he lived until Isaac, and that all the firstborn from Noe to Aaron were high priests. And Salem was afterwards called Jerusalem. The apostle, recalling Melchisedech “without father, without mother,” refers him to Christ, and through him to the Church of the Gentiles, because the glory of the head is referred to the members. Since he blessed Abram the circumcised, and in him Levi, and so Aaron too, from whom the priesthood came afterwards; from which he wishes to gather that the priesthood of the Church, which has the foreskin, blessed the circumcised priesthood of the synagogue. And what he says, “Thou art a priest for ever according to the order of Melchisedech,” our ministry is marked by the word “order”: to be consecrated not through Aaron by sacrificing irrational victims, but by bread and wine being offered, that is, the body and blood of the Lord.
*Strabo:* Melchisedech, who is interpreted “king of justice” and is called “king of peace,” signifies Christ, through whom we have been reconciled, and who at the end of the world is to judge justly.
14.19:
**“Blessed him,”** — as the greater the lesser
**“and said: Blessed be Abram by the most high God,”** — as if this victory is to be assigned to the most high God, and thanksgiving to be shown him for his benefits
14.20:
**“And blessed be the most high God, by whose protection the enemies are in thy hands.”** — or “in his hands”
**“And he gave him the tithes of all.”**
• morally: tithes are given when perseverance is added to good work
• in whom Levi, as the lesser, was tithed
**“he gave him the tithes”** — ISIDORE. So the patriarch, knowing that the priesthood among the people of the Gentiles was better than the Levitical, which was to be born of himself, and that he was to be blessed by the better, gave Melchisedech the tithes of his substance after the blessing, as the people according to the laws gave tithes to the priests who blessed them. Melchisedech is interpreted “king of peace” or “of justice.” For we are reconciled to God through Christ, who is to come to sort the good from the evil. He is the priest who offered himself to God the Father for all, and the true king, who rules his own in the present and in the future will judge justly.
14.21:
**“And the king of Sodom said to Abram: Give me the persons,”** — the vices seek only souls
**“and the rest”** — the spoils
**“take to thyself.”** — he strives to deceive through greed
14.23:
**“That from the very woof thread”** — as if not even the least: he shakes his hands from every gift
**“unto the shoe latchet, I will not take of any things that are thine, lest thou say I have enriched Abram:”** — From the very woof thread, etc. The just man shakes his hands from every gift; in which it is shown that wars are to be waged by the faithful not out of greed but out of charity. He excepts the pay of the soldiers and the shares of those who had fought together with him, partly showing his own justice, partly not denying the pay owed to those who fight lawfully.
14.24:
**“Except such things as the young men have eaten, and the shares of the men”** — he justly gives to each what is his
**“that came with me, Aner, Escol, and Mambre: these shall take their shares.”** — That came with me, Aner, Escol, etc. For faith sometimes uses the testimonies of unbelievers. Whence the apostle: “evil beasts, slothful bellies”; but for the profit of the faithful.

15.1:
**“Now when these things were done, the word of the Lord came to Abram by a vision,”** — by a hidden inspiration
**“saying: Fear not, Abram, I am thy protector, and thy reward exceeding great.”** — Now when these things, etc. “Fear not.” Mystically. The multitude of the vices having been triumphed over, the hope of each of the faithful is strengthened by the Lord, so that it may not waver but await its reward.
15.2:
**“And Abram said: Lord God, what wilt thou give me? I shall go without children:”** — he who has overcome the vices seeks the fruit of good work, as the fruitfulness of a multiplied seed
**“and the son of the steward”** — who dispenses all things and distributes their food to the household
**“of my house is this Damascus”** — From him they say Damascus was named and founded, and that he reigned there.
**“Eliezer.”** — “my God is helper”
**“And Abram said”** — Mystically. It signifies the murmuring of the ancients, who, held in suspense by long waiting, as it were wavered about the coming of him who, as Lord, was to receive the eternal inheritance, and, the seed of believers being multiplied, was to shut out the barren law as the stewardship of a servant born in the house. Their wavering is removed by the prophetic spirit, and their faith, made firm, earns justice. Whence: “Abram believed God, and it was reputed to him unto justice.”
15.5:
**“And he brought him forth abroad, and said to him: Look up to heaven and number the stars, if thou canst. And he said to him: So shall thy seed be.”**
• namely the heavenly
• the Christian people, shining with the light of the resurrection
• Look up to heaven, etc. Above he said, “Thy seed shall be as the sand of the sea,” because in that people some are fleshly and earthly, who are compared to sand because they are dry and barren of good works; others are as shining stars.
• RABANUS. A twofold signifying of the promised seed is given. When the stars are shown, it is said to him, “So will I make thy seed,” that is, the Christian nation, of which thou art to be father in faith, namely to shine with the light of the resurrection. But when the sand is shown it is said, “So shall thy seed be,” etc., that is, the nation of the Jews will be numerous, but dry and barren.
15.6: **“Abram believed God, and it was reputed to him unto justice.”** — because “the just man liveth by faith”
15.7:
**“And he said to him: I am the Lord who brought thee out from Ur”** — “fire.” Mystically: the fire of the Chaldeans is the kindlings of the vices
**“of the Chaldees, to give thee this land, and that thou mightest possess it.”** — he seeks a sign not by tempting but by hoping and by asking the manner; from this the custom grew up among the Jews of asking for signs
15.9:
**“And the Lord answered, and said: Take me a cow of three years old,”** — the Jewish people, pressed under the yoke of the law
**“and a she goat of three years,”** — the same, which was to be a sinner
**“and a ram of three years,”** — which was to reign
**“a turtle also, and a pigeon.”**
• the simple, the innocent; for both birds have simplicity and innocence
• Take me, he said, a cow, etc. ISIDORE. The three-year-old cow is the people set under the yoke of the law; the she goat, the same people that was to be a sinner; the ram signifies it as about to reign.
