These are called three years old because through the joints of the times, from Adam to Noe, and from there to Abram, and from there to David, the nation grew up as to a three-year age. By the turtle and the pigeon the spiritual peoples are figured, the sons of the promise and heirs of the kingdom to come, whose age is not told, who, meditating on eternal things, pass beyond the temporal. The three-year-old animals are divided, the parts being set against each other, because the fleshly, both in the old people and now, are separated from one another. The birds are not divided, because the spiritual are led astray neither by schism nor by heresy, but enjoy peace, whether they live alone like the turtle or with others like the pigeon. The fowls coming down upon the divided bodies signify demons seeking food for themselves from the division of the fleshly. Abram driving away the birds signifies that many fleshly men are to be freed at the end of the world through the merit of the saints. About the setting of the sun fear fell upon Abram, and a great and darksome horror seized him, because about the end of the age a great disturbance from Antichrist will seize the saints. Whence: “There shall be tribulation such as hath not been from the beginning.” So, “when the sun was set,” etc., signifies the day of judgment to come after the end of the age, when through fire the good will be separated from the evil.
**“a cow of three years old, and a she goat of three years, and a ram of three years”** — Because from Adam to Noe, and from there to Abram, and then to David, the people grew up.
15.10:
**“And he took all these, and divided”** — because the fleshly are divided from one another
**“them”** — the animals
**“in the midst, and laid the two pieces of each one against the other; but the birds he divided not.”** — because the spiritual keep the unity of the spirit in the bond of peace
15.11:
**“And the fowls came down”** — demons, troublesome thoughts
**“upon the carcasses, and … drove them away.”** — because many fleshly men will be freed at the end through the merit of the saints
**“Abram”**
• by his merit Israel was freed from its straits
• And the fowls came down, etc. GREGORY. Tropologically. In the very sacrifice of prayer troublesome thoughts thrust themselves in, wishing to snatch or defile it; but with the hand of holy discernment we must guard what we offer outwardly, lest evil spirits and perverse thoughts snatch it away.
15.12:
**“And when the sun was setting, a deep sleep”**
• or “a deep sleep”
• because about the end of the world a great disturbance will be brought upon the saints by Antichrist
**“fell upon Abram, and a great and darksome horror seized upon him.”** — Fear fell upon, etc. AUGUSTINE. This question is to be treated because of those who contend that such disturbances do not fall upon the mind of the wise man. Whether it is such as Gellius recalls: namely that a certain philosopher was disturbed in a great storm at sea, and was noticed by a certain dissolute young man, who, after the danger, mocked him because the philosopher had been so quickly disturbed. He answered that the young man had not been disturbed because he had no need to fear anything for his most worthless soul, since it was not worth fearing anything for. But to the others he brought out a book, in which it was read that the Stoics did not hold that no such disturbance falls upon the mind of the wise man, as if nothing of the kind appeared in their feelings; but that disturbance was defined by them as when reason gave way to such movements; and when it did not give way, it was not to be called a disturbance.
15.13:
**“And it was said unto him: Know thou beforehand that thy seed shall be a stranger”** — the people of Israel
**“in a land not their own, and they shall bring them under bondage, and afflict them”** — strangers
**“four hundred years.”**
• Isidore: in affliction the three hundred years will be completed
• in the last part of this time
• Know thou beforehand, etc. ISIDORE. The people of Israel is prophesied as to serve in Egypt; not that it served the Egyptians for four hundred years, but because this number was completed in that affliction, since it is counted from the time when these things were promised to Abram.
*Augustine:* Know thou beforehand, etc. It is not to be taken as if the people of God were four hundred years in that most hard slavery. But because it was said, “In Isaac shall thy seed be called,” from the beginning of Isaac’s birth to the year of Israel’s going out of Egypt four hundred and five years are counted. So when you have taken from four hundred and thirty the twenty-five which run from the promise to the birth of Isaac, it is no wonder if Scripture wished to call the four hundred and five years by a round sum; for it is wont so to number times that what goes a little over the sum of a number, or is under it, is not counted. So what he says, “they shall bring them under bondage and afflict them,” is not to be referred to the three hundred years, as if for so many years they held them in bondage; but the years are to be referred to what was said, “thy seed shall be a stranger in a land not their own.” For whether in the land of Chanaan or in Egypt, it was a stranger until it should have the inheritance by God’s promise, which happened after they were freed from Egypt. So that by hyperbaton the order of the words is: “Know thou certainly that thy seed shall be a stranger in a land not their own four hundred years”; and “they shall bring them under bondage and afflict them” is put in between, so that this insertion does not belong to the four hundred years. For in the last part of this sum, that is, after the death of Joseph, the people of God was afflicted in Egypt with hard slavery.
15.14: **“But I will judge the nation which they shall serve, and after this they shall come out with great substance.”** — elsewhere: “great”
15.15:
**“And thou shalt go”** — by dying
**“to thy fathers”** — thy holy forerunners
15.16:
**“But in the fourth generation”** — from Caath, son of Levi, to Eleazar, four generations; and from Amram to Phinees
**“they shall return”** — the sons of Abram
**“hither: for as yet … are not at the full”** — so that they must now lose their land
**“the iniquities of the Amorrhites … until this present time.”** — But in the fourth generation, etc. JEROME. But Moses says elsewhere, “In the fifth generation the children of Israel went up out of the land of Egypt”; yet they went out in the fourth generation. For Levi begot Caath, Caath begot Amram, he Aaron, Aaron Eleazar, and he begot Phinees. Caath went into Egypt with his father Levi; Eleazar went out with Aaron. From Caath to Eleazar, four generations. Some, however, begin from Amram and come to Phinees. But they went out in the fifth generation because Juda begot Phares, Phares begot Esron, Esron begot Aram, Aram begot Aminadab, Aminadab begot Naasson, who begot Salmon. Phares went into Egypt with his father Juda; Naasson is entered as prince of the tribe of Juda in the desert, whose son Salmon entered the land of promise. From Phares to Naasson, five generations. Some, however, begin from Esron and come to Salmon.
15.17:
**“And when the sun was set, there arose a dark mist,”** — it signifies the tribulation and straits to come
**“and there appeared a smoking furnace”** — it signifies the judgment by fire, by which the evil are to be separated from the good
**“and a lamp of fire”** — the fire of judgment will separate the good from the evil
15.18: **“That day God made a covenant with Abram, saying: To thy seed will I give this land, from the river of Egypt”** — Rhinocorura, which divides Palestine and Egypt

16.1:
**“Now Sarai”** — grace
**“the wife of Abram, had brought forth no children;”** — free men, who should serve God freely
**“but having a handmaid, an Egyptian, named Agar,”** — Now Sarai the wife, etc. RABANUS. Abram is not an adulterer if he is joined to a handmaid while his wife is living, because the law of the Gospels of one wife had not yet been proclaimed; and he had heard that his race was to be multiplied, but did not know by which woman, for he knew that Sara was barren. Nor was there lustful pleasure in the union, but the godly love of having offspring. His wife too wished it and pressed it, who could not have sons; therefore she desired to receive from another one whom she might adopt in the place of her own.
16.2:
**“She said to her husband: Behold, the Lord hath restrained me from bearing:”** — room is given to fleshly observance, because the time of grace had not yet come
**“go in unto my handmaid, it may be I may have children of her at least.”** — to be adopted by me
**“And when he agreed to her request,”** — Go in unto my handmaid, etc. JEROME. Note carefully that the getting of sons is called in Hebrew “building.” For there it is read: “Go in unto my handmaid, if perhaps I may be built up from her.” This is what is said in Exodus: “And God blessed the midwives, and they built themselves houses.”
*Mystically:* Agar signifies the earthly Jerusalem, in which the old law was practised in a fleshly and servile way; but Sara the grace of the New Testament, which bears free children, citizens of the Jerusalem above. But the grace of the New Testament was long not in the open, and gave the Old Testament, as a handmaid, leave to beget: servants, namely, serving from fear, not love, as if begetting sons of Abraham’s seed, whom it should bind to the worship of the one God and call back from idols, to which the Gentiles offered like sacrifices. But when that people, puffed up by the works of the flesh, refused grace at Christ’s coming and remained unbelieving in slavery, grace prevailing, it was so afflicted and saddened that it lost kingdom and priesthood. Whence, brought into the wilderness, thirsting for the fountain of the law by diligent searching and meditating, it finds nothing, except that, at the warning of the law given through Moses as through an angel, it should return to grace and submit itself.
*Rabanus:* Mystically. These two women are the two Testaments: Agar the Old, which in the synagogue nourished the Jewish people, bound to slavery; Sara the New, which begot the Christian people into the freedom of faith. The handmaid’s sons were multiplied, so that they could not be numbered for multitude, who above are compared to the sand. So this people, jealous in its fierceness and contrary to all good men, above all when, goaded by envy, it persecutes the Christian people through the whole world, is also, scattered far and wide in wandering and trading, burdensome to all.
16.4:
**“And he went in to her. But she, perceiving that she was with child,”** — seeing Israel multiplied according to the flesh
**“despised her mistress.”** — grace, which was to bear free children
16.5: **“And Sarai said to Abram: Thou dost unjustly with me: I gave my handmaid into thy bosom, and she perceiving herself to be with child,”** — as if presuming on an heir
16.6:
**“And Abram made answer, and said to her: Behold thy handmaid is in thy own hand, use her as it pleaseth thee.”** — as if: let the shadow cease, let the truth rule
**“And when Sarai afflicted her,”** — grace destroying kingdom and priesthood, the pride of the Jews will not submit
16.7:
**“And the angel of the Lord having found her,”** — the divine word
**“by a fountain of water”** — leaning on the letter of the law
**“in the wilderness,”** — deprived of its ceremonies
**“which is in the way to Sur”** — consistently, the Egyptian was hastening to go to Egypt by the way to Sur, which leads through the wilderness to Egypt
**“in the desert,”** — in straits
16.8: **“He said to her: Agar, handmaid of Sarai, whence comest thou? and whither goest thou? And she answered: I flee from the face of Sarai, my mistress.”** — as if: I will not submit to grace
16.10: **“And again he said:”** — the angel speaks in the person of God
16.11: **“And again: Behold, said he, thou art with child, and thou shalt bring forth a son: and thou shalt call his name Ismael,”** — “God’s hearing”
16.12: **“He shall be a wild man”** — Or “rustic,” according to others. JEROME: in the Hebrew there is phara, which is interpreted “wild ass.” It signifies that his seed would dwell in the desert, that is, the wandering Saracens, with no fixed seats, who, raiding all the nations whose side borders on the desert, are fought against by all.
16.13: **“And she called”** — She rightly called his name so, because he freely takes counsel for the wretched and comforts the humble. Whence: “Thou considerest labour and sorrow; to thee is the poor man left,” etc. “Verily here have I seen the hinder parts of him that seeth me.” Such is that: “Thou shalt see my back parts: but my face thou canst not see. For man shall not see me and live.” For no one can see that manifestation of the wisdom of God and live. It is that beauty for which he sighs who loves God with his whole heart, his whole soul, his whole mind; to contemplate which he also builds up his neighbour as far as he can, by loving him as himself. But his hinder parts, that is, his incarnation, which he took on in the last times, we now contemplate by desiring through faith and love; in the future we shall enjoy them in eternal contemplation.
16.14:
**“Therefore she called that well, The well of him that liveth and seeth me.”** — Therefore she called that well, etc. To this day the well of Agar is shown in the desert of Arabia between Cades and Barad. It signifies the scripture of the old law and the new, which our Maker, the life of the living, the hope of the dying, gave to mortals in the regard of his loving mercy, so that, taught and corrected from vices, they may deserve to be worthy for ever of the vision of God.
**“The same is between Cades and Barad.”** — the New and Old Testament
16.15: **“And Agar brought forth a son to Abram:”** — because the sons of the flesh too are reckoned as seed
16.16: **“Abram was four score and six years old”** — because he had not yet come to the number of the heavenly citizens, he receives a fleshly son

17.1:
**“And after he began to be ninety and nine years old,”** — that is, after he had begun to desire the fellowship of the heavenly citizens
**“the Lord appeared to him: and said unto him: I am the Almighty God:”** — who can humble and exalt
**“walk before me,”** — according to my good pleasure
**“and be perfect.”** — so that thou mayest serve not from fear but from love
17.2:
**“And I will make my covenant”** — a promise
**“between me and thee: and I will multiply thee”** — in the imitators of thy faith
**“covenant”** — In the Hebrew berith, which signifies not “testament” but “covenant” or “pact.”
17.3:
**“Abram fell flat”** — humble
**“on his face.”** — stretching himself forward
17.4:
**“And God said to him: I am,”** — unchangeably
**“and my covenant is with thee, and thou shalt be a father of many nations.”** — that is, the first way of believing
17.5:
**“Neither shall thy name be called any more Abram:”** — “high father”
**“but thou shalt be called Abraham:”** — “father of many nations,” because all nations were to believe in his seed
**“because I have made thee a father of many nations.”**
• because in thy seed, that is, in Christ, all nations were to believe
• the disposition being changed, the name is changed
**“Neither shall thy name be called any more Abram”** — JEROME. The Hebrews say that God added to Abraham and Sara the letter he from his own name, which among them is the four-lettered one. For he was called Abram, which is “high father”; afterwards he was called Abraham, which is “father of many”; for “nations” is not in the name but understood. Nor is it to be wondered at that, while among the Greeks and us the letter a seems to be added, the letter he is said to be added; for the idiom of the Hebrew tongue is wont to write he and read a, as on the contrary to pronounce e and write a.
17.6:
**“And I will make thee increase,”** — in his successors
**“exceedingly, and I will make nations of thee,”** — “in thee shall all nations be blessed”
**“and kings shall come out of thee.”** — David, Ezechias and others, ruling well themselves and those under them
17.7:
**“And I will establish my covenant”** — of circumcision
**“between me and thee, and between thy seed after thee in their generations, by a perpetual covenant:”** — because it signified something everlasting
**“to be a God to thee,”** — by will, who am so by power
17.8:
**“And I will give to thee, and to thy seed,”** — to the imitators of thy faith
**“the land of thy sojournment, all the land of Chanaan for a perpetual possession,”** — because something eternal is figured by it; or “eternal,” that is, to be held in this age
**“Chanaan”** — It is interpreted “their movement.” Its land is received by the faithful as a possession when the mind, at first driven about by various movements, is changed for the better and afterwards stretches forward to what is before with eyes that do not turn back.
**“for a perpetual possession”** — AUGUSTINE. Scripture calls eternal that whose end is not fixed, or which is not done in such a way that it must not be done afterwards, as far as belongs to the care or power of the doer. Whence: “He will be a slave for ever who will not know how to use a little.”
17.9:
**“Again God said to Abraham: And thou therefore shalt keep my covenant,”** — of circumcision
**“and thy seed”** — thy followers
17.10:
**“This is my covenant”** — he sets out what the covenant is
**“which you shall observe, between me and you, and thy seed after thee:”** — agreed
**“shall be circumcised”** — circumcision is the putting off of the old
**“All the male kind of you shall be circumcised”** — STRABO. For three reasons this is commanded to Abraham. First, that he might please by obedience to the command, through whose transgression Adam had displeased. Second, that by this sign he might be distinguished from the other nations. Third, that, being circumcised in that member in which lust is wont to rule, he might know that chastity was to be kept by him and unchastity cut away.
17.11:
**“And you shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin,”** — because in this part is the propagation of corruption
**“that it may be for a sign of the covenant between me and you.”** — namely, as a witness that I am your God, and you my people, divided from the nations
**“the flesh of your foreskin”** — RABANUS. STRABO. Circumcision done in one member signifies the spiritual circumcision, which is to be shown in the heart and in all the senses. The heart is to be circumcised, lest we think harmful things; the eyes, lest we see vanity; the ears are to be circumcised, that is, stopped, lest they hear blood. And so in all the senses circumcision is to be kept.
*Alcuin:* Therefore circumcision was commended to Abraham, that he might be under law; as Adam was, that he should not eat of the tree, so that it might be proved whether this would be fulfilled or not. For Abraham believed that he would have a son in whom all nations should be blessed, and in whose descendants a pattern of chastity and sobriety should remain. Hence he received the sign of faith there whence Isaac was to be born, a son of God, not of the flesh: not more unsightly for the cutting off of a part of the body, but more glorious by the sign of faith. So to lose something for God is gain, not loss. If Adam had kept God’s covenant, Abraham would not have received this covenant. But because Adam first knew the guilt of disobedience in this member, it was fitting that Abraham secondly should receive the sign of obedience in this member; so that thus it might be shown that the obedient would one day beget sons to life whence the transgressors once begot them to death.
*Allegorically:* Already then, because of the sojourning to come, lest his seed be mingled with the nations, the covenant of circumcision is given as a sign; for it signifies nature renewed through baptism after the stripping off of the old man through Christ, who rose after the sabbath. He commanded the servants too, those born in the house and those bought, to be circumcised, to teach that the grace of redemption belongs to all. There too the parents’ names are changed, so that all things may sound of newness: Abram, “high father”; Abraham, “father of many nations.”
17.12:
**“An infant of eight days old”** — because in the eighth age, that is, in eternity, which follows the sevenfold turning of time, we are stripped of fleshly corruption
**“shall be circumcised among you, every man child in your generations: he that is born in the house,”** — born in the house
**“as well as the bought servant”** — because there is “neither bond nor free”
**“shall be circumcised, and whosoever”** — because there is “neither barbarian nor Scythian”
17.13:
**“And my covenant shall be in your flesh”** — in the putting off of fleshly things
**“for a perpetual covenant.”** — since it leads to eternity
17.14:
**“The male, whose flesh of his foreskin shall not be circumcised,”** — who has not put off fleshly things
**“that soul shall be destroyed”** — will not be counted among the saints
**“out of his people:”** — from the company of the saints; whence: “But thou shalt go to thy people”
**“because … my covenant.”**
• given to Adam in paradise, in whom all sinned
• that is, he has not kept what he promised in baptism
**“The male, whose flesh of his foreskin”** — ISIDORE. It is asked how uncircumcised children, who do not make God’s covenant void, but rather those who neglected to circumcise them, should perish. But they made God’s covenant void not by their own work but by their origin, in the first man, in whom all sinned. For all are born sinners not by their own act but by origin. Therefore all perish who are not freed through regeneration.
17.15:
**“God said also to Abraham: Sarai thy wife thou shalt not call Sarai,”** — that is, “my princess”
**“but Sara.”** — absolutely
**“Sarai thy wife”** — ISIDORE. The promise of the calling of the nations is made plain in Isaac, the son of the promise, that is, of grace, not of nature, because he came of an old father and a barren mother. And because this was to be not through generation, as with Ismael, but through regeneration, circumcision was commanded when a son of Sara was promised, in the type of the Church, not when Ismael was, who is the type of the Jews.
*Jerome:* ISIDORE. They err who think that Sara was first written with one r and that afterwards another r was added, and because r among the Greeks signifies a hundred, they guess many absurdities about this name; when, however they would have the word changed, it must have not a Greek but a Hebrew reason, for it is Hebrew. For no one, naming someone in one tongue, takes the etymology of the word from another. So she was first called Sarai, with shin, resh, yod. So the yod being taken away, the letter he was added, which is read as a, and she was called Sara. For before she was called “my princess,” as the mother of one household; afterwards absolutely “princess,” namely the princess-to-be of all nations. Some very wrongly guess that she was first called “leprosy” and afterwards “princess,” since leprosy is called sarat, which in our tongue seems to have some likeness, but in Hebrew is wholly different; for it is written with tsade and ayin and resh and tau, which plainly differs from the three above, that is, shin, resh and he, with which Sara is written.
17.16:
**“And I will bless her,”** — by exalting the princess, because the Church rules in every nation
**“and of her”** — not of Agar
**“I will give thee a son, whom I will bless,”** — in whose seed all nations shall be blessed
**“and he shall become nations,”** — because Christ shall rule among the nations
**“and kings of people”** — David and others, or those ruling their own movements well
17.17:
**“Abraham fell upon his face,”** — not backwards, like the reprobate
**“and laughed,”** — he rejoiced; whence his son Isaac is called “laughter”
**“saying in his heart: Shall a son, thinkest thou, be born to him that is a hundred years old? and shall Sara that is ninety years old bring forth?”**
• applauding, not disputing; whence Paul: “Nor did he consider his own body now dead, whereas he was almost an hundred years old, nor the dead womb of Sara”
• Abraham fell upon his face, etc. JEROME. A little later follows: “And thou shalt call his name Isaac,” which is interpreted “laughter,” from Abraham’s laughter, not Sara’s. For it is after his son was called Isaac from Abraham’s laughter that Sara is read to have laughed.
17.18: **“And he said to God: O that Ismael may live before thee.”** — for he wished that the sons of the flesh should be reckoned in the seed
17.19:
**“And God said to Abraham: Sara thy wife shall bear thee a son, and thou shalt call his name Isaac,”** — “laughter,” because of the parent’s joy
**“and I will establish my covenant”** — “In Isaac shall thy seed be called,” not in the son of the flesh; because the sons of the promise shall be called sons of God
**“his name Isaac”** — JEROME. It is to be known that four in the Old Testament were plainly called by their names before they were born: Ismael, Isaac, Samson and Josias. Read the Scriptures.
**“with him for a perpetual covenant, and with his seed after him.”** — I will establish my covenant with him, etc. The covenant of the Lord is with Isaac, namely the faithful people, which mother Church has begotten through faith and baptism; and an everlasting covenant, because the possession of eternal life is promised to it alone, which with its head Christ shall possess the kingdom of heaven for ever.
17.20:
**“And as for Ismael”** — the son of the flesh
**“I have also heard thee.”** — in a certain manner
**“Behold, I will bless him,”** — in temporal things, not by an eternal promise
**“and increase, and multiply him exceedingly: he shall beget twelve chiefs,”**
• the twelve tribes of the fleshly Jews
• the twelve apostles, who were of the Jewish people; or the twelve tribes of the people
**“and I will make him a great nation.”** — And as for Ismael I have also heard thee, etc. Ismael signifies the people of the Jews, which was multiplied exceedingly and begot twelve chiefs, when the multitude of the fleshly Jews, begotten from the twelve patriarchs, was divided into twelve tribes.
17.21:
**“But my covenant”** — of the eternal promise
**“I will establish with Isaac,”** — the Christian people
**“whom Sara shall bring forth to thee”**
• namely, with those whom she was begetting by faith
• her oldness changed
**“at this time”** — by the grace of the New Testament
**“in the next year.”** — in the present life
**“in the next year”** — The next year, in which Sara bore Isaac, is the times of regeneration, in which the blood of Christ was shed and the human race restored to life.
17.22:
**“And when he had left off speaking with him,”** — in a visible form taken on
**“God went up”** — he made himself invisible
**“from Abraham.”** — or: “from”
17.23:
**“And Abraham took Ismael his son,”** — prefiguring that the spiritual circumcision belongs to every calling, because all the senses are to be circumcised
**“and all that were born in his house: and all whom he had bought, every male among the men of his house: and he circumcised the flesh of their foreskin forthwith the very same day,”** — because obedience is to be fulfilled without delay
**“as God had commanded him,”** — And Abraham took, etc. God did not intend only that the foreskin of the flesh of Abraham and his offspring should be circumcised, but he was bestowing the gifts of the eternal testament on him whom he had chosen out of all. Whence Paul: “For we are the circumcision, who serve God in spirit.” And elsewhere: “For it is not he is a Jew, who is so outwardly; nor is that circumcision which is outwardly in the flesh.” So let us circumcise by the word of God the ears, the lips, the heart, the foreskin and all the members of the flesh. Of the circumcision of the ears it is said: “He that hath ears to hear, let him hear.” With uncircumcised ears we cannot hear the words of wisdom and truth. Let us circumcise the lips, lest we speak anything shameful or evil or idle. He circumcises the flesh of the foreskin who uses marriage only for the sake of offspring, at fixed and lawful times; he who acts otherwise does not circumcise. But the Church, strengthened by the grace of Christ crucified for her, not only keeps herself from unlawful things but even from those allowed, and as a virgin bride of Christ flowers in chaste virgins, in whom the true circumcision of the foreskin is kept in the flesh. But he who commits no adultery by obscene desires, or by heretical meanings and blasphemous assertions, but keeps the purity of faith in his conscience, is circumcised in heart, and of him it can be said: “Blessed are the clean of heart,” etc. Let the hands be circumcised, lest they do evil; the feet, lest they run to evil; the sight, lest it covet unlawful things; the taste, that it may eat and drink to the glory of God; the smell, that it may take in the odour of Christ and by works of mercy spread the odour of sweetness. Each member too, if it serves God in its offices, is circumcised; if it runs riot beyond the prescribed law, uncircumcised.
*Jerome:* STRABO. It is often asked how women were saved, who were not circumcised. By faith, namely, and the offering of sacrifices, as holy men were cleansed before circumcision. Whence: “purifying their hearts by faith.”
17.24: **“Abraham was ninety and nine years old,”** — renewed: by this number he is hinted to reach the fellowship of the citizens above
17.25: **“And Ismael his son was full thirteen years old”** — not reaching, namely, the fulfilment of the law and the gospel, which is figured by the number four

18.1:
**“And the Lord appeared to him in the vale of Mambre”** — God appears to the humble
**“as he was sitting at the door of his tent,”** — by faith, through which one enters the Church, which is a tent because in it one does service as a soldier for God
**“in the very heat of the day.”** — in the warmth of good desire
**“And the Lord appeared to him”** — ISIDORE. Abraham bears a threefold figure. The first, of the Saviour, who, leaving his kindred, came into the world. The second, of the Father, because he sacrificed his only son. The third (which appears in this place), of the saints, who received the coming of Christ with joy. Abraham’s tent signifies Jerusalem, where for a time the prophets and apostles dwelt, and where Christ, coming, was received by those who believed and hung on the wood by those who did not.
18.2:
**“And when he had lifted up his eyes, there appeared to him three men”** — because to those so disposed faith in the Trinity is made known
**“three men”** — Allegorically. The three men announce the coming of Christ, whom two angels accompany: according to some, Moses and Elias. The one is the lawgiver, who in the law pointed to the Lord’s coming; the other, who is to come at the end, will announce the second coming of Christ and preach his gospel. Whence, when the Lord was transfigured on the mountain, they are seen with him.
**“standing near him:”** — He saw three and adored one, namely showing the Saviour whose coming he was awaiting. Whence: “Abraham saw my day, and was glad.” For he foresaw the mystery of the sacrament to come. Hence he washed their feet, to show the cleansing of the laver that was to come at the end of the world; for the feet signify the last things.
**“and as soon as he saw them he ran to meet them”** — with eagerness for hospitality, leaving us this as an example
**“from the door”** — from the beginning of faith
**“of his tent, and adored down to the ground.”** — one, who had seen three
**“as soon as he saw them”** — GREGORY. Morally. Abraham runs to meet three angels, because the man and lord of the house, namely the spiritual understanding, must by the knowledge of the Trinity go beyond the bars of the flesh, and, as it were, go out of the door of its lowest dwelling. The care of the flesh, which Sara signifies, should not appear outside for display, but behind the man’s back, that is, under the discernment of the spirit, intent only on necessary things, should not know how to uncover itself boldly, but to keep itself modestly in check.
*Gregory:* Abraham could not have seen angels, received them as guests and set food before them, unless they had taken bodies from the air. For they would not appear, nor take food, unless they had a solid body from a heavenly element. Nor is it any wonder that they are called now angels, now the Lord; because those are called angels who minister outwardly, and the Lord is shown who commands inwardly.
18.3:
**“And he said: Lord,”** — perceiving God in the angels, he prefers to speak to the Lord rather than to the angels
**“if I have found favour in thy sight,”** — in good pleasure
**“pass not away from thy servant:”** — lest I enjoy thy vision only in passing
18.4: **“But I will fetch”** — He turns back to the duties of hospitality, which can be shown even to angels when they take on a bodily form from the elements. Understanding this, Abraham adored the Godhead in unity and ministered to the angelic dispensation in its visible form.
18.5:
**“And I will set a morsel of bread, and strengthen ye your heart, afterwards you shall pass on: for therefore are you come aside to your servant.”** — so that I may show you these services
**“And they said:”** — lest they should seem to shun the services of charity
18.6:
**“Abraham made haste”** — lest the old man should seem to serve lukewarmly
**“into the tent to Sara,”** — so that “the unbelieving wife may be saved by the believing husband”
**“and said to her: Make haste, temper together three”** — as if it were said to the Church: gather from all parts
**“measures”**
• jars; the same mystery here and in the Gospel, where the woman leavens three measures
• STRABO. A satum is a kind of measure. The three measures signify the three sons of Noe, from whom the whole race was spread abroad. So the Church is signified, or the gospel teaching, which was to be spread through the whole world and multiplied in the three parts of the world: Asia, Africa and Europe.
**“of flour, and make cakes upon the hearth.”** — because, baked by the fire of the Holy Spirit, they are food acceptable to God
**“cakes”** — in the bread the unity of believers is signified, because bread is made from many grains
**“three measures”**
• These things are said in the type of the Church, which has been gathered from the three parts of the world into the unity of faith, and, as bread without leaven, baked by the fire of the Spirit.
• Of which Sara makes cakes upon the hearth. They signify the three sons of Noe, from whom the whole race of men was born, who, believing in the divine Trinity, were sprinkled with the water of baptism through Sara, that is, the Church, and brought into the one bread of the body of Christ. These are the three measures of meal which the woman in the Gospel leavened. The loaves are unleavened, because the unity of believers must be without the leaven of malice, the weakness of wickedness, and the heat of perverse teaching.
**“upon the hearth”** — They are cakes baked under the ashes, so that, baked by the warmth of the Holy Spirit through penance for sins, they may be made food acceptable to God.
18.7:
**“And he himself ran to the herd,”** — so that the Church might be gathered from the Gentiles, one had to run back to the ancient fathers
**“and took from thence a calf very tender”** — Christ, born of the patriarchs; whence: “It shall please God better than a young calf,” etc.
**“and very good,”** — excellent in the human race
**“and gave it to a young man:”** — he committed it to the order of the prophets to be announced
**“who made haste and boiled it.”** — he foretold with zeal that it was to be accomplished by the passion
**“a calf very tender”** — The tender and fattened calf is the body of Christ, which was sacrificed on the tree of the cross for the salvation of the world. This is the calf that is killed for the prodigal son.
18.8:
**“He took also butter”** — the richness of the gospel, or its teaching
**“and milk,”** — the drink of little ones, namely the old law
**“and the calf”** — Christ who suffered
**“which he had boiled, and set before them:”** — by these sacraments the ministers of Christ are fed
**“but he stood by them”** — because he was looking upon the sacrament of the cross
**“under the tree.”**
• the cross
• Butter and milk, etc. He set them with the flesh of the calf, because milk signifies the old law. Whence: “I gave you milk to drink, not meat,” etc. For he had handed them the command of the law as milk pressed from the breasts of the two tables, that is, the testament of faith, because they could not yet take the solid food of the gospel teaching.
• The richest and fattest butter is the witness of the gospel, which is given to the faithful as oil, for a sign. He set the calf with milk and butter, because neither can the Lord’s body be without the milk of the law, nor this without the gospel.
• And they sat under the tree as a sign of the Lord’s passion, of which they are preachers.
18.9:
**“And when they had eaten, they said to him: Where is Sara thy wife? He answered: Lo, she is in the tent.”**
• because in the Church a woman is not permitted to teach, Sara keeps hidden
• as if: it is not for a woman to come forth in public
• Lo, she is in the tent, etc. STRABO. Abraham is outside with the angels; Sara is in the tent; because it belongs to the strong and learned to preach openly and to instruct by examples, to the weak and unlearned to learn and to be subject.
18.10:
**“And he said to him: I will return and come to thee at this time,”** — having first been refreshed as men, in the unity of the Godhead, by whose kindness the things to come were to be fulfilled, they foretell them
**“life accompanying and Sara thy wife shall have a son. Which when Sara heard,”** — here Sara signifies the synagogue, which, hiding itself in the shadow of the sacraments, does not believe that Christ has come
**“she laughed behind the door of the tent.”**
• because she did not yet give faith
• Which when Sara heard, etc. AUGUSTINE. Sara is rebuked because she laughed, and not Abraham, though he laughed likewise; because his laughter was of wonder, hers of doubt, which he who knows hearts could discern. Sara denies that she laughed, though nothing can be hidden from God; but perhaps she thought them men. But Abraham understood God; though in offering them the services of hospitality, which are needed only by weak flesh, it would be strange if he did not at first think them men, but men in whom he understood God to speak, certain signs of the divine majesty appearing; as Scripture often bears witness that God has appeared in men. But afterwards they knew that they were angels.
**“Sara … shall have a son”** — God promises a son to barren Sara, saying, “About this time I will come,” signifying not the time but the manner of his coming, when through the promised son the faithful people was to be born. Whence: “Rejoice, thou barren, that bearest not,” etc.
18.11:
**“Now they were both old, and far advanced in years, and it had ceased”** — when these fail, a woman ceases to bear, so that the miracle may be commended if a barren woman bears
**“to be with Sara after the manner of women.”**
• the menses
• Now they were both old, etc. The elderly age is younger than that of the old, even if the elderly are called old. Whence, if according to the physicians an elderly man cannot get children of an elderly woman, even if her courses still flow, according to this Abraham wonders at God’s power over the promise of a son; and we can take it that the apostle set down this miracle. For his body was not altogether dead to begetting, if the woman had been of youthful age; but he could not beget of one advanced in age. For afterwards he begot of Cetura, because she was young. For the physicians hold that an old man cannot beget of a woman of more advanced age (even if her courses still come to her), but can of a young one. Again, a woman of advanced age, even if her courses still come to her, cannot bear of an elderly man, but can of a young one. So it was a miracle, because both were old and far advanced in years, and it had ceased to be with Sara after the manner of women.
18.12:
**“And she laughed secretly,”** — disputing about the oracle
**“saying:”** — she follows natural reason
**“shall I give myself to pleasure?”** — GREGORY. Morally. When the care of the flesh is often told not to presume upon itself but to put its whole self into trust in the divine hope, it despises it, and, its own effort ceasing, distrusts that the supports of life will be at hand for it. Whence Sara, hearing God’s promises, laughs; but laughing she is rebuked, and rebuked she is at once made fruitful; and she who could not be made fruitful when strong in youth conceived when broken by old age; because when the care of the flesh leaves off having confidence in itself, against hope it receives from the divine promise what it doubted by human reason that it would have. Whence he who is begotten is rightly called “laughter”; for when our mind conceives trust in the hope above, what does it bring forth but joy?
18.13:
**“And the Lord said to Abraham: Why did Sara laugh,”** — disputing
**“saying: Shall I who am an old woman bear a child indeed?”** — as if: why did she give way more to nature than to divine power?
18.14:
**“Is there any thing hard to God?”** — as if: as I have said, so it shall be
**“According to appointment I will return to thee at this same time,”** — of the coming year; because to the time of the shadow that is past he will succeed who was signified in the shadow
**“life accompanying,”** — anthropopathos, like the rest
18.15:
**“Sara denied, saying: I did not laugh: for she was afraid.”** — namely because she was afraid
**“But the Lord said, Nay: but thou didst laugh:”** — he rebukes her still womanly unbelief
18.16:
**“And when the men rose up from thence, they turned their eyes towards Sodom:”** — because when they had treated with Abraham of the mercy to come, judgment is now threatened against Sodom
**“and Abraham walked with them, bringing them on the way.”** — not knowing the outcome of what was to come; but the Lord, as he wills the godly to know the rewards of the just, so not to be ignorant of the punishments of the wicked
18.17: **“Can I hide”** — The Lord rightly entrusts his secrets to Abraham, whom he knew as the faithful executor of his will and his secrets; from whom he was to be born in the flesh in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. He promises Abraham not only rewards but the justice of his sons’ obedience, and that the promises concerning them will be fulfilled. And again Isaac is promised as to become a great nation, and that in him all the nations of the earth shall be blessed; in which words two things are promised him: the nation of the Jews according to the flesh, and all nations through faith.
18.19:
**“For I know that he will command his children,”** — as if: I make known my judgments to him so that he may make them known to his followers
**“and his household after him”** — not only the rewards, but also the obedience of justice
**“to keep”** — God promised Abraham his sons to this end, that the promises concerning them too may be fulfilled
**“the way of the Lord,”** — the commandments
**“and do judgment and justice:”** — let them depart from evil
18.20:
**“And the Lord said: The cry of Sodom and Gomorrha is multiplied,”** — the plainness of a published crime, which needs no accuser
**“and their sin is become exceedingly grievous.”**
• by habit, as by a stone laid on top
• The cry of Sodom, etc. AUGUSTINE. If we take these words as those not of one doubting but of one angry and threatening, there is no question at all. For God speaks to men in the manner of men, and his anger is without disturbance, because he is unchangeable. But we often say thus in threatening: “Let us see if I do not do it to thee,” and “if I cannot do it to thee,” or “I shall know,” that is, “I shall try whether I cannot.” But disturbance does not fall upon God; but it is the manner of human speech, to which God fits himself so as to suit human weakness.
*Gregory:* Morally. Sin with a voice is guilt in action; sin with a cry is guilt with freedom. “I will go down and see,” etc. Let us not believe the evils of men before we prove them. And behold, he comes down through angels to learn the evils, and, finding them wrapped in so great a crime, he as it were passed over patience and overtook them with the fire of judgment before the day of judgment; he who judges with calm, so that greater crimes are believed slowly, and, when truly known, are punished more quickly.
18.21: **“I will go down and see”** — so as to restrain rashness of judgment, he wished to prove the evils of Sodom before judging them
18.22: **“And they turned themselves from thence,”** — because the Lord speaks in the angels, the style alternates, now in his person, now in that of the angels
18.23: **“And drawing nigh he said: Wilt thou destroy the just with the wicked?”** — through the justice of a few he wishes to obtain mercy for many
18.24:
**“If there be fifty just men”** — some worthy of remission, because the fiftieth is the year of remission
**“in the city, shall they perish withal? and wilt thou not spare that place for the sake of the fifty just, if they be therein?”** — If there be fifty, etc. ISIDORE. The number fifty, from which he comes down as far as ten, signifies penance. Whence the fiftieth psalm too is penitential. So if they were converted they would be saved. But when God sees sinners unwilling to be converted to penance, he at once checks the burning of unbridled lust with the fire of hell. He said that Sodom would not perish, down to ten just men, because if the name of Christ is found in anyone through keeping the ten commandments, he will not perish. For the figure of the number ten also signifies the cross of Christ.
18.25:
**“Far be it from thee to do this thing, and to slay the just with the wicked, and for the just to be in like case as the wicked,”** — that the innocent should perish
**“this is not beseeming thee: thou who judgest”** — thou dost dispose justly
**“all the earth, wilt not make this judgment.”** — he says this by praying, not by inveighing
18.27:
**“And Abraham answered, and said: Seeing I have once begun, I will speak to my Lord, whereas I am dust and ashes.”**
• he tempers the loftiness of the promise with the lowliness of humility
• I will speak to my Lord, etc. GREGORY. Morally. The more the saints look into the inner things of the Godhead, the more they see that they are nothing. Nowhere is Abraham read to have professed himself ashes and dust except when he was found worthy to have speech with God, and said: “I will speak to my Lord, whereas I am dust,” etc. For perhaps he would believe himself to be something if he had not perceived the true being which is above him. Whence David too cries out: “Remember, O Lord, that we are dust,” etc.
*Gregory:* Morally. Wealth does not lift some up through pride, but through works of mercy. Some, when they see themselves abounding in earthly things, do not seek the true riches and do not love the eternal kingdom, because they think temporal things enough. So it is not wealth that is at fault but the disposition; for all things that God made are good. But he who uses good things badly brings it about that, through the gluttony of greed, he dies by the bread by which he should have lived. Poor Lazarus came to rest; torments tortured the proud rich man. Abraham, who held Lazarus in his bosom, had been rich; yet he says: “I will speak to my Lord, whereas I am dust and ashes.” What did he think of his riches, who reckoned himself dust and ashes? We see plainly in what place he had set himself, who reckoned himself dust and ashes even when he spoke with God. With what punishment, then, are they to be struck who do not advance to the highest things and are lifted up over the least?
18.28:
**“What if there be five less than fifty just persons?”** — given over to the five senses and unworthy of remission
**“if there be five”** — Five cities were burnt up by rains of fire; for all who have handled the five senses of the body lustfully are to be burnt in the fire to come.
**“wilt thou for five and forty destroy the whole city?”** — that is, wilt thou not spare all for the sake of those who tame the body with the forty days’ abstinence and use the five senses in order?
**“And he said: I will not destroy it,”** — I will spare it
18.29: **“And again he said to him: But if forty”** — keeping the commandments of the law and the gospel; for four times ten make forty
18.30:
**“Lord, saith he, be not angry, I beseech thee, if I speak:”** — because he seemed to be pressing the Lord by asking for an answer, he tempers what he asks with a preface
**“What if thirty shall be found there? He answered: I will not do it, if I find thirty there.”**
• keeping the law with faith in the Trinity; for three times ten make thirty
• If … shall be found, etc. ALCUIN. It is not necessary to take this of every place; but it could be said of Sodom, because God knew that there were not even ten there; and therefore Abraham was answered so, to heighten the wickedness of Sodom.
18.31: **“Seeing, saith he, I have once begun, I will speak to my Lord. What if twenty be found there?”** — keeping the commandments with love of God and of neighbour, because of ten and two
18.32:
**“I beseech thee, saith he, be not angry, Lord, if I speak yet once more: What if ten should be found there?”** — keeping the commandments of the decalogue
**“And he said: I will not destroy it for the sake of ten.”** — For he knew that there was not even one there besides Lot
**“ten”** — For he knew that there was not even one there besides Lot; this is said to heighten the wickedness, as in Jeremias: “See if you can find a man that executeth judgment,” as if: find even one, and I will spare them.

19.1:
**“And the two angels came to Sodom in the evening, and … was sitting”** — awaiting the coming of any guest
**“Lot … in the gate of the city. And seeing them, he rose up and went to meet them:”** — so that it might appear how hospitable he was
**“and worshipped prostrate to the ground,”**
• understanding that they were angels
• “And the two angels came to Sodom in the evening,” and the rest. That Lot runs to meet the angels and worships on his face, he seems to have understood that they were angels. But again, when he invites them to the refreshment of the body, which is necessary for mortals, he seems to have thought that they were men; and these are to be understood as we have already said above of those who appeared to Abraham.
• And the two angels came, etc. It is to be noted that three angels, an odd number, appear to Abraham, because God delights in an odd number. To Sodom came an even number, that is, two, which is the first number to depart from unity and is the beginning of otherness, as if figuring womanish softness. They came in the evening, because the sun of justice had already set for Sodom.
• By his worshipping he seems to have understood that they were angels; but because he prepares the things that are necessary for mortals, he seems to have thought that they were men; and these are to be understood as those who appeared to Abraham. And note that they appeared in an odd number to Abraham, who was to be multiplied, because God delights in an odd number. In Sodom, which was to be destroyed because of its womanish softness, two appear, because two is the first to depart from unity and is the beginning of alternation. They come in the evening, that is, when the sun of justice had set in them. Through Lot hospitality is commended, of whose virtue the apostle Peter says: “By this some have pleased angels, being received as guests.”
• He runs to meet them; and from this and from many other places of the Scriptures the virtue of hospitality is commended. Of which blessed Peter the apostle too says: “Hospitality do not forget. For by this some, being not aware of it, have entertained angels.”
• And seeing them, etc. When Lot runs to meet and worships the angels, he seems to understand; when he invites them to the refreshment of the body, he seems to think them men. But the same is to be understood of these and of those who appeared to Abraham. And from this place of Scripture and many others the virtue of hospitality is commended. Whence Paul: “Hospitality do not forget. For by this some, being not aware of it, have entertained angels.”
19.2:
**“wash”** — As is wont to be done for guests, so that the dispositions soiled with earthly dust, and with sloth and faint-heartedness as with dusty filth, may be cleansed. Whence in monasteries prayer is said for those who arrive from a journey.
**“And they said: No, but we will abide in the street.”**
• By this word they already prefigured the destruction to come, showing that they were free from the crimes of Sodom and abhorred them
• they signify the destruction to come, while they show that they are free from the crimes of Sodom and abhor them
19.3:
**“He pressed them very much to turn in unto him: and when they were come into his house, he made them a feast,”** — because he saw them clothed or dressed in human form
**“and baked unleavened bread”** — because he was free from the leaven of the wickedness of Sodom
**“He pressed them”** — ALCUIN. The angels enter Lot’s house as if forced, so that his charity, tried and proved, might be rewarded, and so that it might be shown how great a good hospitality is. They entered the hospitable house and freed their host; fire, entering the houses shut to guests, destroyed the sinners.
19.4:
**“But before they went to bed, the men of the city beset the house”** — because the frying pan of lusts, roaring round about, always strives to disturb the calm of chastity
**“both young”**
• the sons of the night wish to darken the sons of light with the works of the night
• the sons of the night try to darken the sons of light with the works of the night
19.8:
**“I have two daughters”** — being disturbed, he wishes to exchange crime for crime
**“who as yet have not known man: I will bring them out to you, and abuse you them as it shall please you, so that”** — it is the custom of the faithful to defend guests from every injury
**“to these men,”** — he thought them only men
**“you do no evil …, because they are come in under the shadow of my roof.”**
• “Lot went out to them, shutting the door behind him,” and the rest. Since Lot wished to prostitute his daughters with this compensation, that his just guests should suffer nothing of the kind from the Sodomites, it is rightly asked whether a compensation of crimes, or of any sins whatever, is to be admitted, so that we do some evil lest another do a worse evil; or whether rather it is to be put down to Lot’s disturbance, not to his counsel, that he said this. And certainly this compensation is admitted most dangerously. But if it is put down to human disturbance and to a mind stirred by so great an evil, it is in no way to be imitated. Lot was disturbed when he wished to exchange crime for crime; for such a compensation of crimes is not to be admitted.
• I have two daughters. AUGUSTINE. Whether a compensation of crimes, or of any sins whatever, is to be admitted, so that we do evil lest worse be done; or whether it is to be put down to Lot’s disturbance, not to his counsel, is rightly asked. And certainly this compensation is admitted most dangerously. But if it was a disturbance of the mind, it is in no way to be imitated.
19.9:
**“But they said: Get thee back thither. And again: Thou camest in, said they, as a stranger,”** — as if: we do not accept a stranger’s judgments
**“was it to be a judge? therefore we will afflict thee more than them.”** — those whom lust cannot overcome by temptation, it presses with heavier goads
**“and they were even at the point of breaking open the doors.”** — because when chastity is attacked almost to falling, it is often kept unharmed within the bars of conscience by the help of the good
19.10:
**“And behold the men put out their hand, and drew in Lot unto them, and shut the door:”** — because the entrance of the heart is fortified by reason against wicked movements
**“and drew in”** — GREGORY. Morally. When the wicked oppose him, Lot is brought back inside the house and protected; because each just man, bearing the snares of the wicked, returns to his mind and remains unafraid. The Sodomites cannot find the door in Lot’s house, because the corrupters of minds find no entrance for blame against the life of the just. Struck with blindness, they go round the house, as it were, because in their envy they search out his deeds and words; but because the strong and praiseworthy action of the just man’s life meets them everywhere, wandering, they grope at the wall.
19.11:
**“And them that were without, they struck with blindness”** — with “unseeing”
**“from the least to the greatest, so that”** — so that they saw nothing blameworthy in the just man
**“they could not find the door.”** — the other things they saw
**“they struck with blindness”** — AUGUSTINE. In Greek, aorasia, that is, “unseeing,” if it can be so called, which makes not everything unseen, but what is not needed. For how would they have tired themselves seeking the door, if they had been struck with a blindness so that they saw nothing? For, troubled by their own calamity, they would have sought nothing further. With this aorasia were struck those who were seeking Eliseus, and those who, walking with Christ after the resurrection, did not know him.
19.12: **“And they said to Lot: Hast thou here any of thine? son in law, or sons, or daughters, all that are thine bring them out of this city:”** — Lot’s household could have been saved by his merit, if they had been willing to go far from the wicked with him
19.13: **“For we will destroy this place, because their cry is grown loud”** — as if: the evil grown in had more power with them than the unaccustomed good
19.14:
**“So Lot went out, and spoke to his sons in law that were to have his daughters, and said: Arise: get you out of this place, because the Lord will destroy this city. And he seemed to them to speak as it were in jest.”**
• whom the love of a wicked habit had bound
• So Lot went out, etc. JEROME. In what follows Lot’s daughters are read to have been virgins, and he himself said to the Sodomites: “Behold, my two daughters, who have not known man,” etc. But now he is said to have had sons in law. But some think that those who had husbands perished in Sodom, and those who were virgins went out with their father. But the Hebrew truth has: “Lot went out and spoke to the betrothed who were to take his daughters.” So the virgin daughters had not yet been joined in marriage.
19.15:
**“And when it was morning,”** — because it is the work of light to withdraw from the wicked
**“the angels pressed him, saying: Arise, take thy wife, and the two daughters which thou hast: lest thou also perish in the wickedness of the city.”** — And when it was morning, etc. ISIDORE. Lot, Abraham’s brother, just and hospitable in Sodom, signifies the body of Christ, which in all the saints groans among the wicked, to whose deeds it does not consent, and from mingling with whom it will be freed at the end of the age.
19.16: **“And as he lingered, they took his hand,”** — those who, from some fleshly affection, put off going out from the company of the wicked, are to be pressed by the frequent warning of the good, lest the examples of the wicked corrupt good manners
19.17:
**“And they brought him forth, and set him without the city: and there they spoke to him, saying: Save thy life:”** — lest thou go back to Sodom
**“look not back,”** — because “no man putting his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God”
**“neither stay thou in all the country about:”** — as the Sodomite, so flee the other vices
**“but … in the mountain,”** — on the summit of the virtues
**“save thyself in the mountain”** — STRABO. The mountain signifies the height of the virtues, to which the angel urges, according to that: “If thou wilt be perfect, go sell all that thou hast,” etc. But whoever sees that he cannot climb up, it is better that he stay in Segor, that is, “the little one,” content with the lay and common life, than that he seize upon the mountain of virtue and go back to worldly things. Virginity is a high mountain, to which the angel urges. If anyone sees that he cannot climb it, let him stay in Segor, that is, in lawful marriage; because it is better to use a middling good than to be hurled down the precipices of lust. Whence: “For fear of fornication, let every man have his own wife.”
19.19:
**“Because thy servant hath found grace before thee, and thou hast magnified thy mercy, which thou hast shewn to me, in saving my life, and I cannot escape to the mountain,”** — he did not yet feel himself fit for the perfection of the virtues
**“lest some evil seize me, and I die:”** — namely, if I take on what I cannot bear
**“and I cannot escape to the mountain”** — Being disturbed, he did not believe the Lord, whom he recognised in the angels, as being disturbed he would have prostituted his daughters.
19.20:
**“There is this city here at hand,”** — Segor, which was so called from Lot’s saying, “It is a little city”
**“to which I may flee”** — Those who are not able to climb to the contemplative life take refuge in the active life, in which they may be saved.
**“it is a little one, and I shall be saved in it: is it not a little one, and my soul shall live?”**
• that is, it is not enough for my weakness to live
• There is this city here. That is, Sodom, which is interpreted “blindness,” expresses worldly desires; but the height of the mountains is the contemplation of the perfect. He went out indeed from Sodom, but yet did not reach the mountains; because many just men flee indeed the enticements of the world, but, set in action, cannot climb to the peak of contemplation; with which agrees what the same Lot says: “There is a city near.” So it is called near, and yet is shown safe for salvation; because the active life is neither wholly separated from the cares of the world nor yet a stranger to the joy of eternal salvation. Otherwise: to flee burning Sodom is to turn aside from the unlawful kindlings of the flesh; the height of the mountains is the stronghold of the continent.
• ISIDORE. There is this city here, etc. Sodom is interpreted “blindness” and expresses worldly desires; the height of the mountains, the contemplation of the perfect. But because many flee the enticements of the world, yet, set in action, cannot climb to the peak of contemplation, Lot went out of Sodom but did not reach the mountains. Whence Lot says: “There is this city here at hand,” etc. It is called near, and yet safe for salvation, because the active life is neither wholly separated from the cares of the world nor a stranger to the joy of eternal salvation.
*Gregory:* Morally. To flee burning Sodom is to turn aside from the fires of the flesh. The height of the mountains is contempt of the world. Or those are on the mountain who cleave to fleshly union, but are not loosed into any pleasure of the flesh except for the care of receiving offspring. But many forsake the crimes of the flesh, and yet, set in the marriage of the flesh, do not keep only the laws of due use. Lot went out of Sodom but did not at once reach the mountains, because the damnable life is left, but the height of conjugal continence is not yet strictly held. In the middle is Segor, to save the weak fugitive; because when married people come together through incontinence, they flee the falls of crimes and are saved with pardon, and find as it were a little city in which they are defended from the fires; because married life is not wonderful in virtues, but only safe from punishments. Whence: “There is this city here,” etc. Married people guard their life as in a little city when they intercede for themselves with constant prayers. Whence it is said to Lot: “Behold also in this I have heard thy prayers”; because when prayer is poured out to God, such a married life is not condemned. Whence: “Defraud not one another,” etc.
19.21:
**“And he said to him:”** — as if: “he that can take, let him take it”
**“Behold also in this, I have heard thy prayers,”** — that is, I yield to thy prayers
19.22: **“Make haste and be saved there, because I cannot do any thing till thou go in thither. Therefore the name of that city was called Segor.”** — that is, “little”
19.23:
**“The sun was risen upon the earth,”** — because the corrupt city was condemned under the light
**“and Lot entered into Segor.”** — fleeing the fires of Sodom
19.24:
**“And the Lord”** — the Father
**“rained upon Sodom and Gomorrha brimstone”**
• stench
• because they had rotted with the stench and heat of lust
**“and fire”**
• burning
• so that the land should be dried up for ever, not grow green again as after the flood
**“from the Lord”**
• from the Son
• by divine judgment, because they had rotted with the stench and heat of lust
**“out of heaven.”**
• by divine judgment
• because the cry of their sin had gone up to heaven
• And the Lord rained upon, etc. GREGORY. Brimstone is the stench of the flesh; fire, the heat of fleshly desire. When the Lord had decreed to punish the crimes of the flesh, he made known the stain of the crime by the kind of vengeance. For brimstone stinks, fire burns. So those who had burned with the stench of the flesh for perverse desires rightly perished by brimstone and fire, so that from a just punishment they should learn what they had done by an unjust desire.
• STRABO. It is to be noted that the water of the flood wiped out the first sinners, who had likewise offended God by the concupiscence of the flesh; but the Sodomites perished by a heavier punishment, namely a flood of fire and brimstone. For though those went beyond measure, they sinned as it were according to nature; but these against nature. Therefore they were condemned by the example of the heaviest punishment.
19.25:
**“And he destroyed these cities, and all the country about,”**
• because it followed the crimes of Sodom
• which did like things
**“all the inhabitants of the cities, and all things that spring from the earth.”**
• in which they delighted
• in which they had taken delight
**“all the inhabitants”** — ALCUIN. The infants were burned with their parents in Sodom, so that the most wicked deed of the Sodomites might be noticed, lest any trace of their origin should remain. And it was provided for them, lest, living long, they should follow the examples of their fathers and be punished more lightly. The parents too are guilty, as much for them as for themselves; for the death of the children is the crime of the parents. Therefore they will be their accusers. And it is some kind of benefit not to be guilty, for one who is not glorious; for it profits one not to be poor who cannot be a king.
19.26:
**“And his wife looking behind her, was turned”** — as if turned back in mind, so as to season the foolish by this example
**“into a statue of salt.”** — for the seasoning of the faithful: the punishment of the wicked is the instruction of the just
**“his wife looking behind her”** — ISIDORE. Lot’s wife is the figure of the kind of people who, called by grace, look back and strive to return to what they had left; of whom it is said: “No man putting his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God.” Therefore they are forbidden to look back. In which it is shown that there is no going back to the old life for those who, regenerated by grace, desire to escape the last fire. The wife, looking back, was turned into salt, made namely an example and a seasoning by which others may be salted. Whence Christ says: “Remember Lot’s wife,” namely that he might season us as with salt, so that we should not be careless but beware prudently.
19.28: **“He looked towards Sodom and Gomorrha, and the whole land of that country: and he saw the ashes rise up from the earth as the smoke of a furnace.”** — through the remains of the burning the memory of the overthrow is pressed upon us, as an example for correction
19.29:
**“Now when God destroyed the cities of that country, remembering Abraham, he delivered Lot out of the destruction of the cities wherein he had dwelt.”** — Scripture commends Abraham, by whose merits it says Lot was freed. But that he is called just is said in a certain manner, by comparison with the Sodomites; living among whom he could not be turned aside to a like life so as to withdraw from the worship of the one true God.
**“Now when … destroyed”** — Scripture hints that God freed Lot rather by Abraham’s merits, so that we may understand that he was called just in a certain manner: chiefly because he worshipped the one true God, and by comparison with the Sodomites, living among whom he could not be bent to a like crime.
**“remembering Abraham”** — It is plain that Lot, whom Scripture calls just, was freed by Abraham’s merits. And it is to be known that he was just not as Abraham was, but by comparison with the Sodomites.
19.30:
**“And Lot went up out of Segor, and abode in the mountain,”** — into which he would not go up before at the Lord’s warning
**“and his two daughters with him, (for he was afraid to stay in Segor,) and he dwelt in a cave, he and his two daughters with him.”**
• And Lot went up, etc. So married people sometimes go up from the lowliness of the active life to the height of the contemplative.
• And Lot went up out of Segor, etc. JEROME. It is asked why, when he first preferred Segor to flight to the mountain and wished the city where he should dwell to be spared, he again passed from Segor to the mountain. We shall answer that the conjecture of the Hebrews about Segor is true: that, often overwhelmed by earthquake, it was first called Bala and afterwards Salisa; and Lot was afraid, saying: “If, while the others stood, this one was often overthrown, how much less will it be able to be saved in the common ruin?” And that this occasion of unbelief was the cause of the incest. For he who had seen the others overthrown and this one stand, and himself rescued by God’s help, ought not to have doubted what he had heard granted to him.
19.31:
**“And the elder said to the younger: Our father is old, and there is no man left on the earth, to come in unto us after the manner of the whole earth.”** — And the elder said to the younger, etc. JEROME. This is said in excuse of the daughters, that they thought the human race had failed, and therefore lay with their father. But what follows does not excuse the father: “and he perceived not when they lay with him, nor when they rose from him.” The Hebrews mark it above with an obelus as superfluous, as if it were incredible, because the nature of things does not allow anyone to have intercourse without knowing it.
*Strabo:* Lot is without excuse: first because he did not believe the angel; then because he was made drunk, and sin was the cause of sin.
*Jerome:* So wicked suggestion and pleasure, like incestuous women, lie in wait for the continent, so that, the occasion taken, they may steep them in the wine of deceit as they grow torpid, and cast them down, as if unknowing, from the state of uprightness.
19.32: **“Come, let us make him drunk with wine, and let us lie with him, that we may preserve seed of our father.”** — Come, let us make him drunk, etc. ALCUIN. Lot’s two daughters had learned that the end of the world was to come by fire. But as girls not fully instructed, they did not know that, the Sodomites being laid waste by fire, much space would remain whole; and they suspected that something had happened such as they had heard of in the times of Noe, and that they were left with their father to restore the human race. And though lying with their father was a great crime, it seemed a heavier impiety if, by keeping chastity, they should blot out the hope of posterity. Therefore they take counsel and soften their father’s sadness or sternness with wine, and each on her own night receives a conception from him unknowing, and they do not repeat it.
19.33:
**“And they made their father drink wine”** — him whom Sodom did not overcome, wine overcame
**“that night: and the elder went in and lay with her father:”** — as Lot was just in Sodom and sinned on the mountain, so some men of the world keep the state of uprightness among the wicked, but when they go up to the height of the life, becoming more careless, they sin gravely
**“but he perceived not neither when his daughter lay down, nor when she rose up.”** — And they made their father drink wine, etc. ISIDORE. Lot in this place signifies the law, which some, begotten from it and set under it, by understanding it wrongly as it were make drunk, and, not using it lawfully, bring forth the works of unbelief. For “the law is good, if a man use it lawfully.”
19.36: **“So the two daughters of Lot were with child by their father.”** — So the two daughters of Lot, etc. JEROME. Moab is interpreted “from the father,” and the whole name has its etymology. But Ammon, for whose name a kind of reason is given, “son of my kindred,” or, as is better in the Hebrew, “son of my people,” is so derived that it is partly the sense of the name and partly the word itself; for Ammon, from which the Ammonites are called, is “my people.”
19.37:
**“And the elder bore a son,”** — idle leisure brings forth such fruits
**“and she called his name Moab: he is the father of the Moabites unto this day.”** — because it is interpreted “from the father,” and signifies those who abuse the law, to whom it is said: “You are of your father the devil”
19.38: **“The younger also bore a son, and she called his name Ammon,”** — which is interpreted “son of my people,” and signifies heretics, of whom it is said: “They went out from us, but they were not of us”

20.1:
**“Abraham removed from thence to the south country,”** — which signifies the heat of tribulation
**“and dwelt between Cades”**
• where Moses brought out of the rock the water of contradiction
• Cades, “fountain of judgment”
**“and Sur,”** — Sur, “straits”
**“and sojourned in Gerara.”** — the land of the Philistines
**“Cades”** — “Fountain of judgment”; Sur, “straits”: by which patience is figured.
20.2:
**“And he said of Sara his wife: She is my sister.”** — while a man has something he can do, he must not tempt God
**“So Abimelech the king of Gerara sent, and took her.”**
• from Pharao’s earlier correction he was sure that she could not be violated
• And he said of Sara, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is often asked how, at that age, Abraham feared to be endangered for Sara’s beauty. But the power of her beauty is to be wondered at, which could still be loved.
• Whose wife the Church is, is hidden from foreigners, not whose sister; because it is hard to understand how the human soul is joined to the Word of God, since he is God, she a creature; for according to this they are bridegroom and bride, or husband and wife. But that Christ and all the saints are brethren by kinship, by divine grace, not by earthly blood, that is, from the father, not from the mother, is both said more pleasantly and heard more readily. For all the saints are brethren to one another through the same grace; but none of them is bridegroom in the fellowship of the others.
*Isidore:* And he said of Sara, etc. He kept silent that she was his wife and said she was his sister, lest he himself be killed and she, made captive, be possessed by foreigners; sure that she would be kept inviolate by God, as with Pharao. Whence Abimelech, warned in sleep, gave her back untouched. Abraham signifies Christ, Sara the Church, which in this sojourning among foreigners lives without spot or wrinkle, for the glory of Christ her husband; whose beauty is the honour of Christ; to whose beauty kings offer gifts, as Abimelech to Sara, wondering at the grace of her form the more because he could love it but not violate it. For the Church is the wife of Christ in hidden secret; for in secret the soul cleaves to the Word of God, so that they are in one flesh. This sacrament of a great marriage, in Christ and in the Church, the apostle commends. But the earthly kingdom, which the kings signify, who are not permitted to violate Sara, did not learn that the Church was the spouse of Christ except when it tried to violate her. For it yielded to the divine witness through the faith of the martyrs, and, corrected, honoured with gifts in later kings her whom in earlier ones it could not corrupt. For what was figured earlier and later in one king, this was fulfilled in this one kingdom by earlier and later kings.
20.3:
**“And God came to Abimelech in a dream by night,”** — though Abraham used human reason, yet he committed himself wholly to God
**“and he said to him: Lo thou shalt die for the woman thou hast taken:”** — he says it by warning him to beware, not by asserting it
20.4: **“Now Abimelech had not touched her, and he said: Lord, wilt thou slay a nation, that is ignorant and just?”** — he does not think he is committing adultery, wishing to take Abraham’s sister in marriage
20.5:
**“Did not he say to me: She is my sister: and she say, He is my brother? in the simplicity of my heart,”** — thinking what was said to be true
**“and cleanness of my hands have I done this.”** — wishing to keep the faith of marriage, not seeking a concubine
20.6:
**“And God said to him: And I know that thou didst it with a sincere heart: and therefore I withheld thee from sinning against me,”** — sinning against our neighbour, we sin against God
**“and I suffered thee not to touch her.”**
• so that thou shouldst come to the crime
• And God said to him, etc. AUGUSTINE. As to what is said to Abimelech for Sara, “And I spared thee, lest thou shouldst sin against me,” it is to be noticed that God did it when he warned him that she whom he thought a sister was Abraham’s wife. And it is to be noted that sin is committed against God when such things are done as men think either not to be sins, or count light, as sins in the flesh.
20.7:
**“Now therefore restore the man his wife,”** — the wrong done is undone when what was lost is restored
**“and he shall pray for thee,”** — so that the unlawful injury may be forgiven thee
**“for he is a prophet:”** — a foreteller of things to come
**“and thou shalt live: but if thou wilt not restore her, know”** — because sin uncorrected will not remain unpunished
20.8:
**“And … forthwith rising up in the night,”** — terrified by the vision
**“Abimelech … called all his servants:”** — lest he should seem to put away a marriage rashly
20.9: **“And Abimelech called also for Abraham, and said to him: What hast thou done to us? what have we offended thee in, that thou hast brought upon me and upon my kingdom a great sin?”** — whatever he committed by this deed he turns back on him who suppressed the truth; for there is little difference whether you commit a crime or allow it
20.10: **“And again he expostulated with him,”** — or “searching out”
20.11:
**“Abraham answered: I thought with myself, saying:”** — as if: I would not tempt God
