**“Perhaps there is not the fear of God in this place: and they will kill me for the sake of my wife:”** — so the Jews killed Christ because of the Church, which is Christ’s sister by the heavenly Father, not by an earthly mother
20.12:
**“otherwise also she is truly my sister”** — JEROME. Since in the Hebrew there is, “Besides, she is truly my sister, the daughter of my father, but not the daughter of my mother,” and it sounds rather as if she was Abraham’s sister, in his excuse we say that such marriages were not yet forbidden by law.
**“the daughter of my father”** — Another translation, more openly: “from my father and not from my mother”; for she was the daughter of Aran, Abraham’s brother, the sister of Lot.
20.14:
**“And Abimelech took sheep and oxen, and servants”** — elsewhere: “and handmaids”
**“and gave to Abraham:”** — because the princes of the earth, having loved the beauty of the Church, gave all that they had in the service of Christ
**“And … took”** — Allegorically. Abraham signifies Christ, Sara the Church. Abraham is honoured because of Sara’s beauty, and Christ because of the Church. Whence: “God is wonderful in his saints.” Sara had a husband, but he was hidden; the Church has Christ, who is not seen in the world, having been received in heaven.
**“and restored to him Sara, his wife.”** — And after, etc. After the word of God was thrust back by Judea, all the faithful are the sister and brethren of Christ. Whence: “Whosoever shall do the will of my Father, that is in heaven, he is my brother, and my sister, and my mother.”
20.15: **“And said: The land is before you, dwell wheresoever it shall please thee.”** — Wheresoever it shall please thee, etc. Those who for a time had put off believing out of terror of the princes, at the command of the same princes betook themselves to the Church, which is Christ’s sister and wife, and spread the glory of Christ and the Church through all parts of the world.
20.16:
**“And to Sara he said: Behold I have given thy brother a thousand pieces of silver: this shall serve thee for a covering of thy eyes to all that are with thee, and whithersoever thou shalt go: and remember thou wast taken.”**
• A thousand pieces of silver, etc. He speaks as if in jest, because she said that he was her brother who was her husband; and he urges her to remember this hereafter, lest, being found out, she should incur a like reproach again.
• A thousand pieces of silver are given to Christ when teachers of the world, eloquent in speech, are taken from the Gentile way of life to hold and preach the faith of Christ. For a thousand, the square of ten, signifies the steadfast and solid teaching of the gospel preaching.
20.17: **“And when Abraham prayed”** — When the son prays to the Father, the barrenness of the princes of the world and of their subject peoples is healed.

21.1:
**“And the Lord visited Sara,”** — the Church, which had long been barren
**“as he had promised: and fulfilled what he had spoken.”** — through the prophets
**“And the Lord visited”** — The figure of circumcision is manifold. For it is, according to the apostle, the seal of the justice of the faith of Abraham and of his seed; and a token of chastising those who should belong to this seed and faith; and a prophecy of the Saviour to be born of this seed, who would cleanse us in the present through baptism from all sin, and in the future, after the resurrection, free us from all the corruption of death. And the number eight suits the glory of the resurrection. For the Lord rose on the eighth day, that is, after the seventh of the sabbath; and we, after the six ages of this world and the seventh of the sabbath, that is, the rest of souls which is meanwhile led in the other life, shall rise as in an eighth time, stripped of all the corruptions and vices of fleshly concupiscence (in which lust reigns most).
21.2: **“And she conceived and bore a son in her old age, at the time that God had foretold her.”** — in the last times Christ was born of a virgin
21.3: **“And Abraham called the name of his son, whom Sara bore him, Isaac.”** — “joy,” because at the birth of Christ the shepherds and angels rejoiced
21.4:
**“And he circumcised him the eighth day,”** — because after the seventh of the sabbath every offshoot of corruption and mortality will be taken away
**“as God had commanded him,”** — He circumcised him, etc. STRABO. Though circumcision was commanded for many reasons, it especially holds out the figure of Christ, who strips us of the old man through baptism, and in the future, after the resurrection, will circumcise all mortality and corruption. And that Isaac was circumcised on the eighth day signifies the eighth age of the world, when the general resurrection of the saints will be celebrated.
21.6: **“And Sara said: God hath made a laughter for me: whosoever shall hear of it will laugh with me.”** — will rejoice with me
21.7:
**“And again she said:”** — the words of one exulting at the benefit given her
**“Who would believe that”** — or “of the hearers”
**“Abraham should hear that Sara gave suck”** — namely, that from bodies already spent a child should be born, and an old woman should give suck against nature; and it is a commending of grace
21.8:
**“And the child grew and was weaned: and Abraham made a great feast on the day of his weaning.”**
• not of his birth, because what has risen sets; nor of his circumcision, for this is not of this time; but of his weaning, where the advance of the mind is understood
• And the child grew, etc. He grows who, disposing ascents in his heart, comes to the solid food of teaching. Whence: “Grow, and thou shalt eat me.”
*Augustine:* And the child grew, etc. He made a feast neither on the day of his son’s birth nor of his circumcision, but on the day of his weaning; because great should be the joy of the spiritual age, when a man has become such as to be fed with solid food, and not like those to whom it is said: “I gave you milk to drink, not meat.”
21.9:
**“And when Sara had seen the son of Agar the Egyptian playing with Isaac her son,”**
• he was teaching him to be slippery and wanton, as he was himself
• so the Jews, the sons of darkness, mock Christians, deriding the death of Christ; which Sara, that is, the Church, takes gravely, and does not receive into her lot the letter of the law, with the fleshly people given to the letter
**“And when Sara had seen”** — JEROME. This is explained in two ways: either that he made games for idols, according to that, “The people sat down to eat and drink, and they rose up to play”; or that, as being of greater age, he claimed the birthright for himself against Isaac in jest; which Sara, hearing it, did not bear.
21.10:
**“Cast out this bondwoman, and her son: for the son of the bondwoman shall not be heir with my son Isaac.”**
• because he did not know that this had been revealed to Sara
• Cast out this bondwoman, etc. It is asked why Sara earlier wished to receive a son of the handmaid, or why she now commands him to be driven out with his mother. She does this not kindled by jealousy but compelled by the mystery of prophecy. For Agar, according to the apostle, begot in bondage the fleshly people; but Sara the spiritual and free, with the freedom with which Christ has made us free. So by this mystery it was signified that the former people, begotten in bondage, would not remain in the house of Sara, that is, the Church, for ever, nor be heir or partner of the Christians, nor possess the kingdom of glory with the noble son, that is, the faithful people.
21.11: **“Abraham took this grievously for his son.”** — Abraham took this grievously, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is asked why Abraham was saddened, when this was a prophecy which he ought to have known rather than Sara. But Sara said this from revelation, because it had first been revealed to her; but he was moved by a father’s affection, and the Lord revealed it to him afterwards. Or perhaps both at first did not know what it was, and prophecy was made through Sara unknowing, when she was moved, with a woman’s mind, by the handmaid’s pride.
21.12:
**“And God said to him: Let it not seem grievous to thee for the boy,”** — as what was revealed to lesser ones the greater should keep silent about
**“and for thy bondwoman: in all that Sara hath said to thee, hearken to her voice: for in Isaac shall thy seed be called.”** — the spiritual
21.13:
**“But I will make the son also of the bondwoman a great nation,”** — because the Jewish people, before the coming of Christ, long flourished both in numbers and in temporal happiness
**“because he is thy seed.”** — the fleshly
**“because he is thy seed”** — AUGUSTINE. It is to be noted that Ismael too is called by God the seed of Abraham; yet the apostle says: “Not the children of the flesh, but the children of the promise, are accounted for the seed.” But this belongs properly to Isaac, who is the son not of the flesh but of the promise; and the spiritual seed is from the promise, not from the flesh.
21.14:
**“So Abraham rose up in the morning, and taking bread”** — the loaves of proposition, the fleshly sacraments of the Jews
**“and a bottle of water,”** — the tasteless understanding of the letter, shut in a dead skin: with these the synagogue is loaded, fulfilling servile commands
**“put it upon her shoulder,”** — and when this was done
**“and delivered the boy,”** — he entrusted him to his mother
**“and sent her away.”** — “the servant abideth not in the house for ever”
**“And she departed, and wandered in the wilderness”** — they wander who do not know the way, which is Christ
**“of Bersabee.”**
• by anticipation
• Taking bread, etc. So when Abraham cast out Agar, taking bread, he put it on her shoulders, and a bottle of water, etc. Agar, going out, put the child on her shoulders, because the sinful, foolish people weighed down the neck of its mother the synagogue, saying: “His blood be upon us and upon our children.” And the loaves signify that the old priesthood would carry the loaves of proposition with it and eat them. But the bottle of water, which runs short, is the Jewish purification that was to run short, or the fleshly teaching shut in a dead skin, that is, in the flesh of the old man, condemned by the sentence of transgression; which neither cools nor heals, but, lukewarm in the heat, causes vomiting. Agar wanders in the wilderness with her son, and the synagogue, driven from its land with its people, wanders through the world without priesthood and sacrifice, and does not know the way, which is Christ. The son perishes with thirst, namely the people having no spiritual purification. She casts her son, dying of thirst, under the tree, and when the angel shows it she sees the fountain; because some of the people are to seek refuge under the shade of the wood of the cross.
*Augustine:* He took bread and a bottle of water, etc. It is asked how he put on her shoulders so big a boy. For he had been circumcised at thirteen years before Isaac was born, when Abraham was ninety-nine; and Isaac was born when his father was a hundred. And Ismael was playing with Isaac when Sara was stirred; surely with a fairly big boy, who had already been weaned; he was certainly more than sixteen years old when he was driven out with his mother. But even if we take what is said, that he played with the little one, as said by way of summing-up, before Isaac was weaned, even so a boy of more than thirteen years could not be put on his mother’s shoulders; but it is to be understood: “he gave her his boy,” etc.
**“put it upon her shoulder”** — JEROME. When Isaac was born, Ismael was thirteen years old, and after Isaac’s weaning he is driven out with his mother. Among the Hebrews there is varied opinion, some asserting that the time of weaning was set at the fifth year, others at the twelfth. So, to choose the shorter age, we reckon that Ismael was cast out with his mother after eighteen years, and that it does not fit that a youth should have sat on his mother’s neck. But it is true that it is an idiom of the Hebrew tongue that every son, in comparison with his parents, is called an infant and a little one. At Rome too, to this day, all sons are called infants.
21.15:
**“And when the water in the bottle was spent,”** — the fleshly observance
**“she cast the boy”**
• from her mind and her care
• when the synagogue cried: “His blood be upon us and upon our children”
**“under one of the trees that were there.”** — She cast the boy, etc. JEROME. What follows, “and she cast the boy under a fir tree, and going away sat over against him a great way off, as it were a bowshot; for she said, I will not see the death of my little one; and she sat over against him,” and at once is joined, “and the boy cried out and wept, and the Lord heard the voice of the boy from heaven where he was, and the angel said to Agar,” should trouble no one. For in the Hebrew this is written first, “I will not see the death of my boy,” etc. So it is read in order that Agar sat over against the boy and lifted up her voice and wept, and God heard the voice of the little one. For while the mother wept and awaited the death of her son, God heard the boy whom he had promised would become a great nation. For the mother laments not her own death but her son’s.
*Augustine:* It is asked how the mother cast a boy of more than fifteen years under a tree. For it seems to be said that she carried him; but it is to be understood that he was cast away from her mind, as one about to die, according to that: “I am cast away from before thy eyes.” In common use too someone is said to be cast away by him with whom he was, so as not to be seen by him or stay with him. And it is to be understood that the mother left her son, the boy not knowing where she went, and hid in the wood, so as not to see her son failing. And what wonder that a boy of that age, his mother long unseen and as it were lost, wept in such a place? Afterwards it is said, “Take up the boy,” not that she should lift him from the ground as if lying there, but that she should join herself to him as companion and hold him by the hand, as people of any age often do when walking.
21.16:
**“And she went her way, and sat over against him a great way off”** — she still sits far off, while she sharpens opinions which she throws far from the truth of the faith
**“as far as a bow can carry, for she said: I will not see the boy die:”** — she would believe them to die whom she saw subjected to the true faith
**“and sitting”** — with zeal
**“over against,”** — against the faith
**“she lifted up her voice and wept.”** — she grieves at the loss of kingdom and priesthood
21.17:
**“And … heard”**
• so that they are not wholly slain; whence: “Slay them not, lest at any time my people forget”
• the mother weeping for the boy
• The boy cries out weeping, and God heard, and, the angel showing it, she sees the fountain: it is said for those who are converted to Christ and, weeping for their sins, are heard; with the eyes of the heart opened they see the fountain of water, that is, Christ, who says: “If any man thirst, let him come to me, and drink.” The angel signifies Elias, through whom the people is to believe. Whence: “Behold I will send you Elias, who shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children.”
**“God … the voice of the boy: and an angel of God called”** — the word of prophecy
**“to Agar from heaven,”** — Scripture
**“saying: What art thou doing, Agar? fear not: for God hath heard”** — so that he is not slain
**“the voice of the boy,”** — of the Jewish people remaining in unbelief
**“an angel of God”** — ISIDORE. Since Scripture first declares him who speaks to Agar an angel, and afterwards the Lord, it is to be believed that it was the Son of God, who spoke through the law and the prophets; who, through obedience to the Father’s will, is called an angel, but by nature is God.
21.18:
**“Arise,”** — it is plain that he was not a burden to his mother but a companion; and that he is held by a parent’s hand shows an anxious affection
**“take up the boy,”** — support him, walking with him
**“and hold him by the hand:”** — the hand is held while it is allowed to practise the works of the flesh
**“for I will make him a great nation.”** — so that he too may have kings from among his own
21.19:
**“And God opened her eyes:”** — “in thy remnants thou shalt prepare their face”
**“and she saw”** — understanding the depth of the sacraments, she believed
**“a well of water, and went and filled the bottle,”** — the mortal heart
**“and gave the boy to drink.”** — the Scriptures being understood, “all Israel shall be saved”
21.20:
**“And God was with him:”** — the concord of the law and the gospel
**“and he grew, and dwelt”**
• the allegory is to be called back to the former state
• in multitude, not in merit
**“in the wilderness,”** — in unbelief
**“and became a young man, an archer.”** — sharpening opinions to fight against the faith
21.21: **“And he dwelt in the wilderness of Pharan, and his mother took … for him”** — the perverse rejoice in the company of their like
21.22: **“At the same time”** — AUGUSTINE. It may be asked, when Abraham made a covenant with Abimelech and the well that he dug was called the well of oath, how it agrees with the truth. For Agar, driven from Abraham’s house with her son, was wandering by the well of oath (as has been said), which is said to have been made by Abraham long after; for there Abimelech and Abraham swore. Agar with her son was driven out earlier. Perhaps it is to be understood that it had already been done, but what Abraham did with Abimelech is recalled by way of summing-up. Unless perhaps he who wrote the book afterwards named the region in which she wandered from the well of oath, as if she wandered in that region in which the well of oath was made, though it was made later. Yet long before the writer’s age the well was so called when the book was written, keeping the ancient name which Abraham had given it. Nor should it trouble us that Agar did not know the well that Abraham had dug, if it was dug before she was driven out; for it could be that he dug a well far from the house for the sake of his flocks, which she did not know.
21.23:
**“Swear therefore by God, that thou wilt not hurt me, nor my posterity, nor my stock: but according to the kindness that I have done to thee, thou shalt do to me, and to the land wherein thou hast lived a stranger.”**
• Palestine, which is now called Salutaris; this is Gerara
• Swear, etc. Often those who are outside, led by the way of life of the faithful, desire to be joined to them and to be shaped for the better by their examples, so as to take thought both for themselves and for the salvation of their neighbours.
21.25: **“And he reproved Abimelech for a well of water,”** — Abraham; because between the faithful and those who are outside there is wont to be contention about the depth of the sacraments
21.26: **“And Abimelech answered: I knew not who did this thing:”** — no one’s crime stains one who does not know of it
21.27: **“And Abraham took sheep and oxen”** — “Render to all men their dues: tribute, to whom tribute is due.” And elsewhere: “Render therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s”
21.30:
**“But he said: Thou shalt take seven ewe lambs at my hand:”** — these are the seven women in Isaias, that is, the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, which the newly baptized receive in the Church through the laying on of the bishops’ hands
**“that they may be a testimony for me,”** — to the teachers who have searched out these sacraments in the Scriptures
21.31:
**“Therefore that place was called Bersabee:”** — “the seventh well,” because of the seven lambs given there; or “well of oath”
**“because there both of them did swear.”** — Therefore that place was called, etc. There is a twofold cause why it was called Bersabee in Hebrew: either because Abimelech received seven ewe lambs from Abraham’s hand, for “seven” is said sabee; or because there they swore, for sabee signifies an oath. If we have read this name above, before this cause, it is said by prolepsis, as with Bethel and Galgala, which were called otherwise before they had these names. It is to be noted from the earlier places and the present one that Isaac was not born by the oak of Mambre, or in the aulon of Mambre (aulon in Hebrew, “oak” in Latin), as is had in the Hebrew, but in Gerara, where Bersabee is a town to this day; which province not long ago, from the division of the governors of Palestine, was called Salutaris. Whence Abraham dwelt in the land of the Palestines many days.
21.32: **“And they made a league for the well of oath.”** — this the faithful enter upon over the fountain of baptism
21.33:
**“And Abimelech, and Phicol the general of”** — army
**“his army arose and returned to the land of the Palestines. But Abraham planted a grove”**
• this is the husbandry which is watered by the rains of the divine fountain
• around the place of the well that was bought
**“in Bersabee,”** — as for an inheritance
**“and there called upon the name of the Lord God eternal.”**
• the Saviour, whom he was awaiting
• But Abraham planted, etc. AUGUSTINE. Abraham, as Stephen says, had not received an inheritance there, “not the pace of a foot.” But inheritance is to be understood as what God was to give freely, not bought for a price. And the space around the well is understood to belong to that covenant of purchase, in which the seven lambs had been given when Abimelech and Abraham swore to each other.
21.34:
**“And he was a sojourner”** — a citizen of the heavenly country is a lodger in the world
**“in the land of the Palestines”** — or “of the Palestines”

22.1:
**“After these things, God tempted Abraham,”**
• so as to make known his perfection, which he himself did not ignore, by a temptation that proves
• so as to make known to him his perfection, of which he himself was ignorant
• From this it appears how ready he is for obedience
• so as to prove how ready he was for obedience
**“and said to him: Abraham, Abraham. And he answered: Here I am.”** — After these things, etc. AUGUSTINE. James says that God tempts no one; but in common use we say “tempt” for “prove.” But James speaks of that temptation by which each is entangled in sin. Whence: “lest perhaps he that tempteth should have tempted you.” For elsewhere it is written: “The Lord your God trieth you, that it may appear whether you love him,” that is, he may make you know. For a man does not know the strength of his own love unless he learns it by trial.
22.2:
**“He said to him: Take thy only begotten son Isaac, whom thou lovest,”** — “God so loved the world, as to give his only begotten Son”
**“and go into the land of vision:”** — where it will be revealed to thee what is foreshown by this sacrifice
**“and there thou shalt offer him for an holocaust”** — the sign of the true holocaust
**“upon one of the mountains which I will shew thee.”**
• of the eminent things of faith, which I will reveal to thee
• Take thy son, etc. ALCUIN. Abraham was not commanded to kill his son at once, but to lead him for three days to be sacrificed, so that the temptation might be increased by the length of time. For through three days, as his cares grew, the father’s heart was tortured, and over a long space the father looks on his son, takes food with him; for so many nights the boy hangs in his father’s embrace, lies in his bosom, and at every moment the grief of killing his son is heaped up in the father’s love.
• Whom thou lovest, etc. From the reminder of his love and the recalling of his name the temptation is heaped up and the father’s love is stirred; and from the memory of the promise, because it was said, “In Isaac shall thy seed be called”; as if, if he were killed, the whole hope of the promise would be made void.
• Go into the land, etc. JEROME. The Hebrews say that this is the mountain on which the temple was afterwards built, on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite. Whence in Paralipomenon: “They began to build the temple in the second month, on the second day of the month, on Mount Moria,” which is therefore interpreted “enlightening” and “shining,” because there is the dabir, that is, the oracle of God, and the law, and the Spirit, who teaches men the truth and inspires prophecies.
22.3:
**“So Abraham rising up in the night, saddled his ass:”** — he prepared the things needed for the holocaust
**“and took with him two young men, and Isaac his son:”** — because two peoples consented to the death of Christ, and the Father spared not his own Son
**“and when he had cut wood”** — because the cross of Christ is made of two pieces of wood joined
**“for the holocaust he went his way to the place which God had commanded him.”** — His ass, etc. The ass signifies the senseless folly of the Jews, which carried all the sacraments and did not know it.
22.4:
**“And on the third day,”** — on the fourth day of the week the betrayal was agreed with Judas; on the fifth he was seized; on the third day, that is, the Parasceve, he was crucified
**“lifting up his eyes, he saw the place afar off.”** — being far from the malice of the Jews
**“And on the third day. Jerome”** — It is to be noted that from Gerara to Mount Moria, that is, the seat of the temple, is a journey of three days, and Abraham is said to have come there on the third day. So they think wrongly that Abraham dwelt at that time by the oak of Mambre, since from there to Mount Moria is scarcely a full day’s journey.
22.5:
**“And he said to his young men: Stay you here with the ass:”** — because the Jews, from their utter slowness, do not understand the mystery of the cross
**“I and the boy will go with speed as far as yonder, and after”** — or “after”
**“we have worshipped,”** — this will be at the end of the world, when the fullness of the Gentiles has come in
**“will return to you.”**
• Stay you here, etc. “Blindness in part has happened in Israel,” that is, “with the ass,” “until the fullness of the Gentiles should come in,” that is, “after we have worshipped.” When the sacrifice of the cross has been preached among the Gentiles, that is, when the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, “we will return to you,” that is, “and so all Israel should be saved.”
• I and the boy, etc. ALCUIN. He wished to slay his son with an undoubting mind. He is to be praised for his constancy in offering and his faith in raising up. For he knew most surely that God cannot deceive, and that though the boy were killed, God’s promise would yet remain safe. Whence the apostle: “By faith Abraham did not waver, when he offered up his only son, in whom he had received the promise, believing that God is able to raise up even from the dead.”
22.6:
**“And he took the wood for the holocaust, and laid it upon Isaac his son:”** — because Christ was forced to carry the cross; whence “the government is upon his shoulder”
**“and he himself carried in his hands”** — in works
**“fire and a sword.”** — good zeal, because it separates father and son
22.7: **“Isaac said to his father: My father. And he answered: What wilt thou, son? Behold, saith he, fire and wood: where is the victim for the holocaust?”** — as far as his innocence goes, Christ seems not to know why he suffers; whence: “Scourges were gathered together upon me, and I knew not”
22.8:
**“And Abraham said: God will provide himself a victim for an holocaust, my son. So they went on together.”** — because the Son obeyed the Father unto death
**“And Abraham said”** — ISIDORE. Abraham, leading his only son to be sacrificed, signifies God the Father. Abraham received his son as an old man; God does not grow old, but the promise concerning Christ had in a manner grown old when he was born. It began from Adam, when it was said, “They shall be two in one flesh,” and was fulfilled in the sixth age of the world. The old age of Sara in the people of God, that is, in the multitude of the prophets, signifies the same: that at the end of times Christ was born of the people of holy souls. Her barrenness signifies that in this world we have been saved by hope, and in Christ, as in Isaac, we have all been born; which offspring the Church brought forth at the end of times not by nature but by grace. For as Abraham offered his only and beloved son as a victim to God, so God the Father delivered up his only begotten Son for us; and as Isaac carried the wood on which he was to be laid, so Christ the cross on which he was to be fixed.
22.9:
**“And they came to the place which God had shewn him, where he built an altar,”** — this is the figure of the altar on which the body and blood of Christ are consecrated
**“and laid the wood in order upon it: and when he had bound”** — because he was led before the governor with bound hands
**“Isaac his son, he laid him on the altar upon the pile of wood.”** — And when he had bound, etc. Isaac, his feet bound, is laid on the altar, and Christ is fixed to the cross; but what was figured by Isaac is passed over to the ram, because Christ is a sheep. For he is the Son because born, the ram because sacrificed. The ram sticks in the briers; the cross has horns. For if two pieces of wood are joined, the form of a cross is given. Whence: “Horns are in his hands.” So the ram sticking by its horns is Christ crucified. And the briers are thorns; the thorns are the wicked, who hung up the Lord; for he was hung among the thorns of sinners. Whence Jeremias: “This people has surrounded me with the thorns of their sins.” Others understand this ram bound in the briers as Christ crowned with thorns before his sacrifice.
22.10: **“And he put forth his hand and took the sword,”** — with which he had cut off every affection of the flesh
22.11: **“And behold an angel of the Lord”** — prophecy, foretelling all the things to come concerning Christ
22.12:
**“And he said to him: Lay not thy hand”** — because the flesh could be crucified; the Godhead could not be touched
**“upon the boy, neither do thou any thing to him: now I know that thou fearest God,”** — I have made thee know. Likewise in what follows it is said, “He called the name of that place, The Lord seeth,” that is, made to be seen, signifying by the cause that which is caused, as “sluggish cold,” which makes men sluggish
**“and hast not spared”** — or “thou hast spared”
**“thy only begotten son for my sake.”** — that is, for obedience to me
**“hast not spared”** — AUGUSTINE. Did Abraham not spare his son for the sake of the angel? But in the angel the Lord was figured, who is God and the Angel of great counsel. For God was in the angel and spoke in his person. This appears more in what follows, when it is said: “And the angel of the Lord called Abraham a second time from heaven, saying: By my own self have I sworn, saith the Lord.” For it is not easily found that Christ would call the Father “Lord,” as his own Lord, especially before the incarnation. For according to the flesh this is fittingly said, according to which it is said in the psalm, “The Lord said to,” etc. But what is said, “The Lord said to my Lord,” is referred to the prophet who speaks; like that, “The Lord rained from the Lord,” that is, our Lord, namely the Son, from our Lord, namely the Father.
22.13:
**“Abraham lifted up his eyes, and saw behind his back”** — because long afterwards the truth of this shadow was to be made plain
**“a ram”**
• “he was led as a sheep to the slaughter”
• ALCUIN. The ram that was sacrificed for Isaac was not imaginary but real. Therefore the angel is thought rather to have brought it from elsewhere than to have created it there from the earth after the work of the six days.
**“amongst the briers”** — he was hung between the two arms of the cross
**“sticking fast by the horns, which he took and offered for a holocaust instead of his son.”** — A ram amongst the briers sticking fast, etc. JEROME. Aquila put “a brier” or “a thorn thicket,” and, as the rendering of the word is, thick shrubs entwined with one another. Whence Symmachus, led by the same opinion, says: “And there appeared after these things a ram held in a net by its horns.” But the Seventy and Theodotion seem to render better, who put the very name sabech: “in the bushes of sabech, by its horns.” For sichon, or “net,” which Aquila and Symmachus put, is written with the letter shin; but here the letter samech is put. Whence it is plain that the word sabech is not a rendering of thick stems and shrubs woven together in the manner of a net, but sounds the name of a bush which is so called in Hebrew.
22.14:
**“And he called the name of that place, The Lord seeth.”** — the Lord sees everywhere; but he said “seeth” for “appeared,” that is, made to see; like that, “Now I know that thou fearest God,” that is, I have made it known; for by the cause is signified that which is caused, as we say “sluggish cold” because it makes men sluggish.
**“Whereupon even to this day it is said: In the mountain the Lord will see.”**
• And he called the name, etc. JEROME. For what is had here, “seeth,” in the Hebrew is written “will be seen.” This passed into a proverb among the Hebrews, so that those set in straits and wishing to be raised up by God’s help say: “In the mountain the Lord will be seen,” that is, as he had mercy on Abraham, he will have mercy on us. Whence too, as a sign of the ram that was given, they are wont to sound a horn.
• When the sacrifice was completed, it is said to Abraham: “In thy seed shall all the nations be blessed.” Which was done when the ram said: “They have dug my hands and feet,” etc. For when the sacrifice was completed it is said: “All the ends of the earth shall be converted to the Lord, and shall adore in thy sight,” etc. So when the ram was sacrificed Abraham called the name of that place “The Lord saw,” that is, made himself to be seen, namely through the incarnation.
22.15:
**“And … called”** — the prophecy repeats the things to come concerning Christ
**“the angel of the Lord”**
• of great counsel; or the angel himself spoke in the person of God
• Christ
22.16:
**“By my own self”** — because I had none greater
**“have I sworn,”** — because it is unchangeably established by God
**“saith the Lord: because thou hast done this thing, and hast not spared thy only begotten son for my sake:”** — because the Father delivered up the Son, he gave him a name which is above every name, that in his name every knee should bow
22.17:
**“I will bless thee, and I will multiply thy seed as the stars of heaven,”**
• the spiritual, fewer and shining
• the Israel of God
**“and as the sand”**
• Israel according to the flesh; because they were to be degenerate and to pass from the good olive into the wild olive
• the fleshly, more numerous and barren
**“that is by the sea shore: thy seed shall possess the gates of their enemies.”** — because Christ went down to despoil hell
22.18:
**“shall … be blessed”** — shall be catechized, that is, baptized
**“And in thy seed”** — in Christ
**“all the nations of the earth”** — the predestined from all nations
22.19:
**“Abraham returned to his young men,”** — at the end of the world faith will return from the Gentiles to the Jews
**“and they went to Bersabee together,”** — then they will live in concord in the Church
22.20:
**“After these things, it was told Abraham that Melcha”** — who was Sara’s sister: Abraham married Sara, but Nachor Melcha
**“Melcha”** — JEROME. Of Melcha, wife of Nachor, daughter of Aran, was born Hus, from whose stock Job came down, as it is written: “There was a man in the land of Hus, whose name was Job.” So some think wrongly that Job was of the race of Esau; for what is had at the end of his book, that it was translated from the Syrian tongue, and that he was fourth from Esau, and the rest that is contained there, is not had in the Hebrew. Second was born of Melcha Buz, of whose race was Balaam the soothsayer, as the Hebrews hand down; who in Job is called Eliu: at first a holy man and a prophet of God, afterwards, through disobedience and the desire of gifts, when he wished to curse Israel, he is called by the name of soothsayer. Whence: “And Eliu the son of Barachel the Buzite was angry,” etc. But Camuel is the father of Damascus; for it is called Aram, which here is written for Syria, and by that very name it is read in Isaias.
22.21:
**“Hus the firstborn,”**
• or Chus, of whose stock was Job; whence: “There was a man in the land of Hus, whose name was Job.”
• from whom the land of Hus is named, according to that: “There was a man in the land of Hus,” etc.
**“and Buz”** — from whom the Buzite is named, whom the Hebrews think to have been Balaam
**“his brother, and Camuel the father of the Syrians,”** — this is not to be referred to him who brought the news, but to him who wrote this long afterwards
22.22: **“And Cased,”** — from whom the Casdim, that is, the Chaldeans, were afterwards called
22.23: **“And Bathuel, of whom was born Rebecca:”** — for whose sake the genealogy is recalled, whom Isaac was to marry; and no wonder if not all these things bear mystical senses, for not all the branches of a tree bear fruit

23.2: **“And she died in the city of Arbee”** — JEROME. “Which is in the valley” is not had in the authentic books. Arboch was little by little corrupted by readers and copyists. Nor is it to be thought that the Seventy rendered the name of the city, a Hebrew one, barbarously and corruptly, otherwise than it is called in its own tongue. For Arboch signifies nothing at all; but it is called Arbee, that is, “four,” because there Abraham, Isaac and Jacob were laid, and Adam the first, as is plainly shown in the book of Josue.
23.7: **“Abraham rose up, and bowed down to the people of the land, to wit the children of Heth:”** — Abraham rose up, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is asked how Abraham bowed down to the people of the land, when it is written: “The Lord thy God shalt thou adore, and him only shalt thou serve.” But it is not said in the commandment, “The Lord thy God only shalt thou adore,” as it is said, “and him only shalt thou serve.” For such service is owed to God alone as is called in Greek latreia. Whence idolaters are condemned, who show this service to idols. Nor should it trouble us that elsewhere an angel forbids a man to adore him and warns him that God rather should be adored. For he had appeared such that he could be adored in God’s place, and therefore the adorer had to be corrected.
23.15:
**“My lord, hear me. The ground which thou desirest, is worth four hundred”** — or “four hundred” (in the ablative)
**“sicles of silver”** — or “sicles” (in the ablative)
23.16: **“And when … had heard this”** — JEROME. In the Hebrew, as we have set it down, the name is first written Ephron, and the second time Ephran. For after he was won over by the price to sell the sepulchre and take the silver, even though Abraham pressed him, the letter vau, which among them is read as o, was taken from his name, and instead of Ephron he was called Ephran. In which it is signified that he was not of perfect virtue who could sell the memorials of the dead. So let those know, who take the price of sepulchres not from those who press them but from the unwilling, that their name is changed and something of their merit perishes, since even he is blamed who took it unwillingly.
23.17:
**“And the field that before was Ephron’s … was made sure”** — first he is called Ephron, that is, “strengthened and perfect”; after the burial place was sold, Ephran, that is, “weak and imperfect”
**“wherein was the double cave, looking towards Mambre, both it and the cave, and all the trees thereof in all its limits round about,”**
• And the field … was made sure, etc. GREGORY. Morally. The double sepulchre hints that the perfect preacher hides the soul that has died to the desires of the flesh under the covering of good work and of contemplation, so that it may lie hidden from fleshly concupiscence as if without feeling; which before, feeling it, lived mortally. Whence: “For you are dead, and your life is hid with Christ in God.” For the active life buries the dead from wicked works; the contemplative more perfectly, since it divides them utterly from all actions. So he who has already tamed in himself the insults of the flesh has still to exercise his mind in the pursuits of holy work; and he who already enlarges his mind through holy works has still to stretch it to the secrets of inmost contemplation. For he is not a perfect preacher who, for the pursuit of contemplation, neglects what is to be done, or, for the urgency of work, puts off what is to be contemplated.
• The double cave, etc. And the wooded field around it is bought by the patriarch from the lords of the land for four hundred sicles of silver, to bury Sara; because for preachers to have leisure for wisdom and to give themselves to action, under the leaves of mystical words as under fruitful trees, a quiet place is not otherwise gained than if, by the gospel teaching shining with the brightness of silver, eternal happiness is urged by them upon the earthly powers. Which is well figured by a hundred multiplied by four, which is moved from the left hand to the right.
23.19:
**“And so Abraham buried Sara his wife,”** — the soul dead to the world, alive to God
**“in a double cave of the field,”** — in the rest of the active and contemplative life
**“that”** — or “which” (masculine)
23.20: **“And the field was made sure to Abraham, and the cave that was in it, for a possession to bury in, by the children of Heth.”** — from whom the Hethites

24.2:
**“And he said to the elder servant”** — the prophetic word, which was sent before the apostles to call the Church from the Gentiles
**“of his house, who was ruler over all he had: Put thy hand under my thigh,”**
• not over, because the flesh of Christ, which is over all, was to come down from there
• Put thy hand, etc. GREGORY. Allegorically. He commands him to put his hand under his thigh and swear by the God of heaven, because through that member the flesh of him was to come down who would be the son of Abraham by his humanity and divine by his Godhead; as if: touch my son, and swear by my God. Whence he commands him to put his hand not over the thigh but under it, because from there was to come down one who would be man but above men. Whence it was not fitting that he should put his hand over the thigh, because no flesh is above that one.
24.3:
**“That I may make thee swear by the Lord the God of heaven and earth, that thou take not a wife for my son,”** — as if: “because you have shewn yourselves unworthy and rejected the word of God, behold we turn to the Gentiles”
**“that thou take not”** — GREGORY. Allegorically. Isaac is forbidden to take a wife from the daughters of the Chanaanites, because no souls of the reprobate are joined to Christ. He is commanded to take a wife from his kindred, because only the Church of the elect was to be joined to Christ, which the Only-begotten, through predestination and foreknowledge, already did not hold a stranger. The servant who is sent to bring the wife is the order of the prophets and apostles and of all teachers, who, while they preach the word, become as it were the providers of each soul that is to be joined to the only Son.
24.4:
**“But that thou go to my own country and kindred,”** — “I will give thee the Gentiles for thy inheritance”
**“and take a wife from thence”** — that is, the Church
24.5: **“The servant answered: If the woman will not come with me”** — and believe; as if: if the foreskin will not be joined to the circumcision, the word of God will be preached only there
24.7:
**“The Lord God of heaven, who took me out of my father’s house, and out of my native country, who spoke to me, and swore to me, saying: To thy seed will I give this land:”** — Judea, to which, after it was preached to
**“he will send his angel”**
• of great counsel
• the guide of thy life
**“before thee, and thou shalt take from thence a wife”** — the Church
**“for my son.”** — for Christ
24.8: **“But if the woman will not follow thee,”** — as if: if, when thou proclaimest it, she will not give way about her wickedness, thou hast delivered thy soul
24.9:
**“The servant therefore put his hand under the thigh of Abraham his lord,”** — honouring Christ, who was to be born from there
**“The servant therefore put”** — JEROME. The Hebrews hand down that he swore by his sanctification, that is, by circumcision. But we say that he swore by the seed of Abraham, that is, by Christ, who was to be born of him, according to that: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham.”
24.10:
**“And he took ten camels of his master’s herd, and departed, … something of all his goods”** — the servant of God must have not only obedience and patience but the other virtues too
**“carrying … with him, and he set forward and went on”** — accompanied by such
**“to Mesopotamia”** — the Gentiles
**“ten camels”** — The divine word must have such with it as obey the commands of God, which is signified by ten, and bravely bear the weight of tribulation, which the camels signify.
**“of all his goods”** — GREGORY. Allegorically. Because those who speak of the Lord show in themselves the riches of the virtues, so that they invite men to follow God the more quickly the more they show their hearers in themselves what they tell of.
24.11:
**“And when he had made the camels lie down without the town near a well”**
• the imitators of Christ dwell with Christ outside the camp, because they do not serve the delights of the tent
• the depth of Scripture
**“of water in the evening,”** — in the sixth age
**“at the time”** — at the right moment, when they may see minds more pliant to receiving instruction
**“when women are wont to come out to draw water, he prayed to the Lord,”** — the preacher must first pray, so that the word of God may run and bear fruit in his hearers
**“saying:”** — Near a well, etc. GREGORY. He stood by the spring and set out by a sentence fixed beforehand which girl was to be chosen; because holy preachers consider the streams of the word. Whence they gather what words they should entrust, or to whom, and of which hearers they may take the confidence of certainty.
24.14:
**“Now, therefore, the maid to whom I shall say: Let down thy pitcher that I may drink: and she shall answer, Drink,”** — I will do what thou and thy fellows urge
**“and I will give thy camels drink also: let it be the same whom thou hast provided for thy servant Isaac:”** — such a soul is to be the bride of Christ
**“and by this I shall understand, that thou hast shewn kindness to my master.”** — Now, therefore, the maid to whom I shall say, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is to be asked how unlawful auguries differ from this petition, by which the servant asks that God show him the one who was to be Isaac’s wife, by whom, when he asked to drink, it should be said: “Drink, and I will give thy camels drink also.” But it is one thing to ask for something that is a sign by its very wonder; another to watch things which happen in such a way that they are not wonderful, but are interpreted by diviners with superstitious vanity. But even this very thing, that some wonder is asked for by which what one wishes to know is signified, whether it should be heard, is no small question. For it belongs to what those are said to do who do this wrongly: to tempt God. Whence: “Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God.” For it was suggested to Christ, as to a man, that he should find out by some sign how much he could do with God; which is done wrongly. From this is distinguished what Gedeon did when the danger of battle hung over him; for that was a consulting of God rather than a tempting. Whence Achaz fears to ask a sign, lest he seem to tempt God, when the Lord warned him here through the prophet; perhaps thinking that he was being tested by the prophet whether he remembered the command by which tempting God is forbidden.
**“Let down”** — Humble thy worldly eloquence to draw up the prophetic word, so that I may bend thy will to my persuasion.
24.15:
**“He had not yet ended these words within himself, and behold Rebecca came out,”** — patience, which would humbly receive the word of God and is therefore to be counted among Christ’s kin
**“the daughter of Bathuel, son of Melcha, wife to Nachor the brother of Abraham, having a pitcher”** — worldly knowledge
**“on her shoulder:”** — in the exercise of works
24.16:
**“An exceeding comely maid,”** — of whom it is said: “The king shall greatly desire thy beauty,” and “The queen stood on thy right hand”
**“and a most beautiful virgin,”** — consenting to no heresy
**“and not known to man:”** — “For I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ”
**“and she went down to the spring,”** — she had humbled herself to draw from the fountain of life
**“and filled”** — with divine sentences
**“her pitcher”** — the words of human eloquence
24.17:
**“And … ran to meet”** — because there is a time of teaching and a time of calling
**“her the servant, and said:”** — the divine word
**“Give me a little water”**
• to the soul pondering its salvation
• GREGORY. Allegorically. Every preacher thirsts for the soul of his hearer; therefore the servant asks, Rebecca gives drink, because the Church of the elect satisfies the desire of the preachers by the strength of her faith. For she who confesses the God whom she hears offers the preacher the water of refreshment and coolness. And it is to be noted that she lowered the pitcher from her shoulder, because that confession is pleasing which proceeds from good work. Or she gave water because in what she believed she did not remain empty; for she soon preached what she heard, and by teaching brought forth many preachers from herself. For the water in the pitcher is the knowledge of preaching in measure; for she strives “not to be more wise than it behoveth to be wise.” The pitcher on the arm is the measure of preaching in work. And she gives drink not only to all his companions but to the camels too, because the word of life is preached not only to the prudent but to fools as well. Whence: “To the wise and to the unwise I am a debtor.” Or water is given to the beasts too, when it is set in order how the care of the flesh is to be had, so that it is not spent on pleasure nor denied to need. Whence: “Make not provision for the flesh in its concupiscences.” And elsewhere: “No man ever hated his own flesh.”
**“to drink”** — or “to drink”
**“of thy pitcher.”** — as if: make the spoils of Egypt vessels in the house of the Lord, fitting the divine sentences to the words of human wisdom
24.18:
**“And she answered: Drink, my lord.”** — as if: I fit my understanding to thee
**“And quickly she let down the pitcher upon her arm,”** — she humbled her eloquence to believing and doing what is said
24.19:
**“And when he had drunk, she said: I will draw water for thy camels also,”** — to those who share in thy labour
**“till they all drink.”** — I will satisfy their desire
24.20:
**“And pouring out the pitcher”** — setting out the understanding to those able to take it
**“into the troughs, she ran back to the well”** — the depth of Scripture
**“to draw water: and having drawn she gave to all the camels.”** — because, bringing forth the good will of the heart, they refresh the teachers with hope
24.21: **“But he musing beheld her with silence, desirous to know whether the Lord had made his journey prosperous or not.”** — a sign of the soul coming back to life and preparing itself for marriage
24.22:
**“And after that the camels had drunk, the man took out golden earrings, weighing two sicles:”** — this is done when the exorcists say to the catechumens, “Ephpheta,” that is, “Be opened,” when they are formed in the two commandments of charity, so that what they hear in word they may have fulfilled in works, namely of the ten commandments
**“and as many bracelets of ten sicles weight.”** — The man took out, etc. JEROME. The beka, which is put here for a didrachma, is half an ounce; but the shekel, which in Latin, though corruptly, is called siclus, is an ounce.
*Gregory:* Allegorically. Because the preacher adorns the hearing of the Church through obedience and her hands through working. The earrings are of two sicles, the bracelets of ten; because the first virtue of obedience is in charity, which is the love of God and of neighbour; and good work is perfected by fulfilling the decalogue, so that when good things begin to be done, no evil things are done.
24.25:
**“And she said moreover to him: We have good store of both straw and hay,”** — because preachers spend spiritual things on their hearers, from whom they receive fleshly things
**“and a large place to lodge in.”**
• the disposition of devotion
• A large place, etc. GREGORY. Allegorically. The Church showed that she had known the law of nature from the former people, and received the preaching in the ample bosom of charity; for the spacious dwelling of the teacher in the heart of the hearer is the breadth of charity. Whence: “You are not straitened in us, but in your own bowels you are straitened”; as if: widen the room of the mind for receiving teaching; narrow it for thinking of fleshly things.
**“both straw”** — GREGORY. Because the Church, receiving spiritual things, gives back earthly wages to the preachers. Whence: “If we have sown unto you spiritual things, is it a great matter if we reap your carnal things?”
24.26: **“The man bowed himself down,”** — ascribing nothing to himself, but to the grace of God
24.28: **“Then the maid ran, and told in her mother’s house, all that she had heard.”** — so the Samaritan woman proclaimed in the city the words of the Lord which she had heard at the well
24.29:
**“And Rebecca had a brother”** — GREGORY. Allegorically. Because the fleshly, joined to the faithful, when they see spiritual gifts, held in wonder, admit the preaching, if not as far as works, yet as far as receiving the faith. For while they see the good shining with miracles, they do not refuse what they hear of eternity, though, not following the Church in manners, they remain in fleshly works.
**“And Rebecca had a brother named Laban, who went out in haste to the man, to the well.”** — And Rebecca had a brother, etc. Because there are fleshly people joined to the faithful, who through their familiarity sometimes come forward to hear the word, and seeing the gifts of God given to the faithful, wonder, and take the word into their heart, which they do not take trouble to fulfil by good manners.
24.32:
**“And he brought him into his lodging: and he unharnessed the camels and gave straw”** — grass for the service of men
**“and hay, and water to wash his feet, and the feet of the men that were come with him.”** — he fulfils the duty of hospitality, lest, the word not being received, the dust be shaken off as a witness of labour made void
24.33:
**“And bread was set before him. But he said: I will not eat, till I tell my message.”** — he does not seek his own things; he will not reap fleshly things unless he has first sown spiritual ones
**“He answered him: Speak.”** — I will not eat, etc. GREGORY. Because there are those who are ready to keep the teachers by temporal wages; but these will not receive them unless they first obtain eternal things. For if they do not find fruit in souls, they scorn to take wages for their bodies. They do not wash their feet, because they relieve the desire of labour by no consolation.
24.34: **“And he said: I am the servant of Abraham:”** — a commending of his person, like that: “Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ”
24.35:
**“And the Lord hath blessed my master wonderfully,”** — a commending of the sender, so that the one sent may be heard for the sender’s sake
**“and he is become great:”** — he subjected men of every kind to his faith
**“and he hath given him sheep”** — the simple
**“and oxen,”** — the prudent
**“silver”** — the eloquent
**“and gold,”** — the wise
**“men servants and women servants,”** — those serving servilely for temporal things
**“camels and asses.”** — those patient in tribulation
24.36:
**“And Sara my master’s wife hath borne my master a son”** — grace; because the son of good will, who was made to him of the seed of Abraham
**“in her old age,”** — in the last age of the world
**“and he hath given him all that he had.”** — whence: “Father, all thy things are mine”
24.37:
**“And my master made me swear, saying: Thou shalt not take a wife for my son of the Chanaanites, in whose land I dwell:”**
• these things have been explained above
• And my master made me swear, etc. AUGUSTINE. The sense is the same; not all the words were said, either the same ones or in that way; which must be said because of those who slander the evangelists, that in some words they do not altogether agree, when the things and the senses are the same. For one man wrote this book, who could have set down what he said above, when Abraham gave his charge, or the rest, if he judged it to belong to the matter; since the truth of a narrative requires only that there be truth of the things and the senses, by which the will (to make which known words are made) appears sufficiently.
24.42: **“And I came … to the well”** — JEROME. In the Hebrew it is written: “Behold I stand by the well of water, and it shall be that the young maiden who comes out to draw,” etc. For “young maiden” in the Hebrew is read alma, as in Isaias, where in our books it is written, “Behold a virgin shall conceive,” etc.; in the Hebrew is read, “Behold an alma shall conceive.” So it is to be noted that alma always signifies a virgin and has the etymology apocrypha, that is, “hidden.” For in Job, where it is written of wisdom, “and it is hid from the eyes of all living,” in the Hebrew it is said naalma. So alma, which is interpreted “hidden,” that is, a virgin guarded with very great care, seems to be of greater praise than virgo. For one can be a virgin in body and not in spirit or mind; but she who is hidden has an addition to virginity, so that she is both a virgin and hidden; and she who is hidden, according to the idiom of the Hebrew tongue, is consequently a virgin too; but she who is a virgin is not at once hidden. This same word we read in Exodus of Mary, Moses’ sister, still a virgin. So let the Jews show anywhere alma put where it sounds “young maiden” and not “virgin.”
24.45: **“And whilst I pondered these things secretly with myself,”** — he tells the miracle so that those who do not believe the word may believe the miracle
24.46: **“And she speedily let down the pitcher from her shoulder,”** — lowering the raised-up eloquence of the world to the prophetic word, which the servant signifies
24.49: **“Wherefore if you do according to mercy and truth”** — these two are often joined, mercy and truth, especially in the psalms
24.50:
**“And Laban and Bathuel answered:”** — God’s disposition being known, the Church from the Gentiles is allowed to come to the faith of Christ, so that he who will not imitate does not presume to oppose
**“The word hath proceeded from the Lord, we cannot speak any other thing to thee but his pleasure.”** — And Laban and Bathuel answered, etc. AUGUSTINE. Either they knew Abraham as a prophet and recognised that what had been said through him was said prophetically by the Lord; or they called the sign which the servant told a speaking of the Lord. For this was said rather of Rebecca; for Abraham had spoken not of Rebecca but of some woman of his tribe or kindred. And this for either case, that the servant should be free from the oath if he did not obtain it; which is not said when something is prophesied, for prophecy ought to be certain.
24.53:
**“And bringing forth vessels of silver”** — the senses of Scripture, with eloquence
**“and gold,”** — the honesty of manners
**“and garments, he gave them to Rebecca for a present. … also to her brothers,”** — because the Gentile world receives temporal things
**“He offered gifts … and to her mother.”** — And bringing forth vessels of silver, etc. GREGORY. Allegorically. After the servant had won the cause of the marriage, he gave all these to Rebecca; because the teachers of the Church give her as many ornaments as the good virtues they have taught. For she who had first received earrings and bracelets now receives vessels of gold and silver and garments; because the Church, which before received faith, obedience and working, growing, grows strong in spiritual things, so that, filled with the spirit of prophecy and the grace of virtues, she grows with enlarged gifts. Gifts are offered to the mother and brother, because the Gentile world, from the time the Church came to the faith, has grown strong in temporal glory. For everywhere Christians feel affliction, Gentiles glory in earthly strength. Her brothers receive gifts; for those who in the Church hold the faith in word, but yet do not follow their profession in manners, are honoured by the faithful because they are called faithful. So the mother and brothers receive gifts, but are strangers to the inheritance; because the unbelieving or the fleshly do not come to the eternal inheritance, but obtain the glory of the bounty above in temporal things.
**“he gave them to Rebecca”** — Rebecca is not adorned with the gold of Bathuel, because the ornaments of the barbarous and unskilled are not worthy; she receives ornaments from the house of Abraham, because patience is adorned from the house of wisdom. From Abraham’s servant she receives earrings, that is, golden words in the ears, and bracelets, that is, golden works in the hands, and other ornaments, by which the various kinds of virtues are figured.
24.54:
**“And a banquet was made, and they ate and drank together, and lodged there. And in the morning, … arose,”** — the zealous preacher does not wish to stay long among the fleshly, because he strives to bring very swiftly the souls converted from the Gentile world to the fellowship of the spiritual
**“the servant … and said:”** — the prophetic word
24.57: **“And they said: Let us call the maid,”** — because faith is of will, not of necessity; and according to the laws, betrothals must be made with the consent of those contracting them
24.59:
**“So they sent … away,”** — patience
**“her, and her nurse, and Abraham’s servant, and his company,”** — wisdom, which says: “The patient man is better than the valiant”; these accompany the prophetic and apostolic word
**“and her nurse”** — It was seemly that a virgin, setting out for her marriage without her parents, should be cherished by the comfort of a nurse.
24.60:
**“Wishing”** — that is, praying earnestly
**“prosperity to their sister, and saying: Thou art our sister, mayst thou increase to thousands of thousands,”** — they were not prophets, nor did they wish such great things out of vanity; but what God had promised to Abraham could not be hidden from them
**“and may thy seed possess the gates of their enemies.”** — this, though they prayed in a fleshly way, was fulfilled spiritually, Christ ruling over all nations
24.61:
**“So Rebecca and her maids, being set upon camels,”** — the inborn vices being subjected to them
**“followed the man:”** — the prophetic word
**“who with speed”** — as if: “we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency may be of the power of God, and not of us”
**“returned to his master.”**
• Christ
• So Rebecca, etc. GREGORY. Allegorically. Because the Church has with her souls of lesser merit, which follow her in manners but are not brought forward to the couch of contemplation. The servant too had some in his company; because with the prophets there were those who lived well but did not have the spirit of prophecy, and with the apostles and teachers those who held to their life and yet did not preach.
• Who with speed, etc. The servant returns with speed to his lord, because preachers, when they win the life of their hearers, give it to God, from whose gift they have it, not to themselves.
24.62:
**“At the same time Isaac was walking”** — Christ
**“along the way”** — humility
**“to the well”**
• the passion of Christ
• the depth of Scripture, through which he is understood who ever lives and sees all things
**“which is called Of the living”** — “I live, saith the Lord”
**“and the seeing:”**
• to whom all things are open
• because in the passion of Christ the Scriptures were revealed
**“for he dwelt”** — by the exceeding charity with which God incarnate loved us
**“in the south country.”**
• Gerara, from which he had been led to be sacrificed
• At the same time, etc. GREGORY. Allegorically. The Living and the Seeing is the Lord, of whom it is written: “I live for ever, saith the Lord.” And elsewhere: “All things are naked and open to his eyes.” The well is the depth of holy Scripture, which waters our minds. The way is the humility of Christ’s passion, through which the streams of Scripture have been opened to us. For unless Christ, incarnate, had been tempted, seized, buffeted, spat upon, crucified and dead, the depth of Scripture would not lie open. So the humility of the passion became the key of the opening, so that we may drink the water of knowledge from the deep. For we understand these things, heard before, now done, which were read before and not understood. Whence: “The lion of the tribe of Juda hath prevailed to open the book and to loose the seals thereof.” But it is to be noted that he does not say “walked” but “walked about.” For he walks about who treads a way by going and returning. In the humility of the passion Christ walked about, because he bore now insults of words, now false witness, now blows, now spittle, now a crown of thorns, now the cross.
**“for he dwelt in the … country”** — GREGORY. Morally. When Rebecca came, Isaac dwelt in the south country, because when the Church came to him Christ remained in the minds of those whom not the cold of sluggishness but the heat of charity held; such as were Anna, Simeon and some of the people of the Jews.
24.63:
**“And he was gone forth to meditate”**
• or “to exercise”
• he had come into the world for the exercise of the passion
**“in the field,”** — the world
**“the day being now well spent:”** — near the end of the world
**“and when he had lifted up his eyes,”** — intent on the salvation of the world
**“he saw camels coming afar off.”**
• the Gentiles, of twisted manners, coming from afar to the faith
• And he was gone forth, etc. JEROME. By the south country he means Gerara, from which he had been brought to be sacrificed. He went forth to be exercised in the field. In the Hebrew is read: “Isaac went forth to speak in the field, the evening now declining”; where it is signified that the Lord prayed alone on the mountain; and that Isaac, who was a type of the Lord, as a just man gone out of his house for prayer at the ninth hour or before sunset, offered spiritual victims to God.
• The day being now well spent, etc. Because he took up the exercises of the sufferings near the end. Whence: “The lifting up of my hands as evening sacrifice.”
*Gregory:* The field is the world, into which Christ went forth, because he deigned to appear visible. Whence: “Thou wentest forth for the salvation of thy people.” Isaac goes out to meditate in the field, because Christ, giving the form of humility, showed the exercise of long-suffering and the examples of passion and patience, as young men practised in the use of arms are wont to drill. The drill of arms is the frequent bearing of the passion. For he who bore blows, spittle, the lance and the cross allowed the passion even to death to be often borne in himself. We call sufferings arms, because through them we are freed from the adversary. Whence: “In your patience you shall possess your souls.”
24.64:
**“Rebecca”** — the Church from the Gentile world
**“also, when she saw”** — the Church saw him who saw her and put off the ugliness of the vices; which we do daily when we search the Scriptures concerning the incarnation of Christ
**“Isaac,”** — Christ
**“lighted off the camel,”**
• from pride
• from the vicious way of the old life
• Lighted off the camel, etc. GREGORY. Rebecca is brought to Isaac on a camel, because Rebecca signifies the Church, the camel the Gentile people, twisted in manners and loaded with the worship of idols. For those who found for themselves, out of themselves, gods to worship, had a burden grow on their back from them, to carry. So the Church, hastening to Christ from the Gentile world, is found in the twisted ways of the old life. On seeing Isaac she gets down from the camel, because, recognising her Redeemer more closely, she humbly forsakes the pursuits of the fleshly life, and herself speaks against her own twistedness, and seeks humility from the height of pride. Sitting on the camel she saw Isaac, because, still leaning on vices, she went up clinging not yet to spiritual but to animal manners. Nor should it trouble us that the servant came with camels carrying his master’s riches; because when preachers stand out in knowledge and life for understanding and bringing forth higher things, they still bear the contradiction of the flesh, “seeing another law in their members, fighting against the law of their mind.” They carry riches on camels, because “lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me, there was given me a sting of my flesh.” So, speaking heavenly things and feeling the contradiction of the flesh from vice, they carry riches on the twisted backs of camels.
24.65:
**“And said to the servant: Who is that man who cometh towards us along the field?”** — he answers that Christ is the Lord
**“And he said to her: That man is my master.”** — Scripture, being searched, answers that Christ is its Lord
**“But she quickly took her cloak, and covered herself.”**
• when the Church knows Christ, she blushes at her foulness
• Who is that man, etc. Rebecca, seeing Isaac, learns who he is by asking the servant, because the Church understands through the sayings of the prophets and apostles what she ought to believe of Christ. She at once covered herself with a cloak, because the more she penetrates the mysteries of Christ, the more she is confounded at her past life. Whence she strives to cover her weakness with a cloak, and she who before was freely carried on the camel, getting down, is covered with shame. To whom, as she is ashamed, it is said: “What fruit therefore had you then in those things, of which you are now ashamed?”
• But she quickly took, etc. JEROME. Another edition has theristrum, which even now is a kind of Arabian garment with which the women of that province are veiled.
24.66: **“And the servant told Isaac all that he had done.”** — because the preacher ascribes to God whatever good he does
24.67:
**“Who brought her into the tent of Sara his mother,”** — he had her in place of the synagogue, from which Christ was born according to the flesh
**“and took her to wife:”** — the marriages of the patriarchs signify the joining of Christ and the Church, or the joining of the soul with the Word of God, of which it is said: “He who is joined to the Lord is one spirit”
**“and he loved her so much, that it moderated the sorrow which was occasioned by his mother’s death.”**
• the Gentile world being taken up softened the grief that could come to him from the synagogue
• He brought her, etc. GREGORY. Isaac brought her into his mother’s tent and took her to wife; as if in the place of the synagogue, from which Christ was born, he loves the Church, so that she who had been near in kindred, that is, in predestination, may become his wife joined in love.
• And he loved her so much, etc. GREGORY. Because from the gain of the Church Christ wiped away the sadness from the loss of the synagogue; for while the Church, coming from the Gentile world, is brought to the couch of contemplation, Judea is held as nothing. Isaac, too, is “laughter”; Rebecca is called “patience.” Laughter is from gladness, patience from tribulation. And though the Church is already held in the contemplation of heavenly joy, she yet has in herself what she grieves for from the weight of the flesh. But Isaac and Rebecca are joined, that is, laughter and patience, according to that, “Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation,” so that prosperous things gladden from contemplation and adverse things trouble from tribulation.

25.1:
**“And Abraham married another wife,”** — not only to multiply offspring, but for a mystical signifying
**“named Cetura:”**
• because a young woman can conceive of an old man
• And Abraham married, etc. ISIDORE. Allegorically. When Sara was dead, Abraham married Cetura: not from incontinence, for he was already very old; nor to provide sons, for seed like the stars of heaven had been promised him through Isaac. But as Agar and Ismael figured the fleshly of the Old Testament, so Cetura and her sons figure the heretics who think that they belong to the New Testament. But both are concubines; Sara alone is the wife. Whence: “One is my dove,” etc.
• Married another wife, etc. JEROME. Cetura in Hebrew is “coupled” or “joined.” Whence the Hebrews suspect that, the name being changed, she is the same as Agar, who, when Sara was dead, passed from concubine to wife. And Abraham’s age seems to be excused, lest the old man be charged with having played the wanton in a new marriage. And the sons of Abraham born of Cetura, according to the historians of the Hebrews, took possession of Troglodytis and Arabia as far as the border of the Red Sea. And it is said that Afer, one of Abraham’s descendants, led an army against Libya and settled there as victor, from whom his descendants called it Africa.
*Allegorically:* After the taking up of the Church, many souls deceived by heretical wickedness cleaved to Christ, who begot not catholics but schismatics, who divided the unity of the Church; whom the sons of Cetura, who are counted below, signify.
*Morally:* Cetura is interpreted thymiama, that is, “incense” or “a good odour.” Abraham takes her in marriage, who could say: “We are the good odour of Christ.” Sin is a stinking thing. If there is anyone in whom there is not the odour of sin but of justice, of sweetness and of mercy, and who says, “Let my prayer be directed as incense in thy sight,” etc., he has married Cetura. For such marriages and such offspring the old are fitter; for the more one is wearied in the flesh, the stronger he is in spirit and the fitter for the embraces of wisdom.
25.3:
**“Jecsan also begot Saba and Dadan. The children of Dadan were Assurim,”** — merchants
**“and Latusim,”** — workers in bronze or metals
**“and Loomin.”**
• phylarchs, that is, princes of tribes
• The children of Dadan, etc. JEROME. They think Assurim is rendered “merchants,” Latusim “workers in the metals of bronze and iron,” Loomin “phylarchs,” that is, princes of many tribes and peoples. Others think the Syrians are named from this Assurim, and that most of Abraham’s sons by Cetura took possession of the regions of India.
25.4:
**“But of Madian was born Epha, and Opher,”** — elsewhere: “Epher”
**“and Henoch, and Abida, and Eldaa: all these were the children of Cetura.”** — these peoples, figuring the heretics, were not gathered into the lot of Isaac, because heretics and schismatics shall not possess the kingdom of God
25.5: **“And Abraham gave all his possessions to Isaac.”** — And Abraham gave, etc. ISIDORE. Because gifts are given to the sons of the concubines, that is, of the fleshly, but heretics or Jews do not come to the promised kingdom, since they follow fleshly gains; Isaac alone is heir, because not the children of the flesh are accounted for the seed, but those of the promise.
25.6:
**“And to the children”** — to Jews and heretics
**“of the concubines he gave gifts, and separated them from Isaac his son,”** — “A man that is a heretic, after the first and second admonition, avoid”
**“while he yet lived, to the east country.”** — where they oppose him of whom it is said, “The Orient is his name”
25.8:
**“And decaying he died in a good old age, and having lived a long time,”** — “the understanding of a man is grey hairs”
**“and being full of days:”** — of light and the works of the day
**“and was gathered”** — in the hope of immortality
**“to his people.”** — the angels, whose fellow citizen he was
**“And decaying he died”** — JEROME. It is badly added in the Seventy, “Decaying, Abraham died,” because it does not befit Abraham to decay or be lessened. That too which we have put, “in a good old age, old and full,” in the Greek books is put “full of days”; which, though it seems to set out the sense, that he went to rest full of light and of the works of the day, yet makes more for the anagogy if “full” is put simply.
25.9:
**“And … buried him”** — they hid his love in their heart
**“Isaac and Ismael his sons”** — the peoples believing from the circumcision and the foreskin
**“in the double cave, which was situated in the field of Ephron the son of Seor the Hethite, over against Mambre;”** — in action as much as in contemplation, for which the teachers of the Church could not have leisure unless that leisure had been bought from the earthly princes by the promise of eternity and the preaching of the truth
25.10:
**“Which he had bought of the children of Heth: there was he buried,”** — commended to memory
**“he”** — Christ
**“and Sara his wife.”** — the first Church
25.11:
**“And after his death,”** — the passion of Christ
**“God blessed Isaac his son,”** — he multiplied the Christian people
**“who dwelt by the well named Of the living and seeing.”** — he lingered in searching out the depths of the Scriptures
25.12: **“These are the generations of Ismael the son of Abraham, whom Agar the Egyptian, Sara’s servant, bore unto him:”** — These are the generations, etc. These peoples are counted before the sons of Isaac; since, though they are of Abraham’s seed, they are yet not counted in the seed; because “that is first which is natural, afterwards that which is spiritual.” Whence after the counting of the fleshly is set the genealogy of Isaac, to whom the promise was made and the succession of the elect was to be spread.
25.13:
**“And these are the names of his children according to their calling and generations. The firstborn of Ismael was Nabajoth,”** — from whom the region from the Red Sea to the Euphrates is called Nabathea
**“then Cedar, and Adbeel, and Mabsam.”** — And these are the names of his children, etc. JEROME. Twelve sons are born to Ismael. The firstborn is Nabajoth, from whom the whole region from the Euphrates to the Red Sea is called Nabathea, which is part of Arabia. For their families, towns, villages and tribes are known by the names of these. From one of these, Cedar, in the desert; and Duma, another region; and Thema to the south; and Cedma, otherwise Chethma, is named toward the eastern quarter. What we read at the end of the chapter according to the Seventy, “He dwelt over against the face of all his brethren,” is truer as we have put it, “He died in the presence of all his brethren,” that is, he died in the hands of his sons, his children still surviving. For sons are called brethren. Whence Jacob: “Lay it here before my brethren and thy brethren, and let them judge between us.” For it is not to be believed that Jacob had any brethren with him besides his own children.
25.16: **“twelve princes”** — The number twelve, as it is hallowed in the apostles and in apostolic men, so it is accursed in the reprobate, spread through the four parts of the world against the faith of the Trinity and the gospel.
25.18:
**“And he dwelt from Hevila”** — India or Ethiopia
