**“as far as Sur, which looketh towards Egypt, to them that go towards the Assyrians. He died in the presence of all his brethren.”** — his sons still living
**“from Hevila as far as Sur”** — The region which the Phison goes round was so called from Hevila, Noe’s grandson, and is a wilderness over against the face of Egypt. Sur too is a wilderness between Cades and Barad, stretching the desert as far as the Red Sea and the borders of Egypt.
25.19: **“These also are the generations of Isaac the son of Abraham: Abraham begot Isaac:”** — this is repeated so that what follows may be joined on more fittingly
25.20:
**“Who when he was forty years old, took to wife Rebecca the daughter of Bathuel the Syrian of Mesopotamia, sister to Laban.”**
• “Father, I pray for them whom thou hast given me”
• though the succession had been promised in Isaac, yet God’s foreordaining was to be fulfilled by prayers
• Of Mesopotamia, etc. A barren region, so called in Greek because it is in the middle between two rivers, the Tigris and the Euphrates. For mesos is “middle,” potamos “river”; hence hippopotamus, that is, “river horse.”
25.21:
**“And Isaac besought the Lord for his wife, because she was barren;”** — because the Church for a long time bore no sons
**“and he heard him, and made Rebecca to conceive.”** — And Isaac besought, etc. JEROME. For “moving” or “clashing” the Seventy put “they were playing” or “kicking”; Aquila, “the sons were fighting in her womb”; Symmachus, “they were carried on the surface, like a ship.”
*Gregory:* What the saints bring about by praying was so predestined that it should be obtained by prayers. For the very predestination of the heavenly kingdom too is so ordered that the elect come to it by labour, so that by asking they may deserve to receive what God had arranged before the ages to give them. For the Lord said to Abraham, “In Isaac shall thy seed be called,” to whom he had also said, “I have made thee a father of many nations”; and again, “I will bless thee, and I will multiply thy seed as the stars of heaven,” etc. Whence it is clear that God had predestined to multiply Abraham’s seed through Isaac; and yet it is written, “Isaac besought the Lord for his wife,” etc. But if the multiplying of Abraham’s race through Isaac was predestined, why did he take a barren wife? Because predestination is fulfilled by prayers. For he in whom God had predestined to multiply Abraham’s seed obtained by prayer that he should have sons.
25.22:
**“But the children struggled in her womb:”**
• “struggled”: the Seventy, “were playing and kicking”
• because within the walls of the Church the elect and the reprobate think differently
**“and she said: If it were to be so with me,”** — as if: what will they do when born, if they wrestle so unborn?
**“what need was there to conceive? And she went to consult the Lord.”**
• perhaps to the altar which Abraham set up, or to a secret place in which she might pray more quietly
• And she went, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is asked where she went, since there were not yet prophets, or priests of the tabernacle or temple of the Lord. Perhaps to the place where Abraham set up an altar. But how answers were given there Scripture is silent: whether through some priest, whom, if there was one, it is strange not to have been named, and no mention to have been made of priests; perhaps, when they had laid their desires before God in prayer, they slept there so as to be warned in sleep; or Melchisedech was still living, whose excellence was so great that it was doubted whether he was a man or an angel. Or perhaps even at that time there were men of God in whom God could be consulted. Whichever of these, or perhaps something else, it was, Rebecca, according to Scripture, consulted the Lord and was found worthy of his answer.
25.23:
**“And he answering said: Two nations”** — the Edomites and the Jews
**“are in thy womb, and two peoples shall be divided out of thy womb,”** — Israel, or the Christian people
**“and one people shall overcome the other,”** — the Edomites, or the Jewish people
**“and the elder shall serve the younger.”**
• the elder by birth, the Jewish people; the younger, the Christian. Or because not all of the Gentiles believed, nor will all of the Jews come together in the unity of faith
• Two nations, etc. In the historical sense the answer is found fulfilled when, through Israel, that is, Jacob, the younger son overcame the Edomites, that is, the nation which Esau propagated, and made them tributaries through David; which they long were, until the king under whom the Edomites rebelled and shook the yoke from their neck; as Isaac prophesied when he blessed the younger in place of the elder, and said the same to the elder when afterwards he blessed him.
25.24:
**“And when her time was come to be delivered,”** — so that the Church might be spread through the gospel
**“behold twins … in her womb.”** — not one understanding was found under the veil of the letter of the law, but a fleshly and a spiritual
**“were found”** — And when her time was come, etc. JEROME. Where we have put “hairy,” in the Hebrew there is seir; whence Esau, as we read elsewhere, was called Seir, that is, “hairy.”
25.25:
**“He that came forth first”** — following the letter
**“was red,”** — a man of blood
**“and hairy like a skin:”**
• accustomed only to outward things
• in the Hebrew seir; whence Esau is called Seir, that is, “hairy”
**“and his name was called Esau. Immediately the other coming forth, held his brother’s foot in his hand,”** — because he was to supplant his brother’s first place
**“and therefore he was called Jacob.”**
• “supplanter”
• Immediately the other, etc. ISIDORE. This was done as a figure; and it is known even to the unbelieving Jews how the people of the Church overcame the people of the synagogue, and the people of the Jews, greater in time, served the lesser people of the Christians. Morally: this can also be said in individuals. There are two nations, namely of vices and of virtues: this the lesser, that the greater, for there are more evil men than good, and more vices than virtues. But yet people overcomes people, and the elder shall serve the younger, namely the flesh the spirit, and the vices the virtues. Esau comes first, red and hairy all over like a skin. Then comes out Jacob, holding his brother’s foot. For the former people was stained with the blood of the prophets and of Christ, surrounded with the filth of sin and wickedness; whose foot the younger held, because the younger overcame the greater people.
25.27:
**“And when they were grown up, Esau became a skillful hunter,”** — practising outward action
**“and a husbandman,”** — not knowing the civil, that is, the ecclesiastical, laws
**“but Jacob a plain man”**
• without spot or wrinkle
• who without guile used guile; another edition, “without guile”
**“dwelt in tents.”**
• he applied himself to spiritual things
• Esau became a skillful hunter, etc. GREGORY. He signifies the life of those who, poured out in outward pleasures, follow the flesh. He is called a husbandman too, because lovers of the world cultivate outward things the more as they leave their inward things uncultivated.
• A plain man, etc. What is said in Greek aplastos the Latins have rendered “plain”; but properly aplastos is “not feigned.” Whence some have rendered “without guile,” saying: “Jacob was without guile, dwelling in a house.” So that it is a great question how he who was without guile received the blessing by guile. But Scripture set this first in order to figure something great; for from this we are most of all compelled to understand spiritual things there, because he who used guile was without guile.
**“plain”** — GREGORY. Because those who flee being scattered by outward cares stay simple in thought and in the dwelling of the conscience. For he dwells in tents who confines himself within the secrets of the mind, and does not yet gape after many things outside, nor withdraw from himself, estranged in thought.
25.28:
**“Isaac”** — God the Father
**“loved Esau,”** — the Jewish people
**“because he ate of his hunting:”** — by the present justice of fleshly observances, which it showed to the one God
**“and Rebecca”** — grace
**“loved”** — from foreknowledge
**“Jacob.”** — the younger people
25.29:
**“And Jacob boiled pottage:”** — simplicity does not seek the fleshpots
**“to whom Esau, coming faint out of the field,”** — And Jacob boiled, etc. JEROME. “Red” or “tawny” is called edom in Hebrew; and because Esau sold his birthright for red food, he took the name of “tawny,” that is, Edom.
25.30:
**“Said:”** — the fool burns with the desire of the gullet for cheap food
**“Give me of this red pottage,”** — the lentil is the food of brute animals, signifying the animal understanding of the law, enticed by which the Jewish people preferred to lack the first place rather than give it up; which even now it strives to obtain from the younger people; given over to temporal things, it hopes for nothing good after death.
**“for I am exceeding faint. For which reason his name was called Edom.”** — “red” or “ruddy,” from whom the Edomites
25.31: **“And Jacob said to him: Sell me thy first birthright.”** — the firstborn are those that open the womb, and the birthright is owed especially to firstborn sons
25.33:
**“Jacob said: Swear therefore to me. Esau swore to him, and sold his first birthright.”**
• the Jew still persists in folly; for temporal things he does not care for eternal ones
• And Jacob said to him, etc. ISIDORE. That Esau sold his birthright to his younger brother for food, and afterwards was deprived of the father’s blessing promised him, signifies the Jewish people, which in Exodus is called the firstborn son of God, and for the gains of the world not only lost the honour of its first place but was not found worthy to win the reward of the heavenly kingdom prepared for it. Whence it is said in reproach: “The kingdom of God shall be taken from you, and shall be given to a nation yielding the fruits thereof.” And the birthright was the priestly garment, clothed in which the elder-born, with the father’s blessing, offered victims to God as high priests. Through the desire of something earthly the Jews went without this gift, together with the glory of the kingdom to come.
• Esau swore to him, etc. GREGORY. It is to be known that the vice of gluttony tempts us in five ways. Sometimes it forestalls the time of need. Sometimes it does not forestall the time, but seeks daintier foods. Sometimes it desires that what is to be taken be prepared more carefully. Sometimes it suits the kind of food and the time, but goes beyond measure in the quantity taken. And sometimes what it desires is base, and yet it sins worse by the very heat of the desire. Jonathan earned the sentence of death because in tasting the honey he forestalled the appointed time of eating. The people led out of Egypt fell in the desert because, despising the manna, they asked for flesh, which they thought daintier. The first fault of the sons of Heli is that, at their wish, the priest’s servant would not receive the meat of the sacrifice boiled, as was the custom, but sought it raw, to serve it up more carefully. And when it is said, “This was the iniquity of Sodom, pride, fulness of bread and abundance,” it is shown that it perished because, with the vice of pride, it went beyond the measure of refreshment. Hence Esau lost his birthright, because he desired with great heat a contemptible food, that is, lentils; and the vice is not in the food but in the appetite. Whence we often take daintier foods without fault, and taste baser ones with the guilt of concupiscence. For Esau lost the first place for lentils; Elias in the desert kept his strength by eating flesh. Hence the devil, because he understands that not food but concupiscence is the cause of damnation, subdued the first man to himself not by flesh but by an apple, and tempted the second by bread. Hence it is that the fault of Adam is often committed even when cheap things are taken. For Adam was not the only one to receive a prohibition to abstain from the apple. For when God points out foods contrary to our health, he forbids them to us as by a sentence; and when, desiring harmful things, we touch them, we taste what is forbidden. But those things are to be taken which the need of nature asks, and not those which the lust of eating suggests.

26.1:
**“And when a famine came in the land,”** — Judea refusing the word of the gospel, the bread of the word of God, as before the prophetic oracles
**“after that barrenness which had happened in the days of Abraham, Isaac went to Abimelech”** — Christ to the Gentiles, who through natural reason believed in the true Maker, whom Abimelech signifies, who is interpreted “my father the king”
**“king of the Palestines to Gerara.”** — which is interpreted “wall” or “enclosure,” so that he might break down the wall of enmities
**“And when a famine came”** — And when a famine came, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is asked when this was done, that Isaac went to Gerara: whether after Esau sold his birthright, for these things are told in a row; or whether, as is often done, the narrator went back to them by summing-up, when, having gone on about his sons, he had come to the place where the lentils are recalled. For the Abimelech is found who had also desired Sara; for his groomsman and the captain of his army, who were recalled there, are recalled here too. But it raises the question whether they could have been alive. For when he became Abraham’s friend, Isaac was not yet born, but promised. Let us suppose that that was done before Isaac was born; then Isaac received his sons when he was sixty years old. And they were young men when Esau sold his birthright; let us suppose them to have been about twenty, and Isaac’s years up to that deed of his sons come to about eighty. Let us take Abimelech too to have been a young man when he desired his mother and became Abraham’s friend; so he could have been about a hundred, if Isaac went to Gerara after that deed of his sons. So from this no necessity compels us to think that Isaac’s journey is told by summing-up. But because it is written there that he was there long, dug wells, contended over them, and grew rich in wealth, it is no wonder if it is said by summing-up, having been passed over so that the account of the sons might first come down to the lentils. And so what is written of Isaac, “God blessed him, and the man was exalted,” etc., is said according to earthly happiness, as what follows teaches. So although these things signify something spiritual, yet as to the way in which they happened, “God blessed him” is put first, so that we may understand that temporal things can neither be given nor should prosper except from the one God.
26.2: **“And the Lord appeared to him and said: Go not down into Egypt,”** — “Woe to them that go down to Egypt for help”
26.3:
**“And sojourn in it,”** — as if: be a stranger in this place, which thou shalt possess as lord in thy successors
**“and I will be with thee, and will bless thee: for to thee and to thy seed I will give all these countries,”** — which was fulfilled spiritually in the Gentile world after the ascension of Christ
26.4:
**“And I will multiply thy seed like the stars of heaven: and I will give to thy posterity all these countries: and in thy seed shall … be blessed”** — in the one, who is Christ
**“all the nations of the earth”** — some from all nations
26.6: **“So Isaac abode in Gerara.”** — still Christ breaks down the wall of enmities through the preachers
26.7:
**“And when he was asked by the men of that place, concerning his wife,”** — whence “heirs indeed of God, and joint heirs with Christ”
**“he answered: She is my sister; for he was afraid to confess”** — so many disciples in the first Church were secret, for fear of the Jews
**“that she was his wife, thinking lest perhaps they would kill him because of her beauty.”** — lest they should blot out the Christian name because of their unbelief
26.8:
**“And when very many days were passed, and he abode there, Abimelech king of the Palestines looking out through a window, saw him playing with Rebecca his wife.”**
• And when very many days were passed, etc. ISIDORE. From the time of Christ to the times of Constantine the faith was preached not in the assembly of the peoples but as it were in hiding places. Christians gathered in secret. At length the princes of the world, seeing through the miracles of Christ his majesty tempered to human weakness, so that they could be joined and be two in one flesh, allowed the sacrament of Christ and the Church to be preached openly, and grieved that it had long been hidden.
• Saw him playing, etc. AUGUSTINE. What it means in the sacrament of Christ and the Church that so great a patriarch played with his wife, so that the marriage was known, let each one surely see, lest he sin in any way in the Church by his telling, if he looks into the secret of her husband in the Scriptures and finds that he hid for a little while, in the form of a servant, the majesty by which he is equal to the Father, so that human weakness could take him in, and in that way fitted himself to his spouse. For what is absurd, nay, what is unfitting to the foretelling of things to come, if a prophet played something fleshly so that the affection of his wife might hold him, when the Word of God was made flesh, to dwell among us?
26.9: **“And calling for him, he said: It is evident she is thy wife: why didst thou feign her to be thy sister?”** — this reproach is, as it were, a leave given to preach
26.10:
**“And Abimelech said:”** — so dangerous a burden
**“Why hast thou deceived us?”** — that is, “deceived”; whence “impostors”
**“Some man of the people might have lain with thy wife,”** — to corrupt the simplicity of the faith by some violence
**“and thou hadst brought upon us a great sin. And he commanded all the people, saying:”** — when peace had been given to the Church, it was decreed by the princes that no one should violate the soundness of the faith
26.12:
**“And … sowed”**
• or “sowed” (another form)
• he preached publicly through his own
**“Isaac”** — Christ
**“in that land,”** — in the Gentile world
**“and he found that same year”** — in the time of the peace obtained
**“a hundredfold:”** — a great gain of the heavenly country
**“and the Lord blessed him.”** — And Isaac sowed in that land, etc. JEROME. Though Isaac sowed in a foreign land, I do not think he had such a yield of barley. Whence I judge better what is had in the Hebrew, and what Aquila translated: “He found in that year a hundredfold reckoned.” And Scripture, keeping silent about the kind of crop that was multiplied a hundredfold, seems to have shown in it the multiplying of all the virtues.
26.13:
**“And the man was enriched,”** — the number of believers was multiplied
**“and he went on prospering and increasing, till he became exceeding great:”**
• the multiplying of barley does not make one great
• “their sound hath gone forth into all the earth”
26.14:
**“And he had possessions of sheep and of herds, and a very great family.”** — many serving him as his household
**“Wherefore the Palestines envying him,”**
• foreign sons
• Wherefore … envying him, etc. ISIDORE. Isaac is Christ, who first wishes to dig the wells which his father’s servants had dug. For Moses dug the well of the law; David, Solomon and the prophets wrote the books of the Old Testament, which the earthly and filthy understanding of the Jews had filled up. When he wished to cleanse their mouth, so as to show that whatever the law and the prophets said was said of him, the Palestines quarrelled, that is, the Jews, strangers to the kingdom of God; and he departed from them. For he cannot be with those who will have not water in the wells but earth. And he says to them: “Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate.” So Isaac, or rather his servants, dug a new well, namely the apostles and evangelists, who, digging the well of the New Testament, found water springing up into life everlasting. For these too they contend who savour earthly things, and they do not allow new wells to be founded nor old ones to be cleansed. So it is said to them: “Seeing you judge yourselves unworthy of the grace of God, from henceforth we will go to the Gentiles.”
26.15:
**“all the wells,”** — all the Scriptures which Moses, David, Solomon and others had searched
**“that the servants of his father Abraham had digged,”** — of God, whom Abraham signified
**“Stopped up at that time …, filling them up with earth:”**
• taking away the spiritual understanding, urging the fleshly
• The wells, etc. … stopped up, etc. GREGORY. Morally. Often when we give ourselves to the divine words, we bear the more heavily the snares of the demons, who sprinkle the dust of earthly thoughts on our mind, so as to darken the eyes of our attention from the light of the inner vision. For we dig wells when we penetrate the depths of Scripture, which the foreigners secretly fill up, because they thrust in earthly thoughts and take away the water of divine knowledge. Whence: “Depart from me, ye malignant, and I will search the commandments of my God.”
26.16: **“Insomuch that Abimelech himself”** — this was done when charity at times grew cold
26.17:
**“So he departed”** — “And when they shall persecute you in this city, flee into another”
**“and came to the torrent of Gerara,”** — through the course of human mortality
**“to dwell there:”** — So he departed, etc. JEROME. “And Isaac went away from there and came into the valley of Gerara and dwelt there”: for “valley” they have “torrent” in the Hebrew. For Isaac, after he had become great, could never dwell in a valley, but in a torrent, of which it is written, “He shall drink of the torrent in the way”; of which Elias drank in the time of famine; but because he was not perfect like Christ, the torrent dried up for him. But Christ too was betrayed at a torrent, hallowing our regeneration and the sacrament of baptism.
26.18:
**“And he digged again other wells,”** — the New Testament, which had been prefigured in the patriarchs and prophets
**“which the servants of his father Abraham had digged, and which, after his death,”** — which testament, after the passion of Christ, the foreigners, that is, the Jews, hid
**“the Palestines had of old stopped up: and he called them by the same names by which his father before had called them.”**
• when the New Testament is shown in the Old, and the witness of Moses and the prophets is confirmed, and the names of the former authors are not changed
• He digged other wells, etc. Morally. ISIDORE. Isaac digs wells among a foreign nation; in which we are warned that in this sojourning we should penetrate the depths of our thoughts, and that, until the water of true understanding comes back, the hand of searching should not grow slack in emptying out the earthy things of the heart. The foreigners, lying in wait, fill up the wells; because unclean spirits, when they see us digging zealously, thrust the troubles of temptations into our thoughts.
**“against the herdsmen”** — JEROME. Aquila and Symmachus translated “adversary” and “opponent.” But in the Hebrew there is Satana. Whence it is plain that Satan is interpreted “opponent.”
26.19:
**“And they digged”** — the apostles
**“in the torrent,”**
• others “in the valley”; but in a valley a well of living water is not found
• the abundance of the Scriptures
**“and found … water.”** — that is, the gospel teaching
**“living”** — that is, springing up into life everlasting
26.20: **“But there also … strove”** — because the Jews resist the gospel teaching, and neither allow new wells to be founded nor wish old ones to be cleansed
26.21: **“And they digged also another;”** — a second
26.22:
**“Going forward”** — because, after the faith of the Trinity began to be preached through the world, their adversaries were overcome by the patience of the saints
**“from thence, he digged another”** — a third
**“well, for which they contended not: therefore he called the name thereof, Latitude,”** — because Isaac, that is, Christ, was spread abroad
**“saying: Now hath the Lord given us room, and made us to increase upon the earth.”**
• Latitude: in the Hebrew Rehoboth. Whence what was said above is proved: “He built Ninive and Rehoboth,” that is, its streets.
• Now hath … given us room, etc. Isaac was spread abroad and filled the whole earth with the knowledge of the Trinity, and set the breadth of the Church in the whole world; yet first known in Judea and named in Israel, afterwards “their sound went forth into all the earth,” that is, of the apostles, who dug wells through the whole world and showed water to all, baptizing all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. He called the wells of Abraham which he opened as his father did. For Moses and the prophets are called among us by their own names, nor are the names of these wells changed.
26.26:
**“To which place when Abimelech, and Ochozath his friend, and Phicol chief captain of his soldiers came from Gerara,”**
• in the Hebrew tongue, “the company of his friends”
• To which place, etc. JEROME. Abimelech does not always have peace with Isaac. Sometimes he is at odds, sometimes he seeks peace. And he signifies the studious and wise of the world, who through the learning of philosophy have grasped much of the truth. He is neither always in dissension with Isaac (who signifies the word of God) nor always in peace. For philosophy is neither contrary to the divine law in everything nor in harmony with it in everything. For many of the philosophers write that there is one God who created all things. And some have even added that he made and rules all things through his Word, and that it is the Word of God by which all things are governed; in which they agree with the Gospel too. And moral and natural philosophy hold almost all that is ours; but they differ when they say that matter is coeternal with God, and deny that God cares for mortal things, saying that his providence is confined above the space of the lunar sphere; and that he lays out the lives of those born by the courses of the stars; and when they say that the world is perpetual and to be closed by no end. And there are many other things in which the philosophers differ or agree with us.
*Jerome:* For Ochozath the groomsman, in the Hebrew there is “the company of his friends,” so that it signifies as much a man as the crowd of friends who had come with the king, among whom was Phicol the captain of his army.
**“Abimelech, and Ochozath, and Phicol”** — ISIDORE. Two came with Abimelech: Ochozath his son-in-law, and Phicol the captain of the army. Ochozath is interpreted “holding,” Phicol “the mouth of all,” Abimelech “my father the king.” These three hold the image of the whole of philosophy, which is divided into three parts: logic, physics, ethics, that is, the rational, the natural, the moral. The rational is that which confesses God as Father of all, as Abimelech is. The natural is that which is fixed and holds all things, as if resting on the powers of nature itself, which Ochozath, who is called “holding,” professes. The moral is that which is in the mouth of all, belongs to all, and, because of the likeness of common precepts, is turned over in the mouths of all; which Phicol signifies, who is interpreted “the mouth of all.” So all these, instructed in these learnings, come to the law of God, saying: “We saw that the Lord is with thee,” etc. They ask for a blessing, not a repayment. Whence follows: “So he made them a feast”; for he who ministers the word is a debtor to the wise and to the unwise.
26.32: **“And behold the same day the servants of Isaac came, telling him of a well which they had digged, and saying: We have found water.”** — And behold the same day, etc. JEROME. I do not know how in the Seventy it is had: “And the servants of Isaac came, telling him of the well which they had dug, and they said to him: We have not found water; and he called its name Oath.” For what etymology is there in its being called Oath because they did not find water? And on the contrary in the Hebrew, with which rendering Aquila and Symmachus agree, it signifies that they found water, and that therefore the well itself was called “Fullness,” and the city Bersabee, that is, “the well of fullness.” For though above we asserted that Bersabee was named from the word of swearing, or from the number seven of the sheep, which is called sabee, yet now, from the finding of water, Isaac, alluding to the name of the city, bent the letter a little, and for the hissing shin of the Hebrews, with which sabee begins, put the Greek sigma, that is, the Hebrew samech. And according to the allegory too, after so many wells, at the end of the virtues, it does not fit that Isaac should not find water.

27.1:
**“Now … was old,”** — it shows the end of the world
**“Isaac”** — God the Father
**“and his eyes were dim, and he could not see:”** — faith has perished from the world, and the light of religion
**“and he called Esau,”** — to receive the law
**“his elder son,”** — the former people
**“Now Isaac was old”** — HIPPOLYTUS THE MARTYR. Isaac bears the image of God the Father; Rebecca, of the Holy Spirit; Esau, of the former people and of the devil; Jacob, of the Church and of Christ. Isaac’s old age signifies the end of the world; his dim eyes, that faith has perished from the world and the light of religion has been neglected. That the elder son is called is the Jews’ receiving of the law. That the father loved his food and his catch is men saved from error, whom every just man hunts by teaching. The word of God is the blessing of the promise and the hope of the kingdom to come, in which they are to reign with Christ and keep the true sabbath. Rebecca, full of the Holy Spirit, knowing what she had heard before she bore, that the elder should serve the younger, bears the form of the Holy Spirit, who was meditating beforehand in Jacob what she knew was to be in Christ. She speaks to the younger son: “Go to the flock and bring me two kids of the best,” prefiguring the Saviour’s coming in the flesh, in which he would free those who were held liable for sins; for kids everywhere signify sinners. Two are commanded to be brought, so that the taking up of two peoples may be signified: tender, namely, and good, docile, that is, and innocent souls. The robe of Esau is faith, that is, the Scriptures of the Hebrews, which were given first to them, with which the people of the Gentiles was afterwards clothed. The skins put round his arms are the sins of both peoples, which Christ, in the stretching out of his hands, fixed with himself to the cross. For he bore in his body not his own sins but those of others.
**“and he called Esau”** — ISIDORE. Esau was a hunter and a husbandman; but Jacob, a plain man, dwelt in tents. Esau signifies the Hebrew people, Jacob the Gentile people; but Isaac, God, who made both peoples his sons, the one through the law, the other through faith. Esau was a husbandman, because the Jew served God for earthly things; to whom it was not said that he should be poor in spirit, meek, peaceable, merciful, suffering persecution, so as to have a plentiful reward in heaven; but, “If you keep my commandments, I will give you rain in due seasons,” and the rest that belongs to the delights of the flesh. He was also a hunter, because by shedding the blood of rams and calves and goats they appeased God. Jacob, a plain man, dwelt in tents, because the elect of the Gentiles strove to please God by faith and will. By the tents we understand the various Churches through the world, or the various orders.
27.3:
**“Take thy arms, thy quiver, and bow, and go abroad: and when thou hast taken some thing by hunting,”**
• men to be set free from error, as the just hunter does by teaching
• Take thy arms, etc. Isaac loved Esau because he ate of his hunting; Rebecca loved Jacob. Isaac figures God, but Rebecca the foreknowledge of God; because God loved the people of the Jews, since he was constantly appeased by their offerings; but, foreknowing that the people of the Gentiles would be much better, he loved it more through the grace of his foreknowledge. While Esau lingered in the hunt, to set food from wild animals before his father and be blessed, the mother brought Jacob to the father to receive the blessing; because the Jews still linger in the legal observances and come late to the faith of Christ, the mother, grace, brought the Gentiles, eagerly receiving the faith, to receive the blessing owed to the Jews. And how they earned the gift of the blessing, the works of Jacob bear witness, which he did to receive the blessing.
27.5:
**“And when Rebecca had heard this,”**
• foreknowledge
• patience
• the Holy Spirit
27.6:
**“She said to her son Jacob:”** — because she had heard, before she bore, “and the elder shall serve the younger”
**“I heard thy father talking with Esau thy brother, and saying to him:”** — She said to her son, etc. By the two kids we can take the confession of sins of the Gentile people, and penance. The kids are of the best, because the confession of sins and penance are very acceptable to God. Whence: “There shall be joy in heaven upon one sinner that doth penance,” etc. By the one sinner he understands the people of the Gentiles; by the ninety-nine just, the Jews, who seemed to themselves just in keeping the law. Whence: “You are they who justify yourselves before men,” etc. They are put in an imperfect number, because the law brought nothing to perfection.
27.15:
**“garments of Esau”** — JEROME. In this place too the Hebrews hand down that the firstborn performed the office of priests and had a priestly garment, clothed in which they offered victims, before Aaron was chosen for the priesthood.
**“She dressed meats”** — ISIDORE. By the savoury meats that are prepared from the kids for Isaac we understand the works of penance, of which it is said: “Bring forth fruits worthy of penance.” The very good garments which Esau, that is, the Jews, had left at home are the best precepts of the law (for example), “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God,” etc., and others without which no one can be just. These the Jews had left at home, that is, in the Old Testament, because they would not keep them. Adorned with these, the Gentile went to God the Father with the food of good works; and with the food he offered loaves; by loaves we often understand the word of God. And he goes well to God with the food of good works who does not cease to urge whomever he can to good works. The mother covered the bare parts of Jacob’s hands and neck with the kids’ skins. For when the skin is drawn off the kid, the flesh remains, from which savoury food is made; and when vices are drawn off the sinner, the good of nature appears with reason, and if these are cooked by faith, savoury foods are prepared for God from the good of nature. By the neck, in which pride appears, the lifting up of the mind is signified; by the hands, works. He puts kids’ skins round his neck who, to lay aside pride and keep the guard of humility, often brings his past sins before the eyes of his mind.
27.20: **“And Isaac said to his son: How couldst thou find it so quickly, my son? He answered: It was the will of God, that what I sought came quickly in my way.”** — How couldst thou find it so quickly, etc. HIPPOLYTUS. Isaac asks Jacob why he has come so quickly, wondering, namely, at the swift faith of believers. Savoury meats are offered, because the salvation of sinners is a sacrifice pleasing to God. That after the eating the blessing follows, and he enjoys its smell, plainly proclaims the power of the resurrection and the kingdom. “Behold the smell of my son is as the smell of a plentiful field”: this is the blessing. With the smell of the name of Christ the world, as a field, is filled. The blessing is “of the dew of heaven,” that is, the rain of the divine word; “and of the fatness of the earth,” the gathering of the peoples; “abundance of corn and wine”: this is the multitude which he gathers from the sacrament of his body and blood. “Let peoples serve him,” that is, the converted Gentiles. “Let tribes worship him”: the peoples believing through circumcision. “He is lord of his brethren,” that is, of the Jews. “His mother’s children worship him,” because according to the flesh he was born of her. “Cursed be he that curseth him, and he that blesseth him shall be blessed.” Christ is blessed from the mouth of a people that does not know the Father, that is, it is said truly; but by the Jews another is thought to be blessed, who is awaited by those who err.
27.25: **“Then he said: Bring me the meats of thy hunting, my son, that my soul may bless thee. And when they were brought, and he had eaten, he offered him wine also, which after he had drunk,”** — And when they were brought, etc. After Isaac took food, Jacob offered him wine. If by food the works of the active life are signified, by wine, which carries minds away, is understood the contemplative life, which makes the minds of the elect strangers to the love of the world. After food and drink Jacob is blessed, because those receive the heavenly blessing from God who strive to please him by good works to the end.
27.27:
**“He came near, and kissed him. And immediately as he smelled the fragrant smell of his garments, blessing him, he said: Behold the smell of my son”** — the world is filled with the smell of the name of Christ
**“is as the smell of a plentiful field,”** — the world is filled with the virtues of the saints
**“blessing him, he said”** — GREGORY. One is sent to hunt so as to be blessed; the other, by his mother’s putting him in his place, is blessed by his father. Which of the little ones is not fed by the deed of the just, according to the history of the sacred reading? But it can be seen that Jacob did not steal the blessing of the firstborn by fraud, but received what was owed him, which he had bought from his brother. But allegorically, Isaac desires to feed on the elder son’s hunting, because almighty God willed to be fed by the good working of the Jews; but while he delayed, Rebecca put the younger in his place, because while the Jewish people seeks good works outside, mother grace brought in the Gentile, so that he might offer to the almighty Father the food of good work and receive the elder’s blessing. She gave food from domestic animals, because the Gentile people, not seeking to please by outward sacrifices, says: “In me, O God, are vows to thee, which I will pay, praises to thee.” Jacob covered his hands, arms and neck with kids’ skins, because a kid is wont to be offered for sin; and the Gentile people, while it does not blush to confess itself a sinner, slew in itself the sins of the flesh. He is clothed with the garments of the elder, because he who is clothed in good working with the precepts of holy Scripture (which were given to the elder people) is the younger who uses in the house what the elder, going outside, left within.
*Gregory:* Allegorically. Isaac, with dim eyes, blessed his son Jacob without knowing him; he foresaw the things that were to come, and did not know him who stood present. For it is clear that the Jews who fully learned the law knew of the coming of Christ. Whence Herod asks of the chief priests where Christ should be born, to whom they at once answered: “In Bethlehem.” So they knew him before, whom, when they despised him at the time of the passion, they did not know. Their earlier knowledge and later ignorance are signified by Isaac’s dimness, who, while he blessed Jacob, foresaw what would befall him in the future, but did not know that he stood present. So the people of the Jews received the mysteries of prophecy, but kept its eyes blind in contemplation, because it did not see him present of whom it foresaw much in the future. For it could not discern, set before it, him the power of whose coming it had announced long before.
*Gregory:* Isaac does not know the son whom he blessed, according to that: “A people which I knew not hath served me,” etc. He did not see him present, and foresaw what was to come to him; because almighty God, when through the prophets he foretold that grace was to be bestowed on the Gentile world, did not see it present through grace, since he then left it in error; and yet, because he was to gather it by the grace of the blessing, he foresaw it. Whence: “Behold the smell of my son is as the smell of a plentiful field, which the Lord hath blessed.” For the field is the world; and because the people of the elect is fragrant with virtues in the whole world, the smell of the son is the smell of a plentiful field. For the flower of the grape smells one way, because great is the strength and repute of the preachers who make drunk the minds of their hearers. The flower of the olive another way, because sweet is the work of mercy, which cherishes and shines. The flower of the rose another way, because wonderful is the fragrance which glows red and smells sweet from the blood of the martyrs. The flower of the lily another way, because the life of the flesh is white from the incorruption of virginity. The flower of the violet another way, because great is the virtue of the humble, who, holding the last places, do not raise themselves from the earth on high through humility, and keep in their mind the purple of the heavenly kingdom. The ear of grain smells another way when it is brought to ripeness, because the perfection of good works is prepared for the filling of those who hunger after justice. And because the Gentile people, scattered through the world in the elect, fills with the smell of good repute by its virtues all who understand, it is rightly said: “The smell of my son is as the smell of a plentiful field, which,” etc. But because it does not have its virtues from itself, there is rightly added: “which the Lord hath blessed.” And because through some it rises to contemplation, through some it grows fat in the works of the active life, there follows: “God give thee of the dew of heaven,” etc. Dew falls from above and finely; and as often as we receive of the dew of heaven, so often, through the pouring in of inner contemplation, we see something finely of the things above. But when we do good works through the body, we are enriched with the fatness of the earth.
27.28:
**“God give thee the dew of heaven,”**
• the rain of the divine word
• by contemplation
**“and of the fatness of the earth, abundance”** — by good works
**“of corn”** — of charity
**“and wine.”** — of fervour in the new way of life
**“and oil”**
• of mercy
• Abundance of corn, etc. ISIDORE. This is the multitude which he gathers from the sacrament of his body and blood.
27.29:
**“And let peoples serve thee,”** — the converted Gentiles
**“and tribes worship thee:”** — the Jews
**“be thou lord of thy brethren,”** — of the Jews, or of the heretics, of whom it is said: “The sons of my mother have fought against me”
**“and let … bow down”** — by worshipping
**“thy mother’s children … before thee.”** — of the Jewish people
**“Cursed be he that curseth thee:”** — deprived of the eternal inheritance
**“and let him that blesseth thee”** — he who shall say with heart and mouth: “Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord”
**“be filled with blessings.”** — present and to come
27.30: **“Isaac had scarce ended his words, when Jacob being now gone out abroad, Esau came,”** — Esau came, etc. Esau returns late to his father, because the former people will be converted at the end. Whence: “They shall return at evening, and shall suffer hunger like dogs.” And elsewhere: “They opened their mouths, as one that devoureth in secret.”
27.32: **“And Isaac said to him: Why! who art thou?”** — for when the New Testament has been made plain and confirmed, the worshipper of the old shadow is now not known
27.33:
**“Isaac was struck with fear, and astonished exceedingly: and wondering beyond what can be believed, said Who is he then that even now brought me venison that he had taken,”** — how great, how prudent, he who in none of his labour gloried in merits
**“and I ate”** — I received gladly all the good things which he brought me
**“of all before thou camest? and I have blessed”** — the sacrament revealed to him, he confirms the blessing
**“him,”** — who blessed me
**“and he shall be blessed.”**
• unmovably
• And I have blessed him, etc. ALCUIN. If the will of a just man is good, why is it that Isaac blessed not Esau, whom he wished, but Jacob, whom he did not wish? The will of a just man is good as far as his conscience goes; but God alone judges of the future. Isaac, in human manner, thought the elder son was to be blessed; but God, who is the knower of hidden things, showed the younger worthy of the blessing, so as to show that the blessing is not man’s but God’s. Therefore in Numbers it is said to Moses and Aaron the priests: “Put my name upon the children of Israel, and I the Lord will bless them.” It is the priest’s to bless; it is God’s to give the effect. And when Isaac understood through the spirit of prophecy that the blessing was destined for the younger, he says: “I have blessed him, and he shall be blessed.”
**“Isaac was struck with fear”**
• When the elder son asks again for the promised blessing, Isaac was struck with fear, and knew that he had blessed one in place of the other; nor is he angry, the sacrament being known, saying, “And I have blessed him, and he is blessed.” This is the first blessing of Isaac, given to the younger people of the Christians. But neither is the elder son wholly despised, because when the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, then all Israel shall be saved. Of which second blessing this is the prophecy: “In the fat of the earth and in the dew of heaven from above shall thy blessing be.” “In the fat of the earth,” that is, in the fruitfulness of things and the power of the kingdom which was in that people; “and in the dew of heaven,” in the words of God: “To them were committed the words of God,” and the testaments of the law. “Thou shalt live by the sword,” because that people, given to blood, carried out slaughter on Christ and the prophets. “And shalt serve thy brother,” that is, the younger, the Christian people; “and the time shall come when thou shalt shake off and loose his yoke from thy neck,” namely when, converted through the knowledge of faith and the grace of Christ, thou hast laid down the burden of the law; when thou shalt then no longer serve the younger, but through faith shalt be called brother.
• So that a certain carrying away of the mind followed, which is called ecstasy, which is wont to happen in revelations of great things. Whence it is to be understood that Isaac was warned spiritually to confirm the blessing in Jacob, he who should rather have been angry because Jacob deceived his father. In Adam too an ecstasy went before, before he said: “They shall be two in one flesh”; which is a great sacrament in Christ and in the Church.
27.34:
**“Esau having heard his father’s words, roared out with a great cry:”** — the former people still grieves that its first place has been taken from it
**“and being in a great consternation, said:”** — and if not with the eternal, at least with the present blessing
27.35: **“And he said: Thy brother came deceitfully”** — in figure and sacrament
27.36:
**“But he said again: Rightly is his name called Jacob; for he hath supplanted me lo this second time: my first birthright he took away before,”** — our birthright is faith, hope, charity, in which the Jewish people grieves that the Christian people has been preferred to it, and that it surpasses it in the height of temporal things
**“and now this second time he hath stolen away my blessing. And again he said to his father: Hast thou not reserved me also a blessing?”** — Rightly is his name called, etc. JEROME. Jacob is interpreted “supplanter.” So from his having deceived his brother by craft he alluded to the name; who was called Jacob before because at birth he grasped his brother’s foot.
27.39:
**“Isaac being moved, said to him: In the fat of the earth,”** — the abundance of all things
**“and in the dew of heaven from above,”** — the knowledge of the Scriptures, with which that people is still rained upon
27.40:
**“Shall thy blessing be. Thou shalt live by the sword”** — by cruelly persecuting the prophets and apostles
**“and … thy brother:”** — the Christian people
**“shalt serve …: and the time shall come, when thou shalt shake off and loose”** — through the knowledge of faith
**“his yoke”** — of the law
**“from thy neck.”** — And thy brother, etc. Because the Edomites were tributaries of Israel, who is called Jacob.
**“and the time shall come”** — This was fulfilled when the Edomites rebelled so as not to be under Juda.
27.41:
**“… hated”** — meanwhile
**“Esau therefore always”** — the Jewish people
**“Jacob”** — Christ and his own
**“for the blessing wherewith his father had blessed him: and he said in his heart:”** — to God, who sees all things
**“will come”** — or “let … come”
**“The days … of the mourning of my father, and”** — that
**“I will kill my brother Jacob.”**
• Christ, whom it crucified, and his disciples
• Because of the incurable hatred of the Jews, the apostles were commanded through the Spirit of counsel to leave Judea and pass over to the Gentiles.
**“and he said in his heart”** — Since Scripture says that Esau thought over his brother’s death in his heart, how, or by whom, were these things told to Rebecca? But it is given to be understood that all things were revealed to her by God.
27.42: **“These things were told to Rebecca:”** — by God, though said in thought; whence it belongs to a great mystery that she wished the younger to be blessed instead of the elder
27.43: **“Now therefore, my son, hear my voice: arise and flee to Laban my brother to Haran:”** — Syria
27.44: **“And thou shalt dwell with him a few days,”** — for the preaching of the gospel among the Gentiles

28.1: **“And Isaac called Jacob, and blessed him, and charged him, saying: Take not a wife of the stock of Chanaan:”** — And Isaac called, etc. AUGUSTINE. Where the Latin books have, “Go into Mesopotamia, to the house of Bathuel,” and the rest, the Greek have, “Flee into Mesopotamia,” etc.; so that it is understood that Isaac too had understood that Esau was thinking of his brother’s death.
28.5: **“he took his journey and went”** — ISIDORE. Jacob, fleeing his brother’s guile, leaving home, country and parents, goes into a far country to take a wife. Likewise Christ, leaving his parents according to the flesh, that is, the Jews, and his country, that is, Jerusalem, and all the regions of Judea, went off to the Gentiles to take the Church for himself; according to that: “I will call that which was not my people, my people,” etc.
28.6:
**“And Esau seeing that his father had blessed”** — God
**“Jacob”** — Christ
**“and had sent him”** — in the apostles
**“into Mesopotamia of Syria,”** — the Gentiles, before proud and lofty
**“to marry a wife thence;”** — the Church
28.10: **“But Jacob being departed from Bersabee, went on to Haran.”** — But Jacob being departed, etc. GREGORY. Morally. To sleep on the journey is, in the passage of the present life, to rest from the love of temporal things, and, in the course of slipping days, to close from the desire of visible things the eyes of the mind, which the seducer opened for our first parents. For guilt opened the eyes of concupiscence, which innocence kept closed. To see angels coming down and going up is to contemplate with how great a love the citizens of the country above cleave to their Maker, or with how great a compassion of charity they come down to our weaknesses. And it is to be noted that he sees the angels sleeping who lays his head on a stone. For on the stone he who, ceasing from outward things, penetrates inner things is he who with intent mind observes the imitation of the Redeemer; for he lays his head on a stone who cleaves to Christ in mind. For those who are withdrawn from the action of the present life and do not reach toward things above can sleep, but cannot see angels, because they scorn to keep their head on the stone; and they sleep in body, not in zeal, because they have laid their head not on a stone but on the earth. Such men often, the more securely they cease from outward things, the more widely they heap up for themselves the din of unclean thought. Whence: “The enemies have seen her, and have mocked at her sabbaths.” For by the command of the law one ceases from outward work on the sabbath. So the enemies mock when they drag those very times of leisure to unlawful things. So the saints sleep more laboriously when they keep watch; because in forsaking the actions of the world they overcome, and daily fight against themselves, lest the mind grow numb through negligence, lest, subdued by idleness, it grow cold to the desires above, lest it serve itself more than is right, lest, sparing itself under the guise of discretion, it languish from perfection; and when it withdraws itself wholly from the pursuit of this world, intent on the virtues through the zeal of quiet, it sleeps while keeping watch. Whence: “No man can serve two masters.” And elsewhere: “No man, being a soldier to God, entangleth himself with secular businesses.” And: “Be still and see that the Lord is sweet.”
28.11:
**“And when he was come to a certain place, and would rest in it after sunset, he took of the stones that lay there, and putting under his head,”** — the head of Christ is God
**“slept in the same place.”**
• so Christ died on the cross
• He took of the stones, etc. ISIDORE. Jacob’s sleeping on the journey is the death of Christ on the cross. The stone put under his head is Christ according to his humanity, which Jacob anointed so that Christ might be signified; for Christos in Greek is unctus, “anointed,” in Latin. And the head of Christ is God. So the stone put under Jacob’s head signifies the humanity of Christ joined to God who took it up. For “the head of the man is Christ; the head of Christ is God.”
28.12:
**“And he saw in his sleep a ladder”** — Christ, who is life
**“standing upon the earth,”** — earthliness
**“and the top thereof touching heaven:”** — he is above in his head who is below in his body
**“the angels”** — the evangelists, the preachers
**“also of God ascending”**
• beyond every creature, to God, through whom all things were made
• so as to find him to whom they ascribe all things
**“and descending by it;”**
• so as to find him made of a woman
• And he saw in his sleep, etc. GREGORY. Allegorically. Jacob signifies the preachers, who not only seek by contemplating the head of the Church, that is, Christ, but come down in pity to his members; which the angels going up and coming down show. Hence Moses often goes in and out of the tabernacle; and he who within is caught up into contemplation is pressed outside by the business of the weak. Within he considers secret things; outside he bears the burdens of the fleshly. He who in doubtful matters always runs back to the tabernacle consults the Lord before the ark of the testament, giving an example to teachers: that when outside they are unsure what to arrange, they should return to the mind as to the tabernacle, and, as before the ark of the testament, consult the Lord about the things they doubt, searching within themselves the pages of the sacred word.
• ISIDORE. “He saw in his sleep,” etc. The angels going up and coming down by the ladder are the evangelists and preachers of Christ: going up, to understand the Godhead, passing beyond every creature, so as to find in the beginning the Word with God, through whom all things were made; coming down, so as to find him “made of a woman, made under the law,” etc. For in that ladder is from earth to heaven, from flesh to spirit; because in it the fleshly, by advancing, as by going up, become spiritual. To feed whom with milk the spiritual come down, because they cannot speak to them as to spiritual men, but as to fleshly. He is above in the head; he is below in his body, that is, the Church. He is the ladder who says: “I am the way.” He is gone up to so as to be understood in the heights, and come down to so as to be fed in his little members. Through him they lift themselves up to await him on high, and humble themselves to proclaim him loftily and temperately.
*Morally:* To sleep on the journey is, on the way of this world, to rest from the hindrance of worldly actions. Jacob, sleeping, saw angels, because those behold divine things who close their eyes to the desire of temporal things; which, well closed, the devil opened, saying: “In what day soever you shall eat, your eyes shall be opened,” etc.
28.13:
**“And the Lord leaning upon the ladder, saying to him: I am the Lord God of Abraham thy father, and the God of Isaac; the land,”** — the Church
**“wherein thou sleepest, I will give to thee”** — to the man
**“and to thy seed.”** — to the Christian people
**“I am the Lord God of Abraham thy father”** — Mystically it signifies the command of the Godhead directed to the humanity of Christ, to whom the land, that is, the Church, is promised, and to his seed, that is, the Christian people. Whence: “Ask of me, and I will give thee the Gentiles for thy inheritance, and the utmost parts of the earth for thy possession.”
28.14:
**“And thy seed shall be as the dust of the earth:”** — numberless
**“thou shalt spread abroad … to the east,”** — the light of faith, or of all good work
**“to the west, and”** — the setting of the vices
**“to the north,”** — the narrowing of pleasure and the mortifying of desire
**“and to the south:”** — the brightness of wisdom and the heat of love
**“and in thee … shall be blessed”** — in Christ
**“and thy seed”** — in the imitators
**“all the tribes of the earth”** — some of all
28.15:
**“And I will be thy keeper”** — “The Lord keep thy coming in and thy going out”
**“whithersoever thou goest,”** — in the preachers
**“and will bring thee back”** — about the end of the world
**“into this land:”** — Judea, which is to believe
28.16: **“And when Jacob awaked out of sleep, he said: Indeed the Lord is in this place, and I knew it not.”** — And when Jacob awaked, etc. Whoever, after the numbness of sloth, has woken up, and through the exercise of good work has truly risen, will understand in the Church the surpassing grace of God and the entrance of the heavenly kingdom.
28.17:
**“And trembling he said: How terrible is this place!”** — because the tabernacle was to be there
**“this is no other but the house of God,”**
• it signifies the temple and the worship of God to come
• because Christ was born in Bethlehem, which he foresaw in the spirit
**“and the gate of heaven.”**
• because there he came down to earth, there he went up to heaven
• because from there is the entrance for believers to take the kingdom of heaven
28.18:
**“And Jacob, arising in the morning, took the stone, which he had laid under his head, and set it up”** — it signifies the resurrection of Christ
**“for a title, pouring oil upon the top of it.”** — according to that: “God, thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness”
**“And … arising”** — AUGUSTINE. That Jacob set up for a title the stone which he had put under his head, and poured oil over it, did nothing like idolatry; because neither then nor afterwards did he frequent the stone by adoring it or sacrificing to it; but it was a sign and a prophecy belonging to the anointing, from which Christ is named.
28.19:
**“And he called the name of the city Bethel,”** — “house of God”
**“which before … Luza.”** — “nut” or “almond.” Others: Ulam Luz was the name of the city before
**“was called”** — And he called the name, etc. JEROME. From what was said, “How terrible is this place,” etc., he gives the place the name Bethel, that is, “house of God,” which before was called Luza, that is, “nut” or “almond.” Whence some think, absurdly, that the Hebrew word Ulam is the name of the city, though Ulam is interpreted “before.” So the order of the reading is this: “He called the name of that place Bethel, and before, Luza was the name of the city.” And the ancient Scriptures are full of the word Ulam, or Elam, which signifies nothing but “before,” or “in front,” or “porch,” or “lintel,” or “doorposts,” etc.
28.20: **“And he made a vow, saying: If God shall be with me, and shall keep me in the way by which I walk, and shall give me bread to eat, and raiment to put on,”** — or “clothing”
28.22:
**“And this stone, which I have set up for a title, shall be called the house”** — not God
**“shall be called the house”** — It is a prophecy of the house of God that was to be there. There too, on his return, he himself sacrificed to God.

29.2:
**“And he saw a well”**
• baptism
• the knowledge of the Scriptures
• the grace of the Holy Ghost, to come through the preaching of Christ to the Church of the Gentiles, which was covered while the Word of God had not yet come and been made flesh
**“in the field,”** — of the world
**“and three”** — because of faith in the Trinity
**“flocks of sheep”**
• of the simple
• “he shall set the sheep on his right hand,” etc.
**“lying”**
• seeking the grace of baptism
• humbly
**“by it:”** — because they long to be filled with the mysteries of Scripture
**“for the beasts were watered out of it,”** — the simple
**“and the mouth thereof was closed with a great stone.”** — by the covering of the letter
**“he saw a well”** — The water of the well is the knowledge of the Old Testament, which the stone closed, because the letter of the law hid the spiritual sense in it; but when Christ came the stone was taken away, since through the preaching of the New Testament the shadow of the law was shut out and the truth of the Gospel laid open.
*Allegorically:* By the well baptism is expressed, by the field the world; by the three flocks lying by the well are signified those who belong to receiving faith in the Trinity, seeking in humility the grace of baptism.
**“was closed with a … stone”** — The hardness of unbelief, which being cast away, the baptism of life is received. And the shepherds are those of the Church, who long for the flocks to be watered when the stone has been removed by Jacob; because, when Christ takes away unbelief from their hearts, those whom he predestined to the sacrament of baptism are washed in the wave of purification.
29.4: **“And he said to the shepherds:”** — the prophets
29.10: **“And when Jacob saw her, and knew her to be his cousin-german,”** — this he had learned from the shepherds
29.11: **“he kissed her”** — AUGUSTINE. It was the custom, especially in that simplicity of the ancients, for kinsmen to kiss their kinswomen; and it is done today in many places. But it can be asked how she received a kiss from a stranger, if Jacob made known their kinship afterwards. So it must be understood either that he, who knew of the kinship, confidently rushed to the kiss, or that the Scripture told afterwards, by recapitulation, what happened when Jacob had first made known who he was.
29.16: **“the name of the elder was Lia: and the younger was called Rachel”** — VICTORINUS THE MARTYR interpreted Rachel and Lia as a likeness of the Church and the synagogue. He thinks Lia, the elder by birth, signifies the synagogue, because she first bore the people of God; who is called blear-eyed, because the law given through Moses was covered and sealed. Rachel, the younger and beautiful, first barren, afterwards fruitful, signifies the Church, which is later in time and holy in body and spirit. Her eyes are comely, because they were found worthy to see the Gospel. But she was long barren, while the synagogue bore the people. For Rachel Jacob served, and Lia was put in her place; because Christ, to take the Church to himself, first joined the synagogue to himself.
29.18: **“seven years”** — Jacob’s service of seven years for two wives signifies the time of the present life, which turns in seven days, in which the Lord took the form of a servant, obedient to the Father unto death. Jacob served, because the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister. He fed sheep, and Christ said: “I am the good shepherd.” He took for himself as wages the speckled cattle; Christ gathered to himself the variety of the different nations. He put three rods, with the bark stripped, in the watering troughs, that by looking at them the sheep might be multiplied; and our Lord set before the faithful people in the water of baptism the names of the three persons, of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost, so that whoever has looked on these with a full heart is made a sheep of God.
29.20:
**“So Jacob served seven years for Rachel: and they seemed but a few days, because of the greatness of his love.”**
• love lightened the labour
• They seemed but a few days, etc. It is to be asked how this was said, since even a short time seems long to lovers. It was said, then, because of the labour of the service, which love made easy.
*Augustine:* Jacob’s four wives are thrown at him as a huge crime. But since it was the custom then, it was not a crime; now, however, it is a crime, because it is not the custom. Some sins are against nature, some against custom, some against precepts. But Jacob did this neither against nature, for he used those women not for the sake of wantonness but for the sake of begetting; nor against custom, for at that time in those lands this was commonly done; nor against a precept, for it was forbidden by no law. Now, however, it is not lawful, by laws and by customs. And if anyone despises these two, even if he uses several women only for the sake of begetting, he still sins and violates human society, to which the begetting of children is necessary. But because men living under other customs cannot take delight in a multitude of wives except through the greatness of lust, they err in thinking that many wives could not have been had except through the burning of fleshly concupiscence.
*Isidore:* So Jacob has two free wives, for both are daughters of the remission of sins, that is, of whitening, which is what Laban means. One is loved, the other is borne with. But the one who is borne with is the first and the more abundantly made fruitful, so that, if not for her own sake, she may be loved for her children’s. For the labour of the just has its greatest fruit in those whom they have begotten to God by preaching amid many tribulations; for whose sake they are in labours and in stripes and often in deaths; for whose sake they have fightings without, fears within; and these they call their joy and their crown. And they are born more easily and abundantly by the word of faith, by which they preach Christ crucified and whatever is more quickly grasped by human thought and does not trouble the weak eyes of Lia. But Rachel, of bright face, goes beyond the mind to God, and sees “in the beginning the Word with God,” and wishes to bear, and cannot; because “who shall declare his generation?”
*Isidore:* Jacob has two free wives because two lives are preached to us in the body of Jesus Christ: one temporal, in which we labour; the other eternal, in which we shall contemplate the delight of God. The Lord showed the one by his passion, the other by his resurrection. Hence Lia is interpreted “labouring,” Rachel “the beginning seen,” or “the Word by which the beginning is seen.” The action of human life, in which we live by faith, is very laborious in its works, and uncertain by what outcome it will come to the profit of those we wish to help. This is Lia, Jacob’s first wife, and blear-eyed; for the thoughts of mortals are fearful, and their foresight uncertain. But the hope of eternal contemplation, having a sure understanding of the truth, is Rachel, well favoured and of a beautiful countenance. Her every devout and zealous man loves, and for her he serves the grace of God, in which our sins, though they be as scarlet, shall be made white as snow. Laban is “whitening,” whom Jacob served for Rachel. For no one turns, under the grace of the remission of sins, to serve justice, except that he may live quietly in the Word by which the beginning, which is God, is seen. So it is for Rachel, not for Lia, that one serves. For no one in the works of justice loves the labour of action or of suffering, nor seeks that life for its own sake; just as Jacob did not seek Lia. Yet, embracing her when she was put in Rachel’s place in the night, for the purpose of begetting, he found her fruitful; and because she could not be loved for herself, the Lord made her to be borne with, so that Rachel might be reached, and then commended her by her sons. So every servant of God set under the grace of the whitening of sins, loving this alone, meditates in his conduct on how to receive the teaching of wisdom. Many think they will soon receive it once they have exercised themselves in the seven precepts that concern the love of neighbour, so that no one is harmed: that is, “Honour thy father and mother; thou shalt not commit adultery; thou shalt not kill; thou shalt not steal; thou shalt not bear false witness; thou shalt not covet thy neighbour’s wife, nor thy neighbour’s goods.” When these have been kept as far as he can, and, in place of the longed-for and hoped-for most beautiful delight of teaching, he has held fast through various temptations, as through the night of this world, to the bearing of labour, then, as in place of Rachel, Lia is unexpectedly joined to him; and he bears with her that he may come to the other, if he loves perseveringly, receiving seven other precepts, as if it were said to him: “Serve another seven years for Rachel,” that thou mayest be poor in spirit, meek, mourning, hungering and thirsting after justice, merciful, clean of heart, a peacemaker. For he would wish, if he could, to come to the delights of beautiful contemplation without any bearing of labour, which must be embraced in doing and suffering. But this cannot be in the land of the dying; which is signified by these words: “It is not the custom in this place,” etc. She is called the elder who is first in time; for in the training of a man the labour of working, which these things are, comes first. Hence: “Thou hast desired wisdom; keep the commandments,” which belong to justice. And justice is that which is of faith, which is amid the dangers of temptations, so that by devoutly believing what is not yet understood one may also gain the merit of understanding. Hence: “Unless you believe, you shall not understand.” For justice is shown to belong to faith, understanding to wisdom. Yet the desire to see the truth clearly is not to be rejected, but called back to order, so that it begins from faith and strives by good works to reach where it tends. For in that in which virtue is busied, it is laborious; in that which it seeks, it is luminous wisdom. “What need is there,” he says, “to believe what is not shown to me? Make plain some word by which I may see the beginning of all things.” For this is what it burns for chiefly and first. To whom it is answered: “What you desire is beautiful and worthy to be loved; but Lia marries before Rachel. Let that ardour avail for this, that the order is not refused but borne with, without which one cannot come to what is loved.” But when it has been reached, there will be had together in this world beautiful understanding and laborious justice. For however keenly and purely the unchangeable good is discerned, still “the corruptible body is a load upon the soul, and presseth down the mind that museth upon many things.” So one must strive toward one thing, but for its sake many things must be borne.
*The same:* Accordingly the life that belongs to the pursuit of contemplation, so as to behold, with the eyes of the mind that are not weak, “the invisible things” that are not of the flesh, “being understood by the things that are made,” and to discern ineffably “his eternal power also and divinity,” wishes to be free of all business, and is therefore barren. For in seeking the leisure in which the pursuits of contemplation are kindled, it does not suffer with the weakness of men who in their troubles desire to be helped. But because it too burns with the charity of bringing forth, it wishes to teach what it knows. It sees its sister abounding in children by the labour of action, and grieves that men run rather to the virtue by which their needs are seen to than to that from which something divine and unchangeable is learned. Hence Rachel envied her sister.
*The same:* Accordingly, because a pure understanding of that divine substance, which is not a body and so does not belong to the sense of the flesh, cannot be expressed in words uttered by the flesh, the teaching of wisdom chooses to suggest divine things somehow, by thinking through any bodily images whatever, rather than to cease from the office of teaching such things; just as Rachel chooses to receive children from her husband and her handmaid rather than to be without children. For Bala, who is Rachel’s handmaid, is interpreted “grown old”; for from the old life of the flesh, given over to the senses, bodily images are thought of even when something is heard about the unchangeable substance of the Godhead. Lia too, set on fire with love of numerous offspring, received children from her handmaid, whose handmaid, Zelpha, is interpreted “gaping mouth”; which signifies those whose mouth gapes to receive preaching while their heart does not gape. Hence: “This people honoureth me with their lips, but their heart is far from me.” And elsewhere: “Thou that preachest that men should not steal, stealest.” But so that even through this condition Jacob’s free wife, labouring, may receive children of the kingdom, the Lord says: “What they say, do,” etc. Hence the Apostle: “Whether by occasion, or by truth, Christ be preached: in this also I rejoice, yea, and will rejoice,” as one who, even when the handmaid bears, is glad at the number of offspring. That offspring was made in the womb of Lia, but brought forth by the kindness of Rachel, when, having received the mandrakes from Lia’s son, she let her husband lie with her sister on the night owed to her own bed.
29.23: **“And at night he brought in Lia his daughter to him,”** — the active life, which bears children by preaching and by the example of good works
29.25:
**“And he said to his father in law: What is it that thou didst mean to do? did not I serve thee for Rachel?”**
• “ewe,” or “the beginning seen”
• the contemplative
29.27: **“Make up the week of days of this match: and I will give thee her also, for the service that thou shalt render me other seven years.”** — that is, celebrate this marriage for seven days, as is the custom; for it would have been unjust, when he had been deceived, to put him off another seven years
29.28: **“He yielded to his pleasure: and after the week was past,”** — the seven days of Lia’s marriage, which being fulfilled, he served seven years
29.29: **“To whom her father gave Bala for her servant.”** — “grown old”
29.32: **“And she conceived and bore a son, and called his name Ruben,”** — “son of vision”
29.33: **“And again she conceived and bore a son, and said: Because the Lord heard that I was despised, he hath given this also to me: and she called his name Simeon.”** — “hearing”
29.34: **“And she conceived the third time, and bore another son: and said: Now also my husband will be joined to me, because I have borne him three sons: and therefore she called his name Levi.”** — “enlargement,” or “addition”
29.35: **“The fourth time she conceived and bore a son, and said: now will I praise the Lord: and for this she called him Juda.”** — praise, that is, the giving of thanks; as there: “I confess to thee, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth,” that is, I give thanks to thee

30.4: **“And she gave him Bala in marriage:”** — ALCUIN. Perhaps every concubine is called a wife, according to the manner of Scripture, but not the other way round
30.6:
**“And Rachel said: The Lord hath judged for me,”** — that is, he has done me justice, making me equal to my sister
**“and hath heard my voice, giving me a son, and therefore she called his name Dan.”** — “judgment”
30.8: **“For whom Rachel said: God hath compared me with my sister, and I have prevailed: and she called him Nephtali.”** — from “wrestling” or “comparison”; for nep sounds both
30.11: **“She said: Happily. And therefore called his name Gad.”** — “in readiness,” or “happiness”
30.13: **“And Lia said: This is for my happiness: for women will call me blessed. Therefore she called him Aser.”** — “blessed”; elsewhere, by the ambiguity of the word, riches can be called so
30.14:
**“And Ruben, going out in the time of the wheat harvest into the field, found mandrakes:”** — fruits beautiful, sweet-smelling and tasteless
**“which he brought to his mother Lia. And Rachel said: Give me part of thy son’s mandrakes.”** — And Ruben, going out, etc. AUGUSTINE. Why did Scripture not keep silent about this deed, when it is not its habit to present such longings of silly women as something great? Unless it moves us to seek something great in them, I can conjecture nothing more than what is suggested by that sense: that I take that fruit to figure a good name; not the one that the few just and wise bestow, but the popular one, by which a greater and more famous notice is gained; not to be looked for for its own sake, but necessary to the aim of good men by which the human race is helped. Hence: “He must have a good testimony of them who are without.” These, though they have little wisdom, for the most part repay the labour of those by whom they are helped with the splendour of praise and the odour of good repute. And to this glory none of those in the Church come first except those who are busied in action and labour. Therefore Lia’s son found these fruits going out into the field, that is, walking honestly toward those who are without. But the teaching of wisdom, which, withdrawn from the din of the crowd, is fixed in the contemplation of truth, would not obtain this popular glory except through those who in the crowds, by acting and persuading, are set over them, not to be over them but to be of profit to them. For when these active men, by whom manifold service is rendered and whose authority is dear to the peoples, bear witness to the contemplative life, the mandrakes, as it were, come to Rachel through Lia; and to Lia through her firstborn son, that is, through the son of her fruitfulness, in whom is all the fruit of laborious action, imperilled amid conflicts. This action many, eminent in good talent and burning with zeal, though they are fit to rule peoples, shun because of its turbulent business, and burn for the leisure of teaching as for the embrace of beautiful Rachel. But because it is good that, becoming more widely known in this life, it should earn popular glory, and yet unjust that it should obtain it if it keeps its lover, fit for administering the cares of the Church, in leisure, and does not share him with the governing of the common good, therefore Lia says to her sister: “Dost thou think it a small matter, that thou hast taken my husband from me, unless thou take also my son’s mandrakes?” By one she signifies all who, though worthy to have the government of the Church committed to them, are kindled with the zeal of contemplating wisdom and wish to be removed from all the troubles of action and to settle in the leisure of learning.
