Hence: “Is it a small matter that thou hast taken my husband?” etc. As if the active life said to the contemplative: It is a small matter that the life of the studious keeps in leisure men who are needed for labour; besides, it seeks popular glory as well. So, that she may obtain all things justly, Rachel shares her husband with her sister that night: so that those who by laborious virtue are suited to the government of peoples, even if they had chosen to be free for knowledge, may take up the trial of temptations for the common good, lest the teaching of wisdom, for which they were eager to be free, be blasphemed, and lest they fail to gain from the unlearned the good esteem which the fruits signify, and which is necessary for the encouragement of learners. But they are compelled against their will to take up this charge. This is signified well enough in that, when Jacob came from the field, Lia met him and, holding him back, said: “Thou shalt come in unto me,” etc.; as if to say: Do you wish good repute to be given to the teaching you love? Do not flee the dutiful labour. Whoever pays attention sees this done in the Church: men come from the whole world, from the works of the world, to pass into the leisure of knowing the truth, as into the embrace of Rachel; but they are taken across by the need of the Church and ordained to labour; as if Lia said: “Thou shalt come in unto me.” And while they chastely dispense the mystery, so that in the night of the world they may beget sons of faith, that life too is praised by the peoples, for love of which they turned and left the hope of the world, and from whose profession they were taken up to the mercy of ruling the people. For they do this in all their labours: that the profession from which they turned, because it has given such rulers, may be glorified more widely; as Jacob did not refuse the night with Lia, so that Rachel might obtain the sweet-smelling and shining fruits. And she too, by the gift of God’s mercy, at last and with difficulty bears; for it is very rare that what “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God,” and whatever is said devoutly and wisely on this matter, is grasped soundly, even in part, without a phantom of fleshly thought.
*Augustine:* And Ruben, going out, etc. Of this kind of fruit I know some think that, taken as food by barren women, it gives fruitfulness, and that this is why Rachel pressed to receive it; which I do not think, not even if she had conceived then. But as it is, since the Lord gave her offspring after two further births of Lia from that night, there is no reason to suspect anything of the mandrake such as we have found in no woman. For when I had seen these fruits myself, and was glad they had come my way because of this passage of the sacred reading (for it is a rare thing), I examined their nature as far as I could; not by some knowledge removed from common sense, which teaches the virtues of roots and the powers of herbs, but as far as sight, smell and taste report; and I found the thing beautiful and sweet-smelling, but tasteless in flavour. So why the woman wanted it so much, I do not know; unless perhaps for the rarity of the fruit and the pleasantness of its smell.
30.18: **“And said: God hath given me a reward, because I gave my handmaid to my husband. And she called his name Issachar.”** — Is is “man,” achar “wages”; so it means “there is wages,” because she had bought the coming in of the husband owed to Rachel with her son’s mandrakes
30.20: **“And said: God hath endowed me with a good dowry: this turn also my husband will be with me, because I have borne him six sons: and therefore she called his name Zabulon.”** — “dwelling.” In the book of Hebrew names it is interpreted, forcedly, “flowing of the night”
30.21: **“After whom she bore a daughter, named Dina.”** — “cause,” because she became the cause of the quarrel at Sichem
30.22: **“The Lord also remembering Rachel,”** — which is interpreted “ewe”
30.26: **“Give me my wives, and my children, for whom I have served thee, that I may depart:”** — as if: by now you ought to be teachers, because of the time
30.29:
**“But he answered: Thou knowest how I have served thee, and how great”** — by works
**“thy possession hath been in my hands.”** — the distribution of gifts
30.30:
**“Thou hadst but little before I came to thee,”** — only as much as nature had given
**“and now thou art become rich:”** — in that which grace has given
**“and the Lord hath blessed thee at my coming. It is reasonable therefore that I should now provide also for my own house.”** — of Judea
30.31:
**“And Laban said: What shall I give thee? But he said: I require nothing:”** — of thy gift
**“but if thou wilt do what I demand,”** — that is, if thou wilt let my sheep hear my voice
**“I will feed … again”** — I will nourish with milk
**“and keep thy sheep”** — from the attack of wolves
30.32:
**“Go round through all thy flocks, and separate all the sheep of divers colours, and speckled: and all that is brown and spotted, and of divers colours,”** — “The queen stood on thy right hand, surrounded with variety”
**“as well among the sheep, as among the goats, shall be my wages.”** — Go round through all thy flocks, etc. JEROME. The sense is much confused in the Septuagint, and to this day I have been able to find none of our writers who explained this place plainly. “You wish,” says Jacob, “that I serve you another seven years: do what I ask. Separate all the parti-coloured and speckled, both sheep and goats, and hand them over into the hands of your sons; and from each flock give me the white and black cattle, that is, those of one colour. So if anything speckled is born from the white and black, which are of one colour, it will be mine; if anything of one colour, yours. I do not ask a hard thing: the nature of the cattle works with you, that white are born from white and black from black; with me is my justice, while God looks on my lowliness and labour.” Laban gladly seized the option given, and doing as Jacob asked, he set a three days’ journey between Jacob and his sons, lest any trickery should arise from the nearness of the cattle. So Jacob devised a new trick, and fought against the nature of white and black colour by a natural art. For he took three rods, of poplar, almond and pomegranate (though the Septuagint has storax, nut and plane), and by stripping them in part made the colour of the rods speckled, so that wherever he had left the bark on the rod the old colour remained, and where he had taken off the bark the white was laid bare. So Jacob watched the time when the cattle were covered; and when after the heat of the day they went eagerly to drink, he put the parti-coloured rods in the troughs, and letting in the rams and he-goats, in the very eagerness of drinking he had the sheep and she-goats covered; so that from the double desire, while they both drink eagerly and are covered by the males, they might conceive offspring such as the shadows of the rams and he-goats mounting above them that they beheld in the mirror of the waters. For from the rods put in the troughs the colour of the images was speckled. Nor is it strange that this should be the nature of females in conceiving: that whatever they have seen or conceived in mind in the utmost heat of pleasure in which they conceive, such offspring they produce; since this very thing is said of the herds of mares among the Spaniards too. And Quintilian, in the controversy in which a matron is accused because she bore an Ethiopian, argues in her defence that this, which we have said above, is the nature of conceptions. And it is found written in the books of Hippocrates that a certain woman was to be punished on suspicion of adultery, when she had borne a most beautiful child unlike both parents and their stock, had not the said physician solved the question, advising them to look whether there was perhaps such a picture in the bedchamber; and when it was found, the woman was freed from suspicion. Jacob, shrewd, kept justice even in his new art. For if all the lambs and kids had been speckled, there would have been suspicion of fraud, and Laban in his envy would openly have opposed it. So he tempered it in such a way that he received the fruit of his labour and Laban was not stripped bare. But when the sheep and goats were covered at the first season (because the spring offspring is better), he put the rods in front, so that they were born speckled; but whatever sheep and goats sought the male late, he did not put them in front, so that the cattle were born of one colour. And whatever was born first was his, because speckled; whatever later, Laban’s, because of one colour. As for what is written, that they conceived at the rods, I cannot express the force of the Hebrew word except by a circumlocution. For laameha means properly the utmost heat in coition, by which the whole body is shaken, and the end is near the accomplished pleasure.
30.33:
**“And … shall answer for me tomorrow”** — in the future
**“my justice … before thee when the time of the bargain shall come: and all that is not of divers colours, and spotted, and brown, as well among the sheep as among the goats, shall accuse me of theft.”** — those who would not imitate, but have persisted in the vices born in them, will not be of my fold
30.37:
**“And Jacob took green rods of poplar, and of almond, and of plane trees, and pilled them in part:”** — the variety could have been made in one kind, but three kinds of wood are set down for the sake of the mystery
**“so when the bark was taken off, in the parts that were pilled, there appeared whiteness: but the parts that were whole remained green: and by this means the colour was divers.”** — And Jacob took, etc. Otherwise. GREGORY. The understanding of the sacred word must be weighed between the text and the mystery with such balance that neither the weight of too much discussion presses it down nor the numbness of carelessness leaves it empty. For many sentences are so pregnant with the conception of allegories that whoever strives to hold them to the history alone is deprived of knowing them through his carelessness. Some so serve outward precepts that if anyone wishes to penetrate more subtly, he finds nothing within, and hides from himself even what is outside. Hence it is well said in the historical narrative by way of signification: “And Jacob took green rods of poplar,” etc. To set green rods of poplar, almond and plane before the eyes of the flocks is, through the course of Scripture, to offer the peoples the lives and sayings of the ancient fathers as an example; which, because by the test of reason they are straight, are called rods. From them he takes the bark in part, so that the inner whiteness may appear, and in part keeps it, so that the outer green may remain as it was. And so the colour of the rods is made varied, because the sayings of the fathers who went before are set before the eyes of our consideration like varied rods; in which, when for the most part we flee the understanding of the letter, we take off the bark, as it were; but when we follow it, we keep it. And while the bark of the letter is drawn off from them, the whiteness of allegory is laid open; while it is left, green examples of the outward understanding are shown. These Jacob put in the troughs of water, because Christ fixed them in the books of sacred knowledge by which we are instructed. The rams with whom they mate look at them, because when our rational spirits are fixed in attention on them, they are mingled with our several actions, so that they beget such offspring of works as the examples of those who went before which they see in the words of the precepts; and the offspring of good work has a varied colour, because, the bark of the letter being drawn off, they keenly consider inward things, and often, keeping it, they shape themselves well in outward things.
*Alcuin:* Why is Jacob not accused of fraud in this place? Without doubt because he did this as a prophet; nor is it to be believed that he did it without spiritual revelation.

31.2: **“And perceiving also that Laban’s countenance was not towards”** — or “toward”
31.7: **“hath changed my wages”** — JEROME. In place of what we have put, “He changed my wages ten times,” the Septuagint put “ten lambs,” although the Hebrew word moin sounds a number rather than lambs; and from what follows this sense is proved: that Laban changed the terms at each birth. If he saw speckled cattle being born, he would say: “I want speckled ones to be born to me in future.” Then Jacob would not put the rods in the troughs, so that the offspring were born of one colour; and when that happened, Laban would say those cattle ought to fall to his share. So the terms were changed up to ten times; and whatever colour Laban had proposed should be born to him was turned to the contrary. Now ten times of bearing in six years would seem incredible; but read Virgil, where it is said: “Twice the flocks are with young.” And the nature of the sheep of Italy and of Mesopotamia is said to be the same.
31.11: **“And the angel of God said”** — or “of the Lord”
31.12: **“And he said: Lift up thy eyes, and see that all the males leaping upon the females, are of divers colours, spotted, and speckled. For I have seen all that Laban hath done to thee.”** — For I have seen all, etc. From this we learn that Jacob did it with no evil guile, but by divine arrangement, or because all things were done in figure. Hence he deserved to be strengthened by an angelic vision.
31.13: **“Now therefore arise”** — GREGORY. After a long servitude the Lord commanded Jacob to return to his country; then, without his father-in-law’s knowledge, he hastened away with his wives and company. But Laban overtook him on mount Galaad, in fury, searching for the idols, and did not find them. In this place Laban bears the type of the devil; for he is interpreted “whitening.” And the devil, though he is dark, transforms himself into an angel of light.
31.19: **“At that time Laban was gone to shear his sheep, and Rachel stole away her father’s idols.”** — She stole her father’s idols, etc. JEROME. Where we read “idols,” in the Hebrew is written theraphim, which Aquila interprets “figures” or “images.” I say this so that we may know what theraphim means in the Book of Judges.
31.21:
**“And when he was gone, together with all that belonged to him, and having passed the river, was going on towards mount Galaad,”**
• by anticipation
• Towards mount, etc. Not that at that time it was called mount Galaad; but by anticipation it is called by the name by which it was afterwards named.
31.23: **“And he took his brethren with him, and pursued after him seven days; and overtook him in the mount of Galaad.”** — Who taking his brethren, etc. By Laban the world can be expressed, which follows Jacob in fury, because it tries to crush the elect, who are the members of Christ. Jacob took away the daughter of the world, or of the devil, when Christ joined to himself the Church from the Gentiles, to whom it is said through the prophet: “Forget thy people and thy father’s house.” In the idols avarice is signified, which is the service of idols. Laban, coming to Jacob, did not find the idol, because when the riches of the world were shown, the devil found in our Redeemer no traces of concupiscence. But what Jacob did not have, Rachel covered by sitting on it; who is interpreted “ewe” and signifies the Church. And to sit is to seek the lowliness of penance; hence: “Rise ye after you have sitten.” So Rachel covers the idols by sitting, because the Church, following Christ, has covered the vice of earthly concupiscence through the lowliness of penance. Hence: “Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered.” So Rachel signifies us, who press down the idols by sitting if we condemn by repenting the faults of avarice; the uncleanness of which does not hinder those who run manfully, but those who walk effeminately are undone by the allurements of the world; which is signified by these words: “It has happened to me according to the custom of women.” For she made known that she was suffering, as it were, the things of women.
31.24: **“And he saw in a dream God saying to him: Take heed”** — he is not to be feared who can do nothing unless permitted
31.25:
**“Now Jacob had pitched”** — had spread out
**“in the mountain:”** — in the loftiness of the precepts
**“his tent”** — the dwelling of passers-by
**“and when he with his brethren had overtaken him, he pitched his tent in the same mount of Galaad.”** — the devil pursues Christ, who says: “I will sit in the mountain of the covenant,” etc.
31.26:
**“And he said to Jacob: Why hast thou done thus,”** — as if: “What have we to do with thee, Jesus, Son of the living God?” etc.
**“to carry away, without my knowledge, my daughters,”** — souls snatched from slavery
**“as captives”** — “he led captivity captive”
**“taken with the sword.”** — of the Word of God
31.27: **“Why wouldst thou run away privately and not acquaint me, that I might have brought thee on the way with joy, and with songs, and with timbrels, and with harps?”** — as if: Why did you hide your coming from me? If I had known you, I would not have crucified you, but would have celebrated your glory with the insignia of a royal triumph
31.28:
**“Thou hast not suffered me to kiss my sons and daughters:”** — “I came not to send peace, but the sword”
**“thou hast done foolishly:”** — when spat upon and buffeted, and therefore unknown
**“and now, indeed,”** — That I might kiss, etc. By the custom of Scripture he calls Jacob’s sons and daughters his own, as it calls kinsmen sons or brothers. Hence in what follows: “And Jacob said to his brethren: Bring hither stones.” In the Gospel too the sons of Mary, the Lord’s mother’s sister, are called his brethren.
31.29:
**“It is in my power to return thee evil:”** — as if: I can pursue your members
**“but the God of your father said to me yesterday:”** — that is, I cannot, except as far as I am permitted
**“Take heed thou speak not any thing harshly against Jacob.”** — let it be granted
31.30:
**“Suppose thou didst desire to go to thy friends,”** — to return into Judea
**“and hadst a longing after thy father’s house: why hast thou stolen away my gods?”**
• he speaks as a Gentile; and it is to be noted that here we first find the gods of the Gentiles, for above Scripture named God
• why does avarice, which is the service of idols, lie hidden with you?
31.31: **“Jacob answered: That I departed unknown to thee, it was for fear lest thou wouldst take away thy daughters by force.”** — It was for fear lest by force, etc. As if: I did not make myself known to you for this reason, lest by the bitterness of persecution you should overcome weak souls newly snatched from you.
31.32:
**“But whereas thou chargest me with theft:”** — of avarice
**“with whomsoever thou shalt find thy gods,”** — idolatry
**“let him be slain”** — let him be banished from our fellowship by common judgment
**“before our brethren. Search, and if thou find any of thy things with me,”** — “For what concord hath Christ with Belial? what agreement hath the temple of God with idols?”
**“take them away. Now when he said this, he knew not”** — he did not love those who sold and bought in the temple; hence he cast them out
31.33:
**“So Laban went into”** — “as a roaring lion, goeth about seeking whom he may devour”
**“the tent”** — of the world
**“of Jacob, and of Lia, and of both the handmaids, and found them not.”** — hence: “For the prince of this world cometh, and in me he hath not any thing”
**“And when he was entered into Rachel’s tent,”** — what he did not find with the greater he strives to find with the lesser. But Rachel, that is, the Church, scorns what Laban counts gain, as the burdens of fools
31.34:
**“She in haste hid”** — covering avarice with the lowliness of penance
**“the idols under the camel’s furniture, and sat upon them: and when he had searched”** — to him trying every kind of snare of temptation
**“all the tent, and found nothing,”** — that is, not prevailing
31.35:
**“She said: Let not my lord be angry”** — it is a natural custom to rise for one’s elders; but I do not rise for you, because I do not honour a follower of avarice
**“that I cannot rise up before thee, because it has now happened to me, according to the custom of women,”** — he who follows the uncleanness of avarice suffers, as it were, the things of women
**“So … was in vain.”** — frustrated
**“his careful search”** — of the tempter
31.36: **“And Jacob being angry, said in a chiding manner: For what fault of mine, and for what offence on my part hast thou so hotly pursued me,”** — the crafty exactor is rebuked, who raised himself against Christ with every kind of temptation, but found nothing in him to blame
31.37:
**“And searched all my household stuff? What hast thou found of all the substance of thy house? lay it here before … brethren,”** — sons
**“my”** — by grace
**“and thy brethren,”** — by nature
**“and let them judge between me and thee.”** — “the saints shall judge nations”
31.38:
**“Have I therefore been with thee twenty years?”** — in the keeping of the ten commandments with twofold charity
**“thy ewes”** — the innocent
**“and goats”** — the penitent
**“barren,”** — empty of good work
**“were not … the rams”** — the strong
**“of thy flocks I did not eat:”** — I broke
31.39:
**“Neither did I shew thee that which the beast had torn,”** — as if: I defended the flocks entrusted to me from the attacks of invisible wolves
**“I made good all the damage:”** — I restored the lost sheep
**“whatsoever was lost by theft, thou didst exact it of me:”** — whatever was done amiss through ignorance you imputed to me; which is not done to the shepherds of the Church
31.40:
**“Day and night”** — I was beset by daily pressure
**“with heat,”** — by the scandals of the brethren
**“was I parched”**
• or “I was pressed”
• Heat and cold have one effect.
**“and with frost, and sleep departed from my eyes.”** — “he shall not slumber that keepeth Israel”
31.41:
**“And in this manner have I served thee in thy house twenty years, fourteen”** — I kept the seven precepts on the love of neighbour and the seven of the Gospel on the love of God
**“for thy daughters, and six”** — wonderful works
**“for thy flocks:”** — for guarding the peoples in the faith
**“thou hast changed also my wages ten times.”** — ungrateful for my benefits, you set against my labour things contrary to the ten precepts
31.42:
**“Unless the God of my father Abraham, and the fear”** — God, who is to be feared by all
**“of Isaac had stood by”** — had come to help
**“me, peradventure now … naked:”** — with no one cleaving to me
**“thou hadst sent me away … my affliction”** — which I suffered in the world
**“and the labour of my hands,”** — of my fellow workers
**“God beheld”** — who did not leave me alone
**“and rebuked thee yesterday.”** — he held you back before you could harm
31.43: **“Laban answered him:”** — what he did not do because he was held back by the fear of God, he says he let go for the sake of fleshly affection
31.44: **“Come therefore, let us enter into a league: that it may be for a testimony between me and thee.”** — here Laban bears the type of the Gentile people coming to the faith, Jacob that of the faithful Jewish people
31.45:
**“And Jacob took a stone,”** — not to worship it as God, but to signify something in it
**“and set it up for a title:”** — the cornerstone, “who hath made both one”
31.46:
**“And he said to his brethren:”** — to his kinsmen
**“Bring hither stones. And they gathering stones together, made a heap,”** — the gathering of stones is the assembly of the faithful
**“and they ate upon it.”**
• signifying the communion of the sacraments
• Bring hither stones, etc. JEROME. A heap in the Hebrew tongue is called gal, and aad is “witness.” In the Syrian tongue “heap” is ygar, “of witness” sedutha. So Jacob called it in Hebrew “heap of witness,” that is, Galaad; Laban called it “heap of witness,” ygar sedutha, in the speech of his own people. For he was a Syrian, and had changed the tongue of his fathers for the speech of the province in which he lived.
*Isidore:* Mystically, among the faithful, both Jews and Gentiles, the witness is the stone standing high, in the likeness of Christ, and the heap of stones, which is the multitude of believers.
31.47:
**“And Laban called it The witness heap:”** — ygar sedutha
**“and Jacob, The hillock”** — Gal-
**“of testimony”** — -aad
31.48: **“And Laban said:”** — the assembly of the faithful is witness between the believing Gentile and the Jew
31.49: **“The Lord behold and judge between us when we shall be gone one from the other.”** — if we violate the covenant made, even when absent in body
31.50:
**“If thou afflict my daughters,”** — by urging strange gods
**“and if thou bring in other wives”** — heretical sects
**“over them: none is witness of our speech”** — of outsiders; or, because of the witness of God, which they ought to hold as if there were no one with them to be witness
**“but God, who is present and beholdeth.”** — as if: he will be judge who is aware
31.51: **“And he said again to Jacob:”** — he confirms it by repeating
31.53:
**“The God of Abraham, and the God of Nachor,”** — not new
**“the God of their father, judge between us. And Jacob swore by the fear”** — of the Lord
**“of his father Isaac.”** — And Jacob swore, etc. That is, by the fear with which he feared God, whom he commended above, saying: “And the fear of my father,” etc.
31.54:
**“And after he had offered sacrifices”** — the sacraments being shared
**“in the mountain,”** — the hearing of spiritual understanding
**“he called his brethren to eat bread.”** — the eating of bread is the signifying of unity
31.55:
**“But Laban”** — who above signified believers, now apostates
**“arose in the night, and kissed his sons, and daughters, and blessed them: and returned”** — elsewhere: “and he returned”
**“to his place.”** — But Laban, etc. That Laban and Jacob went across the river can signify the two peoples coming to the Church through baptism. But while Jacob goes forward, Laban turns back; because, while the sons of light move on in the progress of virtues after baptism, the reprobate turn back from the dignity they had received, after Satan, into apostasy.

32.1: **“Jacob also went on the journey he had begun:”** — not looking back
32.2:
**“And when he saw them, he said: These are the camps of God,”** — the multitude of angels, which is called the host of heaven; strengthened by them he would not fear his brother, secure in their help
**“and he called the name of that place Mahanaim, that is, Camps.”** — These are the camps of God, etc. Where “camps” is put, in the Hebrew there is Mahanaim; so that we may know, whenever it is put as a translation in another place, what place it signifies. And beautifully, as he is about to go to his hostile brother, he is received by choirs of angels accompanying him.
32.3: **“And he sent messengers before him to Esau his brother to the land of Seir to the country of Edom:”** — past temptations having been overcome, like enemies, and following at our back, future ones threaten, like enemies coming to meet us, which we must forestall by praying and by working well; and to accomplish this the persuasive words of human wisdom are sometimes useful
32.4:
**“And he commanded them, saying: Thus shall ye speak to my lord Esau: Thus saith thy brother Jacob:”** — a sharer of nature, not of grace
**“I have sojourned with Laban, and have been with him until this day.”** — everyone who is a citizen of the heavenly country is a pilgrim in the world for the whole time of the present life
32.5:
**“I have oxen,”** — the wise
**“and asses,”** — the foolish
**“and sheep,”** — the simple
**“and womenservants:”** — for whose weakness provision must be made, lest they be led into temptation
**“and menservants,”** — who serve from fear, not love
32.7:
**“Then Jacob was greatly afraid; and in his fear divided the people that was with him,”** — when danger threatens, let us do what human reason has, lest by committing everything to God we seem to tempt him
**“and the flocks, and the sheep, and the oxen, and the camels, into two companies,”** — Then Jacob was greatly afraid, etc. AUGUSTINE. It can be asked how he had faith in God’s promises, since he said this. But it could have happened that Esau overthrew his camp, and that afterwards, after that affliction, God would be present and fulfil what he promised. And we are warned by this example that, though we believe in God, we should still do what must be done for the protection of our safety. Jacob’s words too are to be considered, when he says: “O God of my father Abraham,” etc.; because in these words both human weakness and the faith of piety appear.
32.9: **“And Jacob said:”** — lest he again ascribe everything to human counsel, he adds prayer; because God’s predestination is helped by prayers
32.10:
**“I am not worthy of the least”** — unworthy
**“of all thy mercies,”** — bestowed on me
**“and of thy truth which thou hast fulfilled to thy servant. With my staff I passed over this Jordan;”** — before it was said, “Baptize all nations,” the people of God leaned on the law, which beat and did not pity
**“I passed over … Jordan”** — Through baptism the wall from the Gentiles was joined to the one from the Jews; yet the early Church did not lack fear of the Jews, whom Esau signifies.
32.11: **“Deliver me from the hand of my brother Esau, for I am greatly afraid of him: lest perhaps he come, and kill the mother with the children.”** — Deliver me from the hand, etc. He prays so as to temper hope with fear and console fear with hope; signifying that we should take thought by reason for our own life and that of our household, and yet call on God’s help.
32.13: **“And when he had slept there that night, he set apart, of the things which he had, presents for his brother Esau.”** — he prepares to appease with gifts the one whom he displeased by his ways
32.14:
**“Two hundred she goats,”** — two, the first principle of otherness, pleases Esau
**“twenty he goats,”** — twenty pleases him because of the doubling of ten
32.16: **“And he sent them by the hands of his servants, every drove by itself,”** — so that the gifts might please by their number as by their size
32.18: **“Thou shalt answer: Thy servant Jacob’s: he hath sent them as a present to my lord Esau: and he cometh after us.”** — so that he might be reconciled by the gifts before he was seen by his brother
32.20:
**“And ye shall add: Thy servant Jacob himself also followeth after us: for he said: I will appease him with the presents that go before, and afterwards I will see him, perhaps he will be gracious to me.”**
• these words were put in by the writer. The order of Jacob’s words is: “I will appease him, and after this I will see his face”
• I will appease him, etc. These words were put in by the writer. For it is not the part of a prudent man to uncover his art, and so make himself suspect to those with whom he deals.
32.21: **“So the presents went before him,”** — he did this prudently, so as to learn his brother’s will through the messengers
32.22: **“And rising early he took his two wives, and his two handmaids, with his eleven sons, and passed over the ford of Jaboc.”** — after the water of salvation, a place of solitude is fit for the Church, so that it may be able to contemplate God
32.24:
**“He remained alone: and behold a man wrestled with him till morning.”**
• because in contemplation, as in wrestling, now the sweetness of God is in some way embraced, now it overcomes, so that it is not felt
• And behold a man, etc. GREGORY. Mystically. Jacob, when he returns to his own parents, finds on the way an angel, with whom he had a great contest in wrestling. And whoever wrestles finds himself sometimes above, sometimes below. So the angel signifies God, and Jacob, who strives with him, expresses the soul of the contemplative man; which, when it strives to contemplate God, as in a contest, now seems to overcome, because by understanding and feeling it tastes something of the boundless light; and now gives way, because in tasting it fails again. So the angel is overcome, as it were, when God is grasped by the inmost understanding. But it is to be noted that the same angel, overcome, touched the sinew and made it wither, and from then on Jacob limped on one foot; because almighty God, when he is known by understanding and desire, dries up the pleasure of the flesh. And we who before seemed to seek him leaning, as it were, on two feet, and to hold the world, after knowing the sweetness of God have one foot that remains sound in us, while the other limps; because, the love of the world being weakened, the love of God alone grows strong. So if we hold the angel, we limp on one foot; because while the strength of inward love grows in us, the strength of the flesh is weakened. For he who limps leans only on the sound foot; for he in whom earthly desire is dried up supports himself with all his strength on the foot of the love of God alone, and stands on it; because the foot of the love of the world, which he used to set on the earth, he now carries lifted up. So if we return to our spiritual fathers, let us hold the angel on the way, so as to lay hold on God by inward sweetness.
*Isidore:* And behold a man, etc. In this chiefly is figured the image of the Lord’s sacrament. For that man signifies Christ, over whom, because he willed it, Jacob prevailed, so as to signify the mystery of the passion, in which Jacob, in the offspring of his body, was seen to prevail over God; and to engage in wrestling with his flesh as with a weak man, and to grow strong, when they said: “Crucify him, crucify him.” And yet Jacob obtained a blessing from the angel whom he had overcome; for the giving of the name was the blessing. And Israel is interpreted “seeing God,” which will be in the end the reward of all the saints. The angel touched the breadth of his thigh and made him lame. And so he was both blessed and lame: blessed in the faithful, and lame in the unfaithful. For the sinew or breadth of the thigh is the multitude of his race. For many, degenerating from the faith of the fathers and straying from the precepts of their author, limp in the paths of their error. Hence: “And they have halted from their paths.” And that people, its strength being touched, not only limps but grows numb, so that it can no longer beget.
32.25: **“And when he saw that he could not overcome him, he touched the sinew of his thigh, and forthwith it shrank.”** — because in the contemplative the use of propagating mortality is done away
32.26:
**“And he said to him: Let me go, for it is break of day.”** — as if: it is time for you to come down from the invisible to deal with temporal things
**“He answered: I will not let thee go except thou bless me.”** — because the soul that tastes the inward sweetness always desires to stay in it
32.27:
**“And he said: What is thy name?”** — as if he did not know his former state
**“He answered: Jacob.”** — “wrestler”
32.28:
**“But he said: Thy name shall not be called Jacob,”** — as if: you will be called not a wrestler but a victor, because you persevered in knocking
**“but Israel:”** — the change of name is a blessing
**“for if thou hast been strong against God,”** — persevering in knocking
**“how much more shalt thou prevail against men?”**
• against Esau, whom you fear
• Thy name shall not be called, etc. JEROME. Josephus, in the first book of the Antiquities, thinks he was called Israel because he stood against the angel. But I could not find this in the Hebrew; rather the angel set down the etymology of the name, saying: “For if thou hast been strong against God,” etc. For saruch, which is derived from the word Israel, means “prince.” As if: Your name shall not be called “supplanter,” that is, Jacob, but “prince with God,” that is, Israel. For as I am a prince, so you too, who could wrestle with me, will be called a prince. And if you could fight with me, who am God, or an angel (for many interpret it variously), how much more with men, that is, with Esau, whom you need not fear? As for its being interpreted in the book of Hebrew names, “Israel, a man seeing God,” or “a mind seeing God,” it seems interpreted not so much truly as forcedly. For here Israel is written with these letters: iod, sin, res, aleph, lamed, which is interpreted “prince God” or “straight God.” But “a man seeing God” is written with these letters: “man” is written with three letters, aleph, iod, sin, and is pronounced is; “seeing” with three, res, aleph, he, and is pronounced raa; and el with two, aleph and lamed, and is interpreted “God” or “strong.” So although those who translated Israel as “a man” or “a mind seeing God” are of great authority, and the shadow of their eloquence weighs upon us, we are led rather by the authority of Scripture, and of the angel or God who called him Israel, than by that of any worldly eloquence.
32.30:
**“And Jacob called the name of the place Phanuel, saying: I have seen God face to face, and my soul has been saved.”** — And Jacob called, etc. That too which follows, “And he blessed him there, and Jacob called the name of that place The face of God,” etc.: in the Hebrew it is called Phanuel, so that we may know it is the same place which in the other volumes of Scripture, according to the Hebrews, is read Phanuel.
*Gregory:* It is asked, since the Truth says, “Man shall not see my face,” and “No man hath seen God at any time,” how Jacob testifies, “I have seen God face to face.” For human minds, when the inner eye has been cleansed, when the rust of the vices has been burned away by the fire of tribulation, behold the joy of the heavenly country; so that we may first cleanse by mourning what we have done, and afterwards contemplate the joys we seek. For first, as sorrow burns, the mist is wiped away, and so the mind is enlightened by the boundless light flashing for a moment. In this joy it is swallowed up in a certain security, and as if, after the failing of the present life, caught up beyond itself, it is refreshed in a certain newness. There the mind is sprinkled with dew from above from the boundless fount of vision. There it beholds that it is not sufficient for that to which it is caught up; and, perceiving the truth, it sees that it does not see how great the truth is; and it reckons itself the farther from it the nearer it approaches; because unless it beheld it in some way, it would not perceive that it cannot behold it. So the sight of the soul, while it strains, is beaten back by the flashing of immensity. For that light, filling all things, surrounds all things; and therefore the mind does not widen itself to grasp the uncircumscribed substance, which the poverty of its own circumscription narrows. Hence it quickly slips back to itself, and having looked on certain traces of variety, it is called back to its own inner places. And this, when it is done through contemplation, is not a solid and lasting vision, but a sort of imitation of vision, and is called the face of God. For because we recognise anyone by his face, we call the knowledge of God his face. So Jacob, after he wrestled with the angel, says: “I have seen the Lord face to face”; as if: I have known God, because he deigned to know me. This knowledge will be made most full at the end. Hence: “Then I shall know even as I am known.”

33.1: **“and he divided”** — AQUILA: “He halved them,” so as to make one band of the handmaids with their little ones, and another of the free women with their sons; and to send the handmaids first, the free women second; while he himself, before them all, went to meet his brother to bow down to him.
33.10: **“And Jacob said: Do not so I beseech thee, but if I have found favour in thy eyes, receive a little present at my hands: for I have seen thy face, as if I should have seen the countenance of God: be gracious to me,”** — For I have seen thy face, etc. AUGUSTINE. Did the words of a fearful and troubled mind break out into this flattery, or could they be said without sin? For perhaps, since the gods of the Gentiles, which are demons, are also so called, no prejudice arises from these words against the man of God; because, if these brotherly words were said with a kindly mind, since after the good reception his fear had passed, it could be said in the way that Moses was called a god to Pharao, according to the saying of the Apostle: “For although there be that are called gods, either in heaven or on earth,” etc.; especially since it is said in the Greek without the article, by which the true God is most plainly signified. For he did not say prosopon tou theou, but prosopon theou; which those who are used to hearing and understanding Greek readily understand.
33.14: **“May it please my lord to go before his servant: and I will follow softly after him, as I shall see my children to be able, until I come to my lord in Seir.”** — And I will follow, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is asked whether he promised his brother a lie. For, as Scripture tells, he did not do this, but went on by the road that led to his own people. Or perhaps he promised with a truthful mind, but afterwards, on further thought, chose otherwise.
33.17: **“Socoth”** — JEROME. Where we have “tents,” in the Hebrew is read Socoth. And to this day there is a city across the Jordan by this name, in the district of Scythopolis, about which we wrote in the book of places.
33.18: **“And he passed over to Salem, a city of the Sichemites, which is in the land of Chanaan, after he returned from Mesopotamia of Syria: and he dwelt by the town:”** — And he passed over to Salem, etc. JEROME. A difficulty arises how Sichem is called the city Salem, since Jerusalem, in which Melchisedech reigned, was formerly called Salem. So either both cities are of one name, as we find of many places in Judea, that the same name of city and place is in one tribe and another; or we shall say that this Salem, which is now named for Sichem, is interpreted “finished and perfect,” and the one afterwards called Jerusalem, “peaceful.” This word sounds both, with the accent slightly changed. The Hebrews hand down that the thigh of the limping Jacob was healed there, and that therefore the city gained the name of “healed and perfected.”

34.1:
**“And Dina … went out”** — the weak soul, which, setting aside its own affairs, takes care of other people’s business
**“the daughter of Lia … to see the women of that country.”** — conducting themselves carelessly
**“And … went out”** — GREGORY. Dina goes out to see the women of a foreign country when the mind, neglecting its own pursuits and caring for the actions of others, wanders outside its proper order. Sichem, the prince of the land, overpowers her, because the devil corrupts the mind he finds in outward cares. “And his soul was fast knit unto her,” because he regards it as united to himself through iniquity. And because the mind, coming to its senses from guilt, is moved and tries to weep for what it has committed, the corrupter calls up before its eyes an empty hope and security, so as to take away the profit of sorrow. Hence it is added: “Whereas she was sad, he comforted her with sweet words.” For now he speaks of other people’s graver deeds, now says that what was done is nothing, now that God is merciful, and promises time for penance; so that, while the deceived mind is led on by these things, penance may be put off; so that then it may receive no good things, which now no evil things sadden, and then be more fully swallowed up in torments, which now rejoices in delights.
**“Dina”** — Which is interpreted “that judgment.” For this is the judgment: that because it wanders carelessly of its own accord, it is soon corrupted by the devil.
34.2:
**“And when Sichem the son of Hemor the Hevite,”** — the devil, or the heretic
**“the prince of that land, saw her, he was in love with”** — to lead astray
**“her: and took her away, and lay with her,”** — so as to draw it by temptation and wicked persuasion to his own pursuits; according to that: “Evil communications corrupt good manners”
**“lay with her”** — AUGUSTINE. “And he set his heart on the soul of Dina, Jacob’s daughter, and loved the virgin, and spoke to the virgin’s mind.” How is she called a virgin if he had already lain with her? Unless perhaps “virgin” is a name of age in the Hebrew idiom; or rather, by recapitulation, what was done before is mentioned after. For he could first have set his heart on her soul, and loved the virgin, and spoken to the virgin’s mind, and then lain with her.
34.3:
**“And … was fast knit”** — by habit
**“his soul … unto her,”** — there was made one consent in wickedness
**“and whereas she was sad, he comforted her with sweet words.”** — by promising impunity
34.7: **“Behold his sons came from the field:”** — free of their sister’s corruption
34.8: **“And Hemor spoke to them:”** — so evil spirits, or the authors of wicked doctrine, strive through the corruption of one soul to corrupt many
34.10: **“And dwell with us:”** — the mutual joining of daughters with the undisciplined is the prostitution of seduced and seducing souls to divers schisms
34.12: **“Raise the dowry, and ask gifts,”** — for fleshly dealings fleshly gifts are promised, by which the corrupted soul, delighted, is pressed less toward correction
34.14: **“We cannot do what you demand, nor give our sister to one that is uncircumcised, which with us is unlawful and abominable.”** — as if: “What concord hath Christ with Belial? What agreement hath the temple of God with idols?”
34.15: **“But in this we may be allied with you, if you will be like us, and all the male sex among you be circumcised:”** — outsiders are not admitted to the fellowship of the Church otherwise than if they renounce the devil and share in the sacraments of the Church
34.18: **“Their offer pleased Hemor, and Sichem his son:”** — the ministers of Satan, like their prince, transform themselves into ministers of justice, so as to deceive souls by their superstition
34.20: **“And going into the gate of the city they spoke to the people:”** — or “to the people”
34.21:
**“These men are peaceable”** — in the Hebrew salamim; whence it is plain that what we said above about Salem is true
**“peaceable”** — Where the Septuagint translated “peaceable,” Aquila rendered “finished and perfect,” for which in the Hebrew is read salamim. From which it appears that what we said above about Salem is true.
34.24:
**“And they all agreed, and circumcised all the males.”**
• such were some in the early Church, who said that circumcision and Jewish rites were necessary to the Christian religion; to whom it is said: “If you be circumcised, Christ shall profit you nothing.” These Paul, at the council that was held, slew as in the pain of circumcision, when he separated them by the sword of the spirit from the fellowship of the faithful
• And they all agreed, etc. AUGUSTINE. A little before, Jacob, speaking with Esau, indicates that his sons are children. So it can be asked how they could make such a slaughter, even though the others were in the pain of circumcision. But it must be understood that Jacob lived here a long time, until his daughter grew older and his sons became young men. For it is written: “And he dwelt by the town, and bought the part of the field in which he had pitched his tents of the sons of Hemor, the father of Sichem, for a hundred lambs; and raising an altar there, he invoked upon it the most mighty God of Israel. And Dina the daughter of Lia went out to see the women of that country,” etc. So it appears from these words that Jacob did not stay there in passing, but bought a field, set up a tent and an altar, and so lived there for some time; and that his daughter, when she was already able to have friends, wished to get to know the daughters of the citizens of the place; and that so the slaughter and plunder were done on her account. For the company with Jacob, who had become very rich, was not small; but his sons are named in this deed as its leaders and authors.
34.25: **“And behold the third day, when the pain of the wound was greatest, two of the sons of Jacob, Simeon and Levi, the brothers of Dina, taking their swords, entered boldly into the city, and slew all the men:”** — Taking … two, etc. STRABO. So the shepherds of the Church ought to avenge the sin of the flesh or of the soul with the sword of the spirit, which is the word of God, “being ready to revenge all disobedience.”
34.26: **“And they killed also Hemor and Sichem, and took away their sister Dina, out of Sichem’s house.”** — taking away the soul deceived by heretical wickedness from the fellowship of the devil. Yet this was in itself a crime, which displeased Jacob too; but in the Church it was a prophecy
34.30: **“And when they had boldly perpetrated these things, Jacob said to Simeon and Levi: You have troubled me, and made me hateful to the Chanaanites and Pherezites, the inhabitants of this land: we are few: they will gather themselves together and kill me; and both I, and my house, shall be destroyed.”** — For we are few, etc. AUGUSTINE. He says this because very many wars could arise; not that he had much fewer than would suffice for storming a city.
34.31: **“They answered: Should they abuse our sister as a strumpet?”** — Should they abuse our sister as a strumpet? etc. AUGUSTINE. The zeal of Jacob’s sons in avenging their sister warns the shepherds of the faithful, in the moral sense, to take care of the souls entrusted to them, lest they be violated by bodily sin or by spiritual fornication; and to be ready to avenge all disobedience, and to strike the defiler with the sword of excommunication, lest he escape unpunished.

35.1:
**“In the meantime God said to Jacob: Arise, and go up to Bethel, and dwell there,”** — the house of the devil being destroyed, one must return to the house of God
**“and make there an altar to God, who appeared to thee when thou didst flee from Esau thy brother.”** — he does not say “to me, who appeared to thee,” because perhaps the Son appeared there and the Father says this; or it is to be counted as some figure of speech
35.2:
**“And Jacob having called together all his household, said: Cast away the strange gods that are among you,”** — in the house of God there must be no idols
**“and be cleansed”** — within
**“and change your garments.”** — without
35.3:
**“Arise, and let us go up to Bethel,”** — “be ye built up, … spiritual houses”
**“that we may make there an altar to God:”** — our heart
35.4:
**“So they gave him all the strange gods they had, and the earrings which were in their ears:”** — the amulets of the idols
**“and he buried them under the turpentine tree, that is behind the city of Sichem.”**
• because avarice, which is the service of idols, lies hidden in the hearts of the earthly
• And the earrings which, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is asked why earrings. If they were ornaments, they did not belong to idolatry; but it is to be understood that they were amulets of the strange gods.
35.5: **“And when they were departed, the terror of God fell upon all the cities round about,”** — sent by God, who was guarding his promises in Jacob and his sons
35.6:
**“And Jacob came to Luza, which is in the land of Chanaan, surnamed Bethel: he and all the people that were with him.”** — And Jacob came, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is to be noted that three names of this city are mentioned: Ulammaus, as it was first called when Jacob came there going into Mesopotamia; Bethel, which Jacob himself gave it; and Luza. Nor is it strange; for to many cities and rivers, as to men themselves, names are added or changed for many reasons.
*Jerome:* And Jacob came, etc. See, it is most plainly proved that Bethel was formerly called not Ulam, as was said above, but Luza, that is, “almond.”
35.10:
**“Saying: Thou shalt not be called any more Jacob,”** — wrestling in a dark manner
**“but Israel shall be thy name.”** — this will be at last when we shall see him as he is
**“And he called him Israel.”** — Thou shalt not be called, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is asked, since it was once said, “Thou shalt not be called any more Jacob,” etc., why we read that he was called Jacob afterwards. But this name belongs to that promise in which God is seen as he was not seen before by the fathers; where the old name will not be, because nothing of oldness will remain even in the body itself, and the vision of God will be the highest reward.
*Jerome:* Thou shalt not be called any more, etc. For the name is not yet given him by the angel, but foretold as to be given by God. So what is promised there as to come is shown here to be fulfilled.
35.11:
**“And said to him: I am God Almighty, increase thou”** — by your succession, up to the excellence of the kingdom
**“and be multiplied.”** — in number
**“Nations and peoples of nations shall be from thee,”** — according to the flesh; peoples according to faith
**“and kings”** — the saints, ruling themselves and their subjects well
**“increase thou and be multiplied”** — This promise belongs to the spiritual seed of Jacob, as was already said before of Abraham. For all who supplant vices, and put off the old man with his deeds, and turn the eyes of the mind toward God, rightly belong to Jacob, whose faith and deeds they imitate. And kings come out of his loins, that is, the saints, who according to the will of God truly rule themselves and their subjects, and who are made fruitful in good works from his spiritual seed, that is, from the imitation of his faith.
35.12:
**“And the land which I gave to Abraham and Isaac, I will give to thee,”** — in hope
**“and to thy seed”** — in reality
35.14:
**“But he set up a monument of stone, in the place where God had spoken to him:”**
• as a type of the figure of the Church
• what had been done before is recalled here
**“pouring drink offerings upon it,”** — not to it, as idolaters do
**“and pouring oil thereon:”**
• foreshadowing the sacraments of the Church to come
• But he set up, etc. AUGUSTINE. Either what had been done before was done again in this place, or what had been done before is recalled here. But whichever of these it is, Jacob poured the offering upon the stone, not to the stone. So he did not do as idolaters are wont, who set up altars before a stone and pour offerings to the stone as to a god.
35.16:
**“And going forth from thence, he came in the springtime”** — in which the world was made; also signifying newness of life
**“to the land which leadeth to Ephrata:”** — which is interpreted “fruitful,” because there the bread of life was born; this is Bethlehem
**“Ephrata”** — JEROME. Ephrata and Bethlehem are the name of one city, with a like interpretation; for it is interpreted “fruitful” and “house of bread,” because of the bread which came down from heaven.
35.18:
**“And when her soul was departing for pain, and death was now at hand, she called the name of her son Benoni, that is, The son of my pain:”** — signifying Paul, who was to be born of his tribe, who calls himself “one born out of due time,” that is, born into the Church by force
**“but his father called him Benjamin, that is, The son of the right hand.”**
• because he was to be moved from the left to the right, that is, from persecutor was to become apostle
• And when her soul was departing, etc. ISIDORE. What does it mean that Rachel, when she gave birth, called the same child Benoni, “son of my pain,” unless that from that tribe Paul was to come, who would afflict the sons of the Church in the time of his persecution? Otherwise: by Benjamin the earthly Jerusalem is figured, which is in the tribe of Benjamin; whose people afflicted their mother with grievous pain by shedding the blood of the prophets, and by crying out for the death of Christ: “His blood be upon us and upon our children.”
*Jerome:* “And it came to pass, when she was giving up her soul, for she was dying, she called his name Son of my pain; but his father called his name Benjamin.” In the Hebrew the likeness of the names rings out. For “son of my pain,” the name his dying mother gave, is said benoni; but “son of the right hand,” that is, of strength, to which Jacob changed it, benjamin. Hence those err who think Benjamin is interpreted “son of days.” For the right hand is called iamin and ends in n; but days are called iamim and end in m.
35.19: **“So Rachel died, and was buried in the highway that leadeth to Ephrata, this is Bethlehem.”** — “house of bread”
35.21:
**“Departing thence, he pitched his tent”** — signifying the present Church, where at the Lord’s birth the angels sang, “Glory to God in the highest”
**“beyond the Flock tower.”**
• that is, Ader
• Departing thence, he pitched, etc. JEROME. The Hebrews will have it that this is the place where the temple was afterwards built, and that the tower Ader means “tower of the flock,” that is, of the gathering and assembly. Hence Micheas: “And thou, O cloudy tower of the flock of the daughter of Sion,” etc. And at that time Jacob is said to have had his tents beyond the place where the temple was afterwards built. But if we follow the order of the road, there is a place of shepherds near Bethlehem, where either the flock of angels sang at the Lord’s birth, or Jacob fed his flocks, giving the place its name; or, what is truer, by a kind of prophecy the mystery to come was even then being shown.
35.22:
**“And when he dwelt in that country, Ruben went, and slept with Bala, the concubine of his father:”** — in this is signified the malice of the Jewish people, who defiled the law, which begot into bondage, like a concubine, by abusing it carnally
**“which he was not ignorant of. Now the sons of Jacob were twelve.”**
• signifying the apostolic number
• Ruben went, etc. ISIDORE. This crime would not have been written unless the perversity of the people to come were being foretold. Though in him it was a shameful deed, in the Scriptures it is a prophecy of things to come; because by Ruben is figured the firstborn people Israel, which polluted the bed of the concubine, that is, stained the law of the Old Testament by transgressing it. And that the concubine signified the Old Testament Paul shows, saying: “Abraham had two sons, the one by a bondwoman, and the other by a free woman,” etc.
• Now the sons, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is asked how this is true, since Benjamin was born long afterwards, when they had already passed Bethel and were drawing near to Bethlehem. But it is understood to be said so, when the twelve sons have been mentioned: “These are the sons of Jacob that were born to him in Mesopotamia of Syria”; because among many there was only one not born there, who yet had from there the cause of his birth, because there his mother was joined to his father. For there is no easier solution of this question than to take it by synecdoche.
35.27: **“the city of Arbee”** — JEROME. For Arbee the Septuagint has “plain,” though Hebron is on a mountain. And the same city was anciently called Mambre, from the friend of Abraham.
35.29:
**“And being spent with age”** — that is, full of years
**“he died, and was gathered to his people,”** — of the angels, or of holy souls
**“being old and full of days: and his sons Esau and Jacob buried him.”** — To his people. JEROME. Of the angels, or of holy souls; to whom he was gathered, no anxiety of temptations or danger of sins remaining.

36.2: **“Esau took wives of the daughters of Chanaan:”** — a recapitulation; for this was done before Isaac’s death
36.4: **“And Ada bore Eliphaz:”** — whom the Scripture remembers in Job
36.6: **“went into another country”** — STRABO. It can be asked why Esau is said, after his father’s death, to have gone off to Seir and withdrawn from his brother, when he is already said to have been living there when Jacob came to Seir. But it could have happened that, when Jacob fled into Mesopotamia, Esau, in grief at the blessing snatched from him, withdrew from his father and lived in Seir for the twenty years Jacob was away; and, reconciled to him on his return, came back again from Seir with his brother while his father lived; and when he died, withdrew from his brother, because they were rich and could not dwell together.
36.10: **“And these the names of his sons: Eliphaz”** — the Themanite
36.20:
**“These are the sons of Seir the Horrite, the inhabitants of the land:”** — that is, “free men,” whom the Idumeans drove out, and dwelt in their place
**“Lotan, and Sobal, and Sebeon, and Ana,”** — These are the sons of Seir, etc. JEROME. After he has listed the sons of Esau, he goes further back to those who were princes in the land of Edom before Esau, of the race of the Horrites, which is interpreted “free men.” In Deuteronomy it is written more plainly how the sons of Esau came and, having killed the Horrites, inherited their land.
*Strabo:* The sons of Seir, etc. That is, the “free men,” who, as is read in Paralipomenon, first dwelt in mount Seir; and when they were driven out, the Idumeans dwelt in their place.
36.22: **“And the sister … was”** — JEROME. This is the Thamna of whom it was said above, “And Thamna was the concubine of Eliphaz, the firstborn of Esau,” etc. The Horrites are recalled for this reason, that the firstborn of Esau’s sons took a concubine from their daughters. And as for the names Theman and Cenez and Amalech and the rest, let us know that afterwards the regions and peoples of the Idumeans were named from them.
36.24:
**“And these the sons of Sebeon: Aia and Ana. This is Ana that found the hot waters in the wilderness, when he fed the asses of Sebeon his father:”** — This is Ana, etc. STRABO. Some say simply that he found in the desert hot waters, which we call thermae.
*Jerome:* “This is Ana, who found iamim in the desert, when he fed the asses of Sebeon his father.” Various things are argued among the Hebrews about this passage; among the Greeks and our own writers there is silence. Some think the seas are meant, for it is written with the same letters; and they will have it that, while feeding the asses, he found gatherings of waters, which by the idiom of the Hebrew tongue are called seas, because he found a pool, which is hard to find in the desert. Some think hot waters are signified by this name in the Punic tongue, which borders on the Hebrew. There are those who reckon that he put wild asses to the she-asses, and found a mating of such a kind that very swift asses were born, which are called iamim. Others say that he was the first to have herds of mares covered by asses, so that mules were born against nature.
36.29: **“These were dukes”** — He speaks of those before, who are of Seir; not of those whom he begins to number here, who are of Esau.
36.31:
**“And the kings”**
• It is to be known that he does not mention all the kings that there were before the sons of Israel had kings, of whom the first was Saul, but only all those who reigned before Moses died.
• He speaks according to the time in which the writer lived. For when Seir, who begot these, lived there, Esau had not yet come into that land, and it was not yet called the land of Edom after him.
*Augustine:* It is not strange that, counting from Abraham through Esau, the father of the people of Edom (to whom, through Rahuel the son of Esau, and Zara the son of Rahuel, and Jobab the son of Zara, whom Bela succeeded, who was the first king in the land of Edom, down to the last king whom Moses could name), more generations are found than are counted from Abraham through Jacob down to Moses. For there about twelve are found, but here, down to Moses, about seven. For it could have happened that more are named there because, dying sooner, more succeeded one another. So it happened that Matthew, following one line, counts forty-two generations from Abraham to Joseph; Luke, by another line, not through Solomon as he did but through Nathan, seventy-six. For in the line where more are counted they died sooner than here, where fewer.
36.32: **“Bela the son of Beor,”** — not the one who, as is read in the Book of Numbers, hired Balaam the soothsayer; for he was king of Moab and the son of Sephor; this one was king in Seir and the son of Beor
36.34: **“Husam”** — JEROME. Whom some suspect to be Job, as is added at the end of his book. But the Hebrews assert that he was born of the stock of Nachor, as was said above.
36.35: **“And after his death, Adad the son of Badad reigned in his stead, who defeated the Madianites in the country of Moab:”** — or Cophin

37.2:
**“And these are his generations: Joseph,”** — Christ
**“when he was sixteen years old,”**
• which he began to be before Isaac’s death
• that is, of perfect life and teaching
**“was feeding”** — with the bread of the Gospel
**“the flock”** — the sheep entrusted to him by his father
**“with his brethren,”** — the apostles
**“being but a boy: and he was with the sons of Bala and of Zelpha his father’s wives: and he accused his brethren to his father of a most wicked crime.”**
• which is hatred of a brother; or that they had dealings with the cattle; or he accused Ruben alone, for his father’s concubine, so that by synecdoche we take the whole for the part; for he did not accuse them all
• Joseph, when he was sixteen, etc. AUGUSTINE. How the death of Isaac could find Joseph seventeen years old, as Scripture seems to tell in its order, is hard to find. For if he was seventeen after the death of his grandfather Isaac when his brothers sold him into Egypt, his father Jacob was a hundred and twenty years old in the seventeenth year of his son Joseph. For Isaac begot him when he was sixty years old, as it is written. So Isaac lived afterwards a hundred and twenty years, because he died in his hundred and eightieth year. Therefore he left his sons a hundred and twenty years old, and Joseph seventeen. But Joseph was thirty years old when he appeared in Pharao’s sight. Then followed the seven years of plenty and two of famine, until his father came to him with his brothers. So Joseph was thirty-nine when Jacob entered Egypt, who then, as he told Pharao, was in his hundred and thirtieth year of age. But Jacob was a hundred and twenty years old when Joseph was seventeen; which cannot be true. For if in Joseph’s seventeenth year Jacob was a hundred and twenty, in Joseph’s thirty-ninth year he was not a hundred and thirty but a hundred and forty-two. And if on the day of Isaac’s death Joseph was not yet seventeen, but reached his seventeenth year some time after his grandfather’s death, in which year, as Scripture testifies, he was sold into Egypt, his father must have been more than a hundred and forty-two when he followed his son into Egypt. For Scripture, after it told of the last year of Isaac’s life, the hundred and eightieth, and of his death and burial, then recorded how Esau went away from his brother from the land of Chanaan to mount Seir, and wove in the record of the kings and princes of the people which Esau established or propagated; and afterwards brought in this about Joseph: “And Jacob dwelt in the land of Chanaan; and these are the generations of Jacob: Joseph was seventeen years old, feeding the sheep with his brothers.” Then are told the causes of the dreams, how he was made hateful to his brothers and was sold. So either in that same seventeenth year, or somewhat older, he came into Egypt; and either way the question remains. For if he was seventeen after his grandfather’s death, when his father was a hundred and twenty, then certainly in his thirty-ninth year, when Jacob came into Egypt, the same Jacob must have been in his hundred and forty-second year; but he was a hundred and thirty. So if Joseph was sold at seventeen, he is found to have been sold twelve years before his grandfather died. For he could not have been seventeen except twelve years before the death of Isaac, in the hundred and eighth year of his father Jacob’s life. For when we add to these the twenty-two years he spent in Egypt until his father’s coming, Joseph’s years will be thirty-nine and Jacob’s a hundred and thirty, and there will be no question. But because Scripture told these things after Isaac’s death, Joseph is thought to have been seventeen after his death. Let us understand, then, that Scripture was silent about the life of Isaac, as being very decrepit, while it spoke of Jacob and his sons; and yet Joseph began to be seventeen while Isaac was alive.
• And he was with, etc. In the early Church he did not cast off even those who cleaved to him through the preaching of the false apostles, whom Jacob’s handmaids signify; whom he would not have forbidden when they did miracles in his name.
**“and he was with the sons”** — Joseph, one of the twelve sons of Jacob, loved by his father above the rest, signified Christ, whom God the Father preferred, born according to the flesh, to the other brothers begotten of the stock of Abraham. Hence: “Jacob loved him, because he had begotten him in his old age.” For when the world was growing old, the Son of God was born of a virgin, as the son of old age.
37.3:
**“Now Israel”** — God the Father
**“loved Joseph”** — Christ
**“above all his sons,”** — in the human race
**“because he had him in his old age:”** — that is, he had made him become flesh in the old age of the world
**“and he made him a coat of divers colours.”**
• through the grace of the virtues
• allegorically: a coat of divers colours, that is, the variety of peoples gathered from all nations into the body of Christ
• the Church cleaving to him from all nations
**“he made him a coat”** — JEROME. For the coat of divers colours Aquila translated astragaleion, that is, reaching to the ankles; Symmachus, sleeved; either because it came down to the ankles and was marked out with a wonderful variety by the craftsman’s hands, or because it had sleeves. For the ancients mostly used colobia, that is, garments without sleeves.
*Gregory:* Because Joseph is described as having persevered as a just man among his brothers to the end of his life, he alone is said to have had a coat reaching to the ankles. What is a coat reaching to the ankles but action brought to completion? For the coat, stretched out as it were, covers the ankle of the body when good action rules us before the eyes of God to the end of life. Hence Moses commanded the tail of the victim to be offered, so that we may complete the good work we begin with a persevering end.
37.4:
**“And his brethren seeing”** — the Jews according to the flesh
**“that he was loved by his father,”** — God
**“more than all his sons, hated him, and could not speak peaceably to him.”**
• “This man is not of God, who keepeth not the sabbath”
• And his brethren seeing, etc. The brothers of Christ according to the flesh are the Jews, from whose kindred he took flesh. But because they saw that the grace of virtues was at work in him, which testified to the Father’s special love, they envied him, and could not speak anything peaceably to him, and often laid snares for him, and blasphemed the father of the household, saying that he cast out devils by Beelzebub, the prince of the devils.
37.6: **“And he said to them:”** — elsewhere: “Joseph said to his brethren”
37.7:
**“I thought we were binding sheaves in the field: and … arose as it were,”** — in the resurrection
**“my sheaf … and stood, and your sheaves standing about, bowed down before my sheaf.”**
• to Christ “every knee should bow, of those that are in heaven, on earth, and under the earth”
• I thought we were binding, etc. ISIDORE. This was fulfilled spiritually in Christ. Hence: “All kings shall adore him; all nations shall serve him,” that is, through faith, offering the sheaves of good works. He it is whom sun and moon and stars adore, according to that: “Praise ye him, O sun and moon; praise him, all ye stars and light.” For the excellence of the saints adores him, as the sun; and the brightness of the Church, as the moon; and the multitude of all peoples, in the figure of the stars.
37.8:
**“His brethren answered: Shalt thou be our king? or shall we be subject to thy dominion?”** — as if the Jews said: “We have no king but Caesar”
**“Therefore this matter of his dreams and words ministered nourishment to their envy”** — because he applied the prophecies to himself, saying: “Moses wrote of me,” and the prophets
37.9:
**“He dreamed also another dream, which he told his brethren, saying:”** — the confirmation of things to come is repeated through other images
**“I saw in a dream, as it were the sun,”** — the excellence of the saints
**“and the moon,”** — the brightness of the Church
**“and eleven stars”** — the multitude of peoples
37.10:
**“And when he had told this to his father and brethren, his father rebuked him,”** — this rebuke signifies the hardness of the Jews, who despise Christ because they know he was born from among them
**“and said: What meaneth this dream that thou hast dreamed? shall”** — or “shall”
**“I”** — as the sun
**“and thy mother,”** — as the moon
**“and thy brethren”** — as the stars
**“worship thee upon the earth?”** — Shall I, etc. It can be asked, according to the letter, when he was adored by his father, who is signified by the sun, and by his mother, who is signified by the moon. For Jacob is not read to have adored him when he went down into Egypt, and his mother was already dead. But let us run back to the allegory, which is fulfilled in Christ.
37.11: **“His brethren therefore envied him:”** — the Pharisees
37.12:
**“And when his brethren”** — the Pharisees
**“feeding … flocks,”** — the peoples subject to them
**“abode in Sichem … their father’s”**
• which is interpreted “shoulder,” because they were weighed down by the burden of the law
• And when his brethren, etc., as far as “bring me word,” etc. ISIDORE. Jacob sends his son to take care of his brothers, and God the Father his only-begotten Son to visit the human race, sick with sins. Hence: “God sent his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh.” Joseph was sent to see whether all things were well with the sheep; and Christ says: “I was not sent but to the sheep that are lost of the house of Israel.”
37.13:
**“Israel said to him:”** — God the Father
**“Thy brethren”** — to visit whom the Father sent the Son, to take care of them
**“feed the sheep in Sichem:”** — weighed down by the burden of the law
**“come, I will send thee”** — made flesh
**“to them.”** — to visit them
37.14:
**“I am ready:”** — obedient without delay
**“he said to him: Go, and see”** — to see “if there be any that understand and seek God”
**“if all things be well with thy brethren,”** — the Pharisees
**“and the cattle:”** — those subject to them
37.15:
**“And a man found him”** — the prophetic word
**“there wandering in the field,”** — seeking who would know him, and not finding
37.17:
**“And the man said to him:”** — to him who did not find the Jews whom he sought, the prophetic word answered
**“They are departed from this place:”** — “They are all gone aside, they are become unprofitable together,” etc.
**“for I heard them say: Let us go to Dothain.”** — “falling away”
**“And Joseph went forward after his brethren,”** — following the fugitives
**“in Dothain”** — “Falling away.” For those who were thinking of fratricide were in a great falling away.
37.18:
**“And when they saw him afar off, before he came nigh them,”** — because they would not believe
**“they thought to kill him.”** — so the Jews thought to kill Christ, and took counsel, saying, “Crucify him, crucify him”; which is said in other words too: “Let us put wood on his bread”
37.19: **“And said one to another: Behold the dreamer cometh.”** — the Jews count the words of Christ as dreams
37.20:
**“Come, let us kill him,”** — let us blot out his name
**“and cast him into some old pit:”** — into hell
**“and we will say: Some evil beast hath devoured him: and then it shall appear”** — Jewish savagery; hence: “Behold I send you as sheep in the midst of wolves”
**“what his dreams avail him:”** — his idle talk
37.21: **“Ruben”** — The prophetic word, foreseeing this, which Ruben signifies (who is interpreted “vision of the son”), deterred them with prophetic threats, so that they might keep themselves innocent of the blood of Christ, their brother according to the flesh.
37.22:
**“Do not take away his life,”**
• which dies with the flesh
• the truth
**“nor shed his blood:”** — because it is more damnable to deny the truth than to hide it by keeping silent
**“but cast him into this pit,”** — of silence
37.23:
**“And as soon as he came”** — Christ
**“to his brethren,”** — the Jews
**“they forthwith stript him of his outside coat, that was of divers colours:”**
• the flesh he took up, which is perfect in every virtue
• They stript him, etc. ISIDORE. And the Jews stripped Christ by death of the bodily coat, and of divers colours, that is, adorned with the diversity of all the virtues. And they sprinkled the coat with the blood of a kid, because, accusing him with false witnesses, they brought him into the odium of sin. Joseph is put into the pit, that is, into the cistern; and Christ, stripped of his human flesh, went down into hell.
37.24:
**“And cast him into an old pit,”** — into hell
**“where there was no water.”** — refreshment
37.25:
**“And sitting down to eat bread, they saw some Ismaelites on their way coming from Galaad, with their camels, carrying spices, and balm,”** — despisers of the world, who, coming from the Gentiles to the faith, by the testimonies of the law and the prophets laid sweet-smelling and healing poultices on the sick world
**“and myrrh”** — it is a drop from the myrrh tree, and is itself called myrrh
**“they saw some Ismaelites”** — AUGUSTINE. It is asked why Scripture calls the Ismaelites, to whom Joseph was sold, Madianites as well, since Ismael was the son of Abraham by Agar, while the Madianites were by Cethura. Is it because Scripture had said of Abraham that he gave gifts to the sons of his concubines, that is, of Agar and Cethura, and separated them from Isaac his son into the land of the east, and therefore they are to be understood to have made one people? Or is the opinion of the Hebrews true, who say that Agar and Cethura were one?
37.26: **“And Juda said to his brethren:”** — who signifies the believing Jews, who will neither consent to the death of Christ nor bury it in silence, but set out openly to the Gentiles the communion of the faith
37.27: **“It is better that he be sold to the Ismaelites, and that our hands be not defiled: for he is our brother and our flesh. His brethren agreed to his words.”** — because the Jews left Christ to the Gentiles and thrust him away from themselves
37.28:
**“And when the Madianite merchants passed by,”** — a happy merchant, where salvation is bought and life redeemed from death
**“they drew him out of the pit, and sold him”** — as a cheap slave
**“to the Ismaelites, for thirty pieces of silver: and they led him into Egypt.”**
• because the teachers of the faith preached him in the world
• And they sold, etc. JEROME. The Hebrew truth has “pieces of silver”; for the Lord should not be sold for a cheaper metal than Joseph.
**“they drew him out”** — ISIDORE. Joseph, lifted out of the pit, is sold to the Ismaelites; and Christ, coming back from hell, is purchased by all nations through the commerce of faith. The one is sold off for thirty pieces of silver by the counsel of Juda; and the other is sold for the same number by the counsel of Judas Iscariot.
