37.29: **“And Ruben, returning to the pit, found not the boy:”** — and we, when we go back to the prophetic word, see that so it behoved Christ to suffer and to rise again
37.30:
**“And rending his garments he went to his brethren, and said:”** — the sacraments of the law being opened, it is said to the Jews that Christ is risen
**“The boy doth not appear and whither shall I go?”** — as if: because you have made yourselves, or shown yourselves, unworthy of the word of God, I will pass over to the Gentiles
37.31: **“And they took his coat, and dipped it in the blood of a kid, which they had killed:”** — blaspheming his life, they brought him, as far as lay in them, into the suspicion of sin
37.32:
**“Sending some to carry it to their father,”** — because they defamed him among men, they wished to defame him with the Father too, saying that he was not the Son of God
**“and to say: This we have found: see whether it be thy son’s coat, or not.”** — the Father bears witness to the Son: “This is my beloved Son”
37.33:
**“And the father acknowledging it, said: It is … coat,”** — innocence
**“my son’s … an evil wild beast”** — Jewish savagery
**“hath eaten him,”** — according to that: “The zeal of thy house hath eaten me up”
**“a beast hath devoured Joseph.”** — a beastly people
37.34:
**“And tearing his garments,”** — the sacraments being opened
**“he put on”** — every year, by the tradition of the fathers, the Church remembers the sorrow of the apostles at the death of Christ
**“sackcloth, mourning for his son a long time.”**
• the prophetic lament of Jacob for the death of Christ his son: he mourns the perdition of the Jews more than the passion of his son
• And tearing his garments, etc. ISIDORE. Jacob, weeping for the losses of his posterity, mourned as a father for a lost son, and as a prophet for the ruin of the Jews. He tore his garment, which the chief of the priests did at the Lord’s passion. And the veil of the temple too was torn, so that as a prophet he might show both his people stripped and the kingdom divided.
37.35:
**“And all his children being gathered together to comfort their father in his sorrow, he would not receive comfort, but said: I will go down to my son … mourning.”** — because the Father’s power through the Son defeated hell
**“into hell,”** — for the blindness of the Jews
**“And whilst he continued weeping,”**
• the hardened faithlessness of the Jews
• I will go down, mourning, into hell, etc. It is asked how this is to be understood: whether only the wicked go down into hell, or the good also. If only the wicked, how does he say he wishes to go down mourning to his son? For it is not credible that he is in the pains of hell. Are these the words of a troubled and grieving man, exaggerating even here his own ills? Or is it credible that in hell there were certain hidden and less painful places before the Lord’s passion, to which even the saints went down? For no one could enter paradise until Christ removed the flaming sword.
*Jerome:* “And the Madianites sold Joseph in Egypt to Phutiphar, Pharao’s eunuch, the archimagirus.” Scripture mostly puts archimagiri, that is, chiefs of the cooks, for masters of the army; for magirus in Greek means to kill. So Joseph was sold to the chief of the army and of the warriors, not to Petephres, as is written in the Latin, but to Phutiphar the eunuch. Where it is asked how he is afterwards said to have a wife. The Hebrews hand down that he bought Joseph for his great beauty for a shameful service; and that, after his master’s private parts had withered, he was afterwards taken up, after the custom of the hierophants, that is, of those who speak sacred things, into the priesthood of Heliopolis; and that Aseneth, whom Joseph afterwards took as wife, was his daughter.
37.36:
**“The Madianites sold Joseph in Egypt”** — the teachers from the Gentiles, having received the price of faith, preached Christ in the whole world
**“to Putiphar, an eunuch of Pharao, captain of the soldiers.”** — because a chaste people bought him in the disciplines of the Church, who know how to wage Christian warfare under evil princes

38.1:
**“At that time”** — before Joseph was sold
**“Juda went down from his brethren, and turned in to a certain Odollamite, named Hiras.”**
• At that time, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is asked how these things could have happened. For if it was after Joseph came into Egypt, how could it have happened within twenty-two years (for after so long a time it is gathered that they came with their father to Joseph in Egypt) that the sons of Juda were of an age that they could all take wives? For when his firstborn died he gave Thamar his daughter-in-law to another son; and when he too died she waited for the third to grow up; and when he had grown up he did not give her to him either, fearing that he too would die. Hence it came about that she put herself in the way of her father-in-law himself. How could all these things have happened within so few years, it is rightly asked; unless perhaps, as Scripture is wont, by recapitulation it wishes it to be understood that this began to happen some years before Joseph was sold. For it is put so as to say: “And it came to pass at that time.” Yet here it is asked: if Joseph was sixteen when he was sold, how old could Juda, the fourth son of Jacob, have been, when Ruben, the firstborn himself, could at most have preceded his brother Joseph by five or six years? But Scripture says plainly that Joseph was thirty when he became known to Pharao. So since he is believed to have been sold in his seventeenth year, he had spent thirteen years in Egypt unknown to Pharao. To these thirteen were added the seven years of plenty, and they made twenty. To these are added two years of famine, because in the second year of the famine Jacob entered Egypt with his sons; and these are the twenty-two during which Joseph was away from his father and brothers. How, in that meantime, all that is told of the wife and sons and daughter-in-law of Juda could have happened is hard to find; unless perhaps we believe that as soon as Juda began to grow up he fell in love with the woman he took as wife, before Joseph was sold.
• Juda … from his brethren, etc. Here, like the other patriarchs, he signifies Christ, who went down to the baptism of John. For Hiras is interpreted “seeing God”; Odollamite, “witness in water”; because John, seeing Christ coming to baptism, said: “Behold the Lamb of God.” At this witness the synagogue cleaved to Christ, which the daughter of Sue the Chanaanite signifies; because to her was to be given the land of lowly profession, which is what Chanaan is interpreted. So this synagogue first cleaved to Christ when Peter and Andrew and the other disciples of John became disciples of Christ. The order in which these things were fulfilled the following history signifies, telling how Juda went in to Thamar, who signifies the same as Sue.
38.3: **“And she conceived, and bore a son, and called his name Her.”** — princes who do harm; “of skins”
38.4:
**“And conceiving again, she bore a son, and called him Onan.”**
• useless princes; “their grief”
• And she conceived, etc. The synagogue bore princes who were of use to it like husbands; of whom some were harmful, whom Her signifies, who is interpreted “of skins.” For skin signifies death, because our first parents, clothed in skins, were given over to death. Others were useless, whom Onan signifies, who is interpreted “their grief,” that is, of those whom they do not profit.
38.5:
**“She bore also a third: whom she called Sela.”** — “his letting go”; because the kingdom of the Jews, after it did harm or did not profit, ceased; Judea ceased to have kings
**“also a third”** — ISIDORE. The third son, who is not joined to Thamar, signifies the time from which kings from the tribe of Juda failed that people. He was indeed the son of Juda, but Thamar did not receive him; because the tribe of Juda remained, but no one of it reigned. Hence Sela is interpreted “his letting go.” The holy men do not belong to this signification, who, though they lived at that time, belong to the New Testament, and were useful by prophesying, like David. In that time when Judea had begun not to have kings from Juda, the elder Herod is not to be counted among its kings as a husband of Thamar, since he was a foreigner. She was joined to them by that sacrament of the mystical anointing as by a marriage covenant; but he, a stranger, had received power from the Romans, as had his sons the tetrarchs, of whom one was the Herod who agreed with Pilate at the Lord’s passion. So these foreigners were not reckoned by God in the mystical kingdom of the Jews; so that the Jews themselves cried out publicly: “We have no king but Caesar.” For when the kingdom had failed from the tribe of Juda, the kingdom of Christ was to come, which would do no harm and would profit much. Hence: “The sceptre shall not be taken away from Juda, till he come that is to be sent.” For at that time all the authority of the Jews, and the mystical anointing from which they were called christs, had failed, when, according to the prophecy of Daniel, he came for whom it was laid up; and the Holy of holies was anointed “with the oil of gladness above his fellows.” For he was born in the time of the elder Herod, and suffered in the time of Herod the tetrarch. The figure of him, coming to “the sheep that are lost of the house of Israel,” Juda bore when he went to shear his sheep at Thamnas, which was interpreted “failing.” For already the sceptre had failed from Juda, and all the authority and anointing of the Jews. And he came with Hiras the Odollamite. Odollamite is interpreted “witness in water.” With this witness the Lord came, though he had a greater witness than John; but for the sake of the weak sheep he used this witness in water. For Hiras is interpreted “vision of my brother.” John saw his brother, for Mary and Elizabeth were kinswomen. He saw too his Lord and God, because, as he says: “Of his fulness we have received.” Hence: “There hath not risen among them that are born of women a greater than John the Baptist”; because of all who foretold Christ he alone saw him; for “many just men and prophets have desired to see, and have not seen.” He greeted him from the womb, he knew him more perfectly in the dove; and therefore, as the Odollamite, he bore witness in water.
38.6:
**“And Juda took a wife for Her his firstborn, whose name was Thamar.”** — Juda … a wife for his firstborn, etc. From Juda came the royal tribe, which long ruled over the Jewish people; which Thamar signifies, who is interpreted “bitterness,” because she showed herself bitter to Christ in his passion.
**“Thamar”** — ISIDORE. The Jewish people, to whom kings were given from the tribe of Juda as husbands, which is interpreted “bitterness,” because it gave the Lord a cup of gall. Two kinds of princes not acting rightly among the people, one that harms and the other that does not profit, are signified in the sons of Juda, of whom one was wicked before the Lord, the other spilled his seed on the ground lest he make Thamar fruitful. Nor are there more than two kinds of useless men: those who harm, and those unwilling to profit; and if they have any good in this life, they lose it, as if pouring it on the ground. And because in evil he who harms is worse than he who does not profit, therefore the elder is called wicked, not the younger who spilled his seed. And Her is interpreted “of skins,” such tunics as the first men were clothed in, in the punishment of damnation; Onan, “grief,” that is, of those whom he does not profit, though he has the means to profit them. But it is a greater evil to take life away, which the skin signifies, than not to help it, which “their grief” signifies. Yet God slew both, because he takes the kingdom away from such men.
38.7:
**“And Her, the firstborn of Juda, was wicked in the sight of the Lord:”** — because in wickedness the one who harms is worse than the one who does not profit
**“and was slain by him.”** — because the power of such men was destroyed
38.8: **“Juda, therefore said to Onan his son: Go in to thy brother’s wife and marry her, that thou mayst raise seed to thy brother.”** — by him are signified those unwilling to profit
38.9: **“He knowing that the children should not be his, when he went in to his brother’s wife, spilled his seed upon the ground,”** — so the Jews, by an earthly understanding, adulterate the words of the law, lest their hearers become Christians
38.12:
**“And after many days were past, the daughter of Sue the wife of Juda died: and when he had taken comfort after his mourning, he went up … to the shearers of his sheep, he”** — Christ
**“and Hiras”** — “vision of my brother,” that is, John the Baptist
**“the Odollamite the shepherd of his flock … to Thamnas.”** — “witness in water”
**“to the shearers of his sheep”** — STRABO. The Lord came to shear the sheep, that is, to relieve them of sins; of whom it is said: “Thy teeth are as flocks of sheep, that are shorn.” Thamar changes her dress; for she is also interpreted “changing.” She changes dress and name, and from the synagogue becomes the Church. But the name of bitterness remains; not that in which she ministered gall to the Lord, but that in which Peter wept bitterly. For Juda too is called “confession.” So let bitterness be mingled with confession, so that true penance may be foreshown. By this penance let the Church, established in all nations, be made fruitful. For “it behoved Christ to suffer, and to rise again, and that penance and remission of sins should be preached in his name unto all nations.” The dress of the harlot, too, is the confession of sins. For Thamar signifies the Church called from the Gentiles, sitting in this dress at the gate of Enam, which is interpreted “fountain”; because she ran like the hart to the fountains of waters, to come to the seed of Abraham. She is made fruitful by one who does not know her, according to that: “A people which I knew not hath served me.” She received in secret the ring, the bracelet and the staff, because she is sealed by calling, adorned by justification, exalted by glorification. For “whom he predestinated, them he also called, justified, glorified”; but in secret, where the conception of holy fruitfulness takes place.
38.14:
**“And she put off the garments of her widowhood, and took a veil:”** — it is a veil which the women of Palestine used
**“and changing her dress,”** — from the synagogue the Church is made
**“sat in the cross way, that leadeth to Thamnas: because Sela was grown up, and she had not been married to him.”** — And she put off, etc. It is to be noted too that in the times of the patriarchs widows had their own fixed garments, not such as married women had.
**“sat in the cross way”** — JEROME. “And she sat at the gate of Enam, which is on the way to Thamna.” The Hebrew word Enam is translated “eyes.” So it is not the name of a place, and the sense is: she sat at a crossway, or at a crossroads, where the traveller must look more carefully which way he is to go.
38.16: **“And going to her, he said: Suffer me to lie with thee: for he knew her not to be his daughter in law.”** — for by now, because of its transgressions, he had put the synagogue behind his back
38.17: **“He said: I will send thee a kid out of the flock.”** — the reproach of sin, which is cast at the penitent soul when it is said: “What fruit had you then in those things of which you are now ashamed?”
38.18:
**“Juda said: What wilt thou have for a pledge? She answered: Thy ring”** — the seal of secrets
**“and bracelet,”** — the pledge of faith
**“and the staff”** — the justice of faith
**“which thou holdest in thy hand. The woman therefore at one copulation conceived.”** — she who had remained barren under the ancients, now joined to Christ, bears sons of different merit
38.19: **“And she arose and went her way: and putting off the apparel which she had taken, put on the garments of her widowhood.”** — because in the time of the early Church many of the Jews went back to Jewish observances
38.20:
**“And … sent”** — so that the Jewish people might renounce its old life
**“Juda”** — Christ
**“a kid”** — the reproach of sin
**“by his shepherd, the Odollamite,”** — saying: “Ye brood of vipers,” etc.
**“that he might receive the pledge again,”** — so that he might not lose the sacraments entrusted
**“And Juda sent”** — The promised kid is sent as to a harlot, that is, the reproach of sin, through the Odollamite, as one rebuking: “Ye brood of vipers,” etc. But the reproach of sin did not find her whom the bitterness of confession had changed.
**“which he had given to the woman: but he, not finding her,”** — In this deed of Juda is seen not the sincerity of justice but the faithfulness of a promise. For if he had kept justice by keeping chastity, he would not have gone in, as he thought, to a harlot. But what he promised he faithfully sent by the shepherd.
38.21: **“Asked the men of that place:”** — because Judea, after it cleaved firmly to Christ, did not sit at the crossway, nor is mention made of past sins
38.23: **“Juda said: Let her take it to herself; surely she cannot charge us with a lie:”** — as if: let her have the pledges she received; she whom the confession of sin has made free from the reproach of her fault
38.24:
**“And behold after three months they told Juda, saying:”** — after the confession of the Trinity, the converted Jews are accused by the unconverted, as though they had gone after strange gods and shown that they were not the seed of Abraham
**“Thamar, thy daughter in law hath played the harlot, and she appeareth to have a big belly. And Juda said:”** — who here signifies the Jewish people, unjustly condemning the faith of Christians
38.25:
**“But when she was led to execution, she sent to her father in law, saying: By the man, to whom these things belong, I am with child. See whose ring, and bracelet, and staff this is.”** — accused by the Jews, the Church shows that in her are fulfilled the sacraments of the law and the prophets; and when these are proved, she is freed from infamy
**“But when she was led”** — ISIDORE. But afterwards, by publicly showing the ring, the bracelet and the staff, she overcame the Jews who judged rashly, whom Juda already signified; who today too say that this is not the people of Christ nor the seed of Abraham; but when the proofs of our calling, justification and glorification are brought out, they are confounded, and confess that we rather than they have been justified. For the Church, accused by the Jews as an adulteress of the law, declares that she has the pledges; and she shows the staff, the sign of the passion; the bracelet, the lawful things of the law; and the ring, the pledge of immortality.
38.26:
**“But he acknowledging the gifts, said: She is juster than I:”** — the faith of the Church is praised; for it is recognised that the kingdom of the Jews has failed
**“because I did not give her to Sela, my son. However, he knew her no more.”**
• that is, he did not approve fleshly observances
• But he acknowledging, etc. JEROME. “And Juda knew,” etc. In the Hebrew there is: “She is justified from me”; not that she was just, but that in comparison with him she had done less evil, not by roving lewdness but by seeking sons.
38.27:
**“And when she was ready to be brought to bed, there appeared twins”** — a figure of the two peoples
**“in her womb: and in the very delivery of the infants, one put forth a hand,”** — the Jewish, which exercised its hand in outward things, polluted with the blood of the saints and of Christ himself
**“whereon the midwife tied a scarlet thread, saying:”**
• a figure of the blood to be shed
• And when she was ready, etc. That the first, who is called Zara, put out his hand, and the midwife tied a scarlet thread, and when he drew back his hand the later one, who is called Phares, stretched out his hand and in being born came forth first, signified that Israel would stretch out its hand in the work of the law, and would draw it back polluted with the blood of the prophets and of Christ himself; but the people of the Gentiles would afterwards break forth, so that the first would be last and the last first.
38.29:
**“But he drawing back his hand,”** — because when Christ came they could not perform fleshly sacrifices
**“the other came forth:”** — who signifies the Gentile people
**“and the woman said: Why is the partition divided for thee?”** — the little membrane of the afterbirth, which he broke when he put out his hand so that the other might be born. So the mother wonders at this contest, that the first becomes last and the last first
**“and therefore called his name Phares.”**
• “division”
• Why is the partition divided, etc. JEROME. For “partition” Aquila and Symmachus translated “division,” which in Hebrew is said phares. So he received the name of division from his having divided the little membrane of the afterbirth. Hence the Pharisees too, who had separated themselves from the people as being just, were called “the divided.”
38.30:
**“Afterwards his brother came out, on whose hand was the scarlet thread: and she called him Zara.”** — that is, “east”
**“Zara”** — Is interpreted “east,” because he appeared first; or because very many just men were born of him, as is said in Paralipomenon.

39.1:
**“And Joseph was brought into Egypt,”**
• he returns to the order of what went before
• that is, Christ preached throughout the world
**“and … bought him”** — with the price of faith
**“Putiphar an eunuch of Pharao,”** — the people chaste in faith, which is sometimes compelled to serve worldly princes
**“chief captain of the army, an Egyptian, … of the Ismaelites,”** — because Gentiles proclaimed Christ to Gentiles
**“by whom he was brought.”** — And Joseph, etc. AUGUSTINE. Scripture makes its way back to the order of the things done above, from which it had withdrawn.
39.2:
**“And the Lord was”** — the Father
**“with him,”** — the Son
**“and he was a … man in all things:”** — in deeds and words
**“prosperous … and he dwelt in … house,”** — the Church
**“his master’s”**
• of God, whose servant Christ is according to the flesh
• And the Lord was, etc. GREGORY. Many, puffed up with human wisdom, when they see the divine judgments running contrary to their desires, try cunningly to struggle against them, so as to twist the force of the arrangement from above to their own wish; but they accomplish the will of God by the very means by which they strive to change it; and resisting the counsel of God, they obey it; because what springs back through human effort fights for his arrangement. Hence: “Who catcheth the wise in their craftiness.” Joseph had seen a dream that his brothers’ sheaves adored his sheaf, and that the sun and moon with the other stars adored himself. And when his brothers feared being made subject to his rule, they put him down into a pit and sold him to the Ismaelites. He, brought into Egypt, made subject to slavery, condemned on a charge of lust, helped by the merit of chastity, rescued by the judgment of prophecy, was set over all Egypt. And by wisdom from above he providently gathered grain, and met the coming danger of need. And when famine bristled over the world, Jacob sent his sons into Egypt; they found Joseph set over the distribution of the grain, and were compelled to adore him in order to earn food. Joseph had been sold by them lest he be adored; and he was adored because he was sold; and they were compelled to accomplish the will of God because they strove to change it. And God, just and merciful, ordering the deeds of mortals, grants some things in kindness and permits others in anger; and what he permits in anger he so bears with that he turns it to the use of his counsel. Hence it comes about that what is done without the will of God is not contrary to the will of God; because, while evil deeds are turned to a good use, even the things that fight against his counsel fight for it. Hence: “Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all his wills.” For his works are so great that through everything that is done by men his will is sought out. For often it is accomplished by the very means by which it is thought to be thrust back. Hence: “Whatsoever the Lord pleased he hath done, in heaven and in earth.” Hence Solomon says: “There is no wisdom, there is no prudence, there is no counsel against the Lord.” So in all that we do let us seek out the force of the will from above; and when it is known, we ought to serve it, and follow it as the guide of our journey, lest we serve it even against our will. For the force of the counsel from above cannot be avoided; but he tempers it with great strength who reins himself in under its nods, and he lightens its weight who carries it willingly.
39.3: **“Who knew very well that the Lord was with him, and made all that he did to prosper in his hand.”** — “whatsoever he shall do shall prosper”
39.6: **“Neither knew he any other thing, but the bread which he ate. And Joseph was of a beautiful countenance, and comely to behold.”** — Christ, “beautiful above the sons of men,” in whose hand all things are directed
39.7:
**“And after many days his mistress cast”** — the synagogue
**“her eyes on Joseph,”** — lust, which tries to attack purity; but the chaste man brings back to mind the good things given him, and overcomes the temptation by which he is assailed
**“and said: Lie with me.”** — And after many days, etc. GREGORY. Whoever, lifted up by the successes of the world, feels himself tempted by lust, let him call Joseph to mind and keep himself in the citadel of chastity; who says: “Behold, my master, having delivered all things to me, knoweth not what he hath in his house,” etc. Where it is plain that he suddenly brought back to mind all that he had obtained, and overcame the evil that assailed him. For when pleasure tempts in prosperity, those very things must be set against the temptation, so that we may blush to commit wicked things in that we remember receiving undeserved good things from God; for because pleasure is born of prosperity, let it be struck down by the consideration of the same.
**“his mistress cast”** — ISIDORE. Allegorically. This is a figure of the synagogue, which often committed adultery after strange gods, and wished to hold Christ in the crime of its adultery, so that he would deny that he was God, and keep the precepts of the Pharisees and scribes, who were to it like a husband, rather than those of the law. But not consenting to the unlawful teaching of the synagogue, seized by its hand by the garment of his body, he stripped himself of the flesh and ascended free into heaven. The harlot slandered him when she could not hold him, saying that he blasphemed the temple of God and was a transgressor of the law. But the prison did not terrify him, nor did hell hold him. For where he had gone down as one to be punished, from there he set others free.
39.10: **“With such words as these day by day, … was importunate”** — so the incitements of lust frequently attack chastity
39.12:
**“And she catching the skirt of his garment,”** — because solitude seemed fitting for the crime
**“said: Lie with me. But he leaving the garment in her hand, fled, and went out.”** — But he leaving in her hand, etc. So the allurements of the flesh tempt us and shake the fleshly garment. But the chaste man would rather break all bonds than subject himself to shamefulness.
*Gregory:* Allegorically. “But he leaving in her hand,” etc. Because, while the synagogue, believing Christ a mere man, wished to bind him in an adulterous embrace, he cast the covering of the letter before its eyes, and showed himself plainly to the Gentiles for the knowing of the power of his Godhead. Hence: “Even until this day, when Moses is read, the veil is upon” the eyes of “their heart”; because, that is, the adulteress kept the garment, and lost, stripped, the one she held wrongly.
39.13: **“And when the woman saw the garment”** — the veil of the letter
39.14: **“She called to her the men of her house, and said to them: See, he hath brought in a Hebrew, to abuse us: he came in to me, to lie with me:”** — the one she could not defile, she strives to defame by plausible conjectures
39.15: **“And he heard my voice, he left the garment that I held, and got him out.”** — to the Gentiles
39.19: **“His master hearing these things, and … too much”** — or “excessively”
39.20:
**“And cast Joseph into the prison,”**
• Christ went down into hell
• the innocent to the punishment of the guilty
39.21:
**“But the Lord was with Joseph and having mercy upon him”** — because Christ was free among the dead
**“gave him favour in the sight of the chief keeper of the prison:”** — his own, without whose nod neither are the wicked punished nor the good crowned
39.22: **“Who delivered into his hand all the prisoners that were kept in custody: and whatsoever was done was under him.”** — because to Christ was given power over things above and things below

40.1:
**“After this, it came to pass, that two eunuchs, the butler and the baker of the king of Egypt, offended their lord.”** — because the two peoples sinned, by origin and in act, and so were thrust down into hell as into a prison
**“two eunuchs”** — ISIDORE. Joseph found two eunuchs in the prison, that is, two peoples, of the faithful and of the unfaithful, who were held liable under the sin of Adam’s transgression. They are called eunuchs because they had received a chaste rule of discipline: “The words of the Lord are pure words.” But after the third daylight, when the Lord rose from the dead and, like Joseph, revealed the dark things of the law as dreams, the people of believers was loosed from sins and from the prison of hell and restored to the ministry of the divine law. But the unbelieving people of the Jews, because in their turning they did not believe the wood, is hanged on the wood of transgression.
**“the butler … of the king”** — JEROME. Where we have put “chief of the wine-bearers,” in the Hebrew there is meseth, the word we read a while ago in the name of Abraham’s servant, which we have put, after common usage, as “butler.” And to this day among barbarians it is of the highest dignity to have handed the king his cup.
40.2:
**“And Pharao being angry with them (now the one was chief butler,”** — the Gentile, who gave the new wine of love to drink to the beloved
**“the other chief baker)”** — the Jew, who in Jeremias puts wood on the bread of life
40.3: **“He sent them to the prison of the commander of the soldiers, in which Joseph also was prisoner,”** — the innocent with the guilty
40.4:
**“But the keeper of the prison delivered them”** — to be taught
**“Joseph”** — to Christ
**“and he served them.”** — the words of salvation
**“Some little time passed, and they were kept in custody.”** — the Jews under the law, the Gentiles under tutors and governors, until the time appointed by the Father
40.5: **“And they both dreamed a dream the same night, according to the interpretation agreeing to themselves:”** — the dream is seen not for their merits, but so that Joseph, who lay hidden, might be made known and magnified
40.8: **“They answered: We have dreamed a dream, and there is nobody to interpret it to us.”** — because prophecy was closed until Christ came, who opened the book and loosed its seals
40.9:
**“The chief butler first told his dream:”** — because, few of Juda being saved, the people of the Gentiles ran ahead to salvation
**“I saw before me a vine,”**
• which says, “I am the true vine,” in which the Church is rooted; of which it is said, “and you the branches”
• I saw before me, etc. JEROME. “And behold a vine in my sight, and on the vine three stocks, and it budding.” Three stocks, three shoots, three branches or layers, the Hebrew word signifies, which by them are called syriachim.
40.10: **“On which were three branches,”** — the married, the continent, the rulers
40.11: **“And the cup of Pharao was in my hand:”** — the Church little by little brings forth the bud of faith, flowering in the newly baptized, ripe in the perfect; from which wine too is pressed when it is trodden in the press of the passion; which is given to Pharao, that is, to the powers of the world, to drink, when the passion of Christ is preached to them to be imitated or believed
40.12: **“Joseph answered: This is the interpretation of the dream: The three branches are yet three days:”** — although the prophecy belongs to Christian times, yet it is interpreted according to the outcome of things soon to come
40.16:
**“The chief baker seeing that he had wisely interpreted the dream, said: I also dreamed a dream, That I had three baskets of meal”** — JEROME. For “three baskets,” codrithon, in the Hebrew there is “three baskets of meal”
**“three baskets”** — AUGUSTINE. Where in the Latin books is written “three baskets of meal,” the Greek have codrithon, which is interpreted “common bread.” But this troubles us: how Pharao could have common bread among his foods. For he says that in the uppermost basket were all the works of baking, of which Pharao ate. But it must be understood that the first basket too had common bread, because it had been said, “three baskets of codrithon”; and that those things were on top, and of every kind of baker’s work, that is, in the same uppermost basket.
40.20: **“the birthday of Pharao”** — Pharao and Herod kept their birthdays, because they thought they had been kings from the hour of their birth.
40.21:
**“And he restored the one to his place”** — he who received the Lord’s cup deserved to be set free
**“to present him the cup:”** — even through the vessels of wrath the cup of life is ministered to the vessels of mercy
40.22: **“The other he hanged on a gibbet,”** — he who put wood on the Lord’s bread perished by wood
40.23: **“when things prospered with him,”** — “the prosperity of fools shall destroy them”

41.1:
**“After two years Pharao had a dream. He thought he stood by the river,”**
• which signifies the course of slipping things; he stands upon it who tramples on the love of temporal things
• He thought he stood, etc. AUGUSTINE. As Abraham’s servant said, “Behold, I stand by the well of water.” If this manner of speech is understood in the psalm where it is written, “Who established the earth upon the waters,” men are not driven to think that the earth floats on the waters like a ship. For it is understood that the earth is higher than the water; for where the land animals live is raised higher than the waters.
41.2:
**“Out of which came up seven kine, very beautiful and fat:”** — spiritual graces, which came forth to nourish the infancy of the early Church
**“and they fed in marshy places.”** — lowly; hence: “Upon whom shall my Spirit rest, but upon him that is humble and quiet, and that trembleth at my words?”
**“Out of which came up”** — JEROME. “Behold, out of the river came up seven kine, beautiful to see and choice in flesh, and they fed in achi.” Twice in Genesis it is written “in achi,” and it is neither a Greek word nor a Latin one. The Hebrew too has been corrupted; for it is said ahu, that is, “in the marsh.” But because among the Hebrews the letters vau and iod are alike, and differ only in size, the Septuagint translated ahi for ahu; and according to their custom, to express the double aspiration of heth, the Hebrew letter, they joined the Greek chi.
41.3:
**“Other seven also came up”** — the spirits of wickedness
**“out of the river, ill favoured, and leanfleshed:”** — fit for no nourishment
**“and they fed on the very bank of the river, in green places:”** — tender minds
41.4: **“And they devoured them, whose bodies were very beautiful”** — they consumed all the comeliness of virtues in souls that had the practice of virtues only in appearance
41.5: **“He slept again, and dreamed another dream:”** — the doubling of the dream is the confirmation of the presage
41.6: **“Then seven other ears sprung up thin and blasted,”** — by the leanness of the ears, the famine of the word of God; when charity grows cold at the end of the world, iniquity will abound
41.9:
**“Then at length the chief butler remembering, said:”** — because the mystery which was hidden in God from the ages was made plain when the Mediator appeared in God and preached
**“Then at length”** — Because the Gentile people at last, by the showing of things past, brought itself to the hope of things to come.
41.14: **“Forthwith at the king’s command, Joseph was brought out of the prison, and they shaved him, and changing his apparel, brought him in to him.”** — Christ, rising from death, is shaved, because he is stripped of passibility and mortality as of the superfluity of hair, and is clothed with the garment of immortality
41.15: **“And he said to him: I have dreamed dreams, and there is no one that can expound them: Now I have heard that thou art very wise”** — or “wisest”
41.17:
**“So Pharao told”** — elsewhere: “Pharao”
**“Methought I stood upon the bank”** — The seven years, which are shown by the seven full ears or the seven fat cows, signify the spiritual gifts, by which the richness of faith overflows with generous piety; but the seven barren and hungry ones, the famine of truth and justice in the last time.
41.18: **“And seven kine came up out of the river exceeding beautiful and full of flesh:”** — round and full of fatness
41.27: **“And the seven lean and thin kine”** — he so interprets the dream that it serves both the outcome of the times and the mystical understanding
41.33: **“Now therefore let the king provide a wise and industrious man, and make him ruler over the land of Egypt:”** — Now therefore, etc. We see this fulfilled in this time of grace; because, as the apostolic teaching ministered by the sevenfold Spirit abounded, by divine arrangement bishops and teachers were ordained in every city, who, from the abundance of teaching divinely bestowed on them, wrote the holy books, by which, when the famine of the word abounds and teachers fail, we might relieve our need.
41.34:
**“That he may appoint overseers over all the countries:”** — or “all”
**“the fifth part”** — It is to be noted that the Egyptians gather a fifth part of the fruits into the king’s barns, because the sons of darkness, given over to the five senses, do not care for heavenly things; but the true Israelites give tithes, because they labour to restore the heavenly country, of which a tenth part fell.
*Isidore:* Joseph gathered for seven years all the abundance of fruits, that is, storing the grain of faith in the barns of the saints through the seven gifts, as through seven years; so that when the seven years of want begin, that is, when the iniquity of the seven capital crimes comes upon us under Antichrist, when there will be a famine of faith and of salvation, the saints may then have a plentiful crop of justice, lest their faith fail for want of the word.
41.38: **“And he said to them: Can we find such another man, that is full of the spirit of God?”** — Who is full of the spirit, etc. AUGUSTINE. For the third time, unless I am mistaken, the Holy Ghost is suggested to us in this book: first where it was said, “The Spirit of God moved over the waters”; second where God said, “My spirit shall not remain in these men,” etc.; third when Pharao says that the Spirit of God is in Joseph. Yet we have not yet read “the Holy Ghost.”
41.41:
**“And … said”** — ISIDORE. Joseph, who bore the type of Christ, was granted a chariot, and a crier proclaimed before him, and Pharao set him over the whole land of Egypt. And our Lord, after he was sold off by Judas as Joseph was by his brothers, and rose from the prison of hell, went up into the chariot of the heavenly kingdom, of which it is said, “The chariot of God is attended by ten thousands,” and received from the Father the power of preaching and judging. Hence: “He hath given him a name which is above all names,” etc. He received too the ring, that is, the priesthood of faith, by which the souls of believers are sealed with the sign of salvation, and the figure of the eternal king is printed on our foreheads and hearts by the sign of the cross. He is clothed with a robe of fine linen, that is, with holy flesh more shining than linen, and with the robe of immortality. He received too a chain of gold, that is, good understanding. A crier goes before him, that is, John the Baptist, who said, “Prepare ye the way of the Lord.” He will have another crier too, for he will come with the trumpet of an angel.
**“And again Pharao said to Joseph: Behold, I have appointed thee over the whole land of Egypt.”** — Behold, I have appointed thee, etc. Joseph, brought out of prison, is set over Egypt; and Christ, rising, received “a name which is above all names, that in the name of Jesus every knee should bow.”
41.42:
**“And he took his ring from his own hand,”** — which signifies the priesthood of faith, which is in the power of Christ
**“and gave it into his hand: and he put upon him a robe of silk,”** — which signifies the flesh of Christ, taken from the earth, the Virgin, and brought through divers sufferings to the comeliness of immortality
**“and put a chain of gold about his neck.”** — heavenly wisdom, which like a circle is closed by neither beginning nor end
41.43:
**“And he made him go up”** — so Christ, adorned with divine gifts, ascended the heavens
**“into his … chariot,”** — because he passes beyond all the changeableness of temporal things
**“second … the crier proclaiming”** — John the Baptist, who said, “Prepare ye the way of the Lord”; or the angelic trumpet, which will go before him when he comes to judgment
**“that all should bow their knee before him, and that they should know he was made governor over the whole land of Egypt.”** — The crier proclaiming, etc. “And a crier cried before him, and he set him over all the land of Egypt”; for which Aquila translated: “And he cried in his sight a kneeling.” Symmachus put the Hebrew itself: “And he cried before him abreth.” Hence it seems to me that what is to be understood is not so much “crier” or “kneeling,” which can be taken of the greeting or adoring of Joseph, as what the Hebrews hand down, saying that “tender father” is translated from this word; for ab is said for “father,” reth “delicate” or “most tender”; the Scripture signifying that in prudence he was the father of all, but in age a most tender youth and boy.
41.45:
**“And he turned his name, and called him in the Egyptian tongue, The saviour of the world.”** — so that he might bear more rightly the likeness of Christ, who is the saviour not only of Egypt but of the whole world
**“And he gave him to wife Aseneth the daughter of Putiphare priest of Heliopolis.”** — Joseph, raised on high, takes a wife; and Christ, lifted up into the heavens, joins to himself the Church from the Gentiles, which the daughter of the priest of Heliopolis well signifies, who was a priest of the Gentiles. Heliopolis too is interpreted “city of the sun”; from it he joins to himself a bride, he who “hath set his tabernacle in the sun”
**“Then Joseph went out to the land of Egypt:”**
• And he called, etc. JEROME. “And Pharao called Joseph’s name Phasnecphane, and gave him Aseneth the daughter of Phutiphar, priest of Heliopolis.” Though this name in Hebrew sounds “finder of hidden things,” yet since it is given by an Egyptian, it ought to have the meaning of his own tongue. So Phasnecphane, or, as the Septuagint chose to render it, Psonthomphanech, is interpreted “saviour of the world,” because he freed the world from famine. And it is to be noted that he took as wife the daughter of his former master and buyer, who by that time was high priest of Heliopolis; nor was it lawful for any but eunuchs to be priests of that idol; so that the Hebrews’ suspicion about him, which we spoke of before, is proved true.
• And he gave him to wife, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is often asked whose Phutiphar is meant (by others Petephres, as most have it, and corruptly, as was said above): whether the one whose slave he was, or another. But it is more credible that it was another. For there are many things that trouble us if it is believed to be the former. First, because Scripture did not mention it, though it seems it could not pass over what belonged to Joseph’s glory: that he married the daughter of the man whose slave he had been. Then, how could a eunuch have a daughter? But it is answered: how a wife? For he is believed to have been cut afterwards, either by accident or by his own will. And his usual office is not mentioned, that is, that he was archimagirus, which the Latins interpreted chief of the cooks and some understand as chief of the soldiery. But here too it is answered that he held two honours, the priesthood of the sun and the command of the soldiery; and that elsewhere that honour is fittingly mentioned which suits such deeds; but here, after no small divinity had appeared in Joseph, the honour of his father-in-law had to be named which belongs to no small divinity in the opinion of the Egyptians, namely the priesthood of the sun. But in all these things it is incredible that the one who was set over the keeping of the prison should be set in the office of the priests.
41.46:
**“Now he was thirty years old”** — at this age Christ began to preach the Gospel; before it no one ought to be taken up to the priesthood or the office of preaching
**“when he stood before king Pharao”** — presenting himself in the world by preaching and miracles
41.49:
**“And there was so great abundance of wheat, that it was equal to the sand of the sea,”** — that is, numberless, like sand
**“and the plenty exceeded measure.”** — the usual
41.50:
**“And … Joseph had … born:”** — to Christ
**“before the famine came, … two sons”** — the falling away from the faith which Antichrist will bring about
**“whom Aseneth the daughter of Putiphare priest of Heliopolis bore unto him.”** — And … were born, etc. JEROME. Note, because of the question to be set out afterwards about Joseph’s sons, that before the time of famine in which Jacob entered Egypt he had only two sons, Manasses and Ephraim.
41.51: **“And he called the name of the firstborn Manasses, saying: God hath made me to forget”** — “forgetfulness”; this is the Jewish people, forgetful of its God
41.52: **“And he named the second Ephraim,”** — “fruitfulness,” which signifies the Church from the Gentiles spread through the whole world
41.54:
**“The seven years of scarcity, which Joseph had foretold, began to come: and the famine”** — of the word of God
**“prevailed in the whole world,”** — because “there was none that did good”
**“but there was bread in all the land of Egypt.”** — elsewhere: “there was famine”
41.55: **“And when there also they began to be famished, the people cried to Pharao for food. And he said to them: Go to Joseph:”** — in the distress of spiritual famine the one counsel is that we run back to the barns of Joseph, that is, the holy Scriptures, kept by the holy fathers for us for the comfort of our want
41.56:
**“And the famine increased daily in all the land:”** — elsewhere: “every”
**“and Joseph opened all the barns, and sold to the Egyptians:”** — the grain of the word of God is sold to the Egyptians when they bind themselves over to divine service
**“for the famine had oppressed them also.”**
• of the word of God
• And Joseph opened, etc. Joseph saves Egypt from want of grain, and Christ frees the world from the famine of the word. Christ opened his barns to the whole world, and by the giving out of his grain brought all things under him. Unless Joseph’s brothers had sold him, Egypt would have failed; unless the Jews had crucified Christ, the world would have perished. Joseph is interpreted “increase.” But in that Joseph none had enlargement but Egypt alone; in ours, the whole world. He gave out wheat; ours the word of God. “For their sound hath gone forth into all the earth.”

42.1:
**“And Jacob hearing”** — the Jewish people
**“that food was sold in Egypt,”** — that the teaching of the Gospel was being preached in the world
**“said to his sons: Why are ye careless?”** — Jacob said, etc. ISIDORE. There is grain in Egypt. And God the Father says: “Out of Egypt have I called my son.” The ten go down, that is, the Jews set under the decalogue; whom he knowing is not known by them. The Hebrews are known by Christ, and they do not know him. They gave him money; but Joseph, that is, Christ, gave wheat and gave back the silver; because Christ is bought not with money but by grace.
42.3: **“So the ten brethren of Joseph went down, to buy corn in Egypt:”** — now the Jews set under the decalogue no longer glory in the starving letter
42.4: **“Whilst Benjamin was kept at home by Jacob,”** — Paul being still taken up with the traditions of his fathers
42.5:
**“And they entered into the land of Egypt with others that went to buy.”** — they humbled themselves to the understanding of those of whom it was said: “that they who see not may see”
**“For the famine was”** — of bread in the land, or of understanding
**“in the land of Chanaan.”** — Judea
42.6:
**“And Joseph”** — Christ
**“was governor in the land of Egypt,”** — of the world
**“and corn was sold by his direction to the people.”** — “to another the word of knowledge, to another the word of wisdom, to another interpretation of speeches”
**“And when his brethren had bowed down to him,”** — the whole assembly of the saints adores Christ
42.8: **“And though he knew his brethren, he was not known by them.”** — the Jews were known by Christ; but they did not know him
42.9: **“And remembering the dreams, which formerly he had dreamed, he said to them:”** — in which he saw that the sun and moon and stars adored him
42.15:
**“I shall now presently try what you are: by the health of Pharao you shall not depart”** — understand “all”
**“hence,”** — from the narrowness of the letter
**“until your youngest brother come.”**
• let Paul believe, “the least of the apostles,” as “one born out of due time”
• this was fulfilled when Ananias was sent to baptize him
**“by the health of Pharao”** — AUGUSTINE. What does it mean that Joseph, a wise man, praised not only among men but by the witness of Scripture, swore by the health of Pharao that his brothers would not go out of Egypt unless the younger brother came? Was the health of Pharao cheap even to a good and faithful man? For how much more would he keep faith with the one who had placed him in such honour, if he kept it with the one who owned him as a bought slave! And if he did not care for Pharao’s health, ought he not to avoid perjury by the health of any man whatever? Or is it not perjury? For he kept one of them until Benjamin came, and what he said came true: “You shall not go out until your brother comes.” For what was said could belong to all of them; for how would that one come unless some went back to bring him? But what follows presses the question more, where he swore again, saying: “Send one of you, and fetch your brother,” and the rest, as far as “by the health of Pharao, you are spies.” To this sentence he added an oath because, if they had not told the truth, they would be spies, that is, worthy of the punishment of spies; though he knew they were telling the truth. Nor is anyone a perjurer if he says to one whom he knows to be most chaste: “If you have committed this adultery of which you are accused, God damns you,” and adds an oath to these words. He truly swears no falsehood at all; for there is a condition in what he says, “if you did it,” though he holds it certain that he did not. But someone says: it is true, because if he committed adultery, the Lord damns him; whereas this, “If you do not tell the truth, you are spies,” is not true, since even if they lie they are not spies. But “you are spies” was said as if it had been said, “you are worthy of the punishment of spies,” that is, “you will be reckoned spies by the merit of your lie.” That “you are” could be said for “you will be held” and “you will be reckoned,” countless like expressions teach. Hence too that expression of Elias: “Whoever shall hear by fire, he shall be God”; for he will not be God, but will be held to be.
42.23:
**“And they knew not”** — AUGUSTINE. What does it mean that, when they were speaking among themselves in repentance about Joseph, that they had done evil to him and that this was being paid back to them by divine judgment, since they saw themselves in danger, Scripture adds: “They knew not that Joseph heard; for there was an interpreter between them”? This is to be understood: they thought he did not hear because they saw that the interpreter who was between them told him nothing of what they were saying; for they thought he had been brought in because Joseph did not know their tongue. Nor was it the interpreter’s concern to tell the man by whom he had been placed things that were said not to him but among themselves.
**“And they knew not that Joseph understood, because he spoke to them by an interpreter.”** — It is asked why Joseph, a most gentle man, wished to treat his brothers so, by putting off his recognition, when he could quickly have helped them by making himself known. But he did not do this for revenge, to avenge the evil done to him, but to find out whether by the same goad they would destroy his brother by the same mother, as they had sold himself into foreign provinces.
42.27: **“And one of them opening his sack”** — Joseph’s brothers give silver, because the converted Jews leave the letter that kills and receive the Spirit that gives life; yet the silver is found in the mouth of the sacks, because for the sake of the fruit of spiritual understanding the brightness of eloquence is not forsaken.
42.35: **“every man found”** — Joseph’s brothers gave money in buying the grain, but received it back with the grain; because our Joseph seeks not ours but us. For he gives his gifts freely, and in our buying makes us richer.
42.37: **“And … answered him”** — STRABO. Ruben says: “Kill my two sons if I bring him not again to thee,” etc.; and yet he did not prevail. But Juda, saying, “I will be guilty of sin against my father for ever,” obtained it, because Benjamin was entrusted to him. So it is more to be guilty of sin than to be slain bodily.
42.38:
**“But he said: My son shall not go down with you: his brother is dead, and he is left alone: if any mischief befall him in the land to which you go, you will bring down my gray hairs with sorrow”** — elsewhere: “grief”
**“to hell.”** — You will bring down my gray hairs, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is asked whether he says this, “to hell,” because it would be with sorrow, or whether, even if sorrow were absent, he would go down to hell in dying. For about hell there is a great question, and what Scripture thinks of it must be observed wherever it is mentioned.

43.11:
**“Then Israel said to them: If it must needs be so, do what you will: take of the best fruits of the land”** — or “fruits”
**“in your vessels, and carry down presents to the man, a little balm, and honey, and storax,”** — a kind of resin
**“myrrh, turpentine,”** — the terebinth is a tree whose resin is called by the same name
**“a little balm”** — JEROME. “Some resin and honey and incense and myrrh and terebinth and nuts,” or, as Aquila and Symmachus translated, “almonds.” Where in our books there is “incense,” in the Hebrew there is nechota, which Aquila translated “storax”; from which the house of nechotha that is read in Isaias is plainly understood to be the storeroom of incense or storax, because divers spices were stored in it.
43.23:
**“But he answered: Peace be with you, fear not: your God, and the God of your father hath given you treasure in your sacks. For the money,”** — the wise steward does not lie, because he speaks of the money of the word of God
**“which you gave me, I have for good. And he brought Simeon out to them.”** — Your God, etc. AUGUSTINE. It seems a lie, but it must be believed to signify something. For the silver that is given and is not lessened, which is also called “tried,” is perhaps that of which it is said: “The words of the Lord are pure words, as silver tried by the fire, purged from the earth, refined seven times,” that is, tried perfectly.
43.29:
**“And Joseph lifting up his eyes, saw Benjamin his brother, by the same mother, and said: Is this your young brother,”** — elsewhere: “little”
**“of whom you told me? And he said: God be gracious to thee, my son.”** — Joseph saw, etc. ISIDORE. Paul, when the light shone round about him; who was little, because he did not yet bear the mature age of faith. Hence he is also read to have been a young man while he kept the garments of those stoning Stephen. Joseph wept: the blindness of Paul is the weeping of Christ. Christ washed his face when Paul was baptized, through whom Christ was to be seen by very many.
*Augustine:* The affection of a good mind is always inclined to piety. Hence in Joseph we can consider an abundance of virtues. He was chaste when he spurned the shamelessness of his mistress; wise when by careful inquiry he explored his brothers’ minds, how they felt about his brother by the same mother; just in applying discipline to the guilty; kind in the conversion of the penitent.
43.30: **“And he made haste because his heart was moved”** — or “his”
43.32:
**“And when it was set on, for Joseph apart, and for his brethren apart,”** — as to strangers
**“for the Egyptians also”** — as to natives
**“that ate with him, apart, (for it is unlawful for the Egyptians to eat with the Hebrews, and they think such a feast profane):”** — And when it was set on, etc. Food was set apart for Joseph as for an incomer; and apart for his brothers as foreign by nation; and apart for the Egyptians too as natives, who thought a feast with foreigners profane.
43.34:
**“Taking the messes which they received of him: and the greater mess came to Benjamin,”** — because Paul laboured more than all
**“so that it exceeded by five parts. And they drank, and were merry with him.”**
• “filled,” according to the idiom of the Hebrew tongue
• And they drank, and were merry, etc. AUGUSTINE. Drunkards are wont to bring in this testimony in their own defence, because of Joseph, who is commended as very wise. But this word is used in the Scriptures for fullness. Hence: “Thou hast visited the earth, and hast plentifully watered it”; because this is put in praise of a blessing and a gift of God is recalled, it appears that this drunkenness signifies fullness. For to be made drunk as drunkards are drunk is not useful even to the earth, since it is spoiled by more moisture than suffices; like the life of the drunkard, who does not fill himself to fullness but drowns himself in a flood.

44.2:
**“And … put my silver cup, and the price”** — the brightness of the divine word
**“which he gave for the wheat … in the mouth of the younger’s sack”** — of Paul, who is the least of the apostles
44.5:
**“The cup which you have stolen is that in which my lord drinketh,”** — the accusation so often thrown at the brothers is the expiation of their selling of their brother
**“and in which he is wont to divine: you have done a very evil thing.”** — The cup which, etc. ISIDORE. What does it mean that Joseph’s cup was found in Benjamin’s sack, unless that in the heart of Paul the word of heavenly teaching was already shining, while he was learned in the law? But because he was not subject to God, the cup was inside the sack, the teaching inside the law, the lamp under the bushel. Yet Ananias was sent, laid his hand on him, loosed the purse, and the silver shone out; and when the scales fell, as the cords of the sack, the sack being loosed, that is, the veil of the law being put off, he gained the liberty of grace, and with unveiled face preaches the Gospel of the word.
44.15:
**“And he said to them: Why would you do so?”** — he inflicts words on his brothers in place of blows, lest the crime against a brother remain unpunished
**“know you not that there is no one like me in the science of divining.”** — Know you not, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is often asked what this means. Perhaps, because it was said not in earnest but in jest, as the outcome teaches, it is not to be held a lie. For lies are told by liars in earnest, not in jest; and when things that are not so are said as in jest, they are not thought lies. But what moves us more is what this action of Joseph’s means, by which he so often made sport of his brothers until he revealed to them who he was, and held them in such suspense; which, though it is the sweeter in the reading the more unexpected it is for those with whom it is done, yet, given the gravity of his wisdom, unless something great were signified by this play, as it were, it would neither have been done by him nor told by Scripture, in which there is such holiness and such a purpose of prophesying things to come. So I think it must not be carelessly considered: that so great a misery in the trouble of his brothers Joseph kept up as long as he wished, and drew out with as much delay as he wished, making them the more wretched the more he thought of their coming joy; and what he did to put off their joy, he did so that by the delay it might be heaped up; as if the sufferings of so little a time were not worthy to be compared with the coming glory of the exultation to come, when they should know the brother whom they reckoned they had lost.
44.16: **“And Juda said to him: What shall we answer my lord? or what shall we say, or be able justly to allege? God hath found out the iniquity of thy servants: behold, we are all bondmen to my lord, both we, and he with whom the cup was found.”** — And Juda said to him, etc. AUGUSTINE. Many things in Juda’s account are told otherwise than as Joseph had dealt with them, though he was speaking before him; so that nothing at all was said of the charge of being spies; whether this was kept quiet on purpose, or whether the forgetfulness of distress did it, does not appear. For that too which they said, that they had been asked by Joseph about their father and brother, and had told him when he asked, is strange, if the account itself can arrive at the sense so that it is agreed to be truthful; although, even if there are some false things in it, he could rather have been deceived through forgetfulness than have dared to lie; especially before him, into whose account he put things not as to one who did not know, but which he knew he knew, so as to bend him to mercy.
44.20: **“And we answered thee, my lord: We have a father an old man, and a young boy, that was born in his old age; whose brother by the mother is dead: and he alone is left of his mother, and his father loveth him tenderly.”** — as if: he alone survives of his mother; for so they thought

45.3: **“And he said to his brethren: I am Joseph:”** — so, making himself known to the Jews, who have long not known Christ, about the end of the world, he will show himself pleased with them, who before had felt him justly angry
45.5:
**“Be not afraid, and let it not seem to you a hard case that you sold me into these countries: for God sent me before you into Egypt for your preservation.”**
• for unless Christ had been handed over by the Jews, the world would not have been saved
• God sent me, etc. AUGUSTINE. What does it mean that in other copies it is read thus: “For God sent me before you, that your remnant might remain upon the earth, and to nourish the great seed of your remnant”? For this does not altogether agree, that we should take the remnant of Jacob to be his sons too, since all are safe. Or perhaps it signifies, in a secret mystery, what the Apostle says: “A remnant is saved according to the election of grace.” For to this end Christ was slain by the Jews and handed over to the Gentiles, as Joseph was by his brothers to the Egyptians; hence: “For I also am an Israelite”; “that the fulness of the Gentiles should come in, and so all Israel should be saved.”
45.9: **“Make haste, and go ye up to my father, and say to him: Thus saith thy son Joseph: God hath made me lord of the whole land of Egypt: come down to me, linger not.”** — elsewhere: “you will die”
45.10:
**“And thou shalt dwell in the land of Gessen:”**
• which is interpreted “nearness”; whence it is plain that even if Israel lives in Egypt, it is still not far from God
• others have “Gessen of Arabia,” but it is more truly called Gesem
**“And thou shalt dwell in the land of Gessen of Arabia”** — “Of Arabia” was added. JEROME. It is not in the Hebrew. Hence the error grew that the land of Gessen is in Arabia. Further, as in our books, it is written Iessem with the last letter; which does not at all please me, as signifying “a land rained upon”; for Iessen is turned into “rain”; whereas in most books Gesem is found.
45.16:
**“And it was heard, and the fame was spread abroad in the king’s court: The brethren of Joseph are come: and Pharao with all his family was glad.”**
• who bears the type of the Gentile people, which will rejoice at the end over the conversion of the Jewish people
• And … was glad, etc. These words of Pharao, which he spoke to Joseph about Jacob and his sons, signify the joys of the Gentile people over the conversion of the Jews. For the Church of the Gentiles has great devotion that the people of Israel should come to the faith; to whom, if they turn and become sharers of the faith, it promises the spiritual riches of the virtues and the grace of the Spirit, and whoever receives it will not suffer want of good.
45.17:
**“And he spoke to Joseph that he should give orders to his brethren,”** — Christ commands his apostles
**“saying: Load your beasts, and go into the land of Chanaan.”** — these are a figure of the Gentile people, which, of low birth, afterwards willingly took up the burden of Christ
45.18:
**“And bring away from thence your father”** — invite the faithlessness of the Jews to faith
**“and kindred, and come to me: and I will give you all the good things of Egypt,”** — the abundance of the divine Scriptures, in which the Gentiles abound
**“that you may eat the marrow of the land.”** — the sweetness of spiritual understanding
45.20:
**“And leave nothing of your household stuff:”** — of the Old Testament
**“for all the riches of Egypt shall be yours.”** — the brothers of Joseph
45.21:
**“And the sons of Israel did”** — the apostles are the brothers of Christ
**“as they were bid. And Joseph gave them wagons according to Pharao’s commandment: and provisions for the way.”** — because Christ ordained that those who preach the Gospel should live by the Gospel
45.22:
**“for every one of them”** — for the apostles
**“He ordered also to be brought out … two robes:”** — the knowledge of the divinity and humanity of Christ, to be preached, and the love of God and neighbour
**“but to Benjamin he gave three hundred pieces of silver”** — to Paul, the knowledge of the Trinity and of the cross, which is represented by the letter tau, signifying three hundred
**“with five robes of the best:”**
• that is, the knowledge and governance of the five senses, which was greater in Paul
• But to Benjamin he gave three hundred, etc. JEROME. Three hundred pieces of silver are given to Benjamin, which he receives from Christ, who preaches the Trinity or the cross of Christ. Hence Paul says: “I judged not myself to know any thing among you, but Jesus Christ, and him crucified.” He received five robes, that is, the wisdom of all the senses. So Paul excels in the abundance of his merits; but the brothers too, that is, the other preachers, have their grace, that is, two robes, so that they may confess Christ God and man. Hence “all her domestics are clothed with double garments,” that is, with mystical and moral understanding. Gifts are sent to the father too; and Christ invites his people with promised gifts. Asses carry the gifts, that is, the Gentiles, once useless and toilsome, but now useful; they carry, in the type of Christ, the gifts in the Gospel of the giver of gifts.
45.23:
**“Sending to his father as much money and raiment,”** — through the apostles the treasure of faith and uprightness of morals is sent to the Jews
**“adding besides ten he asses”** — teachers from the Gentiles, instructed in the commandments of the decalogue
**“to carry off all the riches of Egypt,”** — they would imbue the Jews with all the fullness of knowledge
**“and as many she asses, carrying wheat and bread for the journey.”** — which can signify the false apostles, of whom the Apostle says: “Whether by occasion, or by truth, Christ be preached”
45.24: **“So he sent away his brethren, and at their departing said to them: Be not angry in the way.”** — do not quarrel about temporal things
45.25:
**“And they”** — the apostles
**“went up out of Egypt, and came into the land of Chanaan”** — Judea
45.26:
**“And they told him, saying: Joseph thy son is living:”** — Christ was made flesh
**“and he is ruler in all the land of Egypt.”** — he is Lord of the whole world
**“Which when … heard,”** — the coming of Christ
**“Jacob”** — the Jewish people
**“he awaked as it were out of a deep sleep,”** — from the numbness of fleshly life
**“yet did not believe them.”**
• at the first persuading
• Which when Jacob heard, etc. ISIDORE. Jacob, that is, the unbelieving people, was dismayed; but after he came to know the deeds of Christ, his spirit revived, and he who seemed dead is given life by faith in the resurrection of Christ. So the people of the Jews is called to grace by his sons, that is, by Peter, Paul and John. Juda goes to meet him, who is interpreted “confession,” because confession goes before those whom faithlessness possessed before; and so Joseph, that is, Christ, goes to meet him, to receive in the last time the people of the Jews, now old in age, not according to merits but according to the election of grace, and to lay his hand on his eyes and take away the blindness; which he put off so that he who before did not think he should believe might be the last to believe. Hence: because “blindness in part has happened in Israel, until the fulness of the Gentiles should come in, and so all Israel should be saved.”
45.27:
**“They, on the other side, told the whole order of the thing. And when he saw the wagons and all”** — had come to know the fullness of the Gospel and the distribution of gifts
**“that he had sent his spirit revived,”** — which through long blindness had been as if dead

46.1: **“And Israel taking his journey, with all that he had, came to the well of the oath, and killing victims there to the God of his father Isaac,”** — not new
46.2: **“He heard him by a vision in the night calling him, and saying to him:”** — rightly God is seen in the place of peace and concord; for there the Lord commanded blessing
46.3:
**“God said to him: I am the most mighty God of thy father: fear not,”** — you who have me as helper
**“go down into Egypt,”** — secure, to fight against the spirits of wickedness
**“for I will make a great nation of thee there.”** — an imitator of your faith
46.4:
**“I will go down with thee thither,”** — as if: my glory will be with you
**“and will bring thee … from thence:”** — in my power
**“back again”** — to the land of promise
46.7: **“His sons, and grandsons, daughters, and all his offspring together.”** — the plural for the singular, as the singular is wont to be put for the plural; for he had only one daughter, named Dina; or he called his granddaughters daughters
46.15: **“These are the sons of Lia, whom she bore in Mesopotamia of Syria,”** — because their fathers were born there
46.21: **“The sons of Benjamin: Bela and Bechor and Asbel and Gera and Naaman and Echi and Ros and Mophim and Ophim”** — elsewhere: “Ofim”
46.26: **“All the souls that went with Jacob into Egypt, and that came out of his thigh, besides his sons’ wives, sixty-six.”** — All the souls, etc. AUGUSTINE. It must be seen what answer is to be given to those who use this testimony to confirm that souls are propagated from parents together with bodies. For no one doubts that “souls” is said for men, the whole by the part, in a figure of speech. But in what way do we separate that very part, that is, the soul, by whose name the whole man is signified, from what is said, “They came out of his thighs,” so as to take it that only the flesh was born of him, though only souls are named? The manners of speech in the Scriptures must be looked into.
46.27:
**“And the sons of Joseph, that were born to him in the land of Egypt, two souls. All the souls”** — he puts the part for the whole
**“of the house of Jacob, that entered into Egypt, were seventy.”** — And the sons of Joseph, etc. JEROME. “All the souls of the house of Jacob that entered into Egypt were seventy-five,” it says, though Joseph and his sons are excepted. There is no doubt that sixty-six souls, which came out of Jacob’s thighs, entered into Egypt; for the number, reckoned up one by one, proves it, as it is found in the Hebrew volumes. And as for what we read in the Septuagint, “The sons of Joseph that were born in Egypt, nine souls,” let us know that for nine in the Hebrew there are two. For Ephraim and Manasses were born in Egypt before Jacob entered Egypt and the time of famine broke upon them. That too which we read above, “And sons were born to Manasses, whom his concubine bore him, Machir; and Machir begot Galaad; and the sons of Ephraim, the brother of Manasses,” etc., is described as done by anticipation, as it were. For when Jacob entered Egypt they were not of an age to beget sons. Hence it appears that all the souls that entered into Egypt from Jacob’s thighs were seventy; because sixty-six entered after him and found three in Egypt, that is, Joseph with his two sons, and the seventieth was Jacob; lest we seem to speak against the authority of Scripture. Even the Septuagint translators rendered in Deuteronomy that Israel entered Egypt with seventy souls. So if anyone opposes our Scripture, he will make the Scripture contrary to itself. For those same Septuagint translators, who said by prolepsis that seventy-five souls entered with Jacob and his posterity, recorded in Deuteronomy that only seventy went in. And if it is objected how in the Acts of the Apostles it is said that seventy-five souls entered into Egypt, the excuse is easy. For Luke, the writer of that history, sending out the volume of the Acts of the Apostles among the Gentiles, ought not to write anything contrary to the Scripture that had already been spread among the Gentiles; and at that time the authority of the Septuagint was of greater repute than Luke, who was unknown and of little account. And this is to be observed generally: that wherever the apostles or apostolic men speak to the peoples, they make use of those testimonies that had already been spread among the Gentiles; though most hand down that Luke, as a proselyte, did not know Hebrew letters.
46.28:
**“And he sent Juda before him to Joseph,”** — confession is sent ahead to Joseph, that is, to Christ; because “with the mouth confession is made unto salvation”
**“to tell him; and that he should meet him in Gessen.”**
• not into the land of Ramesses
• And he sent Juda, etc. JEROME. “And he sent Juda before him to Joseph, that he should meet him at the city of Heroes, in the land of Ramesses.” In the Hebrew there is neither “city of Heroes” nor “land of Ramesses,” but only Iessen or Gesem. Some of the Jews assert that Iessen is now called the Thebaid; and as for what follows, “He gave them to possess in Egypt the best land, in Ramesses,” they reckon that the district of Arsinoe was so called of old.
46.29: **“And when he was come thither,”** — after confession Joseph comes to meet him, because the mercy of Christ follows after
46.32: **“And the men are shepherds, and their occupation is to feed cattle: their flocks and herds, and all they have, they have brought with them.”** — And the men are shepherds. AUGUSTINE. It is commended in the patriarchs that they were feeders of cattle from their childhood and from their parents; because this is a just service and a just lordship, when cattle serve man and he is lord over the cattle. Hence: “Let us make man to our image and likeness, and let him have dominion over the fishes of the sea, and the fowls of the air, and all the cattle that are upon the earth”; where it is suggested that reason ought to rule over irrational life. But it was either iniquity or adversity that made man the servant of man. Iniquity, as it was said: “Cursed be Chanaan, a servant shall he be to his brethren”; adversity, as Joseph, sold by his brothers, was made the servant of a foreigner. So the first servants, to whom the Latin tongue gave this name, were made by wars. For he who, being overcome, could be killed by the law of war, was called servus because he was saved (servatus). Hence too they are called mancipia, because they were taken by the hand (mancipata). There is also a natural order among men, that women serve men and sons parents; because there too this is justice, that the weaker in reason serve the stronger. So this is plain justice in lordships and servitudes: that those who excel in reason excel in lordship. And when in this world this is disturbed, through the iniquity of men or through the diversity of fleshly natures, the just bear temporal adversity, to have at the end a most well-ordered and everlasting happiness.
46.34: **“You shall answer: We thy servants are shepherds, from our infancy until now, both we and our fathers. And this you shall say, that you may dwell in the land of Gessen, because the Egyptians have all shepherds in abomination.”** — rightly the Egyptians, in whom is the figure of this world in which iniquity abounds, abominate the shepherds of cattle; for “the just man is an abomination to the wicked”

47.9:
**“He answered: The days of my pilgrimage”** — the saints are strangers and pilgrims upon the earth
**“are a hundred and thirty years, few, and evil, and they are not come up to the days of the pilgrimage of my fathers.”** — The days of my pilgrimage, etc. AUGUSTINE. What does it mean that Jacob says to Pharao, “The days of the years of my life, which I sojourn,” etc.? For so the Greek have, where the Latin have “I spend” or “I have.” Did he say “which I sojourn” because he was born in a land that the people had not yet received as an inheritance by the divine promise, and, spending his life there, was in any case in a foreign land, not only when he was a pilgrim, as in Mesopotamia, but also when he was where he was born? Or is it rather to be taken according to that saying of the Apostle: “While we are in the body, we are absent from the Lord”; and that: “I am a stranger with thee and a sojourner, as all my fathers were”? Again he says of all the days of his life: “They are not come up to the days of the years of my fathers, which days they sojourned.” For he wished nothing else to be understood than what the Latin books have, “they lived.” But by this he signified that this life is a sojourning, that is, the dwelling of a pilgrimage. But this befits the saints, to whom an eternal country is promised. So it must be seen how it was said of the wicked: “They will sojourn and hide; they will watch my heel.” For it is more fittingly taken of those who sojourn so as to hide. They do not abide in the house for ever.
47.11:
**“But Joseph gave a possession to his father and his brethren in Egypt, in the best place of the land,”** — or “place”
**“in Ramesses,”** — it is part of the Thebaid
