**“as Pharao had commanded.”** — But Joseph, etc. It must be asked whether the land of Ramesses is the same as Iessen; for they had asked for this, and Pharao had commanded it to be given.
*Isidore:* Allegorically. Joseph gave his father and brothers the best land, Iessen, providing them food, because famine had oppressed the land. So too the Lord, to his parents, that is, to the patriarchs and prophets from whom he is according to the flesh, or to all the saints, of whom he says in the Gospel, “These are my brethren, who do the will of my Father,” gives the best land, of which it is said: “I believe to see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.”
47.12: **“allowing food to every one”** — Joseph measured out wheat to his father; and yet his father did not adore him, either when he saw him or when he received the wheat. How then do we think the dream fulfilled, unless it contains the prophecy of a greater thing?
47.16:
**“And he answered them: Bring me your cattle, and for them I will give you food, if you have no money.”**
• We give cattle for grain when we cut off beastly impulses from ourselves, so that we may give ourselves more richly to the word of truth.
• Bring me your cattle, etc. It is asked, since Joseph was gathering grain on which men might live, on what did the cattle live, when so great a famine had prevailed, and Joseph’s brothers said to Pharao: “There is no grass for the flocks of thy servants,” etc.? If then in that famine the pastures had failed in the land of Chanaan, why had they not failed in Egypt, since the same famine was everywhere? Perhaps, as is reported by those who know the places, in the many marshes of Egypt the pastures could still not be lacking, even when there was a famine of grain, which usually comes about through the flooding of the Nile; those marshes are said to produce pasture more richly when the water of the Nile rises less.
47.18:
**“And they came the second year, and said to him: We will not hide from our lord,”** — or “from our lord”
**“how that our money is spent, and our cattle also are gone: neither art thou ignorant that we have nothing now left but our bodies”** — elsewhere: “bodies”
47.20:
**“So … bought”** — by teaching and by blood
**“Joseph”** — Christ
**“all the land”** — by the body
**“of Egypt, every man selling his possessions, because of the greatness of the famine. And he brought it into Pharao’s hands:”**
• So … bought, etc. Joseph is not charged with injustice or iniquity, since even his faithfulness is commended from this, that he showed favour to no person, but weighed out to each in even balance according to the buyer’s price. Mystically it signifies that all who are in the spiritual Egypt and covet its riches are slaves. For no Egyptian is free who is fleshly and sold under sin; for Pharao made them subject. Hence perhaps it is said: “I am the Lord thy God, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage.” Hence: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body,” etc. And elsewhere: “You are the servants of him whom you obey, whether it be of sin unto death, or of obedience unto justice.” But the Egyptians were brought into slavery willingly, the Hebrews by force. And the Egyptians sold themselves; nor is it the steward’s fault where worthy things are paid back according to merits. Paul did this too, when he handed over to Satan the one who was unworthy of the number or fellowship of the saints. So let no one say that Paul acted too harshly, who cast a man out of the Church, so that, expelled, he might learn not to blaspheme. For the will of man is wicked when, loving earthly things, it despises heavenly things, and for avarice subjects itself to the devil. But God’s permission is just when he leaves to his own choice, that he may fall, the one who, scorning better things, has chosen worse.
• So Joseph bought, etc. The buying of Joseph, who bought the land of Egypt with grain, signifies that Christ redeems the world with teaching and the price of his blood. And as for his saying, “Take seed and sow the fields, that you may have corn,” etc.: the seed is the word of God; the fields are bodies, which, ploughed by the plough of the Gospel and sown with spiritual seed, put forth the fruit of virtues. The fifth part, which was given to the king, is the tax of the five senses, which is to be paid to Christ the king. The four that remain are allowed to the owners for sowing and for food, because the use of the active life is granted to each, so that he may sow the works of the virtues and reap the fruits of justice unto eternal life, which is given us by Christ. Hence it is said to Joseph: “Our life is in thy hand,” because the salvation of the world is in the power of Christ.
47.22:
**“Except the land of the priests, which had been given them by the king:”** — hence we have the example that the possessions of the Church ought not to be sold off, since they have been made over to God by kings, and so are to be counted among no one’s goods
**“to whom also a certain allowance of food was given out of the public stores, and therefore they were not forced to sell their possessions.”** — Except the land, etc. This signifies that the land of the Church, in which are the true priests, is free from worldly tax; which is fed unceasingly by the divine word, and will suffer no loss of spiritual bread.
47.23: **“Then Joseph said to the people: Behold as you see, both you and your lands belong to Pharao: take seed and sow the fields,”** — made slaves, that is, fully subject to God, we receive grain for seed, because we can freely preach the word of God to our neighbours
47.24:
**“That you may have corn. The fifth part you shall give to the king:”** — we give the fifth part when one serves God by governing the five senses
**“the other four you shall have for seed, and for food for your families and children.”** — we keep four when in this life we live praiseworthily according to each one’s means
47.25: **“And they answered: Our life is in thy hand:”** — the salvation of the world is in the power of Christ
47.29:
**“And when he saw that the day of his death drew nigh, he called his son Joseph, and said to him: If I have found favour in thy sight,”** — the burial of the fathers is carefully commended, to stir the memory of the sons
**“put thy hand under my thigh; and thou shalt shew me this kindness and truth, not to bury me in Egypt:”** — he will be buried in Egypt who is sunk into the depth of evils
**“And when he saw that … drew nigh”** — AUGUSTINE. He binds his son by the same oath by which Abraham bound his servant: the one charging where a wife should be taken for his son, this one commending the burial of his body. Yet in both cases two things are named that are greatly to be valued in all the Scriptures: mercy and justice, or mercy and judgment, or mercy and truth; for it is written: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth.” Abraham’s servant said: “Deal mercifully and justly with my master”; and this one: “that thou shew me mercy and truth.” But why so anxious a commending of his body, that he should not be buried in Egypt but in the land of Chanaan beside his fathers, seems strange, and not fitting the great excellence of a prophet, if we measure it by the custom of men. But if we look for the sacraments, we shall find a joy of greater wonder. For sins are signified by the corpses of the dead, since men are commanded after touching them to be purified as from uncleanness. Hence: “He that washeth himself after touching the dead, if he toucheth him again, what doth his washing avail?” So the burial of the dead signifies the remission of sins. Hence: “Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven,” etc. Where then were the corpses of the patriarchs to be buried but in the land in which he was crucified by whose blood the remission of sins was made? For by their deaths the sins of men are signified. And it is said that the place called Abraham’s, where their bodies were laid, is about thirty miles from the place where the Lord was crucified; so that by the very number Jesus Christ is signified, who appeared at his baptism about thirty years old.
47.31:
**“And as he was swearing, Israel adored God”** — AUGUSTINE. Where the Latin books have, “He adored upon the top of his rod,” some have more correctly, “He adored upon the top of his own rod,” or “on the head of his own rod,” or “on the tip,” or “upon the tip of his own rod.” For they are misled by the Greek word, which is written with the same letters whether it signifies “his” or “his own.” But the accents are different, and are not disregarded in the books by those who know these things; for they are of great value for telling them apart; although it could have one letter more if it were “his own,” so that it would be not autou but heautou. And therefore it is rightly asked what was meant. For it would easily be understood that the old man, who carried a rod as that age is wont, bowed himself upon the top of his own rod to adore God, carrying it so that he adored God by bowing his head upon it. What then is “he adored upon the top,” or “the tip, of his rod,” that is, of Joseph’s? Perhaps he had taken the rod from him when he was swearing to him, and while he held it, after the words of the one swearing, before it was given back, he adored God? For he was not ashamed to carry for a little while the emblem of his son’s power, where the figure of a thing to come was being foreshown.
*Jerome:* “And Israel adored toward the top of his rod.” In this place too some vainly pretend that Jacob adored the top of Joseph’s sceptre, that is, that in honouring his son he adored his power; whereas in the Hebrew it is read very differently: “And Israel adored at the head of the bed”; because after his son swore to him, secure about his request, he adored God, turned to the head of the bed. For the holy man, given to God and weighed down with old age, had his bed so placed that his very posture as he lay was ready for prayer without any difficulty.

48.1: **“taking”** — JEROME. “And he took his two sons with him, Manasses and Ephraim.” From this appears what we said above: that Joseph by that time had only two sons, Ephraim and Manasses. And if, many years later, when Jacob was dying, he brought only two to the blessing, certainly at the time when his father and brothers came in, when his sons were little and still nursing and could not beget, he could not have had grandsons by them.
48.2: **“And being strengthened he sat”** — JEROME. “And Israel, strengthened, sat upon the bed.” Why the Septuagint rendered the same word now one way and now another I do not know; but I say boldly that the same word mitta, which here they translated “bed,” above, where he said Jacob adored, they named “rod.”
48.5:
**“So thy two sons who were born to thee in the land of Egypt before I came hither to thee, shall be mine: Ephraim and Manasses shall be reputed to me as Ruben and Simeon.”**
• they will be called sons of Israel
• So thy two sons who were born, etc. “Before I came to thee into Egypt, they are mine.” JEROME. It is plain that seventy souls entered into Egypt, and that Joseph at that time had not nine but only two sons, as Jacob himself testifies. And as for his saying, “Ephraim and Manasses as Ruben and Simeon,” they will be two tribes, and will be called by their own names, and will beget two peoples, and will inherit the land of promise. But when he says, “the rest of the sons whom thou shalt beget after my death,” he shows that they had not yet been begotten. And as for what he adds, “And they shall be called by the name of their brethren in their possessions,” that is, they will not receive land separately, nor lots of their own, but will be mingled into the tribe of Ephraim and Manasses as appendages.
48.7:
**“For, when I came out of Mesopotamia, Rachel died from me in the land of Chanaan in the very journey, and it was springtime: and I was going to Ephrata,”** — or “Effrata”
**“and I buried her”** — He tells Joseph, as though he did not know, where and when he buried his mother; perhaps prophetically recalling that his mother was buried where Christ was to be born.
48.10: **“For Israel’s eyes were dim by reason of his great age, and he could not see clearly. And when they were brought to him,”** — elsewhere: “brought near”
48.12: **“And when Joseph had taken them from his father’s lap, he bowed down with his face to the ground.”** — And when Joseph had taken, etc. ISIDORE. As it was done in Esau and Jacob, when the Lord said, “The elder shall serve the younger,” so too in the sons of Joseph. For the elder, Manasses, that is, “forgetfulness,” signifies the people of the Jews; the younger, that of the Christians. This is Ephraim, which signifies fruitfulness; which befits the younger people, which is the body of Christ, made fruitful in the breadth of the world. Joseph set Ephraim on the left and Manasses on the right. But he, crossing his hands, prefiguring the mystery of the cross, laid them figuratively, the right moved onto the younger and the left onto the elder; so that the likeness of the cross marked over their heads might foreshow a scandal to the Jews and future glory to the Christians; and that, through the mystery of the cross, the elder would become left from right, and the younger right from left.
48.22:
**“I give thee a portion”** — JEROME. “I have given thee Sichem, a special portion above thy brethren, which I took out of the hands of the Amorrhites with my sword and arrow.” Sichima is declined after the Greek and Latin custom; for in Hebrew it is called Sichem, as John the Evangelist testifies, though it is read faultily as Sichar. So because Sichem is translated “shoulder,” he alluded beautifully to the name, saying, “I have given thee one shoulder”; for in the Hebrew “one” is written for “special.” And as for his saying that he possessed it with bow and sword, he calls bow and sword the justice by which, a pilgrim and stranger, he deserved to be freed from danger when Sichem and Hemor were slain. For he feared that the neighbouring towns and fortresses would rise against him because of the overthrow of an allied city. Or thus: “I will give thee Sichem, which I bought with my strength,” that is, with money that I acquired with much labour, “above thy brethren,” that is, without lot I gave it to the tribe of Joseph. For Joseph was buried there, and his tomb is seen there to this day.
*Augustine:* That Jacob says he gives Sichem to his son Joseph as a special portion, and adds that he possessed it with sword and bow, it is asked how this agrees with the letter. For he bought that possession for a hundred lambs; he did not take it by right of war. Is it because his sons had stormed Salem, the city of the Sichemites, and it could become his by right of war, so that it seems a just war against them, because they did the wrong first by defiling his daughter? Why then did he not give it to his elder sons who did this? And then, if he now gives it to Joseph glorying in the victory, why were the sons who committed this displeasing to him then? Why, finally, when he blessed them, did he recall it in reproach? So a prophetic sacrament lies hidden here: because Joseph signified Christ by a certain special signification, and to him is given that land where Jacob buried the strange gods; so that Christ may be understood as one who will possess the Gentiles, who renounce the gods of their fathers and believe in Christ.
*Alcuin:* In the blessings of Jacob the history must be held and the allegory searched out: the history, about the division of the land of promise; allegorically, about Christ and the Church, which were to be revealed in the last times. But first the foundations of the history must be laid.

49.1: **“And Jacob called his sons, and said to them: Gather yourselves together that I may tell you the things that shall befall you in the last days.”** — he suggests, or signifies, that he speaks prophetically. For though this belongs to the division of the land of Chanaan, yet spiritually it is to be referred to Christ, who came at the end of the world
49.3:
**“Ruben,”** — the Jewish people, to whom it is said: “Israel is my firstborn”
**“my firstborn,”** — to the Jewish people, by right of the firstborn, the priesthood and the kingdom were owed
**“thou art my strength,”** — because from the Jewish people came the foundation of faith, and Christ himself
**“and the beginning of my sorrow:”** — because it always did wrong to God the Father, turning its back to him and not its face
**“excelling in gifts,”** — because to it were given the words of God, the giving of the law, and the testament
**“greater in command.”** — for the greatness of its strength, because it reigned more abundantly than the rest
**“Ruben”** — JEROME. “Ruben, my firstborn, thou art my strength and the beginning of my sons, hard to bear and hard in wantonness and wrong; like water, boil not over; for thou wentest up upon thy father’s bed; then didst thou defile the couch when thou wentest up.” In the Hebrew thus: “Ruben, my firstborn, my strength, and the head of my children; greater in bearing and greater in strength; thou art poured out like water; add not; thou wentest up to thy father’s bed, and didst defile the couch in going up.” And the sense is: You are my firstborn, greater among my children; and you ought, by the order of your birth, to have received the inheritance owed to the firstborn, that is, the priesthood and the kingdom. For this is shown in the bearing of burdens and in very great strength. But because you sinned, and like water that is not held in a vessel were poured out by the rush of pleasure, I command you sin no more, and pay the penalty of your sin in the number of your brothers, in that you have lost the rank of the firstborn.
49.4:
**“Thou art poured out”**
• by sinning against Christ
• by the rush of pleasure
**“as water,”** — which is not held in a vessel
**“grow thou not:”** — because, scattered through the world, it is lessened and cut short
**“because thou wentest up”** — the cause for which it deserved these things
**“to thy father’s bed,”** — when you hanged on the cross the body of the Lord, in which the fullness of the Godhead rested
**“and didst defile his couch.”** — by calling him a sinner and a Samaritan and one who has a devil
49.5:
**“Simeon and Levi brethren: vessels of iniquity, waging war.”**
• Simeon and Levi, etc. JEROME. The Septuagint: “Simeon and Levi, brothers, accomplished the iniquity of their contrivance. Let not my soul come into their counsel, and let not my liver vie in their assembly; for in their fury they slew men, and in their desire they hamstrung a bull.” But in the Hebrew it is thus: “Simeon and Levi, brothers, vessels of iniquity are their weapons. Let not my soul enter into their secret, and in their assembly let not my glory be laid waste; for in their fury they slew a man, and in their lust they undermined a wall.” And it signifies that it was not by his counsel that they killed Sichem and Hemor, men in covenant with them, and against the law of peace and friendship shed innocent blood, and, carried away by cruelty as by fury, overthrew the walls of the city that had received them. Hence: “Cursed be their fury, because it was stubborn, and their wrath, because it was cruel. I will divide them in Jacob, and scatter them in Israel.” Levi did not receive an inheritance of his own, but among all the tribes had a few cities to dwell in. Nor did Simeon, as is written in the Book of Josue; but he received some from the tribe of Juda. Some interpret prophetically the men slain as the apostles, and the bull hamstrung as Christ slain by the Pharisees.
• By these the scribes and priests are understood; for from Simeon came the scribes, from Levi the priests, who took counsel to hand Jesus over to death. Hence he adds: “Let not my soul go into their counsel.”
49.6:
**“into their counsel,”** — of the death of Christ
**“Let not my soul go”** — will
**“nor my glory be in their assembly: because in their fury they slew a man,”** — Christ
**“and in their selfwill they undermined”** — with the lance
**“a wall.”**
• the body of Christ, which was built in forty-six days in the womb of the Virgin
• the bulwark, who keeps Israel
49.7:
**“Cursed be their fury, because it was stubborn:”** — because, kindled with fury, they broke out into so great a crime that they offered Christ to Pilate, saying, “Crucify him, crucify him”; and wrath: “If thou release this man, thou art not Caesar’s friend”
**“and their wrath because it was cruel:”** — so that they asked for Barabbas and demanded that Christ be crucified
**“I will divide them in Jacob,”** — they are called divided, because, separated from the others, they come to the faith
**“and will scatter them in Israel.”** — the scattered, who, the city and temple being overthrown, wander unbelieving through the world
49.8:
**“Juda, thee shall … praise:”** — this is Christ, the true confessor, who was born of the tribe of Juda according to the flesh
**“thy brethren”** — the apostles and others, who by adoption are sons of God the Father
**“thy hands shall be on the necks of thy enemies:”** — by the trophy of the cross he both freed his own and bent down the opposing powers
**“the sons of thy father shall bow down to thee.”**
• because many of the sons of Jacob adored Christ, saved through the election of grace
• Juda, thee shall … praise, etc. JEROME. Because Juda is interpreted “confession” or “praise,” it is written accordingly: “Juda, thy brethren shall confess thee,” or “praise thee, and the sons of thy father shall adore thee. Juda is a lion’s whelp; from the shoot, my son, thou art gone up, lying down as a lion and as a lion’s whelp. Who shall rouse him?” Though there is a great mystery about Christ, yet according to the letter it is signified that kings would be begotten from Juda through the stock of David, and that all the tribes would adore him; for he does not say “the sons of thy mother,” but “the sons of thy father.” And what follows, “from the shoot, my son, thou art gone up”: in the Hebrew, “from the captivity, my son, thou art gone up”; to show that he would lead captive peoples, and, according to a holier understanding, that he ascended on high and led captivity captive; or, as I think better, the captivity signifies the passion, the going up the resurrection. “Tying his foal to the vine, and the foal of the ass with a cord.” In the Hebrew it is thus: “Tying his foal to the vine, and his ass, my son, to the sorec”; that is, that he joined the foal of the ass on which Jesus sat, the people of the Gentiles, to the vineyard of the apostles, who are from the Jews; and tied to the sorec, that is, to the choice vine, the ass on which he sat, that is, the Church gathered from the Gentiles. And in saying “my son,” he makes an apostrophe to Juda himself, because Christ would do all things. And where we read “to the vine his foal,” in the Hebrew it can be read “his city”; by the same sense, in other words, the Church is shown, of which it is said: “A city seated on a mountain cannot be hid.”
49.9:
**“Juda is a lion’s whelp:”** — “a child is born to us”
**“to the prey, my son, thou art gone up:”** — you went up on the cross, to lead captivity captive
**“resting thou hast couched”** — in the tomb; or when in the passion, bowing his head, he gave up the ghost, and rested as in a kind of sleep of numbness
**“as a lion, and as a lioness,”** — overcoming the bitterness and onslaught of death
**“who shall rouse him?”**
• but he himself, who said: “Destroy this temple,” etc.
• Resting thou hast couched, etc. ISIDORE. Or the lion’s whelp rested in sleep because it was not by necessity but by power. Hence: “I have power to lay down my life, and no man taketh it away from me, but I lay it down.” And as for what he adds, “and as a lion’s whelp”: for he died from that whence he was born. The natural philosophers say that the lion’s whelp, when it is born, sleeps three days and three nights; then the place of its den, shaken by its father’s roaring, rouses the sleeper. Christ too, lying in the den of the tomb three days and three nights, fulfilled the sleep of death. So Christ well rested as a lion, who overcame not only the bitterness of death but its rule; and as a lion’s whelp, because he rose on the third day. Hence he adds: “Who shall rouse him?” No one, understand, but himself; for he said: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.”
49.10:
**“The sceptre shall not be taken away”** — the kingdom
**“from Juda, nor a ruler from his thigh,”** — by the generations
**“till he come”** — Christ
**“that is to be sent,”** — by the Father
**“and he shall be the expectation”** — the awaited salvation
**“of nations.”**
• whom he redeemed in his blood
• not of the Jews only
**“shall not be taken away”** — For so long were there kings among the Jews from the seed of Juda, until Christ was born of the Virgin. For the first foreign king in the nation of the Jews was Herod, when Christ was already born. So let him who denies that Christ has come show a king of the tribe of Juda in the nation of the Jews.
49.11:
**“Tying … to the vineyard,”** — with the bond of charity and discipline, so that by imitating him one may be made an heir of God and joint heir with Christ
**“his foal”** — the Gentile people, on whom the burden of the law was not laid
**“to the vine.”** — who says: “I am the true vine”
**“and his ass, O my son,”**
• on which he sat: that is, the Church gathered from the Gentiles
• that is, the slow-footed synagogue, weighed down by the burden of the law
**“He shall wash … in wine,”** — in the blood of the passion, which shall be shed for many unto the remission of sins
**“his robe”** — the flesh, or the Church
**“and his garment in the blood of the grape.”** — His garment, etc. The Gentiles, whom he joined to himself. Hence: “As I live, saith the Lord, thou shalt be clothed with all these as with an ornament.” For Christ cleansed us in the blood of the grape when he hung like a cluster on the wood of the cross, and from his side came out water for washing and blood for redemption.
49.12:
**“His eyes are more beautiful”** — the apostles and evangelists, who give the light of knowledge to the Church
**“than wine,”** — than the austerity of the law
**“and his teeth whiter than milk.”**
• the preachers, who cut men off from error, bringing them as by eating into the body of Christ
• His eyes are more beautiful, etc. ISIDORE. Because their teaching surpasses the austerity of the old law, and the precepts of the Gospel are brighter than the commandments of the law.
**“than milk”** — That is, the teaching of the law, which fed the fleshly people with milk like a little child; but whiter are the teachers of the Church, who chew and distribute the strong and solid food of the word. Hence: “Strong meat is for the perfect.” They are well called whiter than milk, because they are white, pure and free from every stain.
49.13:
**“Zabulon”** — “dwelling of strength,” that is, the Church, most strong to endure
**“shall dwell on the sea shore,”** — according to the letter, Zabulon possessed the coast
**“Zabulon … on the sea shore”** — So as to show a refuge to believers and the harbour of faith to those in peril. Made firm against all the bounds of the world, it awaits the shipwreck of the Jews and the storms of the heretics, who are carried about with every wind of doctrine. From there too some apostles were taken. There the Lord often taught. And it reaches as far as Sidon, that is, it comes as far as the Gentiles. Hence: “The land of Zabulon and the land of Nephtali, the way of the sea beyond the Jordan,” etc. Sidon is “hunting,” and from those places were taken the hunters of whom it is said: “I will send them many hunters, and they shall hunt them from every mountain.”
49.14:
**“Issachar”**
• the people of the Gentiles, which the Lord bought with his blood
• “wages”
• JEROME. “He desired a good thing, resting between the lots; and seeing rest that it was good, and the land that it was fat, he put his shoulder to labour and became a husbandman.” In the Hebrew thus: “Issachar a bony ass, lying down between the borders; and seeing rest that it was good, and the land that it was beautiful, he bowed his shoulder to carry, and became a servant under tribute.” Because he had said of Zabulon that he would possess the shores of the great sea and touch Sidon and the other cities of Phenicia, he returns to the inland province, and by his blessing makes Issachar the dweller in it, who was to possess a most beautiful region in Galilee beside Nephtali. He calls him a bony ass, with a shoulder given to carrying, because he would labour very much in working the land and in carrying to the sea the goods that grew within his borders, bringing tribute to kings as well. The Hebrews say that it is signified by a metaphor that, meditating day and night on the holy Scriptures, he gave his zeal to labour; and that therefore all the tribes serve him, bringing gifts as to a teacher.
**“shall be a strong ass”** — brutish, lustful, tamed by no reason; strong, because redeemed and subject to the Redeemer
**“lying down”** — resting in hope
**“between the borders.”**
• beside the possession of Nephtali
• of this life
• elsewhere: “between the borders”
• Lying down between the borders. To lie down is to rest, waiting for the end of the world, and to seek nothing of worldly things but to desire the last things. The strong ass saw rest and the best land when the simple Gentiles raised themselves to strength of work, because they are making for the country of life.
49.15:
**“He saw rest”** — of eternal life
**“that it was good: and the land”** — of the living
**“that it was excellent: and he bowed his shoulder to carry,”** — he who desires to reach the promised rest willingly carries the burdens of the commandments
**“and became”** — therefore
**“a servant under tribute.”** — offering Christ the gifts of his faith and works
49.16:
**“Dan shall judge his people like another tribe in Israel.”** — Judas, in guile and malice a horned serpent
**“Dan shall judge his people”** — ISIDORE. Some think that by these words Antichrist is foretold, who is to come from the tribe of Dan. Others declare these things of Judas the traitor. By the rider and the horse they understand the Lord with the flesh he took; and his falling backward, because he returned to the earth from which it was taken. But because he rose on the third day, he says: “I will look for thy salvation, O Lord.” Hence elsewhere: “Thou wilt not leave my soul in hell, nor wilt thou give thy holy one to see corruption.” Others transfer these things to Antichrist, whom they assert will come from the tribe of Dan, because Dan is called both a snake and one that bites. Hence: “Dan camped toward the north,” signifying him who said: “I will sit in the mountain of the covenant, in the sides of the north,” etc. And elsewhere: “From Dan the snorting of his horses was heard.” He is called not only a snake but a cerastes. For horns are called cerata in Greek, and this serpent is said to be horned; by which the coming of Antichrist is fittingly asserted, who will be armed against the saints with the bite of pestilent preaching and the horn of power. And a path is narrower than a way. So he is a snake in the way, because he urges to walk in the broadness of life those whom he flatters as if sparing them; but in the way he bites, because he consumes such men with the poison of his error. He becomes a cerastes in the path, because those whom he finds faithful and binding themselves to the precepts of the heavenly journey he not only attacks with crafty persuasion but also presses with the terror of power; and after the favours of feigned sweetness he wields the horns of power.
*Jerome:* “Dan shall judge his people as one of the sceptres of Israel. Let Dan be a snake in the way, a basilisk in the path, biting the hoofs of the horse, and his rider shall fall backward. I will look for thy Saviour.” Samson, judge of Israel, was of the tribe of Dan. So he says this foreseeing in the spirit all things: that Samson the Nazarite would grow his hair and triumph over slain enemies; that, in the likeness of a snake and of a basilisk besetting the roads, he would let no one pass through the land of Israel; and that if anyone rash, trusting in his strength as in the swiftness of a horse, wished to plunder it like a robber, he would not be able to escape. And he speaks by the metaphor of the serpent and the rider. So, seeing that so strong a Nazarite died on account of a harlot, and by his death killed many enemies, he thought he himself was Christ. But because he died and did not rise, and Israel was again led captive, he understands that another saviour of the world and of his race must be awaited, so that he may come for whom it is laid up, and “he shall be the expectation of nations.”
49.17:
**“Let Dan be”** — Antichrist
**“a snake in the way,”** — consuming with poison those whom he urges to the broadness of life
**“a serpent”** — armed with the horns of power
**“in the path,”** — that is, for those who make for the country by the narrow way
**“that biteth the … heels”** — because he will strive to lead astray the last ends of the world
**“horse’s”** — of the world, which foams with pride in the course of slipping times
**“that … may fall”** — not knowing to what punishments he is suddenly being led
**“his rider … backward.”** — to the earth from which he was taken
49.18:
**“thy salvation, O Lord.”**
• suddenly he turns to speak in the voice of the elect, as if: I will not, like the unfaithful, wait for Antichrist, but for the true Christ, the redeemer of the world
• because he rose from the dead on the third day
**“I will look for”** — at his coming
49.19:
**“Gad,”**
• Christ, who at his first coming goes to meet Antichrist, to fight before him
• “little robber”
• with the sword of the word; hence: “I came not to send peace, but the sword”
**“being girded, shall fight before him:”** — the people of Israel
**“and he himself shall be girded”** — the brightness of the second coming is signified; because when Antichrist comes, he will go to meet him “backward,” that is, after him, to kill him with the sword of his mouth; and like a little robber, unforeseen, because “the day of the Lord shall so come as a thief,” etc.
**“backward.”** — having returned to his children
**“Gad”** — JEROME. “A little robber shall rob before him, and he himself shall rob.” We have interpreted according to the Hebrew; for where we have put “little robber,” there is written gadud, so as to allude to the name Gad; which can be expressed more meaningfully as “girded” or “ready for action.” The whole of it is this: that Gad, with Ruben and the half tribe of Manasses, returning after fourteen years to his sons, whom he had left in possession beyond the Jordan, found a war of the neighbouring nations against them, and, the enemies being overcome, fought bravely.
*Isidore:* Gad, being girded, shall fight before him. Christ will fight against Antichrist before and behind: before, by the hidden coming of humility; after, by the glory of majesty made manifest. Hence Moses: “Blessed be Gad in his breadth; he hath rested as a lion, and hath seized the arm and the top of the head, and he saw his principality.” For Christ rested in the tomb, humbled the strength and pride of the lofty, and to him was given principality and honour and kingdom.
49.20:
**“Aser,”** — Christ, whose is the depth of the riches of wisdom and knowledge, who for our sakes became poor, being rich
**“shall be fat,”** — because his possession is fertile
**“his bread”** — the flesh, that is, the food of the saints, of which if any man eat, he shall not die for ever
**“and he shall yield dainties”**
• of wisdom
• of the word; or himself, because Aser is interpreted “dainties”
**“to kings.”** — who rule themselves well, hold down the vices, restrain their bodies
49.21:
**“Nephtali”** — JEROME. “A shoot let loose, giving beauty in its offspring.” In the Hebrew it is written thus: “Nephtali, a well-watered field,” signifying that the waters of immortality spring up in that same tribe; or that, above the lake of Genesareth, it is watered by the river Jordan. And the Hebrews will have it that because of Tiberias, which seems to have knowledge of the law, a well-watered field and words of beauty are prophesied. And where we have put “well-watered field” and the Septuagint “shoot let loose,” the Hebrew can be interpreted “a hart let loose,” because of the early fruits and the quickness of the richer land. But it is better if we refer it all to the teaching of the Saviour, because there he taught most.
*Isidore:* Nephtali, a hart let loose, etc. For the apostles and preachers, leaping swiftly like harts, pass beyond the hindrances of the world, and, meditating on lofty things, give words of beauty, that is, preach the teaching of the Saviour.
49.22: **“Joseph is a growing son, a growing son and comely to behold; the daughters run to and fro upon the wall.”** — A growing son, etc. JEROME. “A growing son above the fountain; daughters walking with measured step upon the wall; and they embittered him, and strove, and were angry against him, having arrows. His bow sat in the strong one, and the bands of his hands were broken by the hands of the mighty one of Jacob; thence the stone of Israel shall be fed by the God of thy father”; because in very many places the Septuagint disagree, as is expressed more plainly in the Hebrew. And the sense is: O Joseph, who are called so because the Lord has increased you to me; or, you will be greater and strongest among your brothers (for the tribe of Ephraim was very strong, as is read in the Book of Kings); O, I say, son Joseph, who are so beautiful that the whole crowd of the girls of Egypt looks out at you from walls and towers and windows: your brothers envied you and provoked you to anger, having the arrows of spite and wounded by the darts of jealousy. But you set your bow and weapons of fighting in the Lord, who is a strong fighter; and your bonds, with which your brothers bound you, were loosed by him; so that from your seed the tribe of Ephraim might be born, strong and steadfast, and unconquered like a harder stone, ruling also over the ten tribes of Israel.
49.27:
**“Benjamin a ravenous wolf, in the morning shall eat the prey, and in the evening shall divide the spoil.”** — Benjamin a ravenous wolf, etc. JEROME. “In the morning he shall still eat, and at evening he shall divide food.” Although it is a plain prophecy of Paul, that in his youth he persecuted the Church and in his old age was a preacher of the Gospel, yet in the Hebrew it is read thus: “Benjamin a ravenous wolf,” or “seizing; in the morning he shall eat the prey, and at evening he shall divide the spoil.” Which the Hebrews explain thus: the altar on which victims were sacrificed, and at whose base the blood was poured out, was in the portion of the tribe of Benjamin. So this, they say, signifies that the priests sacrificed victims in the morning, and at evening divided what had been given them by the people under the law; putting the voracious wolf for the interpretation of the altar, and the dividing of the spoils for the priests, who, serving the altar, live by the altar.
*Isidore:* Benjamin a ravenous wolf, etc. One of the doctors referred this to Jerusalem. Benjamin, he says, is interpreted “son of sorrow.” By the lot of inheritance he received the place in which is the earthly Jerusalem, which was rejected because of its unbelief. This is signified in its sons by Benjamin, who receives the blessing last; and that people is the last to be saved, when the fulness of the Gentiles has come in. For Benjamin is called a wolf because that people shed the blood of the prophets and the just; ravenous, because from great hunger and eagerness it ran to the word of God and seized the kingdom of God by violence. He ate the prey in the morning when he alone received the law; for then the first light of knowledge shone on the world. And he eats in the morning, because the law he received in the morning he still eats and meditates on. But following the law of justice, he has not come to the law of faith. At evening he will divide the spoil, that is, at the last time, when he will be converted. Then he will divide the food, understanding that the letter must be divided from the spirit, because the letter kills, but the spirit gives life.
49.28: **“All these are the twelve tribes of Israel: these things their father spoke to them, and he blessed every one, with their proper blessings.”** — All these in the twelve tribes of Israel, etc. It is asked why Jacob made all whom he begot of the free women and the handmaids sons and heirs with equal honour. It is because Christ bestows the heavenly rewards with equal honour and glory on all who are joined to his body by faith. For there is no distinction there, whether Jew or Greek, barbarian or Scythian, bond or free; because Christ is all and in all, who put on the form of a servant and served for the free and for the slave, that he might bestow an equal gift on all. For whoever earns the faith of the Lord is darkened by no stains of fleshly birth. Hence: “I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh.”
49.33:
**“And when he had ended the commandments, wherewith he instructed his sons, he drew up his feet upon the bed, and died: and he was gathered to his people.”**
• the company of the angels
• And he was gathered, etc. STRABO. It must be asked of what people this is said. For of the fathers there is no question; for it is known that he was gathered to Abraham and Isaac. But a people is a multitude, and those so few could not be called a people. So it must be understood that this is said of the angels too, to whose fellowship the saints are gathered when they pass from the world. Hence: “You are come to mount Sion, and to the heavenly Jerusalem, and to the company of many thousands of angels,” etc.

50.3:
**“And while they were fulfilling his commands, there passed forty days:”** — which number befits penance and humility
**“for this was the manner with bodies that were embalmed, and Egypt mourned for him seventy days.”**
• seven multiplied by ten; because “the mourning for the dead is seven days”
• Seventy days, etc. STRABO. The heathen wept for the dead for nine days; hence too the ninth day was called the novendial. When the worshippers of God were buried, they celebrated the funeral rites for seven days. Hence: “The mourning for the dead is seven days, but for a fool all the days of his life.” For seven signifies rest; hence the seventh day is called the sabbath, that is, rest. So they keep the seventh day of the dead, praying that they may rest with the Lord from the labours of the present life. Hence then it is said, “Egypt mourned for him seventy days,” which is seven multiplied by ten; for seven tens are seventy.
• It can also be said that, as the third day of the dead is kept by the faithful, so that the soul, which is of a threefold nature, may rest, so the seventh day is celebrated so that the soul, which sinned through the enticing of the flesh, may be reconciled with the body. For in seven are three and four: three belongs to the soul, which is irascible, concupiscible and rational; four to the body, which consists of four elements.
**“there passed forty days”** — STRABO. Which number befits penance and humility. Hence in the law and in the Gospel it was kept by the prophets and by the Lord himself.
*Augustine:* The forty days of burial that Scripture records perhaps signify penance, by which sins are buried. For not in vain were the forty days of fasting appointed, in which Moses and Elias and the Lord himself fasted, and the Church calls its chief observance of fasting Quadragesima. Hence too in the Hebrew it is written of the Ninivites, “Forty days, and Ninive shall be destroyed”; so that through so many days, suited, that is, to the humbling of penitents, they may be understood to have wept for their sins in fasting and obtained mercy. Nor does this number befit only the mourning of penitents. For forty days after the resurrection the Lord spent with his disciples, going in and out, eating and drinking; which were days of joy. Nor are the Septuagint translators to be believed to have erred, who said, “Three days, and Ninive shall be destroyed.” For, endowed with an authority greater than the office of translators, by the prophetic spirit (by which also they are confirmed to have agreed with one mouth in their translations, which was a great miracle), they put “three days,” though they were not unaware that forty days were read in the Hebrew; so that it might be understood that sins are dissolved and abolished in the glorifying of Christ, “who was delivered up for our sins, and rose again for our justification.” And the glorifying of the Lord is known in his resurrection and ascension. Hence he gave them, though one and the same Spirit, twice: first after he rose, second after he ascended. And because he rose after three days, but ascended after forty days, the Hebrews signify one of these, the one done later, by the number of forty days; and the Septuagint record the other, the three days, which belongs to the same matter, not by the servitude of translation but by the authority of prophecy. So let us not say that one of these is false, and dispute for some translators against others; since those who translate from the Hebrew prove that what they translate is written, and the authority of the Septuagint, which is commended by so great a miracle done by God, is confirmed by so long a standing in the churches.
50.4: **“And the time of the mourning being expired, Joseph spoke to the family of Pharao: If I have found favour in your sight, speak in the ears of Pharao:”** — The time of mourning being expired, etc. AUGUSTINE. As for Joseph’s charging the powerful men of Egypt to say to Pharao in his name, “My father made me swear, saying: In the tomb which I made for myself in the land of Chanaan, there shalt thou bury me,” it is asked how this is true, since these words of his father are not read where he gave charge about his burial. But the words are to be referred to the sense, as other things above were likewise repeated. For words must serve the will that is to be declared and brought to knowledge. And it is never read above that Jacob dug himself a tomb; but perhaps, unless he had dug it, it would not now be said.
50.10:
**“And they came to the threshingfloor”** — where afterwards the people murmured and were consumed by divine fire
**“of Atad,”** — elsewhere: “Achad”
**“which is situated beyond the Jordan: where celebrating the exequies with a great and vehement lamentation, they spent full seven days.”** — And they came to the threshingfloor, etc. This place is beyond the Jordan, and is seventy miles from Hebron. So they passed beyond the place where they were to bury him, and afterwards, having crossed the Jordan, came back to the place of the double cave. Hence it can be asked why he did this. Someone may say it was because they feared wars, as the sons of Israel were led around through the desert for forty years until, having crossed the Jordan, they came to the land of promise. But this was done for the sake of a greater signification. For in the place called the threshingfloor of Atad, the multitude of the sons of Israel, murmuring against the Lord, was afterwards consumed by divine fire. So in so great a mourning it was not so much the death of Jacob as the coming ruin of the people that was being read.
50.22: **“And he dwelt in Egypt with all his father’s house: and lived a hundred and ten years. And he saw the children of Ephraim to the third generation. The children also of Machir the son of Manasses were born on Joseph’s knees.”** — And he lived a hundred, etc. AUGUSTINE. Since Scripture says that Joseph saw in his lifetime these sons of his sons, or grandsons of his sons, how does it join them to the seventy-five souls with whom it says Jacob entered Egypt, when Joseph, in growing old, came to see them born? For when Jacob entered Egypt, Joseph was a young man, and his father at his death left him in about his fifty-sixth year. Hence it is clear that Scripture commends that number, that is, seventy-five, for the sake of a mystery. According to the faith of the history, Jacob entered Egypt with seventy-five souls, not on that one day on which he came; but because Jacob is very often named in his sons, that is, in his posterity, and it is agreed that he entered Egypt through Joseph, his entering is to be taken as lasting as long as Joseph lived, through whom it came about that he entered. For in all that time all who are mentioned could have been born and lived, so that the seventy-five souls are completed down to the grandsons of Benjamin. For as it says, “These are the sons of Lia whom she bore to Jacob in Mesopotamia of Syria,” speaking also of those who were not born, because there she had borne the parents from whom they were born, declaring them born there because the cause by which they would be born was born there, that is, their parents whom Lia bore there; so, since Jacob had in Joseph the cause of entering Egypt, the whole time that Joseph lived in Egypt was Jacob’s entering into Egypt, through his progeny, which was propagated while he lived through whom it came about that he entered.
50.24:
**“After which he told his brethren: God will visit you after my death, and will make you go up out of this land,”** — from the vale of tears
**“to the land”** — of promise, of the living
**“which he swore to Abraham,”** — faith

• All the kings of the Egyptians were formerly called Pharaos, as now the Ptolemies, and the Arsacids the kings of the Persians, and the Caesars Augusti of the Romans. Yet they had their own names: as he under whom Joseph was in Egypt was called Mephres; from whom down to Cenchres, who afflicted the children of Israel and perished in the Red Sea, there were many Pharaos.
**“In the mean time there arose a new king”** — ORIGEN. Allegorically. This is the devil, who “said in his heart: There is no God”; who says to his people, that is, to the apostate angels: “Behold the people of the children of Israel,” etc., that is, of those who can see God with the mind; “it is mightier than we; come, let us wisely oppress it.” The devil perceives that the people of Israel is great and stronger than he, because he has often fought with it and is often overcome. He knows that Jacob wrestled, and by the help of an angel prevailed against the adversary and was strong with God. He perceived too the wrestlings of other saints and endured spiritual combats; he fears lest a war should some day come and they should side with his adversaries, and, having overcome them, depart from his land. It seems to me, from what had been shown to the patriarchs and prophets about the coming of Christ, that he perceives that one is coming who will strip off his principalities and powers, and triumph over them confidently, and afflict them on the wood of the cross.
*Origen:* Morally. First I wish to ask who is the king in Egypt who knows Joseph, and who does not. For while he reigned who knew Joseph, the children of Israel are not said to have been afflicted, nor worn out in clay and brick, nor their males killed and the females kept alive; but when he began to reign who did not know Joseph. If the Lord rules us, and the sense of our mind or soul is enlightened by God, remembering that Christ rose from the dead, in Egypt, that is, in our flesh, our spirit holds the kingdom with justice, and does not wear out the children of Israel, that is, the rational senses or the virtues, in clay and brick, nor grind them down with earthly cares. If our sense loses the memory of these things and does not know Christ, then “the wisdom of the flesh,” which “is an enemy to God,” succeeds to the kingdom. It addresses its people, that is, the bodily pleasures, and, calling the leaders of the vices to counsel, deliberates against the children of Israel how they may be got round, oppressed, afflicted with clay and brick; how they may expose the males and rear the females; how they may build the cities of Egypt and its fortified cities. Nor is it to be thought that the divine books tell the deeds of the Egyptians without cause; but “what things were written, were written for our learning”; so that you who hear these things, if perhaps you are baptized and numbered among the children of Israel, and have received the Lord as king in yourself, and after this wish to turn aside and do the works of the world, to carry out the deeds of the earth and the services of clay, may know that another king has risen in you who does not know Joseph, a king of Egypt. He compels you to his works, to work brick and clay. He, with masters and taskmasters set over you, drives you with whips to earthly works, so that you may build cities for him. He makes you run about the world, troubling the elements of sea and land for greed; beat at the courts with lawsuits; weary your neighbours with quarrels for a little turf of land; lay snares for chastity, deceive innocence, commit foul things at home, cruel things abroad, shameful things within the conscience. In things of this kind know that you are serving as a soldier of the king of Egypt, which is to be driven by the spirit of this world.

• Therefore he set over them masters, etc. ORIGEN. Allegorically. The devil, having called his people together, desires to oppress the rational sense, which is now called Israel in figure. He set over them masters of works, to compel them to learn the works of the flesh; according to that: “They were mingled among the heathens, and learned their works.” He teaches them to build cities for Pharao: Phithom, which signifies “mouth of failing” or “of the abyss”; and Ramesses, which is “the stirring of the moth”; and On, that is, Heliopolis, which is called the city of the sun. The mouth fails from truth and proofs when it speaks a lie. He was a liar from the beginning, and therefore wishes such cities to be built for him. “Mouth of the abyss,” because the abyss is the place of his perdition. His other city is “the stirring of the moth.” For whoever follows him lays up treasure where the moth destroys and thieves break through and steal. He builds also the city of the sun, under a false name, because “he transformeth himself into an angel of light.” In these he busies the minds that were made to see God. Yet he foresees that wars threaten him and that the ruin of his people is ripe. Therefore he says: “The people of Israel is stronger than we.” Would that he might feel us too to be stronger than he: that is, that I may not receive the evil thoughts and desires he sends in, but drive back his fiery darts with the shield of faith, and in all that he suggests say: “Begone, Satan; for it is written: The Lord thy God shalt thou adore, and him only shalt thou serve.” And as for his saying, “Lest perhaps a war befall us, and these side with our adversaries”: from the prophetic voices he foresees the war to come, and that he must be forsaken by the children of Israel, and that they will side with his adversary and be added to the Lord. This is what Jeremias says: “The partridge hath cried, she hath gathered together what she did not bring forth; he hath gathered riches, and not by right; in the midst of his days he shall leave them, and in his latter end he shall be a fool.” So he understands that he is the partridge that gathered what she did not bring forth, and that those whom he gathered without right will leave him and follow Christ, who begot them. He will remain a fool, when the whole creation flees to its maker and parent. Therefore he is indignant, saying: “Lest, overcoming us, they go out of our land.” He does not wish us to go out of his land, so that we may always bear the image of the earthly; lest, leaving him, we flee to him who has prepared the kingdom of heaven, leaving “the image of the earthly” and taking up “the image of the heavenly.” Therefore he set up masters of works, to teach their arts and make us craftsmen of malice. And because there are many masters of malice whom Pharao set over us, who command, exact and wring out earthly works, therefore, when Christ came, he made other teachers fighting against them, who, subduing all their principalities, powers and virtues, might defend the children of Israel from violence, and teach them the works of Israel and to see God with the mind; to leave the works of Pharao, to go out of the land of Egypt, to put off the ways of Egypt and the whole old man with his deeds, and to put on the new, who according to God is created.
*Isidore:* Allegorically. Israel signifies the Christian people, Pharao the devil, who lays on the most heavy yoke of clay and brick, that is, the slavery of earthly and muddy work, with straw mixed in, that is, with light and irrational deeds; so that, all being weighed down with the burden of sins, there may be no one to destroy or overcome his kingdom.

**“And the king of Egypt spoke”** — the devil

**“of the Hebrews: of whom one was called Sephora,”** — “sparrow,” that is, the spiritual law

• And the king of Egypt spoke, etc. ORIGEN. Allegorically. We find these things not only in the world, which is spiritually called Egypt, but in each one of us. The prince of this world does not wish the males to be kept alive, but the females. In the female the flesh and the affections of the flesh are signified; but the male is the rational sense and the intellectual spirit, which can grasp heavenly things, understand God, seek the things that are above. This the prince of Egypt hates and desires to be killed; but he desires the things of the flesh to live, and what belongs to bodily matter, not only to live but to be increased and cultivated. For he wishes all to savour fleshly things, to seek temporal things and those upon the earth; that no one lift his eyes to heaven, no one ask whence he came here, no one remember his country, paradise. So when you see men leading their lives in pleasures, floating in luxury, giving themselves to feasts and lewdness, know that in them the king of Egypt is killing the males and keeping the females alive. But if he sees one in a thousand turned to God, lifting his eyes upward, seeking eternal things, hating delights and luxury, loving continence, this one Pharao desires to be killed as a male; he persecutes him, attacks him with a thousand engines; he hates such men, and does not let them live in Egypt. Hence it is that in this world the servants of God are held in contempt and exposed to insults; hence hatreds and persecutions are stirred up against them.
**“to the midwives of the Hebrews: of whom”** — ORIGEN. He tries also to corrupt the midwives, of whom one was called Sephora, that is, “sparrow,” the other Phua, that is, “red” or “modest”; through them he seeks to have the males killed and the females kept alive. “But the midwives feared God, and did not as he commanded them.” The midwives taught us beforehand to hold a certain form of rational learning. For midwives are physicians, and they tend both the males and the females being born. So common learning is rational knowledge, and it reaches almost every sense, instructs and tends all. If anyone in it is of manly mind, who wishes to seek heavenly things and pursue divine things, he will come, as one doctored and strong, more ready through these learnings to the understanding of divine things. For there is one, like the sparrow, which teaches loftier things and calls upward on the wings of rational teaching. The other, red or modest, is moral: it orders conduct, teaches modesty and uprightness. Yet to me, because Scripture says of them that they feared God and did not do the command of the king of Egypt, they seem to keep the figure of both Testaments; and Sephora, which is interpreted “sparrow,” seems to fit the Law, which is spiritual; and Phua, which is “red” or “modest,” to point to the Gospels, which are red with the blood of Christ and glow red through the whole world with the blood of the passion. By these, then, as by midwives, the souls that are born in the Church are tended, because all the medicines of learning are supplied from the Scriptures. Yet Pharao tries through them to kill the males, when he suggests heresies and wicked doctrines to those studious in the divine Scriptures. But the foundation of God stands firm. For the midwives fear God, that is, they teach the fear of God, which is the beginning of wisdom. So what follows fits more aptly: because the midwives feared God, they made themselves houses. Which according to the letter has no consequence; for a house is not made because God is feared. But if you see how the Scriptures of the New and Old Testament, teaching the fear of God, make the houses of the Church and fill the whole world with houses of prayer, it will seem reasonably written. So these midwives, because they fear God, that is, teach the fear of God, do not do the command of the king of Egypt, but keep the males alive; and yet it is not said that they obeyed by keeping the females alive. And I say confidently: they do not keep the females alive. For neither vices nor luxury are taught in the Church, nor are sins nourished, which Pharao wants when he orders the females to be kept alive; but virtue alone is cultivated and nourished. But let us refer these things to each one. If you fear God, you do not do the command of the king of Egypt; for he commands you to live in delights and to covet present things. You, if you fear God and perform the office of a midwife, if you desire to bring salvation to your soul, keep the males alive; that is, you tend and nurse the inner man who is in you, and by good deeds and understandings gain eternal life.

So the devil, lest the strength of faith prevail, wishes the virtues to be killed and the vices to live; and strives to kill the strong and manly senses of the mind by which we savour divine things, that is, reason, prudence, constancy, innocence and faith; and desires what is womanish, weak, fragile and prone to vice to survive, that is, ambition, violence, lust, anger and things like these, which are the figure of the females.

**“They answered: The Hebrew women are not as the Egyptian women:”**
• They lie from fear of their own death, which is to be punished; but they saved the boys from the fear of God, which is to be rewarded.
• No lie is told without sin; but when it is told joined with mercy, it is pardonable, like the lie of the midwives.
• They answered, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is asked whether such lies are approved by divine authority, because it is written that God dealt well with the midwives. But whether God pardoned the lies for the sake of the mercy, or judged even the lie worthy of reward, is uncertain. For the midwives did one thing in keeping the little ones alive, another in lying to Pharao. In keeping them alive it was a work of mercy; but they used the lie for themselves, lest Pharao harm them, which could belong not to praise but to pardon. Nor is authority for lying given from this to those of whom it is said: “And in their mouth there was found no lie.” For the life of some, far below the profession of the saints, if it has these sins of lies, is borne with for its very progress and disposition, especially if they do not yet know how to wait for heavenly benefits, but are busied about earthly ones. But those whose “conversation is in heaven” I do not think ought to shape the measure of their tongue concerning truth and falsehood by the example of the midwives.
1.20:
**“Therefore God dealt well with the midwives:”** — because they feared God
**“Therefore God dealt well”** — GREGORY. Lying must be shunned with the greatest care, though it is of lighter guilt if someone lies in doing a kindness. But since it is written, “The mouth that belieth killeth the soul,” and “Thou wilt destroy all that speak a lie,” the perfect flee even this, so that not even anyone’s life is defended by their deceit, lest they harm their own soul while striving to profit another’s flesh; though we readily believe that this kind of sin is forgiven. For if any guilt whatever is purged by a following devout work, how much more easily is this wiped away, which piety, the mother of good work, accompanies? But many try to assert from the deceit of the midwives that this kind of lie is not a sin, because the Lord built them houses. In which recompense, rather, it is known what the guilt of a lie deserves. For the reward of their kindness, which could have been repaid in eternal life, was turned aside, for the guilt of the lie, into an earthly recompense; so that in their life, which they wished to protect by lying, they received the good they had done, and had no further reward of wages to wait for. For if it is weighed closely, they lied for love of the present life, not with the intention of a reward. For by sparing they tried to shield the life of the infants; by lying, their own.

**“And because the midwives feared God, he built”** — by granting abundance
**“them houses.”** — according to the letter; or he gave them sons
*Augustine:* In the book of Expressions. “And because the midwives feared God, he built them houses.” Did they not have houses before? Or does this word belong to riches, or rather to some suitable means of household goods? For it seems like what Jacob said to his father-in-law: “Now when shall I too make a house for myself?” For he had said that Laban’s cattle had increased under him, which Laban himself confessed, saying: “God hath blessed me at thy coming.” So “as you too” is understood; for this is what “I too” seems to mean; so that it seems to belong to the making of the house itself that the wages to be fixed are then proposed by Laban.

**“Pharao therefore charged”** — “scattering,” or “opening of the mouth,” or “mouth of the abyss”
**“all his people,”** — to the demons, or to wicked men, or to the vices
**“saying: Whatsoever”** — good work
**“of the male sex,”** — of the virtues
**“shall be born … into the river:”** — the waves of the world
**“ye shall cast … whatsoever of the female,”** — of the vices
**“keep it alive.”** — Pharao therefore charged, etc. ORIGEN. Morally. The Egyptians, whom Pharao charges here, keep only the females alive and hate the males; for they hated the virtues and nourished the vices. Now too the Egyptians lie in wait, if a male is born to the Hebrews, to kill it at once, unless they take care, watch and hide it. Scripture tells that one of the tribe of Levi begot a male, and saw that the infant was goodly, and hid him. So let us not do our justice before men, but with the door shut pray to our Father in secret, and let not the left hand know what the right hand does; lest it be snatched away by the Egyptians, seized, and drowned in the waves. If I give alms because it is a work of God, I beget a male. But if I seek praise from men and do not hide it, it is snatched away by the Egyptians and drowned in the river; and with so much labour and so much zeal I have begotten a male for the Egyptians.
