• After this there went, etc. RABANUS. Hence Josephus says: But Amram, fearing that if caught he would fall to the king’s wrath, and himself perish with the boy and shut out the providence of God, decided rather to see to the boy’s safety in this way, and judged that this was the providence of hiding. He prepared a round vessel woven of withies, of about the size of a cradle, enough for the infant to lie in it roomily. Then they daubed it with pitch; for it is the nature of pitch to keep back the entry of water in wicker vessels. So putting the infant there, and setting it near the river, they left his safety to God. Now Thermuth was the king’s daughter. While she was playing by the bank of the river, seeing that vessel carried by the river, she ordered that cradle to be brought to her. When those who had been sent for this came with the cradle, she took it, and seeing the infant, rejoiced greatly at his size and beauty. For God used such care about Moses that by the very people who, because of his birth, had decreed to destroy the whole race of the Hebrews, he was held worthy of food and care. And Thermuth, the king’s daughter, ordered a woman to be brought to give the infant the breast. When he would not go to her breasts but shunned them, and did this with many women, Mary, standing by what was being done, as if she seemed to be standing among the others by chance, said: In vain, O queen, do you call these women to nurse the infant, who have no kinship with him. But if you order one of the Hebrew women to be brought, I think he will be able to take the breast as from one of his own tribe. And when she was thought to have spoken well, she ordered her to go and bring someone who could suckle him. And she, having received such leave, came back bringing her mother, known to no one. And the infant went gladly, as it were, to her breasts; and at the queen’s request the nursing of the boy was entrusted to her with all diligence. And according to the outcome of events the name was given him because he was saved from the river. For the Egyptians call water moy, and saved ses; so putting this together from both they gave him the name Moses, that is, “saved from the water.” Allegorically. The parents of Moses, whose faith and works the natural law adorned, are the patriarchs, from whom Moses himself and those who received the law of the letter were born. So Moses, born in his parents’ house, is hidden for three months, since the old law lay hidden among the Jewish people for three periods before the coming of Christ, that is, under the judges, under the kings, under the priests, until he came who gave the law and handed it over to the Gentiles through the whole breadth of the world, to be kept spiritually. And Pharao’s daughter is the Church gathered from the Gentiles, which, though she now rejoices in a true parent, that is, God the Father, yet before, when she served idols, followed another father; of whom it was said to her by the divine voice in the Psalm: “Hearken, O daughter, and see, and incline thy ear; and forget thy people and thy father’s house,” etc. So she went out of her father’s house and came to the waters of baptism, to be washed from the sins she had contracted in her father’s house; and coming to baptism she received the law, which was then inside a basket of bulrushes, woven of many twigs or of papyrus and daubed with pitch and slime, because it was fouled, hemmed in by the cheap and earthly traditions of the Jews; until the Church took it up from the marshy and muddy places of fleshly senses, and within the halls of true wisdom and the royal roofs. It spent its infancy among its own, that is, among those who did not know how to understand it spiritually, a little thing and the food of sucklings. But when it came to the Church and was rightly understood through her, it was made stronger. What then is it that she who nursed the boy received wages from Pharao’s daughter, unless that the synagogue, with whom the law was born and nursed, received this wage from the Church: that it should no longer worship idols; seeing those from the Gentiles who had believed so turned to the Lord that they utterly rejected images and no longer worshipped them, it too is taught to blush at worshipping idols?
• And seeing him a goodly child, etc. ORIGEN. Allegorically. Pharao’s daughter is the Church gathered from the Gentiles, to whom it is said through the Prophet: “Forget thy people and thy father’s house, for the king hath greatly desired thy beauty.” This, then, is she who went out of her father’s house and came to the waters to be washed from the sins she had contracted in her father’s house; and at once she received bowels of mercy and had pity on the infant. Coming into the marsh, she found Moses lying, exposed by his own people, and had him nursed. He is nursed among his own and spends his infancy there; grown stronger, he is brought to her and adopted as a son. Moses signifies the Law. So the Church, coming to the waters of baptism, received the Law shut in a thibis and daubed with pitch. Now a thibis is a covering woven of papyrus and twigs, or formed from the bark of trees. So the Law lay shut within coverings of this kind, daubed with pitch and slime, that is, with the cheap and foul senses of the Jews; it lay fouled and smeared until the Church came from the Gentiles and took it up from the muddy and marshy places into the halls of wisdom and the royal roofs. Yet it spends its infancy among its own; for among those who do not understand it spiritually it is little, an infant, and has the food of sucklings. When it comes to the Church, Moses is stronger and more vigorous; for when the veil of the letter is removed, perfect food is found in the reading of it. She receives the wages of nursing from Pharao’s daughter, with whom the law is born and nursed. But what is it that the synagogue receives from the Church? I think it is what Moses says: “I will provoke you to jealousy by that which is not a nation; by a foolish nation I will anger you.” So the synagogue receives this wage from the Church: that it no longer worships idols. For seeing the Gentiles so turned to God that they no longer know idols, it blushes to worship idols any longer. We too, if we have had Pharao for a father, if he begot us in evil works, when we come to the waters, let us take up the law of God. Let not the letters seem foul to us like a dark covering; let us eat what in it is little and for sucklings; let us take up what is perfect and place it within the royal roofs of the heart. We have a great and strong Moses: let us think nothing small of him, nothing cheap, but all magnificent, all excellent, all goodly. For all that is spiritual and of lofty understanding is great.
2.3:
**“And when she could hide him no longer, she took a basket”** — from fiscus, that is, a sack
**“made of bulrushes, and daubed it with slime”** — with the cheap and foul sense of the Jews
**“and pitch: and put the little babe therein, and laid him in the sedges by the river’s brink,”** — in marshy ground only; because in earthly hearts the law lay fouled, as if exposed
2.4: **“His sister standing afar off,”** — Mary, according to the Hebrews
2.5:
**“And behold the daughter”**
• Thermuth, as it is said
• the Church from the Gentiles
**“of Pharao came down”** — of the devil
**“to wash herself”**
• to be baptized
• hence: “Forget thy people, and thy father’s house”
**“in the river:”** — of baptism
**“and her maids”** — “the young maidens have loved thee exceedingly”
**“walked by the river’s brink. And when she saw the basket”** — the hearts of the Jews
**“in the sedges, she sent one of her maids for it: and when it was brought,”** — the first souls of believers
2.6:
**“She opened it and seeing within it an infant”**
• the law suckling its little ones in the literal sense
• And seeing within it, etc. ISIDORE. Moses, that is, Christ, is found by the faithful at the river of washing and the water of baptism. Moses wept; and Christ wept for the sins of the old man whom he had put on. Hence, in raising Lazarus he wept, bewailing the faithlessness or the misery of the Jews. Pharao’s daughter, coming down to the washing of the river, took up the infant; because the Church from the Gentiles, desiring the sanctification of the saving washing, received from the synagogue, its fleshly mother, Christ cast out as an infant; who then seemed little, when he was seen in man. She found Moses shut in a little vessel woven of many wild twigs; and the Church finds Christ laid up in the hearts of the saints, who, woven together in unity out of many persons, are all made one body in Christ, and receiving him, guard him with devout observance.
**“crying, having compassion on it she said:”** — because the law was born and nursed among the Jews
2.7: **“And the child’s sister said to her Shall I go and call to thee a Hebrew woman,”** — the synagogue
2.8: **“She answered: Go. The maid went and called her mother.”** — or “her own”
2.9:
**“And Pharao’s daughter said to her. Take this child and nurse him for me: I will give thee thy wages.”** — that you may no longer worship idols
**“The woman took,”** — the synagogue
**“and nursed the child: and when he was grown up,”**
• in the early Church
• now feeding the strong with perfect sense
**“she delivered him”** — by thrusting him away from herself
**“to Pharao’s daughter.”**
• to the Church from the Gentiles
• And when he was grown up, she delivered, etc. RABANUS. Josephus relates that Pharao’s daughter brought Moses, grown up, to her father, who set his crown on him; which Moses at once threw down, because he saw an image carved on it. Hence the priest who was there wished to kill him, saying that Egypt was to be overthrown through him, as he had learned from an oracle of the demons. But Pharao’s daughter freed him. And when he was of full age, he was sent by Pharao against the Ethiopians. And since he knew that he would march through deserts full of serpents, he took ibises, that is, Egyptian storks. And when he had pitched camp, he brought them out, so that they might devour and drive off the serpents; and so the army passed the night safely. So when he came to the city he was to storm, the queen of the Ethiopians fell in love with him, and by agreement handed the city over to him and married him. Hence it is that Aaron and Mary quarrelled with Moses on account of his Ethiopian wife.
2.10:
**“And she adopted him for a son,”** — received into the royal hall of the heart
**“and called him Moses, saying: Because I took him out of the water.”**
• the Church from the Gentiles receives Christ at the font of baptism
• of baptism
2.11:
**“In those days after Moses was grown up,”** — Christ
**“he went out”**
• from the Father
• or from the Jews
**“to his brethren: and saw their affliction,”** — in the world
**“and an”** — the devil, who does us wrong in this pilgrimage
**“Egyptian striking one of the Hebrews”** — who pass in haste along the way of this world
**“his brethren.”** — We are all brothers in Christ; “we have one Father, God”
2.12:
**“And when he had looked about”**
• foreseeing all things with discernment, because he overcame the proud one by wisdom, not by might
• AUGUSTINE. Of this deed of Moses we have argued enough in the work we wrote against Faustus on the life of the patriarchs: whether there was a praiseworthy disposition in him, by which he committed this sin, as rich ground is praised before useful seeds for a certain wildness of useless weeds; or whether the deed itself is to be justified. Which seems not to be so, because he did not yet hold any lawful power, neither received from God nor ordained by human society. And yet, as Stephen says in the Acts of the Apostles, he thought his brothers understood that God would give them salvation through him; so that by this testimony Moses seems to have been already warned by God (which Scripture is silent about in that place), so that he could dare this.
**“this way and that way, and saw no one there, he slew”** — by his own death
**“the Egyptian”** — the devil
**“and hid him in the sand.”** — in loose and dry minds
*Isidore:* Allegorically. Moses, that is, Christ, in defending us kills the Egyptian, that is, the devil, who does us wrong in this pilgrimage, and buries him, slain, in the sand. For he lies hidden in those who have no firm foundation. But he builds the Church on a rock, and those who hear his word and do it he compares to a wise man who builds his house upon a firm rock; but others he compares to a foolish man who builds upon the sand.
2.13:
**“And going out the next day”** — In this Moses bore the figure of Christ, who in himself, the cornerstone, sought to make peace in the discord of the two peoples. The one who does the wrong and scorns the reconciler is the Jewish people, which rejected the preaching of Christ the reconciler and remained an enemy of the believing people. Hence: “Be thou his disciple; but we are the disciples of Moses.”
**“and he said to him that did the wrong: Why strikest thou thy neighbour?”** — or “brother”
2.14: **“But he answered: Who hath appointed thee prince and judge over us? Wilt thou kill me, as thou didst yesterday kill the Egyptian? Moses feared, and said: How is this come to be known?”** — And Moses feared, etc. AUGUSTINE. “If this word has been so made known.” Two things are to be noted in this expression: that the sentence hangs, and was left so; and then that he put “word” for “deed.”
2.15:
**“And Pharao heard”** — the devil
**“of this word and sought to kill”** — in his members
**“Moses:”** — Christ
**“but he fled”** — in the apostles, to the Gentiles
**“from his sight,”** — from the Jewish people, that is, the spiritual Egypt
**“and abode in the land of Madian, and he sat down by a well.”** — which is interpreted “contradiction” or “answer”; for the Gentiles first contradicted, and afterwards, answering devoutly, obeyed
2.16:
**“And the priest”** — the devil
**“of Madian”** — because before they were subject to the superstition of the Gentiles
**“had seven daughters,”** — the churches from the Gentiles, enlightened by the sevenfold Spirit
**“who came to draw water:”**
• the knowledge of the Law, or worldly knowledge
• of baptism, or of heavenly teaching
• beside the streams of the Scriptures
**“and when the troughs were filled,”**
• the hearts
• humble minds
**“desired to water … flocks.”**
• the apostles
• the people
**“their father’s”** — Those seven daughters, that is, the faithful, after they were turned to the Lord and to be filled from the heavenly fountain, watered the flocks of their father, that is, of God, from the same Gospel fountain from which they themselves had drunk.
2.17:
**“And the shepherds came”** — the philosophers of the Gentiles, the scribes and Pharisees of the Jews, or the priests of the idols
**“and drove them away: and … arose,”**
• in speech
• from death
**“Moses”** — Christ
**“and defending the maids, watered”** — with the water of wisdom
**“their sheep.”**
• or “flocks”
• simple souls
2.18:
**“And when they returned to Raguel”**
• who is also called Raguel and the Cinite
• Raguel, “feeding of God,” or “God his friend”
**“their father, he said to them: Why are ye come sooner than usual?”** — The devil marvels that the Gentiles are turned to God more quickly than to himself, with whom they had long been.
2.21: **“And Moses swore that he would dwell with him. And he took Sephora”** — “beauty,” or “appeasing”
2.22:
**“And she bore him a son, whom he called Gersam,”** — “stranger”
**“saying: I have been a stranger in a foreign country. And she bore another, whom he called Eliezer,”** — “the help of my God”
**“saying: For the God of my father, my helper hath delivered me out of the hand of Pharao.”** — And she bore, etc. Allegorically. Christ joined to himself the Church from the Gentiles, which by the gift of the sevenfold Spirit is one in the Catholic faith; hence: “One is my dove”; which bears a son who is called “stranger,” and another who is “the help of God.” For the saints are strangers upon the earth, but they never lack the help of God.
2.23:
**“Now after a long time the king of Egypt died:”** — Now after a long time, etc. Allegorically. After Moses took a wife in the land of Madian, the king of Egypt died; because when Christ turned the Gentiles to the faith throughout the world, the principality of the devil was destroyed.
**“and … groaning,”** — repenting
**“groaning”** — Morally. Unless the king of Egypt dies in you, you do not know that you are oppressed by the slavery of Egypt and by the works of clay and brick; nor do you groan in heart, nor cry out to the Lord to free you.
**“the children of Israel … because of the works:”** — of the flesh
**“cried out”**
• with heart and mouth
• “The eyes of the Lord are upon the just, and his ears unto their prayers”
**“and their cry went up unto God from the works.”** — that is, because of the works
2.25: **“And the Lord looked upon”** — that is, for the merits of the fathers

3.1: **“Now Moses fed the sheep of Jethro his father in law”** — another reading: “his father in law”
3.2:
**“And the Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire”** — by the word of the Lord
**“out of the midst of a bush:”** — of the Jewish sin
**“and he saw that the bush was on fire and was not burnt.”**
• because through the law the sins of the people were not consumed
• Others understand by the burning bush the Church, which is set aflame by persecutions and, the Lord speaking in her, is not burnt. That the Lord appeared to Moses in the bush shows that he appears to the faithful in the Church, and nowhere else.
• The Hebrews say that God appeared to Moses in a bush so that the Jews could not carve themselves an idol from it. For God always cuts off the occasion of idolatry.
**“And … appeared to him”** — ISIDORE. Allegorically. There was a flame in the bush and it was not burnt. The bush is the thorns of the sins of the Jews; the flame in the bush is the Word of God, that is, the Law given to that people. And the flame does not burn up the bush, because the Law that was given does not consume their sins.
*Gregory:* Morally. Moses, mingled among the Egyptians, was as it were awake to the world, and so he did not hear the voice of the Lord. But when the Egyptian was slain, after he fled into the desert and spent forty years there, he fell asleep to earthly tumults, and so he perceived the divine voice. For when the mind is lulled to sleep from outward things, the word of God penetrates more truly. For a crowd of earthly thoughts, clamouring, shuts the ear of the heart. For a man divided is not wholly equal to both; because if he opens his hearing outwardly, he grows deaf inwardly.
3.3: **“And Moses said: I will go”** — or “I will pass over,” according to the Septuagint, which is fitting; for such a vision suits one who passes over
3.4:
**“And when the Lord saw”** — And when the Lord saw, etc. GREGORY. The angel who is described as having appeared to Moses is called now the Lord, now an angel: an angel, because he serves by speaking outwardly; the Lord, because, presiding inwardly, he gives the speaking its power. For when one who speaks is governed from within, he is called both an angel through his service and the Lord through the inspiration.
**“that he went forward to see, he called to him out of the midst of the bush,”** — He called to him out of the midst, etc. GREGORY. God often speaks through angels by earthly and heavenly substances together, as here, when he joined fire and the bush, and united one thing above with another below. This is done only when something great is signified by the joining. For in speaking to Moses through the kindled bush, he showed that he would be the teacher of the people, who would both receive the flame of the law and not shun the thorn of sin: so that he who would come forth from that people would take the sins of our flesh like the thorn of the bush with the fire of the Godhead, and keep the substance of the humanity unconsumed in the very flame of the divinity.
3.5:
**“And he said: … not”** — or “not”
**“Come … nigh hither, put off the shoes”** — dead works
**“from … feet:”** — the affections
**“thy”** — Put off the shoes, etc. ISIDORE. Because no one, that is, can worthily stand or see God unless he lays aside all earthly and mortal vices. Otherwise: it was the custom of the ancients that if a bridegroom repudiated his bride, he took off his shoes as a sign of the repudiation. So Moses is ordered to take off his shoes, lest he approach shod, as if a bridegroom, to the Church, which is signified in the bush: for this was to be kept for Christ, who is the true bridegroom. Of whom John says: “The latchet of whose shoe I am not worthy to loose.”
**“the place”** — the Church, to which no one comes shod
3.6:
**“And he said: I am the God of thy father, the God”** — The merits of good parents often help their children.
**“of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. Moses hid his face:”** — by bowing
3.7:
**“And the Lord said to him: I have seen the affliction”** — having had pity, that I may free them
**“of my people in Egypt, and I have heard their cry because of the rigour of them that are over the works:”** — I have seen the affliction, etc. GREGORY. Morally. When minds are scattered abroad it is hard for anyone to return to himself. For crooked ways, once they have caught a man, hold him the more delightfully, the more what he likes is not lawful. For when the gift of discipline does not stand in the way, no penalty of retribution is foreseen to frighten him. But with the eyes of the heart shut, the soul is hurled headlong, and the more securely it enters into temporal evils, the more stubbornly it despairs of eternal goods. But this wickedness of the reprobate separates the life of the elect, as grain from chaff, and while it afflicts, it profits them: because while it inflicts violence, it compels them to hasten to things above. This is signified in the people of Israel, with Moses calling and Pharao raging. For Moses was sent to call when Pharao pressed with hard works, so that one by calling might draw, another by raging might drive, so that the people, shamefully fixed in slavery, might be moved, either called or driven. This is done daily when, after the heavenly rewards are preached, the reprobate are allowed to rage against the elect: so that those whom Egypt, that is, the present life, oppressed by flattering, it may help by pressing; so that while God invites, torment may drive.
3.8:
**“And knowing their sorrow, I am come down to deliver them out of the hands of the Egyptians,”** — by suffering with them, by freeing them with my presence
**“and to bring them out of that land”** — And to bring them out of the land, etc. GREGORY. To a rude people something had to be promised from the present life, so that it could be more strongly established in the future. For if it did not receive small things, it would not believe great ones. So God, by bestowing earthly things, persuades also to heavenly ones, so that, receiving what it saw, it might hope for what it did not see.
**“into a good and spacious land, into a land that floweth with milk and honey,”** — He gives earthly things to persuade to heavenly ones, and that he who receives visible things may learn to hope for invisible ones.
**“into a good and spacious land”** — GREGORY. Present prosperity is sometimes given to invite to a better life, sometimes to damn more fully for ever. Hence the land of Chanaan is promised to the Israelites, so that they might at length be invited to hope for eternal things. For a rude people would not believe the promises unless it received something near at hand from the one who promised. So it is drawn not only by hope to things, but sometimes by things to hope. Hence: “He gave them the lands of the Gentiles: and they possessed the labours of the people: that they might observe his justifications, and seek after his law.”
3.9:
**“For the cry of the children of Israel is come unto me: and I have seen … affliction,”** — bodily and spiritual
**“their … wherewith they are oppressed by the Egyptians.”** — by demons, or by wicked men
3.10:
**“But come,”** — incarnate, by his own will
**“and I will send thee to Pharao,”** — to hold back the devil
**“that thou mayst bring forth my people,”** — by predestination
**“the children of Israel out of Egypt.”** — out of the darkness of sin
3.11: **“And Moses said to God: Who am I that I should go to Pharao, and should bring forth the children of Israel out of Egypt?”** — as if to say, it is God’s doing, not man’s, to do this. Hence: “My glory is not mine, but the Father’s who sent me.”
3.12:
**“And he said to him: I will be with thee:”** — the Godhead with the manhood
**“and this thou shalt have for a sign, that I have sent thee: When thou shalt have brought my people out of Egypt, thou shalt offer sacrifice”** — thou shalt have sacrifice offered
**“to God upon this mountain.”** — He who would sacrifice to God must be on the height of the virtues.
3.14:
**“God said”** — or “the Lord”
**“to Moses: I”** — no other
**“AM WHO AM.”** — properly, unchangeably
**“He said: Thus shalt thou say to the children”** — or “to the children”
**“of Israel: HE WHO IS, hath sent me to you.”** — Remaining without any change and steadfast, he gives all things to be moved.
**“He who is, hath sent”** — Moses is sent to Pharao, to punish him and at last to kill him. The Law was sent to destroy the devil.
*Jerome:* Writing to Marcella on the ten names of God, he puts in the sixth place the name ieye, which is read in Exodus: “He who is, hath sent me to you.” For God alone, who has no beginning, holds the name of true being; which was said through the angel to Moses when he asked his name, because in comparison with him who truly is, since he is unchangeable, the things that are changeable as it were are not. For what is said to have been, is not; and what is said to be going to be, is not yet. But God only is, who knows not having been or being going to be. And only the Father with the Son and the Holy Spirit truly is. Compared with his being, our being is not. Hence we also say: “God lives,” because the divine being lives a life that death does not have.
3.15:
**“And God said again to Moses: Thus shalt thou say to the children of Israel: The Lord God”** — not new
**“of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob,”** — To whom three tried and proven witnesses bear witness, whose testimony is true.
**“hath sent me to you: This is my name for ever,”** — because these witnesses live for ever
3.16:
**“Go, gather together the ancients of Israel,”** — the apostles, the early Church
**“and thou shalt say to them: The Lord God of your fathers … hath appeared”** — hidden from ages and generations
**“to me, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, saying: Visiting I have visited”** — the doubling is a confirmation
**“you:”** — weak through sin
3.17:
**“And I have said the word to bring you forth out of the affliction of Egypt,”** — of the world
**“into the land of the Chanaanite, the Hethite, and the Amorrhite, and Pherezite, and Hevite, and Jebusite,”** — which, that is, the vices figured by these nations possessed
**“to a land that floweth”** — the Church
**“with milk”** — the teaching of infants
**“and honey.”**
• by the sweetness of the divine savour
• To a land that floweth with milk, etc. AUGUSTINE. Ought we to take this spiritually, because in the proper sense this was not such a land as was given to the Hebrews? Or is it a manner of speech by which the fruitfulness and pleasantness of the land is praised?
3.18:
**“And they shall hear thy voice:”** — obeying
**“and thou shalt go in, thou and the ancients of Israel,”** — the princes of the Church
**“to the king of Egypt,”** — the prince of the world
**“and thou shalt say to him: The Lord God of the Hebrews”** — of those passing over, who have here no abiding city, who desire to go out of Egypt
**“hath called”** — inwardly as much as outwardly
**“us: we will go … journey”** — Christ, who rose on the third day
**“three days’ … into the wilderness,”** — far from the din of the world
**“to sacrifice unto the Lord our God.”**
• the sacrifice of praise
• who does not enter the city
3.19:
**“But I know”** — yet it is mine to warn, so that he may be without excuse
**“that … will not let you”** — the children of light
**“the king of Egypt”** — of the dark ones
**“go,”** — going back from the darkness
**“but by a mighty hand.”** — open power
3.20:
**“For I will stretch forth my hand”** — to strike
**“and will strike Egypt”** — the world and its prince
**“with all … wonders”** — with plagues
**“my … which I will do”** — which no one else does
**“in the midst of them:”** — so that all may see, lest they can make excuse
**“after these he will let you go.”** — overcome by the plagues
3.21:
**“And I will give favour”** — freely
**“to this people”** — the new one, that is
3.22:
**“But … shall ask”** — what is done at God’s command is not dishonourable
**“every woman”** — the careful soul, as the Church
**“of her neighbour,”**
• from her fellow lodger
• the poets and philosophers are in a manner our neighbours
**“and of her that is in her house, vessels of silver and of gold, and raiment:”**
• the honourable qualities of manners and works
• You shall not go out, etc. AUGUSTINE. That the Lord commanded the Hebrews to take from the Egyptians vessels of silver and gold, and raiment, and added, “And you shall spoil them,” no judgment of injustice can be passed on this command. For it is a command of God, about which there was to be no judging, but obeying. For he himself knows how justly he commanded it; it belongs to the servant to do obediently what he commanded.
• Vessels of silver, etc. We ask silver and gold of the Egyptians, from which to build a tabernacle for God, when we read the poets and philosophers, so that we may read divine Scripture more wisely and more eloquently.
**“and you shall put them”** — by adorning, by instructing
**“on your sons”** — the elder ones
**“and daughters,”** — the younger ones
**“and shall spoil Egypt.”** — by taking away what is useful for the tabernacle of God

4.1: **“Moses answered and said: They will not believe me, nor hear my voice,”** — The Jews also did not believe Christ. Hence: “Who hath believed our report?”
4.2: **“Then he said to him: What is that thou holdest in thy hand? He answered: A rod.”** — The divine power which Moses held while the Jewish people trusted in it before the coming of the Redeemer; or Christ, whom Moses, that is, the law, preached.
4.3:
**“And the Lord said: Cast it down upon the ground. He cast it down, and it was turned”**
• God, remaining in himself, was made mortal man.
• when through the prophets he announced that God would be incarnate
**“into a serpent:”** — ISIDORE: Death, because the beginning of death came through the serpent.
**“so that … fled from it.”** — because when it saw him mortal, it was afraid to believe him God.
**“Moses”** — the Jewish people
4.4:
**“And the Lord said: Put out thy hand and take it by the tail.”**
• Because the people that now refuses to believe will gather itself to the faith in the last part of the Lord’s body, that is, at the end of the world.
• Because him whom it despised as mortal it will confess as Redeemer in the last part of the Church.
**“He put forth his hand, and took hold of it,”** — by believing
**“and it was turned into a rod.”**
• because soon our Redeemer will appear at the judgment with the power of the Godhead
• because Christ rose, death being overcome
• ISIDORE. The serpent persuaded man to death. So death is from the serpent; the rod in the serpent, Christ in death. Moses was afraid and fled. For when Christ died, the disciples were afraid, falling away from the hope they had held. He took hold of the tail, that is, the hinder parts, and it became a rod: because, first slain, afterwards, when all was accomplished, he returned by rising to what he had been, where, death being swallowed up by life, nothing of the serpent appeared in him. Or the serpent’s tail is the end of the world, because so the mortality of the Church rolls on through slippery times (some go, others come) through death, as through the serpent, through whom death was sown; but at the end of the world, as at the tail, we return to the hand of God, and, taken hold of, we shall be restored, and, death the last enemy being destroyed, rising at the right hand of God we shall be the rod of the kingdom.
**“What is that thou holdest in thy hand?”** — GREGORY. Moses is the Jewish people; the rod, the power of the Godhead; the serpent, Christ’s mortality: for since death came through the serpent, mortality is signified by the serpent. Or because it is written, “Be ye wise as serpents,” and because the highest wisdom, that is, the Wisdom of God, was made flesh, his mortality is rightly figured in the serpent. Hence: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so must the Son of man be lifted up.” Moses held the rod, because the Jewish people, before the Redeemer’s coming, trusted in the power of God. He casts it on the ground, because through the patriarchs and prophets it announced that God would be incarnate; the rod is turned into a serpent, because Christ, God remaining in himself, was made mortal in man. But Moses, seeing the serpent, was afraid and fled, because the Jewish people, when it saw Christ mortal, was afraid to believe him God. He is ordered to take hold of the tail, because the people that now refuses to believe will gather itself to the faith in the last part of the Lord’s body, that is, in the later time of the Church, namely at the end of the world; holding the serpent’s tail, because him whom it had before despised as mortal it will confess as its Redeemer in the last part of the Church. At once the serpent returns into a rod, because as soon as the Jewish people has believed in Christ, he will soon appear for judgment in the power of his Godhead, so that now the serpent is a rod: because he who on earth was despised as a man, coming from heaven, will be seen as God above the angels.
4.6:
**“And the Lord said again: Put thy hand into thy bosom. And when he had put it into his bosom, he brought it forth leprous as snow.”**
• because the people, removed from God, became unclean
• Put thy hand, etc. ISIDORE. The white hand, that is, unclean: for whiteness in the skin is leprosy, not brightness. For the very inheritance of God, that is, the people, sent out away from him, became unclean. Hence: “Why dost thou turn away thy hand out of the midst of thy bosom for ever?” etc. But the hand was called back into the bosom and returned to its own colour: so the Jewish people, estranged from the bosom of God, remained outside, unclean. But called back, it will return to its former colour when it acknowledges the Saviour: for “blindness in part has happened in Israel.”
4.7: **“And he said: Put back thy hand into thy bosom. He put it back, and brought it out again, and it was like the other flesh.”** — this will be fulfilled when all Israel shall be saved
4.9:
**“But if they will not even believe these two signs, nor hear thy voice: take”** — this will be explained in what follows
**“water,”** — the people
**“of the river”** — from the flowing, that is, of this world
**“and pour it out upon the dry land, and whatsoever thou drawest out of the river shall be turned into blood.”**
• faith in the blood of Christ
• Take water, etc. ISIDORE. Water signifies the people; hence: “The waters which thou sawest are peoples and nations.” So the people will be turned into blood, that is, into faith in the blood of Christ.
4.10:
**“Moses said: I beseech thee, Lord. I am not eloquent”**
• though instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians
• in comparison with thee: “I am become as a beast before thee”
**“from yesterday and the day before: and since thou hast spoken”** — Since, that is, I began to know the true Word of God, which was in the beginning with God.
**“to thy servant, I have more impediment”** — According to the Hebrews, he had a thin, weak voice; and he needed a loud voice, because royal pride did not let him come near.
**“and slowness of tongue.”** — of eloquence
**“I have”** — I beseech thee, Lord, etc. AUGUSTINE. When Moses says to the Lord, “I pray, Lord, I am not eloquent before yesterday nor before the day before, nor since thou didst begin to speak to thy servant,” he is understood to believe that by God’s will he could suddenly be made eloquent, when he says “nor since thou didst begin to speak to thy servant”: as if showing that it could have happened that one who had not been eloquent before yesterday and the day before should suddenly become so from the time the Lord began to speak with him.
*Origen:* Allegorically. While Moses was in Egypt and was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, he was not thin of voice, nor slow of tongue, nor did he profess himself ineloquent. For, as far as the Egyptians went, he was of a sonorous voice and of incomparable eloquence. But when he heard the voice of God and received the words of the Lord, he feels his voice thin and slight and slow, and his tongue hindered, and he declares himself dumb, when he begins to know the true Word, which was in the beginning with God. For though an untaught man be compared with dumb animals, he will seem eloquent; but compared with the learned and eloquent, foolish and dumb. But if anyone looks to the Word of God and the divine wisdom, he will profess himself a dumb animal before God far more than the cattle are before us. Hence: “I am become as a beast before thee.” So because he advanced so far in understanding as to know himself, which is a great part of wisdom, the divine favour rewards him, saying: “I will open thy mouth,” etc. Blessed are those whose mouth God opens, that they may speak. Hence: “Open thy mouth wide, and I will fill it.” Likewise Paul says: “That speech may be given me, that I may open my mouth.” So God opens the mouth of those who speak the words of God. The devil opens the mouth of those who speak lies, false witness, buffoonery, filthiness, and of whisperers and detractors, and of those who speak idle words. Of Judas it is related that Satan entered into him and put it into his heart to betray him. So he opened his mouth, that he might speak with the Pharisees how he should betray him for money received. And it is no small grace to tell apart the mouth that God opens and the one the devil opens. God also opens the ears of the saints to hear the divine words. Hence: “The Lord will open my ear”; he will open the eyes, as he “opened the eyes” of Agar, and she saw “a well of living water.” Hence Eliseus: “Open, Lord, the eyes of thy servant, that he may see, for there are more with us.” But the ear that is opened through the Lord’s instruction is sometimes open, sometimes shut. Hence: “Thou shalt not receive a vain report.” If vain, profane, filthy things are said, he who knows the Lord’s instruction shuts his ear and says: “But I, as a deaf man, heard not: and as a dumb man not opening his mouth.” But if what is said bears on the good of the soul, if the talk is of God, if it teaches morals, invites to virtues, cuts away vices, let the ears be open and the whole door of the soul. And note that the law used the greatest restraint in saying, “Thou shalt not receive a vain report.” It did not say “thou shalt not hear,” but “thou shalt not receive.” For we often hear vain things: Marcion and Valentius, and all who argue against the Creator, speak vain things; yet we often hear them, in order to answer them, but we do not receive them, because the devil opens their mouth. May the Lord deign to open our mouth, that we may be able to refute the gainsayer and stop the mouth that the devil opens.
4.11:
**“The Lord said to him: Who made”** — outwardly or inwardly
**“man’s mouth? or who made the dumb”** — in fact or in spirit
**“and the deaf, the seeing and the blind? did not I?”**
• as if to say: I who made these things can give thee the use of them.
• Who made the mouth, etc. AUGUSTINE. There are those who slander God, or rather the Scripture of the Old Testament, because God said that he made the dumb. What then do they say of Christ, who says openly: “I am come, that they who see not may see, and they who see may become blind”? And who but an ignorant man would believe that anything could happen to a man in the way of bodily defects that God does not will? But no one doubts that he wills it all justly.
4.12:
**“Go therefore and I will be in thy mouth:”**
• “Take no thought what you shall speak,” etc.
• that I may open it
**“and I will teach thee what thou shalt speak.”**
• The Spirit, that is, will teach all truth.
• Go therefore, etc. AUGUSTINE. Allegorically. When the Lord says to Moses, “But now go thou, and I will open thy mouth, and instruct thee in what thou shalt speak,” it appears that not only the instruction of the mouth but also its very opening belongs to the grace of God. For he does not say, “Open thy mouth, and I will instruct thee,” but promises both: “I will open, and I will instruct.” But in the psalm he says: “Open thy mouth wide, and I will fill it.” There he signifies in man the will to receive what God gives to one who wills, so that “Open thy mouth wide” belongs to the beginning of the will, but “and I will fill it” to the grace of God.
4.13:
**“But he said: I beseech thee,”** — he humbly excuses himself
**“Lord send whom thou wilt send.”** — someone worthier, that is
4.14:
**“being angry”** — Not with unreasoning disturbance, as a man is.
**“The Lord … at Moses, said Aaron the Levite is thy brother, I know that he is eloquent: behold he cometh forth to meet thee,”** — the priest runs to meet the law and rejoices with it
**“and seeing thee shall be glad at heart.”** — at heart, not with the mouth
4.15:
**“Speak to him,”** — as a mediator
**“and put my words”** — as a master
**“in his mouth:”** — that he may say it to the people as a minister
**“and I will be in thy mouth,”** — “For it is not you that speak,” etc.
**“And I will be in … mouth”** — ORIGEN. Not only to Moses is it promised that his mouth will be opened by the Lord, but to Aaron too. For it is said: “I will open thy mouth and his mouth, and will instruct you in what you shall do.”
4.16:
**“He shall speak in thy stead to the people, and shall be thy mouth: but thou”** — as the greater
**“shalt be to him in those things that pertain to God.”** — The Lord being angry at Moses, said, etc. AUGUSTINE. He seems not to have given him, as one distrustful, the fullest power he was going to give, and to have willed that what could have been done through one, had he believed, be done through two. But if you consider carefully, the Lord, being angry, does not seem to have given Aaron by way of punishment. For he says: “Is not Aaron the Levite thy brother? I know that he speaketh well.” In these words it is shown rather that he rebuked him because he feared to go, as if less fit, when he had a brother through whom he could speak what he wished to the people. For he was thin of voice and slower of tongue, though he ought to have hoped for everything from God. Indeed, even when angry he said what he had promised before. For he had said: “I will open thy mouth and instruct thee.” But now he says: “I will open thy mouth and his mouth, and will instruct you in what you shall do.” But because he added, “and he shall speak for thee to the people,” the opening of the mouth seems to have been granted because Moses said he was slower of tongue. But as to the thinness of his voice the Lord willed to grant him nothing, but for this he added the help of his brother, who with a fitting voice would be equal to teaching the people. And when he says, “And thou shalt put my words in his mouth,” he shows that he would give them by speaking. For if only by hearing, as he would speak into the ears of the people; then what he says after, “And he shall speak for thee to the people, and he shall be thy mouth,” here too “to the people” is understood. And when he says “he shall speak for thee to the people,” he points to the leadership in Moses, the ministry in Aaron. And as to his saying, “But thou shalt be to him in those things that pertain to God,” a great mystery is perhaps to be sought here: whose figure Moses bears, as a mean between God and Aaron, and Aaron between Moses and the people.
4.19:
**“And the Lord said to Moses, in Madian: Go, and return into Egypt: for they are all dead that sought”** — to take
**“thy life.”** — And the Lord said, etc. AUGUSTINE, in the book of Locutions. “Now after many days the king of Egypt died. And the Lord said to Moses in Madian: Go, proceed into Egypt,” etc. Many kinds of expression are to be noted in these words. For first he says, “Go, proceed into Egypt,” as if one were not enough. Then, “all are dead that sought thy life,” when Scripture said only the king of Egypt had died; of whom alone it had been said before that he sought to kill Moses. Or did he die last, after the other enemies? If that is so, it is not a manner of speech but the sense.
4.20:
**“Moses therefore took his wife,”** — the Church
**“and his sons,”** — and each of the saints
**“and set them upon an ass:”**
• upon himself, who is the strong ass, who bore our sins
• that they might keep down the folly and wantonness of the flesh
**“and returned into Egypt, carrying the rod of God in his hand.”** — Moses therefore took, etc. AUGUSTINE. As to its being said that Moses set his wife and his infants upon beasts, to go into Egypt, and that afterwards Jethro his father in law met him there with them when he had led the people out of Egypt: it is to be understood that after that killing of Moses or of the infant which was to come from the angel, his wife returned with the little ones. For some have thought that the angel struck terror for this reason, lest the female sex should go along as a hindrance to the ministry divinely laid on him.
4.21:
**“And the Lord said to him as he was returning into Egypt: See that thou do all the wonders … which I have put in … hand:”** — in thy power
**“thy … before Pharao: I shall harden”** — I will let it be hardened
**“his heart, and he will not let the people go.”** — unless compelled
4.22:
**“And thou shalt say to him: Thus saith the Lord:”** — whose servant thou art
**“Israel is my son, my firstborn.”**
• because the first Church was from the Jews
• because in the patriarchs it was the first chosen for the worship of the one God
4.23: **“I have said to thee: Let my son go,”** — caught in the net of sins
4.24:
**“And when he was in his journey, in the inn, the Lord met him, and would have killed him.”** — Moses, or the uncircumcised infant
**“The angel met him”** — AUGUSTINE. Another text has: “And it came to pass on the way at the resting place, an angel met him and sought to kill him; and Sephora, taking a pebble, circumcised the foreskin of her son, and fell at his feet and said: The blood of my infant’s circumcision has stopped. And he departed from him because she said: The blood of the circumcision has ceased.” First it is asked whom the angel wished to kill: whether Moses, because it is said, “An angel met him and sought to kill him”? For whom is he thought to have met, but him who was over them all? Or was he seeking to kill the boy, whom his mother helped by circumcising him, so that he is understood to have willed to kill the infant because he was not circumcised, in order to sanction the command of circumcision by this severity? If that is so, it is at first uncertain of whom he said, “He sought to kill him,” but it is made clear from what follows. It is indeed a wonderful and unusual expression, that he should say first, “He met him and sought to kill him,” of one of whom he had said nothing before. Like this is that: “The foundations thereof are in the holy mountains: the Lord loveth the gates,” etc. For “the foundations” can be understood as “of the Lord” or “of Sion,” because this pronoun “eius” is of every gender; but in Greek it is said autes in the feminine, autu in the masculine and neuter, and the Greek codex has autu, which compels us to understand not the foundations “of Sion” but “of the Lord.” But rather it is to be asked what it means that the angel withdrew from killing either of them because the woman said, “The blood of the infant’s circumcision has stopped.” For it does not say, “He departed from him because she circumcised the infant,” but because the blood of the circumcision stopped; not because it ran but because it stopped: a great mystery, unless I am mistaken.
4.25:
**“Immediately Sephora took”** — as if knowing why he wished to kill
**“and circumcised the fore skin of her son,”** — of the angel; or the blood flowing out on the boy’s feet
**“and touched his feet and said: A bloody spouse art thou to me.”**
• She says this coaxing the angel, as if to say: as I married Moses in the flesh, so I married thee by the shedding of my son’s blood.
• A bloody spouse art thou, etc. According to the history, the Gentile mother, wondering at the strangeness of the thing, could say to Moses, “A bloody spouse art thou to me,” as if to say: the rite of thy nation compels me to shed my son’s blood, which is not the custom of other nations. Mystically, Sephora signifies the Church from the Gentiles, which strips the foreskin of her son, that is, of the Gentile people, with a very sharp stone, that is, the teaching of the Holy Spirit, or that rock of which it is said, “And the rock was Christ,” so that he may be cleansed from all defilement of the flesh and of the spirit, and put off “the old man with his deeds.” For the blood of circumcision stops when this corruptible shall put on incorruption.
4.26:
**“And he let … go”** — angry, that is, at the circumcision of the boy, she returned to Madian to her father. Hence afterwards we read that Jethro met Moses in the desert, saying: “Lo, I and thy wife and thy children.”
**“him”** — the little circumcised one, or Moses
**“after she had said A bloody spouse art thou to me, because of the circumcision.”** — done
4.27:
**“And the Lord said to Aaron:”** — by inspiring, or by warning through someone outwardly
**“Go … to meet”** — to any of the saints, who are members of the High Priest
**“Moses.”** — the Law
**“into the desert”** — that in solitude he may better understand the mystery of the Law.
**“And he went forth to meet him in the mountain of God,”** — the height of the virtues and of spiritual understanding
**“and kissed him.”**
• Because the Law has peace with such men; those who linger in the lowliness of the letter it hates and shudders at.
• And the Lord said, etc. ORIGEN. Aaron meets Moses and went out of Egypt. But it matters where he meets Moses, whose mouth is to be opened by the Lord: he meets him on the mountain of God. Rightly is his mouth opened who meets him on the mountain of God: Peter, James and John on the mountain were found worthy to see the Lord Jesus transfigured, and Moses and Elias with him in glory. You too, unless you climb the mountain of God and meet Moses there, that is, unless you climb up to the lofty sense of the law, unless you take the summit of spiritual understanding, the door is not opened by the Lord. If you stand in the low place of the letter, you have not met Moses on the mountain of God; God has not opened your mouth, nor instructed you in what you ought to speak. Had Aaron not met Moses on the mountain, had he not seen his lofty sense, he would not have spoken to him the words of God nor handed on to him the power of the signs, nor made him a sharer in so great a mystery.
4.28:
**“And Moses told”** — the Law
**“Aaron”** — a true man of the mountain, that is, a spiritual man
**“all the words of the Lord,”** — The Law speaks only the things of God
4.29:
**“And they came together,”** — the law and the priest
**“and they assembled all the ancients of the children of Israel.”**
• whose counsel and wisdom are strong
• that it might have greater authority
4.30:
**“And Aaron spoke all the words”** — “The lips of the priest shall keep knowledge,” etc.
**“which the Lord had said to Moses: and he wrought the signs before the people,”** — the Lord working withal and confirming the word with signs that followed
4.31: **“And the people believed. And they heard that the Lord had visited the children of Israel: and that he had looked upon their affliction: and falling down”** — humble in heart and body

5.1:
**“After these things Moses and Aaron went in, and said to Pharao: Thus saith the Lord God of Israel: Let my people go that they may sacrifice to me in the desert.”** — Not in Egypt. “Love not the world, nor the things which are in the world.”
**“Let my people go”** — ORIGEN. Allegorically. Moses does not want the people to serve God while set in Egypt, but to go out into the desert and serve him there. For while anyone remains in the dark doings of the world and busies himself in the obscurity of affairs, he cannot serve God: “For you cannot serve God and mammon.” So we must go out of Egypt; the world must be left, not in place but in mind, if we wish to serve the Lord. Hence John says: “Little children, love not the world, nor the things which are in the world.”
5.2:
**“But he answered: Who is the Lord, that I should hear his voice, and let Israel go?”**
• He answers this while he is not in the labours of men, nor scourged with men; so pride held him. A little later, as if amended by the scourges, he will say: “Pray for me to the Lord.”
• The ruler of this darkness does not want you to be drawn away from his darkness and led to the light of knowledge.
**“I know not the Lord, neither will I let Israel go.”**
• so raw pride answers
• what fellowship hath light with darkness
• Who is the Lord, etc. It expresses the pride of the devil, who, scorning to be subject to God, says: “I will be like the Most High.” And as if in doubt about the Lord’s birth, he says: “If thou be the Son of God, command that these stones be made bread.” But afterwards the demons, as if compelled, cried out: “Art thou come hither to torment us before the time?” “We know that thou art the Son of God.” After torments they know what before they would not know. Pharao too, when beaten, asks that prayer be made for him to the Lord.
• Who is the Lord, that I should hear his voice, etc. You see what raw pride does; you will see a little later how much it gains under the scourges, how much better he is made when beaten, who now says, “I know not the Lord,” and when beaten will say, “Pray the Lord for me.” So let no one be so untaught in the divine discipline as to think the divine scourges ruin and a penal death. See, even the hardest Pharao gains when beaten: for before the blows he does not know the Lord, and when beaten he asks that prayer be made for him, and gaining in the punishments, he knows how to recognize why he is punished. “I know not the Lord,” he says. In the Gospel, beaten, he amends this word, for the demons cried out: “We know who thou art. Thou art the Son of the living God.” After the scourges he will also let Israel go, and will even urge them to go out. For there is no fellowship of light with darkness, no part of the faithful with the unbeliever.
5.3:
**“And they said: The God of the Hebrews”** — of those passing over, one of whom says: “I am a stranger with thee, and a sojourner as all my fathers were.”
**“hath called us, to go three days’ journey”** — Christ, who rose on the third day
**“into the wilderness”** — The Law is learned in quiet and silence
**“and to sacrifice to the Lord our God:”**
• In the faith of the Trinity the true sacrifice is offered.
• “Offer to God the sacrifice of praise,” etc.
**“lest a pestilence or the sword fall upon us.”**
• The God of the Hebrews hath called us, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is asked how it is said to the people that God commanded that he would cast them out of Egypt into the land of Chanaan, while to Pharao it is said that they wished to go out a three days’ journey to sacrifice in the desert to their God at his command. But it is to be understood that, although God knew what he would do, since he foreknew that Pharao would not consent to let the people go, that was said first which would have happened first if he had let them go: for that all things should happen as the following Scripture bears witness, the stubbornness of Pharao and his people deserved. For God does not lyingly command what he knows the one commanded will never do, so that a just judgment may follow.
• A three days’ journey, etc. ISIDORE. We walk a three days’ journey going out of Egypt, that we may come to the place where we must sacrifice to the Lord. This way is Christ, who says: “I am the way,” etc. For he who confesses Christ with his mouth, and believes in his heart that God raised him up on the third day, will be saved, coming to the place in which the sacrifice of praise is offered.
*Origen:* Morally. We set out a three days’ journey from Egypt if we so keep ourselves from all defilement of soul and body and spirit that our spirit, and soul, and body may be preserved whole unto the day of Christ.
*Origen:* We set out a three days’ journey from Egypt if, taking rational, moral and natural wisdom away from worldly things, we turn it to the divine ordinances. We set out a three days’ journey from Egypt if, purifying in ourselves what is said, done or thought (for these are the three things through which men can sin), we are made clean of heart, so that we can see God. But the prince of Egypt, when he sees himself pressed harder to let the people of God go, seeks in the second place to obtain that they go no further, that they do not go the whole three days. Saying, “Go not far,” he does not want the people of God to be far from him. For he wants them to sin, if not in deed, then in word; if not in word, then in thought. He does not want them to go the whole three days from him. He wants to possess in us one day, in others two, in others the whole three days. Blessed are those who go away from him the whole three days.
*Strabo:* A three days’ journey, etc. At the third station, after they crossed the Red Sea, they came to Etham, which place is also called Mara, because of the bitter waters. Or “of three days,” that is, of three months, because in the third month after they went out of Egypt they came to Sina, where they sacrificed and received the Law, where the tabernacle too was set up.
*Origen:* Now too Moses, whom we have with us (for we have Moses and the prophets), that is, the law of God, wishes to lead you out of Egypt, if you hear him; he wishes to put you far from Pharao, to rescue you from the work of clay and straw, if only you hear him and understand spiritually. He does not want you to remain in the doings of the flesh and of darkness, but to go out to the desert, that is, to a place empty of the disturbances and waves of the world, and to the quiet of silence. For the words of wisdom are learned in silence and quiet. In this place you will be able to sacrifice to the Lord, to know the Law of God and the power of the divine voice. So Moses longs to cast you out of the waves of affairs and the din of the peoples, and out of Egypt, that is, out of the darkness of ignorance, so that you may hear the Law of God and take hold of the light of knowledge.
5.4:
**“The king of Egypt said to them:”** — the prince of this darkness
**“Why do you Moses and Aaron”** — the word of prophet and priest
**“draw off the people from their works?”** — worldly
**“Get you gone to your burdens.”**
• of earthly toil
• Why do you Moses and Aaron, etc. ORIGEN. While the people is with him and works clay or brick, while it is busy with straw, he does not think it perverted, but going on rightly. But if it says, “I wish to go a three days’ journey and serve the Lord,” he says the people is being perverted by Moses and Aaron. Today too, if Moses and Aaron, that is, the word of prophet and priest, urge the soul to the service of God, to go out of the world, to renounce all that it possesses, to attend to the law and the word of God, at once you will hear the like-minded friends of Pharao saying: See how men are led astray and young men are perverted, so as not to work, not to serve as soldiers, not to do anything useful; leaving necessary things, they follow trifles and idleness. What is it to serve God? They do not want to work and they seek occasions for idleness. These were Pharao’s words then; these his friends speak now too, and they persecute not only with words but with blows. He orders the scribes of the Hebrews to be scourged, straw not to be given, the work to be exacted. Our fathers suffered these things, and now the people of God suffers them. Those who have given themselves wholly to the prince of this world prosper; all things, as they think, turn out happily. But for the servants of God not even a small and humble living succeeds. For these are the straws that were given by Pharao. Hence some, worn out, say to Pharao: “Why dost thou afflict thy people?” For overcome by blows they fall from the faith and confess that they are Pharao’s people. “For all are not Israelites that are of Israel.”
5.5:
**“And Pharao said: The people of the land is numerous:”** — the devil envies because the people of God grows
**“you see that the multitude is increased: how much more if you give them rest from their works?”** — so that you do not exercise them in earthly works
5.6:
**“Therefore he commanded the same day the overseers of the works,”** — the demons who are over the various vices
**“and the taskmasters of the people, saying:”** — because they often compel to do evil by force, if they cannot by flatteries
5.7:
**“You shall give straw no more”**
• a cheap and small living
• Straw was given so that, mixed with it, the work might hold together more firmly, or that bricks might be baked with it; and bricks were made most of all in Egypt so that cities might be made of them, because stones are not plentiful there.
**“to this people”** — of the faithful
**“to make brick,”** — the works of clay and of the flesh
**“as before: but let them go”** — that they may get a living from wherever they can
**“and gather straw.”** — as if to say, let them do evil works no less
5.8:
**“neither shall you diminish any thing thereof:”** — having their food for nothing
**“for they are idle, and therefore they cry, saying: Let us go”** — by going away from the devil: for they cannot serve God and Mammon.
5.9:
**“Let them be oppressed, with works,”** — that they may forget their God
**“and let them fulfill them: that they may not regard lying words.”**
• The prince of Egypt calls a lie whatever is said against him.
• Let them be oppressed with works, etc. From the time Moses began to speak to Pharao, the people of God is afflicted the more: from the time the word of God reaches the soul, the devil rises up more fiercely and sends in greater vices. For before the word of God came to reprove the vices, they lasted in peace. But when it came, a great disturbance arises.
5.10:
**“And … went out”** — to tempt
**“the overseers of the works”** — having heard their master’s commands
**“and the taskmasters”** — demons or wicked men
**“and said to the people:”** — by suggesting secretly

**“And they that were over the works of the children of Israel were scourged”** — Both of old and now the officers of the people of God have been afflicted with various persecutions.

**“saying: Why have you not made up the task of bricks both yesterday and today as before?”** — And they … were scourged, etc. The children of Israel were worn down more heavily after they resolved to go out of Egypt; because those who wish to renounce the world and wicked works are assailed by the devil with fiercer temptations.

**“And they met Moses and Aaron, who stood over against them”**

**“And they said to them: The Lord see and judge, because you have made our savour to stink”**

• The word of prophet and priest becomes an accursed savour to unbelievers and to those who are Pharao’s people.
**“before Pharao and his servants, and you have given him a sword to kill us.”**
• a cause of slaying
• The Lord see, etc. GREGORY. Morally. When the divine light enlightens the human heart, temptations soon grow up against it from the devil, so that it feels itself pressed by temptations more than when it did not know the rays of the inner light. Hence the Israelites, after they were called, complain against Moses about their growing labour, saying: “The Lord see and judge,” etc. For from those who wished to depart from Egypt Pharao had taken away the straw, and required work of the same measure. So the mind as it were murmurs against the law, after knowing which it bears sharper goads of temptation; and in that it displeases the adversary, seeing its labours grow, it grieves as if it stank in the eyes of Pharao.
• Because you have made … to stink, etc. ORIGEN. They speak the truth, though they do not know it; as Caiphas, who said, “It is expedient that one man should die for the people,” did not know what he was saying. For as the Apostle says, “We are the good odour of Christ, to some unto life, to others unto death,” so the prophetic word is a sweet savour to believers; but to the doubtful and unbelieving, and to those who confess themselves Pharao’s people, it becomes an accursed savour. Moses himself too says to the Lord: “Since I spoke with Pharao, thou hast afflicted thy people”; because before the word of God is heard, there is no tribulation or temptation; but when the trumpet of preaching has given the signal of war, the battle of tribulations arises. So from the time Moses and Aaron began to speak to Pharao, the people of God is afflicted. From the time the word of God was brought forth into your soul, a struggle of the virtues against the vices is stirred up within you, which before lasted in peace within you. But when the word of God began to make the division in each one, a great disturbance arises, and war is born without treaty, because injustice does not agree with justice, nor drunkenness with sobriety, nor a lie with the truth. So let us not be troubled if we seem an accursed savour to Pharao. For virtue is called the execration of vice. But as Moses stood before Pharao, let us too stand, let us not be bent, having our loins girt about with truth, and our feet shod with the preparation of the Gospel of peace. And we stand confidently if we pray the Lord to set our feet upon a firm rock, lest our feet be moved. Let us stand, that is, resist, according to that: “Whom resist ye, strong in faith,” that Satan may soon be crushed under our feet. For the more steadily and bravely we stand, the weaker Pharao is. But if we begin to be weak or doubtful, he will become stronger. For when Moses lifted up his hands, Amalec was overcome; when he let them drop as if tired, he prevailed. So let us lift up our arms in the power of the cross of Christ, and raise holy hands in prayer, that we may deserve the help of God. Hence James says: “Resist the devil, and he will fly from you.” So let us act so that he not only flees but is crushed under our feet: so Pharao was destroyed in the depth of the abyss. And we, if we go back out of the Egypt of the vices, escape the waves of the world as though on a solid road, through Jesus Christ.

*Gilbert:* God chose for the priesthood not the first tribe or the second but the third, because priests are consecrated in the name of the Holy Trinity, so that they may be eager to keep the faith of the Trinity in themselves and to teach it to others; and because God delights in an odd number.

7.1:
**“And the Lord said to Moses: Behold I have appointed thee the God of Pharao:”**
• that thou mayst command him whatever thou wilt, as God commands his creature: for the saints are gods by adoption, though not by nature.
• in name
**“and Aaron thy brother shall be thy prophet.”** — interpreter
7.2:
**“Thou shalt speak”** — or “thou speakest”
**“to him all that I command thee; and he shall speak to Pharao, that he let the children of Israel go out of his land.”**
• the lust of the world
• Behold I have appointed thee God, etc. AUGUSTINE. Note that when he was sent to the people, it was not said to him, “Behold, I have given thee as a god to the people, and thy brother shall be thy prophet,” but, “Thy brother shall speak for thee to the people.” It was also said, “He shall be thy mouth, and thou to him in the things that are toward God”; it was not said, “Thou to him a god.” But to Pharao Moses is said to be given as a god; by analogy, Aaron is prophet to Moses, but toward Pharao. Here it is suggested to us that the prophets of God speak what they hear from him, and that a prophet of God is nothing other than one who announces the words of God to men who either cannot or do not deserve to hear God.
*Gregory:* Sometimes “God” is said in name, sometimes in essence. In name, as here: “I have appointed thee the God of Pharao.” And elsewhere: “Bring him to the gods.” And elsewhere: “God hath stood in the congregation of gods,” etc. In essence, as here: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” Wishing to distinguish this, Paul says: “Of whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is over all things, God blessed for ever.” For one is called God in name among all things, but in essence above all things; so, to show that Christ is God by nature, he recorded that he is not only God, but God above all things. For any just man is a god, but among all things, because in name; but Christ above all things, because God by nature.
7.3:
**“But I shall harden”** — when the signs and wonders have been shown; or: I will show how hard it is
**“his heart,”** — in this way, that is
**“and shall multiply”** — or “I will fulfil”
**“… signs”** — the lesser
**“and wonders”** — the greater
**“my … in the land of Egypt,”** — But I shall harden his heart, etc. AUGUSTINE. God says constantly, “I will harden Pharao’s heart,” and brings in as it were the cause why he does this: “I will harden Pharao’s heart, and I will fulfil my signs and my wonders in Egypt,” as if Pharao’s hardening were needed for the signs to be multiplied or fulfilled. So God makes good use of evil hearts, for what he wishes to show to the good and what he will do for the good. And although the quality of each heart in its malice, that is, what kind of heart it has toward evil, comes about by its own fault, which has grown up from its free choice, yet that this evil quality should be moved this way or that, whether it is moved wickedly this way or that, comes about through causes by which the mind of man is driven on; and whether these exist or not is not in man’s power, but they come from the hidden providence of God, who justly and wisely orders and governs all that he created. So that Pharao had such a heart that the patience of God did not move him to piety but rather to impiety was his own fault; but that those things were done which his heart, so malignant by its own fault, resisted, the commands of God (for this is what is called hardened, because it did not consent pliably but resisted unbendingly), was of the divine dispensation, by which a plainly just penalty was prepared for such a heart, by which those who fear God might be corrected. For when a gain is set before them (for example) for which a murder might be committed, the greedy man is moved one way, the despiser of money another: the one to commit the crime, the other to beware of it. Yet the setting forth of the gain was not in their power. So causes come to the wicked which are not in their power, but they make of them what the causes find them already made by their own vices, of their own will. “I will harden” can also be taken thus: I will show how hard it is.
7.4:
**“And he will not hear you:”** — hardened
**“and I will lay … hand”** — power, or the Son
**“my … upon Egypt, and will bring forth my army and my people”** — whom I exercise in the contest of this world
**“the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt,”** — those who see God ought not to remain in darkness
**“by very great judgments.”** — done against Pharao

**“And the Egyptians shall know”**
• as if to say, what is thought anger is mercy, namely that the Egyptians may know that I am the Lord.
• by this experience
**“that I am the Lord, who have stretched forth my hand”**
• power
• which I long held back
**“upon Egypt,”** — the children of darkness
7.6: **“And Moses and Aaron did as the Lord had commanded:”** — or “said”
7.7:
**“And Moses was eighty years old, and Aaron eighty-three, when they spoke to Pharao.”**
• And Moses was eighty, etc. STRABO. Because of circumcision, that is, which was ordered to be kept on the eighth day: for eighty has the same meaning as eight, the smaller number beneath it.
• And Moses was eighty years old. When Moses and Aaron spoke to Pharao, Moses was eighty and Aaron eighty-three years old, because the law, offered to the Gentiles through preachers, taught spiritual circumcision; and they themselves were eager to be perfectly cleansed, and so they preached the faith of the Holy Trinity.
**“And Aaron eighty-three”** — GILBERT. Because the true man of the mountain, that is, Christ, fulfilled true circumcision in himself on the eighth day of the resurrection, and, the devil being overcome by faith in the Trinity, filled the world.
7.9:
**“When Pharao shall say to you, shew signs: thou shalt say to Aaron: Take … rod,”** — the cross
**“thy … and cast it down before Pharao,”** — in the faith of the hearers
**“and it shall be turned into a serpent.”**
• wisdom
• When Pharao shall say to you, etc. AUGUSTINE. Here there was no need of the voice, for whose thinness Aaron seemed to have been given to Moses; but the rod was to be cast down to become a dragon. Why then did Moses not do this himself, unless because Aaron’s mediation between Moses and Pharao bears the figure of a great faith? This too is to be noted, that it is written, “Aaron cast down his rod”; perhaps if it had said, “He cast down the rod,” there would be no question; but that it added “his,” when Moses gave it, was perhaps not said in vain. Or was that rod common to both, so that it might be called either one’s?
*Strabo:* The rod of Moses signifies Christ, who took flesh from a royal stock. Hence the same rod, turned into a serpent, devoured all the rods of the sorcerers, because the death of Christ consumed our death.
*Origen:* The Apostle says: “Be zealous for the better gifts,” elsewhere, “for spiritual gifts, but rather that you may prophesy.” Let us too try to take up the zeal for good things, and to wait for the fulness of the gift from the Lord. For to this it is said: “Open thy mouth, and I will fill it.” And to that: “He that pricketh the eye bringeth out tears: and he that pricketh the heart bringeth forth feeling.” I think, then, that Moses coming to Egypt and bearing the rod with which he chastises and strikes Egypt with ten plagues is the law of God, which reproves and amends the world with ten plagues, that is, with the ten commands of the decalogue. The rod by which these things are done, and Egypt subdued, and Pharao overcome, is the cross of Christ, through which the world and the prince of the world is overcome, that is, the devil with the principalities and powers. The rod cast down becomes a dragon or serpent and devours the serpents of the Egyptian magicians. Now the serpent is usually put for wisdom or prudence. Hence: “Be ye wise as serpents.” And elsewhere: “The serpent was more subtle than any of the beasts,” etc. So the cross of Christ, whose preaching seemed foolish, which Moses, that is, the Law, contains, according to that, “For he wrote of me,” after it was cast on the earth, that is, came to the faith of men, was turned into wisdom, and into such wisdom as would devour all the wisdom of the Egyptians, that is, of this world. For see how God made foolish the wisdom of this world, after he made known that Christ crucified is the power and wisdom of God; and now the whole world is caught by him who said: “I will catch the wise in their own craftiness.”
7.10:
**“So Moses and Aaron went in unto Pharao, and did as the Lord had commanded. And Aaron took the rod before Pharao, and his servants, and it was turned into a serpent.”**
• This is the first sign.
• The preaching of the cross seemed foolish, but after it came to the faith of men, it is understood to be wisdom.
• And it was turned, etc. The law of Moses was tasteless, as it were, like a rod; but turned into a serpent, that is, into spiritual understanding, it was made drinkable and delightful.
**“He cast down”** — ISIDORE. Moses cast down the rod before Pharao, and having become a serpent it devoured the serpents of the Egyptians, signifying that the Word would be made flesh, and would empty the serpents of their dire poison by the remission of sins. For the rod is the straight word, royal, full of power, the badge of rule. The rod became a serpent, since he who was the Son of God, born of God the Father, became the son of man, born of a virgin, who, lifted up on the cross like the serpent, poured healing into human wounds. Hence: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert,” etc. For the rod of Moses, turned into a dragon, swallowed up the rods of the magicians; and Christ, after the dignity of his glory, “became obedient unto death.” Through the very death of the flesh he consumed the sting of death, according to that: “O death, I will be thy death.”
7.11:
**“And Pharao called the wise men and the magicians: and they also by Egyptian enchantments and … secrets”** — of the demons
**“certain … did in like manner.”** — And Pharao called, etc. Know that either they deluded the eyes of the onlookers with devilish feignings, so that things remaining in their own nature seemed something else; or, according to Augustine, the demons, though evil, did not lose their nature. So while the sorcerers try to bring something about by their enchantment, they run about through the world and suddenly bring the seeds of the things with which this is done. And so from them, God permitting, they produce new kinds of things.
**“in like manner”** — In the first plague, when the water is turned into blood; and in the second, when the frogs swarm up; and in the third, when the sciniphs rush in; in the fourth, when the cynomia is brought forth; in the fifth, when the hand of the Lord is upon the beasts of the Egyptians, they are said to do the like.
7.12:
**“And they every one cast down their rods, and they were turned into serpents:”**
• lesser serpents: he put one kind for another
• the cunning of the world
• Dragons are named apo tou dorcen, that is, from seeing, because they see more sharply than other animals.
**“but Aaron’s rod devoured”**
• the wisdom of the world, which is an enemy to God
• the cross of Christ, who is a priest for ever
**“their rods.”** — But … devoured, etc. AUGUSTINE. If it had been said, “Aaron’s dragon swallowed their rods,” it would be understood that Aaron’s true dragon swallowed not phantom feignings but rods. For it could swallow what they were, not what they seemed and were not. But because it said, “Aaron’s rod swallowed their rods,” a dragon could swallow rods, not a rod. But the thing is called by the name of what it was turned from, because it was also turned back into it. So it ought to be called what it principally was. What then is to be said of the magicians’ rods? Had they become true dragons, but are called rods by a like reason? Or rather did they seem to be what they were not, by a sorcerous mockery?
