Why then are they called rods and dragons on both sides, so that the manner of speaking differs nothing about those feignings? But it is hard to show. How, even if true dragons were made from the magicians’ rods, were they nonetheless not creators of dragons, neither the magicians nor the evil angels by whose ministry those things were done? For in bodily things, through all the elements of the world, there are certain hidden seminal reasons, which, when a fitting time is given them, break forth into their due kinds, according to their own measures and ends. And those who do such things are not called creators of the animals, as farmers are not creators of crops or trees or the like, though they furnish certain visible occasions and causes for their springing up. And what these do visibly, the angels do invisibly. But God alone is the true creator, who put those very causes and seminal reasons into things.
7.13: **“And Pharao’s heart was hardened, and he did not hearken to them, as the Lord had commanded.”** — And … was hardened, etc. God hardened Pharao’s heart because he so hardened the devil after his sin that he is never softened by the compunction of repentance; as it is said in Job: “His heart shall be as hard as a stone.”
7.14:
**“And the Lord said to Moses: Pharao’s heart is hardened,”**
• hence: “His heart shall be as hard as a stone.”
• for whom it ought to have been softened
7.15:
**“Go to him in the morning,”** — Eagerly, and as it were in the early morning, the devil is to be attacked.
**“behold he will go out to the waters:”** — to deceive the peoples
**“and thou shalt stand”** — thou shalt resist
**“to meet him on”** — not “in”
**“the bank of the river:”** — of the world
**“and … the rod”** — the faith of the cross
**“that was turned into a serpent. thou shalt take in … hand”** — in deed
**“thy”** — Behold he will go out, etc. ORIGEN. At first Moses does not go in to Pharao, but meets him going out to the waters; afterwards he goes in; after this he does not go in, but comes when summoned. Because, whether we have a contest with Pharao over the word of God and the defence of religion, or try to rescue souls besieged by him, and there is a struggle in us in disputing, we ought not at the first onset to go in to the last points of the questions, but must meet the adversary, even at his own waters, that is, the authorities of the Gentile philosophers, so as first to refute them and show that they have erred; then go into the inner parts of the contest. For the Lord says: “Unless a man first bind the strong man, he cannot enter into his house and rifle his goods.” So the strong man must first be bound and tied with the bonds of questions, and so we must go in to plunder the goods and free the souls which he had held by deceit and fraud. And when we have done this often and have stood against him, with our loins girt about with truth, standing in the Lord and acting manfully, the old and crafty artificer will pretend to be beaten and to give way, so as to make us more careless for the contest. He will also feign repentance; he will beg us to go away, but not far: he wants us to be near him in some part. But unless we go far from him, and cross the sea, and say in thought, speech and deed, “As far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our iniquities from us,” we cannot be saved. So let us pray the mercy of God, that he may rescue us too from the land of Egypt, from the power of darkness, and sink Pharao with his army like lead in the mighty waters; and that we, set free, may with joy and gladness “sing a hymn to the Lord: for he is gloriously magnified,” etc.
7.16:
**“And thou shalt say to him: The Lord God of the Hebrews sent me to thee saying: Let my people go”** — predestined
**“to sacrifice to me”** — “Offer to God the sacrifice of praise.”
**“in the desert:”** — in quiet and silence
**“and hitherto … hear.”** — obey
**“thou wouldst not”** — as if it were in his choice either to hold or to let go
7.17:
**“Thus therefore saith the Lord: In this thou shalt know”** — thou shalt find by experience
**“that I am the Lord:”** — whom no one can resist
**“behold I will strike with the rod that is in my hand, the water of the river,”** — in which they killed the little ones of the Hebrews, so that they may drink the blood they shed
**“and it shall be turned into blood.”**
• Behold I will strike, etc. ISIDORE. The plagues were done bodily in Egypt, but they are done spiritually in us. For Egypt is the figure of the world.
• The water of the river, and it shall be turned into, etc. STRABO. The water turned into blood signifies worldly wisdom, in which everyone who remains is killed, as a fish in blood. For worldly wisdom thinks it foolish that God should die for men: so whoever clings to it cannot live.
*Origen:* The water of the river is turned into blood, to which they had handed over the boys of the Hebrews to be killed, so that it might give back a draught of blood to the authors of the crime, and they might taste by drinking the gore of the polluted stream which they had stained with parricidal slaughter. Allegorically too, the waters of Egypt are the wandering and slippery doctrines of the philosophers, which deceived those little in sense and understanding; but when the cross of Christ showed the light of truth, the slaughter of their own is required of them in punishment and the guilt of blood. Hence: “All the blood that hath been shed upon the earth shall be required of this generation.”
7.19: **“The Lord also said to Moses: Say to Aaron, Take thy rod, and stretch forth thy hand”** — make known thy power
7.20:
**“And Moses and Aaron did as the Lord had commanded: and lifting up the rod”** — the cross
**“he struck the water of the river”** — the doctrines of the philosophers
**“before Pharao and his servants:”** — hence: “All the blood that hath been shed upon the earth shall be required of this generation.”
**“and it was turned into blood.”**
• death to those who drink
• And it was turned, etc. RABANUS. The first commandment is about worshipping one God: “Thou shalt not have strange gods before me”; the first plague, water turned into blood. Compare the first commandment with the first plague: water, from which all things are produced, signifies the one God, from whom are all things; blood, mortal flesh. So the water was turned into blood, because they changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of the image of a corruptible man; and this change indeed takes place in the heart of the ungodly.
• Into blood, etc. Because those who think carnally about the causes of things are reproved by corrections of this kind, so that from the quality of the punishments they may recognize their error.
7.21:
**“And the fishes”** — men
**“that were in the river”** — in the philosophical doctrine
**“died: and the river corrupted, and the Egyptians could not drink the water of the river,”** — or “of the river”
7.22: **“And … heart was hardened”** — AUGUSTINE. Pharao’s heart seems to have been hardened because the enchanters of the Egyptians did the like. But what follows teaches how great that hardening was, even when the enchanters failed.
7.24: **“And all the Egyptians dug round about the river for water to drink: for they could not drink of the water of the river.”** — And all the Egyptians dug, etc. Because the Gentile world, confounded in its study of worldly philosophy, when it sees that there is nothing life-giving or wholesome in it, is eager, searching round about, seeking a draught of wisdom, and does not find it until it comes to him who said: “If any man thirst, let him come to me and drink.”

8.2:
**“But if thou wilt not let them go behold I will strike all thy coasts with frogs.”** — A graceful expression, so that the frogs themselves are understood to be the plague.
**“with frogs”** — STRABO. There are three kinds of frogs. One lives in rivers and croaks. The second is very small, which is called the reed frog, of which it is said that if it is thrown into the mouth of a barking dog, it at once falls silent. The third is very large, which is called the bramble frog, very bad and poisonous, which is commonly called crassantium.
*Origen:* The frogs signify the songs of the poets, which with an empty and puffed-up melody, as with the sounds and songs of frogs, brought fables of deceit into the world: for that animal is useful for nothing except that it gives out the sound of its voice in shameless and wearisome cries.
*Rabanus:* The second commandment: “Thou shalt not take the name of thy God in vain.” The name of God is truth; for he himself says: “I am the truth.” He who speaks the truth speaks of God; for he who speaks a lie speaks of his own. For to speak truth is to speak reasonably; to speak vanity is to make a din. So the second commandment is about the love of truth, to which the love of iniquity is contrary. Truth speaks, vanity makes a din. Contrary to this is the second plague, the abundance of frogs, whose chatter signifies vanity. The lovers of truth do not take the name of God in vain, because they do not go back from truth into vanity. But those who contradict the truth and, deceived by vanity, deceive, are frogs, bringing weariness to the ears, not food to the minds. Hear men speaking reasonably: “There are no speeches nor languages, where their voices are not heard.” Hear the frogs: “They have spoken vain things, every one to his neighbour.”
8.6: **“And Aaron stretched forth his hand upon the waters of Egypt, and the frogs came up,”** — the songs of the poets
8.7: **“And the magicians also by their enchantments did in like manner, and they brought forth frogs upon all the land of Egypt.”** — And the magicians also did, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is asked from where, if it had already been done everywhere. But the question is like this one: from where did they turn water into blood, if all the water of Egypt had already been turned into blood? But it is to be understood that the region where the children of Israel lived was not struck with such plagues, and from there the enchanters could draw water to turn into blood, or bring out frogs to show off their magic power; although they could also have done it after those things were finished; but Scripture, in its narrative, joined what could have happened afterwards.
8.8: **“But Pharao called Moses and Aaron”** — scourged, he comes to his senses, who before said: “I know not the Lord.”
8.9:
**“And Moses said to Pharao: Set me a time when I shall pray for thee, and for thy servants, and for thy people,”** — so that the frogs may be understood to have left Egypt by our prayer, not by chance
**“that the frogs may be driven away from thee and from thy house, … and may remain only in the river.”** — in the flowing, that is, the filth of the world
8.12: **“And Moses and Aaron went forth from Pharao: and Moses cried to the Lord for the promise, which he had made to Pharao concerning the frogs.”** — he had agreed
8.13: **“And the Lord did according to the word of Moses: and the frogs died”** — the feignings of the poets destroyed
8.15: **“And Pharao seeing that rest was given, hardened his own heart, and did not hear them, as the Lord had commanded.”** — And Pharao seeing, etc. AUGUSTINE. Here it appears that Pharao was hardened not only because the enchanters did the like, but also because of the very patience of God, by which he spared; which, according to the hearts of men, is useful to some for repenting, useless to others, for resisting God and persevering in evil. Yet it is not useless in itself, but according to the evil heart; according to that: “Knowest thou not that the patience of God leadeth thee to penance? But according to thy hardness and impenitent heart, thou treasurest up to thyself wrath,” etc. For when the Apostle said elsewhere, “We are the good odour of Christ” in every place, he added: “in them that are saved, and in them that perish.” He did not say he was a good odour of Christ to those who are saved, but a bad one to those who perish; he called himself only a good odour. But they are such as to perish by a good odour according to the quality of their heart, which is to be changed by a good will in the grace of God, so that the judgments of God, which harm evil hearts, may begin to profit it. Hence he, his heart changed for the better, sang: “My soul shall live, and shall praise thee: and thy judgments shall help me.” He did not say “thy gifts” or “thy rewards,” but “thy judgments.”
8.16:
**“Stretch forth thy rod”** — Moses chastising Egypt with the rod signifies the law, which reproves the world with the ten plagues of the commandments. The rod too, by which Egypt is reproved and Pharao overcome, is the cross of Christ, by which the world is conquered and the devil overcome or triumphed over. The rod cast down becomes a serpent, which signifies wisdom, according to that: “Be ye wise as serpents,” etc. The rod devoured the serpents of the magicians, and the cross of Christ, whose preaching seems folly, overcomes all the wisdom of the world. Hence: “For he wrote of me.” The rod cast on the ground was turned into a serpent, because when the mystery of the cross came to the faith of men, it made the wisdom of the world foolish.
**“and strike the dust of the earth: and may there be sciniphs”** — the subtleties of dialectic, or the heretics who deceive the unlearned with dialectical syllogisms
**“and may there be sciniphs”** — ORIGEN. This animal is held up on wings, flying through the air, but so fine and tiny that it escapes the sight of the eye, unless one sees sharply. Yet when it has settled on the body, it bores with a most bitter sting, so that one who cannot see it flying feels it stinging. So this animal is compared to the art of dialectic, which bores into souls with tiny and subtle stings of words, and gets round them with such cunning that the one deceived neither sees nor understands by what he is deceived.
*Rabanus:* The third commandment: “Remember to keep holy the sabbath day.” By this is suggested the rest and tranquillity of mind that a good conscience makes. There is sanctification, because there is the Spirit of God. Hence: “Upon whom shall my Spirit rest, but upon the humble and quiet?” etc. So the restless spring back from the Holy Spirit, the stirrers of quarrels, the lovers of slanders, and they do not admit the rest of the spiritual sabbath. So be gentle; let there be no tumult in your heart, with phantasms flying about through corruption and stinging you. Hear God saying: “Be still and see that I am God.” You will not be still because of your restlessness, and, blinded, you demand to see what you cannot. For mark the contrary plague: the sciniphs were born in the land of Egypt from the mud, very tiny flies, most restless, flying without order, rushing into the eyes and denying men rest; when driven off, they come back: so are the phantasms of the restless. Keep the commandment, beware the plague.
8.18:
**“practiced in like manner,”** — they tried to do it, that is, by stretching out their hands holding rods
**“and there were sciniphs”** — The blood is the teaching of the philosophers; the frogs, the feignings of the poets; the sciniphs, the sophisms of the dialecticians: all of which deceived the world.
8.19:
**“And the magicians said to Pharao This is the finger of God.”**
• the Spirit, who gives the divisions of graces
• the working
**“And … was hardened,”**
• infected with a wicked quality
• not amended
• although the magicians fail
**“Pharao heart … and he hearkened not unto them, as the Lord had commanded.”** — The finger of God, etc. ISIDORE. At the third sign the magicians fail, saying, “It is the finger of God”; they bore the type and the animosity of the heretics. Hence: “As Jamnes and Mambres resisted Moses, so these also resist the truth, men corrupted in mind, reprobate concerning the faith,” etc. And these, who were restless through corruption of mind, failed at the third sign, confessing that the Holy Spirit, who was in Moses, was against them. For the Spirit, who is the finger of God, is put in the third place: who, as when appeased he gives rest to the meek and humble of heart, so when angered he harries the unmeek and proud through restlessness, which the most grievous flies signified, under which the magicians failed, saying, “This is the finger of God,” lest they should understand by what they are deceived.
*Strabo:* Note that the magicians were overcome at the third sign, because all faithlessness and worldly wisdom or philosophy is overcome by faith in the Trinity. For though they found philosophy and disputed about the frame of the whole world, they could not come to the knowledge of the Trinity. By the finger the Holy Spirit is understood, not because he is less than the Father and the Son, but because in the finger there are very many divisions, and through the Holy Spirit the division of graces is given.
*Augustine:* When the magicians said to Pharao, “This is the finger of God,” because they could not bring forth sciniphs, they perceived (since they knew the power of their wicked arts) that they had been thwarted not by such arts, as if Moses were more powerful in them, but by the finger of God, who worked through Moses, who is the Holy Spirit. For what one evangelist says, “by the finger of God,” another set out as “by the Spirit of God.” So when the magicians, in whose power Pharao trusted, confessed that the finger of God was in Moses, by which their sorceries are overcome, yet Pharao’s heart was hardened. But why the magicians failed at the third plague is hard to perceive and explain. For they could have failed at the first sign, where the rod was turned into a serpent, and at the first plague, where the water was turned into blood, and at the second, of the frogs, if the finger, that is, the Spirit, of God had willed it. For who would say that the magicians could be hindered by the finger of God at this sign, and not at the earlier ones? So there is certainly a reason why they were allowed to do those things up to this point. For perhaps the Trinity is commended; and, what is true, the greatest philosophers of the Gentiles, as far as is traced in their writings, philosophized without the Holy Spirit, though they were not silent about the Father and the Son.
8.20:
**“The Lord also said to Moses: Arise early, and stand before Pharao:”**
• strong, immovable
• Resist the devil, and he will fly from you.
**“for he will go forth to the waters:”** — the flowing of the world, that is, which Pharao loves; or the peoples, whom he easily deceives
**“and thou shalt say to him: Thus saith the Lord: Let my people go to sacrifice to me.”** — Thus saith the Lord, etc. RABANUS. The fourth commandment: “Honour thy father and thy mother.” Contrary to this is the fourth plague, that is, the cinomia, the dog fly: it is doglike not to acknowledge one’s parents. Hence their whelps are born blind.
8.21:
**“all kind of flies”** — ISIDORE. In the fourth place Egypt is struck with flies. Now the fly is an insolent and restless animal, in which the insolent cares of carnal desires are figured. And Egypt is struck with flies because the hearts of those who love the world are struck with the restlessness of desires. The Septuagint put cynomia, that is, the dog fly, by which doglike manners are signified, in which the lust of the human mind and the desire of the flesh are reproved. The eloquence of men in the courts can also be signified by the dog fly: they tear one another like dogs.
*Origen:* The cinomia is the sect of the heretics who, besides their other wickednesses of deceit, preach pleasure and lust as the highest good. So since the world was first deceived by each of these things, the word and law of God, coming, rightly reproves it with corrections of this kind, so that from the quality of the punishments they may know the quality of their own error.
8.22:
**“And I will make the land of Gessen … wonderful in that day,”** — it is interpreted “nearness”
**“wherein my people is, … so that flies shall not be there: and thou shalt know that I am the Lord in the midst of the earth.”** — And I will make … wonderful, etc. AUGUSTINE. This is to be understood to have been done in the earlier signs too, so that the land in which the people of God lived was troubled by no such plagues. But it was fitting that it be set down plainly here. For from here begin the signs whose like the magicians did not try to do. For it is certain that there were sciniphs everywhere in Pharao’s kingdom, but not in the land of Gessen or Gesem. There the magicians tried to do the like, and could not; so until they failed, nothing was said about the separation of that land; but only from when those things began to be done which they would not even dare to try.
8.23: **“And I will put a division between my people and thy people: tomorrow shall this sign be.”** — by prayers
8.24:
**“And the Lord did so. And there came a very grievous swarm of flies”**
• a multitude of flies
• The rush and crowd of thoughts that meet us most of all at prayer.
**“into the houses of Pharao and of his servants, and into all the land of Egypt:”** — earthly men
**“and the land was corrupted”** — earthly men
**“by this kind of flies.”**
• by doglike manners, by troublesome thoughts
• And there came a … fly, etc. AUGUSTINE. “Fly” is put for a multitude of flies. For I do not know how, through the custom of speaking that has steeped men’s senses, what is said in the singular often seems more than what is said in the plural. For example, “there is soldiery there” means more than “there are soldiers there”; “there is fish there” means more than “there are fishes there.”
8.25: **“And Pharao called Moses and Aaron, and said to them: Go, and sacrifice to your God in this land.”** — Egypt, that is: he did not want them to go where they said, lest they go far from him.
8.26:
**“And Moses said: It cannot be so: for we shall sacrifice the abominations of the Egyptians to the Lord our God:”** — For the Egyptians disdain to eat sheep.
**“now if we kill those things which the Egyptians worship, in their presence, they will stone us.”** — The abominations, etc. The wicked Egyptians abominate good things; that is, the citizens of this world abominate the sheep, that is, the simplicity of the good: for as the good abominate evil things, so the evil abominate good. Hence the good abominate an ungodly man, and the ungodly those who are in the right way.
*Augustine:* The Egyptians disdain to eat sheep; but what the Egyptians abominate the Israelites offer to God, because the simplicity of conscience which the unjust despise as lowest and most abject, the just turn into a sacrifice of virtue; and cultivating the purity and meekness of what is right, they sacrifice to God what the reprobate, abominating it, think folly.
*Augustine:* Moses said that he wished to go into the desert, where the Egyptians would not see their abominations. And this is to be understood as mystically signified, as we said of the shepherds who were abominable to the Egyptians, and so the Israelites received a separate land in Egypt. For so the sacrifices of the Israelites are abominations to the Egyptians, as the life of the just is to the wicked.
*Strabo:* The Egyptians abominate sheep, and worship them because of Jove Hammon, who is painted with a ram’s head. Likewise the Egyptians worship the ox, which is consecrated to Apis, as the cow to Isis. For Apis was the greatest god of the Egyptians, who appeared once a year at a fixed time to their priests. And they, following him with hymns and praises, prophesied as if frenzied.
*Gregory:* Egypt is struck with flies. Nothing is more toilsome than to burn with earthly desires; nothing more restful than to desire nothing in the world. So Israel receives the keeping of the sabbath as a gift; Egypt is struck with a multitude of flies. For he who follows God receives the sabbath, that is, rest of mind, so as not to be wearied by the craving of carnal desire. But Egypt, that is, the world, is struck with flies, that is, with the insolent cares of desires. Hence: “Dying flies spoil the sweetness of the ointment,” because the superfluous thoughts which are constantly born and die in a mind thinking carnal things spoil the sweetness with which each one is anointed within by the Spirit, because they do not let him enjoy it whole. Hence, when the crowd had been put out, he went in and took her by the hand, and the girl arose. So the crowd is put out so that the girl may be raised, because first the multitude of cares is driven from the secret places of the heart, and so the soul that lies dead within will rise. For while each one scatters himself through countless thoughts of desires, he does not gather himself to the knowledge of himself. For no one fully receives the wisdom which is God unless he draws himself back from all the tossing of carnal thoughts. Hence: “Write wisdom in the time of leisure: and he that is less in action shall receive it.” And again: “Be still and see that I am God.”
8.32: **“And Pharao’s heart was hardened, so that neither this time would he let the people go.”** — And … was hardened, etc. AUGUSTINE. When the locust had been taken away, it was said of Pharao: “Pharao hardened his heart, even at this time, and would not let the people go.” Certainly now it is not said, “Pharao’s heart was hardened,” but, “Pharao hardened his heart.” As indeed in all the plagues, the origin of vices is from the will of man. So the hearts of men are moved by causes, some in this way, others in that, often in different ways even by causes that are not different, according to their own qualities, which come from their wills.

9.5:
*Origen:* In the fifth place Egypt is struck by the death of animals or cattle. In this the senselessness or folly of mortals is reproved, who, like irrational cattle, gave the worship and name of God to figures, not only of men but of cattle, carved in wood and stone: worshipping Jove Hammon in a ram, Amulius in a dog, Apis in a bull, and the other monstrous gods which Egypt imitates; so that in those to which they believed divine worship was due, they might see a pitiable punishment.
*Rabanus:* The fifth commandment is: “Thou shalt not commit adultery.” The fifth plague, death among the cattle. Let us compare these. Take a man who wishes to commit adultery, not content with marriage. He will not turn aside the craving of the flesh, which we share with the cattle. For to couple and beget belongs to cattle too; to reason and understand belongs to men. So reason, which presides, ought like a queen to rein in the lower motions, not loosen them without measure. So it is given to cattle by nature to be moved to coupling only at certain times; for in between, the motion itself grows sluggish. But man can always be moved, because he can rein in the motion. To you the Creator gave the dominion of reason; to you he granted the commandments of continence, like reins upon the lower beasts. You hold what the beast cannot, and you hope for what it cannot. You labour in restraining yourself, not the beast; you will rejoice in eternity, not the beast. If the work wearies, the reward consoles. You ought to rein in the inner motion, not let it loose upon everything like a beast. But if you scorn this, and set aside the image of God that is in you, overcome by desire, you will be a beast, the man being let go. Against that: “Do not become like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding.” But perhaps you demand to roam with free lust, reined in by no law. Mark the plague, if you are a beast: at least fear to die.
9.6:
**“The Lord therefore did this thing the next day: and all the beasts of the Egyptians died,”** — so that the worshippers of animals may be confounded
**“but of the beasts of the children of Israel”** — who worship God, not animals
9.7: **“And Pharao sent to see: and there was not any thing dead of that which Israel possessed. And Pharao’s heart was hardened, and he did not let the people go.”** — And Pharao’s heart was hardened, etc. AUGUSTINE. If the cattle of the Israelites had died, there would seem to be a fitting cause why his heart was hardened against God’s command, as if his magicians had killed the cattle of the Israelites; but it was hardened by what should have moved it to fear or to believe, and that hardening went on even to this point.
9.8:
**“And the Lord said to Moses and Aaron: Take to you handfuls of ashes out of the chimney, and let Moses sprinkle it in the air in the presence of Pharao.”** — Take to you handfuls, etc. AUGUSTINE. Another text: “Take you handfuls of embers from the furnace, and let Moses sprinkle it toward heaven,” etc. The earlier signs were done with the rod, which not Moses but Aaron stretched out over the water, or struck the earth with. But now, after two signs coming between, namely the cynomia and the deaths of the cattle, where neither Aaron nor Moses does anything with his hand, it is said that Moses should sprinkle the embers toward heaven; both are ordered to take, but he to sprinkle, not on the earth but toward heaven: as if Aaron (who had been given for the people) ought to strike the earth, or stretch out his hand over the water or the earth, while Moses, who was in the things that pertain to the Lord, is ordered to sprinkle the embers. What of those two earlier signs, where neither Moses nor Aaron does anything with his hand? What does this very difference mean?
*Rabanus:* The sixth commandment: “Thou shalt not kill.” The sixth plague, pustules on the body, blisters boiling up and swarming, the burnings of wounds and the embers of the furnace. For murderers burn with anger and madness. If you could see the souls of murderers, you would lament them more than the rotting bodies of the ulcerated.
9.9:
**“And be there dust upon all the land of Egypt: for there shall be boils … both in men and beasts”** — deceitful and festering malice
**“and swelling blains”** — puffed-up pride
**“in the whole land of Egypt.”** — Boils and blains, etc. ORIGEN. With burning heats they are brought out in the sixth stroke. In the boils deceitful and festering malice is reproved; in the blains swelling and puffed-up pride; in the burning heats the madness of anger and fury.
9.10:
**“And they took ashes out of the chimney, and stood before Pharao, and Moses sprinkled it”** — who was in the things that pertain to God
**“in the air: and there came boils with swelling blains in men”** — rational ones, as it seemed
**“and beasts.”** — foolish
9.15:
**“For now I will stretch out my hand to strike thee, and thy people with pestilence, and thou shalt perish from the earth.”** — And the Lord hardened … heart, etc. ORIGEN. Note that in the sixth plague it is not said, “Pharao’s heart was hardened,” but something more terrible is added. For it is written that “the Lord hardened Pharao’s heart,” etc. Again in the seventh, when hail and fire lay Egypt waste, Pharao’s heart is indeed hardened, but not by the Lord. But in the eighth, when the locust is brought on, the Lord is said to harden Pharao’s heart. And in the ninth, when darkness that can be felt is made; and finally when, the firstborn being destroyed, the Israelites had departed, it is said thus: “And the Lord hardened the heart of Pharao king of Egypt and of his servants, and he pursued them.” But also when Moses is sent from the land of Madian to Egypt and is commanded to do wonders, it is added: “Thou shalt do them in the sight of Pharao: but I will harden Pharao’s heart,” etc. Here it was first said by the Lord: “I will harden Pharao’s heart,” etc. A second time too, after the princes of Israel are listed, it is said: “I will harden Pharao’s heart,” etc. Not in vain was this variety made, that now the Lord is said to have hardened Pharao’s heart, now that it was hardened of its own accord. I see Paul, as one understanding the difference between Pharao’s heart being hardened and the Lord hardening Pharao’s heart, saying in one place: “Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness, and patience, and longsuffering? Knowest thou not that the benignity of God leadeth thee to penance?” etc. Here without doubt he blames him who was hardened of his own accord. But elsewhere, as if putting a question about this, he says: “Therefore he hath mercy on whom he will; and whom he will, he hardeneth,” etc. He also adds to these: “O man, who art thou that repliest against God?” By which, about him who is said to be hardened by the Lord, he answered not so much by solving the question as by apostolic authority, because of the incapacity of his hearers; as he says elsewhere: “And heard secret words, which it is not granted to man to utter.” Hence in what follows he deters one who, not so much by the merit of his studies as by a craving to know, plunges himself curiously into more secret questions, saying: “O man, who art thou that repliest against God?”
*Rabanus:* The seventh commandment: “Thou shalt not steal”; the seventh plague: hail on the crops. For no one has an unjust gain without a just loss. While you steal, you get a garment, you lose faith: a visible gain, an invisible loss; the gain from your blindness, the loss from the Lord’s cloud. For those who steal outwardly with an evil desire are hailed upon inwardly by God’s judgment, and the field of their heart is laid waste.
9.16:
**“And therefore have I raised thee, that I may shew”** — for the vessels of mercy
**“my power in thee, and my name may be spoken of throughout all the earth.”** — for the warning and correction of the good
9.17:
**“yet”** — with thy wonted malice
**“Dost thou … hold back my people: and wilt thou not let them go?”** — And therefore have I raised, etc. AUGUSTINE. The Apostle set down these words where he also says this: “What if God, willing to shew his wrath, and to make his power known, endured with much patience vessels of wrath,” that is, by sparing those whom he had foreknown would be evil, which vessels he calls “fitted for destruction”: “that he might shew,” he says, “the riches of his glory on the vessels of mercy,” who say: “My God, his mercy shall prevent me.” So God knows how to use the evil well; yet he does not create human nature for malice, but bears them patiently as long as he knows it to be fitting; not uselessly, but for the warning or exercise of the good. For see, that the name of the Lord may be proclaimed in all the earth profits the vessels of mercy; so for their benefit Pharao was kept.
9.18:
**“Behold I will cause it to rain tomorrow at this same hour, an exceeding great hail:”** — by which the still tender shoots of the vices are laid waste
**“Behold I will cause it to rain”** — ORIGEN. Up to here the punishments are tempered to the world through the figures of its own errors; after this come strokes from above.
9.19:
**“Send therefore now presently, and gather together thy cattle, and all that thou hast in the field: for men and beasts, and all things that shall be found abroad,”** — the Church
**“and not gathered together out of the fields,”** — by the manners of the rustic
**“which the hail shall fall upon,”** — the hardness of the unbelieving heart
9.20: **“He that feared the word of the Lord”** — or “of the Lord”
9.21: **“Send therefore now”** — AUGUSTINE. God seems to forewarn of this not so much in indignation as in mercy, who even when angry tempers the punishment. But it is puzzling what cattle are now being provided for, if all had died in the earlier plague; because God distinguished between the cattle of the Hebrews and of the Egyptians, so that all the cattle of the Egyptians died, but none of the Hebrews. Or is the question solved by this, that he had foretold that those which were in the field would die, so that these are taken as “all”? And those are understood to have escaped which were in the houses, which those gathered and kept who doubted whether what Moses had foretold the Lord would do might be true; and of these some could again be in the fields, which are now ordered to be gathered into the houses lest they perish by the hail, when Scripture says: “He that feared the word of the Lord among Pharao’s servants,” etc. So this could have been done, since God threatened the death of the cattle, although Scripture was silent about it.
9.22:
**“And the Lord said to Moses: Stretch forth thy hand towards heaven,”** — not toward the earth
**“that there may be hail”** — as above with the embers
9.23:
**“And Moses stretched forth his rod towards heaven, and the Lord sent thunder”**
• the Septuagint: “voices,” that is, teaching
• the terror of threatening
• He does not strike in silence: he sends teaching from heaven, by which the chastised world may recognize its fault.
**“and hail,”** — the rebuke of the wicked
**“and lightning running along the ground:”** — miracles
9.24: **“And the hail and fire”** — of which it is said: “I am come to cast fire on the earth.”
9.26:
**“Only in the land of Gessen, where the children of Israel were, the hail fell not.”**
• And Moses stretched forth, etc. ORIGEN. This too is to be noted, that some strokes Aaron is said to bring on Pharao or Egypt, some Moses, and some the Lord himself. For in the first plague, where he turns the waters into blood, Aaron lifts up the rod and strikes the water. In the second, he strikes the waters and brings out frogs. In the third, he stretches out his hand and strikes the dust of the earth with the rod, and sciniphs are made. In the fourth, the Lord is said to have done it, so that the cynomia came. In the fifth too, when the cattle are destroyed, he is said to have done this thing. But in the sixth, Moses sprinkles the embers, and boils and blains are made. In the seventh, he lifts up his hand toward heaven, and voices and hail are made, etc. In the eighth, likewise he stretches out his hands toward heaven, and the Lord brings on a wind and brings the locusts. And in the ninth too, he stretches out his hand toward heaven, and darkness and gloom are made. But in the tenth, the end and completion of the whole work is ministered by the Lord. For as it is said: “And the Lord struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt.”
• And the Lord sent thunder, etc. ORIGEN. Allegorically. See the tempering of the divine correction: he does not strike in silence, but gives voices and sends teaching from heaven, by which the chastised world may recognize its fault. He gives hail, by which the still tender shoots of the vices are laid waste. He gives fire too, knowing there are thorns and thistles which it had to devour; of which the Lord says: “I am come to cast fire on the earth.” By this fire the kindlings of pleasure and lust are consumed.
*Origen:* There is another difference to be observed. For in the first plague, when the water is turned into blood, it is not yet said to Moses that he should go in to Pharao, but: “Go to meet him,” etc. But in the second, the first having been ministered steadfastly and faithfully, it is said to him: “Go in to Pharao,” etc. In the third, the sciniphs are brought on; the magicians give way, confessing: “This is the finger of God.” In the fourth, Moses is ordered to watch in the morning and stand against Pharao as he goes out to the waters, when the houses of the Egyptians are filled with the cynomia. In the fifth, when the cattle are destroyed, he is ordered to go in to Pharao. In the sixth, Pharao is scorned, and it is not said that Moses and Aaron went in to him, because boils and blains with burning were made even upon the sorcerers, and they could not withstand Moses. In the seventh, he is ordered to watch very early in the morning and stand against Pharao, when he brings forth hail and fire and voices. In the eighth, he is commanded to go in to him, when the locust is brought on. In the ninth, Pharao is again scorned, and Moses is commanded to stretch out his hands toward heaven, so that darkness that can be felt may be made; and he does not go in, but is called to Pharao. Likewise in the tenth, when the firstborn are destroyed, and he is forced to go out of Egypt in haste.
*Origen:* There are many other things to be observed by which the divine wisdom is shown. For at first Pharao is not bent when the water is turned into blood. In the second he seems to be softened a little: for he called Moses and Aaron, saying: “Pray for me to the Lord,” etc. In the third, the magicians give way, saying: “This is the finger of God,” etc. In the fourth, struck by the cynomia, he says: “Go and sacrifice to the Lord your God,” etc. In the fifth, where he is struck by the slaughter of the cattle, he does not give way, but is hardened more. Likewise in the sixth, at the plague of boils. But in the seventh, when he is laid waste by hail and fires, “he called Moses and Aaron, saying: I have sinned this time also, the Lord is just: I and my people are wicked,” etc. In the eighth, when he was pressed by the locusts, he called Moses and Aaron in haste: “I have sinned against the Lord your God, and against you. But now forgive me my sin this time also, and pray to the Lord your God.” In the ninth, when he is covered with darkness, he calls Moses and Aaron, saying: “Go, sacrifice to the Lord your God.” In the tenth, when the firstborn are destroyed, he calls them by night and says: “Arise and go forth from among my people, you and the children of Israel,” etc. And he adds: “And bless me too.” These things cannot be explained except by the same spirit by which they were done, because, according to the Apostle, “the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets”: so the sayings of the prophets are said to be subject not to just anyone for explaining them, but to the prophets.
9.30: **“But I know that neither thou, nor thy servants do yet fear the Lord God.”** — But I know that neither thou, etc. AUGUSTINE, in the book of Questions on Exodus. Pharao had been terrified by the crash of the sky and the hail. Hence he asked Moses to pray for him, confessing his iniquity and that of his people. But Moses sought another fear. For it is easy to fear punishment, but this is not to fear God, that is, with that fear of piety of which Jacob says: “Unless the God of my father Abraham, and the fear of Isaac had stood by me, peradventure now thou hadst sent me away naked.”
9.33: **“And when Moses was gone from Pharao out of the city, he stretched forth”** — or “held out”

10.1: **“And the Lord said to Moses: Go in to Pharao; for I have hardened”** — I have patiently borne with him
10.2:
**“And thou mayest tell in the ears of thy sons, and of thy grandsons, how often I have plagued the Egyptians, and wrought my signs amongst them: and you may know that I am the Lord:”**
• For I have hardened, etc. AUGUSTINE, in the same book. He spoke here as if God had need of anyone’s malice; but it is to be understood as if he said: I was patient toward him and his servants, so as not to take them away, so that my signs might come upon them in order. For since the evil mind became more obstinate through the patience of God, because I was patient toward it, it is said: “I have hardened his heart.”
• The plagues of the Egyptians are the instruction of the children of Israel, lest they be hardened in like manner and suffer the like: “When a pestilent man is punished, the little one will be wiser.”
• There, first, blood flows from the wells and rivers; here, the first plague was under Nero, so that everywhere there was the blood of the dying, either corrupted by diseases in the City or poured out by wars in the world.
• There, the second plague, frogs in the inner rooms, almost destroyed the inhabitants by hunger; here, under Domitian, unbridled henchmen at the bidding of the bloody prince, and want, scattered almost all the Roman citizens.
• There, the third plague, the sciniphs, most savage little flies, which in midsummer fly in swarms through filthy places and settle with a burning bite on the hair of men and the bristles of cattle. Here, the third plague under Trajan stirred up the Jews, who, though before they lay quiet, scattered as if they did not exist, were moved by a sudden heat and ran riot. Besides, many cities fell at the same time by earthquake.
• There, the fourth plague, the dog flies, nurslings of rottenness, mothers of worms; here, under Marcus Antoninus, a pestilence poured over many provinces gave Italy and the city of Rome, and the army of the Romans scattered through various winter quarters, broken up by death, to rottenness and worms.
• There, the fifth plague, of the cattle and beasts of burden. Here, under the persecutor Severus, the very vitals and supports of the commonwealth, that is, the commons of the provinces and the legions of soldiers, were crushed in civil wars.
• There, the sixth plague, swelling blains and running boils; here, the plague that came after the persecution of Maximus, who had ordered that the bishops and clergy especially, the popular crowd being passed over, the leaders of the Churches, be tortured; it swelled up often, and, with anger and faithlessness, rose not through the slaughter of the common people but through the wounds of dying princes and powerful men.
• There, the seventh plague, hail gathered in the air, which was death to men and beasts; here, under Gallus and Volusianus, who succeeded the persecutor Decius, a pestilence was poured through all the spaces of the Roman empire and gave almost the whole human race to death.
• There, the eighth correction, locusts stirred up on every side; here, nations stirred up on every side laid waste the Roman world with slaughter and burning.
• There, the ninth plague, darkness that could be handled, threatening more danger than it did; here, when the persecutor Aurelian was making his decrees, a terrible thunderbolt with dire whirlwinds fell at his very feet, showing what so great an avenger would do, if he were not patient; although within six months three emperors were killed: Aurelian, Tacitus and Florianus.
• There, the tenth and last plague, the killing of the firstborn. Here, the destruction of all the idols, which, made first, they loved among the first things. There, the king proved the power of God, and felt it, and feared, and let the people of God go free; here too he did all these things, and even believed.
*Origen:* The ten plagues with which Egypt is struck through the Israelites can be compared to the times of the Roman empire, because these things were done in a figure of us. The Christian people and the Israelite people belong to the one God; the cause of each was subjected to one: the Synagogue to the Egyptians, the Church to the Romans. The Egyptians persecuted; the Romans persecuted too. There Moses is gainsaid ten times; here there are ten edicts against Christ. There, the various plagues of the Egyptians; here, the various calamities of the Romans.
*The same:* There the people of God was not dragged back to slavery, nor here afterwards forced into idolatry. There the precious vessels of the Egyptians were handed over to the Hebrews; here the precious temples of the pagans gave way to the Churches of the Christians.
*The same:* When the Egyptians, after the ten plagues, pursued the Hebrews who had been let go, destruction by the sea rushed upon them; for us too, as pilgrims, the persecution of the Gentiles remains, until we cross the Red Sea, that is, the fire of judgment, with Christ as leader and judge. And those who persecute the Christians will be drowned, with their king Antichrist, in the pool of everlasting fire.
*Rabanus:* The eighth commandment: “Thou shalt not bear false witness.” The eighth plague: the locust, an animal, that is, harmful with its tooth. For the false witness harms by biting and consumes by lying. Hence: “If you bite and devour one another, take heed you be not consumed one of another.”
10.4:
**“But if thou resist, and wilt not let them go, behold I will bring in tomorrow the locust into thy coasts:”**
• note the expression
• against the inconstancy of men
10.5:
**“To cover the face of the earth that nothing thereof may appear, but that which the hail hath left may be eaten: for they shall feed upon all the trees that spring in the fields.”** — Behold I will bring in, etc. ORIGEN. I think that by this kind of plague the inconstancy of the human race, always at odds with itself and in discord, is refuted. For the locust, though it has no king, according to Scripture, leads an ordered army; but men, though they were made rational, could neither rule themselves in order nor patiently bear the governance of God who rules them.
*Strabo:* The locust, which has longer legs behind, is called locusta as if “long spear” (longa hasta), and in Greek hastago. By the locust, which has no king, is signified the rashness of those who, though punished with various penalties, always remain in their hardness, as if they had no ruler.
10.12:
**“unto the locust”** — Locusts are taken for the restlessness of levity, as souls wandering and leaping for the pleasure of the world.
**“that it may come upon it”** — or “that it may come down”
10.13:
**“And Moses stretched forth his rod”** — Some wonders are done through Moses, some through Aaron, and some through the Lord himself, so that we may know that in some things we must be cleansed through the sacrifices of priests and the prayers of bishops, whom the person of Aaron points to; in some things we must be amended through the knowledge of the law, which the office of Moses points to; but in the harder ones we need the power of the Lord himself.
**“and the Lord brought a burning wind all that day, and night: and when it was morning, the burning wind”**
• the hot south wind, that is, as they think
• the devil’s suggestion
**“raised the locusts:”**
• the tongues of flatterers
• the inconstancy of the human race, at odds with itself and in discord
**“the burning wind raised the locusts”** — GREGORY. The plagues of Egypt shown from heaven were inflicted bodily as its deserts required, but they signified spiritually the evils that daily strike wicked minds; so that by these strokes on outward things afflicted Egypt might be moved and, grieving, weigh what losses of devastation it carelessly bore within. For by the locusts, which harm the crops more than the other small animals, are figured the tongues of flatterers, which corrupt the minds of earthly men by praising them when they bring forth some good things. For the fruits of the Egyptians are the works of the vainglorious, which the locusts destroy, when flattering tongues bend the heart of the doer to craving passing praises. The locusts eat the grass when flatterers extol the words of speakers with applause. They devour the fruit of the trees too, when with vain praises they weaken the works of some who are already, as it were, strong.
10.14:
**“And they came up over the whole land of Egypt:”** — the citizens of the world
**“and rested in all the coasts of the Egyptians innumerable,”** — for flatterers are not worthy of being numbered
10.15:
**“And they covered the whole face of the earth, wasting all things.”** — works
**“was devoured,”** — lifted up by applause
**“And the grass”** — words
**“of the earth … and what fruits soever”** — of works
**“were on the trees,”** — the strong
10.20: **“And the Lord hardened Pharao’s heart, neither did he let the children of Israel go.”** — There remained not, etc. AUGUSTINE. Scripture recorded the kindness of God by which he took away the locusts, and went on to say that the Lord hardened Pharao’s heart, that is, by his kindness and patience, by which that obstinacy came about while he was spared. As all evil hearts of men grow hard by misusing the patience of God.
10.21:
**“And the Lord said to Moses: Stretch out thy hand towards heaven: and may there be darkness upon the land of Egypt,”** — reproving the blindness of the mind, or showing that the reasons of the divine dispensation and providence are most obscure
**“so thick that it may be felt.”**
• By hyperbole: for darkness cannot be felt, but he signified the greatness of the darkness.
• Stretch out thy hand, etc. AUGUSTINE. For the third time it is said to Moses, “Stretch out thy hand toward heaven,” so that the plague of darkness too might come. But it was never said to Aaron that he should stretch out his hands toward heaven. As to its being said to Moses, “Stretch out thy hand over the land of Egypt, and let the locust come up over the land,” I believe this signifies that he who can do more can also do less, but not the reverse.
*Origen:* The ninth plague is darkness, so that the blindness of their mind may be reproved, or that they may understand that the reasons of the divine dispensation and providence are most obscure. For God “made darkness his covert”; and they, searching it boldly and rashly, and asserting one thing after another, rolled down into the thick darkness of errors that can be felt.
*Strabo:* By the darkness is shown the folly of the Jews, who were afflicted and did not know to what end their punishment would come. Hence too by the darkness is signified the secret of the divine judgment, by which he mercifully saves the just and justly condemns the ungodly.
10.23:
**“No man saw his brother,”** — The Greek has: “And not no one saw his brother.”
**“nor moved himself out of the place where he was:”** — not that he did not move at all, but because they could not pass from place to place
10.24:
**“And Pharao called Moses and Aaron, and said to them: Go sacrifice to the Lord: let your sheep only, and herds remain; let your children go with you.”** — Let your sheep only, etc. The Greek has: “Except the sheep and oxen, leave”; and it is an unusual expression, unless “leave” is brought in after a pause and “these” is understood, so that the sense is: Go, except the sheep and oxen, and leave these. For such an ellipsis is often made in the expressions of the Scriptures.
*Rabanus:* The ninth commandment: “Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour’s wife.” The ninth plague, thick darkness. For there is a kind of adultery also in coveting another’s wife, when his own is not enough for someone, so that he tries another’s too. Truly the darkness is thick. For nothing grieves the sufferer so much, nothing would the doer so little wish to suffer. He who does this is truly blinded by a horrible madness.
10.26: **“All the flocks shall go with us: there shall not a hoof remain of them:”** — As if, when the cattle were led away, a hoof could remain; but it is to be understood thus: We will not leave even a hoof.

11.2:
**“Therefore thou shalt tell all the people that every man ask of his friend, and every woman of her neighbour, vessels of silver, and of gold.”**
• Therefore thou shalt tell all the people, etc. AUGUSTINE. No one ought to take an example from this, or so to rob his neighbour. For God commanded this, who knew what each ought to suffer; and the Israelites did not commit theft, but at God’s command performed a service; as when the officer of a judge kills one whom the judge orders. But if he does it of his own accord, he is a murderer, even if he kills one whom he knows ought to have been put to death by the judge. But if the Jews lived apart in the land of Gesem, where the plagues did not happen, how does each ask gold, silver, raiment of a neighbour, man or woman; especially since, where this is first commanded through Moses, it is put thus: “And the woman of her neighbour, and of her fellow lodger,” or “her house-mate” according to another text? Hence it is to be understood that in the land of Gesem too not the Hebrews alone lived, but some Egyptians lived with them, to whom those divine kindnesses could come by the merit of the Hebrews, so that they loved them and readily lent what they asked; yet God did not judge them so free from the wrongs and grindings that the people of God bore that they should not be struck even with this loss, who had not been struck by the other plagues.
• That every man ask, etc. GREGORY. Minds clinging to the habits of carnal life cannot be torn up from the lowest things unless they advance by preaching that leads them step by step. Hence it is that to those set in Egypt, with a loving restraint, condescension is made to their hidden covetousness, and they are ordered to depart taking away their neighbours’ vessels of gold and silver. And when they were led to Mount Sina and had received the law, they soon hear: “Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour’s goods.” Hence too in the law they are ordered to exact “an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth”; yet at some time, when grace is revealed, they are ordered, when struck, to offer the other cheek. For since anger always demands more vengeance than the wrong it receives, while they learn not to repay evils many times over, they might at some time learn to bear them willingly even when multiplied. Hence he forbade the rude people some things, and kept some things in their former use, and these too as a figure of a better life. For in Egypt they used to sacrifice brute animals to idols. So he kept the sacrifice of animals but forbade the worship of idols, so that while they lost something of their custom, they might also have something for comfort. And this, by a wonderful dispensation, he turned into a figure of the spirit. For the sacrifices of those animals signify the putting to death of our carnal life. So by that by which condescension is made to the weakness of a rude people, by that very thing, through the shadowed forms of allegories, a greater strength of the spirit is announced to it.
11.3: **“in the sight of the Egyptians”** — Who, that is, lived with the Hebrews in the land of Gessen and because of them had not been hurt by the nine plagues, and so loved them; but they were afflicted by the tenth plague, when the Hebrews had departed from them.
11.5:
**“And every firstborn in the land of the Egyptians shall die, from the firstborn of Pharao who sitteth on his throne, even to the first born of the handmaid that is at the mill, and all the firstborn of beasts.”**
• or “of beasts”
• Every firstborn shall die, etc. ORIGEN. At the last the destruction of the firstborn is brought on, in which there is perhaps something beyond our understanding, which seems to have been committed by the Egyptians against the Church of the firstborn which is written in heaven. Hence too the destroying angel is sent for this ministry, who spares only those who have both their door posts marked with the blood of the lamb. Again the firstborn of the Egyptians are destroyed: whether we call them the principalities and powers and rulers of the darkness of this world, whom Christ at his coming led in triumph, that is, led captive and took captive, when he triumphed by the sword of the cross; or the authors and inventors of false religions, which the truth of Christ destroyed with their authors.
• The principalities and powers and rulers of this darkness are the firstborn of the Egyptians, because in the last plague, that is, when the end of the world comes, when he shall separate the sheep from the goats, the grain from the chaff, they will be condemned, the licence to roam and to tempt being lost.
*Origen:* Morally. The soul, while it lives in this world in errors, in ignorance of the truth, is set in Egypt. If the law of God begins to come near it, it turns the waters into blood, that is, it turns the fluid and slippery life of youth to the blood of the Old or New Testament. Then the law brings out of it the vain and empty talkativeness against the providence of God, like the croaking of frogs. It also purges its malignant thoughts, and shakes off the stings of cunning like the biting of sciniphs. It drives out too the bites of lusts like the darts of the cynomia, and the folly and understanding like that of cattle, through which “man when he was in honour did not understand,” but “is compared to senseless beasts,” etc. It reproves the boils of sins, the swelling of arrogance, and puts out the heat of fury. After this it applies the voices of the sons of thunder, that is, the teachings of the Gospels and the Apostles, and the chastisement of the hail, to restrain luxury and pleasures, and at the same time the fire of repentance, so that it may say: “Was not our heart burning within us?” It also draws from it the examples of the locusts, by which all its restless and troubled motions are fed down, so that it may learn to do all things according to order. And when it has been sufficiently chastised for its manners, when it has felt the author of the strokes, confessing that “it is the finger of God,” and has received a little knowledge, then especially it sees the darkness of its deeds and the gloom of its errors, and then it will deserve that the firstborn of Egypt be destroyed in it. For every soul, when it comes to the fulness of its age, and the natural law, as it were, begins to defend its rights in it, produces its first motions according to the desire of the flesh, which the kindling force has stirred up from the tinder of lust or anger. Hence the prophet says of Christ, as a singular privilege: “Butter and honey shall he eat; before he do or bring forth evil things, he shall choose the good”; for “before the child know to refuse the evil,” he will resist malice, so as to choose what is good. But David says of himself: “The sins of my youth and my ignorances do not remember.” So because these first motions of the soul, brought forth according to the flesh, rush into sin, rightly in the moral place the firstborn of the Egyptians are set as the first fruits, because they are destroyed if the conduct of the rest of life directs a more amended course. So in the soul which the divine law, having taken it up from its errors, chastises, the firstborn of the Egyptians are destroyed; unless, after all this, persisting in unbelief, it would not be joined to the people of Israel, so as to go out of the deep and escape unharmed, but remains in iniquity and goes down like lead into the mighty waters. “For iniquity,” according to Zacharias, “sitteth upon a talent of lead.” And so he who remains in iniquity is sunk like lead into the deep.
11.7: **“But with all the children of Israel there shall not a dog make the least noise, from man even to beast: that you may know how wonderful a difference the Lord maketh between the Egyptians and Israel.”** — But with all the children of Israel, etc. AUGUSTINE, in the book of Locutions. It is a most elegant expression: for by the dog he signified the lowest, whether of men or of cattle, so setting forth how great a quiet there would be among the Hebrews, while the Egyptians cried out in their bitter bereavement.
11.9:
**“And he went out from Pharao exceeding angry.”** — not with disturbance of mind, but because of the hardness of Pharao, who, touched by so many punishments, did not come to his senses: he was amazed and marvelled
**“But the Lord said to Moses: Pharao will not hear you, that many signs may be done in the land of Egypt.”** — Pharao will not hear you, etc. AUGUSTINE. As if Pharao’s disobedience had been needed for those signs to be multiplied: which were done profitably to strike fear into the people of God and, by the very distinction, to form them to piety. But this was of God, who made good use of the malice of that heart, not of Pharao, who made bad use, that is, of patience.

12.2:
**“This month shall be to you the beginning of months: … the first”** — the greatest
**“it shall be … in the months of the year.”**
• This month, etc. RABANUS. This is April, which among the Hebrews is called Nisan, among the Macedonians Sanctios; and it is called Aprilis as if aperilis, because then the earth is opened (aperitur) to bring forth shoots, grasses and flowers. Or Aprilis from Venus, as if Aphrodis; for Venus is called Aphrodite in Greek. The Hebrews have this as the first. For on the fifteenth before its Kalends was the first day of the world; on the fourteenth, the second; on the thirteenth, the third; on the twelfth, the fourth, on which the sun and moon were made, and then was the first equinox. For the sun in the east and the moon in the west divided the sphere of the world equally.
• On the tenth day of the month the lamb is taken, on the fourteenth it is sacrificed, because the passion of Christ is figured in the law and fulfilled when the grace of the Gospel shines forth. For ten, because of the decalogue, signifies the law; and four, the four Gospels.
*Strabo:* This is Nisan, according to the Hebrews, in which the world was made, whose full moon after the spring equinox is always to be watched for; in which the people of Israel is freed from the slavery of Egypt, and the human race is rescued by the blood of Christ from the power of the devil.
12.3:
**“Speak ye to the whole assembly of the children of Israel, and say to them: On the tenth day of this month let … take”** — from the flock
**“every man … a lamb by their families and houses.”** — because the Jewish nation alone is not enough
12.4:
**“But if the number be less than may suffice to eat the lamb,”** — in the singular, because though each one took one, yet all signified him who was to be the single victim
**“he shall take unto him his neighbour that joineth to his house,”**
• “neighbour,” that is, singular for plural: for he wants it understood not one, but as many as suffice.
• a Gentile
**“according to the number of souls”**
• the whole is to be understood from the part
• of the predestined
**“which may be enough to eat the lamb.”** — of Christ, whose body we eat and whose blood we drink
12.5:
**“And it shall be a lamb”** — “who taketh away the sins of the world”
**“without blemish,”** — “Who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth.”
**“a male,”** — strong
**“of one year:”** — of one year, of which it is said: “Thou shalt bless the crown of the year of thy goodness.”
**“according to which rite also you shall take a kid.”**
• “The lamb shall be for you perfect, a male, of one year,” another text. AUGUSTINE. That expression may trouble someone, as if a lamb could be other than male, not knowing by what necessity it was so translated. For “sheep” ought to have been put, because the Greek has probaton, which in Greek is of the neuter gender, and all that follows could agree with it; as if one said, “The beast shall be for you perfect, male, of one year.” For “male beast” (masculum pecus) could be said in Latin, as “male frankincense” (mascula thura) is said, in the neuter gender. For ovis masculus could not be said, because the word is only feminine; and if ovis mascula were said, it would be more absurd. But if “beast” were put, something else too would be understood; nor would the mystery be kept, that while he speaks of a sheep, he afterwards says, “you shall take it from the lambs and the kids,” in which Christ is signified. For why should we be told that a sheep or lamb is to be taken from the lambs or kids, unless he were signified whose flesh was taken from the just and sinners? Although the Jews try to understand that a kid too is to be taken for celebrating the Pasch, as if it were said: either a lamb from the lambs, or a kid from the kids, if the other is lacking, must be taken. Yet it appears in Christ, now that things are fulfilled, what was figured by that command.
• According to which rite, etc. Because Christ took flesh from the just and sinners, so that no one should despair of pardon; or because Christ was a kid to the Jews who said, “This man is a sinner,” but to us a lamb without blemish; or because he appeared “in the likeness of sinful flesh,” and died for sin, though he had no sin.
*Strabo:* On the tenth day of April he came to Jerusalem, and on the following day he was received by the crowds with palm branches and divine praises. For the three remaining days he was watched by the Jews until the fourteenth day, that is, until the fifth weekday, on which he supped with the apostles, and afterwards was betrayed.
12.6:
**“And you shall keep it until the fourteenth day of this month:”** — the fourteenth moon, because the Jews count days and months by the course of the moon
**“and the whole multitude of the children of Israel shall sacrifice it”** — because at the end of the ages he was sacrificed for us by the Jews
**“in the evening.”** — because Christ is sacrificed at the end of the ages
12.7:
**“And they shall take of the blood thereof,”** — of Christ
**“and put it upon both the side posts,”** — of the mouth and of the heart
**“and on the upper door posts”** — the intentions
**“of the houses,”** — of the minds
**“And they shall take of the blood … and put it upon both”** — GREGORY. The blood is put on when it is drunk not only with the mouth of the body but also with the mouth of the heart, and is thought on with an intent mind toward imitation. For he who so receives the Redeemer’s blood that he does not yet wish to imitate his passion has put the blood on one post; it must be put also on the upper door posts of the houses. For the houses are our minds, in which we dwell by thought; and the upper door post is the intention, which stands out above the action. So he who directs the intention of his thought to the imitation of Christ’s passion puts the lamb’s blood on the upper door posts of the house. Or our houses are the bodies in which we dwell while we live, and we put the lamb’s blood on the upper door post of the houses because we bear the cross of his passion on our forehead.
12.8:
**“And they shall eat the flesh”** — the sacrament of the Lord’s body
**“that night”** — of this world, while we do not yet see one another’s consciences
**“roasted”** — made strong
**“at the fire,”** — of the passion
**“and unleavened bread”**
• good works
• without the corruption of vainglory
**“with wild lettuce.”**
• with weeping and repentance for sins
• They shall eat the flesh, etc. GREGORY. We eat the lamb by night, because now we receive the Lord’s body in the sacrament, while we do not yet see one another’s consciences; yet the flesh is roasted, because, that is, he who cooks flesh in water dissolves it, but fire without water, by baking it through, makes it strong. And fire cooked the lamb’s flesh, because the force of the passion made him stronger for the resurrection and strengthened him to incorruption. But the Redeemer’s sacraments received alone are not enough for the true solemnity of the mind unless good works are joined to them. Hence he adds: “And unleavened bread with wild lettuce.” He eats bread without leaven who does right works without the corruption of vainglory, who carries out the commands of mercy without admixture of sin, lest he wickedly plunder what he seems to dispense rightly. Hence it is said in rebuke: “And offer a sacrifice of praise with leaven.” For he offers praise with leaven who prepares a sacrifice for God from plunder.
• With wild lettuce, etc. Wild lettuces are very bitter; and the lamb’s flesh is to be eaten with wild lettuce, so that while we receive the Redeemer’s body we may afflict ourselves by weeping for our sins, so that the bitterness of repentance may wipe from the stomach of the mind the humour of a wicked life. Hence it is added: “You shall not eat thereof any thing raw, nor boiled in water.” The very words of the history exclude the historical sense. Were they used in Egypt to eat lamb raw, that the law should say, “You shall not eat thereof any thing raw”? And it is added: “Nor boiled in water.” Water signifies human wisdom; hence: “Stolen waters are sweeter.” The raw flesh of the lamb is his manhood left unconsidered and without the reverence of knowing his Godhead. All that we think on subtly we cook, as it were, in the mind. But the lamb’s flesh is to be eaten neither raw nor boiled in water, because our Redeemer is neither to be thought a mere man, nor is it to be thought out by human wisdom how God could become incarnate. For everyone who believes him a mere man eats the lamb’s flesh raw, which he would not cook by the understanding of the Godhead. He who discusses the mysteries of the incarnation by human wisdom boils the lamb’s flesh in water, and seeks to penetrate the mystery of the dispensation through a loose knowledge. So let him eat the lamb’s flesh roasted, so as to know that all things are dispensed through the power of the Holy Spirit.
12.9:
**“You shall not eat thereof any thing raw,”** — thinking him a mere man
**“nor boiled in water,”** — by human wisdom
**“but only roasted at the fire:”** — of the Holy Spirit
**“the head”** — the Godhead
**“with the feet”** — the footsteps of the manhood
**“and entrails thereof.”** — the mysteries of the words and commands
**“you shall eat”** — taking it eagerly
12.10:
**“Neither shall there remain any thing of it”** — undiscussed
**“until morning.”** — of the resurrection
**“If there be any thing”**
• The bones, that is, of which it is said: “You shall not break a bone of it.”
• The lamb’s bones are forbidden to be broken, because the Lord’s bones were not broken on the cross.
**“left,”** — what cannot be understood
**“you shall burn it with fire.”** — you shall reserve it to the Holy Spirit
12.11:
**“And thus you shall eat it: … your reins,”** — the delight of the flesh
**“you shall gird”**
• first
• with the girdle of continence
**“and … shoes”** — the examples of the dead fathers
**“you shall have … on your feet,”** — on the works
**“holding”** — afterwards
**“staves”**
• or “a staff”
• the commands of God and the mysteries of Christ
• pastoral care
**“in your hands, and you shall eat”** — because you do not know how long it is allowed
**“in haste:”** — because they were on a journey
**“for it is the Phase (that is the Passage) of the Lord.”**
• The head with the feet, etc. GREGORY. The head of Christ is God. So to eat the head of the lamb is to receive his Godhead by faith; to eat the feet, to search out the footsteps of his manhood by loving and imitating them; the entrails, the hidden and mystical commands of Christ’s words, which we eat when we take them eagerly. In the word “eat” (vorare, devour) our sloth is reproved, we who neither seek out his words and mysteries by ourselves, and hear them unwillingly when spoken by others. “Neither shall there remain any thing of it until morning,” because his sayings are to be discussed with great care, so that before the day of the resurrection appears, all his commands may be penetrated by understanding in the night of the present life. But because this is very hard, it is rightly added: “If there be any thing left,” etc. We burn with fire what remains of the lamb when what we cannot understand and penetrate of the mystery of his incarnation we humbly reserve to the power of the Holy Spirit; so that no one may proudly dare either to scorn or to pronounce on what he does not understand, but may hand it to the fire, that is, leave it to the Holy Spirit. So since we have learned how the pasch is to be eaten, let us go on to by whom it ought to be eaten: “And thus you shall eat it: you shall gird your reins,” etc. In the reins the delight of the flesh is understood. Hence: “Burn my reins and my heart.” And elsewhere it is said of the devil: “His strength is in his loins.” So he who eats the pasch rightly girds his reins, so that he who keeps the solemnity of the resurrection and of incorruption may be subject to no corruption through vices, may tame his pleasures, rein in his luxury. These things indeed are hard, but narrow is the gate that leads to life, and we have many examples of those who went before. Hence he adds: “You shall have shoes on your feet.” The feet are works. Shoes are the skins of dead animals. Shoes protect the feet. The dead animals from whose skins our feet are protected are the ancient fathers who have gone before us to the eternal homeland. When we look at their examples, we protect the feet of our work. So to have shoes on the feet is to look at the life of the dead, and to guard our footsteps from the wound of sin.
• Holding staves, etc. GREGORY. The staff is pastoral care; and note that they are first commanded to gird their reins, afterwards to hold staves, because those ought to undertake pastoral care who already know how to tame the flowings of luxury in their own body, so that when they preach strong things to others they may not give way to soft desires. “And you shall eat in haste”: that is, know with haste the commands of God, the mysteries of the Redeemer, the joys of the heavenly homeland, and fulfil the precepts of life; because we know that today we may well act, whether tomorrow we may we do not know. So eat the pasch in haste, that is, pant for the solemnity of the heavenly homeland. Let no one grow sluggish on the journey of this life, lest he lose his place in the homeland.
• Phase is Hebrew, pascha Greek; that is, “passage,” because it was first celebrated by the children of Israel as they went out of Egypt; we too must pass from passing things to eternal ones, from earthly to heavenly.
12.12:
**“And I will pass through the land of Egypt that night,”** — note that the firstborn of the Egyptians are struck by night
**“and will kill every firstborn in the land of Egypt both man”** — who seems rational
**“and beast:”** — simple
**“and against all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgments: I am the Lord.”**
• Against all the gods, etc. The Hebrews say that all the idols of Egypt and the temples were broken that night, either by an earthquake or by the flooding of the river Nile.
• But allegorically, as we go out of Egypt the idols of errors fall down, and every cult of wicked doctrines is shaken.
12.13:
**“And the blood shall be”** — because the memory of Christ’s blood keeps Christians safe from the destroyer
**“unto you for a sign in the houses”** — in the minds or bodies
**“where you shall be: and I shall see the blood, and shall pass over”** — I will not strike
**“you: and the plague shall not be upon you”** — eternal
**“to destroy you, when I shall strike the land of Egypt.”** — the citizens of this world
12.14: **“And this day shall be … to you”** — AUGUSTINE. “And you shall keep this day in your generations as a lawful ordinance, eternal” or “everlasting,” which is called eomon in Greek. It is not to be taken as though any day of these present ones could be eternal; but that is eternal which this day signifies; as when we say “eternal God,” we do not call these two syllables eternal, but what they signify. Although it should be carefully searched out how Scripture is wont to use “eternal,” lest perhaps it called “eternal” solemnly something which they would hold it wicked to leave out or to change of their own accord. For it is one thing when something is commanded to be done for a while, as it was commanded that the ark should go round the walls of Jericho seven times; another, when something is commanded to be kept so that no limit is set beforehand. So either he called it eternal because they should not dare to leave it out of their own accord; or he called eternal not the signs of things, but the things that are signified.
12.15:
**“Seven days shall you eat unleavened bread: in the first day”** — which is called the Pasch: for the other days are called the days of unleavened bread
**“there shall be no leaven”**
• or “leaven”
• of malice and wickedness
**“in your houses: whosoever shall eat any thing leavened, … that soul shall perish out of Israel.”** — from the assembly of the saints who see God
**“from the first day until the seventh day,”**
• from the beginning, that is, of life to the end
