• Seven days, etc. Seven is put for the whole, because all time rolls on through seven days: unleavened bread is to be eaten for seven days, that is, through all the time of the present life simplicity is to be kept and malice shunned.
12.16:
**“The first day”** — the beginning of faith
**“shall be holy and solemn,”** — in honour of the passion and resurrection of Christ
**“and the seventh day shall be kept with the like solemnity: you shall do no work”** — servile
**“in them, except those things”** — namely the studies of the holy Scriptures and good works, which prepare the eternal refreshment
**“that belong to eating.”** — the Pasch
12.17:
**“And you shall observe the feast of the unleavened bread:”** — of sincerity and truth
**“for in this same day I will bring forth”** — to the land of the living
**“your army”** — those exercised in good works
**“out of the land of Egypt,”** — from the world
**“and you shall keep this day in … generations”** — or “generations”
**“your”** — your
**“by a perpetual observance.”** — because it signifies eternal rest
12.18:
**“The first month, the fourteenth day of the month”** — When Christ supped with the disciples, he gave his body and blood.
**“in the evening.”** — or “evening”
**“you shall eat unleavened bread, until the one and twentieth day of the same month in the evening.”** — The first month, etc. RABANUS. The evening of the fourteenth day of the first month, on which the Pasch is celebrated and the sacrifice of the lamb is accomplished, signifies the putting off of the old man and the beginning of the new, which is begun in baptism, which figures the death of Christ. Hence: “All we who are baptized in Christ Jesus are baptized in his death,” etc. So from the evening of the fourteenth day of the first month to the evening of the twenty-first, that is, a whole week, we are ordered to eat unleavened bread, because from the receiving of baptism to the end of life we ought to live simply and without guile. Hence Peter: “Laying aside all malice, and all guile, and dissimulations,” “as newborn babes,” etc.
12.19:
**“Seven days”** — through the whole present life
**“any leaven”** — the corruption of sin
**“there shall not be found … in your houses: he that shall eat leavened bread,”** — guile, error of doctrine
**“shall perish”** — for ever
**“his soul … out of the assembly of Israel,”** — of the saints
**“whether he be a stranger”** — who were nourished outside the Church and afterwards received into it
**“or born in the land.”** — who were nourished within the Church
**“in the land”** — of the Church, which is rained upon and tilled by God, that it may bear fruit
12.20: **“You shall not eat any thing leavened: in all your habitations”** — the Churches, or the various orders
12.21:
**“the ancients”** — Note that he does not communicate God’s commands first to boys or young men, but to the elders, because “in the ancient is wisdom, and in length of days prudence.”
**“and said to them: Go take a lamb by your families,”** — the Churches, or the various ranks
12.22:
**“And … a bunch of hyssop”** — of faith, that is, which is compared to a grain of mustard seed, which, received with humble devotion, purges all the affections of the soul
**“dip … in the blood that is at the door,”**
• the intention of the mind, or the forehead of the body
• because this blood is for us the door of life
**“and sprinkle the transom of the door therewith, and both the door cheeks:”**
• as above
• And … a bunch of hyssop, etc. STRABO. Hyssop is a lowly herb, growing in rocks, that purges the chest and the lungs. And it signifies true humility, of which Christ gave us an example in himself. So we dip the bunch of hyssop in the blood when, mindful of Christ’s humility, we are eager to imitate him.
• Dip … in the blood, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is asked what blood he means by the door, since he wants that blood to be understood by whose sacrifice the Pasch is made. Does he command it to be done in this way accordingly, though he was silent about it, that the same lamb be killed by the door? Or, what is more believable, did he say “of the blood that is by the door” because he who is to smear it will set the very vessel in which he catches the blood by the door, so as to have it at hand while he dips?
**“let none of you go out”** — This was kept afterwards; for then they could not, because they were in passage.
**“of the door of his house”** — We ought to keep ourselves by or within the enclosure of the mind while we celebrate the Pasch, lest we wander abroad like Dina and commit fornication with the devil.
**“till morning.”** — the day of judgment
12.23:
**“For the Lord will pass through striking the Egyptians: and when he shall see the blood”** — the faith and defence of Christ’s passion
**“on the transom, and on both the posts,”** — of the mind and of the body. Hence: “The light of thy countenance, O Lord, is signed upon us.”
**“he will pass over the door of the house, and not suffer the destroyer to come into … houses”** — minds or bodies
**“your … and to hurt you.”** — And not suffer, etc. STRABO. Whether the destroyer was a good angel or an evil one need not be asked: for whoever he was, he obeyed the Lord’s command. Yet it is to be known that evil angels are wont to cause such plagues, by God’s permission.
12.27:
**“You shall say to them: It is the victim of the passage of the Lord, when he passed over the houses of the children of Israel in Egypt,”** — in the world
**“striking”** — bodily or spiritually
**“the Egyptians, and saving our houses.”** — from the destroyer, or from the slavery of Egypt
**“And … bowing themselves,”** — humbled
**“the people … adored.”** — giving thanks
12.29:
**“And it came to pass at midnight, the Lord slew every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharao, who sat on his throne, unto the firstborn of the captive woman that was in the prison,”** — in the work prison
**“and all the firstborn of cattle.”** — The tenth commandment is: “Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour’s goods,” etc. Contrary to this is the tenth plague, the death of the firstborn. By another commandment theft is forbidden, by which robbery too is condemned; for it is worse to snatch by force than in secret. So the wish to take away, openly or secretly, has its own commandment; but to covet your neighbour’s goods, even if you seek them by just succession, is not lawful. For those who wish to possess others’ goods as if justly seek to be heirs to the dying. When you praise a thing left you as if possessing it by right, God condemns you as coveting unjustly. For you who seek to become someone’s heir do not want him to have heirs; and among these nothing is dearer than the firstborn. So you are rightly punished in your firstborn, who, coveting others’ goods, seek a shadow of right, as it were, and lose the firstborn of the heart, which are better. The firstborn indeed is faith. For no one does good in whom faith has not gone before. All good works are spiritual sons, but among them faith is the firstborn. So whoever you are that secretly covet another’s goods, inwardly you lose faith. For you serve not with charity but with fraud, as if loving him whom you desire to die, so that you may succeed him.
12.30: **“And Pharao arose in the night, and all his servants, and all Egypt: and there arose a great cry in Egypt: for there was not a house wherein there lay not one dead.”** — For there was not a house, etc. AUGUSTINE. Since only the firstborn died, how was there no house in which there was not one dead? Or had this too been brought about by God, that there should be firstborn in all the houses in which the Egyptians were struck, even those who lived in the land of Jessen? For here it was of men or of animals, not of the land; that is, men and firstborn animals died by a hidden stroke of an angel; nothing had been done in the land or in the sky, like the frog, or the locust, or the darkness. For since the land of Jessen had been free of such plagues, the kindness reached the Egyptians who lived in it with the Hebrews; but by this one all were struck.
12.32: **“Your sheep and herds take along with you, as you demanded, and departing, bless me.”** — give thanks
12.34:
**“The people therefore took dough before it was leavened:”**
• “Purge out the old leaven, that you may be a new paste,” etc.
• Dough, etc. AUGUSTINE. The children of Israel set out from Egypt without leaven, so that, going out of this world, we may cast away the leaven “of malice and wickedness” and “feast with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.”
**“and tying it”** — lest it run out
**“in their cloaks,”** — the ornaments of works, or the defences of faith
**“put it on their shoulders.”** — in the exercise of works
12.35:
**“And the children of Israel did as Moses had commanded: and they asked of the Egyptians vessels of silver and gold, and very much raiment.”**
• In the gold and silver and raiment of the Egyptians are signified certain teachings which, from the very usage of the Gentiles, are profitably sought out; or precious souls with their bodies, which are joined from the Gentiles to the people of God.
• And they asked, etc. AUGUSTINE. This had already been done before the deaths of the firstborn; but now it is repeated by recapitulation, for it was told when it was done. For now how could it happen that these things were lent in such great mourning? Unless perhaps someone says that the Egyptians who lived with the Hebrews were not struck by this plague either.
• Vessels of gold, etc. These signify the teachings which, from the very usage of the Gentiles, are learned with a not unprofitable study; or precious souls from the Gentiles, like vessels of gold and silver with raiment, that is, bodies, which join themselves to the people of God, so as once for all to be freed from this world as from Egypt.
12.37:
**“And the children of Israel set forward from Ramesse”**
• from Boida, as they say
• “the stirring of the moth”
**“to Socoth,”** — tents
**“being about six hundred thousand men on foot,”**
• perfect in good works
• because the glory of the perfect is the beginning
• On foot: fighting men
**“beside children.”**
• The weak are not worthy of being numbered, because they are not fit for war
• And they set forward, etc. ORIGEN. He who prepares to set out from Egypt, who desires to leave the dark doings of the world and the darkness of errors, must first set out from Ramasse, which is interpreted “the stirring of the moth.” If you wish to come to this, that God may be your leader, and go before you in the pillar of the cloud, and the rock may follow, which gives spiritual food and drink, go out of Ramasse, lest you lay up treasure where the moth consumes and thieves break through and steal. As if to say: “If thou wilt be perfect, go sell what thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come follow me.” This is to set out from Ramasse and follow Christ.
• From Ramasse to Socoth, etc. ORIGEN. Let us see what the place of the camp is to which they come. From Ramasse they came to Sochot, which is interpreted “tents.” So when, leaving Egypt, you have shaken off the moths of all corruption and cast away the incitements of the vices, you will dwell in tents, in which, that is, we would not be unclothed, but clothed over. And the dwelling in tents shows that he who hastens to God is unencumbered. But one must not stop even here: the camp must be moved from Sochot too, and one must hasten to Othon, which is interpreted “signs to them”; because here you will hear that God went before them by day in a pillar of cloud, and by night in a pillar of fire; not this in Ramasse, nor in Sochot, which is the second camp. The third is that in which the divine signs are done: this was the three days to which Moses and Aaron were hastening, and Pharao gainsaid them, saying, “Go not far.” He did not want the children of Israel to come to the place of the signs, so that they could enjoy the mysteries of the third day. Hence: “He will revive us after two days: on the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live in his sight.” The first day for us is Christ’s passion; the second, on which he went down into hell; the third, on which he rose. So on the third day he went before them by day in a pillar of cloud, and by night in a pillar of fire. So it is necessary that those who are baptized in Christ be baptized in his death, and be buried with him, and rise on the third day: those, that is, whom he raised up with himself and made to sit in the heavenly places.
• About six hundred thousand, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is asked whether the Hebrews came to so great a number in Egypt through those years which the number, considered in the Scriptures, can show: and how many these were is no small question. For God says to Abraham, before not only Isaac but also Ismael was born: “Thy seed shall be a stranger in a land not their own, and they shall bring them under bondage, and afflict them four hundred years.” If, then, we understand that they were four hundred years with the Egyptians, it was no small space in which the people might so multiply; but Scripture plainly testifies that it was not so many years. For some think that four hundred and thirty years ought to be taken from when Jacob entered Egypt until Moses freed the people, because it is written in Exodus: “The sojourning of the children of Israel, which they sojourned in the land of Egypt and in the land of Chanaan, they and their fathers, was four hundred and thirty years”; and that the years of their slavery were four hundred, because it is written in Genesis: “They shall bring them under bondage, and afflict them four hundred years.” But because the years of slavery are counted after the death of Joseph (for while he lived they did not serve), four hundred and thirty cannot be counted in Egypt. For Jacob entered in the thirty-ninth year of his son, because Joseph was thirty years old when he appeared in the sight of Pharao and began to reign under him. And when the seven years of plenty had passed, in the second year of famine Jacob came into Egypt with his sons, when Joseph was in his thirty-ninth year; who died having filled one hundred and ten years of his life. And he lived after his father’s coming seventy-one; if you take these from four hundred and thirty, there will remain not four hundred years of slavery, but three hundred and fifty-nine. But if we count from when Joseph began to reign under Pharao, so that Israel may in a manner be said to have entered Egypt when his son was exalted there, even so there will be three hundred and fifty, which Tyconius wants taken as four hundred, so that the part is understood from the whole, that is, the fifty from the hundred; and he proves that Scripture is wont to use this rule of speaking. But if, which is more probable, we say that Israel entered Egypt when Joseph began to be sold there, we take away thirteen years more, so that we take three hundred and thirty-seven years for four hundred. But since Scripture says that Caath, the son of Levi, the grandfather of Moses, entered Egypt with his grandfather Jacob, and says that he lived one hundred and thirty years, and his son Amram, the father of Moses, one hundred and thirty-seven, and that Moses was eighty years old when he freed the people from Egypt: even if Caath had begotten Moses’ father in the year he died, and he too had begotten Moses in the last year of his life, the years counted, one hundred and thirty and one hundred and thirty-seven and eighty, make three hundred and forty-seven years, not four hundred and thirty. But if someone says that Caath the son of Levi was born in the last year of Joseph’s life, about seventy years can be added to that sum, because Joseph lived seventy-one years in Egypt after his father’s entry. So too the seventy years of Joseph’s life from Jacob’s entry into Egypt until the birth of Caath, if he is asserted to have been born then, and the one hundred and thirty years of Caath himself, and the one hundred and thirty-seven of his son Amram, the father of Moses, and the eighty of Moses himself, make four hundred and seventeen years, not four hundred and thirty. So the reckoning of Eusebius in his Chronicle seems true: for he counts four hundred and thirty years from that promise by which God called Abraham to go out of his land into the land of Chanaan; because the Apostle too, when he commended Abraham’s faith, did so in that promise in which God promised him that all the tribes of the earth would be blessed in him: “Now this I say, that the testament which was confirmed by God, the law which was made after four hundred and thirty years doth not disannul.” In Exodus too this is shown clearly enough. For it did not say, “The sojourning of the children of Israel, which they sojourned in the land of Egypt, was four hundred and thirty years”; but it said plainly, “which they sojourned in the land of Egypt and in the land of Chanaan, they and their fathers.” So it is plain that the time of the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac and Jacob is also to be counted, from when Abraham began to be a stranger in the land of Chanaan, that is, from that promise in which the Apostle praises his faith, until Israel entered Egypt. For through all that time the fathers were strangers in the land of Chanaan, and afterwards the seed of Israel in Egypt; and so the four hundred and thirty years were completed from the promise to the going out of Israel from Egypt, when the Law was made on Mount Sina, which does not disannul the testament of God. In the seventy-fifth year of his life Abraham, according to Scripture, entered the land of Chanaan, and he begot Isaac when he was a hundred years old. So there are twenty-five years from the promise to the birth of Isaac. To these are added all the years of his life, that is, one hundred and eighty, and they make two hundred and five. Then Jacob was one hundred and twenty years old; for he and Esau were born twins when their father was sixty. And after ten years Jacob entered Egypt, when he was one hundred and thirty years old, and Joseph thirty-nine. So there are two hundred and fifteen years from the promise to Jacob’s entry into Egypt. And Joseph lived afterwards seventy-one; all his years were one hundred and ten. So when seventy-one are added to two hundred and fifteen years, they make two hundred and eighty-six years. There remain, then, one hundred and forty-four or five, in which Israel served in Egypt after the death of Joseph. How much they could multiply in these years, if the fruitfulness of men is considered, with the help of God, who willed them to multiply, it is found no wonder that they went out of Egypt six hundred thousand men on foot. So what God said to Abraham, “They shall bring them under bondage and afflict them four hundred years,” is not to be understood as though they served four hundred years in that hard slavery; but because it is written, “In Isaac shall thy seed be called,” four hundred and five years are counted from the year of Isaac’s birth to the year of the going out. So when you take from four hundred and thirty the twenty-five that are from the promise to the birth of Isaac, it is no wonder if Scripture called four hundred and five years four hundred as a round sum, since it is wont so to count times that what exceeds the number of the full sum a little, or falls below it, is not counted. So what he said, “They shall bring them under bondage and afflict them,” is not to be referred to the four hundred years, as though they served so many years; but the four hundred years are to be referred to what was said, “Thy seed shall be a stranger in a land not their own”; because, whether in the land of Chanaan or in Egypt, the seed was a stranger before they received the promised inheritance, having gone out of Egypt: so that a hyperbaton is to be understood here, and the order of the words is: “Know that thy seed shall be a stranger in a land not their own four hundred years.” And that which is put between, “They shall bring them under bondage and afflict them,” does not belong to the four hundred years. For in the last part of the years of this sum, that is, after the death of Joseph, they were oppressed with hard slavery.
12.38:
**“And a mixed multitude without number”** — they were multiplied above number, because “many are called, but few chosen.”
**“went up also with them, sheep”** — the innocent
**“and herds and beasts of divers kinds, exceeding many.”** — because if they cannot fight, yet they are a help to the fighters
12.39:
**“And they baked”** — binding it together with the fire of the Holy Spirit
**“the meal, which a little before … in dough:”** — that they might be a new paste and unleavened
**“from Egypt:”** — from the world
**“they had brought … and they made earth cakes”** — in humility
**“unleavened: for it could not be leavened, the Egyptians pressing them to depart,”** — The world itself drives us to God, and Satan casts out Satan, lest we be corrupted by the leaven of sin.
**“and not suffering them to make any stay:”** — The Egyptians press us, lest we season the sternness of the law with the savour of the Gospel, or of worldly doctrine.
12.40: **“And the abode of the children of Israel that they made in Egypt, was four hundred and thirty years.”** — from when Abraham went out of his land to dwell in the land of Chanaan until the going out of Egypt, when the Law was made on Mount Sina.
12.43: **“And the Lord said to Moses and Aaron: This is the service of the Phase: No foreigner shall eat of it.”** — A Gentile, a Jew, or one excommunicated from the Church ought not to communicate in the sacraments of the Lord’s body.
12.44:
**“But every bought servant”** — who before served idols, but has been redeemed by the blood of Christ
**“shall be circumcised,”** — from original sins in baptism
**“and so shall eat.”**
• having put off the old man and put on the new
• the Body of Christ
12.45:
**“The stranger”** — who has lately come to the faith and is not yet firm
**“and the hireling”** — who serves Christ for temporal gains
12.46:
**“In one house”** — the Catholic Church, not in the conventicles of the heretics
**“shall it be eaten,”** — or “it shall be eaten”
**“neither shall you carry forth of the flesh thereof”** — because neither Jews nor pagans nor heretics, nor any at all who are outside the Church, are admitted to this communion.
**“out of the house,”** — that is, outside the Catholic Church, lest they communicate with the ungodly and sinners, because they are deprived of the Catholic Church.
**“neither shall you break a bone thereof.”**
• that is, you shall not lessen the Godhead because of the manhood
• Neither shall you break a bone thereof, etc. Christ’s bone was not broken on the cross, because, seeing him already dead, they did not break his legs; or the strength of the Godhead in the flesh is not corrupted by blasphemy, because he is not a mere man, but true God.
12.47:
**“All the assembly”** — the Catholic Church
**“of the children of Israel,”** — not of others
12.48:
**“And if any”** — unbelieving and a stranger to the worship of the Christians
**“stranger”** — of the Gentiles or of the Jews
**“be willing to dwell among you,”** — the worship of religion
**“and to keep”** — the most solemn passage from the world to God
**“the Phase of the Lord, … shall first be circumcised,”** — that he may put off the old man with his deeds
**“all his males”** — For he is strong and a man who can be circumcised of the superfluity of original and actual corruption.
**“and then”** — Not before: “For he that eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh judgment to himself.”
**“shall he celebrate it according to the manner:”** — joined to the heavenly banquets
**“and he shall be as he that is born in the land:”**
• nourished in the Church
• in Catholic nobility
**“but if any man be uncircumcised,”** — because there is no part of uncleanness with cleanness, which cleanses all things
**“he shall not eat thereof.”** — because “God is not a respecter of persons,” nor is there “distinction of the Jew and the Greek”
12.49: **“The same law shall be to him that is born in the land, and to the proselyte”** — who has been received into the colony of the Church
12.51: **“And the same day the Lord brought forth the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt by their companies.”** — the various orders, sexes, professions

13.2:
**“Sanctify”**
• dedicate.
• Because I killed all the firstborn of the Egyptians in your deliverance.
**“unto me every firstborn”** — the beginning of a good work
**“that openeth the womb”** — of the body or of the mind: for God gives both to will and to accomplish, according to his good will.
**“among the children of Israel,”** — who see God
**“as well of men”** — rational and learned
**“as of beasts:”** — irrational, unlearned
**“for they are all mine.”** — because the beginning of all good is from God, whose mercy goes before and follows
13.3:
**“And Moses said to the people: Remember”** — keep in memory how great things the Lord has done for you
**“this day”**
• on which the true light shone forth on the world
• singularly
**“in which you came forth”** — free
**“out of Egypt,”** — out of the darkness of this world
**“and out of the house”** — out of the household of the devil
**“of bondage,”** — devilish
**“for with a … hand”** — in the Son, who is the power and wisdom of the Father
**“strong”** — invincible
**“hath … brought you forth”** — slaves
**“the Lord”** — who is able
**“out of this place:”** — dreadful
**“that you eat no leavened”** — in malice and wickedness
**“bread.”** — that is, of heaven, and the word of God
13.4: **“This day you go forth”** — that you may eat new food
13.5:
**“And when the Lord shall have brought thee into the land of the Chanaanite,”** — which the nations of the vices held before
**“and the Hethite, and the Amorrhite, and the Hevite, and the Jebusite, which he swore”** — he firmly promised, lest anyone should doubt
**“to thy fathers”** — in the flesh or in faith
**“that he would give thee, a land that floweth”** — the present Church, or the homeland to come
**“with milk”** — the teaching of the little ones
**“and honey.”** — with heavenly sweetness; hence: “Butter and honey shall he eat.”
**“thou shalt celebrate”** — spiritually, because it profits nothing to celebrate outwardly unless the true celebration is kept in the mind
**“this manner”** — not another
**“of sacred rites in this month.”** — notable, mystical
13.6:
**“Seven days”** — through all the time of the present life
**“shalt thou eat unleavened bread:”** — of sincerity and truth
**“and on the seventh day”** — when the labour of working is finished
**“shall be the solemnity of the Lord.”** — the true rest of souls
13.7:
**“Unleavened bread shall you eat seven days: there shall not be seen … with thee,”** — and if it happens: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body.”
**“any thing leavened”** — a little leaven corrupteth the whole lump
**“nor in all thy coasts.”** — the bounds of the Church
13.8:
**“And thou shalt tell thy son”** — a disciple, anyone younger
**“in that day, saying: This”** — notable, remarkable
13.9:
**“And it shall be as a sign”** — of the profession of faith
**“in … hand,”** — in deed; perhaps this is rather the sense than a manner of speech
**“thy … and as a memorial before thy eyes:”**
• of the heart, lest thou forget
• “Open thou my eyes: and I will consider the wondrous things of thy law.”
• of thy intention, because: “If thy eye be single, thy whole body shall be lightsome.”
**“and that the law of the Lord”**
• the meditations of the law
• “But his will is in the law of the Lord, and on his law he shall meditate day and night.”
**“be always in thy mouth,”** — of the heart or of the body
**“for with a strong hand the Lord hath brought thee out of the land of Egypt.”** — And it shall be as a sign, etc. AUGUSTINE. What does it mean that, when giving commands about the Pasch, he says, “It shall be for a sign to thee upon thy hand”? Did he wish it to be understood “upon thy works,” that is, that thou oughtest to put it before thy works? For the Pasch, because of the killing of the sheep, belongs to faith in Christ and the blood by which we have been redeemed. And this faith is to be put before works, so that it is in a manner upon the hand, against those who glory in the works of the Law. Hence the Apostle so puts faith before works that good works hang upon it and are gone before by it, not that it is paid back for the merits of good works. For it belongs to grace: “And if by grace, it is not now by works: otherwise grace is no more grace.”
13.10:
**“Thou shalt keep”** — diligently
**“this observance”** — prescribed: do not excuse thyself, to whom religion is prescribed
**“at the set time”** — by God
**“from days to days.”** — until this corruptible put on incorruption and thou come to the fellowship of the angels
13.11:
**“And when the Lord shall have brought thee into the land of the Chanaanite,”** — He explains how he is to sacrifice the firstborn.
**“as he swore to thee and thy fathers,”** — by whose merits thou art brought in
**“and shall give it thee:”** — freely
13.12:
**“Thou shalt set apart”** — to man
**“all that openeth the womb for the Lord, and all that is first brought forth of thy cattle: whatsoever thou shalt have of the male sex,”**
• not of the female, which Pharao loves and nourishes
• of manly and perfect work

13.13:
**“The firstborn of an ass”** — the beginnings of an unclean life
**“thou shalt change for a sheep:”**
• by the innocence of the life that follows
• The firstborn of an ass, etc. GREGORY. The ass signifies uncleanness, the sheep innocence. So to change the firstborn of an ass for a sheep is to turn the beginnings of an unclean life into the simplicity of innocence, so that after the sinner has done those things which the Lord rejects as unclean, he may now, by acting, bring forth what he may lay on God’s sacrifice. For we are all born in sin, and, conceived from the delight of the flesh, we have contracted original guilt; hence too we are entangled in sins by our own will. But he too who after the malice of the flesh is turned to innocence of heart changes the firstborn of the ass for a sheep, that is, the malice of his former life. For he who ceases to be what he was before, and, having laid hold of cleanness of the flesh, guards innocence, has changed the firstborn of the ass for a sheep as an offering to God.
**“and if thou do not redeem it, thou shalt kill it.”**
• that is: if thou art so weak that thou canst not come to true innocence, at least confess and condemn thy sin.
• with the price of an amended life.
13.14:
**“And when thy son shall ask thee”** — According to that: “Ask thy father, and he will declare to thee,” etc. It belongs to fathers, both spiritual and carnal, to know the Law and teach the faith.
**“tomorrow,”** — in the future: a usual expression
13.15:
**“For when Pharao was hardened,”** — of his own accord, or by the Lord
**“and would not let us go, the Lord slew every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn”** — as above
**“of man”** — who is thought learned
**“to the firstborn of beasts:”** — of the foolish
**“therefore I sacrifice”**
• or “I will sacrifice”
• mindful of the kindness
**“to the Lord all that openeth the womb of the male sex,”** — the beginnings of good work and thought
**“and all the firstborn of my sons”** — of works or thoughts
**“I redeem.”** — by correcting, by changing for the better
13.16:
**“And it shall be”** — or “for”
**“as a sign”** — the memory of the kindness
**“in … hand,”** — in working
**“thy … and as a thing hung … for a remembrance:”** — an eternal memory
**“between thy eyes,”** — of the heart, by which the wonders of the Law are seen
**“and as a thing hung”** — The Jews, understanding this wrongly, bound on their heads little tablets or phylacteries, in which they had the ten words written before their eyes.
13.17:
**“And when Pharao had sent out the people, … them not”** — still rude beginners
**“the Lord led”** — to the land of promise
**“by the way of the land of the Philistines which is near: thinking lest perhaps they would repent,”** — to have gone out of Egypt
**“if they should see wars … against them,”** — of the vices, of the demons
**“arise, and would return into Egypt.”**
• the world, which was still neighbouring and near
• When Pharao had sent out, etc. GREGORY. Morally. Often converts, at the very entrance of their conversion, receive tranquillity of the flesh, gifts of prophecy, the preaching of doctrine, the wonders of signs or the grace of healings. Afterwards they are wearied by hard trials of temptations, from which they believed they were free; because if the bitterness of temptations knocked at the beginning, they would easily return to the vices from which they had not gone far. So from those going out of Egypt wars near at hand are withdrawn, because to those leaving the world a certain tranquillity is first shown, lest, troubled in their very tenderness and beginning, they return to what they had left. So first they feel the sweetness of security, first they are nourished by the quiet of peace. But after the sweetness has been known, they bear the struggles of temptations the more tolerably, the more deeply they have known in God what they may love.
• He led them not, etc. AUGUSTINE. Here it is shown that all things ought to be done that can rightly be done by counsel to avoid what is adverse, even when God is most plainly our helper.
13.18:
**“But he led them about”** — as if cherishing them with the sweetness of security
**“by the way of the desert, which is by the Red Sea:”** — baptism consecrated by the blood of Christ, to which the way of the desert, which is Christ, is near
**“and … armed”** — with virtues
**“went up”** — from the valley of Egypt
**“the children of Israel … out of the land of Egypt.”** — And … went up armed, etc. JEROME. Aquila, who is not contentious, as some think, but painstaking, translating word for word, where the Septuagint put, “And in the fifth generation the children of Israel went up out of the land of Egypt,” translated, “and the children of Israel went up armed out of the land of Egypt”; although for what we said, “armed,” by the ambiguity of the Greek word it can be understood as “equipped” or “furnished,” because of the goods with which they spoiled the Egyptians. But where the Septuagint put “in the fifth generation,” those who have carefully examined the books of the Hebrews report that not “fifth” but “five” is written, so that the sense is, “and five the children of Israel went up out of the land of Egypt”; and because this seemed less understandable, “generation” was added. But Aquila, both in the other places and especially in this one, is said to have translated properly, as all the benches of the synagogues agree.
*Augustine:* “And in the fifth generation the children of Israel went up out of the land,” etc. Does he wish a generation to be counted in a hundred years, and so “in the fifth generation,” because they went out after four hundred and thirty years? Or is this rather to be understood by the generations of men, from Jacob himself, who entered Egypt, to Moses, who went out with the people? For Jacob is found first, Levi second, Caath third, Amram fourth, Moses fifth. And the Latin translator calls progenies those which the Greeks name, which in the Gospel are called “generations,” and they are numbered by the successions of men, not by the number of years. But others count not from Jacob through Levi to Moses, but through the tribe of Juda, which was the royal one; so that from Phares, the son of Juda, who entered Egypt with his father Juda, to Salmon, who as leader in that same tribe of Juda entered the land of promise, there are five generations. For Phares begot Esrom, Esrom begot Aram, Aram begot Aminadab, Aminadab begot Naason, Naason begot Salmon.
13.19: **“And Moses took Joseph’s bones with him:”** — Of which Jesus the son of Sirach says that they prophesied after death, because, that is, Joseph prophesied what was to happen to the children of Israel after his death.
13.20:
**“And marching from Socoth they encamped in Etham”** — “signs to them”
**“in the utmost coasts of the wilderness.”** — on the border of Egypt and the desert, where the wilderness begins after Egypt ends
13.21:
**“And the Lord went before”** — God and protector
**“them to shew the way”** — of the heavenly homeland
**“by day”** — the life of the just
**“in a pillar of a cloud,”** — of gentle caressing
**“and by night”** — the life of sinners
**“in a pillar of fire:”** — because he is terrible to the unjust
13.22:
**“There never failed”** — the Hebrews relate that for forty years they were protected by the pillar of cloud by day, lest they be burnt by the heat of the sun.
**“the pillar of the cloud”** — the obscurity of the Old Testament
**“by day, nor the pillar of fire”** — the light of the Gospel
**“And the Lord”** — ORIGEN. When you have received the mystery of the third day, God will begin to lead you and show you the way of salvation.
*Gregory:* In the fire, terror; in the cloud, the gentle caressing of the vision. The day is the life of the just man; the night, of the sinner. Hence: “You were heretofore darkness, but now light in the Lord.” By day the pillar was shown through the cloud, and by night through the fire, because almighty God will appear both gentle to the just and terrible to the ungodly. Coming to judgment, he will soothe the former with the mildness of gentleness, and terrify the latter with the strictness of justice. Otherwise: the pillar of cloud went before the people in the desert, and shone with the brightness of fire not by day but by night, because Christ, giving leadership by the example of his way of life to those who follow, shone with no light to those who trust in their own justice; but on those who acknowledge the darkness of their sins he shone with the fire of his love.
**“by night, before the people.”** — Christ is the cloud and the pillar: because upright and firm, and propping up our weakness; because shining by night, not shining by day, so that “they who see not may see, and they who see may become blind.” The mystery of Christ too is plain as in the day, in the flesh as in a cloud; but in the judgment as in a terror by night, because then there will be great tribulation: like fire he will shine for the just and burn the unjust.

14.2:
**“Speak to the children of Israel: Let them turn and encamp over against Phihahiroth”**
• a place in the desert
• “mouth of the nobles”
**“which is between Magdal”** — Tower: a city on the border of Egypt, to which the Jews fled in the captivity in the time of Jeremias.
**“and the sea over against Beelsephon:”** — a place in the desert
**“you shall encamp before it upon the sea.”** — Phihahiroth which is between Magdal, etc. ORIGEN. Let us see what way is commanded to be chosen. “Turning from Othon,” he says, “make your way between Epanleum and Magdal, which is over against Beelsephon,” etc. Epanleum is interpreted “a winding ascent,” Magdal “tower,” Beelsephon “ascent of the watchtower” or “having a watchtower.” You perhaps believed that God would show a level and soft road; but it is an ascent, and winding. For the road by which one makes for the virtues is not downhill; it is climbed narrowly and with difficulty: “For narrow is the gate, and strait is the way that leadeth to life.” So the road on which one goes is a winding ascent, and an ascent of the watchtower, or having a watchtower. The ascent belongs to deeds, the watchtower to faith. So it is shown that both in deeds and in faith there is much difficulty, much labour: for many temptations meet us, many stumbling blocks, when we wish to do the things of God. Then in faith you will find many winding things, very many questions, the objections of heretics, the contradictions of unbelievers: this, then, is the road to be taken by those who follow the Lord. But there is a tower too on this road, of which it is said: “Which of you having a mind to build a tower, doth not first sit down and reckon the charges that are necessary, whether he have wherewithal to finish it?” This, then, is the tower, steep and lofty with these virtues. Seeing this, Pharao says: “These are wandering.” In Pharao’s eyes he who follows God is said to wander, because the road of wisdom is winding, having many difficulties and windings. If you confess one Father invisible, and his one only-begotten Jesus Christ, and one Holy Spirit, this seems winding, difficult and inexplicable to unbelievers. If you say that the God of majesty crucified is the son of man, who came down from heaven, these things seem winding and difficult; he who hears, unless he hears with faith, says that these are wandering. But be fixed in this faith, knowing that God shows you this road of faith, who says: “Moving the camp from Othon, place it between Epanleum and Magdal.”
14.3: **“And Pharao will say of the children of Israel: They are straitened in the land,”** — Josephus says that on one side an impassable mountain, on the other the sea, hemmed them in.
14.4:
**“And I shall harden”** — as above
**“his heart, and he will pursue you: and I shall be glorified”** — I will appear glorious
**“in Pharao,”** — when he is drowned
14.5: **“And it was told the king of the Egyptians that the people was fled: and the heart of Pharao and of his servants was changed with regard to the people, and they said: What meant we to do, that we let Israel go from serving us?”** — That the people was fled, etc. ORIGEN. Fleeing Egypt, you come to the ascent of work and faith, and to the building of the tower; you come to the sea, and the waves of temptations meet you. For “all that will live godly in Christ shall suffer persecution,” because “the life of man upon earth is a temptation.” But if you follow Moses, that is, the law of God, Egypt pursues you. But see what will happen. “The angel of the Lord,” it says, “who went before the camp of Israel, lifted himself and went behind them. And the pillar of the cloud too lifted itself from before them, and stood behind them, and went in between the camp of the Egyptians and of the Israelites.” This pillar of cloud becomes a wall for the people of God; on the Egyptians it lays darkness. It is not the pillar of fire that is moved over to the Egyptians, that they might see the light, but of cloud, that they might remain in darkness, because they loved darkness, not light. So you too, if you withdraw from the Egyptians, if you flee from the power of the demons, see how great helps are prepared for you, provided you remain strong in faith: let not the horsemen and four-horse chariots of the Egyptians terrify you, nor cry out against the law of God, that is, Moses, saying: “As if there were no graves in Egypt, so thou hast brought us out,” and so on.
14.6: **“So he made ready his chariot,”** — the pride of the rolling world
14.7:
**“And he took”** — about to fight against the faith of the Holy Trinity
**“three hundred”** — another reading: “six hundred”
**“chosen chariots,”** — outstanding in warfare
**“and all the chariots that were in Egypt: and the captains”** — the greater ones
**“of the whole army.”** — of the devil’s army
14.8:
**“And the Lord hardened the heart of Pharao king of Egypt, and he pursued”** — bodily or spiritually
**“the children of Israel:”**
• the saints
• “All that will live godly in Christ shall suffer persecution,” that they may be drawn back.
**“but they were gone forth”** — from Egypt
**“in a mighty hand.”** — by unconquerable power
14.9:
**“And when the Egyptians followed the steps of them who were gone before, they found them encamped”** — of faith
**“at the sea side:”** — the waves of temptations
14.10: **“And when Pharao drew near,”** — by tempting more fiercely
14.11:
**“And they said to Moses: Perhaps there were no graves in Egypt, therefore thou hast brought us to die in the wilderness:”** — the words of men despairing and growing weary in temptation
**“why wouldst thou do this, to lead us out of Egypt?”** — from the power of Satan
14.12:
**“Is not this the word that we spoke to thee in Egypt, saying: Depart from us that we may serve the Egyptians? for it was much better to serve them, than to die in the wilderness.”**
• These are words of temptation and frailty; otherwise they are false. For it is better to begin the good, even if you cannot finish it, than not to depart from the devil.
• Than to die in the wilderness: not reaching the land of promise.
• Perhaps there were no graves, etc. ORIGEN. These are the words of a mind failing in temptation: blessed is he who so receives temptations that no thought of doubt creeps upon him. Even to Peter it is said: “O thou of little faith, why didst thou doubt?” These are words of temptation and frailty; otherwise it is false. For it is better to die in the desert than to serve the Egyptians. For he who dies in the desert, by the very fact that he is separated from the Egyptians, that is, from the rulers of darkness, and from the power of Satan, has made some progress, even if he could not reach the whole. For it is better for one who seeks the perfect life to die on the way than not even to set out. Hence the opinion of those seems mistaken who, while they set forth the steep and dangerous road of virtue, judge that it should not even be begun. For it is better to die on the way than to be slain among the Egyptians and overwhelmed by the salt and bitter waves.
14.13:
**“And Moses said”** — the Law of God
**“to the people: Fear not:”** — as if to say: “Fear not, little flock”
**“stand”** — “in the faith, do manfully.”
**“and see”** — with the eyes of the body and of the mind
**“the great wonders of the Lord, which he will do this day:”** — in the time of grace
**“the Egyptians,”** — the rulers of darkness
**“for … whom you see now, you shall see no more for ever.”**
• because the prince of this world is cast out
• alive, that is: for they saw them dead afterwards
• For the Egyptians, whom, etc. AUGUSTINE. “For as you have seen the Egyptians today, you shall not see them again for ever.” But how are these words to be taken, since the Israelites saw Egyptians afterwards? Is it because those who saw them then did not see them any more, because both those who pursued died, and these all, each on the day of his death; but their descendants saw the descendants of the others? Or is “you shall not see them as today” to be understood, not as today pursuing and enemies, so that there is no question, not even about the “for ever” which he put here; because even if both will see one another at the time of the resurrection, it will not be as today?
14.14:
**“the Lord”** — who alone is able
**“will fight for you,”** — against the powers of the air
**“and you shall hold your peace.”** — you shall be at rest
14.15: **“And the Lord said to Moses:”** — the Spirit asking with unspeakable groanings
14.16:
**“But lift thou up thy rod,”**
• this is the rod by which the wonders were done, which is called Moses’ and Aaron’s, because they worked through it.
• the word of the Law
**“and stretch forth thy hand over the sea,”** — the waves of the gainsayers
**“and divide it:”** — by the lawful lines of disputations, following the straight road of faith
**“that the children of Israel may go through the midst of the sea on dry ground.”**
• Why criest thou to me, etc. GREGORY. It is not our words that make cries in the ears of God, but our desires. For if we ask eternal life with the mouth and do not desire it in the heart, crying we are silent. But if we desire it in the heart, though we are silent with the mouth, being silent we cry. Hence in the desert, when the people clamoured with voices and Moses was silent from the din of words, he is heard though silent, and it is said to him: “Why criest thou to me?” For in desire a secret cry does not reach human ears; it fills the divine ones.
• ORIGEN. Otherwise: if you flee Egypt, that is, the darkness of ignorance, if you follow Moses, that is, the law of God, and the sea meets you, that is, the waves of the gainsayers, strike you too the struggling waves with the rod of Moses, that is, with the word of the Law and watchfulness in the Scriptures; open yourself a way through the adversaries by disputing, and the waves will give way to the victor; and while those who before gainsaid you wonder and stand fixed in amazement, you will cut the straight road of faith with the lawful lines of disputations; and you will advance so far in the word of teaching that your hearers, whom you have instructed with the rod of the law, will now rise against the Egyptians like the waves of the sea, and not only attack them but overcome and destroy them. For he destroys the Egyptian who does not do the works of darkness, who lives not carnally but spiritually, who either drives filthy thoughts from his heart or does not receive them at all, according to that: “Taking the shield of faith, wherewith you may be able to extinguish all the fiery darts of the most wicked one.” So in this way we too can see the Egyptians dead today, and Pharao himself, if we live with such faith that God may crush Satan under our feet speedily, through Jesus Christ.
*Origen:* No voice of Moses is heard, and the Lord says, “Why criest thou to me?” I should like to know how the saints cry to God without a voice: because “God hath sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying: Abba, Father.” And he adds: “The Spirit himself asketh for us with unspeakable groanings.” And again: “And he that searcheth the hearts knoweth what the Spirit desireth.” So when the Holy Spirit asks, the cry of the saints is heard through silence. Moses is ordered to strike the sea with the rod, so that it may give way as the people of God goes in, and the waters which were feared, made a wall on the right and on the left, not only know no harm but even give protection. The liquid takes on solidity, and the floor of the sea dries up into dust. Understand the goodness of the Creator: if you obey his will, if you follow his law, he compels the elements to serve you against their nature. I have heard it handed down from the elders that a separate division of the waters was made for each tribe, and a way of its own for each. And this is shown from what is said: “Who divided the Red Sea into divisions,” etc.; and elsewhere: “There is Benjamin a youth, in ecstasy of mind. The princes of Juda are their leaders: the princes of Zabulon, the princes of Nephthali”: a proper entry seems to be listed for each tribe. The Apostle says that baptism was completed in Moses, in the cloud and in the sea, so that you who are baptized in Christ, in water and in the Spirit, may know that the Egyptians pursue you and call you back to slavery, that is, the rulers of the world and the spirits of wickedness, whom you served before. But you go down into the water and escape unharmed, and you come up new, washed from the filth of sins, ready to sing a new song. The Egyptians who pursue are sunk in the abyss, even if they seem to ask Jesus not to sink them again into the abyss.
14.17:
**“And I will harden”** — as above
**“the heart of the Egyptians”** — not only of Pharao
**“to pursue you: and I will be glorified”** — I will appear glorious
**“in Pharao,”** — when he is sunk
**“and in all his host, and in his chariots,”** — with rolling glory
**“and in his horsemen.”** — the proud
14.18:
**“And … shall know”** — they are compelled to know
**“the Egyptians”** — no other
**“that I am the Lord,”** — not Pharao
14.19:
**“And the angel … removing,”** — the teachers
**“of God, who went before”** — by teaching both in word and example
**“the camp of Israel,”** — the Church fortified against enemies. Hence: “Terrible as an army set in array.”
**“went”** — by setting himself against the danger
**“behind them: and together with him the pillar of the cloud,”** — the knowledge of Scripture, which is the support of the Church
14.20:
**“Stood … between the Egyptians’ camp”** — of the persecutors
**“and the camp of Israel: and it was a dark cloud,”** — to the Egyptians
**“and enlightening”** — the Hebrews
**“the night,”** — the obscurity of the present life, while we see through a glass in a dark manner
**“so that they could not come at one another all the night.”** — And the angel … removing, etc. STRABO. The angel, which is interpreted “messenger,” signifies the teachers, who announce to us the precepts of life and go before the camp of Israel, that is, the Church, with the cloud, that is, the knowledge of the Scriptures, because they preside with the knowledge of the Scriptures. When the Egyptians come upon them, he goes behind, because in time of persecution they set themselves in the way for those under them. And the cloud was dark to the Egyptians, bright to the Hebrews.
14.21:
**“And when … had stretched forth”** — showing, that is, the effect of the divine power in the waters
**“Moses”** — the Law of God
**“… hand”** — the power of correcting and convicting, that is, the gainsaying of the persecutors
**“over the sea, the Lord took it away by a strong and burning wind blowing”** — the Holy Spirit drying up worldly wisdom
**“all the night,”** — of adversity, or of the present ignorance
**“and turned it into dry ground: and the water was divided.”** — All the night, etc. Because through all the time of this life, which the night signifies, the grace of the Holy Spirit makes the waters of baptism passable for the faithful, so that they may pass from the spiritual Egypt into the land of promise; but it chokes the army of the enemies.
*Isidore:* The Red Sea signifies baptism consecrated by the blood of Christ; the enemies following behind die with their king, because past sins are blotted out in baptism, and the devil is choked: the Egyptians press on up to the sea, and sins up to baptism. After the crossing of the Red Sea, the enemies being drowned, the people sings; and the faithful coming up from the font, their sins destroyed, sing a hymn, saying: “Let us sing to the Lord: for he is gloriously magnified,” etc.
14.22: **“And the children of Israel went in through the midst of the sea dried up: for the water was as a wall”** — a defence
14.23:
**“And the Egyptians pursuing”** — sins
**“went in after them, and”** — namely
**“all Pharao’s horses,”** — of the devil
**“his chariots”**
• God’s chariots are all the elect, of whom it is said: “The chariot of God is attended by ten thousands,” etc.
• the devil’s chariots: all the reprobate and the spirits of wickedness
**“and horsemen”** — the demons
14.24:
**“And now … was come,”** — as the light of faith brightens, and God enlightens his people, the darkness of ignorance being sent away
**“the morning watch”**
• in which Christ rose from the dead
• that God might keep watch to guard his people, who before seemed to be asleep
**“and behold the Lord looking”** — God is said to look upon when he does something new and remarkable.
**“upon the Egyptian army”** — of the spirits of wickedness
**“through the pillar”** — which props up the godly, overwhelms the ungodly
**“of fire”** — because terrible to the ungodly
**“and of the cloud,”** — because gentle to his own
**“slew their host.”** — the vices, the power of the wicked
14.25:
**“And overthrew the wheels of the chariots,”** — the din and the rolling of the reprobate
**“and they were carried”** — by their own iniquity
**“into the deep.”** — of the abyss
**“said:”** — having seen the power of God
**“And”** — or “therefore”
**“the Egyptians”** — the demons, or any persecutors
**“Let us flee”** — let us not pursue
**“from Israel:”** — the people that sees God
**“the Lord”** — “Whose wrath no man can resist.”
**“for … fighteth for them”** — to set them free
**“against us.”** — to crush us
14.28: **“And the waters returned, and covered the chariots and the horsemen of all the army of Pharao, who had come into the sea after them,”** — who in baptism, all sins being forgiven, and the power of the devil sunk
14.29:
**“But the children of Israel marched through the midst of the sea upon dry land, and the waters were to them as a wall”** — for a defence
**“on the right hand”** — prosperity
**“and on the left:”** — adversity
14.30:
**“And the Lord delivered … in that day”** — in the time of baptism
**“Israel”** — the baptized people
**“out of the hands”** — from the power
**“of the Egyptians.”** — of the demons, of the vices
**“upon the sea shore, and the … hand”** — unspeakable power
14.31:
**“And they saw the Egyptians”** — the demons or the vices
**“dead”**
• cast down, that is, by the power of baptism
• their power lost
**“mighty … that the Lord had used against them: and the people feared”**
• having seen the miracle
• “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.”
**“the Lord,”** — whose power it had proved
**“and they believed the Lord, and Moses his servant.”** — they understood the faith in the promise

15.1:
**“Then”** — the enemies being drowned
**“Moses and the children of Israel sung this canticle to the Lord: and said:”**
• urging one another on
• Then … sung, etc. ORIGEN. We read many canticles in the Scriptures, but this is the first of all, which is sung after the victory, when the Egyptians and Pharao had been drowned. For it is the custom of the saints, when the adversary is overcome (because they know the victory was won not by their own strength but by the grace of God), to offer God a hymn of glorifying. Yet as they sing they take timbrels in their hands, as is told of Mary and Aaron. And you too, if you have crossed the Red Sea, if you have seen the Egyptians sunk and Pharao hurled into the abyss, can sing a hymn to God with thanks and say: “Let us sing to the Lord: for he is gloriously,” etc. But you will say this more worthily if you have a timbrel in your hand, that is, if you have crucified your flesh with its vices and lusts.
**“Let us sing”**
• with mouth, heart, deed
• a hymn to the victor
**“to the Lord: for he is gloriously magnified,”** — he was magnified in the signs of Egypt, but gloriously magnified because he drowned Pharao and his army; or magnified: the wonders before the passion
**“gloriously”** — THE SAME (Origen). “He is glorified” is not enough: for it is one thing to be glorified, another to be gloriously glorified. For when Christ took flesh for us he was glorified, he who came to seek what had perished; yet not gloriously, because he had no beauty nor comeliness. He was glorified when he came to the cross and bore death. Hence: “Father, the hour is come, glorify thy Son,” etc. So the passion of the cross was his glory, where he was glorified, not gloriously indeed, but humbly. Hence: “He humbled himself unto death, even to the death of the cross.” And elsewhere: “Let us condemn him to a most shameful death.” So in these he was glorified, but humbly, not gloriously. Hence: “Ought not Christ to have suffered these things, and so to enter into his glory?” When he comes in the glory of the Father and of the angels to judge the earth, and slays the true Pharao, that is, the devil, with the spirit of his mouth, when he shines in the majesty of the Father: then he will be gloriously glorified, when all shall honour the Son as they honour the Father.
**“the horse”** — any wicked man
**“and the rider”** — the devil
**“he hath thrown into the sea.”**
• into hell
• He was magnified in the signs of Egypt, but gloriously magnified because he drowned Pharao and his army. Or he was magnified by doing wonders before the passion, by preaching, by dying on the cross; but gloriously magnified when he rose as victor, the devil being conquered and hell despoiled.
• The horse and the rider, etc. ORIGEN. The men who pursue us are horses, and all who are born in the flesh are figuratively horses, and have their riders. There are some whom the Lord mounts, and they go round the whole earth; of whom it is said: “Thy riding is salvation.” Others the devil and his angels mount. Judas was a horse, and when he had the Lord for his rider, he was of the cavalry of salvation. Sent with the other apostles, he gave health to the sick and healing to the languishing; when he laid himself under the devil, who entered into him after the morsel, he was made Satan’s horse and, led by his reins, rode against the Lord. So all persecutors are neighing horses, but they have evil angels as riders, by whom they are driven, and so they are fierce. If you see your persecutor raging exceedingly, know that he is spurred on by his rider, and so he is savage and ferocious.
15.2:
**“… is my strength and my praise,”** — because through him I am strong and worthy of praise
**“The Lord”** — no other
**“and he is become”** — man, that is
**“salvation to me: he is … God”** — the Creator
**“my … and I will glorify”** — by words, by deeds
**“him:”** — not myself
**“the God of my father,”** — of Christ, who says: “I go to my Father and your Father.”
**“and I will exalt”**
• therefore
• not only glorify
**“him.”** — He is my God, etc. ORIGEN. So he will be both my God and the God of my father. Our father, who made us and begot us, is Christ, who says: “I go to my Father and your Father,” etc. So if I acknowledge that he is my God, I will glorify him; if also that he is my father’s, I will exalt him. For it is a loftier understanding how Christ, to bind together and unite the truth of the one God, calls him his God whom by nature he knows as Father.
15.3:
**“The Lord is as a man of war,”**
• overcoming for us, that is, the enemies visible and invisible
• because there is none who can resist his will
15.4:
**“chariots”** — others: “four-horse chariots”
**“Pharao’s … and his army”** — as above
**“he hath cast into the sea: … chosen captains”**
• others: “ternistratores”
• the capital vices, or the demons who preside over those vices
**“his … are drowned in the Red Sea.”** — The Lord is as a man of war, etc. ORIGEN. Another text: “The Lord crushes wars; the Lord is his name.” He crushes not only visible battles, but those too that we have against the principalities and powers and the rulers of this darkness. For the Lord is his name, and there is no creature of which he is not Lord. “Pharao’s four-horse chariots and his army he cast into the sea. The chosen riders, the ternistratores, he sank in the Red Sea.” Pharao, as stronger in malice and holding the kingdom of wickedness, drives four-horse chariots: it is not enough for him to mount one horse, but he drives several at once and forces them with the twisted lash. When you see them fouler in luxury, more savage in cruelty, more hideous in avarice, know that they are of Pharao’s four-horse chariots, which he yokes to his car: in them he is carried and flies through the open plains of crimes with the reins let loose. There are other chosen riders, that is, chosen for malice.
15.5:
**“The depths”** — of hell
**“have covered them, they are sunk to the bottom like a stone.”** — They are sunk to the bottom, etc. ORIGEN. Because such men, that is, were not the stones from which children of Abraham might be raised up, but men who loved the deep and liquid element, that is, the bitter and fleeting pleasure of present things. Hence it is said of them: “They sunk as lead in the mighty waters.” Sinners are heavy, and “iniquity” is read to sit “upon a talent of lead.” Hence the wicked are sunk to the bottom like lead. But the saints walk upon the waters, because they are light and not weighed down by the weight of sin. Christ walked upon the waters, who truly did no sin. Peter walked too, but he doubted a little; for he had something of lead, for which it is said to him: “O thou of little faith, why didst thou doubt?” So all are saved through fire, so that if perhaps anything of the kind of lead has been mixed in, the fire may melt and dissolve it, so that all may be made the best gold, because the gold of that land which the saints are to have is the best; and as the furnace tries gold, so tribulation tries just men. So all must come to the melting pot. For God sits and melts and purifies the sons of Juda. If anyone has brought many good works and a little iniquity, that little is melted and purged as by fire, and the whole remains pure gold. If anyone has brought more lead, more is burnt away, so that it may be melted down more, so that, even if little, yet some purged gold may remain. But he who comes wholly of lead is sunk like lead in the mighty waters.
15.6:
**“Thy right hand, O Lord,”** — Father
**“is magnified in strength: thy right hand,”** — power, or the Son
**“O Lord,”** — Father
**“hath slain the enemy.”** — the devil
15.7:
**“And in the multitude of thy glory”** — because from this thou didst appear very glorious
**“thou hast put down”** — from the throne of pride
**“… adversaries:”** — the devil and the vices
**“thy”** — or “my”
**“thou hast sent thy wrath”** — AUGUSTINE. Another text: “Thou didst send thy spirit, and the sea covered them,” etc. See, now the Spirit of God is mentioned for the fifth time, so that in this number we may take also what was said: “This is the finger of God.” First, where it is written: “The Spirit of God moved over the waters.” Second, where it is said: “My Spirit shall not remain in these men, because they are flesh.” Third, where Pharao says to Joseph: “Since the Spirit of God is in thee.” Fourth, where: “This is the finger of God.” Fifth, in this canticle: “Thou didst send thy Spirit, and the sea covered them.” And let us note that the Spirit of God is mentioned not only for kindnesses but also for vengeance. Hence above: “By the spirit of thy anger the water was divided.” So the Spirit of God was a spirit of anger to the Egyptians, whom the dividing of the waters harmed, so that as they went in they could be overwhelmed by the returning waters. To the children of Israel, whom the divided water profited, that Spirit was not the anger of God. Hence it is signified that the Spirit of God is named differently because of his different workings and effects, though he is one and the same, who is also taken as the Spirit in the unity of the Trinity. I do not think another is signified, but the same, as the Apostle says: “For you have not received the spirit of bondage again in fear; but you have received the spirit of adoption of sons, whereby we cry: Abba, Father”; because by the same Spirit of God, that is, the finger of God, by which the Law was written on tables of stone, fear was struck into those who did not yet understand grace, so that they might be convicted of their weakness and sins through the Law, and the Law might become their pedagogue, by which they might be led to the glory that is in the faith of Jesus Christ. And of this Spirit of adoption and grace, that is, of this work of the Spirit of God by which grace and regeneration into eternal life is imparted, it is said, “But the spirit quickeneth,” when it had been said above, “The letter killeth,” that is, Scripture that only commands, without the help of grace.
15.8: **“And with the blast of thy anger the waters were gathered together: the flowing water stood,”** — against nature
15.9:
**“The enemy said:”** — the devil
**“I will pursue”** — those going back from Egypt
**“and overtake,”** — he says this with the rashness and pride native to him
**“I will divide”** — among various vices or torturers
**“the spoils,”** — the saints snatched away to Christ
**“… soul shall have its fill:”** — will
**“my … I will draw”** — I will lay open
**“my sword,”** — all the ways of deceiving
**“shall slay”** — spiritually
**“them … my hand”** — power, or the multitude of the army
15.10:
**“… wind blew”** — of indignation, or the burning wind
**“Thy … and the sea covered them: they sunk”** — a flood of punishments
**“as lead”** — weighed down by the weight of sins
**“in the mighty waters.”** — in the bitter and fleeting pleasure of present things, or in the gulf of hell
15.11:
**“Who is like to thee,”** — in substance, in power
**“among the strong,”** — or among the gods, of whom it is said: “I have said: You are gods.”
**“O Lord? who is like to thee, glorious in holiness,”** — of the saints
**“terrible”**
• by just judgment
• to the ungodly
**“and praiseworthy,”** — by mercifully sparing
**“doing wonders?”**
• miracles
• Who is like to thee, etc. ORIGEN. He does not compare God to the images of the Gentiles, nor to the demons who falsely take to themselves the name of gods, but he speaks of those gods who are called gods by grace and participation in God, according to that: “I have said: You are gods.” And elsewhere: “God hath stood in the congregation of gods.” But these, though they are capable of God and seem to be given this name by grace, none is like him in power or nature. And as to what is said, “We shall be like to him,” this likeness is brought back not to nature but to grace; as a picture is like him whose image is expressed in it as to grace, but far unlike as to substance. For the one is the form of flesh and the comeliness of a living body; the other a coat of colours and wax laid on boards without sense. So none among the gods is like the Lord, that is, invisible, incorporeal, unchangeable, without beginning and end. None is creator of all things but the Father, creating all things through the Son, and sanctifying all things in the Holy Spirit.
15.12:
**“Thou stretchedst forth thy hand,”**
• “I have spread forth my hands all the day to an unbelieving people.”
• on the cross
**“and the earth swallowed them.”**
• the water, akin to the earth and everywhere held in by the earth
• earthly pleasure, or the death of the crime committed
• Thou stretchedst forth thy hand, etc. ORIGEN. It moves me that he says, “Thou stretchedst forth thy right hand, and the earth swallowed them,” as if the cause of their being swallowed by the earth was that he stretched out his right hand. If you consider how the Lord, lifted up on the cross, stretched out his hand all the day to a people not believing but gainsaying, and how the death of iniquity crushed the unbelieving people who cried, “Crucify him, crucify him,” you will find how he stretched out his right hand and the earth swallowed them. Yet one must not despair altogether. For if he who has been swallowed comes to his senses, he can be vomited out like Jonas. The earth once swallowed us all, and held us in the inner places of hell. So Christ came down not only to the earth, but also to the lower parts of the earth, and there he found us swallowed and sitting in the shadow of death. Leading us out from there, he prepares for us not only the earth, lest we be swallowed again, but the kingdom of heaven.
• … swallowed them, etc. ORIGEN. Even today the earth swallows the ungodly, who always think about the earth, do earthly things, speak of the earth, quarrel, desire the earth, put their hope in it, do not look up to heaven, do not think of what is to come, do not fear God’s judgment nor desire his promises. When you see such a man, say that the earth has swallowed him; and if you see anyone given over to luxury and the pleasures of the body, in whom the mind has no strength, but lust possesses all, say that the earth has swallowed him.
15.13:
**“thou hast been a leader”** — by consoling, teaching, cherishing
**“In thy mercy … to the people”** — bought by the devil with the cheap price of sin
**“which thou hast redeemed:”** — with the precious blood, in the font of regeneration
**“and”** — by the consolation of the Holy Spirit
**“thou hast carried them”** — like the good shepherd, the sheep laid upon his shoulder
**“in … strength”** — by unconquerable power
**“thy … to thy holy habitation.”**
• the land of the living
• the land of promise
15.14:
**“went up”** — rising up
**“Nations … and were angry: sorrows took hold on the inhabitants”** — the demons who dwell in them, who raged with the cup of perversity and luxury
**“of Philisthiim.”** — “falling by drink”
15.15:
**“Then were the princes … troubled,”** — seeing their kingdoms, which are in hell, broken into by him who went down into the lower parts of the earth
**“of Edom”** — which is interpreted “earthly”
**“the stout men of Moab:”** — who are “from the father,” to whom, that is, it is said: “You are of your father the devil.”
**“trembling seized on”** — of Christ despoiling hell
**“became stiff.”** — seeing the strong man bound, and all his goods plundered
**“all the inhabitants”** — the demons
**“of Chanaan”** — which is interpreted “changeable” and “movable”
15.16:
**“Let fear and dread fall upon them,”** — of the cross, on which they were triumphed over
**“in the greatness of thy arm:”**
• stretched out on the cross
• Nations rose up, and were angry, etc. ORIGEN. “The nations heard and were angry; sorrows took hold on the inhabitants of Philisthiim,” etc. ORIGEN. As to the history, it is certain that none of these nations was present at these wonders: how then were Philisthiim and the Moabites and Edom and the other nations he lists terrified with fear or angry? But spiritually you will find that Philisthiim, that is, “falling by drink,” and Edom, that is, “earthly,” tremble; and their princes run about and are afraid, gripped by sorrows, when they see their kingdoms, which are in hell, broken into by him who went down into the lower parts of the earth to rescue those who were held by death. Hence they fear and tremble, because they have felt the greatness of his arm; hence too the inhabitants of Chanaan, that is, “the changeable” and “the movable,” pined away, when they saw their kingdoms moved and the strong man bound. So let fear and trembling come upon them: the demons tremble and fear the cross of Christ, on which they were triumphed over, and their principalities and powers stripped. So fear and trembling will fall upon them when they see the sign of the cross faithfully fixed in us, and the greatness of the arm which the Lord spread out on the cross, as he says: “I have spread forth my hands all the day to an unbelieving people,” etc. They will not fear you otherwise, nor will trembling at you fall upon them, unless they see in you the cross of Christ, so that you say: “But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ.”
**“let them become unmoveable as a stone,”**
• not truly
• by the hardness of unbelief: “For God is able of these stones to raise up children to Abraham.”
**“until … people … pass by:”** — the Gentile one
**“thy … O Lord, … until this thy people pass by, which thou hast possessed.”** — or “acquired,” by redeeming with blood, which the devil had bought with sin
15.17:
**“Thou shalt bring them in,”** — into the land of promise
**“and plant them in the mountain”** — not in the valley
**“of thy inheritance,”** — Thou shalt bring them in and plant them, etc. ORIGEN. The Lord does not wish to plant us in Egypt, nor in low and humble places, but in the mountain of his inheritance. Of this planting the Prophet says: “Thou hast brought a vineyard out of Egypt: thou hast cast out the Gentiles and planted it. Thou wast the guide of its journey in its sight: thou plantedst the roots thereof, and it filled the land. The shadow of it covered the hills: and the branches thereof the cedars of God.” Do you notice how God plants, and where? He does not plant in the valleys, but on the mountains, in high and lofty places. For those whom he leads out of Egypt, that is, out of the world to faith, he does not wish to set again in low places, but wants their way of life to be lofty, and to dwell on the mountains, and not to creep along the ground in them. He no longer wants his vineyard to have its fruits cast down low, but its branches to be led upward, set on high, made into trained vines; and trained not on low trees, but on the lofty and highest cedars of God, that is, the prophets and apostles. If we are joined to these, the vine which God brought out of Egypt, and our branches are spread through their boughs, and, entwined with them, we are made trained vines, bound to one another by the bonds of charity, we shall bear very much fruit. For “every tree that bringeth not forth good fruit shall be cut down, and shall be cast into the fire.”
**“in thy most firm habitation”** — which is not moved
**“which thou hast made, O Lord;”**
• thou, not man
• lest they should have to labour
• In thy most firm habitation, etc. ORIGEN. “In the prepared habitation which thou hast prepared, O Lord.” See the kind goodness of the Lord: he does not wish to lead you into labour, he does not wish you to make yourself a dwelling; he will lead you at once into a prepared habitation. Hence: “Others have laboured, and you have entered into their labours.”
**“thy sanctuary,”**
• or “sanctimony,” that is, the tabernacle of God, or the temple which sanctifies those who come near
• the manhood of Christ
**“O Lord, which … hands have established.”** — because his manhood was not begotten by human work
**“thy”**
• not of man
• Thy sanctuary, etc. ORIGEN. “Thy sanctimony, O Lord,” etc. The tabernacle of God or the temple is called the sanctimony because it sanctifies those who come near. This is said to be made not by the hand of men, but by the hand of God: so for your sake God both plants and builds; he becomes husbandman and builder, lest you should lack anything. Hence the Apostle: “You are God’s husbandry, you are God’s building.” What then is this sanctimony prepared not by the hand of men but of God? “Wisdom hath built herself a house,” that is, the flesh of Christ, not by the hand of man, that is, not by human work: the temple of the flesh is built in the Virgin; but “the stone cut out without hands” grew and “became a great mountain.” This is the sanctimony of the flesh taken up, cut out without hands and without the work of men from the mountain of human nature and the substance of the flesh.
15.18:
**“The Lord shall reign for ever”**
• so that there may never be an end
• for an age
**“and ever.”**
• others: “and yet”
• The Lord shall reign, etc. ORIGEN. “O Lord, who reignest for an age, and for an age, and yet.” Whenever “for an age” is said, a length of time is indeed shown, but that there is some end; and if “into another age” is said, something longer is shown, but yet an end is set. And whenever “ages of ages” are named, perhaps some limit is shown, unknown to us, yet fixed by God. But what he added here, “and yet,” leaves no sense of any limit or end: for whatever you think of in which you suppose the end to consist, the prophetic word always says to you “and yet”; as if it said to you: You think the Lord will reign for the age of the age: and yet. You think for the ages of ages: and yet. And whatever you say of the spans of his kingdom, the Prophet always says to you: and yet.
15.19:
**“For Pharao went in on horseback”** — the henchmen of the devil
**“with his chariots and horsemen into the sea:”** — because he yokes many chariots, in which he may sit and travel the world and run about
**“and the Lord brought back upon them the waters of the sea:”** — the moisture of sin
**“but the children of Israel”** — those who follow Christ
**“walked on dry ground”** — not soaked with the moisture of sin
**“in the midst”** — not turning aside to the right hand or to the left
**“thereof.”**
• another reading: “of it”
• But the children of Israel, etc. ORIGEN. You too, if you are a son of Israel, can walk on dry ground in the midst of the sea. If you are in the midst of a wicked and perverse generation, going like the light of the sun in the midst of sinners, the moisture of sin will not soak you, and as you pass through this world no wave of lust will splash you, no surge of greed will beat on you.
