He who is an Egyptian and follows Pharao is sunk in the waves of the vices. But he who follows Christ and walks as he walked, for him the water becomes a wall on the right hand and on the left. And he goes by the middle way on dry ground; he turns aside neither to the right hand nor to the left, until he comes out into freedom and sings to the Lord the hymn of victory, saying: “Let us sing to the Lord,” etc.
15.20:
**“So Mary the prophetess,”** — or “prophetess”
**“the sister of Aaron, took a timbrel”** — the mortification of the flesh
**“in … hand,”** — in deed
**“went forth”** — from the delight of the flesh
**“and all the women”** — holy souls
**“after her”** — prophecy, which is signified by Mary
**“with timbrels”** — with the mortification of the flesh
**“and with dances:”** — the concord of charity
**“a timbrel”** — STRABO. According to Jerome, it is a kind of trumpet having at the top a reed or pipe, through which it gives a sounding note. The chorus, according to the same, is a single skin with two pipes: through one it is blown, through the other it gives sound; so by both the narrow understanding of the old law is pointed to. For how short and small it is is shown from this, that it is carried in a woman’s hand. According to Cassiodorus, the timbrel is a skin stretched between two pieces of wood, by which the mortification of the flesh is pointed to. And the chorus is a multitude singing together; and it is called chorus as if the song of those of one age (coevorum cantus). So because in the chorus all the voices sound equally, charity is signified by it, by which we are all one in Christ. So whoever renders praise to God in jubilation, let him do this in the chorus, that is, in charity, and with the timbrel, that is, in the mortification of the flesh. Hence: “Praise him with timbrel,” etc.
15.21:
**“And she began the song to them,”** — as a teacher
**“saying: Let us sing”** — hymns of victory
**“to the Lord,”** — to the triumphant one
**“for he is gloriously magnified,”** — as above
15.22:
**“And Moses brought Israel from the Red Sea, and they went forth into the wilderness of Sur: and they marched”** — we must walk in the faith and knowledge of the Trinity
**“three days through the wilderness,”** — the desert of this life
**“and found no water.”**
• teaching to refresh the soul
• And Moses brought, etc. After the crossing of the Red Sea, the baptized are led through the world as through a desert, not yet having the promised homeland, but hoping and waiting through patience, while they are wearied by toilsome and dangerous temptation. But lest they turn back in heart to Egypt, Christ does not forsake them even there; for that pillar too does not depart.
15.23:
**“And they came into Mara,”** — the place, that is, which was already called so because of the bitterness of the waters; or it was said by prolepsis
**“and they could not drink the waters”** — the letter of the Law
**“of Mara, because they were bitter:”** — they are intolerable, as circumcision and the like
**“whereupon he gave a name also agreeable to the place,”** — perhaps he confirmed it, or gave the name
15.24:
**“And the people murmured”** — coming to the faith
**“against Moses,”** — the teachers of the Church
15.25:
**“But he cried to the Lord,”** — with the desire of the heart
**“and he shewed him a tree,”** — of the cross, of the wisdom of Christ
**“which when he had cast into the waters,”** — the letter of the Law
**“into sweetness.”** — of spiritual understanding
**“they were turned”**
• And they came into Mara, etc. ORIGEN. After the crossing of the Red Sea, after the dances and timbrels, after the hymns of triumph, they come to Mara, that is, bitter water, which the people could not drink: they come into the danger of thirst. But Moses cried to the Lord, and he showed him a tree by which the water was made sweet; and there God set for him justices and judgment; where, that is, there was bitterness, where there was thirst, and, what is heavier, amid an abundance of waters, there was no other place worthier and fitter. Besides, as to his saying, “God showed him a tree, and he cast it into the water, and it was made sweet”: as if God could not make the water sweet without a tree, or Moses did not know the tree. But if the Law is taken according to the letter, it is bitter, and is itself Mara. For what is so bitter as that a boy on the eighth day should receive the wound of circumcision, and tender infancy suffer the hardness of iron? For the cup of the law is bitter, so that the people of God, not that which was baptized in Moses in the cloud and in the sea, but that which was baptized in spirit and water, cannot drink and taste it, nor bear the bitterness of the victims, nor the keeping of the sabbath. But if God shows the tree that is to be cast into this bitterness, the water of the Law is made sweet and drinkable. “Wisdom is a tree of life to them that lay hold on her.” So if the tree of the wisdom of Christ is cast into the law, showing how circumcision, the sabbath, the law of leprosy and the like ought to be understood, the bitterness of the law is turned into the sweetness of spiritual understanding, so that the people can drink it which has left idols and fled to God. If it hears the law teaching about sacrifices, it at once shrinks back and cannot drink. So into this bitterness, that is, the letter of the law, God put justices and testimonies, as if he shut up the treasures of his wisdom and knowledge in a little vessel. Hence: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels.” So that this water may be drunk, God shows the tree that is to be cast into it, so that he who drinks may not die, may not feel the bitterness. So if anyone drinks without the tree of life, that is, without the mystery of the cross, without the faith of Christ, without spiritual understanding, he will die of the bitterness. Hence: “The letter killeth,” that is, the water of Mara, if it is drunk not changed and turned into sweetness.
• And he shewed him a tree, etc. AUGUSTINE. Was there a kind of wood having this power? Or could God, who did so many wonders, do this with any wood? Yet what was said, “he showed him,” seems to signify that it was already such. Unless perhaps the place was one where no wood at all was found, and this itself was of the divine help, that the Lord showed him a tree where there was none, and by the wood made the waters sweet, prefiguring the glory and grace of the cross. But even in such a wood, who is to be praised but the Creator and the Shower?
**“There”** — in the letter of the Law, as in a little vessel
**“he appointed him ordinances, and judgments, and there he proved”** — whether he would obey the commandments
**“him”** — the people subject to Moses
15.26:
**“Saying: If thou wilt hear the voice of the Lord thy God, and do what is right before him,”** — by pleasing him
**“and obey his commandments, and keep all his precepts, none of the evils”** — the vices of the world
**“that I laid”** — I allowed to be laid
**“upon Egypt,”** — the world
**“will I bring upon thee: for I am the Lord … healer.”**
• the true physician, not only one who cares for the sick
• of thy soul
**“thy”** — There he appointed him, etc. ORIGEN. Why did he add, “After God had set him justices and judgments, there he tried him, saying: If thou wilt hear the voice of the Lord thy God,” etc.? He seems to explain why he gave the justifications and judgments, namely, to try them, whether they would hear the voice of the Lord God and keep his commandments. For as to the former people, what good or perfect thing was commanded to them, murmuring and gainsaying, who a little later, forgetting the wonders of God, turn to idols? So precepts are given in which they may be tried. Hence: “I gave them statutes that were not good, and judgments in which they shall not live.” For tried in the precepts they are not found faithful; so the commandment was found to be unto death for them which was unto life. For the same thing, if kept, begets life; if not kept, death. So to those who do not keep them the commandments are called not good, and such that they shall not live in them. But with the wood of the cross mixed in, turned into sweetness, and understood and kept spiritually, they are commandments of life. “None of the evils that I laid upon Egypt will I bring upon thee.” He seems to say that if anyone knew the commandments he would suffer no sickness, that is, neither fevers nor other pains of the body. But Job, most just and full of all piety, is covered from head to foot with a very grievous ulcer. But the just do not have those sicknesses which the Egyptians have. For Egypt is the world. So to love the world and the things that are in the world is the Egyptian sickness; to observe months, times, to cling to the courses of the stars, to serve the flesh, to give oneself to luxury and to make leisure for delights, is the Egyptian sickness.
15.27:
**“And the children of Israel came into Elim,”** — after the bitter waters were turned into sweetness
**“where there were twelve fountains of water,”** — the teaching of the twelve apostles
**“and seventy palm trees:”**
• the seventy disciples, by whose preaching the world came to know the palms of Christ’s victory
• every order of teachers perfected in the Decalogue by the sevenfold grace
**“and they encamped by the waters.”** — And the children of Israel came into Elim, etc. ORIGEN. The people is not first led into Elim, where there were twelve fountains of water, in which there was nothing bitter, but very great pleasantness from the thickness of the palms. But first it was led to the salt and bitter waters; and when these were sweetened by the wood shown by the Lord, it comes to the fountains. If we follow only the history, it does not much build us up to know to what place they came first, to what second. But first the people is led to the letter of the law, from which, while it stays in its bitterness, it cannot withdraw. So when it has been sweetened by the tree of life and understood spiritually, it passes from the Old Testament to the New, and to the twelve apostolic fountains, where trees of seventy palms are found. For not only the twelve apostles preached the faith of Christ, but also seventy others, through whom the world came to know the palms of Christ’s victory. So it is not enough for the people of God to drink the water of Marath, though sweetened by the tree of life: the Old Testament alone is not enough to drink; one must come to the New, from which one drinks without scruple or difficulty. The Jews even now are at Marath, that is, at the bitter waters. For God has not yet shown them the tree by which they grow sweet, because unless they believe, they will not understand.

16.1: **“And they set forward from Elim, and all the multitude of the children of Israel came into the desert of Sin, which is between Elim and Sinai: the fifteenth day of the month”** — namely when the Pasch is celebrated
16.2:
**“And all the congregation of the children of Israel murmured”** — "Neither do you murmur, as some of them murmured" etc.
**“against Moses,”** — God
**“and Aaron”** — the priests of God
**“in the wilderness.”**
• of the present life
• THE FIFTEENTH DAY OF THE MONTH etc. ORIGEN. O ungrateful people, it longs for Egypt. He who sees the Egyptians destroyed, and the flesh of Egypt, who sees the flesh of the Egyptians given to the fishes and to the birds. It murmurs against Moses, nay against God; but the first time it is pardoned, and the second, and perhaps the third. But if they cease not, but persist, hear what follows. It is related in the book of Numbers, and the same Apostle recounts it, saying: Neither do you murmur, as some of them murmured, and perished by the serpents. These things are written for us, upon whom the ends of the world are come. But if we cease not to murmur and complain against God, we shall incur a like peril or example of offence. For when we complain of the inclemency of the sky, the barrenness of the fruits, the scarcity of rains, and of the prosperity of some and the ill fortune of others, we murmur against God. But these things are pardoned the first time; on those who persist they are heavily avenged, because serpents shall be sent among them, that is, they shall be delivered to unclean and poisonous spirits, which with hidden bites feed upon the inmost parts of the heart.
*Origen:* The sin of the people is made known for the correction of the readers, that it murmured and was ungrateful for the divine benefits, when it received the heavenly manna. In the second month, on the fifteenth day of the month, which is not written without reason. Recall what was said of the laws of the pasch, and you will find that this is the time appointed there for keeping a second pasch by those who were unclean in soul, or busied in business abroad. Those who were not unclean in soul, or were not travelling far off, kept the pasch on the fourteenth day of the first month; but those far abroad and the unclean keep the second pasch at this time, in which also the manna came down from heaven. On the day on which the first pasch is kept, the manna does not come down, but on that of the second. The first pasch is that of the Jewish people; the second, ours. For we were unclean in soul, who worshipped idols; and strangers and far off, who were strangers and foreigners to the testaments of God, etc. But the manna is given from heaven, not on the day on which the first pasch is kept, but on that of the second. For the bread which came down from heaven did not come to those who kept the first solemnity, but to us who have received the second: for Christ our pasch is sacrificed, who, true man, came down as bread from heaven. Let us meanwhile see what is shown to have been done on this day: On the fourteenth day of the second month the people murmured etc.
16.3:
**“And the children of Israel said to them: Would to God we had died by the hand of the Lord in the land of Egypt,”**
• the ungrateful people longs for Egypt, which sees the Egyptians destroyed
• EGYPT. the world
**“when we sat”** — delighted, at rest
**“over the flesh pots,”** — the manifold refreshments of carnal pleasures
**“WE SAT OVER THE FLESH POTS”** — They had flocks of sheep and herds of oxen, of which they could eat; but they burned with desire for the fish and birds in which Egypt abounds.
**“and ate bread”** — "which is turned into the gall of asps within"
**“to the full. Why have you brought us into this desert,”** — the toil of the present life, and its peril
**“that you might destroy all the multitude with famine?”**
• of carnal pleasures
• brought across through the Red Sea, that is, baptism
16.4:
**“And the Lord said to Moses: Behold I will rain bread from heaven for you”** — the Word of God, the bread which came down from heaven
**“let the people go forth, and gather what is sufficient for every day: that I may prove them whether they will walk in my law, or not.”** — BEHOLD I WILL RAIN BREAD FROM HEAVEN FOR YOU etc. ORIGEN. I should wish first to hold discourse on this scripture with the Jews, to whom the words of God were committed, what they think of what he says: Six days you shall gather continually, but on the sixth day double. It appears therefore that the sixth day is named which is set before the sabbath. But the sabbath is the seventh day. I ask therefore on what day the manna began to be given, and I wish our Lord's day to be compared with the sabbath of the Jews. For it appears from Scripture that the manna is first given on the Lord's day, gathered six days continually; on the seventh, which is the sabbath, it ceases. Since therefore God rained manna on the Lord's day, and not on the sabbath, let the Jews understand that even then our Lord's day was preferred to their sabbath, and it was shown that the grace of God would not come down to them from heaven on it, and the heavenly bread, which is the word of God, would not reach them. Whence: The children of Israel shall sit many days without king, without prince, without victim, without sacrifice, without priest. But on our Lord's day the Lord always rains manna, that is, heavenly words, which are joyful to us. Those unhappy ones sigh even for manna, as their fathers did, and do not deserve to receive it: for they cannot eat what is small as coriander seed, and white as hoar frost. For they perceive nothing small, fine and spiritual in the word of God, but all fat and gross. "For the heart of this people is grown gross." The interpretation of this name also sounds this: for manna is interpreted 'What is this?' The very force of the name invites to learning, that when you hear the Law of God read, you may always inquire and say to the teachers: What is this? You therefore, if you wish to eat manna and receive the word of God, know that it is small and very fine, as coriander seed: for it has something of the herb, with which it can nourish and refresh the weak. For he that is weak eateth herbs. It has also something of stiffness, and therefore is like hoar frost; but of whiteness and sweetness very much. What is whiter, more splendid, than divine learning? What sweeter, more pleasant than the words of God, which are above honey and the honeycomb?
**“BREAD”** — Namely the manna: it is a manner of speech, because bread is put for food; and Scripture loves to say 'breads' in the plural rather than 'bread' in the singular.
**“THAT I MAY PROVE”** — This temptation is a proving, not a seducing to sin; nor are they proved so that God may know, but he shows them to themselves, that they may become humbler in asking help and in acknowledging the grace of God.
16.5:
**“But the sixth day”** — this present life
**“let them provide”** — namely let them lay up whereby they may live in the future
**“for to bring in: and let it be double to that they were wont to gather”** — that it may suffice for the present life and the future
**“every day”** — BUT THE SIXTH DAY etc. ORIGEN. On the sixth day let double be gathered for storing, as much as may suffice also for the sabbath. The sixth day is this life in which we now are. In six days God made this world. On this day therefore we ought to lay up as much as may suffice in the future. For if you acquire anything of good work here, if you store up anything of justice, mercy and piety, this will be food to you in the future. For he who here acquires ten talents shall there receive ten cities, and "what things a man shall sow, those also shall he reap." The rich of this world store up those things which in this world, nay with this world, are corrupted; but good things stored up remain until the morrow. But it is written: Those who were unfaithful kept some of the manna, and worms bred out of it and it putrified; but what was laid up for the sabbath day remained whole. And you therefore, if you treasure up for the present life and the love of the world, worms straightway breed, of which it is said: "Their worm dieth not"; these avarice begets, and the blind lust of riches, in those who have money, and seeing their brethren in need, shut up their bowels from them. Whence the Apostle charges the rich not to be highminded, nor to trust in the uncertainty of riches etc.; nor do worms come to be in us from anywhere else than from the manna, that is, the word of God. Whence: If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin etc. If therefore anyone sins after receiving the word of God, the word itself becomes a worm which ever digs at his conscience, and gnaws the secrets of his breast.
16.6:
**“And Moses and Aaron said to all the children of Israel: In the evening”**
• of the sabbath, when it began to dawn towards the first day of the week
• at the coming of Christ, which is at the end of the world
16.7:
**“And in the morning you shall see the glory of the Lord”**
• because the angels at the sepulchre announced the glory of the resurrection
• IN THE EVENING YOU SHALL KNOW etc. ORIGEN. In the evening you shall know that I am the Lord. But in the morning you shall see the majesty of the Lord. Let the Jews answer me: How is the Lord known in the evening, and his majesty seen in the morning? Where was he acknowledged in the evening, and his majesty seen in the morning? But this is not understood except in the Gospel, in which: "In the end of the sabbath, when it began to dawn towards the first day of the week, came Mary Magdalen and the other Mary" to "the sepulchre", and they found the stone rolled back from the monument, an earthquake made, and the monuments opened, and the centurion and the guards of the sepulchre saying: Indeed this was the Son of God. In this evening the Lord was acknowledged, because he himself was the Lord. He was acknowledged in the power of the resurrection, and in the morning his glory was seen. When the other women had come very early in the morning, the first day of the week, they found angels sitting at the sepulchre with great brightness, and saying: He is not here, but is risen from the dead. Come and see the place etc. His majesty therefore was seen in the morning, because the resurrection also was announced by angels.
**“for he hath heard your murmuring against the Lord”** — not against me
16.8:
**“And Moses said: In the evening the Lord will give you flesh”** — of the world, in which "the Word was made flesh".
**“to eat, and in the morning bread”** — the Word of God
**“to the full”** — of the soul
**“for he hath heard your murmurings”**
• namely he has known all things, even if he does not punish at once
• from whom nothing is hidden
**“with which you have murmured against him”** — who sent us, who works in us
**“for what are we? your murmuring is not against us, but against the Lord.”** — YOUR MURMURING IS NOT AGAINST US etc. AUGUSTINE. Not by this did they mean that they were worth as much as God; for they said: What are we? Nor was that saying of this kind, where Peter says to Ananias: Hast thou dared to lie to the Holy Ghost? Thou hast not lied to men, but to God. For he does not say: Hast thou dared to lie to me? Thou hast not lied to me, but to God. Had he said that, it would have been like. Nor did he say thus: Hast thou dared to lie to the Holy Ghost? Thou hast not lied to the Holy Ghost, but to God. For speaking thus, he would deny that the Holy Ghost is God. But now, when he had said: Hast thou dared to lie to the Holy Ghost?, while that man thought he had lied to men, he showed that the Holy Ghost is God, adding: Thou hast not lied to men, but to God.
16.9:
**“Moses also said to Aaron: Say to the whole congregation of the children of Israel:”** — because it belongs to the priests to announce the Law and the will of God to the people
**“Come”** — well pleasing
**“before the Lord: for he hath heard your murmuring.”** — who hears all things
16.10: **“And when Aaron spoke to all the assembly of the children of Israel, they looked towards the wilderness: and behold the glory of the Lord appeared in a cloud.”** — flesh having been assumed
16.12:
**“I have heard”** — I have known
**“the murmuring of the children of Israel: say to them: In the evening”** — for in the evening Christ died and was buried
**“AND IN THE MORNING”** — On a new day, when Christ, the sun of justice, by his coming restored for believers the things that were lost.
**“you shall eat flesh, and in the morning”** — who rose in the morning
**“you shall have your fill of bread: and you shall know”** — then you shall know
**“IN THE EVENING YOU SHALL EAT FLESH”** — ORIGEN. Morally. We can understand that for each of us it is morning and the beginning of the day, the time when we are first enlightened and kindled to the light of faith. At this time we cannot eat the flesh of the word, that is, we are not yet capable of perfect doctrine; but after long exercises, after much progress, when we are now near the evening, that is, the perfection of faith, then we are made capable of more solid food. Let us therefore make haste to receive the manna, which yields in the mouth a savour according as each wishes. Whence: Be it done to thee according to thy faith. And you therefore, if you receive with all faith and devotion the word of God which is preached in the Church, be it done to you whatever you desire. If you are troubled, it consoles you, saying: A contrite and humbled heart, O God, thou wilt not despise. If you rejoice for the hope to come, it heaps up joys for you, saying: "Be glad in the Lord, and rejoice, ye just." If you are wrathful, it says: Cease from anger, and leave rage. If you are in pains, it heals you, saying: The Lord "healeth all thy diseases." If you are wasted by poverty, it says in consolation: The Lord raiseth up the needy from the earth, and lifteth up the poor out of the dunghill. Yet if anyone receives it faithlessly, and does not eat it but hides it, worms breed out of it. Nor be troubled that the word of God is brought to this, that it should be thought to become a worm. For he himself says: "I am a worm, and no man." For as it is he who becomes to some "for the fall", but to others "for the resurrection", so also it is he who in the manna becomes sweetness of honey to the faithful, a worm to the unfaithful. For he is the word of God, which rebukes the minds of the wicked, and bores into the conscience with the darts of correction. For it is he who becomes fire to those to whom he opens the Scriptures, who say: "Was not our heart burning within us" etc. To others he is fire, with which he burns up the thorns from the bad earth, that is, consumes wicked thoughts in the heart; and therefore for sinners neither does the rebuking worm ever die, nor is the burning fire quenched. But to the just and faithful he remains sweet and pleasant. Whence it is said: "O taste, and see that the Lord is sweet" etc.
*Origen:* Another text: In the evening you shall eat flesh, and in the morning you shall be filled with bread. Let the Jews say: what consistency is there, that in the evening they should eat flesh without bread, or in the morning bread without relish? What of divine gift, what tempering of heavenly grace is shown in this? This is that in which they can acknowledge God, who eat flesh in the evening without bread, and say that the majesty of God appears. If again bread is eaten without flesh, let them keep these things for themselves, they who, resting content in the quails, think God is acknowledged. But we, for whom at the end, toward the evening of the world, the Word was made flesh, say that God is acknowledged only in that flesh which he took from the Virgin: for this flesh of the Word of God no one has eaten, neither in the morning nor at midday, but toward evening. Whence: Little children, it is the last hour. In the morning, he says, you shall be filled with bread. For us therefore the bread is the Word of God: He is the living bread, which came down from heaven, and giveth life to the world. But that he says this bread is given in the morning, though he was incarnate toward evening, is to be understood thus: that the Lord came toward the evening of the world and near the end, but by his coming, since he is the sun of justice, he restored a new morning for believers; namely a new light of knowledge, in which those are filled with bread who have received his precepts. Nor wonder that the word of God is called both flesh and bread, and is called milk and herbs, and is named diversely according to the measure of believers and the capacity of those who receive it. Or after the resurrection made in the morning, he filled believers with bread, because he granted for the instruction of the Church the books of the Law and the prophets, before unknown, so that he himself is the bread in the Gospel, but the other books of the Law and the prophets or of the histories are called many loaves, with which believers from the gentiles are filled. Whence: They shall go up into the mountain and shall drink wine, they shall be anointed with ointment. So therefore fittingly we receive flesh toward evening and are filled with bread in the morning, because neither could we eat flesh in the morning. For it was not yet the time. Nor at midday: for scarcely do the angels eat flesh at midday, and perhaps the midday time is granted to that order.
**“that I am the Lord your God.”** — Some such thing is signified in Elias, when the raven brought him food. Perhaps by flesh in the evening and bread in the morning is signified he "who was delivered up for our sins, and rose again for our justification": for toward evening he died through weakness and was buried; but in the morning he appeared to the disciples, he who rose in power.
16.13:
**“So it came to pass in the evening, that quails coming up”**
• in Greek: ortygometra
• this is the promised flesh
**“covered the camp: and in the morning, a dew”** — namely the manna, the promised bread
**“lay round about the camp.”** — THE QUAIL COVERED THE CAMP etc. ISIDORE. By the food of birds is figured the preaching sent from God, which runs through sounding words, as feathered fowl through the air, by which they are fed through faith who journey to the heavenly fatherland. Or the words of the old law, which fed the carnal people as with flesh, through words sent from God, as through fowl. Whence also they are given in the evening, because all things granted to them carnally were to have an end. But in the manifest light of faith the manna is given, which is Christ, namely the living bread which came down from heaven, who is rained on the whole world through the gospel clouds: no longer to the murmuring and tempted Synagogue, but to the believing and hoping Church.
16.14:
**“And when it had covered the face of the earth, it appeared in the wilderness small”** — fine, because the mystery of the incarnation is unknown to human senses
**“and as it were beaten with a pestle, like unto the hoar frost on the ground.”**
• because the body of Christ cools from the heat of vices
• LIKE UNTO THE HOAR FROST etc. The hoar frost, which signifies Christ. For the manna was first given on the Lord's day, and Christ rose on the Lord's day.
**“BEATEN”** — That is: most clean. For as wheat or millet, or other such thing, is pounded with a pestle in a little mortar, and stripped of its husks, so the body of Christ, through the tribulation of the passion and the pestle of the cross, was stripped of mortality. Or the small manna is the fineness of heavenly doctrine, which is beaten with a pestle, that the literal sense may be stripped off.
16.15:
**“MANHU”** — GREGORY. What is designated by the manna given from above to the children of Israel, but the wonder at the sweetness on high? For sweet is the food which is received from on high: it is called manhu, which is interpreted 'What is this?', which we say when we behold, not knowing it, what we wonder at. The soul therefore receives the manna from on high when, lifted up by the voice of compunction, it is astonished at the new aspect of the eternal refreshment, so that, filled with the divine sweetness, it may rightly answer 'What is this?', because while it is lifted above lowly thought, it beholds the things on high and wonders at them as unwonted. And when by this voice the deafness of our torpor is broken, the habit of the old life is changed, so that the soul, breathed upon by the Spirit on high, both seeks in the highest what it had despised and despises in the lowest what it used to seek.
**“for they knew not what it was. And Moses said to them: This is the bread”** — living, which came down from heaven
16.16:
**“This is the word, that the Lord hath commanded: Let every one gather of it as much as is enough to eat: a gomor”** — a measure of five sextarii, which Josephus calls the assarion
**“for every man, according to the number of your souls that dwell in a tent, so shall you take of it.”** — ACCORDING TO THE NUMBER etc. Scripture often calls men souls, the whole by a part; but not readily fleshes for men, but flesh, as there: I will not fear what flesh can do, which in the same psalm it says more plainly: "what man can do to me". But it will not be said: according to the number of your fleshes, as it said: according to the number of your souls.
16.17: **“And the children of Israel did so: and they gathered, one more, another less.”** — according to the capacity of understanding
16.18:
**“And they measured by the measure of a gomor: neither had he more that had gathered more: nor did he find less that had provided less: but every one had gathered, according to what”** — because to each one his measure of understanding suffices for salvation, if he remain in the faith
**“to eat”** — to understand
**“they were able, had gathered”** — ACCORDING TO WHAT etc. Because in the present life each one ought to learn as much as he can, lest he leave anything unexamined, lest he begin to learn when he cannot.
16.20:
**“And they hearkened not to him, but some of them left until the morning, and it began to be full of worms”** — the evil of avarice is marked, and he who is given to it will be handed over to be consumed by worms
**“and it putrified, and Moses was angry with them.”** — Christ, or the Law, which forbids this, saying: "Lay not up to yourselves treasures on earth".
**“THE MORNING”** — The beginning of the other life, in which it will not be permitted to give time to doctrine, but the manna will putrify and be full of worms, that is, it will beget eternal punishment for them.
16.21:
**“Now every one of them gathered in the morning”** — zealously, as a zealous workman begins to work in the morning
**“as much as might suffice to eat: and after it grew hot”**
• on the day of judgment
• appearing more manifestly
**“the sun”** — Christ
**“it melted.”** — AND AFTER THE SUN GREW HOT etc. Because then the understanding of all Scripture will lie open, because now we see through a glass in a dark manner, but then we shall see face to face.
16.22:
**“But on the sixth day”** — the present life
**“A DOUBLE PROVISION”** — Namely the things needful for soul and body. For in the seventh, which is understood as the age of the dead, there will be no place for working.
**“that is, two gomors”** — that one may be kept for the sabbath
16.23:
**“And he said to them: This is what the Lord hath spoken: the rest of the sabbath sanctified to the Lord”** — that you may give yourselves to him alone
**“tomorrow,”** — the parasceve before the sabbath
**“Whatsoever work is to be done, do it: and the meats that are to be dressed”** — to be prepared for bodily or spiritual eating
**“dress them: and whatsoever shall remain, lay it up until the morning.”** — whereon you may live on the sabbath, namely while it is permitted to work
**“THE REST OF THE SABBATH”** — By hearing the word of God and doing it, or by living well, and showing mercy to others: what was laid up for the sabbath was not corrupted, because good things done for the rest to come remain whole in the life to come. Otherwise worms bred, and what was kept putrified. For those who treasure up for the present life and the love of the world, for them breeds the worm that dieth not.
16.25:
**“And Moses said: Eat it today, because it is the sabbath of the Lord”** — or: to the Lord
**“today it shall not be found in the field.”** — because it will not be permitted to work after this life
16.26:
**“six days”** — the whole present life
**“Gather it: but on the seventh day is the sabbath of the Lord”** — or: to the Lord
**“therefore it shall not be found.”** — because after this life it will not be permitted to work
16.29:
**“See that the Lord hath given you the sabbath, and for this reason”** — because it will not be permitted to work on it
**“on the sixth day he giveth you a double provision”** — of the present life and the future
**“let each man stay at home”** — that is: let him rest, and not go forth to work
**“and let none go forth”** — to work
16.31:
**“And the house of Israel called the name thereof Manna”** — because the Word of God has something of the herb whereby weakness may be nourished
**“and it was like coriander seed white”** — because the Word of God which was made flesh remains pure and bright
16.32:
**“And Moses said: This is the word, which the Lord hath commanded: Fill a gomor of it, and let it be kept unto generations to come hereafter, that they may know the bread”** — or: the bread (singular)
**“wherewith”** — or: wherewith (singular)
**“I fed you in the wilderness”** — the desert of the present life
**“when you were brought forth out of the land of Egypt.”** — from the bondage of the devil
16.33: **“And Moses said to Aaron: Take a vessel, and put manna into it, as much as a gomor can hold”** — a measure of three modii
16.34:
**“As the Lord commanded Moses. And Aaron put it”** — the priests
**“in the tabernacle”** — the Church
**“to be kept.”**
• for an everlasting memorial
• AND THOU SHALT LAY IT UP etc. AUGUSTINE. It can be asked where Aaron would lay it up before the Lord, when there was no tabernacle, nor had the ark of the testament yet been made. Or perhaps he said thou shalt lay it up of the future, so that it may be understood that it could be laid up before the Lord then, when the ark was to be? Or rather is before the Lord said of what is done by the very devotion of offering, in whatever place it were put? For where is God not? But what he adds: And Aaron laid it up before the tabernacle to be kept, asserts rather the former sense. For in this way Scripture spoke by prolepsis of what was done afterward, when the tabernacle of the testimony began to be.
16.35:
**“And the children of Israel”** — of the divine vision
**“ate”** — or: did eat
**“manna forty years”** — The whole time of the present life, in which we live according to the New and Old Testament: for four times ten make forty.
**“till they came to a habitable land”** — of the living, where the saints dwell in rest, the desert of this world crossed over
**“with this meat”** — aforesaid
**“were they fed, until they reached the borders of the land of Chanaan.”**
• He explains what land he meant.
• The Septuagint: until they came into the region of Phenice.
• THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL etc. AUGUSTINE. Another text: And the children of Israel ate manna forty years, until they came to the land which was inhabited. But Scripture signifies in this place, by prolepsis, recording what was done afterward, that the children of Israel ate manna only in the desert. For this is what it says: until the land which was inhabited, that is, which is no longer desert; not that as soon as they came to a habitable land they left off eating manna, but that they did not before. For it is signified that the manna ceased when the Jordan was crossed, where they ate the bread of the land. But having entered the habitable land before they crossed the Jordan, they could eat either manna only, or both foods: for this can be understood, because the manna is not said to have ceased except when the Jordan was crossed. But why in the desert they also desired flesh, when they went out of Egypt with many cattle, is a great question. Unless perhaps it be said that in the desert there were no pastures, and so, the cattle being less fruitful, they spared the cattle, lest, all failing, things needful even for the sacrifices should be lacking; or whatever else can be said whereby the question may be solved. Yet it is more fittingly believed that they did not desire the flesh which they could have from the cattle, but that which was lacking, namely from the waters, which they did not find in the desert. Whence ortygometra was given them, that is, birds which many Latins interpret as quails, though the ortygometra is another kind of bird, though not altogether unlike quails. For God knew what they desired, and with what kind of flesh he would satisfy them.
**“MANNA”** — The body of Christ, namely the Word of God, which we now perceive in a dark manner, but then face to face.

17.1:
**“Then all the multitude of the children of Israel setting forward from the desert of Sin”** — which is interpreted temptation
**“SIN”** — Here Sin is taken specially as one mansion, of those five which were from the Red Sea to Mount Sinai, which Josephus describes by name. For generally that desert also is called Sin, as also Raphidim.
**“by their mansions, according to the word of the Lord, encamped in Raphidim”** — soundness of judgment
*Jerome:* Raphidim is a place in the desert near Mount Horeb. But it is to be known that the whole wilderness as far as Mount Sinai is called Sin, and from the whole province the place of one mansion also took its name, as Moab also is the name both of a city and of a province. In this wilderness there are five mansions: Suph, and the wilderness of Sin, Alus, Depheca, Raphidim. Whence it is well said that all the multitude of the children of Israel set forward from the wilderness of Sin, by their mansions, according to the mouth of the Lord, and came into Raphidim. Whence it is plain that several mansions are shown by the name of one region.
**“THEN SETTING FORWARD”** — ORIGEN. All that will live godly in Christ suffer persecution and are assailed by enemies; and he who makes the journey of this life ought always to be ready and to stand in the camp. Whence: all the synagogue of the children of Israel set forward from the desert of Sin according to their camps by the word of God. There is indeed one Synagogue of the Lord, but it is divided into four camps, which are described in Numbers as set about the tabernacle of the Lord. Armed therefore, serving as a soldier in the camp of the Lord, entangle not thyself with secular businesses, and keep watch always in the camp of the Lord, that it may be said of thee that thou hast set forward by the word of the Lord from the desert of Sin, and mayest come into Raphidim. Now Sin is interpreted temptation; Raphidim: soundness of judgment. He who goes out well from temptation comes to soundness of judgment. For in the day of judgment he will be sound. Whence: To him that overcometh, I will give of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God. He comes therefore to soundness of judgment who orders his words with judgment.
17.2:
**“And they chode with Moses,”** — the Law
**“and said: Give us water, that we may drink.”** — elsewhere: that we may drink
**“And Moses answered them:”** — elsewhere: to whom Moses answered
17.3:
**“were thirsty”** — in the desert
**“So the people”** — which ought to hunger and thirst after justice
**“there for want of water, and murmured against Moses, saying: Why didst thou make us go forth out of Egypt, to kill us and our children, and our beasts with thirst?”** — SO THE PEOPLE WERE THIRSTY etc. ORIGEN. Another text: The people, he says, thirsted for water, and they murmured against Moses. It sufficed to say that it thirsted: what need was there to add water? The addition is not superfluous. There are therefore divers thirsts, and each has his own. They who are good hunger and thirst after justice. Others also say: My soul hath thirsted after thee, O God. But they who are sinners suffer not a thirst of water, nor a famine of bread, but of hearing the word of God. The people therefore thirsted for water, which ought to have thirsted for justice. But God, the instructor of infants, the master of the foolish, corrects faults and amends errors, saying to Moses that he should take the rod, strike the rock, and bring forth waters. For he wishes them now to drink from the rock, and to advance, and to come to the inner mysteries. For they murmured against Moses; therefore the Lord commands that he show them the rock from which they shall drink. For if there is anyone who, reading Moses, murmurs against him, and the law according to the letter displeases him, because in many things it seems not to hold together, Moses shows him the rock which is Christ, that he may drink from it and refresh his thirst. But this rock gives no waters unless struck; but struck, it brings forth fountains. For Christ, struck and slain on the cross, brought forth the fountains of the New Testament. Whence: I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock shall be dispersed. For had he not been struck, and had not blood and water come out of his side, we should all suffer thirst for the word of God. Whence: "And they drank of the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ."
*Isidore:* The thirsting people murmured against Moses for water: therefore God commands that he show them the rock from which they may drink. But if anyone, reading Moses, murmurs against him, and the letter of the law displeases him, Moses shows him the rock which is Christ, and leads him to it, whence he may drink and refresh his thirst.
17.4: **“And Moses cried to the Lord, saying: What shall I do to this people? Yet a little more”** — elsewhere: a little
17.5:
**“And the Lord said to Moses: Go before the people, and take with thee of the ancients of Israel: and the rod wherewith”** — The Septuagint: 'in which' for 'with which'; a very frequent manner of speech in the Scriptures
**“thou didst strike the river, take in thy hand, and go.”**
• GO BEFORE THE PEOPLE etc. Not Moses alone leads the people to the waters, but also the ancients of the people. For not the Law alone announces Christ, but also the prophets, and the patriarchs, and all the elders.
• AND THE ROD etc. TAKE IN THY HAND. AUGUSTINE. Aaron, not Moses, is read to have struck the river with the rod. For Moses with the same rod divided the sea, not the river. What then does it mean: Take the rod wherewith thou didst strike the river? Did he perhaps call the sea a river, and must an example of this manner of speech be sought? Or was what Aaron did rather attributed to Moses, because God commanded Moses what Aaron should do, and in the one was the authority, in the other the ministry? Whence: He shall be to thee for the people, and thou to him in those things that pertain to God.
17.6:
**“Behold I will stand there before thee, upon the rock Horeb”** — the mountain which is also Sinai
**“and thou shalt strike the rock, and water shall come out of it”** — when the side of Christ was opened, "there came out blood and water"
**“that the people may drink”** — "And they drank of the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ."
**“AND THOU SHALT STRIKE THE ROCK”** — Christ, who on the cross was struck by the Jews: to whom the rod came, that is, the wood of the passion, that water might flow for the faithful.
17.7: **“And he called the name of that place Temptation, because the chiding of the children of Israel, and for that they tempted the Lord, saying: Is the Lord”** — or: God
17.8:
**“And Amalec came”** — the devil, shutting off the way to the heavenly fatherland
**“and fought against Israel in Raphidim.”** — AND AMALEC CAME etc. STRABO. Amalec was the son of Ismael, from whom the Amalecites, who are also the Ismaelites, are themselves the Saracens. Now he is interpreted drinking, or licking, blood, and signifies the devil, who always assails the saints going out of Egypt and making for the land of promise, and desires to drink the blood of souls.
*Origen:* The war waged with the Amalecites is described. The people is said to have fought and conquered. Before it ate bread from heaven and drank from the rock, the people is not said to have fought, but it is said to it: The Lord will fight for you, and you shall hold your peace. There is therefore a time when the Lord fights for us, and does not suffer us to be tempted above that which we are able, nor lets us, unequal in strength, come to a strong encounter. Job also, when already perfect, fulfilled the contest of his temptation; and you therefore, when you begin to eat manna, the heavenly bread of the word of God, and to drink water from the rock, and when you have come to the inner things of spiritual doctrine, expect the fight, prepare yourself for war.
17.9:
**“And Moses said to Josue: Choose out men: and go out and fight against Amalec”** — AND MOSES SAID etc. ORIGEN. Another text: And Moses said to Jesus: Choose thee men etc. Up to this point no mention was ever made of the blessed name of Jesus. Here first Moses called Jesus, and said to him: Choose men for thyself. Moses calls Jesus, the law invokes Christ, that he may choose for himself mighty men from the people: Moses could not choose, but Jesus alone, who says: You have not chosen me, but I have chosen you. He is the leader of the chosen, and the prince of the mighty. He contends with Amalec. For he enters into the house of the strong, and binds the strong, and plunders his vessels.
**“tomorrow I will stand”** — firm, immovable, according to that: "You that stand in the house of the Lord".
**“on the top of the hill”** — as being near to heaven, and not in the valley; whence: "I have lifted up my eyes" to him who dwelleth in heaven.
**“having the rod”** — which God gave, that the enemies might be beaten
**“in … hand,”** — power or work
**“I WILL STAND ON THE TOP OF THE HILL”** — ORIGEN. Moses, he says, went up not to the top of the mountain, but to the top of the hill. For it was kept for him to go up to the top of the mountain then, when Jesus was to go up, and with him Moses and Elias, and there to be transformed in glory. Now therefore, as not yet glorified by the transformation of Jesus, he does not go up to the top of the mountain, but to the top of the hill. And when Moses lifted up his hands, Israel overcame. Moses lifts up his hands, he does not stretch them out. Jesus, who, exalted on the cross, embraced the whole world, says: I have spread forth my hands to an unbelieving people. To lift up the hands is to lift up one's acts to God, that one may have acts not cast down and lying on the ground, but pleasing to God and raised to heaven. He therefore lifts up his hands who lays up treasure in heaven. For where the treasure is, there is the eye, there the hand. He lifts up his hands who says: "The lifting up of my hands, as evening sacrifice." If therefore our acts be lifted up, Amalec is overcome. Whence: Lift up the hands which hang down, and the feeble knees. If the people keeps the law, Moses lifts up his hands, and the adversary is overcome. If it keeps not the law, Amalec prevails. Since therefore our wrestling is against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the world of this darkness, if you would conquer, lift up your hands, that is, your acts; let your conversation be not on earth, but in heaven. Lift up you also your hands to heaven to God, fulfil the command of the Apostle: "Pray without ceasing"; and then shall be done what is written, that as the calf licketh up the green grass in the fields, so shall this people lick up the people that is upon the earth; where it is brought in that the people of God fought not so much with hand and arms as with voice and tongue, and laid the enemies low by prayer. Lift up therefore your acts, be instant in prayer: this is the fight of the Christian by which he overcomes the enemy. But I think that by this figure two peoples are signified, of whom one, from the gentiles, lifts up the hands of Moses, and raises on high the things he wrote and their understanding, and so conquers. But the other, that is, the Jewish people, does not lift up the hands of Moses from the earth, nor understands anything high or lofty in him, and so is overcome by the adversaries.
**“my”** — HAVING THE ROD etc. AUGUSTINE. Now it is called the rod of God, which was first called Aaron's, and afterward is said to be Moses'. For as the spirit of Elias, which is the Spirit of God, of which Elias is said to partake, and the justice of God, which is ours. Whence: Not knowing the justice of God, and seeking to establish their own, that is, as prepared for themselves by themselves.
17.10:
**“Josue did as Moses had spoken, and he fought against Amalec”** — the devil
**“Moses”** — the Law which God gave
**“and Aaron”**
• mountain of strength
• Christ
**“and Hur”** — fire, the Holy Ghost
17.11:
**“And when Moses lifted up his hands”** — in the figure of the cross, in which enemies are triumphed over
**“Israel overcame”** — We ought to pray with working, if we wish to overcome the enemies, and for the heavenly reward, not for earthly gain.
**“but if he let them down a little, Amalec overcame.”**
• because when good works are let go, that is, turned to earthly things, the enemy follows as victor
• AND WHEN MOSES LIFTED UP etc. STRABO. Because when the law is understood mystically, and the passion of Christ is weighed spiritually, the devil is overcome and put to flight. But when the hands are let down, that is, the precepts of the Law are practised less zealously, the enemy follows as victor.
17.12:
**“And Moses' hands were heavy: so they took a stone,”**
• on which are seven eyes, which is also the stone of help
• the Church, or Christ
**“and put under him, and he sat on it”** — rested
**“and Aaron and Hur stayed up his hands on both sides.”** — because the Law has been spiritually fulfilled in Christ and the Holy Ghost
**“And it came to pass that his hands were not weary until sunset.”**
• the end of the world
• SO THEY TOOK etc. GREGORY. Moses sat on the stone when the law rested in the Church, but it had heavy hands, because it did not bear sinners mercifully, but struck them with severe strictness. Now Aaron is mountain of strength, Hur is interpreted fire. The mountain of strength is Christ, of whom it is said: "In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the top of mountains." But the fire is the Holy Ghost, whom Christ came to send upon the earth. Aaron therefore and Hur, by holding up the heavy hands of Moses, make them lighter, because the mediator of God and men, coming with the fire of the Holy Ghost, showed us the heavy commands of the law (which, while they were held carnally, could not be borne) to be bearable through spiritual understanding. For he made as it were the hands of Moses light who turned the weight of the commands of the law to the truth of confession, according to that: "I desire not the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live." Hence it is said to the sinful soul: If a man put away his wife, and she go from him, and marry another man, shall he return to her any more? shall not that woman be polluted, and defiled? but thou hast prostituted thyself to many lovers: nevertheless return to me, saith the Lord. Behold, he has given the example of a shameful woman, showing that after shame she cannot be received; but he overcomes the very example by mercy, when he says that the woman who commits fornication cannot be received, and yet waits to receive the soul that commits fornication. Let us weigh the weight of so great a goodness. He says what cannot be done, and shows that he can do this very thing against custom. Behold, he calls even those whom he declares defiled; those he seeks even to embrace, by whom he complains that he has been forsaken. He bent therefore the hardness of the law to mercy, since those whom it justly condemns, he himself mercifully frees.
17.13:
**“And Josue put to flight”** — Christ
**“Amalec”** — the devil
**“and his people”** — the demons, the vices, or any persecutors whatever
**“by the edge”** — it is a manner of speech
**“of the sword”** — of the Word of God
17.14:
**“And said”** — or: therefore
**“the Lord to Moses: Write this for a memorial in a book, and deliver it to the ears of Josue: for I will destroy the memory”** — here through the saints, and wholly in the judgment: "their memory hath perished with a noise."
**“Amalec”** — a brute people, or licking blood
**“from under heaven.”** — FOR I WILL DESTROY etc. RABANUS. In this he signifies that almighty God, through the law (which Moses signifies, and which proclaims Christ), destroys the memory of the spiritual enemies. Whence: "Their memory hath perished with a noise."
17.15:
**“AND MOSES BUILT AN ALTAR”** — All who are victors over the devil ought to build in their hearts altars of faith, on which to offer spiritual victims.
**“and called the name thereof, The Lord”** — not man
**“my exaltation”**
• because, lifted up from the earth, he draws all things to himself.
• strength
17.16:
**“Because the hand”** — power
**“of the Lord alone”** — whence: Thou hast wrought all our works for us.
**“and the war of God shall be against Amalec”** — the evil spirits
**“from generation”** — of the Jews
**“to generation.”**
• of the gentiles
• until the end. For then it will truly be fulfilled. Whence: "O death, I will be thy death", "thy bite" etc.

18.2:
**“He took”** — Amalec being overcome
**“Sephora”** — the Church
**“the wife of Moses”** — of Christ, or of the preachers
**“whom he had sent back”** — that he might be more free for the work of the Lord
18.3:
**“And her two sons”** — both peoples
**“of whom one was called Gersam, his father saying: I have been a stranger in a foreign country.”** — because he signifies those who say: "I am a stranger with thee, and a sojourner as all my fathers were".
18.4:
**“And the other Eliezer: For the God of my father, said he, is my helper”** — because he signifies those who say: "Thou art my helper and my deliverer: O Lord, make no delay".
**“and hath delivered me from the sword of Pharao.”**
• of the devil
• AND WHEN HE HAD HEARD etc. That Moses, when about to free the children of Israel, sent away his wife and sons, whom he afterward received back in the desert, signifies that preachers, when they are sent to the work of preaching, ought to unburden themselves of temporal care; but when afterward they are taken up to the episcopate or to another dignity, then they ought to bear care for those subject to them, in spiritual as well as temporal things.
18.5: **“And Jethro the kinsman of Moses came with his sons and his wife, to Moses into the desert, where he was camped by the mountain of God.”** — AND JETHRO CAME etc. ORIGEN. Another text: After these things Moses came to the mountain of God, and went out of the camp to meet Jethro coming to him, and does not lead him to the mountain of God, but to his own tent. For the priest of Madian could not go up into the mountain of God, nor yet go down into Egypt, nor could the wife of Moses; but now she comes to him with the sons. For no one could go down into Egypt and undergo the contests of the Egyptians, unless he were a proven athlete, and one who, striving in the contest, refrains himself from all things. Moses, because he was a great and mighty athlete, went down into Egypt to the contests and exercises of the virtues, and so did Abraham. Jacob also, who by his very name is an athlete, when he had gone down into Egypt, was made as the stars of heaven in multitude. For others, going down into Egypt turns out the contrary. I know that Jeroboam, fleeing from Solomon, went down into Egypt, and divided and corrupted the people of God, because, going down into Egypt, he received from king Susachim for wife the sister of his wife Tethimene.
18.7: **“And he went out to meet his kinsman, and worshipped”** — showed him reverence
18.8:
**“Moses told”** — the first preachers
**“his kinsman”** — to the gentile people, or to the preachers from the gentiles.
**“all that the Lord had done to Pharao”** — to the devil
**“and the Egyptians”** — or to the ministers of the devil
**“in favour of Israel”** — the saints who see God
**“and all the labour”** — which Paul relates befell him, when he glories in his infirmities
**“which had befallen them in the journey”** — by which one passes over from the world to heaven
18.9: **“And he rejoiced”** — because of the faithful there is "one heart and one soul".
18.10: **“And he said: Blessed is the Lord,”** — to whom all things are ascribed, not to us
18.11:
**“Now I know”** — in this miracle
**“that the Lord is great above all gods”** — of the gentiles, whom they worshipped; or above the saints, who by participation in beatitude are well called gods
18.12:
**“So Jethro the kinsman of Moses offered”** — ate bread
**“holocausts”**
• when they leave the world wholly
• "A sacrifice to God is an afflicted spirit" etc.
**“and sacrifices to the Lord”**
• when they use worldly things lawfully
• JETHRO OFFERED etc. AUGUSTINE. And Jethro the father in law of Moses took holocausts and sacrifices for the Lord etc. Took is put for offered: or perhaps it is the sense, not a manner of speech, so that he is understood to have taken those things which Moses is understood to have offered; although Moses is not read to have sacrificed, nor Aaron, nor any of the Hebrews who were brought out of the land of Egypt: but yet it was said above that Moses set up an altar. But we read that Jethro was a priest of Madian, that is, of the nation of Madian. And it is a wonder if at his coming Moses began to sacrifice, and not rather he himself who was a priest.
**“and Aaron came”** — the priestly order
**“and all the ancients”** — of the first people
**“of Israel, to eat bread”** — of the Word
**“with him before the Lord.”**
• for the honour of the Lord
• AND AARON CAME etc. ORIGEN. Another text: There came, he says, the elders, Aaron, and all Israel, to eat bread with the father in law of Moses in the sight of God. Not all eat bread in the sight of God, but they who are elders, who are ancients, that is, who are perfect and proved by their merits, who, whether they eat or drink, do it to the glory of God. Whatever therefore the saints do, they do in the sight of God: the sinner flees from the sight of God. Adam, after he sinned, fled from the sight of the Lord, and being asked, answered: I heard thy voice, O Lord, and I hid myself, because I was naked. Cain went out from the face of the Lord, because he was unworthy of the sight of the Lord. Moreover, they who receive a fuller knowledge of God, if they do evil, do it before God. Whence: To thee only have I sinned, and have done evil before thee. He who does evil before God straightway repents, and says: I have sinned. He who departs from the sight of God knows not how to be converted and to cleanse his sin by repenting. This therefore is the difference between doing evil before God, and departing from the sight of God.
• BEFORE THE LORD etc. AUGUSTINE. It is asked where, since there was neither the tabernacle nor the ark of the testament, which were instituted afterward; nor can we take this as said of the future, as was said of the manna which was put in a vessel, namely a golden one. Therefore we ought to take that as done before God which was done in the honour of the Lord.
*Origen:* Not in vain did Jethro come to Moses, nor in vain did he eat bread with the ancients of the people in the sight of God; he gives Moses a sound and useful counsel, that he should choose men and appoint princes of the people who worship God, mighty, and hating pride. For such ought they to be as are not proud, and hate pride; that is, that not only should they themselves be without vice, but in evil men they should hate the vices: I say not the men, but the vices.
18.13:
**“And the next day Moses sat, to judge the people”**
• as a master
• the doctors of the Law, who, sitting, that is, being at rest in mind, judge amid the tumult of the people
**“who stood by Moses”** — as men to be judged, to be taught
**“from morning until night.”** — from the beginning of the world to the end: for the law, natural or written, was never lacking
18.14:
**“And when his kinsman had seen all things that he did among the people, he said: What is it that thou dost”** — elsewhere: does
**“among the people?”** — among the common people
18.16: **“And when any controversy falleth out among them, they come to me to judge between them, and to shew the precepts of God, and his laws.”** — TO SHEW THE PRECEPTS etc. It can be asked how Moses said this here, when as yet no law of God had been written; unless because the law of God is everlasting, which all who live piously consult, that what they find in it they may do or command or forbid, according as it has commanded by that unchangeable truth. For must it be believed that Moses, though God spoke with him, was wont to consult the Lord on each point, if there was anything in the disputes of so great a multitude, which held him in the business of judging from morning until evening? And yet unless he consulted the Lord presiding over his mind, and attended to the eternal law, he could not judge justly.
18.19: **“But hear my words and counsels, and God shall be with thee.”** — BUT HEAR MY WORDS etc. AUGUSTINE. The first question is why God suffered his servant, with whom he himself spoke so many and such great things, to be admonished by a foreigner. In which Scripture admonishes us that, through whomsoever the counsel of truth is given, it ought not to be despised. It is to be seen also whether perhaps God willed Moses to be admonished by a foreigner at that point where he could be tempted by pride. He sat in the loftiness of a judge: for Jethro himself indicates this sense, when he bade those be chosen for judging who hated pride. Then, how much what Scripture says elsewhere is to be observed: "My son, meddle not with many matters", appears clearly enough here. The words of Jethro also are to be considered. For he says: Now therefore hear me, I will give thee counsel, and God shall be with thee. Where it seems to me to be signified that the mind too intent on human actions is in a manner emptied of God, with whom it is made the fuller, the more freely it reaches out to things above and eternal.
18.20: **“And to shew the people the ceremonies and the manner of worshipping, and the way wherein they ought to walk, and the work that they ought to do.”** — BE THOU TO THE PEOPLE etc. THE SAME. But what he adds: Be thou to the people in those things that pertain to God, and thou shalt bring their words to God; and thou shalt testify to them the precepts of God and his law; and thou shalt show them the ways in which they shall walk, and the works which they are to do, shows that these things are to be done with the whole people. For he does not say: Thou shalt bring the words of each one to God, but their words, since he had said above: Be thou to the people in those things that are to God. After these things he admonishes that the business of individuals which they had among themselves be left aside, able men having been chosen, who worship God, just men who hate pride, whom he had appointed over thousands, others over hundreds, others over fifties, others over tens. Thus he removed perilous occupations from Moses. Nor did he burden these, since a thousand had one over them, and under them ten others, and under these twenty, and under these a hundred others, so that scarcely anything that needed to be judged would come to each of those set over them. An example of humility also is suggested, in that Moses, with whom God spoke, did not disdain or despise the counsel of a foreigner; although whether Jethro himself, since he was not an Israelite, is to be counted among the men who worship the one God and are religiously wise, as Job, is rightly asked; nay, it is held the more credible. For the words are set down ambiguously, whether he sacrificed to the true God among his people when he saw his son in law, or whether Moses himself worshipped him; although, as to the worship, if it had been expressly set down, it would seem to be an honour paid to the father in law, as is wont to be shown to men for the sake of honouring them. But whom he calls grammatoysagogas, whom decurions, cannot easily be known, since we have this name in no use, either of offices or of masters. For some have interpreted them teachers of letters, namely those who bring in to letters, as the Greek word sounds. Here certainly it is signified that before the Law was given the Hebrews had letters, but when these began to be I know not whether it can be traced. Some think they began from the first men, and were brought down to Noe, and thence to the parents of Abraham, then to the people of Israel; but whence this can be proved I know not.
18.21:
**“And provide out of all the people able men”** — or: wise
**“such as fear God, in whom there is truth, and that hate avarice”**
• he prescribes the form of a good judge
• AND PROVIDE etc. He is instructed by a foreigner for the guarding of humility, lest he who was learning so many secrets of God from God himself should be lifted up, and think he had no need of human counsel. It was prefigured also that the teaching of the gentiles would overcome the knowledge and pride of the Jews; and that the faithful from the gentiles would suggest the things lacking in the law to be completed, and would bring a spiritual understanding to the law of God. Moses knew also that the law would hear this people, and would do whatever it said, and that the lessening of the law also would come about at the suggestion of the Gospel.
**“and appoint of them rulers of thousands”** — who allot good things to those subject to them, who in Greek are called chiliarchs, in Latin millenaries
**“and of hundreds”** — who in Greek are hecatontarchs
**“and of fifties”** — who also are pentecontarchs
**“and of tens.”** — who are over tens
18.22:
**“Who may judge”** — the private causes of the people
**“the people at all times:”**
• who in Greek are decarchs
• "Blessed are they that keep judgment, and do justice at all times"
**“and when any great matter soever”** — weighty and common questions
**“shall fall out, let them refer it to thee, and let them judge the lesser matters only: that so it may be lighter for thee”** — intent on many things: the sense is less for each one
**“the burden being shared out unto others.”** — AND APPOINT OF THEM etc. ORIGEN. Thou shalt ordain them, he says, tribunes and centurions etc. And they shall judge the people at every hour; but what is weightier they shall refer to thee. Let the princes of the people and the elders of the common people hear, who ought to judge the people at every hour, to sit always and without ceasing in judgment, to settle quarrels, and reconcile those at variance, to call back the discordant into favour. Let each learn his office from the holy Scriptures. Moses, he says, is to be in those things that are to God, and to set forth the word of God to the peoples. But the other princes, whom he called tribunes because they are over a tribe, or centurions, or fiftymen, are over lesser judgments, settling those that pertain to individuals. And this figure I think is to be kept also in the world to come. Whence: When the Son of man shall sit on the seat of his majesty, you also shall sit on twelve seats etc. You see therefore that not only does the Lord judge, to whom the Father hath given all judgment, but he appoints princes to judge of the lesser causes. But the word that is weightier they shall refer to him. Therefore the Lord says of one that he shall be in danger of the council; but of another: "He shall be in danger of hell fire." But also of every idle word they are said to render an account. And he did not say that we shall render the account to God, as of perjury: "But thou shalt perform thy oaths to the Lord." "The queen of the south" also "shall rise in judgment with the men of this generation, and shall condemn them." Behold another kind of judgment: "He that hath ears to hear, let him hear"; for all these things are a shadow of heavenly things and an image of things to come.
*Origen:* As it is written: The eye is not filled with seeing, neither is the ear filled with hearing, neither can we be filled with considering the things that are written, with which they edify us, in how many ways they instruct us. For when I behold that Moses, a prophet full of God, to whom God spoke face to face, took counsel from Jethro his father in law, the priest of Madian, I am struck with exceeding wonder. For Moses heard the voice of his father in law, and did whatever he said to him. He did not say: Since God speaks to me what I ought to do, how shall I take counsel from a man, from a gentile man, a stranger to the people of God? And he listens not to who speaks, but to what he speaks. We therefore, if we find anything wisely said by the gentiles, let us not despise the sayings together with the name of the author; nor, because we hold the law of God, does it become us to swell with pride and despise the words of the prudent, but proving all things, let us hold that which is good. But they who are over the peoples today, I do not say if anything has now been revealed to them by God, but if they have any merit in the knowledge of the law, disdain the counsel of an inferior, even of a priest, much less of a layman, much less of a gentile; but Moses, who was meek above all men, took the counsel of an inferior, to give princes a form of humility, and to mark the image of a sacrament to come. He knew that it would one day be that the gentiles would bring good counsel, bringing to the law in Moses a good and spiritual understanding, and that the law would hear them, doing all things they said. For the law cannot do, as the Jews say, because the law is weak in the flesh, that is, in the letter, and can do nothing according to the letter. "For the law brought nothing to perfection." But according to this counsel which we bring to the law, all things can be done spiritually, and sacrifices offered, which now cannot be done carnally; the law of leprosy can be kept spiritually. As therefore we understand, perceive and give counsel, the law does all things: but according to the letter, not all, but few.
18.23:
**“If thou dost this, thou shalt fulfill the commandment of God”** — or: of the Lord
**“and shalt be able to bear his precepts”** — or: uphold
18.24: **“And when Moses heard this, he did all things that he had suggested unto him.”** — MOSES DID etc. A man familiar with God, most wise, not ashamed to be taught by a lesser man and a gentile, gave a pattern to teachers, that they be not ashamed to be instructed by anyone whatever.
18.26: **“And they judged the people at all times: and whatsoever was of greater difficulty they referred to him, and they judged the easier cases only.”** — WHATSOEVER etc. Others: But the weighty word they referred 'upon Moses'. For so the Greek has it, which the Latins have rendered 'to Moses'. By that very manner of speech, in which it is said 'upon Moses', it was also figured, as though a burden laid upon him is signified. 'But the weighty word' is said for 'the weighty question'.

19.2:
**“For departing out of Raphidim, and coming to the desert of Sinai”** — a bush, or temptation
**“they camped in the same place, and there Israel pitched their tents over against the mountain.”**
• IN THE THIRD MONTH etc. ORIGEN. Another text. But of the third month of the going out of the children of Israel from the land of Egypt: on this day they came into the wilderness of Sina, and they set forward from Raphidim, and came into the wilderness of Sina, and Israel encamped there over against the mountain; and Moses went up into the mountain of God, and the Lord called him from the mountain, saying: Thus shalt thou say to the house of Jacob, and tell the children of Israel etc. And a little after: Go down and charge the people, and thou shalt purify them today and tomorrow, and let them wash their garments, and let them be ready against the third day. For on the third day the Lord will come down upon mount Sina before all the people. On this day the law is found to be given, which was written on tables of stone by the finger of God, as what follows teaches. But this third day appears to be of the third month from the going out of the children of Israel from Egypt. From the day on which they kept the pasch, that is, sacrificed and ate the lamb, which was the fourteenth of the first month, up to this on which the law is given, fifty days are numbered: namely seventeen of the first month, the rest from the fourteenth itself; then all thirty of the second month, which make forty-seven; and the third of the third month, which is the fiftieth from the solemnity of the slain lamb. And so in this shadow of what was to come, counting from the feast day of the slain lamb, the law was given on the fiftieth day, written by the finger of God. So in the very truth of the New Testament, from the feast of the slain Lamb, Jesus Christ, fifty days are numbered to when the Holy Ghost was given from on high, who is the finger of God.
• ON THIS DAY etc. Namely on the forty-seventh day after they went out of Egypt, that is, on the first day of June, they came to mount Sina; and there, the two days having been passed in which they were sanctified, on the third, that is, the fiftieth, they received the Law: and this is Pentecost.
*Rabanus:* In Sina there was one mansion, but the greatest of all. For there the law was received, the tabernacle set up. There Exodus and the greatest part of Leviticus and almost all the books of the Law were written.
19.3:
**“And Moses went up to God.”** — It is proper to the saints to love the mountains and dwell in them, whose "conversation is in heaven".
**“And the Lord called unto him from the mountain, and said: Thus shalt thou say to the house of Jacob”** — to the active
**“and tell the children of Israel:”**
• to the contemplative
• AND MOSES WENT UP etc. GREGORY. Another text. And Moses went up into the mountain, and the Lord came down to him. The mountain is the height of contemplation, into which we go up, that we may be lifted up to gaze on the things that are beyond our weakness. But the Lord comes down, because to the saints who make much progress he opens some little of himself.
19.4:
**“You have seen what I have done to the Egyptians,”** — He recalls the punishments of the Egyptians, and the benefits he bestowed on his people, that they may fear the almighty and love the benefactor.
**“how I have carried you upon the wings”** — most swiftly
**“of eagles”**
• of Moses and Aaron
• As the eagle enticing her young to fly, etc.
• THE WINGS OF EAGLES etc. Allegorically. He calls so the teachings of the two Testaments, which carry us from the lowest things to the heavenly.
19.5:
**“If therefore you will hear”**
• Before he gives the Law, he allures them with promises, that they may receive it willingly.
• with the ear of the heart
**“my voice, and keep”** — diligently
**“my covenant,”** — as it were 'an act of peace'
**“you shall be my peculiar possession above all people.”** — a special people, whom I will feed, defend, and nourish as my own flock.
19.6:
**“And you shall be to me a priestly kingdom, and a holy nation.”**
• Whence Peter: "A chosen generation, a kingly priesthood", and "a holy nation, a purchased people".
• A KINGDOM etc. Allegorically. Namely the members of the high priest, who are to come into the kingdom of heaven.
19.7: **“Moses came, and calling together the elders of the people, he declared all the words which the Lord had commanded.”** — HE DECLARED ALL etc. GREGORY. It is to be noted that the Law is not thrust upon the unwary or the ignorant: but when the rewards owed to those who keep it have been set forth, and the past benefits and wonders which they have already experienced, and when the people of its own accord vows itself to keep the law, the law is given to those who ask it, so that, according to their promise, those who violate it may be judged as guilty of their vow, and may not plead violence done to them.
19.8:
**“And all (the people) answered”** — or: all
**“And when Moses had related the people's words to the Lord,”** — Prelates bring back the vows of their subjects to the Lord when they attribute their good things to him, and bless him in all things.
19.9:
