**“The Lord said to him: Lo, now will I come to thee in the darkness of a cloud”** — the obscure knowledge of the law.
**“that the people may hear me speaking to thee”** — not to the people, which cannot understand me
19.10:
**“And he said to him: Go to the people, and sanctify them”** — command that they be sanctified
**“today, and tomorrow,”** — namely in the present life and in the life to come
**“and let them wash”** — from sins
**“their garments.”**
• the bodies in which souls are clothed
• Blessed is he that keepeth his garments, lest he walk naked.
19.11:
**“And let them be ready”** — through the knowledge of the natural law
**“against the third day:”** — as being about to receive the Law and the worship of the holy Trinity
**“for on the third day (the Lord) will come down”**
• about to give the knowledge of the law
• condescending to human frailty
**“the Lord”** — that they may know the Law is given by God, not by man
**“in the sight of all the people upon mount Sinai.”**
• GO TO THE PEOPLE etc. ORIGEN. Go down and charge the people, and purify them today and tomorrow, and let them wash their garments, and let them be ready against the third day etc. He who wishes to come to the word of God, let him hear what the Lord commands. He ought to come sanctified and with washed garments. For if you bring soiled garments, it will be said to you: "Friend, how camest thou in hither not having on a wedding garment?" No one therefore can hear the word of God unless first sanctified, that is, holy in body and spirit, and with washed garments. For a little after he is to go in to the wedding supper, to eat of the flesh of the lamb, and to drink the cup of salvation. No one goes in to this supper with soiled garments. Whence: At all times let thy garments be clean. For your garments have been washed once by the grace of baptism; you have been purified in body, cleansed from all defilement of the flesh and of the spirit. What therefore God has cleansed, do not you make unclean. Hear the kind of sanctification: come not near, he says, to a woman today and tomorrow, that on the third day you may hear the word of God: this is what the Apostle says: "It is good for a man not to touch a woman", saving however the remedy of marriage for the weak. But because the time is short, it remaineth that they who have wives be as if they had none.
• SANCTIFY THEM etc. RABANUS. He who desires to come to the sight of God, let him sanctify himself by faith and conversation, and wash his garments, that is, his works, today and tomorrow, namely in the present and in the future, that he may come to the glory of the resurrection, which the third day suggests.
• FOR ON THE THIRD DAY etc. On this day the law was given, written on tables of stone by the finger of God; this is the third day of the third month from the going out of the children of Israel from Egypt. From the day therefore on which they kept the pasch, that is, the fourteenth of the first month, until the law was given, fifty days are numbered: namely seventeen of the first month, the rest from the fourteenth; and all thirty of the second, which are forty-seven; and the third of the third month, which is the fiftieth from the slaying of the lamb; as from the passion of Christ until the Holy Ghost is given fifty days are numbered. For the finger of God signifies the Holy Ghost.
*Isidore:* On the fiftieth day after the pasch the Law was given to Moses: on the fiftieth day after the passion of the Lord, which that Pasch figured, the promised Spirit was given, coming down upon the apostles and those who were with them, set at a hundred and twenty, the number of the age of Moses; and, the tongues of the believers being divided, the whole world was filled with the gospel preaching. There the law is said to be written by the finger of God, and the Lord says of the Holy Ghost: "By the finger of God I cast out devils." All the people beheld the voices, the lamps, and the mountain smoking, the thunders, the lightnings, and the sound of the trumpet resounding. In the voices and thunders are understood the allurements of the promise, or the terror in the preaching; in the lamps, the brightness of miracles; in the sound of the trumpet, the strong preaching of the saints: all which were fulfilled at the coming of the Holy Ghost, when the disciples thundered forth precepts and signs in variety of tongues. Now Sinai is interpreted 'bush', which signifies the Church, in which the Lord speaks to Moses. And that the Lord, when about to give the law, came down in fire and smoke, signifies that he enlightens the faithful by the showing of his brightness, and darkens the eyes of the unbelieving with the smoke of error. He is seen also in darkness, because the wicked, who savour earthly things, did not know him coming down, that is, being born in humility, for the darkness of their malice; or because he spoke the truth of the law to the unbelieving through darkness, that seeing they may not see, and hearing may not understand.
19.12:
**“And thou shalt appoint certain limits to the people”** — lest anyone dare to climb the mountain of sacred Scripture beyond his understanding, but let him be content with his measure, according to the gift he has received from God
**“round about, and thou shalt say to them: Take heed you go not up into the mount, and that ye touch not the borders thereof: every one that toucheth”** — beyond his strength
**“the mount”** — the height of Scripture
**“dying”** — eternal
**“he shall die.”**
• fallen into heresy or blasphemy against God
• TAKE HEED YOU GO NOT etc. RABANUS. First he forbids the people to go up into the mountain, and threatens death. Now he commands that they go up into the mountain when the trumpet sounds; restraining, namely, human boldness, and inviting to obedience: because at the voice of preaching we ought to raise ourselves to the things above, and not presume of our own accord in searching into the sacraments, but follow the calling of God.
19.13:
**“No hands shall touch him,”** — that is: no one shall imitate his madness
**“but he shall be stoned to death”** — he shall be pressed by the hard words of the Church
**“or shall be shot through with arrows:”**
• as it were by the sharpest rebukes
• the words of the wise are as goads
**“whether it be beast”** — the fool is compared to beasts
**“or man”** — wise in his own esteem
**“he shall not live.”** — or: he shall die
**“When the trumpet shall begin to sound,”** — it signifies preaching
**“THE TRUMPET”** — As it were 'vocina', from voice, or from calling; or from the cheek.
19.14: **“And Moses came down from the mount to the people, and sanctified them. And when they had washed their garments,”** — AND WHEN THEY HAD WASHED etc. It is not enough for the virtue of contemplation to cleanse one's works with the tears of penance, unless chastity of mind and body follow. Whence: "Blessed are the clean of heart: for they shall see God" etc. And: "For wisdom will not enter into a malicious soul".
19.15:
**“He said to them: Be ready against the third day,”** — the faith of the holy Trinity
**“and come not near your wives.”** — to any carnal pleasure or worldly care
19.16:
**“And now the third day was come,”** — in which the faith of the holy Trinity was to dawn
**“and the morning appeared: and behold thunders began to be heard”** — the sound of preaching
**“and lightning to flash,”** — miracles
**“and a very thick cloud”** — the same is signified by the cloud and the smoke
**“to cover the mount, and the noise of the trumpet sounded exceeding loud, and (the people) feared”** — "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom"
**“the people that was in the camp.”** — of the warfare of God
19.17:
**“And when (Moses) had brought (them) forth”** — by advancing or leading them forward to greater and better things
**“them, Moses, to meet God from the place of the camp,”** — God meets him who comes to meet him: for by free will we are moved toward God, but we are not advanced unless his mercy go before and follow.
**“they stood at the bottom of the mount.”** — as being near to the height
19.18:
**“And all mount Sinai was on a smoke”** — because the Law is obscure to the unbelieving
**“because the Lord was come down upon it in fire,”** — as a light to the just, or because the Law is fiery.
19.19:
**“And the sound of the trumpet grew by degrees louder and louder, and was drawn out to a greater length: Moses spoke,”** — by asking
**“and God answered him.”**
• by teaching
• AND ALL MOUNT SINAI etc. GREGORY. The Lord, when about to give the Law, came down in fire and smoke, because he enlightens the humble by the brightness of his showing, and darkens the proud by the darkness of error. First therefore the mind is to be cleansed from the desire of temporal glory and from all carnal concupiscence, and then raised to the keen gaze of contemplation. Whence, when the law is received, the people is forbidden to approach the mountain, that, since with a mind still weak it desires earthly things, it may not presume upon the sublime. Whence it is rightly said: "If a beast shall touch the mount, it shall be stoned." For a beast touches the mount when the mind, subject to irrational desires, raises itself to the heights of contemplation; but it is struck with stones, because, not bearing the highest things, it is slain by the blows of the weight from above. They therefore who strive to lay hold of the summit of perfection, when they desire to hold the citadel of contemplation, let them first prove themselves by exercise in the field of work, that they may know carefully whether they now inflict no evils on their neighbours, whether they bear with equanimity those inflicted, whether, when temporal goods are set before it, the mind is not loosed in gladness, and, when they are withdrawn, is not wounded with too great grief; and then let them weigh whether, when they return within to themselves, in searching out spiritual things they do not draw with them the shadows of bodily things, or, if perhaps drawn, drive them away with the hand of discretion; whether, desiring to see the uncircumscribed light, they press down all the images of their own circumscription; and whether, in that which they seek to reach above themselves, they overcome what they are.
*Gregory:* The sacred words, at the beginning of their narratives, express qualities, and the ends of matters; sometimes from the position of a place, sometimes from the position of a body, sometimes from the quality of the air, sometimes from the quality of the time, they signify what they will set down of the action to come. For from the position of places they express the merits of what follows and the ends of matters, as it is said of Israel: That it could not hear the words of God on the mountain, but received the precepts in the plains; indicating the following weakness of the people, which could not go up to the highest things, but slackened itself in the lowest by living negligently. From the position of a body, as in the Acts of the apostles Stephen declares that he saw Jesus, who sits at the right hand of power, standing. For to stand belongs to one who helps, and he is rightly seen to stand who gives aid in the war of the contest. From the quality of the air, as when, at the Lord's preaching, the Evangelist would say that none of Judea would then believe: And it was winter. For it is written: Iniquity shall abound, and the charity of many shall grow cold. He took care therefore to express the time of winter, to show that the cold of malice was in the hearts of the hearers. Of Peter also, when he was about to deny, it is set down first that it was cold, and standing at the fire of coals he warmed himself. For he had already grown torpid from the heat of charity, and, his weakness burning, he warmed himself at the love of the present life, as at the coals of the persecutors. From the quality of the time, as Judas, who was not to return to pardon, is said to have gone out at night to the perfidy of the betrayal, since, as he went out, the evangelist says: "And it was night." And to the wicked rich man it is said: This night do they require thy soul of thee. Solomon also, who was not to persevere, is said to have received wisdom in sleep and in the night. Hence it is that the angels come to Abraham at midday; but when about to punish Sodom they are recorded to have come in the evening.
19.20:
**“And the Lord came down”** — showing something of himself in contemplation
**“upon mount Sinai, in the very top of the mount, and he called Moses”** — that he might advance through contemplation
**“unto the top thereof. And when he was gone up thither,”** — AND THE LORD CAME DOWN etc. GREGORY. Moses goes up into the mountain, and the Lord comes down. The mountain signifies contemplation, into which we go up, that we may be lifted up to see the things that are beyond our weakness. But into it the Lord comes down, because to us, when we make much progress, he opens some little of himself to our senses; if indeed little or anything can be said of him who, being ever one and the same, cannot be understood in part, and yet is said to be partaken of by his faithful, though in his substance no part is in any way admitted. But because we cannot express him in perfect speech, in the manner of our humanity, as it were hindered by the weakness of infancy, we sound him forth in some measure by stammering.
19.21:
**“He said unto him: Go down”** — from the height of contemplation, according to that: "For whether we be transported in mind, it is to God; or whether we be sober, it is for you."
**“and charge the people: lest they should have a mind”**
• forgetful of his frailty
• of his capacity
**“to pass the limits to see the Lord,”** — There is need of great discretion, lest anyone wish to search into the divine nature beyond what he can; whence: He that is a searcher of majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory; and: "Thou hast found honey, eat what is sufficient for thee".
**“and of them should perish”** — led astray by heresy or by any error
**“a very great multitude.”** — because few are fit for contemplation and the divine vision
19.22:
**“The priests also that come to the Lord, let them be sanctified”** — in mind and body
**“lest he strike them.”** — with a bodily stroke, or a spiritual
19.23:
**“And Moses said to the Lord: The people cannot come up”** — for the weakness of understanding
**“to mount Sinai: for thou didst charge, and command, saying: Set limits”** — show them set
**“about the mount, and sanctify it.”** — show it sanctified, lest the unsanctified presume to approach.
19.24:
**“And the Lord said to him: Go, get thee down: and thou shalt come up, thou and Aaron”** — the Law and the priesthood
**“with thee: but let not the priests and the people pass the limits,”** — the lesser, less capable of understanding, and not penetrating the secrets of Scripture
**“nor come up to the Lord, lest he kill them.”** — if they approach unworthy.

20.2:
**“I am the Lord thy God,”** — This is not a commandment, but he says whose the commandment is.
**“who brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage.”** — the devil's
**“I AM THE LORD THY GOD”** — ORIGEN. He who despises the present world, namely Egypt, and, translated by the word of God, is not found, because he hastens to the world to come, of him God says: I am the Lord God etc. Not to those only who set out from Egypt, but to those who no longer serve the Egyptians, brought out of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. The business of the world, the acts of the flesh, are the house of bondage; as to leave worldly things and to live according to God is the house of freedom. Whence: If you continue in my word, you shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free. Egypt therefore is the house of bondage; Judea and Jerusalem, the house of freedom. Whence: "That Jerusalem, which is above, is free." As therefore the earthly Egypt is called the house of bondage for the children of Israel in comparison with Judea and Jerusalem, which is to them the house of freedom: so in comparison with the heavenly Jerusalem, which is the mother of freedom, the whole world and the things that are in it are called the house of bondage; and because from the paradise of freedom we came through sin to the bondage of the world, the first word of the decalogue is of freedom: I am the Lord thy God, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt etc. This voice you will not be able to hear in Egypt, even if it be enjoined you to keep the pasch, to gird your loins, to take sandals on your feet, to hold a staff in your hand, and to eat unleavened bread with bitterness. But neither in the first mansion, nor in the second, nor in the third, nor when you have crossed the Red Sea, even if you have come to Mara and the bitterness has been turned for you into sweetness, nor in Elim, where there were twelve fountains of water and seventy palm trees, even if you have passed Raphidim and gone up by the other stages, are you yet judged fit, but when you have come to mount Sina. Scarcely therefore will you at length deserve to receive the precepts of freedom, and to hear: I am the Lord thy God, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. Yet this is not a word of command, but shows who it is that commands. The first commandment therefore is: Thou shalt have no other gods but me.
*Augustine:* It is asked how the ten precepts of the law are to be divided. Whether there are four, up to the precept of the sabbath, which pertain to God, and the six remaining, of which the first is: Honour thy father and mother, which pertain to man? Or rather are those three, and these seven? For they who say those are four separate what is said: Thou shalt have no other gods but me, so that another precept is: Thou shalt not make to thyself an idol etc., where images are forbidden to be worshipped. But they will have it one: Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife, Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house, and all to the end. But they who say those are three and these seven will have it one, whatever is commanded of worshipping the one God, lest anything else besides him be worshipped for God: and these last are divided into two, so that one is: Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife, another: Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house. Yet that the precepts are ten neither party doubts, because Scripture testifies it. But to me it seems more fitting to take those as three and these as seven. Because those which pertain to God seem to suggest the Trinity; and what is said: Thou shalt have no other gods but me, this very thing is more perfectly unfolded when images are forbidden to be worshipped. But the coveting of another's wife and the coveting of another's house differ so much in sinning that to that in which it is said: Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house, other things were joined, Scripture saying: nor his field, nor his servant, nor his handmaid, nor his oxen etc. And it seems to have distinguished the coveting of another's wife from the coveting of any other thing of another's, when it began both thus: Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife, Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house, and to this joined the rest. But it did not, when it had said: Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife, join other things to this, saying: nor his house, nor his field etc.; but all these appear to be joined, as contained in one precept, and distinguished from that in which the wife is named. But as for that where it is said: Thou shalt have no other gods but me, it is plain that the diligent carrying out of this matter is in the things set down after it. For to what does: Thou shalt not make to thyself an idol, nor any image etc., pertain, but to what is said: Thou shalt have no other gods but me?
*Isidore:* God gives Moses the law of our innocence and of the acknowledging of himself, which consists in ten words, written on tables of stone by the finger of God. Three are those which pertain to the love and knowledge of the Trinity, seven to the love of neighbour, by which human society is not hurt. The first pertains to God the Father: The Lord thy God is one God; that, hearing this, you may worship one God the Father, and not pour out fornication upon many feigned gods. The second to the Son: Thou shalt not take the name of thy God in vain; that is, do not think that Christ the Son of God is a creature, because every creature is made subject to vanity; but equal to the Father, God of God, light of light.
20.3:
**“Thou shalt not have strange gods before me.”**
• though there be gods many and lords many, thou shalt have no other gods but me
• THOU SHALT NOT HAVE STRANGE GODS etc. ORIGEN. The first commandment is: Thou shalt have no other gods but me; and there follows: Thou shalt not make to thyself an idol, nor any likeness etc. Some think all these together are one commandment; and if it be reckoned so, the number of ten commandments will not be filled. The first commandment therefore is: Thou shalt have no other gods but me. The second: Thou shalt not make to thyself an idol, nor any likeness etc. Let us begin therefore from the first commandment: Thou shalt have no other gods but me. Had he said: 'There are none', the saying would seem more absolute. But because he says: Thou shalt have none, he did not deny that there are, but forbade that they be gods to him to whom these precepts are given. From this I think Paul took: For although there be that are called gods, either in heaven or on earth etc. In other places also you will find them named, as there: "A great King above all gods", and: "The God of gods, the Lord". Of lords the same Apostle says: "Whether thrones, or dominations, etc." But dominations are nothing else than a certain order and multitude of lords. In which the Apostle seems to open the sense of the law, as if he should say: Though there be many lords, who rule over other nations, and many gods who are worshipped by others, yet to us there is one God, and one Lord. Whence, when the Most High divided the nations and scattered the sons of Adam, he appointed the bounds of the nations according to the number of the angels of God. The angels therefore, to whom the Most High committed the nations, Scripture calls lords or gods: gods, as given by God, and lords, as having received power by lot from the Lord. Whence it is said to them: "I have said: You are gods, and all of you the sons of the most High. But you like men shall die, and shall fall like one of the princes": imitating, namely, the devil, who was made prince of all to his ruin. Whence it is plain that transgression made them execrable, not nature. To thee therefore, O Israel, who art the portion of God and his lot, thou shalt have, he says, no other gods but me: because truly God is the one God, and truly the Lord is the one Lord; but on the others created by him he conferred this name not by nature, but by grace. These things are not said only to Israel according to the flesh, nay to you who have been made Israel by seeing God with the mind, and circumcised in heart, not in flesh. If yet you so act as to be worthy to be the portion of God, and to be measured in the lot of his inheritance; otherwise let them be an example to you who had been called to this, that they might be the portion of God, and, their sins requiring it, were scattered through all nations, and, brought out of the house of bondage, now serve not the Egyptians only, but all nations. For he who sins is the servant of sin.
20.4:
**“Thou shalt not make to thyself a graven thing”** — an idol, which is nothing, because it is taken from the likeness of no existing thing, but idly feigned
**“nor the likeness of any thing”** — of an existing thing, which is not nothing
**“that is in heaven above”** — as of the sun and moon and such like
**“or in the earth beneath”** — of man, ox and the like
**“nor of those things that are in the waters”** — of fishes
**“under the earth.”** — THOU SHALT NOT MAKE TO THYSELF A GRAVEN THING etc. ORIGEN. Thou shalt not make to thyself an idol, nor any likeness etc. Idols are one thing, gods another. For of gods the Apostle says: "For there be gods many, and lords many" etc. But of idols: "That an idol is nothing in the world." But of likenesses he did not add that they are nothing. But here it is said: Thou shalt not make to thyself an idol, nor the likeness of anything. It is one thing therefore to make an idol, another a likeness. For example: if anyone in gold and silver, wood or stone, makes the form of a four-footed beast, or a serpent, or a bird, and sets it up to be prayed to, he has made not an idol but a likeness. But he who makes what is not, namely a form which the eye has not seen, but the mind feigns for itself; as if anyone forms the head of a dog or a ram on human members, or two faces in the one figure of a man, or the hinder parts of a horse or fish to a human breast: he who does this makes not a likeness, but an idol. For he makes what is not, nor has anything like itself. Therefore the Apostle says: "that an idol is nothing in the world." For the form is not taken from any of the things that exist, but is what the idle and curious mind has found. But a likeness is when something is formed of the things that are either in heaven, or in earth, or in the waters; but not as it is easy to declare of the likenesses of the things that are on earth or in the sea, so too of the heavenly, where one may say this can be perceived of the sun and moon and stars, whose forms the gentiles express. But Moses, learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, desired to forbid even the things that were among them in secret, as Hecate, and other forms of demons, which the Apostle calls "the spirits of wickedness in the high places", of which perhaps it is said: "My sword is inebriated in heaven." For by these forms and likenesses they invoked demons to drive away or avoid evils. But it is to be known that when you have resolved to keep this commandment and to have only one God and Lord, this is to declare war on all the others, which you renounced in baptism, confessing God alone, Father and Son and Holy Ghost. But confessing this, unless we love the Lord our God with all our heart, cleaving to him with all our soul, with all our strength, we are not made the portion of the Lord, but, set on the border, we have those offended whom we flee, and do not make him propitious to whom we flee. To whom the prophet says: Woe to the double-minded. And again: How long do you halt on both feet? By those therefore we are beaten as runaways, and by our Lord we are not defended, as unstable. Whence: Thy lovers have become thy enemies. Many are the lovers of the soul, taken with her beauty, with whom she played the harlot, saying: I will go after my lovers, that give me my wine etc. These she offended by returning to her former husband. Unless therefore you abide with your husband in all faith, you are suspected for the crimes you have committed; he marks all your movements, looks and gait; he can bear to see in you nothing wanton any longer, nothing loose or prodigal. If therefore you neglect the grace received, and even entangle yourself in worldly business, straightway the unclean spirit returns with seven more wicked, that he may not be cast out again, and the last things become worse than the first. There is therefore no agreement of the temple of God with idols. If we are God's, we ought to be such that God dwells and walks in us. Whence: You that carry the vessels of the Lord, go out, and touch not the unclean thing: I will receive you etc. He says therefore: Thou shalt have no other gods but me.
20.5:
**“Thou shalt not adore them, nor serve them.”** — THOU SHALT NOT ADORE etc. To worship is one thing, to adore another. One can adore unwillingly, either flattering idolatrous kings, or overcome by torments, though he knows that an idol is nothing. But to worship is to give oneself over to these with all affection and zeal. He cuts off both therefore, that you may neither worship with affection, nor adore in outward show.
**“I am the Lord thy God, mighty, jealous,”**
• not bearing that the soul espoused to me should be marked with any suspicion
• I AM THE LORD etc. See the kindness of God: that he may teach us and make us perfect, he does not refuse the frailty of human affections; he does and suffers all things for our sake, he speaks with the affections known and familiar to us.
*Origen:* Every woman is either under a husband and subject to the laws of the husband, or she is a harlot, and uses the liberty of sinning. He who goes in to a harlot knows that he has gone in to one prostituted and open to all. Therefore he cannot be indignant at others. He who uses lawful marriage does not suffer his wife to sin, but is kindled with jealousy to guard the chastity of the marriage, that he may become a lawful father. So every soul is either prostituted with demons, and has many lovers that they may go in to her, now the spirit of fornication, now of avarice; after this will come the spirit of pride, and very many others. Yet one does not envy another nor is moved with jealousy, but they invite one another. Whence: He bringeth with him seven other spirits more wicked than himself etc. So the soul that is prostituted to demons suffers no jealousy of her lovers. But if she has been joined to a lawful husband, that is, to Christ, even if she was at one time a sinner, he does not suffer her to sin any more, nor can he bear that she should play with adulterers; his jealousy is stirred up over her, and he defends the chastity of the marriage. But if he sees her violating the rights of marriage, and seeking occasion of sinning, he gives her a bill of divorce. Whence: For your iniquities I have put away your mother; he who speaks these things is both jealous, and says this moved with jealousy. This also is a new kind of his goodness, that he receives her even after adultery, returning and repenting with all her heart. Whence: If a woman go from her husband, and sleep with another man, shall she return again to her husband etc.? And elsewhere: And after thou hadst played the harlot in all these things, I said: Return etc. If therefore this jealous God seeks and desires your soul to cleave to him, if he watches, rebukes and is indignant, as though using a certain jealousy toward you, know that there is hope of salvation for you. But if you despise the rebuke, his jealousy departs from you, according to that: Therefore jealousy departeth from thee etc. See the mercy and goodness of God; when he wills to have mercy, he says he is indignant and angry, as he says by Jeremias: With pain and scourge thou shalt be chastised, Jerusalem, that my soul depart not from thee. For he scourgeth every son whom he receiveth. But this is the terrible thing, this the last, if we are not rebuked for our sins. For when we pass the measure of sinning, even the jealousy of God will be taken away from us, and he is angry no more.
**“visiting the iniquity”** — For after the sin he says: "Hearken, O daughter, and see, and incline thy ear" etc., as a merciful father and physician.
**“of the fathers”** — of the devil and his angels
**“upon the children”**
• not upon the fathers, who are unworthy of correction
• namely those who sinned at the suggestion of the devil and his angels
**“unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me”**
• because companions are taken in by men when they sin
• VISITING THE INIQUITY etc. ORIGEN. Rendering the sins of the fathers upon the children etc. The heretics say that this is not the word of a good God, who says that one is punished for the sins of another; yet they call the God of the law just. Nor can they show how he is just, if he punishes one when another sins. But our inner man is said either to have God for Father, if he lives according to God; or the devil, if he does his will. Whence: You are of your father the devil, and the desires of your father you will do. As therefore the seed of God is in us when, keeping the word of God, we do not sin, according to that: He who is of God sinneth not, because the seed of God abideth in him; so when we are persuaded by the devil to sin, we receive his seed; when we do what he persuades, he has now begotten us. For we are born his sons through sin. But because we scarcely sin without help, as no one commits adultery alone, but an adulteress must become partner, and, if not more, someone, man or woman, must be joined for the service of the crime: all these, begotten as it were one from another according to the order of persuasion, draw their lineage from the devil; as in the betrayal of the Lord the devil entered into the heart of Judas, and begot the first son of sin, who could not do this alone; he went therefore to the Scribes and Pharisees and the high priests. From Judas therefore is born the third and fourth generation of sin. Let us see therefore how God renders the sins of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation, and not upon the fathers themselves. For nothing is said of the fathers. The devil therefore, because he has now passed the measure of sinning, like a garment clotted with blood, will not be clean in this world, and is not scourged for sin: for all things are kept for him in the future. Whence: "Art thou come before the time to torment us?" But the sins are rendered upon the sons whom he begot through sin, who, set in the flesh, are scourged, because "God desireth not the death of the sinner, but rather that he be converted and live". Mercifully therefore he renders the sins of the fathers upon the children, because the devil and his angels, who are made the fathers even of sin, are unworthy to be corrected in the present: their sons, and those who through them have been taken into the fellowship of sin, receive in the present what they have done, that, being purged, they may not be made companions of the devil in punishment. Whence: "I will visit their iniquities with a rod." But my mercy I will not take away from them. For God is jealous, and does not wish the soul which he espouses to himself in faith to remain in the defilement of sin, but to be quickly purged. But if she will not be purged, he will laugh at their destruction, saying to them: "Depart from me, you cursed, into everlasting fire" etc. Let us know therefore that we are rebuked in the present, that in the future we may rest. Whence: When we are chastised, we are rebuked by the Lord, that we be not condemned with this world.
*Origen:* In this saying the heretics are wont to taunt us, that it is not the word of a good God, who judges one for the sins of another. But they who will call the God of the law who commands these things not good, yet call him just. Nor can they themselves show how it may seem to agree with justice if, when one sins, another is punished.
*Isidore:* The first commandment forbids stealing away. The second, error. The third slays the love of the world. The fourth, impiety. The fifth, cruelty. The sixth, fornication. The seventh, rapacity. The eighth destroys falsehood. The ninth, the covetousness of the world. The tenth, the knowledge of adultery. And it is to be noted that as the Egyptians are struck with ten plagues, so the tables are written with ten precepts, by which the people of God are to be ruled and the demons slain. For the law was written on two tables, to signify the two Testaments, or because there are two precepts of love, of God and of neighbour, on which dependeth the whole law and the prophets. For on one are three precepts, which pertain to the love of God; but on the other seven, which pertain to fellowship with neighbour. And the tables were of stone, because the heart of the Jews was of stone, insensible, hard, dull. Whence: I will take away the stony heart, and will give them a heart of flesh. And the Apostle says: "Not in tables of stone, but in the fleshly tables of the heart", which, namely, may feel and understand.
20.6:
**“And shewing mercy”** — because they do not need correction; for they who love do not sin
**“unto thousands”**
• unto all
• the finite for the infinite
**“to them that love me”** — not those who hate
**“and keep my commandments.”** — "If any one love me, he will keep my word". And: "Perfect charity casteth out fear".
20.7:
**“Thou shalt not take the name of thy God in vain:”**
• namely by swearing by the name of the Lord for nothing
• by thinking Christ to be only a creature
**“for (the Lord) will not hold him guiltless”** — even if men hold him so
**“the Lord”** — "the just judge"
20.8: **“Remember that thou keep holy the sabbath day.”** — The third commandment, pertaining to the Holy Ghost, by whose gift eternal rest is promised and sanctification is perfected.
20.9: **“Six days shalt thou labour,”** — the six thousand years in which there is labour
20.10:
**“But on the seventh day is the sabbath”** — in the rest of the blessed kingdom; of the sabbath of the Jews it is said: Your sabbaths my soul hateth.
**“of the Lord thy God: thou shalt do no work on it, thou”** — because after this life is the true rest
**“nor thy son, nor thy daughter, nor thy manservant, nor thy maidservant,”**
• no sex is excluded, no age, nor any condition
• carnal and spiritual
**“nor thy beast,”** — the unlearned
**“nor the stranger”** — who has newly come to the Law
**“that is within thy gates”** — the enclosure of the Church
20.11:
**“For in six days the Lord made”** — signifying that in the perfection of the number six we must do works, that afterward we may enjoy eternal rest
**“heaven and earth, and the sea, and all things that are in them,”** — according to the letter or spiritually
**“and rested”** — in us
**“on the seventh day: therefore the Lord blessed the sabbath day,”** — because he will bless us perfectly when he has given eternal rest
20.12:
**“Honour thy father and thy mother,”** — This is the first on the other table, that children honour their parents with the office of piety. For he who does not show honour to his parents, whom can he obey?
**“that thou mayest be longlived upon the land”** — of the living, or the present one
**“which the Lord thy God will give thee.”** — HONOUR THY FATHER etc. This is the first of the seven commandments which pertain to neighbour. And well are they seven. For the number seven is made of three and four. The three befits the soul, which is irascible, concupiscible, rational. The four, the body.
20.13:
**“Thou shalt not kill.”**
• By hand, or by mind, or by withholding the help or counsel of life from him to whom you can or ought to give it.
• The judge does not kill the guilty man, but the law which commands it.
• THOU SHALT NOT KILL etc. AUGUSTINE. And as to what is said: Thou shalt not kill, it is not to be thought that it is done against this precept when the law kills, or God commands someone to be killed. For he does it who commands what it is not lawful for the minister to refuse.
20.14:
**“Thou shalt not commit adultery.”** — that is: that thou be not joined to any one except in the bond of marriage: for by the part he wishes the whole to be understood.
**“THOU SHALT NOT COMMIT ADULTERY”** — AUGUSTINE. It is asked also how Thou shalt not commit adultery differs from what is said a little after: Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife. For in what is said: Thou shalt not commit adultery, that could be understood; unless perhaps in those two precepts, of not committing adultery and not stealing, the deeds themselves are marked; but in these last, the coveting itself; which differ so much that sometimes he commits adultery who does not covet his neighbour's wife, when for some other cause he is joined with her; and sometimes he covets and is not joined with her, fearing the penalty; and this perhaps the law wished to show, that both are sins.
*Augustine:* Again it is wont to be asked whether fornication also is held under the name of mechia. For this is a Greek word, which Scripture now uses for the Latin. For in Greek it calls none moechi but adulterers. But the Law was given not to men only, but also to women. For let not the woman think nothing is commanded her here because it is said: Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife, as though she might lawfully covet the husband of her neighbour. If therefore here, from what is said to the man: Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife, what pertains to the woman also is understood, how much more by what is said: Thou shalt not commit adultery is each sex bound, since the precept itself can be referred to both, as "Thou shalt not kill", Thou shalt not steal, and the things which in like manner, no one sex being expressed, seem to sound to both; because the more honoured, that is, the male, is the one expressed. And hence a woman who has a husband is an adulteress by lying with one who is not her husband, even if he has no wife. A man also is an adulterer by lying with her who is not his wife, even if she has no husband. But whether, if a man who has no wife does it with a woman who has no husband, he is held by the transgression of this precept, is rightly asked. For if he is not held, fornication is not forbidden in the Decalogue, but only mechia, that is, adultery, although every adultery is fornication. Whence: Whosoever shall put away his wife, excepting the cause of fornication, maketh her to commit adultery. For here he called it fornication if she who has a husband sins with another, which is mechia, that is, adultery. But whether every fornication can be called mechia in the Scriptures, no example of the manner of speech occurs to me. But if not every fornication can be called mechia, where in the Decalogue that fornication is forbidden which men who have no wives commit with women who have no men or husbands, whether it can be found, I know not. But if by the name of theft every unlawful taking of another's thing is well understood (for he who forbade theft did not permit robbery, but wished the whole to be understood from the part, whatever is unlawfully taken of the things of one's neighbour), then by the name of mechia also every unlawful lying together, and the unlawful use of those members, ought to be understood as forbidden.
20.15:
**“Thou shalt not steal.”** — any taking of a thing whatever, which is the vice of rapacity
**“THOU SHALT NOT STEAL”** — ISIDORE. But again it is asked how Thou shalt not steal differs from what is said a little after of not coveting the things of one's neighbour. Not that every one who covets his neighbour's thing steals, but every one who steals his neighbour's thing covets it. In that general precept, where it is commanded not to covet the thing of one's neighbour, that which pertains to theft could also have been contained.
20.16:
**“Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour.”**
• which is the crime of lying and falsehood
• THOU SHALT NOT BEAR etc. AUGUSTINE. In what is said also: Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour, it is wont to be asked whether every lie is forbidden; lest perhaps this precept be not against those who say one ought to lie then, when the lie profits someone and does no harm to him to whom you lie. For such is not against your neighbour; so that Scripture might seem to have added this for that reason, which could have said briefly: Thou shalt not bear false witness, as it said: "Thou shalt not kill", "Thou shalt not commit adultery", Thou shalt not steal. But it is a great question, and cannot quickly be unfolded, how this is to be taken: "Thou wilt destroy all that speak a lie", and: "Be not willing to make any manner of lie", and the like.
20.17: **“Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house: neither shalt thou desire his wife, nor his servant, nor his handmaid, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor any thing that is his.”** — He forbids even the will to commit adultery: for to do is one thing, to desire another. Whence there are two precepts: "Thou shalt not commit adultery", and: Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife.
20.18:
**“And all the people saw the voices and the flames, and the sound of the trumpet, and the mount smoking:”**
• sight, because it holds the primacy among the senses, is mingled with all. For so we say: Hear and see, smell and see, touch and see.
• We also, hearing the voices of the doctors, ought to direct the eye of the mind.
• AND ALL THE PEOPLE etc. AUGUSTINE. It is wont to be asked how the people saw the voice, since the voice seems to pertain not to sight but to hearing. But to see is wont to be put for the general sense of body and soul. Whence: When Jacob saw that there was food in Egypt, from which he was namely absent. Though some have thought that to see the voice is nothing else than to understand, which is the sight of the mind. But if here it had been said briefly that the people heard the voice, and the lamps, and the voice of the trumpet, and the mountain smoking, a greater question would arise, how they heard the lamps and the smoking mountain, which pertains to the sense of seeing. Unless one should say it ought not to have been said so briefly, but the whole said: they heard the voice and saw the lamps, and heard the voice of the trumpet, and saw the smoking mountain. For there were two kinds of voice, and from the clouds, as the thunders, and the trumpet; if yet he called that the voice which was sent forth from the clouds; and hence it is better that in the things which pertained to the sense of hearing the general sense, that is, of seeing, was set (since Scripture wished to embrace the whole briefly), than that in the things which pertain to the sense of seeing hearing should be understood, in which manner we are not wont to speak. For we are wont to say 'See what it sounds'; we are not wont to say 'Hear what it shines'.
**“and being terrified and struck with fear,”** — as unworthy to approach
**“they stood afar off,”** — He describes the form of a good hearer, who promises that he will hear and fulfil the precepts of the master.
20.19:
**“Saying to Moses: Speak thou to us,”** — as if: teach us
**“and we will hear:”** — that is: we will obey
**“let not the Lord speak to us,”** — at the day of judgment, saying: Depart, you cursed, into everlasting fire.
**“lest”** — it can quickly happen
**“we die.”**
• by everlasting death
• SPEAK THOU TO US etc. It is signified that fear pertains rather to the Old Testament, as love to the New, although the New lies hidden in the Old, and the Old lies open in the New. But how it is granted to such a people to see the voice of God, if this is to be taken as to understand, when they fear that God should speak to them lest they die, does not sufficiently appear.
20.20:
**“And Moses said to the people: Fear not: for to prove you”** — to yourselves or to others, not to himself, who knows all things
**“God is come,”** — through signs and wonders
**“and that the dread of him”** — "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom."
**“might be in you, and you should not sin.”**
• restrained, if not by love, at least by fear.
• FEAR NOT etc. AUGUSTINE. So they were to be restrained from sins, namely by fearing lest they suffer sensible punishments; because they could not yet love justice; and they were tried by the Lord, that it might appear of what kind they were, not to God, from whom it was not hidden, but among themselves and to themselves.
20.21:
**“And the people stood afar off. But Moses went to the dark cloud”** — namely where more express signs were done, by which God was known. For how was he in a cloud whom the heavens of heavens do not contain?
**“wherein God was.”** — AND THE PEOPLE STOOD etc. GREGORY. In some places of Scripture the history is to be kept, and the allegory. And often the allegory alone is to be sought. Sometimes the history alone is to be held, that the slower may be fed by the history, and the swifter by the allegory. Whence, when the people, while God spoke, beheld the lamps, the sound of the trumpet and the smoking mountain, terrified, it asked that the Lord should speak to it through Moses, and it stood afar off. Moses went to the dark cloud in which God was, because the people cannot pierce the darkness of allegory: for it belongs to very few to search out the spiritual understanding. For because the minds of the carnal are often fed by the history alone, while God spoke, the people stood afar off; but because the spiritual pierce the cloud of allegory, that they may know the words of God spiritually, Moses went to the dark cloud in which God was.
20.23: **“You shall not make gods of silver, nor shall you make to yourselves gods of gold.”** — YOU SHALL NOT MAKE GODS etc. What was said in the first precept is repeated, and by the silver and golden all images are understood, as in the Psalm: "The idols of the gentiles are silver and gold, the works of the hands of men."
20.24:
**“An altar”**
• faith
• that is: you shall have faith in the incarnation of my son.
**“of earth”** — the humanity of Christ
**“you shall make unto me, and you shall offer upon it your holocausts”** — the works of the virtues
**“and peace offerings, your sheep”** — simple things
**“and oxen”** — strong and perfect things
**“in every place where the memory of my name shall be:”**
• namely in the universal Church; not in the conventicles of the heretics.
• AN ALTAR OF EARTH etc. He shows that, images having been forbidden, an altar is to be built of earthly matter for this reason, that victims and sacrifices may be offered on it to the one God.
*Gregory:* To make an altar of earth to God is to hope in the incarnation of Christ. For then our gift is received by God, when on this altar our humility, that is, upon faith in the Lord's incarnation, has set whatever it works. On an altar of earth therefore we set the gift offered, if we ground our acts on faith in the Lord's incarnation.
**“I will come to thee,”** — by hidden inspiration
**“and will bless thee.”** — with bodily blessing and spiritual.
20.25:
**“And if thou make an altar of stone unto me, thou shalt not build it of hewn stones:”**
• heretics, schismatics
• that is: not worshipping God through heresy and schisms
• OF HEWN STONES etc. ISIDORE. The hewn stones are they who cut unity and divide themselves from the fellowship of the brethren: these Christ does not receive into his body, the figure of which body the building of the altar signifies. The unhewn stones, of which the altar is commanded to be built, are they who are made solid in unity through faith, of whom it is said: You are living stones, built together into spiritual houses. On these no iron has been laid, because they are uncorrupted and have not received the fiery darts of the wicked one. All make one altar in the unity of faith and the concord of charity.
**“for if thou lift up a tool upon it”** — of corruption or of cutting
20.26: **“Thou shalt not go up by steps unto my altar, lest thy nakedness be discovered.”** — of unbelief

21.1: **“THESE ARE THE JUDGMENTS”** — From here on the things which pertain to neighbour are unfolded more distinctly. The manner of speech is to be noted: though it was said to Moses: These are the judgments which thou shalt set before them, the rest are said to the people: If thou buy a Hebrew servant etc.
21.2:
**“If thou buy a servant”** — shalt have given over to the service of God
**“a Hebrew,”** — who in mind passes over from this world
**“six years shall he serve thee:”** — by the perfection of the active life
**“in the seventh”** — in contemplation
**“he shall go out free”** — from the bondage of the world
**“for nothing.”** — because this too is ascribed to the grace of God
21.3:
**“With what raiment”**
• with the intention of working well
• not changed for the worse
**“he came in, with the like let him go out:”** — persevering to the end
**“if having a wife,”** — good working
**“his wife also shall go out with him.”** — Let it not be forsaken in the contemplative life
21.4:
**“But if his master”** — the preacher
**“gave him a wife,”** — good working
**“and she hath borne sons and daughters:”** — strong and tender fruits
**“the woman and her children”** — or: children
**“shall be her master's:”** — Good working and its fruit will be credited to the preacher.
**“but he himself shall go out”** — to contemplation
**“with his raiment.”** — with the intention of desire
21.5:
**“And if the servant shall say: I love my master”** — namely I keep the preacher's words with careful mind
**“and my wife”** — action
**“and children,”** — fruits
**“I will not go out free:”** — that is: I will not pass over to contemplation
21.6:
**“shall bring him (to the gods)”** — let him imbue him with the sayings of the ancient fathers, who were priests of God
**“The owner”** — the preacher
**“and he shall bore his ear through with an awl:”** — namely the mind, with the fineness of the divine word, lest in the things he does he seek to please men
**“and he shall be his servant”** — in the active life, by serving men
**“for ever.”**
• that after the world he may be free
• IF THOU BUY A HEBREW SERVANT etc. AUGUSTINE. Lest Christians should demand this of their masters, the Apostle commands servants to be subject to their masters, lest the name of the Lord and his doctrine be blasphemed. For it is plain from this that it was commanded in a mystery, that God commanded the ear of him who had refused his freedom to be bored with an awl at the post.
• SIX YEARS etc. ISIDORE. Allegorically. Serving in the six ages of this world, on the seventh day, that is, the eternal sabbath, we shall be freed, if yet we have willed to be free while in this world we serve sin. But if we have not willed it, the ear will be bored in witness of disobedience, and with our wife and children, whom we preferred to freedom, that is, with the flesh and its works, we shall serve sin for ever.
*Gregory:* Allegorically. It is to be known that, though the active and the contemplative life are both of the grace of God, the one is to us of necessity, the other of will. For no one knowing God enters into his kingdom unless he first works well. But they can enter without the contemplative who do not neglect the good things they can do. Hence it is said by Moses: If thou buy a Hebrew servant etc. Hebrew is interpreted 'passing over', and a Hebrew servant is bought when one who already passes over in mind from this world is made subject to the service of God. So Moses passed over that he might see the sight, and David says: "I passed by, and lo, he was not." This bought servant is commanded to serve six years, so that in the seventh he may go out free for nothing. For the number six signifies the perfection of the active life; the number seven, contemplation. He serves six years therefore, in the seventh he goes out free, because through the active life which he has perfectly shown forth he passes over to the freedom of the contemplative life. And it is to be noted that they go out free for nothing, because after they have done all things they say they are unprofitable servants; as the active life therefore was theirs by gift, so the contemplative will be of grace. With what raiment he came in, with the like let him go out: because it is needful that each one persevere in what he has begun until the end of the work, in the intention with which he began. For he passes over well to the contemplative who in the active did not change the raiment of his intention for the worse; and there are some who, after they are joined to the service of God, love to work. Others, after they have come to the service of God, learn to work well. He who first was zealous to have good works is the Hebrew servant bought with a wife, and for the most part he can pass over to the contemplative, yet not forsake the active life. Whence it is added: If having a wife, his wife also shall go out with him. For the wife goes out with him to freedom when he does not abandon the good action by which he may profit others. But if his master gave him a wife, and she hath borne sons and daughters: the woman and her children shall be her master's; but he himself shall go out with his raiment. The master gives a wife to the bought servant when the preacher joins to good action him whom he has given over to God. And preachers are called masters, as it is said to Eliseus of his preacher: Dost thou know that thy master will be taken from thee? The wife of the bought servant bears sons and daughters when good action brings forth for him strong and tender fruits. But the woman remains with her children to the master, and the servant goes out with his raiment, because good action and its fruit are reckoned to the preacher for reward. But he himself, persevering in the intention of desire, goes out by the grace of God to contemplation. And if the servant shall say: I love my master etc. The servant loves his master when he keeps the preacher's words with careful mind. Loving also his wife and children, he refuses to go out free, when, loving the active life and its fruits, he will not pass over to the contemplative; because, considering that he has the good works of his ministry in servitude, he refuses to pass over to the rest of freedom; but let his master bring him to the gods, and set him to the door and the posts, and bore his ear with an awl, that he may be a servant for ever. For he who has resolved to persevere in the active life is brought by the Lord to the gods when he is imbued by his preacher with the sayings of the ancient fathers, who have been priests to us in the way of God. He is led also to the door and posts of the tabernacle, both that he may hear something of the entrance of the eternal tabernacle, and may know finely the day of the dreadful judgment, lest by the good works he does he seek to please men. And so his ear is bored with an awl, that is, the mind with the fineness of the fear of God, that, pierced by the point of the word, in all that he does he may know how to attend to the entrance of the kingdom, and bear as it were an ear bored at the door and post of the tabernacle. And he shall be a servant for ever, that after the world he may be free: "Because the creature also itself shall be delivered from the servitude of corruption, into the liberty of the glory of the children of God." For then shall there be true liberty for us, when our adoption has come to the glory of the children of God. But now not only is the active life in servitude, but contemplation itself, by which we are rapt above ourselves, does not perfectly obtain the freedom of the mind, but imitates it, because that inmost rest is seen in a dark manner.
21.7:
**“If any man sell his daughter to be a servant,”** — The law of the bondwoman is one, of the daughter another, because a daughter is sold out of greater necessity than a bondwoman.
**“she shall not go out as bondwomen”** — Hebrew bondwomen, namely after six years, because she has been humbled
21.8:
**“If she displease”** — having been humbled
**“the eyes of her master to whom she was delivered, he shall let her go:”** — free
**“but to a foreign nation”** — to the gentiles, or to heretics
**“he shall have no power to sell her,”** — or: power
21.9:
**“But if he have betrothed her to his son”** — in firm marriage
**“he shall deal with her after the manner of daughters.”** — by dowering her
21.10:
**“And if another”** — this one being put away
**“he take for him, he shall provide the maid”** — humbled by the son
**“a marriage, and raiment, and the price of her chastity”** — taken away
21.11:
**“If he do not these three things,”** — Namely if he himself has not humbled her, nor fixed her as wife to his son, nor cast her off when another was brought in by the son.
**“she shall go out free”** — it will suffice not to be held in servitude
**“without money.”** — as the Hebrew servant
*Augustine:* If any man sell his daughter to be a servant, she shall not go away as bondwomen depart. But if she please not her master, because he has not named her, he shall reward her. But to a foreign nation he is not master to sell her, since he has despised her. But if the son has named her, he shall do to her according to the justification of daughters. But if he take another for him, he shall not defraud her of the things that are needful, and her raiment, and her converse. But if he do not these three things to her, she shall go out free without price. They have made a most obscure place of an unusual manner of speech. But I will open it as I can. If any man sell his daughter to be a servant, that is, that she be a household servant (whom the Greeks call oiketen), she shall not go away as bondwomen depart. It is to be understood: She shall not depart in the way that Hebrew bondwomen depart after six years. For the law kept in the males must be understood as given also for the Hebrew woman. Why then shall she not depart so, unless because she is understood to have been so humbled in her service that her master has joined himself with her? Whence it follows: But if she please not her master, because he has now not named her, that is, has not made her his wife, he shall reward her; this is what he said above: She shall not go away as bondwomen depart. For she is bidden to receive something, because she has been humbled, because he did not so join himself with her as to make her his wife, that is, to name her to himself. But to a foreign nation he is not master to sell her, since he has despised her; that is, not because he has despised her is he therefore master to sell her; that is, he is not so much master that he may lawfully sell her to a foreign nation. 'He has despised in her' is the same as 'he has despised her'. And he despised her, that is, humbled her by lying with her and not making her his wife. But if the son has named her, he shall do to her according to the justification of daughters; that is: if he has joined her as wife to his son, he shall give her a dowry as to a daughter. But if he take another for him, that is, has not assigned this one as wife to his son, he shall not defraud her of the things that are needful, and her raiment, and her converse, since she did not remain wife to his son, in the manner he would give if he had not named her to himself. But where we have said: he shall not defraud her converse, the Greek has homilian, that is, speech, so calling lying together more modestly; that is, he shall give a reward for the lying together. So also Daniel, signifying lying together, says: "Under what tree didst thou see them conferring together?" And elsewhere: "Then they that feared spoke to you." But if he do not these three things to her, she shall go out free; that is: if he has neither humbled her himself by lying with her, nor joined her to his son, nor cast her out when another was taken by the son. She shall go away free, that is, it will suffice her not to be held in servitude. She shall go away receiving nothing, as the Hebrew servant. For it will not be lawful for the master to couple her to a man not a Hebrew, since it is not lawful for her to be handed to a foreign nation. But if he has coupled her to a Hebrew servant, it is understood that she will go out with him free, not separated from her husband.
**“SELL HIS DAUGHTER”** — STRABO. The daughter is devout subjection born of good will, which commits itself to the teaching of some doctor; whom the doctor ought either to teach himself, or hand over to a dear disciple to be taught, adorned with many precepts, as it were dowered. If he will do neither, let him send her away free, and not sell her to a foreign nation, that is, to heretics.
21.12:
**“He that striketh”** — with the material sword or the spiritual
**“a man with a will”** — with wicked will
**“to kill him,”** — in soul or in body
**“dying”** — bodily or spiritual
21.13: **“But he that did not lie in wait for him, but God delivered him into his hands:”** — by a hidden equity
21.14:
**“If a man on set purpose”** — namely willingly
**“kill his neighbour,”** — by scandalizing, or by leading into heresy
**“and by lying in wait for him:”** — as is read of Joab
**“thou shalt take him away from my altar”** — thou shalt separate him from the communion of the body of Christ
**“that he may die.”** — BUT HE THAT DID NOT etc. RABANUS. For homicides not done willingly six cities of refuge are appointed: Cedes in Galilee, of mount Nephthali, and Sichem in mount Ephraim, and Cariatharbe, which is Hebron, in mount Juda; and beyond the Jordan, over against Jericho toward the east, Bosor, which is in the plain of the wilderness, of the tribe of Ruben, and Ramoth in Galaad, of the tribe of Gad, and Gaulon in Basan, of the tribe of Manasses. These were appointed for the children of Israel and the strangers, that they might not die, even at the hand of the neighbour desiring to avenge the blood shed, until he set forth his cause before the people. Mystically: if anyone through lying in wait or hatred has struck another with the sword of malice, and seduced him into the death of the soul, he himself will be liable to eternal death. Whence: He that shall scandalize one of these little ones that believe in me, it were better for him etc. And: Whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer. And we know that no murderer hath eternal life. This one is commanded to be taken from the altar of the Lord, because, being unworthy of the Lord's sacraments, he is deservedly removed from communion. But he who has hurt someone through carelessness or ignorance has a city of refuge, namely the catholic Church, where, repenting, he may be zealous in good works through all the time of the present life; and if he has set his hope in the death of the high priest, that is, Christ, he will be saved.
*Augustine:* But if unwillingly, but God delivered him into his hands etc. This is said as if, even though not willing to kill, he could kill, where God delivered him into his hands. It is understood therefore that God alone did it, and for this alone, because God did it, it is said: but God delivered him into his hands. But when he kills willingly, both he himself kills and God delivered him into his hands. This therefore is the difference: that there God alone did it; but here both God and man, because of the will of the doer. But not as God, so man. For God did it justly, but man is worthy of punishment: not because he killed him whom God did not will to be killed, but because he did it through iniquity. For he did not lend his ministry to God commanding, but served the lust of his own malice. In the same deed therefore God is praised for his hidden equity, and man is punished for his own iniquity. For not because God "spared not even his own Son, but delivered him up for us all" did Judas therefore justly deliver him.
21.15:
**“He that striketh”** — afflicting bodily or spiritually
**“his father”** — carnal or spiritual
**“or mother, shall be put to death.”** — eternal; or let him die, repenting, to such a sin
21.16:
**“He that curseth”**
• gainsaying by word or deed, or by calling down evil
• by blaspheming
**“his father”** — God
**“or mother,”** — by cutting the unity of the Church
21.17:
**“He that shall steal”**
• or: shall have stolen
• by seducing from the truth
**“a man, and sell him,”** — shall have made liable to the devil
**“being convicted of guilt, (shall be put) to death”** — eternal
21.18:
**“If men quarrel,”** — that is: if two wise men contend
**“and strike”**
• shall have provoked
• shall have stirred so that he swerve from the faith
**“the one his neighbour with a stone”** — with hardness of mind, or by not counselling mercifully
**“or with his fist,”** — with scrupulous questions
**“and he die not,”** — not swerving wholly from the faith
**“but keepeth his bed:”** — charity being hurt in him
21.19:
**“If he rise again and walk abroad upon his staff,”** — charity which is not wholly extinguished
**“quit”** — clean of crime
**“shall he be that struck him, yet so that he make restitution for his work, and for his expenses upon the physicians.”**
• IF MEN QUARREL etc. RABANUS. That is: if anyone, contending with his neighbour, has provoked him by hardness of mind, or namely by despising him through niggardliness, or by not counselling him, and he, made weak by sadness, has languished from the fervour of love, let the guilty one, through confession, spend the works of penance and the expense of the promised amendment upon the physicians, that is, the doctors, who may raise up the weak man with the staff of consolation and restore him with the poultices of preaching to the former state of love.
• In correction discretion is necessary, lest he who ought to correct should kill, or drive into despair or hatred.
21.20:
**“He that striketh his bondman”** — the disciple committed to him
**“or bondwoman”** — the people subject to him
**“with a rod,”** — with excessive correction
**“and they die under his hands,”** — in his keeping
21.22:
**“If men quarrel,”** — disputing "to the subverting of the hearers"
**“and one strike a woman”** — the weak soul conceiving the word of God
**“with child,”** — with the word of God
**“and she miscarry indeed,”** — has lost the word conceived
**“but live herself:”** — not wholly dead in faith
**“he shall be answerable for (so much) damage”** — because he neglected those whom he could have gained for God
**“as the woman's husband shall require,”** — Christ, or the doctor of the Church
**“and as arbiters (shall award)”** — the prelates of the Church
21.23:
**“But if her death ensue thereupon,”** — so that she has gone away after Satan
**“he shall render life for life.”** — to be punished at the day of Judgment; or let him labour even to death to restore her to the faith
21.24:
**“Eye”** — the understanding
**“for eye,”** — the understanding having been troubled
**“tooth for tooth,”** — by which the word of God is broken small and made fine, because he broke it small and divided it ill
**“… hand”** — with which he works ill
**“for hand,”** — in power and act
**“foot for foot,”** — because he gave a stumbling block
21.25:
**“Burning”** — in the fire of hell
**“for burning,”** — because he delivered a soul to hell
**“wound”** — any hurt of the soul
**“for wound, stripe”** — a lesser hurt
**“for stripe.”** — IF MEN QUARREL etc. RABANUS. If anyone, after the word has been conceived, has hurt someone's soul through carelessness or fraud, so that it cannot bring forth whole the living seed of good work, even if the soul itself has continued still living in faith, he will need, according to the ministry of the Gospel, to restore by penance the damage done. But if the soul itself, slain by error, after bringing forth the untimely birth, that is, the deadly work, has persevered in unbelief, without doubt its seducer, as a true murderer, will be guilty of eternal death.
*Augustine:* Since he would not have the unformed offspring pertain to homicide, he certainly did not reckon it a man. Here there is a question about the soul: whether what is not formed cannot be understood to be even ensouled, and therefore it is not homicide, because it cannot be said to be deprived of life if it does not yet have a soul. For he follows and says: But if it was formed, he shall give life for life, that is, he shall die. According to that: "Eye for eye", and "tooth for tooth", and the like, namely by the equity of retaliation, which the Law established for this reason, to show what vengeance is due. For otherwise it would not be known what pardon remits, so that it might be said: "Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors." Debtors therefore are shown by the Law, that when there is forgiving, it may appear what is remitted: for otherwise we would not remit. If therefore that unformed offspring already was, but still in some manner formlessly ensouled, since the great question of the soul is not to be rushed, the Law therefore would not have it pertain to homicide, because it cannot yet be called a living soul in a body which lacks sense, if such it is in flesh not yet formed, and therefore not yet endowed with senses.
*Origen:* But if two men strive, and strike a woman with child, and her infant come forth not yet formed, he shall suffer loss, as much as the husband of the woman shall lay upon him, and shall give for his soul. But if it was formed, he shall give life for life, eye for eye etc. First let us see of that which came forth not yet formed, how one of those striving is commanded to be struck with the loss of money, when two are spoken of. What too of this, that the husband of the woman lays it 'on him', and not 'on them'; and 'he shall give', and not rather 'they shall give'? But if the infant came forth already formed, we easily understand giving life for life: namely that the sin be avenged by death. But what follows it is worth the pains to unfold. For it does not seem that even a formed infant, struck by the heel of one striving, lost an eye in the womb; and teeth it had none at all. For if we refer this to the mother, how does the miscarrying woman lose an eye, or suffer in her teeth? But grant that she miscarried being struck either in the eye or in the tooth, and received a stripe or a wound; what do we say also of burning for burning? Could the woman standing by the striving men be burned, that burning should be paid for burning? In Deuteronomy also these things cannot easily be unfolded. Yet in the Scriptures the members of the soul are named by the same words and offices with which the members of the body are used or called. Whence: Thou seest the mote in thy brother's eye, and the beam that is in thy own eye thou seest not. And elsewhere: "He that hath ears to hear, let him hear." And: "How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace." Let not the likeness of the words therefore trouble us. There are therefore two striving, two disputing about doctrines or questions of the law, and quarrelling over battles of words. Whence the Apostle: Contend not in words etc. And elsewhere: Avoid questions of the law, knowing that they beget strifes. Because therefore these strive in a question "to the subverting of the hearers", they strike a woman with child, and cast out the infant formed, or still unformed. The woman with child is the name for the soul which has newly conceived the word of God. Whence: From thy fear, O Lord, we have conceived in the womb and brought forth. They therefore who conceive and at once bring forth are to be counted not women, but men, and perfect. Whence: If the earth hath brought forth in one day, and a nation is born together in one day. This then is the generation of the perfect, which is conceived and born on the same day. And men bring forth according to that: "My little children, of whom I am in labour again, until Christ be formed in you." The perfect therefore and men bring forth at once, that is, they bring the word of faith conceived to works. But the soul which conceives and keeps in the womb and does not bring forth is called a woman. Whence: The pains of childbirth have come upon her, and there is not strength to bring forth in her. This one therefore, when two strive among themselves and bring forth scandals, is struck and scandalized, so that she casts away the word of faith which she had faintly conceived, not yet formed. For in some the word is formed, in some not formed. Whence: "Until Christ be formed in you." For Christ is the Word of God. He therefore who struck it out shall suffer loss. Of the losses of doctors therefore the Apostle says: If any man's work burn, he shall suffer loss etc. And the Lord himself in the Gospel: What doth it profit a man, if he gain the whole world, and lose his own soul? Whence it seems to be shown that certain sins pertain to loss, yet not to destruction, because he who has suffered loss is said to be saved, though by fire. Whence John says that certain sins are unto death. But which are unto death, which not unto death, cannot easily be discerned: for "who can understand sins?" But when it is related that on five pounds other five were gained, and on two, two, he who loses the reward of this gain is said to be struck with loss, as he who gave a cause of scandal to the weaker and womanly soul. And he shall give according as her husband shall lay upon him, and he shall give with honour to the soul of the learner. The husband is the master, Christ, or he who for Christ is the doctor of souls. He therefore shall suffer loss who contends "to the subverting of the hearers", for the soul which did not yet have a formed infant; which can be taken of the scandal of a catechumen. It can also be that he who hurt her may instruct and restore to the soul what she lost, and with honour and modesty, namely with meekness, not with strife, as when he brought the scandal. But when it was formed, he shall give life for life. The formed infant can be seen as the word of God in the heart of the soul which has received the grace of baptism, or which has received the word of God more evidently and clearly. He therefore who struck shall render life for life at the day of judgment, namely before that judge who can destroy both soul and body in hell. As one who is conscious to himself of so great a scandal, let him lay down his soul for the soul of the one scandalized, and give his labour even unto death how she may be restored to the faith. Let him lay down eye for eye: if he hurt the eye of the soul, that is, troubled its understanding, let his eye be taken away from him who is over the Church, that is, his understanding. If he hurt the tooth, which, receiving the food of the word of God, was wont to break it small or grind it with the grinders, that it might send on a fine sense to the belly of the soul; if he has troubled and pulled out this tooth, so that by its grinding the soul cannot receive the word of God finely and spiritually, his tooth shall be taken away who does not break small and divide well the foods of the word. For this perhaps it is said of the Lord: "Thou hast broken the teeth of sinners." And elsewhere: "The Lord shall break the grinders of the lions." So therefore the soul is said to be hurt and struck through its members. He demands also hand for hand, and foot for foot. The hand is the power of the soul by which it can hold and grasp something, as its act and strength; and the foot that by which it walks to good or to evil. Because therefore the scandalized soul is cast down not only in faith but also in acts, which are signified by the hands, his hands are taken away with which he does not work well, and the feet with which he does not walk well. He will receive also burning, because he burned the soul and delivered it to hell. Through each of these it is shown that the striker, all his members cut off, is to be cut off from the body of the Church, that the rest seeing it may have fear and not do the like. Therefore the Apostle, when he describes the doctor of the Church, among other things commands "no striker", lest, striking women with child, that is, beginning souls, he should lay down life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth etc. Of such it is said: "Woe to them that are with child, and that give suck in those days", in which even the elect are scandalized, if it can be. Yet it is to be known that it is not for the perfect to be scandalized, but for women or little ones. Whence: If anyone shall scandalize one of these little ones etc.
21.26:
**“If any man strike the eye”** — the gaze of the right understanding of the hearer
**“of his manservant or maidservant, and leave them but one eye, he shall let them go free”** — as unworthy to rule those whom he has hurt
21.27:
