**“Also if he strike out a tooth of his manservant or maidservant,”** — of the discretion by which Scripture is broken small for the food of the soul
**“he shall in like manner make them free.”** — to another master
21.28:
**“If an ox”** — any animal that can wound, the whole by a part
**“with his horn”** — with unbridled speech or action
**“gore a man or a woman,”** — the disciple of any doctor
**“and they die, he shall be stoned:”** — he shall be corrected with hard threatenings
**“and his flesh shall not be eaten,”** — that is: no one shall imitate him; for he eats the flesh of a dead animal who imitates dead works.
21.29:
**“But if the ox”** — the disciple of any doctor
**“was wont to push with his horn yesterday and the day before,”** — this he puts for time past, the part for the whole, after the manner of Scripture
**“and they warned”** — they who see, or are hurt
**“his master, and he did not shut him up,”** — by correcting, by bridling
**“and he shall kill”** — by word or example
**“a man”** — the stronger
**“or a woman”** — the weaker
**“then the ox shall be stoned, and his owner”** — the master
**“also shall be put to death.”**
• by casting out from the Church
• they will show him slain
21.30:
**“And if they set a price upon him,”** — by the penance of satisfaction
**“he shall give for his life”** — to be redeemed
**“whatsoever is laid upon him.”** — by God, or by the prelates of the Church
21.31:
**“a son”** — a disciple
**“or a daughter”** — a woman disciple
**“If he have gored, he shall fall under the like sentence.”** — IF THE OX WAS WONT TO PUSH etc. RABANUS. That is, if the master, that is, the spirit, does not restrain the proud motion of the mind, and it brings destruction to souls, or harm to bodies, the guilt redounds upon the keeper. Whence: The heart of man shall instruct his mouth, and shall add grace to his lips.
21.32:
**“If he assault a bondman or a bond woman,”**
• any one, as a servant obedient to God or to his prelate, or still serving through fear of punishment
• who serves God only for temporal things, and neglects the inheritance of the heavenly fatherland
**“THIRTY SICLES”** — That is, according to the commands of the law, he shall make amends through faith and hope and charity.
**“OF SILVER”** — He shall make good the brightness of the divine word, by which they had been instructed in the faith of the Trinity and the knowledge of the decalogue.
**“and the ox shall be stoned.”** — he shall make good by hard corrections, or he shall be rebuked
21.33:
**“If a man open a pit,”** — the depth of knowledge
**“and dig one,”** — by penetrating the heights of knowledge
**“and cover it not,”** — by covering it before little ones
**“and an ox fall into it”** — a clean mind scandalized
**“or an ass”**
• an unclean one
• the whole by a part: a usual manner of speech
21.34:
**“The owner”** — the searcher of deep things
**“of the pit shall pay the price of the beasts:”** — through worthy penance
**“and that which is dead shall be his own.”**
• that is: it shall be imputed to him
• IF A MAN OPEN etc. To open a pit is to penetrate the secrets of sacred Scripture with strong understanding. But by the ox and the ass, a clean animal and an unclean, the faithful or the unbelieving is taken. He therefore who digs pits, let him cover them, lest an ox or an ass fall in there; that is, he who understands the heights of Scripture, let him cover the lofty senses by silence from those who do not grasp them, lest by the scandal of the mind he slay either a faithful little one, or an unbeliever who could have believed. For from the death of the beasts he owes the price, because he is convicted of having lost it. Whence the guilty one is held to do penance. For whoever, coming to the deep streams of wisdom, does not cover this before the dull hearts of the hearers, is adjudged guilty of punishment, if through his words a clean or unclean mind takes scandal. The pit therefore is to be covered before little ones, that is, deep knowledge is to be veiled.
21.35:
**“If an ox”** — a disciple
**“one man's (ox) another's ox”** — his fellow labouring with him in the field of the Lord
**“of another gore,”** — shall have seduced
**“and he die:”** — fallen into error or fault
**“they shall sell the live ox,”** — namely they shall subject him to penance and punishment
**“and shall divide the price,”** — that is: they shall suffer with one another and do worthy penance
**“and the carcass of that which died they shall part between them.”** — by grieving with the penitent. Whence: "Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not on fire?"
**“IF ONE MAN'S OX GORE ANOTHER MAN'S OX”** — This is not to be kept in the ox alone, but in every beast: for the whole is understood by the part. But this cannot be done with the flesh of slain beasts which are not eaten.
21.36:
**“But if he knew that his ox was wont to push”** — a corrupter of the brethren
**“yesterday and the day before, and did not keep in”** — corrected
**“him his master:”** — the master
**“he shall pay ox for ox,”** — that is: let him be zealous to reform him who was deceived to a sound understanding
**“and shall take the whole carcass.”** — that is: let him transfer all the penance to himself, because the error of the disciple is the master's

22.1:
**“If any man steal”** — by withdrawing from the Church
**“an ox”** — a wise man labouring in the field of the Lord
**“or a sheep,”** — a simple one
**“and kill”** — namely shall have wholly extinguished faith in him
**“or sell it:”** — to heretics or demons
**“he shall restore five oxen for one ox,”**
• the greater the advantage in possession, the greater the grief in the loss
• he shall subject the senses of the body to penance
• for what justice is there according to the letter, that five should be rendered for an ox, four for a sheep
**“and four sheep for one sheep.”**
• that is: let him do penance all the time of his life, which is passed in four seasons; or let him afflict by penance what consists of four elements and four humours.
• IF ANY MAN STEAL etc. STRABO. According to the letter, five oxen are rendered for one ox, four sheep for one sheep, because the ox has five uses, the sheep four. For the ox is sacrificed, ploughs, feeds, gives milk, and its hide too serves divers uses. But the sheep is sacrificed and feeds, and gives milk and wool. But allegorically by the ox any Jew is understood; if any Jew sells him, he shall be subject to the penalty of the law, which is contained in five books. By the sheep, the Christian, who imitates Christ, of whom it is said: He was led as a sheep to the slaughter. If anyone sells him, let him render four sheep, that is, do penance according to the teaching of the four Gospels.
22.2:
**“If a thief, breaking open”** — the heretic
**“a house”** — the Church
**“or undermining it”** — overturning it secretly
**“be found, and be wounded so as to die”** — anathematized
**“he that slew him shall not be”** — he shall be subject to no fault
**“guilty”** — in his breast
**“IF A THIEF BREAKING OPEN”** — AUGUSTINE. If a thief be found digging through and be struck and die, it is not homicide to him. But if the sun be risen upon him, he is guilty etc. It is understood therefore not to pertain to homicide if a thief by night is killed; but if by day, that it pertains. For this is what he says: if the sun be risen upon him etc., because it could be discerned that he had come to steal, not to kill, and therefore he ought not to be killed. This is found also in the ancient secular laws, than which however this is more ancient: namely that a thief by night may be killed with impunity in any manner whatever; but one by day, if he defends himself with a weapon: for then he is more than a thief.
22.3:
**“But if when the sun is risen”** — of truth
**“he did this, he hath committed murder,”** — He shall be guilty of the crime.
**“and he shall die.”** — by eternal death
**“If he have not wherewith to make restitution for the theft,”** — namely something of sound doctrine, by which he may be converted to the faith of Christ
**“he shall be sold.”** — that is: he shall be delivered to the power of the devil and to all torments
22.4:
**“If that which he stole be found with him, alive”** — that is, not wholly departing from the faith
**“either ox, or ass, or sheep:”** — as above
**“he shall restore double.”** — that is: he shall repent in body and mind
22.5:
**“If hurt”** — by invading
**“any man”** — a bishop or priest
**“a field or a vineyard,”** — another's parish
**“and put in his beast”** — carnal appetite, by which he seeks to invade the dignity of another
**“to feed upon that which is other men's:”** — let it lay waste, for the sake of avarice
**“he shall restore the best of whatsoever he hath in his own field, or in his vineyard, according to the estimation of the damage.”** — that is: whatever labour and profit he spends in his own parish, he loses for such an invasion, or shall give it to restore the loss
22.6:
**“If breaking out”** — namely exceeding measure
**“of fire”** — chastisement most sharp or immoderate
**“STACKS OF CORN”** — Tender hearers, not yet reaching the ripeness of fruit; he who rebukes their vices bitterly and without discretion, as it were sends fire among the ears of corn and does not let them come to ripeness.
**“and catch stacks of corn”** — the gatherings of those already advanced
**“or corn standing in the fields,”** — still growing and tending to ripeness
**“he that kindled the fire shall make good the loss.”**
• by repenting and, if he can, by restoring to the former state
• IF A FIRE BREAKING OUT etc. We kindle a fire when we prepare correction for those under us, that we may consume the thorns of vices. But it is to be seen that, while we pursue vices, we do not hurt virtues, and harm before their ripeness those who had begun to bring forth the fruit of good works. He therefore who has committed this, let him do worthy penance, and what he hurt through sloth let him zealously restore.
22.7:
**“If a man”** — a preacher
**“deliver”** — by teaching
**“money unto his friend”** — of the divine word or of faith
**“or any vessel”**
• of right faith and good work
• the books of the ancient fathers, who are the vessels of God
**“to keep, and they be stolen away from him that received them:”** — by the fraudulence of heretics
**“if be found”** — uncorrected
**“the thief,”**
• not a man
• a heretic
**“he shall restore double.”** — he shall repent in body and soul, or shall be punished for ever
22.8:
**“If the thief be not known, the master”**
• who received the money to keep
• the master
**“of the house shall be brought to the gods,”** — the priests or the catholic doctors
**“and shall swear that he did not lay his hand upon his neighbour's goods,”** — by his own wickedness
22.9:
**“To do any fraud,”** — by subverting someone of the flock of the Lord
**“either in ox,”** — as above
**“or in ass,”** — in a foolish one
**“or sheep, or raiment,”** — of the works of the virtues
**“or any thing that may bring damage: the cause of both parties to the gods”** — of the accuser and the accused
**“shall come: and if they give judgment, he shall restore double”**
• as above
• namely he shall fully discharge faith and confession, that he who strayed through understanding too little may, being fully instructed, be faithful in all things.
22.10:
**“If a man”** — Christ, or a higher prelate
**“deliver to his neighbour”** — to a bishop or priest
**“ass,”** — an unclean one
**“ox,”** — a clean one
**“sheep,”** — a simple one
**“or any beast,”** — a dull one
**“to custody,”** — spiritual
**“and it die,”** — shall have wholly departed from the faith
**“or be hurt,”** — scandalized in something
**“or be taken”** — deceived
**“by enemies,”** — heretics, demons
**“and no man saw it:”** — because it was done secretly
22.11:
**“There shall be an oath between them,”** — for clearing suspicion
**“that he did not put forth his hand to his neighbour's goods:”** — who committed it to him
**“and the owner shall accept of the oath;”** — the devotion; but his good zeal also shall restore him to eternal life.
**“and he shall not be compelled to make restitution.”** — because he is innocent
22.12:
**“But if it were taken away by stealth,”** — while the father slept
**“he shall make the loss good to the owner.”** — because he ought to have kept it
22.13:
**“If it were eaten by a beast,”** — incorporated into the devil
**“let him bring”**
• lest the whole be devoured
• let him at once pour out prayers for him, and admonish him and be zealous to heal him
**“to him”** — the Lord
**“that which was slain, and he shall not make restitution.”** — because he did what he could
22.14:
**“If a man borrow of his neighbour any of these things,”** — as if a bishop should have corrupted another's cleric or parishioner
**“and it be hurt”** — in part
**“or die”** — in the whole
**“the owner”** — who received the loan
**“not being present,”** — namely negligent
**“he shall be obliged to make restitution.”** — IF A MAN BORROW etc. We ask a loan of our neighbour when for an eternal reward we take up the care of the Lord's flock. But if we always set the fear of God, as of one demanding the money, before the eyes of the heart, we are as it were always in his presence. Whence: "Knowing the fear of the Lord, we use persuasion to men." And elsewhere: As before God, in Christ we speak. The death or hurt of the beast therefore is not imputed to the shepherd if he has carried on its care vigorously, and as with God present; otherwise he shall be compelled to make good the loss. Whence: He shall not go out from thence till he repay the last farthing.
22.15: **“But if the owner be present,”** — because he used what diligence he could
22.16:
**“If a man seduce a virgin not yet espoused”**
• by expounding according to the sense of a party
• canonical knowledge not yet expounded by another
**“and lie with her: he shall endow her”** — because unless he has acquiesced through the catholic faith, it will not be lawful to enjoy union with her.
**“HE SHALL ENDOW HER”** — The historical sense of a passage, from which the discourse is born. If therefore the historical sense builds up the kingdom of charity and scatters that of covetousness, there is no need for it to be expounded allegorically. Yet the reader ought to honour the passage with the dowry of right faith and leave it untouched by his own exposition.
22.18:
**“Wizards”** — the fellow workers and helpers of the devil
**“WIZARDS”** — Those who act by the illusions of the magic art and devilish feignings, or heretics, because they are to be excommunicated from the fellowship of the faithful who truly live, until the sorcery of error die in them.
**“thou shalt not suffer to live.”** — as if: to be living in the Church.
22.19:
**“Whosoever copulateth with a beast”** — that is, shall have been mingled with the vices of the foolish and senseless, whose fellowship separates from God and joins to the devil, which is the worst fornication.
**“dying”** — eternal
22.20:
**“He that sacrificeth”**
• bodily or spiritually
• namely the idolater
**“to gods,”** — to demons, because the gods of the gentiles are devils
**“shall be put to death,”** — let him be excommunicated from the Church, or he shall be punished for ever
**“save only to the Lord.”** — The Lord thy God shalt thou adore, and him only shalt thou serve.
22.21:
**“A stranger”**
• "I am a stranger with thee, and a sojourner as all my fathers were".
• who makes for the heavenly fatherland
**“thou shalt not molest, nor afflict him: for yourselves also were strangers in the land of Egypt.”**
• in the world
• THOU SHALT NOT MOLEST A STRANGER etc. He commends love of neighbour for the compassion of mercy, lest, moved by the goad of fury or avarice, we neglect the law of nature. But what we would that men should do to us, the same let us do to them; and what we would not have done to us, let us not do.
22.22:
**“a widow”** — who at the day of judgment awaits Christ, whom she has not now present.
**“or an orphan”** — to whom the world, his father, is dead, and Babylon, his mother.
22.23:
**“they will cry out”** — in heart
**“to me,”** — who am their defender
**“and I will hear”** — by judging
22.24:
**“And my rage shall be enkindled, and I will strike you with the sword,”** — with the spiritual sword or the material
**“and your wives shall be”** — actions
**“widows, and your children”** — fruits, or according to the letter
22.25:
**“If thou lend money”**
• material or spiritual
• the knowledge of the law
• IF THOU LEND MONEY etc. He warns the preachers of the gospel not to seek beyond what is useful, but, having food and clothing, to be content with these, according to that: "Freely have you received, freely give."
**“to any of my people”**
• the faithful
• the gentile
**“that is poor”** — in spirit
**“that dwelleth with thee”** — in the same faith
**“thou shalt not be hard upon them”** — by exacting immoderately the fruit of what was committed, or of the divine word
**“as an extortioner, nor oppress them with usuries.”** — with any overabundance, because after receiving grace he ought not to be turned back to the observance of the law, because Christ is the end of the law.
22.26:
**“If in pledge”** — the confession of sin
**“of thy neighbour”** — who has sinned against thee
**“thou take”** — namely
**“a garment,”** — with which he is covered against the cold of impiety
**“before sunset”** — before the sun of justice sets for thee through grief of heart
**“IF IN PLEDGE”** — AUGUSTINE. He has put the genus for the species: for it is said as if he had given a pledge of any garment whatever, whereas Scripture testifies by what follows that it speaks specially of him who has no garment but that with which he is covered at night.
*Gregory:* The pledge is the confession of sin. For our neighbour becomes our debtor when he sins something against us, because sins are called debts, according to that: "I forgave thee all the debt, because thou besoughtest me", and "Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors." And we receive a pledge from our debtor when we hold from him who has sinned against us the confession of the sin, by which we are asked to release the sin. For he who confesses sin and asks pardon has as it were already given a pledge for the debt. Which we are commanded to give back before sunset, because before the sun of justice sets for us through grief of heart, we ought to give back the confession of pardon to him from whom we receive the confession of fault, that he who remembers he has offended against us may feel that what he offended has been at once released by us.
22.27:
**“For that same is the only thing wherewith he is covered, the clothing of his body,”** — elsewhere: with which the clothing of his flesh is covered
**“neither hath he any other to sleep in:”** — secure, the sin being released
**“if he cry to me,”** — thou not pardoning
**“I will hear him, because I am compassionate.”** — willing the life of the sinner, not his death
22.28:
**“Of the gods”** — the priests, the doctors, who rule the Church: for though all detraction is pernicious, against them it is more pernicious.
**“thou shalt not speak ill, and the prince of thy people”** — according to the letter; or to Christ, whose government is upon his shoulder
**“THOU SHALT NOT SPEAK ILL OF THE GODS”** — AUGUSTINE. Thou shalt not curse the gods. It is asked whom he called gods: whether the judges who judge the people, as it was said to Moses, who had been given as a god to Pharao, so that by way of explaining it follows: And thou shalt not curse the prince of thy people. Or according to that of the Apostle: For although there be that are called gods, either in heaven or on earth, as there are gods many and lords many; for by adding 'as there are', he wished those to be understood as gods who are even worthily so called, to whom however latria, that is, the service which pertains to religion, is not due, but to the one true God, who is God to us? But these are forbidden to be cursed, not commanded to be honoured with sacrifices or any services of latria.
22.29:
**“thy tithes”** — the perfections of works
**“and thy firstfruits”** — the beginning will to do
**“Thou shalt not delay”** — God loveth a cheerful giver.
**“to pay:”** — to consecrate to divine grace
**“the firstborn of thy sons”** — the beginning of works
**“THY TITHES”** — ISIDORE. By the firstfruits of the crops or of the firstborn are shown the first beginnings of good works, or the good will, which is prior to the work, which the Pelagians offend by attributing it to themselves. But God, when he commands it to be offered to him by us, shows that it pertains to his grace. But in the tithes the number ten signifies perfection, because number grows up to it. And therefore, as in the firstfruits the beginnings of our wills, so in the tithes we are commanded to refer the completions of our works to God, by whom both the beginning of good work and the effect of perfection are given.
22.30:
**“with the firstborn of thy oxen also and sheep”** — the strong and the simple
**“Thou shalt do the same:”** — the whole present life, in which we ought to beget good works to offer to the Lord in the octave of the resurrection
**“seven days let it be with its dam,”** — the Church
**“the eighth day”** — of the resurrection
**“thou shalt give it to me.”** — who demands it
22.31:
**“You shall be holy men to me:”** — removed from all worldly action
**“the flesh”** — the books of heretics, consecrated to demons, or any carnal men, that is, corrupted by idolatry or heresy or by human conversation
**“that beasts”** — heretics or demons
**“have tasted of before,”** — deceived
**“you shall not eat,”**
• by incorporating into the members of Christ
• the faithful must not communicate with the table of devils
**“but shall cast it to the dogs.”** — to the fellowship of the unclean, barking against the Church; whence: "Let him be to thee as the heathen and publican."

23.1:
**“Thou shalt not receive the voice of a lie”** — by consenting, or by speaking
**“neither shalt thou join”** — by associating thyself with him
**“… hand”** — thy work
**“thy (hand) to bear false witness for a wicked person.”** — "A false witness shall not be unpunished"
23.2:
**“Thou shalt not follow”** — as if: do not defend thyself because thou sinnest with many, or say that it is therefore no sin
**“the multitude”** — the people; but namely the doctors, who, though they be fewer, are yet of sounder counsel
**“to do evil: neither in judgment (shalt thou yield) to the opinion of the most part”** — while thou sittest as judge
23.3: **“Neither shalt thou favour a poor man in judgment.”** — while thou sittest as judge
23.4:
**“If thou meet thy enemy's ox or ass going astray, bring it back to him.”**
• These things are so plain of themselves that they would be obscured by exposition.
• As if he should say: Love your enemies, and so on.
• NEITHER SHALT THOU FAVOUR A POOR MAN etc. Namely, that thou favour not the poor man against justice for the sake of mercy. Mercy is good, but it ought not to be against judgment. And Scripture calls judgment that which is just. But lest anyone think from this sentence that God forbids mercy, there follows fittingly: If thou meet thy enemy's ox etc. As if: show mercy even toward thy enemies, when thy power is free from judging. For when thou bringest back thy enemy's straying ox and restorest it, thou dost not sit as judge among any.
23.5:
**“If thou see the ass of him that hateth thee lie underneath his burden, thou shalt not pass by,”** — by neglecting
**“but shalt lift him up with him.”** — Do good to them that hate you.
23.6:
**“Thou shalt not go aside”** — by accepting persons
**“in the poor man's judgment.”** — Judge right things, ye sons of men.
23.7:
**“Thou shalt fly lying.”** — "Thou wilt destroy all that speak a lie".
**“LYING”** — The Lord loves truth and judgment, and exhorts his people to carry these out, "because he is not a respecter of persons".
**“The innocent and just person thou shalt not put to death:”** — because the Lord will avenge the blood of his servants
**“because I abhor the wicked.”** — not the just
23.8:
**“Neither shalt thou take bribes”**
• in judgment or in testimony
• Blessed is he who "shaketh his hands from all bribes"
**“which blind”** — with inward blindness
**“even the wise,”** — Nothing is more wicked than the covetous man; nothing more unjust than to love money.
**“and pervert the words of the just.”** — as they think
23.9:
**“A stranger”** — who, while he is in this world, is absent from the Lord
**“thou shalt not molest, for you know the hearts of strangers:”** — namely how easily they are saddened, having nothing whereby to console themselves
**“for you also were strangers in the land of Egypt.”** — Let each one weigh from his own condition how he should have mercy on others. Whence: Forgive, and you shall be forgiven etc.
23.11:
**“But the seventh year thou shalt let it alone,”** — thou shalt sow indeed, but shalt not gather
**“and suffer it to rest, that the poor of thy people may eat, and whatsoever shall be left, let the beasts of the field eat it:”** — boars, stags
**“so shalt thou do with thy vineyard and thy oliveyard.”**
• Namely thou shalt prune and till, but shalt not gather the fruit.
• SIX YEARS THOU SHALT SOW etc. AUGUSTINE. It is asked what the poor gather, if in the seventh year the land is so spared that it is not even sown. For what is said: The poor of thy nation shall eat, does not pertain to the vineyard and the oliveyard, because from unsown land they can take nothing, where crops cannot spring. For of the vineyard and the oliveyard he says afterward that the like is to be done. Therefore that is understood of the tilled fields, which serve for corn. Or is it to be taken thus: Six years thou shalt sow thy land, and shalt gather; but the seventh thou shalt not gather; so that 'thou shalt sow' is understood even though it is not said, so that sowing and gathering pertain to the six years, but to the seventh, letting alone what was sown? For what will the poor have from it, whose leavings he gave even to the wild beasts, namely to those which can feed on those crops, that is, boars, stags, and such like? Which yet would not be said, except for the sake of signification. For God has no care for oxen. Which is not so understood as if he does not feed those which "neither sow, nor reap", but because it is no care of his to move man by a precept how he should look to his ox: how much less then is it his care to give precepts about wild beasts, since he himself feeds them with the riches of nature, who feeds them also through the other six years, when the things sown are gathered?
• SIX YEARS THOU SHALT SOW THY GROUND etc. In the number six the perfection of works is expressed, in the number seven the rest of souls. Well therefore are we commanded to sow our land six years and gather its crops, because in the present life, which consists of six ages, we ought to till the land of our flesh and sow in it the seeds of the virtues, that in the future we may receive eternal life. And that the poor of the people and the beasts of the field are commanded to eat what grows in the seventh year from our past labour signifies that through the service of almsgiving and charity a reward is prepared in the future. Which the vineyard and the oliveyard also, that is, the works of grace and mercy, prepare. If therefore we are beneficent not only to friends but also to beasts, that is, to enemies, in the future, when there will no longer be time for working, we shall obtain rewards. Whence: "He who soweth in blessings shall also reap of blessings" eternal life.
23.12:
**“Six days shalt thou labour,”** — all the time of the present life, in which there must be labour
**“the seventh day thou shalt cease”** — in the rest of the soul loosed from the body
**“that thy ox may rest”**
• which has borne the labour of working strongly
• the disciplined
**“and thy ass”**
• the dull
• of whom it is said: Issachar a strong ass bowed his shoulder to carry.
**“and the son of thy handmaid may be refreshed”** — of the Church, which serves us as a handmaid; or of the synagogue, which serves with her children: for many Jews were converted to the Lord.
**“and the stranger.”** — the gentile, taken from the wild olive and grafted into the good olive; or he who was in the world as a stranger and sojourner.
23.13:
**“Keep all things that I have said to you. And by the name”** — but by his own name
**“of strange gods you shall not swear,”** — In the Gospel the oath is wholly forbidden.
**“neither shall it be heard out of your mouth.”** — AND BY THE NAME OF GODS etc. He permits swearing by his own name, not that it is good to swear. But he knew that men were prone to swearing: he does not wish them to swear by the names of strange gods and be led by frequent swearing to their worship. So too God does not approve victims, yet would rather they be sacrificed to him than to idols.
23.14:
**“Three times every year”** — Namely in April, in June and in September
**“you shall celebrate feasts to me.”**
• The Pasch, Pentecost, Scenopegia
• THREE TIMES etc. Worshipping the faith of the holy Trinity: for at the Pasch the Son is sacrificed, at Pentecost the Spirit is given, at Scenopegia the power of the Father's majesty is declared.
23.15:
**“the feast of unleavened bread”** — in which Christ is sacrificed
**“Thou shalt keep. Seven days shalt thou eat unleavened bread, as I commanded thee, in the time of the month of new corn, when thou didst come forth out of Egypt:”** — of April, when, according to Josephus, they gathered ears of corn, and parching them with fire and rubbing them with their hands they offered the firstfruits to the Lord; of which they laid a little on the sacrifice, the rest was the priest's; which done, everyone was free to reap.
**“thou shalt not appear empty before me.”** — of good works
23.16:
**“And the feast”** — This was in June, when the loaves of the firstfruits were offered.
**“of the month of the firstfruits of thy work, whatsoever thou hast sown”** — or: shalt have sown
**“in the field. The feast also in the end of the year, when thou hast gathered in all thy corn out of the field.”** — Three times every year etc. That is, all the time of the present life and in the confession of the holy Trinity, through faith, hope and charity, you shall show forth the services of good works to God your creator. For we celebrate the Pasch in the month of new corn when, freed from Egyptian bondage by the blood of the spotless lamb, we pass through the spiritual waters from the old man into the new, not in the oldness of the letter, but in the newness of the spirit, by which we come into the land of promise through the grace of Christ. And we celebrate the feast of the month of firstfruits when we consecrate to the Lord the will of our works and the firstfruits of our words. The feast also in the end of the year, when, the crops gathered, that is, the fruits of the virtues, we strive to come to the end of life and the entrance of the heavenly kingdom, keeping the remembrance in tabernacles for seven days, because we acknowledge that through all the time of the present life we are sojourners, and seek rest not here but in the future, taking diligent care not to appear empty in the sight of God.
**“THE FEAST ALSO IN THE END OF THE YEAR”** — Namely when the crops are ripe, when the fruits of the whole year have been gathered, namely in September, which the Hebrews call Thesseri, the Macedonians Ytheneos; at the beginning of which the Jews, keeping holiday, sound the trumpet more than in all the months, and offer more; in which is the day of expiations, and the day of scenopegia on the fifteenth day, which is the feast of Tabernacles.
23.17: **“Thrice a year shall all thy males appear before the Lord thy God.”** — For females ought to be kept hidden.
23.18:
**“Thou shalt not sacrifice upon leaven”** — of malice and wickedness
**“the blood of thy victim,”** — that is: thou shalt offer a pure sacrifice without corruption.
**“neither shall the fat remain”** — that is, the fatness of good works and the fruitfulness of virtues, or spiritual understanding
**“of my solemnity until the morning.”** — on the day of judgment, because then there will be no place for working, for striving after virtues, or for searching the Scripture
23.19:
**“the firstfruits of the corn of thy ground”** — the beginnings of good works
**“Thou shalt carry to the house of the Lord thy God.”** — because there is no place of true sacrifice outside the catholic Church
**“Thou shalt not boil”**
• Josephus says it is not lawful for it to be killed before the eighth day.
• O Herod, O Jews
• punish by the passion
**“a kid”**
• And the Septuagint: a lamb
• Christ, who is a kid to the Jews, a lamb to us
**“in the milk of his dam.”**
• in infancy, or at the time of conception
• THOU SHALT NOT BOIL A KID etc. AUGUSTINE. How it is to be understood according to the proper sense of the words I know not whether it can be found. For if we take it that a lamb is forbidden to be boiled in milk for the sake of some signification, there is no custom of boiling so. But if in the days when it is suckled, which of the Jews ever kept this, not to boil a lamb unless it had ceased to suck? And what is in the milk of his dam, as if, even if this were understood, it could be boiled without transgression of this precept if, its mother having died when it was born, it were suckled by another ewe? That the precept is for the sake of some signification, therefore, no one doubts. But even the things that can be done in observance were not commanded so without cause. For they signify something: but how this is to be observed according to the proper sense of the words either does not exist or does not appear. Yet I approve the understanding of it concerning Christ, who was foretold by this prophecy not to be killed by the Jews as an infant, when Herod, seeking to kill him, did not find him; so that 'thou shalt boil', which is said, pertains to the fire of the passion, that is, tribulation. That too perhaps is not absurd which others say, that this was commanded by way of prophecy, that the good Israelites should not join themselves to the wicked Jews, by whom Christ suffered as a lamb in the milk of his mother, that is, at that time in which he was conceived. For women are said to gather milk from the time they conceive: but Christ was born, the ninth month completed and the tenth begun, on the eighth of the kalends of January, and was conceived in the first month, namely on the eighth of the kalends of April, which was also the time of his passion, in the milk of his mother, that is, on the day on which he was conceived. Or: upon those still little and sucking thou shalt not bring the passion; as if it were said to Christ, who spared such disciples still. Whence: "If therefore you seek me, let these go their way." Whence the Evangelist adds: "That the word might be fulfilled which he said: Of them whom thou hast given me, I have not lost any one." Whence it appears that they, if they had suffered then, would have perished; but afterward they suffered, not as lambs in milk, but as rams in the flock.
*Strabo:* Morally. The kid, that is, the sinner, is not to be boiled in the milk of his mother, that is, softened by flatteries, but to be sharply rebuked and reproved.
23.20:
**“Behold I will send my angel,”**
• Josue
• Behold I will send etc. RABANUS. Josue signifies the leader of the people, who is therefore called an angel, because he is sent to announce the will of the Lord: for angelos in Greek is called messenger.
23.21:
**“Take notice of him, and hear his voice,”** — Whence: As we obeyed Moses, so will we obey thee.
**“and do not think him one to be contemned: for he will not forgive when thou hast sinned, and my name is in him.”** — because he was of the children of Israel, which is interpreted 'a man seeing God', or because he was called Jesus. But mystically our saviour and redeemer can be understood, who is the angel of great counsel, and the messenger of his own and his Father's will, in whom the name of God truly is, because he is true God.
23.22: **“But if thou wilt hear his voice, and do all that I speak, I will be an enemy to thy enemies, and will afflict them that afflict thee.”** — I WILL BE AN ENEMY etc. GREGORY. The root of all evil is pride, of which it is said: Pride is the beginning of all sin. Its first offspring are the seven principal vices: vainglory, envy, anger, sadness, avarice, gluttony, lust. And because our Redeemer grieved that we were taken captive by these seven vices of pride, he came full of the Spirit of sevenfold grace to the spiritual battle of deliverance.
23.23:
**“And my angel shall go before thee, and shall bring thee in unto the Amorrhite, and the Hethite, and the Pherezite, and the Chanaanite, and the Hevite, and the Jebusite, whom I will destroy.”** — AND MY ANGEL SHALL GO BEFORE THEE etc. RABANUS. Josue brought the Israelite people into the land of promise, casting out seven nations, and destroying their idols and altars. Mystically, the true God exterminates these nations with their images when he expels from our hearts the seven principal vices and every idol of the enemy, that we may securely possess the land of our nature.
**“WHOM I WILL DESTROY”** — JOHN CHRYSOSTOM. Each vice has in our heart its own dwelling, which claiming for itself, in the recess of our soul it exterminates Israel, that is, the contemplation of the highest things, and does not cease to oppose. For virtues cannot dwell with vices; but when the vices have been overcome by the Israelites, that is, by the virtues, the place which the spirit of concupiscence or fornication possessed, chastity will hold. That which fury had seized, patience will claim. That which sadness working death had occupied, saving gladness full of joy will possess. That which sloth laid waste, fortitude will till. That which pride trod down, humility will honour. And so, each vice being expelled, their places, that is, their dispositions, the contrary virtues will possess, which are called the children of Israel, that is, souls seeing God; who, when they have expelled all the passions of the heart, are to be believed not so much to have gained others' possessions as to have recovered their own; because, according to the old tradition, the sons of Sem received by lot the land of the Chanaanites in the division of the world, which the Chanaanites possessed by violence. Whence by the just judgment of God they were driven out. The will of the Lord also assigned the possession of our heart not to vices but to virtues, which, after the transgression of Adam, when the vices grew insolent, as the Chanaanites, were driven from their own region. But when through the grace of God they are restored by our diligence and our labour, they do not so much occupy another's land as receive back their own.
23.24: **“Thou shalt not adore their gods, nor serve them. Thou shalt not do their works, but shalt destroy them, and break their statues.”** — that all memory of them may be destroyed
23.25:
**“And you shall serve the Lord your God, that I may bless”** — "For the lawgiver shall give a blessing; they shall go from virtue to virtue: the God of gods shall be seen in Sion".
**“your bread”** — of the word of God
**“and your waters,”** — of doctrine
**“and may take away sickness”** — of sin
**“from the midst of thee.”**
• the heart
• I WILL BLESS YOUR BREAD AND YOUR WATERS etc. AUGUSTINE. Another text: I will bless thy bread and thy wine etc. Although these promises can also be understood spiritually, yet when they are understood according to the temporal happiness of men, they pertain to the Old Testament; so that whatever precepts, except those which signify something in a sacrament, are found to pertain to good morals, the same; yet the promises are carnal and earthly. But in the future rewards will be given pertaining to the New Testament, which the wicked will not receive.
23.26:
**“There shall not be one fruitless nor barren”**
• without the fruit of virtues and works
• On account of men's sins, barrenness of women and of animals and of the land itself often comes about.
**“in thy land:”** — the body
**“the number of thy days”**
• Wicked men shall not live out half their days.
• not of nights, namely that thou mayest die "old and full of days"
**“I will fill.”** — namely in the stability of eternity
23.27:
**“I will send my fear before thee,”** — that is: before thee, to terrify the people
**“and will destroy all the people to whom thou shalt come: and will turn the backs of all thy enemies before thee.”** — not according to the letter, but it signifies the terrors of the enemies, with which God harries their foes.
23.28:
**“Sending out hornets before, that shall drive away the Hevite, and the Chanaanite, and the Hethite, before thou come in.”**
• SENDING OUT HORNETS etc. AUGUSTINE. I will send wasps etc. God promises this, and the book of Wisdom says it was fulfilled, where it says: He sent wasps, forerunners of his host. But we do not read that it was done either in the time of Moses, or under Josue, or under the judges, or under the kings. Therefore perhaps the wasps are to be understood as the stings of fear by which the nations were harried, that they might give way to the children of Israel. For God speaks, in whose speech, if something is said figuratively which was not fulfilled according to the proper sense, it does not hinder the faith of the history, in which the truthfulness of the narrator is seen; as neither is the narrative of the Evangelists hindered according to the proper sense if something is said figuratively by Christ.
• I WILL NOT CAST THEM OUT FROM THY FACE etc. STRABO. These nations signify the vices, which are extinguished in the saints neither together nor at one time, lest the monsters of the earth be multiplied, that is, lest they be lifted up into pride, and vainglory, and the like. For when the saints fight against the greater vices and conquer, they leave the lesser, and these are permitted to rule, lest through elation they fall more grievously. Whence a sting of the flesh was given to Paul for the guarding of humility.
**“THE SEPTUAGINT”** — Another text: I will send wasps before thee, and it shall cast out the Amorrhites etc. He turns from the plural to the singular number. And it is understood that the wasp shall cast out the Amorrhites, namely as the locust, as the frog; not that there is one, but by the singular the plural is understood.
23.29: **“I will not cast them out from thy face in one year: lest the land be brought into a wilderness, and the beasts multiply against thee.”** — God would not destroy all the nations at once, lest, the land being brought to a wilderness, the beasts should rage more cruelly against them.
23.31:
**“And I will set thy bounds from the Red Sea”** — which is in the East
**“to the sea of the Palestines”** — namely the Mediterranean, which is the Great Sea and the Tyrrhene Sea
**“and from the desert”** — beyond Bethlehem there is only one little city, which is called Thecue, otherwise Theone: after it at once follows the waste of the desert.
**“to the river”** — the Euphrates
**“I will deliver into your hands”** — elsewhere: thy
**“the inhabitants of the land,”** — demons or vices
**“and will drive them out from before you.”** — that they may not dare to resist
23.32:
**“Thou shalt not enter into league with them”** — No participation of justice with iniquity, nor of the temple of God with idols
**“nor with their gods”** — idols or demons
23.33:
**“Let them not dwell in thy land”** — body or soul tilled by God
**“lest perhaps they make thee sin against me, if thou serve their gods:”** — The Greek has duleuses, not latreuses; whence it is understood that dulia also is due to God as Lord, but latria to none but God, as God.
**“which undoubtedly will be a scandal to thee.”** — of the soul

24.1:
**“And he said to Moses:”** — not the Lord, but the angel who spoke with Moses in the figure of God
**“Come up to the Lord, thou, and Aaron, Nadab, and Abiu,”** — namely four, in whom the men of the gospel are signified
**“and seventy of the ancients of Israel,”** — who, helped by the grace of the Holy Ghost, fulfil the ten of the law, and go up to contemplation
**“and you shall adore afar off.”**
• COME UP TO THE LORD, THOU, AND AARON etc. AUGUSTINE. Up to: The people answered with one voice, saying: All the words of the Lord which the Lord hath spoken we will do and will hear. Up to this place of Scripture the justifications are understood, which were given to the people to be observed. And they begin, as far as the very words of Scripture show, where this name of justifications took its start, from the Hebrew servant, whose ear is bored at the post. In all which justifications it is to be considered that they cannot be drawn to the conduct of life and the conversation of good morals. For in them are many sacraments, signifying something rather than instructing our life. And the Latins say that those are justifications which the Greeks call diocemata.
• THOU, AND AARON etc. STRABO. Moses and Aaron and Nadab and Abiu: by these four the men of the gospel are signified, namely those who follow the gospel precepts. But by the seventy (which consists of seven taken ten times, or of ten multiplied seven times) are signified those who, helped by the grace of the Holy Ghost, fulfilling the ten of the law, make for the contemplation of the Creator. Or according to the letter, those of whom it is said: Take to thee seventy men etc., of whom were Eldad and Medad.
24.2:
**“And Moses alone”** — because the unity of the Church alone deserves to see God
**“shall come up to the Lord,”** — He searches out the height of contemplation, and the sentence of the will on high.
**“but they shall not come nigh; neither shall the people come up with him.”**
• Weak hearers who are entangled in earthly things: for such cannot reach the knowledge of the divine law.
• AND MOSES ALONE etc. RABANUS. First it is commanded that Moses and Aaron, Nadab and Abiu, and the seventy ancients go up to the Lord. And at once it is added that Moses alone go up to the Lord, the others not come nigh, but adore afar off. Where morally we are instructed to weigh our strength, and not to reach for the citadel of contemplation beyond our power, but as far as the divine clemency calls and the rule of Scripture invites.
*Gregory:* Moses, that he might receive the sublime precepts of God, climbs the heights; and that he may penetrate the inner things, he is hidden from outward tumults; because holy men who are compelled by necessity to serve outward offices always zealously flee to the secrets of the heart. And there they go up the summit of inmost thought, and receive the law as on the mountain, while, the tumults of temporal actions set aside, on the height of their contemplation they search out the sentence of the will on high.
24.3:
**“So Moses came and told the people all the words of the Lord, and all the judgments: and all the people answered with one voice: We will do all the words of the Lord, which he hath spoken.”** — The Septuagint: we will do and will hear.
**“WE WILL DO”** — AUGUSTINE. It is to be noted that the people again answered: All the words which the Lord hath spoken we will do and will hear, when the order seems to require: we will hear and will do. But it is a wonder if some sense does not lie hid here. For if 'we will hear' is put for 'we will understand', one must first render to the words of God the service of doing, that it may lead, by the merit of devotion, to the understanding of the things done at his command. But it is to be seen whether this people is like that son who said to his father who bade him: I go into my vineyard, and went not. For "the Gentiles" who wholly despised God, afterward justified by the obedience of one, "who followed not after justice, have attained to justice".
24.4:
**“And Moses wrote all the words of the Lord:”** — not the ten precepts, which were handed down on the tables and written, but others
**“and rising in the morning he built an altar”** — It is understood that the altar built of twelve stones signified that the people itself is the altar of God, as it is the temple of God.
**“to the Lord at the foot of the mount, and twelve titles according to the twelve tribes of Israel.”** — Perhaps twelve altars. But in another translation it is read that one altar was built of twelve stones.
24.5:
**“And he sent young men of the children of Israel,”**
• who have overcome the wicked one
• not boys, not old men, of whom levity hinders the one, weakness the other
• perhaps Nadab and Abiu, because the priests had not yet been chosen from the tribe of Levi
**“and they offered holocausts, and sacrificed pacific victims”** — sacrificing themselves wholly, and therefore renouncing the world altogether
**“to the Lord, twelve calves.”** — They signify the twelve apostles, who filled the world with the lowings of preaching; or the one Christ, who by the faith of the Trinity filled the four parts of the world.
24.6:
**“Then Moses took half of the blood, and put it into bowls:”** — because by the blood of Christ the vessels of the Church, that is, the apostles and their followers, were redeemed and consecrated
**“BOWLS”** — Cratera is named from joining together, because the ancients made themselves cups by joining rods together: for cratin in Greek is said for to be joined. And crateres are cups having handles.
**“and the rest he poured”** — to signify that no sacrifice pleases God unless it is offered in the faith of the passion of Christ, and consecrated by it
**“upon the altar.”**
• the Church, which is the altar and temple of God
• TOOK etc. AUGUSTINE. It is to be noted that Scripture now for the first time says plainly that Moses sacrificed, since the people was brought out of Egypt. For it was said first of Jethro, though ambiguously. And it is to be observed that the book of the Testament is read with the blood of the victim, in which the justifications were written. For it is plain afterward that the decalogue was written on tables of stone.
24.7:
**“And taking the book”** — Because in it is contained the right of the law written, which was set forth to the people to observe.
**“of the covenant,”** — of the law by which we are bound in covenant to God
**“he read it in the hearing of the people: and they said: All things that the Lord hath spoken we will do,”** — The Septuagint: we will do and will hear; they answer not otherwise the third time
24.8:
**“And he took the blood and sprinkled it upon the people,”** — signifying that the people was to be washed by the blood of Christ
**“and he said: This is the blood”** — Every testament is confirmed by the death of the testator: the Gospel also is confirmed in the blood of Christ.
**“of the covenant”** — as if the testament will be confirmed by the death of Christ, which is signified in this blood
24.9:
**“Then Moses and Aaron, Nadab and Abiu went up,”** — In the number four the four gospels are signified, and the four parts of the world that were to believe through the gospels.
**“and seventy of the ancients of Israel”** — who pertain to the Holy Ghost
24.10:
**“And they saw the God of Israel: and under his feet as it were a work of sapphire stone”** — in which the heavenly life is signified
**“UNDER HIS FEET”** — God is not contained in a place, nor does he set his members in the posture of a body, as it belongs to our body to sit, lie, stand, and the like, which are of the body only. But God is a spirit. That therefore he showed himself spiritually, or expressed himself bodily by signs, is not his substance appearing, which is what he himself is; but the taking of visible forms is subject to his omnipotence.
24.11:
**“Neither did he lay his hand upon those of the children of Israel, that retired afar off,”** — that is, he did not hide himself from them: for God to put his hand is to hide himself that he be not seen; whence he says to Moses: I will put my hand till I pass etc.
**“and they saw God, and they did eat and drink.”** — they eat and drink in the place of God: signifying sweetness and fullness in the kingdom of eternity: "For blessed are they that hunger and thirst after justice, etc."
24.12:
**“And the Lord said to Moses:”** — because the law is grasped only by the more perfect, and is preached to one nation
**“Come up to me”** — because the law is lofty, hidden from human doctrines
**“into the mount,”** — of the height of the law
**“and be there:”**
• abide
• that, abiding with me, thou mayest hear more freely what thou art to teach below
• COME UP TO ME INTO THE MOUNT etc. BEDE. Being about to speak of the figure of the tabernacle, its vessels and utensils, let us first look attentively at the situation of the place and the circumstances of things: For all things happened to them in figure etc.: for they are written for us, etc. The Lord therefore, about to give the law to Moses, first invites him to the top of the mountain, that, abiding with him on high, he may hear more freely the things he is to teach when he returns to the lower places; and may gather from the height of the place how lofty, how hidden from human doctrines is the law which he receives, and that it can be understood or kept only by those who have separated themselves from earthly contagions by living more loftily. Whence he bids the people wait below until he returns, to suggest that the secrets of the law are heavenly, and to be grasped only by the perfect; yet let not the weak despair, if they listen to the greater, according to that: "Thy justice is as the mountains of God." In the Gospel also the Lord called together the heralds of grace on a mountain and instructed them, appearing to them on a mountain after the resurrection, and sending them to preach to the whole world: "Going", he says, "teach ye all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost" etc. But because the law was to be committed to one people only, the grace of the Gospel to be preached to all, Moses alone goes up to receive the law; but the teaching of the Gospel the apostles all heard together, set on the mountain with the Lord, the crowds also listening. The coming of the Holy Ghost also, by which the truth of the Gospel has now been given more manifestly, not the apostles only, but a very great crowd of the faithful received in the upper room of mount Sion, in the division of various tongues, that it might be signified that the Church throughout the world would speak God in the tongues of all nations.
**“and I will give thee tables of stone,”** — because it is to be kept by the strong with fixed intention; and when their examples are set before us for imitation, the law is shown as it were written in stone. Hence it is that Daniel saw a stone cut out without hands, and Peter says: Be you also as living stones built up, a spiritual house etc.
**“and the law,”** — in them
**“and the commandments which I have written: that thou mayst teach the children of Israel.”** — AND I WILL GIVE THEE etc. BEDE. Like this is that: "Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you." Neither Moses, therefore, nor the apostles, nor anyone, ought to teach other things than what the Lord taught and prescribed by the decree of his counsel to be observed, in which he willed us to have eternal life; as nothing of these ought to be passed over, but all that he commanded must be committed to the hearers.
24.13:
**“rose up”** — By this it is certain that Josue was among those who went up the mountain.
**“Moses and Josue”** — Christ
**“the minister”** — who came not to destroy the law but to fulfil
**“his”** — of the law
24.14:
**“Said to the ancients: Wait ye here”** — in the plains; namely you who cannot go up into the mountain
**“till we return to you. You have Aaron”**
• the mountain of strength, Christ
• the faith of the incarnation of Christ
**“and Hur”**
• the consolation of the Holy Ghost
• fire or light, that is, the Holy Ghost
**“with you: if any question shall arise,”** — namely if any adversity or temptation shall assail
**“you shall refer it to them.”** — MOSES AND JOSUE ROSE UP etc. AUGUSTINE. Josue, not mentioned among those four, suddenly appears with Moses, and goes up with him to receive the tables of the Law; and suddenly again is hidden, that is, passed over in silence, and Moses received the Law, and he appears again with him. Perhaps it signifies that the New Testament is hidden in the Law, and sometimes appears to those who understand? But that he is already called Jesus: since in the book of Numbers Scripture says that he received this name when they were already near to entering the land of promise, Scripture anticipates by prolepsis, that is, preoccupation, what was done afterward. For all these things were written after they were done; and therefore, when what is now recorded was done, he was not yet called Jesus, but when it was written.
*Bede:* Josue signifies Christ in name and action, who is called the minister of Moses, because Christ came not to destroy the law, but to fulfil. He follows the footsteps of Moses in all things, because he is typically designated in all that Moses wrote, and is found, if he is well sought, as an inseparable companion. Whence: "If you did believe Moses, you would perhaps believe me also."
*Bede:* Aaron is mountain of strength, Hur is interpreted fire or light. Aaron therefore signifies Christ, Hur the Holy Ghost; of the former Isaias says: In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the top of mountains. And the latter appeared upon the apostles in the light of fire. Moses therefore, going up to the Lord, left the mountain of strength and the light of fire in the plains to rule the people. We therefore, if we cannot follow the doctors to contemplation, let us take care that we be not drawn back by any temptation from the neighbourhood of the mountain of God, but insist as we can on the works of the virtues, cleaving steadfastly to the sacraments of Christ, with which we have been imbued; and let us keep undefiled the grace of the Spirit by which we are sealed. And if any question shall assail, let us call on the help of the Redeemer, who is wont through the gift of the Holy Ghost to protect and deliver from all evils. Nor is it to be doubted that, if we persist, through the mountain of strength our lowliness and weakness will be exalted and made stronger than all enemies. Through the light of the Holy Ghost also our ignorance is enlightened, and the mind burns with love of the Creator.
24.15:
**“And when Moses was gone up, a cloud covered”** — the divine protection
**“the mount,”** — AND WHEN MOSES WAS GONE UP etc. BEDE. As the mountain designates the height of perfection which was to be written in the law, so the cloud by which the mountain is covered suggests the grace of divine protection: which each enjoys the more, the more he goes up with the eyes of the heart unveiled to search out the wonders of the Law. For the cloud covered not only the mountain which Moses went up, but also overshadowed the people walking through the deserts, which could not go up to the higher places. Whence: "He spread a cloud for their protection" etc. Because the Lord protects all who fear him, the little with the great, with heavenly blessing.
24.16:
**“And the glory dwelt”** — the enlightening
**“of God upon Sinai”** — 'my amphora' or 'my measure', because the Law of God is the perfect rule of living, and renders to each according to his works
**“covering”** — from the temptation of the devil
**“it with a cloud”** — with the divine protection
**“six days:”** — because in the law of God we are commanded to work six days
**“and the seventh day”**
• because on the seventh day we are commanded to rest
• because after the perfection of works the law promises eternal rest
**“the Lord called him”** — because to Moses and the other clean of heart, by the grace of God revealing, the obscurity of the heavenly sacraments is accessible. Whence: "Come ye to him and be enlightened."
**“out of the midst of the darkness.”**
• namely of the obscurity of the sacraments
• In God there is no darkness, but he dwells in light inaccessible, which no one can see.
• COVERING IT etc. BEDE. For six days it is covered by the cloud and the glory of the Lord: because he who carries out the commandments of the Lord by just works is held worthy of divine protection. For the Lord who bade him go up surrounded him with his cloud and brightness, because he who grants the gift of working well himself enlightens those who work well, that they fail not, and protects them, that they be not scorched by the temptations of the devil as by the heats of the sun. On the seventh day he called him to the higher things, because after the perfection of works the Law promises eternal rest, that we who stand by the Lord in the height of right action may go up to his vision and converse, according to that: "For the lawgiver shall give a blessing; they shall go from virtue to virtue: the God of gods shall be seen in Sion." In this life also, after the perfection of the active life, they go up to the grace of divine contemplation, such and so little as can yet be given to mortals. Whence it is said of Moses that he spoke with the Lord face to face, as a man with his friend. Of him therefore it is specially understood that for six days on the mountain he was protected by the cloud and the glory of the Lord; on the seventh, called to converse with the Lord, he climbed higher, because through the works which he had received from God he deserved to be the more enlightened and overshadowed from all evils, that he might come to the more sublime gifts of the divine vision and converse.
24.17:
**“And the sight of the glory of the Lord was like a burning fire upon the top of the mount”** — because it irradiates the minds of the faithful with the knowledge of the things above, and kindles them with love
**“in the eyes of the children of Israel.”**
• who, desiring to see God, fix the eyes of the mind on the memory of his brightness
• AND THE SIGHT etc. BEDE. The sight of the glory of the Lord appeared like a burning fire, because it enlightens the hearts of the elect with the gifts of heavenly knowledge, and inflames them with the ardour of its charity. In the cloud therefore the glory of the Lord appears, because it protects us from the heat of temptations. In the darkness, because the power of his majesty can be wholly comprehended by no one: for the peace of God surpasseth all understanding. In the burning fire, because it irradiates the minds of the faithful with the knowledge of the things above, and kindles them with hope and love. This glory the children of Israel behold from afar and from below; Moses by going up penetrates it, because the perfect see the divine mysteries finely. But let us, mindful of our frailty and sloth, if we cannot enter in by comprehending, take care to behold it near at hand by believing, hoping and loving. For the children of Israel have their eyes from afar on the mountain of the Lord and on the sight of his glory, when the weak, desiring to see God, fix the eyes of the mind on the memory of eternal brightness; who, abiding in the neighbourhood of the mountain of God into which they know Moses has gone up, restrain themselves with such moderation of living that they never withdraw the step of their work from the imitation of the highest men, though they cannot fully follow them.
24.18:
**“And Moses, entering”** — the preachers
**“into the midst of the cloud,”** — the hidden things of the divine power, or wisdom
**“went up”** — with sublime understanding
**“into the mount,”** — the height of wisdom
**“and he was”** — Moses also
**“there forty days, and forty nights.”**
• because they alone fulfil the decalogue whom the grace of the gospel helps.
• AND MOSES ENTERING THE MIDST etc. BEDE. Moses, entering the midst of the cloud, goes up into the mountain, when the preachers of the divine Law, among whom he himself is foremost, penetrate, the Lord leading, to behold loftily the hidden things of divine wisdom. And he was with the Lord forty days and nights, that by this number he might learn that they alone could fulfil the decalogue of the Law, which he had received with his people, whom the grace of the Gospel, to be written in four books, should help. For four times ten make forty; or because at some time the same precepts of the decalogue would be opened by divine grace to the knowledge of all nations, which are contained in the four parts of the world, that through their observance they may come to eternal salvation.

25.2:
**“Speak to the children of Israel, that they bring firstfruits to me:”**
• beginnings
• The Pelagians do not offer the firstfruits of good things to God, but, imputing them to themselves, say that they have something good without the grace of God.
**“of every man that offereth”** — "For God loveth a cheerful giver".
**“of his own accord,”** — not with sadness or of necessity
**“you shall take them.”**
• "I will freely sacrifice to thee, and will give praise, O Lord, to thy name: because it is good".
• THE LORD SPOKE TO MOSES etc. BEDE. We offer the firstfruits of good things to God when, attributing wholly to divine grace the good that we do, we profess with all our heart that we cannot have even the beginning of a good action or thought except from the Lord. But evil things are always both begun and finished by us at the devil's instigation, and are not to be released except by the Lord's gift.
25.3:
**“And these are the things you must take:”**
• precious things in silver and gold and silk, and the other things of which the vessels of the tabernacle are to be made
• AND THESE ARE THE THINGS etc. BEDE. All the things which the Lord commanded to be offered to him materially for making the sanctuary, we also, who desire to be spiritual children of Israel, imitators of the people that sees God, ought to offer spiritually, that through these voluntary offerings we may make a sanctuary for him in ourselves, that he may deign to dwell in our heart and consecrate it as a dwelling for himself.
**“gold”** — the brightness of true wisdom
**“and silver”** — the lustre of sacred eloquence
**“and brass,”**
• the public preaching of faith, or of confession
• the confession of the mouth unto salvation
25.4:
**“Violet”**
• hearts lifted up on high
• heavenly conversation
**“and purple,”** — the passion of the body, for which we ought to be ready for Christ
**“and scarlet twice dyed,”** — the burning love of God and neighbour
**“and fine linen,”** — the chastity of the flesh
**“goats' hair,”** — the habit of penance and mourning
25.5:
**“And rams' skins dyed red,”**
• the doctors of the Lord's flock, baptized in their own blood
• We offer rams' skins when we believe that our bodies will be incorruptible and glorified.
**“and violet skins”** — These we offer when we hope that after death we shall have spiritual bodies in heaven.
**“and wood”** — when, the thorns of sins being cleansed away, namely with clean flesh and soul, we serve God alone
**“setim”** — the firmness of the saints, who are corrupted by no vice
25.6:
**“Oil”** — the shining fruits of charity and mercy
**“to make lights:”** — that is, to be compounded: for cinnus is a kind of compound of divers mixtures; hence concinno, that is, I compound, is said
**“spices for ointment”** — spreading far and wide the good name of good work as an example of living well
25.7:
**“stones”** — miracles
**“Onyx, and precious stones to adorn”** — The works of the virtues and of miracles by which the ephod and the rational, that is, the works and thoughts of the saints, are adorned.
**“the ephod”** — works
**“and the rational.”**
• thoughts
• ONYX STONES etc. BEDE. These we offer when we preach with worthy praise the miracles of the saints with which they adorned their thoughts devoted to God and their works of virtue, and take them up, when there is need, in aid of our faith. For because we carry burdens on our shoulders, by the ephod, that is, the superhumeral, they suggest the works and labours of the just. But because the seat of the thoughts is in the breast, in the rational, which is the priestly vesture of the breast, the clean thoughts of the elect are expressed. The onyx stones therefore and the gems adorn the ephod and the rational when the acts and thoughts of the holy Fathers are distinguished also by miracles. Or in the onyx stones, which are said to be of the colour of blood, the merits of martyrdom added to good works are signified.
25.8:
**“And they shall make me”** — of themselves
**“a sanctuary,”** — a tabernacle
**“and I will dwell in the midst”** — common to all
25.9:
**“According to all the likeness”** — not in part: if we desire the fellowship of the angels, we ought to imitate their life on earth, as far as our hurtful bodies do not hold us back.
**“of the tabernacle which I will shew thee”** — of the heavenly fatherland, to the likeness of which the Church is commanded to be built
**“and of all the vessels”** — of the angels, each one
**“for the service thereof: and thus you shall make it:”**
• AND THEY SHALL MAKE ME etc. BEDE. The Lord showed Moses the tabernacle on the mountain, and the vessels consecrated for its service, because to him who abode with him so long he openly showed with how great humility, piety and purity the angelic powers rejoice to obey. These are the perfect tabernacle of him who has always dwelt in them. Whose likeness of life also, and common conversation before God, is promised to us in the resurrection: whoever of us now strive to imitate their life, namely by praising and loving God and neighbour, and calling even enemies to God; to whom it is said: But you, brethren, are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit. The tabernacle therefore shown to Moses on the mountain is the heavenly fatherland, which then consisted of the angels alone, but after the ascension received a glorious multitude of holy souls.
• OF ALL THE VESSELS etc. BEDE. The vessels of the tabernacle are the several persons of the angels, of whom Jerusalem, the mother of us all, consists in true peace and unity.
**“ACCORDING TO ALL THE LIKENESS”** — BEDE. We ought to imitate the angels by loving God and neighbour. They too come to the help of the wretched, if not of angels, who are all blessed, at least of men. They are humble, they are meek, peaceable, they obey the divine precepts. Imitate these as far as you can, that you may build in yourself a sanctuary for the Lord according to the pattern which was shown on the mountain, that God may both dwell in you now, and after this life bring you into that tabernacle which you imitate.
25.10:
**“an ark”** — the body of Christ, which was corrupted by no contagion of sin, whose length was the endurance of the passion
**“of setim wood”** — with most pure members, though "in the likeness of sinful flesh"
**“Frame”** — AND THUS YOU SHALL MAKE etc. BEDE. An ark is commanded to be made, in which the incarnation of Christ is figured, in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. It is framed of setim wood, which is light and incorruptible and differs little in quality from the white thorn, because the body of Christ consists of members clean from all vice. This wood is like thorns, because he came not in sinful flesh, but "in the likeness of sinful flesh".
**“the length whereof”** — long-suffering patience
**“shall be of two”** — the teaching and the working of Christ, of which one was not without the other
**“cubits and a half”**
• We do not have the full cubit, because we cannot imitate his works to the full.
• because he bore long-sufferingly the slowness of the disciples
**“THE LENGTH WHEREOF”** — BEDE. It is asked of what size is this cubit which Moses set in the tabernacle, Noe in the ark. According to Josephus: it is not to be thought that a Jew endowed with talent, most learned in the divine and secular Scriptures, could have been ignorant of this. He says therefore: The ark was made of a length of five palms, a breadth of three. Whence it is plain that he designates that cubit which two palms make.
**“the breadth,”**
• the breadth of charity, which is one but divided into two commandments
• of the charity by which he took care to unite his own
**“a cubit and a half”** — because in this life we are not able either to love God perfectly or to comprehend how much he loves us
**“THE BREADTH A CUBIT”** — BEDE. The breadth of one cubit is for the dispensation of the Lord's charity, by which he took care to unite the elect in God. Whence: That they may be one in us. And a little after: that the love wherewith thou hast loved me may be in them, and I in them. It has also a half, because in this life we are not able either to love God perfectly or to comprehend the love which God has toward us, because we love in part, as we know in part. The ark therefore has one cubit and a half, because the Lord loves us with a single goodness, to be joined to himself and the Father, and embraces with equally kind goodness the capacity of our love such as it can be in this life, until we enter into his vision, where we may love him with all our heart.
**“the height, likewise, a cubit and a half.”**
• For the single hope by which we await the coming of the glory of the future resurrection; or because he admonishes us to rejoice amid adversities for the sake of the rewards to come.
• THE HEIGHT, A CUBIT etc. BEDE. The ark has a cubit in height, because Christ knew most fully, while he was in corruptible flesh, how great a glory was to be either for himself or for his members. It has also a half, because he willingly took into himself the devotion of our flesh; because we love the fatherland to come with devout intention, but do not yet perfectly grasp what its happiness is, and this little we have only from him.
*Bede:* Mystically. The length of the ark suggests the long-suffering of Christ, and the patience with which he conversed among men. The breadth, the breadth of the charity with which he came to us and dwelt with us. The height, the hope of the sublimity to come, by which he foresaw that after his passion he was to be glorified, or would glorify. Whence the length of two cubits, namely for the teaching and the works by which he shone in the world. Whence: "Which Jesus began to do and to teach." And elsewhere: "How came this man by this wisdom and miracles?" But that the ark had a half in its length can signify the slowness of human frailty, which could not worthily grasp the sublime words or works of Christ. Whence: "These things his disciples did not know at the first" etc., namely his deeds. And elsewhere: "This word was hid from them" etc. The ark therefore had two cubits of length, because he appeared in the flesh renowned in word and deed. But the half cubit, because he bore long-sufferingly the slowness of the disciples.
25.11:
**“And thou shalt overlay it with the purest gold within and without”** — because his humanity was full of power within, and without showed forth the works of the Holy Ghost
**“and over it thou shalt make a golden crown round about:”** — because he waited for the time when he would overcome, for us, the death he had taken up together with the author of death, and ascend to the Father as victor, crowned with glory and honour
25.12:
**“And four”** — the four books of the Gospels, which are compared to rings, because the eternal Wisdom of God which they preach, which man received, neither begins nor ends
**“golden rings”** — with the brightness of wisdom
**“which thou shalt put at the four corners of the ark”** — because the sacraments of the incarnation are spread through all the regions of the world, and the Gospel is preached
**“let two rings be”**
• because two evangelists cleaved to him while he preached in the flesh, two others cleaved to Christ after the resurrection and ascension
• John and Matthew, who cleaved to Christ as he preached
**“on the one side,”** — the right
**“and two”** — namely Mark and Luke, who, believing afterward, were made disciples of the apostles
**“on the other.”** — the left
25.13:
**“Thou shalt make bars also”** — the doctors, who carry God about by preaching
**“of setim wood,”** — because they ought to be pure and strong
25.14:
**“And thou shalt put them in”** — the Gospels
**“through the rings that are”** — namely girding it
**“in the ark”** — of the Church
25.15:
**“And they shall be always in the rings, neither shall they at any time be drawn out of them.”**
• because it is needful that those who preach heavenly things to others never hold back the mind from the memory of sacred Scripture, or the hands from the observance of the commandments
• that they may never cease from reading
• AND FOUR RINGS etc. GREGORY. The ark is the Church. The four golden rings at the four corners are the four books of the Gospel, by which it is preached through the four parts of the world; the bars of setim wood, which are put into the rings for carrying, are the strong and persevering doctors, who, ever cleaving to the sacred books, proclaim the unity of the Church. To carry the ark with the bars is for good doctors, by preaching, to bring the Church to the rude minds of unbelievers. These are commanded to be overlaid with gold, that when they preach to others they may shine with the brightness of knowledge. These shall always be in the rings, nor ever be drawn out, that those who keep watch in the office of preaching may never withdraw from the study of reading. For the bars are commanded always to be in the rings of the ark for this, that when the ark is to be carried no delay may arise over putting in the bars; because when something spiritual is asked of the pastor, it is shameful if he seeks to learn then, when he ought to untie the question; but let the bars cleave to the rings, that the doctors, ever meditating the words of the Lord, may lift the ark of the Testament without delay, and teach whatever is needful. Whence Peter: Being ready always to satisfy every one that asketh a reason of that hope and faith which is in us.
• TWO RINGS etc. BEDE. Because in the figure of the four living creatures, two, which are signified by the man and the calf, signified the passion and death; two, which by the lion and the eagle, the victory, namely by which he destroyed death. For as man, God appeared made mortal through the incarnation. As calf, he was offered for us on the altar of the cross. Again, he was made lion by overcoming death, eagle by ascending. There are therefore two rings on one side and two on the other, because two evangelists suggest the taking up of human frailty in the Lord; and two the victory by which he triumphed over the frailty taken up and over death. For as it were the left side had two rings, when two evangelists figured the incarnation and passion of Christ; the right side also two, when two others expressed the resurrection and ascension, which pertain to the glory of the life to come.
25.16:
**“And thou shalt put in the ark the testimony which I will give thee.”**
• because we ought to speak and believe of the incarnation only those things which the Lord himself deigns to reveal to us through the authors of sacred Scripture
• THE TESTIMONY WHICH etc. BEDE.
