• OF RAMS' SKINS etc. BEDE. The rams are the doctors, the leaders of the Lord's flock. Whence: "Bring to the Lord, O ye children of God: bring to the Lord the offspring of rams." As if to say: O angels, appointed to this office, bring to the Lord into heaven the imitators of the apostles. Hence also the sixth station of the people that went out of Egypt is named Elim, that is, rams, in which there were twelve fountains and seventy palm trees, that namely by name and appearance it might hold a figure of the apostles.
**“dyed red;”** — by martyrdom
**“DYED RED”** — BEDE. The rams' skins are dyed red to cover the roof of the tabernacle when the apostles and apostolic men do not cease to teach even unto martyrdom, that they may the more safely protect those subject to them from the dangers of temptations, while they suffer persecution even unto death for justice' sake; and the rams' skins dyed red cover the tabernacle and defend it from storms when the preachers fortify the hearts of the weak by the example of their passion and patience, lest they fail amid pressures.
**“and over that”** — Over those dyed red are laid the violet ones, in which eternal life is figured.
**“again another cover of violet coloured skins.”**
• of those, namely, whose "conversation is in heaven", and with the concupiscence of the flesh mortified
• OF VIOLET SKINS etc. BEDE. Violet is of the colour of the sky; the skin is a part and token of a dead animal. By the violet skins therefore is expressed the virtue of those who, having mortified the allurements of the flesh, lead a heavenly life on earth, and, set among men, imitate angelic purity, because they neither marry nor are given in marriage: "These are they who were not defiled with women: for they are virgins." Rightly therefore the violet skins hold the highest place, and the heavenly colour is nearest to heaven, that the choirs of virgins may be designated as about to follow the Lamb in spiritual nearness, and to sing to him the praises of hymns. And well is it said of the veils of the curtains and the hair curtains that, though set on high, they hang let down to the ground, although the curtains did not reach to the ground. The pillars also and the boards, set up on high, had their bases placed below. But of the skins dyed red and the violet skins it is said that they covered the roof on high, but not that they were bent down to the ground; because the other kinds of virtues have something in common with those who are on earth, but the contest of martyrdom and the glory of virginity, raised up from earthly things, are joined to the citizens above. For the martyr set in torments desires to leave all worldly things and the world itself, and to come to see the Maker of the world and the joys that are beyond the world. The celibate also, while for regard of a greater reward they pass beyond the common law by which it is said: "Increase and multiply, and fill the earth", choose a seat higher than the other faithful and than the world itself, since these were purchased from among all as firstfruits to God and the Lamb, who in Latin are rightly named 'virgins', as it were 'distinguished by virtue', or 'celibates', as it were 'blessed of heaven', that is, imitating the life of heaven.
**“THOU SHALT MAKE ALSO A COVER”** — STRABO. The first covering was of the curtains, of fine linen, purple and scarlet; the second, of the eleven hair curtains; the third, of the rams' skins dyed red, that is, Parthian-dyed; the last was of violet skins. The curtains covered in such a way that they came down to the sides, yet did not reach to the ground. But the hair curtains covered the roof and the sides, and reached to the ground. The skins dyed red or violet covered the roof only, and did not come down to the sides.
26.15:
**“Thou shalt make also the boards”** — He shows the position of the boards.
**“of the tabernacle standing upright”**
• persevering
• the saints, fortifying the Church by example and doctrine
**“of setim wood,”**
• OF SETIM WOOD etc. BEDE. These boards signify the apostles and their successors, by whose word the Church has been spread abroad. For breadth is the spreading of the faith and its sacraments, which before were known in Judea only. Although in the breadth of the boards the enlarging of the heart of the saints can be understood, by which they despise the world, kindled to seek heavenly things, and love both friends in God and enemies for God's sake. Whence: "Our mouth is open to you, O ye Corinthians, our heart is enlarged." Of that also, which he was wont to use for the advancement of the tabernacle, that is, of the Church, Paul says: So that from Jerusalem round about as far as unto Illyricum, I have replenished the gospel of Christ. And the boards were made of setim wood, that is, of thorns, which signify the cares of the world, delights, pleasures, or also the prickings of sins. Whence: As if a thorn should grow in the hand of a drunkard, that is, in the works of a fool. Because therefore the preachers strove to purge themselves of the prickings of vices, and to strip themselves of all the cares and delights of the world, that with free mind they might be enlarged into the love of God and neighbour, and might run far and wide to preach the word: rightly is it said that the boards of the tabernacle were made of thorn wood, which namely had put off all their thorny prickles, and shine with whiteness alone. For the saints were conceived and born in the sin of the first transgression, to whom also that general condemnation pertains: Thorns and thistles shall thy land bring forth to thee. But stripped of the thorns of sins by the grace of Christ, they have been fitted into the structure of the house by a worthy exercise of virtues.
• Because they are incorruptible, excellent in whiteness, light, differing little from the white thorn except in size, and are hardly found except in the lands of Arabia, where the tabernacle was made; nor was the Hebrew name translated, because this wood is scarcely found among other peoples.
26.16:
**“Let every one of them be ten cubits in length, and in breadth one cubit”** — the perfection of good
**“and half.”** — the beginning of the knowledge of God
*Bede:* EVERY ONE had TEN CUBITS in length, in breadth a cubit and a half; but the length is the height, which had ten cubits, because the doctors tend to perfection through the observance of the decalogue, labouring in the vineyard of Christ for the daily penny, insisting on doctrine namely for this, that they may restore the image of their Maker and King, which they lost when Adam sinned, and by living rightly recover his name, which they had lost by sinning. For in a penny the name and image of the king are wont to be contained: a penny also is so called from its being made up of ten coins, and our beatitude is perfected by the love of God and neighbour. For God is often figured by the number three because of the Trinity which he himself is. Man by the number seven, because he has a body of four elements. But the substance of the soul is wont in Scripture to be comprehended by a threefold distinction. Hence it is that we are commanded to love God with all the heart, with all the soul, with all the strength. The boards therefore have ten cubits of height, because the rulers of the Church serve God with this intention, that they may deserve to see him for ever, and strive to stir up their hearers to this by word and work, as it were to raise them up. That the boards had a cubit and a half each in breadth: the full cubit shows the perfection of work; the half, the beginning of the knowledge of God; because the just can give themselves perfectly to almsgiving, prayers and fastings and the like. For meanwhile we know God by faith, but we hope for the full knowledge of him in the future. Whence: This is eternal life, that they may know thee the only true God etc. And elsewhere: "For we know in part, and we prophesy in part." He does not say: We labour in part, and we preach in part. But the cubit will be filled, the Lord promising: I will deliver him, and I will glorify him; and I will shew him my salvation.
26.17:
**“In the sides of the board shall be made two mortises,”** — in prosperity and in adversity the inviolate rights of charity, that holding with the arms and the same embraces of charity the greater and the lesser who have gone before us or followed us in Christ, we may tend to the summits of perfection
**“whereby one board may be joined to another board: and after this manner shall all the boards be prepared.”** — IN THE SIDES etc. BEDE. The mortises in the sides of the boards signify humility in the minds of the just, by which above all they are joined to one another in brotherly charity. For while with a contrite and humbled heart they prepare in themselves a receptacle for the love of their neighbours, and show themselves worthy to be loved with piety and devotion, all the boards of the tabernacle are as it were coupled to one another by the joining of the mortise. When indeed the tabernacle has been set up and the framework of boards duly ordered, the shape of the mortise is not seen, but the steadiness of the wall shows with how great strength it has united the boards: because the humility of the saints, by which they are leagued together, cannot be seen from without, but from the most peaceful state of the Church it is plain what it works within. By which dispensation of divine grace it is brought about that we sincerely love those who were faithful at the beginning of the world, as we receive with the bosom of love those whom we see in the present, and believe ourselves to be received by them.
26.18:
**“Of which twenty”** — four times five make twenty: the Law is contained in five books, the grace of the New Testament in four Gospels, and the doctors with wonderful agreement of truth make plain the secrets of the Law fulfilled in the Gospel, and the sacraments of the Gospel prefigured in the Law
**“shall be in the south side”** — the Jewish people, because "in Judea God is known"
**“which looketh southward.”** — OF WHICH TWENTY etc. BEDE. How great the length of the tabernacle was is not specially expressed, but it is found from this, that the walls were framed of twenty boards, each of which has a cubit and a half of breadth. For twenty cubits, and twenty times half a cubit, make thirty, which Josephus writes was the length of the tabernacle. And well is the length of the tabernacle comprehended by this number, because there are three virtues in which the perfection of the Church chiefly consists: faith, hope and charity, which are multiplied by ten that thirty may be filled, while to the virtues of the mind are joined the good works which are contained in the decalogue, lest anyone think the virtues suffice him without work.
26.19:
**“For which forty sockets of silver”**
• for the brightness of the heavenly word
• "The words of the Lord are pure words: as silver tried by the fire"
**“thou shalt cast, that two sockets”** — because of the agreement of prophetic testimony and gospel preaching
**“may be put under every board at the two corners.”**
• FOR WHICH FORTY SOCKETS etc. BEDE. The sockets by which the boards were held up are the words and books of the Law and the prophets, by which the apostles and evangelists proved that what they wished to write and preach was true and divine. Whence: Then was fulfilled that which was spoken by the prophets. And elsewhere: "Now all this was done that the scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled." And Peter says: "We have the more firm prophetical word."
• BEDE, GREGORY. By the silver sockets of the boards the order of the prophets is signified: who, since they first spoke of the Lord's incarnation, rose as sockets from the foundation, and bore the weight of the building laid upon them, and sustain the boards, that is, the apostolic preaching spread abroad in the world, as firm and cast; because the life of the apostles is instructed by their preaching and made solid by their authority. Whence two sockets joined are put under each board, because while the prophets agree in their words concerning the incarnation of Christ, they build up the preachers who follow, that the more they do not disagree among themselves, the more strongly they may fix those. They are commanded to be cast of silver: for the brightness of silver is kept by use, without use it turns to blackness; and the sayings of the prophets before the coming of Christ were not in the use of spiritual understanding, since they could not be seen through their obscurity, and therefore remained as it were black; but after Christ, coming, wiped them before our eyes with the hand of his incarnation, whatever of light lay hid in them shone out, and he gave the sense of the fathers who went before into use, because he expounded words by things.
*Bede:* Well are two sockets put under each board, that the agreement of prophetic testimony may be shown in all that the Apostles said. Or two are put under at the two corners, that, the corners being well supported, the whole board may stand rightly: because the beginning of every apostolic and gospel word is foreshown in the prophetic books, and the end of every life of the apostles and their successors, from the beginning of faith to the end of the present life, is set in the mystical tables of the Old Testament.
26.20:
**“In the second side also of the tabernacle”** — the gentiles, who were numb with the darkness and cold of unbelief until the coming of Christ
**“that looketh to the north, there shall be twenty boards,”** — IN THE SECOND SIDE ALSO etc. BEDE. The south side, which looks southward, signifies the ancient people of God, which long ago receiving the light of the knowledge of the law glowed with the love of God. The second side, which looks to the north, signifies the gentiles, who until the time of the incarnation were numb with the darkness and cold of unbelief; of whose calling it is said: "I will say to the north: Give up: and to the south: Keep not back." As if to say: "I will say" to the people of the gentiles, long cold without faith: "Give" of thy sons, who may come to the faith of my confession and love; and to the people of Israel, which already enjoys the light of my knowledge: "Keep not back" the gentiles from being received into the lot of election.
**“TWENTY BOARDS”** — BEDE. And each side had boards of one number, measure and making, because one and the same faith, hope and charity is preached to both peoples by the apostles, and each is called to the promised land of the heavenly kingdom; concerning both they receive the general precept: "Go ye into the whole world, and preach the gospel to every creature", that is, to uncircumcision and circumcision, and without any difference it is added: "He that believeth and is baptized, shall be saved."
26.21: **“TWO SOCKETS”** — A socket (basis) is a foundation, from the Greek baseio, that is, I found. By the sockets the prophets are signified, on whose authority the apostles and all the doctors lean; and they are called two because of the concord of the prophets, who all held one mind.
26.22:
**“But on the west side”**
• which signify the end of each one, or of the Church in general
• by which the end of good works is signified
**“of the tabernacle thou shalt make six boards,”**
• for the perfection of the work, because in six God completed the adornment of the world
• the saints who were through the six ages of the world
• BUT ON THE WEST SIDE etc. BEDE. The western quarter, which, receiving both walls, completes the building of the tabernacle, signifies the fulfilment of the Church at the end of the world, to which the faith and working of both peoples, as the breadth of the twin wall, will persevere and reach. For never, even before the incarnation, were there lacking those of the gentiles who believed, nor are some faithful ever lacking from the people of the Jews, though condemned. If anyone however presume to deny this, let us say that the spiritual doctors of both Testaments, who bring forth out of their treasure new things and old, are to abide in the Church until the end of the world.
*Bede:* But on the west side etc. Well is the tabernacle completed in the western quarter, where the day is closed and the stars set, because of the death, namely, of each of the elect, or the general end of the world. For to him the sun as it were sets who passes from this light through the darkness of passing death to the joys of eternal light and life. The sun sets for the whole Church in the west, that it may rise more truly in the east when the darkness is past, when, the life of the present world being ended at the Lord's coming, the true day of eternity will at once appear, and because, the just reigning with the Lord, the reprobate perish for ever. Of this quarter of the tabernacle it is said in what follows that it looks toward the sea, namely the Red Sea, in which the army of Pharao was drowned, and Israel, saved, went up to mount Sinai, where it made the tabernacle. This quarter looks toward the sea when the Church, crowned after the perfection of the good, freely beholds the vices or the punishments of the wicked which by Christ's help it has escaped. Whence: "And they shall go out, and see the carcasses of the men that have transgressed against me" etc. For the waves of the sea, deep, turbulent, bitter, signify sins, by which the reprobate, wickedly delighted, are plunged into the abyss of perdition. Nor must it be passed over that when the tabernacle was built at Sinai it had the Red Sea to the west, and when it was brought in by Josue into the land of promise and set up in Silo, it had the great sea in the same quarter: because the saints, serving the Lord in this life and making a tabernacle in themselves, with fixed mind despise the proud boasting of the wicked as soon to fall, and, set with the Lord in the fatherland to come, behold their perpetual punishment without any lessening of their happiness, that they may render him greater thanks, not only for the good things he has given but also for the evils from which he has delivered them.
*Bede:* Well does the western quarter, which is said to look toward the sea, consist of six boards, because in the number six the completion of good work is noted, since in it the Lord completed the adornment of the world; in it he created man in the beginning; in it he restored the human race by his passion; or because there are six ages of the world, in which we must be perfected in good works, that we may come to eternal rest and the glory of the resurrection.
26.23: **“AND AGAIN OTHER TWO”** — BEDE. That again two other boards, besides the first six, are commanded to be set up in the corner at the back of the tabernacle, which receive the wall coming from the eastern quarter and are joined to the wall of the western quarter, pertains to the reward of the life to come, which after the labours and times of this life is secure, or made secure, divided into the sabbath rest, that is, the rest of souls after their release from bodies, and the glory of the resurrection common to both peoples, to be bounded by no end.
26.24:
**“And they shall be joined together from beneath unto the top,”** — because the one charity of the elect tends to heavenly things, and comes to the same end
**“and one joint shall hold them all. For the two boards also”** — because the glory of the rest and immortality to come is firmly joined to our conversation through faith, hope and charity
**“AND THEY SHALL BE JOINED”** — BEDE. Because the whole life of the elect tends to heavenly things by one faith and charity, and comes to one end of the divine vision, the whole word of the holy preachers agrees in one voice of right doctrine. For the joining of the boards would come apart from one another if what one prophet or apostle had said another denied.
**“that are to be put in the corners the like joining shall be observed.”**
• FOR THE TWO BOARDS ALSO etc. BEDE. The corner boards are joined in all things to the boards of the walls, because the glory of the rest and immortality to come is most firmly joined to the conversation of the present life through faith, hope and charity; nay, our conversation endures steadfast and unshaken because it believes, hopes for and loves the conversation to come, because it is held up by the frequent help of the citizens above, lest it fall by the turbulent blasts of demons. And these boards, which designate the perfection of good work or the rewards to come, are each held up by two sockets, because the prophets with harmonious voice foretold that all these things also would be, for the confirmation of the gospel and apostolic preaching.
• Here the measure of the sockets is not given, but Josephus says that the boards stood four fingers off the ground, by which it is understood that the sockets were of four fingers.
• Historically. Josephus writes that the tabernacle had ten cubits of breadth, and that its boards were raised from the ground by a measure of four fingers, from which he seems to wish it understood that the sockets of the boards were of that height. He again speaks of the chapter we have set out, and of the bars of the boards. The six boards made the nine cubits of the back wall, to which were joined two other boards, cut from half a cubit, which they set as corner pieces after the pattern of the larger boards. And each board has golden rings standing out on the outer face, as if fixed to one another in order by certain roots, looking round about, and through them gilded bars were put, each having a size of five cubits; and they were at the joinings of the boards, and the head of each bar went into the head of another bar, as in the manner of a shell, because of the back of the walls set lengthwise; there was one row going through all the boards, by which the sides of each wall were held together with hooks, in mortises made to one another and put into one another. Which was so carefully devised that the tabernacle was neither moved by the winds nor troubled by any other cause, but kept immovable in secure rest.
26.25: **“And they shall be in all eight boards, and their silver sockets sixteen, reckoning two sockets for each board.”** — because the prophets with harmonious voice foretold that all these things would be, for the confirmation of the gospel or apostolic preaching
26.26:
**“Thou shalt make also five bars of setim wood”** — the five books of Moses, by which the Church is wonderfully fortified
**“to hold together the boards”** — lest they waver under the winds
26.27:
**“and five others”** — because of the five books of the Law, by which the same thing is commanded to all
**“on the other side,”** — because the Law instructed in faith and works not only the former people of God, but us also in the New Testament, understood spiritually
**“and as many”** — because the Law well understood preaches to us the very completion of good work, when we go out of the flesh to the rewards to come
**“at the west side:”** — THOU SHALT MAKE ALSO BARS etc. BEDE. The five bars which hold the boards of the tabernacle are the five books of the Law, by whose defence the Church is held up against every assault, and this on both sides, because the letter of the law not only instructed the former people of God to faith and good works, but also instructs us, serving God in the New Testament, the same letter being spiritually understood, with the grace of greater sweetness, to faith and the working of virtues in the present, and kindles us in the future to the hope of perpetual reward. There are bars of the same number at the western quarter, because the law well understood preaches to us the very completion of good work, when we go out of the flesh to the rewards to come; as to the rich man asking: Master, what good shall I do that I may have life everlasting?, the good Master answered: If thou wilt enter into life, keep the commandments; nor did he add anything but the commandments of the Law.
26.28: **“which shall be put along by the midst of the boards”** — namely of the tabernacle
26.29:
**“The boards also themselves thou shalt overlay with gold,”**
• in this is signified the purity and cleanness of the saints
• because the word of the preachers shows beforehand the light of heavenly wisdom and beatitude
**“and shalt cast rings of gold for them,”**
• which signify the crown of the highest beatitude that will be rendered to the saints for the urgency of their labour
• because eternal and shining beatitude
**“through which the bars may hold together the boardwork:”**
• The bars hold together the boardwork through the golden rings when the words of preaching, through the promise of the heavenly kingdom, complete the state of the Church, that it may not fear the disturbances of the world.
• THE BOARDS ALSO THEMSELVES etc. BEDE. The gilded boards of the tabernacle shine forth when the whole word of the preachers shows beforehand the light of heavenly wisdom and beatitude, which for the glory of its brightness is compared to gold, for its eternity to a ring. Whence: "There is laid up for me a crown of justice." Each board has five rings: not because the distinction of the heavenly fatherland is divided into five, but because the perpetual brightness of that kingdom is contained written in Genesis, in Exodus, in Leviticus, in the book of Numbers, and the same in Deuteronomy. And five golden rings were fixed in each board of the tabernacle, because the hearts of the just, much enlarged through love, read in all the books of the Law not only the correction of works but also the light of the reward above.
**“which bars thou shalt cover with plates of gold.”**
• with spiritual understanding
• WHICH BARS THOU SHALT COVER WITH PLATES etc. BEDE. The bars are covered with plates of gold when in the words of the divine law, which according to the letter seem strong and plain for confirming the life of the faithful, a higher understanding, shining with gospel brightness, is shown to be within. For when we read that the flood destroyed the wicked, and that Noe with his own was saved in the ark, it is plain that God loves justice and hates iniquity, delivers the godly from temptation, and punishes the wicked with just vengeance. And such a reading, like incorruptible bars, holds together the tabernacle of the Lord, because it fortifies the minds of the faithful against the onset of temptations. But the wooden bars are clothed with plates of gold when the spiritual understanding is shown to be full of mysteries.
26.30:
**“And thou shalt rear up the tabernacle”** — the minds of the elect
**“according to the pattern”** — of angelic purity
**“that was shewn thee in the mount.”** — THOU SHALT REAR UP THE TABERNACLE ACCORDING etc. BEDE. The pattern of the tabernacle was shown to Moses on the mount, because, tarrying in secret with the Lord, he saw the sublime life of angelic purity and immortality, after the likeness of which he was commanded to order human conversation, so far as it was possible to imitate it, that, giving ourselves on earth after the example of the angels to divine praise, unanimous peace, sincere chastity and the other virtues, we may deserve to be their fellows in heaven. Whence: They are equal to the angels, and are the children of God, being the children of the resurrection. The pattern of angelic conversation therefore, which he saw on the mount of contemplation, he showed by the precepts of the law, by observing which we may come to the fellowship of the angels in heaven. He also gave a pattern of the more perfect life and of the blessed reward in the figure of the tabernacle and of the priestly and Levitical ministry. And the tabernacle is reared up according to the pattern shown on the mount when the elect order their work and mind after the imitation of the angelic purity which he was found worthy to contemplate.
26.31:
**“Thou shalt make also a veil of violet and purple, and scarlet twice dyed, and fine twisted linen, wrought with embroidered work and goodly variety:”**
• this variety of beauty befits heaven
• THOU SHALT MAKE ALSO A VEIL OF etc. BEDE. Even according to the letter this befits the beauty of the heavenly sight. For if you consider the beauty and the flames of the stars, the manifold appearance of the clouds, and the rainbow itself, drawing a thousand varied colours from the opposite sun, you will note in the sky many more and fairer paintings than in the veil of the tabernacle.
• THOU SHALT MAKE ALSO A VEIL etc. Thus far the south, north and west walls have been expounded. In what follows it is shown how the eastern side was composed; but first we must speak of the middle wall which divides the holy of holies from the former tabernacle; by which, namely, are distinguished the sanctuary and the sanctuary of the sanctuary, which the Apostle interprets as heaven, saying that after the veil was the second tabernacle, into which once a year the high priest alone entered, bearing blood in his hand. The veil therefore is heaven, the high priest Christ, who, rising again, ascended into heaven in the blood of his passion. And well is heaven intimated by this veil, in which is the likeness of the colours by which heaven is distinguished. For the clear sky is violet, and contains the flames of the stars, and the diversity of the planets, of which some are fiery, as Mars, some white, as Jupiter, some blue, as Saturn; and the rainbow draws a thousand colours from the opposite sun.
*Bede:* THOU SHALT MAKE ALSO A VEIL etc. Josephus says that this veil, by which the tabernacle was divided in the middle, was so placed that twenty cubits of the length belonged to the former house, but ten to the second. Which agrees in all things with the measures of Solomon's temple, which, being sixty cubits in length and twenty in breadth, had the third part of the length, that is, twenty cubits, separated for the inner house, that is, the holy of holies, so that the length and breadth of that same inner house were one. So the inner part of the tabernacle had a like length and breadth, that is, of ten cubits each. Of the mystical sense of this veil the Apostle speaks, explaining why "into the first tabernacle the priests always entered, accomplishing the offices of sacrifices; but into the second, the high priest alone, once a year, not without blood." This veil signifies heaven. Into the first tabernacle the priests entered daily through the year with sacrifices, which signifies the age of this life, where the saints, always serving the Lord, as priests of God expiate the daily errors of their frailty, without which they can by no means be in this life, the daily sins without which they cannot be in this life, with daily victims of works and libations of tears. But by the high priest, who once a year entered the holy of holies with the blood of victims, understand him to whom it is said: "Thou art a priest for ever according to the order of Melchisedech"; who, offered once for our sins, himself priest and victim, entered heaven by his own blood, that he may appear before the face of God for us.
26.32:
**“which thou shalt hang up before four pillars of setim wood,”**
• the angelic spirits, who fully practise the four principal virtues, whom we imitate after our small measure
• WHICH THOU SHALT HANG UP BEFORE FOUR etc. BEDE. The four pillars before which this veil is hung are the powers of heaven, illustrious in the four excellent virtues, that is, fortitude, temperance, prudence, justice, which are kept otherwise in heaven by the angels and holy souls. For there it belongs to justice to be subject to God; to prudence, to prefer or equal no good to God; to fortitude, to cleave most strongly to God; to temperance, to be delighted by nothing harmful. But here justice is exercised in succouring the wretched, prudence in guarding against snares, fortitude in bearing troubles, temperance in restraining wicked delights; this will not be there, where there is no evil at all.
**“which themselves also”** — because the angels were created incorruptible and not mortal, or because they keep the unstained purity of their condition
**“shall be overlaid with gold,”** — clothed with the grace of the highest brightness
**“and shall have heads of gold,”**
• minds enlightened by the presence of his vision
• WHICH THEMSELVES ALSO SHALL BE OVERLAID WITH GOLD etc. BEDE. The pillars before which the veil is hung are gilded, because, set within the veil of heaven, the powers of the angels are clothed with the grace of the highest brightness. They have heads of gold, because they have the mind by which they are ruled enlightened by the presence of the divine knowledge and vision.
**“but sockets of silver.”**
• because they stand on the praise of the Creator as on a foundation, which they pay without ceasing
• BUT SOCKETS OF SILVER etc. GREGORY. Sockets clothed with silver hold up the four pillars of the tabernacle, because the preachers of the Church, adorned with the divine word, carry the sayings of the four evangelists in mouth and work, that they may offer themselves as an example in all things.
• Let this be read in place of the interlinear. BEDE. The pillars have sockets of silver because their whole nature stands on this as on a foundation, that they sing praises to their Creator, and tell his will as fellow citizens to us who are still on pilgrimage, set as it were outside the veil. Whence we too, rejoicing with them, say in exhortation in their praises: "Bless the Lord, all ye his angels" etc. For by gold the splendour of wisdom is shown, by silver the brightness of words.
*Gregory:* He commands the sockets of the four pillars to be of silver. For in silver the brightness of the divine word is understood. Whence: "The words of the Lord are pure words: as silver tried by the fire." Sockets clothed with silver therefore hold up the four pillars, because the preachers of the Church, adorned with the divine word, carry the sayings of the four evangelists in mouth and work, that they may offer themselves as an example in all things.
26.33:
**“And the veil shall be hanged on”** — for the eternal counsel of the Godhead, in which it was when the world was created, or because the firmament of heaven cannot be dissolved
**“with rings,”**
• the eternity of counsel
• AND THE VEIL SHALL BE HANGED ON etc. BEDE. Because it was in the eternal counsel of the Godhead when the world was created, in which the heavenly nature holds the first place; or because the firmament of heaven was so made that it may never be dissolved. For what the Lord says: "Heaven and earth shall pass", is to be taken of the airy heaven. Of which Jeremias: "The kite in the air hath known her time." For that heaven will perish by fire at the judgment, which it is plain perished in the flood. Whence Peter: The heavens were before, and the earth out of water, and through water, consisting by the word of God, whereby the world that then was, being overflowed with water, perished. But the heavens which now are, by the same word are kept in store, reserved unto fire against the day of judgment.
**“within”** — namely
**“which”** — the veil
**“thou shalt put the ark of the testimony,”**
• Christ Jesus, privy to secrets
• WITHIN WHICH THOU SHALT PUT THE ARK OF THE TESTIMONY etc. BEDE. Within this veil the ark of the testament was put, because Christ, privy to the Father's secrets, after his passion and resurrection, ascending to the heaven of heavens, sits at the right hand of the Father.
**“with which”** — veil
**“SHALL BE DIVIDED”** — BEDE. Because the Church, which consists of angels and men, is partly on pilgrimage below, partly reigns above, it still has its citizens separated from one another by the dividing veil of heaven.
26.34:
**“And thou shalt set the propitiatory”**
• because Christ was given by the Father to be the propitiation for our sins; whence: Who died, yea that is risen also again, who is at the right hand of God, who also maketh intercession for us.
• a propitiation for sins
**“upon the ark of the testimony”** — Christ
26.35:
**“and the table without the veil:”**
• it signifies the temporal benefits of God, by which in the present we are refreshed and enlightened
• because in this life only do we need them, that we may come to the bread of angels and the true light of the world
**“and over against the table the candlestick in the south side of the tabernacle;”** — which signifies the ancient people of God, which first received the light of divine knowledge and the fervour of divine love
**“for the table”** — Scripture
**“shall stand in the north side.”**
• AND THE TABLE WITHOUT etc. BEDE. The table and candlestick of the tabernacle signify the temporal benefits of God, by which in the present we are refreshed and enlightened, that, strengthened and helped by these, the grace of merits increasing, we may be able to enter to eat the bread of angels in heaven and to the true light of the world. These are both outside the veil, because in this life only do we need the Scriptures and the doctors, or the other sacraments of our redemption. But in the future, where Christ will show us plainly of the Father, and we shall see him as he is, there will be no need of outward support, since God, dwelling in his elect, enlightens them as light and satisfies them as the bread of life, and, bringing them into the joy of the kingdom, exalts them with perpetual beatitude.
• We said that the south side of the tabernacle signifies the ancient people of God, which first received the light of divine knowledge and the fervour of divine love; but the north part, the Church gathered from the gentiles, which sat in darkness. By a right distinction therefore the candlestick, which is placed in the south part, signifies the grace given to the former people; but the table, which stands in the north part, the benefits of God given to us. And rightly is the candlestick set over against the table, because the Scripture of the Law and the prophets looks to the Gospel, bearing witness to it.
26.36:
**“Thou shalt make also a hanging in the entrance of the tabernacle”** — the beauty of the primitive Church, which was adorned with divers flowers of virtues
**“of violet,”** — because it thought on heavenly things
**“and purple,”** — because it was ready to die for Christ
**“and scarlet twice dyed,”** — because it burned with the love of God and neighbour
**“and fine twisted linen,”** — cleanness of heart and mind
**“with embroidered work.”** — THOU SHALT MAKE ALSO A HANGING etc. BEDE. Having set out the account of the veil which divided the sanctuary and the sanctuary of the sanctuary, he returns to set out the eastern side of the sanctuary, which he had left off when he described its other sides, namely the south, the north and the west. The hanging therefore in the entrance of the tabernacle, woven with goodly variety, signifies the primitive Church, woven of divers flowers of virtues. Whence: And the multitude of believers had but one heart and one soul etc. There was violet in it, because it thought on heavenly things and led a heavenly life on earth. There was purple in it, because it was ready to die for Christ. There was scarlet twice dyed in it, because it burned with the love of God and neighbour. There was fine twisted linen in it, because it rejoiced in continence of flesh and mind.
*Bede:* According to the letter the tabernacle was a house consecrated to God, having thirty cubits of length, ten of breadth, and likewise ten of height, having a roof level throughout, as houses are built in Egypt and Palestine: whose south, north and west walls were framed of wooden boards, gilded on both sides. On the eastern part, where the entrance was, there was one bar, which went through the midst of the boards from corner to corner, that is, from the last top of this wall to the top of the other wall, on which the curtains of the tabernacle and the roof lay, where also the hanging was, hung on five pillars. And the house was covered above and on every side with curtains woven with wonderful variety, ten, which were properly called the tabernacle. This was covered on every side with curtains of hair reaching to the ground. And another covering was made for the roof of rams' skins dyed red, and over this another covering of violet skins. For there was a veil diversified with embroidered work, hung on four pillars, by which the sanctuary and the sanctuary of the sanctuary were divided, within which the ark of the testament was placed, and over against the ark, outside the veil, the altar of incense. Likewise in the middle of the sanctuary itself the candlestick. In the south part the altar of holocaust. Outside, before the entrance of the sanctuary, the brazen laver between this altar and the tabernacle, and round about all, the court of the tabernacle, having a hundred cubits of length and fifty of breadth.
26.37:
**“And thou shalt overlay with gold five pillars”**
• the five books of Moses, by whose authority the whole Church is strengthened
• the doctors, of whom it is said: "And with great power did the apostles give testimony of the resurrection" etc.
• The pillars are five because of the five books of Moses, with which the doctors fortify their preaching, chiefly those who instructed the primitive Church, which, gathered from the Hebrews, knew only the authority of the law, the gospel Scripture being not yet disclosed.
**“AND FIVE PILLARS”** — BEDE. The pillars on which the hanging is hung are the doctors, whose mind, the more strongly it is raised to things above, the more firmly by teaching lifts others to the love of things above. For as the apostles and apostolic men are signified by the boards because of their breadth or doctrine, because, going into the whole world, they preach the gospel to every creature; or extend charity even to enemies: so because of the unconquerable strength of their mind and their intention ever raised to heavenly things, they are figured by the name and making of pillars. Whence: "James and Cephas and John, who seemed to be pillars" etc.
**“of setim wood,”** — because the preachers are sound within by firmness of heart
**“OF SETIM WOOD”** — BEDE. The pillars are commanded to be made of setim wood and covered with gold, because the preachers, sound within by firmness of heart, failing in nothing, ought to be conspicuous without by the brightness of their works. Or because they teach that the strength of their action is protected by divine help, since in all things they seek the glory of the Father who is in heaven, and in all that they speak they preach Christ. Whence: "For we preach not ourselves, but Jesus Christ."
**“before which the hanging shall be drawn: their heads shall be”** — because Christ is all in all; the others receive of his fulness.
**“of gold,”** — not gilded, because Christ is full of grace and truth
**“and the sockets of brass.”**
• the prophets, by whom the word of the apostles is made firm
• because of their unconquerable confidence, or because their word, while the world grows old, is consumed by no age, because he came not to destroy the law or the prophets, but to fulfil.
**“THEIR HEADS SHALL BE OF GOLD”** — BEDE. The golden heads signify Christ, who "is the head of the body, the Church", "the beginning, the firstborn from the dead"; nor unfittingly by the five heads of the pillars is the one head of the Church signified. For there were as many heads as pillars, because Christ, the head of all the saints, remaining ever indivisible in himself, divides the grace of the Spirit to each according to their capacity. Of which it is said: "Now he hath lifted up my head above my enemies." The heads of the pillars are commanded to be not gilded, like the pillars and boards, but of gold, because all the saints partake of the Spirit and of heavenly glory; but he himself is full of grace and truth, to whom God doth not give the Spirit by measure. "For the Father loveth the Son." The pillars of the tabernacle have sockets of brass and heads of gold, because the apostles and apostolic men were made firm in faith by the words of the prophets, and raised by desire to see the face of the Creator. Again they have heads of gold but sockets of brass, because whatever they received through God by the heavenly authority given them, they learned to be sacraments foretold by the prophetic word. Because we are speaking of the eastern quarter, something must be recalled of the exposition of the single bar, which we said was stretched from the corner of the boards to the corner of the other wall, and held together the whole steadiness of the walls, lest by the force and thrust of storms it be bent this way and that. It is written in what follows, where Moses is related to have fulfilled what was commanded: He made also another bar, which went through the midst of the boards from corner to corner. This bar therefore was stretched from the first top of the boards to the top of the other side, through the ten cubits of the breadth of the tabernacle, firmly set on the boards at each end, that by this that quarter of the tabernacle too, which consisted not of boards but of pillars, might stand no less fixed than the others, though the wind drove against it. This bar signifies Christ, who came from corner to corner, because from the Jewish people, which he first chose to save, he extended himself, being propitious, to the gentiles. Whence, as in the prophets he is called the corner stone, in the law also he can be called the corner bar: the corner stone because of the tabernacle, which is built for him of incorruptible wood, that is, of the souls of the elect free from corruption.

27.1:
**“Thou shalt make also an altar”**
• properly, namely, of holocaust
• The hearts of the elect, which are consecrated by the Lord for offering sacrifices of works.
**“OF SETIM WOOD”** — BEDE. Namely because the hearts in which the Holy Ghost dwells ought to be clean and incorrupt.
**“which shall be five cubits long and as many broad,”** — that all the senses may be exercised in the service of God in the length of patience and the breadth of charity
**“that is, foursquare,”** — This squaring of five cubits on each side signifies the fathers of both Testaments, who strove to keep the five senses of the body in all purity according to the precepts of the Law and the Gospel.
**“and three cubits high.”** — because the hearts of the elect tend to heavenly things through faith, hope and charity
**“AND THREE CUBITS”** — BEDE. This is about the stature of a man; how then was the altar served, which elsewhere is forbidden to have steps, lest the nakedness be uncovered? But that was said of the altar which is built of earth or of stones, where the steps, built together with it, would belong to the altar; but now it is commanded to be made of boards. And if something be set beside it for the hour of ministering, on which the minister may stand, it does not belong to the altar.
27.2:
**“And there shall be horns”** — the four virtues, or the four Gospels, by which the Church is fortified
**“at the four corners”** — the quarters of the world
**“of the same:”**
• from the inmost root of the heart of the elect
• THE HORNS AT THE FOUR. BEDE. The altar of holocaust has four corners, because the Church is spread abroad through the four quarters of the world, which, because of the one heart and one soul of the multitude of believers, is designated in the figure of one altar: from which there are four horns, since the hearts of the just are fortified by four virtues. Of which: She teacheth temperance and prudence, and justice and fortitude, which are such things as men can have nothing more profitable in life. These horns are drawn out from the altar itself when the faithful do not show the defences of the virtues to the eye, but they are begotten from the root of the heart, God being witness. Four horns at the four corners of the altar, when in all the ends of the world the Church, by the spiritual power of the virtues inviolable against all the snares of enemies, nay stronger, stands fast.
**“and thou shalt cover it with brass.”** — because the virtue of the faithful, once begun, is faithfully held to the end. For brass, incorruptible for a long time, designates perseverance.
27.3:
**“And thou shalt make for the uses thereof pans to receive the ashes,”**
• brazen pots, therefore, in which they received the ashes of the hearth and the burnt coals of the holocaust
• the faithful who turn over in their mind the examples of the Lord's passion, or the departure of the just who have gone before, who, the contest finished, rejoice without end
• AND THOU SHALT MAKE FOR THE USES etc. BEDE. By the divers vessels of the altar we understand the divers persons of the faithful, ordered to the service of the Creator through their manifold actions or thoughts. First pans to receive the ashes are commanded to be made. And the ash of the victims is taken in a great mystery, as the "ashes of a red heifer" "being sprinkled" testify, which, according to the Apostle, "sanctify such as are defiled, to the cleansing of the flesh"; in which the sacrament of the Lord's passion, or the sacrifices of the perfected virtue of the just, are understood. Rightly therefore is the ash of the sacraments sprinkled for the consummation of the Lord's passion or the perfection of the virtue of justice, when, offered wholly in the service of God through the fire of the Holy Ghost, they have deserved to finish good works and to be caught up into eternal life to receive their rewards. Whence Moses: This, he says, is the law of the holocaust. It shall be burnt upon the altar all night until the morning. The fire shall come forth from the same altar. The priest shall be vested with the tunick and the linen breeches, and, taking up the ashes which the devouring fire hath burnt, and putting them beside the altar, he shall put off his former vesture. And, being clothed with others, he shall carry them forth without the camp, and shall cause them to be consumed to dust in a most clean place. But the fire on the altar shall always burn. The holocaust therefore "shall be burnt upon the altar" when in the heart of the elect one, who has vowed himself wholly to God, namely in flesh and heart, a good work is prepared with the glowing fire of charity: which is done "all night until the morning", that is, through the whole time of this life until the morning of the world to come. "The fire shall be from that altar", because we ought to burn only from that charity which the Lord bestows on the Church through the Spirit. Lastly the sons of Aaron, because they wished to offer to God strange fire, and not that which had once been given from heaven, were slain by heavenly fire; because they who do heavenly works not with the intention of a heavenly reward but for temporal favour or advantage are struck by the sentence of heavenly wrath. "The priest shall be vested with the tunick and the linen breeches": that is, Christ, who is wont to kindle in us the fire of his charity, and through it to make the victims of our good action acceptable. He is clothed with linen, because to stir us up to works of virtue he sets before us the examples of his incarnation, purity and death, which are signified by linen. The priest takes up the ashes which the fire has burnt, and puts them beside the altar, when the Lord puts an end to laborious works, and does not bid the just, caught up from this life, strive any longer for eternal life, but receive the crown of justice in eternal life. Putting the ashes beside the altar, he puts off his former vesture, when, bringing back to remembrance for the just the good things they have done, he no longer shows them the habit of his passion to be imitated, but is clothed with other vesture, of which he says: "He will gird himself, and make them sit down to meat", that is, he will cause them to be refreshed in eternal rest for an eternal reward. Clothed therefore with other vesture, he will carry the ashes forth without the camp, when, ready to reward the labour of the elect, he will cause whatever good they had done to be seen in that life, taken away from here. The place without the camp signifies the entrance of perpetual life. Whence: By me, if any man enter in, he shall be saved: and he shall go in, and go out etc. And elsewhere: "May the Lord keep thy coming in and thy going out" etc., the coming in, namely, into this life of the Church, the going out into that where the pastures of eternal fulness are found. The place set without the camp is understood in that life, since it is said to be most clean, which is not found in this life. The most clean place therefore without the camp is the mind of the just taken away from this life and rejoicing in the other: in which the ash of the holocaust is consumed to dust, when there the reward of good works is so rendered that all labour is wholly finished. Whence: God shall wipe away all tears from the eyes of the just. The labour of works ceasing, the charity by which they were done will never cease, but will be more ardent when it shall see for ever him whom it loves; rightly is it added: "But the fire on the altar shall always burn." And a little after: This is the perpetual fire which shall never go out on the altar. When therefore the holocaust has been consumed to dust, the fire will go out from the altar, namely because, every kind of labouring being taken away, charity, never to be quenched, will burn.
**“and tongs”** — for trimming the fire of the altar
**“TONGS”** — BEDE. The tongs are the preachers, who are wont by exhorting to kindle the fire of charity in us as on the altar of God. And they use as it were a twin tooth when they instruct us by the harmonious pages of both Testaments, and set in the heart the words of charity by which they inflame us to eternal desires. Or with the tongs, that is, a double iron, they trim the fire of the altar when they pour in the virtue of twofold charity, and bid us burn and shine by its grace.
**“and fleshhooks,”**
• firepans, by which the fire and coals were carried from the altar of holocausts to the altar of incense
• AND FLESHHOOKS etc. BEDE. The fleshhooks, which in Greek are called creagrae, were kept for the ministry of the altar, that by them the flesh of the victims, cooked, might be brought out of the cauldrons and carried to the eating of those to be refreshed. Their use befits the preachers, whose ministry is to refresh the souls of the faithful with the word, to give the milk of simple doctrine to the unlearned, to serve solid food to the more perfect. For they who know the sacraments of Christ and take them up for imitation are as it were filled with the flesh of the saving victim; because it belongs to the doctors to commit to each person his ministry with discretion. Rightly is Moses commanded to make fleshhooks for the priests, with which they may arrange the flesh of the victims as is fitting, and offer some for all to eat, and leave others to be consumed by the fire of the altar. For there are in the word of God some things which he has granted for the banquet of our refreshment; but some of so great depth that they lie open to the Holy Ghost alone, and pass the measure of our capacity.
**“and firepans:”** — the hearts of neighbours imitating charity
**“FIREPANS”** — They were appointed for this, that by them the holy fire might be carried evening and morning from the altar of holocaust to the altar of incense, for putting on the incense; because the doctors carry as it were fire from the altar of holocausts to the altar of incense when by teaching they lead their hearers on from virtue to virtue, and, their merits growing, to higher things and the inner secrets of the divine vision. They also who imitate the hearts of neighbours glowing with piety become firepans, because they strive to kindle in their own the flame of the heavenly sacrifice which they behold in the minds of their brethren.
**“all its vessels”**
• the hearts of the saints
• because they obey perseveringly, and instruct others with a clear voice. For brass is lasting and sounding.
27.4:
**“And a grate of brass in manner of a net:”**
• that through the many openings the fire may go out freely to devour the victim
• prepared to receive the holocausts, because the elect prepare a place for the Lord in their inmost heart, where they set devout thoughts for him
**“at the”** — that the words of God and of truth may confirm the Church spread through the four quarters of the world
**“four corners of which shall be four rings of brass,”**
• because: "Their sound hath gone forth into all the earth"
• the books of the Gospels, which promise their hearers the crown of perpetual life
• AND A GRATE etc. BEDE. The altar was commanded to be made wholly hollow, as appears in what follows, but having in the middle a grate throughout, divided in the manner of a net, on which the flesh of the victims to be burnt was placed, and beneath it a hearth, in which, the wood being laid, fire might always burn, ready to devour the holocausts. And over against the hearth there was a door in the eastern part of the altar, by which wood could be put in to feed the fire, and coals or ashes could be taken out, as we have seen it expressed in the picture of Cassiodorus the senator, which he himself mentions in his exposition of the Psalms: because he also made four feet for each altar, namely of holocaust and of incense. Both of which we think he learned, like the position of the tabernacle and the temple, from the doctors of the Jews.
27.5:
**“which thou shalt put under the hearth of the altar:”** — that they may lift up the minds of the humble with the defence of their consolation
**“UPON THE HEARTH”** — BEDE. The altar has a hearth beneath the grate, in which it receives the wood and the fire of the holocausts, because the same hearts of the elect receive within them the heavenly words, by which, warmed and inflamed through the gift of the Holy Ghost, they render to God vows of pious thoughts pleasing to him. For the priest lays wood on the hearth of the altar when the doctor brings to the desiring minds of the faithful the testimonies of the Scriptures, by which they are confirmed in faith and love. He adds fire to the wood when he declares that the understanding of the word and the efficacy of working are to be sought from God. And the wood burns on the altar when "the charity of God is poured forth in our hearts". And the holocaust laid on this fire is consumed when all the good we purpose to do is made acceptable through the virtue of love, the grace of the Holy Ghost granting it. Whence the grate which bears the holocausts is commanded to be made like a net, that through its many openings the fire beneath may freely pass through to consume the victims wholly. For it is necessary that we open our hearts to the grace of God, and as it were with many doors thrown open earnestly pray that through each good thing we begin, as through each piece of his victims, he may deign to enlighten us with his mercy and kindle us into love. For the Pelagians, who presume to accomplish something without the grace of God, do not set on the altar of the heart a grate like a net, but as it were set a solid wall between themselves and the fire of the Holy Ghost, lest they be warmed by charity. "Not solid but empty" etc., namely that it might have ample room, to receive the holy fire, and wood for the fire, or holocausts to be consumed by fire. Thou also, if thou wilt be an altar of God, empty thyself of every contagion of worldly things, that thou mayest have in thee spacious room for the wood of heavenly words and the victims of virtues, and mayest take the flame of the Holy Ghost, by which the victims of the Church may be consecrated to the Lord and brought to the end of perfection.
*Bede:* If anyone is moved, according to the letter, as to how the wood of the altar could remain unburnt with so great a fire near it, let him take Jerome's answer. The wood of the altar, he says, which is of the wood of paradise, is not burnt by the fire near it, but is made purer; nor is it strange to believe this of the sanctuary and the inner parts of the temple and the altar of incense, since even anchiton, a kind of wood or something like wood, the more it has burned, the cleaner it is found.
27.6:
**“Thou shalt make also bars for the altar of setim wood,”** — the doctors, who in a manner carry the Church, while they preach the faith and the sacraments of truth either to those who do not know them, or strengthen those who know, confirming what they have received
**“two, which thou shalt cover with plates of brass:”**
• because of the sound and urgency of preaching
• that they may preach the word to both peoples, namely of the Jews and of the gentiles
• THOU SHALT MAKE ALSO BARS etc. The doctors, namely, who with harmonious mouth and work call Judea and the gentiles into the one grace of faith. Or there will be bars on each side of the altar for carrying it, when the preachers teach the minds of the faithful to hold the constancy of the virtues in prosperity and in adversity.
27.7: **“And thou shalt draw them through rings,”** — The bars are put into the rings that the altar may be carried, when the doctors raise up the hearts of the faithful by exhorting them through the words of the Gospel, which, though heaven and earth pass away, shall not pass.
27.8:
**“Not solid, but empty”** — If thou wilt be an altar of God, cast away all contagions; make thy heart spacious, that thou mayest take the wood of heavenly words, and the victims of virtues, and the fire of the Holy Ghost.
**“and hollow”** — empty, namely, both of all iniquity and of temporal care
**“in the inside shalt thou make it, as it was”** — as, namely, is the case with the angels and holy men
**“in the mount”** — of contemplation
**“shewn thee.”** — AS IT WAS SHEWN THEE IN THE MOUNT etc. BEDE. All the things that Moses mystically marked out for us to do in the building of the altar and the tabernacle, he first saw done with perpetual observance among the citizens above, in that heavenly conversation in which he was with the Lord forty days. For there is no doubt that he could have seen before the throne of God that altar which Isaias saw, most full of the true coals of inner brightness, and the holy tongs which the same prophet saw, with one of which the angel took a coal from the altar, with which he cleansed his lips, by the grace of the same Spirit by which the angels are inflamed to love God always in heaven, and sins are forgiven to men on earth, and the gifts of the virtues are granted. He commands the altar therefore to be made hollow and empty, as was shown to Moses on the mount, because as the angels and the spirits of the just in heaven are empty of sins and full of piety and justice, so we too on earth ought to decline from evil and do good: which we are bidden to do as by the exhortations of the heavenly word, so by the mystical figures of the tabernacle and the vessels and the ceremonies.
27.9:
**“Thou shalt make also the court”** — the first lessons of beginners
**“of the tabernacle, in the south side whereof southward there shall be hangings of fine twisted linen:”**
• because for beginners the allurement of flesh and spirit is first to be put to flight, that they may be cleansed from all defilement
• THOU SHALT MAKE ALSO THE COURT etc. BEDE. As the holy of holies designates the part of the Church that is in heaven, and the former tabernacle the perfect life of the faithful in this world, so the court of the tabernacle, which was outside, the first lessons of beginners. Whence the hangings of this court were of fine twisted linen, because the first care must be given by beginners that they bridle the allurements of flesh and spirit together. Whence: "Let us cleanse ourselves from all defilement of the flesh and of the spirit." For fine linen springs green from the earth, but when pulled up it is dried, beaten, boiled, twisted, and by great and long working brought to a white colour: so our flesh, that it may come to the virtue and beauty of chastity, must pray, fast, watch and labour with all continence, that it may dry up its inborn delights and rise to that worth of virtue which we desire. And the linen is twisted lest it be easily loosed, when not only is the wantonness of the flesh restrained, but its whole memory is rooted out of the inmost heart.
**“one side shall take up a hundred cubits in length.”**
• The hundred, which passes from the left hand to the right, signifies the heavenly life.
• A HUNDRED CUBITS etc. BEDE. It is well known that the hundred, which in reckoning on the fingers passes from the left hand to the right, often signifies in the Scriptures the heavenly life, because as the right hand is preferred to the left, so the heavenly life to the present. Noe completed the building of the ark in the hundredth year, because the Lord builds the Church in this life and will perfect it in the future. To Abraham at a hundred is born Isaac, the son of promise, because the blessing of the inheritance, which is promised to all the families of the earth in his seed, will be rendered in the future and heavenly fatherland. He himself sojourns a hundred years in the land of promise, because we who are made sons of Abraham through faith must sojourn in the present in hope of the inheritance above. Isaac grew old in Gerara, which is interpreted 'sojourning', and found in that same year a hundredfold, because whoever of us, sons of the promise, do good things while sojourning in this life, are soon, when we have gone out of the body, received into the heavenly life. The side of the tabernacle therefore has a hundred cubits in length, because all who belong to the members of the Church must take on the labour of penance and temporal continence for the sake of eternal life in heaven.
27.10:
**“And twenty pillars with as many sockets of brass,”** — the sockets: the fear of the Lord, which is the beginning of wisdom
**“the heads of which with their engraving shall be of silver.”** — not silvered
**“AND TWENTY PILLARS”** — BEDE. The pillars on which the hangings are hung are the doctors, who lift up the hearts of their hearers from earthly things to heavenly, and as it were stretch out the garments of the Lord carefully, lest any doubleness remain, but that with simple and clean intention they may shine before the Lord like hangings of fine linen. And the pillars were of brass, but clothed with silver, as is declared in what follows. Of brass, indeed, because of the perseverance of virtue or the sound of preaching; clothed with silver, because they sound nothing but the word of God.
**“WITH SOCKETS”** — BEDE. By the brazen sockets of the pillars, the beginning of wisdom, that is, the fear of the Lord, of which Jesus the son of Sirach says: The root of wisdom is to fear the Lord; and he beautifully added: And the branches thereof are longlived; because the manifold shoots of the virtues, which spring from the fear of the Lord as the work and engraving of the pillars from the sockets, will never lack the fruit of reward.
27.11:
**“TWENTY PILLARS”** — Why the pillars of the court were twenty has been said above, where boards of the same number are commanded to be made on one side of the tabernacle.
**“and sockets of brass of the same number, and their heads”** — as above
27.12:
**“But in the breadth of the court, that looketh to the west,”** — because the active life sets, and rest follows, and reward
**“there shall be hangings of fifty cubits,”**
• because the number signifies rest, and the remission which the saints await through good works. For jobel is interpreted remission
• because our sevenfold shall be joined for ever to the vision of the holy Trinity; whence: "But it is good for me to adhere to my God."
**“BUT IN THE BREADTH OF THE COURT”** — BEDE. The breadth of the court which looks to the setting of the sun, where, the day's labour ended, the welcome sleep of night succeeds, signifies the time in which, the active life ceasing after death, the rest of the elect and eternal reward follow. In the vineyard of the householder also, when it was evening, the labourers received the reward of their labour, because each of the just at the end of this life obtains entrance into eternal life. Whence: "Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord. From henceforth now, saith the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours" etc. Therefore the western side of the court has hangings of fifty cubits and ten pillars, because the number fifty signifies rest, because of the fiftieth year, which was given to liberty and rest and remission. Whence also it is called the jubilee. For jobel is interpreted 'remitting' or 'begun'. Ten also designates the rewards above, where human nature, raised immortal in both its substances, rejoices in the presence of the divine vision. For God is Trinity. Our body subsists of four elements. The inner man by the number three. When therefore we are bidden to love God with all the heart, all the soul, all the strength, our sevenfold also will be joined for ever to the vision of the holy Trinity, according to that: "But it is good for me to adhere to my God." This is the penny which the tillers of the Lord's vineyard, their labours finished, receive for their reward. Because therefore the holy preachers promise us, when this life is ended, the presence of the Creator and eternal rest, and so raise our desires from the lowest things to seek heavenly ones, they lift up as it were on the western side of the court the hangings of fifty cubits of breadth, ten pillars raising them.
27.13:
**“In that breadth also of the court,”** — the beginning of good conversation
**“which looketh to the east,”** — faith
**“there shall be fifty cubits.”**
• because at the very entrance those who are catechized must hope for remission of sins and rest
• IN THAT BREADTH ALSO OF THE COURT etc. BEDE. The breadth of the court looking to the east signifies the beginning of good conversation, which begins from faith: which because of the first receiving of heavenly grace is said to look to the east. Whence: "The Orient from on high hath visited us: to enlighten them that sit in darkness and in the shadow of death." In this quarter there are fifty cubits, because at the very entrance of conversion all who are catechized are taught to hope for remission of sins and rest; the number fifty pertains to remission. Whence in the psalm of the same number penance and confession and remission of sins are described, so that he who had sinned against the Lord and done evil before him, by knowing his iniquity, is washed by him and made whiter than snow, and again received the joy of the salvation of God, that is, of Christ whom he had offended, and was strengthened by his principal Spirit, lest he fall any more. The eastern breadth of the court therefore has fifty cubits when the first confession of faith rejoices in the remission of sins and the hope of rest and peace to come. In the creed of the apostles also we confess that we believe the holy Church, the remission of sins, and the resurrection of the flesh. Which afterward the universal synod expressed more fully, saying: I confess one baptism for the remission of sins, I look for the resurrection of the dead, and the life of the world to come.
27.14:
**“In”** — or: in
**“which there shall be for one side hangings of fifteen cubits,”** — because it consists of seven and eight. Seven signifies the present life, which revolves in seven days. Eight, the life to come, which is of those who rise again, to which one comes through this.
**“and pillars”** — the preachers, who hang the hangings on themselves while they teach their hearers to seek the things that are above, not the things upon the earth
**“three”** — because of faith, hope and charity
**“and sockets”** — who are founded in the fear of God
**“as many.”** — FIFTY CUBITS etc. BEDE. By the fifty cubits of the eastern quarter the beginnings of believers are generally signified, because they are celebrated in the remission of sins and the hope of the beatitude to come; whose special distinction is added, which, well considered, is added toward the same end. For it follows: In which there shall be hangings of fifteen cubits etc. For fifteen, which consists of seven and eight, designates the joys of eternal life, which, beginning from the sabbath rest of souls, is perfected in the resurrection of bodies. For the Lord, resting in the sepulchre on the seventh day of the week, rose again on the eighth day, that is, after the seventh day of the week. And that on one side of fifteen cubits there were three pillars with as many sockets figures the preachers, excelling in faith, hope and charity, and making the mind firm in the steadiness of fear. He therefore who is about to enter the court of the tabernacle has on each side hangings of fifteen cubits hung on three pillars, because whoever, about to enter the Church, has purposed to learn the sacraments of faith, whether he turn the gaze of his mind to the Church of the gentiles or to the Synagogue, will find on both sides doctors of the faithful, strong in faith, lofty in hope, fervent in charity, founded in the fear of the Lord, promising their hearers the rest of souls and the resurrection of bodies: which they hang on themselves like hangings of fine twisted linen when by their example they teach them to seek the things that are above, not the things upon the earth, and to keep spirit and soul and body whole and blameless unto the day of the Lord.
27.15: **“And in the other side there shall be hangings of fifteen cubits,”** — in which the rest of souls and the resurrection of bodies is signified
27.16:
**“And in the entrance of the court”** — of the Church
**“there shall be made a hanging of twenty cubits”** — which is five taken four times; and there are five senses of the body, which he who enters the Church must subject to the divine commands.
**“of violet,”** — with the hope of heavenly things
**“and purple,”** — with the endurance of temporal things
**“and scarlet twice dyed,”** — with the ardour of perfect charity
**“and fine twisted linen,”** — and with continence of the flesh
**“with embroidered work:”**
• because the virtues themselves bestow mutual brightness on one another by kindred fellowship
• OF VIOLET etc. BEDE. Rightly in this entrance of the court the hanging is made, not as in the other court, of fine twisted linen, but of four most noble colours: namely violet and purple, and scarlet twice dyed, and fine twisted linen, with embroidered work; because to those who are catechized the face of the Church shines without, but its virtue will appear brighter and worthier to those who enter it through the sacraments of baptism. For no one becomes highest of a sudden, but by degrees we tend from lesser things to more perfect. Violet signifies the hope of heavenly goods; purple, the endurance of temporal evils; scarlet twice dyed, the ardour of perfect love; fine twisted linen, continence of the flesh. Which colours are diversified one with another in embroidered work, because each virtue of the faithful grows by the fellowship, as it were the kinship, of the virtues near it, although single colours could befit single elect persons. For he who gazes more loftily on heavenly things is violet; he who suffers more for justice' sake is purple; he who blazes with more fervent charity toward God and neighbour, scarlet twice dyed; he who spiritually grows white with virginal integrity of the flesh, fine twisted linen. And when the just, in the same faith and gospel piety, rejoice together in one another's virtues, it is as if a hanging, woven with fair variety of colours, adorned the entrance of the Lord's court.
**“it shall have four pillars,”** — because they who enter the Church must order their faith and action according to the rule of the Gospels
**“with as many sockets.”** — AND IT SHALL HAVE FOUR PILLARS etc. BEDE. In the entrance of the court there are four pillars, because we enter the unity of the Church only through the faith and sacraments of the Gospel, which are contained in four books. Whence the beginnings of the four Gospels are recited to those to be catechized, and they are skilfully instructed concerning their figures and order at the opening of the ears, that they may know thenceforth and remember which and how many are the books by whose words they must chiefly be instructed in the faith of the Trinity. In which entrance a hanging of twenty cubits is made, which is four taken five times. And there are five senses of the body. Well therefore at the entrance of the court is a hanging of twenty cubits hung on four pillars, because all who enter the Church must order their faith and their acts alike according to the rule of the Gospels, that, holding back from the allurements of the flesh, they may subject the senses of the body to the divine commands. For not only is this hanging raised on four pillars, but it also has in its length the number five multiplied, when any humble and pious hearers coming to the faith, desiring not only to be imbued with the words of the Gospel but also to lead the gospel life, spend all the senses of the body in the obedience of charity.
27.17:
**“All the pillars”** — the doctors
**“of the court”** — heavenly
**“round about shall be garnished with plates of silver,”**
• with the observance and proclaiming of the divine words
• "The words of the Lord are pure words: as silver tried by the fire" etc.
**“silver heads,”**
• with minds
• because they must subject themselves to the divine precepts as to a silver head
• who must apply themselves in body and mind to the labour of preaching
**“and sockets of brass.”**
• because they are to be established in the fear of the Lord
• because it lifts up its arms to good works for the sake of eternal unity
• ALL THE PILLARS etc. BEDE. He presses home more carefully what he had said, that he may earnestly admonish the reader that no one can be counted among the doctors of truth, namely the pillars of the heavenly court, who has not learned to have, like brass, an unconquerable patience amid adversities; unless he has adorned himself, fortifying himself on every side with the observance and proclaiming of heavenly words as with plates of silver; unless he has put himself under the divine precepts with all subjection, as under a silver head, and established himself in the fear of God as on a brazen socket.
27.18:
**“In length the court shall take up”** — the Church
**“a hundred cubits, in breadth fifty,”** — because it hopes for rest in the grace of the Holy Ghost
**“the height shall be of five cubits,”** — because of the five senses of the body, because in the body we shall receive what we have done in the body
**“and it shall be made of fine twisted linen,”** — with chaste heart, namely, and work
**“and shall have sockets of brass.”**
• fixed, namely, in the fear of God
• IN LENGTH etc. BEDE. The Church has a hundred cubits of length, which lifts up its arms to good works for the sake of eternal life. Fifty of breadth, because it hopes for everlasting rest in the grace of the Holy Ghost, which he willed to be signified by the number fifty, when he consecrated Pentecost, that is, the fiftieth day of the Paschal feast, by his coming. The height is five cubits, according to the number of the senses of the body, because then every one shall receive the proper things of his body, according as he hath done, whether it be good or evil.
