With all these things Aaron and his sons were to be clothed, but distinctly, so that he himself should use all these, but the sons the last three which are properly assigned to them, when it is said: "Moreover for the sons of Aaron thou shalt prepare linen tunicks" etc.
**“And thou shalt consecrate the hands of them all,”**
• with the oil of unction, that the consecration may be perfected through the grace of the Spirit; yet the former things were not without his grace, but he who mounts higher and is set further above needs greater grace
• that all the works of the priests may be consecrated
**“and shalt sanctify them,”** — that they may be holy who serve or minister to the Lord
**“that they may do the office of priesthood unto me.”** — otherwise they cannot be priests
28.42:
**“Thou shalt make also linen breeches,”** — breeches not reaching to the ankles
**“to cover the flesh of their nakedness from the reins to the thighs:”**
• THOU SHALT MAKE ALSO LINEN BREECHES etc. BEDE. The breeches which are made to cover the nakedness of the body or flesh properly designate that portion of chastity which holds back from the conjugal union, without which no one can either receive the priesthood or be consecrated to the ministry of the altar: that is, if he has not either remained a virgin or dissolved the bonds of marriage; which is commanded to no one of necessity, but is to be offered to God voluntarily. Whence: "All men take not this word." And: "He that can take, let him take it." And a little after he promises to those who have left wife or other kin and the hindrances of the world for his sake a hundredfold in this world, and in the world to come life everlasting. Whence Moses is not commanded to clothe Aaron and his sons with this vestment, as is said of the former ones: Thou shalt vest Aaron thy brother with all these etc. But: Thou shalt make linen breeches, to cover the flesh of their nakedness etc. Thou shalt make breeches for the high priest and his sons; thou shalt teach the rule of chastity; thou shalt make known that those who are to enjoy the priesthood must abstain from the embrace of a wife. Yet thou shalt lay the yoke of this continence forcibly on no one; but whoever wish to become priests and serve the altar, let them of their own will cease to be servants of wives. And when they have done this, so that, having once taken up the purpose of continence, they have consented to be ministers of the sanctuary and the altar, the divine law will be at hand, which, as it were laying on the rest of the habit befitting priests, will instruct abundantly how they ought to live or teach, and, rejoicing at their spontaneous devotion, will add above the beauty worthy of the priesthood: of wisdom, patience, meekness, mercy, spiritual zeal, humility, the fear of the Lord, and the rest of such adornment. Otherwise "being guilty of iniquity they die", if namely, living wantonly, they usurp the priestly degree. Which sense is confirmed by the following words, when it is said: And when thou hast washed the father with his sons with water etc., as far as: and they shall be priests to me by a perpetual ordinance. For neither here is anything commanded about the breeches to be received from Moses; whence it is plain that Aaron himself and his sons had first put on this kind of vestment, and so came in to be washed, vested, anointed and consecrated by the hand of Moses. Where it is to be noted that Moses, about to consecrate them, first washed them with water, and so put on them the habit of the priest, because it is necessary that he who is to be promoted to the office of the altar should wash himself with streams of tears or compunction greater than usual, that the cleaner he has come to receive the degree, the more perfectly he may fulfil it when received.
• These pertain to Aaron and his sons. And so it comes about that Aaron is clothed with all eight vestments: linen breeches, a linen tunic, a violet tunic, the ephod, the rational, the girdle, the mitre, the golden plate. But the sons with four only: breeches, the strait linen garment, the girdle and the mitre.
28.43:
**“And shall use them”** — of their own accord, not compelled
**“Aaron and his sons”** — high priests, priests
**“when they shall go in to the tabernacle of the testimony,”** — not always, at least when they shall go in to the tabernacle
**“or when they approach the altar to minister in the sanctuary, lest being guilty of iniquity”** — of wantonness
**“they die.”** — by death of soul or body
**“It shall be a law for ever”** — because it signifies eternal things

29.1:
**“And thou shalt also do this, that they may be consecrated to me in priesthood.”** — AND THOU SHALT ALSO DO THIS etc. BEDE. Thus far it is marked out what the habit of Aaron and his sons ought to be. There follows the manner of consecration by which they, or the tabernacle with all its furniture, must be dedicated: namely by offering to the Lord a calf and two rams, wheaten loaves also, not only unleavened but tempered with oil, with the oil of unction added; all of which show in figure the devotion of good works and the cleanness of faith, or the grace of divine enlightening, with which the priests must be consecrated.
**“Take a calf”** — these animals, slain, show the slaying of Christ and the sprinkling of his blood, through which we are to be washed from sins and quickened in good works
**“from the herd,”** — of the patriarchs
**“and two rams without blemish,”** — because Christ was slain for both peoples
**“TAKE A CALF”** — STRABO. Every high priest or priest ought to offer a bull, that is, firmly to believe and imitate the passion of Christ. And two rams, that he may believe that the same Christ consists of body and soul. And unleavened loaves, that is, cleanness of life; and tempered with oil, that among all the virtues he may not neglect the works of mercy, or may believe that he has them not from himself but from the gift of grace.
29.2:
**“and unleavened bread,”** — a kind of bread without leaven, hardened in the likeness of a little cake, tempered with oil; and oil signifies the fatness of grace, or the unction of the spirit, or of mercy. Whence the Apostle: "Therefore let us feast, not with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness; but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth."
**“and a cake without leaven tempered with oil, wafers also unleavened anointed with oil:”** — that the works of the priesthood may be not only cleansed of the leaven of malice and wickedness, but also worthy of the divine sight by the fatness of charity
**“AND A CAKE”** — BEDE. We offer to the Lord for our consecration a cake tempered with oil when all that we do grows fat in the devotion of the heart through the inner grace of the Spirit. Wafers anointed with oil, when we show outwardly without doubt, as an example of living, that what we do is spiritual; by which oblations our consecration is perfected, while through good works and pure thoughts we acquire, God granting it, the merit of holiness.
29.3:
**“And thou shalt put them in a basket and offer them: and the calf”** — that he may firmly believe the passion of Christ
**“and the two rams.”** — because in Christ is a true body and a true soul
29.4:
**“and Aaron,”** — the high priests
**“and his sons”** — the priests, imitators of the high priest
**“thou shalt bring to the door”** — or: entrance
**“of the tabernacle of the testimony. And when thou hast washed the father with his sons with water,”**
• because they who are to be consecrated are to be cleansed with the water of tears
• AND WHEN THOU HAST WASHED THE FATHER WITH HIS SONS etc. BEDE. They are commanded first to be washed, then to be adorned with vestments, because whoever takes up the office of priest ought to wash himself in the flood of tears, that he may draw near worthy to the divine ministry.
*Bede:* In this washing the baptism of the sacred font could be understood, if it followed that one chosen for the priesthood was then first washed with the water of baptism for the remission of sins, and the Apostle did not gainsay it, saying: "Not a neophyte: lest being puffed up with pride, he fall into the judgment of the devil."
29.5:
**“thou shalt clothe Aaron with his vestments, that is,”** — these have been set out above
**“with the linen garment”** — with bodily continence
**“and the tunick,”** — the violet one, namely with heavenly hope
**“and the ephod”** — with the weight of work
**“and the rational,”** — with wisdom of mind
**“which thou shalt gird with the girdle.”**
• every concupiscence being tamed
• THOU SHALT CLOTHE AARON etc. BEDE. It is to be noted that whereas in Exodus Aaron is declared to be clothed with eight vestments, in Leviticus a ninth seems to be added: namely the girdle with which the linen tunic was girt before the violet one was put on. For so it is written: And when he had washed them, he vested the high priest with the strait linen garment, girding him with the girdle, and putting on him the violet tunick; and over it he put the ephod, which, binding with the girdle, he fitted to the rational.
*Bede:* It is to be noted that the four excellent colours of which the habit of the priest was made are fitted by a fitting comparison to as many elements of the world. Fine linen or flax to the earth, because it springs from it; purple to the waters, because it is dyed from sea shellfish. Violet and scarlet to the air and fire, because of the likeness of colour. The scarlet twice dyed, because fire is of twofold power: for it shines and burns. The Hebrews say that the high priest bore in his habit the figure of all the elements, because, sacrificing, he ought to pray for the whole world; to which we perhaps can add that in every man the figure of all the elements is contained: of fire in warmth, of air in breath, of waters in moisture, of earth in the solidity of the members. Whence man is called in Greek microcosmos, that is, 'lesser world'. And gold in the same habit signifies the rational power of the inner man. Whence on it properly was written Holy of the Lord, because by this alone does he rise to the knowledge of the Creator. Whence: In the inner man, that Christ may dwell by faith in our hearts. And therefore Scripture shows us the high priest of the Old Testament so vested, that the high priest of our time may know that he ought to intercede for the whole human race, but chiefly for those who have known the truth and bear the sign of faith on their foreheads: I desire therefore, first of all, that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all men: for kings, and for all that are in high station. But if in the high priest whom Moses consecrates we understand Christ, rightly does he have in his habit the figure of the whole world and of man together: for he upholds all things by the word of his power. And he is "the Lamb of God, who taketh away the sins of the world", and a priest for ever, illustrious with every adornment of holiness, not which, born in the flesh, he received by the exercise of labour, but which, incarnate in the womb of the Virgin, he had at once, the grace of the Holy Ghost going before. Of whose priesthood the Apostle says: "But this, for that he continueth for ever, hath an everlasting priesthood" etc. Commending also the vestments and adornments of the virtues, he says: For it was fitting that we should have such a high priest, holy, innocent, undefiled etc. And he had on his head a plate of gold, and on it Holy of the Lord engraved, because he came in the name of the Father, saying: "I am in the Father, and the Father in me"; and: "He that seeth me seeth the Father also."
29.6:
**“And thou shalt put the mitre upon his head,”** — that the four senses may be kept with discretion and directed to God
**“and the holy plate”** — on which is the ineffable name of the Lord, which adorns and protects all things
29.7:
**“And the oil of unction”** — of the Holy Ghost; whence: "God, thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows."
**“thou shalt pour upon his head:”**
• the head of the man is Christ, the head of Christ is God
• the mind, that the inner man may be consecrated
**“and by this rite shall he be consecrated.”** — then
29.8:
**“His sons also”** — the priests, or vicars of Christ
**“thou shalt bring,”** — that, removed from the people, they may cleave to God
**“and shalt put on them the linen tunicks,”** — with the continence of chastity
**“and gird them with a girdle:”** — that justice may be the girdle of his loins, and faith the girdle of his reins
29.9:
**“to wit, Aaron and his children, and thou shalt put”** — Moses does all these things, that is, the law, according to whose institution all things are done
**“mitres upon them:”** — the guard of all the senses
**“and they shall be”** — so consecrated
**“priests to me by a perpetual ordinance.”** — because it signifies the perpetual religion, that is, the Christian
**“After thou shalt have consecrated”** — consecrated
**“their hands,”**
• with which they handle holy things
• that they may work all good things and no evil
• AFTER THOU SHALT HAVE CONSECRATED THE HANDS etc. AUGUSTINE. Another reading. What is: And thou shalt perfect the hands of Aaron and his sons? Did they signify power by the hands, that they themselves also might be able to sanctify something? And the power itself was perfected by the signification by which they were commanded, namely, to be sanctified by Moses.
29.10:
**“thou shalt present also the calf before the tabernacle of the testimony.”** — because, as the Law had foretold, Christ was slain
**“And Aaron and his sons shall lay their hands upon his head,”**
• because he bore our sins
• THOU SHALT PRESENT ALSO THE CALF etc. AUGUSTINE. Another reading: And thou shalt bring the calf to the door of the tabernacle, and Aaron and his sons shall lay their hands upon it etc. See whence it was said that their hands were to be perfected, that is, their power completed, that they themselves also might sanctify, as is done when they lay their hands on the calf to be slain.
29.11: **“and thou shalt kill him in the sight of the Lord, beside the door of the tabernacle of the testimony.”** — because he was offered to God for an odour of sweetness
29.12:
**“And taking the blood of the calf, thou shalt put it upon the four horns of the altar”**
• the four principal virtues
• upon the four just, shining with virtues
**“with thy finger,”**
• that is, with the Holy Ghost, who fills all with his gifts
• because he is the power of God
**“and the rest of the blood thou shalt pour at the bottom thereof.”** — the lower in the Church
29.13:
**“Thou shalt take also all the fat”** — carnal desires
**“that covereth the entrails, and the caul of the liver,”** — These you will find fully set out in Leviticus; we pass them over, hastening to other things.
29.14: **“But the flesh of the calf and the hide and the dung thou shalt burn abroad, without the camp,”** — Christ suffered without the city
29.15:
**“One ram also”** — Christ, leader and shepherd of the sheep
**“thou shalt take, upon the head whereof Aaron and his sons shall lay their hands.”** — because the priests delivered Christ to death
29.18: **“IT IS AN OBLATION TO THE LORD, A SWEET SAVOUR”** — AUGUSTINE. The sacrifice of the victims of cattle is often called an odour of sweetness to the Lord, not because God is delighted by the smell of smoke, but because what is signified by these delights God spiritually when it is shown forth spiritually, as the odour of God is understood spiritually. For he does not draw in an odour, as we do, with bodily nostrils.
29.20:
**“And when thou hast sacrificed him, thou shalt take of his blood,”** — because by the slaying of Christ the hearing of the Jewish people was purged and renewed
**“and put upon the tip of the right ear of Aaron and of his sons, and upon the thumbs of their hand”** — in which purged works are signified
**“and the great toes of their right foot,”** — that their goings may be right and pure
**“and thou shalt pour the blood”** — of the animals
29.22: **“Thou shalt take the fat of the ram, and the rump, and the fat”** — that the sacrifice may be consummated and perfected
29.26:
**“Thou shalt take also the breast of the ram”** — that every sense and thought of his may be consecrated to the Lord
**“wherewith Aaron was consecrated,”** — for this pertains to the high priest
29.27: **“And thou shalt sanctify both the consecrated breast,”** — or: of consecration
29.29:
**“And the holy vesture, which Aaron shall use, his sons shall have after him,”** — that his successors may imitate his religion and holiness
**“that they may be anointed in it, and their hands consecrated.”** — their works
29.30:
**“Seven days”** — continuous, namely, in which the priesthood is dedicated
**“shall he wear it who shall be high priest”** — the highest, namely, who could be only one
**“AND THAT SHALL ENTER”** — AUGUSTINE. How does he say that it is proper to this one alone to enter the tabernacle of the testimony to minister in the holy places, since those things too which are outside the veil by which the holy of holies is veiled are called holy, and that too is called the tabernacle of the testimony where the holy things are, that is, the table and the candlestick, where the following priests also minister at the table and the candlestick and the altar itself? How does he speak of one successor of Aaron who enters the tabernacle of the testimony to minister in the holy places? For if he had said 'to minister in the holy of holies', there would be no question. For into that, where the ark of the testimony is, the high priest alone entered; unless perhaps by the very fact that he says that one enters the tabernacle of the testimony to minister in the holy places, he does not wish it to be understood of the holy of holies, because those too are called holy. For not all things that are holy can also be called holy of holies, but the things that are holy of holies are certainly holy. And this one, who once a year went into the holy of holies, signifies Christ. And that which was prefigured in the holy of holies, that over the ark which held the Law there was the propitiatory, where the mercy of God is understood to be signified, by which he becomes propitious to the sins of those who do not fulfil the Law: this seems to be signified also in the very vesture of the priest, which itself also signifies the sacraments of the Church, who on the logion, that is, the rational, placed on the breast of the priest, set judgments; and on the plate, the sanctification and abolishing of sins; as if the rational on the breast were like the ark in which the Law was, and the plate on the forehead like the propitiatory which was over the ark, and that in both that might be kept which is written: "Mercy exalteth itself above judgment."
29.33: **“That it may be an atoning sacrifice, and the hands of the offerers may be sanctified. A stranger”** — a gentile or heretic, or one whose life is estranged from the Church
29.34:
**“And if there remain of the consecrated flesh, or of the bread till the morning, thou shalt burn the remainder”** — if anything be left over, it shall be burnt with fire
**“at the fire,”** — of the Holy Ghost
29.35: **“All that I have commanded thee thou shalt do unto Aaron and his sons. Seven days shalt thou consecrate their hands:”** — that their works may be clean at all times
29.36: **“And thou shalt offer a calf for sin every day for expiation. And thou shalt cleanse the altar”** — which is outside the veil
29.37:
**“Seven days shalt thou expiate the altar”** — which is outside the veil
**“and sanctify it, and it shall be most holy.”** — by the anointing
29.44: **“I will sanctify”** — I alone, namely, and not another

30.1:
**“Thou shalt make also an altar”**
• it designates the spiritual life of the perfect
• THOU SHALT MAKE ALSO AN ALTAR etc. BEDE. The commands for the consecration of Aaron and his sons being fulfilled, Scripture returns to give commands also about the making of the altar of incense, on which Aaron was to burn the daily incense. If in the altar of holocaust, of which it was spoken above, the life of the just is generally signified, who daily crucify their flesh with its vices and concupiscences and offer it as a living victim, what does this altar, made for burning incense, designate but the special life of the just? For not in vain were the flesh of animals burnt on that, incense burnt on this; but on that were figured those who do not walk according to the desires of the flesh, but, as it were sacrificing these to the Lord, dedicate all the senses of the body to his will through the fire of the Spirit. But on this are figured those who, with greater perfection of mind, all the allurements of the flesh being quenched, offer to the Lord the solid vows of prayers: having nothing of the flesh to resist, nothing of the consciousness of sin to trouble their minds, longing, amid the outpouring of sweet tears, to come and appear before the face of the Lord. Whence this altar was set within, near the veil and the ark, that one outside before the tabernacle, because the former shine forth before all in the sight of the Church as an example of virtues; the latter, by the ardour of a loftier desire, draw near even in the body to the contemplation of the beatitude to come.
**“AN ALTAR”** — BEDE. Fittingly also the altar of incense, the more it excelled in the brightness of its metal, the less it was in size: for the holier, the fewer.
**“to burn incense,”** — the vows of prayers
**“of setim wood”** — the hearts of the elect, fortified by the firmness of true faith
**“OF SETIM WOOD”** — BEDE. Fittingly is each altar commanded to be made of setim wood, like the white thorn and incorruptible, because there is one firmness of true faith, by which the hearts of all the elect must be fortified and prepared to receive the fire of love and to offer to God the libations of the virtues. For the Apostle says to all in general: "Let us cleanse ourselves from all defilement of the flesh and of the spirit, perfecting sanctification in the fear of God"; as if to say: let us take away from ourselves the thickets of vices and the stings of tickling prickings, which the earth of our body has made to spring up for us from the sin of the first transgression, and, cutting them as with the axe of chastisement, let us cultivate our inner and outer man, that we may be worthy, having received the fire of the Holy Ghost, to offer the victim of the virtues in the sight of God. Fittingly one fire, not different, burned the victims on that and the frankincense on this, because there is one spirit, who quickens the minds of all the faithful with the varied grace of his gifts.
30.2:
**“having a cubit”** — the long-suffering of patience, as was said in the exposition of the altar of holocaust
**“in length”** — the perseverance of the saints in good work
**“and another of breadth,”**
• the amplitude of love
• HAVING A CUBIT etc. BEDE. The length and breadth of the altar is of one cubit, because the perfect bear temporal evils with the sole regard of perpetual refreshment, and bestow through charity on their neighbours what good things they can. Again, because charity is patient and kind: patient, to bear injury done by a neighbour; kind, to bestow the office of piety even on the one who does injury.
**“that is, foursquare,”** — that it may be stable and firm on every side
**“and two cubits in height.”**
• with the hope of heavenly rewards, namely of soul and of body
• because meanwhile there is the rest of souls, and in the resurrection also the beatitude of bodies
**“FOURSQUARE”** — BEDE. Rightly is the altar of incense made foursquare in length and breadth, because the soul of the perfect, the virtues being leagued with one another, is as able to bear a brother as to love him, and as able to love as to bear. And it has two cubits in height, because the elect hope to receive a double reward in the future, one of souls, the other of bodies. Whence: In their land they shall receive double, everlasting joy shall be unto them.
**“Horns”** — They signify the eminence of the virtues and of faith, by which we overcome the assaults of the devil, saying: "Through thee we will push down our enemies with our horn."
**“shall go out of the same.”** — HORNS SHALL GO OUT OF IT etc. BEDE. The horns signify the eminence of faith and virtue, by which the Church overcomes the wars of vices. Whence: "And I will break all the horns of sinners: but the horns of the just shall be exalted." Whence in the law only horned animals are decreed to be clean and fit to eat. For those which chew the cud and divide the hoof are known to be horned, because they only can be incorporated into the Church of God by spiritual union who are proved unconquered against the wars of vices by the strength of faith and virtue. And the horns go out of the altar of incense itself when the elect do not show the works of the virtues to the face of men in appearance only, but exercise them from the inner root of the mind with fixed and unmoved affection. But on the other hand the hypocrites, with horns borrowed from elsewhere, having an appearance of godliness, deny the power thereof.
30.3:
**“And thou shalt overlay it with the purest gold,”** — because the perfect shine with the light of inner wisdom, and show in all they do that the splendour of charity is in them, and that they think on and seek before all things the kingdom of God and his justice
**“AND THOU SHALT OVERLAY IT”** — BEDE. Fittingly is that one commanded to be clothed with brass, this with gold. For brass is more sounding and lasting than other metals; but gold, as much as it is surpassed in sound, so much does it surpass the other metals in brightness. Whence rightly the brazen altar, on which flesh was burnt and the blood of victims poured out, signifies those who, the pleasures of the flesh being tamed and as it were sacrificed to God, carry through perseveringly the way they have begun, and sound it forth to their neighbours to be kindled by frequent words of preaching. But gold signifies those who are enlightened by a fuller grace of the brightness above, but open less to others what they taste in secret of the inner sincerity: they are less able to utter with how great sweetness of God they are refreshed in the hidden place of his face.
**“as well the grate thereof as the walls round about and the horns.”**
• the confidence of the strength of the just
• AS WELL THE GRATE etc. BEDE. Well are the grate of the altar, the walls and the horns clothed with gold. For the grate was within, in the middle of the altar, prepared to receive the incense. But the walls appeared outside; the horns too, appearing outside, stood out higher with a special peak. The grate is gilded when the grace of Christ shines in the inner man through faith. The walls are gilded when the same grace of the Lord's love is spread abroad outwardly through good works. The horns are gilded when the confidence of the strength of the just, by which they have learned either to bear the adversaries of truth strongly through patience, or to repel or correct them wisely through prudence, glitters in all things with the brightness of inner light. And because such can say: "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith" etc., rightly is it added: "And thou shalt make a crown of gold" etc.
**“And thou shalt make to it a crown of gold round about,”**
• that the saints may await eternal rewards for the good things they remember they have done
• that all things may be shown worthy of heavenly reward, and nothing remain to be corrected by purgatorial fire after release from the flesh
• AND THOU SHALT MAKE A CROWN etc. BEDE. The altar of incense has a crown round about in those who are less in merits and do not dare to declare openly that the reward of the good fight and service and faith is laid up for them: yet they do all things with the intention of well pleasing God, but in the hope of receiving reward.
30.4: **“and two rings of gold,”** — the love of God and neighbour, which never falleth away
30.5:
**“The bars also themselves”** — the sayings of the fathers who went before, by which, lifted up from the earth, they are advanced to heavenly things
**“thou shalt make of setim wood, and shalt overlay them with gold.”**
• because the intention of the just directs them to the entrance of heaven
• AND TWO RINGS etc. BEDE. In these rings the four books of the Gospel can be taken, by whose faith and doctrine the saints are carried, and, lifted up from earthly thoughts, are borne through the wilderness of this life with the daily fruits of works to the heavenly fatherland, as has been set out of the altar of holocaust, the ark and the table. But there were four rings there; here two are said to be made on each side. There therefore the number of the evangelists more plainly; here another mystery, which looks to the love of God and neighbour. For the altar is surrounded with golden rings on each side because the heart of the elect is made firm on this side and that by the love of God and neighbour. Which is compared to rings, because when prophecy and knowledge and tongues shall cease, charity will never cease. There are two rings on each side because each commandment of charity is distinguished by a twofold virtue. For love of God is perfected by sincerity of faith and cleanness of life. "For without faith it is impossible to please God", and "faith without works is dead". Whence: But my just man liveth by faith, that is, he who has the works of justice with the faith of truth comes to life. Brotherly love too consists in patience and kindness. Whence: "Charity is patient, is kind" etc. And elsewhere: Forgive, and you shall be forgiven; give, and it shall be given to you. Into these rings gilded bars are put, that the altar may be carried, when such receive with the ready bosom of the mind the bright examples and sayings of the fathers, by which, raised from earthly things, they are caught up to the love of eternal things. And that in merit and mind they draw near to heavenly things, what follows shows: "And thou shalt set the altar" etc.
30.6:
**“And thou shalt set the altar over against the veil”** — heaven, which the Lord entered when death was overcome
**“that hangeth before the ark”** — that is, Christ
**“of the testimony, before the propitiatory wherewith the testimony is covered, where I will speak to thee.”**
• The altar stands before the propitiatory by which the testimony is covered when the saints draw near to the vision of God by purity of mind, who, though in a mortal body, have their conversation in heaven.
• because the saints daily contemplate Christ
30.7:
**“And shall burn”** — by stirring up to prayer
**“incense”** — prayer; whence: "Let my prayer be directed as incense in thy sight."
**“upon it Aaron,”** — Christ, or the priests of our order
**“sweet”** — to God
**“smelling,”** — because to the compunct it is sweet to weep and pray
**“in the morning. When he shall dress”** — by calling on the help of God at the beginning of good work
**“the lamps,”** — of the Word of God
**“he shall burn it:”** — by admonition
30.8:
**“and when he shall place them in the evening,”**
• the completion
• AND SHALL BURN INCENSE etc. BEDE. Incense or thymiama signifies prayer, according to that: "Let my prayer be directed as incense in thy sight." And elsewhere: "Golden vials full of odours, which are the prayers of saints." And because Aaron, as was said above, signifies the high priest, that is, Christ, and the priests of our order, Aaron will burn sweet smelling incense on the altar in the morning, when Christ will stir up the hearts of the faithful, enlightened with the splendour of new grace, to the sweetness of prayer; or the sharers of his priesthood, by earnest exhortation, stir up the faithful to entreat the face of their Creator. The priest burns the incense not only in the morning but also in the evening. For in the morning incense is burnt, that at the beginning of every good which by God's inspiration we purpose to do, we may call on his help, by which we may complete it. In the evening, that when we complete what was well begun, we may give thanks to him from whom we began.
• IN THE MORNING WHEN HE SHALL DRESS etc. BEDE. In the morning Aaron burns incense on the altar when Christ inflames the hearts of the faithful with the grace of compunction in those sacraments which they can understand. He burns it also in the evening, when he places the lamps, when even from those things which they cannot yet grasp, since it is not doubted that they are holy and divine, he forms them to the love of heavenly things, where all things are laid open. The incense smells sweet when, touched from on high by sudden compunction, they delight to give themselves only to tears and prayers.
*Bede:* AND SHALL BURN INCENSE etc. In the morning, the sun being risen, we see all things clearly round about; in the evening we are in darkness, and therefore we need the light of a lamp. By the morning therefore those sacraments or sayings of the Redeemer which we are able to discern clearly according to the order of human reason, after our small measure, and behold as it were in the day. But in those where human reason fails, and the authority of Scripture alone is to be sought, there the eye of the understanding is darkened as in the night. But the lamp of the word of God helps our feet, lest perhaps they stumble and stray from the way of truth. Whence Peter: "We have the more firm prophetical word, whereunto you do well to attend, as to a light that shineth in a dark place."
**“he shall burn an everlasting incense before the Lord throughout your generations.”** — because it is necessary that the mind after prayer and weeping beware of idle words or deeds, and keep itself in the same freshness of devotion even when prayer is ended; as it is said of Anna, namely: Her countenance was no more changed.
30.9:
**“You shall not offer upon it incense of another composition,”**
• nothing is to be asked in prayer but what God has commanded and has promised to give
• YOU SHALL NOT OFFER etc. BEDE. In what follows it is marked out by name of what spices this incense is to be compounded: namely stacte and onycha, galbanum of sweet savour, and the clearest frankincense; all of which are known to pertain to the signifying of the eternal goods to be sought chiefly from the Lord. Incense therefore of another composition than the Lord appointed is not to be offered on the golden altar, because in praying we ought to seek from the Lord nothing but what he himself commanded, who promised to give it, nor to believe anything else of him than he himself taught.
**“nor oblation and victim,”** — which pertain to beginners, in whom carnal things are still to be sacrificed
**“neither shall you offer libations.”** — of wine, which signify the cup of doctrine, or the chalice of the passion, or the fervour of love
*Bede:* No victim is to be offered upon it, nor libations poured. For all these pertain to the outer altar, which designates the life of beginners and of those who are advancing. For the life of the perfect is of such loftiness that nothing carnal is found in it to be sacrificed to the Lord. And the libations of wine designate the virtue of spiritual grace, namely either the cup of doctrine, or the chalice of the passion, or chiefly the fervour of love, or the receiving of the Holy Ghost himself, or something of this kind. But whenever the wine of libations is offered with the flesh of victims, it designates the holiness of those who still have something of carnal concupiscences which is opposed to purity of spirit and is kindled by spiritual fire on the altar of the heart. But the perfect, who can say: "For thee my flesh and my heart hath fainted away: thou art the God of my heart, and the God that is my portion for ever", the libations of victims ceasing, which pertains to the brazen altar set outside, offer within on the golden altar only the spices of heavenly desire, because, secure of the remission of sins, they mourn only for the delay of the everlasting kingdom, and every night water their couch with the sweet streams of tears.
*Bede:* We can interpret these altars so as to take the brazen one, on which flesh is burnt and the blood of victims poured out, as the whole Church of this time, in which no one is without sin, not even an infant of one day; there is no one who, born of the sin of transgression, has not need to be reborn in Christ and to be cleansed by the fire of his spirit. But the golden altar signifies Christ, who ineffably so took true flesh from Adam as to be free from the sin of Adam's flesh; whence both altars were made of the same kind of wood, but not both covered with gold. On this altar too nothing carnal was offered, but only spices, because Christ poured out prayers and tears not for his own errors but for our salvation. For as the ark placed within the veil signifies the man God sitting at the right hand of the majesty, so the altar placed outside the veil, but near its entrance, can express the same mediator of God and man, dwelling among men in his humanity, but by the power of his divinity entering the inner parts of heaven. The altar of incense stood in the sanctuary where the candlestick and the table were, because "the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us". The ark stood within the veil, because Christ after his passion and resurrection was taken up into heaven, and sits at the right hand of God. Upon the horns of whose altar Aaron prays in the blood which was offered for sin, and makes atonement upon it, when the priests, praying for the people or for their own ignorance, trust that they are to be helped through the Son of God and saved through the sacrament of his passion. Whence: By him therefore let us offer the sacrifice of praise always to God, that is to say, the fruit of lips confessing to his name; which can be taken of all the elect, the members, namely, of the high priest, who pray to the Father in spirit and in truth.
30.10:
**“And shall pray”** — he will cause to pray
**“Aaron”** — Christ
**“upon the horns of the altar”** — the virtues of the elect
**“once a year,”** — the priest went daily into the Holy place to burn incense; but once a year with blood, with which he sprinkled the horns of the altar.
**“with the blood”** — his own
**“of that which was offered”** — to the Father
**“for sin,”**
• of the human race
• AND SHALL PRAY etc. BEDE. Because Christ our priest offered his blood once in the year for the sins of all, when namely he preached the acceptable year of the Lord, that is, the whole time in which he deigns to join the Church to himself. Once also he gave to each believer the laver of baptism, in the mystery of his blood, for loosing the bonds of sins. And beautifully is he commanded to pray once a year with the blood of the oblation upon the horns of the altar, but to burn incense on it daily, because Christ, who daily renews the faithful, kindling them with the grace of inner compunction, once redeemed them by the victim of his blood when death was overcome. The faithful themselves too, who wash away daily sins with daily prayers and tears, rejoice that they have been once absolved from all sins in the sacrament of his passion. Aaron will pray upon the horns of the altar, because Christ not only prayed for men while dwelling among men, but also now, sitting at the right hand of the Father, intercedes for us. Dwelling also by faith in the hearts of the elect, while he stirs them up to pray, he is rightly said to pray. Aaron prays upon the horns of the altar when he commends the elect to the Father through the remembrance of the virtues they have practised. Lastly, as if touching the horns of the golden altar, he speaks of the devotion of the disciples: "Thine they were, whom thou gavest me out of the world, and to me thou gavest them; and they have kept thy word" etc. And he added: "I pray for them: I pray not for the world." And because for the merits and intercessions of lofty men the Lord has mercy on our weakness, rightly is it added: "And shall make atonement upon it in your generations."
**“and shall make atonement”**
• the Lord
• through the justice of the saints
**“upon it in your generations. It shall be most holy to the Lord.”**
• of Christ to be born it is said to the virgin mother: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee" etc.
• AND SHALL MAKE ATONEMENT etc. BEDE. Aaron makes atonement upon the altar of incense when God is made propitious for the sake of the justice of the saints, which we seek as intercessor and patron for ourselves. Whence it is said to Ezechias: I will save this city, and will protect it for my own sake, and for David my servant's sake. As Moses, interceding for the people, made remembrance of the fathers, and, as if praying upon the horns of the altar, took care to appease the Lord, saying: Be appeased upon the wickedness of thy people, and remember Abraham, Isaac and Israel etc.
30.11: **“And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying:”** — AND THE LORD SPOKE etc. The altar of incense being described, there remains the description of the brazen laver in which the priests about to enter the tabernacle should wash their hands and feet; but one command is put first.
30.12:
**“When thou shalt take the sum”**
• that is: when thou hast numbered them, going on an expedition
• AUGUSTINE: this was punished in David, because God had not commanded it
**“of the children of Israel,”** — of all the elect, whose names are written in the book of life
**“according to their number, every one of them shall give a price”** — the homage of diligent service
**“for their souls to the Lord, and there shall be no scourge among them, when they shall be reckoned.”** — because they are perpetually damned who obtain the number of the faithful in name only
**“WHEN THOU SHALT TAKE”** — BEDE. David forgot this precept when he numbered the people, and therefore by numbering brought a scourge upon the people itself. But mystically, the sum of the children of Israel signifies the sum of all the elect, whose names are written in heaven; and each gives a price to the Lord for their souls when they diligently serve him in good works; otherwise, being numbered, they will incur the scourge, because perpetual vengeance awaits those who, joined to the number of the faithful in name only, do not offer the Lord the perfect works of faith. Of such it is said: He shall not give to God his ransom, nor the price of the redemption of his soul. For the ransom of a man's soul are his riches.
30.13:
**“And this shall every one give that passeth at the naming,”**
• written in heaven
• that is: to the family: for those who passed were named
**“half a sicle”** — that is, ten obols, namely the observance of the Decalogue and the faith of Jesus Christ
**“according to the standard”** — according to the will of the offerer
**“of the temple.”** — the ordering of the law
**“HALF A SICLE”** — BEDE. That is, ten obols, namely the observance of the decalogue and the faith of Jesus Christ. For he who rightly understands this knows that in it is all the multitude both of faith and of work and the promise of reward to come. Lastly, in the first three the love of God, in the seven following the love of neighbour is contained; and, the Apostle witnessing: Love is the fulfilling of the law. The name of Jesus also among the Hebrews and Greeks begins with ioth and iota, each of which is the mark of the number ten. And they offer ten obols as the price of the soul who, believing in Jesus Christ, bear on their forehead and in their profession the sign of his name, which begins from the number ten. Perhaps therefore it was said that one iota cannot pass from the law, because the virtue of the decalogue which is contained there, and the faith of the name which is signified there, can be corrupted by no disturbance of unbelievers.
30.14:
**“He that is counted”** — truly
**“in the number”** — of the people of God
**“from twenty years and upwards,”** — understanding the Law spiritually, and fulfilling it helped by the grace of the Gospel
**“shall give the price.”** — HE THAT IS COUNTED IN THE NUMBER etc. Twenty signifies the joining of both Testaments, namely of the law, which is written in five books, and of the Gospel, which is written in four: for four times five make twenty. From twenty years therefore each is counted in the number of the people of God, because he alone is worthy of the fellowship of the elect who, helped by the grace of the Gospel, fulfils according to his measure and capacity the decrees of the law spiritually understood, and awaits the eternal rewards promised in heaven.
30.15:
**“The rich man”** — great in merits and perfect
**“shall not add to half a sicle, and the poor man”** — little and imperfect
**“shall diminish nothing.”**
• the Decalogue is laid on all equally
• THE RICH MAN SHALL NOT ADD etc. BEDE. Because whether one be great in merits and perfect, or little and set in the course of advancing in virtues, the law of the Decalogue, by which they are to love God and neighbour, is laid on all equally.
30.16:
**“And the money received”** — whatever good we do
**“which was contributed”** — to God
**“by the children of Israel,”** — by the just
**“thou shalt deliver unto the uses of the tabernacle of the testimony,”** — of the faithful to come
**“that it may be a memorial of them”** — in the remembrance of God, that he may deign to become propitious
**“before the Lord, and he may be merciful to their souls.”** — AND THE MONEY RECEIVED etc. BEDE. This is done when whatever good we do is kept in the eternal remembrance of our Creator and Judge, that from the fruits of the good things we have offered him he may become propitious to us. The same money is kept for the use of the tabernacle when by the works of the just both the manners and the acts of the faithful who follow are confirmed, and the lesser strive to become such as they know those to have been whom they hear to be reigning with the Lord. It is indeed to be noted that the money was to be given not according to the estimation of the crowd, but according to the standard of the temple. The standard of the temple is the ordering of the divine law, which the Lord commanded to be kept in his Church, and promises eternal rewards to those who keep it. If anyone strives to serve God according to the pleasure of human will, because he has not offered the money of devotion according to the standard of the temple, his oblation being rejected, he will be struck with the scourge of strict vengeance.
30.18:
**“Thou shalt make also a brazen laver”**
• Moses set this laver, because the law of God preached to all the faithful the grace of compunction
• "Every night I will wash my bed: I will water my couch with my tears."
• the unfailing washing of compunction and tears, with which priests and all the saints ought often to be washed
**“with its foot,”** — the desire of the heavenly life
**“to wash in:”** — "Every night I will wash my bed, with my tears" etc.
**“and thou shalt set it between the tabernacle of the testimony”**
• because no one becomes highest of a sudden
• because there are two kinds of tearful compunction: namely for sins, and from desire of the heavenly fatherland
**“and the altar. And water being put into it,”**
• AND THE LORD SPOKE etc. BEDE. In this laver (labium or labrum, for both are said) the water of baptism can be understood, by whose washing those who enter the doors of the Church must be cleansed. But because it was set between the tabernacle of the testimony and the altar of holocaust, and because the same priests were commanded to wash in it twice daily, that is, morning and evening, when they went in to the altar to offer incense to the Lord, whereas one is washed with the water of baptism once only, we more fittingly take this laver as the washing of compunction and tears, which we always need, chiefly when we come to minister the heavenly mysteries. For the altar of holocaust, on which the flesh of the victims was burnt to the Lord, signifies the quenching of carnal concupiscences by the fire of the Holy Ghost; but the altar of incense, the purity of those who, the allurements of the flesh being wholly put to sleep, shed tears of love only in the expectation and desire of entering heaven. Rightly is the laver set near the altar of holocaust, in which the priests, being washed, enter that tabernacle and burn incense to the Lord. For the state of tears and compunctions is distinguished in two ways: because first each one converted asks pardon weeping for his sins; and when he has long fulfilled this with worthy fruits of penance, secure of pardon, he longs with gaping desires for the time to be at hand when he may go in to see the face of the Creator, and does not bear without tears the length of this life or the delay of that, saying: "Woe is me, that my sojourning is prolonged" etc. And elsewhere: "My soul hath thirsted after the strong living God" etc. And a little after: "My tears have been my bread day and night" etc. The altar of holocaust therefore signifies the tears of penitents; the altar of incense, those of men rejoicing in the good things they have done with God's help, and desiring the rewards which they trust they will receive. Which weeping excels the former as much as gold excels brass, as much as the holy of holies, where the ark of the Lord was, excels the former tabernacle, in which were the candlestick and the table of the Lord. The laver was set near the altar of holocaust, in which those who went in to the altar of incense were washed, because no one becomes highest of a sudden, but, as merits advance, each must first overcome the wars of vices, and so obtain from God the compunction of tears, that he who shed bitter tears for fear of punishments may shed sweet tears for entrance into the kingdom.
• The laver was a vessel in which those washed who were about to enter the temple of God and to sacrifice, and to receive the holy vestments and put off their own, and likewise those about to go out; made of the mirrors of the women who watched at the entrance of the tabernacle.
**“WITH ITS FOOT”** — BEDE. The foot on which the laver was set signifies the desire of the heavenly life, the cause of which is so great that perfect men wash themselves with daily tears, and taste by sighing the joy of inner rest which they cannot by seeing. And that by this laver (which was set between the tabernacle and the altar) the tears of the perfect are figured these words testify: And water being put into it, Aaron and his sons shall wash their hands in it etc. No one of the people is commanded to be washed there, but the high priest and his sons, that is, the priests of the lesser degree, because of great men, as the life is more perfect, so the compunction is loftier. But this compunction befits not the ministers of the altar alone. For Peter says to all the faithful: Be you also as living stones built up, a spiritual house, a holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices. And John: Blessed is he that hath part in the first resurrection. In these the second death hath no power. And what victims they ought to offer Paul shows, saying: I beseech you by the mercy of God, that you present your bodies a living sacrifice etc.
30.19:
**“Aaron shall wash in it”** — the high priest
**“and his sons”** — the lesser
**“their hands”** — works
**“and feet:”**
• affections
• SHALL WASH IN IT etc. Christ too was washed with the water of this laver before he went in to offer at the altar and burned the incense of his sacred body for our salvation on the altar of the cross: for he shed tears for love of us, as at the raising of Lazarus.
30.20:
**“when they are going”** — to minister
**“into the tabernacle of the testimony, and when they are to come to the altar, to offer on it incense”** — prayers
30.21:
**“lest perhaps they die.”**
• if they come unclean
• eternally
**“It shall be an everlasting law to him,”** — The laver and the priesthood of Aaron have been destroyed, but what they signified remains for ever: in the life of the faithful the altar and the incense remain, as many other things which the law commanded to be celebrated perpetually.
**“and to his seed by successions.”**
• that is: to all the saints, because Christ came not to destroy the law but to fulfil
• that is: to those who believe in him in whom Aaron believed. For this is the seed which the Lord hath blessed.
• LEST PERHAPS THEY DIE etc. BEDE. For eternal death is to be feared if anyone chosen for the ministry of the altar does not render the incense of prayers, but presumes to enter the most holy mysteries without the washing of compunction, and to handle the holy table of the Lord with common hands. Let them wash their hands and feet therefore in the water of the brazen laver, and so go to the altar; let them wash their acts and goings with tears, then put forth their hands to touch the mysteries of God, and set the going of their feet in the court of the Lord. This is commanded to those also who partake of the sacraments, that they examine their acts and thoughts and wash them with the tears of compunction. "For he that eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh judgment to himself."
30.23:
**“saying: Take spices, of principal myrrh”**
• of principal mortification, namely, which is done with pure intention for God alone; whence: "My hands dropped with myrrh" etc.
• TAKE SPICES OF PRINCIPAL MYRRH etc. STRABO. Zmyrna in Greek, in Latin is called myrrh, which is a tree in Arabia of five cubits, whose shoots the Arabs burn, that they may sprout and bear fruit better. From whose fumes they would contract incurable diseases, did they not counter them with the smoke of storax. The gum of this tree is properly called stacte, by misuse also myrrh.
**“and chosen, five hundred sicles, and of cinnamon half so much,”** — which is of ashen colour, and signifies the humility by which we understand that we are ash and shall return into ash. Cinnamon is a shrub, and grows in India or Ethiopia, only two cubits high. And it is called cinnamon because in the manner of a cane it has slender and folded stalks of ashen or black colour, which when broken give off a visible breath; and the slender is dear, but the thick cheap and despised. Calamus is an aromatic kind near Libanus.
30.24:
**“of cassia”**
• this grows in watery places, and grows to a great size, and gives a good odour; and it signifies faith, which grows through baptism
• OF MYRRH, CINNAMON, CALAMUS, CASSIA etc. These four kinds signify the four principal virtues, by which, with the oil of unction and the grace of God's mercy, the Church is to be dedicated and sanctified.
**“also five hundred sicles by the weight”**
• let the measure be just and right
• because all things are to be done according to the rule of the Church
**“of the sanctuary, of oil of olives the measure hin:”** — a sextarius
30.25: **“And thou shalt make the holy oil of unction, an ointment compounded after the art of the perfumer,”** — the chrism with which the tabernacle is anointed, namely the faithful people of the Church, that is, those in whom the Godhead dwells as in a tabernacle. By the ointment also can be understood the virtues of the saints, or the odour of justice spread far and wide.
30.26: **“and therewith thou shalt anoint the tabernacle of the testimony, and the ark of the testament,”** — All these have been set out above.
30.29:
**“And thou shalt sanctify all, and they shall be most holy: he that shall touch them shall be sanctified.”** — AND THEY SHALL BE MOST HOLY etc. AUGUSTINE. When, namely, they have been anointed. What difference then will there be from those inner things which are covered by the veil?
**“HE THAT SHALL TOUCH THEM”** — The like was said above of the altar of sacrifices, which is to be so understood that the people might touch the tabernacle when they offered victims or any gifts, and by touching were sanctified because of that oil with which all things were anointed: not as the priests, who were also anointed with it that they might perform the priesthood.
30.32:
**“The flesh of man shall not be anointed therewith,”** — because these things do not befit those who love the pleasure of the flesh
**“and you shall make none other of the same composition, because it is sanctified,”** — to God alone
**“and shall be holy unto you.”** — sanctifying
30.33:
**“What man soever shall compound such, and shall give thereof”** — because holy things are not to be given to dogs
**“to a stranger,”** — to a heretic or gentile or Jew
**“he shall be cut off from his people.”** — from the company of the saints, to which he ought to be joined
30.34:
**“And the Lord said to Moses: Take unto thee spices, stacte,”** — a drop of the myrrh tree
**“ONYCHA”** — Onycha is said to be a little shellfish of sweet odour, the size of a human nail. Whence also it is called onyche in Greek, because onyx in Greek means nail.
**“GALBANUM”** — Galbanum is said to be the juice of the fennel-giant, and the best grows in Syria; it is gristly and less woody, and by its odour demons are put to flight.
**“AND FRANKINCENSE”** — Thus in Greek, it is called libanum in Latin, from Libanus, a mountain of Arabia: for there is another Libanus, of Phenicia, on which are the cedars.
**“and the clearest frankincense.”** — The best frankincense, namely that which is called male, because it is round in the manner of a human testicle; whose tree grows in Arabia, of the quality of the maple, with tangled and twisted withes. But mystically these four kinds signify the kinds of the holy virtues.
**“All shall be of equal weight.”** — that all the virtues may agree
30.35:
**“And thou shalt make incense”** — the prayer of the virtues
**“compounded by the work”** — with variety of virtues and works and prayers
**“of the perfumer,”** — of Christ and his disciple
**“well tempered together,”** — all these kinds were mixed into one, and incense was made, which in Hebrew is called sithirach
**“carefully, and pure, and most worthy of sanctification.”**
• The prayers of the saints ought to be pure, and retain nothing bodily, but seek only heavenly things.
• BY THE WORK OF THE PERFUMER etc. AUGUSTINE. We must not think that an ointment is made, but incense or a burnt offering of perfume, which is set on that altar of incense where it was not lawful to sacrifice, and it was within in the holy of holies.
30.36:
**“And when thou hast beaten all into very small powder,”** — with the pestle of examination
**“thou shalt set of it before the tabernacle of the testimony,”**
• where the ark was
• AND THOU SHALT MAKE INCENSE etc. GREGORY. We make incense compounded of spices when on the altar of good work we give off the odour of a multitude of virtues; which is made mixed and pure, because the more virtue is joined to virtue, the more purely is the incense of good odour shown forth. Whence it well follows: And when thou hast beaten all into very small powder, thou shalt set of it before the tabernacle of the testimony. We grind spices into very small powder when we pound our good works as in the mortar of the heart with hidden examination, and go over them minutely, that they may be truly good. To reduce spices to powder therefore is to grind the virtues by thinking them over, and to go over them to the fineness of hidden examination. And it is to be noted that of the same powder it is said: Thou shalt set of it before the tabernacle of the testimony, because our good things truly please in the sight of the judge when the mind grinds them by thinking more finely, and as it were makes powder of the spices, lest the good that is done be coarse and hard; which, unless going over it breaks it small, does not scatter its odour more finely.
*Isidore:* The incense, which is compounded of four most fragrant kinds ground to the greatest fineness, that is, stacte, onycha, galbanum and frankincense, signifies the prayers of the faithful; although these four seem to signify the four elements, so that frankincense, which is clear, may be compared to the air, stacte to the waters, galbanum and onyx to earth and fire; that through these the incense of all things which are in heaven and beneath heaven, and on earth, and in the waters, may be pleasing to God.
**“in the place where I will appear to thee. Most holy shall this incense be to you.”** — so made
30.37:
**“Such a composition”** — of works or prayers
**“you shall not make for your own uses, because it is holy to the Lord.”**
• dedicated, namely, to God alone
• SUCH A COMPOSITION YOU SHALL NOT MAKE etc. RABANUS. Because, namely, we must not use the divine prayers and praises in human flatteries: for God alone is to be served so. Whence above it is forbidden that the flesh of man be anointed with it.
30.38:
**“What man soever shall make the like,”** — that he may wish divine worship to be paid to himself
**“to enjoy the smell thereof,”** — with delight

31.2:
**“Behold, I have called”** — as dear and known to me
**“BESELEEL”** — Which is interpreted in the shadow of God; as if to say: "The Lord is my light and my salvation: whom shall I fear?" From him David is said to have drawn his origin, and the name of the embroiderer, because Beseleel built the tabernacle with embroidered work.
31.3: **“And I have filled him with the spirit of God,”** — with spiritual gifts
31.4:
**“to devise whatsoever may be artificially”** — skilfully
**“made of gold,”** — with wisdom
**“and silver,”** — with eloquence
**“and brass,”**
• with the steadfastness and resounding of preaching
• AND I HAVE FILLED HIM etc. AUGUSTINE. Are these works which seem to belong to craftsmanship to be attributed to the gift of the Holy Ghost, or is this also said significatively, so that they pertain to the divine Spirit of wisdom and understanding and knowledge which are signified by these things? Yet here too, though he is said to be filled with the Spirit, the divine Spirit of wisdom and knowledge, the Holy Ghost is not yet read of.
31.5:
**“of marble,”** — with unwearied fortitude
**“and precious stones, and variety of wood.”** — of the saints, with whom the tabernacle is built
31.6:
**“And I have given him for his companion Ooliab”** — my protection, father
**“OOLIAB”** — Which is interpreted 'my protection', as if he said by the name: "The Lord is the protector of my life: of whom shall I be afraid?" And well do they build the tabernacle who trust so constantly in the Lord.
*Strabo:* It is to be noted that in the building of the tabernacle the mystery of the Trinity is shown, as in the baptism and in the transfiguration. For in the baptism the Father sounded in the voice, and the Son was baptized; the Spirit appeared in the form of a dove. Ooliab also, which is interpreted 'my protection, father', signifies the person of the Father; Beseleel, which is 'in the shadow of God', the person of the Holy Ghost, of whom it is said: "And the power of the most High shall overshadow thee." For by the power of the most High the Holy Ghost is understood. Whence the Lord says: "I know that virtue is gone out from me." And the command, that is, the word, by which the tabernacle was commanded to be made, is the Son, through whom the Father works all things in the power of the Holy Ghost.
**“the son of Achisamech of the tribe of Dan. And I have put wisdom in the heart of every skilful man, that they may make”** — or: they may make
31.13:
**“Speak to the children of Israel, and thou shalt say to them: See that you keep my sabbath: because it is a sign between me and you in your generations:”**
• through all generations
• SEE THAT YOU KEEP MY SABBATH etc. In vain do the Jews glory in the legal observance. For it is plainly said that it is a sign, namely of the rest and beatitude to come; or of the rest of the saints in the present, in which they rest from the tumult of worldly works and vices.
**“that you may know that I am the Lord, who sanctify you.”** — in the keeping of the sabbath
31.14:
**“Keep you my sabbath: for it is holy unto you: he that shall profane it,”** — by troubling the rest of the soul
**“dying”** — of soul and body
**“shall be put to death: he that shall do any work in it,”** — servile, namely sin
**“his soul shall perish out of the midst of his people.”** — of the saints
31.17:
**“between me and the children of Israel,”** — the children of the promise, namely, and those who will see God face to face as he is
**“and a perpetual sign. For in six days the Lord made heaven and earth, and in the seventh he ceased from all work.”** — signifying that we ought first to complete good works, and after them to rest for ever
31.18:
**“And the Lord, when he had ended these words in mount Sinai, gave to Moses two tables”** — for the love of God and neighbour they were given to the people
**“TWO TABLES”** — Though God spoke many things, only two tables of stone are given to Moses, which are called the tables of testimony, because all the other things that God commanded are understood to hang on those ten precepts which were written on the two tables, if they are diligently sought and well understood; as those ten themselves hang on two, namely the love of God and neighbour, on which dependeth the whole law and the prophets.
**“of testimony, of stone,”** — because to a stony
**“written with the finger of God.”** — the Holy Ghost

32.1:
**“And the people seeing that Moses delayed to come down from the mount,”** — it thought he had perished, or that something had befallen so that he could not return
**“gathering together against Aaron, said: Arise, make us gods, that may go before us: for as to this Moses, the man that brought us out of the land of Egypt, we know not what has befallen him.”** — MAKE US GODS etc. Gods in the plural, though only one calf was made, after the likeness, namely, of the ox Apis which they worshipped in Egypt; but he who practises idolatry subjects himself to all vices, and serves as it were as many gods and demons as vices.
32.2:
**“And Aaron said to them:”** — He did not dare to resist, because he knew the people were ready to kill
**“Take the golden earrings”** — because this gold was purer and dearer
**“from the ears of your wives, and your sons and daughters, and bring them to me.”**
• He commanded a hard thing, that he might call them back from their purpose
• AND AARON SAID TO THEM etc. AUGUSTINE. Aaron is understood to have commanded hard things, that in this way he might call them back from their purpose. Yet that very hard thing was done, that there might be gold for making the idol; which I have thought should be noted on account of those who are saddened if they are bidden by God to do some such thing for the sake of eternal life, or to bear it with an even mind.
32.3: **“And the people did what he had commanded,”** — even though it was hard
32.4: **“And when he had received them, he fashioned them by founders' work, and made of them a calf”** — Because they had adored an ox in Egypt, perhaps they would not have taken up another idol.
32.6: **“And rising in the morning, they offered holocausts, and peace victims, and the people sat down to eat, and drink, and they rose up to play.”** — AND THE PEOPLE SAT DOWN etc. Eating and drinking drove them to play, play to idolatry, because if the fault of vanity is not carefully restrained, the unwary mind is devoured by iniquity. Whence: He that contemneth small things shall fall by little and little. For if we neglect to heal small things, led astray insensibly, we boldly commit even greater ones.
32.7:
**“And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Go, get thee down: thy people hath sinned.”**
• no longer mine
• by kinship of the flesh, or by the affection of care
32.8:
**“They have quickly strayed”** — as light and unstable
**“from the way”** — by which one goes to God
**“which thou didst shew”** — before
**“them: and they have made”** — they compelled to be made
**“to themselves a molten calf, and have adored it, and sacrificing victims to it, have said:”** — in their heart
**“These are thy gods, O Israel, that have brought thee out of the land of Egypt.”** — as it were they ascribed my benefit to an idol
**“THESE ARE THY GODS”** — AUGUSTINE. The Lord, showing Moses what the people had done about the calf and the idol which they had made of their gold, says that they said: These are thy gods, O Israel, that have brought thee out of the land of Egypt. Which they are not read to have said. But God showed that this was their mind; for they bore in their heart the sense of these words, which could not lie hid from God.
32.9: **“And again the Lord said to Moses: I see that this people is stiffnecked:”** — of untamable pride
32.10:
**“Let me alone, that my wrath may be kindled against them,”** — The saints withstand the wrath of God when they receive from him that they should oppose themselves; otherwise nothing resists the wrath of God.
**“and that I may destroy them, and I will make of thee a great nation.”**
• a generation of saints
• LET ME ALONE etc. GREGORY. What is it to say to a servant: Let me alone, but to give him boldness to pray? As if to say: Weigh how much thou availest with me, and know that thou canst obtain whatever thou prayest for the people. In Job, however, it is said: "God, whose wrath no man can resist", whereas Moses resisted the wrath of God, who restrained the onset of the stroke from above by offering his own death, saying: Forgive this trespass, or else strike me out of thy book which thou hast written. Aaron too tempered the fire of the divine punishment with the smoke of incense; and Phinees, slaying those who were wanton with strangers, offered his zeal to the divine indignation and appeased the fury with the sword; David, offering himself to the smiting angel, obtained the grace of appeasement before the time set. But the wrath of God cannot be resisted when it moves itself (so to speak) from the marrow, nor does anyone's entreaty set itself against it profitably when God has once disposed something in anger from his inmost being. Hence it is that Moses, who wiped away the guilt of the whole people by his prayers and appeased the force of the divine anger, coming to the rock of Horeb and distrusting about the giving of water, could not enter the land of promise, the Lord being angry; and he afflicts himself over this matter and is troubled with desire, and could not drive from himself the anger of the vengeance disposed, he who, God willing, had removed it from the people. Hence David, the people being laid low, restrained by prayer the sword of the angel, whereas before, weeping and wailing, with bare feet, he mourned his son, and until he received in full the vengeance of the crime committed could not temper the wrath of God for himself.
*Gregory:* It can edify the reader according to the history if he weighs how in good rulers the authority of ruling and the kindness of consoling are mingled. For discipline or mercy is much forsaken if one be held without the other. But toward their subjects there ought to be in doctors or rulers both justly consoling mercy and piously severe discipline. For see Moses piously loving and strictly severe. For when it was said: "Go down: thy people hath sinned", as if to say: He who has fallen into such a sin is no longer mine; and it was added: Let me alone, that my wrath may be kindled against them etc., often setting himself against the wrath of God he says: Either forgive them this trespass, or strike me out of thy book. Let us weigh with what bowels he loved the people, for whose life he asked to be struck out; and with how great zeal for righteousness, when he had obtained pardon, coming to the people, he says: "Put every man his sword upon his thigh" etc. See, he who asked the life of all with his own death extinguished the life of a few with the sword; within he burned with the fires of love, without he was kindled with the zeal of severity. So he loved those over whom he was set that he did not spare himself for them; so he pursued the offenders that he laid them low even when the Lord spared them; a strong envoy on both sides, he pleaded the cause of the people with God by prayers, the cause of God with the people by swords. Loving within, he withstood the divine wrath by supplicating; severe without, he consumed the fault by striking. He succoured all the more quickly in the punishment of a few. But God heard him the more quickly pleading for the people because he saw what he was about to do against the people for God. In ruling the people therefore Moses mingled both, that neither discipline should be lacking to mercy nor mercy to discipline.
32.11:
**“But Moses besought the Lord his God, saying:”** — out of mercy he prays humbly for the people; afterward out of discipline he takes severe vengeance for God
**“Why, O Lord, is thy indignation kindled”** — not mine
**“against thy people, whom thou hast brought out of the land of Egypt?”** — whom thou createdst and cherishedst with many benefits
32.12: **“Let not the Egyptians say, I beseech thee: He craftily brought them out,”** — because he could not destroy them otherwise
32.13:
**“Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, thy servants, to whom thou sworest”**
• thou didst promise firmly, it may not be changed
• REMEMBER ABRAHAM, ISAAC etc. He brings in the fathers, who are loved, on behalf of the sons, who offend and do not deserve to be heard, because the good deeds of the holy fathers often come to the help of the sons.
**“by thy own self,”**
• because thou hadst no greater
• by whom men do not dare to swear falsely
**“saying: I will multiply your seed as the stars of heaven: and this whole land that I have spoken of, I will give to your seed, and you shall possess it”** — what it signifies
32.14:
**“And the Lord was appeased from doing the evil”**
• affliction
• AND THE LORD WAS APPEASED FROM DOING THE EVIL. AUGUSTINE. He wished evil here to be understood as punishment, as in that: Their departure was taken for misery. According to this both good and evil are said to be from God, not according to the evil by which men are evil. For God is not evil, but he brings evils upon the evil, because he is just.
32.15:
**“And Moses returned”** — to rule the people and correct them
**“from the mount,”** — of contemplation
**“carrying the two tables of the testimony in his hand,”**
• in work
• elsewhere: in his hand
32.16: **“and made by the work of the Lord: the writing”** — the divine precepts
32.18:
**“But he answered: It is not the cry of men encouraging to fight,”** — against the devil or sin
**“nor the shout”** — which warns to flee vices, according to that: "Fly fornication."
**“of men compelling to flee: but the voice of singers”** — before the idols
32.19:
**“And when he came nigh to the camp, he saw the calf, and the dances:”** — of men playing and singing
**“and being very angry, he threw the tables out of his hand, and broke them”** — because he judged them unworthy to have the precepts of God read to them
**“AND BEING VERY ANGRY”** — AUGUSTINE. Moses, being angry, seems to have broken the tables of testimony written by the finger of God. Yet by a great mystery the repetition of the Testament was figured, because the Old was to be abolished and the New established. It is indeed to be noted how greatly he laboured in supplication to God for the people, who was so severe in avenging.
*Augustine:* It is asked why the tables which the Lord wrote and made were broken, but those which were hewn by the hand of man lasted. But in this it is signified that God adorned the first man with reason and wit. He gave a wise and understanding heart, that he might know and fulfil without difficulty and error. By doing this therefore he as it were wrote and hewed certain tables; but man broke them when he gave in to the devil and made himself unworthy of that grace. He is commanded therefore to hew tables again, that is, to prepare the breadth of the heart to receive the commandments of God; and because he so violated free will that he can no longer do good of himself without the grace of God, let him strive to labour toward the virtues: for Adam was overcome in delights; Job overcame the devil on the dunghill.
32.20:
**“And laying hold of the calf”** — the body of the devil, that is, the idolaters
**“which they had made, he burnt it,”** — with the fire of zeal and of the Holy Ghost
**“and beat it”**
• with the edge of the word of God, or with a hammer
• AND LAYING HOLD OF THE CALF etc. ISIDORE. In the calf the body of the devil is signified, that is, men in all nations, for whom the devil is the head, that is, the author, of these sacrileges. A golden calf, because the rites of idolatry seem to have been instructed by the wise, of whom it is said: Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools; and they changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of the image of a corruptible man etc.; and by such wisdom this golden calf, as it were, as even the wise men of the Egyptians were wont to adore figments. In the calf therefore is signified the whole body of the devil, that is, the whole fellowship of gentiles given to idolatry; this sacrilegious fellowship Christ burnt with the fire of which he says: "I am come to cast fire on the earth" etc. And elsewhere: There is no one that can hide himself from his heat; while the gentiles believe in him, the devilish form is melted by the fire of his power. Then the body is broken small, that is, scattered from that gathering of wicked conspiracy, it is humbled by the word of truth; and, broken small, it is cast into water, that the Israelites, that is, the preachers of the Gospel, may carry them over from baptism into their members, that is, into the Lord's body. Whence it is said to Peter: Kill and eat, when it could likewise have been said 'cut up and drink'; so the calf, by the fire of zeal and the edge of the word and the water of baptism, was swallowed up rather by those whom it was trying to swallow.
**“to powder, which he strowed into water,”** — of baptism
**“and gave thereof to drink”** — that they might blush to worship what they saw cast into the draught
**“to the children of Israel.”** — to the preachers of the Gospel
**“AND GAVE THEREOF”** — The Hebrews relate that when the children of Israel drank the water tainted with the powder of the calf, those who had committed idolatry showed the powder of gold on their beards; by which sign they appeared guilty or free of the crime, and the guilty were slain.
32.24:
**“And I said to them: Which of you hath any gold? and they took and brought it to me: and I cast it into the fire, and this calf came out.”**
• he spoke briefly
• AND THEY GAVE IT ME etc. AUGUSTINE. He spoke briefly, not saying that he himself had fashioned it so that a molten calf came out; or did he lie for the sake of excuse, from fear, as though he had cast the gold into the fire to perish, and without his doing it the form of a calf came out? Which is not therefore to be believed, because the truth could not lie hid from Moses, with whom God spoke, and he did not convict his brother of a lie.
32.25:
**“And when Moses saw that the people were naked (for Aaron had stripped them by occasion of”** — that is: by occasion of
**“the shame of the filth, and had set them naked among their enemies),”**
• FOR AARON HAD STRIPPED etc. It is to be noted that all that evil which the people did is ascribed to Aaron himself, because he consented to do what they had wickedly asked.
