For it is rather said that Aaron stripped them, because he gave way to them, than that they stripped themselves, who demanded so great an evil.
• By the ornaments of which the idol had been made, he had either shown their evil will, which before lay hid, or had betrayed the help and protection of God.
32.26: **“Then standing in the gate of the camp, he said:”** — with the severity of justice
32.27:
**“And he said to them: Thus saith the Lord God of Israel: Put every man”** — strong, vigorous
**“his sword”** — of preaching
**“upon his thigh:”** — the pleasures of the flesh
**“go, and return”** — run about rebuking
**“from gate to gate”** — from vice to vice, through which fault enters the mind
**“through the midst”** — equally, that they spare none
**“of the camp,”** — of the Church
**“and let every man kill his brother, and friend, and neighbour.”**
• with the sword of rebuke, nor let him spare those whom he loves by kinship
• PUT EVERY MAN HIS SWORD etc. GREGORY. To put the sword upon the thigh is to set the zeal of preaching before the pleasures of the flesh, so that when one strives to speak holy things, he must take care to tame suggestions. To go from gate to gate is to run about rebuking from vice to vice, through which fault enters the mind. To pass through the midst of the camp is to live within the Church with such evenness that he who reproves the faults of offenders does not rest in the favour of anyone. Whence it is added: Let every man kill his brother, and friend, and neighbour. He kills these who, when he finds things to be punished, spares from the sword of rebuke not even those whom he loves by kinship of the flesh. If therefore he is called God's who is stirred up by the zeal of divine love to strike vices, surely he denies that he is God's who refuses to rebuke the life of the carnal as much as is needful.
32.28: **“And the sons of Levi did according to the words of Moses, and there were slain that day about three and twenty thousand”** — By this number it shows the threefold form of sins. For every sin is committed either by deed or by word or by thought.
32.29: **“And Moses said: You have consecrated your hands this day to the Lord, every man in his son and in his brother,”** — not sparing, namely, their near ones
32.31: **“And returning to the Lord, he said: I beseech thee: this people hath sinned a heinous sin, and they have made to themselves gods of gold:”** — AND THEY HAVE MADE TO THEMSELVES GODS etc. AUGUSTINE. He put the plural for the singular, as there: "These are thy gods, O Israel, that have brought thee out of the land of Egypt." But this manner of speech is not found except where it can also be said or understood of several. For it is not that, because the calf was one, several could not therefore be made, or that it was not therefore like many idols. By this manner of speech it was said that the thieves reviled the Lord, though Scripture testifies that one did this; but he was not the only thief. Nay more, when this manner of speech is made with proper names (in which way we have not yet found it made in the divine Scriptures), several are understood there, as some have said Phedras and Medeas, though there was one Phedra and one Medea, but they called Phedras and Medeas all who were like Phedra and Medea. So not without cause, nor at random as is done faultily by the unskilled, but in a certain manner and by certain rules are these manners of speech put in.
32.32:
**“either forgive them this trespass,”** — he said this indeed in security, because he will not be struck out
**“or if thou do not, strike me out of the book that thou hast written.”** — EITHER FORGIVE THEM etc. AUGUSTINE. He said this indeed in security, that the reasoning might be concluded from the consequents, that is, that because God would not strike Moses out of his book, he would forgive the people that sin. But it is to be noticed how great an evil Moses saw in that sin, which he believed was to be expiated by so great a slaughter, he who so loved them that he poured out those words to God for them.
32.33:
**“And the Lord answered him: He that hath sinned against me,”** — or: to me
**“him will I strike out of my book:”** — as if to say: Thee I will not strike out, because thou hast not sinned.
32.34: **“But go thou, and lead this people whither I have told thee: my angel shall go before thee. And I in the day of revenge”** — of the Roman captivity, or of the general judgment
32.35:
**“The Lord therefore struck the people for the guilt of the calf which Aaron had made.”** — Yet Aaron was not struck: he is spared, that he may be changed for the better.
**“WHICH AARON HAD MADE”** — AUGUSTINE. It is asked, since above Aaron was said to have stripped the people, why vengeance was not taken on him, neither when Moses commanded that every one the armed men met from gate to gate should be killed, nor afterward when the Lord struck the people for the making of the calf which Aaron had made; and it was not said 'which they made', but which Aaron made; and yet Aaron was not struck. Nay more, that which God commanded about his priesthood before the sin was fulfilled; but he commanded him and his sons to be washed, and so they were ordained in the priesthood. So he knows whom he spares until a change for the better; and whom he spares for a time, although he has foreknown that he will not be changed for the better; and whom he does not spare, that he may be changed for the better; and whom he does not spare so as not even to await his change. For "his judgments are incomprehensible, and his ways unsearchable".

33.1:
**“And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Go, get thee up from this place, thou and thy people”** — not mine
**“which thou hast brought”**
• not I
• as was said above
**“out of the land of Egypt,”** — GO, GET THEE UP FROM THIS PLACE, THOU AND THY PEOPLE etc. AUGUSTINE. God, being angry, seems to say: Thou and thy people which thou hast brought out; otherwise he would have said: Thou and my people which I brought out. But when they demanded the idol, they spoke thus: This Moses, the man that brought us out of the land of Egypt etc.; and because they set their deliverance in a man, this is turned back on them when it is said: Thou and thy people which thou hast brought out of the land of Egypt; which is a charge against them, not against Moses. For Moses wished them to put their hope in the Lord, and to know that they were freed from that bondage by his mercy; and yet there was in him so great merit through the grace of God that he said to him: Let me alone, that I may be angry against them. But whether it be of one commanding, when he says: Let me alone, or as of one asking, either seems absurd. For if God commanded, the servant disobediently did not obey; and it was not fitting for God to ask this of a servant as a favour, since he could crush them even against his will. By these words therefore God signifies that it profited that people very much with him to be so loved by that man; that in this way we might be admonished, when our merits weigh us down so that we are not loved by God, that we can be relieved with him by the merits of those whom he truly loves. For when it is said by God to a man: Let me alone, and I will crush them, this is: I would crush them were they not loved by thee; as if to say: Do not love them, and I will crush them, because thy love intercedes that I may not do it. The Lord would have to be obeyed when he says: Do not love them, if he had said this commanding, and not rather admonishing and expressing what was calling him back from their punishment: and yet, even with him interceding, he does not leave the people without the scourge of discipline. For I know not how, so that Moses himself might so love them, God loved them more hiddenly, who terrified them with open voice.
**“into the land concerning which I swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob,”** — Here he shows that he does this for the fathers, not because these are worthy.
33.2:
**“And I will send an angel as thy forerunner,”** — whom we can understand as Christ, who is the angel of great counsel, who visited the human race by the presence of the flesh, and forgave sins
**“I WILL SEND AN ANGEL”** — AUGUSTINE. God is with the just by visiting, having mercy and strengthening; but with the wicked by avenging and punishing. And the sense is: I cannot be with these for thy sake, so as to avenge and punish; nor for their sake, so as to visit and strengthen; I will send my angel at least.
33.3:
**“that thou mayst enter into the land that floweth with milk and honey.”** — the Church, abounding in simple and perfect doctrine
**“For I will not go up with thee,”** — because they are unworthy of my grace and of the consolation of my presence
**“because thou art a stiffnecked people: lest I destroy thee”** — thy people
**“in the way.”** — GO, GET THEE UP etc. AUGUSTINE. At once, as though he were still speaking to Moses himself, by a hidden turning, which in Greek is called apostrophe, he says to the people: I will send my angel before thee etc. A great and wonderful depth of sacrament: as though an angel could have greater mercy than the Lord, so as to spare a stiffnecked people; and yet through an angel, he himself being as it were absent, who can be absent nowhere, he says he will fulfil what he swore to their fathers; as though here too showing that he does this because he promised to the fathers, not because these were worthy. What then does it signify, unless perhaps that he is therefore not with those who are stiffnecked, because only humility and piety receive him as propitious and saving? And for God to be with stiffnecked men is nothing else than to be present avenging and punishing. Whence: "Turn away thy face from my sins", because if he turns toward, he overturns. For as wax melteth before the fire, so let the sinners perish at the presence of the Lord.
33.4:
**“And the people hearing these very bad tidings,”**
• most sorrowful
• because it had offended God
**“mourned: and no man put on his ornaments according to custom.”**
• that it might show its penance by its dress also
• it was sorry for its offence
33.5:
**“And the Lord said”** — having pity, namely, on the mourners
**“to Moses: Say to the children of Israel: A stiffnecked people”** — of untamed pride
**“thou art; once I shall come up in the midst of thee, and shall destroy thee.”** — He threatens the Babylonian captivity, or the Roman, or the vengeance of the last judgment.
**“Now presently lay aside thy ornaments,”** — the manifest presence of God, by which he appeared to that people through the angel; or that which was within the camp in their midst, to which the people flocked for the sake of consulting in prayer
**“that I may know what to do to thee.”** — that is: I will make thee know how much evil thou hast committed, by which thou art deprived of my presence and the visitation of angels. For from that day God did not appear so manifestly to that people.
33.7: **“Moses also taking the tabernacle, pitched it without the camp afar off, and called the name thereof, The tabernacle of the covenant. And all the people that had any question went forth to the tabernacle of the covenant, without the camp.”** — TAKING THE TABERNACLE etc. This is to be taken by prolepsis, if it is taken of that tabernacle which was shown to Moses on the mount and made by Beseleel and Ooliab at the Lord's command. Or there was another tabernacle to which they already gathered for judgment.
33.8:
**“And when Moses went forth”** — the preacher, speaking lofty things
**“to the tabernacle,”** — of the dwelling above
**“rose up”** — in will
**“all the people, and every one stood in the door”** — at the going out, that is, of the bodily dwelling
**“of his pavilion,”** — a pavilion is a tent, so called from its likeness to a winged creature
**“and they beheld”** — elsewhere: they looked back at
**“the back of Moses, till he went into the tent.”**
• of the heavenly dwelling
• AND WHEN MOSES WENT FORTH etc. GREGORY. The Hebrew people, freed from Egyptian bondage, when they saw the pillar of cloud as God spoke, stood each at the doors of his tabernacle and adored. Whence it is said: "And when Moses went forth to the tabernacle, all the people rose up, and every one stood in the door of his tabernacle." For what is it for the people to behold the pillar of cloud, and to stand at the doors of their tabernacles and adore, but that when the human mind beholds those higher and heavenly things in some manner in a dark way, it already goes out of the enclosure of the bodily dwelling by lifted thought, and humbly adores him whom, if it cannot see, it yet already wonders at his power through the enlightening of the spirit? And when Moses enters the tabernacle, the people behold his back and stand at the door of their pavilions, because when the preacher speaks lofty things of God, he already enters in some manner the tabernacle of the dwelling above; the office and power of whose preaching, if the weak cannot fully weigh, they yet as it were behold his back, because they follow by understanding the last things they are able; but in those very least things which they can grasp, they already as it were go out of their pavilions and stand at the doors, because they strive to leave the dwellings of the flesh and go forward to those joys of eternal life of which they hear.
• AND THEY BEHELD THE BACK etc. STRABO. Moses holds the figure of the law. The Jewish people therefore beheld the back of Moses, because it would understand nothing mystical, nothing spiritual in the law, but only the surface of the letter. Therefore his face was hidden, that is, the true and pure knowledge. When he had entered the tabernacle, the pillar of cloud came down and stood at the door. Another translation says that when Moses wished to enter the tabernacle, the cloud set itself before him and prevented him. But here it is said that when he had entered, the cloud spoke with him before the door. It is to be known therefore that he entered some part, namely the court, and then, before he entered the tabernacle, the cloud set itself in the way: in this place therefore it signifies those who are less perfect in knowledge and work and cannot penetrate the inner things of the Scriptures. But elsewhere, when he entered the midst of the cloud, he held the figure of the perfect, namely those who search out the secrets of the mystical senses.
33.9:
**“And when he was gone into the tabernacle of the covenant, the pillar of the cloud came down,”** — the enlightening of the Holy Ghost
**“and stood at the door,”** — because the people behold heavenly things in some manner in a dark way
33.11:
**“And the Lord spoke to Moses face to face,”** — in manifest vision
**“as a man is wont to speak to his friend.”** — AND THE LORD SPOKE FACE TO FACE etc. Scripture speaks according to the opinion of the people, which thought that Moses spoke with God mouth to mouth, whereas he spoke and appeared to him through a subject creature, that is, through an angel and a cloud. For no one, either of men or of angels, has been able to see his substance as it is. Whence: "Now to the king of ages, immortal, invisible" etc. And elsewhere: He inhabiteth light inaccessible.
**“And when he returned into the camp, his servant Josue the son of Nun, a young man, departed not”**
• because if he went aside for the needs of the body, he returned at once
• Christ is with his Church until the consummation of the world, and is always proclaimed in the law, though hidden.
**“from the tabernacle.”** — not that he remained in the tabernacle, but in some place of the court appointed for him
33.12: **“And Moses said to the Lord: Thou commandest me to lead forth this people, and thou dost not let me know whom thou wilt send with me, especially whereas thou hast said: I know”** — I have approved
33.13:
**“If therefore I have found favour in thy sight, shew me thy face, that I may know thee, and may find grace before thy eyes:”**
• IF THEREFORE I HAVE FOUND FAVOUR etc. AUGUSTINE. By these words Moses shows that he did not see God with that familiar sight he desired, because all those visions of God which were offered to the sight of mortals, and from which came a sound by which mortal hearing might be reached, were shown forth by things assumed, as God willed, in the form he willed, so that in them the divine nature itself was perceived by no bodily sense, which is invisible, everywhere whole, and contained in no place. And because on two precepts, namely the love of God and of neighbour, the whole Law depends, therefore Moses showed his desire in both: in the love of God, where he says: If I have found favour in thy sight, shew me thyself etc.; in the love of neighbour, where he says: And that I may know that this nation is thy people etc.
• It was said before: Thou hast found favour in my sight; again he asks that he may find favour. For one grace does not suffice the saints. For there is the grace which goes before, that they may know and love God. There is that which follows, that they may keep themselves clean and inviolate and advance.
33.14: **“And the Lord said: My face shall go before thee, and rest”** — eternal life
33.17:
**“And the Lord said to Moses: This word also, which thou hast spoken, will I do: for thou hast found grace before me, and thee I have known by name.”**
• properly and specially thou hast pleased me
• AND THEE I HAVE KNOWN etc. AUGUSTINE. Because I know thee above all etc. Does God know some more and some less? Or is it according to what is said to some in the Gospel: I know you not? It is according to another knowledge of God, by which God is said to know the things that please him and not to know the things that displease him, not because he is ignorant of them but because he does not approve them; as an art is rightly said not to know faults, since it disapproves them; and God knew Moses above all because Moses pleased God above all. It is to be noted that Moses himself had said to God before: Thou hast said to me: I know thee above all; which God is read to have said to him after he himself said this. But before, it is not read; that we may understand that not all things are written which God spoke with him; but it must be sought more carefully in the earlier parts of Scripture whether it is truly so.
33.19:
**“He answered: I will shew thee all good,”** — eternal rest, in which is all good in the vision of God, as the Psalmist says: "I shall be satisfied when thy glory shall appear."
**“I WILL SHEW”** — When Moses had said to the Lord: Shew me thy glory, he answered: I will pass before thee in my glory etc. Whereas a little before he himself had said: I will go before thee, and will give thee rest; which Moses seems to have taken thus: I will go before thee, as though he would not be present with the people on the way; and therefore he said: If thou thyself dost not come with us, bring me not out of this place etc. But God did not deny him this either, saying: This word also which thou hast spoken will I do. How then, when Moses had said to him: Shew me thy glory, does he seem to say again, as about to go before and not to be together with them: I will pass before thee, unless because this is something else? For he is understood to say: I will pass before thee, of whom it is said: When the hour was come that Jesus should pass out of this world to the Father etc. Which passing is called the Pasch; he passes before all the saints from this world to the Father, to prepare the mansions which he will give them in the resurrection of the dead, because, about to pass before all, he was made the firstborn from the dead. And he greatly commends his grace when he says: And I will proclaim in the name of the Lord in thy sight, as in the sight of the people of Israel. Moses, when he heard these things, signified the people. For in the sight of that nation, scattered everywhere, the Lord Christ is proclaimed among all the gentiles.
**“and I will proclaim”** — through my preachers and apostles I shall be called upon
**“I WILL PROCLAIM”** — AUGUSTINE. And he said "I will proclaim", not: I will be proclaimed, putting an active verb for a passive, by an unusual kind of speech, in which perhaps he wished to signify that he himself does this, that is, that it is done by his grace that the Lord is proclaimed among all the gentiles.
**“in the name of the Lord”** — of my Son, whose incarnation they will preach
**“before thee:”** — O Jewish people
**“and I will have mercy on whom I will,”** — The mercy of God is free and spontaneous to all. For when he has mercy it is grace; when he permits hardening it is just judgment, though hidden.
**“and I will be merciful to whom it shall please me.”** — AND I WILL HAVE MERCY etc. AUGUSTINE. What he added: And I will have mercy on whom I have had mercy, and I will show mercy to whom I have shown mercy, shows more expressly the calling by which he called us into his kingdom and his glory, not for our merits but for his mercy. For since he promised that he would bring in the gentiles, saying: I will proclaim in the name of the Lord in thy sight, he commends that he does this mercifully. Whence: "For I say that Christ Jesus was minister of the circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises made unto the fathers. But that the Gentiles" etc. This therefore was foretold: I will have mercy on whom I have had mercy etc. By which words he forbade man to glory as of the merits of his own virtues, that "he that glorieth may glory in the Lord". For he does not say: I will have mercy on such or such, but on whom I shall have been merciful, that he may show that no one has deserved the mercy of so great a calling by preceding works or merits. For Christ died for the ungodly. But whether he wished to repeat the same thing when he added: I will show mercy to whom I have shown mercy, or, as others have translated: to whom I shall be merciful, or whether there is some difference, I know not. For by this repetition God can show the firmness of his mercy, as it is said: Amen, Amen; and: So be it, so be it; and the repetition of Pharao's dream, and many like things; or that in both peoples, that is, the Gentiles and the Hebrews, God so foretold that he would show mercy.
33.20:
**“And again he said: Thou canst not see my face:”** — the very power of the divine essence
**“for shall not see me”** — through his uncircumscribed essence
**“man”** — in mortal flesh
**“and live.”**
• with immortal flesh
• THOU CANST NOT SEE etc. AUGUSTINE. After the commendation of his mercy he answers what had been said to him: Shew me thy glory, or Shew me thyself. Thou canst not, he says, see my face. For man shall not see my face and live; showing that God as he is cannot appear to this life of corruptible flesh, that is, be seen as he is. For in that life he can, where, that one may live, one must die to this life.
• FOR MAN SHALL NOT SEE etc. GREGORY. John also says: "No man hath seen God at any time." For as long as one lives mortally here, God can be seen through certain images, but cannot through the very form of his nature. Hence it is that Moses, who spoke with God face to face, as a man is wont to speak with his friend, says: If I have found favour in thy sight, shew me thyself openly. For if he with whom he spoke were not God, he would say 'shew me God', and not 'shew thyself'. But if he was God, why did he ask to see him whom he saw? But he thirsted to behold through the brightness of his uncircumscribed nature him whom he had already begun to see through certain images. The fathers of the Old Testament therefore saw God, and yet "no man hath seen God at any time", because to those living in this flesh he could be seen through certain circumscribed images, and could not be seen through the uncircumscribed light of eternity. But if to some living in this flesh, yet growing with inestimable virtue, the brightness of the eternal God can be seen by the keenness of contemplation, yet man shall not see him and live, because he who sees the wisdom which is God dies utterly to this life, lest he be held by love of it. But there have been some who said that even in that region of beatitude God is beheld in his brightness but not seen in his nature. But he himself promises to those who love him, saying: "He that loveth me shall be loved of my Father: and I will love him, and will manifest myself to him." As if to say: You who behold me in your nature, it remains that you see me in my nature. And elsewhere: "Blessed are the clean of heart: for they shall see God." Hence Paul says: "We see now through a glass in a dark manner: but then face to face" etc. But because Peter says: "On whom the angels desire to look", there are some who suppose that not even the angels see God, whereas the Lord said: Their angels always see the face of my Father; but the angels both see God and desire to see him. For if they so desire to see that they do not enjoy their desire, desire without fruit has anxiety, and anxiety punishment. But the angels are strangers to all punishment, because punishment and beatitude never agree. Again, when we say that they are satisfied with the vision of God, according to that: "I shall be satisfied when thy glory shall appear", it is to be considered that loathing is wont to follow satiety. But lest there be anxiety in desire, they are satisfied while desiring; and lest there be loathing in satiety, being satisfied they desire; they desire therefore without labour, because satiety accompanies desire, and they are satisfied without loathing, because satiety is ever kindled from desire.
33.21:
**“And again: Behold, he said, there is a place”** — the Church
**“with me,”** — because truth is beheld from the catholic Church alone, he says that the place from which it is seen is with him.
**“and thou shalt stand”** — firmly
**“upon the rock.”**
• myself, namely
• BEHOLD, HE SAID, A PLACE etc. AUGUSTINE. Again, with a clause put between, Scripture saying, And the Lord said, there follows: Behold a place with me. What place is not with God, who is absent nowhere? But signifying the Church, as commending it as his temple: And thou shalt stand, he says, upon the rock. Because upon this rock, says the Lord, I will build my Church; as soon as my glory shall pass, thou shalt stand, namely, upon the rock; because after the passing of Christ, that is, his passion and resurrection, the faithful people stood upon the rock.
• Moses is set on the rock that he may contemplate the face of God. For he who does not hold the solidity of faith does not know the divine presence. Of which solidity it is said: "Upon this rock I will build my Church."
*Gregory:* There is a place with me etc. The place is the Church, the rock the Lord, Moses the Jewish people, which did not believe when the Lord preached on earth. It therefore stood on the rock beholding the back of the Lord as he passed, because namely after the Lord's passion and ascension, brought into the Church by faith, it deserved to perceive Christ, and knew the back parts of him whose presence it did not see.
*Gregory:* There is a place with me etc. The Church, namely, from which alone truth is beheld, sacrifice is received; it alone intercedes for those who err. Whence it is commanded of the victim of the lamb: In one house shall you eat it, neither shall you carry forth of the flesh thereof out of the house; because in the one catholic Church the true victim of the Redeemer is sacrificed, and the holy thing is not given to dogs. It alone is that in which good work is done fruitfully. Whence also only those who laboured within the vineyard received the reward of the penny. It alone is that which guards those set within it with the strong bond of charity. Whence the water of the flood raised the ark indeed to higher places, but all whom it found outside the ark it destroyed.
33.22:
**“And when shall pass”** — from the world to the Father
**“my glory, I will set thee in a hole of the rock,”**
• and I will set thee in the cleft of the rock. It signifies a most firm defence.
• I will make thee firm in the faith of the passion of my Son.
• with a most firm defence
**“and protect thee”** — "For day and night thy hand was heavy upon me" etc.
**“with hand”** — elsewhere: right hand
**“my, till I pass:”**
• I shall ascend to heaven
• after I have passed
33.23:
**“And I will take away”**
• elsewhere: I will lift
• I will take away the veil from thy heart
**“my hand, and thou shalt see my back parts:”** — thou wilt believe, namely, the incarnation
**“but my face”** — my presence in the flesh
**“thou canst not see.”** — blindness being laid upon thee
**“AND PROTECT WITH HAND”** — AUGUSTINE. And I will cover thee with my hand until I pass, and I will take away my hand, and then thou shalt see my back parts better; but my face shall not be seen by thee. Whereas he had said: Thou shalt stand upon the rock as soon as my glory shall pass, where he is understood to have promised his own firmness on the rock after his passing, how is what he says to be taken: I will set thee in the cleft of the rock, and I will cover thee with my hand until I pass, and I will take away my hand, and then thou shalt see my back parts; as though, he being already set on the rock, he covers him with his hand and then passes, whereas he cannot be on the rock except after his passing? But a recapitulation of a thing passed over is to be understood, which Scripture often uses. For afterward he said what is first in the order of time, which runs thus: I will cover thee with my hand until I pass, and then thou shalt see my back parts. For my face shall not be seen by thee; and thou shalt stand upon the rock as soon as my glory shall pass, and I will set thee in the cleft of the rock. For this was done in those whom Moses then signified, that is, in the Israelites who afterward believed in Christ, that is, as soon as his glory passed; because when he had risen from the dead and ascended into heaven, and, the Spirit being sent, the Apostles spoke with all tongues, many of those who had crucified Christ were pricked to the heart. For blindness in part has happened in Israel, as had been said: I will cover thee with my hand until I pass. Whence: Thy hand was heavy upon me by day, namely when Christ did divine miracles; by night, when as man he died. But afterward, pricked in heart, they said: What shall we do? And they were bidden by the Apostles to do justice and to do penance; but before they were blinded, so that they did not know. "For if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory." That this too was a prophecy the thing itself shows, because of the rock or its cleft, of the laying on of the hand and the sight of the back parts, nothing is read to have followed in visible deed. For at once Scripture adds: And the Lord said to Moses, while he was still speaking the things above; then it joins on what the Lord says afterward: Hew thee two tables of stone etc.

34.2:
**“Be ready in the morning,”** — at the beginning of good work
**“that thou mayst forthwith go up into the mount,”** — the spiritual understanding, namely, of the law
**“and thou shalt stand with me”** — "Without me you can do nothing."
**“upon the top of the mount.”** — the eminence of contemplation
34.3:
**“Let no man”** — unworthy
**“go up with thee: and let not any man be seen throughout all the mount: neither the sheep”** — the simple and unskilled
**“nor the oxen”** — those entangled in earthly cares
**“let them feed over against it.”** — the pasture of holy Scripture and the freshness of contemplation
34.4: **“Then he cut out two tables of stone, such as had been before: and rising by night he went up into the mount Sinai,”** — he passes from human darkness to the mount of spiritual understanding
34.5: **“And when the Lord was come down”** — The human mind cannot contemplate God unless he come down to it.
34.7:
**“who keepest mercy unto thousands: who takest away iniquity, and wickedness, and sin, and no man of himself is innocent before thee. Who renderest the iniquity”**
• any whatever
• original
**“of the fathers to the children,”** — not baptized
**“and to the grandchildren,”** — imitating, namely
**“unto the third and fourth generation.”**
• the vengeance extends to those who have seen what they wickedly followed
• WHO RENDEREST THE INIQUITY etc. GREGORY. Since it is written: What is it that you use among you this parable as a proverb in the land of Israel, saying: The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the teeth of the children are set on edge? As I live, saith the Lord, this parable shall be no more to you a proverb in Israel: as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine: the soul that sinneth, the same shall die; what is it that is said: Who renderest the iniquity of the fathers to the children and to the grandchildren? We draw original sin from our fathers, and unless we are saved through the grace of baptism we bear even the guilt of our parents, because we are still one with them. He renders the iniquity of the fathers on the children when for the fault of the parent the soul of the offspring is polluted by original sin. And again he does not render the iniquity of the fathers on the children, because when we are freed from original guilt through baptism, we have no longer the faults of our parents but those we ourselves commit. Otherwise: he who imitates the iniquity of a wicked parent is bound also by his offence; but he who does not imitate it is not weighed down by his offence. Whence it comes about that the wicked son of a wicked father pays not only his own sins which he adds, but also his father's, when, not ignorant of God's anger, he does not fear to add his own malice. And it is just that he who does not fear, under a strict judge, to imitate the ways of a wicked father, should be compelled also to pay for his faults. Whence: The soul of the father is mine, the soul of the son is mine: the soul that sinneth, the same shall die; because sometimes sons perish even from a father's sin. But when original sin is blotted out, they are not held in soul by the wickedness of their parents. For why is it that little children are often seized by demons, but that the flesh of the son is punished by the father's penalty? For the wicked father is struck in himself and despises it. He strikes him therefore in his children, that he may be sharply burned, and the father's pain is rendered through the flesh of the children, that by the children's punishment the father's wicked mind may be punished. But when not little children but sons already grown are struck even for their parents' fault, they pay the penalties of those whose deeds they have followed. Whence it is rightly said: Unto the third and fourth generation; because up to that generation, which the sons imitate, they can see the life of their parents; the vengeance extends to those who have seen what they wickedly followed.
34.8: **“And Moses making haste, bowed down”** — understanding that he is earth and ashes
34.9:
**“said: If I have found grace in thy sight, O Lord, I beseech thee, that thou wilt go”** — merciful and propitious
**“with us (for it is a stiffnecked people), and take away”** — by punishing and pardoning
**“our iniquities”** — against our neighbour
**“and sin,”** — against ourselves
**“and possess us.”** — as thy inheritance
34.10: **“The Lord answered: I will make a covenant in the sight of all. I will do signs such as were never seen upon the earth,”** — This was never given to the Jews according to the letter: it is therefore to be taken of the day of judgment, in which God will do what has never been seen.
34.11: **“Observe all things which this day I command thee: I myself will drive out before thy face the Amorrhite, and the Chanaanite, and the Hethite, and the Pherezite, and the Hevite, and the Jebusite.”** — By these nations the seven vices are designated, with which we are forbidden to join fellowship.
34.13:
**“But destroy their altars,”** — lest anyone begin to worship
**“break their statues,”** — that no monuments of idolatry may remain
34.14: **“THE LORD, JEALOUS”** — AUGUSTINE. For the Lord God is jealous, his name is a jealous God; that is, the very name by which he is called the Lord God is jealous, because God is a jealous one: which God does not do by the fault of human disturbance, being always and wholly unchangeable and tranquil; but by this word he shows that his people will not commit fornication with strange gods unpunished. For this word is said figuratively, from a husband's jealousy, which guards a wife's chastity and destroys everyone who goes a whoring from him.
34.17: **“Molten gods”** — the whole from a part
34.18:
**“The feast of the unleavened bread”** — the Pasch
**“thou shalt keep. Seven days”** — the whole present life
**“shalt thou eat unleavened bread,”** — of sincerity and truth
34.19:
**“All that openeth the womb”** — the beginning, namely, of goods both bodily and spiritual
**“of the male kind”** — manly, namely, and strong
**“shall be mine. Of all beasts, both of oxen”** — the strong and patient
**“and of sheep,”** — the simple and innocent
34.20:
**“The firstling of an ass”** — the first work of uncleanness
**“thou shalt redeem with a sheep:”**
• with the simplicity of innocence
• THE FIRSTLING OF AN ASS etc. ISIDORE. By the ass uncleanness, by the sheep innocence is designated. To exchange the firstlings of the ass for a sheep, therefore, is to turn the beginnings of an unclean life to the simplicity of innocence, that after the sinner has done those things which the Lord rejects as unclean, he may now, by acting, bring forth things which he may lay clean upon the sacrifice of God.
**“but if thou wilt not give a price for it, it shall be slain.”** — because the unclean mind, if it be not changed for the better, will be slain by perpetual death
**“The firstborn of thy sons thou shalt redeem: neither shalt thou appear before me”** — in the tabernacle, namely, which signifies the Church
**“empty.”** — of the offerings of good works and virtues
34.21:
**“Six days shalt thou labour,”** — through the whole time, namely, of his life, because man is born to labour, and the life of man upon earth is a warfare
**“the seventh day”** — in the rest, namely, of souls
**“thou shalt cease to plough and to reap.”** — THE SEVENTH DAY etc. AUGUSTINE. When he was giving commands about the sabbath, why did he add something about sowing and harvest? For he seems to say: In the time of sowing and harvest. Or perhaps he commanded the rest of the sabbath to be so kept that not even those times should have an excuse which are very necessary to farmers for food and life? It is just even in the time of sowing and harvest, when work presses much, that there be rest on the sabbath; and so, by these times which demand most work, it was signified that one ought to cease on the sabbath at all times.
34.22:
**“The feast”** — Pentecost
**“of weeks thou shalt keep with the firstfruits of the corn of thy wheat harvest, and the feast”** — of tabernacles, namely, which is called scenopegia
34.23:
**“Three times in a year”**
• in spring, namely, in summer, in autumn
• because we ought to offer all our goods in the faith of the holy Trinity
34.24:
**“For when I shall have taken away the nations”** — the vices
**“from thy face, and shall have enlarged thy borders,”** — all narrowness of mind and body being shut out
**“no man shall lie in wait against thy land when thou shalt go up, and appear in the sight of the Lord thy God thrice in a year.”**
• This never happened to the Jews according to the letter.
• This will be fulfilled in the life to come, when neither visible nor invisible enemy will be able to harm the saints.
• NO MAN SHALL LIE IN WAIT AGAINST THY LAND etc. AUGUSTINE. What he said: No man shall covet anything of his land etc., he wishes to be understood thus: that each might go up secure, and not be anxious about his land, God promising a guard, that no one would covet anything from it because of him who went up, nor should he fear his absence from it. And here he shows clearly what he said above: Thou shalt not appear empty in the sight of thy God; because he said it of that place where God was to have the tabernacle or the temple.
34.25:
**“Thou shalt not offer”** — because the sacrifice ought to be pure and without any corruption.
**“upon leaven”** — of malice and wickedness
**“the blood of thy sacrifice:”**
• elsewhere: of my sacrifice
• THOU SHALT NOT OFFER etc. AUGUSTINE. What is it that he says: Thou shalt not slay the blood of my sacrifices upon leaven? Does he in this place call his sacrifices those which are slain at the pasch, and command that there be no leaven in the house then, when the days of unleavened bread are?
**“neither shall there remain in the morning any thing of the victims”**
• of the flesh, namely, of the lamb which was sacrificed at the Pasch
• because we ought so to complete our sacrifices in the present that we may not begin to sacrifice at the judgment to come, when it will not be the time for working but for receiving the reward.
**“of the solemnity of the Phase.”** — or of the Pasch
34.26:
**“The first of the fruits of thy ground thou shalt offer”** — ascribing the beginnings of all goods not to thyself
**“in the house”** — the Church
**“of the Lord thy God. Thou shalt not boil”** — as above
**“a kid in the milk of his dam.”** — THOU SHALT NOT BOIL A LAMB etc. AUGUSTINE. See, again I do not know how it can be understood. Yet it is a great prophecy of Christ even if it could be done according to the letter: how much more if it cannot? For in the sayings of God not all things are to be referred to the proper sense of works, as neither that about the rock and its cleft and the laying on of the hand; but this is plainly to be required of the faithfulness of the narrative, that the things it says were done were truly done, and the things it says were said were truly said. Which is required also of the narrators of the Gospel, since they relate that Christ said certain things which he said in parables; yet that he said this is not a parable but a historical narrative.
34.27: **“And the Lord said to Moses: Write thee these words,”** — what he had said before when he received the tables which he broke, he repeats in this way also, not recapitulating what was done, but commending that it was done again.
34.28:
**“And he was there with the Lord forty days and forty nights:”** — FORTY DAYS etc. ISIDORE. Moses fasted forty days, and Elias, and the Lord himself. For it is commanded us from the law, from the prophets, and from the Gospel, which has testimony from these. Whence on the mount between the two persons the Saviour shone forth in the middle, that we may bridle our greed from all the allurements of the world as by the fast of temperance, as long as the perfection of the Decalogue is preached through the four parts of the same world, that is, to the whole world, so that ten taken four times may mark the number forty.
**“bread”**
• bodily, namely
• By the name of bread he signifies all food, the whole from a part, as also by the name of water all drink.
**“he did not eat, nor drank water, and he wrote upon the tables the ten words of the covenant.”** — AND HE WROTE UPON THE TABLES etc. AUGUSTINE. It is said of Moses that he himself wrote, to whom God also said a little before: "Write thee these words." But when he first received the Law, whose tables he cast down and broke, he was neither said to have hewn them, nor was he told to write, nor is he related to have written them, as it is now said: He wrote upon the tables the words of the testament etc.; but then it was said: And he gave to Moses, as soon as he had ceased to speak to him in mount Sinai, two tables of testimony, tables of stone written with the finger of God; and a little after: And Moses returned, he says, and came down from the mount, and the two tables, and the tables were the work of God, and the writing of God was graven in the tables. A great question arises how those tables which Moses was, the Lord foreknowing it, to break, are said to be not the work of man but of God, and not written by man but by the finger of God; but the later ones, which were to last long and to be in the tabernacle and in the temple of God, were by God's command hewn and written by man. Was the grace of God signified in the former, not the work of man, of which they were made unworthy, turning back in heart to Egypt and making an idol, whence they were deprived of that benefit, and therefore Moses broke the tables? But by these later ones are signified those who glory in their own works. Whence the Apostle: For they, not knowing the justice of God, and seeking to establish their own, have not submitted themselves to the justice of God; and therefore the tables were written by human work, which remained with them, signifying the same men who would glory in their own works, not in the finger of God, that is, in the Spirit of God. Certainly then the repetition of the Law signifies the New Testament. But that one signified the Old, whence it was broken and abolished. Especially because when the Law is given the second time it is given with no terror, as that was, amid the din of fires, clouds and trumpets. Whence the people, terrified, say: Let not the Lord speak to us, lest we die. Whence it is signified that there is fear in the Old Testament, love in the New. How then is this question solved, why those were the work of God, these the work of man, and those written by the finger of God, these written by man? Or perhaps is the Old Testament rather signified in the former for this reason, that God there commanded, but man did not do? For "the Law" was set in the Old Testament to convict transgressors, which "entered in that sin might abound". For it was not fulfilled by fear, since it is not fulfilled except by charity. And therefore it is called the work of God, because God established the Law, God wrote it: not the work of man, because man did not obey God, and the Law rather made him guilty. But in the second tables man made the tables through the help of God. Whence the Lord says: I am not come to destroy the Law, but to fulfil. And the Apostle: Love is the fulfilling of the Law. That therefore was made easy for man in the New Testament which in the Old was hard, for him who has the faith that worketh by charity, that finger of God, that is, the Spirit of God, writing it within in the heart, not outside on stone. Whence: "Not in tables of stone, but in the fleshly tables of the heart"; since "the charity of God", by which the precept is truly fulfilled, "is poured forth in our hearts by the Holy Ghost, who is given to us". This then is the Law first given, where the Old Testament is signified, which is the work of God only, and written by the finger of God. Whence the Apostle says: "Wherefore the Law indeed is holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good." The Law therefore, holy and good, is the work of God: where man does nothing, because he does not obey, but is rather weighed down by guilt, the Law threatening and condemning. But man is blessed when this "holy and just and good commandment" is also his work, but through the grace of God.
34.29:
**“And when Moses came down from the mount Sinai, he held the two tables of the testimony, and he knew not that his face was horned”**
• The face of Moses glorified: the law made bright with divine mysteries.
• with certain rays of brightness which human sight could not bear
**“from the conversation of the Lord.”** — because, namely, he had spoken so long with the Lord
**“AND WHEN HE CAME DOWN”** — ISIDORE. Moses goes up again into the mount, and again God gives him the law on other tables hewn after the pattern of the former. But those which he first received he broke without delay, which bore the image of the ancient Law, which ceased after no long interval because of the people's sin. But those hewn after the pattern of the former signified the New Testament; which were not broken, because the New Testament remains for ever; whence they are fittingly marked by ten words, that by that number the figure of the cross may be expressed, which ten signifies, being formed in the shape of a cross. For Christ came not to destroy the law but to fulfil it, namely through the passion of the cross, whose image was on the tables.
*Isidore:* As Moses comes down with the tables, his face is seen glorified, but yet it is covered with a veil; in which it signified that the law was covered with a mystic veil and hidden from unbelievers. For the word of the law has the knowledge of glory, but secret; it has also the horns of the two Testaments, with which it goes armed against the doctrines of falsehood. For when Moses is read, the veil is upon their heart; and plainly, while unbelievers take the Scripture of the law and the prophets carnally, the whole face of Moses is covered with a kind of veil, so that they cannot bear the glory of the law as it speaks; but if they be turned to God, the veil shall be taken away; the killing letter will die, the quickening spirit will be quickened. For the Lord is a Spirit, and the law is spiritual. Whence: "Open thou my eyes: and I will consider the wondrous things of thy law."
34.30:
**“And Aaron and the children of Israel seeing the face of Moses horned,”** — with the two testaments, namely, which were in the face of Moses, that is, in the law: the old openly, namely, the new hiddenly
**“were afraid to come near.”** — because the Jews do not understand but shrink from the light of the divine mysteries in the law
34.33: **“And having done speaking, he put a veil upon his face.”** — because "even until this day, when Moses is read, the veil is upon the hearts of the Jews"
34.34:
**“But when he went in to the Lord, and spoke with him, he took it away until he came forth,”**
• because when they are turned to the Lord the veil is taken away
• AND AARON AND THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL SEEING etc. ORIGEN. It is written that Aaron and all the children of Israel saw Moses, and his face was glorified, and the colour of his countenance, and they feared to come to him. And after a little Moses put a veil upon his face. But when he went in before the Lord to speak to him, he took away the veil. Setting this out the Apostle says: Now if the ministration of death, engraven with letters upon stones, was glorious, so that the children of Israel could not steadfastly behold the face of Moses for the glory of his countenance, which is made void: how shall not the ministration of the Spirit be rather in glory? And a little after: And not as Moses put a veil upon his face, that the children of Israel might not steadfastly look on the face of his countenance. For their senses were made dull etc. Who would not be afraid of the mark of a dull heart? The face of Moses is glorified, but the children of Israel cannot steadfastly look on his face. The people of the Synagogue cannot steadfastly look. But if anyone has a life more eminent than the crowd, he can. For now too the veil is set on the reading of the Old Testament, and Moses speaks with glorified countenance. But we cannot gaze on the glory, because we are still the people, and have nothing more of zeal, nothing more of merit, than the rest of the common folk. But when anyone shall be turned to the Lord, the veil shall be taken away. Our turning therefore is the cause of the veil's being taken away. While therefore, reading the divine Scriptures, we do not understand, while they are obscure and shut, we are not yet turned. For to those turned, the veil will at once be taken away. Everyone who, when the words of the law are recited, is occupied with common tales, is turned away; and he who is anxious about the business of the world, about money, about gains, about the cares of possessions and the desire of riches, who strives after the glory of the world and the honours of the age, is turned away. He too who seems a stranger to these, but stands and hears the words of the Law intent with face and eyes, yet wanders in heart and thought, is turned away. What then is it to be turned? If we turn our backs on all these things, and give ourselves to the word of God with zeal, acts, mind and care. For let us meditate on the law day and night, and, leaving all, give ourselves to God and be exercised in his testimonies; this is to be turned to the Lord. But which of us seeks the divine writings with as great labour and zeal as he sought human ones? Some, as soon as they have heard what is read recited, go away at once. There is no inquiry with one another about the things that have been read, no conferring. They do not ask their fathers to tell them, nor the priests to declare to them. Others do not even wait patiently until the lessons are recited in church; others do not even know if they are recited, but in the remoter places of the church are occupied with worldly tales: on whom there is no longer a veil upon the heart, but a wall and rampart is set. For if he who is present, hears, attends, and goes over and discusses what he hears, asks and learns, can scarcely come to the freedom of knowledge, he "who stoppeth his ears lest he hear", and turns his back to the face of the reader, how is he to be said to have a veil laid upon his heart, to whom not even the very veil of the letter by which the sense is veiled, which is the sound of the voice, has come? The face of Moses therefore is made glorious: for the things he speaks have glory, but it is covered and hidden, and "all his glory is within".
*Origen:* Consider this too, that in the law the countenance of Moses is glorified, though it is covered with a veil. But his hand, put into his bosom, became leprous. In which the form of the whole Law seems to me to be most fully marked out. For in the countenance the word of the law, in the hand the works are signified. Because therefore no one was to be justified by the works of the law, nor could the law lead anyone to perfection, the hand becomes leprous and is hidden in the bosom, as having nothing of perfect work. The face therefore is glorified, but covered with a veil, because its word has the glory of knowledge, but hidden. Whence: "The uncertain and hidden things of thy wisdom thou hast made manifest to me." The face of Moses therefore has glory, the hand disgrace. Lastly he is commanded to loose his shoe, so that there was no glory in his feet, although this was done not without mystery. For the feet are the last part of man. It was shown therefore that in the last times Moses would loose his shoe, that another might take the bride, and she would be called "the house of the unshod" until the present. Moses therefore has nothing glorious in the law but his face alone. But in the gospel he is glorified wholly. Whence: There appeared Moses and Elias in glory, speaking with him. Here it is not said that his countenance was glorified, but that he appeared wholly in glory speaking with Jesus, where is fulfilled what was promised him on mount Sina: Thou shalt see my back parts. For he saw the things that were done in the latter days and rejoiced, because he not only came down from the mount glorified in countenance, but went up from the mount glorified wholly; and he saw now present him of whom he had said: The Lord your God will raise up to you a prophet of your brethren, like unto me etc., and making good his words. And lest he should hesitate in anything, he hears the Father saying: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased: hear ye him." Moses said: Him you shall hear; the Father, saying: "Hear ye him", shows him present. Moses also rejoices, because he too in a manner lays down the veil, turned to the Lord, when what he foretold is evidently fulfilled, or when the time has come for the things he had covered to be revealed through the Spirit. But let us see what the Apostle says: "Now the Lord is a Spirit: and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty." I think that the Word of God, according to what profits the hearers, is named now the way, now the truth, now the life, now the resurrection, now also flesh, and now Spirit. For although he truly received the substance of flesh from the virgin, in which he bore the cross and began the resurrection, yet the Apostle says: And if we have known Christ according to the flesh, but now we know him so no longer: because therefore now his word calls us to a subtler understanding, and wishes us to perceive nothing carnal in the law, he says that he who wishes to take away the veil should turn to the Lord, not as to flesh but as to spirit, that he may come from carnal things to spiritual, and from bondage to liberty, for "where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty". But elsewhere he says: I judged not myself to know anything among you, but Jesus Christ, and him crucified. To these he did not say that the Lord is a Spirit, and the wisdom of God, because they could not know Christ according as he is wisdom, but according as he was crucified. But those to whom he said: We speak wisdom among the perfect, not of this world, but the wisdom of God in a mystery, which is hidden, did not need the Word of God according as "the Word was made flesh", but according as he is wisdom hidden in a mystery. To those therefore who are called to spiritual understanding it is said: "Now the Lord is a Spirit: and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty": by which, namely, turned to the Lord and freed from the bondage of the world, we may seek the liberty of knowledge.
**“and then he spoke”** — with veiled face
**“to the children of Israel all things that had been commanded him.”** — AND THEN HE SPOKE etc. AUGUSTINE. After Moses came down from the mount, the works of building the tabernacle and of the priestly vesture are commanded; before giving any command about the making of these, he spoke to the people about the keeping of the sabbath. Where it rightly moves us, since he had received the ten words of the Law on the tables which he himself hewed and wrote, why, after he came down, he admonished the people about the sabbath alone. For if, because of the same precepts of the Law, it was superfluous for the people to hear them again, why was not this also superfluous, since it is read among those same ten precepts? Or is this too like the veil with which he covered his face, because the children of Israel could not gaze on the brightness of his countenance? For of the ten precepts he commanded this alone to the people, which is said there to be figurative: for the other nine we do not doubt are to be kept in the New Testament as there. But that one about the sabbath was so far veiled and commanded in mystery that today it is not kept by us. But let us gaze only on what is signified. In that rest, where servile works are bidden to cease, great is the height of the grace of God. For good works are then done with rest when faith worketh by charity: but fear hath torment, and in torment what rest? Whence: "Fear is not in charity." But "charity is poured forth in our hearts by the Holy Ghost, who is given to us". Therefore the sabbath is a holy rest to the Lord: to be ascribed, namely, to the grace of God, not to us as from ourselves. Otherwise our works will be such that they are either human sins or done with fear, not with love; and therefore servile works without rest are everlasting. For not in vain was the sabbath of sabbaths instituted. Above, when God spoke first of the anointing of the tabernacle, he said that by the same unction all those things were sanctified and made holy of holies. But the altar of holocausts, sanctified by the same unction, he had said was made holy of the holy. And there seemed to be this difference, that he had called none of them holy of holies except what is separated from the holy only by the veil, namely where the ark of the testament and the altar of incense were. Now, when he repeated the same things, he said of the anointed tabernacle and the things that were in it that they were sanctified by that unction and made holy. But the altar of holocaust, which he had said before was made holy of the holy, he now said was made holy of holies by the same unction. Whence it is understood that holy of the holy and holy of holies are the same; and by this, that all those anointed things, that is, the whole tabernacle and whatever was in it, which he before called holy of holies, mean just as much as what he now calls holy: nor is each of them called after that unction only holy of the holy, but also holy of holies, like the altar of holocaust; so that now there is no difference, so far as this name is concerned, between the things that were within the veil, namely where the ark of the testimony was, and the rest that are outside, except that those were so called the holies of holies, or the holy of holies, that they were so called even before the unction; but the rest were sanctified by unction that they might receive this name.
34.35: **“And they saw that the face of Moses when he came out was horned, but he covered his face again, if at any time he spoke to them.”** — the fulness of this sabbath will be in eternal beatitude

35.2: **“Six days you shall do work: the seventh day shall be holy unto you, the sabbath, and the rest of the Lord: he that shall do work”** — servile
35.3:
**“You shall kindle no fire”** — of covetousness or lust or anger
**“in any of your habitations”** — minds or bodies or any gatherings whatever
35.5:
**“Set aside with you”** — The Seventy: Take from among yourselves; because all these things, namely, are within us.
**“firstfruits to the Lord.”**
• let the rest, namely, be yours
• SET ASIDE WITH YOU etc. ORIGEN. Another reading: Take from among yourselves a redemption for the Lord. Let every one that has conceived in his heart offer firstfruits to the Lord. Moses does not wish you to offer to God anything that is outside you: From among yourselves, he says, take, and offer firstfruits to the Lord, as each has conceived in heart, gold, silver etc. The spiritual law requires gold for the tabernacle, and other materials which we have within us and can bring forth from ourselves. For Scripture says: The word is nigh, in thy mouth and in thy heart. For if thou confess the Lord Jesus, and believe in thy heart that God hath raised him up from the dead, thou shalt be saved. If therefore thou hast believed 'in thy heart', thy heart and thy understanding are the best gold. Thou hast therefore offered gold for the tabernacle, the faith of thy heart. If thou hast confessed, the word of confession is silver. These are within thee; these, even if thou art naked, thou canst have. And what he adds: Each as he has conceived in heart, looks to this. For thou wilt not be able to offer God anything of thy understanding or of thy word unless thou hast first conceived in heart the things that are written; unless thou hast been attentive and heard diligently, thy gold cannot be proved, nor thy silver. For it is required to be proved. Whence: "The words of the Lord are pure words: as silver tried by the fire, purged from the earth, refined seven times." If therefore thou hast conceived in heart the things that are written, thy gold, that is, thy understanding, will be proved, and thy silver, that is, thy word, will be proved.
*Origen:* You who are accustomed to be present at the divine mysteries know how, when you receive the body of the Lord, you keep it with caution and reverence, lest any little of it fall. For if it fall, you believe yourselves guilty, and rightly you believe it: how do you think it a lesser sin to have neglected the word of God than his body? They are commanded therefore to offer beginnings, that is, firstfruits. He who offers what is first necessarily has himself what remains. See how much he must abound in gold or silver and all the other things that are commanded, so that we may both offer to the Lord and have left over for ourselves. For first my understanding ought to understand God, and offer him the firstfruits of its understanding, that it may consequently know the rest; let the word also do this; all these things that are in us do it.
**“Let every one that is willing and hath a ready heart, offer them to the Lord:”**
• "For God loveth a cheerful giver."
• LET EVERY ONE THAT IS WILLING etc. ORIGEN. Another reading: Let each of you, he says, as he has conceived in heart, offer firstfruits to the Lord. I ask what are the firstfruits of gold, or the firstfruits of silver? And how do firstfruits seem to be kept of fine linen, scarlet and purple? Or how is each to offer as he has conceived in heart? There are those who conceive in heart the things that are read. There are those who do not conceive at all, intent on the works of the world or the reckonings of gain. The women only chatter, make a din with tales, and do not allow silence to be; they think of their children, or of wool, or of household needs. They learn to go about from house to house, speaking not only wordily but curiously things which they ought not. How then do they conceive? No one conceives in heart but he who is free in heart, free in mind and wholly intent. Otherwise he cannot offer to God. And it is just that each be found to have his portion in the temple of the Lord. For it is not hidden from the Lord what each offers. How glorious for thee, if it be said in the temple of the Lord: This gold, with which the ark of the testament is covered, is his. The silver, of which the sockets and pillars are, is his; the brass of which the rings and the laver and certain parts of the pillars were made, or the stones of the ephod and the logion, or the purple with which the high priest is adorned, and the scarlet, are his; and every other thing one by one. How unseemly, how wretched, if the Lord, visiting the tabernacle, find nothing of thy gift, know nothing offered by thee. So undevout, so unfaithful hast thou lived, that thou hast placed nothing of remembrance of thee in the temple of the Lord. For as the prince of this world comes to each one seeking whether he may find anything of his acts in us, and, if he finds it, claims us for himself: so if the Lord, coming, find something of thine in his tabernacle, he defends thee as his and calls thee his own.
**“gold”** — faith
**“and silver”** — confession
**“and brass,”** — interpretation from tongue to tongue
**“BRASS”** — ORIGEN. It seems to be put for fortitude; I think it can also be taken for the voice. For the word is one thing, the voice another. For a word is called speech supported by reason. But the voice is the same whether it be spoken in Latin or in Greek, whether loudly or softly. Whence: "I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal." To speak with tongues therefore and to interpret from one tongue into another is the offering of brass. For it is necessary that the tabernacle of the Lord have all things, and that nothing be lacking in the house of God. The offering of brass therefore is the voice which turns another's sense into another tongue. But the word is that which brings forth one's own sense. Let all things therefore be offered to God: sense, word and voice.
35.6:
**“Violet”**
• We are bidden, namely, to offer ourselves, who consist of four elements.
• which is referred to the air
**“purple,”** — which to water
**“and scarlet twice dyed,”** — because to fire, of twofold nature
**“and fine linen,”**
• which is referred to the earth, because it springs from the earth
• twisted, namely, not loosened by luxury and delights; whence: I chastise my body, and bring it into subjection.
• VIOLET, PURPLE etc. ORIGEN. Let us look at the rest: violet, purple, scarlet doubled, and fine twisted linen. These hold the figure of the four elements of which the world and the human body consist, that is, of air, fire, water, earth. Violet is referred to the air, which the colour itself shows; and scarlet to fire; purple to water, because it takes its juice from the waters; fine linen to the earth, from which it springs. We too therefore have all these things in ourselves, since we are bidden to offer firstfruits to the Lord from them. Therefore he says: Take from among yourselves, and you shall bring firstfruits to the Lord.
• AND SCARLET TWICE DYED etc. ORIGEN. Let us see why the scarlet is doubled. This colour indicates the element of fire, which has a twofold power: one by which it gives light, another by which it burns. This is the reason of the history. Mystically too fire is twofold. For there is fire in this world and in the world to come. The Lord says: "I am come to cast fire on the earth." This fire gives light. He will say in the future: Depart into everlasting fire etc. That fire burns. But this which he came to cast "enlighteneth every man that cometh into this world"; yet it has something which burns. Whence: Was not our heart burning within us, whilst he opened to us the Scriptures? But I know not whether that fire in the world to come, which burns, has anything that gives light. But let us see how we can offer this doubled fire. If thou art a doctor and buildest the tabernacle, that is, the Church of God, and it is said to thee: Behold, I have given my words in thy mouth as fire: if then, teaching and building the Church of God, thou dost only rebuke, reprove and chastise, and upbraid the sins of the people, but bringest forth nothing of consolation from the divine Scriptures, explainest nothing obscure, openest nothing of more sacred understanding, thou hast offered scarlet, but not doubled. For thy fire only burns, it does not give light. Again, if in teaching thou openest the mysteries of the Law and discussest its secrets, but dost not reprove the sinner, nor correct the negligent, nor hold the severity of discipline, thou hast offered scarlet, but not doubled. For thy fire only gives light, it does not kindle. He therefore who offers rightly and divides rightly offers scarlet doubled, so as to mingle with the light of knowledge a little fire of severity.
*Origen:* If anyone worthily understands the going out of the Hebrews from Egypt, and the passing of the Red Sea, and all the way that is made through the desert, and each station of the camps, so as to receive also the law of God written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, and understands in these the increases of the virtues, and fulfils each in himself, he can come to the understanding of the tabernacle. Of which the Apostle says: For there was a tabernacle made the first, wherein was the candlestick, and the setting forth of loaves, which is called the Holy. And after the veil, the second tabernacle, which is called the Holy of holies, having a golden censer, and the ark of the testament, and in it the two tables, and the manna, and the rod of Aaron that had blossomed. But what he adds: "Of which it is not now the time to speak particularly", some refer to that time in which he was writing to the Hebrews. Others think that because of the greatness of the mysteries he denies that the whole time of the present life is fit for it. But after his manner he opens a few things to many, that it may be shut to the negligent, but found by those who seek and opened to those who knock. Whence again he says: For Jesus is not entered into the holies made with hands, the patterns of the true: but into heaven itself, that he may appear now in the presence of God "through the veil, that is to say, his flesh". Since then he interpreted the veil of the inner tabernacle as the flesh of Christ, and the Holies themselves as heaven or the heavens, and Christ as the high priest who he says entered once into the Holies, having obtained eternal redemption: from these few things, if anyone knows how to understand the sense of Paul, he has opened to us a great sea of understanding. David too says: I shall go over into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God. And elsewhere: "Lord, who shall dwell in thy tabernacle? or who shall rest in thy holy hill? He that walketh without blemish, and worketh justice." That is not the tabernacle which the prophet desires, made of skins and curtains and coverings of haircloth and the other materials of our use. For how is it true that no one dwells in this tabernacle but "the innocent in hands and clean of heart", when in the material tabernacle the worst priests, sons of pestilence, often dwelt, and the ark of the testament was taken and held by the Philistines? He therefore must be innocent in hands and clean of heart who dwells in the tabernacle which God pitched, and not man. The Lord also mentions not one tabernacle but several, and not temporal but eternal, saying: "That when you shall fail, they may receive you into everlasting dwellings." And the Apostle: Desiring to be clothed upon with our habitation that is from heaven. Follow therefore, leaving the earth, the prophetic and apostolic sense, and, what is greater, the word of Christ, that with all thy mind thou mayest ascend into heaven, and there seek the magnificence of the eternal dwelling or tabernacle, whose figure is shadowed forth on earth through Moses; to whom the Lord says: See, he says, that thou make all things according to the pattern which was shewn thee in the mount. The whole people therefore is commanded, each contributing according to his strength, to make the tabernacle, that all may in a manner be one tabernacle. And the contribution is made not of necessity but of free will: Thou shalt make, he says, a sanctification, and thence I will be seen by you. God therefore wishes us to make him a sanctification. For he promises that if we make him a sanctification he will be seen by us. Whence the Apostle: Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see God. And he who has been sanctified in body and spirit, through purity of heart and body, will see God. Let us make therefore a sanctification for the Lord, all of us one, and each one one. For let us all make one, that is, the Church which is holy, "not having spot or wrinkle", but having for pillars, namely, its doctors and ministers, of whom it is said: Peter and James and John, who seemed to be pillars, gave to me the right hands of fellowship, and to Barnabas. In the tabernacle the pillars are joined by bars put between them; in the churches the doctors are joined in fellowship by right hands given to one another. But these pillars are silvered, and their sockets. And two sockets are assigned to each pillar: one which is called the head and is set on top; the other which is truly called the socket and is put under the pillar as a foundation. Those pillars are silvered which preach the word of God and receive it through the Holy Ghost: "The words of the Lord are pure words: as silver tried by the fire." And these preachers have the prophets for sockets. For they set the Church "upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets", using whose testimonies they confirm the faith of Christ. And the head of the pillars is he of whom the Apostle says: The head of the man is Christ. By the hangings, which are set in loops and hung from rings and tied with cords after the manner of curtains, stretched twenty-eight cubits in length and four cubits in breadth, is had the people of believers, which clings and hangs on the cords of faith. For a threefold cord is not broken, which is the faith of the Trinity, from which the Church hangs and is held up. And the measure of one court is stretched twenty-eight cubits in length and four in breadth, in which the law set into the four Gospels is marked. For seven signifies the law, which, when joined with four, four times seven make the number twenty-eight. These courts are ten, that they may hold the whole number of perfection and signify the decalogue of the law. And now the kinds of violet and fine linen and purple unfold many and divers works. Thence the hangings; thence the outer and inner veil; thence the whole vesture of the priest and high priest made of gold and gems, by which we can understand the kinds of virtues with which the Church is adorned. Faith is compared to gold, the word of preaching to silver; brass to patience; to incorruptible wood the knowledge which comes through the wood, or the incorruption of chastity which does not grow old; to fine linen virginity, to scarlet the glory of confession, to purple the brightness of chastity, to violet the hope of the kingdom of heaven. And what or of what sort are the vestments of the priests he declares, saying: "Let thy priests be clothed with justice" etc. And the Apostle: "Put ye on the bowels of mercy"; and he designates nobler vestments: Put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh.
*Gregory:* In the building of the tabernacle, that the silver pillars might stand within, pins of brass were commanded to be made round about outside, by which the tabernacle might be held tied. Of which it is written: Thou shalt make the pins of the tabernacle and of the court with their little cords. The fathers of the Old Testament, who stood far off from the incarnation of Christ by intervals of time, seemed to be outside; but from the blood of Abel the passion of the Church began, and the Church of the elect who went before and who follow is one. But because it is said to the disciples: Many kings and prophets have desired to see the things that you see, and have not seen them, to have stood as it were outside, for the ancient fathers, is not to have seen bodily the presence of the Redeemer. They were outside therefore, but not divided from the Church, because in mind and in the work of preaching they held the loftiness of the Church, which we behold not by waiting for it but by having it. For as we are saved in the passion that is past, so they were saved by faith in the same passion to come. They therefore were outside, not outside the mystery, but outside the time. Whence in the building of the tabernacle, that the silver pillars might stand within, pins of brass were fixed outside round about, by which the tabernacle might be held tied, and cords were tied to the pins, that the tabernacle might remain fixed; because, that the apostles might stand firm in the light of their word, and the whole tabernacle, that is, the Church, might stand in the integrity of faith, the fathers of the Old Testament and the prophets were fixed outside like pins, that with the cords of their words they might bind faith to our minds, and this tabernacle of God might remain unshaken. They were therefore before the time of this Church, but yet they bind those who are in it, because while they preached the heavenly mysteries to come, after they were shown they made them credible to all. That the pillars therefore may stand immovable within, the pins hold the cords outside; because the preaching of those who could both see and preach it before it happened obtained that the holy apostles should perfectly believe the mystery of life. The pillars were made of silver, the pins of brass, because what the apostles clearly preach, this the prophets spoke obscurely under a mystical understanding. Rightly therefore are they marked by brass, because they were not clear in preaching. But the apostles, because they had the light of preaching in the mystery of the Redeemer, are expressed by silver pillars. And it is to be noted that silver sounds and shines, but brass sounds and does not shine; because the preachers of the New Testament spoke openly, and could also show the things they spoke of.
