But the preachers of the Old Testament, because they spoke obscure things of the heavenly mystery through the shadows of allegories, gave as it were a sound without light.
*Origen:* After this the men took from their wives, all to whom it seemed good in mind, and brought gems and earrings and rings and hairpins and bracelets. These gifts too they offer to God who conceive understanding in heart, who have a mind given and intent to the word of God. And the men offer from their wives earrings and gems and bracelets. The woman is taken as the flesh, the man as the rational sense. Good are these women who obey their husbands; good is the flesh which no longer resists the spirit, but obeys and consents. Therefore if two or three of you shall agree concerning anything whatsoever you shall ask, it shall be done to you, says the Lord. They offer therefore earrings from their wives when hearing is offered to the Lord; and bracelets, that is, right works, good works, which are done through the flesh. These the rational sense offers to the Lord. And hairpins, he who knows well how to discern what is to be done, what avoided, what pleases God or what displeases, what is just, what unjust. These are the hairpins which they offer to God, because they are wise women, and they made whatever was needed for the vestments of the high priest. But those women who offered their earrings that the calf might be made were foolish, who turned away their hearing from the truth and turned it to fables and impiety; and therefore they offered their earrings that the head of the calf might be made. And in the book of Judges too we find an idol made from the earrings of women. Blessed therefore are these women, blessed the flesh, which offers to the Lord its earrings, bracelets and rings, and all the works of its hands which it does in the commandments of the Lord. And he with whom incorruptible wood was found offered it to the Lord. If anyone loves Christ in incorruption, he offers incorruptible wood to God. Blessed therefore is he with whom an incorrupt understanding or an incorrupt body is found, and offers this to God. Whence also he said well: He with whom incorruptible wood was found. Of gold he did not say, nor of silver, with whom it was found: for understanding and word can be found with all. Nor of the four colours: it belongs to all to consist of four elements according to the body. But incorruptible wood, that is, the grace of incorruption and virginity, can be found with few. Whence: "All men take not this word, but they to whom it is given."
**“AND GOATS' HAIR”** — ORIGEN. Goats' hair is offered. This kind of beast is commanded in the law to be offered for sin. But hair is a dead thing, bloodless and lifeless; he who offers this shows that the sense of sin is now dead in him, and that sin no longer lives and reigns in his members.
35.7:
**“And rams' skins dyed red,”**
• which show anger dead in the offerer
• the mortification of sin
**“RAMS' SKINS”** — ORIGEN. Rams' skins also are offered, which some before us have set for anger; and because the skin is a token of a dead animal, he who offers rams' skins to the Lord shows anger dead in himself.
35.9:
**“onyx stones, and precious stones, for the adorning”** — or: adornment
**“the ephod”** — or: of the ephod
**“and the rational.”** — or: of the rational
35.10:
**“Whosoever of you is wise,”** — A sacrifice is not received without the salt of wisdom.
**“let him come”** — of his own accord
35.21:
**“offered”** — God does not want forced services: he is served by love, not by fear; with the mind, not with the body.
**“with a mind”** — in which all these things are
**“most ready and devout firstfruits to the Lord, to make the work of the tabernacle of the testimony.”** — of the Church, namely
35.22:
**“Men”**
• the strong
• the rational sense, namely, with the obedient flesh
**“with women”** — the weak; but God does not despise the works or vows even of such
**“gave bracelets”** — which are named from armus, the shoulder: for they bind the arms, and signify the strong works of the virtues which the holy doctors offer.
**“and earrings,”**
• the obedience, namely, of subjects
• good hearing
**“and rings”** — the secrets of the precepts, which the doctors seal and lay up to be brought forth in their time, while the less learned are not able to grasp them.
**“and tablets:”** — good works which are done through the flesh
**“every vessel of gold was set aside to be offered to the Lord.”** — from earthly uses
35.23: **“If any man had gold, violet,”** — as above
35.24:
**“metal of gold and silver”** — of the word
**“and brass,”** — of the voice
**“they offered it to the Lord, and wood”** — incorruption, namely, and virginity
**“of setim for divers uses.”** — WHATSOEVER FOR THE SERVICE etc. GREGORY. In the adorning of the tabernacle men with women offer gifts, because in completing the worship of holy Church both the lofty deeds of the strong and the least works of the weak are counted. The faith of holy Church too is compared to gold, the word of preaching to silver. But what is shown by the bracelets, which bind the arms, but the works of prelates labouring strongly? By the earrings the obedience of subjects is expressed. By the rings, the sealing of secrets; for masters often seal what they consider cannot be grasped by hearers. By the tablets, the adornments of the first working. By the vessel of gold set aside for the gifts of the Lord, the understanding of the Godhead, which is as far parted from the love of lower things as it is raised to love eternal things alone. By violet, the hope of heavenly things. By purple, blood and the endurance of sufferings shown for love of the perpetual kingdom. What by the scarlet twice dyed but charity, which is dyed twice by perfection, because it is adorned with the love of God and neighbour? What by fine linen but the spotless incorruption of the flesh? What by goats' hair, of which the roughness of haircloth is woven, but the hard affliction of penitents is signified? While then some by bracelets and rings exercise a strong mastership, others by earrings and tablets show devout obedience and right working. Others by the vessel of gold set apart hold an illustrious and subtler understanding; others by violet, purple and scarlet do not cease to hope and believe the heavenly things they have heard, even those which they do not yet know by subtler understanding. Others by fine linen offer the incorruption of the flesh. Others by goats' hair bewail harshly what they gladly committed; as if the mysteries of the gifts, joined together into one work of the craftsman, are brought forth in the tabernacle of the Lord, that is, the Church, as he himself has given.
35.25:
**“The women also”** — the flesh subject to the soul
**“that were skilful”** — For there are unskilled women, from whose earrings the calf was made, and the idol in the book of Judges.
**“gave what they had spun,”** — the works of the hands
**“violet and purple and scarlet,”** — scarlet, namely
35.26:
**“and goats' hair,”** — the mortification of sin
**“of their own accord.”** — not of sadness or of necessity
35.27:
**“But the princes”** — who have advanced so far that they deserve to be set over peoples
**“offered onyx stones, and precious stones, for the ephod”** — in which good work is signified
**“and the rational,”** — in which the rational sense
35.28:
**“and spices”** — that they may say: "We are the good odour of Christ unto God."
**“and oil for the lights,”** — because the lamp of those whom he has set over peoples ought not to be hidden, but set upon a candlestick, that it may shine to all that are in the house.
**“and for the preparing of ointment, and to make the incense of most sweet savour to God.”**
• THE PRINCES OFFERED etc. ORIGEN. The princes offered their gifts, namely gems, emerald stones, stones of filling, and stones for the ephod. Those are called stones of filling which are set in the logion, that is, which are placed on the breast of the high priest, with the names of the tribes of Israel inscribed. And the logion, that is, the rational, which is placed on the breast of the high priest, has the form of the rational sense which is in us. In this are set the stones of filling, which cling and are joined to the stones of the ephod, so that from these the adornment of the bound ephod is continued, in which is the token of good acts. Action therefore is joined with reason, and reason with actions, that there may be harmony in both: He that shall do and teach, he shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven. Let there be in us then a word hanging on acts, and let acts adorn the word: for this is the adornment of the high priest; but for fulfilling these, princes are required. This adornment is theirs who have advanced so far that they deserve to be set over peoples.
• Morally. Let him have in the inner chambers of the breast the altar of incense, that he may say: "We are the good odour of Christ unto God."
• Morally. Let him have the ark of the testament, in which are the tables of the law, that we may meditate on the law of God day and night, and his memory may be made an ark and library of the books of God. Within it too let there be laid up the pot of manna, namely the subtle and sweet understanding of the word of God. Let there be also the rod of Aaron, that is, priestly doctrine and the flowering severity of discipline. But above all glory let him have the high priest's adornment. For that part in him which is more precious than all can perform a high priesthood within him, which some call the principal part of the heart, others the rational sense or intellectual substance; or in whatever way that portion of ours is named by which we are capable of God, let it be adorned in us like a high priest with precious vestments and ornaments, with the poderis of fine linen; which vestment is drawn down to the feet, covering the whole body: in which it is signified that first of all he be wholly clothed with chastity.
• Morally. After this let him take the ephod set with gems, in which is the brightness of works, that seeing your good works they may glorify your Father who is in heaven.
• Morally. Let him take the logion, which can be called the rational, laid upon the breast, marked out by a fourfold order of stones. Let the golden plate too shine on the forehead, which is called the petalum, on both of which truth and manifestation are said to be placed. I perceive in those things placed on the breast the gospel word, which in a fourfold order sets out to us the truth of faith and the manifestation of the Trinity, referring all things to the head, that is, to the nature of one God. In these therefore is all truth and all manifestation of truth. If therefore thou wilt bear the high priesthood, let the gospel word and the faith of the Trinity always be held in thy breast, with which the apostolic word agrees both in virtue and in number; so that the name of the Lord may always be held on the head, and all things be referred to one God.
• Morally. Let the high priest also have his inner coverings, let him have his nakedness covered, and be holy in body and spirit, and pure in thoughts and works.
• Morally. Let him have also bells round the border of his vestment, that going into the holy place he may sound, and not go in with silence; and set on the edge of the vestment, that he may never be silent about the last times and the end of the world. Therefore let him sound, dispute and speak, that, mindful of his last end, he may not sin. So therefore let the inner man be adorned, that he may enter not only into the holy place but into the Holy of holies, where the propitiatory and the Cherubim are, whence God may appear to them. The Holy can be those things which holy conversation can have in the present world. But the Holy of holies, into which one enters only once, I think is the passing into heaven, where the propitiatory and the Cherubim are, where God appears to the clean of heart. As I understand it, Abraham dwelt in tabernacles, and Isaac and Jacob, which they had set up within themselves for God, who adorned themselves with so great and such splendours of virtues. Kingly purple shone in them. Whence it was said by God to Abraham: Thou art a king among us. The scarlet shone when his right hand was ready to slay Isaac, his only son, for God. And the violet, when, ever gazing on heaven, he followed the Lord of heaven. In the rest also he was likewise adorned. So it is commanded in the law that the people go out on a certain day of the year and keep the feast day of tabernacles, dwelling in tabernacles, having branches of palms and boughs of willow and poplar, and branches of a leafy tree, that is, of myrtle. The palm is the sign of victory in the war which the flesh and the spirit wage with each other. The poplar and willow trees are, both in virtue and in name, shoots of chastity: which if thou keep whole, thou canst have also the branches of the shady and leafy tree, which is eternal and blessed life, when the Lord shall have set thee in a place of pasture by the water of refreshment.
*Origen:* The princes also offer oil to serve for the lamps and the chrism. For the lamp of those who are set over peoples ought not to be hidden or put under a bushel, but on a candlestick, that it may shine to all that are in the house. The princes also offer the composition of the incense, which is compounded by Moses for an odour of sweetness to the Lord, that it may be said of them also: For we are the good odour of Christ.
*Origen:* Morally. Each one can set up a tabernacle in himself. For if, as some before us have said, this tabernacle holds the figure of the whole world, and each can have the image of the world, why not also of the tabernacle? Each therefore ought to fit to himself pillars of virtues, silver pillars, that is, rational patience. For there seems to be a patience which is not rational. For he who does not feel an injury, and therefore does not repay it, seems patient, but is not rational. That patience has pillars, but not silver ones. But he who suffers bravely for the sake of the word of God is adorned with silver pillars. He can stretch out courts in himself by enlarging his heart. Whence: "Be you also enlarged." He can fortify himself with bars, namely bind himself with the unanimity of love. He can stand on silver sockets when he is set on the steadfastness of the word of God, the prophetic and apostolic word. He can have on the pillar a gilded head, that is, the faith of Christ. For "the head of every man is Christ". And he can stretch out ten courts in himself when he is enlarged not in one word only of the law, nor in two or three, but can enlarge the amplitude of spiritual understanding in the whole decalogue of the law; or when he has brought forth the fruit of the Holy Ghost: joy, peace, patience, benignity, goodness, modesty, faith, continence, with charity added, which is the greatest of all.
*Origen:* Morally. Let him have an altar fixed in himself, on which he may offer the victims of prayers and the sacrifices of mercy, on which with the knife of continence he may slay pride as a bull, cut the throat of anger as a ram, and sacrifice wantonness and all lust as he-goats and kids. Let the priest know, however, how to separate from these the right shoulder, that is, good works, right works, lest anything left-handed be kept back; and the whole breast, a right heart and a devout mind consecrated to God; and the jaws, for speaking the word of God. Let him know that a candlestick of light is to be placed for him in the holy place, that he may have lamps always burning, and loins girt, that he may be as a servant who waits for his lord to return from the wedding. Of these lamps it is said: "The light of thy body is thy eye."
*Origen:* Morally. Let him place the candlestick also in the south, so that it looks toward the north. For, the light being kindled, that is, with a watchful heart, he ought always to look toward the north, from which the evils of all the earth are kindled. Watchful therefore and careful and burning, let him always look out against the wiles of the devil, and whence temptation may come, whence the enemy may rush in, whence he may creep in secretly, who "as a roaring lion goeth about seeking whom he may devour".
*Isidore:* Morally. Let the table of proposition also, having twelve loaves, be placed in the north part looking toward the south: the loaves are the apostles, whose word he ought to use unceasingly, and to look toward the south, whence the Lord comes.
35.29:
**“All both men and women”** — "My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God."
**“with devout mind offered gifts, that the works might be done which the Lord had commanded by the hand of Moses. All the children of Israel”** — There is no child of Israel who does not offer something in the tabernacle.
**“dedicated voluntary offerings to the Lord.”** — No forced offering is received in this tabernacle.
35.31: **“And hath filled him with the spirit of wisdom and understanding and knowledge”** — elsewhere: with the Spirit of God, with wisdom and understanding and knowledge
35.34:
**“He hath given”** — For this is the gift of God.
**“BESELEEL”** — Beseleel is called shadow. Hur: fire. Uri: my light. Juda: confession. Ooliab: my protection, father; Achisamech is interpreted 'strengthening my brother'; Dan 'judgment' or 'judging'. Because the holy doctors, who by their preaching proclaim and build the house of God, trust in God's defence. Whence: "In the shadow of thy wings will I hope" etc. And kindled with spiritual zeal they pour the light of faith and knowledge into their hearers and show the rule of confession; they have also the protection of God the father, and in justice and judgment they strengthen their brethren by exhorting them.
35.35: **“Both of them hath he instructed with wisdom, to do carpenters' work and tapestry, and embroidery in violet and purple, and scarlet twice dyed, and fine linen, and to weave all things, and every new thing”** — which signify the new man, not the old

36.1:
**“Beseleel therefore and Ooliab and every wise man, to whom the Lord gave wisdom and understanding, to know how to work artificially,”** — with skill
**“made the things that are for the uses of the sanctuary”** — of the Church
**“BESELEEL THEREFORE MADE”** — RABANUS. It is to be noted that not only one of the kingly tribe, but one born of a handmaid, was chosen for the mastership of the works of God. For Beseleel was of the tribe of Juda, who was the son of Lia; Ooliab of the tribe of Dan, who was the son of Bala, the handmaid of Rachel: because even the lowly born are chosen for the dignity and government of the Church. "For God is not a respecter of persons." It can also be signified in this that the doctors of the Church are taken not only from the Jews but also from the gentiles. Whence in the book of Numbers Juda pitched his camp about the tabernacle on the east, and Dan on the north. For in the east the Lord first set up the Church from the Jews, afterwards from the gentiles, who were of the kingdom of him who said: I will set my seat in the north. For he willed that these too should receive ecclesiastical dignity and belong to the unity of his body.
36.2:
**“And when Moses had called them, and every skilful man, to whom the Lord had given wisdom,”**
• All things in the tabernacle are made by the wise, because all the works of the Lord are in wisdom.
• AND WHEN MOSES HAD CALLED THEM etc. ORIGEN. And after the people offered, Moses, he says, called every wise man to the building, and the master builder, that they might put together each of the things that are written. But he called wise women too, he says, that they might make what was fitting in the tabernacle of the Lord. You see therefore that all things that are made are made by the wise, both wise women and wise men. For all the works of the Lord are made in wisdom. It is not enough for us if we offer; there is need also that we work with wisdom the things that are in us, that we know how to mingle gold with fine linen, and to double the scarlet, or mingle it with purple. For what does it profit thee if thou have this, and know not how to use it, nor understand how thou oughtest to fit and bring forth each thing in its time and in its place?
**“and such as of their own accord had offered themselves to the making of the work,”** — AND SUCH AS OF THEIR OWN ACCORD etc. AUGUSTINE. And all who of their own accord wished to go to the works, that they might finish them etc. Moses mentioned certain men to whom he said the Spirit was given from God, by which they could accomplish those things; and yet many are understood to have come of their own accord to the same works, to whom it was neither commanded, nor are their names recorded as spoken by the Lord to Moses. Not only those therefore had this gift from God who are mentioned by name, but perhaps those chiefly and more excellently. But in all these is to be praised a mind not drawn to the work servilely, but freely and of its own accord devoted.
36.3: **“He delivered all the offerings of the children of Israel unto them. And while they were earnest about the work, daily in the morning”** — zealously, as children of God, not children of the night and of darkness
36.4: **“Whereupon the workmen being constrained to come,”** — WHEREUPON THE WORKMEN etc. Note that the wise makers of the works were holy in their conduct also: for they could, had they wished, have taken away much, but modesty forbade them, or religion struck them with fear.

37.1:
**“And Beseleel made also the ark”** — the Church
**“THE ARK”** — ISIDORE. In the ark of the testament was a golden pot, the tables also and the rod of Aaron. The ark, namely the Church, has two tables of stone, that is, the perpetual firmness of the twofold Testament; and the golden pot, that is, the flesh of Christ, pure and sincere, which keeps hidden in itself the manna of perpetual Godhead and bears the everlasting sweetness of the angelic bread; and the rod of Aaron, that is, of our true high priest, the saving standard of immortal memory, ever flowering with greenness.
**“of setim wood,”** — Holy in mind and body, who have within the two tables of the testament, that is, the observance of the Law and the Gospel.
**“having two cubits and a half in length, and a cubit”** — the second, namely
**“and a half in breadth; the height also was of one”** — or: of one
**“cubit”** — or: of a cubit
**“and a half”** — or: of a half
37.2:
**“and he overlaid it with the purest gold within and without.”** — because the Church ought to shine like gold, as much within with the splendour of life as without with the brightness of wisdom and doctrine
**“and he made to it a crown of gold round about”** — A CROWN OF GOLD etc. Because, in that the Church is spread through the four parts of the world, she is proclaimed girded with the four books of the holy Gospel; yet she is enclosed within the circuit of one crown, that is, within the firmness of the same faith, that is, its unity.
37.4: **“THE BARS ALSO”** — ISIDORE. Because strong and persevering doctors are to be sought like incorruptible wood, who, ever clinging to the instruction of the sacred volumes, may proclaim the unity of the Church and, as if put through the rings, carry the ark; who are commanded also to be covered with gold, that while they sound in speech to others, they themselves also may shine with the splendour of life.
37.6:
**“He made also the propitiatory,”** — Christ
**“HE MADE ALSO THE PROPITIATORY”** — ISIDORE. The propitiatory set upon the ark of the testament is Christ, who intervenes between God and men as mediator and propitiator. Whence: Whom God hath proposed to be a propitiation, through faith in his blood. This propitiatory is set over the ark, because Christ is the head of the Church.
**“that is, the oracle, of the purest gold,”** — because Christ, who is the wisdom of the Father, did no sin
**“two cubits and a half in length, and a cubit”** — or: of a cubit
**“and a half”** — or: a half
37.8: **“cherub”** — Cherub is interpreted fulness of knowledge, namely the love of God and of neighbour.
37.9:
**“spreading their wings, and covering the propitiatory,”** — because the Old and New Testament cover, under the figures of riddles, both the sacraments of Christ and the mysteries of the Church
**“and looking one towards the other, and towards it.”** — because the two Testaments with one accord proclaim the sacraments of Christ
37.10: **“He made also the table”** — on which we are fed with the nourishment of the Scriptures
37.23:
**“he made also the seven lamps”** — AND THE SEVEN LAMPS etc. It signifies the Holy Ghost, who with sevenfold grace enlightens the Church standing in the unity of faith; or Christ bearing the seven churches, in which the splendour of the sevenfold Spirit shines forth.
**“WITH THEIR SNUFFERS”** — Which in Isaias are called tongs: the two Testaments, namely, by which sins are cleansed, and which are joined within themselves by the union of the Holy Ghost.
37.25: **“He made also the altar of incense of setim wood,”** — The body of Christ, or any saints in whom the divine fire ever burns and the flesh is ever consumed.
37.29: **“He compounded also the oil for the ointment of sanctification,”** — the grace of the Holy Ghost, having in itself peace and mercy through the coming of the Saviour; whence the light of truth is kindled in our hearts.

38.8:
**“He made also the laver of brass”** — vehement compunction
**“with its foot,”** — with the fear of God
**“of the mirrors”** — the divine precepts
**“of the women”** — of holy souls
**“that watched”** — watching with continual love for the entrance of the eternal kingdom
**“at the door”** — the entrance
**“of the tabernacle.”**
• not made with hands
• HE MADE ALSO THE LAVER OF BRASS etc. GREGORY. Moses sets a laver of brass in which the priests may be washed when about to enter the holy of holies, because the law of God bids us first be washed through compunction, that our uncleanness may not hinder us from penetrating the cleanness of the secrets of God. And the laver is made of the mirrors of the women who keep watch unceasingly at the door of the tabernacle. For the mirrors of the women are the precepts of God, in which holy souls ever look, and if there are any spots of foulness in them, they detect them; they correct the faults of their thoughts, and as it were compose their faces, shining back from the image returned. For while they attend skilfully to the Lord's precepts, they recognise in them what in themselves pleases or displeases the heavenly husband. And so long as they are in this life they cannot enter the eternal tabernacle. But yet the women keep watch at the door of the tabernacle, because holy souls, even when weighed down by the infirmity of the flesh, yet with continual love watch for the entrance of the inner way in. Moses therefore set for the priests a laver made of the mirrors of the women, because the law of God offers a washing of compunction for the spots of our sins, by which holy souls have displeased the heavenly bridegroom. It gives us heavenly precepts to look into, and if we attend to them diligently, we see the spots of our inner image. And seeing the spots, we are pricked with the sorrow of penance. And being pricked, we are washed as it were in the laver made of the mirrors of the women. Then therefore are we truly pricked concerning ourselves, if we weigh carefully the deeds of the fathers who went before, so that, that glory being beheld, our own life grows foul in our eyes. Then are we truly pricked, when we search out the precepts of God carefully, that we may strive to advance by those things by which we know those whom we venerate to have advanced.
38.15: **“and on the other side, for between the two he made the entry of the tabernacle,”** — of the Church, which is set in the desert of this life
38.19:
**“And the pillars in the entry were four”** — the four are the evangelists, made solid with the firmness of faith
**“with sockets of brass, and their heads and gravings of silver.”** — with the brightness of the divine word
38.20: **“THE PINS ALSO”** — STRABO. The pins, according to the letter, were fixed at the top of the pillars, to which cords were tied, which raised the curtains from the ground; made fast by certain loops above, and tied below to the said pins, they stretched out the curtains, lest they gather a wrinkle. But mystically the cords signify holy Scripture, of which Solomon says: "A threefold cord is not easily broken"; because holy Scripture, consisting of history, morality and allegory, can be broken by no doctrines of heretics. The pins, made in the manner of a tongue, signify the tongues of the doctors who expound Scripture to the peoples. They also raise the curtains from the ground and stretch them out, because they teach those subject to them to follow and imitate heavenly things, and to gather no wrinkle of evil or of fraud.

40.2:
**“In the month”**
• April, namely, in which the Jews celebrate the pasch
• of the second year
**“the first,”** — in the beginning of grace
**“the first day of the month, thou shalt set up the tabernacle of the testimony,”** — IN THE FIRST MONTH etc. STRABO. The first month of the year is Nisan itself, which is also April, in which the Jews celebrated the pasch, and the tabernacle was set up. But allegorically the first month marks the beginning of grace, when the tabernacle of God, that is, the Church, was set up, when Christ, namely crucified, brought forth from his side the mysteries of blood and water, by which the Church is dedicated and consecrated. And it is to be noted that this was the first month of the second year: for the first year was before the law; the second year under the grace of the Gospel, which the Lord blessed. Whence: "Thou shalt bless the crown of the year of thy goodness." For that was the year of goodness in which the salvation of mankind appeared through the humanity of Christ: in this year therefore the tabernacle of God was set up, that is, the Church founded and exalted.
*Rabanus:* RABANUS. The first year is all the time of the law before the incarnation of Christ; the second, from his coming to the consummation of the world. As it were in the first month, on the first day of the month, the tabernacle is set up, when in the beginning of his grace the adornment of the Church is built through Christ, and the beauty of the new Jerusalem is shown to the faithful. And as in the first year the cost was made ready for the work to come, so the word or work of all the elect from the beginning of the world to the coming of the Lord, fitting for the building of the Church, is gathered through the writers of the Old Testament, that the doctors of the Gospel may use these in the confirming of faith.
40.9:
**“And thou shalt take the oil of unction and”** — with spiritual grace
**“anoint the tabernacle”** — the Church
**“with its vessels,”** — the several persons, namely, of the saints, who are vessels unto honour; whence Paul is called a vessel of election.
**“THOU SHALT ANOINT THE TABERNACLE”** — STRABO. The tabernacle with its vessels is consecrated with the oil of unction, because holy Church ought to dedicate and consecrate to the grace of the Holy Ghost whatever she does with her virtues. For the oil of unction is compared to spiritual grace, by which the works of all the virtues are consecrated.
40.12:
**“And thou shalt bring Aaron”** — the prelates
**“and his sons”** — the subjects
**“to the door”** — the apostles
**“of the tabernacle of the testimony,”**
• of the Church or of the heavenly kingdom
• AND THOU SHALT BRING AARON etc. STRABO. The doors of the tabernacle, that is, of holy Church, are the apostles, through whom one must enter the court of heaven: to these are to be brought Aaron and his sons, that is, the whole company of the saints, and chiefly of the prelates, that they may imitate them and follow their footsteps.
**“and having washed them with water”** — of compunction
40.13:
**“with the holy vestments,”** — with virtuous works
**“that they may minister to me,”** — being made worthy
40.14: **“thou shalt clothe them”** — lest they walk naked, and their shame appear
40.18:
**“And Moses reared it up, and placed the boards and the sockets and the bars, and set up the pillars”** — The bar not only binds the walls, but also strengthens the pillars of the entry, lest they fall or bend from their upright state; because the Lord both joined each people in one faith of love, and strengthens their doctors, that they may persevere in faith and love and preaching. Nor is it strange if Christ is understood both by the heads themselves and by the bar holding the heads together, because by ruling he is the head of each of the elect. Whence: The head of the man is Christ. And because he not only raises each one to seek heavenly things, but also holds all together, and strengthens them with the bond of peace, that they may not be bent from their upright state nor be separated from one another by disagreeing. Like to this is that the Lord is called lamb and shepherd and door, though the shepherd feeds the lamb, and both enter by the door; since properly he is the Word in the beginning, but none of these properly, but figuratively. Shepherd, because he leads to the pastures of life; door, because only through him does one come to the Father; lamb, because he saves from Egypt. So here too he is figured by the heads because of the rule by which he is over each, and by the bar because of his general providence, because he strengthens all.
*Bede:* BEDE. So the soul receives divers names according to its divers actions: while it quickens the body, it is named soul; while it wills, it is mind; while it knows, it is understanding; while it recalls, it is memory; while it judges, it is reason; while it breathes, it is spirit; while it perceives, it is sense.
40.33: **“He set up also the court round about the tabernacle and the altar, drawing the hanging in the entry thereof. After all things”** — or: all
40.35:
**“Neither could Moses”** — the Jewish people
**“go into the tabernacle of the covenant,”** — the secrets of the Scriptures
**“the cloud covering all things,”** — with the depth of Scripture
**“and the majesty of the Lord shining, for the cloud had covered all.”**
• NEITHER COULD MOSES etc. STRABO. Moses therefore in this place, as in many others, holds the figure of the Jewish people. Moses therefore, the cloud standing in the way, could not enter the tabernacle, because the Jewish people never availed to penetrate the sacraments of Scripture. For the cloud of the Lord lay upon the tabernacle by day, and fire by night. In this place the fire signifies the knowledge of the divine mysteries. For holy Scripture is light to the holy and to those who confess their ignorance; but to the wicked and to those who boast of knowledge it is a cloud, because it blinds them.
• In the tabernacle of the Lord were boards, in whose rings were set bars of setim wood, by which they could be lifted and carried from mansion to mansion; all of which are full of mysteries. By the tabernacle we understand the present Church, in which are the boards, namely the saints full of humility, to which five bars are fixed, that is, the spiritual knowledge of the five books of Moses, by which they lift up themselves and others to the brightness of eternal blessedness. By the bars therefore, as we have said, we understand the five books of Moses, which are Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, the book of Numbers and Deuteronomy, in which are contained the beginning of the world, and the middle, and the consummation. In Genesis is described the creation of the world; in Exodus the re-creation; in Leviticus the administration of the sacraments of the Church; in the book of Numbers the gospel preaching; in Deuteronomy the last blessing. Whence also it ends in blessings. There is therefore in Genesis the order of creation; in Exodus the mystery of re-creation; in Leviticus the holiness of ecclesiastical administration; in the book of Numbers the strengthening of the gospel preaching; in Deuteronomy the consummation of the eternal blessing. Among these five books of Moses Exodus excels, which we now have in hand. For in it are fully contained both the things that befell the children of Israel in figure, and the mysteries of Christ and of the Church. Here first, however, it treats of the actual going out of the carnal children of Israel from the historical Egypt; in which is signified the spiritual going out of the spiritual Israelites from the true Egypt, namely from the darkness of vices. It treats also of the passing of the Red Sea, and the drowning of Pharao and his army, and the deliverance of the people of God; in which is figured baptism consecrated in the blood of Christ, in which the vices of the devil are drowned and the souls of the faithful delivered. It treats also of the battle of the Israelites with Amalec; in which the victory of Christ and of his own, and the confusion of the devil, is figured. At length, the catalogue of the mansions being described, it treats of the law given on mount Sina: in which it is hinted to us that, lifted up from earthly things, we should learn to be subject to heavenly disciplines. It treats again of the building of the tabernacle and its vessels, of the vestments of the priests and the unction: in which is understood the present Church, and the divers persons of the faithful appointed to divers offices, as the vessels were appointed to divers uses or offices, and the most sweet perfumes of the sacraments and of hallowed prayers. Of these so far. Now it is to be said that according to the order of the history and according to allegory this book is fittingly the second in the Pentateuch: for after it treated in Genesis of the creation of heaven and earth, and of the going in of the children of Israel into Egypt, it is fitting that it should next treat of their going out. Behold what is fitting according to the order of the history. According to allegory also it is not unfittingly done. For after it spoke of the carnal generation, by which through the sin of the first man we are born children of the devil, it is fitting that it should at once add of the spiritual regeneration, by which through the justification of the second man, that is, Christ, we are born again children of God. And this book is called Exodus in Greek, Ellesmoth in Hebrew, Exitus or Egressus in Latin; because it treats of the going out of the children of Israel from Egypt. But it can be asked why this book is called Exodus, because it treats of their going out, when at the beginning it treats not of their going out but of their going in. To which it can be said that, although it intends specially to treat of their going out, yet because much time flowed between the going out, of which it treats here, and the going in, with which the first book ends or had ended, in order to join its narrative more fittingly, it briefly first repeats of the going in, and so descends better to the going out. So we too in our discourses, when a long interruption has been made and we are about to say other things, repeat what went before, that we may better continue what was said. These things considered, the matter is to be seen, which is the bodily going out of the children of Israel from Egypt and the spiritual going out of the saints from the world. By its intention it admonishes us to go out spiritually from conformity to the world, as they who went out bodily from Egypt, that as we were conformed to the world, so we may be conformed to God. The manner is this: touching briefly on the going in of the children of Israel into Egypt, it treats of their multiplying; then of the new king who knew not Joseph and began to afflict the people; then of the plagues of Egypt; at length of their going out and the passing of the Red Sea and the drowning of the Egyptians. At length it comes to mount Sina, on which the law was given, and treats of the tabernacle and its vessels, and of the vestments of the priests, and the unction, and so it ends. Note that although the history which Moses set himself to describe is one and undivided, yet they divide it by chapters and parts or by books, that weariness may be taken from the readers; as a traveller divides the way, which is undivided, by days' journeys, that the labour may be lessened and weariness be absent.
*Augustine:* AUGUSTINE. A very wonderful thing is to be noted: that when the cloud came down and filled the tabernacle (which yet is called the glory of the Lord), Moses could not enter the tabernacle, who on mount Sina, when he first received the Law, entered into the cloud where God was. He figured therefore one person then, another now: then, of those who become partakers of the inmost truth of God; but now, of the Jews, to whom the glory of the Lord which is in the tabernacle (which is the grace of Christ) is set against them like a cloud, since they do not understand it; and therefore they do not enter the tabernacle of the testimony. And this is to be believed to have been done once, as soon as the tabernacle was set up, for the sake of this signification or of some other. For the cloud was not always so over the tabernacle that Moses could not enter; since indeed the cloud was not removed except when this sign was given them of setting out, that is, of moving the camp from the place where they were, and going whither the cloud led by day, the flame by night. Which two in turn also remained over the tabernacle where they had pitched the camp, the cloud by day, the flame by night.

1.1:
**“And called”** — The Seventy: called again
**“HESYCHIUS”** — AND CALLED etc. According to the Seventy: Called again. As according to them God called Beseleel again by name when he commanded the tabernacle to be made according to the pattern which was shown in the mount: so now too he commanded a certain image of the intelligible sacrifices to be described; for this calling again hints at a certain dispensation of things or words looking to higher things.
**“the Lord Moses, and spoke to him from the tabernacle of the testimony,”** — heaven, or Scripture, in which are images and figures of the mysteries in testimony of things to come
**“saying:”** — AND CALLED etc. HESYCHIUS. By the conjunction he joins what follows to what went before, namely the beginning of this book to the end of the preceding one. For the work of one and the same day is contained in each. The book of Numbers also, because it has nothing between itself and Leviticus, has a like opening, that is: "And the Lord spoke to Moses in the desert of Sinai" etc. The people therefore did nothing after the history of Leviticus before the history of Numbers: for they had not changed place, because they had not yet dedicated the tabernacle, nor had much time passed. For in the first month of the second year, at the beginning of the same month, they began to act. But in Exodus and Genesis, because much time had flowed between the death of Joseph and the going out of the children of Israel, the conjunction does not hold the beginning, but a fitting opening is arranged for their dispensation: "These are the names of the children of Israel that went into Egypt."
**“ORIGEN”**
• AND CALLED etc. In the beginning, setting forth the laws of sacrifices and gifts, he says: If a man offers a gift to God, he shall offer of oxen or of cattle, that is, lambs and kids. But if of birds, turtles or young of the dove. But if not a man but a soul offers a gift to God, let it offer of fine flour unleavened loaves baked in the oven, or fine flour from the frying pan tempered with oil, or from the gridiron. Then he says that leaven ought not to be offered, nor honey mixed with the sacrifices, but every sacrifice or gift salted with salt. Secondly he commands the sacrifices of firstfruits to be offered fresh and cleansed. After these, under the same tenor of the law, he adds concerning the saving sacrifices: first of oxen, secondly of sheep, in which it is lawful to offer, whether lambs or kids, males or females. Nothing besides these did he decree to be offered in the saving sacrifices. But we must see what it is that he said: A man of you etc., as though one not a man could offer, when it would have sufficed to say: If any of you offer. And in what follows he says: If a soul offer a gift. In the later passages, when God speaks a second time to Moses of the sacrifices to be offered for sin, he adds: If the high priest sin, let him offer this or that. But if the whole Synagogue, if a prince, if one soul sin, it is commanded what each is to offer. Let us not think this distinction of persons or things empty. For blessed are the eyes which, the veil of the letter cast away, can see the spirit; and blessed they who bring clean inner ears to hear these things.
• AND CALLED etc. That God does not love the sacrifices of the Jews Isaias shows, saying: To what purpose do you offer me the multitude of your victims, saith the Lord? I am full: I desire not holocausts of rams, and fat of fatlings, and blood of calves and rams and buck goats. Who required these things at your hands? What therefore he had commanded, he refuses. Whence Amos: Did you offer victims and sacrifices to me in the desert? Yet they had often offered them, but those he did not hold pleasing he rejected as though not offered. Hence Jeremias: Eat ye flesh, for I spoke not to your fathers, and I commanded them not concerning the matter of holocausts. But the same who had commanded denies it, because they who had received it passed over the intention of the giver. For the law was subtle, and hidden under the veil of the letter, that those searching it might both amend themselves and understand things to come. The image therefore of rational and intelligible sacrifices is described, and plainly this calling hints at a dispensation of words, or of things looking to higher things.
1.2:
**“Speak to the children”** — to the Jews
**“of Israel,”** — carnal or spiritual: For it is not he that is a Jew outwardly, nor is that circumcision which is outwardly in the flesh: but that which is in secret; whose praise is not of men, but of God.
**“and thou shalt say to them: The man”**
• mankind
• It belongs to man, that is, to the rational, to appease God by offering, because a victim without reason does not please.
• HESYCHIUS. It is possible for the same one to be called a man and to do the things of beasts; whence: "Man when he was in honour did not understand."
**“that shall offer”**
• willingly
• with the works of the active life, of which he treats here; but of contemplation in what follows, where birds are commanded.
**“among you a sacrifice”** — Hostia is named from hostis, the enemy, or from ostium, the door by which it was brought, or because it was immolated before battle; but after victory, victima.
**“to the Lord of the cattle,”** — as if: such as they are, such things they offer.
**“that is, of oxen”** — with works of piety
**“and sheep,”**
• with the simplicity of innocence
• under the name of sheep he included the kind of goats also.
**“OF OXEN AND SHEEP”** — HESYCHIUS. He designates the simple man, who has no sharpness either for malice or for virtue, but is drawn by another. For these animals are gentle, and easily follow those who draw them. Whence these can be gifts only of the Jews, who, if they work nothing of virtue, it suffices that they do no evil. Of whom: "Men and beasts thou wilt preserve, O Lord." The first rank is given to men; salvation is granted to beasts also.
1.3:
**“If it be a holocaust,”** — a work, namely, wholly perfect
**“his offering, and of the herd,”** — of the stock of the Patriarchs
**“a male”**
• Christ, having nothing of womanly frailty
• strong and manly works
**“without blemish”** — "Who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth."
**“he shall offer at the door of the tabernacle of the testimony,”**
• because: "He suffered without the gate", and: "He came unto his own, and his own received him not."
• the apostolic doctrine, according to which we must live and work
**“to make the Lord favourable to him”**
• For he was made a curse, that he might free us from the curse.
• The Seventy: acceptable before the Lord
• THE MAN THAT SHALL OFFER etc. ORIGEN. Allegorically. The man whom he sets first to offer to the Lord he understands as mankind, which offers the fatted calf, namely that which the father slew for the son who returned after wasting all his substance, made a great feast and had gladness, that the angels in heaven might rejoice over one sinner doing penance. This one, because he had no substance of his own to offer, since he had squandered all, offered the calf sent from heaven; of the herd, that is, of the generation of the Patriarchs; a male, having nothing of womanly frailty; without blemish, "who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth". At the door of the tabernacle, not within, because: "He came unto his own, and his own received him not." He was offered at the door also because he suffered outside the camp, that is, outside the city. For the wicked husbandmen cast the son of the householder out of the vineyard and slew him: here therefore he is offered at the door of the tabernacle of the testimony, acceptable before the Lord. For what is so acceptable to God as the victim of Christ, who offered himself? He shall put his hand upon the head, because he laid the sins of mankind upon his own body. For "he is the head of the body, the Church". But perhaps it is not without cause that it was said above, at the door of the tabernacle of the testimony, and below, at the altar which is at the door of the tabernacle of the testimony; as though it did not suffice to have marked the same place once; but perhaps he wished it to be understood that the blood of Christ was not only shed in Jerusalem, where were the altar and its base and the tabernacle of the testimony, but also sprinkled the altar on high which is in heaven, where is the Church of the firstborn, according to that: He made peace through the blood of his cross, both as to the things on earth and the things that are in heaven; so that the victim was twofold. Paul says to the Hebrews: "through the veil, that is to say, his flesh". And again he interprets the inner veil which Jesus penetrated. If therefore as high priest he entered through two veils, the sacrifice also is twofold, which saves both earthly and heavenly things.
• OF THE HERD A MALE etc. ISIDORE. Allegorically. The first sacrifice is the calf, that is, Christ; of the herd, that is, begotten of the stock of the patriarchs; who with the plough of his cross subdued the earth of our flesh, and enriched it with the seed of the Holy Ghost, with the harvest of the virtues.
• The proud calf is our flesh: this we offer when we keep it chaste. At the door of the tabernacle: where it will receive the hearing of divine things. Let the gift be male, let it not know womanly concupiscence; let it flee frailty, dissoluteness and softness. The hand is put upon the victim that it may be acceptable to the Lord, namely the bridle of continence and the hand of discipline, according to that: I chastise my body, and bring it into subjection: lest perhaps, when I have preached to others, I myself should become a castaway. It is slain before the Lord when the members are mortified. The sons of Aaron the priest offer the blood. The priest is in thee, and his sons are thy mind and thy sense, which alone understand the Lord and are capable of his knowledge. He wishes therefore that thou offer a rational sense and thy chaste flesh. Whence: A living sacrifice, holy, pleasing unto God, your reasonable service. For this is the offering of blood at the altar by the priest or his sons, when one is made chaste in body and spirit. For there are those who offer flesh in holocaust not through the ministry of the priest. For not knowingly, nor according to the law which is in the mouth of the priest, are they chaste in body, unchaste in mind. For either they are stained by the lust of glory, or polluted by greed or avarice, or troubled by other vices. For there is not in them the counsel and prudence which perform the priesthood before God; but they are as the foolish virgins, who were chaste in body, but had not the oil of charity and peace and the other virtues.
**“ORIGEN”** — Allegorically. The man that shall offer etc. The man who was made to the image and likeness of God lives rationally. Morally: he offers a calf, a sheep, a kid, a pair of turtles and two young pigeons, when he has kept chaste wedlock, and understood the mystery by which the eyes of the bride are said to be as doves upon brooks of waters, and her neck as the turtle's.
1.4:
**“And he shall put”**
• He bore our sins in his body upon the tree
• the offerer, who is not designated by name
**“his hand”** — workings
**“upon the head of the victim,”**
• the beginning of good thought, that the perfection of work may follow at once
• "He is the head of the body, the Church."
**“and it shall be acceptable,”** — to God
**“and help to its expiation.”** — IF IT BE A HOLOCAUST etc. HESYCHIUS. Morally. God requires sacrifice that it may profit us, not himself. Whence: I beseech you that you present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing unto God, your reasonable service etc. The sacrifice pleasing to God therefore is the mortification of our bodies, by which we both abstain from sins and acquire virtues. This some do most fully, others in part: those who mortify themselves wholly and renounce the world become a holocaust, while through the intelligible fire they offer themselves wholly to God, made no longer earthly but heavenly. If therefore such a one has done the justice of the law which is according to the letter, he is fittingly named an ox, who bears the yoke of earthly works, sustaining the law as a yoke, of which Peter says: "Why tempt you God to put a yoke upon the necks" etc.? Paul also says: Thou shalt not muzzle the mouth of the ox that treadeth out the corn. Which he expounds thus: Doth God take care for oxen? or doth he say this for our sakes? because he that plougheth should plough in hope. The gift must be male, lest the worker of the law be in any way made womanish. Without blemish, lest he mingle a stain of iniquity or of pretence. At the door of the tabernacle of the testimony: for our conversation ought to be in heaven. In the conscience also dwell the thoughts, which at length bear testimony for us or against us. To make the Lord favourable. But according to the Seventy he says: this acceptable to the offerer; namely, if it be truly acceptable to us, and our heart, judging rightly and clinging to no passion, has proved the gift worthy to be received, then we can pray in the sight of the Lord, that is, obtain remission. Whence: In his sight we shall persuade our hearts, for if our heart reprehend us, we know that God is greater than our heart, and knoweth all things etc. And he shall put his hands upon the head of the victim etc. What we call hostia is in Greek called karpoma, in which the intelligible holocaust is signified. For he bears fruit spiritually who through spiritual conversation is made a holocaust: because of which he who offers puts his hand on the head of the victim, which signifies the beginning of the aforesaid conversation, of which he who offers is himself the cause by his promise. For he offers of his own accord, because it is a gift, and every gift is voluntary. For if he transgresses his promise, he accuses himself when he pays the penalty. And thus it will be acceptable and help to his expiation, when by the laying on of the hand he has shown that he offered of his own accord, not of necessity.
1.5:
**“And he shall immolate”**
• He will have faith in the death of Christ in his mind.
• He will break the wantonness of the flesh.
**“the calf”** — which, being lively, signifies spiritual gladness: "For God loveth a cheerful giver."
**“before the Lord,”** — by the rule of the mind, where God sees
**“and the sons of Aaron the priest shall offer”** — The elect are members of the true priest, that is, Christ; whence: "You are a chosen generation, a kingly priesthood."
**“the blood thereof, pouring it”**
• thus
• cleansing their hearts in this faith
**“round about the altar,”**
• ORIGEN. "Because it cannot be that a prophet perish out of Jerusalem."
• THE SONS OF AARON etc. ORIGEN. Of the race of Aaron were Annas and Caiphas, and others who pronounced Christ guilty of death, and shed his blood at the base of the altar: for he was slain there where the altar and its base were. Whence: "It cannot be that a prophet perish out of Jerusalem."
**“which is before the door”** — the apostolic doctrine
**“of the tabernacle”**
• by the priests
• AND HE SHALL IMMOLATE THE CALF etc. HESYCHIUS. For we ought not only to offer our own conscience and conversation to God, but also, as pleases him, by mortifying the body, tending not to lower things but to higher. For this is what the sons of Aaron do before the Lord, slaying and offering the blood; but he who offers is not designated by name. For anyone can bring an offering, that is, promise; but to fulfil the promises, as it were to slay the ox and pour out the blood, belongs to the sons of Aaron alone, by the dignity of the priesthood. And Aaron is interpreted secret or mountainous. Whoever therefore has built himself a temple of God, lofty in virtues, ought to be called a son of Aaron and a priest. For a priest is made by unction, and we are all priests who keep the dignity of the mystic unction. Whence John: "You have the unction from the Holy One." And Peter: "But you are a chosen generation, a kingly priesthood" etc. These pour out the blood, that is, they do not spare the soul, hearing that: "He that shall lose his soul for me shall find it." For blood signifies the soul, according to that: "The life of the flesh is in the blood." Round about the altar, that is, the Lord's body: because as the sacrifice is laid upon the altar, so the priests work every virtue of the soul upon the body of Christ, that is, in imitation of him. Whence: "You shall make an altar of earth unto me." For the body of Christ is of our earth. And elsewhere: If thou make an altar of stone unto me, thou shalt not build it of hewn stones: for if thou lift up a tool upon it, it shall be defiled. For the flesh of Christ was neither hewn nor smoothed by human hand. At the door of the tabernacle round about, that we may imitate him in all things. And by the door of the tabernacle we understand the apostolic doctrine, by which we enter into the heavenly tabernacle in which God dwells. Whence Isaias: Look down, O Lord, from heaven. As Christ is called the door, so is the apostolic doctrine which he bestows.
1.6:
**“And when they have flayed”**
• HESYCHIUS. that is, riches scattered for Christ
• the veil of the letter
**“the victim,”**
• of the Word of God
• by showing what befits each, what is the progress of each
**“the joints”** — by consecrating all the senses of the body to the Lord, or by examining each with sure discernment
**“they shall cut into pieces”** — When we dedicate our life to God, we lay upon the fire the members of the victim cut into pieces.
1.7:
**“And they shall put”**
• as faithful dispensers
• mingling in the discourse of the Godhead
**“fire on the altar,”** — of the Holy Ghost, by which works and vows are to be thoroughly tried and examined
**“having before laid in order a pile of wood”**
• with the examples of the Fathers, in imitation of whom all things are to be done
• the passion of Christ even to the wood of the cross; there the dispensation of the flesh was ended
1.8:
**“and laying in order thereupon the parts that are cut out,”** — not sharing them with the lowest and unworthy
**“to wit, the head,”**
• the chief part of the mind and understanding, and what is chiefly to be consecrated to the Lord
• that is, the mind, which is cherished in the health of body and soul, and gathers into one the motions of each, ought not to be divided
**“and all things that cleave to the liver,”** — in which, according to the natural philosophers, is the beginning of all desire, and the seat of the heat by which foods are digested. And all our intention and desires are to be devoted to the Lord.
1.9:
**“the entrails”**
• with unclean thoughts
• the conscience
**“and feet”** — dusty deeds, because we scarcely do anything without sin
**“being washed”**
• otherwise they are not to be offered
• the consummation of the sacrament being received
**“with water”** — with tears of compunction
**“and the priest shall burn them upon the altar”** — Christ
**“and a sweet savour to the Lord.”**
• because upon the altar
• AND WHEN THEY HAVE FLAYED etc. ORIGEN. Allegorically. The priest draws off the skin by which the members are covered, who separates the veil of the letter from the Word and lays bare the inner members of spiritual understanding, and does not set them in a low place, but on the altar. For he does not open the mysteries to the unworthy and earthly, but to those who are the altar of God, in whom the divine fire is always kindled and the flesh consumed. He divides the calf limb by limb who explains in order and distinctly what is the progress: to have touched the hem of Christ, to have washed his feet with tears and wiped them with the hair, and how much more to have anointed his head, or what prerogative it has to have leaned upon his breast; to set out the reasons of these. To fit some things to beginners, others to those advancing in the faith of Christ, others to those already perfect in knowledge and charity: this is the dismembering of the calf. He also who knows how to show what are the beginnings of the law, what the progress in the prophets, what the perfection in the Gospels; with what milk little ones are nourished, with what oil the weak are cherished, with what solid food the athletes of Christ are fattened. He fittingly arranges the holocaust of the calf by distinct members, and puts wood under the altar for the fire to burn, who shows not only the bodily virtues of Christ, but in some measure his Godhead. For the Godhead of Christ is from above, whither this fire hastens. Fittingly therefore the heavenly fire consumed all things that were done in the body of the Saviour, and restored all to the nature of his Godhead. Yet this fire is kindled with wood applied: for he suffered even to the cross; but when he was hung on the wood, the dispensation of the flesh was ended. For rising from the dead he ascended into heaven, which way of his the nature of fire shows. Whence: If we have known Christ according to the flesh; but now we know him so no longer. For the holocaust of his flesh, offered through the wood of the cross, joined earthly things to heavenly and human to divine. Morally. He commands the entrails with the feet to be washed with water, in signification of baptism. He washes the entrails who cleanses the conscience; he washes the feet who receives the consummation of the sacrament. For he that is clean needeth not but to wash his feet, but is clean wholly; nor can anyone have part with Jesus unless he has washed his feet.
**“HESYCHIUS”** — Morally. AND WHEN THEY HAVE FLAYED etc. The skin is drawn off when we are stripped of riches and of all worldly things. Whence: Skin for skin, and all that a man hath he will give for his life. The members are cut up when the conversation of each is built up to the increase of the body in the measure of the member. The sons of Aaron put fire under when they kindle the spirit, laying in order a pile of wood, namely the meditations and teachings of the Scriptures, by which the Spirit of God is nourished and continually kindled, that it be quenched by no whirlwinds. Whence: "Extinguish not the spirit. Despise not prophecies." And by the pieces we understand the soul and body. For though they are of one living being, they are set against each other. The flesh lusteth against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh etc. And the head signifies the mind. Whence Isaias: "The whole head is sick, and the whole heart is sad." For these are said to suffer with each other, and our rational part, dwelling in both, is cherished in the health of both. The head is not divided, because the mind ought not to wander through divers things, but be guarded by the peace of God, according to that: The peace of God, which surpasseth all understanding, keep your hearts etc. All things that cleave to the liver, or the fat according to the Seventy, by which namely the appetites of the desires are moved. For it lies over the kidneys and the groin, which are the organs of coition. And these we offer when we use the desires not bodily but spiritually. We lay them on the altar with wood put under, that we may fit them to the spiritual Scriptures which were spoken of the altar of the Lord's body. The entrails, that is, the hidden thoughts, being washed with the water of baptism or the tears of penance, and the feet, that is, the actions. Upon the altar: in this it becomes a sweet savour to the Lord. Our sacrifice becomes a holocaust to the Lord and an odour of sweetness when we offer all things upon the intelligible altar, imitating Christ as far as we can.
**“GREGORY”** — Morally. And when they have flayed etc. We draw the skin off the victim when we remove the surface of virtue from the eyes of the mind. We cut the joints into pieces when, distinguishing finely and limb by limb, we consider its inward parts. If we are sometimes afflicted by the impulse of unlawful thought, it is for this reason, that we are gladly busied in certain acts of earthly thought, though lawful. And when earthly action is touched by desire even in the least things, the strength of the devil growing, our mind is defiled by temptation. Whence the members of the victim, cut into pieces, the head and the things about the liver, are commanded to be burned with fire, but the feet and entrails first to be washed with water. For we offer ourselves a sacrifice to God when we immolate the works of our life, distinguishing them by virtues. We burn the head and the things contained about the liver when in our sense, by which the whole body is ruled, and in our hidden desires, we burn with the flame of divine love. And yet it is commanded that the feet and entrails be washed: for by the feet the earth is touched, by the entrails dung is carried; because often, already kindled by desire for eternity, we gape with the whole sense of devotion after the appetite of our mortification. But because we still do something earthly through infirmity, we also bear in the heart many unlawful things which we have already subdued. And when unclean temptation defiles our thoughts, the entrails of the victim carry dung. But that they may be burned, they are washed, because weeping washes away the unclean thoughts, which heavenly love may burn in the acceptance of the sacrifice. And whatever the mind suffers, whether in the struggle it has experienced or from the memory of its former conversation, is washed, that it may burn the more sweetly in the sight of God the more it has begun to stand before him, laying nothing earthly, nothing slippery, in the ark of its prayer.
1.10:
**“And if the offering be of the flocks,”** — He still instructs the active life.
**“AND IF OF THE FLOCKS”** — AND IF OF THE FLOCKS etc. HESYCHIUS. With a few things changed, he says the same. And it is to be noted that he commanded the Israelite to offer not only of oxen but also of sheep. A holocaust therefore is made not only of the ox which works the commandments, but also of the sheep, that is, the simple and one without malice. Whence Jeremias: "I was as a meek lamb that is carried to be a victim" etc. Let the offering be of goats also: for it is possible for a sinner to give his effort to simplicity, and, made as it were a sheep, to offer the holocaust of his conversation to God who commands it; though the Jews did not think this, thinking that the son inherits the sin of the father. Whence: "The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father" etc.
**“of sheep”**
• the simple
• by which innocence and simplicity are signified
**“or of goats,”** — By the roughest hair of goats is signified the habit of penance, which is to be offered to the Lord.
**“a holocaust,”** — Morally: he who repents ought to offer a perfect work.
**“a lamb of a year”** — Christ, who was offered in the acceptable year to the Lord; whence: "Thou shalt bless the crown of the year of thy goodness." And elsewhere: And it shall be a lamb without blemish, a male, of one year: according" etc.
**“and without”** — or: without
**“blemish”** — because "he did no sin"
**“he shall offer”** — A LAMB OF A YEAR AND WITHOUT BLEMISH etc. ISIDORE. Allegorically. The lamb offered is Christ, innocent, crucified. Whence: "Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who taketh away the sin of the world." Well is the kid offered, because through the death of Christ the devil, the author of sin, is slain.
1.11:
**“And he shall immolate it at the side”** — if not straight on
**“of the altar”**
• Christ
• The memory of the Lord's passion, in which every sacrifice is to be offered and every good thing done
**“that looketh to the north”**
• because this part or region is cloudy
• the saints, cold with fear: for they are afraid of all their works, uncertain to what end they will be brought, and how they are weighed before God
**“AT THE SIDE OF THE ALTAR THAT LOOKETH TO THE NORTH”** — That is, the altar looks to the gentiles, because the passion of Christ was celebrated for the gentiles. And we offer sacrifice at the northern part of the altar when we believe, keeping it in memory, that the passion of Christ was made for the gentiles.
**“before the Lord:”** — AND HE SHALL IMMOLATE IT AT THE SIDE etc. HESYCHIUS. This he did not command concerning the oxen, but that they be immolated before the Lord. Whence the words seem to have contrariety and difference, since both are a holocaust but have a different place. According to the letter, therefore, he gave the same place to both. For the altar of holocausts was set before the tabernacle at the side of the door, that the entrance to the holies might not be blocked for those ministering, as is said in Exodus: And he put the veil at the door of the tabernacle of the testimony, and he set the altar of holocausts about the door of the tabernacle. Whatever therefore was offered for sacrifice stood at the side of the altar on the north, and so the sacrifice was celebrated before the Lord, that is, in sight of the holies: for the holy of holies is called the face of God, because the glory of God dwelt in it. Whence the priest was commanded to enter into it once a year. The difference of the words therefore was necessary for contemplation. For the altar is Christ; the sheep, those who study simplicity. The offering of sheep, therefore, is not offered simply straight before the intelligible altar, as that of oxen, but at the side. For he offers straight on who fulfils the commandments; but at the side he who abstains from evils; as into a royal hall it is better to enter by the straight door, yet it is good to enter even from the side. For to offer to God in any manner is good. To the north he necessarily added. For this part is almost always cloudy. For those are darkened by cloud, that is, ignorance, who give themselves wholly to innocence; therefore it is called a holocaust even without the working of justice.
**“the blood”** — the soul; whence: "The life of the flesh is in the blood." This we ought not to spare, but lay down for Christ.
**“thereof shall pour”** — that is, they shall consecrate their souls to the Lord: for the seat of the soul is in the blood.
**“upon the altar”**
• Christ
• that they may consecrate all their acts by the memory of the passion
**“the sons of Aaron”** — mountainous or secret
1.12:
**“And they shall divide”**
• by discerning
• they arrange all the senses, or the power of contemplation, with sure discernment
**“the joints, the head,”** — the mind
**“and all that cleave to the liver,”** — in which is desire
**“and shall lay them upon the wood,”** — the examples of the Fathers
**“under which is to be put”** — as the foundation of every good
**“the fire”** — of the Holy Ghost
1.13:
**“But the entrails”** — the hidden thoughts, which are sometimes foul with the dung of sin
**“and the feet”** — the actions, which often touch the earth
**“they shall wash with water.”** — of baptism or of compunction
**“And all being offered,”** — to God the Father
**“shall burn it”** — with the fire of the Holy Ghost
**“the priest upon the altar”**
• Christ
• THE PRIEST SHALL BURN IT ALL UPON THE ALTAR etc. He commands the offerer to lay all these things upon the altar, that we may fit our whole man to the spiritual Scriptures which were spoken of the intelligible altar of the Lord's body, and may study to live in imitation of him.
1.14:
**“But if”** — The instruction of the contemplative life begins.
**“of birds”** — the contemplatives
**“the oblation of a holocaust to the Lord be, of turtles”** — with the holiness of chastity
**“or of young”** — with knowledge, namely, and spiritual meekness
**“of the pigeon,”**
• with simplicity
• BUT IF OF BIRDS etc. ISIDORE. Allegorically. The turtle is the flesh of Christ, according to that of Solomon: "Thy cheeks are beautiful as the turtledove's." The dove signifies the Holy Ghost. Whence: He upon whom thou shalt see the Spirit descending as a dove, this is my Son. The turtle and the dove therefore are the flesh of Christ joined to the Spirit. These three sacrifices the man, that is, Christ, offers: namely of oxen, of cattle and of birds.
**“HESYCHIUS”** — Wonderful is the subtlety of the words, not only because it describes the differences of ways of life, but signifies some according to the law, some above the law. For the offerings of oxen and sheep are according to the law, though they are called voluntary; because even if to offer is in the power of the offerer (for man is of free will), yet not what sort he works. It is necessary therefore either to offer an ox or a sheep, that is, either to work justice or to abstain from evils. Whence above: The man among you that shall offer a sacrifice to the Lord of the cattle, that is, of oxen and sheep, shall offer victims. But birds are not numbered with the aforesaid offering. For this sacrifice is more perfect and greater, and of few. For the birds are men given to contemplation, who, if of necessity they mix themselves in earthly business, soon fly back to heavenly things. Whence: They sow not, neither do they reap, and your heavenly Father feedeth them. Let such a one offer of turtles and doves, that is, in knowledge and spiritual meekness, that the knowledge of the law may not exceed, busied in vain things: for the turtle signifies knowledge. Whence Jeremias: "The turtle, and the swallow, and the stork have observed the time of their coming: but my people have not known the judgment of the Lord." And the dove, clean and simple, signifies the Holy Ghost and declares what they ought to be who study to contemplate the holy Scriptures. Whence Ezechias: I will meditate like a dove. One priest offers, not many, because contemplation is of few. Whence he offers at the altar, while the rest are offered at the tabernacle of the testimony. For contemplatives put earthly things after, contemplate and savour heavenly things, "where Christ is sitting at the right hand of God".
1.15:
**“the priest shall offer it”** — whence not many: for contemplation is of few
**“at the altar”** — the Lord's body
**“and twisting back the head to the neck,”**
• Christ, who is our head, is never torn away from his body, that is, the Church.
• TWISTING BACK TO THE NECK etc. Morally. The head is twisted back to the neck and not cut off, when the flesh is so wasted with fastings and watchings that life is not wholly broken. Whence the Apostle says "a living sacrifice".
**“and breaking the place of the wound,”**
• or: the neck
• the skin, namely
**“he shall make run down”** — The Seventy: he shall strain it out; where, namely, he who wishes to offer his whole soul to God may despise the cares of the present life part by part and perfectly
**“the blood upon the brim”** — others: the base, that is, the Gospel, in which we must chiefly despise the present life
**“of the altar”**
• of Christ
• AND BREAKING THE WOUND etc. That is, the skin which lies over the neck being broken, not much separated from the body; he does not command that the bird be killed, but broken off or broken back. For little by little the head, that is, the mind, is to be divided from the skin, that is, from the flesh. Whence the blood is not poured out, but runs down.
1.16:
**“But the crop”**
• the swelling
• that he may lay aside swelling and wholly superfluous inquiry; whence: "Knowledge puffeth up."
**“of the throat and the feathers”**
• pride
• lightness and instability
• "Seek not the things that are too high for thee."
**“he shall cast beside”** — outside
**“the altar”** — because not necessary but superfluous
**“at the east side,”** — because the inquiry into lofty things seems to be toward the east
**“in the place where the ashes are wont to be poured out”**
• that he may know that these things are worthy of ashes and of remaining on the earth, not of ascending into heaven
• AT THE EAST SIDE etc. We ought to remember our first condition: for the first father was made toward the east in the happiness of paradise, but, his sin requiring it, rolled down into the miseries of this life, he was made a worm and ashes. While we think on this and weigh that we are such, we cast as it were the crop and feather into the place of the ashes, that is, the discernment of mind by which we do not doubt that we have lost happiness and shall return to ashes.
1.17:
**“And he shall break”** — because the members must be bruised and afflicted
**“the pinions”** — the pinions (ascellae) are named from motion: for in them the arms are moved, for we say cillere for to move
**“thereof, and shall not cut, nor divide it with a knife,”**
• The Seventy: as an ox or a sheep; for let the spirit and soul and body be kept whole without blame
• Nothing is to be cut with the knife of heretical depravity, but done with the hand of good work.
**“and shall burn it upon the altar, on the wood,”** — of doctrine
**“fire”** — of the Holy Ghost
**“being put under: it is a holocaust”** — wholly burnt
**“and oblation of most sweet savour to the Lord.”** — AND SHALL NOT CUT etc. He shall not make the bird, like the ox or the sheep, by divisions. For the contemplative clings only to heavenly things, nor does his flesh lust against the spirit. Whence: "My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God." For he is offered whole upon the intelligible altar, and upon the wood under which the fire is put. Otherwise the sacrifice is not received, unless it is seasoned with meditation on the law. And thus it becomes a holocaust and a most sweet savour to the Lord, because he smells our sacrifice if the life and conversation of each is offered to him according to the law.

2.1:
**“A soul”**
• Three sacrifices the man, that is, Christ, offers; the fourth the soul, that is, the Church.
• not a man
• the Church
• the Gentile
• some poor man
