**“when it shall offer an oblation of sacrifice to the Lord, of fine flour”** — fine flour, which is the most delicate meal, of which the best bread is made. This is wisdom, best among the gifts of God. "And the spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and of understanding."
**“shall be its offering, and it shall pour upon it”** — ascribing whatever it knows to the grace of the spirit
**“oil”** — almsgiving
**“and put frankincense”**
• prayer
• that wisdom may be increased before God; whence James: "If any of you want wisdom, let him ask of God."
• A SOUL WHEN etc. By the better part he signifies the whole man: for he requires a spiritual and perfect hearer, because the soul is capable of wisdom, not the flesh.
**“ISIDORE”** — Allegorically. The soul offers the fourth sacrifice. The fine flour signifies the Church, which is gathered from many persons as from grains, separated by the mill of the law and the Gospel between the letter and the spirit, united through the water of baptism, anointed with chrism, and made solid by spiritual fire; through humility it becomes an acceptable victim.
**“ORIGEN”** — ORIGEN. A soul etc. Namely one which has neither calf, nor sheep, nor kid, nor a pair of turtles or two young pigeons: this is the sensual man, who, if he is not pressed by sins nor cast headlong through vices, yet has nothing spiritual in himself, or, figuratively, the flesh of the Word of God. The sensual man perceiveth not the things that are of the Spirit of God; but the spiritual man judgeth all things. This one therefore who is named a soul cannot offer all things, because he cannot examine all things; but only fine flour and unleavened loaves, that is, this common life in husbandry and in the other uses of life. Yet he offers fine flour tempered with oil. For every soul needs the oil of divine mercy or grace.
**“HESYCHIUS”** — HESYCHIUS. A soul when it shall offer etc. The soul signifies the whole man, as there: "All the souls that went with Jacob into Egypt" etc. And Luke says: And we were in all in the ship two hundred threescore and sixteen souls. Perhaps by the soul he signifies the Gentile. For above he commanded the children of Israel to offer sacrifices with blood. But here, commanding him who is without the law to offer, he does not say 'man', as above, but soul. The Gentile was sensual, not understanding the things that are of God; but the mercy of God calls him to the offering, that he may receive salvation, when he arranges sacrifices for sins; he who has neither sheep nor goat, he commands to offer a turtle or a dove; he who has not that, fine flour. For he is saved no longer by works, as one poor in virtues, but by the knowledge of God alone, which, though it is the beginning of salvation, yet frankincense and oil are to be put upon it, that the grace of God may be mingled with alms and prayers. Whence the angel says to Cornelius: Thy prayers and thy alms are ascended before the Lord. In frankincense the inner passions are cured, and by its smoke eyes that water from infirmity are healed. For prayer heals the passions of the soul, cures the inner eyes of ignorance, and drives away the tears that rise from the sickness of sin.
2.2:
**“THE SONS”** — The ministers of the Church. Because whatever we offer we ought to confer with the holy doctors of the Church. Whence Paul conferred the Gospel with the apostles, lest he had run in vain.
**“and one of them”** — Christ, who offers us to God
**“taketh a handful of the flour and oil”** — of mercy and charity
**“and all the frankincense”**
• because we ought always to pray; whence: "Pray without ceasing."
• AND ONE OF THEM etc. The unity of the Church takes a handful of the flour, because according to the capacity of his sense each of the faithful ought to seek the knowledge of Scripture. Whence: "Not to be more wise than it behoveth to be wise, but to be wise unto sobriety."
• MORALLY. And one of them etc. It is to be noted that a handful of the flour and oil, but all the frankincense, is commanded to be offered, because wisdom, which is marked in the flour, and charity or mercy, which is marked in the oil, cannot be full in this life. Whence: "We see now through a glass in a dark manner"; and "now I know in part" etc. A part of the oil also is offered, because mercy is never fulfilled; for even if thou have mercy as much as thou canst, yet thou oughtest to wish more. Charity also, which is figured by oil, is begun in the present and will be perfected in the future. But all the frankincense is burned, because one perseveres always in prayer.
**“OF THE FLOUR”** — Of knowledge or of the acquaintance of God. For that knowledge is acceptable to God which faith can grasp; and as he who wishes to grasp more in a handful gains nothing, for all runs out, so faith is the measure of the knowledge of God. "For he that cometh to God must believe", and what is not of faith is sin.
**“and shall put it a memorial”**
• the knowledge of God, according to that: "He manifesteth the odour of his knowledge by us in every place."
• A MEMORIAL etc. The perfect knowledge of the acquaintance with God, of which we shall be mindful, which is never destroyed; and it does not destroy that which is now as contrary, but shows by its fulness that it is a very small part: "For when that which is perfect is come, that which is in part shall be done away."
**“upon the altar for a most sweet savour to the Lord.”** — "We are the good odour of Christ in them that are saved" etc.
2.3:
**“And the remnant”**
• the secret of the mystery, which the crowd cannot grasp
• of the knowledge hidden in Christ
**“of the sacrifice shall be Aaron's”** — his, namely, who can understand lofty things and hold the law of God as secrets, storing up lofty mysteries until he bring them forth to hearers at the fitting time
**“and his sons'”** — the imitators
**“holy of holies”** — surpassing all knowledge
**“of the offerings of the Lord.”** — OF THE SACRIFICE etc. HESYCHIUS. Namely of that perfect knowledge, hidden in heaven and laid up in Christ, "in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge". Aaron is interpreted mountainous, that is, understanding the loftier things of God; or secret, as having in himself the law of God and his words: such a one can offer such a sacrifice. Holy of holies, it is of the offerings to the Lord: for what remains is a portion, yet surpassing all knowledge, and it raises to perfection.
2.4:
**“But when thou offerest”** — by believing, preaching, venerating
**“a sacrifice”** — Christ
**“baked in the oven,”**
• the Virgin's womb
• we shall offer from the oven when we discourse of the incarnation of Christ
**“of flour,”** — the knowledge of God
**“loaves”**
• the Gospel doctrine, which is solid and perfect
• the words of the apostles
**“to wit, without”** — or: without
**“leaven,”** — worldly knowledge
**“tempered”** — abundantly
**“with oil”**
• the mercy of Christ
• because it proclaims with what charity Christ was or is incarnate and suffered
**“and unleavened wafers”** — the proclamations of the Prophets
**“anointed”**
• not tempered
• BUT WHEN THOU OFFEREST etc. HESYCHIUS. Allegorically. The sacrifice is Christ immolated for us. Baked in the oven: namely in the virgin's womb. For the oven receives bread and fire: so the virgin's womb received from heaven the bread of life, that is, the Word of God, and the fire of the Holy Ghost. Whence: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee" etc. If therefore thou offerest the gift of the incarnation of Christ, which was made in the virgin's womb, it is not acceptable to God unless it be made of fine flour, that is, of the knowledge or acquaintance of God. For of this matter we receive the speech from the apostles and from the prophets. The words of the apostles are loaves, of the prophets wafers. For as loaves are fitter than wafers for nourishing, so much do the words of the apostles excel the words of the prophets. And both are unleavened, without the leaven of worldly knowledge. Yet both are made in oil: for with one accord it was written by them of Christ's mercy; because the apostles and prophets wrote, but the apostles wrote more fully, who showed fulfilled what those announced as to come.
**“WAFERS”** — A broad and thin bread, which signifies prophecy and the law: for as much as the solidity of bread differs from the thinness of the wafer, so much the Gospel from the words of the law and the prophets. Yet these are anointed with oil, because the law and prophecy foretold the charity of Christ, with which he came for the salvation of mankind.
2.5:
**“If thy oblation”** — dispensation
**“be from the fryingpan,”** — the cross
**“FROM THE FRYINGPAN”** — For as the fryingpan is midway between the fire and the food, so in a manner is the cross between the impassible Godhead and the humanity which was roasted with the fire of the passion. And as in the fryingpan soft things harden and hard things soften, so in the passion of the cross stony hearts were softened, and soft and loose ones made solid. To offer sacrifice from the fryingpan therefore is to discourse with veneration of the mystery of the cross.
**“of flour”** — of the knowledge of God
**“tempered with oil,”** — because by the grace of God, having mercy, he tasted death for us
**“and without leaven,”** — of outward doctrine
2.6:
**“Thou shalt divide”** — by distinguishing the several parts of the passion: namely the betrayal, the spittle, the buffets, the crown of thorns etc.
**“it into little pieces, and shalt pour oil upon it.”**
• Christ suffered for us, that we should follow his steps.
• IF THY OBLATION etc. HESYCHIUS. Allegorically. The oblation from the fryingpan is the dispensation of the passion from the cross. The fryingpan is consumed by fire, and renders the foods laid upon it fit for eating either at once or after a long interval; the cross also, strong above all things, subjected every creature to the crucified, and made the flesh fit which before the passion did not seem fit for eating. For if he had not been crucified, we should not eat the sacrifice of his body, which we now do in memory of his passion. Whence it is said to Ezechiel: Take unto thee a frying pan of iron, and thou shalt set it for a wall of iron between thee and the city: namely Jerusalem, which was most offended at the cross of the Lord, and therefore withdrew from the knowledge of him. OF FLOUR TEMPERED WITH OIL: because he died and had mercy on us. WITHOUT LEAVEN: without stain. THOU SHALT DIVIDE IT INTO LITTLE PIECES: that we may divide the discourse of his sufferings, which proceeded by parts, and diligently distinguish the blows, namely the buffets, the spittle and the wounds. AND THOU SHALT POUR OIL UPON IT: that as he died mercifully for us, we too may have mercy on our brethren even unto death.
2.7:
**“And if from the gridiron”** — death and burial. For in the oven is marked the birth, in the fryingpan the passion, in the gridiron the death.
**“the sacrifice be,”** — We offer sacrifice from the gridiron when we piously remember the death of Christ.
**“in like manner the flour”** — knowledge or understanding separated from the chaff, ground or made fine
**“shall be tempered with oil”**
• for out of mercy he died and rose again
• AND IF etc. HESYCHIUS. As in the fryingpan we take the cross, so in the gridiron the death and burial. For the fryingpan is put over a fire burning and kindled, but the gridiron over coals burning and kindled long before: so the death of Christ was not the beginning of the passion, but its continuance. This gift is made of fine flour, that is, of the knowledge of God. For Christ who died according to the flesh must be preached God and immortal. The gift is made in oil, because he who discourses of both the death and the resurrection must add mercy also: for out of mercy he bore death and dispensed the resurrection.
**“MORALLY”** — And if etc. He offers fine flour who studies to live well in some of the uses of common life. This is to be tempered with oil, because every soul needs the oil of mercy, nor can it escape the present life unless heavenly mercy be present. And the oven expresses the weight of temptation; the fryingpan, the constancy and strength of the mind; the gridiron, manifold assault.
2.8: **“which thou shalt offer to the Lord, delivering it to the hands of the priest.”** — of Christ, through whom we offer
2.9:
**“And when he hath offered”** — to the altar which is in heaven
**“it, he shall take a memorial”** — the abundance of knowledge or of perfect acquaintance, of which we shall always be mindful when we shall be capable of it
**“out of the sacrifice, and burn it upon the altar for a sweet savour to the Lord.”** — keeping it with him even for the future
2.10:
**“And whatsoever is left shall be Aaron's and his sons',”** — that is, to know as much as he has commanded us also to search out shall be Aaron's and his sons', namely of those who can think or perceive lofty things of God
**“holy of holies”** — for every good conscience is holy; or the holy of holies is that which discourses of the knowledge of God as it ought
2.11:
**“Every oblation that is offered to the Lord shall be made without leaven,”**
• with heretical corruption
• of outward doctrine: "Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees."
**“EVERY OBLATION THAT IS OFFERED”** — ORIGEN. Someone may say: It went almost better with the ancients, to whom pardon was granted by divers sacrifices; with us there is only one pardon of sins, through the laver of baptism; after sin, no mercy. For it befits the Christian, for whom Christ died, to be of stricter discipline: oxen, goats and sheep were slain, and birds, and fine flour was tempered with oil; for thee the Son of God was slain, and does it delight thee to sin again? Yet do not despair: thou hast heard how many sacrifices for sins there are in the law; hear how many remissions there are in the Gospels. The first is in baptism. The second is in martyrdom. The third through almsgiving. Whence: Give what you have, and behold all things are clean unto you. The fourth, because we forgive our brethren. Whence: If you forgive your brethren from your hearts, your Father also will forgive you etc. The fifth, because we convert "a sinner from the error of his way", according to that: "He who causeth a sinner to be converted from the error of his way" etc. The sixth through abundance of charity. Whence it is said: Many sins are forgiven her, because she hath loved much. And elsewhere: "Charity covereth a multitude of sins." The seventh through hard and laborious penance, when the sinner washes his bed with tears, and they become his bread day and night, and he is not ashamed to confess his sin to the priest of the Lord and seek medicine, according to him who says: "I said: I will confess against myself" etc. Hence James: Is any man sick among you? Let him bring in the priests of the Church. Thou therefore, when thou comest to the grace of baptism, hast offered a calf, because thou art baptized in the death of Christ. When thou art led to martyrdom, thou hast offered a goat, because thou hast slain the devil, the author of sin. When thou hast done alms and spent the affection of mercy on the needy, thou hast honoured the holy altar with fat kids. If thou hast forgiven thy brother from the heart, and laid aside the swelling of anger, and had a meek and simple mind, thou hast sacrificed a ram or a lamb. If, instructed by the divine readings, meditating like a dove, and watching in the law of the Lord, thou hast converted a sinner from the error of his way and called him back to the simplicity of the dove, and, joining him to the saints, made him imitate the fellowship of the turtle, thou hast offered a pair of turtles or two young pigeons. But if thou hast loved thy neighbour not only as thyself, but as Christ, who says: Greater love than this no man hath, that a man lay down his life for his friends etc., know that thou hast offered unleavened loaves of fine flour, worked with the oil of charity, without the leaven of malice and wickedness, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. If thou hast been in the bitterness of weeping, if thou hast wasted thy flesh and dried it up with much abstinence, so as to say: My bones are grown dry like fuel for the fire, thou hast offered in sacrifice fine flour from the fryingpan or from the gridiron. In this way thou offerest more truly and perfectly, according to the Gospel, the sacrifices which Israel can no longer offer according to the law.
**“neither shall any leaven or honey”** — of philosophic eloquence
**“LEAVEN OR HONEY”** — Nothing voluptuous, nothing sweet pleases God, but what has something of sharpness and severity. Whence the Pasch is eaten with bitter herbs.
**“OR HONEY”** — Of Gentile eloquence, which is sweet in sound, not in substance. Whence: The lips of a harlot are like a honeycomb dropping. But what is said in the Canticles, "Honey and milk are under thy tongue", does not contradict the present words. For it says 'under the tongue', not 'on the tongue', to show that the wisdom of the pagans and the letter of the Jews are subject to the tongue of the Church, that is, to its doctrine. He does not wish the whole doctrine of these to be offered. Whence he says: It shall not be burnt in the sacrifice, that is, the holocaust: you shall offer only their firstfruits. For we offer the firstfruits of that wisdom, not the whole, as Paul says to the Athenians: As some also of your own poets said, For we are also his offspring. For what he found fitting to the knowledge of God he did not reject; yet he did not multiply testimonies further, because "it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe". Whence Moses says: But they shall not be put upon the altar; and though it might have been said they shall not be placed, he says: They shall not be put upon it for a savour of sweetness; signifying that if we try to gain the knowledge of the Godhead from outward things, such a sacrifice does not ascend to the altar, but is pressed down among earthly things, because it is of the earth.
2.12:
**“You shall offer only the firstfruits of them and gifts:”** — The elements of letters and the other things which the philosophers found, which are necessary to the divine words; the arts are therefore to be learned, that through them the divine Scripture may be brought forth as by an instrument.
**“but they shall not be put upon the altar, for a savour of sweetness.”** — because they are earthly
2.13:
**“Whatsoever sacrifice thou offerest, thou shalt season it with salt,”** — that whatever we offer to the honour of Christ we may season with the salt of reason and discretion
**“neither shalt thou take away the salt of the covenant of thy God from thy sacrifice. In all thy oblations thou shalt offer salt.”** — THOU SHALT SEASON IT WITH SALT etc. Apostolic wisdom. Whence: "You are the salt of the earth" etc. As every food is seasoned with salt, so is the word of preaching with apostolic doctrine. Therefore salt is commanded to be offered in every sacrifice, that we may live according to the apostolic doctrine and institution and the imitation of its work. Whence Paul says: "Be ye followers of me, as I also am of Christ." And elsewhere: "Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets." Whence also the lawgiver did not say simply salt, but the salt of the covenant of thy God. For as the covenant is rational, so also the salt is rational. He wished therefore to remind us of the Gospel testament and the apostolic salt. Oil is offered in the sacrifice if we offer with cheerfulness, not out of sadness or of necessity. "For God loveth a cheerful giver."
2.14:
**“But if thou offer a gift of the firstfruits”**
• ORIGEN. of the first fruits, as fine flour, let it be fresh and new
• with the beginnings of good works and of doctrine
**“of thy corn”** — or: of the fruit
**“to the Lord, of the ears yet green,”** — the untaught
**“thou shalt dry”** — thou oughtest to consecrate by scorching
**“it at the fire,”** — of the Holy Ghost
**“and break it small”** — by separating the letter from the spirit
**“like meal, and so shalt thou offer thy firstfruits to the Lord,”** — BUT IF THOU OFFER A GIFT OF THE FIRSTFRUITS etc. ORIGEN. In the second place the offering of the firstfruits, that is, of the beginnings, of the corn is commanded, which the law of God bade to be done on the day of Pentecost: but to them the shadow was given, for us the truth was reserved. And on the day of Pentecost, the sacrifice of prayers being offered, the Church received the firstfruits of the Holy Ghost, the apostles. And truly these were fresh, because it was new. Whence also they were said to be "full of new wine". Dried at the fire: for fiery tongues sat upon every one of them.
**“HESYCHIUS”** — HESYCHIUS. But if thou offer etc. He commands not only those who have remained in it to offer the acquaintance or knowledge of God, but the untaught also. Whence the Apostle: Immediately, when he was called, he preached. He is a firstfruit to God who has newly begun to believe, who formerly offered him no fruit of knowledge. Such ones, because they do not yet bring forth the mysteries finely so as to offer meal or fine flour, must offer things green and dried and broken. For as with moist fruits, not yet fit for the mill to become meal or fine flour, we break them with fire and separate the chaff: so those who do not yet have solid knowledge nor subtle theology need the fire of the Holy Ghost, that they may separate the chaff of the letter, whereby they may possess sufficient knowledge of God. And we must pour oil over it and put on frankincense: for through almsgiving and prayer divine knowledge is perfected in us.
2.15:
**“pouring oil upon it”**
• of mercy
• almsgiving
**“and putting on frankincense”** — prayer: "Let my prayer be directed as incense in thy sight."
2.16: **“Whereof the priest shall burn”** — as above

3.1:
**“And if his oblation be a sacrifice of peace offerings,”** — ORIGEN. The saving offering, which is offered only of oxen and sheep or goats. For for sins the soul is commanded generally to offer; but after this it goes through various persons, so that if the high priest offend and offer for sin, he shall offer a calf, not as for a gift.
**“and he will offer of the herd, whether male”** — that is: strong works
**“or female,”**
• weak ones
• for both must live worthily if they wish to be saved
• WHETHER MALE OR FEMALE etc. HESYCHIUS. Above, only males are offered in holocaust. By the holocaust therefore the highest virtues are designated: namely to be a virgin, to renounce the world, and the like, which are the sacrifices of few. But the victims of peace offerings are the lesser virtues and the common vows of the faithful, by which God is appeased. Whence females are offered with males, that is, weak works with stronger.
**“without blemish”** — of the stain of sin
**“he shall offer before the Lord.”**
• in the good pleasure of the Lord
• AND IF HIS OBLATION BE A SACRIFICE etc. ORIGEN. Passing over the rest, he speaks of the saving sacrifices which are offered of animals, that is, oxen and goats and sheep, and nothing further is substituted for immolation; not even birds, which were substituted above in the offering of gifts. For he who offers saving victims is already conscious of his salvation. He must therefore offer great and perfect things. Whence the Apostle: "But strong meat is for the perfect."
**“HESYCHIUS”** — HESYCHIUS. And if his oblation be a sacrifice etc. According to the laws there are divers ways of life of men; there are virtues ordered in the manner of ladders, so that one attains some, another all, that each may be raised from the earth; which the difference of the sacrifices signifies. Whence here one offers a holocaust, that is, himself wholly, as Paul, who is nailed to the cross with Christ; another the sacrifice of peace offerings, or the saving sacrifice, who desires salvation but cannot ascend to lofty things. For he who cannot be a virgin, if he lives in holy wedlock, receives life from the Lord who says: "All men take not this word", and is necessarily ranked among the saved. So also of the contempt of things, of justice, of taking food with thanksgiving. For he is great who does great things; small, not least, he who can attain salvation, namely by middling things. According to the two kinds of ways of life therefore, he sets two definitions of voluntary sacrifices. For he says in Exodus: You shall make an altar of earth unto me, and you shall offer upon it your holocausts and peace offerings, your sheep and oxen etc. He adds the peace offerings as of the second rank and virtue. He therefore who thinks it suffices him if he be saved, offers indeed of the oxen. And the oxen are those who do the things of the law; he offers a gift, male and female, without blemish. But he does not command him who offers a holocaust to offer a female; not that the female is deprived of the way of life, but because to savour perfect things belongs to men, that is, to the stronger. Whence: "Who shall find a valiant woman?" For strength is scarcely found in women. The sacrifice of peace offerings is of men and of women: for they must live worthily that they may come to salvation.
3.2: **“And he shall lay his hand”** — as above
3.3:
**“And they shall offer of the sacrifice of peace offerings, for an oblation to the Lord, the fat”**
• anger: for this covers the heart
• anger, which we offer when we temper it, or when we are angry for God and turn our anger back into his cause
**“THE FAT”** — HESYCHIUS. The intelligible fat must be offered, that is, desire, which the Greeks call epithymia, which covers first the upper belly, then the lower, that we may offer the desire both of thinking and of doing: for thought goes before, fulfilment follows. And this we do in the belly, that is, in the heart, in which we first set before us actions as though we craved them; then we hasten to accomplish them as though we digested them. Let us therefore propose nothing wicked, fulfil nothing. And well does he describe the fat which covers the belly over the upper belly, that is, the appetite, since the greatest part of desire is about the appetite or purpose. And to the lower belly he joined the two kidneys, because there is a certain kinship of the kidneys and the heart. Whence: "Burn my reins and my heart." Elsewhere also they are joined: Who triest the reins and the hearts. For physicians set the motion of anger in the heart, but say that the memory of this thing lies in the kidneys, in which the female also is the cause; whence also they have communion with the thighs. He wishes therefore the desire of marriage also to be offered to God, that it may be for the sake of offspring, not of fornication, that marriage may be honourable and the bed undefiled. Let us offer anger also to God, that we may be angry against sin. Whence: "Be angry, and sin not." Hence Moses, being very angry, cast down the tables and broke them. And because concupiscence is in the liver, he commands the lobe, that is, the top, to be taken away and offered with the kidneys: that we may offer to God the firstfruits of our thoughts, and sanctify the lump by the first portion.
**“that covereth the entrails,”** — the heart and liver and what cleaves to the heart
**“THE ENTRAILS”** — The Seventy: The belly, that is, the heart. Of which it makes mention a second time according to the Seventy, because according to the physicians it has a twofold working: by one part it draws in nourishment, which they call the upper belly; by the other it separates the purgation, which they call the lower belly. The kidneys are the ministers of the genital seeds, communicating with the belly and the thighs. He commands therefore to be offered first the fat which is over the belly, and the two kidneys, and the fat which is over them, that is, over the thighs, which are near the kidneys: for they are placed in the middle between the thigh and the belly.
**“and all the fat that is within:”** — The Seventy: all the fat that is in the belly
3.4:
**“the two kidneys”**
• in which is the force of lust
• in which is the power of generating
**“THE CAUL OF THE LIVER”** — That is, of the liver, in which is delight or concupiscence. Whence according to the Seventy: The lobe of the liver shall be taken away with the kidneys. For the liver supplies the power of working in the kidneys.
**“with the two little kidneys.”** — in which is the seat of heat and the beginning of desire, in which the appetite of gluttony is marked, which we offer when we rein it in with the love of God
3.5:
**“And they shall burn them upon the altar”** — the altar on high
**“for a holocaust, the wood”** — the examples of the Fathers
**“fire”**
• of the Holy Ghost
• living according to the commandments of the Spirit
• because the foundation of every good
**“being put under, for an oblation of most sweet savour to the Lord.”** — whom it pleases to bring fruit to perfection, not only a hundredfold or sixtyfold, but also thirtyfold
3.6:
**“But if his oblation be of the flock,”** — in the sheep innocence is figured, as also in the lamb
**“and the sacrifice of peace offering, whether male”** — strong works
**“or female,”** — weak works
**“he offer, they shall be without blemish.”** — from the stain of sin
3.8: **“He shall put his hand”** — as above
3.9:
**“And they shall offer of the victim of peace offerings a sacrifice to the Lord: the fat”** — of desire or of concupiscence
**“and the rump”** — the tail is the end of the body: this is immolated when a good work is brought to its end
**“whole,”** — AND THE RUMP etc. The Seventy: The loin whole without blemish, namely that one thing be not offered to God and another to the adversary. For it suffices this one for pardon not to do the things that are of virtue; but if he works evil, he does not obtain pardon. Whence: Be ye simple as doves. For doves have exceeding simplicity, no malice. He who offers sacrifice of the oxen does not need to offer the loin to God, which he binds up and exercises in good works. He who immolates of the goats has no loin without blemish to offer, because he once stained it with sin. He therefore who was not in sins can offer a loin without blemish, not he who was a sinner. For this cause in the sacrifice of peace offerings he distinguished goats from lambs.
3.10:
**“with the kidneys, and the fat that covereth the belly and all the vitals,”** — these have already been expounded
**“and both the little kidneys, with the fat that is about the flanks, and the caul”** — The Seventy: the lobe
**“of the liver with the little kidneys.”** — BUT IF OF THE FLOCK etc. HESYCHIUS. Whom he commands to offer an ox, whom again a sheep, and whom a goat, we have said above. For the ox is he who works the commandments of the law; sheep, the simple; goats, because simple, formerly sinners, now penitent. But there he mingled goats with sheep, saying: And if the offering be of the flocks, of sheep or of goats etc. But the Seventy: If his gift be from the sheep, from the lambs and kids, he shall offer it without blemish. For the sheep seems to be the kind of lambs and kids. Whence Amos: I am of the peoples, and the Lord took me from the flocks of the sheep; since 'of the peoples' is properly said of one who feeds on goats. Because therefore the law speaks of some as lambs, of some as goats: and lambs are only the simple who have sinned in nothing, but goats the simple who have sinned and been converted: rightly in a manner the sacrifice in holocaust is one. For he who after sin wishes to savour perfect things ought to live as one who has not sinned before. But in the sacrifice of peace offerings, though he had kept the rest the same in sheep and goats and oxen, he set this one thing more in sheep: that he commanded to be offered not only the fat and the caul of the liver, or according to the Seventy the lobe of the liver and the kidneys, but also the rump, or also according to the Seventy, the loin without blemish with the kidneys. For because as a simple one he left out many things which he ought to have done, he ought to use his virtue in doing good, not, as a simple one, only in avoiding evil; that it may be manifest that he does not leave out the things he can know. Rightly are the simple made cautious, who from simplicity can easily be drawn to another's will; so that they offer not only the kidneys and the fat that is over them, but also the loin which is in the kidneys. For the loin signifies strength. Whence Roboam says: My little finger is thicker than the back of my father. And elsewhere: You shall gird your loins. In the loins also is the working of generation.
3.11:
**“And the priest shall burn them upon the altar, for the food of the fire”**
• spiritual
• the fire consuming the sacrifices, swallowing up death in victory
3.12:
**“If a goat”**
• the simple one who sinned before and repented
• which signifies the habit of penance
3.13:
**“He shall put”** — let him who offers penance give his effort to good works in the beginning
**“his hand upon the head thereof, and shall immolate it in the entry of the tabernacle of the testimony; and the sons of Aaron shall pour the blood thereof round about upon the altar.”** — as above
3.14:
**“And they shall take of it for the food of the fire”** — of the Holy Ghost
**“of the Lord, the fat”** — anger, as above
**“that covereth the belly,”** — because anger hinders the mind so that it cannot discern the truth
**“and that covereth all the vital parts:”** — the heart and liver and what cleaves to them
3.16: **“And the priest shall burn them upon the altar, for the food of the fire, and of a most sweet savour. All the fat”** — that all our desire may be offered to the Lord, not partly to the world. No man being a soldier to God entangleth himself with secular businesses.
3.17:
**“By a perpetual law”** — not because the figure is always to be observed, but what is understood by it
**“for your generations,”** — through each age
**“and in all your habitations:”**
• in the Churches or in any places whatever
• that is: in every way of life, whether in company or solitary
**“neither fat”** — the appetite or desire of the flesh
**“nor blood”** — all reason and understanding of the mind, which the blood signifies, are to be consecrated to God: for the soul is in the blood.
**“shall you eat at all.”** — NEITHER FAT etc. We ought not to have our own concupiscence, that is, carnal: For every man is tempted by his own concupiscence, being drawn away and allured. He forbids blood to be eaten, lest we kill anyone. For to eat blood is of beasts, that is, of the cruel. And at all is added for this reason, that we may spare both our neighbours and ourselves. But the soul ought to be immolated to God; whence he commanded the blood to be poured about the base of the altar.

4.2:
**“Speak to the children of Israel:”** — because this is commanded to all
**“The soul”**
• man in general, or the prelates of the Church and the perfect. But in what follows he makes an exception, saying: "If the priest that is anointed."
• for the body alone is not the cause of sin
**“that sinneth through ignorance”** — of the good
**“THE SOUL THAT SINNETH”** — ORIGEN. Rightly he calls it the soul which he describes as sinning: for he would not call the spirit that which he said would sin, nor the man, in whom, sin intervening, the image of God would not stand. It is not therefore the spirit that sins. For the fruit of the spirit, as the Apostle says, is charity, joy, peace, patience and the like. But elsewhere he says: He that soweth in his flesh, of the flesh also shall reap corruption; but he that soweth in the spirit, of the spirit shall reap life everlasting: since therefore he who sows is one, and that in which he sows another. For one sows in the flesh when one sins, that corruption may be reaped thence; or in the spirit, when one lives according to God, that life eternal may be reaped. It is plain that it is the soul which sows either in the flesh or in the spirit, and which can rush into sins and be turned away from them. For the body is its follower to whatever it chooses, and the spirit its guide to virtue, if it will follow it.
**“HESYCHIUS”** — HESYCHIUS. The soul that sinneth etc. The lawgiver omitted nothing necessary: he assigned the differences of ways of life, and in the offering of sacrifices the ways of living; at length he sets forth the sacrifice of Christ, through which remission and redemption of sins was given to us. And it is to be noted that he said the sin was the soul's, against those who accuse the body as the cause of sin. But if the soul is free from it, the luxury of the flesh harms it nothing. Rather, if the soul rules well, it at once ceases and withdraws. But if the soul sins through ignorance, yet it is not compelled by the flesh, but by negligence and the imitation of worse things, through which it thinks harmful things useful. It is to be noted also that in many things he mingles the priest as one like the others, offering for sins: for Christ ought in all things to be made like unto his brethren, that he might become a merciful and faithful priest. But the lawgiver calls the sin of the priest the sin of the people. For the sensible priest, being negligent or sinning or not punishing, makes the people sin; but the intelligible priest in no way did sin. Yet, as far as we can, let us fit what is said to the intelligible priest. For if anyone abuses the patience of God, God seems to give him licence to sin. Whence Isaias: Why hast thou made us to err, O Lord, from thy ways? why hast thou hardened our heart etc.? Habacuc also complains of the like: Why lookest thou upon them that do unjust things, and holdest thy peace when the wicked devoureth the man that is more just than himself etc.? The lawgiver seems therefore to signify the priest to whom it was said: "Thou art a priest for ever according to the order of Melchisedech"; and who was anointed by the Father, according to that: "Therefore God, thy God, hath anointed thee." He offered himself a sacrifice for our sins. Whence Paul says: Christ was offered once to exhaust the sins of many. Yet he offers himself for his own sin, because he took our sin upon himself. Whence: Him that knew no sin, for us he hath made sin.
4.3:
**“If the priest”**
• he passes from the genus to the species
• Christ, who is a priest for ever
**“that is anointed”** — with the oil of gladness above his fellows
**“shall sin,”** — Christ is said to sin when we sin who are his members.
**“making the people to offend,”**
• by the long-suffering of patience: for while he does not punish at once, he is thought either not to care for these things or not to know them, and so the wicked are emboldened to worse; whence the patience of God leadeth thee to penance or to patience: but thou treasurest up to thyself wrath etc.
• IF THE PRIEST etc. ORIGEN. It is to be observed that in the sin of the high priest the lawgiver does not add that he sinned ignorantly or unwillingly: for ignorance cannot befall him who was advanced to teach the rest.
**“ORIGEN”**
• ORIGEN. If the priest etc. Terror and mercy together are shown in the divine laws. So that nothing is safe, not even the high priest himself. He who is high priest, who is anointed, who kindles the divine altars with sacred fires, who immolates gifts and saving victims, who intervenes as propitiator between God and men, not even he is free from the contagion of sin. But see the mercy of God. Whence Paul: Every high priest taken from among men is ordained for men, that he may offer sacrifices. And after: The law maketh men priests who have infirmity, that they may offer as for their own, so also for the people's infirmity; not namely men who could not sin at all, otherwise they would not be men, but who imitate him "who did no sin". In which it is chiefly to be wondered at, not that the priest does not sin, but that he recognises his sin. For it is not he who thinks he has not sinned, but he who amends; and he more easily pardons sinners who is bitten by the consciousness of his own infirmity.
• Morally. If the priest etc. The high priest is the sense of piety and religion, which in us performs as it were the priesthood through the prayers we pour out to God: if this offends, it makes the people of good acts offend, which is within us. Nor do we do anything rightly if the sense, the leader of good works, is depraved. Therefore for the amendment of this a singular victim, the fatted calf, is required. Likewise the Synagogue, that is, the amendment of our virtues, is restored by the death of Christ.
**“he shall offer”** — to the Father
**“for his sin”** — which he took upon himself, who bore our sins in his body upon the tree.
**“the calf”**
• his flesh
• The Seventy add: of the oxen, that is, of the fathers who were glorious in the justice of the law
• who on the cross scattered our enemies
**“without blemish”** — "Who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth."
**“to the Lord.”** — A CALF WITHOUT BLEMISH etc. A second time we find a calf offered by the high priest in holocaust, once for a gift and once for sin; but that for a gift is consumed upon the altar of holocaust, while that for sin is burned outside the camp and in a clean place, only the fat and the kidneys being offered on the altar. This perhaps is Jesus, who through his blood made peace both as to the things on earth and the things in heaven. In heaven, for a gift; but on earth, where sin reigned from Adam to Moses, offered for sin. And this is to have suffered outside the camp, namely of the angels of God. Whence Jacob: These are the camps of God. Outside these is all this earthly place in which we dwell, in which Christ suffered.
4.4:
**“And he shall bring it to the door of the tabernacle of the testimony”**
• the cross
• because he gave himself up to the cross; whence: "He was offered because it was his own will."
• the doctrine and tradition of the apostles, according to which the sacrifice was made. For this is the entrance to heaven, which is the tabernacle of the testimony. Whence Isaias: He spreadeth out the heavens as a tent to dwell in.
**“before the Lord,”** — the Father looking on, to whom it is said: "Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit."
**“And he shall lay his hand”** — For he offered himself; no one compelled him. Whence: I have power to lay down my life etc.
**“upon the head thereof,”** — the beginning of the passion
**“and shall sacrifice it to the Lord.”** — for our sins
4.5:
**“He shall take also of the blood of the calf, and carry it”** — whence Paul: "By his own blood he entered once into the Holies."
**“into the tabernacle of the testimony.”**
• heaven. He rose from the dead bearing the scars of his passion, and so entered.
• HE SHALL TAKE ALSO etc. He carried the blood of the calf into the tabernacle, that is, into heaven, when, ascending the heavens after the resurrection, he stood before the face of the Father, as it were offering the blood of the passion, interceding for us.
4.6:
**“And having dipped his finger”** — who is the power of God. This is dipped in blood, because the passion of the Lord's flesh is wrought by the power of the Godhead, which the withdrawing of the sun, the rending of the rocks and many like things prove.
**“in the blood, he shall sprinkle with it seven times”** — He sprinkled seven times when he wiped away our sins fully by the shedding of his blood, or enriched us with the sevenfold spirit.
**“SEVEN TIMES”** — Namely for the remission of sins and the supplying of spiritual gifts. And the blood signifies the passion, according to that: I am innocent of the blood of this just man. And elsewhere: "His blood be upon us" etc. Of this sprinkling Peter says: And the sprinkling of the blood of Christ.
**“before the Lord,”** — these things were done before the Lord, because he fulfilled the will of the Father in all things
**“before the veil of the sanctuary.”**
• the humanity or flesh of Christ
• BEFORE THE VEIL etc. He calls the Lord's flesh by many names, because its working is manifold. Whence the Lord himself named himself by transferred words, now sacrifice, now shepherd, again vine, then bread of life and grain of wheat. So Moses too called his flesh the veil. Whence Paul: He hath dedicated for us a way through the veil, that is to say, his flesh. It is called the veil of the sanctuary also for this reason, that in it the flesh of the holy of holies is figured.
**“THE VEIL”** — The humanity of Christ. For as the veil was between the holy of holies and the outer tabernacle, so the flesh of Christ is between us, who are the outer tabernacle, and the Godhead, which is signified by the holy of holies. Before the veil of the testimony therefore the priest sprinkled the blood of the calf, because Christ bloodied his flesh with the blood of the passion.
4.7:
**“And he shall put some of the same blood upon the horns”** — the four principal virtues
**“UPON THE HORNS”** — This altar signifies the seat of God, that is, the Seraphim. Whence Isaias: One of the Seraphims flew to me, and in his hand was a live coal, which he had taken with the tongs off the altar etc. Thymiama, according to the Seventy, the compositions of all the virtues. For where is it fitting that the virtues be compounded but in the seat of God? For from heaven they come down to us. Whence James says: "But the wisdom that is from above." And the four virtues, wisdom, justice, fortitude, temperance (because the kinds of the other virtues come together in them) are named horns. These God anoints with his own blood, strengthening them namely with greater and more perfect virtue, that they may prevail against the adverse powers and forces.
**“of the altar”**
• the Seraphim
• of the body of Christ
• OF THE ALTAR etc. Of the angelic powers. For if men render to God a pleasing odour of good works, how much more the holy angels, abiding in purity of nature? And though they did not commit a sin that should be expiated by the blood of Christ, yet through his blood they have been set at peace with us, and their number restored.
**“of the sweet incense”** — The Seventy: of the composition, namely of the virtues
**“most acceptable to the Lord, which is in the tabernacle of the testimony.”** — heaven
**“And he shall pour all the rest of the blood at the foot”** — the Gospel
**“AT THE FOOT”** — The base, the lower part of the altar, signifies weak men. For by the blood of Christ not only was the number of the angels restored, but man also was redeemed. Therefore Christ is called the redemption of the angels also.
**“OF THE ALTAR OF HOLOCAUST”** — The body of Christ: for he himself is the priest, he the sacrifice, and he the altar. For as he works many things, so he is fittingly called by many names. Whence Paul: We have an altar, whereof they have no power to eat who serve the tabernacle; this is the body of Christ, of which it is not lawful for the Jews to eat. This altar is at the entry of the tabernacle, that is, of heaven, because through him we have entrance into heaven.
4.8: **“AND THE FAT”** — Mystically. The delights and desires of the flesh; all of which, however, are not to be received into Christ, such as the desire of gluttony and coition; but those which he had, he had from us, as thirst, hunger and the like. And these he offered to the Father, to whose glory he transferred them, and set them forth as an example to us, that we may refer our desires to God.
4.9: **“The two little kidneys, and the caul that is upon them, which is by the flanks, and the fat of the liver”** — The Seventy: the lobe of the liver
4.10: **“as it is taken off from the calf of the sacrifice of peace offerings”** — as he signifies above it is to be understood
4.11:
**“But the skin and all the flesh with the head”** — because the beginning
**“and feet”** — because the end
**“and the bowels”**
• the mind
• ORIGEN. He shows that Christ assumed the substance of humanity whole.
**“and the dung,”**
• The Seventy: with the belly and the dung
• the sin of mankind
• THE TWO LITTLE KIDNEYS etc. HESYCHIUS. These things are done also in the sacrifice of peace offerings, or the saving sacrifice. And he divides the sacrifice in two, that it may be lawful for all to imitate the sacrifice of Christ, both for those who are of a lower way of life, to whom the sacrifice of peace offerings is fitting, and for those who follow higher things, for whom it suffices if they imitate what follows.
• But the skin and all the flesh with the head and the feet etc. This he commands, that thou divide not Christ, as some do, saying: He who was of Mary suffered; he who was of God did not suffer. But to us there is one God, Jesus Christ, by whom are all things. For the flesh in the Lord is the whole humanity, according to what is said: "The Word was made flesh." Whence he says: Its flesh with the head and the feet, or the extremities according to others, that by these words we may believe that he who suffered for us is the first and the last. "For he is before all, and by him all things consist." With the bowels and the dung. The Seventy: with the belly and the liver. And the belly signifies the mind. Let us by no means doubt, therefore, that he who suffered for us had a human mind, as some heretics do, who said Christ was apsychos, without a soul. The dung is the sin of mankind, which the Crucified took upon himself. Dung, though it is unclean, does not pollute the one who carries it, nor is it of our nature, though it is in us: so our sins which the Lord bore were foreign to him, and did not pollute him.
• THE BOWELS AND THE DUNG etc. ORIGEN. Perhaps in comparison with the heavenly bodies the human body is called dung. But also that basket of dung which is put to the roots of the fig tree bears witness to the mystery of the dispensation taken up in the body; nor are the inward parts said to be lacking. For though he bore the lowly form of a servant, yet in him is the fulness of the Godhead. The same also is to be understood of the calf of the synagogue.
• Since the figure of the Lord's passion appears in each particular, the lawgiver figures its mystery more fully in what follows.
4.12:
**“and the rest of the body he shall carry forth without the camp”** — because the Lord suffered outside the camp, that is, outside the city
**“into a place”** — Golgotha
**“clean”**
• because there we were cleansed
• who cleansed the whole world
**“where the ashes are wont to be poured out,”** — because in it the sins of mankind were quenched, and the heat of sin grew cold
**“and he shall burn them upon a pile of wood;”** — of the Scriptures: for whatever things were done in the time of the passion fulfilled the Prophecies; whence: "Now all this was done that the Scriptures of the Prophets might be fulfilled"; and elsewhere: That the Scripture might be fulfilled, he said: I thirst.
4.13:
**“And if all the multitude of the children of Israel”**
• the Synagogue, or the common people who cried: "Crucify, crucify"; and: "His blood be upon us, and upon our children."
• It is plain that the whole Synagogue can offend through ignorance; whence: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.
**“shall be ignorant, and through ignorance shall do that which is against the commandment of the Lord,”** — not knowingly, as the priests; whence Peter: "I know that you did it through ignorance" etc. But the priests sinned knowingly, seeing all things foretold in the Scriptures, and therefore offending more grievously.
4.14:
**“and afterwards”** — converted to penance through the preaching of the apostles
**“shall understand their sin,”** — this is not said of the priest
**“they shall offer for their sin”**
• when, knowing its sin, it is converted to the sacrifice of Christ
• by believing in the Crucified, who redeemed mankind
**“the calf”** — Christ
**“and shall bring it”**
• the same things also are to be understood of the calf of the Synagogue
• namely, let it offer and show its faith to the doctors of the Church
**“to the door of the tabernacle.”** — as above
4.15:
**“And the ancients of the people shall put their hands upon the head thereof before the Lord.”**
• The chief priests and Pharisees gathered a council, that they might deliver Jesus to death and kill him; whence Caiphas: It is expedient that one man should die for the people.
• because the princes of the Jews and the chief priests delivered Christ to Pilate to be crucified
• as the priest in his sacrifice
• AND IF ALL THE MULTITUDE etc. HESYCHIUS. He commands the same in the sacrifice of the multitude and of the priest: namely that a calf be immolated and burned outside the camp, and the blood offered in the tabernacle. Whence he shows most plainly that the sins of the priest and of the common people are the same; wherefore the same sacrifice is offered for both. This also which is changed shows that the sacrifice is one. For of the priest he did not say: 'If he come to know his sin.' For God was not ignorant of the sin, which he took on flesh that he might take upon himself. But of the multitude, that is, of the Synagogue or of the common people, he added: and afterwards shall understand their sin. First therefore it was ignorant, but afterwards it knew. Whence: If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin, as being ignorant. But now they have no excuse for their sin, as knowing. When therefore they knew their sin, they turned to the sacrifice of the only-begotten. In the sacrifice of the priest also he himself puts his hand upon the head of the calf, but here the ancients. For in the sacrifice of Christ the ancients of the people and the Scribes and Caiphas acted (who said: It is expedient that one man should die for the people etc.), and Christ, who gave himself up for us to dispense our remission. Whence he says: Doing so as he did also before. And the priest praying for it, the Lord will be merciful. For Christ was made a propitiation for us in his blood. For he prayed for his very crucifiers: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.
**“And the calf being immolated in the sight”** — good pleasure
4.16:
**“the priest that is anointed shall carry”** — with the oil of gladness above his fellows
**“of the blood thereof”** — with the blood of Christ the horns of the altar, that is, the arms of the cross, were sprinkled
4.17: **“And shall dip his finger”** — what has been expounded, do not expound; do not do what is done
4.18:
**“And he shall put of the same blood”** — which is mankind, which was sprinkled and redeemed with the blood of Christ, by which Christ daily saves and redeems
**“on the horns of the altar”** — the four virtues
4.19:
**“And all the fat thereof he shall take off,”** — as above
**“and shall burn it upon the altar:”** — the faith of the cross
4.20:
**“doing so with this calf, as he did also with that before:”** — he shows plainly that these things are to be done and understood in the same way
**“and the priest praying for them,”** — Christ, who intercedes for us
**“the Lord will be merciful unto them.”** — the Father
4.21:
**“But the calf itself he shall carry forth without the camp,”** — because Christ suffered without the gate; we must go forth therefore without the camp, bearing his reproach
**“and shall burn it”** — because Christ was roasted with the fire of the passion
**“as he did the former calf: because it is for the sin of the multitude.”**
• of the Synagogue or of mankind
• HE SHALL CARRY FORTH THE CALF etc. HESYCHIUS. The conclusion of the law suffices us to make plain the present passage; for nothing is commanded here to be changed for the sin of the multitude. It is manifest that he understands the same sin of the common people and of the priest; therefore he ordained the same sacrifice in each.
4.22:
**“If a prince shall sin,”**
• of him to whom more is committed, more is required
• endowed with wisdom, who ought not to be ignorant
4.23:
**“and afterwards shall come to know his sin,”**
• by himself or through another
• otherwise he does not repent
**“he shall offer”** — for sin
**“a sacrifice”** — not a holocaust
**“to the Lord, a buck goat”**
• as a greater victim for a greater sin
• The Seventy: chimarros
• because a sacrifice for sin
**“A BUCK GOAT”** — Not a she goat, namely an easy or middling penance, but a hard and rough one: for the more one excels in understanding, the more, if he sins, does he bear a greater penalty for a greater fault.
**“of the goats without blemish.”**
• The penance must be without blemish, that is, without the sin of which he repents, lest by vow or deed he incline himself to something else.
• IF A PRINCE SHALL SIN etc. HESYCHIUS. As in the voluntary sacrifices he ordained the sacrifices according to the differences of ways of life, so for sins too he commands the sacrifices to be equal to them, whose greatness is set not only from the sin but from the person of those sinning. For the servant who knew the will of his lord and did it not shall be beaten with many stripes; he that knew it not, with few; because to whom much is committed, of him more is required. This is the prince who, if he sins, shall offer a buck goat. But if anyone of the people, that is, an unlearned man or a commoner, not one who is set apart perhaps for meditating the law of the Lord (for this one too is a prince), he offers a she goat for a lesser sin. The buck goat is of the masculine gender, the she goat of the feminine: he distinguishes the force of the sacrifice. The Seventy have chimarros or chimarra in the Greek, which in Latin is interpreted a kid of the goats, namely a male, and a she goat of the kids, a female. And chimarros and chimarra are the young of the goats, winter-born, which are born about the time of winter: for they bear twice, namely in winter and in summer. In winter is signified the sadness of penance: for the penitent brings forth sons in sadness and weeping; but they are not strangers to the sacrifice. The penitents therefore offer winter kids, as tossed and struggling against sin with divers waves; who, if they persevere, and do not in despair abandon the helm as in a storm, will be delivered. Whence: Pray that your flight be not in the winter or on the sabbath: by winter penance is designated, by the sabbath the rest of the good. For the sabbath was given for rest from evil.
**“ORIGEN”** — ORIGEN. Morally. This prince can be called the force of reason which is within us; which, if it sins so that we do something foolish, let us fear that sentence: You are the salt of the earth. But if the salt lose its savour, it is good for nothing any more but to be cast out and to be trodden on by men.
4.24:
**“And he shall put his hand upon the head thereof: and when he hath immolated it”** — HE SHALL PUT HIS HAND etc. Making the sin manifest by himself and offering his confession: but he himself, according to the Seventy, does not slay it, but others; because he needs the help of others that his penance may be received. Nor is the priest commanded to slay it; for he says: And when he hath immolated it etc., and does not add who ought to immolate it; for in the sacrifice of penance it is lawful to use the help of another, as James: "Pray one for another, that you may be saved."
**“in the place where the holocaust is wont to be slain before the Lord, because it is for sin,”**
• sin must be confessed in the sight of the Lord; whence: "I have acknowledged my sin to thee."
• WHERE IS WONT etc. Because the worthy penance of sinners and the strong works of the just please God alike.
4.25:
**“shall dip”** — fulfilling the work of the passion, through which penance profited
**“The priest”** — Christ
**“his finger in the blood of the victim”** — of Christ immolated for us
**“for sin, touching therewith the horns”** — the cross; whence: "Horns are in his hands"; or the angelic powers, higher than the human.
**“of the altar of holocaust,”**
• of the Lord's body
• THE HORNS etc. Upon the cross are offered the firstfruits of the blood which is offered for sin, because the work and effect of the cross is the perfect remission of our sins.
**“and pouring out the rest at the foot thereof.”** — men to be expiated
**“AND POURING OUT THE REST”** — Namely assigning all penance to the gospel preaching, whose intention is that he who repents may correct himself and be saved. Whence at the beginning of the Gospel the Lord providently says: Do penance: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.
4.26:
**“But the fat”**
• that all the desire of the penitent may look upward: for then the penance of the offerer can be reckoned in the sacrifice of peace offerings.
• but the rest shall remain to the priests to eat
**“he shall burn upon it, as is wont to be done with the victims of peace offerings:”** — HESYCHIUS. Whatever things are common to both sacrifices are to be understood in common.
**“and shall pray”**
• the priest, namely
• For we are not fit to forgive sins to ourselves: for Christ gains propitiation for us.
**“for him, and for his sin, and it shall be forgiven him.”** — he sets down the final cause, namely of the things said above
4.27:
**“And if a soul shall sin”** — one
**“through ignorance,”** — which is not busied in meditation of the law
**“of the people of the land, doing any of those things that by the law of the Lord are forbidden,”** — He does not say that if he transgress in one, he is made or is guilty of all.
**“and offending,”**
• AND IF A SOUL SHALL SIN etc. ORIGEN. Doing one of all the commandments of the Lord, which shall not be done. Long did amazement hold me astonished at this saying. For I do not see it said consistently: if a soul shall sin and do one of the commandments of the Lord, which shall not be done. For if it is a commandment of the Lord, how ought it not to have been done, since commandments are given that they may be done? Yet I see that all the translators have put it alike. It is not therefore an error of translation, but a deep sense. For some commandments of the Lord are given that they may be done, some that they may not be done; but human necessity demanded that among those which ought to be done there should be inserted those which ought not to be done. A lamb is commanded to be immolated at the Pasch, not that God required the victim of a lamb every year, but that he might mark that the lamb ought to be immolated "who taketh away the sin of the world". This therefore he willed, that he did not will. Whence: To what purpose do you offer me the multitude of your victims etc.? Yet he commanded how these things should be done. He who has offered these carnally is a soul of the people of the land, which sins unwillingly, doing one of the commandments of the Lord which shall not be done. And when the sin is made known to it, it brings its gift before the Lord, when it has known that God does not seek such a sacrifice; because a sacrifice to God is an afflicted spirit, and God desires mercy rather than sacrifice. It brings its gift when it knows how to immolate the sacrifice of praise.
• OF THE PEOPLE OF THE LAND etc. ORIGEN. To distinguish it from him who is not of the earth. For this cannot fit him who said: Our conversation is in heaven etc. For that soul is not of the people of the land which has nothing with the earth, which converses in heaven, "where Christ is sitting at the right hand of God", which desires to be dissolved and to be with Christ, but judges it needful to remain in the flesh for our sake.
4.28:
**“and shall come to know his sin, he shall offer a she goat”** — chimarra
**“without blemish”**
• a middling penance
• that he may abstain from sin while he cleanses sin
4.29:
**“And he shall lay his hand”** — that is, let him add working at once to the first thought of penance
**“upon the head of the victim that is for sin, and shall immolate it in the place of the holocaust.”** — that it may be received as in holocaust
4.31: **“But taking off all the fat, as is wont to be taken away of the victims of peace offerings, he shall burn it upon the altar, for a sweet savour to the Lord: and he shall pray”** — These being offered, our penance and offering do not suffice unless the great priest pray for us.
4.32:
**“But if he offer of the flock a victim for his sin, an ewe,”**
• who is simple among the people
• because he sinned through simplicity
**“to wit, without blemish,”**
• that the penance may be clean
• BUT IF OF THE FLOCK etc. HESYCHIUS. To the offering of the she goat which those of the people offer he joined the ewe. For among the people there can be some simple ones, to whom the sacrifice of the sheep is fitting, which is shown in the sacrifices of holocaust and of peace offerings. For not only the prince, that is, loftier knowledge, or the commoner, but if anyone among the people is simple, if perchance he sins, he must repent for the redemption of his sin. And he commanded not a ram but a female to be offered for this reason, that he assigned the sacrifice of females to the common people. In these he plainly testifies that the prince who excels in knowledge should show not only the simplicity of the dove, but also the wisdom of the serpent. But he who is among the people, though simple, if perchance he sins, is not pardoned unless he has washed away his sin by the offering of penance. The rest need no exposition. For when sacrifice is made for sin, he commands like things of the she goat and the ewe.
4.33: **“He shall put his hand upon the head thereof”** — do not expound what has been expounded: "For thou hast yet a great way to go."

5.1:
**“If any soul sin,”**
• any soul, not of the people of the land as above
• here sacrifice is not commanded to be offered for sin
**“and hear the voice of one swearing,”** — falsely
**“and is a witness,”** — of the matter that is sworn
**“either because he himself hath seen, or is privy to it: if he do not utter it,”** — to the priest, or to one who may profit him, not harm him
**“he shall bear his iniquity.”** — IF ANY SOUL SIN etc. AUGUSTINE. He seems to say that a man sins who hears someone swear falsely, and knows that he swears falsely, and keeps silence. And he knows it then if he was a witness of the matter sworn, namely either saw it, or was privy to it, that is, knew it in some way; either he beheld it with his eyes, or he who swears told him: for so he could be privy. But between the fear of this sin and of betrayal there is often no small temptation. For we can, by admonishing or forbidding, call back one ready for perjury from so grave a sin. But if he does not listen, and swears falsely in our presence, whether he is to be betrayed, even if when betrayed he runs into danger of death, is a most difficult question. But because he did not express to whom it is to be told, whether to him to whom the oath is made, or to the priest, or to someone who not only cannot pursue him by inflicting punishment, but can pray for him, it seems to me that he frees himself from such a sin who tells it to such as can rather profit the perjurer than harm him, namely by correcting or by praying, if he himself applies the medicine of confession. Yet it is to be noted that for this sin he did not command sacrifice to be offered, but at once added: The soul that toucheth any unclean thing etc.
**“HESYCHIUS”** — HESYCHIUS. If any soul sin etc. He does not repeat what he said above, treating generally of every sin and commanding what they ought to offer. For when he said: "If a soul shall sin of the people of the land" etc., he showed carnal Israel, which, knowing the commandments of the law of God, ought not to have transgressed in anything; but having transgressed, ought to repent. But now, saying: If any soul sin, he does not add "of the people of the land". For he speaks of the sins from which even the gentiles must abstain, that is, things offered to idols, things strangled, blood and fornication, as you will find also in what follows. Above also he shows the sin of one offending by himself, but here one defiled by the sins of others: for this the touching of an unclean carcass and of one taken by a beast hints, showing most plainly that we ought not to consent to the sins or error of another, but reprove them.
5.2:
**“The soul that toucheth”** — by imitating
**“any”** — what proceeds from the heart defiles a man
**“unclean thing,”** — the sin of another
**“either that which hath been killed”**
• spiritually
• it signifies the spiritual vices which are committed at the devil's prompting, such as hatred, envy and the like
**“by a beast,”** — the devil, namely
**“or of itself”** — by its own concupiscence
**“died,”** — in carnal sins, which are gluttony, lust etc., which proceed from human concupiscence
**“or any other”** — it signifies those who desire and care only for earthly things and think nothing of heavenly: he therefore is defiled who imitates such
**“creeping thing,”** — which goes upon its breast and belly
**“and forgetteth”**
• one suffering a flux of blood or of seed, and menstruous women and certain others. It signifies those of whom the lawgiver treats more finely a little after.
• for forgetfulness is the defilement of the soul
**“his uncleanness, he is guilty, and hath offended:”**
• by consenting or by doing
• THE SOUL THAT TOUCHETH etc. HESYCHIUS. Morally. He shows unclean touchings not of the body but of the matter. Whence: Not that which goeth into the mouth defileth a man, but the evil thoughts that come forth from the heart, namely murders, adulteries and the like, these are the things that defile a man; therefore they are called unclean. For the carcass signifies a man dead in sin. Whence: "Let the dead bury their dead." He is taken by a beast who has been enticed by the devil to sin. The Seventy added unclean: for not everyone who is taken by a beast is in every way slain, as Peter; but he can say with David: "Our soul hath been delivered as a sparrow out of the snare of the fowlers."
**“GREGORY”** — GREGORY. Morally. To utter an oath is to bind ourselves by vow to divine service, when we promise good works and pledge to do well. When we vow abstinence and the torment of the flesh, we swear to do ourselves hurt. But because there is no one who does not sometimes sin even among pious vows, for sin an ewe lamb or a she goat is commanded to be offered: by the ewe lamb the innocence of the active life, by the she goat, which pastures on the highest rocks, the contemplative life is marked. He therefore who sees that he does not fulfil his promises ought to raise himself either by the innocence of good work, or to the lofty pasture of contemplation. And it is to be noted that the ewe lamb is commanded to be offered of the flocks, but the she goat not of the flocks, because the active life is of many, the contemplative of few. And when we do what we see many doing, we give as it were an ewe lamb of the flocks. But if the offerer's strength does not suffice for the ewe lamb and the she goat, in the remedy of penance let two young pigeons or two turtles be offered. Young pigeons have moaning for song. By the two young pigeons or the two turtles therefore the twofold moaning of penitents is designated, namely because we have neglected right things and done wicked ones: we offer one turtle for sin when we moan for our fault; of the other we make a holocaust when for the good things we have left undone we burn, kindling ourselves utterly with the fire of sorrow.
5.3: **“And if he touch any thing of the uncleanness of man,”** — Not every uncleanness of man pollutes him who touches it.
5.4:
**“The soul that sweareth, and uttereth”** — openly pronouncing
**“with his lips,”** — The Seventy: distinguishing with his lips, that is, defining and setting it apart from the other things which are not held by a mere word.
**“that he would do either evil”** — as Herod to the daughter of Herodias
**“or good,”** — and has not done it
**“and the same”** — to do good or evil
**“bindeth with an oath and his word, and having forgotten it”**
• at first unaware
• THE SOUL THAT SWEARETH etc. AUGUSTINE. Why is it that for silent perjury, or the touching of a carcass or of anything unclean, he commands no sacrifice, but for one who swears falsely without knowing it he decrees an ewe lamb or a she goat to be offered? Or ought this sacrifice to be understood for all the things said above? For when all had been set out, he brought in the sacrifice of expiation.
**“afterwards understandeth his offence,”** — in all the things that have been said
5.6:
**“And offer of the flocks”** — because of the people
**“an ewe lamb,”**
• perfect innocence
• fitting for the simple
**“or a she goat,”** — perfect penance
**“and shall pray”**
• the Father
• that is: he will make us pray, or the saints for us
**“for him the priest,”** — Christ
**“and for his sins.”**
• He uses the accustomed words, recalling to memory the things which he received in the prayer for sins.
• UNDERSTANDETH HIS OFFENCE etc. HESYCHIUS. It is to be noted that offence sometimes signifies what is presumed against God alone, as in holy things or in oaths. Sometimes the lawgiver calls every sin that comes to knowledge an offence. And wherever there is knowledge of sin, whether it is put before or added after, it is called an offence. For when the offence is known, one offends against God. For not in vain does the lawgiver use this word: for as at the beginning he designated the differing ways of life of men through holocausts and saving sacrifices, that he might open many ways, so he appointed not one but many kinds of offerings for sin, that he might set forth several modes of penance; since we cannot all do all things, nor does every penance suit every sin, or fit it. For how will an old man or a sick man bear sackcloth, fasting, tears, continual prayer and the like? But he has another mode of repenting, as what follows shows: But if he be not able etc.
**“HESYCHIUS”** — HESYCHIUS. Let us add this, that if a prince sins in any of these things, he should offer a buck goat of the goats, namely a penance worthy of himself, who ought neither to have sinned, nor to have shared with others, nor to have provoked his subjects to sin. What therefore ought not to happen he left undiscussed.
5.7:
**“But if he be not able to offer a beast,”**
• an ewe lamb or a she goat
• BUT IF etc. HESYCHIUS. He who cannot afflict himself continually, eat ashes like bread, mingle his drink with weeping and the like, let him in repenting offer himself to the contemplation of God and the study of the law, consecrating his whole mind to heavenly conversation, shunning earthly things most fully; whence remission of sins and justification are hoped for. Therefore one is made for sin, that is, for the cleansing of sin, the other for a holocaust, because he sanctifies himself most fully to God.
**“let him offer”** — the contemplative life, and meditation intent on the law
**“two turtles,”** — let him leave the world: for the turtle, wandering alone, signifies solitude
**“or two young pigeons”**
• cleanness and simplicity
• continual moaning and mourning in mind and body
**“to the Lord, one for sin,”** — for the cleansing of sin
**“and the other for a holocaust,”**
• because the whole way of life is consecrated to God
• because sacrifice was not offered for sin. But when he spoke of the holocaust he named the turtle, and did not say two.
5.8:
**“And he shall give them to the priest:”** — Christ: for the things that are according to him and are offered through his mediation are acceptable.
**“who, offering”** — No one offering can become a holocaust unless he has first been free from sin: he sets down the manner of freedom, saying: he shall twist back.
**“the first for sin, shall twist back the head”** — the mind
**“of it to the little pinions, so that to the neck”** — The Seventy: to the vertebra, namely to the whole body, because the firmness of the neck is the health and substance of the body.
**“it stick, and be not altogether broken off.”**
• whence he says: "Destroy this temple" etc.
• HE SHALL TWIST BACK THE HEAD etc. GREGORY. Allegorically. The death of Christ availed for the joining of his body, that is, the Church, not for its separation. For he is the mediator of God and men, and our head, and the victim of true cleansing; and while he bore death here for us, he clung the more truly. After the cutting therefore the head of the turtle clings to its body, because not even death can divide Christ from the Church. The persecutors brought death, that they might cut off from him the devotion of the faithful; but thence faith grew, when they saw him crucified and buried, when they believed they had divided him from the love of all. But the head of the turtle was cut, yet not cut off from its body: for by this, that he bore death for us, he joined us all to himself more truly in his very death.
• BE BROKEN OFF etc. He wishes us not to serve the body, but to be broken off or twisted back, lest the law of sin reign in our members. But because we ought not to hold our body in hatred, nor reckon it, as the heretics do, a making of the devil, but to set it under the mind, he does not command the body to be separated from the neck: for both are the creature of one and the same.
**“GREGORY”** — GREGORY. Morally. He shall twist back etc. In the sacrifice of God we ought to be a turtle, that our head may be twisted back to the pinions, that is, the sense to the virtues. By the head we understand the mind, because as the head rules the body, so the mind rules the actions. But the head clings to the neck and is not wholly cut off, because our mind is to be separated from the delight of the flesh, not from the necessary care of the flesh, lest we make provision for the flesh in its lusts: the head of the turtle therefore is to be partly cut off and partly cling to the neck.
5.9:
**“And of its blood he shall sprinkle the side of the altar,”** — of the body of Christ
**“and whatsoever is left, he shall let it drop at the bottom thereof, because it is for sin.”** — THE BOTTOM etc. The Seventy: The base, which is the Gospel; because according to the intention of the sacrifice of Christ and of the Gospel, sacrifice ought to be offered for sins. Whence he adds: Because it is for sin: for nothing so rescues from sin as the imitation of Christ and obedience to the gospel preaching.
5.10:
**“And the other he shall burn”** — wholly renouncing the world
**“for a holocaust, as is wont to be done: and the priest shall pray for him,”** — Wonderful is God the lawgiver, who condescends to human weakness and has found a way by which the weak may merit no less.
5.11:
**“And if be not able”** — The Seventy: shall not find, because, namely, abusing the riches of power, he has spent unseasonably
**“his hand”** — AND IF BE NOT ABLE etc. That not every time is easy for penance, namely when we abuse penance itself and, returning to sin, abolish its fruit, the lawgiver hints, saying: And if his hand be not able etc.
**“to offer two turtles, or two young pigeons,”** — Much less therefore can he offer a kid or a sheep.
**“AUGUSTINE”** — AUGUSTINE. It is asked whether what is said is to be taken everywhere: that if his hand be not able to offer a sheep, he ought to offer a pair of turtles or two young pigeons; and if he be not able for this either, a certain quantity of fine flour. For if it is understood everywhere, it cannot be said that the priest has not a calf, or the synagogue or the prince has not a goat or a sheep.
