And if it is so, what need was there afterwards to say that silent perjury, or the touching of an unclean thing, and perjury done through ignorance were purged by the sacrifice of an ewe lamb or a she goat, when the same precept is in that generality to which these could have belonged? But if these are distinguished, so that it was lawful for them to offer turtles or doves, or, if these were lacking, fine flour, but where this is not said it was not lawful, it does not seem that the poor were helped, since there could be many offences not specially expressed which are referred to that generality, where the needy would be burdened if it were lawful to offer only the she goat and the ewe lamb, and not also those little birds and fine flour. Unless perhaps someone says that these expressly named are distinguished from those mentioned generally because here he said ewe lamb, there sheep, so that age makes some difference: provided only it be understood that the poor were helped, so that if they had not those four-footed beasts they might offer the said birds or fine flour for sins of ignorance. But if it troubles anyone why, when he had concluded generally all sins of ignorance, and had distinguished the sacrifices not by the difference of the sins, which he had not made, but by the difference of the persons, he afterwards would also distinguish the sins and command sacrifices according to their variety and diversity, as though all did not belong to that generality: the exception afterwards made is to be understood thus, that whatever remain, these which are specially mentioned being excepted, we understand in that generality; which manner of speech is found not only in the holy Scriptures. Such is that: "Every sin that a man doth is without the body." For he seems to have left out no sin; yet afterwards he excepts: But he that committeth fornication sinneth against his own body; which according to the custom of speech would be said thus: Every sin that a man doth, fornication excepted, is without the body; but he that committeth fornication sinneth against his own body. And here, when he had first spoken generally of all those sins of ignorance which were to be expiated by the sacrifices he mentioned, afterwards he excepted those to which, set out distinctly, he would apply a certain purgation of sacrifices, so that all the rest besides these should belong to that generality.
**“he shall offer for his sin the tenth part of an ephi of flour.”** — by believing perfectly in the holy Trinity. For the ephi contains three measures, and ten is perfect.
**“OF AN EPHI”** — HESYCHIUS. Allegorically. It is a measure of three measures, that is, containing three bushels. Christ therefore is he who offers the sacrifice, and he himself is the sacrifice. Because the ephi, a measure of three bushels, hints at the Trinity; because it is one measure, since in it is one Godhead; but it has three measures, that is, three perfect persons and as many subsistences; so that we do not sin if we call the flesh of the Lord a part, on account of the inseparable union of the incarnate Word; for it is a part of the Trinity, because its glory and power are indivisible. Whence the Apostle: "In him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead corporeally." And John: Whosoever denieth the Son, the same hath not the Father. He that confesseth Jesus hath the Father also. Christ therefore is the ephi, having in himself the fulness of the Trinity: the tenth of it is his flesh, in which is shown the loftiness of his Godhead in respect of his humanity; for which reason it is also called a part; and the Word was incarnate in a whole man, who also fulfilled the law. Ten is perfect, and contains the ten commandments of the law. Whence also the law assigned to the priest, that is, to Christ, the chief tenth of the tithe, as having the firstfruits of our lump. He therefore who after transgression wishes to do penance, let him do it in the hope of Christ, who says: I say not to thee, till seven times, but till seventy times seven times. In which he does not take away the hope of penance from those who sin often; therefore he fills a handful for a memorial of him who offered, that is, mindful of his word by which he says: They shall not perish for ever, and no man shall pluck them out of my hand; the handful, that is, the memorial, that is, the word according to which he promised that they who are under his hand shall not perish.
**“He shall not put”** — He whose penance is stained ought to fear lest perhaps he be not received, as unworthy of mercy and compassion.
**“oil upon it,”** — the gladness of cheerfulness
**“nor put any frankincense thereon,”**
• nor let him put the hope of salvation in prayers
• HE SHALL NOT PUT UPON IT etc. As if to say: this is not perfect penance; therefore it has not oil, that is, the spiritual gladness of cheerfulness, nor frankincense, because neither is he to trust in prayers. But let him who offers deliver the oblation to the priest, that is, commit the hope of salvation to the divine goodness.
**“because it is for sin.”** — BECAUSE IT IS FOR SIN etc. Because he does not know whether the prayer of one who often transgresses is of good odour. Whence: "Who knoweth but he will return, and forgive, and leave a blessing behind him?" He does not allow him therefore to despair, nor yet to presume, lest they be negligent again.
5.12:
**“And he shall deliver it to the priest:”** — Christ
**“who shall take a full handful thereof,”** — by which the written mercy is signified
**“A HANDFUL”** — In the handful is signified the Scripture, by which one writes. And it is written: "I say not to thee, till seven times, but till seventy times seven times." By the handful therefore it is hinted that God is to be entreated to remember his written mercy, that he may give it to us, as he commands it to be given to brethren: for by this the great priest will cleanse him who prays.
**“and shall burn it upon the altar”** — The altar is his body, which took on every sin, even that which seemed not to be purged; therefore he adds: because it is for sin, showing that Christ will take on all sins.
5.13:
**“praying”** — because he is a merciful and faithful priest, who prays for the sins of the people
**“for him and making atonement: but the part that is left he himself”** — alone
**“shall have for a gift.”** — that is, by his grace he will save the offerer
5.14: **“And spoke”** — Here, in most copies, the sixth chapter begins.
5.15:
**“If a soul, transgressing the ceremonies through mistake in those things that are sanctified to the Lord,”** — namely, has usurped what is owed to the holy things, or to the priests, or to the offerings
**“shall sin, he shall offer”** — Let him believe firmly, let him have full trust in the redemption of the blood of Christ: for this is the ram sticking fast by the horns among the briers.
**“for his offence”** — He calls an offence what is in the conscience, and what has been committed in swearing or in doing holy things, because it is equally against God.
**“a ram”** — the Saviour
**“without blemish”**
• who did no sin
• IF A SOUL TRANSGRESSING etc. HESYCHIUS. One must abstain from every sin, but chiefly from that which is committed against holy things: and how horrible it is the offering bears witness. For nowhere from the beginning of the history, except in this place, is a ram commanded to be offered, in which the necessity and usefulness of the sacrifice is shown: no buck goat is offered here, no she goat, no sheep, no pair of turtles or two young pigeons.
• THE CEREMONIES THROUGH etc. ORIGEN. There are many kinds of sanctification. There is the oil with which only the tabernacle is anointed. And the incense, of which it is said: Whosoever shall make such a composition shall perish from his people. The loaves of proposition also only the males eat who are of the stock of Aaron. But mystically he sins in the things that are sanctified who irreverently usurps anything in a holy place, or handles divine things unworthily.
**“out of the flocks, that may be bought for two sicles,”**
• with the love of God and of neighbour, with innocence
• The Seventy: For fifty sicles of silver, by the holy sicle. For no one gains the Lord's sacrifice except through the Holy Ghost, because "no man can say the Lord Jesus but by the Holy Ghost". And fifty signifies the coming of the Holy Ghost, because on the day of Pentecost, that is, the fiftieth, he came to the apostles. The Seventy: By the holy sicle. In the sicle, or the holy one, he signified the power and working of the Holy Ghost. The sicle is of twenty obols; the number twenty is not liable to sin. Whence those who went out of Egypt, when they were twenty years old, did not undergo the penalty of the people's sin. For the spiritual man is clean from every sin.
**“FOR TWO SICLES”** — The two sicles are the two precepts of charity, by which the sinner buys himself confidence of remission. For penance avails nothing without the grace of remission. Whence according to the Seventy the ram is bought for fifty sicles, because through penance and the observance of the twin charity perfect rest is gained, when the remission of sins is given.
5.16:
**“And he shall make good the damage itself which he hath done, and the fifth part”** — it signifies the five senses, of which one is the fifth part, as taste, in which the tongue also is understood: this the penitent ought to offer, that with heart and tongue he may confess and praise God
**“he shall add besides, delivering it to the priest, who shall pray for him, offering the ram, and it shall be forgiven him.”** — AND THE FIFTH PART etc. HESYCHIUS. He who abuses a holy vessel, or food, or ointment is said to sin in holy things; let him both restore the thing itself and deliver the fifth part of it to the priest. We have five senses: if we have sinned through any of them, if with the eye, namely in the temple and in a holy place, we have abused it by adultery, with the tongue in detracting, with the ears in hearing evil, with the smell in smelling evilly, with the touch in touching evilly, the first thing is to abstain wholly from that sin, and offer penance through the ram, that is, to ask Christ to rescue us from the sin committed against him. Then let us offer the fifth part, that is, whatever sense by which the sin was committed, to Christ, that we may no longer exercise that sense in evil, but consecrate it to God. For so he will intercede for our sin.
5.17:
**“The soul”** — simply, not of the people; whoever he be, gentile or Jew, having knowledge of the law or not
**“that sinneth through ignorance, and doth one”** — any
**“of those things which by the law of the Lord are forbidden, and of sin”** — of any
**“being guilty, understandeth”** — afterwards
**“his iniquity,”**
• For thus he dashes the sin back upon himself.
• THE SOUL THAT SINNETH etc. HESYCHIUS. He seems to have forgotten what he had commanded: for for the sins for which he commanded a she goat or a sheep to be offered, he now seems to command a ram to be offered; but he neither forgot the earlier things, nor commanded contrary things. For there by the soul he signified the Gentile; but here him who through ignorance transgresses the commandments of the law.
**“AUGUSTINE”** — AUGUSTINE. It is asked how this offence is distinguished from those which he included generally: for to certain kinds of sins certain sacrifices of expiation seem to be applied. But here he does not express the sin specially, but seems to be dealing in generality, for which he appointed as sacrifice for the priest a calf, as also for the synagogue; for the prince a goat; and for any soul, that is, man, a she goat or a sheep, and only female cattle. Then he excepts certain kinds of sins, and expressed by name what is to be offered for which: as for perjury heard and kept silent, for the touching of a carcass and of an unclean thing, and for false swearing through ignorance, an ewe lamb or a she goat or a pair of turtles or two young pigeons, or the tenth part of an ephi of fine flour. But for him who through forgetfulness usurped any of the holy things, a ram, and the restitution of the same thing, and fifths. But now, no species of sin being expressed, adding generally: Any soul that shall offend, and do against any of the precepts of the Lord the things which ought not to be done (as he said in that generality): One of the precepts of the Lord which shall not be done, and shall not know it, and shall offend, that is, shall sin unwillingly through ignorance, he commands a ram to be offered, not a she goat or a female sheep, as he had appointed in such a generality of sins. What then does this mingling mean? Unless that what he says here: For he hath offended with an offence, an offence before the Lord; by this that he says, before the Lord, he wished the offence to be understood in those things which are done before the Lord, that is, by which the Lord is served in the tabernacle. Whence above: But he sinned in holy things, that is, usurped some of the holy things, which also he commanded to be restored; and by this it is not only so that one can sin in these. For in many other ways one can offend through ignorance in the things that are shown in the service of the Lord: this kind of offences he wished afterwards to mention generally, and therefore here and there he commanded a ram to be offered. And it is often said: before the Lord, and it is understood that sacrifice is shown to the Lord, namely firstfruits, or some things in the sacred services.
5.18:
**“He shall offer of the flocks a ram without blemish”** — HE SHALL OFFER A RAM etc. Allegorically. Above he commanded the penitent to offer a she goat; here he commands a ram to be immolated, because it profits nothing to immolate the roughness of penance unless thou hast studied to have full confidence in the immolation of Christ.
**“to the priest, according to the measure and estimation of the sin:”** — because the scourges of penance are measured according to the quality and quantity of the fault
**“and he shall pray for him,”** — for the man, namely: he put soul for man, as he is wont
**“because he did it ignorantly:”** — according to that: I obtained mercy, because I did it ignorantly.

6.2:
**“The soul that shall sin, and despising the Lord,”** — the precepts of the Lord, while he either neglects them or thinks he does not avenge
**“shall deny to his neighbour the thing delivered to his keeping, which was committed to his trust;”** — ORIGEN. Anything committed to him, or the soul and body received from God, or the image and likeness of God, or the rational sense, or any motion whatever.
**“or shall by force any thing”** — robbery: extortioners shall not possess the kingdom of God.
**“extort, or commit oppression;”** — let us abstain from deceit, let us beware of avarice
6.3:
**“or shall find a thing lost,”** — A THING LOST etc. ORIGEN. The Seventy: perdition. Heretics labour to find perdition in the Scriptures, whereby they may build up error; but perhaps, hearing the words of the Church, they come to their senses, and understand that what they had found is perdition, and give it back, that is, leave the alien error to its author.
**“THE SOUL THAT SHALL SIN”** — HESYCHIUS. The sin that is committed in holy things and in an oath is the same, because it is expiated by the same sacrifice, that is, the ram. And he joined the sin of the oath and that done in holy things, because each pertains to the Lord. For he who swears falsely does wrong not only to his neighbour but to God himself, whom he set up as mediator. Nor is it a small guilt in the sight of God fraudulently to deny a deposit, or to extort anything by force, or to oppress, or, when one has found a thing lost, to forswear it. For many think this is without sin. But if anyone does not return what he has found, it is like robbery.
**“ORIGEN”** — ORIGEN. The soul that shall sin etc. I think that we have received our soul and body as a deposit from God; and, what is a greater deposit, he has committed to thy soul his image and likeness: this must be restored as whole as it is plain it was received from thee. If thou art merciful, as thy Father also is merciful, the image of God is in thee, and thou keepest the deposit whole; and if thou art perfect, as thy Father also is perfect, and the likenesses which are in God by nature are present to thee by imitation, the deposit of the divine image is safe with thee. If on the contrary thou art cruel, impious, violent and the like, casting away the image of God thou hast taken up the image of the devil, and hast denied the good deposit. Whence: O Timothy, keep the good deposit. I add this also, that we have received Christ as a deposit, and the Holy Ghost: we must see therefore that we do not use the holy deposit unholily, and, when sins solicit us to consent to them, swear that we have not received the deposit, which if we had, we could not consent to sin. The rational sense too which is in me is committed to me, that I may use it for the understanding of divine things. Talent, understanding, memory, judgment, reason and all the motions that are within me seem committed to me, that in them I may use them for the things which the divine Law commands. But if the talent, skilful and keen, is turned to evil arts, and abuses the things of God in what he does not will, this is to forswear the deposit and turn benefits into faithlessness. There are robbers good and evil. Good, who take the kingdom of God by force; evil, of whom it is said: The spoil of the poor is in your house. Whence: extortioners shall not possess the kingdom of God. Some also, according to spiritual understanding, seize blameworthily, as others seize the kingdom of heaven praiseworthily. If anyone not yet purged of vices, nor yet separated from filthy acts, wishes to thrust himself secretly into the company of the saints and hear the discourse in which perfect and mystic things are treated, he has not rightly seized the knowledge of the secret and perfect things. For no one putteth new wine into old bottles.
6.5:
**“all that he would have gotten by fraud, in the principal, and the fifth part besides”** — AND THE FIFTH PART etc. Namely the tongue, in which is one of the five senses: this is offered, that he may not sin henceforth, because through it each of the aforesaid was committed.
**“ORIGEN”** — ORIGEN. The Seventy: not the fifth part, but fifths, so that twice five may be rendered in one added. Five is taken for the five senses. And the five senses can be restored in this way: if we have abused them in worldly things and in what we did not according to God, let us restore them to holy acts, and add five others, that is, the senses of the inner man; that, clean of heart, we may see God, and hear what Jesus teaches, and catch the odour, that we may be the good odour of Christ; that we may taste him of whom it is said: "O taste, and see that the Lord is sweet"; that we may handle, according to John, of the word of life. To all these let us add one, that we may refer them all to the one God.
**“to the owner, whom he wronged.”** — for against him he suffered the damage, and against God himself it was done by deceit and perjury
6.6: **“Moreover for his sin he shall offer a ram without blemish out of the flock, and shall give it to the priest, according to the estimation and measure of the offence:”** — as above
6.7: **“and he shall pray for him before the Lord, and he shall have forgiveness for every thing”** — "Every night I will wash my bed."
6.9:
**“Command Aaron and his sons: This is the law of a holocaust:”** — a continual fire
**“It shall be burnt upon the altar all night”**
• in the darkness of the present life
• that is: in the ignorance of this life, we who have been made the holocaust of God, let us kindle fire, that we may live spiritually.
**“until morning:”**
• charity ought to burn in us at all times until the morning of the life to come, when the sun of justice shall rise upon us
• not that it was not kindled in the day: for the holocaust was made twice each day; but he kept silence about the day fire as manifest, and added the night fire.
**“the fire”** — of charity
**“shall be of the same altar.”**
• as if it shall be nourished on the altar
• AND THE LORD SPOKE etc. HESYCHIUS. Here he speaks of the continual sacrifice, which in Exodus the priests are commanded to offer daily. For he says: "This is" the sacrifice "which thou shalt make upon the altar: two lambs of a year old every day continually"; and a little after: "by a perpetual oblation unto your generations". And he adds: Thou shalt make a holocaust of one lamb in the morning, and the other thou shalt make in the evening. By this therefore we understand that it is in the will of those who are of the common people whether they wish to offer a holocaust. Whence that sacrifice, their gift, is named as a voluntary offering: for perfect wisdom is not required of all. But the priest ought to be perfectly wise, who is commanded to offer the perpetual sacrifice, that is, the continual holocaust, morning and evening, that he may begin from perfect wisdom and end in the same, and order his whole life to perfection.
6.10:
**“shall be vested”** — Thus
**“with the tunick”** — of justice
**“The priest”** — anyone perfectly wise, because the priesthood is the pattern of perfection
**“and the linen breeches,”**
• with chastity
• Linen, not woollen: he wills the tunic and the breeches to be linen, not woollen. For a linen garment is supple and soft and clings to the body, but woollen is rough; because justice and chastity are supple and cling closely to the soul. A linen garment also can easily be had; so too the virtues, if one will seek to attain them.
**“and he shall take up”** — clothed with these
**“the ashes”** — the virtues completed in work
**“of that which the devouring fire”** — of the Holy Ghost
**“hath burnt, and putting them”** — that a like sacrifice may be offered: let us too, with the Spirit working with us, set down virtues in turn, let us go up from virtue to virtue, because otherwise we shall not come to the prize; whence the holocaust consumed by fire is put beside the altar.
**“beside the altar,”**
• Christ, who as just judge will render
• AND HE SHALL TAKE UP THE ASHES etc. The ash is the completion of good work. Aaron carries the ashes out of the camp, who after this life present their good works to God the Father through Christ the great high priest. And there they are reduced to dust while he stands before the face of God for us. For the camp is the present life, in which we ever fight against the spirits of wickedness. They are put beside the altar when the completion of good works is laid up in the ark of the heart. For the altar in this place signifies the heart. Whence: For our glory is this, the testimony of our conscience.
6.11:
**“Shall put off his former vestments,”** — the old way of life
**“and being clothed with others,”**
• not content with the preceding good things, we add others
• with justice, truth and the other virtues; whence: "Let thy priests be clothed with justice."
**“without the camp,”** — of the present life
**“shall carry them forth”** — before God
**“and in a very clean place”** — sending them ahead to the judgment to come, which is a place clean from all corruption
**“shall cause them to be consumed to dust.”** — standing before the face of God for us
6.12:
**“the fire”** — he who wishes to offer the working of perfect wisdom as a holocaust, let him not allow the fire of the Holy Ghost to fail through negligence
**“And on the altar”**
• which is the body of Christ
• of the heart
**“shall always burn,”**
• with the fire of the Holy Ghost
• THE FIRE ON THE ALTAR etc. AUGUSTINE. He does not wish the fire to be wholly put out, but, when the holocaust has burned until morning, the remains taken away, to be renewed again, whereby the other things laid on it may burn.
**“and the priest shall feed it,”** — Christ, or any faithful preacher, a member of the true priest
**“putting wood on it”** — the examples of the saints, and the testimonies of Scripture
**“in the morning”**
• the night of blindness being put to flight
• when he was judged
**“every day; and laying on the holocaust,”** — himself
**“shall burn thereupon the fat”** — the fattening of the new life makes peace for us with God, and renders a most sweet odour
**“of the peace offerings.”** — AND THE PRIEST SHALL FEED IT etc. Allegorically. In the morning Christ was judged, in the evening crucified. Fire therefore is put under morning and evening, because the charity of God is nourished in us while we recall Christ judged in the morning and crucified in the evening.
**“GREGORY”** — GREGORY. Tropologically. The altar of God is our heart, on which fire is commanded always to burn, because it is necessary that the flame of charity ascend from it unceasingly. To it the priest puts wood, lest it be put out: namely any preacher of Christ, a member of the supreme priest; and each of the faithful ceases not to gather in his heart the examples of the saints and the testimonies of Scripture; with these we ought to nourish and stir up the fire if perchance it languishes. Wood is put under in the morning when the night of blindness is put out. Or, because the morning is the first part of the day, let each of the faithful, putting earthly thoughts aside, think on this in the beginning. And laying on the holocaust, he shall burn thereupon the fat of the peace offerings. For whoever kindles this fire of charity in himself lays himself upon it as a holocaust, and burns up every vice which lived wickedly in him. For then he considers his inward parts, and slays his reprobate life with the sword of immolation, when he has laid himself upon the altar of his heart and kindled himself with the fire of charity. Of the victim of peace offerings he shall burn the fat of the peace offerings, because the fattening of the new life makes peace between us and God and renders a most sweet odour. And because the same charity remains unquenchable in the hearts of the elect, it is well added: This is the perpetual fire etc. This fire fails not from the altar, because in the future the fervour of charity increases in the minds of the saints. For by eternal contemplation it comes about that the more God is seen, the more he is loved.
**“AND LAYING ON THE HOLOCAUST”** — AND LAYING ON THE HOLOCAUST etc. AUGUSTINE. We must see whether no day was passed over on which a holocaust and the saving fat were not found; or whether it was not laid on except in the morning, on whatever day it was laid on. For if we understand it daily, what if no one offered? But if the priest provided the daily holocausts as from the public store or from his own, upon them were laid the things which the Lord commanded, offered by the people for sins, to be laid upon the holocausts; and it was not necessary for one offering a sacrifice for sin to offer a holocaust also on which it might be laid, except where a pair of turtles or two young pigeons are offered. For there he determines that one be offered for sin and the other for a holocaust, and first for sin, then for a holocaust. It is asked also whether the holocaust which he commanded to be laid on in the morning burned through the whole night until the next morning; or whether, since he says it ought to burn all night, the holocaust is the evening one, and he began from that to speak of the law of the holocaust, so as to begin from the evening holocaust; which is strange if he kept silent and did not admonish that such things were offered in the evening.
6.13:
**“This is the perpetual fire”** — because after this life the fervour of charity burns in the minds of the saints
**“which shall never go out on the altar.”** — of the heart
6.14:
**“This is the law of the sacrifice and libations, which the children”** — alone
**“of Aaron shall offer”**
• lofty in wisdom
• THIS IS THE LAW etc. The lawgiver seems to repeat what he said, renewing the memory by the repetition of the command, and showing the usefulness and necessity of the law. Yet he puts in something new, in which he hints that the command is necessary and inexcusable. As therefore he repeated the sacrifices concerning the holocausts, mingling with them continuance, as is that: The fire on the altar shall always burn and never go out; so in the sacrifice of fine flour, that is, of theology, he adds that it must be eaten only in a holy place and by males.
**“before the Lord,”** — according to the will of God, not disputing superfluously in the divine word
**“AND BEFORE THE ALTAR”** — According to what Christ, who is the true altar, has revealed. In these things therefore let us set our theology which Christ incarnate handed down to us, that we may think of the Father in him and of him in the Father, and that the Spirit is the Son's and proceeds from the Father.
6.15:
**“The priest shall take”** — Christ
**“a handful of the flour”** — because the sum of knowledge is with God
**“that is tempered with oil, and all the frankincense”** — namely with almsgiving and prayer, to which theology is compared; nor do they fall from the truth who speak of heaven
**“that is put upon the flour: and he shall burn it on the altar for a memorial”** — because that knowledge will remain for ever, because, being perfect, it will not be destroyed as ours is
6.16:
**“And the part that is left”** — handed down to us
**“of the flour shall eat”** — by understanding and working
**“Aaron with his sons, without leaven:”**
• of Jewish or gentile doctrine
• AND THE PART THAT IS LEFT etc. That we may not wholly cease from theology, because the sum of knowledge is kept for the future.
**“and he shall eat it”** — he shall work
**“in the holy place of the court of the tabernacle.”** — of heaven, in which God dwells
**“IN THE HOLY PLACE”** — The Church, which is the entrance and vestibule of heaven. In it one must speak of the Godhead. Whence: "In the churches bless ye God." Each one is a household church to himself when he ceases from earthly business: here he can speak to himself of God and exercise theology. Such are they to whom part of the sacrifice is given, namely to meditate and speak of God.
6.17:
**“And therefore it shall not be leavened, because part thereof is offered for the burnt sacrifice of the Lord. It shall be most holy, as that which is offered for trespass and for sin.”** — because they shall possess the contemplation of the holy of holies
**“AS FOR SIN”** — He hints that this sacrifice is like that which is for sin and trespass: for discourse of God is held chiefly for the expiation and cleansing of the soul, when to the oil and frankincense, that is, to almsgiving and prayer, the sacrifice of the word of God, that is, of theology, is joined.
6.18:
**“THE MALES ONLY”** — It is not for all to dispute of God, but for those who have nothing womanish, nothing loose, in thoughts or works. It is lawful and everlasting. For we ought not to presume to dispute of God while through worldly fancies we decline from the dignity of males.
**“EVERY ONE THAT TOUCHETH”** — HESYCHIUS. This cannot stand according to the letter: for if a murderer or a profane man touches it, will he be sanctified? For no one is excepted. But Christ, in whose type these things went before, is immolated: whoever touches his flesh, that is, whoever with faithful heart has set his whole hope of salvation in his passion and resurrection, will at once be sanctified.
**“HESYCHIUS”** — HESYCHIUS. Every one that toucheth etc. Every remembrance of God bestows sanctification. Whence: For it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer. But when he says that he who touches is sanctified, he plainly shows that in disputing of God, that is, in theologizing, it suffices us only to touch. For he who wishes to be warmed, if he puts his hand into the fire, will suffer burning instead of warming.
6.20:
**“This”** — every sacrifice of the priest signifies the sacrifice of Christ
**“is the oblation of Aaron”** — of Christ
**“and his sons'”**
• the faithful
• namely of many priests. But it is offered by one anointed, because the firmness of every priest is the sacrifice of Christ
**“which they must offer to the Lord, in the day of their anointing:”** — that is, of the incarnation, by which he anointed him with the Holy Ghost and with power; whence: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee."
**“THIS IS THE OBLATION”** — THIS IS THE OBLATION etc. AUGUSTINE. Other are the sacrifices which he mentioned in Exodus, by which the priests are sanctified for seven days that they may perform the priesthood. Another is that which he now mentions, which the high priest offers when he is appointed, that is, when he is anointed. Whence he adds: In the day when he shall anoint him, not 'them', though he commands the second priests also to be anointed. This sacrifice is everlasting, namely through the succession of priests; or because what it signifies is everlasting.
**“the tenth part of an ephi”** — The ephi: the humanity of Christ; the ephi indeed, holding three measures, signifies the Trinity; if yet the ephi is the Lord's flesh, that the eminence of the Godhead may be shown, and the inseparability of the Lord's flesh with it, nonetheless the sacrifice is perpetual. For by one oblation he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified: "Whereby he is able also to save for ever."
**“they shall offer of flour”** — because Christ after the incarnation taught to offer the perfection of good works in the faith of the Trinity
**“for a perpetual sacrifice,”** — The Law is an everlasting sacrifice insofar as it is spiritual: for it is not in a place which is overthrown, or in a time by which it is changed, but in the faith of the offerer and the heart of the one sacrificing.
**“half of it in the morning,”** — because he stood before the governor
**“and half of it in the evening:”** — because, the passion accomplished, he lay in the sepulchre
**“FOR A SACRIFICE”** — FOR A SACRIFICE etc. ORIGEN. The law of Moses is the sacrifice of the priest, which is divided into two parts, namely the letter and the spirit. The letter is offered in the morning, namely in the first time of the law, when the light brought forth a new light and a new day; in the evening the spirit is given, namely at the coming of Christ, the spiritual understanding of the law. The oil marks mercy, which ought to abound in priests. In a fryingpan, because he wills the priest to be dry and parched with much continence, in whom there is nothing slack, nothing luxurious.
**“IN THE MORNING”** — The passion of the Lord began when in the court of Caiphas he was struck with blows, and it was drawn out until evening; for darkness interrupting it from the sixth hour to the ninth hour, it is divided into morning and evening.
6.21:
**“which in a fryingpan”** — the cross, which made the Lord's flesh fit for our eating
**“tempered with oil shall be fried.”** — out of mercy he suffered
**“he shall offer”** — standing before the Father and offering his passion for us
**“it hot,”** — with the fire of charity
**“for a most sweet odour to the Lord.”** — because he gave salvation to mankind, than which nothing was sweeter to the creator of nature
6.22:
**“And the priest that rightfully succeedeth his father”** — Christ, who succeeded to the old priesthood, as the Gospel to the law.
**“THE PRIEST THAT HIS FATHER”** — The Seventy: The priest anointed in his stead from among his sons shall do these things. For Christ is in place of Aaron, not in his room, because he transferred the priesthood to himself and took it away from Aaron. From among his sons, because he descended from Jacob through Mary, and from the same tribe.
**“THAT HIS FATHER”** — "One Lord Jesus Christ, by whom are all things." For the Lord of glory was crucified, and the passion is of the incarnate Word, which was in the flesh of Christ, who emptied himself wholly, taking the form of a servant, and obedient to the Father unto the death of the cross.
**“and it shall be wholly burnt on the altar.”** — because the passion of Christ is not to be discussed rashly, but reserved to the spirit of knowledge
**“WHICH IN A FRYINGPAN”** — WHICH IN A FRYINGPAN etc. GREGORY. Morally. No sacrifice is such to God as zeal for souls. Whence: "The zeal of thy house hath eaten me up." Therefore the fine flour tempered with oil is fried in a fryingpan. For the priest who succeeds his father offers it hot for a most sweet odour to the Lord. The fine flour is fried with oil in the fryingpan when the clean mind of the just is burned through the zeal of a holy odour. And it is commanded to be tempered with oil, because in Greek eleos is called mercy, which burns and shines in the sight of God. Let the strictness of holy zeal therefore burn and grow bright with the virtue of mercy. For it loves even what it pursues. Whence it is offered hot for a most sweet odour to the Lord. For if zeal has not love, the fine flour in the fryingpan has lost its heat. The priest who succeeds his father offers it, he namely who shows himself a son of God by his conduct and does not fall away from his nobility. It is wholly burned on the altar, that it may become a holocaust. A holocaust is wholly burnt, and every holocaust is a sacrifice, but not conversely. There are many good things done that are sacrifices but not holocausts. For those who so work the things that are of God that they do not leave the things that are of the world offer a sacrifice, not a holocaust. But those who forsake all things that are of the world, and with their whole mind are kindled with the fire of divine love, become a sacrifice and a holocaust to God. The fine flour in the fryingpan therefore is the mind of the just, which in the affliction of spiritual zeal is fried through solicitude for souls, and is reckoned to God as a holocaust.
6.23:
**“For every sacrifice of the priests”** — the mystery of the incarnation is not to be discussed rashly, but reserved to the spirit of knowledge
**“FOR EVERY SACRIFICE”** — Whatever things he commands to be done in the sacrifice of peace offerings, he commands to be done in this also.
**“shall be consumed with fire,”** — because it is a holocaust
**“neither shall any man eat thereof.”**
• The Seventy: it shall be whole
• that is, it shall not be divided: for the sacrifice of Christ is undivided; for what is eaten is divided by the teeth.
• NEITHER SHALL ANY MAN etc. What is eaten is diminished. He diminishes the sacrifice of Christ who says he died for his own sins, since he did no sin.
**“ORIGEN”** — ORIGEN. Neither shall any man eat. The sacrifice in this place is to be taken as the Word itself and doctrine, of which no one eats, that is, disputes or reworks; but it is a holocaust. For whatever he said, whatever he ordained, endures by an eternal consecration.
6.25:
**“Say to Aaron”** — because to offer sacrifice for sin, that is, penance, belongs to the holy
**“and his sons: This is the law of the victim for sin: in the place where the holocaust is offered,”** — in the Church
**“it shall be immolated”** — because he who offers penance already imitates him who offers his whole self
**“before the Lord,”** — whom what is offered according to him pleases
**“It is holy of holies.”**
• therefore
• otherwise he would not bring into the holy of holies the penitent who was cast out through sin
6.26:
**“The priest that offereth it”** — Christ, who took our sins upon himself, rightly offers our penance
**“shall eat it”**
• it belongs to the priests to be eaten
• because Christ took our penance into himself and converted it
**“in a holy place, in the court of the tabernacle.”** — the Church, in which Christ works the salvation of penitents, which is called his food: "My meat", he says, "is to do the will of the Father who sent me", that is, the salvation of mankind.
**“THE PRIEST THAT OFFERETH SHALL EAT IT”** — THE PRIEST THAT OFFERETH SHALL EAT IT etc. AUGUSTINE. Not what he lays on, for that is consumed by fire, but what remains of it. But he says afterwards: All the things that are for sin, of whose blood something has been brought into the tabernacle of the testimony to make atonement in the holy place, shall not be eaten, but shall be burned with fire. How then do the remains of the sacrifices for sins belong to the priests to be eaten? Wherefore it is to be understood that those are excepted with whose blood the altar of incense is touched. For this he commanded to be done of the calf which the priest offers for his own sin, and of the calf for the sin of the synagogue, that the flesh which remained should be burned outside the camp: this too he now briefly recalls.
**“ORIGEN”** — ORIGEN. Some of the victims are God's alone; some are Aaron's and his sons'; some his and his sons' and his daughters', so that it is lawful for the priest's wife also to eat. Of these some are the priests' and their sons' and daughters', but of which it is lawful for the children of Israel also to eat. And in those of which it is lawful for the children of Israel to eat, the priests and their sons have a share; yet it is not lawful for the children of Israel to eat of every victim of which the priest eats. The first victim therefore is the holocaust. For the first ought to be none but that which is offered to almighty God. The second is that which is eaten by the priests. The third, that of which the children of Israel may eat, namely the clean only. For only the clean are commanded to eat of the sacrifices. Mystically seek these victims within thyself, having within thyself herds of oxen, which are blessed in Abraham, and flocks of sheep and goats, in which the patriarchs were blessed and multiplied. There are within thee also the birds of heaven. Do not wonder: understand that thou art another world, and that within thyself are the sun and moon and stars. Whence it is said to Abraham: Look up to heaven and number the stars, if thou canst, for their multitude. So shall thy seed be as the stars of heaven: namely those who, begotten of his faith, live rationally and keep the divine laws and precepts. The Saviour also says: "You are the light of the world." Doubt not therefore that the sun and moon are within thee; hear something greater, lest thou neglect thy life as cheap. This world has its governor, who dwells in it, almighty God. Whence he says: Do not I fill heaven and earth? Hear what the Almighty says of men: I will dwell in them, and walk among them. He adds something more concerning thy person: I will be a Father to them, and they shall be my sons and daughters. Where the holocaust is slain, which is offered to God alone, there also is the victim for sin; that namely he who has sinned and repents, and offers the victim of a contrite spirit, may understand that he stands in a holy place and is joined to the things that pertain to God. He offers before the Lord, or in the sight of the Lord, who does not go out from the sight of the Lord, as Cain, but stands confidently, nor does he turn from his gaze through the consciousness of sin. Therefore he says this victim is holy of holies. Hear something greater. What is the victim which is offered for sins and is holy of holies, but the Only-begotten of God, my Lord Jesus Christ? He is the victim for sins and the holy of holies. The priest that offereth it shall eat it. This is the priest who eats and consumes the sins of the people, who is a priest for ever. And our God is a consuming fire, namely of human sins. Those he consumes, those he devours, those he purges. Whence elsewhere he says: And I will purge thee with fire to purity. For he took our sins upon himself, and in himself ate them up as fire. The priest that hath offered it shall eat it in a holy place, in the court of the tabernacle. For it follows that, according to him who gave the priesthood to the Church, the priests of the Church should take on the sins of the people and, imitating the master, grant remission of sins. Who ought to be so perfect and so learned in their offices that in a holy place, by not sinning themselves, they may consume the sins of the people. Moses had come into a holy place, to whom it was said: The place whereon thou standest is holy ground. And in the Church the place is made faith, charity, a good conscience. The priest shall eat the flesh of the sacrifice in the court of the tabernacle of the testimony when he can understand what is the reason or what the mysteries in the things that are written of the courts of the tabernacle of the testimony: to which no one draws near, which are open to none but the priests, who by knowledge and mystic understanding can penetrate their secrets. There are other more secret doctrines in the Church, which it is not lawful even for the priests to approach, namely where the ark is laid up and the pot and the tables of the testament, but only for the one high priest, and for him once a year, at fixed times and with mystic purifications. There are others to which the Levites also can come. There are others too which the children of Israel can approach, that is, the laity, yet not foreigners, unless they have already been enrolled in the Church of the Lord. For the Egyptian shall enter into the Church of God in the third generation, that is, in the faith of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost, by which everyone believes who is joined to the Church of God. But it is to be known that, although some of the victims are granted to the priests to eat, yet not all. For some part is offered to God and given to the fires of the altar; because if it is granted us to know some things from the Scriptures, yet some are reserved to God, which surpass our senses; lest they be brought forth by us otherwise than the truth holds, we do better to reserve these to the fire.
6.27:
**“Whatsoever shall touch the flesh thereof shall be sanctified.”**
• the fasting, watchings, haircloth, tears, prayer and almsgiving of penance: of these penance consists; he who touches these is rightly sanctified.
• WHATSOEVER SHALL TOUCH etc. Although the oblation is another's, that is, the penitent's, he shall be sanctified even if he does not repent. Likewise if a little child has been baptized who has not yet sinned of himself, he is cleansed from original sin.
**“If with the blood thereof”** — in baptism: for as the life of the flesh is the blood, so baptism is the force of penance, without which penance does not profit.
**“a garment”** — the flesh, which is the garment of the soul
**“be sprinkled, it shall be washed”** — by that very sprinkling
**“in a holy place.”**
• the Church: the sprinklings of the gentiles are outside and therefore do not wash; or whoever are outside
• IF WITH THE BLOOD etc. That is: if the substance of the flesh has been stained with sins. Whence: The garment mingled with blood shall be burnt, and be fuel for the fire of hell; namely, it shall be washed in a holy place, that is, it shall have hope in baptism, which not only washes away the past but instructs that one may repent of the future.
6.28:
**“And the earthen vessel”** — whence: In a great house there are vessels of wood and of earth, namely sinners
**“wherein it was sodden shall be broken:”**
• whence: Thou shalt break them in pieces like a potter's vessel
• because he received good things wickedly
• by the terror of the Judgment
• AND THE EARTHEN VESSEL etc. The weak one, namely the feeble, who after penance done falls back into sins: this one is to be broken by the terror of the Judgment.
**“but if the vessel be of brass,”** — the strong and solid one, who does not return to sins; and he is scoured, that is, inflamed with the heat of the Holy Ghost
**“it shall be scoured,”** — it shall not be broken
**“and washed with water.”**
• because, seeing another penitent, he is moved to compunction
• the compunction of tears
6.29: **“Every male of the priestly race shall eat of the flesh thereof,”** — EVERY MALE etc. The priest offering and eating the whole sacrifice is Christ, who offers our penance and eats the salvation of sinners. But the flesh of the sacrifice, because it pertains to penance, every male of the priests eats, namely the strong and vigorous, to whom it is said: Do manfully, and let thy heart take courage, and wait thou for the Lord.
6.30:
**“For the victim”** — of the calf, that is, of the Synagogue, or for the sin of the high priest
**“that is slain for sin, the blood of which is carried into the tabernacle of the testimony to make atonement in the sanctuary, shall not be eaten, but shall be burnt with fire.”** — SHALL NOT BE EATEN etc. Because it pertains to Christ, who by his own authority and by the power of his own Godhead grants remission. For his passion, through which remission is procured for us, was not of a mere man, but of God incarnate. Therefore it is not eaten by men, but consumed by fire; because to give remission belongs to God alone, who is signified by fire: for our God is a consuming fire.

7.1:
**“This also is the law”** — namely that which was said for sin
**“A TRESPASS”** — A TRESPASS etc. HESYCHIUS. Sometimes he calls it a sin recognised; sometimes that which is committed against God himself, which is hard to be pardoned. Whence: If one man shall sin against another, the priest will pray for him; but if against God, who shall pray for him? Necessarily therefore a ram is offered in sacrifice, signifying him of whom it is said: "Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who taketh away the sin of the world", who alone can release what is committed against himself. But the ram is not wholly made a holocaust, as the calf offered for the people and for the priest, which likewise signifies Christ. But there the remission of mankind is dispensed generally; therefore of necessity the whole sacrifice of Christ is offered. But here it is made for those for whom sacrifice and remission are procured. Whatever therefore can be saved is received into the sacrifice of Christ: namely peace and holiness, without which no man shall see God. For the offerings of the inward parts are the thoughts, which being set at peace, we have peace with all. And the offering of the kidneys and of the lobe of the liver and of the thighs is holiness.
**“ORIGEN”** — ORIGEN. Some say that a trespass is when we do not do what we ought, but a sin when we do what we ought not; but this is not observed everywhere.
7.2:
**“Therefore where the holocaust is immolated,”** — for the virtue of the just and the worthy penance of sinners please God equally, which restored David and Peter to their former rank
**“the victim also for a trespass shall be slain: the blood thereof shall be poured round about the altar.”** — THE BLOOD THEREOF etc. HESYCHIUS. Whatever things are done in the sacrifice of peace offerings, he commands to be done in this also.
7.3:
**“They shall offer thereof the rump”** — GREGORY. The rump is the end of the body: and he immolates well who brings the sacrifice of good work to its end.
**“and the fat”** — namely, Christ came down to save him who commits grievous sins
7.4:
**“The two little kidneys,”** — Christ wills the inner man of the penitent to be cleansed and to have chastity.
**“and the fat which is by the flanks,”** — The Seventy: the lobe of the liver
**“and the caul of the liver”** — that he may not have his own concupiscence, but offer it wholly
7.6:
**“Every male”** — not soft, not womanish, not weak
**“of the priestly race”** — succeeding by lawful generation, excelling namely in life and knowledge
**“shall eat this flesh in a holy place, because it is most holy.”** — As if this sacrifice differs not in vain from those for sin, because it is for a trespass, namely what is committed against God.
7.7:
**“ORIGEN”** — ORIGEN. As for sin etc. Likewise the fat of the ram which is about the kidneys and which covers the inward parts is commanded to be laid upon the altar, that whatever in thee is gross and covers thy inward parts thou mayest offer to the fires of the altar; that, thy inward parts purged, thou mayest say: "Bless the Lord, O my soul, and let all that is within me bless his holy name." For otherwise they cannot have the spiritual sense or praise God. But if thou hast purged thy inward parts from every vice of lust, thou hast slain the victim for trespass and offered a sacrifice for an odour of sweetness. It shall be the priest's that offereth it and hath made atonement for the trespass. Let the priests learn that a portion is given them with those whom they have brought to penance and made such that God is merciful to them. For the merit of those subject to them will be the reward and glory of such priests. Let the priests understand therefore where the true portion is given; let them give themselves to this, nor entangle themselves in superfluous acts; but let them know that they have a part with God in nothing else but in what they offer for sin, that is, in turning the sinner from the way of sin.
**“the same shall be the law of both these sacrifices: it shall belong to the priest that offereth it.”** — TO THE PRIEST etc. Christ, who was made a propitiation for us. In him therefore every sacrifice is ministered and done, and what follows from penance is referred to him. For he came to save us, saying: I came not to call the just, but sinners.
7.8:
**“The priest”** — Christ, namely, received the outward substance in his members, that is, in the poor.
**“that offereth of holocaust”** — of a man: for he does not add of oxen or sheep or the like; by which he hints at the spiritual holocaust.
**“the victim”** — THE VICTIM OF HOLOCAUST etc. HESYCHIUS. Not of oxen or sheep or the like, but of a man: for where the sacrifices are considered not from those who offer but from what is offered, animals are necessarily mentioned; but here, because he wished to bring in the person of the Lord more openly, he set the priest offering the holocaust of a man. For Christ alone offers the intelligible holocausts, in imitation of whom our victim and way of life is formed, in regard to whom we have patience in sufferings.
**“SHALL HAVE THE SKIN”** — The surrounding of riches, which they ought to offer to the true priest who wish to become a holocaust. Satan named the surrounding of riches a skin, saying: Skin for skin, and all that a man hath he will give for his life. This Job gave as a skin, that he might keep patience, which is called a skin, from which many useful things are made.
7.9:
**“And every sacrifice of flour”** — of theology
**“that is baked in the oven,”** — in which he signifies the Virgin's bearing
**“and whatsoever on the gridiron”**
• in which the resurrection is signified
• AND WHATSOEVER ON THE GRIDIRON etc. Because these are nearest to the theology of the incarnation, they necessarily belong to the offering priest, that is, to Christ born, suffering, and risen.
**“or in the fryingpan”** — which signifies the cross
7.10:
**“Whether they be tempered with oil,”**
• that is, if it be of a rich man, who has wherewith to be merciful
• that is, whether he be eloquent or not. For oil signifies eloquence; whence: "Her throat is smoother than oil."
**“or dry,”** — that is, of a poor man, who has not what to give, or lacks wisdom
**“to all the sons of Aaron in equal measure”** — because God receives alike the good devotion of poor and rich, of simple and wise
**“it shall be divided, one as much as another.”** — WHETHER TEMPERED WITH OIL etc. ORIGEN. The saving sacrifice is commanded to be made in oil. Upon the sacrifice for sin oil is not put, because it is for sin. Therefore it has neither the oil of gladness nor the frankincense of sweetness. For mourning befits sinners, not gladness or the odour of sweetness; because it is said in the person of the sinner: My sores are putrified and corrupted, because of my foolishness. The heart of man is an oven, which, if vices or the devil have kindled it, will not bake but burn up. But if he has kindled it who came to cast fire on the earth, it does not burn up the loaves of the Scriptures to perdition, but bakes them for sacrifice. Perhaps those things are said to be baked in the oven which are well hidden and cannot easily be brought forth to the crowd. For there are many such things which, if they are not baked in the oven, are raw and cannot be eaten, as in the vision of Ezechiel. For it is not to be believed that there is a living creature in the form of a lion, or of a calf or of an eagle, by which God is carried. There are three things in which sacrifices are prepared: in the oven, in the fryingpan, on the gridiron. The oven, according to its form, signifies the deeper things in the divine Scriptures; the fryingpan, those things which, if often turned over, can be understood and explained; the gridiron, those that are open. For there is in the divine Scriptures history, morality, the mystic sense, as body and soul and spirit. This too the basket of perfection signifies, in which three loaves are commanded to be had. For in the divine Scripture foods are set before the hearers in three ways. In the Gospel also it is said: Friend, lend me three loaves. One is baked in the oven, another in the fryingpan, the third on the gridiron.
**“HESYCHIUS”** — HESYCHIUS. He speaks of a sacrifice of fine flour tempered with oil which is put neither in the oven nor in the fryingpan nor on the gridiron: this is theology which is not referred to the humanity of Christ, but concerns the Father or the Holy Ghost, or the Son himself according to the Godhead. Therefore he assigned this to the sons of Aaron, who advance to theology through meditation on the Scriptures, equally, that all may think the same of God. This sacrifice the heretics do not taste, since they savour divers things. There is a sacrifice of fine flour not tempered with oil, when the tenth part of an ephi without oil and frankincense is offered for sin, namely by those who cannot offer a buck goat or a sheep or turtles or doves. This, even if it signifies the sacrifice of the Saviour, he assigned to the sons of Aaron as commanded not for the sake of theology but for the profit of the offerer.
7.11:
**“This”**
• The seventh chapter begins here in most copies.
• He divides the saving sacrifice into two parts: one of praise, the other of vow.
7.12:
**“If for thanksgiving”** — The Seventy: for praise; whence: "Offer to God the sacrifice of praise, and pay thy vows to the most High."
**“IF FOR THANKSGIVING”** — According to the letter: let the oblation be for thanksgiving when one who has been delivered from great tribulation gives thanks, as Moses after the passing of the Red Sea. Mystically also, he who has not committed the greater crimes pays praises to the mercy of God, who has kept him free from horrible crimes.
**“they shall offer”** — that is: let them have the gospel knowledge, which is perfect and solid.
**“loaves”** — the apostolic books
**“without leaven”** — the corruption of foreign doctrine
**“tempered with oil,”** — that whatever he knows may be ascribed to grace and the mercy of God
**“and wafers”** — the prophetic books, which do not proclaim the mercy of God so plainly, mingling threats because of the Jewish obstinacy; properly wafers are not said to be tempered but anointed.
**“AND WAFERS”** — A bread, namely thin and broad, which signifies the knowledge of the Prophets. And as much as the solidity of bread differs from the thinness of the wafer, so much the knowledge of the Old and of the New Testament: the loaves therefore are sprinkled with oil, the wafers anointed, because the light and grace of the New Testament is greater than of the Old.
**“and fine flour fried,”** — theology, namely, but with almsgiving; which he calls fine flour because of its fineness
**“and cakes tempered and mingled with oil.”** — AND FINE FLOUR FRIED etc. Namely the divine wisdom, which is baked with the fire of charity. For Christ, the wisdom of God, gave himself up to death because of his exceeding charity.
7.13:
**“loaves”**
• namely twisted in the manner of a ring. These are the expositors of divine Scripture, the knowledge of whose exposition we ought to have.
• the perfection and firmness of faith; for leaven strengthens bread.
**“of leavened bread also”**
• not unleavened
• With worldly knowledge, wherever it is necessary, as grammar, rhetoric, dialectic.
7.14:
**“Of which one”** — because: "One Lord, one faith, one baptism"; whence the Apostle: Let us all be of one mind in the Lord etc.
**“shall be offered to the Lord for firstfruits, and shall be the priest's”** — of Christ, to whom the one loaf belongs, because our faith is to him and through him and in him.
**“that shall pour out the blood of the victim.”** — IT SHALL BE OFFERED TO THE LORD etc. The Seventy: And he shall offer of all his gifts the praise of God; to the priest that poureth out the blood of the saving offering it shall be his. For "it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy". To Christ, who ministers and perfects the sacrifice, the firstfruits are to be offered.
7.15:
**“And the flesh of it shall be eaten the same day, neither shall any of it remain until the morning.”**
• because the mysteries, namely of the incarnation, are to be searched out and imitated in the present life; nothing ought to remain undiscussed until the morning, that is, the beginning of the other life.
• THE FLESH OF IT etc. ORIGEN. There is a food of the soul of milk, a food of herbs, a food of flesh. Whence: I gave you milk to drink, not meat. And elsewhere: He that is weak, let him eat herbs. And elsewhere: Strong meat is for the perfect. The flesh of the saving sacrifice which is offered for the praise of the Lord is therefore commanded to be the priest's. For solid food and perfect knowledge are assigned to the priests, because they ought to be perfect in all things, in doctrine, in conduct, in virtues; otherwise they shall not eat of the flesh of the sacrifices. The flesh which is assigned to the priests from the sacrifices is the word of God which they teach in the Church of God. They are admonished therefore not to bring forth yesterday's things, but always to find new and spiritual things through the grace of God. If what thou learnedst yesterday from the Jews thou bringest forth today in the Church, thou hast eaten yesterday's flesh of the sacrifice. Above also, in the oblation of the firstfruits: Let them be, he says, new and old.
• UNTIL THE MORNING etc. The world to come, where there will be the true day that succeeds the night of this world: he does not wish our life, through which we must be saved, to be left imperfect; for in the future it will not be lawful to work.
7.16:
**“If by vow, or of his own accord,”** — One offers by vow when he vows that he will serve God and renounce the world. Of his own accord, when he is suddenly converted and, divinely inspired, is pricked to the heart.
**“any man offer a sacrifice,”** — IF BY VOW OR OF HIS OWN ACCORD etc. Every sacrifice of peace offerings, or saving sacrifice, is voluntary. Whence it was placed above among the gifts. But the sacrifice of thanksgiving or praise, though it is a species of it, is not called voluntary because it is rational; because, since we are rational, we owe to the Creator a rational sacrifice as in a manner a chief debt.
**“it shall in like manner be eaten the same day:”**
• the present life, the present world, is called 'today'; whence: "Today if you shall hear his voice."
• in the present the vow is to be paid: for in the future it cannot be paid; whence: Whatsoever thy hand is able to do, do it earnestly.
• THE SAME DAY etc. Because some have described after the end of this life another such, bringing in a certain age of a thousand years in which Jerusalem will be built and its temple, and the holy of holies restored, and sacrifices offered. But if anyone believes this, and in a manner eats it in his mind, hoping that he will eat at that time, which is impossible, his oblation is not received, because it is polluted; he contracts sin also. Whence he says: Whatsoever soul shall defile itself with such meat.
**“and if any of it until the morrow”** — The morrow signifies the time after the vow: for until the end of life we can fulfil our vow.
**“remain, it is lawful to eat it.”** — AND IF ANY OF IT etc. ORIGEN. The two days on which it is lawful to eat the flesh of the sacrifice I think can be understood as the two Testaments, in which it is lawful to seek out every word that pertains to God. For this is the sacrifice, to be sought and discussed. If anything remains which divine Scripture has not decreed, no third scripture ought to be received, which here is named the third day; but what remains let us give to the fire, that is, reserve to God; because in the present life God willed us to know all things which "now we know in part; but when that which is perfect is come, the things that are in part shall be done away". Let us not therefore take to ourselves the knowledge of all things.
7.17: **“THE THIRD DAY”** — The world to come, in which is the general resurrection, which the resurrection of Christ signified. When the morning of the third day has come, then what remains shall be consumed by fire. For whatever saving thing we have left imperfect, or whatever evil we have done, as wood or hay or stubble, shall be consumed by fire: but we shall suffer loss.
7.18:
**“If any man of the flesh of the victim of peace offerings”** — that is: Scripture beyond the two Testaments
**“shall eat on the third day,”** — that is: has hoped for a time of working well after this life, and therefore put it off
**“it shall be of no effect,”** — or: it shall become
7.19:
**“The flesh”** — any virtue, as chastity and justice and the like
**“that hath touched any unclean thing”**
• has done anything evil
• as chastity kept for vainglory
**“shall not be eaten,”**
• no one shall imitate it
• THE FLESH THAT etc. ORIGEN. The holy flesh is understood as the divine words. And it often happens that clean flesh is touched by something unclean: as if someone makes a pure and sincere discourse, worthy of the mystery of the Godhead, of God the Father and his Only-begotten and the Holy Ghost, and of all rational creatures as made by God that they might understand him, and does not consistently assert the resurrection of the flesh. His first discourse is solid food: it is holy flesh. But he who denies the resurrection of the flesh, because it is foreign to the faith, joined to what went before, pollutes his flesh. It is commanded therefore that such flesh be not eaten to which the uncleanness of unbelief is joined. Whence: Let us feast with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. The second kind of uncleanness is that he who eats the flesh be not unclean and his uncleanness be upon him: as if there be one of flourishing and ardent natural talent, he will not at once seem fit to receive the mysteries of the word of God. He must first be separated from profane and unclean works, that he may become capable of learning, if first he has become capable of holiness. The third kind of uncleanness is that by which one who is clean touches something unclean, and is polluted not so much by his own sin as by another's contagion: as if someone is joined in fellowship with an envious or angry man or an adulterer, and does not by his own acts take part in his crimes; yet he sees him hate his brother, lie in wait for another's wife and do the like, and does not depart from his company: this is he who touches an unclean thing, whether a soul, or a bird, or a carcass, and is polluted by another's uncleanness.
**“but shall be burnt with fire:”** — of the judgment to come
**“he that is unclean”** — the hypocrite
7.20:
**“The soul that is defiled”** — the hypocrite's
**“that shall eat”** — by working fraudulently
**“of the flesh”** — that is: of the virtues which are dedicated to God
**“of the sacrifice of peace offerings, which is offered to the Lord, shall perish from his people.”** — that he may be called not a sheep but a ravening wolf
7.21:
**“And that which hath touched”**
• by imitating
• by consenting
**“the uncleanness of man,”** — of a clever one
**“or of beast,”** — OR OF BEAST etc. Unclean beasts are they who are intent on unclean and earthly actions. Whence fornicators are called "stallions".
**“or of any thing”** — as of divination by dreams and the like
**“that can defile,”** — by working unclean things
**“and shall eat of such kind of flesh, shall perish from his people.”** — from the fellowship of those who are to be saved
7.23:
**“Say to the children of Israel: The fat”** — desire, namely, which is wholly to be referred to God
**“of a sheep,”** — of the simple, the innocent
**“and of an ox,”**
• of the strong
• who works the commandments of the law
**“and of a goat”**
• because by the goat are signified the sacrifices which are made for sins
• of penitent sinners
**“you shall not eat.”**
• because the desire of such is harmful, nor does he command it to be offered to God, because the desire of sinners shall perish.
• THE FAT OF A SHEEP etc. That is, the good intention or desire neither of the strong, nor of the innocent, nor of the penitent is to be depraved by a sinister interpretation, as though it were done through hypocrisy; lest anyone wish to destroy the merit of another, and as it were diminish it by eating.
7.24:
**“The fat of a carcass that hath died of itself,”** — because he sins of his own accord, no one prompting
**“and of a beast that by another beast”** — the devil prompting
**“was caught,”** — because he neglected the guarding of himself, not hearing what is said: "Be sober and watch" etc.
**“you shall have for divers uses.”**
• because we ought to transfer them to virtue, as to justice or chastity or almsgiving or any good working, namely by melting them down and refining them
• AUGUSTINE. He said above: All the fat shall be the Lord's; and we had asked whether all the fat of the body, of clean animals at least (for of the unclean there is no question), and what was done with the fat which he forbade to be eaten. But now he has said what was done with the fat of a carcass and of one caught by a wild beast, namely that it be for every work for which such a thing is necessary. Whence the question remained what was done with the fat of those which are clean for eating. But when he says that every soul shall perish from its people which eats the fat of those of which offering is made to the Lord, he seems to forbid only the fat of those of which sacrifice is made. But the Jews do not find what to do with the fat, whence they abstain, and how it is to be thrown away, since it is said: All the fat shall be the Lord's; if they wish to understand here not the fat of the sacrifices only, but also of those of which no sacrifice is made, though clean; because through certain unchastities or other vices they have chosen for themselves the death of sin.
• FOR DIVERS USES etc. Not only by imitating the works of the good, but also by drawing those of the wicked to us as an example. For we read that Herod celebrated his birthday and defiled the banquet with blood: such a desire we have in use that we may beware of it; but on the contrary let us remember with mourning and affliction the day of our birth, on which we were in paradise. The Pharisee in his pride says: I give thee thanks that I am not as the rest of men etc. Let us on the contrary say: O God, have mercy on me, because I am not like thy servants who lead the angelic life on earth.
7.25:
**“If any man eat the fat that should be offered for the burnt sacrifice of the Lord,”** — compelling or persuading him who has offered himself not to strive after heavenly desire, but to incline to his own pleasure
**“he shall perish out of his people.”** — from the congregation of the saints
7.26:
**“the blood”** — the soul: as if to say, do nothing toward the death of thy neighbour
**“Moreover of any creature whatsoever you shall not take for food, whether of birds”** — the just, whose "conversation is in heaven".
**“or of beasts.”**
• sinners, who obey the belly
• IF ANY MAN THE FAT etc. ORIGEN. Allegorically. As if: Let no one scandalize one of these little ones that believe in me etc. Blood is forbidden to be eaten, as if: Boast not against the broken branches, lest thou also be cut off; and they, if they abide not in unbelief, shall be grafted in. And by blood the people of the Jews is rightly understood. For it descended not from the faith nor from the spirit of Abraham, but only from his blood.
7.29:
**“Speak to the children of Israel, saying: He that offereth a victim of peace offerings to the Lord,”** — victims of peace offerings: thanksgivings. These we ought to season with charity, with which every good work is seasoned.
**“let him offer therewith a sacrifice also,”** — that is: charity
**“that is, the libations thereof.”** — HE THAT OFFERETH A VICTIM etc. ORIGEN. Another reading: He that offereth the sacrifice of his saving offering to the Lord, let him bring his gift to the Lord in the sacrifice of his saving offering. His hands shall offer the sacrifice, a victim to the Lord, the fat which is upon the breast and the lobe of the liver; he shall offer them so that the gift be set before the Lord; and the priest shall lay the fat which is upon the breast of the saving offering, and the breast shall be Aaron's and his sons'; and the right shoulder you shall give as a separation to the priest from your saving sacrifices. He of the sons of Aaron who offers the blood of the saving offering and the fat, his shall be the right shoulder for a portion. For the breast of laying on and the shoulder of taking off I have received from the children of Israel from your saving sacrifices, and have given them to Aaron the priest and his sons, an everlasting ordinance from the children of Israel. And the sacrifice which is called saving no one offers to the Lord but he who is whole, and, conscious of his salvation, renders it to the Lord.
**“ORIGEN”** — ORIGEN. The sacrifice which is called saving only one who is whole and conscious of his salvation offers in thanks to the Lord: one sick in mind, one languid in works, cannot offer it. That leper of the Gospel could not offer until he was cured; but when he was cleansed by the Lord, he was commanded to offer the gifts at the altar which Moses commanded for a testimony to them. The clean therefore can offer. But how shall his hands offer the victims to the Lord? Not 'the man', but 'the hands', that is, his works. For these commend the victim to the Lord. For if thy hand is closed to giving, thou art still a leper and canst not offer. Where we have victim, the Greeks have holocarpomata, which signifies 'all the fruit', which the unfruitful cannot offer, who bears not the fruit of justice and mercy and the like. And as to what he says: The fat which is upon the breast, understand the breast as the heart, from which all evil thoughts are to be taken away (for thence they proceed), that the clean heart may see God. He commanded the lobe of the liver also to be offered, in which is wrath or greed. He offers the lobe of the liver who cuts off wrath and fury from himself. The fat which is upon the breast is laid on the altar; the breast to Aaron and his sons; the right shoulder he commanded to be separated. Of what sort is the breast of the priest, full of wisdom and divine understanding; of what sort too the shoulder which the children of Israel offer to him for their salvation. These are forms which are not performed in the Church, but read. For they would not be read unless edification were offered to the hearers from them. If therefore the priest through doctrine, through much solicitude, and through the labour of watchings has converted a sinner and taught him to follow better things; if, I say, he has done such a work, he who is saved by his labour ought to give thanks to God and offer the victim of the saving offering, because he has obtained salvation. And he says the breast of laying on and the shoulder of taking off. For when all grossness has been taken from thy heart, and it has been cleansed from every covering, which is to be given to the fire, it remains that the grace of the Holy Ghost be laid upon it, and then it will become the breast of laying on. And the shoulder will be of separation. If thou knowest how to discern what are the works of light and of darkness, if thou hast separated thy works from darkness, that they may be in the light, thy shoulder is made one of separation. Or when thou hast separated thyself from every brother walking disorderly. Or when they who bear the vessels of the Lord have gone out from the midst of sinners.
7.30:
**“He shall hold”** — he himself, not another for him, because: "The justice of the just shall be upon him."
**“in his hands the fat”**
• desire
• The Seventy: the fat which is upon the breast and the lobe of the liver
**“of the victim, and the breast:”** — thought or faith
**“and when both”**
• because faith in Christ and clean thought are to be consecrated to him
• faith and confidence, which are joined to fortitude, which are signified in the breast: these he ought to offer who desires to be saved, because: Without faith it is impossible to please God.
**“HE SHALL HOLD IN HIS HANDS THE FAT”** — JEROME. TO FABIOLA. Which is upon the breast and the lobe of the liver etc. Of the saving victims the priests offer the fat, and receive the breast and the right shoulder for food. Sense is in the heart, the heart in the breast; pleasure, according to the natural philosophers, is in the liver; whence Pliny: the lobe set against pleasure, and pleasure bursting out through the windows of the eyes. After therefore they have made a fat holocaust, and burned the concupiscence of lust with the fire of the Holy Ghost, they receive the breast and the shoulder as a reward: in the breast, clean thoughts, the knowledge of the law; in the shoulder, good working and the fight against the devil, and the armed hand, that what they have conceived in mind they may prove in work. For Jesus began to do and to teach. The breast also is called addition, or chief, or excellent. "For the lips of the priest shall keep knowledge" etc. This ought to be chief, and by the addition of spiritual grace he forms such a man as can resist the gainsayers and have nothing of left-handed work in himself. Let the shoulder be right and separated, that the works of the priest may be separated from all by comparison of virtues. The other three, besides the firstfruits of the victims, which are given to the priest from the private and the public shambles, where not religion but the force of necessity is: the shoulder, of which we have already spoken, the jaw and the belly. The jaw signifies the eloquent and learned man, that what he conceives in the breast he may set forth with the mouth. The belly, the receptacle of foods, pierced through with the priestly dagger in the Madianite harlot, condemns all the labours and momentary allurements of gluttony by the end of dung, showing to minds consecrated to God that all we devour is cast out into the privy. Whence: Meat for the belly, and the belly for the meats: but God shall destroy both it and them. The dust of the calf which the children of Israel worshipped he receives as drink in contempt of superstition, that he may learn to despise what he sees himself cast into the privy.
**“he hath offered and consecrated to the Lord, he shall deliver them to the priest,”** — The Seventy: He that offereth a saving sacrifice to the Lord shall offer his gift to the Lord of his saving sacrifice.
