Which, expounding, he adds: He shall hold in his hands the fat of the victim; or according to the Seventy: His hands shall offer of it to the Lord. For he himself must work the things that pertain to his salvation, because: The justice of the just shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him.
7.31:
**“who shall burn the fat upon the altar,”** — he wills all our desire to become a holocaust
**“THE BREAST SHALL BE AARON'S”** — ISIDORE. The breast is given to the priest, that he may have clean thought and the knowledge of doctrine; the right shoulder, that he may have good works, and go forth with armed hand to the fight against the devil, and accomplish by the example of works what he has conceived in heart. There is given also from the private offering the jaw, that he may be strong in eloquence; and the belly is given, that he may quench luxury and despise gluttony.
**“and his sons'.”** — who are lofty in life
7.32:
**“The right shoulder also”**
• let him who desires to be saved offer faith and working
• as if Christ, who offered his blood and life for us, will receive our good working
**“OF THE PRIEST”** — AUGUSTINE. Of Christ, figured in the priest. Whence the priest alone can complete the sacrifice. For to begin is our good; to complete and bring to its end is of divine grace. It is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy, to direct actions. Whence also it is named the arm of God. Whence rightly he received the shoulder, or according to the Seventy, the arm.
7.33: **“He among the sons of Aaron that offereth the blood and the fat, he shall have the right shoulder also for his portion.”** — HE THAT OFFERETH THE BLOOD etc. It is Christ who offers the true blood and fat of the peace offerings, namely the souls and desires of the saved; who is of the sons of Aaron, namely the singular priest and chief in all things, to whom falls the right shoulder for his portion, that is, every good action and perfection.
7.34:
**“For the breast”** — This is right faith, or holy knowledge, which lifts us from earthly things to heavenly.
**“that is elevated”** — because, namely, the knowledge of the priest ought to excel
**“and the shoulder that is separated”**
• This is the good working which separates the just from the reprobate.
• because the work of the priest ought to be separate and singular
**“I have taken of the children of Israel, from off their victims of peace offerings, and have given them to Aaron the priest and to his sons, by a law for ever.”** — because its signification endures for ever
7.35:
**“This”** — the things said above
**“is the anointing of Aaron and his sons,”** — namely of those who through the things that have been said advance to the dignity of the priesthood
7.36:
**“and the things that the Lord commanded to be given them by the children of Israel, by a perpetual observance”** — unshaken
**“in their generations.”**
• THIS IS THE ANOINTING etc. HESYCHIUS. These things seem therefore to pertain to the anointing of the priests, but the lawgiver does not intend this at present. For what fellowship have the aforesaid sacrifices with the anointing of the priests? But he wished only to show their dignity, and what progress they afford to those who keep them. For what he says: This is the anointing of Aaron and his sons in the ceremonies of the Lord, goes back to what was above; that thou mayest know that if anyone keeps them, he will come to that dignity of the priest, and not otherwise. For this is the anointing in the ceremonies of the Lord, as though it is acquired from the aforesaid sacrifices. Whence he adds: In the day when Moses offered them, that they might do the office of priesthood, and the things which he commanded to be given them by the children of Israel. In these therefore he gave us the anointing. In these God called us on the day when he offered them, namely on which day he anointed them that they might do the office of priesthood, through the anointing namely which has now been spoken of. For those who live more holily and loftily are more excellent among the people. Whence he fittingly adds: By a perpetual observance in your generations, that thou mightest know that with God this observance is unshaken. No one excels in dignity or wisdom or lofty things, but he who has done the things he commanded above. For so one becomes a priest according to the knowledge of Christ the true priest, who showed a spotless and perfect life. And what he understood by the aforesaid anointing he shows in what follows: "This is the law of holocaust" etc.
• The anointing of Christ is in part common to his own. For they too are partakers; whence we too are called Christians by participation in Christ. But he excels by inestimable dignity. He himself is anointed substantially, but we by his working and grace: his sons therefore are anointed with Aaron, but not such things in their anointing as are done in the anointing of Aaron, as is made manifest in what follows; and this is understood of Christ. For the lawgiver, knowing that these mysteries pertain to the Church, commanded the whole assembly or Synagogue to be called together, which the Greeks call Ecclesia. For the Synagogue cannot have this law unless it come together to the Church, in which the truth of these figures is kept.
**“ORIGEN”** — ORIGEN. When the lawgiver had set forth: This is the anointing of Aaron and of his sons etc., he did not add what it was, nor explain how he anointed; but this indeed he does in what follows. But now, after he said: This is the anointing of Aaron, he adds nothing of the anointing, that he might show that these things which he had said above, namely the breast of laying on and the shoulder of separation, are the very anointing of Aaron and his sons; lest we should think those things said of flesh, that he might teach that they too were set under the sacrament of anointing. Afterwards he repeats what he had set out above, saying: "This is the law of holocaust" etc. This is what was set out above, and it seems to be a recapitulation of the sacraments which were narrated above, as also that, namely: This is the anointing, is a foretaste of what follows: for in passing he touches on other things both to be said and already said; to be said, there: This is the anointing; said, there: "This is the law."
7.37:
**“This”** — of perfect wisdom
**“is the law of holocaust, and of the sacrifice”** — of middling justice
7.38: **“which the Lord appointed to Moses in mount Sinai, when he commanded the children of Israel that they should offer their oblations to the Lord in the desert of Sinai.”** — THIS IS THE LAW etc. HESYCHIUS. Thou seest the differing ways of life which join to God: namely the honour, perfect in wisdom, which is signified by the holocaust; or the middling justice, which works the things that are for salvation. For the law understood that the sacrifices of peace offerings, whether through holocaust or through oblation, are rightly useful for the priestly dignity. Whence on the day on which he commanded the law of anointing, he added the things that concern the sacrifices, and at the same time briefly recalled them all. On mount Sinai: which is interpreted 'bush' or 'temptation'. And temptation is like a bush: for it is a rough shrub and hard to grasp; so the crown of a good life is scarcely had in temptations and tribulations. Whence: Blessed is the man that endureth temptation; for when he hath been proved, he shall receive the crown of life.

8.2:
**“TWO RAMS”** — The passion of Christ is signified, who is the leader of the people. And well are two rams immolated, because Christ twice committed to us the mysteries of his passion: first when he ate the mystic lamb at the supper; secondly when he established the same mysteries in the consecration of the bread and wine.
**“a basket”** — a vessel made of interwoven wicker, and it signifies Scripture, which is made up of a manifold texture of sentences.
**“with unleavened bread”** — divine wisdom, "in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth"
8.3:
**“And thou shalt gather together all the congregation to the door of the tabernacle.”** — This was done when, at the preaching of the apostles, five thousand believed on one day after the resurrection, two thousand on another.
**“AND THOU SHALT GATHER TOGETHER”** — Moses called together the whole synagogue; though the Lord had chosen and commanded, yet the synagogue is called together. For in ordaining a priest the presence of the people is required, that all may know and be certain that he who is more excellent than all the people, more learned, holier, more eminent in virtue, is chosen for the priesthood. He washed him therefore and clothed him. With what clothing? With a tunic, and he girded him with a girdle. And again: He clothed him with a tunic reaching to the ankles, or, as we read elsewhere, an inner one. And I see the high priest clothed with two tunics. But Jesus forbids the apostles to be clothed with two tunics, though Moses and Jesus, that is, the law and the Gospel, ought to agree. Others say that Jesus' command not to have two tunics is not contrary to the law, but more perfect than the law: as when the law forbids murder, but Jesus cuts off anger; and when the law forbids adultery, but Jesus cuts off concupiscence. I do not enter into the narrowness of this understanding; I close up the pontifical sacraments: something more seems to me to be shown from this form. That high priest whom Moses then ordained knew that circumcision was spiritual; yet he kept that of the flesh also, because he could not be uncircumcised; he had therefore two tunics, one of the carnal mystery, the other of spiritual understanding. For he could not be the high priest of those who then were unless he offered carnal works or sacrifices, though he knew they ought to be spiritual. Fittingly therefore he had two tunics. But the apostles, who were to say: If you be circumcised, Christ shall profit you nothing, and were wholly to reject the literal observance, are rightly forbidden to have two tunics; one suffices them, and that the inner one; but the tunic of the law which is outside he did not will, because Jesus permits them to have one, and that the inner.
8.5: **“He said: This is the word”** — the gospel word; whence Peter: This is the word which was preached to you, namely the gospel mysteries
8.6:
**“And immediately he offered Aaron”** — Christ, who is offered to the Father; whence Daniel: He was offered in his sight, who is offered with us and for us
**“and his sons:”** — who imitate him; whence: "Be ye followers of me, as I also am of Christ."
**“and when he had washed them,”**
• because this offering is celebrated through Christ: for Christ was baptized that the water of baptism might be sanctified.
• AND WHEN HE HAD WASHED THEM etc. JEROME. Even then the sacraments of baptism signified the cleansing of the world and the holiness of all things. They do not receive the vestments unless washed, nor are they adorned for sacred things unless they are born again new men in Christ. For new wine is put into new bottles. Moses washes, that is, the law. Whence: "They have Moses and the prophets: let them hear them." From Adam to Moses all sinned. We are washed by the precepts of God, and, made ready for the coming of Christ, we lay aside the garments of skins, that we may put on the linen garment, having nothing of death in it, but wholly white; that, rising from baptism, we may gird our loins in truth, and all the foulness of our former sins may be covered. Whence: "Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered." After the breeches and the linen tunic we are clothed with the violet garment, ascending from earth to the heights. This is the undertunic, according to the Seventy, which signifies that the reason of lofty things is open only to the greater and perfect. This the Prophets had, Moses and Aaron and all to whom it is said: Get thee up upon a high mountain, thou that bringest good tidings to Sion. The first washing of sins, the grace of baptism, the more secret doctrine, do not suffice unless we have works, that is, the ephod, which is joined to the rational, that it be not loose nor slack. For reason needs works and works need reason, that what we conceive in mind we may accomplish in work.
**“ORIGEN”** — ORIGEN. Let Moses wash thee, that is, the law, which washes thee and rinses away thy filth. The law consecrates priests. He cannot be a priest whom the law has not appointed. If thou hast been washed by Moses, thou canst come to the vestments which Moses brings forth. But for the priestly insignia not only vestments are needed, but girdles also. Adam and his wife were clothed with garments of skins: with such it was fitting that the sinner be clothed, which were tokens of the mortality which he had contracted by sinning, and of the frailty which came from the corruption of the flesh. But if thou hast been cleansed of these by the law of the Lord, Moses will clothe thee with the garment of incorruption, that thy shame may nowhere appear, and this mortal may be swallowed up by life. Let us see in what order the high priest is appointed.
8.7:
**“He vested the high priest”**
• the preceding things are common to Aaron and his sons, that is, to Christ and to us: but these befit God alone and the true priest: he vested the high priest etc.
• The third is the girdle, most like the skin of a serpent which it casts off in summer, so woven in the round like a long purse, under a weft of scarlet, purple and violet and fine linen, for beauty and strength, so distinguished with many-coloured work that you would think the divers flowers and gems not woven but added by the craftsman's hand. With this belt the linen tunic is bound between the navel and the breast; it has a breadth of four fingers and, coming down in great part to the legs, when there is need of quickness for the sacrifices it is thrown back over the left shoulder.
• The sixth in Hebrew is ephod, that is, the superhumeral: for wherever in Exodus or Leviticus the superhumeral is read, in the Hebrew it is ephod. Samuel, however, a Levite still of tender age, and David before the ark, wore an ephod. But one is woven of violet, fine linen, scarlet, purple and gold; another, in the likeness of the priests, simple and of linen. Plates of gold, that is, leaves, are beaten out to a wonderful thinness, from which threads are cut and twisted, with the weft of three colours, violet, scarlet, purple, and the warp of fine linen; whence is made a little mantle of embroidered beauty and wonderful brightness, in the manner of the caracallae, but without hoods. Over the breast nothing is woven; a place is left for the rational. On each shoulder single stones are set, bound in gold, which in Hebrew are called soom, by Aquila and Symmachus and Theodotion onyx stones, by the Seventy emeralds. Josephus calls them sardius stones, agreeing with the Hebrew, so as to show either the colour of the stones or their country. On each are six names of the Patriarchs, by whom the Israelite people is divided: on the right shoulder the elder sons of Jacob, on the left the younger; that the high priest, going into the Holy of Holies, may carry on his shoulders the people for whom he is to pray.
• The seventh is small, but the most holy of all: in Hebrew it is called hosen, in Greek logion, in Latin rationale. It is a short cloth woven of gold and the four colours of which the superhumeral also is made, having the size of a palm in the square, doubled, lest it tear. In it are set twelve stones of wonderful size and price in four rows, three stones in each line. In the first, sardius, topaz, emerald; in the second, carbuncle, sapphire, jasper; in the third, ligure, which perhaps is also hyacinth, agate and amethyst; in the fourth, chrysolite, onyx, beryl. On each are written the names of the twelve tribes according to their ages. Of these stones the heavenly Jerusalem is built in the Apocalypse: by their names or appearance the order or diversity of the virtues is indicated. At the four corners of the rational are four rings of gold, having opposite them on the superhumeral four others, so that ring comes against ring, and they are joined to each other with violet bands. And lest the size and weight of the stones break the threads, they are bound and enclosed in gold. Chains also are made of gold, which for beauty are covered with little golden pipes, and have on the rational above two larger rings, which are fastened with golden hooks of the superhumeral, and below two others. For behind, on the superhumeral, against the breast and stomach, on each side were rings of gold, which were joined with the golden rings of the rational, so that the rational was joined to the superhumeral and to beholders was thought one woven work.
• The eighth is the plate of gold, on which is written the name of the Lord in four Hebrew letters, Yod, He, Vau, He, which among them is called ineffable. This is added in the high priest over the linen cap common to all the priests, that it may be bound on the forehead with a violet band, and the name of God may crown and protect all the beauty of the high priest.
• And the pomegranates and bells set in the lower parts show lightnings and thunders, or earth and water and all the elements sounding together with one another, and so interwoven with each other that all are in each.
**“HE VESTED”** — JEROME. TO FABIOLA. Let us learn first the common vestments of the priests and of the high priests. Linen breeches, by which the privy parts are hidden down to the knees, whose upper part is tightly bound below the navel, lest, while unencumbered they slay victims or carry burdens, the thighs be by chance uncovered and what is covered be laid open. Hence also they are forbidden to go up the steps of the altar, lest the people below see the privy parts of those going up. These, according to Josephus, were woven of twisted fine linen for strength, and cut and sewn, because such a work cannot be made on the loom.
**“JEROME”**
• JEROME. The second is the poderis of linen, that is, a garment to the ankles of double fine cloth, which Josephus calls of byssus: this clings to the body, so close and with tight sleeves that there is no wrinkle in the garment, and it comes down to the legs. Soldiers are wont to have such linen shirts, which they call camisiae, fitted and bound to the limbs, that they may be unencumbered for everything. This tunic the priests use, having the beauty of the clothed and the quickness of the naked; and it is called the linen one.
• JEROME. The Hebrews refer the four colours to the four elements, of which all things subsist. Fine linen they assign to the earth, because it is produced from the earth; purple to the sea, because it is dyed with its shellfish; violet to the air, for the likeness of colour; scarlet, which in Hebrew is thola, that is, the little worm, to fire and the ether. For they recall that this was done so that the high priest might pray to the Creator not only for Israel but for the whole world, which consists of earth and water and air and fire: for these are the elements of all things. Whence the first vestment is of linen, signifying earth; the second violet, showing the air, which is raised little by little from earthly things to the heights; and the violet vestment reaching from the head to the ankles indicates the air poured from the heavens to the earth. That the said colours are woven with gold they wish to figure this: that the vital heat and the providence of the divine mind penetrate all things.
• JEROME. In the violet tunic pomegranates and bells, because the knowledge of the high priest ought to be so great that his steps and movement and all things may be sounding, and the truth which he has conceived in mind he may sound forth in his bearing; whatever he does, whatever he speaks, may be doctrine. Without bells, divers colours, gems and the flowers of the virtues he neither enters the Church nor is high priest.
• JEROME. THE SUPERHUMERAL. The superhumeral and the two emerald or onyx stones which cover the shoulders above they interpret as the two hemispheres, of which one is above the earth and the other below the earth; or the sun and moon which shine above.
• The two stones on the superhumeral are Christ and the Church, containing the names of the twelve apostles who were sent to preach. Or the letter and the spirit, in which are all the mysteries of the law: on the right the spirit, on the left the letter. Through letters we come to words, through words to sense. A beautiful order, signifying sacraments by the very habit: in the shoulders works, in the breast reason. Whence also the priests eat the breast.
**“THE SAME”** — THE SAME. The fourth is a round cap, which the Greeks and our people call tiara, some galerus. It has no point at the top, nor does it cover the whole head down to the hair, but leaves a third part bare from the forehead; it is bound with a band lest it slip; it is of byssus, and so skilfully covered with a linen cloth that there are no traces of the needle outside. These four both the priests and the high priests use. The remaining four belong properly to the high priests. The first of which, and here the fifth, is the tunic to the ankles, wholly violet, having sleeves of the same colour sewn on; the opening by which it is put on, which is commonly called the capitium, has very firm borders lest it tear. And in the lower part are seventy-two bells and as many pomegranates, woven of the same colours as the girdle; between two bells one pomegranate, and between two pomegranates one bell; that when the high priest goes into the Holy of Holies he may be all sounding: if he did not do this, he would die at once.
**“ORIGEN”** — ORIGEN. In Exodus, where the priestly vestments are commanded, I find there are eight kinds which are prepared for the high priest; but here only seven: for the eighth is left out, which is the girdle-cloth, or, as we read elsewhere, the linen breeches. But perhaps because in this kind of garment, by which the thighs are covered or the loins bound, there is a token of chastity, those parts were not always bound in those priests. For sometimes indulgence is given for the posterity of the race. But in the priests of the Church I see another sacrament. For they can beget sons in the Church. Whence: "My little children, of whom I am in labour again" etc. And elsewhere: For in Christ Jesus, by the gospel, I have begotten you. In such generations they sometimes use the breeches and abstain, when they see that they cannot have fruit in their hearers, in whom the seed would perish and make no offspring. When therefore they see them incapable, or feigned and hypocrites, they put on the girdle-cloth, they use the breeches, lest that which is holy be given to dogs, and pearls be cast before swine.
**“with the strait linen garment,”** — with the garment of immortality
**“girding him with the girdle,”** — that the loins may be girded in truth, and the foulness of sins covered
**“and putting on him the violet tunick,”** — This is proper to the high priest, and signifies that the reason of lofty things is open only to the perfect.
**“and over it”** — The Seventy: He put upon him the hyponis (in most copies: hyphonis; elsewhere: hypodytes), and girded him according to the fashion of the hyponis, and bound him to it.
**“AND PUTTING ON HIM THE TUNICK”** — The Seventy: He put on the tunic and girded the girdle and clothed him with the hypodytes. He follows out the incarnation of Christ. For he took on the whole man, namely body and soul: the tunic he called earthly, because it is of the earth; the hypodytes heavenly, because the hypodytes is the poderis, and violet, which is the heavenly colour: for he took on both and saved both.
**“the ephod”**
• works
• that is, the "sweet yoke" of Christ, that is, the gospel life which, showing it, he himself carried upon his shoulders, of which he says: "Take up my yoke upon you, and learn" etc.
**“HE PUT THE EPHOD”** — Moses puts upon the high priest the superhumeral, which is the adornment of the shoulders by the drawing round of the garment: and the shoulders are tokens of labour and work. He wills therefore the high priest to be adorned in works. For knowledge alone does not suffice, but he that shall do and teach shall be called great.
**“AND BINDING IT WITH THE GIRDLE”** — AND BINDING IT WITH THE GIRDLE etc. ORIGEN. He girded him according to the making of the superhumeral. He had already said above: He girded him with a girdle over the tunic. What is that double girdle? Let him be bound in word, unencumbered for all things in work; let him have nothing slack, nothing loose. Let him be girded with the virtues of the mind, bound from bodily vices; let him fear no lapse of the soul, none of the body: let him always use both girdles, that he may be holy in body and spirit. He is girded according to the making of the superhumeral, because he uses the girdle of virtue according to his works.
8.8:
**“And binding it”** — that, cleaving together, they may help each other: for reason needs works and works need reason.
**“with the girdle,”**
• the girdle by which the breast of the priest is bound, and the linen tunic, that is, earth and ocean, it is thought
• with the mystery of the incarnation, by which we are girded and strengthened.
**“he fitted it to the rational, on which was Doctrine and Truth.”**
• that, cleaving together, they may help each other: for reason needs works and works need reason.
• that he may teach what he has conceived in mind
• HE FITTED THE RATIONAL etc. JEROME. The rational, set in the middle, indicates the earth, which, like a point, though it has all things in itself, is walled about by all the elements.
• ORIGEN. He put upon him the logion, which is the rational, and upon the logion manifestation and truth. It does not suffice the high priest to have wisdom and to know the reason of all things unless he can manifest to the people what he knows. Therefore manifestation is laid upon the rational, that he may be able to answer everyone that asks him a reason of the faith and truth. Truth also is laid on, that he may not build up what he has thought out by his own wit, but what the truth holds. Another adornment is to be added, whence it is necessary that he receive a crown: he receives therefore the cidaris, which is the covering or adornment of the head. After this the mitre is put on before the face, that is, at the forehead of the high priest, the sanctified plate of gold on which the name of God is graven. But this adornment of the head, in which the name of God is set, is put on after those things by which the lower members of the body had been adorned. For above all things that can be perceived or understood of the world or of creatures, the knowledge of God excels as of the author of all things. And because he is the head of all, therefore this adornment is put upon the head above all: for nothing is added to the head of the high priest after these.
**“JEROME”** — JEROME. The rational is twofold, open and hidden, simple and mystic; it has twelve stones and four rows, that is, four virtues: prudence, fortitude, temperance, justice, which cling to each other; and while they are mingled together they make twelve. Or the four Gospels, full of eyes and enlightening the world: in one, four, and in four, each. Whence doctrine and truth are in the breast of the priest. When one is wrapped in a manifold garment, it follows that he should bring forth in speech the truth which he holds in heart. Therefore the rational is also truth, that is, it is knowledge, that he may know what is to be taught; and manifestation and doctrine, that he may manifest what he has conceived in mind. First the superhumeral, after it the rational. Whence: "By thy commandments I have had understanding." First we do, then we teach, lest doctrine be destroyed by empty works. Sow for yourselves in justice, reap the fruit of life, enlighten yourselves with knowledge. First one must sow, and afterwards reap the fruit, that we may claim knowledge for ourselves. Nor does this suffice unless reason cleave to works and works to reason, and, these going before, doctrine and truth follow.
**“THE SAME”** — THE SAME. The twelve stones are either the zodiac circle or the twelve months, and in each row the several seasons, and three months each. And beautifully what is in the middle is called the rational. For all things are full of reason, and earthly things cling to heavenly. Rather the reason of earthly things and of seasons, of heat and cold, and the twofold temperateness between both, comes down from the course and reason of heaven. Whence the rational is bound with the ephod. In the rational is manifestation and doctrine, or truth, because in the reason of God there is never a lie, and truth itself is shown by many signs and proofs. Whence it came about that we should know the reason of the sun and moon, of the year, the months and seasons and hours, of storms, fair weather and winds, and of all things, receiving the wisdom implanted by God, he himself, the dweller and teacher, showing us the knowledge of his dwelling and his workmanship.
8.9:
**“The mitre”**
• according to the Seventy: the mitre
• Above all, the cidaris and the violet band show heaven.
**“also he put upon his head:”** — the head of Christ is God
**“and upon it over the forehead he put the plate of gold, consecrated”**
• the dignity of the incarnate Word, who was made our priest
• The plate of gold on the forehead of the high priest and the name inscribed signify that all things that are upon the earth are governed by the will of God. For it was just that the high priest of God, bearing the type of all creatures in his vestments, should show that all things need the mercy of God; and that when he sacrificed, the whole condition of things should be expiated, where he prayed by voice and habit not for children, parents and kin, but for every creature.
**“HE PUT THE PLATE”** — HE PUT THE PLATE etc. JEROME. The learning of all things profits nothing unless it be crowned by the knowledge of God, which is ever with him and the Father. Whence he put the plate upon the cidaris.
**“JEROME”** — JEROME. All things are imperfect unless a driver be sought for the chariot, and the Creator, standing over the creatures, himself rule what he made. What was once shown in the plate is now shown in the sign of the cross: the blood of the Gospel is more precious than the gold of the law. Then, according to Ezechiel, the sign thau was fixed on the forehead of those that sigh; now, bearing the cross, we say: "The light of thy countenance, O Lord, is signed upon us" etc.
8.10: **“He took also the oil of unction, with which he anointed the tabernacle with all the furniture thereof.”** — HE TOOK ALSO THE OIL OF UNCTION etc. He is the Son of God who anoints and who is anointed: anointing by the word of the Godhead, according to which he has all things in common with the Father and the Holy Ghost. He is anointed by the Father, according to that: "God, thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness" etc. The Holy Ghost anointed him, according to Isaias: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me etc. And what the Father and the Holy Ghost do, these the Son also does. He anoints therefore according to the Godhead, he is anointed according to the humanity. Whence Daniel too sees him offered, but does not see one offering, because he offers himself. Moses therefore anointed and offers, bearing the figure of Christ.
8.11:
**“SANCTIFYING”** — SANCTIFYING etc. ORIGEN. It signifies the heavenly creation enriched by our sanctification, that is, through the Lord's flesh taken from us. Whence: That the manifold wisdom of God may be made known to the principalities and powers through the church etc.
**“had sprinkled the altar seven times, he anointed”** — because the whole anointing is the fulness of the Spirit, who is designated in seven operations
**“it, and all the vessels”** — the apostles and their imitators, as it is said of Paul: This man is to me a vessel of election.
**“thereof, and the laver”** — or: laver
**“with the foot thereof,”** — Penance, which is set under baptism, because its grace, which we often weaken, we raise and prop up by penance.
8.12: **“And he poured it upon Aaron's head, and he anointed and consecrated him.”** — POURING IT UPON THE HEAD etc. The head of Christ is the Godhead. For as the head is not divided from the feet, so neither the Godhead of Christ from his humanity after the anointing. Whence he says: "God, thy God, hath anointed thee" etc. For so God is anointed and sanctified.
8.13:
**“His sons also, being offered, he consecrated, and vested them with linen tunicks, and girded them with girdles, and put mitres on them, as the Lord had commanded.”** — HIS SONS ALSO etc. ORIGEN. Mark the difference of the lesser priests from the greater. To these are not given the double vestments, nor the superhumeral, nor the rational, nor the adornment of the head, but only the cidaris and the girdle which binds only the tunic. They receive therefore the grace of the priesthood and perform the office, but not as he who is adorned with the superhumeral and the rational, who shines with manifestation and truth, who is graced with the ornament of the golden plate. I think therefore that it is one thing in priests to perform the office, another to be furnished and adorned in conduct. For anyone can perform the solemn ministry to the people, but few are they who, adorned in conduct, doctrine and wisdom, are fit to manifest the truth, and who bring forth the knowledge of the faith not without the ornament of understanding and the brightness of assertions, which the adornment of the golden plate set on the head designates. One therefore is the name of the priesthood, but not one the dignity according to the merit of life or the virtues of the soul. In these things therefore which the divine law says, let each priest look at himself as in a mirror; if he sees himself adorned in all the things said above, and such and so great in knowledge and in acts or in doctrine, let him know that he holds the high priesthood not only in name but in merit. Otherwise let him know that a lower rank is set for him, even if he has received the name of the first.
**“AND HE VESTED THEM WITH TUNICKS”** — Like tunics and girdles, or belts, and cidares or mitres are put upon the sons of Aaron: for they put on him, they are girded with him, they bear him on the head. For the loins are girded in truth, which is Christ, and they put on the breastplate of justice; and Christ is justice, as also the helmet of salvation, for he is the salvation of God.
8.14:
**“He offered also the calf”** — Christ
**“for sin: and when upon the head”** — the Godhead: this is done when the priests and doctors of the Church preach of the Godhead of Christ and proclaim it to their hearers.
**“HE OFFERED ALSO THE CALF”** — HE OFFERED ALSO THE CALF etc. HESYCHIUS. What the force of this law is, how it is taken in the sacrifice of Christ, has been set out above. There only Aaron lays his hands on the calf; but here his sons also, already anointed. When, offered in baptism, we are anointed for him, we are made sharers of the Lord's passion, of which baptism bears the image. For we are baptized in the death of Christ: for we are buried together with him by baptism into death. And necessarily the sons of Aaron, as sharing with him in the sacrifice, lay on their hands.
**“AUGUSTINE”** — AUGUSTINE. When he mentioned the sacrifices for sins, he said a calf was to be offered for the sin of the priest who made the people sin; but afterwards, when it is said how the things which the Lord commanded were done toward Aaron and his sons, a calf is said to be offered for sin. But above he commanded the horns of the altar of incense to be touched with the blood of the calf, and some of the blood to be sprinkled before the veil, and the rest poured at the base of the altar of holocausts; but afterwards, when Aaron is sanctified, nothing is said of the sprinkling of the blood before the veil; of the horns of the altar it is said, but 'of incense' is not added; and it is added that the blood is to be poured at the base of the altar, nor is it said at the base of which, as though it must necessarily be taken of that whose horns were touched with blood. Since therefore it is set down ambiguously, one is free to understand it done as had been commanded of the calf for sin: that we understand the horns touched to be not of the altar at whose base its blood was poured, but of the altar of incense, and the blood poured at the base of the altar of sacrifices.
8.15:
**“He immolated it: and taking the blood, and dipping his finger in it, he touched the horns”** — of the passion of Christ
**“of the altar”** — of incense, namely
**“round about; which being expiated and sanctified, he poured the rest of the blood at the bottom thereof.”**
• of the altar of holocausts, namely
• the doctrine of the Gospel, because the passion of Christ is to be received and believed according to the Gospel
8.18:
**“He offered also a ram”** — the leader of the perfect way of life
**“for a holocaust: upon whose head”** — as above
**“HE OFFERED ALSO A RAM”** — HE OFFERED ALSO A RAM etc. HESYCHIUS. The law, having the priest figure Christ in many things, now commands him to immolate a calf for sins and burn it outside the camp. For so the sacrifice of Christ was made for the washing away of our sins. But now a ram for a holocaust, because the world is crucified to him, and the way of life that renounces the world, which is the holocaust, has Christ for teacher and example; because of which he says: He that taketh not up his cross and followeth me is not worthy of me, that is: he who does not so renounce the world as I teach (for this is to follow him) is not worthy of me. Why then is the holocaust divided, and its feet and entrails, or according to others the belly, washed? The interpretation of the holocaust made at the beginning of the book has sufficiently fulfilled this. There he said the parts of the offerings were made, signifying that body and soul ought to be offered. But these divisions too are in us, because the flesh lusteth against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh; but not in Christ. Therefore the law made no mention of division in that sacrifice. And the priest offers a calf for sin, a ram for a holocaust, by which it is signified that the perfect way of life, which is the holocaust, is offered in the ram. For this one gives leadership to the sheep going in and going out, as Christ is the leader of the perfect way of life; and therefore he commanded the sheep to go in and out through him.
8.21:
**“having first washed the entrails and the feet,”** — the inner sacraments washed from the dung of the letter, that it may become acceptable and saving food
**“and the whole ram together he burnt upon the altar,”** — of the cross
8.22: **“He offered also the second ram, in the consecration of priests: and Aaron and his sons put their hands upon the head thereof.”** — HE OFFERED THE SECOND RAM etc. The ram signifies the handing down of the mysteries and the mystic pasch which Christ celebrated with his disciples. It is called the second because after the lamb immolated at the supper he offered himself. Whence Aaron laid his hands on the head of the ram with his sons, because Christ celebrated a common supper with his disciples; but Moses offered this sacrifice specially, because more than the others he expressed the figure of Christ, who chiefly made his own sacrifice.
8.23:
**“And when Moses had immolated it, taking of the blood, he touched the tip of the ear”** — in which obedience is marked
**“the right”** — that we may obey in good things
**“of Aaron, and the thumb of the hand”** — of working
**“his right, and in like manner of the foot.”**
• of good will
• HE TOUCHED THE TIP OF THE EAR etc. If by Aaron we take Christ, the tip of his ear was touched with blood, because he obeyed the Father even unto death. If the priests of the Church, their ears are to be touched and the thumbs of their hands and feet, that they may consecrate to the Lord the eminence of their actions and their going.
• HE TOUCHED THE TIP etc. What the effect of this sacrifice is, the anointing of the ears and hands and feet shows; for it is celebrated because of our obedience and good actions and way of life, that, free of Adam's disobedience, we may attain the obedience of the Only-begotten.
**“OF THE RIGHT HAND”** — That we may be strengthened in good action. For things which are anointed are strengthened; those not anointed are destroyed. For where there was no anointing with the blood of the immolated lamb, Egypt was struck. But first the priest, and afterwards his sons, were anointed with blood, because Christ first received the blood at the supper, then gave it to his disciples.
8.24:
**“He offered also the sons of Aaron: and when with the blood of the ram that was immolated he had touched the tip”** — that the end may be completed in good
**“of the right ear of every one of them, and the thumbs”** — that good working may be strong
**“of the right hand and of the right foot, the rest he poured on the altar”** — the body of Christ, that is, the Church
**“HE POURED ON THE ALTAR”** — For when he drank and gave the apostles to drink, he poured the intelligible blood upon the altar, that is, his body. And the Church is the body of Christ. Whence Mark: And taking the chalice, giving thanks, he gave it to them, and they all drank of it, and he said to them: This is my blood of the new testament, which shall be shed for many.
**“round about.”** — No one is excepted.
8.25:
**“The fat”** — desire
**“and the rump,”** — the completion
**“and all the fat that covereth the entrails, the caul of the liver, and the two kidneys with their fat, with the right shoulder, he separated.”** — BUT THE FAT etc. What these signify in the saving sacrifice, or that of peace offerings, has been said. But the Seventy put loin for rump, little belly for entrails, and the lobe of the liver for the caul of the liver: and not in vain are they mentioned now also in the ram.
8.26:
**“OUT OF THE BASKET”** — The Seventy: The basket of completion, which is the tongue of the Lord, which brought in the chief and perfect doctrine. For he came not to destroy the law but to fulfil it. This is well called a basket because of the texture of his doctrine, since he had said many things in parables. And it was both the dish and the table of the whole doctrine. Rightly therefore he sets forth the mystic bread from the basket of completion.
**“of unleavened bread, which was before the Lord,”** — because the mystic Pasch of Christ is a saving victim
**“A LOAF”** — The apostolic doctrine, and that of the law and the prophets. For the law and the prophets and the apostles make memory of him. For the law says: "This is the bread which the Lord hath given us." And the Prophet: "Bread is given him" etc. But the prophetic and legal doctrine nourish less than the apostolic. Whence Paul: God hath set some in the church, first apostles, secondly prophets. And the apostles bring in the testimonies of the law and the prophets, by which the cakes and wafers are set under them.
**“he put them upon the fat and the right shoulder,”**
• because it is necessary to offer every desire and good work in the ministry, if thou wilt receive it according to God and the intention of the law.
• AND THE RIGHT SHOULDER etc. GREGORY. The priest by the precept of the law is commanded to receive the right and separated shoulder, that his working may be not only useful but also singular; nor may he do right things only among the wicked, but may surpass those subject to him who work well, as in the honour of rank, so in the virtue of conduct. To him the breast also is given with the shoulder, that what he is commanded to take from the sacrifice he may learn to immolate of himself; that he may not only think in the breast the things that are right, but may invite the beholders to lofty things by the shoulder of work. Let him seek no prosperity of the present life and fear no adversity; let him despise the allurements of the world in regard of inward terror, and scorn its terrors, considering the allurement of inward sweetness; which Moses also says in what follows.
8.27:
**“delivering all together to Aaron”** — first, because Christ began his mysteries, and afterwards handed them to us to be celebrated
**“and to his sons: who, after they had lifted them up before the Lord,”** — The mystery which he handed to us when he lifted his flesh into heaven. Thy name is as oil poured out.
8.28: **“he took them again from their hands, and burnt them upon the altar of holocaust, because it was the oblation of consecration, for a sweet odour of sacrifice to the Lord.”** — "Thy name is as oil poured out", O Lord
8.29:
**“And he took the breast,”** — as in the sacrifice of peace offerings; and so to the intelligible Moses is offered the breast of the ram, by which faith and confidence are figured.
**“elevating”** — because it is of elevation
**“it before the Lord, of the ram of consecration, for his portion, as the Lord had commanded him.”** — AND HE TOOK THE BREAST etc. AUGUSTINE. Above, because he was commanding generally, if the priest had sinned, he commanded the priest himself, anointed and consecrated, that is, the high priest, to offer these things; but now Moses offers and receives the breast of laying on, because the fat was laid on from it, as he mentioned of the saving sacrifice. Since then the high priesthood seems to have begun from Aaron, but Moses was not a priest, how did he do these things? But if he was, how did the high priesthood begin from Aaron? Yet the Psalm in which it is said: "Moses and Aaron among his priests" affirms that he was a priest. Yet Aaron is commanded to receive the priestly vestment, which contains a great sacrament, and his successors, before anything is commanded about sanctifying and ordaining the priests; when, Moses going up into the mount, the priests are commanded not to go up, that is, the sons of Aaron, not because they already were, but because they were to be. Were both therefore then high priests, Moses and Aaron, or rather Moses, and Aaron under him? Or was the latter also high because of the pontifical vestment, the former because of a more excellent ministry? For from the beginning it is said: He shall be to thee in the things that pertain to the people, thou to him in the things that pertain to God.
8.30:
**“And taking the ointment”**
• of the Holy Ghost
• Because the anointing of the Spirit and the blood of the Only-begotten are of one working, rightly he joined the things by which all the elect are sanctified.
**“and the blood”**
• of the Son
• the passion of Christ
**“that was upon the altar,”** — the body of Christ
**“he sprinkled”** — Christ offered himself as a sacrifice for our sanctification by the sprinkling of his own blood.
**“Aaron”**
• first, because the highest
• HE SPRINKLED UPON THE ALTAR etc. Whatever good things are in us are to be brought back to him as our head. Whence: "For them do I sanctify myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth." Plainly therefore he called his passion sanctification, which sanctification is given to us.
**“and his vestments,”**
• the aforesaid
• AND TAKING THE OINTMENT etc. AUGUSTINE. It is asked who anointed the priest after the death of Moses, who succeeded only one who had died. Was it one who was already anointed among the second priests? For the oil of the high and the second priest was the same. Only that high priest whose supremacy appeared took the vestment; and if so, did he take it himself, or did another clothe him, as after the death of Aaron Moses clothed his brother's son? If then he was clothed by him, was the high one clothed by a second? For the vestment was such that it had to be put on by another; or was it put on the first time as afterwards? For sometimes he laid it aside and took it up again. A second therefore could clothe the first, by serving, not by excelling.
**“and”** — after
**“his sons and their vestments.”**
• As many of us as have been baptized have put on Christ.
• AND UPON HIS SONS etc. AUGUSTINE. It did not appear which of the sons should succeed the high priest. For Scripture does not determine the firstborn or the elder, unless it was done by some divine token; though it seems to have come from contention that afterwards there were several high priests, because when the more excellent contended, the honour itself was given to several for the sake of ending the strife.
8.31:
**“And when he had sanctified them in their vestments, he commanded them, saying: Boil”** — All our works ought to be thoroughly cooked with the fire of charity.
**“the flesh before the door of the tabernacle,”**
• of heaven, in which God dwells
• in the Church, which is the entrance of heaven, not outside, lest the things done be published to the profane
**“and there eat it. The loaves”** — of the word of God
**“also of consecration”**
• For unless Christ, entreated by the mouth of the priests, has come and sanctified the supper, the sacrifice of the Lord is in no way made.
• AND THERE EAT IT; THE LOAVES etc. He commanded the flesh to be eaten with the loaves, that we may understand the body of Christ, who is flesh, and the bread which came down from heaven: this ought to be celebrated only in the Church.
8.32:
**“And whatsoever shall be left of the flesh and the loaves, fire shall consume.”**
• as if: whatever the human mind cannot grasp of the divine commandments, let it leave to the Holy Ghost.
• AND WHATSOEVER etc. This we see done in the Church, and what remains unconsumed given to the fires. But he does not say on how many days it remained unconsumed, so that always, if it remains, it is given to the fire; hinting that if we fail in eating the sacrifice, and cannot search out whether the things we see are the very body of the Lord, yet we should not leave them, but give them to the fire, that the Holy Ghost may eat what we cannot. And he eats when we think that things are possible to him which are not possible to us.
8.33:
**“And you shall not go out of the door of the tabernacle”** — namely, there shall be your dwelling
**“OUT OF THE DOOR”** — Morally. It signifies that through the whole time of the present life one must not withdraw from the tabernacle, but persevere in the service of God.
**“for seven days, until the day”** — of Pentecost
**“wherein the time of your consecration shall be expired.”** — of the pouring in of the Spirit
**“AUGUSTINE”** — AUGUSTINE. At the door of the tabernacle of the testimony you shall sit seven days, day and night, lest you die. The idiom of the Scriptures is to be noted, which puts sitting for dwelling and abiding. For not because it is said of Semei that he sat in Jerusalem three years is it to be thought that through all that time he sat on a seat and did not rise. Hence also seats are so called where men have their abode: for habitation took this name.
**“For in seven days the consecration is finished:”** — FOR IN SEVEN DAYS etc. HESYCHIUS. The fiftieth is completed by seven multiplied by itself with one added. Whence Luke says: To whom also he shewed himself alive after his passion by many proofs, for forty days appearing to them and speaking of the kingdom of God; and eating together with them, he commanded them that they should not depart from Jerusalem etc. See how he consecrated or perfected them, appearing and teaching of the kingdom of God and eating with them; and saying not to depart from Jerusalem, he does not allow them to go out of the door of the tabernacle, does not allow them to preach, until they receive the promise of the Holy Ghost on the fiftieth day. Which fulfilled, Peter at once preached, and there were added to the faith "about three thousand souls". And they kept the command in every particular, and fulfilled what follows: Observing the watches of the Lord etc.
8.35:
**“Day and night”** — in prosperity and adversity
**“shall you remain in the tabernacle”** — in the service of God
8.36: **“And Aaron and his sons did all things which the Lord spoke by the hand of Moses.”** — AND AARON AND HIS SONS DID etc. Aaron is joined to his sons, nor does he go out of the door of the tabernacle. For he was to be preached, and to preach in them, as he himself consecrates and is consecrated in his members.

9.1:
**“And when the eighth day was come, Moses called Aaron and his sons, and the ancients of Israel, and said to Aaron:”**
• AND WHEN THE EIGHTH DAY WAS COME etc. The eighth day after the dedication signifies the day of Pentecost, on which the Holy Ghost came. And the seven days from the dedication hint at the seven times seven days which were from the resurrection to Pentecost, namely forty-nine, the very day of Pentecost being added as it were an eighth.
• Pentecost, which fell on the day of the resurrection, which bears the figure of the future and of the consummation of the present world, which turns in seven days: for it was fitting that the Spirit should come on the same day on which Christ rose. Then he says Aaron and his sons and the elders were called: for then the spectacle of the Church was called together, in which is Aaron, that is, Christ, and his sons, who are of lofty way of life and therefore ministers of the priesthood, and the elders, that is, the presbyters: for of these the body of the Church consists.
9.2:
**“Take of the herd”** — of the patriarchs and prophets
**“the calf”** — Christ
**“for sin, and a ram”** — of whom it is said: Thou shalt be my leader, and shalt nourish me.
**“for a holocaust, both without blemish,”** — "Who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth."
**“and offer them before the Lord.”**
• TAKE OF THE HERD A CALF etc. Aaron takes a calf for a holocaust and a ram, and offers them to the Lord. For then Christ made known his sacrifice, when the Spirit, coming, gathered the Parthians, Medes, Elamites and the firstfruits of all nations to the upper room of the apostles.
• Aaron offers a calf and a ram when the doctors of the Church proclaim the mysteries of the passion and make known that they were celebrated for the salvation of mankind.
9.3:
**“And to the children of Israel”** — the elders, the presbyters namely, the doctors who instruct the life of those who come together in the Church
**“thou shalt say: Take ye a he goat”**
• the sacrifice for penance
• Christ, who bore our sins
**“TAKE YE A HE GOAT”** — The apostles offered a he goat on the day of Pentecost, when Peter, proclaiming penance, said: Be converted and do penance.
**“for sin, and a calf, and a lamb,”**
• "who taketh away the sins of the world"
• these the priest offers when he immolates to God the strong works and the works of innocence
**“both of a year old,”** — a perfect and completed life
**“and without blemish, for a holocaust;”**
• this is referred to all
• through these the holocausts are completed
9.4:
**“also a bullock”** — He understands a middling way of life, which yet can save those who offer it.
**“and a ram for peace offerings: and immolate them before the Lord,”** — Every work of virtue ought to be done as with God looking on, and not be corrupted or in any way spoiled.
**“for the sacrifice”** — namely divine wisdom, which is to be applied in all good works, whether they be strong, or fitting to penance and innocence
**“of every one of them flour”** — theology with almsgiving
**“tempered with oil, offering;”** — or: you shall offer
**“for today the Lord will appear to you.”** — on the day of Pentecost the Holy Ghost will appear: "Now the Lord is a Spirit."
**“AUGUSTINE”** — AUGUSTINE. Take ye one he goat of the goats for sin, and a ram and a calf and a lamb of a year for a holocarposis without blemish, and a calf of the oxen, and a ram for a sacrifice of the saving offering before the Lord, and fine flour tempered with oil, because today the Lord will be seen in you. Four kinds of sacrifices of animals he commended above: the holocaust, the one for sin, the saving one, and the one of completion; but the sacrifice of completion pertains to the sanctification of the priest; the other three are here commanded to be offered. And this is said to the elders of Israel, that they may pertain to the whole people. But the sacrifice for sin has here three beasts: the he goat, the ram and the calf. To the holocaust belongs the lamb; to the saving sacrifice, the calf and the ram. It is not therefore to be distinguished so that only the he goat is understood for sin, and three in holocaust, ram, calf and lamb; but rather the first three for sin, he goat, ram, calf, and the lamb in holocaust; because above he commanded a he goat to be offered for the sin of the prince, and for each one's own sin, when he sins before the Lord by doing one of the things which ought not to be done, a ram; for the sin of the whole Synagogue a calf. It is fitting therefore that when he speaks to the senate of what the whole people ought to offer, a he goat should be commanded for the princes, and a ram for each one's own sin, and a calf for the sin of the whole Synagogue, which namely is done by the common will of all. And in the saving sacrifice he commands a calf and a ram to be offered, which are the chief. But in giving precepts about the saving sacrifices he commanded them to be offered from wherever, whether male or female, provided only they were offered of none but sheep and goats. If it is asked why he commanded two, the calf and the ram, it is hard to find, unless perhaps he willed the calf to be the saving sacrifice of the whole people, the ram for each one as for individuals. He seems above to have commanded two kinds of saving sacrifice: one which he called the saving sacrifice as in the name of all; the other where he said: If anyone offer the sacrifice of his saving offering. Where we find a difference, because in that which he called saving he did not say that the fat of the breast was to be offered to the Lord and the breast also and the right shoulder given to the priest, as in that which he called of his saving offering; because he offered the saving sacrifice for the whole people. It is not yet 'of his saving offering', which perhaps is understood as the private one of individuals, not the public one of all. For Moses offered the saving sacrifice, and it is not said 'of his saving offering', because he offered for the whole people. And where all are, there also are individuals, but not conversely.
9.5: **“They brought therefore all things that Moses had commanded before the door of the tabernacle:”** — For all come together to the Church who seek the mercy of God, who correct themselves from error, not only from the streets and lanes, but from the highways also and hedges, that the royal supper may be filled.
9.6:
**“Moses said: This is the word which the Lord hath commanded: do it, and his glory will appear to you.”**
• the Spirit; whence Paul: But we, beholding the glory of the Lord with open face, are transformed as by the Spirit of the Lord.
• THIS IS THE WORD etc. The word, namely the thing commanded: Do this for a commemoration of me. And he says word, because the dispensation of this mystery is considered more in a word, or consisted in it, and chiefly in the Lord's word transferring the things that appear into something else greater and intelligible. Whence of the manna also he says: This is the bread which the Lord hath given you to eat; this is the word which the Lord hath appointed. In these things therefore he signifies that while they performed the holy mystery and celebrated the Lord's supper, the Holy Ghost came. For it was the Lord's day, on which the apostles were to celebrate the sacred mysteries; following whose traditions we assign the Lord's day to the divine assemblies. Likewise we find Christ also made manifest after the resurrection through the mystic supper and the breaking of bread.
9.7:
**“And he said to Aaron: Approach to the altar, and offer sacrifice for thy sin: offer”** — what thou hast taken on
**“a holocaust,”** — thyself
**“and pray”** — "Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit."
**“for thyself”** — who hast taken on sin
**“and for the people:”**
• for whom thou wast made a propitiation
• Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.
• AND OFFER FOR THY SIN etc. AUGUSTINE. Another reading: Make for thy sin, and thy holocaust etc. It is strange how he says first that it must be made for sin, then the holocaust, when above he commands the sacrifice for sin to be laid upon the holocaust, except what he commanded of birds. Perhaps what was done first, that is, the holocaust, he mentioned later? Do that first, afterwards that. But which is to be done first he shows above when it is said: Lay the sacrifice for sins upon the holocaust. Though it troubles us that Scripture says Aaron did so as to mention first the one for sin, then the holocaust. Whether he did it first, or Scripture put these out of order, would be uncertain, had not what he said gone before. For how could it be laid upon the holocaust unless the holocaust were first laid on? And he commanded this also of the saving sacrifice; but because he does not say this everywhere, not through all the saving sacrifices, nor through all those for sin, it can perhaps be said that this was not commanded as a rule, but only in the saving sacrifice when it is of oxen. There he commands it, and in the sacrifice for sin when it is made of a female of the sheep. But the others, whether saving or for sin, need not be laid upon the holocaust.
• OFFER THE HOLOCAUST etc. He does not say the holocaust of completion, as above, when it was offered that he might be completed by sanctification, that he might perform the priesthood which he was performing.
• It is indeed to be noted that when sacrifices are offered for the people, sacrifices for sin were commanded to be offered, and a holocaust, and a saving sacrifice. But for the priest there was offered one for sin and a holocaust of completion, not a saving one. But the one of completion was offered when the priests were sanctified. And these Moses offered for Aaron and his sons; but afterwards Aaron, already performing the priesthood, is commanded to offer for himself a calf for sin and a ram for a holocaust, not of completion: for then it was offered that he might be completed by sanctification and be able to perform the priesthood; when he was performing it, there was no need to complete him again.
9.8: **“And forthwith Aaron, approaching to the altar, immolated the calf for his sin.”** — AND FORTHWITH AARON etc. HESYCHIUS. For what cause these sacrifices are performed here also we have said above; nor is it necessary to say again what we discussed in order in the Lord's sacrifice, which, though it is one, yet grants us not only the remission of sins but also a life perfect and complete in philosophy. Necessarily therefore it ought to be reckoned in the calf which is for sin and in the ram which is immolated for a holocaust. Whence in the person of the priest we behold both offered.
9.9: **“And his sons brought him the blood of it:”** — The sons of Aaron are the faithful people, who offer the blood of the calf when they worthily remember and venerate the passion of Christ.
9.10: **“AUGUSTINE”** — AUGUSTINE. It troubles us also that when Aaron made the gifts of the people which are mentioned above, not all that had been foretold are said to be immolated, but only the he goat for sin and the holocaust, where yet he did not express that lamb. And the two others, which we said pertain rather to the sacrifice for sin than to the holocaust, namely the ram and the calf, he passed over in silence. Where he understood the whole from a part, that in the he goat alone we might take also the things that followed. When he was narrating the people's saving sacrifices, how Aaron made them, he says of the calf and the ram: And he slew the calf and the ram, the saving sacrifice of the people, and the sons of Aaron brought the blood, and he poured it at the altar round about; and the fat from the calf, and from the ram the loin, and the fat covering the belly, and the two kidneys and the fat that is above them, and the lobe that is in the liver; and he put the fat upon the breasts, and laid the fat on the altar: and the breast and the right shoulder Aaron offered as an oblation before the Lord. Now he speaks in the singular, not the plural, though he speaks of two animals. What therefore he says, the two kidneys, is to be understood of each animal; and so they make four; and so the rest. But as to what he says: And he put the fat upon the breasts, though he did not lay these upon the altar (for they were owed to the priest with the right shoulders), is it to be understood: He put the fat which is upon the breasts? For he put them, as if he laid them upon the altar, taken off from the breast. For so he had commanded above. Then follows: And he laid the fat upon the altar, and the breast and the right shoulder Aaron offered as an oblation before the Lord: now bringing it in the singular, saying breast, both from each animal, as if he had said breasts.
9.12: **“He immolated also the victim of holocaust: and his sons brought him”** — as above
9.14:
**“having first washed the entrails with water,”** — the thoughts, which are often stained
**“and feet”** — Which touch the earth and gather dust; which the Lord washed for his disciples when they returned from preaching.
9.15: **“Then offering for the sin of the people, he slew the he goat: and expiating the altar,”** — AND OFFERING FOR THE SIN OF THE PEOPLE etc. HESYCHIUS. Of what these bear the figure, and how the he goat for sin signifies the sacrifice of penance, the holocausts the crucified way of life, the fine flour theology, and the saving or peace offering the life which can save us even when moderately wise, the preceding discussion of the sacrifices before the anointing of the priest shows. He therefore who does not know the explanation of this ordinance will find it by searching there finely point by point. But we add these things necessarily, because the lawgiver considered that the Holy Ghost would descend at Pentecost upon the apostles gathered into one and doing all things according to the law. Whence rightly he commanded the sacrifices of the priest to go before and those of the people to follow. For the doctrine of the Church must begin from the sacrifice of the Only-begotten, that priests may be brought in teaching what the passion of the Lord has profited us; then the word of penance, necessary for all, is brought in. Whence the Lord too preaches one doctrine, that is, penance, and adds after it the perfect ways of life and theology, by which we can be saved, even though we do not live loftily in them: it is fitting also that the Church be gathered and receive the manifestation of God. These things without doubt the disciples were doing at Pentecost, for which reason they were gathered together; and though they did not preach openly, because they did not go out of the door of the tabernacle until they were endued with power from on high, they did these things within themselves, and did not cease to meditate on what they should teach the Church.
9.17:
**“adding in the sacrifice the libations”** — fine flour, oil and the rest, which they add in the sacrifice of the victim
**“which are offered withal, and burning them upon the altar, besides the ceremonies of the morning holocaust.”** — namely of the lamb, which were offered daily morning and evening
9.19:
**“The fat”** — good desire
**“also of the bullock, and the rump”** — perfect work
9.20:
**“they put upon the breasts. And after was burnt”** — with the fire of the Holy Ghost
**“the fat upon the altar,”** — of the cross or of the heart
9.21: **“the breasts”** — All these things are to be offered to God in faith, which the breast signifies: without this no sacrifices please.
9.22:
**“And stretching forth his hands to the people, he blessed them.”** — AND STRETCHING FORTH HIS HAND etc. AUGUSTINE. He served standing at the altar. Thence therefore he came down where he stood. And the altar was three cubits high and had no step, because God had forbidden it, lest the privy parts be uncovered, which would surely happen if the step were part of the altar, that is, if it clung to it joined fast. For the altar would be one with the step; but because the height of the altar is so great that unless the priest stands on something he cannot minister fitly, it is to be understood that for the hour of ministering something was set and taken away which was not part of the altar; nor was it against the command of the Lord, who forbade steps to be there.
**“And so the victims for sin, and the holocausts, and the peace offerings being finished, he came down.”**
• from the place where he stood serving the altar
• AND SO BEING FINISHED etc. HESYCHIUS. Plainly he wishes to set forth the whole figure of the Church. Whence it is said that, these being finished, he came down; as if, the sacrifices set forth, he came down from the chair of mastership, as the priests are wont to do, to whom the figure of the true Aaron is entrusted. And in praying he lifted his hands to heaven. Whence Paul: "I will that men pray in every place, lifting up pure hands." Stretching out or lifting up his hands therefore, he blessed them, because through prayer the priests bless the people. But whence they give the blessing, what follows shows: And Moses and Aaron went in etc. Because the priests bless from the intelligible tabernacle, that is, from heaven, saying with Paul: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who hath blessed us with spiritual blessings in heavenly places in Christ. The Lord also, blessing the five loaves or the seven, looked up to heaven. And it is to be noted that not Aaron alone, but with Moses, blesses. For the priests do not bless by their own power, but because they bear the figure of Christ, and through him who is in them they bestow the fulness of blessing; and not only he who has obtained the priesthood, but whoever has Christ in himself and bears his figure through good conversation, as Moses, is fit to give blessing.
9.23:
**“And went”** — before they blessed
**“Moses”** — Christ, through whom Aaron blesses
**“and Aaron into the tabernacle of the testimony,”** — heaven, from which they bless
**“and afterwards came forth and blessed the people.”** — AND WENT IN etc. He set first went in, and adds came forth, because the priest goes into the tabernacle when he prays for himself or for the people, or gives himself to divine contemplation. He comes forth when he teaches or blesses the people, when he returns to his conscience, searching himself lest perhaps he have offended in preaching.
**“And the glory of the Lord appeared to all the multitude:”**
• AND THE GLORY OF THE LORD APPEARED etc. In the form of fire, as on the day of Pentecost. Whence he adds: And a fire came forth from the Lord. Whence Luke: "There appeared to them parted tongues as it were of fire."
• TO ALL THE MULTITUDE etc. Like to which Luke says: "And when this was noised abroad, the multitude came together, and were confounded in mind": not only came together, but were afraid. Whence here follows: And they were all astonished and wondered etc.
9.24:
**“and behold a fire, coming forth”** — he plainly shows the Holy Ghost, who appeared in fire
**“from the Lord, devoured”**
• SYMMACHUS: consumed
• received gladly
**“the holocaust and the fat that was upon the altar: which when the multitude saw, they praised the Lord,”**
• This was fulfilled when "the apostles spoke with divers tongues", and all who heard them were astonished and praised the Lord.
• THAT WAS UPON THE ALTAR etc. He hints that it is necessary to lay the aforesaid sacrifices and their expositions upon the intelligible altar of the body of Christ, that our imitation may breathe there; and then the nourishments of the intelligible fire, that is, the Holy Ghost, will be present, of whom it is said: The Lord our God is a consuming fire.
**“falling on their faces.”**
• Repenting humbly: for they said: "What shall we do, men and brethren?"
• they fell on their face, that is, some cast down the face of the mind to the earth, saying: These men are full of new wine.

10.1:
**“And Nadab and Abiu, the sons of Aaron, taking”** — These signify the heretics, who kindle strange fire, namely of covetousness and of wicked doctrine, in the Church, and will be consumed by the fire of divine vengeance.
**“their censers, put fire therein, and incense on it, offering before the Lord strange fire”** — which did not come forth "from the Lord" our God
10.2:
**“And fire coming out”** — the fire of punishment
**“from the Lord devoured them, and they died before the Lord.”** — AND NADAB TAKING etc. AUGUSTINE. By fire going out from the Lord the sons of Aaron died, because they dared to put incense to the Lord with strange fire applied, which was not lawful; for by the fire divinely kindled on the altar and thereafter kept, all things were to be kindled which needed to be kindled in the tabernacle. When they were dead, therefore, Moses says: This is what the Lord said etc. They approach the Lord who perform the priesthood in the tabernacle. And the Lord is sanctified in them also by punishing, that it may be known that he will spare others less if he spares not them, according to that: If the just man shall scarcely be saved, where shall the ungodly and the sinner appear? Or rather according to that: To whom more is given, of him more is required. And that: The servant who knew the will of his lord and did it not shall be beaten with many stripes. And: To him that is little, mercy is granted; but the mighty shall be mightily tormented.
**“ISIDORE”** — AND TAKING etc. They offer strange fire who, despising the tradition of God, covet strange doctrines and bring in the teachings of human institution. To whom it is said: You reject the commandment of God, that you may keep your own tradition. He also kindles strange fire who, nourishing in the sanctuary of his heart the fire of bodily or worldly desire, dares to approach the altars of the Lord. These receive no kindling save from that fire which the Lord came to send upon the earth, which ever kindles us, that we may be enlightened in our senses, lest we burn with vices.
**“HESYCHIUS”** — Here he understands that those who teach strange things, who blaspheme against the Spirit, who wickedly interpret the Scripture inspired by him, are punished by invisible fire. They are called sons of Aaron, having namely the habit of doctors and feigning a spiritual mastership. Whence also their tongues are called fire, because the Spirit came in the form of fiery tongues. They lay incense and aromatics upon the censers, or upon the fires of tongues, namely the doctrines of the Law and the prophets, of which it is said: "The odour of thy ointments above all aromatical spices." But they offer strange fire, because they do not interpret according to the intention and power of the Spirit. To these, therefore, fire comes forth from the Lord, not that which kindles the sacrifices, which is called the glory of the Lord, but the fire of punishment. For the Church has both: this for the enlightenment of the just and the perfecting of the sacrifices, that for the punishment of the ungodly. This the priests bring upon blasphemers, succeeding by the ministry of the Spirit (who rests in them), as Paul punishes Hymeneus and Alexander, who taught strange things. Before the Lord, that is, seeing, they are so condemned, lest by their example they give others cause of death. Before the Lord: a wonderful thing, where they ought to have lived, there they die; because, wickedly interpreting the divine Scriptures, they lie under a curse from that whence they could have merited life.
10.3:
**“And Moses said to Aaron: This is what the Lord hath spoken: I will be sanctified”** — by purging them
**“in them that approach to me,”**
• by ministering, by abundance of knowledge or by some ministry
• That is: I will appear holy in them that minister to me, by avenging their offences and not sparing.
**“and I will be glorified in the sight of all the people.”** — I will be praised and magnified; whence David says: The Lord is just, and hath loved justice: his countenance hath beheld righteousness.
**“THIS IS WHAT THE LORD HATH SPOKEN”** — When the Lord said to Moses: Go down and charge the people, lest they should have a mind to pass the limits to see the Lord, and a very great multitude of them should perish. The priests also that come to the Lord, let them be sanctified, lest he strike them. The people do not approach, because they do not bear the force of contemplation. The priests who approach are commanded to be sanctified, that they may become worthy to see and contemplate. Whence Paul: Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see God.
**“AUGUSTINE”** — Another reading: This is what the Lord said: I will be sanctified in them that approach to me, namely those who performed the priesthood in the tabernacle. He is sanctified also by punishing, that hence it might be known that he will spare others less if he spares not them, according to that: If the just man shall scarcely be saved, where shall the ungodly and the sinner appear? Or according to that: To whom more is given, of him more is required. The servant who knew the will of his lord and did it not shall be beaten with many stripes. But where the Lord said this above is not found; yet in Exodus Moses says to the Lord: Thou hast said, I know thee above all; which is found to have been said not before but afterwards. But because Moses would never say this falsely, it is understood that he said it before also, though it was not written. Whence it appears that not all things are written which the Lord spoke to those through whom he gave us the Scripture.
**“And when he heard this, he held his peace,”** — he was pricked at heart
**“of Aaron shall offer”** — the Church, which is the body of the true Aaron
10.4:
**“And Moses called Misael”** — or: Misadai
**“and Elisaphan, the sons of Oziel, the uncle of Aaron, and said to them: Go and take away your brethren from before the sanctuary,”** — from the fellowship of faithful priests
**“and carry them without the camp.”**
• the Church
• AND MOSES CALLED etc. Misael: 'the handling of God'. Elisaphan: 'the enlightening of God' or 'the mirror of God'. To these it is rightly commanded that they take Nadab and Abiu without the camp: for these signify the saints who, enlightened by God, handle him with the hands of faith and contemplate God with perfect faith. Whence they are well called sons of Oziel, who signifies the Gospel. Whence he is said to have been the uncle of Aaron, because great is the kinship of the Gospel and the Law. For the Gospel is the exposition of the Law; and the sons of the Gospel thrust the heretics, truly dead, out of the camp of the Church.
• Or Misadai and Elisaphan: the first, Misadai, is 'the handling of God'; Elisaphan is interpreted 'the watchtower of my God'. Whoever knows how to handle God and to behold, namely, the flesh and the divinity of Christ, as Thomas, who, touching the flesh with his hand, said: My Lord and my God, can take away the fire of strange doctrine from the face of the saints, that is, of the priests.
