The tunics of the priests are the conversation and life which they put on with the habit of the priesthood. They are cast out therefore, with the priesthood, from the fellowship of the priests and also of the people. Whence he adds: Without the tabernacle, that is, the church of the people. The sons of Aaron's uncle do these things.
• AARON, that is, David, through whom are understood the prophecies, which make Christ manifest and in a manner bring him forth to those who know him not. And the brother of prophecy is the Gospel: for what was done in the Gospels was foretold by the prophets. The sons therefore of the brother of Aaron's father, that is, of the Gospel, cast out such men. Whence John: "If any man come to you, and bring not this doctrine, receive him not into the house."
10.5: **“And they went forthwith and took them as they lay, vested with linen tunicks,”** — made ready, namely, to sacrifice; because heretics are wont to bear the habit of holiness before them, but they are cast out of the camp of the Church with their linen tunics, that is, with their feigning and hypocrisy
10.6:
**“And Moses said to Aaron, and to Eleazar and Ithamar, his sons: Uncover not your heads,”**
• of the mitre
• as if: Do not mourn the dead.
**“and your garments”** — the dispensation of Christ
**“rend not,”** — that is, to make degrees among the persons, or to rend the Church by heresies
**“lest perhaps you die,”** — as they did
**“and upon all the congregation”** — When a prince or priest sins, the people are often punished.
**“indignation arise.”** — from the sin of the masters
**“Let your brethren, and all the house of Israel,”** — the Church
**“bewail”** — When we see anyone punished by divine vengeance for sin, we ought to grieve and suffer with them.
**“the burning which the Lord has kindled:”**
• UNCOVER NOT YOUR HEADS etc. To the letter. Because they had lately been consecrated to God, he commands them not to put off the holy garments, but to stand by ready to serve God.
• ALLEGORICALLY, however: that they make no division of persons in Christ. For the head of Christ is God; and Christ consists of divinity and humanity: for the mitre of the head, that is, of the divinity, is the humanity, by which the divinity was covered as with a cap. This is not to be taken away, nor a division of persons to be preached in Christ, but one person of two substances.
**“AUGUSTINE”** — Uncover not your heads etc. That is, that they put not off their mitres, which are the coverings of the head. For mourners did contrary to the custom of their adornment, as in our custom the head which is kept uncovered is covered in mourning. He forbids them, therefore, to mourn those in whose punishment the Lord was sanctified, that is, his fear was commended. Yet he permits others to mourn them; but these ought not to mourn now, the seven days not yet being completed, during which they were not to go out of the tabernacle. It may also seem that those sanctified with that oil ought to mourn no one. Whence he adds: Let your brethren and all the house of Israel bewail the burning.
10.7:
**“But you”** — because lately consecrated; it is mystically hinted that, though we suffer with our neighbours, we ought yet to accord with the divine judgments
**“shall not go out of the door of the tabernacle,”** — the knowledge of doctrine
**“otherwise you shall perish, for the oil of the holy unction is on you.”** — as if: You are priests of the Lord.
**“HESYCHIUS”** — We are not ignorant what the mitres signify, because the head of every man is Christ, and the head of Christ is God. Of necessity the mitre signifies the humanity of Christ. He shows therefore what the priests and doctors ought to keep, that is, that they deny not the divinity of Christ nor gainsay his humanity, because he is God of God and the Word of the Father. For this is not to take the mitre from the head; but neither let them refuse or blaspheme the dispensation of Christ, as though rending the priestly stole. For all of us who have been baptized have put on Christ. Let the priests above all do this, lest they die, lest they bring the wrath of God upon the people. For the vices of those set over others are a stumbling block to those beneath them. He commands the house of Israel, that is, the whole Church, to bewail the burning. For if the loss of anyone at all is a harm to the Church, how much more that of priests. But you shall not go out of the door of the tabernacle. Above he commanded them not to go out of the tabernacle for seven days only; these fulfilled, eight days are kept. Here again he threatens that they go not out. Yet he does not contradict himself, because this is another going out. Whence he adds: That you die not, which he did not add above. For because those offering the fire of strange doctrine perished, he tells the others not to go out of the doors of the knowledge of Christ, but to follow his precept in all things, lest they die. This he commands the priests, to whom the mystery of the word has been entrusted by the gift of the Holy Ghost. Whence it follows: For the oil of unction is on you, of which John says: "His unction teacheth you of all things."
**“And they did all things according to the precept of Moses.”** — what the spiritual Moses commands, the Church keeps
10.9:
**“Wine”**
• "Be not drunk with wine, wherein is luxury."
• any single vice whatever
• as if: Lest your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting and drunkenness and cares.
**“and any thing that may make drunk”** — every vice that overturns the mind
**“you shall not drink, thou nor thy sons,”** — the priests who succeed
**“when”** — Note that he forbids vice at every time.
**“you enter into the tabernacle of the testimony,”**
• the handling of heavenly things
• WINE AND ANY THING etc. HESYCHIUS. Until now the Church keeps this law. For he did not command them to abstain from wine altogether, but when we go up to the tabernacle of the testimony or to the altar, that is, when we touch the mystery of heavenly doctrine; of which the altar is a figure, as the tabernacle is of the handling of heavenly things. Whence Paul to Timothy: Use a little wine for thy stomach's sake and thy frequent infirmities. And he who uses a little abstains from much wine and drunkenness at the time of the mystery and of doctrine. The priests also keep the same. Whence this commandment is delivered to the sons of Aaron too, that is, to those who have attained higher things. And Paul writes the like to the Ephesians: "Be not drunk with wine, wherein is luxury." Drunkenness also overturns sobriety and perverts the mind, so that it does not understand what it does. Whence Isaias: Woe to you that rise up early in the morning to follow drunkenness; and a little after he adds: "Wine in your feasts, and the work of the Lord you regard not." But they who regard not the works of the Lord, how do they discern between holy and profane, clean and unclean, or how can they exhort and enlighten the people from the Scriptures? Wishing to show the authority of this commandment, he says that God spoke it, that is, inspired it spiritually.
• WINE AND ANY THING etc. They are commanded to abstain from those things which cast down or overturn the state of the mind when they enter the tabernacle. But let us never be drunk, but ever sober in mind and body.
**“lest you die:”** — spiritually
**“because it is an everlasting precept through your generations:”** — WHEN YOU ENTER INTO THE TABERNACLE etc. AUGUSTINE. When then was it lawful for them to drink, who needed daily to enter the tabernacle and approach the altar in continual service? For if anyone says that sacrifices were not wont to be laid on every day, what will he say of the daily entry into the tabernacle for the candlestick and for setting the loaves of proposition upon the table? If it is answered that the tabernacle of the testimony is to be understood as that in which was the ark of the testimony, the high priest also needed to enter that for the burning of the incense. For he did not enter once in the year only, but once in the year with the blood of purification, and daily for the incense. Or did God command that they should not drink wine at all? Why then did he not say briefly: You shall not drink wine, but added: When you enter the tabernacle of the testimony etc.? Was it because the cause of not drinking was not to be kept silent, and chiefly because God foreknew that there would afterwards be many, even high priests, at one time, not by succession, who would serve all that ministry in turn, when surely those did not drink whose turn it was to serve, while the others drank? Nothing else is to be understood here, since when he forbade the priests to drink wine and strong drink, he said: A lawful thing for ever in your generations. It is doubtful whether this is connected with the sense before, that is, so that it pertains not to drinking wine, or with the one after, where there follows: To distinguish between the holy and the defiled, the clean and the unclean etc., so that this is the lawful office of the priests for ever in their generations.
10.10:
**“And that you may have knowledge to discern”** — which a drunken man cannot have, because drunkenness takes away their heart
**“between holy and unholy, between unclean and clean:”**
• from sin
• because a drunken man knows not how to rule himself nor teach another
• THAT YOU MAY HAVE KNOWLEDGE TO DISCERN etc. AUGUSTINE. This also is set down ambiguously, that he says: To distinguish between the holy and the defiled, the clean and the unclean: whether from this, that things are holy and clean, or defiled and unclean? Or from this, that persons are holy and unclean? That is, whether he willed the priests to distinguish among the sacred rites themselves, which were done rightly or not rightly? Or among the men themselves, to be approved or disapproved? Or is it rather to be referred to both?
10.11:
**“And may teach”**
• It belongs to priests to teach and instruct those beneath them.
• Not only "that you may have knowledge".
**“the children of Israel all my ordinances which the Lord hath spoken”**
• by divine inspiration
• the authority of the precept
• He does not say 'which I have spoken'; he speaks of himself as of another.
**“to them by the hand of Moses.”** — by the living voice of one speaking and writing
10.12:
**“And Moses spoke to Aaron, and to Eleazar and Ithamar, his sons that were left: Take the sacrifice”** — AQUILA: the gift that is left of the corn
**“that is remaining of the oblation”** — the fine flour
**“of the Lord, and eat it without leaven”** — of eternal doctrine
**“beside the altar,”** — The body of Christ
**“because it is holy of holies.”**
• TAKE THE SACRIFICE etc. HESYCHIUS. That the breast signifies confidence and faith, and the shoulder the action and correction of the conversion promised by them, was shown when we treated of the sacrifice of peace offerings or the saving sacrifice. And why the sacrifice that remains of the oblation is assigned to Aaron and his sons, that is, what is left of the fine flour without leaven beside the altar. The sacrifice of fine flour, which everywhere signifies the doctrine of theology, he wills to be without leaven, lest it be mixed with outside doctrine. He shows also that our theology is in part: for its fulness is in heaven; therefore he commanded what remained, that is, what is left over, to be eaten, to show that the sum is with him and kept beside the altar, that is, the body of Christ. For from it theology is ministered to us. But what remained of the fine flour shall be Aaron's and his sons'; but what is of the peace offerings shall be Aaron's and his sons' and his daughters', or according to the Septuagint, his house's, that is, of all the people. For theology belongs to few, namely the lofty and those who approach the Lord and follow Christ; but what pertains to the peace offerings and saving sacrifices belongs to the whole people.
• TAKE etc. That is, the hidden and deep sacraments of Scripture, which the crowd does not grasp, are to be kept and eaten by the perfect beside the altar, that is, beside the faith and authority of the Lord's passion.
10.13: **“And you shall eat it in a holy place:”** — as above
10.14:
**“For the breast”** — It signifies the confidence and faith of those who offer.
**“also that is offered, and the shoulder”** — the action of conversation and correction
**“that is separated, you shall eat in a most clean place,”**
• in the mind, in the Church
• THE BREAST ALSO etc. AUGUSTINE. The breast of separation and the arm of oblation you shall eat in a holy place. Though a single name is given to each, yet both could be called of separation, because they are separated for the priest; and both of taking away and removal, because they are removed and taken from those for whom it is offered, that they may be given to the priest. We read above, indeed, of the breast of imposition and the arm of taking away, because nothing of the arm was laid upon the altar; but the fat of the breast was laid upon the altar.
**“thou and thy sons, and thy daughters”** — For the strong and the weak in faith are to be fed and strengthened by true faith and good works.
**“with thee. For to thee”** — the greater
**“and thy children”** — the lesser
**“they are set aside, of the victims of peace offerings”**
• those acquiring salvation
• which are namely the Saviour's, that is, Christ's, of whom it is said: "My eyes have seen thy salvation."
**“of the children of Israel:”** — who namely see God
10.16:
**“While these things were a doing, the buck goat”**
• namely the oblation of penance
• the sinner
**“that had been offered”** — when penance was enjoined
**“for sin, when Moses sought for it, burnt”**
• by the intelligible fire of the Holy Ghost, against whom they sinned
• because he did not repent well
**“he found it: and being angry”** — because the things offered for sin by the people were to be eaten by the priests, the fat and kidneys being taken from them
**“with Eleazar and Ithamar,”** — because perhaps the ministry of suggesting it pertained to them
10.17:
**“Why did you not eat the sacrifice for sin”** — as if: Why have you not caused penance for the sin committed to be performed?
**“in a holy place.”** — the Church
**“which is most holy, and given to you,”** — the vicars of Christ
10.18:
**“Especially whereas none of the blood thereof hath been carried within the holy places,”** — because the blood of Christ was carried into heaven, in the sight of the Father, for our blood
**“and you ought to have eaten it in the sanctuary, as was commanded me?”** — that is, as I commanded: for Moses is a figure of Christ
**“WHILE THESE THINGS WERE A DOING, THE BUCK GOAT”** — HESYCHIUS. Because every sin is blotted out by penance, and those who committed the aforesaid sin of other doctrine and blasphemy were not saved, the lawgiver sets out the cause of their death. While these things were a doing, the buck goat etc.; because, namely, the sons of Israel and of Aaron did not eat in the holy place what was for sin, that is, did not cause the penance of the sin committed to be performed in the Church. To these this is commanded whom Christ has appointed his vicars in the Church. For he himself offered the blood of his oblation, which was offered for our blood, into the holy place, that is, into heaven, in the sight of the Father. And this sacrifice ought to be eaten in the holy place, that is, the church, for the propitiation of sins. Whence he adds: As was commanded me, that is, as I commanded. For Moses bears the person of Christ. He found it burnt, because they had sinned against the Holy Ghost: the oblation for penance was taken away by the intelligible fire of the Holy Ghost. For to those who sin wilfully there is left no sacrifice for sin. For as true penance merits pardon, so feigned penance provokes God; because the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee from the deceitful. And this the holy Fathers have called the unforgivable sin and blasphemy against the Holy Ghost: to persevere in crimes to the end of life, to despair of one's salvation, to distrust the power and mercy of the Redeemer.
**“ADAMANTIUS”** — While these things were a doing, the buck goat etc. "Not to sin belongs to God alone; to amend, to the wise man"; but rarely will you find one who corrects himself: rare is the confession of sin, rare is penance. Nature and shame resist, because all flesh is liable to fault. And each one blushes to confess his sin, while he thinks more of present things than of future. Moses wishes to find the soul empty of sin, that it may lay down the spoils of error and depart naked of fault without shame of itself; but an unreasoning impulse forestalls it, and the flame of the swiftest motion feeds upon the soul and burns up its innocence. For present things outweigh future, pleasant things serious, glad things sad, and hasty things slower. For iniquity is swift, suggesting occasion to do harm; virtue is slow and delaying, and judges before it begins what is seemly, what is honourable. Iniquity hurries all things headlong. But penance is sluggish and bashful, punished by shame of the present. For it looks only to future things, whose hope is late and whose fruit is slow. Meanwhile shamelessness runs ahead, and penance is shut out by the hope of present things, and its affection is burnt up and abolished. The law seeks it and finds it not. For it is burnt up by the heat and smoke of iniquity. Hence he is angry, and says that penance ought to have been eaten in the holy of holies. He rebukes the priests as sluggish. Aaron answers that the priestly judgment ought to be provident, and that this office is not easily to be entrusted to a conscience not sound, lest the last error be worse than the first. For in a foul vessel either oil or wine is easily spoiled. And how could sin be burnt up in the sight of the Lord, to whom all things are open, where there was strange fire? As if: He does not please God who keeps injustice shut up in his heart and declares that he does penance. Strange fire is lust, avarice and every wicked desire. This fire burns, it does not cleanse. For in whom it is, if they offer in the sight of the Lord, the heavenly fire consumes them, as Nadab and Abiu, together with the things that had been offered for sin. He therefore who wishes to be cleansed, let him remove the strange fire and offer himself to that fire which burns up the fault, not the man. This fire dried up the flowing blood of the woman with the issue of blood; this dried up the fault of the thief. For it is a consuming fire; it heals those who confess simply and purely. Judas said: "I have sinned in betraying innocent blood", but he had in his breast the strange fire, inflamed by which he ran to the halter. And he was unworthy of the remedy, because he did not repent with a pure mind. But the priests do not take away the fault of those who offer deceitfully, nor can they feast upon them, whose food is the remission of sins. Whence the true priest says: My meat is to do the will of my Father, that is, that sinners, converted and penitent, be saved. No sacrifice is acceptable to God unless it be true and sincere.
**“AUGUSTINE”** — Truly, since six beasts are commanded to be offered for the people, of which he first mentioned four, the he goat, the ram, the calf and the yearling lamb, of which it is plain that the he goat is for sin, and plain also that the yearling lamb is for a holocaust, let us see whether the two in the middle, the ram and the calf, set down ambiguously, pertained to the sacrifice for sin and were joined to the he goat, or rather to the lamb, so as to be offered in holocaust. What seemed to us on this we have set out. But afterwards, that the six animals might be completed, he mentioned a calf and a ram for the saving sacrifice; and yet in what follows, when they were immolated and mentioned, no mention is made of the ram and calf which he had placed between the goat and the lamb, but only that calf and that ram are mentioned which he had commanded to be offered for the saving sacrifice; so that there would be believed to have been not two beasts but four. Perhaps he named again those two which he had placed before between the he goat and the lamb, and there was not another calf and another ram for the saving sacrifice; so that, when he had said the he goat for sin, and the ram and the calf, not saying for what, and the yearling lamb for a holocaust, he wished afterwards to say what was to be done with the calf and the ram, that is, neither for sin like the he goat nor for a holocaust like the lamb, but they were commanded to be brought in for the saving sacrifice to be burnt. But the question will remain why a he goat was offered for the sin of the Synagogue, when the Lord, speaking from the beginning of the sacrifices which were to be offered for sin, commanded a calf to be offered for the sin of the Synagogue, just as for the sin of the priest, not a goat but a calf; with whose blood, as for the sin of the priest, the horns of the altar of incense were touched; and what the cause was that Moses offered a calf for the sin of Aaron, and Aaron himself another calf, as it behoved to be done for the sin of the priest according to the precept of the Lord. But for the sin of the people not a calf, as had been commanded, but rather a he goat is offered. It seemed to us, therefore, that not the he goat alone was commanded to be offered for the sin of the people, but the ram and the calf also, so that to these three 'for sin' should be understood; because there were also princes among the people, for whom the he goat was to be offered, and individuals could have their own sins, for which the ram; and all one common sin, for which the calf, as it had been commanded from the beginning that a calf should be offered for the sin of the whole Synagogue. And therefore, when they were immolated, he named only the he goat, that the others too might be understood, the whole from a part, all of which had been for sin.
10.19:
**“Aaron answered:”** — mildly, because he saw Moses angry
**“This day hath been offered the victim”**
• in the time of grace
• of which: "Today if you shall hear his voice, harden not your hearts."
**“for sin, and the holocaust before the Lord: and to me what thou seest has happened: how could I eat it, or please the Lord in the ceremonies, having a sorrowful heart?”** — AARON ANSWERED etc. Aaron seems to say this in the person of the Church, whose figure he bears, as also Christ's. As if: because after the coming of the Saviour they were appointed to minister, and to offer for penance, and to expound the prophetic life. Otherwise: the teachers perished, and in them these things befell the Church, so that she mourned the death of priests and masters. Whence she could not eat for sin today nor pray; and it would displease the Lord.
**“AUGUSTINE”** — Aaron answered etc. If today they have offered what is for their sin, and their holocausts before the Lord, and such things have befallen me, and I eat what is for sin, will it be pleasing to the Lord? etc. Aaron seems to have said that, when the sons of Israel first offered for their sin, it ought not to have been eaten by the priests but wholly burnt; not making from this a rule for the rest. For thereafter they themselves ate the sacrifices for sins. And it is to be believed that Aaron said these things by divine inspiration, which Moses approved as divinely spoken. What then of the other sacrifices of the same day, that is, of the ram and the calf, which we said were also offered for sin? Is there no question of the calf, since it behoved to be done so, that some of its blood should be offered in the holy place, whence the horns of the altar of incense should be touched, and it followed that it should be wholly burnt? What then of the ram? Is it that, because Moses first sought the goat, what was answered about the goat is to be understood also of the ram, which in order he was going to seek, had not the priest's answer pleased him? But what should he seek about the calf, since it could be done under that law which the Lord had commanded about the calf for the sin of the whole Synagogue, as about the calf for the sin of the priest, that is, that it should be wholly burnt without the camp? For Moses in anger said: Why did you not eat what was for sin in the holy place? For since they are holy of holies, it was lawful for you to eat this, that you may take away the sin of the Synagogue and pray for it before the Lord. For none of its blood was brought into the holy place before the face; you shall eat it within, in the holy place etc. When he says: None of its blood was brought into the holy place before the face, he distinguishes that which is done for the sin of the priest or of the Synagogue: not of the goat, of whose blood, since it was not commanded to be brought in to touch the horns of the altar of incense, it ought not to have been wholly burnt but eaten by the priests. But why this was done, Aaron answered, and it pleased Moses.
**“THIS DAY”** — As if he said: If they had sinned this before the remission of the Saviour, perhaps it would be forgiven, since knowledge was not yet made manifest to the world. Whence: If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin.
10.20: **“Which when Moses had heard he was satisfied.”** — the Church, namely, keeping his doctrine

11.2:
**“Say to the children of Israel: (Keep all things that I have written to you, that I may be your God)”** — because it is a common commandment of the whole people
**“These are the animals which you are to eat of all the living things of the earth.”** — in distinction from the heavenly ones: for there is the lion, the calf, the eagle and the man, according to the vision of Ezechiel; but there all are clean and holy.
11.3: **“THE HOOF DIVIDED”** — They divide the hoof who set themselves with firm step of innocence and justice according to the two Testaments. The Jews chew the words of the law, but do not cleave the hoof, because they do not receive the two Testaments, nor believe in the Father and the Son and the Holy Ghost. The heretics divide the step of faith: they cleave the hoof, believing in the Father and the Son, but they do not chew the cud of the doctrine of truth.
11.4:
**“But whatsoever cheweth the cud”** — he discerns not cattle but the manners of men: and those are clean who chew the cud, that is, who ever carry the precepts of God in their mouth.
**“and hath a hoof, but divideth it not, as the camel, and others, that you shall not eat”**
• he condemns a life shapeless and twisted with crimes
• In the camel pride is designated, which belongs properly to fools; and folly is contrary to wisdom. The hare, as timid, is contrary to fortitude; the cherogrillus, as rapacious, to justice; the swine, as filthy, to chastity. Let us not eat the flesh of these; let us not follow the virtues they seem to have. And by these four general virtues understand all. Let us not touch their carcasses, that is, let us not share in sins.
**“THE CAMEL”** — The Jew swollen with pride, to whom it is said: Straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel. These chew the cud because they meditate on the letter, but they do not divide the hoof because they do not distinguish the letter from the spirit.
11.5: **“The cherogrillus which cheweth the cud, but divideth not the hoof, is unclean.”** — a spiny animal larger than the hedgehog
11.6:
**“The hare”**
• timid, weak; whence: Woe to them that are of a fearful heart, and to the slack hands.
• he rejects the effeminate; whence the Comic poet: Thou art a hare thyself and lookest for dainties
**“also: for that too cheweth the cud, but divideth not the hoof.”** — THE CHEROGRILLUS WHICH etc. THE HARE etc. Both are taken of the people of the Jews. For these animals are said to be weak. Whence Solomon: "The rabbit, a weak people." And David: "The rock is a refuge for the hedgehogs", or cherogrilli. Whence the one is swift and timid; the other weak indeed but rapacious, and they call it deadly, that is, the cherogrillus, which fits the people of the Jews, of whom it is said: "Their feet are swift to shed blood."
11.7: **“And the swine”** — it signifies those to whom it is said: The dog is returned to his vomit, and the sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mire.
11.8:
**“The flesh of these”** — feigned virtues
**“you shall not eat, nor their carcasses”** — sins
11.9:
**“These are the things that breed in the waters,”** — of baptism; of which Isaias: "Behold the Gentiles are as a drop of a bucket"; the Septuagint: The Gentiles as many waters.
**“and which it is lawful to eat. All that hath fins,”** — a lofty and heavenly life
**“and scales, as well in the sea, as in the rivers, and the pools, you shall eat.”**
• ignorance, but such as is easily taken away, as is said of Paul: "There fell from his eyes as it were scales, and he received his sight."
• THESE ARE THE THINGS etc. HESYCHIUS. As in the freewill sacrifices, which are also called gifts, he signified by various oblations the workers of the law and the simple or the contemplatives, and those who are saved from the Gentiles, to whom the sacrifice of fine flour is assigned as to the simple; which he hints when he says: If a soul shall offer to the Lord, and did not add 'of the people of the land', as in the other sacrifices; so, wishing by abstinence from foods to show what sort those ought to be who meditate on the law, by chewing the cud and dividing the hoof he expressed the Jew, who ought to fulfil the commandment of the law, divide the letter from the spirit, and understand the law spiritually. But by the things said in the present chapter he shows that he speaks of the Gentiles. Whence he did not set down the names of the fishes, because the Church does not wish the names of her own to be written upon the earth. Whence: "Let these things be written unto another generation", that is, in the heavens.
• ALL THAT HATH FINS etc. ISIDORE. Among fishes, whatever has not fins and scales is abominable: the rough are held for clean. For bristly and shaggy, firm and grave manners of men are approved. Those without these are called unclean, to whom are ascribed light and slippery, weak and effeminate manners.
• He joins fins also with scales: for whatever fishes are finned are also scaly. So those whose ignorance can be loosed have also lofty knowledge and heavenly life. But with those who are not such, take not even food.
**“GREGORY”** — Morally. Fishes that have fins and scales are wont to leap above the waters. In the finned fishes, therefore, are figured the elect souls, which alone pass into the body of the heavenly Church; which, propped by the fins of virtues, leap by heavenly desire to contemplation, though they slip back into themselves through the frailty of the flesh. They alone therefore pass, as chosen food, into the body of the elect, who, while they serve lower things, climb by the leaps of the mind to things above, lest they ever lie hid in the depths of cares, where they have no care of the highest love, as of the free air. They therefore who are busied with temporal things then dispose outward things well when they carefully take refuge in inward things, and love not the din of disturbance, but rest within themselves in the bosom of tranquillity.
11.10: **“BUT WHATSOEVER HATH NOT FINS”** — There are also fishes having a shell for a skin, whose scale cannot be taken away; because they neither lay down the scales of ignorance at the word of God nor receive the knife of the spirit; and though they be found in the sea of baptism or in the rivers of penance, yet they are abominable among the things that move and live in the waters, because by living ill they corrupt the regeneration and life which they received in baptism.
11.12: **“All that have not fins and scales, in the waters, shall be unclean.”** — THEIR FLESH etc. HESYCHIUS. When he forbids the swine, he reproves a life filthy and rejoicing in uncleanness. When the hare, he condemns effeminate men. Who will make food of the weasel? But he marks theft. Who of the lizard? But he hates inconstancy of life. In the stellio he abhors the spots of minds. He hates the hawk, the kite, the eagle, that is, robbers living by violence. He abhors the vulture, that is, those who seek prey from another's death. He forbids the raven, that is, black pleasures. When he forbids the sparrow, he rebukes intemperance. When the owl, the shifting things that flee the light. When the charadrion, intemperance of tongue. When he forbids the swan, he forbids the pride of the lofty neck. When the bat, those who seek the darkness of night.
11.13:
**“Of birds these are they which you must not eat, and which are to be avoided by you: The eagle,”** — which lives by the death and plunder of other birds
**“and the griffon, and the osprey,”**
• a great bird
• OF BIRDS THESE ARE THEY etc. He adds what pertains to the life of contemplatives. For as in the offering of sacrifices he assigned them a chapter of their own, so also in foods. For truly it is abominable that anyone given to contemplation should of his own will have such spots as the lawgiver signifies in these birds. For he says: The eagle and the griffon etc. By these he figures robbers, and those who wickedly pursue another's food and rejoice in unjust things. Some of these live by plunder; others enter houses and carry off what they find. Like these are they who creep into houses and lead captive silly women laden with sins.
11.14:
**“And the kite, and the vulture,”** — a bird like the eagle, but larger
**“THE VULTURE”** — He who delights in wars. Whence it follows an army, awaiting the carcasses of the dead: for he who gives himself to contemplation ought not to be fed by another's mourning.
11.15: **“And all that is of the raven kind”** — who is without affection; whence the raven, once sent out by Noe, does not return; like whom is Judas.
11.16:
**“THE OSTRICH”** — The ostrich is a bird, but cannot fly, and is ever about the ground, as some who are soldiers to God and entangle themselves with worldly business.
**“and the owl”**
• Septuagint: the glaux
• The night raven seizes prey only at night. Such are the Gentiles who gape after the works of night, "which are fornication, uncleanness, immodesty."
**“THE OWL”** — This, they say, sees sharply in the night and little in the day. Such are they who glory in the contemplation of the Law and cannot take in the light of the Gospel.
**“THE LARUS”** — The larus is an animal dwelling both in the water and on land: for it flies and swims. To this are likened those who reverence circumcision and baptism.
**“THE HAWK”** — The hawk is among the birds of prey, but it grows tame and does its plundering with men. This they imitate who seem gentle, but strive to plunder together with the powerful, the covetous and the rapacious.
11.17: **“THE CORMORANT AND THE IBIS”** — These are long-necked, and draw their food (as is said) from the depth of the earth or the water, and are not to be imitated. For he who gives himself to contemplation ought to reach toward higher things and not be anxious about lower.
11.18: **“And the swan, and the bittern,”** — it is a bird in Africa having a long beak
11.19:
**“THE HOUP”** — This is mournful and loves mourning. But the sorrow of the world worketh death. And he who loves God ought to rejoice, pray without ceasing, in all things give thanks.
**“also, and the bat.”** — THE BAT. It flies about the ground and uses wings for feet; which is foreign to those who contemplate, lest their contemplation be busied with earthly things.
11.20: **“Of things that fly, whatsoever goeth upon four feet, shall be abominable to you.”** — OF THINGS THAT FLY, WHATSOEVER etc. Those who seem to be like the contemplatives, but cleave like creeping things to earthly desires, even if they walk on four feet, that is, if they feign the preaching of the Gospel, which calls to penance, are abominable, because they do not truly embrace the common life, but serve pleasures.
11.21: **“But whatsoever walketh upon four feet, but hath the legs behind longer, wherewith it hoppeth upon the earth,”** — BUT WHATSOEVER etc. Because, while they are in the flesh, they "walk not according to the flesh", but leap away from filthy actions, and mingle with earthly men to instruct and teach them, as the Lord with sinners and publicans. We must have legs higher than our feet, lest we halt on both feet, as the Jews in the law and the prophets; but let us have straight legs, like the Cherubim, of whom it is said: Their legs were straight, and their feet winged.
11.22:
**“THE BRUCHUS”** — Which leaps, but less than the attacus or the locust, which leap more. Such are they who converse with sinners, for their conversion, not for consent or imitation.
**“THE OPHIOMACHUS”** — Which fights with serpents: and our fight is with the old serpent and his angels.
**“and the locust, every one according to their kind.”** — namely of all these animals
11.23: **“But of flying things whatsoever hath four feet only,”** — that is: those who abuse the preaching of the Gospel and are defiled with the filth of earthly life
11.24:
**“And whosoever the carcasses”** — actions in which is death
**“of them shall touch,”** — by sharing in them
**“shall be defiled, and shall be unclean until the evening:”**
• as above
• until he do penance; whence: "In the evening weeping shall have place."
11.25:
**“And if it be necessary that he carry any of these things when they are dead,”** — THAT HE CARRY ANY etc. As he who calls evil good, and bitter sweet: for by praising the evil from which he ought to have forbidden, he makes it his own and carries it.
**“he shall wash his clothes,”** — the body or action; whence: "Blessed is he that watcheth and keepeth his garments."
11.26:
**“Every beast that hath a hoof, but divideth it not,”** — as the Jews do not divide the letter from the spirit
**“nor cheweth the cud,”** — by meditating constantly on the word of God
**“shall be unclean: and he that toucheth it, shall be defiled.”** — EVERY BEAST etc. HESYCHIUS. The law passes over no sin: whatever things are forbidden in the Gospel are expressed in the riddles of the Law, that in the mouth of two witnesses every word may stand, and that in both laws you may praise God, and, as he forbids, flee evil.
11.27:
**“That which walketh upon hands of all animals which go on all four, shall be unclean: he that shall touch their carcasses”**
• with whom, by the imposition of the hand, their death is shared
• THAT WHICH WALKETH UPON HANDS OF ALL ANIMALS etc. He who passes over to the doctrine or conversation of the Gospel, but walks upon his hands, namely laying on hands for the sake of filthy lucre, is rightly compared to all the beasts, so that you may call him adulterer, or covetous, or murderer and the like: for by wicked imposition he shares with them all.
**“shall be defiled until evening.”** — until he do penance
11.28:
**“And he that shall carry such carcasses,”** — HE THAT SHALL CARRY SUCH etc. By bearing false witness, by calling the unworthy worthy and the unclean clean.
**“shall wash”** — with the tears of penance: "Every night I will wash my bed: I will water my couch with my tears."
11.29:
**“These also shall be reckoned among unclean things, of all that move upon the earth, the weasel,”** — he forbids theft
**“and the mouse,”** — gluttony
**“THE MOUSE”** — Gluttony. For the mouse, for the gluttony of its belly, shuns no dangers.
**“THE CROCODILE”** — Which, hard of skin and malicious, feeds on mud.
11.30:
**“The shrew,”** — it is an animal born for mockery, crafty, rapacious, gluttonous
**“THE CHAMELEON”** — It shows pity, and through weakness feigns itself gentle, though it is cruel.
**“and the stellio,”** — the askalabotes, small indeed but venomous
**“and the lizard,”** — which dwells in tombs
**“and the mole:”** — THE MOLE. A blind animal born of the earth. For it is produced, as they say, from earth rained upon and muddy, but first corrupted.
11.31:
**“All these are unclean.”** — not these alone, but these chiefly
**“He that toucheth their carcasses shall be unclean until the evening.”**
• as above
• HE THAT TOUCHETH etc. If they were unclean by nature, he would be unclean who touched even the living. The carcasses of such are actions, that is, guile, theft, doubleness and the like, in which is the death of the soul.
11.32:
**“And upon what thing soever any of their carcasses shall fall, it shall be defiled, whether it be a vessel of wood,”** — a light and middling life
**“or a garment,”** — that which suffices for covering
**“AND UPON WHAT THING SOEVER SHALL FALL”** — HESYCHIUS. The lawgiver uses a wonderful division. For some sin from negligence, others from zeal. Whence Solomon: Woe to them that are zealous for wine, and give themselves to draining cups. These he rightly placed among those who touch carcasses. But those who offend through negligence and stupor of soul and failing of virtues, as David, seeing the wife of Urias washing herself, shining in beauty, fell into adultery: upon these the carcasses fall. For they did not set themselves to sin, but fell into it, as receiving a carcass falling from above. But those who wholly received it and did not resist are unclean: Whether it be a vessel of wood or a garment.
**“or skins”** — the one who suffers
**“or haircloths;”** — the penitent
**“or any thing in which work is done,”** — of virtue
**“they shall be dipped in water,”** — of the laver or of tears
11.33:
**“But an earthen vessel,”** — who is wholly earthly
**“into which any of these”** — a carcass, that is, sin unto death
**“shall fall,”** — so as to rule over the inward man
**“shall be defiled, and therefore is to be broken.”** — because its uncleanness cannot easily be purged, and needs much labour and contrition and a kind of reforming
11.34:
**“Any meat which you eat, if water be poured upon it,”**
• if any of these shall fall in
• IF WATER BE POURED etc. AUGUSTINE. From the vessel, namely, which was made unclean by the unclean carcasses, if perhaps it had water.
• the water of baptism. For the discourse is of the baptized: of unbelievers he makes no mention. Whence Paul: I wrote to you not to keep company with fornicators; I mean not with the fornicators of this world etc.
**“shall be unclean; and every liquor that is drunk out of any vessel,”** — any man whatever
**“shall be unclean.”** — ANY MEAT etc. By meat and drink he understands good works. Therefore he said: The meat which you eat, and the liquor that is drunk etc., because both the meat and drink of evil actions are forbidden, that no one may share in them. If then upon the good actions which are in every vessel, that is, in every man, any carcass whatever shall fall, of necessity the action will be unclean. For if upon a good action pride, guile, hypocrisy or any carcass, that is, a thing deadly to him who shares in it, shall fall, this too will be unclean: for an evil intention falling upon a good action defiles it.
11.35:
**“WHETHER IT BE OVENS”** — By this the masters are designated, in whom the foods of sacred doctrine are cooked by the working and fire of the Holy Ghost. Nor is it strange: for Moab is called a pot: "Moab is the pot of my hope."
**“or pots with feet,”** — certain vessels
**“POTS WITH FEET”** — Because they who teach not to steal, steal; and they who preach not to commit adultery, commit adultery: yet the doctrine is clean. Whence: Fountains etc.
11.36:
**“But fountains”** — rich doctrines
**“and cisterns,”** — tongues speaking middling things and having a borrowed doctrine
**“and all gatherings together of waters”** — an abundance of words gathered from wherever
**“shall be clean.”** — in itself
**“He that toucheth their carcasses shall be defiled.”** — as above. For what such men have said we ought to do, not what they have done.
11.37:
**“If it fall upon seed corn,”** — those to be baptized
**“it shall not defile it.”** — where ignorance excuses
11.38:
**“But if any man”** — the baptizer
**“with water”** — of baptism
**“pour upon the seed, and afterwards it be touched by the carcasses, it shall be forthwith defiled.”**
• Because: "They have no excuse."
• IF THEY FALL etc. HESYCHIUS. He leaves nothing undiscussed. He discusses all things to the perfection of the spiritual law, though it seem imperfect to those who look only at the letter of the law. He sets out therefore the difference of the unbelievers who are not yet baptized. They are called seed, whoever receive the preaching. Whence the Lord says: The good seed are the children of the kingdom. Seed corn is that which is to be sown: these are those not yet baptized, who are to be baptized. If a carcass fall upon these, because they have not yet received the caution of the mysteries, nor the whole knowledge of God, so as to be able to guard themselves from sins, they are said to be clean, because they are excused through ignorance. Upon whom the water of baptism has been poured, if any carcass whatever fall upon them, they become unclean.
11.39:
**“If dead”** — in sin
**“be any beast, of which it is lawful for you to eat,”** — that is, to be joined to the conversation of the living
**“he that toucheth the carcass thereof,”** — by imitating
**“shall be unclean until the evening:”** — until the heat of sin fail
11.40:
**“And he that eateth”** — shall defend
**“or carrieth any thing thereof, shall wash his clothes,”** — actions
**“and shall be unclean until the evening.”** — HE THAT TOUCHETH THE CARCASS etc. We ought to abhor the life of the wicked and imitate that of the just. For he who touches the life of the wicked will be unclean until he repent. He who eats, that is, defends it as an advocate and transfers it into himself by helping, let him wash his garments, that is, his wicked actions, until he repent.
11.41:
**“All that creepeth upon the earth”** — savouring earthly things
**“shall be abominable, neither shall it be taken for meat.”** — ALL THAT CREEPETH etc. The lawgiver set this out above, but repeats it, admonishing the hearer to frequent meditation of the law.
11.42:
**“Whatsoever upon the breast”** — others: upon the belly
**“goeth on four feet,”**
• abusing the preaching of the Gospels by living luxuriously
• given to gluttony
**“or hath many feet,”** — Affirming future salvation for himself even from other writings and varied doctrine.
**“or traileth on the earth, you shall not eat, because it is abominable.”** — to be avoided
11.43: **“Do not defile your souls, nor touch aught thereof, lest you be unclean,”** — as those things are, if you touch them
11.44:
**“For I am the Lord your God:”** — to whose image you are made, that you may savour heavenly things
**“be holy because I am holy. Defile not your souls”** — He notes that there is no defilement in dead bodies.
**“YOUR SOULS”** — In which is the image, which suffers no defilement nor is joined to weak animals, because they rule over all.
**“by any creeping thing, that moveth upon the earth.”** — it is good for a man to be humbled, but to decline to earthly wisdom is evil; whence he adds: that moveth upon the earth
11.45:
**“For I am the Lord, who brought you out of the land of Egypt,”** — from the evil works of darkness
**“that I might be your God.”** — to whom if you wish to cleave, you ought to be holy as I am:
11.47:
**“HESYCHIUS”**
• Whatever is made by God is clean by the very authority of its institution. For in the animals are painted the manners of men, their acts and wills, from which they become clean or unclean.
• He said to Noe: "Everything that moveth and liveth shall be meat for you" etc. In Genesis also it is said: God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good. But here certain things are forbidden as evil and are decreed unclean. Yet these are not contrary to one another: for the Lord both restrains the gluttony of the Jews for a while, and the spiritual exposition of the precepts instructs them what sort they ought to be. For the law, rationally understood, is the nourishment of the rational soul. And as in what went before he figured the offerers by the oblations, so now by the things that are eaten he expresses the eaters.
**“AND KNOW WHAT YOU OUGHT TO EAT”** — Not these foods cleanse or defile us, but we ourselves: for we give life to what is eaten; and as every food is good, and nothing to be rejected that is received with thanksgiving, so we give life to the things that are eaten, that is, that nourish the soul, namely good actions, if we use them well; if ill, we put them to death. For he who makes alms out of plunder puts it to death and takes away its power; and they who abstain from foods but slander their brethren put their abstinence to death.

12.2:
**“Speak to the children of Israel, and thou shalt say to them: If a woman having received seed”** — of the man
**“IF A WOMAN HAVING RECEIVED SEED”** — ISIDORE. The week is the present life, because in a week of days the world was completed, in which we cannot be wholly pure; but on the eighth day, that is, in the time of the world to come, he will be clean who has acted manfully. For his mother who has borne a male is made clean. But he who has had nothing manly, but has remained slack and effeminate, will be purged neither in the week of the present world nor in the future.
**“shall bear a man child,”** — He excepted her who conceived and bore without receiving seed.
**“she shall be unclean seven days, according to the days of the separation of her flowers.”** — SHE SHALL BE UNCLEAN etc. Because, namely, the sower is unclean, as heir of Adam, who was unclean through transgression, and so was mingled with his wife. For after he went out of paradise he knew his wife, and so the human race is propagated. Seven days: because Adam (from whose seed she receives uncleanness) defiled our life, which turns in the number of seven days. And he defiled life by bringing in the curse and misery and taking away blessedness. Whence: "Cursed is the earth in thy work" etc. Whence the lawgiver added: According to the days of the separation of her flowers. The Septuagint: According to the days of the separation and purging of her flowers. Symmachus: According to the days of the separation of affliction. Aquila: Of the separation of misery. Theodotion: Of the separation of her pain. And misery and affliction and pain began to be when Adam, separated from paradise, fell into this misery.
12.3: **“And on the eighth day the infant shall be circumcised:”** — ON THE EIGHTH DAY etc. The eighth day, since it succeeds the seventh, which is the image of the present life, is a figure of the world to come, in which we shall circumcise the flesh of the foreskin, laying aside all the works of the flesh, no more to sin nor eat nor drink nor marry, because we shall be "as the angels of God". For what "is sown in corruption shall rise in incorruption". It is sown a natural body, it shall rise a spiritual body. The uncircumcised shall perish from his people, because without circumcision the flesh is abominable and unclean. Circumcision therefore cleanses, in which the resurrection is foreshown. But it is to be noted that the law, commanding circumcision, was silent about its uncleanness. It called the mother unclean until the circumcision, perhaps because Eve was seduced by reason of disobedience; and disobedience brought on us uncleanness and filth.
12.4:
**“But she three and thirty days”** — that they may make forty, seven being added
**“shall remain”** — Septuagint: she shall sit, that is, she shall remain: for it was not that she might not rise for so many days.
**“in the blood of her purification.”** — not of defilement
12.5:
**“But if a maid child”** — who is fined double
**“she shall bear, she shall be unclean two weeks, according to the custom of her monthly courses, and she shall remain in the blood of her purification sixty-six days.”**
• THREE AND THIRTY DAYS etc. Seven being added, they make forty. In forty days the male is said to be formed. And two things are proved by these: that the substance of the human race is clean, because it was created by God; therefore he says that the woman sits in clean blood, or the blood of her purification; but because through the succession of Adam's transgression she received seed and conceived, she shall touch no holy thing, nor enter into the sanctuary, until the days of her purging be fulfilled, that is, the forty in which the child is formed. For by the image of God our nature is cleansed, though defiled. We are not commanded, therefore, to enter the sanctuary or touch the holy thing, except because the image of God, once given to our race, afforded entry to the holy things; for the saving of which the Lord was incarnate, and, forty days being fulfilled, he took it up to heaven, as he formed man in the womb, to whom he gave it: then our nature ascended to the true sanctuary. These things are plainly proved by what follows concerning the female sex: for since females are said to be formed in the womb on the eightieth day, he commanded the same number for the fulfilment of the purging or purification of those who receive seed, thus: If she shall bear a maid child, she shall be unclean etc. And it is to be noted that he would not say fourteen days, but two weeks, that in the seven days we may understand human life, and in the monthly flow its affliction, pain and misery. And he well said two weeks, because the female sex is fined double. For she has the whole curse of Adam, and there is added to her: In sorrow shalt thou bring forth children etc. She sits sixty-six days in the blood of her purification, until eighty be fulfilled. For fourteen added to sixty-six make eighty, in which the female is formed. Our race, therefore, defiled by the curse, does not enter into the holy things except through the image of God. For this reason women receiving seed are kept from the holy things during the days of the forming of their little ones; while they have them in the womb they ought not to be kept away. For it is uncertain whether they will bear a female or a male.
• EVERY HOLY THING etc. What does he wish the sanctuary to be understood as, since none but the priests might enter the tabernacle, and that as far as the second veil; and beyond the veil, where the ark was, the high priest alone went in? Perhaps the place before the tabernacle, where the altar of sacrifices is, could be called the sanctuary. For often the court too is called a holy place, as when it is said: In the holy place they shall eat them. Thither perhaps the women entered, offering their gifts to be laid upon the altar.
**“AUGUSTINE”** — What difference is there between the seven days in which he calls her unclean and the thirty-three in which she shall sit in clean blood? Is the difference this, that she is still in blood, though clean, so that it differs in this: that while she is unclean, wherever she sits she makes it unclean; but when she now sits in clean blood, only she may not touch what is holy and enter the sanctuary? For this is what he says: According to the days of the withdrawal of her purging; since he says elsewhere that the uncleanness of a woman who is purged by her monthly courses is of seven days, when everything upon which she sits shall be unclean. And he says of her withdrawal, since she withdrew somewhat, lest she defile all things, while she passed those days of her uncleanness. If she bore a female, the law doubles it, and made fourteen; the rest, in which she sat in clean blood, it also made double, sixty-six, so that in all there were forty for the birth of a male, eighty for a female.
12.6:
**“And when the days of her purification are expired, for a son, or for a daughter, she shall bring a lamb of a year old for a holocaust,”** — what these signify has been said above
**“and a young pigeon”** — the meditation of the law
**“or a turtle”** — contemplation
**“for sin, to the door of the tabernacle of the testimony, and shall deliver them to the priest:”** — AND WHEN THE DAYS ARE EXPIRED etc. He discloses his intention: namely, that natural motions do not cause defilement, but sin, of which David says: "For behold I was conceived in iniquities" etc., calling nature his mother, and signifying that the uncleanness of the sin of Adam and Eve descended into the whole human race. Therefore Moses, the days of purification being fulfilled, commanded a holocaust to be immolated for sin, plainly showing that the image of God gives perfection to our race. For the days of cleansing show the forming; the holocaust, the perfection.
**“AUGUSTINE”** — Is it a sin to have given birth? Or is that offspring from Adam shown here, of which the Apostle says: "From one unto condemnation", and that by one man sin entered into the world etc.? Whence: For I was conceived in iniquities etc. Why then does Scripture say not that what was born is purged, but she who bore it? The purging is referred to her from whom the origin was drawn, because of the fountain of blood; yet it could not be done without the purging of the offspring, which sprang from the blood. For to what does what he said above pertain: For a son or a daughter she shall offer a lamb of a year etc., if nothing was done by this sacrifice for those who were born? But if anyone tries to divide it, so as to say that it is not to be joined thus: For a son or a daughter she shall offer a lamb of a year etc., but rather to be read thus: When the days of her purging are fulfilled for a son or for a daughter; so that there follows, in another sense: She shall offer a lamb of a year without blemish for a holocaust, and a young pigeon for sin, that is, for her own sin, when the days of purging are fulfilled for a son or for a daughter; he who thinks it should be so divided will be refuted from the Gospel, where they did some such thing for the Lord born of the virgin, rather for the custom of the Law than for the need of expiating sin. Thus it is read: "To do for him according to the custom of the Law"; it is not said 'for his mother', but "for him", although those things were done which are commanded here concerning two turtles or two young pigeons. For so too he was baptized with the baptism of John, which was the baptism of penance for the remission of sins, though he had no sin. Rightly therefore some have interpreted this so as to say not 'over a son or over a daughter', but 'for a son or a daughter'. And it is to be noted how poor the Lord willed to be born: that for him there was offered not a lamb and a young pigeon or a turtle, but a pair of turtles or two young pigeons, according to the Gospel, which the Scripture of Leviticus then commanded to be offered if the hand of the offerer had not a lamb, which is great enough.
**“BEDE”** — Our Lord, though he was God, was made for us not only man but also poor, though he was rich, that he might grant us to be partakers of his riches and his divinity. And it is good to consider why these birds above all are commanded to be offered as a victim. For Abraham too, long before the law, offered them for a holocaust, and in very many ceremonies of the law he who is to be cleansed is commanded to be cleansed by them. The dove, then, indicates simplicity, the turtle chastity. For if the turtle by chance lose her mate, she seeks no other after. Whence in the Canticles: "Thy cheeks are beautiful as the turtledove's." And elsewhere: "Thy eyes are doves' eyes." Each bird has a moan for its song, and signifies in this the sorrow of the saints, to whom it is said: You shall lament and weep etc. You shall weep, but the world shall rejoice. The simple and modest conversation of the faithful, therefore, is a sacrifice pleasing to the Lord. And he who labours in groaning, who washes his couch with tears, slays a victim most acceptable to God. But because the turtle moans wandering alone, the dove in flocks, the one signifies the secret tears of prayers, the other the assemblies of the Church. The child Jesus is first circumcised, and after an interval of days is brought to Jerusalem with a victim; because, now a young man, he first trod down all corruption of the flesh by dying and rising again; then, after an interval of days, with that same flesh now immortal, which he made a victim for us, he ascended to the heavenly Jerusalem. And each one of us is first cleansed from all sins by the water of baptism, as by a true circumcision, and so, as the grace of the new light advances, enters to the holy altar to be hallowed by the victim of the body and blood of Christ, which, singularly simple and chaste, is figuratively expressed by the immolation of the dove and the turtle. The whole Church also at the end of the world will first put off by the common resurrection the stain of mortality and corruption, and afterwards, commended to the Lord by the victims of good works, will come to the heavenly Jerusalem.
12.7: **“Who shall offer them before the Lord, and shall pray for her, and so she shall be cleansed from the issue of her blood.”** — FROM THE ISSUE etc. As though someone should ask whence she shall be cleansed who has lawfully given birth, he says: from the issue of her blood, that is, disobedience, whence uncleanness and punishment flowed forth; through the meditation and contemplation of the law, the neglect of which brought uncleanness upon men.

13.1: **“AND THE LORD SPOKE”** — God speaks once, and two things are heard: Moses hears the Spirit, as the loftier; Aaron the letter, as the lower, who announces the letter to the people. Whence: He shall speak in thy stead to the people, and shall be thy mouth; but thou shalt be to him in those things that pertain to God.
13.2:
**“The man”** — THE MAN: sometimes is taken in the excellent sense, of him who keeps the image of God and the dignity of nature; sometimes of the sinner, in whom the dignity is disfigured, as here.
**“in whose flesh”**
• the inward
• by carnal pleasure
**“and skin”**
• the outward
• IN WHOSE FLESH etc. He carries leprosy in flesh and skin who strives to urge carnal or outward things, as the Corinthians, who think the resurrection to come will be in the pleasure of the flesh, and that sins are not imputed to those who remain in the faith, though they live carnally.
**“shall arise a different colour”** — Septuagint: a scar of signification, that is, sin in the flesh, which signifies that the soul suffers with the body.
**“OR AS IT WERE SOMETHING SHINING”** — One leprosy is very or moderately obscure, the passion not yet boiling over, which needs very much deliberation. Another is very clear and plain, whose knowledge is open.
**“that is, the stroke of the leprosy,”**
• which is the transgression of the law: for the leper is cast out of the tabernacle for the leprous part; so he who offends in one is guilty of all.
• He bears leprosy in the body who detracts from the Church, as the Carpocratians, who deny the resurrection of the flesh, and the Novatians, who condemn marriage and take away penance from those who sin.
**“THE STROKE OF THE LEPROSY”** — ISIDORE. Leprosy is false doctrine; the lepers are heretics, who, not having the unity of the true faith, profess various errors of doctrine, mingling true with false, and stain the Church as leprosy stains bodies by spreading.
**“OR ANY ONE”** — Of the kindred according to the spirit, from whom they have the priesthood, in whom is perfect and full philosophy, so that they can discern subtle things and the hidden motions of the soul.
13.3:
**“And if he see the leprosy in his skin, and the hair”** — that is: the thoughts into open knowledge of sin
**“THE HAIR”** — The thoughts by which the soul is adorned and the mind covered, by which they are begotten, as the head begets the hairs by which it is adorned and covered. Whence: The very hairs of your head are numbered. Hence the Nazarites do not shave the head, because they have no superfluous thoughts; but to lay aside holy ones is holy loss.
**“into white”** — the white leprosy is the darkened and ill-cleansed conscience of heretics
**“turned in colour, and the appearance of the leprosy itself lower than the skin and the rest of the flesh:”** — natural strength failing and weakness appearing
13.4:
**“But if there be a shining whiteness”** — suspicion of sin
**“in the skin, and not lower than the other flesh,”**
• than itself
• LOWER THAN THE FLESH etc. Lower than itself; whence rightly it does not merit pardon. For to be overcome by another greater is bearable; but not to work the good commanded by God (for the Lord divides as he will), so that one becomes worse than himself, this is unbearable.
**“and the hair”** — the thoughts
**“be of the former colour,”** — of the former manner
**“he shall shut him up”**
• for the sake of trial and amendment
• he shall not remove him, though the sin has come under suspicion
**“HE SHALL SHUT HIM UP”** — He is shut up a second time, that he may be studiously inspected, and that, a double trial being passed, a strict judgment may be made. For the sin was manifest to the priest, but he did not know whether the mind consented to the passion, but conjectured; therefore he inspected again. Hence the Lord after the denial asks a third time how Peter's mind stands, that we may not judge quickly but inquire often. He is shut up seven days. For the number seven signifies the fulness of the present life, which is passed in seven days; when that is completed, sin and servitude will cease. Whence the seventh is named rest in the divine Scriptures.
13.5: **“And the seventh day he shall look on him: and if the leprosy”** — of the spirit
13.6:
**“And on the seventh day, he shall look on him: if the leprosy be somewhat obscure,”** — by the iniquity by which we are darkened in mind
**“and not spread in the skin, he shall declare him clean,”** — as a physician
**“HE SHALL DECLARE HIM CLEAN”** — So Paul removed from the tabernacle of the saints, and delivered to Satan, him who committed fornication at Corinth, because the passion was manifest; whom, when he had inspected him a second time and seen him repent, he commanded to be received.
**“because it is but a scab: and he shall wash”** — by baptism or penance
13.7: **“But if, after by the priest”** — from whom sin is not hidden
13.10:
**“And he shall view him. And when there shall be a white colour in the skin,”**
• manifest prevarication
• AND WHEN THERE SHALL BE A WHITE COLOUR etc. The manifest transgression of the letter of the law which is proper to the Jews, as in sacrifices and purifications and the like. For there is also one common to the Gentiles, concerning adultery, robbery, avarice and the like.
**“and it shall have changed the look of the hair,”** — things done from the zeal of the mind
**“and the living flesh itself shall appear:”** — because he offends the law in some point
13.11:
**“It shall be judged an inveterate leprosy,”** — because he grows old in sin and is not corrected, because he carries on a continual quarrel within himself, while he partly defends the law and partly despises it.
**“and grown into the skin. The priest therefore shall declare him unclean, and shall not shut him up, because he is evidently unclean.”** — He shall show him defiled, he shall not shut him up, because the uncleanness is manifest.
13.12:
**“But if spring out”** — through the whole
**“the leprosy, running about”** — the prevarication of the law
**“in the skin,”** — because it is the transgression of the sabbath, of circumcision or of such things: for the letter restrains the outward man, it does not hurt the soul.
**“BUT IF IT SPRING OUT”** — HESYCHIUS. He shows the Jewish people to be leprous in part, as a transgressor of the law in part; whence the priest expels him as unclean. But the Gentile, leprous in the whole body, who transgresses the whole law, he does not expel, but judges him clean, because he was not subject to the yoke of the law.
**“JEROME”** — But if it spring out etc. In this leprosy, as it were flowering and white, he designates divers crimes. For when the pleasure of worldly life is reckoned as it were white and flowering, then the grievous contagion of vices rages in the body: for the spots either of avarice or of lust lie open. But the crime of avarice can easily be cut away. Whence: Give alms, and all things are clean unto you. Lust also is cleansed by fasts and abstinence. But let healing be applied to all through the priest. For one is cleansed by the oblations of sacrifices; another is that which is cleansed more easily; another that which is cleansed when set without the camp; another that which is not cleansed at all.
**“and cover all the flesh from the head to the feet,”** — so that one wholly departs from the letter of the law from the head to the feet, that is, from the first to the last commandment
13.13:
**“The priest shall view him,”** — Christ, whom it pleases
**“and shall judge that the leprosy which he has is very clean: because it is all into whiteness”** — the brightness of the conversation of the Gospel, according to that: "Let your light shine before men."
**“turned, and therefore the man shall be clean.”** — the filth of the law being left behind
13.14: **“But when the live flesh shall appear in him,”** — LIVE FLESH etc. The Jewish commandment, which is said to live as far as the commandment goes, or because, well understood, it brings life.
13.15: **“Then by the judgment of the priest he shall be defiled, and shall be reckoned among the unclean: for live flesh, if it be spotted with leprosy, is unclean.”** — FOR LIVE FLESH, IF WITH LEPROSY etc. ISIDORE. He bears leprosy in the live flesh who holds anything false concerning the soul, which is the life of the flesh; as the Luciferians, who say the soul is propagated from the substance of the flesh, and the Arabians, who think the soul dies with the body.
13.16:
**“And if again it be turned into whiteness,”** — into the spiritual understanding
**“and cover all the man,”** — so that he retains nothing of the carnal law
13.18:
**“When also the flesh and the skin in which an ulcer”** — sin
**“has been, and it has been healed,”** — through penance
13.19:
**“And in the place of the ulcer,”** — in the action or counsel by which sin is carried on
**“there appeareth a scar,”** — A SCAR etc. ISIDORE. They bear leprosy in the scar of a healed wound who, after the knowledge of the faith and the medicine of God which they receive in Christ, show again some token of error or of the faithlessness of old doctrine.
**“white, or somewhat red,”**
• the following of sin
• bright and manifest
**“WHITE”** — Because it is from the wound of the transgression of the law: for the law is white, and not warmed by the sun of justice.
**“SOMEWHAT RED”** — Because it is from prevarication of the Gospel, as to eat what is offered to idols, or blood, or what is strangled; and both are done against Christ, whose are the Law and the Gospel.
13.20:
**“And when he shall see the place of the leprosy lower than the other flesh,”** — that is, the mind lower or inferior to itself
**“and the hair turned white,”** — that is, the mind manifestly changed to malice
**“HE SHALL DECLARE HIM UNCLEAN”** — Because the sin is in habit, and an evil feeding upon the soul has settled through the ulcer. Whence he called it leprosy blossoming from the wound.
13.21:
**“But if the hair”** — of the penitent
**“be of the former colour, and the scar somewhat obscure, and be not lower than the flesh that is near it, he shall shut him up seven days.”** — in which the suspicion may be settled
13.22:
**“And if it spread,”**
• or: shall spring out
• that is: shall have proclaimed and multiplied his sin
**“he shall judge him to have the leprosy:”** — to the uncleanness which grew by later action
13.23:
**“But if it stay in its place,”** — so that he sins no more over this of which he repents
**“it is but the scar of an ulcer,”** — which shows what he has suffered, not what he suffers; whence Rahab is still called the harlot, Paul the persecutor.
13.24:
**“The flesh also and skin that fire”** — of envy
**“hath burnt, and after it is healed hath a white”** — through penance
**“or a red scar,”**
• from wrath and murder
• THE FLESH ALSO etc. He seems to repeat what was said above, but says partly the same things and partly adds; for he sets down another passion but the same token. For he treated of the ulcer which is begotten and grows by some sickness of neglected flesh. The ulcer of our flesh, then, is pleasure, drunkenness, gluttony and the like, which arise from the body running riot and itching in itself. But now he treats of a greater stroke, that is, the burning of fire; of which it is said: Fire shall consume the adversaries.
13.25:
**“The priest shall view it, and if he see it turned white, and the place thereof is lower than the other skin: he shall declare him unclean,”** — he shall judge him defiled
**“BECAUSE THE EVIL OF LEPROSY IN THE SCAR”** — The Manichaeans have leprosy in the scar of a burning, who burn their bodies in the torment of abstinence, and through unbelief beget thence not cleanness but leprosy.
13.26: **“But if the colour of the hair be not changed,”** — that is: if he has not returned to iniquity
13.27:
**“And on the seventh day he shall view him: if be grown”** — by later action
**“meanwhile the leprosy, he shall declare him unclean.”** — he shall judge him defiled
13.28: **“But if the whiteness stay in its place, and be not very clear, it is the sore of a burning, and therefore he shall be cleansed.”** — he shall be judged clean
13.29:
**“A MAN OR WOMAN”** — He namely who errs concerning the divinity, as the heretics, who not only deny the Father to be the maker of the world, but even affirm him the author of evils, as Manes.
**“in whose head”** — Christ, whom the age of a perfect man adorned
**“OR THE BEARD”** — ISIDORE. They bear leprosy in the beard who think perversely of the apostles and disciples of Christ and feign to preach false things: for the beard is the ornament of a man, and the apostles are the doctors of the body of Christ.
**“ISIDORE”**
• We find that the lawgiver set down six kinds of leprosy. The first is of the head and beard. The second, of the bald forehead and the bald crown. The third, of the flesh and skin. The fourth, of the skin and body and of the white scar with redness. The fifth, of the ulcer and scar. The sixth, of the ulcer in the head. He bears leprosy in the head who sins concerning the divinity of the Father, or concerning the head itself, which is Christ. For the head of Christ is God, the head of man is Christ. This the Jews and the Valentinians bear, who bear leprosy in the bald place also, because they defend the faithlessness of their error with open wickedness.
• He sets down divers colours of leprosy: pale, red and white, livid, black, and flowering. The pale marks a feeble and frail faith, when one, the colour of whole health being lost, languishes with the sickness of error. The red shows a mind stained with the blood of murder. The white, heretics who call themselves clean, or who glory in false virtues. The livid, envy. The black, a conscience blackened with the smoke of idolatry. The flowering over the whole body signifies avarice, which stains every kind of men, as it were the whole body. There is also a leprosy which has redness with paleness, namely wrath and fury with weakness of mind. For some faint-hearted men are lightly angered, forswear themselves, lie. And paleness signifies a lying tongue and weakness.
13.30:
**“And if the place be lower than the other flesh,”** — a more wretched presumption from blasphemy
**“and the hair yellow, and thinner than usual: he shall declare them unclean, because it is the leprosy of the head and the beard;”** — that is: if he has bent his mind a little to blasphemy; so the hair is thin, and does not flower but grows yellow.
13.31:
**“But if he perceive the place of the spot is equal”** — so that rash impiety did not show itself
**“with the flesh that is near it,”** — because it often happens that one speaks impious things against his will
**“and the hair black: he shall shut him up seven days,”** — HE SHALL SHUT HIM UP etc. Not so much for punishment as for the sake of strict trial: for time is to be kept in all cases, and more strictly in those whose tongue runs unbridled about the divinity.
13.32:
**“And on the seventh day he shall look upon it. If the spot be not grown,”** — the impiety
**“and the hair keep its colour, and the place of the blemish be even with the other flesh:”** — For the thought cannot be known, whether he acted impiously of his own will or against it.
13.33: **“The man shall be shaven all but the place of the spot,”** — that is, let his other words be considered, that it may be known whether he spoke by surprise, as is wont to happen, or malignly and impiously.
13.34:
**“If on the seventh day the evil seem to have stayed”** — the impiety
**“IF ON THE SEVENTH DAY”** — Because the word in which one offends, if he who sinned once denies it, ought not to be judged: for who judges him guilty who denies that he uttered with his will what he confessed with his tongue?
**“and not lower than the other flesh, he shall cleanse him, and being washed”** — through penance
**“his clothes”** — because he defiled the stole of baptism
**“he shall be clean.”** — AND HIS CLOTHES BEING WASHED HE SHALL BE CLEAN etc. JEROME. Some things committed before baptism are washed away in baptism. Others are committed after baptism, which, whether they be graver or lesser, the sight of the priest yet cleanses: for what is slight can be loosed by the priest with pardon. What are graver are to be purged by ecclesiastical discipline and prayer. What are incurable are reserved to God the judge. Hence it is that each one is commanded to offer for his cleansing according to what he has, that is, according as he knows himself to have offended, let him not cease to make satisfaction as he can. There is a leprosy which cannot be cleansed at all, and therefore must be driven out of the camp. This is the crime of blasphemy, which is committed against the Holy Ghost, of which it is said: "He that hath sinned against the Holy Ghost, it shall not be forgiven him" etc.
13.35: **“But if after his cleansing the spot spread again in the skin,”** — so that he speaks impiously again
13.36:
**“He shall seek no more whether the hair”** — with what mind he spoke impious things
**“be turned yellow, because he is evidently unclean.”** — because he is returned to his vomit
13.37:
**“But if the spot be stayed, and the hair be black,”** — that mourning may go forth from the mind, as the hair from the head
**“THE HAIR BLACK”** — That is: if he has mourned his impiety and done true penance: for mourners and penitents are disfigured with black garments.
13.38: **“If a whiteness appear in the skin of a man or a woman,”** — because this stroke does not reach the soul
13.39:
**“The priest shall view them. If he find that a darkish whiteness”** — ignorance of the things of the law
**“shineth in the skin, let him know that it is not the leprosy,”** — because these were not given for justification but for servitude
**“but a white blemish, and that the man is clean.”** — A MAN OR WOMAN etc. HESYCHIUS. In the prevarication of divine doctrine, using very great distinction, he deals more mildly when speaking of the doctrines of the Jewish law, whose transgression he calls a darkish and shining whiteness.
