As therefore we call the transgression of the letter of the law a white scar, so let us call ignorance of it a darkish whiteness: not wholly, that is, nor of those things that are common with the law of the Gospel or with the natural law. For these are not venial; but of certain partial and small commandments, such as of the cleansing of a woman in her courses, of the offering of one after childbirth. This ignorance, therefore, as a small scar, he called a darkish whiteness; he who has such ignorance has no need to be cleansed. For these things do not pertain to justice. Whence God gave them precepts that were not good, and judgments in which they shall not live.
13.40:
**“The man from whose head”** — the mind
**“the hair falleth off,”** — the thoughts grow thin
**“he is bald and clean:”**
• without the doubleness of fraud
• BALD AND CLEAN. Simple, not foolish: for there is no one to whom at least a few hairs do not remain.
13.41:
**“And if the hair fall from his forehead, he is bald before”** — that is: If in the fore part, through simplicity, he has betrayed the glory of virtues which it were better to hide, the passion is tolerable and near to pardon.
**“and clean.”** — namely if he sins from simplicity
13.42:
**“But if in the bald head”** — in simplicity of every kind
**“or in the bald forehead”** — in part
**“a white”** — because it is against the rule of the law
**“or reddish colour be risen,”** — because it is against the Gospel
13.43:
**“And the priest perceive this, he shall condemn him”** — For no one is so simple as not to know evil.
**“undoubtedly”** — or: doubtfully
**“of leprosy”** — or: pre; and est is redundant
**“which is risen in the bald part.”** — of simplicity
13.45:
**“Shall have his clothes hanging loose,”** — because the virtues are dissolved
**“his head bare,”** — because he has lost the helmet of salvation
**“his mouth covered with a cloth,”**
• lest by speaking he spread the stench of sin, lest he presume to teach
• WHOSOEVER THEREFORE etc. ISIDORE. Heretics are cast out of the Church until they are purged. With tunics unsewn, that is, with their secrets made manifest, they are commanded to sit. With head bared, that their nakedness may be seen by all. With mouth shut, that they may speak impious things no further.
**“and he shall cry out that he is defiled and unclean.”**
• with the intention of the heart
• by confessing his sin
13.46:
**“All the time that he is a leper and unclean, he shall dwell alone without the camp.”** — that he may be confounded, and that he may not spread the infection to others; whence: "Let him be to thee as the heathen and the publican."
**“HE SHALL DWELL WITHOUT THE CAMP”** — So John shuts the intelligible leper out of the intelligible dwelling: He that bringeth not this doctrine, receive him not into the house, nor say to him, God speed you.
**“HESYCHIUS”** — These things are ridiculous interpreted according to the letter: for why is the leper cast out of the camp, who rather needs comfort and mercy? Because he is wretched, why are his clothes unsewn, his head bared, his mouth veiled? But the leper is the sinner, whose loosened garments signify the loosened virtues of the soul, which could have kept it from the heat and frost of sin. The head is bared, because the helmet of salvation is lost. The mouth is covered, lest by speaking a horrid odour be spread, and lest he presume to teach others whose folly appears, lest it be said to him: "Thou that preachest that men should not steal, stealest"; "But to the sinner God hath said: Why dost thou declare my justices?" etc.
13.47:
**“a garment”**
• the body
• the garments of the soul ought always to be clean; whence Solomon: "At all times let thy garments be white."
**“woollen”** — which is more useful
**“or linen”** — which is less
13.48:
**“In the warp,”**
• the soul
• divine grace
• IN THE WARP etc. JEROME. The warp is the soul, which, while it is twisted by the spindle of temptation into the fineness of threads, is drawn tight by the solidity of a firmer virtue. The soul therefore stands erect like the warp; the sense of the body lies beneath like the woof: some are sins of the body, others of the soul.
**“and the woof,”**
• the sense of the body
• our intention
• A WOOLLEN GARMENT etc. HESYCHIUS. Woollen: things precious and warming the soul; linen: things cheap and little warm. Woollen is virginity; linen, conjugal chastity. Woollen: to renounce the world, to live the philosophic life in the desert, to strive for the truth even unto death. Linen: largeness in possessions, honesty or modesty in civil life. Whence: "She hath sought wool and flax" etc. And: "She hath made for herself clothing of tapestry" etc. And garments are of warp and woof. The woof is our intention. For the grace of God stands, into which our intention is woven, that a precious garment may be made, namely virtues and good works.
**“HESYCHIUS”** — Those who attend only to the letter wonder why the lawgiver speaks of the warp and the woof and leaves aside the things that can edify, saying: What do the warp or the woof or such leprosy pertain to the edification of the soul, or what harm do they do? Let us seek therefore the fruit of understanding which lies hid under the leaves of the vine. For so far does the lawgiver cultivate us, even concerning that which is wont to befall about the virtues.
**“or a skin, or whatsoever is made of a skin,”**
• Leprosy in a linen garment: perversity of manners in a bitter mind, whence some rage as if for justice, and drag the sinner more to despair than to health. Leprosy in a woollen garment signifies those who for flattery will not correct offenders, but consent, or who live softly. Leprosy in the warp: as the warp sustains the woven work, so the soul sustains the body. Leprosy in the woof: the sins which are committed through the body: for the soul is in the body as the warp in the woof. The skin is the outward carnal conversation; whence the Lord made garments of skins for our first parents after the sin. Leprosy in the skin: an evil example in the conversation of this life.
• A SKIN OR WHATSOEVER etc. The temptation of tribulation, which mortifies a man; but as of a dead skin some useful thing is made, so of things mortified are made patience, humility and proof. He forbids therefore that in perfect virtue (which is the garment), great or middling (which is the woollen or linen), a spot be found white or red, in the warp and in the woof; he desires us also to bear temptations without these. If any such thing has befallen, let the priest inspect it, and not at once repel it, nor proudly decree it unclean from suspicion, nor rashly receive it as clean.
13.49:
**“If it be infected with a white or red spot,”** — IF A WHITE etc. Septuagint: Greenish and flaming, that is, pride, which flowers for a little; whence: As the green herbs they shall quickly fall; or vainglory. For Christ wills the virtues to be without vainglory.
**“infected, it shall be accounted the leprosy,”** — not: it shall be judged
13.50: **“And he shall look upon it and shall shut it up seven days:”** — doing nothing proudly, nothing without discretion
13.52:
**“And therefore it shall be burnt”**
• in the judgment to come
• he hints at the time to come
**“with fire.”** — signifying the flames of hell
13.54:
**“He shall give orders, and they shall wash”** — through penance
**“that part wherein the leprosy is, and he shall shut it up other seven days.”**
• after the washing
• that he may discover whether the spot of pride or vainglory remains
13.55:
**“And when he shall see that the former colour is not returned,”** — that is: has not passed over to penance
**“nor yet the leprosy spread, he shall judge it unclean, and shall burn it with fire,”** — because he is not corrected
13.56:
**“But if somewhat dark”** — namely an uncertain and doubtful leprosy
**“HE SHALL TEAR IT OFF”** — By penance he shall cut away the passion: pride is torn off when humility is applied; vainglory, when flattery and vain praise are removed.
**“and divide it from that which is sound.”** — from the garment of solid virtue
13.57:
**“And if after this”** — after the washing and penance
**“there appear in those places that before were without spot,”** — in the garments, the warp, and the other things aforesaid
**“a flying and wandering leprosy: it must with fire”** — of hell
**“be burnt.”** — A FLYING AND WANDERING LEPROSY etc. Sometimes we know that we have done evil and shun it. But that very fault creeps into other acts which held us in others. For there are some who, subject to carnal uncleanness, return to themselves, acknowledge their guilt, and when they have corrected themselves are puffed up by the good of chastity; and those whom the uncleanness of the deed held in the body, the uncleanness of pride holds in the mind. For the flying leprosy has not fully left the garment, but has changed its place. And each faithful one is a garment of the Church. So he who is proud of riches, being corrected, distributes all to the poor, but takes pride thence in his heart, and the flying leprosy has changed its place. Another, often given to immoderate words and unseemly mirth, is rebuked by a preacher, and while he wishes to be grave and is immoderately restrained from joy, he becomes wrathful. The vice of unseemly mirth, therefore, through immoderate restraint passes over into the vice of wrath.
13.58:
**“If it cease, he shall wash”** — For once cleansed, he wishes to be washed again, that he may be seen to be cleansed.
**“the parts that are pure, the second time,”** — by a second penance

14.1:
**“SPOKE”** — Because he has taught how to purify the spots springing up among the virtues, he adds how the leper is cured; where he shows that above he treated of the leprosy of the soul.
**“the Lord to Moses”** — alone
14.2:
**“This is the rite of a leper,”**
• simply
• THE LORD SPOKE TO MOSES. Note that he speaks the things concerning cleansings to Moses alone, not to Aaron as well. For he signifies chiefly Christ, who alone cleanses all leprosy. For here he treats not of a special but of a general leprosy; whence he says simply: This is the rite of a leper; for he cured every sin.
**“when he is to be cleansed: he shall be brought to the priest:”** — Christ
14.3:
**“Who going out of the camp”** — Christ came to us, who were without the camp
**“when he shall find that the leprosy is cleansed,”** — us, namely, cleansed from error, that is, ready to be cleansed
14.4:
**“Shall command him that is to be purified, to offer for himself two living sparrows,”** — TWO SPARROWS. Namely the divinity and humanity of Christ; which is clean, because he had no sin, and living, because it was not liable to death from sin.
**“which it is lawful to eat,”** — WHICH IT IS LAWFUL TO EAT etc. Because: "The Word was made flesh", and: Unless we eat the flesh of the Son of man, we shall not have life in us.
**“CEDAR WOOD”** — The cross, which is strong against all things, as the cedar is strong and incorruptible.
**“and scarlet,”** — an incorrupt mind and a steadfast faith
**“SCARLET”** — Septuagint: Twisted scarlet, namely the passion, because scarlet is red; twisted, woven together of passibility and impassibility.
**“and hyssop.”** — the prayer of the saints
**“HYSSOP”** — The grace of the Holy Ghost, which works together with our cleansing. Whence: "Thou shalt sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed" etc.
14.5:
**“And one of the sparrows”** — that namely which is passible and can be slain
**“he shall command to be immolated in an earthen vessel”** — for us, who were made of clay
**“over living waters:”** — OVER WATERS etc. Of baptism. All we who are baptized in Christ are baptized in his death.
14.6:
**“But the other that is alive, with the cedar wood, and the scarlet”** — with martyrdom
**“and the hyssop, he shall dip in the blood of the sparrow that is immolated:”** — HE SHALL DIP IN THE BLOOD etc. Because all things are comprehended in the power of baptism. The living sparrow is dipped in the blood of the slain sparrow, because we are baptized not in the passion of a man only, but of God and man.
14.7:
**“SEVEN TIMES”** — For the sevenfold Spirit, in whom is all cleansing and remission. Or that the soul may be purged of seven devils.
**“and he shall let go the sparrow”** — the impassible divinity
**“AND HE SHALL LET GO THE SPARROW”** — Because in a manner it is held under the contemplation of the human understanding.
**“living, that into the field”** — the breadth of contemplation
14.8:
**“And when he hath washed”** — by penance
**“HIS CLOTHES”** — Works, and whatever virtues he had, because sin defiles these also.
**“he shall shave all the hair of his body,”** — the thoughts, which were all unclean
**“and washed with water.”** — of tears or of baptism
**“AND BEING PURIFIED”** — Truly; yet above it was said that the leprosy was cleansed, but it is to be understood thus: fit to be cleansed.
**“he shall enter into the camp, yet so that he tarry”** — because he is advanced little by little to better things
**“without his own tent”**
• in which he sups with God as the bride with the bridegroom
• the attaining of the mysteries
**“WITHOUT THE TENT”** — The fellowship of the saints, from which sinners are shut out. Whence: With such a one not so much as to eat.
14.9:
**“THE HAIR”** — The thoughts which afford adornment to a man, as rational and debating many things, as the hairs of the head do.
**“and his beard”** — which contains discernment: for the beard is a distinction between the two sexes.
**“AND HIS EYEBROWS”** — Which set the contemplative man upon lofty and more divine things; which the eyebrows, set in the higher parts, signify.
**“and the hair of all his body.”** — OF ALL HIS BODY etc. Even of the privy parts, that nothing of the old thoughts may remain, that, wholly new and as it were newborn, he may put off the old man and put on the new. For as new hairs succeed when the hairs are shaved, so new thoughts sprout toward better things when the old are shaved.
**“And having washed”** — by penance, not by baptism: for there is "one Lord, one faith, one baptism".
14.10:
**“ON THE EIGHTH DAY”** — On which the Lord rose, on which the leper enters the camp, which the patriarch Jacob saw when the angels met him; whence he called the place the camp of God.
**“On the eighth day”** — After he commanded sacrifice to be offered without the camp for the cleansing of the leper on the first day, on which the priest goes out, on the eighth day he substitutes other sacrifices. For these have the same force as the first, because all time is bounded in weeks. The eighth, therefore, is also the first which follows. And it is to be noted that he shows leprosy, that is, sin, to be shunned above all, since he commands it to be purged so carefully.
**“he shall take two lambs without blemish,”**
• Whence: "It shall be a lamb without blemish, a male, of one year."
• LAMBS WITHOUT BLEMISH etc. All these figure the sacrifices of the Saviour, who was a victim for us. The sacrifice is made of both sexes, because he saved both sexes.
**“JEROME”** — In the two lambs, the two comings of Christ, by which we must believe that we are cleansed from the leprosy of sins: for first he came and suffered; secondly he will come in glory.
**“OF A YEAR OLD”** — He commands the sacrifice to be of a year, as perfect: for in the aforesaid animals those of a year are perfect; whence also they are then fit for generation.
**“AND THREE TENTHS”** — For he who is cleansed in the sacrifice of the Only-begotten ought to be signed with faith in the Trinity: three tenths, namely in the Trinity, the Father and the Son and the Holy Ghost, having perfection in each person: for the number ten is perfect.
**“OF THE FLOUR”** — Of the Only-begotten. For though the passion was the Only-begotten's, yet the work is of the whole Trinity. Whence we are baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost, while we are baptized in the death of Christ.
**“for a sacrifice, tempered with oil,”** — because he suffered for us mercifully
**“ISIDORE”** — There is a leprosy of sin which is cleansed by the oblations of sacrifices, that is, by a contrite and humbled heart; there is one of idolatry, which is washed away by the water of baptism; there is one of heretics, who are kept without the camp seven days, that they may be purged by the knowledge of the sevenfold Spirit; there is a leprosy which is taken away by the sight of the priest through doctrine. But there is one which cannot be cleansed at all, namely of those who sin against the Holy Ghost and will not repent and obtain pardon.
**“and a sextary of oil apart.”**
• Septuagint: a cotyle
• because faith is from the mercy and grace of God
**“A SEXTARY OF OIL”**
• Because each of the aforesaid things is understood and done by faith. For a sextary is a measure, holding neither more nor less: for what is more is poured out; if it is less, it is not a sextary. So faith is given to the measure of our mind, and holds neither more nor less than is distributed by God: for what is more or less is outside faith.
• The fatness of God's mercy and grace; and though he could not show the most bright face of holiness, let him not put out the lamp of faith.
14.11: **“And when the priest that purifieth the man, hath presented him, and all these things before the Lord,”** — because he who is cleansed is brought to the entrance of the knowledge of God
14.12:
**“He shall take a lamb,”** — Christ
**“and offer it for a trespass offering”** — of him whose ears are leprous
14.13: **“He shall immolate the lamb, where the victim for sin is wont to be immolated, and the holocaust, that is, in the holy place: for as that which is for sin, so also that for a trespass pertaineth to the priest”** — the true one
14.14:
**“UPON THE TIP”** — That it may fortify the hearing and make it wary, that it may no more hear the voice of the serpent.
**“AND OF HIS FOOT”** — That our movement and way may be directed in the sight of God. For when these aforesaid are guarded through the blood of the Lamb and faith in him, which is given us through his mercy and compassion, the intelligible leprosy is put to flight.
14.16: **“AND SPRINKLE IT SEVEN TIMES”** — Such a priest is confident with God, since he could cleanse and forgive; whence he sprinkles seven times, because it is the number of remission and grace.
14.17:
**“And the rest of the oil in his left hand,”** — as was said above
**“he shall pour upon the tip of the right ear of him that is cleansed,”** — AND THE REST etc. That the faith of the priest may be shown in works. For it does not exert its force otherwise than with the hand taken up, that is, confirmed and sealed by action. And he puts oil into the left hand, and dips the right finger in the oil, that he may walk by the armour of justice on the right hand and on the left, by honour and dishonour, by evil report and good report.
14.18: **“And upon his head.”** — in the head he signifies the whole body; and he shows by this anointing that he who is cleansed is Christ's, God's
14.19: **“And he shall pray for him before the Lord, and shall offer the sacrifice for sin:”** — AND SHALL OFFER THE SACRIFICE etc. By what has been said of trespasses the things that are for sin can be established: for they are neighbouring and common, as in a common matter.
14.20: **“And put it on the altar with the libations thereof, and the man shall be rightly cleansed.”** — THE HOLOCAUST etc. The sacrifice of Christ first cleanses us from trespasses and sins, and then our holocaust is made. For when, sanctifying our body and soul by intelligible cleansing, we have been made spiritual, then we are made worthy of the ascent of the altar: for then we receive full cleansing and need no other. For there are degrees of cleansings: one frees from the defilement of leprosy, another brings into the camp, another presents those most fully cleansed at the altar.
14.21:
**“But if poor”** — weak in body or in mind
**“he be, and his hand cannot”** — though he would, because either old or infirm
**“find the things aforesaid:”** — sacrifices fit for strict penance
**“he shall take a lamb”** — for the penitent must before all things be kind
**“for an offering for trespass, that the priest may pray for him, and a tenth part of flour tempered with oil”**
• He who abstains from evil things has a tenth part of fine flour tempered with oil.
• the theology of Christ, who mercifully tempered himself to our flesh.
**“for a sacrifice, and a sextary of oil,”** — faith
14.22:
**“And two turtles or two young pigeons,”**
• These are easily found.
• continence
• the meditation of the Law: these draw back both body and soul from earthly works, as do the things done in strict penance; whence they are brought in in their place.
14.23:
**“And he shall offer them on the eighth day of his purification to the priest, at the door of the tabernacle of the testimony before the Lord.”**
• BUT IF HE BE POOR etc. JEROME. If he has not the riches of heavenly anointings (for example), if he could not keep virginity, let him keep the marriage bed undefiled; if he could not bear the trophy of martyrdom, let him at least keep himself unconquered.
• BUT IF HE BE POOR etc. He condescends wonderfully, granting pardon to poverty; he commands sacrifices suited to the poor man, lest he be dismayed if sacrifices beyond his strength be required. Yet who has not bread or money wherewith to buy a lamb or a dove or a turtle? By occasion of these, therefore, we are called to spiritual things, that we may understand leprosy as malice, penance as cleansing. Works of penance are necessary which may avail to blot out sins. Whence: Bring forth fruits worthy of penance. But there are many who cannot pay what the strictness of penance requires. For it requires assiduous prayer, alms, vigils, holy fasting, and that he can say: My tears have been my bread day and night. And: "Every night I will wash my bed: I will water my couch with my tears" etc. And: "I did eat ashes like bread" etc. He pardons those who will but cannot, and seeks out another way of penance, that is, other kinds of sacrifices.
14.25:
**“And the lamb being immolated,”** — before the Lord
**“he shall put of the blood thereof upon the tip of the ear”** — that the hearing may be clean
**“right, of him that is cleansed, and upon the thumb of his hand”** — that the works may be clean
**“and of his right foot:”** — lest he walk to evil
14.27: **“And dipping the finger of his right hand in it, he shall sprinkle it seven times”** — that he may receive the Holy Ghost, or that seven devils may be cast out
14.28: **“And he shall touch the tip of the right ear of him that is cleansed, and the thumb of his right hand and the great toe of his right foot, in the place of the blood that was shed for trespass.”** — HE SHALL PUT UPON THE TIP etc. ORIGEN. You see how it belongs to the last and highest purification that the ear be purified, that the hearing may be kept pure and clean; and the right hand, that the works may be clean, mixed with no filth; and the feet, that they may be directed only to good work, and incur no further the slip of youth. The priest sprinkles of the oil seven times before the Lord: for after all things that were celebrated for the purification, after he has been converted and reconciled to God, after the victims were immolated, it was in order that the power of the sevenfold Spirit should enter into him, according to that: "Restore unto me the joy of thy salvation, and strengthen me with a perfect spirit." Or since the Lord testifies in the Gospel that the hearts of sinners are besieged by seven devils, he fittingly sprinkles seven times before the Lord in the purification, that the expulsion of the seven wicked spirits from the heart of the purified may be declared by the oil shaken seven times from the fingers. So therefore purification is given to those converted from sin through all the aforesaid things; and the gift of the grace of the Spirit is given, which is designated by the image of oil, that he who is converted from sin may not only obtain purification, but, filled with the Holy Ghost, may receive the first robe and the ring, and be restored in all things as a son to the Father.
14.33:
**“And the Lord spoke to Moses”** — the Law
**“and Aaron”**
• the Prophets
• because these things pertain to both
14.34:
**“When you shall be come into the land of Chanaan,”** — of the Gentiles, which were promised to Abraham, according to that: I have made thee a father of many nations etc.
**“which I will give you for a possession,”** — to those preaching the Law and prophecy, as to the apostles, who taught the Gentiles
**“if there be the plague of leprosy in a house,”**
• the household churches
• the congregations of heretics
14.35:
**“He whose house it is, shall go and tell”** — as Nympha or Priscilla
**“the priest,”** — Peter or Paul, who could judge sins
**“saying: as it were the plague of leprosy”** — of impious doctrine
**“it seemeth to me there is in my house,”** — the Church
**“CHANAAN”** — HESYCHIUS. The land of the Chanaanites was promised to Abraham, which seven nations possessed, signifying the unclean spirits; of which it is said: He taketh seven other spirits more wicked than himself, and they dwell there. The Gentiles which were promised to Abraham possess his land, to whom it was said: I have made thee a father of many nations. When therefore Moses and Aaron, that is, the Law and the Prophets, enter among the Gentiles, God through them expels the intelligible Chanaanites and gives them the land for an inheritance, that there the Law and Prophecy may reign, and those who preach them. Then he whose house it is goes and tells the priest that leprosy seems to be in his house. Such houses are the household churches of individuals. Whence Paul: Salute Priscilla and Aquila, and the church in their house. He goes therefore to the priest, who has the judgment of discernment. For sometimes he whose house it is is not a priest, which is plain there: Salute Nympha, and the church in her house.
14.36: **“And he shall command, that they carry forth all things out of the house, before he go into it,”** — that is: Let those who were in the house withdraw and show themselves free of that evil, lest they become partakers of the punishment; for this is what he says: "Lest all things become unclean that are in the house."
14.37:
**“And if he see in the walls”** — the divers orders by which the Church is sustained; whence James and John and Cephas are called pillars of the Church, as ministers of the sacred things and doctors.
**“thereof as it were little dints,”** — namely the repute of the ministers growing vile and made lower by sin
**“with paleness or redness,”** — Septuagint: with greenness, that is, vainglory, which vanishes quickly like grass.
14.38: **“He shall go out of the door of the house, and forthwith shut it up seven days,”** — correcting with moderate rebuke, that the penitent may merit pardon and be absolved: for the number seven signifies pardon in the sevenfold Spirit.
14.39: **“And returning on the seventh day, he shall look upon it. If he find that the leprosy is spread,”** — the doctrines of impiety
14.40:
**“WITHOUT THE CITY”** — Not only without the house, because they are to be cast out of the universal Church, which is the city of the living God.
**“into an unclean place:”** — among the heretics, who receive all the works or doctrines of impiety
14.41:
**“And that the house itself be scraped”** — AND THAT THE HOUSE ITSELF BE SCRAPED etc. They scrape the house who understand and discern the Scriptures, and scrape off with the razor of discernment what has been craftily darkened.
**“on the inside round about, and the dust be scattered”**
• a particular doctrine
• the remnants, that nothing at all may remain
**“of the scraping without the city”** — the general Church
**“into an unclean place:”** — among the heretics, as unclean things and brought in by the unclean
14.42:
**“AND OTHER STONES”** — The doctrines of truth, of which it is said: Living stones are rolled upon the earth. And elsewhere: If any man build upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones etc.
**“be laid in the place of them that were taken away, and the house be plastered with other mortar.”** — with an exposition that expresses the law
14.44:
**“The priest going in perceive”** — knowing not by hearing but by inspection
**“that the leprosy is returned, and the walls”** — the orders of ministers
**“full of spots,”** — THAT THE LEPROSY IS RETURNED, AND THE WALLS FULL OF SPOTS. That is: if, the wicked doctrines being cast out, the doctrine of impiety is found again sprinkled even in a subtle exposition.
**“it is a lasting leprosy, and the house is unclean:”** — I have hated the assembly of the malignant.
14.45:
**“And they shall destroy it forthwith,”** — they shall condemn not only the doctrines but the authors themselves
**“and the stones and timber thereof,”** — of whose doctrine that church consisted
**“and all the dust they shall cast without the town”** — the holy city Jerusalem
**“into an unclean place:”** — of the heretics
14.46:
**“He that entereth”** — communicating among whom
**“into the house”** — the conventicle of heretics
**“when it is shut,”** — which is subject to punishment
**“shall be unclean until the evening:”**
• penance
• "In the evening weeping shall have place."
14.47:
**“And he that sleepeth in it,”** — shall have rested in such doctrine
**“and eateth”**
• the bread of mourning
• the mysteries of the destroyed church
**“any thing, shall wash”** — by penance or baptism
**“his clothes.”** — works
14.48: **“But if the priest going in perceive that the leprosy is not spread in the house, after it was plastered again, he shall purify it, it being cured,”** — BUT IF THE PRIEST GOING IN etc. Remember what you have read in the cleansing of the leper. For it plainly appears that he expresses the church of the heretics, which acts against the dispensation of the incarnation of Christ; and therefore for cleansing the house he adds such sacrifices, in which the mysteries of the flesh and passion of Christ can be expressed, and the sins committed against them healed.
14.54:
**“This is the law of every kind of leprosy and stroke.”**
• a recapitulation
• he puts the kind first
**“THIS IS THE LAW”** — Because he has set out the laws of leprosy at length, he necessarily recapitulates: first he sets out the kind, then the parts.
14.55:
**“Of the leprosy”** — of impious doctrine, which is worse than all
**“of garments”** — of virtues
**“and houses,”** — of churches
14.56: **“OF THE LEPROSY”** — Of impious doctrine, which befalls laymen also; therefore it was added: A man or woman in whom there shall be the stroke of leprosy etc. For if he had meant priests only, he would not have added woman. After these he set the leprosy which is in the virtues: for these are the garments of the soul. Then that which is, namely, in the doctors of the Church, who are the walls of the house. Lastly he makes mention of the scar and of blisters breaking out, describing the true leprosy, that which is in sins, whether doubtful or manifest.
14.57:
**“That it may be known when a thing is clean”** — when one sins ignorantly; whence: "If you were blind, you should not have sin."
**“or unclean.”** — when one sins knowingly.

15.2:
**“Speak to the children of Israel, and say to them: The man”** — who ought to be strong
**“that hath an issue of seed,”**
• superfluity of speech
• THE MAN THAT HATH etc. The SEPTUAGINT thus: To a man, a man, to whom there shall have happened etc. Whenever the lawgiver doubles something, he shows how anxious he is about it, that no one may pass over that commandment; as there: Man, man of the children of Israel etc. And it is to be noted that he says 'to a man, a man', not 'to a human being, a human being': he signifies strength in him who commands the law. For the perfect are called men. Whence Solomon: But a perfect man who shall find? And Paul: Until we all meet unto a perfect man etc.
**“shall be unclean.”** — who in the multitude of words shall not want sin
15.3:
**“And then shall he be judged subject to this evil, when at every moment”** — when he has often given himself to perversity of sense and outpouring of words
**“cleaveth”** — the seed
**“to his flesh, and gathereth there, a filthy humour.”** — GREGORY. THE MAN THAT HATH etc. What is speech but seed? Which, while it is sent forth in order, the mind of the hearer, as the womb of one conceiving, is made fruitful for the offspring of good work. If it is untimely, defiling, it loses for him who sends it the power of begetting. Seed flowing unfitly defiles the members of the body, when speech, through which knowledge ought to be born in the hearers, if it come forth disorderly, fouls even what it rightly perceived. He is unclean therefore who suffers this flux, because he is defiled by much speaking. Whence Paul, being about to say 'out of season' to his disciple, first set down 'in season', saying: "Be instant in season, out of season." And as to what he says: Then shall he be judged subject to this evil etc., then namely he will be proved to be subject to the uncleanness of the issue of seed, that is, of harmful doctrine, when he has more frequently given himself to perversity of sense and superfluous outpouring of words, whereby he seeks temporal glory rather than the fruit of everlasting reward.
15.4:
**“Every bed”** — the disciples, in whose obedience the masters rest
**“on which he sleepeth, shall be unclean, and every place on which he sitteth.”** — in the chair of pestilence
15.5:
**“If any man touch his bed,”** — who shall have heard his disciples
**“shall wash”** — of penance
**“his clothes: and being washed with water,”** — of tears
**“he shall be unclean until the evening.”** — the completion of penance
**“HESYCHIUS”** — Because there are many kinds of wicked doctrine, when the lawgiver had signified some in the healing of leprosy, others in the distinction of foods, he sets out by this commandment those who teach from shamelessness. There are some who temper the speech of doctrine according to their own passions, and commend it to others whom they love. He who so teaches corrupts his doctrine and does not make sons for God: therefore he is said to suffer an issue of seed. The bed on which he sleeps is defiled, that is, the disciple in whom, diligently obeying, the spirit of the master rests. Whence Paul said of Titus: His spirit was refreshed by you all. Of those, then, who teach unchaste things, and spurn the procreation of children and lawful marriage, and so bring in fornication and flow with seed: some by obeying become a bed, who are so unclean that Moses does not command the cleansing of those whom he knew to be so affected with the disease that they could not do penance. If any man touch his bed, that is, if he be a partaker of his doctrine, following his disciples.
15.6:
**“If a man sit where that man hath sitten,”** — in the chair of evil doctrine
**“he also shall wash his clothes: and being washed with water,”** — of tears
**“he shall be unclean until the evening.”** — until the penance be completed
15.7: **“He that toucheth his flesh,”** — his carnal doctrine
15.8:
**“If his spittle”** — flowing doctrine
**“such a man cast”** — by thrusting himself in
15.9:
**“The saddle”**
• the saddle-cloth
• the disciples subject to such doctrine
• Septuagint: the saddle of an ass. By which is understood the more negligent disciple, and one of soft heart, easily changed. For saddles are soft.
15.10:
**“And every one that toucheth whatsoever has been under him”** — under his doctrine
**“shall be defiled”** — by obeying
**“until the evening. He that carrieth any of these things,”** — taking sins upon himself
**“shall wash his clothes: and being washed with water, he shall be unclean”** — not for ever
**“until the evening.”** — he takes away despair
15.11:
**“Every person whom shall touch”** — by mingling himself
**“such a one, not having washed”** — by penance
**“his hands before,”** — works
15.12:
**“a vessel”** — which is filled with his doctrine
**“of earth,”** — wholly earthly and tending to mud, which is easily corrupted
**“if he touch,”** — he has not sat upon it, as laying the whole doctrine upon it, but a certain part
**“it shall be broken:”** — because it is wholly corrupt and not fit for penance
**“but a vessel of wood”** — which is stronger
**“shall be washed with water.”** — because it is not so weakened that it may not be healed through penance
15.13:
**“If he be healed,”** — from this corruption, that he may not bear it further
**“HE SHALL NUMBER SEVEN DAYS”** — Because remission of sins is given through the sevenfold Spirit, of whose seven gifts they stand in need who ought to be perfectly cleansed.
**“after his cleansing, and having washed his clothes, and all his body in living water,”** — of which it is said: "Out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water", that is, of doctrine which leads to life.
15.14:
**“And on the eighth day”** — The grace of Christ, which shone forth with the resurrection on the eighth day, without which it profits not to offer sacrifice.
**“TWO TURTLES”** — A sacrifice worthy of doctors. For the turtle designates meditation; the dove, often breeding and simple, the Holy Ghost. For the doctor must beget spiritually: worthily therefore he dedicated this sacrifice to priests and masters.
**“and he shall come before the Lord, to the door of the tabernacle of the testimony,”** — the apostolic doctrine, that he may not thereafter transgress it
**“And he shall give them to the priest:”** — that he may yield to another priest, because he defiled the priesthood
15.15:
**“Who shall offer one for sin,”** — of wicked doctrine contrary to the divine law
**“and the other for a holocaust,”** — that he may act wisely in future
**“and he shall pray for him before the Lord, that he may be cleansed of the issue of his seed.”** — BEFORE THE LORD etc. According to the will and law of God, against which he sinned: by repenting, by offering sacrifices of prayers, and thereafter by living rightly and being perfectly wise.
15.16:
**“The man”** — even the strong
**“from whom the seed of copulation goeth out,”** — for the begetting of children
**“shall wash”** — because he begets in sin
**“all his body with water:”** — the whole man, as elsewhere by the soul the whole man is signified
**“and he shall be unclean until the evening.”**
• the end of the ages
• THE MAN FROM WHOM THE SEED GOETH OUT etc. HESYCHIUS. Unless a man be born again of water and the Spirit, he shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven. For the sin of one passed into all. Whence David says: In sins did my mother conceive me. Therefore the lawgiver commanded the man from whom the seed goes out for the begetting of children, and the woman also who conceives, to be washed. For the body, defiled by original sin, transfuses an unclean seed. But he is called unclean until the evening, because at the end of the ages Christ cleansed the human race with water.
• Because many of the Jews were lustful, he commands so many and so great things, that at least under compulsion they might seek holiness. And as by him who suffers an issue of seed we understand the corrupter of doctrine, so by him from whom the seed of copulation goes out we understand one sowing the doctrine of the Jews. For as he is unclean by origin who, though healthy, has shed natural seed, so their sound doctrine seems clean because of the law, but is not, because it teaches according to the letter, and the law helps no one fully. And by the women who come together with them we take the Jews, who ever cleave to the traditions of their doctors.
15.17:
**“The garment or skin”** — women or Jews
**“THE GARMENT OR SKIN”** — He expresses the misery of original sin, by which the defiled human race defiles even insensible things. He expresses the women who are mingled with men for the sake of lust, for the temporal use they afford; and as a garment and skins also, grown old, are thrown away, so the custom of a woman is rejected when the friendship grows old.
**“that he weareth, he shall wash with water,”** — of baptism or by penance
15.19:
**“The woman”** — the effeminate soul
**“who at the return of the month hath her issue of blood,”** — the corruption of idolatry
**“THE WOMAN WHO AT THE RETURN”**
• By the monthly courses wicked thoughts are designated. For she who suffers her courses touches no other's flesh and defiles herself with her own. So wicked thoughts and wills, though they be not fulfilled in deed, are held with God as done, and are punished.
• He intends to call back both women and men from lust, and finds an occasion which may keep men away from women through vain and many seasons. Those who each month pay the tribute of nature he says are unclean seven days; and those who simply touch them are unclean until the evening; but those who sleep with them are unclean not one day but seven. Of necessity, therefore, continence is meanwhile enjoined on both; and according to this sense the Jew in the flesh can be helped by the letter. But the issue of blood of the soul, which the effeminate woman signifies, is idolatry, which is the corruption of the human race.
**“seven days”** — the whole of time
**“shall be separated.”** — SEVEN DAYS etc. It signifies the whole of time, up to the fulfilment in which the Gospel was declared. For men were separated from God until the preaching of the Gospel should join them.
**“Every one that toucheth”** — made a partaker
15.20:
**“And every place”** — of obedience
**“on which she sleepeth,”** — shall have rested
**“or sitteth,”** — by teaching as a master
15.21:
**“He that toucheth the garment”** — otherwise: the bed
**“HE THAT TOUCHETH THE GARMENT”** — So must we abstain from idolatry, that we touch neither idolaters nor their disciples or abettors, whom they use as beds or vessels, nor have communion with them.
15.22: **“any vessel on which she sitteth,”** — as above. To expound things already expounded is the mark of an idle man.
15.24:
**“If a man copulateth with her”** — by communicating, or sacrificing, or consenting.
**“in the time of her flowers, he shall be unclean seven days:”** — all the time of his life
15.25:
**“The woman that hath an issue of blood many days”** — This is she who in the Gospel, suffering an issue of blood, spent all her substance on physicians.
**“out of her ordinary time,”**
• by sacrificing to idols or suggesting the same to others
• in which idolatry prevailed, but even after the light of godliness shone forth by the doctrine of the Gospel
**“or that to flow after the monthly courses”** — to teach the error of idolatry
**“ceaseth not,”** — THE WOMAN THAT HATH etc. Since we have said that he who suffers an issue of seed is one teaching obscene and corrupting things, and he from whom the seed of copulation goes out is one using the Jewish doctrine, there remain those who spread the doctrine of the Gentiles, which is fitly called an issue of blood, as the seduction of idolatry: for the demons rejoice in blood.
**“as long as to this”** — passion
15.26: **“Every bed on which she sleepeth,”** — Remember what you have read.
15.29: **“SHE SHALL OFFER FOR HERSELF TO THE PRIEST”** — Above he commanded him who suffers the issue of seed to take two turtles or doves for a sacrifice, because he occupied the place of a master; and here also her who suffers the issue of blood, because she too was a master of idolatry.
15.31:
**“You shall teach”** — masters
**“YOU SHALL TEACH”** — This he did not ordain either of the lepers or of those who touch carcasses.
**“therefore the children of Israel”** — those beneath you
**“to take heed of”**
• "Fly fornication."
• He shows why he said this.
**“uncleanness,”** — of mind or body
**“UNCLEANNESS”** — Every sin is an uncleanness of the soul, but idolatry above all.
**“that they may not die”**
• by the death of impiety
• spiritually or bodily
**“TABERNACLE”** — The inward man, in which is the image of God: also "the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us".
15.32:
**“This is the law of him that hath the issue of seed,”** — who sows corrupt doctrine
**“THIS IS THE LAW”** — He is wont to bind together things which cohere with one another and have a common intention, to show how they ought to be understood, and which things are joined with which in the knowledge of the understanding.
**“AND THAT IS DEFILED BY COPULATION”** — He who teaches the Jewish precepts, and teaches good things badly, is unclean, while he brings forth out of season the things that pertain to the letter, and as one clean uses unclean things. Whence: "All things are clean to the clean" etc.
15.33:
**“AND OF THE WOMAN THAT IN HER MONTHLY TIMES”** — These are they who teach impiety, since the human race was held by the error of idolatry in the monthly courses, that is, in the separation of malice.
**“or that hath a continual issue of blood, and of the man”** — the faithful
**“that sleepeth with her.”** — mingled with idolatry

16.1: **“AND THE LORD SPOKE TO MOSES”** — He makes one body of the law and gathers what coheres into one. For when he had set out the manifold differences of contrary doctrine, now he refutes it by one law, setting a common precept against it and showing the cause of its death. For the strange fire is doctrine strange to God; therefore they were consumed by the divine fire who offered strange fire: for they act against the Holy Ghost who teach wicked things. Whether then one teach idolatry, or corrupt the divine commandments by expounding them wickedly, or so use the Jewish doctrine as to be defiled, out of season, namely, following the letter against the intention of the law itself, he offers strange fire to God: therefore, consumed by the spiritual fire, he does not escape the swift penalty of transgression; but when these have died and failed, that which follows will obtain greater holiness. Whence after their death the Lord speaks these things to Moses.
16.2:
**“And he commanded him,”** — So ought priests to enjoin these things on one another.
**“saying: Speak to Aaron thy brother,”**
• He sets forth a law common to all who search into the divine mysteries, but first to the priests.
• SPEAK TO AARON etc. How much God spares us, how anxious he is for our salvation, we said in what went before. Doctrine is the guardian and guide of our salvation. About this, therefore, the lawgiver is most diligent: not only that the doctors may not go beyond bounds in the precepts of the Lord, or in Jewish fables, or in any phantasm of idolatry, but that they may not fall into impiety by occasion of theology, as the heretics, who, searching out divine and lofty things by their own sense, have been cut off from the body of ecclesiastical moderation; which is guarded against by the present words.
**“that he enter not at all times into the sanctuary,”** — the divine contemplation, in which the holy of holies dwells
**“which is within the veil”** — the flesh of Christ, who was a propitiatory for us through his own blood
**“before the propitiatory,”** — Septuagint: the face of the propitiatory, that is, the divinity; whence: "Thou canst not see my face" etc.
**“with which the ark is covered, lest he die,”** — Curiously inquiring into secrets, as: Seek not the things that are too high for thee; whose faith brings salvation, the discussion of them peril.
**“BEFORE THE PROPITIATORY”** — Septuagint: Before the face of the propitiatory. Plainly then he forbids priests, or anyone whatever, to search out the divinity of Christ, to enter the inner parts of the veil. Christ has a veil, that is, the flesh, which covers the divinity, as the visible veil covers the holy of holies. He calls the flesh of Christ also the ark of the testimony, alluding by many names to many effects. And hence David says: Arise, O Lord, into thy resting place: thou and the ark of thy sanctification. This is the ark which gave the testimony of Christ under Pontius Pilate; this is also the propitiatory.
**“for I will appear in a cloud over the oracle,”** — Or the propitiatory, that is, the flesh of Christ, or the Gospel. For he is called by many names, and it is not tautology, but for divers effects there are divers names. He calls the flesh a veil, because it covers the divinity of Christ. Sometimes an ark, which the Lord expounds, saying: Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up. Sometimes a cloud, because it is clean, light and fine. Whence Isaias: The Lord will ascend upon a swift cloud etc. Whence: I will command my clouds to rain no rain. In the cloud, therefore, is understood both the flesh of Christ and the preaching of the Gospel. Let us seek nothing more than what the word of the Gospel delivers to us, or what we receive from the Lord's flesh.
16.3:
**“Unless he first do these things: He shall offer a calf for sin,”**
• He enters by the sacrifice of Christ, who was immolated for us.
• HE SHALL OFFER A CALF FOR SIN etc. The beginning of divine preaching is Christ and his passion; had this not been, and had he not freed men from error, Gentile as well as Jewish, none could speak of the divinity of the Father. For no one knoweth the Father but the Son, and he to whom the Son will reveal him.
**“HE SHALL OFFER A CALF FOR SIN”** — A wonderful order. For when he had said that one must not always enter into the holy places, lest we presume to approach rashly and heedlessly, he shows when and how we should enter.
**“and a ram”** — Christ, who is the leader of the sheep; he was immolated in the place of Isaac.
**“he shall offer for a holocaust.”** — the perfection of virtues
16.4:
**“With a linen tunick”** — justice
**“he shall be vested; with linen breeches”** — chastity
**“he shall cover his nakedness: he shall be girded with a linen girdle,”** — fortitude
**“and a mitre”** — wisdom, because the organ of wisdom is in the head
**“of linen”** — it signifies a faculty of virtues, and an acquisition swift, ready and pleasing: therefore he commands all to be of linen.
**“he shall put upon his head:”** — A LINEN TUNICK etc. LINEN BREECHES etc. A GIRDLE etc. He who is to speak of God, and to see him so far as is possible, let him be armed with all the virtues, of which four are general: justice, chastity, fortitude, wisdom.
**“BREECHES”** — Where it is related how Moses vested his brother Aaron, nothing is said of the breeches: the law does not put its hand to our genitals and privy parts; we ourselves ought to cover our more secret parts and those worthy of shame, and reserve the continence of purity and of the thighs to God as judge. Of the other virtues, namely wisdom, fortitude, justice, humility and the like, others can judge; chastity conscience alone knows, and human eyes cannot be certain. Whence: "Now concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord"; as if Moses should say: I do not vest anyone with breeches, nor lay necessity upon anyone: he who wishes to be a priest, let him vest himself. Let us ourselves therefore take up the breeches, let us ourselves cover our privy parts, that they may lie open to none, lest, when we enter into the Holy of Holies, if any shame appear, we die the death.
**“JEROME”** — TO FABIOLA. According to the Hebrews, the account of the thighs and of generation pertaining to the flesh is assigned to the earth through it. Whence: "Earth thou art, and into earth thou shalt go"; and the causes of this thing, how from a tiny seed and the foulest beginnings so great a beauty, whether of men or of divers things, is born, are wrapped up and do not lie open to human eyes. Therefore the thighs are veiled with linen breeches.
**“AFTER HE IS WASHED”** — With the water of baptism. For he must first be regenerated by water and the Spirit, and so be clothed with the aforesaid virtues, that he may put on Christ, who was immolated as a ram for a holocaust, that is, the perfection of virtues. For he, according to the Apostle, is the perfect man and the measure of the age. These attained, he enters into the Holy of Holies, not discussing the substance of God, but desiring to understand the dispensation of Christ.
16.5:
**“And he shall receive from the whole multitude of the children of Israel”** — wonderful sacraments
**“two buck goats for sin, and one ram”** — because Christ is the shepherd of the sheep
**“for a holocaust.”**
• the perfection of virtues
• AND HE SHALL RECEIVE FROM THE WHOLE etc. Christ was immolated for us from the children of Israel according to the flesh. Whence Paul: Of whom is Christ according to the flesh. Two buck goats for sin: for Christ was offered to exhaust sins. And one ram for a holocaust, because he was offered for the perfection of virtues and the advancement of life. Whence Paul: You are become dead to the law by the body of Christ.
16.6:
**“And when he hath offered the calf and prayed for himself,”** — for the man whom he took on
**“and for his own house,”** — because he redeems the just also
16.7: **“He shall make the two buck goats to stand before the Lord in the door”** — he himself is the door of heaven
16.8:
**“And casting lots upon them both, one to the Lord, and the other to the emissary goat:”** — TWO BUCK GOATS etc. Because Christ was offered both for sinners and for the just, rightly he is called a he goat as for sinners, and a calf for the just. Whence he says: When he has offered the calf, he shall pray for his house, that is, for the just, who are the house of God.
**“THE TWO BUCK GOATS TO STAND”** — Some say that one goat was to be sacrificed to the Lord, the other to the devil; as if the law did not most strongly forbid it, saying: Thou shalt have no strange gods.
**“AUGUSTINE”** — TWO BUCK GOATS. The goat to be immolated is taken by some in a good sense, the one to be sent away in an evil sense; because he who sends it into the desert washes his clothes when he returns, and his body with water, and so enters the camp. But he who burns the flesh of the other goat without the camp is also washed. The allegorical signification must therefore be handled strictly.
**“HE SHALL MAKE THE TWO BUCK GOATS TO STAND”** — Because Christ is God and man, suffering according to the humanity, impassible according to the divinity, two goats are taken and set before the Lord in the door of the tabernacle. For he is the true door that leads to the door of the tabernacle which is in heaven. Aaron casts a lot upon both, by which we may understand the divinity and the humanity to be distinguished, that the one may suffer and the other strengthen the sufferer: one to the Lord, the other to the emissary goat, Christ.
16.9:
**“That whose lot fell to the Lord, he shall offer”**
• The true Aaron, "a priest for ever according to the order of Melchisedech", will offer.
• to the Father
**“it”** — himself
**“for sin:”** — of the human race
16.10:
**“But that whose lot was to be the emissary goat,”** — upon which the lot of sending away came, in which the divinity of Christ is signified
**“he shall present alive”** — keeping him impassible, that he may intercede: for no one can forgive sins but God alone.
**“before the Lord, that he may pour out prayers upon him,”** — or: him
**“INTO THE WILDERNESS”** — That is, into the bosom of the Father, where none approaches but he himself and the Holy Ghost: he went away, therefore, that is, he restrained his power of working, and bore our iniquities, not that he might have them but that he might consume them. For God is a consuming fire.
**“and let him go into the wilderness.”** — Into the wilderness, of which it is said: "A desert land, and where there is no way, and no water" etc. There the enemy has no place where God abides. For the divinity is said to have gone away into heaven at the time of the passion, not changing place, but in a manner restraining its power, that the wicked might accomplish the passion.
16.11:
**“After these things are duly celebrated, he shall offer”** — Christ
**“the calf”**
• the flesh
• The lawgiver makes manifest that the sacrifice of Christ is indeed of the flesh, by the power of the divinity, and in the good pleasure of the Father, and is a propitiation for our sins, and is performed for the ministering of the Spirit.
**“THE CALF”** — When Christ is offered for the freeing of the Jewish people, he is called a calf, because he observed the justification of the law. Whence he says: "I am not come to destroy" the law, "but to fulfil"; who was made of a woman, that he might redeem them who were under the law. Rightly therefore he is called a calf, as one yoked under the commandments of the law.
**“and praying for himself”** — the humanity which he had taken on to be saved
**“and for his own house,”** — his kindred
**“he shall immolate it:”** — the high priest of his own sacrifice
16.12:
**“And taking the censer,”** — a learned tongue filled with the fire of the Spirit
**“which with the burning coals of the altar”**
• of the Cherubim, where is the intelligible fire
• WITH THE BURNING COALS OF THE ALTAR etc. With the spiritual words which John wrote at the supper after Judas went out, in which he sets out how he, since he is in the Father and the Father in him, sends the Spirit; how the Father is the husbandman, he the vine, the apostles the branches; and many other things which kindle to godliness like coals of fire.
**“he hath filled, and taking up with his hand the compounded”** — because it is for many and from many
**“perfume”** — prayer: "Let my prayer be directed as incense in thy sight."
**“PERFUME”** — Prayer: "Let my prayer be directed as incense in thy sight." For Christ prayed for his disciples.
**“TAKING UP WITH HIS HAND”** — Septuagint: He shall fill his hands with incense of fine composition; praying, namely, for fine spiritual things, not earthly.
**“for incense, he shall go in within the veil into the holy place:”**
• because the flesh is visible, but he is invisible
• Septuagint: he shall offer within the veil
16.13:
**“That when the perfumes are put upon the fire, the cloud and vapour thereof may cover the oracle, which is over the testimony, and he may not die.”** — THAT WHEN THE PERFUMES ARE PUT etc. Aaron, by the dignity of the priesthood, signifies Christ and the other priests. Christ puts upon the fire, that is, doctrine, the aromatics, that is, prayer; and the vapour of the cloud, that is, the power of prayer, covers the oracle, that is, the flesh, from which comes to us the propitiation of sins in Christ, who is also the testimony. And every priest also, speaking of Christ, puts in the fire of spiritual doctrine the aromatics of prayer, whose power covers the oracle which is over the testimony, and does not permit him to seek concerning the passion of Christ the things that are above the power of the seeker; and he will not die, namely by immoderate questions.
**“AND HE MAY NOT DIE”** — His flesh did not see corruption, because it was covered by the vapour of the aromatics, namely by the power of prayer, of which it is said: Thou wilt not give thy holy one to see corruption.
16.14:
**“He shall take also of the blood of the calf, and sprinkle with his finger”** — it signifies the power of the divinity
**“TOWARDS THE PROPITIATORY”** — Because Christ, who is called the propitiatory and the east, suffered for our propitiation and enlightening. Whence: "Behold a man, the Orient is his name." And elsewhere: The Orient from on high hath visited us. Or towards the propitiatory, that is, in the sight of the Father; seven times, because he granted us remission of sins and the Holy Ghost.
16.15:
**“And when he hath killed the buck goat”** — Christ
**“for the sin of the people,”** — of the human race
**“he shall carry in the blood thereof within the veil,”** — with the Father
**“as was commanded with the blood of the calf,”** — in which the Gentiles are shown to be subjected to the yoke of the cross
16.16:
**“And may expiate the sanctuary”**
• the human race
• AND WHEN HE HATH KILLED etc. Because Christ was made of the common mass of men, he is rightly called a he goat, because this animal is rough and shaggy with hair, and the human race is for sin. Whence he fittingly says: And when he hath killed the buck goat for the sin of the people, that is, of the human race, which once was not a people but now is a people, since Christ took its firstfruits. That he might show, therefore, that Christ bears the firstfruits principally of the Jews, but also of all nature which is in sin, he took both a calf and a he goat; and because there is one sacrifice and one effect, of necessity the same things are done with the he goat and the calf. For you see that the he goat is slain before God, that is, the Father, and the blood is brought into the inner parts of the veil, that is, to the same Father, and the sanctuary is expiated, namely the mass of the human race, which from the beginning was holy, and the tabernacle of the Holy Ghost.
**“from the uncleanness of the children of Israel, and from their transgressions, and all their sins. According to this rite shall he do to the tabernacle of the testimony, which is fixed among them in the midst of the lots”**
• or: of the filth
• Septuagint: of their uncleannesses
16.17:
**“Let no man”**
• not that all were then shut out
• No Gentile or Jew or Levite or priest: for they have all gone aside, they are become unprofitable together.
**“be in the tabernacle”**
• the intelligible one: no one lived holily
• IN THE TABERNACLE etc. What above he called the sanctuary, here he calls the tabernacle of the testimony. For by the same reason both the holy place and the tabernacle of the testimony are said of the mass of the human race. For if the tabernacle of the testimony is heaven, it is rightly named the holy place: our man is heavenly, of whom Paul says: "As we have borne the image of the earthly" etc. He is here rightly named the holy place who is in the midst of uncleannesses, because Christ is assailed by the passions of the flesh.
**“THE SANCTUARY”** — The human race, by taking flesh, that he might pray through the cross in the proper sanctuary of the flesh.
**“UNTIL HE COME OUT”** — Namely, sending forth his spirit in human manner and leaving the flesh in the tomb.
16.18:
**“And when he is come out”** — relieving our captivity and making us sit in the heavenly places
**“at the altar”** — namely of incense, which is the seat of the Cherubim
**“that is before the Lord, let him pray for himself, and taking the blood of the calf, and of the buck goat, let him pour it upon the horns thereof round about:”** — AND TAKING etc. Because by his passion he sanctified the horns of the altar, that is, the four principal virtues.
16.19:
**“LET HIM EXPIATE”** — They are expiated by the sacrifice of Christ. Whence: But the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these.
**“and sanctify it from the uncleanness”** — the cause why it ought to be cleansed
**“FROM THE UNCLEANNESS”** — As regards the powers of the heavens, they need not be expiated, being in everlasting sanctification. But because the smoke of our sins often ascends, of which it is said: "There went up a smoke in his wrath", and of Ninive: "The wickedness thereof is come up before me", rightly he expiates the choirs above from our uncleannesses, that he may take away the abominable odour. Therefore he does not sprinkle simply, but seven times, because the heavenly things are cleansed by the pardon of our sins.
16.20:
**“After he hath cleansed the sanctuary, and the tabernacle, and the altar, then let him offer the living goat:”** — Christ according to the divinity
**“AFTER HE HATH CLEANSED”** — Morally. AMBROSE also says in the epistle to Simplician: As there are two in the field, one is taken and the other left, so the two goats: one is sacrificed, and the other sent away into the desert, useful to none, nor to be eaten by the sons of the priests. For as of foods what is good is eaten, and what is bad or useless is thrown away, so too we call good things fit for feasting those which are fit to eat. It will not please the Lord, therefore, if the priest eat a sacrifice in which there is fraud of oblation, not the sincerity of diligent confession. Therefore this goat is to be sent away into the desert, where our fathers wandered and did not come to the land of promise, but their memory perished from the earth. Lastly there are works fit for feasting. Whence: The sabbaths of the earth shall be meat for you. For works fit for feasting and refreshing are rest in God.
16.21:
**“And putting both hands”** — AND PUTTING BOTH HANDS. The laying on of hands ministers blessing in the sacrifice, or remission of sins, or the Holy Ghost, which cannot be in that upon which the lot of the devil falls. There are many circumstances also that contradict that opinion.
**“AND PUTTING”** — That it may be shown that the impassible, immortal Word took in the flesh a sufficient sacrifice for us, rightly all sins are laid upon him, because he bore our sins in his body. Septuagint: He shall lay them upon the head of the living kid. In which is signified the crown of thorns pressed upon his head. For by thorns sins are signified.
**“let him confess all the iniquities of the children of Israel,”** — because he bore all our sins
**“and all their offences and sins: and praying that they may light”** — to God
**“on his head, he shall turn him out by a man ready for it, into the desert.”** — BY A MAN READY etc. Christ, who is all things of his own sacrifice: priest, sacrifice, worship and altar. Ready, according to that: "And I do not resist: I have not gone back. I have given my body to the strikers." Christ therefore, immolating himself by the living kid, himself by a ready man, that is, by his own power, sends the living goat into the wilderness, namely the immortal and impassible divinity, to places pathless to us and deserted by all malice. Whence John: Jesus "knowing that the Father had given him all things into his hands, and that he came from God and goeth to God."
**“ADAMANTIUS”** — IN THE HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS. He says that the goat which is immolated to the Lord signifies those who are destined to the lot of the Lord, as that Lazarus who is carried by the angels into the bosom of Abraham; but that the goat which is sent away into the desert signifies the reprobate, or the Jewish people, who are cast away from the face of the Lord for their sins, as the rich man clad in purple, buried in hell. And the man ready, Christ or his angels. Whence each one receives what he deserves.
16.22:
**“And when the goat hath carried all their iniquities”** — Christ, who bore our sins
**“into an uninhabited land,”** — into heaven
**“and shall be let go”** — who before was taken among men
16.23:
**“Aaron shall return”** — Christ, the true one of the mountain
**“into the tabernacle of the testimony.”** — into heaven
**“and putting off the vestments, which he had on him before”** — the filth of mortality and passibility, with which he was clothed for our sins
16.24:
**“He shall wash his flesh”** — He will make his flesh manifest as washed.
**“in a holy place.”** — in heaven
**“and shall put on his own garments.”** — of his glory; whence: "The Lord hath reigned, he is clothed with beauty."
**“And after that he has come out”** — from the world
**“and hath offered”** — to the Father
**“his own holocaust,”**
• himself
• which none could offer but he
**“and that of the people, he shall pray”** — appearing before the face of God for us
**“both for himself, and for the people:”** — his members
16.25:
**“and the fat”** — the fatness of charity
**“that is offered for sins, he shall burn”** — that the holocaust may be made fat
**“upon the altar”** — himself
16.26:
**“He”** — Christ
**“that hath let go the emissary goat, shall wash”** — immortality and impassibility being taken on
**“his clothes,”** — before foul
**“and his body with water, and so shall enter into the camp.”**
• of the angels, or of the Church, of which it is said: "Terrible as an army set in array."
• HE THAT HATH LET GO etc. ORIGEN. Has desire, or any wicked thought, come up into your heart? Cast it away: it is the lot of the apopompaeus. And you will cast it away if you have with you the hand of the ready man, that is, if the divine reading be in your hands and the precepts of God before your eyes: then you will truly be ready. Likewise if the other vices have come up into your heart, drive them out: send them into the desert. But if mercy, justice and peace and the like come up into your heart, these are of the lot of the Lord; they are offered at the altar; the high priest receives them and reconciles God to you. He, therefore, in whom is the lot of the apopompaeus is not slothful nor busied with worldly things, but ready, prompt and watchful. And if he seems to be defiled, because he has touched the unclean, he shall wash his garments and shall be clean. This pertains morally to each one of us. The ready man is the reason itself which is within us, by which we have the discernment of good and evil; which, if it seems to be defiled because it learns and handles what is evil, yet if it cast these away, then, purified and washed by better thoughts, it will be seen to be clean. Christ also is said to wash his garments and be made clean, because of that: I saw Jesus the high priest clothed with filthy garments. If this is understood of the taking of flesh, the same figure can be kept in the washing of the garments also.
16.27: **“But the calf and the buck goat, that were sacrificed for sin, and whose blood was carried into the sanctuary,”** — or: into the sanctuary
16.29:
**“And this shall be to you an everlasting ordinance: The seventh month, the tenth day of the month, you shall afflict your souls,”** — The days will come when the bridegroom shall be taken away from them, and then they shall fast.
**“and shall do no work, whether it be one of your own country, or a stranger that sojourneth among you.”** — IN THE SEVENTH MONTH etc. ORIGEN. In which is the solemnity of propitiation, and in which alone the high priest alone, clothed in all the pontifical vestments, enters once in the year into the holy of holies. For, leaving the people, he enters where the propitiatory is, and above the propitiatory the Cherubim, where is the ark of the testimony and the altar of incense, to which access belongs to the high priest alone. The high priest is Christ, who was with the people the whole year, of whom it is said: He hath sent me to preach the gospel to the poor, and to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord; and once on this day of propitiation he enters into the holy of holies, that is, his dispensation fulfilled, he pierces heaven and enters to the Father, that he may make him propitious and pray for all who believe in him. The day of propitiation remains for us until the sun sets, that is, until the world receives its end. For we stand before the doors, waiting for our high priest, who tarries within the holy of holies and prays for the sins of those who wait for him, upon whom his lot has come, that they may be the portion and choice of the Lord, not for that part which for its unworthiness is spurned and cast away. Whence the goat is called apopompaeus, that is, cast away and rejected.
16.30: **“Upon this day”** — on which Christ suffered
16.31: **“a sabbath”** — "You shall do no servile work therein."
16.32:
**“And the priest shall make atonement”** — Christ, because the priests of the Jews could not: for it was impossible that sins should be taken away with the blood of oxen or goats.
**“that is anointed,”** — "God, thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows."
**“and whose hands are consecrated to do the office of the priesthood”** — "Thou art a priest for ever according to the order of Melchisedech."
**“in his father's stead;”** — obedient to the Father unto death
**“and he shall be vested with the linen robe and the holy vestments,”** — In place of the priests of the Jews, who could not accomplish these things; from whom is Christ according to the flesh.
16.34: **“And this shall be an ordinance for ever, that you pray for the children of Israel, and for all their sins once in a year.”** — because Christ died once for our sins.

17.1:
**“And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying:”**
• This law is given to all in common.
• AND THE LORD SPOKE TO MOSES, SAYING etc. By the present law it is shown that the Lord speaks not to Moses only but to all in common: he wishes all to know what is expedient for all, namely that the law is temporal, and that when its time is fulfilled it is kept to no purpose. And the perfect fulfilment of the time is the destruction of the place in which he commanded sacrifices to be offered; by intimating that he who has sacrificed outside the camp, or abroad, only outside the tabernacle of the testimony, perishes from his people; so that when the tabernacle and the place are destroyed, the sacrifices have an end. But holy actions and those that edify the human mind, as to honour father and mother, and love one's neighbours, and the like, he did not confine to a place, because they always profit and agree with the Gospel. Whoever therefore now performs the figures of the destroyed place sheds blood and stains the common conversation; they sin in common, as those who shed blood. They shed the blood also of those whom by their example they send into error.
17.2:
**“Speak to Aaron and his sons, and to all the children of Israel, saying to them: This is the word, which hath commanded”** — the authority of the precept
**“the Lord”** — not man
17.3: **“Any man whosoever of the house of Israel”** — ANY MAN WHOSOEVER etc. As if: the figures of the law are temporal and are in a certain place, which being destroyed they cannot remain.
17.4:
**“And offer it not at the door of the tabernacle of the testimony”** — where alone it is lawful to offer
**“an oblation to the Lord, of blood”** — of murder
**“shall be guilty: as if he had shed blood, so shall he perish from the midst of his people.”** — IF HE KILL AN OX etc. AUGUSTINE. He does not speak of those who kill for the use of eating: for he forbade private sacrifices, lest anyone dare to be a priest to himself, but should bring it thither where he might offer through the priest. For he forewarned that this was to be guarded against in custom. Though then it was not lawful to offer sacrifices except in the tabernacle, to which the temple succeeded, Elias yet sacrificed outside the temple, when he both obtained fire from heaven and overcame the prophets of the demons. But when he who established the law commands something to be done which he forbade in the law, the command itself is held for law, because it is given by the lawgiver. For the Spirit of God, who was in Elias, whatever he did in this matter could not be against the law, because he is the giver of the law.
17.7:
**“And they shall no more sacrifice their victims to devils, with whom they have committed fornication.”**
• by departing from the true bridegroom
• WITH WHOM THEY HAVE COMMITTED FORNICATION etc. He calls idolatry fornication, because God has espoused our souls to himself. Departure from him, therefore, is called fornication. He frightens also those who commit fornication in the flesh, when he compares the sin of fornication to the worship of idols and the offering to demons.
**“It shall be an ordinance for ever to them and to their posterity.”** — AND THEY SHALL NO MORE etc. Though it was said by the Lord: Thou shalt not make to thyself an idol, nor any likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or in the earth beneath, or under the earth, they made a molten calf and offered sacrifice to it, longing to feast on the sacrifice. The law therefore, as their pedagogue, commands them to sacrifice to God, that, busied with this, they might abstain from the sacrifice of idolatry. Yet it ordained such sacrifices as signified mysteries to come.
17.8:
**“And thou shalt say to them: The man”** — Septuagint: man, man
**“whosoever of the children of Israel, and of the strangers who sojourn among you, that offereth a holocaust”** — now perfected, not only begun
17.9: **“And bringeth it not to the door of the tabernacle, that it may be offered to the Lord, shall perish from among his people.”** — ANY MAN WHOSOEVER etc. AUGUSTINE. If the same commandment is repeated, it is shown to be necessary and useful; but yet above he commanded only him to be punished who killed in order to make a sacrifice but did not complete it. For he says: He that killeth an ox or a sheep, whether in the camp or without the camp etc., where he is forbidden what is attempted. But here he says: He that offereth a holocaust or a victim etc., now signifying the perfected sacrifice; yet they are struck with equal penalty. For he who begins, and would do it if it were allowed, differs nothing from him who has done it. For to both the penalty is assigned, that he be cast out of his people, and not glory in circumcision, nor be called of the race of Israel, but be reckoned among those who have the foreskin. They therefore who now celebrate the figures of the law outside the temple boast themselves Israelites or Jews in vain.
17.10:
**“Any man whosoever”** — Septuagint: man, man
**“OF THE STRANGERS”** — The Gentiles, who are not joined to the Jews, but are among us. For we were among them, having their law and prophets and the promised inheritance, yet cleaving not to them but to God. Therefore, according to the Septuagint, he said 'man, man', to show that both those in circumcision and those in uncircumcision who cleave to God ought to keep this commandment.
**“that sojourn among them, if he eat blood, I will set my face against his soul, and will cut him off from among his people:”** — IF HE EAT BLOOD etc. By blood we understand murder: hatred of a brother is murder: for "whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer". We must abstain therefore from all blood, that is, from all hatred of brethren; because against such a soul, which eats such blood, according to that: "Who devour my people as they eat bread", God sets his face, namely Christ, who is the image of the Father. For "he that seeth" the Son "seeth the Father also". For he is the judge, of whom it is said: "But the countenance of the Lord is against them that do evil things, to cut off the remembrance of them from the earth." And he cuts off him who eats blood from his people, namely from the common race of men, because as one unmerciful and impious he sends him with the wicked spirits into everlasting fire, which is prepared for the devil and his angels. And to show how merciful we ought to be to one another, how loving, he shows that he shed his own blood for our expiation, saying: "I have given it to you", namely the blood of Christ.
17.11:
**“Because the life of the flesh”** — the carnal life, which ends with death
**“THE LIFE OF THE FLESH”** — There is something vital in the blood, because through it chiefly one lives in this flesh, which is spread through all the veins of the body. He called the very life of the body the soul: not the life which departs from the body, but that which ends with death. In which manner of speech we call this life temporal, not eternal, mortal, not immortal; whereas the soul is immortal which is carried "by the angels into the bosom of Abraham", and to which it is said: "This day thou shalt be with me in paradise." According to this the Apostle says: Neither do I count my life more precious than myself, where he shows himself ready to die for the Gospel. For he was making the soul which departs from the body more precious when he acquired so great merit.
