**“is in the blood: and I have given it”** — the blood of Christ
**“to you, that upon the altar”** — the cross, on which the blood was shed
**“my”** — otherwise: upon it
**“you may make atonement with it for your souls, and the blood”** — of Christ
**“for the soul”** — his own, which was fashioned by himself and taken on with the flesh
17.13:
**“ANY MAN WHOSOEVER”** — HESYCHIUS. God has great care for us, that we do not harm one another: therefore he commands him who is struck to offer the other cheek, and to let go the tunic to him who takes the cloak, and not to contend in judgment, lest from contention we wish even to harm, but to correct him by suffering. Therefore the lawgiver recapitulates the commandment of blood, that he may take away the various frauds and cunning ways of harming, saying: If by hunting or fowling etc.
**“BY HUNTING”** — By fraud that pertains to blood and life. Whence: They will hunt after the soul of the just, and will condemn innocent blood. And again: "Our soul hath been delivered as a sparrow out of the snare of the fowlers." This is, if he sees him sin who through weakness or simplicity is exposed to hunting and guile.
**“or fowling, he take a wild beast or a bird,”**
• any common man, carnal and brooding on passions, but without experience of common causes
• OR A BIRD etc. When, namely, he who removes himself from earthly things, which it is lawful to eat. For such the violent and covetous eat. Whence: If you bite and devour one another, take heed you be not consumed one of another. Or since they were just before, they are rightly reckoned among the clean.
**“which is lawful to eat, let him pour out”** — by praying, by confessing; whence: "In his sight I pour out my prayer."
**“the blood”** — the sin which he sinned
**“its blood, and cover it with earth.”** — that is: the sins which have been committed from the frailty of the brethren, do not expose; but the blood of him who has been seen to be caught, give to the earth, covering it, namely, with pardon and compassion; and he eats it who defames his neighbour's sin, because sin is the death of the soul.
**“COVER IT WITH EARTH”** — The earth covers the sins of those who confess, as remaining below and mortified by penance; whose cry is forbidden to ascend to heaven, whither the cry of the Sodomites ascended, who would not repent.
17.15:
**“The soul that eateth that which died of itself,”** — dead in sin
**“or has been caught by a beast,”**
• By the devil, which is worse: for he is so far dead that the demons hold him captive.
• THE SOUL THAT EATETH etc. Above it was said: He that toucheth carcasses caught by beasts, that is, he who has shared in such things; but here it is said: The soul that eateth: that is, has made the whole sin his own and fulfilled his will from it.
**“whether he be one of your own country or a stranger, shall wash his clothes”** — the outward man
**“and himself”** — the inward
**“with water”** — of baptism or of tears
**“and shall be defiled until the evening: in this manner”** — aforesaid
**“he shall be clean.”** — or: shall be made

18.2:
**“Speak to the children of Israel, and thou shalt say to them: I am”** — who command this
**“the Lord your God.”** — whose servants you are
**“I AM THE LORD YOUR GOD”** — As if: Know your Creator; keep his precepts diligently.
18.3:
**“According to the custom”** — Septuagint: the pursuits
**“of the land of Egypt, in which you dwelt, you shall not do: neither shall you act according to the manner of the country of Chanaan, into which I will bring you,”** — ACCORDING TO THE CUSTOM etc. He discloses the intention of the whole law: namely that we abstain from evil things and hold to good.
**“nor in the ordinances”** — religions
**“of them shall you walk.”** — NOR IN THE ORDINANCES etc. For he commands them to abstain not only from fornication, avarice and pride, but also from divinations and auguries and the superstitions of all nations.
18.4:
**“You shall do my judgments,”** — that is: the things I command from judgment and discernment
**“and shall observe my precepts, and shall walk”** — by advancing
**“in them.”** — He says this a second time, in which he hints at the Old and New Testament.
18.5:
**“Keep my laws and my judgments, which if do”** — Not the hearers of the law are just, but the doers.
**“a man, he shall live in them. I am the Lord your God.”** — HE SHALL LIVE IN THEM etc. Because in them is true life for those who believe in Christ; because: "He that seeth the Son and believeth in him hath life everlasting." This he did not add to the former judgments and precepts: for the law does not give life unless the Gospel come upon it.
18.6:
**“No man”**
• as rational: for he who approaches is not a man but a beast.
• He sets forth the kind, and places the species under it.
**“shall approach to her that is near of kin to him, to uncover her nakedness. I am the Lord.”**
• NO MAN etc. He forbids us craftily to approach those who sin in the law by occasion of kinship, so as at length to betray their shameful deeds; whence he adds: I am the Lord.
• NO MAN etc. Septuagint: Man, man shall not approach to any of the household of his own flesh etc. For as man is twofold, so the precepts are twofold, teaching the inward and the outward man. The law forbids the outward man to be mingled with kindred, as the Gentiles were, whose inheritance Israel was to receive; who was so dissolute and given to the pleasures of the flesh that one man would take many wives; that so at least they might abstain from foreigners. The lawgiver goes through in order the degrees from which they ought to refrain, lest the generations be confounded and the inheritances perish. He calls the union of such persons shame, to show it abominable and horrible. And it is to be noted that, when in the beginning of this law he had said: I am the Lord your God, he repeated: I am the Lord, signifying that he is joined to us in the flesh and a partaker of our kinship: it is damnable therefore to offend so great a kinship.
**“I AM THE LORD”** — Not making manifest the sins of men, but blotting out and covering what has been blotted out or uncovered by confession.
18.7:
**“The nakedness of thy father, or the nakedness of thy mother”** — by sinning with the mother
**“thou shalt not uncover”**
• lest the generation be confounded, lest the same be son and brother
• By this manner of speech he forbade lying with these persons.
**“THE NAKEDNESS OF THY FATHER AND OF THY MOTHER”** — He forbids lying with the mother. For there is the shame of the mother and the father. For afterwards he forbids it where he says: Thou shalt not uncover the nakedness of thy father's wife: for it is the nakedness of thy father. Where he set out how in the mother there is the shame of both, that is, of the father and the mother. For in the stepmother there is that of the father only.
18.8: **“Thou shalt not uncover the nakedness of thy father's wife: for it is the nakedness of thy father.”** — He forbids us to reveal any sins entrusted to us by kinsmen or friends, lest we suffer the curse of Cham, who laid open his father's nakedness to his brethren. By fathers we understand those of whom Paul says: "An ancient man rebuke not, but entreat him as a father"; brothers too, and mothers and sisters, of whom he added: "Young men as brethren, old women as mothers, the younger as sisters." Lastly, since we have kinship with all the faithful, according to that: "We being many are one body in Christ, and every one members one of another." According to the Septuagint, ten degrees of kinship are enumerated, of which number are all the commandments of the law; showing that whoever reveals the shame of spiritual or carnal kindred is a transgressor of the whole law. For he sins against charity, which is "the fulfilling of the law".
18.9:
**“The nakedness of thy sister by father or by mother, whether at home”** — of the father
**“OR ABROAD SHE BE BORN”** — AUGUSTINE. Of the mother, if, conceived by a former husband, she came into the house with the mother; but he forbids dealing with such a sister. If it is not lawful to reveal the shame of a sister from either parent, how much more from both. But what is it that, after the prohibition of lying even with one's granddaughters, whether by son or by daughter, has been set between, there follows: Thou shalt not reveal the nakedness of thy father's wife's daughter. For if he had said thus far, we should understand that lying was forbidden even with the daughter of the stepmother whom the stepmother had borne by a former husband; and she would not be sister, either by father or by mother, to him to whom it is forbidden. But when he added: She is thy sister by the same father, thou shalt not reveal her shame, he makes it manifest that the prohibition was made concerning a sister, since she was of the father and of the stepmother, of whom he had already spoken above; but perhaps he wished to forbid more plainly what he said above obscurely.
18.11: **“The nakedness of thy father's wife's daughter, whom she bore to thy father,”** — THE DAUGHTER OF THY FATHER'S WIFE etc. AUGUSTINE. Lest he seem to forbid lying with the daughter of a stepmother by a former husband, since she is not sister, either by father or by mother, to him to whom it is forbidden, he added: by the same father.
18.14:
**“Thou shalt not uncover the nakedness of thy father's brother:”**
• otherwise: of thy uncle
• THE NAKEDNESS OF THY FATHER'S BROTHER etc. AUGUSTINE. It is asked whether this is forbidden while the brother is living or dead. If while the brother is living, this is contained in the general precept by which a man is forbidden to approach another's wife. Why then does he distinguish the household persons so carefully by their own prohibitions? For what he forbids concerning the father's wife, that is, the stepmother, is not to be taken of the father living, and not rather of the father dead: for while the father lived, who did not know it to be forbidden, since every other man's wife is forbidden? He seems therefore to speak of those persons who, having no husbands, could come together in marriage unless it had been forbidden by the Law, as the custom of the Persians is said to be. But if it is understood to be forbidden when the brother is dead, then no seed will be raised up to the dead brother. It is to be taken thus, therefore: It is not lawful to marry the wife of a deceased brother if the deceased left offspring; or it is forbidden to marry a brother's wife to whom a bill of divorce has been given: for someone might think it lawful for him to marry such a one and not fear adultery.
**“neither shalt thou approach to his wife, who is joined to thee by affinity.”** — NEITHER SHALT THOU APPROACH etc. Septuagint: And to his wife thou shalt not go in. Hence they call this the shame of his father's brother, that is, of the uncle, namely the privy parts of the wife.
18.17:
**“Thou shalt not uncover the nakedness of thy wife and her daughter.”** — that is: lest thou think it lawful for thee to have both.
**“Her daughter's daughter or her son's daughter thou shalt not take,”**
• He forbids the granddaughter of thy wife by thy son or by thy daughter to be taken to wife.
• THE NAKEDNESS OF THY WIFE etc. In the mother desire is understood, in the daughter action, in the granddaughter death. For desire brings forth sin, and sin death or another sin; as David from desire committed adultery, and for the adultery committed murder.
**“to discover her shame: because they are her flesh, and such copulation is incest.”** — TO REVEAL HER SHAME etc. As if: sin is familiar and akin to you. Whence we ought to suffer with one another and bear our burdens, that we may fulfil the law of Christ, who bore our sins.
18.18:
**“Thy wife's sister for a harlot, to rival her,”** — FOR A HARLOT, TO RIVAL HER etc. Septuagint: For her jealousy; as if this jealousy were between sisters, as if it were not also between those not sisters. Or rather lest it be done with this mind, that a sister be brought in upon a sister for jealousy? God has called us in peace: let us have peace with all, above all with our neighbours. Also with the Jewish way of life it is not fitting to take on the ecclesiastical, nor to celebrate the typical Pasch with the true, nor circumcision with baptism. Whence Paul: If you be circumcised, Christ shall profit you nothing. The Jewish way of life, therefore, being put to death, he ought to be joined to the Church, which is the sister of the law, has the same doctors, the same prophets. But the Jewish way of life is jealous, because its riches have passed over to the Church. Whence Paul says: "They are zealous in your regard not well"; for the former wife is jealous because the second comes in. Whence Lia says: "Dost thou think it a small matter that thou hast taken my husband from me?"
**“thou shalt not take, neither shalt thou discover her nakedness, while she is yet living.”**
• By publishing their works: yet you shall not spare them, if the hearers be not scandalized.
• THY WIFE'S SISTER etc. AUGUSTINE. He does not forbid bringing in any other wife upon the first, which was lawful for the ancients because of the abundance of propagation, but a sister; which Jacob nevertheless did, because it had not yet been forbidden by the law, or because he had been deceived by the fraud of substitution; and her whom he took afterwards he came to by agreement; but it was unjust that the first should be put away, lest he should make her commit adultery.
18.19: **“Thou shalt not approach to a woman having her flowers,”** — TO A WOMAN HAVING HER FLOWERS etc. Though he had sufficiently forbidden this above, he repeats it here also, perhaps lest in what went before it seem to be taken figuratively, where such things are forbidden as, the observance of the shadows being removed, are to be kept in the New Testament. In Ezechiel also, among those things which are sins not figuratively but manifestly, approaching a woman in her courses is forbidden, and it is the merit of justice if one does not approach; in which matter nature is not condemned, but what is harmful to the offspring to be conceived is forbidden.
18.20:
**“With the wife”** — wisdom
**“of thy neighbour”** — the Gentile, who is neighbour in nature
**“thou shalt not lie,”** — by communicating
**“nor of seed”** — of action, of doctrine
**“be defiled with mingling.”**
• so far as to be defiled
• WITH THE WIFE OF THY NEIGHBOUR etc. Here he forbids adultery again, which is forbidden also in the Decalogue; whence it appears that those were forbidden in such a way that, even when their husbands are dead, they may not marry the wives whose shame he forbids to be revealed.
18.21:
**“Thou shalt not give any of thy seed to be consecrated to the idol”** — Septuagint: to the prince
**“Moloch,”** — OF THY SEED etc. These things are fittingly joined. For the lawgiver intends to restrain one subject to the law from lust, sensible as well as intelligible; whence both the woman in her courses is forbidden and the neighbour's wife, because in such a mingling there is adultery, not marriage. Whence he adds: Nor be defiled with mingling of seed. But marriage is honourable, and the bed undefiled. Since therefore he was speaking of twofold fornication, rightly he adds: Thou shalt not give of thy seed to the idol Moloch etc. And by seed we understand not only children and kindred, but every action and doctrine, which we ought not to consecrate to idols, because the root of all evils is covetousness, which is the service of idols. Nor ought we to teach the things that pertain to idolatry. For so we go not in to a woman in her courses, nor are mingled in the error of the Gentiles.
**“nor defile the name”** — Let this be referred to each of the things aforesaid.
**“of thy God:”**
• whose glory is singular and unchangeable
• NOR DEFILE etc. Not only by living luxuriously, or sacrificing to idols, but also by bringing the philosophy of the Gentiles into the Church. For what agreement hath the temple of God with idols?
18.22:
**“Thou shalt not lie with mankind as with womankind,”**
• because it is against nature
• because you ought not to make effeminate one who acts manfully and is strong
**“because it is an abomination.”** — SYMMACHUS: unspeakable
18.23:
**“Thou shalt not copulate with any beast, neither shalt thou be defiled with it.”** — namely with the actions of beastly men, so as to be defiled with unspeakable pleasures
**“A woman shall not lie down to a beast, nor copulate with it: because it is a heinous crime.”** — A WOMAN SHALL NOT LIE DOWN TO A BEAST etc. The law is laid down not only for men but also for women. Whence: "Who shall find a valiant woman?" For as the male signifies the soul strong and constant in virtues, so the woman designates one who keeps her dignity: for she was made as a help to the man; and she who is such ought not to be defiled by the coupling of beasts.
18.24:
**“Defile not yourselves with any of these things”** — aforesaid
**“with which all the nations have been defiled, which I will cast out before you,”**
• The greatness of the punishment shows the greatness of the fault.
• DEFILE NOT YOURSELVES etc. The punishment of the defiled shows how great the defilement is in the things aforesaid. Nor is it to be passed over heedlessly that he gathers into one the things that are joined to one another, to show that he who is defiled in one offends in all.
• ALL THE NATIONS HAVE BEEN DEFILED etc. The demons, who for their multitude are called all the nations. Who, though they rejoice in every sin, rejoice chiefly in fornication and idolatry, because in these both body and soul are stained, and the whole man, who is called earth. But God has visited the earth, that is, the race of men.
18.25:
**“And with which the land is defiled: the abominations of which I”** — the defilement
**“will visit,”** — "The Orient from on high hath visited us."
**“that it may vomit out”** — even bringing forth hornets against them
**“its inhabitants.”** — the demons, who said: If thou cast us out, send us into the herd of swine.
18.26:
**“Keep ye my ordinances and my judgments, and do not any of these abominations: neither any of your own nation,”** — who was nourished in the law and taught from infancy
**“nor any stranger that sojourneth among you.”** — who was added to you from outside, not nourished within
18.27:
**“For all these detestable things the inhabitants of the land have done, that were before you,”** — the demons, who are more ancient in their creation
**“and have defiled it.”** — namely the human earth, suggesting disobedience to Adam; and daily they suggest evil things
18.28:
**“Beware then, lest you also”** — because you have been visited by the Lord
**“in like manner it vomit out,”** — the intelligible earth; whence: Depart from me, you cursed, into everlasting fire, which was prepared for the devil etc. And again: "Depart from me, all ye workers of iniquity" etc.
**“if the like things”** — the like
18.29:
**“Every soul that shall commit any of these abominations, shall perish”** — now, and utterly in the future
**“from the midst of his people.”** — EVERY SOUL etc. For those who commit such things after the preaching of the Gospel find no other medicine of the evil; nor will they be in the lot of men but of demons.
18.30:
**“Keep my commandments. Do not the things which they have done, that have been before you,”** — by whose punishment you ought to be frightened
**“and be not defiled therein. I am the Lord your God.”**
• He says this a third time: for in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word stands.
• KEEP MY COMMANDMENTS etc. As if: The commandments are mine, not man's; to whose image you are made, which you ought not to defile, "for you are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwelleth in you".

19.2:
**“Speak to all the congregation of the children of Israel, and thou shalt say to them: Be ye holy,”**
• because you are the temple of God
• Rightly he sets holiness first, because it is the foundation of virtue.
**“because I the Lord your God am holy.”**
• as if: Without holiness you cannot be with me.
• BE YE HOLY etc. ORIGEN. We must ask what this name 'holy' signifies. The vessels of the ministry are called holy, and the holy vestments; places too in the cities or the suburbs assigned to the priests are called holy, and the firstborn of oxen or of cattle. If therefore we consider in what sense these are called holy, we shall see how we should strive to be holy. A firstborn ox is born to me; it is not lawful to employ it on common work, because it is holy to the Lord. What is holy, therefore, ought to serve none but God alone; for common uses we ought to use common things. He therefore who has vowed himself to God, separated from the business of the world and from those who live carnally, that he may please him to whom he has approved himself, is called holy. For while he is mingled with the crowd he cannot be holy. Be ye holy etc.: as if: Be separated even from a brother walking disorderly, and from all the desires of the world. So you will be firstborn calves. Let not sin work through you, nor malice lay its yoke upon you; serve only the uses of the priesthood; because I am holy, that is, far from all things which work and are worshipped, whether in heaven or on earth; I surpass every creature that I have made: be you therefore set apart from those who are not holy. The Greek word hagios also sounds 'without earth', that you may have your conversation in heaven.
19.3:
**“Let every one fear his father, and his mother.”** — LET EVERY ONE etc. He builds upon the foundation; as if: Be holy, that the Holy One may dwell in you, and pay the dignity of nature by honouring father and mother.
**“Keep my sabbaths.”** — MY SABBATHS etc. Wishing to recapitulate the commandments of the law, that is: Thou shalt not kill, Thou shalt not steal etc., he says: Keep my sabbaths. For the true sabbath is to cease from all evil. Whence Moses: "You shall do no servile work therein."
**“MY SABBATHS”** — God, wishing to teach us of the intelligible rest and of the consummation of the world, when it is impossible to prepare food or to work, or to be busied about anything bodily, says through Moses: Today is the sabbath of the Lord; you shall not find it in the field etc. Note that he does not say 'sabbath' but sabbaths, because the intelligible rest is quiet and free not from one but from all carnal things: therefore in this place the name of sabbaths was first set in the divine Scripture, that you may know that the sabbath is full and perfect rest.
19.4:
**“Turn ye not to idols,”** — that is: to condescend to those whom the vain and profane law of idols weighs down.
**“nor molten gods”** — Statues of any animals, or treasures of money, which those who gather them adore as gods, nor do they presume to take anything thence.
**“make to yourselves. I am the Lord your God.”** — You will need no other.
19.5:
**“If ye offer in sacrifice a peace offering”** — or of saving offerings, namely by working the things that pertain to salvation
**“to the Lord, that he may be favourable,”** — acceptable to God
19.6: **“On the same day”** — namely in the present life
19.7: **“If after two days any man eat thereof,”** — so that he thinks he will complete after this life what he has done too little
19.8:
**“And shall bear his iniquity, because he hath defiled the holy thing of the Lord,”** — because he works imperfectly and slanders the divine law
**“and that soul shall perish”** — Because he led an imperfect life, which would have saved him if he had completed it.
**“from among his people.”**
• of those to be saved
• IF YE OFFER etc. He repeats almost all the chapters of the law, that he may fix their memory in the hearers, but above all the most necessary, as this commandment which he set forth above when he treated of sacrifices. He took the saving sacrifice, in which it is necessary to work the things that pertain to salvation; and that it may be acceptable, godliness and chastity must be offered. For this, according to the Apostle, is good and acceptable in the sight of God our Saviour, who will have all men to be saved. And to eat on the day of the immolation and on the next is to work in the present life whatever pertains to salvation: for today and tomorrow are taken for the present world. Whence James: You that say: Today or tomorrow we will go into such a city etc. The third day, because on it the Lord rose from the dead, bears the figure of the world to come and of the resurrection, in which it will not be lawful to work, but to receive the reward of works. He therefore who lives here as though he will work there, as though he would eat the sacrifice on the third day, is forbidden by the lawgiver to do this, because he leaves virtue imperfect, as though he could perfect it there.
19.9:
**“When thou reapest”** — The field is the world, the reaping doctrine, the reapers the doctors.
**“the corn of thy land, thou shalt not cut down”**
• thou shalt bruise
• otherwise: thou shalt thresh
19.10:
**“Neither in thy vineyard the bunches”** — the just, the saints
**“and grapes that fall down”** — the things which are not understood
**“shalt thou gather, but to the poor”** — the Gentiles
**“and the strangers to take”** — to be handled diligently
**“shalt leave them. I am the Lord your God.”**
• for you poor and a stranger in the world
• because I have given all things, I desire something to be given me
• WHEN THOU REAPEST etc. That we may have love for one another, that we may be lovers and merciful to the poor, is commanded in the present chapter. For we ought to give to the needy, and not exact debts violently, and to grant the remnants of our goods, imitating God the giver of all things. Therefore he wills those who reap or gather grapes to leave something to the poor man and the proselyte, lest they seem ungrateful to the giver of all, who gave riches to some and willed others to live on the remnants of others, that so he might prove the stewardship of the rich and the patience of the poor. For he does not cast away the poor and the proselytes, for whom he has provided food even thus. Whence he adds: I am the Lord your God, namely who make men rich, who for you become poor, who for the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor will at length arise.
• Allegorically. When thou reapest etc. He shows plainly that the doctors of the Jews do not grasp the interpretation of the whole law, but leave certain things to the poor man and the proselyte, namely to the Gentiles, to whom it is said: Blessed are the poor in spirit etc.; who are proselytes too, because they thrust themselves into the kindred of Abraham. What is said therefore: "Thou shalt not kill", "Thou shalt not commit adultery", let the doctors of the Jews reap. But the things which have a spiritual interpretation, such as cleansings, sacrifices and the like, let them grant to the doctors of the Church, and the things which fall from them as they reap, that is, which they themselves do not understand.
• NEITHER IN THY VINEYARD etc. The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel, which ought to have brought forth grapes and brought forth thorns; yet once it had a few bunches, that is, the saints of divers times, whom the Jews cannot gather and treasure in their riches, who do not imitate their life, but leave them to the poor man and the proselyte. For as many as were just among them are with us. Whence their memorials are celebrated every year by us and not by them, that the divine word may be proved by experience.
19.11:
**“You shall not steal.”** — in which the neighbour is hurt
**“You shall not lie,”** — in any manner
**“YOU SHALL NOT LIE”** — He shows the kinship of sins. We think many things small which are very great, as lying and perjury, which are joined with theft; and rightly, because these work together with theft.
**“YOU SHALL NOT STEAL”** — AUGUSTINE. What he says: You shall not lie, nor do calumny, is set in the Decalogue. In this precept there seems to be contained: neither shalt thou bear false witness; because calumny cannot be done without a lie, which is comprised under false witness. But it is asked whether by some compensation it should be done (as seems right to almost all) that one should lie for safety where no one is hurt. Is one then likewise to steal, even when it is for the good of him from whom it is done? As if one should steal the sword from a man wishing to kill himself. So the calumny which Joseph brought upon his brethren concerning the cup was made for a greater joy to come; upon whom he had also laid the false charge of spying. For perhaps it is not theft except when the neighbour is hurt by something of his secretly taken away; and calumny, when the neighbour is hurt by the charge of a false crime. But we cannot say that a lie is a lie only then. For when it is spoken by one who knows, it is a lie, whether anyone or no one is hurt. And it is said absolutely: You shall not lie; as that: Thou shalt not make to thyself an idol, Thou shalt not commit adultery, Thou shalt not steal. But idolatry or adultery and theft, as it has been defined, cannot be just. And: Thou shalt not kill; because when a man is justly killed, the law kills, not you. Can it likewise be said, when a man lies justly, that the law lies? The midwives lied, and God rewarded them with good things. Rahab lied, and was delivered. Or is it that from the time it was said in the Law: You shall not lie, from then it was not lawful to lie in such a case or cause? But rather a lie was forbidden because it was unjust, not unjust because it was forbidden. Perhaps then, as the midwives were rewarded not because they lied but because they freed the infants, and because of this mercy the sin was venial, yet not none at all; so Rahab was delivered for the deliverance of the spies, for which the sin was venial. But let no one think that in other sins, if they are done for the deliverance of men, pardon can be so granted: for many evils intolerable and detestable follow such an error.
19.12:
**“Thou shalt not swear falsely by my name,”** — THOU SHALT NOT SWEAR FALSELY etc. Septuagint: You shall not take up my name unjustly. An oath is unjust not only when it is broken, but also when it is unjustly kept, as the oath of Herod to the daughter of Herodias: such oaths ought not to be made, or if they are made, kept.
**“nor profane the name of thy God. I am the Lord.”** — NOR PROFANE etc. By doing evil, because you cannot transgress the oath. For God, by whom you swear, so wills good things that, if he threaten evil, he does not inflict it if he sees men repent, that he may bestow mercy. Whence he adds: I am the Lord, namely merciful, compassionate, and ready to repent of the evil.
19.13:
**“Thou shalt not calumniate thy neighbour,”** — by transferring his glory to yourself
**“THOU SHALT NOT CALUMNIATE”** — AUGUSTINE. All the things which are forbidden to be committed against the neighbour are to be referred to this one thing which was said: Thou shalt not harm thy neighbour. For as to what follows: Thou shalt not take by force, unless it be referred to this, that one may not harm by taking by force, it happens that one may harm by not taking by force: for a sword is to be taken by force from a madman.
**“nor oppress him by violence.”** — NOR OPPRESS HIM BY VIOLENCE etc. Little by little he instructs the hearer, and joins things that seem small to great ones, so that those who are frightened by the defined penalty of evils may abstain from the lesser. For those who are joined in the commandment are joined also in the penalty. For he who offends in one is guilty of all. Therefore he joins violence to calumny. Nor does it matter how one loses his goods, whether by fraud or by power or in any other way.
**“The wages of him that hath been hired by thee shall not abide”** — the wages of the work which he has earned
**“with thee until the morning.”**
• THE WAGES OF HIM THAT HATH BEEN HIRED SHALL NOT ABIDE etc. The wages, namely, by which perhaps he lives with wife and children and parents. If it is put off, his food fails; even if he receive it on the morrow, he has suffered violence and calumny, because meanwhile he had nothing to live on.
• THE WAGES OF THE HIRED etc. The wages of the preacher are from the word of preaching, which ought not to abide with us, that is, be idle, until the morning, namely the world to come, which succeeds this night, in which is light unquenchable. For from the progress of the disciple the wages of the master grow.
19.14:
**“Thou shalt not speak evil of the deaf,”** — the disobedient; whence Isaias: Hear, ye deaf, and ye blind, come that ye may see. These are not to be cursed but taught and corrected.
**“nor before the blind”** — the ignorant
**“put a stumblingblock:”**
• by saying or doing wicked things
• THOU SHALT NOT SPEAK EVIL OF THE DEAF etc. To speak evil of the deaf is to disparage one who is absent and does not hear. To put a stumblingblock before the blind is to do a thing that is indeed discreet, but to give occasion of scandal to one who has not the light of discretion.
**“but thou shalt fear the Lord thy God, because I am the Lord.”** — who forbids these things
19.15:
**“Thou shalt not do that which is unjust, nor judge unjustly. Respect not the person of the poor,”**
• O judge
• so as to decline from justice for poverty's sake, because "God is a just judge", and you ought not to be more merciful than he
**“nor honour the countenance of the mighty.”** — Because no one is mightier than God, whose the judgment is, whose person you bear in judging.
**“But judge thy neighbour according to justice.”** — THOU SHALT NOT DO THAT WHICH IS UNJUST etc. The law sets down the highest and perfect justice chiefly in the present things, proceeding by a straight road: first providing for the poor, then instructing the mighty and the princes. For it shows that one ought not to respect persons, nor commit theft or calumny, nor perjure oneself; which, though they sometimes befall the rich and mighty, are yet the proper sins of the poor, who seem to be driven to them by poverty. Whence Solomon: "Or being compelled by poverty, I should steal, and forswear the name of my God." But to oppress by violence, to withhold wages, and to mock the deaf and the blind belong to the rich and mighty.
19.16:
**“THOU SHALT NOT BE A DETRACTOR”** — HESYCHIUS. Septuagint: Thou shalt not walk in guile among thy people. David too joins murder to guile. Whence: "The bloody and the deceitful man the Lord will abhor." For guile is a hidden sword; so let us swiftly flee guile, which is joined to so great a crime.
**“nor a whisperer among the people. Thou shalt not stand against the blood of thy neighbour.”** — THOU SHALT NOT STAND etc. As if: Thou shalt not join thyself to those who lie in wait for their neighbours; as many, allied with others, do what they cannot do by themselves.
19.17:
**“Thou shalt not hate thy brother”** — any man whatever
**“in thy heart,”** — though you feign craftily to hate him that you may correct him; whence: Yet do not esteem him as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother.
**“but openly”** — not by disparaging secretly
**“reprove him, lest thou incur”** — by consenting
19.18:
**“Seek not revenge,”** — Revenge is mine, and I will repay, saith the Lord.
**“nor be mindful”** — so as to avenge
**“SEEK NOT REVENGE”** — That is: lest you be carried away by the lust of avenging while you rebuke, so as to wish to rejoice or be consoled at another's evil; but rather to take counsel for him whom you rebuke. Whence, according to the Septuagint, there follows: Thou shalt not be angry with the children of thy people. For so anger is rightly defined as the lust of avenging.
**“Thou shalt love thy friend”** — Septuagint: neighbour
**“as thyself.”** — This is the confirmation and abridgement of the whole law: for love is the fulfilling of the law.
**“I am the Lord.”** — who have true charity toward you. "Greater love than this no man hath, that a man lay down his life for his friends."
19.19:
**“Keep ye my laws. Thy cattle”** — the common people
**“thou shalt not make to gender with beasts of any other kind.”**
• with Jews and Gentiles
• THY CATTLE etc. These things seem ridiculous according to the letter, and were not observed by the prophets and spiritual men. Whence David says: Set my son Solomon upon my mule. But according to the letter it behoved them to abhor what was born of such a mingling. The valiant woman also found wool and flax, and wrought by the counsel of her hands.
**“Thy field”** — the Church committed to thee
**“thou shalt not sow with different seeds.”** — with catholic and heretical doctrine
**“Thou shalt not wear a garment that is woven of two sorts.”** — the worship of Christ and of idols: "You cannot serve God and mammon."
19.20:
**“If a man carnally lie with a woman”** — made a partaker of doctrine, and mingled with it through the way of life of the law
**“with copulation of seed”** — through the word of a teacher
**“that is a bondservant”** — through fault
**“and marriageable,”** — through nature
**“MARRIAGEABLE”** — Septuagint: Kept for a man, that is, the Synagogue kept for the law, which could not be espoused to Christ before the letter of the law died. Whence: You are become dead to the law by the body of Christ, that you may belong to another. The Synagogue is the bondwoman, according to that: "Abraham had two sons: the one by a bondwoman, and the other by a free woman."
**“and yet with a price”** — of the blood of Christ
**“not redeemed, nor with freedom”** — with the freedom wherewith Christ hath made us free
**“THEY BOTH SHALL BE SCOURGED”** — Septuagint: There shall be a visitation for them, that is, they shall be freed from the servitude of the law, according as it is said to the children of Israel who were to be freed from Egypt: "Visiting I have visited you."
**“and they shall not be put to death, because she was not a free woman.”** — AND THEY SHALL NOT BE PUT TO DEATH etc. For though they acted according to the letter, not according to the spirit, because they did not know the intention of the lawgiver, they more easily obtained pardon.
19.21:
**“And for his trespass he shall offer to the Lord, at the door of the tabernacle of the testimony, a ram:”**
• Christ
• IF A MAN CARNALLY LIE etc. Note how great is the difference of freedom and servitude. For with a free woman espoused, death is the penalty of adultery; but with a marriageable bondwoman, and, according to the Septuagint, kept for a man, that is, espoused, a sacrifice is commanded to be offered, not death inflicted. Yet these things are to be understood spiritually.
**“IF A MAN CARNALLY LIE”** — When he forbade cattle to be mingled with cattle of another kind, that is, those who are under the yoke of Christ to take up the yoke of the law, he fitly added this, showing that even before the coming of Christ whoever was outwardly mingled with the Jews needed the sacrifice of the true ram.
19.22:
**“And the priest shall pray for him”** — Christ
**“and for his trespass”** — otherwise: sin
19.23:
**“When you shall be come into the land, and shall have planted in it fruit trees, you shall take away the firstfruits of them:”** — not approving the beginnings of works
**“the fruit that comes forth”** — the works that are beginning
19.24: **“But in the fourth year,”** — at the coming of Christ
19.25:
**“And in the fifth year”** — when the apostles were preaching
**“you shall eat the fruits thereof, gathering the increase thereof. I am the Lord your God.”**
• WHEN YOU SHALL BE COME etc. He continues in his purpose, showing that the Jews had no good fruit before the coming of Christ, when he says the fruit is not to be eaten in three years nor clean, but is to be cleansed in the fourth year; and what the cleansing is, is not said. But what is said is to be understood spiritually.
• WHEN YOU SHALL BE COME INTO THE LAND etc. He calls the divine Scripture the land, which the Jews first received. Whence they were commanded to plant fruit trees. And the planting of trees is the meditation and preaching of the law, according to what is said: "I have planted, Apollo watered" etc. Good indeed were the commandments, like fruit trees, but they did not do what they ought, following only the letter. The fruit, therefore, that is, the working of the law, was unclean for three years: from Abraham to David, from David to the transmigration, thence to Christ, as Matthew distinguished. In the fourth year he commends the fruit of the law as holy and praiseworthy, yet not yet eatable by the Jews. For the fruit of the law in the fourth year, that is, at the coming of Christ, was holy and praiseworthy, which the Holy of holies wrought, whose works were praiseworthy and glorious. Whence also at the paralytic carrying his bed they glorified God, who had given such power to men: but the Jew did not yet eat, because he was not converted. But in the fifth year, that is, when the apostles were preaching, all who believed ate its fruit.
• AND SHALL HAVE PLANTED etc. MORALLY. GREGORY. Fruit trees are works fruitful in virtues. We take away the foreskins when, suspicious of the weakness of beginning, we do not approve the beginnings of our works. The fruits that sprout we do not fit for our eating, because when the beginnings of a good work are praised, this ought not to feed the mind of the worker, lest, while praise is sweetly taken, the fruit of the work be eaten out of season. He therefore who has received praise for virtue begun eats, as it were, the fruit of the planted tree before its time. Whence: "It is vain for you to rise before light: rise ye after you have sitten." To rise before light is to rejoice in the night of the present life before the brightness of the eternal reward.
19.26:
**“You shall not eat with blood.”**
• Septuagint: You shall not eat upon the mountains, as the Gentiles ate at the feasts of the idols.
• YOU SHALL NOT EAT etc. He scrapes away the whole leaven of the Jews and the Gentiles. Whence now he forbids the servitude of the law, now the error of the Gentiles.
**“ALLEGORICALLY”** — Not to eat upon the mountains is not to be fed on proud thoughts, of which Isaias: "Every mountain and hill shall be made low." Not to divine by birds is not to attend to those things that snatch away the seed of godliness. To cut the hair roundwise is to consecrate the thoughts to demons. To shave the beard is to corrupt the perfection of virtue by working feignedly. Not to cut the flesh is not to take up delights which both harm the soul and corrupt the body. Marks: wicked doctrine, which is fixed in the soul and is hardly done away.
**“You shall not divine nor observe dreams.”** — YOU SHALL NOT DIVINE etc. By a part he signifies the whole, condemning all superstitions of this kind. For he who cares to observe such things seems to defame God, as though he had given more knowledge to birds than to men.
19.27:
**“Nor shall you cut your hair roundwise: nor shave your beard.”**
• Septuagint: thou shalt not mar the look of thy beard.
• NOR SHALL YOU CUT YOUR HAIR ROUNDWISE etc. As the barbarians do: each one ought to be content with natural adornments, lest he seem to accuse the Creator as unable to perfect his work; nor to grow and vow locks in honour of demons, as the pagans are eager to offer the heads of boys to demons; which he seems chiefly to forbid here.
19.28:
**“You shall not make any cuttings in your flesh, for the dead,”** — As the Gentiles, having no hope of resurrection; whence: That you be not sorrowful, even as others who have no hope.
**“neither shall you make in yourselves any figures or marks:”** — MARKS. The lawgiver takes care even of our comeliness, that we may not abuse the flesh even in those things which disfigure the body.
19.29:
**“Make not a common strumpet”** — who oughtest to correct her
**“thy daughter,”** — THY DAUGHTER: the carnal one, or the soul. Whence: "Deliver, O God, my soul from the sword: my only one from the hand of the dog." She, by departing from God, commits fornication with demons.
**“lest the land be defiled,”**
• that is: the inhabitants of the land.
• The body, which is of earth, in which all iniquity rules when the soul commits fornication.
**“and filled with wickedness.”** — Septuagint: with fornication.
19.30:
**“My sabbaths”** — holidays from all evil
**“keep ye, and reverence my sanctuary.”** — lest you enter unworthily
**“I am the Lord.”**
• who dwell in the holy ones
• MY SABBATHS etc. From the one sabbath every lawful rest is called a sabbath. So from one general abstinence the lawgiver is eager to run through the particulars, commanding us to abstain from all evil. Whence he adds: Reverence my sanctuary. For as those who approach worthily sanctify it, so those who presume wickedly and approach unclean defile it, so far as in them lies, as Nadab and Abiu. Whence the Apostle: "Therefore are there many infirm and weak among you" etc. Hence is added: I am the Lord, namely holy and dwelling in the holy, and judging wrong done to holy things.
19.31:
**“AFTER WIZARDS”** — Septuagint: Ventriloquists, that is, pythons or false prophets, who bring forth from the belly of their heart certain fables and stinking doctrines.
**“neither of soothsayers”** — NEITHER OF SOOTHSAYERS etc. Septuagint: Poisoners, who namely call upon the names of demons, and sometimes cure the body that they may kill the soul.
19.32:
**“Rise up before the hoary head,”**
• by deferring
• that the younger also may rise up for thee
**“and honour the person of the aged man:”**
• in age or in wisdom
• BEFORE THE HOARY HEAD etc. In the ancient is wisdom, and in length of days prudence. Hence Paul says: "Let the priests be esteemed worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine."
19.33:
**“If a stranger dwell”** — newly converted
**“in your land,”** — the cultivation of virtues, good doctrine
**“and abide among you,”** — made faithful
**“do not upbraid him:”** — because he was an unbeliever
19.34:
**“But let him be among you as one of the same country:”** — nourished and taught in the faith
**“and you shall love him as yourselves:”** — "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself."
**“for you were”** — before the faith
**“strangers also”** — aliens from God
**“in the land of Egypt.”**
• in the world
• IF A STRANGER DWELL etc. The land given us by God is namely the cultivation of virtues and good doctrine. If therefore anyone wishes to be converted to our faith and enrolled as a citizen of our land, let us not afflict him nor lay a heavy yoke upon him, as the Pharisees, of whom it is said: They bind heavy and insupportable burdens; but with a finger of their own they will not move them. Let him be to us as one of the country, namely one who has been nourished in the faith and grown in godliness. Hence Peter said to those who wished to circumcise the believers from among the Gentiles: "Why tempt you God, to put a yoke upon the necks of the disciples?"
**“I am the Lord your God.”** — who will all to be saved and none to perish
19.35:
**“Do not any unjust thing”** — by respecting persons
**“in judgment,”** — Judge right things, ye sons of men.
**“in rule,”** — the kind of the species that follow
**“in weight,”** — of metals
**“or in measure.”** — of wine or oil or millet
19.36:
**“Let the balance”** — by which silver and the like are weighed
**“be just and the weights equal, the bushel just, and the sextary equal.”** — DO NOT ANY UNJUST THING etc. In what went before he commands justice to be kept in judgment; here in weights and measures; and let us use the bounds of justice for justice: for these are the bounds for sellers and buyers, as the laws are for judges, that all injustice against the neighbour may be guarded against. For what possessions of land and treasures of money are to the rich man, this a measure of wine and wheat and the like is to the poor.
**“ORIGEN”** — MORALLY. DO NOT ANY UNJUST THING etc. In the judgment of the mind we ought not to act unjustly, nor corrupt the measures of natural justice, judging our own sins one way and our neighbour's another. For in what judgment we judge, we shall be judged; and with what measure we mete, it shall be measured to us again. Let us have also divine balances and divine measures just; that is, let us keep the laws of divine Scripture holily and justly, adding nothing of ours, taking away nothing of theirs, lest it be said to us: Why do you transgress the commandment of God for your traditions?
**“I am the Lord.”** — not another
**“your God,”**
• whose servants you are
• by whom you were created
**“that brought you out of the land of Egypt.”**
• who in many things have done your will
• Be not ungrateful, but
19.37:
**“Keep”**
• as a treasure
• lest one tittle or one jot pass away

20.2:
**“Thus shalt thou say to the children of Israel:”**
• the Jews by birth
• He had already said this above, but here he adds the penalty.
**“If any man of the children of Israel,”** — by birth
**“or of the strangers that dwell in Israel,”** — proselytes
**“give of his seed to the idol Moloch,”** — the idol of the Moabites, which is interpreted 'king'.
**“dying let him die: the people”** — not only, but the prince also
**“of the land shall stone him.”** — THE LORD SPOKE etc. The law often repeats the same things, that it may fix their memory in the reader; yet it inserts certain new things, lest it seem superfluous, but that by inquiring into the new the things already said may be inquired into more studiously. Whence above, in forbidding certain things, it was silent about the penalty, that, asking what or of what kind it is, we may diligently search it out in what follows. For when above it forbade sacrifice to Moloch, it repeats the same, adding the penalty: namely the people of the land shall stone him, not the princes only. Nor content with this, it adds: "I will set my face against him" etc.
20.3:
**“And I will set my face against him: and I will cut him off from the midst of his people,”** — of the saints
**“because he hath given of his seed”** — carnal; or the disciple whom he has begotten in teaching
**“to the idol”**
• Septuagint: to the prince
• to the prince of this world, who worketh in the children of unbelief
**“Moloch, and hath defiled my sanctuary, and profaned my holy name.”** — HATH DEFILED MY SANCTUARY etc. Whoever consecrates his seed to idols defiles the sanctuary of God and his name, because he devotes to demons the image of God which he has. He defiles also, as far as in him lies, him who gave the image and breathed in the spirit of life, while the image of God is prostituted to an unclean spirit. He who fills his son or disciple with avarice, which is the service of idols, likewise defiles the sanctuary and the name of God. In the same way one may reason of the other vices, lest anyone defile with any uncleannesses the body, which is the temple of Christ and the dwelling of the Holy Ghost. For he commands such a one to be punished by all, because he is the enemy of all and opposes the glory of all.
20.4:
**“And if the people of the land neglecting,”**
• who has been nourished in knowledge: for this is the fruitful earth.
• AND IF NEGLECTING etc. He stirs up others against him and frightens them, if they neglect a penalty so studiously commanded, God himself being angry and passing sentence.
**“and as it were little regarding my commandment, let alone the man”** — who harms himself and others
**“that hath given of his seed to Moloch,”** — Septuagint: to the prince
20.5:
**“I will set my face against that man, and his kindred,”** — the imitators of his life and doctrine
**“and will cut off both him and all that consented with him, to commit fornication with Moloch, out of the midst of their people.”**
• Not only those who do are punished, but those who consent to the doers.
• AND WILL NOT KILL HIM etc. HESYCHIUS. It is evil to allow even those who are outside to commit fornication away from God and cleave to the devil, but much more from the midst of the people: for this is to yield the whole flock to the wolf. And those who consent, namely who could accuse or reprove or warn and do not, will not escape judgment. God sets his face upon him, of which it is said: "The countenance of the Lord is against them that do evil things" etc.
20.6:
**“The soul that shall go aside after magicians,”** — Septuagint: ventriloquists
**“and soothsayers,”** — Septuagint: poisoners
**“and shall commit fornication”**
• by departing from God
• THE SOUL THAT SHALL GO ASIDE etc. It is a great sin to go aside to magicians and soothsayers: for this is to depart from God. And there are intelligible magicians, who prophesy false things in the name of the Lord. There are soothsayers, deceivers and flatterers, who with poisonous words corrupt the hearing of many and turn them from the truth.
**“with them, I will set my face against that soul,”** — "But the countenance of the Lord is against them that do evil things."
**“and destroy it out of the midst of its people.”** — as above
20.7: **“Sanctify yourselves,”** — because whoever do these things are defiled
20.8:
**“Keep my precepts,”** — which those persuade you to transgress
**“and do them, because I am the Lord that sanctify you.”** — as if: those defile, speaking against the law.
20.9:
**“He that curseth his father, or mother,”** — Ungrateful for the benefits of nature, and to the Creator, who is the father of all.
**“dying let him die:”**
• A heavy penalty, because a heavy fault; he shows the sentence to be right when he adds: father and mother etc.
• HE THAT CURSETH etc. ORIGEN. Of these things he gave precepts above, but did not set down with what penalty he would warn the disobedient: the same things therefore are repeated, and the penalty of each is decreed. There, then, are the precepts; here are given the justifications and judgments, by which what is just is adjudged to the sinner. And it is to be noted that he did not at once set penalties with the first precepts, because precepts ought to be kept from love, not fear. If you have despised them, you will be punished not so much as a man as a despiser. He kindly calls on the son, lest he punish him as a despising servant.
**“ORIGEN”** — He that curseth etc. The name of father or mother is a great mystery. God is your father according to the spirit, the heavenly Jerusalem your mother. First, God is your father, who begot your spirit. Secondly, the father of your flesh is your father, by whose ministry you were born in the flesh. Whoever then curses father or mother, dying let him die. You must return like grace to your parents. If you are insolent to your carnal father, you will be so to the spiritual also. Of the mother likewise. As a servant insolent to his bodily master dishonours God also, who lends his name to the carnal master. In no way, therefore, ought we to gainsay father or mother: let them say, let them do what they will. How can we return grace to those by whom we were begotten, nourished, instructed, by whose means we came to know God? What then is to be expected for those who deny that God is the author of the world, and turn what is said of the heavenly Jerusalem to some earthly city with depraved senses?
**“he hath cursed his father, and mother, let his blood be upon him.”** — HIS BLOOD etc. Because he himself is the cause of his death. If he is so punished who curses his carnal father, how will he be punished who has blasphemed Christ, and has not obeyed him who said: "Unless a man be born again of water and the Holy Ghost" etc.? He will die the death, namely; alienated from the kingdom of heaven, he is guilty. For nothing heavy, nor toilsome or laborious, has been commanded him.
20.10:
**“If any man commit adultery with the wife of another, and defile the wife”**
• otherwise: spouse
• the Church
**“of his neighbour,”** — of the priest, the bishop, nay of Christ
**“let them be put to death, both the adulterer and the adulteress.”** — IF ANY MAN COMMIT ADULTERY etc. AUGUSTINE. Here he would have no difference between any man whatever and the neighbour, though he often puts 'neighbour' for 'man'; and it follows of necessity: if one must abstain from the wife of any man, much more from the wife of one's neighbour. Or perhaps it is a repetition showing how great an evil it is to commit adultery with the wife of any man: for this is to commit adultery with the wife of one's neighbour. For nothing is nearer to man than man.
**“IF ANY MAN COMMIT ADULTERY”** — HESYCHIUS. Bodily adultery is evil; spiritual is worse: the one does insult to the flesh, the other to the spirit; the one to man, the other to God. He commits adultery spiritually who corrupts the doctrines of the law; he commits adultery with a man's wife who corrupts the Church of Christ, of which it is said: "For I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ." And he commits adultery by sowing a wicked doctrine, not Christ's. The priest also, or any doctor, is the husband of the Church committed to him by Christ. If any of these has stained the Church, he does wrong to his neighbour, that is, to Christ, who entrusted this care to him.
20.11:
**“IF A MAN LIE WITH HIS STEPMOTHER”** — These things were said and expounded above, where it was said: "Thou shalt not uncover the nakedness" of thy father etc. But here he touches plainly on him who does the same as his neighbour, and, not ashamed of the fellowship of sin, betrays it; on whom the lawgiver ordained the penalty of death. And he joined the man to the stepmother, because what is offended by the son against the father, this is committed by the father against the son, and the impiety is alike on both sides.
**“ORIGEN”** — Above it was said: Thou shalt not uncover the nakedness of thy stepmother. But because the penalty of the law or precept was not written beneath, he repeats the same that he may write the penalty beneath. The Apostle says: A man making void the law of Moses dieth without any mercy under two or three witnesses: how much more, do you think, he deserveth worse punishments who hath trodden underfoot the Son of God etc. In the law the adulterer or adulteress could not say: We ask penance, we beg pardon. They had to die for each of the crimes to which the penalty of death was ascribed. But among Christians, since it is not commanded that they be punished bodily, neither has power been given to bishops to condemn to present death, which the priests had in the law. Do we say then that the law of Moses was cruel, and that the Gospel of Christ has relaxed it for the worse? God forbid. But in both is the kindness of God, by a different dispensation. In the law adultery was punished by death, that those who were punished here might be punished no further: the law then was full of mercy, which willed to purge by present punishment and shut out the future. But now bodily punishment is not inflicted for purging, but the priest enjoins penance; and whether each one bears it so as to merit pardon, let him see to it himself. For with what measure he has meted, it shall be measured to him again, according to that: Thou wilt give us for our drink tears in measure. There are therefore sins which lead to death. Hence it follows that as often as one commits them, so often he dies. The Apostle signifies that there are many deaths, saying: Who hath delivered and doth deliver us out of so great deaths etc., that is, out of the deaths of sin. He seemed to be immortal as to this common death who said: Out of so great deaths he hath delivered us etc. For if he has delivered, and delivers, and will deliver, there will never be a time when he dies whom God will always deliver. We must see, therefore, lest perhaps it be heavier for us, who are punished with the death of the soul, than for those who were punished bodily; because for us punishment remains in the future, while the punishments once paid set them free. He therefore who has committed it once, let him not add it a second time: for with the just judge there is a measuring of punishment not only by quality but also by quantity.
20.12: **“If any man lie with his daughter in law, let both die,”** — because the sin is alike
20.13:
**“If any one lie with a man”** — perfect in virtues
**“as with a woman,”** — making us effeminate with him by words and examples
**“IF ANY ONE LIE WITH A MAN”** — This sin is a wrong to nature; whence it is decreed to be punished with death. For spiritually he is a male who is strong in mind. For in the divine Scripture a man is named who is perfect in virtues; let us beware of making him effeminate by wicked words or actions, lest we be dissolved with him and die together.
20.14:
**“If any man after marrying the daughter,”** — action
**“her mother”** — desire
**“marry, he hath done a heinous crime: alive”** — knowingly
**“he shall be burnt”** — repenting
**“with them:”** — desire and action
**“neither shall so great an abomination remain in the midst of you.”** — IF ANY MAN AFTER MARRYING etc. He decrees a cruel penalty for this offence. For of those who are born of the mother, as regards those whom the daughter has borne, since there is one father, it is uncertain whether they are brothers or uncles. Let so uncertain a mingling, therefore, be shunned. But because desire is the mother of every sin, if there be any desire in us, let us not join action to it. For he who does this is burnt with fire, both his desire and his action. For if by the Spirit we mortify the deeds of the flesh, we shall live.
20.15:
**“He that with any beast”** — with beastly lust
**“or cattle shall copulate,”** — by deliberating and persevering
**“dying”** — eternal
**“let him die, the beast also ye shall kill.”**
• When the beast is dead, sin does not work.
• HE THAT WITH ANY BEAST etc. Very great strictness is exercised against those who were so wicked and given to lust as to desire unheard-of crimes; whence he decreed the penalty of death for men or women mingled with four-footed beasts. To the faithful also this law will not be superfluous, if we understand the four-footed beasts as wicked wills bent to the earth, which have not hands as men have, because they lack every human action; whence they have no kinship with us. A man or woman, therefore, who cleaves or couples with them not from weakness of nature but by deliberation is guilty of death. They too are said to die when those die; for they do not subsist by themselves, nor is there any substance of sin, but it works in sinners.
**“AUGUSTINE”** — HE THAT WITH ANY BEAST etc. It is asked how the beast is guilty, since it is neither rational nor capable of law. Or, as metaphorical words are transferred from animal to animal, as a wind is called wicked or the sea angry, so here too is it transferred from the rational to the irrational? For the beasts were commanded to be killed for this reason, that, defiled by such a crime, they renew the unworthy memory of the deed.
20.17:
**“If any man take his sister, the daughter of his father, or the daughter of his mother, and see her nakedness, and she behold her brother's shame: they have committed a crime: they shall be slain,”** — that the rest may be frightened
**“in the sight of their people, because they have discovered one another's nakedness, and they shall bear their iniquity.”**
• the penalty of iniquity
• the sin itself will be the penalty
• IF ANY MAN TAKE HIS SISTER etc. HESYCHIUS. This seemed tolerable, because Abraham said of Sara: She is my sister by the father, and not by the mother. But Moses, enumerating those who were born of Thare the father of Abraham, nowhere made mention of Sara. And if Abraham married his sister, yet he did this before he knew God. Well therefore did the law forbid such a union.
• IF ANY MAN TAKE HIS SISTER etc. Tropologically. He sees and takes the nakedness of his sister by the father and not by the mother who admires and imitates a shameful action of his father or his mother, in which they offended; not only searching out what he ought not, but joining himself to the wickedness of the parents, which is called his sister as being begotten of the same parents. And because sons publish the sins of their parents by doing the like, rightly the penalty is inflicted in the sight of the people, or according to the Septuagint: In the sight of the sons of their race, namely of those who think to imitate such things, that the affliction of one may be the correction of many.
• AND SEE HER NAKEDNESS etc. AUGUSTINE. That is, shall have known her by lying with her, as there: Adam knew his wife, that is, was joined with her. And as to what he says: They shall bear their iniquity, that is, the sin itself will be the penalty.
20.18:
**“If any man lie”** — shall have cleaved with delight
**“with a woman in her flowers, and uncover”** — shall have made it plain to others
**“her nakedness, and she open the fountain of her blood,”** — the whole error of idolatry and of the sacrifices
**“both shall be destroyed out of the midst of their people.”**
• that he may not be of the people of God who has defiled the image of God, nor that be named wisdom
• IF ANY MAN LIE WITH A WOMAN etc. The lawgiver intends to urge continence, that we may not, after the manner of beasts, be continually mingled with women, but, as though under constraint, come little by little to the practice of continence. And it is strange that now he commands such to be cut off from their people, when above he laid upon the same a law of purification. Let us consider, therefore, the menstruous wisdom of the Gentiles, removed from God, disputing of the flight of birds and the course of the stars and the measures of the heaven: to sleep with this, that is, to delight in it, or to uncover it and bring forth what is hers, and to hear one setting out the fountain of the whole error, is impious. Therefore such a one shall be slain out of the midst of his people, that he may not be named man who, by not knowing the image of God and himself, has estranged the Creator from himself. She too shall be slain, that she may not be named wisdom; because: The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God.
20.19:
**“Thou shalt not uncover the nakedness of thy aunt by thy mother, and of thy aunt by thy father: he that doth this, hath uncovered the shame of his own flesh, both shall bear their iniquity.”**
• THE NAKEDNESS OF THY AUNT BY THY MOTHER etc. He forbids sons to be mingled with the sisters of their parents, that the generations may not be confounded and reverence may be shown to parents. Allegorically. But according to the spirit we ought to veil both the sins of our parents and of those who are joined with them, as brothers and sisters, from whom the parents cannot lie hid naked. Whence he adds: He hath uncovered the shame of his own flesh.
• SEPTUAGINT: They shall die without children, that is, without virtues, which is the worst barrenness.
20.20:
**“If any man lie with the wife of his uncle by the father, or of his uncle by the mother, and uncover the shame of his near akin, both shall bear their sin: they shall die without children.”**
• which is the greatest penalty
• Not that the children of such shall be killed, but the children are forbidden by the law to succeed them.
• IF ANY MAN LIE WITH THE WIFE OF HIS UNCLE etc. HESYCHIUS. He shows that the fellowship of marriage was given to the human race for the sake of children; for what he now forbids as abominable, in Deuteronomy he compels and commands, saying: When brethren dwell together, and one of them dieth without children, the wife of the deceased shall not marry to another, but his brother shall take her etc.; as Booz took Ruth by the law of kinship. But for the sake of lust he forbids such a union. And the spiritual interpretation is like what went before.
**“AUGUSTINE”** — IF ANY MAN LIE WITH THE WIFE OF HIS UNCLE etc. Whoever shall have slept with his kinswoman, and uncovered the shame of his kindred, shall die without children. It is asked how far this kinship is to be observed, since it is lawful to take a wife in a distant degree, and always has been. But it is to be understood that it is not lawful in those degrees which he forbade, according to which it was said: Whoever shall have slept with his kinswoman etc., where he passed over some things to be understood, as the sister by both parents, and the wife of the mother's brother, that is, of the maternal uncle. For of the wife of the paternal uncle he forbade first. They shall die without children: perhaps it is to be understood that it was established by law that the sons who were born of these should not be reckoned, that is, should succeed their parents by no right.
20.22:
**“Keep”** — with the will
**“my laws”** — all
**“and my judgments,”** — KEEP MY LAWS etc. It is not enough to keep part of the law; we must observe all the precepts and judgments.
**“and do them: lest you also”** — as the nations
**“vomit out”** — cast out
**“the land”** — as God judged in the son of the Israelitess who blasphemed
20.23:
**“Walk not”** — by advancing to the worse
**“after the laws”** — the superstitions which they think lawful
**“of the nations,”** — of the demons, who ruled over many
**“which I will cast out before you.”**
• The prince of this world is cast out.
• WALK NOT etc. These things are to be observed not only by the Jews but by all the nations, if they wish to serve God.
**“For they have done all these things,”** — they compelled them to do
**“and I abhorred them.”** — by casting them out of the hearts of men
20.24:
**“But to you I say: Possess the land”** — of the living, which they once had
**“of them which I will give you”** — by grace, not by merits
**“for an inheritance,”** — to be possessed for ever
**“a land flowing”** — abounding
**“WITH MILK”** — With the delights of blessedness, than which nothing is sweeter, nothing more pleasant; and they will be without all labour and sorrow, as milk and honey, which are prepared without our labour.
**“I am the Lord your God, who have separated you from other people.”** — I AM THE LORD, who said: Be not solicitous, saying: What shall we eat, or what shall we drink, or wherewith shall we be clothed? for after all these things do the heathens seek. But those who follow a loftier way of life and reward ought to be separated from the other nations.
20.25:
**“Therefore do you also separate the beast”** — the common people
**“clean from the unclean, and the clean fowl”** — the contemplatives
**“from the unclean: defile not your souls with beasts, or birds, or any things that move on the earth,”**
• Here he makes no distinction: for all were unclean.
• THEREFORE SEPARATE etc. Morally. The law calls the common people beasts or cattle, the contemplatives birds. Every common man is judged clean by many for his simplicity; likewise with the contemplatives; but it is not so: for the common man ought to be wise in good and simple in evil; for he alone is clean. The contemplative also ought to have a clean conscience and a faith unfeigned. Those who have not these are turned aside to vain babbling, "understanding neither the things they say, nor whereof they affirm". Diligently, therefore, are the clean separated from the unclean, that we may follow the clean and flee the unclean. And it is to be noted how discreetly the lawgiver here distinguishes among the four-footed beasts and the birds, and not among the creeping things of the earth. For all things that move upon the earth are unclean; they savour earthly things, namely those "whose god is their belly".
**“and which I have shewn you to be unclean.”**
• If they seem to be unclean.
• AND WHICH I HAVE SHEWN YOU etc. AUGUSTINE. He seems to say that these things are not unclean by nature, but for some sign of a sacrament, because he says that he showed them to be unclean, as though they would not be unclean to them unless they had been shown.
20.26:
**“You shall be holy unto me,”** — undefiled
**“because I am holy,”** — made a pattern of life for you
20.27:
**“A man, or woman,”** — he takes care for both sexes, who created both
**“in whom there is a pythonical or divining spirit, dying let them die:”** — He who is corrupted corrupts others.
**“WITH STONES”** — Because they seduce the simple people with vain errors, whereby they feed their belly and desire to please their hearers; such as are many today in the Church, of whom Paul says: For such serve not Christ our Lord, but their own belly; and by pleasing speeches and good words seduce the hearts of the innocent.
**“they shall stone them:”** — the people, whom they harm most

21.1:
**“The Lord said also to Moses: Speak to the priests the sons of Aaron, and thou shalt say to them: Let not a priest incur an uncleanness”** — By the letter he commands the priests to abstain from the defilements of the dead.
**“at the death of his citizens:”** — that is: namely by mourning the dead, or by deadly sins.
21.2:
**“But only for his kin, such as are near in blood,”**
• for whom we ought to take greater care
• over whom the priestly dignity often sets a son
21.3:
**“And for a maiden sister, who hath had no husband:”**
• namely estranged from the priest's house
• LET NOT A PRIEST INCUR AN UNCLEANNESS etc. That is: he will leave out nothing of the things which it is expedient for the priest to teach, and they will not obey, who die from disobedience; but only for his kin and those near etc. For the priest must use diligence for the people, lest they sin, but above all for his kindred and his house. For if any man have not care of his own, and especially of those of his house, he hath denied the faith etc. When these sin, therefore, the priest is of necessity defiled, as one who daily, nay always, ought to provide for them the things that pertain to salvation, and to watch over them lest they sin in things worthy of death. In the father and mother also the same is to be understood. For often the priestly dignity makes a son a doctor. Who hath had no husband: for if the kindred of priests have separated themselves, so that another house is made in them, when they sin the priests are not defiled. For so long as they cleave to them, keeping the law of nearness and kinship, they are rightly partakers of their defilement: for the sin of those who dwell together cannot be unknown.
**“BUT ONLY FOR HIS KIN”** — JEROME to Fabiola. The priest shall not go in to any soul that is dead. He shall not approach, namely, where there is sin, and in sin death: "The soul that sinneth, the same shall die." Though he be mighty and rich, and offer a multitude of victims, if he is dead he is not touched by the high priest, nor seen. But if he revives, and at the voice of the Saviour comes forth from the tomb, and goes forth loosed from the bands of sins, the high priest goes in to him, abides with him, and dines with him when he has risen. For his father and his mother he shall not be defiled. Affection compels us to do many things, and while we regard the nearness of bodies we offend the Creator of body and soul. But he who loves father or mother above Christ is not worthy of him. Many monks, while they have pity on their parents, have lost their souls. It is not lawful to be defiled for father or mother: how much less for brother, sister, cousins, household and servants. We are a kingly and priestly race; let us attend to that Father who never dies, or who dies for us; who, living to God, died, that he might give life to us who were dead. If we have anything of Egypt which the prince of the world can recognise as his own, let us leave it with the cloak to the Egyptian woman who holds it. A young man clad in linen followed the Lord when he was bound. He would have fallen into the snares had he not, unencumbered and naked, escaped the onset of the pursuers. Let us render to parents what is the parents', if indeed they live, if they glory that their sons serving God the Father are preferred to themselves. But this is understood of the greatest high priest, as is shown in what follows. To the lesser something is allowed.
21.5:
**“Neither shall they shave their head,”** — wisdom
**“nor their beard,”** — the perfection of wisdom
**“nor in their flesh make”** — That is: Let them not be scandalized when anyone sins, nor ought they to take carnal wisdom from this.
**“incisions.”**
• The incision is the wisdom of the flesh; therefore Paul says of the Jews who savour carnal things: "Beware of the concision."
• NEITHER SHALL THEY SHAVE THEIR HEAD etc. The law forbids priests to grieve too bitterly for the dead, as having the hope of the life to come and teaching the people; therefore they must watch not only in their own sins and have a sound mind, but also in others', which were reckoned above. The head and beard signify wisdom and perfection. Whence Christ is called our head, in whom alone we are rightly wise. Fitly the beard signifies perfection, the head wisdom, because the beard grows on those coming to the years of discretion and of youth. Sinners are called dead, according to that: When we were dead in sins, Christ hath quickened us together with himself. The head or beard of the priest, therefore, must not be shaved for the dead, because the thoughts, which adorn wisdom as the hairs the head, must not be corrupted by another's sin, but kept whole, that he may be able to exhort, reprove, rebuke.
**“NEITHER SHALL THEY SHAVE THEIR HEAD”** — JEROME to Fabiola. But the high priest shall not uncover. He who has the mitre, and bears the name of God on his forehead, and is adorned with the diadem of a king, and has come to the perfect age of Christ, and is ever to be protected by his glory, shall not rend his garments, because they are white, because they are undefiled. Thamar, her chastity lost, rent her tunic; Caiphas, his sacrifice lost, publicly tore his garments. He shall not go in to any soul that is dead, and he shall not go out of the holy places, lest he defile the sanctification of his God. We shall render account even for an idle word. Whatever does not edify the hearers turns to the peril of the speakers. If we say anything blameworthy, we go out of the holy places, and defile the name of Christ in which we flatter ourselves. How much more then the high priest (who must be without crime, and of such virtues that he ever abides in the holy places), ready to offer victims for the people, the mediator of men and God, and confecting the flesh of the Lamb with sacred mouth, because the holy oil of Christ his God is upon him, let him not defile his garments. For as many of us as are baptized in Christ have put on Christ; let us keep the tunic which we have received; we shall keep the holy in the holy. That dweller of the mountain who went down from Jerusalem to Jericho was not wounded before he was stripped. He shall take a virgin to wife etc. The high priest to whom these precepts are given is understood by some to be Christ, of whom it is said: "Thou art a priest for ever according to the order of Melchisedech." And in Zacharias: Hear, O Jesus the high priest etc. This is he from whom the filthy garments of our sins are taken away, that he may receive "the glory which he had before the world was". But lest we be thought to do violence to the Scripture, let us interpret in the members what is referred to the head, and so let us discourse of the true light, that it may be derived to those to whom Christ has granted to be light.
21.6:
**“They shall be holy to their God, and shall not profane his name:”** — Whence Malachias: O priests that despise my name. And a little after: "You offer polluted bread upon my altar."
