**“PROFANE HIS NAME”** — Which is great among the Gentiles. But you, says Malachias, have profaned it, in that you say: The table of the Lord is despised. For by sin of the sacrifice the priests profane the name of God.
21.7:
**“A harlot or a vile prostitute”** — the Synagogue, of which Isaias says: "How is the faithful city become a harlot?"
**“they shall not take to wife,”** — A HARLOT OR A VILE etc. Any priest whatever; for of the high priest he will say afterwards that he shall take none but a virgin to wife.
**“nor one that has been put away from her husband:”** — THAT HAS BEEN PUT AWAY etc. Because she is found blameworthy, the priest ought not to take her to wife, lest he preach her absence according to the letter.
21.8: **“LET HIM THEREFORE BE HOLY”** — If the priests keep the sanctification already given them by God, they sanctify God himself, who, though he is holy by nature, willed to be sanctified by the partakers of his glory.
21.9:
**“of a priest”** — of Christ
**“the daughter”** — the Synagogue
**“THE DAUGHTER OF A PRIEST”**
• It is grievous for anyone's daughter to commit fornication, but above all a priest's, who ought to have his children subject in all chastity.
• The Synagogue is called not only the wife but also the daughter of God; but corrupting both, she has become estranged. Whence: The daughter of Sion shall be left as a covert in a vineyard etc. And elsewhere: "Their mother hath committed fornication"; and that she has been burnt with fire the traces of the burning show.
21.10:
**“The high priest, that is to say, the priest that is the greatest”**
• anointed above his fellows
• THE HIGH PRIEST etc. Christ, "great is our Lord, and great is his power", who for us was made priest and victim.
**“among his brethren,”**
• I will declare thy name to my brethren.
• Christians: Whosoever shall do the will of my Father, he is my brother etc.
**“upon whose head the oil of unction hath been poured,”**
• "God, thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows."
• Septuagint: Scripture calls the oil Christ, that is, Christ himself.
**“and whose hands have been consecrated for the priesthood,”** — Septuagint: perfected
**“CONSECRATED”** — The other priests consecrated or perfected, namely their hands, in the blood of a calf and a ram; but he with his own blood, with crucified hands.
**“and who hath been vested with the holy vestments,”** — "The Lord hath reigned, he is clothed with beauty: the Lord is clothed with strength" etc.
**“shall not uncover his head,”**
• because mourners stripped off their ornaments
• of the mitre
• by stripping off the ornament
**“he shall not rend his garments:”**
• which was the custom of mourners
• He will not suffer the Church to be rent by heresies.
**“HE SHALL NOT REND HIS GARMENTS”** — HESYCHIUS. For from the time the Word was made flesh he is wholly in his flesh, nor was he ever separated from it, whether crucified or buried. Of his better garments it is said: "Clothed" with "light as with a garment"; "the deep like a garment is its clothing." This is the habit of the high priest, by which he is shown clothed with the depths of wisdom and with the light of knowledge; these are truly holy garments.
21.11:
**“Nor shall he go in at all to any dead person: not even for his father, or his mother,”** — the Jewish people, of whom he was according to the flesh
**“shall he be defiled:”**
• TO ANY DEAD PERSON etc. Septuagint: a dead soul. "The soul that sinneth, the same shall die." By this death above all the Gentiles perished, who had neither law nor doctrine; but he bore the sins of all, and yet remained undefiled.
• FOR HIS FATHER etc. ADAMANTIUS. Every man is defiled in father and mother. Christ alone entered clean into this generation; he was not defiled in his mother, because he was begotten without concupiscence, since Joseph only rendered a service, whence he earned the name of father; besides, the true Father of all is God, the mother the heavenly Jerusalem. Whoever then sin are defiled in the Father, against whom they commit sins. They are defiled in the mother who, after they have believed, harm the Church in anything, or stain the freedom of the heavenly mother with the unworthy servitude of sin.
**“AUGUSTINE”**
• TO ANY DEAD PERSON etc. Septuagint: He shall not go in to any dead soul. How he calls a dead body a dead soul is hard to understand: yet the body destitute of the soul has taken the name of its ruler, since it is to be restored to it, as the building which is called a church is still called a church when the people have gone out. But since the body of a living man is not called a soul, how is it called a soul when it is dead? Further, if we understand the dead soul as the soul separated from the body, so that we call the separation itself death (as we are said to be dead to sin because we do not use sin, so the soul is dead to the body because it does not use it), how can one go in to a dead soul, which the priest is forbidden? Or is the temporal life the soul which is dead in the body when the soul departs, which cannot die? Not because that life was the soul, but because it subsisted by its presence, it took its name: for the soul of all flesh is its blood, which is dead in the body of the dead. For it did not depart when the soul departed. He forbade, therefore, the high priest to go in to the funeral of his father or mother, which he did not forbid the second priest. He shall not go out of the holy places, namely while their funerals are being celebrated. He was forbidden to go out of the holy places as during the seven days in which he was being sanctified, but not always. Certainly if high priests are not forbidden to marry wives and beget sons, a great question arises: since he calls a man unclean from conjugal intercourse until the evening, even when he has washed his body, and the high priest is commanded, for the continual incense, to go in twice daily within the veil where the altar of incense was, nor was it lawful for any unclean person to approach the holy things, how could the high priest fulfil this daily if he begot sons? Of sickness it can be answered that by the grace of God he did not fall sick. It follows, then, either that he was continent, or that on some days he left off the incense, or, if that could not be left off, since it could be put on only by the high priest, that he was not made unclean by conjugal intercourse, by the merit of his especial sanctification; or, if what he says in what follows of all the children of Israel, that he who has met with any uncleanness may not approach the holy things, pertains to him also, it remains to take it that on some days incense was not put on, and this as a sin.
• It may be asked why the priest is forbidden to go in to the funeral of his father. For how could he be high priest while his father was not yet dead, since the law commands them to succeed their fathers? But it was necessary, before the high priest was buried, that another be at once put in his place, because of the continual incense. And of sickness we can say that perhaps high priests were not wont to die save suddenly, without preceding sickness, as Scripture testifies of Aaron.
21.12:
**“Neither shall he go out of the holy places,”** — Though he condescends to sinners, yet he is holy and rests in the holy, because he did not desert heaven, although he eats with publicans and sinners.
**“lest he defile the sanctuary of the Lord,”** — the Holy Ghost: for this is the oil of holy unction.
**“because the oil of the holy unction of his God is upon him. I am the Lord.”** — who, the lawgiver of this law, adds what sort the law is: He shall take a virgin etc.
**“AUGUSTINE”** — I AM THE LORD who sanctify. Of Moses also it was said: And thou shalt sanctify him. But Moses sanctifies by visible sacraments through the mystery; the Lord by invisible grace through the Spirit, where is the whole fruit even of the visible sacraments: without this sanctification the visible sacraments profit nothing. But the invisible sanctification profits without the visible. For one would more tolerably say that without them this does not exist, than that, if it exists, it does not profit, since this is the whole usefulness of those. And the invisible can exist without the visible. To Simon Magus the visible, namely baptism, did not profit, because the invisible was not present; but to those to whom the invisible was present it profited, even if they did not receive the visible sacraments. Yet it is not shown where Moses, who visibly sanctifies the priests, was himself sanctified by sacrifices or oil. But no one denies that he was sanctified invisibly. The same can be said of John the Baptist, who appeared as baptizer before he was baptized; whence it was clear that he was sanctified, though it is not found to have been done visibly before he baptized. This of the thief also, to whom, crucified with him, the Lord said: "This day thou shalt be with me in paradise." For he was not granted so great a happiness without invisible sanctification. From these it is gathered that invisible sanctification was present to some and profited them without the visible sacraments, which have been changed according to the diversity of times; but that visible sanctification, which is made through visible sacraments, can be present without the invisible but cannot profit. Nor yet is the visible sacrament therefore to be despised. For he who despises it cannot be sanctified invisibly: hence Cornelius and those who were with him, already sanctified by the Spirit, were baptized; nor was visible sanctification judged superfluous because the invisible had gone before.
21.13:
**“A virgin”** — the Church: "For I have espoused you to one husband" etc.
**“HE SHALL TAKE A VIRGIN UNTO HIS WIFE”** — JEROME to Fabiola. A widow is she whose husband is dead; a divorced woman, she who is cast out by a living husband; a harlot, she who lies open to the lust of many. He shall take a virgin to wife of his own race, not a foreigner, lest the grain of noble seeds degenerate in bad soil. Not a harlot, who has been exposed to many; not one cast out, who was unworthy of a former marriage; not a widow, lest she remember former pleasures; but that soul which has no spot nor wrinkle, which, reborn in Christ, is renewed from day to day. Whence: "For I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ." I would not have the disciple and wife of the high priest have anything of the old man. If we be risen with Christ, let us mind the things that are above, forgetting the past, eager for the future. Unhappy Simon, who after baptism thought of his former marriage and had not come to virginal purity, was unworthy of the fellowship of Peter.
21.14:
**“A widow”**
• the Synagogue
• having lost God
**“or one that is divorced,”**
• from God through idolatry
• others: cast out
• A WIDOW OR ONE THAT IS DIVORCED etc. ADAMANTIUS. He who sins is cast off; even if the bishop is silent, whether from ignorance or negligence, grace does not profit the man. Christ does not take to wife a soul cast off, nor one defiled, namely one that has only willed and desired the sin; because the great high priest requires a wholly pure soul to join to himself and make one spirit. He who sins unto death is cast off; he who sins venially is defiled.
**“or defiled,”** — Note that he does not wish his faithful to share in the observances of the Jews.
**“or a harlot,”**
• heresy, which lies open to the lust of many
• DEFILED, OR A HARLOT etc. She who goes after lovers, namely the demons, who desire to corrupt the beautiful soul, that is, the one made to the image of God.
**“he shall not take, but a maid”** — a virgin, that is, the Church or the soul
21.15:
**“He shall not mingle”**
• the faithful
• Let him not cast pearls before swine.
**“the stock”** — Septuagint: seed, that is, the Word of God.
**“of his kindred”** — Septuagint: with his race, namely the human
**“with the common people”** — with Jewish manners
**“of his nation:”** — of which he was according to the flesh
**“for I am the Lord who sanctify him.”** — Therefore he does not need the sacrifices and purifications of the Jews: I am the sacrifice and purgation for all.
21.17:
**“Say to Aaron: Whosoever of thy seed throughout their families, hath a blemish,”** — of sin
**“he shall not offer bread to his God.”** — WHOSOEVER OF THY SEED etc. To take these things according to the letter seems too absurd. Such blemishes are not in a man's power or will. By the blemishes of bodies, therefore, he describes the vices of minds: for when the prelate takes up the cause of the people, he comes as a physician to the sick. If he himself is sick, with what presumption does he wish to heal? He therefore ought to be drawn forward as an example who, dead to all passions, lives spiritually; by whose purpose the body is neither wholly broken by weakness nor too much by insolence.
21.18:
**“IF HE BE BLIND”** — Ignorant of the light of contemplation, pressed by the darkness of the present life, who, while he does not diligently look upon the light to come, knows not whither to stretch the step of his work.
**“or if he be lame,”** — who cannot do what he knows ought to be done
**“IF HE BE LAME”** — Who, namely, sees whither he ought to go, but through weakness of mind cannot do what he desires.
**“if he have a little, or a great, or a crooked nose,”** — discernment, by which we distinguish virtues from vices
**“IF HE HAVE A LITTLE OR A GREAT NOSE”** — He has a little nose who is not fit to hold the measure of discernment: for with the nose we discern scents and stenches. The great and crooked nose is an immoderate subtlety of discernment, which, growing out more than is needful or fitting, confounds the rightness of action.
21.19: **“IF HIS FOOT BE BROKEN”** — He who cannot go the way of God and is without good work; not as the lame man, who at least held to it with weakness.
21.20:
**“IF HE BE CROOKBACKED”** — Pressed with earthly care, not looking back to things above, looking only on things below.
**“OR BLEAR EYED”** — The blear-eyed, whose wit shines forth to the knowledge of the truth, but carnal working darkens it. For in the blear-eyed the pupils are sound, but with the humour flowing down the eyelids grow thick, and by its frequent pouring the sight even of the pupil is spoiled.
**“IF HE HAVE A PEARL IN HIS EYE”** — He has a pearl in his eye who is not allowed to see the light of truth, because he is blinded by arrogance of wisdom or justice: for the black pupil sees, the white does not see; because the sense of human thought, if it understands itself foolish or a sinner, grasps the knowledge of inward brightness: if it attributes to itself the whiteness of justice or wisdom, it shuts itself out from heavenly knowledge.
**“IF A CONTINUAL SCAB”** — In whose mind, namely, the wantonness of the flesh rules without ceasing. For in the scab the heat of the bowels is drawn to the skin, in which lust is signified; because likewise the temptation of the heart leaps forth into action.
**“IF A DRY SCURF”** — He has a dry scurf in his body who is wasted by avarice in his mind; which, if it is not checked in small things, spreads without measure. The scurf takes hold of the body without pain and fouls the comeliness of the members; avarice also, while it delights the soul, ulcerates it, because while it strives to acquire it is kindled to enmities; it causes no pain in the wound, because it promises abundance from the fault to the burning mind; the comeliness of the members is fouled, because through it the beauty of the other virtues is depraved; it roughens as it were the whole body, because through all vices it supplants the soul. For covetousness is the root of all evils.
**“OR A RUPTURE”** — Others: heavy; because, namely, he does not practise filthiness in deed, but is still burdened in mind by continual thought; who with all his thoughts flows down to wantonness, as carrying in his heart the weight of filthiness.
21.21: **“Whosoever hath a blemish,”** — any of the aforesaid
21.23:
**“Yet so that within the veil”** — the body of Christ
**“he enter not, nor approach to the altar, because he hath a blemish, and he must not defile my sanctuary.”**
• to scandalize the people
• The priest must be spotless in mind and conversation; whom, as Moses commanded to be clean of twelve blemishes, according to the Septuagint, so Paul warned him to keep himself from twelve, saying: Not proud, not soon angry, not violent etc. For he is the steward of God, who ought to excel those beneath him in virtues.
• This is done in the Church also: if anyone has been stained and has left off by repenting, he is not forbidden to communicate in the holy things; but to minister, or approach the veil and the altar, is not lawful. For the veil and the altar are the body of Christ. Whence Paul: We have an altar whereof they have no power to eat who serve the tabernacle. And elsewhere: Having confidence in the entering into the holies through the veil, that is, his flesh.
**“WHOSOEVER HATH”** — Whoever is subject to any of these vices is forbidden to offer bread to the Lord, lest he be unable to wash away the offences of others whom his own offences still lay waste.
**“AUGUSTINE”** — All doubt is taken away. None of the high or second priests ought to approach the holy things if he is unclean. It follows, then, that the priest was continent, lest because of the begetting of sons he should on some days not put on the continual incense, which the high priests alone put on twice daily, morning and evening. For after conjugal intercourse, even with the body washed, he was unclean until the evening, by whom the incense had to be put on.
**“I am the Lord who sanctify them.”** — saying: Be you perfect, as also your heavenly Father is perfect.
21.24:
**“Moses therefore spoke to Aaron, and to his sons and to all Israel, all the things that had been commanded him.”**
• the things which were said before
• MOSES THEREFORE SPOKE etc. He commends the dignity of Moses: for to others God speaks few things, but to him all things, because he is just and is the image of Christ. He warns us also to attend to the greater and more perfect, who continually enjoy the eternal vision.

22.2:
**“Speak to Aaron and to his sons, that they beware of those things that are consecrated of the children of Israel, and defile not the name of the things sanctified to me,”**
• He does not show it vile and defiled by handling it profitably.
• AND DEFILE NOT etc. By acting disorderly they scandalize the people, who think the ministry of God, and justice, and judgment superfluous.
**“WHICH THEY OFFER”** — Which they offered, namely, to the priests, to be offered by them to the Lord. Note the kind of sanctification which is made by the vow and devotion of the offerer; but whether men are said to sanctify themselves in the same way, when they vow themselves in some matter, is to be observed.
**“I am the Lord.”** — who am angry and avenge
22.3:
**“Say to them and to their posterity:”** — He wishes not only the priest but every minister of the holy things to observe this law.
**“Every man of your race that approacheth”** — as long as it shall last
**“THAT APPROACHETH”** — As if: let him not only abstain from the ministry, the mystic office, but not even touch what has been offered: for the clean must approach clean things.
22.4:
**“The man of the seed of Aaron,”** — the Christian adopted in baptism and made kinsman and brother; whence they are called "a chosen generation, a kingly priesthood, a holy nation".
**“that is a leper, or that suffereth a running of the seed, shall not eat of those things that are sanctified to me, until he be healed.”**
• as was said above
• He does not wish the defiled to eat holy things before they are healed. And he wishes not only the priests but also those who minister to abstain from receiving the holy foods until they have repented.
**“THAT IS A LEPER”** — He does not abhor the sensible leper, who suffers in vices, but the spiritual; which he sets out there: He that toucheth anything unclean by occasion of the dead; or, according to the Septuagint: Every uncleanness of the soul, that is, sin.
**“and he whose seed goeth from him as in generation,”** — WHOSE SEED GOETH FROM HIM. JEROME. TO FABIOLA. If any of the priests has had an issue of seed, he is forbidden to approach the priestly table; on the contrary, the widow, with whom, as with Sara, it had ceased to be after the manner of women, is received for her continence and chastity and is fed from the treasury of the temple; if she has children, she is given back to her offspring; that true widows may be ministered to and sustained by the priestly foods, held by the love of no other.
22.6:
**“shall be unclean until the evening:”** — penance
**“and shall not eat those things that are sanctified: but when he hath washed his flesh with water,”** — with the tears of penance: "Every night I will wash my bed: I will water my couch with my tears" etc.
22.7: **“And the sun is down, then being purified, he shall eat of the sanctified things, because it is his meat.”** — The meat which I will give is my flesh.
22.8:
**“That which dieth of itself, and that which was taken by a beast, they shall not eat,”** — One must not be partaker of the table of the Lord and of the table of devils.
**“nor be defiled therewith, I am the Lord.”** — namely "the bread which came down from heaven".
22.9:
**“LET THEM KEEP MY PRECEPTS”** — The precepts of the Lord are to those who keep them the cause of justification and salvation; but to those who transgress, of sin and death, and above all in the receiving of the holy things. "For he that eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh judgment to himself."
**“that they may not fall into sin, and”** — so
**“die in the sanctuary, when they shall have defiled it.”** — This is the cause of death.
**“I am the Lord who sanctify you.”** — who namely receive the penitent into the communion of the saints, and except the defiled.
22.10:
**“No stranger”**
• who does not receive the law of the Gospel
• who, being kin to the devil, is a stranger to God
**“shall eat of the sanctified things: a sojourner of the priests, or a hired servant,”**
• The Jew, who seeks the fruit of the observance of the law carnally.
• A SOJOURNER etc. He who lives in the Church not purely nor diligently, as one about to move away, but for the sake of glory or gain, is spoken of as a hireling: who is not the shepherd, whose own the sheep are not.
22.11:
**“But he whom the priest”**
• Christ
• who forbade the wicked to share in the holy things, permits the converted to approach
**“hath bought,”** — "For you are bought with a great price" etc.
**“and he that is his servant, born”** — The home-born servant, who was nourished in the house and brought up in the faith of the Church.
**“in his house,”** — the doctrine of the Gospel, which is "silver tried by the fire, purged from the earth" etc.
**“these shall eat of them.”** — of the mystical and life-giving loaves
22.12:
**“If the daughter”** — the soul regenerated in baptism
**“of a priest”** — of Christ, who is "a priest for ever according to the order of Melchisedech".
**“to any of the people”** — to sin
**“be married,”** — embracing, namely, the fellowship of the Jew, the Gentile or the heretic.
**“MARRIED TO ANY OF THE PEOPLE”** — It is not enough to be nourished in the faith of Christ: we must abide and grow in it, and not be mingled with any of the strangers, that is, with doctrine estranged from God, whether by law or by action; nor, because we are of faithful fathers, therefore presume upon the holy things, but where we too persist as faithful.
**“of those things that are sanctified, nor of the firstfruits,”** — the body of Christ
22.13:
**“But if she be a widow,”** — utterly leaving and burying error
**“or divorced,”** — from those whose fellowship she abhors
**“and having no children”** — evil works
**“return to the house”** — the Church
**“of her father,”** — Christ
**“as she was wont to do when she was a maid,”** — while she was fervent in the faith and was young in virtues; of whom it is said: "The young maidens have loved thee."
**“she shall eat of her father's meats: no stranger”** — He who is not a son of Christ or of the Church, lest the holy thing be given to dogs and pearls to swine.
22.14:
**“He that eateth of the sanctified things”** — of the mystery of the body and blood
**“through ignorance,”**
• not knowing its power and dignity
• HE THAT EATETH OF THE SANCTIFIED THINGS etc. The holy of holies, the mysteries of the body of Christ, of whom it was said: "The Holy which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God." From this he not only forbade strangers and sojourners to approach, but it is forbidden to receive it through ignorance. And he receives it through ignorance who does not know its dignity and power. Whence Solomon: When thou shalt sit to eat with a prince, consider diligently what is set before thy face.
**“shall add the fifth part with that which he ate,”** — SHALL ADD THE FIFTH etc. Septuagint: Upon it. The fifth, therefore, is commanded to be added not from elsewhere, but from it and with it or upon it: this is the word spoken by Christ himself over the Lord's mystery. He removes us from ignorance, lest anyone think it carnal or earthly. This is well called the fifth, because the spirit and the word which he delivers compose our five senses, and bring forward to the mystery not only taste but hearing and sight, touch and smell, that we may suspect nothing earthly of the things that are heavenly.
**“and shall give it to the priest into the sanctuary.”** — AND SHALL GIVE IT TO THE PRIEST INTO THE SANCTUARY. The sanctification of the mystical sacrifice, and its translation from sensible to intelligible things, must be given to the priest, because by his power and word the things that are seen are sanctified, so as to surpass all the senses.
22.15:
**“And they shall not profane”** — by adding the fifth
**“OF THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL”** — It signifies the faithful people, who see God through this mystery; and whatever they consecrate to God in the Lord's sacrifice are holy of holies, because of them the body of Christ is confected. For he is the firstfruits of our lump: therefore rightly he subsists from our firstfruits.
22.16:
**“Lest perhaps they bear the iniquity”** — in eating: because they ought to understand not common but mystical food.
**“of their trespass,”** — What is committed against God is properly called a trespass in the law; whence he adds: "I am the Lord who sanctify you."
**“when they shall have eaten the sanctified things. I am the Lord who sanctify them.”** — Against whom he acts who receives holy things impiously; who set forth my mystery for sanctification, not for defilement.
22.17: **“And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying:”** — AND THE LORD SPOKE TO MOSES, SAYING etc. He commands not only that the priests be clean, but that the oblations of the people be clean, that the faithful may know that the oblation is intelligible, because he ought to live holily and be undefiled, as the priest of Christ. Teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost, teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you. He therefore who has promised a holocaust, which is the perfect life, let him see that such an oblation be undefiled: for otherwise it will not be received.
22.18:
**“Speak to Aaron, and to his sons, and to all the children of Israel, and thou shalt say to them: The man of the house of Israel, and of the strangers who dwell with you, that offereth his oblation, either vows”** — promised from necessity
**“paying, or offering of his own accord,”** — "I will freely sacrifice to thee" etc.
22.19:
**“To be offered by you, it shall be a male”** — manly, strong, steadfast in offering
**“without blemish”** — from sin
**“of the calves,”** — he offers of the oxen who fulfils the law in deed
**“or of the sheep,”** — which the simple man offers
**“or of the goats.”** — which the penitent offers
22.20:
**“If a blemish”** — of sin
**“it have, you shall not offer it, neither shall it be acceptable.”** — THE MAN OF THE HOUSE OF ISRAEL etc. According to the letter also, if you offer an ox or a sheep or a goat or anything of this kind, by giving firstfruits to the priests, or feeding the poor, or building divine edifices, or doing anything that pertains to God himself (for therefore it is called a holocaust), let this oblation be undefiled; yet he does not name the defilement, that we may understand the spiritual defilement which comes of robbery, injustice, avarice and the like.
22.21:
**“The man that offereth a victim of peace offerings to the Lord, either paying his vows, or offering of his own accord, whether of calves”** — as above
**“or of sheep, shall offer it without blemish, that it may be acceptable: there shall be no blemish in it.”**
• THE MAN THAT OFFERETH etc. He commanded the oblation of the people to be clean; he adds what sort the ministers ought to be and offer.
• OF PEACE OFFERINGS etc. Things which avail for salvation and peace, even if one cannot live the philosophic life rightly, as he who has left all, who strives for virginity and the like. For star differeth from star in glory.
22.22:
**“IF IT BE BLIND”** — He who is ignorant of God and his ministry, and cannot expound it to others. Whence he acts negligently about himself, about others, and about the ministry. Whence Isaias: His watchmen are all blind, they are all ignorant: dumb dogs not able to bark.
**“IF BROKEN”** — In foot or hand: he whose action, namely, or will is weak or distorted is not worthy of salvation and the sacred altars.
**“IF IT HAVE A SCAR”** — It marks the detractor: for this disease is the worst, and the sharpest wound is not easily soothed.
**“IF BLISTERS”** — Septuagint: A tongue cut; he who for his filthy life has lost confidence in teaching. To the sinner God hath said: Why dost thou declare my justices? etc.
**“or a scab, or a dry scurf:”** — A SCAB, OR A DRY SCURF. The fornicator is signified, who stains his body. For he that committeth fornication sinneth against his own body.
**“you shall not offer them to the Lord, nor burn any thing of them upon the Lord's altar.”** — YOU SHALL NOT OFFER THEM TO THE LORD etc. Septuagint: They shall not offer these to the Lord. For such are not to be offered to the ministry of the altar. He does not add the sacrifice of peace offerings, as above, that we may understand this to be said of the ministers of the altar, who ought to be a holocaust and lead a perfect and consummated life.
22.23:
**“An ox or a sheep, that hath the ear and the tail cut off,”**
• He has his tail cut off who does not think of the last things.
• THE EAR AND THE TAIL etc. He has his ear cut off who is disobedient, who delights in shameful words and opposes good things.
**“voluntarily”** — that sins may be mortified and they may live to God and be joined to thee
**“thou mayst offer:”**
• Septuagint: thou shalt slay for thyself
• VOLUNTARILY etc. For such a one either works the commandments, and is called an ox, or is simple, and is called a sheep. Therefore we do not wholly oppose them, or reckon them among enemies in part; but we teach and exhort.
**“but a vow may not be paid with them.”** — that is: such cannot be offered for the ministry; yet if they repent, they are to be received.
22.24:
**“Any beast that hath the testicles bruised,”** — who, as malice grows, bruises in himself the offspring of virtues and the things by which a man may be known
**“or crushed, or cut”** — OR CRUSHED etc. He who yields to the temptations brought upon him and loses the strength of the soul. For one ought not to suffer these things, nor believe the enemy who afflicts. Whence: Why go I sorrowful whilst my enemy afflicteth me?
**“AND TAKEN AWAY”** — He who by one wicked action kills himself as with a knife, deprived of union with God, of the offspring of virtue and the signs of manhood: for the other is he who is bruised little by little.
**“you shall not offer to the Lord: in your land”** — Our land is good conversation, which we receive from God to be cultivated.
22.25:
**“From the hand of a stranger”** — who comes to the Church from outsiders, taught outside
**“you shall not offer bread”** — corrupt
**“to your God,”** — incorruptible
**“nor any other thing that he would give: because they are all corrupted, and defiled: you shall not receive them.”** — Because you serve an incorrupt God and a Church which is without spot.
22.27:
**“A bullock, or a sheep, or a goat,”** — the grace of the Gospel; whence Paul: "By the gospel I have begotten you."
**“when they are brought forth, seven days”** — the whole present life, which turns in seven days
**“they shall be under the udder”** — that they may be nourished with the milk of doctrine
**“of their dam:”** — of the Church
**“And on the eighth day”** — of the resurrection, because then soul and body will be a holy sacrifice.
**“and thenceforth, they may be offered to the Lord.”** — A BULLOCK, OR A SHEEP, OR A GOAT etc. Nature is the mother of all. Under her is every kind of men, of sinners namely and of the just, for seven days. For if anyone works the commandments, whether he be simple or a sinner, for seven days, that is, in the age of the present life, he must bear the laws of nature; but on the eighth day of the resurrection he will not be under this mother, but a perfect victim of the Lord, which he cannot be in this life, where all things are uncertain and changeable. Whence Solomon: Praise not any man before death.
22.28:
**“Whether it be a cow, or a sheep,”** — the figurative Pasch
**“THEY SHALL NOT BE SACRIFICED”** — It signifies the Pasch of the law, because Moses delivered these to the Jews to be immolated on the day of the Pasch, saying: Thou shalt immolate the phase to the Lord thy God, of sheep and of oxen etc.; this Pasch they cannot celebrate who have received the true one.
**“the same day with their young ones.”** — With the true Pasch, which is called the young for the newness of the time, and because the figure at length brought forth the truth.
22.29:
**“If you immolate a victim for thanksgiving to the Lord,”** — the conversation of the Gospel, which gives thanks to the Lord; whence: "So let your light shine before men, that" etc.
**“that he may be favourable,”** — namely acceptable
22.30:
**“You shall eat it the same day it is immolated;”** — by working, by contemplating
**“there shall not any of it remain”** — anything uncorrected or unfinished
**“until the morning”** — at the beginning
**“of the next day.”** — of the world to come, in which it is not lawful to work
**“I am the Lord.”** — who here establish the law, there judge; here entrust the talents, there demand the account.
22.32:
**“Profane not my holy name,”** — Those defiled: my name "is blasphemed through you".
**“that I may be sanctified”** — in things to come, not in things present
**“in the midst of the children”** — the true
22.33:
**“And who brought you out of the land of Egypt,”** — that you may not return
**“that I might be your God:”** — that you might know me as God; which will be when he shall be "all in all".

23.3:
**“Six days shall ye do work: the seventh day, because it is the rest of the sabbath,”**
• in imitation of the Lord, that you may rest on the sabbath
• THESE ARE THE FEASTS OF THE LORD etc. If you attend closely to the present passage, you will find the lawgiver setting spiritual things even into the letter. For he says: These are the feasts of the Lord, which you shall call holy. And he added: Six days shall ye do work; in which he shows that the first feasts are in good works. For God made things very good in six days. The second festival, of the seventh day, is the rest, which no one will be able to celebrate unless he has done good works worthy of God. For it was not set before in vain: Six days shall ye do work. For if anyone has acted in imitation of God, which is to work six days, he rests on the intelligible sabbath.
**“shall be called holy. You shall do no work on that day:”** — on which there is no working, but enjoying the reward of works
**“it is the sabbath of the Lord in all your habitations.”** — The present life is a pilgrimage; there is the everlasting and true habitation, because: "In my Father's house there are many mansions."
23.4:
**“These also are the holy days of the Lord,”** — of the triumphant one
**“which you must celebrate in their seasons.”**
• THESE ARE THE HOLY FEASTS etc. Not to the Lord, as all the others, but properly the Lord's, on which, the enemy being overcome, he saved mankind and brought it back from captivity.
• At the time of the Lord's passion; whence this month shall be the beginning of months in the months of the year: for it is the beginning of the new life and of holy conversation; the evening on which the Lord suffered. Whence: "Little children, it is the last hour."
23.5:
**“The first month, the fourteenth day of the month at evening, is the phase of the Lord:”**
• He does not say this of the festivals of the Jews, who serve figures, but of the faithful.
• THE FOURTEENTH DAY etc. Let us ask the Jews why he did not command the festival to be kept on the fourteenth day, on which he appointed the figurative pasch, but, making memory of it, defined that it be on the day of unleavened bread, which came after it. For he wishes it known what the difference is between the figure and the truth. He therefore makes mention of the fourteenth, which held the figure, but commands the feast to be kept on the fifteenth, on which Christ our pasch was sacrificed.
**“IS THE PHASE OF THE LORD”** — Because the Lord suffered, he did not straightway end the times, but left the remnants of the last and evening hour, that the sound of the apostles might go forth into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world. At evening also, or in the middle of the evening, going before the proper pasch, he celebrated his cross, because beyond the mystical he delivered the true pasch to the disciples. It was therefore night already when Judas, having received the morsel, went out to betray him. On the following day he fulfilled the pasch. Whence the lawgiver appointed this festival on the fifteenth day, and proclaimed the solemnity of unleavened bread.
23.6: **“And the fifteenth day of the same month is the solemnity of the unleavened bread of the Lord. Seven days shall you eat unleavened bread.”** — SEVEN DAYS etc. If we wish truly to celebrate the pasch, we ought for seven days, that is, always, to be unleavened of all malice, and above all of Jewish error. Whence the Apostle says: "Not with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness: but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth."
23.7:
**“The first day shall be most solemn unto you, and holy: you shall do no servile work therein:”**
• NO SERVILE WORK etc. "Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin." We ought not to serve sin when we celebrate the pasch, in which Christ freed us from sin.
• YOU SHALL DO NO SERVILE WORK etc. He does not permit servile things to be done on the other days on which he forbade us. Whence he adds: "But you shall offer sacrifice in fire to the Lord."
23.8: **“But you shall offer sacrifice in fire to the Lord seven days.”** — SACRIFICE IN FIRE etc. Septuagint: holocaustomata; where it is hinted that he commands ceasing from all servile things; moreover he named not only the first but also the seventh, that he might comprehend the whole of human life, because that is the beginning, this the end, in which all things can be comprehended.
23.10:
**“Speak to the children of Israel, and thou shalt say to them: When you shall have entered into the land”** — the Gospel life or doctrine, whose fruits are first and purest
**“which I”** — not another
**“will give you, and shall reap your corn,”**
• Receiving the Word; whence: "The harvest indeed is great, but the labourers are few."
• by teaching, by converting, by gathering to the faith
• by proclaiming with their own mouth
**“you shall bring sheaves of ears, the firstfruits”** — The body of Christ, who is the highest and the firstfruits of the harvest
**“of your harvest”** — of preaching
**“to the priest:”** — Christ, who immolated himself
23.11:
**“Who shall lift up”** — by raising from the dead
**“the sheaf”** — his own body: for Christ is risen, the firstfruits of them that sleep.
**“before the Lord, that it may be acceptable for you, the next day after the sabbath,”**
• of the resurrection, because the first day is that of the Lord's passion
• THE NEXT DAY etc. He could have said the second of unleavened bread, but lest he lead our attention to the following day, namely the morrow of the first, he said the next day, signifying the resurrection which followed the passion, as day follows day.
23.12:
**“And on the same day that the sheaf is consecrated, a lamb without blemish of the first year shall be killed for a holocaust of the Lord.”**
• mystically, namely: let the mystical lamb be immolated
• AND ON THE SAME DAY etc. Of the resurrection, that is, of the lifting up of the sheaf; that is, when we celebrate the resurrection, we ought not to forget the Lord's sacrifice, from which the sheaf was offered.
23.13:
**“And the libations shall be offered with it,”** — because without him they cannot be understood spiritually
**“two tenths of flour tempered with oil for a burnt offering of the Lord, and a most sweet odour:”** — WITH OIL etc. For the perfect humanity and the perfect divinity must come together into one: in oil, that is, through the mercy which he had toward us; for so the sacrifice is found an odour of sweetness to the Lord, if we understand the things concerning him that are worthy.
**“libations also of wine, the fourth part of a hin.”** — LIBATIONS ALSO OF WINE etc. Behold the intelligible oblation of Melchisedech, which is accomplished in bread and wine: thence the fourth part of a hin is offered, that by the fourth part the Gospel doctrine may be signified; and by the libation the Lord's word, in which he says: This is my blood, which shall be shed for many unto remission of sins.
23.14:
**“A LOAF”** — The oblation of the present gifts, which is the mystery of Christ, reconciled us to God and prepared new food.
**“PARCHED CORN”** — Septuagint: You shall not eat parched citrea. For the precepts of Christ are not only new, but citrea, that is, soft. Whence: My yoke is sweet etc. Or rubbed with the hands and cleansed: for so others interpret citrea, because the precepts of Christ seek action and correction.
**“or frumenty of the harvest, you shall not eat, until the day that you shall offer thereof to your God. It is a precept for ever”** — Neither place nor time changes the mystery of Christ.
23.15:
**“You shall count therefore from the morrow”** — the Lord's day: for this is the morrow of the sabbath, on which is the resurrection.
**“wherein you offered the sheaf of the firstfruits, seven full weeks.”** — which being ended, we merited the coming of the Holy Ghost.
23.16:
**“FIFTY DAYS”** — This is the Lord's day, on which we celebrate the festival of Pentecost, which the Jews celebrate neither according to the letter nor according to the spirit, who do not even number the days according to the law.
**“and so you shall offer a new sacrifice”** — As it were excluding the old sacrifices, he brings in the Gospel of the law.
**“to the Lord.”** — YOU SHALL OFFER A NEW SACRIFICE etc. New, not old, not worldly. For the Spirit, coming, renewed the whole of human life, because he confirmed the institution of Christ and perfected in them the confirmation of life. Whence: "He shall receive of mine, and shall shew it to you." Therefore he came on no other day than that on which the resurrection was, and the intelligible sheaf was offered, to show that the new conversation was perfected by the resurrection of Christ and the coming of the Holy Ghost.
23.17:
**“Out of all your dwellings,”** — the Churches
**“your”** — YOUR DWELLINGS etc. Because there is a chief dwelling, of which it is said: "Blessed are they that dwell in thy house, O Lord." And elsewhere: "One thing I have asked of the Lord, this will I seek after: that I may dwell" etc.
**“loaves”** — Septuagint: set apart, because foremost in all wisdom and set apart from the worldly.
**“two loaves of the firstfruits,”**
• The Law and the Gospel, which contain the food of souls.
• LOAVES OF THE FIRSTFRUITS etc. For first the Lord perfected and taught the Gospel with the law. You have heard that it was said to them of old: Thou shalt not kill. But I say to you: Whosoever is angry with his brother shall be in danger of the judgment. Here he joined the law to the Gospel. Hence Luke says: "Which Jesus began to do and to teach" etc.
**“of two tenths of flour leavened, which you shall bake”** — OF TWO TENTHS etc. Of the doctrine, namely, which teaches through the divinity and the perfect humanity; nor can they be baked otherwise than through such doctrine.
23.18:
**“SEVEN LAMBS”** — For the seven gifts of the Holy Ghost, which he calls lambs, because the Holy Ghost is one with Christ, of whom it is written: "Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who taketh away the sin of the world"; therefore: "No man can say the Lord Jesus, but by the Holy Ghost."
**“without blemish of the first year, and one calf”** — Christ
**“from the herd,”** — of the Patriarchs: for of these he was born according to the flesh.
**“and two rams,”** — AND TWO RAMS etc. By which the enemy is tossed. These are the higher commandments and virtues, which the others follow as sheep (for example): Go, sell all that thou hast, and give to the poor.
**“and they shall be for a holocaust with their libations”** — WITH THEIR LIBATIONS etc. Which are knowledge and correction. Whence: Now thanks be to God, who manifesteth the odour of his knowledge by us, because we are the good odour of Christ etc.
23.19:
**“You shall offer”** — because it is the festival of the Holy Ghost, who consummates all things and wills all sacrifices to be perfect.
**“also a buck goat”** — he brings in the word of penance
**“for sin, and two lambs of the first year for sacrifices of peace offerings.”** — AND TWO LAMBS etc. The commandments of peace and holiness. Whence: "Follow peace with all men, and holiness" etc. Because these were spoken in the apostolic word, he commands them to be offered with the loaves of the firstfruits, which signify the doctrine of Christ. Whence in what follows: "And when the priest hath lifted them up with the loaves of the firstfruits."
23.20:
**“And when the priest hath lifted them up with the loaves of the firstfruits”** — for the refreshment of souls
**“before the Lord, they shall fall to his use.”** — THEY SHALL FALL TO HIS USE etc. To the use of the priest, that is, of Christ, who is our priest and our Lord; his are the loaves of the firstfruits and the lambs of the commandments; he himself spoke in Paul; he himself offered all the things that were spoken; he first proclaimed peace to the disciples and kept holiness, as the holy of holies.
23.21:
**“And you shall call this day most solemn,”** — Here note its excellence.
**“MOST SOLEMN”** — On which the calling of the Gentiles was not only foretold but fulfilled: when the Parthians and Medes and Elamites and the other nations heard the apostles speaking in divers tongues the wonderful works of God.
**“and most holy.”** — OTHERS: holy, or of the holy
**“You shall do no servile work”** — which serves sin
**“therein.”** — On which the Spirit came, because: Where the Spirit is, there is liberty.
23.22:
**“And when you reap the corn of your land,”** — because these things are full of piety, they are to be kept even according to the letter
**“you shall not cut it to the very ground:”**
• It signifies the things which are lacking to us for full and perfect knowledge.
• AND WHEN etc. He seems to have said the same things above, but there: You shall not finish your reaping; here, however, he says: You shall not cut it to the very ground; and the very change of words hints at a difference.
• THE CORN OF YOUR LAND etc. Of conversation, whose reaping is after the resurrection of Christ and the coming of the Holy Ghost; yet the word of preaching does not deliver all the knowledge which we are to have in the future. For there are things which cannot now be revealed to us. Whence he set this law among the aforesaid festivals.
**“neither shall you gather the ears that remain;”** — that is: do not try to gather the things which escape our knowledge, as it were falling from the reaper's hand.
**“but for the poor and for the strangers”** — to Christ, who was made poor and a stranger for us.
**“you shall leave them.”** — FOR THE POOR AND FOR THE STRANGERS etc. Septuagint: for the poor and the proselyte, that is, for Christ, who had not where to lay his head, and "came unto his own, and his own received him not". He alone understands the things that remain. Whence: O the depth of the wisdom and of the knowledge, how incomprehensible are his judgments etc.
23.24:
**“Say to the children of Israel: The seventh month, on the first day of the month,”** — that is: at the beginning of the consummation
**“THE SEVENTH MONTH, ON THE FIRST DAY OF THE MONTH”** — The number seven signifies consummation, either spiritual or general. Hence God rested on the seventh day, and by his rest signified ours. Whence: He that is entered into that rest hath rested from his works, as God did from his. But the beginning of the consummation of the times is the coming of the Lord. Whence: "Little children, it is the last hour." This time he calls the first of the seventh month, as the beginning of the consummation is also rest to us, whom he made to cease from evil works and freed from the heavy yoke. Whence: Come to me, all you that labour and are burdened etc. And learn of me, because I am meek and humble of heart, and you shall find rest to your souls.
**“with the sound of trumpets, and it shall be called holy.”**
• because in it the called and adopted are sanctified
• WITH THE SOUND OF TRUMPETS etc. Because it preaches the resurrection of the Saviour, which is the memorial of the general resurrection, which according to the Apostle will be "with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God".
23.25: **“You shall do no servile work therein,”** — YOU SHALL DO NO SERVILE WORK etc. As if: there is no need of doing the servile things which you did before. But as you have yielded your members to serve iniquity unto iniquity, so now yield them to serve justice unto sanctification: for this is the true holocaust.
23.27:
**“Upon the tenth day of this seventh month shall be the day of atonement,”** — from sins
**“it shall be most solemn,”** — of all
**“and shall be called holy:”** — of the holy ones
**“and you shall afflict your souls on that day,”**
• by repenting
• that you may be healed
**“and shall offer”** — by building perfect good things upon it
**“a holocaust,”** — the consummated life
**“to the Lord.”** — UPON THE TENTH DAY etc. From these things we understand that propitiation and deliverance from sins are acquired in humility and affliction of soul. This we ought to do from the evening, that is, to begin from penance, which Christ made the beginning of his preaching: upon penance a good life is to be built, and consummated in virtues. Whence he added: And you shall offer a holocaust to the Lord.
23.28:
**“You shall do no servile work”** — you shall cease from evils
**“A DAY OF PROPITIATION”** — It signifies two things: that in this time we shall receive propitiation, and therefore in it we ought to abstain from all evil.
23.29: **“Every soul that is not afflicted on this day, shall perish from among his people:”** — Because he does not follow the humility of Christ, who humbled himself unto death.
23.30:
**“And every soul that shall do any work,”** — earthly
**“the same will I destroy from among his people.”** — of the saints
23.31: **“You shall do no work therefore on that day:”** — YOU SHALL DO NO WORK THEREFORE etc. It signifies that we must always cease from evil and superfluous things. Whence the Lord too allows us neither to plead a cause, nor to think what we shall eat, or what we shall drink, or what we shall put on: for he proclaimed the true sabbath of sabbaths.
23.32:
**“It is a sabbath”** — Septuagint: A sabbath of sabbaths, namely, that we may understand that which exceeds the weakness of the Jews.
**“of rest, and you shall afflict your souls”** — YOU SHALL AFFLICT etc. It is a recapitulation of humility, which is the foundation and base of the virtues. Whence the Lord says: Whosoever shall humble himself as this little child, he is the greater in the kingdom of heaven.
23.34: **“Say to the children of Israel: From the fifteenth day of this same seventh month, shall be kept the feast of tabernacles”** — that in this life we may keep holiday from evils, in which we ought to be as in tabernacles
23.35:
**“The first day shall be called most solemn and most holy:”**
• He who knows how to use present things as in a tabernacle, for him the first day, that is, the beginning, begins from the sanctification of the calling.
• FROM THE FIFTEENTH DAY etc. The festival begins with this number, which is composed of seven and eight, of which the one signifies the present age, the other number the age to come: therefore, commanding the festival to be consummated in seven days, he made mention of another day most solemn and most holy, and did not announce it with the seven, but set it apart; for the age to come follows the present as another thing. He therefore appointed the festival of tabernacles for seven days. For whoever uses the present world as a tabernacle can keep festival in it and rejoice in the hope of the age to come. For if the earthly house is dissolved, a building not made with hands is had in heaven.
**“You shall do no servile work therein,”** — Because none serve in the world who understand that the things in it are passing.
23.36:
**“And seven days”** — at all times
**“you shall offer holocausts”** — a perfect conversation
**“to the Lord.”** — from whom it is
**“The eighth day also”** — the life to come
**“it shall be most solemn,”** — to those who do the aforesaid things
**“and most holy,”**
• because the saints will be called into the prepared dwellings
• THE EIGHTH DAY ALSO etc. Note that the same things are said of the first and of the eighth, because the day of the resurrection is the second, and the beginning of the age to come. The first, in Christ, is the beginning of conversation and the opening of things to come; but the eighth succeeds the present age, which is signified in the seventh. Moreover the saints have their rest, and the life to come, in this life. Whence it was said to the apostles: "The kingdom of God is within you."
**“and you shall offer holocausts”** — which, namely, you prepared here, that is, yourselves
**“OF ASSEMBLY”** — Septuagint: Going forth, because hence is the departure, there the dwelling. Whence: I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ.
**“and congregation:”**
• all the saints being gathered together from every side
• For you shall all be as the angels of God.
23.37:
**“These are the feasts of the Lord, which you shall call most solemn and most holy, and shall offer on them oblations to the Lord, holocausts”** — "Mortify your members."
**“and libations”** — continual prayers
23.38:
**“Besides the sabbaths”** — on which we turn aside from evil
**“of the Lord, and your gifts, and those things that you offer by vow,”** — which is wont to be done in danger
**“or which voluntarily”** — by will alone
**“you shall give to the Lord.”** — THESE ARE THE FEASTS OF THE LORD etc. Paul agrees with the lawgiver, saying: "Always rejoice. Pray without ceasing. In all things give thanks." Moses also, setting forth the most solemn and most holy festivals, mixed in daily libations and sacrifices. Therefore he expressed those festivals by names, but immediately added: And shall offer on them oblations to the Lord etc. For he wished us "always to rejoice" and to keep festival and to pray. For this is the daily libation and holocaust, which we offer when we present our bodies a living sacrifice to God, and say with the Apostle: "For I am even now ready to be sacrificed, and the time of my dissolution is at hand"; therefore he adds: Besides the sabbaths of the Lord etc. Because when we have turned aside from evil, it is also over and above the justices which we promise to God according to the time: for sometimes we promise a fast, sometimes an oblation of sufferings, either in dangers or voluntarily.
23.39:
**“So from the fifteenth day of the seventh month,”**
• of the fulness of the times
• FROM THE FIFTEENTH etc. The fifteenth, composed of seven and eight, signifies the preaching of the Gospel, which consists of the present life and the life to come: this it orders, that it prepares.
**“when you shall have gathered in all the fruits of your land, you shall celebrate the feast of the Lord”** — being free from evils
**“seven days”** — as long as you live
**“on the first day”** — because it signifies the resurrection
**“and the eighth”** — no longer on the seventh
**“ON THE FIRST DAY”** — Which is the eighth; it is also the first of the age; moreover the first on which preaching is dispensed and sins cease, and in the end it bestows eternal rest. Then, having proclaimed the festival for seven days, he called the first day a rest, is silent about the following ones, to signify that labour must be given to the virtues; he transfers the rest to the eighth day, because rest is kept in the future for the faithful who do the law.
23.40:
**“And you shall take to you on the first day the fruits of the fairest tree,”** — ON THE FIRST DAY THE FRUITS etc. The fruit is Christ. Whence: "There shall come forth a rod out of the root of Jesse" etc., who fits the virtues to their time. "He shall be like a tree which is planted near the running waters, which shall bring forth its fruit in due season."
**“and branches”** — young branches
**“AND BOUGHS OF TREES”** — All the fruits, namely, of the virtues, but above all mercy, which ought to be continual and abiding. Whence: Let not oil depart from thy head.
**“of thick leaves,”** — AND BRANCHES OF PALM TREES etc. The youthful shoots of justice, because: "The just shall flourish like the palm tree"; because nothing of the palm is cast away, nor of those who live justly, he adds: "and boughs of trees of thick leaves" etc.
**“and willows”** — the branches, namely, of continence and chaste wedlock. For the willow bears no fruit.
**“OF THE BROOK”** — Of the present life, namely, which flows like a brook, boiling with temptations and tribulations. Whence: He shall drink of the torrent in the way, therefore shall he lift up the head; hanging, namely, on the cross.
**“and you shall rejoice before the Lord your God.”** — by believing in him, by suffering for him
23.41:
**“And you shall keep the solemnity thereof”** — There is no rejoicing for the wicked, saith the Lord.
**“seven days in the year. It shall be an everlasting ordinance”** — that is: the precept and institution of the Lord, which is always to be observed
23.42:
**“And you shall dwell in bowers seven days:”** — that the whole present life may be held, namely, for a bower
**“every one that is of the race of Israel, shall dwell in tabernacles:”** — The true Israelite, who with Abraham has left all things and dwells in tabernacles with Isaac, the co-heirs of the promise.
23.43:
**“That your posterity may know, that I made the children of Israel to dwell in tabernacles,”**
• as if: Let them not forget my benefit, and the Egyptian bondage and the deliverance.
• Morally, that they may imitate him who said: The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air nests: but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head.
**“when I brought them out of the land of Egypt.”** — from the earthliness of the world, from the bondage of Pharao

24.2:
**“Command the children of Israel, that they bring unto thee the oil”** — almsgiving, by which the other good things are watered
**“of olives,”** — by one's own labours
**“the finest and clearest,”** — that it may desire nothing of human praise
**“to furnish the lamps”** — the virtues
24.3:
**“Without the veil of the testimony”** — before Christ, who says: What you did to one of my least, you did to me.
**“in the tabernacle of the covenant.”**
• heaven
• COMMAND THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL etc. The candlestick is the Gospel life, in which the virtues shine as a lamp. Whence: No man lighteth a lamp and putteth it under a bushel etc. To these lamps oil is joined, that is, almsgiving, by which the other virtues are watered lest they be put out. This oil the foolish virgins did not have; therefore they were shut out. This ought to be the purest, of olives, that we may not give alms from robbery or for human praise. Whence: Of the firstfruits of thy fruits give to the poor. The lamps burn without the veil, that is, before Christ, who says: What you did to one of my least, you did to me. In the tabernacle, that is, in heaven, where the merciful hide their treasures.
**“And Aaron shall set them”** — Christ, the true priest, who has compassion on the poor.
**“from evening until morning”** — continually; whence: Let not oil depart from thy head.
**“UNTIL MORNING”** — Of the world to come, namely: for then there will be no time for praying or giving alms. Whence: "Say not to thy friend: Go, and come again, and to morrow I will give to thee." For you know not "what the day to come may bring forth".
**“before the Lord,”** — "Thy Father, who seeth in secret, will repay thee."
**“by a perpetual service and rite in your generations.”** — that this law may last for ever
24.4:
**“upon the most pure candlestick”**
• the Gospel conversation
• UPON THE CANDLESTICK etc. Christ, who is the true light and "enlighteneth every man that cometh into this world": "Who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth." Upon him burns the lamp, that is, the Holy Ghost, who appeared upon the disciples in fiery tongues: to him we ought to offer the purest oil, that is, a clean life, knowing that not all can kindle it, but only Christ and his sons, who, full of the Spirit, says: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me." Who also says: "I am come to cast fire on the earth, and what will I but that it be kindled?" Breathing it forth, as though kindling it, he says: "Receive ye the Holy Ghost." But this lamp is not kindled except through a clean life and conversation, or once kindled it is quickly put out. Whence: "Extinguish not the spirit" etc.
**“They shall be set before the Lord continually.”** — Let them shine as lamps before God, free from all error and hypocrisy, and not before men.
24.5:
**“Thou shalt take also fine flour,”** — Because the first preachers ought to be zealous for the fruits of the virtues.
**“and shalt bake twelve loaves thereof,”** — the apostles and their followers, who minister the food of the Word of God, or the bread of the Word
**“two tenths shall be in every loaf:”** — that all may be perfect
24.6:
**“six and six one against another”** — for the concord of charity
**“upon the table,”** — the Church
**“the most clean,”** — without spot or wrinkle
24.7:
**“And thou shalt put upon them the clearest frankincense,”** — prayer
**“that the bread may be for a memorial of the oblation of the Lord.”** — namely, that the memory of the sacred oblation may be in the sight of God
24.8:
**“Every sabbath they shall be changed before the Lord,”** — because, those taken up into rest, new preachers are put in their place
**“being received of the children of Israel by an everlasting covenant:”**
• THOU SHALT TAKE ALSO FINE FLOUR etc. BEDE. The twelve loaves on the table of the tabernacle are the twelve apostles and all who follow their doctrine in the Church. And because until the consummation of the world they refresh the people of God with the loaves of the Word, therefore the twelve loaves of proposition never depart from the table of the Lord. These are commanded to be made not of any flour, but of fine flour. For those who minister the Word of life must first be zealous for the fruits of the virtues, that what they admonish they may keep or commend by doing. These are well set one against another upon the table for the concord of charity and fellowship. For the Lord too sent them two by two to preach, because holy preachers are never divided, either in asserting the truth or in the affection of love. The clearest frankincense is put on for a memorial of the oblation of the Lord, because pure prayer is added over pious action and the doctrine of the Lord, that, these two being duly joined, the memory of the sacred oblation may always appear in the sight of God. The loaves which were set on the table of the Lord through the seven days of working are changed every sabbath, because the teachers of holy Church, the time of their labour being completed, are rewarded with eternal rest in heaven, and leave others to the work of their labour under the same hope of reward. The loaves were baked before the sabbath, according to Josephus. Divided two and two, and offered on the sabbath morning, they were set upon the table, six turned toward each other, with two golden patens full of incense set upon them, which remained until the next sabbath; and then others were brought, those were given to the priests, and, the incense being burnt in the sacred fire in which all the holocausts were made, other incense was put on: because first the rest of a devout conversation is to be received by us, and eternal life is promised, yet so that through labours and good works of life we hasten toward it.
• THOU SHALT BAKE TWELVE LOAVES THEREOF etc. ORIGEN. The word of the Lord is bread, but of many forms. One teaches the common people in public about works of mercy and beneficence, which seems common. There is another, secret, discoursing of faith or of the knowledge of things. This is clean and made of fine flour, and is to be set before the Lord upon the clean table, to be set apart for the priests alone. You therefore, if you have the knowledge of secret things, that is, of the faith of God, if you can discourse knowingly of the mystery of Christ, of the unity of the Holy Ghost, offer to God loaves of fine flour; if you instruct the people with common admonitions and morally, you have offered common loaves. One loaf is made of two tenths. It is not said of what measure the tenths are. What then is this thing whose measure and manner is neither named nor grasped? The number ten is everywhere perfect, because the whole reckoning and origin of number arises from it. In this, then, God is rightly shown as the author and origin of all things; but if in the Church we speak of the Father alone, we make a loaf of one tenth. If of the Son alone, likewise. But if I say that the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, and that the Father and the Son are one, I offer one loaf of two tenths of clean fine flour. Who gives life to the world; also by receiving and preaching the Old and New Testament and the one Lord of both, I offer one loaf. The name of its measure, that is, of the substance, I cannot grasp or find; yet by confessing the Father and the Son one, I offer one loaf of two tenths, not so that one loaf is made of one tenth and another of the other, so that there are two separate tenths, but the two tenths are one mass and one loaf, because I do not separate the Father from the Son, nor the Son from the Father. The loaves are set out in two rows, lest the discourse of the Father and the Son be confused. Now there is one loaf, because there is one substance; two rows, that is, the properties of the persons. For we call him the Father who is not the Son, and him the Son who is not the Father; and so we keep two tenths in one loaf, and before God we confess two rows. But it belongs to a great shepherd to keep these measures, and to join or distinguish the discourse of the Father and the Son as is fitting, so that one loaf appears. And twelve loaves of their measure are commanded to be made, according to the number of the tribes of Israel, in which the form of the whole rational nature is contained. For its general orders are thought to be twelve, which are figured in the twelve tribes; among which there was a certain royal order, which is named Juda; another fellow-priestly, which is called Levi, in which order the temple of God and the altar were placed. Another order, Issachar, and others, whose reckoning it is not the time now to explain. Yet each tribe has its loaf before God. And although some tribes descended from a concubine, and are partly free and partly servile, yet for all a loaf of two tenths is set upon the table, namely the clean one, upon the holy and pure mind.
24.9:
**“And they shall be Aaron's and his sons', that they may eat them in the holy place:”** — not everywhere
**“because it is most holy”** — the Church, or holy bodies, according to that: The temple of God is holy, which you are.
24.10:
**“And behold there went out the son of a woman of Israel,”** — of spiritual wisdom
**“whom she had of an Egyptian,”** — of worldly wisdom
**“among the children of Israel,”** — Catholics
**“and fell at words in the camp with a man of Israel.”** — attacking the spiritual through worldly knowledge
24.11:
**“And when he had blasphemed the name, and had cursed it,”** — saying the Son is less than the Father, and the like
**“he was brought to Moses:”**
• AND BEHOLD THERE WENT OUT etc. The woman of Israel, spiritual wisdom, ought not to come together with the Egyptian, that is, with outward wisdom. For he who is born, that is, taught, of such a union is the son of the Egyptian, that is, of worldly wisdom, and strives to maintain what he learned in it. Such a one sometimes quarrels in the camp of the Church with the Israelite who has dedicated himself wholly to the wisdom of God, not seeking the wisdom of this world nor of the princes of this age; and the son of the Israelite woman blasphemes the name, making no mention of Christ. But it is to be noted that he does not determine what name or whose. For the name of Christ was as yet unknown; of which Gabriel says: And his name shall be called Jesus. Of which name Paul says: He hath given him a name which is above every name etc. But when one who trusts in such wisdom blasphemes the name of Christ, saying he is unequal to the Father, he is driven out of the Church. They that heard put their hands upon his head, because the head of man is Christ, the head of Christ is God, who is blasphemed in Christ.
• AND BEHOLD etc. ORIGEN. Two strive: one wholly an Israelite, who strives and does not sin; the other for the greater part, that is, from his father, an Egyptian, whose sin is marked. The Israelite strives reasonably. In Exodus also the Israelite prevails and the Egyptian falls. He who defends the truth and the faith of the Church strives as a whole Israelite with the Egyptian; he who in part believes Christ and receives the Scriptures, but does not grasp the sense wholly and faithfully, is from his mother an Israelite, but from his father an Egyptian. But he who is a Christian and a Catholic by belief of the faith and by profession of the name is an Israelite on both sides. And he who is a Christian by profession, but heretical and perverse in his understanding of the faith, has an Israelite mother and an Egyptian father. Moreover, when one reads the Scriptures and follows the letter and rejects the spiritual understanding, he has an Israelite mother, that is, the letter; and the carnal sense, which he follows, he has as an Egyptian father: therefore he strives against the Catholic, who is an Israelite according to the letter and the spirit. He who is of the Egyptian father names the name and curses, because he denies that the Creator of the world is the Father of Christ. But we, who follow the letter and the spirit, say that one must neither curse according to the letter nor blaspheme according to the spirit. For railers against God and against their neighbour shall not possess the kingdom of God. Whence through Moses God punishes the railer so severely. Therefore he did not say before whose name he named in cursing, whether of God or of man, lest, if he spoke of God, anyone should think he had given licence concerning men. For those who curse, even if not from the heart, not from a wicked wish or mind, yet incur uncleanness of the lips, according to the word of Isaias, and defilements of the mouth. But this man, though of an Israelite mother, yet begotten of an Egyptian, went out and, naming the name, cursed; I think that if he had not gone out, he would neither have striven nor cursed in naming. For he went out from the truth, went out from the fear of God, from faith, from charity: for through these one goes out of the camp of the Church, even if he is not cast out by the voice of the bishop; as on the contrary someone is sent out by an unjust judgment, but if he did not go out before, that is, did not act so as to deserve to go out, he is not harmed. For sometimes he who is sent out is within, and he who is without seems to be kept within.
**“now his mother was called Salamuth”** — retribution, or peaceable
24.12:
**“And they put him into prison, till they might know what the Lord would command.”**
• in the Gospel
• The law keeps blasphemers to be judged by the Gospel.
• AND THEY PUT HIM INTO PRISON etc. Moses does not pronounce sentence against the blasphemer on his own authority, but, reserving it to the command of God, sends him to prison: for the law hates him who blasphemes, against whom it often preaches the Trinity, but not openly as the Gospel does; therefore it reserved him for the judgment of the Gospel. He that doth not believe in the Son is already judged.
24.13: **“And the Lord spoke to Moses,”** — agreeing with the law
24.14: **“Saying: Bring forth the blasphemer without the camp, and let them that heard him, put their hands upon his head,”** — because he blasphemed against the Lord, who is the head of Christ
24.15:
**“And thou shalt speak to the children of Israel: the man, the man”** — THE MAN, THE MAN etc. AUGUSTINE. It is an idiom, as though it were said: This man or that, that is, whatever man. Not, as some think, that "the man, the man" is said as if in praise, as though: a man, not of any sort, like one who is also similar to a sinner, but one who is truly a man. That this sense is not true, but that this is an idiom of the Scriptures, is plainly shown here, since it is said of one who is blamed, not of one who is praised.
**“that curseth”** — knowingly
**“his God, shall bear his sin:”** — the penalty of a venial sin
24.16:
**“And he that blasphemeth”** — knowingly
**“the name of the Lord,”** — of the Spirit: for the Lord is a Spirit.
**“dying let him die:”**
• AQUILA: The man who blasphemes his God shall also take iniquity upon himself, and he who names the name of the Lord shall die the death.
• THE MAN, THE MAN etc. AUGUSTINE. If he curse his God, he shall receive sin. But he who names the name of the Lord, dying let him die; as if it were one thing to curse his God and another to name the name of the Lord, and that were a sin, but this so great a wickedness as to be worthy even of death. Although in this place what is said, the name of the Lord, is to be understood as done with cursing, that is, that he names it in cursing. What then is the difference between that sin and this so great crime? Or perhaps by repeating it he showed that this itself is no light sin but to be punished with death? But because he brought it in with a distinction, saying not "for naming" but "but naming", it has become somewhat obscure. And therefore, if this is rightly understood, the kind of idiom is to be noted.
**“all the multitude of the people shall stone him, whether he be a native”** — nourished in the Church
**“or a stranger.”** — newly joined
**“HESYCHIUS”** — Septuagint: The man, the man, who curses God shall receive sin; but he who names the name of the Lord, dying let him die; as though to curse God were less, and to name the name of God more grievous. But he is God and Lord. Whence: "The Lord thy God is one God." And elsewhere: "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with thy whole heart." What is that name of his whose naming is punished? Why are the names of God made manifest in the Scriptures, if those who name them are so punished? But blasphemy which is committed knowingly is avenged with the greatest penalty. Whence: He that shall sin against the Spirit, it shall not be forgiven him; that is, he who blasphemed in knowledge, which is the gift of the Holy Ghost. Whence: And to another is given by the Spirit the word of knowledge. He therefore curses who blasphemes unknowingly, and receives sin, that is, the penalty of sin, because he did not have the knowledge he ought to have had. But he names the name of the Lord who blasphemes in knowledge; and this he does who has acquired knowledge of him through the Spirit. For "no man can say the Lord Jesus, but by the Holy Ghost". Therefore he is justly punished without mercy, whether he was taught by the fathers as a native, or has newly learned as a stranger. And such a one names and blasphemes, as the son of the Israelite woman named and blasphemed.
24.17:
**“HE THAT STRIKETH”** — Septuagint: He that striketh the soul of a man etc., that is, he who draws him to iniquity. By soul he understands the animal man, who perceiveth not the things that are of the Spirit of God.
**“AUGUSTINE”** — He that striketh the soul of a man and he die etc. He does not say: "He that striketh a man and he die", but: the soul of a man, though it is rather the body that is struck. Whence: "Fear ye not them that kill the body" etc. He therefore calls the soul the life of the body, which comes through the soul; and hereby he wished to show the murderer, who strikes the soul of a man, that is, by striking deprives the man of life. Why then did he add: And he die, if by this very thing he already showed the murder, that he struck the soul of a man, that is, that the man was deprived of life by the striker? Or did he wish to explain how what he said, that the soul of a man was struck, is to be taken, and so says: And he die, as though he said: that is, he die? For this is what it is for the soul of a man to be struck.
24.18:
**“He that killeth a beast,”** — who lives as a beast; who is compared to senseless beasts, and is become like to them.
**“shall make it good, that is to say, shall give beast for beast.”** — although he made a common and dull man go astray, he shall make amends with himself
24.19:
**“He that giveth a blemish”** — of sin
**“to any of his neighbours:”** — has not drawn him wholly to impiety
**“as he hath done, so shall it be done to him:”** — according to the fault, he shall bear the penalty
24.20:
**“Breach for breach,”** — BREACH FOR BREACH etc. Septuagint: Bruising for bruising, that is: if by teaching, persuading, scandalizing, he has bruised some virtue of his neighbour.
**“eye for eye,”** — if he has blinded the eye of knowledge
**“TOOTH FOR TOOTH”** — The power of speaking. For teeth are taken for words. Whence: The sons of men, whose teeth are weapons and arrows etc. And: "His eyes are more beautiful than wine, and his teeth whiter than milk." For the words of the Gospel are clearer and plainer than the milk of the law.
**“shall he restore.”** — in the judgment to come
