True things therefore mixed with false in any disputation or narration of anyone, appearing as it were in the colour of one body, signify leprosy, which varies human bodies with true and false patches of colour as it were.
**“and whosoever hath an issue of seed,”**
• who, namely, burns with the wantonness of carnal desires
• abounds in superfluous thoughts
**“or is defiled”** — in deed
**“by the dead:”** — who, namely, follows the impiety and the examples of those dead in sins, and is stained with their filth
5.3:
**“Whether it be man or woman, cast ye them out of the camp,”** — of the Church
**“lest they defile”** — by the contagion of manners
**“it”** — the guilty with the innocent
5.6:
**“Say to the children of Israel: When a man or woman shall have committed any of all the sins that men are wont to commit, and by negligence shall have transgressed the commandment of the Lord, and offended,”** — AND THE LORD SPOKE etc. A MAN OR WOMAN etc. RABANUS. In this chapter we are admonished that if we offend in anything through negligence, we should wash it away by confession and penance and restore the loss. And if we have brought loss on a neighbour, let us repent before him and restore the loss. But if he does not survive, let us make satisfaction to the Lord by confessing, repenting and giving alms.
**“AUGUSTINE”** — Another reading: Man or woman, whoever shall have done any of all human sins, and despising shall have despised and offended, that soul shall declare the sin which it sinned, and shall restore the trespass: the principal, and he shall add the fifths of it over it, and shall render it to him against whom he offended. But if the man have no kinsman, so that he may render the trespass to him, the trespass which is rendered to the Lord shall be the priest's, besides the ram of propitiation, by which he shall make entreaty in it for him. Here those sins are to be understood whose commission is in such things as could be restored with money. For he would not otherwise say how they are to be restored, unless they had been of pecuniary loss. For he commands the principal and the fifths to be restored, that is, the whole of whatever it is, and its fifth part, besides the ram which was to be offered in sacrifice to expiate the trespass. And he commands that what is restored be the priest's, that is, the principal itself and the fifth, if there is no kinsman of him against whom it was committed. Where it is understood that what is to be the priest's is then to be rendered to the Lord, if he who suffered the loss does not survive, nor his kinsman, that is, his heir; but of the man himself he said nothing. But when he says: If he have no kinsman, he briefly hints that his kinsman is then sought if he himself is not there. And if there is no kinsman either, it shall be restored to the Lord, lest the offence remain unpunished. Yet it is not to go into the sacrifice, but to be the priest's: so indeed the words of Scripture are to be distinguished. But if the man have no kinsman, so that he may render the trespass to him: for what he added, "to him", belongs to the idiom. Or perhaps he said "to him" meaning what pertains to him, that is, what he himself possesses. Then follows: The trespass which is rendered to the Lord shall be the priest's. And he says trespass when the thing is rendered which was taken away through the trespass.
5.7:
**“They shall confess their sin, and restore the principal itself, and the fifth part”** — that is, with the same sense of the body by which we brought evil, let us strive to render good things
**“over and above, to him against whom they have sinned.”** — THEY SHALL RESTORE THE PRINCIPAL ITSELF etc. AUGUSTINE. It is asked how in Exodus we read: If anyone steal a calf or a sheep, he ought to restore five calves or four sheep, if he has killed or sold it; but if what he took be found alive with him, double is to be restored; whereas here he commands the principal and the fifth to be restored. Which is far even from the double; how much more from the fourfold or fivefold. Unless perhaps, because here he says: Man or woman, whoever shall have done any of all human sins, he wished human sins to be understood as sins of ignorance. For it can happen that through negligence a man carries over another's property into his own, which is a sin for this reason, that if he had paid careful attention it would not have been committed. And these he wished to be restored with the principal and the fifth, not fined as thefts. For if we understand here thefts and frauds which are committed not through ignorance but with the intent of stealing and defrauding, and therefore called human because they are done against men, then (unless I am mistaken) this will be the solution of the question: that he who did it does not render fourfold because he is not caught or convicted, but, when people do not know by whom it was done, or whether it was done, he himself declares his trespass. For when he had said: Man or woman, whoever shall have done any of all human sins, and despising shall have offended, that is, has committed these things in contempt, he added: That soul shall declare its sin which it sinned, and shall restore the trespass, the principal and the fifths of it. Perhaps, then, only so much, because he declared it; and therefore he was not to be punished with the penalty with which a thief caught or convicted must be punished.
5.8:
**“But if there be no one to receive it, they shall give it to the Lord, and it shall be the priest's, besides the ram that is offered”** — to the Father
**“for expiation,”** — of the human race
**“BESIDES THE RAM”** — The offering of the ram signifies the passion of Christ, in which we trust above all, because without him we can do nothing. He is the priest who reconciles us to the Father by the offering of his flesh. Therefore we offer our gifts to him, by whose intercession we may merit pardon.
5.9:
**“All the firstfruits also,”** — of good will, of words and of works
**“which the children of Israel offer,”** — the true Israelites, who look upon God with the mind
**“belong to the priest:”**
• not to another
• Who offered himself for us of his own accord.
**“TO THE PRIEST”** — To Christ, namely, to whom it is said: "Thou art a priest for ever according to the order of Melchisedech." Reserving all things, namely, to his judgment, lest perhaps one judge an uncertain matter. Whence: "Judge not before the time, until the Lord come" etc.
5.10:
**“And whatsoever into the sanctuary”** — the Church
**“is offered”** — to the Father
**“by every one, and is delivered into the hands of the priest,”** — of Christ, because whatever is offered in the Church pertains to his dignity and grace.
5.12:
**“Speak to the children of Israel, and thou shalt say to them: The man”** — the teacher
**“whose wife”** — the one subject, who ought to have obeyed his master in all things, as a wife her husband
5.13:
**“Shall have slept with another man,”** — mingling, namely, with heretics
**“and her husband cannot discover it,”** — or: detect
**“but the adultery is secret,”** — the fornication of faith
**“and by witnesses be proved”** — namely, be convicted by judicial order
**“cannot, because she was not found”** — by the true master
**“in the adultery:”** — namely, in an open act of heresy
5.14:
**“If the spirit of jealousy”** — namely, the zeal of justice and of the lost sheep
**“stir up the husband”** — the lawful master
**“against his wife, who either is defiled,”** — by heresy
5.15:
**“OF BARLEY MEAL”** — RABANUS. The barley meal signifies the knowledge of the old law, which is well compared to barley, because as barley, cleansed from the chaff with great labour, is brought to meal, so the letter of the law, ground by the millstone of discernment, gives forth the meal of the spiritual sense; and rightly the tenth part of a measure is offered, because the law consists of ten commandments, of which any commandment is a tenth part, against which the wicked wife is said to have acted. The woman therefore is offered to the priest with the oblation of the tenth part when she is reserved for the judgment of Christ, according to the law divinely given, to be condemned or freed.
**“he shall not pour oil thereon,”** — of flattery or of indiscreet mercy
**“HE SHALL NOT POUR”** — RABANUS. etc. It is not fitting that the impenitent be anointed with the oil of flattery or of indiscreet mercy, nor with the frankincense of superfluous praise or of disordered prayer; but that vice be pursued earnestly and in order with the zeal of justice according to the Lord's precept.
5.16: **“The priest therefore shall offer it,”** — because she is kept to be judged by divine judgment
5.17:
**“And he shall take holy water in an earthen vessel,”** — the divine wisdom, namely, contained in the lowly letter of the Law
**“HOLY WATER”** — To this water the priest mixes a little earth from the pavement of the tabernacle, when by the decree of Christ the remembrance of the patriarchs, prophets and apostles is found brought in.
5.18: **“And when the woman shall stand before the Lord, he shall uncover her head, and shall put on her hands the sacrifice of remembrance, and the oblation of jealousy: and he himself shall hold the most bitter waters,”** — showing the punishment of sin
5.19: **“And he shall adjure her, and shall say: If another man hath not slept with thee, and if thou be not defiled by forsaking thy husband's bed, these shall not hold thee”** — or: shall not hurt
5.23: **“And the priest shall write these curses in a book, and shall wash them out with the most bitter waters, upon which he hath heaped the curses,”** — AND THE PRIEST SHALL WRITE etc. Because, namely, the punishment of sinners is set out in holy Scripture. And whoever drinks it piously and faithfully, dreading the punishments of sinners which are told in it and abstaining from sins, for him the most bitter water will become salvation. But he who despises it, his belly swelling, his thigh shall rot, and he shall be a curse and an example, because he will be punished by the just judgment of God, and his desires and acts will be to him a reproach.
5.24: **“And he shall give them her to drink.”** — AND HE SHALL GIVE HER TO DRINK: that her sin may be made manifest, either here for correction or in the future for damnation. For there is nothing hidden that shall not be revealed. Hence the Lord says: The word that I have spoken, the same shall judge you in the last day.
5.25:
**“The priest shall take from her hand the sacrifice”** — This is done when the confession of the holy Trinity is found in the sacrifice of the Law, which is worthily offered on the altar of faith.
**“of jealousy,”** — of flattery
5.27:
**“And when she hath drunk them, if she be defiled, and having despised her husband be guilty of adultery, the waters of malediction shall go through her, and her belly swelling, her thigh shall rot:”** — carnal pleasure and act
**“and the woman shall be a curse, and an example”** — of fear and abstinence
5.28: **“But if she be not defiled, she shall not be hurt, and shall bear children.”** — good works

6.3:
**“From wine”** — in which is wantonness
**“and from every thing that may make drunk”** — the mind
**“they shall abstain.”** — from every earthly pleasure
**“They shall not drink vinegar of wine, or of any other drink, nor any thing that is pressed out of the grape:”** — by falling back into the pleasure of past vice
**“nor shall they eat grapes either fresh or dried.”**
• lest they grow pale with abstinence for vainglory
• AND THE LORD SPOKE etc. FROM WINE AND FROM EVERY etc. ISIDORE. In the twelfth station, that is, Sinai, the Nazarites are commanded not to drink or eat wine and strong drink and everything that can make drunk. In the Proverbs too it is commanded that the mighty and the wrathful drink no wine, lest they forget wisdom. In the Nazarites the life of the continent is marked; to them wine is forbidden, that is, wantonness; and strong drink, that is, every earthly pleasure. For strong drink is made from diverse kinds, as pleasure from the diverse passion of vices. For those do not drink wine but drink strong drink who, to deceive men, feign certain shadows and images of virtues. They eat dried grapes who stain themselves with the pallor of abstinence before human eyes, that they may take glory from men. They drink vinegar who after holiness of life slip back into the oldness of past vices and delight in the corruption of the old wickedness.
6.5: **“NO RAZOR”** — That is: he shall keep neither guile nor malice in his mind, lest, namely, the hair of the head, that is, the thought of the mind, be defiled; but let him keep innocence to the end of life. For otherwise the vow will not be acceptable. But he that shall persevere shall be saved.
6.6: **“NOT TO ANY DEAD”** — That is: he shall not imitate one dead in sins, nor enter the way of his iniquity, lest he lose his labour. For not he who begins, but he who finishes, shall be crowned.
6.7:
**“NEITHER FOR HIS FATHER”** — That is: let no carnal affection draw him back; every person, every dignity, every kinship is to be set after the service of Christ.
**“THE CONSECRATION OF HIS GOD”** — That is: the grace of the Holy Ghost is poured forth in his heart. Whence: Grieve not the Holy Spirit of God, whereby you are all sealed.
6.8:
**“All the days”** — elsewhere: on all the days
**“ALL THE DAYS”** — That is: let him persevere to the end without the defilement of sin and trespass.
6.9:
**“BUT IF ANY MAN DIE”** — That is: if he has wished to imitate one defiled by mortal sin, and has gone down as far as consent, let him know that his continence must needs be defiled and his head shaved, that is, his mind cleansed from wicked thought and harmful delight.
**“HE SHALL SHAVE IT FORTHWITH”** — In the time, namely, of compunction, when he knows he has offended, let him strive at once to amend himself, and always fear a like fall.
6.10:
**“And on the eighth day”** — by which the time of the resurrection is signified
**“TWO TURTLES”** — The turtles signify chastity, the young pigeons simplicity. He therefore who wishes to come to the resurrection of the good, let him offer to the true priest, that is, Christ, chastity of mind and body, and simplicity in the catholic faith, through which he enters the Church, that he may be expiated through the help of so great a high priest.
6.11:
**“And the priest shall offer one for sin,”** — he will make him groan, namely, for sins through fear of hell
**“and the other for a holocaust,”** — that he may sigh, namely, with desire of eternal life
**“AND SHALL PRAY”** — Our advocate with the Father. Or because he will make us pray, according to that: "The Spirit asketh for us with unspeakable groanings."
**“for him, for that he hath sinned by the dead: and he shall sanctify his head”** — the mind rescued from carnal desire
6.12:
**“And shall consecrate to the Lord the days of his separation,”** — that all may be holy and spotless
**“offering a lamb of one year for sin:”** — an innocent life for a criminal one, simplicity for craftiness
**“SO THAT THE FORMER DAYS”** — Let him presume nothing of his former conversation, but trust in the grace of God alone, by whose gift he receives pardon and everlasting rest.
**“HIS SANCTIFICATION WAS PROFANED”** — When the just man shall turn himself away from his justice and do iniquity, all his justices shall be forgotten.
6.13: **“This is the law of consecration. When the days which he had determined by vow shall be expired, he shall bring him to the door of the tabernacle of the covenant,”** — THIS IS THE LAW etc. After the lawgiver has instructed the Nazarite how he is to be cleansed if his consecration is defiled by the dead, he adds how, after the vow is completed, he should present himself to the Lord with an oblation to give thanks; mystically hinting that the life of the continent, with the oblation of work and cleanness of heart, will please the Lord in a good end.
6.14:
**“A LAMB OF A YEAR OLD”** — He offers this who puts all his hope in his immolation, of whom it is said: Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who taketh away the sins of the world. He offers him for a holocaust when for his love, by mortifying the flesh, he consecrates to the Lord his whole life kindled with the ardour of charity.
**“and one ewe lamb of a year old without blemish for a sin offering,”** — others: for sin
**“AUGUSTINE”** — Another reading: And he shall offer his gift to the Lord, a lamb of a year without blemish for holocausts, and one ewe lamb of a year without blemish "into sin". This some would not translate, as though avoiding an unusual expression, and said "for sin", not "into sin", although the sense in that expression is not to be disturbed. For "into sin" was said because what was offered for sin was called sin. Whence: Him that knew no sin, for us he hath made sin, that is, a sacrifice for sin. As therefore the lamb "into holocaust", so also the ewe lamb "into sin", so that the animal itself was sin, that is, a sacrifice for sin; as of the ram, which follows, he says "into saving", which he makes plain afterward by repeating. For he also says "for sin" what he had said before "into sin"; and "this sacrifice of saving" what he had said before "into saving".
**“RABANUS”** — Tropologically. He offers a lamb for a holocaust who shows God simplicity of heart with the devotion of charity; a ewe, who shows an example of innocence; and a ram as a peace victim, when he rules himself well in the way of God and subjects the rebellious flesh to the command of the soul.
**“AND ONE EWE”** — He offers a ewe for sin who faithfully believes that Christ, the innocent, was offered for the sin of the human race.
**“AND ONE RAM”** — This is done when he trusts that he is the one who by the dispensation of the flesh made peace between things heavenly and earthly, emptying every principality and power: whom "God hath exalted, and hath given him a name which is above every name" etc.
6.15:
**“A basket”** — the Scripture
**“also of unleavened bread,”**
• of spiritual nourishment
• of the Gospel doctrine
**“tempered with oil,”** — of gladness, the grace of the Holy Ghost
**“AND WAFERS”** — The old law, dictated by the Holy Ghost and tempered for human profit.
**“without leaven”**
• of malice and wickedness
• Without leaven: because spiritual grace lies open in the law and in the Gospel to those who understand rightly.
6.16:
**“WHICH HE SHALL OFFER”** — Presenting the merit and labour of each, his meditation and observance of the law, in the sight of God by rewarding it, at the entrance of the heavenly life, the contest of good work being finished.
**“the priest”** — Christ
6.17: **“But the ram he shall immolate for a sacrifice of peace offering to the Lord, offering at the same time the basket of unleavened bread, and the libations that are due by custom.”** — BUT THE RAM etc. Showing him, namely, worthy of the reward of everlasting rest, as the prince and best leader of himself or of others, who has ruled and led himself well in the path of God's commandments, according to the doctrine of the Scriptures and the grace of the spiritual gifts.
6.18:
**“Then shall the Nazarite be shaved”** — the mind, namely, of one abstaining from superfluous thoughts
**“before the door of the tabernacle of the covenant of the hair of his consecration: and he shall take his hair,”** — the thoughts of presumption
**“and lay it upon the fire,”** — of divine love
**“GREGORY”** — What is it that the Nazarites grow their hair, except that through a life of great continence the thoughts of presumption grow? But what is it that, the devotion being completed, the Nazarite is commanded to shave his head and put the hair in the fire of the sacrifice, except that we then reach the height of perfection when we so conquer outward vices that we also cut off superfluous thoughts from the mind? To burn these in the fire of the sacrifice is to kindle them with the flame of divine love, so that the whole heart burns in the love of God, and, burning up superfluous thoughts, consumes as it were the hair of the Nazarite by the perfection of devotion.
6.19:
**“And shall take the boiled shoulder of the ram, and one cake”** — by revealing the obscure mysteries of the Scriptures
**“AND THE BOILED SHOULDER”** — The strength, namely, of work, boiled and proved in the fire of tribulation, the high priest makes his holy one offer to God the Father.
**“unleavened out of the basket,”** — the knowledge of Scripture
**“and one wafer”** — AND ONE WAFER: helping him, namely, by the gift of the Holy Ghost to complete in work the knowledge of the law.
**“unleavened, and he shall deliver them into the hands of the Nazarite, after his head is shaven.”** — that is: when he has stripped him of the corruption of the flesh and freed him from the burden of cares.
6.20:
**“And receiving them again from him, he shall elevate them”** — HE SHALL ELEVATE: he will present to the Father, namely, the good things which the continent man has wrought, and will have them rewarded with everlasting reward.
**“in the sight of the Lord:”** — of the Father
**“and they being sanctified shall belong to the priest,”** — SHALL BELONG TO THE PRIEST: because whatever the Nazarite has willed well and completed in deed pertains to his glory. For he it is who worketh in us both to will and to accomplish.
**“as the breast,”** — because our wisdom is his own gift
**“which was commanded to be separated, and the shoulder.”** — the mortification of carnal pleasure
**“After this”** — the aforesaid
**“AFTER THIS”** — That is: after right intention, discreet promise, perfection of work, retribution of reward.
**“the Nazarite may drink wine.”** — DRINK WINE: to drink in the spiritual gift fully and freely; whence: "Thou shalt make them drink of the torrent of thy pleasure."
6.21:
**“This is the law”** — the aforesaid
**“of the Nazarite, when he hath vowed his oblation to the Lord in the time of his consecration,”** — of consecrated abstinence
**“besides those things”** — which, namely, he will do of his own accord
6.22:
**“And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying:”** — AND THE LORD SPOKE etc. Moses signifies the law, Aaron the priesthood, and his sons the order of the Church. The Lord therefore teaches through the law the order of priests how they should build up the people by preaching and strengthen them by frequent prayer and blessing.
**“RABANUS”** — Moses has a manifold signification. He bears the figure of the Jewish people when he holds the serpent's tail; for it signifies that the Jews will come to the faith of Christ at the end of the world. He signifies the law also, as we showed above. He bears the person of Christ, who frees his elect from the spiritual Egypt through the water of baptism, when he leads the people out of Egypt through the Red Sea, when he completes, sets up and anoints the tabernacle.
6.24:
**“Bless”** — by the pouring in of the spiritual gifts
**“thee the Lord”** — whose it is to keep; whence: "Unless the Lord keep the city, he watcheth in vain that keepeth it."
**“BLESS THEE”** — It is to be noted that in this blessing the name of the Lord is brought in three times, that the holy Trinity may be understood, from whom and through whom and in whom all good things are to be sought and obtained, because of him and by him and in him are all things.
**“AND KEEP THEE”** — May he keep by his grace the blessing which you have received. "Unless the Lord keep the city, he watcheth in vain that keepeth it."
6.25: **“SHEW”** — The showing of God's face is propitiation, and the showing of true salvation; whence: "Shew us thy face, and we shall be saved."
6.26: **“The Lord turn his countenance to thee, and give thee peace.”** — TURN etc. The turning of the face signifies mercy, the turning away, wrath. Whence: "Look thou upon me, and have mercy on me." And elsewhere: Why turnest thou thy face away, and forgettest our want? We must pray therefore that he whose help we turn away from us by sinning would deign, by his goodness, to make his face shine upon us, that, rescuing us from our enemies, he may grant everlasting peace.
6.27: **“THEY SHALL INVOKE”** — It is the priests' part to invoke the name of the Lord; the Lord's to accomplish what is asked. Let no one therefore ascribe to himself what the Trinity alone grants to whom it will.

7.1:
**“And it came to pass in the day that had finished”** — completing it with his blood
**“Moses”** — Christ
**“the tabernacle”** — the Church
**“THE TABERNACLE”** — Allegorically. The Church, or the perfect, in whom the spices of virtues and prayers are burnt; or the humanity of Christ, in which he presented to the Father the victim of our redemption. For he himself is priest, himself victim and altar, because, holding death in his power, he took it up of his own will. Whence: No man taketh my life away from me, but I lay it down, and I take it up again.
**“and set it up,”** — to seek glory
**“and had anointed”** — with the oil of gladness
**“and sanctified it”** — with spiritual grace
**“with all its vessels,”** — the elect ordained to diverse ministries
**“the altar likewise and all the vessels thereof,”** — of the altar
7.2:
**“The princes of Israel offered”** — THE PRINCES OF ISRAEL etc. The patriarchs, prophets and apostles, who by doctrine, example and good working offered gifts pleasing to God, and contributed with glad mind whatever good they could to the building of the Church. Tropologically too they can be called princes who, instructed in the apostolic doctrine, rightly rule the senses of the body as well as the affections of the mind; whose gifts are most pleasing to God because brought with one accord. Whence: If two of you shall consent upon earth concerning any thing whatsoever they shall ask, it shall be done to them by my Father.
**“and the heads of the families,”** — of the various orders or churches
7.3:
**“Their gifts before the Lord, six wagons covered,”**
• covered with boards, that they may receive the loads within, or spread with cloths, that they may more worthily receive the furniture of the tabernacle
• Covered wagons, adorned with faith and the affection of mercy, that they may be acceptable to God. There are twelve oxen. For those who labour in the service of the saints do all things honourably and in order under the yoke of the apostolic doctrine. Or by the oxen we take the teachers who work worthily in the Lord's field, of whom it is said: "Thou shalt not muzzle the mouth of the ox that treadeth out the corn." For those who keep the apostolic rule by living and preaching are to be counted worthy of double honour.
**“SIX WAGONS”** — The wagons which the children of Israel offered to the Levites for carrying the tabernacle signify the temporal comforts which devout peoples render to preachers, that without care or hindrance they may be free for the divine service, and that they who preach the Gospel may live by the Gospel. For if they sow spiritual things, it is no great matter if they reap temporal things.
**“with twelve oxen. One wagon”** — because one office of charity is accepted, ministered as well by mind as by body: "For God loveth a cheerful giver."
**“ONE OX”** — Because unity of faith and simplicity of intention with devout labour please most in teachers. Nor should it be passed over that twelve embraces each man, and the fulness of time, and the site of the world. For man consists of three qualities in the soul and four in the body; and if you multiply three by four, or the reverse, twelve will come out. The world too is bounded by twelve winds, the year by twelve months, and the day by twelve hours. From all these we gather that every man, in every place, at every time, ought to hasten to the tabernacle of God with due service.
7.9: **“BUT TO THE SONS OF CAATH”** — It is written above that the sons of Caath must carry on their own shoulders the tabernacle of the covenant, the holy of holies, the ark, the altar, the table, the candlestick and all their vessels wrapped in cloths; that the office of the Gersonites is to carry the curtains of the tabernacle, and the roof and the other covering, and over all the violet covering, and the hanging that hangs in the entry of the tabernacle, the curtains of the court, and all that pertains to the brazen altar, the cords and the vessels of the ministry; and of the Merarites, to carry the boards of the tabernacle, its bars, pillars and their vessels, and the pillars of the court round about with their sockets, pins and cords. Note therefore that the things which are holy are not laid on dumb animals to be carried, but on rational ones. The harder and heavier things, then, are laid on dumb animals, and among these there is a difference. For those who keep the harder and heavier ministries have more animals. For four wagons are given to the sons of Merari; but for the sons of Gerson, who are nearest to the sons of Caath, two suffice. Whence it is shown that more serve the harder and coarser works, as it were like animals. But to the things which are seen to by rational men, few of the less learned come. The mystical secrets lie open to the priests alone; no animal man comes near, nor even those who seem to have some exercise and learning.
7.10:
**“And the princes offered for the dedication of the altar”** — the consecration of the church
**“OFFERED”** — Each one ought to offer according to his power faith, doctrine and good working for the progress and honour of the Church.
**“IT WAS ANOINTED”** — In the time of the incarnation, when after the resurrection and ascension the disciples received the outpouring of the Holy Ghost.
7.11: **“THE PRINCES”** — The preachers, leaders on the right way, who, though they offer the same doctrine of faith and the same examples of good work, yet distribute their offerings according to the diversity of place and time.
7.13:
**“And his offering was a dish”** — a vessel in which vinegar is put
**“of silver weighing one hundred and thirty sicles,”**
• A DISH etc. These have a narrow mouth, and signify the narrowness of the letter of the law and the obscurity of the prophets.
• The various vessels made for offering libations are the various distinctions of the word according to the various capacity of the hearers. For the wise are to be taught one way, the foolish another, the rich one way, the poor another, the healthy one way, the sick another; the rude people of the Jews one way under the shadow of the law, the Christian another in the truth of the Gospel.
**“A SILVER BOWL”** — The spiritual knowledge is in the law and in the Gospel, which was written and put forth for the salvation of men by the ministry of spiritual grace; hence the sacrifice is rightly made, because nothing is so acceptable to God as meditation on the law with the carrying out of work.
**“RABANUS”** — The bowl was formerly made of glass: for hyalim is Greek, vitrum Latin; and, being broad at the top, it signifies the light of the Gospel, by which all the mysteries of the law and the prophets are explained; also the apostolic doctrine, by which all the riddles of the law became clear. And well are the dishes of one hundred and thirty sicles of silver, because of the Decalogue of the law and the age of the lawgiver, which was one hundred and twenty years. The bowls too are of seventy sicles, where the number ten multiplied seven times shows that the commandments are to be fulfilled by the grace of the Holy Ghost, who was given more manifestly in the New Testament.
7.14:
**“A LITTLE MORTAR”** — The heart of the elect, full of divine wisdom, containing the spices of the virtues. Whence it is said: For the multitude of believers had but one heart and one soul.
**“OF TEN”** — Because with the fulfilling of the ten commandments they send forth the odour of doctrine and prayer, that they may merit to receive the penny of eternal life.
7.17:
**“And for the sacrifice of peace offerings, two oxen, five rams, five he goats, five lambs of a year old.”**
• AN OX OF THE HERD etc. These signify the diverse persons of the Fathers who went before, who are examples to us. For some performed the offices of teacher, others were set over subjects in leadership and kingship, others were either most holy or most pleasing by the simplicity and meekness of their conversation, others most acceptable by penance done bravely and worthily.
• Tropologically. He offers an ox who spends useful labour on his neighbours in the Church of God; a ram, who directs himself and others in the way of justice; a lamb of a year old, who is simple and innocent. All these for a holocaust, for the love of God alone and the desire of eternal life. He offers a buck goat for sin who does not cease to repent and pray for his sins. For a sacrifice of peace offerings he offers two oxen who with good works fulfils the two precepts of charity, namely love of God, by keeping his commandments, and of neighbour, by providing for his needs; on which dependeth the whole law and the prophets. And he offers five rams, five buck goats, five lambs of a year old, who leads the five senses of the body bravely in the way of truth, restrains them from sins, and sets forth examples of simplicity.
7.35: **“And for victims”** — or: for the sacrifice
7.42: **“The sixth day the prince of the sons of Gad, Elisaphat”** — or: Eliasaph
7.78: **“The twelfth day the prince of the sons of Nephtali, Achira”** — others: Ahira
7.85: **“Each dish weighing a hundred and thirty sicles of silver, and each bowl seventy sicles: that is, putting all the vessels of silver together, two thousand four hundred sicles, by the weight of the sanctuary.”** — TWO THOUSAND FOUR HUNDRED. Allegorically. In the silver vessels, which all together have two thousand four hundred sicles by the weight of the sanctuary, we take the perfect doctrine of the word of God, which consists in the two Testaments; to which, if we rightly obey, the four-horse chariot of the virtues, that is, prudence, justice, fortitude and temperance, will bring us to eternal beatitude. For the thousand doubled shows that the two Testaments show us the way to beatitude; and the four hundred, that with the perfection of good works we come there in the chariot of the virtues: for unless one runs by good acts, one does not come there.
7.86: **“LITTLE MORTARS”** — Allegorically. The twelve golden little mortars, each of which has ten sicles, and all together one hundred and twenty sicles of gold, signify that the hearts of the elect keep the knowledge of the law in all things according to the apostolic doctrine. For twelve tens make one hundred and twenty, the number with which the first Church in Jerusalem received the Spirit the Paraclete. Whence is added: By the weight of the sanctuary. For the sanctuary is the Church, following whose rule of faith and understanding we believe that all things written in the law and the prophets are wholesome for us. But whatever is thought and understood or kept outside the unity of the Church brings forth the damnation of the soul.
7.87:
**“OXEN OUT OF THE HERD”** — The oxen, rams and lambs, comprised in the number twelve, signify those who, either in the office of teacher, or in the rule of some honour, or living simply, strive to do all things according to the apostolic and prophetic doctrine.
**“TWELVE BUCK GOATS”** — These are they who strive to perform penance according to the rule of the apostolic faith.
7.88:
**“OXEN TWENTY-FOUR”** — In these is signified spiritual knowledge with the perfection of good works, because twenty-four, the number of hours in which the course of a day is run, signifies that the light of knowledge and faith is necessary to every Christian.
**“SIXTY”** — Sixty, that is, six times ten, shows the perfection of the commandments. For it is necessary that prelates, subjects and penitents do all things according to the doctrine of the Church, so that their oblation may keep the rite and order of peace offerings, and they may merit the grace of God, not his offence.
7.89:
**“And when Moses entered”** — the preachers, the teachers of the people
**“into the tabernacle of the covenant,”** — namely, by meditating on holy Scripture, whence God speaks
**“AND WHEN HE ENTERED”** — GREGORY. What is it that Moses so often goes in and out, except that he who within is rapt into contemplation is pressed outside by the affairs of the weak? Within he considers the secrets of God, outside he carries the burdens of the carnal. He who on doubtful matters always runs back to the tabernacle consults the Lord before the ark of the testimony, giving an example to teachers, that when outside they are in doubt what to order, they should always return to the mind as to the tabernacle, and consult God as before the ark of the testimony; and in the things about which they are in doubt within themselves, they should search the pages of the sacred word within. Whence: Christ clings to prayer on the mountain, works miracles in the cities; laying down for good rulers the way of imitation, that if they already seek the highest things by contemplating, they should yet be mingled with the needs of the weak by compassion. For charity rises wonderfully to the heights when it draws itself mercifully to the low things of neighbours; and the more kindly it comes down to the lowest, the more strongly it runs back to the highest.
**“FROM THE PROPITIATORY”** — Because through the grace of divine propitiation, after the fault of transgression, God opened to us the way of truth.
**“BETWEEN THE TWO CHERUBIMS”** — Because God did not appear to Moses in his own substance, but through an angelic vision. Whence: The law ordained by angels in the hand of a mediator. Or because through both Testaments he instructs us with a harmonious voice to the faith of truth. Or because through the Son, who appeared in the flesh in the midst of the two Testaments, the Father spoke to the human race.

8.2:
**“THE SEVEN LAMPS”** — The seven gifts of the Holy Ghost, which always remained in Christ and are distributed in the members according to his will.
**“let the candlestick be set up on the south side. Give orders therefore that the lamps look over against the north, towards the table”** — the sacred Scripture of the Gospel
**“TOWARDS THE TABLE”** — The table and the candlestick: the temporal benefits of God by which we are refreshed and enlightened, so that, strengthened by these, as the grace of merits grows, we may come to eat the bread of angels in heaven and to see the true light of God. These are without the veil, because only in this life do we need Scriptures and teachers and the other sacraments; but in the future the Lord will show us plainly of the Father. The south side of the tabernacle signifies the ancient people of God, which first received the light of divine knowledge and the fervour of love; the north, the Church gathered from the Gentiles, which remained longer in darkness. Rightly therefore the candlestick, which is on the south side, signifies the grace given to the former people; and the table on the north side, the benefits of God given to us. Well therefore is the candlestick set over against the table, because the Scripture of the law and the prophets looks toward the grace of the Gospel, bearing witness to it.
8.3: **“And Aaron did so, and he put the lamps upon the candlestick,”** — UPON THE CANDLESTICK: namely, upon Christ, the firstborn from the root of Jesse, "upon" whom rested "the spirit of wisdom and of understanding, the spirit of counsel and of fortitude" etc.
8.4:
**“OF GOLD”** — Because Christ is singularly free from sin and renowned for works of justice; and the members, who imitate his innocence as they are able, will be perfected in the future.
**“BEATEN”** — Because Christ from his conception and birth was perfect God and man, bore the pains of the passions, and so came to the glory of the resurrection; and all who will to live godly in him, as metal widened by beating, come through the insults of the passion to the grace of immortality.
**“THE SHAFT”** — Christ, namely, from whom the branches proceed, because from him the just receive whatever good they have. Whence: "Without me you can do nothing."
8.6: **“TAKE THE LEVITES”** — Mystically. He instructs the ecclesiastical order how it is duly to be advanced to the dignity of the priesthood.
8.7:
**“According to this rite: Let them be sprinkled with the water of purification,”** — namely of baptism, or of tears, by which the stains of sins are washed away
**“and let them shave”** — not: pluck out; because the roots remain, from which they may grow again.
**“all the hairs of their flesh.”** — the thoughts of the old life
**“THE HAIRS OF THEIR FLESH”** — GREGORY. The hairs of the flesh are any superfluous thoughts of human flesh or of the old life, which we so cut from the mind that we are wearied by no grief at their loss. And Levite is said to mean taken up. The Levites therefore must shave all the hairs of the flesh, because he who is taken up into the service of God ought to appear before the eyes of God clean of all thoughts of the flesh, lest the mind put forth unlawful thoughts and make the beautiful appearance of the soul unsightly as with darkening hairs. But however high the virtue of holy conversation has raised anyone, there still grows in him from the oldness of life something to remove. Whence the hairs of the Levites themselves are commanded to be shaved, not plucked out. For when the hairs are shaved, the roots remain in the flesh and grow, that they may be cut again. Because superfluous thoughts must be cut off with great zeal, but they cannot be cut off utterly. For superfluous things are always being produced, which the spirit cuts back with the steel of carefulness. But we do this more finely in ourselves when we penetrate the heights of contemplation.
**“THEY SHALL HAVE WASHED”** — They have cleansed, namely, their works, that their conversation may be clean in the sight of God and blameless before men.
8.8:
**“They shall take an ox”** — the Lord's body
**“AN OX”** — The Mediator of God and men, by whose immolation our sins are blotted out. In both oxen his incarnation is signified. For the passion of Christ is one, but it obtained two things for us, namely expiation from sins and sanctification, that he might offer us to God sanctified in the flesh and quickened in the spirit. Whence Paul: But you are washed, but you are sanctified in the name of the Lord Jesus. By these two oxen, of which one is offered for sin and the other for a holocaust, two kinds of actions can be expressed: by one we wash away by the lament of penance the evil we have done; by the other we merit the grace of God and the reward of beatitude by the fruits of good works and virtues.
**“of the herd,”** — begotten of the patriarchs and prophets
**“THE OFFERING”** — The sacrament of the passion, which, understood and handled with spiritual knowledge, is most wholesome to the faithful and most pleasing to God; if only the minister of God shows himself clean and worthy within and without for receiving such mysteries.
8.9: **“AND THOU SHALT BRING”** — The Levites are brought before the tabernacle of the covenant when those chosen for the office of the altar are brought forward according to the apostolic doctrine, by which the true tabernacle is entered; if, namely, they have begun well according to the doctrine and examples of the saints, and have persevered to the end.
8.10: **“And when the Levites are before the Lord, the children of Israel shall put their hands upon them:”** — THEY SHALL PUT. Because they ought to give assent to the choice of their devotion, and at their command to press on in good works.
8.11:
**“And Aaron shall offer”** — the true one of the mountain, that is, Christ
**“the Levites, as a gift in the sight of the Lord from the children of Israel,”** — taken up
**“FROM THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL”** — The choice, namely, is to be made under the testimony and knowledge of many, that a worthy examination may be held, so that no one can find fault. For they ought to have a good testimony even from them that are without.
8.12: **“The Levites also shall put their hands upon the heads of the oxen, of which thou shalt sacrifice one for sin, and the other for a holocaust to the Lord, to pray for them.”** — THE LEVITES ALSO etc. Because the ministers of the Lord hasten to consecrate to the Lord by their own labour the beginnings of good works, that, whether penance is to be done or the pursuits of virtues exercised, they may carry them out effectually.
8.14: **“THOU SHALT SEPARATE”** — The minister of the Lord ought not to be content with the discipline of the common people. He ought to be set apart and conspicuous in manners and doctrine.
8.17:
**“EVERY FIRSTBORN IN”** — Allegorically. ORIGEN. The firstborn of the Egyptians are the beginnings of vices, by which human life is corrupted. For every soul, when it has come to the fulness of age and a certain natural law, as it were, has begun to defend its rights in it, produces its first motions according to the desires of the flesh, which the force of incitement stirs up by the tinder of concupiscence or anger. Whence it is said of Christ as something proper and special: "Butter and honey shall he eat", before he does or utters evil things, he shall choose the good. For before the child know good or evil, he will resist evil, that he may choose what is good. But David says of himself: "The sins of my youth and my ignorances do not remember." Because therefore the first motions of the soul, brought forth according to the flesh, rush into sin, they are rightly called the firstborn of the Egyptians, which are extinguished. But let the conversation of the rest of life direct a more amended course.
**“For all the firstborn of the children of Israel, both of men and of beasts, are mine. From the day that I slew every firstborn in the land of Egypt,”** — The vices, which are the firstborn of the devil, or the works of the flesh by which nature is defiled, being extinguished, good manners are to be put in their place. Moreover, the minister of God ought to be instructed in more perfect manners than the multitude of the people. For therefore, for the firstborn of the Egyptians, the firstborn of the Israelites are commanded to be offered to the Lord; and again, for the firstborn of the children of Israel, the Levites are taken into the service of the Lord; so that for a sinful life a just life, and for a just life a holy, proven and perfect one may be shown, that the true Levite may be worthily fitted to the altars of Christ and to the divine mysteries.
8.19: **“And have delivered them for a gift to Aaron and his sons out of the midst of the people, to serve me for Israel in the tabernacle of the covenant, and to pray for them, lest there should be a plague among the people, if they should presume to approach unto my sanctuary.”** — TO SERVE etc. Let the ministers of the Lord see how necessary it is for them to keep the rights of their office, and not to gape after earthly gains or pleasures, they whose proper part is to serve the tabernacle and pray for the people, lest there be a destroying plague among them; otherwise they cast both themselves and the people headlong into perdition, and it is said to them: "I will not receive a gift of your hand."
8.22: **“That being purified they might go into the tabernacle of the covenant to do their services before Aaron and his sons. As the Lord had commanded Moses”** — so was it done touching the Levites
8.24:
**“This is the law of the Levites: From twenty-five years old and upwards, they shall go in”** — when the wars of the vices rise up against each one
**“to minister in the tabernacle of the covenant.”** — let them serve, namely, in the Church, not preside
8.25:
**“And when they shall have accomplished the fiftieth year of their age,”** — that is: when they shall have inward rest
**“they shall cease to serve:”** — the war of the vices being laid to rest
8.26:
**“And they shall be the ministers of their brethren”** — keepers of souls
**“in the tabernacle of the covenant, to keep the things that are committed to their care,”**
• by God
• FROM TWENTY-FIVE. ISIDORE. The Levites are commanded to serve the tabernacle from the twenty-fifth year, and from the fiftieth they become keepers of the vessels. By the twenty-fifth year, in which the flower of youth springs up, the wars against each of the vices are marked. By the fiftieth, the inward rest of the mind, the war being subdued, is marked. By the vessels of the tabernacle, the souls of the faithful. The Levites therefore serve the tabernacle from the twenty-fifth year, and from the fiftieth become keepers of the vessels, so that those who still endure the struggles of assailing vices through the consent of delight should not presume to take up the care of others. But when they have subdued the wars of temptations, when they are already secure within themselves of inward tranquillity, let them be allotted the keeping of souls. But who subdues these perfectly, when Paul says: I see another law in my members, fighting against the law of my mind etc.? But it is one thing to endure wars bravely, another to be overcome feebly. In the former virtue is exercised, lest it should be lifted up; in the latter it is wholly extinguished, so that it cannot stand.

9.3:
**“LET THEM MAKE”** — BEDE. Let the children of Israel make the phase in its season, the fourteenth day of this month etc. Whereas in the Old Testament the paschal time is observed by three marks, namely that it be celebrated after the equinox, and in the first month, in its third week, that is, from the evening of the fourteenth moon (which is the beginning of the fifteenth) to the evening, that is, the end, of the twenty-first moon, a fourth rule has been imposed on us by the resurrection of Christ: that when, the equinox passed, we have seen the moon of the first month rise in the evening on the fourteenth, we do not at once make the pasch, but, waiting for the Lord's day, on which he himself celebrated the pasch, that is, the passage from death to life, by rising, we celebrate the pasch on it. And if anyone objects that the Lawgiver set down no mention of the equinox, but only of the first month and the third week, let him know that, although he does not name the equinox expressly, yet in commanding the pasch to be made from the full moon of the first month he declares the passing of the equinox. Since it is agreed that the moon which first shows its full orb after the equinox has passed is the moon of the first month. As often, therefore, as we have the Lord's day as soon as the fifteenth moon comes, our paschal time differs in nothing from the legal one, although we keep the pasch with other kinds of sacraments. And as often as the same Lord's day falls on the second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth or seventh day from then, not even then do we destroy the law and the prophets. For as the observance of so many paschal ceremonies, so also the time in which it was commanded to be done, breathes of sacred mysteries. For first we take care, according to the decree of the law, that the equinox be passed, so that the solemnity (in which Christ, the power of darkness destroyed, opened to the world the way of light) may by the very order of time show outwardly what it holds within; and that the feast which promises us the light of eternal beatitude may be celebrated chiefly then, when the sun, advancing by its yearly increase, takes its first victory over the shadow of night. Then we attend to the first month of the year, which is also called the month of new things, in which to celebrate the pasch; that is, the month in which this world was formed and the first man set in the seat of paradise; because through this solemnity we hope to receive again the first robe and the first kingdom from which we departed into a far country. Whence Peter: But we look for new heavens and a new earth according to his promises. And elsewhere: "Behold, I make all things new."
**“BEDE”**
• Then we observe the third week, which accords with the Lord's resurrection, which took place on the third day, and in the third age of the world, that is, when with the coming of heavenly grace his whole dispensation in the flesh appeared to the world, consummated by the glory of the resurrection. For he enlightened the first times of the world by the natural law through the fathers, the middle by the written law or the prophets, the last by the spiritual gift through himself.
• The very turning of the moon also signifies to us a heavenly sacrament. For the moon, being of round shape, receives light from the sun. Therefore it is always bright on the half of its orb which it has toward the sun, but always dark on the other half. From the first to the fifteenth it has increase of light toward the earth, but lack toward the heavens; from the fifteenth to the last, the reverse. This turning of it rightly signifies the mysteries of the paschal joy, by which we are taught to turn all the glory of our mind away from earthly things and hang it on the light of heavenly grace alone. Or the light of the moon, growing to human eyes, hints at the grace of the virtues with which the Lord, appearing in the flesh, shone upon the world; of which it is said: And Jesus advanced in age and wisdom and grace with God and men. But turning back toward the heavens, it hints at the glory of the resurrection and ascension, which in itself came at once to perfection, but in the mind of the faithful grows by certain advances of its light until the end of the world. For the Lord, rising, appeared first to individuals, then to two, then to more, now to seven, now to eleven, now to twelve, now to more than five hundred brethren together, and last to all the disciples; and, about to ascend into heaven in their sight, he commanded them to be "witnesses" of his dispensation "even to the uttermost part of the earth".
• To these marks of the Pasch or Phase taken from the law, we heirs of the New Testament also join the Lord's day, because it excels both by the creation of the first light and by the triumph of the Lord's resurrection.
• The seven days of the moon also, that is, from the fifteenth day to the twenty-first, through which that Lord's day runs in natural order, signify the whole Church throughout the world redeemed by the paschal mysteries. For seven signifies universality. Whence: "Seven times a day I have given praise to thee." That is: "His praise shall be always in my mouth." Whence John too, writing to the seven churches of Asia, shows the mysteries of the universal Church; whence, writing exhortations to each, he watchfully repeats: He that hath ears to hear, let him hear what the Spirit saith to the churches; as if: What I say to one, I say to all.
**“The fourteenth day of this month in the evening, according to all the ceremonies and justifications thereof.”**
• And well does the moon, when it grows to our eyes, gradually withdraw from the sun, but when toward the heavens, return to it by equal spaces. For this is what he says: "I came forth from the Father, and am come into the world", and "again I leave the world, and I go to the Father." And David says: "His going out is from the end of heaven, and his circuit even to the end thereof." Because therefore the moon, by the increase of light which, going out from the sun, it turns to our gaze, signifies Christ's doctrine and virtues in the flesh up to the passion; and by gathering back its light, returning to the sun, gradually to the face of heaven invisible to us, shows the miracles of the resurrection and the later glory, the fifteenth is rightly fitted to the paschal joy.
• Or in the moon growing toward men the active life is shown, in the one turned back toward the heavens the contemplative. Or in this turning, love of neighbour; in that, of God. Or the advance of light turned hither admonishes us to do good works outwardly; turned thither, to do the same works with regard only to the heavenly reward. Hither, that "your light may shine before men, that they may see your good works"; thither, "that they may glorify your Father who is in heaven". On the first day of the week, which is the proper solemnity of the New Testament, we are instructed to bear all things for Christ, and death itself, patiently, in the hope of our future resurrection in Christ. Because if the Spirit of him that raised up Jesus from the dead dwell in us, he shall quicken also our mortal bodies. And whose Spirit (because his grace is sevenfold) can fittingly be understood by the same number of seven lunar days through which the Lord's day, the first of the week, is carried round.
**“THE SAME”** — In the name too of Pasch or Phase we are morally admonished to pass over from vices to virtues. In the month of new things (in which the grown fruits, by their coming, announce the ceasing of the old), that we put off the old man with his deeds and put on the new, and, quickened by the variety of diverse virtues and veiled by their leaves as by the shade of a pleasant tree, spring up as glad and fruitful crops. At the full moon, that, bearing the perfect splendour of faith and understanding, we may be separated from the darkness of sin. In the light turned back toward the heavens, which begins from the fifteenth moon, that the greater we are, the more we may humble ourselves in all things, saying: By the grace of God I am what I am. And because this grace of the heavenly gift was poured forth more manifestly in the third age of the world, by a most beautiful sequence of the figure, in the third week of the moon its light, which until then had grown toward the earth, begins to grow toward heavenly things. Beautifully we are commanded to observe this week at the Pasch, that, mindful of the grace received, we may through each step of the spiritual passage repay the giver of it.
9.6: **“But behold some who were unclean by occasion of the soul of a man, who could not make the pasch”** — or: Phase
9.7:
**“Said to them: We are unclean”** — on account of the touching of some dead body
**“by occasion of the soul of a man. Why are we kept back that we may not offer in its season the offering to the Lord among the children of Israel?”** — BUT BEHOLD SOME WHO WERE UNCLEAN BY OCCASION OF THE SOUL OF A MAN etc. AUGUSTINE. When at the time of the Pasch some were unclean by occasion of the soul of a man, and asked how they should make the Pasch, since they had to be purified from uncleanness for seven days according to the law, Moses consults the Lord. And he received the answer that whoever this had befallen, or who, being far off, could not come, should make the Pasch in another month, because of the fourteenth day of the month, where the number of the moon was observed. But if it is asked what they would do if perhaps such uncleanness befell them even at the second month, I think that what was said of the second month was to be held as a rule, so that they would observe it in the third month. Or perhaps, if they had not kept the Pasch, it would not count as a fault.
9.8: **“STAY THAT I MAY CONSULT”** — GREGORY. Moses often runs back to the tabernacle on doubtful matters, leaving the crowds. To return to the tabernacle is to enter the secret place of the mind, the tumults of outward things being set aside. For there the Lord is consulted, and what is to be done publicly outside is heard silently within. Good rulers also do this daily, when they know they cannot discern doubtful matters, and, returning to the secret place of the mind as to a kind of tabernacle, having looked into the divine law, consult the Lord as if before the ark set there. And what they first hear within in silence they afterward make known outside in action. For that they may serve outward things without offence, they take care to run back unceasingly to the secret places of the heart, and so hear the voice of the Lord as by a hidden inspiration, while in the meditation of the mind they are drawn away from the carnal senses.
9.10:
**“Say to the children of Israel: The man that shall be unclean by occasion of a soul,”** — the Gentile, defiled in soul with all vices, and having committed fornication with demons
**“or shall be in a journey afar off”** — from God, because without the faith of one God, without the Law
9.11:
**“In the second month, on the fourteenth day of the month in the evening,”** — of the world
**“THE MAN THAT SHALL BE UNCLEAN”** — ISIDORE. It is commanded that those who dwelt farther off, or had been unclean in soul, should make the Pasch in the second month, because the Gentiles, having committed fornication with all the demons, were unclean and far from God. But, cleansed by wholesome confession, they are commanded to pass over to the nativity of Christ as to the second month.
**“they shall eat it with unleavened bread and wild lettuce:”** — RABANUS. He is unclean in soul who is defiled by diabolical deceit through the worship of idols and the enormity of sins. He is on a journey far off who, hearing the word of salvation, chooses to forsake idols and receive the faith, but has not yet come to baptism, by which one enters the Church, that is, Jerusalem, the city of peace, where are the house and the holy of holies. For the flesh of the lamb is commanded to be eaten in one house, because outside the Church it is not lawful to eat the body of Christ. The Gentile people therefore (because it could not keep the first Pasch according to the law), in the second month, that is, in the time of grace, now cleansed from all uncleanness of sins and restored to the house, where it is lawful to make the Phase, eats the lamb at the evening of the world with unleavened bread and wild lettuce.
**“WITH UNLEAVENED BREAD”** — He eats unleavened bread who does right works without the corruption of vainglory, and the commandments of mercy without admixture of sin.
**“WILD”** — Because when we receive the body of Christ we ought to be pricked with compunction for sins, that the bitterness of penance may wipe away the love of a perverse life.
9.12:
**“They shall not leave any thing thereof until morning,”** — of the resurrection
**“ALL THE CEREMONIES”** — Whatever was commanded historically in the law in the celebration of the Pasch, the Church observes spiritually.
**“THEY SHALL OBSERVE”** — Because his sayings are to be carefully examined, that they may be penetrated in the present life by understanding and working.
9.13: **“SHALL BE CUT OFF”** — He instructs those who were under the law by threatening, lest they neglect to observe the time of the Pasch. He admonishes us also to make the spiritual Pasch in its time, of which Paul says: "Behold, now is the acceptable time" etc. Because whoever has not celebrated with worthy faith the redemption of the human race, which was made by the immolation of the true lamb, and has not turned his life to better things, and has not passed over from vices to virtues in the time of this mortality, will have no part in the glory of the resurrection to be given at the end to the true worshippers of Christ, but will be cut off from the fellowship of the saints.
9.14: **“THE SOJOURNER”** — He shows that there is no respect of persons with God. For whoever, converted to the catholic faith and washed with the baptism of Christ, has entered the unity of the Church can share in the ecclesiastical mysteries.
9.15:
**“A CLOUD”** — ISIDORE. Christ is the pillar, who is upright and firm and props up our weakness, shining by night, not shining by day, that they who see not may see, and they who see may become blind. The sacrament of Christ too is manifest as in the day, in the flesh, as in a cloud; but in the judgment as in the terror of the night. Because then there will be great tribulation, like fire, and it will give light to the just and burn the unjust.
**“MYSTICALLY”** — The incarnation of Christ, whose clemency protects the tabernacle of the Church, whose goodness orders its state, whose prudence directs its passage on the way of this world.
**“GREGORY”** — In the fire, terror; in the cloud, the gentle charm of vision. The day is the life of the just, the night that of the sinner. Whence: You were heretofore darkness, but now light in the Lord. In the day therefore the pillar is shown by a cloud, in the night by fire, because God will appear gentle to the just, terrible to the unjust. These, coming in the judgment, he will soothe with the mildness of gentleness; those he will terrify with the justice of strictness. The pillar of cloud went before the people in the desert, shining with the splendour of fire not in the day but in the night, because Christ, by the example of his conversation, giving leadership to those who follow, shone with no light to those who trust in their own justice, but shone with the fire of his love on those who acknowledge the darkness of their sins.
9.18: **“At the commandment of the Lord”** — at the sign, namely, of the cloud for standing or moving, by which God commanded them either to stand or to move
9.19: **“And if it was so that it continued over it a long time, the children of Israel kept the watches of the Lord,”** — keeping, namely, the precept of the Lord
9.22: **“But if for two days or a month”** — others: But if for two days or a month
9.23: **“BY THE WORD”** — The signification of the cloud, which was the sign of the divine will, like the voice of one speaking.

10.2: **“Make thee two trumpets of beaten silver, wherewith thou mayest call together the multitude when the camp is to be removed.”** — MAKE THEE TWO TRUMPETS etc. ISIDORE. And a little after: When a broken sound shall ring out, the camps shall move etc. By two trumpets the army is led, because by the two Testaments or the two precepts of charity the people is called out to the readiness of faith. These are commanded to be made of silver, that the words of preachers may shine with the brightness of eloquence and confound the mind of the hearers by no obscurity of their own. And they are beaten, because those who preach the life to come must grow through the blows of present tribulations. And well is it said: When a broken sound shall ring out, the camps shall move. Because when a finer and more detailed preaching is handled, the minds of the hearers are roused more ardently to the struggles of temptations.
10.4: **“IF THOU SOUND BUT ONCE”** — RABANUS. To sound the trumpets once is to put forth the word of doctrine according to the unity of faith and the concord of the catholic sense. At this sound the princes and the heads of the multitude ought to come together, so that those who preside over the rest, united in faith and love, may faithfully confer about their own salvation and that of their people, and show an example of peace and concord; lest there be among them "envying and contention", but that "all speak the same thing in the same mind and in the same judgment".
10.5: **“THE FIRST”** — To whom, namely, the light of faith first shone. When, therefore, the preachers of the Gospel were ordained, it is said to them first: Go ye not into the way of the Gentiles, but go ye rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel; to whom Christ himself preached the Gospel in person. But after the resurrection, appearing to the disciples, he says: Going therefore teach ye all nations etc. The tribe of Juda therefore, with the others who dwelt with it on the east, first moved camp; then the others according to their order. Because the first Church had first to be built in Judea, and afterward the nations from all the peoples of the world called to the faith.
10.7: **“BUT WHEN TO BE GATHERED TOGETHER”** — RABANUS. In the calling together of the people, the sound of the trumpets is commanded to be plain and not broken, because he who preaches the word of faith to a multitude ought to speak simply and openly, so that many may understand and be edified; lest, if he preaches obscurely and strangely, the hearers go away empty. Whence Paul: Brethren, if I come to you speaking with tongues, what shall I profit you, unless I speak to you either in revelation, or in knowledge, or in prophecy, or in doctrine? etc. And a little after: "Let all things be done to edification." For a word too obscure or ambiguous ought to be said in the manner of the common people, so that it may be understood even by the unlearned. For what does correctness of speech profit, if it does not edify the hearers? For we speak to no purpose if we are not understood by those for whose sake we speak. He therefore who teaches should avoid all words that do not teach; and if instead of them he can say correct words that are understood, let him rather choose those. But if there are none, or they do not occur at the moment, let him use less correct words, provided the matters are correctly taught and learned. And not only in private conversations, but still more when the people is called together. And the best manner of learning is that by which it comes about that he who hears hears the truth and understands it; and it is the mark of a good disposition to love the truth in words, not the words. For what does a golden key profit if it does not open? For we seek nothing but that what is shut may lie open.
10.8:
**“THE SONS OF AARON”** — The preachers, namely, preach the word of God and show the way of justice to the hearers, that they may set the step of good work in the path of God's commandments and flee the road of the wicked.
**“the priests shall sound the trumpets:”** — because it is proper to priests to preach the Gospel
10.9:
**“If you go forth to war”** — the care of earthly things, namely, being cast away
**“out of your land against the enemies”** — the demons
**“YOU SHALL SOUND”** — By rousing, namely, those subject to them to penance and to the compunction of tears, and by provoking the hearts of the hearers to implore the mercy of God.
**“aloud with the trumpets, and there shall be a remembrance of you before the Lord your God, that you may be delivered out of the hands”** — the power
**“of your enemies.”** — of the demons
10.10: **“IF AT ANY TIME YOU SHALL HAVE A BANQUET”** — RABANUS. Note that he commanded the trumpets to be sounded in adversity and in prosperity, because every time is fitting for the word of God. For now it is to be read, now to be sung to God; now it is fitting to pray, now to teach, now to exhort, now to rebuke; because the speech of teachers is to be tempered according to the quality of the hearers. Whence: "I will bless the Lord at all times, his praise shall be always in my mouth." And elsewhere: "Preach the word, be instant in season, out of season" etc.
10.11: **“THE SECOND YEAR, IN THE SECOND MONTH, THE TWENTIETH DAY OF THE MONTH”** — JEROME. At the twelfth station the children of Israel came into the desert of Sinai, on the forty-seventh day from their going out of Egypt. Whence in Exodus: In the third month of the departure of the children of Israel out of Egypt, on this day they came into the wilderness of Sinai. For departing out of Raphidim, they came into the desert of Sinai, and they camped in the wilderness, and Moses went up to God. And the Lord called unto him from the mountain etc. And again: Go, he says, to the people, and sanctify them today and tomorrow, and let them wash their garments, and let them be ready against the third day etc. Let us reckon the number, and we shall find that the law was given on mount Sinai on the fiftieth day of the departure; whence also the solemnity of Pentecost is celebrated, and the sacrament of the Gospel is completed by the descent of the Holy Ghost. At this station are described the middle part of Exodus, the whole of Leviticus, and no small precepts of Numbers, and the distribution of the people by each tribe, and the offering of the princes. And Sinai is interpreted "of the bramble", not one, as above in the wilderness of Sin, but many; so that there is the beginning, here the perfection; there a single number, here a manifold. For it is one thing to possess one grace, another to possess all. Israel therefore, after the familiar speech with the Lord, having stayed by mount Sinai one year and four days, went out with a wonderful ordering of the camps into the wilderness of Pharan, which is interpreted "wild ass" or "wildness"; and there it gave way to the evil beast, loathing the heavenly bread and desiring the flesh of the Egyptians, when a sudden fire devoured many, and at the intercession of Moses the devouring flame was swallowed up by the ground. Then they receive quails and devour them to nausea. Seventy elders are chosen, and go to the door of the tabernacle; two remain, Eldad and Medad, not neglectful of the command, but bowed down by humility, judging themselves unworthy of the honour; whence also, though absent, they prophesy. And when the people was filled, while the meat was yet in their mouth, "the wrath of God came upon them, and he slew the fat ones amongst them, and brought down the chosen men of Israel", that they might not run swiftly to evil. Whence the place was called "the graves of lust", or according to the Septuagint, "of the memory of desire". From these we are taught, we who leave worldly knowledge and have despised the Egyptian fleshpots, that we ought not to murmur against the heavenly bread of Scripture, nor seek the poisons of the Egyptians, who are of great flesh, but the simple food of manna. But if we wish to seek them again, we shall devour to nausea, and at once be tormented by the fire of the Lord, and our desire will be turned into tombs, so that we are whited sepulchres, which outwardly appear to men beautiful, but within are full of dead men's bones and of all filthiness.
10.12:
**“And the children of Israel marched by their troops from the desert of Sinai,”** — of the bramble
**“and the cloud rested in the wilderness of Pharan.”** — wild ass, or wildness
10.13: **“And the first moved their camp according to the commandment of the Lord by the hand”** — or: by the hand
10.20: **“And in the tribe of Gad, the prince was Helisaphat”** — others: Eliasaph
10.27: **“And in the tribe of the sons of Nephtali, the prince was Achira”** — elsewhere: Ahira
10.29: **“And Moses said to Eliab”** — others: Hobab
10.31: **“WE ARE GOING TOWARDS THE PLACE WHICH THE LORD WILL GIVE”** — GREGORY. Often we can better persuade the proud to useful things if we say that their progress will profit us rather than them, if we ask that their bettering be bestowed on us rather than on them. For the pride of such a one is easily bent to good if his bending is believed to profit others. Whence Moses, who was going on with God ruling him and the pillar leading, when he wished to lead his kinsman out of the conversation of the Gentiles and bring him under the dominion of God, said: We are going towards the place which the Lord will give us etc. And when he had answered: I will not go with thee etc., he at once added: Do not leave us: for thou knowest in what places we should encamp in the wilderness etc. It was not ignorance of the way that straitened the mind of Moses, which the knowledge of the Godhead had opened out to the knowledge of prophecy, whom the pillar and the divine converse instructed. But the provident man, speaking to a proud hearer, asked for comfort that he might give it; he sought a guide on the way for one whose guide he might become to life. He so acted, then, that the proud hearer might be the more devoted to the voice persuading him to better things, the more he was thought necessary; and from the very place where he believed he was going before his exhorter, he might bow to the words of the one exhorting.
10.33:
**“So they marched from the mount of the Lord three days' journey,”** — by the faith of the Trinity, showing the way of truth in three times
**“and the ark of the covenant”** — the incarnation of Christ
**“AND THE ARK OF THE COVENANT”** — RABANUS. The ark of the covenant of the Lord goes before the children of Israel for three days, providing places for the camps, because the incarnation of the Lord directs the journey of the present life for the elect from the beginning of the world, and truly gives leadership to the holy land; which before led the fathers of the Old Testament in figure, and now in truth shows us the way of justice. The three days' journey, therefore, is the faith of the holy Trinity. In three times, before the law, under the law, under grace, it shows the path of truth and justice to those who follow.
10.34: **“THE CLOUD ALSO”** — The divine protection, which by the grace of the Holy Ghost defends the elect from the beginning of the world and guards them for the rest to come.
10.35: **“AND WHEN IT WAS LIFTED UP”** — By the example of Moses the rulers of the people are called on always carefully to commend the flock entrusted to them to the Lord at the beginning of the work and at its completion, that he may protect his own sheep and drive back the enemies.

11.1: **“THE MURMURING OF THE PEOPLE”** — RABANUS. The fire of the Lord, kindled, devours the murmuring people, because the fire of the Lord's great vengeance will torment in the future those who, with a tongue set on fire by hell, murmur or detract. Whence it is said by Wisdom: "The whisperer and the double-tongued is accursed." The fire devours the uttermost part of the camp, namely the end of present actions. Whence: "The Lord shall judge the ends of the earth." But he who persists uncorrected until death shall be burned with perpetual punishment both in soul and in body.
11.4: **“For a mixt multitude of people, that came up with them, burned with desire, sitting and weeping, the children of Israel also being joined with them, and said: Who shall give us flesh to eat?”** — carnal works, to be boiled down by the labours of tribulations that are seen
11.5:
**“We remember the fish that we ate in Egypt free cost: the cucumbers come into our mind, and the melons,”** — earthly sweetnesses
**“and the leeks”** — the difficulties of the present life, which is passed not without grief, and yet is loved with tears
**“THE MELONS AND THE LEEKS”** — GREGORY. The minds of the carnal, for love of the world, are ready to bear certain hard things as though they were soft and delightful. While in this life they strive to lay hold of the heights of things, the Lord commands a ceasing from the labours of the world and persuades them to the sweetness of rest; and yet the mad mind of the wicked rejoices more to pursue harsh things carnally than to hold soft things spiritually. It is fed more by the bitterness of weariness than by the sweetness of rest. So the Israelites, while they received the refreshment of manna from above, desired from Egypt the fleshpots, melons, leeks and onions. For does not the manna signify grace of most sweet savour, given from above for the refreshment of the inner life to those who are well at leisure? The fleshpots, carnal works, to be boiled down by the labours of tribulations that are seen, as by fires. The melons, earthly sweetnesses. The leeks and onions, which are eaten with tears, the difficulty of the present life, which is passed not without grief and is loved with tears. Forsaking the manna, therefore, they sought leeks and onions with melons and flesh, because perverse minds despise the sweet gifts of grace given through rest, and for carnal pleasures covet the laborious journeys of this life, full even of tears. They scorn to have that wherein they may rejoice spiritually, and with longing seek that wherein they may groan carnally.
11.16:
**“And the Lord said to Moses: Gather unto me seventy men”** — SEPTUAGINT: chosen by tongues
