**“of the ancients of Israel, whom thou knowest to be ancients”** — by gravity of manners
**“GATHER UNTO ME SEVENTY MEN OF THE ANCIENTS OF ISRAEL”** — GREGORY. Just as those are commonly called young who are weighed down by no gravity of counsel, so Scripture calls those old, not who are ripe by length of time alone, but by gravity of manners. Whence: "Venerable old age is not that of long time, nor counted by the number of years: but the understanding of a man is grey hairs. And a spotless life is old age." Hence it is said to Moses: Gather unto me seventy men of the ancients of Israel, whom thou knowest to be ancients of the people. In which words old age of heart is noted, since such old men are commanded to be chosen as are known. For if old age of body were sought, they could be known by as many as could see them. But when it is said, whom thou knowest to be ancients of the people, it is plain that old age of mind, not of body, is chosen.
11.17:
**“That I may come down”** — in the cloud of the flesh
**“and speak with thee: and I will take of the spirit”** — the Holy one, namely, who is in thee by grace etc.
**“THAT I MAY COME DOWN”** — ISIDORE. At the thirteenth station the Spirit came down upon seventy chosen men, and the Lord came down from the cloud and took of the Spirit that was upon Moses, and put it upon the seventy men. For when Christ came down in the cloud of the flesh, the grace of the Holy Ghost was poured out through faith upon the peoples, upon the chosen out of the seventy nations, and there came upon all that gift of heavenly power which had once been in Moses and the prophets.
**“that they may bear with thee the burden of the people, and thou mayest not be burthened alone.”** — AND I WILL TAKE OF. AUGUSTINE. Another text: And I will take of the spirit which is in thee, and will put it upon them, and they shall bear with thee the onset of the people, and thou shalt not carry them alone, etc. Many Latins did not translate as it is in the Greek, but said: I will take of thy spirit which is in thee, and will put it upon them, or will put it in them; and they made the sense laborious to understand. For it may be thought to be said of the man's own spirit, by which human nature is completed when the body is joined to it, which consists of body and spirit, which they also call the soul. Whence Paul: What man knoweth the things of a man, but the spirit of a man that is in him? So the things also that are of God no man knoweth, but the Spirit of God. And what he then adds: Now we have received not the spirit of this world, but the Spirit that is of God, shows that the Spirit of God is other, of whom the spirit of man is made partaker by the grace of God. Although (as others have interpreted) the Spirit of God can also be understood when it is said, of thy spirit which is in thee, because he who is of God becomes ours also when we receive him; as it was said of John: "In the spirit and power of Elias." For the soul of Elias had not been rolled back into him. But if certain heretics think so, what do they say to that which is written: The spirit of Elias hath rested upon Eliseus, when he already had his own soul, unless that it is said of the Spirit of God, so that he worked through the one such things as he worked through Elias, not withdrawing from the one in order to fill the other, nor, being divided, less in the one so that he could be in the other? For it is God who can be as great, or whole, in all in whom he has willed to be through that grace. But now, since it is written: And I will take of the spirit which is upon thee, and it is not said, of thy spirit, it is more easily resolved; because we understand that he meant to signify nothing else than that they too would have help from the same Spirit of grace from whom Moses had it, so that these also might have as much as God willed, not so that Moses should therefore have less.
11.21: **“SIX HUNDRED THOUSAND”** — AUGUSTINE. Another text: Six hundred thousand footmen, among whom I am, and thou hast said: I will give them flesh, etc. It is asked whether Moses said this distrusting or inquiring. But if we suppose he said it distrusting, it is asked why the Lord did not reproach him for it, as he did at the rock from which the water flowed, where he seems to have doubted of the power of the Lord. But if we say he inquired the manner in which it should be done, the Lord's answer, in which it is said: Is the hand of the Lord unable?, seems to be as of one reproving him for not having believed. But I think it better understood that the Lord so answered as one who would not tell the manner he was asking, but rather show his power by the deed itself. For it could also have been objected by cavillers against Mary when she said: How shall this be done, because I know not man?, that she believed less, though she asked the manner and did not doubt of the power of God. But what was answered her: The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow thee, might also have been answered as here: Is anything impossible to the Holy Ghost, who shall come upon thee?, as if the same sense were kept. But Zachary, saying such things, is charged with unbelief and punished with the penalty of his voice stopped. For God judges not of words but of hearts; otherwise Moses could have been excused, were there not a clear sentence of God against him that he said such things distrusting: Hear, ye unbelievers. Can we bring you forth water out of this rock? And when Moses had lifted up his hand, he struck the rock twice with the rod, etc. For this he took that rod with which he had done so many miracles, and struck the rock with it, and thence obtained the effect of the accustomed power. The words therefore in which he says: Can we bring you forth water out of this rock? could be taken as though it were said: Surely out of this rock, according to your unbelief, water cannot be brought forth; so that then by striking it might be shown that what they in their unbelief did not believe could be done by God. Especially since he had said: Hear, ye unbelievers. But God, who is the inspector of the heart, showed with what mind they were said. For the Scripture says: Because you have not believed me, to sanctify me before the children of Israel, etc. And by this Moses is understood to have spoken as though he struck at uncertainty, so that if the effect did not follow, he might be thought to have foretold this when he said: Can we bring you forth water out of this rock?; which would have lain wholly hidden in his mind, had not the sentence of God betrayed it. Contrariwise, therefore, we ought to understand here that the words of Moses about the promised flesh were those of one asking how it should be done, not of one distrusting, since no sentence of God followed to punish, but rather one to teach.
11.22: **“Shall then a multitude of sheep and oxen be killed”** — but he seeks the manner; he does not distrust
11.24:
**“Moses therefore came, and told the people the words of the Lord,”** — SEPTUAGINT: Moses went out to the people and spoke the words of the Lord. For he is within while he is taught by him; when he speaks to the crowds, he is shown to go out of doors.
**“MOSES THEREFORE CAME”** — ORIGEN. Another text: Moses, it says, went out to the people, and spoke the words of the Lord. While Moses hears the words of God and is taught by him, he is within, and abides in the inner and secret places. But when he speaks to the crowds and ministers to the people, he who cannot stand within is said to go out of doors. For every teacher of the Church, if he treats of the deeper mysteries and brings forth the hidden things of wisdom among the perfect, is within. But when he speaks to the crowds the things that profit those who are without, and which the common people can hear, he goes out of doors and speaks to the people the words of God. Paul was within when he said: We speak wisdom among the perfect, etc. Going forth to the people he says: "Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth", and: "He that stole, let him now steal no more", and the like, etc.
11.25:
**“TAKING AWAY OF THE SPIRIT”** — It is not to be understood as though he cut a material and bodily substance into seventy portions and gave a particle to each. For it is impious to understand this of the nature of the Holy Ghost. But Moses and the Spirit that was in him were as a lamp of most bright light, from which God kindled seventy, to whom the splendour of the principal light came, and its source suffered no loss from the drawing off.
**“And when the spirit had rested on them”** — for purity of heart and capacity of understanding
**“HAD RESTED”** — ORIGEN. And the spirit rested upon them, and they all prophesied, etc. The Spirit is not read to have rested save in the saints. For he rests in those who are clean of heart, who purify their souls from sin. Just as he does not dwell in a body subject to sins, even if he once dwelt there. For he cannot suffer the fellowship of evil. And it is certain that in the time of sin an evil spirit is in the heart of each, and plays its part. When place is given it through evil thoughts and concupiscences, the Holy Ghost, saddened (so to speak), is put to flight. Whence: "Grieve not the Holy Spirit of God, whereby you are sealed" etc. Sinning, therefore, we grieve the Holy Ghost. Doing well, we prepare him rest. What, therefore, he says of the seventy elders, that the Spirit rested in them, set forth the praise of their life and their virtues.
**“they prophesied”** — he sets forth the praise of their life
**“ORIGEN”** — And the Spirit rested in them, or upon them, and they prophesied, etc. The Spirit works continually and suffers no idleness where worthy matter for working is supplied. In all, therefore, who prophesied the Spirit rested, but not as in the Saviour, for which reason it is said of him: There shall come forth a rod out of the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise up out of his root, and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and of understanding, etc. For see that upon no other is the Spirit of the Lord described to have rested with this sevenfold virtue; by which the substance of the divine Spirit (since it could not be by one name) is explained by divers words, and is prophesied to rest upon him. Hence John also says: He who sent me to baptize with water said to me: He upon whom thou shalt see the Spirit of God descending, and remaining upon him, he it is. For he added "and remaining upon him", that this might be a sign in the Saviour which could not be shown in another. For of him alone was it said: Who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth. For because he alone is the one who did no sin, therefore in him alone the Spirit remained and abode. It is clear therefore that all the rest were under sin, nor is it fitting that we should say the Spirit remained in them in the time of sin. For Moses himself, when he had already received the Spirit, bears witness that he sinned, when he said: Hear, ye unbelievers. Can we bring forth water for you out of this rock? For in these words he did not sanctify God, that is, he did not trust in the power of God. When therefore he spoke these things, he spoke not by the Holy Ghost but by the spirit of sin. It is certain therefore that the other prophets at times had the Spirit of God, at times had not. Hence David also says: "And take not thy spirit from me", in which he shows that it can be taken away. But in what follows he asks for it again as taken away: "Restore unto me the joy of thy salvation, and strengthen me with a perfect spirit." No one says, either, that Solomon judged judgments, or built the temple to the Lord, otherwise than in the Holy Ghost; or again that in the Holy Ghost he made temples to demons, or bent his side to impious women. The prophet Abdo too was sent by the Lord to Bethel, and spoke the words of the Lord in the Spirit of God; yet not in the same Spirit did he transgress the command of the Lord, by which he was forbidden to eat bread in Bethel; and therefore he was slain by a lion. But I (though I do not pronounce it in every case) think there are also certain common doings of men which, though they are not without sin, yet do not seem worthy that the Holy Ghost should be present in them; as lawful marriages are indeed without sin, yet when conjugal acts are done the Holy Ghost is not given, even if a prophet performs them. For there are many other things in which human strength alone suffices, and the matter neither needs nor befits the presence of the Holy Ghost.
11.26: **“THERE REMAINED”** — Not by neglect of the Lord's command, but by the devotion of humility, judging themselves unworthy of receiving so great a gift; therefore God, the judge of hearts, judged them worthy and showed them so.
11.29:
**“But he said: Why hast thou emulation for me? O that all the people might prophesy,”** — He willed all to prophesy who did not grudge the good he had.
**“and that the Lord would give them his spirit!”** — WHY, HE SAITH, HAST THOU EMULATION FOR ME, etc. GREGORY. The loving mind of pastors, because it seeks not its own glory but the Author's, wishes to be helped by all in what it does. For the faithful preacher wishes, if it could be, that the truth which he alone is not sufficient to speak should sound from the mouths of all. Whence when Josue wished to withstand the two who remained in the camp and prophesied, it is said to him by Moses: Why hast thou emulation for me? O that all the people might prophesy, and that he would give them his spirit! For he willed all to prophesy who did not grudge others the good he had.
11.32: **“A MULTITUDE OF QUAILS”** — RABANUS. The carnal people of the Jews, having taken the heavenly food, desired flesh; but God so tempered the judgment as to punish the wicked, and not to deny nourishment to the frail, and in the very grant to hint at something spiritual. For he gave them to eat not of wild beasts, not of four-footed or earthly animals, but of birds, that they might learn to desire heavenly things rather than earthly, spiritual rather than bodily. For the nature of birds came forth from the waters, but acquires for itself a dwelling in the air. Those therefore who eat birds are warned to lift the heart from the lowest things to the highest, that though they live in earthly bodies, they may always seek heavenly things in mind, according to that of the Apostle: Walking in the flesh, we do not war according to the flesh. "But our conversation is in heaven."
11.34:
**“THE GRAVES OF LUST”** — ISIDORE. The thirteenth station is at the graves of lust, where the people, loathing the heavenly bread, desired the flesh of Egypt, and a sudden fire devoured many. By which we are taught, we who leave the conversation of the world and the Egyptian fleshpots, that is, the heats of carnal desires, not to murmur against the heavenly bread, nor seek the poisons of the Egyptians, who are of great flesh, but the simple food of manna; that is, that we lead a pure and heavenly life. For if, after receiving the angelic manna, which is the heavenly life or doctrine, we again seek the flesh of Egypt, that is, the carnal pleasures of the world, and the nausea of former lust, we shall at once be tormented by the fire of the Lord, and our desire will be turned into tombs, so that we are whited sepulchres, which outwardly appear beautiful, but within are full of dead men's bones and of all filthiness.
**“And that place was called, The graves of lust: for there they buried the people that had lusted. And departing from the graves of lust, they came unto Haseroth, and abode there.”** — THEY CAME UNTO HASEROTH, etc. JEROME. The fourteenth station is in the wilderness of Pharan, which is turned "courts". In this Aaron and Mary murmur against Moses because of the Ethiopian woman. And mark this, prudent reader, that after virtue was completed in the number twelve (because Israel grew proud and at the graves of lust desired the flesh of Egypt), it lays the foundation again and enters the courts, that is, the forecourts, of virtue; showing us that those who stand can fall, and those who have fallen can rise again. For Jesus is set for the fall and for the resurrection of many. Who says by the Prophet: Shall not he that falleth rise again?
**“ISIDORE”** — The fourteenth station is in the wilderness of Haseroth. In this Aaron and Mary offended by detracting from their brother because he had taken a foreign wife; and at once Mary, struck with leprosy, broke out white; because the priestly people, disparaging the Church gathered from the Gentiles before Christ the Saviour, is covered with the leprosy of sin. Nor does it return to the tabernacle of God until the fulness of the Gentiles has come in. For then it will receive its former health, when the knowledge of the sevenfold Spirit has brought it back to pardon.

12.1:
**“And Mary spoke”** — Mary
**“and Aaron took”** — the priestly people, the carnal priesthood
**“against Moses,”** — Christ
**“because of his wife the Ethiopian,”**
• the Church gathered from the Gentiles
• AND MARY SPOKE, etc. ORIGEN. Mary is the Jewish people; Moses is the law of the Lord, which passes into marriage with the Ethiopian, namely the Church gathered from the Gentiles. This the spiritual law took to wife, and therefore Mary, that is the Synagogue, is indignant and detracts together with Aaron, namely with the priests and Pharisees. That people therefore disparages her to this day, and she seems base to it, because she does not teach among us circumcision of the flesh, nor the keeping of the sabbath, nor of the new moon, nor sacrifices of blood, but circumcision of the heart and rest from sinning, and feast days "with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth", and sacrifices of praise, and the slaying of victims not of cattle but of vices. Of these things, therefore, God judges, and confirms the marriage of the Ethiopian, and allows Moses to dwell gladly with her; he casts Mary out of the camp and makes her afar off, that is, far from the tabernacle of the testimony, with whom Aaron is cast out, and she herself is made leprous. Look upon that people; see how great a leprosy of sin is in it, how great a darkness of understanding, how great a foulness of observance. But this leprosy is not perpetual. For when the week has begun to be fulfilled, she will be called back to the camp. For at the end of the world, when the fulness of the Gentiles has come in, all Israel shall be saved, and the leprosy of Mary shall cease. For she will recover the beauty of faith and receive the splendour of the knowledge of Christ, and her countenance will be restored, when there shall be one fold and one shepherd.
• MYSTICALLY, not only the Jews but the heretics who do not receive the law and the prophets detract from Moses. They charge him also with being a murderer, because he slew the Egyptian, and with blasphemous mouth patch together many other things against the other prophets too. Therefore they are leprous in soul, and are cast out of the Church of God. Or: the heretics who detract from Moses. Or: churchmen who detract from their neighbours.
**“ORIGEN”**
• Because Aaron and Mary detracted from Moses, they were rebuked, and Mary was even made leprous. For so great was the care of correction that while Mary was in her leprosy for a week, the people of God did not make its journey to the land of promise, nor was the tabernacle of the testimony moved. In which I am warned not to detract from a brother, not to disparage, not only the saints, but any neighbours whatever. Whence: Sitting thou didst speak against thy brother, and didst lay a scandal against thy mother's son. And elsewhere: The man that in private detracted his neighbour, him did I persecute. By these words of divine Scripture, as by certain swords sharp on both sides, the vice of slander and disparagement is cut away. For leprosy follows detractors and evil-speakers.
• Everyone too who understands the writings of Moses ill, and receives the spiritual law carnally, detracts from him; he also who thinks carnally of the words of the spirit.
**“THE ETHIOPIAN”** — AUGUSTINE. Of the Ethiopian wife of Moses it is asked whether she is the daughter of Jethro, or whether he married another, or took another besides. But it is credible that she was the same; for she was of the Madianites, who in Paralipomenon are called Ethiopians, when Josaphat fought against them. For in those places the people of Israel is said to have pursued them, where the Madianites dwell, who are now called Saracens; but now hardly anyone calls them Ethiopians, as the names of places and peoples are commonly changed by age.
12.8:
**“For I speak to him mouth to mouth: and plainly, and not by riddles and figures doth he see the Lord. Why then were you not afraid to speak ill of my servant Moses?”**
• IF THERE BE etc. ORIGEN. Hear how great a benefit detractors confer. For we never find the Lord to have praised Moses so much as now, when he is detracted from. Whence: If there be among you a prophet of the Lord, I will make myself known to him in visions, and I will speak to him in dreams; not so with my servant Moses, etc. See what the detractors brought upon themselves, what upon him: shame for themselves, praise for him; leprosy for themselves, splendour and glory for him. Yet before he took the Ethiopian, it is not written that God spoke to him in open sight and not in a riddle. When she had been taken, God says: Mouth to mouth will I speak to him, in open sight and not in a riddle. For when Moses is joined to our Ethiopian, the law of God is now known not in figure as before, but in the very appearance of truth. And the things that were before signified in a riddle are now fulfilled in truth. Whence: We know that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all in Moses were baptized, in the cloud and in the sea, etc. You see how Paul resolves the riddles of the law and teaches the appearances of the riddles, saying (because the rock was in a riddle with Moses before he was joined to the Ethiopian) that now in open sight the rock is Christ. For now God speaks mouth to mouth through the law. Before, baptism was in a riddle in the cloud and in the sea; now in open sight it is of regeneration, in water and the Spirit. Then manna was food in a riddle; but now in open sight the flesh of the Word of God is meat indeed. Now therefore Moses, joined to the Ethiopian, whether he to us or God to him, speaks not in a riddle but in open sight.
• DOTH HE SEE THE LORD, etc. Another text: And he sees the glory of the Lord. Moses saw the glory of the Lord when the Lord was transfigured on the mount, and Moses was present with Elias and talked with him. Therefore he rightly adds: Why were you not afraid to speak ill of my servant Moses? This is said to those who seem to receive the Gospel, but disparage Moses. And they are deservedly reproved, because though they learn through the Gospel that Moses with Elias saw the glory of the Lord, they dare to disparage the law and the prophets. Let us not detract from the law, then, nor be hearers only, but doers, that we may be glorified with Moses. They therefore prepare matter for disparaging Moses who do not expound the law spiritually. For those who hear the rite of sacrifices, the keeping of sabbaths or the like recited in the Church are offended, and say: What do Jewish precepts profit us? Let the Jews look to them. Pains must therefore be taken that the law be understood and explained spiritually, lest Moses be disparaged by the unskilled. But let us turn to the Lord, that he may take from us the veil of the letter, lest the face of Moses seem misshapen to us, but comely and glorious; so that we may not only not slander him, but glorify him for the greatness of his meanings.
12.9: **“And being angry”** — God is angry with detractors
12.10:
**“The cloud also that was over the tabernacle departed: and behold Mary”** — the Jewish people
**“appeared white”** — the cloud, that is, the visitation of God, departing
**“THE CLOUD ALSO DEPARTED”** — ORIGEN. And the cloud departed from the tabernacle, etc. The cloud departed before Mary was filled with leprosy, to show that if the grace of the Holy Ghost is in anyone and he slanders and detracts, it departs from him after the slander, and his soul is filled with leprosy. For that people once had in itself the glory of God. Allegorically. But after they stretched out the tongues of blasphemers, or of blasphemy, against the true Moses, that is, Christ, the cloud departed from them and passed over to us on the high mountain, when the Saviour was transfigured, and a bright cloud overshadowed the disciples, and a voice out of the cloud said: This is my beloved Son, etc. After this, therefore, Mary was made leprous as snow. While the cloud was present she was not leprous; for while the visitation of God was in that people, it was not leprous.
**“MORALLY”** — Let us also fear lest perhaps we put this cloud to flight from us by thinking evil, speaking evil, doing evil, and the leprosy of sin appear in us.
**“AND WHEN HE HAD LOOKED”** — ORIGEN. Another text: And Aaron looked upon Mary, and behold Mary was leprous, etc. He wishes in this to show that that people was formed in the womb of its mother the Synagogue, yet could not come to a whole birth. As an abortion is an imperfect birth, so that people was placed for some time within the womb of its mother, that is, the institution of the Synagogue. But with sins intervening it could not be wholly formed and quickened. Therefore they were cast off, sin consuming (as he says) the half of her flesh. Yet an abortion is called good, not absolutely, but sometimes when compared with others. Whence Ecclesiastes: An abortion is better than he who walks in vanity. And elsewhere he says the dead are better than the living. If you compare an abortion with these, you would say it is good above both. But he names no other living than those of whom it is said: "Surely all things are vanity: every man living." For not all life is in vanity, but that which is according to the flesh, and according to errors and pleasures. Above this is every man who is dead to this life and says: "But the world is crucified to me, and I to the world." Of whom it is said: You are dead therefore with Christ, etc. Above these the abortion is said to be, because though it seems to have come in the flesh, yet it took up no beginnings of vanity. Another seems better even than this, of whom Ecclesiastes says: And best of all above these is he who is not yet born; that is, who has not come into life even to the closing of the fleshly womb and to bodily birth. But when Ecclesiastes says: I praised all the dead rather than the living, and those who live until now, he plainly shows that he calls those better who are dead to the world, and those lower who are alive to the world. But according to the letter the dead are not more to be praised than the living. For one is praised for what he has done of good will. But common death comes to no one from his will. How then is anyone praised for what he suffers against his purpose? Otherwise Pharao, drowned in the sea, would be praised above Moses, who escaped, and the Egyptians above the people of the Lord, which passed over dryshod. If therefore thou hast renounced the world, if thou hast cast off vices, if thou art not moved to sin, thou shalt be as one dead. The death of life is praiseworthy; for no one is praised for the common death which comes from the law of nature. And Paul, knowing that among the orders spoken of above there is an abortion, says of himself: And last of all, as by one born out of due time, he was seen also by me; numbering himself above the living and above the dead, yet after those who are not yet born. Mary therefore was as an abortion; for that people could not be formed to perfection in the law. Whence: The law brought nobody to perfection. For the Apostle calls back certain who had fallen from faith and been turned as it were into an abortion to the institutions of a perfect birth: "My little children, of whom I am in labour again, until Christ be formed in you" etc.
12.12: **“Let her not be as one dead, and as an abortive that is cast forth from the mother's womb. Lo, now one half of her flesh is consumed with the leprosy.”** — that is: the leprosy has devoured
12.13: **“AND HE CRIED”** — ORIGEN. Another text: And Moses cried out to the Lord, saying: Lord, I beseech thee, heal her, etc. Who ought to pray for the health of his people but Moses? Perhaps this was what he spoke of with the Lord on the mount of the transfiguration, asking that when the fulness of the Gentiles had come in, all Israel might be saved.
12.14:
**“And the Lord answered him: If her father had spitten upon her face, ought she not to have been for seven days at least”** — elsewhere: for seven days
**“covered with blushing? Let her be separated seven days”** — the week of this world
**“without the camp,”** — the Church
**“HAD SPITTEN”** — To be spat upon in the face is a sign of repudiation. Whence the next of kin who refuses the marriage has his shoe taken off and is spat upon in the face. Hence Isaias: All nations are as a drop of a bucket, and are counted as spittle. It is shown, therefore, that that people too, like the other nations which are counted as spittle, is cast off. For if you consider its former honour, the pontifical order, the insignia of the priests, the Levitical mysteries, the majesty of the temple, and their having fellowship on earth with heavenly things, what an honour that was, what a glory! But now they shudder in great disgrace, without temple, without altar, without sacrifice, without prophets, without priesthood, without heavenly visitation. Whence it is plain that the father, spitting, covered their faces with ignominy. They are separated therefore seven days without the camp, that is, through the week of this world. For in the week of days the substances of the whole visible creation appear to have been brought forth. For then the things that were not were made. In the week of the whole world, by a certain secret dispensation known to God alone, the things that were then brought forth are unfolded. In this week (because Mary is set apart) the camp of the children of Israel is not moved, but they stand shut up in one place, and none of them sets forth, until Mary is cleansed of her leprosy.
12.15:
**“Mary therefore was put out of the camp seven days:”** — the week of this world
**“and the people moved not from that place until Mary was called again.”** — because none of them sets forth until Mary is cleansed of her leprosy
**“SEVEN DAYS”** — ORIGEN. Mary indeed, with Aaron the high priest interceding, is healed on the seventh day. But we, if we slander, shall remain leprous until the end of the world's week, that is, until the resurrection, unless while it is the time for penance we are corrected, turned to Jesus, and supplicating him through penance.
12.16:
**“And marched”** — Mary being cleansed
**“the people from Haseroth,”** — it is interpreted: perfect house
**“PHARAN”** — RABANUS. Note that Pharan is not the special name of a station, but of a wilderness containing several stations, as is shown in the catalogue of the stations, when it is said: The children of Israel departing from Haseroth camped in Rethma, then in Remmonphares; so that all the stations in order, as far as Asiongaber and as far as the thirty-second station, are comprised under the name of the wilderness of Pharan. From Rethma, therefore, which was fifteenth in order, to the thirty-second, these are contained.
**“and pitched their tents in the desert of Pharan.”** — PHARAN is interpreted "visible mouth", in which can be understood that the Word was made flesh, and the invisible was made visible; and this is signified, that after the end and perfection of all things that were to be done toward that people had come, then it passed over and came to him whom, the Word made flesh, it did not believe before.

13.2: **“Send men to view the land of Chanaan,”** — SEND MEN, etc. RABANUS. Twelve spies are sent to the holy land. The cluster is carried on wood, where the passion of Christ too is briefly shown. The people of the Jews murmurs, dreading the onset of the giants. There is fighting against Amalec and the Chanaanite, and, God willing it, it is overcome. It hears what sacrifices it ought to perform in the holy land. Dathan and Abiron and the sons of Core rise up against Moses and Aaron, and are swallowed by a chasm of the earth. Between the dead and the living the high priest goes in, armed with the censer, and the running wrath of God is stopped by the voice of the priest. The rod of Aaron brings forth both flower and leaves, and the dryness grown green is consecrated for an everlasting memorial. Not yet was there a temple or keepers of the temple, not yet had priests and Levites offered sacrifices, and the mystic word describes their portions. A red heifer is burned for a holocaust, and its ash is a sprinkling of expiation.
13.10: **“Of the tribe of Zabulon, Geldehel”** — elsewhere: Geddihel
13.13: **“Of the tribe of Aser, Sur”** — elsewhere: Schur
13.14: **“Of the tribe of Nephtali, Nabdi”** — elsewhere: Naabi
13.18: **“View the land, of what sort it is:”** — the land, namely, to be contemplated
13.19: **“GO YOU UP BY THE SOUTH SIDE”** — AUGUSTINE. Another text: And he said to them: Go up from this wilderness, and you shall see the land, what it is, and the people that dwells upon it, whether it is strong or weak, whether they are few or many. He is understood to have explained what he had said, whether it is powerful or weak, that is, whether they are few or many. For how could they, looking out from a mountain, perceive the strength of human forces? There can also be another sense, much more fitting to the truth. When he says: You shall go up into the mountain, he spoke of the very land which they wished to explore. For they could not easily be understood as spies unless they searched out everything as travellers. For if we suppose that they viewed and explored the land from the top of a mountain, how could they inquire into all the things that Moses commanded? How could they enter the cities which they are read to have entered, and take the cluster from that valley, on account of which it is called the valley of the Cluster? The land, therefore, is explored in itself, because it was itself what was to be explored, and there was there a certain lower place, from which valley the cluster was taken.
13.23:
**“And going forward as far as the torrent of the cluster of grapes,”** — of Christ, who hung from the wood of the cross
**“they cut off a branch with its cluster of grapes, which two men carried upon a lever.”**
• two peoples
• WHICH THEY CARRIED, etc. ISIDORE. Two bring the cluster on wood from the land of promise, because Christ hanging on the wood of the cross, promised to the Gentiles, was born according to the flesh of the land of his mother Mary. The two bearers who walked under the burden of the cluster are the two peoples: of whom the first, the Jewish, is blind and turned away, ignorant of the grace of him who hangs, and weighed down by the burden of him who is hung, to whom as judge it shall be subjected. Whence: "Let their eyes be darkened that they see not: and bow down their back always." But he who came behind bore, that is signified, the people of the Gentiles, which, believing and having Christ before its eyes, always sees him whom it carries, and follows as a servant his lord and a disciple his master. According to that: If any man will come after me, let him take up his cross and follow me. This is the cluster which, by the crushing of the cross, poured out the wine of his blood shed for our salvation, and gave the Church to drink of the pressed cup of his passion. Whom, in the pomegranate, mother Church followed with the companion grace of the gift; having within herself by the number of the seeds the multitude of peoples, by the redness, that is, the seal of the blood of Christ shining; having also the divers charisms of the Holy Ghost. Judging themselves unworthy of these, the unbelieving did not merit to receive the land of the flesh of Christ, flowing with milk and honey, which his servants, that is, the Christians, obtained through faith. Of whose doctrine it is said: "How sweet are thy words to my palate" etc. They brought the fig with the cluster from the land of promise, that is, the image of the law with the figure of Christ. For of him it is said: My beloved is as a cluster of Cyprus; because neither can Christ be without the law, nor the law without Christ.
**“Of the pomegranates also”** — by which the Church is figured, which signifies Christ
**“OF THE POMEGRANATES ALSO”** — Which signify the law, because neither is Christ without the law, nor the law without Christ.
13.25: **“THEY THAT WENT TO SPY OUT THE LAND”** — ISIDORE. The spies, who, sent to a fruitful land, frightened the people so that they did not believe they could possess the promised land, signify the scribes and Pharisees. For as those were sent by Moses carefully to consider the fertility of the soil, so these were sent by the law and the prophets, that by searching the Scriptures they might watch for the Lord's coming, in which was the land, that is, the holy flesh, in which they could obtain the kingdom of God, and the abundance of spiritual fruits, and eternal life. But as those frightened the people by despair so that they did not believe, though God promised, so these persuaded the people of the Jews not to believe in Christ, longing to return to the Egypt of this world, rejecting the manna of faith, and seeking the black pots of sins, and the rejected onions of blasphemies, and the melons of vices and lusts withering in corruption.
13.26: **“TO THE DESERT OF PHARAN”** — RABANUS. The wilderness of Pharan contains eighteen stations. At the last of these the spies returned to Moses and reported what they had seen, carrying the cluster with pomegranates and figs. And in what follows it is written: Departing from Asiongaber they camped in the desert of Sin. This is Cades, which is interpreted not "holy", as many think, but "changed" or "transferred" etc. At this station Mary dies and is buried, and because of the waters of contradiction Moses and Aaron offended the Lord and are forbidden to cross the Jordan.
13.27: **“And they related and said: We came into the land to which thou sentest us, which in very deed floweth with milk and honey”** — of the doctrine of Christ it is said: "How sweet are thy words to my palate! more than honey to my mouth."

14.6: **“But Josue the son of Nun, and Caleb”** — who was of the tribe of Juda
14.7: **“THE LAND WHICH WE HAVE GONE ROUND IS VERY GOOD”** — ORIGEN. What is this land, holy indeed and good, but inhabited by the wicked? Who are the enemies who dwell in the land of the saints? How are they to be cast out, that these may succeed and dwell there? The Gospels promise the saints the kingdom of heaven. And the Apostle says: "But our conversation is in heaven." In heaven, therefore, is the inheritance promised to the saints. Do you think, then, that there is now no inhabitant there who must be expelled? From the days of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven suffereth violence, etc. Unless there were some to be expelled from it, it would never be said that the kingdom of heaven is to be seized by violence. And unless we had a battle with some, the Apostle would not say: "Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood" etc. Of these too it is said: My sword hath been inebriated in heaven. It is necessary, therefore, that you conquer the spiritual wickednesses which are said to be in the heavenly places, who are the true Chanaanites, and expel them from the heavenly places, that you may dwell in their stead. Know, however, that there are giants. Everyone who resists God is called a giant, which those principally do. Whence: Who shall take the spoils from the giant? And elsewhere: No man can enter into the house of a strong man and rifle his goods, unless he first bind the strong man. By comparison, therefore, of human nature and demonic nature, we are locusts. Especially if our faith is doubtful and unbelief terrifies us, they will truly be giants and we locusts. But if we follow Jesus and believe his words, they will be as nothing in our sight. For he exhorts us, and says: If God loves us, he will bring us into this land, because it is good and its fruit wonderful. The figure therefore went before in the fathers; it is fulfilled in us. They cast out the giants and obtained their land, all the land of Judea, and the city of Jerusalem, and mount Sion. But to us it is said: For you are not come to the things that are visible, but to the invisible. For you are come to the mount of the living God, and to the heavenly city Jerusalem, and to the multitude of angels. And elsewhere: That Jerusalem which is above is free, which is our mother. We believe, therefore, that there is a heavenly Jerusalem, and that this earthly one is after its type; and the things written of this earthly one we refer spiritually to that heavenly one. And as they cast out of the earthly Jerusalem the Chanaanites and Pherezites and the other nations, so we too, who are come to the mount of God and to the heavenly kingdoms, must expel from them the opposing powers and the spiritual wickednesses in the heavenly places. And as they cast the Jebusite out of Jerusalem, and what was called Jebus was afterwards called Jerusalem, so we must expel the Jebusite from Jerusalem, and so obtain its inheritance. They conquered with visible and bodily arms, we with invisible and spiritual ones. Whence: Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, etc. Put on the breastplate of charity and the helmet of salvation, and take up the shield of faith and the sword of the spirit, which is the word of God. With such arms, following Jesus as leader, as the fathers trod on the necks of the nations, you too shall tread on the necks of the demons. For he says to those who follow him: "Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions." Jesus therefore wills always to do wonderful things; he wills to conquer giants by means of locusts, and by those who are on earth to overcome the heavenly wickednesses. This is perhaps what is said: That he who believes in him shall not only do the things that he himself did, but greater. For it seems to me greater if a man set in the flesh, frail and perishable, yet armed with the faith of Christ and his word, overcomes legions of demons; although it is he himself who conquers in us, yet he says it is more that he conquers through us. Only let us always be ready and armed with these arms, and let our conversation be in heaven, every movement of ours, act, thought and speech be heavenly. For the more ardently we ascend there, the more headlong they will descend. And the higher we are, the lower they. If our life is holy and according to God, it brings death to them. If slothful and luxurious, it makes them mighty against us, as giants. And the more we are spread out on earth, the wider spaces we yield to them in heaven. Let us increase, therefore, that they may be diminished; that as we enter, they may be driven out, and as we ascend, they may fall.
14.9: **“NEITHER FEAR YE”** — AUGUSTINE. Caleb and Jesus Nave, speaking to the people that they should not fear to enter the land of promise, said: But fear ye not the people of the land, for they are food for us. For their time is departed from them, but the Lord is among us; fear them not. Since it is said: they are food for us, that is: we shall consume them. But in what is added: For their time is departed from them, but the Lord is among us, they carefully did not say: The Lord is departed from them. For they were wicked. But since even to the wicked, by a hidden dispensation, a time of flourishing and reigning is given, the time departed from them. But the Lord is among us: they did not say: Time is departed from them and ours has succeeded; but: the Lord is among us, not time. For they had time; these had the Lord, the creator of times and dispenser of all things.
14.10: **“And when all the multitude cried out, and would have stoned them, the glory of the Lord appeared over the roof”** — The majesty of the Lord covered them in the clouds of heaven.
14.12:
**“I WILL STRIKE THEM THEREFORE”** — ORIGEN. This threat is not wrathful but prophetic. For the people of the nations was to be taken up, but not through Moses; therefore Moses excused himself. For he knew that the nation which is promised was to be called not through him but through Jesus, and was to be named not the Mosaic but the Christian people. Therefore he entreats with many words for his own people.
**“ORIGEN”** — I WILL STRIKE THEM THEREFORE. This threat is made by the Lord, not to show the divine nature passible and subject to anger, but that the charity which Moses had toward the people, and the goodness of God, which is above every mind, might appear. For God is written to be angry and to threaten, that man may know that he has so much place with God, and so much confidence, that if there is even some indignation in God, it may be softened by human observances; that man can obtain so much from God that he changes his own decrees. For the goodness which follows the anger both shows the confidence of Moses with God and teaches that the divine nature is foreign to the vice of anger. And the word contains a mystery to be fulfilled in the future, by which God promises that, this people being cast off, he will raise up another.
14.18: **“The Lord is patient”** — others: as thou hast sworn, saying: The Lord is patient
14.22:
**“But yet all the men that have seen my majesty,”** — He dispenses the manner of correction with balanced moderation.
**“and the signs that I have done in Egypt, and in the wilderness, and have tempted me now ten times,”** — or: many times
14.31: **“YOUR CHILDREN”** — ORIGEN. But their children who are here with me, whoever know not good or evil, etc. Our fathers were that former people; we are their children. Because they sinned, they were cast off and fell; but we their children have risen up in their place and been raised, we who knew not good or evil. For we are of the Gentiles, and we knew neither the goods that come from God nor the evils that are begotten of sin. Whence: See then the severity and the goodness of God: towards them indeed that are fallen, the severity; but towards thee, the goodness, if thou abide in goodness, etc.
14.33: **“Your children shall wander in the desert forty years, and shall bear your fornication,”** — that is, the punishment of fornication
14.34:
**“According to the number of the forty days,”** — he expounds the mystery of the number
**“A YEAR FOR A DAY”** — ORIGEN. As a year for a day you shall receive your sins for forty years. I fear to discuss this mystery. For I see that in it is comprised the reckoning of sins and punishments. For if to each sinner a year of punishment is assigned for the sin of one day, and according to the reckoning of the days on which one sins so many years are spent in torments, I fear lest perhaps for us, who sin daily, not even the ages themselves, or even the ages of ages, can suffice to pay the penalties. In this, that that people for the offence of forty days is tormented forty years in the desert, and is not permitted to enter the holy land, there seems to be shown a likeness of the future judgment, where the reckoning of sins is to be examined; where there will perhaps be some compensation of good works, or of those things which each received in his life, as is said of Lazarus. But no one knows this wholly save him to whom the Father has given all judgment.
**“ORIGEN”**
• Someone perhaps may deny that it befits the goodness of God to repay a year of torments for a day's sin; indeed he may say that even if he repaid a day for a day, though it were just, it would not seem kind. But if a wound is inflicted on the body, or a bone broken, or the joining of the sinews loosened, these wounds are wont to befall bodies within the space of one hour, and afterwards, many torments and pains having been gone through, to be healed with difficulty in a long time. For how many swellings in the place, how many torments are produced? But if it happens that in the same wound or the same fracture someone is wounded again and broken more often, with how many pains and how many torments can he be cured? And in how long a time, if indeed he can be, is he brought to health? And scarcely will he ever be so cured as to escape either weakness of body or the ugliness of the scar. Pass from the example of the body to the wounds of the soul, which as often as it sins is so often wounded, by sins as by darts. Whence: Take the shield of faith, wherewith you may be able to extinguish all the fiery darts of the most wicked one. And it suffers not only the wounds of darts, but also fractures of the feet, when snares are prepared for its feet and its steps are supplanted. How long do you think such wounds as these can take to be healed? O that we could see how the soul is wounded by each sin! An evil word inflicts a wound, though not on the tongue; the soul is wounded also by evil thoughts and desires. And it is broken and crushed by the works of sin. If we saw all these and felt the scars of the wounded soul, we would resist sin even unto death. But as the possessed or the mad do not feel if they are wounded (because they lack the natural senses), so we, made mad by the desires of the world or drunk with vices, do not feel how great wounds, how great bruisings of the soul we acquire by sinning. And therefore it is a fitting reckoning that the time of punishment, that is, of cure and medicine, be extended, and that for each wound the spaces of healing be prolonged according to the quality of the blow. So therefore let both the equity and the kindness of God become evident in the very torments of the soul, so that he who has sinned, hearing these things, may come to his senses and sin no more. For conversion in the present life and fruitful penance bestow a swift medicine, which not only heals the past wound but does not allow the soul to be wounded by sin any further.
• I will add another thing: if I am a sinner, will the punishment be the same for me if I have sinned once as if twice and thrice, and if more often? No; for according to the manner and number and measure of the sin, the quantity of the punishment also is to be measured. Whence: He will give us for our drink tears in measure. And the measure will be that which each has sought for himself in this life by sinning either less or more. The cup in the hand of the Lord, of pure wine, is said to be full of mixture. For it is mixed for each one, and judgment is made not only from the evils he has done but also from the goods. Yet though both are mingled, its dregs (which I think are called the portions of evils) shall not be wholly emptied out. But these things are in the hand of God; ours rather is quickly to amend and repent, to bewail the past, to beware of the future. For when thou shalt be converted and lament, thou shalt be saved. For we have an advocate, who intercedes for us, far more excellent than Moses, who yet was heard for that people. And perhaps Moses is written to have obtained pardon for the former people for this reason, that we may trust much more that our advocate Jesus will obtain pardon for us from the Father.
14.40: **“WE ARE READY”** — RABANUS. O wonderful insolence of the human mind and dreadful folly of a blinded heart! God commands them to believe his promises and trust in his power, and so to enter the land. Human folly distrusts and spurns the wholesome warnings. Contrariwise, he denies his help to them when they will to invade the land against the will of God. Like these are those who do not believe the promises of God and do what is forbidden. But the spiritual Amalecites and Chanaanites, who dwell in the mountains of pride, smiting them pursue them as far as Horma. Amalecite means the people "licking blood"; Chanaanites, "traffickers" or "moved". Horma is interpreted "anathema". The wickednesses of the air, therefore, which thirst for our blood and wish to entangle us in earthly business, if we persevere in sins and climb the mountain of pride, cut us down with fiery darts and pursue us as far as perpetual anathema. Let us not therefore presume upon ourselves, but, considering our weakness, follow the command of God in all things. For so shall we overcome all enemies; so shall we receive the joys of the heavenly fatherland which are promised to us.
14.43:
**“The Amalecite”** — licking blood
**“and the Chanaanite”** — trafficker, or moved
**“are before you, and by their sword”** — spiritual, fiery
14.44:
**“But they being blinded”** — by wickedness of mind
**“went up to the top of the mountain.”** — of pride
14.45:
**“And the Amalecite came down, and the Chanaanite that dwelt in the mountain:”** — of pride
**“and smiting and slaying them pursued them as far as Horma.”** — anathema

15.4:
**“Whosoever immolateth the victim, shall offer a sacrifice”** — spiritual knowledge in meditation on the law
**“of fine flour, the tenth part of an ephi, tempered with oil”** — with charity and mercy
15.5:
**“and wine”** — spiritual grace, or the communion of Christ's passion
**“of the same measure he shall give to pour out in libations for the holocaust or for the victim, for every lamb.”** — A SACRIFICE OF FINE FLOUR, etc. The faith of Christ's incarnation, which is most fully commended in the law, or the keeping of the Decalogue.
**“JEROME”**
• JOSEPHUS. The law commands that in private and public sacrifices most pure flour also be added: with a lamb one measure of an assaron, with a ram two, with a bull three, and mixed with oil upon the altar. For those who sacrifice also offer oil: with an ox half a hin, with a ram a third part of this measure, and a fourth with a lamb. Now the hin is an ancient measure of the Hebrews, holding about two ancient choes, according to which they offered oil. And the ephi (as is read in Ruth) is a measure of three bushels. And the hin (as those wish who have written of weights and measures) holds the measure of a sextarius; which is so named because it is the sixth part of a congius.
• Allegorically. A sacrifice is commanded to be added for each kind of animal that is offered. Because we, who shall enter the land of the Church by the grace of the Lord, ought to add spiritual knowledge in meditation on the divine law for each kind of good works. The measure of the ephi, therefore, which has three measures, signifies the faith of the holy Trinity, of which we ought to offer the tenth, that is, the faith of Christ's incarnation, which is most fully commended in the law, or the keeping of the Decalogue. We are commanded, therefore, to offer oil, that is, charity and mercy, and wine for a libation, that is, spiritual grace and the communion of Christ's passion. And these according to the portion of the measure of the hin, that is, according to the distribution of perfect devotion. For the number six, because it is perfect, signifies the perfection of each thing. What else therefore is it, in the offering of a lamb, to offer the tenth part of an ephi of fine flour tempered with oil according to the fourth part of a hin, and wine of the same measure to pour out in libations, but to show simplicity of manners with the knowledge of the law and evangelical prudence? For simplicity does not please without prudence, nor prudence without simplicity. Whence: "Be ye wise as serpents and simple as doves." For folly as well as cunning is abominable to God.
15.7:
**“and wine”** — spiritual grace
**“AND FOR THE RAMS THERE SHALL BE”** — AUGUSTINE. In the offering of a ram two tenths of fine flour are offered, and of oil and wine the third part of a hin. Because the ram signifies the order of rulers, it is well offered with two tenths, when anyone holding the Decalogue of the law in understanding and in deed is appointed to the office of ruler. And the third part of a hin of oil and wine is shown forth when charity and mercy and the grace of spiritual doctrine are spent by him on those subject to him.
15.8:
**“But when of oxen”** — preachers
**“thou makest a holocaust or victim,”** — others: a host
15.9:
**“Thou shalt give for every ox three tenths of flour”** — the knowledge of the law, practice and doctrine
**“tempered with oil”** — with charity
15.10:
**“and wine”** — spiritual grace
**“BUT WHEN OF OXEN”** — RABANUS. In the offering of an ox, three tenths of fine flour and half a hin of oil and wine. The ox signifies the order of preachers, who till the Lord's field, and with the gospel ploughshare root out the thorns of vices and multiply the harvest of virtues. These are offered with three tenths of fine flour, because, holding the Decalogue of the law in knowledge, doctrine and work, they are true asserters of the faith of the holy Trinity. These ought to have charity, and to give an example by counselling their neighbours through mercy, that is, to profit them by divine grace as far as mortals can, that they may come to perfection and holiness of life, according to that: Be ye holy, because I am holy. But what is lacking in this life, let them hope to have perfected in them in heavenly beatitude by the grace of the Lord.
15.12:
**“For every ox”** — preachers
**“and ram”** — leaders of the Church
**“and lamb”** — the meek and simple
**“and kid.”** — penitents
15.13:
**“Both they that are born in the land,”** — born in the Church
**“and the strangers,”** — coming from the Gentiles or the Jews
15.18:
**“When you are come”** — by faith
**“into the land”** — the Church
15.20:
**“Of the things you eat.”** — the domestic disciplines which each one exercises in himself
**“As firstfruits of your barnfloors:”** — the beginnings of loving labour toward others
15.21: **“So also shall you give firstfruits of your dough to the Lord.”** — WHEN YOU ARE COME INTO THE LAND, ETC. RABANUS. When anyone enters the present Church through faith, he must diligently work the land of his flesh, that is, his bodily life, in the fear of God, and bring forth the fruit of virtues for eternal refreshment. We are commanded, therefore, to consecrate to God firstfruits not only of the barnfloors but also of the dough; that is, not only of the office of preaching but also of the domestic disciplines which each one skilfully exercises in himself, to dedicate to the Lord the beginning of good will. For whether someone strives after virtues in himself, or spends loving labour on others, let him impute it not to himself but to divine grace, so that to him may be consecrated the beginning of every good from whom the completion of perfection is hoped for.
15.22:
**“And if through ignorance”** — or: not willingly, another text
**“AND IF THROUGH IGNORANCE”** — AUGUSTINE. Since it is commanded how sins are to be expiated which are committed not willingly, it is rightly asked what are these sins of the unwilling: whether those committed by the ignorant, or those which they are compelled to do? For these too are commonly said to be done against the will. But one wills that which he does for the sake of something, when he wills to live, if someone threatens death unless he does it: he wills therefore to do it because he wills to live. And therefore not seeking for its own sake to swear falsely, but to live by swearing falsely. If it is so, I do not know whether such things can be called sins of the unwilling, such as are here said to need expiation. For if it is carefully considered, perhaps no one wills sinning itself, but it is done for the sake of something else which he who sins wills. For all men who knowingly do what is not lawful would wish it were lawful; so far does no one seek sinning for its own sake, but for the sake of that which follows from it. If these things are so, there are no sins of the unwilling except of the ignorant, which are distinguished from the sins of the willing.
15.24:
**“And the multitude have forgotten to do it: a calf”** — Christ
**“they shall offer out of the herd,”** — of the stock of the patriarchs
**“a holocaust for a most sweet savour to the Lord, and the sacrifice and libations thereof,”** — bread and wine in memory of Christ's passion
**“as the ceremonies require, and a buck goat”** — Christ in the likeness of sinful flesh
**“for sin”** — of the human race
**“SHALL OFFER A CALF”** — RABANUS. The children of Israel offer a calf of the herd for a holocaust when the faithful peoples believe and confess with full faith the body of Christ immolated on the altar of the cross for the salvation of the human race. They offer its sacrifice and libations as the ceremonies require when in the sacrament they offer bread and wine in memory of his passion, and, partaking, trust that they have truly received his body and blood. And the buck goat for sin, when they believe that he took humanity and the likeness of sinful flesh, and offered himself for sins. The priest himself prays the Father for the sins of the people, and they are forgiven it, because in the days of his flesh, offering prayers and supplications to God, he was heard for his reverence.
15.25:
**“And the priest shall pray”** — Christ, our advocate
**“for all the multitude of the children of Israel: and it shall be forgiven them, because they sinned not willingly, offering notwithstanding a burnt offering”** — prayer with fasting and almsgiving
15.27: **“But if one soul shall sin ignorantly, he shall offer a she goat of a year old for his sin.”** — doing penance, namely, earnestly, and withdrawing wholly from sin
15.28:
**“And shall pray for him”** — or: for the sin
**“the priest”** — Christ, namely
**“THE PRIEST”** — Christ, who "by his own blood entered once into the holies, having obtained eternal redemption".
15.30:
**“But the soul that through pride”** — despising the command of the Lord
**“committeth any thing, whether he be a citizen or a stranger (because he hath been rebellious against the Lord) shall perish from among his people:”** — from the number, namely, of those who belong to God
15.31: **“BUT THE SOUL THAT”** — AUGUSTINE. Another text: Whatever soul shall sin with a high hand of pride, of the natives or of the proselytes, provokes God; that soul shall be exterminated from his people, because he has despised the word of the Lord and scattered his commandments: that soul shall be crushed with crushing, its sin is in it. What the sins are that are done with a high hand of pride he explained, saying: Because he has despised the word of the Lord. It is one thing, therefore, to despise the precepts of God, another to esteem them highly but to act against them either in ignorance or unwillingly; which two perhaps pertain to the sins done by the unwilling, of which he advised above how they should be expiated, God being propitiated. Then he added the sin of pride, when anyone does wrong by being proud, that is, by despising the command; which kind of sin he did not say ought to be purged by any kind of sacrifice, as judging it incurable by that cure which was carried out through those sacrifices, such as are here commanded to be done. Which, if they are regarded in themselves, can heal no sin. But if the things of which these are sacraments are inquired into, the purging of sins can be found in them. What is written, therefore: The wicked man, when he is come into the depth of sins, contemneth, signifies him whom Scripture here says to offend with a high hand of pride. This, therefore, cannot be abolished without the punishment of him who commits it, and therefore cannot be unpunished, even if it is healed by repenting. For the very affliction of the penitent is the punishment of sin, though medicinal and wholesome. For the sin is rightly judged great when pride despises the command. But on the contrary, that it may be healed, God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart; but because it is not done without punishment, such things are here said: For he here, he says, provokes God, because God resists the proud. And: that soul shall be exterminated from his people, because such a one is not at all in the number of those who belong to God. Because he has despised the word of the Lord and made his precepts void. He shall be crushed with crushing. And he adds why he is crushed, saying: His sin is in him; and therefore if he applies by repenting the contrition due to such a sin, God will not despise a contrite heart. Although in the Greek it is not said in this place, he shall be crushed with crushing, because it could be taken as though he were extinguished by being crushed in every way, or worn away, so that he should not be. But the soul is immortal; and if that which is worn away were wholly made not to be, it would not be said of wisdom: Let thy foot wear the steps of her doors. But that distinction is to be considered, whether no one sins except either in ignorance, or overcome, or in contempt; of which it is long to dispute now.
15.35: **“And the Lord said to Moses: Let that man die the death, let them overwhelm him with stones”** — by the sentences of the spiritual
15.36:
**“And when they had brought him out, they overwhelmed him with stones, and he died”** — judged
**“as the Lord had commanded.”** — AND WHEN THEY HAD BROUGHT HIM OUT etc. ISIDORE. The wicked cavil that by the command of God he was so cruelly slaughtered by the whole people because he gathered sticks on the sabbath. But all things happened to them in figure. And they are written for our correction. For he who dared to violate the sabbath day by gathering sticks, and was therefore punished, signified him who today, sealed in Christ, is found doing carnal work, that is, gathering together wood, hay, stubble for food of the eternal fire. Who, if he is caught, is stoned and slain, because he is judged by the spiritual.
15.40: **“FRINGES IN”** — The children of Israel are commanded to make fringes of blue at the four corners of their cloaks, so that as circumcision in their bodies is the sign of the Jewish nation, so their garment too may have some difference; and that those who by the command of God differ from the other nations in dress may be warned to differ also in religion. We too are instructed that the commandments which seem to be least in the dress of the law, if they are done for the sake of the heavenly life (which the blue riband signifies), profit much. For he who despises the least things falls away little by little. Whether therefore we eat or drink, or whatsoever else we do, let us do all to the glory of God.

16.1: **“And behold Core the son of Isaar, the son of Caath, the son of Levi, and Dathan and Abiron the sons of Eliab, and Hon the son of Pheleph”** — elsewhere: Phelech
16.14: **“TO CALL DATHAN AND”** — AUGUSTINE. What is it that Dathan and Abiron, called by Moses in the sedition, answered proudly and insultingly: Is this a small thing, that thou hast brought us into a land flowing with milk and honey, to kill us in the wilderness, because thou art over us, thou art prince? And thou hast brought us into a land flowing with milk and honey, and given us a lot of field and vineyards? After this they added: Thou wouldst have cut out the eyes of those men: we do not go up. Whose eyes did they mean? Whether of the people of Israel, as if: if thou hadst so provided, thou wouldst have cut out their eyes, that is, they would so love thee that they would pluck out their eyes and give them to thee, according to that of the Apostle: "If it could be done, you would have plucked out your own eyes, and would have given them to me." And then they added full contumacy: We do not go up, that is: We do not come, because he had called them. Or rather the eyes of those men, that is, of the enemies, who were reported as exceedingly fierce and terrible, as if: Even if thou hadst done this, we would not obey thee; except that one mood of the verb is put for another, so that they said not: We will go up, but: We do not go up, by a certain kind of idiom?
16.26: **“DEPART FROM THE TENTS”** — AUGUSTINE. Another text: Go up from the midst of this congregation, etc. It is to be noted that the Lord commands a bodily separation to be made then, when vengeance already threatens the wicked. So Noe with his house is separated from the rest who were to perish by the flood; so Lot with his own is separated from the Sodomites who were to be consumed by fire from heaven; so the people itself from the Egyptians who were to be overwhelmed by the waves of the sea; so these now from the congregation of Core, Dathan and Abiron, who before had willed to break themselves off by sedition: with whom, however, the saints, living and conversing before, and with the others whom God reproves, could in no way be defiled by them. Nor were they commanded to separate themselves when the Lord delayed vengeance, or applied such a one by which the innocent could not be endangered, as by the bites of serpents, or the slaughter of the dying, by which God struck whom he willed, as he willed, the other being untouched; not as by the water of the flood, or the rain of fire, or the water of the sea, or the gaping of the earth, by which he could consume them alike when mixed together (not because God could not preserve his own there; but what need was there of the trial of a miracle where a separation could be made), so that water, or fire, or the gaping of the earth might carry off those it found. And so at the end the wheat shall be separated from the cockle, that, the flames burning the wicked, the just may shine as the sun in the kingdom of their Father.
16.30: **“But if the Lord do a new thing, and the earth opening her mouth swallow them down, and all things that belong to them, and they go down alive into hell,”** — into the lower parts of the earth
16.31: **“THE EARTH BROKE ASUNDER”** — ISIDORE. By Dathan and Abiron and Core are signified heretics and schismatics, who, drawing many with them, deceive them; despising the priests of Christ and separating themselves from the fellowship of the clergy and the people, they dare to build churches, and make another altar and another prayer with unlawful words, profaning the truth of the Lord's victim by false sacrifices. And because they strive against the will and ordinance of God, for the audacity of their rashness they are swallowed alive, the joints of the earth being broken; and not only the leaders, but all their accomplices and abettors shall perish in eternal fire, the vengeance prepared.
16.33:
**“And they went down alive into hell”** — into the lower parts of the earth
**“THEY WENT DOWN”** — AUGUSTINE. Another text: And they went down, themselves and all things whatsoever were theirs, alive to the lower regions. It is to be noted that the lower regions are so called according to an earthly place, that is, in the lower parts of the earth; for the name of the lower regions is put in various senses, and it is commonly taken especially of the dead. But since these are said to have gone down alive to the lower regions, and from the narrative itself it appears what was done, it is manifest that here the lower parts of the earth are named by the word for the lower regions, in comparison with this upper earth on whose face we live. Just as, in comparison with the upper heaven, where the dwelling of the holy angels is, Scripture says that the sinning angels, thrust down into the darkness of this air, are reserved to be punished as in the prisons of hell.
16.37:
**“Command Eleazar”** — and not Aaron
**“the son of Aaron the priest to take up the censers that lie in the burning, and to scatter the fire of one side and the other: because they are sanctified”** — because through those who sinned an example was given to the rest, that they might fear
**“COMMAND ELEAZAR”** — AUGUSTINE. Another text: And the Lord said to Moses and to Eleazar the son of Aaron the priest: Take the brazen censers out of the midst of the burnt, and sow this strange fire there; because they have sanctified the censers of these sinners in their souls; and thou shalt make them beaten plates, a covering round about for the altar, because they were offered before the Lord and are sanctified, and are made for a sign to the children of Israel. Why did the Lord speak not to Moses and Aaron, as above, but to Moses and to Eleazar the son of Aaron? This reason occurs to me meanwhile: because the question was about the lineage of the priests, that is, of what stock they ought to be; whence those of another stock, because they dared to usurp the priesthood to themselves, perished by a wonderful punishment. God willed to speak not to Aaron, who was already high priest, but to Eleazar, who was to succeed him and already held the second priesthood, so as thus to commend the line of descent that was to be in the successions of the priests. Whence in what follows he adds: And Eleazar the son of Aaron took the brazen censers, as many as those who were burnt had offered, and added them as a covering round about the altar, a memorial to the children of Israel, that no stranger who is not of the seed of Aaron may approach to put incense before the Lord; and he shall not be as Core and as his conspiracy, etc. In this way therefore God willed to commend not the priesthood, which was already in Aaron, but the lineage of the succession. And when he says: Sow the strange fire, it is to be understood: scatter it there. And what he added: Because they have sanctified the censers of these sinners in their souls, is a sentence expressed by an unusual idiom. But it is to be noted that they are said in a new manner to be sanctified in the punishment of those by whom this sin had been committed, because through them an example was given to the rest of what they should fear.
**“TO TAKE UP THE CENSERS”** — ORIGEN. Core bears the figure of those who rise up against the faith of the Church and the doctrine of truth. He with his company offered incense of strange fire in brazen censers. The fire, therefore, is commanded by the Lord to be scattered, and beaten plates to be made of the censers, because they are sanctified, and the altar to be surrounded with them, because they were offered before the Lord and sanctified. This seems to me to be figured: that the brazen censers hold the figure of divine Scripture, upon which the heretics, putting strange fire, that is, an understanding foreign to God and contrary to the truth, offer to God an incense not sweet but execrable. And therefore a pattern is given to our priests, that (if anything of the kind arises) the things that are foreign to the truth be wholly shut out of the Church of God. But if any things are found in the very words of the heretics from the meanings of divine Scripture, let them not be rejected; for they are sanctified, and offered to the Lord.
16.38:
**“In the deaths of the sinners: and let him beat them into plates, and fasten them to the altar, because incense hath been offered in them to the Lord,”** — as though it is rather to be regarded before whom they were offered than by whom
**“ORIGEN”** — What is commanded of the censers of the sinners, that they be joined to the altar, can also be understood in another way. They are called brazen, because where there is true faith and the whole preaching of the word of God, they are called either silver or gold; so that the gleam of gold declares the purity of faith, and silver tried by fire signifies the words of the Lord examined by fire. But these brazen censers, that is, the voices of the heretics, if we bring them to the altar of God, where the divine fire is, where the true preaching of faith is, the truth itself will shine the better from comparison with false things. For if I refute the sayings of Marcion or Basilides or any heretic with the words of truth and the testimonies of the Scriptures, as with the fire of the divine altar, their impiety will appear more evident in me from the very comparison. For if the doctrine of the Church were simple, and were not split from without by any assertions of heretical dogmas, our faith would not seem so clear and so tried. Therefore those who contradict assail the catholic doctrine, that our faith may not grow torpid with idleness but be polished by exercises. Whence: There must be heresies, that they who are approved may be made manifest; as if: The altar must be surrounded by the censers of the heretics, that the difference of the faithful and the unfaithful may be made manifest to all. For when the faith of the Church has begun to shine like gold, and its preaching has gleamed like silver tried by fire, the voices of the heretics will be the more basely sordid with the cheapness of dark brass. For good things are known more by comparison with worse. Who would know that light is good, unless we felt darkness? Who would know the sweetness of honey, unless he had tasted bitterness? Finally, if you take away the devil himself and the opposing powers, will not the virtues of the soul be unable to shine forth without an adversary? So too the glory of faithful priests cannot shine forth unless the reprobation and punishment of the unfaithful commend it. Each of the just also seems to be held more glorious with God by comparison with the rest. Of Noe it is written that he was a just and perfect man in his generation; in which it is shown that he was not perfect wholly, but in his generation, that is, in comparison with the rest. Likewise Lot: the worse the Sodomites became daily, the more just he appeared. And when those who had viewed the land had returned, and ten with lying words had struck the people with despair, and two, that is, Caleb and Jesus, had reported good things and exhorted them to remain in their purpose, it was not so much their own confession that brought them immortal merit as the fear of their companions. For the virtue of their soul would not have shone so splendidly in them, had not the cowardly fear of the rest been laid open.
**“BECAUSE IT HATH BEEN OFFERED”** — AUGUSTINE. And why he willed a covering round about the altar to be made of them, he added, saying that they were offered for a sign to the children of Israel. He did not wish, therefore, to reprove in them that they were offered by such men, but rather that this should be thought on and regarded: before whom they were offered, that is, that it was before the Lord; so that the name of the Lord before whom they were offered might avail more in them than the most evil desert of those by whom they were offered. And this Scripture already mentioned in Exodus also, when it tells of the altar being made. Whence it is understood that the kinds of things done are distributed through the books, not the order of times woven together. For of the rod of Aaron too, how the thing was done, that flowering and budding it should divinely show the choice of his priesthood, is read in this book; and yet in Exodus it is said, that it should be put in the holy of holies with the manna in the ark, when the command is given about making the tabernacle; which was commanded long before the tabernacle itself was made and finished and stood. And it stood in the first month of the second year after they went out of Egypt, and this book begins from the second month of the same second year, on the first day of the same month.
