Whence it is clear that these things (if we consider the order of the books) are related by recapitulation, that is, by a recalling of past things; which those who attend less carefully think were done in the same order in which they are told.
16.39: **“THEN ELEAZAR TOOK”** — ORIGEN. With God nothing is idle, but things thought fit to be thrown away have some necessary work. The Scripture relates, therefore, that by the command of God Eleazar took the brazen censers which those who were burnt had offered, and they made of them rings and set them about the altar for a memorial to the children of Israel, that no stranger may approach to put incense before the Lord. For divine counsels are not as human counsels: if this cause were judged among men, and were held before the princes of the churches concerning those (for example) who, teaching things different from the churches, have borne the punishment of divine sentence or vengeance, would it not be judged that what they spoke, what they taught, what they wrote, should all perish together with the ashes of them all?
16.40:
**“lest he should suffer as Core suffered, and all his multitude”** — others: congregation
**“AS HE SUFFERED”** — ORIGEN. An example is given to posterity also, that no one by the presumption of a proud spirit should seize the office of high priest not given him by God. But let it fall to him whom no human ambition, no corrupt favour, no damnable largess has taken up.
16.42:
**“And when they were gone into it, the cloud covered it, and the glory of the Lord appeared.”** — in tribulation, namely; for the glory of the Lord cannot appear to one sleeping and idle.
**“THE CLOUD COVERED IT”** — ORIGEN. For we do not read before that the cloud covered the tabernacle, and the majesty of the Lord appeared, and received Moses and Aaron within the cloud, except when the people rose up against them and wished to stone them. Let us learn from this how great a benefit there is for Christians in persecution, how God protects them and the Holy Ghost is poured in. For then the glory of the Lord is most present when the cruelty of men is stirred up; and then we have peace with God when we are assailed by men for justice' sake; for where sin abounded, grace did more abound. The cloud therefore covered the tabernacle, and the congregation rushed upon Moses and Aaron, and the glory of the Lord appeared. Though they are of great merit and strong in virtues, the glory of God does not appear to them except in tribulation and danger, and almost in death itself. The Apostle too merited to obtain the glory of the Lord in these things; whence he reckons that he was in tribulations above the rest, was thrice stoned, and suffered shipwrecks, and perils of the sea and of rivers.
16.43: **“MOSES AND AARON”** — ORIGEN. In Sodom indeed at least ten were required, by whom those who dwelt in the Pentapolis might scarcely be saved. But now if two are found such as Moses and Aaron were, they suffice for the whole nation of the Israelites to be saved. What then is more in these two? What so great virtue, what merit, that six hundred thousand and more should be delivered? I think that in Moses the law is signified, which teaches man knowledge and the love of God; but in Aaron the form of supplicating and beseeching God. If ever, therefore, God is indignant with us or with the whole people, and vengeance is already going forth, and the law of God returning into our heart warns and teaches us to be converted to penance and to make satisfaction for our offences, at once the wrath will cease and the Lord will be appeased, as though Moses and Aaron were interceding for us and supplicating for the whole people. But if our hearts are hardened, and we neither turn nor are humbled in the sight of the Lord, so as to soften his wrath in the confession of supplications, but say on the contrary: God has no care for the life of mortals, nor do these things pertain to God; he left us long ago, nor does he know these things; then Moses and Aaron are not in us, namely the knowledge of the law and the fruit of penance, by which we can escape destruction.
16.46:
**“said”** — seeing in spirit what was being done
**“Moses”** — The law, which teaches man knowledge and the love of God.
**“to Aaron: Take the censer,”** — human flesh
**“and putting fire in it”** — the soul, namely, with which Christ was born
**“from the altar, put incense”** — Christ immaculate
**“upon it, and go quickly to the people to pray for them:”** — lest, namely, the destruction should go further
**“GET YOU OUT FROM THE MIDST”** — ORIGEN. Moses and Aaron, therefore, are commanded to go out of the midst of the congregation, that it may perish. But let us see what they do. They are holy and perfect, and disciples of the Gospel rather than of the Law; therefore they love even their enemies and pray for their persecutors. For as those rush upon them, these fall upon their face, and Moses says to Aaron: Take the censer, and put fire upon it, put in incense, etc. Let those see, therefore, who accuse God and the law alike, how Moses and Aaron did first what the Gospel afterwards taught. Moses loves his enemies and prays for his persecutors. The virtue of the Gospel, therefore, is found in the law, and the Gospel rests on the foundation of the law. Nor do I call the law the Old Testament, if I understand it spiritually. The law is the Old Testament only for those who understand it carnally. For them it is old and has grown old, because it cannot keep its strength. But for us, who expound it spiritually, it is always new, and both are to us a New Testament, not by the age of time but by the newness of understanding. Whence John says: Little children, "a new commandment I give unto you, that you love one another", though he knew that the commandment of love had been given in the law. But because charity never falleth away, and the commandment of truth does not grow old, he declares it always new. For it always makes those who keep it new in spirit; but to the sinner, and to one who does not keep the covenants of charity, even the Gospels grow old. Nor can there be a New Testament for him who does not put off the old man and put on the new, created according to God. Moses exhorts the high priest to offer incense in the camp and pray for the people. For the people had already begun to be destroyed. Moses saw in spirit what was being done. Understand the people of Israel in the camp, arranged in order of tribes and families, and a certain power sent from God, not at random, but having begun to destroy the people from the first part, and proceeding in order, a slaughter of death. Consider after this the high priest, clad in the pontifical vesture, carrying the censer and fire with incense, hastening to the place to which death had come through the destroying angel, and standing where death had made an end of the first and threatened the last. Behold the high priest standing and by a kind of interposing separating the living from the dead, and the destroying angel put to shame by the power of his propitiation and the mystery of the incense, and in this death ended and life restored. But having considered the history, go up to the loftier heights of this word, and see how the true high priest Jesus, taking the censer of the flesh, and fire of the altar set upon it, namely a magnificent soul, and incense also added, which is the immaculate spirit, stood between the living and the dead and checked death, destroying him who had the empire of death, so that he who believes in him may not die but live for ever. This mystery, then, that was to come afterwards, he who was destroying the people already then dreaded; he recognized the figure of the censer, the fire, the incense, and foresaw what manner of victim was to be offered to God by him who had stood between the living and the dead. The image saved them; to us the truth of salvation has come. For that angel would not have been put to shame by the vestments of the high priest of purple and wool woven with fine linen; but he understood the vestments of the great high priest to come, to which the whole creation is inferior, and yielded. And I think this pattern was fulfilled not only at the first coming of the Lord, but will be fulfilled at the second also: the Son of man will come again, and will find some dead and some living. And we can understand that some will be found in this state of life, when many have gone before dead. Or let us understand the bodies as the dead and the souls as the living; and then perhaps Christ will stand between the living and the dead, when he shall set the sheep on his right hand and the goats on his left, and shall say to those on the right: "Come, ye blessed of my Father" etc. But to those on the left: Depart, ye cursed, into everlasting fire, etc. For those are dead who are sent into everlasting fire, and those living who are sent to the kingdom.
16.47:
**“When Aaron had done this,”** — Christ, the great priest
**“and had run”** — the form of supplicating and beseeching
16.48:
**“And standing”**
• with an upright heart
• lest death should range further
**“between the dead”**
• through the excess of their crimes
• sinners
**“and the living,”**
• in works of justice
• the just
**“AND STANDING BETWEEN”** — GREGORY. Aaron, to appease the wrath of God, took the censer and stood between the living and the dead, because it is the business of the priest to pour out prayer to God, both for the just that they may not fall and for sinners that they may rise again. Whence: Let my prayer be directed as incense in thy sight.
**“ISIDORE”** — Aaron, taking the censer, ran to meet the shattering, and standing between the living and the dead, shut out the deadly plague by putting himself in its way, like a kind of wall. This priest is Christ, who, beholding the ruin of death in the world, ran to meet it from the highest heaven, and came to meet it as a giant to run the way. And he stood between the living and the dead, because he was born and died; and so, taking the censer of the passion and holding it forth for an odour of sweetness, he stayed the destruction of eternal fire and bore hostile death.
**“and the plague”** — SEPTUAGINT: the destruction; or, as is contained in other copies: the breaking.
**“AND THE PLAGUE CEASED”** — ORIGEN. Another text: And the destruction ceased, or the breaking, which is more fitting. For breaking happens in earthen vessels, which are sinners. Whence: The sons of Sion, who are more honourable and exalted in gold, how are they esteemed as earthen vessels, etc.? And in a great house there are vessels of wood and of earth, and some unto honour, some unto dishonour, which can be broken. Whence the Apostle of earthen vessels: If any man therefore shall cleanse himself from these, he shall be a vessel unto honour, sanctified and profitable to the Lord, prepared unto every good work. In which he shows that the vessel which is made and he by whom it is made are one and the same man. Understand, therefore, that a man's purpose is that which works; the rest of the man is the vessel itself, which is made unto honour or unto dishonour. When therefore our mind has chosen the things that are good and draws us to good conversation, it makes us a profitable vessel. But when it has neglected, and our purpose has fallen away from good things, we are made a vessel unto dishonour. If our understanding is of clay, and thinks always of clay and earthly things, we are made an earthen vessel, the work of the potter's hands. Whence: Shall the thing formed say to him that formed it: Why hast thou made me thus? For a clayey and earthly mind does not grasp the mysteries.
**“ceased”** — Our body too is called an earthen vessel, or the letter of the law, in that the Apostle says: Having this treasure in earthen vessels. Because the Lord bestows the treasure of grace through the Holy Ghost on those set in the body. And in the words of the law, which are despised because they seem set forth with no grammatical art, is hidden the treasure of the wisdom and knowledge of God.

17.2:
**“Speak to the children of Israel, and take of every one of them a rod by their kindreds, of all the princes of the tribes, twelve rods, and write the name of every man upon his rod.”** — OF ALL THE PRINCES, etc. Every prince has a rod, because without it he cannot rule the people. Whence Paul, because he was a prince of the people, said: "What will you? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in charity?"
**“ORIGEN”** — All the princes of the tribes must have rods. There is one only high priest, Aaron, whose rod budded; this is Christ, whose rod of the cross not only budded but also flowered and brought fruit to believers: nuts, it says, a fruit which in its first covering is bitter, in the second is fortified, in the third feeds. Such, therefore, in the hearing of Christ, is the doctrine of the law and the prophets. The first face of the letter is bitter, which commands circumcision of the flesh, and sacrifices, and the rest; all which cast away like the bitter rind of the nut. Secondly you will come to the defence of the shell, in which is signified either moral doctrine or the reckoning of continence; which are necessary for the guarding of the things that are kept within. Yet they are at some time to be broken and loosed; for abstinence from food and chastisement of the body are necessary to a corruptible body. But when it has been broken and dissolved, and at the time of the resurrection made incorruptible and spiritual, no corruption of the body will any longer have dominion, not now by the labour of affliction nor by the chastisement of abstinence, but by its own quality. Now, therefore, abstinence is necessary, but afterwards it is not to be sought. In the third place you will find the hidden sense of the mysteries of the wisdom and knowledge of God, by which the souls of the saints are nourished even in the future. For this is the pontifical fruit, of which it is promised to those who hunger and thirst after justice that they shall be filled. So, therefore, through all the Scriptures runs the reckoning of a threefold sacrament; so Wisdom too admonishes that we describe her in our heart in three manners; so Isaac dug three wells, of which the third is named breadth or largeness. And because the rod of the nut is a priestly sacrament, I think Jeremias (who was one of the priests of Anathoth) saw a rod of the nut tree, and prophesied the things that are written of the rod of the nut tree and of the boiling caldron; as though he showed by these that in the rod of the nut tree is life, and in the kindled caldron is death. For life and death are set before our face. And life is Christ in the sacrament of the nut; but death is the devil in the figure of the caldron. If therefore you sin, your portion will be with the kindled caldron. If you do well, in the rod of the nut tree with the great high priest. In the Canticle of Canticles too the bride is said to go down into the garden of nuts, and with the nuts to have found an abundance of priestly fruits.
17.5: **“HIS ROD SHALL BLOSSOM”** — ORIGEN. God promised one fruit in the rod, and gave many, that we may observe the liberality of God to be larger than his promises. The man, he says, whom I shall choose, his rod shall bud. But when it comes to the thing, not only is this promise fulfilled, but many things are added. For it says: and it brought forth leaves, and put forth flowers, and budded nuts; whereas only a bud was promised. As in these God gave his promise fourfold, and bestowed many more and more precious things than he promised, so in all places of Scripture where some promise is contained, it will be prepared manifold in the future, and that will truly be fulfilled which eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither hath it entered into the heart of man. Whether therefore you speak of earth or heaven, or this sun and the brightness of visible light, all these the eye has seen and the ear has heard. Pass beyond, therefore, all the things you see, that you hear, whatever even can be thought, and know that that is laid up for those who love God which cannot even ascend into the thought of your heart. Whence I think that nothing bodily is to be thought of in the promises. For the nature of bodily matter does not escape the sense of one who thinks; but they are things contained in the wisdom of God alone.
17.8:
**“He returned on the following day, and found that the rod had budded”** — of the cross
**“FOUND THAT THE ROD OF AARON WAS BUDDED”** — GREGORY. When Aaron, who was of the tribe of Levi, was despised for the priesthood, and another was believed worthy to offer holocausts, twelve rods according to the twelve tribes are commanded to be put in the tabernacle; and the rod of Levi grew green, and showed what virtue Aaron had in his office. In which it is hinted that all of us who lie in death until the end of the world remain in dryness, like the rest of the rods. But while all the rods remained in dryness, the rod of Levi returned to flower, because the body of the Lord, namely of the true priest, placed in the dryness of death, burst forth into the flower of the resurrection; by which flower Aaron is rightly shown to be priest, because by this glory of the resurrection the Redeemer, who sprang from the tribe of Juda and of Levi, is shown to be an intercessor for us. The rods of the twelve tribes remain in dryness, because the body of the Lord lives after death, but our bodies are still deferred from the glory of the resurrection until the end of the world.
**“ORIGEN”**
• The dry rod buds when the dead body comes to life again, to which four things will be granted: sown in corruption, it shall rise in incorruption; sown in weakness, it shall rise in power; sown in dishonour, it shall rise in glory; sown a natural body, it shall rise a spiritual body. These four things the rod of the dry body will bud forth in the resurrection.
• We can also understand thus the differences of the things that budded on the rod. He who believes in Christ first dies, and afterwards is born again, and so the dry rod buds. The first bud is the first confession of a man in Christ. Secondly it puts forth leaves, when, reborn, he receives the gift of grace and the sanctification of the Spirit. Then it brings forth flowers, when he advances and is adorned with sweetness of manners, and pours out the fragrance of mercy and kindness. At length it brings forth fruits of justice, by which not only he himself may live, but he may give life to others, namely by bringing forth from himself the word of faith and of the knowledge of God, that he may gain others. So, therefore, each of the faithful buds from the rod of Aaron, which is Christ; and these four differences of theirs are marked in other places of Scripture as four ages. Whence John says: I have written to you, children; and I have written to you, young men; and I have written to you, youths; and I have written to you, fathers. In which he sets down differences not of bodily age but of the soul's progress, as we have observed in the bud of the priestly rod. But all these are had not so much in the rod of Aaron as in that which came forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise up out of his root, upon whom the Spirit of God shall rest. Nor does it seem idle that the rod is said to come forth and the flower to rise up. For though Christ is one in substance, yet he becomes different to each, according as the one in whom he works has need. To him who is slothful he becomes a rod for discipline, and in the rod he is said not to rise up but to come forth. For he must come forth to one who is slothful, and pass over to another state, as a rod, that is, compelled by the severity of a more rigid doctrine. But in the just man, who flourishes like the palm tree, Christ is said to rise up. If anyone therefore needs stripes, he comes forth to him in the rod. But to him who advances to justice he rises up in the flower, until he brings forth the fruits of the Spirit, which are charity, joy, peace, patience and the other virtues.
**“THE ROD”** — GREGORY. The flesh of Christ, which, cut off from the root of Jesse and put to death, quickly lived again after the dryness of death. In the rod, the power of one reigning; in the flower, beauty. Whence: "I am the flower of the field, and the lily of the valleys." Others think this rod which flowered without moisture is Mary, who without intercourse brought forth the Word of God. Whence: "There shall come forth a rod out of the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise up out of his root", namely Christ, who, bearing the type of the passion to come, made purple with the white light of faith and the blood of the passion; the flower of virgins, the crown of martyrs, the grace of the continent.
**“of Aaron for the house of Levi: and that the buds swelling it had bloomed blossoms, which spreading the leaves, were formed into almonds.”** — AND THE BUDS SWELLING, etc. ORIGEN. But by this reckoning, by which the good things of the promises are given greater than the promises, the punishments which are foretold to sinners are inflicted with multiplied torments. Unless someone should think that some third thing can be done, gathering some comfort from the things contained in the threat to David, where a destruction of death to come was foretold for three days, and the time of punishment was shortened to six hours. But these things can avail there where a time of penance and a place of satisfaction is granted. Yet it is written that God repays to the wicked their sins unto the third and fourth generation, but shows mercy to the good, not only unto the third and fourth, but according to Scripture unto a thousand generations.

18.1:
**“And the Lord said to Aaron: Thou, and thy sons, and thy father's house with thee shall bear the iniquity of the sanctuary:”** — SEPTUAGINT: You shall take the sins of the holy things; because, namely, by the things which the high priest offers for each one's sin, he purifies him.
**“and thou and thy sons with thee shall bear the sins of your priesthood.”**
• the sacrifices offered for sins, which are due to the priests
• I add further that unless someone has a holy purpose and carries on the pursuit of holiness, he does not know how to do penance for sin or seek a remedy. Those who are not holy die in their sins; those who are holy do penance for their sins, feel their wounds, understand their falls, seek the priest and purification through the high priest. Therefore it is carefully and significantly said that the high priests and priests take the sins not of anyone whatever, but of the holy. For he is holy who has his sin cured through the high priest.
**“THOU AND THY SONS”** — AUGUSTINE. Another text: Thou and thy sons and thy father's house shall receive the sins of the holy things, and the sins of your priesthood. These are the sins of the holy things which are called sacrifices for sins. And sins of the holy things is said, not such as holy men commit, but from this, that they are holy things. It is said of the holy things because they are offered in the holy places, and the sacrifices for sins are called sins: therefore they are called sins of the holy things. And the sins of your priesthood, that is, the same things that are offered for sins: as he declares also in Leviticus, and says they belong to the priest.
**“ORIGEN”**
• Another text: Thou and thy sons and thy father's house with thee shall take the sins of the holy ones. Those who are better take up the faults of the lower. Whence: You that are stronger, bear the infirmities of the weak. If an Israelite sins, that is, a layman, he cannot himself take away his own sin, but seeks a Levite, or a priest, or a high priest, that he may receive remission of sins. But a priest or high priest, if he offends, can himself purge his own sin, provided he does not sin against God. For of sins of this kind we do not easily see remission of sins signified in the letter of the law.
• Jesus our high priest, who has passed into the heavens with his sons, that is, the apostles and martyrs, takes the sins of the holy ones. For he came to take away the sins of the world by his death. Their sons too take away the sins of the holy ones. Whence Paul: I most gladly will spend myself for your souls. And elsewhere: For I am even now ready to be sacrificed. And a victim is sacrificed for this, that the sins of those for whom it is slain may be purged. And of the martyrs John writes in the Apocalypse that the souls of those who were slain for the name of Jesus stand by the altar. And he who stands by the altar is shown to perform the office of a priest, that is, to supplicate for the sin of the people. I fear therefore that perhaps, since there are no martyrs, and the victims of the saints are not offered for our sins, there may be no remission, and that may befall us which the Jews say of themselves. For having neither altar nor temple nor priesthood, and therefore not offering victims, our sins, they say, remain in us; therefore we do not obtain pardon. But we ought to say that because the victims of the martyrs are not offered for us, therefore our sins remain in us. For we do not merit to suffer persecution for Christ. For the devil, knowing that remission of sins comes about through the passion of martyrdom, does not wish to stir up against us a public persecution of the Gentiles, because he envies our glory; or perhaps God knows that we are not fit for martyrdom.
• It is to be asked how some are called holy and yet it is written of their sins. For it is not (as some think) that as soon as a man has begun to be holy he cannot sin and is at once without sin. For it is said by Ezechiel: Begin ye at my sanctuary. For if the saints are without sin, how do they first succumb in the punishment of sinners? And elsewhere: The just is first accuser of himself. The Apostle too, who writes in the beginning: "To all that are at Rome, the beloved of God, called to be saints", afterwards says to the same: Destroy not the work of God for meat. And to the Corinthians: Paul, called to be an apostle of Jesus Christ, to the church of God that is at Corinth, to them that are sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints. Afterwards he says to the same: For whereas there is among you envying and contention, are you not carnal, and walk according to man? And a little after: It is absolutely heard that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as the like is not among the heathens, and you are puffed up. In which he leaves no one free, while he ascribes fornication to some, to others being puffed up and the crime of pride, and he sets down many things of this kind and worse in what follows. But there are many differences among the holy. For those same are called holy and sinners who have vowed themselves to God and separated their life from the common crowd, that they may serve the Lord. A man of this kind, according to this, that he has given himself over to the Lord with his other acts cut off, is called holy. But perhaps in this, that he serves the Lord, he does not do all things as befits, but offends in some. For if he who separates himself from all acts in order to attain the discipline of medicine or philosophy is not at once so perfect that he does not err in anything, but rather scarcely reaches perfection by erring very often, and yet when he has given himself to such schools it is certain that he is numbered among physicians and philosophers; so he who is given over to the pursuits of holiness, according to what he has purposed, is called holy. But according to this, that he must offend in many things while by practice and diligence the habit of sinning is cut away, he is called a sinner.
18.7:
**“BUT THOU AND THY SONS”**
• etc. ORIGEN. Another text: But thou and thy sons with thee before the tabernacle of the testimony, keep your watches and those of the altar, of the tabernacle, etc. The things that are written should be diligently observed, and especially by those who glory in the priestly order. But who observes and does the things that are commanded to priests, and who uses the priestly order and speech but does not observe the works, he alone can know who searches the hearts and reins. And they are commanded to observe not only the things that are without, but especially those that are within the veil; as though the priests should have care both to fulfil the evident and manifest commands of the divine law and to behold the hidden mysteries with all clear-sightedness. But if you wish to refer the tabernacle of the testimony to man (for Paul calls the body of man a tabernacle), the inner part of the veil, where the inaccessible things are covered, we shall call the principal part of the heart, which alone can receive the mysteries of truth. And the two altars, that is, the inner and the outer (since the altar is a token of prayer), I think signify what the Apostle says: I will pray with the spirit, I will pray also with the understanding. For when I pray in the heart, I go in to the inner altar. Whence: But thou when thou shalt pray, enter into thy chamber, and having shut the door, pray to thy Father in secret. He who prays thus goes in to the altar of incense, which is within. But he who with a clear voice, and words uttered with sound, to edify the hearers, prays in spirit, offers a victim on the altar which is without, set up for the holocaust of the people. The priests therefore ought especially to care for the things that are covered within the inner veil, that nothing defiled be found there, namely the inner man and the secrets of the heart, that they may remain spotless there. The cherubim and the propitiatory are to be understood as the knowledge of the Trinity. For cherubim is interpreted multitude, that is, perfection of knowledge; and what other perfection of knowledge is there than to have known the Father and the Son and the Holy Ghost? These things therefore are to be cared for by the priests, that they may be kept uncontaminated and unhurt. And the urn having the heavenly food of manna is the treasure of the divine word. The golden ark in which are the tables of the testament is our mind, in which we ought to have the law of God written: this ought to be golden, that is, pure and precious, in which the law of God may be "written, not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God; not in tables of stone, but in the fleshly tables of the heart". Whence: "Who shew the work of the law written in their hearts." For God wrote with his finger in their hearts the natural law which the Lord gave to the human race, and wrote it in the minds of all. From which we take beginnings and certain seeds for searching out the truth, which, if we cultivate them well, will bring us the fruit of life.
• Allegorically. The more perfect, namely, in the Church, and the holy doctors, whose office is to handle with their hands the divine sacraments and the holy vessels, that is, to winnow the mystic words of Scripture and bring them forth to understanding. But the rest of the crowd should diligently meditate on what it can grasp and what the discretion of the masters commands.
**“IF ANY STRANGER”** — Not of the tribe of Levi. For Ozias, of the tribe of Juda, because he usurped the priesthood, was struck with leprosy.
18.8:
**“And the Lord said to Aaron: Behold I have given thee the charge”** — AND THE LORD SAID, etc. ORIGEN. Another text: The Lord spoke to Aaron, saying: Behold I have given you the firstfruits for keeping. Others however say: for observing; but more truly: for keeping. And it is to be asked how, according to the law, the firstfruits are kept? For the priests receive them not to keep them but to consume them. This therefore is not applied to the law of the letter but to the law of the spirit. For spiritual firstfruits can be kept; literal ones cannot. Christ is truly the firstfruits which are given us for keeping. For it is blessed that the soul which has received Christ should always keep him and always have him. But the things that were offered in the law were consumed, and digested in the belly, into the privy; but not so these firstfruits. He who eats and tastes the bread which came down from heaven shall not die for ever. For this is the bread which, though it is always eaten, always remains, nay, is increased. For the more fully you take the word of God, the more it will abound.
**“OF MY FIRSTFRUITS”** — Literal firstfruits are consumed; spiritual ones are kept. For the more fully you take the word of God, the more it will abound.
**“All things that are sanctified by the children of Israel,”** — not by proselytes, not by Gentiles
**“ALL THINGS THAT ARE SANCTIFIED BY THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL”** — ORIGEN. Another text: Of all things that are sanctified to me by the children of Israel, etc. God does not wish to receive firstfruits except from those sanctified of Israel. For works worthy of God are found among the Gentiles: some have cultivated the virtues of the soul, and prophecy has done something in a few. God wishes to receive good deeds from those whose mind sees God and who are holy through faith in God. But a Gentile, even if he has something honourable in his manners (because he ascribes it not to God but to himself), is not sanctified nor received among the firstfruits.
**“ORIGEN”**
• But according to the letter he seems to exclude the proselytes, and wishes only the sanctified of the children of Israel to offer firstfruits. And I think a proselyte is so called from this, that he is not permitted to enter the Church. For it is written: "Thou shalt not abhor the Edomite, because he is thy brother: nor the Egyptian, because thou wast a stranger in his land. They that are born of them, in the third generation shall enter into the church of God." Until, therefore, the Egyptian or the Edomite bears fruit and makes sons of the first and second and third generation, he does not enter into the Church; but the begetting of sons makes him enter. And note that he does not say "if sons or daughters are born to them", but "if sons are born to them". Only sons are those who make the fathers enter into the Church.
• Three times in the year every male is commanded to appear, not the female.
• You will hardly find saints to whom God gives exceptional testimony having begotten daughters. Abraham and Isaac did not beget daughters. Jacob alone begot one daughter, and she was a reproach to her brothers and parents, and stirred up in her brothers the fury of vengeance.
**“BY THE SONS”** — Not by the daughters. For not idly does he elsewhere name daughters too with sons, and elsewhere make no mention of daughters. Which, however, are to be referred especially not to sex but to the distinction of souls.
**“I have delivered to thee and to thy sons for the priestly office, by everlasting ordinances.”** — spiritually understood, namely
18.9:
**“These therefore shalt thou take of the things that are sanctified,”**
• because they are not holy of themselves
• THESE THEREFORE SHALT THOU TAKE, etc. THE SAME. And let this be yours of the things that are sanctified of the holy things, of the sacrifices, etc. The Holy Ghost is so holy that he is not sanctified. For sanctification does not come to him from elsewhere, nor did he receive a beginning of holiness. The same is to be understood of the Father and the Son. For the Trinity alone is the substance which is holy not from without but by its own nature. For every creature, sanctified either by the condescension of the Holy Ghost or by reason of merits, is called holy. Whence: "Be ye holy, because I am holy" etc. For the same holiness is not to be set in God and in man. For of God it is said, that thou art holy; but to men, as to those who were not always so, it is commanded that they become holy. And where we have "be ye holy", in the Greek is had "become ye holy". But our interpreters put "be ye" indifferently for "become ye". Each one of us therefore, from the time he has given himself over to God with a true heart, is made holy. But truly and always holy is God alone. Whence: For both he that sanctifieth and they who are sanctified are all of one. And do not think that contrary which we read of Christ, whom the Father sanctified and sent into this world. For he who is sanctified according to the flesh is Christ, not according to the spirit. According to the spirit and the flesh alike he says: I sanctify myself for them; so that he who sanctifies is understood according to the spirit, he who is sanctified according to the flesh, yet one and the same Christ. From all the fruits, therefore, sanctified firstfruits are to be offered, but to the spiritual high priest. And the fruit of the spirit is charity, joy, peace, patience etc. And the firstfruits of charity are that one love God with the whole heart and with the whole soul and with the whole mind. From this fruit of charity I ought to have secondly that I love my neighbour as myself. Those firstfruits of charity, therefore, are offered to God through the high priest; those which are in the second place are left for my uses; and in the third place, from this fruit I ought to love even my enemies.
**“ORIGEN”**
• The law commands the firstfruits of all flocks to be offered to the priests, so that everyone who possesses a field, a vineyard and an olive yard, a garden, and whatever is worked on the land, and who rears herds of any cattle, should offer to God all that is first. For he says that what is given to the priests is offered to God; for this is taught from the law, that no one lawfully uses fruits or cattle unless firstfruits of each are offered to God in the priests. This law, therefore, I think must of necessity be observed according to the letter, like some others. For there are some commands that must of necessity be observed even in the New Testament. Yet there are those who say: If anything is observed according to the letter, why not all? But if they are to be understood spiritually, all are to be discussed spiritually. But we, tempering the extravagance of both assertions, will set forth by the authority of the Scriptures what is to be observed in these things. For it is written: "The law of the Lord is unspotted, converting souls: the testimony of the Lord is faithful, giving wisdom to little ones"; "the commandment of the Lord is lightsome, enlightening the eyes"; "the fear of the Lord is holy, enduring for ever and ever"; "the justices of the Lord are right, rejoicing hearts"; "the judgments of the Lord are true" etc. Unless each of these were different, Scripture would not have given its own differences to each, so as to say one thing of the law of the Lord, another of the commandment, another of the justifications, another of the judgments. One thing therefore is the law, another the precept, another the testimony, another the judgment, another the justification. Whence elsewhere: "This is the law, and the commandments, and the justifications, and the precepts, and the testimonies, and the judgments, which the Lord commanded Moses." Let us attend more carefully, therefore, to the things recited in the law. For wherever a commandment is written to be, it is not at once to be taken as law. Justifications too are not at once to be thought law or commandment. For a testimony or justice is to be taken not confusedly as one with the rest, but distinctly. When therefore it is said that the law has a shadow of things to come, it is not therefore that the commandment or justice or judgments are shadows of things to come. For neither is it written "this is the commandment of the Pasch", but "this is the law of the Pasch". In the bodily sheep, therefore, I ought to understand that there is a shadow of the good to come, and that Christ our Pasch is sacrificed; likewise too you will find it written of the unleavened bread and of the other observances of feast days. Since therefore all these things are written in the law under the title of law, I ought to ask what is the unleavened bread of the good things to come? And I find the Apostle saying: "Not with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness" etc. It is written also: "This is the law of circumcision." I ask therefore what shadow of the good things to come is contained in circumcision? Lest Paul say to me in the shadow of circumcision: If you be circumcised, Christ shall profit you nothing. Each of these things, therefore, which the Apostle says are not to be observed according to the letter, "you will find marked with the title of law in Moses".
• But where it says: "Thou shalt not kill, thou shalt not commit adultery" and the like, it did not set before them the title of law. For these are commandments, and therefore they are not emptied out among the disciples of the Gospel, but fulfilled. For not the commandment, but the law is said to have a shadow of the good things to come.
• But note that law is said in two ways: for generally all these things, commandment, justifications, precepts, testimonies, judgments, are called law; but specially, some part of the things written in the law, as said above. And law is signified generally when it is said: "I am not come to destroy the law, but to fulfil." And elsewhere: "Love is the fulfilling of the law." For he named all the things written in the law the law.
• Elsewhere too he says: Thou shalt follow justly after that which is just. And what need is there to seek allegory even in these, when the letter edifies?
• I ask also whether some things which stand according to the letter must necessarily be understood allegorically too? For it is written in the law: "Wherefore a man shall leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife" etc. That these contain allegorical mysteries Paul declares, saying: "This is a great sacrament" etc. But that it ought also to be kept according to the letter the Lord himself shows, saying: "It is written: For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife, and they two shall be in one flesh." What therefore God hath joined together, let no man put asunder. And that Abraham had two sons, the one by a bondwoman and the other by a free woman, who doubts that it stands according to the letter? But the Apostle added: Which things are said by an allegory.
• For it is useful to offer firstfruits to the priests of the Gospel, so that those who preach the Gospel may live by the Gospel. For it is impious that one who enters the Church of God, who knows that the priests and ministers stand by the altar and the word of God, or serve in the ministry of the Church, should not offer the priests firstfruits of the fruits of the earth which the Lord gave by bringing forth his sun and supplying the rains. For he who believes the fruits are given him by God knows how to honour God from his gifts by rewarding the priests. Whence: "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites; because you tithe mint, and cummin, and anise, and have left the weightier things of the law: hypocrites, these things you ought to have done, and not to leave those undone." The Lord therefore wills these things not to be left undone according to the letter. To the disciples too he says: "Unless your justice abound more than that of the scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven." What therefore he wills from the Pharisees, much more from the disciples. But what he does not will to be done by the disciples, neither by the Pharisees. "Whence it was said to them of old: Thou shalt not kill"; this the Pharisees keep; but to the disciples it is said: "Whosoever is angry with his brother shall be in danger of the judgment."
• Christ has redeemed us from the curse of the law, not from the curse of the commandment or of the testimony or of the judgments; that is, that we should not be subject to circumcision of the flesh and the observance of sabbaths and the like, which are contained in the law, not in the commandments. Our justice therefore abounds more than that of the scribes and Pharisees. If they dare not taste of the fruits of the earth before they offer firstfruits to the priests and set apart tithes for the Levites, shall I, doing none of these things, so abuse the fruits of the earth that the priest and the Levite and the altar of God have no feeling of it?
• Peter and Paul too offer through themselves the firstfruits of believers. Whence Paul says: "That from Jerusalem round about as far as unto Illyricum, I have replenished the gospel of Christ", where Christ was not named, lest they should build upon another man's foundation. All therefore whom he taught he offers as his fruits, and daily seeks new fields to cultivate and new country to sow. Whence he says: "I long to come unto you, that I might have some fruit among you also, even as among other Gentiles." From all these he marks out the choice ones, and chooses and offers the firstfruits of each church.
• Every doctor too, because he teaches, preaches and instructs his hearers, seems to cultivate the field of his Church, that is, the hearts of believers. He has also the fruit of his cultivation, and in the fruit some choice and special one whom he may offer as firstfruits, and another for the firstborn, another for the tithes.
• Someone perhaps has firstborn and lower ones whom he can offer neither for firstfruits nor for firstborn, but for tithes.
**“and are offered to the Lord. Every offering, and sacrifice, and whatsoever is rendered to me for sin and for trespass, and becometh holy of holies, shall be for thee and thy sons.”** — EVERY OFFERING, etc. ORIGEN. It belongs to the wise scribe, learned in the kingdom of God, to know how to bring forth from these treasures new things and old; and how to cast away wholly the letter that killeth and seek the spirit that quickeneth, so as to confirm the useful and necessary doctrine of the letter, or, the history remaining, to bring in a mystic sense as well, as in the present place.
18.10: **“Thou shalt eat it in the sanctuary: the males”** — strong in faith
18.11:
**“But the firstfruits,”** — virgins
**“which the children of Israel shall vow and offer, to thee”**
• Aaron
• the true high priest, namely, that is, Christ
**“I have given, and to thy sons,”** — the apostles, the greater, namely, and the lesser powers
**“and to thy daughters,”** — holy souls or peoples
**“BY A PERPETUAL LAW”** — How can that be eternal which is visible? For the things which are seen are temporal. But the firstfruits which are offered to Aaron are visible; circumcision too and the unleavened bread and the Pasch are visible; necessarily they are not eternal but temporal. The invisible circumcision, therefore, which is in secret, is eternal, and the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. So too these things, for him who is a Jew not openly but in secret, who keeps the law in spirit, not in the letter, are called eternal ordinances according to the inner man.
18.12:
**“All the best of the oil, and of the wine, and of the corn, whatsoever firstfruits they offer to the Lord, I have given them to thee.”**
• ALL THE BEST, etc. ORIGEN. We have shown that the command concerning the firstfruits of crops or cattle ought to stand even according to the letter. Let us see how it is understood spiritually. For here he says: All the firstfruits of oil, wine and corn. The firstfruits of all these, which shall have been offered to the Lord, I have delivered them to thee. But if all firstfruits belong to the high priest, a high priest is to be sought to whom those firstfruits also ought to belong which we find in other places. And of Christ we read that he is the firstfruits of the dead; he is therefore in some part firstfruits. The Apostle also says of certain ones that they are the firstfruits of Asia, and others the firstfruits of Achaia. It follows that Cornelius, with those who received the Holy Ghost with him, is called the firstfruits of the Church of Caesarea, and perhaps of all the Gentiles, of whom he first believed and first merited the Holy Ghost. And the field is called the world. And the field is not of earth alone, but human hearts, which the angels have received to cultivate. The fruits of their cultivation, therefore, they themselves possess, namely those who live under stewards and authors and have not yet come to the full perfection of age. But the perfect, as chosen and special ones, they offer as firstfruits to the great high priest. We find that Cornelius himself, before he received the doctrine of the word or the grace of baptism from Peter, heard from an angel that his prayers and alms had ascended to God; whence through the angel he seems to have been offered to God as firstfruits.
• Christ is the firstfruits of firstfruits. Cornelius the firstfruits of the Gentiles. Others the firstfruits of churches, as some the firstfruits of Asia, others of Achaia.
• But even if I merited to offer a great sense and worthy of the supreme high priest, so that something excellent out of what we say and teach might please the supreme high priest, the angel who presides over the Church could choose something from all our sayings and offer it to the Lord in place of the firstborn or firstfruits from the little field of our heart. But would that we might not merit to be condemned for the things we say; this grace would suffice us.
**“ORIGEN”**
• Each of the angels will be present at the consummation of the world in the judgment, bringing with him those over whom he presided, whom he helped, whom he instructed, for whom he always saw the face of the Father who is in heaven. And I think it will be inquired there whether the angel failed in the cultivation of men, or whether human sloth did not answer worthily to the angelic cultivation. There will therefore be a judgment of God in this also, whether by the negligence of the ministers who were sent to minister and help for the sake of those who receive the inheritance of salvation, or by our own idleness, so many falls befall us. There will therefore be a judgment of God both on men and on angels. And perhaps some who come from the multitude of believers will be judged with Paul and compared with his labours and fruits, and perhaps he will be found stronger than some angels. Whence: Know you not that we shall judge angels? Not that Paul judges angels, but the work of Paul will judge some. Hence perhaps Peter said: On whom the angels desire to look. Although the apostles too use the angels as helpers in completing the office of preaching. Whence in the Acts of the Apostles it was said that it was Peter's angel who knocked at the door. Likewise, therefore, it is understood that there is an angel of Paul and of any apostle, and of each in order or according to merits; who in the labours and doctrine either of the apostles or of the other doctors must have the first parts, and bring to the Lord's threshing floor the fruit of the souls which have profited through them, together with those through whom they worked. There will therefore be, in the gathering of fruits, that is, in the choosing of believers, he who was the special and outstanding firstfruits of that Church; and the higher of that Church, the firstborn offered by that archangel. All, therefore, that is foreshadowed in the law (since the law has a shadow of the good things to come) will be fulfilled in another manner through the ministries of angels in the truth of the good things to come, so that the things formed in Israel according to the flesh may be fulfilled in the true Israelites. For the name of Israel reaches to the angels, who are more truly called Israel, inasmuch as they are more truly the mind seeing God; for this is what Israel is interpreted. For as certain names of nations or princes are referred to evil angels, as Pharao king of Egypt, Nabuchodonosor king of Babylon or the Assyrian, so the things written of holy men and of a religious nation are referred also to the holy angels. Whence Isaias of Nabuchodonosor: "And I will bring the sword upon a great nation, and upon the prince of the Assyrians." And elsewhere, as of the prince of some nation: "How art thou fallen, O Lucifer, who didst rise in the morning?" And as to what we read in Genesis of God speaking to the angels: "Come, let us confound their tongue", it is to be thought that divers angels produced divers tongues and speeches in men. For example: one impressed on one man the Babylonian tongue, another the Egyptian, another Greek; and so perhaps they themselves were the princes of divers nations, who seemed to be the authors of the tongue and speech. But the tongue first given through Adam, that is, Hebrew, remained in that part of men which is the portion not of an angel or prince but of God.
• The angels therefore offer firstfruits from among us, and each cultivates what he has zealously converted to God from the errors of the Gentiles, and each one is in the portion or care of this or that angel. And as from the beginning, when God divided the sons of Adam, he appointed the bounds of the nations according to the number of the sons or angels of God, and each nation was made subject to this or that angel, but Israel is the portion of the Lord and the lot of his inheritance; so I believe it will be at the end of this world and the beginning of the other age, that the Most High will again divide the sons of Adam; and those who cannot be so clean of heart as to see God himself and be the portion of the Lord will either see the holy angels and be according to the number of the angels of God. It is desirable therefore that each should so advance as to be chosen among the firstfruits or firstborn and offered to God as his portion. If less, let him at least merit to be the portion of the holy angels, provided he is not found among those of whom it is said: "They shall go into the lower parts of the earth: they shall be delivered into the hands of the sword, they shall be the portions of foxes", that is, of demons. For these are the foxes that destroy the vineyards; of whom was Herod, of whom it is said: "Go and tell that fox." Let us flee, therefore, earthly acts and earthly understanding, lest we go into the lower parts of the earth. For they go in who receive the law of God and the goods of the promises with an earthly understanding, and do not rouse the souls of the earthly to the expectation of heavenly things, that they may seek the things that are above, not the things that are upon the earth.
• The angels offer firstfruits, each one, I believe, of his own nation and of his own church; to whom John in the Apocalypse seems to write, namely to the angel of the Church of Ephesus, Smyrna, Laodicea etc. Each therefore offers the firstfruits of his nation or of his church, which was committed to him to dispense; or perhaps there are also other angels from without, who gather the faithful from all nations. And let us consider whether perhaps, as in some city where there are not yet Christians, if someone teaches and instructs, and afterwards becomes chief bishop there; so the holy angels, those whom they have gathered from divers nations, if they have made them advance, may become princes and rulers in the future? so that Christ may be called King of kings and Lord of lords. For these are the kings of those whom they rule and make to advance. They themselves therefore offer some to the high priest, some to the sons of the high priest, that is, to the higher powers and archangels, some to the Levites, that is, to those a little lower; if the angelic orders are distinguished as the Israelites were, since they are said to serve the shadow and example of heavenly things. Perhaps, therefore, in the future, when all the fruits shall be gathered to the threshing floor, some will be the portion of the true high priest, that is, Christ; others, of the Levites, set apart either for angels or for other heavenly powers; some also the portion of men who in this life were prudent dispensers of God. Whence to him to whom the Lord had entrusted five pounds and who had made ten he says: "Have thou power over ten cities" etc. For what is understood here by power over cities but the government of souls? Whence it seems to me that among the angels some hold principality and power over others, others are subject and obey the power. So neither does he to whom the power of ten cities or of five is given come to this power undeservedly. All things therefore are done with God by reason and judgment, and not by favour but for merit is one set as prince of many, another subject to principality.
• As Christ is King of kings, so he is the firstfruits of firstfruits which are offered not to the high priest but to God; because he offered himself a victim to God, and rising from the dead sits at the right hand of God. And he is called the firstfruits and firstborn of every creature. Whether this ought to be understood so through each creature, as among men he is called and understood the firstfruits of them that sleep, or with a loftier and more divine understanding, it is not for the present time to pursue.
**“THE SAME”** — The fields of the angels are our hearts; each of them offers firstfruits to the Lord from the field which he cultivates.
18.13:
**“All the firstripe of the fruits, that the ground bringeth forth,”**
• human hearts
• ALL THE FIRSTRIPE OF THE FRUITS, etc. AUGUSTINE. All the firstborn things whatsoever shall be in their land, however much they shall offer to the Lord, shall be thine. Here he calls firstborn not the first or firstling young of cattle. For these in Greek are named prototoka or prototosa; but these, protogennemata. But in Latin two names have not been found for these two things, and therefore some have translated these protogennemata as firstfruits. But firstfruits are plainly so called and are something else. These three, therefore, are distinguished thus: that prototoka or prototosa are the firstling young of animals and of men; protogennemata, the first fruits taken from the land or from the tree or from the vine; but firstfruits, from the fruits indeed, but those already brought in from the field, as from the lump, from the vat, from the jar, from the cask, which were taken for firstfruits.
18.15:
**“Whatsoever is firstborn of all flesh,”** — The firstborn are those who are not defiled with women, or the martyrs.
**“WHATSOEVER IS FIRST”** — ORIGEN. Perhaps those can be called firstborn who are not defiled with women, or even the martyrs. The virgins too can be called the firstfruits of the Church, and the tithes those who are continent after marriage.
**“which they offer to the Lord, whether it be of men,”** — the rational
**“or of beasts,”** — the unlettered and simple
18.19:
**“All the firstfruits of the sanctuary which the children of Israel offer”**
• archangels, angels, apostles, and any doctors of the Church
• ALL THE FIRSTFRUITS, etc. RABANUS. In both testaments oblations and tithes are assigned to the ministers of the altar for their necessities, lest they should dare to dwell in earthly possessions or seek gain from the ministry. Whence: "Freely have you received, freely give. Do not possess gold, nor silver, nor money." But mystically the tithes signify the observance of the law, or the sincerity of the integrity of faith, or the perfection of good work, which those ought most to have who give themselves to the divine ministry. For in the number ten is comprised the knowledge of the creature and of the Creator; because seven looks to human nature, namely three showing the power of the soul. Whence: "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with thy whole heart, and with thy whole soul, and with thy whole strength." And the body consists of four elements. And if you join seven to the number three, which expresses faith and the confession of the Trinity, you will complete ten.
**“to the Lord, I have given to thee and to thy sons and daughters, by a perpetual ordinance. A covenant of salt”** — of wisdom, the divine seasoning
**“A COVENANT OF SALT”** — RABANUS. He names as a covenant of salt the whole of the oblations which pertain to the ministry or the right of the priests. Whence in Leviticus: "Whatsoever sacrifice thou offerest, thou shalt season it with salt" etc. Mystically it is shown that wisdom befits the priests and preachers of the divine law; not worldly but apostolic, of which Paul says: "We speak wisdom among the perfect: yet not the wisdom of this world" etc. Of which it is said to the apostles: "You are the salt of the earth." For as all food is seasoned with salt, so all speech with apostolic wisdom. To Aaron therefore and his sons there is an everlasting covenant of salt, because wisdom is necessary not only to bishops, but also to priests, deacons and all orders; and this before God, that is, that it may please God pure and simple, without cunning and malice. For the wisdom of this world is an enemy to God.
**“it is for ever before the Lord, to thee”** — to the bishops
**“and to thy sons.”** — to the priests, the deacons
18.20: **“And the Lord said to Aaron: You shall possess nothing in their land, neither shall you have a portion among them: I am thy portion and inheritance”** — "The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup" etc.
18.21:
**“And to the sons of Levi”** — who live continently after marriage
**“I have given all the tithes of Israel”** — of the true one, namely

19.1: **“And the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying:”** — AND THE LORD SPOKE, etc. AUGUSTINE. And the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: This is the distinction of the law, whatsoever the Lord has appointed, etc. There is no distinction except between two or more. For singleness does not admit distinction; nor did he mention the distinction of just any thing, but added: of the law; and not of just any law. For it is constantly read in Scripture of each thing of which something is lawfully commanded: This is the law of this or that; not the universal law which contains all things that are lawfully commanded. But here, when he had said: this "is the distinction of the law", he added: "whatsoever the Lord has appointed", namely by commanding, not by creating. For some translated: whatsoever the Lord commanded. If therefore this is the distinction of the law, whatsoever the Lord commands, great is this distinction, and it is rightly understood to understand or distinguish the two testaments. For the same things are in the Old and in the New Testament: there overshadowed, here revealed. For not only are the sacraments different, but also the promises there seem to be set forth as temporal, by which a spiritual reward is secretly signified; but here spiritual and eternal things are manifestly promised. And what more certain distinction is there between temporal and carnal goods and spiritual and eternal ones than the passion of Christ? In whose death it shone out that transitory happiness is not to be hoped for and desired as a great gift, since God, by the only-begotten Son (whom he willed to suffer such things), declared by an open distinction that something far other is to be sought from him and awaited. This passion, therefore, as the distinction of the two testaments, is fittingly enough figured by what is said of the slaying of the red heifer. The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: "This is the distinction of the law, whatsoever the Lord has appointed"; then he begins to command, adding these things, saying: "Speak to the children of Israel." It can also be punctuated thus: And the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: "This is the distinction of the law, whatsoever the Lord has appointed, saying"; not whatsoever the Lord has appointed in creating, as heaven and earth and sea and all things that are in them, but whatsoever the Lord has appointed in saying, in two, namely, testaments; so that there then follows: Speak to the children of Israel, and let them take to thee a red heifer without blemish. The red heifer signifies the flesh of Christ. The female sex, fleshly weakness; red, bloodied by the passion. And when he says, let them take to thee, he shows in Moses himself the figure of the law; because according to the law they seemed to themselves to kill Christ, because he broke the sabbath and profaned the observances of the law.
19.2:
**“This is the observance of the victim, which the Lord hath ordained. Command the children of Israel, that they bring unto thee a red cow of full age,”**
• because all his working is perfect
• A RED COW, red, namely, with the blood of the passion. Whence: "My beloved is white and ruddy." White, namely, from the divinity; ruddy from the blood; white also through justice of life.
**“A COW”** — By the male strength is signified, by the female weakness. By the cow is figured the weakness of the Lord's incarnation, taken up for sacrifice. For he was crucified through weakness, yet he liveth by the power of God.
**“GREGORY”** — Morally. We slay the red cow when we extinguish the flesh from the wantonness of pleasure; which we offer with hyssop, cedar wood and scarlet, because with the mortification of the body we burn the sacrifice of faith, hope and charity.
**“in which there is no blemish, and which hath not carried the yoke:”** — "Who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth."
**“THERE IS NO BLEMISH”** — AUGUSTINE. Without blemish. For the other victims signified this flesh, where likewise cattle without blemish were commanded to be immolated. For he was in the likeness of sinful flesh, but not sinful flesh. But here, where God willed more evidently to commend the distinction of the law, it was too little to say without blemish, unless it were said: which has no blemish in itself. And if it was said for the sake of repetition, perhaps it is not in vain that the repetition itself commended the thing more firmly; although it would not stray from the truth if it is understood to have been added, which has no blemish in itself, when it had already been said, a heifer without blemish, because the flesh of Christ had no blemish in itself, but had it in others, who are his members. For what flesh in this life is without sin save that one alone which had no blemish in itself?
**“NOR HATH CARRIED”** — Everyone who sins is the servant of sin; because therefore Christ never sinned, he did not carry the yoke.
**“AUGUSTINE”** — And there is no yoke laid upon her, etc. For she was not subjugated to iniquity; finding those subjugated to it, he freed them and broke their bonds. Whence: "Thou hast broken my bonds: I will sacrifice to thee the sacrifice of praise" etc. For upon his flesh no yoke was laid who had power to lay down his life and to take it up again.
19.3:
**“AND YOU SHALL DELIVER”** — The cow is delivered to the priest to be immolated, because the Lord incarnate made himself a sacrifice for our redemption, given into the hands of the Jewish people.
**“AUGUSTINE”**
• "And thou shalt give her to Eleazar the priest" etc. Why not to Aaron? Perhaps it was prefigured that the passion of the Lord would come not in the time that then was, but in the posterity of this priesthood.
• And they shall cast her out of the camp. So the Lord, about to suffer, was cast out of the city.
• Into a clean place, because he had no evil cause. And they shall slay her in his sight; so the flesh of Christ was slain in the sight of those who were to be the priests of the Lord in the New Testament.
**“SHALL IMMOLATE”** — Morally. No one will be able to immolate the red cow (whose ash is the expiation of the people) save one who has not done earthly works, and has not drawn the yoke of offence, and has not been bound with the chains of sins.
**“in the sight of all:”** — WHO SHALL BRING HER FORTH, etc. AUGUSTINE. Because Christ suffered without the gate, that he might lead us out of the conversation of the present life as out of a city.
**“IN THE SIGHT OF ALL”** — GREGORY. Because Christ was as it were extinguished in the sight of all. He was immolated in the sight of the Father, because what before the eyes of men was punishment, this before the eyes of the Father was sacrifice.
19.4:
**“And dipping his finger in her blood,”**
• AND DIPPING HIS FINGER, etc. AUGUSTINE. Another text: And Eleazar shall take of her blood and shall sprinkle of her blood seven times over against the face of the testimony. Because Christ according to the Scriptures shed his blood for the remission of sins, therefore over against the face of the tabernacle of the testimony, because it was not made known otherwise than it had been foretold by the divine testimony. And therefore seven times, because that number pertains to spiritual cleansing.
• GREGORY. In the finger the discernment of working is signified. To dip the finger in the blood of the cow is to consecrate our works in the passion of the Lord, that we may imitate his passion which we know. For he suffered, leaving you an example that you should follow his steps.
**“GREGORY”**
• Eleazar the priest immolates and dips his finger in the blood, because the Jewish people, on the part of the reprobate, persecuted the humility of the Lord even to the passion; but in the elect it imitated the working of his humility. And he shall sprinkle over against the door of the tabernacle etc. The tabernacle signifies the synagogue. He therefore who has dipped his finger should sprinkle over against the door of the tabernacle; that is, whoever imitates the ways of his passion should give to the synagogue, which does not believe and resists, a sign of living well by good examples and right preaching.
• Seven times, etc. In the number seven perfection is signified or understood. Whence also all time is completed in seven days, and the Holy Ghost is called sevenfold. To dip the finger in the blood seven times, therefore, is to imitate the mystery of the passion by perfect working. And to sprinkle seven times over against the synagogue is to announce the passion to unbelievers by perfect preaching.
**“SHALL SPRINKLE”** — GREGORY. The same will show to the resisting people, by right preaching and works, the examples of Christ's passion.
**“SEVEN TIMES”** — Because of the seven gifts of the Holy Ghost, which through the blood of Christ are distributed over the peoples of the Church, in which they are purged from every offence.
19.5:
**“And shall burn her in the sight of all,”** — SHALL BURN HER IN THE SIGHT OF ALL, etc. GREGORY. By the skin and flesh and blood and dung are signified the sacrifices held in the Old Testament which announced the weakness of the Lord. Because all of them, understood afterwards spiritually by the fathers, are called dung according to the outward mystery. Whence Paul: "I count all things as dung"; which are delivered to the flame. For though at first they were shown forth carnally, afterwards through the Holy Ghost they were consumed by the fire of understanding.
**“AUGUSTINE”** — And they shall burn her in his sight. I think that the burning pertains to the sign of the resurrection. For it is the nature of fire to move upward, and that which is burned is turned into it. For the very word cremare is a word brought from Greek into Latin, from hanging up. And what is added, in his sight, that is, in the sight of the priest, seems to signify that the resurrection of Christ appeared to those who were to be of the royal priesthood.
**“delivering up to the fire her skin, and her flesh, and her blood, and her dung.”** — HER SKIN, etc. AUGUSTINE. And what follows, her skin and flesh and her blood with the dung shall be burned, sets forth how she shall be burned; and it is signified that not only the substance of the mortal body of Christ, which is intimated by the mention of skin and flesh and blood, but also the contumely and abjection of the people, which is signified in the dung, will be turned into glory, which the flame of the burning signifies.
**“GREGORY”** — By the skin and flesh the outward working of Christ is signified. By the blood, the subtle and inner power quickening the outward deeds. By the dung, weariness, thirst, hunger and the fear of death, and whatever he willed to suffer from humanity. For whatever he had from the defect of mortality was as dung in him, to be cast away; all which are to be burned with fire, that is, to be understood according to the truth of the Holy Ghost, so that the things he did bodily may be perceived as ordered by the incorporeal spirit of the Godhead.
19.6:
**“wood”** — the cross
**“CEDAR WOOD ALSO”** — The cedar is a tall and incorruptible wood. Hyssop is a very lowly herb, which yet warns against the swelling of the lung. By the cedar, therefore, lofty persevering contemplation is signified; by hyssop, the humility of a meek heart. For he who is raised by contemplation to heavenly things ought to condescend to the lower by the compassion of humility; nor should he lift himself up because of what he has, but should gladly spend it in preaching on those who have it not.
**“AUGUSTINE”** — And the priest shall take cedar wood and hyssop and scarlet and cast them into the midst of the burning of the heifer etc. The cedar wood is hope, which dwells firmly in heavenly things. Hyssop is faith, which is a lowly herb clinging with its roots to the rock. Scarlet is charity, which bears witness to the fervour of the spirit by its fiery colour. These three we ought to cast into the resurrection of Christ, as into the midst of that burning, that our life may be hidden with him.
**“GREGORY”**
• By the cedar can be understood hope, which seeks lofty things. By hyssop (which by its smell also purges the uncleanness of the stomach), faith, which bears adverse things with very even mind and cleanses whatever had been contracted from former sins. And by the scarlet, charity. Let each of us, therefore, cast into the flame which devours the cow the cedar, the hyssop and the scarlet twice dyed; that is, let him show forth faith, hope and charity in the sacrifice of the Lord's passion, lest he hear of the passion of his Redeemer to no purpose. Hence Paul: "And now there remain faith, hope, and charity: but the greater of these is charity." Whence here too the scarlet is put last, because when faith and hope are completed and we have come to the eternal fatherland, charity alone will be multiplied in us at the last.
• Let the cedar be cast into the flame which devours the cow; that is, let the perseverance and loftiness of our contemplation be burned with the fire of the Lord's passion. Let the hyssop be cast in; that is, let the humility of our heart draw the truth of meekness from mingling with the Lord's passion. Let the scarlet twice dyed be cast in; that is, let the charity which rouses us to love God and our neighbour compel us to contemplate the Lord's passion continually, that in it it may learn the right works it is to do.
• In the scarlet twice dyed the virtue of charity is expressed, which, kindled by the flame of holy love, is commanded to be shown forth by two precepts, namely the love of God and of neighbour. The scarlet therefore is twice dyed when charity is formed by the twofold precept, so that God is loved in such a way that the neighbour is not forsaken, and the neighbour in such a way that God is not despised.
• This priest who burns the cow's flesh, skin, blood and dung can signify the order of the Jewish priesthood, with the people under it, consenting to the death of the Lord. Whence it follows: And then after washing his garments and his body.
**“HYSSOP”** — ISIDORE. Baptism, because they were sprinkled with hyssop dipped in the blood of the lamb.
**“AND SCARLET TWICE DYED”** — ISIDORE. The scarlet twice dyed is the blood of Christ, by which we are washed in mind and body. These three purge: the cedar, that is, the faith of the cross; hyssop, baptism or martyrdom; scarlet, the sacrament of the Lord's blood.
**“THE PRIEST”** — GREGORY. All of us who believe in Christ are priests. Whence: "But you are a chosen generation, a kingly priesthood" etc. The lofty things, therefore, which we reach by contemplation, and what we do from the meekness of humility, and what we show forth through the fire of charity, we ought to dip in the blood of Christ's passion, so that all that is in us may imitate him from whom it is; because outside the imitation of the passion it is not so much virtue as vice.
19.7:
**“And then after washing his garments,”**
• from the works of unbelief
• AND THEN AFTER, etc. THE SAME. It can be understood that this priest is both washed in his garments and yet unclean until the evening, because the Jewish people, on the part of those who believed, is clean; on the part of those who did not believe, remains unclean until the evening. He washes his garments and body, therefore, because by believing he cleanses his outward works and inner mind from wicked actions; and he returns fully to the camp then, when he is called back perfectly at the end. But because, while Judea partly persists in unbelief, the Gentile world enters into faith and understands the mysteries of the divine incarnation, he rightly adds: And a man that is clean shall gather up the ashes of the cow etc.
**“AUGUSTINE”** — The priest shall wash his garments and wash his body with water, and afterwards shall enter the camp, and the priest shall be unclean until the evening. The washing of the garments and the body is the cleansing of the outward and inward things; this is the priest. Then follows: He who burns her shall wash his garments and wash his body with water, and shall be unclean until the evening. In him who burns her I think those are figured who buried the flesh of Christ, committing it to the resurrection as to a burning.
**“and his body,”** — cleansed, namely, by the water of baptism and by penance
**“he shall enter”** — by the knowledge of faith
**“into the camp,”** — of the Church
**“and shall be unclean until the evening.”** — the end of the world: then indeed the remnant shall be saved.
**“UNTIL THE EVENING”** — AUGUSTINE. At evening the priest enters, because the unbelieving people, which until the evening, that is, the end of the world, is set outside the commandments of life as outside the camp, defiled with wicked works, washed by the water of baptism and by penance, returns to knowledge at the end of the world as into the camp.
19.8:
**“He also that hath burned her,”** — Those who offer the heifer are unclean, and those who laid hold of Christ.
**“shall wash his garments,”** — the outward works
**“and his body,”** — the inner mind
**“and shall be unclean until the evening.”** — the end of the world
19.9:
**“shall gather up”** — by acknowledging
**“And a man that is clean”**
• The Gentile, clean by faith; whence: "Purifying their hearts by faith."
• AND SHALL GATHER UP. AUGUSTINE. And a clean man shall gather the ashes of the heifer, the remains, namely, of the slaying and of the burning, that is, the fame which followed the passion and resurrection of Christ; because there are remains for the peaceable man. Christ was ashes, because he was condemned by the unbelieving as dead; and yet he cleansed, because he was believed to have risen by the unbelieving. And because this fame shone out most among the other nations, which were not of the fellowship of the Jews, it is said: a clean man shall gather the ashes of the heifer; clean, namely, from the slaying of Christ, which made the Jews guilty. And he shall lay them up in a clean place, that is, shall handle them honourably; yet without the camp, because the gospel word shone out outside the celebration of the Jewish custom.
• They are clean who preach the passion of Christ to the Gentiles.
**“GREGORY”**
