• The priest burns the cow, a clean man gathers the ashes; because the Jew slew the weakness of the Lord, the Gentile understands his subtle mysteries.
• The clean man pours out the ashes of the cow in a most pure place when any learned man taken from among the Gentiles seeks out the hearts of the Gentiles made clean through humility and does not cease to hand on to them the mysteries of the Redeemer. And when this is done the faith of the Gentiles is multiplied, the divine power is known, the discipline of the precepts is held. Whence he adds: that they may be reserved for the multitude of the children of Israel. For Israel is interpreted a man seeing God, and the Gentile world well converted is called Israel, which now contemplates God by faith.
**“the ashes of the cow,”** — the most subtle sacraments of the incarnation
**“SHALL POUR THEM FORTH”** — Because the Gentile does not cease to preach the sacraments which he has come to know, but makes them manifest to those who know them not.
**“WITHOUT THE CAMP”** — Because all the Gentile world is outside the law, outside the sacrifice, outside the synagogue.
**“IN A MOST CLEAN PLACE”** — Because the secrets of the Lord's incarnation are not to be handed on to wicked and polluted minds, but to those who, coming to the faith, have cleansed their heart.
**“FOR THE MULTITUDE OF THE CHILDREN”** — AUGUSTINE. Another text: And it shall be to the congregation of the children of Israel for keeping. The water of aspersion is purification. Afterwards he declares more fully how the water of aspersion was made from this ash, by which they were cleansed from contact with the dead, that is, from the iniquity of this dying or deathly life. But what follows is strange. And he who gathers, it says, the ashes of the heifer shall wash his garments and shall be unclean until the evening. How shall he be made unclean by this, who came to it clean? Unless that those also who seem to themselves clean in the Christian faith acknowledge that all have sinned and need the glory of God, being justified freely by his blood. Yet he said that this man washes his garments, not his body also. I believe that by the gathering of that ash and laying it up in a clean place (if these things are understood spiritually) he wishes him to be understood as already cleansed within. As Cornelius, hearing and believing what Peter preached, was so cleansed that before visible baptism he received, with his own who were present, the gift of the Holy Ghost also. But neither could the visible sacrament be despised, so that being washed outwardly too he should in a manner wash his garments.
**“TO BE RESERVED”** — Because the more subtle sacraments, handed on to the clean hearts of the Gentiles, are turned into a fortification of the mind. Because while we attend by imitation to the secret and subtle things of his working, we provide cleanness for ourselves by this.
**“that they may be reserved for the multitude of the children of Israel, and for a water of aspersion: because the cow was burnt for sin.”**
• On account of working, the ashes are for our keeping; but on account of baptism, for a water of aspersion.
• Then we providently keep the ashes for our keeping when we carefully consider our Redeemer, who suffered for our iniquities. For we weigh what he will render to the good, who willed to die for the wicked; what we, brought to the justice of faith, owe to his grace, who, set in iniquity, received the intercession of his death.
19.10:
**“And when he that carried the ashes of the cow, hath washed his garments,”** — not his body also
**“he shall be unclean until the evening.”** — some stain of this life being contracted, even after full remission of sins
**“The children of Israel, and the strangers”** — Gentile proselytes
**“SHALL OBSERVE THIS”** — AUGUSTINE. And it shall be to the children of Israel and to the proselytes who are added an everlasting ordinance, etc. What else does it show but the baptism of Christ, which the water of aspersion signified, to be of profit to both Jews and Gentiles, that is, to the children of Israel and to the proselytes, as to the natural branches and to the wild olive grafted into the fatness of the root? But whom does it not move that after the washing it is said of each one: and he shall be unclean until the evening? Not here only, but in all or nearly all such cleansings; where I do not know what is to be understood, except that every man, after the fullest remission of sins, by remaining in this life contracts something whereby he is unclean until the end of life, where this day is in a manner closed, which the evening signifies.
**“that dwell among them,”** — as grafted into the fatness of the root
19.11: **“HE THAT TOUCHETH THE CORPSE”** — AUGUSTINE. He that toucheth the dead body, etc. He begins to say how men made unclean are purified by that water of aspersion. He that toucheth, it says, a dead man, every soul of a man, shall be unclean seven days. This one shall be purified on the third and on the seventh day, and shall be clean. And here I understand nothing else than that the touching of a dead man is iniquity. And I think the uncleanness of seven days is said on account of soul and body: the soul in the number three, the body in the number four; according to which I think it is said by the prophet: For three crimes and for four I will not turn.
19.12:
**“Shall be sprinkled with this water on the third day,”** — that Christ may be believed to have risen from the dead on the third day
**“and on the seventh, and so shall be cleansed. If he were not sprinkled on the third day, he cannot be cleansed on the seventh.”**
• in the kingdom, namely, of the saints, the Lord coming
• IF ON THE THIRD DAY, etc. AUGUSTINE. But if he is not purified on the third day and the seventh day, he shall not be clean; everyone who has touched a dead man, of any soul of a body, and has died having touched the dead before he is or has been purified, defiles the tabernacle of the Lord; that soul shall be cut off from Israel. It is to be noted that it is very hard to find in these books anything written more evidently of the life of the soul after death. Here, then, when he says that if he has died before purification, the uncleanness remains on him and that soul is cut off from Israel, that is, from the fellowship of the people of God, what else does he wish to be understood than that punishment remains for the soul even after death, if while it lives it has not been cleansed by this sacrament by which the baptism of Christ is figured? Because the water of aspersion, it says, has not been sprinkled upon him, he is unclean; his uncleanness is still in him. Still, that is, even after death.
19.13:
**“Every one that toucheth the corpse of a human soul, and is with this mixture sprinkled”** — fortified, namely, by faith in this grace
**“not, shall profane the tabernacle of the Lord, and shall perish out of Israel:”** — from the kingdom of the saints
**“SHALL PROFANE THE TABERNACLE”** — As far as in him lies; according to that: Extinguish not the spirit, though that cannot be extinguished. For if he wished the tabernacle to be understood as made unclean by this, he would command it to be cleansed.
19.15:
**“The vessel”** — any man
**“that hath no cover,”** — the veil of silence
**“THE VESSEL THAT HATH NO COVER”** — GREGORY. The covering of the lid or the binding is the censure of discipline; whoever is not held down by it is rejected as an unclean and polluted vessel. For he is defiled as a vessel without lid or binding who, lying open through the pursuit of display, is covered by no veil of silence.
**“nor binding”** — the censure of discipline
19.16: **“IF ANY MAN IN THE FIELD”** — AUGUSTINE. Another text: Everyone who touches upon the face of the field one wounded, or dead, or the bone of a slain man, or a tomb, etc. It is asked what he understands by wounded, or dead? For if he meant one thing by wounded and another by dead, care must be taken lest he who touches a living wounded man be thought unclean too; which is surely absurd. But because the dead also can be wounded, he is understood to have distinguished the dead themselves, so that we understand either a wounded dead man, that is, one killed by a wound, or one dead without a wound.
19.17: **“And they shall take”** — the clean, namely
19.18:
**“in which when a man that is clean”** — a minister of Christ, that is, one who bears his person
**“shall dip hyssop,”** — faith
**“he shall sprinkle therewith”** — others: with it
19.19: **“And in this manner he that is clean shall purify the unclean on the third and on the seventh day. And being expiated the seventh day, he shall wash both himself and his garments, and be unclean until the evening.”** — HE SHALL WASH BOTH HIMSELF, etc. And he shall wash his garments, and shall be washed with water, and shall be unclean until the evening. The water of aspersion is one thing, and that with which he washed his garments another. And he shall be washed with water, which I think is to be understood as spiritual, by signification, not by its proper nature. For without doubt it was visible, like all the shadows of things to come. But he who is rightly washed by the sacrament of baptism (which that water of aspersion figured) is cleansed spiritually, so that he is clean in body and spirit. And as to his saying that the water of aspersion is sprinkled with hyssop, which herb we have said signifies faith, what else occurs but what is written: "Purifying their hearts by faith"? For baptism does not profit if faith is lacking. And he said these things are done by a clean man, where the ministers are signified who bear the person of the Lord, who is truly the clean man. For of these ministers he will say in what follows: And whoever sprinkles the water of aspersion shall wash his garments, that is, shall keep them, and in body. And he who touches the water of aspersion shall be unclean until the evening; and whatever the unclean man touches shall be unclean, and the soul that touches it shall be unclean until the evening.

20.1: **“And the children of Israel, and all the multitude came into the desert of Sin, in the first month: and the people abode in Cades. And Mary died there, and was buried in the same place.”** — AND THE CHILDREN CAME, etc. ISIDORE. The thirty-third station is in the desert of Sin; this is Cades. And Sin is interpreted "holy", by antiphrasis, as a grove is called lucus when it is least lucid, or war bellum when it is horrid. At this station Mary dies and is buried, who signifies prophecy dead; as Moses and Aaron signify the end of the law and of the priesthood, which cannot come to the land of promise nor lead the people out of the wilderness of this world; which Christ alone does, that is, the Saviour, the Son of God.
20.11:
**“And when Moses had lifted up”** — the Jew placed under the law of Moses
**“his hand, striking with the rod”** — fastening him to the wood of the cross
**“STRIKING WITH THE ROD”** — AUGUSTINE. That water was brought out of the rock the Apostle explained, saying: "And all drank the same spiritual drink: and they drank of the spiritual rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ." Signified, therefore, is the spiritual grace flowing from Christ, by which the inner thirst is watered. But that the rock is struck with the rod figures the cross of Christ; for when the wood came to the rock grace flowed; and that it is struck twice signifies the cross more evidently. For the cross is two pieces of wood.
**“twice”** — because of the two pieces of wood of the same cross
**“the rock,”** — Christ
**“there came forth water”** — of spiritual grace
20.12: **“BECAUSE YOU HAVE NOT BELIEVED”** — ISIDORE. Here Moses offends the Lord and is forbidden to cross the Jordan; for, troubled by the murmuring of the people, he struck the rock with the rod doubtingly, as though God could not bring water out of the rock, which he had done before. Here Moses signifies the Jewish people placed under the law. For as Moses, striking the rock with the rod, doubted of the power of God, so that people, placed under the law given through Moses, fastened Christ to the wood of the cross, but did not believe him to be the power of God. But as from the stricken rock water flowed for the thirsty, so the wound of the Lord's passion was made life for believers. This carnal doubting of the divinity of God, therefore, God commands to die in the height of Christ himself, when he orders the death of Moses' flesh to take place on the mountain. For as Christ is the rock, so also the mountain: Christ the rock, lowly strength; the mountain, eminent greatness. For the prudence of the flesh lives when the humility of Christ in the cross is despised, as a rock that is struck; for Christ crucified is unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Gentiles foolishness. The prudence of the flesh dies when Christ is acknowledged exalted, as the eminence of a mountain. For unto them that are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God.
20.13: **“This is the Water of contradiction, where the children of Israel strove with words against the Lord, and he was sanctified in them.”** — THIS IS THE WATER, etc. AUGUSTINE. What is said of that water which flowed from the rock: This is the water of contradiction, because the children of Israel railed before the Lord, and he was sanctified in them. First they railed when they spoke against the benefit of God by which they had been brought out of Egypt; and afterwards he was sanctified in them, when his holiness was declared in the miracle. Or perhaps he showed two kinds of men, those who contradict the grace of Christ and those who receive it, so that to the former it is the water of contradiction. For of him it is said: "for a sign which shall be contradicted".
20.17: **“And we beseech thee that we may have leave to pass through thy country. We will not go through the fields, nor through the vineyards, we will not drink the waters of thy wells,”** — freely, namely; but: we will pay the price; which he declares in what follows.
20.22: **“TO MOUNT HOR”** — The thirty-fourth station is at mount Hor, in the furthest borders of Edom, into which Aaron went up according to the command of the Lord. And he died in the fortieth year of the going out of Israel from Egypt, namely when the new people was about to enter the land of promise. And although on the mountain he left the priesthood to his son Eleazar, and the law brings those who have fulfilled it to the summit, yet that very loftiness is not beyond the Jordan, but in the furthest borders of earthly works. And the people mourns him thirty days. Aaron is mourned; but Jesus is not mourned. In the law is the descent to hell; in the Gospel, the ascent to Paradise.

21.1: **“And when king Arad the Chanaanite, who dwelt towards the south, had heard this, to wit, that Israel was come by the way of the spies, he fought against them, and overcoming them carried off their spoils.”** — AND WHEN HE HAD HEARD. The Chanaanite heard that Israel had come to the place of the spies, where once the people had offended; he joined battle and led Israel captive. And again in the same place there is fighting; by a vow the victor is vanquished, the vanquished overcome. In which it is understood that when enemies have attacked us, destitute of the help of God, and taken us captive, we should not despair; for it may come about that we conquer where we were conquered.
21.3: **“ANATHEMA”** — AUGUSTINE. And he anathematized him and his cities, and the name of that place was called Anathema; so that the victor should carry off nothing thence for his own uses, but vow the whole to punishment. For to anathematize is what is commonly called to devote. And the origin of this word is in the Greek tongue, from those things which, vowed and paid, that is, promised and rendered, were set up aloft in the temples: apotoianathome, that is, to set up aloft, either by fixing or by hanging.
21.4: **“And they marched from mount Hor, by the way that leadeth to the Red Sea, to compass the land of Edom. And the people began to be weary of their journey and labour:”** — THEY MARCHED, etc. The thirty-fifth station is in Salmona. The thirty-sixth station is in Phinon. These two are not found in the order of the history. In these, Aaron being dead, Israel murmurs against God and Moses, loathes the manna, is wounded by serpents. And beautifully is Salmona interpreted "little image", because there the image of Christ was expressed by the brazen serpent which hung on the wood. And Phinon is interpreted "mouth", because when we know his passion, what we believe with the heart we pronounce with the mouth. For with the heart we believe unto justice, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.
21.8: **“And the Lord said to him: Make a brazen serpent, and set it up for a sign: whosoever being struck shall look on it, shall live.”** — MAKE A BRAZEN SERPENT, etc. ISIDORE. The bites of the serpents were healed when the brazen serpent was lifted up and looked upon, because Christ triumphed over the ancient serpent on the gibbet and shut out his poisons, so that he who truly and expressly looks upon the image of the Son of God and his passion may be healed. Whence: "As Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert" etc. The brazen serpent is hung on the wood because brass is more durable than the other metals; and Christ, dead through his humanity in the serpent, lives through his divinity, as being of brass.
21.10:
**“And the children of Israel setting forwards camped in Oboth.”**
• magicians or pythons
• AND THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL SETTING FORWARDS CAMPED, etc. The thirty-seventh station is in Oboth, which is rendered "magicians" or "pythons". Because after the image of God, which is shown in the reason of the heart, and the confession of faith, which is uttered with the mouth, serpents and evil arts rise up. But let us, keeping our heart with all watchfulness, stop our ears, that we may not hear the voices of enchanters and the songs of the sirens.
21.11:
**“And departing thence they pitched their tents in Jeabarim, in the wilderness, that faceth Moab toward the east.”**
• AND DEPARTING THENCE, etc. JEROME. In Jeabarim, a heap, namely of stones passing over. These are the saints who hasten to pass through this world to other stations. For there are holy stones which roll over the earth, light and polished, and by their roundness like the wheels of chariots. There are others to be taken out of the way, lest they strike the feet of those who walk. Whence Isaias: "Lift up the stones from the head of the streets."
• And as to its being said, in the borders of Moab, and written above, in the wilderness of Moab, which faces Moab toward the rising of the sun, it shows according to the letter that up to this point they were in the borders of the Edomites, and now come to the boundary of Moab, from one province, namely, to another. For not always is one virtue to be striven after; but one must go from virtue to virtue and pass from one to another. For they cleave to one another and are so joined that he who lacks one lacks all. And this belongs properly to those who consider the rising of the sun of justice.
21.12:
**“And removing from thence, they came to the torrent Zared:”**
• a strange descent
• THEY CAME TO THE TORRENT ZARED, etc. The thirty-ninth station was in Dibongad, as is written in the series of the stations, which is interpreted "temptation strongly understood". But in place of this, in the order of the history, it is said that from Jeabarim they came to the torrent Zared. Then they camped beyond the Arnon, which is in the wilderness of the borders of the Amorrhite, on the boundaries of the Moabites and the Amorrhites. And afterwards they came to the well where they sang this song: "Spring up, O well, which the princes dug" etc. And from the wilderness to Mathana, then to the torrents of God, and after to the high places, and from the high places to the valley which is in the country of Moab. Some, interpreting these places in the borders of the Amorrhites, think they are not stations but crossings, and that an extraordinary exposition ought not to prejudge the catalogue of the stations. Others, comparing spiritual things with spiritual, will not have regions signified, but by the names of the places the progress of virtues: that after the magicians and the gatherings of stones we often come to the torrent Zared, which is interpreted "a strange descent", and placed in the descent pass over to the Arnon, that is, the curse, which is set in the borders of the Amorrhites, who are bitter enemies, or speak much. And if we pass the boundaries of Moab (who was born or begotten of incest and departed from the true father), there meets us the well which no common or ignoble man dug, but princes and leaders, who prophesy singing where they are to pass over in the desert, namely to Mathana, that is, the house of Juda; to Nahaliel, that is, the torrents of God; then to Bamoth, which is interpreted "high places" or "death coming", when we are made conformable to the death of Christ. Afterwards there meets us the valley of humility, which yet is set on the top of mount Phasga, which is interpreted "hewn", namely having nothing shapeless or rough, which looks toward the wilderness, which in Hebrew is called Sinen; because, set on the summit of the virtues, we look upon the ruins of the whole world and the desolation of all sins. Dibongad is interpreted "temptation strongly understood". After Dibongad there is fighting against Sehon king of the Amorrhites and Og king of Basan. And when we have come to the summit and have drunk from the fountain of the princes, going up the mountains of Phasga, let us not be proud, but fear the wilderness set before us.
21.13: **“Which they left and encamped over against Arnon,”** — the curse
21.14: **“IN THE BOOK OF THE WARS OF THE LORD”** — AUGUSTINE. He did not say in what book it is written, or of what prophet or patriarch; nor is it to be denied that there were already books, either of the Chaldeans, whence Abraham came out, or of the Egyptians, where Moses had learned all their wisdom, or of any other nation, in some one of which books this could have been written. Yet it is not therefore to be taken into those scriptures to which divine authority is committed. For it was lawful for divine authority to take a true testimony whence it would; but it does not therefore confirm that all things written there are to be received. But why this is mentioned in this place does not plainly appear, unless perhaps, since a war was waged so that boundaries should be set there between two nations, the men of that place said because of its greatness that it was a war of the Lord, so that it was written in some book of theirs: the war of the Lord.
21.16:
**“When they went from that place, the well appeared whereof the Lord said to Moses: Gather the people together, and I will give them water.”** — WHEN THEY WENT FROM THAT PLACE, THE WELL APPEARED WHEREOF THE LORD SAID, etc. ORIGEN. What is it that the Lord earnestly commands Moses to gather the people, that he may give them waters from the well to drink? As though they would not come together of their own accord to drink. The Spirit says through Solomon in the Proverbs: "Drink water out of thy own cistern, and the streams of thy own well; and let not the waters overflow thee outside thy fountain." Although in other copies we have read: "and let thy waters be poured out outside thy well." Each one therefore has within himself a well, nay many wells and many vessels of water. Whence he says: "Out of thy own vessels and out of the fountain of thy wells." Abraham had wells, and Isaac. In the Gospel the Saviour sat upon a well, resting after his labour and saying: "That if anyone drinks of the waters which the earthly well contained, he will thirst again. But whoever drinks of those which Jesus gives, there will become in him a fountain of living water, springing up into life everlasting." And elsewhere it is said: "He that believeth in him, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water." He therefore who believes in him will have in himself not a well but wells, not only fountains but rivers; not such as are wont to bestow mortal life, but such as bestow eternal. According to these things, therefore, which we read in the Proverbs, "where wells with a fountain are numbered or named, the word of God is to be understood": a well, if it covers a deep mystery; a fountain, if it flows out to the peoples. And it is to be asked how Wisdom in the Proverbs speaks of wells in the plural and of a fountain in the singular: "Drink waters from the fountain of thy wells?" Let us see, therefore, of what wells he called one the fountain. I think that the knowledge of the unbegotten Father can be understood as one well, and the knowledge of the only-begotten Son as another; for the Son is other than the Father, nor the same as the Father. Whence: "It is another that beareth witness of me, the Father." The third well is the knowledge of the Holy Ghost; for the Spirit is other than the Father and the Son. Whence: "The Father will send you another Paraclete, the Spirit of truth." There is therefore this distinction of three persons in the Father and the Son and the Holy Ghost, which is brought back to the plural number of wells; of which there is one fountain, because there is one substance and nature of the Trinity.
**“ORIGEN”** — Those wells also can be seen of whose knowledge he speaks who was filled with the Wisdom of God: For he hath given me the true knowledge of the things that are, that I should know the knowledge of the world, and the virtues of the elements, the beginning and ending and midst of the times, the alterations of their courses and the changes of seasons, the revolutions of the year and the dispositions of the stars, the natures of living creatures and the rage of wild beasts etc. You see how many wells there are in the knowledge of things. There is a well, the knowledge of plants; and perhaps the nature of each plant has its own well. Again there is a well, the knowledge of animals; and perhaps each species of animals has its own well; and each of these (since they have a deep knowledge) are rightly said to be wells. And while the mystery of Christ was hidden from ages and generations, the knowledge of these things is rightly called wells. But when God has made them manifest to believers through the Holy Ghost, all these become fountains and rivers, so that the knowledge of them is no longer held in secret, but waters believers and satisfies them. Therefore, I believe, the Saviour said that he who believes in him and drinks the water of his doctrine, in him there will be no longer a well nor a fountain, but rivers of living water. For as one well, that is, the word of God, becomes wells and fountains and rivers, so the soul of man, which is to the image of God, can have in itself and bring forth wells and fountains and rivers. But the wells which are in our soul need one to dig them, that they may be cleansed and what is earthy be taken away, so that those veins of rational senses which God has set in them may bring forth pure and sincere streams. For while earth covers them, the pure wave of water cannot flow forth. Therefore it is written that the servants of Abraham dug wells, but the Philistines covered them with earth. Isaac too, who had received his father's inheritance, dug his father's wells and removed the earth which the Philistines had thrown in. And note that while Abraham lived the Philistines dared not fill up the wells or throw earth in; but when he was dead they grew strong and laid snares for his wells; but they are restored by Isaac. The servant of Abraham too found Rebecca at the wells, who is interpreted "patience". She becomes the wife of Isaac, but at the wells. Likewise Jacob, when he came to Mesopotamia having his father's command not to take a foreign wife, found Rachel at the wells, and Moses Sephora. If therefore you have understood what and of what kind are the wives of the saints, if you wish to lead or take patience in marriage, or wisdom and the other virtues of the soul, and to say what is said of wisdom: Her have I sought to take for my bride, be constantly about these wells, and there you will find a spouse of this kind; because it is certain that the virtues dwell by the streams of the living word. There are therefore many wells within the soul, and very many others in each of the words and senses of the scriptures. This one, then, is the more eminent, which not any men whatever dug, but princes, and those higher than these whom he called kings. Therefore hymns are sung to God at this well; and it is written that this is the well whereof the Lord said to Moses: Gather the people, and I will give them water from the well.
**“GATHER THE PEOPLE TOGETHER”** — Allegorically. The law calls you to the well, Christ, namely the Son of God, subsisting indeed in his own substance, yet named with the Father and the Spirit by the one fountain of the Godhead. To this well, therefore, that is, to the faith of Christ, the law calls you together. Whence he himself says that Moses wrote of me. And it calls us that we may drink the waters and sing a song to him; that is, believe with the heart unto justice and confess with the mouth unto salvation.
21.17:
**“Then Israel sung this song: Let the well spring up.”**
• SEPTUAGINT: Begin to him the well; that is: confess the well to be at the beginning of all things.
• Or thus: so that the words are directed from the person of Moses to the people. Give a beginning to your heart, that you may begin to understand what the well is from which the spiritual waters are to be drawn and the people of believers refreshed. Begin, therefore, to him, that is, to Israel, this well, so that if anyone sees God with the heart he may draw the mystic sense from the depths. To this well Moses, that is, the law, gathers; to which someone seems to come, but unless he is gathered by Moses he is not accepted by God. Marcion seems to himself to have come, and Basilides and Valentinus; but because they did not come through Moses, nor received the law and the prophets, they cannot praise God from the fountains of Israel. Such, therefore, do not come to the well which the princes dug and the kings hewed out. And there is a salt valley in which there are wells of bitumen. And every heresy and every sin is in the valley, and in the salt valley. For sin does not go up on high, but always descends to the depths and to the lower things. Every heretical sense, therefore, and every act of sin is set in the valley, salt and bitter. For what sweet, what pleasant thing can sin have? But if you have come to a heretical opinion and the bitterness of sin, you have come to the wells of bitumen, which is the food and nourishment of fire. If you taste the water of these wells, if you receive a heretical sense and the bitterness of sin, you will prepare in yourself the fuel of fire and the burnings of gehenna. To such it is said: "Walk in the light of your fire" etc. The princes dug it and the kings hewed it out. The princes therefore dug, the kings hewed out; which is said from hewing out, not from cutting down. For that is said to be hewn out which is cut or shaped in stone. The princes, as being lower, dug, that is, sank a certain depth as into the softness of earth. But these whom he calls kings, as stronger, penetrate not only the depth of the earth but the hardness of the rock, that they may reach the deeper waters and search out the very veins of the abyss, knowing that the judgments of God are a great deep. These are the apostles, one of whom says: "But to us God hath revealed them by his Spirit." For the Spirit searcheth all things, yea, the deep things of God. Those, therefore, who through the Holy Ghost can search the deep things and penetrate the profound mysteries of the well are said to be kings, who hewed out the well in the rock, because they penetrated the hard and difficult secrets of knowledge. The princes therefore dug this well and the kings of the nations hewed it out, that is, the apostles, who gathered the nations to obedience of faith and opened to all the knowledge of Christ, in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. For they fulfilled the command of God, teaching all nations and baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost. And by this they hewed out, that is, laid open, the knowledge of the well. These things too which we have in hand are a well for us, and all the scripture of the law and the prophets, the gospel too and the apostolic, together are one well, which none can dig or hew out but kings and princes, who namely can take away the earth and remove the surface of the letter, and from the lower rock, where Christ is, bring forth spiritual senses as living water. They are called kings because they have expelled the kingdom of sin and set the kingdom of justice in their members. For it befits him to teach the rest who has first done what he teaches. Whence: "He that shall do and teach, he shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven." And to be great in the kingdom is to be a king.
**“LET THE WELL SPRING UP”** — ORIGEN. Begin to him the well; that is, set the well as the beginning of all things, because he himself is the beginning and the firstborn of every creature.
21.18:
**“The well, which the princes dug,”** — others: kings
**“THE PRINCES”** — The same can be called princes and kings; or we understand the prophets as princes. For they set the sense and prophecy of Christ, buried, in the depth of the letter. Therefore it is said of them: "But if you will not hear in secret, your soul shall weep." And elsewhere: "O how great is the multitude of thy sweetness, O Lord, which thou hast hidden for them that fear thee!" The kings are the apostles, who search the deep things of God and rule the churches. Whence Christ too is called King of kings.
**“and the chiefs of the people prepared by the direction of the lawgiver, and with their staves. From the wilderness to Mathana.”** — their gifts
**“AND THE CHIEFS PREPARED”** — ORIGEN. The kings of the nations, it says, hewed it out in their kingdom, while they ruled over them. For they cannot dig this well, nor open the hidden veins of living water, unless they are first lords of the barbarous nations. Whatever was wild in them in their acts, whatever barbarous in their manners, they tamed and subjected to the royal sense, that they might act not in the manner of the Gentiles but lawfully. These truly are kings, probing the depths of the well and searching out the secrets of the word of God.
21.19:
**“From Mathana unto Nahaliel:”**
• from God
• He who drinks from this well advances to this, that he has gifts to offer to God, of which it is said in the law: "My gifts, my presents." From the things, therefore, which God has given, there is offering to God. And he gave the knowledge of himself, and man offers him his faith and affection.
• When we have offered the things that are from God, we obtain the things that are from God. For when we have offered our faith and affection, then he bestows the divers gifts of the Holy Ghost, of which it is said: "But all things are of God."
**“THEY MARCHED”** — ORIGEN. Setting out from the well they came to Mathana, which is interpreted "their gifts". For God asks faith and affection from man. Whence: "And now, Israel, what doth the Lord thy God require of thee, but that thou fear the Lord, and walk in his ways, and love him" etc. These gifts must be given by us to the Lord after we have drunk the knowledge of his goodness from the depth of the well. And note that the prophet says "require of thee", that those may blush who deny that it is in the choice of man to be saved. For how would God require of man, unless man had in his power what he ought to offer to him who requires it? There are therefore things that are given by God and things given by man. It was in man to make five pounds of one; from God, that man should have the pound from which he could make ten pounds. And when he had offered from himself, he received from God no longer money but power and the kingdom of ten cities. God asked Abraham to offer him his son. He offered him fearlessly, laid him on the altar, drew the knife to slay him; but at once he is stopped, and a ram is given instead of his son for the victim. You see, therefore, that the things we offer to God remain to us; but they are required of us that our affection and faith may be proved.
**“UNTO BAMOTH”** — Bamoth, the coming of death; by which, namely, we die with him that we may live with him, and mortify our members which are upon the earth. For we are buried together with him by baptism into death. For he who keeps the order of the saving way ought to make his journey through each of these and after many to come to this place.
**“from Nahaliel unto Bamoth.”** — ORIGEN. The same, and from Bamoth, it says, into the grove which is in the plain of Moab, from the top of the mount of Cesi, which looks toward the desert. If we walk by this journey, which consists not so much in the names of places as in the progress of the soul, after all things we come into the grove, or according to others into Ranan, which is interpreted "ascent" or "top of the mountain". Through these things, therefore, one comes to that famous grove of paradise and the pleasant delights of the ancient dwelling, or to the summit of perfection and beatitude, so that we may say that he has raised us up together with him and made us sit in the heavenly places with Christ. You see how far one comes from the well; by what stations, nay progresses, the journey of the soul to heaven is prepared.
21.21:
**“And Israel sent”** — others: Moses
**“AND HE SENT”** — THE SAME. Israel sends ambassadors to the king of the Amorrhites, namely the proud king, who said: "By the strength of my own hand I have done it, and by my own wisdom I have understood, and have removed the bounds of the people" etc. And: "I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars" etc. That proud and lifted-up one too is as it were his only-begotten, of whom it is written: "Who is lifted up above all that is called God, or that is worshipped" etc. Every one, therefore, who is lifted up is a son of this lifted-up one, or his disciple and imitator. Whence: "Lest being puffed up he fall into the judgment of the devil." In which it is shown that every one lifted up will be condemned like the devil. We therefore, who wish to pass through this world that we may come to the holy land promised to the saints, send with peaceable words to Sehon, promising that we will not dwell in his land nor tarry with him, but only pass through, going by the king's way, or the royal way, turning aside nowhere, neither into field nor into vineyard, nor drinking of his vat. For when we come to the water of baptism and receive the seals of the first faith, we renounce the devil and his pomps and all his works and all his services and pleasures; which is foreshadowed when it is said: "That Israel turn not aside into his field nor into his vineyard, nor drink of his vat." For the faithful no longer drinks of diabolical discipline, not of astrological, not of magical, or of that doctrine which is against the piety of God. For he has his own fountains, and will drink of the fountains of Israel, of the fountains of the Saviour, not of the vat of Sehon. Nor, leaving the fountain of living water, does he gather to himself broken or crushed cisterns.
**“messengers to Sehon king of the Amorrhites,”** — that is, of the unbelieving, namely who lead God into bitterness
**“TO SEHON THE KING”** — Sehon, who is interpreted "unfruitful tree" or "lifted up". This is the king of the Amorrhites, who are interpreted "leading into bitterness" or "speaking". This is the devil, lifted up and unfruitful, of whom it is said: "The prince of this world cometh, and in me he hath not any thing." And elsewhere: "Now shall the prince of this world be cast out"; not because he created the world, but because sinners are in the world. And he himself is the prince of sin, according to what is said: "That the whole world is seated in wickedness", and he himself is the prince of the world.
21.22:
**“I beseech thee that I may have leave to pass through thy land: we will not go aside into the fields or the vineyards, we will not drink waters”** — diabolical discipline, or that contrary to piety
**“of the wells, we will go the king's highway, till we be past thy borders.”** — THE KING'S HIGHWAY, etc. Who says: "I am the way, and the truth, and the life." Of whom it is said: "Give to the king thy judgment, O God." By this one must walk and turn aside nowhere, neither into field nor into vineyard; that is, neither to diabolical works nor to diabolical senses; we wish to pass peaceably through the world. But this rather stirs up the prince of the world, that we say we do not wish to remain with him or tarry or touch anything of his. Thence he is angry and moves persecutions and threatens perils of torment. Thence he says: "Sehon gathered his people" etc.
21.23:
**“AN ARMY”** — With princes, namely, and judges of the world, and all the ministers of wickedness, who always assail the people of God.
**“TO JASA”** — In Jasa or Isaar, which is interpreted "fulfilment of the commandment". For if we come to the fulfilment of the commandments, we overcome the proud and lifted-up one. For to fulfil the commandment is to overcome the devil and his army. For nothing will be able to harm us if we come into Isaar, that is, if we keep the precepts of our Lord Jesus Christ.
21.24:
**“And he was slain by them with the edge of the sword, and they possessed his land from the Arnon”** — a city
**“WITH THE EDGE OF THE SWORD”** — "For the word of God is living and effectual, and more piercing than any two edged sword" etc. Of which the Apostle says: "And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God." By the edge of this falls Sehon, that is, the devil.
**“HIS LAND”** — Every earthly region is called the land of Sehon. But Christ and his Church have dominion in all the land of Sehon.
**“FROM THE ARNON UNTO THE JEBOC”** — Jeboc is a city and the end of the kingdom of Sehon, as the Arnon is its beginning. And Arnon is interpreted "their curses"; Jeboc, "wrestling". For he who wishes to go out of the kingdom of the devil must wrestle with his ministers. But if he has conquered, Jeboc will no longer be the city of Sehon but of Israel. Hence Jacob, when he had come to a certain place, a contest was prepared for him, and having wrestled there all night, when he had prevailed his name was called Israel.
21.25:
**“So Israel took all his cities, and dwelt in the cities of the Amorrhite, to wit, in Hesebon, and in the villages thereof.”** — SO ISRAEL TOOK, etc. AUGUSTINE. Here Israel possessed the cities of the Amorrhites which it overcame in war, because it did not anathematize them. For if it had anathematized them, it could not possess them, nor take anything thence for its own uses. And note how just wars were waged: for an inoffensive passage was refused, which was owed by the right of human society; but now, that God might fulfil his commands or promises, he helped the Israelites here, to whom the land of the Amorrhites was to be given. For when Edom likewise refused passage, the Israelites did not fight with that nation, that is, the sons of Jacob with the sons of Esau, because he had not promised that land to the Israelites; but they turned aside from them.
**“ISRAEL”** — He who is Israel in Christ, not in the flesh, but seeing openly, dwells in all the cities of the Amorrhites, when the churches of Christ are spread through the whole world. But each of us too was formerly a city of king Sehon, who is interpreted "lifted up". For folly, pride, impiety and all things that are on the side of the devil reigned in us. But when the strong man was overcome and his goods plundered, we were made cities of Israel and the inheritance of the saints; if only the power that before had dominion, and the unfruitful tree, and the lifted-up king, is wholly cut down in us, and we are under him who says: "Learn of me, because I am meek and humble of heart." In Hesebon and its villages etc. He enumerates one by one the cities of the proud and unfruitful king, and names Hesebon, the chief city of his kingdom, which is interpreted "thoughts". Rightly, therefore, the greatest part of the devil's kingdom and the most of his power reigns in the thoughts, because from the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries and the like, which defile a man. Necessarily, therefore, this city is burned up with the fire which the Saviour came to send upon the earth, and wills that it be kindled.
**“ISIDORE”** — In the thirty-ninth station war is waged against Sehon king of the Amorrhites and Og king of Basan. Sehon is interpreted "temptation of the eyes". This is the devil, who transforms himself as into an angel of light, and through heresies and schisms lies with things like the truth, that he may deceive the unwary. Him the Amorrhites, that is, the embittering, have as king. For unless a certain pretence of truth went before, there would be no embittering heresies nor schisms in the Church. This king each one slays when he condemns pretence and loves truth. Og is interpreted "shutting in"; and Basan, "confusion". For the devil acts to shut the way to God by setting idols in the way, lest Christ be believed in. Shutting in goes before as king; confusion follows as the people. For those who are now shut in so as not to believe in Christ will be confounded when Christ appears. Therefore this station, that is, Dibongad, is interpreted "temptation strongly understood". Because if the pretence which embitters the Church through schism or heresy is overcome, and the shutting in which closes the way of faith through sacrilege, the temptation is understood, and being understood is strongly overcome.
21.26:
**“The city Hesebon”** — thoughts, namely
**“was the city of Sehon the king of the Amorrhites, who fought against the king of Moab:”** — from the father, or paternal water
**“OF SEHON THE KING”** — Sehon, that is, of one speaking; for those who act under the devil know how to speak, but they speak vain things, as astrologers and some natural philosophers. But the kingdom of the faithful, which is from God, is not in speech but in the power of God.
**“MOAB”** — RABANUS. Moab, who is interpreted "from the father" or "paternal water", conceived of incest and drunkenness, the father as it were absent and unknowing, signifies worldly knowledge, which has its own sense as author. And because it is begotten by the making of God, it seems to be born of the father. But because it is adulterous and an adversary of the people of God, it is begotten of incest, and in a cave, and by night. Whence according to Isaias: "In the night it perished", that is, in everlasting error. Ar too, the city of the Moabites, which is interpreted "adversary", signifies that this wisdom, hostile to God, is consumed by the fire of truth, the word of the Church fighting against it; by which also the inhabitants of the high places of the Arnon are devoured. For Arnon is interpreted "curse" or "their enlightening". Because those who trust in eloquence or human wisdom, which seems bright to the children of darkness, fall and are consumed.
**“and took all the land, that had been of his dominions, as far as the Arnon.”** — the curse, or their enlightening
21.27: **“THEREFORE IT IS SAID”** — ORIGEN. Another text: For this, it says, the speakers in riddles shall say: Come into Hesebon, that the city of Sehon may be built and set up; for a fire went out from Hesebon and a flame from the city of Sehon, and devoured as far as Moab, etc. Sehon was king, whose city was Hesebon. This is therefore the order of the words, as if the speakers in riddles said: Come, that Hesebon may be built and set up, which was the city of king Sehon. A riddle is called figurative speech; speakers in riddles, those who speak figuratively. These are the law and the prophets. Whence: "I will open my mouth in parables: I will utter propositions from the beginning." And Isaias: "The words of this book, he says, shall be as the words of a book that is sealed." The book is sealed because it is entangled with figures and wrapped in riddles. Come into Hesebon that it may be built: the first fell, overthrown and burned; another is to be rebuilt. If you see a Gentile in comeliness of life and in error of religion, say that this is Hesebon, the city in the kingdom of king Sehon. For the unfruitful and lifted-up king reigns in his thoughts. If Israel approaches him, that is, a son of the Church, applying the darts of the word of God, drawing the sword of the spirit against him, and destroys in him all the fortifications of Gentile dogmas and burns up all the arguments of the lifted-up with the fire of truth, say that Hesebon, the city of king Sehon, is overthrown. Yet it is not left deserted. For when all the children of Israel have overturned evil thoughts and impious senses in men, they build up good thoughts and pious senses; they put in the doctrine of truth, the rite of religion, the order of living and honesty of manners. And then truly these speakers in riddles say to one another: Come, let us build Hesebon, which was the city of Sehon. For the children of the Church, because they understand the riddles of the law spiritually, are called speakers in riddles. Whence: "Lo, I have set thee this day over the nations and over kingdoms, to root up and to pull down, to build and to plant." For he overthrows Hesebon, roots up impure thoughts; but he rebuilds and replants chaste thoughts, so that Hesebon is made not of the Amorrhites but of the children of Israel.
21.29:
**“Woe to thee Moab: thou art undone, O people”**
• gathering
• WOE TO THEE, MOAB, etc. Chamos is interpreted "gathering" or as it were "handling". Dibon, "understanding temptation abundantly" or "their flowing". Iophe, "blowing" or "breathing". Medaba, "from the forest". Woe therefore to those who, trusting in the spiritual Moab, gather to themselves the treasures of worldly wisdom and lift themselves up against the power of God. Whose boldness shall not prevail, but shall flee and be delivered into captivity to the king of the spiritual Amorrhites. For their yoke shall perish from Hesebon unto Dibon; that is, from the root of thought to the depth of understanding their knowledge shall flow away; and weary, blowing out vanities of words and breathing the fetid odour of putrid sense, they shall come into the forest, where there are no fruitful trees but beasts; against which it is said: "Deliver not up to beasts the soul that confesseth to thee."
21.30:
**“Their yoke is perished from Hesebon unto Dibon,”** — understanding temptation abundantly, namely, or their flowing
**“they came weary to Iophe Nophe,”** — blowing or breathing
**“and unto Medaba.”** — from the forest
21.32:
**“And Moses sent”** — the law
**“some to take a view of”** — preachers
**“Jazer: and they took the villages of it,”** — a gathering of peoples
**“JAZER”** — That is, their strength: namely the strongest dogmas of the heretics, built up by the art of dialectic.
**“AND THEY POSSESSED”** — By converting them from error and teaching the precepts of the Lord, that from their correction and progress they might acquire for themselves the heavenly fatherland.
21.33:
**“And they turned themselves, and went up by the way of Basan,”** — of foulness
**“and Og came against them”** — shutting in
**“OG THE KING OF BASAN”** — ORIGEN. To Og king of Basan they neither deign to send ambassadors nor ask of him to pass through his land, but at once fight with him and overcome him and his people. Basan is interpreted "foulness". Rightly, therefore, neither are ambassadors sent to this nation nor is passage asked through its land. For there ought to be no passage or approach of ours to foulness, but it is to be fought from the beginning at once and wholly avoided. And Og is interpreted "shutting in". He holds the figure of all carnal and material things, held by the desire of which the soul is shut out from God; against which war is commanded to be waged so that nothing living be left in him. None, therefore, ought to be left living by the children of Israel in the kingdom of foulness and disgrace. It befits Israelite virtue to cut away impious things, and to build up pious and honourable things. But of the kingdom of Sehon it is not written that none be left alive, nor of the kingdom of Moab. For perhaps we need some of those things for the exercises and struggles of this life; otherwise we ought to have gone out of this world. But of Basan, that is, foulness, we need nothing at all; all the works of foulness are to be shaken off. For in nothing can that be honourable which is foul.

22.2: **“AND BALAC SEEING”** — AUGUSTINE. In what Scripture says, that after Israel had conquered the Amorrhites and possessed all their cities, Balac king of the Moabites sent ambassadors to hire Balaam to curse the people of Israel, it is sufficiently shown that not all the Moabites had come under the dominion of Sehon king of the Amorrhites when he overcame them in war. Since the nation of the Moabites remained until that time, when Balac reigned as king of Moab. And as to what Moab said to the elders of Madian, that is, the Moabites to the elders of the Madianites: Now this congregation will lick up all who are round about us; they were not one nation, but neighbours said to neighbours that it was to be guarded against alike; but two neighbouring nations.
22.4: **“He said to the elders of Madian: So will this people destroy all that dwell in our borders, as the ox is wont”** — the preacher
22.5: **“He sent therefore messengers to Balaam the son of Beor, a soothsayer, who dwelt by the river of the land of the children of Ammon, to call him, and to say: Behold a people is come out of Egypt, that hath covered the face of the earth, sitting over against me.”** — HE SENT THEREFORE, etc. ORIGEN. War threatens you, king Balac; you ought to prepare arms and an army, and go to meet them equipped with arms. But you send many gifts to Balaam the diviner and promise greater, saying: "Come, curse the people which came out of Egypt." And Balaam refers this to God and is forbidden to come; the king sends ambassadors again and puts all his hope in Balaam, that he may hurl curses at the people in place of darts; if perchance by words the people might be overcome whom the king's army could not overcome. What consequence or counsel does this history have? What king ever, with battle threatening him, laid aside arms and fled for refuge to the words of a diviner and soothsayer? First, then, it must be confessed that in some things words avail more than bodies. For what an army cannot accomplish is accomplished by words; and I do not say holy words or words of God, but certain words which are current among men. How to name them I do not know. Yet they are composed by a useless art, whose name may be whatever pleases each one. There were enchanters and magicians in Egypt. What man can by strength of body change a rod into a serpent, or water into blood? Which they did; for Moses had done it first. But because the king of Egypt knew that these things were done by a certain art of words that is current among men, he thought Moses had done this not by the power of God but by magic art, and had pretended it was done by the power of God. At once he calls together the enchanters and magicians of the Egyptians, and makes a contest between him who worked by the power of God and those who invoked demons. The contrary power does the like; but the serpent made by the power of God swallowed up the others. For demonic power could not restore to good the evil it had made from good. It could make a serpent from a rod, but not return a rod from a serpent. Therefore they are all consumed by that which had been turned into a serpent by the power of God, and by divine power it is returned to its own nature, that nature might confess God. The enchanters of the Egyptians turned water into blood, but could not turn blood into water. But the power of God turned not water but the whole river into blood, and at the prayer of Moses returned it to its own nature. The magicians brought forth sciniphs, but could not drive them away; but Moses brought them forth and removed them. For the contrary power can do something evil, but cannot restore to wholeness. And there are differences among magicians: some avail more, others less. Balaam was famous in magic art and mighty in incantations. For he had not the power or art of words for blessing, but for cursing. For demons are invited for cursing, not for blessing. As one experienced in such things, then, he was most renowned in the east. For otherwise the king would not have presumed that this could be done by words which could scarcely be accomplished by iron and battle line. Certain, therefore, and having often made trial, laying aside the instruments of war he sends to the diviner, saying: "Behold a people is come out of Egypt and hath covered the face of the earth" etc. The king also seems to have heard that the children of Israel are wont to conquer enemies by prayer, not by arms; not so much by iron as by prayers. For Israel moved no arms against Pharao, but it was said to him: "The Lord will fight for you, and you shall hold your peace." Against the Amalecites too, not so much the force of arms as the prayer of Moses availed. These things the king of Moab had heard. For it is written: "Nations rose up and were angry; sorrows took hold on the inhabitants of Philisthiim. Then were the princes of Edom troubled, and the princes of the Moabites" etc. He thought therefore within himself, saying: "Because no arms can be matched with the prayers of this people, I must therefore seek prayers that can overcome their prayers." It is written therefore: "And Moab said to the elders of Madian: Now this congregation will lick up all who are round about us, as the calf licks up the grass of the field." Because as the calf tears off the grass of the field with its mouth, and with its tongue as with a sickle cuts whatever it finds, so the people fights with mouth and lips, and has its arms in words. Balac therefore sends to Balaam, that he may oppose words to words and prayers to prayers. And do not wonder whether there is such a thing in magic art. For Scripture marks out this art in order to forbid it, as it signifies that demons exist but forbids them to be worshipped; because the masters of magicians are evil spirits. For none of the holy spirits obeys them; one cannot invoke the great Michael or Raphael or Gabriel; much less, then, can one invoke the Father or the Son or the Holy Ghost. We alone have received this power. But he who has been made partaker of the Holy Ghost ought not to invoke unclean spirits, lest the Holy Ghost flee from him. Magicians are those who invoke Beelzebub. This the people knew, who, lying against the Lord, said: "By Beelzebub the prince of devils he casteth out devils." But the Saviour, knowing that it is true that Beelzebub is the prince of devils, did not reprove them for a lie in this, but answered: "If I by Beelzebub cast out devils, by whom do your children cast them out?" It is clear, therefore, that there are certain evil demons who, invoked by magicians, are present with them for evil, not for good. For they are ready to do evil, but know not how to do good. These, therefore, by a certain art and composition of words, took Balaam into friendship; from whose friendship great fruit was seen among men. The king therefore sends to him, saying: "Come hither and curse me the people" etc.
22.6: **“I KNOW THAT HE IS BLESSED”** — ORIGEN. I do not believe he knew that whomsoever Balaam blessed would be blessed; but he said these things for the sake of flattery, so that by extolling his art he might make him readier for himself. For the magic art does not know how to bless, nor do demons. Isaac and Jacob and all the saints know how to bless. None of the wicked knows how to bless.
22.7:
**“IF BY ANY MEANS I MAY”** — He seems not to trust wholly in Balaam, terrified by the fame of the mighty works which were done among the people of God.
**“And the ancients of Moab, and the elders of Madian, went, having of divination”** — SEPTUAGINT: divinations, namely the price of divination
**“THE PRICE OF DIVINATION”** — Others: divining instruments, in the arts which human curiosity has composed. There are certain things which Scripture has named divining instruments. And Gentile custom calls them tripods or cauldrons or by words of this kind, which, as though consecrated to this, are wont to be moved and handled by them. But divine Scripture in the prophets names the Ephod in the native tongue, which they report to be the garment of those prophesying. Yet prophecy is one thing in divine Scripture, divination another. For it says: There is no soothsaying in Jacob, nor divination in Israel. Divination therefore is wholly renounced; for it is fulfilled by the work and ministry of demons. Balaam therefore, having received the divining instruments, when the demons were wont to come to him, sees them put to flight and God present; whom he therefore says he consults, because he does not see those accustomed to obey him. God therefore comes to Balaam, not because he is worthy, but that those who were wont to be present for cursing and doing evil might be put to flight. For hence God was providing for his people.
22.8:
**“He answered: Tarry here this night, and I will answer whatsoever the Lord shall say to me. And while they stayed with Balaam, God came and said to him:”**
• GOD CAME, etc. It is not said whether this was done in sleep, although it is clear that it was done by night. For afterwards Scripture says: "Balaam rising up" etc.
• Let no one glory if God speaks to him. For he knows how to speak with such, since he speaks even with the reprobate. And when he speaks through angels, he himself speaks.
**“ORIGEN”** — God came and said to him, etc. It can be objected: Let Balaam invoke demons, let him curse the people; let the demons invoked do what they can. Can God not defend the people from the demons and check their force? What need was there that he should come to Balaam and forbid the demons even to attempt to harm the people? Though not all things that may occur are to be brought forward, we shall say however that he does not will to condemn them before the time. For they too know that their time comprises this present age. Whence: "Art thou come hither to torment us before the time?" Therefore he did not remove the devil from the principality of this age, because his works are necessary for the perfecting of those who are to be crowned. So too he does not will to draw the other demons away by force from the intent of their purpose before the time. Therefore he does not permit them to be invoked through Balaam, lest perhaps, invoked, they should be destroyed before the time, and perish with God defending the people. For it is one thing if a demon awaits from God someone to be tempted, as Job, and receives power by a certain limit, and it is said to him: I give thee all that he hath in thy power, but touch not himself. It is another if, at a magician's demand, extorting by certain adjurations, the demons rage without any restraint. In which, if their freedom of choice is kept, they will destroy the people of God; if it is taken away, this will be for God to have condemned a rational creature, and brought judgment before the time, and hindered all who, striving against them, could be crowned. For if freedom of choice is taken from the demons, none will assail the athletes of Christ, and there will be no contest; no reward, no victory. So therefore God acts, that the people still raw, and lately begun to be drawn away from the worship of demons, may not be delivered to demons; and that the demons invoked may not bring answers to the magician, and the race of demons not be stripped of the power of choice. Therefore God comes first and forbids Balaam to invoke demons, if only he had ceased from covetousness. But because he persists in the desire of money, God, indulging the power of choice, permits him to go; yet he put his word into his mouth, forbidding the curse to be made through demons, so as to give place to blessings; and in place of curses he makes him bring forth blessings and prophecies which edify the other nations too. For if his prophecies were written by Moses, how much more by those who dwelt with him in Mesopotamia, among whom he was held in great esteem as among the disciples of this art. From him the race and institution of the magi is said to flourish in the parts of the east. They, having in writing all the things that Balaam had prophesied, had this among the rest: That a star shall rise out of Jacob and a man shall spring up out of Israel. Therefore the magi, when the Lord was born, recognized the star and understood that the prophecy was fulfilled, more than the Jews, who despised the oracles of the holy prophets. They therefore, recognizing that the time was at hand, came and adored. And it was a proof of great faith that they venerated a little child as a great king.
22.16: **“THUS SAITH BALAC”** — Balac means "shutting out" or "devouring". In which is signified some contrary power of this world, which desires to shut out and devour the spiritual Israel, and uses no ministers but the high priests and scribes and Pharisees. It invites these, it promises reward; and they, like Balaam, feign to refer all things to the Lord and to act from zeal for God. For they say: Search the scriptures, and see that out of Galilee a prophet riseth not. "We have a law; and according to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God."
22.18:
**“Balaam answered:”** — a vain people; this signifies the scribes and Pharisees of the Jews
**“If Balac would give me his house full of silver and gold, I cannot alter the word of the Lord my God, to speak either more or less.”** — IF BALAC WOULD GIVE ME, etc. AUGUSTINE. In that Balaam said, when more honourable messengers had been sent to him a second time: If Balac would give me his house full of gold and silver, I cannot transgress the word, etc., he has no sin at all; but what follows is a grave sin. For he ought now to have been constant, since the Lord had said: "Thou shalt not go with them" etc., and not to give them hope that the Lord, as though like Balaam bent by gifts and honours, could change his sentence against the people whom he had called blessed. But he showed himself overcome by covetousness, when he wished the Lord to speak to him again about this matter, of which he already knew his will. For what need was there to add: "And now stay here this night" etc.? But the Lord, seeing his covetousness overcome by gifts, permitted him to go, that he might restrain his avarice by the beast on which he rode; confounding his madness by this very thing, that the ass did not dare to transgress the Lord's prohibition made through the angel, which he by covetousness was trying to transgress, although fear held down his covetousness. For God came to Balaam by night and said to him: If the men have come to call thee, arise, follow them, etc. Why after this permission of the Lord did he not consult him again, as after that prohibition, unless because his covetousness was apparent, though it was held down by fear? Then the Scripture says: "And the Lord was angry", because he went; and the angel of the Lord rose up, and the rest that follows until the ass spoke. Nothing here seems more wonderful than that he was not terrified when the ass spoke, but even answered her (as one accustomed to such ministers) with his anger continuing. Afterwards the angel speaks to him, reproving his way; and when he saw him he was terrified and adored. Then he was permitted to go, that prophecy might be brought forth through him. For he was not permitted at all to say what he wished, but what the Spirit compelled. But he himself remained reprobate. Whence: "Having followed the way of Balaam of Bosor, who loved the wages of iniquity."
22.20:
**“God therefore came to Balaam in the night, and said to him: If these men be come to call thee, arise”**
• God yields to covetousness; he lets him go in the desire of his heart.
• GOD THEREFORE CAME, etc. Balaam is troublesome to God, and almost extorts permission to go to curse the children of Israel and invoke demons; to whom God had already come.
• IF TO CALL, etc. Balaam was a diviner, namely by the ministry of demons and magic art sometimes foreknowing future things. He is asked by Balac to curse Israel. The ambassadors come; they carry divining instruments in their hands; the nations stand astonished and earnestly awaiting what Balaam will answer, whom they believed worthy of divine converse. See how the wisdom of God made a vessel prepared for dishonour profit not one nation but almost the whole world. And to this man, to whom demons were wont to appear, God appears, forbidding the journey of evil work. Balaam is stupefied and wonders at the authority of the one forbidding. For evil was not wont to displease the demons. He sends back the ambassadors, saying that he can do nothing but the word which God shall give in his mouth. The ambassadors return; he inquires again; again he is troublesome, again he desires to hear. For the covetous does not easily go without reward. What then does he hear the second time? If these men have come to call thee: "Arise and go with them." In which God yields to the will of his covetousness, according to that: "So I let them go according to the desires of their heart" etc. But the counsel of the divine dispensation is fulfilled; for it is said to him: Whatever word I shall put in thy mouth, that shalt thou speak. If he had not been unworthy, the Lord would have put his word not in his mouth but in his heart. But because in his heart was the desire of reward and the covetousness of money, the word of the Lord is put not in the heart but in the mouth. For it was being brought about by a wonderful dispensation that the words of the prophets, which were contained within the Israelite court, should reach the Gentiles through Balaam, since all the nations believed him; and that he should bring forth to the nations the secret mysteries of Christ and a great treasure, not so much with heart and sense as with mouth and speech.
**“ORIGEN”** — It is difficult in the explanation of the history how, when it is said "God came to Balaam by night" the first time and asked who the men were who had come to him, and he had answered that they were sent by Balac, saying: Come and curse me the people, the Lord answered: "Thou shalt not go with them" etc. The second time he is said to have come by night and said: "that he should go with them" etc., but that he should speak the word which God would give in his mouth. And the third time the angel of God met him as he went, etc. To whom yet his way seems untimely, so that he would even have killed him had the ass not turned aside; and yet, blamed because he willed to go, he is permitted by him to go, only that he should bring forth the word alone which God would give in his mouth. But before we come to the matter it is to be said that in the letters of the Hebrews the name of God, this God or Lord, is said to be written differently. For any god whatever is written one way, and another way the God of whom it is said: "Hear, O Israel, the Lord thy God is one God." This God of Israel, then, the one God and creator of all, is written with a certain sign of letters, which among them is called the tetragrammaton. When it is written under this sign, there is no doubt that it is said of the true God. But when in common letters, it is uncertain whether it is said of the true God or of any of the others. Those therefore who read Hebrew letters say that God is not here set under the sign of the tetragrammaton; let him who can inquire into it. And that God said, as though asking: Who are these men? it is asked why he seems not to know. And again that he says: "Thou shalt not curse the people", for it is blessed; as though he had said: Thou shalt not curse my people. We meanwhile shall say that by the wisdom of God all things are so ordered that nothing is idle with God, whether good or evil. God did not make malice; yet though he could forbid it when found out by others, he does not forbid it, but uses it with them for necessary causes; for through those in whom it is he proves those who strive toward the glory of the virtues. For if malice were destroyed, there would be none to go against the virtues; and virtue, if it had no contrary, would not shine forth nor be tried; and not proved nor tried, neither would it be virtue. Take away the malice and envy of the brothers of Joseph, and at the same time you will destroy the dispensation of God and the things done in Egypt for the salvation of all nations. If Joseph is not sold, the dream of Pharao will not be expounded; no one will understand what God revealed to him. No one will gather corn in Egypt; Egypt and the bordering regions will perish, and Israel himself and his seed seeking bread. For he will not enter Egypt, nor will the wonders of God be done; there will be no plagues upon the Egyptians, nor the mighty works which God did through Moses and Aaron. No one will cross the Red Sea dryshod; manna will not be given, nor water from the rock, nor the law on mount Sinai; the things related in Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy for the knowledge of the human race; they will not come to the land of promise, none will enter it. Take away the malice of king Balac, by which he desires Israel to be cursed, and the cunning by which he invites Balaam to devote the people, and you will take away the dispensation of God and the favour of his providence; nowhere will there be the prophecies of Balaam. Take away the malice of Judas and the betrayal, you will take away likewise the cross of Christ and the passion; nor are the principalities and powers despoiled, nor triumphed over in the wood of the cross. If there had not been the death of Christ, there would have been neither his resurrection, nor any firstborn from the dead, nor hope of resurrection for us. Let us suppose the devil had not sinned, or after sinning had lost the will of malice: the contest against the wiles of the devil will be taken from you, nor will there be the crown of justice and victory for him who strives lawfully. If there are no opponents there will be no contests, nor will rewards be set for the victors. Not only, therefore, does God use the good for good work, but also the wicked. There are vessels unto honour, there are vessels unto dishonour; yet both are necessary. And they are rational and of free choice, and no one is made a vessel of honour by chance or fortuitously. But he who lives most wickedly will become a vessel of dishonour, not by the maker but by himself, having given causes for dishonour. The maker therefore did not make them to be such, but disposes their minds according to their purpose by the justice of his providence and by a certain ineffable reason. As in great cities men of the foulest life are condemned to do the lowest and laborious works, which yet are necessary: either they serve the furnaces of the bath to kindle the fires, that you may enjoy comfort or delights, or they clean the sewers, or do things of this kind, so that you may have a pleasant dwelling in the city. So God indeed did not make malice; yet, found out by the intent of the purpose of those who turned aside from the right way, he did not will to take it away wholly; foreseeing that, though it would be useless to him who used it, he would yet make it useful to those against whom it was exercised. Therefore we ought to flee wholly, lest malice ever be found in us. But in others we must strive to overcome it, not destroy it, because those in whom it is contribute something of necessary work to the whole. For nothing is idle, nothing empty with God; for if the purpose of a man is good, he uses it for good things; if evil, for necessary things. But you will be more blessed if from the virtue that is in you the whole of this life obtains some good, according to that: "That you may shine as lights in the world, holding forth the word of life unto glory." Lights therefore are necessary to this world; and what is so delightful and so magnificent as the work of the sun and moon, by which the world is enlightened? For the world needs also angels who are over the beasts and preside over the birth of animals, the planting of plants and shrubs and the growth of the rest; and who preside over holy works, who teach the understanding of eternal light and the knowledge of the hidden things of God and the science of divine things. See therefore that you are not found among the angels who preside over beasts, if you have led a beastly life, or among those who preside over earthly works, if you have loved bodily and earthly things. But take pains how you may be taken up into the fellowship of Michael, who always offers the prayers of the saints to God. And you will be taken up into this number, or into this office, if you are instant always in prayer and watch in it. Or into the office and fellowship of Raphael, who presides over medicine: when you see one wounded, namely by sins and by the arrows of the devil, apply the cure of words and the medicine of the word of God, that you may heal the wounds of sin through patience. He who does such things in this world offers himself to be formed by the maker in the future a vessel of election, profitable to the Lord, prepared unto every work. He who does the contrary has offered himself a vessel unto dishonour of the divine dispensation. Therefore I think that in the divine volumes are written the deeds of the good and of the wicked, and the scriptures are woven of left-handed and right-handed acts, that we may understand that with God neither the works of the wicked nor of the good are idle.
**“and go with them: yet so, that thou do what I shall command thee.”** — The counsel of the divine dispensation is fulfilled.
22.21: **“Balaam arose in the morning, and saddling his ass went with them.”** — BALAAM AROSE, etc. ORIGEN. Allegorically. If you see a contrary power assailing the people of God, you will understand who it is that sits upon the ass. And if you see how men are driven headlong by demons, you will understand what the ass is. For you understand Jesus sending his disciples to the ass that was tied, and to the colt, that they might loose them and bring them, that he himself might sit upon her. Perhaps this ass, that is, the Church, formerly carried blasphemy, but, loosed by the disciples, carries Christ, that with her he may enter the heavenly Jerusalem. Whence: "Behold thy king cometh to thee, meek, and sitting upon a beast of burden": the believers, namely, from the Jews; "and a young colt": namely the believers from the Gentiles.
22.22:
**“And God was angry. And an angel of the Lord stood”** — sent by the Lord
**“AND AN ANGEL OF THE LORD STOOD”** — Who was present, namely with the children of Israel; of whom it is written: "My angel shall go before thee."
22.23:
