**“The ass seeing the angel standing in the way, with a drawn sword, turned herself out of the way, and went into the field.”** — who was outside the walls of the vineyards
**“THE ASS SEEING THE ANGEL”** — The magician sees demons, the ass sees the angel; not because she is worthy to see, as neither to speak, but that Balaam may be confuted. Whence: "The dumb beast rebuked the folly of the prophet."
**“GREGORY”** — Balaam strives to reach his purpose, but the animal over which he presides hinders his wish; because the ass saw the angel whom the human mind does not see. Often the flesh, made slow by troubles, by its own scourge points out to the mind the God whom the mind, presiding over the flesh, did not see; so that it hinders those who, in anxiety of spirit, desire to advance in this world and strive swiftly, until it makes known the invisible one who meets it. Whence it is well said by Peter: He had a check of his madness, the dumb beast used to the yoke, which, speaking with man's voice, forbade the folly of the prophet. For the insane man is rebuked by the dumb beast of burden when the lifted-up mind is reminded by the afflicted flesh of the good of humility which it ought to hold. But Balaam did not obtain the good of this correction, because, going on to curse, he changed his voice, not his mind.
22.25: **“TO THE WALL”** — That is, the wall of that vineyard in which the angel was not, since he was on the other side, in the furrows of the vineyards, according to the Septuagint.
22.26: **“TO A NARROW PLACE”** — No longer in the furrows of the vineyards, but between the walls themselves, that is, in the way, he withstood him, so that he could go neither to the right nor to the left.
22.27: **“SHE FELL UNDER THE FEET”** — Because, hurt, she did not go back nor turn aside in either direction, because she was not terrified from one side, but the angel was in the middle of the way in the narrow place.
22.28:
**“AND HE OPENED”** — That Balaam might be reproved by her and confuted by the voice of a dumb beast, who seemed a diviner and wise.
**“AND SHE SAID”** — ISIDORE. Allegorically. The ass on which Balaam sits sees the angel and speaks. That is, the brutish Gentile world, which formerly Balaam, that is, the seducer to idolatry, as a brute animal resisting with no reason, subjected to what error he would; it saw the angel whom man could not see, and saw and bore it and spoke; that we might know that at the coming of the great angel that Gentile people, the nature of its hardness and stolidity being changed, would speak with tongues loosed to God.
**“ORIGEN”** — Allegorically. The ass on which Balaam sat (because Scripture says: "Men and beasts thou wilt preserve, O Lord") can be understood as a part of the believers, which for its folly or innocence is compared to animals. Whence: Not many wise, not many mighty, not many noble; but the foolish things of the world hath God chosen, that he may confound the wise. These, therefore, were held subject and bound by most wicked masters, the scribes and Pharisees; but they are loosed by the Lord, not indeed by himself, but by his disciples. Whence: "Go ye into the village that is over against you, and you shall find an ass tied" etc. As therefore in the Gospel it is not the Lord himself but his disciples who loose the ass, so here the mouth of the ass is opened not by God himself but by the angel. And as in the Gospel those who do not see reprove those who speak; whence: "Father, I give thee thanks, because thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them to little ones." The scribes and Pharisees therefore sat upon the ass and held her bound. With them, therefore, the angel is angry; and unless by a certain foresight of things to come, he would have slain them and saved the ass, which saw and reverenced him who came to the vineyard and stands among the ruins. Yet she pressed the feet of him who sat upon her against the wall. Therefore perhaps that ancient rider cannot walk, nor will he come to him who says: "Come to me, all you that labour and are burdened." Yet the ass came, brought by the disciples; and on her, on whom Balaam, greedy of reward, then sat, Jesus now sits. Do not wonder if you see him whom we have said signifies the scribes and teachers of the people prophesying of Christ. For Caiphas said: "It is expedient for you that one man should die for the people." But, it says, because he was the high priest of that year, he prophesied. Let no one therefore be lifted up if he prophesies, if he merits foreknowledge; because prophecies shall be made void, tongues shall cease, knowledge shall be destroyed; but there remain faith, hope, charity, and the greater of these is charity, which alone never falleth away.
22.29:
**“Balaam answered: Because thou hast deserved it, and hast served me ill: I would I had a sword that I might strike thee.”** — others: kill
**“HE ANSWERED”** — Truly he was carried away, so full of covetousness, that he was not terrified by the miracle of so great a portent, and answered as though speaking to a man; whereas God had not turned the soul of the ass into a rational nature, but had made to sound from her what pleased him, to restrain his madness. Perhaps prefiguring that the foolish things of the world God chose to confound the wise, for the spiritual and true Israel.
22.32: **“And the angel said to him: Why beatest thou thy ass these three times?”** — the faithful, namely, the foolish, the innocent
22.33: **“And unless the ass had turned out of”** — from
22.38: **“He answered him: Lo, here I am: shall I have power to speak any other thing but that which God shall put in my mouth?”** — LO, HERE I AM: SHALL I SPEAK ANY OTHER, etc. ORIGEN. Balaam is set down in the scriptures now as blameworthy, now as praiseworthy. He is blameworthy when, forbidden by God to come to the king, he persists in coming, and, greedy of reward, consults God again until he is left to his covetous desires and goes in his own wills. He is culpable when he builds altars, lays victims on them for demons, and with magic apparatus demands divine counsels; when he gives the most wicked counsel by which the people may be deceived. He is shown praiseworthy when the word of God is put in his mouth, when the Spirit of God is upon him, when he prophesied of Christ, when he foretells to Jews and Gentiles the future mysteries of the coming of Christ, when instead of curses he blesses the people and extols the name of Israel above visible glory with mystic utterances. It is difficult, therefore, to define, to determine his person; to whom not only this diversity belongs, but also what he himself says of himself as though prophesying: Let my soul die among the souls of the just, and let my seed be like the seed of the just. Through Micheas also it is said: "O my people, remember what Balac the king of Moab purposed against thee", and what Balaam the son of Beor answered him, from the cords to Galgal, that thou mightest know the justice of the Lord. He shows therefore that through these things the justice of the Lord would be known. Therefore Balaam the son of Beor answered all those things concerning king Balac which are related in writing. Who, think you, will be found who can show from these very answers of Balaam that the justice of God is made manifest in them? For if the word of God was put in his mouth, and the Spirit of God came upon him, and the justice of God is known from his answers, the things said by him are to be believed prophetic and divine; although it is hard to find that the Spirit of God came upon any of the prophets. But either the vision which he sees, or the taking up of the word of God, or the word of God came to him, and certain other things we read of the prophets; but that the Spirit of God came upon any of the prophets I do not remember to have read. Of David indeed it is written thus: "And the spirit of God appeared," or "shone forth," "upon David from that day forward"; yet the Spirit of God did not come upon David. But of Saul it is written thus: "The spirit of the Lord shall come upon thee, and thou shalt prophesy with them, and shalt be changed into another man." Again of the same: "The spirit of the Lord departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the Lord troubled him." Again: it came to pass, when the evil spirit was upon Saul, David took the harp and played, and it was well with him, and the evil spirit departed from him. That which is written may therefore seem a middle case: And the Spirit of the Lord came upon him. We shall try, therefore, to unfold Balaam in the person of the Pharisees and scribes and those like them. From Mesopotamia, he says, Balac king of Moab hath called me, from the mountains of the east, etc. He calls Mesopotamia the land which lay between the rivers of Babylon, of which it is said: "Upon the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept: when we remembered Sion." If anyone therefore is between the rivers of Babylon, if anyone is flooded with the streams of lust and washed round with the heats of luxury, he is said not to stand but to sit. Whence: Upon the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept, when we remembered Sion. But neither can they weep unless they have first remembered Sion. For the remembrance of good things makes the causes of evils lamentable. For unless one remembers Sion, unless he looks upon the law of God and the mountains of the scriptures, he does not begin to weep for his evils. From these rivers, therefore, Balaam is called, and from these mountains of the east he is invited. These mountains are not the holy mountains of which it is said: "The foundations thereof are in the holy mountains." And elsewhere: "Mountains are round about it: so the Lord is round about his people." But those of which it is said: Dark mountains, etc. And elsewhere: "O dark mountain", and again: "Behold I come against thee, O destroying mountain." These are the mountains in which is every height that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God. From these mountains Balaam is called. Such as the mountains are, such an east they have; for they have the rising of their own light. He who transforms himself as an angel of light has that light of which it is said: "The light of the wicked shall be put out." And as the light of the wicked, and of him who transforms himself as an angel of light, is contrary to that light which said: "I am the light of the world", so too this east is contrary to that of which it is said: "Behold a man, the Orient is his name." From the borders of that east, then, not of this, Balaam came, enlightened by that Lucifer of whom it is said: "How art thou fallen, O Lucifer, who didst rise in the morning?"

23.7:
**“And taking up his parable, he said: Balac king of the Moabites hath brought me from Aram, from the mountains”** — in which is every height exalting itself against the knowledge of God
**“FROM ARAM”** — SEPTUAGINT: From Mesopotamia, which is washed by the rivers of Babylon. Whence: "Upon the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept: when we remembered Sion."
**“of the east:”** — of the devil, namely of Lucifer, who rose in the morning
**“Come, said he, and curse Jacob:”**
• the active
• COME, HE SAID, AND. ORIGEN. Come, he says, and curse me Jacob. In the Latin words the repetition seems almost superfluous; but in the Greek, with the name Israel, there is the addition of a preposition, namely: over-curse me Israel; so that he seemed to demand a curse with greater intensity against Israel than against Jacob. For while one is only Jacob, that is, placed in works, he is assailed with lower curses; but when he has advanced and sharpened the inner man to see God, he is assailed with over-curses, that is, with the more vehement darts of curses. And then indeed the mouth of Balaam was full of cursing and bitterness, and under his tongue labour and sorrow. He sat in ambush with the rich, he awaited reward from the king, that in secret places he might kill the innocent. But God, who alone does wonderful things, works salvation from enemies. For he put the word into his mouth, though his heart could not yet receive the word of God; for there was still in his heart the covetousness of reward. Whence after the word of God which he had in his mouth, he said to Balac: "Come, and I will give thee counsel" etc. For he had the word of God not in his heart but only in his mouth. And therefore he speaks the word of God.
**“make haste and detest”** — others: over-curse
**“Israel.”** — the contemplative
23.8:
**“HOW SHALL I CURSE”** — ORIGEN. How shall I curse him whom the Lord does not curse? Or how shall I over-curse him whom God does not over-curse? The Lord does not curse Jacob nor Israel; but do you think he curses anyone? To the serpent he says: "Cursed art thou among all the beasts of the earth"; and to Adam: "Cursed is the earth in thy work"; and to Cain: "Cursed art thou upon the earth, which hath opened her mouth to receive the blood of thy brother" etc. He will say also to those who shall be on his left: "Depart from me, you cursed, into everlasting fire"; and when he says: "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites", and the like, he seems to reprove with curses. What is it, then, that the Apostle says: "Bless, and curse not"? Does he himself, who sets an example of life for men, do what he does not wish done by men? It is not so. For God, when he curses, marks the desert of him who is cursed and brings forth sentence, as one whom neither the quality of the sin nor the disposition of the sinner deceives. But man, who cannot know these things nor recognize the purpose and mind of another, if he utters a curse in the manner of one speaking or bringing forth sentence, there cannot be a just cause of cursing where the disposition of the sinner is unknown; and especially he utters curses when he is provoked by reproaches and injuries. Which vice the Apostle cuts away, lest we provoke curses with curses and reproaches with reproaches, commanding that we bless and do not curse; not that the truth of judging, which is not hidden from men, and the authority of pronouncing, are destroyed.
**“WHOM GOD HATH NOT CURSED”** — Who yet marks the desert of him who is cursed and brings forth sentence, whom neither the quality of the sin nor the disposition of the sinner deceives. But man knows neither, and often curses when provoked by reproaches. Therefore the Apostle says: "Bless, and curse not", that the vice of reproaching may be cut away.
23.9:
**“I shall see him from the tops of the rocks, and shall consider him from the hills. This people shall dwell alone, and shall not be reckoned among the nations.”**
• FROM THE TOPS, etc. As if it ought not to be cursed for this, that its life is lofty and heavenly. No one understands it unless he has ascended to eminent knowledge.
• ORIGEN. From the tops of the mountains I shall behold him, and from the hills I shall understand him. As though because Israel is set on lofty hills and high mountains, that is, in a high and arduous life, to behold and understand which no one is fit unless he ascends to eminent knowledge. Therefore God does not curse him, because his life is most lofty, not lowly and cast down. Which seems to be said not of the carnal Israel, but of him whose conversation, while he walks on earth, is in heaven. Or if these things are referred also to that people, it is rightly said, I shall behold and I shall understand, so that the future time is signified in which all Israel, coming to the faith of Christ, shall be saved. And he shall be beheld from the mountains and from the hills, that is, those who, rising with Christ, have practised a lofty and heavenly life on earth.
**“I SHALL SEE HIM”** — The act of Jacob, that is, of the active, is seen; the contemplation of Israel, that is, of the contemplative, is only understood. Or in the future resurrection Jacob shall be seen, that is, the body; Israel understood, that is, the soul and spirit of those who rise.
**“THIS PEOPLE ALONE”** — Because it is not mingled with other men, nor reckoned among the other nations, ennobled by certain privileges, observances and ordinances of its own; as the tribe of Levi is not mingled with the others. This people shall dwell alone, etc. The spiritual Jacob and Israel truly dwells alone among the nations. For if we have come to mount Sion and to the city of the heavenly Jerusalem, and have come to the spiritual Judea, which is the portion of God, and, set on earth, have our conversation there, truly we are not reckoned among the other nations, nor are their borders mingled with ours. Even if Sodom and Egypt are restored to their former state, and whatever else of the kind is written in the prophets, yet when Jacob and the spiritual Israel have gone up with the Church of the firstborn, none shall be equalled or mingled with them. For unless one has been grafted among the branches as a wild olive and made partaker of the fatness of the root of the olive, how can he be associated with Jacob or Israel? Since without that root no one can be called either Jacob or Israel; neither can anyone of Jacob or Israel be called Jacob or Israel if he sins; nor will anyone from the Gentiles, if he has entered the Church of the Lord, be any longer reckoned among the Gentiles.
23.10:
**“Who can count”** — No one, namely, except him "who telleth the number of the stars", and brought forth all things in measure and weight and number.
**“WHO CAN COUNT”** — THE SAME. Who has searched out the seed of Jacob? And who has numbered the people of Israel, etc.? This is like what the Lord said to Abraham: "Look up to heaven and number the stars of heaven, if thou canst"; and he said: "So shall thy seed be." And Abraham believed God, and it was reputed to him unto justice. Abraham, then, or any man whatever, or even perhaps of the angels and higher powers, cannot number the stars nor the seed of Abraham, since it is said: "So shall thy seed be." But God ("who telleth the number of the stars, and calleth them all by their names", and who said: I have commanded all the stars) can search out the seed of Jacob and number the dust of Israel. For he alone knows who is truly Jacob and who truly Israel. For he does not regard the Jew openly, nor circumcision in the flesh, but him who is a Jew inwardly and circumcised in heart. He alone, therefore, can number and search out; who, according to incomprehensible wisdom, after that heavenly form which he alone can know, set also these numbers which we have in hand, in which he commanded that according to their kindreds and the houses of their families, by name, all the males should be numbered by their polls from twenty years old and upward, every one who goes forth in strength; and their number is gathered as sacred, sacred namely and pleasing to God then, when it is numbered at his command. But if anyone wishes to number contrary to the command of the Lord, though he be David, though a great prophet, he acts against the law and is reproved by a prophet, and suffers the things that are written in the second book of Kings.
**“the dust”** — seed innumerable
**“LET MY SOUL DIE”** — ORIGEN. He seems to prophesy of himself; but according to the letter it was not done either in Balaam or in that Israel, nor could it be done; for he died not among them but by them.
**“ORIGEN”** — Let my soul die among the just. This fits rather the person of those who at present, though they are held a vain people, because they are without the grace of the Holy Ghost, yet when the fulness of the Gentiles has come in, all this prophecy which is spoken of Israel will be fulfilled in the spiritual Israel, and his soul will die with the souls of the just. For they will receive into themselves the faith of Christ, that they may be baptized into his death, and buried together with him by baptism into death. And let my seed be as the seed of the just. For not they themselves, but their seed becomes as the seed of the just, who, believing from the Gentiles, are justified in Christ. Therefore neither circumcision availeth anything, nor uncircumcision, but faith that worketh by charity.
**“GREGORY”** — Let my soul die the death of the just, and my last end be like to them, etc. Many within the Church have long prayers to God, but have not the life of those who pray; and they weep in prayer, but in the time of temptation, when they are assailed by pride, they swell with haughtiness. Likewise they succumb to the storm of avarice, of luxury, of anger, nor do they remember that they wept for desire of the eternal kingdom. Which Balaam showing of himself says: Let my soul die the death of the just, etc. But after his compunction he gave counsel against the life of those to whom he had asked to be made like even in dying; and by occasion of avarice he forgot what he had wished concerning innocence. For often the wicked are pricked to justice to no profit, as the good are tempted to fault without harm. For it comes about by divine dispensation that the former do something of good which does not profit them, whence they may trust amid the evils which they commit most fully; and the latter, who are tempted but do not consent, through weakness fix the steps of the heart more truly in justice through humility. The one is plain in Balaam; of the other Paul says: "I see another law in my members, fighting against the law of my mind" etc. The one, therefore, is pricked, yet does not draw near to justice. The other is tempted, and yet fault does not defile him; because neither do imperfect good things help the wicked, nor do unconsummated evils condemn the good. For prayer which perseverance does not hold has not the weight of virtue. Whence: "Their faces were no more changed in different ways."
**“AND LET MY LAST END BE”** — This can be understood of the magi, who first came from the east to adore Christ, who were of the seed of Balaam by succession of race and by tradition of discipline. For it is clear that they recognized the star which Balaam had foretold would rise in Israel.
23.11:
**“And Balac said to Balaam:”** — the second prophecy of Balaam
**“WHAT IS THIS”** — Balac, hearing against his hope blessings instead of curses, and bearing it no further, interrupted the words of the one prophesying.
**“What is this that thou dost? I sent for thee to curse my enemies: and thou contrariwise blessest them.”** — Allegorically. The bitter king does not wish blessing, but seeks curses. For he is of the mind of him to whom it is said: "Cursed art thou among all the beasts of the earth."
23.12: **“He answered him:”** — in whose mouth God put the word
23.13:
**“BALAC THEREFORE SAID”** — He thinks him terrified by the multitude of Israel and therefore not daring to curse, and that a change of place will profit him.
**“THOU CANST NOT SEE”** — The madman thought the Israelite grace could be hidden by the obstacle of a place, not knowing that "a city seated on a mountain cannot be hid".
23.14:
**“And when he had brought him to a high place, upon the top of mount Phasga, Balaam built seven altars, and laying on every one a calf and a ram,”** — others: with calves and rams
**“HE BUILT”** — The thing was being done with profane sacrifices, and divination was sought by magic art. Yet God, willing grace to abound where offence abounded, deigned to be present, not at the sacrifices, but coming to meet him. And there he gives his word, and foretells mysteries and things to come, where the faith and working and wonder of the Gentiles most hung; so that those who will not believe our prophets may believe their own diviners.
23.15: **“STAND HERE BY”** — He stood by the holocaust, set in his idolatry; therefore he fell the more. He therefore seems to stand who had fallen the more, when he seemed to stand in idolatry.
23.19:
**“God is not a man, that he should lie,”**
• who is hindered by vices, so that what he speaks is not true
• GOD IS NOT AS, etc. ORIGEN. God is not deceived as a man, nor terrified as a son of man. As though you think that God is deceived like a man in the things he speaks. "For men are hindered by many vices, so that what they speak is not true. For they speak when angry, or from fear, or covetousness, or for the sake of boasting; but God, in whom there is no passion, whatever he has said, says according to the deserts of the causes." And therefore he cannot be deceived, because whatever is brought forth by reason cannot lack reason. He therefore is not one who speaks in vain like a man, nor is he terrified, or does he terrify, as a son of man. In men terror changes the sentence; but God, who is above all things, can be terrified by none so as to change his sentence; nor does he terrify as a son of man. For men for boasting's sake raise false alarms and threats even against those whom they cannot harm. But God terrifies by reason, that he may correct man in the tribulation of hearing, that, terrified by the word of threatening, he may be amended, lest the vengeance of his evils come upon him.
**“nor as the son of man, that he should be changed.”** — changeable through the vice of human frailty
**“Hath he said then, and will he not do? hath he spoken, and will he not fulfill?”** — HATH HE SAID THEN, etc. ORIGEN. The same: when he has said, will he not do? will he speak and not abide? Though men do not do what they say, being changeable through the vice of human frailty, God is unchangeable. But someone says: When God spoke of Nineve, that it should be overthrown after three days, why did he not abide by his word? And in the things he spoke of David, to whom death had been promised for three days to waste the people, and within one day, even to the hour of the midday meal, it ceased? Perhaps the things that are said by way of question will be seen not to be defined, but to show something in between; and the disposition of an irrevocable sentence is not shown; so that this seems said more moderately: Hath he said, and will he not do? It is written in Jonas: "And Jonas preached and said: Yet three days", or forty according to the Hebrews, "and Nineve shall be destroyed." It is to be observed, therefore, that it is not found in the words of God, which he spoke to the prophet, "yet three days and Nineve shall be destroyed"; so that the word said and not done seems uttered rather by Jonas than by the Lord. In the second book of Kings too: the word of the Lord, it says, came to Gad the prophet, saying: "Thus saith the Lord: I give thee thy choice of three things, choose one of them which thou wilt, that I may do it to thee. And Gad came to David, saying: Either seven years of famine shall come to thee in thy land, or thou shalt flee three months before thy enemies, or for three days there shall be a pestilence in thy land." Observe therefore how, in these three threats too, God is not found to have spoken of death for three days. For it is set in the words of Gad, not in the commands of the Lord. And the things that are said through a prophet are not always to be received as said by God. God spoke many things through Moses; yet Moses commanded some things by his own authority. Whence: "Because of the hardness of your heart Moses wrote you this precept" etc., down to: "What therefore God hath joined together, let no man put asunder." You see therefore here that God neither commanded nor willed divorce to be made; but that Moses, because of the hardness of the Jews, wrote that a bill of divorce was to be given. Hence Paul says: "The Lord commandeth, not I." And elsewhere: "For I speak, not the Lord." And again: "I have no commandment of the Lord; but I give counsel." And again: "That which I speak, I speak not according to God." Likewise, therefore, in the other prophets: some things the Lord spoke and not the prophets, some the prophets and not the Lord. The objection therefore seems to be resolved, since the Lord revokes and changes for the better not so much his own words as the prophet's. But I think rather that the former solution fits the senses of the whole of Scripture; and especially those in which God says he is patient and of much mercy and repenting of the evil; or most of all in those which are pronounced generally by Jeremias, in which it is shown that for his many mercies and incomprehensible goodness God speaks and does not do, speaks and does not abide, thus: "I will suddenly speak, that is, I will speak definitely, against a nation and against a kingdom, to root up and to pull down and to destroy it. If that nation shall repent of their evil, I also will repent of the evil that I thought to do to them. And I will suddenly speak of a nation and of a kingdom, to build up and plant it. If it shall do evil in my sight, that it obey not my voice, I will repent of the good that I have spoken to do unto it." How then can we prefer to these things, which are said absolutely through Jeremias, those which are said in suspense through Balaam, unless because those are to be confirmed for the negligent and the despisers, but these are to be noted more secretly by the more perfect?
23.20:
**“I was brought to bless,”** — by God, who put the truth in my mouth
**“the blessing I am not able to hinder.”** — For he cannot, even if he would, turn the word of God with a human tongue.
23.21:
**“THERE IS NO IDOL”** — Another translation: "There shall be no labour in Jacob, nor shall sorrow be seen in Israel"; in the world to come, namely.
**“ORIGEN”** — There shall be no labour in Jacob, nor shall sorrow be seen in Israel, etc. The state of the life to come is announced. For this life is not passed without labour and sorrow. For Paul is beaten with rods thrice, stoned once, and suffers innumerable things; but in the future sorrow and sadness and groaning shall flee away. Which yet is referred not to all, but only to those who shall be of the merits of Jacob and Israel; as the poor Lazarus, who passed this life in labour and sorrow, whence where the rich man is tormented, he rests. He is in the true Israel and in the true Jacob, upon whom labour and sorrow do not come. But that rich man was Israel according to the flesh, of whose brothers he said: They have the law and the prophets; let them hear them.
**“in Jacob,”** — the active
**“neither is there an image to be seen”** — a likeness of an existing thing
**“in Israel.”** — the contemplative
**“The Lord”** — He that keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep.
**“his God”** — who does not forsake his Israel
**“is with him, and the sound of the victory”**
• the preaching of the Gospel, by which the trophy of the cross is announced
• THE LORD HIS GOD, etc. THE SAME. The Lord his God is with him, and the glorious things of the princes are with him, etc. God never forsakes his Israel. The glorious power of the princes is principality and true kingdom; since there are also some princes who are to be driven out of their principality, or perhaps have already been driven out, and these who are truly Israel are to be brought in. After all those glorious things which those princes had in heaven, who kept not their principality but forsook their everlasting dwellings, this Israel and Jacob, who wrestled and conquered, shall receive them.
**“AND THE SOUND”** — The admonition of preaching, because in you the king, that is, Christ, triumphs over the devil.
23.22:
**“God hath brought him out of Egypt,”**
• from the power of darkness
• of this world
**“GOD HATH BROUGHT”** — THE SAME. God who brought him out of Egypt; as the glory of the unicorn to him, etc. That Israel was brought out of this earthly Egypt; but the spiritual Israel out of the Egypt of this world and out of the power of darkness. And his glory is as of the unicorn. The unicorn is said to be an animal formed according to its name, in whose strength and power Christ is understood. And horn is often put for kingdom. Whence: "The four horns are four kingdoms." Under the name of unicorn, therefore, it seems to be shown that all that is his is one horn, that is, one kingdom. For the Father has put all things under his feet, until the last enemy, death, is destroyed, and as the unicorn he holds one kingdom of all, and of his kingdom there shall be no end. There goes out, therefore, glory to the spiritual Israel as the glory of the unicorn. Whence: "Father, grant them that as I and thou are one, so these also may be one in us"; when, namely, he will reform the body of our lowness, made like to the body of his glory.
**“WHOSE STRENGTH”** — Whose? Christ's, all of whose is one horn, that is, one kingdom; whose glory belongs to the spiritual Israel. For he himself says: "Father, grant them that as I and thou are one, so they may be one in us."
23.23:
**“There is no soothsaying in Jacob,”** — who wrestles against principalities and powers and the rulers of this world
**“THERE IS NO SOOTHSAYING IN”** — ORIGEN. There is no soothsaying in Jacob, nor divination in Israel. It seems to me that the foreknowledge of future things, as far as regards the thing itself, is something in between, that is, neither properly good nor properly evil; since foreknowledge of future things can sometimes come to the knowledge of men even from the side of the devil. But when the time and opportunity and the will of God are there, foreknowledge is also given to men by God through the prophets. Therefore that cannot properly be called good which is sometimes from the evil one, nor properly evil which is sometimes from God. In the book of Kings it is written that the ark of God was taken by the foreigners and brought into Azotus, and they brought it into the house of Dagon. And Dagon was found fallen on his face to the ground before the ark; and the hand of the Lord was heavy upon the Azotians, and he struck them in the hinder parts. After this it went into Accaron, and the Accaronites said to their diviners and priests: Tell us how we shall send back the ark to its place. They answered: "If you send it back, send it not empty, but give it what you owe for sin, and then you shall be healed, and he will forgive you; otherwise his hand will not depart from you." And after a little: "Make a cart, and take two kine that have calved, on which there hath come no yoke, and yoke them to the cart, and shut up their calves at home; and put the ark upon the cart, and the vessels of gold which you have offered for sin, and all its holy things, and let it go. And look: if it go up by the way of its own coasts towards Bethsames, then he hath done us this great evil; but if not, we shall know that it is not his hand hath touched us, but it hath happened by chance." See therefore how, by judgments set before them, they consider whether the cause of the evils came from the hand of God and for the injury to the ark, or happened by chance. It follows: "When they had put the ark of the Lord upon the cart, the kine took the straight way that leadeth to Bethsames, and turned not aside neither to the right hand nor to the left." Who then, looking carefully at these things, would call the foreknowledge which was foretold of the oxen's going straight either fortuitous or composed by art, and not ministered by demons? Who feared the power of the ark, by which even the worship of demons was destroyed, their images and temples falling down. There is therefore a certain working of demons in the ministry of foreknowledge, which is gathered by certain arts by those who have given themselves over to demons; and it seems to be grasped and understood now through lots, as through auguries; now from the contemplation of entrails, which they call auspices, and by tricks of this kind. Which arts have deceived men away from God, so that Manasses, the son of the most just Ezechias, deceived by this error, built an altar to all the host of heaven in both courts of the house of the Lord; to the spiritual wickednesses, namely, set in the heavenly places. And such were the things he awaited, of which it could be said: That they were done in all power and lying signs and wonders, so that even the elect might be deceived. All these things, then, I do not doubt are done by the working of demons, who direct the movements of birds or beasts or entrails, or of lots, according to the signs which they themselves have taught to be observed by those to whom they handed down this art. From all which the man of God, who is numbered in the portion of God, ought to be wholly a stranger, which the demons secretly contrive; lest he be again joined to the demons and filled with their spirit and power, lest he be brought back to the worship of idols. It is better to be ignorant than to learn from demons. It is better not to learn even from a prophet than to inquire of diviners. For divination is not given divinely, but is so called by antiphrasis, as being done through men filled with demons. But the rite of the Gentiles believed everything divine which is uttered by any spirit whatever. Yet God commands us to learn nothing from these, lest we become their partners. Whence Christ, disdaining to receive testimony from demons, said: Hold thy peace, and go out of him. Paul too, when the woman having a spirit of divination cried out: These men are the servants of the most high God, etc., being grieved said: I command thee in the name of Jesus Christ to go out from her; because he judged it unworthy that testimony should be given to his preaching by the spirit of divination. We ought therefore to grieve the more whenever we see souls deceived by those who believe a spirit of divination, or a ventriloquist, or demons of this kind, as a divine spirit. There shall be no soothsaying in Jacob, then, nor divination in Israel. It follows: In time it shall be told to Jacob and to Israel what God shall accomplish. That is, when it behoves, when it is expedient, future things are told by God through the prophets, by the Holy Ghost. If they are not told, it is not expedient to foreknow them. Those, therefore, who inquire into future things by divers arts and invocations of demons desire to learn what is not expedient. And for the utter destruction of divination or augury we shall add this also, that all these animals or birds are judged fit and worthy for the ministry of demons. For dragons and other serpents are said to minister to the pythons; and to the augurs and to those who take auspices from slain victims, wolves bring all things, or foxes, or hawks, or crows, or eagles, or the like; which Moses, I believe for these causes, marked as unclean.
**“nor divination in Israel. In their times”** — in which it behoves and is expedient
**“IN ISRAEL”** — Who sees God by purity of faith and cleanness of mind; nor would he receive Balaam himself, but he does not dare to reject the word which God put in his mouth. For unless the word had been from God, he would not have revealed it to his servant Moses, far away, when Balaam said these things.
**“it shall be told to Jacob and to Israel”** — the spiritual, not the carnal
23.24:
**“Behold the people shall rise up as a lioness, and shall lift itself up as a lion: it shall not lie down till it devour the prey,”**
• "The kingdom of heaven suffereth violence, and the violent bear it away."
• THE SAME. Behold the people shall rise up as a lion's whelp, and shall exult as a lion. He seems to describe the confidence of the people believing in Christ, and the freedom which it has in faith, and the exultation which it bears in hope. For it is compared to a lion's whelp when it tends toward perfection, glad and swift; but to a lion when it already holds the things that are perfect. For as the lion and the lion's whelp fear no animal, but all things are subject to them, so the perfect Christian, who takes up his cross and follows Christ, saying: "The world is crucified to me, and I to the world", despises all things that are in the world, imitating him who is called the lion of the tribe of Juda and the lion's whelp. For as he himself is the light of the world and granted his disciples to be the light of the world, so, since he is the lion and the lion's whelp, he gave to those who believe in him the name of lion and of lion's whelp.
**“BEHOLD THE PEOPLE AS”** — Others: Behold, as a lion's whelp he shall rise up, and as a lion he shall exult. For he is a whelp when rational infants lately born receive milk without guile; but an exulting lion when the perfect man puts away the things of a child.
**“SHALL LIFT ITSELF UP”** — He says the people shall be lifted up in the future; for of the one he saw he would have said: it is lifted up.
**“IT SHALL NOT LIE DOWN”** — ORIGEN. He shall not sleep until he eat the prey and drink the blood of the wounded. These things cannot stand according to the letter. For how should this people, so praiseworthy, so magnificent, drink the blood of the wounded, when even those called from the Gentiles are commanded to abstain from blood as from things sacrificed to idols? But except we eat the flesh of the Son of man and drink his blood, we shall not have life in us. For his flesh is meat indeed and his blood is drink indeed; in which is spirit and life; who was wounded for our sins. We drink his blood, not only in the rite of the sacraments, but also when we receive his words, in which is spirit and life. He himself, then, is the wounded one, whose blood, that is, the words of doctrine, we receive. And all those are wounded who have preached his word to us. For when we read their words, that is, of his apostles, and obtain life from them, we drink the blood of the wounded. Whence: they drank the purest blood of the grape; of that grape, namely, of which it is said: I am the true vine, the disciples the branches, the Father the husbandman. You therefore are the true Israel, because you know how to drink the blood both of that grape which is of the true vine and of its branches which the Father purges; whose fruit is rightly called the blood of the wounded, which we drink from their words. If only we are as lion's whelps rising up, and as an exulting lion.
**“and of the slain”**
• Christ was slain for our offences
• others: of the wounded
**“drink the blood.”** — the words of Christ and of the apostles; whence: The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life.
23.27: **“And Balac said to him: Come and I will bring thee to another place; if peradventure it please God that thou mayest curse them from thence.”** — Balac thinks the diviner lacks the advantage of place for cursing rather than the will.
23.28:
**“And when he had brought him upon the top of mount Phogor,”** — of delight
**“AND WHEN HE HAD BROUGHT”** — ORIGEN. And Balac took Balaam himself to the top of mount Phogor, which stretches toward the desert. Those whom God calls he sets on the top of mount Sinai. Balac, contrary to God, on the top of mount Phegor, which is interpreted "delight". On the top of delight and lust, therefore, Balac sets men; for he is a lover of pleasure more than of God, and wishes to shut them out from God; for he is called, or is interpreted, "shutting out" and "devouring". Therefore Phegor stretches toward the wilderness, that is, toward the business which is a wilderness and deserted by God.
**“which looketh towards the wilderness,”** — business deserted by God
23.29: **“BUILD ME”** — THE SAME. The things which the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God. Yet because the law of God commanded sacrifices and handed down to Israel the rite of sacrificing, perhaps it is asked why these things, which seem dedicated to demons, are commanded to be offered to God? And the answer will be ready. Because as the giving of a bill of divorce was not of the will of God, who did not wish what he had joined to be separated, but Moses wrote it because of the hardness of the Jews, so it can be seen of this too. For God does not eat the flesh of bulls or drink the blood of goats, who says: I spoke not to thee of sacrifices and victims in the day that I brought thee out of the land of Egypt. But Moses, because of their hardness, to take away the Egyptian custom, commanded them these things, that those who could not abstain from sacrificing might sacrifice at least to God and not to demons. There is perhaps a more secret reason for sacrificing to God, for the destruction, namely, of the sacrifices which are offered to demons; so that, because souls are wounded through those, they might be healed through these; as those who have skill in medicine confirm. For they report that the poisons of serpents are driven out by medicines made from serpents. So, therefore, the poison of the sacrifices of demons is driven out by the sacrifices offered to God; so the death of Jesus does not allow the death of sin to have dominion over believers. But while the time allowed it, sacrifices were set against sacrifices; when the perfect victim came, which should take away the sin of the whole world, the sacrifices which were offered one by one to God seemed superfluous, since by one victim all the worship of demons was driven away. But Balaam, either according to the purpose of his heart, which he had not amended, or according to the figure by which he bore the person of the teachers and Pharisees of the unbelieving people, still sets up victims, in which men put their hope who do not receive the faith of Christ.

24.1:
**“And when Balaam saw that it pleased the Lord that he should bless Israel,”** — AND WHEN BALAAM SAW, etc. When he saw no demon, no contrary power standing by, heeding his victims, and the ministers of malice which he used for cursing shut out, he could understand thence also that it was good in the sight of the Lord to bless Israel. But that people which is now vain, and the teachers who, not believing in Christ, hold the people in vanity, will see in the last days, when the fulness of the Gentiles has come in and all Israel has begun to come to the faith of Christ: those who now have eyes and see not will then lift up their eyes to higher and spiritual senses, and will see and understand that it is good in the sight of the Lord to bless Israel, arranged in its parts and houses and families, each one in his own order to obtain the glory of the resurrection.
**“he went not as he had gone before, to seek divination: but setting his face towards the desert,”** — HE WENT NOT AS, etc. That is, he does not consider the will of God by foolish senses, as he was wont, in dumb animals and beasts. But he will recognize that God has no care for oxen, nor for sheep, nor for birds and other animals; namely, understand that the things written are written for the sake of men.
24.2: **“THE SPIRIT RUSHING UPON HIM”** — AUGUSTINE. And the Spirit of God came upon him, that is, upon Balaam. The Spirit of God was not made as though he were a thing made; but he came to be upon him, that is, it came about that he was upon him. As: He that cometh after me is preferred before me, that is, it came about that he was before me, that he was set above me, because he was before me. As: The Lord was made my helper; for the Lord is not a thing made, but it came about that he helped me. And: The Lord is become a refuge for the poor, that is, it came about that the poor fled to him. And: The hand of the Lord came upon me, that is, it came about that it was upon me; and many like things.
24.3:
**“He took up his parable”** — because: "A veil is upon their heart"; they neither see nor understand.
**“and said: Balaam hath said:”** — a vain people, or one casting them headlong
**“BALAAM HATH SAID”** — ORIGEN. Balaam the son of Beor hath said. The man who truly sees hath said, hearing the words of the strong one, who saw the vision of God in sleep; his eyes were opened. It is a wonder how Balaam is held so worthy that, taking up his parable, he should pronounce these things of himself. For how is he one who sees, who serves divination and auguries, who studies magic? Unless perhaps because the Spirit of God came to be in him and the word of God was put in his mouth, such great things are said of him. For neither Moses nor any of the prophets is easily found raised up with such praises. Whence these things seem rather to fit that people at the time when, turned to the Lord, it puts away the veil that was upon its heart. For God is a spirit; therefore he says his eyes were opened, as though those formerly shut are opened through the Spirit of God who came upon him, the veil being taken away. Now therefore is the time when he truly sees and truly hears the words of the strong one, and sees the vision of God in sleep; that is, he will see fulfilled the times which were marked out in sleep to the prophet Daniel, and the visions which were brought to him in sleep he will understand with opened eyes, so that he can say: "But we all, beholding the glory of the Lord with open face" etc. Perhaps these are the eyes which elsewhere are called the eyes of earth, that is, the senses of the flesh, of which the serpent said to Eve: "For God doth know that in what day soever you shall eat thereof, your eyes shall be opened." And a little after: "Their eyes were opened." For some are the eyes which are opened through transgression; others those by which Adam and Eve saw before the transgression, by which the woman saw that the tree was good to eat. Christ therefore came into this world for judgment, that they who see not may see, and they who see may become blind; because in sinners the eyes which are better do not see, but those which are called the senses of the flesh and which were opened by the counsel of the serpent. It was the work of Christ, therefore, that those who do not see with the better eyes the things that are good, but with those opened by the counsel of the serpent the things that are evil, should become blind; and that those who were blind in those which the serpent opened should see the good things of the Lord in those which Jesus came to open. For unless the sight of evil things is first shut, the gaze on good things will not lie open. Hence too it is said: Who made the seeing and the blind? Seeing, namely, according to the Spirit of Christ; but blind according to the counsel of the serpent. It is apparent, therefore, that Balaam (because his eyes had been opened) speaks of himself: The man who truly sees hath said, and hearing the words of the strong one. And likewise the other ears are to be shut and opened. But if anyone wishes to take these things according to the history, he can say that in this, that Balaam saw that it is good in the sight of the Lord to bless Israel, his eyes were opened and he was made a man who truly sees. For he saw true things which were to come to Jacob or Israel. He heard the words of the strong one when God came to him and said to him in sleep: The word which I shall put in thy mouth, take heed that thou speak. And this will be the vision of God which he saw in sleep; and therefore he says his eyes were opened, because he could see what he saw.
**“the son of Beor”** — of the one impelling, that is, the devil, who impels to sin
**“WHOSE EYE IS STOPPED UP”** — Because in sleep, his bodily eyes being shut, he saw these things by angelic ministry; but the eyes of the mind he has partly open, partly shut; who recognizes future mysteries, but does not correct his error. So the wicked do one thing in knowledge, another in manners; show one thing in the mouth, another in work.
24.5:
**“How beautiful are thy tabernacles, O Jacob,”**
• who is perfect in act and work
• of those, namely, who always walk and find no certain end of the journey
**“HOW BEAUTIFUL ARE THY TABERNACLES”** — ORIGEN. How good are thy houses, O Jacob, and thy tabernacles, O Israel, etc. He does not praise earthly houses, which they did not have beyond the other nations. But the people was divided by tribes, the tribes by peoples, the peoples by kindreds, the kindreds by houses of families; the houses were numbered by the number of men and by heads. That is, every male who was from twenty years old and upward, who could go forth to war; these things, foreseeing in spirit, he extolled. Nor is the sense to be regarded of the letter alone; for he speaks taking up a parable. For if you consider the divisions and orders of the peoples which will be in the true Israel in the resurrection, when each shall rise in his own order; if you can behold its tribes and kindreds, in which you will understand a kinship not so much of flesh and blood as of mind and spirit; then good are the houses of Jacob and the tabernacles of Israel. And a house is a thing founded and stable and enclosed by certain bounds; tabernacles are of those who are always on the way and walk and have not found the end of the journey. Jacob, therefore, is to be held in the persons of those who are perfect in acts; but Israel are those who study wisdom and knowledge. Because, therefore, the exercises of acts are closed by a certain end (for the perfection of works is not without end) when one has fulfilled all that he ought to do, the very perfection of works is called a good house. But of those who study wisdom and knowledge (because there is no end; for what end will there be of God, and what bound of wisdom? for the further one approaches, the deeper he will find it, for the wisdom of God is incomprehensible) he does not praise their houses, because they have not come to the end; but he wonders at the tabernacles in which they always walk and advance; and the more they advance, the more the way of advancing is increased and stretches out into the immeasurable. Therefore he names the tabernacle. And if anyone has begun some progress in knowledge, and knows something by experience, he knows that where he has come to some contemplation and knowledge of spiritual things, there the soul tarries as in a tabernacle. When therefore from these it searches out other things it has found, and advances to other understandings, as though the tabernacle were lifted, it tends to higher things and there sets the seat of the mind, fixed with stability of sense; then from these it finds others which the consequence of the former senses has laid open; and so, always stretching forth to the things before, it goes by tabernacles. For there is never a time when the soul, kindled by the spark of knowledge, can be idle and rest; but it is always called on from good things to better, and from better to higher. This journey of the wisdom of God, therefore, he has described with great and much comeliness, saying: "As shady groves, and as gardens beside the rivers" etc.
**“and thy tents, O Israel!”** — who study wisdom and knowledge
24.6:
**“As woody valleys,”** — By these rivers the tabernacles of Israel are flooded, like those which the Lord pitched.
**“AS WOODY VALLEYS”** — Others: Shady groves. To those who walk the journey of the wisdom of God, the groves are the whole assembly of the just and the choir of the prophets. For under the shade of the senses which they find written among them their souls are refreshed, and in their doctrine they delight as though walking through the shades of groves.
**“AS GARDENS NEAR THE RIVERS”** — THE SAME. And as a garden beside the rivers. These find gardens beside the rivers like that in which is the tree of life. For the rivers are the evangelical or apostolic scriptures, or the helps of the heavenly powers toward such souls. For they are watered by them and flooded, and are nourished to all knowledge and acknowledgment of heavenly things. For although Christ is the river which makes glad the city of God, and the Holy Ghost is not only himself a river but is in those to whom it is given that "rivers flow from their belly", the Father too says: They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water; from which, namely, these rivers proceed. Flooded by these rivers, the tabernacles of Israel become as the tabernacles which the Lord pitched; he compares tabernacles, then, to tabernacles. For we can say that the houses of Jacob are the law and the tabernacles of Israel the prophets. For he praises not Jacob himself but his houses, nor Israel but his tabernacles, when his eyes have been opened. For as long as the veil is set upon the reading of the law and the prophets, neither the tabernacles seem good nor the houses praiseworthy; but when it is understood that the law and the prophets are spiritual, the letter that kills being removed, and the spirit that quickens perceived, the bodies and souls together of the believing people gathered from the Gentiles seem also to be praised. Let the house of Jacob be said of bodies, as is read in a certain little book, that Jacob is the house of Israel, that is, his body is called Jacob and his soul Israel. The body of Jacob, therefore, is praiseworthy in continence and chastity; but the tabernacles of Israel are perfect souls, to which the name of Israel belongs from seeing God. These tabernacles, therefore, are as the tabernacles which God pitched; those, namely, which he showed Moses when he was building the tabernacle, saying: See that thou make all things according to the pattern which was shown thee on the mount; that in imitation of these Israel, and each of us, might make tabernacles. Hence it seems to have come about that Peter and Andrew and the sons of Zebedee were found fishermen by trade, but Paul a maker of tents; and those are changed into fishers of men, and Paul, called an apostle through Christ, by a like transformation of his trade is transferred to setting up heavenly tabernacles. For he makes tabernacles by teaching the way of salvation and of the blessed mansions in heaven, and builds churches from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum. And he makes tabernacles after the likeness of those which God showed Moses on the mount. But each one who has gone out of Egypt and dwells in the desert ought to dwell in a tabernacle and keep the feast. For as the commemoration of the going out of Egypt is made by the Pasch and the unleavened bread, so the memory of the dwelling in the desert is made by tabernacles. For your fathers dwelt in tabernacles in the desert; these things must be done according to the words of the law and the prophets and the Psalms. For when the soul advances from the things that are written, and, forgetting the things that are behind, stretches forth to those that are before, and from the increase of virtues and the imitation of progress, it is rightly said to dwell in a tabernacle.
**“watered, as tabernacles”** — of which it is said: "That" "they may receive you into everlasting dwellings."
**“which the Lord hath pitched,”** — because they are not carried about with every wind of doctrine
**“as cedars”** — angels
**“CEDARS”** — Of God, namely, which hold up the branches of the vine transplanted out of Egypt, on which rests that fruit whose shadow covered the hills.
**“by”** — beside
**“the waterside.”** — the divine wisdom
24.7:
**“Water shall flow”** — many peoples, or doctrine
**“out of his bucket,”** — from the nation, or from the primitive Church
**“and his seed shall be in many waters. Shall be removed”**
• from the kingdom, namely
• AND HIS SEED, etc. THE SAME. A man shall come forth from his seed and shall rule over many nations, and his kingdom shall be exalted above Gog. God brought him out of Egypt, "as the glory of the unicorn" etc. Christ came forth from the seed of Israel according to the flesh, who rules among the nations. Whence: Ask of me, and I will give thee the Gentiles for thy inheritance, etc. Gog is interpreted "upon the roofs", and here it is not put for a nation, as is thought, but, as in many places, the Hebrew word itself has been left untranslated. For the sequence of the speech is such: and his kingdom shall be exalted upon the roofs, and his kingdom shall grow. To be exalted upon the roofs is said of the perfection of believers; to grow, of their multitude. In those, therefore, who are perfect, the kingdom of Christ is exalted upon the roofs, that is, over those who are in the heights. For perhaps there are some in heaven who advance more in some things, and those who are in the kingdom of Christ are exalted higher. Whence: "He that is on the housetop, let him not come down to take any thing out of his house"; for those who have come to lofty perfection ought not to come down to the lowly things of this world, which is called a house. And elsewhere: "That which you hear in the ear, preach ye upon the housetops." And his kingdom grows while the number of the Church is multiplied, until the Father puts all enemies under his feet and destroys the last enemy, death.
**“for Agag”** — the king, namely, of the Amalecites, whom he spared
**“his king”** — Saul
24.8:
**“HATH BROUGHT HIM”** — God brought him out of Egypt, after the death, namely, of Herod. Whence: "Out of Egypt have I called my son"; which seems taken from this place and inserted in the Gospel, or from the prophet Osee.
**“God hath brought him out of Egypt,”** — After the death of Herod; or the Father brought him out of the world to himself, that he might make a way for those who were to ascend from this world to God.
**“whose strength is like to the rhinoceros.”** — WHOSE STRENGTH IS LIKE, etc. For, casting out all the kingdoms of demons, he founded his one kingdom in glory, as of the true unicorn; for the horn signifies kingdom.
**“THEY SHALL DEVOUR”** — He shall eat the nations of his enemies, and shall take the marrow of their fatness, etc. The nations, namely, which his enemies possessed, he shall eat, the power of the enemy destroyed; and shall take the marrow of their fatness, when from these he thins the gross and carnal sense and turns it to spiritual understanding. And fatness is put in a bad sense, according to that: "The heart of this people is grown gross." And elsewhere: "The beloved grew fat and kicked." He eats the nations, therefore, and has as food those who believe in him. Whence: "My meat is to do the will of him that sent me"; whose will, namely, was that the nations should be converted to the faith. And subtlety is praiseworthy, because the spirit of wisdom, which is understanding and holy, is said to be both one and manifold, and subtle.
**“AND PIERCE THEM WITH ARROWS”** — SEPTUAGINT. And with his darts he shall shoot the enemy. For Christ by his words conquered the devil and overcomes and breaks all who contradict. For everyone who sins is his enemy while he sins. But if, pierced by the words of God, he recognizes his sins and is pricked, and is converted to penance, he is said to be pierced by his darts.
24.9:
**“Lying down he hath slept as a lion,”**
• Balaam prophesies also of the passion of Christ:
• when, set on the cross, he triumphed over the principalities and powers
• Christ a lion in the perfect, a lion's whelp in the little ones.
**“LYING DOWN HE HATH SLEPT”** — If you have understood how great rest the journey of wisdom has, how much grace and how much sweetness, do not pretend otherwise, do not neglect it; set out on the journey, nor shudder at the loneliness of the desert; for to one dwelling in such tabernacles the heavenly manna will come, and you will eat the bread of angels. Only begin; soon the angels will come into your fellowship, whom the cedars signify.
**“and as a lioness, whom to rouse”** — Christ the whelp, when, namely, he rose from the sleep of death.
**“WHOM TO ROUSE”** — SEPTUAGINT. Who shall rouse him? For now he is said to be raised by the Father, now he himself says he raises up the temple of his body; therefore the disposition is signified as of one asking.
**“HE THAT BLESSETH”** — Those who bless Christ bless, taken up into the communion of the Father's blessing. But those who curse are cursed. The Jews who cursed Christ are lamentably cursed. For what could befall those who curse wisdom, truth and life, but that they lie exiled from all these? For all these are Christ.
**“shall also himself be blessed: he that curseth thee shall be reckoned accursed.”** — HE THAT CURSETH THEE, etc. ORIGEN. I think that not only he curses Christ who utters a word of cursing against him; but also he who under the name of Christian does evil, lives foully, and by dishonest words or deeds causes his name to be blasphemed. As he blesses God not only who causes the name of God to be blessed by words alone, but by acts, life and manners.
24.10:
**“And Balac being angry against Balaam, clapped his hands together and said:”** — the fourth prophecy
**“I called thee to curse my enemies, and thou on the contrary hast blessed them three times.”** — like things were set down before in the preface above
24.11: **“THE LORD HATH DEPRIVED”** — The Lord shows that even Balac understood that Balaam was no longer deceived by the ministry of demons, but was being transferred to better things by the power of God.
24.13:
**“If Balac would give me his house full of silver and gold, I cannot go beyond the word of the Lord my God, to utter any thing either good or evil out of my mouth”** — others: out of the heart
**“I CANNOT GO BEYOND”** — Balaam, knowing that answers were not brought him by the accustomed ministers but by him who has power over all, rightly seems to protest that he cannot go beyond the word of the Lord or utter anything good or evil from his own mouth. For he who speaks cannot be changed by sacrifices or gifts, with whom there is no change. And therefore the priest cannot be changed by reward where God is not moved by gifts. Yet Balaam, about to depart, begins again to prophesy: "And he says: I give thee counsel" etc.
24.14: **“I WILL GIVE THEE COUNSEL”** — ORIGEN. Come, I give thee counsel what this people shall do to thy people in the last days. And taking up his parable he said, etc. I would ask what is the sense or order of the words. For he does not seem to give counsel, but says what this people will do to thy people in the last days. Since it would seem to have been fittingly said: Come, I will prophesy to thee what this people will do to thy people; and it would be consistent, so that Balaam seemed to prophesy of the things which the people of Israel would do to the people of Balac or to the other nations, that it would leave none safe of the cities of Moab. This prophecy also, which he joins concerning Christ and says: "A star shall rise out of Jacob" etc., would seem fittingly placed if he said: Come and I will prophesy to thee. Counsel, then, is to be understood thus: I give thee divine counsel; namely, what is to be fulfilled in the last days, now revealed to me, I open to thee and make manifest, that thou mayest know what this people will do to thy people; this is the counsel of God I make manifest to thee. Likewise also I think is to be understood what the Apostle says: "Who hath known the mind of the Lord? Or who hath been his counsellor?" For here "who" is taken not for none, but for rare and exceptional. For the Son knew the mind of God, who says: "No one knoweth the Father but the Son, and he to whom it shall please the Son to reveal him." What the Father knows, therefore, the Son knows, both his counsel and his mind. The Spirit too, who searches the deep things of God, knows his mind. The Son, therefore, who knows the mind of God is his counsellor; not that the Son or the Spirit gives counsel to one ignorant what he should do, but is partaker and knower of his counsel and will. Balaam therefore, because he was making Balac partaker of the counsel which God had revealed to him, says: "Come, I give thee counsel"; as one who truly sees and has truly heard.
24.15:
**“Therefore taking up his parable, again he said: Balaam the son of Beor hath said: hath said”**
• not "saith": Thus saith the Lord, as is the custom of the prophets.
• BALAAM HATH SAID, etc. ORIGEN. Balaam the son of Beor hath said: The man who truly sees and truly hears the words of God, knowing the knowledge of the Most High, etc. I have not easily found this written of any of the prophets. I wonder therefore how it is written of Balaam, to whom it was not even granted to say what is in use among the prophets: Thus saith the Lord; but he says: Balaam hath said, etc. How does he know the knowledge of the Most High, who even taught Balac how to cast a stumblingblock before the children of Israel, that they should eat things sacrificed and commit fornication? For of the apostles it is hardly found said that they know the knowledge of the Most High; although Paul said he had heard secret words which it is not granted to man to utter, he did not profess to have the knowledge of the Most High. In Ecclesiasticus it is said: "All wisdom is from the Lord God." Which perhaps we can understand thus, as though the wisdom of the world, which shall be destroyed, and of the princes of the world, and any by which false knowledge is commended, were also from God. But in what follows it is read: The learning of wickedness is not wisdom; where it is taught that every discipline which asserts falsehood, even if it seems vehement and probable, yet ought not to be called wisdom. But all wisdom is from God; that is, every skill which is held necessary for human use in any art, or the knowledge of anything whatever, is given by God. Whence it is said in Job: "Who hath given to women the wisdom of weaving and the skill of embroidery?" And of Beseleel the Lord says: "I have filled him with the spirit of wisdom and understanding, that he may understand every work and be an architect to work in silver and gold" etc. This knowledge, therefore, is from the Most High. How not geometry, from which the knowledge of architecture is derived? In Zacharias too a geometrical line is spoken of, with which the angel measures Jerusalem. What of music, the skill of which, and the discipline of melody and rhythms, David so attained that from all these he found sounds by which he soothed even the king vexed by an evil spirit? Of the knowledge of medicine I think there is no doubt. For what knowledge is more from God than that of health, in which also the powers of herbs and the qualities and differences of juices are known? The knowledge of Balaam, therefore, for which he was called from the mountains of Mesopotamia from the east, has its origin from the Most High. Whence he knew the natures of animals or the movements of birds or the differences of sounds; and what he received for the knowledge of good things he turned to the uses of evil things; as if a physician became a poisoner, and in place of remedies brought diseases, in place of health deaths. But that we may know more fully that the knowledge of all wisdom draws its origin from God, but is turned aside to evil by men of evil purpose or even by demons mingling certain corruptions with the wisdom of God, it is to be noted that the Lord gave Daniel and his companions knowledge and understanding and prudence in every art of letters; and to Daniel he gave understanding in every word and vision and dreams; and they were found by the king ten times wiser than the sophists and philosophers and enchanters and magicians who were in all his kingdom. From all these things it is gathered how Balaam spoke of himself; namely, so that it is understood that the origin of all knowledge took its beginning from him, but by the vice of human malice, with the demons conspiring and stealing in, the things granted for profit were turned to destruction.
**“GREGORY”** — The man hath said whose eye is stopped up, the hearer of the words of God hath said, who hath beheld the vision of the Almighty, who falleth, and so his eyes are opened. The wicked man does not know the evils he does except when he has begun to be punished for them. Balaam gave counsel against the Israelites; but afterwards in punishment he saw what he had first committed in fault. But the elect, because they ought not to sin, their eyes, providing, lie open before the fall. But the wicked man opened his eyes after the fall, because after the fault he now perceives in punishment that he ought to have avoided the evil which he did.
**“the man whose is stopped up”** — because he does not know his own evils which he does, except when he is punished
**“eye”** — the inner
24.16:
**“The hearer of the words of God hath said, who knoweth the doctrine of the Highest, and seeth the visions of the Almighty, who falling hath his eyes opened:”**
• because he does not lift his intent from earthly things
• because by contemplation he stretches his eyes in consideration
**“WHO FALLING”** — Often the wicked man wonders at the eternal judgments; when he hears the preaching of the heavenly fatherland he loves it, and is astonished at the works of the divine disposition. Lying down, therefore, he considers the miracles, because he weighs the power of God in knowing it, but does not love it in living.
24.17:
**“I shall see him,”**
• Christ, of whom: A star shall rise out of Jacob etc.
• I SHALL SEE HIM, BUT, etc. Another text: I shall show him, and not now; I shall bless him, and he does not draw near. These things are referred to those whose person he bears. Because the teachers of the law and the scribes show Christ promised in the law and the prophets, but not now, that is, when he came; but when the fulness of the Gentiles has come in, then they will show, then they will bless him whom now they blaspheme. But the time in which these things shall be is far off, and at the end of the world. Therefore he says: I shall show him, that is, to the people which will then be saved; but not now.
**“NOT NOW”** — While I speak these things; because when the fulness of time came God sent his Son.
**“I shall behold him, but not near. A star shall rise”**
• which the magi saw in the east
• the divinity of Christ
**“out of Jacob and shall spring up”**
• "There shall come forth a rod out of the root of Jesse."
• A STAR SHALL RISE OUT OF JACOB, etc. ORIGEN. Of this star it is said in the Gospel that it came and stood over where the child was. But whether it departed thence, or vanished, or was taken up, or what at all became of it thence, is not said. But perhaps as at the baptism the Spirit descended upon Christ as a dove and remained upon him, and the voice of the Father was heard: "This is my beloved Son", so too the star which came over where the child was and stood remained in Christ. And as we receive that the Spirit of God came upon him there and remained in him, so that the Spirit of God never withdrew from him, so the star which came and stood over him never departed. Therefore I think that star was a token of his divinity. The order of the prophecy too shows the same, when of the divinity it says: A star shall rise out of Jacob; but of the humanity: A man shall rise up out of Israel; so that both may appear evidently prophesied.
**“a sceptre”** — of which it is said: "Thou shalt rule them with a rod of iron" etc.
**“from Israel: and shall strike the chiefs”**
• the spiritual wickednesses
• the vices, namely, in them
**“AND SHALL STRIKE THE CHIEFS”** — Fastening the principalities and powers to the cross; otherwise he could not save the Moabites, unless he had first laid waste the leaders of impiety.
**“of Moab, and shall waste”** — he shall lead captive the one leading captive
**“SHALL WASTE ALL”** — THE SAME. And he shall make a prey of all the sons of Seth. This is Seth the son of Adam, of whom it is said: "God hath given me another seed for Abel, whom Cain slew." For from him is the whole human race; for those who were of Cain perished in the flood. The sons of Seth, therefore, are all men. He takes as prey, therefore, all the sons of Seth, the demons conquered; those, namely, who were held under their dominion; whom Christ leads as the prey of victory and brings back as the spoils of salvation. Whence: "Ascending on high, he led captivity captive." The captivity, namely, of the human race, which the devil had taken to perdition, Christ led captive and called back from death to life.
**“all the children of Seth.”** — the human race
24.18:
**“And Idumea shall be his possession:”**
• the flesh, which before fought against the spirit
• AND IDUMEA SHALL BE. THE SAME. And Edom shall be his inheritance; Esau his enemy, etc. Edom is the same as Esau. He, according to the history, is the enemy of Israel. But at the coming of Christ he himself will be his inheritance; that is, he will be received to the faith, he will not be shut out from the inheritance of Christ. Spiritually, therefore, by Edom is understood the flesh, which is adverse to the spirit and is its enemy. But at the coming of Christ, when the flesh has been subjected to the spirit through the hope of the resurrection, it too will come to the inheritance; for not the soul only, but the flesh too, which had once been an enemy, will through obedience to the spirit be a sharer of the future inheritance.
**“the inheritance of Seir shall come to their enemies,”** — it shall obey, namely, reason and virtue
**“Israel.”** — the soul
**“but shall do manfully.”** — in virtues, sloth cast off
**“BUT ISRAEL SHALL DO MANFULLY”** — ORIGEN. And Israel has done in strength; because, namely, then Edom or Esau, that is, the nature of the flesh, will be called into the fellowship of the inheritance, when Israel, that is, the soul, has been made in strength, fittingly filled with virtues. For if the soul does not come to the virtues, but persists in sloth, neither will the flesh come to the inheritance, but to the judgment of him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna.
24.19:
**“Out of Jacob”** — that is, Christ according to the flesh
**“shall he come that shall rule, and shall destroy”**
• wholesomely
• saying: "He that shall lose his life for me shall find it."
**“the remains”** — the remnant shall be saved
**“of the city.”**
• of the world
• of the heretics or philosophers, who fortify their dogmas against God
• AND SHALL DESTROY THE REMAINS, etc. THE SAME. He shall destroy him that is delivered from the city. Let us see if perhaps it can be explained in this way. Let us understand the city here as the world; as in the Gospel it is said of the prodigal son who wasted his father's substance: "He went, it says, and cleaved to one of the chief citizens of that country", by whom, received, he is sent into the field to feed swine. This city, therefore, of which he was a chief citizen, is the world. He therefore who is delivered from this city, that is, whom Christ delivers from this world, he destroys, saying: "He that shall lose his life for me shall save it." Wholesomely, therefore, Jesus destroys him whom he rescues from this world. If therefore we wish to come to salvation and be delivered from the world, let us lose our souls by a necessary and profitable loss. For he loses his soul according to Christ who bridles its desires, cuts away its covetings, chastises luxury and dissoluteness, and in nothing does his own will, but God's. By these things the soul is said to perish. For its former life perishes, and the new begins which is in Christ; with whom if we die, we shall also live together.
24.20:
**“And when he saw Amalec, he took up his parable,”** — as above
**“and said:”** — the fifth and last vision of Balaam
**“AMALEC THE BEGINNING OF NATIONS”** — This cannot be referred to the historical Amalec. For he was not first in antiquity; but to the spiritual one, who is named Amalec by turning peoples aside from God and making Gentiles out of worshippers of God. And he is called the beginning of nations because he gave the beginning for men to become Gentiles, changing the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of the image of corruptible man. For as in the people of God Christ is the beginning, so in the people which turns aside from God and becomes Gentile, Amalec.
**“ORIGEN”** — Amalec the beginning of nations, and their seed shall perish.
