This, then, the day of propitiation requires. For when the soul has been afflicted and humbled in the sight of the Lord, Christ is propitious, whom God hath proposed to be a propitiation in his blood, through faith.
29.6: **“Besides the holocaust of the calends with the sacrifices thereof, and the sacrifice”** — or: holocaust
29.12: **“AND ON THE FIFTEENTH DAY”** — ORIGEN. The last festival day, of which he rejoices in man, is that of tabernacles. He rejoices over you, then, when he sees you dwelling in tabernacles, not having a mind fixed and founded upon the earth, nor possessing earthly things, and as it were a shadow, for an inheritance; but set in passing and saying: "I am a sojourner and a stranger, as all my fathers were." "For Abraham, Isaac and Jacob dwelt in tabernacles." When, then, you are ready to stretch yourself forth to the things before, until you come to the land flowing with milk and honey, God rejoices in you and keeps a festival day over you; this indeed in the present. But in the future, if you wish to consider how the festival days are kept, forget all worldly things; picture to yourself how heaven and earth pass away, and the whole fashion of the world passes. But a new heaven and a new earth is founded. Remove the light of this sun, and give to that world which is to come sevenfold the light of this sun, nay, God himself. Set there the angels of glory standing by and all the powers of the heavens. Consider how the festival days of the Lord can be kept there, what festivity is there, what joys there, what greatness of gladness. For although the festivities which are carried on spiritually in the soul are great and true, yet they are in part, not wholly; as we know in part and we prophesy in part. Whence: "Let no man judge you in meat or in drink, or in respect of a festival day." He did not say: on a festival day. For in part we celebrate the festival day in this world; for the corruptible body is a load upon the soul, and presseth down the mind that museth upon many things. "But when that which is perfect is come, that which is in part shall be done away."

30.2:
**“If any man make a vow to the Lord,”**
• IF ANY MAN, etc. Over the soul which has come to the perfect man no one rules in vows, but it has its freedom in them.
• THE SAME. The angels have care of the souls which are in the Church of God; whom we have shown too to come to judgment with men, that it may be established whether men sinned by their own desire or by the negligence of their guardians. It seems to me, then, that some souls live under them as daughters, others as wives. If any one, then, vows something over-hastily and less fittingly, it is the guardian's part to check and blunt the boldness of the one vowing. And if he does not do so, the soul will be freed from fault, but he himself will be guilty of the vow. But this concerns the lower. To the more perfect God himself is present; as it is said of the people of Israel: The Lord himself led them. But after they sinned and were made lower than themselves, they are handed over to an angel. Whence Moses said: "If thou thyself go not with us, lead us not out from this place." And of the just man God says: I am with him in tribulation. And elsewhere he says: "Fear not to go down into Egypt, for I will be with thee." The Lord, then, is present to the just and the elect; but angels to the lower. But we must strive to meet unto the perfect man and use the freedom of vows, that we may be one spirit with the Lord himself, that he may abide in us and we in him; that nothing womanish, nothing of tender age, may be found in us, nor need we be left by the Father under tutors and governors.
**“ORIGEN”** — A law of vows is set down, and Moses seems to use a new beginning in this law. For he says: A man, a man, whoever shall vow to the Lord, etc. As though it would not have sufficed to say: a man who shall vow a vow to the Lord. For there is one, the inner man, who is renewed from day to day according to the image of God; but another, the outer, who is corrupted. But when one comes to this progress, that the law of God is taken up and vows are offered, these none can offer but he who has something in himself to offer to God. It is not enough for the outer man to take up the law of God and offer vows alone, because he cannot have anything worthy of God; but the inner, who has in himself something to offer to God, in whom is the dwelling of the virtues, of understanding, of knowledge, and the renewal of the divine image. When he has recovered his own beauty, which was made by God from the beginning, and the restoration of the virtues with the beauty of the former form, he can offer vows; and then he is called not man alone, but a man, a man. For he who does not cultivate the inner man, does not build him up with virtues, does not adorn him with manners, does not seek the wisdom of God and spends no labour on the scriptures, cannot be called a man, a man, but only a man, and an animal man; because the inner man, which is truer and nobler in him, [is overwhelmed] with carnal vices and the cares of this world. Whence each must act, if he sees the inner man in himself weighed down by the filth of sins, that he may quickly rescue him from all defilement of flesh and blood; let him be converted to penance, recall to himself the memory of God and the hope of salvation. For these things are not to be sought from without. Within us is the occasion of salvation. Whence: "Lo, the kingdom of God is within you." For within you is the power of conversion. For when, converted, you groan, you shall be saved, and you will be able worthily to pay your vows to the Most High and be called a man, a man. A vow is when we offer something of our own to God. God wishes to receive something from us, and so himself to bestow on us, that he may not bestow his gifts on the undeserving. Whence: "And now, Israel, what doth the Lord thy God require of thee, but that thou fear the Lord thy God, and walk in his ways, and love him with all thy heart" etc. These things God requires of us; and if we do not first offer them we shall receive nothing from him. If we give glory, we shall receive glory. For he says: "Them that glorify me I will glorify." If we offer our justice, we shall receive the justice of God; and if we offer our chastity, that is, of the body, we shall receive from him chastity of the spirit; and if we offer our mind, we shall receive his mind. Whence the apostles: "But we have the mind of Christ." So then we shall be called not only a man, but a man, a man; for each is adorned with the perfection of his name. Divers vows are read in the scriptures. Anna vowed to God the fruit of her womb, and consecrated Samuel in the temple. Jephte vowed whatever should meet him after the victory, and when his daughter met him he paid a lamentable vow. Others vow calves or rams or houses or other things lacking reason. But he who is called a Nazarite vows himself. For this is the vow of the Nazarite, which is above every vow. For a son or daughter or beast or estate is outside us. To offer oneself to God, and to please him not by another's labour but by one's own, is more perfect and more eminent than all vows. He who does this is an imitator of Christ. For he gave the earth, the sea and all that is in them; the heaven too, the sun and moon and stars, for the service of men; rains and winds and whatever is in the world he bestows on men; and after that himself. For God so loved the world as to give his only-begotten Son for the life of the world. For what great thing does man do if he offers himself to God, when God first offered himself? If, then, you take up your cross and follow Christ; if you say: 'I live, now not I, but Christ liveth in me'; if your soul desires to be with Christ and does not delight in the world, you have offered yourself, that is, your soul, to God. So does he who lives in chastity; whence the virgin thinks how she may be holy in body and in spirit. Those, then, are called holy who are vowed to God. Whence a ram, if it is vowed to God, is called holy, nor may it be yoked to common work. If, then, you vow yourself to God, you must imitate the calf, that you do only what pertains to the divine worship.
**“or bind himself by an oath: he shall not make his word void but shall fulfil all that he promised.”** — BIND HIMSELF BY AN OATH, etc. AUGUSTINE. This does not pertain to every swearing, but to that where one vows abstinence from some thing which was lawful to use by the law, but by the vow he makes it unlawful for himself.
30.3:
**“If a woman vow any thing, and bind herself by an oath, being in her father's house, and but yet a girl in age:”**
• Still little, namely, and having only the beginnings of divine learning.
• IF A WOMAN, etc. That is, if the soul is womanish and still tender, over whose vows the man, truly the father, rules, the fault is not always in her, but sometimes goes back to the husbands or parents.
**“AUGUSTINE”** — Rightly is it asked in this place also about the vow of virginity. For women who are virgins too are wont to be called women in scripture; and the Apostle seems to speak of the father when he says: "Let him keep his virgin, and give his virgin in marriage" etc. And in this way, where some have understood "his virgin" as his own virginity, yet they show this by no like manner of speaking in the scriptures, since it is most unusual.
30.4: **“if her father knew the vow that she hath promised, and the oath wherewith she hath bound her soul, and held his peace, she shall be bound by the vow:”** — THE OATH WHEREWITH, etc. SEPTUAGINT. And the determinations which they determine against their soul. Not that by such vows they harm their soul; but it is said against the soul, that is, against the animal delight, as there: "You shall afflict your souls."
30.5: **“NEITHER SHALL SHE BE BOUND”** — SEPTUAGINT. The Lord will cleanse her, because her father refused; that is, he will hold and judge her clean; as it is said: "The priest hath cleansed her", and "with cleansing thou shalt not cleanse the guilty", that is, thou shalt not call him clean who is unclean.
30.6:
**“IF SHE HAVE A HUSBAND”** — That is, if she is grown up and able for a husband, to conceive the seed of the word of God and to take in the secrets of spiritual doctrine. Whence: "For I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ."
**“AUGUSTINE”** — Because the Lord commanded that the woman be under her father before she marries, and under her husband when married, the law did not wish her so to vow anything against her soul, that is, in abstinence from lawful things, that in these same vows a woman's authority should prevail, but rather a man's. So that if her father has already allowed her while yet unmarried to pay her vows, if she marries before she has paid them, and it is known to her husband and does not please him, she should not pay them; and that altogether without sin, because the Lord has cleansed her, as he says, that is, has judged her to be made clean. Nor is this to be thought to be done against God, since he himself has commanded and willed it.
30.10: **“If the wife in the house of her husband hath bound herself by vow and by oath,”** — THE WIFE IN THE HOUSE OF HER HUSBAND, etc. AUGUSTINE. He spoke before of her who vowed in her father's house and married before she paid. Of her, then, who vowed in her husband's house he speaks thus: If in the house of her husband her vow or determination which is against her soul with an oath, and her husband hears it, etc. It is manifest, then, that the law wished the woman to be under her husband in such a way that no vows of hers which she has vowed for the sake of abstinence should be paid by her, unless the husband is the author by permitting. For since he wished it to pertain to the husband's sin if he first permitted and afterwards forbade, even here (yet he did not say that the woman should do what she had vowed because she had first been permitted by her husband) he said it was the sin of the husband who refused what he had first granted; yet he did not therefore allow the woman to disregard the vows if the husband afterwards forbade. But whether these things pertain also to vows of continence and to abstinence from intercourse is rightly asked; lest perhaps only those things are to be understood as vowed against the soul which are in foods and drinks. Which too seems signified there: Is not the soul more than the meat? And when fasting is commanded it is said thus: "You shall afflict your souls." But I do not know whether anywhere a vow concerning abstinence from intercourse is read to be called a vow against the soul. Above all since here the law gives the authority to the husband, not to the woman, who is subject to the husband: that she should pay her vows if the husband approves the vows, but if he refuses, she ought not. The Apostle, when he spoke of things of this kind, gave no greater authority to the husband than to the wife. But let the husband, he says, render the debt to his wife, and the wife also in like manner to the husband. The wife hath not power of her own body, but the husband. Since, then, he gives equal power to each, he hints that the rule about lying together does not pertain to those vows where they do not have equal power, but the husband greater, and almost his alone. For the law does not say that the husband ought not to pay his vows if the wife forbids, but the wife if the husband forbids. Moreover these are called justifications; and we remember that in those justifications which are recorded under this name in Exodus many things are commanded which cannot be taken in their proper sense nor observed in the New Testament, such as the boring of the servant's ear and the like. Whence here too something is understood to be said figuratively: so that, since there are many irrational abstinences of ceremonies, hostile to truth, perhaps he wished this to be understood: that they are ratified when they are rational, that is, when reason approves them, which as a husband ought to rule every animal motion; which arises not only in desiring but also in abstaining; so that if it is decided by mind and reason, then let it be done; but if it is disapproved, let it not be done. But if reason afterwards disapproves what it first decided was rightly to be done, let it be a sin of counsel; yet even so, only if that motion consents to reason.

31.2:
**“Revenge first the children of Israel on the Madianites,”** — the saints, to the citizens of the city above
**“REVENGE”** — ORIGEN. Stumblingblocks had befallen the children of Israel through the shiftiness of the Madianites, who had suborned women to deceive them so that they should sin. Those, then, were punished for their sin, yet more moderately and sparingly; but these, who had been the cause of sinning, much more vehemently. Whence it is plain that it is far graver to give the cause of sin than to sin. Whence it is said: "That it were better for that man not to have been born, or that a millstone should be hanged about his neck and he be drowned in the depth of the sea, than that he should scandalize one of these little ones." And a stumblingblock is where a deceit unto sinning is put in the way of one walking rightly.
**“AND SO THOU SHALT BE GATHERED”** — At the last, he says, thou shalt be gathered to thy people, etc. This is against the Samaritans, who deny the resurrection of the dead and do not receive the faith of the world to come. For no one is gathered to those who are not. It is established, then, that there is some people to which he says Moses is to be gathered.
31.4: **“Let a thousand men be chosen out of every tribe of Israel to be sent to the war.”** — A THOUSAND MEN, etc. Mark the magnificence of the divine power. The children of Israel, when they were six hundred thousand armed men, were all conquered, because there was sin in them. But now twelve thousand conquer as victors; because Israel does not conquer by multitude, but justice and godliness are in them, which conquer. Whence: One shall chase a thousand, and two ten thousand. You see, then, that one saint by praying avails more than countless sinners by fighting. For the prayer of the saint pierces heaven; how then should it not conquer the enemy on earth? Let us, then, seek and keep justice; let us put on the breastplate of justice, girt with truth, and take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the spirit, and above all the shield of faith, wherewith we may quench the fiery darts of the wicked one. For furnished with such arms we shall put to flight the camps of the devil.
31.8:
**“And their kings Evi, and Recem, and Sur, and Hur, and Rebe, five princes of the nation:”**
• The error of unbelief is slain by the wood of the cross.
• AND THEIR KINGS, etc. ORIGEN. The kings of the Madianites are slain; and those who before were conquered by women, now, expiation having been had and penance done, conquer kings; so much does conversion to God and the correction of sins avail. And it was the care of the divine scripture to record the names of the kings: Evi and Recem and Sur and Ur, Sorophoc. For these reign among the Madianites, whom everyone who serves as a soldier of God must utterly extinguish. For Evi is interpreted "beastly" or "wild". Beastly and wild manners, then, you must utterly destroy, that you may please him who has proved you and come to beatitude, the wildness of all wrath having been put to death. I think that the divine scripture did not relate these names for the sake of the history, but fitted them to causes and things. For what fool puts the name "beastly" on his son? But the divine word looked rather to the instruction of souls, wishing to show that we ought to war against vices of this kind and put these kings to flight from the kingdom of our body, lest sin reign in our mortal body. For names are fitted to things even among the Gentiles and barbarians. It is known why Abram was called Abraham, and Sarai Sara, and Jacob Israel. And Joseph was surnamed by Pharao in a barbarous tongue Photophanec, which he composed in his own tongue from the revelation of secrets or dreams. Daniel too in Babylon is named Baltassar; and Ananias and Azarias and Misael, Sidrach, Misach and Abdenago. Moses, then, named the king of the Madianites according to what he did. A beastly wildness, he says, is what reigns among the Madianites; nor it alone. There is another king named Recem, that is, emptiness, which reigns there. For there is much emptiness and vanity in this world, which the soldier of God overcomes and conquers if he does nothing emptily, nothing superfluously, remembering that men shall render account even of an idle word in the day of judgment. In this life of man almost everything that is said or done is idle and empty. Empty is every act and speech in which there is not within something for God or for the commandment of God. And there is another king of Madian, Ur, that is, provocation. You see what kind they are who reign among the Madianites; who, namely, must be fought down, nay destroyed, by those who follow God. For it is not so much the names of kings as of the vices that reign in men which are related in the law; and not so much the wars of nations as of the carnal concupiscences which war against the soul are described. Lastly, those who reign in vices are said to be five kings, that it may be plain that every vice which reigns in the body hangs on the five senses. These, then, must be destroyed from the kingdom of the Madianites, that vices may no longer reign through them, but justice; nor the eyes see unto stumbling, but unto edification. Whence: If thy eye scandalize thee, pluck it out, etc. Yet he does not command the eye of our body to be dug out, nor the hand or foot to be cut off, but the sense which perceives carnal things and wantons in concupiscences; that the eyes may see right things, the ears hear right things, our taste taste the word of God, the hands feel and handle of the word of life. And so, the kings of the Madianites being destroyed, let justice reign in us, that is, Christ, who of God is made unto us justice and peace and redemption.
**“BALAAM ALSO”** — It is plain that the women of the Madianites who had deceived Israel were suborned by the counsel of Balaam. Whence he is slain here as the author of the crime.
**“ORIGEN”** — It was said above that Balaam returned into his place. But perhaps he came back, though the scripture did not say so. Or perhaps he returned into his place from the place where he was making sacrifices, into the place, namely, where he had lodging as a stranger. For it was not said: into his house, or into his country. But of Balac it was said: to himself, where he dwells as lord.
31.15: **“Said: Why have you saved the women?”** — WHY HAVE YOU SAVED THE WOMEN, etc. RABANUS. Mystically. He keeps a woman for booty returning from war who, restraining wicked acts outwardly and destroying them with good zeal, hides carnal delight in the secret of the breast. But Moses, that is, the law, reproves this. For he who hides the delight of the flesh in the hidden places of the body easily goes astray into the guilt of wicked working. All the males, then, and the little ones too, and all the women who have known men, are commanded to be slaughtered; because we ought utterly to kill the foul appetite and delight of the flesh, which conceives iniquity and brings forth sin. But the girls and the women who are virgins, that is, the part of delight which is not prone to sinning but burns for the good, let us keep; that we may desire the things that are pleasing to God and study to accomplish them.
31.16:
**“BY THE COUNSEL OF BALAAM”** — Here it is shown more plainly that the women were suborned at the suggestion of Balaam.
**“ISIDORE”** — Balaam did not doubt that, a plenty of women being offered, the Israelites would fall into the ruin of fornication; because he knew that the concupiscible parts of their soul were corrupted. So the demons try each one, laying snares for those affections of the soul in which they perceive us to be sick.
31.18: **“But the girls, and all the women”** — or: the females
31.21:
**“Eleazar also the priest spoke to the men of the army, that had fought, in this manner:”** — Note that the word of God is spoken only to those who are men of valour.
**“ELEAZAR ALSO”** — Note that Eleazar speaks not to all the people but to the men of valour who were returning from the battle. And the men of valour are those who go forth to war, who strive in the contest and abstain from all things; but the others are not men of valour.
31.22: **“Gold, and silver, and brass, and iron, and tin, and lead,”** — GOLD AND SILVER, etc. The time of war is in this world, against the spiritual wickednesses and the carnal concupiscences. The choir of angels watches us, and the godly expectation of the heavenly powers hangs upon us: when or how we return from the battle, who brings more gold or silver, who looks carefully at precious stones. They seek also those who bring brass, who iron, who lead, or a wooden or earthen vessel, or anything of this kind necessary for the uses of a great house. According to the things, then, that each has brought, the merit of his mansion will be assigned him. Yet all these are proved, some by fire, others by water; the fire shall try every man's work, of what sort it is.
31.24: **“AND YOU SHALL WASH”** — ORIGEN. You see how everyone who comes out of the battle of this life needs purging. Those who fought for the children of Israel slew the Madianites; in which they pleased God, whose will they fulfilled; yet by this very thing they are said to have been made unclean, whence they are commanded to wash their garments and be cleansed and so enter the camp. Those, then, who fight are polluted, because they touch unclean enemies. If, then, I have conquered the devil, and the unclean thoughts which he suggests I have either driven back as they come or, when they have entered within me, killed lest they come to effect, treading on the head of the dragon, yet by this very thing I am polluted, that I strove to tread upon the polluted. Yet I am blessed because I overcame. Whence: "No one is clean from filth." We all, then, need purification, nay purifications. For many and divers purifications await us. But these things are mystical and unspeakable. For who will be able to tell what purifications are prepared for Peter and Paul and the like, who laid low so many enemies, took so many spoils, who return from the slaughter with bloody hands, whose foot is dipped in blood, and who washed their hands in the blood of sinners, slaying in the morning all the sinners of the land? For they destroyed divers nations of demons; and unless they had conquered them they would not have freed the captives nor brought them to the obedience of Christ. Blessed is he who succeeds in these battles and slays the Madianites, that he may be justified by their blood. He sheds the blood of demons who rescues captives. But he will be purified in the kingdom of God, that he may enter clean into the city of God, or of the Lord.
31.27: **“THEM THAT FOUGHT”** — Allegorically. ORIGEN. There are some in the people of God who serve as soldiers, who, namely, do not entangle themselves with secular business. These go forth to war against the fortified nations and the spiritual wickednesses on behalf of those who are weaker, whether in age or sex or purpose. And they fight with prayers, fasts, justice, godliness, meekness, chastity and all the virtues of continence. And when they have returned as victors to the camp, even the unwarlike, who are not called to the fight or cannot go out, enjoy their labours. But it is to be known that all things which are taken from these nations must be changed; and perhaps whatever is taken from this world or captured in battle is unclean and needs purification; and some pass through fire, for others the purification of water suffices. And men and beasts are taken from the battle when every understanding is taken captive to the obedience of Christ through the word of God; in which those fighting take captive the understanding of those who think contrary things. Yet few are they who can fight and carry through these battles. Of six hundred thousand armed men who seem to serve God, only twelve thousand are chosen; the rest are left in the camp. Behold how many there are in the Church who can fight for the truth and resist the gainsayers, who know how to handle the wars of the word. Blessed are they who can fight for the people of God and bring back spoils from the enemies. Yet the rest of the people, which seems unwarlike, if it stays quietly in the camp, acts in silence, does not depart from Moses but remains in the law of God, shall have part of the spoils. For the portion will be made equal, not by number, but as much is given to all the people as to the twelve thousand who took the spoils. Who, hearing these things, is not stirred to fight for the Church and resist the enemies of the truth, who assail the dogmas of the Church or teach men to give themselves to pleasure and luxury? He, then, who fights these down, or destroys vices in himself or in his neighbours, will take many spoils, fifty times multiplied over the rest; for so much does the quantity of the number seem to be increased when twelve thousand are compared with six hundred thousand. Yet each part is commanded to offer to God: those indeed who conquered, one out of five hundred; but those who stayed at home, one out of fifty. And each number is sacred. Whence one had to be given out of five hundred, and another out of fifty, etc. And seven weeks, with one added, make the fiftieth day, which is called the festivity of Pentecost. Likewise, as seventy weeks [exceed] seven, so much more excellent is the number five hundred than fifty.
31.48: **“AND WHEN THEY WERE COME”** — ORIGEN. That there are differences and advances of merits in the people of the faithful we gather both in other places and here from what is written: And there came to Moses all who had been appointed princes by tribes in the army, tribunes and centurions, and said to Moses: We thy servants have gathered the sum of our warriors, and not one of us has dissented, and we have offered a gift to the Lord, etc. The chosen princes, then, who were appointed over the army, speak to Moses and offer gifts to the Lord for things well done, saying: We thy servants are they who received the sum of the warring children of Israel, namely the twelve thousand who were chosen out of all the tribes to fight against the Madianites. There are, then, in the people of God many warriors and many unwarlike; and among the warriors some who are called the sum of the warriors, more eminent, namely, among the warriors; and again higher than these, those who are appointed over them as princes and prelates over each thousand of the chosen. There is, then, much diversity in the order of the warriors. Among the unwarlike too there is some difference. For some are so unwarlike that they can never become warriors; [others] hope, when they have come, namely, unto the perfect man and the measure of age, to come even into the sum of the warriors and be chosen among the twelve thousand, or be princes of the chosen. Consider that all the present age is filled with wars and pressed hard by the invisible battles of the demons; but that in the people of God there are some robust in faith, armed with virtues, who carry through wars of this kind and, always set in readiness, protect from the enemies by word and example even those who cannot fight, if only faith is not lacking in them; for it is impossible to be saved without faith. Among the warriors themselves there are others ready and unencumbered, so that they entangle themselves in no secular business, meditating on the law of God day and night. These are called the sum of the warriors. And it was not said of the common number of warriors that no one among them dissented, but of those who are called the sum of the warriors. For in such there is no dissension, no discord. For of these it was said: "The multitude of believers had but one heart and one soul" etc. These are they who by fighting had taken very much gold, and offer to God all the gold and ornament, whether of the head or of the arms or of the fingers, that is, whatever they have in understandings or works; knowing that his gifts are his presents. Therefore not one dissented (for those dissenting cannot offer; whence: if thou offer thy gift at the altar, and there thou remember that thy brother hath any thing against thee, leave there thy gift, etc.), that they may lift up their hands to God without anger and dissension. For in music, if the harmony of the strings is fitted concordantly, it gives back a sweet sound; if there is any dissonance, the sweetness of the song is corrupted. So if the soldiers of God dissent, all things are unpleasing to God, even if they carry through many wars and bring back many spoils. For it will be said: Go first to be reconciled to thy brother, etc. For if in anything you dissent from the commandments of God, you cannot conquer the enemy either. For in that very thing in which you dissent from God you are already conquered by the devil. If, then, you wish to conquer and to be of the sum of the warriors, cleave to God, agree with him, saying: "Who then shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation? or distress?" etc. He who is such can conquer the Madianites and slay all the sinners of the land, that is, of the flesh: fornication, uncleanness, passion, concupiscence, avarice and the like. And so he will be worthy to offer every golden vessel, a torque or a bracelet or a ring or an armlet or a little chain. The torque is the ornament of wisdom; for in Proverbs it is said of wisdom that he who has acquired it should put a golden torque about his neck. The bracelet and the ring are ornaments of the hands, in which works are signified; likewise the armlet. But the little chains signify the connexions of word and doctrine.
31.49:
**“We thy servants have reckoned up the number of the fighting men,”** — Who also defend others in the Church from enemies both visible and invisible.
**“whom we had under our hand, and not so much as one”** — The multitude of believers had but one heart and one soul.
31.50:
**“Therefore we offer”** — Those in discord cannot offer; whence: "Go first to be reconciled to thy brother, and then coming thou shalt offer thy gift."
**“as gifts to the Lord what gold every one of us could find in the booty, in garters and bracelets, rings”** — ornaments, namely, of works
**“and armlets and chains,”** — made of gold and silver
**“THAT THOU MAYST PRAY FOR US”** — ORIGEN. That thou mayst make God propitious for us. If we should say that God is made propitious to men on account of gold, it is judged absurd and impious; for this is called a disgrace even in a good man. By gold, then, are signified virtues and good works, which alone are worthily offered to God, and for which alone it befits him to be propitiated.
31.51:
**“And Moses and Eleazar the priest received all the gold”** — the virtues of the soul and good works
**“AND THEY RECEIVED”** — And Moses and Eleazar the priest received the gold from all the tribunes and centurions, and brought it into the tabernacle of the testimony, a memorial for the children of Israel before the Lord. Note that the things said are referred not to visible sight but to the memory of the mind. For blessed is he who remembers that he has done some good work before the Lord and offered gifts well pleasing to God, namely the virtues of the soul and the ornaments of godliness.

32.1: **“AND THE SONS OF RUBEN”** — ORIGEN. All things that are said are to be weighed not only by the speech that is spoken but by the person of the speaker. If a boy speaks, we fit our souls to the hearing of boyish speech, nor do we expect more in what is said than a boy could perceive. But if a man speaks, at once we consider whether the things said are worthy of a man; and if he is learned, we weigh the sayings too with regard to his learning; but if he is unskilled and unlettered, we take what is said otherwise. But if he is an elder, or of much skill and proved (as those who are versed in learning), far greater will be the expectation of his sayings. But he who speaks these things is the Holy Ghost. For whence could Moses relate the things that were done from the beginning of the world, or are to be done at the end, but by the inspiration of the spirit of God? Whence could he have prophesied of Christ? For Christ says: If you did believe Moses, you would perhaps believe me also; for he wrote of me, etc. This, then, must be understood according to the majesty of the speaker. Whence Abraham says: They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them; signifying not men set in the body, but the things written by them, dictated by the spirit of God. Let us, then, the veil being removed, so understand the letters of Moses that they seem to be spoken to each one; that if the hearers understand and observe them, they may not go into the place of torments, like the rich man who scorned to hear, but into the bosom of Abraham, where Lazarus rests. Yet to know these things clearly I think belongs to the Holy Ghost himself, who inspired them, and to Jesus Christ, who says: "For he wrote of me"; and to the Father, whose ancient counsel is shown to the human race not bare but veiled by the letters. But let us now come to the judging of the things that seem to lie hid. There are two ways of going out of Egypt. For when anyone is led from the darkness of errors to the light of knowledge, and is converted from earthly conversation to spiritual ordinances, he seems to have gone out of Egypt and come to the wilderness; to that state of life, namely, in which through silence and quiet he is exercised in the divine laws and steeped in the heavenly words; instructed and directed through which, when he has crossed the Jordan, he may hasten as far as the land of promise, that is, through the grace of baptism as far as the Gospel ordinances. The soul also goes out of Egypt when it leaves the darkness of this world and the blindness of bodily nature and is transferred to another world, which is shown as the bosom of Abraham, as in Lazarus, or paradise, as in the thief, or whatever other places or mansions God knows there to be; passing through which the soul that believes God, and coming as far as the river which makes glad the city of God, receives beyond it the lot of the inheritance promised to the fathers. Since, then, the going out of Egypt is marked in two ways, and the passing to the desert, and thence the going out to the inheritance of the holy land, let us see what is meant by the inheritance of Ruben and Gad and the half tribe of Manasses, which is handed over through Moses and decreed outside the Jordan. In the twelve tribes of the children of Israel the figure of the whole human race is mystically embraced, or of all who have come to the knowledge of God. Of these, part obtains an inheritance outside the Jordan through Moses, but part beyond the Jordan in the land of promise through Jesus. And indeed those to whom an inheritance is given outside the Jordan are firstborn, though less noble, though not blameless. For Ruben is the firstborn of Jacob, though he defiled his father's bed; and Gad, though from a handmaid. Manasses too, whose half tribe obtains an inheritance outside the Jordan, though born of an Egyptian, is yet firstborn. All these, then, are firstborn, and therefore they signify the former people, who receive an inheritance outside the Jordan not through Jesus but through Moses.
32.4:
**“The land, which the Lord hath conquered in the sight of the children of Israel, is of a very fertile region for the feeding of beasts: and we”**
• GREGORY. Those whom the many hindrances of the world occupy do not desire the dwelling of the heavenly fatherland.
• THE LAND WHICH THE LORD HATH CONQUERED, etc. GREGORY. There are many in the Church who disdain to be little, and, set in a place of humility, do not cease to be swollen within themselves. These are lifted up by honours, enjoy pleasures, and are spread wide by a multitude of things. They desire to be over others and to be feared by many; they neglect to live rightly and desire to have the fame of a good life; they seek flatteries, swell with favours; and because they delight in the plenty of present things, they do not seek the joys to come. And while manifold activity occupies them and shows them estranged from themselves, yet if any trial of the faith arises, because they are held by it in outward show, they defend it with words and labours and lay claim to the heavenly fatherland, yet do not love it. These Ruben and Gad and the half tribe of Manasses well signify; because, possessing many flocks and beasts, while they coveted the plains about the Jordan, they would not have an inheritance in the land of promise, saying: The land which the Lord hath smitten in the sight of the children of Israel is a most fertile region for the feeding of beasts, etc. Those, then, who possess very many beasts shrink from crossing the Jordan, because those whom the many entanglements of the world occupy do not seek the dwelling of the heavenly fatherland. But the faith (which they hold in outward show) rebukes them, lest they grow numb, idle, with delight, and by their example break others away from the endurance of labour and the zeal of longsuffering. Whence it is said to them through Moses: Shall your brethren go to fight, and will you sit here? etc. But because they are ashamed not to defend what they confess, they hasten to the contest for the faith, and claim it not for themselves but for their neighbours. We will build folds for the flocks and stalls for the beasts, etc. These, presently coming as strong men on behalf of others, free the land of promise from the enemies, and leave it, and return outside the Jordan to feed their herds; because, against the faith of baptism, with their whole mind and desire they serve perishing things; because they do not love the inheritance of the land of promise, that is, the fruit of faith. And so they fight for it in such a way as to set down their pledges outside it; for because they have their little ones outside, they have no affection for dwelling in it. Whence they return to the plains, because they slip down from the height of the mountains, as from the hope of heavenly things; or outside the land of promise they nourish brute animals, namely the irrational motions of the mind, with vain desires; because they do not know the brightness of the eternal light while they are blinded by transitory things.
**“VERY MUCH CATTLE”** — ORIGEN. They have many beasts and flocks, etc. The former people could not come to the inheritance of that land which flows with milk and honey, nor acknowledge the Word made flesh, because it had many beasts and flocks. For the animal man cannot perceive the things that are of the spirit of God, nor judge spiritually; because man, when he was in honour, did not understand, but was compared to senseless beasts. That people, then, received an inheritance through Moses, namely the land of two kings; for Moses could not slay more than two kings, whose land he might divide to the peoples having many animals and many flocks. But to those who cross the Jordan Jesus divides the land. For although they had animals and flocks, they were not so many as to shut them out from crossing the Jordan; but with their very wives and infants they strive to cross and come to the promises of the fathers. But all these things hold the others back, so that they cannot cross the Jordan nor enter the faith of Christ, which is the land of promise.
32.7: **“Why do ye overturn the minds of the children of Israel, that they may not dare to pass into the place which the Lord will give them?”** — ORIGEN. Note that Moses, that is, the Law, rebukes those who wish to stay beyond the Jordan.
32.16: **“But they coming near, said: We will make sheepfolds,”** — elsewhere: we were making
32.29: **“IF THEY PASS”** — ORIGEN. Another reading: If the sons of Ruben and the sons of Gad cross the Jordan with you, all armed for battle before the Lord, and you have taken the land in your sight, you shall give them the land of Galaad, etc. Land is taken in many ways. And this land on which we dwell was not called land from the beginning, but dry land, and afterwards land; as this visible heaven was first called firmament, afterwards heaven. Yet in the beginning of the creation God is said to have made heaven and earth, and afterwards the dry land and the firmament. Here Aggeus says: "Yet one little while, and I will move the heaven and the earth and the sea and the dry land." You see how he sets the earth as one thing, the dry land as another. In many places too the earth is taken in a good sense, but the dry land rarely. For Adam too after sin is thrust down into a place which is named the dry land; for before he was in the earth; for paradise is not in the dry land but in the earth. To the meek too in the Gospel not the dry land but the earth is promised: "Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the land." The seed too which yields fruit a hundredfold, sixtyfold, thirtyfold is called earth, not dry land. And I think that it is progress to come from the dry land to the earth, as it was progress that the dry land should be called earth. For while we are unfruitful and bear no fruit of justice, chastity or godliness, we are dry land. But if, cultivating ourselves, we raise up the crop of virtues, from dry land we are made earth, which, having received the seed of the word of God, bears fruit. There is, then, a certain earth even in the kingdom of God, which is promised to the meek, and an earth which is named of the living. There is an earth set on high, of which it is said to the just: "He will exalt thee to inherit the land." The inheritance of this land the soul obtains going out of the Egypt of the world: in one place those who lived under the law, in another those who were ordered through the faith and grace of Christ. Yet those who seem first and ordered through Moses do not obtain the inheritance unless they first cross with those whom Jesus orders, and fight with them against the enemies and settle them in their seats; and so they obtain the inheritance which they merited under Moses as leader. Whence Paul: "And all these, being approved by the testimony of faith, received not the promise, God providing some better thing for us, that they should not be perfected without us." As though these nine and a half tribes said it of those two and a half tribes. Therefore they did not receive the promise of that land which was decreed them outside the Jordan through Moses, God providing some better thing for us, that they should not be perfected without us. And therefore they cross with us armed and help to fight down the enemies. But only the armed men cross, namely the strong and mighty. The slothful and unwarlike band remains outside the Jordan. But the strong, leaving the animals and flocks and all hindrances, fight with us until our enemies are conquered, until we take the inheritance of the promised land. For the holy fathers help us with prayers, exhort and strengthen us by examples, and by their writings, which they left for a memorial, instruct us how we should fight against the hostile powers and endure the contests. They fight, then, for us, and go first armed. For we set them before us, and seeing their brave deeds we arm ourselves for the spiritual battle and fight. So lastly those who serve under Jesus as leader destroy thirty kings and more, and receive their lands by lot. The spiritual wickednesses in the heavenly places being driven out too, they receive the inheritance of heaven, Christ fighting for them. There can yet be a third manner of exposition: that among the children of Israel, that is, among the people of the Church, some are understood to be spiritual, and to receive within the Jordan the inheritance of the land flowing with milk and honey, taking the sweetness of wisdom and knowledge; whose land is surrounded and watered by the river of God, which is filled with the waters of divine understanding. But others are carnal, abounding in beasts and cattle, that is, in gross and dull senses; to such the Apostle says: "Are you so foolish that, whereas you began in the spirit, you would now be made perfect by the flesh?" And: "O senseless Galatians, who hath bewitched you that you should not obey the truth?" But each of us, unless he arms himself and, casting away brute and beastly senses, hastens to spiritual understanding, will remain outside the Jordan; nor will he be able to go through the river of wisdom, which makes glad the city of God, that is, the soul capable of God; nor does he attain the inner things of the word of God, which are sweeter than honey and the honeycomb; but he will obtain only that land in which two kings were slain, where it is said to him: I judged not myself to know any thing among you, but Jesus Christ, and him crucified. But he who can cross the Jordan and penetrate to the inner things, following the Lord Jesus Christ, will slay thirty kings and more; those strong ones of whom it is said: "The kings of the earth stood up, and the princes met together, against the Lord" etc. These being laid low, you will know the more secret mysteries, until you come to the seat of God and to Jerusalem, the city of the living God; not that which is in bondage with her children, but that which is above, which is free, which is the mother of us all.

33.1:
**“These are the mansions of the children of Israel, who went out of Egypt”**
• that is: by working
• THESE ARE THE MANSIONS, etc. ORIGEN. God created divers differences of foods for the diversity of animals or of human desire. Whence the animals too know their proper foods: the lion uses some, the hart others. Among men too, he who is sound and strong requires strong food and is confident to eat all things; the weak delights in herbs and does not bear strong food; but the little one, if not by voice, yet by the thing itself, requires only milk. And the food of the rational nature is the true word of God. But here too there are differences: not everyone is nourished by the same word. For some there is in the word of God a fitter food of milk, namely doctrine such as the moral, which is wont to be given to the untaught. These gladly receive a reading in which nothing is obscure, for example Esther, Judith, Tobias, and the precepts of wisdom. If Leviticus is read to them, the mind is at once offended, as though it were not its food. For he came to learn to worship God and receive the precepts of justice and godliness, and he hears the commandments of sacrifices and the rites of immolations. Another gladly embraces the evangelists, the Apostle, the Psalms, as remedies for his infirmity. If these things which we have in hand are read to him, he will judge that they profit nothing for his infirmity or the salvation of his soul, but will refuse them as heavy and burdensome foods. But as a lion, if he had understanding, would not blame the abundance of herbs created, nor call it superfluous because he uses flesh; nor ought a man, because he uses foods fit for himself, to blame God for making serpents as food for harts; so in rational foods the scripture is not to be refused which seems more obscure and unfitting for beginners, little ones, the weak, and those less strong to understand. Let each take what he feels wholesome for himself. He says, then: These are the mansions of the children of Israel, from the time they went out of the land of Egypt with their power, in the hand of Moses and Aaron. And Moses wrote their departures and their mansions by the word of the Lord, etc. Who then would dare to say that these things which are written by the word of the Lord have nothing of usefulness or salvation, but relate only a history? In two ways can anyone go out of Egypt spiritually: either by leaving the Gentile life and coming to the knowledge of the divine law, or when the soul departs from the dwelling of this body. For these mansions look to both. Of those mansions which the soul, stripped of the body, nay rather clothed again with its own body, is to have, it is said: "In my Father's house there are many mansions" etc. There are, then, many mansions which lead to the Father; in each of which what usefulness the soul's sojourn has, what learning or illumination it receives, only the Father of the world to come knows, who says: "I am the door; no man cometh to the Father but by me." But let us return to the things that are done among us and in us. The children of Israel were in Egypt in the works of Pharao; they were afflicted with clay and brick, until groaning they cried to the Lord, and he sent them his word through Moses and led them out of Egypt. We, then, when we were in Egypt, that is, in the errors of this world and the darkness of ignorance, working the works of the devil in the concupiscences and pleasures of the flesh, the Lord had mercy and sent his word, that is, his only-begotten Son, to lead us from the ignorance of error to the light of the divine law. But first of all behold the reason of the mystery. In the going out of the children of Israel from Egypt there are forty-two mansions; and the coming of Christ into the world is made through forty-two generations. Whence: from Abraham to David fourteen generations, etc. The forty-two mansions of generations, then, which Christ made descending into the Egypt of this world, those make who ascend out of Egypt. In forty-two mansions, then, the children of Israel come to the beginning of taking the inheritance, where Ruben and Gad and the half tribe of Manasses receive the land of Galaad. As Christ by forty-two fathers, as by mansions, descended as far as us, so the children of Israel by as many mansions ascended as far as the beginning of the promised inheritance. Let us begin, then, to ascend by those by which he descended, and to make our first mansion that which he made last, who was born of the virgin. The first mansion, then, for those going out of Egypt, the worship of idols being left, will be to believe that Christ, born of the virgin and of the Holy Ghost, the Word made flesh, came into the world. After this let us strive to ascend to each step of faith and the virtues, and tarry at each, until, when we have come to the highest summit of instruction, the promised inheritance is fulfilled. The soul too, going from the Egypt of this life toward the land of promise, proceeds by certain ways and makes certain mansions. Whence: "I poured out my soul upon me, for I shall go over into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God." Of these mansions he says elsewhere: "How lovely are thy tabernacles, O Lord of hosts! my soul longeth and fainteth for the courts of the Lord." And elsewhere: "My soul hath long been a sojourner." Understand, then, what these sojournings of the soul are, in which it grieves that it sojourns too long. And it will understand more truly what was the reason of its sojourning when it has returned into its rest, that is, into paradise. Whence: "Turn, O my soul, into thy rest" etc. These, then, are the mansions by which one goes to heaven. But who is so aware of the divine secrets that he can describe the mansions of this ascent, and the labours or rests of each place? Who would relate that after the first and second and third mansion Pharao and the Egyptians still pursue, although they do not overtake, although they are drowned? How would he tell that the people of God, made safe, after some mansions first sang a song, saying: "Let us sing to the Lord, for he is gloriously magnified"? Who could or would dare to fit these things one by one to the going out of the soul? And how did the old people fall, whose conversation and dwelling had been with the Egyptians, while the new came safe to the kingdom, which did not know the Egyptians, except the priests and Levites? For he who is in the priesthood or the order of the Levites, and has God alone as his portion, does not fall in the desert but comes to the land of promise. Names are given to the mansions; for it did not seem fitting that all other things should use their names, but the ascent of the soul should not have the names of its mansions. It has, then, mystical names, and one leading it: not Moses, who did not know where he was going, but the pillar of fire and the cloud, namely the Son of God and the Holy Ghost; when all the Egyptians and Amalecites and all who assailed it have been drowned; that through each of the mansions which are said to be with the Father it may be more fully enlightened, until it becomes used to bearing the gaze of that light which enlightens every man, and to entering the brightness of majesty. If, then, we understand that the true advances of the soul set in this life are taught by these things; which, converted from the Gentile life, follows not so much Moses as the law of God, nor Aaron but that priest who remains for ever; before it comes to the perfect it dwells in the wilderness, where it is exercised in the precepts of the Lord, that its faith may be proved; and, one temptation overcome, it comes to others, as from mansion to mansion, when it has borne faithfully what has befallen. For so, through each trial of life and faith, its advance is said to have mansions, according to that: "They shall go from virtue to virtue", until it comes to the highest step of the virtues, and the river of God is crossed, and the promised inheritance received. But what usefulness does it bring to those who read and meditate on the law of God day and night to know how that place was called in that wilderness where they put in, when the names are described a second time, though in some cases changed, and are commanded by the word of the Lord to be described by Moses? This is done so that he might show two ways of the soul: one by which, set in the flesh, it is exercised in the virtues through the law of God, and, advancing by certain steps, ascends from virtue to virtue, as from mansion to mansion; the other, by which, about to ascend to heaven after the resurrection, it does not climb suddenly nor untimely, but through many mansions, enlightened everywhere in each with the light of wisdom, comes to the Father of lights himself.
**“BY THEIR TROOPS”** — SEPTUAGINT. With their power: with Christ, namely, who is the power of God and the might of God. With him, then, one ascends who descended to us that we might ascend. For he who descended is the same also that ascended; and who says: "I will go down with thee into Egypt"; therefore there was not a weak one in their tribes.
**“of Moses and Aaron”** — For the hand of Moses, which signifies the knowledge of the law, does not suffice: the hand of Aaron too is sought, which signifies skill in sacrificing to God.
**“UNDER THE HAND OF MOSES AND AARON”** — ORIGEN. For when we go out of Egypt we ought to have not only the knowledge of the law and of faith, but also the fruits of works by which God is pleased. For if, going out of Egypt and converted to God, I cast away pride, by the hands of Aaron I have sacrificed a bull to God; if I destroy wantonness, a goat; if lust, a calf; if folly, a sheep. If, then, the vices of the soul are fought against, the hand of Aaron works in us; and the hand of Moses, when we are enlightened from the law to understand these things. Both hands, then, are necessary, that there may be found in us the perfection not only of faith and knowledge but also of acts and works. Yet they are not two hands, but one; for he said "in the hand", not "in the hands". For the work of both hands is one, and the accomplishment of perfection is one.
33.2:
**“Which Moses wrote down according to the places of their encamping, which they changed by the commandment of the Lord.”** — that we may always read and see how many departures and mansions await us
**“WHICH HE WROTE DOWN”** — And Moses wrote their departures and mansions by the word of the Lord: that, namely, reading how many departures and mansions await us, we may prepare ourselves for this way, and not spend our time sluggishly; lest, while we tarry in vanities and delight in each of the things which come to sight, hearing, touch, smell and taste, the time pass and we do not complete the space of the way, but fail in the midst, as in the desert. For to this end we came into this world, that we might pass from virtue to virtue, and not remain on earth for earthly things, like him who said: "Soul, thou hast much goods; eat, drink, make good cheer." For the Lord said to him: "Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be taken from thee." He did not say "in this night" nor "in this day", but "this night". For he is destroyed in the night, like the firstborn of the Egyptians, because he loved the world and its darkness, a companion of the rulers of the world of this darkness. And this world is called darkness and night for those who live in ignorance, so that they do not receive the light of truth and do not pass from Ramesses to Soccoth.
33.3:
**“Now they departed from Ramesses”**
• 'troubled commotion' or 'commotion of the moth'. For all things that are in the world are set in perturbation and corruption.
• This order and distinction of the mansions is very necessary and to be observed by those who follow God and think on the advances of the virtues. The first departure, then, is made from Ramesses, whether the soul setting out from this world and going to the world to come, or from the errors of life to the way of virtue and the knowledge of God. It sets out from Ramesses, which is interpreted "troubled commotion" or "commotion of the moth"; because in this world all things are set in commotion and perturbation and corruption. In which the soul must not stay, but set out and come to Soccoth, that is, tabernacles. The first advance of the soul, then, is that it be taken away from earthly commotion and know that, as a sojourner and one making a journey, it must dwell in tabernacles; whereby, set as it were in readiness, it can meet the ambushers unencumbered and free. And then, when it feels itself prepared, it sets out from Soccoth and puts in at Buthan.
**“NOW THEY DEPARTED”** — The children of Israel, still set in Egypt, made the Pasch on the fourteenth day, and a certain beginning of festivity. On the following day, then, which is the first of the unleavened bread, the fifteenth, namely, of the first month, they set out from Ramesses and come to Soccoth, to keep there the festivities, or the day, of the unleavened bread. Who would understand these things? Who would know them even in part? As the Apostle says: "We know in part, and we prophesy in part." For who will understand how we keep the festival days in part, so that no one may judge us in respect of a festival day or a new moon or a sabbath? For every festival day which is kept here is carried on in part, not wholly. But when you have gone out of Egypt, then you will have the perfect festivity. Know, however, that after that Pasch which was once made in Egypt, another is found kept in the desert when the law was given, and after this none kept anywhere but in the land of promise.
**“the first month, on the fifteenth day”** — Because on the fourteenth they kept the Pasch in Egypt, and a certain beginning of festivity, slaughtering the lamb the day before they set out.
**“WITH A MIGHTY HAND”** — Where there is no human or earthly work, but divine, there a high hand is named; for by the hand work is understood.
33.4:
**“and they were burying”** — The dead were burying their dead; the living were following their Lord.
**“AND UPON THEIR GODS”** — All the gods of the Gentiles are devils, on which the Lord will execute vengeance in the day of judgment; he does so now too, when one who had been deceived by them into worshipping idols, converted by the word of the Lord, worships the Word, that is, God; or when the fornicator is converted to chastity and bewails that he has erred; the demon [is punished] by the very tears of his penance; or from pride to humility, from luxury to frugality. With how great torments do you think they are driven if they see someone sell all that he has and give to the poor and take up his cross and follow Christ; or when they see the clouds of their fraud laid open through the knowledge of the divine law? For sin is not accomplished without them. We, then, must act with all diligence lest we raise up again in ourselves the firstborn of the Egyptians, or their gods, whom the Lord has extinguished, if we give them place to work in us the things which the Lord hates. For so the Lord will punish the gods of the Egyptians, by our amended conversation.
33.5:
**“they camped in Soccoth.”**
• IN SOCCOTH, etc. In tabernacles; for while we sojourn in the body we dwell in tabernacles.
• When we have gone out of Egypt, that is, out of the world, we first pitch tabernacles, knowing that we hasten to further things and to the holy land, namely the heavenly.
33.6:
**“FROM SOCCOTH”** — ORIGEN. They set out from Soccoth and put in at Buthan, which is called a valley. For in these is the advance of virtue, which is acquired by exercise and labour, and is proved not so much in prosperity as in adversity. One comes, then, to the valley; in valleys and lower places the contest is had against the devil and the powers of the air. Abraham fought in the valley of the salt pits against the barbarian kings and obtained the victory. Our traveller too, then, descends to those who are in the depths, and to the enemies, not that he may tarry there, but that he may obtain the victory.
**“INTO ETHAM”** — Etham, "sound strength" or "profession", in which we take up strength and vigour lest we faint on the way.
33.7:
**“Departing from thence they came over against Phihahiroth, which looketh towards Beelsephon, and they camped before Magdalum.”** — greatness, or tower
**“DEPARTING FROM THENCE”** — THE SAME. And setting out from Buthan they put in at Airoth, which is interpreted "villages". For one does not yet come to the city, nor are perfect things held yet, but certain small ones. This is the advance: that one comes from small things to great. One comes, then, to the mouth, that is, to the first entrance of the village, which is the judgment of conversation and abstinence. And Airoth is set over against Beelsephon and over against Magdalum. Beelsephon is interpreted "ascent of the watchtower" or "of the tower". From small things, then, one ascends to great. The soul is not yet in the watchtower itself, but over against the watchtower, that is, set in sight of the Church; for it begins to watch and look forward to the hope to come and the breadth of advances. And little by little it grows, while it is nourished more by hope than wearied by labours. The fourth mansion, then, is over against Magdalum, not yet in it, which is called magnificence. It has, then, in sight the ascent of the watchtower and the magnificence of things to come, by which it is fed and nourished. For it is in advances, not in arrival.
**“JEROME”** — The fourth mansion is Phihahiroth, which is interpreted "mouth of the nobles", which is written with the letter beth. Some wrongly think Airoth means villages; and the error is manifest, that for the aforesaid element they read the letter ain. Beelsephon is interpreted "house of the north", or "ascent of the watchtower", or "having secrets"; Magdalum, "greatness of the tower". Strength having been taken up, then, we are ennobled, or we serve as soldiers in the Lord, and despise the secrets of the devil, and turn aside from his magnificence and towering pride. For he is not from the south, whence the Lord comes, and from the noonday, where the bridegroom lies among the flowers; but the possessor of the north, the coldest wind, whence evils burn forth; who, though he is coldest, is called by the name of the right hand, falsely taking to himself the name of virtue and of the right hand, though he is wholly on the left.
33.8:
**“And departing from Phihahiroth,”** — 'Mouth of the nobles': for strength having been taken up we are ennobled in the Lord, and we despise Beelsephon, that is, the lord of the north, and turn aside from his pride.
**“they passed through the midst of the sea into the wilderness: and having marched three days through the desert of Etham, they camped in Mara.”**
• Mara is interpreted bitterness: that the pleasure and luxury of life may be ended in bitterness, and sweetness be repaid through the wood of the cross, as through torment.
• After this they set out from Airoth, cross through the midst of the Red Sea, and put in at the bitternesses. For the time of advances is perilous. What a grievous temptation it is to pass through the midst of the sea, to see the waves swell into a mound, to hear the crash of the raging billows! Yet if you follow Moses, that is, the law of God, the waters will become a wall to you on the right hand and on the left, and you will find a dry way in the midst of the sea. That heavenly journey too which the soul makes can meet waves. For part of the waters is above the heaven, part under the heaven. We meanwhile endure the waves and billows of those which are under the heaven. God will see whether those are quiet and always calm and stirred by no blasts. But when we come to the passage of the sea, even if we see Pharao and the Egyptians pursuing, let us not tremble at all; let us believe in the one true God, and him whom he sent, his Son Jesus Christ. Let us believe Moses too, that is, the law of God and the prophets, and we shall see the Egyptians lying on the shore of the sea, and shall sing to the Lord, who threw the horse and the rider into the sea. They put in, then, at the bitternesses; but do not be afraid. For all chastisement for the present seems not to bring joy but bitterness, but afterwards yields to those exercised by it the most sweet fruit of justice. The unleavened bread too is eaten with bitterness. Nor does one come to the land of promise except through bitternesses. For as physicians put certain bitter things into medicines for the soothing of the sick, so the physician of souls willed us to suffer the bitternesses of this life; because the end of bitterness acquires the sweetness of health, as the end of worldly sweetness [acquires] a bitter end. Do not shrink, then, from putting in at bitterness.
**“IN MARA”** — JEROME. The fifth mansion is Mara, that is, bitterness. They could not come to the whirlpools of the sea and see Pharao perishing with his army unless they had had nobilities in their mouth, that is, virtues in the confession of the Lord. After the preaching of the Gospel, after the tabernacles of those passing over, after strength taken up, after the nobility of confession, dangers again meet us. Ambushes, then, are always to be guarded against, the mercy of God invoked, that we may escape the pursuing Pharao and he may be choked in the baptism of the spiritual cloud. To those come out of the Red Sea the wilderness of Sur meets them, which is also called the desert of Etham, in which, going out three days, they had no water, and they come to Mara, so called from bitterness. The spring had water that was not sweet. The people murmurs, seeing water and not enduring to drink it. Mara signifies the waters of the killing letter; to which if the confession of the cross and the sacraments of the Lord's passion are added, the bitterness will be turned into sweetness. Whence: The Lord appointed for the people a law and judgments, and tried them. For where there is greatness of grace, there is greatness of peril. Do not be terrified if after victory you come to bitterness; because those keeping the true Pasch eat it with bitternesses; and temptation brings forth proof, proof hope, hope salvation. Among physicians too the antidote which tempers noxious humours is named from bitterness, which is shown to be sweet by restoring health. As, on the contrary, pleasure and luxury are tempered with bitterness. Whence that which for a time makes your throat fat, at the last you will find more bitter than gall.
33.9:
**“And departing from Mara, they came into Elim,”** — Rams: these are the apostolic leaders of the Christian flock.
**“INTO ELIM”** — And setting out from the bitterness they came into Elim, where there are twelve fountains of waters, and there were seventy palm trees. You see after the bitternesses and roughnesses of temptations how pleasant are the places that receive you. You would not have come to the palms unless you had borne the bitternesses of temptations; nor to the sweetness of the fountains unless you had overcome the sad and rough things. Not that in these is the end of the journey and the perfection of all things; but God, the dispenser of souls, puts some refreshments among the labours, by which the soul, refreshed, is made readier for the remaining labours. Elim is interpreted "rams"; rams are the leaders of the flock. These are the apostles, leaders of the flock of Christ, who are also the twelve fountains. But because Christ chose not only them but also seventy others, therefore seventy palm trees are written to be there; for they too are named apostles. Whence Paul: "Then by all the apostles." Let this pleasantness after bitterness, this rest after labour, this grace after temptation receive you.
**“where there were twelve fountains of waters,”** — the apostolic doctrine of the living
**“and seventy palm trees”** — the other disciples, namely, who yet were called apostles
33.10:
**“BUT DEPARTING FROM THENCE ALSO”** — Because after the apostolic doctrine and the sweet fruits of triumphs past perils sometimes appear.
**“But departing from thence also, they pitched their tents by the Red Sea. And departing from the Red Sea,”** — And setting out from Elim they put in beside the Red Sea. Note that they do not now enter into the sea; it sufficed to have entered once; but they put in beside it, and see the sea indeed and the waves, but fear its motion and onset.
**“THE RED SEA”** — JEROME. In Hebrew: Iamsuph. To those going on a certain bay of the sea meets them, beside which they pitched their tents; which is another thing than crossing the sea. For after the Gospel discipline, after the sweet foods of triumphs, the sea and past perils sometimes appear. Iamsuph is compounded of "sea" and "red". For suph is called red, and also bulrush. Perhaps, then, they came to a certain marsh full of sedge and rushes. And all gatherings of waters are called seas. This mansion is not found in Exodus, but it is written that from the Red Sea they came into the desert of Sin, which is between Elim and Sinai, on the fifteenth day of the second month of their going out of Egypt, that is, thirty days after they went out of Ramesses.
33.11:
**“They camped in the desert of Sin.”**
• 'bush' or 'hatred': because when we come to the place of the Church, of which God speaks to us, we incur the hatred of the enemy.
• And setting out from the Red Sea they put in at the desert of Sin. Sin is interpreted "bush" or "temptation". There the hope of good things begins now to smile, where the Lord appeared from the bush and gave answers to Moses and the beginning of visitation to the children of Israel. For there is wont to be temptation in visions. For the angel of iniquity is wont to transform himself into an angel of light; and therefore one must act carefully, that you may discern visions. Whence Jesus Nave, when he saw a vision, asks him who appeared: Art thou ours, or of our adversaries? So, then, the soul setting out, when it has found the discernment of visions, will be proved to be spiritual. For among the gifts of the Holy Ghost is the discerning of spirits.
**“IN THE DESERT OF SIN”** — JEROME. And setting out from the Red Sea they camped in the desert of Sin. This is the eighth mansion, though according to Exodus the seventh. But it is to be known that the whole wilderness as far as mount Sinai is called Sin, and the place of that mansion took its name from the whole province; as Moab is the name both of a city and of a province. In this wilderness there are five mansions: Iamsuph, and the wilderness of Sin, and Daphca, and Alus, and Raphidim. And Sin is interpreted "bush" or "hatred". For when we have come to the place of that mansion of which the Lord speaks to us, we incur the hatred of the enemy, and we see the bush burning and not consumed: the Church set aflame by persecutions and, the Lord speaking in her, not perishing. And note that in this mansion, in which are our winepresses, whence the eighth psalm is entitled, we pluck the desert of the bush; because many are the children of the desolate, more than of her that hath a husband.
33.12:
**“And they removed from thence, and came to Daphca.”** — Because after we have come to the place of the Church, we begin to knock at the sacraments, that they may be opened to us.
**“TO DAPHCA”** — In Hebrew Phichaici, that is, knocking. After the answers of the Lord, after the eighth number of the resurrection of Christ, we begin to knock at the sacraments.
**“ORIGEN”** — Setting out from the desert of Sin they came into Rapheca, which is interpreted "health". Note the order of the advances. When the soul has been made spiritual and has the discernment of visions, it comes to health, so that it may rightly say: Bless the Lord, O my soul, who healeth all thy diseases. Many are the diseases of the soul: avarice, namely, pride, boasting, fear, inconstancy and the like.
33.13:
**“And departing from Daphca, they camped in Alus.”**
• Leaven, which the woman of the Gospel mixes in three measures of meal.
• And setting out from Rapheca they come into Alus, that is, labours. Nor wonder if labours follow health; because the soul is healed to this end, that it may labour with delight and it may be said to it: Thou shalt eat the labours of thy fruits; blessed art thou, and it shall be well with thee.
**“THEY CAMPED”** — JEROME. The tenth mansion is not found in Exodus, and it is believed to be contained in the wilderness of Sin, the same book relating: All the multitude of Israel set out from the wilderness of Sin by their mansions, by the mouth of the Lord, and came into Raphidim. Whence it is plain that several mansions are shown by the name of this region. In this wilderness the people murmurs for hunger, and turning sees far off the glory of God in the cloud; it receives the quail in the evening, but in the morning manna. And note that in the tenth mansion leaven is set, and after the eating of flesh manna is given, and the scripture is fulfilled: Man ate the bread of angels.
33.14: **“And departing from Alus, Raphidim”** — 'Loosing of the strong' or 'slackening of the hands', because there Amalec was scattered.
33.15:
**“And departing from Raphidim,”** — IN RAPHIDIM. JEROME. They camped in Raphidim. This is called the eleventh mansion in Exodus, after the departure from the wilderness of Sin. In it the people complains for the burning of thirst, and a spring breaks forth and flows from the rock of Horeb, and it receives the name of temptation. Moses goes up into the mountain; Jesus fights against Amalec, and the enemy is overcome by the sign of the cross. When the hands of the one praying are let down, the enemy pursues as victor. Moses sits on the stone of Zacharias, which has seven eyes, and in the volume of Samuel is called Abenezer, that is, the stone of help. Aaron and Hur, that is, the mountainous and the shining, hold up each of his hands. The adversary being conquered, Jethro arrives, brings Sephora and both sons, gives the counsel of the seventy elders; and in a type of the Church gathered from the Gentiles, the lightening of the law is accomplished at the suggestion of the Gospel. Well is Raphidim called the loosing or the healing of the strong, because of Amalec scattered or Israel healed; or the slackening of the hands, according to the Syrians, because of the offence of the people, which murmured against the Lord in this place. After the leaven, then, of Alus and the lump of the Church, the temptations of demons are wont to rise up.
**“ORIGEN”** — After this they come into Raphidim, which is interpreted "praise of judgment". Well does praise follow after labours, namely the praise of judgment. The soul, then, becomes worthy of praise which judges and discerns rightly; which, namely, judges all things spiritually and is judged by no one.
**“IN THE DESERT OF SINAI”** — JEROME. Sinai, the twelfth mansion. At once let the number of the apostles come to your mind. One of many, but greater than all; it is not separated in order, it excels in merit. They come to it on the forty-seventh day, the scripture saying: In the third month of the going out of the children of Israel from Egypt, on this day they came into the wilderness of Sinai.
**“they camped in the desert of Sinai.”** — Afterwards one comes into the desert of Sina. Sina is a certain place of the desert which above he named Sin. But here rather the place of the mountain which is in that desert is called, which from the name of the desert is called Sina. After the soul, then, has been made of praiseworthy judgment, and has begun to have right judgment, the law is given to it by God, because it is capable of the divine secrets and the heavenly visions.
33.16:
