**“and bless you”** — in number and in merit
**“as he hath spoken.”** — who does not lie
1.12:
**“I am not able”** — unbearable
**“alone to bear your business, and the charge of you”** — unbearable
**“and your differences.”** — The meekest man does not bear discord or brawling, as contrary to himself
**“I ALONE AM NOT ABLE”** — AUGUSTINE. See how much is to be observed what scripture says elsewhere: "My son, meddle not with many matters." Consider too the words of Jethro giving counsel. For he says: "Hear my words and counsels, and God shall be with thee." It seems to be signified that a mind too intent on human actions is in some way emptied of God, by whom it is made the fuller the more freely it stretches out to things above and eternal.
1.13:
**“LET ME HAVE FROM AMONG YOU”** — Let you give, not I; as if: I do not wish to command you, but to obey.
**“men”** — strong in vigour and age
**“wise”** — he that is understanding shall possess governments
**“and understanding,”** — in divine things, in worldly things; that from their former life their future may be proved to all; that they may be promoted by the testimony of many
**“and such whose conversation is approved among your tribes, that I may appoint them”** — whom you shall have chosen
**“I MAY APPOINT THEM”** — Note: he gives the election to the subjects, he keeps the appointment to himself; lest the people despise or hate, if it was not allowed to have whom it wished.
1.15:
**“And I took”** — you having chosen first
**“out of your tribes”** — not strangers
**“men”** — strong
**“wise”** — namely, who act wisely
**“and honourable,”** — who are more feared
**“TRIBUNES”** — Over thousands, in Greek chiliarchs, who teach their subjects of the hope, namely, of the eternal reward.
**“and centurions,”**
• who, filled with the Holy Ghost, labour that others may be filled
• the Greeks [say] decarchs, who teach the ten commandments of the law
• Rightly are they set over [them] who, endowed with the number one hundred, that is, with perfection, rule as it were a hundred, while they lead them to perfection.
**“AND CENTURIONS”** — Centurions, in Greek hecatontarchs, who hand on the heavenly commandments to the perfect.
**“AND OFFICERS OVER FIFTIES”** — In Greek pentecontarchs, who announce the works of penance.
**“OVER TENS”** — Who by the perfection of the denarius, awaiting the denarius of the vineyard, prepare many sharers of the same denarius.
**“who”** — each
**“might teach you all things.”** — the necessary things
1.16:
**“And I commanded them, saying: Hear”** — No one is to be judged unless first heard.
**“them, and judge that which is just:”** — Judge justly, sons of men; as if: lest you accept persons.
1.17:
**“BECAUSE IT IS GOD'S”** — Not of men; as if: in judging you are vicars of God, who does not accept persons.
**“And if any thing seem hard”**
• to discern
• AND IF ANY THING SEEM HARD, etc. The greater ones ought to discern and judge all greater and difficult things, the lesser ones the small and easy.
1.18: **“And I commanded you all things”** — not only the things aforesaid
1.19:
**“And departing from Horeb, we passed through the wilderness,”** — the wilderness
**“AND DEPARTING”** — GILBERT. These things have been fittingly expounded in their own places; but to expound things expounded is the part of the idle, not of the studious.
**“the terrible and vast wilderness, which you saw, by the way of the mountain of the Amorrhite, as the Lord our God had commanded us. And when we were come into Cadesbarne,”** — AND WHEN WE WERE COME INTO CADESBARNE, etc. That in the second year of its going out the people came into the desert of Pharan, which is Cades, where, the spies having returned with the fruits of the land and announcing what they had seen, they murmured against Moses and Aaron, and therefore, afflicted with the weariness of a long journey and with mortality, they perished: this place will give manifest judgment. Where it is to be noted that the forty-two mansions which they had from Egypt as far as the Jordan seem to fit only three courses of years, namely the first, the second, and the fortieth of the going out of Egypt. The first, by a certain distinction, contains twelve: the first, Ramesses, entered on the fifteenth day of the first month; the last, the wilderness of Sinai, reached on the first day of the third month, and not left for eleven continuous months for the sake of building the tabernacle and teaching the law. Of which twelve mansions only nine are expressed by name in Exodus; three are signified without distinction under the name of the desert of Sin (which is said to be between Elim and Sinai). The second year comprises twenty-one mansions; of which, all being comprehended without distinction in the order of the history under the name of the wilderness of Pharan, only the first and second and last, that is, the graves of lust, Haseroth, and Cades, are distinguished by name. But in the catalogue of mansions all alike are shown, how many they are in number, or by what name they are called. The first mansion, that is, the graves of lust, was entered in the second month of the same second year, on the twenty-second day of the month. For in the second year (as the scripture says), in the second month, on the twentieth day of the month, they moved the camp from the desert of Sinai, and the cloud rested in the wilderness of Pharan. They set out from the mountain of the Lord a journey of three days, until they came to the place of the mansion which, by the merit of the people lusting for flesh, received the name of the graves of lust. On what day or month of the same year the last of these, that is, Cades, was entered is not said; yet that it lies in the wilderness of Pharan, because it was reached in the same year, is not passed over in silence. For it is written: The people did not move from that place until Mary was called back. And setting out from Haseroth, having pitched their tents in the desert of Pharan, where the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Send men to view the land of Chanaan. Which, lest it be thought commanded and done at the very next mansion after Haseroth, [it is shown] fulfilled in the last of those which are contained under the name of Pharan. Below it is written: "And the spies of the land, returning after forty days, having gone round the whole country", came to Moses in Pharan, which is Cades. In Deuteronomy too Moses says to the people: When you were come into Cadesbarne I said to you: You are come to the mountain of the Amorrhite, etc. And you said: "Let us send men who may view the land" etc. And that they reached the same mansion in the second year of their going out, from which yet, by the sin of murmuring, they deserved to turn back and wander long through the desert and fall here and there, Moses bears witness in what follows, saying: You abode in Cadesbarne a long time; and setting out thence we came into the wilderness that leadeth to the Red Sea, as the Lord had said to me; and we compassed mount Seir a long time. And below: The time that we walked from Cadesbarne to the torrent Zared was thirty-eight years, until the whole generation of the men of war was consumed. And Zared is not the name of any mansion of the forty-two, but of a torrent, to which (as is read in the book of Numbers), having passed the thirty-eighth mansion, named Ijeabarim, they came; leaving which, he says, they camped over against the Arnon, which is in the desert and juts out in the borders of the Amorrhite; which it is not hidden was done in the fortieth year. This last [year] contains ten mansions of the very long way through the desert; of which the first, regained with great labour, is the same, namely that Cades of the desert of Sin, which thirty-eight years before, their fault requiring it, they left behind them, turning back; of which it is written: "The children of Israel came into the desert of Sin in the first month, and the people abode in Cades; and Mary died there, and was buried in the same place. And when the people wanted water, they came together against Moses and Aaron" etc., as far as this: "This is the water of contradiction" etc. It is to be noted that the same Cades is set both in the desert of Pharan and in the desert of Sin, as the scripture relates; whence we conjecture that the part of the desert of Pharan where Cades is is specially called Sin. But this Sin is not that which they passed through as soon as they had crossed the Red Sea, between Elim and Sinai, but another altogether, and written among the Hebrews with other letters. The second mansion of the same fortieth year is mount Hor, on which Aaron died on the first day of the fifth month; the last, the plains of Moab upon the Jordan over against Jericho, where they abode meditating Deuteronomy until, Moses being dead, under Josue as leader they crossed the Jordan on the first day of the tenth month. The mansions of the first year, then, are twelve, of the second twenty-one; of the last ten, that twenty-first, which is Cades, being itself one, and nine others; together, in all, forty-two.
1.22: **“And you came all to me, and said: Let us send men who may view the land, and bring us word what way we shall go up, and to what cities we shall go.”** — AND YOU CAME TO ME, etc. In the book of Numbers it is written that the Lord said to Moses that he should send men to view the land. But here the people is read to have said: Let us send men to view the land. But the people suggested this first to Moses; Moses referred the counsel to the Lord, according to whose command he afterwards sent the spies.
1.23:
**“And because the saying pleased me, I sent of you twelve men, one of every tribe:”** — I SENT OF YOU TWELVE MEN, etc. ISIDORE. The twelve spies sent to spy out the fertile land, who terrified the people, bear the figure of the scribes and Pharisees. For as those were sent by Moses to view carefully the fertile land, so these by the law and the prophets, that through the searching of scripture they might watch for the coming of Christ, in whom was the land, that is, the holy flesh, in which they might obtain the kingdom of God and the fertility of spiritual fruits, and life eternal. But as those terrified the people with despair, lest they trust in God's promise, so the scribes and Pharisees persuaded the people not to believe in Christ, returning to the Egypt of this world, rejecting the manna of faith, seeking the black pots of sins and the rotten onions of blasphemers and the melons withering with the corruption of vices and lusts. And the cluster which two carried is Christ hanging on the wood of the cross, promised to the Gentiles, brought from the land of promise, from the womb of the virgin. The two bearers who go under the burden of the cluster are the two peoples. The former, the Jewish, blind and turned away, ignorant of the grace of him who hangs, and pressed by the burden of the one suspended, is put under it as he judges, according to that: "Let their eyes be darkened that they see not, and bow down their back always." But the latter, the Gentile, believing in Christ, having him always before his eyes, and following as a servant his Lord and a disciple his master, and hearing that saying of the Gospel: "If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me." This is the cluster which poured out the wine of its blood for our salvation in the crushing of the cross, and gave the Church to drink the pressed cup of its passion. This is the cluster which the pomegranates, that is, mother Church, followed; having a number of grains, that is, a multitude of peoples, and the redness of the blood of Christ glittering with its seal; it has also distinct grains, namely divers charisms. Judging themselves unworthy of all these, the unbelievers would not receive the land of the flesh of Christ flowing with milk and honey; which his servants, that is, the Christians, have obtained, of whose doctrine the Church sings: "How sweet are thy words to my palate! more than honey to my mouth." And the fig signifies the law, as the cluster bears the figure of the Saviour; because neither is Christ without the law, nor the law without Christ.
**“TWELVE MEN”** — Allegorically, these signify the teachers of the Church, of whom some pervert the people by teaching wicked things, others profit them by preaching right things.
1.25:
**“Taking of the fruits thereof, to shew its fertility, they brought them to us, and said: The land is good,”** — the flesh of Christ
**“which the Lord our God will give us.”**
• freely
• for our salvation
1.26: **“And you would not go up,”** — one goes up into the land of promise, one goes down into Egypt
1.27: **“You murmured in your tents,”** — with wicked hearts
1.30:
**“The Lord God, who is our leader, for you”** — you will lend the hand: he [will give] the effect
**“himself will fight, as he did”** — as if: from things done before, trust about things to be done
1.31:
**“And in the wilderness”** — where there was the greatest straitness
**“(as thou hast seen) hath carried”** — with affection
**“thee the Lord thy God, as a man is wont to carry his little son,”**
• whom he tenderly loves, and does not let labour
• he was never lacking
1.32:
**“And yet for all this you did not believe”** — ungrateful for benefits
**“the Lord your God,”**
• who did great things in you
• who is the leader and companion of labour
1.33:
**“Who went before you in the way,”**
• by the sign of the cloud
• when, namely, the pillar of the cloud stood still
**“and marked out the place, wherein you should pitch your tents, in the night”**
• In the blindness of this world he gives the light of the Holy Ghost
• that they who see not may see
**“shewing you the way by fire,”** — BY NIGHT SHEWING, etc. Night is the day of the sinner; [day] the life of the just. In the pillar of fire, the damnation of the wicked, to whom the Lord will appear terrible in the judgment. In the pillar of the cloud, a light and gentle vision, by which the elect will be consoled.
**“and in the day”** — that they who see may become blind
**“IN THE DAY BY THE PILLAR OF A CLOUD”** — In the heat of this world, overshadowing and sustaining by the strength and propitiation of his flesh.
1.34:
**“And when the Lord had heard the voice of your words, he was angry”** — God is said to be angry when we do the things that are worthy of anger and vengeance
**“HE SWORE”** — God is not passible, nor subject to the vice of wrath. But by these things the charity of Moses toward the people is made manifest, and the goodness of God, which surpasses all understanding.
1.35:
**“SHALL NOT SEE”** — The like is said of those who, invited to the supper, excused themselves: None of those men that were invited shall taste of my supper.
**“Not one of the men of this wicked generation shall see the good land, which with an oath”** — The most wicked generation does not possess the good land, because it does not believe the incarnation of Christ.
**“I promised”** — not to the wicked, but to the good. I owe nothing, then, to the wicked
1.36:
**“Except Caleb the son of Jephone: for he”** — shall possess
**“shall see”** — with the mind
**“it,”** — the flesh of Christ
**“and to his children,”** — his imitators
**“because he hath followed the Lord.”** — by obeying, by believing
1.37:
**“Neither is his indignation against the people to be wondered at,”** — NEITHER IS IT TO BE WONDERED AT, etc. Here Moses says that the Lord, angry with him because of the people, said that he should not enter the land of promise; whereas in the book of Numbers it is read: "The Lord said to Moses and Aaron: Because you have not believed me, to sanctify me before the children of Israel, you shall not bring these people into the land which I will give them." But the following sentence seems to solve the question: "This, he says, is the water of contradiction, where the children of Israel strove with words against the Lord" etc. For the strife and rebellion of the people was the cause of the wrath and vengeance both against the people and against Moses and Aaron.
**“since the Lord was angry with me also on your account,”** — striving at the water of contradiction
**“and said:”** — the law brought no one to perfection
**“NEITHER SHALT THOU GO IN”** — ISIDORE. In Mary prophecy seems to have died; in Moses and Aaron, the law and priesthood of the Jews, who could not go up to the land of promise nor lead the believing people out of the wilderness of this world; but only Jesus, that is, the Saviour, the true Son of God. In the thirty-third mansion Moses offended the Lord. For, troubled by the murmuring of the people, doubting, he struck the rock, as though God could not give water from the rock, because he had not done so before. Moses in this place bears the figure of the people set under the law. For so the people fastened Christ to the wood of the cross, not believing him to be the power of God; as Moses, when he struck the rock, doubted of the power of God. But from the rock struck water flowed, and the wound of Christ was given back as life to believers. For the rock was Christ. This carnal despair about the divinity of Christ the Lord commands to die in the height of Christ himself, when he commands Moses to die on the mountain. For Christ is the rock, Christ the mountain: the rock, lowly strength; the mountain, towering greatness. Of this mountain it is said: A city seated on a mountain cannot be hid, etc. The prudence of the flesh lives when the humility of Christ on the cross is despised as a rock struck. The prudence of the flesh dies when Christ is acknowledged as exalted, as the eminence of a mountain.
1.38:
**“But Josue”** — the true Jesus
**“the son of Nun, thy minister,”** — Christ came not to destroy the law, but to fulfil
**“the land”** — by the election of grace
**“by lot”** — In my Father's house there are many mansions
1.39:
**“Your children,”** — the Gentiles, poor in spirit, whom you despised
**“captives,”** — by the devil
**“should be led away, and your sons”** — not servants
**“who this day of good”** — of God
**“and evil”** — of the devil
**“know not”** — you were heretofore darkness, but now light in the Lord
**“the difference, they shall go in:”** — by free will
**“and to them I will give”** — through grace
**“the land”** — of the living, or myself
**“and they shall possess it.”** — for ever
1.41:
**“And you answered me: We have sinned against the Lord: we will go up and fight, as the Lord our God hath commanded. And when ready”** — trusting in their own strength
**“armed you went unto the mountain,”**
• AND WHEN READY ARMED, etc. This sentence strikes at human pride, which presumes on its own strength and does not trust in the power of God. For the Amorrhites, that is, the embittering, are the spiritual enemies who dwell on the mountains of pride and kill the presumptuous from Seir to Horma, that is, from the filth of vices to the damnation of punishments. For Seir is "hairy"; Horma is interpreted "anathema". For whoever does not fear to be polluted with the filth of vices must, according to his merits, be handed over to the fires of Gehenna. For the demons wish to entangle us in earthly desires; and if we persevere in sins and do not cease to go up the mountain of pride, they cut us down with fiery darts and lead us to perpetual anathema. Therefore let us not, after the manner of the Pelagians, presume on our own power, but, considering our infirmity, let us obey the Lord in all things, that, the enemies having been overcome, we may obtain the promised joys of the heavenly fatherland.
• We must beware lest, murmuring against the Lord, we go up the mountain of pride, thinking that we can be saved by our own strength; lest we be at once handed over to the Amorrhites, that is, to the demons.
1.42:
**“The Lord said to me: Say to them: Go not up,”** — on the mountain of pride
**“and fight not,”** — I am humility
**“with you:”**
• who are proud, disobedient
• by counselling
**“lest you fall”** — laid low
**“before your enemies.”**
• the demons
• they that trouble me will rejoice when I am moved
1.43:
**“I spoke,”** — by counselling
**“and you hearkened not:”** — with the ear of the heart
**“but resisting the commandment of the Lord, and swelling with pride,”** — advancing for the worse
**“you went up into the mountain.”** — of pride
1.44:
**“And coming out,”** — from ambush
**“the Amorrhite”** — the embittering, that is, the devil
**“that dwelt in the mountains,”** — of pride
**“and meeting you, chased you,”**
• with fiery darts
• with the spiritual sword
• the filth of vices, which are shaggy and bristling
**“Horma.”** — anathema
1.45:
**“And when you returned”**
• from pride
• as though penitent
**“and wept before the Lord, he heard not”** — unworthy to be heard
**“you, neither to your voice”** — not to his

2.1:
**“And departing from thence we came into the wilderness that leadeth to the Red Sea, as the Lord had spoken to me: and we compassed mount Seir a long time.”** — AND DEPARTING, etc. GILBERT. We pass quickly over things expounded in other books, that we may tarry on those that are to be expounded.
**“MOUNT SEIR”** — Seir is a mountain in the land of Edom, on which Esau dwelt, in the region of Gebalene, where the Horrhite dwelt before, whom Chodorlahomor slew; which received from Esau, hairy and shaggy, the name Seir, that is, "of the hairy one". The Horrhites, like the other nations which those overcame who descended from the seed of the patriarchs, express the wicked spirits or vices, which those can overcome who press on in the footsteps and teachings of the holy fathers and carry on spiritual warfare under Christ the king; of which it is said: "Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers" etc.
2.8:
**“And when we had passed by our brethren”** — kinsmen
**“the children of Esau,”** — of Jacob's brother
2.9:
**“to the children of Lot”** — the Moabites
**“I have given Ar”** — it is interpreted "he raised up"; which is now the metropolis
**“in possession.”** — TO THE CHILDREN OF LOT I HAVE GIVEN AR IN POSSESSION, etc. Ar is the metropolis of the Moabites, upon the bank of the torrent Arnon, once possessed by a most ancient nation, the Emims; afterwards held by the children of Lot, that is, the Moabites, the inhabitants having been overthrown. It is shown today on the top of a mountain; but the torrent, coming down through steep places, flows into the Dead Sea. Allegorically. Ar is interpreted "he raised up"; Emims, that is, "the terrible". These are the demons, who raise up strifes and contentions and prepare the darts of wickedness against the faithful. The Enacims too, begotten of the stock of Enac and equalled to the giants in tallness, according to their name signify the demons. For [Enac] is interpreted "necklace on a lofty neck". For, lifted up with the haughtiness of pride, they ascribe all the equipment of their warfare to their own strength. Therefore they easily yield to those who trust in the strength of God and say with the Psalmist: "The Lord is my strength and my praise" etc.
2.10:
**“The Emims”** — that is, the terrible
**“tall,”** — of the strong
**“that like the race of the Enacims,”** — Necklace on a lofty neck
2.12:
**“The Horrhites”**
• or Orim
• horrible in the hugeness of their bodies
2.14: **“And the time that we journeyed from Cadesbarne till we passed over the torrent Zared, was thirty-eight years: until all the generation of the men that were fit for war was consumed out of the camp, as the Lord had sworn:”** — FROM CADESBARNE, etc. JEROME. Cadesbarne is a place in the desert which is joined to the city of Petra in Arabia, where Mary died, and Moses, the rock having been struck, gave water to the thirsting people. The tomb of Mary is shown there even today; and the princes of Amalec too were slain there by Chodorlahomor.
2.26:
**“to Sehon”** — the devil
**“the king of Hesebon”** — which are spoken in baptism
**“with peaceable words, saying:”** — SO I SENT MESSENGERS, etc. Allegorically. Sehon signifies the devil, for [the name] is "useless sprout" or "unfruitful tree" or "lifted up". Israel [signifies] the Christian people, which desires to pass through the way of this world and come to the heavenly kingdoms. This people sends to Sehon, promising with peaceable words that it will not dwell in his land, but only pass through and go by the king's way. This each one promised when he first came to the water of baptism and received the first seals of the faith. For he renounced the devil and his pomps and works and all his service and pleasures. This is what is said: "that Israel will not turn aside into his field or into his vineyard, and will not drink water from his cistern"; that is, will no longer take up the discipline either of astrology or of magic or of any doctrine that is against godliness. But he will drink from the fountains of the Saviour; he will not forsake the fountain of living water to drink from the fountain of Sehon; but he will go by the king's way, which is Christ, who says: "I am the way, the truth and the life", and the King, according to that: "Give to the king thy judgment, O God." He will not turn aside into his field or into his vineyard; to his works, namely, or to his wicked senses. The Amorrhites are interpreted "speaking" or "embittering", because they provoke God to bitterness and trust only in words, like the poets, astrologers, philosophers, who speak empty things. But the kingdom of God is not in speech, but in power. The faithful wish to pass through in peace, and to be peaceable even with the enemies of peace; although they offend the prince of the world the more, the more they say they do not wish to tarry with him nor touch anything of his. Thence, exasperated, he persecutes the more, stirs up dangers, threatens tortures, gathers his people, demands to fight against Israel. His people are the princes and judges of the world and all the ministers of wickedness, who persecute the people of God. But he too comes into Jasa, which is interpreted "fulfilment of the commandment". For he who has come to the fulfilment of God's commandments will not fear Sehon or his raging army. For to fulfil the commandments of God is to overcome the devil and his army. For so God crushes Satan under our feet and gives us power to tread upon serpents and scorpions and upon all the power of the enemy.
2.27:
**“We will pass”** — as pilgrims and strangers
**“through thy land,”** — the world, which is seated in wickedness
**“we will go along by the highway:”** — which is Christ, common to all
**“we will not turn aside neither to the right hand”** — as over-just
**“nor to the left.”** — as the unjust
2.30:
**“because the Lord thy God had hardened his spirit,”** — he had allowed him to be hardened, his sins requiring it
**“BECAUSE HE HAD HARDENED”** — By long patience, not correcting. Whence in Exodus: "I have hardened the heart of Pharao"; and in the Psalm: "He turned their heart to hate his people." And the cause of the hardening is added: that he might be delivered into thy hands, that is, that he might be crushed by thee; which would not happen unless he resisted, nor would he resist unless he were hardened. If we seek the justice of this thing, his judgments are unsearchable; but there is no iniquity with God.
**“and fixed”**
• Septuagint: "had strengthened", which is taken also in a bad sense
• in a bad sense
• he turned their heart to hate his people, and to deal deceitfully with his servants
**“his heart, that he might be delivered”** — to be conquered
2.32:
**“And Sehon came out”** — the devil
**“to meet us”**
• the faithful
• with the demons or visible enemies
**“at Jasa.”** — which is the fulfilment of the commandments
2.33:
**“And delivered”** — to be conquered
**“him the Lord our God to us: and we slew him with his sons”**
• the demons
• the princes of this world and any evil men
• AND WE SLEW HIM WITH HIS SONS, etc. These are the true Israelites, not in the flesh but in the spirit. They dwell in all the cities of the Amorrhites, since the churches of Christ are spread through the whole world; and each of us was a city of king Sehon, because folly, pride, impiety and all that the devil suggests reigned in us. But when the strong one was conquered and his vessels plundered, we were made cities of Israel, the inheritance of the saints; the unfruitful tree having first been cut down and the lifted-up king cast down, and the meek one reigning in us, who says: "Learn of me, because I am meek and humble of heart" etc. The names of the places too agree. For Aroer is interpreted "lifting up", Arnon "heap of testimony". From Aroer, then, which is upon the bank of the torrent Arnon, etc.: because every person of whatever dignity, trusting in the state of pride or in worldly pomp, with the persecutors who straiten Christians with various tribulations, as far as the conventicles of heretics, who fight against the Church with depraved testimonies of the scriptures, but cannot prevail to resist, are delivered conquered into the hands of the saints, with their dwellings.
2.34: **“And we took all his cities at that time, killing”** — in that they were evil; and: overturn the wicked, and he shall not be
2.36:
**“From Aroer,”** — which is lifting up
**“which is upon the bank of the torrent Arnon,”** — heap of sadness
**“a town”** — namely
**“that is situate in a valley, as far as Galaad.”** — Heap of testimony

3.1: **“Then we turned and went up by the way of Basan: and Og the king of Basan came out to meet us with his people to fight in Edrai.”** — THEN WE TURNED AND WENT UP, etc. To Og the king of Basan they do not even deign to send envoys, nor ask passage through his land; at once they fight with him, overcoming him and his people. Basan is interpreted "foulness". Rightly, then, neither are envoys sent to this nation nor is passage asked. For there ought to be no passage or going up for us to foulness, which must be fought down at once and wholly guarded against. Since Og is interpreted "shutting in", it signifies carnal things, by desire of which the soul is shut out and separated from God. Against these one must so make war that no vice be left. For nothing ought to be left in the kingdom of foulness. For foul things must be cut away, that honourable and religious things may be built up. In the kingdom of Sehon or of Moab this is not commanded. For perhaps we have need of something from those, as the manifold use of the present life requires. Otherwise we should have to go out of this world. But of Basan, that is, of foulness, we leave nothing, because we need nothing. For that which is foul cannot be honourable.
3.3:
**“So the Lord our God delivered into our hands, Og also the king of Basan,”** — of foulness
**“and all his people:”** — many vices subject to foulness
3.4:
**“of Argob”** — which is cursed loftiness
**“the kingdom of Og in Basan.”** — SIXTY CITIES, etc. It confirms the sense above. For the number sixty, like the number six, signifies perfection. And well does he record sixty cities laid waste in the region of Og king of Basan, that is, of the devil, who is the king of foulness; because it signifies that the delight of all vices must be perfectly destroyed. Argob, that is, "cursed loftiness", signifies earthly pride, which reigns in the children of wrath. The cities having been destroyed, he says the men and women and children were killed, the cattle and spoils taken; because, the fortress of the devil having been overcome, whatever we perceive as wanton must be crushed, with its little thoughts, by the zeal of God. But whatever we find fit for the service of God in the simplicity of pure sense or in the adornment of the members, we ought to keep.
3.6:
**“And we utterly destroyed them, as we had done to Sehon the king of Hesebon, destroying every city, men”** — the rebellious
**“and women”** — wantonness
**“and children:”** — weak thoughts
3.7:
**“But the cattle”** — simple ones, useful for the service of God
**“and the spoils”** — the adornment of words
3.11:
**“For only Og king of Basan remained of the race of the giants. And”** — in Hebrew, Raphaim
**“his bed of iron is shewn, which is in Rabbath of the children of Ammon, nine cubits”** — it commends his greatness
3.12:
**“AND WE POSSESSED THE LAND AT THAT TIME”** — GREGORY. There are many in the Church who disdain to be little, and, set in a place of humility, do not cease to be swollen within themselves. These are lifted up by honours, enjoy pleasures, are spread wide by a multitude of things; they desire to be over others and to be feared; they neglect to live rightly and covet the fame of a right life. Yet if any trial of the faith arises, they defend it with words and clamours, and lay claim to the heavenly fatherland, yet do not love it. Such the sons of Ruben and Gad and the half tribe of Manasses express, who, possessing many flocks and beasts, covet the plain country beyond the Jordan and will not have an inheritance in the land of promise, saying: "The land which the Lord hath smitten in the sight of the children of Israel is of a most fertile region" etc. Those who possess very many beasts will not cross the Jordan; because those whom the many hindrances of the world occupy do not seek the heavenly dwelling. But the faith which they hold in outward show rebukes them, lest they grow numb with idleness, lest by their example they draw others away from labour and longsuffering. Whence it is said to them through Moses: "Shall your brethren go to fight, and will you sit here? Why do ye overturn the minds of the children of Israel?" But because they are ashamed not to defend the faith which they confess, they hasten to the contest, and claim it not for themselves but for their neighbours. Whence they say to Moses: "We will make sheepfolds" etc. They add: armed and girded we will go to the battle. Presently, then, they free the land of promise from the enemies, and leave it, and go beyond the Jordan to feed their beasts; because against the faith of baptism they serve perishing things with all their desire. For they so fight as to set down their pledges, in which they have affection, outside the land of promise. Therefore they return to the plains from the height of the mountains, as from the hope of heavenly things, and outside the land of promise they nourish brute animals, namely vain desires and irrational motions of the mind.
**“RUBEN AND”** — AUGUSTINE. Ruben is the firstborn of Jacob, though he defiled his bed. Manasses too, whose half tribe remains outside the Jordan, though born of an Egyptian woman, is firstborn. So they designate the former people, which receives its lot not through the true Jesus but through Moses, outside the Jordan; both first, and outside the Jordan, and set apart from the rest. "We have, they say, many beasts and flocks." For this cause the former people cannot come to the land flowing with milk and honey, nor acknowledge the Word made flesh. For the animal man does not perceive the things that are of the spirit of God, but is compared to senseless beasts; for which he receives an inheritance outside the Jordan, namely the land of two kings. For Moses could slay only two kings, whose land he might divide to those having many flocks. Jesus divided the land to those who crossed the Jordan, who had flocks indeed, but not so many as to keep them back beyond the Jordan; but with their very wives and infants they strive to cross and come to the fatherland.
3.25: **“I will pass over therefore, and will see this excellent land beyond the Jordan, and this goodly mountain, and Libanus.”** — mount Libanus, namely: this is a mountain of Phenicia, the boundary of Judea toward the north
3.28: **“Command Josue, and encourage and strengthen him: for he shall go before this people, and shall divide unto them the land which thou shalt see.”** — COMMAND JOSUE, etc. Allegorically. It was done by a great dispensation of God, that Moses, who is the type of the law, should not bring the people into the land of promise; because the law brought no one to perfection. But Josue is the type of Christ, which is interpreted "saviour". For Christ saved his people; fittingly, as leader and prince, he brought them into the land of promise.

4.2:
**“You shall not add”** — as the scribes and Pharisees, who for their traditions forsook the commandment of God
**“to the word”** — He does not forbid adding truth to truth, but wholly removes falsehood
**“YOU SHALL NOT ADD TO THE WORD”** — He teaches the rule of equity and strikes down every heresy. For he forbids adding anything of wicked intent to right doctrine or taking away anything of truth. For one must go by the king's way, not to the right hand or to the left; because the ways of the Lord are right, and the just shall walk in them. Likewise John says: "If any man shall add to these things, God shall add unto him the plagues written in this book. And if any man shall take away, God shall take away his part out of the book of life."
4.3: **“Your eyes have seen all that the Lord hath done against Beelphegor,”** — the idol of the Ammonites
4.4: **“But you that adhere to the Lord your God, are alive”** — with eternal life
4.7:
**“Neither is there any other nation so great, that hath gods so nigh”** — by appearing manifestly, by helping with signs and wonders
**“them, as our God is present to all our petitions.”** — NEITHER IS THERE ANY OTHER, etc. There is no other nation so great in dignity, namely of gifts, not in multitude of peoples. For the nation of the Jews did not surpass other nations in number or power, but in the prerogative of the fathers and the divine favour.
4.9:
**“Keep thyself therefore, and thy soul carefully. Forget not the words that have seen”** — have understood
**“THAT HAVE SEEN”** — Sight holds the first place among all the senses; therefore it is put for every sense.
4.11:
**“And you came to the foot of the mount, which burned”** — hyperbole
**“even unto heaven:”** — the airy [heaven], which the water of the flood occupied
4.12: **“And the Lord spoke to you from the midst of the fire. You heard the voice of his words, but you saw not any form at all.”** — lest, namely, wishing to imitate it by carving, thou shouldst make thyself an idol
4.16:
**“Lest perhaps being deceived you might make you a graven similitude, or image”** — this of men
**“A GRAVEN SIMILITUDE, OR IMAGE”** — AUGUSTINE. Perhaps by these two words he signified one thing. Or he called a likeness a statue, or an image not expressed by imitating the features of any man. For that a thing made by such expression is called an image no one would doubt; so that every image is a likeness, but not conversely. For in twins who are alike, there is the likeness of each in the other, not an image. But if a son is like his father, he is rightly called an image, so that the father is the prototype, that is, the first figure, from which that image is seen to be expressed. Of these images some are of the same substance, as a son; others not, as a picture. Whence that which is written: "God made man to his own image" is to be so understood that the image which was made is not of the same substance. For if it were of the same, it would be said not made but begotten. And that he did not add "and likeness", as above, seems to have been done because where there is an image, [there is also] a likeness. Whence here too Moses forbids a likeness and an image to be made. But in the Decalogue it is said that no likeness is to be made, nor is an image mentioned. For if there is no likeness, there is no image; since if there is an image, there is a likeness. Lastly, where he forbade a likeness and an image, he wished men to be understood, where a likeness can be made, not properly of this or that man, but of anyone; and an image, that is, properly of this or that man. But when he spoke of irrational animals, he said only "likeness". For no one sets up for himself one dog or the like, looking at which he paints or fashions an image, as is customary with men.
4.17: **“The similitude of any beasts,”** — this of animals
4.18: **“Or of creeping things, that move on the earth, or of fishes, that abide in the waters under the earth:”** — THAT ABIDE IN THE WATERS UNDER THE EARTH, etc. AUGUSTINE. Did he wish water to be understood as earth because of its handleable bodiliness, as there: "God made heaven and earth", and there: "My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth"? Or is it said "under the earth" for this reason, that unless the earth were higher than the waters it could not be inhabited by men or have the animals of the earth?
4.19:
**“Lest perhaps lifting up thy eyes”** — nor didst thou see a likeness in heaven, lest etc.
**“to heaven, thou see the sun and the moon, and all the stars of heaven, and being deceived by error thou adore and serve them, which created”** — others: distributed
**“the Lord thy God for the service”** — for use
**“of all the nations, that are under heaven.”** — WHICH THE LORD GOD CREATED, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is not said as though God commanded them to be worshipped by all nations and not worshipped by his people alone; but that he foreknew that the nations would show them worship, and yet, foreknowing, created them; but that his own people would be one that would not worship them. Or let the use be understood which is commended in Genesis, that they be for signs and seasons and days and years; which use the people of God has in common with all nations, but not the worship which other nations have.
4.23:
**“Beware lest thou ever forget the covenant of the Lord thy God, which he hath made with thee: and make to thyself a graven likeness of those things which to make”** — or: to be made
**“A GRAVEN LIKENESS”** — AUGUSTINE. Here, speaking generally, he set down likeness and was silent about image; because if there is no likeness, there is no image.
4.24: **“Because the Lord thy God is a consuming fire,”** — he consumes sins, and hands the reprobate to the fires of Gehenna
4.26:
**“I call this day heaven”** — the angels
**“and earth to witness,”**
• men
• Metonymically: by that which contains it signifies that which is contained.
4.30: **“IN THE LATTER TIME”** — He foretells the conversion of Israel to the faith of Christ: that after the fulness of the Gentiles has come in, all Israel may be saved.
4.32: **“Ask of the days of old, that have been before thy time from the day that the Lord God created man upon the earth,”** — ask, understood
4.33: **“That a people should hear the voice of God speaking out of the midst of fire, as thou hast heard, and lived:”** — FROM THE TOP OF HEAVEN, etc. AUGUSTINE. Why he did not likewise say "from the top of the earth to the top of the earth" is hard to discern; as in the Gospel, where it is said: "They shall gather the elect from the tops of the heavens to the ends of them." But perhaps here he wished it to be understood that neither among men nor among angels had that been heard which was done among the people, as what follows shows. But how then would that in the Gospel be understood, "from the tops of the heavens to the ends of them", since this is said of the last gathering of the elect?

5.2:
**“The Lord our God made a covenant with us in Horeb.”**
• the writing of the law
• THE LORD OUR GOD, etc. AUGUSTINE. Is it said for this reason, because those do not enter into the land of promise? For all are dead, nor do they pertain to this testament, whose census was then made when they were numbered from twenty years and upward to fifty years, able for war. How then did the Lord speak to those who are alive today? Is it because many of nineteen or eighteen years and under could have been there then, who would remember this, free from the penalty which the Lord appointed for those who were numbered, namely not to enter the land of promise? But surely he addresses those who, although they were not twenty years old and upward when God was speaking on the mountain, so that they could be numbered, yet could have been nineteen and under, down to boyhood, who could see and hear and retain in memory the things that were done and said.
5.3: **“Not with our fathers”** — Abraham, Isaac and Jacob
5.5:
**“I was the mediator and stood between”** — not in place, but by the office of interpreting, reporting the words of God to the people and of the people to God
**“the Lord and you at that time, to shew you his words, for you feared the fire, and went not up into the mountain, and he said:”** — BETWEEN YOU AND GOD, etc. AUGUSTINE. As though the Lord were in a place, that is, on the mountain, whence they too heard the voices; he who is wholly everywhere, nor draws near or withdraws by intervals of place. But his manifestations in the creature, which is not what he is, are not otherwise shown to human senses. Moses, then, was not in the middle by an interval of place; but it pleased the people to hear the rest of God's words through him, after it was terrified, hearing from the midst of the fire the voice of God speaking the decalogue of the law.
5.7:
**“Thou shalt not have strange gods”** — it forbids idolatry
**“in my sight.”** — from whom nothing is hid
5.9:
**“a jealous God,”** — avenging and jealous
**“visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon their children”** — the first motions of the senses
**“unto the third”** — the working
**“and fourth generation,”** — the boasting
**“to them”** — not to others, but
**“that hate me,”**
• with inherited impiety
• VISITING THE INIQUITY OF THE FATHERS, etc. ISIDORE. There are some who explain it so as to turn the sentence to the human soul; saying that the father in us is the light prick of the senses and the incentives of vices; the son, if thought has conceived the sin; the grandson, if you have accomplished the conception in deed; the great-grandson, if you glory in the things accomplished; according to that: "The wicked man, when he is come into the depth of sins, contemneth." Or it can be understood thus: that he is of such great mercy that he does not punish at once, but defers the sentence a long time.
• TO THEM THAT HATE ME, etc. To them, namely, who hate God with inherited impiety. For it is perverse that the sins of the fathers be imputed to sons who do not sin; since it was said through Ezechiel: "The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father" etc.
5.10:
**“And shewing”** — so quickly
**“mercy unto many thousands, to them that love me,”** — with true love
**“and keep”**
• in this love is proved
• whence: if you love me, keep my word, or my commandments
**“my commandments.”** — as a treasure
5.11:
**“Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord”** — the first commandment forbids idolatry, the second perjury
**“thy God”** — the Son
**“in vain:”** — by swearing for a thing that is not, or by giving the name of the Lord to wood or stone and the like
**“for he shall not be unpunished that upon a vain thing”** — every creature is made subject to vanity
**“taketh his name.”**
• thinking Christ, namely, a mere man
• THOU SHALT NOT TAKE THE NAME OF THE LORD THY GOD, etc. The first commandment pertains to the Father, by which it is said in what follows: Hear, O Israel, the Lord thy God is one God; so that, hearing this, you may worship the one God the Father and not take up many gods. The second pertains to the Son, of whom it is said here: "Thou shalt not take the name of thy God in vain"; that is, do not think the Son of God to be a creature; for every creature is made subject to vanity; but believe him equal to the Father, God of gods, God with God, through whom all things were made. The third [pertains] to the Spirit, by whose gift eternal rest is promised; for the Holy Ghost is spoken of [here]: "Therefore God sanctified the seventh day." For on the other days of works sanctification is not named, except on the sabbath, on which God rested. Rightly, then, this commandment pertains to the Spirit, both because of the name of sanctification and because of the eternal rest pertaining to the gift of the Holy Spirit. For it is said thus: "Remember that thou keep holy the sabbath day. Six days shalt thou labour" etc. In the work of six days the working of six thousand years seems to be marked; in the seventh, the time of eternal quiet, in which after good works eternal rest is promised. Whatever, then, we do, if we do it for the sake of the future rest, we observe the sabbath.
5.12:
**“Observe the day of the sabbath,”** — that thou mayst do all things for the sake of the sabbath, that is, the eternal rest pertaining to the gift of the Holy Ghost
**“to sanctify it, as the Lord thy God hath commanded thee.”** — by doing all things holily, by ceasing from the din of vices
5.13:
**“Six days shalt thou labour,”** — all the time of working good and perfect things
**“and shalt do all thy works.”** — befitting thy nature
5.14:
**“work”** — servile
**“thou nor thy son nor thy daughter,”** — who serves by love
**“nor thy manservant nor thy maidservant,”** — who namely is still pressed by fear
**“nor thy ox,”** — the Jew, or the wise
**“nor thy ass,”** — the Gentile and the foolish
**“nor any of thy beasts,”** — men and beasts thou wilt preserve, O Lord
**“nor the stranger”**
• one newly converted
• I am a stranger and a sojourner, as all my fathers were
**“that is within thy gates:”** — of thy Church: the Lord loveth the gates of Sion above all the tabernacles of Jacob
5.15:
**“Remember that thou also”** — to God or to the devil
**“didst serve in Egypt,”** — the world
**“and brought thee out”** — to filial fear
**“from thence the Lord God”**
• almighty
• by the Son made manifest
5.16:
**“Honour”**
• this is the greatest and first commandment in the second table
• with the duty of piety and honour
**“thy father and mother,”**
• carnal or spiritual
• according to the letter; or God and the Church
**“that thou mayst live a long time,”** — with eternal life, for which one must labour
**“and it may be well with thee in the land,”** — of the living
**“which the Lord thy God will give thee.”**
• freely
• HONOUR THY FATHER, etc. After three precepts follow seven which pertain to the neighbour. Among the seven it is first, but in the order of all it is the fourth: Honour thy father, etc. For from his parents man opens his eyes, and this life takes its beginning from their love. Whence this commandment is called the greatest and first in the second, namely table. We are commanded, then, to honour our parents and to show them the duty of piety and reverence. For he who does not do this to his parents, how will he do it to others? The fifth: Thou shalt not commit adultery; that is, besides thy lawful wife thou shalt be joined with none. The sixth: Thou shalt not kill. He too kills who sees his neighbour dying of hunger or nakedness and does not help as far as he can. The seventh: Thou shalt not steal; in which he forbids all robbery. The eighth: Thou shalt not bear false witness; he abhors the crime of lying and falsehood. The ninth: Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife; in which he forbids even the adulterous thought. The tenth: Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's goods; in which he strikes at ambition and concupiscence. The first, then, forbids stealthy encroachment; the second, error; the third, love of the world; the fourth, impiety; the fifth, fornication; the sixth, cruelty; the seventh, rapacity; the eighth, falsehood; the ninth, the thought of adultery; the tenth, the covetousness of the world. And it is to be noted that as the Egyptians are struck with ten plagues, so the people of God is ruled by ten precepts, and the demons are slain.
5.17:
**“Thou shalt not kill.”**
• he that hateth his brother is a murderer
• in deed or in will, or by withholding what thou canst supply
5.18: **“Neither shalt thou commit adultery.”** — It forbids adultery, carnal or spiritual. Fornication is idolatry and the wicked exposition of the scriptures.
5.19: **“And thou shalt not steal.”** — in act or in habit, or by avarice with the talent entrusted
5.20:
**“Neither shalt thou bear false witness against thy neighbour.”**
• the worst kind of lying
• it forbids falsehood
5.21:
**“Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife:”** — by will alone: whosoever shall look on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her
**“nor his house, nor his field, nor his manservant, nor his maidservant, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor any thing that is his.”**
• in the tenth commandment he forbids the covetousness of every thing
• he condemns ambition and concupiscence
5.22:
**“These words the Lord spoke to all the multitude”** — no one is excepted
**“adding”** — on the tables
**“nothing more: and he wrote them in two tables”** — there are two testaments, two precepts of love
**“of stone,”** — because the hearts of the Jews are hard and senseless
**“which he delivered unto me.”** — IN TWO TABLES, etc. ISIDORE. In the two tables are signified the two testaments, or the love of God and of the neighbour, on which the whole law hangs and the prophets. For on one table three precepts pertain to the love of God, on the other seven to fellowship with the neighbour. The stone tables signify the stony hearts of the Jews, of which it is said: "I will take away from you the stony heart, and will give you a heart of flesh", namely one able to feel and to understand.
5.29:
**“Who shall give”** — but I
**“such”** — grace poured in
**“them to have a mind, to fear me,”** — with chaste fear
**“and to keep”** — not stony, but able to feel
**“all my commandments”** — that not one jot may pass
**“at all times, that it may be well with them and with their children for ever?”** — WHO SHALL GIVE THEM TO HAVE SUCH A MIND, etc. God wishes it to be understood that this benefit is granted by his grace, that in all things the justice of God may be from faith, not as from one's own law. Whence: "I will take away from them the stony heart, and will give a heart of flesh", that is, one with feeling. For flesh has feeling, but stone does not. And elsewhere: "He hath made us fit ministers of the new testament, not in the letter, but in the spirit."
5.32: **“Keep therefore and do the things which the Lord God hath commanded you: you shall not go aside neither to the right hand, nor to the left.”** — so that you add anything or take away

6.3: **“Hear, O Israel, and observe to do the things, that it may be well with thee, and thou mayst be greatly multiplied, as the Lord the God of thy fathers hath promised thee a land flowing with milk and honey.”** — with all plenty
6.4: **“Hear, O Israel, the Lord thy God is one God.”** — in manifestation; three in persons; it neither has division nor admits solitude
6.5:
**“Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with thy whole heart,”** — with the understanding
**“and with thy whole soul,”** — with the life
**“and with thy whole strength.”**
• with the powers, or with affection
• THOU SHALT LOVE THE LORD THY GOD, etc. AUGUSTINE. Charity will not be taken away, but fulfilled. When it has contemplated what it believed and obtained what it hoped, in that fulness this precept will be fulfilled. For while there is in us anything of carnal concupiscence which is bridled even by restraint, God will not be loved altogether with the whole soul. For the flesh does not lust without the soul, although the flesh is said to lust, because the soul lusts carnally. But then there will be no law in the members fighting against the law of the mind, but God will be loved by the soul with the whole heart, the whole mind. And this perfection ought to have been commanded to man, although in this life it cannot be had. For one does not run rightly if he does not know how he is to run. And we run by hoping, believing and desiring, by giving alms and praying, that running we may be helped; and so let us hear the precepts of perfection, and not neglect to run toward the fulness of charity. Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with thy whole heart, etc., and thy neighbour as thyself. On these the whole law hangs and the prophets. The end of the precept, then, is the twofold love, namely of God and of the neighbour; and if you understand yourself whole, that is, soul and body, and your neighbour likewise whole (for man consists of soul and body), no kind of things to be loved has been passed over in these two. For since the love of God runs before, its measure is prescribed, that all other things should flow together into him. Of love of yourself nothing seems to be said; but where it is said "as thyself", that you should love yourself is not passed over. And he loves in order who does not love what is not to be loved and loves what is to be loved; and does not love more what is less to be loved, nor equally what is to be loved more or less, nor more or less what is equally to be loved. Every sinner, in so far as he is a sinner, is not to be loved; but every man, in so far as he is a man, is to be loved for God's sake; but God for his own sake. And if God is to be loved more than every man, each one ought to love him more than himself. Likewise another man is to be loved more than our body; because all these things are to be loved for God's sake, and another man can enjoy God with us, which the body cannot, because it lives through the soul, by which we enjoy God. And all are to be loved equally; but since you cannot do good to all, you must take thought chiefly for those who, by the occasion of places and times or of anything else, are more closely joined to us.
• The soul is of a threefold nature; therefore it is commanded to love in a threefold way. God does not wish his love to be shared, or that we love God and gold together, or wife or children. No one can serve two masters. He is to be loved above all; love of him is set first.
**“GREGORY”** — THOU SHALT LOVE THY GOD WITH THY WHOLE, etc. Through the love of God the love of neighbour is begotten, and through the love of neighbour the love of God is nourished. For he who neglects to love God does not know how to love his neighbour. And we are more fully perfected in the love of God if in the bosom of his love we rejoice in charity toward our neighbour. About to say, then, "thou shalt love thy neighbour", he set first "thou shalt love the Lord thy God"; that first he may fix in us the root of his love, and afterwards brotherly love may spread its branches. And that the love of God grows together with the love of neighbour, John shows, saying: "He that loveth not his brother whom he seeth, how can he love God whom he seeth not?" The love of God is born through fear, but in growing it is changed into affection. And that it may be shown how far each is from the charity of neighbour or how far he has advanced in it, God presses some down with scourges, props up others with successes. For often those pursue us when we are wretched who venerate us beyond comparison when we are happy. But when one loves or is loved in prosperity, it is uncertain whether the prosperity or the person is loved. For in good times a friend is not known, and in evil times an enemy is not hidden.
6.7:
**“And thou shalt tell them to thy children, and thou shalt meditate upon them”** — on them
**“sitting”** — at home or abroad
**“in thy house, and walking on thy journey,”** — abroad
**“sleeping”** — in all things, namely, that thou shalt do
6.8:
**“And thou shalt bind”** — that thou mayst fulfil them in work and give an example to others
**“them as a sign on thy hand, and they shall be”** — that thou mayst have them in memory
**“and shall move between thy eyes.”**
• that thou mayst meditate on them day and night
• of the heart
• AND THOU SHALT BIND THEM, etc. The Pharisees, wrongly interpreting this, wrote the Decalogue, that is, the ten words, on parchments, and carried them bound on the forehead; which the Babylonians do even today, that they may be thought religious. Whence: "They make their phylacteries broad, and enlarge their fringes."
6.9: **“And thou shalt write them in the entry, and on the doors of thy house.”** — going in and going out thou mayst always meditate on them
6.12: **“Take heed diligently lest thou forget the Lord thy God, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. Thou shalt fear the Lord thy God, and shalt serve him only, and thou shalt swear by his name.”** — He does not command to swear, but forbids swearing by the name of another god. But it is better not to swear at all; not that true swearing is evil, but lest by readiness in swearing you fall into perjury. For he who swears can forswear himself; but he who does not swear at all is far from perjury.
6.13: **“THOU SHALT SWEAR BY HIS NAME”** — They are permitted to swear by the name of God, lest perhaps, swearing by idols and naming them constantly, they should begin to worship them.
6.16: **“Thou shalt not tempt”** — this was set against the devil tempting Christ when he said: cast thyself down
6.22: **“And he wrought signs and wonders great and very grievous”** — in the opinion of those who bore them

7.1:
**“When the Lord thy God shall have brought thee into the land, which thou art going in to possess, and shall have destroyed”** — the seven principal vices and their offspring
**“seven nations”** — the seven principal vices and their offspring
**“MANY NATIONS”** — ISIDORE. The seven nations are the seven principal vices, which the spiritual soldier, overcoming them through the grace of God, is commanded to exterminate. They are said to be of greater number because the vices are more than the virtues. In the catalogue they are called seven nations; in the conquest they are set down without number: but when he shall have destroyed many nations before thee. For the people of carnal things, which is multiplied from the sevenfold tinder of the vices, is more numerous than Israel. From gluttony: revelling, drunkenness. From fornication: filthy speech, scurrility, jesting and foolish talk. From avarice: lying, fraud, thefts, perjuries, desire of filthy lucre, false witness, violence, inhumanity and rapacity. From anger: murder, clamour and indignation. From sadness: rancour, faintheartedness, bitterness, despair and sloth. From acedia: idleness, drowsiness, importunity, restlessness of mind and body, instability, wordiness and curiosity. From vainglory: contentions, heresies, boasting and presumption of novelties. From pride: contempt, envy, disobedience, blasphemy, murmuring, detraction and many others. These, though they are of greater number than the virtues, yet when the principal ones are overcome all are quieted and are destroyed by a perpetual death. And that these plagues are stronger we feel in temptation; for the delight of carnal passions fights more strongly in our members than the pursuits of the virtues, which are acquired with the utmost contrition of heart and body. We possess the regions of these nations with the army of Israel, that is, we overcome the vices with the virtues, so that in our heart chastity may hold the place of fornication, patience the place of fury, saving joy the place of sadness, fortitude dwell in the place of acedia, humility in the place of pride; so, each vice being driven out, in their place may reign the sons of Israel, that is, souls seeing God. But when God spoke to Abraham of things to come, he is read to have numbered not seven but ten nations, whose land is promised to his seed. Namely, when the idolatries of the Gentiles, the blasphemy of the Jews and the error of the heretics are cast off, to which those are subject before the knowledge of God and the grace of baptism who dwell in the spiritual Egypt. But he who goes out from there and through the grace of God comes to the spiritual desert will be freed from the assault of three nations, [and] does battle against seven.
**“much more numerous than thou art, and stronger than thou:”** — THE HETHITE, AND THE GERGEZITE, etc. JEROME. The Hethite, fearing or astonished; the Gergezite, that is, a husbandman drawing near, or casting out a husbandman, or a stranger approaching; the Amorrhite, that is, bitter or speaking; the Chanaanite, possessing, or possession, or merchants, or movable; the Pherezite, hoping or scattered; the Hevite, that is, gathering stones; the Jebusite, that is, trodden down, or their manger.
**“SEVEN NATIONS”** — It was promised to Abraham that ten should be destroyed. For then there were ten; but when the sons of Israel crossed over to the Jordan, three had already been destroyed: for the sons of Lot destroyed the giants, the sons of Esau the Horrites, and the Cappadocians part of the Hevites.
**“AND STRONGER”** — Spiritual wickednesses are subtler and have more power to deceive than [our] weakness has to withstand.
7.3:
**“Neither shalt thou make marriages with them. Thy daughter”** — thy thought; namely, thou shalt not join it to the vices
**“thou shalt not give to his son,”** — or: to his own
7.5: **“But thus rather shall you deal with them:”** — despise their cunning
7.8: **“and hath kept his covenant,”** — elsewhere: oath
7.9: **“And thou shalt know that the Lord thy God, he is a strong and faithful God,”** — he deceives no one who hopes in him
7.10: **“And repaying forthwith them that hate him, so”** — all time compared with eternity is as a point
7.14: **“BARREN”** — There were some barren women among the Jews, but so few that in comparison with the fruitful ones there seemed to be none.
7.20:
**“Moreover hornets also”** — the stings of fear
**“the Lord thy God will send among them, until he destroy and consume all that have escaped thee, and could hide themselves.”** — MOREOVER HORNETS ALSO, etc. It is nowhere read in the history that God sent hornets or wasps before them against their enemies; but by stinging animals he signifies the stings of fear, by which he put their terrified enemies to flight.
7.21:
**“Thou shalt not fear them, because the Lord thy God is in the midst of thee, a God mighty”** — almighty in delivering his own
**“and terrible:”** — against his adversaries
7.22:
**“He”** — not another; to him alone is the victory ascribed, by whom the enemies are overcome
**“will consume these nations in thy sight by little and little and by degrees. Thou wilt not be able to destroy them altogether: lest perhaps the beasts of the earth should increase upon thee.”** — THOU WILT NOT BE ABLE, etc. He shows that one must beware lest perhaps, when sins have been driven out of our flesh, a spiritual beast should rise up, that is, boasting, pride, vainglory, which are rooted out with more difficulty than carnal vices. For Lot, who held firm in Sodom, was defiled by fornication on the mountain. When a vice has been driven out, let a virtue be planted at once, lest the unclean spirit return and find the house empty.
**“GREGORY”** — To some God gives greater goods, and does not give lesser ones, so that they may have something for which to reproach themselves, and while they desire to be perfect and cannot, they may not at all exalt themselves in the things they have, who of themselves are not able to have even small things. Hence it is that he destroyed strong and powerful adversaries, but kept the Philistines and Chanaanites for a long time, that Israel might be trained by them, having those against whom to fight, lest it exalt itself over the greater ones it had overcome. The same mind, then, is strong by virtue and is harassed by infirmity, so that while it seeks what it cannot have, it may humbly keep what it has. The heavenly country too suffered losses in part among its citizens and in part stood firm, so that the elect angels, seeing others fallen through pride, might stand the more firmly as they stood the more humbly. So it is done in each soul, that at times the least losses confer the greatest gains.
7.26:
**“Neither shalt thou bring any thing of the idol into thy house,”** — an image or a statue skilfully wrought and well polished
**“lest thou become an anathema,”**
• by adoring and worshipping
• estrangement
**“ANATHEMA”** — From "apo tou anatithenai", that is, from setting up or hanging up, as offerings were hung up in temples and were estranged from those who gave them.

8.2:
**“And thou shalt remember all the way through which the Lord thy God hath brought thee for forty years through the desert, to afflict thee and to prove thee, and that might be made known”** — to thee or to others; for to God all things are open
**“FOR FORTY YEARS”** — For this reason he allowed them to be afflicted for forty years, that they might know how great was their frailty.
**“the things that were in thy heart, whether thou wouldst keep his commandments or no.”** — TO AFFLICT THEE, etc. AUGUSTINE. Here is said more plainly what elsewhere is obscured by a manner of speaking, that is: "The Lord our God trieth you, that he may know whether you love him", that is, that he may make it known; which is now said openly: "to prove thee, and that the things that were in thy heart might be made known", etc. For he does not say "that he might know"; and if he had said it, it would have to be understood "that he might make it known".
8.3:
**“He afflicted thee with want, and gave thee manna for thy food, which neither thou nor thy fathers knew: to shew that not in bread alone doth man live, but in every word”** — the Word was made flesh, etc.
**“MANNA”** — The flesh of Christ, refreshed by which we may come to the true land of promise. For forty years we eat manna, that is, through the whole of our time, which turns in four seasons, we are fed with the sacrament of the Lord's body.
**“that proceedeth from the mouth of the Lord.”**
• NOT IN BREAD ALONE DOTH MAN LIVE, etc. Spiritual food is commended, by which souls that are to live for ever are filled. The manna given from heaven signifies the flesh of Christ, who says: "I am the bread of life; this is the bread that came down from heaven"; "for the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us." He that eateth this flesh hath everlasting life.
• NOT IN BREAD ALONE MAN, etc. He signifies the twofold substance of our nature. For man consists of soul and body; the body, which is from the earth, [lives] by earthly food, but the soul lives by the word of God. And the spirit of God quickens the spirit of man, if only the man is in the body of the Church, that is, of Christ, and in the faith of the Son of God. Therefore he adds that his raiment did not fail for age, because the conversation of the new man ought to abide in newness of life; while the foot is not worn, because the step of his works is kept unharmed; for the Lord knoweth the way of the just, and the way of the wicked shall perish.
8.4:
**“Thy raiment”**
• conversation
• the habit of the virtues, which God does not wish to fail with age
**“and thy foot”** — the step of good works or of faith
8.5: **“That thou mayst consider in thy heart,”** — what is just
8.7:
**“For the Lord thy God will bring thee into a good land, of brooks and of waters, and of fountains: in the plains of which”**
• in the Church, the rivers of doctrine
• the middling
**“and the hills”** — from the hills, that is, the doctors, they flow into the minds of the hearers
8.8:
**“A land of wheat,”** — of the Gospel doctrine
**“and barley,”** — of the doctrine of the law, which is wrapped in the hard husk of the letter
**“and vineyards,”** — of fervent doctrine, which gladdens the heart of man
**“wherein fig trees”** — the sweetness of wisdom
**“and pomegranates,”** — a heaping up of virtues
**“and oliveyards”** — works of mercy
**“grow: a land of oil”** — of mercy
**“and honey.”** — of sweet-flowing charity
8.9:
**“thy bread”** — which came down from heaven
**“the stones are iron,”** — firm doctrine, or the unconquerable saints
**“and out of its hills”** — the eminent saints
**“are dug mines of brass:”** — the sonority of preaching
8.10:
**“That when thou hast eaten, and art full, thou mayst bless”** — by giving thanks
**“the Lord thy God”** — from whom are all things
**“for the excellent land”** — the Church
8.11:
**“Take heed, and beware lest at any time thou forget the Lord thy God, and neglect his commandments”** — the ten moral commandments of the law written on the tables
**“and judgments”** — the discernment of good and evil
**“JUDGMENTS”** — Those which were commanded the people through Moses at various times after the law was given, which in Exodus are called justifications.
**“and ceremonies, which I command thee this day:”** — circumcision
**“AND CEREMONIES”** — Circumcision, the rite of the sacrifices. Whence Ambrose on the epistle to the Romans: "The law", he says, "is threefold: the first part concerns the sacrament of the Godhead; the second accords with the natural law, which forbids sin; the third is of the feasts of the law, that is, sabbaths, new moons and circumcision."
8.15:
**“And was thy leader in the great and terrible wilderness, wherein there was the serpent burning with his breath, and the scorpion and the dipsas, and no waters at all: who brought forth streams”** — namely, of doctrine
**“out of the hardest rock,”**
• "And the rock was Christ."
• AND THE DIPSAS, etc. A kind of asp which in Latin is called situla; whomever it bites dies of thirst. It is so small that when it is trodden on it is not seen. Its venom kills before the one who is to die feels it. Mystically: the various serpents are heresies, differing indeed among themselves, but all deadly.
8.16:
**“And fed thee with manna”** — with the body of Christ
**“which thy fathers knew not.”** — of the old law
**“And after he had afflicted and strengthened thee,”** — or: proved
8.17: **“Lest thou shouldst say in thy heart:”** — by attributing to thyself
8.18:
**“But remember”** — to whom all things are to be attributed
**“that he might fulfil his covenant,”** — promise
**“concerning which he swore to thy fathers,”** — by firmly promising

9.5: **“For it is not for thy justices, and the uprightness of thy heart that thou shalt go in to possess their lands: but because they have done wickedly, they are destroyed at thy coming in: and that the Lord might accomplish his word, which he promised by oath to thy fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.”** — FOR IT IS NOT FOR THY JUSTICES. AUGUSTINE. These are they who did not deserve to perish in the desert, because they knew not the right hand or the left. Yet now they are called stiffnecked. That, then, was said in a mystery, and the merits of these men were not commended; for lest anyone think that those who had been deservedly praised before were suddenly made blameworthy, a little after it is said of them: "Remember, and forget not", etc. And if some were such, but some faithful and good, even so the land of promise is not given to those who knew not the right hand or the left in such a way that we should understand it as though they had not offended the Lord. For their fathers too, who died and did not enter the land of promise, are found to have been such that there were some good men among them. Whence the Apostle says that some of them, not all, offended, and recounts their sins. And that they were like their parents, what is added shows: "For in Horeb also thou didst provoke the Lord", where those provoked the Lord who by their own desert were not brought into the land of promise.
9.10: **“And the Lord gave me two tables of stone written with the finger of God, and containing all the words that he spoke to you in the mount from the midst of the fire, when the people were assembled together.”** — AND THE LORD GAVE ME, etc. AUGUSTINE. In Exodus it is read that the Lord gave Moses the tables, but that Moses wrote [the second] at his dictation, the Lord giving him the power to write. It is to be noted that the tables which the Lord gave, on which man did not labour, were broken; but those which were made by human labour remained whole. Allegorically: because the law which the Lord gave to the Jews, since they were unwilling to work, did not remain; but the Gospel, which was given to the Gentiles, since they work and exercise themselves spiritually, endures for ever.
9.12:
**“And said to me: Arise, and go down from hence quickly: for thy people”** — as though not mine, since it offended me
**“quickly”** — as being fickle
**“the way”** — Christ, who is the way, the truth and the life
**“that thou hast shewn them,”** — therefore without excuse
9.13:
**“And again the Lord said to me: I see that this people”** — of untamed pride
**“is stiffnecked:”** — whom thou holdest back by prayers
9.14:
**“Let me alone that I may destroy them, and abolish their name from under heaven, and set thee over a nation,”**
• the understanding of the law
• the Gentile people converted to the faith
9.15: **“And when I came down from the burning mount, and [held] the two tables of the covenant”** — because the precepts are to be held or fulfilled in work
9.16:
**“And saw that you had sinned against the Lord your God, and had made to yourselves a calf”** — they made a calf because they saw the Egyptians worship oxen
**“molten, and had quickly forsaken his way, which he had shewn you:”** — through me

10.4:
**“AND HE WROTE”** — AUGUSTINE. In Exodus Moses is related to have written the ten words of the law on the tables; in Deuteronomy, God himself. In Exodus also [it is said] that the former tables were written with the finger of God, but the second were kept in the ark and in the tabernacle. We have said that they signify the two testaments: so that in the Old Testament the law might be commended as the work of God, where man did nothing, because the law cannot be fulfilled [by man]; for the work of the law is truly done by charity, not by fear, which is the grace of the New Testament. But on the second tables man is read to have written the words of God, because man can do the work of the law through the charity of justice, which he cannot do through the fear of punishment. When therefore it is read in Deuteronomy: "And he wrote", etc., namely "in the tables, according as he had written before", etc., God is read to have written both tables, and not man. In Exodus [too] the Lord says: "I will write on the tables the words that were in the former", etc. Exodus alone, then, raises the question; for a little after it is said: "Write thee these words", etc., and after a few [words] it adds: "and he wrote upon the tables the words of the covenant." For if it be understood thus: "Write thee these words", namely other words, which are not written on the tables but in the book of the law, certainly what follows: "And he was there with the Lord forty days and forty nights; he neither ate bread, and he wrote upon the tables the ten words of the covenant", shows that Moses wrote on the tables, not God; unless by force we understand "the Lord" and not Moses, and so there will be no difference of the testaments, since God wrote both the former and the second tables. Yet the former, without doubt, God, not man, both made and wrote; for it was not then said to Moses: "Hew thee two tables", but thus it is read: "Moses came down from the mount, and the two tables in his hands; and the tables were the work of God, and the writing [of God]." Above too it had been said: "He gave Moses tables of stone written with the finger of God." But Moses is commanded to hew the second, that they may be understood to be hewn by human work, although God wrote [them]. And both are said of the second tables for this reason: that God by his grace does the work of the law in man, and man, receiving the grace of God through faith (which belongs to the New Testament), is a fellow worker with God who helps him.
