Therefore in the first only the work of God is mentioned, because the law is spiritual and holy, and the commandment holy, where there is no work of man, because the unbelievers do not submit themselves to the help of God's grace, but wish to establish their own justice, and the law is to them for damnation; which the breaking of the tables signifies. And for this reason above God promised that he would write, and in Deuteronomy he is related not only to have promised but also to have written. For God works in us both to will and to accomplish and to perfect, and we work out our salvation with fear and trembling; and he helps the choice of the good will.
**“THE TEN WORDS, WHICH”** — GILBERT. Fittingly the words of the law end in the number ten. For ten consists of eight and two: there are eight beatitudes, two commandments of charity. It consists also of seven and three, because the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit fill out faith in the Trinity. It is divided also into six and four, as unfolding the perfection of works and the fulfilment of the four Gospels.
10.6:
**“Eleazar his son”** — by the privilege of age
**“INTO MOSERA”** — In the book of Numbers he is written to have died on mount Hor; but perhaps the place has two names. For Beroth of the sons of Jacan is a place in the desert, as is Mosera, where Aaron died, as is read in the books of places; and it is shown to this day at the tenth milestone from the city of Petra, on the top of the mountain.
10.8: **“THE TRIBE OF LEVI”** — Unless the whole royal priesthood, which belongs to the New Testament, were signified by this [tribe], a man who was not of that tribe would not dare to say: "The Lord is my portion"; and elsewhere: "The Lord is the portion of my inheritance."
10.13: **“And keep the commandments of the Lord, and his ceremonies, which I command thee this day, that it may be well with thee?”** — as if [to say]: lest thou think he needed thy service and therefore commanded such things
10.14: **“Behold heaven is the Lord's thy God, and the heaven of heaven, the earth and all things that are therein.”** — THE HEAVEN OF HEAVEN, etc. Some say there are three heavens: the airy, the ethereal and the starry. Some, seven: first the airy, second the ethereal, third the Olympian, fourth the fiery, fifth the firmament, sixth the watery, seventh that of the angels.
10.16:
**“Circumcise therefore the foreskin”**
• the superfluities of the heart
• every evil will
**“of the heart”** — "With all watchfulness keep thy heart"
**“of you, and your neck”** — with the swelling of pride
**“stiffen no more.”**
• or: further
• CIRCUMCISE, etc. It signifies spiritual circumcision, that is, the guarding of the mind and true abstinence; as if [to say]: when you have extinguished the lust of the flesh, cut away also the superfluities of the mind. All the senses are to be circumcised. Whence Moses complains that he is uncircumcised of lips; and Stephen to the Jews: "Uncircumcised", he says, "in heart and ears", etc. He then is truly circumcised who stops his ears lest he hear blood, and shuts his eyes lest he see evil; who does not offend in his tongue; whose heart is not weighed down with surfeiting and drunkenness; who washes his hands among the innocent and keeps back his feet from every evil way; who chastises his body and brings it into subjection, and keeps his heart with all watchfulness. We need this twofold circumcision, and let us not seek vainglory from it, lest we be clean without and unclean within and suffer the penalties of feigned holiness, like the Sichemites, who imitated the circumcision of the patriarchs not for love of God but for the sake of lust. Therefore they gained no reward, but on the third day perished within the ruins of their city. For such men, at the time of the resurrection, when the virtues in which they trusted are made void, die for ever.
10.17:
**“God”** — against whom it is foolish to be proud
**“of gods, and the Lord of lords, a great God and mighty and terrible,”** — whom you ought to imitate
10.19: **“And do you therefore love strangers,”** — as he does, that you may be the sons of your Father who is in heaven
10.20:
**“Thou shalt fear the Lord thy God,”** — as sons
**“and serve him only:”** — spiritually
**“to him thou shalt adhere,”** — "But it is good for me to adhere to my God"
**“and shalt swear”** — it is a permission
**“by his name.”** — not of idols
10.21:
**“He”**
• whom alone thou oughtest to praise
• "In the Lord shall my soul be praised"
**“is thy praise, and thy God, that hath done for thee these great”**
• lest thou be ungrateful
• which no other has done
**“and terrible things,”** — to the enemies
**“which thy eyes have seen.”** — do not dare to doubt
10.22: **“WENT DOWN”** — One goes down into Egypt, [for] the descent is easy; one goes up to Jerusalem, because narrow is the way that leads to life, and virtue strives toward the heights.

11.1:
**“Therefore love the Lord thy God”** — all the commandments of the law are consummated in the love of God
**“and observe his precepts and ceremonies, his judgments and commandments at all times.”** — he that shall persevere shall be saved
11.2: **“Know this day the things that your children know not, who saw not the chastisements of the Lord your God, his great doings and strong”** — power or working
11.3: **“The signs and works which he did in the midst of Egypt to king Pharao,”** — whom he drowned in the Red Sea
11.10:
**“For the land, which thou goest to possess, is not like”** — which [lies] low
**“the land of Egypt,”** — like the prosperity of the present life
**“FROM WHENCE THOU CAMEST OUT”** — In mind, Moses leading, that is, the law teaching [us] to despise earthly pleasures, and to enter the land of promise with Jesus leading.
**“from whence thou camest out, where, when the seed is sown, waters are brought in to water it after the manner of gardens.”** — AFTER THE MANNER OF GARDENS, WATERS, etc. Because all carnal men strive to multiply for themselves present happiness and abundance of temporal things.
11.11:
**“But it is a land of hills”** — by the height of the virtues
**“and plains,”** — by the cleanness of good works
**“expecting rain from heaven.”** — of divine grace
11.12:
**“And the Lord thy God”**
• filling it with heavenly gift
• propitiation
• "The eyes of the Lord are upon the just"
**“doth always visit it, and his eyes are on it from the beginning of the year unto the end thereof.”** — "His mercy shall follow me all the days of my life"
**“FROM THE BEGINNING”** — From the beginning, namely, of good will to the perfection of good work he directs the course of life. For it is God who works in us both to will and to accomplish, according to his good will.
11.14:
**“He will give the rain”** — of preaching; whence: "I will command my clouds to rain no rain"
**“to your land, the early”**
• because at the beginning of the year
• at the end
**“and the latter,”** — at the end
**“that you may gather in your corn,”** — temporal sustenance
**“and your wine, and your oil,”** — THE EARLY, etc. Because to his elect in the former time he gave the understanding of the law. He bestows the latter rain because in the last time he has opened to us the mystery of his incarnation.
**“AND THE LATTER”** — Because it is the last hour when his preaching reached us, who says: "The lifting up of my hands, an evening sacrifice."
11.20: **“THOU SHALT WRITE THEM UPON”** — THOU SHALT WRITE THEM UPON. AUGUSTINE. According to the letter no one of the Israelites is recorded to have done this, nor could he do it, unless perhaps he divided them over many parts of his house; or it is a hyperbolic manner of speech, as many things are said.
11.24:
**“Every place, that your foot shall tread upon, shall be yours. From the desert,”** — which is in the south
**“and from Libanus,”** — in the north
**“from the great river Euphrates”** — which is in the east
**“unto the western sea”** — the Tyrrhenian; these are the bounds of the land of promise
11.25:
**“None shall stand against you:”** — to harm us
**“the Lord your God shall lay the dread and fear of you upon all the land”** — earthliness
**“that you shall tread upon,”** — lest it be proud
**“as he hath spoken to you.”** — who does not lie
11.26:
**“Behold I set forth”** — that you may choose what you will
**“in your sight this day a blessing”** — of grace
11.27: **“A blessing,”** — which is of free will
11.29:
**“And when the Lord thy God shall have brought thee into the land, whither thou goest to dwell, thou shalt put the blessing upon mount Garizim, the curse upon mount Hebal:”** — it is interpreted old abyss
**“MOUNT GARIZIM”** — Garizim is interpreted division or stranger; Hebal is interpreted old abyss. For those who separate themselves from vices and judge themselves strangers and pilgrims in this world deserve also the eternal blessing. But those who cast themselves into the abyss of the old life, serving carnal desires, will be subject to the eternal curse.
11.30: **“Which are beyond the Jordan, behind the way that goeth to the setting of the sun, in the land of the Chanaanite who dwelleth in the plain country over against Galgala,”** — which is the hill of the foreskins, because there the people was circumcised by Josue
11.31:
**“For you shall pass over the Jordan,”** — baptism
**“to possess the land,”** — of the living
**“which the Lord your God will give you,”** — freely
**“that you may have it and possess it.”** — lest you lose the land

12.2: **“Destroy all the places in which”** — the shrines and idols which they worship in [these] places
12.3: **“Overthrow their altars, and break down their statues,”** — that no memory may remain
12.6: **“And you shall offer in that place your holocausts and victims, the tithes and firstfruits of your hands and your vows and gifts, the firstborn of your herds and your sheep.”** — TITHES, AND, etc. It is to be asked how he commands the tithes of all fruits and the firstlings of all cattle not to be eaten except in the city where the temple will be, when he commanded them to be given to the Levites.
12.13: **“Beware lest thou offer thy holocausts in every place that thou shalt see:”** — BEWARE, etc. He cuts off the occasion of sacrificing to idols. For he commands victims to be offered in the temple and at the altar of the Lord for this reason, that where religion is whole, there fitting worship may be shown. Mystically, he intimates that no gift is acceptable to God outside the Catholic Church. For this is the place which God chose to put his name there and to dwell in it.
12.17:
**“Thou mayst not eat in thy towns the tithes of thy corn,”** — good will
**“and thy wine,”** — spiritual grace
**“and thy oil,”** — mercy
**“the firstborn of thy herds and thy cattle, nor any thing that thou vowest, and that thou wilt offer voluntarily, and the firstfruits of thy hands:”** — WITHOUT EATING, etc. He forbids murder. Blood is put for the soul, because the seat of the soul, that is, of human life, is in the blood.
**“IN THY TOWNS”** — That is, thou shalt not assign to thy own merits what thou hast received by divine bounty, nor to thy own strength, but to God, by whose gift thou hast these things.
12.18:
**“But thou shalt eat them before the Lord thy God in the place”** — with the affection of humanity and innocence
**“which the Lord thy God shall choose,”** — this precept is general, that all should keep it
**“thou and thy son and thy daughter, and thy manservant, and maidservant, and the Levite that dwelleth in thy cities: and thou shalt rejoice”** — with heavenly joy: "Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice"; "He that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord"
12.19: **“TAKE HEED THOU”** — "Let him that is instructed in the word communicate to him that instructeth him, in all good things." For those who preach the Gospel ought to live by the Gospel.
12.23:
**“Only beware of this, that thou eat not the blood, for the blood is for the soul: and therefore thou must not eat the soul with the flesh:”** — that is, ascribing [it] to earthliness
**“ONLY BEWARE OF THIS”** — According to the letter the Apostles commanded this; but in the blood murder and the hatred of brothers is forbidden. For whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer.
**“FOR THE BLOOD”** — Because something vital is in the blood, and through it most of all one lives in this flesh, since it is diffused through all the veins, he calls it the soul, that is, the life of the body, which is ended by death. Mystically it is intimated that, when carnal men departing from their former conversation are joined [with us] in the unity of faith and good works, we should not turn their errors to our own use, but pour them out; that is, when they are brought forth through confession, ascribe them to earthly frailty and cast them away as unworthy of spiritual men.

13.1: **“If there rise in the midst of thee a prophet or one that saith he hath dreamed a dream, and he foretell a sign and a wonder,”** — IF THERE RISE, etc. He wishes it to be understood that the things said by diviners not according to God, even if they come to pass, are not to be so received that what they [command] be done; nor does he show that the things which so happen are outside his own power. But why he permits it he sets down: to make known, namely, how much they love God, [known] to themselves, not to him who knows all things.
13.3:
**“Thou shalt not hear the words of that prophet”** — a Gentile or a heretic
**“THAT IT MAY APPEAR”** — The Seventy: "to know whether you love". But the Latin translators [render] it "that he may know whether you love"; but the sense is the same. For what is said, "he tempts you to know", is this: by tempting he makes you know.
13.5:
**“And that prophet or forger of dreams shall be slain:”** — by eternal death
**“because he spoke to draw you away from the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, and redeemed you from the house of bondage: to make thee go out of the way, which the Lord thy God commanded thee: and thou shalt take away the evil out of the midst of thee.”** — "If thy eye scandalize thee, pluck it out and cast it from thee. It is better for thee", etc.
13.9: **“But thou shalt presently put him to death. Let thy hand be first upon him, and afterwards let all the people put their hands [to him].”** — by hard reproof and strong sentence
13.16:
**“And all the household goods”** — of [their] pursuits
**“that are there, thou shalt gather together in the midst of the streets thereof, and with the city itself”** — of the devil, which is Babylon the great, with which all the kings of the earth have committed fornication
**“shalt burn them, so as to consume all”** — with everlasting fire

14.1:
**“Be ye children of the Lord your God: you shall not cut yourselves,”**
• as the priests are read to have done in the book of Kings
• as the heathen cut their hair and consecrate it to the dead
• YOU SHALL NOT CUT YOURSELVES. To this day many nations cut themselves at the funerals of the dead.
• Be not sorrowful, even as others who have no hope. For to do these things belongs to those who despair of the resurrection.
**“nor make any baldness for the dead;”** — NOR MAKE ANY BALDNESS, etc. The hairs of your head are numbered, that is, the thoughts, which one must not take away from the honour of the head and offer to the devil, as some offer their bodily hair to the devil.
14.3: **“Eat not the things that are unclean.”** — EAT NOT THE THINGS THAT, etc. It is not that the animals are unclean, but that by signifying they express the manners, namely, the acts and wills of men.
14.5:
**“The hart and the roe, the buffle,”** — the buffles are those which by another name are called bisons
**“the tragelaph,”** — the goat-stag, like a goat and a stag
**“THE CAMELOPARDALUS”** — It is sprinkled with white spots, like a camel in the head, with a horse's neck and the feet of a buffle, in the rest like a pard; it is born in Ethiopia.
14.6:
**“THAT [DIVIDETH THE HOOF] IN TWO”** — He, namely, who, receiving the two testaments, establishes himself with the firm step of justice and innocence.
**“EVERY BEAST”** — The Church receives and incorporates into its members those who divide the hoof, who know how to have the discernment of good and evil, and who chew the cud, that is, meditate on the law day and night.
14.7:
**“THE CAMEL”** — The Jew, who strains out a gnat and swallows a camel; who chews the cud of the letter, but has not a cloven hoof, because he does not divide the letter from the spirit: these are the scribes and Pharisees.
**“the hare,”** — swift, timid
**“and the cherogril:”** — weak, rapacious, deadly
**“THE HARE, THE CHEROGRIL”** — By the cherogril and the hare he signifies the multitude of the Jews; for each animal is weak and infirm.
**“BECAUSE THEY CHEW THE CUD”** — The Jews chew the cud of the words of the law, but do not divide the hoof, because they do not believe in the Father and the Son, nor receive the two testaments. But certain heretics divide the hoof, but do not chew the doctrine of truth in the mouth.
14.8:
**“The swine also, because it divideth the hoof, but cheweth not the cud, shall be unclean, their flesh”** — by feigned virtues
**“you shall not eat,”** — that is, you shall not receive such into fellowship
**“and their carcasses”**
• carcasses, that is, sins
• that is, you shall not imitate dead works
**“you shall not touch.”** — by communicating [with them]
14.9:
**“These shall you eat of all that abide in the waters:”** — of baptism
**“All that have fins and scales, you shall eat.”**
• ignorance, which will quickly be taken away
• THAT HAVE FINS, etc. Those who meditate on the law of the sublime life. Because ignorance of the divine law had long been among the Gentiles, he joins scales to the fins. For as fish are scaled and finned, so to those in whom there is temporal ignorance the knowledge of the sublime, heavenly life is quickly added.
**“THESE SHALL YOU EAT”** — By these are understood the Gentiles, who are reborn in the waters of baptism.
14.11: **“All birds that are clean you shall eat.”** — he sets down a proper chapter on the contemplatives, as in the sacrifices
14.12:
**“The unclean eat not: to wit, the eagle, and the grype,”** — those who seize what belongs to others and rejoice in unjust gains
**“and the osprey,”** — the falcon
**“AND THE GRYPE”** — This is a four-footed beast, like an eagle in head and wings, in the rest of the body like a lion; it abounds in the Hyperborean mountains, and is most hostile to horses and to men.
14.13:
**“The ringtail, and the vulture,”** — which rejoices in wars and deaths
**“and the kite according to their kind:”** — of the rapacious
14.14: **“And all of the raven's kind:”** — which is without affection, like Judas toward his master
14.15:
**“And the ostrich,”** — the Seventy: glaucus
**“THE OSTRICH”** — Which is not lifted from the earth, but is entangled in worldly business.
**“THE OWL”** — Which sees sharply by night and not by day; like those who glory in the knowledge of the law and do not take in the light of the Gospel.
**“THE LARUS”** — Which flies like a bird and swims like a water creature; who, namely, venerates circumcision and baptism. To such Paul says: "If you be circumcised, Christ shall profit you nothing."
**“THE HAWK”** — Those who seem gentle but are allied with the powerful and the avaricious.
**“according to its kind:”** — the gerfalcon, in the common tongue; it seizes the eagle
14.16: **“THE SWAN AND THE IBIS”** — These are said to have long necks and to draw their food from the depth of the earth. But we ought to seek the bread which came down from heaven, and not be solicitous what we shall eat.
14.17:
**“And the cormorant,”** — the Seventy: the pelican
**“THE NIGHT CROW”** — Which creeps and works by night; signifying those who are given over to the works of the night, which are fornication, uncleanness, the worship of idols and the like.
14.18:
**“The bittern,”** — not the calander lark, as they think
**“THE HOOP”** — Which loves mourning. But the sorrow of the world worketh death; and we ought to rejoice in the Lord, and in all things give thanks.
**“THE BAT”** — Which flies about the earth and walks on its wings. But our conversation ought to be in heaven.
14.19: **“Every thing that creepeth,”** — intent on the earth, though it feigns contemplation
14.20:
**“All that is clean, you shall eat.”**
• share in honest works and manners
• without sin
14.21:
**“But whatsoever is dead of itself,”** — defiled by sin
**“eat not thereof.”**
• by consenting or by doing the same
• abstain from dead works
**“TO THE STRANGER, THAT”** — As if [to say]: leave unclean things to pagans and heretics. Hence in the Gospel the demons are permitted to go into the herd of swine, and it is said: "Let the dead bury their dead", etc.
**“or sell it to him: because thou art the holy people of the Lord thy God. Thou shalt not boil”**
• thou shalt purge
• who will be set on the left hand
**“a kid”** — the sinner
**“IN THE MILK”** — With middling but more austere disciplines, that they may restore by bitter things the sweet things they have lost.
**“of his dam.”** — the Church
**“BUT WHATSOEVER”** — Mystically, the Church is commanded by the mystical Man to keep herself in holiness and to shun all the uncleanness of sin; but she may let the stranger, that is, the Gentile, remain in his filth.
14.22: **“THE TITHES”** — As if [to say]: the good things which thou doest according to the precepts of the divine law, do them and set them apart for the Lord, that thou mayst do all things to his praise.
14.23:
**“of thy corn,”** — of the body of Christ, or of preaching
**“and thy wine,”** — of the blood of Christ, or of gladness of mind
**“and thy oil,”** — of works of mercy, or of the chrism
**“and the firstborn of thy herds”** — by greater works
**“and thy sheep:”** — by simplicity
**“THE FIRSTBORN”** — That is, the beginnings of good work, which are to be tithed, that is, consecrated to the Lord.
14.24: **“CARRY”** — As if [to say]: let those who are far from the perfection of the saints, and cannot ascend the summit of the virtues nor give themselves to contemplation, do humbly and devoutly what they can, and make themselves friends of the mammon of iniquity and treasures in heaven, that they may be received into the eternal dwellings, where there is feasting and rejoicing with friends, that is, the saints and elect of God.
14.26:
**“And thou shalt buy with the same money whatsoever pleaseth thee, either of the herds or of sheep, wine also and strong drink,”** — everything that can inebriate except wine
**“and all that thy soul desireth: and thou shalt eat before the Lord thy God, and shalt feast, thou and thy house:”** — AND THOU SHALT BUY WITH THE SAME, etc. Spiritually he commands that we always persevere in good works, so that after this life we may return to our house, that is, to the heavenly fatherland.
14.28:
**“The third year”** — one [year] coming between
**“thou shalt separate another tithe of all things that grow to thee at that time, and shalt lay it up”** — thou shalt not carry it to the place which the Lord chose
**“ANOTHER”** — Besides that one, namely, which thou eatest with thy household and the Levites in the place which the Lord chose.
14.29: **“AND THE LEVITE SHALL COME”** — He shows plainly that this tithe was not to be shared by him who offers it, but only by those to whom he commands it to be paid out, among whom he set the Levite first.

15.1:
**“In the seventh year thou shalt make a remission,”** — IN THE SEVENTH YEAR, etc. In this chapter piety and love are commended, that we may have mercy on our neighbours and await our reward from the Lord. For in due time we shall reap, not failing, if while we have time we work good to all men, but especially to those who are of the household of the faith. Whence: "Forgive, and you shall be forgiven; give, and it shall be given to you."
**“IN THE SEVENTH”** — Because remission is by the sevenfold Spirit. Almost all the solemnities of the law are in the number seven. For the sabbath is on the seventh day; and Pentecost, when seven weeks are finished; the seventh year also is celebrated; and the jubilee follows after seven times seven years.
15.2:
**“Which shall be celebrated in this order.”** — the moral precepts
**“He to whom any thing is owing”** — within the Church
**“from his friend or neighbour”**
• in God
• "One is your Father, who is in heaven"; "one is Christ"
15.3:
**“Of the foreigner or stranger”** — who is of another religion
**“OF THE FOREIGNER AND”** — Though all are our neighbours, yet mercy is to be spent most of all on those who are members of Christ with us. For he that hath the substance of this world and spends it not on his needy brother, how doth the charity of God abide in him?
15.4: **“And there shall be no poor nor beggar at all”** — mystically, as if the money of the word should be dispensed largely to all
15.6:
**“Thou shalt lend”** — thou shalt lend the word of God
**“THOU SHALT LEND TO MANY NATIONS”** — Because thou shalt be richer than all nations. The Church too, which abounds in spiritual riches, herself teaches and has no need to be taught.
15.7:
**“If one of thy brethren that dwelleth within the gates of thy city in the land which the Lord thy God will give thee, come to poverty: thou shalt not harden thy heart,”** — as one unmerciful
**“nor close thy hand,”** — by avarice; but thou shalt stretch it out by mercy
15.9: **“BEWARE LEST PERHAPS”** — AUGUSTINE. The Seventy: "Attend to thyself, lest there be a hidden word of iniquity in thy heart, saying: The seventh year draweth nigh, the year of remission; and thy eye be malignant toward thy needy brother." Splendidly he called this a hidden word, since no one dares to say what he could think: that a loan is not to be given to the needy because the year of remission draws nigh; when God for mercy's sake commanded both, namely that it be lent when anyone is in need and that it be remitted in the year of remission. How will he remit mercifully, or how is it to be remitted, if he cruelly thinks that it is not to be given at the time when it is to be given?
15.12:
**“When thy brother a Hebrew man, or Hebrew woman is sold to thee,”**
• in faith
• "Come over to me, all ye that desire me"
**“and hath served thee six years,”** — by the perfection of the active life
**“in the seventh year”**
• not [the year] of the general remission, but whatever [year] fell seventh from the sale
• in eternal rest
**“thou shalt let him go free:”**
• WHEN [THY BROTHER] IS SOLD TO THEE, etc. ISIDORE. If a Hebrew boy has come into servitude, it is commanded that he serve six years and be freed in the seventh. If he will not, because of his wife and children, his ear will be bored and he will be a servant for ever. This is not said of the present world but of the future: because, serving in the six ages of this world, on the seventh day, that is, in the eternal sabbath, we are freed, if only we have willed to be free while in the world we serve sin. But if we will not, our ear will be bored in testimony of disobedience, and with our wife and children, whom we preferred to being freed, that is, with the flesh and its works, namely sins, we shall serve for ever.
• WHEN [THY BROTHER] IS SOLD TO THEE, etc. A Hebrew is a passer-over, one who strives, namely, toward the eternal fatherland and passes from vices to virtues, from earthly things to heavenly. If such a one sells himself to thee, that is, binds himself to thy teaching, thou shalt teach him to strive to work in the present life so that he may come to rest. This is: he shall serve thee six years. In the seventh year thou shalt let him go free, nor suffer him to go away empty; as promising him eternal rewards and true freedom in the other life. But if he say: "I will not go out", because he loves thee and thy house, that is, if he has done the good things he did not for eternal reward but for human praise, as one loving the present life, thou shalt bore his ear with an awl, that is, thou shalt prick his mind with the terror of judgment, at the door of the house; because the judgment will be at the going out of this life and the going in of the other; and he shall serve thee for ever, that is, thou shalt teach him that if he has loved the world more than God he is to be delivered over to eternal punishments.
• Lest Christian servants demand this of their masters, the Apostle commands servants to be subject to their masters, lest the doctrine of God be blasphemed. For it is understood to be said mystically, where the ear of him who refuses freedom is commanded to be bored with an awl.
**“GREGORY”** — Though the active life and the contemplative are [given] us by the grace of God, the one is of necessity, the other of will. For no one who knows God enters the kingdom without the active life, but many do without the contemplative. "If thou buy a Hebrew servant", etc. A Hebrew, that is, one passing over, is bought when each one who passes over in mind from the world is subjected to the service of God. He is commanded to serve six years, that in the seventh he may be freed for nothing. In six the perfection of the active life is expressed, in seven the contemplative. He serves six years and goes out free in the seventh, because through the active life perfectly carried through he passes to the freedom of the contemplative life. For nothing: because when we have done well we are unprofitable servants. As therefore the active life is of gift, so also is the contemplative. With what raiment he came in, with such let him go out: because it is necessary that each one persevere in what he has begun. For he passes well to the contemplative life who in the active has not changed the course of his intention. But some love to work well before they are joined to the service of God, others after they have come to his service. He then who had good working before was bought with a wife. He can pass to the contemplative life and yet not forsake the active; whence the wife goes out with him. For passing to contemplation he does not leave the affection of good work by which he may profit others. "The woman and her children shall be her master's." When the servant is bought, the master gives him a wife, when the preacher joins to good action him whom he has delivered to the Lord. For preachers are called masters; whence: "Dost thou know that the Lord will take away thy master from thee?" The wife bears sons and daughters when good action begets strong or tender fruits. This woman with her children remains to the master; the servant goes out with his raiment: because good action and its fruits are credited to the preacher, while he himself, with the intention of desire, goes out free to contemplation through grace. If the servant say [I love my master]: he loves his master when he guards the preacher's words with careful mind; he loves his wife and children, namely the active life and its fruits. The master brings him to the gods and sets him to the door and the posts, and bores his ear with an awl, that he may be a servant for ever: because the preacher imbues him with the sayings of the ancient fathers, at the door and posts of the tabernacle, that he may hear of the entry into the eternal tabernacle and acknowledge the terror of judgment, lest he seek glory from men for his good works. The ear is bored with an awl when his mind is pierced by the subtlety of the fear of God, so that, transfixed by the point of the word, it may ever attend to the entry of the kingdom, as though bored at the door and post of the tabernacle. He will be a servant in the world, that he may be free after the world. For now not only is the active life in servitude, but even contemplation does not obtain freedom of mind, because it sees the inmost rest in a dark manner.
15.16:
**“because he loveth thee,”** — the preacher
**“and thy house,”** — the Church
15.17:
**“Thou shalt take an awl,”** — the subtlety of divine fear
**“and bore through his ear”** — the disobedient mind
**“in the door of thy house,”** — at the entry of the Church, that he may be mindful of the heavenly tabernacle
**“and he shall serve thee”**
• by working well in the active life
• the present world
**“for ever: to thy womanservant”** — to the weaker and less learned
15.18:
**“Turn not away from them”** — thy solicitude
**“thy eyes when thou makest them”** — in contemplation
**“free:”** — free from the servitude of the active life
**“because according to the wages of a hireling”** — that they may receive eternal wages
**“he hath served thee six years:”**
• the preacher
• by rewarding
**“that the Lord thy God may bless thee in all the works”** — in good words or deeds
15.19:
**“Of the firstlings,”** — the first beginnings of good will and working
**“that come of thy herds and thy sheep, whatsoever is of the male sex”** — what is strong and manly
**“thou shalt sanctify”** — by attributing
**“the Lord thy God”** — not to thyself
**“Thou shalt not work with the firstling of a bullock,”**
• as if [to say]: do not allow a neophyte to teach in the Church
• in things to be preached
• while the good working of the first time is still weak
**“and thou shalt not shear the firstlings of thy sheep.”**
• that is: thou shalt not strip the firstlings of innocence that they may be seen and praised by men
• nothing is to be shown as an example except what is a pattern
**“OF THE FIRSTLINGS”** — He shows the difference among the Greeks between "firstlings" and "first-borne"; he shows also that where among the Latins Christ is called firstborn, among the Greeks he is called prototokos.
**“AUGUSTINE”** — OF THE FIRSTLINGS. Those are called firstborn which first open the womb and come forth at the first birth. But in Greek "prototoka" are those which belong to the first bearing of the female, as it were "first-borne" [protoparta], not "protogena", that is, first-begotten. Whence Christ is not called "monotokos" of the Father, but "monogenes", that is, only-begotten, namely the only one. But where in Latin he is called the firstborn from the dead, in Greek he is called "prototokos", not "protogenes", as though the Father had both begotten one equal to himself and brought forth a creature. For in that he is called the firstborn of every creature, that is, "prototokos", it can be understood according to the new creature, of which it is said: "If then any be in Christ a new creature"; of which he is the first, because he first so rose that he dies no more, which is promised at the end to the new creature which is in him. Yet it raises a difficulty that in Proverbs it is said: "Firstborn, I say to thee, son." For if the father speaks to the son, he calls the same one firstborn whom [he calls] only-begotten: [firstborn,] because we too are sons of God; but he is only-begotten because he alone is of the substance of the Father, equal and coeternal.
**“THOU SHALT SANCTIFY TO THE LORD THY GOD”** — Not to thyself, but to the giver of all, because every best gift is from above. But what is light in our thought, or spotted in our conversation, or lame in the progress of works, or blind through ignorance of mind, or deformed or feeble in any part, we ought not to sacrifice to God, that is, impute to him, but to ourselves.
**“THOU SHALT NOT WORK”** — GREGORY. To plough with the firstling of a bullock is to publish the beginnings of good conversation in the exercise of action. To shear the firstlings of the sheep is to strip the good things that are beginning of the hidden covering of reason. For if we begin to practise anything good and strong, we ought not quickly to show it. And what is simple and harmless ought not to be stripped of its veil. [Let them be kept] for the divine sacrifices alone, [lest,] mingled with carnal life, they become known too soon, and the mind, deceived when its good things are praised, fail to detect the evils that are in them.
15.20: **“In the sight of the Lord thy God”** — that is, thou shalt take care to please God alone with thy good work
15.21:
**“But if it have a blemish,”** — of crime
**“or be lame,”** — in the step of good work
**“or blind,”** — by ignorance
**“or in any part disfigured or feeble, it shall not be sacrificed”** — shall be imputed
**“the Lord thy God”**
• from whom is all good; but to thee, from whom is all evil
• BUT IF IT HAVE, etc. There are some works which, though they please God less, yet profit the neighbour; and if they cannot be offered to God, they can be eaten. For though they please God less, because the intention (which God looks on) is darkened, yet they help neighbours by example, like the roe and the hart. The roe goes by leaps; the hart is an enemy to the serpent, and leaping over rough and thorny places it climbs the mountains. And therefore they are taken in a good sense.

16.1:
**“the phase to the Lord thy God:”** — the Pasch
**“out of Egypt by night.”**
• out of the world
• The first month, namely, of the Hebrews, which among them is called Nisan, among the Greeks Xanthicus, among the Latins April, in which the paschal lamb was slain.
• HE BROUGHT THEE OUT, etc. Mystically. Let us too, freed from the Egypt of the world, having put on the new man, walk in newness of life, consecrating the firstfruits of good works and celebrating the phase, that is, the good passage, that leaving Egypt we may come to the land of promise.
**“OBSERVE THE MONTH”** — Because in it the handfuls of ears, that is, the firstfruits, were offered to the Lord by the priest.
16.2:
**“And thou shalt sacrifice”** — the lamb
**“the phase to the Lord thy God, of sheep,”** — of simplicity
**“and of oxen,”** — of working
**“in the place which the Lord thy God shall choose,”** — in the Church
**“that his name may dwell there.”** — AND OF OXEN, etc. He adds oxen, though he had commanded concerning the sheep only, which he ordered to be taken from the sheep and the kids or goats, because of Christ, who according to the flesh was from the just and from sinners. For he does not say "from the sheep or the goats", but "from the sheep and the goats", though properly a sheep is not understood [to come] from the goats; lest the Jews should say that a goat was to be understood. Why then are oxen added? Is it because of the other sacrifices which are to be offered in the days of unleavened bread?
16.3:
**“Thou shalt not eat with it leavened bread:”** — through the whole present life
**“seven days shalt thou eat without leaven, of affliction”** — in the vale of tears
**“LEAVENED BREAD”** — Corrupt doctrine or the old conversation; whence: "Let us feast with the unleavened bread, not with the old leaven", etc.
**“the bread, because thou camest out of Egypt in fear: that thou mayst remember the day of thy coming out of Egypt, all the days of thy life.”** — SEVEN DAYS, etc. Through the whole time of the present life: as they ate unleavened bread for seven days, so let us live purely and simply in the seven days of this life, in which daily the lamb is slain and the Pasch celebrated, if, being renewed, we keep nothing of the old corruption. For what else is leaven but the corruption of nature? For what is leavened departs from its natural sweetness and is corrupted by an adulterate sourness.
16.4:
**“No leaven shall be seen”** — [unclear in the edition: "alia statum"]
**“in all thy coasts for seven days, neither shall any of the flesh of that which was sacrificed the first day in the evening remain until morning.”**
• until the day, that is, [the end] of the world
• NO LEAVEN SHALL BE SEEN, etc. "Let us feast not with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness", etc. As if [to say]: leave the old man and put on the new.
• THERE SHALL NOT REMAIN, etc. In this life all the sacraments of the Lord's incarnation are to be searched out, and all his precepts are to be fulfilled, before the morning, that is, the end of the world, comes.
16.5:
**“in any one of thy cities,”** — namely, of the congregations of Jews, heretics and Gentiles
**“which the Lord thy God will give thee:”**
• will subject [to thee]
• THOU MAYST NOT IMMOLATE, etc. In one house the paschal lamb is eaten and in one place the phase is immolated, that is, the Catholic Church; outside it the Pasch is not rightly celebrated.
• He forbids celebrating the mysteries of Christ in the conventicles of heretics.
16.6:
**“But in the place which the Lord thy God shall choose,”**
• the Church
• by his grace
• "You have not chosen me, but I have chosen you"
**“at the going down”** — of Christ
**“of the sun,”** — the death
**“at which time thou camest out of Egypt.”** — out of the world
**“IN THE EVENING”** — In the last age of the world, when the true Sun set in the passion and loosed the Egyptian captivity, when Christ our Pasch was sacrificed.
16.7:
**“in the place”** — the Church
**“which the Lord thy God shall choose, and in the morning rising up thou shalt go into thy dwellings.”** — through the whole laborious life
**“THOU SHALT GO INTO THY DWELLINGS”** — When the service of the Lord is done, in the morning of the resurrection we shall pass into the eternal tabernacles, that we may rest from all labour, rejoicing over the blessing received (or: the retribution).
16.8:
**“Six days shalt thou eat unleavened bread:”**
• of sincerity and truth
• not with the old leaven, etc.
**“and on the seventh day,”** — God rested on the seventh day
**“because it is the assembly”** — of the saints
**“of the Lord thy God, thou shalt do no work.”** — servile
**“ON THE SEVENTH DAY”** — The eternal rest, which seven signifies because of the sabbath, where there is no labour, no reckoning of working.
16.9:
**“seven weeks”** — when they are finished the Holy Spirit is to come
**“Thou shalt number unto thee”** — this the Jews keep neither according to the letter nor according to the spirit
**“from that day, wherein thou didst put the sickle to the corn.”**
• SEVEN WEEKS, etc. In Leviticus more fully: you shall number therefore from the day after the sabbath seven full weeks, unto the day after the completion of the seventh week.
• We too celebrate Pentecost, that is, the coming of the Holy Spirit, who is the finger of God, by which the law was written on the tables.
**“AUGUSTINE”** — SEVEN WEEKS, etc. If this Pentecost was commanded to be observed by the whole people, are we to believe that all were commanded to put the sickle to the harvest on one day? But if each one observes this fiftieth day for himself, counting from the day on which he puts in the sickle, it is not one for the whole people. But that one is one, which is counted from the immolation of the Pasch to the day of the giving of the law on Sinai.
16.10:
**“And thou shalt celebrate the festival of weeks”** — on which you shall receive the Holy Spirit
**“the Lord thy God”** — to whom thou owest all things
**“a voluntary oblation”** — "God loveth a cheerful giver"
**“of thy hand,”** — of thy own working
**“which thou shalt offer according to the blessing of the Lord thy God.”** — the multiplying of good works
16.11:
**“And thou shalt feast”** — with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth
**“before the Lord thy God,”** — well pleasing
**“thou, and thy son, and thy daughter, and thy manservant,”** — there is no respect of persons with God
16.12: **“And thou shalt remember that thou wast a servant in Egypt: and thou shalt keep and do the things that are commanded.”** — having here no abiding city
16.13:
**“Thou shalt celebrate”** — thou with thine
**“seven days, when thou hast gathered in thy fruit of the barnfloor and of the winepress.”**
• THE SOLEMNITY, etc. He who uses the present world as a tabernacle can keep festival and rejoice in it because of the expectation of the future. For if the earthly house of this habitation be dissolved, he will have a house not made with hands in heaven.
• WHEN THOU HAST GATHERED, etc. It signifies that, when the perfection of all goods is consummated and many virtues are gathered, one must rejoice and exult with friends. When each one who here was generous in giving shall exult over the retribution received, then truly the solemnity of tabernacles will be kept, not of changeable ones but of eternal; whence: "that they may receive you into everlasting dwellings."
16.14:
**“And thou shalt make merry in thy festival time,”** — small and great are there
**“thou, thy son, and thy daughter, thy manservant,”** — and the servant free from his master
**“that are within thy gates.”** — of the Church
16.15: **“in all thy fruits,”** — in the fruits of the virtues
16.16:
**“Three”** — in the faith of the Trinity
**“times in a year”** — pleasing through good works
**“shall all thy males appear before the Lord thy God in the place which he shall choose: in the feast of unleavened bread, in the feast of weeks, and in the feast of tabernacles.”** — in the judgment
**“No one shall appear with his hands empty before the Lord:”**
• it is a fearful thing to fall into his hands
• THY MALES. Not female. For nothing soft and fragile and weak ought to be in our conversation; God requires of us all things strong. But if in the faith of the Trinity, Father and Son and Holy Spirit, with regard to the eternal reward, we toil in good works in the time of the present life, we set a male in the sight of the Lord.
**“NO ONE SHALL APPEAR”** — AUGUSTINE. As if he said: he who has not provided, by doing well, the reward of the life to be merited will appear empty in the sight of the Lord; whence: "But coming they shall come with joyfulness, carrying their sheaves." For they come carrying their sheaves to the examination of judgment who show in themselves the right works by which they merit life.
16.17:
**“But shall offer”** — the fruit of labour
**“every one according to what he hath,”** — he gives as much as he can
**“according to the blessing of the Lord his God, which he shall give him.”** — every best gift is from above
16.18:
**“Judges”** — of the Church
**“and magistrates”** — unmoveable
**“thou shalt appoint in all thy gates,”** — the sayings of the Apostles and Prophets
**“which the Lord thy God shall give thee, in all thy tribes: that they may judge the people with just judgment,”** — of the divine law
**“IN ALL THY GATES”** — That those coming from every side may find at once at the entry men ready, from whom they may receive just judgments.
16.19:
**“And not to either part”** — either by prayer or by price
**“go aside. Thou shalt not accept person nor gifts: for gifts blind the eyes of the wise,”** — THE EYES OF THE WISE, etc. Among men, not with God; to whom it is said: "Woe to you that are wise in your own eyes."
**“and change the words of the just.”**
• not harsher than is fair, nor slacker
• "There is a way which seemeth just to a man", etc. "You are they who justify yourselves before men."
16.20:
**“Thou shalt follow justly after that which is just:”**
• elsewhere: thou shalt carry out
• THOU SHALT FOLLOW JUSTLY AFTER THAT WHICH IS JUST. GREGORY. He carries out unjustly what is just who is stirred to the defence of justice not by zeal for virtue but by love of temporal reward, and does not fear to sell the justice he professes. To carry out the just justly, then, is in asserting justice to seek justice itself.
**“that thou mayst live”** — for ever; and elsewhere
**“and possess the land,”** — of the living
**“which the Lord thy God shall give thee.”**
• in the future
• freely; whence: "But the grace of God, life everlasting"
16.21:
**“Thou shalt plant no grove,”** — the beautiful but empty eloquence of the philosophers
**“nor any tree near the altar”** — the mystery of the Passion or of the Incarnation of Christ; as if [to say]: thou shalt not dispute of the mysteries of Christ according to the arguments of worldly wisdom
**“THOU SHALT PLANT NO”** — He cuts off the occasion of idolatry. For the Gentiles used to sacrifice in groves and adore statues in shrines.
**“GROVE”** — ISIDORE. A grove is leafy trees, unfruitful, planted for the delight of the sight alone: [that is,] the Gentiles, who compose their reasoning with the beauty of words, not to turn [men] from vices but to delight them. But we, around the altar of God, that is, the Lord's faith, compose nothing unfruitful in words, nothing enticing, but preach the pure knowledge of truth. Whence: "Not in the persuasive words of human wisdom, but in the showing of the Spirit and of power."
**“NEAR THE ALTAR”** — Mystically. He forbids setting up near the altar of faith the unfruitfulness of idle speech or of depraved works and the darkness of ignorance; nor does he permit the fiction of falsehood or error to be joined to Catholic truth.

17.1:
**“an ox,”** — one who works strongly
**“or a sheep,”** — one who is simple
**“wherein there is blemish,”** — any sin which fouls the other goods
17.2:
**“any of thy gates,”** — the Church, [whose gates] lead to heaven
**“which the Lord thy God shall give thee, man or woman that do evil in the sight of the Lord thy God, and transgress”** — even if it be hidden from men
**“his covenant,”** — the law
**“WHEN THERE SHALL BE FOUND”** — The law most of all detests error and idolatry. For the greatest crime is to spend the honour of the Creator on the creature; which the Gentiles do, or bad Catholics, who, though they do not depart from the Church, are found rather to serve the devil through various vices than to fight for God through good things. These he commands to be overwhelmed with stones, whom he foresaw to be damned by an irrevocable sentence.
17.3:
**“So as to go”** — departing from God
**“and serve strange gods, and adore them, the sun and the moon, and all the host of heaven, which I have not commanded:”** — which fights for the Creator
17.4: **“And this is told thee, and hearing it thou hast inquired diligently,”** — doing nothing without discernment
17.5:
**“Thou shalt bring forth the man or the woman, who have committed that most wicked thing, to the gates of thy city,”** — where judgments are held, lest anyone be condemned without judgment
**“and they shall be stoned.”** — by a strict sentence
17.6:
**“By the mouth of two or three witnesses shall he die”** — the testimony of one is received neither by the laws nor by the canons
**“BY THE MOUTH OF TWO OR THREE WITNESSES”** — By the attestation, namely, of the Law, the Prophets and the Gospel; according to that: "The word that I have spoken, the same shall judge him in the last day." In the title of the cross also three tongues bear witness that Christ is king of the Jews: Hebrew, Greek and Latin.
**“that is to be slain. Let no man be put to death, when only one beareth witness against him.”**
• LET NO MAN BE PUT TO DEATH, etc. So great is the concord of the Old and New Testament that neither [stands] without the other.
• In every judgment the authority of divine Scripture is first to be sought.
17.7:
**“The hands of the witnesses”** — not of the witness
**“shall be first upon him to kill him, and afterwards the hands of the rest of the people:”** — that is, that the rest may be afraid
17.8:
**“If [there be] a hard”** — this too is to be kept in the Church
**“and doubtful matter in judgment, if thou perceive, between blood and blood, cause and cause, leprosy and not leprosy: and of the judges within thy gates”** — in thy city
**“thou see the words do vary:”** — note: he grants the faculty of appealing
**“to the place, which the Lord thy God shall choose.”**
• the Church
• IF [THERE BE] A HARD, etc. He instructs the priests of the Church of God to conduct ecclesiastical judgments reverently according to the power given them by God and to discern justly, not at their own pleasure but according to the decree of the law, lest by respecting persons they change the sentence.
17.9:
**“And thou shalt come to the priests of the Levitical race,”** — the lawful ones, namely
**“and to the judge,”** — the high priest
**“that shall be at that time: and thou shalt ask of them, and they shall shew thee the truth of the judgment.”** — not declining to one side
17.10:
**“And thou shalt do”** — by obeying
**“whatsoever they shall say, that preside in the place, which the Lord shall choose, and what they shall teach thee,”** — "Obey your prelates"
17.11: **“ACCORDING TO HIS LAW”** — Note: it is not said to thee that thou shouldst obey unless they teach according to the law; whence: "The scribes and the Pharisees have sitten on the chair of Moses."
17.12:
**“But he that will be proud, and refuse to obey the commandment of the priest, who ministereth at that time to the Lord thy God, and the decree of the judge, that man shall die, and thou shalt take away the evil”** — the example of evil
**“from the midst of Israel:”** — THE COMMANDMENT OF THE PRIEST, WHO, etc. Of Christ, who is a priest for ever according to the order of Melchisedech, who appointed vicars in his place, to whom he says: "He that heareth you heareth me; and he that despiseth you despiseth me", etc. Rightly then he undergoes the sentence of damnation who despises the power of the Godhead.
17.13:
**“And all the people hearing it”** — the sentence
**“shall fear, that no one afterwards swell with pride.”**
• the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom
• when he is punished
17.14:
**“When thou art come into the land,”** — of promise
**“which the Lord thy God will give thee, and possessest it, and dwellest in it, and shalt say:”** — thou, not I
**“I will set a king over me,”** — not God, but a man
**“as all nations have that are round about:”**
• "The wicked walk round about"
• the Gentiles, who are born, yet not reborn
• WHEN THOU ART COME, etc. AUGUSTINE. It may be asked why the people displeased God when it desired a king, since here it is found to be permitted. But it is to be understood that it was rightly [judged] not to be according to the will of God, who did not command this to be done but permitted it to those who desired it. Yet he commanded that it should not be a foreigner, but a brother from the same people, a native, not one of another race. And where he says "Thou mayst not", it is to be understood: "you ought not".
• I WILL SET, etc. As [it is] for the inhabitants of the earth: the inhabitants of the earth set up a king for themselves against the will of God.
17.15:
**“him”** — he permits it, does not command it
**“Thou shalt set whom the Lord thy God”** — by some judgment, as Saul
**“shall choose”** — by canonical election
**“out of the number of thy brethren.”** — not from a foreign sect
**“Thou mayst not”** — that is, thou oughtest not
**“make a man of another nation king,”** — a foreigner
**“that is not thy brother.”** — by kinship
17.16:
**“And when he is made king, he shall not multiply horses to himself,”**
• the pomp and ambition of the world
• "Vain is the horse for safety"
**“nor lead back”** — by example, by domination, by persuasion
**“the people”** — varying and changeable
**“into Egypt,”** — the appetite of the world
**“being lifted up with the number of his horsemen,”**
• by manifold pride and human or worldly power
• "like the dust which the wind driveth from the face of the earth"
**“especially since the Lord hath commanded you to return no more the same way.”** — but by another way, understood, return into your country
17.17:
**“He shall not have”** — cares
**“many wives,”** — even if several
**“that may allure his mind,”** — it seems to touch foreign wives
**“nor of silver and gold”** — he rebukes avarice
**“NOR OF SILVER AND”** — "Lay not up to yourselves treasures on earth."
**“immense sums.”**
• beyond the measure of necessity
• not for beasts of burden
• sinking him that carries them into hell
**“HE SHALL NOT HAVE WIVES”** — AUGUSTINE. It is manifest that Solomon transgressed this precept; but David had several and did not pass over the precept. For it was permitted to have several, not very many, such as allure the mind to multiply [them]. But when it is added, "that his heart be not lifted up", it seems that to have foreign wives was forbidden. Yet the multiplying of wives is forbidden generally; it was permitted to the king to have several, but not to multiply them, lest by multiplying he come to foreign women.
17.18:
**“But after he is raised”** — rest, gravity, maturity belong to kings
**“to the throne of his kingdom, he shall copy out to himself the Deuteronomy of this law”** — not of another's [law]
**“in a volume, taking the copy of the priests of the Levitical tribe,”** — where nothing is darkened, nothing corrupted
17.19:
**“And he shall have it with him, and shall read it all the days of his life,”** — use makes the master
**“that he may learn to fear the Lord his God,”**
• by reading
• with chaste fear; "the fear of the Lord is holy, enduring for ever and ever"
**“AND SHALL READ IT”** — Note with what assiduity priests ought to read, when kings read assiduously.
**“and keep his words and ceremonies, that are commanded in the law;”** — Reading itself is light [and] life; whence: "The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life."
17.20:
**“And that his heart be not lifted up”** — lest he swell in heart
**“with pride”** — which follows power
**“over his brethren,”** — let him [not] decline through friendship or hatred or any occasion, but rule with a rod of iron
**“nor decline to the right or to the left,”** — bodily and spiritually
**“that he and his sons may reign a long time”** — in the flesh or by imitation
**“OVER HIS BRETHREN”** — As if he says that he is a brother. We all have one Father, God, to whom we say: "Our Father who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name."
**“OVER ISRAEL”** — It is a blessing to reign over Israel, that is, by reigning to make Israel, namely, those who see God.

18.1:
**“The priests and Levites shall not have,”** — "No man, being a soldier to God, entangleth himself with secular businesses"
**“and all that are of the same tribe, part nor inheritance with the rest of Israel, because they shall eat the sacrifices of the Lord, and his oblations,”**
• let them not be anxious about food or clothing
• as if one should ask: whence then shall they live?
• THE PRIESTS SHALL NOT HAVE, etc. Both in the Old and in the New Testament the ministers of the altar are commanded to live from oblations and tithes, and it is not granted them to dwell upon acquiring earthly possessions. Whence: "Do not possess gold nor silver", etc.; and a little after: "For the workman is worthy of his meat"; and elsewhere: "They that serve the altar partake with the altar." For it is not fitting that those who ought always to serve the altar in the divine office, whose inheritance is God, should gape after earthly gain. What then can be lacking to him who has him who has all things?
18.2:
**“And they shall receive nothing else of the possession of their brethren: for the Lord”** — who possesses all things
**“himself is their inheritance, as he hath said to them.”** — that with so great a surety they may be secure
**“THEIR INHERITANCE”** — For good working, so that what he has conceived in mind he shows in work; whence: "Jesus began to do and to teach."
18.3:
**“THEY SHALL GIVE TO THE PRIEST”** — Because we ought devoutly to share with our teachers in bodily comforts and spiritual gains. Whence: "Let him that is instructed in the word communicate to him that instructeth him, in all good things."
**“THE MAW”** — The belly, the receptacle of foods, [signifies] all the labours of men and the momentary allurements of the gullet, whose end he condemns, and he shows to minds consecrated to God that all we devour is cast into the privy. Whence: "Meat for the belly, and the belly for the meats; but God shall destroy both it and them."
18.4: **“THE FIRSTFRUITS”** — The firstfruits of the fruits: the husbandman that laboureth must first partake of the fruits.
18.5: **“For the Lord thy God hath chosen him of all thy tribes, to stand and to minister to the name of the Lord thy God, him and his sons for ever.”** — "firm in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God"
18.6: **“IF [A LEVITE] GO OUT”** — As it were he deserts city and house who serves God freely and sets forth the Gospel without charge.
18.7:
**“He shall minister in the name of his God, as all his brethren”** — his kinsmen
**“the Levites do, that shall stand”** — firmly
**“at that time before the Lord.”** — well pleasing
18.8:
**“He shall receive the same portion of food”** — "They that serve the altar partake with the altar"
**“BESIDES THAT WHICH”** — GREGORY. The Seventy: "Besides the sale which is according to family." What sale he means is obscure, unless perhaps because he commanded the tithes and firstborn to be sold by those who dwelt far off, lest they be forced to carry many things to the place of the invocation of the Lord or drive cattle, so that they might be bought there afresh with the price. And he had ordered that the Levite who dwelt in that city from which those tithes and firstborn were due should have a part there. And therefore he said that this was due to the Levite according to family, because by the succession which passes from the parents, what was shown to the parents must be kept toward him.
18.9: **“WHEN THOU ART COME”** — AUGUSTINE. Since the inspections of portents are forbidden, it is to be asked how the portents which are forbidden to be inspected are distinguished from those which are given divinely, so that it ought to be said what they signify; such as the miracles found in the Scriptures signifying what pertains to the rule of faith: as the fleece dry on the floor that was rained on, or rained on in the dry, or the rod of Aaron that flowered and bore nuts, and the like. For as the divinations which he forbids in what follows are distinguished from the divinations of the prophets, so are the inspections of prodigies from the significations of miracles.
18.10:
**“SOOTHSAYERS”** — Those who go round altars with nefarious prayers and seek divination in the entrails of animals.
**“OMENS”** — As it were "avigeria", which are carried on in the voices of birds; or "avigarria", from the chattering of birds.
18.11: **“PYTHONIC SPIRITS”** — Ventriloquists, from whose belly demons speak; so called from Pythius, that is, Apollo, whom they believed to be the god of divination.
18.12: **“For the Lord abhorreth all these things, and for these abominations he will destroy them”** — beware lest he destroy thee likewise
18.13:
**“Thou shalt be perfect,”**
• in human measure
• "Be you perfect, as also your heavenly Father"
**“and without spot”** — of crime
**“with the Lord thy God.”** — "With the holy thou wilt be holy"
18.14: **“thou shalt possess,”** — or: you shall possess
18.15:
**“a prophet of thy nation”** — Josue, or the others following
**“and of thy brethren like unto me:”** — a true man
18.18:
**“I will raise up a prophet”** — Christ
**“to them out of the midst of their brethren”** — of the seed of David
**“like to thee: and I will put my words in his mouth,”** — who came not to destroy the law but to fulfil it
**“I WILL RAISE THEM UP A PROPHET”** — Though it can be taken historically of the prophets who after Moses were filled with the Spirit of God among the people of Israel, yet it is better taken of the Lord of the prophets, of whom the crowds that he had filled said: "This is of a truth the prophet that is to come into the world"; and elsewhere: "A great prophet is risen up among us."
18.19: **“And he that will not hear his words, which he shall speak in my name, I will be the revenger.”** — avenging with perpetual punishment
18.20:
**“But the prophet,”** — the false [prophet]
**“who with pride”** — of vainglory
**“being corrupted shall speak in my name”** — that he may be believed
**“things that I”** — in whose name he speaks
**“did not command him to say, or in the name of other gods,”** — elsewhere: of strange [gods]
18.21:
**“And if in silent thought thou answer: How shall I know the word”** — that I may discern
**“that the Lord hath not spoken?”** — through him

19.2:
**“three cities”** — that thou mayst stand out
**“Thou shalt separate to thee”** — an example to others
**“THREE CITIES”** — Faith, hope and charity, to which all penitents ought to flee.
**“in the midst of the land, which the Lord thy God will give thee in possession,”** — Moses appointed three cities of refuge beyond the Jordan for slayers who did not commit homicide willingly; he commands three others to be separated on this side of the Jordan. Mystically he intimates that before the reception of baptism he who wishes to be saved from sin and freed from spiritual enemies must confess the faith of the Holy Trinity with a sincere mind, and after baptism work manfully in faith, hope and charity. And so, living religiously in the world, which was made in the number six, after the perfection of good works he awaits eternal rest in the sabbath-keeping.
19.3:
**“Paving diligently the way: and thou shalt divide the whole province of thy land equally into three parts:”** — by preaching the faith of the Trinity equally to all
**“AND EQUALLY INTO THREE”** — That he who is to be saved may escape more easily. Let preachers too, by word and example, take care to counsel sinners, and equally in the whole land of the Church impart the faith of the Trinity to all, that they may know that the way of truth and the gate of faith lie open to them, and that they are deservedly to be damned if they will not enter.
19.5:
**“But to have gone with him simply to the wood”** — of sins
**“to hew wood,”**
• the twisted and unfruitful vices
• with the axe of correction
**“and in cutting down the wood the axe”** — rebuke
**“slipped out of his hand,”** — the power or working of the one hewing
**“and the iron slipping”** — a harsher word
**“from the handle”** — [from] moderation
**“struck his friend, and killed him: he”**
• by an insult uttered
• into despair
• has cast [him] out of the spirit of charity
**“to one”** — in the unity of the sacrament
**“of the cities aforesaid,”**
• of faith, hope and charity
• by repenting
**“BUT TO HAVE GONE WITH”** — By an example he shows what kind of slayer is to be saved.
**“GREGORY”** — We go to the wood with a friend whenever we turn with a neighbour to examine his faults; and we hew wood simply when with pious intention we cut away the vices of offenders. The axe flies from the hand when correction draws itself into harshness; the iron leaps from the handle when in correction the speech goes forth too harsh. He kills his friend by striking him who by an uttered insult slays his hearer from the spirit of love; for the mind of the one corrected breaks out thence into hatred. But let him who incautiously strikes the wood and kills his neighbour flee to the three cities that he may live: because if, turned to penitence, he is hidden under hope, faith and charity, he is not held guilty of homicide. And when the kinsman of the slain finds him, he will not kill him: because when Christ comes, who joined himself to us by sharing our nature, he will not exact vengeance from him whom faith, hope and charity hide under his pardon. For a fault is more quickly forgiven that is not committed with malice.
**“AMBROSE”** — In the book On Flight from the World: It is plain that it was fittingly provided, because the Levites are fugitives from this world, that they may please God. Hence it was said to Abraham, "Go forth out of thy country", etc., who had the Levites in his loins; and the Lord is [the portion] of the Levites. This is what he says to the Apostles: "If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me." This is the true flight of the priest: the renouncing of his household, that he who longs to serve God may deny himself to his own. Rightly then the ordinance of the eternal law commends fugitives to fugitives, that those who have forgotten this world may receive those who, condemning their sins and works, look for the forgetting of their former life and desire to abolish the worldly things they have done. There is also another reason: because the Levites are ministers of God. And therefore their cities are assigned by the laws to fleeing slayers, because to them belongs the right of executing the divine commands concerning those who have committed a mortal crime. Hence the Apostle, as a Levite: "To deliver", he says, "such a one to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved." Struck by the Levitical sword, let the sense of the flesh die, that your soul may live.
19.6:
**“Lest perhaps”**
• or: perhaps
• it can quickly happen
**“the next kinsman”** — Christ
**“of him whose blood was shed, pushed on by his grief should pursue, and apprehend him, if the way be too long, and take away the life”** — in the day of judgment, or in the present
**“of him who is not guilty of death,”**
• because he did not kill with malice
• as if [to say]: he killed not by design but by chance
19.7:
**“Therefore I command thee,”** — faith, hope and charity
**“that thou separate three cities at equal distance one from another.”** — as much as each one believes, so much he hopes; and as much as he hopes, so much he loves
19.9:
**“(Yet so, if thou keep his commandments, and do the things which I command thee this day, that thou love the Lord thy God, and walk in his ways at all times) thou shalt add to thee other three cities, and shalt double the number of the three cities aforesaid:”**
• AND THOU SHALT ADD TO THEE THREE, etc. In the book of Jesus Nave six cities of refuge are appointed for such slayers: Cedes in Galilee of mount Nephtali; Sichem in mount Ephraim; and Cariatharbe, which is Hebron; and beyond the Jordan, Bosor of the tribe of Ruben; and Ramoth in Galaad of the tribe of Gad; and Gaulon in Basan of the tribe of Manasses.
• These three cities beyond the Jordan are given for refuge to the more perfect prudence: that first we may flee guilt by conforming the disposition of the mind to the image of God. For so we were created, God saying: "Let us make man to our image and likeness." This then is the first law of that city. Then, if through the frailty of the flesh and the allurements of the world we cannot so form our mind, let us lighten sin by reverence for the fatherly generation and by the devotion of offspring. Charity covers a multitude of sins. He then who could not be to the image of God, let him be to the fulness of charity. That city shuts out guilt; this one looses it. This, finally, is the law of the second city: "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with thy whole soul." But if again you are straitened, and there are little ones who cannot receive the abundance of charity and grace, thou hast the third city, that the dread of the divine piety may make thee sober and fear may bend thee. And this is the third law: "Thou shalt adore the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve." These then are the chief virtues, and therefore they are set beyond the Jordan, [virtues] of few, not of many: that thou mayst express [God] as an image its archetype, love [him] as a son his father, adore [him] as a subject his king. But [as for] those who have crossed the Jordan (and the Jordan is called their descent): those, then, who have descended from those higher virtues to these lower things, that is, in whom integrity, charity, humility have wavered, have refuges proper to man to seek, so that those who are liable to faults and bent by vices not voluntary may hope that the Lord can be reconciled to them, and may ask pardon; may hope that they can be corrected if they follow the precepts of the heavenly sacraments, by which we are either formed to innocence or recalled from guilt. These then are the following cities within the Jordan: that we may make God propitious to us, follow what he commands, avoid what he forbids. Let there be, then, the zeal of propitiating the Godhead, the obedience of following the precept, the caution against forbidden transgression; by which we may venerate the propitiating mercy of God and his admonishing providence, either by the obedience of things commanded or by declining things forbidden.
**“LIKEWISE”** — AMBROSE. Now the refuges of the six cities are these: that the first city is the knowledge of the Word, and the form of living according to his image. For whoever has entered that knowledge is clean from punishment, according as God also says: "Now you are clean by reason of the word which I have spoken to you"; and elsewhere: "This is eternal life, that they may know thee, the only true God, and him whom thou hast sent", that is, Christ. This city is as it were a metropolis, to which the other five cities of the Levites are subject, so that by the number by which the world was formed, by the same number a remedy may be provided against worldly vices and the shipwrecks of this world. The second city and the second remedy is that he who cannot foretaste the knowledge of that good, and is slower either in wit or in the grasp of faith (since one strives to the height of knowledge with swift vigour of mind and sharpness of wit), may at least consider the works of the Lord, and from the things that are made contemplate the author of so great a work: how from these goods which are in the constitution of this creation (for they are very good, as the Lord said) that highest and eternal good may be grasped. What order of things, what discipline, what glory! Is not one provoked by these (however slow his wit) to love his author? For if we love the parents who begot us, how much more ought we to love the creator of our parents and our own author! Therefore the working power of God, even if it is not seen, is yet reckoned from his works, and his works betray the worker, that he may be understood who is not comprehended. Whence the Lord too: "Though you will not believe me, believe the works." These things too, then, are good, that we may be the more desirous of him who is seen to have bestowed on us so great a beauty of this fabric. The third order, that of the third city, is the contemplation of the royal power, that we may be subject to the king through fear, if we do not defer [to him] as to a parent. For through fear of the ruler he who is ungrateful for salvation often becomes obedient to power, so that he who would not and could not acknowledge the grace of piety may acknowledge the necessity of sobriety. Necessity therefore corrects him whom piety ought to have called forth.
19.10:
**“That blood may not be shed,”** — of one who sins unknowingly
**“innocent, in the midst of the land which the Lord thy God will give thee to possess, lest thou be guilty of blood.”** — if thou hast furnished refuge
19.11:
**“But if any man hating his neighbour,”** — "Whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer"
**“lie in wait”** — maliciously
**“and strike him,”** — in body or in soul
**“and he die, and he flee to one of the cities aforesaid,”**
• BUT IF ANY MAN, etc. He who strikes someone with malice and leads him into the death of the soul is guilty of eternal death. Whence: "He that shall scandalize one of these little ones that believe in me", etc.; and elsewhere: "Whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer, and hath not eternal life." Such a one is torn from the altar as unworthy of the Lord's sacraments, and does not merit pardon except through condign penance. But he who kills not willingly has cities of refuge, namely the Catholic Church, where, restraining himself in the strait of penance, let him strive in good works through all the time of the present life; and if he has set his hope on the death of the high priest, namely his Redeemer, he will at length merit to be saved.
• He who keeps brotherly hatred in his heart cannot do fruitful penance nor make God favourable to him.
19.12:
**“The ancients of his city shall send, and take him out of the place of refuge,”** — from the participation of the altar
**“and shall deliver him into the hand of the kinsman”** — of Christ
**“of him whose blood was shed, and he shall die.”** — by eternal death
19.13: **“Thou shalt not pity him, and thou shalt take away the innocent blood”** — the guilt of innocent blood
19.14: **“THOU SHALT NOT TAKE NOR REMOVE”** — Allegorically. Whence: "Pass not beyond the ancient bounds which thy fathers have set", that is, the rules and definitions of living of the fathers who went before.
19.15: **“ONE WITNESS SHALL NOT RISE UP”** — This we ought to keep both historically and against the impious or heretics when we need the testimonies of the Scriptures: we bring two witnesses, that is, the Old and the New Testament, or three, that is, the Gospel, the Prophets, the Apostle; and so the word stands.
19.21:
**“Thou shalt not pity him, but shalt require life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand,”** — knowledge, because he took knowledge from his brother
**“foot”** — the step, or the will
**“LIFE FOR”** — For he who made a soul err is not worthy of pardon.
**“TOOTH FOR TOOTH”** — The power of words. For teeth signify words, according to that: "The sons of men, whose teeth are weapons", etc.; and elsewhere: "His teeth whiter than milk", that is, than the law.
**“HAND FOR HAND”** — Working: so that those things, namely, whether useful or harmful, which he perverted in another [are required of him].

20.1:
**“If thou go out to war”** — the errors of Gentiles or heretics
**“against thy enemies, and see horsemen and chariots, and the numbers of the enemy's army greater than thine, thou shalt not fear them: because the Lord thy God is with thee, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt.”** — BECAUSE THE LORD YOUR GOD IN THE MIDST, etc. Mystically. AUGUSTINE. The Seventy: "Because the Lord your God shall go before with you, he shall fight together with you against your enemies, and shall save you." See how in spiritual conflicts also the help of God is to be hoped for and sought, not that we may do nothing, but that, being helped, we may work together [with him]. For he says: "He shall fight with you", to show that they too would act.
20.2:
**“And when the battle is now at hand, shall stand”** — spiritual or bodily
**“the priest”** — firm, undaunted, one who ought to strengthen [others] in the spiritual war
**“before the army,”** — the first to fight, for himself and for others
**“and shall speak to the people in this manner:”** — that is to be proved
20.3:
**“Hear, O Israel, you this day”** — in the present life
**“against your enemies”** — visible and invisible
**“join battle, let not your heart be dismayed,”** — "Fear ye not them that kill the body, and are not able to kill the soul"
20.4:
**“Because the Lord your God”** — stronger than they
**“in the midst of you”** — common to all
**“is, and for you”** — who are to be delivered
**“against your enemies”**
• demons or vices
• he will give the strength and the will to fight
20.5:
**“the captains”** — the greater doctors
**“also through every band”** — of those subject [to them]
**“that hath built”** — with virtues
**“a new house,”** — the body
**“and hath not dedicated it?”** — that is, has not brought the virtues to perfection
**“WHAT MAN IS THERE, THAT HATH BUILT A HOUSE”** — AUGUSTINE. He is not better in war who has already dedicated his buildings, or has drunk of his new vineyard, or has married his bride. But because human affection is held by these things, these things are said to those going forth to war, so that he who is affected by them may show himself when he turns back, lest on account of these things he act less bravely, fearing to die before he accomplishes them. For as far as the woman is concerned, it is better that she marry another untouched than as a widow; but these things were instituted for the testing of their spirits.
20.6:
**“What man is there, that hath planted a vineyard,”** — the fervour of a new conversation
**“and hath not as yet made it to be common,”** — by bringing it forth as an example to others
20.7:
