**“What man is there”** — still held, namely, by the cares of the world
**“let him go,”** — if he is held by affection for it
**“and return”** — from the purpose of contemplation
**“to his house, lest he die in the war,”** — let him not go forward to the spiritual war, lest he act less bravely
20.8:
**“What man is there that is fearful”** — "A double minded man is inconstant in all his ways"
**“and return to his house,”**
• from the purpose of contemplation
• the custom of his former life
**“lest he make to fear”** — if he should fail
**“the hearts of his brethren,”** — who wish to begin the same
**“as he himself is possessed with fear.”**
• WHAT MAN IS THERE THAT IS FEARFUL, etc. He teaches that no one can take up the profession of contemplation or of spiritual warfare who still fears to be stripped of earthly works, lest through weakness of mind he turn back and by his example call others back and by his terror weaken them. Let them return to their house who are of a double heart, who cannot fight the battles of the Lord. For a double minded man is inconstant in all his ways. Let such not even take up the beginning of renunciation: it is better for them to remain in the active life than, pursuing contemplation tepidly, to involve themselves in greater danger. The same is said to him who has married a wife, who has planted a vineyard, that is, the offshoots of children; for the servant of a wife cannot serve contemplation, nor can he attain the pursuit of contemplation who is held in the delight of the flesh. For no man, being a soldier to God, entangleth himself with secular businesses, that he may please him to whom he hath engaged himself.
• It is better to avoid a profession, or persecution, than to succumb in it. Nor ought anyone to come to disputation against heretics unless he is learned and perfect, lest, being overcome, he scandalize others.
20.9:
**“And when the captains of the army shall hold their peace, and have made an end of speaking, every man shall prepare their bands to fight.”**
• the people subject [to him]
• by exhorting
20.10:
**“If at any time thou come to fight against a city,”** — the conventicles of heretics, or the world, or the outward man, which are adverse to the spirit
**“thou shalt offer”** — by preaching
**“it first peace.”**
• "Peace be to this house"
• the word of peace, coming into the fellowship of faith
• Christ, our peace, who hath made both one
20.11:
**“If they receive it, and open to thee”** — willingly
**“the gates,”**
• the senses and affections
• of the heart, that it may receive Christ as guest
**“all the people that are therein, shall be saved,”**
• from death
• by obeying
• the preacher
• of good works and the fulfilment of the precepts
20.12:
**“But if a covenant”** — of the peace of faith
**“they will not make, and shall begin war against thee,”** — of disputation
**“thou shalt besiege it.”** — with the testimonies of Scripture
20.13:
**“And when the Lord thy God shall deliver”** — by whose help thou overcomest
**“it”** — conquered
**“into thy hands,”** — power
**“thou shalt slay all”** — those strong in error, resisting the faith
**“that are therein of the male sex,”** — with the vigour of resisting
**“with the edge of the sword,”** — which is the word of God
20.14:
**“Excepting women and children, cattle”** — namely, those who are easily converted by preaching and are quiet and do not resist the truth
**“and other things, that are in the city. And all the prey”** — every good that we do we ought to turn to the profit of the brethren
**“to the army”** — to the soldiers of Christ
**“thou shalt divide, and thou shalt eat”**
• thou shalt be filled when thy glory, or God's, shall appear
• those whom thou hast subjected to God
**“the Lord thy God”** — not thy own strength
20.15: **“So shalt thou do to all cities that are at a great distance from thee,”** — of a different religion
20.16:
**“But of those cities”** — the Catholic churches
**“NONE AT ALL”** — No vice is to be spared in our conversation, lest before the eyes of the Lord we appear corrupted and abominable by pleasures, and the enemies, exulting over our ruin, say: "Well done, well done, to our mind: we will swallow him up."
20.19:
**“When thou hast besieged a city”** — the false fortification of the philosophers
**“a long time, and with bulwarks”** — of the Scriptures
**“hath compassed it to take it, thou shalt not cut down the trees”**
• by judging without discernment; whence: "Instruct such a one in the spirit of meekness"
• men apt in the fruits of knowledge and virtues
• physics, ethics, logic, from which comes much profit
**“that may be eaten of, neither with axes”** — with the edge of a sharper judgment
**“a tree,”** — fruitful
20.20:
**“But if there be any trees”** — fictions and voluptuous songs
**“that are not fruitful, but wild,”** — of a rustic and disordered sense
**“and fit for other uses, cut them down, and make engines,”**
• thou shalt pluck [them] out from wicked study; whence: "with such a one not so much as to eat"
• the Gentiles are to be overcome out of their own books

21.1:
**“the corpse of a man”** — the Body of Christ
**“slain, and it is not known who is guilty of the murder,”**
• WHEN THERE SHALL BE FOUND, etc. A corpse is a body without a soul, and [so is] a soul without God, who is its life. In the land which the Lord thy God will give thee: that is, in the Church. Guilty of the murder: the author of the sedition. The ancients: those greater in life and wisdom. The judges and priests, whose office it is to judge, that is, to discern, of each matter. They shall measure from the place of the corpse: that is, with the utmost discernment they will search out the author of the sedition. They shall take a heifer of the herd: that is, the flesh of Christ which he took from the fathers; "which hath not drawn in the yoke", because he did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth; "nor ploughed the ground", namely, he admitted no stain of sedition. And they shall bring her into a rough and stony valley: namely, a despised and most shameful death; whence: "Let us condemn him to a most shameful death." "Which never was ploughed", because the death of Christ was without fault; "nor sown", that is, [it received not] the cockle of sin which the enemy oversowed. We can take the rough valley as the Gentile world, which was rough [and] stony, because it adored stones; in which the neck of the heifer was struck, because the death of Christ was accomplished for the salvation of the Gentiles. The neck is the strength of the flesh, which he laid down in death. They shall wash their hands over the heifer: that is, they will purify their works through confidence in the passion of Christ.
• IT IS NOT KNOWN WHO IS GUILTY, etc. The devil, who is invisible and therefore is said to be unknown. For it is known that he put it into the heart of Judas to betray him.
21.2: **“THY ANCIENTS”** — The Apostles and doctors, who by the attestation of Scripture perceived that no nation was so ready for slaughter as the race of the Jews, who shed the blood both of the prophets and of the Lord.
21.3:
**“And the ancients of that city which they shall perceive to be nearer than the rest”** — the Apostles and apostolic men, by whom she is preached crucified for the expiation of our sins
**“shall take a heifer”** — the flesh of Christ
**“of the herd,”** — of the patriarchs and prophets
**“that hath not drawn in the yoke,”** — of sin
**“nor [ploughed] the ground,”** — brought forth without the seed of man, born of a virgin
21.4:
**“And they shall bring her”** — Jerusalem, which Isaias calls the valley of vision
**“into a rough”** — hard and untamed, most rough with the thorns of vices
**“and stony valley,”**
• because it did not perfectly yield to the holy doctors; whence: "Jerusalem, that killest the prophets"
• "and stonest them that are sent unto thee"
**“that never was ploughed,”** — of the Gospel; but for fruit it brought forth thorns, and for grapes wild grapes
**“nor sown: and there they shall strike off the head of the heifer:”** — where they crucified the flesh of Christ
21.5:
**“And the priests the sons of Levi shall come,”** — the Apostles and their followers, to whom it is committed to rule the ecclesiastical order and to preach
**“whom the Lord thy God hath chosen”** — "You have not chosen me, but I have chosen you"
**“to minister to him,”** — by preaching
**“and to bless in his name,”** — not in their own
**“and that by their word every matter should be decided, and whatsoever is clean or unclean should be judged.”** — be discerned
21.6: **“And the ancients of that city shall come to the person slain, and shall wash their hands over the heifer that was killed in the valley,”** — AND THEY SHALL WASH THEIR HANDS, etc. That is, they will show their works to be clean in the passion of Christ. For although they daily imitate the sacraments of that same passion, they have hearts and works most clean from all the fraud of the Jews.
21.7:
**“And shall say: Our hands did not shed this blood,”** — of Christ
**“nor did our eyes see it.”** — nor did we consent
21.8:
**“Be merciful to thy people Israel,”** — namely, that thou mayst make [them] Israel
**“whom thou hast redeemed, O Lord, and lay not innocent blood to their charge,”**
• the punishment
• of the innocent blood
**“in the midst of thy people Israel.”** — thus
**“And the guilt of blood shall be taken from them:”** — of Christ
**“BE MERCIFUL”** — By their office they bless the people, that vengeance be not repaid for the crime, but salvation for the redemption.
21.9: **“And thou shalt be free from the innocent's blood, that was shed, when thou shalt have done what the Lord hath commanded thee.”** — the expiation aforesaid
21.10:
**“If thou go out to fight”** — spiritual
**“against thy enemies,”** — demons or Gentiles
**“and the Lord thy God deliver them into thy hand, and thou lead them away captives,”**
• falsehood being overcome
• to the yoke of Christ; whence: "bringing into captivity every understanding"
**“IF THOU GO OUT TO FIGHT”** — ISIDORE. Let the Jews say how they keep these things. What is the reason for the woman to be made bald and her nails pared? What if she were found without hair and nails?
21.11:
**“And seest in the number”** — in Gentile conversation
**“of the captives”** — thy own, namely
**“a beautiful woman,”**
• useful knowledge
• the soul
• created by God
**“and lovest her, and wilt have her to wife,”**
• that is, to join her to the body of the Church
• with true charity
• for the help of Christ
• Others thought that this woman fair of form signifies the rational discipline found among the Gentiles. For from it all the uncleanness of superstition must be cut away, that it may be taken up for the study of truth. For the disciplines of the Gentiles have nothing clean, because there is no discipline among them with which something of uncleanness or superstition is not mixed.
**“A BEAUTIFUL WOMAN”** — As Paul, who took from Menander: "Evil communications corrupt good manners"; and from Aratus: "In him we live, and move, and are; for we are also his offspring."
21.12:
**“Thou shalt bring her into thy house:”**
• the Church
• care and providence
• with the razor of the word of God
**“and she shall shave her hair,”**
• superfluous thoughts
• superfluous things, like the fictions of the poets
• whatever is dead in works
• every sin of unbelief, which is dead and superfluous
**“and pare her nails,”** — cruelty or rapacity
21.13:
**“And shall put off the raiment,”**
• the trappings of falsehood or vanity
• the worship of idolatry
• the former error
**“wherein she was taken:”** — humbled
**“and shall remain in thy house, and mourn for”** — she will show [it] to be damnable and worthy of weeping
**“her father”**
• error
• that is, the devil, who is a father by imitation, not by nature
**“and her mother”**
• every worldly memory and the carnal allurements
• human curiosity
**“one month: and after that thou shalt go in unto her,”** — that thou mayst beget spiritual offspring
**“and shalt sleep with her, and she shall be thy wife.”** — received into fellowship
**“ONE MONTH”** — That is, thirty days, that after the faith of the Trinity and the work of the law she may deserve to be joined to the Church; for three tens make thirty.
**“AND AFTER THAT”** — When neither in the head, that is, the senses, nor in the hands, that is, the works, will there be anything superfluous or unclean.
21.15:
**“If a man have”** — God
**“two wives,”** — the people of the Jews and of the Gentiles
**“one beloved,”** — the Church from the Gentiles, which by faith and devotion deserved to be loved
**“and the other hated,”** — the synagogue, which is unbelieving and ungrateful
**“THE OTHER HATED”** — Reason, which does not indulge the body nor serve pleasure, but renounces the hidden things of dishonesty.
**“and they have had children by him,”** — faithful
**“and the son of the hated be the firstborn,”**
• holy, as the first-born of a holy mother; whence: "The wicked are alienated from the womb, they have gone astray", etc.
• IF A MAN HAVE TWO WIVES, etc. Christ joined to himself in marriage two wives, namely the people of the Jews and of the Gentiles. By the name of the hated one is [meant] the synagogue, ever contentious, stiffnecked, uncircumcised in heart; the beloved is the church of the Gentiles. But he cannot prefer the son of the beloved to the son of the hated, that is, [he cannot prefer] the church of the Gentiles, or its sons, to the apostles and the other firstlings, who are sons of the synagogue. He acknowledges the firstborn of the hated and gives him double, because to the firstlings, the sons of the synagogue, he gave the law and the prophets and the knowledge of his name, and preached the Gospel first to them. For this is the firstborn of his children.
**“ONE BELOVED”** — Animality, which seems sweet and delightful, desires all things voluptuous and is affected by no sorrow.
**“THE FIRSTBORN”** — The Apostles and apostolic men, who hold the place of the firstborn, whose authority the Church follows.
21.16:
**“his substance”** — spiritual gifts
**“of the beloved”** — voluptuous and slack
**“of the hated”** — austere and severe
21.17:
**“he shall acknowledge”** — that is, he shall hold
**“BUT THE SON OF THE HATED”** — This is to be done according to the letter, lest anyone follow the motion of his own mind, whether love or hatred, rather than nature.
**“A DOUBLE PORTION OF ALL”** — The Apostles received a double portion of all, being endowed with doctrine and working.
**“for the firstborn, and shall give him a double portion of all he hath: for this is the first of his children, and to him are due the first birthrights.”** — To the others he will give that they may live, not that they may abound; as Abraham set the son of the handmaid over nations, [but] on the son of Sara he heaped not only temporal but spiritual things.
21.18:
**“If [a man] have begotten”** — by faith
**“a man”** — a preacher
**“of his father”** — of God, or the preachers
**“or mother,”** — of the Church, or of the law
**“and being corrected,”** — often admonished
**“slighteth obedience:”** — IF A MAN HAVE [A SON], etc. Obedience is better than sacrifices, and to hearken rather than to offer the fat of rams; "because it is like the sin of witchcraft to rebel", etc. Moses [commands] the disobedient and vicious son to be overwhelmed with stones; the Gospel too reproves such men with hard rebukes as with stones: "Ye brood of vipers, who hath shewed you to flee from the wrath to come?"
21.19:
**“They shall take him”** — that they may correct him
**“and bring him to the ancients of his city,”** — to whose authority one must submit
**“and to the gate”** — the Church, by which one goes to heaven
**“of judgment,”** — of discernment
21.20: **“And shall say to them: This our son is rebellious and stubborn, he slighteth hearing our admonitions,”** — so in the Church the lesser bishops do toward the greater, referring the greater cause
21.21:
**“with stones”** — with hard rebukes
**“The people of the city shall stone him:”** — that, corrected publicly, he may blush the sooner
**“and he shall die,”** — to sin, that he may live to God
**“that you may take away”** — thus
**“the evil”** — the sin
**“out of the midst of you,”** — lest he corrupt others by his example
**“and all Israel hearing it may be afraid.”** — "The pestilent man being scourged, the wise shall become wiser"
21.22:
**“When a man hath committed a crime”**
• a Christian
• namely, a mortal crime
**“for which he is to be punished with death,”** — of torments or of excommunication
**“and being condemned”** — to guilt
**“IS HANGED”** — His torment being seen by the people; whence: "Them that sin reprove before all, that the rest also may have fear."
21.23:
**“His body shall not remain upon the tree, but shall be buried the same day: for he is accursed”** — punished for sin
**“of God”** — who said: "In what day soever thou shalt eat of it, thou shalt die the death"; who hates sin and death
**“that hangeth”**
• by persevering
• fixed [to it]; not as Judas, as some have held
**“on a tree:”** — sin, because the first sin was at a tree
**“and thou shalt not defile”** — with the filth of sins
**“thy land,”** — the flesh
**“which the Lord thy God shall give thee in possession.”**
• HIS BODY SHALL NOT REMAIN, etc. That is, he ought not to be left in the same damnation, but called back by the exhortation of the doctors, so that reconciliation be denied to no one while he lives.
• CURSED OF [GOD], etc. AUGUSTINE. Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us (for Adam fell at the tree of transgression; therefore he merited for himself and his posterity the curse of which it is said: Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree); for he took on him a curse, that is, an execrable and most shameful death.
**“AUGUSTINE”** — He is accursed of God that, etc. Certain heretics turn this sentence to a calumny of the passion of Christ, not understanding that death is from the punishment of sin. Whence it too is called sin (not that a man sins when he dies), as speech formed by the tongue is called a tongue, and writing a hand, whence we say: His hand is proved and choice. Sin therefore is called not only the evil work which is worthy of punishment, but death itself, which was brought about by sin. That sin, then, by which he would be guilty of death Christ did not commit; but the other, that is, death, which was inflicted for sin, he took upon himself for us. This hung on the tree; this was cursed by Moses; that is, death was condemned that it might not reign, and cursed that it might perish. Through Christ such sin of ours was condemned, that we might be freed, lest, sin reigning, we should remain condemned. Why then does Faustus wonder that sin, [that is,] the mortality of the flesh, was cursed, without sin in Christ? Yet it came from the sin of man even in Christ; for he took a body from Adam, from whom came Mary, who bore Christ. And God said: In what day you touch it, you shall die the death; this is the curse which hung on the tree. He denies that Christ was cursed who denies that he died; whence the Apostle: "Our old man is crucified with him"; and he was made a curse for us. And every sin is a curse, whether the sin itself on which punishment follows, or the punishment itself. And Christ took on himself the punishment of our [sins]. The flesh of Christ was not [flesh] of sin, because it had not come into Mary through a male by the propagation of mortality; but because death is from sin, he was nonetheless mortal from the virgin, from whom he had the likeness of sinful flesh; whence: "that of sin he might condemn sin in the flesh"; and elsewhere: "Him that knew no sin, for us he hath made sin." The curse is the companion of sin: cursed therefore is every one that hangeth on a tree. Unless God hated sin and death, he would not send his Son to take it on and destroy it. Rightly then that is called a curse which God hates: this hung on the tree.
**“THOU SHALT DEFILE”** — With the tears of penance we ought to wash away the stench of sins, lest it breed scandal for others and torment for ourselves.

22.1:
**“Thou shalt not see”** — these things are to be done according to the letter out of the kindness of nature
**“an ox,”**
• the worker
• because he was called from the yoke of the law to faith
**“thy brother's”** — of Christ, who says: "Go, tell my brethren"
**“or his sheep”** — the simple Catholic
**“go astray:”** — sinning through heresies
**“and pass by,”** — be neglected
**“but thou shalt bring them back”** — by calling back
**“to thy brother.”**
• to Christ
• from whom he departs
• THOU SHALT NOT SEE [THY BROTHER'S] OX, etc. Morally. Thy brother is the doctor of the Church; if thou seest his disciple go astray, whether the learned, who is signified by the ox, or the unlearned, who is signified by the sheep, do not neglect it, but exhort him, so that thou mayst reconcile him to his brother and master. Bring him into thy house, that is, apply care. And if he is not near, that is, [not the doctor] of thy church, but the doctor of another.
22.2:
**“And if thy brother be not nigh, or thou know him not: thou shalt bring them to thy house,”**
• domestic care
• in the unity of the Church
**“and they shall be with thee until thy brother seek them,”** — coming to judgment
**“and receive them.”** — when thou returnest [them]
22.3:
**“Thou shalt do in like manner with his ass,”**
• the Gentile
• the unlearned
**“and with his raiment, and with every thing”** — the outward works of the unlearned, which if we see go astray we ought to direct into the way of justice
**“that is thy brother's, which is lost:”** — from him
**“THOU SHALT DO IN LIKE MANNER WITH”** — With the Gentile, namely, whose vileness and uncleanness we ought not to despise.
**“HIS RAIMENT”** — The people, with which the doctor is adorned. According to the letter also all these and similar things are to be kept.
22.4:
**“If thou see the ass”** — the Gentile
**“thy brother's”** — the Jew learned in the law
**“or his ox to be fallen down”** — by an unforeseen sin
**“in the way,”** — of the present life
**“but shalt lift it up”**
• "Bear ye one another's burdens"
• nature gave a different clothing to each sex
22.5:
**“A woman shall not be clothed with man's apparel, neither shall a man use woman's apparel: for he that doeth these things is abominable before God.”**
• A WOMAN SHALL NOT BE CLOTHED, etc. AUGUSTINE. Another edition: "The vessels of a man shall not be upon a woman." He wished vessels of war to be understood, that is, arms. But mystically the Apostle expounds this: "I suffer not a woman to teach" in the Church; for neither priesthood nor teaching is granted to women in the Church, lest she be clothed with man's apparel. But neither ought a man to be clothed with woman's apparel. For he who is a man and bears the government of the Church ought to have nothing womanish or soft in his doctrine.
• It is against nature for a man to do womanish things, to curl his locks, to twist his hair. Whence: "If a man nourish his hair, it is a shame unto him; but to a woman her hair is given for a covering." Let not a man then be clothed with woman's apparel, namely, with loose and dissolute working.
**“A WOMAN”** — [The woman,] whose colour, motion, gait and strength are naturally different, who is not permitted to teach nor to have dominion over the man; nor may she usurp the office of preaching.
22.6:
**“If as thou walkest by the way,”** — of the present life
**“in a tree,”**
• the Scripture which speaks of the contemplative [life]
• the contemplative
**“or on the ground,”** — that which [speaks] of the active
**“thou find a bird's nest”** — the words of the history
**“and the dam upon the young”**
• the history
• with the spiritual understanding already manifest
**“or upon the eggs”** — not manifest, as not yet come forth
**“sitting: thou shalt not take her with her young:”** — because in some places the history is to be passed over, so that the young alone, that is, the sense of the spiritual understanding, may refresh us
**“IF AS THOU WALKEST BY THE WAY”** — GREGORY. We pass through the present life as through an unclean way. The bird's nest in a tree or on the ground is the words of the history, either in the contemplative or in the active life: the precepts of the active life are a nest on the ground, those of the contemplative in a tree. The mother sits on the young or the eggs when the history cherishes the spiritual understanding, and brings forth some things in full speech, as it were young birds; but others [it so sets forth] that by them it may lead the mind of the reader to higher things, as it were containing eggs beneath it from which to bring forth young. For they are cherished that young may be born of them; and there are certain things of the contemplative life which are seen through certain images, that afterwards they may be seen in their own power and nature. Whence: "We see now through a glass in a dark manner", etc. Though a wife is not to be had except for the sake of children, Paul yet says: "For fear of fornication let every man have his own wife", so that, namely, they might rise thence to better things, that is, to the lawful bond of marriage. Here too preachers send fear before and so lead to love; but perfect charity casteth out fear, and the young begin to live when they do not succumb to fear. The law too was [as] eggs when it said: "Eye for eye, tooth for tooth"; it brought forth young when it said: "Seek not revenge, nor be mindful of the injury of thy citizens." But it is to be noted that it is said: thou shalt not take her with her young, but shalt let her go, keeping the young which thou hast caught; because sometimes the history is to be let go, that the spiritual understanding may refresh us, not the historical use. We read that the gold and silver of the Egyptians were taken by the Israelites by a deceitful request, and that carnal sacrifices were offered to God. But in this nest of words the mother is to be let go, the young are to be kept. For when we draw from worldly men vigilance of wit for the defence of truth, and their eloquence into the use of rectitude, we take gold and silver from the Egyptians, that we may be made rich and they poor. Whence: "Bringing into captivity every understanding unto the obedience of Christ." And when we tame our bodies through abstinence, we offer carnal sacrifices. We let go, then, the examples of the history, but from it we keep the allegorical sense in the mind.
22.7: **“But shalt let her go, keeping the young which thou hast caught: that it may be well with thee, and thou mayst live a long time.”** — he lives a long time who through spiritual understanding grasps the years of eternity
22.8:
**“When thou buildest”** — with virtues
**“a new house,”** — for God: thy own conversation, or the congregation of others prepared for thy preaching
**“thou shalt make a battlement to the roof”** — the fortification of right faith and of divine protection, or the guard of humility
**“round about: lest blood be shed in thy house, and thou be guilty,”** — who couldst have preserved [him] by doctrine and example and didst neglect it
**“A NEW HOUSE”** — That is, the Church. The battlement of the roof, that is, the guard of the virtues. Lest blood be shed in thy house: that is, lest thou be held guilty when another sins.
**“LEST [BLOOD] BE SHED”** — Through carelessness and desires; whence: he who gathers virtues without humility is like one who carries dust into the wind.
22.9:
**“Thou shalt not sow”** — thou shalt establish
**“thy vineyard”** — the Church
**“with divers seeds:”** — with another's doctrine
**“lest both the seed which thou hast sown, and the fruit of the vineyard, be sanctified together.”** — or: be choked
**“THE VINEYARD”** — The doctrine, or the people committed to the doctors, where the wine of spiritual grace ought to abound.
**“WITH DIVERS”** — That is, heretical. The good seed is the word of God; the wicked seed is that which the enemy sowed. Care must be taken, then, lest anything of error be mixed in and the seed of God be corrupted.
22.10:
**“with an ox”**
• the Jew placed under the yoke of the law
• the Gentile, who belongs to the Gospel
**“THOU SHALT NOT PLOUGH”** — ISIDORE. He ploughs with an ox and an ass who receives the Gospel together with the observance of the Jews, which went before in shadow. In the ox too [is signified] the life of those who work well, in the ass the sloth of the foolish. As if [to say]: do not join a fool to a wise man in preaching, lest through him who cannot accomplish the matter he hinder him who is able. But the fool and the wise are well joined so that one commands and the other obeys, not so that they announce the word of God with equal power.
22.11:
**“Thou shalt not wear a garment”** — "Beware of false prophets, who come to you in the clothing of sheep", etc.
**“that is woven of woollen”** — with the simplicity of innocence
**“and linen together.”** — namely, with the subtlety of malice
**“THOU SHALT NOT WEAR A GARMENT”** — MORALLY. Wool is simplicity, linen subtlety. The garment that is made of wool and linen hides the linen within and shows the wool on the surface. He is clothed with a garment of wool and linen who under speech of innocence hides the subtlety of malice. Allegorically. He mixes wool or purple with linen garments who lives disorderly and in professions of a diverse kind; as if a nun should have the ornaments of a wife, or a wife bear the hope of a virgin. And what was figured then in garments is now declared in manners.
22.12:
**“Thou shalt make strings in the hem”**
• hyacinth fringes
• in all that thou doest be mindful of the precepts of God
**“STRINGS”** — For distinction, namely, as the sign of circumcision separates the Israelites from the rest. But superstitious masters, catching at the favour of the people and worldly gains from silly women, enlarged their fringes and bound thorns to them, that whether walking or sitting they might be pricked and so be moved to serve God. Whence: "They make their phylacteries broad, and enlarge their fringes."
22.13:
**“If [a man] marry”** — that is, has received a people to rule
**“a man”** — a doctor
**“a wife,”** — through ambition of a greater principality
**“it,”**
• committed to him
• IF A MAN MARRY, etc. AUGUSTINE. It appears how the law wished wives to be subject to their husbands and almost servants: because when the husband bears witness against the wife, so that she is stoned if it is established as true, he himself is not stoned in turn if it is found false, but is chastised and fined and commanded to keep her for ever. But in other causes he who wished to harm by false testimony is struck with the same penalty with which the other was to have been struck.
22.14:
**“And seek occasions to put her away, laying to her charge a very ill name,”** — of heresy or disobedience
**“and say: This woman”** — to be ruled
**“I took to wife,”** — that I might beget spiritual fruit
**“and going in to her, I found her not a virgin:”** — of which: "For I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ"
22.15:
**“Her father”** — God
**“and mother shall take her,”** — the Church
**“and shall bring with them the tokens”** — the works of the divine testaments
**“of her virginity”** — of whole faith
**“to the ancients of the city”** — the masters of the Church
**“that are in the gate:”**
• judging the cause of the people
• by whose judgment hidden things are made manifest
**“FATHER AND MOTHER”** — The doctors of the Church, who as father and mother cherish the people: fathers by authority, mothers by piety.
22.16: **“And the father shall say: My daughter”** — the Church
22.17:
**“He layeth to her charge a very ill name, so as to say: I found not thy daughter a virgin: and behold these are the tokens of my daughter's virginity.”** — of whole faith and working
**“And they shall spread the cloth”** — the works of the divine law, by which they prove [her] uncorrupted
22.18:
**“And the ancients of that city shall take”** — the doctors
**“that man, and beat him,”** — they will chastise [him] by the authority of the Church
**“AND BEAT”** — It is no wonder if the man who accuses falsely is commanded to be beaten and to pay a fine, but the girl, if she is guilty, to be stoned: because through the woman was the beginning of sin, who seduced the man; and she sinned doubly, first against God, afterwards against the man; the man only against God.
22.19:
**“Condemning him besides in a hundred sicles of silver, which he shall give”** — to God, who has care of you
**“to the damsel's father, because he hath defamed by a very ill name a virgin of Israel:”** — of those who see God
**“and he shall have her to wife,”** — lest, leaving her, he pass over to another church
**“and may not put her away all the days of his life.”**
• that is, if that people is found defiled by error or corrupted by vices and incorrigible
• A HUNDRED SICLES, etc. The perfection of doctrine and solicitude which he should spend on the people subject to him, or [the perfection] of penance. For a hundred is perfect; fifty is consecrated to penance.
22.20: **“But if what he charged her with be true, and virginity be not found in the damsel:”** — they will condemn [her] by the judgment of the Church
22.21:
**“They shall cast her out of the doors of her father's house,”** — the threshold of the universal Church
**“and with stones”** — of hard anathema, because she did not fear to corrupt the Catholic faith
**“the men of the city shall stone her to death, and she shall die:”** — by eternal death
**“because she hath done a wicked thing”** — heresy
**“in Israel, to play the whore”** — by departing from the true spouse
**“in her father's house:”** — the Church
**“and thou shalt take away”** — lest by consenting thou make [it] thy own
22.22:
**“If [a man] lie”**
• according to the letter he deters adulteries
• by corrupting
**“a man”** — a heretic or a Jew
**“with the wife”** — the Church
**“of another,”** — of Christ, to whom she is joined by faith and love
**“they shall both die,”** — by repenting of sin; or, the impenitent will be assigned to eternal torment
22.23:
**“If a damsel”** — namely, the ecclesiastical people, or the Christian soul espoused by the word of God
**“that is a virgin”** — by the pledge of faith
**“a man”** — Christ
**“and some one find her”** — a Jew or a heretic or a schismatic or even a pagan
**“in the city, and lie with her,”** — staining [her] with error
**“IF A DAMSEL THAT IS A VIRGIN”** — In this chapter, as in the two preceding and the two following, he condemns bodily fornication.
22.24:
**“Thou shalt bring them both out to the gate of that city,”** — the judgment of the elders of the Church
**“and with stones”** — with hard rebukes or sentences
**“and they shall be stoned: the damsel,”** — the people or the soul
**“because she cried not out,”**
• by calling to her help the doctors of the Church, who would reprove the corrupter
• consenting to error
**“being in the city:”** — where she would quickly be heard and freed by the doctors
**“the man, because he hath humbled the wife”** — from the dignity of faith
**“of his neighbour.”** — of Christ
22.25:
**“But if in the field”**
• outside the Church, and not received into the fellowship of the saints
• among the Gentiles
**“a man find a damsel”** — a soul
**“that is betrothed,”**
• imbued with faith through catechism
• to God
**“and taking hold of her,”**
• in that place
• by corrupting [her] with the seed of error
• the seducer
• punished by anathema
22.26:
**“The damsel”** — because she could not resist the seducer, nor had a doctor to help her
**“shall suffer nothing, neither is she guilty of death: for as a robber riseth”** — from ambush
**“against his brother, and taketh away his life,”** — with a spiritual sword
**“so also did the damsel suffer:”** — under compulsion of force
**“SHALL SUFFER NOTHING”** — But she will be called back to the faith she began, freed from her enemies through the grace of baptism.
22.27:
**“She was alone in the field:”** — outside the fellowship of the Church
**“she cried, and there was no man”** — for many such resist
22.28:
**“If a man find”** — some doctor
**“a damsel that is a virgin,”** — a disciple
**“who is not espoused,”** — to whom, namely, the counsel of the Church is not present
**“and taking hold of her,”** — that is, has presumed to join [her to himself]
**“lie with her,”** — or: with her
22.29:
**“He that lay with her shall give to the father”** — to God
**“of the maid fifty sicles of silver,”** — perfect penance
**“and shall have her to wife,”** — under his care and providence
**“because he hath humbled her:”** — especially where the disciple has bound himself by vow
**“HE MAY NOT PUT HER AWAY”** — AUGUSTINE. It is rightly asked whether this is a punishment, that he cannot put away all his life her whom he disorderly and unlawfully defiled. For if we understand that she cannot, that is, ought not, be put away all her life, once she has been made his wife, it occurs [to us] that Moses permitted giving a bill of divorce and putting away. But in the case of those who unlawfully violate he would not allow it, lest he seem to have done it in mockery and rather to have feigned that he married her. This too he commanded of her whose husband had falsely accused her concerning the tokens of virginity not found.
22.30:
**“No man shall take”** — that is, he shall not seduce a soul joined to God the Father
**“a man”** — the preacher
**“a wife,”** — the Church
**“of his father,”** — of Christ
**“SHALL NOT TAKE”** — Our Father is Christ, whose Church is the wife. It is not lawful for a man to transfer to himself the dignity of this Spouse, nor to violate his bride so as to turn her love to himself, seeking from the gift of virtues or from preaching his own praise, not God's, to whom it is fitting to say: "Not to us, O Lord, not to us; but to thy name give glory."

23.1:
**“An eunuch shall not enter,”** — who has not the seed of the word, nor can beget good works
**“whose testicles are broken or cut away, or yard cut off, into the church of the Lord.”** — the fellowship of the saints
**“AN EUNUCH”** — All who live softly and do not perform a manly work cannot remain in the congregation of the saints, nor are they worthy of entry into the kingdom of heaven, which suffereth violence, and the violent bear it away.
23.2:
**“A mamzer, that is to say, one born of a prostitute, shall not enter into the church of the Lord,”** — the consortium of the saints
**“until the tenth generation.”** — the observance of the decalogue
**“A MAMZER”** — Degenerate in sense and manners; or one whom the depravity of heretics has made degenerate in the reception of the sacraments, or whom the rite of Gentilism or of Judaism has stained. He will be received into the Church when with whole faith he has kept the decalogue of the law according to the institution of the Gospel. Whence: "If thou wilt enter into life, keep the commandments"; and elsewhere: "I am the door; by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved."
23.3:
**“The Ammonite”** — who were born of incest
**“and the Moabite, even after the tenth generation”** — AUGUSTINE. That is, for ever, because ten is the close of the numbers
**“THE AMMONITE”** — AUGUSTINE. Another edition: "The Ammonite and the Moabite shall not enter into the church of the Lord, and even to the tenth generation he shall not enter into the church of the Lord, and even for ever." How then did Ruth the Moabitess enter? Perhaps it mystically prophesied that she would enter, in saying "even to the tenth generation". For they are counted from Abraham, when Lot lived, who begot the Moabites and Ammonites; and from Abraham ten generations are found down to Salmon, who begot Booz, the husband of Ruth. For these are: from Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, Judas, Phares, Esrom, Aram, Aminadab, Naasson, Salmon, who begot Booz, to whom Ruth bore sons in the church of the Lord. But why is "even for ever" added? Is it because afterwards no soul of the Ammonites and Moabites entered that church of the Hebrews? Or rather was "even to the tenth generation" so said that he wished it to be understood always, by ten, as the whole, and expounded it by saying "and even for ever"? But if so, Ruth seems to have been admitted against desert. Or did he forbid Ammonites and not Ammonitesses, that is, men to be admitted, not women? Especially since, when the Israelites overthrew that nation, they were commanded to kill all the men, and of the women only those who had known man, since they had drawn the people into fornication; but the virgins they spared, not imputing to them the fault for which that nation deserved to be overthrown, which he also recalls here. As if it were asked why he would not have the Moabites and Ammonites admitted, he adds: because they did not meet you with bread and water in the way when you came out of Egypt, and they hired against thee Balaam the son of Beor from Mesopotamia to curse thee. These faults they did not impute, even then when that nation was conquered, to the women, whom they preferred to keep.
**“shall not enter into the church of the Lord for ever:”** — He signifies that heretics are ever to be driven from the Church; as if [to say]: a man that is a heretic, after the first and second admonition, avoid.
23.4:
**“Because they would not meet you with bread and water in the way, when you came out of Egypt:”** — out of the world
**“and because they hired”** — as heretics stir up persecution against the faithful people through the devil
**“against thee Balaam, the son of Beor, from Mesopotamia in Syria, to curse thee.”** — BECAUSE THEY WOULD NOT [MEET] YOU, etc. The Hebrews relate that these nations, being near, met them as they came out of Egypt with bread only, though they knew that they were labouring most of all with thirst in the desert; and therefore they were subjected to this curse. Mystically they designate the heretics, who offer to those fleeing from the Egypt of this world to the true land of promise polluted bread, not sweetened with the water of wisdom; and therefore they are estranged from the church.
23.5:
**“And the Lord thy God would not hear Balaam, and he turned his cursing into thy blessing, because he loved thee.”**
• freely, namely
• AND HE TURNED, etc. Because persecution is often the cause of greater prosperity; for to them that love God all things work together unto good.
23.7:
**“Thou shalt not abhor”**
• THOU SHALT NOT ABHOR THE EDOMITE, etc. The Edomite, bloody or earthy, signifies the flesh, whose matter is earthy. The Egyptian, that is, dark, [signifies] the sickly body. We ought not to abhor our flesh, but to cherish it and furnish it with necessaries, yet not make provision for it in its desires. He is thy brother, he says, because we are of flesh and soul. Let us not abhor the Egyptian, that is, the body, in whose land we were strangers; for the soul, which has a heavenly origin, dwells in the body as a stranger. Whence the Apostle: "While we are in the body we are absent from the Lord." "They that are born of them", etc.: that is, they will little by little become spiritual.
• Thou shalt not abhor the Edomite, etc. By the Edomite and the Egyptian is signified the present life; for though, renouncing it, we turn away from the Egyptian land, that is, the former conversation and the concupiscence of the world, yet while we are subject to the necessities of this world we do not altogether extinguish the Egyptian nation, but, in a manner separated, we are content with daily food and clothing. In the third generation they will enter into the Church, because a secular man can be joined to the saints when he has perfectly believed in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, or when he has been adorned with hope, faith and charity.
**“the Edomite,”** — the present life
**“because he is thy brother:”** — bloody or earthy; this is our flesh, which is from the earth
**“nor the Egyptian,”** — dark, that is, the sickly body
**“in his land.”** — our fatherland is paradise
23.8:
**“They that are born of them, in the third generation”** — in perfect faith in the Trinity
**“shall enter into the church of the Lord.”** — elsewhere: of God
23.9:
**“WHEN THOU GOEST OUT”** — He instructs the spiritual soldiers of Christ, to whom it is said elsewhere: "[Every one that striveth for the mastery] refraineth himself from all things."
**“against thy enemies,”** — the demons
**“to war, thou shalt keep thyself from every evil thing.”** — harmful
23.10:
**“If there be among you”** — IF THERE BE AMONG YOU. AUGUSTINE. The law sets many things in sacraments and shadows of things to come. For a certain material formlessness in the seed, which when formed will render a human body, is set as a signification of a formless and untaught life, from which formlessness one must be cleansed by the form and teaching of doctrine. Therefore that purification was commanded after the effusion of seed; for no sin is committed in sleep. Or if anyone thinks it a sin, supposing that it happens only from such desire (which is false), are the customary monthly courses of women also sins, which the law commands to be expiated? [No,] but only because of that material formlessness which, when conception takes place, is added as it were to the building of the body. And thereby, when it flows formlessly, the law wished to signify the mind flowing unbecomingly and dissolute without the form of discipline, which it signifies is to be formed when it commands the flux to be purified. Lastly, to die is not a sin, and to bury the dead is a duty of humanity, and yet purification was commanded: not because the dead body is sin, but it signifies the sin of the soul deserted by justice.
**“GREGORY”** — Mystically. If there be among you a man, etc. The nightly dream is hidden temptation, by which through dark thought something shameful is conceived, but is not fulfilled in deed. He who is defiled in a nightly dream goes out of the camp, so that he who is defiled in thought may judge himself unworthy of the fellowship of the faithful and despise himself in comparison with the good. He is washed with water toward evening, when, seeing his failing, he turns to the laments of penance, so that by weeping he may wash out what the hidden defilement accuses. But after the setting of the sun let him return to the camp, that is, when the heat of the ardour cools, let him take confidence toward the fellowship of the good and be restored to the merits of the faithful. [The text breaks off: "perfumenda".]
**“a man”**
• by hidden temptation
• by dark thought
**“that is defiled by night”** — by consenting
**“in a dream,”** — judging himself unworthy of the fellowship of the faithful
23.11:
**“And shall not return, before he be washed in the evening”** — the heat of temptation being overcome, namely
**“with water:”**
• of penance
• of tears
**“and after sunset”** — when the temptation cools
**“he shall return”** — to the fellowship of the faithful
23.12:
**“THOU SHALT HAVE A PLACE”** — For God loves bodily cleanness. Therefore he commanded that nothing foul remain in the camp.
**“Thou shalt have”** — GREGORY. Mystically. Thou shalt have a place, etc. From the womb of our mind, weighed down by corruptible nature, certain superfluities of thoughts burst out, as it were the burden of the belly. But we ought to carry a paddle under our girdle, so that, ever girded to reprove ourselves, we may have about us the sharp goad of compunction, which may dig the earth of our mind with the pain of penance and hide what bursts out of us foul.
**“a place”** — the conscience, in which thou art pricked
**“without the camp,”** — of the saints
23.13:
**“Carrying a paddle”**
• the sharp goad of compunction
• compunction of heart, or the memory of chastity
**“AT THY GIRDLE”** — For the loins are girt with a girdle. Therefore by the girdle is signified the crushing of evil will; whence Job: "He looseth the girdle of kings, and girdeth their loins with a cord."
**“And when thou sittest down, thou shalt dig round about, and with the earth that is dug up thou shalt cover”** — lest it appear before the eyes of God
**“THOU SHALT COVER”** — Considering earthly frailty we ought to cover our filth.
23.14: **“That which thou art eased of: (for the Lord thy God walketh in the midst of thy camp,”** — of the Church, which is like an army set in array
23.15:
**“Thou shalt not deliver”**
• one fleeing from the servitude of the devil or of sin
• by rejecting him or by casting him into despair
**“THOU SHALT NOT DELIVER THE SERVANT”** — AUGUSTINE. The Seventy: "Thou shalt not deliver a servant to his master, who is set by thee from his master." Not that his master set him, that is, entrusted him, for then he would say "deposited"; but he said "set by", that is, joined to this one when he had departed from that one. He forbade, then, fugitives to be returned, not to be received. How can this be thought, unless we understand these things to be said to a nation and people, not to one man? Assuredly he forbade one fleeing from another nation to this one, to which he was speaking, from his master, that is, from his king, to be returned; which the foreigner Achis king of Geth kept when David fled to him from the face of his master, that is, of king Saul. He explains this by saying: He shall dwell among you in every place where it shall please him.
23.16:
**“He shall dwell with thee in the place that shall please him,”** — in the Church, or under whatever order of the faithful
**“and in one of thy cities”** — of the churches or of the [ways of] conversation
**“shall rest:”** — in the peace of the Church
**“give him no trouble.”** — because he is rather to be cherished, lest he despair
23.17:
**“There shall be no whore”**
• joined to the fornication of heretics
• Spiritually he intimates that it is not lawful for a Christian soul to mingle itself with the errors of heretics; it is not lawful for a son of God to give himself up to impurity and lust.
**“THERE SHALL BE NO WHORE”** — AUGUSTINE. The Seventy: "There shall be no harlot of the daughters of Israel, and there shall be no fornicator of the sons of Israel." He plainly forbids men and women to commit fornication, showing that it is a sin, even when not with the spouses of others, to be joined with those who are not one's spouses; for in forbidding there to be harlots he forbids approaching them, whose shame is publicly for sale. But in the Decalogue, under the name of "moechia", by which nothing but adultery is usually understood, he does not seem to have forbidden it openly; whence what seemed [right] to us we treated there.
**“among the daughters of Israel,”** — the souls that are the temple of the living God
**“nor whoremonger”** — whence: "Fly fornication"
**“among the sons of Israel.”** — who have been adopted by God
23.18:
**“THOU SHALT NOT OFFER”** — AUGUSTINE. The Seventy: "Thou shalt not offer the hire of a harlot nor the exchange of a dog in the house of the Lord thy God for any vow, for it is an abomination to the Lord thy God." Both, namely, not one. For concerning the dog he forbids the exchange of the firstborn to be made, which he commands to be made also concerning unclean animals, that is, horses, asses and those that help man; whence they are also called beasts of burden. But concerning the dog he would not. Why does he except the dog alone here? For he seems to have rejected the hire of a harlot because he forbade there to be a harlot of the daughters of Israel, or any of the sons of Israel to use a harlot; and lest anyone should think this could be expiated if he offered something from it in the temple, it had to be said that it is an abomination to the Lord.
**“Thou shalt not offer”** — soon he shows that as the hire of a brothel is an abomination, so also is the gift of rapacity
**“THE PRICE OF A DOG”** — Of the rapacious dog. The Most High approveth not the gifts of the wicked. He who offers sacrifice of the substance of the poor is as one who sacrifices the son in the presence of his father.
23.19:
**“THOU SHALT NOT LEND”** — He removes usury and avarice and commands [us] to spend charity.
**“to thy brother.”**
• desiring a reward
• the Catholic
• the Jew
**“to usury”** — There is a money which is forbidden to be given to usury, because it is the vice of cupidity to wish to exact what you know you did not lend. This the Lord had, and gave it to be paid out from it to the poor, and invited us to the liberality of bounty. The other is that which we ought to give to usury; whence: "Shouldst thou not then have committed my money to the bankers, and at my coming I should have received my own with usury?"
**“money,”** — of the word of God
23.20: **“But to the stranger.”** — But to the stranger: the unbeliever or the wicked man, to whom we give money at usury when for the word of preaching we exact faith, penance and good working.
23.21:
**“When thou hast made a vow”** — "Vow ye, and pay to the Lord your God"
**“THOU SHALT NOT DELAY”** — Whence Solomon: "It is ruin to a man after vows to retract", or to delay.
**“to pay it: because will require”** — as a debt
**“it the Lord thy God. And if thou delay,”** — to pay
**“it shall be imputed to thee for a sin.”** — the delay itself
23.23: **“But that which is once gone out of thy lips, thou shalt observe, and shalt do as thou hast promised to the Lord thy God,”** — therefore thou art bound by right
23.24:
**“Going into the vineyard”** — the sacred Scripture, or the Catholic Church
**“GOING INTO THE VINEYARD”** — In the church of another bishop one may correct or confirm some; it is not lawful for him to rule the whole people or to handle great affairs.
**“of thy neighbour,”**
• of Christ
• he provides for necessity, forbids avarice
• believe the Incarnation of Christ, share in his sacraments
**“OUT”** — It is not lawful to carry grace outside the Church, because the flesh of the lamb is commanded to be eaten in one house.
23.25:
**“If thou go into”** — by meditating
**“the corn”** — the law
**“of thy friend,”** — of Christ, who is the true friend
**“thou mayst break”** — by expounding he will bring the rigour of the letter back to the spiritual sense
**“the ears, and rub them in thy hand:”** — that is, thou shalt not transfer it to another sense
**“but not reap them with a sickle.”** — IF THOU GO INTO THY FRIEND'S CORN, etc. There are some scriptures which imbue faith historically, some instruct holy conversation morally; some show venerable mysteries not according to the history but according to the allegorical [sense]. Cautiously then must one enter the corn of one's neighbour, that by discerning thou mayst pluck food, [and] not by rushing incur the judgment of the reaped harvest.

24.1:
**“a man”** — anyone
**“a wife,”**
• the care of earthly business
• Mystically. If a man take a wife, etc. Christ took to himself a wife when he joined the synagogue to himself, whom by giving the law he espoused in judgment and justice and mercy; but she found not favour because of unbelief and the uncleanness of idolatry. For he wrote a bill of divorce, that is, the Gospel, in which it is declared how unworthy she was of spiritual fellowship, when she delivered Christ to be crucified [and] chose Barabbas. The bill of divorce was given into her hand when power was given to crucify. Therefore she was cast out of the house, that is, the Church; whence: "Many shall come from the east and the west, and shall sit down with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven; but the children of the kingdom shall be cast out into the exterior darkness." And what follows, "And when she is departed, and marrieth another husband", etc., signifies that, although the apostles after the passion and resurrection of Christ called her to faith and penance and wished to join her in spiritual nuptials, she remained abominable, as unworthy and defiled with error. Whence: "To you it behoved us first to speak the word of God; but because you reject it", etc.
**“IF A MAN TAKE”** — GREGORY. Morally. A man takes a wife when he takes up the care of earthly business. He perceives uncleanness when he feels that it is polluted by sins. He shall send her out of his house: that is, he casts the love of it out of his mind. When she has gone out she takes another, because the earthly business which thou forsakest another covets. To him too she comes into hatred, and he profitably puts her away. Whence it follows well: If he put her away, or be dead, etc. Each one either puts away the earthly care or dies: that is, either does not succumb to it from the heart, or through it utterly succumbs in the life of the soul. Whether then the following husband puts her away or dies, the former will not take her back to wife, because she is defiled: namely, that he who has once left earthly care may not return to it again, which he himself by his own judgment has defiled, who before forsook it because he knew it to be polluted.
**“AUGUSTINE”** — There were many causes in the law for putting away wives. Christ excepts fornication alone; the other troubles he commands to be borne for the sake of the faith and chastity of marriage. And he calls him an adulterer who marries her who is bound to a husband, that is, as long as her husband lives; when he is dead she is loosed. The husband too, if he puts her away, may not marry another. But if it is lawful neither for her to marry nor for him to take another while the wife he put away is living, much less is it lawful to commit fornication with anyone. More blessed indeed are the marriages which, either without begetting children or with earthly offspring despised, can keep continence by mutual consent. Nor is that against [the precept] by which the Lord forbids a spouse to be put away. For he does not put her away who lives with her not carnally but spiritually, so that they that have wives may be as if they had none.
**“and have her, and she find not”** — because earthly business, before it is had, is strongly loved, before it is known to be foul
**“favour in his eyes, for some uncleanness:”** — the sin which he knows in her
**“HE SHALL WRITE A BILL”** — For the hardness of your heart Moses wrote this precept: preferring, namely, to allow divorce rather than that murder be committed.
**“of divorce, and shall give it in her hand, and send her out of his house.”**
• that is, he will cast the love of it out of his mind
• because the earthly business which one forsakes, another covets
24.3:
**“And he also hateth her, and hath given her a bill of divorce, and hath sent her out of his house”** — by not succumbing to it from the heart
**“or is dead:”** — by succumbing to it in the soul
24.4:
**“The former husband cannot take her again to wife: because she is defiled,”** — by his own judgment, because he formerly put her away as defiled
**“and is become abominable before the Lord: lest [thou cause] to sin”** — or: to be defiled
**“LEST TO SIN”** — He defiles his land who stains his body with carnal concupiscences. Therefore it is necessary that the ambition of the present life be tamed quickly, lest it be able to dominate. And when earthly business has once been rejected, it is not to be sought again, lest he look back who had put his hand to the plough.
24.5:
**“WHEN [A MAN] HATH TAKEN”** — As if [to say]: whoever binds himself to carnal desires, let him know that he is not fit for the government of the Church and for spiritual warfare. For no man, being a soldier to God, entangleth himself with secular businesses, that he may please him to whom he hath engaged himself. Whence: "Impose not hands lightly upon any man."
**“a man lately a wife,”** — carnal delight
**“he shall not go out to war,”** — against the demons
**“neither shall any business”** — of ecclesiastical care
**“be enjoined him publicly, but he shall be free without fault”** — which he would have incurred if he had undertaken to rule a church
24.6:
**“Thou shalt not take”** — thou shalt take away
**“THOU SHALT NOT TAKE”** — In place of a pledge, then, let not the upper nor the lower millstone be taken; because those who preach to a sinner ought to preach with such dispensation that they neither, leaving hope, withdraw fear, nor, withdrawing hope, leave fear.
**“ISIDORE”** — He takes the upper millstone who says to one weeping for sin: Thou shalt have no pardon for what thou hast committed. He takes the lower who, flattering sin, says: Do as much evil as thou wilt; God is merciful and ready to pardon. Both millstones are held profitably if there is hope with correcting fear, and fear with hope.
**“GREGORY”** — THOU SHALT NOT TAKE IN PLACE OF A PLEDGE, etc. We sometimes say "take" for "take away"; whence also we call the birds that seize others hawks [accipitres]. Whence: "If a man devour you, if a man take from you", that is, seize. The debtor's pledge is the confession of the sinner. This is taken when the confession of sin is withheld from the sinner. The upper and the lower millstone are hope and fear. Hope bears up to high things, but fear presses the heart down. One millstone without the other is held uselessly. In the breast of the sinner, then, hope and fear ought always to be joined; because he hopes for mercy in vain if he does not fear justice, and he fears in vain who does not trust.
**“to pledge”** — of the sinner's confession, which is the pledge of amendment
**“the nether”** — fear, which lies unmoving like a sluggish millstone
**“and the upper millstone”** — hope, which turns with wondrous swiftness and grinds and breaks the corn received for the use of men
24.7:
**“If any man be found”** — a seducer
**“soliciting”** — to sin
**“his brother of the children of Israel, and selling him,”** — when we sin we are sold to the devil
**“shall take a price,”** — the end of his intention
**“he shall be put to death,”** — spiritually
**“and thou shalt take away the evil”**
• he shall be excommunicated
• THOU SHALT TAKE AWAY THE EVIL. AUGUSTINE. Scripture says this constantly when it commands the wicked to be killed, as there: "Put away the evil one from among yourselves", that is, according to the Greek, the wicked one in the masculine gender, not "this evil"; namely, him who has committed some such thing that he is worthy of excommunication. For excommunication now does in the Church what killing did then. Although that apostolic saying can be understood otherwise, that each one should put away evil, or the evil one, out of himself. Which sense would be more acceptable if "this evil" or "this wicked thing" had been written, not "this wicked one". But as it is, it is more credible that it was said of a man than of a vice; although it could elegantly be understood that a man puts away from himself the evil man, as it is said: "Put off the old man"; expounding which he says: "He that stole, let him now steal no more."
24.8:
**“Observe diligently”** — from heretics, whose speech spreadeth like a canker
**“that thou incur not the stroke of the leprosy,”**
• of sin or error
• "The scribes and the Pharisees have sitten on the chair of Moses: what they say to you, do"
**“THE STROKE OF THE LEPROSY”** — Note that this infirmity befalls men because of sin, as to Ozias, who usurped the priesthood.
**“but thou shalt do whatsoever shall teach thee”** — against sin or heresy
**“the priests of the Levitical race,”** — it appears that every priest was a Levite, though not every Levite was a priest
**“according to what I have commanded them,”** — not what they add or invent
24.9:
**“Remember”** — that you may beware
**“what the Lord your God did to Mary, in the way when you came out of Egypt.”** — that is, to the synagogue murmuring against the Ethiopian woman, that is, the Church
24.10:
**“When thou shalt demand”** — he forbids violence and commends mercy
**“WHEN THOU SHALT DEMAND”** — AUGUSTINE. It belongs to the work of mercy that the one taking the pledge should not enter the house, lest there be disturbance of the debtor; and he admonishes the debtor to bring forth the pledge to the creditor. But it is a difficulty that he commands the pledge to be restored to the needy man on the same day, because he has nowhere to sleep. Why does he not rather command the creditor not to take what is to be restored the same day? What if he wished it to be done for compelling the debtor? How would he press himself to repay, when he knows he will receive the pledge back the same day? Or perhaps he wished this done for memory's sake, lest he forget to repay? And then would he not repay, if he truly had not [the means]? Especially since he is overcome by the mercy of the creditor, to whom he ought not to be ungrateful if he has received back the pledge in which to sleep. The creditor too, when he has not repaid, ought to believe that he has not [the means], who needs even this mercy, that the pledge be restored to him, having nowhere to sleep.
24.14:
**“Thou shalt not refuse”** — according to the history he commends the affection of mercy and the works of equity toward the poor
**“THOU SHALT NOT REFUSE”** — Let him who preaches the Gospel live by the Gospel. "For the workman is worthy of his hire."
**“the hire of the needy, and the poor, whether he be thy brother,”**
• to whom scrip and purse are forbidden
• who is poor in spirit
**“or a stranger”** — "I am a stranger in the land, and a sojourner, as all my fathers", etc.
**“that dwelleth with thee in the land,”** — of exile
**“and within thy gates”** — the Church: "The Lord loveth the gates of Sion above all the tabernacles of Jacob"
**“is:”** — waiting
24.15:
**“But thou shalt pay him the price of his labour the same day,”**
• the husbandman that laboureth must first partake of the fruits
• "If we have sown unto you spiritual things, is it a great matter if we reap your carnal things?"
**“before the going down of the sun,”** — the end of the world
**“because he is poor,”** — in this world
**“and with it maintaineth his life:”** — until he receive eternal rewards
**“lest he cry”** — in deed, if not in voice
24.16:
**“THE FATHERS SHALL NOT BE PUT TO DEATH”** — AUGUSTINE. The law too says that each one is to be put to death for his own fault. What is it then that is said: "visiting the sins of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation"? Is it to be understood of children not yet born, because of original sin, which the human race drew from Adam? But here a distinction is made concerning children already born, that each should die in his own sin. For he who is already born draws nothing from a sinning father. But when it is said there, "of them that hate me", it is manifest that that condition can be changed if the children have not imitated the deeds of their parents. For that [sin] from Adam too is repaid temporally, because all die on account of it; but not eternally to those who have been regenerated by grace and have remained in it to the end. Although it is rightly asked, if the sins of the fathers are repaid upon the children to those who hate God, why unto the third and fourth generation, passing over the first or second, or not also to the rest, while impiety and the imitation of evil parents continue? Did he wish universality to be understood by seven? Yet he did not set down the seven itself, saying "unto the seventh generation", but the cause of its perfection. For seven is called perfect for this reason, that it consists of the first three, namely the first whole odd number, and the first four, the first whole even number. Similarly I think is to be understood that [saying], "for three crimes and for four I will not turn it away"; for he wished all impieties to be understood, not three or four.
**“for the children, nor the children for the fathers,”** — "The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father", etc.; "The soul that sinneth, the same shall die"
24.17:
**“THOU SHALT NOT PERVERT”** — AUGUSTINE. The Seventy: "Thou shalt not pervert the judgment of the stranger and the orphan and the widow. Thou shalt not take the widow's garment in pledge." Why does he not say: and thou shalt not take their garment in pledge? What is the reason that he forbade the judgment of the three to be perverted, but the garment to be taken in pledge from the widow alone? Unless because the judgments of all those are to be done who have none by whom they may be defended; but he admonishes that the true widows are those who are poor. Whence: "If any widow have children or grandchildren, let her learn first to govern her own house", etc.; and he straightway added: "But she that is a widow indeed and desolate, let her trust in God", etc. He called her a true widow who has none by whom she may be sustained, who is destitute of husband and offspring and all help. For he would not call a rich woman desolate. By the very fact too that he forbids her garment to be taken, he shows her poor; for a creditor would more gladly take silver than a garment. But if she has many things and superfluous, how is she a widow indeed? For the true widow is desolate, and not given to delights. And whatever rich women will not marry, continence is praised in them; desolation is not commended.
**“the judgment of the stranger”** — who cannot defend himself in a foreign land
**“nor of the fatherless,”** — who lacks parents
**“neither shalt thou take away for a pledge the widow's”** — who lacks a husband; nay, poor and utterly desolate, who is the true widow
**“OF THE WIDOW”** — The widow is the soul formerly joined to the devil, from which, when converted, the garment of faith is not to be taken.
24.18:
**“Remember that thou wast a slave in Egypt,”** — the world
**“and delivered thee”**
• in the blood of the Son
• from the power of darkness
**“the Lord thy God from thence. Therefore I command thee”** — lest thou be ungrateful, namely
**“to do this thing.”** — he commends mercy
24.19:
**“When thou hast reaped the corn”** — by meditating on the law
**“in thy field, and hast forgot and a sheaf”** — a spiritual sense
**“left,”** — not being able to understand [it]
**“THOU SHALT NOT RETURN”** — By envying the Gentiles, who are strangers to the testaments of God.
**“to take it away: but the stranger,”** — "Now you are no more strangers and foreigners, but you are fellow citizens with the saints"
**“and the fatherless and the widow”** — which thou hast neglected
**“thou shalt suffer to take it away: that may bless”** — multiply thee and thine
**“thee the Lord thy God in all the works of thy hands.”** — "he that will not work, let him not eat"
24.20:
**“IF THOU HAVE GATHERED THE FRUIT”** — Even if the proud and the wicked gather [them], he does mercy who leaves it with this intent, that the needy may have it. Moreover, when these things are commanded to the people, those who are not in need are admonished not to seek them; but if they do seek them, they are to be judged as robbers of the poor.
**“of thy olive trees,”** — of the Scriptures
**“thou shalt not return to gather whatsoever remaineth on the trees: but shalt leave it for the stranger,”** — as above
24.21:
**“If thou make the vintage of thy vineyard,”** — under which the saint rests
**“THY VINEYARD”** — The vineyard from which is gathered the wine that gladdens the heart of man.
**“thou shalt not gather the clusters that remain,”** — spiritual sentences
**“but they shall be for the stranger,”** — who have left the devil, the father of the wicked
**“the fatherless, and the widow.”** — who has fled the marriage of the devil
24.22: **“Remember that thou also wast a bondman in Egypt,”** — sold under sin

25.1:
**“IF THERE BE A CONTROVERSY”** — AUGUSTINE. The Seventy: "But if there be a dispute between men, and they come to judgment, and the judges justify the just and condemn the wicked, then it shall be, if he that acts wickedly be worthy of stripes, thou shalt set him in the sight of the judges, and they shall scourge him before them according to his wickedness; by number, forty, they shall scourge him and shall not add." It is to be noted that he called him wicked whom he commanded to be punished not with death but with a few stripes. For some think that what is done against a man is not impiety, [as] adultery, which yet is punished with death; but there is a light impiety, which is worthy of the scourge, and there is a grave one, which is worthy of death. So too of the sins which seem to be committed not against God but against man, some are worthy of death, some of the scourge.
**“between men, and they call upon”** — themselves
**“the judges: to him whom they perceive to be just, the prize of justice”** — the victory
25.3:
**“THE NUMBER OF FORTY”** — Forty is completed by ten taken four times; and we consist, according to the body, of the four elements; the precepts of the decalogue are understood by ten. He commands, then, that the judgment or punishment by which the sin of the flesh is struck be ordered according to the precepts; and he wishes all the precepts to be understood in the decalogue.
**“ISIDORE”** — In forty is figured this time, in which the Church, spread through the four parts of the world, lives under the decalogue. We beat offenders with the number forty if in this time we scourge them with the stripes of penance. The sinner then ought to be worn down by temporal scourges, that in the judgment he may be found purged. Blessed is the man who is corrected by the Lord; for no punishment in eternity can afflict those whom the discipline of penance has struck here. If we are beaten here for sins, there we are found without sin.
25.4:
**“Thou shalt not muzzle”** — that is, thou shalt not withdraw sustenance from the preacher, that he may be wholly free for prayer and preaching
**“the ox”** — of the one preaching
**“THE OX”** — ISIDORE. In the ox is expressed the life of those who work, of whom it is said: "The workman is worthy of his hire." Scripture wishes, then, carnal things to be furnished [to those] from whom we receive spiritual things, who, being occupied in doctrine, cannot provide necessaries for themselves.
**“that treadeth out”** — the hearts of the hearers, or the rigour of the Scriptures
**“on the floor”** — the Church
**“thy corn”** — the Scriptures
25.5:
**“WHEN [BRETHREN] DWELL”** — AUGUSTINE. The Seventy: "But if brothers dwell together, and one of them die, and he have no seed, the wife of the deceased shall not [marry] one not near; her husband's brother shall go in to her, and take her to himself as wife, and dwell with her. And the child, whatever shall be born, shall be established from the name of the deceased, and his name shall not be blotted out of Israel." The law, then, seems to have commanded this, that seed be raised up to the brother who is dead. But where it says "shall be established from the name of the deceased", it seems said so that he who is born should have the name of the deceased, to whom he is propagated. Whence it seemed to us better to solve the question in the Gospel about the two fathers of Joseph according to the custom of adoption: one of whom Matthew records, namely him who begot him; the other Luke, namely him whose son he was; because Joseph took the name of neither of them. Unless perhaps "shall be established from the name of the deceased" is understood not that he takes his name, but that [he is established] from his name, that is, as the son not of him by whom he was begotten but of him to whom seed is raised up. And where it is said "his name shall not be blotted out of Israel", it can be understood not that the boy takes his name, but that he will not seem to have died without posterity; and therefore his name, that is, his memory, will remain. For neither, if he himself had begotten a son, would he have given him his own name so that his name should not be blotted out of Israel; but he would not depart this life without children; and this, which he himself could not do, is commanded to be fulfilled from his wife. For even if he were not a brother, a near kinsman took the wife of the dead, as Booz took Ruth, that he might raise up seed for him by whom the wife had not borne. Yet he who was born of her was established from the name of the deceased, because he was called his son lest his name be blotted out; yet he is not called by his name. More abundantly, then, the Gospel question can be solved in two ways: that one of them was so near to the other for taking his wife that this one could have some [men as] ancestors and that one others. For if they had been sons of brothers, they would have had one grandfather; but according to Matthew, Mathan is the grandfather of Joseph; according to Luke, Mathat. But if anyone thinks the likeness of the name so great that the scribes erred by one letter, so that there came to be as it were a small and almost no difference, what would he say of their fathers? For according to Luke Mathat was the son of Levi; according to Matthew Mathan was the son of Eleazar. So going upward the fathers and grandfathers and ancestors are different, as far as Zorobabel, who is about the twentieth going upward from Joseph in Luke, the eleventh in Matthew. He is believed to be the same for this reason, that his father in both is called Salathiel. Yet it could have happened that there was another of the same name, having a father of the same name as the other had; because thereafter, going upward, they are different. For in Luke Zorobabel has the grandfather Neri, in Matthew Jechonias; and from there there is no agreement as far as David: in Matthew it runs through Solomon, in Luke through Nathan. But it seems difficult that there was no one nearer to take the wife of his kinsman than one who was a kinsman from David in so distant a degree, since David in Luke is about the fortieth from Joseph, in Matthew the twenty-seventh. Or if kinsmen by the blood of women were sought for this, it could have happened that someone so near begot Joseph of the wife of a kinsman who died without children, and he had one father by nature, another by law; and in the fathers and grandfathers and ancestors no nearness would appear, because they were near not through males but through females. But if it were so, not even David would occur as the one father; or if anyone contends that he could, we answer that Scripture is not accustomed to set women in place of males in a genealogy; whence the evangelist set in none. For where mothers are mentioned, they are not mentioned except with the fathers. Therefore either a nearer [kinsman] was lacking to join to himself the wife of the deceased, so that the origin of the kinship is found [only] in David, or adoption made the other father whom Joseph could have.
**“brethren together, and one of them”** — Christ, who says: "Go, tell my brethren"
**“without children,”** — because he has not yet filled up the number of the elect
**“WITHOUT CHILDREN”** — He suffered and ascended into heaven, the synagogue still remaining barren.
**“dieth, the wife”**
• the Church
• the synagogue
**“of the deceased”** — of Christ
**“shall not marry to another:”** — to a philosopher or a heretic
**“but shall take her”** — to be his own
**“BUT SHALL TAKE HER”** — He who is able to rule, in whose face, if he is unwilling, the woman spits. For him who does not care to profit others by spiritual gifts, the Church, reproaching him even for these goods of his, as it were spits in the face.
**“his brother”** — the choir of the apostles
**“and raise up”** — by preaching, by exhorting
**“seed for his brother:”**
• the faithful, the saints, the sons of God
• namely, faith and good works from the synagogue
25.6:
**“the first son”** — the holy one
