5.5: **“AND THE PEOPLE”** — ADAMANTIUS. Those who had not been obedient to the commandments of the Lord are called uncircumcised; from which it is understood that those are called uncircumcised who do not obey the commandments of God. But because God loves every soul, he sent Jesus the Son of God to circumcise both the worthy and the unworthy: not the son of Nave, who did not truly and perfectly circumcise the people, but Jesus the Son of God, who truly cleansed body and soul from every defilement of sin.
5.6: **“During the forty years of the journey in the wide wilderness, were uncircumcised: till they were consumed”** — whose fathers, disobedient to the law, disdained to circumcise them
5.7: **“The children of these succeeded in the place of their fathers, and were circumcised by Josue:”** — by Jesus Christ
5.8:
**“Now after they were all circumcised, they remained in the same place of the camp, until they were healed.”** — that is, until they did with love what before seemed difficult
**“NOW AFTER”** — "And the children of Israel, being circumcised, rested in the same place, sitting in the camp until they were healed." It is not enough to be circumcised. After circumcision there is need to be healed and for a scar to form over the wound. To be circumcised through Jesus, then, is to lay aside vices and depraved habits and the worst ways, and to cut off whatever is at variance with the rule of honesty. But in doing this we are constrained by a certain difficulty, and with a certain pain of mind we avoid the fault of habit by a new way of life. In this time, then, we are said to remain as it were in the pain of our circumcision until the scar forms and we are healed, that is, until we fulfil the new ways without difficulty and what before seemed unaccustomed and difficult turns into habit; and then it will rightly be said to us: "This day have I taken away the reproach of Egypt from you."
5.9:
**“And the Lord said to Josue: This day have I taken away from you the reproach of Egypt.”** — all the vices and sins of the Egyptians
**“And the name of that place was called Galgal,”** — that is, revelation; because while one walks in the foreskin of unbelief through the desert of this life he is blind; but as soon as he is circumcised his eyes are opened
5.10:
**“And the children of Israel abode in Galgal,”** — after the second circumcision and the healing
**“AND THEY KEPT”**
• After the reproach of Egypt was taken away, the children of Israel kept the Pasch on the fourteenth day of the month. For neither before circumcision, nor after it before they were healed, could they eat the flesh of the lamb. You see then that no unclean man keeps the Pasch, no uncircumcised man; whence: "Christ our pasch is sacrificed; therefore let us keep the feast, not with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth."
• ISIDORE. After the circumcision of the Gospel, at once in the place of revelation the Pasch is celebrated and the lamb is sacrificed that taketh away the sins of the world; and, the manna of the figurative law failing, the people first eats the bread of the body of Christ, which the incorrupt land of promise, that is, the Virgin Mary, brought forth, whose grain, falling into the earth, brought forth much fruit. Note the order: after, with Jesus Christ as leader, we pass through the streams of the laver, and are signed by faith with the spiritual circumcision, then at last we celebrate the Pasch, that is, we believe that Christ was sacrificed for the salvation of the world, and, believing, we are at once fed with the bread of the Lord's [body].
5.11: **“AND THEY ATE”** — ADAMANTIUS. When the people went out of the land of Egypt, they carried dough with leaven in their garments. When this had failed, manna was given them. But when they came to the holy land and took the fruits of the province of palms, the manna failed them, and they began to eat of the fruits of the land. Three kinds of food, then, are described in general: one on which we feed when going out of the land of Egypt, but this suffices for a short time; after this the manna succeeds; the third we take from the holy land. The fruit that we carry with us from Egypt is this small schooling, or perhaps that of the liberal letters, which can help somewhat. In the wilderness, that is, in the state of this life, we feed on manna while we are instructed in the learning of the divine law. But those who have merited to enter the land of promise, that is, to obtain the promises of Christ, will eat fruit from the region of palms. For he truly will find the fruit of the palm who, the enemy being conquered, shall come to the promises. For however much we may understand in the divine letters, far more sublime will be the things which we shall see not in a riddle but face to face; because eye hath not seen, nor [ear heard], what things God hath prepared … But if the law is taken according to the letter, the children of Israel are found, when they were using better things (for they received manna from heaven by promise), to have received worse; they to whom, when the foods of Egypt failed, a better food, that is, manna, had succeeded. For how is it thought that, the better food ceasing, a worse succeeded?
5.12:
**“And the manna ceased after they ate”** — because "when that which is perfect is come, that which is in part shall be done away"
**“of the corn of the land,”** — of the living
5.13:
**“And when Josue was in the field of the city of Jericho,”** — AUGUSTINE. The Seventy: "In Jericho": not in the city itself, namely, which was not yet taken, but in the field belonging to it
**“he lifted up his eyes,”** — we first lift up our eyes when we begin to see Christ
**“and saw a man standing over against him, drawn”** — the ready sentence by which Jericho was to be punished
**“AND SAW A MAN”** — ADAMANTIUS. "It came to pass, when Jesus was in Jericho, looking up with his eyes he saw a man standing over against him, and a drawn sword was in his hand; and Jesus going to him said to him: Art thou ours, or of the adversaries?" Looking up with his eyes he saw the prince of the host of the power of God, as though he had not looked before; but then, when he was to see the prince of the host of the Lord, he did not see him as a common man, but understood him to be a certain power. He is not yet certain whether what is seen is a divine power or an opposing one; therefore he says: "Art thou ours, or of the adversaries?" "And he said: I am the prince of the host of the power of the Lord; now I am come." When Jesus heard this he adored and said: "Lord, what dost thou command thy servant?" Jesus teaches the same as the Apostle: "Believe not every spirit, but try the spirits if they be of God." Jesus therefore knew not only that he was of God, but that he was God. For he would not have adored unless he had known God. For who else is the prince of the host of the powers but Christ? For the whole host of heaven, whether angels or archangels or virtues or dominations, ever [fights]; all things were made through him, and they serve under him as prince, who is the prince of princes and bestows principality on princes; who says: "Have thou power over ten cities", etc.; who, having received the kingdom, returned.
**“holding a sword,”** — to cut away the filth of our flesh
**“and he went to him, and said: Art thou one of ours, or of our adversaries?”** — believe not every spirit; hence it is said to Jeremias: "If thou wilt separate the precious from the vile, thou shalt be as my mouth"
5.14:
**“And he answered: No: but I am prince of the host of the Lord,”** — Christ is the prince of the heavenly host, because "all things were made by him" and he gave to each his principality
**“FELL”** — It can be asked whether he prostrated himself to an angel and called him Lord, or rather, because he understood that it was God, understanding by whom he had been sent, he called him Lord and prostrated himself to him.
**“Josue fell on his face to the ground.”** — because he understood that it was God
5.15:
**“Loose, saith he, thy shoes”** — every mortal bond
**“LOOSE, SAITH HE”** — ISIDORE. Jesus is in Jericho. The enemies still hold the city, not yet taken; and yet it is said to Jesus: "Loose, saith he, thy shoe; for the place in which thou standest is holy ground." How is Jericho holy ground, which is held by the enemies? But perhaps wherever the prince of the power of the Lord comes, he sanctifies the place. I dare further and say: where Moses stood, the place was not of itself holy, but the presence of the Lord who was with him had sanctified the place; therefore it is said to him: "The place in which thou standest is holy ground", etc. And we, if by life and merits we draw near to God and are made worthy that God should stand by us, will be told to loose from the feet of our soul whatever mortal bond is in them. For these are the feet which Jesus washed, and unless he wash them we shall have no part with him. If then we loose from our soul and senses every bond of mortal guilt, at once God gladly cleaves to us and stands by us.
**“from off thy feet.”** — namely, of the soul, which unless Jesus wash we shall have no part with him
**“For the place whereon thou standest is holy.”** — because, namely, I am there

6.1:
**“Jericho”** — the world
**“NOW JERICHO”** — THE SAME. Jericho is surrounded, and it must be taken. No sword is drawn against it, no bow or ram is aimed at it, nor are darts hurled; only trumpets are applied by the priests, and by them the walls of Jericho are overthrown. Jericho signifies this world. Whence: a certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among robbers: he was the figure of Adam, who was thrust out of paradise into the exile of this world. The blind also who were in Jericho, whom God enlightened, signified those who in this world were oppressed by the blindness of ignorance. Jericho, then, that is, the world, is to fall. For the consummation of the world has long since been published in the holy volumes; and the consummation will come about by the voices of trumpets; whence the Apostle: "For the trumpet shall sound, and the dead" who are in Christ [shall rise] first; and the Lord himself shall come down from heaven with commandment, and with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God. Then therefore Jesus will conquer Jericho with trumpets and lay it low, so that out of it the harlot alone is saved and all her house. Jesus therefore will come, and with the voice of trumpets. But even now let us pray that he come and destroy that world which is seated in wickedness, and all the things that are set in the world; because all that is in the world is the concupiscence of the flesh, and the concupiscence of the eyes, and the pride of life. But let him save this one alone, who received his spies, who set his apostles, received in faith and obedience, in the upper places; and let him join this harlot with the house of Israel. But let us no longer reckon her old fault: once she was a harlot; but now she is joined as a chaste virgin to one husband, Christ. Whence: "I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ." For, that she might escape and not perish with Jericho, she received from the spies a most powerful sign of salvation, the scarlet cord; for through the blood of Christ the Church is saved.
**“ISIDORE”** — JERICHO is interpreted moon. And the moon signifies the world, because, as the moon wanes in its monthly courses, so this world, running toward the consummation of the times, falls by daily waning. In the ark the Church is figured; the strong preachers in the trumpets of brass. For the Israelites, bearing the ark, go round this city of Jericho for seven days with brazen trumpets sounding, and its walls fall at the presence of the ark and the sound of the trumpets. For in this time, which revolves in the succession of seven days, while the ark is carried, that is, while the Church, going round the whole world, is moved, at the voices of the preachers, as at the sound of the trumpets, the walls of Jericho, that is, the obstacles of the world's pride and of the haughtiness of unbelief, fall; until at the end of the times the last enemy, death, is destroyed, and from the perdition of the wicked the one house of Rahab, that is, the Church, is freed, cleansed from the filthiness of fornication, through the window of confession, in the blood of remission. For this harlot dwells in Jericho, that is, in this mortal body, that is, in the world; who, that she may be saved, puts out the scarlet through the window of her house, as through the mouth of her body, which is the sign of the blood of Christ, confessing unto salvation through the remission of sins. Those who were found in her house were saved from the destruction of the city; and whoever are found within the Church are saved. Outside this house, that is, outside the Church, no one is saved.
**“was close shut up and fenced,”** — by worldly cunning, or blocked up
6.2:
**“And the Lord said”** — the Father
**“to Josue”** — to Christ
**“Behold I have given into thy hands”** — power
**“Jericho”** — the world
**“and the king thereof,”** — the prince of this world
**“and all the valiant men.”** — the demons, or any who are mighty in the world
6.3:
**“Go round about the city, all ye fighting men,”** — the preachers
**“once a day: so shall ye do for six days.”** — through the whole time of the present life
6.4: **“And on the seventh day the priests”** — for the consummation of the world has long since been published in the holy volumes
6.5:
**“And when the voice of the trumpet shall give a longer and broken tune,”** — which now sounds, now is silent
**“AND WHEN JOSUE”** — ADAMANTIUS. Jericho is overthrown by the trumpets of the priests: for as soon as the blare of the trumpets sounded, the walls were cast down. For we see that the strength of the world and its defences have been destroyed by the priestly trumpets: namely, the worship of idols, the deceit of divinations supplied by the art of demons, the contrivances of augurs, soothsayers and magicians, by all which, as by walls, the world was surrounded. Besides, it was fortified as by tall and strong towers by the various doctrines of the philosophers, their most lofty assertions and disputations. But Jesus Christ, coming, sent priests, that is, his apostles, bearing the beaten trumpets of preaching, the holy, magnificent and heavenly doctrine. Matthew first sounded the priestly trumpet in his Gospel. Mark also and Luke and John sang with these trumpets. Peter resounds with the two trumpets of his epistles; James also and Jude and John sound the trumpet through their epistles, and Luke describing the acts of the apostles. Last, Paul, thundering forth fourteen epistles, overthrew as with trumpets the walls of Jericho, and all the engines of idolatry and the doctrines of the philosophers.
**“and shall sound in your ears, all the people shall shout together with a very great shout, and the walls of the city shall fall to the ground.”** — because at the consummation of the world the trumpet shall sound, and the dead who are in Christ shall rise first, and the Lord himself shall come down from heaven with the trumpet of God
6.16:
**“And when in the seventh going about sounded with the trumpets”** — of preaching
**“the priests, Josue said to all Israel: Shout.”** — others: Make jubilee
6.17:
**“And let this city be”** — the world
**“AND LET THE CITY BE”** — ADAMANTIUS. "Keep yourselves from the anathema, lest perhaps you covet and take of the anathema, and make the camp of the children of Israel an anathema, and crush yourselves and all the synagogue of the Lord." As if [to say]: see that you have nothing worldly in you, nor bring anything of the world with you to the Church, but let all worldly conversation be an anathema to you. Do not mingle worldly things with divine; as if [to say]: "Love not the world, nor the things which are in the world"; whence: "Be not conformed to this world", etc. For those who do these things take of the anathema. Those Christians also who celebrate the solemnities of the Gentiles bring the anathema into the Church; and those who inquire into the lives and deeds of men from the courses of the stars, and those who observe the flight of birds and the like, pollute the camp of the Lord and cause the people of God to be conquered. For a little leaven corrupteth the whole lump.
**“an anathema, and all things that are in it, to the Lord.”** — that no one take anything thence for himself
**“Let only Rahab the harlot live, with all”** — the Gentiles converted to the faith, who before played the harlot with idols
**“that are with her in the house: for she hid the messengers”** — the preachers
**“whom we sent.”** — go "into the whole world and preach the gospel to every creature"
6.18:
**“But beware ye lest you touch ought of those things that are forbidden,”** — that is, bring nothing worldly with you into the Church
**“and you be guilty of transgression, and all the camp of Israel be under sin, and be troubled.”** — "A little leaven corrupteth the whole lump."
6.20:
**“So all making a shout,”** — making jubilee
**“SO ALL MAKING A SHOUT”** — THE SAME. All the people is said to have shouted with a great shout, or, according to others, to have made jubilee with a great jubilee. Of this jubilee it is said: "Make jubilee to God, all the earth"; and elsewhere: "Blessed is the people that knoweth jubilation." He did not say "that worketh justice" or "that knoweth mysteries", but "that knoweth jubilation". In other places the fear of the Lord makes good or blessed, but only one man: "For blessed, he says, is the man that feareth the Lord." Elsewhere also many are made blessed, as the poor in spirit, or the meek, or the peacemakers, or the clean of heart. But this beatitude, poured out, makes blessed a whole people, namely, that which knoweth jubilation. Whence this jubilation seems to me to signify a certain affection of concord and unanimity; which, if it fall upon two or three disciples of Christ, whatsoever they shall ask in the name of the Saviour shall be done for them. But if the beatitude be so great that the whole people remain of one mind, say the same thing, in the same mind and the same judgment, when such a people lifts up its voice with one accord, there will happen what is written in the Acts of the Apostles: that a great earthquake was made where the apostles were praying with one mind with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus; and by this earthquake all earthly things would fall and the world itself would be overthrown. To this Jesus exhorts, saying: "Have confidence, I have overcome the world." Under his leadership, then, the world is now conquered for us, and its walls have fallen, on which the men of the world relied.
**“AND SOUNDING”** — Let each of us fulfil these things in himself. Thou hast Jesus in thee as leader through faith. "Make thee beaten trumpets" from the holy Scriptures; draw thence thy meanings, thence thy words; for that is why they are called beaten trumpets. Sound on them, that is, in psalms, in hymns, in spiritual canticles. If thou sound on such trumpets and carry the ark of the testament round seven times, that is, if thou do not separate the mystical precepts of the law from the trumpets of the Gospel; if also thou require of thyself the consent of jubilation, that is, if the people of thy thoughts and senses always utter a concordant and harmonious voice; and if thou do not sometimes speak the truth and sometimes lie in flattering; if thou art not now soft with slackness, now savage with anger; and if within thee the flesh does not lust against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh: send forth the voice of jubilation, because the world is conquered for thee. Hence Paul said: "But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom the world is crucified to me, and I to the world."
**“when the voice and the sound thundered in the ears of the multitude, the walls forthwith fell down:”** — the worship of idols, the deceit of divination and the like
**“THE WALLS FORTHWITH FELL DOWN”** — At the coming of Jesus the walls of Jericho were overthrown; that is, at the coming of Christ the world is conquered; whence Paul: that which was contrary to us he took out of the way, fastening it to the cross; and despoiling the principalities and powers, he hath exposed them confidently, triumphing over them on the wood of the cross. From these words I understand that the heavenly virtues, principalities and powers, seeing the battle of Jesus, the strong man bound and his goods plundered, sounded the heavenly trumpets, because, the prince of the world being bound, the world is conquered; and the heavenly host gave the voice of jubilation to the king in his triumph. Truly, then, the people of the Gentiles is set free, which knows this jubilation and acknowledges and believes the mysteries.
6.23: **“AND WENT IN”** — ADAMANTIUS. "Jesus saved alive Rahab the harlot and all the house of her father, and she was added to Israel unto this present day", etc. How was she added unto this present day? For this is the custom of holy Scripture, to say it of things that remain until the end of life or of the world: as "this is the father of the Moabites unto this present day", that is, until the end of the world; and "this word was spread abroad among the Jews unto this present day", that is, as long as the world stands. But how was Rahab added to the house of Israel unto this present day? Is her posterity ascribed to the mother, so that she seems to be preserved in her offspring? Or is it rather to be understood that she has truly been joined to Israel unto this present day? For the branch of the wild olive is set, that is, grafted, into the root of the good olive and joined to Israel unto this present day; because we who were taken from the Gentiles into their root, who once played the harlot, worshipping wood and stone for God, have been made above through the faith of Christ, but that people below through unbelief. For he who has in himself Christ, who is the head of all, is made the head; but those who denied him are made the tail, and those who were first are made last.
6.25: **“But Josue saved Rahab the harlot and her father's house, and all she had, and they dwelt in the midst of Israel”** — because the branches cut from the wild olive have been grafted into the root of the fatness of the olive

7.1:
**“But the children of Israel transgressed the commandment, and took to their own use of the anathema. For Achan”** — in Paralipomenon: Achar; in Josue: Acham, or Achor
**“AND WAS ANGRY”** — ADAMANTIUS. It is not to be passed over idly that, when one sinned, wrath came upon the whole people. This happens when the priests who preside over the people wish to seem kind toward the offender, and, fearing the tongues of sinners lest perhaps they speak ill of them, unmindful of priestly severity, they will not rebuke the sinner publicly before all that the rest may have fear, nor do they put away the evil from among themselves, nor deliver such a one to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved; and while they spare one, they work the destruction of the whole Church. "For by one diseased sheep the whole flock is infected." Let us then watch over one another, and let the conversation of each be known especially to the priests and ministers. For we are all one body in Christ. Thou who presidest art the eye of this body, that thou mayst look round on all things and foresee all things to come. Thou art the shepherd of the Lord's sheep: dost thou see them carried over precipices and hanging over steep places, and not run to meet them? Dost thou not call them back? Dost thou not at least deter them with a cry? We do not say this so that someone should be cut off for a light fault; but if, perhaps admonished or corrected once, twice and a third time, he does not amend, let us use the physician's discipline. If we have anointed with oil, if we have soothed with plasters, softened with poultices, and yet the hardness of the swelling does not yield to the medicines, the only remedy left is cutting. Whence: "If thy hand scandalize thee, cut it off, and cast it from thee." This is what he says: that if I, who seem to be thy right hand and am called a priest and seem to preach the word of the Lord, do anything against the rule of the Gospel, so as to cause scandal to the Church, the whole Church, agreeing together in consent upon this, should cut me off and cast me from it. For it is better for thee, the Church, to enter into the kingdom of heaven without me, thy hand, who by doing evil caused scandal, than to go with me into hell.
**“AUGUSTINE”** — It is usually asked how vengeance is justly taken on some for the sins of another, since it is said in the law that neither fathers are to be punished for the iniquities of their sons, nor sons for those of their fathers. Was that precept given to men when they judge, that they should not punish one for another? But the judgments of God are not of that kind, who by his high and invisible counsel knows how far to extend even a temporal punishment of men and a wholesome terror. For nothing dreadful, so far as pertains to the governance of the whole world, befalls mortals when they die, who must die sometime; and yet among those who fear such things discipline is established, so that each one in the people does not care for himself alone, but they show diligence toward one another, and, as of one body and one man, the members are solicitous for one another. Nor yet is it to be believed that in the punishments inflicted after death one can be condemned for another; but that this punishment is inflicted only in those things which were to have an end, even if they did not end in this way. So also it is shown how closely the whole is bound together in the fellowship of the people, so that they are reckoned not singly in themselves but as parts in a whole. Through the sin of one, then, and the death of a few, the whole people was admonished to seek, as in a whole body, what had been lost. At the same time it was shown how much evil would have come about if the whole congregation had sinned, when not even one could be so judged that the rest could be secure from him. But if Achan had been found and seized by someone and brought, guilty of the crime, to the judgment of Jesus, it is not to be thought that a human judge would have punished anyone else, who was not bound up in the fellowship of his deed, for him or with him. For it was not lawful to go beyond the commandment of the law which was given to men, lest by his own judgment, which has been granted or permitted to man over man, he should think one to be punished for another. But God judges by a far more secret judgment, who is able even after death, which man cannot, either to free or to destroy. The visible afflictions of men, then, or their deaths, since they can both hurt and help those on whom they are brought, God knows in the secret of his providence how to dispense justly to each, even when he seems to avenge the sins of some on others. But the invisible punishments, which hurt and do not help, no one pays for the sins of others when God is judge; as, when man is judge, no one ought to pay these visible ones except for his own fault. For this God commanded the human judge: that in the things which pertain to human judgment he should do what God himself does in his own judgment, whither human power does not aspire.
7.15: **“And whosoever he be that shall be found guilty of this fact, he shall be burnt with fire with all his substance,”** — with a vehement punishment, which the iron furnace of Egypt signifies
7.21:
**“For I saw among the spoils a scarlet garment exceeding good,”** — the adornment of worldly conversation
**“and two hundred sicles of silver, and a golden rule of fifty sicles: and I coveted them, and I took them away, and hid them in the ground in the midst of my tent, and the silver I covered with the earth that I dug up.”** — A GOLDEN RULE ALSO. "He stole a golden tongue and put it in his tent." I do not think there was so great a force of sin in that theft of a little gold that it should stain so numerous a Church of God; but there is much grace in words, much beauty in the speeches of the rhetoricians or philosophers, who are all of the city of Jericho, that is, of this world. If then you find among the philosophers perverse doctrines adorned with the assertions of brilliant speech, this is the golden tongue. But then let not the glitter of the work deceive thee, let not the golden beauty of speech carry thee away. Remember that Jesus commanded all the gold that should be found in Jericho to be anathema. If thou read a poet weaving gods and goddesses in a shining poem, be not delighted by the sweetness of eloquence: it is a golden tongue. If thou take it away and put it in thy tent, that is, if thou bring into thy heart the things that are asserted by them, thou wilt pollute the whole Church of the Lord. We ought then to examine diligently lest anyone have a Jericho tongue hidden in his tent; and let us cast away the evil from among ourselves; [the evil] which, even if we cease [to examine], God will expose, so that he confess of his own accord and say: "I have stolen a golden tongue and pure dextraria" [so the edition]. The dextraria are works in which nothing divine is mingled, but all is done according to man; [whereas] we confess Christ God and man. What was stolen from Jericho is called pure, that is, without God, which was to the thief the cause of sin. A GOLDEN RULE ALSO. The Seventy: "tongue": of the heretics, namely, their doctrines, or the superstitious studies of worldly letters. For this is the golden tongue, fitted with brilliant speech. This the heretics stole from Jericho as a golden rule, who have tried to bring the sect of the philosophers into the Church; by whose anathema many perish and are extinguished, as with a heap of stones, by the multitude of sins; whose leader is the devil, who, having conquered some of the faithful through their impiety, is overcome again and conquered, and, hanged by the people of God, is slain by the power of the cross.
**“ISIDORE”** — Jericho signifies the world; he hides of its anathema in his tent who brings worldly manners into the secret places of the Church; who, remaining under the worship of God, loves the solemnities or spectacles of the world; who seeks out sorcerers, soothsayers and augurs, or does the other things that were held in Jericho, that is, in the world.
7.25: **“AND STONED HIM”** — AUGUSTINE. It is asked, since the Lord commanded that he who had committed the theft, when he had been caught, should be burned with fire, why Jesus rather had him stoned. Or ought he to have died thus? How did Jesus understand the words of him who commanded? For another could not easily have understood so; therefore we must rather ask why the Lord called the stoning fire than believe that Jesus did otherwise than the Lord had commanded. For who could be wiser to understand the words of the Lord, or more obedient to do them? But by the name of fire punishment could be signified, as there: "He brought us out of the iron furnace", namely out of hard tribulation. Two reasons occur to me, not that both are so, but one of them, why he was not burned with manifest fire with all his household. If the Lord judged his sin to be such that, expiated by that punishment, he would not punish it for ever, that punishment was called fire because of the purgation itself. Nor would anyone be moved to tend toward this understanding if visible fire had burned him up; but everyone would rest in what is seen to be openly fulfilled, and would inquire no further. But now, because of the words of God and the deed of Josue, by which those words could not be transgressed, the stoning is rightly said to have been fire, that it may be recognized that that man was purged by that punishment, so as not to be punished hereafter; which the vessels in Leviticus signify, which are commanded to be purged with fire. But if that sin was such that the fire of hell would receive him even after this life, Jesus therefore wished him to be stoned, that what was said by the Lord, "he shall be burned with fire", might be understood as what the Lord would do, not what was to be done by them. For it was not said: You shall burn with fire, etc. Since, then, it was said so that God might seem rather to have foretold what was to befall him than to have commanded what should be done to him by men, Jesus, who understood the divine words as a prophet, and who did this very thing prophetically, could not do better than to kill him with stones rather than with flames, lest the words of the Lord, which he wished to be understood as spoken of something else, should seem fulfilled by [these] fires. Nor ought it to trouble us that God foretold that not only he but all that were his should be burned with fire; for he says: "He shall be burned with fire, and all that he hath." For all these can be understood as the works which he said were to be burned with him. For as the Apostle says of certain works consumed by fire, "but he himself shall be saved": if this man's sin is to be so understood that he is also punished with eternal fire. His sons, then, and his daughters, with the cattle and all that he had, the people overwhelmed with stones together, when it punished him. Yet Jesus did this not by human judgment but by the prophetic spirit: whether so understanding "all that he hath" that he judged not even the sons excepted, applying the punishment of stoning in place of fire; or [understanding] his works, which after his death were to be burned in him, signifying them not only by the other things that were his but also by the sons. Nor is it therefore to be believed that they, who were innocent of their father's sin, are to be burned after death with the fire of hell. For death, which awaits all, although it comes from the first sin, because we are so born that we must needs die, is hastened for some; whence: "He was taken away lest wickedness should alter his understanding." By what judgment or mercy of God, then, it was inflicted on his sons, or on those thirty-six men, when all were strangers to his sin, lies hidden with him in whom there is no iniquity. But this is plain: that the people had to seek terribly what was lost; and the others feared to imitate his deed the more, the more human weakness shuddered at being given over to so great and so just a hatred of the people, and at dying with those, consumed with it by its own sin, whom it thought to leave behind for the hope of continuing its line.

8.1: **“TO THE TOWN OF HAI”** — ADAMANTIUS. First, because of sins, we were conquered, and those who dwelt in Hai killed many. For Hai is interpreted chaos, which is the dwelling of the demons, whose king is the devil; against whom Jesus comes. He divides the people into two parts: some he sets in front, others behind, to come unexpectedly upon the backs of the enemies. The first are the Jews, of whom it is said: I am not sent but "to the lost sheep of the house of Israel"; and elsewhere: "to the Jew first, and to the Greek", that is, to the Gentile, afterwards. The Jewish people, then, is that which is set first and as it were fleeing with Jesus; but the latter is the Gentile, coming as it were unexpectedly. For who would have hoped that the Gentiles would be saved? It smites the adversaries more fiercely from behind; and so both peoples shut in the crowd of demons in the middle and conquer it. Those who follow Jesus seemed to flee from the burden of the law, the observance of the sabbath, the circumcision of the flesh and the like; but again, he does not flee who follows Christ, the perfection and fulness of the law.
8.2:
**“LAY AN AMBUSH”** — AUGUSTINE. When one has undertaken a just war, one for whom it is lawful to make war (for it is not lawful for all), whether he conquer in open battle or by ambushes makes no difference to justice. And just wars are usually defined as those that avenge injuries, if the nation or city that is to be attacked in war has either neglected to punish what was wickedly done by its own people, or to restore what was taken away by injuries. But this kind of war also is just which God commands, with whom there is no iniquity, and who knows what ought to be done to each. In which war the leader of the army or the people itself is to be judged not so much the author of the war as its minister.
**“AUGUSTINE”** — It is to be asked whether every will to deceive is to be reckoned a lie; and if so, whether there can be a just lie, by which he is deceived who deserves to be deceived; and if not even this is found just, it remains that what was done concerning the ambushes be referred to the truth according to some signification.
8.15: **“AND FLEEING”** — ADAMANTIUS. What do you think Jesus fleeing signifies? Let us see whether there is some such thing that we conquer by fleeing. That there is some perfect virtue in flight Paul shows, saying: "Fly fornication." You see then that there is a certain kind of fornication which we ought to flee if we wish to live chastely in Christ. This flight, then, brings forth salvation. In like manner we ought to flee anger, avarice, envy, spite, detraction and the like. This is the army of Hai which Jesus taught us to flee; whence: "If they persecute you, flee into another." For he wishes us to flee enemies of this kind; and if by fleeing we escape the contagion of these evils, the angels, seeing our devotion and the purpose of our mind, and that we suffer the harassment of the demons, rise up and slay them, smiting them from behind. For Jesus is with those who flee rather than with those who pursue. For he loves those who flee fornication, deceit, lying and the like.
8.24: **“So all being slain that had pursued after Israel in his flight to the wilderness, and falling by the sword in the same place, the children of Israel returned and laid waste the city.”** — SO ALL. ADAMANTIUS. "They smote them with the edge of the sword, until there was not left of them one that should be saved", etc. It shows us that of those whose dwelling is chaos, that is, the demons who reign in the abyss, we ought to leave none at all, but slay all: not their substance, namely, but the work and endeavour by which they make men sin. For this is their life, if we sin, and their destruction, if we do not sin. The saints, then, slay the inhabitants of Hai and let none go, who keep their heart with all diligence, lest evil thoughts proceed from it, and [keep] their mouth, lest an evil word proceed thence: this is to leave none to escape, when not even an evil word escapes. Let us then destroy all who dwell in chaos, that is, the opposing powers, and leave none to escape. For so we shall keep the feast day to God and rejoice in glad solemnity. When therefore you read in the Scriptures of the battles of the just, the slaughter of the slain, and that the saints spare none of the enemies, and that if they spared any it was reckoned to them as sin, as to Saul, who kept alive Agag king of Amalec, they are to be understood as we have expounded: that these wars are waged against sin. For how will they be just if they keep even a little sin in themselves? Therefore it is said of them that they left not one; whence: "You have not yet resisted unto blood, striving against sin." Hence it is said elsewhere: "Sanctify war", and "Fight the battles of the Lord". For what is it to sanctify war, unless, all the enemies of the soul, that is, the vices, being slain, "and the members which are upon the earth being mortified", and all evil desires cut off, one be made "holy in body and in spirit", and, doing valiantly, come to the sight of the living God and be crowned for the palm of victory by the merit of virtue?
8.28: **“And he burned the city, and made it a heap for ever.”** — not only this according to the letter, but the place of the demons will be uninhabitable for ever, when no one will sin any more nor sin reign, when the devil and his angels shall go "into everlasting fire"
8.29:
**“And he hung the king thereof on a gibbet until the evening and the going down of the sun. Then he commanded, and they took down his carcass from the gibbet: and threw it in the very entrance of the city, heaping upon it a great heap of stones, which remaineth until this present day.”** — HIS KING ALSO. ADAMANTIUS. The king of Hai is hanged on a twofold tree: the devil, namely, on the cross of Christ, which was twofold, that is, consists in a twofold reason; because visibly the Son of God was crucified in the flesh, but invisibly the devil with his principalities and powers. Whence the Apostle: "That which was contrary to us he took out of the way, fastening it to his cross; and despoiling the principalities and powers, he hath exposed them confidently, triumphing over them on the wood of the cross"; although in other copies it has "triumphing over them in himself", yet among the Greeks it has "on the wood". Twofold, then, is the reason of the Lord's cross: one in which Christ, crucified, left us an example; the other in which that cross was the trophy over the devil, on which he was crucified and triumphed over. Whence: "But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom the world is crucified to me, and I to the world." You see how the Apostle sets forth the twofold reason of the cross. For he says that two things contrary to each other are crucified: himself, namely, the saint, and the world of sins; as we said, Christ and the devil. "For we are crucified to the world when the prince of the world, coming, finds nothing in us; and the world is crucified in us" when we do not receive the concupiscences of sin. But someone will say: if the devil and his army have been slain, how does he still prevail against the servants of God, and "as a roaring lion go about seeking whom he may devour"? But the coming of Christ, one indeed, has been completed in humility; another is hoped for in glory; and this first coming in the flesh is mystically called in the Scriptures his shadow. Whence: "The breath of our mouth, Christ the Lord, to whom we said: Under thy shadow we shall live among the Gentiles." Whence we understand that many things are foreshadowed in his first coming whose fulfilment will be completed in the second. And the Apostle says that "he hath raised us up together with him, and hath made us sit together in the heavenly places": which we do not yet see fulfilled, but they are now foreshadowed here through faith, because in mind and hope we are lifted up from earthly and dead works and daily raise our heart to heavenly things; but in the second coming the things we now believe and hope will be fulfilled. Thus, then, the devil has been conquered and crucified, but for those who have been crucified with Christ; but for all he will be crucified when that shall be fulfilled which the Apostle says: "As in Adam all die, so also in Christ all shall be made alive." This, then, is also the mystery of the resurrection to come. For then too the people will be divided into two parts, and some will be first, others last: whoever have joined together in one to Jesus; and there will be no more devil, nor death. Whence: "We who are alive, who are left unto the coming of the Lord, shall not prevent them who have slept; for the Lord himself shall come down from heaven with commandment, and with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God; and the dead who are in Christ shall rise first; then we who are alive", etc. And of the devil he says: "The enemy death shall be destroyed last", etc.
**“ADAMANTIUS”** — The Seventy: "on a twofold tree". This is the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, on which the good one, that is, Christ, and the evil one, that is, the devil, hung: but the evil one that he might perish, the good one that he might live by power; because "he was crucified through weakness, yet he liveth by the power of God"; and not only that he might live, but that he might give life. He is "the last Adam, a quickening spirit".
8.30:
**“Then Josue built an altar to the Lord God”** — he had to offer to God something worthy of so great a victory
**“THEN JOSUE BUILT”** — ADAMANTIUS. "Jesus built an altar to the Lord God of Israel", etc. All of us who believe in Christ are called living stones, according to that: "But you are living stones", etc. And as the stronger stones are laid first in the foundation, that the weight of the building may be set upon them, and the second, a little weaker, are placed next; those still weaker [are set] a little higher; and then, by comparison, the stones that are weakest are placed in the upper parts, near the very top: the same is to be understood of the living stones. "The apostles and prophets" are in the foundations; whence: "Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the chief corner stone." And Christ himself is the foundation of the spiritual building; whence: "For other foundation no man can lay, but that which is laid, which is Christ Jesus." Blessed then are they who have raised holy buildings upon so noble a foundation. But in this building there must be an altar. Whoever then, being living stones, give themselves to prayers and supplications and offer the victims of entreaty, of these Jesus builds an altar. But see what praise is ascribed to the stones of the altar, as the lawgiver Moses said that the altar was to be built of whole stones on which no iron had been laid. Each one's conscience knows who is whole, incorrupt, unpolluted, unspotted in flesh and spirit, on whom iron has not been laid, that is, who has not received the fiery darts of the wicked one but has quenched and repelled them with the shield of faith; or who it is that has never received the iron of fighting, of war, of strife, but has always been peaceable, quiet, meek and formed in the humility of Christ. These are the living stones of which the altar is made, that Jesus may offer upon them holocausts and sacrifices of salvation. But there is still lacking what Jesus adds to all these. "Jesus wrote", he says, "upon the stones of the altar the Deuteronomy, the law of Moses", etc. But how could he do this? But our Jesus wrote in living and whole stones the Deuteronomy, that is, the second law. Whence he himself says: "It was said to them of old: Thou shalt not kill. But I say to you: whosoever is angry with his brother is a murderer", etc. You see the Deuteronomy which Jesus wrote "in living and whole stones, not in tables of stone but in the fleshly tables of the heart, not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God"; whence: "For when the Gentiles, who have not the law, do by nature those things that are of the law, these, having not the law, are a law to themselves, who shew the work of the law written in their hearts", etc. And now, through these things that we speak, Jesus writes the Deuteronomy in the hearts of those who receive with whole faith and all their mind, as in whole stones.
**“AUGUSTINE”** — How could he write a great book upon stones, and the children of Israel remaining there until he had written it out? But our Jesus needs no long delay to fix the second law in the hearts of believers who are worthy of the building of the altar.
8.31:
**“As Moses the servant of the Lord had commanded the children of Israel, and it is written in the book of the law of Moses: an altar of unhewn stones”**
• These living stones are the apostles, both whole and undefiled, making one altar because of unanimity and concord, praying with one mind. Upon this altar Jesus offers sacrifice to the Father. We too can be made stones of the altar. For Christ does not forsake us, and the Spirit helps our prayers and offers our prayers to the Father.
• to all the faithful, who are living stones
**“which iron had not touched”** — because incorrupt in flesh and spirit
8.32:
**“And he wrote upon stones the Deuteronomy of the law of Moses,”** — the Gospel, namely, in the hearts of believers
**“which he”** — by giving the sacraments of the faith
**“had ordered before the children of Israel.”**
• These are the heavenly virtues, the angels, that is, the Church of the firstborn, who stand by in such things
• who "always see the face of the Father"
8.33:
**“And all the people, and all the ancients, and the princes and judges stood on both sides of the ark, before the priests”**
• who live in priestly religion
• ALL THE PEOPLE, etc. "And all Israel, and the elders and judges and scribes, went on this side and that of the ark of the testament of the Lord", etc. The ark of the testament of the Lord is that in which the tables of the law, written by the hand of God, are kept; and around it walks he who is truly Israel, nor is he far from it; but the levites and priests carried it on their shoulders. For all who live in priestly religion and holiness, not only those who sit in the priestly seat but rather those who act in a priestly way, whose portion is the Lord, they are the priests and levites of the Lord, who carried the law on their shoulders, namely by fulfilling in work the things that are written in the law.
**“that carried the ark of the covenant of the Lord,”** — by fulfilling in work the law that was in the ark
**“both the stranger”**
• the catechumen, or he who now strives to be joined to the faithful
• BOTH THE STRANGER, etc. "But both the proselyte and the native together, and half were beside mount Garizim"; and who are the half who, though they are saved, yet could not walk beside mount Garizim, but walk beside mount Hebal? Mount Garizim has the blessings; mount Hebal the curses, which hang over sinners. For they set, as is written in Deuteronomy, six tribes to bless on mount Garizim, the nobler and choice ones, that is, Simeon, Levi, Juda, Issachar, Joseph and Benjamin; but six more ignoble to curse, among whom is Ruben, who went up to his father's bed, and Zabulon, who is the last son of Lia. I see two kinds of those who hasten to salvation through faith: one of those who, kindled with desire for the heavenly promises, strive with the greatest zeal lest even the highest beatitude pass them by, desiring not only to obtain the blessing and be made "partakers of the lot of the saints", but always to stand in the sight of God. But others, even if they tend toward salvation, do so not so much for love of the blessings or promises as lest they go into hell; as if they said: It is enough for me not to go into everlasting fire, not to be cast out "into the exterior darkness". Those halves, then, that walk beside mount Garizim, which was chosen for the blessing, signify those who come to salvation not from fear of punishment but from desire of the blessing and the promise. And nobler are those who do good from desire of the good itself and of the blessing than those who do it from fear of punishment. But Jesus alone is able to discern such minds out of the whole people, and to set some on mount Garizim for the blessings, others on mount Hebal for the curses: not that they may receive the curses, but that, fearing the curses prescribed and the punishments appointed for sinners, they may beware of incurring them.
**“and he that was born among them,”** — the Christian
**“half of them by mount Garizim,”** — who works well for love of the good and of the promised blessing
**“and half by mount Hebal,”** — who do well for fear of punishment and of the curse that is to be avoided
**“as Moses had commanded”** — the law
**“the servant of the Lord. And first he blessed the people of Israel.”** — he gave the grace of understanding, that in the law we may have the mind of Christ
8.34: **“AFTER THIS HE READ”** — ADAMANTIUS. It is related that Jesus read all the words of the law, the blessings and the curses, etc. I think that whenever Moses is read to us, and through the grace of the Lord "the veil of the letter is removed", and we begin to understand and love [it], because "the law is spiritual", the Lord Jesus reads the law and recites these things in the ears of the people, commanding that we not follow "the letter that killeth, but hold the spirit that quickeneth". Jesus, then, reads us the law when he reveals the secrets of the law; whence: but we have the mind of Christ, that we may know the things that are given us from God.
8.35:
**“He left out nothing of those things which Moses had commanded, but he repeated all before all the multitude of Israel,”**
• of the "perfect", namely, to whom belongs "strong meat"
• NOTHING OF THOSE THINGS. "There was not a word of those which Moses commanded which Jesus did not read in the ears of the whole church of Israel"; it is added also: "to the women and infants and proselytes". For our Jesus knows that there are ears besides these fleshly ones, of which he says: "He that hath ears to hear, let him hear." In these ears, then, Jesus reads the law. If then we understand the women and infants and proselytes separately, and perceive them to be as it were a certain following of the Church, as "in a great house there are also vessels of wood and of earth", we say indeed that strong meat is given to the strong men, of whom it is said: "But strong meat is for the perfect", of whom the church is prepared which "hath not spot or wrinkle". But those whom he calls women, infants and proselytes we understand to be those who still "have need of milk", or who, being also weak like women, "eat herbs". But if one takes the whole church together, the men are understood as those who stand perfect in all things, "armed against the deceits of the devil"; the women, those who do not yet of themselves do what is profitable but by following the examples of the better, who are their head; "for the head of the woman is the man". The infants will be those who, having lately received the faith, are nourished with the milk of the Gospel; and the proselytes, the catechumens, or those who already strive to be joined to the faithful.
**“with the women”** — the lowest; he that is weak, let him eat herbs
**“and children and strangers”** — the catechumens, who have need of milk

9.2: **“GATHERED THEMSELVES TOGETHER”** — ADAMANTIUS. From the things that were done let us contemplate the wars and triumphs of the Lord Jesus; although we see these too visibly fulfilled in him. For the kings of the earth, the senate, the people and the Roman princes came together to fight against the name of Jesus and Israel at once. For they decreed by their laws that there should be no Christians. Every city, every order assails the Christian name. But as then all those kings, coming together, could do nothing against Jesus, so now too neither these princes nor the opposing powers have been able to prevent the race of Christians from spreading more widely and deeply. For it is written: "The more they oppressed them, the more they multiplied." And we trust that not only have the invisible enemies been unable to overcome us, but that swiftly, our Lord Jesus conquering, Satan will be crushed under the feet of his servants.
9.3: **“BUT THEY THAT”** — ADAMANTIUS. "In my Father's house there are many mansions." Many too are the differences of those who are in salvation or come to it. Whence I think the Gabaonites are a certain small portion of those who are to be saved, but not without the mark of some infamy. For they become hewers of wood and carriers of water for the service of the people and the altar, because they came with guile to the children of Israel, clothed in old rags and shoes, bringing food of stale bread. These, then, come to Jesus with their oldness, yet asking to be saved. For there are in the Church those who believe indeed and assent to the divine precepts, who are devout and dutiful toward the servants of God and ready enough for the adornment or ministry of the Church, but in their own conversation foul and wrapped in vices, and, by no means "putting off the old man with his deeds", apply no amendment or renewal of morals. To these, then, Christ Jesus grants salvation, but they do not escape a certain mark of infamy. Similar is what is said of such in the book of the Shepherd: that there is a certain tree called the elm, which bears no fruit, yet carries the fruitful vine; and so it is necessary, because it serves the fruit-bearing vine. So the Gabaonites have not put off the old man with his deeds, but they minister to the saints and serve and render some usefulness, and so they receive salvation from Jesus with the interposition of an oath. And note that the heretics who do not receive the Old Testament say at this place: "See that Jesus son of Nave had nothing of humanity, that, granting salvation to men who had come to him as suppliants, he inflicted on them the mark of infamy and the yoke of servitude." But Jesus judged fittingly according to the measure of their faith. For Rahab the harlot, who believed with whole faith with all her house and received the spies with full devotion, was received wholly into the fellowship of the people and "added to the children of Israel". But these, who loved not so much the fellowship of the Israelite people as, from fear of their own destruction, came deceitfully to Jesus, how could they by servile guile merit freedom of life and fellowship in the kingdom? Therefore, though they said, "We have heard how great things the Lord did for you through the Red Sea and in the desert", they yet did nothing worthy of so great a faith. Jesus therefore, seeing their purpose narrow in faith, keeps toward them a most just moderation, so that they who have little faith merit salvation, yet do not receive the height of the kingdom or of freedom, because their faith is ennobled by no addition of works. "But faith without works is dead." But we must take care, while we have power, that, casting away the old filth and the old rags of vices, we be joined to Israelite freedom. For it is commanded in the law that a Hebrew boy, if he should fall into servitude, may not serve more than six years, but in the seventh is to be let go free; so great was the care of freedom among the Israelites. Thou then, if thou art a Hebrew boy and hast fallen into servitude (for he is a boy who through easiness of mind falls into servitude; "but whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin"; into this servitude a manly and perfect mind does not fall, but a boyish and easy one), thou then, if thou art a Hebrew boy, that is, one of the faithful already baptized, and hast afterwards lapsed into sin, let it suffice thee to have served six years. In the seventh see that thou serve not, but return to thy freedom. Seven signifies the law of the commandments, six the world. While, then, thou savourest "the things that are of the world" and art occupied with them and "thinkest according to the flesh", thou must needs serve sin. When then thou comest to seven, that is, to the knowledge of the law, then seek thy freedom; lest, if thou persevere in sins, with the mark fixed in thy ear, because thou hearest not the words of God moving thee and calling thee back to thy former freedom, thou become the servant of sin for ever.
9.4:
**“Cunningly devising”** — desiring to become allies of the Israelites not sincerely nor wholly
**“took for themselves provisions, old sacks,”** — namely, the old filth and the old rags of the vices
9.5: **“And very old shoes,”** — namely, "the old man with his deeds"
9.6:
**“And they went to Josue,”** — to Jesus Christ
**“who then abode”** — "I am with you even to the consummation of the world."
**“in the camp”** — among the saints, who are always ready to fight against the powers of the air
**“at Galgal, and said to him, and to all Israel with him:”** — namely, in revelation, of which it is said: "Open my eyes", etc.
**“desiring to make peace with you. And the men of Israel answered”** — elsewhere: the children of Israel
9.9: **“They answered:”** — they confess that they have heard and know the divine wonders, yet they do nothing worthy of wonder at such great powers
9.19:
**“WE HAVE SWORN TO THEM”** — AUGUSTINE. It is asked how the Hebrews believed the oath was to be kept to the Gabaonites, to whom they had sworn as to men coming from a far land, as those had lied. For they knew they would be overthrown in war if it were known to the Hebrews that they dwelt in that land which they were to receive. To them, then, lying that they had come from a far land, they swore; but after they learned that they dwelt where they were to overthrow all whom they found according to God's command, they yet would not break the oath; and although they had learned that those had lied, they chose to spare them, when they could have said that they had sworn as to those whom they believed them to be, that is, men coming from afar, and that when they learned otherwise the command of the Lord concerning them had to be fulfilled, that they should be overthrown like the rest. But God approved this, nor was he angry with those who spared them, although they had not asked him who those men were, and though they had chosen to deceive. Whence they are to be believed, even if they wished to deceive for their own safety, yet to have feared God in his people without deceit. Therefore the Lord was not angry with those who swore or those who spared, and afterwards avenged these same Gabaonites, as men of his own people, on the house of Saul, as the history of the Kings shows. And because the oath was kept thus, though to lying men, so that the sentence was bent toward clemency, it did not displease God. For if, on the contrary, they had sworn to kill some whom they thought to be Gabaonites dwelling in the land, and had afterwards learned that they were foreign to that land and had come to them from afar, it is not to be thought that they would not have spared them, for the sake of fulfilling the oath; since for the sake of that very clemency of sparing, holy David, after he had sworn to kill Nabal, knowing indeed whom he was going to kill, chose to spare him and not fulfil the oath by the harsher law, judging it more pleasing to God if he did not do what he had sworn when disturbed by anger than if he had done it.
**“ISIDORE”** — The Gabaonites signify those who believe and seem to be devoted toward the servants of God or to have zeal for the Church, yet have no amendment or devotion or renewal in their morals. Such show only a certain sign of salvation within the Church for a time; but among the spiritual, that is, among the saints of God, they do not obtain the eternal kingdom or freedom.

10.1: **“When Adonisedec king of Jerusalem had heard these things, to wit, that Josue had taken Hai, and had destroyed it (for as he had done to Jericho and the king thereof, so did he to Hai, and its king),”** — he who seeks the friendship of Jesus [must bear] the enmities of many patiently; whence: "Son, when thou comest to the service of God, prepare thy soul for temptation"
10.3: **“Therefore Adonisedec king of Jerusalem sent to Oham”** — elsewhere: Oham
10.4: **“COME UP TO ME”** — When the soul joins itself to the word of God, at once it suffers as enemies those whom before it had as friends, and not only men but also the opposing powers. Let him know, then, who seeks the friendship of Jesus, that he must bear the enmities of many. Whence: "All that will live godly in Christ shall suffer persecution", etc. And elsewhere: "Son, when thou comest to the service of God, prepare thy soul for temptation." The Gabaonites too are assailed for the friendship of Jesus, though they are hewers of wood and carriers of water: that is, though thou be last in merits in the Church, yet by this very thing, that thou belongest to Jesus, thou art assailed by five kings. But the Gabaonites are neither abandoned nor spurned by Jesus or by the leaders and elders of the Israelites; but help is brought to their weakness. And this is done in us; whence: "Comfort the feeble-minded, support the weak"; likewise: "You that are stronger bear the infirmities of the weak." So, then, Jesus with the leaders and princes is present to those who are assailed by the opposing powers for his name. And not only does he give help in the war, but he also lengthens the day and the spaces of light and drives off the coming of night.
10.5: **“SO BEING ASSEMBLED TOGETHER THEY WENT UP”** — AUGUSTINE. It is asked how the king of Jerusalem, Adonibezec, and the others with whom he besieged the Gabaonites, are according to the Seventy first [called] kings of the Jebusites, when they came together against them, but afterwards are called kings of the Amorrhites by the Gabaonites themselves, when they sent messengers to Jesus to come to their help. But as we have looked into it, according to the Hebrew they are called in both places [kings] of the Amorrhites; since it is certain that the king of Jerusalem, which was called Jebus, as the metropolis of that nation, was a Jebusite, and Scripture records seven nations to be exterminated, one of which is said to be of the Amorrhites. Unless perhaps this name was universal of all, or rather of the greater part, so that not one but several of these seven were reckoned under this name, although there was one of the seven which was properly called of the Amorrhites. So there is a certain part which is properly called Libya, although this name befits the whole of Africa; and a certain part which is properly called Asia, although some have reckoned Asia half the world, others a third part. The Chanaanites also are mentioned as one nation among those seven, and yet the whole of that land is originally called the land of Chanaan.
10.7: **“AND JOSUE WENT UP FROM GALGAL”** — AUGUSTINE. When the Gabaonites, besieged by the kings of the Amorrhites, had sent to Jesus to come to their help, Jesus went up from Galgal, he and all the people of warriors with him, all mighty in strength; and the Lord said to Jesus: "Fear them not, for I have delivered them into thy hands; none of them shall stand", etc. Where the Lord was not even consulted whether they should go to them, but of his own accord he foretold the coming victory to his own, who rightly wished to bring help. So he could have been moved, unconsulted, against the Gabaonites when they lied, had not that oath pleased him which compelled them to spare those made subject. For they had believed God concerning what they had heard he promised to his people, that he would overthrow those nations and they would obtain their land; and this faith of theirs he in a manner rewarded, because he did not betray them.
10.10: **“And the Lord troubled them at the sight of Israel: and he troubled”** — elsewhere: he crushed
10.12: **“Then Josue spoke to the Lord, in the day that he delivered the Amorrhite in the sight of the children of Israel, and he said before them: Move not, O sun, toward Gabaon, nor thou, O moon, toward the valley of Ajalon.”** — THE SUN AGAINST GABAON. ADAMANTIUS. We wish, if we can, to show how our Lord Jesus Christ prolonged the light and made the day longer, whether for the salvation of men or for the destruction of the opposing powers. From the time the Saviour came, it was the end of the world; in short, he says: "Do penance, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand." But he held back and checked the day of consummation. For God the Father, seeing that the salvation of the nations could stand through him alone, says to him: "Ask of me, and I will give thee the Gentiles for thy inheritance", etc. While, then, the Father's promise is being fulfilled and the Church grows and the fulness of the Gentiles comes in, that at last all Israel may be saved, the day is lengthened and the setting is put off; nor does the sun ever go down, but it is always rising, while the sun of justice pours the light of truth into the hearts of believers. But when the measure of believers is fulfilled, and the worse and faded age of the last generation has come, and, iniquity abounding, the charity of many grows cold, and faith is found in few, then the days will be shortened. The same Lord, then, willed to lengthen the day when it is the time of salvation, and to shorten it in the time of tribulation and perdition; while, then, he lengthens the space of light, so let us walk honestly as in the day.
10.13:
**“And the sun stood still”** — namely, of justice, which knows no setting
**“and the moon,”** — the brightness of the Church
**“till the people revenged themselves of their enemies.”** — visible or invisible
**“Is not this written in the book of the just? So the sun stood still”** — Christ, pouring in the light of truth
**“in the midst of heaven,”** — of the Church
**“and hasted not to go down the space of one day.”** — because he is always rising for the faithful
10.14: **“There was not before nor after so long a day, the Lord obeying the voice of a man, and fighting for Israel.”** — So, while we fight against the demons, the sun of justice stands by us, who says: "I am with you even to the consummation of the world."
10.16:
**“For the five kings were fled”** — immersed in the five senses of the body and in earthly deeds
**“FOR THE FIVE WERE FLED”** — ADAMANTIUS. What is it that he says there were five kings, and that these fled into a cave? There is a twofold fight for Christians: for the perfect, such as Paul was and the Ephesians, as he himself says: "Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of darkness"; but for the lower, against flesh and blood: those, namely, who are still assailed by carnal vices and frailties; which I think is indicated in this place too. For war was declared on the Gabaonites by five kings: on those, that is, who are imperfect, by the five bodily senses; for through some one of these each must needs fall into sin. These five kings assail the Gabaonites, that is, carnal men. And that they are said to have fled into caves can perhaps indicate this, since a cave is a place dug into the depth of the earth: the sense is that when, set in the body, they have sunk themselves in earthly deeds, and have done nothing for the work of God but all for the service of the body, they are said to have fled into caves. Yet it must be known that the very kingdoms whose kings are now conquered by Jesus and flee into caves afterwards come into the lots of the saints and are called the portion of the Lord, as the kingdom of Jerusalem or Lachis or Hebron. In which it is indicated that when the five senses set in the body have been conquered through Jesus, and unbelief has departed from them, and they have died to sin, the soul afterwards uses them as ministers to do the works of justice. So it comes about that in Jerusalem, where a most wicked king reigned, afterwards David, mighty of hand, reigns, or Solomon the peaceful king. For malignant powers sit by or stand by the bodily senses, to solicit the soul to concupiscences and to render foul services; if the faith of Christ has overcome them and they have been hanged on the wood of his cross, these being slain and driven from the kingdom, then the soul is made a portion of God, and Jerusalem the kingdom of God, and a temple is built in it to the Lord. Whence: "For we ourselves also were some time unwise, incredulous, erring, slaves to divers desires and pleasures", etc. For this is Jerusalem's having once been under king Adonibezec, or other cities under other kings.
**“ADAMANTIUS”** — Jesus killed the enemies not teaching cruelty, as the heretics think, but designating future sacraments in them: that when he destroyed the kings who hold the kingdom of sin in us, as we have yielded our members to serve iniquity unto iniquity, so we may yield them to serve justice unto sanctification. This too is blamed as cruel, that Jesus says: "Put your feet upon their necks and kill them." But this is not cruelty; rather it is found to be humanity and kindness. Would that thou too mightest put thy feet upon serpents and scorpions and upon all the power of the enemy, and tread down the dragon and the basilisk that once reigned in thee, that, all being slain that reigned in thee by the work of sin, Jesus Christ alone may reign in thee.
10.17: **“And it was told Josue”** — to Jesus Christ
10.19:
**“And stay you not, but pursue after the enemies”**
• the opposing powers that stand by the senses
• BUT STAY YOU NOT, etc. ADAMANTIUS. The wars of Jesus and the slaughter of kings and enemies are a shadow of heavenly things: namely, of the wars which Jesus Christ wages with his army and his majesties [so the edition], that is, the people of believers, and their leaders, against the devil and his angels. For it is he who in Paul and in the Ephesians "fights against the rulers of darkness". And see, heretic, how the new agrees with the old. To the ancients was promised the kingdom of the holy land flowing with milk and honey, which was then inhabited by most wicked inhabitants and kings. Jesus comes into this land with his army, and with the Israelite leaders he takes it by storm, slays all and holds it, and for the merit of victory receives their kingdoms. To thee through the Gospel are promised not the kingdoms of the earth but of heaven. Nor are they empty; for they have inhabitants, sinners and demons, against whom the apostolic trumpet urges thee to battle. And as there Jesus said that the war would be against the Amorrhites, Pherezites, Hevites and Jebusites, so here too Paul says: "Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood": that is, we shall not fight as the ancients did, nor must we wage battles on earth with men, "but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the world of this darkness". Now thou understandest in what places these contests are to be stirred up for thee; or, if thou dost not understand, hear more plainly: "against the spirits of wickedness in high places". Thou hast heard who must be driven by thee in war from the heavenly places, that thou mayst take by lot the places of the kingdom of heaven for thy inheritance. This too the Lord says in the Gospel: "From the days of John the kingdom of heaven suffereth violence, and the violent bear it away." Canst thou then likewise bring a charge against our Saviour, that is, of driving out the possessor violently and plundering the possession? Why then do you accuse what Jesus the successor of Moses did? And would that Jesus might open to us the treasure of his wisdom, that we might see of which of the heavenly spiritual enemies that assail Israel that prince of Maceda bore the figure, and he of Lachis, and he of Lebna; or of what vice or error within me, by which the soul is entangled, each of those bears the form whom the people of God slew under the leadership of Jesus: those, namely, who hear his commandments, to whom he gives the power to tread upon serpents and scorpions and all the power of the enemy. Let us pray, then, that our feet may be so beautiful and so strong that they may tread on the necks of the enemies, and so tread down the head of the serpent that it cannot bite our heel. For he who fights under Jesus as leader ought to merit what is written of those warriors: "And all the people returned to Jesus safe, and not one of the children of Israel muttered with his tongue." For he who serves under Jesus ought to return safe from the battle, and receive no wound from the fiery darts of the wicked one, nor be polluted in heart or thought.
• And that he adds that no one muttered with his tongue seems to be said because no one boasted of the victory nor ascribed it to his own strength. For they know that Jesus gave the victory; whence: "Yet not I, but the grace of God with me"; and elsewhere: "When you shall have done all these things, say: We are unprofitable servants." Would that my Lord Jesus would grant me to tread down the spirit of fornication and the neck of the spirit of anger and of fury, and the demon of avarice, and boasting, and to crush with my feet the spirit of pride; and when I have done these things, to hang the sum of the work done not on myself but on his cross, according to that: "By whom the world is crucified to me", etc.; "yet not I, but his grace which is in me". If I do this, there will be said to me what the ancient Jesus says: "Do manfully and be of good heart; fear not, neither be ye dismayed at their sight; for the Lord God" hath delivered all your enemies into your hands.
• LEBNA too is interpreted whiteness, which is understood in different ways. For there is the whiteness of leprosy and the whiteness of light. And Lebna had the whiteness of leprosy under wicked kings; but when it came to the Israelite people it received the whiteness of light.
• LACHIS also is interpreted way, which is both praiseworthy in the Scriptures and blameworthy; whence: "The way of the wicked shall perish"; and elsewhere: "Make straight steps for your feet." First, then, the city of Lachis was the way of the wicked; when that was destroyed, afterwards, the Israelites reigning, it came to the right way.
• HEBRON: joining, or marriage. The joining of our soul was first with that most wicked husband, the devil; when he died, it was freed from the law of the former, and joined to a good and lawful husband, of whom Paul says: "I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ." So, then, the meaning of these very names accords with the twofold state; so it is better to understand the Israelite wars and the overthrow of cities and kingdoms; so Jesus appears the more religious in having overthrown each city, so that nothing was left in them that breathed, nor any who was saved, nor any who escaped: so that, namely, no sense of malice may breathe again in the soul, nor any feeling of anger or concupiscence be saved; let there be no evil word to escape from the mouth. So the cities of Juda are built; for even now Jesus destroys and builds the soul of each. For the first work of God is to root out evils, the thorns and briers of the vices; for while they occupy the land, it cannot receive the holy seeds. It is necessary, then, first to root out the plant of sin, which the heavenly Father did not plant, and to burn it with fire. The second work is to plant. Moses says that God planted a paradise; but even now he plants in the souls of believers. For in the soul from which he has cut out anger he plants meekness; from which he has cut out pride, he plants humility; from which he roots out wantonness, he plants chastity; ignorance being uprooted, he plants knowledge. Such is said to be the planting of God, rather than [that] of senseless trees. For it is first the work of the word of God to destroy the devilish buildings. For he builds in each one the towers of pride and the walls of haughtiness, which the word of God destroys, that we may be made God's husbandry and God's building, set upon the foundations of the apostles and prophets, and may merit to be made heirs of the holy land, in the Israelite portion, our enemies being destroyed.
**“ADAMANTIUS”** — "All these things happened to them in figure, and they are written for us." When he who is a Jew outwardly and circumcised in the flesh reads these things, he thinks only wars are described, and the destruction of enemies, and that the Israelites under the leadership of Jesus conquered and plundered the kingdoms of the nations.
