This sense is best there: You were sold gratis, and: "Thou hast sold thy people for no price"; because the wicked merited that the people be delivered to them not by worshipping God, so that the worship itself might seem the price. But as to what is said, and you shall be redeemed without money: it does not say without price, but without money, that the price of the redemption may be understood to be the blood of the immaculate Lamb. For by money the Prophet signified all wealth, because they were to be redeemed by the price of the blood of Christ, not by a price of money.
**“AND THE LORD BEING ANGRY”** — ORIGEN. When one serves God he is not delivered into the hands of plunderers; but when he forsakes God and serves his own passions, he is delivered up to shameful affections and "to a reprobate sense, to do those things which are not convenient", because he "is filled with all iniquity, wickedness, fornication" and the like. For if we sin against the Lord and worship our pleasures and desires as God, we are delivered into the hand of the devil by apostolic authority, as he himself says: "I have delivered such a one to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved." Not only through angels does God deliver sinners into the hands of enemies, but also through the prelates of the Church, who have the power of loosing and binding. And they are delivered to the destruction of the flesh when for their sins they are separated from the body of Christ. And they are delivered in two ways: when, namely, the sin is manifest to the Church, and one is driven out of the Church by the priests, that, marked by men, he may blush, and, being converted, that may come about which follows, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord; or, when the sin is not manifest to men, but God, who seeth in secret, seeing his mind serving vices and passions, and that he is not worshipped in his heart, but avarice or lust or the like, himself delivers such a one to Satan. For he turns away and flees from his evil thoughts and unworthy desires, and leaves the house of his heart empty. Then the unclean spirit which had gone out of the man, finding his house empty and swept, takes with him seven other spirits more wicked than himself, and entering in they dwell there, and the last state of that man becomes worse than the first. So it is to be understood that God delivers those whom he delivers, not because he himself delivers anyone, but he forsakes the unworthy and does not dwell in them. And the soul is said to be delivered from this, that it is found empty of God and is invaded by the wicked spirit. Let us watch, then, and purge ourselves of vices, that we may keep God within us, lest we be delivered to the devil.
2.21: **“I also will not destroy the nations which Josue left, when he died”** — AUGUSTINE. The cause is plain why Jesus did not destroy all those nations: that there might be, namely, those in whom these might be proved. And they could have been of profit, if, tried in them, they were not found reprobate, but were found such as the Lord commanded them to be. For the nations would be taken away if they lived so, nor would wars be necessary for them.
2.22:
**“That through them I may try Israel, whether they will keep the way of the Lord,”** — the words of the writer explaining why those nations were not destroyed
**“and walk in it, as their fathers kept it”** — AUGUSTINE. Who were, namely, with Jesus while he lived; for when they were dead, another generation arose which began to offend the Lord, for the proving of whom the nations were not destroyed.
2.23: **“The Lord therefore left all these nations, and would not quickly destroy them, neither did he deliver them into the hands of Josue.”** — as though Jesus should not seem to have left those nations by human counsel

3.1: **“These are the nations which the Lord left, that by them he might instruct Israel, and all that had not known the wars of the Chanaanites”** — AUGUSTINE. This, then, was the cause, for their trial, that they might learn wars, that is, that they might make war with as great piety and obedience to the law of God as their fathers, who pleased God even in making war; not because war is desirable, but because piety is praiseworthy even in war.
3.3: **“The five princes of the Philistines, and all the Chanaanites, and the Sidonians, and the Hevites that dwelt in mount Libanus, from mount Baal Hermon to the entering into Emath.”** — AUGUSTINE. Satrapies are so called as it were small kingdoms over which satraps presided; which name in those parts is, or was, one of a certain honour.
3.4: **“And he left them, that he might try Israel by them”** — AUGUSTINE. Not that God, the knower of all things, even of things to come, might know, but that they themselves might know, and by their own conscience might either glory or be convicted.
3.5: **“IN THE MIDST OF THE CHANAANITE”** — AUGUSTINE. In Deuteronomy God says of these nations: I will not cast them out in one year, lest the land be brought into a wilderness and the wild beasts multiply against thee. By little and little I will cast them out, until thou be increased and grow and inherit the land. He could have kept this promise of his toward the obedient, so that the extermination of those nations should take place as the Israelite portions grew, since their multitude would not suffer the lands from which the adversaries were exterminated to be deserted. But as to what he says, lest the wild beasts multiply against thee, it is a wonder if he did not mean bestial desires and lusts to be understood, which are wont to arise from a sudden success of earthly felicity. For God could not exterminate men and be unable [to exterminate] beasts.
3.7: **“And they did evil in the sight of the Lord, and they forgot their God, and served Baalim and Astaroth.”** — because they treasured up wrath for themselves
3.8:
**“And the Lord being angry with Israel, delivered them”** — by just judgment
**“DELIVERED THEM INTO THE HANDS”** — ADAMANTIUS. And the Lord delivered them into the hands of Chusan Rasathaim king of Mesopotamia. Chusan Rasathaim is interpreted their humiliation. They were delivered to him, then, that he might humble them; and because they acted impiously on the heights of the mountains against the most High, they were delivered by him into humiliation. Nor did divine providence of old only deliver to be humbled those who were impiously exalted, that contraries might be cured by contraries with a wholesome medicine, but it does the same now too in its Church. There is now too a Chusan Rasathaim, king of Mesopotamia, to whom are delivered, to be humbled and afflicted, the souls which, despising Christian humility, have lifted themselves up into pride, which is very hateful in the sight of God. For pride is the beginning of departing from God; but "God resisteth the proud, and giveth grace to the humble." If anyone, then, despising the humility of Christ (who for our sakes, being God, was made man and humbled even unto death), is lifted up and leaps forward to the powers and dignities of the world, and does not shrink from the arts by which these are attained, even if they be against faith and religion, it comes about that he does evil in the sight of the Lord; and when he has obtained the highest insignia of power, and has climbed to the very summit of pride, thence cast down he is delivered to Chusan Rasathaim, namely to one of the princes of the air, as elsewhere to Pharao, and elsewhere to Chiram, that he may humble him who had been too much exalted, and afflict him until he come to his senses and seek the Lord, because while he was in pride he knew him not.
**“into the hands of Chusan Rasathaim king of Mesopotamia”** — Anyone, even a little or least one, even if he has enjoyed no dignity, can labour under the vice of pride; and nothing is so foul, so execrable, as a poor man proud and a rich man lying. The disease of pride sometimes penetrates the very priestly and levitical order; and in us, who are set as an example of humility, and in the circle of the altar as on a watchtower for those who look on, the vice of arrogance stinks; and from the altar of the Lord, which ought to be fragrant with the sweetness of incense, the foulest odour of pride breathes forth.
**“and they served him eight years”** — as long, namely, as they served Baalim. For the affliction of penance ought to be according to the measure of the fault.
3.9:
**“And”** — being set in tribulation
**“they cried to the Lord, who raised them up a saviour”**
• unless they had cried, a saviour would not have been raised up for them
• "They cried to the Lord in their affliction, and he delivered them out of their distresses, and he brought them out of darkness", etc.
• AUGUSTINE. Note that he calls a man a saviour, through whom God saves.
**“and delivered them, Othoniel”**
• The Seventy: Gothoniel, which is: my time of God
• some one, namely, of the archangels, sent to the help of those who receive the inheritance of salvation
• hysterologia, namely a species of hyperbaton
• See the kind Lord mingling mercy with severity, and weighing the measure of punishment with a just and clement balance. He does not deliver sinners up for ever; but as long, it says, as they served Baalim, so long do they serve Chusan Rasathaim, that is, eight years. Learn this, thou who knowest that thou hast erred: as long as thou hast sinned, so long humble thyself to God in the confession of penance. Do not wait for Chusan Rasathaim to humble thee and for necessity to wring penance from thee unwilling. Forestall the hands of the torturer, because if thou correct thyself, the Lord is kind, who will temper vengeance to him who forestalls it by repenting. And it is to be noted that while they served Chusan Rasathaim and did not cry to the Lord, no one was raised up who could save them. When, then, they cried, he raised up for them as saviour Gothoniel, who is interpreted my time of God, through whom that people was rescued from servitude, and peace was restored to the people, which pride and the various crimes of the people had put to flight.
• And Gothoniel seems to me to be one of the heavenly host and the archangelic troops who are sent to the help of those who receive the inheritance of salvation. For there are saving angels, who are signified by Gothoniel or Aod.
**“to wit, the son of Cenez”** — it is shown of what family, of what nobility he is
**“the younger brother of Caleb”** — of a wonderful man, namely, who was the companion of Josue
3.10:
**“AND THE SPIRIT OF THE LORD WAS IN HIM”** — It is great praise of the first judge that the spirit of the Lord came upon him and that he judged the people by the Spirit of God; which I do not well remember to have been said of another. There are today judges of the churches, to whom is given even the judgment of souls. But I know not whether any is worthy "to be filled with the Spirit of God".
**“AND THE SPIRIT WAS IN HIM”** — ADAMANTIUS. After, namely, they cried to the Lord. Who among us sends forth so strong, so just a cry to the Lord that the people may merit to receive a judge whom the Spirit of God may fill, so that he may hold right judgment? Whence the book itself is called of Judges, of those, namely, who judged the people of Israel: wonderful men, namely, as Josue was. So too the book of Kings, in which it is told how each of the kings reigned and what he did, even evil, that the princes or judges of the Church may imitate their good deeds and beware of their evil.
**“and he judged Israel. And he went out to fight, and [the Lord] delivered”** — because the spirit of the Lord was in him
3.11:
**“And the land rested forty years”**
• Great is the bounty of the divine clemency: for the sins of many they served eight years; for the justice of one they rested forty.
• AUGUSTINE. As much time, namely, as the beginnings of the Roman empire had in peace, under Numa Pompilius only.
**“and Othoniel the son of Cenez died.”** — because, namely, the people was unworthy to have such a judge; whence follows: But the children of Israel did evil again, etc. Consider that, because they were unworthy to have such a prince, he is therefore taken from them.
3.12: **“And the children of Israel did evil again in the sight of the Lord: who strengthened against them Eglon king of Moab”** — Thou seest that our sins give and restore strength to the enemies, when we do evil in the sight of the Lord, and our adversaries are strengthened by the Lord. In spiritual things too the contrary powers would not grow strong against us, nor the devil himself, unless we gave him strength from our vices, and by sinning made him room to enter and to rule in us; whence: "Give not place to the devil."
3.13: **“And he joined to him the children of Ammon, and Amalec”** — most wicked enemies, to fight against Israel with him
3.14: **“THEY SERVED EIGHTEEN YEARS”** — ADAMANTIUS. After eighteen years the children of Israel cried again to the Lord, and he raised up for them a saviour, Aioth the son of Gera, the son of Jemini, a man ambidextrous. He who is raised up to save Israel has nothing left-handed in him, but both his hands right: a worthy prince of the people, a worthy judge of the Church, who does nothing left-handed, whose "left hand knoweth not what the right hand doth". On both sides he is right-handed: in faith, in acts; he has nothing of those who are placed on the left, to whom it shall be said: Depart from me, ye workers of iniquity, I know you not; go into everlasting fire, etc.
3.15:
**“ADAMANTIUS”** — The divine Scripture almost marks the measures too: above, eight years; here it says eighteen. And it is certain that the times of chastisement are bounded according to the measure of the sin and the delay of conversion. For these eighteen years of servitude also passed, and it is not said that they cried to the Lord or were converted from their wickedness, but afterwards.
**“A SAVIOUR”** — ADAMANTIUS. The saviours or judges who are raised up to set free the children of Israel signify the princes of the heavenly host, whom God sends forth to the aid of those who have cried to him with their whole heart and have bent the divine clemency toward them by the conversion of penance. For it is written that when our fathers had served Pharao a long time, they cried to the Lord, so that he himself said: The cry of the children of Israel is come up to me; and, sending Moses, he brought them out visibly. The destroying angel too was sent, who should lay waste all the firstborn of Egypt but touch none of the Israelites. And so it is plain that it was a heavenly power which, the Egyptians being laid waste, brought the children of Israel out of servitude. Under Sennacherib king of the Assyrians too an angel of the Lord is sent, who, having laid low a hundred and eighty-five thousand of the enemy in one night, set free both the city from the siege and the people from destruction. Similarly, then, when we sin, or are delivered into captivity for our sins, let us cry to the Lord not with the mouth but with the mind, so that the sorrow of the heart may bring forth a fountain of tears from the eyes; like him who said: "Every night I will wash my bed; I will water my couch with my tears." If we are so converted from evil things that we touch them no more, the Lord will send us his heavenly power, through which we may be set free from the devilish power; which may do all things for us right and prosperous, which may make us leave the left way that leads to perdition, and call us back to the right way, which says: "I am the way, the truth and the life."
**“called Aod, the son of Gera”** — which is interpreted praise
**“the son of Jemini, who used the left hand as well as the right.”**
• having nothing left-handed, whose "left hand knew not what the right hand did"
• WHO [USED] BOTH, etc. According to the spiritual understanding all the saints are called ambidextrous; the devil and his princes ambi-left-handed. For all that they do is left-handed and perverse, and assigned to the eternal fire with those who are on the left.
3.16: **“And he made himself a two-edged sword, with a haft in the midst of the length of the palm of the hand, and was girded therewith under his garment on the right thigh.”** — ADAMANTIUS. Whatever Aioth the ambidextrous does is right. He is right-handed with hands and feet. For he carries the sword on the right thigh, that he may come to the king of Moab and kill him.
3.17: **“And he presented the gifts to Eglon”** — "rolled, or a wheel-track". This is the discourse of the philosophy that judges pleasure the highest good
3.19: **“Then returning from Galgal, where the idols were, he said to the king: I have a secret message to thee, O king.”** — AUGUSTINE. He does not lie; for a deed is called a word, and he had a secret deed for the king.
3.20:
**“AOD WENT IN TO HIM”** — ADAMANTIUS. Aioth is interpreted praise: for using a cunning art and a praiseworthy deception he slew Eglon, who is interpreted rolled or a wheel-track. The judges of our people ought to be such as was Aioth, who is interpreted praise, that they may cut away all rolling motions and the wheel-tracks of the evil way, and slay the king of the Madianites [so the edition], who is interpreted flux or outpouring. And who is the prince or leader of the flowing and dissolute nation but the discourse of that philosophy which judges pleasure the highest good? Him the evangelical and prophetic discourse kills, which is compared to a sword; which is shut up in their belly and inmost vitals by the disputations of the ambidextrous doctor, that, shutting them in with the assertion of the truth, he may put out every sense of perverse doctrine and gross understanding which lifts itself up against the spiritual knowledge of Christ; that every judge of the Church, doing this and fighting with the word of God, may become a praiseworthy Aioth, to whom the Lord may say: "Well done, good and faithful servant, because thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will place thee over many things."
**“Now he was sitting in a summer parlour alone, and he said: I have a word from God to thee.”** — because the Lord, who had raised him up as saviour for his people, had commanded him to do this
3.21:
**“And Aod put forth his left hand, and took the dagger”** — the evangelical or prophetic discourse
**“from his right thigh”** — by disputing, namely, that he might put out every sense of perverse doctrine and gross understanding
3.22: **“IT WAS CLOSED UP WITH THE ABUNDANCE OF FAT”** — AUGUSTINE. It is rightly asked how king Eglon was very slender, and the fat closed the wound when he was struck. But it is to be understood as said in that manner of speech by which things are wont to be understood by the contrary, as a grove [lucus] is so called because it least gives light, and to abound is said of what is not, and he blessed the king, that is, he cursed, as was said in the book of the Kingdoms of Naboth. For in that translation which is not according to the Seventy but from the Hebrew, we find thus: "Now Eglon was exceeding fat."
3.25: **“THEY TOOK A KEY”** — AUGUSTINE. How did the servants of king Eglon open with a key what Aod had not shut with a key? Or if he had shut it with a key, how had he not taken it with him, so that these could not open with a key? Accordingly either another key was brought, or the kind of fastening was such that it could be shut without a key but not opened without a key. For there are certain such, like those which are called [unclear in the edition: "verrudata"].
3.30: **“And Moab was humbled that day under the hand of Israel: and the land rested eighty years from wars.”** — AUGUSTINE. Twice, namely, the time of the Romans under king Pompilius, which was memorable
3.31:
**“AFTER HIM WAS”** — AFTER HIM WAS. ADAMANTIUS. The Seventy: Semegar, that is, a stranger there. For all men of God are strangers in this world, like him who said: I am a sojourner with thee in the land, and a stranger, as all my fathers were. This Semegar, then, the Holy Ghost calls a sojourner there, that is, here. For what is there to the Holy Ghost, who is in heaven, is here to us.
**“After him was Samgar the son”** — AFTER HIM WAS, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is asked how after Aod Samgar fought for Israel and is said to have saved it. For it had not been taken captive or bound by the yoke of servitude. But he saved it thus: not because the enemy had done harm, but lest he should be allowed to do harm; who, it is to be believed, had begun to make trial by war and was repulsed by this man's victory.
**“of Anath, who slew of the Philistines six hundred men with a ploughshare.”**
• The number six, which multiplied reaches six hundred, signifies the world finished in six days. He, then, is said to have struck six hundred with the plough, to whom the world is crucified through the cross of Christ.
• Thou too, be the husbandman of thy soul. Use the plough which Semegar uses. But when thou hast put thy hand to the plough, look not back; that is, after thou hast taken up thy cross and followed Christ, after thou hast renounced the world and the things that are in the world, seek not again the things which for Christ thou hast counted as dung. For if thou hast thy hand ever on this plough, so that thou say confidently: "But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ", etc., a thousand shall fall at thy side, and ten thousand at thy right hand, etc., but they shall not come nigh thee.
**“WHO SLEW”** — WHO SLEW. ADAMANTIUS. Semegar smote the Allophyli, six hundred men, with the plough-handle, or the foot of the plough. I see another kind of praise in Semegar. He fights with a plough; Aod, it says, with a sword; yet he too conquers and lays low the Allophyli. It can be, then, that the judge of the Church does not always bring forth the sword, that is, does not always use the severity of the word and the sharpness of correction, but imitates the husbandman, as it were furrowing the earth of our soul with a plough, and often breaking it up with clement admonition, to fit it to receive the seeds. The Allophyli are slain thus too, when we do not use arguments and sharpness against adversaries, but drive vices and sins out of the minds of the hearers by a rustic and simple admonition.

4.1: **“And the children of Israel again did evil in the sight of the Lord after the death of Aod”** — AND THE CHILDREN [OF ISRAEL] AGAIN, etc. As though for the sins of the people the good leader died; for the man of God is taken away from sinners and the unworthy. But someone says: When is the Church of God without a judge? If the former departs, another is brought in; [but] not always the prince of the people. The judge of the Church is given by the decision of God, but as our merits demand. If our acts are evil and we work evil in the sight of the Lord, princes are given us according to our heart. Whence: They have made a king, but not by me, and a prince, and not by my counsel. This seems said of Saul, whom the Lord himself had chosen and had commanded to be made king. But because he had been chosen not according to the will of God, but according to the desert of the sinful people, he denies that he was appointed by his will or counsel. So in the Church a ruler powerful either in word or in work is granted by God according to the merits of the people; or, if the people do evil in the sight of the Lord, such a judge of the Church is given, under whom the people suffer a famine and thirst of the word of God: not a famine of bread nor a thirst of water, but of hearing the word of God. Let us so act and pray, then, that we be not condemned by the indignation of God to this famine and thirst, that he be not taken from us who instructs us in the word of God and in work. For if we do evil in the sight of the Lord, Aod will die for us, and Semegar will be taken away, and our praise will be darkened, and we shall be delivered into the hands of Jabin king of Chanaan, who is interpreted sense or prudence. If, then, we do not like to have God in our knowledge, God will deliver us up to a reprobate sense, filled with iniquity, wickedness, fornication, avarice, etc. Thou seest who they are and of what sort, who are delivered up to a reprobate sense and to Jabin, the prince of the Chanaanites.
4.2:
**“And the Lord delivered them up into the hands of Jaban king of Chanaan, who reigned in Asor”** — sense or prudence; for those who do not like to have God in their knowledge are delivered up to a reprobate sense.
**“INTO THE HAND OF JABAN KING”** — ADAMANTIUS. The prince of the host of Jabin was Sisara, who is interpreted the sight of a horse. For he is animal, not spiritual, and sees nothing but the things that are animal. This is his sight. For he is ever looking on [them], and therefore the animal man, who is according to the flesh, ever persecutes him who is according to the spirit, until the animal man understands and examines all things, and understands whence help is to be asked for him, and cries to the Lord; until for that soul which has cried to the Lord prophecy is raised up, which Debbora signifies, and according to the grace and understanding of prophecy either the people of the Church is governed, or the sense of each soul.
**“and he had a general of his army named Sisara.”** — that is, the sight of a horse
4.3:
**“And the children of Israel cried to the Lord.”** — ADAMANTIUS. Observe that the children of Israel know not how to cry to the Lord unless they are delivered into the hands of Jabin king of Chanaan, or afflicted by Sisara the prince of his host.
**“For he had nine hundred chariots set with scythes”** — by which a stiff-necked people might be afflicted
4.4:
**“And there was Debbora a prophetess”** — this is read of none of the judges
**“AND THERE WAS”** — AND THERE WAS. ADAMANTIUS. According to the Apostle: All Scripture inspired of God is profitable to teach, to reprove, to instruct in justice. It is asked, then, what of doctrine or reproof or discipline this Scripture has, which is inspired of God. For what does it profit if we read that Debbora, a woman, a prophetess, the wife of Lapidoth, judged Israel, etc.? First, then, this very thing, that while there were very many judges in Israel, it is said of none that he was a prophet, as it is of Debbora a woman, gives in this a consolation to the female sex, that it may not despair for its weakness of being able to receive prophecy, but may believe that it is purity of mind, not difference of sex, that confers this grace.
**“DEBBORA”** — A bee, or speech; which signifies prophecy, which composes the sweet combs of heavenly doctrine and the sweet honey of the divine word. Whence: How sweet are thy words to my palate, more than honey to my mouth. And elsewhere the prophet says that the judgments of the Lord are precious above gold and much precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb.
4.5:
**“And she sat under a palm tree, which by her name”** — because the just shall flourish like the palm tree; whom prophecy, by instructing, brings forth to the palm of the heavenly calling
**“was called, between Rama”** — which is interpreted the heights
**“and Bethel”** — the house of God
**“AND SHE SAT UNDER A PALM TREE”** — AND SHE SAT UNDER A PALM TREE. ADAMANTIUS. See in what places prophecy sits: between the heights, namely, and the house of God. Nothing lowly or mean can be found about the seat of prophecy; as Solomon says that it stands at the high gates of the cities, or dwells on the battlements of the walls, or moves freely in the high towers. It is said, then, to dwell between the house of God and the heights. For it does not teach us to seek the things that are upon the earth, but those that are in heaven, where Christ is, sitting at the right hand of God. Thither it exhorts us to go up; thither prophecy labours to move its disciples.
4.6:
**“And she sent”** — first
**“and called Barac”**
• the former people
• that is, a flash of lightning, which, namely, has a light that does not abide, for it quickly ends. This is the former people, which first of all was called by prophecy, through the prophets, to hear the words of God and to receive the gifts of the law; which shone indeed with the splendour of the law, but did not abide nor keep a continual brightness of light.
**“the son of Abinoem out of Cedes in Nephtali: and she said to him: The Lord God of Israel hath commanded thee: Go, and lead an army to mount Thabor, and thou shalt take with thee ten thousand fighting men of the children of Nephtali”** — a hart let loose
4.8:
**“And said to her”** — to prophecy
**“Barac:”** — the former people
**“If thou wilt come with me, I will go:”** — a false promise
**“if thou wilt not come with me, I will not go.”** — a true excuse
**“IF THOU WILT COME”** — IF THOU WILT COME. AUGUSTINE. What is it that Barac, answering Debbora, says: If thou wilt go with me, I will go, and if thou wilt not go with me, I will not go; for I know not the day in which the Lord prospereth the angel with me? As if he could not hear the day from the prophetess?
4.9:
**“She said to him: I will go indeed with thee, but at this time the victory shall not be attributed to thee”** — it shows that the palm of the first victory was not with that people
**“because into the hand of a woman”** — Jahel
**“ADAMANTIUS”** — ADAMANTIUS. I will not go up unless thou go up with me. Thou seest how prophecy brought the words of God to those former ones, and tells them that precepts are given them, to go up into the mountain; but they excuse themselves and say: I will not go up unless thou go up with me. And of the excuse indeed it is true, of the promise false. For they do not go up into the mountain of the Lord. But that they promise to go up with prophecy is false. For they did not follow prophecy so as to believe in Christ, of whom all prophecy is. Debbora therefore says to him: I will go with thee, but the primacy shall not be thine at this time. The Lord will deliver Sisara into the hand of a woman, etc. It shows openly that the primacy was not with that people, nor the palm of victory, but Sisara is delivered into the hand of a woman whose name is Jahel.
4.15: **“And the Lord struck a terror”** — AUGUSTINE. See how the Scripture shows that God acts in the hearts of men to give to things the issue he has appointed. For he terrified Sisara, that he might deliver him up.
4.18:
**“And Jahel went forth”** — a foreign woman
**“to meet Sisara”** — who before had had a covenant of friendship with him
**“and said to him: Come in to me, my lord, come in, fear not. He went in to her tent, and being covered by her with a cloak”** — The Seventy: with skins
**“AND JAHEL WENT FORTH”** — AND JAHEL WENT FORTH. ADAMANTIUS. Jahel, a foreign woman, signifies the Church, which is gathered from the foreign nations. For Jahel is interpreted ascent, because there is no other ascent to heaven but through the Church of the manifold wisdom of God. She, then, while she ascends from bodily things to spiritual and from earthly to heavenly, kills Sisara, who bears the figure of the carnal vices and of the animal man. For Sisara is interpreted the sight of a horse, of which it is said: Do not become like the horse and the mule, who have no understanding. With a stake, then, she kills him, that is, with the point and power of the wood of the cross; and well is she said to have pierced his jaws with the stake. For the mouth which spoke of carnal things, and the doctrine which set forth the glory of the flesh, which persuaded the wise of the world that they should live in delights and pleasure, and had deceived by the flattery of luxury, is pierced through by the wood of the cross; because the way of pleasure which philosophy had preached as broad and spacious, Christ has shown to us as the strait and narrow way of salvation. So, then, Jahel, that is, the Church, delivered to eternal sleep Sisara, the prince of the vices, covered with skins, that is, lulled by the mortification of the members.
4.19:
**“Said to her: Give me, I beseech thee, a little water, for I am very thirsty. She opened a bottle of milk”** — of moral doctrine, which befits little ones
**“GIVE ME, I BESEECH THEE”** — GIVE ME, I BESEECH THEE. ADAMANTIUS. Sisara asked for water, but Jahel gave milk. The food of milk is called in holy Scripture the doctrine which is delivered to beginners as to little ones. For the deep and more secret sacraments are not to be delivered at once to disciples, but the correction of morals, the amendment of discipline, the first elements of a religious conversation and of simple faith. This is the milk of the Church; these are the first elements of the little beginners. But this food gives life and salvation to those who tend to the good; but to those who are pleased with contrary things, to whom luxury, lust, avarice and all impiety are dear, death. By the same foods, then, the good are nourished and the wicked choked; and where there is life for the pious, there is death for the impious; as wine helps the healthy, and gladdens the heart of man, of the healthy man only, but brings ruin to the fevered. So it is to be understood that Sisara, the animal man and prince of the vices, was killed by the doctrine of the Church, which he did not receive in faith.
**“SHE OPENED A BOTTLE”** — SHE OPENED A BOTTLE. ADAMANTIUS. Let each soul lull and kill Sisara in itself with this evangelical and apostolic milk. For if anyone, taught by this, has mortified his members which are upon the earth, avarice, fornication and the like, he will be seen to have slain Sisara in himself; so that each may show these things to be fulfilled not only in the person of the Church but also in his own soul. Because, then, the former people began to pursue Sisara, but he was slain by a woman, that is, the Church of the Gentiles, and the palm of victory was given into her hand, at the consummation of all things, that is, at the end of the world, a canticle also will be sung to the Lord by Debbora, in which the primacy will be given to Jahel, that is, to the Church of the Gentiles; yet the praise of Debbora will not be silent, but one prize of victory will be given to the first and to the last.
4.21:
**“So Jahel Haber's wife took a nail of the tent”** — The Seventy: a palm, that is, the wood of the cross, by whose point and power the Church killed the devil; which Barac, that is, the former people, could not do by the precepts of the law.
**“and taking also a hammer: and going in softly, and with silence, she put the nail upon the temples”** — The Seventy: the jaw
4.22:
**“And behold Barac pursuing after Sisara”** — who had first begun to pursue
**“came: and Jahel went out to meet him”** — the Church from the Gentiles, which, as he passed by, had snatched the victory before him
**“and said to him: Come, and I will shew thee the man whom thou seekest. And when he came into her tent,”** — Note that it does not follow, when Scripture says that a man went in to some woman, that he had intercourse with her, though it is wont so to speak; here, then, went in to her is said properly, that is, into her house.
**“AND JAHEL WENT OUT TO MEET”** — AND JAHEL WENT OUT TO MEET. ADAMANTIUS. Jahel, that is, the Church, goes to meet the former people as it pursues Sisara. For Israel followed after the law of justice, but did not come unto the law of justice. The Church, then, goes to meet him too, showing him its work and the victory accomplished, and invites him into the fellowship of the overthrown enemy; because when the fulness of the Gentiles shall have come in, then all Israel shall be saved. The primacy, then, is in the hand of a foreign woman; yet Barac too is not shut out from the fellowship of the glory, who indeed began first but came last to the faith. Nay, while he is coming, the foreign Jahel in a manner snatches the victory from him as he passes. The same pattern went before in Esau and Jacob. For while Esau followed the things of the field and lingered in the woodlands, Jacob, coming before him and offering his father the food prepared by the counsel of the woman his mother, received the blessing of the primacy. In the Gospel too, while the Lord was going to raise the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, the woman with the issue of blood, coming before, by her faithful touch first obtains health.

5.1:
**“And sung”** — the praise of the victory
**“Debbora”** — who had foretold in song that Sisara would be overcome
**“and Barac son”** — the husband of Debbora, who is also given as Lapidoth. Lapidoth is interpreted flash, Barac thunderbolt; because before he avenged Israel he shone among the people like a flash, namely by his merits and the prerogative of his works; but after he avenged Israel he was called thunderbolt, that is, smiting.
**“AND DEBBORA SUNG”** — AND DEBBORA SUNG. ADAMANTIUS. If we remember what was said above, what Debbora signifies, what Barac, what Jahel too, who alone cast down the adversary, or what Sisara, who was laid low by the foreign woman with the power of the wood, we understand that all these are sacraments which are to be consummated through the Church in the last times, and that in this canticle there is described as it were an epinikion, that is, a praise, of the victory, namely, of that time when the last enemy, death, shall be destroyed. For then Debbora will exult, that is, the glory of prophecy will be made illustrious, because the things it foretold will be fulfilled; then Jahel, that is, the Church, will overcome the common enemy of all; and when the fulness of the Gentiles shall have come in, Barac, that is, the remnant of Israel, will be saved and received into the fellowship of the victory. Then, if we are worthy, we shall sing this canticle filled with mystical and prophetic sacraments.
5.2: **“THE SAME”** — THE SAME. In the beginning of the princes in Israel, in the willingness of the people, bless ye the Lord, etc. The blessing, it says, with which we bless the Lord takes place at the beginning [from] the princes in Israel, then in the willingness of the people. For example: when we first come to the worship of God and receive the beginning of heavenly doctrine, these beginnings are to be taken from the princes of Israel; and by the princes of Israel, that is, of the Christian people, I think the angels are to be understood, of whom it is said: Their angels always see the face of the Father who is in heaven. For example: if a boy goes to school, he is received by the master as a pupil, but he does not at once take the beginning of learning from the master himself; but when he has received from him only the first elements, he is handed over to others to be taught, as it were to the princes of that school, so that when he has been taught by them as far as is in them, he may at last receive the more perfect precepts of the teacher himself. Recalling, then, the beginnings of our instruction, prophecy says that when the princes have begun to work in us from the beginning, we then follow on with will and purpose, and, increased by progress, come at last to bless God himself. In the beginning, it says, of the princes in Israel. It is the beginnings that are said to be helped by the princes. After this we must strive with our own will and purpose, that we may merit to bless the Lord. For when the people of Israel was beginning to go out of Egypt and to cross the Red Sea, nothing was done by its own labour, but all through the princes, that is, through the angels. Whence: You shall hold your peace, and the Lord will fight for you. The destroying angel fought for them, who killed the firstborn of the Egyptians; of the Israelites he did not make even a beast to mutter. But we must not always wait for the angels to fight for us; only in the beginning are we helped by these princes; but in the course of time we ourselves too must go out armed to the battle. For before we learn wars, before we think of fighting the battles of the Lord, we are upheld by the angel princes; before we obtain the provision of the heavenly bread and are filled with the flesh of the immaculate Lamb, before we are inebriated with the blood of the true vine that came up from the root of David, while we are little ones and are fed with milk, so as to hold the word of the beginnings of Christ, we live as little ones under the angels as guardians and stewards. But afterwards it is said to us: Put you on the armour of God, that you may be able to stand against the deceits of the devil. The Apostle does not suffer us any longer to lie hidden under the wings of those who give suck; he invites us to the fields of the contests. Thou seest how all things are done in order in the people of God: in the beginning the princes help. When thou hast been helped by them and taught, now do of thine own accord the things thou hast learned from the princes. For rightly, when the first things are digested and the rudiments laid aside, it is committed to our will, that either the praise may be deservedly ours, as sought by our own virtue, or the blame which comes through our sloth.
5.3:
**“Hear”** — with the inner ears
**“O ye kings”** — he calls kings those whom he calls together to hear the word of God
**“give ear”** — the outer [ears]
**“ye princes.”** — The Seventy: satraps
**“HEAR, O YE KINGS”** — HEAR, O YE KINGS. ADAMANTIUS. Give ear, all ye satraps. As the satraps are inferior to the kings, so too to give ear seems to be inferior to hearing. For to hear belongs to the inner man; whence: He that hath ears to hear, let him hear. But to give ear belongs to the outer and bodily hearing. Therefore those who ought to hear are called kings; but those who [ought] to give ear, satraps.
**“ADAMANTIUS”** — ADAMANTIUS. Exult, people of God; hear the marks of thy nobility. Thou art called to hear the word of God not as a commoner but as a king. For thou art a royal and priestly race; whence Christ your King is called "King of kings and Lord of lords". But if thou exultest in the title of nobility, learn by doing what each one becomes a king. Thou makest thyself king of all if Christ reigns in thee. For a king [rex] is so called from ruling [regendo]. If, then, the mind reigns in thee and the body obeys, if thou keepest down the vices with the bridle of sobriety, thou art deservedly called a king, because thou rulest rightly; and, made such, thou wilt worthily be called as a king to hear the divine words.
**“It is I, it is I, that will sing to the Lord”** — ADAMANTIUS. That is the voice of the just man, of tuneful voice and sincere mind, so that his song delights the divine hearing: who has in himself no hoarse sound of sin at all, and nothing of offence in his tongue, nothing of grossness in his spirit.
5.4:
**“O Lord, when thou wentest out of Seir”** — The Lord is said to have gone out of Seir and passed through Edom because, the Idumeans being unwilling to receive the law, he gave it on mount Sinai.
**“and passedst by the regions of Edom, the earth”** — on mount Sinai, namely
**“trembled, and the heavens and the clouds dropped water”** — the heavens, trembling before the face of the Lord, are said to have sweated and dropped waters
5.5: **“The mountains melted before the face of the Lord, and Sinai”** — trembled and smoked, understand
5.6:
**“In the days of Samgar the son of Anath”** — or Enaph, or Sanaph
**“in the days of Jahel the paths rested”** — Sisara, namely, having been slain by Jahel, the ways were opened, and without any fear they went to the house of the Lord, not as before by by-paths
**“IN THE DAYS OF SAMGAR”** — IN THE DAYS OF SAMGAR. The paths are said to have rested which in the days of Samgar, the leader of Israel, had been seized by the enemy, and they dared not go up to the house of the Lord to pray; from whom it is not written that Samgar fully set them free.
**“and they that went by them, walked through by-ways.”** — they failed
5.7:
**“The valiant men ceased”** — the preachers of the law
**“and rested in Israel: until Debbora arose”** — who by preaching and exhorting might teach, and by counselling might set free from the enemy
5.8:
**“The Lord chose new wars”** — because he made the unarmed strong and triumphant
**“and he himself overthrew the gates of the enemies: a shield and spear”** — because neither shield nor spear could be found in Israel, since Jabin king of Chanaan had taken their arms from them
**“was not seen among forty thousand of Israel.”** — ADAMANTIUS. Not human, namely, but divine; for I do not think according to man
5.9:
**“My heart”** — he brings in God speaking
**“loveth the princes of Israel”** — in the Hebrew: the teachers
**“MY HEART”** — MY HEART. ADAMANTIUS. My heart toward the things that are ordained for this Israel. As if: my heart, my mind and my whole soul tends to that and looks forward to that which is ordained and prepared for Israel. Whence: I count all things that are in the world as dung, that I may gain Christ, who has prepared all those things which eye hath not seen nor ear heard.
**“O you that of your own good will”** — the teachers of the law, who of their own accord offer their lives to danger
**“O YOU THAT OF YOUR OWN GOOD WILL”** — Of whom it is said: You that of your own accord offered your lives to danger, etc., because they subjected themselves to the law of God and to its service, meditating day and night on his law.
5.10:
**“you that ride upon fair asses”**
• in the Hebrew: she-asses. These are the teachers of Israel, on whose doctrine the people is said to mount and rest.
• ADAMANTIUS. The bodies, namely, made subject to the soul, shining with the splendour of chastity and modesty
**“YOU THAT RIDE UPON FAIR [ASSES]”** — YOU THAT RIDE UPON FAIR [ASSES]. ADAMANTIUS. Ye mighty of the people, bless the Lord, you that mount upon the beasts, etc. Our body is a beast: for it is given to the soul for a beast and for service. It is said to the inner man. He who mounts upon the beast, that is, his body, and is made superior to the bodily desires, and has governed the motions of the body with the bridle of reason, [is called] to bless the Lord.
**“and you that sit in judgment”**
• in the Hebrew: sitting upon judgment
• by the knowledge of the law
**“and walk in the way”** — of the law, not straying, namely
**“Speak.”**
• that is, praise
• He calls the people sitting upon the she-asses to bless the Lord.
5.11:
**“Where the chariots were dashed together, and the army of the enemies was choked, there let the justices of the Lord be rehearsed, and his clemency towards the brave men of Israel.”** — ADAMANTIUS. The sacrifice acceptable to God, which is offered in justice and equity.
**“WERE DASHED TOGETHER”** — As if: although God is to be praised always and everywhere, is he not rather to be praised and blessed here, who overthrew our enemies, as the Egyptians in the Red Sea?
**“THERE LET [THE JUSTICES] BE REHEARSED”** — ADAMANTIUS. The Seventy: The just were strengthened in Israel. In other nations those who are stronger in bodily might are called mighty in battle; but in Israel those who are more just, because justice, even when weak in strength, conquers; but injustice, even if it has many strong warriors, is overcome. In our nation, then, either we overcome through justice, or we are conquered through injustice.
**“Then the people of the Lord went down to the gates”** — of the house of the Lord, namely; because, having blessed and praised the Lord in the place of the victory, they went down to the house of the Lord to praise him there, offering prayers and sacrifices.
**“and obtained the sovereignty.”** — this is not in the Hebrew
5.12:
**“Arise, arise, O Debbora, arise, arise, and utter a canticle. Arise, Barac”**
• ADAMANTIUS. Prophecy rises up at the coming of Christ and makes the peoples rise up to the faith.
• ARISE, ARISE, O DEBBORA, etc. It is not in the Hebrew, but: awake, namely, with the spirit of prophecy. For the perfect teachers call on Debbora to awake with the spirit of prophecy and of praise.
**“and take hold of thy captives”**
• in the Hebrew: take thy prey.
• He takes captivity from the enemies who keeps the answers of the heavenly Father.
**“O son of Abinoem.”** — ADAMANTIUS. Of the answer of the father.
5.13:
**“The remnants of the people are saved,”** — The remnant of Israel shall be saved.
**“the Lord among the valiant ones”** — against the Egyptians and their other enemies
**“hath fought.”** — in the Hebrew: The Lord fights for me among the valiant. And it is the voice of the whole people.
5.14:
**“Out of Ephraim he destroyed them into Amalec”** — In Exodus it is read: "Josue put Amalec and his people to flight by the edge of the sword", etc.
**“and after him”** — Josue
**“out of Benjamin”** — Saul, namely, at the command of the Lord, destroyed Amalec; which Debbora prophesied long before.
**“into thy people, O Amalec.”** — this "O Amalec" is not in the Hebrew, but has been added for the sake of opening the sense.
**“Out of Machir there came down princes”** — to lay Sisara low, namely
**“and out of Zabulon”** — came down, namely
5.15:
**“The captains of Issachar”** — the teachers of the law, namely
**“were”** — for war
**“with Debbora, and followed the steps of Barac”** — because a certain part of them remained with Debbora to praise God, and a part followed Barac to exhort the people and to overcome Sisara
**“who exposed himself to danger, as one going headlong, and into a pit.”** — throwing himself, namely, into the torrent Cison and pursuing the enemies
**“Ruben being divided against himself, [there was found a strife] of courageous men”** — of the proud
5.16:
**“Why dwellest thou between two borders”** — thine own, namely, and those of the neighbouring cities
**“that thou mayest hear the bleatings of the flocks?”** — As if: thou desirest to serve the flocks in which thou aboundest, and delightest rather to hear their bleatings than to go to meet the enemy with thy brethren, and in pride thou gainsayest the command of the Lord.
**“Ruben being divided against himself, there was found a strife of courageous men.”**
• against the command of the Lord
• he says this in rebuke, because Ruben and Gad stayed behind:
**“BEING DIVIDED AGAINST HIMSELF”** — BEING DIVIDED AGAINST HIMSELF. The voice of Debbora rebuking Ruben, who did not obey the command of the Lord with his brethren to overcome the enemy, but, terrified and unbelieving of the words of the Lord, divided himself from them, and therefore was found magnanimous, that is, proud. Whence he is rebuked in the spirit of prophecy thus: Why dwellest thou between two borders, etc. But in the Hebrew two is not found.
5.17:
**“Galaad rested beyond the Jordan, and Dan applied himself to ships.”** — Seeing Ruben and Gad failing their brethren, he took to flight in ships.
**“Aser dwelt on the sea shore, and abode in the havens.”** — he rebukes Aser because he took to flight by ship rather than bring help to his brethren
5.18: **“But Zabulon and Nephtali offered their lives to death in the region of Merome.”** — the rest failing, these two tribes offered their lives to death in the region of Merome, that is, of the height, because they offered themselves to danger for the people of God.
5.19:
**“The kings came”** — a mockery of the enemy
**“and fought, the kings of Chanaan fought”** — who, namely, were subject to Jabin
**“in Thanach by the waters of Mageddo”** — the province in which is the torrent Cison, by the waters of Mageddo
**“and yet”** — a scoffing, because they did not save even their lives
**“they took no spoils.”** — because among ten thousand of Israel there was neither shield nor spear
5.20:
**“War from heaven was made”** — with hail and fire
**“against them, the stars remaining in their order and courses fought against Sisara.”** — the angels, who fought against Sisara
5.21:
**“The torrent of Cison dragged their carcasses, the torrent of Cadumim, the torrent of Cison.”** — It is the voice of the people magnanimously exhorting itself to tread on the necks of its enemies:
**“DRAGGED THEIR CARCASSES”** — Into the Red Sea, which is Cadumim, which is interpreted of the ancients, because the ancient miracles were done there, when the children of Israel crossed and the Egyptians perished; so that in place of the carcasses of the Egyptians the fishes and beasts of the Red Sea might have the carcasses of the Chanaanites.
5.22: **“The hoofs of the horses were broken whilst the stoutest of the enemies fled amain, and fell headlong down.”** — by hailstones sent from heaven; as if the hoofs of the horses, struck by the stones, were broken; which thou mayest think befell the horsemen
5.23:
**“Curse ye the land of Meroz, said the angel of the Lord:”** — Michael, who through Debbora commands to curse Meroz, that is, the contrary power which presided over the Chanaanites. For Meroz is interpreted secret. For while the other angels fought for Israel, the apostate angels not only did not fight but even opposed.
**“curse the inhabitants thereof, because they came not to the help of the Lord, to help his most valiant men.”** — of the warriors
5.24:
**“Blessed among women be Jahel the wife of Haber the Cinite”** — the holy women, namely, Sara, Rebecca, Rachel, Lia and the like
**“and blessed be she in her tent.”** — of the Lord
5.25:
**“He asked her water”** — she acted wisely and prudently
**“and she gave him milk, and offered him butter in a dish fit for princes.”** — that the enemy might trust himself to her the more firmly; she gave milk indeed, not wine, because the house of Rechab drank no wine.
5.28: **“His mother looked out at a window, and howled: and she spoke from the dining room.”** — a mockery
5.31: **“And the land rested for forty years.”** — ADAMANTIUS. The land rests while sin rests. But the land, that is, those who dwell on the land, is moved when sins move and trouble the souls of men.

6.1:
**“And did”** — ADAMANTIUS. While there was justice in the land it is said to have rested; but when iniquity grew and they did evil in the sight of the Lord, he delivered them into the hand of Madian.
**“the children of Israel evil in the sight of the Lord: and he delivered them into the hand of Madian”** — of the demons
**“seven years”** — with a perfect and condign penance
**“AND [THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL] DID”** — AND [THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL] DID. ADAMANTIUS. The Madianites are not said to have prevailed over the people of God while it kept the commandments. When, then, it began to neglect them, the enemy at once prevailed. Against us too, who are called Israel according to the spirit, the spiritual enemy rises up when we neglect the commandments of God; and we are delivered to the enemies when we are forsaken by the grace of God.
6.2: **“And they were oppressed”** — by spiritual affliction
6.3:
**“And when Israel had sown, Madian and Amalec, and the rest of the eastern nations came up”**
• "He that soweth in the flesh, of the flesh also shall reap corruption"
• It often happens too that one who, toiling much in spiritual work, has brought forth very many fruits, and has filled his barns with the crop of justice, and has laid up many good works in the chamber of his conscience, yet, if he grows negligent and after his labour inclines more readily to pleasure, all those seeds of good things will be spoiled, lust having the mastery. Therefore it is said: With all watchfulness keep thy heart. The heart, therefore, is to be kept from every sin, especially in time of persecution. For if anyone then denies the faith, he has lost all the fruits of justice, made suddenly naked and empty; and what was long sought and gathered with much and hardly won labour, all that labour is suddenly poured out, according to that: All his justices which he hath done shall not be remembered. Let us pray, then, that we may be able to endure persecution, because tribulation worketh patience, and patience trial, and trial hope. For our trial extends not only to stripes, but even to the shedding of blood, because Christ, whom we follow, shed his blood for our redemption, that we might go forth thence washed in our own blood. For the baptism of blood alone is that which renders us purer than the water of baptism, of which it is said: I have a baptism wherewith I am to be baptized, which you know not. He called, then, the shedding of his blood a baptism. And if I do not offend in teaching these things, I fear that this baptism is more eminent than that baptism which is given through water. For of those who receive that one, very few keep it unspotted to the end of life; but he who has been baptized with this can sin no more. And if it is not rash to hear something in such matters, we can say that by that baptism past sins are purged, by this future ones too are destroyed. And the prince of this world, coming to such a soul, finds nothing; nay, he is lulled by the shedding of blood, and dares not accuse in anything the soul made glorious by its death, washed in blood.
**“AND WHEN [ISRAEL] HAD SOWN”** — AND WHEN [ISRAEL] HAD SOWN. ADAMANTIUS. Israel according to the flesh suffered these things. It sowed the land, but because it had been delivered to its enemies for its sins, it reaped corruption instead of crops. But we, who are named Israel according to the spirit, sometimes sow, and the enemies cannot spoil what is sown nor lie in wait for our husbandry. But there is a time when our sowings are spoiled. Whence: He that soweth in the flesh, of the flesh also shall reap corruption; but he that soweth in the spirit, of the spirit shall reap life everlasting. The Madianites, then, spoil the seeds of those who sow in the flesh, and their fruits are destroyed and perish. But what is sown in the spirit the Madianites cannot spoil. For the demons cannot go up to the spiritual fields and violate the fallow lands of the spirit, namely of those who do not sow upon thorns, but break up for themselves fallow ground.
6.8: **“And he sent unto them a prophet”** — AND HE SENT UNTO THEM, etc. AUGUSTINE. Why the name of this prophet is not given, the cause is hidden; yet I do not think there is none. But because after the words with which he reproached the people for disobedience, the Scripture follows, saying: And an angel of the Lord came and sat under the oak that was in Ephra, it is not absurdly understood that this angel was signified by the name of a man, so that after he had spoken these words he came to the oak and sat there. For angels are often spoken of by the name of men; but that angels are called prophets does not come to mind, though one who is a prophet is often found to be called an angel. But if prophetic sayings of angels are known, that is, by which they foretold things to come, why could not an angel be called a prophet?
6.11:
**“And an angel of the Lord came, and sat under an oak, that was in Ephra, and belonged to Joas the father of the family of Ezri. And when Gedeon his son was threshing”** — in the shade of the oak, that is, of the cross
**“and cleansing”** — from vices
**“wheat”** — virtues
**“AND WHEN GEDEON”** — AND WHEN GEDEON. ISIDORE. Gedeon signifies Christ, who, set under the shade of the holy cross, in the predestined mystery of the incarnation to come, by the rectitude of judgment as with a rod separated the election of the saints from the chaff of the vices.
6.14: **“And the Lord looked upon him, and said: Go in this thy strength, and thou shalt deliver Israel out of the hand of Madian: know that I have sent thee.”** — AUGUSTINE. He speaks with the authority of the Lord by whom he was sent
6.17:
**“And he said: If I have found grace before thee, give me a sign that it is thou that speakest to me.”** — because the devil "transformeth himself into an angel of light"
**“GIVE ME A SIGN”** — GIVE ME A SIGN. ADAMANTIUS. A learned man, and having the example of Jesus his predecessor, he acts more cautiously. For he knew that the angels of darkness can transform themselves into angels of light; therefore he tries the spirit, whether it be of God. For the spiritual man examines all things. So his predecessor Jesus Nave, when he had seen the prince of the heavenly host, asks: Art thou ours or of our adversaries? Therefore Gedeon tests the angelic vision by the diversity and change of signs.
6.18: **“AND BRING A SACRIFICE”** — AND BRING A SACRIFICE. AUGUSTINE. It is to be noted that Gedeon does not say to the angel: I will offer thee a sacrifice, but: I will offer my sacrifice, and lay it before thee. Whence it is to be understood that he offered the sacrifice not to the angel but through the angel. Which the angel showed, who did not take it from him as for himself, but said to him: Take the flesh and the unleavened loaves and lay them upon that rock, and pour out the broth. And when he had done this, the angel of the Lord put forth the tip of the rod that was in his hand and touched the flesh and the unleavened loaves, etc. So the angel himself fulfilled in the sacrifice the office of one ministering. For the fire which a human minister would have set under it without a miracle, as a man, he himself set under it wonderfully, as an angel. Then at last Gedeon knew that he was an angel of the Lord. For the Scripture adds this at once: And Gedeon saw that he was an angel of the Lord. Before, then, he was speaking as with a man, whom yet he believed to be a man of God, so that he wished to offer the sacrifice before him, as if to be helped by the presence of his holiness.
6.19:
**“SO GEDEON WENT IN”** — SO GEDEON WENT IN. GREGORY. Gedeon, while he was threshing the wheat from the chaff, saw an angel, at whose command he boiled a kid, put it on the rock, and poured the broth of the flesh over it. These the angel touched with his rod, and fire coming out of the rock consumed them. To beat the wheat with a rod is, by the rectitude of judgment, to separate the grains of the virtues from the chaff of the vices. To those who do this an angel appears, because the Lord makes known inward things the more, the more zealously men cleanse themselves from outward things. He commands the kid to be killed, that is, every appetite of our flesh to be sacrificed, and the flesh to be put upon the rock, and the broth of the flesh to be poured over it. The rock signifies Christ, of whom it is said: And the rock was Christ. We put the flesh upon the rock when we crucify our body in imitation of Christ. He also pours the broth of the flesh over it who in the conversation of Christ has emptied out even his carnal thoughts themselves. For it is as if the broth melted from the flesh were poured upon the rock when the mind is emptied of the flow of carnal thoughts. That the angel touches with the rod is because the power of the divine help does not forsake our intention. Fire comes out of the rock and consumes the broth and the flesh, because the spirit breathed from the Redeemer burns our heart with so great a flame of compunction that it burns up all that is unlawful in it of work and thought. For the perfect mind watches carefully, not only to refuse to do perverse things, but also to wipe away all that basely melts in it through thoughts.
**“and boiled a kid”** — every appetite, namely, of the flesh
**“and made unleavened loaves of a measure of flour: and putting the flesh in a basket, and the broth of the flesh”** — the carnal thoughts
**“into a pot, he carried all under the oak, and presented to him.”**
• as to a minister
• SO GEDEON WENT IN, etc. AND PRESENTED TO HIM, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is asked why Gedeon dared to offer a sacrifice apart from the place where God had commanded. For he forbade sacrifice to be made to him outside his tabernacle, to which the temple succeeded. And in the time of Gedeon the tabernacle was in Silo. But it is to be known that he at first thought the angel a prophet, and consulted him about offering a sacrifice to the Lord. If he had forbidden it, it would not have been done. But because he assented, Gedeon followed the authority of God. For God so established those legal ordinances as to give laws not to himself but to men. Whence what he himself commanded apart from them was fulfilled not by transgressors but by the obedient, as by Abraham in sacrificing his son. So Elias sacrificed outside the tabernacle of the Lord, to convince the priests of the idols, by the command of the Lord, who bade him do this by revelation and inspiration. And yet the custom of sacrificing apart from the tabernacle had grown so frequent that even Solomon is found to have sacrificed on the high places, and his sacrifice was not rejected. And yet those kings are censured who among their praiseworthy works did not destroy the high places, where against the law of God the people had been wont to sacrifice; and he who destroyed them is the more praised. Thus God bore with, rather than forbade, the custom of his people by which, though apart from his tabernacle, they offered not to strange gods but to their own God, hearing those who offered even so. But what Gedeon did was brought about through the angel, that it might be done prophetically, so that in the prophecy that rock might be set forth; to which sacrifice was not offered, but from which fire is recorded to have come out to consume the sacrifice. For whether by the water which the rock poured forth when struck in the desert, or by fire, the gift of the Holy Ghost is signified, which Christ has poured out most richly upon us. Whence: "If any man thirst, let him come and drink. He that believeth in me, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water. Now this he said of the Spirit which they should receive who believed in him." And elsewhere: There appeared to them parted tongues as it were of fire, etc. And the Lord himself says: I am come to cast fire on the earth.
6.20: **“And the angel of the Lord said to him: Take the flesh and the unleavened loaves, and lay them upon that rock”** — Christ, in imitation of whom we crucify our body
6.21:
**“The angel of the Lord put forth the tip of the rod, which he held in his hand, and touched the flesh and the unleavened loaves: and there arose a fire”** — the spirit, namely, breathed from the Redeemer
**“from the rock, and consumed the flesh and the unleavened loaves.”** — ISIDORE. Because in the flesh of Christ the sins of the whole world were blotted out, [the rock] namely struck with the rod, that is, crucified; and it purged not only deeds but also desires. For the flesh of the kid signifies the guilt of the deed, the broth the allurements of desire. The fire went out of the rock because the flesh of Christ, filled with the divine Spirit, burned up all sins; whence: "I am come to cast fire on the earth", etc.
6.25: **“That night the Lord said to him: Take a bullock of thy father's, and another bullock of seven years, and thou shalt destroy the altar of Baal”** — higher, or devourer
6.26: **“AND THOU SHALT TAKE THE BULLOCK”** — AND THOU SHALT TAKE THE BULLOCK. ISIDORE. The one which his father had assigned to the idols Gedeon killed, and he sacrificed another of seven years to God. In which he shows that after the coming of Christ all the sacrifices of heathenism are to be abolished, and now only the sacrifice of the passion of Christ is to be offered to God for the redemption of the people. For he is the bullock of seven years, full, namely, of the sevenfold Spirit.
6.32:
**“From that day Gedeon was called”** — ISIDORE. Going about in the womb: this is Christ, who, incarnate in the womb of the Virgin, was within the womb
**“Jerobaal”** — that is, strong against Baal through the substance of weakness, and outside the world through the power of majesty
6.33:
**“Now all Madian”**
• outside judgment
• from judgment
**“and Amalec”** — a licking people, that is, given to the belly and the gullet
**“and the eastern people”** — ADAMANTIUS. The Seventy: the sons of the east, that is, false Christians
**“NOW ALL”** — NOW ALL. ADAMANTIUS. There came together against Israel the Madianites, who are interpreted outside judgment, who, namely, are outside the judgment of God, and have sinned without the law and shall perish without the law; and Amalec, that is, a licking people, an earthly nation, namely, given to the belly and the gullet: carnal Israel, namely, came together against the spiritual. The sons of the east too are mixed with them. For every one who takes upon himself the name of Christ is made a son of the east. For of Christ it is said: Behold a man, the Orient is his name. But not always do those who have the name of Christ remain in the Church of Christ. When the heretics, who are reckoned by the name of Christ, assail the Church and the faith, the sons of the east with the Madianites and Amalec assail the people of God, with the pagans, namely, and the Jews.
**“and passing over the Jordan, camped in the valley of Jezrael.”** — ADAMANTIUS. In low and humble places, namely, do they pitch their camp who wish to assail the people of God.
**“IN THE VALLEY OF JEZRAEL”** — IN THE VALLEY OF JEZRAEL. ADAMANTIUS. Which is interpreted the seed of God. For the adversaries do not dare to go there where the fruits of the spirit are already born, but where the seed of God still lies and the fruit has not yet come up. For some fell by the wayside, and the birds of the air snatch it away; these, namely, are they who hear the word of God and receive it with joy; but the devil comes and takes away the word, or seed, out of their heart. So, then, these come and seek to take away the seed of God from the heart of those in whom it is sown, because they find them set in the valleys and following low things. For they receive the word of God lowly and unworthily and with a Jewish understanding. But he who goes up from the lowness of the letter to the heights of the spirit, from him the Madianites or Amalecites snatch nothing, nor the sons of the east either, because he is set on the summit of spiritual understanding.
6.34:
**“But the spirit of the Lord came upon Gedeon”**
• The Seventy: The Spirit of the Lord strengthened Gedeon
• "The spirit of wisdom and of understanding, the spirit of counsel and of fortitude", etc., filled him
**“and he sounded the trumpet and called together the house of Abiezer, to follow him.”** — ADAMANTIUS. The Seventy: And he called Abiezer after him; who, namely, was nowhere. And it is interpreted 'the help of our father'; he seems, then, to have called not some man but the help of the most high Father.
6.36: **“And Gedeon said to God: If thou wilt save Israel by my hand, as thou hast said”** — ISIDORE. He did not ask this sign as one unbelieving, but foresaw the mysteries to come and diligently searches them out, that he may believe the mystery the more when he has understood the oracle.
6.37:
**“I will put this fleece of wool”** — the people of the Jews
**“on the floor.”**
• where the harvest is to be cleansed and the chaff separated from the wheat
• of the whole world, namely, in which the superstition of the Gentiles was parched in its fruitless worship
**“If there be dew on [the fleece] only”** — of the word of God, which was given in the time of the law
**“[on the] fleece, and it be dry on all the ground beside”** — because no moisture of the divine word watered the other nations
**“IF THOU WILT SAVE”** — IF THOU WILT SAVE. If thou wilt save Israel by my hand, as thou hast said, behold I will put a fleece of wool on the floor, etc. Since there are many and innumerable signs which he could have asked to confirm the promise, it is asked why, after the angelic voice and the heavenly promise, he asked this new sign; [and,] having obtained it, he wrings the fleece into a basin; [and] why, in reversed order, he asks a second sign; especially since it is said: "Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God." But the issue of the matter teaches that it was not done against the commandment. For God would not have granted the petition if it had been against the law. The reason, then, of this mystery is to be seen. Now I remember that one of our predecessors said that the fleece of wool is the people of Israel; and the rest of the ground the rest of the nations; and the dew which fell upon the fleece the word of God, which was sent from heaven to that people alone. For the dew of the divine law had come upon Israel only; but dryness held all the nations, which no moisture of the divine word watered.
**“ON THE FLOOR”** — ON THE FLOOR. THE SAME. Not just anywhere, not in a field nor in a woodland, but on the floor, where the harvest is. The harvest indeed is great, but the labourers are few. He foresaw by the Holy Ghost that Christ gathers his people on the floor and cleanses it there, holding the fan in his hand. Not without cause, then, did so great and such a man, of whom even the Apostle makes mention in the catalogue of the prophets, choose the floor for laying the fleece. Nor without cause did he wring the fleece into a basin and fill it with water. For Christ laid aside his garments and, girding himself with a towel, put water into a basin and washed the feet of the disciples. Thou seest, then, that the prophets foreshadowed these things which were to be fulfilled in the last times through Christ. The water put into the basin, then, was the dew of heavenly grace, with which the feet of the disciples are washed. Whence he says: Now you are clean by reason of the word which I have spoken to you.
**“I shall know that by my hand, as thou hast said, thou wilt deliver Israel.”** — But we too, if we offer our feet, Jesus is ready to wash the feet of our soul and to cleanse them with the heavenly dew, the grace of the Holy Ghost, the word of doctrine. For he willed not the apostles only to be clean, but also all who believe through his word; and he says to all with Peter: If I wash thee not, thou shalt have no part with me. For no one has part with Jesus unless washed and clean. Lay aside, I pray, O Lord, the garments which thou didst put on for me; gird thyself for me; put water into a basin, and wash the feet of thy servants; wash away the filth of thy sons and daughters; wash the feet of our soul, that, imitating and following thee, we may put off the old garments, saying: I have put off my garment, how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet, how shall I defile them? For when thou hast washed my feet, thou wilt at once make me sit at table with thee and hear: You call me Master and Lord, and you say well, for so I am, etc. I will, then, wash the feet of my brethren. Therefore I draw water from the fountains of Israel; nay, I wring it out of the Israelite fleece, now from the fleece of the book of Judges or the book of Kings, now from the fleece of Isaias or Jeremias; and I put it into the basin of my soul, conceiving the sense in my heart, and I take the feet of those who offer themselves to be washed, that, all purified by the word, we may not be cast out of the bridal chamber for filthy garments, but with white garments, washed feet and clean heart, may sit at the banquet of the bridegroom Jesus Christ.
**“IF THERE BE DEW ON THE WHOLE FLEECE”** — IF THERE BE DEW ON THE WHOLE FLEECE. AUGUSTINE. In the trial of Gedeon the Lord showed what he wished to foretell: namely, that the fleece rained upon, with the whole floor round about dry, figures the first people of Israel, among whom were the saints with heavenly grace, as with a spiritual rain; and that afterwards the floor rained upon, with the fleece dried, figures the Church of God spread through the whole world, having heavenly grace not in a fleece, as in a veil, but in the open, the former people being as it were estranged from the dew of the same grace and dried up.
6.38:
**“And it was so. And rising before day wringing the fleece, a vessel”**
• of the heart
• Christ "put water into a basin, and washed the feet of the disciples"
**“he filled with the dew.”** — with the sense of the word
6.39:
**“And he said again to God: Let not thy wrath be kindled against me if I try once more, seeking a sign in the fleece. I pray that the fleece only may be dry”** — the Jewish people
**“and all the ground”** — the Gentiles
**“wet with dew.”**
• of the divine word
• When, namely, the sheep of the house of Israel shall have perished and denied the fountain of living water, let the dew of faith dry up in the sinners of the Jews.
• I PRAY THAT THE FLEECE ONLY, etc. ADAMANTIUS. In the reason of the second sign too, in which he says that the dew should come down upon all the ground, but dryness remain upon the fleece: see all this people, which has been gathered from the Gentiles through all the earth, having now the divine dew in itself, and filled within with dew, and watered by the writings of the prophets, and growing green with the evangelical moisture; but that fleece, that is, the Jewish people, suffering the dryness of the word of God, according to that: The children of Israel shall sit many days without king, without prince, without prophet, etc. The Prophet too, describing the coming of Christ, says: He shall come down like rain upon the fleece, and as showers falling gently upon the earth. For Christ came down like rain upon the fleece of the people of the circumcision, and as showers falling upon the earth, that is, upon the rest of the earth; but dropping also upon us, and bringing to us Gentiles the drops of the heavenly dew, that we too might drink, who were upon the earth dried up with continual drought. Holy Gedeon, then, beholding this order of the mystery with the prophetic spirit, asks the second sign too in reversed order. For he knew that the divine dew, which is the coming of the Son of God, would be not only for the Jews but afterwards for the Gentiles also, because by the unbelief of Israel salvation comes to the Gentiles. And this is why, instead of the dryness of the fleece, the whole earth is watered with the grace of the divine dew.

7.2:
**“And the Lord said to Gedeon: The people that are with thee are many”** — In human wars a more numerous army affords safer help, but it is not so in divine ones. For the work of divine power is not clear if it is propped by human supports. "The king is not saved by a great army."
**“and Madian shall not be delivered into their hands: lest Israel should glory against me, and say: I was delivered by my own strength.”** — lest he ascribe my victory to himself
7.3:
**“Speak to the people, and proclaim in the hearing of all, Whosoever is fearful and timorous, let him return.”** — As if: let him leave the contests to brave men, lest he give the rest an example of fear and dread.
**“WHOSOEVER IS FEARFUL AND TIMOROUS”** — WHOSOEVER IS FEARFUL AND TIMOROUS. ADAMANTIUS. Jesus cries the same today: He that is fearful and timorous of heart, let him not come to me to the wars. For he says: He that taketh not up his cross and followeth me is not worthy of me; and: He that hateth not his father and mother, brothers, sisters and children, yea and his own life also, is not worthy of me. Again: He that doth not renounce all that he possesseth cannot be my disciple. So he separates the fearful and timorous from his camp. Let the soldier of Christ, then, drive out fear and dread, and say confidently: If armies in camp should stand together against me, my heart shall not fear; and: The Lord is my light and my salvation, whom shall I fear? etc. Let not this malice frighten you, which is easily overcome by those who serve faithfully. In this camp women are wont to conquer, not by strength of body but by the power of faith, like Debbora, and Judith, who restored to her country the safety which the men had lost. Virgins too in their first youth have borne the tortures of tyrants for martyrdom.
