In those, then, who serve God, strength not of body but of soul is sought, because the victory is won not with darts of iron but with the weapons of prayers, and faith in the contest gives endurance. Whence: Stand therefore, having on the breastplate of justice, having your loins girt about with truth; and take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit; in all things the shield of faith, etc. So armed we ought to take up the standards of the cross of Christ and follow him. Yet if in persecution thou seest thyself inferior in strength to the cruelty of the tyrant, it is [permitted] in the service of Christ to give place to wrath, to flee from place to place; nor is a military offence charged to thee in this. Whence: If they persecute you in one city, flee into another. For the sum of the matter is not to deny Jesus, whom thou hast once confessed. And he confesses who flees for this reason, that he may not deny. In the Apocalypse, when those are enumerated who are to be cast into the pool of fire with the unbelievers and fornicators and sorcerers, the fearful and timorous are counted. So among great and abominable crimes the crime of fear and dread is set.
**“THE SEVENTY”** — THE SEVENTY. He is fearful who, as from a growing vice, is terrified by thought alone before he sees evils, rolling a chill dread through his limbs, so that he is undone not so much by the sight of evils as by hearing and expecting them. Therefore according to the Seventy he is called fearful of heart; for this vice remains fixed in the heart and in the inner parts of the mind. But he is timorous who trembles at the first sight of the encounter, yet is not terrified with his whole heart, but can be restored and given courage again.
**“So two and twenty thousand men went away from mount Galaad and returned home”** — the catechumens, namely, who give way in terror before baptism
7.4:
**“And the Lord said to Gedeon: The people are still too many, bring them”** — to be tried
**“to the waters”** — of baptism
**“THE PEOPLE ARE STILL”** — THE PEOPLE ARE STILL. ADAMANTIUS. The people are still many; bring them down to the water, and there I will try them for thee. As I see, those who were first rejected had not even gone down into the water, but still showed themselves catechumens, and were so deterred by the vice of dread that they did not even go down to the saving laver. Therefore they were rejected. But these second ones come to the water, to be tried there. And the Lord said to Gedeon: Every one that shall lap the water with his tongue, as a dog lappeth, thou shalt set him apart, etc. In almost all the deeds of the ancients great mysteries are signified, as here. For those who go down to the water, that is, to the grace of baptism, must not go forward on to the ground, nor bend the knees and yield to the temptations to come, but stand constantly, and lift up the hands that hang down and the feeble knees, and make straight steps with their feet. Thou hast come to the water of baptism; this is for thee the beginning of the spiritual fight. If thou art slack, if thou canst easily be bent, how wilt thou fight? How wilt thou stand against the wiles of the devil? Therefore the Apostle cries: Stand fast, and be not held again under the yoke of bondage. He, then, is approved, he is chosen, who, after he has come to the waters of baptism, knows not how to be bent to bodily and earthly necessities, who does not indulge vices, nor is laid prone through the thirst of sin.
7.5:
**“And when the people were come down to the waters, the Lord said to Gedeon: They that shall lap the water with hand and tongue,”**
• that is, with work and word
• that is, who draw in the rightness of doctrine and do not bend the rightness of works
**“as dogs are wont to lap”** — which above all animals love their masters
**“THEY THAT WITH HAND AND TONGUE”** — THEY THAT WITH HAND AND TONGUE. He says that they lap the water with hand and tongue, because the soldiers of Christ ought to work with hand and tongue, that is, with work and word. For he that shall do and teach shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven. He brings in too the likeness of the dog lapping, because above all other animals it is said to keep love for its own master, and its affection is said not to be blotted out either by terror or by injuries. There are, then, three hundred only who bear the image of this sacrament. These are the chosen, the approved, and the consecrated for victory, who can overcome the adversaries even by the very sacrament of the number. For they are three hundred, who are multiplied by three hundreds, and bear the number of the perfect Trinity.
**“thou shalt set apart by themselves: but they that shall drink bowing down their knees”** — slack, namely, in works
**“shall be on the other side.”** — who, namely, do not make straight steps with their feet
7.6:
**“And the number of them that had lapped water, casting it with the hand to their mouth, was three hundred men.”** — in the number, namely, of the perfect Trinity
**“AND THE NUMBER WAS”** — AND THE NUMBER WAS. AUGUSTINE. And the number of those who lapped with their hand, with their tongue, was three hundred men. Most Latin codices do not have with their hand, but only with their tongue, because they so understood what was said above, as dogs. But the Greek has both, with their hand, with their tongue, that it may be understood that they cast into the mouth water caught up with the hand, like dogs, which do not draw the water they drink with the mouth applied, as oxen do, but snatch it into the mouth with the tongue; as these too did, but casting the water into the mouth with the hand, which they received with the tongue. And the translation from the Hebrew has this more plainly: And the number of them that had lapped water, casting it with the hand to their mouth, was three hundred men. For men do not drink so as to draw water with the tongue without the work of the hand, like dogs; nor indeed had these been commanded to do this; but when they had gone down to the water to drink, many drank on bended knee, because it was done more easily and with less labour. But a few did not bend the knee but stooped, and drank like dogs, the water cast into the mouth with the hand. Their number, because they were three hundred, signifies the cross, because of the Greek letter tau. By which too it was prefigured that the Gentiles would rather believe in Christ crucified, because it is a Greek letter. Whence the Apostle signifies all the Gentiles by the name of the Greeks, saying: "To the Jew first, and to the Greek"; because among the tongues of the Gentiles the Greek so excels that all are fittingly signified by it. This number is to be noticed also in the home-born servants of Abraham, by whom he set free his brother from the enemy, when Melchisedech blessed him in a great mystery. For what is over, the eighteen, seems to signify at what time it would be done, that is, in the third, which was to be under grace. For the first is before the law, the second under the law, the third under grace. And the single times are signified by the number six, because of its perfection; for three sixes are eighteen. Whence too the woman who had been in infirmity eighteen years, bent over, the Saviour raised up. And that these were so approved that they were said to be like dogs in drinking signifies that God chose the contemptible and the ignoble; for the dog is held in contempt. Whence: It is not good to take the bread of the children and to cast it to the dogs. David too calls himself a dog, as something contemptible.
7.7: **“And the Lord said to Gedeon: By the three hundred men, that lapped water, I will save you, and deliver Madian into thy hand: but let all the rest of the people return to their place.”** — because "praise is not seemly in the mouth of a sinner"
7.13:
**“And when Gedeon was come, one told his neighbour a dream: and in this manner related what he had seen: I dreamt a dream, and it seemed to me as if a hearth cake of barley bread rolled”** — AUGUSTINE. Because through the contemptible things of the world the Saviour confounded his enemies
**“IT STRUCK IT, AND BEAT IT DOWN”** — IT STRUCK IT, AND BEAT IT DOWN. GREGORY. Of this battle it is said through the Prophet: "Thou hast overcome the yoke of their burden, and the rod of their shoulder, and the sceptre of their oppressor, as in the day of Madian." For the Lord, rescuing the Gentiles, overcame the yoke of their burden when by his coming he set them free from the servitude of the devil. He overcame the rod of their shoulder when, the human race being redeemed, he checked his smiting, which pressed them down heavily from perverse work. He overcame the sceptre of their oppressor when he cast down from the heart of the faithful the kingdom of the devil, who exacted the tributes of punishment due for sins. The coming of the Redeemer, then, is compared to the victory of this fight, because it is signified in that victory of Gedeon. For Gedeon signifies the coming of the Redeemer, of whom it is said: Lift up your gates, O ye princes, and be ye lifted up, O eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter in; the Lord who is strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle. This Gedeon prophesied by deed and by name: for Gedeon is interpreted going round in the womb. For Christ by the power of his majesty went round all things, but by the grace of his dispensation came into the womb of the Virgin; who, redeeming us by his dispensation, embracing all things by his divinity and taking humanity within the womb, was incarnate in the womb and was not shut in, because he was within the womb by the substance of weakness, and outside the world by the power of majesty. And Madian is interpreted from judgment: for his enemies were driven back not from the judgment of him who drives back, but from the judgment of him who judges justly. Therefore they are called from judgment, because, being strangers to the grace of the Redeemer, they bear even in their name the desert of just damnation. Against these Gedeon goes to battle with three hundred. In the hundred the fulness of perfection is wont to be understood. What, then, in the three hundred but the perfect knowledge of the Trinity? For with these the Lord destroys the adversaries of the faith, with these he goes down to the wars of preaching, who can know divine things and think perfectly of the Trinity, which is God. And it is to be noted that the number three hundred is contained in the letter tau, and is marked by the figure of the cross; which holds the figure of the cross, to which, if what stands out above in the cross were added to the cross line, it would be no longer the figure of the cross but the cross itself. Because, then, this number is contained in the letter tau, and by it shows the figure of the cross, rightly in these three hundred following Gedeon are signified those to whom it is said: If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me. They who follow the Lord take up the cross the more truly, the more keenly they both tame themselves and are tormented with the compassion of charity toward their neighbours. Whence: "Mark tau upon the foreheads of the men that sigh and mourn." Or by the three hundred this is signified, that the iron of the enemies is overcome by the wood of the cross.
7.16:
**“And he divided the three hundred men into three parts, and gave them trumpets”** — of preaching
**“in their hands, and pitchers”** — the bodies
**“empty, and lamps”** — the brightness of miracles
**“AND HE DIVIDED THE THREE HUNDRED”** — AND HE DIVIDED THE THREE HUNDRED. They were led to the river to drink the waters, and those who drew them on bended knees were removed from the purpose of the war. For by the waters the doctrine of wisdom is signified, and by the knee standing upright right working. Those, then, who bend the knee while they drink the waters are kept from the war, because Christ goes to battle against the enemies of the faith with those who, while they draw in doctrine, do not bend the rightness of works. For all are related to have drunk water then, but not all to have stood with upright knee; and those were rejected who bent their knees in drinking, because not the hearers of the law are just before God, but the doers. For because slackness of works is signified by the bending of the knees, it is rightly said: Lift up the hands which hang down and the feeble knees, and make straight steps with your feet. They go forth, then, to war with Christ as leader who show by work what they proclaim with the mouth, who draw in the streams of doctrine spiritually, and yet do not bend in carnal fashion to perverse works. In the trumpets is the cry of the preachings; in the lamps the brightness of the miracles; in the pitchers the frailty of bodies. For our leader led such with him to the battle of preaching as, despising the safety of their bodies, would lay low the enemies by dying, and would overcome their swords not with arms but with patience. For our martyrs came armed to the battle under their leader, namely with trumpets, pitchers and lamps: they sound with trumpets while they preach; they break the pitchers while they set their bodies, to be dissolved in suffering, against the swords of the enemy; they shine with the lamps while after the dissolution of their bodies they flash with miracles. And at once the enemies are turned to flight, because when they see the bodies of the dead martyrs flash with miracles, broken by the light of truth they believed what they were assailing. They sounded the trumpets, then, that the pitchers might be broken; the pitchers were broken that the lamps might appear; the lamps appeared that the enemies might be turned to flight; that is, the martyrs preached until their bodies were dissolved; these were dissolved that they might flash with miracles; they flashed that they might lay the enemies low by the divine light, lest, standing up, they should resist God, and that, made subject, they might fear him. And it is to be noted that the enemies stood before the pitchers but fled the lamps, because the persecutors of the faith resisted the preachers while they were still in the body; but after the dissolution of their bodies, when the miracles appeared, they were turned to flight, because, terrified with dread, they ceased from the persecution of the faithful: namely, by the preaching of the trumpets, the pitchers of the bodies being broken, they feared, having seen the lamps of the miracles. It is to be noted too that it is written there that they held the trumpets in the right hand and the pitchers in the left. For we are said to hold as on the right whatever we weigh as great, and as on the left what [we weigh] as nothing. Well, then, did they hold the trumpets in the right hand and the pitchers in the left, because the martyrs of Christ hold the glory of preaching as great, but the profit of their bodies as least. But whoever makes more of the profit of the body than of the grace of preaching holds the trumpet in the left hand and the pitcher in the right.
7.17: **“And he said to them: What you shall see me do, do you the same.”** — "Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example that you should follow his steps."
7.18:
**“When the trumpet shall sound”** — preaching
**“in my hand”** — with work, because work ought not to disagree with preaching
**“do you also blow the trumpets on every side of the camp, and cry out: To the Lord and to Gedeon.”** — AUGUSTINE. Because, namely, that was being done which would please the Lord and Gedeon
7.20:
**“And when they sounded their trumpets in three places round about the camp, and had broken their pitchers, they held in their left hands”** — because he holds the profit of the bodies as least, but the grace of preaching as great
**“AND THEY BROKE THEIR PITCHERS”** — AND THEY BROKE THEIR PITCHERS. ADAMANTIUS. They carry pitchers and lamps and a horn trumpet in their hands, and so they come to that innumerable multitude of enemies, among whom were camels like the sand of the sea. And when they had come to the battle they sounded the horn trumpets, and let the pitchers fall from their hands, and they were broken. Then, seizing the lamps, they rush upon the adversaries and at the same time blow the trumpets. See how the chosen soldiers of God fight with lamps. For so Christ had armed them, saying: "Let your loins be girt, and lamps burning in your hands"; and: So let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works, etc. With such lamps lit, then, the soldiers of Christ ought to fight, shining with the light of works. And he sounds the trumpet who speaks of heavenly things, discourses of spiritual things, and reveals the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven. He speaks with a trumpet who [speaks] of great and greatest things, who opens the knowledge of Christ to human ears. And the trumpet is called of horn because it is said of the saint: "His horn shall be exalted in glory." Therefore the trumpet of each is called of horn, because it discourses of the manifold knowledge of Christ and the sacraments of his cross, which is signified in the horn. With this trumpet, then, serving and fighting, we conquer the foreigners and turn the enemies to flight, even if their multitude be like the locusts. For the multitude of the demons is compared to locusts, which have a seat neither in heaven nor on earth. Let there go before, then, in this war the light of works and of knowledge, virtue, the preaching of the divine word. Let us too fight, singing together in hymns and psalms and spiritual canticles and crying to the Lord, that we may merit to obtain the victory from him.

8.27:
**“AND GEDEON MADE THEREOF”** — AND GEDEON MADE THEREOF. AUGUSTINE. It is asked what the ephud or ephot is. If indeed it is a priestly vestment, as most say, or rather an over-vestment, which in Greek is called ependyma or epomis, which may better be understood as the superhumeral, it rightly perplexes one how Gedeon made it of so much gold. For it is written: And the weight of the golden earrings which he had asked was a thousand seven hundred sicles of gold, besides the bracelets and collars and purple coverings which were upon the kings of Madian, besides the collars that were on the necks of the camels; and Gedeon made it into an ephud, and set it up in his city, and all Israel went a whoring after it, etc. How, then, could this garment be made of so much gold? For the mother of Samuel too made him an ephud bad, which indeed they have translated a linen ephud, when she gave him to the Lord to be brought up in the temple; where it appears more evidently that this is a kind of vestment. Or is it said, he set it up in his city, so that it might be understood that it was made of gold? For it is not said placed, but set up, because it was so solid that it could be set up, that is, being placed, it stood. When Gedeon, then, had done this unlawful thing, all Israel went a whoring after it, that is, by following it against the law of God.
**“And Gedeon made an ephod thereof, and put it in his city Ephra. And all Israel committed fornication with it, and it became a ruin to Gedeon and to all his house.”**
• Whence it is not idly asked, since it was not an idol, that is, the image of some false god, but an ephud, that is, one of the sacraments of the tabernacle, which belonged to the priestly vesture, how the Scripture speaks of the fornication of the people venerating these things. It is because, namely, apart from the tabernacle of God, where were those things which God had commanded to be made there, it was not lawful for anything like them to be made outside. Therefore it became a scandal to Gedeon and his house, that is, so that he departed from God, whom he had offended; because this too was a certain kind of idol, that anything made with hands should be worshipped as God outside the tabernacle of God, since those very things which were commanded to be made in the tabernacle were referred rather to the worship of God than worshipped as God or as the image of God.
• Although by the ephud, in that manner of speech which signifies the whole by a part, all the things can be understood which Gedeon set up in his city, as for the worship of God, like the tabernacle of God; and so by the ephot, because this is the mark of the priestly honour; so that the sin of Gedeon would be this, that outside the tabernacle of God he made something like it, where God might be worshipped: not that he set up an ephud of solid gold as if to be adored, but that of that gold he made the things which belonged to the ornaments or instruments of the sanctuary, all of which are signified by the ephud. The ephud itself too was not commanded to be made of gold alone; but this is the superhumeral of the priestly vesture, and it has something of gold. For it was commanded to be made of gold and hyacinth and purple and scarlet and fine linen. But because the Seventy set these things down in such a way that, having mentioned all that Gedeon had received of the spoils, they add: and Gedeon made it into an ephud, it seems that this was made of the whole of it; whereas by that manner of speech which signifies a part by the whole it can be understood thus: he made it into an ephud, as if, "thence he made an ephud", or "of it he made an ephud", not, namely, using all of it up on the ephud, but spending of it as much as was sufficient. For in that translation which is from the Hebrew it is read thus: And Gedeon made an ephod thereof. For what among the Seventy is ephut is read in the Hebrew ephot. But not all the priests used such a superhumeral, which was of gold, hyacinth, purple, scarlet and fine linen, but only the high priest. That, then, which was given to Samuel by his mother while he was still a boy was not such; whence it is called ephut bad, that is, linen. But I think Gedeon made that which was the chief vestment of the priest, by which the other works of the sanctuary too were signified, which he set up in his city apart from the tabernacle of God. And therefore it became a scandal to him and his house, so that his numerous offspring of sons perished, as the Scripture afterwards testifies.
**“AUGUSTINE”** — AUGUSTINE. It is to be understood that it was said by prolepsis that Gedeon made an ephot against the law of God of the gold which had been taken from the conquered enemies, so that it might be said at once whence the gold was and what was made of it. For this sin was committed at the end of the days of Gedeon, when the evils followed which the Scripture joins on, after it has said for how many years the land rested in the days of Gedeon.
8.33: **“BUT AFTER [GEDEON] WAS DEAD”** — BUT AFTER [GEDEON] WAS DEAD. AUGUSTINE. And it came to pass, when Gedeon was dead, that the children of Israel turned away, and went a whoring after Baalim, and they set up for themselves Baalberith as a covenant, that he should be their god, etc. Both Baalim and Baalberith are to be understood as idols. The transgression and fornication of the people after the death of Gedeon, then, is greater than while he lived, apart from the ephut; which, even if it was done unlawfully, was yet of the sacraments of the tabernacle; but this idolatry has not even a false defence of their fathers' religion. Whence, even if the ephut was made at the end of the time of Gedeon, yet before this God bore with it so patiently that peace continued in the land; because, though what he had forbidden had been done, yet he had not gone far from him who had commanded something of the kind to be made in his tabernacle in his honour. But now he would not have the graver things committed, and the open fornication of the people after idols, go unpunished.

9.4: **“And they gave him seventy weight of silver out of the temple of Baalberith: wherewith he hired to himself men that were needy, and vagabonds, and they followed him.”** — ISIDORE. So Antichrist will hire many with gifts to favour him
9.5:
**“And he came to his father's house in Ephra, and slew his brethren”** — ISIDORE. the believers, whom Christ begot in faith
**“the sons of Jerobaal, seventy men”** — of the seventy tongues
**“upon one stone: and there remained only Joatham the youngest son of Jerobaal”** — the remnant of Israel shall be saved
**“AND THERE REMAINED”** — AND THERE REMAINED. ISIDORE. The younger son, who escapes the sword of the enemy by fleeing, signifies the remnant of Israel, which will believe in the last time and escape the sword of Antichrist. He goes up to the top of mount Garizim, because no one can either prophesy or escape the persecution of Antichrist unless he has first gone up into the mountain of blessing, that is, into the height of faith and virtues. For this is mount Garizim, which was appointed by Moses for blessing.
9.7: **“This being told to Joatham, he went and stood on the top of mount Garizim”** — which was appointed for blessing
9.8:
**“The trees went”** — wandering, unfruitful men, prepared for the eternal burning
**“THE TREES WENT”** — THE TREES WENT. ISIDORE. If this deed were not mystical, what need was there to know that Gedeon had seventy sons and many wives, and also a concubine, from whom he had received one son, and a wicked one? Gedeon, then, signified Christ; the wives, the nations which have cleaved to Christ through faith; the seventy sons, the seventy tongues of the world, in which the Lord begot sons for himself through faith; the concubine, the Synagogue, which in the last times will believe in Antichrist, of which it is said: Who say they are Jews, and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan. From it in the last times the wicked son, that is, Antichrist, is to be begotten, the son of the handmaid, that is, of the sinful Synagogue. For whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin. He, gathering the wicked to himself, like Abimelech, will wickedly usurp the kingdom; and, having slain the noble sons, namely the faithful from divers nations and tongues, he will bring in persecution, to kill all the saints.
**“to anoint a king over them: and they said to the olive tree:”** — of the grace of the Holy Ghost
**“Reign thou over us.”** — AND THEY SAID TO THE OLIVE TREE: REIGN. ISIDORE. The trees of the forest are unfruitful, vain, wandering men, prepared for the eternal burning. Over these neither the olive nor the fig nor the vine deigns to reign, because they do not deserve it. For the olive signifies the grace of the Holy Ghost and the anointing of peace; the fig the law, which the householder planted in his vineyard: God, namely, who is the father of the household, that is, of all believers; who planted a vineyard, that is, the people of the Jews, and in this vineyard a fig tree, that is, the law; which cast the first people to the ground, like the dry and useless untimely figs, and afterwards brought forth other fruits, that is, the Christian people, which it led with glory and honour to the due ripeness of the evangelical discipline and to the most sweet fatness of Christ.
9.10: **“And the trees said to the fig tree:”** — the divine law
9.12:
**“And the trees said to the vine:”** — Christ, who said: "I am the true vine"
**“THE SAME”** — And the vine is Christ, who said: "I am the true vine." Because, then, the people which serves Antichrist is given up to a reprobate sense, that it may believe a lie, that is, Antichrist, since it would not believe the truth, that is, Christ, it is rejected from the reign of the vine, that is, of Christ, and from the olive, that is, the grace of the Holy Ghost, and from the fig, that is, the sweetness of the divine law.
9.14:
**“And all the trees said to the bramble:”** — Antichrist, or the devil
**“AND ALL [THE TREES] SAID”** — AND ALL [THE TREES] SAID. ISIDORE. The bramble is a kind of briar, which is commonly called bear's thorn, very rough and thorny, by which Antichrist is signified, who will lay waste the human race with all roughness and fierceness; and fire shall come out of the bramble, that is, iniquity out of Antichrist, and shall devour all who trust in him together with him.
9.15: **“And it answered them: If indeed you mean to make me king, come ye and rest under my shadow: but if you mean it not, let fire come out from the bramble, and devour the cedars of Libanus.”** — AUGUSTINE. It is of a more vehement threat, and in a manner of more present efficacy, if one says: If thou wilt not do what I will, let my wrath rage against thee, that is, let it rage now, why do I hold it back? As if he should say: it will rage, threatening future punishment in the manner of a promise.
9.18:
**“And you are now risen up against my father's house, and have killed his sons seventy men”** — the faithful of the seventy tongues
**“upon one stone, and have made Abimelech the son of his handmaid king”** — of the sinful Synagogue
**“over the inhabitants of Sichem, because he is your brother.”** — the son, namely, of perdition, as you are too
9.19:
**“If therefore you have dealt well, and without fault with Jerobaal”** — with Christ
**“and his house”** — with the faithful
9.20:
**“But if unjustly: let fire come out from him”** — of iniquity
**“and consume the inhabitants of Sichem, and the town of Mello: and let fire come out from the men of Sichem, and from the town of Mello, and devour Abimelech.”** — Antichrist himself will destroy both himself and others
9.21: **“And when he had said thus he fled, and went into Bera”** — ISIDORE. In the persecution of Antichrist none escapes but he who flees and goes up into the mountain of blessing. This is the mountain which the saints surround, which Moses in Deuteronomy appointed for the blessings.
9.23: **“AND THE LORD SENT A SPIRIT”** — AND THE LORD SENT A SPIRIT. AUGUSTINE. And God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of the Sichemites. Whether this word signifies God commanding or permitting cannot easily be determined. For where here is put sent forth, the Greek has exapesteilen, which is also in the Psalm where it is read: "Send forth thy light"; although in some places our translators, where exapesteilen is, have translated sent, not sent forth. It can be understood thus, then: that God sent forth the evil spirit as one willing to go between them, that is, gave power to the evil spirit to disturb their peace. But it is so far from absurd that an evil spirit should even be sent by the Lord for justice' sake, to punish, that some have translated exapesteilen even as sent in.
9.32: **“ARISE THEREFORE IN THE NIGHT”** — ARISE THEREFORE IN THE NIGHT. AUGUSTINE. And now arise by night, thou and thy people with thee, and lie in wait in the field; and it shall be in the morning, as soon as the sun riseth, thou shalt make haste and stretch out against the city. Some Latin [codices] have thou shalt make haste [maturabis], some thou shalt rise early [manicabis]. But what the Greek has cannot be said in one word, which is, thou shalt rise at dawn; and perhaps maturabis was said from the morning [matutino] time, although it is also wont to be said at other times for hastening a thing. But manicabis does not occur to me as a Latin word. But this perplexes one, that when it had said, as soon as the sun riseth, it added, thou shalt rise at dawn, since dawn itself, which in Greek is called orthros, signifies the time before the sun, which is now most commonly said when it has begun to grow white. So, then, it is to be understood that what is put as morning is understood as the dawn itself. But as soon as the sun riseth was added to express that it was to be done not when the sun had already risen, but when the brightness of the rising sun appeared. For the dawn grows white from nothing else but when the light of the returning sun has begun to touch the part of the sky which we see in the east. Hence it is that in the Gospel one evangelist says that one and the same thing was done at dawn, while it was yet dark, another at the rising of the sun; because that light of dawn, however little, comes from the sun rising, that is, coming toward its rising, and is known to belong to the sun, casting its brightness from the nearness of its presence. Which light some unlearned men thought was not the sun's, but that which was first created, before God made the sun on the fourth day.

10.1: **“AFTER ABIMELECH”** — AFTER ABIMELECH. AUGUSTINE. How was a man of the tribe of Issachar the uncle of Abimelech, when Abimelech had as father Gedeon, of the tribe of Manasses? How, then, were Phua and Gedeon brothers, so that Phua could be the uncle of Abimelech, whose son Thola succeeded Abimelech himself? Gedeon and Phua could, then, have had one mother, from whom they were born of different fathers, and been brothers, sons of one mother, not of one father. For women were wont to marry from some tribes into others. Whence Saul too, though he was of the tribe of Benjamin, gave his daughter to David, a man of the tribe of Juda; and a priest of the tribe of Levi married the daughter of king Joram, a man of the tribe of Juda. Hence Elizabeth and Mary are read in the Gospel to be kinswomen, though Elizabeth was of the daughters of Aaron. From which it is understood that some woman of the tribe of Levi married into the tribe of Juda, whence that kinship arose between the two, so that the flesh of the Lord should be propagated not only from the royal but also from the priestly stock.

11.1: **“THERE WAS AT THAT TIME JEPHTE”** — AUGUSTINE. Jephte is interpreted opening, who signifies Christ. For he opened to his disciples their understanding, that they might understand the Scriptures. This Jephte his brethren drove out of their father's house, as sons of a lawful wife [driving out] the son of a harlot. This the chief priests, scribes and Pharisees did against Christ, who seemed to glory in the observance of the law, as though he were undoing the law and therefore were not a lawful son; and as regards the nation, his mother can be called the synagogue of the Jews, which often committed fornication with idols. But they, as observers of the law, seemed lawful, while he seemed to act against the law. Therefore, as lawful sons, they seemed to themselves to have rightly cast out one not lawful: for according to this that people is said to commit fornication, because, not keeping the precepts of the law, it did not show faith as to a husband.
11.2:
**“Now Galaad had a wife of whom he had sons: who after they were grown up, thrust out Jephte”** — Christ
**“saying:”** — AUGUSTINE. They prevailed, namely, over the weakness of Christ, because he so willed it, that he should suffer at their hands the things he ought. As Jacob too, signifying this same thing, prevailed over the angel, with whom he wrestled that he might foreshow this very thing, the Lord.
**“Thou canst not inherit in the house of our father”** — AUGUSTINE. as if [they said]: This man is not of God, who keepeth not the sabbath; but boasting themselves to be lawful sons they said: We are not born of fornication; we have one Father, God
**“because thou art born of another mother.”** — AUGUSTINE. Because he hid how great he was, and lay hidden from them in their raging. "For if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory." He fled, because they saw the weakness of the dying, but not the power of the rising.
11.3:
**“AND HE DWELT IN THE LAND OF TOB”** — AUGUSTINE. He dwelt in the land of Tob, that is, in the good land, or rather the best. For what in Greek is agathon, in Latin is called best. And Tob is interpreted this, wherein the resurrection seems to be understood. For what land is better than the earthly body clothed with the excellence of immortality and incorruption?
**“and there were gathered to him needy men, and robbers, and they followed him as their prince.”** — AND THERE WERE GATHERED etc. AUGUSTINE. Before his passion he ate with publicans and sinners, saying: They that are whole need not the physician, but they that are sick. Crucified also among thieves, he carried one of them from the cross into paradise. But after he rose and began to be in the land of Tob, wicked men were gathered to him for the remission of sins, who walked with him, because they lived according to his precepts. This also is done daily, when the ungodly flee to him, that they may be justified and learn his ways.
11.5:
**“And as they pressed hard upon them, the ancients of Galaad went”** — AUGUSTINE. [Galaad means] casting off, or revelation: because at first they cast Christ off, but afterwards he will be revealed to them.
**“IN THOSE DAYS [THEY] MADE WAR”** — AUGUSTINE. They who had cast Christ off, turned again to him, received salvation in him. Whence in the Acts of the Apostles, when Peter exhorted them to turn to him whom they had persecuted, many were compunct in heart, desiring salvation from him whom they had estranged. For what is to be delivered from enemies but to be saved from sins? For so he says: Do penance, and be baptized every one of you in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and your sins shall be forgiven you. Or rather that calling of the Jews is signified which is hoped for at the end; which seems to be marked when it is said: and it came to pass after days, that is, after a time, as though that is not to be understood which was done when the Lord's passion was recent, but what is to come afterwards. To this seems to pertain that the elders of Galaad came to Jephte, so that by old age the last times are signified.
11.6: **“And they said to him: Come thou and be our prince, and fight against the children of Ammon.”** — [Ammon,] which is interpreted 'son of my people' or 'son of sorrow'. These are they who of that very nation remained unbelieving, or who are assigned to hell, or the devil and his angels.
11.7:
**“And he answered them:”** — an elegant answer; it expresses the prophecy more evidently
**“Are not you the men that hated me, and cast me out”** — in your opinion
**“of my father's house”** — David
**“and now you are come to me constrained by necessity?”** — as if: then we came to thee to persecute, now we come to follow.
11.8:
**“AND THE PRINCES SAID”** — AND THE PRINCES SAID. AUGUSTINE. Something like this was figured in Joseph, whom his brethren cast off by selling him, and when they were afflicted with famine they turned to his help and mercy. But here the signification of things to come shines out more fully, because not those very brethren who cast out Jephte came to him, but the elders of Galaad, making supplication for the whole people; just as the same nation is called Israel, whether in those who were then and rejected Christ, or in those who afterwards returned to his help. For it is said to a hostile people, whether in its elders or its younger, or in its posterity, drawing out long hatreds and at last converted in those who are then to be converted: Did not you hate me, and cast me out of my father's house? For they thought they had cast Christ out of the house of David, in which "of his kingdom there shall be no end."
**“AND FIGHT AGAINST THE CHILDREN”** — AND FIGHT AGAINST THE CHILDREN. AUGUSTINE. That Jephte is sought as leader against the children of Ammon, that when these are conquered they may be delivered, and that they desired to make war under him as leader: since Ammon is interpreted 'son of my people' or 'people of sorrow', either those enemies are signified who of that very nation remained in unbelief, or all who are predestined to hell, where "there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth," as for a people of sorrow; although by the people of sorrow the devil and his angels are fittingly understood, either because they gain eternal misery for those whom they deceive, or because they themselves are assigned to eternal misery.
11.9:
**“I WILL BE YOUR PRINCE”** — I WILL BE YOUR PRINCE. AUGUSTINE. That is, a king, which that nation did not yet have in the time of the Judges. But they began to have Saul as king, and afterwards his successors. For in Deuteronomy, when they are instructed what king they ought to have if it should please them, he is not named there king but prince; but Jephte signified him who is the true king.
**“AUGUSTINE”** — AUGUSTINE. A king, namely, as was written in the title of the cross. For after Jephte delivered them from their enemies, he was not made king over them, that we might understand these things to pertain rather to Christ than to Jephte himself, of whom Scripture closes the narrative thus: And Jephte judged Israel six years, and died etc. He judged Israel, then, as the other judges did; he did not reign there as prince, as those did who are contained in the volumes of Kings.
11.11:
**“Jephte therefore went with the princes of Galaad, and all the people made him their prince.”**
• a judge, namely, not a king
• because "he is the head of the body, the Church"
11.12:
**“And he sent messengers to the king of the children of Ammon”** — AUGUSTINE. He sends messengers of peace, as the Apostle, in whom Christ spoke, says: "If it be possible, as much as is in you, having peace with all men."
**“to say in his name, What hast thou to do with me, that thou art come against me, to waste my land?”** — AUGUSTINE. The teaching of Christ admonishes us how we are to walk, that is, to live, among those who are not "called to be saints according to his purpose." "For the Lord knoweth who are his."
11.24: **“ARE NOT THOSE THINGS WHICH [HE] POSSESSETH”** — ARE NOT THOSE THINGS WHICH [HE] POSSESSETH. AUGUSTINE. Shalt thou not possess whatsoever Chamos thy god hath given thee to inherit etc. Which some Latins have translated thus: Shalt thou not possess whatsoever Chamos thy god hath given thee etc. Wherein Jephte seems to have affirmed that the god called Chamos could give some inheritance to his worshippers. But some have it thus: Shalt thou not possess whatsoever Chamos thy god possessed? As though he could possess any such thing. Or perhaps it is said according to this, that the nations are set under angels, according to the canticle of Moses. Is that angel, under whom the children of Ammon were, called Chamos? Who would dare to affirm this, since it can be understood as said according to the opinion of him who thought that his god possessed this, or had given it to him for a possession?
11.29:
**“Therefore the spirit of the Lord came upon Jephte”** — in this it is signified that the Spirit is imparted to the members of Christ
**“and going round Galaad, and Manasses”** — the members of Christ are signified, advancing to carry off the victory over the enemies
**“AND GOING ROUND GALAAD”** — AND GOING ROUND GALAAD. AUGUSTINE. Galaad is interpreted 'casting off', Manasses 'necessity of passing over'. There are, then, those casting off, that is, despising, [to be passed over] by those who advance; necessity too is to be passed over, lest perhaps, when he who advances has passed the despisers, he should yield to those who terrify. The watchtower of Galaad also is to be passed over, for Galaad is also interpreted 'revelation'. Now a watchtower is a height for looking forth or looking down, that is, looking from above. The watchtower of Galaad, then, seems to signify pride of revelation; whence: "And lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me" etc. Therefore this too is to be passed over, that is, one must not remain in it, because of the danger of falling. These being passed, the enemies are easily overcome; which it signifies by saying, and passing from the watchtower of Galaad, and passing over to the children of Ammon.
11.30: **“IF THOU WILT DELIVER THE CHILDREN OF AMMON”** — IF THOU WILT DELIVER THE CHILDREN OF AMMON. AUGUSTINE. Whomever he had in mind, Jephte does not seem to have had his daughter in mind. For he would not say: Alas, my daughter, thou hast hindered me etc. For he shows that he was hindered from fulfilling what he had had in mind. But whom could he have in mind, who had no sons? Or did he have his wife in mind, and God did not will this to be done, and [so it came about] that he should not leave [the vow] unpunished, lest anyone afterwards should dare it; and that by great providence, from what befell, a great sacrament of the Church should be figured? From both, then, the prophecy was fitted: namely from what he had in mind in vowing, and from what befell him against his will. For if he had his wife in mind, the wife of Christ is the Church. But because the wife of this Jephte could not be a virgin, in that his daughter rather met him, both the rashness of the vow did not remain unpunished and the virginity of the Church was figured. To whom it is said: Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace.
11.31:
**“WHOSOEVER SHALL FIRST”** — WHOSOEVER SHALL FIRST. AUGUSTINE. Concerning the daughter of Jephte there is wont to be a great question for some who piously seek and desire to know what it means; for some who oppose the Scriptures with unskilled impiety, it is a charge, that the God of the law and the prophets delights even in human sacrifices. But neither did those sacrifices delight him in which holocausts of cattle were offered. But because they were significative, and certain shadows of things to come, he wished to commend to us the things signified by these sacrifices. And this also was a useful reason why they were changed and are now not only not commanded but forbidden to be offered: lest we should think that God truly delights in such things according to carnal affection.
**“Whosoever shall first come forth out of the doors of my house, and shall meet me when I return in peace from the children of Ammon, the same will I offer a holocaust to the Lord.”**
• But whether it was fitting that things to come should be signified even by human sacrifices is rightly asked: not that we ought in this matter to shudder at the deaths of men who must die at some time, but that those who would gladly accept this being done to themselves might be commended to God for an eternal reward. But if this were true, this sacrifice would not displease God. Yet Scripture testifies that it displeases him. For though he willed and commanded all firstborn to be his, yet he willed the firstborn of men to be redeemed from him, lest they should believe that their firstborn were to be immolated to God. Whence: Thou shalt not do in like manner to the Lord thy God; for they have done to their gods all the abominations which the Lord hateth, when they burned their sons and daughters with fire to their gods. Not only, then, does God not love, but he even hates such sacrifices, in which men are immolated. But those he loves and crowns, when the just man contends for the truth even unto death, or is slain by enemies whom he has offended for justice' sake, rendering them good for evil, that is, love for hatred. Such, he says, is the just blood, from the blood of Abel unto the blood of Zacharias. But chiefly, that he himself shed his blood for us and offered himself a sacrifice to God; and so he offered it, that he was slain by enemies for justice' sake. Imitating him, the martyrs contended even unto death for the truth, of whom it is said: As gold in the furnace he hath proved them, and as a victim of a holocaust he hath received them. Whence the Apostle: For I am even now ready to be sacrificed. But not as Jephte immolated his daughter to the Lord, but as it was commanded that cattle be offered, and forbidden that men be immolated. This seems more like that which Abraham did, which the Lord specially commanded to be done; not generally did he ever command such sacrifices to be made to himself, nay, he forbade them altogether to be made. What Jephte did, then, differs from the deed of Abraham, because the one offered his son at command, the other did what is forbidden by the law and is enjoined by no special command. In the very son of Abraham too the Lord showed that he did not delight in such sacrifices, when he forbade the father, whose faith he had proved by commanding, to slay his son, and set by a ram, by which the sacrifice might lawfully be completed according to the custom fitting the time.
• But if this moves anyone, how Abraham piously believed that God delights in such sacrifices, if they are offered unlawfully, and he therefore thinks that Jephte too rightly believed that such a sacrifice could be acceptable to God: first let him consider that it is one thing to vow of one's own accord, another to obey one who commands. For if something to his loss, beyond custom, is commanded a servant by his lord, and he does it with praiseworthy obedience, it does not follow that he is not to be punished if he has presumed to do it of his own accord. Then Abraham had ground to believe that [it was] beyond the divine command [that he] not spare his son, not believing that God gladly accepts such victims, but that he had commanded it in order to raise up the slain, and thereby, as a wise God, to show something. Whence his faith is praised in the Epistle to the Hebrews, because he believed this of God, that he could raise up his son. But this man, God neither commanding nor demanding it, and against the lawful precept of God, of his own accord vowed a human sacrifice. For he says: Whosoever shall come forth from the doors of my house to meet me etc. In these words he did not vow some beast which could be offered according to the law. Nor was it the custom that cattle should come to meet leaders returning with victory. Dogs indeed are wont to run to meet their masters; of these, since he did not vow them, he could not have thought, lest he seem to have vowed, to God's injury, a thing not only unlawful but also contemptible and unclean according to the law. Nor does he say 'Whatsoever shall come forth' but 'Whosoever shall come forth', where he had only a man in mind. Not, however, perhaps his only daughter, though who could go before her in so great glory of her father, unless perhaps his wife? For as to his saying not 'whosoever' [in the feminine] but whosoever [in the masculine] shall come forth from the doors of my house, Scripture is wont to put the masculine gender for either sex, as it was said of Abraham: Rising up from his dead, when his wife had died.
• Since, then, Scripture seems to have passed no judgment on this vow and deed, as on Abraham when at command he offered his son, but only to have left it written for readers to judge; as with the deed of Juda, when he went in to his daughter-in-law, unknowing indeed, but as far as in him lay he committed fornication, because he thought her a harlot, and Scripture neither approved this nor reproved it, but left it to be weighed by consulting the justice and law of God: so concerning the deed of Jephte it gave sentence on neither side, that our understanding might be exercised in judging. We might now say that such a vow displeased God, and that it was brought to that vengeance, that his only daughter above all should meet her father. For if he had hoped and willed this, he would not, on seeing her, at once have rent his garments and said: Alas, thou hast hindered me, my daughter etc. Then, so long a delay of sixty days being given to his daughter, the Lord did not forbid him the death of his only and dearest one, as he did Abraham, until by performing it he bereaved himself, but did not appease God by the immolation of a human being; and therefore this penalty was rendered to the father, lest the example of such a vow be left unpunished, so that men should either think they vowed some great thing to God when they vowed human victims, and, what is more horrible, those of their children; or those same vows should be not true but rather feigned, since, as by the example of Abraham, they would hope, knowing that God would forbid such vows to be fulfilled. We might, I say, say this, unless two testimonies of the Scriptures held us back, that we should search diligently into this deed, committed to memory in books of so great authority, lest we judge rashly. One, that Jephte is mentioned among such men that we should fear to blame him, when it is said: For the time would fail me to tell of Gedeon, Barac, Samson, Jephte etc. The other, that Scripture set first, saying: And the spirit of the Lord came upon Jephte etc. And added: And Jephte vowed a vow to the Lord etc., so that all the things that were done afterwards seem to be understood as works of the spirit of the Lord which came upon him.
• But whether, because after it was said: The spirit of the Lord came upon Jephte, these things followed, that he vowed that vow and conquered the enemies and paid the vow, all are to be ascribed to the spirit of the Lord, so that this sacrifice too should be held as if the Lord had commanded it, as to Abraham, I would not easily say, since after Gedeon made the ephod no prosperity is recorded. But after Jephte vowed the vow, his victory followed, for which he had vowed, and having obtained it, he paid the vow. For again it is to be considered that Gedeon, though not after he made the ephod, yet after he tempted the Lord (which is certainly a sin), with great slaughter of the enemies overcome, gained salvation for the people. For thus it is written: And Gedeon said to the Lord: Let not thy wrath be kindled against me, if I try once more in the fleece. For he feared the wrath of God, because he knew that he sinned in tempting, which God manifestly forbids in his law. Yet this sin was followed both by the evidence of a wonderful sign and by the prosperity of victory. For God had already determined to succour the afflicted people, and he used the mind of this leader whom he had taken for this work, not only faithful and pious but also failing and offending, both to foretell what he willed and to fulfil what he had said.
• For not only through these, who, though they sinned, are reckoned among the just, but also through Saul, wholly reprobate, God bestowed many things on his people; upon whom also the spirit of the Lord leapt, and he prophesied. For he did not know how to act justly, in that, namely, he raged against David, a holy man. The spirit of the Lord works through the good and the bad, through the knowing and the unknowing, what he knows and has determined is to be done; who also through Caiphas, not knowing what he said, prophesied that Christ must die for the nation.
• For who did it but the spirit of the Lord, caring to foretell things to come, that it should come into the mind of Gedeon, wishing to tempt the Lord and not believing what the Lord had already spoken to him, [to ask] this above all, of the fleece first wet with rain then dry, and of the floor first dry then watered? So that what falls short in faith may be ascribed to his offence; but that God used such a mind of his is to be left to his mercy and wonderful providence.
• But if anyone says that Gedeon did and said all things knowingly by prophetic revelation, that through him such signs might be shown, and that he did not fail in faith, and believed what the Lord had already promised him, but by a prophetic action willed to make trial in the fleece, and that therefore the trial was blameless, like the guile of Jacob; and that what he said to the Lord: Let not thy wrath be kindled against me, he did not say because he feared wrath, but because he trusted that he would not be angry, since he was doing what he perceived was to be done at the Spirit's dictation: let him say as it seems [to him], provided that he does not dare to excuse from sin the deed of the ephod which Scripture blamed, whatever it may signify.
• For that, too, the three hundred men, pertaining by their very number to the sign of the cross, took earthen pitchers and shut burning torches in them, which being broken, the lights suddenly terrified the multitude of the enemies, Gedeon seems to have done as of his own will. For Scripture does not say that the Lord moved him to do it; and yet so great a sign, who but the Lord inspired to be done? He prefigured that the saints would have the treasure of the evangelical light in earthen vessels. Whence: We have this treasure in earthen vessels; which being broken in their passion, a greater brightness of their glory shone forth, which overcame the enemies by the unlooked-for brightness of Christ.
• Whether, then, through the knowing or through the unknowing, the spirit of the Lord wrought the signification of things to come in prophetic times. Nor were their sins therefore not sins; because God, who uses even evil things well, used them to signify what he willed.
• If, then, it was not a sin either to vow or to pay a sacrifice of any human death, or even a parricidal one, because it signified something great and spiritual, in vain did God forbid such things and say that he hates them, since even those things which he commanded to be done are referred to the signification of spiritual things. But human sacrifices did not please God, when one is slain not for justice, as one who lives rightly or will not sin, but a man is immolated by a man like a chosen victim, in the manner of cattle.
• But if anyone says that, because the victims of cattle, now customary, though referred to a signification, made men less intent on seeking the great sacrament of Christ and the Church, God therefore, wishing to rouse the minds of men by a notable and unlooked-for thing, the more so because he had forbidden such sacrifices to be offered to him, took care that something be offered to him in which the very wonder should beget a great question, and the question should demand study to search out the mystery; and that the mind of man, piously searching the depth of the prophecy, should draw up Christ, as a fish with a hook, from the deep of the Scriptures: to this reasoning we do not object. But it is one question concerning the mind of the one vowing, another concerning the providence of God, who uses most well a mind of whatever kind.
• [If] therefore the spirit of the Lord, which came upon Jephte, commanded him to vow this, which Scripture has not disclosed, whose commands it is not lawful to despise, not only is folly not to be blamed, but obedience to be praised.
• For in this way, even if a man should kill himself, which it is wicked to do by human will and counsel, it is to be understood to be done obediently, not wickedly.
• But if Jephte, following a human error, thought a human sacrifice should be vowed, his sin indeed was justly punished in his only daughter, which he himself seems to show, rending his garments and saying: Alas, my daughter, thou hast hindered me etc.
• Yet this error has some praise of faith, because he feared God, so as to pay what he had vowed, and did not decline the sentence of the divine judgment upon himself: whether hoping that the Lord would forbid it, as he did to Abraham, or resolving to do his will, understood even when he did not forbid, rather than to despise it.
• Although here it is rightly asked whether it is more truly understood that God did not will this to be done, and that God would rather be obeyed in it if it were not done, since he had shown that he did not will this, both in the son of Abraham and in the lawful prohibition. But yet, if Jephte did not do it for that reason, he would seem rather to have spared himself in his only daughter than to have followed the will of God. He rather understood, then, in that his daughter met him, God as avenger, and faithfully submitted himself to just punishment, fearing a fiercer vengeance for evasion. For he believed that the soul of his good and virgin daughter was well received, because she did not vow herself to be immolated, but had not resisted her father's vow and will and had followed the judgment of God. For death, as it is not to be inflicted on oneself by anyone of his own accord, nor on anyone else of one's own accord, so when God commands it is not to be refused, by whose ordinance it must be undergone at some time. Nor does anyone who shrinks from suffering it labour to avoid it altogether, but only to put it off.
**“AUGUSTINE”** — AUGUSTINE. But among praiseworthy men is not only Jephte but also Gedeon, of whom Scripture likewise says: The spirit of the Lord strengthened Gedeon etc.; that he made an ephod we not only do not approve, but openly, Scripture judging it, reprove. Nor yet is any injury done to the spirit of the Lord, who strengthened him. Yet he is mentioned among those who by faith conquered kingdoms, wrought justice; because holy Scripture, whose faith and justice it truly praises, is not hindered from noting their sins. For in this too, that Gedeon, asking a sign, as he spoke, made trial with the fleece, I know not whether he did not transgress this precept: Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God. But yet even in his trial the Lord showed what he wished to foretell; nor was it in vain that among the faithful and those working justice he merited such testimony, for the good and faithful life in which it is to be believed he died.
**“ISIDORE”** — ISIDORE. Jephte signifies Christ, who, departing from the face of his brethren, that is, the Jews, received the princedom among the Gentiles; because he fulfilled all the sacraments of human salvation as one sworn, and offered his own flesh, as a daughter, for the salvation of Israel. And he swore to the Father and vowed, according to that: "How he swore to the Lord, he vowed a vow to the God of Jacob": namely that he would fulfil the sacrament of religion in the passion of his flesh for the salvation of the human race. These things, then, were so done by Christ that they seem to be fulfilled by the religion of an oath.
11.37: **“AND MAY BEWAIL MY VIRGINITY”** — AND MAY BEWAIL MY VIRGINITY. AUGUSTINE. The chaste virgin, that is, the Church, will become a holocaust in the resurrection, when in her entire that will be done which is written: "Death is swallowed up in victory." Then the true Jephte will deliver the kingdom, that is, the Church, to God and the Father, when the sixth age of the world is completed; therefore a delay of sixty days was asked. For the Church is gathered out of all the ages: namely from Adam to the flood, from the flood, that is, from Noe, to Abraham; thence to David; then to the transmigration of Babylon; from the transmigration to Christ; thence to the end of the world. Through these six ages, as through sixty days, the holy virgin weeps her virginity; because, though virginal, yet there were sins to be bewailed. Whence through the whole world she cries: "Forgive us our debts, etc." These sixty days she preferred to call two months, because of the two men: one through whom came death, the other through whom came the resurrection of the dead; because of whom also two testaments are spoken of.
11.39:
**“And the two months being expired”** — AUGUSTINE. Sixty days, that is, the six ages in which the virgin Church is gathered and laments her sins, saying daily: "Forgive us our debts."
**“she returned”** — in the general resurrection
**“to her father”** — Christ, whose daughter is the Church
**“and he did to her as he had vowed”** — delivering, namely, the kingdom to God and the Father
**“and she knew no man.”** — "I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ"
**“FROM THENCE CAME A FASHION”** — FROM THENCE CAME A FASHION. AUGUSTINE. But as to what was done by precept in Israel, that from days to days they assembled to lament the daughter of Jephte four days in the year, I do not think it signifies anything after the holocaust is fulfilled, which will be in eternal life, but the past times of the Church, in which the mourners were blessed. By the four days its universality is figured, because of the four parts of the world through which it is spread far and wide. But as to the proper sense of the history, I do not think the Israelites decreed this, except because they understood that in this matter the judgment of God was shown rather to strike the father, lest anyone thereafter should vow such a sacrifice. For why was lamentation decreed, if that vow was a matter of joy?
11.40:
**“That from year to year the daughters of Israel assemble together, and lament the daughter of Jephte”** — signifying the past times of the Church, in which "Blessed are they that mourn."
**“the Galaadite for four days.”** — because of the four parts of the world through which the Church is spread

12.1: **“But behold there arose a sedition in Ephraim.”** — This is to be referred to the last judgment, according to that: "Those that would not have me reign over them, bring hither, and kill them before me."
12.7: **“AND HE JUDGED”** — AND HE JUDGED. As those two months, because of the sixty days, signify the number six of the six ages, so here six times seven multiplied figures this same thing, as far as pertains to the six ages of the world. For six times seven are forty-two; nor was it in vain that Jephte himself judged the people six years.
12.8: **“After him Abesan judged Israel”** — or: Abethlan
12.13: **“After him Abdon, the son of Illel, a Pharathonite, judged Israel”** — better: Hellelphara the Thecuite

13.2: **“NOW THERE WAS A CERTAIN MAN”** — NOW THERE WAS A CERTAIN MAN. ISIDORE. Samson has certain things in type of Christ: namely, that his birth is announced by an angel. For thus the angel of the Lord said to the Virgin: "Mary, thou hast found grace with God. Behold thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and shalt bring forth a son" etc. Samson also is called a Nazarite, and of Christ it was said that he shall be called a Nazarene. Samson delivered the children of Israel from the hand of the enemies, and Christ his people from their sins. Samson is interpreted their sun, and of Christ it was said by the Prophet: Unto you the sun of justice shall arise, and health in his wings.
13.4: **“NOR ANY UNCLEAN THING”** — NOR ANY UNCLEAN THING. AUGUSTINE. The unclean thing is the loosening of discipline which had begun to be in Israel, and had already brought them down to eating those things which God had forbidden among the animals. For they were already passing over even to the worship of idols.
13.6: **“And when she was come to her husband she said to him: A man of God came to me, having the countenance of an angel, very awful. And when I asked him who he was, and whence he came, and by what name he was called”** — AUGUSTINE. This Scripture passed over in silence above
13.7: **“AND WHEN SHE WAS COME”** — AND WHEN SHE WAS COME. AUGUSTINE. What the woman says was told her by the angel, that the child shall be a Nazarite of God from the womb until the day of his death, is not read as said by the angel; and what is read as said, He shall begin to save Israel from the hand of the Philistines, is not mentioned by the woman. She did not, then, tell something that she heard; and yet she is to be believed to have told nothing that she did not hear. But rather Scripture did not set down all the words of the angel when it brought him in speaking to the woman. And it was said, From the womb until the day of his death, for this reason: because those were called Nazarites in the law for a time who had a vow, according to what Scripture had commanded by Moses. Hence it is that this was commanded him, that iron should not come upon his head, and that he should not drink wine and strong drink: for these Samson kept all his life, which those who were called Nazarites observed for certain days, vowing and paying the vow.
13.19: **“THEN MANUE TOOK”** — THEN MANUE TOOK. AUGUSTINE. From what Scripture says, that Manue did not know that it was the angel of the Lord, it is manifest that his wife too believed him a man. When, then, he said to him: Let us now constrain thee, and make ready in thy sight a kid of the goats, he invited him as a man, namely that he might feast with him on what he had made a sacrifice. For to make a kid is not wont to be said except when a sacrifice is made. He too so answered: If thou constrain me, I will not eat of thy bread; where he shows that he had been invited to a feast. Then he added: And if thou wilt make a holocaust, offer it to the Lord; because, namely, he had said: Let us make ready in thy sight a kid of the goats. But not every sacrifice is a holocaust: for of a holocaust nothing was eaten, because the whole was burnt, and therefore it was called a holocaust. But the angel, not being about to eat, advised that a holocaust rather be made, yet not to himself but to the Lord: because, namely, Israel at that time had been accustomed to sacrifice to false gods. Whence too it had then offended God, so as to be delivered to enemies for forty years.
13.20: **“AND WHEN [MANUE] SAW THIS”** — AND WHEN [MANUE] SAW THIS. GREGORY. What is it that at the vision of the angel the man is fearful, the woman bold, except that when heavenly things are shown to us, the spirit indeed shakes itself with dread, but yet hope is confident? For hope raises itself to see greater things from that very thing by which the spirit is troubled, which sees first the things that are above; because when the mind, thus lifted up, beholds the higher things of the heavenly secrets, all the firmness of human strength trembles.
13.22: **“WE SHALL CERTAINLY DIE”** — WE SHALL CERTAINLY DIE. AUGUSTINE. What is it that, after the angel who was speaking with them was made manifest to Manue and his wife, Manue said to his wife: We shall die the death etc.? Because, namely, of what is written: No man can see my face and live. They thought, then, as men, that they had seen God, so great a miracle having been done, that he stood in the fire of the sacrifice who before had spoken with them as a man. But did they call God in the angel, or the angel himself God? For thus it is written: And Manue took a kid of the goats, and made a sacrifice, and offered it upon a rock to the Lord who doth wonderful things, and Manue and his wife looked on etc. From these words, then, because he did not say: We shall die the death because we have seen the angel of the Lord, but, We have seen God, the question arises: whether they understood God in the angel, or called the same angel God? For that third [possibility], that they had thought him God who was an angel, cannot be said, since Scripture openly says: Then he knew that it was the angel of the Lord. But whence did they fear death? For it was not written: No man seeth the face of an angel and shall live. Or was Manue, in this very thing, that he had known God in the presence of the angel, so troubled that he feared death? But as to what his wife answered him: If the Lord would kill us, he would not have received holocausts and sacrifice at our hand, nor have shown all these things, nor have done these things for us as we heard: did they believe that the angel himself had received the sacrifice, because they saw him stand in the flame of the altar? Or did they understand by this that the Lord had received it, because the angel did this to show himself an angel? Whichever of these it be, the angel had already said: But if thou make a holocaust, offer it to the Lord, that is: not to me but to the Lord. That the angel stood in the flame of the altar, then, is rather to be understood as having signified that the angel of great counsel, in the form of a servant, that is, in the man whom he was to take up, would not receive a sacrifice, but would himself be the sacrifice.

14.5: **“THEN [SAMSON] WENT DOWN”** — THEN [SAMSON] WENT DOWN. ISIDORE. Samson, when he went to the foreigners for the sake of seeking a wife, slew a lion; and Christ, about to call his Church from the Gentiles, overcame the devil, who says: Rejoice, for I have overcome the world. From the mouth of the slain lion the honeycomb is drawn, because, as we behold, the kings of the earthly kingdom who before had raged against Christ, their fierceness now destroyed, proclaim the sweetness of the Gospel and furnish it defences.

15.8: **“AND HE MADE A GREAT SLAUGHTER OF THEM”** — AND HE MADE A GREAT SLAUGHTER OF THEM. THE SEVENTY. Samson smote the foreigners leg upon thigh: that is, so wonderfully that in astonishment they laid the leg of one foot upon the thigh of the other.
15.12: **“SWEAR, HE SAID”** — SWEAR, HE SAID. AUGUSTINE. What is it that Samson says to the men of Juda: Swear to me that you will not kill me, and deliver me to them, lest perhaps you fall upon me? Which expression some have translated thus: lest perhaps you come against me. But that he said this lest he be killed by them is shown by what is written in the book of Kings, when Solomon commanded that a man be killed, saying: Go, fall upon him. Which is not understood for this reason, that it is not our custom so to speak. For so what the military authorities say: Go, lift him up, and it means 'kill him', who would understand, except one who knew the custom of that expression? It is also commonly said among us: compendiavit illi ['he cut him short'], that is, he killed him; and no one understands this except one who has been used to hearing it. For this is the general force of all expressions: that as languages themselves are not understood unless they are learned by hearing or reading, so neither are the modes of expression.
15.15:
**“And finding a jawbone, even the jawbone of an ass”** — simple and patient preachers
**“which lay there, catching it up”** — holding [them] in the hand of his power
**“he slew therewith a thousand men”** — from vices
15.16: **“WITH THE JAWBONE”** — WITH THE JAWBONE. GREGORY. The jawbone of the ass signifies preachers. For our Redeemer, holding in the hand of his power the simplicity and patience of the preachers, slew the carnal [to free them] from vices; and the jawbone, cast to the ground, afterwards poured forth waters, because the bodies of the preachers, given over to death, showed great miracles to the peoples.
15.19: **“Then the Lord opened a great tooth in the jaw of the ass, and waters issued out of it.”** — because, after the bodies of the preachers died, they showed great miracles
15.20: **“AND HE JUDGED”** — AND HE JUDGED. GREGORY. Whom does Samson signify in this deed but the Redeemer? What is Gaza but hell? What the Philistines but the faithlessness of the Jews? Who, when they saw the Lord dead, and his body laid in the sepulchre, at once appointed guards, and rejoiced that the author of life was held by the bars of hell, as though they had caught Samson in Gaza. But Samson at midnight not only went out but also carried off the gates; because our Redeemer, rising before the light, not only went out free from hell, but also destroyed the bars of hell. He carried off the gates and went up to the top of the hill, because by rising he took away the bars of hell, and by ascending he entered the kingdom of heaven.

16.2:
**“And when the Philistines had heard this”** — the Jews
**“and it was noised about among them, that Samson was come into the city”** — Christ
**“they surrounded him”** — guarding the sepulchre
16.3:
**“But Samson slept till midnight”** — because Christ rose before the light
**“and then rising he took both the doors of the gate, with the posts thereof, and the bolt”** — because he destroyed the bars of hell
16.19: **“AND SHE CALLED A BARBER”** — AND SHE CALLED A BARBER. ISIDORE. That the crafty woman shaved Samson's head and gave him over to the Allophyli to be mocked, that he was taken captive, that he was blinded and appointed to the mill: in these not Christ but those are figured who only glory in the name of Christ and are continually entangled in evil deeds. For the man is understood as the rational sense; but the woman signifies the flesh. For if we consent to the woman, that is, to our flesh, when lust flatters, or to other evil works, we are stripped bare of the grace of the Holy Ghost, which is signified by the Nazarite's hair, and are deceived. For thus, the grace of Christ being violated, the proud and sinners are mocked by the devil, as Samson was when his hair was cut. But if anyone returns by doing penance, his hair returning, that is, grace flowering again, he is restored to strength, and, the pillars of covetousness and lust being overthrown, he has cast down the enemies, and, the combat renewed, he will triumph most mightily over the demons unto the end.
16.21: **“AND WHEN [THEY] HAD SEIZED HIM”** — AND WHEN [THEY] HAD SEIZED HIM. GREGORY. Samson, having lost his eyes, is appointed by the Allophyli to the mill. It is to be known that first the understanding is dulled, and afterwards the captive mind wanders through outward desires, so that the blind mind knows not whither it is led and willingly submits itself to the allurements of the flesh. But sometimes the desires of the flesh first boil up, and after long use close the eye of the heart by unlawful works. For often the mind discerns rightly, and yet does not boldly raise itself against perverse things, and, struggling, is overcome, while, judging the very thing it did, it is overpowered by the delight of its flesh. For that most often the eye of contemplation is first lost, and afterwards through the desires of the flesh the mind is subjugated to the labours of this world, Samson witnesses, taken by the Allophyli, who after he lost his eyes was appointed to the mill; because the malignant spirits, after they have dug out the keenness of contemplation within by the goads of temptations, send [the mind] outside into the round of labour.
16.30: **“AND MANY MORE”** — AND MANY MORE. GREGORY. In this place Christ is signified by Samson. For Samson, while he lived, slew few; but in overthrowing the temple, dying, he slew a very great multitude of adversaries; and when our Lord preached, few of the Jews believed, but innumerable peoples of the Gentiles followed the way of life when he died. For the proud he bore with while he still lived subject to suffering; but having died [and risen] to impassible life, he laid them low. This Samson long ago expressed figuratively in himself, who slew few while he lived, but, the temple being destroyed, killed many when he died: because the Lord extinguished few from the loftiness of pride while he lived, more when the temple of his body was dissolved; and the chosen [so the edition] from the Gentiles, whom he bore with by living, he laid low all together by dying.

20.18: **“AND THEY CONSULTED”** — AND THEY CONSULTED. GREGORY. He who does not judge himself does not know what he may rightly judge in another. Even if perhaps he knows by hearing how he ought to judge rightly, yet he cannot rightly judge the merits of others, to whom the conscience of his own innocence affords no rule of judgment. Hence it is that when the tribe of Benjamin had been overwhelmed in a crime of the flesh, all Israel, gathered together, wished to avenge the iniquity, and yet was laid low in battle once and again. But when [the Lord] was consulted whether they ought to go to avenge it, it was commanded. Israel, which went on according to the command of the divine voice, lost once and a second time, and at last almost utterly destroyed the sinning tribe. What is it, then, that they are inflamed to avenge the crime and are first laid low, except that those by whom the faults of others are struck must first themselves be purged, so that those who hasten to correct the vices of others may come to the vengeance already clean? Whence: "He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her." For they were going to punish the sins of others, and had left their own. They are called back, then, to conscience, that they may first correct their own and then reprove those of others.
