Whence it is necessary that, while the divine vengeance ceases against us, conscience itself should reprove itself and raise itself against itself to the laments of penance, lest it be lifted up against the good and humble [so the edition] toward itself; but let it be rigid against itself, and submissive to all the good.

1.1:
**“There came”** — For the fewness of spiritual teachers, to whom the authority of judging is given, there came a famine of the word of God, when the law too was corrupted by the traditions of the Jews.
**“And a certain man … went”** — Rabanus. Christ, that is, born in Bethlehem Juda, visited the sojourning of this world, with his wife, that is, the Church, and with two children, namely the two orders of the prophets and the apostles, who were freed from the slavery of sin by the blood of Christ.
**“A certain man … went”** — Rabanus. Some understand him as the decalogue, and his wife as the Synagogue, and the two sons as the royal and the priestly honour, which won themselves a union not only in the nation of the Jews but also of the proselytes, as was done in the time of David and Solomon and others.
**“to sojourn in the land of Moab”** — that is, in the country of the devil, who is the prince of this world
1.2:
**“He was named Elimelech”** — “My God is king”: this is Christ, to whom it is said: “Hearken to the voice of my prayer, O my King and my God.”
**“and his wife, Noemi”**
• beautiful
• “Thou art beautiful, O my love”, and so on
**“Mahalon”** — Who is “from the window”, or “from the beginning”. This is the choir of the prophets, through whom the first light of faith went forth into the world from the window, who were also the first preachers of the true light, that is, of Christ.
**“and the other Chelion”** — Chelion: consummation. These are the apostles, who brought the riddles of the prophets to the consummation of full understanding. These are rightly Ephrathites, and sprung from Bethlehem Juda, who, filled with the heavenly bread, gathered the fruit of preaching through the preaching of the gospel. For Ephrathite is interpreted “fruitful”, Bethlehem “house of bread”, Juda “confession”. Whence: “Give you them to eat.” Again: “Going, preach the gospel of the kingdom of God.” And elsewhere: “I have chosen you out of the world, that you should go, and should bring forth fruit.”
**“Ephrathites of Bethlehem Juda. And entering into the country of Moab”** — Judea, which made ill use of the law
1.3:
**“And Elimelech the husband of Noemi died: and … remained”** — in the exile of this world
**“she”** — the Church
**“with her sons”** — with the teachers
1.4:
**“And they took wives of the women of Moab”** — because the apostles joined to themselves the fellowship of two peoples, namely of the Jews and of the Gentiles
**“of which one was called Orpha”**
• her neck
• these are the faithful from among the Jews, who first received the strength of faith and the fortitude of working
**“Ruth”** — She is interpreted “seeing”, or “hastening”, or “failing”; in whom is signified the obedience and believing of the Gentiles, of whom it is said: “A people which I knew not hath served me”, and so on. And elsewhere: Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands to God. So the two peoples were called by the holy preachers to the fellowship of faith and of God’s elect, that out of divers flocks there might be one fold.
1.5:
**“And they both”** — the apostles and prophets
**“died, to wit, Mahalon and Chelion”** — in this sojourning, after the Lord’s ascension
**“died”** — After the completion of their holy labour, that is, they had passed from the exile of this world to the heavenly kingdom, that, the commandment of the decalogue being fulfilled, they might receive the penny of blessedness.
**“and the woman was left alone, having lost”** — the Church
**“both her sons and her husband”** — the prophets and apostles, whose temporal or bodily presence she lacked
1.6: **“And she arose to go from the land of Moab to her own country with both her daughters in law: for she had heard that the Lord had looked upon his people, and had given them food”** — of life
1.7:
**“she went forth … with both her daughters in law”** — The Church takes earnest pains to bring the peoples whom the apostles and prophets instructed in their time to the unity of the faith and the fellowship of the Christian religion; for she has learnt from the Scripture that the just man “is not forsaken”, “nor his seed seeking bread”, the bread “that came down from heaven”.
**“Wherefore … out of the place of her sojournment”** — out of the world
**“with both her daughters in law”** — with each people
**“and being now in the way”** — in Christ, or in his commandments
**“to return”** — firmly
1.8: **“Go ye home”** — The Church does not act without discernment, nor receive anyone without discernment; whence: Believe not every spirit, but try the spirits if they be of God. These things can also fit the Synagogue, which draws back those coming to the faith of Christ; and above all this, that, overcome by the truth, she knows herself weak and worn out, saying: Return, my daughters.
1.11:
**“But she answered them: Return, my daughters: why come ye with me? have I”** — elsewhere: have I then
**“have I any more sons”** — Rabanus. The voice of the Synagogue confessing the truth and not keeping silent about the guilt that has come upon her, who, forsaken by her husband, that is, David, and deprived of her sons, that is, kings and princes, confesses that after the coming of Christ she is barren and too weak to conceive sons to God.
1.12: **“Return again, my daughters, and go your ways”** — elsewhere: my daughters, and go your ways
1.14: **“And they lifted up their voice”** — By these women, one of whom, grieving and mourning, departs from her mother in law, while the other clings to her with a steadfast mind, believers are signified: some of whom, having received the grace of baptism and the fellowship of faith, fall back into their former errors, whom Orpha signifies, who went back to her gods; but others, with settled purpose, keep the grace they have received, whom Ruth signifies.
1.16: **“for whithersoever thou shalt go, I will go”** — So the Church called from the Gentiles, leaving her country, that is, abandoning idolatry, fleshly life and desires, professes that her God is he in whom the saints believed, and that she will go where the flesh of Christ ascended, and suffer for his name in this world even unto death, and be with the people of the saints and prophets and patriarchs; whence: “Rejoice, ye Gentiles, with his people.”
1.18: **“Then Noemi, seeing”** — Noemi, seeing, and so on. The Gentile people follows the preachers with steadfast mind into the holy land and into Bethlehem, the city of God, where it is prepared to receive the bridegroom born of the stock of Abraham, in whom all nations or tribes of the earth shall be blessed.
1.20: **“But she said to them: Call me not Noemi”** — Call me not, and so on. The Synagogue acknowledges her calamity, which she deservedly suffers after the coming of Christ, and shrinks from being called beautiful, because she sees the times of her prosperity ending.
1.22: **“So Noemi came with Ruth the Moabitess her daughter in law, from the land of her sojournment: and returned into Bethlehem, in the beginning of the barley harvest”** — In the beginning of the barley harvest, and so on. That is, when it turns the order of his incarnation to the mystery of Christ’s passion. For the barley harvest expresses the time of the Lord’s passion, which fell in the month of new corn, that is, in the first month. Rightly then they come to Bethlehem at that time, when the law preaches that Christ, whom it teaches was born in Bethlehem, was slain at the pasch, that is, in the month of new corn. Holy Church too labours with all her strength to steep those whom she calls to the faith in the merit of the incarnation, passion and resurrection. The barley harvest expresses the believing of the Jews, who, the sacrament of the passion being accomplished, came first to the faith at the apostles’ preaching; who elsewhere are read to have been fed by the Lord with five barley loaves.

2.1:
**“Now her husband Elimelech had a kinsman, a powerful man, and very rich, whose name was Booz”** — “The strength of God”; whence: “And his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, God the Mighty, the Prince of Peace, the Father of the world to come.”
**“Now her husband … had”** — This man, the kinsman of Elimelech, is Christ, the lamb of the law and the lawgiver, because he was promised through the law and born of the patriarchs, and of the nation of the Jews according to the flesh. Whence: “God will raise up to you a prophet of your brethren; him you shall hear as myself.” He is the powerful one who vanquished the prince of the world and subdued the whole world to his rule; and very rich, because he is “possessor of heaven and earth”, and “in him are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge”. For he is “the power of God and the wisdom”.
2.2:
**“And Ruth the Moabitess said to her mother in law: If thou wilt, I will go into the field”** — the Church
**“and glean the ears of corn”** — The ears left behind signify the faithful who, the rest having been taken up to heaven, are left to us as an example
**“that escape the hands of the reapers”** — The harvest is the saints, who are gathered to be laid up in God’s barn. The reapers are the angels.
2.3: **“She went therefore and gleaned the ears of corn after the reapers. And it happened that the owner of that field was Booz, who was of the kindred of Elimelech”** — And it happened, and so on. Because holy Church belongs to Christ, whose bride and body she is; of whom it is said: “The Lord is my strength and my praise.” And elsewhere: “The Lord who is strong and mighty: the Lord mighty in battle.” He is the kinsman of Elimelech, who, born of Bethlehem and of the stock of David, has witness from the law and the prophets. He brought the words of salvation to his household; at his birth the angels sang: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will. When he came into Jerusalem, the crowd met him, crying out: “Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord.”
2.5: **“And Booz said to the young man that was set over the reapers: Whose maid is this?”** — because Christ, as if not knowing, asks about the faith of the Gentiles of any of the teachers who is set over the lesser priests, when he stirs him up to preach
2.7:
**“And she desired leave to glean the ears of corn that remain, following the steps of the reapers: and she hath been in the field from morning”** — because from the beginning, that is, of faith, to the perfection of good work
**“till now, and hath not … home for one moment”** — of the old superstition
**“gone”** — And she desired leave, and so on. Because holy Church perseveres in the field of divine reading after the reapers and preachers, gathering the mysteries of the Scriptures, so as to store the testimonies and examples of the virtues in the bosom of her mind. Or that field is the discipline of heavenly study; the harvest, spiritual understanding; the reapers, the preachers; the ears left behind, the sentences of the Scriptures, which, being much hidden in mystery, remain as it were fuller, for the exercise of one who meditates. So the Gentile people ardently longs for the Church’s discipline, that it may be admitted to the meditation of the divine law and the fellowship of the saints, and be refreshed by the teachings or examples of the saints.
2.8: **“do not go to glean in any other field”** — As if to say: Do not depart from the state of faith, do not follow the errors of heretics or schismatics, but rather join thyself to holy souls, that thou mayest reap the holy Scriptures by meditating and fulfilling them in deed, and mayest drink the draught of divine wisdom from the books of the two Testaments, whence the young men, that is, the saints, drink.
2.10: **“She fell on her face”** — The Church of the Gentiles gives thanks to the Saviour, who has deigned to regard her. He answers her that it pleases him that, her husband, that is, the devil, being dead, she has left her idolatrous parents and the land of her birth, that is, fleshly desires, and has joined herself to the people of the saints, which was unknown to her before, when she followed the lust of the old man.
2.12:
**“The Lord render unto thee for thy work, and mayest thou receive a full reward of the Lord the God of Israel”** — that is, by faith; whence: “This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he hath sent.”
**“to whom thou art come, and under whose wings thou art fled”** — the two Testaments, with which God protects those who flee to him; whence: “In the shadow of thy wings will I hope.”
2.13: **“And she said: I have found grace in thy eyes, my lord, who hast comforted me and hast spoken to the heart of thy handmaid, who am not like to one of thy maids”** — I have found, and so on. Note the humility of the Church of the Gentiles, which knows herself unequal to so great a grace, and does not dare to make herself equal to the first Church. Whence she says: “For the whelps also eat of the crumbs that fall from the table of their masters.” And elsewhere: “Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldst enter under my roof: but only say the word, and my servant shall be healed”, and so on.
2.14:
**“At mealtime”** — The hour of eating was when it was said to the apostles: “Going, teach ye all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost.” For it had been said by the Lord: “Go ye not into the way of the Gentiles.”
**“come thou hither, and eat of the bread, and dip thy morsel in the vinegar”** — Dip thy morsel, and so on. In the law, that is, which, so long as it was meditated upon, persevering in the former people, corrupted by the conditions or traditions of the Pharisees, lost its native savour. In this the Church dips her morsel, that is, she learns that the mysteries of Christ’s incarnation are in the Old Testament; and so she believes the more firmly, because she knows it was prefigured long before.
**“So she sat at the side of the reapers”** — because the Gentile Church joins herself to the holy preachers through faith
**“and she heaped to herself frumenty, and ate and was filled”** — because the knowledge of the divine law refreshed her devout mind
**“and took the leavings”** — because she chewed over each word that she heard with fine discernment
2.15: **“And she arose from thence, to glean the ears of corn as before”** — because she kept the words she had heard in her heart, and laboured earnestly in meditating, that she might take in greater things
2.16:
**“some of your handfuls”** — Note the humility of the householder, who not only lets the ears of the testimonies that are left be gathered, but also bestows handfuls of knowledge with unasked largess.
**“And let fall some of your handfuls of purpose, and leave them, that she may gather them without shame, and let no man rebuke her when she gathereth them”** — Some of your handfuls, and so on. Because he does not despise the weakness of the Gentile people, nor reproach it with its former errors, but by the shrewdness of his care leads it on to edification.
2.17:
**“She gleaned therefore in the field till evening: and beating out with a rod and threshing what she had gleaned”** — because holy Church with the rod of discernment draws the spiritual sense out of the letter of the law
**“about the measure of an ephi”** — When in reading she learns the catholic faith through the confession of the holy Trinity. In the measure of an ephi, which contains three bushels, is signified the one substance of the godhead and the property of the three persons.
2.18:
**“Which she took up and returned”** — Because she shows her faith to mother Church. Or the Church shows the Synagogue the grace she has received by the gift of her bridegroom, to stir her up to come to her.
**“gave her of the remains”** — “My heart hath uttered a good word”: that is, the food of preaching, from the fulness of the heart.
2.19: **“And her mother in law said to her: Where hast thou gleaned today, and where hast thou wrought? blessed be he that hath had pity on thee”** — Blessed, and so on. The Synagogue, the Church of the Gentiles preaching, acknowledges the goodness and power of the Lord and the strength of her protector, and at length, the truth compelling her, blesses the name of the Lord, because he has kept for the dead the kindness which he showed to the living.
2.20:
**“And Noemi answered her: Blessed be he of the Lord: because the same kindness”** — of bounty
**“which he shewed to the living”** — to the Jews, when they enjoyed his benefits
**“he hath kept also to the dead”** — to the Gentiles, who were buried in sins
**“And again she said: … our kinsman”** — to the Synagogue according to the flesh, to the Church by union of the spirit
**“The man is”** — Christ
**“The man is our kinsman”** — Mother Church recognizes the kinsman by the free benefits bestowed on the people of the Gentiles, and, hearing the name, remembers the ancient benefits; whence: “I remembered the days of old, I meditated on all thy works.”
2.21: **“And Ruth said, He also charged me, that I should keep close to his reapers, till all the corn should be reaped”** — He charged me, that I should keep close, and so on. Because Christ charges all who come to him to join themselves rather to his faithful for the harvest of the spiritual crop than to strangers; to which counsel the mother in law consents, saying: It is better, my daughter; as good and useful the Synagogue cannot deny it.
2.22:
**“And her mother in law said to her: It is better for thee, my daughter, … with his maids”** — with holy souls
**“to go out to reap …, lest in another man’s field some one”** — of the heretics
**“may resist thee”** — the teaching of the schismatics, as quarrels and contentions
2.23:
**“So she kept close to the maids of Booz: and continued to glean with them, till … the wheat”** — the grace, though not that which is given to rational creatures for refreshment, in which the flesh and blood of Christ is offered, of which it is said: “Unless the grain of wheat falling into the ground die, itself remaineth alone.”
**“all the barley”** — the letter of the law, which was given to the Jews as to beasts for fodder
**“till all the barley”** — That is, she cleaves to the teachers in the meditation of the Scriptures until she has stored the knowledge of the Old and New Testaments in the cell of her heart, whence she might have food enough for the soul.

3.1: **“After she was returned to her mother in law, Noemi said to her: My daughter, I will seek rest for thee, and will provide that it may be well with thee”** — The first Church conferred with the Gentile Church on how she might come to union with Christ.
3.2: **“he winnoweth barley in the threshingfloor”** — The Synagogue of the Jews, where the law is stored up. Christ winnows it when, preaching the Gospel on the threshingfloor, he threshes out the counsels and wills of each towards himself. Whence: “But Jesus did not trust himself unto them, for that he knew all men, and because he needed not that any should give testimony of man.”
3.3:
**“Wash thyself therefore”** — with the water of baptism, or with the tears of penance
**“and anoint thee”** — with chrism, or the anointing of the Holy Spirit
**“and put on thy best garments”** — with the adornment of the virtues
**“and go down to the barnfloor: but let not the man see thee, till he shall have done eating and drinking”** — Here, that is, Christ dwells and calls the human race back to himself, that is, by dying for you, where he won all things; whence: “If I be lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself.”
**“let not the man see thee, till”** — Because the faith of the Gentiles did not appear to the Church before Christ had fulfilled the mystery of his incarnation, when, living bodily among men, he took food and drink, and at last, supping with his disciples, imparted to them the sacraments of his body and blood. But when the mystery of Christ’s dispensation was fulfilled, the Church of the Gentiles came confidently to the faith.
3.4:
**“thou shalt … lift up the clothes”** — As if to say: Know Christ, who suffered for thee, and come with a devout mind; uncover the covering of the letter of the Old Testament, in which the sacrament of Christ’s incarnation is held; and when thou hast learnt the salvation promised thee there, flee humbly to his help, that thou mayest remain there for all time.
**“and he will tell thee what thou must do”** — because thou must learn the order of thy salvation from him. But if thou refer Noemi’s words to the Synagogue, thou wilt find in the law and the prophet that after the passion the Church of the Gentiles is to come to the faith.
3.5: **“She answered: Whatsoever thou shalt command, I will do”** — the Church’s obedience deserves the fulfilment of her desire; whence: “O woman, great is thy faith: be it done to thee as thou wilt.”
3.7:
**“And when Booz had eaten”** — Christ ate and drank when at the supper he handed on the sacraments of his body and blood to the apostles; whence, because the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he himself also hath partaken of the same.
**“he went to sleep by the heap of sheaves”** — heap
**“the heap”** — The testimonies of the Scriptures; whence: “The Son of man indeed goeth, as it is written of him.” Or beside the troops of faithful souls whom by his death he called back from hell. To this bed the Church hastened, and, uncovering the cloak, and so on.
**“and she came softly and uncovering his feet, laid herself down”** — because, the world being wrapped in darkness, she showed the Church’s swift faith for us to imitate
3.8:
**“And behold, when it was now midnight the man was afraid, and troubled: and he saw a woman”** — the Church
**“lying at his feet”** — humbly worshipping the sacrament of the incarnation
3.9:
**“And he said”** — Christ
**“Who art thou?”** — he asks for the Church’s confession
**“And she answered: I am Ruth thy handmaid: spread thy coverlet over thy servant, for thou art a near kinsman”** — The Church desires above all things the grace of faith and of Christ’s protection.
**“spread thy coverlet”** — She who asked that the cloak be spread over her deserved to receive a blessing. For he who fully receives the grace of faith will possess blessing and virtue alike.
3.10:
**“And he said: Blessed art thou of the Lord, my daughter, and thy latter kindness has surpassed the former”** — by which, taking counsel for thyself, thou didst cast away idolatry
**“because thou hast not followed”** — because after thou camest to Christ thou hast steadfastly persevered
**“young men either poor or rich”** — heretics or schismatics, who have no ripeness of counsel, because they are always unstable and uncertain
3.11: **“Fear not therefore, but whatsoever thou shalt say to me I will do to thee”** — “Ask, and you shall receive”; “Seek, and you shall find.” Whatever faith rightly asks, the kindness of Christ grants.
3.12:
**“Neither do I deny myself to be near of kin, but there is another nearer than I”**
• because the faithful are firmly persuaded that the Church is full of virtues; of whom it is said: “Who shall find a valiant woman?”
• But there is another than I, and so on. John the Baptist, who was thought to be the Christ, but did not usurp the name of bridegroom, but kept it for Christ, saying: “He that hath the bride is the bridegroom”, and so on. He is nearer because he was born first in the world. Or this kinsman is the decalogue of the law, which seemed nearer to the Synagogue than the Gospel, because it was given especially to that people and is earlier in time.
3.14:
**“So she slept at his feet till the night was going off”** — because, resting in the hope of the incarnation, she waited patiently until the darkness of unbelief should withdraw
**“And she arose before”** — Because before the Jews, steeped in the teaching of the law, knew the rights of their nature, the Church of the Gentiles, shaking off the sleep of her sloth, rose again at the dawn of the newborn faith and hastened to the grace of Christ.
**“Beware lest any man know that thou camest hither”** — do not seek praise for thy way of life. When thou dost alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doth.
3.15:
**“And again he said: Spread thy mantle”** — Enlarge thy faith
**“wherewith thou art covered”** — practise in deed what thou receivest in heart
**“and hold it with both hands. And when she spread it and held it, he measured six measures of barley”** — He measured six measures, and so on. Because the measure of perfect working is granted according to the capacity of understanding, that she may be enriched within and without by the divine gift. The number six can also signify this, that in the sixth age the Lord granted the Church of the Gentiles the barley of the law spiritually understood.
**“and laid it upon her”** — namely, seasoned with Christ’s gifts and adorned with the fruits of the virtues
3.16: **“And came to her mother in law; who said to her: What hast thou done, daughter? And she told her all that the man had done to her”** — the great works of God, that is, so as to stir the first Church to praise, or the Synagogue to conversion
3.17:
**“And she said: Behold he hath given me six measures of barley: for he said: I will not have thee return empty”** — The Church promised confidently, because the truth will not cease to fulfil the promises, which says: “He that believeth and is baptized shall be saved.”
**“to thy mother in law”** — the first Church, or the Synagogue

4.1:
**“Then Booz went up to the gate, and sat there”** — Because Christ brings to fulfilment the prophecy written of his incarnation
**“went up to the gate”** — Because he took flesh in the virgin’s womb, in which he would appear. Of this gate it is said: “This gate shall be shut, it shall not be opened, and no man shall pass through it: because the Lord the God of Israel hath entered in by it.”
**“Turn aside for a little while”** — Because Christ saw the law set up bodily for the Jews, and bade it turn aside to him, because he bent it to bear witness to the mystery of his dispensation. Otherwise: he saw the kinsman going by, when he saw the coming of his forerunner hastening on after the manner of human life, and mercifully turned him to the office of forerunner.
**“and sit down here, calling him by his name”** — that is, through Gabriel, saying: his name shall be called John
4.2:
**“And Booz taking ten men”** — for a witness of his second coming
**“of the ancients of the city”** — the fathers of the Old Testament, that is, those who kept the decalogue, and knew that Christ’s incarnation was foreshadowed there
4.3: **“he spoke to the kinsman”** — Fittingly he offered the part of Noemi’s field to the lawyer to buy, when he showed the masters of the Synagogue the part of the people that remained to be saved, grace having now appeared, that they might acknowledge their weakness, and commit what they themselves could not do to the true physician to be done; whence it is said to the lepers: Go, show yourselves to the priests; and as they went, they were made clean.
4.5: **“to raise up”** — He signifies no other possession of the people than the joining of the Church in marriage to Christ, who raised up the ancient name of sons of God, which the saints had at the beginning. Whence: “The sons of God seeing”, and so on; and Luke says: “Adam, who was of God”; which name he raised up in the Church of the Gentiles by the grace of God. Whence: “He gave them power to be made the sons of God”, and so on. This name the decalogue of the law could not raise up among the nations. But if thou refer this to John the Baptist, thou wilt find him yielding his right of kinship and saying: “I baptize with water; but there hath stood one in the midst of you, whom you know not, the latchet of whose shoe I am not worthy to loose.” And elsewhere: “I am not Christ, but … I am sent before him. He that hath the bride is the bridegroom.” The law too yields to the Gospel. For the law entered in, that sin might abound, grace abounding more. There is indeed a setting aside of the former commandment, because of its weakness; but a bringing in of a better hope, by which we draw nigh to God, through Jesus Christ.
4.8: **“So Booz said to his kinsman: Put off thy shoe. And immediately he took it off from his foot”** — Put off his shoe, and so on. The shoe is the veil of the mysteries. The law took off the shoe from its foot and gave it to Christ, because it could not make the sacraments plain through the masters of the people, but kept this to be done by Christ. So John claimed the shoe not for himself but for Christ, because he understood that the bride belonged to Christ alone; whence he says: “I am not worthy to loose the latchet of his shoe.”
4.9: **“You are witnesses”** — So Christ has witnesses enough from both Testaments, that the people of the Gentiles, which the decalogue, now ended, could not make fruitful spiritually, he himself made fruitful with the seed of the word, possessing all that the earlier and later saints had.
4.11:
**“Then all the people that were in the gate, and the ancients answered”** — And the ancients, and so on. Isidore. The blessing of the ten ancients shows that all nations are to be blessed in the name of Jesus. For iota, which is the first letter in the name of Jesus, signifies ten among the Greeks.
**“The Lord make this woman”** — They pray for prosperity for the Church of the Gentiles, that she may receive the grace of fruitfulness that the first parents of the Israelites had.
**“Rachel”** — The beauty of inward contemplation, having inward understanding of the truth. Whence Rachel, “well favoured and of a beautiful countenance”, whom every devoutly zealous man loves and for whom he serves Laban, who is interpreted “whitening”, which he compares to the grace of God, who says: “If your sins be as scarlet, they shall be made as white as snow.”
**“Lia”** — The action of this life in which we live is laborious, from faith, and uncertain as to the outcome by which it will come to the profit of those whom we wish to help. This is Lia, the first wife of Jacob, who is recorded to have had weak eyes.
4.12: **“And that the house may be, as the house of Phares”** — Phares, and so on. Because the Gentile people held the grace, and in the birth went before the brother who had first put out his hand. For Israel first put out its hand in the work of the law, and drew it back defiled with the blood of the prophets and of Christ himself. But afterwards the people of the Gentiles broke forth, that “the first should be last, and the last first”. Thamar too is interpreted “changing” or “bitterness”. For the Church of the Gentiles, both in name and in bearing, which was foul and bitter in idolatry, becomes sweet and beautiful in penance.
4.13:
**“Booz therefore took Ruth, and married her”** — because the Church joined to Christ bears spiritual offspring; whence: “The barren hath borne many: and she that had many children is weakened.”
**“to conceive and to bear”** — The Church is always made fruitful by the gift of the Holy Spirit, and as some depart to everlasting light others will succeed, so that the Christian name may remain for ever, and the most holy mother may have comfort from new offspring in her old age. As the patriarchs and prophets departed, too, the evangelists and apostles succeeded them. Whence: “Instead of thy fathers, sons are born to thee.”
4.14: **“And the women said to Noemi”** — the Synagogue
4.15:
**“For he is born of thy daughter in law”** — The daughter in law of the Synagogue is the Gentile Church, which married Christ, born of the Synagogue. Him, namely, she could not bring forth through the law; received through the mystery of prophecy, she carried him hidden, figured under a veil, and performed the office of a nurse, because she lacked the privilege of a mother.
**“is much better to thee”** — That is, than the multitude of those who were nourished in the Old Testament by the teaching of the law, who, namely, did not believe the word of the Lord, “and they sacrificed their sons and their daughters to devils”, and at last killed Christ and persecuted the apostles.
4.16: **“and she carried it, and was a nurse unto it”** — The spiritual lineage of the generation is shown. For Obed is interpreted “serving”; Isai, “sacrifice in the sun”, or “incense”; David, “strong of hand”, or “desirable”. For he who serves God earnestly offers him a pleasing sacrifice and incense of sweetest odour through works of virtue and zeal in prayer; and so, strengthened by faith and devotion, he is desirable and pleases God.
4.17: **“And the women her neighbours”** — The powers of heaven, which rejoice in the fruitfulness of the Church, and call his name Obed, that is, serving, whom they desire to serve the King on high with them.
4.22: **“These are the generations”** — There are ten generations from Juda’s son to David. From which thou knowest that the purpose of the whole divine law tends to Christ, who was born of the seed of David, to proclaim his coming and to show the perfection of the law in him: “For the end of the law is Christ, unto justice to every one that believeth.” So before the law Jacob says of Christ’s incarnation: The sceptre shall not be taken away from Juda, nor a ruler from his thigh, till he come that is to be sent, and so on. And to David, because Christ is of the seed of Juda, it was said: Of the fruit of thy womb I will set upon thy throne. It is plain, then, that the oracle of all the prophets and patriarchs belongs to the dispensation of our Lord Jesus Christ.

1.1:
Samuel wrote the first book of Kings up to his death; then David; after [him] Solomon; finally the prophets.
Twenty-two letters are found among the Hebrews, according to whose number twenty-two volumes are reckoned among them, among which the book of Kings is held third in order after Judges. Fittingly is Kings placed after Judges: because now there are rulers of the Church, afterwards the kingdom; or because judgment will go before, and everlasting empire will follow.
**“There was a man”** — by strength of mind
**“one”** — not wandering, not changeable
**“of Ramathaim”**
• which is interpreted 'their height'
• First the generation of the prophet is to be told historically; then the allegory is to be continued. Elcana, the father of Samuel, was of the stock of Levi, but not of the generation of Aaron the priest. For he was, according to Paralipomenon, the son "of Jeroam, the son of Eliel, the son of Thau, the son of Suph, the son of Elcana, the son of Mahath, the son of Amasai, the son of Elcana, the son of Joel, the son of Azarias, the son of Sophonias, the son of Thahath, the son of Asir, the son of Abiasaph, the son of Core, the son of Isaar, the son of Caath, the son of Levi, the son of Israel." His mother too is shown to be of the tribe of Juda from this, that he is called an Ephrathite from Ephrata, the wife of Caleb, who was of the tribe of Juda, not from Ephraim; as David is called the son of an Ephrathite man, that is, of Isai, who was not of Ephraim but of Juda. He, being strong among the citizens of Ephraim [Ephrem], dwelt in the city Ramathaim Sophim, which is in the Thamnitic region near Diospolis, whence was Joseph, who in the Gospel is said to be of Arimathea. And he had two wives, Anna and Phenenna. Fittingly too is the barrenness of Anna mentioned, whose childbearing was the more renowned: as Sara was first barren and Agar the Egyptian bore; and Rachel, for whom Jacob long served, was long barren, while her sister rejoiced in the number of her offspring.
**“ARMATHAIM OR RAMATHAIM”** — It is interpreted 'two heights', so that two tribes may be understood, namely the royal and the priestly, from which his father and mother came.
**“RAMATHAIM”** — ORIGEN. Or Armathaim, which is found in other codices, is interpreted 'their height'. Sophim, watchtower or rock. Ephraim, fruitfulness. He is said to have dwelt in mount Ephraim and in Ramathaim Sophim, on high, namely in the contemplation of the virtues, so that the loftiness of his mind might not be cast down, nor its unity torn, by any thoughts of vices lying beneath and barking round about. Therefore he is said to be not of the valleys or of the plains, but of mount Ephraim, that is, the fruitful, in which the nobility of all the virtues is known to bear fruit.
**“ORIGEN”** — He had two wives, of whom the nobler, that is, Anna, was barren, as Sara the nobler wife of Abraham. But the second, that is, Phenenna, was fruitful, as Agar the Egyptian. Elcana, then, who is the possession of God, is made a father first by the second wife, because God had shut up the womb of Anna, which afterwards he opened. Phenenna is interpreted 'conversion', Anna 'grace'. Whoever, then, wishes to be the possession of God, let him have these two wives, and the first the nobler, that is, grace. For she is first joined to a man through faith. Whence: "By the grace of God you are saved through faith." Then let him be joined to Phenenna, that is, to conversion, because after the grace of faith follows amendment of morals. Phenenna first bears sons, because we bring forth our first fruits through conversion; for unless we are turned from evil, we are not made fathers by Anna. The sons of Phenenna do not stand at the altar; yet they are not made empty, because they eat of the divine sacrifices. He, then, who is converted from sin begets from conversion works of justice; and afterwards Anna, that is, the soul, roused by good zeal, prays that she may have sons who stand before God, that is, sons of grace. For he who is free for God "and meditates on his law day and night" is a son of grace. Hence in the Gospel Martha is busy about much serving, fulfilling works of justice, and as it were begets sons of conversion. Mary, sitting at the Lord's feet, hears his word, and chooses the best part, and begets a son of grace, who may say: "But it is good for me to adhere to my God." Anna begets a son Samuel, of whom it is said: "And Samuel among them that call upon his name"; who is called 'there is God himself'; for where the spirit of grace is, there is God. For unless the works of conversion go before, we cannot beget the gifts of the Holy Ghost. Let us pray for this offspring in imitation of Anna, as she herself did.
**“Sophim,”** — watchtower or rock
**“SOPHIM”** — Watchmen, who perhaps are the prophets, whose son is Elcana.
**“ARMATHAIM”** — Sophim, heights or watchtower: this is the heavenly Jerusalem, coming from which he taught contemplation and by his death made [us] possess it.
**“of mount”**
• not of the valleys, not of the plains, not of the hills
• of the height of the virtues
**“Ephraim,”** — fruitfulness
**“and his name was Elcana,”** — possession of God
**“ELCANA”**
• JEROME. He is interpreted 'possession of God', who is called a man by strength of mind, and one: not changeable, not wandering, but firm and unconfused. All too are fittingly called one who have one wisdom, who confess one Jesus Christ, who are filled with one Spirit of God. Whence: "All run indeed, but one receiveth the prize." Each of the foolish is not one but many; whence: 'A fool is changed as the moon.' But God is called one not in number, but because he is never changed. Whence: "But thou art always the selfsame, and thy years shall not fail."
• Allegorically: the possession of God, who is the Son of God, saying: "The Lord possessed me"; who is well called one man, not in number, but because he is never changed, nor is God made other than himself.
**“the son of Jeroham,”**
• merciful
• Jeroham: merciful.
**“the son of Eliu,”**
• my God
• Eliu: my God.
**“the son of Thohu,”**
• sealed
• Thohu: sealed.
**“the son of Suph,”**
• pouring out
• Suph: pouring out; because, coming to us through mercy, sealed in his passion, he says: "My God, my God," where, emptying himself, he poured himself out. Whence: "Thy name is as oil poured out": poured out from his invisible things to our visible things.
**“an Ephraimite:”** — from Ephrata the wife of Caleb, not from Ephraim
**“AN EPHRAIMITE”**
• Fruitful, because he abounds in the gifts of the Holy Ghost.
• From Ephrata the wife of Caleb, or from the city Ephrata, which afterwards was called Bethlehem; or from Ephraim, as some say, because he was of Ramatha, a city of Ephraim, which is situated on mount Sophim, which is a mountain in the tribe of Ephraim.
1.2:
**“And he had two wives,”**
• namely conversion from evil, and grace
• AND HE HAD TWO WIVES etc. Phenenna is the Synagogue, which, fruitful at first, bore sons to God through the law, but now because of unbelief remains unfruitful. Anna, the barren one, is the Church of the Gentiles, which, once barren of spiritual offspring, now redeemed by the grace of Christ (for Anna is interpreted grace), bears sons to God through baptism and the Holy Ghost.
**“the name of one was Anna,”** — grace
**“and the name of the other Phenenna.”** — conversion
**“Phenenna had children:”** — works of justice
**“but Anna”**
• who was the first and nobler
• that the more desired, the more welcome the birth might be
**“had no children.”** — sons of grace, who in contemplation always stand before God
1.3:
**“And this man went up”** — it is for the strong to go up, as for the weak to go down
**“out of his city upon the appointed”**
• at the Pasch, namely, at Pentecost, at the solemnity of tabernacles. Whence: "Three times a year shall all thy males appear before the Lord" etc.
• in the law
• obeying, namely, the law
**“days,”** — in the works of the saints no mention is made of night, because they are not children of the night or of darkness
**“to adore and to offer sacrifice”** — as a Levite
**“to the Lord of hosts in Silo.”** — a city in the tribe of Ephraim, where the ark of the Testament and the tabernacle of the Lord were from the time of Josue to the time of Samuel
**“SILO”** — It is at the ninetieth milestone from Neapolis, in the region Athabitana [so the edition].
**“OPHNI”** — Barefoot, or madness of conversion.
**“And the two sons of Heli, Ophni and Phinees, were there priests of the Lord.”** — PHINEES, a mute mouth, signifies the scribes and Pharisees, who are called sons of Heli because Heli bears the type of the priesthood. They, because they did not receive him whom the law and the prophets foretold, turned to the madness of unbelief, deserved to have a mouth mute from the confession of Christ. And because they would not raise up the seed of faith to Christ, their dead brother, they deserved to be unshod and to be outside the lot of those of whom it is said: "Your feet shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace." And because they tried to claim the name of bridegroom for themselves, not for Christ, usurping the Church, they remained stripped of all dignity, unshod of the examples of the patriarchs and prophets. Whence Silo, where the priests were, is interpreted 'his dismissal' or 'petition', because they petitioned Pilate to release Barabbas to them. Deservedly, then, were they dismissed and forsaken by God.
1.4:
**“Now the day came, and Elcana offered sacrifice, and gave to Phenenna his wife, and to all her sons and daughters, portions:”** — because after the victims were offered the Levite ate with his wives and sons and daughters
**“TO PHENENNA AND HER SONS AND DAUGHTERS, PORTIONS”** — That is, garments, which they changed at the festivals. But to Anna he gave one portion, sorrowful, because she had no sons to whom he might give more.
**“TO PHENENNA”** — That is, to the Synagogue and her sons he gave portions, that is, temporal goods, according to that: He gave them the lands of the Gentiles; and because the words of God were first committed to them. To Anna, that is, to the Church of the Gentiles, he gave one portion, namely among the Gentiles [so the edition: "ingentium"]. Well does it say sorrowful, because the Lord had shut up her womb; for the time of having mercy on her had not yet come, that she should be made fruitful by spiritual grace. As Phenenna despised Anna, so the Synagogue despised the Gentile world. Many of the Gentiles awaited the coming of the Redeemer, as we find in Job; and because they persevered in prayer, at last the Redeemer brought consolation to Anna weeping and not taking food, saying: Anna, why weepest thou? etc. Better to the Church is her husband, that is, Christ, than the ten sons whom the Synagogue brought forth to God; because she sometimes loves Christ more, that is, his grace, than those whom she bore carnally.
**“TROPOLOGICALLY”** — Elcana is the preacher whom the Lord possesses; Phenenna and Anna the active and the contemplative life. Phenenna, fruitful in sons and daughters, is the active, begetting strong works and weak ones. Phenenna is interpreted 'conversion', because the active life must turn itself with care to the actions by which it may profit its neighbours. For the active life is to give bodily bread, or [the bread] of doctrine, to the hungry; to correct the erring; to call back the proud to the way of humility; to take care of the sick; to dispense to each what is fitting. Anna is interpreted 'grace', because contemplation is had through grace. She is barren because, since no one can penetrate it as it is, and no one suffices to preach what he perceives in it, it comes about that no one begets many sons by preaching it. The contemplative life is to hold fast the love of God and neighbour with the whole mind, to rest from outward action, to cleave to the desire of the Creator alone, so that it now pleases one to do nothing. Whoever wishes to be made the possession of God, let him take these two wives: the active first, the contemplative afterwards. Especially let the teacher pass from the embraces of Phenenna to the embraces of Anna, and give portions to each, joining virtues to virtues.
1.6:
**“Her rival also afflicted her,”** — as Agar [afflicted] Sara
**“and troubled her exceedingly, insomuch”** — for it is the solace of the wicked to carp at the life of the good
1.7:
**“And thus she did every year, when the time returned that they went up to the temple of the Lord: and thus she provoked her: but Anna wept,”** — "My tears have been my bread day and night"
**“and did not”** — glad
**“eat.”** — bodily; and elsewhere: I mingled my drink with weeping
1.9:
**“So Anna arose after she had eaten and drunk in Silo: And Heli”** — he was the high priest, and after Samson ruled the people of Israel forty years, but according to the Seventy twenty
**“the priest sitting”** — that he might minister the word of God to those going in and out of the temple. For the priests have the keys of knowledge
1.10: **“As Anna had her heart full of grief, she prayed to the Lord, shedding many tears,”** — he that is mocked by his friend, as I am, says Job, shall call upon the Lord, and he will hear him
1.13:
**“Now Anna spoke in her heart,”** — because God is found not by the voice only but by the heart. Whence: "The Lord hath heard the desire of the poor: the preparation of their heart" etc.
**“and only her lips moved, but her voice was not heard at all. Heli therefore thought her to be drunk,”** — temulenta [drunk], from temetum, which the ancients called wine
1.14:
**“And said to her: How long wilt thou be drunk?”** — HOW LONG [WILT THOU BE] DRUNK etc. Man seeth the face, God the heart. Heli, who looked only at her mouth, thought her drunk. But the Lord, who saw her heart, had regard to her prayer. And here a form of praying is handed down to us: that we should pray not in much speaking but in compunction of heart and the shedding of tears; because: "A sacrifice to God is an afflicted spirit: a contrite heart" etc.
**“digest”** — digest, that is, sleep it off
1.15: **“Anna answering, said: Not so, my lord: for I am an exceeding unhappy woman, and have drunk neither wine nor any strong drink”** — today, namely
1.16: **“Count not thy handmaid for one of the daughters of Belial:”** — without yoke; and it is to be noted here that drunkards are called sons of Belial
1.18:
**“And she said: Would to God thy handmaid may find grace in thy eyes. So the woman went on her way, and ate, and her countenance”** — because she persevered firmly in what she had begun, namely in her vow; so we too ought to persevere, if we wish to be heard by the Lord
**“AND HER COUNTENANCE WAS NO MORE CHANGED”** — RABANUS. Another translation: her face fell no more, because she most surely believed that she had been heard.
**“RABANUS”** — For the Church was by no means changed from faith and love of the Redeemer by turning aside to other ways.
1.19: **“AND THE LORD REMEMBERED HER”** — RABANUS. Because Anna devoutly asked of the Lord, she conceived and bore. So the Church, praying through natural understanding, conceived the mystery of the Incarnation in the heart and brought it forth by the mouth of confession.
1.20:
**“And it came to pass when the time was come about,”** — the return of the year
**“Anna conceived and bore a son, and called his name Samuel:”**
• 'petition' or 'his name is God'
• RABANUS. Samuel: 'petition of God' or 'his name is God'; because [God was] the author, namely, of his birth, because to the barren woman praying he granted a son, who should serve him in the temple all his days.
• ANNA BORE A SON: that is, the Church from the nations first nourished with milk the son whom she conceived through faith, that is, by simple understanding, in her hearers. The three calves signify the three times in which the Church awaited Christ. The three bushels of flour are faith, hope and charity, which the Church offered; or the three sons of Noe, from whom the Church offered many to God through faith. These gifts the Church of the Gentiles offers for the child, to show that she has borne the child, that is, has received the faith of Christ and wishes to show it by works. And she brought him to Silo, into the house of the Lord, when with perfect faith in the incarnation she joined herself to the primitive Church from the Jews.
**“AND CALLED HIS NAME SAMUEL”** — That is, God; Anna's firstborn, a prophet. Who is this but the Lord's man?
1.23:
**“AND I PRAY THAT THE LORD MAY FULFIL HIS WORD”** — What thou hast willed; or his [word], which he promised through Heli when he said: God grant thee thy petition etc.
**“So the woman stayed”** — SO THE WOMAN STAYED etc. Anna will not bring the child to the house of God before he is weaned; because the Church advances no one to the priesthood while he shares the milk of infancy and is not capable of solid food and spiritual understanding.
1.24:
**“And after she had weaned him, she carried him with her, with three calves”** — in sacrifice, namely of pious confession
**“WITH CALVES”** — 'In' for 'with', as there: in silver and gold.
**“and three bushels of flour”** — by exercise of good working
**“and a bottle of wine”** — by the grace of instruction, namely, and instructed in the faith of the Holy Trinity, that he might be able to say: We will render the calves of our lips, and might worthily offer the sacrament of the body and blood of the Lord
**“AND THREE BUSHELS OF FLOUR, AND A BOTTLE OF WINE”** — [The bottle] which holds three bushels. It is not understood that she offered all these to God at once, but some to God, some to the priest, that he might gladly receive the child into the ministry.
**“JEROME”** — In the Hebrew: with a bushel of flour; but it has been corrupted by the fault of the scribes. For if she offered three bushels of flour with three calves, she acted against the law, in which it is said: "One calf of the herd, one ram, seven lambs of a year old without blemish," and in their sacrifices fine flour tempered with oil, three tenths for each calf, two tenths for the ram, one tenth for a lamb. And this tenth part was a tenth of an ephi; whence it is understood that Elcana did not offer three bushels of flour with three calves, but nine tenths.
1.26: **“And Anna said: I beseech thee”** — namely, that thou receive him well.
1.28:
**“Therefore I also have lent him to the Lord all the days”** — namely, as long as he lives
**“AND ANNA ADORED”** — She is not found praying in this canticle except in two phrases only. One is where she says: "I have joyed in thy salvation." The other there: "For there is no other [God] besides thee." But the just man prays without ceasing, because he does not cease to do well. Whence: "The lifting up of my hands, as evening sacrifice." He lifts up his hands who lifts up his deeds. When Moses lifted up his hands Israel overcame, but when he let them down Amalec overcame; because while the servant of God lifts up his deeds the people of God overcomes, but if he lets them down Amalec, the enemy of God, overcomes.

2.1:
**“My heart hath rejoiced”** — "Rejoice in the Lord always" etc.
**“in the Lord”**
• because not in the praise of men, not in vanity
• MY HEART HATH REJOICED IN THE LORD etc. RABANUS. AUGUSTINE. Let the Church say this, full of grace, fruitful in offspring, which she knows was prophesied of herself beforehand.
**“and is exalted”** — because
**“my horn”** — the horns of the just shall be exalted; because from the tips of the cross of Christ these horns are kept for the just; with them we toss and destroy the demons that lie in wait for our soul
**“HORN”** — The kingdom of the Church, because it rises above the adversities of the world and the desires of the flesh, as a horn rises beyond the flesh.
**“in my God:”** — not in herself
**“my mouth is enlarged”**
• MY MOUTH IS ENLARGED etc. The mouth of the Church is the preachers, whose teaching is enlarged over the enemies, because it surpassed the knowledge of the scribes and Pharisees.
• MY MOUTH IS ENLARGED etc. RABANUS. AUGUSTINE. Because the word of God is not bound: not bound in pressures, not bound in its heralds.
• RABANUS. AUGUSTINE. [In] Christ, whom the old man Simeon embraces as a child and knows as great, saying: "Now thou dost dismiss thy servant, O Lord, according to thy word in peace," because: "My eyes have seen thy salvation." If I shall have joyed in the salvation of God, then my mouth shall be enlarged: namely, through meditation on the word of God one comes to the lifting up of the heart. Whence: "Our mouth is open to you, O ye Corinthians, our heart is enlarged." From the breadth of the heart wisdom is ministered to the mouth.
**“over my enemies: because I have joyed in thy salvation.”** — "For he shall save his people from their sins"
2.2:
**“There is none holy”** — THERE IS NONE HOLY etc. ORIGEN. Besides thee, O Lord, because no one is made [holy] except by thee; although there be that are called many gods and many lords, yet none of them is by nature that which God is, because he alone is he who says: I am who am. For a shadow, in comparison with a body, is not; or smoke, in comparison with fire.
**“AS THE LORD IS”** — RABANUS. AUGUSTINE. He does not say 'none but the Lord', but none is as the Lord, holy and sanctifying, just and justifying.
**“for there is no other beside thee,”** — unchangeable, namely, as thou art
2.3:
**“Do not multiply”** — DO NOT MULTIPLY etc. She rebukes the Jews and the wise of the world, who exalt themselves against the knowledge of God.
**“to speak lofty things,”** — higher things, transcending the capacity of the understanding
**“boasting:”** — RABANUS. SOLOMON. "Seek not the things that are too high for thee"; and elsewhere: 'God is in heaven, and thou upon earth: therefore let thy words be few.'
**“let old matters depart from your mouth:”** — vain talk or foul talk
**“OLD MATTERS”** — Things which pertain to the old man, that is, to carnal conversation. Seek knowledge, which is not but from God, because he is the Lord of knowledge: "In whom are all the treasures of wisdom."
**“for the Lord is a God”** — the Spirit searcheth all things
**“A GOD OF ALL KNOWLEDGE”** — RABANUS. AUGUSTINE. He knows you even where no one knows. Whence: "For if any man think himself to be something, whereas he is nothing, he deceiveth himself." These things are said to the adversaries of the city of God, belonging to Babylon, trusting in their own strength; of whom are the Jews, who, not knowing the justice of God, that is, that which God gives to man, who alone is just and justifying, and seeking to establish their own, as though prepared for themselves from themselves, not imparted by the Lord, have not submitted themselves to the justice of God. But the God of knowledge and judge of consciences sees the thoughts of men, that they are vain; vain because they are properly men's, and are not from him from whom men are.
**“TO HIM ARE THOUGHTS PREPARED”** — Because he withdraws himself from thoughts which are without understanding; or, to him are thoughts prepared, that is, made manifest. Whence: "The Lord knoweth the thoughts of men."
2.4:
**“The bow of the mighty”** — that is, the intent of the Jews, or the discipline of the philosophers, because they presumed on themselves and mocked the simplicity of faith
**“THE BOW OF THE MIGHTY”** — THE BOW OF THE MIGHTY. RABANUS. AUGUSTINE. That is, the intent of those who seem to themselves so powerful that without God's help they can fulfil the divine commandments.
**“AND THE WEAK”** — AND THE WEAK. RABANUS. AUGUSTINE. Those who trust in the mercy of God say: Have mercy on me, O God, for I am weak. The Gentile people was weak when it was a stranger to the testament of God; but now it is girt with strength, since, clothed with the shield of faith and the helmet of salvation and the sword of the spirit, it will be able to extinguish the fiery darts of the devil.
2.5:
**“They that were full”**
• filled
• The filled are the same as the mighty, that is, the Israelites, to whom were committed the words of God; but the sons of the handmaid were diminished, who withdrew themselves and did not believe in the Saviour, and in those very breads, that is, the divine words, perceived only earthly things. But the Gentiles, to whom the law was not given, after they came through the New Testament to those words, by hungering much passed over the earth, because in them they savoured not earthly but heavenly things. In the Greek: thus those full of bread were diminished, and the hungry passed over the earth.
**“THEY THAT WERE FULL”** — The Jews, filled before, namely with the mysteries of the [divine] words, have hired themselves out for bread, that is, have separated themselves from God, or have torn themselves from their own seats, lest they should receive the gospel which treats of the bread that came down from heaven.
**“before for bread”** — or: for loaves
**“have hired out themselves: and the hungry”** — the Gentiles
**“are filled,”** — and the hungry are filled: that is, the Gentiles, formerly in want, now taste the bread of the word of God, for it is sweet. They were fed with the knowledge of God until the barren bore many: in the Hebrew sabba, which signifies seven and many.
**“so that”** — it is the cause why it was so done
**“THE BARREN HATH BORNE MANY”** — In the number seven the universality of the Church is designated; whence John too writes to seven Churches, showing that he writes to the fulness of one. Whence: "Wisdom hath built herself a house, she hath hewn her out seven pillars." The Church was barren among the Gentiles before this offspring which we behold arose. We behold too the earthly Jerusalem, formerly fruitful, now weakened; because whatever sons were in her were free by her strength [so the edition]; but now, because the letter is there and the spirit is not, having lost her strength she is weakened.
**“MANY”** — RABANUS. For many, in the Hebrew and in the Seventy is found: seven. The Jews say that when Samuel was born the firstborn son of Phenenna died, and, as each son was born to Anna, a son of Phenenna died. But Phenenna had seven; Anna, however, five. But the Hebrews count the two sons of Samuel among the sons of Anna.
2.6: **“RABANUS”** — He killeth and maketh alive the barren, or the same [people]; which he repeats, adding: he bringeth down to hell and bringeth back again. Whence: "If you be dead with Christ, seek the things that are above." They are killed unto salvation to whom it is said: "Mind the things that are above, not the things that are upon the earth," as are, namely, those who, hungering, passed over the earth. "For you are dead," he says, unto salvation, namely, "and your life is hid with Christ in God." The same, then, are made alive, or living, as Christ "was delivered up for our sins, and rose again for our justification." And because he says: Thou wilt not leave my soul in hell: God brought the same down to hell and brought him back. By this his poverty we are made rich.
2.7:
**“MAKETH POOR”** — Jesus, who for our sakes was made poor; and he makes the same rich with the glory of the resurrection.
**“and maketh rich,”** — that is
**“he humbleth”**
• the proud
• "God resisteth the proud, and giveth grace to the humble"
**“and he exalteth.”** — the humble
2.8:
**“He raiseth up”** — quickly, that his flesh might not see corruption
**“the needy from the dust,”** — Christ, who for us was made poor, that we might be made rich
**“THE NEEDY FROM THE DUST”** — Christ from corruption. Whence: "Nor wilt thou give thy holy one to see corruption."
**“FROM THE DUNGHILL”** — RABANUS. [From] the Jewish people, in which, when the Apostle had said that he persecuted the Church: The things that were gain to me, he says, for Christ I counted as dung.
**“and lifteth up the poor”** — above the rich
**“WITH PRINCES”** — RABANUS. To whom it is said: You shall sit on twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.
**“and the throne of glory”** — that he may give them an inheritance, that is, a seat of glory
**“THE THRONE OF GLORY”** — By sitting in equality with the Father; and because: 'The Father hath given all judgment to the Son'; and because: "Of his kingdom there shall be no end."
**“hold.”** — because: "He shall rule from sea to sea"
**“For the poles of the earth are the Lord's,”** — that is, the four quarters of the world
**“THE POLES OF THE EARTH”** — Namely the four quarters of the world, in which he has spread the world of the Church, which from the rising of the sun to its going down praise the name of the Lord.
**“MYSTICALLY”** — The preachers, upon whom the world, that is, the Church, is established by their faith; of whom it is said: "Under whom they stoop that bear up the world."
2.9:
**“the feet of his saints”** — that is, the works of the elect
**“he will keep”** — he will direct in the way of justice
**“and the wicked in darkness”** — of hell: "Where there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth"
**“shall be silent,”** — they shall cease from arrogance
**“because not by his own strength”** — but by God's
**“shall man prevail.”** — the faithful people
2.10:
**“SHALL FEAR THE LORD”** — That [the Greek says] he will make his adversary weak can also be understood, from the ambiguous Greek, as his own adversary. For when the Lord begins to possess us, our adversary becomes his, and is overcome by us, not by our strength, because not in his own strength is a man mighty.
**“shall fear the Lord”** — SHALL FEAR THE LORD etc. The adversaries are the Jews, upon whom the Lord thundered in the heavens, that is, in the apostles, when he terrified them by threatening hell, confirming the threats with signs; whence many were converted. Or they shall fear in the judgment him whom, opposing him here, they despised; upon whom he will thunder, saying: 'Depart into everlasting fire'; and lest this befall all, the Lord daily thunders in the heavens, that is, in the Scriptures and the teachers.
**“his adversaries”**
• the Jews
• sinners
**“and upon them”**
• the Jews
• sinners
• the damned
**“in the heavens”**
• the apostles
• the holy Scriptures
• the judgment
**“SHALL HE THUNDER IN THE HEAVENS”** — RABANUS. Because the just retribution will be in the day of judgment; but meanwhile he thunders from his clouds, which he filled with the Holy Ghost after he ascended into heaven.
**“The Lord”** — but afterwards
**“shall judge the ends of the earth,”**
• not only the midland regions but also the farthest
• man's last things
**“THE ENDS OF THE EARTH”** — Man's last things: because the things that are changed for better or for worse in the middle time will not be judged, but the last state in which he shall have been found.
**“and he shall give empire”**
• the Church
• of ruling the flesh
**“to his king,”**
• Christ
• the Christian people
**“AND HE SHALL GIVE TO HIS KING”** — That is, to Christ. Empire, that is, the Church. Whence: "I will give thee the Gentiles for thy inheritance." Or empire, that is, the power of judging, because: "He hath given all judgment to the Son."
**“TO HIS KING”** — RABANUS. The Christian people, to whom he gives the power of ruling the flesh, that in it he may overcome the world, who for its sake shed his blood.
**“and shall exalt the horn of his Christ.”** — the horn of Christ, namely of the head and the members: the sublime kingdom will be shown, which is now despised by the unbelievers.
**“OF HIS CHRIST”** — Of the Christian people anointed with chrism; yet the whole body with its head is one Christ. This Anna prophesied, the mother of Samuel, in whom was then figured the change of the old priesthood, and now fulfilled, when the fruitful was weakened, that the barren might have a new priesthood in Christ.
2.11: **“And Elcana went to Ramatha, to his house: but the child ministered in the sight of the Lord before the face of Heli the priest.”** — HELI is interpreted 'stranger'. For he is a stranger to God who does not correct those subject to him. Ophni, 'infamy of conversion'; and deservedly is he so called who puts off being converted to better things. Phinees, 'stopping of the mouth' or 'sparing the mouth'. We read of two priests Phinees: one just, the son of Eleazar; the other unjust, the son of Heli. Priests who guard their mouth, lest anything perverse come forth from it, are signified in the son of Eleazar. But those who have a mouth stopped, either by unskilfulness or by consciousness of sins, are figured in the son of Heli.
2.12:
**“NOW THE SONS OF HELI”** — Josephus relates that the priest Heli had two sons, Ophni and Phinees, injurious toward men and impious toward the divinity, and they spared no iniquity: some gifts from those who offered they set apart for themselves on account of [their] honour, others they took by way of plunder; they offered insults to the women who came together for religion's sake, doing violence to some, persuading others with gifts; and their life differed in nothing from the worst tyranny. Whence Heli too was condemned for their iniquity, because he punished them with too little severity of correction; although indeed he restrained and rebuked them with gentleness, yet with the mildness of a father, not with the severity and authority of a high priest. Let priests learn, then, that they will be punished for the crimes of the people, and the fault of those under them will be imputed to them.
**“were children of Belial,”** — without yoke, without master
2.18:
**“But Samuel ministered before the face of the Lord: being a child girded with a linen ephod.”**
• with a superhumeral
• not that with which the high priest was clothed; for that was marked with four colours: violet, scarlet, fine linen and gold
• which had been granted to the lower orders
2.19: **“AND A LITTLE COAT”** — The coat which Anna, that is, grace, made and gave to the child is the beginning teaching, by which the faithful receive their first rudiments. Whence: "I gave you milk to drink, not meat." But the linen superhumeral signifies chastity and continence with good works. For he who desires to minister to the Lord must live chastely and continently and exercise himself in good works.
2.25: **“If one man shall sin against another,”** — IF ONE MAN SHALL SIN etc. One does not sin against a man in the same way as one sins against God; because to sin against a man, that is, against a neighbour, is lighter and more venial. But to sin against God, that is, to withdraw from his worship, is the sin of impiety, which is more hardly punished and more slowly forgiven. And when one sins against a man, by appeasing the man he makes God placable to himself. But when one sins against God, who shall pray for him? That is, through whom shall he make God propitious to himself? Not that no pardon is to be hoped for by those who sin in the divine office; but greater is the punishment and slower the pardon for those who offend in things consecrated to God than if they had hurt their neighbour by word or deed, because the greater the glory, the heavier the offence.
2.29: **“Why have you kicked away my victims, and my gifts which I commanded to be offered in the temple: and thou hast rather honoured thy sons than me, to eat the firstfruits”** — not content with the part granted you
2.30:
**“Wherefore thus saith the Lord the God of Israel: I said indeed that thy house, and the house of thy father should minister in my sight, for ever.”** — not that the shadow is eternal, but the truth
**“But now saith the Lord: Far be this from me: but whosoever shall glorify”** — as Samuel
2.31:
**“Behold the days”** — of the New Testament, in which there is no priest according to Aaron
**“come: and I will cut off thy arm,”** — the dignity and strength of the priesthood
**“and the arm of thy father's house,”** — Aaron
**“OF THY FATHER”** — Aaron, namely. For who else was in the Egyptian bondage who after the deliverance was chosen for the priesthood? For whoever is of his race, when he sees the priesthood of the Christians flourishing throughout the world, but taken away from himself, wastes away with grief and sorrow.
**“that there shall not be an old man”** — a high priest
2.32:
**“And thou shalt see thy rival”** — the Christian people
**“RIVAL”** — RABANUS. The rival of the house of Heli was Sadoc the priest, who received the priesthood when Abiathar was cast out by Solomon. Whence: "Solomon cast out Abiathar from being the priest of the Lord, that the word of the Lord might be fulfilled, which he spoke concerning the house of Heli."
2.33:
**“THAT THY EYES MAY FAINT”** — RABANUS. AUGUSTINE. That, namely, there may always be one of the house of Heli in the house of the Lord, who, seeing another put in the dignity of the priesthood and himself put out, may faint in mind and waste away. But this change of the priesthood, which was figured by Samuel, was fully completed in Christ. For after Samuel there were priests of the race of Aaron, Sadoc and Abiathar and others, up to the time of Christ.
**“and thy soul be spent: and a great part”**
• this was fulfilled when Saul commanded the priests of his stock to be slain
• either by unbelief or by the sword of Titus
2.34:
**“And this shall be a sign to thee,”** — of the change of the priesthood; for the death of the sons signifies the death not of a man but of the priesthood
**“that shall come upon thy two sons, Ophni and Phinees: In one day they shall both of them die.”** — in battle
2.35:
**“And I will raise me up a faithful priest, who according to my heart”** — whence: "I do always the things that please him"
**“AND MY SOUL”** — AND MY SOUL. RABANUS. AUGUSTINE. God has no soul, but he is said tropically to have a soul, as hands and feet and the other members of the body. Now it can be said of Samuel that he obeyed God in all things. But Christ pleased God the Father in all things. Whence: "I do always the things that please him"; for whom the Father built a house, which house are we, if we hold fast the confidence and grace and glory of hope unto the end. But it cannot be said of Samuel that a faithful house was built for him, to walk all days before the Lord's anointed, that is, Samuel, since we read in what follows that his sons turned aside after avarice; unless perhaps we take his house to be the Jewish people, which served the Lord all the days of his priesthood. Whence: "And all the house of Israel rested following the Lord."
**“shall do, and I will build him a faithful house,”** — the Church, or the heavenly Jerusalem
**“and he shall walk”**
• the house
• shall live
• from death to life
2.36:
**“IT SHALL COME TO PASS”** — IT SHALL COME TO PASS. RABANUS. This is not said properly of the house of Heli but of the house of Aaron, of whose race even to this day they come and are converted.
**“that whosoever shall remain in thy house, shall come that he may be prayed for, and shall offer a piece of silver,”** — the confession of the mouth
**“and a roll of bread,”** — the saving sacrifice, carnal things being cast off
**“and shall say: Put me, I beseech thee, to somewhat of the priestly office,”** — that is, the people itself, mighty with Christ as priest. Whence: "But you are a chosen generation, a kingly priesthood" etc.
**“A MORSEL OF BREAD”** — A MORSEL OF BREAD. RABANUS. "The bread that I will give is my flesh, for the life of the world." Because he had said that he gave food to the house of Aaron from the victims of the Old Testament, which were the sacrifices of the Jews, he says that a morsel of bread must be asked for, to eat; which is the sacrifice of the Christians and the food of souls.

3.1: **“Now the child Samuel ministered to the Lord before Heli, and the word of the Lord was precious”** — PRECIOUS. RABANUS. Rare. Whence: In those days there was no manifest vision; for because of the sins of the people and of the prelates the Lord did not appear through visions or through angelic answers, as he appeared to the fathers.
3.2: **“And it came to pass one day when Heli lay in his place, and his eyes were grown dim”** — through very great age
3.3: **“THE LAMP”** — THE LAMP. RABANUS. Which burned in the tabernacle before the light of day. For at daylight it was put out, but it gave light until morning. Or this signifies that Heli would remain in blindness until he was utterly put out with his offspring, that is, died. But mystically the blindness of Heli signifies the blindness of the Jews, who did not acknowledge the Saviour present, nor the brightness of his miracles, nor his teaching, until the priesthood was overthrown with the people and the temple.
3.4: **“And the Lord called Samuel.”** — it can be understood by the threefold calling, because he was to be prophet, leader and priest
3.7: **“Now Samuel did not yet know the Lord,”** — because the divine word, the mystery of prophecy, had not been revealed to him
3.11: **“And the Lord said to Samuel: Behold I do a thing in Israel: and whosoever shall hear it, both his ears shall tingle.”** — [BOTH HIS EARS] SHALL TINGLE etc. RABANUS. It is the threat of God upon Heli and upon his house, because, namely, for the sin of the sons of Heli the house was deprived of the priesthood of the Lord. Whence: The ears of the hearers shall tingle with vehement amazement.
3.14:
**“Therefore have I sworn to the house”** — or: to the house
**“of Heli, that the iniquity [of his house] shall not be expiated”** — which they committed against Christ
3.17: **“MAY GOD DO SO AND SO TO THEE, AND ADD SO AND SO”** — It was a proverb among the Hebrews. And the sense is: if thou hide from me, may the evil which the Lord hath spoken to thee concerning me come upon thy head.
3.19: **“AND NOT ONE [OF HIS WORDS] FELL”** — AND NOT ONE [OF HIS WORDS] FELL. RABANUS. Because nothing of the things which the Lord spoke was void. For empty words fall to the ground, to be held as nothing and trodden under foot in the contempt of all. Whence Job: "The light of my countenance fell not to the earth"; because he had been accustomed to hold his countenance in such gravity that it was not loosened by contemptible mirth. But whenever he showed himself cheerful to those present, he did it for a certain reason of their profit.
3.20: **“FROM DAN TO BERSABEE”** — FROM DAN TO BERSABEE. RABANUS. JEROME. By the boundaries of Judea he takes in the whole of the people. Dan is a little village at the fourth milestone from Paneas, which is so called to this day; the boundary of the province of Judea toward the north, from which the Jordan, breaking forth, took its name from the place. For the Hebrews call a river or stream Ior. Dan is interpreted 'judgment' or 'judging'. Bersabee, in the tribe of Juda or of Simeon, is a large village at the twentieth milestone from Hebron, lying toward the south, in which a garrison of the Romans is stationed; from which the boundaries of Judea, beginning, stretch as far as Dan. Nor should anyone wonder if he finds cities of Juda in the tribe of Simeon or of Benjamin. For the tribe of Juda, strong and warlike, often overcoming its adversaries, held the princedom among all the tribes. Therefore the lots of other tribes are counted in its portion. Otherwise, Scripture shows that Simeon dwelt in the midst of the tribe of Juda.
3.21: **“ISRAEL”** — ISRAEL: a man seeing God, or strong with God; these are the believers. The Philistines, falling with drink: namely the demons, who, made drunk with the cups of pride, have themselves fallen and hasten to pervert men. Against them Israel, that is, the faithful, lest they yield, but that they may overcome, encamp by the stone of help, that is, the law of Christ, where the stone, that is, Christ, is found, of whom: "The stone which the builders rejected." But while the faithful meditate on the law of the Lord that they may find him their helper, the Philistines come into Aphec, that is, new fury: then, because the unclean spirits see the faithful press more on the divine laws, they therefore contrive sharper and new combats; whence those who trust in their own strength and glory in human wisdom, and through this despise the grace of the gospel, the unclean spirits easily lay low, as it were four thousand.

4.1:
**“And it came to pass in those days, that the Philistines gathered themselves together to fight: and Israel went out”** — a man seeing God, or strong with God
**“to war against the Philistines, and camped by the Stone of help.”** — BY THE STONE OF HELP. The stone of help, which Samuel afterwards set up as a sign, when the Lord first helped him.
**“APHEC”** — APHEC. RABANUS. JEROME. It is a place near the village of Esrom, of the city of Jezrael, where Saul fought, in the lot of Aser; and it is interpreted new fury, or seizing; for those who deserved the wrath of the Lord were seized by the enemies.
4.4:
**“AND THEY BROUGHT FROM THENCE THE ARK”** — The children of Israel brought the ark where it was taken. And the faithful from the Jews carried the two testaments over to the Gentiles.
**“SITTING UPON THE CHERUBIMS”** — For there was a table upon the ark, which the cherubims covered with their wings, where the Lord appeared through an angel and spoke. Cherubim is the fulness of knowledge, which is found in Christ and in the two testaments.
4.5: **“WITH A GREAT SHOUT”** — The great shout is the voice of the preachers, strengthened by miracles, brought forth from the two testaments; and the earth rang with the voice of the preaching, the wise of the world; the demons too groaned, believing that they were overcome.
4.8: **“FROM THE HAND OF [THESE HIGH] GODS”** — The Jews worship one God, but the Gentiles speak after their own fashion.
4.9: **“Take courage and behave like men,”** — strong
4.11: **“And the ark of God was taken:”** — AND THE ARK OF GOD WAS TAKEN. The ark taken by the foreigners signifies that the testament would pass over to the Gentiles.
