4.12: **“And there ran a man of Benjamin out of the army, and came to Silo the same day, with his clothes rent, and his head strewed”** — a sign of mourning
4.18:
**“AND WHEN HE HAD NAMED THE ARK OF GOD”** — AND WHEN HE HAD NAMED THE ARK OF GOD. RABANUS. Josephus relates these things thus: when Heli heard that the ark had been taken by the enemies, troubled with grief, falling from his seat he died, having lived ninety-eight years, of which he held the princedom forty. On that day the wife of Phinees his son died, since she could not bear to live after the fall of her husband. And she bore a son of seven months, whom they called Ichabod, that is, inglorious, because at that time such a misfortune had befallen.
**“And when he had named the ark of God,”** — Heli was the first to hold the princedom from the house of Ithamar, the son of Aaron. For before, the priests were of the house of Eleazar, from whom the son received the honour from the father; and Eleazar handed it to Phinees his son. After him Abiezer his son received the honour, which he left to Bozi his son, whom Ozi his son succeeded; and after him Heli held the priesthood; [afterwards] those of the house of Eleazar received it again.
**“he fell from his stool”** — whoever turns backward from faith and truth must fall and die. But mystically, when the ark of the Lord passed over to the Gentiles, the priesthood of the Jews perished.
**“HE FELL FROM HIS STOOL”** — And when Heli falls from his seat, the seat of the high priest remains empty, and the glory of the priests is put out.
**“AND DIED”** — Heli dies, the sons die too, because the high priesthood fails with the old priesthood.
4.19: **“THE WIFE OF PHINEES”** — The wife of the priest did not die before she bore a male child; nor did the Synagogue wholly perish before the primitive Church, which was from it, believed.
4.20:
**“And when she was upon the point of death”** — AND WHEN SHE WAS UPON THE POINT OF DEATH etc. By an evident sign it is figured that, when the carnal priesthood of the Jews was put out, the carnal Synagogue, which clung carnally to it, is put out.
**“FEAR NOT, FOR THOU HAST BORNE A SON”** — The believers console the Synagogue, but she, despairing, gives no heed, and reckons the new offspring not to glory but to ignominy. Whence it follows: and she called the child Ichabod. Chabod: glory; Ichabod: the glory has fallen. For the glory was carried away when the ark was taken. Whence: "The kingdom of God shall be taken from you, and shall be given to a nation yielding the fruits thereof."

5.1:
**“INTO AZOTUS”** — INTO AZOTUS. RABANUS. Which is also Asdod, one of the five cities of the Palestinians, assigned indeed to the tribe of Juda but not held, because it could not drive out the natives. And it is interpreted 'fire of the father' or 'burning'. And well is the place so called where the idol Dagon was, because the coming of the ark into Azotus was the burning of the devil, the father of all enemies or of the wicked. Dagon, which is interpreted 'fish of sadness', signifies the devil, who in the sea of this world devours sinners, who in Job also is named Leviathan and Behemoth.
**“AZOTUS”** — It is the place in which Samuel set up the stone, as is shown in what follows.
5.3:
**“And when the Azotians arose early the next day, behold Dagon”** — after the testament of God came to the Gentiles, at once the idols fell down
**“lay upon his face on the ground before the ark of the Lord: and they took Dagon, and set him again”** — there were many defenders of idolatry
5.4:
**“AND THE HEAD”** — The pride of the devil, which is the beginning of all sin.
**“of Dagon, and both the palms of his hands were cut off upon the threshold:”** — that is, the faith by which idolatry is destroyed
**“UPON THE THRESHOLD”** — UPON THE THRESHOLD. RABANUS. It signifies the end fixed beforehand, in which idolatry would cease. For the threshold is the end of a journey.
**“ONLY THE STUMP REMAINED”** — They found only the back, all the members being broken, which expresses the flight of idolatry. For he who flees gives his back to the pursuer. Whence: "For thou shalt make them turn their back" etc.
5.5: **“in its place. For this cause neither the priests of Dagon, nor any that go into his temple tread on the threshold of Dagon”** — out of reverence for their god
5.6:
**“And the hand of the Lord was heavy upon the Azotians, and he destroyed them, and smote them in the more secret part of the buttocks”**
• since they were Sodomites
• AND SMOTE THEM IN THE MORE SECRET PART OF THE BUTTOCKS. Those who receive the testament of God and love the hinder things of this life will justly be tormented in the hinder parts by those very things, which they ought to esteem as dung. For those who take up the testament of God and, looking back to the hinder things, do not strip themselves of the old vanity, are like those who put the ark of the testament beside their idols. And the old things indeed fall even against their will, because: "All flesh is grass"; but the ark remains for ever, namely the testament of the kingdom of heaven which is to follow, where the word of God is for ever.
5.8:
**“And sending, they gathered together all the lords”** — that is, the princes
**“of the Philistines to them, and said: What shall we do with the ark of the God of Israel? And the Gethrites answered:”**
• priests and diviners.
• winepresses, or oppressing
**“LET IT BE CARRIED ABOUT”** — LET IT BE CARRIED ABOUT. That if, wherever it goes, the stroke accompanies it, we may know that the plague is from God. Which was done by the will of God through their counsel, that the plague might be common, since the guilt was common.
5.9: **“THE LOWER BOWELS”** — The inward parts; hence extales, where the plague was.

6.1: **“Now the ark of God was in the land of the Philistines seven months.”** — SEVEN MONTHS. The number seven signifies the whole of time, which runs on by the number of seven days; and it signifies that the testament of God will remain among the Gentiles until the consummation of the world.
6.4:
**“They answered: What is it we ought to render unto him for sin? and they answered:”** — or: to them
**“According to the number of the provinces of the Philistines you shall make five golden emerods,”** — FIVE EMERODS etc. RABANUS. The five golden emerods and five mice which the Philistines made after their plague and brought to the ark signified that the carnal, given to the five senses of the body, when they have been chastised by the Lord, acknowledging their own crimes confess that they were justly struck, and, though compelled, are changed for the better. This the five cities of the Philistines well signify: Azotus, Gaza, Ascalon, Geth, Accaron, expressing namely those who follow the acts of the outward man. Gaza is a city of the Hevites, in which the Cappadocians dwelt after the former inhabitants were slain. Among the ancients it was the boundary of the Chanaanites near Egypt, and it fell to the lot of Juda, but it could not hold it, because the Enacim, that is, the giants of the Allophyli, resisted most strongly. And it is to this day a notable city of Palestine; yet Gaza is said to be destined to be an everlasting heap, because first it was utterly destroyed and another was built in another place. Ascalon, a noble city of Palestine, was assigned to the tribe of Juda, but it could not overcome its inhabitants. Geth is now a large village called Gethan. Between Antipatris and Thamna there is also another town of this name. Accaron is in the tribe of Dan or in the tribe of Juda, on the left of the Chanaanites, but it did not drive out the former inhabitants; and to this day a large village is called Accaron, between Azotus and Thamna, facing the east. Some think Accaron is the Tower of Strato, afterwards called Caesarea. Azotus is interpreted 'fire of my father' or 'burning'; Gaza 'strength'; Ascalon 'infamous fire' or 'ignoble fire'; Geth 'winepress'; Accaron 'teaching of sadness' or 'of barrenness'. For every concupiscence, infamous and ignoble, inflamed by the devil, urged on by the contrary powers, and pressed out by the winepress of wickedness, pours forth the wine of bitterness in perverse teaching and wicked working. And therefore it tends to death, where there is true sadness and perpetual barrenness.
6.7:
**“A CART”** — The cart is the cross of Christ; the ark, sacred Scripture.
**“TWO KINE”** — TWO KINE. ISIDORE. The kine bearing the ark signify the saints who renounce the world, who have drawn no yoke of sin. For as the kine did not turn aside from the straight way through affection for their calves, so the holy fathers do not swerve from their good purpose through such affection.
**“that have calved, on which there hath come no yoke,”** — of sin
**“tie to the cart,”** — the chariot of God is ten thousandfold
**“and shut up”** — as remaining in the world
**“their calves”** — the parents' sons
6.9: **“BETHSAMES”** — BETHSAMES. RABANUS. It is a priestly city in the tribe of Benjamin, which is shown to this day to those going from Eleutheropolis to Nicopolis, at the tenth milestone toward the east. There is another Bethsames in the tribe of Nephthali, in which the old inhabitants remained.
6.10: **“They did therefore in this manner: and taking two kine”** — the saints renouncing the world
6.12:
**“THAT LEADETH”** — THAT LEADETH. RABANUS. Going, namely, by the king's way to Bethsames, that is, into the house of the sun, namely the heavenly Jerusalem, where the sun of justice ever shines.
**“AND TURNED NOT ASIDE”** — AND TURNED NOT ASIDE. RABANUS. That is, they were neither lifted up by prosperity nor broken by adversity. If, then, we tend toward the dwelling of the eternal sun, let us not turn aside from the way of God for carnal affections. But it is to be weighed that the kine of God, set under the cart, go on and low, and yet do not turn their steps from the way. So the preachers of God, and any of the faithful, ought to be within the Church: that they may suffer with their neighbours through charity, and not swerve from the way of God through compassion. For to go to Bethsames with the ark set upon one is to draw near with heavenly knowledge to the dwelling of the inner light. Which we truly do when we do not turn aside for affection for our dear ones. For so ought those to go who, set under the yoke of the sacred law, now carry the ark of the Lord through inward knowledge: that, grieving with the needs of their kin, they do not turn aside from rightness. Whose grace ought so to hold our mind, that it be neither hard if it is not touched by affection, nor, touched too much, slackened into weeping.
**“BETHSAMES”** — BETHSAMES: 'house of the sun'. This is the Church, lighted by the "sun of justice." For the Bethsamites to reap the wheat in the valley is for the teachers of the Church to handle the corn of the word of God in humility. The stone in the field of Josue: Christ in his Church; the wood of the cart: the cross of Christ. To immolate the kine upon the stone is to mortify those converted from the world in the imitation of Christ.
6.14: **“And the cart came into the field of Josue a Bethsamite, and stood there. And there was a great stone, and they cut in pieces the wood of the cart, and laid the kine upon it”** — the Levites or the priests, because it was not lawful for others
6.17: **“And these are the golden emerods, which the Philistines returned for sin to the Lord: For Azotus one, for Gaza one, for Ascalon one, for Geth one, for Accaron one:”** — FOR AZOTUS ONE etc. ISIDORE. The five cities gave five emerods and five mice. But the remaining cities of the provinces, and the towns that were without wall, [gave] mice only. Whence: From the fenced city to the village that was without wall etc.
6.18:
**“And the golden mice according to the number of the cities of the Philistines, of the five provinces, from the fenced city to the village that was without wall, and to Abel”** — JEROME. Mourning
**“ABEL”** — ABEL. It is a city on the border of Israel, which, called Bethsames before, is now called Abel, either because of the mourning made there over the men of Bethsames, or to distinguish the city from Abel Beth Maacha, from which the wise woman cried out to Joab: They that ask, let them ask in Abela.
**“the great (the stone) whereon they set down the ark of the Lord, which was”** — continually
6.19:
**“BUT HE SLEW”** — BUT HE SLEW. Who, though they were not Levites, dared to look upon the ark. Lest the people should suffer this, in Exodus they stood afar off; Moses alone went up to the Lord.
**“of the men of Bethsames, because they had seen the ark of the Lord: and he slew of the people”** — AND HE SLEW OF THE PEOPLE etc. In the Hebrew: he smote of the people seventy men and fifty thousand men. The seventy men [were] judges, the Hebrews say. It was lawful for no one to see the ark uncovered except the high priest; they were struck, then, because they were unworthy, or had approached unworthily, or had not guarded the ark.
**“seventy men”** — the elders, namely the chief men of the people
6.20:
**“And the men of Bethsames said: Who shall be able to stand before”** — presence
**“the Lord this holy God? and to whom shall he go up”** — worthily
6.21: **“AND THEY SENT MESSENGERS”** — AND THEY SENT MESSENGERS. RABANUS. The transfer of the testament of the Lord from the Jews to the Gentiles is signified; because, since they defiled the law with carnal observance and the superstitions of the Pharisees, they refused the teaching of Christ and his disciples. Whence: "To you it behoved us first to speak the word of God: but because you judge yourselves unworthy, behold we turn to the Gentiles."

7.1:
**“And the men of Cariathiarim came”**
• of the Gentile Church
• RABANUS. Cariathiarim is the city of forests, one of the cities of the Gabaonites, belonging to the tribe of Juda, at the ninth milestone for those going from Aelia to Diospolis. From it was Urias the prophet, whom Joakim slew in Jerusalem, as Jeremias writes.
**“CARIATHIARIM”** — CARIATHIARIM. RABANUS. It is interpreted town of the woods, of which it is said: "Until I find out a place for the Lord, a tabernacle for the God of Jacob. Behold we have heard of it in Ephrata: we have found it in the fields of the wood." For the place of the Lord is the tabernacle of the breast of the Christian people. For the city of the woods, that is, the assembly of the Gentiles, is a fit place to receive the ark. In the house of Abinadab, which is interpreted 'my father of his own will', and it can say: willingly, namely, to thee.
**“and fetched up the ark of the Lord and carried it into the house of Abinadab”** — which is interpreted 'my father of his own will'
**“GABAA”** — GABAA. RABANUS. The hill of humble souls. Whence: "Let the mountains receive peace for the people: and the hills justice." The mountains are the greater souls, the hills the lesser. Or again Gabaa is interpreted loftiness, where Eleazar the priest is appointed.
**“ELEAZAR”** — ELEAZAR. RABANUS. 'Help of God'. And well is he who is called by this name chosen to keep the ark of the Lord, because holy men ascribe whatever good they have to God, not to themselves. Whence: "Our sufficiency is from God," who hath made us fit ministers of the new testament.
7.2:
**“And it came to pass, that from the day”** — after the testament abode in the Church, the just were multiplied, who were enlightened by it as days
**“THE TWENTIETH YEAR”**
• It was [the twentieth year] when, in the seventh year of Saul's reign, it was brought into the camp from Cariathiarim.
• RABANUS. It is not to be understood that the twenty years during which the ark abode in Cariathiarim are to be reckoned up to the eighth year of the reign of David, in which, a great multitude of the people being gathered, he brought it into Jerusalem. For it is found in what follows that in the time of Saul it was taken from this city into the camp against the Philistines; and since it is certain that David brought it into Jerusalem from the house of Abinadab, it remains to be understood that in the days of Saul it was brought back from the camp into the aforesaid city; whence afterwards, in the reign of David, it was brought to Jerusalem. The sense, then, is that from the time the ark abode in Cariathiarim it was the twentieth year when in the time of Saul it was carried into the camp. Or it was the twentieth year when all the house of Israel had rested following the Lord, having cast away their idols and serving him; which Josephus testifies it did through the whole time of Samuel, namely twenty-seven years, and in the first time of the reign of Saul, which, by the same Josephus' testimony, he held twenty years. For when the spirit of the Lord had departed from Saul and an evil spirit drove him to persecute David, some part of the army and of the people followed him.
7.3:
**“And Samuel spoke to all the house of Israel, saying: If you turn to the Lord with all your heart, put away the strange gods from among you, Baalim”** — ascending or higher
**“and Astaroth”** — Astaroth: the making of explorations. He who is a true Israelite puts away from himself every making of the malignant spirits, and boasting and pride, and serves the Lord alone, because there is no fellowship of light with darkness.
7.4:
**“MASPHATH”**
• It is a city in the tribe of Juda near Cariathiarim.
• RABANUS. The Church, gathered in unity of faith under the new priesthood, drawing the waters of tears, pours them out before the Lord in making satisfaction. The prophet judges the people in Masphath, because the teacher teaches most those whom he has seen to be intent on contemplation and on the love of the heavenly country.
7.5: **“And Samuel said: Gather all Israel to Masphath”** — MASPHATH. RABANUS. Watching, or contemplation, or intent, or the place of judgment. And this place well befits so holy a man, who judged in justice and truth and governed the people with the highest prudence.
7.6: **“THEY DREW WATER, AND POURED IT OUT”** — That, as water poured out does not return, so they too should not return to idolatry.
7.9:
**“A SUCKING LAMB”** — The lamb offered for the people gives the victory to God; and through the passion of Christ, the demons being overcome, peace is given to the faithful.
**“RABANUS”** — An innocent life kindled with the fire of charity.
**“and Samuel cried to the Lord for Israel, and the Lord heard”** — the ears of the Lord [are open] to the prayers of the just
7.10: **“THUNDERED”** — THUNDERED. RABANUS. When the Lord thunders through the preachers of the gospel, the spiritual enemies are turned to flight before Israel, that is, the people of God; and they pursue them as far as the house of knowledge, that is, until all error is purged away and God is truly known.
7.11: **“BETHCHAR”** — BETHCHAR. RABANUS. House of knowledge, or house of the lamb.
7.12:
**“And Samuel took a stone,”** — as a sign of victory
**“AND LAID IT BETWEEN MASPHATH”** — Another edition: between new Masphath and old, and he called its name Abenezer, or Abongener, that is, stone of help. This is the mediation of the Saviour, through which one must pass from the old Masphath to the new: that is, from the intent by which false happiness is awaited in a carnal kingdom to the intent by which, through the New Testament, true happiness is awaited in the kingdom of heaven, than which nothing is better; thus far God helps.
**“and laid it between Masphath”** — Masphath: intent. Sen: of teeth. The stone between these: Christ, set between the intent of the Old Testament and the preaching of the gospel; himself a stone because of firmness; of help, because he helps his own when they fight against the demons.
**“THUS FAR [THE LORD] HATH HELPED”** — Because those who go beyond these bounds, as the heretics, do not merit the help of God.
7.14:
**“And the cities, which the Philistines had taken from Israel, were restored to Israel, from Accaron to Geth, and their borders: and he delivered Israel from the hand of the Philistines, and there was peace”** — AND THERE WAS PEACE. "Christ is our peace, who hath made both one," through whom they who were afar off are made nigh.
**“between Israel and the Amorrhites.”** — bitter, or speaking
7.16:
**“And he went every year about to Bethel”** — house of God
**“and to Galgal”** — revelation
**“GALGAL”**
• It is the city where Josue circumcised the people the second time and celebrated the Pasch, and, when the manna failed, Israel used bread of wheat; where too the stones were carried over from the bed of the Jordan; where the tabernacle of the testimony was for a long time. It fell to the lot of Juda, and to this day the place is shown at the second milestone from Jericho, venerated by the men of that region. But some suppose another Galgal near Bethel.
• It is interpreted rolling or revelation. Well, then, did the prophet judge Israel in Bethel and in Galgal and Masphath, and, returning to Ramatha to his house, judged Israel there and built there an altar to the Lord: giving an example that judgment is to be done in the house of God, not indiscreetly or with a malicious mind, but according as Scripture has revealed, and with good intent and brotherly love; and that so we are to return to Ramatha, into our house, that is, to the inward parts of the breast, that we may be free for contemplation and offer on the altar of faith pleasing victims of work and truth.
**“and to Masphath,”** — intent
7.17:
**“And he returned to Ramatha,”** — a lofty sign, or vision of death
**“HE BUILT AN ALTAR TO THE LORD”** — The law commanded that an altar not be built except where the Lord had chosen; but lest they should sacrifice to gods he built an altar, in which he is reproved [so the edition].

8.1:
**“And it came to pass when Samuel was old,”** — because, weighed down with age and cares, he could not celebrate the solemnities
**“HE APPOINTED HIS SONS”** — HE APPOINTED HIS SONS. RABANUS. Because, according to Josephus, he set one in Bethlehem, the other in Bersabee.
8.2:
**“Now the name of his firstborn son was Joel:”** — beginning, or God was
**“ABIA”** — ABIA. RABANUS. The Lord is father, or he was father. Fittingly, then, those who did not persevere in the justice they had begun, and neglected the fatherhood of the Lord, were named 'God was' and 'father was', to signify that they were unworthy of the fatherhood of God.
8.3: **“And they walked not”** — AND THEY WALKED NOT etc. Because for a gift they oppressed justice, turning aside to feasts and costly banquets.
8.5: **“And they said to him: Behold thou art old,”** — as if [to say]: worn out by age, thou canst not be over affairs
8.7: **“And the Lord said to Samuel: Hearken to the voice of the people in all that they say to thee. For they have not rejected thee,”** — "He that despiseth you despiseth me"
8.9:
**“Now therefore hearken to their voice: but yet testify to them,”** — that is, give testimony to them
**“and foretell them the right of the king,”** — exaction and domination
8.12: **“And he will appoint of them to be his tribunes,”** — judges
8.13: **“Your daughters also he will take to make him ointments, and to be his cooks,”** — kitchen-maids
8.15: **“Moreover [he will take the tenth of] your corn, and of the [revenues of your] vineyards”** — which the vines bring forth as the year returns
8.19: **“But the people would not hear the voice of Samuel, and they said: Nay”** — namely, we will hear thee
8.22: **“And the Lord said to Samuel: Hearken to their voice, and make them a king. And Samuel said to the men of Israel: Let every man go to his city.”** — until God shows what we are to do

9.1:
**“Now there was a man of Benjamin whose name was”** — son of the right hand
**“Cis, the son”** — hard, or vomiting of a man, or a man vomiting
**“of Abiel,”** — my father God
**“the son of Seror,”** — little one, or turbulent
**“the son of Bechorath,”** — thy firstborn
**“the son of Sared,”** — descending, or descent
**“the son of Aphia,”** — liberality of the Lord
**“the son of a man of Jemini,”** — he had two names; and it was a family belonging to the tribe of Benjamin
9.2:
**“And he had a son whose name was Saul,”**
• petition
• RABANUS. That Saul, seeking his father's asses, came to the prophet, by whom he was anointed, signifies that the Jews, following the folly of carnal sense, seek after the luxury of the world through devious errors. For the ass is a brutish and wanton animal. And coming to the prophet, that is, to Moses, they hear that the asses are found, that is, that the goods of the earth are owed to them; by whom also the oil of anointing and the helm of the kingdom are promised, in which for a time they might rescue their brethren from the hand of the enemies.
**“WHOSE NAME WAS SAUL”** — Saul, who, God being offended, was made king over Israel, signifies the Jews. For as he became hard and proud and rigid, so as to oppress them with a servile burden rather than free them, so the people of the Jews, though anointed in its priests and kings, was yet a son of the handmaid, who bore unto bondage, and could not attain perfect freedom through the anointing, especially because it would not receive the true and meek king, through whom it could have been freed. Saul, then, is interpreted petition, who was of the stock of Benjamin, because [he was] the son of Cis, the son of Abiel, the son of Seor, the son of Bethoreth, the son of Sared, the son of Aphia. Benjamin: son of the right hand. Cis: hard, or vomiting of a man, or a man vomiting. Abiel: my father God. Seor: little one, or turbulent. Bechoreth: thy firstborn. Sared: descent. Aphia: liberality of the Lord. Israel, then, God's firstborn son, and God his father, was a son of the right hand, because by the help of God he prevailed over his enemies; but because, ungrateful and hard, he went down from the liberality of the Lord, he broke out into blasphemy, and from great became little, and from peaceful turbulent.
**“a choice and goodly man, and there was not among the children of Israel a goodlier person than he:”**
• according to the justice of this life
• THERE WAS NOT A GOODLIER. RABANUS. According to the justice of the present life.
• RABANUS. This pertains rather to Christ, of whom it is said: "Behold my servant, my elect, whom I have chosen"; and elsewhere: "Who among the sons of God shall be like to God?"
9.4:
**“And through the land of Salisa, and had not found them, they passed also through the land of Salim,”** — the city of Melchisedech
**“and they were not there: and through the land of Jemini,”** — that is, Benjamin
9.5:
**“And when they were come to the land of Suph”** — the great-grandfather of Samuel
**“Saul said to the servant that was with him: Come, let us return, lest perhaps my father forget”** — put out of mind
9.7:
**“And Saul said to his servant: Behold we will go: but what”** — Saul thought that he would not tell of the asses except for a price
**“shall we carry to the man of God? the bread is spent in our bags:”** — bags, or scrip
9.8:
**“OF A SICLE”** — A stater is a sicle, which has twenty obols, that is, ten denarii.
**“LET US GIVE”** — Although they resolved to give, we do not read that Samuel received it. Yet if he had received it, it would not be reckoned as the price of divination but as the stipend of a prophet.
9.9:
**“Now in time past, in Israel ... he spoke thus”** — NOW IN TIME PAST IN ISRAEL HE SPOKE THUS etc. As Bede says, these are not the words of the historian but of Esdras.
**“THE SEER”** — He is called a prophet because through the spirit he foreknows things to come.
9.11: **“And when they went up the ascent to the city,”** — THE ASCENT. A clivus is the winding ascent of a mountain.
9.16:
**“AND THOU SHALT ANOINT HIM TO BE RULER”** — Saul anointed signifies 'Christ' [that is, the anointed]; who himself too was called Christ; whence: "Why didst thou not fear to put out thy hand against the Lord's anointed?"
**“over my people Israel: and he shall save my people”** — that Christ may save his people from the power of the demons
**“out of the hand of the Philistines: for I have looked down upon my people,”** — at the coming of Christ
9.19: **“And Samuel answered Saul, saying: I am the seer, go up before me to the high place, that you may eat with me today, and I will let thee go in the morning: and tell thee all that is in thy heart.”** — ALL THAT IS IN [THY HEART]. RABANUS. The Hebrews hand down that it was in Saul's heart that he would be king, since he had seen in a vision that he was set on the top of a palm tree, which is the sign of one about to reign.
9.22:
**“Then Samuel taking Saul and his servant,”** — THEN [SAMUEL] TAKING etc. RABANUS. That Samuel led Saul to the high place and gave him refreshment signifies the prophets, calling the people of the Hebrews by their teaching to higher things, that, refreshed with spiritual knowledge, it may stand on the summit of the virtues and not slip back into vices.
**“THE PARLOUR”** — A dining room, [named] from the three couches of those reclining.
9.24: **“OF PURPOSE”** — That is, by forethought. It is given to be understood that they had already eaten, though not fully, because, the Lord having revealed that Saul would come, the banquet was put off.
9.27: **“AND AS THEY WERE GOING DOWN”** — They went down from the high place, that in some more secret place he might speak of the kingdom and anoint him.

10.1: **“TOOK A LITTLE VIAL”** — TOOK A LITTLE VIAL. A lenticula is a four-cornered earthen vessel having a hole in the side; by which the frailty of the kingdom is designated.
10.2: **“When thou shalt depart from me this day, thou shalt find two men by the sepulchre of Rachel in the borders of Benjamin to the south, leaping”** — for the sake of delight and exercise
10.3:
**“And when thou shalt depart from thence, and go farther on, and shalt come to the oak of Thabor, there shall meet thee three men going up”** — for the sake of prayer
**“to God to Bethel,”** — where Jacob set up the stone
10.5: **“After that thou shalt come to the hill of God”** — the hill of God is the place where the prophets dwelt
10.6: **“AND THOU SHALT PROPHESY”** — AND THOU SHALT PROPHESY. The Jews hand down that he prophesied of the world to come, of Gog and Magog, of the rewards of the just and the punishments of the wicked.
10.7: **“WHEN THEREFORE THESE SIGNS SHALL HAPPEN”** — WHEN THEREFORE THESE SIGNS SHALL HAPPEN. As if [to say]: by these signs thou wilt be able to know that God has willed thee to be king; therefore act royally in all things, because the Lord is with thee.
10.8:
**“And thou shalt go down before me to Galgal, (for I will come down to thee,) that thou mayest offer an oblation, and sacrifice victims of peace: seven days shalt thou wait,”**
• it is understood: for the consecration of thy kingdom. So the seven days were appointed not for waiting but for sacrificing
• SEVEN DAYS. It is understood: in the consecration of thy kingdom; as in the consecration of the priests victims were offered for seven days.
10.9: **“AND ALL THESE THINGS CAME TO PASS”** — AND ALL THESE THINGS CAME TO PASS. It signifies that all things which Moses and the prophets foretold came to pass for the Jews. And they, holding the books of the law and the prophets, seem to divine, since they are known to pronounce the future mysteries of Christ and the Church written in them.
10.12:
**“AND WHO IS HIS FATHER”** — AND WHO IS HIS FATHER. As if: who is greater than he in dignity and wisdom? He can therefore move among the prophets as a father and master.
**“AND WHO IS THEIR FATHER”** — That is, of the prophets: it is understood, but God?
**“MYSTICALLY”** — The elders of Israel, rejecting Samuel, asked a king for themselves; and the scribes with the Pharisees, rejecting Christ the true priest, cried out: "We have no king but Caesar." Whence Samuel is interpreted 'his name is God', Saul 'asked' or 'petition', because he was demanded by the people: Barabbas is understood. Cis: 'hard' or 'vomiting'. Abiel: my father God. For the Jews, hard and vomiting, in confessing God the Father deny the Son; but he who denies the Son denies also the Father who sent him. Saul, seeking his father's asses, was taken up into the kingdom; and the Saviour, 'sent' by the Father 'to the sheep that were lost of the house of Israel', was set up as king over all the people. For the asses are the same as the sheep. Saul received the shoulder, and Christ the princedom. Saul was anointed by Samuel, and the Only-begotten was anointed by the Father with spiritual anointing. Saul stood above [the people] from the shoulder, because Christ our head is above us.
10.16: **“And Saul said to his uncle: He told us that the asses were found. But of the matter of the kingdom he told him not”** — lest he should seem to boast, or lest he should beget envy against himself
10.25: **“And Samuel told the people the law of the kingdom,”** — what the king ought to exact from the people, what the people ought to give the king

11.1: **“And it came to pass about a month after this that Naas, the Ammonite came up, and began to fight against Jabes Galaad.”** — NAAS, JABES GALAAD. Jabes: sense; Galaad: heap of testimony. Naas, that is, the serpent, namely the devil, goes up against the sense instructed by the testimonies of Scripture.
11.2:
**“AND NAAS ANSWERED THEM”** — AND NAAS ANSWERED THEM. The war of Naas signifies the war of the heretics against the Church. Naas is interpreted serpent; Ammon: pressing, or straitening, or people of sorrow; Jabes: dried up; Galaad: heap of testimony. Naas, then, signifies the old serpent, who is the prince of the Ammonites, that is, of the heretics. For this is the people of sorrow, which has not the joy of the Holy Ghost; which arranges a covenant with the people of the Church, that it may pluck out the right eyes, namely the sight of the sound and orthodox faith. It leaves the left eye, that they may perceive only perverse things. But the mind of the faithful, dried from the filth of vices, gathers a heap of testimony, that is, the sentences of holy Scripture, by which it may manfully resist the enemy.
**“On this condition will I make a covenant with you, that I may pluck out all your right eyes,”**
• the understanding of faith
• for the use of war, that they might not see the enemy with the left eye, hidden under the shield
11.3:
**“And the ancients of Jabes said to him:”** — dried up
**“Allow us seven days, that we may send messengers”** — namely the teachers of the Church, who ought to set the shield of faith against the enemies
11.8:
**“And he numbered them in Bezec:”** — AND HE NUMBERED THEM IN BEZEC. RABANUS. In the city Bezec, namely of Adonibezec. To this day two villages are called Bezec, at the seventh milestone from Neapolis for those going down to Scythopolis. Bezec is interpreted 'want', and signifies the fewness of the elect. Whence: "Many are called, but few chosen." Our king too, Christ, who is priest and prophet, directing the battle line against the enemies, chooses soldiers from both peoples, distinguished by faith in the Trinity and by perfection; he puts the enemies to flight and smites them with the sword of the spirit from the morning of dawning faith, until the Church spreads the light of knowledge and the ardour of charity through the whole world.
**“and there were of the children of Israel three hundred thousand: and of the men”** — distinguished by faith in the Trinity
**“of Juda thirty thousand.”** — illustrious by faith in the Trinity and knowledge of the law
11.9:
**“And they said to the messengers that came: Thus shall you say to the men of Jabes Galaad: Tomorrow,”** — in the future
**“when the sun shall be hot, you shall have relief.”** — of justice
11.11:
**“And it came to pass, when the morrow was come that Saul put the people in companies: and he came into the midst of the camp in the morning watch,”** — at the beginning of brightening faith
**“and he slew the Ammonites until the day grew hot, and the rest were scattered”** — THE REST WERE SCATTERED. Because the congregation of the wicked, not joined by the unity of charity and faith, is separated by mutual dissension. Whence: "Thy enemies, O Lord, shall perish, and shall be scattered."

12.3: **“Speak of me before the Lord, and before his anointed”** — Saul
12.5:
**“And he said to them: The Lord is witness against you, and his anointed is witness this day, that you have not found in my hand”** — in deed
**“any thing.”** — of evil
12.11:
**“And the Lord sent Jerobaal,”** — who is also Gedeon: fear of a man
**“and Badan,”**
• that is, Samson, the strongest
• chief, or in judgment
**“and Barac,”** — lightning, or thunderbolt
**“Jephte,”** — opening, or opened, or an opening
**“and Samuel,”** — named, or asked of God
12.17:
**“HARVEST”** — HARVEST. RABANUS. The gathering, namely, of the Gentile people to the faith.
**“THUNDER”** — THUNDER. That is, thunders and rains; it is not usual in Judea for it to rain in the summer season.
12.18:
**“And Samuel cried unto the Lord,”** — at the coming of Christ
**“and the Lord sent”** — namely Christ
**“thunder”** — persuasive preaching
**“and rain”** — the words of the gospel or of the law
12.20: **“And Samuel said to the people: Fear not, you have done all this evil: but yet depart not”** — but follow the Lord as your leader
12.21: **“And turn not aside after vain things”** — the desires of the world
12.23:
**“And far from me be this sin against the Lord, that I should cease to pray for you,”** — although you have offended me and God
**“and I will teach you the good and right way.”** — Christ, the Word of God
12.24:
**“Therefore fear the Lord,”** — as sons
**“and serve him in truth and with your whole heart,”** — not of necessity

13.1:
**“Saul was a child of one year”**
• that is, humble, as a little one and a suckling
• SAUL WAS A CHILD OF ONE YEAR. RABANUS. He speaks by anticipation of Isboseth the son of Saul, of whom it is said in what follows: "Isboseth was forty years old when he began to reign over Israel, and he reigned two years." But if the whole time in which Samuel and Saul reigned is reckoned from the death of Heli, forty years are found up to the death of Saul. When, then, Saul began to reign, he had a son of one year, who after his father's death reigned two years in Israel, and, slain by robbers, left the kingdom to David.
• The time of Samuel is joined with the time and reign of Saul. For the historians could not count him in the number of the judges, since he was a prophet and had not judged the people the whole time of his life, as the others had.
**“when he began to reign, and he reigned two years over Israel.”** — justly, namely, and gently; for afterwards he was more a tyrant than a king
13.2:
**“And Saul chose him three thousand men of Israel: and two thousand were with Saul in Machmas,”** — to this day a large village is shown in the borders of Aelia, distant from it eight miles, near the town of Rama, and it keeps its ancient name; and it is interpreted 'humility'
**“GABAA”** — GABAA. It is the city of Phinees the son of Eleazar, where Eleazar himself was buried, and it is interpreted 'hill of the cousin'. Fittingly were three thousand Israelites chosen to fight against the Philistines. For they alone are fit to fight against the enemies of the Church who have perfect faith in the Trinity, in which they may stand above their enemies.
**“and in mount Bethel: and a thousand with Jonathan in Gabaa of Benjamin,”** — The Philistines are the heretics, who, conspiring with equal consent against the Church, try to lay it waste; to whom some, having forsworn the faith, join themselves, others, while they fear to confess the faith openly, lie hid as it were in caves. The various sects, bound together by one bond of impiety, run about to deceive. The horsemen are those swollen with power who help the heretics. The common people as the sand: the multitude gathered by heretical persuasion. The men remaining with [unclear in the edition: "lavi"]: the catholics cleaving firmly to Christ.
13.5:
**“The Philistines also were assembled to fight against Israel, thirty thousand chariots, and six thousand”** — elsewhere: six hundred
**“horsemen, and a multitude of people besides, like the sand on the sea shore for number. And going up they camped in Machmas”** — humility, or handling
**“at the east of Bethaven.”** — house of idolatry, or useless house
13.6: **“And when the men of Israel saw that they were straitened, (for the people were distressed,) they hid themselves in caves, and in thickets, and in rocks, and in dens, and in pits.”** — THEY HID THEMSELVES etc. RABANUS. Certain Israelites, namely, having hidden themselves, who had left Saul and the people that was with him, some part of those who are called 'Hebrews', terrified with fear, fell away from Saul and from the men who were with him, and went down into the camp of the Philistines; whence in what follows: But the Hebrews also that had been with the Philistines yesterday and the day before, and had gone up with them in the camp, returned to be with Israel, who were with Saul and Jonathan. All the Israelites also who had hidden themselves in mount Ephraim, hearing that the Philistines had fled, joined themselves with their own in the battle.
13.13:
**“And Samuel said to Saul: Thou hast done foolishly, and hast not kept”** — Samuel by the Lord's command had bidden him wait for him until he should come to anoint him king, and [that] victims [were] to be offered for seven days, as in the consecration of a priest; and because he did not keep this he is rightly rebuked
**“THOU HAST DONE FOOLISHLY”** — THOU HAST DONE FOOLISHLY. RABANUS. It seems to some that Saul sacrificed blamelessly, because Samuel, though waited for according to the agreement, did not come. But he who inquires diligently finds that he was justly blamed and guilty of disobedience. Among the Hebrews it is divided thus: "And thou shalt go down before me to Galgal; for I will come down to thee." Then is added: 'To offer oblations and sacrifice victims of peace, seven days shalt thou wait until I come to thee and show thee what thou art to do.' Samuel, then, did not command that he be waited for seven days, but wished to be waited for seven days to offer oblations and sacrifice victims of peace; which Saul did not do, and therefore he is deservedly blamed and accused of folly.
**“the commandments of the Lord thy God, which he commanded thee. And if thou hadst not done thus,”** — AND IF THOU HADST NOT DONE THUS etc. AUGUSTINE. It is not to be taken as if the Lord had prepared Saul to reign for ever and then would not keep this for him when he sinned. For he knew that he would sin; but he had prepared his kingdom, in which there should be a figure of the eternal kingdom. Whence he added: And now thy kingdom shall not stand for thee. What was signified in him, then, stood and will stand; but it will not stand for him, because he was not to reign for ever, nor his offspring, so that at least through his posterity, succeeding one another, what was said might seem to be fulfilled: For ever.
13.14:
**“But thy kingdom”** — BUT THY KINGDOM etc. The rejection of Saul: the taking away of the kingdom of the Jews. David, surviving him: Christ, who would succeed to the people of the Jews.
**“shall not continue. The Lord hath sought him a man”** — The man signifies David, or the Mediator of the New Testament himself, who was figured in the chrism with which David and his offspring were anointed.
**“according to his own heart: and him hath the Lord commanded to be prince over his people, because thou hast not observed that which the Lord commanded.”** — He sought for himself: not as not knowing where he is, but through a man he speaks after the manner of men, because by so speaking he seeks us. For not only to God the Father but to his Only-begotten himself, "who came to seek that which was lost," we were already so known that "we were chosen in him before the foundation of the world." He will seek for himself, then, it says: [that is,] he will have as his own. Whence in the Latin tongue this verb takes a preposition and is said acquirit, which is clear enough. Even without the preposition quaerere is understood as acquirere, from which gains are called quaestus.
13.19:
**“Now there was no smith to be found in all the land of Israel,”** — NOW THERE WAS NO SMITH etc. The devil too, through pagans, through heretics, and through false Christians, strives to prevent there being teachers in the Church who may make spiritual arms and give them to us for fighting. For the pagans forbade Christians to be instructed in the liberal arts. The heretics too persuaded princes that the catholic defenders of the Church should be driven into exile, that they might more easily seduce the desolate people. Now too the old enemy turns prelates away from diligence in learning, that he may more easily deceive both them and those under them. The devil is bound by a double guilt: pride, by which he fell, and envy, by which he strives to cast others down. And Philistines is interpreted 'double ruin', Hebrews 'passing over'. "For we have not here a lasting city" etc.
**“for the Philistines had taken this precaution,”** — that they might the more easily overcome
**“lest the Hebrews should make them swords”** — with which they might defend themselves
13.20: **“So all Israel went down to the Philistines, to sharpen every man his ploughshare”** — the ploughshare: the controversy of the heretics sharpens the sense of the good

14.3: **“JONATHAN”** — Gift of the dove. These are they who are filled with the gift of the Holy Ghost, through whom the Lord scatters the assemblies of the heretics and turns them to flight. His armourbearer: the disciples of the spiritual, who take their journey not by the plains but by the steeps; because the priests cannot go against the enemies unless, walking by the narrow way between both Testaments, and between prosperity and adversity, as between two rocks on the right and the left, they go forward and climb with the whole effort of the mind to the heights of contemplation. Jonathan does not go over to the enemies unless provoked, because the catholics do not stir up contention against the heretics unless they are first provoked to the combat. Jonathan, then, lays the enemies low in the field of tillage, and the teachers overcome the heretics in meditation on Scripture.
14.4:
**“Now there were between the ascents, by which Jonathan sought to go over to the garrison of the Philistines, rocks standing up on both sides, and steep cliffs like teeth on the one side, and on the other, the name of the one was Boses,”** — flourishing
**“and the name of the other was Sene:”** — straitening him
14.24: **“And the men of Israel were joined together that day; and Saul adjured the people, saying: Cursed be the man that shall eat food”** — Saul proclaimed a fast, lest, if they ate, the vengeance on the enemies should be delayed
14.27:
**“But Jonathan”** — BUT JONATHAN. The gift of the dove: here he signifies those who, having received the grace of the Holy Ghost, prepare to spurn the allurements of the world. For he cannot fight manfully against the spiritual Allophyli, that is, the demons, who does not know how to turn away from the sweetness of the world.
**“had not heard when his father adjured the people: and he put forth the end of the rod, which he had in his hand, and dipt it in a honeycomb: and he carried his hand to his mouth, and his eyes were enlightened.”** — beaten back before by the excessive heat and the battle and the fasting
**“WERE ENLIGHTENED”** — WERE ENLIGHTENED. AUGUSTINE. Not for seeing, for he saw before, but for discerning, because he had touched what was forbidden; whence he was confounded. By which deed everyone who wishes to fight for God is warned to despise all the allurements of pleasures: 'For the lips of a harlot drop honey', that is, carnal pleasure brings forth delight. Of which Jonathan is mystically thought to have tasted, and, caught by the lot, he was scarcely freed by the prayers of the people. Whence it is plain that he who is overcome by the pleasure of the world needs the suffrages of the saints and the prayers of the brethren.
14.31: **“So they smote that day the Philistines from Machmas to Aialon.”** — elsewhere: Haylon
14.33:
**“And they told Saul that the people had sinned against the Lord, eating with the blood.”** — because, having slain the beasts, they cooked and ate the flesh not yet well cleansed of blood
**“THE PEOPLE HAD SINNED AGAINST THE LORD, EATING WITH THE BLOOD”** — They are said to have sinned against the Lord and to have eaten with the blood because, when the victims were slain, they did not offer the fat and the blood to the priests at the sanctuary according to the law, though they had the sanctuary with them. For when the place of the sanctuary was far off, the blood was commanded to be poured on the ground, namely of those victims which they prepared for their own eating. But when the sanctuary was present, it was poured on the altar of the Lord. Whence in Deuteronomy: "Thou shalt pour the blood of thy victims on the altar: and the flesh thou thyself shalt eat." This the people did not do; therefore it is said: they sinned against the Lord and ate with the blood.
14.34:
**“SLAY THEM UPON”** — SLAY THEM UPON. That the blood may flow to the ground. Or he ate with the blood because they ate before the evening sacrifice, which after a slaughter it was the custom to make before food. Or they sinned in this, as some hold: that they did not bring their victims to the door of the tabernacle.
**“AND SLEW THEM”** — AND SLEW THEM. The slaying of the animals is baptism, in which the old man dies. The great stone upon which the slaying was done is faith, without which the old man does not die. The slaughtering on the ground is the baptism of the heretics, whose blood they eat when they gather to themselves those washed without purification of sins. These animals taken from the Philistines signify either those brought back from the heretics or those converted from the Gentile world: the former the unskilled rebaptize, the latter they baptize otherwise than the Church hands down. Christ, as Saul, commanded that these, as oxen and sheep, be slain in his faith as upon a great stone, that is, that [men] of different kinds be baptized.
14.35:
**“And Saul built an altar to the Lord”** — that he might intercede for the sin of the people
**“AND HE THEN FIRST BEGAN TO BUILD AN ALTAR TO THE LORD”** — Because [he did it] obediently and rightly. But above, when he was rebuked by Samuel, he is not said to have built [an altar] to the Lord, because he built it disobediently.
14.38: **“And Saul said: Bring hither all the corners”** — BRING HITHER ALL THE CORNERS etc. He calls the princes the corners of the people, to whom the peoples on either side clung as walls to corners.
14.44: **“MAY GOD DO SO AND SO TO ME”** — An oath of the Hebrews, which is understood by the contrary. As if he should say: let the evil that is due to thee be imputed [to me] if I do not kill thee.
14.45: **“And the people said to Saul: Shall Jonathan then die, who hath wrought this great salvation in Israel?”** — WHO HATH WROUGHT [THIS GREAT] SALVATION etc. Good deeds done in the past profit much; for unless his past good deeds had helped Jonathan, he would not have escaped the evils hanging over him. For God is not unjust, that he should forget good deeds.

15.3: **“Now therefore go, and smite Amalec, and utterly destroy all that he hath: spare him not, nor covet any thing that is his: but slay both man and woman, child and suckling, ox and sheep, camel and ass.”** — OX AND SHEEP etc. The Lord commands the beasts of Amalec to be destroyed for this reason: that there be no memory of him even in his beasts. For the Lord had said that he would blot out the memory of Amalec from under heaven; and because his memory was not wholly blotted out, Saul sinned by disobedience. Of Amalec it is said in Deuteronomy that 'he slew the hindmost of the people of God, who sat down weary'. The Hebrews explain the weary as those unclean according to the law, remaining outside the camp; whose foreskins, as they hand down, they cut off and threw toward heaven in mockery of God.
15.6: **“SAUL SAID TO THE CINITE”** — SAUL SAID TO THE CINITE. The Cinite is Jethro himself, the kinsman of Moses, from whom were the Cinites who dwelt with Amalec. For they were kindred and had an inheritance in his land. The Cinite showed kindness to the children of Israel because he cherished Moses in the land of Madian and gave him counsel how he should govern the multitude of the people.
15.7:
**“And Saul smote Amalec”** — a brutish nation, a licking people
**“from Hevila,”** — grieving, bringing forth, stupid, or from the beginning
**“until thou comest to Sur,”** — a strong wall, containing, directed, straitness, bitterness, or continence
15.8: **“And he took Agag”** — house, or roof, or festively solemn
15.9: **“And Saul and the people spared Agag”** — to display the glory of his triumph
15.11: **“It repenteth me”** — IT REPENTETH ME etc. GREGORY. By this rebuke the pride of the king is cast down, which every prelate can turn to his own correction. When Saul esteemed himself little in his own eyes, he was made head in the tribes of Israel. As if [to say]: when thou didst behold thyself little, I made thee great above the rest; but because thou beholdest thyself great, thou art esteemed little by me. Whereas David, when he despised the power of his kingdom by dancing before the ark of the Lord, said: "I will play, and I will make myself meaner than I have done: and I will be little in my own eyes." If, then, the saints, even when they do mighty things, think meanly of themselves, what will they say who swell without works of virtue? But any works whatever are nothing unless they are seasoned with humility. A wonderful action done with elation does not lift up but weighs down. For he who gathers virtues without humility carries dust in the wind; whence, while he is seen to carry something, he is the worse blinded. Let us not, then, look at those above whom we already are, but at those below whom we still are, that we may always ascend to greater things out of humility.
15.12: **“And when Samuel rose early, to go to Saul in the morning, it was told Samuel, that Saul was come to Carmel, and had erected for himself a triumphant arch”** — an arch where he might describe the triumph of his glory
15.17:
**“WHEN THOU WAST A LITTLE ONE”** — WHEN THOU WAST A LITTLE ONE. GREGORY. He is little in his own eyes who, while he considers himself, weighs himself unequal to the merits of others. For he sees himself great who stretches himself above the merits of others. But Saul did not abide in the good he had begun, because he swelled with the pride of power. But David, always thinking humbly of himself, and setting himself after the same Saul by comparison, when he found a chance of striking him spared him, and humbly prostrated himself before the raging adversary, saying: "Whom dost thou pursue, O king of Israel, whom dost thou pursue? A dead dog and a living flea." Yet he had already been anointed king; he had already learned that, Saul being rejected, he was kept for the helm of the kingdom. Let those learn, then, how they ought to humble themselves to their neighbours who do not yet know in what place they are held with God, if the elect humble themselves to those whom they know they are already set before. And this is proper to the elect: to think of themselves below what they are. Whence: "If I was not humbly minded, but exalted my soul." And elsewhere: "Whosoever is a little one, let him come to me" etc. For he who does not think himself humble does not lay hold of the wisdom of God.
**“A LITTLE ONE”** — Saul at first saw himself little; but lifted up by power he no longer saw himself little; preferring himself by comparison with the rest, because he could do more, he esteemed himself great above all. But when little with himself, he was great with God; when great with himself, he was little with God. Whence: 'Have they made thee ruler? Be not lifted up, but be among them as one of them.'
15.20: **“And Saul said to Samuel: Yea I have hearkened to the voice of the Lord”** — he answered proudly; he added evil to evil, because he strove to defend his fault, and thereby heaped it up
15.22: **“And Samuel said: Doth the Lord desire holocausts and victims, and not rather that the voice of the Lord should be obeyed? For obedience is better than sacrifices”** — OBEDIENCE IS BETTER etc. Because by victims another's flesh, but by obedience one's own will, is slain. So much the sooner, then, does each one appease God, the more he immolates himself with the sword of the precept, the pride of his own choice being repressed. And disobedience is called the sin of witchcraft, that the greatness of the virtue of obedience may be shown from the contrary. For if to resist is as the sin of witchcraft, and to refuse to obey as the crime of idolatry, obedience alone is that which possesses the merit of faith, without which anyone is convicted of unbelief. Whence Solomon: "An obedient man shall speak of victory." For while we humbly submit to another's voice, we overcome ourselves in the heart. But it is to be known that evil is never to be done through obedience; but sometimes the good which is being done ought to be left off. For the tree in paradise which God forbade to be touched was not evil; but that man, well created, might grow through the merit of obedience, it was fitting that he should forbid him even from a good thing. It is to be noted also what is said there: Of every tree of paradise thou shalt eat etc. For he who forbids those under him one good thing must grant many, lest the mind, repelled from all, perish as it were fasting. It is to be known also that obedience is sometimes nothing if it has something of its own; but sometimes it is very small if it has nothing of its own. For when a higher place is commanded, he empties the virtue of obedience for himself who still pants for it with his own desire. But when reproaches or insults are commanded, unless the mind desires this of itself, it lessens for itself the merit of obedience, because it comes down to this unwillingly. Hence Moses humbly refuses the princedom of the people; but Paul boldly says: "For I am ready not only to be bound, but to die also in Jerusalem."
15.26: **“And Samuel said to Saul: I will not return with thee”** — I WILL NOT RETURN WITH THEE etc. Another edition: I will not return with thee, says Samuel, because thou hast despised the word of the Lord, and the Lord hath despised thee, that thou be not king over Israel. And Samuel turned his face to go away, and Saul took hold of the hem of his double cloak and tore it. And Samuel said to him: The Lord hath torn the kingdom of Israel from thy hand this day, and will give it to thy neighbour, good above thee; and Israel shall be divided in two, and he will not be turned nor will he repent; for he is not as a man that he should repent; [a man] threatens and does not abide [by it].
15.27:
**“BUT HE LAID HOLD UPON THE SKIRT OF HIS MANTLE, AND IT RENT”** — BUT HE LAID HOLD UPON THE SKIRT OF HIS MANTLE, AND IT RENT. As in the passion of the Lord the high priest rent his garment, so too Saul [rent] the garment of the prophet. For the rending done by both powers, namely the royal and the priestly, shows that the kingdom and priesthood of the Jews could not stand, because they would not receive the true king and priest, that is, Christ.
**“AUGUSTINE”** — He to whom he said: The Lord despiseth thee, that thou be not king over Israel, and: The Lord hath rent the kingdom of Israel from thy hand this day, reigned forty years, namely as long as David too reigned; and he heard this in the first time of his reign. We understand, then, that it was said because none of his stock was to reign; and we look to the stock of David, from whom Christ was born according to the flesh. Saul is also a figure of the people of Israel, which was to lose the kingdom to Christ, who would reign spiritually through the New Testament; of whom it is said: "He will give it to thy neighbour, good" above thee, that is, better; or above thee because he is good; whence: Until I make thy enemies thy footstool, among whom is Israel too. From whom, as his persecutor, Christ took away the kingdom, although there was there also an Israel in which there was no guile, as it were the wheat of that chaff. For thence were the apostles, thence the martyrs, of whom the first was Stephen; thence the Churches magnifying God. Whence follows: and Israel shall be divided in two: namely into Israel hostile to Christ and Israel cleaving to Christ; into Israel belonging to the handmaid and Israel belonging to the free woman. These two were at first together, until the barren, made fruitful by grace, should cry: "Cast out the bondwoman and her son." Because of the sin of Solomon, indeed, in the reign of his son Roboam, Israel was divided in two, until that whole nation was overthrown by the Chaldeans. But what has this to do with Saul, since it should rather have been threatened to David himself, whose son Solomon was? Lastly, the Hebrew nation is not divided among itself, but scattered over the lands in the same error. But the division which God threatened, under the person of Saul, who bore the figure of that kingdom and people, to the same kingdom and people, is signified to be eternal and unchangeable by what is added: And he will not be turned, nor will he repent; for he is not as a man that he should repent; [a man] threatens and does not abide. For where it is read that he repents, a change of things is signified, the divine foreknowledge remaining unchangeably; where, then, he is said not to repent, it is understood that he does not change. For whoever have passed over or will pass over to Christ were not of them according to the foreknowledge of God, [though they were] according to the one and same nature of the human race.
15.28:
**“HATH RENT”** — HATH RENT. Although afterwards he reigned forty years; but then he merited that it be rent from his stock and handed to a better, that is, David; and from Saul, that is, the Jews, the kingdom is taken away and handed to Christ.
**“And Samuel said to him: [The Lord] hath rent”** — He corrects the king for disobedience, because he did not fulfil the command of the Lord, and foretells the loss of the kingdom. And deservedly does he lose the kingdom who does not know how to hold it; but he rules well who obeys his superior and sets his authority before those beneath him.
**“the kingdom of Israel from thee this day, and hath given it to thy neighbour”** — Christ, who is of the Jews according to the flesh, as Saul also was
15.29:
**“But the triumpher”** — the Lord, to whom every victory is ascribed
**“in Israel will not spare, and will not be moved to repentance:”** — because he is unchangeable and judges all things according to justice and truth
15.33: **“And Samuel said: As thy sword hath made women childless, so shall thy mother be childless among women. And Samuel hewed him in pieces before the Lord in Galgal.”** — AND [SAMUEL] HEWED HIM IN PIECES etc. When some read in the Scriptures that the saints spared none of the enemies, they call them cruel, and do not understand the mysteries overshadowed in these words: namely that, fighting against vices, we should leave none at all. For if we spare [any], it will be reckoned to us as a fault, as to Saul, who kept the king of Amalec alive. But the saints, as Samuel, leave no sin unpunished.
15.35: **“And Samuel saw Saul no more”** — it is understood: in the attire of one reigning

16.3: **“And thou shalt call Isai to the sacrifice, and I will shew thee what thou art to do, and thou shalt anoint him whom I shall shew to thee.”** — Christ was anointed with the oil of gladness above his fellows
16.5:
**“And he said: It is peaceable: I am come to offer sacrifice to the Lord, be ye sanctified,”** — that is, wash your garments
**“and come with me”** — that I may sacrifice
**“And he sanctified Isai”** — that is, he made them cleanse themselves
16.7: **“And the Lord said to Samuel: Look not on his countenance, nor on the height of his stature: because I have rejected him, nor [do I judge] according to the look”** — LOOK NOT etc. NOR ACCORDING TO THE LOOK etc. The elder sons of Isai being rejected, the least is chosen for the kingdom; because, the Jewish priesthood and the kingdom of the former people being spurned, Christ, the head of the lesser people, was made king and priest.
16.10: **“Isai therefore brought his seven sons before Samuel: and Samuel said to Isai: The Lord hath not chosen any one of these.”** — this is the sabbath-keeping nation, rejected
16.11: **“A YOUNG ONE, WHO KEEPETH THE SHEEP”** — From the care of cattle David was made king of men; but Christ was transferred from the sheepfold of the Jewish people to the kingdom of the Gentiles.
16.12:
**“He sent therefore and brought him. Now he was ruddy and beautiful to behold,”**
• "Who is this that cometh from Edom, with dyed garments from Bosra?"
• "Thou art beautiful above the sons of men"
**“and of a comely face. And the Lord said: Arise, and anoint him”** — "God, thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows"
16.13:
**“Then Samuel took the horn of oil, and anointed him in the midst of his brethren: and the spirit of the Lord came”** — Saul being rejected
**“upon David”** — Christ, who is "strong of hand" (because he overcame the devil and the world) "and desirable". Whence: "The desired of all nations shall come"
16.15:
**“And the servants of Saul said to him:”** — all the subjects of the king are called servants or boys; only the counsellors are called friends
**“Behold now an evil spirit from God troubleth thee.”** — AN EVIL SPIRIT OF THE LORD etc. ISIDORE. So too was called the sleep of the Lord, which came upon the soldiers of Saul when David took away the spear and the cup from the head of the sleeper: not that the Lord himself slept, but because it had been poured in by his will, that no one might perceive the presence of David. The evil spirit of God, then, is so called, that is, the minister of God, to do in Saul what the judge of all decreed that he should suffer.
16.16: **“SKILFUL IN PLAYING ON THE HARP”** — SKILFUL IN PLAYING ON THE HARP. David was learned in the songs of music. The reasonable and measured concord of different sounds signifies the unity of the Church, which resounds daily in various modes. David restrained the evil spirit with his harp: not that there was such power in the harp, but in the figure of the cross of Christ, which was borne by the wood and the stretching of the strings, which even then put the demons to flight. But tropologically we are instructed by this deed to have compassion on our neighbour. For often a proud rich man is to be appeased by the soothing of exhortation; because often hard wounds are softened by light fomentations, and the fury of the mad is brought back to health when the physician soothes them. David, taking up his harp, calmed the madness of Saul. By Saul the powerful, by David the life of the saints is signified. When, then, Saul is seized by the unclean spirit, his madness is tempered by David's singing; because, when the sense of the powerful is turned to fury through elation, it is fitting that it be called back to health of mind by the calmness of our speech, as by the sweetness of the harp.
16.23: **“So whensoever the evil spirit from the Lord was upon Saul, David took his harp, and played with his hand, and Saul was refreshed,”** — SAUL WAS REFRESHED. For before he was vexed by the demon even to suffocation. Boethius relates that a certain philosopher by the touch of the harp drove a demon from a possessed body.

17.1:
**“Now the Philistines gathering together their troops to battle, assembled at Socho”** — a town in the tribe of Juda, and it is interpreted branch, or humility, or temptation
**“AZECA”** — AZECA. It is a city of the Chanaanites in the tribe of Juda, as far as which Josue smote the five kings. And today a town between Eleutheropolis and Aelia is called Azeca, which is interpreted 'strength' and 'snare'.
**“in the borders of Dommim.”** — or: Duina
**“DUINA OR DOMMIM”** — It is a village in the tribe of Juda in the borders of Eleutheropolis, distant from it twenty-seven miles. Duina is interpreted 'silence' or 'joy'.
17.2:
**“And Saul and the children of Israel being gathered together came to the valley of Terebinth”** — the terebinth is a tree from which flows a most excellent tear of resin; whence by medicinal skill it glues together things that are loosened.
**“OF TEREBINTH”** — The terebinth is in Sichem, near Neapolis, under which Jacob hid the idols.
17.4:
**“And there went out a man baseborn”** — because born of a giant father and a Gethite mother
**“BASEBORN”** — Because he was born of an ignoble father but a noble mother.
17.5: **“And he had a helmet of brass upon his head, and he was clothed with a coat of mail with scales”** — joined and linked together with hooks
17.6: **“And he had greaves of brass”** — that is, of iron
17.8: **“And standing he cried out to the bands”** — troops
17.12:
**“Now David was the son of that Ephrathite of Bethlehem Juda before mentioned, whose name was Isai, who had eight sons,”**
• EIGHT SONS. In Paralipomenon only seven are mentioned; but he had brought up and nourished as a son Nathan the prophet, the son of Samaa. Before Samuel too seven sons of Isai are said to have been brought, and the eighth to be in the pastures. Among those brought was Nathan, who is also Jonathan, of whom it is said in the last part of Samuel: "And Jonathan the son of Samaa the brother of David slew him." And it is to be noted that wherever the prophet is named, Nathan is written, not Jonathan.
• Some suppose that Jonathan, the son of David's brother, is Nathan the prophet; but it is false, because this Jonathan gave counsel to Amnon to lie with his sister, which did not become a prophet. ISIDORE too says that Nathan the prophet was of the Gabaonites.
17.14: **“But David was the youngest. So the three”** — BUT DAVID WAS THE YOUNGEST, and the eighth, who is chosen for the kingdom: this is Christ, who "emptied himself, taking the form of a servant"; because also through the glory of the resurrection he obtained the kingdom among the Gentiles.
17.16:
**“Now the Philistine came out”**
• the devil
• falling by drink
**“morning”** — by prosperity
**“and evening,”** — by adversity
**“and presented himself forty days.”** — the whole time of the present life, in which we sin against the decalogue through the four elements
17.17: **“And Isai said to David his son: Take for thy brethren an ephi of frumenty”** — it is a measure of three bushels
17.21: **“For Israel had put themselves in array, and the Philistines who stood against them were prepared.”** — FOR [ISRAEL] HAD PUT [THEMSELVES] IN ARRAY etc. The fight of the Philistines against Israel can be taken as the fight of the demons against the Church. And Goliath signifies the pride of the devil, which David, that is, Christ, laid low in single combat, and rescued the people of God. He slew the lion and the bear: namely the devil and Antichrist, the one now lying in wait secretly, the other afterwards raging openly. Pride provoked humility, the devil Christ. David received arms of war, which because of his age and small stature he could not carry, and cast them off. He took five stones from the river and put them in the shepherd's vessel. Armed with these he conquered. So Christ, in the time of the revelation of the New Testament, to insinuate and commend grace, laid aside the bodily sacraments of the law, which were not imposed on the Gentiles, which we read in the old law and do not observe, but understand to have been sent before and set for some signification: these he laid aside as burdens of the law, and he took the law itself. For the five stones signify the five books of Moses. He took five stones from the river, that is, from this world; for the mortal world flows away. The stones were, as it were, in the river among the first people; there they lay idle and profited nothing. The river passed over them; but David took grace, that the law might be useful, which cannot be fulfilled without grace. "For love is the fulfilling of the law." Because, then, grace makes the law to be fulfilled: for grace is signified by milk. For this is what is free in the flesh, where the mother seeks not to receive but to give; she gives freely and is saddened if there be lacking one to receive. David showed that the law cannot work without grace when, wishing to join those five stones, by which the law in five books is signified, to grace, he put them in the shepherd's vessel in which milk used to be drawn. Armed with these he went forth against the proud one. He took one stone and cast one: he struck him in the forehead, and he fell, [struck] in that place of the body where he did not have the sign of Christ. He took five, he sent one: five books were chosen, but unity conquers. "Love, then, is the fulfilling of the law," as the Apostle says: Supporting one another in charity, careful to keep the unity of the spirit in the bond of peace. When he had laid him low, he took away his sword and cut off his head. Christ slew the devil with his own members, when the magi believed, whom he held in his hand and by whom he slaughtered others, turning their tongues against the devil; and so Goliath's head is cut off with his own sword.
17.23:
**“And as he talked with them, that baseborn man whose name was Goliath shewed himself coming up,”** — revealed, transfigured, or migrating
**“the Philistine, of Geth, from the camp of the Philistines: and he spoke according to the same words, and David heard them.”** — Christ
17.25:
**“And some one of Israel said:”** — the saints seeing God
**“Have you seen this man that is come up?”** — in pride
17.26:
**“And David spoke to the men that stood by him, saying: What shall be given to the man that shall kill this Philistine, and shall take away the reproach from Israel? for who is this uncircumcised Philistine,”** — unclean
**“that he should defy the armies of the living God?”** — the saints fighting for God
17.28: **“I KNOW THY PRIDE”** — I KNOW THY PRIDE. He thought there was swelling in him because of Samuel's anointing, as though he had taken boldness from it; and he feared lest, if he engaged with the Philistine, he should be killed. Whence he adds: thou art come down to see the battle; that is, in this thou appearest proud, that though thou hast no custom of fighting, thou inquirest into the deeds of battle as a soldier.
17.29:
**“And David said:”** — understand: worthy of rebuke
**“IS THERE NOT CAUSE TO SPEAK”** — IS THERE NOT CAUSE TO SPEAK. As if he should say: there is, because it is not a wish to fight, but that I may know what I did not know. Yet he had taken boldness from this, that he had received the Holy Ghost, having experienced God's help in the lion and the bear; and therefore he boldly offered himself for single combat, not so much desirous of victory as an avenger of the blasphemies against God and the injuries to the people.
17.34:
**“And David said to Saul: Thy servant kept his father's sheep, and there came a lion,”** — the devil
**“or a bear,”** — Antichrist
**“and took a ram”** — any prelate
**“out of the midst of the flock:”** — of the Lord's [flock]
17.37: **“And David said: The Lord who delivered me out of the paw of the lion”** — power
17.39: **“And David having girded his sword upon his armour, began to try if he could walk in armour: for he was not accustomed to it. And David said to Saul: I cannot go thus, for I am not used to it. And he laid them off,”** — the sacraments of the law, as burdensome
17.40:
**“And he took his staff, which he had always in his hands: and chose him five”** — the law of Moses, written in five books
**“smooth stones out of the brook”** — he joined it, namely, to grace, which is signified by the milk that is drawn in the shepherd's vessel
17.41:
**“And the Philistine came on, and drew nigh against David, and his armourbearer before him.”**
• AND THE PHILISTINE CAME ON etc. AGAINST DAVID etc. Allegorically: the Philistines are the demons; Goliath is their head, who before the coming of the true David could not be overcome. Geth, the city of Goliath, is interpreted winepress: this is the world, or hell, in which, as in a winepress, he will trample those bound by sins; who, having left the heavenly rest, as it were of the seventh [day], fell into this world made in six days. The height of Goliath is the pride of the devil, through which he obtained princedom over the children of pride, lifting himself up like a palm. The arms of Goliath are the devil's cunning for doing harm. David was sent by his father to visit his brethren, and Christ by God the Father to the sheep that were lost of the house of Israel. David brought to his brethren an ephi of frumenty, that is, a measure of three bushels, and Christ commended the mystery of the Holy Trinity to believers. David brought ten little cheeses to the tribune, and Christ delivered the decalogue to the Jews. Eliab: my God father: the Jews, falsely claiming to have God as father, who, envying Christ, lost the birthright. The staff of David, the cross of Christ. Goliath, struck in the forehead, falls and is put under David himself; and the devil is struck in the forehead of his own when the sign of the cross is fixed in that place, and he is subjected in the members to Christ. David brought Goliath's sword to Jerusalem, and Christ transferred those whom he snatched from the devil's power into the Church for its defence. Saul inquires about the house of David and about him as though unknown, though David had long been attending him; and the Jews knew that Christ would come, and him whom in his bodily presence they could approve as the Son of God by his mighty works, as though ignorant, they say: Who art thou? And where is thy father?
• Morally: when the members of the true David overcome the proud heretics, who bring forward the sentences of sacred Scripture, by those same sentences which they bring forward, they as it were behead the lofty Goliath with his own sword.
17.42:
**“And when the Philistine looked, and beheld David, he despised him. For he was a young man, ruddy,”** — by passion
**“and of a comely countenance.”** — "beautiful above the sons of men"
17.46:
**“This day, and the Lord will deliver thee into my hand,”** — power
**“and I will slay thee, and take away thy head from thee: and I will give the carcasses of the army of the Philistines this day to the birds of the air,”** — which eat up the seed by the wayside
**“and to the beasts of the earth:”** — of which: "Deliver not up to beasts the souls that confess to thee."
17.49:
**“And he put his hand into his scrip, and took a”** — unity conquers
**“stone, and cast it with the sling, and fetching it about struck the Philistine in the forehead: and the stone was fixed in his forehead,”** — where he did not have the sign of Christ
17.51:
**“He ran, and stood over the Philistine,”** — the devil
**“and took his sword,”** — namely those whom the devil held in his hand, by whom he slaughtered others
**“AND TOOK HIS SWORD”** — AND TOOK HIS SWORD. GREGORY. The catholic man too gathers the testimonies of Scripture which the heretic brings forward, and from them convicts the obstinacy of his error, as David [did]: the type of the Lord, who is interpreted strong of hand.
