But Goliath, revealed or migrating, signifying the pride of the heretics: these things they spoke by deeds which we disclose by words. Goliath came to battle with a sword, David with a shepherd's scrip; but David slew Goliath with his own sword. We too, who are members of the true David, overcome the heretics by their own sentences.
**“and drew it out of the sheath, and slew him”** — with his own sword
17.54:
**“And David taking the head of the Philistine”**
• it is anticipation; for he did this afterwards
• THE HEAD OF THE PHILISTINE etc. David took the head of the Philistine to Jerusalem to terrify those who trusted that they were unconquerable by the strength and height of their walls, that they should not disbelieve that they would be conquered by him.
**“brought it to Jerusalem: but his armour he put in the tent”** — whence afterwards he received it from Achimelech the priest
**“his own.”** — the Lord's: 'his own' is added superfluously, because he put the arms not in his own but in the Lord's tabernacle
17.55:
**“OF WHAT FAMILY”** — OF WHAT FAMILY. AUGUSTINE. That Saul and Abner did not know David, who had stayed a long while with them, was caused by the beard which had grown on the young man while he was absent.
**“is this young man descended? And Abner said: As thy soul liveth”** — AS THY SOUL LIVETH. Like this is that: Naboth blessed God and the king; as if [to say]: may thy soul not live, O king, if I know; or, may I see thy death if I know. Also the conjunction 'if' is sometimes put for 'not', according to that: "If they shall enter into my rest," that is, they shall not enter; whence it can be expounded thus: if I know, that is, I do not know.

18.1: **“AND JONATHAN LOVED HIM”** — AND JONATHAN LOVED HIM. Jonathan, a warlike man, loved David, a youth fit for battles. Jonathan signifies those from the Jews who believed in Christ, and, having received the grace of the Holy Ghost, left all for Christ and followed him. Whence Peter: "Behold we have left all things, and have followed thee." For so Jonathan gave David his garments, from the coat to the girdle, when the believers brought all that they had into the service of Christ.
18.7:
**“And the women sung as they played, and they said: Saul slew his thousands,”**
• SAUL SLEW HIS THOUSANDS etc. This was the seedbed of hatred against David. So the Jews, hearing that Christ, whom they had crucified, was preached in the Churches, and that believers rejoiced in his praise for the victory by which he overcame the old enemy, took it ill.
• SAUL HIS THOUSANDS: namely those who were slain fleeing.
**“and David his ten thousands.”** — DAVID HIS TEN THOUSANDS: namely the Philistine, by casting down whom alone he put all to flight.
18.10:
**“And the day after the evil spirit from God came upon Saul,”** — that is, the Jews
**“and he prophesied”** — that is, in the manner of the possessed, he uttered strange things
**“in the midst of his house. And David”** — Christ
**“played”** — with evangelical sweetness
**“with his hand as at other times.”** — "Jesus began to do and to teach."
**“AND [SAUL] HELD”** — So the Jews tried to bring death on Christ as he preached the gospel. But while he withdrew for the salvation of the Gentiles, they harmed only themselves.
18.13: **“Therefore Saul removed him from him, and made him a captain over a thousand men, and he went out”** — first into battle, in the royal manner
18.18: **“And David said to Saul: Who am I, or what is my life,”** — he hints secretly that he is worthy
18.21:
**“And Saul said: I will give her to him,”** — AND SAUL SAID: I WILL GIVE etc. ISIDORE. Saul, a cunning dissembler, sought to bind David to Michol his daughter if he would offer him a hundred foreskins of the Allophyli; but he offered two hundred. And so Saul, while he exposed him to danger, glorified him the more. So the Jews, while they strove against the will of God to kill Christ, wrought the salvation of the Gentiles. David first brought the foreskins of the foreigners, and so received Saul's daughter as wife; and Christ did not take the Synagogue before he had become glorious among the Gentiles. For he first cut away among the nations the pollution of the flesh, and afterwards was joined to the Synagogue. "For when the fulness of the Gentiles shall come in, then all Israel shall be saved." And he offered double foreskins for the Jews and the Gentiles, namely those gained; or because the number of believing Gentiles is greater than that of the Jews. The hatred of Saul against David grew so much that, as David played according to custom for his relief, he tried to pierce him with a javelin. By Saul the elation of the Jews, by David the humility of Christ is signified. When, then, Saul is seized by the unclean spirit, his madness is tempered by David's singing; because, when the sense of the Jews is turned to fury through blasphemy, it is fitting that it be called back to health by the calm of evangelical speech, as by the sweetness of the harp.
**“that she may be a stumblingblock to him, and that the hand of the Philistines may be upon him. And Saul said to David: In two things”** — one thing is that he laid the giant low; the other, if he should bring a hundred foreskins of the Allophyli
18.25: **“And Saul said: Speak thus to David: The king desireth not any dowry, but only a hundred foreskins”** — heads, according to some, because the summit of a thing is called the foreskin.
18.27:
**“And after a few days David rose up, and went to Accaron with the men that were under him, and he slew of the Philistines two hundred men, and brought their foreskins”** — HE SLEW etc. AND BROUGHT THEIR FORESKINS etc. So Christ was glorified among the Gentiles before he joined the Synagogue to himself; and he first cut away uncleanness among the Gentiles. "For when the fulness of the Gentiles shall come in, then all Israel shall be saved."
**“and numbered them out to the king, that he might be his son in law. Saul therefore gave him Michol”** — the Synagogue

19.3: **“And I will go out and stand beside my father in the field”** — IN THE FIELD. Where Saul had been accustomed to come for counsel, where it had been agreed that David should be killed.
19.11:
**“Saul therefore sent”**
• the kingdom of the Jews
• SAUL THEREFORE SENT etc. This pertains not to the cross of Christ but to the passion. For Christ was crucified, and died, and was buried. And that burial was as it were the house to which the kingdom of the Jews sent to guard [him], when guards were set at the sepulchre of the Lord. That the house was guarded that David might be killed, since Christ was killed not in the sepulchre but on the cross, is referred to his body. For to take away the name of Christ is to kill Christ; for Christ would not be believed in if the lie of the guards had prevailed, who said: While we were asleep his disciples came and stole him away. But neither could Saul kill David, nor the kingdom of the Jews take away the memory of Christ. But those who presumed against Christ on the strength of Saul, that is, of the kingdom of the Jews, struck against the stone of stumbling, as against the image; and to them the lamb seemed a kid, because him in whom they found no sin they persecuted as a sinner.
**“his guards”** — soldiers to guard the sepulchre
**“by night to the house”** — the sepulchre
**“of David”** — of Christ
**“to watch him, that he might be killed”** — that is, that his memory and faith might be taken away from the hearts of men
19.12: **“She let him down through a window.”** — because the house was surrounded with guards
19.13:
**“And Michol took an image”** — the stone of stumbling
**“and laid it on the bed, and a goat's skin with the hair”** — because to the Jews the lamb seemed a kid
**“A SKIN WITH THE HAIR”** — From it a little pillow was sewn, which with its unshorn hair might counterfeit the head of a man wrapped up in the bed.
19.14: **“And Saul sent officers”** — ministers who obey the one commanding
19.18: **“IN RAMATHA”** — IN RAMATHA. It is the city of Saul in the tribe of Benjamin, at the sixth milestone from Aelia toward the north, over against Bethel. Another Rama is in the tribe of Aser. These names well fit the things done in them, because the sayings of the prophets have both the loftiness of knowledge and the beauty of eloquence.
19.19:
**“And it was told Saul by some, saying: Behold David is in Najoth”**
• it is a place in Ramatha where David sat
• beauty
**“in Ramatha.”** — lofty
19.20: **“So Saul sent officers to take David: and when they saw a company of prophets”** — who were prophesying at that time
19.22: **“Went also himself”** — HE SENT MESSENGERS etc. WENT ALSO HIMSELF. RABANUS. Saul too and his messengers signify the Jews, who, while they desire to oppose Christ, have in their mouth the sacraments of the law and the prophets as testimony to Christ, and dispute with the Church as with prophets about the Scriptures, as those prophesied with the prophets.
19.24:
**“HE PROPHESIED”** — HE PROPHESIED. These prophets were religious men called Nazarenes, who did not drink wine and were always free for singing hymns and psalms.
**“with the rest before Samuel,”** — hidden
**“NAKED”** — NAKED. The Jews too, stripped of faith and priesthood and kingdom, have the law and the prophets in their mouth.
**“all that day and night. This gave occasion to a proverb: What! is Saul too among the prophets?”**
• WHAT! IS SAUL TOO etc. That is called a proverb which is often turned over in the mouths of speakers. For it seemed a wonderful thing that so profane a man should prophesy. And we too, when we see the unlearned teaching, rightly say: Is Saul too among the prophets?
• RABANUS. A great question arises here: since in what precedes it is read, and Samuel saw Saul no more until the day of his death, how is he said here to have prophesied before Samuel? Which the Hebrews solve in two ways: namely that Samuel hid himself, that he might not be seen by him. Or he did not see him, namely clothed in the royal attire with which he was clothed, when it was said, he saw him not until the day of his death; and so he did not see him clothed, namely, in royal attire. And that he stripped himself is to be understood not of all his garments but only of the royal ones.
• RABANUS. Again it is asked how those who had been sent to seize a man and lead him to death merited to be partakers of the prophetic spirit; and likewise Saul himself, seeking innocent blood? But Balaam too prophesied, and many will say in that day: "Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name" etc. To whom it will be said: "I never knew you: depart from me, you that work iniquity." It is not wonderful, then, that a reprobate man prophesied for a passing moment. But mystically Saul and his messengers signify the heretics, who have something of the spiritual gifts, as the testaments of the law and the gospel, and baptism. Which, when they come to the Church, is not to be violated in them, or given as though they did not have it; but they must acknowledge the unity in the bond of peace, without which, whatever they have, though it be holy and venerable, yet they themselves are the more unworthy the less well they have used those gifts.

20.3: **“BUT ONE STEP”** — He calls the wall a step, by which, in the middle between himself and the enemies, he escaped through the window of the house where the besiegers were.
20.5:
**“And David said to Jonathan: Behold tomorrow is the new moon,”** — the Jews celebrate the calends with victims, feasts and rest
**“and I according to custom to sit”** — as the king's son-in-law
**“am wont beside the king to eat: let me go then that I may be hid in the field till the evening of the third day.”** — for they kept the festival of the new moon three days
20.11: **“And Jonathan said to David: Come and let us go out into the field.”** — they went out from the city into the field that they might more securely enter into the covenant of the Lord, that is, the oath
20.13:
**“May the Lord do so and so to Jonathan and add still more. But if my father shall continue in malice against thee, I will discover it to thy ear, and will send thee away, that thou mayest go in peace, and the Lord be with thee,”** — may he exalt thy kingdom
**“as he hath been”** — before
20.16: **“Jonathan therefore made a covenant with the house of David: and the Lord required it at the hands of David's enemies.”** — AND THE LORD REQUIRED IT AT THE HAND. It is prolepsis, that is, anticipation; for this was done long after, when, Saul having been slain, the kingdom was transferred to the house of David, and those who had persecuted the innocent were punished by God. Then the Lord required it at the hand of the enemies, namely why they afflicted a holy man. Then they were compelled to render account, because they had hated him so long a time. Which can be understood of Absalom and of Seba the son of Bochri, of Saul and of the other enemies of David. Or the Lord required at the hand [of the enemies], that is, of David['s], why they too were not willing to enter into a covenant of peace with him with whom they saw the Lord to be. And Scripture anticipated these things in order to prove true what it had said, when the Lord shall have rooted out the enemies of David: namely that the enemies of David were rooted out from the earth, not by David avenging himself, but by the Lord avenging him.
20.17:
**“AND JONATHAN [SWORE] AGAIN”** — AND JONATHAN [SWORE] AGAIN. RABANUS. That he might be shown free from the destruction of David's enemies, because he loved him according to the law of God. And though, prevented by death, he could not have the earthly kingdom with him as he hoped, without any doubt he received the fellowship of the heavenly kingdom with him whom he loved for his virtues, since he too was a man of virtues.
**“to swear”** — that is, to swear strongly
20.19:
**“For thy seat will be empty till after tomorrow. So thou shalt go down quickly, and come to the place, where thou must be hid on the day when it is lawful to work,”** — on the day before the calends
**“and thou shalt remain beside the stone, which is called Ezel.”** — seeing God, or the strength of God
20.22: **“If I shall say to the boy: Behold the arrows are on this side of thee, take them up: come thou to me, because, there is peace to thee, and there is no evil, as the Lord liveth.”** — king Saul
20.30:
**“Then Saul being angry against Jonathan said to him: Thou son of a woman that is the ravisher of a man,”** — that is, an adulteress
**“do I not know that thou lovest the son of Isai”** — DO I NOT KNOW THAT THOU LOVEST etc. As if he should say: thou lovest my enemy, opposing me, in which thou showest that thou wast conceived of an adulterous union. For those lawfully born love their fathers more closely.
20.34: **“So Jonathan rose from the table in great anger, and did not eat bread on the second day after the new moon. For he was grieved for David, because his father had put him to confusion.”** — reproaching him that he was the son of an adulteress
20.36: **“FETCH ME THE ARROWS WHICH I SHOOT”** — FETCH ME THE ARROWS WHICH I SHOOT. What is it that Jonathan, wishing to save David while he lay hidden in the field beside the stone, shot two arrows as a sign, which a little boy, not knowing what he was doing, gathered and brought back into the city, except that the Father had hidden in the letter of the law, the Jews not knowing it, his only-begotten Son, to be sent for the salvation of the human race? David, then, was hidden in the field, and Christ in the world: "He was in the world, and the world was made by him, and the world knew him not." He sat beside the stone, because he was written in the tables of the law. Whence: "The Lord thy God is one" and: "Thou shalt not take the name of thy God in vain." Saul at the feast judged him to be a son of death, and Jewish perfidy at the paschal feast treated of the death of the Lord. When, then, the morning had dawned, Jonathan came into the field according to the appointment with David, and a little boy with him; he shot one arrow and shot another; and God the Father, as the morning of faith dawned, first brought forth the testimony of the law concerning Christ, then sent the prophets. Jonathan's boy gathered the arrows and brought them to his master, not knowing what he was doing. So the Jewish people, carrying the books of the law and the prophets, honoured them as divinely written, but knew not him whom Moses and the prophets had foretold.
20.42: **“And Jonathan said to David: Go in peace:”** — understand: let them be firm; excessive grief fails in speaking

21.1:
**“And David came to Nobe to Achimelech”** — ACHIMELECH: my brother king. The apostles, whom the King of kings calls his brethren. David was alone, and Christ in his passion. David says: I have appointed my servants to such and such a place. And Christ said: "After I shall be risen again, I will go before you into Galilee." David came by a defiled way, and Christ passed undefiled through the unclean actions of the Jews. David says: And it shall be sanctified this day in my vessels. And the vessels of the Lord, that is, the apostles, were sanctified by faith from the contagion of the Jews.
**“the priest: and [he] was astonished,”** — because he came without soldiers
**“Achimelech”** — Achimelech is the same as Achias, the grandson of Heli
21.4: **“And the priest answered David, saying: I have no common bread”** — 'laos' in Greek is people; hence lay loaves, that is, popular
21.5:
**“And David answered the priest, and said to him: Truly, as to what concerneth women, we have refrained ourselves from yesterday and the day before, when we came out, and the vessels of the young men were holy.”** — from intercourse, namely
**“Now this way is defiled,”** — in the Hebrew: lay
**“THIS WAY IS DEFILED”** — THIS WAY IS DEFILED. RABANUS. In the Hebrew: this way is lay. As if [he said]: it is written in the law that a stranger shall not eat of them; why dost thou ask whether the young men are clean, who, even if they were clean, ought not to eat? The way, then, is lay, because thou askest in a lay manner; but it too is sanctified this day in the vessels. In the vessels, that is, he said he was sanctified in his mind, because he would not eat of them unless the necessity of the body and the danger of life pressed him.
21.6: **“THE PRIEST THEREFORE GAVE THEM”** — THE PRIEST THEREFORE GAVE THEM. As far as pertains to prophecy, this was fulfilled in Christ, who, placed in the flesh, while he avoided the cruelty of the Jews, passed over to the apostles, with whom he took the food he desired. "For with desire he desired to eat the Pasch." He took away the arms of Goliath, that is, of the devil. For, being stronger, he plundered the spoils of the strong one. But on those by whom Christ was received the devil brought persecution, tribulation and death. For all that will live godly in Christ suffer persecution. Whence: "If they have persecuted me, they will also persecute you."
21.7:
**“WITHIN THE TABERNACLE”** — WITHIN THE TABERNACLE. RABANUS. In the Hebrew: bound before the Lord. For perhaps he had vowed that he would stay some days in the tabernacle of the Lord and be free for prayers.
**“DOEG, AN EDOMITE”** — DOEG, AN EDOMITE. RABANUS. He was keeper of the camels, that is, of an unfruitful and crooked flock, and he is interpreted 'movement' or 'anxious'; who also struck Achimelech the high priest, who is interpreted 'my brother king'. By name and deed he signifies Judas, through whom the devil wrought fraud against Christ the true king, that, he being destroyed, the Church too might suffer, and the disciples of Christ and the priests be slain for his name. But in the house of Achimelech Abiathar alone, the chief of the priests, escaped; because no one can harm Christ, the prince of priests, who ascended victorious into heaven.
21.8: **“And David said”** — he fed Saul's mules
21.12:
**“BUT DAVID LAID UP”** — BUT DAVID LAID UP. ISIDORE. RABANUS. Achis is interpreted 'how is it?', by which ignorance is signified. For it is the word of one swearing and not acknowledging. Which was fulfilled in the Jews, who, when they saw Christ, did not acknowledge him. Before them he changed his countenance and went away. For there were there the carnal precepts of the law, there was the sacrifice according to Aaron; but he instituted from his body and blood the sacrifice "according to the order of Melchisedech." He changed his countenance in the priesthood, he changed it in the precepts, giving another testament, carnal working being made void. He slipped down between their hands when they seized and crucified him. And he stumbled against the doors of the gate, that is, he humbled himself to the beginning of our faith: the door of the gate is the beginning of faith; from faith the Church begins and reaches even to hope. That the spittle ran down upon his beard as of a madman, the Apostle discloses, saying: "We preach Christ crucified, unto the Jews indeed a stumblingblock, and unto the Gentiles foolishness." For spittle signifies weakness, because: "The foolishness of God is wiser than men." The spittle flows down the beard; for as weakness is shown in spittle, so strength is shown in the beard. He covered, then, his strength with the body of his weakness; and what was weak outwardly appeared as spittle, while the divine strength lay hidden within as the beard.
**“these words in his heart, and was exceedingly afraid”** — lest, moved by envy, he should contrive some evil

22.1: **“David therefore went from thence and fled to the cave of Odollam. And when [they] had heard of it”** — AND WHEN [THEY] HAD HEARD OF IT. RABANUS. It signified that our Redeemer, having accomplished his passion and the redemption of the human race, first set up the Church in Judea from the Israelite people, from which he also took flesh; where his brethren, that is, the apostles, and his father's house, that is, those who believed from the Jews, came to him. And there gathered themselves unto him all that were in distress etc. To whom, namely, he says: "Come to me, all you that labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you."
22.2:
**“And all that were in distress gathered themselves unto him”** — of sins, namely, not having the breadth of charity
**“OPPRESSED WITH DEBT”** — OPPRESSED WITH DEBT. RABANUS. By the tax, namely, of sins, which they pay to the devil while they make their members serve iniquity unto iniquity. Such must do penance in bitterness of mind and come to David, that is, to Christ, desired by all nations, that he may become their prince. "For he it is who is the Judge of the living and the dead," and the prince of peace: 'Of whose kingdom there shall be no end.'
22.5: **“AND GAD SAID”** — AND GAD SAID. RABANUS. Gad is brought in unexpectedly; for no mention is made of him in what precedes, as also Elias, where it is said: "And Elias the Thesbite of the inhabitants of Galaad said." From the mouth of the Lord, then, Gad the prophet told David not to stay among the Gentiles in a polluted land, but to return to the land of Juda, where according to the will of the Lord he should endure persecution.
22.7: **“He said to his servants that stood about him: Hear me now, ye sons of Jemini:”** — that is, of Benjamin
22.8: **“That all of you have conspired against me, and there is no one to inform me, especially when even my son hath entered into league with the son of Isai? There is not one of you that pitieth my case, nor that giveth me any information: because my son hath raised up my servant against me, plotting against me”** — an enemy
22.17:
**“And the king said to the messengers”** — the emissaries are those who are sent by the king's command to kill the guilty
**“that stood about him: Turn, and kill the priests of the Lord, for their hand is with David, because they knew that he was fled,”** — David and his servants
22.18: **“And the king said to Doeg: Turn thou, and fall upon the priests of the Lord. And Doeg the Edomite turned, and fell upon the priests and slew in that day eighty-five men that wore the linen ephod.”** — that by the garb of religion the king's mind might be moved to pity

23.1: **“And they told David, saying: Behold the Philistines fight against Ceila, and they rob the barns.”** — the corn carried off from the threshing floors
23.5:
**“David therefore, and his men, went to Ceila, and fought against the Philistines, and brought away their cattle,”** — to be loaded from the threshing floor
**“and made a great slaughter of them: and David saved”** — that is, the Lord
23.6: **“Now at that time, when Abiathar the son of Achimelech fled to David to Ceila, he came down having an ephod with him.”** — which Moses had made at the Lord's command, as also the rational, in which were doctrine and truth, in which too David consulted the Lord
23.11: **“Will the men of Ceila deliver me into his hands? and will Saul come down, as thy servant hath heard? O Lord God of Israel, tell thy servant. And the Lord said: He will come down.”** — HE WILL COME DOWN etc. RABANUS. If thou stay here, Saul will come down, and the men of Ceila will deliver thee into his hands; so he disclosed their will. And the men of Ceila, ungrateful for the benefits of David, whom he freed from the hands of the Philistines, signify the unbelief and inconstancy of the Jews, who, ungrateful to their Redeemer, lie in wait for him with the powers of the world. And Ceila is interpreted 'cast to the sling' or 'excelling for itself': "The wicked walk round about" and: "A fool is changed as the moon."
23.12: **“And David said: Will the men of Ceila deliver me, and my men, into the hands of Saul? And the Lord said: They will deliver thee up.”** — they have it in their will to deliver [thee]
23.14: **“But David abode in the desert in strong holds, and he remained in a mountain of the desert of Ziph,”** — Ziph: a squalid or cloudy or darkening mountain; and one of the posterity of Caleb was so called.
23.16: **“And Jonathan the son of Saul arose, and went to David into the wood, and strengthened his hands”** — Jonathan [strengthened David's]
23.19: **“THE ZIPHITES”** — THE ZIPHITES. RABANUS. They betrayed to Saul David hiding among them, and treated with him of his death. And Ziphites is interpreted 'flourishing' or 'budding', and they signify those Jews who, coveting the flower of the earthly kingdom, treated with their princes of the death of Christ, how they might seize him through his lost disciple and hand him over to the governor to be killed; and those flourishing in the world, namely the powers of this world, betray Christ in his members.
23.29: **“Then David went up from thence, and dwelt in strong holds of Engaddi.”** — fountain of the kid, or eye of temptation

24.2: **“Saul therefore took three thousand chosen men out of all Israel, and went out to seek after David, and his men, even upon the most craggy rocks, which are accessible only to wild goats.”** — ibexes are animals which, falling from the rocks, catch themselves on their horns
24.3:
**“And he came to the sheepcotes,”** — a place so called
**“which were in his way. And there was a cave,”** — AND THERE WAS A CAVE etc. RABANUS. The king, caught by an unforeseen ambush in what he was contriving against the innocent, fell into the pit which he had made. But David, returning good for evil, did not kill him, but as testimony of the deed cut off the hem of his robe, though it would have been easier to destroy his adversary than to deceive him. David hid in the cave that he might not be found. And he who hides in a cave is covered with earth, that is, with flesh. And Jesus lay hidden in the flesh which he had received from the earth, that his divinity might not be found by the Jews: "For if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory." They, then, not knowing God, persecuted the man. Christ fled into the cave from the face of Saul; for so long did the Jews persecute him, until he was laid in the monument which was hewn in a rock. Saul goes into the cave to purge his belly, because the Jews sent forth the malice they had conceived against Christ as a foul odour, and showed their evil thoughts by worse deeds. David chose to save Saul rather than destroy him, whom, hidden in the cave, he had in his power, by Saul's own testimony. So too Christ, when he was in the cave of the flesh, had the persecuting people in his power, and did not kill them, of whom it was written: Slay them not. He silently cut off the edge of the robe, because Christ did not kill the Jews but took away the glory of the kingdom. For the cutting of the robe is the cutting off of the kingdom; whence, when Saul tore the garment of Samuel, Samuel said: "The Lord hath rent the kingdom of Israel from thy hand."
**“into which Saul went, to ease nature.”** — SAUL. GREGORY. Morally. What is signified by Saul but bad rulers? What by David but good subjects? For Saul to purge his belly is for wicked superiors to extend the malice conceived in the heart even to works of wretched odour, and to show the harmful things thought within by carrying them out in outward deeds. Yet David feared to strike him; because the minds of pious subjects, keeping themselves from every plague of detraction, strike the life of their superiors with no sword of the tongue, even when they rebuke their imperfection. For if at times through weakness they can scarcely refrain from speaking of some extreme and outward evils of their superiors, yet they speak humbly, and as it were silently cut off the hem of the robe; because, while they disparage the dignity set over them, though harmlessly and secretly, they as it were soil the garment of the king set over them; but yet they return to themselves and reprove themselves for the slightest laceration by word. For David's heart struck him because he had cut off the hem of Saul's robe. For the deeds of a superior are not to be struck with the sword of the mouth, even when they seem rightly to deserve rebuke. But if at any time the tongue slips against them even in the least things, it must be checked by the affliction of penance, that it may return to itself, and, when it has offended against the dignity set over it, may dread the judgment against itself of him who set that superior over it. For when we offend against superiors, we oppose the ordinance of him who set them over us. Whence Moses, when he knew that the people complained against himself and Aaron, said: "For what are we? Your murmuring is not against us, but against God."
24.4: **“And the servants of David said to him: Behold the day, of which the Lord said to thee: I will deliver thy enemy unto thee, that thou mayest do to him as it shall seem good in thy eyes. Then David arose, and secretly cut off the hem of Saul's robe.”** — the chlamys is a military cloak, which is also called pirotica because it is pointed on both sides, where it reaches to the ankles.
24.6: **“AS THE LORD LIVETH”** — AS THE LORD LIVETH. Josephus supplies what is lacking in the letter: those who were with him reproached him, for he was saving an enemy who wished to destroy him; and he calmed them, saying: As the Lord liveth etc.
24.14: **“After whom dost thou pursue, O king of Israel? After whom dost thou pursue? After a dead dog”** — ignoble, powerless

25.1: **“And Samuel died, and all Israel was gathered together, and they mourned for him, and buried him in his house in Ramatha. And David rose and went down into the wilderness of Pharan.”** — PHARAN. RABANUS. It is a town in Arabia, near the Saracens who were in the wilderness. Through it the children of Israel passed when they had moved camp from mount Sinai. And it is toward the south, and is distant from Aila toward the east three days' journey. Scripture records that Ismael dwelt in the wilderness of Pharan, from whom are the Ismaelites, who are now called Saracens. We read too that Chodorlahomor smote those who were in the wilderness of Pharan.
25.3: **“NABAL”** — NABAL. RABANUS. A hard and very bad man, he signifies the Jews, who, drunk with the grape of gall and the bitterness of the cluster, stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart, always resisted the Holy Ghost, and, following the law carnally, became fools. For Nabal is interpreted fool or madman. Therefore, rejecting Christ and the apostles, who sought the refreshment of faith and good work, they said: As to this man, we know not from whence he is; but we are the disciples of Moses. But Abigail, most prudent and comely, signifies that people which was converted to God. She is interpreted 'my father's exultation'; whence: "There shall be joy in heaven upon one sinner that doth penance."
25.7: **“I heard that thy shepherds were shearing”** — because the patriarchs were shepherds of sheep, therefore at the shearing of sheep the Jews feasted festively in memory of them
25.10:
**“But Nabal answering the servants of David, said: Who is David?”** — contemptuously
**“and what is the son of Isai? servants are multiplied now a days”** — are multiplied
25.14:
**“Abigail”** — Her David, after the death of her husband, who perished mad in his folly, joined to himself, "a bride having neither spot nor wrinkle".
**“the wife of Nabal one of the servants told, saying: Behold David sent messengers out of the wilderness, to salute our master: and he rejected”** — despised
25.17: **“Wherefore consider, and think what thou hast to do: for evil is determined against thy husband, and against thy house, and he is a son of Belial”** — that is, of the devil
25.18:
**“Then Abigail made haste and took two hundred loaves, and two vessels of wine, and five sheep ready dressed, and five measures of parched corn”** — measures; [polenta] from pollen, which is flour
**“MEASURES OF PARCHED CORN”** — MEASURES OF PARCHED CORN. A satum is a kind of measure containing a bushel and a half. Polenta is the finest flour. Raisins are what is called grape which, before it ripens, is long dried in the sun and so kept. Cakes of dry figs, that is, bindings of the fruits of fig trees.
25.24: **“And she fell at his feet, and said: Upon me let this iniquity be, my lord:”** — by soothing [him] she calls down on herself the sin which David would have if he avenged himself
25.26:
**“Now therefore, my lord,”** — I am come to thee
**“the Lord liveth, and thy soul liveth, who hath withholden thee from coming to blood, and hath saved thy soul”** — innocent
25.28:
**“Forgive the iniquity”** — which I called down on myself if thou avenge thyself; namely, do not avenge thyself.
**“of thy handmaid: for the Lord will surely make for my lord a house”** — it signifies the kingdom
25.29:
**“For if a man at any time shall rise, and persecute thee, and seek thy life, the soul of my lord shall be”** — THE SOUL OF MY LORD SHALL BE etc. By a most beautiful comparison she distinguished the state of the just and of the reprobate: the souls of the former she calls living, those of the latter seized by spiritual death. "For the soul that sinneth, the same shall die." The former she likens to bundles, the latter to the stone of a sling. For a bundle is bound tight that it may be kept; a stone is put in a sling that it may be cast away. So the elect are bound tight by the pressures of tribulations, that, admonished by them, they may be knit more closely to one another by mutual charity, and, united by the hands of the Redeemer, may be kept for ever. The reprobate, the more widely they are let go in their pleasures, the farther they are cast from the glory of the divine vision: "For they are cast off from the hand of God." And wonderfully does she describe the almighty providence of the heavenly protector, when she says that the soul of the holy man is kept with him as in the bundle of the living. For as it is easy for anyone to keep a bundle of grass or hay held in the hand, so is the power of our Saviour [able] to keep and guard the elect from the beginning to the end. Whence: "And no man shall pluck them out of my hand." And as a bundle is bound, so the glory of the saints is bound tight by true charity and surrounded by divine protection. But literally, the soul of David, though many persecuted him, was always kept in the lot of the living; but his enemies, as a stone whirled in a sling, troubled with unstable motion, were taken away from their borders or from human affairs.
**“kept, as in the bundle”** — literally, a bundle of vines lives in water when it is prepared for transplanting
25.31: **“This shall not be an occasion of grief to thee,”** — that is, into weeping
25.37: **“But early in the morning when Nabal had digested his wine, [his wife] told”** — WHEN NABAL HAD DIGESTED HIS WINE, [HIS WIFE] TOLD [HIM]. Morally. GREGORY. We correct the wrathful better if we turn aside from them in the very commotion of their wrath. For when disturbed they do not know what they hear; but when they return to themselves, they receive the words of exhortation the more willingly, the more they blush that they were borne with so calmly. But to a mind drunk with fury everything right that is said seems perverse. Whence Abigail laudably kept silent about his fault to Nabal when drunk, and laudably spoke of it when his wine was digested. For he could come to know the evil he had done because he had not heard it while drunk.
25.39: **“And when David had heard that Nabal was dead, he said: Blessed be the Lord, who hath judged”** — this David said out of love of justice, not out of lust for vengeance.
25.44: **“But Saul gave Michol his daughter, David's wife, to Phalti, the son of Lais, who was of Gallim.”** — TO PHALTI THE SON. RABANUS. As the Hebrews hand down, Phalti did not know her; because if he had known her, David would not afterwards have received her back, since it is forbidden in the law. For Phalti was of Gallim, that is, of cleansing, that is, of the law. For he was a teacher of the law, of Baurim, that is, of the chosen, when Michol was given to him. For he is called Phalti, going, when she is taken away; Phaltiel, that is, escaping by God, because he kept him, that he should not touch her, lest he become a transgressor of the law; yet he followed her weeping as far as Baurim, for joy that he had not touched her.

26.3: **“And Saul encamped in Gabaa Hachila”** — it is a place on a hill
26.5: **“SLEEPING”** — SLEEPING. RABANUS. The Jews persecute Christ, and in persecuting they sleep, because they do not watch in heart. For the sleep of the heart is hardness: they sleep in the old life, they do not watch in the new. Christ came; he did not kill them, but took away the cup of water, that is, the grace of the law, and the sceptre of the kingdom, that is, the power by which they protected themselves in temporal things and raised themselves up against God. But our David, going forth victorious from their camp, ascended to the height of heaven.
26.10: **“unless the Lord shall strike him, or his day shall come to die, or he shall go down”** — by plague or something of the kind
26.12: **“So David took the spear, and the cup of water which was at Saul's head”** — or: his
26.19:
**“Now therefore hear, I pray thee, my lord the king, the words of thy servant: If the Lord stir thee up against me, let him accept of sacrifice:”** — he must be appeased with sacrifice and prayer
**“but if the sons of men,”** — stir thee up against me
**“they are cursed in the sight of the Lord, who have cast me out this day, that I should not dwell in the inheritance of the Lord, saying: Go, serve strange gods.”** — what need is there for me to dwell among strangers, but that the king of Israel seeks my death
26.21:
**“And Saul said: I have sinned, return, my son David,”** — as if [to say]: I was stirred up against thee neither by God nor by the sons of men, but by myself
**“for I will no more do thee harm, because my life hath been precious in thy eyes this day: for it appeareth that I have done foolishly, and have been ignorant in very many things.”** — the counsels of God, who preserves thee and delivers me into thy hands
26.24: **“And as thy life hath been much set by this day in my eyes, so let my life be much set by in the eyes of the Lord, and let him deliver me from all distress.”** — that this might be done, he often spared his enemy
26.25:
**“Then Saul said to David: Blessed art thou, my son David: and truly doing”** — already prevailing over me, thou shalt prevail more
**“thou shalt do,”** — that is, thou shalt do abundant things
**“and”** — already
**“prevailing thou shalt prevail.”** — so that thou reign

27.2: **“And David arose and went away, both he and the six hundred men that were with him, to Achis the son of Maoch, king of Geth.”** — not him from whom the man escaped, but his son, who loved him for the fame of his valour
27.8:
**“And David and his men went up, and pillaged Gessuri, and Gerzi,”** — these districts were not under the power of Achis.
**“and the Amalecites:”** — securely, namely, and quietly, because there was no one to plunder [them]
27.9: **“And David wasted all their land, and left no man alive”** — lest they should accuse him before Achis
27.10: **“And Achis said to him: Whom hast thou gone against today? David answered: Against the south of Juda”** — feigning that he held his own nation hateful
27.11: **“And David saved neither man nor woman,”** — that is, he did not allow to live

28.2: **“And David said to Achis: Now thou shalt know what thy servant will do.”** — for thee against thy enemies
28.3:
**“Now Samuel was dead,”** — NOW SAMUEL WAS DEAD etc. RABANUS. Samuel is read above to have died, but it is repeated because of his raising up, for the condemnation of Saul, who, having forsaken God, consulted a python against the law.
**“and all Israel mourned for him, and buried him in Ramatha his city.”** — above he is said to have been buried in his house, that is, in his family and kindred
28.6:
**“AND HE CONSULTED THE LORD”** — AND HE CONSULTED THE LORD. RABANUS. As the Hebrews hand down, an oracle was sought from God by fasting and praying, and God revealed things to come to them through dreams; which Saul is not read to have done.
**“and he answered him not, neither by priests, nor by dreams”** — NEITHER BY PRIESTS, NOR etc. RABANUS. In the Hebrew: Neither by doctrine nor by ephod: namely that which the priest wore on his breast, on which was written doctrine and truth.
28.7: **“And Saul said to his servants:”** — who are said to have been disciples of Samuel, with whom Saul prophesied.
28.9: **“And the woman said to him: Behold thou knowest all that Saul hath done, and how he hath rooted out the magicians and soothsayers from the land: why then dost thou lay a snare for my life, to cause me to be put to death?”** — MAGICIANS AND SOOTHSAYERS etc. Magicians use human blood and the touch of the dead in their sorceries and divinations; soothsayers divine by words alone, that is, by incantations. Pythian Apollo is called the patron of these arts, from whom [come] pythonesses, that is, diviners. These Saul destroyed as though from zeal for the law, because, as they say, compelled by the demons they proclaimed that David would be king.
28.11: **“And the woman said to him: Whom shall I bring up to thee? And he said, Bring me up Samuel.”** — WHOM SHALL I BRING UP etc. AUGUSTINE, TO SIMPLICIAN. Thou askest whether an evil spirit could have raised up the soul of a just man, so that it should be seen and speak with Saul? Is it not more to be wondered at that he took up the Lord and set him on the pinnacle of the temple? However he did it, it was done; unless one should say that the devil had easier licence to take up the living Lord whence he would and to set him where he would than to raise up the spirit of Samuel. But if this does not disturb us, because the Lord willed and permitted it to be done without any diminution of his power and divinity, as he suffered himself to be crucified and killed by the Jews, it is not absurd to believe that by some dispensation it was permitted that, not by the mastery of magic art or power, but by a hidden dispensation which escaped the pythoness and Saul, the spirit of the just man should show itself to the sight of the king, to strike him with the divine sentence. Or the spirit of Samuel was not truly raised from his rest, but some phantasm and imaginary illusion made by the machinations of the devil, which the prophet [so the edition] calls Samuel, as images are wont to be called by the names of the things they represent, as a picture of Cicero or Sallust; as the cherubim over the ark of the testament, made of metal for the sake of signifying a great thing, were called cherubim, though the heavenly powers are those that are called cherubim. Also, when anyone sees a dream, he does not say, I saw an image of Augustine, but, I saw Augustine, although at the time when he saw such a thing Augustine did not know of it. Pharao too said that he had seen in his dreams ears of corn and kine, not images of ears or kine. Perhaps, then, an image of Samuel appeared through the feigned contrivances of him who "transformeth himself into an angel of light." But if it moves anyone how true things were foretold to Saul by an evil spirit, that too can seem wonderful, that the demons acknowledged Christ, whom the Jews did not acknowledge. For when God wills that even weak spirits should know some true things, temporal things only, pertaining to this mortality, it is easy and not unfitting that the Almighty and just, for the punishment of those to whom these things are foretold, that they may suffer the evil that threatens before it comes, should by the hidden ordering of his mysteries impart to such spirits something of divination, that they may foretell to men what they hear from the angels. But they hear only so much as the Lord, the governor of all, commands or allows. Whence also the spirit of python in the Acts of the Apostles bears witness to Paul and proclaims him an evangelist. Yet they mingle deceits, and pronounce the truth with the aim not of teaching but of deceiving. Hence perhaps that image said that Saul would be with him, which is false; for between the good and the wicked after death a great chaos is fixed. Or it said, thou shalt be with me, for this reason: that it might be referred to the like condition of death, because each was a man and could die; already dead, he foretold death to the living.
28.13: **“And the king said to her: Fear not: what hast thou seen? And the woman said to Saul: Gods”** — the plural for the singular
28.19: **“And the Lord also will deliver Israel with thee into the hands of the Philistines: and tomorrow thou and thy sons shall be with me”** — that is, dead, which is true; or in rest, which is false; he says it to make himself believed and to render him secure
28.21:
**“And [the woman] came”** — from the secret chamber where she practised sorcery
**“to Saul (for he was very much troubled) and said to him: Behold thy handmaid hath obeyed thy voice, and I have put my life in my hand”** — that is, I exposed myself to danger
28.24: **“Now the woman had a fatted calf”** — fattened

29.2: **“And the lords of the Philistines marched with their hundreds”** — whence centurion, and he who is tribune
29.3: **“And the princes of the Philistines said to Achis: What mean these Hebrews? And Achis said to the princes of the Philistines: Do you not know David, who was the servant of Saul the king of Israel, and hath been with me many days, or years, and I have found no fault in him”** — of unfaithfulness
29.4: **“But the princes of the Philistines were angry with him, and they said to him: Let this man return, and abide in his place, which thou hast appointed him, and let him not go down with us to battle, lest he be an adversary to us, when we shall begin to fight: for how can he otherwise appease his master, but with our heads?”** — cut off
29.5: **“Is not this David, to whom they sung in their dances, saying: Saul slew his thousands, and David his ten thousands?”** — SAUL SLEW HIS THOUSANDS. Envying the glory of David, they say that he fought only among ten thousands, as of lesser power, but Saul among thousands, as innumerable; nor do they add how many were struck, envying their praise, or lest they should frighten their own. In the most ancient books it is not 'thousands' but only a thousand and ten thousand.
29.6: **“Then Achis called David, and said to him: As the Lord liveth, thou art upright and good in my sight: and so is thy going out, and thy coming in with me”** — is acceptable to me

30.1:
**“Now when [they] were come”** — These are the Amalecites whom Saul ought to have destroyed, and, guilty of disobedience, he lost the kingdom.
**“David and his men to Siceleg on the third day, the Amalecites had made an invasion on the south side upon Siceleg”** — THE AMALECITES HAD MADE AN INVASION etc. GREGORY. It is to be considered what it means that the Amalecites invade Siceleg and take booty. The Amalecites are called a licking people, by whom the minds of worldly men are designated, which, by coveting earthly things, as it were lick them while they delight in them. The licking people takes booty, as it were, when those who love earthly things heap up gains for themselves from the losses of others. And they do this while David is absent, because they neglect to have the Redeemer before the eyes of the heart. The Egyptian boy grows weary on the way, because the lover of the present world, covered with the blackness of sin, is often left by that same world weak and despised, so that he cannot run with it, but, broken by adversity, grows torpid. Him David finds, because Christ, truly strong of hand, turns to his love those whom he finds despised by the glory of the world. He feeds him with food, because he refreshes him with the knowledge of the word, because he makes him even his preacher. And because he could not follow the Amalecite, he becomes the guide of David, because he whom the world has deserted not only receives God in his converted mind, but by preaching leads him even into the hearts of others. With him as guide David finds the Amalecite feasting and destroys him, because Christ, through the preaching of those whom the world disdained to have as companions, destroys the gladness of the world.
30.9: **“So David went, he and the six hundred men that were with him, and they came to the torrent Besor: and some being weary stayed there.”** — in the Hebrew it says not that the weary remained, but those commanded
30.10: **“But David pursued, he and four hundred men: for two hundred stayed, who being weary could not go over the torrent Besor.”** — FOR TWO HUNDRED STAYED etc. The two hundred weary men who were left with the baggage signify the weak of the Church, who cannot run on the way with the spiritual men; but because they have faith and keep good works, they receive from Christ the reward of blessedness with the perfect.
30.15: **“And David said to him: Canst thou bring me to this company? And he said: Swear to me by God, that thou wilt not kill me, nor deliver me into the hands of my master, and I will bring thee to this company.”** — securely
30.16:
**“And when he had brought him, behold they were lying spread upon the face”** — the face [facies] of a man is so called because it makes him known.
**“of all the ground, eating”** — securely
30.17: **“And David slew them”** — These are the Amalecites whom Saul ought to have destroyed, and, guilty of disobedience, he lost the kingdom.
30.24: **“And no man shall hearken to you in this matter. But equal shall be the portion of him that went down to”** — elsewhere: to
30.26: **“Then David came to Siceleg, and sent presents”** — that he might draw them into friendship, and they might make him king, as they also did

31.2: **“And the Philistines fell upon Saul, and upon his sons, and they slew Jonathan, and Abinadab and Melchisua the sons of Saul.”** — THEY SLEW JONATHAN, ABINADAB AND MELCHISUA etc. RABANUS. Jonathan, Abinadab, who is also Jessui, and Melchisua. But Isboseth was at home, who is said to have been born in the year in which Saul was made king, who is also read to have been forty years old when he began to reign; whence it is gathered that Saul reigned forty years. And Jessui is interpreted 'equal', because they are recorded to have been equal in merits with their father. Abinadab, 'my father of his own will'; for his father Saul by doing evil of his own will brought it about that he perished together with his sons.
31.4: **“Then Saul said to his armourbearer: Draw thy sword, and kill me: lest these uncircumcised come, and slay me, and mock at me. And his armourbearer would not: for he was struck with exceeding great fear. Then Saul took his sword, and fell upon it.”** — THEN SAUL TOOK HIS SWORD etc. With the sword with which, against the command of God, he spared the Amalecites, he deservedly killed himself. So he who, having received power for the common good, either does not use it or abuses it, surely pierces himself with his own sword, and with that by which he ought to have been defended from the enemy he rather helps the enemy.
31.5: **“And when his armourbearer saw this”** — Doeg, according to the Hebrews, who, seeing Saul dead and fearing David, killed himself
31.6: **“So Saul died, and his three sons, and his armourbearer, and all his men”** — of his household
31.7: **“And the men of Israel, that were beyond the valley, and beyond the Jordan,”** — this valley around the Jordan is large and level
31.11: **“Now when the inhabitants of Jabes Galaad had heard”** — THE INHABITANTS OF JABES, whom Saul had defended from their adversaries, repay what they can. Let us too, as far as we can, rescue our benefactors, slain by the sword of sin, from the reproach of the Philistines.

1.1: **“Now it came to pass, after Saul was dead, that David returned from the slaughter of the Amalecites”** — AMALECITE. RABANUS. The Hebrews say this man was the son of Doeg. For Amalecite and Edomite are one, because the firstborn son of Esau was Eliphaz, and his son was Amalec. And he had the diadem and the bracelet entrusted to him by his father.
1.2: **“And on the third day, there appeared a man who came out of Saul's camp, with his garments rent, and dust strewed on his head: and when he came to David, he fell upon his face”** — the whole from a part: for a man does not fall upon his face alone, but falls wholly toward the side on which his face is
1.6: **“And the young man that told him, said: I came by chance upon mount Gelboe, and Saul leaned upon his spear:”** — being wearied, he was propping himself up
1.9: **“And he said to me: Stand over me, and kill me: for anguish is come upon me, and as yet my whole life is in me.”** — the whole vigour of life
1.10: **“So standing over him, I killed him: for I knew that he could not live after the fall”** — the wounding
1.12:
**“And they mourned, and wept, and fasted until evening for Saul, and for Jonathan his son, and for the people of the Lord”** — the priests
**“and for the house of Israel”** — in general
1.15: **“GO NEAR”** — Everyone who plots evil against his neighbour, or rejoices at his destruction, deserves from the heavenly judge the penalty of just retribution. For "he that diggeth a pit shall fall into it," and "the mouth that belieth killeth the soul." But this man was lying that he had killed Saul.
1.16: **“And David said to him: Thy blood”** — thy condemnation
1.18:
**“Also he commanded that they should teach the children of Juda the use of the bow”** — elsewhere: lamentation
**“THE CHILDREN OF JUDA”** — The children of Juda are the children of confession, whom the true David wills to be armed with the bow of Scripture, lest through ignorance they fall in the sight of the demons.
**“THE BOW”** — RABANUS. Because the Philistines are archers, by which art they had killed Saul, he wills them to learn the same art of war. Or he commanded that they should teach the kings of Juda strength, namely that they should be strong and intent in the fear of the Lord, lest they perish as Saul did.
**“IN THE BOOK OF THE JUST”** — RABANUS. It is read, or it is written: they declare that this book is found nowhere, like the book of the wars of the Lord, of which mention is made in the book of Numbers, and the songs of Solomon and his discourses on the nature of trees, herbs, beasts, birds, creeping things and fishes. Or what is said in the book of the Chronicles: "Now the rest of the acts of Solomon, first and last, are written in the books of Nathan the prophet, and of Ahias the Silonite, and in the vision of Addo the seer against Jeroboam the son of Nabat," and many volumes of this kind, which it proves were written but which it is certain do not exist today. For when Judea was laid waste by the Chaldeans, the library was consumed by the enemy's fire. But a few books were repaired or restored by Esdras the high priest, through the diligence of prophecy. This Esdras was a scribe in the law of God, who devised readier shapes of letters than the Hebrews had had until then. And there are some who say that the Book of the Just is the Book of Kings, in which are contained the just prophets Samuel, Gad and Nathan, in which it is written how Saul, departing from the fear of the Lord, perished through disobedience.
1.19:
**“CONSIDER, O ISRAEL”** — Thou who hast remained, [consider] for what fault they were slain, and beware lest thou too perish in their crime. Or CONSIDER how glorious they were who were wounded for thy freedom.
**“are slain upon thy mountains: how are the valiant fallen?”** — as if to say: right there among the enemies.
1.20:
**“GETH”** — A winepress, namely "Jerusalem that killest the prophets," to which the death of the Lord and of the apostles was a mockery; and for this reason the true David commands that his passion be not announced to them.
**“publish it not in the streets of Ascalon: lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice, lest the daughters of the uncircumcised triumph.”** — he forbids that anyone should rejoice at such a fall, [and] that the fall of the people of God should be spread abroad in the cities of the enemies
1.21:
**“Ye mountains of Gelboe”** — indignant at the fall of the valiant, he abhors the very place of the slaughter
**“MOUNTAINS”** — RABANUS. Others [read] 'high places', namely because, O Saul, thy disobedience was reckoned as idolatry in the high places, since it is the crime of idolatry to refuse to obey.
**“YE MOUNTAINS OF GELBOE”** — They were most fertile before the curse; they say they lie under the curse to this day, and testify that it never rains there.
**“RABANUS”** — David, king and prophet, who did not return evil to his persecutors, when Saul and Jonathan had fallen in battle, cursed the mountains of Gelboe in his lamentation: Ye mountains of Gelboe, let neither dew nor rain etc. What fault did the mountains commit? But because Gelboe is interpreted 'a running down', and through Saul, anointed and dead, the anointing and death of our mediator is expressed, by Gelboe are fittingly signified the proud hearts of the Jews, which, while they flow away in the desires of this world, mixed themselves in the death of the anointed, that is, of Christ. And because in them the anointed king dies in time, they are dried up from all dew of grace. Of them it is said that they cannot be fields of firstfruits. For the proud mountains of the Hebrews do not bear the first fruits, since at the Redeemer's coming they for the most part remained in unbelief and would not follow the beginnings of the faith. For holy Church, made fruitful in her firstfruits by the multitude of the gentiles, scarcely at the end of the world receives the Jews whom she finds, and gathering the last ones lays them up as the remnants of the harvest. Whence: THE REMNANT OF ISRAEL SHALL BE SAVED. Yet the mountains of Gelboe can be cursed by the prophet's mouth, so that, while the fruit dies as the earth dries up, the possessors of the land might be struck with the loss of barrenness, that they themselves might receive the sentence of the curse who, as their iniquity required, had deserved to have the death of the king take place among them.
1.22:
**“FROM THE BLOOD OF THE SLAIN”** — Blood and fat give strength to the body. So those by whom Saul and Jonathan were slain gave strength to their subjects, as though [they had been slain] not by rustics. Or thus: Saul was rejected by God, and basely slain by the uncircumcised, as though he were not anointed with oil, because of the blood of the slain, namely of the seventy-five priests who burned fat to the Lord, whom Saul ordered to be killed though innocent.
**“from the fat of the valiant, the arrow of Jonathan never turned”** — or: returned
**“back, and the sword of Saul did not return empty.”** — THE ARROW OF JONATHAN etc. and THE SWORD OF SAUL etc. He shows that Jonathan and Saul were warlike and most valiant, and praises in them the comeliness of their form and the constancy of their mind.
**“RABANUS”** — Allegorically. First the prophet David figuratively bewails Saul and Jonathan, who, though they were mighty and always prevailed over their enemies, being wounded and struck down in the midst of the battle, fell. So also Christians bewail those who, fighting against the demons, slip in the slipperiness of the world (for Gelboe is interpreted 'slippery mountains'), and, giving up the hope of recovery, kill themselves with their own blade of despair, as Saul did falling upon his sword. But the Philistines, that is, the demons, carrying off the spoils of virtues from the slain, ascribe the victory to their own strength, since such things befall the just by the promise of God. But our David in his elect groans at the fall of those who fall, and forbids it to be published in the cities of the aliens, that is, he commands the faithful to guard themselves warily, that they may have the shield of faith, the breastplate of justice, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the spirit, which is the word of God, with which they may resist their adversaries, lest, shamefully overcome again, they give joy to their enemies.
1.23: **“Saul and Jonathan, lovely, and comely in their life, even in death they were not divided: they were swifter than eagles”** — hyperbole
1.24: **“Ye daughters of Israel, weep over Saul, who clothed you with scarlet in delights,”** — namely from the spoil of the enemies
1.25:
**“How are the valiant fallen in battle?”** — in sin, understood
**“Jonathan [slain] in thy high places”** — as above

2.2: **“SO DAVID WENT UP”** — RABANUS. The going up of David with his two wives into Hebron signifies 'the calling together of two peoples into the catholic Church'. For Hebron is interpreted 'marriage'. And the Church alone is the bride of the heavenly king. Thither David led every man with his household, because each of the faithful is called into that fellowship through the preaching of the gospel, where there is no distinction of Jew and Greek.
2.4:
**“AND THE MEN CAME”** — RABANUS. Because, while the proud and contemptuous spurn the grace of God, the elect, by the fame of preaching and the pursuit of virtues, confess that Christ is king among his people, to whom has been given "all power in heaven and on earth."
**“and anointed David there, to be king over the house of Juda.”** — this is written more fully in Paralipomenon
2.5: **“AND HE SAID TO THEM”** — RABANUS. He is very pleasing to our Redeemer who by condemning them gives over to oblivion the works of the wicked, who are dead in sins, and does not imitate the things that displease the Lord, but remembers to do what he has commanded.
2.7: **“Let your hands be strengthened, and be ye men of valour: for although your master Saul be dead, yet the house of Juda hath anointed me to be their king.”** — as if [to say]: I will be to you in place of Saul
2.8:
**“ISBOSETH”** — RABANUS. [Isboseth], who is interpreted 'son of confusion', reigned over all Israel with the help of Abner, who is interpreted 'lamp of the father'. AND ONLY THE HOUSE OF JUDA FOLLOWED DAVID, because, while only those who believe and truly confess follow Christ, among the rest the error of confusion reigned, at the instigation of the devil, who "transformeth himself into an angel of light."
**“LED HIM ABOUT THROUGH THE CAMP”** — In the Hebrew it says: he led him over into Manaim, which is interpreted 'camp'. That is, he led him over beyond the Jordan and established him as king in Naim [so the edition].
2.9: **“And made him king over Galaad, and over Gessuri”** — Gessuri, in the Hebrew Assuri, that is, over the tribe of Aser
2.11: **“AND THE NUMBER WAS”** — RABANUS. It is well said that David reigned seven days [so the edition] and six months in Hebron, which is interpreted 'marriage' or 'everlasting vision', because Christ reigns in the Church, which is his person, through the whole time of this life, which runs its course in the sevenfold number of days, according to that: "Behold I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the world"; and because after the fulfilment of the six, that is, the perfection of good work, he leads his elect to the true sabbath, that is, the everlasting rest, where they shall enjoy the perpetual vision of God. Now Hebron is a city in the tribe of Juda which was once called Arbe, although in the Greek manuscripts it is wrongly given as Arboc, as also in ours, whereas in the Hebrew it is read Arbe, that is, 'four', because Abraham and Isaac and Jacob were buried there, and the great Adam, although some suppose he [was buried] in the place of Calvary. This was once the metropolis of the Philistines and the dwelling of the giants, afterwards a priestly city and [a city] of refuge. It lies on the southern side, about twenty-two miles from Aelia, where the oak of Abraham, which is also the terebinth, which is also Mambre, was shown until the reign of the emperor Constantine, and his mausoleum [is seen] at the present time. And though a church has now been built there by our people, the place of the terebinth is worshipped round about by all the nations with superstition, because under it Abraham received the angels as guests. It was first called Arbe, afterwards Hebron, from one of the sons of Caleb; and it was founded seven years before Tanis, the city of Egypt.
2.12: **“And Abner the son of Ner went out”** — AND ABNER WENT OUT etc. RABANUS. Josephus explains this passage thus: Abner moved forward a very choice army, to engage with the tribe of Juda. For he was angry against those by whom David had been ordained king. Against him came Joab, sent by David, the son of Sarvia his sister; he was set as captain of the host against Abner. With him were his brothers Abisai and Asael and all David's armed men; and coming to a certain spring in the city of Gabaon, he drew up his line for battle. And when Abner said to him that he wished to test which of them had the stronger army, it was agreed between both that they should send twelve men to fight; and when the swords were drawn, David's men, holding the heads of the enemy, pierced their loins and sides with their swords, until all perished as if in one appointed danger. When these fell, the rest of the army also gave way, and Abner's people were beaten. And Joab did not cease to pursue the fleeing, commanding the armed men to hasten and not to slacken in killing. His brothers also fought most readily; among whom Asael was the more renowned, who had such glory in swiftness of foot that he outran even horses in running. He pursued Abner, turning aside to neither side.
2.14: **“And Abner said to Joab: Let the young men rise”** — AND ABNER SAID TO JOAB etc. Abner, of the tribe of Benjamin, captain of Saul's army, provoked the young men of David to battle; and Saul, not yet an apostle, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Pharisee, provoked the apostles to the contest, and was present at the killing of Stephen.
2.18:
**“And there were the three sons of Sarvia there, Joab, and Abisai, and Asael: now Asael was a most swift runner,”** — NOW ASAEL etc. GREGORY. Asael signifies those whom vehement fury seizes and drives headlong. They are to be avoided the more cautiously in that same onset of fury, the more madly they are carried away. Whence Abner, that is, 'lamp of the father', flees, because the tongue of teachers, which shows forth the heavenly light of God, when it sees anyone's mind carried along the steep places of fury, refrains from returning the darts of words against the angry man, as if unwilling to strike the pursuer. But when the wrathful are mitigated by no consideration, and like Asael do not cease to pursue, it is necessary that those who try to restrain the furious should not rouse themselves to fury, but show whatever there is of calm; and some things they should put forward subtly, by which they may obliquely pierce the mind of the furious man. Whence Abner pierced his pursuer not with the point but with the butt of the spear. For to strike with the point is to oppose with the onset of open rebuke; but to strike with the butt of the spear is to touch the furious man calmly with certain things, and as it were to overcome him by sparing him. And Asael at once falls, because agitated minds, when they both feel themselves spared and yet are touched inwardly, under calm, by the reason of the answers, immediately fall from that to which they had raised themselves. Because, therefore, struck by gentleness they spring back from the onset of their fury, they die as it were without the steel.
**“like one of”** — or: of
2.21: **“And Abner said to him: Go to the right hand or to the left, and lay hold on one of the young men”** — or: young men
2.23: **“But he refused to hearken to him, and would not turn aside: wherefore Abner struck him with a back [stroke]”** — turned around
2.25: **“And the children of Benjamin gathered themselves together to Abner: and being joined in one body, they stood on the top of a hill”** — of a higher place
2.26:
**“And Abner cried out to Joab, and said: Shall thy”** — the Hebrew does not have 'thy'
**“sword rage unto utter destruction? knowest thou not that it is dangerous to drive people to despair?”**
• "The one safety of the vanquished is to hope for no safety"
• when men despair, life is disregarded and they fight with all their strength
**“KNOWEST THOU NOT”** — In the Hebrew: knowest thou not that the end will be bitter if thou strivest to destroy the people?
2.27: **“And Joab said: As the Lord liveth, if thou hadst spoke”** — that is, if thou hadst sought peace

3.1: **“Now there was a long war”** — THERE WAS A LONG [WAR]. RABANUS. The house of David is the heavenly Jerusalem, which partly is a pilgrim on earth, partly reigns with the Lord in heaven. But the house of Saul, the proud and wicked king, is Babylon, which makes all nations commit fornication. Between these there is a long war, because she who is according to the flesh persecutes her who is according to the spirit. But the house of David rejoices in the growth of her children even in persecution; the house of Saul fails in its iniquity, and at length, according to its deserts, will be sunk in the depth of the abyss.
3.2:
**“And sons were born to David in Hebron:”** — though he had many [wives], yet when they were with child and about to give birth, they were sent there, namely to Hebron
**“AND SIX WERE BORN”** — The six sons who were born to David in Hebron signify the perfection of the saints, who daily arise from the spiritual marriage of Christ and the Church through the grace of the Holy Spirit.
**“and his firstborn was Amnon”** — elsewhere: Ammon
3.5:
**“And the sixth Jethraam of Egla the wife of David.”** — Egla alone is called wife, whom he took in marriage according to the law
**“OF EGLA”** — RABANUS. This is Michol, who alone is called wife, because David obtained her as his first wife in his youth. She is said to have died in childbirth. Whence it is written in what follows: "Therefore Michol the daughter of Saul had no child to the day of her death," [for] she died in the very childbirth.
3.7: **“Why didst thou go in to my father's concubine?”** — he feared that by claiming the concubine he might usurp the kingdom
3.8:
**“And he was exceedingly angry”** — the anger was the cause, by the will of God, that the kingdom was transferred to David
**“for the words of Isboseth, and said: Am I a dog's head”**
• that is, vile and abominable
• a dog's head, that is, a chief of fools, and as it were of those barking against the Lord's anointed
3.14: **“And David sent messengers to Isboseth the son of Saul, saying: Restore my wife Michol, whom I espoused to me for a hundred foreskins of the Philistines.”** — above, two hundred are read, but Saul asked for a hundred
3.16: **“And her husband followed her, weeping”** — because he was losing her whom he had not known, since she, loving David, was always sad
3.17: **“Abner also spoke”** — ABNER ALSO SPOKE. RABANUS. Abner exhorts all Israel to leave Isboseth the son of Saul and come over to David, because the holy teachers, who are called lamp of the father, full of the light of faith and knowledge, exhort all nations to spurn the worship of idols, to leave the error of confusion together with its author the devil, and to hasten to come to the true David, that is, Christ. For Joab too, who, speaking to Abner in guile, struck him in the groin and killed him, signifies the ancient enemy, who subverts the faithful by fraud and kills them through the contagion of lust. For Joab is interpreted 'enemy' or likewise 'father'. For the devil is the head of all the wicked. Whence: "You are of your father the devil." Of this killing David is guiltless, because "God tempteth no man," who "will have all men to be saved." "But by the envy of the devil death came into the world." The person and name of Joab can also signify the people of the Jews, who were always enemies of the preachers and persecuted the faith of Christ everywhere.
3.27: **“And when Abner was returned to Hebron, Joab took him aside to the middle of the gate, to speak to him treacherously: and he stabbed him”** — the Jews or heretics also killed certain prelates of the Church for the defence of the faith
3.28:
**“And when David heard of it, after the thing was now done, he said: I am innocent,”** — lest he should seem to consent to the killing
**“and my kingdom, before the Lord for ever of the blood of Abner the son of Ner”** — he marks the faithlessness and wretchedness of the Jews
3.29:
**“And may it come upon the head of Joab”** — namely the princes and priests of the people
**“and upon all his father's house:”** — namely the synagogue of Satan and the generation of the wicked, that "all the just blood that hath been shed upon the earth" may be required of them
**“and let there not fail from the house of Joab one that hath an issue of seed”**
• flowing with various desires
• ONE THAT HATH AN ISSUE OF SEED etc. According to the letter he seems to imprecate the outflowing of lust, the plague of leprosy, effeminacy, falling under the enemy's sword, and begging.
**“or that is a leper, or that holdeth the distaff”** — the instability of heresy and of worldly pleasure
**“THAT HOLDETH THE DISTAFF”** — AUGUSTINE. By the winding of words are marked those who strive to defend their deceit.
**“or that falleth by the sword”** — by divine vengeance
**“THAT FALLETH BY THE SWORD”** — "He that striketh with the sword shall perish with the sword." Heretics pierce with the sword of the mouth, having first been pierced with the sword of impiety.
**“or that wanteth bread.”** — which came down from heaven
3.38: **“The king also said to his servants: Do you not know that a prince”** — who wished to make me king over all the house of Israel
3.39:
**“But I as yet am tender”** — TENDER [delicatus]. The ancients called things consecrated to the gods 'delicata', which we now call 'dedicata'.
**“as yet”** — not yet perfectly established

4.1:
**“And Isboseth the son of Saul heard that Abner was slain in Hebron: and his hands were weakened”** — strength
**“and all Israel was troubled.”** — not knowing whom he should rather follow
4.2: **“NOW TWO MEN”** — RABANUS. These two men were captains in Isboseth's army, and after Abner's death, as the Hebrews hand down, they took counsel with Miphiboseth to kill Isboseth and make him king. But Miphiboseth betrayed the plan; therefore it is brought in thus: And Jonathan the son had a son that was lame of his feet etc. And they, struck with fear, fled into Gethaim, and were there until that time, namely when, returning from there, they entered the house of Isboseth.
4.5: **“AND THE DOORKEEPER”** — RABANUS. The doorkeeper cleanses wheat when the guard of the mind, by discerning, separates virtues from vices; and if she falls asleep, she admits the plotters to the death of her own lord, because when the care of discretion has ceased, it opens the way to the evil spirits to kill the soul. They, entering, take away the ears of corn, because they carry off the seeds of good thoughts, and they strike in the groin, because they kill the strength of the heart with the delight of the flesh. For to strike in the groin is to pierce the life of the mind with the delight of the flesh. For Isboseth would not have fallen by an unforeseen death if he had not set a woman at the entrance of the house, that is, a soft guard at the approach of the mind. For a strong and wakeful sense ought to be set before the doors of the heart, which neither the sleep of negligence may overpower nor the error of ignorance deceive. Whence he is fitly called Isboseth who, with a woman as guard, is laid bare to the swords of the enemy. For Isboseth is called man of confusion. And the man of confusion is he who is not fortified with a strong guard of the mind, because while he thinks he is practising virtues, the vices creeping in kill him unawares. With all strength, therefore, the approach of the mind must be fortified, lest the enemies pierce it through the opening of a neglected thought.
4.6: **“And they entered into the house secretly taking ears of corn.”** — as if on account of firstfruits, that they might seem to be bringing them to the king and the guile might not be detected

5.1: **“THEN [THEY] CAME”** — So all nations come together to Christ and, as if coaxing, say: We are thy bone and thy flesh, when they love and venerate in him the incarnation which he took from our nature in the virgin's womb.
5.3:
**“The ancients also of Israel came”** — THE ANCIENTS OF ISRAEL. RABANUS. Prophets [and] apostles run together to Christ with equal faith and devotion.
**“AND THEY ANOINTED DAVID”** — RABANUS. David is said to have been anointed twice, and Christ took the sovereignty first among the Jews, afterwards among the gentiles.
5.4:
**“David was thirty years old when he began to reign,”** — at this age the Lord was baptized and began to have disciples
**“AND HE REIGNED FORTY YEARS”** — RABANUS. It is asked why forty years and six months are not counted in the sum. This is resolved by the Hebrews in two ways. For they say that David fled from his son Absalom for six months, and these were subtracted from the sum of his reign. They say also that for six months in Hebron he laboured under bodily infirmity, and therefore these ought not to be counted. For they say that he reigned in Hebron from the time when, having conquered the Amalecites, he sent presents from their spoils to the ancients of Juda, namely those who were in Hebron and in Bethel and wherever David had stayed. And that David began to reign at thirty years signifies that our Lord, when he was thirty years old, came to baptism and began to preach the gospel of the kingdom, whose kingdom is everlasting and his power eternal.
