And the number forty, which consists of four tens, signifies the perfection of times and things.
5.5: **“IN JERUSALEM”** — The Hebrews hand down that Sem, the son of Noe, whom they say was Melchisedech, founded Salem. This the Jebusites afterwards held, from whom it took the name Jebus. Hence JERUSALEM, as if Jebus-Salem, which afterwards from Solomon was called Hierosolyma, as if Hierosalomonia, and which was afterwards called Aelia by Aelius Hadrian.
5.6:
**“And the king and all the men that were with him went to Jerusalem to the Jebusites”** — who was of the race of the Chanaanites
**“the inhabitants of the land: and they said to David: Thou shalt not come in hither unless thou take away the blind and the lame”** — these the Jebusites had set upon the wall to mock David
**“THE BLIND AND THE LAME”** — As if [to say]: they are enough against thee; this they said trusting in their walls. Or thus: thou shalt not come in unless thou take away us, whom thou thinkest unarmed like the blind and the lame, and over whom thou thinkest to triumph.
5.7:
**“But David took the castle of Sion, the same is the city of David.”**
• that he might show his strength at the beginning of his reign
• RABANUS. David, casting out of Jerusalem the Jebusite, the inhabitant of the land, signifies Christ casting the opposing powers out of the hearts of the faithful and abiding there. For Jebusite is interpreted 'trodden down', Jerusalem 'vision of peace'. For not only did he gain the trophy of glory by destroying all the principality of the devil through the mystery of the cross, but he also gave his faithful power over all the might of the devil. Whence: "Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions" etc. Fittingly, then, David, the blind and the lame being cast out, dwelt in the castle of Sion and named it his city, because when Christ has driven the evil spirits and the crowd of vices out of the soul, he dwells there. And it is rightly called the castle of Sion, that is, 'of watching', that it may rightly be said of it: "His place is in peace, and his abode in Sion: there hath he broken the bow, the shield, the sword, and the battle."
• David took the castle of Sion, having first taken away the blind and the lame, who hated the soul of David. So the Lord gained the primacy in the Church of the gentiles, the scribes and Pharisees having first been rejected, who, blind and lame, hated the soul of Christ, that is, tried to take away his life.
**“BUT DAVID TOOK THE CASTLE”** — As Josephus says, when all were hastening to climb up, Joab the son of Sarvia got ahead of them all, and climbing to the summit he cried out to the king, claiming the chief command of the army. So the king, having driven the Jebusites out of the highest citadel and building the city, called it Hierosolyma, and dwelt in it all the time of his reign.
5.8:
**“For David had offered that day a reward”** — the chief command of the army
**“to whosoever should strike the Jebusites”** — namely whoever should climb up into the citadel by the hills below it and take it
**“and get up to”** — because, though the lower city was already taken, he could not get the citadel
**“OF THE TOPS OF THE HOUSES”** — That is, of the roofs. He calls 'gutters' the aqueducts made of lead or tile, through which the water went over the wall through the whole city.
**“and take away the blind and the lame”** — who were upon the wall
5.9: **“AND BUILT ROUND ABOUT FROM MELLO”** — That is, from the place so called; understand 'a wall'; and 'inwards', understand 'another wall'; that is, he fortified the city with a double wall.
5.11: **“AND HIRAM SENT”** — Hiram, 'living on high'. This is the gentile world exalted in Christ; it sends messengers to David, that is, teachers to Christ, and through them cedar trees, that is, the incorruptible and strong, and craftsmen, that is, those by whose art minds are incorrupt and squared like stones by the four virtues. So the house of David, that is, the Church of Christ, is built, and it is known that God has confirmed our David king over Israel, that is, over those who see God.
5.13:
**“CONCUBINES”** — [Concubines are] the churches of heretics, which boast that they abide under the title of the Christian name. But because they follow Christ for carnal gain, they are called not wives but concubines. But now, if kings have several wives or concubines, it is sin, because the figures have passed away, on account of which this was once pardonable.
**“and wives”** — the various churches
**“AND THERE WERE BORN TO DAVID”** — If Christ is signified by David, not unfittingly are Christians understood by his sons, those who are from the Jews and the nations, to whom the interpretations of the names agree: Samua 'boldness', Sobab 'turning', Jabaar 'he chose', Elisua 'salvation of my God', Nepheg 'applying to the mouth', Japhia 'he enlightens' or 'shows', Elisama 'my God hearing', Elida 'my God knows', Eliphaleth 'my God saving'.
5.14:
**“And these are the names of them, that were born to him in Jerusalem, Samua,”** — in First Paralipomenon: Simmaa
**“and Sobab, and Nathan, and Solomon,”** — these four sons were of Bethsabee, daughter of Ammiel
5.15:
**“And Jebahar,”** — in Paralipomenon: Jebaar
**“and Elisua, and Nepheg,”** — in Paralipomenon: Napheg
5.16:
**“And Japhia,”** — in Paralipomenon: Japhie
**“and Elisama, and Elioda,”** — in Paralipomenon: Eliade
**“and Eliphaleth.”** — in Paralipomenon: Eliphaleg.
5.20: **“BAAL PHARASIM”** — It is interpreted 'division of enemies'. The place can be said to have been so called because the Philistines left their idols in the place where they were divided.
5.21: **“And they left there their idols: which David took away”** — and also burned [them], as is declared in Paralipomenon
5.23:
**“And David consulted the Lord: Shall I go up against the Philistines, and wilt thou deliver them into my hands? He answered: Go not up against them.”** — elsewhere: against them
**“OF THE PEAR TREES”** — In the Hebrew 'of the weeping', that is, of the idols, namely where the idols were in which they trusted, which are called 'of the weeping' because they are worthy of weeping and lead their worshippers to weeping and misery.
5.24:
**“And when thou shalt hear”** — or: when thou shalt hear that their idols are crushed and trodden down by the angelic powers
**“IN THE TOPS OF THE PEAR TREES”** — Pirus [the pear tree] is so called from the Greek pyr, which is fire. The holy pear trees: the top is the loftiness of their life, in which, as the Holy Spirit breathed, the sound of preaching thundered. Which is [the sound] of one going, that is, the gift of him coming in the flesh. IN THE TOPS OF THE PEAR TREES, that is, above the height of the saints: while this sound is heard, the spiritual Philistines are overcome by our David.

6.1: **“And David again gathered together all the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand.”** — AND DAVID AGAIN GATHERED etc. David [signifies] Christ, the ark signifies the Church. David sought to bring the ark into his city, but, a cause intervening, he turned it aside elsewhere for a time and afterwards fulfilled what he had vowed; because the Lord, appearing in the flesh, preached the gospel to his own nation, but "blindness in part has happened in Israel, until the fulness of the gentiles should come in, and so all Israel should be saved." David gathered thirty thousand chosen men out of Israel, because the Lord established the primitive Church out of Israel, associating to himself not all but the chosen; "for not all that are of Israel are Israelites, but the children of the promission are accounted for the seed." They are called thirty thousand, that is, perfect in the firmness of faith, work and hope. For three, on account of the confession of the Trinity, pertains to faith; ten, on account of the decalogue, to works; a thousand, on account of its perfection, to the hope of eternal life, than which nothing is higher, as no number is greater than a thousand. For if thou sayest ten thousand, or thirty, or even a thousand thousand, thou dost not go beyond the thousand itself in counting, but multiplyest it, either by itself or by leading it more often through smaller numbers. Multiply three, then, by ten, lest "faith without works be dead"; likewise thirty by a thousand, that faith which worketh by charity may hope for its reward nowhere but in heaven. The chosen out of Israel, then, signify 'peoples rightly believing, working and hoping'. And the men of Juda who were with David signify 'the apostles and teachers', clinging as it were more familiarly to Christ's side; attended by these the Lord rejoices to bring the ark, that is, to enlarge the Church and to set it in the hearts of those who had not believed. The ark is set upon a new cart, that the grace of the new Testament may be poured into those renewed in baptism, and "new wine" be entrusted "to new bottles." The ark was indeed first in the house of Aminadab, who was in Gabaa, because the same faith which the preacher of the Church now [proclaims] flourished also before the time of the Lord's incarnation in those who followed the devotion of the patriarchs. For Aminadab, who is interpreted 'my God willing', signifies either 'Abraham the father of faith' or 'Moses the lawgiver', each of whom keeps the ark in Gabaa, because by a lofty example of virtue he fortifies the breasts of believers. Whence Gabaa too is interpreted 'hill', which is a place in the city of Cariathiarim. When the ark was brought out, David and all Israel played before the Lord with various instruments and kinds of musicians, because, as the proclamation of the new grace begins, the Lord invites all to render praises of humility to God the Father, saying: "If any man minister to me, let him follow me"; "to one is given by the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge, to another divers kinds of tongues" etc. But as the ark advanced with these and such kinds of gifts, that is, as the primitive Church grew, they came to the floor of Nachor, that is, the floor prepared in the Church of the gentiles to be consecrated by the truth of faith, of which it is said: "He will thoroughly cleanse his floor," where the priest who incautiously touched the ark, as if to correct it, soon fell struck by the Lord; because the people of the Jews, while it envies the gentiles, is deprived of the gift of salvation. While it wishes to mix the law with the gospel, it loses the grace of both. He held it because the oxen kicked. For the oxen to kick is for 'the preachers of the gospel' to act more freely concerning the faith, and not to walk according to the custom of the law, but to interpret the sabbaths, new moons, circumcision and victims spiritually. These, as if erring, they tried to correct who, coming down from Judea, taught the brethren: "Except you be circumcised after the manner of Moses, you cannot be saved."
6.2:
**“WHO SITTETH OVER IT UPON THE CHERUBIMS”** — Over the ark was a tablet which two cherubim covered with their wings, between whom the Lord appeared and spoke.
**“And David arose and went, with all the people that were with him of the men of Juda to fetch the ark of God, upon which the name of the Lord of hosts is invoked, who sitteth over it upon the cherubims.”** — GREGORY. In the history of David, king and prophet, in which he is said to have brought the ark of God, humility is shown approved, pride condemned and rashness punished. For David, who was not ashamed to dance humbly before the ark, soon deserved to receive the promise of the Son of God to be born of his stock; and the wife who despised his humility paid the penalty of perpetual barrenness. The priest also who rashly touched the ark purged the guilt of his daring by an untimely death. Here it is to be considered how greatly he sins who approaches the body of the Lord guilty, if he is punished with death who laid hold of the ark, the figure of the Lord's body, with less veneration than he ought.
**“GREGORY”** — Often, because they cannot be understood, the deeds or words of the better displease the worse. But they ought the less rashly to be blamed by them, the less they can be truly grasped. Often something is done by the greater by way of dispensation which is thought an error by the lesser. Often many things are said by the strong which the weak judge, because they do not understand them. This is well signified by that ark of the testament tilted by the kicking oxen, which the Levite, believing it would fall, wished to raise, and soon received the sentence of death. For what is the mind of the just man but the ark of the testament, which is tilted by the kicking oxen, because often even he who rules well, while he is shaken by compassion for his subjects, is moved from love alone to the condescension of dispensation. But in this, which is done by dispensation, the tilting of strength is thought a fall by the unskilled. Whence the subjects also put forth the hand of reproof against it, but by their very rashness they forthwith fail from life. The Levite, then, stretched out his hand as if helping, but by sinning lost his life, because when the weak reprove the deeds of the strong, they are rejected from the very lot of the living. Sometimes holy men say certain things condescending to the least, and put forth certain things contemplating the highest; and while the foolish do not know the force either of the condescension or of the height, they boldly blame these. And what is it to wish to correct a just man for his condescension, but to raise the tilted ark with the proud hand of reproof? What is it to blame a just man for speech not understood, but to think the movement of his strength the lapse of error? But he loses his life who proudly lifts up the ark of God, because no one presumes to correct the right things of the saints unless he first thinks better things of himself. Whence the Levite also is called Oza, that is, 'strong of the Lord', because the presumptuous, unless they believed themselves strong in the Lord, would not judge the deeds or words of the better as weak.
6.7:
**“And the indignation of the Lord was enkindled against Oza, and he struck him for his rashness.”** — that is, he was struck upon the shoulders, on which according to the law he ought to have carried the ark
**“And he died there before the ark of God”** — WHO DIED THERE etc. When the priest had died, he did not dare to turn the ark aside to himself into the city of David, but turned it aside into the house of Obededom the Gethite; because, when the Jews rejected the word, lest the preaching heard and not received should harm them the more, the apostles passed over to the gentiles. Whence the place of the floor of Nachor, which signifies 'the faith of the gentiles prepared for the grace of the Lord', is named the striking of Oza, because by their offence salvation came to the gentiles. For Obededom, who is interpreted 'a serving man', signifies him of whom it is said: "A people which I knew not hath served me: at the hearing of the ear" etc.; and, as it were, the death of Oza is set before it: "Thou wilt deliver me from the contradictions of the people." Geth also is interpreted 'winepress', signifying 'the cross', on which the true vine deigned to be trodden and pressed. From which the people can be called Gethite that says: "But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of the Lord."
6.11: **“THREE MONTHS”** — By which, namely, 'faith', 'hope' and 'charity' are signified. For as a month is filled up with days, so the single virtues come to perfection by their own equal steps. These months do not cease to run "until the fulness of the gentiles come in." At length David, returning, will bring the ark back into the city of the Lord, because Christ, through the preaching of Elias and Henoch, will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, sacrificing oxen and rams, that is, crowning in the blood of martyrdom those who thresh the floor of the Lord and lead the flock of sheep.
6.12: **“And it was told king David, that”** — or: that
6.13: **“And when they that carried the ark of the Lord had gone”** — on their shoulders, lest they be struck as Oza was
6.14:
**“ON INSTRUMENTS 'ARMIGATA' [so the edition]”** — That is, bound to the shoulder [armum ligatis] while they are touched by the hands of the bearer. Another kind of instrument is that which is made with water.
**“EPHOD”** — Not in a pontifical but in a linen garment, for the sake of humility. Flax, brought forth from the earth, comes with much labour to the whiteness of a garment; and the humanity assumed by the Word triumphed amid the scourges.
6.16:
**“And when the ark of the Lord was come into the city of David, Michol”**
• 'all water' or 'water from all'
• AND WHEN THE ARK OF THE LORD WAS COME INTO THE CITY etc. While all rejoice and sound hymns at the entrance of the heavenly ark, Michol the daughter of Saul alone is absent, and from the spectacle despises David humbled; because, when the Jews believe at the end of the world, many will follow Christ in profession but Antichrist in deed. To them it fits that Michol (who, to figure 'the instability of the carnal', is interpreted 'all water') is called not the wife of David but the daughter of Saul, because those who serve Christ as far as faith [only] are not to be crowned in his kingdom, but to be condemned with the anathema of his persecutors, whom they imitate. But though the wicked be angry and despise the humility of the Church, nonetheless the ark of the Lord enters its place and is set in the midst of the tabernacle which David had pitched for it; that is, the faith of the Church is preached, advances, and is set in the hearts of all whom God has foreordained to eternal life. David offers holocausts and peace offerings before the Lord: Christ commends the faith and devotion of the Church to the Father, he who "is at the right hand of God, who also maketh intercession for us"; who, after the example of David, blessing the faithful and humble, feeds them with the food of the saving mystery. He distributes to each one cake of bread, namely of him who "cometh down from heaven, and giveth life to the world"; and one piece of roasted beef, namely of that fatted calf which was slain for the returning son and roasted in the fire of the passion, saying: "My strength is dried up like a potsherd"; and fine flour fried with oil, namely the flesh most pure from the stain of sin, but, for the sake of human salvation, most rich in delights, cooked in the frying pan of the cross. Fittingly one cake of one bread [and] one piece of roasted flesh is given, because there is "one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father" almighty. Otherwise: the faithful receive these gifts when, many being one bread and one body in Christ, each of them chastises the wantonness of his flesh and brings it into subjection. They cook [it] in the fire of the Spirit, and make the fruits of good works, most rich with the oil of mercy, to seethe with compassion for their neighbour. But on the contrary the daughter of Saul, having entered the king's chamber, gives no fruit of conceived seed, because those who receive the word of God with the ear only await the day of perpetual death without the offspring of good work.
**“the daughter of Saul, looking out through a window, saw king David leaping and dancing before the Lord”** — because the gesture of the body belonged to the voice of the singer. Whence: "We have piped to you, and you have not danced"
6.19:
**“And he distributed to all the multitude of Israel both men and women, to every one, a cake of bread”** — it is a small three-cornered loaf
**“and a piece of roasted beef”** — from bos [ox] is named the bubalus, wild and untamed
**“and fine flour fried with oil”** — small loaves first baked, then fried in oil
6.20:
**“And David returned to bless his own house”** — as before he blessed the people, so now he blesses his household, that is, distributes the feast
**“and Michol the daughter of Saul coming out to meet David, said:”** — AND MICHOL THE DAUGHTER OF SAUL CAME OUT etc. GREGORY. It is good to consider what great gifts of virtues David had received, and in all these how strong he kept himself by humility. For whom would it not lift up to break the jaws of lions, to tear apart the arms of bears, to be chosen when his elder brothers were passed over, to be anointed to the government of the kingdom when the king was rejected, to lay low with one stone Goliath, feared by all, to bring back the numerous foreskins proposed by the king when the aliens were slain, to receive at length the promised kingdom, and to possess the whole people of Israel without any gainsaying? And yet, when he brings the ark of God back into Jerusalem, as if forgetting that he was set over all, mingled with the people he dances before the ark. And because to dance before the ark had been (as is believed) the custom of the common people, the king whirls himself in the dance in divine service. Behold, he whom the Lord preferred singularly to all makes himself equal to the least beneath the Lord and despises himself by showing himself abject. The power of the kingdom is not called to mind; he does not fear to grow vile by dancing in the eyes of his subjects; he does not acknowledge himself set in honour above the rest before the ark of him who had given the honour. Before God he did weak or the lowest things, that by humility he might make firm those brave things which he had done before men. What others think of these deeds I do not know; I am more amazed at David dancing than fighting. By fighting he subdued the enemy; by dancing before the Lord he conquered himself. When Michol, the daughter of Saul, still mad with the swelling of royal birth, despised him humbled, saying: How glorious was the king today, uncovering himself before the handmaids of his servants, and was naked, as if one of the buffoons, she forthwith heard: I will play before the Lord, who chose me rather than thy father; and a little after: I will both play and make myself meaner than I have done, and I will be humble in my own eyes. As if he should say: I seek to be vile before men, because I seek to keep my nobility before God through humility. There are some who think humbly of themselves, who, placed in honours, weigh themselves as nothing but dust and ashes, but shrink from appearing vile before men, and, against what they think of themselves within, cloak themselves outwardly as it were with a stiff comeliness. And there are some who desire to be seen as vile by men, and despise all that they are by showing themselves cast down, but within themselves swell as if from the very merit of the vileness they have shown, and are the more lifted up in heart the more they press down elation in appearance. Both these wars of elation David detected with great circumspection and overcame with wonderful virtue. For that, thinking humbly of himself within, he does not seek honour outwardly, he intimates by saying: I will play and make myself meaner. And because through showing himself vile outwardly he does not swell inwardly, he adds: and I will be humble in my own eyes; as if he should say: such as I show myself outwardly, such I regard myself inwardly. What then will they do whom learning lifts up, if David, who knew that the Redeemer would come of his flesh and announced his joys by prophesying, nevertheless pressed down in himself the neck of the heart with the strong heel of discretion, saying: and I will be humble in my own eyes?
**“How glorious was the king of Israel today, uncovering himself before the handmaids of his servants”** — GLORIOUS etc. David, when he brought the ark over into Jerusalem, was mocked by Michol. And Christ, when he brought the New Testament over into his Church, was a mockery to the Jews on the cross; he appeared naked while, hiding his power from them, he showed the infirmity of the flesh as a linen ephod. The handmaids of the servants bear the person of the saints, among whom he was made more glorious through the triumph of the cross; and while Michol mocks him, he appears more glorious to the handmaids, while she, in the type of the Synagogue, remained barren.
**“AND WAS NAKED”** — Naked not altogether, but of his royal garments; and because he was not ashamed to humble himself before the Lord, he soon deserved to receive the promise of the Son of God to be born of his stock.

7.3:
**“ALL THAT IS”** — It is plain that the Spirit of prophecy does not always shine upon the minds of the prophets: "For the Spirit breatheth where he will." Hence Eliseus says: "The Lord hath hid it from me, and hath not told me." Which God orders by a dispensation of mercy, because while he gives and withdraws the Spirit of prophecy, he both lifts up the minds of the prophets to the heights and keeps them in humility, that, receiving the Spirit, they may find what they are from God, and again, not having the Spirit of prophecy, they may know what they are of themselves.
**“GREGORY”** — He who takes care to correct others ought to be clean of vices in himself, that he may not think on earthly things, that he may not yield to the lowest desires, so that he may see the more clearly what others must flee, the more truly he himself avoids these through knowledge and life. The eye which dust weighs down does not see clearly a blemish in a limb, and hands that hold mud cannot wipe away the filth laid upon [something]. Which, according to the ancient translation, is well said by way of signification to David, labouring in outward wars: "Thou shalt not build me a temple, because thou art a man of blood." He builds the temple of God who gives himself to correcting and instructing the minds of his neighbours. We are the temple of God, who are built up for the true life by his indwelling. Whence: "The temple of God is holy, which you are." But the man of blood is forbidden to build the temple of God, because he who still lies upon carnal acts must needs be ashamed to instruct the minds of his neighbours.
7.5: **“Go, and say to my servant David: Thus saith the Lord: Shalt thou build me a house to dwell in?”** — as if [to say]: not, "because thou art a man of blood"
7.7:
**“In all the places”** — Silo, Galgala, Nobe and the other places where the tabernacle and the ark of the Lord were placed
**“that I have gone through with all the children of Israel, did ever I speak a word to any one of the tribes of Israel, whom I commanded to feed my people Israel, saying: Why have you not built me a house of cedar?”** — DID EVER I SPEAK A WORD etc. To any judge of the tribes of Israel: WHOM I COMMANDED TO FEED MY PEOPLE ISRAEL, WHY HAST THOU NOT BUILT ME A HOUSE OF CEDAR. Therefore he commanded that no house of cedar be built for him by any of the judges, because all fought against the enemies and were shedders of blood. But thy son, upon whom the wars of enemies shall not press and who shall not be a man of blood: "He shall build me a house."
7.9: **“And I have been with thee wheresoever thou hast walked, and have slain all thy enemies from before thy face: and I have made thee a great man, like unto the name of the great ones that are on the earth”** — Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, Moses and Josue, whose names are famous on the earth
7.10:
**“And I will appoint a place”** — heaven
**“AND I WILL APPOINT A PLACE”** — He describes the time of Solomon, in which the children of Israel had peace on every side and were not afflicted as in the time of the Judges.
**“for my people Israel”** — the spiritual [Israel]
**“and I will plant them, and they shall dwell therein, and shall be disturbed no more: neither shall the children of iniquity [afflict them] any more”** — he who hopes for such great goods on earth is foolishly wise
7.11: **“From the day that I appointed judges over my people Israel: and I will give thee rest from all thy enemies. And the Lord foretelleth to thee, that the Lord will make thee a house”** — that is, sons succeeding thee
7.12:
**“And when thy days shall be fulfilled, and thou shalt sleep with thy fathers, I will raise up thy seed”**
• Christ
• which [is] not of Solomon
7.14:
**“I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son: and if he commit any”** — in his members
**“iniquity, I will correct him”** — Solomon
**“with the rod of men”** — by the sword of enemies
**“and with the stripes of the children”** — by afflictions of the body
**“of men.”** — who deserve such things
7.16: **“AND THY HOUSE SHALL BE FAITHFUL”** — This is truly said of Christ. For the house of Solomon was full of foreign women worshipping false gods and driving Solomon himself to the same. But in Christ these things are fulfilled, who is "of the seed of David according to the flesh." The Jews understand the son of David promised in this place to be Solomon, and still, with wonderful blindness, say that they hope for another. There was indeed another image of the thing to come in Solomon, because he built the temple and had peace according to his name; for Solomon is interpreted 'peaceable'. At the beginning of his reign he was praiseworthy, but he foretold Christ, he did not show him; whence certain things are written of him as though foretold of [Christ] himself, while Scripture paints in him the figure of things to come. For in the Psalm which is entitled with his name many things are said which cannot fit him, but evidently fit Christ: for in Solomon is the figure, in Christ the truth. For it is known within what bounds the kingdom of Solomon was enclosed, whereas there it is read: "He shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river unto the ends of the earth." But Christ took the beginning of his rule from the river, where, baptized by John and pointed out by him, he began to be acknowledged by the disciples, who called him not only master but also Lord. Nor did he begin to reign while his father was still living (which befell none of those kings) for any other reason than that it might appear that he is not the one whom the prophecy foreshows, saying: When thy days shall be fulfilled and thou shalt sleep with thy fathers, I will raise up thy seed after thee etc. For this is the true peaceable one, who is prophesied to be raised up not before, as Solomon was, but after the death of David; who built a house to God not of wood and stones but of men. Whence: "The temple of God is holy, which you are." For the blessing of the Lord upon the seed of David is to be hoped for for ever; whence with most certain hope it is said, so be it, so be it, according to that: "Blessed be the Lord for evermore. So be it. So be it." And the repetition itself is the confirmation of hope. Whence David: "And thou hast spoken also of the house of thy servant for a long time to come." Then he added: "Now begin, and bless the house of thy servant for ever," because then he was to beget a son, from whom his progeny would be reckoned to Christ. Therefore, since according to the Seventy it was said in the words of Nathan: "And the Lord will tell thee that thou shalt build a house for him," afterwards David himself says: "Because thou, O Lord God almighty, God of Israel, hast revealed to the ear of thy servant, saying: I will build thee a house." For this house we build by living well, and God by helping. When the last dedication of this house shall come, that will be fulfilled which was said by Nathan: "And I will appoint a place for my people Israel, and I will plant them, and they shall dwell apart, and shall be troubled no more; and the son of iniquity shall not afflict them any more, as from the beginning, from the days when I appointed judges over my people Israel." For there were judges before there were kings, and the son of iniquity, that is, the foreign enemy, afflicted the people at intervals of time; and periods of peace are found there longer than Solomon had, who reigned forty years. For under the judge Aod, the son of iniquity [having] afflicted the people, there was peace for eighty years. These things, then, were not promised under Solomon, nor did any of those kings reign in such peace that that nation was not troubled. The place of so peaceful and secure a dwelling, then, is eternal, where there will be the true Israel, that is, seeing God.
7.18:
**“And David went in, and sat before the Lord.”** — namely the ark of the Lord
**“AND SAT BEFORE THE LORD”** — To sit before the Lord is to confess his benefits in humility.
**“And said: Who am I, O Lord God, and what is my house, that thou hast brought me thus far?”** — to the kingdom
7.19: **“But yet this hath seemed little in thy sight, O Lord God, unless thou didst also speak of the house of thy servant for a long time to come: for this is the law of Adam, O Lord God.”** — THE LAW OF ADAM, O LORD, namely of man: that he serve thee in simplicity of heart and purity, and thou do to him according to thy mercy, as thou hast done to me.
7.21:
**“For thy word's sake,”** — namely which thou didst promise to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob
**“and according to thy own heart”** — thy mercy, namely BECAUSE THERE IS NONE LIKE TO THEE
**“thou hast done”** — for me
**“all these great things, so that thou wouldst make it known”** — what thou art about to do
7.23:
**“WHAT IS THERE”** — On the earth, other than the chosen [nation], for whose sake the Son of God came into the world as into Egypt, that by the exchange of his blood he might redeem to himself an acceptable people, a pursuer of good works. And by the God of that same people we understand the Lord's man, whom he took up out of Egypt, that is, the world, through the virgin's womb.
**“as thy people Israel, a nation upon earth, whom God went to redeem for a people to himself, and to make him a name, and to do for them great and terrible things, upon the earth, before the face of thy people, whom thou redeemedst to thyself out of Egypt, the nation and its god.”** — in the Hebrew: from the nations and their gods; as if [to say]: thou didst destroy the Egyptians in the Red Sea and didst execute judgments on their gods
**“OUT OF EGYPT”** — 'From the nation and its god', or 'the nation and its god': the nation Israel and its god Moses, of whom [it is said]: "I have appointed thee the God of Pharao."
7.25: **“And now, O Lord God, raise up for ever the word that thou hast spoken, concerning thy servant and concerning his house”** — accomplish it in deed, namely the son of David, through whom my house may be established for ever
7.26: **“That thy name may be magnified for ever, and it may be said: The Lord of hosts is God over Israel. And the house”** — the Church
7.27:
**“Because thou, O Lord of hosts, God of Israel, hast revealed to the ear of thy servant,”** — Nathan
**“saying:”** — through the prophet
**“I will build thee a house.”** — namely because THOU HAST REVEALED TO THE EAR OF THY SERVANT
**“Therefore hath thy servant found in his heart”**
• the boldness of heart
• FOUND HIS HEART. Nothing is more fleeting than the heart, which is found when it is held in by discretion.

8.1:
**“THE BRIDLE”** — Christ, triumphing over the powers of the air, broke the bridle of error which they had put upon the human race.
**“THE BRIDLE OF TRIBUTE”** — There were five cities of the Philistines which made Israel tributary. These David took for himself and made tributary, as is read in Paralipomenon: "David smote the Philistines, and humbled them, and took Geth and her towns out of their hand" etc.
8.2:
**“And he defeated Moab, and measured them with a line, casting them down to the earth:”** — hyperbole
**“CASTING THEM DOWN TO THE EARTH”** — For the men living on the earth were not humbled so far that, when the line was stretched over them, they appeared level with the ground, but [they were made] so vile and despised that they were worth no more than land that has no men. And he put 'line' for 'lot', because land is wont to be measured with a line, according to that: "and by lot divided to them the land by a line of distribution." It signifies that he divided the regions of the Moabites to whom he would as freely as a possessor his own fields. And he measured two lines, one to put to death and one to save alive: it signifies that he could kill whom he would and spare whom he would. And that he made Moab, which is interpreted 'from a part', and Syria of Damascus and the other regions tributary, signifies that Christ holds and presses all nations under his dominion and exacts the tribute of good works. For Damascus, a noble city of Phenicia, is called by the same word as Maseth, the son of Abraham's handmaid, and is interpreted 'cup of blood'; and Syria 'lofty' or 'moist'. For she who before, moist with lust, insatiably thirsted for human blood, now, cleansed by the baptism of Christ and lofty in the advance of virtues, desires the cup of his blood.
**“and he measured with two lines, one to put to death”** — the Lord Jesus condemns whom he will for their sins, and quickens whom he will, condemning their sins
8.6: **“And David put garrisons in Syria of Damascus”** — that is, [men] who might make it safe for him
8.11: **“AND KING DAVID DEDICATED”** — So Christ sanctifies to the Lord all whom he calls together from the gentiles, making some as gold, that is, of spiritual understanding, others as silver, that is, shining with the brightness of eloquence, others as brass, resounding with preaching, that they may faithfully serve his tabernacle.
8.13:
**“David also made himself a name”** — namely he raised for himself a triumphal arch
**“KILLING EIGHTEEN [THOUSAND]”** — That in certain manuscripts twelve thousand are said to have been slain has grown up by the fault of the scribes. For David truly slew eighteen thousand in the valley of the Saltpits, but Joab twelve thousand, as is written in the title of the fifty-eighth psalm. And it is signified that Christ, by the strictness of his examination, extinguishes in those who think wrongly of him the folly of immoderate savour.
8.16: **“And Joab the son of Sarvia was over the army: and Josaphat the son of Ahilud was recorder:”** — RECORDER. He acted in the king's stead, by whose judgment the laws were written. The scribe wrote down the words from the king's mouth.
8.17: **“THE PRIESTS”** — Priests [sacerdotes], as if 'sacred leader' [sacer dux]. And the sons of David held the leadership in the tribe of Juda.
8.18: **“And Banaias the son of Joiada was over the Cerethi and Phelethi: and the sons of David were the priests”** — CERETHI etc. They stood by the king guarding his body, and they are interpreted 'killing' and 'quickening', since according to their judgment the worthy were kept for life, others were led to death.

9.1: **“And David said: Is there any one, think you, left of the house of Saul, that I may shew kindness to him for Jonathan's sake?”** — IS THERE ANY ONE, THINK YOU etc. Behold, David did not forget the oath and covenant which he made with Jonathan, but fulfilled to the son the mercy which he had promised to the father. David also signifies Christ; Jonathan, who is interpreted 'gift of the dove' or 'gift of the Lord', [signifies] 'the grace of the Holy Spirit'. Jonathan, then, had a little son named Miphiboseth, lame of both feet, whom David called to himself, when the predestination and foreknowledge of God chooses for the ministry of God him whom it sees weak in word and deed for pursuing the desires of the world and worldly business; because him whom the world spurns through the pride of elation, God acquires on account of the devotion of humility. For Miphiboseth is interpreted 'shame from the mouth'. For he whose speech and presence the pride of the world despises will, by the gift of God, appear useful for spiritual ministry in the Church. And what does it mean that David, questioning Siba, the servant of Saul, about his stock, found Miphiboseth, but that Christ, sifting the number of the elect, makes those come to him who, despised, have left the world? For Siba is interpreted 'he came out', Machir 'selling' or 'from weakness', Ammiel 'his people God', Lodabar 'he the word'. And so our David, choosing the contemptible things of this world, and the things that are not, that he may bring to nought the things that are, finding them saleable to the world and set in weakness, joins them, made worthy by the word of preaching, to his people, and grants them royal honour among his sons. Whence David also gave the fields of Saul and the services [of Siba] to Miphiboseth, and commanded him to be at his table with his sons; because Christ, who "raiseth up the needy from the dunghill, that he may sit with princes, and hold the throne of glory," taking contemptible persons out of the world, makes them possessors of virtues and refreshes them daily at the table of the Scriptures. And such beget a son who is called Micha, that is, 'who is this?', because they come to the wonder of the people, who, lately despised in the world, appear glorious in the Church.
9.3: **“And the king said: Is”** — or: is there
9.11: **“And Siba said to the king: As thou my lord the king hast commanded thy servant, so will thy servant do: and Miphiboseth shall eat at thy table”** — or: my

10.2: **“And David said: I will shew kindness”** — I WILL SHEW KINDNESS etc. When David fled from the face of Achis king of Geth, he came to Naas king of Ammon, who showed him kindness. From Naas, then, he came into the cave of Odollam, where his father and mother and all his house came to him. Thence he went on to Moab and left with him his father and mother and all his house. And as to what Achis king of Geth said: "Shall this fellow come into my house?" "David therefore went from thence, and fled to the cave of Odollam", it must be understood: from the house of Naas. If it is asked why he returned to Achis, whom he had first fled, it is to be understood that he to whom he returned was the son of him whom he fled; whence in what follows Achis, with whom David was going down to battle, is said to have been the son of Maoch. For he took this patronymic not from his father but from his mother, who was called Maacha.
10.4:
**“Wherefore Hanon took the servants of David, and shaved off the one half of their beards”**
• and the devil snatches away their former strength
• WHEREFORE HANON TOOK THE SERVANTS OF DAVID etc. These things signify the war of the devil against the Church. For Hanon, that is, 'their grief', signifies 'the devil', who is the ruler of the Ammonites, that is, of the evil spirits, that is, of a people of sorrow, always set in straits, who desires to press men down or straiten them. Hanon, then, shaves half the beard of David's messengers when the devil stains the speech or conduct of certain preachers by corrupting it. He cuts their garments even to the groin when he reveals in the eyes of men the shameful deeds to which he persuades them. These must needs sit in Jericho until their beard grows, lest they be a reproach to others and an anathema to all, that is, until the increase of virtues springs up in them and they are held worthy to be presented to their king. But our David does not suffer his soldiers to be unavenged, but, gathering an army, avenges the injury of his own; and not only does he confound the adversaries through the victory of his saints, but also at the last judgment delivers them to everlasting fires.
**“and cut away half of their garments even to the buttocks, and sent them away.”** — and the devil strips bare the dignity of chastity and reveals the shameful things to which he persuaded
10.5: **“When this was told David, he sent to meet them: for the men were sadly put to confusion, and David commanded them, saying: Stay at Jericho”** — under the ban of penance
10.15: **“Then the Syrians seeing”** — elsewhere: Then the children of Ammon seeing that the Syrian was afraid, and
10.17: **“And when this was told David, he gathered all Israel together, and passed over the Jordan, and came to Helam: and the Syrians set themselves in array against David, and fought against him”** — elsewhere: Israel

11.1:
**“And it came to pass at the return of the year, at the time when kings go forth to war,”**
• AT THE TIME WHEN [KINGS] ARE WONT etc., that is, in spring, when, the harshness of the cold being driven off, fodder is found for the beasts.
• In the Hebrew it reads thus: at the time when the kings had gone forth to war, David sent Joab etc. That is, the kings of Rohob and Istob, Soba and Maacha, who were kings of Syria and wished to fight against David, hired by the king of Moab [so the edition], had gone forth to battle against David, but they were defeated.
**“that David sent Joab and his servants with him, and all Israel, and they spoiled the children of Ammon, and besieged Rabbath”** — or: Rabba
11.2:
**“In the mean time it happened [one day] that David arose”** — "strong of hand" or "desirable to see"
**“IN THE MEAN TIME IT HAPPENED”** — David sinned grievously, for which God both rebuked him through the prophet and he himself washed it away by repenting. But that one, desirable to all nations, walking as it were upon the roof, "set his tabernacle in the sun," and loved the Church washing herself upon the roof, that is, cleansing herself from the filth of the world and by spiritual contemplation passing over and treading down the house of clay. And having begun with her the acquaintance of the first meeting, he killed the devil, separated from her, and joined her to himself for ever. Let us hate the sin, then, but not extinguish the prophecy. Let us love that David as much as he is to be loved, who by mercy freed us from the devil. Let us love this penitent, who healed so grievous a wound of sin by the confession of humility.
**“from his bed after noon”** — the world now declining
**“and walked upon the roof”** — he set his tabernacle in the sun, namely the body which he assumed he laid open to all
**“of the king's house: and he saw a woman washing herself”** — on account of the menstrual flow, as some will have it
11.3:
**“BETHSABEE”** — ISIDORE. 'Well of fulness' or 'seventh well'. And the Church is called 'well of living water', and to this well the name of the number seven is joined in signification of the Holy Spirit, by reason of Pentecost, on which day the Holy Spirit was sent from heaven. To forty-nine, that is, seven times seven, one is added, since unity is commended. Whence: "careful to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace." By the spiritual gift, then, that is, the sevenfold, the Church has been made a well of fulness, because there has been made in her a fountain of water springing up into life everlasting, of which "whosoever drinketh shall not thirst for ever."
**“GREGORY”**
• Still weighed down by the burden of corruptible flesh, we cannot so live that no delight of sin can strike at us. But it is one thing to be touched unwilling, another consenting. Holy men guard themselves with the more watchful circumspection, the more they disdain to be struck by evil motions even in passing, so that if the heart should by chance desire anything unlawful, the eye, held in by the mastery of discipline, would refuse to see it. For as temptation is often drawn in through the eyes, so sometimes, conceived within, it compels the eyes outwardly to serve it. For very often a thing is looked at with an innocent mind, but in the very sight the soul is pierced with the sword of concupiscence. For David did not look at the wife of Urias of set purpose because he had desired her, but rather desired her because he looked incautiously. By a just weighing of retribution, he who uses the outward eye negligently is blinded in the inward. And often concupiscence already rules within, and the enticed soul demands like a tyrant that the bodily senses serve its uses, and compels the eyes to serve its pleasures, and opens the windows of light to the darkness of blindness. Whence holy men, when they feel themselves struck by evil delight, restrain by the mastery of discipline the very eyes through which the image of beauty enters the mind, lest sight serve as pander to a wicked thought. And if this is ever neglected to be guarded carefully, the uncleanness of thought passes over into act.
• Often a thing is a virtue in history [and] a fault in signification, just as sometimes a fault in the deed is a virtue in the writing of prophecy. For who would not detest that David, walking on the roof, desired Bethsabee, the wife of Urias? Whom, returning from battle, he urges to go home and wash his feet; who at once answered, saying: The ark of God is under skins, and shall I rest in my house? Whom David received at his own table and gave him the dishes by which he was to die. David, then, holds the figure of him of whom it is written: "He hath set his tabernacle in the sun." He orders Bethsabee to be brought to him, that is, the law of the letter, joined to the carnal people, to associate to himself by spiritual understanding. For Bethsabee is called 'well of seven', because through the knowledge of the law, by the infusion of spiritual grace, perfect wisdom is ministered to us. And Urias signifies 'the Jewish people', [he] who is interpreted 'my light of God'. For the Jewish people, which is lifted up by the knowledge of the law it received, glories as it were in the light of God. But David took his wife from him and joined her to himself, because the Redeemer, appearing strong of hand, when he made known that the law spoke spiritually of him, by this, that it was held according to the letter, showed it to be estranged from the Jewish people and joined it to himself, because he declared himself to be preached by it. Yet he urges Urias to go home and wash his feet, because, incarnate, he commands the Jews to return to their conscience and wipe away the filth of their works with weeping, that they may understand the commands of the law spiritually, and, after so great hardness of precepts finding the fountain of baptism, may run to the water after their labour. But Urias, who remembers that the ark of the Lord is under skins, answers that he cannot enter his house; as if he should say: I see the commands of God in carnal sacrifices, and I do not seek to return to conscience through spiritual understanding. For he says as it were that the ark of God is under skins, because he understands the precepts of God only in performing the ministry of carnal sacrifice. Yet when he will not return home, David calls him to the table, because, though the Jews scorn to return to their conscience, Christ nevertheless preaches spiritual things, saying: "For if you did believe Moses, you would perhaps believe me also; for he wrote of me." For the Jew holds the law which speaks of his divinity, in whom he disdains to believe. Whence also Urias is sent to Joab with letters by which he is to be killed, because the Jew carries the law by whose conviction he is to die. For when, retaining the commands of the law, he strives to fulfil them, he himself brings the judgment by which he is condemned. What, then, in this deed is more wicked than David? What purer than Urias? But in the mystery, what is holier than David? What more faithless than Urias? Because he through the fault of his life signifies the innocence of prophecy, and this one through the innocence of his life expresses fault in prophecy. For the power of the sacred word so narrates things done as to express things to come; so approves a thing in the deed as to gainsay it in the mystery; so condemns things done as to urge that they be done mystically.
• The sins of David and of Peter are set down in Scripture to this end, that the fall of the greater may be a caution to the lesser. Penance and pardon are made known to this end, that the recovery of the lost may be the hope of the perishing. Let no one be proud at David falling from his state; let no one despair at David rising again from his lapse. Wonderfully does Scripture by the same word press down the proud by which it lifts up the humble. For it related one deed, and in a different manner called back the proud to the fear of humility, the humble to the confidence of hope. An inestimable medicine of a new kind, which, applied in the same way, both dries up swellings by pressing and fills up dry places by lifting. It has terrified us by the fall of the greater, but strengthened us by their restoration. So the mercy of the divine dispensation both represses us when proud and props us lest we fall through despair. But perhaps the reader's mind is moved [to ask] why God does not guard from vices those whom he chooses and takes up to the height of spiritual gifts. But many, through the gifts of virtues received, through the grace of good works bestowed, fall into pride, and yet do not know that they have fallen. Against them, then, the ancient enemy, who already rules within, is permitted to rage without, that those who are lifted up in thought may be laid low through the lust of the flesh. And sometimes it is less to fall in corruption of the body than to sin by silent thought from deliberate elation. But because pride is thought less shameful, it is less avoided. Men blush at lust the more because all alike know it to be shameful. Therefore many, falling through or after pride into lust, blush from their open fall at the evil of their hidden fault, and correct the greater, since, laid low in the least, they are more heavily confounded. For they see themselves guilty among the lesser who believed themselves free among the graver. So by the gracious dispensation of the Lord, the evil spirit often drags those let loose from fault to fault, and the more he strikes, the more he loses him whom he had taken, and is overcome by that whereby he is seen to have conquered. It is good to consider with how great favour of mercy God holds us within the fortified bosom of grace. Behold, he who was lifted up by virtue returns to humility through vice. And he who is lifted up by virtues received is wounded not with a sword but with a medicine. For virtue is a medicine, vice a wound. Because, then, we make a wound of the medicine, he makes a medicine of the wound, that he who is struck by virtue may be cured by vice. For we turn the gifts of virtues to the use of vices; he takes up the enticements of vices into the citadel of virtues, and strikes the state of health that he may preserve it, that we who flee the humility of the healer may at least cling to him when we fall. But many, the more they fall in many things, are bound the more tightly; and when the ancient enemy strikes them with one vice so that they fall, he binds them with another lest they rise. Let a man consider, then, with what adversary he wages war, and if he perceives that he has already offended in something, let him at least fear to be dragged from fault into fault, and let the wounds by which he often kills be zealously avoided, because it is very rare that our enemy serves the salvation of the elect even by his wounds. For the Lord often subjects the elect to the tempter to instruct them, as after the enclosures of paradise, after the secrets of the third heaven, lest Paul should be exalted by the greatness of the revelations, there was given him an angel of Satan. But it is arranged by this temptation that those who could have perished lifted up may be saved humbled. By the secret order of dispensation, then, the kindness of God is perfected by that whereby the iniquity of the devil is permitted to rage, because it obeys the nods of heavenly grace by that whereby it exercises the wrath of its own will.
**“the daughter of Eliam, the wife of Urias the Hethite”** — that is, of the devil, who falsely said 'my light of God', and therefore was deservedly cut off from the land of the living. For Hethite [means] 'cut off'
11.4: **“And David sent messengers, and took her, and she came in to him, and he slept with her: and presently she was purified from her uncleanness”** — that is, from the menstrual flow
11.8:
**“And David said to Urias: Go into thy house, and wash thy feet.”** — after labour use the baths: he put a part for the whole body, for so great a man did not go about barefoot
**“And Urias went out from the king's house, and there went out after him a mess of meat from the king.”** — that, delicately refreshed and stirred by desire, he might sleep with his wife, and so the adultery might lie hidden
11.25: **“And David said to the messenger: Thus shalt thou say to Joab: Let not this thing discourage thee: for various is the event of battle”** — or: of war
11.27: **“And the mourning being over, David sent and brought her into his house, and she became his wife”** — now the obstinacy of the fault has no occasion of defence, and therefore the prophet is rightly sent

12.1: **“And the Lord sent Nathan to David: and when he was come to him, he said to him: There were two men in one city, the one rich, and the other poor.”** — when the prelates of the Church rebuke the powerful, they first bring in certain similitudes as if about another's business
12.5: **“And David's anger being exceedingly kindled against that man”** — after the similitudes the powerful pronounce a right sentence against themselves as if against another
12.7:
**“And Nathan said to David:”** — at length let the prelates, in fitting ways, strike the powerful for their own guilt, when they are no longer raised up in any defence of themselves, being bound by the sentence of their own mouth
**“Thou art the man. Thus saith the Lord the God of Israel: I anointed thee king over Israel, and I delivered thee from the hand”** — elsewhere: house
12.13:
**“And David said to Nathan: I have sinned against the Lord.”** — he who humbly confesses will soon obtain pardon
**“And Nathan said”** — AND NATHAN SAID. Yet all the things that were foretold to him for his sin he afterwards endured. God blots out the offence but does not leave it unpunished. For either man, repenting, punishes it in himself, or God, avenging it with the man, strikes. The sin, therefore, is not spared, because it is not remitted without punishment. So David deserved to hear after his confession: The Lord hath taken away thy sin; and yet, afflicted afterwards with many torments, fleeing, he paid the guilt of the fault he had committed. So we are absolved by the wave of salvation from the fault of our first parent, but even when absolved we still die in the flesh; because God cuts away our offences, either through us or through himself, even when he remits them. For from his elect he is careful to wipe away by temporal affliction the stains of iniquities which he does not wish to see in them for ever.
12.14:
**“Nevertheless, because thou hast given occasion to the enemies of the Lord to blaspheme [his] name”** — among the gentiles it is held wicked if anyone claims another's wife for himself by force, especially one who rules
**“for this thing”** — because he had set such a king over [them]
12.16: **“And David besought the Lord for the child: and David kept a fast, and going in by himself lay upon the ground.”** — let us too fast and lie upon the ground, until the desire of sin be utterly abolished
12.25: **“And he sent by the hand of Nathan the prophet, and called his name, Amiable to the Lord”** — in the Hebrew Idida, that is, beloved of the Lord, on account of the Lord, namely on account of the free mercy by which he deigned to love him, though he was born of an unlawful union [manzer].
12.26: **“And Joab fought against Rabbath”** — when it is written with the addition, Rabbath, as here; when without the addition, Rabba
12.27:
**“And Joab sent”** — AND JOAB SENT. This victory of David, which Joab began and he himself completed, signifies the victory of our king. For the captain wages war against the enemies when the order of preachers sets the shield of faith against the powerful of the world. But the victory is referred to Christ, to whom all power and might of the kingdom is ascribed: "For it is God who worketh in us both to will and to accomplish." David, then, took the crown of the king of the hostile people and made himself a diadem, when Christ, taking the kingdom from the devil, prepared for himself a comely ensign. For the crown of David is the assembly of the catholic people, which crowns and encircles our head, that is, Christ, with faith and conduct. For all the labour, contest and victory of the saints is referred to his honour. Rabbath is the royal city of Ammon, which is now called 'Philadelphia', and is interpreted 'multitude'. And in the gospel it is said: "That many shall come from the east and the west, and shall sit down with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven."
**“THE CITY OF WATERS”** — On account of the abundance of water that was there, or, as some say, of peoples.
12.30: **“AND HE TOOK THE CROWN OF THEIR KING”** — In Paralipomenon it reads thus: "David took the crown of Melchom from his head, and found in it the weight of a talent of gold, and most precious stones, and he made himself a diadem of it." For Melchom is not a proper name, but is interpreted 'their king'. Melchom, as the Hebrews will have it, is the idol of the Ammonites, the gold and gems of whose diadem David is said to have melted down and purified according to the law, and to have made himself a diadem.
12.31:
**“And bringing forth the people thereof he sawed them”** — that is, he cut them through the middle with a saw
**“and drove over them chariots armed with iron”** — with cutting wheels
**“and divided”** — them
**“with knives”** — knives through them
**“and made them pass through the form”** — the likeness
**“of bricks.”** — in the way in which [things] are passed through bricks while still soft, that they may be shaped

13.1: **“And it came to pass after this, that Amnon loved the very beautiful sister of Absalom the son of David, whose name was Thamar”** — or: Amon
13.5: **“And Jonadab said to him: Lie down upon thy bed, and feign thyself sick: and when thy father shall come to visit thee, say to him: Let [my sister Thamar], I pray thee, come”** — or: I beseech
13.6: **“So Amnon lay down, and made as if he were sick: and when the king came to visit him, Amnon said to the king: I pray thee let my sister Thamar come, and make in my sight two little messes”** — LITTLE MESS [sorbitiuncula]. It is what is fit for supping.
13.14: **“But he would not hearken to her prayers, but being stronger overpowered her”** — OVERPOWERED HER. The incest of Amnon, David's elder son, with his sister Thamar, and the murder of Amnon his brother by Absalom, warn us always to act warily, lest vices rule in us and the prince of sin (who promises false peace to those in danger), finding us unprepared, slaughter us unawares. For Absalom is interpreted 'father of peace' or 'peace of the father', Amnon 'giving', Thamar 'bitterness'. For he who gives his members to lust and serves iniquity unto iniquity falls into the bitterness of sin, though the enemy show himself as a father of peace and promise prosperity for such deeds. It is necessary, therefore, that we quickly return to penance, lest perhaps the devil, through the evil spirits, conspire for our death and deliver us to everlasting death.
13.15: **“AND [HE] HATED HER”** — Let us too hold the crime committed in greater hatred than we loved it before it was done, and by this we shall the sooner obtain pardon, provided we do not offend again in another vice, as Amnon did, who, because after the incest he did not avoid drunkenness, therefore did not escape death.
13.37: **“But Absalom fled, and went to Tholomai”** — THOLOMAI. He was the father of Maacha, Absalom's mother, whom the Hebrews say David took in battle, and, her hair and nails being cut off, joined to himself as wife according to the law, and of her begot Thamar and Absalom.
13.39:
**“And king David ceased to pursue after Absalom”**
• because he ceased to go out after Absalom, or because he knew Amnon to be shameful and worthy of death
• AND [KING DAVID] CEASED etc. In the Hebrew: The king ceased to go out after Absalom. For David is said to have wished to go out after Absalom to call him back, but thinking that as often as he saw him he would bring the death of Amnon to mind, he ceased to go out.

14.1: **“And Joab the son of Sarvia, understanding that the king's heart was turned to Absalom,”** — because he saw him sighing for Absalom
14.2: **“sent to Thecua”** — of which was Amos the prophet, whose grandmother this widow is thought to have been
14.6: **“And thy handmaid had two sons: and they quarrelled with each other in the field, and there was none to part them: and the one struck the other, and slew him.”** — THY HANDMAID etc. The Hebrews say this woman really had two sons, and they strove over the inheritance, and one was killed by the other. Yet the woman put herself in the person of David, and the sons in the person of Amnon and Absalom, and the kindred that rises against the son in the person of David's other sons.
14.7: **“And behold the whole kindred rising against thy handmaid, saith: Deliver him that hath slain his brother, that we may kill him for the life of his brother, whom he slew, and that we may destroy the heir: and they seek to quench my spark”** — my remnant, from the likeness of fire
14.9: **“And the woman of Thecua said to the king: Upon me, my lord, [be] the iniquity”** — UPON ME, MY LORD. As if [to say]: because one rose against the other, upon me be the iniquity, if there must be any; but upon thee let there be none, who art without fault; and as I am without fault if one son of mine was killed by the other, so art thou too, if Absalom killed Amnon, who was worthy of death.
14.13:
**“And the woman said: Why hast thou thought such a thing against the people of God”** — namely Absalom, and those who were with him, who as if captives and cast out were not brought back to the inheritance of God, and could be compelled in a foreign land to serve strange gods
**“and [why] hath the king spoken this word”** — AND [WHY] HATH [THE KING] SPOKEN etc. From this is made plain what was said a little above: THE KING CEASED TO GO OUT AFTER ABSALOM.
14.14: **“We all die, and like waters that return no more, we fall down into the earth: neither will God have a soul to perish”** — as if [to say]: God calls back sinners because they are held captive by the devil, and thou, who oughtest to imitate him, castest off
14.16: **“And the king hath hearkened to deliver his handmaid out of the hand of all that sought”** — or: wished
14.17:
**“Then let thy handmaid say, that the word of my lord the king be made as a sacrifice.”** — that is, firm and accepted
**“For even as an angel of God, so is my lord the king, that he is neither by blessing nor cursing”** — of men
**“moved.”** — from what is right
14.22: **“And Joab falling down to the ground upon his face, adored, and blessed the king: and Joab said: This day thy servant hath understood, that I have found grace in thy sight, my lord, O king: for thou hast fulfilled the request of thy servant.”** — in very many [manuscripts] 'my lord, O king' is inserted
14.24: **“But the king said: Let him return into his house, and let him not see my face.”** — lest his presence, bringing the death of Amnon to mind, bring sorrow upon me
14.26: **“And when he polled his hair (now he was polled once a year,”** — they say that in the Hebrew it is 'at an appointed time', namely on the thirtieth day

15.1: **“Now after these things”** — NOW AFTER THESE THINGS. He stayed two years in Jerusalem and did not see the king; in the third he was brought in before the king; in the fourth he made himself chariots and horsemen; and when that was past he drove his father out of the kingdom. Nor was [David] driven out of the kingdom for the seduction and killing of the priests, but for adultery and homicide, as Nathan foretold all things.
15.7:
**“And after four years,”**
• in the Hebrew truth, forty
• of [his] return
• AND AFTER FORTY YEARS etc. It was the fortieth year since Saul overthrew the city of Nobe and killed ninety-five priests on account of David. Therefore the fortieth year is set here, to show that divine vengeance was stirred up against David because he deceived Abimelech the priest and was the cause of so great a slaughter. In faulty manuscripts 'four' is read, not 'forty', but in the Hebrew truth not 'four' but 'forty'. But if anyone contentious asserts that there were four years from the time Absalom killed Amnon until he said to his father: I WILL GO AND PAY MY VOWS WHICH I HAVE VOWED TO THE LORD IN HEBRON, [it is] plain that, after Amnon was killed, Absalom was in Gessur with king Tholomai for three years, and, called back to Jerusalem, stayed two years without seeing his father, and in the sixth year saw his father's face, when he raised rebellion against him. For he said, lying, that he had vowed vows, as if he would pray in the place where Abraham, Isaac and Jacob rest.
15.24:
**“And Sadoc also came”** — the priest
**“and all the Levites with him carrying the ark of the covenant of the Lord, and they set down the ark of God.”** — AND THEY SET DOWN THE ARK. That God might be consulted by Abiathar the priest whither David ought to go.
**“And [Abiathar] went up”** — to prayer, that he might be seen by all
15.25:
**“And the king said to Sadoc:”** — because no answer was given
**“SADOC”** — This just man bears the person of the saints who at the time of the Lord's passion departed indeed in body, but were not separated in love.
15.27: **“And the king said to Sadoc the priest: O seer,”** — that is, prophet, namely when, having consulted God, he foretold things to come to the people
15.28: **“Behold I will lie hid in the plains of the wilderness, till there come word from you to certify me.”** — what I should do
15.30: **“But David went up by the ascent of mount Olivet, going up and weeping, with his head covered”** — lest he should be seen to weep
15.32: **“And when David was come to the top of the mountain, where he was about to adore the Lord, behold Chusai came to meet him”** — CHUSAI. David's friend Chusai is interpreted 'hastening'; he, returning to Jerusalem, scattered the counsel of Achitophel, and signifies the hidden disciples of the Lord from among the Jews, Nicodemus, Joseph and the like.

16.1: **“And when David was a little past the top of the hill, behold Siba the servant of Miphiboseth came to meet him with two asses, laden with two hundred loaves of bread, and a hundred bunches of raisins, and seven [so the edition] cakes of figs”** — he calls cakes of figs 'palatae' because they were pressed in masses between two boards which they call 'palae', from which 'palatae' are named
16.2:
**“And the king said to Siba: What mean these things? And Siba answered the king: My lord, O king, the asses”** — are
**“[are] for the king's household to sit on,”** — the king's sons [to sit] upon them
16.10:
**“And the king said: What have I to do with you, ye sons of Sarvia?”** — WHAT HAVE I TO DO WITH YOU etc. Abisai alone had said: I WILL GO AND CUT OFF HIS HEAD. And David answered Abisai and Joab: WHAT HAVE I TO DO WITH YOU etc. Do you wish to kill this man as you killed Abner?
**“Let him alone and let him curse.”**
• in the Hebrew there is not LET HIM ALONE THAT HE MAY CURSE, but only LET HIM CURSE
• LET HIM ALONE. GREGORY. He who, pressed by insulting words, cannot keep the virtue of patience, or [cannot] suffice [for it], let him call to mind the deed of David, who, when Semei pressed him with revilings and the armed nobles strove to avenge him, said: WHAT HAVE I TO DO WITH YOU, YE SONS OF SARVIA etc. And a little after: LET HIM ALONE THAT HE MAY CURSE ACCORDING TO THE COMMAND OF THE LORD etc. By which words he shows that he was suffering his son rising against him for the sin of Bethsabee. And fleeing, he brought back to mind the evil he had done, and believed the insulting words to be not so much revilings as helps, by which he judged he could be purged and have mercy shown him. For then we bear well the revilings brought against us, when in the secret of the mind we run back to the evils we have committed. For it will seem light that we are struck by injury, while we see what we have deserved by penalties; and so it comes about that thanks rather than anger are owed to insults, by whose intervention, with God as judge, a heavier penalty is turned aside.
**“For the Lord hath bid”** — by permitting
**“him curse David: and who is he that shall dare say,”** — repenting
**“why hath he done so?”** — because he has done all things justly
16.11: **“And the king said to Abisai, and to all his servants: Behold my son, who came forth from my bowels, seeketh my life: how much more now a son of Jemini [shall curse me]? let him alone that he may curse”** — for I have deserved it
16.13:
**“SEMEI”** — This is Nabat, the father of Jeroboam, according to the Hebrews, who is called 'son of Jemini', and he curses David out of zeal for the house of Saul. And the name of his grandfather was Jemini. Semei himself was of the tribe of Ephraim, son of Joseph. Whence he says to David: "I am come first this day of all the house of Joseph"; but Semei, as is read above, was of the kindred of Saul, and Saul of Benjamin. In Esther "Semei the son of Cis" is read, because his father was called both Cis and Gera. He is read here [as] son of Jemini, that is, of Benjamin, but is said to have come first of the tribe of Joseph because he dwelt in the tribe of Joseph.
**“by the hill's side went over against him, cursing, and casting stones at him, and scattering earth.”** — to defile them
16.17: **“And Absalom said to him: Is this thy kindness”** — in the Hebrew 'mercy': as if [to say], thou seemest to be of no mercy, since thou hast forsaken thy friend
16.21:
**“And Achitophel said to Absalom: Go in to the concubines of thy father”** — GO IN TO THE CONCUBINES. Absalom defiled David's concubines. So also the scribes and Pharisees corrupt the Jewish common people with superstitions, and so make it estranged from the true David.
**“ACHITOPHEL”** — It is interpreted 'ruin of a brother'. Judas, working the ruin of Christ, gave counsel to the Jews against Christ; each perished by hanging.

17.2:
**“And coming upon him (for he is now weary, and weak handed) I will defeat him.”** — for fear
**“And when all the people is put to flight”** — from our face
**“that is with him, I will kill the king who will be left alone.”** — because of the flight of his companions
17.3:
**“And I will bring back all the people, as one man”** — that is, in concord
**“is wont to return: for thou seekest but one man: and all the people shall be in peace.”** — Whence: "It is expedient that one man should die" etc.
17.6: **“And when Chusai was come to Absalom, Absalom said to him: Achitophel hath spoken after this manner: shall we do it or not? what counsel dost thou give?”** — what sayest thou?
17.9:
**“Perhaps he now lieth hid in pits, or in some other place where he list: and when any one shall fall”** — whether small or great
**“at the first”** — that is, in the newness of thy reign
**“every one that heareth it shall hear”** — that is, shall have heard it
17.10:
**“AND THE MOST VALIANT”** — In the Hebrew: "the most valiant himself, whose heart is as that of a lion, shall melt for fear." Understand: not this most valiant David. Whence: FOR ALL ISRAEL KNOW THY FATHER TO BE MOST VALIANT.
**“ISIDORE”** — According to the allegory it must be considered what it means that Absalom the parricide pursues his father. First the father fled, secure of victory, and lamented the destruction of the parricide, whom he knew would perish. For it is written that David fled from the face of his son. And of the people of Jerusalem the Lord says: "I have brought up children, and exalted them: but they have despised me." And his son is the Jewish people, which betrayed him. Now Absalom is interpreted 'peace of the father'. What seems strange in the history? Namely, how he who persecutes his father can be understood or called 'peace of the father'? But Absalom signifies 'Jerusalem', which is called 'vision of peace', from whose face Christ fled when he forsook her and passed over to the gentiles.
**“ABSALOM”** — Others take Absalom [for] 'the traitor', whom Christ bore with as though he were ignorant of his thoughts, and shared with him the supper, in which he committed to the disciples the figure of his body and blood. And in the very betrayal he received a kiss from him. Therefore Absalom is called 'peace of the father', because the father had the peace which he did not have.
17.11: **“But this seemeth to me to be good counsel: Let all Israel be gathered to me [so the edition], from Dan to Bersabee”** — the two bounds of the land of promise
17.13:
**“And if he shall enter into any city, all Israel shall cast ropes round about that city, and we will draw it into the river, so that there shall not be found”** — hyperbole
**“so much as one small stone”** — a small stone
17.14: **“And Absalom, and all the men of Israel said: The counsel of Chusai the Arachite is better than the counsel of Achitophel: and by the will of the Lord the profitable counsel of Achitophel was defeated, that the Lord might bring evil upon Absalom.”** — ACHITOPHEL etc. He who, departing from David, passed over to Absalom signifies the heretics who leave the truth and follow error. Achitophel is interpreted 'my brother falling', and Gilonite 'removed', against whom it is said: "In the Lord I put my trust: how then do you say to my soul: Get thee away from hence to the mountain like a sparrow?" And rightly such end their life in the snare of the devil, of their own malice, who corrupt another's [life] with wicked persuasions; as Achitophel, who in another's house plotted against David's life, perished by hanging in his own house. "For he that diggeth a pit shall fall into it," and: "the unjust shall be caught in their own snares."
17.15: **“CHUSAI”** — The Arachite, David's old friend, signifies believers from the gentiles, who, though they were at one time seen to be with Absalom, yet not sharing in his works nor consenting to the wicked suggestions of Achitophel, remained faithfully with David. Chusai is interpreted 'Ethiopian', Arachite 'my length'. Whence: "[If] the Ethiopian change his skin," and elsewhere: "Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands to God," because the gentile people, after it put off its blackness of sins, never drew back from behind the Lord. And that Absalom defiled by rape David's concubines, left to keep the house, signifies that the apostate angel seduces with heretical depravity certain ones who seem to rule and guard the people of God. To them, however, David does not go in any more, but provides food for them, placed in ward. And they, living in widowhood, are shut up until the day of their death; because when heretics, straying from the way of truth, pretend to return, they are not worthy to dwell with Christ, but shut up and separated from his fellowship they must be estranged. Yet he "who maketh his sun to rise upon the good and bad, and raineth upon the just and the unjust" does not refuse to provide such with food in this world, that they may be converted by occasion of his benefits.
17.17:
**“And Jonathan and Achimaas stayed by the fountain Rogel: there went a maid”**
• as if about to wash clothes
• JONATHAN AND ACHIMAAS STAYED etc. RABANUS. That Jonathan, who is interpreted 'gift of the dove', and Achimaas 'his brother', [sent] to spy out the deed of Absalom and report the decree to David, fleeing Absalom, turned aside into the house of a certain man in Bahurim who had a well in his court, and went down into it etc., is not to be believed to be without mystery.
