For these two signify those who are reborn through the grace of the Holy Spirit and are enrolled in the number of the brethren, who, believing, flee from Absalom when they seek to escape the evil spirits. They stand by the fountain Rogel, which is interpreted 'sad' or 'downward', when they seek mourning and contempt in the world for the desire of the heavenly kingdom. They turn aside into the house of the man in Bahurim, which place is interpreted 'chosen' or 'living', when they bring back to memory the times of youth. 'They go down into the well which was in the court', when they humbly submit themselves to penance, which is necessary to all before the end of the present life. 'The woman spreads a covering over the mouth of the well', when the Church, by the assiduity of prayers, hides the offences of youth and ignorance of her children. 'As it were drying sodden barley', when she binds the wantonness of the flesh by the rigour of continence. 'And so the thing lies hid', that is, the transgression of human life, since through assiduity of prayers in the compunction of tears and through chastisement of the body all offences are hidden, and men, protected from the persecution of the enemy, will be freed.
17.18: **“But a certain boy saw them”** — the son of the same maid, as is said
17.19: **“And a woman took, and spread a covering over the mouth of the well, as it were to dry sodden barley”** — barley dried, pounded in a mortar and husked; from it is made a food fit for those who lack teeth; this is ptisana
17.20: **“And when Absalom's servants were come into the house, they said to the woman: Where is Achimaas and Jonathan? and the woman answered them: They passed on in haste, after they had tasted a little water. But they that sought them, when they found them not”** — or: found
17.23: **“But Achitophel seeing that his counsel was not followed, saddled his ass, and arose and went home to his house and to his city, and putting his house in order, hanged himself”** — Josephus says he did this very thing rather from greatness of mind than from smallness of mind
17.24: **“But David came to the camp”** — in Hebrew Manaim, namely where the angels met Jacob
17.25: **“Now Absalom appointed Amasa in Joab's stead over the army: and Amasa was the son of a man who was called Jethra of Jezrael, who went in to Abigail the daughter of Naas, the sister of Sarvia who was the mother of Joab.”** — who is also called Isai and Jesse, as the Jews relate
17.27: **“And when David was come to the camp, Sobi the son of Naas”** — namely the son of Naas, the king with whom Saul fought; Naas too showed kindness to David when he was fleeing from the face of Saul; and when Hanon, who had shaved his servants, was killed by David, this Sobi was set by the same David in his brother's place
17.28:
**“brought him beds”** — of beds
**“and tapestry, and earthen vessels, and wheat, and barley, and meal, and parched corn,”** — pure meal
**“and beans”** — a kind of pulse
**“and lentils, and fried pulse”** — boiled or new
17.29: **“and honey”** — Christ, after he left the Jews, is honoured with spiritual gifts among the gentiles

18.1: **“And David having reviewed his people, appointed over them captains of thousands”** — over a thousand
18.2: **“and sent forth a third part of the people under the hand of Joab, and a third part under the hand of Abisai the son of Sarvia Joab's brother, and a third part under the hand of Ethai, who was of Geth.”** — this man is thought to be the son of that Achis with whom David had friendship
18.3: **“And the people answered: Thou shalt not go forth: for if we flee away, they will not much mind us: or if half of us should fall, they will not greatly care: for thou one”** — alone
18.5: **“And the king commanded Joab, and Abisai, and Ethai, saying: Save me the boy Absalom.”** — not in age but in smallness of understanding
18.8: **“And the battle there was scattered over the face of all the country, and there were many more of the people whom the forest”** — namely the beasts that were in the forest, or the forest itself by its roughness
18.9:
**“And it happened”**
• AND IT HAPPENED. RABANUS. Absalom, fleeing on a mule, was hung in an oak by the hair of his head, because the Jews, leaning on the folly of carnal understanding, corrupting the law through the superstition of the Pharisees, found the occasion of death through the very [law] which they had received for the correction of life. Whence: "There is one that accuseth you, Moses, in whom you trust." And Joab fixes three lances in the heart of Absalom, when the devil puts avarice, pride, and envy or faithlessness into the heart of the Jewish people, which are for them above all the cause of perdition. For out of pride, in contempt of God, they fashioned idols; out of cupidity they preferred transitory things to virtues; out of faithlessness and envy they spurned not only the sayings of the law and the prophets but also the presence of the Saviour himself. Whence: "We have no king but Caesar," and: "If thou release this man, thou art not Caesar's friend." Absalom after death is cast into a great pit, and every wicked man after the death of the flesh into the lake of hell. Over him a heap of stones is piled, while the hardness of his mind is reproached. David bewailed Absalom when he was dead; and for the destruction of the Jewish people Christ, "seeing the city, wept over it," and, pitying its misery, persevered even to the death of the cross in teaching it and caring for its salvation.
• The scribes and Pharisees, the princes of the Jews, were condemned by a hidden judgment on the wood of the cross on which they hung the Lord; and they who seemed to sit upon carnal understanding as upon an irrational mule passed into the dispersion of the nations; they lost both the sovereignty and the people alike.
18.18: **“Now Absalom had reared up for himself, in his lifetime, a pillar, which is in the king's valley: for he said: I have no son”** — namely [the son] who had been a rebel with Absalom
18.21: **“And Joab said to Chusai: Go, and tell the king what thou hast seen. Chusai bowed down”** — a common noun, that is, 'Egyptian'
18.23: **“He answered: But what if I run? And he said to him: Run. Then Achimaas running”** — so indeed by conversion the last become first in faith and love
18.25: **“And crying out he told the king: and the king said: If he be alone, there are good tidings in his mouth.”** — or: his

19.22:
**“And David said: What have I to do with you, ye sons of Sarvia? why are you a satan this day to me?”**
• that is, an adversary
• WHAT HAVE I [TO DO WITH YOU] etc. David feared that if Semei were killed, the rest who had likewise offended the king would not wish to make him their king.
**“shall there any man be killed this day in Israel? do not I know”**
• elsewhere: I do not know
• shall I kill those today who have made me king over them?
19.24: **“WITH UNWASHED FEET”** — In the Hebrew: 'not made'. For Miphiboseth, according to the Hebrews, had made himself wooden feet, which he used in place of natural ones. For he was lame.
19.27: **“Moreover he hath also accused me thy servant to thee, my lord the king: but thou my lord the king art as an angel of God, do what pleaseth thee.”** — as to knowledge, because like an angel thou knowest the will of God
19.29: **“THOU AND SIBA DIVIDE”** — In the Hebrew: I have said, thou and Siba divide the land. Because David, unmindful of the covenant and oath he had made with Jonathan, pronounced so unjust a judgment, therefore Roboam and Jeroboam divided his kingdom. For Miphiboseth is read in the book of Samuel and is interpreted 'mouth of shame'. But in Paralipomenon the same Miphiboseth is read as Meribbaal, that is, 'striving with the Most High', because, namely, [God] had brought David back in peace. And in saying: Let him take all, for as much as my lord is returned peaceably into his house, he spoke indignantly and with twisted words against the Most High.
19.37:
**“But I beseech thee let thy servant return, and die in my own city, and be buried by the sepulchre of my father, and of my mother. But there is thy servant Chamaam”** — in the Hebrew: Chanaan
**“BUT THERE IS THY SERVANT CHAMAAM”** — But in the Hebrew it is: Behold thy servant Chanaan. Chanaan is interpreted 'sighing'. So long as he was with his father, he was called 'sighing'; but after he passed over to the teaching of David, he was called not Chanaan but Chamaam, that is, 'faithful'.
19.42: **“And all the men of Juda answered the men of Israel: Because the king is nearer to me”** — or: more favourable

20.2:
**“And all Israel departed from David, and followed Seba the son of Bochri.”**
• So heretics, wishing to split the people of God, being first condemned by the Church, die in their depravity [before] they can fulfil what they had begun.
• condemned by the Church, they die in their depravity before they can fulfil what they had begun
20.7: **“So Joab's men went out with him, and the Cerethi and the Phelethi”** — two legions
20.8:
**“And when they were at the great stone which is in Gabaon, Amasa coming met them. And Joab had on a close coat”** — that is, a breastplate
**“of equal length with his habit, and over it was girded with a sword hanging down to his flank, in a scabbard, made”** — or: made
20.9: **“And Joab said to Amasa: God save thee, my brother. And he took Amasa by the chin with his right hand as if to kiss him.”** — AND HE TOOK etc. To hold the chin with the right hand is to flatter as if out of kindness; but he puts his left hand to the sword who strikes secretly out of malice.
20.18:
**“And she again said: A saying was used in the old proverb:”** — in the Hebrew 'proverb' is not found
**“They that inquire, let them inquire in Abela”** — as if [to say]: this is the city of counsel
20.19:
**“Am not I she that answer truth in Israel?”** — AM NOT I [SHE] etc. RABANUS. This is the word of the law, in which it is commanded that the children of Israel, entering the land of Chanaan, should first offer peace, and make tributary those who accepted peace, but destroy those who did not accept it. Therefore the wise woman is said to have cried out: AM NOT I SHE THAT ANSWER TRUTH IN ISRAEL etc. As if [to say]: why dost thou destroy this city before thou offer peace according to the law? Why dost thou not keep among Israelites the law which was kept toward foreigners?
**“And thou seekest to destroy the city, and to overthrow a mother of cities in Israel.”** — which is the mother of counsel
20.22: **“AND THEY CUT OFF THE HEAD OF SEBA”** — RABANUS. The return of the people to David after the killing of Absalom signifies the return of the former people to Christ after the death of the wicked teachers, who long reigned in the Synagogue of the Jews and turned the people away from hearing the truth. Now Seba is interpreted 'sect', from 'cutting' [secando], not from 'following' [sectando]; and Bochri 'my firstborn Israel', of whom it is said: "Israel is my son, my firstborn." [The people], having followed Seba, that is, 'error', separated itself from the house of David, that is, the Church. But at the suggestion of the wise woman, that is, 'of spiritual teaching', it cut off from its heart the head of Seba, that is, 'the devil', and returned to David, that is, 'Christ the Son of God'.
20.24: **“But Aduram over the tributes: and Josaphat the son of Ahilud was recorder.”** — the same as chancellor

21.1:
**“And there was a famine in the days of David for three years successively: and David consulted the oracle of the Lord. And the Lord said: It is for Saul, and his house, and blood,”** — or: of bloods
**“because he slew the Gabaonites.”** — AND THERE WAS [A FAMINE] etc. RABANUS. The famine that came in Israel on account of the Gabaonites signifies 'barrenness of good works' in subjects on account of the negligence of teachers, who do not provide them the food of the word of God while they serve earthly things. The Gabaonites, then, are killed when the pursuit of right conduct and the reformation of penance after a fall is withdrawn from the unwary, namely by heretics or evil spirits. For Gabaon is interpreted 'hill of grief'. The Gabaonites are killed when the slothful, after committing crimes, are deluded by the devil with a vain hope of security, who say: "Let us do evil, that there may come good: whose damnation is just." But Respha, who is interpreted 'course', the daughter of Aia, who is interpreted 'his father', taking haircloth spread it upon the rock etc., because the loving solicitude of the saints, succouring such, gives itself to the rigour of fasting and the urgency of prayers, until it obtains from heaven the mercy of God upon them, restraining wicked men and evil spirits, lest they further corrupt their life by wicked suggestion.
21.2: **“AND SAUL SOUGHT”** — Saying, namely, that Josue had let the Gabaonites live for nothing, and had unjustly taken away their spoil from the children of Israel and Juda. And the cause of this vengeance upon the Gabaonites was Abimelech the priest.
21.8:
**“So [the king] took”** — SO [THE KING] TOOK etc. [These were they] who, while still boys, together with Doeg the Edomite killed the priests and the Gabaonites, namely Armoni and Miphiboseth.
**“the two sons of Respha the daughter of Aia, whom she bore to Saul, Armoni, and Miphiboseth: and the five sons of Michol the daughter of Saul, whom she bore to Hadriel the son of Berzellai, that was of Molathi.”** — THE SONS OF MICHOL, namely whom Michol, David's wife, who is also called Egla, adopted among her sons, whom her sister Merob bore to the son of Berzellai.
21.18:
**“There was also a second battle in Gob”** — a city which is also [called] Gazer
**“GOB”** — Which is interpreted 'pit', because, as one is cast into a pit of lions, so David cast himself against Goliath.
**“against the Philistines: then Sobochai of Husathi slew Saph”** — it is a place
21.19:
**“And there was a third battle in Gob against the Philistines, in which Adeodatus the son”**
• David, namely, who was chosen by God for the kingdom
• AND THERE WAS A THIRD [BATTLE] etc. RABANUS. Josephus speaks thus of the third battle: After this encounter the Philistines fought again; and when David sent an army against them, Ephan his kinsman showed himself most valiant. For fighting alone against each of the most valiant of the Philistines he slew them, and turned others to flight, of whom also many fell in the battle. But whether he called Ephan Adeodatus, or someone else, is also uncertain.
**“of the Forest”** — because God took him from the forest where he was feeding the sheep
**“an embroiderer of Bethlehem”** — because his mother was of the race of Beseleel, [and] he was of Bethlehem
21.20:
**“A fourth battle was in Geth, where there was a man of great stature, that had six fingers on his hands and feet, that is, four and twenty, and he was of the race of Arapha”** — the Jews say that Orpha, Noemi's daughter-in-law, was the mother of the giants
**“A FOURTH BATTLE”** — [The slaying of] Goliath, which David did at first in the time of Saul, is repeated. For in Paralipomenon he is read to have fought principally against the Philistines only three times.
**“RABANUS”** — The four battles of David and his servants against the Philistines signify the battle of Christ, which is carried on at every time of this life in his members against persecutors and spiritual wickednesses. For though the pride of the world or the insolence of the evil spirits rise up against the Church of God, yet every principality of the adversaries gives way and is brought to nothing, as the true David commands and orders the battle of his servants. Whence: "Vain is the salvation of man. Through God we shall do mightily: and he shall bring to nothing them that afflict us."
**“OF BETHLEHEM”** — Because Noemi and Ruth, from whom David sprang, returned to Bethlehem in a time of plenty, and because Ruth was joined to Booz for the sake of bread, that place was called 'house of bread'. Or because Noemi, having returned there with her daughter-in-law, obtained abundance of bread in the house of Booz.

22.1:
**“And David spoke to the Lord the words of this canticle, in the day that [the Lord] delivered him:”** — it is an anticipation
**“AND [DAVID] SPOKE”** — RABANUS. The seventeenth Psalm alone is found in the books of Kings, because it signifies that kingdom where we shall have no adversary. For its title is: "In the day that the Lord delivered him from the hand of all his enemies, and from the hand of Saul." For David signifies him "who was made of the seed of David according to the flesh," who in his body, which is the Church, still suffers enemies. Whence: "Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?" And his body will be wholly delivered when "the enemy death shall be destroyed last," that one may come to the kingdom of God. This psalm cannot fit one person. For first the prophet speaks, giving thanks because he is delivered from grievous danger by divine mercy, here: THE PANGS OF DEATH HAVE SURROUNDED ME etc. Secondly the Church speaks, which before the Lord's coming suffered innumerable calamities, [and] afterwards God, having pity, granted the medicine of the holy incarnation and by the benefit of baptism gathered the Christian people from the whole world, there: GOD WHO HATH GIRDED ME WITH STRENGTH. Thirdly the voice of the Saviour, of wonderful mercy, glides in, where his power is described with most beautiful allusions, there: THE LORD LIVETH, AND MY GOD IS BLESSED. Fourthly, again the words of the catholic Church are brought forth, and with great exultation the gifts granted by the Godhead are praised.
22.7: **“In my distress I will call upon the Lord, and I will cry to my God: and he will hear out of his holy temple”** — the temple of God [is] the Son of God
22.8:
**“The earth shook and trembled.”** — sinners
**“The foundations”** — the hopes
**“of the mountains”** — of the proud
**“were moved, and shaken, because he was angry with them.”** — they recognized the wrath of God
22.9:
**“A smoke went up from his nostrils”** — the compunction of penitents
**“and a devouring fire out of his mouth: coals were kindled by it.”** — the hearts of men inflamed by the Holy Spirit
22.10:
**“He bowed the heavens”** — he sent the apostles as messengers of his coming
**“and came down,”** — "He took the form of a servant"
22.11:
**“And he rode upon the cherubims”** — the fulness of knowledge
**“and flew: and slid upon the wings of the wind.”** — the knowledge of the saints
22.14: **“The Lord shall thunder from heaven”** — through the apostles
22.15:
**“He shot arrows”** — the evangelists
**“and scattered them: lightning”** — miracles
22.16: **“And the overflowings of the sea appeared, and [the foundations of the world] were laid open”** — the faith of the Church made manifest
22.17:
**“He sent”** — his Son
**“from on high”** — or: from heaven
**“and took me”** — the Church
22.18: **“He delivered me from my most mighty enemy,”** — the devil
22.20: **“And he brought me forth into a large place,”** — charity
22.27: **“With the elect thou wilt be elect: and with the perverse thou wilt be perverted.”** — because thou dost not favour him, thou seemest perverse
22.30: **“For in thee I will run girded: in my God I will leap over the wall.”** — of sins, which is between God and men
22.34: **“OF HARTS”** — Harts [are] 'spiritual men', on account of their swiftness in leaping over the briars, that is, the entanglements of the world.
22.38: **“I will pursue after my enemies”** — Christ [pursues] the unbelievers, the elect man the vices
22.41: **“My enemies thou hast made to turn their back to me,”** — whence: "Until I make thy enemies thy footstool"
22.44: **“Thou wilt save me from the contradictions of my people”** — of the Jews
22.45: **“The sons of the stranger will resist me,”** — the Jews, "born of their father the devil"
22.48: **“God who giveth me revenge”** — in the judgment, when I shall render to the wicked according to their deserts
22.49:
**“Who bringest me forth from my enemies, and liftest me up from them that resist me: from the wicked man”** — the devil
**“thou shalt deliver me.”** — my Church
22.51:
**“Giving great salvation to his king, and shewing mercy to his anointed”** — to the Saviour
**“David, and to his seed”** — to the elect

23.1:
**“Now these are David's last words. David the son of Isai said:”**
• because David devoutly sang this praise to the Lord at the point of death
• LAST etc. RABANUS. Because they signify the last praise of confession, which the saints will sing for ever when the enemy is overcome and the victory over death is accomplished.
**“The man to whom it was appointed concerning the Christ of the God of Jacob, the excellent psalmist”** — or: psalter-player
**“THE EXCELLENT PSALMIST”** — Because he prophesied most brilliantly of the Christ of God, and of his incarnation and the redemption of the human race.
23.2:
**“The spirit”** — holy
**“of the Lord hath spoken by me, and his word”** — the Son
23.3: **“IN THE FEAR OF GOD”** — He who exercises dominion over his subjects in the fear of God brings forth works of light illumined by the sun of justice, nor does anything dark remain in them; but, watered by the shower of heavenly grace, living in the flesh he bears fruit, the shoots of virtues.
23.4:
**“As the light of the morning,”** — of the Church
**“when the sun riseth,”** — Christ rising from the dead
**“in the morning without clouds”** — of unfaithfulness
**“shineth”** — with miracles
**“and as by rain”** — by preaching
**“the grass springeth out of the earth.”** — the faithful man from the Church
23.5:
**“Neither is my house so great with God, that he should make with me an eternal covenant. For he is all my salvation, and all my will”** — consists in his power
**“NEITHER IS THERE OUGHT THEREOF THAT SPRINGETH NOT UP”** — RABANUS. "He that shall meditate on the law of the Lord day and night shall be like a tree which is planted near the running waters, which shall bring forth its fruit in due season, and all whatsoever he shall do shall prosper."
23.6:
**“But transgressors shall be plucked up as thorns”** — "Every tree that bringeth not forth good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire"
**“all of them”** — especially Jews and heretics, plucked up from the land of the living, are delivered to the eternal burning
23.7: **“AND IF A MAN WILL TOUCH THEM, HE MUST BE ARMED WITH IRON”** — Namely he who, sharing in the sins of others, is pressed by the weight of iniquities on account of the hardness of his heart, and is pierced by the darts of sins; and his works, worthy of eternal fires, shall be brought to nothing.
23.8:
**“These are the names of the valiant men of David. David sitting in the chair was the wisest chief among the three.”**
• Jesbaam the son of Achamoni, as is read in Paralipomenon
• THESE ARE THE NAMES OF THE VALIANT MEN OF DAVID etc. ISIDORE. A catalogue of valiant men is woven in the figure of the saints, who, though they advance in loftiness of virtues, yet do not attain to the excellence of the divine Trinity. For this is what is written: HE ATTAINED NOT TO THE THREE FIRST. "For who in the clouds can be compared to the Lord: or who among the sons of God shall be like to God?"
**“OF THE VALIANT MEN OF DAVID”** — Of these valiant men Josephus says: The first of all was Eusebius the son of Achimee, who, often bursting into the line of the enemy, did not cease until he had killed nine hundred. After him was Eleazar the son of Dodi, who had been with the king in Sarpha. He, when the Israelites feared the army of the Philistines and fled, alone withstood it and killed many, so that his sword stuck to his right hand with the blood of the slain. And the Israelites, seeing the Philistines turned to flight, came down from the mountains and pursued them, and a famous victory came to the Israelites. The third was Semeias the son of Eli, who, in the place of the jawbone, when the Hebrews fled, alone bore [the onset of] the army of the Philistines, laying some low and turning others to flight.
**“He was like the most tender little worm of the wood”**
• who says: "I am a worm and no man" etc.
• HE WAS LIKE THE MOST TENDER etc. RABANUS. "The rod out of the root of Jesse" brought forth a flower without the work of marriage, who from one man, bearing the type of the gentiles, at one onset, that is, by the command of his word, drove out a legion of demons.
**“THE MOST TENDER LITTLE WORM OF THE WOOD”** — RABANUS. The warlike and modest virtue of the man is signified, because, as the little worm of the wood appears tender indeed and frail and small, yet bores and consumes the strongest wood (whence from 'boring' [terendo] it took the name teredo), so he, at home affable to all, quiet and humble, in public combat showed himself sturdy and unbearable to his enemies. Yet the Hebrew supposes this chief of the valiant to be David, of whom it is said: sitting in the chair the wisest etc. His wisdom is shown in 'the wisest', his humility in the example of the little worm, his strength in the killing of eight hundred.
**“who killed eight hundred men at one onset.”** — In Paralipomenon, three hundred; but what is less there is supplied here.
23.9:
**“After him was Eleazar the son of his uncle”** — David's
**“the Ahohite, one of the three valiant men that were with David when they defied the Philistines, and they were there gathered together”** — Paralipomenon: in Aphec domum [so the edition]
23.11:
**“And after him was Semma the son of Age of Arari.”** — Semma: 'hearing'; Age: 'meditating' or 'speaking'; Ararite: 'mountaineer'; who bears the person of Christ or of his preachers.
**“And the Philistines were gathered together in a troop: for there was a field full of lentils.”** — Paralipomenon: "of barley"
23.12: **“HE STOOD”** — RABANUS. Christ, standing with the Holy Spirit in the field of the Church, protects the weak as barley, or surely defends the modesty of chastity in the continent, as lentils, with the sword of his mouth against lust.
23.13:
**“Moreover also before this the three who were princes”** — Abisai, Sobochai, Jonathan
**“THE THREE WENT DOWN”** — The three valiant men named above: Jesbaam the son of Achamoni, whom Josephus names Eusebius the son of Achimee; and Eleazar the son of Ahohi, whom he says is the son of Dodi; and Semma the son of Age, whom he calls Semeias the son of Eli. But the Hebrews think these three were Abisai the son of Sarvia, and Sobochai the Husathite, and Jonathan the son of Samaa the brother of David, who were mentioned above in the battles with the Philistines. With this opinion what follows seems to agree: Abisai also the brother of Joab, the son of Sarvia etc. For hence it appears that Abisai was chief and is named among the three that follow.
**“JOSEPHUS”** — When the king was in Jerusalem, the army of the Philistines came upon him. Then David went up into the citadel to consult the Lord about the war. And the camp of the enemy was pitched in the valley, as far as Bethlehem, which is twenty stadia from Jerusalem. David then said: We have good water in my country; and he especially praised that which was by the well at the gate. He wondered whether there were anyone who would bring him a cup of it, which he would desire more than great wealth. When these three men heard this, bursting through the midst of the enemy, they came to Bethlehem, and drawing the water they returned through the enemy camp to the king, the Philistines being astounded at the confidence and greatness of those who so despised them.
**“among the thirty, went down and came to David in the harvest time into the cave of Odollam: and the camp of the Philistines was in the valley of the giants.”** — that is, the valley of Raphaim
23.15: **“And David longed, and said:”** — that he might test his men
23.16: **“BUT HE WOULD NOT DRINK”** — GREGORY. It must be considered that he who has committed unlawful things should abstain even from some lawful ones, that by this he may make satisfaction to his creator; that he who has committed forbidden things may cut off from himself even things allowed, and reprove himself in the least who remembers that he has sinned in the greatest. The law of the old Testament forbids another's wife to be coveted, but does not forbid under penalty that brave deeds be commanded of soldiers by a king, or that he desire water. But David coveted another's wife and took her away, and fitting stripes followed his fault, and the evil he committed he corrected by the laments of penance. When long after he was encamped against the troops of the enemy, he desired water from their cistern. His chosen soldiers, bursting through the ranks of the enemy, brought unharmed the water he had desired. But the man, taught by scourges, forthwith reproved himself for having desired water at the peril of his soldiers, and pouring it out he offered it to the Lord. For the water poured out was turned into a sacrifice to the Lord, because he slew the fault of concupiscence by the penance of his self-reproof. He, then, who did not fear to covet another man's wife, afterwards dreaded even having coveted water.
23.17: **“Saying: The Lord be merciful to me, that I may not do this: shall I drink the blood of these men that went, and the peril of their lives?”** — BUT HE OFFERED IT TO THE LORD, SAYING: [THE LORD] BE MERCIFUL etc. He gave his soldiers an example of fortitude and constancy, conquering nature, not drinking though thirsty, that the army might learn to bear thirst. But mystically he did not thirst for water, but foresaw Christ to be born of the virgin in Bethlehem, whose laver and blood he thirsted for; so he did not drink the water but poured it out. For he thirsted for the eternal fountain, which is not sought by the perils of others, but washes away the perils of others.
23.19:
**“And the noblest of three, and was their chief, but to the three”** — first
**“THE THREE FIRST”** — They would have them understood as wisdom, humility, fortitude. For David sat as the wisest, he himself the little worm of the wood, that is, humble; he killed eight hundred as one strong. To these three virtues none of the valiant men of David attained.
23.20:
**“And Banaias the son of Joiada a most valiant man, of great deeds, of Cabseel.”**
• elsewhere: master
• AND BANAIAS etc. Who was master from Cabseel, that is, from the congregation of God, over the Cerethi and Phelethi, who are interpreted 'killing' and 'quickening'. He slew the two lions of Moab, whom Paralipomenon names the two Ariels of Moab. These, then, were most valiant men in the kingdom of Moab, whence they are also called 'lions'. For Ariel is interpreted 'lion of God'.
**“He slew the two lions of Moab,”** — who protected Moab against David
**“IN THE MIDST OF A PIT”** — Josephus here says more plainly that it was, namely, a very deep cistern, levelled in the winter time with a heap of snow. Into this a lion fell unawares, and, shut in, cried out with a great roar. And Banaias, who came with the rest to the sight, leaped down into the cistern and killed the lion. Banaias, who is interpreted 'the Lord a builder', signifies Christ, who builds the Church. Whence Paul: "You are God's building." He, in the time of snow and cold, namely when the grace of Christ shone upon the world and the cold of charity had chilled men, killed the lion, that is, the devil. But the Hebrew understands this lion as Joab, who was slain in the midst of the cistern, that is, in the house of the Lord, where he was holding the horns of the altar. And the altar is called a cistern because, as the water of a cistern washes and cleanses, so the sanctuary of the Lord purges sins. In the days of snow, because by death he expiated sin. Whence: "Thou shalt wash me" (which was fulfilled in the midst of the cistern) "and I shall be made whiter than snow", which was fulfilled in that he says: IN THE DAYS OF SNOW.
23.21:
**“He also slew an Egyptian,”** — Semei, who cursed David
**“AN EGYPTIAN”** — That is, an imitator of the Egyptian blaspheming God, whom Moses, at the Lord's command, killed: for that one blasphemed God, this one the prophet and king.
**“a man worthy to be a sight, having a spear in his hand.”** — who in Paralipomenon is read to have been five cubits in stature
**“WORTHY TO BE A SIGHT”** — For he was watched, that if he went out of Jerusalem he should be killed.
**“A SPEAR”** — The law of God, on which, if he had meditated, he would not have perished, remaining in Jerusalem. But because he despised the king's command, Banaias went down to him with a rod, that is, in the uprightness of justice, and wrested from him the spear which he did not hold rightly.
23.23:
**“And he was renowned among the three valiant men,”** — Abisai, Sobochai, Jonathan, to whom he could be made equal
**“who were the most honourable among the thirty.”** — WHO WERE [MOST HONOURABLE] AMONG THE THIRTY etc. Let it disturb no one that in the sum not thirty but thirty-seven are read; for thirty and seven are read in this way. Namely these seven valiant men: David, who is called Adeodatus, Abisai, Sobochai, Jonathan, Eleazar, Semma the son of Age of Arari, and Banaias. Behold seven. And these are the thirty: Asael, Elehanan and the rest.
**“But to the three”** — first
**“he attained not: and [David] made him”** — Christ
**“of his counsel”** — on whom the Godhead conferred all knowledge
**“privy”** — privy to the secret
**“David [made him] for himself.”** — the Father
23.39:
**“Urias the Hethite, thirty and seven in all.”** — honouring faith [and] the observance of the decalogue, the grace of the sevenfold Spirit working
**“URIAS THE HETHITE”** — He is set last because of what follows: AND THE ANGER OF THE LORD WAS AGAIN etc. For vengeance had already been taken on David and on his house, but not on the people, who either did not withstand David or consented.

24.1:
**“And the anger of the Lord was again”** — Satan
**“kindled against Israel.”**
• Paralipomenon: "And Satan rose up against Israel: and moved David to number Israel"
• AND THE ANGER [OF THE LORD] WAS AGAIN etc. GREGORY. The acts of rulers are ordered according to the qualities of their subjects, so that often, for the evil of the flock, the life even of a truly good shepherd offends. For David, praised by the testimony of God, privy to the secrets of God, puffed up with the swelling of sudden elation, sinned in numbering the people, and the people received the penalty, because the hearts of rulers are ordered according to the deserts of the peoples. But the just judge corrected the vice of the sinner by the punishment of those for whose cause he sinned. But because, being proud of his own will, he was not free from the fault, he himself also received vengeance. For the wrath which struck the people in body laid him low too with grief. For the deserts of rulers and peoples are so joined that often from the fault of the shepherds the life of the peoples becomes worse, and from the desert of the peoples the life of the shepherds is changed. But because rulers have their own judge, let subjects not rashly judge the life of those who rule. For the Lord in his own person "poured out the money of the changers, and overthrew the chairs of them that sold doves," signifying that through the masters he judges the life of the peoples, through himself the deeds of the masters; although the vices of subjects too, which are overlooked by the masters or cannot be judged, are reserved for his judgment. While, then, the matter is carried on with faith kept safe, it is a merit of virtue to bear whatever is of the superior. Yet it ought to be humbly suggested, if perchance what displeases may be amended. But care must be taken lest an inordinate defence of justice pass over into pride, and while rectitude is directed incautiously, humility, the mistress of rectitude, be lost, lest one despise him as set over him whom perhaps he reproves in something. Against this swelling of pride let one's own infirmity be unceasingly regarded. For we neglect to examine our strength truly, and because we believe strong things of ourselves, we judge our prelates strictly. For the less we know ourselves, the more we see those whom we strive to reprove. These are evils one by one, which are often committed by subjects in prelates, often by prelates in subjects; because prelates think their subjects less wise, and subjects judge the deeds of their rulers and think they would act better if they happened to hold the government. Whence rulers see less prudently what is to be done, because the cloud of elation darkens their eyes; and often a subject made prelate does what he reproved while he was a subject, so that, because he does the things he had judged, he may at least blush that he judged them. As, therefore, prelates must take care lest the higher place of singular wisdom lift up their hearts, so subjects must see to it that the deeds of their rulers do not displease them. And if the life of masters is rightly reproved, it is fitting that subjects should venerate them even when they displease. But one must carefully see that thou dost not desire to imitate him whom it is necessary to venerate, or scorn to venerate him whom thou disdainest to imitate. For the narrow way of rectitude and humility must be held, so that the deeds of masters may so displease that the mind of the subjects does not withdraw from reverence for the mastership.
24.2: **“And the king said”** — made [so] by the pomp of pride
24.3:
**“And Joab said to the king: The Lord thy God increase thy people”** — so many
**“as many more as they are now.”** — that it may be twice as great
24.9: **“AND JOAB GAVE UP THE SUM OF THE NUMBER”** — It must be noted that in Paralipomenon is read: "Of Israel a thousand thousand and a hundred thousand, and of Juda four hundred and seventy thousand," which it is to be understood that Joab numbered but would not show, except as many as are written in the book of Samuel.
24.11: **“And David arose in the morning, and the word of the Lord came to Gad the prophet”** — THE WORD OF THE LORD CAME TO etc. In Exodus it is written: "When thou shalt take the sum of the children of Israel according to their number, every one of them shall give a price for their souls to the Lord, and there shall be no scourge among them" etc. David, forgetting to do this, offended God, and there was a plague in Israel. Hence Josephus says: When the prophets declared to David that God was angry, he besought him to be propitious and grant pardon. God therefore sent the prophet Gad to him bearing three conditions of punishment: namely whether he would have famine arise in the province for seven years, or be overcome by his enemies in fighting for three months, or have disease and sickness come upon the Hebrews for three days. And when the prophet, pressing him, demanded an answer to report to the Lord, the king, thinking that if he chose famine he would seem to do it against others, since he himself had much corn and would not suffer want, while for the rest there would be distress; and if he chose three months' victory of the enemies, he himself, having very valiant men and guards about him, would fear nothing, but the army would be exposed to slaughter; he chose rather a suffering common and equal to all, saying: It is much better to fall into the hands of God than of enemies. This the prophet reported to the Lord, who sent destruction upon the army of the Hebrews. They died not in one way, so that the sickness could easily be known, but death [came] upon all; one died upon another, others died while burying, and the evil, hanging secretly over them, swiftly brought destruction. The pestilential sickness beginning at the morning hour, seventy thousand were consumed by the hour of the midday meal. And the angel of the Lord was by the threshingfloor of Areuna the Jebusite. In Paralipomenon also it is written: "And the angel of the Lord stood by the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite." And David, lifting up his eyes, saw the angel of the Lord between earth and heaven, with a drawn sword in his hand turned against Jerusalem. And both he and the ancients, clothed in haircloth, fell prone to the earth.
24.13: **“EITHER SEVEN YEARS”** — And it seems that those who are not fed with the bread of the word of God through the grace of the sevenfold Spirit suffer famine seven years; and those who have not been regenerated in the name of the Trinity cannot resist the enemies, that is, the demons, but, unbelieving, die by the pestilence of impiety.
24.16:
**“And when the angel of the Lord had stretched out his hand over Jerusalem to destroy it, the Lord had pity on the affliction, and said to the angel that slew the people: It is enough: now hold thy hand. And the angel of the Lord was by the threshingfloor of Areuna the Jebusite”**
• it is Jerusalem itself
• Areuna is interpreted 'ark', Ornan 'light to us'. Fittingly, then, David, wishing to appease the Lord, is bidden to set up an altar on the floor of Areuna or Ornan, because God is not otherwise appeased by man unless in the ark of the heart, through the light of right faith and true love, he sets up the altar of humility, on which he may offer the sacrifice of oblation and praise. Whence: "The sacrifice of praise shall glorify me," and: "A sacrifice to God is an afflicted spirit" etc. The floor of Areuna or Ornan is Jerusalem itself.
**“BY THE THRESHINGFLOOR OF AREUNA”** — The threshingfloor of Areuna is the Church of the gentiles, in which, after the true David has raised the altar of faith, the death of impiety at once ceases. This floor David bought for fifty sicles, because Christ, through the grace of the sevenfold Spirit, all offences being remitted, sanctified the gentile world into an everlasting house for himself.
24.24: **“And the king answered him, and said: Nay, [not] as thou wilt, but I will buy it of thee at a price, and I will not offer to the Lord my God holocausts free cost. So David bought the floor, and the oxen, for fifty sicles of silver.”** — in Paralipomenon is read: "And David gave Ornan for the place six hundred sicles of gold of very just weight." For it is to be understood that he bought the oxen for fifty sicles of silver, but the floor for six hundred of gold
24.25: **“And David built there an altar to the Lord, and offered holocausts and peace offerings: and the Lord became merciful to the land, and the plague was stayed from Israel.”** — AND OFFERED HOLOCAUSTS etc. Hence in Paralipomenon: "The tabernacle which Moses made in the desert, and the altar of holocausts, was at that time in the high place of Gabaon. And David could not go to the altar there to pray to the Lord; for he was seized with exceeding great fear, seeing the sword of the angel of the Lord. And David said: This is the house of God" etc. In this place, according to the Hebrews, Abraham wished to offer his son, when a ram suddenly appeared, which he took and offered in place of his son.

1.1:
**“Now king David was old”** — AND KING DAVID WAS OLD. Does it not seem to thee, if thou follow the letter that kills, to be a fiction or a farce of Athens? A cold old man is wrapped in clothes and is not warmed except by the embrace of a young girl. Bethsabee was still living, Abigail survived, and the other wives and concubines. All are rejected as if cold, and the aged man grows warm in the embraces of one alone. Abraham was much older than David, and yet while Sara lived he did not seek another wife. Isaac had twice David's years, and with Rebecca, now an old woman, he never grew cold. I say nothing of the earlier men before the flood, who after five hundred years, with limbs not merely aged but almost decayed, never sought girlish embraces. Moses, the leader of the people of Israel, had a hundred and twenty years, and did not change Sephora. Who then is this Sunamitess, wife and virgin, so fervent that she could warm the cold, so holy that she did not provoke the warm to lust? Let Solomon expound his father's delights, and the peaceable one the embraces of the warrior: "Get wisdom, get understanding; forsake her not, and she shall keep thee. Love her, and she shall preserve thee." Almost all the powers of the body are changed in old men, and while wisdom alone increases, the rest decrease: fasts, sleeping on the ground, running here and there, receiving of strangers, defence of the poor, urgency of prayers, visiting the sick, labour of the hands from which alms are supplied; and all things that are exercised through the body become less when the body is broken. Nor do I say this as though in the young, and those of still firmer age, who by labour and most ardent study, and also by holiness of life and frequency of prayer, have attained knowledge, wisdom grows cold, which in very many old men withers with age; but that youth sustains many wars of the body, and amid the incentives of vices and the ticklings of the flesh is smothered like fire in green wood and cannot fill out its own brightness. But the old age of those who have furnished their youth with honest acts and have meditated in the law of the Lord day and night becomes more learned with age, wiser with the passage of time, and reaps the sweetest fruits of its old studies. And the very name Abisag indicates the more ample wisdom of old men. For it is interpreted 'my father superfluous', that is, abounding, or 'roaring of my father'. The word 'superfluous' is ambiguous, but here it signifies that wisdom is more ample and overflowing in old men; elsewhere 'superfluous' is put as if 'not necessary'. And Abisag is properly called 'roaring' too, because the wave of the sea resounds, and, so to speak, a roar is heard coming from the deep. By which it is shown that the thunder of the divine word abides in old men most abundantly and beyond the human voice. And Sunamitess is called 'scarlet', to signify that wisdom is warm and glows with divine reading. Which, though it points to the sacrament of the Lord's blood, also shows the fervour of wisdom. Whence that midwife in Genesis binds a scarlet thread on the hand of Phares, who, from his having divided the wall that before separated the two peoples, obtained the name of divider, that is, Phares. And Rahab the harlot, in the type of the Church, hung up the cord containing the mystery of blood, that when Jericho perished her house might be saved. Whence it is said of the saints: "These are they that came of the heat of the house of Rechab," and elsewhere: "I am come to cast fire on the earth" etc., which, kindled in the hearts of the disciples, compelled them to say: "Was not our heart burning?"
**“and advanced in years: and when he was covered with clothes, he was not warm.”** — AND WHEN HE WAS COVERED etc. David suffered excessive cold, either because he was born of elderly parents, or because he had shed much blood in battle, or rather because, from the time he saw the angel slaying the people, he wasted away with vehement dread; whence he remained in the affliction of cold until death.
1.4: **“And the damsel was exceeding beautiful”** — wisdom or contemplation, embracing which they grow aflame in love of her
1.5: **“ADONIAS”** — He signifies the Jewish people, which seems to be the elder son, because it received the law first, and, spurning the gentile people, which was called later by the grace of God, thought that it alone would reign with the Lord. For Adonias is interpreted 'the Lord a ruler'. But the people of the Church, with the true Solomon, that is, our peaceable one, whose body it is, is by divine ordinance put in the kingdom in its place, from which the elder son, that is, the former people, is deservedly cast down for faithlessness.
1.11: **“BETHSABEE”** — It is interpreted 'daughter of the oath'. And it signifies the ancient Church that was under the law, of whose stock the true Solomon was promised to be born. Nathan is interpreted 'gift', and figures the old prophecy.
1.22: **“As she was yet speaking with the king, Nathan the prophet [came].”** — or: prophet
1.23:
**“And they told the king, saying: Nathan the prophet is here. And when he was come in before”** — or: into
**“the king”** — or: presence
1.26: **“But me thy servant, and Sadoc the priest, and Banaias the son of Joiada, and Solomon thy son”** — or: servant
1.32: **“King David also said: Call me Sadoc”** — that is, the just one
1.38: **“THE MULE”** — [The mule of] David: some say [it signifies] the Church, others the Synagogue, on account of its unfruitfulness.

2.5:
**“THOU KNOWEST ALSO WHAT”** — David instructs Solomon concerning the just recompense of those who were a comfort to him, or who unjustly harmed him, whom he himself patiently bore. And the prophecy indicates what must be done to the wicked or the good in the future, which the true Solomon will fulfil. Meanwhile, however, the patience of God often allows the good to be afflicted, the reprobate to enjoy delights.
**“what he did to the two captains of the army of Israel, to Abner the son of Ner, and to Amasa the son of Jether: whom he slew, and shed the blood of war in peace, and put the blood of battle”** — or: of war
2.13: **“AND SOLOMON SAT”** — Solomon bears the figure of Christ. For he builds the temple, as Christ the Church. He had peace according to his name, as the Lord himself too is called the king of peace, making peace to those far off and peace to those near. And there is no doubt that in wisdom and riches and glory he bore the type of the Saviour.
2.19: **“Then Bethsabee came to king Solomon, to speak to him for Adonias: and the king arose to meet her, and bowed to her, and sat down upon his throne.”** — THEN BETHSABEE CAME TO SPEAK FOR ADONIAS. Adonias, through the intervention of Bethsabee, who is interpreted 'daughter of fulness', longed to corrupt Abisag the Sunamitess, because the Jewish people, through the observance of the law with which it was sated, wished to violate the spiritual understanding, or the Church, which is an incorrupt virgin joined to our David; and because it did not deserve her fellowship, it incurred the death it deserved. Nor did Bethsabee, interceding with Solomon for Adonias, profit him anything, nor the law which the Jews think to be their helper with God.
2.26: **“ABIATHAR ALSO”** — Abiathar, expelled from the priesthood yet not killed, signifies the Jews, whose priesthood, though abolished, they themselves have not been destroyed, for the sake of those of them who will believe at the end of the world.
2.28: **“AND JOAB FLED”** — Joab, who, fleeing to the altar, was killed there at Solomon's command, signifies the masters of perverse doctrine, who, because they destroy churchmen by plots, as Joab [did] Abner and Amasa, will be driven from the altar of faith and punished with everlasting death. But to David and his seed be peace for ever; that is, the enemies of Christ being abolished, the throne of David, that is, the Church, enjoying eternal peace, will remain for ever.
2.36: **“The king also sent, and called for Semei, and said to him: Build thee a house in Jerusalem, and dwell there: and go not out from thence any whither.”** — AND GO NOT OUT. The true Solomon commands us who dwell in Jerusalem never to go out. And if those before subject to us flee from us, let us not therefore go out to follow the footsteps of the fugitives, lest while we wish to save those fleeing we ourselves perish; but rather let the dead bury the dead, and while we may, let us pluck out and cut off from us the eye, hand or foot that scandalizes.

3.1: **“And the kingdom was established in the hand of Solomon, and he made affinity with Pharao the king of Egypt: for he took his daughter, and brought her into the city of David”** — FOR HE TOOK HIS DAUGHTER etc. The daughter of Pharao, whom Solomon joined to himself in marriage, signified 'the Church from the gentiles'.
3.2: **“BUT YET THE PEOPLE SACRIFICED IN THE HIGH PLACES”** — The people sacrificed chiefly on the mountains, either to God or to demons.
3.4:
**“He went therefore to Gabaon”** — it is interpreted 'lofty hill' or 'high'
**“HE WENT THEREFORE TO GABAON”** — In Gabaon was the greatest high place, where was the tabernacle which Moses made, and the brazen altar, upon which Solomon, offering a thousand victims, deserved the divine oracle.
3.5: **“And the Lord appeared to Solomon in a dream by night, saying: Ask what thou wilt that I should give thee.”** — the grace of God requires the free will of man
3.8: **“And thy servant is in the midst of the people which thou hast chosen, an immense people, which cannot be numbered nor counted”** — or: borne
3.11:
**“And the Lord said to Solomon: Because thou hast asked this thing, and hast not asked for thyself long life or riches,”** — such things the reprobate seek
**“nor the lives of thy enemies, but hast asked for thyself wisdom to discern judgment,”** — such a prayer is not in vain with God
3.14: **“And if thou wilt walk in my ways, and keep my precepts, and my commandments, as thy father walked, I will lengthen thy days.”** — AND IF THOU WILT WALK etc. I WILL LENGTHEN THY DAYS. Without keeping the commandments of God, no one can attain long days, that is, beatitude.
3.16:
**“Then there came two women that were harlots”**
• fittingly harlots came to him whom afterwards they deceived
• THEN THERE CAME TWO WOMEN. GREGORY. After the Lord illumines the darkness of our error with the light of his knowledge, he soon tests [us], visiting [us] with the sting of temptation; because by approaching he advances our hearts to virtues, and by withdrawing he allows them to be shaken by temptation. For if after the gifts of virtues it is shaken by no temptation, the mind glories that it has this of itself. That it may have the gifts of firmness, then, and acknowledge its infirmity, it is lifted to the heights by the approach of grace, and by the withdrawal it is proved what it is of itself. Whence Solomon, after receiving wisdom from God, is struck by the dispute of the harlots. Because often, when the regard of the inward bounty illumines our mind with the virtues granted, slippery thoughts soon trouble it, so that she who, lifted up, exults in the immense gift, may also, struck by temptation, find out what she is. So Elias too, visited from above, opened the heavens by his word, and suddenly, proved weak, fleeing through the deserts, dreaded one woman. So Paul, penetrating even to the third heaven, beholds the secrets of paradise, and returning to himself labours against the war of the flesh. He bears another law in his members, by whose rebellion in him he grieves that the law of the spirit is wearied. After the giving of the gift, then, God tests man, because he both lifts him up by bestowing the gift and, withdrawing it a little, shows him to himself. This we suffer so that we may be reformed to the substance of the promised incorruption.
• Some judge that this is to be understood of the Synagogue and the Church, and referred to that time when, after the cross and resurrection, the true Solomon, that is, the peaceable one, began to reign both among the Jews and among the gentiles. For Osee took a wife of fornications, then an adulteress. For Christ came for this, to give harlots in marriage and to make of two flocks one fold. These are the two rods which are joined in Ezechiel, and of which it is said by Zacharias: "And I took unto me two rods, one I called Beauty, and the other I called a Cord." That woman too in the gospel who washed the feet of Jesus with tears, wiped them with her hair, and to whom all sins were forgiven, signifies the Church gathered from the gentiles. Yet the Church "has no spot or wrinkle"; nor do we say that she remained a harlot, but that she had been, according to what is said: 'When Jesus was in the house of Simon the leper', not one who was then a leper but who had been before. Note too what the Church says against the Synagogue: I AND THIS WOMAN DWELT IN ONE HOUSE etc., because after the resurrection of the Saviour one [Church] was gathered from both peoples. And elegantly he added: I WAS DELIVERED OF A CHILD WITH HER IN THE CHAMBER. For the Church from the gentiles, which did not have the law and the prophets, gave birth in the house of the Synagogue, and did not go out of the chamber but went in. Whence: "The king hath brought me into his chamber," and: "I will bring thee into my mother's house, and into the chamber of her that bore me."
• GREGORY. By the nursing mothers is signified the order of teachers, by their sons the person of the disciples. For masters watchful in knowledge but asleep in life, while they neglect to do what they say, kill through the sleep of torpor their hearers, whom they nourish through the vigils of preaching, and by neglect overlay those whom they seemed to feed with the milk of words. Whence, while they live reprehensibly and cannot have disciples of praiseworthy life, they try to draw others' disciples to themselves, that, by showing that they have good followers, they may excuse before the judgments of men the evils they do, and cover their deadly negligence by the life of their subjects. Whence the woman who killed her own son sought another's; but the sword of Solomon found the true mother, because the wrath of the judge at the last examination will show for whom the fruit lives or perishes. And note that the living son is first ordered to be divided, that afterwards he may be given back to the mother alone; because in this life the life of the disciple is allowed to be as it were shared, while from it one is permitted to have merit with God, another praise with men. But the false mother did not fear that he whom she had not borne should be killed, because arrogant masters, ignorant of charity, if they cannot obtain the fullest name of praise from others' disciples, cruelly persecute their life. For, kindled with envy, they do not wish those to live for others whom they see they cannot possess. Whence: LET IT BE NEITHER MINE NOR THINE. For those whom they do not see serving them for temporal glory, they begrudge to live for others through the truth. But the true mother is anxious that her son at least be with a stranger and live, because truthful masters allow that others have the praise of mastership from their disciples, provided these do not lose integrity of life. By which bowels of pity this same true mother is recognized, because mastership is wholly approved in the examination of charity. She alone deserved to receive the whole who as it were gave up the whole; because faithful superiors, since from good disciples they not only do not begrudge others praise but even pray for the profit of their advancement, themselves receive their sons whole and living, when at the last judgment they obtain perfect recompense from their life.
**“RABANUS”** — If thou consider Pilate washing his hands and saying: "I am innocent of the blood of this just man," and the centurion confessing: "Indeed this was the Son of God," and those who before the passion desired through Philip to see the Lord, thou wilt not doubt that the first to give birth was the Church, and that afterwards was born the people of the Jews, for whom the Lord prayed: "Father, forgive them" etc., and: "There believed in one day three thousand," and another five thousand.
3.18:
**“And the third day, after that I was delivered, she also was delivered, and we were together.”** — the multitude of believers had one heart
**“And no other person with us in the house, only we two.”** — of the blaspheming Jews, or of the gentiles serving idols
3.19:
**“DIED”** — RABANUS. For while she follows the observance of the law and couples the grace of the gospel with the law, she is covered with the darkness of error.
**“And this woman's child died in the night: for in her sleep she overlaid him.”**
• because she could not say: "I sleep, and my heart watcheth"
• Read the epistle to the Galatians and see how the Synagogue hastens to make the sons of the Church her own
3.20:
**“SHE TOOK MY CHILD”** — The living one, namely, not to possess him but to kill him. For she did this not from love of the son but from hatred of her rival.
**“from my side, while I thy handmaid was asleep, and laid it in her bosom: and laid her dead child in my bosom.”** — through the ceremonies of the law
3.21:
**“And when I rose in the morning to give suck”** — of doctrine
**“to my child, behold it was dead: but considering him more diligently when it was clear day,”** — CONSIDERING HIM MORE DILIGENTLY etc. RABANUS. It is long to show how, through Paul and other churchmen, the Church understood that he who was held under the law was not her son, and knew in the light him whom she did not see in the darkness. The two women, in one of whom love burned, in the other pretence crept in, figure the Church and the Synagogue, or heretical depravity, each of which [the latter] both kills her own by wicked nursing and entices others until she destroys them. Between the two women the Lord, while he decides what is just by the spirit of his mouth, restores to each what is due.
3.24:
**“The king therefore said:”** — Christ
**“THE KING THEREFORE SAID”** — JEROME. RABANUS. Feigning ignorance, he measures human affections according to the dispensation of the flesh, as also there: "Where have you laid him?" And elsewhere: "Who touched me?"
**“Bring me a sword. And when they had brought a sword before the king, he said:”** — I came not to send peace, but the sword
3.25: **“DIVIDE THE CHILD”** — JEROME. RABANUS. The Lord tests the nature of nature, and wills, according to the will of each, to divide the living son between the law and grace, not that he approves this, but he says he wills it in order to expose the calumny of the Synagogue.
3.26: **“But the woman whose child was alive, said to the king:”** — BUT THE WOMAN SAID etc. RABANUS. The Church, which knows him to be hers, willingly yields him to her rival, that he may at least live with her, lest, divided between the law and grace, he be struck by the blade of Christ. Whence: 'Behold, I Paul tell you, that if you keep the law, Christ shall profit you nothing'.

4.12:
**“Bana the son of Ahilud, who governed Thanac”** — elsewhere: Thane
**“and Mageddo, and all Bethsan, which is by Sarthana beneath Jezrael, from Bethsan unto Abelmehula over against Jecmaan.”** — or: Zeelmaan
4.21:
**“And Solomon had under his dominion,”** — Christ, in whose dominion are all the kingdoms of the earth
**“all the kingdoms from the river to the land”** — "He shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river unto the ends of the earth"
**“of the Philistines, even to the border of Egypt”** — "The kings of Tharsis and the islands shall offer presents"
**“who brought him presents”** — of faith and good works
**“and served him”** — "All nations shall serve him"
**“all the days of his life.”** — For ever and ever; and: of his kingdom there shall be no end
4.22:
**“THE PROVISION OF SOLOMON”** — The refreshment of Christ, who is fed by right faith and the good works which are offered to him daily by the catholic Church.
**“for each day was thirty measures of fine flour”** — the faith of the holy Trinity, which is contained in the law of the Lord
**“and threescore measures of meal”** — the perfection of good works
4.23:
**“Ten fat oxen”** — the teachers of the decalogue
**“TWENTY OUT OF THE PASTURES”** — The preachers of the new Testament, who have as it were a doubled decalogue in themselves, since they preach the new and old Testaments equally, full of love of God and neighbour.
**“and a hundred rams”** — the leaders of the Christian flock, who with their subjects hasten to attain eternal glory
**“besides venison of harts, roes, and buffles, and fatted fowls.”** — BESIDES VENISON. The venison of various animals are those who from various nations are daily caught in the nets of the gospel by spiritual hunters and brought in as food for the Saviour.
4.24: **“For he had all the country which was beyond the river, from Thaphsa to Gazan, and all the kings of those countries: and he had peace on every side round about.”** — "His empire shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end of peace"
4.25:
**“And [they] dwelt”** — under his defence
**“Juda”** — truly confessing
**“and Israel”** — seeing God
**“without any fear”** — namely, all earthly things and the threats of enemies being despised
**“every one under his vine”** — which cheereth the heart of man
**“and under his fig tree”** — with the sweetness of the love of God and neighbour
4.26:
**“And Solomon had forty thousand stalls of chariot horses”** — because in the people of the law and of the gospel they were fed at the mangers of the Scriptures, that they might become fit for the cavalry of the most high king
**“FORTY THOUSAND”** — By forty are designated the times of the ancient law, for receiving which Moses fasted forty days, and the people that was instructed by it was forty years in the desert.
**“AND TWELVE THOUSAND”** — This number signifies the present time, in which the apostolic teaching of the new Testament nourishes the people.
4.27:
**“And [they] fed them”** — by word and example
**“the foresaid governors of the king”** — the preachers
**“and they furnished the necessaries also for king Solomon's table, with great care in their time,”** — giving in their time the measure of divine wheat
4.28: **“BARLEY”** — Lest anything be lacking in the king's house, the order of preachers labours in writing and speaking, that there may be abundance at the Lord's table whereby the faithful may be fed.
4.29: **“And God gave to Solomon wisdom”** — to Christ, in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge
4.31:
**“And he was wiser”** — because [he is] the fountain of wisdom
**“than all men”** — who share in wisdom
**“wiser than Ethan the Ezrahite, and Heman, and Chalcol, and Dorda the sons of Mahol, and he was renowned in all nations round about.”** — because his name is admirable in all the earth
4.32:
**“Solomon also spoke three thousand parables”** — Christ handed down the fulness of faith in the law and the gospel, the whole of which, while it is discussed in manifold ways through the senses of allegories under the mystery of the Trinity, is called as it were three thousand parables
**“and his poems were five thousand [so the edition].”** — HIS POEMS etc. and HE TREATED etc. It is certain that neither the poems nor the discourses of Solomon exist today.
**“FIVE THOUSAND”** — On account of the five senses: he who rules them well in various virtues is blessed, and through them sings as it were five thousand poems to the Lord.
4.33:
**“And he treated about trees from the cedar that is in Libanus”** — by the cedar is understood the loftiness of the elect. Whence: "The just shall flourish like the palm tree: he shall grow up like the cedar of Libanus" etc.
**“THE HYSSOP”** — Hyssop, a lowly herb clinging to the rock, signifies the humility of Christ, who treated from the cedar to the hyssop, because he came down from the excellence of heavenly glory to the humility of the flesh. By the cedar too the pride of the wicked is designated. Whence: "The voice of the Lord breaketh the cedars." From the cedar to the hyssop, then, Christ treats, because he judges the hearts of the proud and of the humble. He also treated about wood [super lignis] when he hung on the cross. For then he bowed the cedar, that is, the arrogance of the world, down to the humility of the hyssop, that is, to the foolishness of the cross: "For the word of the cross, to them indeed that perish, is foolishness; but to them that are saved, it is the power of God." And a little after: "For seeing that in the wisdom of God the world by wisdom knew not God, it pleased God by the foolishness of our preaching to save them that believe."
**“that cometh out of the wall: and he discoursed of beasts, and of fowls, and of creeping things, and of fishes.”** — AND HE DISCOURSED etc. RABANUS. For all things are naked and open to Christ, nor is there any creature invisible in his sight. He knows the thoughts of men and tells the multitude of the stars; to him the abyss lies open, and hell is not hidden before him. And he discourses when he sets before us the reason of each thing and makes manifest in the Scriptures the sacraments hidden from ages and generations, that we may consider the beatitude of the angels, the profit of men, the cunning of the demons, and, rejecting what is evil, follow what is good.
4.34: **“And they came from all nations to hear the wisdom of Solomon”** — Hence Isaias: And all nations shall flow unto it, and many people shall go and say: "Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord"

5.3:
**“Thou knowest the will of David my father, and that he could not build a house to the name of the Lord his God”**
• TO BUILD A HOUSE. BEDE. The house which Solomon built was a figure of the Church, which from the first elect to the last is daily built by the grace of the peaceable king, that is, Christ; which partly is a pilgrim from him on earth, partly, after its pilgrimage, already reigns with him in heaven, where after the last judgment it will reign whole. To it belong the angels, likeness to whom is promised us in the future. Whence: "They are equal to the angels, and are the children of God, being the children of the resurrection." To it belongs Christ himself also. Whence: "Destroy this temple, and in three [days] I will raise it up." "But he spoke of the temple of his body." And of us the Apostle says: "Know you not that you are the temple of God" etc. If, then, he was made a temple according to the flesh, and we are made the temple of God by the indwelling Spirit, it is certain that that temple was a figure of all of us and of the Lord himself, that is, of the members and the head: but of him as the chief cornerstone, elect, precious, laid in the foundation; of us as living stones built up upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, that is, Christ. This will appear better when the order of the building of the temple itself is considered, so that in some things the figure pertains to him himself, in some to all the elect, in some it shows the unspoiled happiness of the angels in heaven, in some the help of the angels bestowed on men, in some the contests of men rewarded with the angels.
• This spiritual house the tabernacle made in the desert also signifies. But [there is a difference], because that house [was made] on the journey by which they were coming to the land of promise, this was built in the land itself and in the city of Jerusalem; that, so that, carried often from place to place by the ministry of the Levites, it might at length be brought into the land of the promised inheritance; this, so that, set up at once in the homeland itself and in the royal city, it might stand ever on an inviolable foundation until it fulfilled the office of heavenly figures laid upon it. In that can be figured the labour and exile of the present Church, in this the future rest and beatitude. Or, because that was made by the children of Israel alone, this by proselytes also and gentiles, in that can be expressed principally the fathers of the old Testament and the ancient people of God,
• in this the Church gathered from the gentiles. Although each building, discussed more closely, shows in manifold figures both the daily labours of the present Church and the eternal rewards in the future, and the joys of the heavenly kingdom, and also the election of the primitive Church and the salvation of all nations in Christ.
5.6:
**“Give orders therefore that thy servants cut me down cedar trees out of Libanus, and let my servants be with thy servants: and I will give thee the hire of thy servants whatsoever thou wilt ask.”** — GIVE ORDERS THEREFORE THAT THEY CUT ME DOWN CEDAR TREES OUT OF LIBANUS etc. The servants of Hiram cutting cedars for Solomon from Libanus are the chosen teachers from the gentiles, who, by correcting them, cut down from the pomp of pride those who rejoice in the things and glory of the world, and transfer them to the service of Christ; with whom the servants of Solomon press on in the said work, because the first teachers from the gentiles needed to be instructed by the teaching of the apostles, who learned from the Lord, lest, if they began to teach without masters, they should be masters of error. For Solomon wished the servants of Hiram to cut the wood for this reason, because in cutting they were more skilled than his servants. He also wished his own to be present, to show the measures to the cutters. The apostles too knew the word of the gospel more surely from him himself, but the gentiles, converted from error to the truth of the gospel, knew the errors of the gentiles better, and therefore fought them more skilfully.
**“FOR THOU KNOWEST HOW THERE IS NOT”** — BEDE. We must speak first of the workmen of the temple, who they were and whence, and of the material itself. "For all these things happened to them in figure, and they are written for us." Solomon, about to build a house to the Lord, sought help from Hiram king of Tyre, who was ever a friend of David, and had already begun to have peace with Solomon himself; and he found him ready in all things, so that he gave him craftsmen and timber and gold as he needed. And Solomon repaid every year very many measures of wheat and oil. Solomon, that is, 'peaceable', both by name and by the most tranquil state of his kingdom signifies Christ, of whom it is said: "His empire shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end of peace." And Hiram, who is interpreted 'living on high', [signifies] gentiles glorious in life and faith. Or, because he was a king and helped Solomon with royal power in the building of the temple, he signifies the lords of the world converted to the faith, by whose aid the Church is increased and is raised up by princely decrees against heretics and schismatics [and] pagans. Solomon, then, asks help from Hiram in the work of the temple, because the Lord, coming in the flesh and wishing to build the Church, chose helpers not from the Jews only but also from the gentiles. For from both peoples he took ministers of the word. Hiram sent Solomon cedar wood cut from Libanus, and fir, to be set in the house of the Lord, because the converted gentile world sent to the Lord men famous in the world, but cast down and humbled from the mountain of pride by the axe of rebuke, who, instructed to the rule of gospel truth, were placed in the building of the Church each according to his merit or time. He also sent craftsmen, that is, philosophers converted to true wisdom, who were set over the peoples to be ruled for the sake of learning; such was in the times of the apostles Dionysius the Areopagite, and Cyprian, a most learned teacher and most valiant martyr. He sent also gold, namely men famous for wisdom and talent, in return for whom he awaits the gifts of heavenly grace: the wheat, namely, of God, the oil of charity, of the anointing and illumination of the Holy Spirit.
5.10: **“So Hiram gave Solomon cedar trees, and fir trees, according to all his desire.”** — SO HIRAM GAVE SOLOMON etc. Tyre, whence king Hiram [came], is an island given to trade, where there were excellent workers of timber, who gave precious timber receiving provisions. For they live not by tilling the land but by trading. There is mount Libanus, from whose timber the house of the Lord was made. Whence [the temple] too is called Libanus, there: "Open thy gates, O Libanus."
5.13:
**“And king Solomon chose workmen out of all Israel, and the levy was of thirty thousand men.”**
• because it was enjoined on each what he should do
• AND KING SOLOMON CHOSE WORKMEN OUT OF ALL ISRAEL etc. Not in vain did he choose workmen out of all Israel, because those who build the house of God by example and word are not to be chosen from the one stock of Aaron the priest, but sought from the whole Church, and promoted without respect of persons. When they are ordained to instruct the unbelievers and call them into the college of the Church, vigorous and chosen men are sent as it were to cut the materials of the temple in Libanus. The thirty thousand cutters signify those who are perfect in the faith of the Trinity, which befits teachers most of all. But because the thirty thousand were so ordered that ten [thousand] pressed on the work each month, the sacrament of the ten is rather to be opened. Ten thousand are sent from Israel to cut timber for the work of the house of the Lord, for those who are ordained to the instruction of the ignorant must keep the ten precepts of the law in all things and show them to their hearers to be kept. The rewards to come in heaven also are figured by the denarius, which they themselves must hope for and make known to their hearers as to be hoped for. And the three months, whose interval was laid on the individual cutters of timber, typically announce the perfection of the three gospel virtues: almsgiving, prayer and fasting. For by almsgiving are comprehended all things which we work kindly toward the brethren to fulfil the love of neighbour; by prayer all things by which through inward compunction we are joined to our creator; by fasting all things by which we keep ourselves from the contagion of vices and the enticements of the world, that with free mind and chaste body we may always be able to cleave to the love of God and neighbour. These are the three months of the workmen of the temple; for because a month is completed by the fulness of the days of the lunar circle, by it is rightly shown the fulness of virtue, in which the mind of the faithful is looked upon by the Lord with daily illumination, as the moon by the sun.
**“WORKMEN”** — These workmen were proselytes, their masters from the Jews, because he did not make anyone of Israel to serve.
5.14:
**“And he sent them to Libanus, ten thousand every month by turns, so that two months they were at home.”** — the month of cutting [is] almsgiving, by which we profit our neighbours; the two, prayer and fasting
**“And Adoniram”** — Adoniram: 'my Lord on high'. This is Christ, who is set over the workmen of the temple, to order in which months each should go out to work and in which return to care for his own house; when he more familiarly informs the minds of preachers, that they may discern when they ought to build the Church by preaching, or by performing other offices of piety, and when to return to examine their conscience, as if to inspect their own house, that by prayers and fasts it may be worthy of the heavenly inspector and visitor.
5.15:
**“And Solomon had seventy thousand to carry burdens, and eighty thousand”**
• AND SOLOMON HAD SEVENTY THOUSAND etc. Nor should it be passed over that the seventy and eighty thousand burden-bearers and stonecutters, with their overseers, were not Israelites, but proselytes, that is, strangers who dwelt among them. Whence in Paralipomenon: "Solomon numbered all the proselytes, and there were found a hundred and fifty-three thousand six hundred. And he made seventy thousand of them to carry burdens on their shoulders" etc. Now they were called proselytes in Greek who passed from other nations into the fellowship of the people of God, having received circumcision. The workmen of the house of the Lord, then, were of Israel, and of the proselytes, and of the gentiles: of Israel the thirty thousand who were sent to cut cedars from Libanus; of the proselytes these stonecutters; of the gentiles Hiram and his servants, who cut timber with the servants of Solomon. Every kind of men, then, through whom the Church was to be built, went before in the building of the temple.
