For Jews, proselytes and gentiles converted to the truth build the one Church of Christ by right living and teaching.
• Seventy thousand and eighty thousand workmen: seventy, namely, on account of the sabbath rest of souls, for the seventh day is consecrated to the sabbath, that is, to rest; eighty on account of the hope of resurrection, which went before in the Lord on the eighth day, that is, after the sabbath, and in us is hoped for on the eighth day and in the eighth age to come.
**“to hew stones in the mountain,”**
• cutters of stones
• And note that some cut stones on the mountain, some carried burdens. For the gifts of the spirit are diverse, and some have greater constancy in teaching and reproving the insolent; some are gentler, for consoling the fainthearted; some, endowed with both virtues, come together for the work of the house of the Lord. Whence: "Rebuke the unquiet, comfort the feebleminded" etc.
**“TO HEW STONES”** — BEDE. Latomi are cutters of stones, and signify the same as the cutters of timber, that is, preachers, who work the minds of the ignorant with the chisel of the word of God, and change them from their native crookedness and deformity, and, regularly instructed, fit them to the unity of the faithful, that is, to the building of the house of God. Timber and stones are cut on the mountain and carried to the mountain of the house of God, because we are all born on the mountain of pride, who draw our origin from the sin of Adam, who sinned proudly. But we are hewn out of the mountain of pride by being catechized and receiving the sacraments of faith, and are carried to the mountain of the house of the Lord, because, rescued from the power of darkness, we come to the citadel of virtues, which is in the unity of the Church.
5.16:
**“BESIDES THE OVERSEERS”** — The overseers are the authors of sacred Scripture, by whose mastery we are instructed to teach the ignorant, to rebuke the contemptuous, and to bear one another's burdens.
**“THREE THOUSAND”** — On account of the faith of the Trinity, which the holy words preach. That in Paralipomenon three thousand six hundred are written looks to their perfection. For the six, in which the adornment of the world was completed, signifies perfect good works; and because holy Scripture teaches that the works of justice are to be had with the faith of truth, the overseers of the works of the temple were rightly three thousand six hundred.
5.17:
**“And the king commanded, that they should bring”**
• AND THE KING COMMANDED THAT THEY SHOULD BRING etc. To build the house of the Lord, first timber and stones are cut from the mountain, because those whom we seek to instruct in the faith we must first teach to renounce the devil and the transgression in which they were born. Then great and precious stones are to be sought and laid in the foundation, so that, the former conversation being renounced, we may look into their life and conduct in all things, and set before our hearers for imitation those whom we know to cleave specially to the Lord through the virtue of humility, and whom we see, squared by stability of mind, to endure unmoved against all onsets of temptations, great and precious in fame and merit.
• Namely men eminent in action and holiness, who cleave more familiarly to Christ, so that the more firmly they hope in him, the more strongly they may be able to direct the life of others, which is to bear the breadth of the wall. These are the prophets [and] apostles, who received the word and sacraments of truth visibly or invisibly from the very wisdom of God. Whence: "Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets."
**“great stones, costly stones”**
• GREAT STONES, COSTLY STONES. Or the great, precious, squared stones are the first masters, who heard the word of salvation from the Lord himself; and the rows of stones or timbers laid above are the following priests or teachers, by whose preaching the Church grows and is adorned with virtues.
• BEDE. RABANUS. And of what colour the stones were, David shows in Paralipomenon, saying to Solomon: 'I have prepared every precious stone and Parian marble in great abundance'. He calls Parian marble white, such as the island of Paros produces. Whence the Poet: "Olearos and snowy Paros" etc. Whence Josephus: "He raised the temple up to the vault, built of white stone." The white marble of which the house of the elect is built signifies clean action and a conscience chastened from every blemish of corruption. Whence: "Let us cleanse ourselves from all defilement of the flesh and of the spirit, perfecting sanctification in the fear of God."
**“FOR THE FOUNDATION”** — The foundation is Christ; whence: "Other foundation no man can lay, but that which is laid, which is Christ Jesus." Who is rightly called the foundation of the house of God, because, as Peter says: "There is no other name under heaven given to men, whereby we must be saved." On him are brought great and precious stones, that is, all the perfect, who faithfully cleave to him and bravely bear the necessities of the brethren, and are bent from their rectitude by no adversity, nor even by death; whom the Church receives not only from Judea but also from the gentiles. Whence it is added: which the masons of Solomon hewed etc.
5.18:
**“which the masons of Solomon, and the masons of Hiram hewed.”** — who prepare or lay on the cement
**“THE MASONS OF SOLOMON, AND THE MASONS OF HIRAM”** — Because the teachers of the Church were from both peoples, and so lofty that they were the teachers even of those lofty teachers themselves, and as it were squaring them prepared them for raising the building of the house of the Lord. For not only Jeremias, Isaias and the other prophets of the circumcision, but also Job with his sons, who were of the gentiles, minister the greatest pattern of life and patience [and] the greatest proclamations of saving doctrine to the teachers who follow, that, superfluous words, deeds and thoughts being cast away, they may become worthy to bear the burden of the Church.
**“AND THE GIBLIANS”** — RABANUS. BEDE. Byblos is a city of Phenicia, of which Ezechiel [says]: "The ancients of Gebal, and the wise men thereof" etc. For which in the Hebrew is had Goel or Gebal, which is interpreted 'defining' or 'discriminating'. For those who prepare the hearts of men for the spiritual building which the soul constructs out of virtues are then able to have or teach their hearers faith and works of justice, if they have first, taught by the sacred pages, learned by a certain definition of truth what faith is to be held, by what path of virtues one must go. In vain does he usurp the office of teacher who does not know the discernment of faith. Nor does he build a sanctuary for the Lord but a ruin for himself who presumes to teach what he himself has not learned.
**“TO BUILD”** — After the foundation composed of such [stones], the house is to be built with timber and stones prepared and set in order, which have been drawn from their place or root; because after the first rudiments of faith, after the foundations of humility laid in us after the example of lofty men, the wall of good works is to be added on high, and, as it were with rows of stones laid one on another, we must advance from virtue to virtue.

6.1:
**“AND IT CAME TO PASS”** — BEDE. RABANUS. Mention is made of the going out of Egypt, when the tabernacle began to be built, so that it may be known how many years passed between the building of each house, and that a spiritual sacrament may be known to be in the sum of the time. For four times a hundred and twenty make four hundred and eighty. Four befits gospel perfection, because there are four evangelists; a hundred and twenty the teaching of the law, on account of the same number of years of the lawgiver. In which number of men also the primitive Church received the Holy Spirit, showing that those who use the law lawfully, that is, who, recognizing the grace of Christ in it, embrace it, are filled with the grace of his Spirit, because they recognize [it] more fully in his love. By the tabernacle which Moses and the children of Israel made in the desert is signified the Synagogue; but by the temple which Solomon and the children of Israel built with proselytes and gentiles, 'the Church of the gentiles'. And the worship and religion of the tabernacle lasted four hundred and eighty years, and so the temple began to be built; because the Scripture of the Old Testament abounds with such perfection that, to him who understands it well, it contains in itself all the mysteries of the new Testament. Many fathers of the Old Testament also lived so perfectly that they are thought in no way inferior to the apostles and apostolic men. And the tabernacle lasted until the building of the temple for four hundred and seventy [so the edition] years, that is, a hundred and twenty multiplied by four; because from the time the law was given until the incarnation of Christ there were not lacking men who in the law kept gospel perfection in all things in mind and deed, nor Scripture in the old that made known the grace of the new Testament.
**“IN THE FOURTH YEAR”** — In the fourth year of king Solomon the house began to be built, because, after the dispensation of Christ's incarnation was completed, written in the four gospels, the Holy Spirit being sent, the structure of the Church began.
**“IN THE MONTH ZIO, THE SAME IS THE SECOND MONTH”** — That [it was] in the second month looks to the election of the gentiles, which began to build second after Israel. Whence also the second month was allowed in the law for keeping the Pasch to those who, unclean in soul or far off on a journey, could not keep it in the first month. There we are designated, who, unclean by the death of our soul and still far off from the people of God, could not keep the first [Pasch], which was done in the flesh and blood of a lamb. But today we celebrate the second Pasch, which is done in the body and blood of the Redeemer.
**“in the month Zio (the same is the second month),”** — Namely May; for April, in which the Pasch is celebrated, is the first among the months of the year with the Hebrews. Whence it is plain that as soon as the Pasch was finished he began to build the house of the Lord, and the people, consecrated by the mystic solemnity, put their hands to the mystic work.
**“HE BEGAN TO BUILD A HOUSE”** — BEDE. Where the temple was built is made manifest in Paralipomenon thus: "And Solomon began to build the house of the Lord in Jerusalem in mount Moria, which had been shewn to David his father, in the place which David had prepared in the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite." The house of the Lord, then, is built in the vision of peace, because the Church, spread over the world, stands in one faith and fellowship of truth. For God is not under a rending of minds, but 'his place is in peace'. It is built on a mountain, that is, Christ, of whom it is said: "And in the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the top of mountains," and elsewhere: "A city seated on a mountain cannot be hid." For he is the mountain of mountains, who, sprung from the earth according to the flesh, surpasses by the height of his dignity the power and holiness of all earthly things. On him the city or house of the Lord is built, because if our hope and faith do not fix their root in him, they are nothing. He is rightly called mount Moria, that is, 'of vision', because those whom he keeps for the eternal vision of brightness he deigns to see and help while they labour in this life. For he is the place in which Abraham offered his son to the Lord and, for the devotion of obedience, deserved to be seen by him, whence it received its name. Lastly, where the Lord says: "Take thy son, whom thou lovest, Isaac, and go into the land which I shall shew thee" etc., in the Hebrew is had 'the land of Moria'. And because the sacrifice of Isaac was a type of the Lord's passion, the temple is rightly built in the same place, because the Church, dedicated through the faith and mysteries of the Lord's passion, grows into a holy temple in the Lord. Which had been shewn to David his father: for the Lord to come in the flesh had been shown to David, as to the other prophets, who through that very incarnation would wash from sins the Church called from the gentiles and consecrate the unbelieving house to himself. In the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite: the floor signifies the Church. Whence: "And he will thoroughly cleanse his floor." And Ornan, that is, 'enlightened', a Jebusite by nation, signifies the gentiles, to be enlightened by the Lord and changed into sons of the Church. Whence: "You were heretofore darkness, but now light in the Lord." Jebus, which is also Jerusalem, is interpreted 'trodden down', Jerusalem 'vision of peace'; while the gentile Ornan reigns in it, it is called Jebus. When David bought in it the place of the holocaust, and Solomon built the temple of the Lord, it is called Jerusalem; because the gentile world, ignorant of divine worship, is trodden down and mocked by the demons, but when the grace of the creator has looked upon it, it finds in itself the place and name of peace. Whence: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God." While Ornan, then, reigned in this city, it was called Jebus; but when he sold the place of the floor, with the oxen and threshing sledges, to king David, it received the name Jerusalem; because the gentile world, persisting in its obstinacy, is trodden down, as vile and abject, by the evil spirits; but when it has learned to sell all things and offer them to the true king, it can no longer be trodden down by demons or vices, but is made possessor of the inward peace which it has with its creator.
**“of the reign of Solomon over Israel, he began to build a house to the Lord.”** — WHICH DAVID HAD PREPARED etc. For David had prepared by singing psalms, the other prophets had prepared by prophesying, the place for the true Lord, namely Solomon, in which he might build the house; because they instructed the hearts of their hearers in faith, warning them to receive the incarnate Son of God with faithful devotion. Whence: "Lift up your eyes, and see the countries, for they are white already to harvest. And he that reapeth receiveth wages, and gathereth fruit unto life everlasting: that both he that soweth and he that reapeth may rejoice together." As if [to say]: lift up your eyes and see the place which is prepared for building the house; and he who builds by teaching receives wages and gathers precious stones unto life everlasting; that both he who prepares the place for the building and he who builds may rejoice together, that is, the prophet foretelling the one to come and the apostle preaching the Lord come may obtain one reward together.
6.2:
**“IN LENGTH”** — The length of the house signifies 'the longanimity of the Church', by which it patiently bears adversities until it comes to the homeland. This is sixty cubits, because six signifies the perfection of good works; because we ought so to bear adversities through longanimity that through good works we may deserve to enter the promised homeland.
**“TWENTY CUBITS”** — On account of the twofold distinction of charity, by which we love God and neighbour.
**“IN BREADTH”** — The breadth signifies 'charity', which with the enlarged bosom of the mind loves friends in God and enemies for God's sake, until, these being turned to peace or utterly extinguished, it rejoices with friends alone in the Lord.
**“in breadth,”** — BEDE. Note that the thirty cubits of height reached not to the roof of the temple, but to the lower upper room. For it is plainly written in Paralipomenon that the height was a hundred and twenty cubits, of the sacraments of which matter it will be more fittingly treated in what follows, where the order of the reading comes to the middle and third upper room.
**“THIRTY CUBITS”** — On account of faith in the Trinity, in whose vision all the desires of our hope are suspended. Each number is multiplied by ten, because through faith and the keeping of the law patience is exercised wholesomely, charity burns manfully, and hope is caught up loftily to eternal things.
**“IN HEIGHT”** — The height signifies 'the hope of future recompense', for which it despises prosperity or adversity, until it sees the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.
6.3:
**“And there was a porch before the temple of twenty cubits in length, according to the measure of the breadth of the temple,”**
• AND THERE WAS A PORCH BEFORE THE TEMPLE OF TWENTY CUBITS IN LENGTH etc. Of this it is written thus in Paralipomenon: "And the porch in the front, which was extended in length according to the measure of the breadth, of twenty cubits." It is plain, then, that this porch was made at the eastern part of the temple. For the temple faced the east, as did the tabernacle, and had its door on the east, over against the door of the temple, according to Josephus, so that the equinoctial sun, rising, would pour its rays in straight lines through the three doors, namely of the porch, the temple and the oracle, upon the ark of the Testament.
• The temple figures the Church; the porch, which, being before the temple, received the light of the sun first, [figures] that part of the Church which preceded the Lord's incarnation, in which the patriarchs and prophets first received the rising sun of justice, and bore witness to the Lord to be born in the flesh by living, preaching, being born and dying.
• OF TWENTY CUBITS IN LENGTH ACCORDING TO THE MEASURE etc. Because the ancient just waited in patience and longanimity for the time when the incarnate Lord would bring the grace of the gospel, beholding and saluting his promises afar off. The porch, then, by its length equalled the breadth of the temple, because through longanimity of mind they desired to come to the enlargement of the Church in the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus.
• The porch had ten cubits in breadth, because such men, though they had not yet received the words or mysteries of the gospel which were to be handed down by Christ, yet kept the precepts of the decalogue with the perfect love of an enlarged heart.
• In the very front of the porch were the first just, namely Abel and Henoch; in its innermost part, and as it were near the wall of the temple, the forerunner of the Lord, Simeon, Anna and the rest, who, though they deserved to see his birth, yet could not hear his teaching and receive his sacraments.
6.4: **“WINDOWS”** — [The windows are] the holy teachers, to whom, going out of themselves in mind to God, it is granted to see the secrets of heavenly things more especially. While they make public what they see in secret, like windows receiving the light of the sun they fill all the inner parts of the temple. Whence they are said to have been oblique, that is, wider within, because he who perceives even for a moment the radiance of heavenly contemplation soon enlarges the bosom of his heart by chastening it more, and prepares it by skilful exercise for grasping greater things.
6.5:
**“And upon the wall of the temple he built floors round about, in the walls of the house round about the temple and the oracle”** — AND UPON THE WALL OF THE TEMPLE HE BUILT FLOORS ROUND ABOUT etc. These floors are called pinnacles of the temple in the gospel, where the Lord is tempted by the devil. We read also that James the brother of the Lord was raised onto the pinnacle of the temple, from which he might preach to the people. But whether it was the custom of teachers to sit on the floors and speak to the crowd below we nowhere read. These three floors, then, signify as many grades of the faithful, namely of the married, the continent and virgins, distinguished by the height of their profession, but all belonging to the house of the Lord by the fellowship of faith and truth and cleaving to it with fixed mind. The highest floor, then, is narrower than the rest, the middle wider than the highest, narrower than the lowest; because the higher profession of virtue ought to hold a higher way of living. For those who, having renounced marriage, consecrate virginity to the Lord must show conduct worthy of virginity: abstain from idle words, anger, quarrelling, detraction, immodest dress, revellings, drinkings and the like; give themselves to vigils, holy prayers, readings, almsgiving and the like; that those who hold in profession the state of the future life, in which 'they shall neither marry nor be married, but shall be as the angels in heaven', may study to imitate its state in the present as far as is possible to mortals. And the lowest is of greater breadth, because it is not said to the married: "Sell all that thou hast, and give to the poor," but: 'If thou wilt enter into life, keep the commandments: thou shalt not kill, thou shalt not commit adultery' etc. The continent hold the middle place, as much lower than virgins as higher than the married; their glorious portion built up the primitive Church. Whence: "The multitude of believers had but one heart and one soul" etc. That the greatest part of these had left the embraces of their wives the history of blessed Stephen testifies, where it calls the women strong in the same religion not their wives but their widows.
**“SIDES”**
• That is, battlements, lest anyone should easily fall from there to the lower parts; which we read befell king Ochozias in Samaria. These signify the daily defences of divine protection toward us. Whence: "The angel of the Lord shall encamp round about them that fear him" etc. Ochozias, it says, king of Samaria, who had separated himself from the house of David, went up into the upper room but fell through the lattice. Because, though heretics or schismatics seem to climb some citadel of good action, yet because they do not have the joining of the unity of the Church, as if through open and not solid defences of the sides they slip down to the depths of vices, while, destitute of divine help, they perish in the pride of their obstinacy.
• That is, walls or lattices or battlements; the teachers sitting on the floors, who preached to the people standing round below. Whence the Lord: "Preach upon the housetops." And Solomon: "It is better to sit in a corner of the housetop." Doma in Greek, roof in Latin.
6.6:
**“The floor”** — virgins
**“that was underneath, was five cubits in breadth, and the middle floor”** — the continent
**“was six cubits in breadth, and the third floor”** — the married
**“BEAMS”** — BEDE. The beams [so the edition: 'Domus'] that bear the floors signify 'the preachers', who, while they hold a lofty and honourable place in the Church of God, by their preaching raise the weaker from the desire of the lowest things, and lift them up to desire and hope for heavenly things, and by interceding help them to persevere. And we read in Paralipomenon that the beams of the temple, like the rest of its interior, were clothed with gold. This was done in such a way that those parts of the beams which are within the temple were covered with plates of gold, while those which appeared outside were not gilded but showed the appearance and form of cedar, on which, however, they carried the floors laid upon them. What stood out on the outside, then, designates the life of the saints, which is made known to us; but what shone gilded within, the brightness by which in the heavenly homeland they rejoice in the sight of their creator. The golden brightness of the beams was open only to those who had entered the temple, because how great is the multitude of the sweetness of God, which he has hidden for them that fear him, and has wrought for them that hope in him, those alone know who have deserved to enter the heavenly kingdom. And yet we, seeing the life, passions and teaching of the saints, that is, reading them in the Scriptures, are stirred up to do well, and are as it were lifted from the earth upon the heads of the beams that appear outside. For though we cannot yet behold the inward glory of the saints, yet from what we have been able to see outwardly we faithfully cleave to the lofty members of the Church. We can also understand these things of the saints still set in this life, whose purity of love, by which they shine in the secret of the heart before the Lord, we cannot behold, and yet from the things which they show outwardly by speaking, doing or suffering we find the help of salvation.
**“BEAMS ON THE OUTSIDE”** — They were of such length that their heads stood out on the outside: in the lowest row of seven cubits, in the middle of six, in the highest of five; so that the floors were put together on their heads, not fixed into the walls of the temple but laid next to the walls upon the beams that had come out of the walls.
6.7:
**“And the house, when it was in building, was built of stones hewed and made ready,”** — AND THE HOUSE, WHEN IT WAS IN BUILDING etc. These things pertain properly to that part of the Church which, after the labours and contests of the world, has deserved to be brought in to the eternal rewards. For nothing defiled shall enter into that city.
**“AND [NEITHER] HAMMER NOR AXE”** — Because here we are beaten by adversities and exercised by the discipline of truth, that there we may be disposed in fitting places according to merit, and, chastisement ceasing, may be bound to one another by the glue of love alone and be filled through and through with one Spirit. But though it is said that Noe was a perfect man in his generations, and blessed are the undefiled in the way, and such like, no one can walk the way of this life truly perfect and without stain. 'For there is no man that doth good, and sinneth not'. But according to the measure of this time those are called 'perfect' and 'undefiled' who are then truly perfected, when, freed from the bonds of the body, they come to the immortal beauty of the house of the Lord.
6.8:
**“The door for the middle side was in the wall on the right hand of the house,”**
• THE DOOR FOR THE MIDDLE SIDE etc. BEDE. Some, understanding this place wrongly, think that the door of the temple was on the south, not noticing that if Scripture had wished to signify this it would not say: The door for the middle side was in the wall on the right hand of the house, but thus: and the house had a door to the south. But now it signifies something else. For by the part of the house on the right hand it means the southern side of the temple, in the eastern part of which was the door, made in the very corner near the ground, entering which they at once went up step by step to the higher parts, having their way and ascent through the inside of the wall, until by such a passage they came to the middle room, and from the middle to the third. And, though Scripture does not say so, they had very many windows on the south, by whose light those going up made their way sure and without stumbling. This place looks properly to the body of the Lord which he took from the virgin. For the door of the middle side was in the part of the house on the right hand, because "one of the soldiers with a spear opened his side." And holy Church believes it was the right side that was opened by the soldier. And the evangelist said "opened", as of the door of the middle side, through which a way to heavenly things might be laid open to us. Then he added thus: "And immediately there came out blood and water," water, namely, by which we are washed in baptism, and blood, by which we are consecrated in the holy chalice. For by this door we have the ascent into the middle room, and from the middle into the third, because through faith and the mysteries of our redemption we ascend from the present conversation of the Church to the rest of souls after death, and from the rest of souls, when the day of judgment comes, to the immortality of bodies, that we may live for ever in great beatitude of body and soul. This passage was made invisibly, so that only those who entered knew it, though those placed outside saw [it] through the door itself; because the acts of the faithful in this world and the celebrations of the sacraments even the reprobate can behold; but the secrets of faith and the inward grace of love no one knows except him who by these climbs to heavenly things with the Lord as guide: "For he who saith that he knoweth God, and keepeth not his commandments, is a liar."
• The door of the temple is the Lord, because 'no man cometh to the Father but by him'. Whence: "I am the door. By me, if any man enter in, he shall be saved." The door of the porch is the prophetic word, which led those entering as it were by a straight path to the door of the tabernacle, because it preached the grace of Christ by which he was to redeem the world. The whole making of the porch, then, signifies the faithful of that time; and the door in the porch expresses the teachers, who laid open to the rest the light of life and the gate of entering to God. And fittingly one door, on account of the faith and love of truth harmonious in all the saints.
**“THEY WENT UP TO THE MIDDLE ROOM”** — BEDE. Note that the thirty cubits of height of which we read above reached to the middle room; then thirty were added up to the third, until one came to the roof of the porch which was round the temple on the south, north and west, according to Josephus. Then sixty cubits were counted up to the highest roof of the temple, and so the whole height of the house, according to Paralipomenon, was completed in a hundred and twenty cubits. The porch also which was before the front of the temple, to the east, had, according to the same book, the same sum of cubits in height; which book calls the aforesaid porches storehouses and chambers. David, it says, gave Solomon his son a description of the porch and the temple and the storehouses and the upper room and the chambers in the secret places of the house of propitiation; where it also mentions the outer houses which were outside the court of the priests round about the temple, thus: "As also of all the courts which he had in his thought, and of the chambers round about, for the treasures of the house of the Lord, and for the treasures of the holy things." And that the whole height of the temple was a hundred and twenty cubits signifies that the primitive Church in Jerusalem, after the Lord's ascension, received the grace of the Holy Spirit in this number of men; because fifteen, which consists of seven and eight, is wont to be referred to the signification of the life of faithful souls which is now led in the sabbath [of rest] and will be perfected at the end of the world by the resurrection of immortal bodies. And fifteen drawn into a triangle, that is, counted with all its parts, makes a hundred and twenty. Fittingly, then, by the number a hundred and twenty the great beatitude of the elect in the future is designated. Aptly the third upper room of the house of the Lord is completed with this, because after the present labours of the faithful, after the rest of souls received in the future, the full felicity of the whole Church will be fulfilled in the resurrection. To which it pertains that the Lord, rising from the dead and ascending to heaven, sent the Holy Spirit in tongues of fire upon this number of men, by which he made those who were separated by divers tongues have a common speech through the kinship of tongues. For the Church, rising in its time and ascending to heaven in incorruptible flesh, will be fully and perfectly illumined by the gift of the Holy Spirit when God shall be all in all, for proclaiming the great works of God, because with harmonious mind and voice all will praise together the glory of the divine majesty.
6.9:
**“WITH ROOFS”** — BEDE. Laquearia are panels put together and adorned with great beauty, fixed to the beams from beneath; and because the house of the Lord had been made of threefold height, it had threefold roofs.
**“So he built the house, and finished it: and he covered the house with roofs”** — The loftier saints, namely, whose work and teaching, set before all in the temple, stand out as it were high and far off; and who, by interceding and exhorting, protect the souls of the weak lest they fail.
**“OF CEDAR”** — The cedar is a tree that does not rot, of pleasant odour, of shining appearance, which when kindled drives away and kills serpents by its brightness. These things befit the perfect, whose patience is invincible, whose fame of virtues is eminent, whose presence is most welcome to the good, whose authority is most constant for refuting and confounding the enemies of truth, and who shine forth with singular eminence both in this life and in the future.
**“of cedar,”** — It signifies the battlements which had been made round about on the highest roof of the house, lest anyone coming to the higher parts should suddenly slip to the bottom. Which Moses commanded to be made in every house; and these above are called sides, where it is said: and he made sides round about. In which are figured the divine defences which help us daily, still labouring in the world and striving according to our capacity toward higher things, lest we fail. In the same way too we understand this place, but with this distinction: that in this life, amid the frequent temptations of the unappeased enemy or the obstacles of our frailty, we are continually defended by the gift of heavenly mercy lest we fall; but in that life we climb to the highest roof of the temple, so that we neither wish nor are able to sin any more, nor are affected by any pain of death or fear of a tempting adversary. Of the present helps of the Lord, as of the sides of the floors, the Lord himself says: "I am with him in tribulation, I will deliver him, and I will glorify him." And of the future grace by which the heavenly city is illumined the prophet says: "Praise the Lord, O Jerusalem" etc., as far as "[who hath placed] peace in thy borders" etc. And fittingly this floor is five cubits high, because in that homeland the presence of the divine brightness so fills us that our sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch have nothing sweet except to love God with the whole heart, the whole soul, the whole strength, and our neighbour as ourselves.
6.10: **“And he built a floor over all the house five cubits in height,”** — A FLOOR OVER ALL THE HOUSE. BEDE. Here the highest roof of the house itself is called that floor which was laid over the highest beams. The temple had no ridge on top, as neither had the tabernacle, but it was level, as houses are made in Palestine and Egypt. And the floor with which the house was covered signifies the same as the roofs, that is, men eminent in the resurrection, and coming by singular holiness to the very summit of virtue; of one of whom it is said: "Among them that are born of women there hath not risen a greater than John the Baptist"; of whose equal it is said: "He shall go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elias."
6.15:
**“And he built the walls of the house on the inside, with boards of cedar”**
• AND HE BUILT THE WALLS OF THE HOUSE etc. BEDE. Within, indeed, the house was clothed with cedar. For outside, the stone of which it was made shone with such brightness as if it were covered with white pebble. But mystically the walls of the temple are the faithful peoples of which the universal Church consists. Their spreading over the world is designated by the breadth of the walls, their hope and intention raised to heavenly things by the height. Or the breadth of the wall, which consists of rows of stones laid one on another, [designates] the state of the present Church, where the elect, all built on the foundation of Christ, succeed one another in order through the courses of time, and, bearing one another, fulfil the law of Christ, which is charity. For while those who are instructed by preceding masters instruct others, as it were with rows of living stones laid on one another in the house of God, they are borne by others with fixed constancy in such a way that they themselves suffice to bear others, down to the last just, who, set on the highest summit of the house, are borne by others but have none to bear.
• The walls are covered within with boards of cedar when the hearts of the faithful overflow with the love of virtues. For as the cedar signifies the perfect, so in fitting places [it signifies] the loftiness of the virtues by which one comes to the same perfection.
**“FROM THE FLOOR”** — All things are covered with timber FROM THE FLOOR OF THE HOUSE TO THE TOP OF THE WALLS AND TO THE ROOFS, when the elect, from the first rudiments of faith to the perfection of good action and to the entrance of the heavenly homeland, toil in good works; when from the first just to the last at the consummation of the world all study the virtues by whose merit they may dare to say: "We are the good odour of Christ unto God."
**“AND HE COVERED THE FLOOR OF THE HOUSE”** — This is written more fully in Paralipomenon thus: "He paved also the floor of the temple with most precious marble, of great beauty." Whence it is plain that he did not lay the fir boards with which he covered the floor on the earth, but first covered it with marble, then laid the boards above, and added a third [layer] clothed with gold over these two, as is read in what follows. And as the height of the wall rising up and reaching to the roofs signifies the advances of virtues by which the elect come to the heavenly kingdom, or the very choirs of the elect succeeding one another through various times, so the evenness of the floor [signifies] their harmonious humility, by which, while still set in temporal life, they live together in fellowship at the bidding of charity. The floor was paved with most precious marble of great beauty, and the same marble was covered with fir boards; because the life of the just must first be fortified in the heart with firmness of faith, then adorned in deed with the breadth of virtues. For what use has the beauty of most precious marble covered with boards of wood, unless it tacitly signified something and showed that the amplitude of good works must be propped by the strength of faith [unclear in the edition: "in temeritate"]? And the fir, on account of its height and durability, fittingly signifies the mind of the elect, spurning the lowest desires and cleaving to the contemplation of heavenly things, and excelling singularly also in the virtue of patience. And the plates of gold laid over the marble and the fir boards [signify] the breadth of charity, from a pure heart and a good conscience and an unfeigned faith, which, as gold is more precious than other metals, so, more eminent than the other virtues, shines with singular light in the temple of God. Whence the Apostle, when he had enumerated, as it were a pavement, very many goods of the virtues which are to be kept by humble men, saying: "Put ye on the bowels of mercy, benignity, humility, patience" etc., added: "But above all these things have charity" etc.
6.16:
**“And he built up twenty cubits with boards of cedar at the hinder part of the temple,”**
• the western [part]: for the temple had its entrance from the rising of the sun, and toward the setting the inner house, that is, the holy of holies
• AND HE BUILT UP TWENTY CUBITS etc. That he says the boards which separate the inner house from the outer were built from the floor to the upper parts signifies not up to the roofs, which were suspended thirty cubits on high from the floor, as has been said, but only up to twenty cubits of height, as will be said. And the rest above these boards was open and empty up to the roofs, ten cubits in height and twenty cubits in length, according to the breadth of the house. Through which empty space the smoke of the incense from the altar of incense was wont to rise into the holy of holies and penetrate to cover the ark of the Lord. The former house, into which "the priests always entered, accomplishing the offices of sacrifices," is the present Church, in which, daily applying ourselves to pious works, we offer to the Lord sacrifices of praise. The inner, which was made at the hinder part of the temple, is eternal life in heaven. The outer, indeed, is the conversation of our exile; the inner, the perpetual solemnity of the blessed which is held in the presence of the highest king. Whence: "Enter thou into the joy of thy lord"; but [it is] later in time, because [it comes] after the labours of the world.
• And the boards that divide the two are the barriers of heaven, whose opening we daily sigh for and knock at with pious urgency that they may be opened; and if we are not permitted to enter before death, yet we have open the door of divine mercy, by which we send before us the incense of prayers, alms, fasts and other good things. For this is it that the cedar wall of the inner house had an empty space throughout its upper parts, through which the smoke of incense might enter, because the eyes of the Lord are open upon his house day and night, and his ears attentive to the prayer of his servants, and this throughout the whole breadth of the Church spread over the world.
6.17:
**“FORTY CUBITS”**
• Ten drawn four times make forty. Whence the people freed from Egypt, in the figure of the present Church, laboured forty years in the desert and was refreshed with heavenly bread, and so came to the promised homeland. For it is exercised by temptations for forty years, to intimate the labours of the Church, in which she toils throughout the whole world in keeping the law. It is fed with manna from heaven through the same forty years, to show that the sufferings of the Church are to be lightened by the hope of the heavenly denarius and of eternal beatitude, where "they that hunger and thirst after justice shall have their fill." The Church, then, is fed in the present and afflicted with adversities, that, "rejoicing in hope, she may be patient in tribulation." Whence Christ too fasted forty days before the death of the flesh, and as many after the resurrection feasted with his disciples, "appearing to them by many proofs, and speaking of the kingdom of God." By fasting he showed our labour in himself, by eating his consolation in us. Fasting he cried: "Take heed, lest your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting and drunkenness." But eating: "Behold I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the world." "I will see you again, and your heart shall rejoice" etc. For while we take the way of God we fast from the vanity of the present world and are refreshed by the promise of the future.
• This number is set in signification of present labour, as fifty of future rest and peace. For there are ten precepts by which one comes to life. For by ten is signified the life which we desire and for which we labour; and by four the world, in which we strive to acquire it. Whence: "He gathered them out of the countries, from the rising and from the setting of the sun, from the north and from the sea."
6.18:
**“AND ALL [THE HOUSE WAS COVERED] WITH CEDAR”** — The cedar signifies the invincible beauty of the virtues. With this wood the whole house is clothed within when the hearts of the just shine with the love of good works alone.
**“HAVING THE TURNINGS”** — The house has in its cedar boards its turnings and joints skilfully made, when the elect are bound to one another by the most beautiful bond of charity, 'that they may have one heart and one soul'. For the turnings which are set on the joints of the boards, that one floor may be made of all, are the offices of charity, by which the holy brotherhood is joined and put together into the one house of Christ throughout the whole world.
**“CARVINGS”** — The works of the saints show forth by manifest expression, as an example to others, what they are. Whence Paul by deeds and words sets himself forth as an example.
**“ALL WAS COVERED WITH BOARDS OF CEDAR”** — The stones of the wall or floor, and the boards and the gold, signify the life of the saints; but the living stones are the saints cemented by the strength of faith into one and the same rule; the cedar or fir boards, [those] joined to one another in one faith by the breadth of various virtues according to the gifts of the Holy Spirit; the plates of gold are those having the charity that surpasses knowledge, and rejoicing together in its most pleasing brightness. These three the Apostle embraces in one sentence, saying: "For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision availeth any thing, nor uncircumcision: but faith that worketh by charity." For the stone signifies 'invincible faith', the cedar 'fragrant action', the gold 'love that transcends all'. And the stone wall is clothed with cedar boards when the profession of faith is adorned with good works, lest it seem idle or dead. But because the law [was] written on stone, the teaching of the gospel confirmed by the wood of the cross, whence also that people was circumcised in the foreskin with a stone, we are consecrated on the forehead with the sign of the cross. The stone walls of the temple, or the floor paved with precious marble, can signify those who lived faithfully and perfectly in the law; and the cedar or fir boards the saints of the new Testament, who, denying themselves and taking up their cross, follow the Lord. And because the common glory of heavenly recompense awaits the saints of both times, to the stones and precious woods is added a third kind, of golden plates. Nor let it seem contrary that we said above that the porch which was before the temple figures the ancient faithful, the temple itself those who were after the Lord's incarnation, and the inner house the joys of the heavenly kingdom promised to both; but now we say that the stone walls designate the ancient people of God, the cedar boards the new, the golden plates the rewards of both in heaven, since the same walls of the temple, both in the porch and in the temple itself and in the Holy of Holies, were alike made of stones and gold. For manifold is the repetition of the same figures in diverse things. But this too must be said: that there were in the law and before the law very many who served the Lord according to the law, not killing, not fornicating, not bearing false witness, not stealing, honouring father and mother, and loving their neighbours as themselves. These belonged to the stone walls of the porch. There were others more perfect, who, leaving the business of the world and taking up the cross, followed the Lord: "They had trial of mockeries and stripes, moreover also of bands and prisons" etc. And those who before the manifest times of the gospel led the gospel life, before the entrance of the temple, shone as it were as cedar boards in the porch; and because the same heavenly kingdom receives them in common, though in distinct mansions, the porch of the temple was covered with gold after the stone and the cedar. Now too there are many who, content with the legal precepts aforesaid, believe it suffices them if they deserve to come to life. There are others who, striving toward perfection, sell all they have and follow the Lord, who says: "You who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of man shall sit on the seat of his majesty" etc. The former, belonging to the walls of the temple made of white [stone], the latter to the cedar boards, await from the Lord the rewards of perpetual light as plates of gold with which to be adorned. There are in the secret parts of the temple precious stones, there are boards of aromatic wood, and one [and the other] covered with gold; because those who walked in the law of the Lord and those who perfectly received the grace of the gospel enjoy eternal life alike.
6.19:
**“AND THE ORACLE”** — BEDE. The oracle where the ark was had twenty cubits in length and breadth and height, that is, square; because in the heavenly homeland, where the eyes of the saints see Christ the king, charity alone, of divine and future grace, shines through all. Whence it follows: AND HE COVERED AND OVERLAID IT WITH MOST PURE GOLD, because he filled the walls of the heavenly city with the grace of charity.
**“And he made the oracle in the midst of the house, in the inner part,”** — This has been explained above: namely that the inner house signifies the secret places of heaven, and the ark of the covenant the Saviour, in whom we have the covenant of peace with the Father, who, ascending into heaven after the resurrection, set the flesh taken from the virgin at the Father's right hand.
6.20:
**“Now the oracle”** — it signifies the cedar wall which separates the oracle, that is, the holy of holies, from the outer house, as was said before
**“NOW THE ORACLE”** — And fittingly the inner house is twenty cubits long, for the mystery of the twofold love of which we have already spoken, which in this life for the most part illumines the minds of the elect, but in that homeland, the works of the other virtues ceasing, reigns alone.
**“was twenty cubits in length, and twenty cubits in breadth, and twenty cubits in height. And he covered and overlaid it with most pure gold. And the altar also he covered with cedar.”**
• AND THE ALTAR ALSO. Namely of incense, which was before the oracle, of which it is added: And the whole altar of the oracle he covered with gold. Whence it is understood that the same altar, made of stone, was clothed with cedar, then covered with gold. For the altar of incense, which was in the outer house but near the door of the inner, is a type of the perfect, who, still held in the world in the flesh, but with all desire suspended to heavenly things, send up as it were the rising smoke of burnt frankincense into the holy of holies; because, burning with heavenly love, they knock at the ears of their author with frequent voices of prayer, and the smoke of incense comes to the upper parts through the wide open empty space, because the cleaner and nearer to heaven they are, the sooner they receive from the Lord what they ask.
• This altar signifies the life of the perfect, who, set as it were in the neighbourhood of the oracle, having forsaken the lowest delights, direct their care to the entrance of the heavenly kingdom alone. Whence on this altar they burned not the flesh of victims but incense only, because such no longer need to slay in themselves the sins of the flesh and the enticements of thoughts, but offer only the perfumes of prayers and spiritual desires through the fire of inward love in the sight of the creator. And what stone, cedar and gold signify has been said above.
6.21:
**“AND THE HOUSE BEFORE THE ORACLE”** — BEDE. The house before the oracle was covered with gold, because the perfect in this life cannot yet hear openly of the Father, that is, cannot yet see openly, but adorn their faith and work of justice with divine love, through which they may deserve the full knowledge of God. The plates of gold with which the house is covered are the works of manifold piety which chaste love spends in the service of the creator or of a brother's need.
**“And the house before the oracle”** — We have said that the house before the oracle signifies the present Church, where we so burn with the love of our Redeemer that we cannot yet see him face to face. Whence fittingly this house is covered with most pure gold, but set apart from the oracle by a middle wall placed between. For it is called an oracle when divine or angelic speech is granted to men with the revelation of secrets. Whence fittingly the oracle was made in the secret parts, that is, in the inner house, because in the heavenly homeland the vision and speech of the angels and the very presence of God will be revealed to us. Whence: "I will love him, and will manifest myself to him," and again: "The hour cometh when I will no more speak to you in proverbs, but will shew you plainly of the Father."
**“he overlaid with most pure gold, and fastened on the plates with nails of gold,”** — by the precepts of charity or the promises of eternal brightness
**“WITH NAILS OF GOLD”** — And the nails are the precepts of charity or the promises of eternal brightness, by which we are held in the exercise of virtues, lest we fail, by the gift of Christ's grace. Whence it is written in Paralipomenon: "He made also nails of gold, so that every nail weighed fifty sicles." For by fifty is signified 'remission of sins' and 'the grace of the Holy Spirit' and 'eternal rest', because the fiftieth psalm is of penance, the fiftieth year the jubilee of remission, and on the fiftieth day after the Pasch the Holy Spirit, coming, consecrated the primitive Church. And each nail by which the golden plates were fastened on the walls of the house of the Lord was of fifty sicles, because the heavenly words by which we advance and are preserved in the love of good works promise us pardon of sins and the grace of the Holy Spirit and an eternal sabbath rest in the future. These indeed are the nails of love. There are other nails of fear, by which beginners mortify the enticements of vices and the pleasure of carnal things, namely the words of truth, by whose instruction we are taught to crucify the flesh. Whence the prophet: "Pierce thou my flesh with thy fear" etc. And again, coming to perfection, he says of the nails of love: "But it is good for me to adhere to my God" etc.
6.22: **“And there was nothing in the temple that was not covered with gold,”** — AND THERE WAS NOTHING IN THE TEMPLE etc. These things are explained more fully in Paralipomenon, where the porch which was before the front of the temple is said to have been gilded within, and the upper rooms covered with gold. The porch before the temple was gilded, because the fathers of the old Testament pleased God through charity. The temple was gilded, because the same "charity is poured forth in our hearts by the Holy Ghost, who is given to us." The inner house was gilded, because in the heavenly homeland charity alone reigns; but there the more truly and securely, as God himself, who is charity, is seen present; there the more surely, as the mediator of God and men himself, who alone is privy to the Father's secrets, is always beheld as the ark of the testament. And that the upper rooms were covered with gold looks to the same. For as the inner house signifies the life of the saints in the sight of the creator, whence: "Thou shalt hide them in the secret of thy face, from the disturbance of men," so the upper rooms on high [signify] that the same life is in heaven and not in this world. Whence: "Seek the things that are above, where Christ is sitting at the right hand of God." "Mind the things that are above, not the things that are upon the earth."
6.23:
**“CHERUBIMS”** — It is a name of angelic dignity, and is said in the singular 'cherub', in the plural 'cherubin'. By the cherubim, then, can be understood the angelic ministries which always stand by the creator in heaven.
**“OF OLIVE TREE”** — Because the angels are anointed with spiritual grace, lest they ever dry up from the love of God, whom he who created them at once filled with the light of heavenly wisdom. Whence also they are called 'cherubim', that is, 'multiplied knowledge' or 'multitude of knowledge'.
**“of olive tree”** — They were made of olive wood, because they give us the light of knowledge with the help of the flame of the love of God, which is poured forth in our hearts by the Spirit.
**“OF TEN CUBITS”** — BEDE. They are ten cubits in height, because they enjoy the denarius of eternal life, having the inviolate image of the creator, holiness and justice and truth, in which they were created, being kept. For the denarius consists of ten obols and was wont to contain in itself the name and image of the king. Therefore it befits the figure of the heavenly kingdom, where the angels remain always in the image of the creator to which they were made, and elect men receive the image which they lost by sinning. Whence: "When he shall appear, we shall be like to him: because we shall see him as he is."
6.24:
**“One wing of the cherub was five cubits,”**
• ONE WING OF THE CHERUB WAS FIVE CUBITS etc. Wings, when they are set in the figure of holy men, signify 'their virtues', by which they fly to heavenly things and have their conversation there. But when they are set in signification of the angels, [they signify] the grace of the perpetual and unfailing felicity of those who always persist in heavenly places and in the ministry of their author; or that they are endowed with the lightness of a spiritual nature, so that wherever they will they arrive at once as if by flying; and here they are figured with wings, and were shown winged to the prophets. And fittingly it is said that one wing of the cherub was five cubits and the other wing of the cherub five cubits, because the angelic powers keep with unwearied devotion the law of God written in five books, namely loving their God with all their strength, and their neighbours as themselves: "For love is the fulfilling of the law." Their neighbours are the angelic spirits, and elect men their fellow citizens. Whence each wing is of the same measure, because with the same devotion with which they love one another in God they also desire our fellowship as we ascend to them. And so the wings together complete ten cubits when, in showing forth twofold charity, they rejoice in the presence of the creator.
• Because amid all the variety of passing things holy men stretch out the senses of the body in the service of the creator, having their eyes ever toward the Lord, hearing and desiring the voice of his praise and telling all his wondrous works, having his words sweet to their palate more than honey and the honeycomb, running in the odour of his ointments, while breath remains in them and the spirit of God in their nostrils, not speaking iniquity nor sounding forth folly; and so, going "by the armour of justice on the right hand and on the left," they come to the heavenly denarius which is promised to the labourers of the vineyard.
**“THE OTHER WING OF THE CHERUB”** — They have two wings, because the testaments declare that they have always stretched toward heavenly things and arrived there with unwearied purpose, alike through prosperity and adversity; because they show that their hearers must do the same.
6.25:
**“ALSO TEN CUBITS”** — BEDE. They are ten cubits high, because they preach that God must be served through the observance of the Decalogue, because they show that those who serve God faithfully are to be rewarded with the denarius of the eternal kingdom.
**“AND THE WORK WAS THE SAME IN BOTH THE CHERUBIMS”** — Two cherubim were made to signify the fellowship of charity, because charity cannot stand between fewer than two. Whence also the disciples are sent two by two to preach, that those who preach the word of faith may before all things hold the virtue of love. The two cherubim are of one measure and work, because there is no dissension of will in the heavenly homeland, where all are illumined by one and the same vision and glory of the present God.
**“and the work was the same in both the cherubims,”**
• Because the writers of both testaments served God with the same chastity of work and devotion of inward charity, they preached God with harmonious voice and faith; and what the New narrates as done concerning the Lord's incarnation, passion, resurrection, the calling of the gentiles, the expulsion of the Jews, the manifold tribulation of the Church, the same the Old, if rightly understood, preached as to be done. The inner wings of the cherubim, then, touched one another above the ark, because they agree in equal witness concerning the Lord. Likewise with their outer wings this one touched one wall, that one the other, because the Old Testament was written properly for the ancient people of God, the New for us who came to faith after the Lord's incarnation; and we are rightly compared to the second wall, that is, the northern, to whom it was given after the cold and darkness of idolatry to know the light of truth.
• BEDE. By the two cherubim the two testaments can be figured. The cherubim were made in the oracle, because in the counsel of divine providence, inaccessible and incomprehensible to us, it was disposed before the ages when and how and by what authors sacred Scripture should be composed. Note indeed that Moses, when he made the tabernacle, made two golden cherubim, which he set on the propitiatory over the ark; but Solomon added two others much greater, to set in the temple, and under their wings the ark in the midst, with the propitiatory and the former cherubim. In the tabernacle, then, there were two cherubim, in the temple four. But both signify the same; but the work was repeated and made more august by Solomon, to teach that, the Church being multiplied after the Lord's incarnation, the loftiness of the heavenly citizens would be laid open more widely, who so praise the creator for their own beatitude that they also rejoice at our rescue and introduction to the same beatitude. For they stretch their wings to one another above the ark when they refer to the praise of the Saviour the good they have received. They stretch their other wings to the walls of the oracle when they delight to see holy men also with them, and touch as it were with the tips of their wings those whom they exult to have been sharers and imitators of their purity in this life. And they touch the two walls equally with their wings, because [the heavenly court] has with it the faithful of both peoples as possessors of the heavenly hall; not that there is in that homeland a local distinction between the two peoples, but because the festivity of inward beatitude is greater from the fellowship of a united brotherhood.
6.27:
**“IN THE MIDST OF THE TEMPLE”** — BEDE. It is manifest from what has been said why the cherubim, who always dwell in heaven, were set in the midst of the inner temple. They stretched out their wings as if to fly, because they always have their mind ready for the service of the divine will. And that one wing of one cherub touched the wall, and the wing of the second cherub the other wall, pertains to that ministry of charity which the angels show to us. That the other wings touched one another in the midst of the temple expresses that grace of love by which they embrace one another.
**“AND [THEY] STRETCHED FORTH THEIR WINGS”** — And the cherubim stretch out their wings to each wall of the oracle, because, rejoicing in the heavenly homeland, they stir up the just of both peoples, by the vision of their glory too, to the praise of the creator; and they rejoice not only in the felicity of the just whom they have with them within, but also take care of us who, still set outside, cry to the Lord out of the depths. Whence it is written of them in Paralipomenon: "And they stood upright on their feet, and their faces were turned toward the outward house." Because, namely, they never strayed from the way of truth in which they were set as soon as they were created; and they desire us, rescued from the hardship of this pilgrimage, to come to their fellowship. So, then, they stand upright on their feet, so they stretch out their gold-covered wings to the walls of the oracle, that they have their faces turned to the outer house; because the angels so perpetually keep their innocence, so exult in the beatitude of holy souls in heaven, that they do not cease to bring help also to those whom they see still pilgrims on earth, until they bring them into the heavenly homeland. "For they are all ministering spirits, sent to minister for them who shall receive the inheritance of salvation."
**“And the cherubims stretched forth their wings”** — They have their faces turned to the outer house, because the writers of them [the testaments], now reigning with the Lord and praising him, take care for the salvation of us who still stand outside, and "are saved" not in fact but "by hope", interceding for us.
6.28:
**“And he overlaid the cherubims with gold.”**
• he raised them up with immortal brightness, filled them with the light of love
• AND HE OVERLAID THE CHERUBIMS WITH GOLD. They were surrounded with gold, because the authority of the testaments was confirmed by the illustrious works of their writers, and the knowledge of the divine Scriptures was made manifest throughout the world; or the inward glory of the heavenly hosts. For the cherubim signify both, namely the angels and the testaments.
6.29:
**“And all the walls of the temple”** — namely the peoples of holy Church, with whom, set upon the foundation of Christ, he has filled the compass of the whole world, and does not cease daily to increase the begun building of faith with a new progeny of members, as by the addition of precious stones
**“he graved round about with divers figures and carvings,”** — because: "To one is given by the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge, to another faith, to another the grace of healing" etc. Also charity, joy, peace, longanimity etc. These are the carvings of holy minds
**“HE GRAVED WITH DIVERS CARVINGS”** — BEDE. The walls are carved with the lathe when the faithful are strong with a ready mind to do what the Lord commands, saying this in every particular: "I will bless the Lord at all times," and: "My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready" etc. They are carved with the lathe when they so attend to the virtues that they are turned from their path by no adversities or blandishments. For because turning surpasses the other arts in speed, and itself keeps for itself the rule by which it works without error, well is the devout life of the saints signified by it, which is always ready for the service of the Lord and, exercised by long use of the virtues, has learned to fulfil it without any byway of straying.
**“And he made in them cherubims”**
• BEDE. Because the Lord makes the elect direct their life to the rule of the Scriptures, in which is the multitude of knowledge.
• BEDE. He makes cherubims when he teaches them in this world to imitate the angelic chastity after their own measure, which is carried on above all [unclear in the edition: "pignus laudibus"] divine, by true love of God and neighbour
**“AND PALM TREES”** — BEDE. He makes palm trees when he fixes the memory of the eternal reward in the minds of the saints, that they may fall the less from the citadel of justice the more they have the wage of justice always before their eyes.
**“AND DIVERS FIGURES”** — He makes divers figures, as it were standing out from the wall and coming forth, when he grants the faithful all the manifold workings of the virtues: "namely the bowels of mercy, benignity, humility, patience, modesty" etc. "But above all these things have charity, which is the bond of perfection." When these virtues have come into such habit in the elect that they seem implanted by nature, what else is it than that they come forth like the figures of the house of the Lord standing out from the wall? For they no longer learn the words and works of truth from others from without, but, having them fixed in themselves by the root, they bring forth, always ready from the inmost heart, the things that are to be done or taught. Now we have said that the evenness of the floor signifies 'the humble concord of brotherhood', where, though they be Jews or gentiles, barbarians and Scythians, free and bond, noble and ignoble, all glory that they are brethren in Christ and have the same Father in heaven. For the most concordant humility of the heavenly citizens is doubtful to none. Solomon therefore covered the floor of the house with gold, in the oracle within and in the temple without, because Christ filled the angels and the souls of the just in heaven with the full gift of perfection, and set apart the citizens of the heavenly homeland, pilgrims in the world, from the vileness of mortals by the eternal seal of love. Whence: "By this shall all men know that you are my disciples, if you have love one for another."
6.31:
**“And in the entrance of the oracle”** — AND IN THE ENTRANCE OF THE ORACLE etc. BEDE. There was one entrance, but it was shut by two doors, and opened when they were unbarred, just as both the temple and the porch before the temple had only one way in, because: "One Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God"; one entrance into the present Church through baptism, one into the heavenly kingdom, to be hoped for through the works of faith. That there was one entrance is witnessed by what is written below of the ark: "And whereas the staves stood out, and the ends of them were seen without in the sanctuary before the oracle, they were not seen any further without." Where it is plainly shown, unless I am mistaken, that there was one entrance of the oracle, made over against the ark which was in the midst of it. The little doors of this entrance signify in many ways. For they designate the angelic spirits by whose ministry we are brought into the heavenly homeland, and the apostles, to whom were given the keys of the kingdom of heaven, who, having received from the Lord the power of binding and loosing, admit the worthy within the gate of the kingdom and put out the unworthy by excommunicating them. The works of justice too, by which one comes to the heavenly kingdom, can be figured by the doors through which one entered into the holy of holies. Whence: "The keeping of her laws is the firm foundation of incorruption: and incorruption bringeth near to God. Therefore the desire of wisdom bringeth to the everlasting kingdom." With all these it fitly agrees that the little doors are of olive wood, because both angels and perfect men show themselves glorious in the house of God by the fruit of mercy and the works of light. Indeed all the elect open for themselves the way into the heavenly homeland by the armour of light and piety.
**“he made little doors of olive tree”** — TWO LITTLE DOORS. BEDE. There are two little doors because angels and holy men love God and neighbour, and cannot enter the gate of life except through twofold love; or because the same gate of life is unbarred for the faithful of both peoples, namely the Jews and the gentiles.
**“AND POSTS OF [FIVE] CORNERS”** — They have posts of five corners, because the heavenly hall receives not only the souls of the elect, but also opens its doors at the judgment to bodies endowed with immortal glory. For there are five senses of the body. Or each post of the oracle is five cubits high, because the entrance of the heavenly homeland is laid open to those alone who serve the Lord with all the senses of body and heart: of the body, namely, when through them they do something for it; of the heart, when they think soberly and justly and piously of the things which they decide to do through those same senses of the body.
6.32:
**“And two doors of olive tree”** — he says the same more plainly; for there was one entrance, but it was shut and opened by two doors
**“and posts of corners.”** — in most [copies] it is wanting
**“and he carved upon them figures of cherubims, and figures of palm trees,”** — all these were set forth and explained above in the adornment of the walls of the temple
**“CARVINGS”** — It could be called a carving made in the joint of the boards, but it is taken broadly.
**“and carvings very much projecting:”** — BEDE. 'Anaglypha' in Greek are called 'celaturae', carvings, in Latin, because to the works of the virtues which the Church exercises throughout the world in holy and perfect men, those above all to whom the care of the faithful is committed and the keys of the kingdom of heaven given ought to apply themselves with all diligence, that as much as they are above the rest in rank so much they may excel in the merit of good action. For they have on themselves the figure of the cherubim carved when they imitate in mind and work, as far as they can, the angelic life on earth. They have figures of palm trees when they meditate with fixed intention on the heavenly retribution; for the palm is the adornment of the victor's hand. They have carvings very much projecting when they show to all most certain proofs of good works, which no one can interpret amiss. And all these are covered with golden plates when, beyond the other flowers of the virtues, the brightness of love shines preeminent in the great members of the Church. To these little doors a veil was added, as is written in Paralipomenon: "He made also a veil," it says, "of violet, purple, scarlet, and silk: and wrought cherubims in it." For the sake of beauty, namely, that among the gilded walls silk too might shine, but in the same signification as the little doors. It was hung before the ark and the entrance of the oracle, that, as the little doors were opened at fitting hours, so the veil too might be drawn back for those coming who entered into the holy of holies. The careful drawing back of this veil, then, signifies the opening of the law and of the heavenly kingdom which was given us through the incarnation of Christ. Whence when the Lord was baptized the heavens were opened, to show that through the baptism which he consecrated for us we must enter the gate of heaven; and when he died on the cross likewise "the veil was rent in the midst from the top even to the bottom," showing that the figures of the law were now ended, and the truth of the gospel and the heavenly secrets, and the very entrance of heaven, were no longer to be prophesied and signified figuratively, but to be opened at once to all who from the beginning of the world up to that time had passed from the world in the faith of truth. For on the fortieth day after the Lord's resurrection all sought heaven with him, and, every veil removed, received many mansions in the Father's house according to their merits. For us too, who were yet to be, the entrance was unbarred in that same hour, but only through inward desires of inward goods, through faith and the sacraments of the Lord's passion, through the fervour of sincere love, through the mortification of the concupiscence of the flesh, and through the daily help of the angels. Whence that same veil, under which one entered into the oracle, was made of violet, purple, scarlet and silk, and cherubims were woven into it. For violet, which imitates the colour of the sky, is compared to the desires of heavenly things. Purple, which is made from the blood of shellfish and displays a bloody hue, signifies the sacrament of the Lord's passion, which we must imitate by carrying our cross. In the scarlet of red colour is expressed the virtue of love, of which it is said: "Was not our heart burning within us" of Jesus "whilst he spoke to us in the way" etc. Silk, which springs green from the earth and by the long labour of craftsmen puts off its native greenness and is brought to whiteness, suggests the chastisement of the flesh, whose inborn moisture, as it were, the Apostle bids to be dried up, saying: "Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth; fornication, uncleanness" etc. And to what grace of whiteness he would have it brought he shows elsewhere, saying: "I beseech you that you present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing unto God" etc. Cherubims are woven in and made with the same colours when, in all that we do piously, we are protected by the Lord's gift from the poisoned darts of the demons through the guard of the angels. Cherubims are woven in when, in the good things we do, we use the multitude of knowledge unceasingly, looking always to the divine words, and, lest perhaps we stray from the path of the virtues, rule our steps continually by beholding them.
6.33:
**“AND HE MADE IN THE ENTRANCE”** — As the entrance of the oracle, by which one came to the ark of the Lord and the cherubims, signifies 'the entrance of heaven', by which we desire to be brought to the vision of God and of the heavenly citizens, so the entrance into the temple [signifies] the beginnings of our conversion to God, when we enter into the present Church. This designates our entrance to faith, that one to hope. Whence the posts of this entrance are foursquare, on account of the four books of the gospel, by whose teaching we are instructed in the faith of truth.
**“POSTS FOURSQUARE”** — BEDE. Foursquare, namely on account of the four principal virtues: prudence, fortitude, justice, temperance, on which, as on a most firm foundation, the whole structure of good acts rests. For prudence is that by which we learn what we should do and how it befits us to live. Fortitude, that by which we fulfil what we have learned is to be done; these the prophet briefly embraces, saying: "The Lord is my light and my salvation, whom shall I fear?" Light, namely, that he may teach what we ought to do; salvation, that he may strengthen us to do it. Temperance is that by which we discern, lest we give ourselves more or less than is just to prudence and fortitude. And because whoever uses prudence, fortitude and temperance is truly just, justice follows fourth after prudence, fortitude and temperance.
6.34:
**“And two doors”** — the love of God and of neighbour
**“ONE OF EACH SIDE”** — Because they look toward one another, so that the one cannot be had without the other: the outer door is brotherly love, the inner divine, because the former is first in time, the latter higher in dignity, and through the former one enters the latter; for in the love of neighbour one learns how the creator ought to be loved.
**“EACH DOOR WAS DOUBLE, AND SO OPENED WITH FOLDING LEAVES”** — BEDE. Because in each love two things are chiefly to be observed. In the love of God, the faith of truth and purity of working: "For without faith it is impossible to please God," and: "Faith without works is dead." In the love of brotherhood, patience and kindness. Whence: "Charity is patient, is kind," that is, that it may forgive the injuries of neighbours and do good to them. Whence: "Forgive, and you shall be forgiven. Give, and it shall be given to you." This love we desire to be spent on us, saying: "Give us this day our daily bread, and forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors."
**“and each door was double, and so opened with folding leaves.”**
• Each door was opened holding one another, because the virtues are joined and cannot be separated; for neither faith without works nor works without faith please, nor does it suffice to bear injuries for one who does not impart necessaries to him whom he bears with, nor to supply necessaries for one who does not know how to forgive from the heart the troubles brought upon him. For the opening of the doors does not signify a separation of the virtues, but that through their joining the entrance of the Church lies open to us more and more, that the more we abound in them the more truly we may be joined to the companies of the saints; just as the dividing of the Red Sea, by which the people of God escaped the pursuing Egyptian, signified not a division of baptism but an opening, by which, all sins being extinguished, we pass over to the shore and firm ground of the virtues.
• BEDE. It is to be noted that in the entrance of the oracle there are said to have been two doors, but not double; but in the entrance of the temple, that is, of the former house, there were two doors such that each was double, because in the present Church it is needful for us to enter and lead such a life that we keep the love of God and neighbour through faith and working, through patience and kindness.
