8.13:
**“And Baria”** — otherwise: Bar
**“and Sama were heads of the kindreds that dwelt in Aialon: these drove away the inhabitants of Geth.”** — because they avenged their brethren the sons of Ephraim
8.23: **“And Abdon, and Zechri, and Hanan,”** — otherwise: Chanan
8.33:
**“And Ner begot Cis, and Cis begot Saul. And Saul begot Jonathan, and Melchisua, and Abinadab,”** — otherwise: Aminadab
**“and Esbaal.”** — otherwise: Hisbaal

9.12: **“And Adaias the son of Jeroham, the son of Phassur, the son of Melchias, and Maasai”** — otherwise Maasia, otherwise Masa
9.14: **“And of the Levites, Semeia the son of Hassub, the son of Ezricam, the son of Hasebia”** — otherwise: Asebia
9.15:
**“Bacbacar”** — otherwise: Bacbacar
**“also the carpenter,”** — who exercised his craft in the house of the Lord and was of the tribe of Levi
9.16:
**“And Obdia the son of Semeias, the son of Galal,”** — otherwise: Calaal
**“the son of Idithun:”** — IDITHUN. That is, David's singer. For singers of the sons of Levi kept watch at the king's gate toward the east by their turns, and in turn came together to sing psalms with David; because before the temple was built the ark of the testament was in the palace, and there the keepers served.
**“and Barachia the son of Asa, the son of Elcana, who dwelt in the suburbs of Netophati.”** — the name of a place, and it is interpreted 'renowned', where Caleb the son of Bara dwelt
9.17: **“And the porters were Sellum, and Accub, and Telmon, and Ahimam”** — otherwise: Chiman
9.19:
**“BUT SELLUM THE SON OF CORE”** — The first Chora is written with aleph and sounds Chora; the second with he, and sounds Chore. Chora is interpreted 'crying out', Chore 'bald'; this is he who in Numbers stirred up sedition against Moses.
**“KEEPERS OF THE DOORS”** — Because they kept the outer door of the tabernacle. But their fathers, who are written below and who have titles in the Psalter, kept the inner door and were singers.
9.20: **“PHINEES”** — The grandson of Aaron, who was still living, as the Hebrews hand down, and ordered the courses of the ministers. And there are twenty-four courses, which David ordered for the ministry of the tabernacle. Whence in the gospel: "Zachary, of the course of Abia."
9.26: **“To these four Levites were committed all the number of the porters, and they were over the chambers and treasures of the house of the Lord.”** — TO THESE FOUR LEVITES etc. Who these four Levites were, to whom all the number of the porters was committed, is shown when it is said: "And of Hosa, that is, of the sons of Merari, Semri the chief" etc., as is had in the twenty-sixth chapter. The four chiefs of the porters are the holy teachers who, keeping the door of faith by the four gospels, open it to believers and shut it to blasphemers; to whom with Peter the keys of heaven were committed. These keep the doors toward the four winds, because they call the nations to the faith through the four quarters of the world and watchfully keep the Church.
9.28:
**“Of their stock”** — of the congregation of the Levites
**“OF THEIR STOCK SOME ALSO WERE OVER THE VESSELS OF THE MINISTRY”** — Mystically, from the company of the holy preachers are ordained those who keep unsleeping watch over the vessels of the Lord, that is, the souls of the faithful, in which the will of God is ministered daily. Under their keeping are the fine flour, wine and oil, with which the sacraments of the body and blood of the Lord are made, and the grace of the Holy Spirit is given by spiritual anointing. They compound in the Church the frankincense of prayers and the spices of virtues, and render acceptable wine in the sight of the Lord.
9.29:
**“Some of them also, who had the vessels of the sanctuary committed to them, had the charge of”** — which belonged to the sacrifices
**“the fine flour, and wine, and oil, and frankincense, and spices.”** — with which the ointments and incenses were made
9.31:
**“And Mathathias”** — Christ, "the firstborn of the dead, and the prince of the kings of the earth"
**“a Levite,”** — of the Lord God
**“the firstborn of Sellum”**
• uprooting or division
• scattering or destroying
**“MATHATHIAS WAS OVERSEER OF THOSE THINGS THAT WERE FRIED IN THE FRYING PAN”** — Because Christ is the author of the heavenly sacraments, where daily bread and wine are offered in memory of his passion, and [he is] the head of all who after his example crucify their flesh and give it up to suffering for his name.
9.32: **“WERE THE LOAVES”** — They were baked two and two separately before the sabbath, according to Josephus, and on the sabbath morning were set upon the table; of which we spoke more fully in Leviticus.
9.34: **“THE HEADS OF THE LEVITES BY THEIR FAMILIES, CHIEFS, ABODE IN JERUSALEM”** — It is fitting that the more anyone is set over others, the more devout he should be in the divine offices. He keeps well the chief place of the ministry who is zealous to abide in Jerusalem, that is, in the vision of peace, so as to flee the tumult of the world and the pleasures of the flesh, and to have quiet of mind in the contemplation of God, saying with the psalmist: "I rejoiced at the things that were said to me."
9.35: **“JEHIEL”** — He who in Kings [is] Abiel, the father of Cis the father of Saul; and it is interpreted 'my father is God'. Jaiel [is] 'forsaken of God', perhaps for the difference of merits. And it is to be noted that among the sons of Jaiel, Cis and Ner are called brothers and are, and so it is had in Kings. But in what follows it is said that Ner begot Cis: not that he begot him, but that he brought him up.
9.38: **“And Macelloth begot Samaan: these dwelt over against their brethren in Jerusalem, with their brethren.”** — because neighbours and near kin, though outside
9.39:
**“And Ner begot Cis: and Cis begot Saul: and Saul begot Jonathan, and Melchisua, and Abinadab,”** — ABINADAB. This one, who in Kings is related to have been slain with his father, is called Aminadab. And Abinadab is interpreted 'my father [is] a vow'; Aminadab, 'my people [is] a vow'.
**“and Esbaal.”** — fire [is her] husband
**“ESBAAL”** — 'Fire [is her] husband'; this is Isboseth, that is, 'man of confusion'.
9.40:
**“And the son of Jonathan was Meribbaal:”** — striving against the husband
**“MERIBBAAL”** — 'Striving against the husband'; this is Miphiboseth, which is interpreted 'reproach from the mouth'.
9.41: **“And the sons of Micha were Phithon, and Melech,”** — otherwise: Malech
9.43:
**“And Mosa begot Banaa: whose son Raphaia begot Elasa,”** — otherwise Elasa
**“of whom was born Asel.”** — otherwise: Asel
9.44: **“And Asel had six sons, whose names are, Ezricam, Bocru, Ismahel, Saria, Obdia, Hanan: these are the sons of Asel.”** — otherwise Hesel

10.1:
Many things being omitted which the history in the book of Samuel tells of Samuel and Saul, he records the fall of Saul and his family; mystically hinting that there is no need to describe the life of him whose impious conduct deserved to receive a swift end, and figuratively showing the end of the kingdom of the Jews and of the old priesthood. He has passed over to David, whose deeds and ordering of the kingdom he weaves together, who bears the type of the true David possessing the kingdom of heaven and earth. When he is at hand, the Philistines after their manner fight against Israel and conquer; because as grace drew near the gentiles, as before, assailed the chastity of the Israelite faith, now by showing evil works, now the worship of idolatry, as Balaam taught Balac to cast a stumblingblock before the children of Israel, to eat and to commit fornication.
**“Now the Philistines fought against Israel, and the men of Israel fled from the Philistines,”** — or Palestinians
**“and fell down wounded in mount”** — pride
**“Gelboe.”**
• lust; for Gelboe signifies 'slippery'
• AND THE MEN FLED etc. Those who seemed strong in the contemplation of God, while incautiously they follow the works and teaching of the gentiles. Secular learning also helped not a little toward the perdition of the heretics. Whence someone says: The philosophers, the patriarchs of the heretics, have stained the purity of the Church with perverse doctrine.
10.2:
**“AND WHEN THEY CAME NEAR”** — The gentiles rushed in from every side upon the kingdom of Juda and its sons, and corrupted the priests, scribes and Pharisees, that is, its sons and the seducers of that kingdom; the heretics also forbade them to preach or worship simply the grace of the Holy Spirit.
**“pursuing after Saul and his sons, they slew Jonathan,”** — the house of the dove
**“and Abinadab,”** — or Aminadab
**“ABINADAB”** — Lest we should praise with worthy confession the Father who adopted us to himself by a spiritual gift: which the slaying of Abinadab, that is, 'my willing father', signifies.
**“MELCHISUA”** — Lest we should believe that future salvation is in the kingdom of Christ. For Melchisua is interpreted 'my king [is] salvation'. The philosopher who seduced Arius as it were killed Melchisua; he who [seduced] Macedonius, Jonathan; he who [seduced] Manichaeus, Abinadab; because the master of corruption taught this one to deny the omnipotence of Christ the true king, that one to detract from the gifts of the Holy Spirit, the other to blaspheme the goodness of the supreme Father.
10.3:
**“And the battle grew hard against Saul,”** — the gentiles strove with all their strength that the kingdom of Juda should be taken away
**“and the archers reached him,”** — deceitful and crafty men
**“and wounded him with arrows.”**
• by hidden deceptions
• not with swords, that is, by open assault
10.4:
**“And Saul said to his armourbearer:”** — AND SAUL SAID TO HIS ARMOURBEARER etc. The Hebrews say this was Doeg the Edomite, who, seeing that Saul was dead, and fearing David, killed himself; but that the young man who brought Saul's diadem and bracelet to David was the son of Doeg, and that Doeg himself was the servant with whom Saul sought his father's asses.
**“TO HIS ARMOURBEARER”** — [The armourbearers are] the teachers of the law. For as the arms and arrows of the Philistines [are] the deceptions of the wicked, so the arms of the Israelites [are] the words of spiritual doctrine, with which the people of God ought to have fortified itself against dangers. Saul, wounded to the point of despair, preferred to perish by the sword of his armourbearer rather than by that of the uncircumcised; because the princes of the Jews, having once taken up the purpose of dying in their sins, preferred to be destroyed by their teachers, who loosed the commandments of the law, rather than be defiled by fellowship with the gentiles. Whence: "They went not into the hall, that they might not be defiled, but that they might eat the pasch."
**“Draw thy sword, and kill me: lest these uncircumcised come, and mock me. But his armourbearer would not, being struck with fear: so Saul took his sword, and fell upon it.”** — BUT HIS ARMOURBEARER WOULD NOT etc. It is not to be doubted that among the reprobate teachers of the law there were some who would not pervert the sharpness of the word to kill their hearers; and yet the hearers themselves, who had received things rightly spoken from their masters, by despising or blaspheming them turned them to their own ruin; and when their death was seen, that is, their obstinacy in sinning, the ministers of the word themselves too, grown worse over time, made the testimonies of the law, which they had feared to interpret wrongly, an occasion of ruin for themselves. Heretics also, bloodied by the darts of their sins, when they drag the divine words into argument for their error, turn their arms against their own breast to their death. Any catholic too, when he defiles the art which he learned for the common good with the contagion of pride, vainglory, love of money or any vice, pierces himself with his own sword, because he has fallen upon that by which he ought to have been defended from the enemy.
10.5: **“AND WHEN HIS ARMOURBEARER SAW”** — The unlearned, ignorant of the remedies of true humility and of the laver of baptism, seeing their masters in Judea overcome in the spiritual contest, and no small crowd nearest to their hearing put to flight from the ancient seat of its constancy by the pursuing adversary, troubled by the ruin of their elders lost the works of virtues and the defences of spiritual knowledge which they had had; and the sins of the gentiles came and corrupted by perverse indwelling all the pursuits of virtue among the unbelieving Jews. The unclean spirits came and occupied the hearts which constancy of faith had deserted. The nations came and by believing made their own the once excellent pursuits of the Jews. Whence: "The kingdom of God shall be taken from you, and shall be given to a nation yielding the fruits thereof."
10.6: **“So Saul died, and his three sons, and all his house fell together.”** — that he might reign no more, and to show that the nation of the Jews had lost the kingdom
10.10:
**“AND FASTENED HIS HEAD IN THE TEMPLE OF DAGON”** — The Philistines fastened Saul's head in the temple of Dagon, when the malignant spirits plunge the soul dead in sins into the abyss of hell. For Dagon is interpreted 'fish of sadness'. And he is fitly called a fish of sadness who, plunged into hell, is tormented with eternal pain. So far did the enemies, visible or invisible, pursue Judea with the arms of impiety that they took away the primacy of the kingdom by the root and snatched away the defences of the sacred law. Its overthrow they spread far and wide to their accomplices as a sign of triumph and a cause of joy; and the armour of the heavenly warfare, taken from the Jews, they set equal with their household gods, that is, with the doctrines of demons, either by interpreting spiritual things carnally, or by tossing the divine letters about at will as if they were common. And the nation itself, deprived of the kingdom, as though brought to nothing under the power of its enemies, they set up for a derision and a public byword; which is to have hung up the trunk of Saul's body on the wall of Bethsan, that is, of the house of the enemy, for a show. Heretics also [do the same], when they defraud those laid low by the arrows of sins of the protection of charity, which is the art of the virtues. The unclean spirits as it were cut off Saul's head when they persuade men to follow their own sense rather than that of holy Scripture. They strip him of his arms when they pervert the divine words by a devilish spirit. They put Saul's arms in the temple of Astaroth, which is interpreted 'the making of spies' and signifies the doctrine of the demons who go about seeking whom they may devour, when they change the works by which the faithful had served into the service of their own malice; they hang up the limbs, wholly without light and life, on the wall of the enemy's house.
**“And they put his armour in the temple of their god, and fastened his head in the temple of Dagon.”** — First they fastened his head, but afterwards sent it into their land to be carried round for a show. But in Kings it is said that "they hung the body of Saul on the wall of Bethsan"; but the Hebrews hand down that the house of Dagon is called Bethsan, which is interpreted 'house of the sleeper', and that the head and body of Saul were hung there. For the Bethsan in Judges and Josue, which is interpreted 'house of security', is another.
10.11:
**“And when the men of Jabes Galaad had heard this, to wit, all that the Philistines had done to Saul,”** — WHEN THE MEN OF JABES HAD HEARD THIS etc. That is, the men of the Church, remembering that Judea, from which preachers had been sent to them, was mocked by the gentiles, rose up acting manfully, and walking with virtues amid the darkness of the erring, forbade the gentiles to rejoice in mocking her, saying: "If the firstfruit be holy, so is the lump also: and if the root be holy, so are the branches"; "Boast not against the broken branches." The corpses are the carnal, or any carnal things; the bones, the strong, or the works of virtues. They bury the bones in the grove of Jabes when what they find of virtue or firmness in the weak they do not despise as nothing, but join to the fruitful works of the saints: if they know any among the carnal to be zealous for virtues, they number them in the fellowship of the saints. For by the grove the fruit of the good is expressed. But that we read in Kings that the men of Jabes burned the bodies of Saul and his sons signifies that the saints leave the fall of the Jews to the judgment above. Whence: "O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and of the knowledge of God" etc. According to that: "If anything be left, it shall be burnt."
**“GALAAD”** — [Jabes,] which is interpreted 'dried up', and signifies the Church, which the heat of the sun of justice has dried from every flow of concupiscence. Hence it is described as set on a mountain which is called Galaad, that is, 'heap of testimony', to signify the lofty life of the saints confirmed by fitting testimonies of the Scriptures. This is the city which Saul at the first beginnings of his reign freed from the siege of the enemies.
10.12:
**“All the valiant men of them arose, and took the bodies of Saul and of his sons, and brought them to Jabes, and buried their bones under the oak that was in Jabes, and they fasted seven days.”**
• AND THEY FASTED SEVEN DAYS. That they might come to rest. For after the six ages of this world, in which we labour in the flesh, follows the seventh, of the rest of souls. Mystically, over the blindness of the Jews who observe the sabbath carnally, their fellow tribesmen, that is, the faithful, grieve continually, and as it were fast seven days. But when the mystery of the eighth day, of the resurrection, has been received, both will rejoice in an everlasting festival.
• But morally, holy men abhor the death of the impious and hand over their examples to the burial of oblivion. They fast seven days, that is, they pass all the time of this life, which turns by the sevenfold number of days, in continence, and abstain from all evil, lest they die in like manner.
10.13:
**“So Saul died for his iniquities,”** — the kingdom of the Jews was ended, because they often transgressed the law and worshipped idols
**“because he transgressed”** — or had transgressed
10.14: **“and did not hope in the Lord: therefore he slew him, and transferred his kingdom to David the son of Isai.”** — to David: to Christ and the Christian people

11.1:
**“Then all Israel gathered themselves”** — the faithful
**“to David”** — Christ
**“in Hebron, saying: We are thy bone, and thy flesh.”** — the faithful love and venerate their own nature in Christ. Whence: "All the kindreds of the Gentiles shall adore in his sight" etc.
11.3:
**“And all the ancients of Israel came to the king in Hebron, and David made a covenant with them”** — of justice, of keeping the commandments, and of future reward
**“THE ANCIENTS”** — The prophets [and] apostles run together to Christ with equal devotion; whence: "The princes of the people are gathered together, with the God of Abraham."
**“before the Lord: and they anointed him king over Israel”** — because the confession of all believers is one, and one is the religion of their warfare
11.4: **“And David and all Israel went to Jerusalem, which is Jebus”** — under Abraham this was called Solima; but some say that Homer afterwards called it Hierosolyma
11.5:
**“And they that dwelt in Jebus said to David: Thou shalt not come in here. But David took the castle of Sion, which is the city of David.”**
• AND THEY SAID etc. Setting the blind and the lame and the lepers on the walls in contempt of the king, and saying that the blind and the lame forbade him.
• Mystically, David casting the Jebusite out of Jerusalem signifies Christ driving the demons out of the hearts of the faithful and setting his dwelling there. For Jebusite is interpreted 'trodden down', Jerusalem 'vision of peace'. Whence he also says to his disciples: "Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents" etc. Well then is it written in Kings that, the blind and the lame who hated David's soul being cast out, he took the castle of Sion and called it his city; because when Christ drives out of the soul the malignant spirits and the crowd of vices, enlightening it with wisdom, it is rightly called the castle of Sion, that is, of watching, and vision of peace; of which it is rightly said: "In Judea God is known: his name is great in Israel. And his place is in peace."
11.8:
**“And he built the city”** — because he fortified it with walls
**“AND JOAB”** — For he fortified the city by the diligence of a soldier. Yet Josephus says that David fortified the upper city and, joining the castle to it, made one body and surrounded all with a wall; and that he set Joab over the work of the walls, drove out the Jebusites and called it Hierosolyma. For Iero in Hebrew is 'fortification'. Christ too first preached the gospel in Judea and strengthened the Church with the fortification of his faith. Joab, who built the rest of the city, signifies the apostles and apostolic men who after the Lord's ascension converted very many of the gentiles. Whence: "We are God's coadjutors: you are God's husbandry."
11.11: **“JESBAAM”** — Josephus names him Eusebius, and they say he was the son of Achimee, who, often breaking into the line of the enemy, did not cease until he had slain eight hundred. Others understand him to be David, because Jesbaam is interpreted 'sitting among the people', and Achamoni 'most wise'; whence in Kings it is written: "Sitting in the chair, the wisest." But there he is compared to the little worm of the wood, because his wisdom was lessened on account of the sin which he had committed against Urias. Hence there [he is said] to have slain eight hundred at one onset, but here three hundred; for his fame was lessened by the sin.
11.12: **“THE AHOHITE”** — Ahohi, as the Hebrews hand down, was the brother of Isai the father of David, whose son was Eleazar, who was mightiest among the three, whom Josephus says were Eusebius the son of Achimee, and Eleazar the son of Addi, and Semeias the son of Eli.
11.17: **“AND DAVID LONGED”** — GREGORY. Morally. It is to be thought on most earnestly that he who remembers that he has committed unlawful things should strive to abstain even from some lawful ones, so that he who committed what was forbidden may cut off from himself even what is granted, and may reprove himself in the least things who offended in the greatest. The old law forbade coveting another's wife; it does not forbid under penalty that brave deeds be commanded of soldiers by a king, or that water be desired. David, pierced by the sword of concupiscence, took away another's wife, and corrected the evil he had done by the laments of penance; who, when long afterwards he sat against the wedges of the enemy, desired to drink water from their cistern, which chosen soldiers, breaking out among the troops of the enemy, brought unharmed. But, taught by scourges, he at once reproved himself for having desired water at the peril of his soldiers, and poured it out to the Lord, because the water poured out was turned into a sacrifice. For he slew the guilt of concupiscence by the penance of his self-reproof. He therefore who once did not fear to covet another's wife afterwards trembled even because he had desired water. For he who remembered that he had done unlawful things was stern against himself and abstained even from lawful ones.
11.21: **“Among the three second he was more renowned, and their chief: but yet he attained not to the first three.”** — BUT YET HE ATTAINED NOT TO THE FIRST THREE etc. Here it appears that Abisai was chief among the three that follow, but did not attain to the first three, Jesbaam, Eleazar and Seminaa. But mystically it is signified that none of the saints, though he excel in virtues, attains to the equality of the power of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit: "For who in the clouds can be compared to the Lord?" etc.
11.22:
**“Banaias the son of Joiada a most valiant man, who had done many acts, of Cabseel: he slew”** — challenged by them
**“the two Ariels of Moab:”** — lions of God
**“ARIEL OF MOAB”** — That is, lions, as is said in Kings: that is, the strongest men in the kingdom of Moab, as lions.
**“and he went down, and slew a lion in the midst of a pit”** — which unawares had fallen into a pit full of snow
**“SLEW A LION”** — The Hebrew judges this lion to be Joab, who was slain in the house of the Lord holding the horns of the altar. For the altar is called a pit [cisterna], because as the water of a cistern cleanses, so the sanctuary of God expiates the sins of men. The Egyptian man whom the book of Kings calls 'worth looking at' [is] Semei the son of Gera, who cursed David, who was of Bahurim, that is, 'of the chosen'. He is called an Egyptian because he imitated the Egyptian blaspheming God whom Moses killed: that one blasphemed God, this one the king and prophet. 'Worth looking at', because he was watched, so that if he went out of Jerusalem he should be killed; having a spear in his hand, that is, the law of God, on which if he had meditated, remaining in Jerusalem, he would not have perished. But because he made the king's command void and went out, Banaias went down with a rod, that is, with the rightness of justice, and wrested from him the spear which he did not hold rightly.
**“IN THE TIME OF SNOW”** — [Snow,] by which can be signified the grace of Christ which shone upon the world, and the cold of charity with which men grow cold. Banaias, which is interpreted 'the Lord the builder', signifies Christ, of whom it is said: "The Lord buildeth up Jerusalem" etc. He did many works who says: "My Father worketh until now, and I work." He is of Cabseel, that is, of the congregation of the Lord, because the whole company of the saints belongs to him; who, coming down from heaven and made man, slaying by his death the lion, that is, the devil, who possessed the world torpid with the cold of its unbelief, plunged him into hell. He, overcoming by the rod of the cross the Egyptian, that is, Antichrist, blackest with sins, that is, abusing the five senses of the body for crimes, condemned him, guilty by his own wickedness, by everlasting power. In the days of snow, because by his death he expiated sin. Whence: "Thou shalt wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow."
11.24:
**“These things did Banaias the son of Joiada, who was most renowned among the three valiant ones,”** — worthy to be named
**“AMONG THE THREE”** — Abisai and Sobochai and Jonathan, to whom he was equal in strength, who was over the thirty, as the Hebrew affirms.
11.25: **“the first among the thirty, but yet he attained not to the three: and David made him of his council.”** — as an intimate and faithful counsellor
11.29: **“Sobochai a Husathite, Ilai an Ahohite,”** — otherwise: Ahothites
11.31: **“Ethai the son of Ribai”** — or Ribai
11.32: **“Hurai of the torrent Gaas, Abiel”** — or Aliel
11.34:
**“The sons of Assem”** — otherwise Assen
**“a Gezonite, Jonathan the son of Sage”** — otherwise: Saga, otherwise: Saie
11.37:
**“Hesro”** — otherwise Ezro
**“a Carmelite, Naarai”** — otherwise Naara
11.38: **“Joel the brother of Nathan, Mibahar”** — otherwise Mibaar
11.42: **“Adina the son of Segar”** — otherwise: Sechar
11.44: **“Ozia an Astarothite, Samma, and Jehiel, the sons of Hotham an Arorite,”** — otherwise: Araorites

12.1:
**“These also came to David to Siceleg,”** — THESE ALSO CAME. Up to this point he has enumerated the valiant men of David who helped him to reign over Israel.
**“WHO WERE MOST VALIANT AND EXCELLENT WARRIORS”** — According to the letter it signifies that they were nimble and vigorous in every kind of warfare. But mystically it describes the soldiers of Christ as not sluggish but zealous, in prosperity and in adversity, on the right hand and on the left.
12.4: **“And Samaias the Gabaonite, the bravest among the thirty, and over the thirty. Jeremias, and Jeziel, and Johanan, and Jezabad”** — otherwise Zozabad
12.5: **“And Eluzai, and Jerimuth, and Baalia, and Samaria, and Saphatia”** — otherwise Sapthia
12.7:
**“And Joela”** — otherwise: Joelam
**“and Zabadia, the sons of Jeroham”** — otherwise: Joroam
12.8:
**“And from Gaddi”** — of the tribe of Gad
**“there went over to David, when he lay hid in the desert, most valiant men, and excellent warriors, holding shield and spear: their faces were like the faces of a lion,”** — by strength of mind
**“and they were swift like the roes upon the mountains.”** — SWIFT. He says it of sharpness of sense or agility of body. But mystically, those who profess the warfare of Christ ought not to be children in sense, but to provide good things, not only before God but also before all men.
12.14:
**“These were of the sons of Gad, captains of the army: the least”** — the teacher of the Church, who is called 'the least' for humility
**“over a hundred soldiers”** — of Christ, who are zealous for the virtues of the perfect
**“was captain, and the greatest over a thousand.”** — who is strong in knowledge and teaches by word and example, worthy of eternal blessedness, which is designated by the thousand
**“THE LEAST AND THE GREATEST”** — This signifies the teachers of the Jews and of the gentiles, of whom Paul, of the tribe of Benjamin, says: "Peter, James and John, who seemed to be pillars, gave to me and Barnabas the right hands of fellowship" etc. These, coming to Christ, were proved in all things. Whence: "But whom do you say that I am?" Peter answered for all: "Thou art Christ, the Son of the living God." To whom the Lord: "Thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church." And elsewhere: "Receive ye the Holy Ghost. Whose sins you shall forgive, they are forgiven them."
12.15:
**“THEY PASSED OVER THE JORDAN”** — The Jordan, in which Christ was baptized, signifies baptism. This the teachers pass over in the first month, when it is wont to overflow its banks; because when the Lord appeared in the flesh and hallowed the acceptable year, after he had hallowed baptism by his own baptism, they spread it through the whole world by preaching and baptizing.
**“and put to flight all that dwelt in the valleys toward the east and toward the west.”**
• unwilling to come to the citadel of the virtues and the summit of wisdom
• AND PUT TO FLIGHT ALL etc. Because by the preaching of the gospel they put to flight the Jews, whom the eastern quarter signifies because of the rising of the knowledge of the law, or the gentiles, in whom natural prudence set, while they ascribe the worship of God to idols. Whence: "Thou hast made my enemies turn their backs upon me, and hast destroyed them that hated me."
12.19: **“AND OF MANASSES”** — These seven princes, namely, who came from Manasses signify the first teachers of the Church coming from Judea, who, enlightened by the sevenfold Spirit, help our David against the rovers, that is, the heretics or the malignant spirits, who do not cease to snatch from the Church and take captive whom they can. Whence: "Now thanks be to God, who always maketh us to triumph in Christ Jesus."
12.20:
**“So when he returned to Siceleg,”** — sent back by the Philistines as they went against Saul
**“there fled to him of Manasses, Ednas, and Jozabad,”** — otherwise: Josabaath
**“and Jedihel”** — otherwise: Jediel
**“Heled,”** — otherwise: Heleth
12.21: **“These helped David against the rovers:”** — who laid waste Siceleg and led away his wives captive
12.22: **“THE ARMY OF GOD”** — That is, the one which came out of Egypt, that is, six hundred thousand; so the Hebrews explain it. But mystically, in the army of our David the number of the faithful grows daily, until those are made up who are predestined to eternal life.
12.23: **“TO TRANSFER THE KINGDOM”** — Because the holy teachers most of all desire that the worship of the old law be transferred into the spiritual understanding of the gospel, and that all things be made new.
12.27: **“JOIADA ALSO THE PRINCE”** — The Hebrews hand down that this was Phinees the son of Eleazar, in comparison with whom Sadoc is called a young man, as lesser in age and merit.
12.28: **“Sadoc also a young man of excellent disposition, and the house of his father, twenty-two princes.”** — it signifies the number of the priests who were ordained in the house of Sadoc's father, that is, of the Levitical [order]
12.32: **“And of the children of Issachar men of understanding, that knew all times to order what Israel should do, two hundred principal men: and all the rest of the tribe followed their counsel.”** — AND OF THE CHILDREN OF ISSACHAR. They hand down that there were teachers of the law in the tribe of Issachar, who taught the several times of the ceremonies to be observed and prescribed what Israel should do. These signify the teachers of the Church, whose precepts those under them obey.
12.38:
**“All these men”** — that is, the aforesaid
**“MEN OF WAR”** — That is, the apostles and apostolic men come together to our David and are joined to him spiritually, and others, both of the Jews and of the gentiles, striving with one heart and equal vow, that David may be made king and they themselves may be the kingdom of Christ.
12.39: **“THREE DAYS”** — That is, holding at all times the faith of the Trinity, and receiving what the first teachers, that is, the apostles, had prepared as food out of divine Scripture, and giving thanks for the bestowal of all good things.

13.1:
**“And he took”** — arranged
**“counsel, David,”** — Christ
**“WITH THE CAPTAINS OF THOUSANDS AND OF HUNDREDS”** — With the apostles [and] evangelists, who transferred the faith of the incarnation from the Jews to the salvation of the gentiles. For this is to transfer the ark of the Lord to himself from the hill of Cariathiarim, which is in Juda and is interpreted 'city of woods': that is, to lead the faith of the Lord from the height of the Scriptures placed among the Jews, where the woody shade of figures abounds, to the understanding of the gentile people, where the Church is founded.
13.3: **“WE SOUGHT IT NOT”** — Because [unclear in the edition: "interpretatur"] that people could not open the spiritual sense of the old Testament, which lay hid, as it is now revealed to the apostles and prophets: namely, that the gentiles are "fellow heirs and partakers of the promise of the Lord".
13.5:
**“FROM SIHOR”** — Sihor is a river of Egypt, because, as they say, it is drawn off from the Nile, and it is interpreted 'new and troubled firmament'. Whence: "And now what hast thou to do in the way of Egypt, to drink the troubled water?"
**“until you enter into Emath, to bring the ark of God from Cariathiarim.”**
• Cariathiarim [so the edition: 'Chariathiarim']: a city of Damascus, which in Amos [is] Emathabaal, that is, Emath the great, which is now called Epiphania. And by Sihor and Emath he takes in the whole land of promise. By Sihor, that is, the brook or torrent, he signifies the southern part of Egypt; by Emath, the northern.
• Cariathiarim, which elsewhere [is] Cariathbaal, 'city of forests', one of the cities of the Gabaonites in the tribe of Juda, at the ninth milestone from Aelia for those going to Diospolis; of which was Urias the prophet, whom Joachim killed in Jerusalem, according to Jeremias. A son of Sobal is also called Cariathiarim, as is shown above.
13.6: **“ALL ISRAEL”** — Chosen, [that is,] more noble. And the number of these men is contained in Kings, where we read: "And David gathered together all the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand."
13.9:
**“And when they came to the floor of Chidon,”** — in Kings Nachon, for which Aquila [has] 'prepared floor'; and Chidon is interpreted 'shield', and is said to be the place where it was said to Josue: "Lift up the shield against the city of Hai"
**“AND WHEN THEY CAME TO THE FLOOR OF CHIDON”** — They came to the floor of Chidon, that is, 'shield', because in the Church the protection of God is sure. Whence: "O Lord, thou hast crowned us as with a shield of thy good will." Where the priest, touching the ark too incautiously, was struck by the Lord, here also the people of the Jews, which envies the gentiles and, while it would mix the law with the gospel, loses both. The priest being slain, David turned aside the ark of the Lord into the house of Obededom the Gethite; because when the Jews rejected the word of God, the apostles turned to the gentiles. Hence too the place of the floor of Nachon, which shows the preparation of the gentiles, is called the striking of Oza; because, that [people] being left, salvation was made for the gentiles. Obededom, which is interpreted 'serving man', signifies the gentile people, of which it is said: "A people which I knew not hath served me." [unclear in the edition: "Abiecto quoque Iudeorum quasi percussio Oze permittitur sic"]: "Thou wilt deliver me from the contradictions of the people." Geth, which is interpreted 'winepress', signifies the cross, on which the true vine was trodden and pressed. Hence the people of the gentiles can be called Gethite, as though it said: "God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ."
13.11: **“BECAUSE THE LORD HAD DIVIDED OZA”** — The Hebrews hand down that Aminadab the priest commanded his sons Oza and Ahio to carry the ark on their shoulders according to the precept of the law. But because they did not carry it, nor give it to the Caathites to be carried, the Lord struck Oza and divided him. For, as they say, his arm withered and [his] shoulders, on which the ark should have been carried, and a distinction was made between obedience and disobedience.
13.13: **“And for this reason he brought it not home to himself, that is, into the city of David, but turned it aside into the house of Obededom the Gethite.”** — INTO THE HOUSE OF OBEDEDOM THE GETHITE etc. Because he too was a Levite. And the cause being known for which Oza was struck, David commanded the ark to be carried on the Levites' own shoulders, as appears in what follows. It is to be noted how greatly he offends who receives the body of the Lord unworthily, if a devout priest perished who laid hold of the ark, the figure of the Lord's body, with less veneration than he ought. But allegorically David signifies Christ, the ark the Church, which Christ wills to bring into his city. Whence: "I was not sent but to the sheep that are lost of the house of Israel." And elsewhere: "Blindness in part has happened in Israel" etc.
13.14: **“And the ark of God abode in the house of Obededom three months”** — by faith, hope and charity

14.3: **“AND DAVID TOOK OTHER WIVES”** — David's many wives signify the many nations which are joined through faith in Christ; the concubines, the churches of the heretics, which glory in the title of the Christian name. But because they follow Christ for carnal gain, they are called not wives but concubines. Now, if kings have several wives it is a crime, because the figures have passed away.
14.8:
**“And the Philistines hearing that David was anointed king over all Israel, went up all to seek him:”** — not out of devotion of faith but by the guile of wickedness; therefore they did not fear to come, because, that is, they would not believe
**“AND THE PHILISTINES HEARING”** — When the grace of the gospel was spread abroad and the kingdom of Christ preached everywhere, the nations rose up on every side, gainsaying the gospel of peace.
**“and David heard of it, and went out to meet them.”** — showing the gifts of his kindness; but he who was ungrateful got death for himself
14.11: **“And when they came up to Baalpharasim, David defeated them there, and said: God hath divided my enemies”** — when he joined the faithful to himself by the election of grace and drove out the unbelievers
14.15:
**“And when thou shalt hear the sound of one going in the tops of the pear trees, then shalt thou go out to battle. For God is gone forth before thee to strike the army of the Philistines.”**
• IN THE TOPS OF THE PEAR TREES. But in the Hebrew, 'of the weeping ones', that is, of the idols in which they trusted, because they lead to eternal weeping. When, he says, thou shalt hear the sound of one going in the tops of the weeping ones, that is, when thou shalt hear that the idols of the pagans, in which is all their strength, are being destroyed by the angels, then thou shalt go into battle, because the Lord before thee will strike the camp of the Philistines.
• The invisible God, who in his majesty is above all things, shows his presence through invisible things. Whence: "The invisible things of him, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made." It is hinted also to the faithful that they should seek the help of God in all things, and trust that they will prosper in the contest when they feel the coming of the Lord to be with them. And the tops of the pear trees signify the height of the saints. God gives a sign to the holy teachers sent to preach, that they should follow with the ministry of devotion those whom the Holy Spirit directs by warning beforehand.
14.16:
**“So David did”** — Christ
**“as God had commanded him,”** — the Father
**“and he smote the army of the Philistines”** — of the demons, or the principality of the world
**“from Gabaon”** — hill, or height
**“as far as Gazera.”** — his hedge, or division
**“FROM GABAON AS FAR AS GAZERA”** — Christ strikes those who stand on the hill of pride, and breaks the hedge of their hardness, dividing their obstinacy, that he alone may have dominion in the whole world. Whence there follows: And the name of David was renowned etc.
14.17: **“And the name of David was renowned”** — "He hath given him a name which is above all names"

15.1:
**“He made himself also houses”** — churches
**“in the city of David,”** — the catholic Church spread through the whole world
**“and he built a place for the ark of God,”** — because in the present Church he commends the mystery of the incarnation and passion
15.2: **“Then David said: It is unlawful that the ark of God should be carried by any but by the Levites, whom the Lord chose to carry it, and to minister to himself for ever.”** — THEN DAVID SAID: IT IS UNLAWFUL etc. Christ does not will that the unworthy should discharge the ecclesiastical office, but that men learned in knowledge and approved for uprightness of morals should carry the ark of God, that is, the Church, on the shoulders of devout labour, and exalt it. Whence: "Do the work of an evangelist, fulfil thy ministry."
15.3:
**“And he gathered all Israel together”** — all the faithful
**“into Jerusalem,”** — the Church, that there, namely, they may venerate the mysteries of the incarnation
**“HE GATHERED ALL ISRAEL TOGETHER INTO JERUSALEM”** — Not only David but also all the prophets in the Church of Christ by words and deeds made room for the incarnation, that, coming, it might be the more quickly received, since it had been prophesied before.
15.4:
**“and also the sons of Aaron,”** — the prelates
**“and the Levites.”** — of lesser dignity
15.14: **“SO THE PRIESTS WERE SANCTIFIED”** — The ministers of the new Testament ought to be clean in life and doctrine; to whom it is said: "Be ye holy, because I am holy." They ought, by the words of right faith and the example of their work, to commend to the faithful the incarnation of Christ and the redemption of the human race etc.
15.16:
**“TO WIT, WITH NABLAS”** — Nablum in Hebrew, psalterium in Greek, laudatorium in Latin. The psaltery has a swelling belly in its upper part, so that the strings of the cords, tied on and struck in measured order, may give back a most sweet song. To this the cithara seems contrary, which holds at the bottom what the psaltery holds at the head. The psaltery with ten strings is the Church with the Decalogue of the law. Opposed to it is the cithara, which is made with twenty-four strings in the shape of the letter delta, as the most skilled hand down, and is set going by the fingers in various modes. This signifies the Church, which with the teachings of the twenty-four elders has a threefold form in the shape of the letter delta and signifies the faith of the holy Trinity. And through the hands of the apostles and evangelists it is figuratively set going in the various measures of the old and new Testament, in one way in the letter, in another in the sense.
**“AND HARPS”** — The lyre is so called apo tou lirein, that is, from the variety of voices, because it makes different sounds. This signifies the Church, which in the variety of different disciplines, historically, allegorically, tropologically, and by anagoge, gives forth a sweet sound, but does not depart from the simplicity of harmony. And cymbals make a sound when struck against each other. Whence: "Praise him on high sounding cymbals" etc. The well-sounding cymbals are our lips, which, struck against each other, give back the sweet harmony of the human voice.
15.18: **“and with them their brethren: in the second order, Zacharias, and Ben, and Jaziel, and Semiramoth, and Jahiel,”** — or Jahiel
15.20: **“And Zacharias, and Oziel, and Semiramoth, and Jahiel, and Ani, and Eliab, and Maasias, and Banaias, sung mysteries upon psalteries.”** — on the psaltery they preached the coming of the Saviour, which by a wonderful secret of the Godhead he arranged for the salvation of men
15.21:
**“And Mathathias, and Eliphalu, and Macenias, and Obededom, and Jehiel, and Ozaziu sung a song of victory for the octave upon harps.”**
• triumph and palm to God the victor
• FOR THE OCTAVE. That is, they signified the coming of the Lord in the day of judgment, in which, the week of the world being ended, he will come to judgment. Hence the sixth Psalm, which is sung with the trembling of judgment, is headed by such a title. And this number contains great sacraments. Eight souls went into Noe's ark and were saved when the world perished. David, whom the Lord chose, was the eighth son of Jesse. On the eighth day circumcision purifies; on the eighth day, that is, the Lord's day, Christ rose.
15.22: **“And Chonenias chief of the Levites, presided over the prophecy, to give out the tune.”** — because, full of the spirit of prophecy, he recalled the melodies and words to the memory of the singers
15.24:
**“And Sebenias, and Josaphat, and Nathanael, and Amasai, and Zacharias, and Banaias, and Eliezer, priests,”** — AND SEBENIAS AND JOSIAS [so the edition: 'Iosias'] etc. These seven priests sounding with trumpets before the ark are the holy preachers, full of the grace of the sevenfold Spirit, who preach the gospel in the Church of Christ and preach the sacrament of the incarnation to their hearers.
**“SOUNDED WITH TRUMPETS”** — There is one trumpet for gathering the people, another for leading [the march], another for victory, another for pursuing enemies, another for the shutting up of cities, etc. And the customary trumpet, among those skilled in these things, is formed in this way: it is blown into through three brass pipes at a narrow head, so that through four brass voice-channels, which over a brass base put forth four voices, they give out a most mighty bellowing. These signify the gospel, inspired from God by the threefold confession of the three Persons at the narrow head, that is, at the birth of Christ, [sending forth] through four brass voice-channels, that is, through the four evangelists, on a brazen, that is, a steadfast foundation of faith and work, a most mighty voice in the world, as the voice of a trumpet that gathers.
15.25:
**“So”** — after "the fulness of the Gentiles shall have come in" to the faith, the ark of God will return into the city of David; that is, it will be turned to the Jews by the grace of Christ, at the preaching of Elias and Enoch
**“David, and all the ancients of Israel, and the captains over thousands, went to bring the ark of the covenant of the Lord”** — crowned with martyrdom
15.26:
**“And when God had helped the Levites that carried the ark of the covenant of the Lord,”** — crowned with martyrdom
**“they offered in sacrifice seven bullocks,”** — [unclear in the edition: "triturante"] the ark of God, full of the sevenfold Spirit
**“and seven rams.”** — leaders of the Lord's flock
15.27:
**“AND DAVID WAS CLOTHED WITH A LINEN EPHOD”** — Christ makes manifest the example of his incarnation and passion, before hidden from the Jews. For linen, which springs from the earth and comes by manifold labour to the whiteness of a garment, shows the truth of the human flesh triumphing amid the scourges; and this is: David was clothed with a linen ephod.
**“GREGORY”** — It is pleasing to consider what great gifts of virtues David had received, and how strong he kept himself in humility in all things: [he] whom it did not lift up to break the jaws of lions, to tear apart the arms of bears, to be chosen when his brothers were passed over, to be anointed king when the king was rejected, to lay low the dreadful Goliath with one stone, to bring back the many foreskins proposed by the king when the foreigners had been slain, at length to receive the promised kingdom, to possess all Israel without gainsaying. Yet when he brings back the ark of God to Jerusalem, forgetting that he was set over them, he mingles with the people and dances before the ark. And because to dance before the ark had been, as is believed, the custom of the common people, in the service of God he whirls himself round in a dance. Behold, he whom the Lord preferred to all despises himself under the Lord by making himself equal with the least and showing himself abject. The power of the kingdom is not brought back to mind; he does not fear to grow cheap to his subjects; he does not acknowledge himself as set over others in honour before the ark of him who had given the honour. Before the Lord he did weak or base things, that by that humility he might make firm the man who had done strong things before all. What others think I do not know; I am more amazed at David dancing than fighting. By fighting he subdued the enemy, by dancing himself. And when the daughter of Saul, still mad with the swelling of royal birth, despised him humbled, saying: "How glorious was the king of Israel today, uncovering himself before the handmaids of his servants, and was naked, as if one of the buffoons", she heard: "I will play before the Lord, who chose me rather than thy father", and a little after: "I will play, and I will be made yet more vile than I have been" etc. As if [to say]: I seek to grow vile before men, because I seek to keep the kingdom for myself before the Lord through humility. There are some who think humbly of themselves and, placed in honours, consider that they are nothing but dust, but they shrink from appearing vile to men, and cloak with stiff outward comeliness what they think inwardly. There are some who desire to seem vile to men and wholly despise what they are by showing themselves abject, but inwardly they swell on account of the merit of the vileness they have shown, and are as much lifted up in heart as they press down elation in appearance. Both these wars of elation David detected with great circumspection and overcame with wonderful virtue. For he who, thinking humbly of himself within, does not seek honour without, says: "I will play, and I will be made yet more vile." And because by showing himself vile outwardly he did not swell inwardly, he adds: "And I will be little in my own eyes." As if [to say]: such as I show myself outwardly in despising myself, such I regard myself inwardly.
15.29: **“MICHOL THE DAUGHTER OF SAUL”** — While all rejoice and resound with hymns at the entry of the ark, Michol the daughter of Saul alone is absent; nay, from the watchtowers she despises David humbled; because when the Jews believe at the end, some will follow Christ by profession, Antichrist by work. To these it fits that Michol, who is interpreted 'all water' to figure the instability of the carnal, is called not David's wife but Saul's daughter. For those who serve Christ in appearance are not crowned with him, but are condemned with the persecutors whom they imitated. But though the wicked despise the humility of the Church, nonetheless the ark of God comes to its place.

16.1: **“AND SET IT IN THE MIDST”** — The ark is set in the midst of the tabernacle which David had pitched for it; that is, the faith of the Church is preached, advances, and is planted in the hearts of the faithful whom God foreordained to eternal life.
16.2: **“And when David had made an end of offering holocausts and peace offerings, he blessed the people in the name of the Lord.”** — HE BLESSED THE PEOPLE. Christ commends to the Father the faith and devotion of the Church, he who also "at the right hand of the Father intercedeth for us", and as the true David blesses and feeds with the food of the saving mystery.
16.3:
**“AND HE DISTRIBUTED TO ALL”** — These gifts the faithful receive when the many, one bread and one body in Christ, chastising the wantonness of their flesh and bringing it into subjection, bake it in the fire of the Holy Spirit, and make the fruits of good works, made most rich by the oil of mercy, glow with compassion for their neighbour. But on the contrary the daughter of Saul, entering the king's chamber in vain, bears no fruit; because those who receive the word of God with the ear only die without the offspring of good work.
**“a cake”** — one, because "one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all" etc.
**“of bread,”** — "which cometh down from heaven, and giveth life to the world"
**“and a piece of roasted beef,”** — of the fatted calf roasted in the fire of the passion
**“AND FINE FLOUR FRIED WITH OIL”** — Flesh most clean, that is, from the salt of sin, toasted in the frying pan of the cross for the cause of human salvation, full of the oil of charity: "For God so loved the world as to give his only begotten Son", who suffered out of charity.
16.4:
**“And he appointed some of the Levites to minister before the ark of the Lord,”** — showing a clean heart with pure conduct
**“and to remember his works,”** — meditating on the law of God according to the rule of faith day and night
**“and to glorify”** — by preaching, rejoicing and work
**“and praise”** — worthily
16.7: **“In that day David made Asaph the chief to give praise to the Lord with his brethren.”** — IN THAT DAY HE MADE etc. Because Christ set the order of teachers at the summit of ecclesiastical dignity. For Asaph is interpreted 'gathering'. Asaph, then, and his brethren are the apostles and apostolic men appointed to gather the faithful, of whom it is said: "Thou shalt make them princes over all the earth." And the writer of the history inserted the manner of praise which David himself composed, saying: Give ye glory to the Lord etc.
16.8: **“GIVE YE GLORY TO THE LORD, AND”** — Alleluia is set as the title of this Psalm, and according to Jerome it is of the neuter gender. Allelu: 'praise ye'; ia signifies the invisible God. It is one of the ten names of God, as Jerome hands down in the letter to Marcella.
16.36:
**“Blessed be the Lord God of Israel from eternity to eternity: and let all the people say Amen, and a hymn”** — the aforesaid
**“to God.”** — AND LET ALL THE PEOPLE SAY AMEN. That is, the gentile [people], which was still unbelieving when he sang this, yet was brought in by the power of prophecy, that out of love of the whole it should say amen, amen, that is, so be it, so be it; as today amen is answered to the priests when they pray, that the devout intention of the priests and the sound devotion of the people may agree in prayer, according to that: "Amen, amen I say to you, that if two of you shall consent upon earth concerning any thing whatsoever they shall ask, it shall be done to them" etc.
16.37: **“So he left there before the ark of the covenant of the Lord, Asaph and his brethren, to minister in the presence of the ark continually day by day”** — no man, being a soldier to God, entangleth himself with secular businesses
16.39:
**“And Sadoc the priest, and his brethren”** — kinsmen
**“the priests before the tabernacle of the Lord in the high place, which was in Gabaon,”** — IN THE HIGH PLACE WHICH WAS IN GABAON etc. Some say that the tabernacle of God, after the children of Israel entered the land of Chanaan, was first in Silo, then in Nobe, afterwards in Gabaon, at last in Sion. Others [say] that a place in Jerusalem was called Gabaon, and that there David set the tabernacle and the ark. For Gabaon is interpreted 'hill'. And they think the place was called high because of the dignity of the divine worship. But in the book of Places we read that Gabaon was the chief city of the Hevites in the tribe of Benjamin. And now a village of the same name is shown at the fourth milestone from Bethlehem toward the west, near Rama and Ramon, where Solomon, having offered victims, merited the divine oracle. And it was set apart for the Levites.
16.43: **“TO BLESS”** — [unclear in the edition: "Generationi filiorum vacaret"]; others take the blessing by antiphrasis. And the house [is] Michol the daughter of Saul, whom David rebuked because she despised him dancing before the ark of the Lord.

17.2: **“And Nathan said to David: Do all that is in thy heart: for God is with thee.”** — AND NATHAN SAID etc. It is plain that the spirit of prophecy does not always enlighten the minds of the prophets. Whence Eliseus: "Let her alone, for her soul is in anguish, and the Lord hath hid it from me" etc. Which comes about by divine dispensation, that receiving the Spirit they may find what was of God, and losing it, what was of themselves.
17.4: **“Go, and speak to David my servant: Thus saith the Lord: Thou shalt not build me a house to dwell in.”** — THOU SHALT NOT BUILD, "because thou art a man of blood." For he who would correct others ought to be clean in himself, so that he flees earthly desires, and sees the more clearly what is to be fled the more truly he himself turns from these by knowledge and life. A hand that holds mud could not wipe away dirt laid upon [another]. This is well said, according to the order of the ancient translation, by a divine voice and by way of signification to David toiling in outward wars: Thou shalt not build me a temple, because "thou art a man of blood." He builds the temple of the Lord who gives himself to correcting the minds of his neighbours. "We are the temple of God", who are established for true life by his dwelling. Whence: "The temple of God is holy, which you are." The man of blood does not build the temple of God. For he who still broods over carnal things must needs be ashamed to instruct the minds of his neighbours.
17.6: **“abiding with all Israel? Did I ever speak to any one of the judges of Israel, whom I commanded to feed my people”** — he commanded a house of cedar to be built for him by none of the judges, who fought against enemies and were all men of blood
17.8: **“And I have been with thee whithersoever thou hast gone: and have slain all thy enemies before thee, and have made thee a name like unto the name of one of the great ones that are famous in the earth.”** — Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses and Josue, whose names [are] famous
17.9: **“And I have given a place to my people Israel: they shall be planted, and shall dwell therein, and shall be moved no more, neither shall the children of iniquity waste them, as at the beginning”** — NEITHER SHALL THE CHILDREN OF INIQUITY etc. Foreign enemies [came] at intervals of time, as of old, now peace, now war. Yet there are found there longer times of peace than Solomon had. For under Aod there were eighty years of peace. Far be it, then, that these things be taken of Solomon.
17.11:
**“And when thou shalt have ended thy days to go to thy fathers, I will raise up thy seed”** — "a just branch to David" etc.
**“after thee, which shall be of thy sons: and I will establish his kingdom.”**
• AND WHEN THOU SHALT HAVE ENDED etc. I WILL RAISE UP THY SEED etc. But Solomon began to reign while his father was reigning, which happened to none of those kings; so that it appears that he is not the one whom this prophecy foreshows. But Christ, the true peacemaker, truly reigned after the death of David.
• AUGUSTINE. He who thinks this promise fulfilled in Solomon errs. He attends to what is said here, He shall build me a house, because Solomon built a noble temple; and he does not attend to what is said, His house shall be faithful etc. Let him attend, then, to Solomon's house full of foreign women worshipping false gods, and the king himself, once wise, seduced into the same idolatry. Nor let him dare to think that God either said or promised this falsely, or did not foreknow that Solomon's house would be such. But in Christ, who was made of the seed of David according to the flesh, we see these things fulfilled; we do not seek another, as the Jews do. For they do not understand this promised son of David to be Solomon, but, he who was promised being made known, they say they hope for another. There went before indeed some image of the thing to come in Solomon, who built the temple and, according to his name, had peace, and at the beginning of his reign was praiseworthy.
17.12:
**“He shall build me a house,”** — of living stones
**“HE SHALL BUILD ME A HOUSE”** — A house, that is, the Church: the house of David because of the race, the house of God because of the temple of God made of men, not of stones, where the people may dwell for ever with God and in God, and God with the people and in the people. Therefore, whereas according to the Septuagint it was said through Nathan: "And the Lord will tell thee that thou shalt build a house for him", afterwards it is said through David: "For thou, O God of Israel, hast revealed to the ear of thy servant, saying: I will build thee a house." For this house both we build by living well, and God by helping. Whence: "Unless the Lord build the house, they labour in vain that build it."
17.14: **“AND HIS THRONE SHALL BE MOST FIRM”** — It can be taken of the son of Isai by hyperbole. But Christ, who was born of the seed of David, is exalted "above all principality, and power, and virtue", to whom "the Father hath given a name which is above all names, that in the name of Jesus every knee should bow."
17.21:
**“For what other nation is there like thy people”** — Christian
**“Israel? one nation upon earth, to which God went”** — made man
**“to deliver”** — from the power of the devil
**“and make it his own people,”** — acceptable
**“and by his greatness and terribleness”** — by miracles
**“to cast out the nations”** — otherwise: the peoples
**“from before them, whom out of Egypt”** — the spiritual [Egypt]
17.24: **“And let it remain, and thy name be magnified for ever: and let it be said: The Lord of hosts is the God of Israel, and the house of David his servant remaineth with”** — otherwise: before
17.25:
**“For thou, O Lord my God, hast revealed to the ear”** — of the inner heart
**“of thy servant, that thou wilt build him a house:”** — that is, by multiplying his progeny; therefore thou hast given him confidence to speak of thee and to preach thy glory

18.1: **“AND HER DAUGHTERS”** — The lesser cities belonging to the chief city. For there were five notable cities of the Philistines: Azotus, Gaza, Ascalon, Geth and Accaron. These, because they were in the land of promise and had been assigned to the children of Israel, but had by no means been possessed by them until David, nay, often forced Israel to serve them, David humbled and made tributary. These five cities signify the five senses of the body, because, while the old nature reigns in us, they afflict us with various torments. But when the true David reigns in us they become tributary, and the flesh is forced to serve the spirit.
18.2: **“And he defeated Moab, and the Moabites became David's servants, offering him gifts.”** — but of Christ it is said: "All the kings of the earth shall adore him"
18.3:
**“At that time David defeated also Adarezer king of Soba of the country of Emath,”** — a city of Syria belonging to the chief city Emath, which is also Epiphania; and that David laid Syria waste Josephus shows
**“ADAREZER”** — [Adarezer,] which is interpreted 'comely help', king of Soba, which is interpreted 'kindled' or 'turning', signifies the vices of the gentiles kindled with natural heat, against which Christ fights and conquers "with the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God".
18.4: **“AND HE HOUGHED ALL”** — Christ hamstrings the height of human wisdom that resists him with the pride of the world; yet what he finds fitting and apt for preaching he keeps for himself.
18.6: **“IN DAMASCUS”** — Damascus, a noble city of Phenice, is interpreted 'cup of blood'; Syria, 'lofty' or 'moist'. For the gentile world, at first fluid with lust and proud in spirit, thirsted for human blood; now, cleansed by the baptism of Christ and exalted by progress in virtues, it longs for the cup of his blood.
18.7:
**“David also took”** — Christ
**“the golden quivers, which the servants of Adarezer had, and brought them to Jerusalem.”** — QUIVERS etc. The teachings of the gentiles, in which the liberal disciplines are contained, which Christ took away from the gentile world and turned to the service of the Church; for they are of use for overthrowing error and confirming truth.
18.8: **“Moreover from Thebath and Chun the cities of Adarezer much brass, of which Solomon made the brazen sea, and the pillars, and the brazen vessels.”** — SOLOMON etc. Because, then, our peaceful king turned the old manner of speech, from the humbling of the overthrown gentile world, to the use of the Church, for the cleansing grace of baptism and the strengthening of faith through the preaching of godly doctrine. For Thebath is interpreted 'a little one came', and Chun 'beauty'. For he who knows himself to be little is made fair and comely in the beauty of the virtues.
18.11:
**“And king David consecrated all the vessels of gold, and of silver, and of brass to the Lord,”** — Christ sanctifies to the Lord all whom he calls from the gentiles, some distinguished in understanding, others splendid in eloquence, others resounding in preaching, that they may serve faithfully in his tabernacle
**“And”** — or with
**“the silver”** — or with silver
**“and the gold”** — or with gold
18.12:
**“And Abisai the son of Sarvia slew”** — as a most valiant man
**“of Edom in the Vale of the saltpits”** — IN THE VALE OF THE SALTPITS. In Kings it is written thus: "And David made himself a name when he returned after taking Syria, in the Vale of the saltpits, eighteen thousand being slain"; because, namely, he set up for himself a triumphal arch. He also made himself a name, because, Syria of Damascus and Syria of Sobal being conquered, he is said to have set up a second.
**“EIGHTEEN THOUSAND”** — But in some copies it is found that David slew not [eighteen but] twenty-eight thousand in the Vale of the saltpits, which came about by the fault of scribes. And Joab laid low twelve thousand, as is written in the title of the fifty-eighth Psalm. But here Abisai is said to have slain eighteen [thousand]; but the victory is ascribed to David for the royal dignity. And because Christ by the strictness of his examination extinguishes, in those who think wrongly of him, the folly of an immoderate taste. Whence: "He that turneth his tongue shall fall into evil."
18.15: **“And Joab the son of Sarvia was over the army, and Josaphat the son of Ahilud was recorder.”** — 'recorder', that is, they were remembrancers, who brought back to the king's memory the causes noted down
18.16:
**“And Sadoc the son of Achitob, and Ahimelech”**
• 'my brother [is] king'
• who in Kings [is] Abimelech, that is, 'my father [is] king'
**“the son of Abiathar, were the priests: and Susa the scribe.”** — who in Kings [is] Saraia; and Susa is interpreted 'joy', Saraia 'prince of the Lord'
**“AHIMELECH”** — That is, 'my brother [is] king', who in Kings [is] Abimelech, that is, 'my father [is] king'. [The king] of the Church instructs the priests, that those who by the order of dignity hold the place of a father may by humility be reckoned brothers, and may not lord it over the clergy.
18.17:
**“And Banaias the son of Joiada was over the bands of the Cerethi, and Phelethi:”** — destroyers
**“THE PHELETHI”** — 'Wonderful' or 'life-givers'; whom some say were seventy judges, after the manner of those whom Moses chose in the desert at the Lord's command. Others say that the Cerethites were appointed to punish the guilty, but the Phelethites to defend the innocent.
**“and the sons of David were the first at the king's hand.”** — in Kings we read, or it is written, that "the sons of David were priests"; but here they are called first and there priests, because of their nobility and precedence
**“AND THE SONS OF DAVID”** — The sons of David, that is, of Christ, are the faithful whom holy Church bears to him, who are "a chosen generation, a kingly priesthood", first at the king's hand, because by good works they merit for themselves the kingdom of heaven, the nearer to God the holier they are.

19.1: **“And it came to pass that Naas the king of the children of Ammon died,”** — HANON, which is interpreted 'their sorrow', signifies the devil, who seems to be ruler of the Ammonites, that is, of the demons, that is, of a people of grief and set in anguish. He shaves half the beard of David's messengers by staining the speech or conduct of the preachers; he cuts their coats as far as the knees or the groin when he reveals in the eyes of men the shameful deeds which he had persuaded. These sit in Jericho until their beards grow, that is, [being] the reproach and shame of others and made accursed by all, until by good endeavour the forms of the beards, that is, of the virtues, grow again, that they may be held worthy of the presence of their king, whose "countenance is against them that do evil things, to cut off the remembrance of them from the earth."
19.4: **“So Hanon shaved and cut off the hair of David's servants, and cut their coats from the buttocks to the feet, and sent them away.”** — in Kings it is written that "he shaved off one half of their beards, and cut away half of their garments even to the buttocks"; but it is not yet different, because what is lacking here is had there

20.1:
**“And it came to pass after the revolution of a year, at the time when kings use to go forth to war,”** — in the Hebrew: when kings had gone forth to war, namely against David
**“that Joab gathered together an army, and the strength of the warriors, and wasted the country of the children of Ammon:”**
• JOAB GATHERED AN ARMY. Joab began the war, David finished it. For Christ wages war when the order of preachers sets the shield of faith against the powerful of the world; but the end of the contest and the triumph are referred to Christ, who "worketh in us both to will and to accomplish". He fitted to himself the crown which he took from the devil, that is, the faithful, who surround him as a crown. Whence: "Thou shalt bless the crown of the year of thy goodness."
• [He took] the crown and made himself a diadem, because he purified it by melting according to the law. But the Hebrews hand down that, because it was unlawful for a Jew to take any gold or silver from idols, since the law forbids idolatry, Ethai the Hethite, who had come from the Philistines to David, snatched the crown from the head of Melchom, so that it might be lawful for a Jew to take from the hand of a man what it was not lawful [to take] from the head of an idol.
**“and he went on and besieged Rabba.”** — a city of the kingdom of Ammon which is now called Philadelphia. And Rabbath is interpreted 'many', because "many shall come from the east and the west, and shall sit down with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven"
20.2:
**“And David took the crown of Melchom from his head,”** — of the idol, which is interpreted 'their king'
**“and found in it a talent weight of gold, and most precious stones, and he made himself a diadem of it: and the spoils”** — that is, the spoils
20.4:
**“After this there began a war at Gazer”** — in Kings Gob, that is, 'lake' or 'locust'; and Gazer, 'ordering'; because as locusts [destroy] grass, so the sons of Arapha destroyed the sons of Israel
**“against the Philistines: in which Sobochai slew”** — in Kings, of the stock of Arapha, because they were the sons of Orpha, the daughter-in-law of Noemi, of the land of Moab
**“WAR”** — It is to be noted that in Paralipomenon three wars of David are chiefly read of, in Kings four. For there the fourth war is where, as David was fighting against the Philistines, Jesbibenob, who was of the race of Arapha, the iron of whose spear weighed three hundred ounces, and who was girded with a new sword, attempted to strike David; Abisai the son of Sarvia was a defence to him, and struck and killed the Philistine. But there are also three divisions of times, past, present and future, and four changes [of seasons]: spring, summer, autumn, winter. And the war of Christ is waged at every time of life against enemies visible or invisible in his members, and is triumphed in him. Whence: "Through God we shall do mightily: and he shall bring to nothing them that afflict us."
20.6: **“AND ANOTHER WAR ALSO HAPPENED IN GETH”** — In the book of Kings thus: "The third was in Gob against the Philistines, in which Adeodatus the son of Saltus, an embroiderer, a Bethlehemite, slew Goliath the Gethite" etc. Gob is interpreted 'lake', because David put himself against Goliath as into a den of lions; who is Adeodatus, that is, chosen for the kingdom. Son of the forest [saltus], namely that in which he fed the sheep; embroiderer, because his mother was of the race of Beseleel; Bethlehemite, because [he was] of Bethlehem, in which Booz was known to Ruth on account of bread; whence the place was called the house of bread. That David himself is Adeodatus is plain where it is said: "These were born of Arapha in Geth, and fell by the hand of David and of his servants." But the Hebrews judge Arapha, the mother of the giants, to be Orpha, the daughter-in-law of Noemi.

21.5: **“And he gave David the number of them whom he had surveyed: and all the number of Israel was found to be eleven hundred thousand men that drew the sword: and of Juda four hundred and seventy thousand fighting men.”** — AND ALL THE NUMBER OF ISRAEL WAS FOUND TO BE A THOUSAND THOUSAND. In Kings thus: "That there were found of Israel eight hundred thousand strong men, and of Juda fifty [so the edition: 'quinquaginta'] thousand fighting men." But the Hebrews assert that this number was found by Joab, but that the writer wished to show [unclear in the edition: "nisi quantum"] is written in the books of Samuel, in which only the survivors of the slaughter are contained.
21.6:
**“But Levi”** — because of the dignity of the priesthood
**“and Benjamin”** — because they had lately fallen almost to extermination
21.7: **“AND HE STRUCK ISRAEL”** — Death, which first came because of sin [so the edition: 'veni'], raged among the people; because often the life of the shepherd offends for the evil of the flock. David, lifted up with pride, sinned by numbering the people, and the people received the punishment; because the hearts of rulers are disposed according to the deserts of the people. But the just judge, by punishing them, rebuked the fault of the sinner on whose account he sinned. But because, being proud by his own will, he was not free of the fault, he received the punishment of the fault. For the wrath which struck the people in body laid low the ruler with grief of heart.
21.8: **“I HAVE SINNED EXCEEDINGLY”** — In Kings thus: "I have sinned very much in this action. But I pray thee, O Lord, to take away the iniquity of thy servant, because I have done exceeding foolishly." In which it is to be noted that David offended in numbering the people because he did not observe the precepts of the law. For in the book of Numbers the Lord commands Moses: "Take the sum of the children of Israel by their kindreds, whatsoever is of the male sex, from twenty years old and upward" etc. But because David commanded all to be numbered generally, he incurred the indignation of God. In Exodus also the Lord says to Moses: "When thou shalt take the sum of the children of Israel according to their number, every one of them shall give a price to the Lord for their souls" etc. Forgetting to do this, David offended God.
21.13: **“And David said to Gad: I am on every side in a great strait: but it is better for me to fall into the hands of the Lord, for his mercies are many, than into the hands of men.”** — AND DAVID SAID. If he chose famine, he would seem to act against others, because, having much grain, he would not suffer want with the others. If he chose to be overcome by enemies for three months, having most valiant men about him he would fear nothing, while the army would be exposed to slaughter. He therefore chose a suffering common to himself and to others, in which the fear would be equal for all.
21.14: **“SEVENTY THOUSAND MEN”** — Only the heads of the people and the elders were numbered. But the Hebrews affirm that as many thousands of the whole people were slain as the number written in Paralipomenon exceeds the number which is in Kings. For they say that in Paralipomenon both those who remained and those who were slain were numbered, but in Kings only the living.
21.15:
**“And he sent an angel to Jerusalem, to strike it:”** — by divers and hidden sicknesses
**“and as he was striking it, the Lord beheld, and took pity”** — Sadoc the priest, as they say, praying for the people
**“for the greatness of the evil: and said to the angel that destroyed: It is enough, now stop thy hand. And the angel of the Lord stood by the thrashingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite.”** — of Areuna the Jebusite. For Areuna is interpreted 'threshingfloor', and Ornam sounds in Latin 'light to us'
21.18:
**“And the angel of the Lord commanded Gad to tell David, that he should go up, and build an altar to the Lord God in the thrashingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite.”** — this is Jerusalem
**“AND BUILD AN ALTAR”** — Well is David, when he would appease the Lord, commanded to build an altar on the threshingfloor of Areume or Horne; because God is not appeased by man unless on the floor [so the edition: 'arca'] of the heart, by the light of right faith and true love, he set up for him an altar of humility, on which to offer the sacrifice of praise.
21.25: **“So David gave Ornan for the place, six hundred sicles of gold of most just weight.”** — SO DAVID GAVE etc. In Kings thus: "So David bought the floor and the oxen for fifty sicles of silver." Hence the Hebrews suppose that the oxen [were bought] for fifty sicles of silver, but the floor for six hundred [sicles] of gold. But others think that the floor bought for fifty sicles expresses the place of the altar where he offered holocausts, but the floor bought for six hundred sicles is the place of the whole temple which Solomon afterwards built, and its courts.
21.26: **“And he built there an altar to the Lord: and he offered holocausts and peace offerings, and he called upon the Lord, and he heard him by sending fire from heaven upon the altar of the holocaust.”** — under Moses, David, Solomon and Elias fire came down from heaven upon the altar; but under Manue the angel brought forth flame from the rock
21.30:
