As by Cyrus, the first king of the Persians, Christ is signified, because he loosed the captivity of the people of God and commanded the temple to be restored, so by his successor Artaxerxes, who with the same devotion commanded Jerusalem to be rebuilt, we understand him who builds the Church through the office of the preachers. Hence well is Artaxerxes interpreted 'light trying in silence'. For the Lord is the light of life, who tries the hearts of the faithful in silence, when at times he enlightens them with the sweetness of heavenly grace, at times clouds them with the pressures of the present life, that, taught by temporal adversities, they may desire eternal goods more ardently.
• Memorable is this year in which Jerusalem was permitted to be built, and long ago foreshown by the prophecy of Daniel, when the angel said to him that seventy weeks were shortened upon his people and upon the holy city. And a little after: "From the going forth of the word, to build up Jerusalem again, unto Christ the prince, there shall be seven weeks, and sixty-two weeks." And a little after: "And he shall confirm the covenant with many, in one week: and in the half of the week the victim and the sacrifice shall fail." The weeks therefore [are reckoned] from the twentieth year of Artaxerxes, when he gave leave to build Jerusalem; at which time, as Julius Africanus writes, a hundred and twenty-five years of the kingdom of the Persians had passed, and as many remained incomplete up to Alexander the Great, when he killed Darius. For it was the hundred and eighty-fifth year of the captivity of Jerusalem; and they reach up to the times of the Lord's passion, through which the legal sacrifices were ended. And each week has seven years, and they make four hundred and fifteen [so the edition], namely according to the course of the moon, so that each [year], in a new and unwonted manner, has no more than twelve lunar months. Hence the angel says that seventy weeks are not numbered but shortened upon the people, which are four hundred and seventy-five solar years; of which whole sentence of the prophet I have taken care to treat as fully as I could in the book of times.
2.10: **“And Sanaballath the Horonite, and Tobias the servant, the Ammonite, heard it, and it grieved them exceedingly, that a man was come, who sought the prosperity of the children of Israel.”** — AND [THEY] HEARD etc. Heretics and all the enemies of the Church are grieved whenever they see the elect labouring for the catholic faith or the correction of manners, by which the walls of the Church are renewed. For the diversity of minds and things is to be noted. Above it was said that those who had remained of the captivity in Judea were in great affliction and reproach; Nehemias too [is said] to have spent a long [time] [so the edition: 'in invium'] with weeping and prayers, because the wall of Jerusalem was broken down and the gates burnt. But now, the case reversed, the enemies are grieved and afflicted because they understand that its buildings are to be restored and its citizens freed from the insults of the enemies; whence: "You shall lament and weep, but the world shall rejoice: but your sorrow shall be turned into joy." And while the world that rejoiced weeps, the sorrow of the just is turned into joy, when they see the affairs of the Church grow and those who had strayed by sinning return by repenting.
2.13: **“I VIEWED THE WALL”** — He goes about surveying the divers places of the destroyed city and anxiously examines how each ought to be repaired. It belongs also to spiritual doctors often to rise by night and, while the others rest, to look into the state of the Church with skilful search, that they may watchfully inquire how they may correct and raise up the things which have been defiled or cast down by the wars of vices. And the wall of Jerusalem lies broken down when the life of the faithful is defiled with earthly and low affections. The gates are consumed by fire when those who ought to have opened the entrance of life to others, abandoning the common master of truth, grow sluggish with idleness with the rest and serve temporal cares.
2.17: **“THAT JERUSALEM IS DESOLATE”** — BEDE. These things are plain and fit the spiritual sense: for the doctors, nay all who burn with the zeal of God, are in the greatest affliction as long as they see Jerusalem, that is, the vision of peace, which God left and commended to us, deserted through the wars of dissensions, and the gates of the virtues, which according to Isaias praise ought to occupy, cast down by the prevailing gates of hell and held in reproach.

3.1:
**“THEN ELIASIB ROSE UP”** — The high priest, that is, the pontiff of that time, the son of Joachim, who after his father, Jesus the son of Josedec, held the pontificate for no short time. And rightly did the restoration of the city begin from the great priest and his brethren, that those who went before in grade of order might become an example to others in good works. And well is it added to the priests building: And even unto the tower of a hundred cubits they sanctified it, unto the tower of Hananeel. For the priests build in the number of a hundred cubits when they kindle all whom they instruct with love and desire of eternal things. For the hundred, which in counting on the fingers passes from the left hand to the right, figures the heavenly goods, which in comparison with earthly ones are as the right hand to the left.
**“AND THEY BUILT”** — BEDE. The old translation has: And they built the gate and the sheep pool; of which name John makes mention, saying: "Now there is at Jerusalem a pond, called Probatica, which in Hebrew is named Bethsaida" etc. Nor does anything hinder us from understanding that the same place is designated here, since the name probatica is not far from the name of the flock; for in Greek a sheep is called probaton. Jerome makes mention of this place in the Book of Places, saying: Bethsaida is a pool in Jerusalem which is called probatica, and is interpreted by us 'of cattle'. It once had five porches. Twin pools are also shown, of which one is wont to be filled by the winter rains, the other, wonderfully reddish, as if with bloody waters, bears witness in itself to the signs of its ancient work. For they say that the victims were wont to be washed in it by the priests, whence also it received its name. From all which it seems that the flock gate was near the sheep pool, so that through the one the victims might be brought, in the other washed.
**“BEDE”** — According to the letter it seems that the flock gate was first built or sanctified by the priests because it was in the neighbourhood of the temple itself and belonged properly to them. For it seems fitting that the building of the city should begin from the temple; because it is necessary that before all things we build in ourselves constancy of faith and love toward God, then add the works of piety which belong to the love of our neighbour, and in the third, that is, the last place, those which look to the general provision of this life; of which the Apostle says: "Having food, and wherewith to be covered, with these we are content." This too seems probable, that it is called the flock gate because through it the cattle to be offered in the temple were brought in. For the priests build the flock gate at the beginning of building the city of God when the preachers before all things imbue their hearers with the faith of truth which works through love, through which they may bring in the victims of good works and offer them to God on the altar of the heart. And they sanctify the building of this gate, extended through a hundred cubits as far as the tower of Hananeel, that is, of the grace of God, when from the beginning of faith to the firmness of good action, which is not perfected except by God inspiring and helping, they stretch forward with the sole intention of the inner reward.
**“They sanctified it, and set up the doors thereof: even unto the tower of a hundred cubits they sanctified it, unto the tower of Hananeel.”** — because it belongs to the priests to make their works worthy of special sanctification before others, and to act earnestly that those who are joined to them may sanctify the name of the Lord in themselves by living well
3.3:
**“But the fish gate the sons of Asnaa built: they covered”** — they finished
**“BUT THE FISH GATE”** — Which, namely, looks toward Joppe and Diospolis, that is, Lydda, nearer the sea than all the ways of Jerusalem; which is now said to be called the gate of David, and to be the first of the gates to the west of mount Sion. With this opinion Paralipomenon seems to agree, where it is written of Manasses king of Juda: "After this he built a wall without the city of David, on the west side of Gihon in the valley, from the entering in of the fish gate round about to Ophel, and raised it up exceeding high." Typically, as the flock signifies the faithful of the Lord, so are they wont to be called fish too. Whence: "Feed my sheep", and: "Come after me, and I will make you to be fishers of men"; of whom it is said: "They chose out the good into vessels, but the bad they cast forth" etc. The fish gate therefore is built when the faithful serve those works of the virtues by which they may lead their neighbours who behold them, rescued from the waves of turmoil and worldly concupiscence, into the tranquillity and peace of the spiritual life. The fish gate is built in Jerusalem when those grades are ordained in the Church through which the elect, separated from the reprobate as good fish from bad, are brought into the fellowship of everlasting peace. Sophonias makes mention of this gate, saying: "The voice of a cry from the fish gate, and a howling from the Second." And by saying 'from the Second' he signifies the gate of the second wall in the same quarter. For that the wall of the city was doubled in the times of Ezechias Paralipomenon shows thus: "He also, acting diligently, built up all the wall that had been broken, and built towers upon it, and another wall without." Typically, Sophonias heard the voice of a cry from the fish gate and a howling from the Second, because he foreknew that both were to be cast down by the enemies. For he saw that the faith and works of the doctors, through which the rest were to be rescued from the waves of corruptible life and brought into the Church, were to be laid low to the earth by the snares of the devil, that is, deprived of heavenly joys through the desire of earthly pleasure. And well did he hear the voice of a cry and howling from both gates, namely the First and the Second, the inner and the outer, because he saw that outwardly works and inwardly hearts were to be overthrown by the devil's attack. But because "the Lord lifteth up them that are cast down", Nehemias relates that the fish gate was restored after its ruin; because if some of the preachers fall by sinning, there will not be lacking up to the end of the world those who, succeeding, by living and preaching well open the gates of justice to the faithful with the Lord's help.
**“THEY COVERED”** — This verse is repeated also of the other gates that were built, because it is necessary that whoever has begun the structure of good work should carry it to the roof of good perfection, and set up the defences of skilful watch as doors, locks and bars. For doors are set up in gates that, being opened at the fitting time, the citizens may have the means of going in and out; locks and bars, that the doors being shut the enemy may not enter. So in good works doors must be set, that our fellow citizens, that is, our neighbours, "seeing" them "may glorify the Father who is in heaven", and may themselves too learn to walk by our examples and to enter the walls of the virtues with us. Locks and bars too must be set against the snares and assault of the enemies, that we may be defended on every side with diligent industry, lest perhaps the enemy, let in, storm the citadel of virtue; whence: "A brother that is helped by his brother, is like a strong city: and judgments are like the bars of cities." When therefore both peoples, namely of the Jews and of the gentiles, agree together in brotherly charity in Christ, they build one Church, namely the city of God; and as bars defend the gates of cities, so the doctrines of truth defend from the incursion of unbelievers the churches throughout the world, which make up the one catholic [Church]. Again, we set locks and bars to our gates when we take care not to betray the secrets of our faith to swine and dogs, that is, to unclean minds, or do our justice for the sake of human favour and let those in to see our good things who bring us more danger by praising [so the edition: 'lavando'] than they take away saving help from us by seeing.
**“it, and set up the doors thereof,”**
• of foresight
• which being opened, citizens or enemies can go in or out
**“and the locks,”** — by which the enemy is kept off
**“and the bars.”** — the defences of diligence
3.6: **“AND THE OLD GATE”** — Of which John says: "Dearly beloved, I write not a new commandment to you, but an old commandment which you had from the beginning. The old commandment is the word which you have heard." And the old gate is built in Jerusalem when the word of faith and love, which was handed down from the beginning of the Church, is either recovered in those who err or established in those who have lately believed.
3.8: **“And next to him built Eziel the son of Araia the goldsmith, and next to him built Ananias the son of the perfumer: and they left Jerusalem unto the wall of the broad street.”** — UNTO THE WALL etc. That is, the firmness and defence of perfect love in the hearts of the elect, to which its instructors come by building when, advancing in the works of charity, they say: "I have run the way of thy commandments" etc., namely by that enlargement of the enlightened mind by which they love both the friend in God and the enemy for God's sake.
3.13:
**“AND THE GATE OF THE VALLEY”**
• BEDE. The valley of Josaphat, which was also called Gehennom, that is, the valley of Ennom, is on the eastern side of the city, through which the brook Cedron, swollen by rains or snows, flows down from the northern to the southern quarter. In the western part of the same city too there is read to be the valley of Gihon, in Paralipomenon, where it is said of king Manasses: "After this he built a wall without the city of David, on the west side of Gihon in the valley." And Gihon is the name of the fountain where Solomon was anointed king outside the city. Whether then Esdras signifies in this place this valley or that or any valley of the city, [it does not matter]. Mystically. The gate of the valley is built in Jerusalem when, to the elect lately imbued with the knowledge of the faith, or to those who had erred and have been restored in the chastity of faith, the virtue of humility is enjoined by the doctors of truth among other things to be observed, through which they may deserve to be exalted by the greater grace of God. "For God resisteth the proud, and giveth grace to the humble"; whence: "The vales shall abound with corn", that is, the humble with the gift of the refreshment above.
• BEDE. Well is the gate of the valley built after the old gate and the wall of the broad street; because after the rudiments of the catholic faith, which works through love, it is necessary that humility be impressed on us to be held as the guardian of the virtues, that the greater we are, the more we may humble ourselves in all things.
**“and a thousand cubits”** — perfect working
**“AND A THOUSAND”** — BEDE. They say that the site of the city of Jerusalem slopes with so gentle a declivity both toward the east and the west that the rain falling there, flowing down like a river through the eastern gates and carrying with it all the filth of the streets, swells the brook Cedron in the valley of Josaphat. That seems to be called the gate of the dunghill through which filth and uncleanness were wont to be carried out; nor is it of less virtue and usefulness that unclean things be carried out of the city of the Lord than that clean things be brought in. They build therefore the gate of the dunghill in Jerusalem who ordain those in the ministry of the Church through whom the filth of vices may be purged from the minds of the elect and men of corrupt mind kept away from the Church, the shower of heavenly grace helping them and weakening all impurity, that all who work iniquity may be cut off from the city of the Lord. And because it is of great perfection when one advances from God through humility so as to be able keenly to look into his errors and effectively to purge them, it is rightly said that those who built the gate of the valley built a thousand cubits in the wall up to the gate of the dunghill. For the thousand signifies perfection, the cubit working, which is done by the hands and arms; and those come by building in the wall of the holy city from the gate of the valley to the gate of the dunghill by a thousand cubits who, having received the grace of humility, give themselves over to good works with such diligence of perfection that they cast out from themselves all the rubbish of harmful action, useless speech and even superfluous thought.
**“in the wall unto the gate of the dunghill.”** — who, namely, cast out from the soul the filth of vices and of a corrupt mind
3.14: **“And the gate of the dunghill Melchias the son of Rechab built, lord of the street of Bethacharem: he built it, and set up the doors thereof”** — as above
3.15:
**“And the gate”**
• through which, by the rushing abundance of rain, the dung of the city is carried out
• the doctors who preach the faith of the Trinity
**“of the fountain”**
• Siloe
• of God the Father, of whom the Son is born
**“AND THE GATE OF THE FOUNTAIN”** — BEDE. Writers relate that from that brow of mount Sion which, with a sheer rock, faces the eastern quarter, within the walls and at the roots of the hill, the fountain of Siloe bursts forth, which flows to the south, not with continuous waters, but bubbles up at certain hours and days, and comes with a great sound through hollows of the earth and caves of the hardest rock; which alone, and not perpetually, the city uses. And Siloe, which is interpreted 'sent', where the man born blind was enlightened, signifies Christ, who was sent by God the Father for our enlightening; whose fountain can be understood to be the Father, from whom he was born. Of whom: "For with thee is the fountain of life; and in thy light we shall see light." The gate of the fountain is built in Jerusalem when doctors are ordained in the Church who preach to the peoples the faith of the divine eternity; and the walls of the pool of Siloe, when the most firm and impregnable testimonies of the Scriptures, by which the sacrament of the Lord's incarnation is designated, are set in order in the mind of the faithful. Which walls, namely, of the divine Word reach to the king's garden when, the mysteries of the Lord's dispensation being known, we have begun, with the supreme King's help, to bring forth the shoots of the virtues. They reach up to the steps that go down from the city of David when one has learned to advance from the general life of the faithful to heavenly things by spiritual desires. For the steps which go down from the city of David to the lower parts of Jerusalem are the helps of divine inspiration or protection, by which we are stirred little by little to come to the walls of the heavenly kingdom. For David made steps by which we go up to his city, when the divine pity taught us the order of the virtues by which we seek heavenly things, when it gave us the gift of carrying out those very virtues; whence: "In his heart he hath disposed to ascend by steps." And a little after: "They shall go from virtue to virtue: the God of gods shall be seen in Sion." To these steps therefore the builders of the holy city come by building after the walls of the pool of Siloe and after the king's garden, when, after the mysteries or sacraments of the Lord's incarnation have been shown, by which the heathen world, blind from birth, was loosed and enlightened, after the shoots of good work have been begun through faith, the holy doctors more diligently show their hearers in due time the advances of the virtues by which they may ascend to the vision of their Maker, namely strong of hand and desirable, which is signified by the name David. Which steps father Benedict understands to consist chiefly in humility, when, interpreting the ladder shown to the patriarch Jacob, with angels ascending and descending by it, as designating our way to heavenly things, he compares its steps to the increase and advances of good works which are done through humility.
**“Sellum the son of Colozai, lord of the street”** — of the neighbourhood
**“of Maspha, built: he built it, and covered it, and set up the doors thereof, and the locks,”** — the firm testimonies of Scripture by which the sacrament of the Lord's incarnation is preached
**“and the bars, and the walls of the pool”** — those, namely, who, with the help of the supreme King, bring forth the shoots of the virtues
**“of Siloe”** — which is interpreted 'sent'; this is Christ, sent by the Father for our enlightening
**“unto the king's garden, and unto the steps”** — the helps of divine inspiration or protection, or the increase of good works which are done through humility
**“that go down from the city”** — the heavenly
**“FROM THE CITY OF DAVID”** — The city of David according to the letter is called mount Sion, which, set on the south, overtops the city as a citadel; and the greater part of the city lies below the mount, set on the plain of a lower hill. Hence in the Book of Kings: "But David took the castle of Sion, the same is the city of David." And a little after: "And David dwelt in the castle, and called it the city of David."
3.16:
**“NEHEMIAS BUILT”** — BEDE. After the gate of the fountain and the walls of the pool of Siloe, which reach to the king's garden and up to the steps that go down from the city of David, the measure of the holy city is stretched even as far as over against his sepulchre; because he who preaches the faith of the holy Trinity and the dispensation of the divine incarnation and the fruitfulness of the Church cleaving to Christ, of which it is said: "My sister is a garden enclosed" etc., ought to impress on them not only the steps of good works by which they may ascend to heaven, but also the Lord's passion, that through him who died for them and rose again they may know that they too will rise from the region and "shadow of death" to life and ascend to the heavenly kingdom.
**“After him built Nehemias the son of Asboth, lord of half the street of Bethsur, as far as over against the sepulchres of David,”** — OVER AGAINST THE SEPULCHRES OF DAVID etc. Note that David was buried not in Bethlehem, as some think, but in Jerusalem, for a sure reason of mystery. For as, born in Bethlehem and anointed king, he figured that Christ would be born there of his seed and be adored by the magi in the person of a king, so, dying and buried in Jerusalem, [he figured] that he would suffer and be buried in the same city.
**“and to the pool, that was made with great labour, and to the house of the mighty.”** — TO THE POOL etc. The pool, namely divine Scripture, which, made by the work of the Holy Spirit, ministers to us the washing of sins and the saving draught; which, if it be turned for us by the Lord into wine, that is, into spiritual sense, inebriates us with the more pleasing sweetness of truth; where also is the house of the mighty, because whoever are refreshed by the frequent streams of the divine word, by hearing and doing, are made strong against all the snares of the devil. After the sepulchre of David therefore is placed the pool made with great labour, to which the house of the mighty is adjacent; because through the Lord's passion the abyss of the Scriptures has been opened to us, by whose abundance the hearts of the faithful have been strengthened and the city of Christ made impregnable to all enemies. For when the waters fail or are taken away by the enemy, a city is easily taken; and if the ancient enemy takes from us the fountain of the word of God, he at once breaks into the citadel of the mind.
3.19:
**“And next to him Azer the son of Josue, the lord of Maspha, built another measure,”** — the second wall, that is, the firm defence of the mind
**“AND [HE] BUILT”** — BEDE. Up to here the first wall of the city is built; from here the "second measure", that is, of the inner wall, begins. Hence it is said that very many of the builders built over against their own house. For very many houses of the city were either near or joined to the inner wall. After the construction of the outer wall, therefore, there follows in our city the measure of the second wall, when, after the perfection of works and tongue, which can appear to all, we strive the more to please God in the inner parts of the mind, lest we conceive anything in the soul by which we may offend the eyes of the inner Judge.
**“OVER AGAINST THE GOING UP OF THE STRONG CORNER”** — This is Christ, who in his faith and love united the people of the Jews and of the gentiles, whence he is called the corner stone. Over against whose going up the second measure is built when through the medicine of pious thought we tend to the vision of him, when also, held back in this life, we often sigh with desire of his vision. There follow very many ranks of builders who are related to have built the second measure, because the greatest structure of the Church is in the defence of inner virtue, namely when we guard our heart with all watchfulness, because life proceeds from it. But to draw each thing to a spiritual understanding is too long.
3.26:
**“And the Nathinites”** — dedicated to God by the profession of perfection of life
**“THE NATHINITES”** — The Gibeonites are meant, who served in the ministry of the house of the Lord with faithful devotion according to the ordering of Josue the son of Nun.
**“dwelt in Ophel,”** — in the defence and height of the virtues
**“IN OPHEL”** — BEDE. It was a tower not far from the temple, of enormous height. Hence it received the name Ophel, that is, 'of darkness' or 'cloudy', because it thrust its head into the clouds. Finally, where it is written in Zacharias [so the edition]: "And thou, O cloudy tower of the flock", it is well called the tower of Ophel. In what part of the city this tower was the Book of Paralipomenon shows, saying that Manasses built "a wall without the city of David, on the west side of Gihon in the valley, from the entering in of the fish gate round about to Ophel". It was fitting therefore, according to the situation of the place, that the ministers of the temple should dwell in a tower near the temple. Mystically, the Nathinites dwell in Ophel, that is, in the cloudy tower, when those who have been dedicated to God by the profession of a more perfect life ever dwell in action and thought in the defence and height of the virtues, and "their conversation is in heaven". Wondering at whom the common people say: "Who are these, that fly as clouds" etc.? Again, the Thecuites dwell in Ophel, whoever, distinguished by the habit of religion, penetrate with enlightened heart the hidden things of the Scriptures, of which it is said: "Dark waters in the clouds of the air", that is, mystical knowledge in the prophets, and read and meditate on them assiduously.
**“as far as over against the water gate toward the east,”** — whence: "The Orient from on high hath visited us."
**“and the tower”** — Christ, who is "a tower of strength against the face of the enemy".
**“that stood out.”** — OVER AGAINST THE WATER GATE etc. BEDE. That is, the Lord, who daily waters us with the grace of his mercy, lest we slip and fail in the hardships of the present life. This gate the psalmist desired, saying: "As the hart panteth after the fountains of water; so my soul panteth after thee, O God." Which gate is fittingly set toward the east, because the Lord, who inebriates us with the torrent of his pleasure lest we thirst, himself enlightens us by the gift of visitation lest we be darkened in the darkness of errors; whence: "The Orient from on high hath visited us: to enlighten them that sit in darkness, and in the shadow of death." He defends us from the enemy by the safeguard of his protection. Hence there follows: And as far as the tower that stood out; of which, namely, it is said: "Thou hast conducted me; for thou hast been my hope, a tower of strength against the face of the enemy." The Nathinites therefore dwell in Ophel as far as over against the water gate toward the east and the tower that stands out, when the faithful, given to sacred readings, rejoice to be inebriated with the grace of the divine pity and defended from the enemy by its help. And because after the present gifts of the virtues one ascends to see the brightness of the Lord, it is rightly added: After him the Thecuites built.
3.27:
**“After them”** — the preachers
**“the Thecuites built”** — the trumpeters
**“another measure over against, from the great tower”**
• of contemplation
• FROM THE TOWER etc. The structure of the city reaches from the great and eminent tower up to the wall of the temple, when the just, from the height of contemplation, which in this life, temporal things being despised, lifts the mind up to heavenly desires, truly ascend in that life to behold the brightness of the Lord's incarnation, the glory of the divine eternity too being opened. And because Thecua is interpreted 'trumpet' or 'horn', the Thecuites 'trumpeters', it is fittingly said that the Thecuites built this. For it belongs to the doctors, whose sound has gone forth into all the earth, to open the present or future gifts of God in his city, that is, to the faithful.
**“UNTO THE WALL OF THE TEMPLE”** — That is, the body of Christ, of which it is said: "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up"; which, namely, the persecutors had destroyed in death, but which, raised and exalted to heaven, its lovers do not cease to see in glory.
3.28:
**“AND UPWARD FROM THE HORSE GATE”** — BEDE. Jeremias signifies that this gate is in the eastern quarter of the city, writing typically of the Church: "And the city shall be built to the Lord from the tower of Hananeel", and a little after: "unto the torrent Cedron, and unto the corner of the horse gate toward the east". The priests build at the horse gate when they furnish sufficient examples of living to those who enter the doors of the Church to curb the wanton motions of the flesh or of the soul; or when they so order the thoughts with which they treat of their own and their people's food or clothing that they do not hinder the freedom of the mind with which they seek heavenly things. Hence well is it said of the workers: Every man over against his house; which phrase is often repeated in this building. Nor must we labour in explaining how in the Church each one ought to build a wall over against his own house and fortify his mind against the snares of the devil, lest he be able to break in from elsewhere, while each defends his body and mind with strong faith in God. Each one too builds over against his own house if he defends those who are committed to him with diligent guard of regular discipline, lest they be deceived by the incursion of vices or the persuasion of heretics.
**“FROM THE HORSE GATE”** — Horses, when they are taken in a good sense, like asses, camels and mules, show the peoples of the gentiles converted to the Lord, or the cares of temporal things subjected, namely, to the dominion of the soul.
**“THE PRIESTS BUILT”** — And the priests build the wall of the city of God at the water gate [so the edition] when the doctors, after the calling of the Jews, come by sowing the word of God to the bringing of the gentiles into the Church.
**“BEDE”** — It is long to discourse mystically on each of the buildings or builders, which the skilled reader can also recognize by himself. Only this is to be noted: that those who build the gates and towers through which the citizens may enter or the enemies be kept off are the prophets, apostles and evangelists, through whom the form of faith and right working, by which we may enter the Church, is ministered to us, and by whose words we learn to refute and repel the adversaries of the truth. But those who build the rest of the city are the pastors and doctors, whom the Apostle put in the second place, through whose diligence, as through great architects of the Church, the catholic faith is kept to this day throughout the whole world. And as Nehemias, enumerating in order all the builders of the city, commends them to perpetual memory, so Christ, the comforter of our poverty, writes in heaven the names of all who build the Church in the elect etc.

4.1:
**“And it came to pass, that when Sanaballath heard that we were building the wall, he was very angry: and being moved exceedingly, he scoffed at the Jews,”** — the confessors of the faith
**“AND IT CAME TO PASS”** — BEDE. Plainly this is the anger of heretics. These are the words of those who surname themselves Samaritans, that is, keepers of the law of God, though they are contrary to God and his laws, as separated from the house of David, that is, from the unity of Christ and the Church, through heresies and schisms and evil works; who fear that the walls of faith be built, lest their impiety be overthrown. This is the scoffing of all who say that they know God, but in their works deny him. For the Samaritans so served the Lord as not to renounce their own gods. Whom they imitate today who are Christians in such a way that they have their belly for their God, or follow avarice, which is the service of idols, or, bound over to the other allurements of the world, serve the creature rather than the Creator. Such men therefore, like heretics, do not wish the walls of the Church to be renewed, lest, as the state of piety grows, they be compelled to depart from their impiety. Such are wont to call the Jews, that is, the confessors of the faith, feeble and easily overcome by those who act, while in the daily struggle of souls they love vices rather than virtues to win the palm of victory. And because there are among the heretics those who deny pardon even to penitents, it is rightly added in their person: Are they able to raise up stones out of the heaps of the rubbish, which are burnt? For burnt stones are built up out of heaps of rubbish when those who, conquered by the fire of persecutions, denied the faith, or, subjected to the delights of vices, lost the cleanness of their work, by God's mercy come to their senses, so as to recover the integrity of the catholic faith by constant profession and, amended in their manners, obtain the ornaments of the virtues.
4.2:
**“and said before his brethren, and the multitude of the Samaritans:”** — of the heretics, namely, who say that they keep the law of God
**“What are the feeble Jews doing? Will the Gentiles let them alone?”** — the gentile persecutors of the Church
**“Will they sacrifice and make an end in a day? Are they able to raise up stones out of the heaps of the rubbish, which are burnt?”** — of those, namely, who, conquered by the fire of persecution, denied the faith, or, subjected to the works of vices, lost the cleanness of body or of work
4.3:
**“But Tobias”** — 'good of the Lord', not in truth but in pride
**“BUT TOBIAS ALSO”** — BEDE. The person and words of this Tobias befit heretics. The person indeed, because his patriarch Ammon was born of incest, of drunkenness, by night and in a cave; and the origin of heretics is begotten of carnal pleasure and uncleanness, of the darkness of errors or of crimes, of private conventicles and not of the public creed of the Church. And that the same Tobias, that is, 'good of the Lord', not by merit and truth but by the elation of pride, says that the wall will be leapt over by a fox: heretics are called foxes, according to that: "Catch us the little foxes that destroy the vines." Which is: detect and bring to light the rotten and deceitful cunning of heretics, by which they strive to corrupt the fruitful minds of the faithful.
**“the Ammonite, who was by him, said: Let them build: if a fox go up,”**
• rising against the assertion of their faith
• the heretic, according to that: Catch us the little foxes
**“he will leap over”** — he will overcome, namely, and quickly put under his feet all the confidence of their teaching, which they boast is founded in Christ as if defended by firm stone
**“their stone wall.”** — the defence of the Church
4.4: **“Hear thou, our God, for we are despised: turn their reproach upon their own head,”** — like this imprecation is what the prophet says: "His sorrow shall be turned on his own head."
4.9: **“AND WE PRAYED”** — This is the one refuge against the enemies of the Church: namely prayer to God and the diligence of the doctors, who, meditating day and night in his law, fortify the hearts of the faithful against the snares of the devil and his soldiers by preaching, consoling and exhorting.
4.10:
**“And Juda said:”** — the tribe of Juda
**“THE RUBBISH IS VERY MUCH”** — BEDE. Heaped up, namely, in the place of the wall, which first had to be carried out, that the foundations of the wall might be laid in the living earth; which befits the house of the gospel, whose builder dug deep and, the heap of earth being carried off, laid the foundations upon a rock, which are cast down by no force of waters or winds. For first the earth of earthly desires must be carried out of our heart, then the firm and impregnable wall of works must be built upon the foundation of faith. For he who raises the building of holy action upon the earth and rubbish of weak thoughts is deceived, and, when the storm of temptation breaks upon him, is shown to have built a ruin instead of a house or city.
4.11: **“THE ENEMIES SAID”** — These things are wont to be done in the spiritual building. For the unwearied enemy remains with his attendants, namely the unclean spirits and malignant men, who strive to hinder and overthrow in us, when we are unwary, the works of the virtues and of faith, and to slay the mind of the faithful with the sword of wicked suggestion. But against these the armour of God must be taken up by us, that we may be able to resist in the evil day and to stand perfect in all things.
4.13: **“I PLACED IN THE PLACE”** — That is, that the workers, surrounded by a band of armed men, might build more freely and securely. For the grades of the faithful are divided. Some build up the Church, adorning it within with good works; others, armed with the weapons of sacred reading, keep watch against the heretics who attack. These with religious devotion strengthen their neighbours in the truth of the faith; those carry on the necessary struggle against the darts of the devil or of the vices, and with pastoral solicitude keep the lurking wolves away from the Lord's fold.
4.15: **“And it came to pass, when our enemies heard”** — In the spiritual building too, if we are clothed with apostolic arms, the counsel of the devil and his angels, who desire to overthrow us, will be scattered
4.16:
**“HALF”** — BEDE. It is to be noted that not only did half of the young men do the work and half stand ready for battle, but the same young men who did the work were girded with the sword. For so great is the cunning of the ancient enemy, so great the fury of his malice against the Church, that not only the preachers of the truth but the people of God itself ought always to keep watch against him and stand as it were in battle array. For the builders have their loins girded with the sword when those who preside take care to persist in good works or to order those committed to them by the rule of discipline; for this is fittingly to place living stones in the building of the holy city: [those] who strive to restrain in themselves the looseness of luxury with the edge of the word of God.
**“And it came to pass from that day forward, that half of their young men did the work, and half were ready for battle, with spears, and shields, and bows, and coats of mail, and the rulers were behind them in all the house of Juda.”** — Nor is it to be passed over that when David or Solomon built the same city, nothing is said of armed builders or attacking adversaries; but, destroyed for sins, it is rebuilt with greater labour and diligence. And like this is the spiritual building which is carried on in the salvation of souls: that, born again in baptism through faith and the confession of the holy Trinity, we are made without labour, by the grace of God, his city and house; and if afterwards, the devil persuading or seducing, we fall back into sins, and the victorious enemy casts down the walls of the virtues with the fire of vices, it is necessary to repair the buildings of good works with a heavier zeal of affliction, of vigils and of a stricter life. For we do without the allurements of vices more hardly once we have experienced them than when they are unknown; and it is less labour to beware of an unknown pleasure of the flesh than to reject a known one.
4.22: **“AND LET [THEM] BE TO YOU”** — BEDE. Note how great zeal they had in working, who persisted in labour even by night, like Paul, who worked night and day with his own hands, lest he should burden any of the believers by seeking food; unless perhaps they so succeeded one another by turns in working that some laboured by day in the work of the wall, others kept the watches of the night against the attacks of the enemies. For the builders of our city also do both at once. For those who build up the Church by instructing the faithful also drive away from the Church the unbelievers and gainsayers by refuting them.

5.1:
**“AND THERE AROSE”** — BEDE. The people desired to build the wall, but was hindered by famine, which not only the scarcity of crops but also the avarice of the princes had caused, which exacted from the same people greater tributes than it could pay. Which we see done daily among us. For many among the people of God desire to obey the divine commandments, but are held back by want of temporal things, by the example of those endowed with the habit of religion, when they themselves exact an unbearable tax of worldly things from those over whom they preside, and fulfil or contribute nothing to their salvation, either by word or example or work of piety. And would that some Nehemias, that is, a comforter coming from the Lord, might in our days restrain our manners, kindle our hearts to divine love, and, turning our hands from our own pleasures, turn them to building the city of Christ.
**“BEDE”** — For three reasons the cry of the people is increased. Some, forced by famine, wished to sell their sons to the richer; others, sparing their children, rather [to sell] their fields and houses. Some, forbidding the sale of children and fields, urged only this: that they should borrow money for the king's tributes, pledging their fields and vineyards, until, fruitfulness returning, they could repay to the lenders what they had received on loan.
5.7: **“AND I REBUKED”** — BEDE. As the best leader of the heavenly army and a wise architect of the city of God, he declared that he had first done himself what he wished the nobles and magistrates of the people to do: namely to give alms to the poor and to seek nothing from them except the keeping of the law and the building of the city. In this reading we need not seek allegory, but must diligently keep the text of the letter by doing it; namely that, besides the daily fruits of alms, when a general famine comes on, we give what we can to the needy, and remit the tributes which we were wont to exact from our subjects as by right, that the Father may forgive us our debts.
5.13: **“MOREOVER I SHOOK”** — To this sentence a terrible close is added. For whoever does not show mercy to the poor, or exacts as if justly from those who have not, is shaken out of his house, that is, out of the company of the Church, in which he thought he would remain for ever; and of his labours, that is, of the fruits of the good works in which he thought he had laboured laudably, he will receive nothing at all. For labours without piety could not be fruitful before God.

6.2: **“LET US MAKE [A LEAGUE]”** — BEDE. The enemies of the holy city persuaded Nehemias to come down into the plains and enter into a covenant of peace with them, calves being slain together in witness of the covenant agreed; but he, lest the religious work be neglected, perseveres in the mountains. So heretics and false catholics wish to have fellowship of peace with true catholics, not that they themselves may go up to the citadel of catholic faith and working, but rather that they may compel those whom they see dwelling on the summit of the virtues to come down to the lowest things of works or of wicked doctrines. And well do they wish to make a pact with Nehemias in one plain, because they desire all to be loosened accordingly into the same liberty of the broader life which they follow. Well do they wish to make the same pact with him with calves slain together, because false brethren long to offer to God the victims of their prayer or action together with true catholics, that, believed to be true faithful, they may through the victim of communion corrupt the true catholics. But Nehemias, holding the person of the faithful doctors, consents neither to come down to the profane nor to be defiled by their victims, but persists devoutly in the works of the virtues begun; and the more sharply they strive to terrify him, the more he becomes terrible to them by working well. Hence in what follows it is said: For all these thought to frighten us etc. Likewise therefore let us in the spiritual structure, because the cunning enemy always tries to hinder our hands, take care always to strengthen them with divine help.
6.10: **“AND I WENT IN”** — Assailed by the snares of the enemies, Nehemias enters the house of Semeias as of a friend and brother, but finds him himself a lier in wait and an enemy, as one corrupted by the gifts and friendship of foreigners. For the elect always have fightings without, fears within; and not only the apostles but the prophets too led a life full of suspicion, in perils from their own nation, in perils from the gentiles, in perils from false brethren.
6.15: **“OF THE MONTH OF ELUL”** — BEDE. Which according to the Hebrews is the sixth, and among the Romans is called September. And rightly is the wall of the holy city completed in the sixth month of the year, that by this time too the perfect action of the faithful, either of penance or of innocence, may be designated. For by the number six the perfection of good work is designated: either because God finished the creation of the world on the sixth day and rested on the seventh; or because he willed that we should toil in good works in the six ages of this world, but hope in the seventh, which is in the other life, for the sabbath of souls. Rightly too is it completed on the twenty-fifth day of the same month because of the five senses of the body, by whose ministry we ought to work good things outwardly. For as the simple five is wont to signify these senses, so, multiplied by itself and brought to twenty-five, it shows them with greater perfection. We finish therefore the walls of Jerusalem on the twenty-fifth of the sixth month when, all the senses of our body being diligently bound over to the divine ministries, we bring the pursuits of the virtues we have begun firmly to their end, and effectively complete, with God's help, whatever we have begun to do faithfully for the defence of the catholic peace. Well too are the walls said to have been completed in fifty-two days. For the fiftieth is the psalm of penance and remission, in which the prophet, praying for the building of this city, says: "Deal favourably, O Lord, in thy good will with Sion; that the walls of Jerusalem may be built up." On the fiftieth day of the Lord's resurrection the Holy Spirit came, through whom the devotion of repenting is given to us and pardon to the penitent. And there are two commandments of charity, namely the love of God and of neighbour, by which, the forgiveness of sins having been given us through the same Holy [Spirit], we are commanded to labour for eternal life. And therefore the citizens rebuilding the wall restore it in fifty-two days, because this is the perfection of the just in this life: that by repenting they chastise through the grace of divine inspiration what they have done amiss, and thenceforth adorn themselves with good works in the love of God and neighbour.
6.16: **“ALL THE NATIONS”** — BEDE. But those who wished to terrify the builders of the holy city, that they might hold them back from the work, fear when the construction is completed, and fall in spirit, knowing that that building had been begun and completed with God as its author. So in the Church, when the structure of the virtues has risen firm, the unclean spirits fear, and their temptation is repelled by our strength and turns to our victory. Heretics too and false catholics, by the constant faith of the good working through love, are either corrected and amended or, being exposed, are guarded against and expelled from the Church.

7.1:
**“Now after the wall was built, and I had set up the doors, and numbered the porters, and singing men,”**
• the singers are those who preach the sweetness of the heavenly homeland with pious voice
• NOW AFTER etc. Mystically. When the wall of the Church has been built, new peoples being gathered to the faith or those who had erred being corrected, the doors of regular discipline must at once be set up, lest the devil, who goes about as "a roaring lion", [should be able] to break into the fold of God.
**“I NUMBERED THE PORTERS”** — The porters, namely those who have received the keys of the kingdom of heaven, that they may receive the worthy and humble but keep the proud and unworthy from entering the city above, saying: "Thou hast no part nor lot in this matter. For thy heart is not right in the sight of God."
**“and Levites:”** — the Levites are those who always watch over the service of divine worship
7.3:
**“LET NOT THE GATES OF JERUSALEM BE OPENED TILL THE SUN BE HOT”** — That is, during the whole time of the night, lest either the enemy break in in the darkness, or some careless citizen going out be taken by the enemy and perish. Which the keepers of souls ought also to do, watching through the whole night of this world, lest, while they act negligently, the devil break in, troubling the band of the faithful, or snatch anyone to destroy him. But when the sun of justice appears and the light of the future blessedness shines forth, there will no longer be need of the bolts of continence, because no further means of attacking or tempting will be given to the adversaries, condemned with their prince to eternal vengeance; whence: "And the gates thereof shall not be shut by day: for there shall be no night there" etc.
**“AND I SET WATCHMEN”** — The keepers of souls are not to be appointed from the neophytes or from the common people, but from those who, freed by the grace of God from the struggle of vices, already have their mind in Jerusalem, that is, in the vision of tranquil peace, whose "conversation is in heaven".
**“And while they were yet standing by, the gates were shut, and barred: and I set watchmen of the inhabitants of Jerusalem, every one by their courses,”**
• For when some, their course finished, are taken from this light, others are at once put in their place, that there may never be lacking those who surround the peace of the Church by keeping watch because of fears in the night, according to that: "Instead of thy fathers, sons are born to thee."
• These things fit typically that time when, the word of God having been sown far and wide by the apostles, the whole world received the new shoot of faith, but the peoples were not yet built up in the Church, being still rude, imbued only with the hearing of the word and the sacraments. Therefore, gathering not only the nobles but also the common people, he carefully took care to number them, that, the sum of all being seen, he might decide who should dwell in Jerusalem, who in the other cities.
**“EVERY ONE”** — For so the keeping of the Church is perfected, if each so bears the solicitude of all the faithful as to bestow the care of more diligent zeal especially on those over whom, with God as author, he has been set.
7.73:
**“And the seventh month of the Scenopegia was come, under Esdras and Nehemias.”**
• Nehemias, namely, seeking to provide and arrange who should dwell in the city which he had built
• THE SEVENTH MONTH. BEDE. Which was not far off. For when the wall had been completed on the twenty-fifth day of the sixth month, only five days remained to the beginning of the seventh month, which from the first day to the twenty-second was wholly consecrated with lawful ceremonies; which being duly celebrated, he then returned with the princes and the people to arranging the dwellers of the city.

8.1:
**“And the children of Israel were in their cities. And all the people were gathered together as one man”** — with the same faith and love
**“AND [ALL THE PEOPLE] WERE GATHERED TOGETHER”** — BEDE. The devotion and concord of the people is to be noted: as one man, that is, with the same faith and love, they came together to the temple of God and asked the high priest to bring the book and unfold the commandments of the law which they should do, that, the city being built, the structure of work pleasing to God might also rise, lest, as before, the city should perish through neglect of religion. And well was the city built in the sixth month, and in the seventh the people gathered in it to hear the law. For six days in the law are for working, the seventh for resting; and this is our rest, acceptable to the Lord after good work: that, abstaining from servile work, that is, from sin, we give our effort to hearing and fulfilling his commandments. Hence at the beginning of the seventh month the solemnity of trumpets was appointed, by whose sound the people, amid prayers and victims, might be more ardently stirred to the memory of the law. Mystically, too, when the city has been built the divine reading must follow and the trumpets sound more frequently, that the people, initiated by the heavenly sacraments, may be instructed in due time more skilfully by the sacred words also how it ought to live.
**“BEFORE THE WATER GATE”** — BEDE. I think the water gate is spoken of in the court of the priests, by which the temple was surrounded on every side in a square, chiefly toward the eastern quarter of the temple, where was the brazen sea for washing the hands and feet of those entering the temple, where were the ten brazen lavers for washing the victims, where also was the altar of holocaust, between which and the temple Zacharias the son of Barachias was stoned. But the people had not leave to enter the gate of this court, but only the priests and ministers of the Lord. And the people were wont to stand outside this gate, and chiefly in the street which was on its eastern side, to hear or to pray. Well then was the people gathered before the water gate, as one to be given spiritually to drink of the streams of the Scriptures through its high priest.
8.4:
**“AND ESDRAS STOOD”** — Paralipomenon seems to make mention of this place, where it is said that "Solomon stood before the altar of the Lord in the presence of all the multitude of Israel, and stretched forth his hands. For Solomon had made a brazen scaffold, and had set it in the midst of the hall, five cubits long, and five cubits broad, and three cubits high: and he stood upon it." For by 'in the midst of the hall' he means in the midst of the court of the priests, by which the greater hall of the outer courts was surrounded on every side of the temple; of which it is written in the same book: "He made also the court of the priests, and a great hall" etc. But Solomon, as king, made a brazen scaffold; Esdras, as of lesser power, a step of wood; as Solomon or Moses made the altar of holocaust of brass, and the children of the transmigration of stone. But it is not to be thought that the step of wood has less of sacrament than the brazen scaffold. For as brass, for its long endurance or sweetness of sound, fits the divine sacraments, which fail by no length of ages [so the edition: 'sacramentorum'] and "their sound hath gone forth into all the earth", so wood fits the same because of the trophy of the Lord's passion.
**“And Esdras the scribe stood upon a step of wood”**
• AND ESDRAS STOOD etc. BEDE. The high priest stands on the step of wood which he made to speak from, when by singular imitation of the Lord's passion he makes himself higher than the rest. Hence rightly he preaches the word of God with confidence. For if he does not imitate the passion of the Lord, he has not yet ascended the step of wood from which he may stand above others. Hence it is necessary that, timid and blushing, he preach to others for doing what he himself has not done etc.
• When the prelates surpass their subjects as much in work as in honour, these, stirred by their examples, devoutly carry out the grade of their life, and, piously admonished by them, delight to shed tears for their sins or from desire of the heavenly homeland. Hence it is well added: For all the people wept etc.
8.5: **“And Esdras opened the book before all the people: for he was above all the people: and when he had opened it, all the people stood.”** — for he who receives the grade of doctor ought by the merit of perfection of life to surpass the action of the common people
8.10:
**“And he said to them: Go, eat fat meats, and drink sweet wine,”** — namely, the freedom of action divinely bestowed and the sweetness of hearing the word of God. For mulsum is wine sweetened with honey; whence in Greek too it is called oenomeli
**“GO AND EAT”** — He commands that we strengthen the weaker consciences of our neighbours by the example of pious action and the sweetness of devout admonition, that "their soul may be filled as with marrow and fatness, and they may praise the name of the Lord with joyful lips". According to the letter too, when on feast days, after prayer, reading and the exercise of the Psalms are completed, we refresh the flesh, we ought to remember the poor and the pilgrims.
**“BE NOT SAD”** — The doctors, who stir the minds of their hearers to tears with sacred readings, and likewise console them while they promise the joys that will follow.
8.11: **“FOR IT IS A HOLY DAY”** — While, namely, we give our effort to hearing and fulfilling the words of the Lord; on which day, though suffering adversities outwardly, we ought to rejoice in hope. Whence: "As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing" etc.
8.14:
**“And they found written in the law, that the Lord had commanded by the hand of Moses, that the children of Israel should dwell in tabernacles”**
• as sojourners and pilgrims upon the earth
• AND THEY FOUND etc. BEDE. These things are written more fully in Leviticus, and that they were commanded to be done in memory of the long journey, in which the Lord, leading the people out of Egypt, made them dwell in tabernacles for forty years through the desert, daily setting forth to them the precepts of the law through Moses. And the pitching of tabernacles, which in Greek is called scenopegia, was commanded to be done every year for seven days, that is, from the fifteenth day of the seventh month up to the twenty-second. We ought to search out the sacrament of this observance, since Christ deigned to be present at this festival and, addressing the people flocking together, dedicated it with sacred words. Our fathers too were freed from Egyptian bondage by the blood of the lamb and led through the desert forty years into the land of promise, when through the Lord's passion the world was freed from the service of the devil and the primitive Church was gathered by the apostles; which was led as it were through the desert forty years to the heavenly homeland, because, imitating the forty days' fast of Moses and Elias and of the Lord himself, it led a continent life, always thirsting for the eternal homeland, and, separated from all the allurements of the world, kept watch in daily meditation of the divine law. We too ought to dwell in tabernacles, going out of our dwellings, that is, leaving the pleasures of the world, to confess that we are pilgrims on earth and have our homeland in heaven, and to desire it with all our vows; and this on the feast day in the seventh month, that is, in the light of heavenly joy, the grace of the Holy Spirit, which is sevenfold, filling our heart. We are commanded to dwell in tabernacles seven days, because through all the time of this life, which runs in seven days, we must remember that we are sojourners on earth and pilgrims, as our fathers were.
**“on the feast,”** — namely, in the light of heavenly joy
**“in the seventh month:”** — full of the grace of the Holy Spirit
8.15:
**“and that they should proclaim and publish the word in all their cities, and in Jerusalem, saying: Go forth to the mount,”** — we too must go forth from a certain dwelling of general thoughts to meditate on the height of the Scriptures
**“and fetch branches of olive,”** — the fruits of mercy, by which, refreshing the poor, we may shade ourselves from the heat of vices
**“and branches of the most beautiful wood, branches of myrtle, and branches of palm, and branches of thick trees,”**
• that is, the ornaments of the other virtues
• OF THE MOST BEAUTIFUL WOOD etc. Which, namely, the Hebrews call cedar. And he brings himself branches of myrtle and a shade who can say: We are the good odour of Christ unto God in every place.
• BRANCHES OF THE MOST BEAUTIFUL WOOD AND BRANCHES OF MYRTLE etc. The fruits of charity, which is the most beautiful among all the virtues, through which Christ too ascended the wood of the cross for our salvation; whose passion, while we imitate it as far as we can, we are protected, as by a roof, with the branches of the most beautiful wood and of myrtle, in the mortifying of vices and lusts. For the magi, offering myrrh to the Lord, taught that they "that are Christ's have crucified their flesh, with the vices and concupiscences".
**“BRANCHES OF PALM”** — BEDE. We bring branches of palm, which is the adornment of the victorious hand, when we bear a mind victorious over vices and unconquered by all enemies, that "we may stand before the throne, and in sight of the Lamb, clothed with white robes, and palms in our hands".
**“to make tabernacles”** — of all these we make tabernacles when, delighted with good works, we draw the whole mind away from worldly allurements
8.16: **“EVERY MAN ON THE TOP OF HIS HOUSE”** — BEDE. On the top of his house, that is, on the roof of the houses; because in Palestine they have no ridges on their houses, but the tops of all the houses are level, with beams and boards laid over them. So each of us, going forth, makes tabernacles on the top, that is, on the roof of his house, when, rising in mind above the dwelling of his flesh, he tramples harmful affections by diligent meditation on the light and freedom above. We do the same in our courts when, with a mind burning for heavenly things, we stand as it were outside the world, whose dwelling we desire to leave the more speedily; and in the courts of the house of God, when, even though it is not yet granted to enter the hall of the dwelling above, we yet place the whole memory and seat of our thought in its neighbourhood; and in the street of the water gate, when, with enlarged heart in the way of God's commandments, "as the hart panteth after the fountains of water, so our soul panteth after the living God"; and in the street of the gate of Ephraim, that is, 'fruitful' or 'increasing', when we so advance in the breadth of a free heart that, the gate of justice being opened to us by the Lord, we may ever grow in him unto salvation and deserve to abound in the greater fruits of good action.
8.18:
**“And Esdras read in the book of the law of God day by day, from the first day till the last, and they kept the solemnity seven days, and in the eighth day”** — which signifies the gathering of the saints in the resurrection
**“SEVEN DAYS”** — BEDE. The Scenopegia was kept for seven days, that is, from the fifteenth moon of the seventh month up to the twenty-first; on the eighth day, that is, the twenty-second of the month, a gathering of the people was again held, distinguished by a greater festivity. Hence in Leviticus: "From the fifteenth day of the seventh month, when you shall have gathered in all the fruits of your land, you shall celebrate the feast seven days: on the first day and the eighth shall be a sabbath, that is, a rest" etc. Esdras therefore read to the people in the book of the law of God for the seven days of the Scenopegia, because this is the true solemnity of the mind: that day by day, that is, through all the good works with which we are enlightened by God, we give ourselves with attentive heart to reading, hearing and doing his words. And this solemnity begins on the fifteenth day of the month, when the moon is fullest by night, when, namely, all the darkness of our mind is dissolved by the most clear light of Christ; and there follows it the eighth day of the sabbath, that is, of rest, which will be in the time of the resurrection in the future life; by whose joy we are meanwhile lifted up in hope, [and] shall then enjoy in very reality, when the whole company of the saints, namely of angels and men, gathered in that longed-for assembly in the sight of God and never to be separated, shall exult.

9.1: **“AND IN THE DAY”** — BEDE. The devotion of the corrected people is to be noted. For the solemnity having been duly completed, with only one day between, they at once came together of their own accord in fasting and penance, that they might diligently do what they had heard was to be done, namely by separating themselves in mind and body from the fellowship of those who are strangers to the Lord, lest through their fellowship they should fall back into like evils, which they had hardly escaped after a long time. Let us therefore treat in mutual conversation among ourselves whatever we have learned is to be done in the public synaxis or hearing, and skilfully search out how we can fulfil each thing by chastisement of heart or body. And the diligence of the correction of life is chiefly proved when it is added: And they rose up to stand etc.
9.3: **“AND THEY ROSE UP”** — Who would not wonder that so great a people had so great a care of piety that four times in the day, that is, in the morning, at the third, sixth and ninth hour, at which they were to give themselves to prayer or psalmody, it gave itself to hearing the divine law, by which, its mind renewed toward God, it might return purer and more devout to beseeching his mercy; and in the night four times, shaking off the torpor of sleep, it rose to confess sins and ask pardon. Hence, as I think, a most beautiful custom has grown up in the Church: that at each of the hours of divine psalmody a reading from the Old and New Testament is said in the hearing of all, and so, strengthened by the apostolic and prophetic words, they bend their knees to earnest prayer; and in the night hours, when there is rest from other labours, ears are lent more freely to the divine readings.
9.6: **“AND ESDRAS SAID”** — Up to the end of his prayer or confession it is shown more fully, Esdras praying, how what was said above was done: that they confessed their sins and the sins of their fathers.
9.38: **“And for all this we ourselves make a covenant”** — WE MAKE A COVENANT. He shows with how great devotion all their persons made a new assembly after the feasts of the Scenopegia: namely that, purged with their whole intention from the contagion of crimes, they might join themselves to the divine covenant and confirm the condition of the holy covenant by word and writing, and so, separated from the fellowship of the impious, might more securely fill up the work which they had long since begun, that is, that they might set up fit citizens of the city from [those separated from] the number of the impious.

10.1: **“THE SUBSCRIBERS”** — Another translation: "Nehemias, who is called Athersatha." For he had two names. Hence it is added in the singular: The son of Hachelai; which is said more plainly above: "And Nehemias said, and he is Athersatha."
10.31:
**“And if the people of the land bring in things to sell, or any things for use, on the sabbath day to sell, we will not take it of them on the sabbath, or on the sanctified day. And we will leave the seventh year, and the exacting of every hand.”**
• ON THE SABBATH DAY. BEDE. We too must always keep a spiritual sabbath, always rest from servile work, that is, from sin, always be still and see that the Lord himself is God, that after such a sabbath of conscience, freed from sins, we may come to the sabbath of future glory. But the peoples of the land seek to profane our sabbath by bringing in things to sell on the sanctified day, since the unclean spirits strive to stain the cleanness of our heart and to thrust in the allurements of vices, the price of our consent being received, by which they may defile the day of greatest sanctification, that is, cloud the light of pious action or thought with errors. But we ought altogether to avoid trade of this kind, the walls of our city being shut, that is, by the guard of a more perfect life.
• All the things contained in this chapter belong to the care of the house of the Lord and its ministers and ministries; and it is the best order of religious life, and to be imitated by us spiritually. For first they cleansed themselves from the defilement of the nations; then they were sanctified by the observance of the sabbath, which stands out among the first things of the law; and for the rest they turn all the care of acting to the service of divine worship. For first it is necessary to be cleansed from evils, then to be adorned with good acts.

11.1:
**“And the princes of the people dwelt in Jerusalem: the nobles dwelt in the midst of the people without lot. But the rest of the people cast lots, to take one part in ten that should dwell in Jerusalem the holy city: the tenth part of the people is chosen to dwell in Jerusalem, because the city was empty, and nine parts in the cities.”**
• the lofty life of the elect, which we cannot follow by imitating, we ought to make ours by rejoicing with it and venerating it
• AND [THE PRINCES] DWELT. BEDE. Now the arrangement is completed which was begun as soon as the city was made, but could not be finished up to this time, the people not yet having been numbered nor the solemnities of the seventh month fulfilled: [namely] who should dwell in the holy city, who in the others. Mystically, the princes of the Church ought to surpass the people in the merits of life as much as they surpass them in height of power. For the other cities of Israel signify the devout life of the people; but the dwelling of the Jerusalemites signifies specially the acts of those who, the struggle of vices now overcome, draw near with free mind to the vision of the peace above; whence: "The Lord loveth the gates of Sion above all the tabernacles of Jacob." Hence too, accordingly, the tenth part of the people obtains by lot a dwelling in Jerusalem, while the other [nine of] ten remain in their cities; because it belongs to the perfect, that is, to those who keep the precepts of the decalogue entire in the love of God and neighbour, to draw near in mind to the heavenly secrets and to imitate the peace of the highest blessedness amid the whirlwinds of this passing life, while for those who keep the general commandments of God the door to eternal life lies open. For such dwell as it were in the cities delivered to them by the Lord, because they fortify themselves against the snares of the devil in the keeping of the divine law. But of those who wholly renounce the world and follow the Lord, [it is said that] they dwell as in the citadel of Jerusalem and near the temple and the ark of the Testament, because they draw nearer to the grace of the Creator. The whole people blesses, because the dwelling of the holy city fell to them not by the choice of human providence but by the outcome of the lot, as the possession of the other cities also was given to the children of Israel in the time of Josue; because both small and great receive small and great things not by the freedom or diligence of their own will but by the gift of the hidden Judge and Giver.
11.2:
**“And the people blessed all the men that willingly offered themselves to dwell in Jerusalem.”** — AND [THAT THEY MIGHT] DWELL IN JERUSALEM. BEDE. By these words it is shown that all Israel, that is, the ten tribes, dwelt in their cities, in which the priests and Levites also held the portion decreed to them by the law. But of the tribes of Juda and Benjamin, whomever the lot chose dwelt together in Jerusalem, and [some] of the priestly and Levitical tribe. For the tribe of Benjamin dwelt there of old; the tribe of Juda from the times of David, when he also made it the metropolis of the whole kingdom; to which tribes the tribe of Levi was also added from the time that the ark of God was brought there and the temple and altar built. For in what follows in this book you will find that he reckons the inhabitants of Jerusalem from these tribes only, of all of whom he also takes or adds the sum; and, their catalogue being finished, he adds in which cities the other part of the same ten tribes dwelt. For there follows: Of the children of Juda dwelt in Cariatharbe etc.
**“BEDE”** — Juda is interpreted 'confessing' or 'confession', Benjamin 'son of the right hand', Levi 'added' or 'taken up'; all of whose tribes dwell partly in Jerusalem, partly in the subject cities given them by God, because the advances of the faithful are many and divers, for which there are also many mansions in heaven. Some are content to keep the general commandments of God, namely not to kill, not to commit adultery, not to steal, and the like. Others strive to lay hold of the citadel of the perfect life; but each according to his calling praises and confesses the grace of his Creator, and they are sons of the kingdom which is at the right hand of God, and are taken up by him into life. "Of those who are in the field, one shall be taken, and one shall be left."
11.30:
**“Zonoa, Odollam, and in their villages, in Lachis and its precincts, and Azecha and its villages. And they dwelt in Bersabee”** — which is on the southern side, namely the border of the tribe of Juda
**“unto the valley of Ennom.”** — which is the border of Juda to the north, by Jerusalem on the east
11.36: **“And of the Levites, divisions of Juda and of Benjamin.”** — and it signifies that the Levites received their lot in the possession of the children of Juda and Benjamin according to the decree of the law

12.1: **“Now these are the priests and the Levites that went up with Zorobabel the son of Salathiel:”** — NOW THESE ARE etc. BEDE. Here are described the chiefs of the priests together with their brethren, that is, the lesser priests and Levites, who went up from the Babylonian captivity with Zorobabel and Jesus the son of Josedec; and when these are set out, those also are added who from then on succeeded one another in the chiefship of the priests up to the beginning of the reign of the Macedonians. For there follows: Josue begot Joacim etc. And Jeddoa, who is put last among these, Josephus writes was chief of the priests in the time of Alexander the Great, and, going to meet him with his brethren, was received humbly and honourably; whom he himself names Jaddus and says was the father of Onias the high priest, of whom it is written in the Book of Machabees. Not that Nehemias, the author of this Book, could have lived in the flesh up to those times, but because he knew the infancy of him who long after his death came to the priesthood. For at the end of this book mention is made of the sons of Joiada the son of Eliasib [so the edition: 'filii Eli ab'], that one of them was son-in-law of Sanaballath the Horonite; whose son-in-law's name is indeed passed over in silence, but because Joiada is the grandfather of Jeddoa, it is clear that the son-in-law of whom the word is was the father or the uncle of the same Jeddoa, and therefore that he could have been born while Nehemias was still living.
12.7: **“Adaia. These were the chiefs of the priests, and their brethren, in the days of Josue.”** — IN THE DAYS etc. BEDE. The succession of the chiefs of the priests and Levites who were at that time is described, that we may know that, a copious number of citizens having been gathered in Jerusalem, there was an excellent company of priests and Levites who would be sufficient for the ministry of the temple and the altar, for confessing and praising God, for the guarding of the same temple and city, and for instructing the people. Nor was it done without the understanding of a more sacred mystery that the rebuilt city deserved so great a number of citizens in every grade and order as it is not read to have lost. For so the Church often receives greater increase from losses, when, one having fallen into sin through carelessness, more, terrified by his example, become more cautious to persist in the chastity of faith. Often the same who have sinned, after doing penance, bear greater fruits of good works; often the Church, laid waste by heretics, after it has recovered the light of truth through the earnestness of catholic doctors, has begotten more sons to know and defend the reason of truth. For Athanasius, Ambrose, Hilary, Augustine and the others such would never have composed so many and such magnificent treatises if the manifold error of the heretics had not arisen against the right faith. But while the heretics strove to build up a lie with the testimonies of the Scriptures, the fathers were compelled to refute them by the authority of the same Scriptures and to set forth how they are rightly to be understood. Hence we, reading their writings, receive as it were more watchful keepers at the gates and porches of the city and temple, as it were more abundant ministers for the office of the altar and of the Lord's victims; because by their discourses we are instructed for the keeping of faith and good action and for serving more intently in the sight of the divine majesty.
