For Aman, because he had not a garment worthy of the feast, deserved to be cast out.
7.7: **“went … into the garden set with trees”** — As the king hastens into the garden, that is, invites the elect with him to the delights of paradise, he strives to entreat the queen for his life, but had not a fitting time. For the remedies of salvation are sought too late when the dangers of death are at hand. Whence Solomon: “Then shall they call upon me, and I will not hear: they shall rise in the morning, and shall not find me.”
7.8:
**“And when the king came back out of the garden set with trees, and entered into the place of the banquet, he found Aman was fallen upon the bed on which Esther lay, and he said: He will force the queen also in my presence, in my own house. The word was not yet gone out of the king’s mouth, and immediately they covered his face”** — confusion and shame, according to that: “Let them be clothed with confusion and shame, that desire evils to me”
**“and immediately they covered”** — Aman’s entreaty is called forcing, because in the day of judgement the prayer of the wicked is provocation. Whence: “When he is judged, may he go out condemned; and may his prayer be turned to sin.” Then the oppression with which they oppressed the humble will be cast in their teeth.
7.9:
**“Harbona”** — He signifies the teachers of the law, who foretold the crimes and deceits of the Jews. Whence Moses: “I know that after my death you will do wickedly, and will quickly turn aside from the way that I have commanded you.” And in the gospel: “There is one that accuseth you, Moses, in whom you trust.”
**“one of the eunuchs that stood waiting on the king, said: Behold the gibbet which he hath prepared for Mardochai”** — “He that diggeth a pit, shall fall into it: and he that rolleth a stone, it shall return to him”
**“in Aman’s house”** — Aman signifies the wicked raging against Christ and persecuting his Church. But Christ had been promised to them in the law; so the law, which was given for the keeping of life, was turned for them into death, by which they strove to blot out Christ and kill his confessors; and those who wished to oppress the innocent by the law received, with the law itself accusing them, the sentence of just judgement: “Whosoever have sinned in the law, shall be judged by the law.”
**“being fifty cubits high”** — on the fiftieth day after the sacrifice of the lamb the law was given on mount Sina
7.10: **“So Aman was hanged on the gibbet”** — “His sorrow shall be turned on his own head”, etc.

8.1:
**“On that day”** — On that day. Esther holds the house of Aman, the enemy of the Jews, when the Church possesses the world which the devil, the enemy of Christians, had possessed. Whence: “When a strong man armed keepeth his court”, etc. Mardochai comes in before the face of the king when daily the souls of the saints go in from their sojourn in this present life to the contemplation of the divine majesty.
**“king Assuerus gave”** — the true king
**“to queen Esther”** — to the Church
**“the house of Aman”** — The dignity and honour which the Jews had by their knowledge of the law and the prophets and by the worship of religion. Whence in Proverbs: “The substance of the sinner is kept for the just.” And in the gospel: “The kingdom of God shall be taken from you, and shall be given to a nation yielding the fruits thereof.”
**“the Jews’ enemy, and Mardochai came in before the king. For Esther had confessed to him that he was her uncle”** — spiritual father
8.2:
**“And the king took the ring”** — the seal of faith, which they would not receive
**“And the king took”** — By the earnestness of the masters in praising and preaching, they receive from the Lord “grace for grace” in the sight of the Creator of all, whence he has nourished the hearts of the faithful.
**“which … from Aman”** — from the Jews and the persecutors of the faith
**“he had commanded to be taken again … and gave it to Mardochai”** — as it is said of the Jews, so it can be taken generally of all the persecutors of the Church
**“gave it to Mardochai”** — To the preachers of the gentiles, that they might hold fast to him and minister to the gentiles.
**“And Esther”** — the Church
**“set Mardochai”** — the preachers
**“over her house”** — to keep
8.3: **“she fell down at the king’s feet”** — Because holy Church daily entreats almighty God, through faith and the mysteries of the incarnation, for the deliverance of her children, that the boldness of the enemies may be crushed and the innocence of the faithful set free.
8.4: **“But he, as the manner was, held out the golden sceptre with his hand, which was the sign of clemency”** — he bestows the clemency of his goodness
8.5:
**“And said: If it please the king, and if I have found favour in his sight, and my request be not disagreeable to him, I beseech thee, that … by new letters”**
• by the teachings of the gospel
• I beseech, etc. Because the doctrine of the gospel, which is preached in the name of Christ in the whole world, is declared to be confirmed with the seal of the Holy Ghost; filled with whose gift the preachers themselves remained unconquerable and glorious triumphers over their enemies.
**“the former”** — all the sects of old errors
**“letters of Aman the traitor and enemy of the Jews”** — of the old enemy
8.9:
**“Then the king’s scribes and secretaries were called for”** — Then the scribes, etc. Because the teaching of the gospel was so set down by the writers of the new Testament, the Lord mediating, that the faith of the holy Trinity was most fully contained in it, and the whole perfection of the decalogue shown in the two precepts of charity.
**“now it was the time of the third month which is called Siban”** — which among the Hebrews is called Siban, among the Greeks Theen, among the Latins May
**“the three and twentieth day of the month, and letters were written, as Mardochai had a mind, to the Jews, and to the governors, and to the deputies, and to the judges, who were rulers over the hundred and twenty-seven provinces, from India even to Ethiopia”** — Who … the hundred, etc. By these the whole world is signified. For the number ten multiplied by twelve makes a hundred and twenty, and the number seven joined to them completes the fulness of the whole sum. So the keeping of the decalogue, spread through the whole world by the tradition of the apostles, is poured into the hearts of the faithful, or is made perfect, by the grace of the sevenfold Spirit.
**“to province and province, to people and people, according to their languages and characters, and to the Jews, according as they could read and hear”** — for the first teachers spoke in these tongues; whence: “We have heard them speak in divers tongues the wonderful works of God”
8.10: **“And these letters which were sent in the king’s name, were sealed with his ring, and sent by posts”** — the preachers, runners of the highest king
8.11:
**“to them”** — to the preachers
**“the king gave orders”** — of heaven and earth
**“to speak to the Jews”** — bringing them into the unity of the faith, in the spirit, not the flesh
**“in every city, and to command them to gather themselves together”** — “The multitude of believers had but one heart and one soul”
**“and to stand”** — strong in faith
**“for their lives”** — to be saved
**“and … all their enemies”** — the Jews who are in the synagogue of Satan, pagans, heretics, demons
**“with their wives”** — their pleasures
**“and children”** — works
**“and all their houses … to kill and destroy”** — worldly ambition
**“to kill”** — Lest the shoots of an evil seed should sprout again. In like manner the Lord commanded the seven nations which dwelt in the land of promise to be killed, and afterwards the Amalecites to be utterly destroyed, that he might take away from them every occasion of stumbling. Whence David says: “In the morning I put to death all the wicked of the land”, etc.
8.12:
**“And one day of revenge was appointed through all the provinces, to wit, the thirteenth”** — which signifies faith in the Trinity with the keeping of the ten commandments
**“of the twelfth month Adar”**
• that is, the month of March
• of the last age of the world; whence: “Upon whom the ends of the world are come”
8.13:
**“And this was the content of the letter, that … in all lands and peoples that were subject to the empire of king”** — heavenly
**“Assuerus”** — “O Lord, all things are in thy power, and there is none that can resist thy will”
8.14:
**“So the swift posts went out carrying the messages, and the king’s edict”** — heavenly
**“was hung up in Susan”** — on high, spurning the pride of the world
**“in Susan”** — For the overthrowing of the pride of the world. For Susan is interpreted riding, or overturning. Whence the Saviour says: “Have confidence, I have overcome the world.”
8.15:
**“And Mardochai … out of the palace, and from the king’s presence”** — from contemplation to action
**“going forth … shone in royal apparel”** — given by the king above
**“to wit, of violet”** — because they await heavenly grace
**“and sky colour”** — or, of wild beasts
**“wearing a golden crown”** — of the eternal dignity which they gain through wisdom
**“on his head”** — in mind
**“and clothed with a cloak of silk and purple”** — the royal dignity which they merited, purpled with blood
**“And all the city”** — “Glorious things are said of thee, O city of God”
**“rejoiced”** — in action
**“and was glad”** — in contemplation
8.16:
**“to the Jews”** — true
**“But … a new light”**
• of gladness
• the knowledge of the faith
**“seemed to rise”** — to the eyes of the mind
**“joy”** — within themselves
**“honour”** — among others
**“and dancing”** — solemnities
8.17:

9.1:
**“So … of the twelfth month”** — when the Son of God was incarnate and the preaching of the gospel was spread through the whole world
**“which as we have said above is called Adar … on the thirteenth day”** — when the Church is made known by the light of faith and of good works through the preaching of the gospel
**“when all the Jews”**

**“and their enemies were greedy after”** — or: lay in wait for

**“And they gathered themselves together”** — in the unity of the faith

**“and town”** — the suburbs
**“and place”** — of the hermits, or their hiding places

**“And no one”** — of the enemies

9.3:
**“And the judges of the provinces, and the governors, and lieutenants”** — “And all kings of the earth shall adore him”, etc.

9.4:
**“For they knew him to be prince of the palace, and to have great power”** — by signs and wonders

**“and was spread abroad through all men’s mouths”** — And to have great power. Because the praiseworthy action of the teachers and the power of their miracles gave honour and reverence to the multitude of the faithful. Whence in the Acts of the apostles: “Many wonders also and signs were done”, etc. Whence it is read elsewhere: “And fear came upon every soul.” Again: “No man durst join himself unto them; but the people magnified them.”
9.5:
**“So the Jews made a great slaughter of their enemies”** — spiritual
**“So the Jews made a great slaughter”** — So the Jews made a great slaughter. Not only does he judge, by the divine sentence of the Holy Ghost, that the other workers of iniquity, who persevere in their sins and care not to receive the remission of sins, are to be damned; but also that the carnal Jews, transgressors of the decalogue, will feel in the torments of hell the guilt of the cross of Christ which they contracted by their unbelief.
**“and killed them, repaying according to what they had prepared to do to them”** — so that some, converted to good, ceased to be what they had been, and the obstinate perished
9.6: **“whose names are these”** — We do not search out the interpretations of these names with much labour, nor force them to serve allegory. For the type lies in a part, not in the whole. If the type were in the whole, it would not be history. The historian must set out the true order of the thing done, neither stopping short nor going beyond; the allegorical interpreter must choose the striking parts that fit the spiritual sense.
9.10: **“And when they had slain them, they would not touch the spoils of their goods”** — none of the elect deigns to imitate the wickedness or the acts of the wicked
9.12:
**“And he said to the queen: The Jews have killed five hundred men in the city of Susan”** — who care not for the remission of the Holy Ghost
**“besides the ten sons of Aman”** — the carnal Jews, transgressors of the decalogue, to be tormented for the crucifixion of Christ
**“how many dost thou think they have slain in all the provinces?”** — who wrought so great a slaughter in Susan
9.13:
**“And she answered”** — And she answered, etc. Esther, who strives with such constancy to root out her enemies, expresses the zeal and skill of the Church, which pursues her enemies with a peaceable mind and endeavours without end to subject them to God. Whence: “I will pursue after my enemies, and overtake them”, etc. First she kills five hundred men, then three hundred: that is, she shows that those who care not to receive the remission of their sin, and those who do not honour the faith of the holy Trinity with good works, are worthy of everlasting death.
**“If it please the king”** — “thy will be done”, not mine
**“let it be granted to the Jews”** — Abraham says the like: “Seeing I have once begun, I will speak to my Lord”
9.15: **“And on the fourteenth day of the month Adar the Jews gathered themselves together, and they killed in Susan three hundred men: but they took not their substance”** — of vices
9.16:
**“Moreover through all the provinces which were subject to the king’s dominion the Jews stood for their lives, and slew their enemies and persecutors: insomuch that the number of them that were killed amounted to seventy-five thousand, and no man took any of their goods”**
• by false teaching or wicked working
• Insomuch, etc. All who receive the law carnally with the five bodily senses, and refuse to understand it spiritually, though through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Ghost it is especially full and perfect, are overcome and laid low as in two days.
9.17:
**“Now the thirteenth day of the month Adar”** — Now the thirteenth day, etc. Note that some of the Jews kill on the thirteenth day and leave off on the fourteenth and keep the solemnity; some kill for two days, that is, the thirteenth and fourteenth day of the same month, and rest solemnly on the fifteenth. For some of the saints, after finishing the labours by which they serve God by believing well and living well, now, before the time of judgement, have in their souls the sabbath of everlasting rest. Others, lasting on in the flesh until the last day of the resurrection, having overcome all their enemies and being suddenly changed, receive the rest of souls and bodies. Whence the Apostle: “The dead who are in Christ, shall rise first. Then we who are alive, who are left, shall be taken up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ, into the air”, etc. For the fourteenth, which contains twice seven, signifies the perfect rest of souls; but the fifteenth, embracing seven and eight, signifies the rest of souls and bodies.
**“was the first day with them all of the slaughter, and on the fourteenth day”** — which signifies the perfect rest of souls
**“they left off”** — to labour against one another, the victory being won
**“Which they ordained to be kept holy day”** — because “nor mourning, nor crying, nor sorrow shall be any more”, etc.
**“so that all times hereafter they should celebrate it with feasting, joy, and banquets”** — the heavenly refreshment; whence: “With the voice of joy and praise; the noise of one feasting”
9.18:
**“But they that were killing in the city of Susan”** — as it were lasting on and striving, and while living awaiting eternal life
**“were employed in the slaughter on the thirteenth and fourteenth day of the same month”** — of spiritual and bodily enemies
**“and on the fifteenth day they rested”** — which signifies the rest of body and soul. For seven signifies the sabbath, that is, the rest of souls; and eight the resurrection, rest and immortality of bodies
**“And therefore they appointed that day to be a holy day of feasting”** — because “nor mourning … shall be any more”
**“and gladness”** — “Thou shalt make them drink of the torrent of thy pleasure”
9.19: **“But those Jews that dwelt in towns not walled and in villages, appointed the fourteenth day of the month Adar for banquets and gladness, so as to rejoice on that day, and send one another portions of their banquets and meats”** — because charity makes all things common, and what was each one’s was all men’s
9.20:
**“And Mardochai wrote all these things”** — that is, he commended in writing these things to be believed, and the commandments or the things to come
**“and sent them comprised in letters to the Jews that abode in all the king’s provinces, both those that lay near”** — the Jewish people
**“and those afar off”** — the gentiles
9.21:
**“That they should receive the fourteenth and fifteenth day of the month Adar for holy days”** — that they should believe they were to be received
**“and always at the return of the year should celebrate them with solemn honour”** — lest the solemnity to come be blotted out by any forgetfulness
9.22:
**“Because on those days the Jews revenged themselves”** — they were revenged, God taking vengeance
**“of their enemies, and their mourning and sorrow … into mirth”** — “Your sorrow shall be turned into joy”
**“and joy”**
• “They went from the presence of the council, rejoicing”
• “For we are saved by hope”
**“were turned … and that these should be”** — in hope
**“days of feasting and gladness”** — “A certain man made a great supper, and invited many”
**“and”** — meanwhile
**“they should send one to another portions of meats”** — for the awaiting of the common resurrection and refreshment
**“and … gifts to the poor”** — communicating to the necessities of the saints
**“should give”** — willingly, “not with sadness, or of necessity”, but with a generous mind
9.23: **“And the Jews undertook to observe with solemnity all they had begun to do at that time, which Mardochai”** — the order of preachers
9.24:
**“Aman”** — the enemy of the Church
**“the son of Amadathi of the race of Agag, the enemy”** — in will
**“and adversary”** — in deed
**“of the Jews”** — of the true

9.25:
**“And afterwards Esther went in to the king, beseeching him that his endeavours might be made void by the king’s letters: and the evil that he had intended against the Jews, might return upon his own head”** — “The unjust shall be caught in their own snares”
**“And so both he and his sons were hanged upon gibbets”** — that is, they foretold that they would be tormented through the cross of Christ
9.28:
**“These are the days”** — Because the rest of souls and the resurrection of bodies is rightly kept firmly and celebrated by the faithful. Or because the holiday of the rest of souls and of the resurrection of bodies is rightly kept and celebrated by the faithful.
**“throughout all generations”** — the successions of the times
**“all”**
• or: many
• throughout all generations
**“provinces in the whole world”** — of the Church
**“shall celebrate”** — foreshowing the festival to come

• their successors
• their imitators

9.29:
**“wrote”** — admonishing

9.32: **“And all things which are contained in the history of this book”** — of the divine Testaments

10.1:
**“And king Assuerus made all the land, and all the islands of the sea”** — the islands: “The kings of Tharsis and the islands shall offer presents”
**“tributary”**
• whence: “Render to God the things that are God’s, and to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s”
• And king Assuerus. Christ, who, cut out of the mountain without hands, grew into a great mountain and filled the whole world. For in the history he did not make all the land tributary, since he did not even have it.
10.2:
**“And his strength and his empire, and the dignity and greatness wherewith he exalted”** — before the faithful and the unfaithful
**“Mardochai”** — the order of preachers

10.3:
**“And how Mardochai”** — a true Jew, not openly in the flesh but inwardly in the spirit
**“of the race of the Jews, was next after king Assuerus: and great among the Jews, and acceptable”** — pleasing and accepted
**“to the people of his brethren”** — the Christians
**“seeking the good”** — eternal
**“of his people”** — whom he rules
**“and speaking those things which were for the welfare”** — in this world and the world to come: “how beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace, of them that bring glad tidings of good things!” And elsewhere: “Pray ye for the things that are for the peace of Jerusalem.”
**“of his seed”** — of his spiritual children

1.1:
**“There was a man”** — as if to say: good among the wicked
**“in the land of Hus, whose name was Job,”**
• in the land of the gentiles, to the praise of Job, who was good among the wicked, as Lot in Sodom: “As the lily among thorns, so is my love among the daughters”
• Allegorically. Job, ‘grieving’, that is, Christ, who carried our sorrows. Hus, ‘counsellor’. So he dwells in the land of Hus, that is, in hearts given to the counsels of life. Whence: “I wisdom dwell in counsel.” Simple and upright: we forsake gentleness for justice, and justice for gentleness; but Christ as man kept both fully, fearing God. Whence: “And he shall be filled with the spirit of the fear of the Lord.” He also avoided evil, not that by doing it he touched it, but that finding it in the world he condemned it. Seven sons: by this number perfection is signified. The sons, the strong apostles; the daughters, the weak faithful; or those who hold the faith of the Trinity; or, after the strong apostles, three daughters, that is, the three orders of the faithful in the Church, pastors, the continent and the married, that is, Noe, Daniel and Job. What is said generally of the daughters is said distinctly of the animals. Seven thousand sheep: the perfect innocence of those who came to grace from the pastures of the law. Three thousand camels: the whole gentile world coming to the fulness of faith; or the Samaritans, who chew the cud in that they receive the law in part, but do not divide the hoof, because in part they despise it; and of these the Lord brought many to faith, as he did the Hebrews. The oxen: workers of the faith. The asses: the simplicity of the gentiles, on which the Lord sits as he goes to Jerusalem, that is, leading them to the vision of peace. Of both it is said: “The ox knoweth” (that is, the Jew, pressed by the yoke of the law) “his owner” (that is, God, whom he worshipped but did not know), “and the ass” (that is, the brutish gentile, driven where the seducer willed) “his master’s crib” (that is, the fodder of the law). So what he said above of the sheep and camels he repeats in the oxen and asses. Five hundred: this number is made of fifty taken ten times; fifty signifies rest, ten perfection; because to the faithful of both peoples the perfection of rest is promised.
• Allegorically. The household is put after the animals, because first he chose the foolish things of the world, so that not eloquence but the cause itself might persuade to the faith; afterwards the shrewd too were gathered in.
**“There was a man in the land of Hus”** — Morally. By Job is meant Christ, that is, the head and the body; so after the history, having seen from the head what we are to believe, let us see from the body what we are to hold in living. Job in the land of Hus, that is, ‘grieving’ in ‘counsel’: he who does not consider the things above exults in these things as though they were good; but he who attends to the eternal things he has lost grieves, and finds counsel to despise these; and the more the knowledge of counsel grows to forsake these, the more grows the grief that he does not yet reach the eternal. Whence Solomon: “he that addeth knowledge, addeth also labour,” because he who knows the highest things which he does not have grieves the more over these lowest. But he who seeks the eternal is simple in work, not double like one who seeks praise from good deeds. Whence Isaias: “Woe to the sinner that goeth on the earth two ways,” as when the work is God’s and the intention the world’s. Upright in faith in the highest things which he perceives within; this he begins from fear but completes by charity. Whence: “fearing God and avoiding evil”: when charity follows fear, he fully avoids evil who out of love of God begins to be unwilling to sin, not he who does so from fear. For he sins in what he would do if he could do it unpunished; because by fear vice is held down, by charity the virtues spring up. Whence he adds: “And there were born sons.” When the Spirit makes the mind fruitful, seven virtues are born in it: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, the fear of God. But these sons have three sisters, when whatever they do they join to faith, hope and charity, without which one does not come to the perfection of ten. These virtues are followed by every kind of thought of good works. Whence he adds: “And his possession was.” We possess seven thousand sheep when we feed our innocent thoughts within us, in perfect purity of heart, with the pasture of truth sought out. We possess three thousand camels when whatever is lofty and crooked in us we bow down to humility under the knowledge of the Trinity, so that bearing one another’s burdens we may have compassion on our brother’s weakness. Or the camels are the good management of earthly things, in which there is something of God and something of the world, though done for eternal things; yet they are not without disturbance of the mind. With the head, by chewing the cud, they agree with the law, because by managing these well they seek heavenly things; with their feet they creep, because what they do is of the world; they do not divide the hoof, because they do not lift themselves wholly from earthly things. So when we subject our earthly occupations to the knowledge of the Trinity, we possess camels, as it were, by faith. The yoke of oxen: virtues in concord, ploughing up the hardness of the heart. We possess she asses when we hold down wanton motions, or when within us we govern simple thoughts, which are slow and do not run among subtler things, but bear the brothers’ burdens the more gently, and humble themselves to outward works; of both there are five hundred. For whether in what we wisely understand or in what we humbly do not know, while we seek eternal rest we are held within the number of the jubilee.
**“and that man was simple and upright”** — Simple and upright and fearing God, etc. The person is described as fit before his battle is told, so that such a man may be seen able to conquer.
**“simple”** — Simple: the simplicity of the dove must be instructed by the wisdom of the serpent, and the serpent’s wisdom tempered by simplicity. Hence the Spirit appeared in a dove and in fire, because those who are full of him so serve the gentleness of simplicity that they are kindled against evils by the zeal of uprightness.
**“and fearing God”**
• to fear God is to pass over nothing that ought to be done
• The animals are called legal, that is, clean according to the law, which both chew the cud and divide the hoof; the camels have the one but lack the other, and so they agree with the law and disagree. The mystery is understood here insofar as through Job we are instructed in faith as to what Christ was to be; the moral sense, insofar as through Job it is foreshown what every believer ought to be.
**“fearing God”** — Fearing God: Solomon: “he that feareth God, neglecteth nothing.” Avoiding evil: Solomon again: “he that shall offend in one, shall lose many good things.”
**“and avoiding evil.”** — because good things mixed with evils are not acceptable to God; for he neither did evil nor consented to evil
1.2:
**“And there were born to him seven sons”** — by seven he signified the whole
**“and three daughters”**
• how great he was, who possessed so much without love of it, as was plain when he lost so much without grief
• how good he was, who did not greedily heap up for so many heirs
1.3:
**“And his possession was”** — first he set out the riches of the heart, then the wealth of the body, which usually draws the mind in different directions; whence riches are said to choke the word of God; but this man, though so occupied, gave himself to divine sacrifices
**“seven thousand sheep, and three thousand camels, and five hundred yoke of oxen, and five hundred she asses, and a family exceeding great:”** — which might have made him more sparing
**“a family exceeding great”** — A family exceeding great: the countless crowd of thoughts, which, like maidservants when the mistress, that is, reason, is away, leave their work and make a din; but when she returns they work in silence. If we rule these well, the mind is not overcome by their number.
**“and this man was great among all the people of the east.”**
• that is, richer than the rich, for the people of the east are known to be very rich
• The people of the east are all who are in Christ by faith, of whom the prophet says: “the Orient is his name”; all these the God-man surpasses.
**“among all the people of the east”** — Among all the people of the east: that is, among the angels who cleave to the light of the east; we are great when we are their companions.
1.4:
**“And his sons went”** — Allegorically. His sons went: that is, the apostles throughout the world, serving the banquets of the word of God, each in his day, that is, according to the measure of his enlightened understanding. The sisters, that is, the weaker, are refreshed by Scripture, which in its obscure places is food, broken by exposition, and in its plain places is drink, swallowed as it is.
**“and made a feast”**
• great wealth breeds discord among brothers; but the father so trained them that, though they would divide their father’s goods, they were of one mind
• Morally. The sons make feasts, because each virtue feeds the mind after its own manner. In his day, because each virtue has its own enlightenment: wisdom has one day, understanding another, and so the rest. Many have a taste of eternal things but cannot understand them. Wisdom therefore feeds in its day when it refreshes the mind with the hope and certainty of eternal things; understanding in its day, when it enlightens the heart about what it has heard; counsel in its day, when it fills the reason and forbids it to be headlong; fortitude in its day, when it gives the fearful confidence against adversity; knowledge drives out ignorance; piety teaches works of mercy; the fear of the Lord holds the mind down lest it be proud of present things, and strengthens it with the hope of things to come. They feed one another, because one supports another, and without that each is badly destitute. Wisdom is less if it lacks understanding; understanding is useless without wisdom, for if without it it penetrates higher things, its own lightness lifts it up to fall more heavily. Counsel is worthless without fortitude, because what it finds by deliberation it cannot bring to act without strength. Fortitude, which can do more, rushes headlong without the restraint of reason. Knowledge is nothing without piety, because he who does not carry out the good he knows is judged more heavily. Piety without the discernment of knowledge does not know how to have mercy. Fear without the others avails nothing, because, trembling at everything, it is numb to good works.
• The three sisters, that is, faith, hope and charity, the virtues call into all that they do, that they may rejoice in it; they gain strength as from food when they become more confident through good works; they are inebriated as with drink after food when they long to be steeped in the dew of contemplation. But from these very goods evils also arise, such as pride, or when the mind takes delight in them; and a certain security comes too, and from it torpor. So he adds: “And when the days were gone about.” To sanctify the sons when the feast is over is, after the exercise of the virtues, to direct the intention of the heart, and to cleanse all that is done by strict reconsideration, lest one be deceived by the quality of evil, so that things which are evil are thought good; or by the quantity of good, so that it is believed sufficient when it is not perfect. But this he finds better by praying than by examining; for the mind raised up by compunction judges more surely everything beneath it. Whence he says: “And rising up early.” He rises early who, flooded with the light of compunction, leaves the human night and opens his eyes to the true light. He offers for each when he offers prayers to God for each virtue: lest wisdom exalt, lest understanding stray, lest counsel confuse by multiplying itself, lest fortitude through confidence throw headlong, lest knowledge puff up, lest piety turn aside from what is right, lest fear, trembling more than is just, despair.
**“by houses every one”** — Mystically, by houses: as Peter through Rome, Philip in Samaria. In his day, that is, according to the measure of his understanding; for Paul taught in one way among the Greeks, Peter in another among the Romans, though they did not disagree in faith.
1.5:
**“And when … were gone about”**
• Allegorically. And when … were gone about: the days of the feast go about when the mysteries of the preaching are completed; when all is done, Job offers for his sons, because Christ prayed to the Father for the apostles returning from preaching, and by sending the Holy Spirit sanctified them, cleansing whatever fault could be in them.
• He rises early to offer, because as he prays for them he scatters the night and enlightens their minds, lest they be defiled in secret by any taint of sin from their preaching by ascribing it to themselves. Whence he adds: “Lest perhaps my sons have sinned, and have blessed,” that is, cursed, “God.” To curse God is to give oneself glory for his gift. Hence also after the preaching the Lord washed the apostles’ feet, because in a good work the dust of sin is gathered, such as inward pride, which the Lord wipes away. “Perhaps” is said, not that he does not know all things, but from our doubting, as: “shall he find, think you, faith on earth?” “So did Job all days,” because he always offers for us, while he shows the Father on our behalf his incarnation, by which he washes away sins.
• When the days of the feast were gone about: because after the seven brothers had finished their feasts, Job is said to offer seven sacrifices. For it is plain that he does this on the eighth day, on which one full of the sevenfold Spirit is shown serving the Lord in hope of the resurrection.
**“the days of their feasting were gone about, Job sent to them”** — what he would do when present, when even absent his care is not lacking
**“and sanctified them:”** — because he knows that feasts can hardly be held without fault, for pleasure and talkativeness almost always attend banquets
**“and rising up early offered holocausts for every one of them.”**
• that is, seven sacrifices
• Offered holocausts: a holocaust means wholly burnt; that is when the whole mind is kindled with the fire of compunction on the altar of love, and burns up the defilements of thought as of its offspring; which none knows how to do but he who, before thought passes into deed, bridles his inner motions, and guards his mind with a manly watch, not a womanish one like Isboseth’s. Whence Solomon: “With all watchfulness keep thy heart, because life issueth out from it.” For the virtues, that is, the good things we do, are weighed by the source of the intention. For he said: “Lest perhaps they have sinned and blessed,” that is, cursed, “in their hearts.” He curses in his heart who does right works with no right intention, who thinks he has of himself what he is, or, if he has it from God, seeks his own praise from it. The things that are good before men the devil defiles in three ways.
• First he corrupts the intention of a good work, so that one does good for the favour of men. Whence the prophet: “Her adversaries are become her lords” (Lamentations: literally “in the head”), that is, they rule at the beginning of the thought. If he cannot do this, if the good is well begun, he sets himself more secretly against it in the doing, as on the road; as though to kill one going securely, he puts praise in the way, which, though not sought, delights when offered; or anger, which in zeal for what is right troubles the mind too immoderately; or sadness, or immoderate gladness. Whence David: “In this way wherein I walked, they have hidden a snare for me.” But if he neither corrupts the beginning nor trips one up on the road, as though driven off he lies in wait more craftily at the end. Whence: “they will watch my heel”; and the serpent, if its head, that is, the beginning of its suggestion, is caught, lies in wait for the heel, that is, it strives to deceive at the end. In all things, then, each ought to look about him and persevere in this. Whence: “So did Job all days,” that the tunic may cover the ankle, that is, that good action may cover us before the eyes of God to the end of life.
**“For he said: Lest perhaps my sons have sinned”** — he does not affirm it, because we ought not to judge rashly of the hearts of others
**“and have blessed God in their hearts.”** — he had taught them to be perfect in work and word, for whom he feared only on account of thought; how sternly would he correct works, who is so careful to cleanse hearts!
**“So did Job all days.”** — perseverance in holy work is indicated, and he is praised for perseverance; for in every sacrifice the tail of the victim is commanded to be offered
1.6:
**“Now on a certain day”**
• from the ministries to which they had been sent, confined in place, where yet they see the face of the Father; they stand by, and so they go out to us
• the person having been described with ample praise, he begins to show Job’s victory
• Allegorically. Nothing is said to be done before the Lord “on a certain day” because there is change of time with him; but he uses our words in condescension, so that while he speaks of the eternal in temporal terms he may raise our minds, accustomed to temporal things, to the eternal. Or Satan was present “on a certain day” because God saw darkness in light; and he who sees all things, good and evil, at once is not diverse in the things he orders in diverse order, nor is his light darkened by the presence of darkness. Satan was among the sons of God because he is pierced by the very force of justice with which the good spirits are filled; he is transfixed by the ray with which they are flooded that they may shine. Among the sons of God, because, although in a different way, he still serves God. Whence in the book of Kings: “I saw the Lord sitting on his throne” (that is, upon the angels, over whose minds he presides on high and orders all things below) “and all the army of heaven standing by him on the right hand and on the left,” that is, good and evil angels; because not only the good angels serve God but also the evil, who try men and weigh down those who wish to be converted. Of these a lying spirit springs forward into the midst, by whom King Achab, as his deserts required, is deceived.
**“on a certain day”** — On a certain day: at the beginning, the quality and the end of a thing are expressed; so now Job’s temptation is said to begin from a day, because he is led to victory; and so in other places. Now a thing is signified by the quality of the time, as that the angels appear to Abraham at midday, and Judas goes out by night; now by the place, as that Israel, being weak, hears the law not on the mountain but below; now by the quality of the air, as when it is said “it was winter” when he preaches to those who will not believe, and “it was cold” as Peter’s denial drew near; now by the position of the body, as that Stephen saw Jesus standing.
**“when the sons of God came”**
• that is, the elect angels
• that is, the angels of God
**“to stand before the Lord”** — by spiritual presence and inward contemplation they are always with God
**“was present among them”**
• in the knowledge of his nature
• Mystically. On the day the Lord saw Satan, because by his incarnation he rebuked the ways of his folly, which he had, as it were, not seen when for so long he had borne his wickedness in the ruin of men. “Whence comest thou?” Because by his coming he laid bare his ways and, holding them in check, rebuked them. On this day the sons of God stand before God, because then, called to their homeland, they already stand before the Godhead by his foreknowledge. “I have gone round about the earth and walked through it,” because he had pressed his footprints into the hearts of the gentiles and gone round as though by right, because he found none who resisted him fully; but now he is held down by him who in the flesh is without sin, whose astounding pride and fearful weakness is set before him by God. “Hast thou considered?” For on earth there is none like him, because the others are adopted by grace, he is God by nature, though in the form of a servant. For the Lord to say this is to declare to the proud one what he should wonder at and grieve to consider; to curb his pride he lists that man’s virtues. Simple and upright Christ came, to give men an example of life: simple, that he might not yield to evil spirits; upright, to overthrow pride; fearing God, to wipe away the uncleanness of life, avoiding evil.
**“Satan also”**
• by nature and by service
• They too were sent from their ministries, confined in place, where yet they always stand by and “see the face of the Father.” So they go out to us by their ministry, yet by spiritual presence and inward contemplation they are always with God.
**“was present”** — Because although by pride he went out, yet he did not lose a nature like theirs; so he was present among them, because God, with the gaze by which he beholds all spiritual things, sees Satan too in the order of the higher nature; yet Satan does not see God, who is seen by the clean of heart, as a blind man does not see the light by which he is shone upon.
1.7:
**“And the Lord said to him”** — And the Lord said to him: the Lord and Satan do not converse by the breath of the voice, since they are bodiless, as we do, who stand in the secret of the heart as though behind the wall of the body until we come out through the tongue. Nor is the speech of a bodiless nature of one kind. God speaks to the angels when his will is breathed into them. The angels speak to God when they marvel at what is above them, to the praise of God; their loud voice in the ears of God is their wonder at God’s power in praising him. Holy souls speak to God by their desires, which do not disagree with God; not that they do not know what is to come, but the more ardently they cleave to him, the more they receive from him to ask of him what they see he wills to do; and if they did not ask, they would be out of accord with his will; and God answers them when by his foreknowledge he strengthens them amid their desires with the certainty of the reward. But God speaks to the devil in four ways. He reproves his ways, as “Whence comest thou?” He sets the justice of his elect against him, as “Hast thou considered my servant Job?”; which is to make them such that he may envy them. He allows him to tempt innocence, as “All that he hath is in thy hand”; which is to let loose his malice against the faithful for their proving. Sometimes he forbids him to dare to tempt, as “Put not forth thy hand upon him”; which is to restrain him from the onset of immoderate temptation. The devil speaks to God in three ways. He tells his ways, as “I have gone round about the earth”: to say what he has done is to know that he cannot hide his acts from him. He accuses the innocent with feigned crimes, as “Doth Job fear God in vain?”; which is to complain against the good and envy their progress, and to seek chinks for doing harm. He asks that innocence be tempted, as “Stretch forth thy hand”; which is to pant with the heat of his malice for the affliction of the good.
**“Whence comest thou?”**
• Whence comest thou? He does not ask of the good, because we ask only what we do not know; and for God not to know is to reject; as a good man too is said not to know how to lie, not because he does not know, but because he despises it. So to say “Whence comest thou?” is to reject his ways as though unknown. “I have gone round about the earth”: by the circling round, the anxiety of toil is signified. He goes about the earth toiling who did not stand at rest in heaven; and he does not fly over it but walks through it, because he has fallen from the flight of spiritual power, weighed down by the heaviness of his own malice. Of his members also it is said: “The wicked walk round about,” that is, they are wearied in toil over outward things.
• The devil strives not against Job, but against God, with Job in between. Hence Job was not first asked of God; but God praised him in his sight.
*Morally:* Morally. Satan among the sons of God, because he thrusts himself among the good thoughts that are from God, to disturb them; but God uncovers him to us as he lurks. Whence it is said: “Whence comest thou?”; which is to lay open his snares to us. “I have gone round about the earth”: he searches fleshly hearts to sow evil in them; nor does he fly over but walks through, because he does not quickly leave the one he tempts, but lingers to press in the footprints of wickedness. Against him Job is praised: “Hast thou considered my servant?”: the man whom God makes good and strengthens he praises, as it were, in Satan’s hearing; whence he rages the more fiercely, saying: “Doth he fear in vain?”, as if to say: why do you praise one whom you protect? He would deserve praise if, with me disregarded, he stood against me by his own strength. Whence he maliciously asks: “But stretch forth a little.” While good things abound the mind is lifted up a little, as though its good were from itself; the devil seeks these good things wickedly, but God allows the trial for good, so that while the man is shaken in those goods, knowing his weakness, he may be made firm in God. Whence he adds: “Behold, all the substance that he hath is in thy hand.”
**“And he answered and said: I have gone round about the earth, and walked through it.”**
• the devil strives not against Job, but against God, with Job in between
• for there are few places where his footprints have no room
1.8:
**“And the Lord said to him: Hast thou considered my servant Job,”**
• that is, for Job was not first asked of God, but the Lord praised him in his sight
• as if to say: I have set up such a man, by whom you must be overcome
1.9:
**“And … answering, said”** — another reading: answering
**“Satan …: Doth Job fear God in vain?”**
• the devil, because he finds no evils to accuse, turns good things into evil, as though they were not done with a good mind; as if to say: he is defended from me not by his own strength but by yours, and so he fears in vain
• him whom he cannot accuse in his works he accuses in his intention, as though deceived
• Doth … in vain, etc. Mystically. The devil had sensed that the Redeemer had come; but because of the lowly things he suffered, whatever he suspected of his Godhead came, for his pride, into doubt; and he believed him not God born, but guarded by God’s grace: “Hast not thou made a fence?” He calls the house fenced because by tempting he could not penetrate his conscience, and his substance, because he did not presume to attack his elect.
1.10:
**“Hast not thou made a fence for him”** — as though it is not by his own strength that he stands, but by your fence, and so Job fears God in vain
**“and his house”** — he calls the mind a house
**“and all his substance round about,”** — on every side
**“blessed the works of his hands,”** — by multiplying them
**“his possession”** — His possession: as if, because he has received so many goods on earth, he behaves innocently for their sake, but he would be innocent if he stood amid adversity; because he cannot reprove him in the day, he wishes to in the night of adversity. Knowing then that not Job’s strength but every man is more truly proved by adversity, he asks that he be tempted. “But stretch forth”: he does not ascribe to himself even the power to strike; his will, which is from himself, is always wicked; his power, which is from God, is just. Whence: “an evil spirit from the Lord” upon Saul: of the Lord by leave, and evil by will.
1.11:
**“But stretch forth”** — give power
**“thy hand”** — Thy hand: he complains that the number of the faithful grows as the apostles preach; for Satan to say this is to think such things in envy and to grieve, wasting away, over them.
**“touch all”** — Touch all: because it is outward things he asks to have crushed, and he thinks it little unless he harm the soul.
**“to thy face”** — To thy face: the face of the Lord is the regard of grace. So he says: if you take away the gifts he loves, he will not seek your regard, that is, of your grace, your favour, but will despise it with cursing.
1.12:
**“Then the Lord said to Satan: Behold, all that he hath is in thy hand:”**
• he gives leave to tempt
• Behold, all, etc. Only upon him …: that is, I grant his goods to be tempted outwardly, but within I keep him for myself.
**“Then the Lord said”** — Then the Lord said: God is not overcome, provoked by the devil’s request, but grants the enemy, to his grief and his deceiving, what profits his servant.
**“Behold, all that”** — Behold, all that: with loving dispensation he lets loose and restrains; he gives up his substance, protects his body; and though afterwards he would give up the body, yet not everything at once, lest heaped together they should destroy what, divided, could be borne. Or the Lord knew Job was strong, and yet he divided the battles, so that he might be the more wonderful a victor when the conquered enemy readied himself again for new battles.
*Mystically:* Mystically. “But stretch forth”: he thought that through sufferings Christ could sin. “Behold, all that he hath is in thy hand.” Satan’s hand is not power but temptation. First Judea, which had been his possession, was taken away by unbelief and turned against him; afterwards his flesh too was crucified.
**“only put not forth thy hand upon his person.”** — here he bridles the devil
**“went forth”** — Went forth: that is, he attained the wishes of his desire.
**“And … went forth”** — Or he goes forth when what is permitted him with a good intention is carried out by him with a wicked one.
**“And Satan went forth”** — Whither? He went out from him who is everywhere. But as long as Satan, held down by the power of God, could not carry out what he desired, he stood, as it were, before his face; he goes out when he is let loose to carry out his desire.
**“And … went forth from the presence”** — Because, while he cannot prevail as far as the heart, shut out from within he wanders outside; even if he troubles the mind, he is outside, because he does not destroy but instructs.
1.13:
**“Now upon a certain day”** — Now upon a certain day: times are suited to temptations. He chose a fit time for tempting, when he found his sons at a feast; the gladness of fulness is a forewarning of trouble.
**“when his sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in the house of their eldest brother,”** — Allegorically. Now upon a certain day when his sons and daughters, etc.: the apostles and all the faithful. The elder son is the Jewish people, begotten by the law; the younger, the gentiles, called at the end. So the apostles feast in the house of the firstborn, because they still fed on the delights of holy Scripture in the gathering of the Jewish people alone, to whom it was then said: “Go ye not into the way of the Gentiles.”
**“were eating and drinking”** — Morally. To eat is to rejoice in good works; to drink wine is to burn with heavenly desire.
**“of their eldest brother”** — Morally. First there is born in the heart wisdom, which is faith; for then we are wise if we believe all that the Lord says. Whence: “If you will not believe, you shall not understand.” So the other virtues are filled with the holy word in the house of faith, that is, in the mind, without which there are no good things, even if they seem good; and in the house of wisdom, because unless they do prudently what they desire they are not virtues. But when this is not done the devil takes away the oxen and asses and kills the servants. The oxen are the weightier thoughts, which by working the heart yield richer fruit; but these the enemy sometimes corrupts by slipping in the delight of pleasure. The asses feeding: the simple motions of the heart, nourished in purity, guarded from doubleness. But to these too the devil shows subtleties, so that while praise is sought from them, simplicity is lost. Or the oxen ploughing: thoughts of charity, which cut into the hearts of the hard by ploughing, that is, by preaching; but these thoughts the enemy kills through the torpor of negligence; or, if they are on their guard, he snatches something in that which prevails over thought for a moment. The asses: the gentleness of patience, for which the devil lays snares out of what it most loves, so that from there its great patience may be troubled. But the elect return to themselves and afflict themselves heavily for a slight movement; yet when he troubles patience even for a moment, he exults that he has taken the asses. In what is to be done, reason, the guardian, weighs what suits each thing; but when the enemy troubles suddenly, forestalling one’s watchfulness unexpectedly, he kills the servants, the guardians, as it were. One escapes, that is, the discernment of reason returns to the mind and announces what is lost, so that what the forestalled mind lost the afflicted mind may recover.
1.14:
**“a messenger”** — this messenger is reason; yet each time another and another, because it announces one thing and another
**“The oxen were ploughing”** — Mystically, the oxen ploughing, that is, the good working well; the asses, those living simply; these are beside the oxen because they feed on their understanding. The Sabeans taking them captive, that is, the demons; the servants, that is, beginners, not yet of manly constancy; with the sword, that is, with despair of eternity. The messenger who escapes is the prophetic word, which says: “my people is led away captive, because they had not knowledge”; because when the evils it foretold come about, it returns, as it were, safe to the Lord; for it is known to have foretold truly the captivity of the weak.
**“and the asses feeding beside them”** — how craftily the losses are announced, so that by recalling the fruit of the work the cause of grief may grow; whence here too the Greeks read ‘she asses in foal’
1.15:
**“And … rushed in”** — while we suffer outwardly we flee for comfort to divine grace; this is said to come from the Sabeans and from God, that there may be no comfort, so that, left destitute on every side, he may break out in despair into insult
**“the Sabeans”** — neighbours sometimes bring comfort, but these persecute
**“and took all away”** — because adversities strike harder if, when they are many, they are also announced suddenly; so the devil has them announced
**“and … the servants”** — And the servants. Morally. He calls servants that wariness of diligence by which one provides for these things, and which is struck in them too.
1.16:
**“And while he was yet speaking, another came”** — or: another
**“and said:”** — he incites him not only by the loss of his goods but by the messengers’ words, when it is craftily said “the fire of God,” as though he were suffering his vengeance, whom he used to appease with so many victims; so that, thinking he had served in vain, he might grow proud against God
**“The fire of God”** — The fire of God, etc. Mystically. Heaven: the teachers of the law, the priests, from whom the fire of envy falls on the sheep and the servants, that is, the innocent and the weak. The servant returns safe, because the prophecy is plain to have spoken truly: “zeal hath taken hold of the unlearned people.”
*Morally:* The fire of God fell, etc. The sheep: the innocence of thoughts. Fire from heaven, that is, from the powers of the air, the flame of envy rushes in, and often kindles clean thoughts with the heat of lust; and it is the fire of God, not as doing it but as permitting it; and because by a sudden assault one’s watchfulness is overwhelmed, the guarding servants are killed. But discernment alone, that is, reason, announces the losses to the mind and calls the master, as it were, to lament.
1.17:
**“And while he also was yet speaking, there came another, and said: The Chaldeans made three troops”** — The Chaldeans, etc. Mystically. The Chaldeans are interpreted ‘fierce’, that is, the persecutors of Christ; three troops, because the Pharisees, Herodians and Sadducees divided themselves to put questions to the Lord; and they drew after them the camels, that is, the crooked minds of fools, and the servants, because any who could use reason yielded to their authority; and true is the prophetic word which says: “they that held the law knew me not,” and: “The kings of the earth stood up, and the princes met together, against the Lord and against his Christ.” They struck the servants with the sword, that is, with wicked persuasion, etc.
**“and have fallen upon the camels”** — The camels, etc. The camel, an animal clean in part, because it chews the cud, but in part unclean, because it does not divide the hoof, signifies the good management of earthly things, in which the enemy lies in wait in more ways; and he strikes such cares now with sluggish, now with headlong action; now he confounds them with slow or immoderate speech; almost always he weighs them down with too great a mass of thoughts. So the Chaldeans carry off the camels in three troops, that is, by unlawful work, superfluous speech and disordered thought they lay waste the pursuits of earthly management. Often the mind attends to what it owes itself and what its neighbours, and neither neglects itself through immoderate care for others nor puts others aside through care of itself; but while it does both skilfully, some cause suddenly arises that overwhelms all its watchfulness, and discernment alone brings back to the mind what it must weep for.
**“and taken them, moreover they have slain the servants with the sword, and I alone have escaped to tell thee.”** — To tell thee, etc. Evils are announced, many and sudden, so that with wound inflicted on wound he may bear it impatiently; and the crafty enemy tries him not so much by the loss of things as by the order of the messages. First he announces lesser evils, then greater, at last the death of his sons, lest, once bereaved, the loss of things should seem cheap, when there were no heirs for whom to keep it. So he hears worse things step by step, that every wound may find a place in his heart.
1.18:
**“Thy sons and daughters”** — Mystically, the sons and daughters, as was said, are the apostles and the people subject to them, who fed on Scripture in Judea. The wind, that is, strong temptation, bursts out from the desert, that is, from the hearts of the Jews or from unclean spirits; and shook the four corners on which the house stands: the priests, the scribes, the elders of the people, the Pharisees. The house, that is, Judea, falling in its persecution of the Lord, overwhelmed the apostles in despair. And true is the word about the persecuting people: “What is the meaning that my beloved hath wrought much wickedness in my house?”; and of the apostles: “my neighbours stood afar off”; and: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep shall be dispersed,” etc.
**“in the house of their … brother”** — At the feast of the elder brother Satan overwhelms the sons, because through the negligence of the elders he seeks an entrance to the death of the younger; and he gains more strength against others when he sees those who by their watch are set over others giving themselves to mirth. Not that they were given to the belly; but at feasts the good intention of the mind is less fervent and foresees less.
1.19:
**“A … wind came on a sudden”** — It is hiddenly said that he moved the elements against him at whose nod they were moved; though the devil, having once received power from God, can shake the elements for the purposes of his wickedness, as fire and water serve those condemned to the mines.
**“from the side of the desert”** — Morally. The side of the desert: the multitude of the demons, forsaken, from whom the wind, that is, strong temptation, rushes and overturns the conscience from its calm. The house of the mind stands on four corners, that is, prudence, temperance, fortitude, justice. These are the four rivers of paradise, which temper it against the heat of fleshly desires. But often through sloth prudence grows cold, and, being tired, foresees less; and often through delight in present things we refrain less from what is unlawful; often fear troubles fortitude; often some love turns the mind from the uprightness of justice; and when these are shaken the conscience is troubled. In the mind which is raised up on these four, the other virtues, the heart’s offspring as it were, feed one another; for the Spirit, which first of all shapes the mind with those four, equips it against each temptation with seven virtues: against folly with wisdom, against dullness with understanding, against rashness with counsel, against fear with fortitude, against ignorance with knowledge, against hardness with piety, against pride with fear. But while the mind enjoys this plenty securely, it presumes as though from itself, not from God; and so it is subtly withdrawn, that it may see in its weakness whence it had what it could not keep. So the seven virtues are struck by their contraries, that is, when the conscience is troubled the sons die for a time; and though they are troubled outwardly by temptation, they live within by the perseverance of the intention. The three sisters die too, because when one thinks oneself burdened beyond one’s strength one grows numb, as it were, in the love of God. While one fears too much, hope is weakened; while one is too much tormented by questions, faith is troubled; but yet the right intention keeps them alive within. So the servant, that is, the mind’s discernment, escapes, and deals with the mind so that what it had begun to lose it may keep by repentance.
**“A violent wind came … from the side of the desert”** — Behold again, lest he grieve any less over human adversity, or likewise over that from above, he shows the wrath named in the air: a wind rushed in.
1.20:
**“Then Job rose up”**
• he who stood firm before stands when all is lost, and this is Job’s rising up
• Wonderful is God’s dispensation for keeping humility and watchfulness: for one who is secure grows slack in ease, but when tempted he wakes up. Whence: “Then Job rose up.” To sit belongs to one at rest, to rise to one who fights; then discernment too makes progress, and learns to distinguish virtues from vices more subtly. Whence he adds: “He rent his garments.” The garments are the works that cover us, lest we blush at our nakedness; when grief makes us weep over our fault, we judge them more strictly, as with an angry hand. Then too all pride and superfluity of thoughts fall from the mind, which is to fall with the head shaven, that is, with thoughts of presumption held down, to feel how weak one is in oneself. It is hard to do great things and not to have confidence in oneself about great things; and thoughts are the henchmen of this pride, as of a tyranny. The Nazarites let their hair grow, as through continence of life thoughts of presumption grow; when their vow is fulfilled they are commanded to shave the head and put the hair into the fire of the sacrifice, because one comes to perfection when he so overcomes outward vices as also to cut away superfluous thoughts from his mind, which he burns with the fire of divine love, so that the whole heart, burning in the love of God, may consume them in the perfection of devotion.
**“Then … rose up”** — Mystically. When the house fell and the sons were dead, that is, when Judea was lost and the apostles dead with fear, Job rose up, that is, Christ from the dead. Or he who lay patient raised up the judgment of justice against the reprobate. He rent his garment, that is, Judea, which, awaiting his coming, had clung to him; he divided it, taking some to faith and leaving others. With his head shaven: the head is the height of the priesthood, the hairs the subtlety of the sacraments; whence Ezechiel: “take thee a sharp knife … and cause it to pass over thy head, and over thy beard”; in this Christ is signified, who shaved the head, that is, took away the sacraments of the law from the Jewish priesthood, and the beard, because, forsaking the kingdom of Israel, he cut off from it the comeliness of strength. The earth is the sinful gentile world. So with his head shaven he fell to the ground, because, forsaking Judea, when he took away its sacraments from its priesthood he came to the knowledge of the gentiles. What falls comes suddenly to the bottom; whence for Christ to fall is to have come unexpectedly to the gentiles, as it is said: “the Spirit of the Lord fell upon them,” that is, came unexpectedly. He worshipped, that is, made them worship, as: “the Spirit himself asketh for us with unspeakable groanings.” But Christ also, in himself, according to the form of a servant, prayed to the Father.
**“and rent his garments”**
• another reading: his tunic
• see, he felt the pain of the scourge
**“and having shaven his head fell down”** — or: went out
**“and having shaven his head”** — And having shaven his head. Mystically. It is thought great constancy if one does not feel evils; others, feeling them too much, grieve without measure; but virtue is in the middle; insensibility of heart is not virtue, as limbs that are numb do not feel pain when cut. Whence the prophet: “Thou hast struck them, and they have not grieved.” Lest he break off love of neighbour, he spent mourning on his sons; lest he forsake love of God, he prayed amid his groans. Lest he be proud, not feeling it, he fell down; lest he be estranged, he worshipped the one who struck him. It was the custom of the ancients that those who kept the comeliness of their body by letting their hair grow cut it off in time of affliction, and conversely those who had cut it in time of peace let it grow as a show of affliction. So Job is shown to have kept his hair, since he cut it for the purpose of grief; so that while the hand from above struck him in everything, he might of his own will also darken himself with the various signs of penance, and show that he consented to the divine power.
**“fell down upon the ground”** — Falling down he worshipped, because he offers true prayer who humbly sees that he is dust. Whence he also says: “Naked came I out of my mother’s womb.” Naked in faith first grace brought us forth; naked the same receives us. When, buffeted by vices, one flees naked as it were to mercy, and, being sometimes stripped of some virtue, is better clothed by humility itself, ascribing what he has not to himself but to God: “the Lord gave” the good things, and his power also takes them away; which is done for a time so that the humble man may have them better.
1.21:
**“and said:”** — see, in his grief he did not go too far against the judgment of the one who scourged him, but prays
**“Naked came I out”** — The earth brought me forth naked as I came in here; the earth will receive me naked as I go out from here. He takes comfort from the condition of things, that he has not lost what was his own but recalls what he received and must leave; he foresees the time when he did not yet have these things, how he will go out. He comforts himself also by the justice of God.
**“of my mother’s womb”**
• the mother is the earth, which brought forth all
• Mystically. The mother of Christ is the Synagogue, which held him in itself covered by the letter, and did not see him naked in his Godhead; but from her he came naked to the gentiles. See Joseph, whom the Synagogue, believing him a mere man, tried to hold fast in an adulterous embrace; he left her the covering of the letter and showed himself plainly to the gentiles. But naked shall he return when at the end of the world God will make himself known to the remnant of Israel. “The Lord gave”: to Judea, when she believed he would come; “hath taken away,” when she despised him coming.
**“and naked shall I return thither: the Lord gave”** — not the devil; for he knows that nothing is permitted him unless God allows; so what wonder if he who gave took back his own?
**“and the Lord hath taken away:”**
• not the devil
• he teaches us to give thanks amid scourges, as he himself, drawing near to his passion, gave thanks
**“as it hath pleased the Lord so is it done:”**
• the last comfort: he knows that God is the judge here; hence he knows that nothing but what is just pleases him
• In a matter that displeases, it is a great comfort if it is done by the ordering of him to whom nothing pleases but what is just; why then murmur at a just thing? As though, after stating his case against his adversary, at the end of his speech he blesses the judge: “blessed be the name of the Lord.” What he felt was right he concluded with the blessing of the Lord; whence the devil blushes, who even in bliss was contumacious toward God, while man, even when struck, sings him a hymn. So Job conquers the proud enemy by humility, the cruel one by patience, and inflicted sharper wounds than he received.
**“as it hath pleased the Lord”** — As it hath pleased the Lord. Morally. When we are troubled we ought to run back to the judgment of God and render greater praise, because when buffeted we know ourselves more truly.
1.22:
**“In all these things Job sinned not by his lips,”** — because even by not speaking we can sin in thought
**“In all these things … sinned not”** — In all these things … sinned not. Morally. The grieving mind guards itself lest it murmur at the fire that tries it. What was said of the virtues may be taken of those things which are given for a show of virtue, the gifts of the Spirit: prophecy, tongues, healings, which are also withdrawn lest the mind be lifted up. For the spirit of prophecy was not always in the prophets. Whence Eliseus says: “the Lord hath hid it from me.” And Amos: “I am not a prophet,” because that was then true; but the Spirit fills me when humble. And he says: “And now hear thou the word of the Lord.” Whence in the gospel: “He upon whom thou shalt see the Spirit descending, and remaining upon him, he it is that baptizeth.” For in others he comes, but in Christ alone he singularly remains. But how is this his sign, when he himself says of the apostles: “he shall abide with you”? But in Christ he always remains by substance for all things; in the elect by grace, not for all things. For there are some gifts of the Spirit without which one does not come to life, such as humility, faith and so on, according to which the Spirit always remains; others by which holiness of life is declared for the benefit of others, such as prophecy, healing, tongues, according to which the Spirit does not always remain, but sometimes withdraws himself from the showing of signs, so that he may be held more humbly. So concerning those that are for life let us fear lest they perish; concerning those for show, when they are sometimes withdrawn without danger, let humility comfort itself, saying: “The Lord gave”; because we show that we had them rightly when we bear their removal with an even mind.
**“In all these things Job sinned not”** — Whence: “Who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth.” Testimony is borne to Job both of mouth and of heart: in heart he did not swell, he did not murmur; in tongue he was not contumacious.
**“nor spoke he any foolish thing against God.”** — he speaks foolishly against God who amid scourges says he is innocent; which is proudly to accuse the justice of God who strikes

2.1:
**“And it came to pass, when on a certain day”** — the same day as before, historically and mystically
**“the sons of God came, and stood before the Lord, and Satan came among them, and stood in his sight,”** — so that he might be seen by God, not see God himself, because he is unclean of heart
2.2: **“Whence comest thou?”** — This is not as before; for since it is known that he has returned from the war to which he had been let loose, it is nothing else than that the weakness of his pride is rebuked, as if to say: you who raise yourself against God are conquered from below and by weak flesh. Hence, listing Job’s goods with triumph, he adds “and still keeping his innocence,” as if to say: you have exercised your malice, but he keeps his innocence, and you who wished to lessen him have served his progress.
2.3:
**“And the Lord said to Satan: Hast thou considered my servant Job, that there is none like him in the earth, a man simple, and upright, and fearing God, and avoiding evil, and still keeping his innocence?”** — Innocence, etc. Morally. He keeps innocence who even after a fall, stirred by a spark of reason, faithfully repents.
**“But thou hast moved me against him”** — not that God is stirred up, but in our way of speaking, who do not strike unless moved; God’s very striking is called being moved
**“But thou hast moved me”** — Allegorically. How was the Father, with whom he is one, moved against Christ by Satan? Because Christ as man would not have suffered had Adam not sinned; when Satan moved Adam he moved God against Christ. “Without cause,” because he bore the punishment without fault of his own; but not without cause, because he paid what another had stolen.
**“that I should afflict him without cause.”** — not without cause, because the virtue of patience and glory grew in him, and what lay hidden in him was shown to us as wonderful; but without cause, because in him sin is not punished; or without cause, that is, it did not come about as you hoped
2.4:
**“And Satan answered, and said”** — a thing less dear
**“for skin,”**
• that is, a dearer one
• Skin is given for skin, because often when a blow comes at the eye we put up a hand, so as to be wounded in it rather than in the more tender part; knowing this to be the usual way, he says: “Skin for skin, and all that a man hath,” as if Job bears so many scourges outside himself with an even mind because he dreads being struck himself, and through care for himself feels less for his own; whence he asks that he himself be struck: “Put forth thy hand”; which God rightly permits, so that, often defeated, he may be silenced.
**“Skin for skin”** — The devil, from the miracles, thought him the Son of God, but from the lowly things, a mere man. So, judging him by others who, instead of shepherds, think little of others’ losses, as though unmoved by the many things taken away, since they are outside him, he tempts him with the pain of his own flesh, as though he would grieve for himself who did not for others. When he asks for this to be done, he says it with his desires. These things he also brought on him through his members, by words and desires, through whom he said: “Let us put wood on his bread,” that is, let us apply the stock of the cross to his body by fastening it there.
**“and all”** — that is, whatever, one by one, all
**“that a man hath”** — he will lay it out without grief, provided only that he keep his life safe
**“he will give for his life:”** — this the devil suspected of Job, which he often saw in others
2.5:
**“But put forth thy hand”**
• that is, if you do not believe that he bears outward things patiently for this reason: whoever fears for his life loves something. Let me loose on his life and you will see
• But put forth thy hand. Morally. Often the devil, after he has assailed the mind, stops for a time, so as to burst in suddenly on it when secure; so he asks for Job again, whom God, by keeping him, grants him.
**“touch his bone and his flesh”** — Touch his bone and his flesh. Morally. By the bone and the flesh he understands the bodily life; by the soul, reason, as above.
*Allegorically:* Allegorically. Satan had power through his own over the flesh of Christ, but keeps his soul, not that he does not tempt it, but that he does not overcome it. Or “the soul,” that is, the dear and elect, he loses from his right when he kills him; “from the sole of the foot to the top of the head,” because from the beginning of the world he brought hard things on his members, and in his raging reached even their head, that is, Christ.
**“and then thou shalt see that”** — or: since
**“he will bless thee to thy face.”** — or: has blessed
2.6: **“And the Lord said to Satan: Behold he is in thy hand,”** — Behold he is in thy hand, etc. He allows us to be tempted, that we may see ourselves weak; and yet he guards us.
2.7:
**“So Satan went forth”** — Went forth, etc. Morally. Having received leave, from the sole, that is, from the least things, coming to greater, he tears the whole body of the mind with the temptations he brings, but does not reach the soul; because among the delights it undergoes the intention resists, and the deliberation of what is right is not bent to the softness of consent. Yet those delights too must be wiped away by the harshness of penance, which is to scrape the corrupt matter with a potsherd. For the potsherd is the rigour of strictness, the corrupt matter the flow of unlawful thought. Or the potsherd is mortal frailty, which he holds in his hand who always has it before his eyes, and by considering how soon it is to be dissolved he scrapes away the corrupt matter. Corrupt matter from a wound, a wicked thought from temptation: even if it is not brought to effect, yet it is not to be thought of as little. Whence: “whosoever shall look on a woman to lust after her,” etc. So fault must be cut away not only from the deed but also from the thought. Hence the angel appears to Jerobaal (Gedeon) threshing in the floor, who, rising, sacrifices a kid upon a rock. After the victim he poured out the broth of the flesh, the thoughts coming from fleshliness, which he also slays with the fleshliness. But because battle arises from victory, so that when a thought is overcome the mind is buffeted by pride, Job, scraping the matter, sits laid low in humility on a dunghill, that is, he thinks humbly of himself, and looks back with penance on what he has done amiss, lest any pride arise.
**“from the presence of the Lord, and struck Job with a very grievous ulcer,”** — see, scourges must be weighed by these two, their quantity [and their weight]; they are lightened if they are many and not heavy, or if heavy and not many
**“from the sole of the foot even to the top of his head:”** — his
2.8:
**“And he took a potsherd and scraped the corrupt matter, sitting on a dunghill.”**
• he increases his abasement, to show himself humbler
• Allegorically. He took a potsherd. The potsherd in his hand is Christ’s flesh, from the clay of our substance, which, baked in the fire of the passion, rose stronger; with it he wiped away the corrupt matter, that is, sin.
