By flesh and blood also the sins of the flesh are marked; corrupt matter, from putrid blood, signifies sins made worse by age. Sitting on a dunghill, because “the weak things of the world hath God chosen”: having spurned the proud Jews, he rests among the gentiles, that is, among penitents, who by weeping over their evils heap up their dung before them, as it were, by casting themselves down. But he who did so much for men endures much in his members from the fleshly, who are like a wife in the bosom of the Church by faith; and so with evil ways and words they press harder, and, received as it were into the bed of faith, they cannot be escaped. These are the crowd that presses on Jesus, but only the humble woman touches him. These urge evils, either from fear, like Peter while still fleshly: “Lord, be it far from thee”; or from pride, like Joab the son of Sarvia asking David for the death of Semei. But worse are those who do it from pride, like Job’s wife, who in pride counsels her husband.
**“he took a potsherd”** — Historically. A potsherd is made of clay, and the matter of the body is clay. So he wiped clay with clay, with a fragment of an earthen vessel, considering, in a broken earthen vessel, what he is who in carelessness swells. For through the things about the body the mind is puffed up, forgetful of human frailty, as happens in honours. Job, from the evils about him, increases his abasement, and sits not on clean ground but on a dunghill, weighing what the substance of the flesh is, and from the stench of the place he feels that the flesh will soon return to stench. What softness did he give his healthy flesh, who put to his wound not cloth or fingers but a potsherd? But the just man is pressed down here by God so that he may be gloriously rewarded; and it is shown what the wicked may expect, when he whom the judge praises is so pressed.
2.9:
**“And his wife said to him”** — Allegorically. He shows that the devil’s first temptation was made in Job’s possessions and sons; the second he shows in the affliction of the body and the persuasion of his wife, and in a fitting order. For if he had first been afflicted in body he would have thought little afterwards of the taking away of his goods. The devil keeps back the wife, so as to conquer at least through her, he who conquered the first man through his wife; but as Job stood victor in the first temptation, so he remained victor in this. In the same way in Christ: first he is tempted in the apostles, he is afflicted in his own person, and in his members; and Christ is received whole.
**“And his wife said to him:”**
• And his wife said to him, etc. The devil attacks in two ways: by tribulation, to break, by persuasion, to soften. So, beaten in tribulation, he runs back to the art by which he conquered Adam, and to the height by a ladder, that is, through the woman, who, being near the man, tries to creep up on him. But he does not hear her as one set over him, but teaches her as one subject to him; and so he takes the weapons from the enemy, and they become weapons of virtue for him as he instructs her.
• Morally. Even in prosperity, yet more amid the ills of the body, fleshly suggestion touches the mind. This is the wife who after the wounds counsels Job ill. Hence Jeremias: “Abroad the sword destroyeth” (that is, outward vengeance strikes), “and at home there is death alike,” because even then the conscience is not clean of temptations. But even if this suggestion wearies the good man and sometimes carries him off to delight, he soon blushes and rebukes himself, saying: “Thou hast spoken like one of the foolish women,” and fortifies himself by considering the gifts: “If we have received good things,” etc. But when someone, seeing so many vices besetting him, fortifies himself the more with virtues, certain vices come at him under the guise of virtues, that is, the friends meet as though to comfort, but break out into insults: as immoderate anger would seem justice, and loose remissness mercy, and fear humility, and unbridled pride freedom. Such begin with a smooth surface, but slide into harshness.
**“Dost thou still continue”** — Allegorically. She reproves his simplicity, because he despises earthly things and desires eternal. As if to say: why do you simply seek eternal things and groan badly over these? Falling away (despise the eternal) escape present evils, or escape by dying. But those who suffered these things are a pattern of uprightness to them. Whence he says: “Like one of the foolish,” etc. Struck outwardly they endure the perverse; inwardly they teach: there strong, here merciful; there they drive back enemies, here they protect their own; and it is a great thing to do both in the battle line.
**“in thy simplicity? bless God and die.”** — by death you will end this affliction; or “die,” that is, you will live, by contraries
2.10:
**“And he said to her: Thou hast spoken like one of the foolish women: if we have received good things at the hand of God,”**
• that is, the gifts of God, that is, temporal or eternal
• If we have received good things: that is, if we are making for eternal goods, why should we not bear present evils?
**“evil”** — that is, scourges
**“why should we not receive?”** — or: receive
**“In all”**
• In all: because the saints, in all that they suffer outwardly and inwardly, do not go too far either at God’s wrongs or at the insults of the wicked.
• “Dost thou still continue?” She repeats Eve’s words, as if saying: forsake simplicity, that is, despise obedience by eating what is forbidden. “Bless God and die,” that is, by overstepping the commandment live beyond what you were made.
• See the order: after the wounds the enemy brought in words, because when the force of pain grows heavier, a wicked persuasion more easily takes hold of someone; for this reason he who took away the rest kept back the wife.
**“like one of the foolish”** — Because the fault is in the understanding, not the sex, he does not say ‘one of the women’ but ‘one of the foolish women’; for to think wickedly belongs to a folly that has befallen, not to the condition of nature.
**“if we have received good things”** — If we have received good things: it is a great comfort in evils to remember goods, lest there be utter despair; as in times of joy the foresight of evil tempers pride. Whence it is said: “In the day of good things be not unmindful of evils: and in the day of evils be not unmindful of good things.”
**“In all these things”** — We sin with our lips in two ways: when we say unjust things, or when we keep silent about just things. But Job neither said proud things against the one who struck him nor kept silent about right things against the one who counselled him. He had patience, giving thanks to God, and taught, by reproving his wife’s folly; and so the beaten enemy is roused the more fiercely, and because the wife has been silenced he stirs up others to insults.
2.11:
**“Now when … heard”**
• because he could not be overcome by the things above, he therefore attacked him with others, namely friends, so that they might afterwards be believed
• Allegorically. The friends signify the heretics, who meet for contention against the body of Christ, that is, against the afflicted Church, grieving at the falls of her members and bearing with others under the name of Christ; which is an increase of grief. From their own place, which is pride, for unless they swelled in heart they would not strive to assert wicked things; conversely the place of the good is humility. So they come from their place, because they are moved by pride against the Church, and their perverse action is gathered from their names. Eliphaz, Baldad, Sophar, as was said above, and the places they come from fit. Theman: ‘southern’; Suhe: ‘speaking’; Naama: ‘comeliness’. He comes from the south who desires more ardently to be wise than he ought; and they desire this heat of wisdom not to live well but to speak proudly. Hence they take on comeliness, that is, the appearance of the good, from learning: hypocrites, not wishing to be learned, but to seem so.
**“heard”** — Heard. Morally. He does not say they heard because these vices hear, but the devil, who tempts by them, understands these things.
**“three friends”** — This number, morally or mystically, signifies the three troops of the Chaldeans, that is, the attack that is made in deed, word and thought; for he attacks all these.
**“all the evil that had befallen him, they came every one from his own place, Eliphaz”** — contempt of God
**“the Themanite,”** — southern
**“and Baldad”** — old age alone
**“the Suhite”** — his speaking
**“and Sophar”** — the scattering of the watchtower, or scattering the watchman
**“the Naamathite.”** — comely
**“For they had made an appointment”** — They had made an appointment both among themselves and toward the stricken man; this shows how great was their charity; but their good intention is darkened by an indiscretion that sprang up
**“they had made an appointment”** — They had made an appointment: because they agree in falsehood, and while they teach their own doctrine they seem to comfort. But they truly comfort in present affliction who instruct about eternal things. The heretics are called friends because they are to be named not from their wickedness but from our kindness, as: “Friend, whereto art thou come?”
*Morally:* They had made an appointment, because certain vices join with one another against us, such as pride and anger, remissness and fear, which, though they are different, yet tend to the same end, that is, the overthrow of the spiritual Job.
2.12:
**“And when they had lifted up their eyes afar off”** — Morally. The vices lift up their eyes when, under the guise of virtues, they prepare to ensnare the faithful and pretend, as it were, to counsel them
**“And when they had lifted up their eyes”** — Allegorically. Those who are below lift up their eyes if they consider the deeds of the Church; and her, placed in grief, who spurns these things and seeks the eternal, they do not know, because what they see in her they do not read again in their own heart; they who love these things despise the eternal. The garments of the heretics are those who cling to them in concord, who always rush into worse things and are divided from one another into many parts. When the garments are rent the body is shown, because when their followers are cut off by discord the malice is laid bare which was covered by concord.
*Morally:* But if from the distress of vices and the love of zeal we grieve within, the things that creep in on the glad do not prevail with the sad; whence he adds: “And when they had lifted up,” etc. The vices do not know the afflicted, from whom, rejected, they spring back, though they knew, that is, penetrated, the glad; and the more the devil sees himself detected in them, the more he hides them under the image of virtues. And this is: “And crying out they wept”: piety is signified by the weeping, discretion by the rending of the garments, the zeal of works by the dust on the heads, humility by the sitting. The appearance of piety leads to cruelty, if it forbids a fault to be punished by discipline, so that afterwards it is punished eternally. Discretion deceives, as if for weakness we take more food, as though discreetly, and indiscreetly stir up the wars of the flesh. Sometimes zeal for good works makes for the restlessness of toil. Humility kills usefulness, when a man thinks himself weaker and more useless than he is and ceases to profit others. But compunction subtly examines these vices lurking under the guise of virtues; for he who truly grieves within foresees well what is to be done outwardly and what is not; and every din of suggestions falls silent by the force of compunction. Whence: “No man spoke; for they saw his grief.” For if the heart truly grieves, the vices do not clamour against us. But the vices themselves are often changed to the use of virtues: as anger, if subjected to reason, is turned to the service of holy zeal; pride, if it bows to the fear of God, defends justice with free authority; strength of body, wicked before, if it is converted, profits much in the exercise of good works. Hence Job sacrifices for his friends, and those whom he bore as enemies he receives as fellow citizens through sacrifice; for when we subdue evil thoughts and turn them into virtues, we change enemies into friends, as it were, through the victim of the intention.
**“they knew him not”** — because they had not seen him further in this state
**“and crying out they wept,”** — they take Job’s show of misery upon themselves, so as to be better believed
**“crying out they wept”** — Historically. Because the plague had changed the appearance of the stricken man, a voluntary grief changes the appearance of the comforters; for he cannot comfort a grieving man who does not join in his grief, but draws him by clinging to it. So seeing his body torn they rend their garments; seeing him changed they defile their heads with dust; so that Job may the more readily hear them when he sees something of his own affliction in them. Yet the comforter must see to it that by grieving too much he does not weigh down the afflicted and drive the grieving man to despair; perhaps Job’s friends grieved too much, not knowing the mind of the stricken man, as though he had fallen away in heart.
**“and rending their garments they sprinkled dust upon their heads towards heaven”** — see, the compassion of piety
**“they sprinkled dust”** — Dust: earthly understanding; the head: the mind; heaven: the commandment of the word from above. To throw dust upon the head towards heaven is to corrupt the mind with worldly understanding and to think earthly things about heavenly words. Day: understanding; night: ignorance; seven: the whole.
2.13:
**“And they sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no man spoke to him a word: for they saw that his grief was very great.”** — So they sit, that is, they pretend to stoop to the weakening Church, both in the things in which they understand the true light and in those in which they have ignorance; and so they prepare the snares of deceit. On the ground, because they show an appearance of humility, so as to urge proud things; or the ground is the incarnation of Christ, which some heretics do not deny, but they differ from us either about the Godhead or about the manner of the incarnation; so because they do not deny it, they sit with Job on the ground, as it were. Days and nights, because whether in what they understand truly or in what they understand foolishly, they do not contradict the incarnation. No man spoke, because enemies are silent if we neglect to beget sons of God by preaching; but if we speak right things, then they heap grave insults on us and break out against us in a cry of grief. They speak indeed the seeds of errors when they see the hearts of the faithful grow numb; but when they see them minding high things, seeking from the distress of the world, with grief, a return to heaven, they warily bridle their tongue. And this is: “they saw that his grief was very great”; because they are afraid to speak wicked things when the grief of the love of God pierces hearts, because then they would not profit, and would lose even those they held, who are well trained.
**“seven days”** — It is not known whether they stayed continuously, or persisted for so many days with frequent visits.
**“no man spoke”** — No man spoke: for there are many who are slow to begin speaking but set no measure to what they have begun, speaking without discretion; and though they came with a good intention, headlong speech spoiled the good of a devout mind. Hence each must weigh the good he does in the scale of discretion, which is to divide what is offered; otherwise what is thought virtue is guilt. It was great charity to have come in concord to an afflicted friend; long-suffering to have kept silent with him so long; humility to have sat on the ground; compassion to have sprinkled their heads with dust; but because they spoke incautiously, what was well begun became evil at the end, and unless they are cleansed by sacrifice they must be punished.

3.1:
**“After this Job opened his mouth, and cursed his day”**
• After this Job opened, etc. He makes us attentive, as to hidden things which were covered in closed vessels, but are uncovered when their mouth is opened, so that we may be refreshed by their inmost fragrance. Up to here, a threefold exposition; from here on, as each place requires. He cursed his day: see, this is not according to the surface of the history, because it is both evil and impossible. For the day on which he was born no longer existed, and it is idle to curse a thing that does not exist, and harmful if it did exist; nor can a past day now be turned into darkness, nor can the rest that follows fit it; nor would an untimely birth (as he says afterwards) enjoy rest. So here nothing is according to the letter.
• After this, that is, after all the things told above which he suffered, while even his friends were silent. So since he patiently gave thanks in all things and taught well, he is not now to be believed, with no one urging him, to break out into cursing from impatience; but he says this calmly, because amid evils he praised God.
• So Job’s curse is not malice but justice, not agitation but teaching. For he sees his friends weeping and, judging by themselves (they sought the prosperity of the world), thinking him broken by evils, and, knowing nothing of inner salvation, despairing and weeping for him on that account. And he lays down a remedy: “Let the day perish wherein I was born,” not made; for man was made on the day of justice, but born on the day of fault: Adam was made, Cain was the first born. So the day on which he was born is the whole time of mortality, under which eternity does not appear to those who live; let this, then, perish, and eternity appear. To perish is said in two ways: not to be, or to be in an evil state. This time of ours will so perish as not to be; whence “time shall be no longer.” For when it is said: “and their time shall be for ever,” it is put for failing, as time fails by moments; yet here he wishes it so to perish as to be in an evil state, for otherwise it could not be wrapped in bitterness, as he says afterwards. But the soul or an angel is so immortal that it cannot die. For it dies by vice or by punishment, by which it loses living in bliss; yet it never ceases to live in its essence. So the day he wishes to perish is the apostate angel, who has indeed already perished from glory, but it is still wished that, thrust back into punishments, he may lose even the leave to tempt. That day was well made by nature, a night by its deserts. The day is dark when it entices with prosperity, but ends in night because it draws to evils. It shows a day when it promises better things: “you shall be as Gods,” but brought on the night of mortality. A day when, promising good things, it appears as an angel of light; a night when it darkens the hearts of those who consent with errors. So Job, in his own grief weeping for the cause of the whole human race, brings back to mind the origin of fault, and tempers the grief of punishment by the consideration of justice. He sees whence man fell, and says: “Let the day perish, and the night in which,” etc., as if: let the hope brought by the devil perish, which shone with the promise of godhead, but like the night darkened immortality. Let the enemy perish who promised light but brought on the darkness of sin.
**“cursed”** — A curse is spoken in two ways: by the judgment of justice, or by the spite of revenge. The first is praised, the second forbidden. God uses the first, as: “cursed is the earth in thy work,” “I will curse them that curse thee.” The saints too, seeing God’s judgment within, curse not with a wish for vengeance but with God’s justice. Whence Peter: “Keep thy money to thyself, to perish with thee.” And Elias to the two captains of fifty: “If I be a man of God, let fire come down … and consume thee.” Against the other kind, which is done in malice, the Apostle says: “bless, and curse not,” and: “nor railers … shall possess the kingdom of God.”
*Morally:* Job, seeing how much man, after his fall, is lifted up by prosperity and how much he is pressed by adversity, runs back to unchangeableness, and declares by cursing how much he despises this state. “Let the day perish”: the day is the prosperity of the world, which ends in night, because it leads to tribulation. Or the day is the delight of sin, the night the blindness of the mind. Man is spoken of in three ways: by nature, by fault, by weakness. So man is born in the day and conceived in the night, because he is not carried off to the delight of sin unless he is first weakened by the darkness of the mind. But let the day perish, that is, let the delight of sin be destroyed by the vigour of justice; and the night, that is, what the blinded mind commits by consent when it does not warily see through the allurements of delight, let penance extinguish. But lest the fault which begins to allure run on to destruction, “let the day be turned into darkness,” that is, at the beginning of the love let it be seen to what end of perdition it carries one away, and let it be tormented by penance. If it is so punished, “let not God regard it” in judgment to punish it, and “let not the light shine upon it.” He shines light upon one whom he reproves; but one is covered, as it were, who is not called back to the judge’s memory. Whence “whose sins are covered,” lest they be shown then in the sight of all. Let it not be shone upon, but let them cover it, that is, the day of delight, lest it be seen by him who sees all things. “Darkness,” that is, the laments of penance, or God’s hidden judgments, by which we are absolved, forestalled by grace, though we know not that we merit it; “and the shadow of death,” that is, the death of Christ according to the flesh, which destroyed our fault. Hence he was one day and two nights in the tomb, because he joined the light of his single death to the darkness of our fault. True death is called that by which the soul is separated from God; its shadow, that by which the flesh is separated from the soul. Otherwise the shadow of death is called forgetfulness, which makes a thing not to be in memory, as death makes what it takes not to be in life. Or the devil is called death, and his change, which is from his own form, as a shadow from a body, the shadow of death. But because no sin is unpunished, even where mercy helps, let man punish this; whence follows: “let a mist overspread it,” that is, confusion of mind, of which it is said: “there is a shame that bringeth glory”; “and let it be wrapped up” on every side in the bitterness of penance. But if the day, that is, the delight of sin, is so punished, what of the night, that is, consent to the fault?
3.3:
**“Let the day perish”** — first of the day, afterwards of the night
**“wherein I was born, and the night in which it was said: A man child is conceived.”** — let it be so understood, namely that the prosperity it promises be understood as adversity; for as the enemy is when raging, so is he when flattering
3.4: **“Let that day be turned into darkness, let not God regard it from above, and let not the light shine upon it.”** — that is, let the blindness of its error so overwhelm it that it may not rise again to the light of penance through God’s remembrance
3.5:
**“Let darkness, and the shadow of death cover it,”** — that is, forgetfulness, which blots out memory as death blots out life
**“let a mist overspread it,”** — now because it has fallen from the light, now it is confounded within by mist
**“and let it be wrapped up in bitterness.”** — afterwards it will be tormented with the endless punishment of hell; for what is wrapped up does not show its end; and this punishment will begin when the judge comes
3.6:
**“Let a darksome whirlwind seize upon that night,”** — let the tempest carry off the apostate angel from the sight of the judge to punishments; of which it is said: “and a mighty tempest shall be round about him”
**“Let a darksome whirlwind seize upon that night”** — Like the whirlwind of a storm is the roused spirit of mourning, which clouds the mind with sadness. This is the spirit that breaks the ships of Tharsis, that is, the force of compunction, which confounds with wholesome terror minds given to the sea, that is, to the world.
**“let not … regard it”** — Let not … regard it: man is redeemed because, being flesh and spirit, he had something weak by which he sinned, which an angel had not; besides, the angel perished by his own malice, man by another’s. So he says “let not God regard it”; and because it brought on darkness, let it bear without end what it did, nor receive the light which it lost without being persuaded.
**“that night … darksome”** — Morally. He who flatters himself in sin is possessed by the night; he who punishes it possesses the night, and better if the sin is held down as it begins. But what we punish, we hope will not be thrown up to us by the judge; whence “let it not be counted,” etc. The year of our enlightenment is completed when the judge comes and the pilgrimage is finished. The days of the year are the several virtues; the months are the manifold deeds of the virtues, or the collection of the virtues of each good man. But because with these he fears lest the judge weigh the evils too, he prays that then he may so reward the good as not to look into the evil. For if this night is numbered with the days, all things are now darkened; and that it may not be numbered then, let us examine it now, lest any fault be unpunished, lest anyone defend what he has done, adding wickedness to wickedness. Whence he adds: “Let that night be solitary, and not worthy of praise.” For there are those who praise and defend evil things, and so the fault is doubled and does not remain solitary. Against which it is said: “Hast thou sinned? do so no more.” To sin, that is, to defend evil, as Adam did, who, sought out for penance, added an excuse to his fault: “The woman, whom thou gavest me,” etc., as if: you were the occasion of sin, who gave the woman. But he pursues fault well who desires no prosperity of the world. Whence it is said: “Let them curse it who curse the day”; that is: they strike the night well by penance who trample on the light of prosperity, who do not have the day of delight. Or the day is the enemy’s suggestion; and they truly punish it as done who in his very smooth suggestion detect the snares of the deceiver, who rouse Leviathan the more against themselves. For others, whom he possesses securely, he sleeps; but for these he wakes for every battle. But because when the vices are conquered some very small thing remains which cannot be conquered, lest the victor be lifted up, he adds: “Let the stars be darkened with the mist of that night”; because even if they shine with virtues they drag remnants of the night, even resisting, so that from it they may shine better; whence, unwilling, they are humbly darkened. Hence the Chanaanite, not slain, becomes tributary to the tribe of Ephraim in the land of promise; because when we enter heavenly things with hope, vices remain among the best things, which yet serve us for the use of humility, lest he be proud who cannot conquer even small things. Whence again: “These are the nations which the Lord left, that by them he might instruct Israel,” that is, vices in which virtue is always exercised; and while it fears to be conquered the pride of virtue is held down, and in small things it learns that it does not by itself conquer greater. Or “let the stars be darkened with the mist of that night,” because the night, that is, consent to fault, handed down from Adam to us, so troubles the eye that even those who shine in the world like stars cannot see the eternal light as it is. And this is: “let it expect light and not see it”; because with however much ardour they leap up, yet in this flesh they will not see the light as it is, because of the blindness of condemnation in which we are born.
**“let it not be counted in the days”** — Allegorically. The year is grace from above, in which is the manifold life of the virtues, like days in the year. Or the year is the multitude of the redeemed, which is completed by the gathering of all the good, as the year by its days; which in Isaias is called “the acceptable year of the Lord.” The days are the several elect; the months, the many churches which make one catholic Church. But the night is not counted among these, that is, the devil; because he beholds the coming of Christ, but does not believe in it unto pardon with the elect. Whence “nowhere doth he take hold of the angels.” Or the days are the angelic spirits remaining in the light; the months their orders and dignities, such as the thrones and the rest; but the devil is brought back neither to the light nor to their order, but is shut out from that homeland for ever. Whence he adds: “Let that night be solitary,” because it is separated from that throng; or he loses man, whom he had made his companion, and, when the elect are redeemed by grace, he is handed over alone with his body to hell.
3.7: **“and not worthy of praise”** — Not worthy of praise: man, when laid low, worshipped idols, in which he praised the demons as the darkness of the night; but now that the idols are rejected it is not worthy of praise.
3.8:
**“Let them curse it who curse the day,”** — Let them curse it who, etc. In the old translation: “Let him curse it who curseth the day, who is ready to take the great whale.” The devil, who now lies hidden as night, at the end will be seen as day, when he will be lifted up above all that is called God or worshipped. But now he destroys his malice who at the end will destroy his power by his coming; who in the waters (namely of baptism) extinguishes the great whale, that is, his strength. Or “let them curse it,” that is, the night, the elect angels, announcing its darkness by condemning it, “who curse the day,” that is, who show that its feigned brightness, by which it presumed to become equal to God, is to be despised; “who are ready to raise up,” that is, to let loose, so that he may act with all his strength against the Church; for now he is held bound in the abyss and pressed down; and he who proudly lifted himself above the others has sunk, laid low, under their rule, so that now, bound by their ministry, he lies hidden, and at the end, loosed, he will wage open war.
**“a leviathan”** — Leviathan: that is, ‘their addition’, that is, of men, in whom after suggestion he does not cease to add evils. Or ‘reproach’, because when he promised to add godhead to Adam he also took away what he had. He is called by the prophet the crooked serpent, because he is soft, pouring in snares as through the smooth coils of words; and a bar, because he is hard through malice and strikes to death. When roused he will act openly; meanwhile, secretly. “With the mist of that night let the stars be darkened,” that is, the hypocrites, who shine by their works to the eyes of men. These are they whom the tail of the dragon, that is, the final persecution of Antichrist, draws; these are darkened, because the enemy’s malice so prevails over them that they are wrapped in open evils, being outwardly what they are within.
3.9:
**“Let … be darkened”** — or: obscured
**“let it expect light”** — Let it expect light: this is according to his members, that is, the wicked who have faith and either do wicked things or good things with no right heart; and secure, because in their own and many people’s opinion they are holy, they await the day of the Lord, not in vain indeed. Of them the prophet says: “Woe to them that desire the day of the Lord.” The light, then, that is, Christ, who says: “I am the light of the world.” The dawn rising is the Church, which forsakes the former darkness and comes into the light of justice. Its rising is the beginning of eternal brightness. So in the judgment there is still dawn, in the kingdom day, whose rising in the light of the Lord’s coming the wicked will not see, because, pressed by darkness, they will not know with how great a light it rises. Whence: “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God.” Or in the present they do not see the rising of the dawn who, when they see works, do not weigh the intention, imitating what they may be praised for outwardly, not what may raise them within to the light. Or this is a prophecy of Judea, which awaited Christ by prophesying, but did not know him when he came.
**“nor the rising of the dawning of the day”** — Nor the rising of the dawning of the day. Morally. The rising of the dawn is the new birth of the resurrection, by which the saints will rise with the flesh to see the eternal light. But however much the elect shine here, they cannot penetrate what that glory of the new birth will be to them. This night did not shut but opened the doors of the womb, because it unlocked the desires of concupiscence to human conception unto sin. And when these doors, that is, the desires of fleshly concupiscence, are unlocked, we are dragged to countless evils of corruption. Whence, weighed down, we groan; because justice requires that what we did willingly we should bear unwillingly.
3.10:
**“Because it shut not up”**
• another reading: shut
• Because it shut not up: this is of the head itself. Paradise is the womb from which the human race came forth, growing by its offspring, conceived there in Adam its origin. The serpent opened its doors, because he burst into the bars of the mind, fortified by warnings from above, and dissolved God’s commandment in it. So Job, in his punishment, thinks again on the fault, and grieves at what the night, that is, the enemy’s dark suggestion, brought into the minds of men, and that man consented to him. He says that he did not shut who opened, and did not take away who brought on; because he would, as it were, take away if he kept still, and would shut if he ceased from bursting in; for the wicked one would, as it were, have been giving us gain if he had not brought losses, as we say robbers give life to their captives if they do not take it away.
3.11:
**“Why did I not die in the womb”** — Why did I not die in the womb? It is not to be believed that so great a man wishes he had perished as an untimely birth; but these words are to be weighed inwardly. Sin is done in the heart in four ways, and completed in deed in four. In the heart there is suggestion, by the enemy, as the serpent persuaded in paradise; then delight, through the flesh, as there too Eve was delighted; afterwards consent, by the spirit, as there too Adam consented; then defence, through pride, as Adam too, when sought out, excused himself; he feared indeed, but also swelled. For when punishment is feared but the face of God, being lost, is not loved, fear is from swelling, not from humility; because he is proud who does not forsake sin if he may go unpunished. In deed, first the fault is committed in secret; afterwards it is laid open before men without shame; then it is brought into habit; afterwards it is fed either by false hope or by despair. In so many ways the human race weeps for its fall. “Why did I not die in the womb?” The womb in which man is conceived in sin is evil suggestion; but would that he had died in it, that is, had known that he would die, lest the suggestion draw him to delight.
**“when I came out of the belly”** — When I came out of the belly. Morally. Because delight snatched the conceived sin outside; but [why did I not] fall in that delight rather than lose my wits as far as consent to the deed? He was received on the knees, because through the consent of the spirit, with all the senses subject to it as knees, he completed the fault. He was also suckled at the breasts, when he is fostered by empty confidence and smooth excuses. So too in deed. The womb is hidden fault. He comes out who does not blush to do openly what he did in secret; whence: “they have proclaimed abroad their sin as Sodom.” But why did I not wish to put myself to death from the life of the flesh in hidden iniquity, or, when I came out into action, why did I not at least then know myself lost? He is fostered on the knees to grow who, not ashamed of his open evil, is strengthened by wicked habits, so as to thrive for worse things. But why these things? that is, would it were not so! He is suckled, because after the fault has come into habit he feeds himself with false hope of God’s mercy, lest he return to amendment; for after habit, even if he wishes, a man resists sin more weakly; whence, enervated, he bends to false comforts, as though God spares these things too; to which is added the flattery of many like him; whence: “if sinners shall entice thee, consent not to them.” Besides, despair feeds the soul with the milk of error. The first three ways, in their order, are more easily corrected, the fourth with more difficulty. Hence Christ raised three dead: in the house, one who lies hidden in sin; outside the gate, one whose iniquity is made public; buried under the mound, that is, one weighed down by the mass of habit. A fourth he hears of as dead and does not raise, because one pressed by evil habit hardly rises again if he is fed with flattery; which is: “let the dead bury their dead,” that is, overwhelm them with favours; or if despair feeds the soul with the milk of error. So Job sees to what great precipices of this exile man has come down, after he lost paradise through fault, and accuses himself of having sinned in the first parent. If that had not been, he adds what rest he could have enjoyed: “For now I should have been asleep and still, and should have rest in my sleep”: if man had not sinned in paradise, he would at some time have passed without death to the homeland of the angels, to which the redeemed are to be carried after death; and had fault not come forth, the saints would rest in peace of heart, and, all clamour, unrest and tumult of temptations removed, would withdraw within the secret of the mind to the contemplation of God; who now cry out as though awake, while they bear the strife of their own flesh against the spirit.
3.13:
**“now”** — in the eternal present
**“For … I should have been asleep”** — in eternal rest
**“and still,”** — I would not complain
**“For now”** — By “now,” which belongs to the present time, he signifies what stands always in the present, that is, eternal rest.
**“and should have rest in my sleep”** — I would rest in eternal goods
3.14:
**“With kings and consuls of the earth, who build themselves solitudes:”** — by despising the tumult of earthly desires
**“should have rest … with kings”** — Should have rest with kings: that is, with the angels, who rule those beneath them; who are also consuls, because they counsel us by announcing God’s will. Or he calls kings the holy preachers, who rule themselves; and consuls of the earth, because they counsel earthly men well. So he says that if man had not sinned, he would have gone up, even unredeemed, to where the apostles and holy preachers arrive after the redemption with great labour; who are not kept waiting like the ancients, but enter heaven soon after death. “Who build themselves solitudes”: every earthly man is crushed in heart by dense tumults of thoughts, and trampled by the press of desires as by crowds. But to build solitudes is to drive the tumults of earthly desires from the secret of the heart and to pant for the love of inward rest, so that one can say: “One thing I have asked … this will I seek after,” etc.
3.15:
**“Or with princes, that possess gold,”**
• divine knowledge
• With princes, that possess gold. The princes are the rulers of the Church. Gold: wisdom, by which eternal goods are bought, as temporal ones with gold. The houses are the consciences. Silver: the divine words. So the princes, that is, the rulers succeeding in the place of the apostles, possess gold by living wisely, and fill the house of conscience with the divine words with which they instruct them. So Job, foreseeing the future, considers with wonder with which elect he would have rested in eternity without toil, had no one sinned through pride. And he says: “For now I should have been asleep and still,” etc.; because if no rottenness of sin had corrupted Adam, he would not have begotten from himself sons of hell, but those alone would have been born from him as elect who are now to be saved by redemption. He who foresaw the future now recalls the past.
**“and fill their houses”** — consciences
**“with silver:”** — with the divine word
3.16:
**“Or as a … untimely birth”** — Or as an untimely birth: because what is born untimely, before its time, is dead and at once hidden away. These are the saints with whom he considered he could have rested, who were from the beginning of the world before the time of the redemption, and yet put themselves to death to the world. The first time, before the law, which brought forth fathers dead to the world, was as the womb of an untimely birth; and they themselves were as dead from the womb, who without the tables of the law feared God by nature and, believing in the Redeemer to come, slew their pleasures.
**“hidden”** — Hidden: because, few being recorded by Moses, the greater part of them is withdrawn from knowledge; and they are said no longer to exist, because their great number is kept in no written record among us. Or those who, conceived through the law, did not see the light of the Lord’s coming, to which, faithfully believed in, they could not attain. In them the inward conception produced the form of faith, but did not bring it to fitting sight. Now he lays open the rest of this light, and shows in plainer words what is daily done there concerning the conduct of the wicked.
**“not”** — another reading: now
**“I should … be, or as they that being conceived”**
• under the law
• Or as they that being conceived: we call ‘conceived’ not only those who had the written law, but all from Abraham, to whom the promises were openly made, whom the spirit of prophecy shone upon, as Job himself.
**“have not seen the light.”**
• or: the light
• in respect of this light and rest
3.17:
**“There”** — in a manner, in the present
**“the wicked cease”** — in the hope of that light
**“from tumult,”** — of vices
**“and there the wearied in strength are at rest.”** — of the virtues
**“There the wicked cease from tumult”** — There the wicked cease from tumult: that is, in the light of Christ, for which the ancients waited, the gentiles cease from the crowd of the world’s desires, and with a calm mind already foretaste eternal rest. And this is: “and there the wearied in strength are at rest.” Those strong in the unclean world are said to be not wearied in strength. He who is strengthened in the love of God wholesomely fails in his own strength, and the more strongly he seeks the eternal, the more, wearied, he dies to earthly things. Whence: “My soul longeth and fainteth for the courts of the Lord.” By saying “there” he shows the light as the place in which the elect are held.
3.18:
**“And they sometime bound”**
• in the rest of the saints
• in glory
• And they sometime bound: the just, though at rest from desires, are yet bound while in the body by the trouble of their corruption; for the body weighs down the soul and the flesh fights against the spirit. There are bodily bonds too: hunger, thirst and the like, which cannot be loosed here, but they will be loosed from all of them “into the liberty of the glory of the children of God.” See the steps: the wicked, converted, cease; the trained rest in the inmost bosom; loosed from the bonds of corruption, they come to freedom. But what they do here meanwhile he adds: “they have not heard the voice of the oppressor.” The oppressor is the devil, who once paid man the coin of deception and daily exacts the debt of death. His voice is temptation: he hears who is tempted and resists; he hearkens who consents. The same is said of inward peace, because what the mind greatly loves it repeats more often.
**“together”** — all
**“without disquiet,”**
• they rested
• this is of the future
**“have not heard”** — even if they heard
3.19:
**“The small and great are there,”** — in the world
**“The small and great”** — The small and great: because here there is a distinction of works, there there will be one of dignities. Whence: “In my Father’s house there are many mansions.”
**“and the servant is free from his master.”** — he does not fear the judge
**“the servant”** — The servant: he who sins is the servant of sin, who here is never made free while he fears the judge; but there he will be free, where there will be no doubt of pardon. There will indeed be memory of fault there, not such as defiles the mind, but such as, without hurt, binds it more closely to bliss and joy; as when healed we recall our pains without pain, and so give the more thanks to the physician.
3.20:
**“Why is light given to him that is in misery”**
• as if: because man lost so great a glory, he is therefore wretched, and so prosperity does not profit the wretched, rather it harms him
• Having contemplated the rest where one is free from the master, he despises the prosperity of the world, which draws one back from it. “Why is light given to him that is in misery,” that is, prosperity in the misery of the pilgrimage? Because even if it does not wholly crush the just man, yet it divides his mind between the love of God and the care of himself. Whence he adds: “and life to them that are in bitterness of soul.” Bitterness belongs to every just man, either weeping for what he has done amiss, or because he is kept back from his homeland. Such a man longs to die wholly to the world; but because the world does not always die to such a one, but its glory is given to the sad and groaning, he complains: “and life to them that are in bitterness.” For such a man fears to be held by the world; because unless in some way he lived to it, it would not love him for its own use; as the sea keeps living bodies within it, but soon casts out the dead. So to those who wish to die wholly to the world, the world itself still lives, when, loving though unloved, it binds them by certain occupations. For the saints often desire to extinguish themselves from all life of temporal glory, but by God’s hidden judgment they are often compelled to be occupied in honours laid on them or to preside in government.
**“and life”** — that he may live in some way
3.21:
**“That look for death”**
• they desire to die to the world
• That look for death: that is, they desire to put themselves wholly to death to the world; but by God’s hidden judgment it does not come, because they are compelled to be occupied in honours that bind them, which they bear out of the fear of God; within there is the desire of piety, and outwardly the ministry of their order is fulfilled, lest through pride they contradict God’s disposition; and so they profit many, and, seeing themselves imperfect, they rise the higher through humility; and because they are kept back from their desires, by the very delay they are enlarged for them. Whence, to express the desire of those who seek, he adds: “as they that dig for a treasure.”
**“and it cometh not,”** — that death
**“as they that dig for a treasure:”** — eternal rest, or the knowledge of the Godhead, that is, wisdom
**“as they that dig for a treasure”** — As they that dig for a treasure: because he who seeks a treasure by digging, when he has dug deeper, thinking himself now near the treasure, burns the more for the work at hand; so the just man, the nearer he is to the end and the reward, the more delightedly he sweats at the work. Or because no one dies perfectly to the world unless he is hidden from visible things within the invisible places of the mind. Those who desire mortification are compared to those digging for treasure, because we die to the world through invisible wisdom, which is dug out like a treasure; for wisdom does not lie on the surface of things but lies hidden in the invisible. This is sought by digging the heart, that is, that the mind may cast every earthly thing out of itself and so recognise the treasure of virtue that lay hidden from it. And because they seek death as a treasure, they rejoice greatly when, as a body in the grave, so the soul, dead to the world, is hidden in divine contemplation, where it is at rest from all the din of the world. Or he who digs for treasure rejoices if he finds a grave, where of old the dead were laid away with riches; because he who seeks wisdom finds, in the just once buried to the world, examples of contemplation, by which he grows rich.
3.22: **“And they rejoice exceedingly when they have found the grave.”** — examples of contemplation
3.23: **“To a man whose way is hidden”** — To a man whose way is hidden: see, when it was asked “why is light given to him that is in misery,” he shows here that the way is hidden to man, because if he now does well, he does not know what he will do at the end. Or sometimes things thought to please God displease him. “And God hath surrounded him with darkness,” because, though he desires heavenly things, yet he does not know what is disposed within concerning him. There is also about him the darkness of ignorance: he is forgetful of the past, does not find the future, hardly knows the present, cannot penetrate the inner workings of God’s dispensation. But he who looks hard at this darkness weeps and with every effort seeks the light above. Whence it sometimes happens that in devout weeping the brightness of inner joy breaks out. Whence follows:
3.24: **“Before I eat I sigh: and as overflowing waters, so is my roaring:”** — Before I eat I sigh, etc. To eat is to be fed by the light of contemplation, which none has but he who first groans in this exile, as where there are no goods, and sighs with desire. He describes the force of his tears: “and as overflowing waters.” Overflowing waters are borne with violence in many rolling waves; so in mourners there are many rolling waves, while they do not know what is decreed by God, while they recall their past and dread the future, and fear lest they go astray in their good deeds. When the scourges of God chastise them they suspect they have offended. Whence he adds:
3.25: **“For the fear”** — For the fear: for they weep because they fear to be forsaken, and lest the loving stroke be not of discipline but of vengeance. Whence: “Who knoweth the power of thy anger?” For sometimes it is grace that we call wrath, and sometimes wrath that we call grace. Hence it is needful to fear in all things: in prosperity, lest these things be given for greater blinding, not for comfort, as is wont to happen to the good; lest in adversity it be the beginning of punishment.
3.26:
**“Have I not dissembled? have I not kept silence? have I not been quiet? and indignation is come upon me.”**
• Have I not dissembled? Although we always sin in thought, word and deed, yet when one is raised up by prosperity the mind is carried away more unbridledly through these three: because when it goes ahead with power it thinks high things of itself; and because no one resists, the tongue is unbridled; and because it may do what it likes, it thinks everything it likes rightly lawful. But the holy man then all the more holds back his heart from glory, lest by pride he lose what he does rightly in power (as the king of Babylon, lifted up above men over the city he made, was made lower than men); he restrains his tongue too from insults to his inferiors, and his work from the wandering of restlessness, holding himself back from lawful things. For he alone does not fall into unlawful things who warily restrains himself from the lawful. So Job sets forth what he was like in power, as an example.
• Have I not dissembled? Power held must be thought of for its usefulness and dissembled because of swelling; and the powerful man must know that he has power in order to do good. “Have I not kept silence?” See what he is in his mouth. “Have I not been quiet?” See what he is toward unlawful works. Or to keep silence is to hold back the mind from the voice of desires; to be quiet in power is to leave off the din of earthly business; because he who is not free of these hides from himself the light of the vision of God. Hence fish without fins are not eaten, because those that have fins leap above the waters; and only these pass into the body of the Church as food, because in that they serve lower things, they sometimes climb up to higher things with the mind, lest they lie always hidden in the depths; who then order outward things well when they flee to inward things and rest in the bosom of a calm mind; as Jacob is said to have dwelt at home, while Esau is called “a skilful hunter.” But it is plain that he scourges even those who do these things, in order to purge them, because our perfection is not without fault; whence he adds: “and indignation is come upon me.” Hence, with great art, being about to speak of the blows, he first set out his right deeds, so that each may consider what punishment awaits the wicked if he so chastises the just here; as: “if the just man shall scarcely be saved, where shall the ungodly appear?”

4.1: **“Then Eliphaz … answered”** — Job’s friends had come out of piety, but they spring forward into words of contention, not with a wicked intention, but because they believe he has been struck for iniquity. They ought rather to have weighed his words by his past life, and, even if they thought otherwise, to have spoken humbly; not to add a wound to the stricken man by immoderate words, but to join him in weeping, not to show off their knowledge. Yet their sayings are in many things right and strong and great in themselves; whence the Apostle uses their authority; yet the Lord rebukes them, but by comparison with a better, saying: “you have not spoken the thing that is right before me, as my servant Job hath.” Although wonderful things are said, they are said proudly against the holy man’s adversity; so Paul weighs them by their worth, God rebukes what was spoken incautiously by the character of the persons. Among right things they slide into perverse ones; so heretics hide evil things in good, that they may be received, and infect good things with evil, that they may corrupt.
4.2:
**“If we begin to speak to thee,”**
• this is said because he was about to speak against him
• If we begin to speak, etc. They begin softly, but break out into harsh things. So heretics put forward smooth words, lest they be guarded against, but bring in harsh ones after.
**“perhaps thou wilt take it ill,”**
• he judges others by himself
• by these words it is plainly hinted that they had made up their minds to offend him
**“but who can withhold the words he hath conceived?”** — or: can, as if none, according to what is felt
**“but … the words he hath conceived”** — But … the words he hath conceived: the perfect do not even conceive perverse things in their heart which they must hold down by silence; others conceive wicked things, but hold them back with great force of silence; others both conceive them and at once bring them out, light in their thinking, headlong in their tongue. Of these is Eliphaz, who from his own experience thinks the same of all.
**“who can withhold”** — Who can withhold: as though he wished to hold back; by which he hints that in speaking he will give offence.
4.3:
**“Behold thou hast taught many,”** — or: many
**“Behold thou hast taught many”** — Behold thou hast taught many: they are certain goods which even he who wants to accuse admits. How great was he before, who, though occupied in ordering so many of his own affairs, also freely taught others, showing right things by deed and word. But what the accuser says good of him he turns to an accusation, saying: “But now the scourge is come,” etc., as if: you have not kept the right things you used to say. But note that the wicked speak even of the good deeds of the just, which, being known, they cannot deny, lest they seem wicked, and so that they may be the more believed in the evils they bring in; and they turn these very goods into a heap of guilt. Here, then, Job is rebuked as having said right things but not kept them, as though a wicked man by his own testimony; lower down he is noted as speaking badly, that he may be silent. And these are the two ways in which the wicked attack the good: saying either that they speak wicked things, or that they do not hold to the good they speak.
**“and … the … hands”** — those wishing to fail in some good
**“thou hast strengthened the weary”** — you taught those who were weary of working to persevere
4.4:
**“them that were staggering”**
• tottering, doubtful
• those who doubted whether to begin, or whether to persevere in what they had begun
**“Thy words have confirmed”** — drew them to the good side
**“and … the trembling knees”** — in which fear first appears
**“thou hast strengthened”** — or: strengthened
4.5:
**“But now”** — see, what you teach is not in you
**“the scourge is come upon thee”** — tribulation
**“and thou faintest:”**
• you did not strengthen yourself
• so quickly
**“it hath touched thee”** — the scourge
4.6:
**“Where is thy fear, thy fortitude, thy patience, and the perfection of thy ways?”**
• which you pretended to have toward God
• Thou faintest, etc. Where is thy fear? As if he wondered at virtues lost, which he puts in fitting order. As in the way of the world boldness begets strength and fear weakness, so in the way of God boldness begets weakness and the fear of God strength; because he who is joined to God is raised by a certain power above all things. Fortitude is shown only in adversity; whence patience is added, because he has made progress in fortitude, as it were, who bears others’ evils unmoved. From patience perfection is born; whence man is said to possess his soul in patience, that is, to live rightly in all things and to master all the motions of the mind by virtue; for he who conquers himself is strong against all things. But since he has rebuked him by inveighing, he now adds, as though exhorting:
4.7:
**“Remember, I pray thee,”**
• as if: it appears that they were not true in you
• as if to say: you suffer what you deserved
**“Remember, I pray thee”** — Remember, I pray thee: but this too he does reprehensibly. For the innocent and upright are often utterly destroyed here, even if they are kept for eternal things. But those who serve God not for an eternal but for an earthly reward invent for themselves what they seek, and, presuming to teach, when they preach earthly security they show by all their labours what they love.
**“who ever”** — of the past
**“being innocent”** — innocent in deed and upright in heart
**“perished”** — that is, is afflicted by losing his goods
4.8:
**“On the contrary I have seen those who work iniquity, and sow sorrows”** — frauds, which bring sorrows
**“and reap them,”** — while they profit, while they prosper in them
**“On the contrary I have seen those”** — On the contrary I have seen those: he sows sorrows who speaks them; he reaps them who prevails by speaking frauds. Or he sows sorrows who does perverse things; he reaps who prospers in them. These do not perish, as he says, but live here more happily than the just. For God allows some to prevail here, so that the life of the just may be more cleanly purged; others he punishes soon, lest he be thought to neglect human affairs and pass over many evils, so as to strengthen the hearts of the innocent who are faint-hearted. He would have spoken more truly of all at the end; it could have been said generally that the innocent and upright does not perish, because even if he is worn down here, he is restored with true salvation with God; and the wicked perish, because even if they grow high here, at the end they will be struck the harder. But because he says “Remember,” it is plain that past things are brought back to mind, not future things foretold.
4.9:
**“by the blast”** — judging
**“Perishing … of God”** — at some time
**“Perishing by the blast of God”** — Perishing by the blast of God: we blow air when we draw it from outside in and give it back from inside out. So God is said to blow in requital, because from outward causes he conceives within the counsel of judgment, and from inward counsel sends forth the sentence outwardly; that is, from our evils which he sees outside he disposes judgment within, and from the inward conception brings about condemnation outside. Or God is said to blow, that is, to be angry, by a likeness, because when we are angry we are puffed up by the blast of fury. So God blows in anger when he thinks of vengeance, when after long patience he who is calm in himself seems stormy to the guilty, since they are troubled before him by their guilt. Typically. The same of the heretics. The lion: the devil, for his cruelty. The lioness: the city of the world, Babylon, joined to the lion. The whelps: all the reprobate begotten by them. From these the saints guard themselves; but the heretics, secure, think they have overcome everything. As if to say: we are not scourged because we conquer the strength of the devil, and the voice, that is, the glory of the world, and the teeth, that is, the persuasion of the reprobate. The tiger, again the devil, for his manifold cunning; or the ant-lion, weak against those who resist, strong against those who consent; which they say has perished because it has no prey in them. They repeat this for joy, because what is said for joy is often repeated. Such men think they surpass all by wisdom. Whence he adds: “Now there was a word spoken to me,” etc. Heretics pretend to hear hidden things, whence they also preach secretly, so that their preaching may be thought holier, not equal to others’. “By stealth,” because they do not enter by the door with the others, but seek chinks of wicked understanding; and because a thief fears the light, he adds:
4.10:
**“The roaring of the lion”**
• which is plain in you
• The roaring of the lion. After warning him gently, he rebukes him openly. The roaring of the lion, that is, the severity and terror of Job himself; the voice of the lioness, the talkativeness of his wife; the teeth of the whelps, the greed of his sons, is destroyed. He exults at the roaring as at a thing condemned. He compares Job also to the tiger, for the spots of pretence. For the hypocrite, who seems upright, has hidden vices which, breaking out sometimes, change his colour. The prey is the glory of the just, which he snatches for himself. So, thinking that holy Job had held the goods he knew in him through hypocrisy, he says: “The tiger hath perished,” that is, the variety of your pretence is extinguished, because the flattery of praise has been taken away. For ‘tiger’ the Septuagint here reads myrmicoleon, which in Latin is ‘lion of ants’, or, more expressly, ‘ant’ and ‘lion’. It is a small animal which, hiding in the dust, lies in wait for ants and eats them; but to birds and other animals it is an ant, by which it is eaten. By this he notes that Job was timid against the lofty and bold against those under him; but now his pride has no prey, because, being struck, he is kept from hurting others.
**“and the voice of the lioness”** — of his wife
**“and the teeth of the whelps of lions”** — the greed of his sons
4.11: **“The tiger hath perished for want of prey,”** — the glory of the just is the just’s own, but to the wicked it is a prey, not their own, which they sometimes usurp
4.12:
**“Now … to me”** — because I am so great
**“there was a word spoken … in private”** — which, revealed to me, no one knows, because it was without voice and without sound
**“and … by stealth as it were”** — faintly and secretly
**“my ears … received the veins of its whisper.”** — but because a thief fears the light, he adds: “In the horror,” etc.
4.13:
**“In the horror of a vision by night, when deep sleep is wont to hold men,”** — when the senses are asleep, imaginings do not thrust themselves on the soul through the senses
**“In the horror of a vision by night”** — In the horror of a vision by night: they say they perceived the veins of the divine whisper in the dread of a night vision, because, to boast of lofty things, they say they could hardly grasp them. But while they so mark out lofty things, they are witnesses against themselves of wickedness; for in a night vision things are seen doubtfully.
**“when deep sleep is wont to hold”** — When deep sleep is wont to hold: that is, while all below sleep in torpor, we keep awake to perceive high and heavenly things. And when they see this sometimes despised, they pretend to fear what they say. Whence he adds:
4.14:
**“Fear”** — of mind
**“seized upon me, and trembling,”** — of body
**“Fear seized upon me”** — Fear seized upon me: to seem wonderful in high things, they pretend to be terrified at what they invent; and yet they are bold to bring out what they assert they could hardly hear. Whence: “And when a spirit passed before me,” etc.
**“and all my bones”** — if there was any strength
4.15:
**“And when a spirit passed before me,”** — because he knew him to be incomprehensible, he says he passed
**“stood up”** — what wonder if here, in the presence of a spirit, the hairs stand on end, when even the bones are terrified
**“the hair of my flesh”** — superfluous and empty thoughts
4.16:
**“There stood one”**
• because he alone is unchangeable
• There stood one, etc. To show that they have known incomprehensible things, they say that the spirit did not stand but passed; and they pretend that they saw an unknown face, to show that they are known to him who cannot be known by the human mind.
**“whose countenance I knew not,”** — because I did not fully know him, but as through an image
**“an image before my eyes”**
• namely the Son, who is the image of the Father and the art in the creation and government of things, is perceived first, and through him the Father also
• An image before my eyes: because heretics often picture to themselves in images the God whom they cannot behold spiritually.
**“and I heard the voice as it were of a gentle wind:”**
• all these things that follow, to the end of his speech, he perceived in the vision
• The voice as it were of a gentle wind, etc. Because they rejoice that they are more intimate than the rest in knowing his secrets. For they do not teach what God speaks openly, but what is breathed to them, as it were, secretly. The things said above can truly be brought forward by those who think rightly; so we repeat them in the person of Job’s friends, who, even if they err in their correction, yet do not err in their knowledge of the truth; or of the heretics, who hold not the life of knowledge but only its words. Here Eliphaz is shown to be of great knowledge, but he was not humble in it, because he arrogated to himself spiritually the common good.
**“there was a word spoken to me”** — There was a word spoken to me: the Son of God; “in private,” because he “was with God.” This is said to the faithful when he is made known to believers. Or the word is the speech of inward inspiration through the Spirit hidden in the heart, which cannot be known except by him who can have it. Whence of this Spirit it is said: “whom the world cannot receive,” because it loves visible things, while the Spirit ascends to invisible things alone. So what few hear within is unknown to the greatest part of men. Or “in private,” because it sounds silently in the heart without the din of speech. “And by stealth as it were,” because swiftly and secretly; for unless the mind is hidden from outward things it does not penetrate inward ones. It receives not the whisper but its veins. The whisper is the inward speech itself; the veins are the ways by which it comes to our mind, because sometimes it pricks us with love, sometimes with terror, and in other ways. So to hear the veins of the whisper by stealth is to know faintly and secretly the hidden ways of divine inspiration. Or he who whispers speaks secretly and does not utter his voice but imitates it. So when God now intimates something of himself to us, he whispers, not as he is; but he will speak in the future, when he shows himself as he is. Or the veins of the whisper are all created things, by which we gather knowledge of the Godhead. But these too by stealth, because we weigh even his wonderful works only swiftly and faintly; but the more the uplifted mind considers God’s power, the more, held back, it dreads his uprightness. Whence he adds: “In the horror of a vision by night,” etc., that is, in the dread of hidden contemplation, in which nothing is seen plainly, but as it were in images. But to this none attains unless fleshly desires are held down. Whence: “when deep sleep is wont to hold men.” He is awake who attends to the cares of the world; he sleeps who flees them restlessly. This is Jacob, who sleeps on his journey and sees angels; that is, in the course of this life he closes his eyes to worldly things, which fault opened in the first parents to covet. And no one is brought to see inward things unless he is withdrawn from the things that entangle outwardly; whence: “Be still and see that I am God.” But the more the mind, raised in contemplation, beholds higher things above itself, the more terribly it trembles in itself. Whence: “Fear seized upon me … and all my bones,” that is, the stronger deeds; because they do not think their good things worthy of the examination of him whom they behold, which by themselves seemed of some value. Whence it is said: “All my bones shall say: Lord, who is like to thee?” The flesh has no word, because weak things are wholly silent before you; but the strong things praise the great one and tremble. Hence it is that Manue, having seen the angel, fears, but the woman dares; because when heavenly things are seen, the spirit which sees first is struck with dread, but yet hope presumes; because hope rises up to greater things from that by which the spirit is troubled. So because, when God’s justice is seen, our goods too seem foul, he rightly says: “Fear seized upon me, and all my bones were affrighted.” Hence Paul too, not conscious to himself of his merits, does not presume with God as judge. But when the uplifted mind gazes on inward things it cannot stand above itself for long, because, if the spirit carries it to the heights, the flesh weighs it down by the weight of its corruption. Whence: “And when a spirit passed before me.” The spirit passes while we are present, because we see invisible things not steadily but swiftly; nor is the mind fixed long in the sweetness of contemplation, because, beaten back by the light, it is called back to itself; and, advancing with great strength, it sees that it cannot see what it ardently loves; yet it would not love ardently unless it saw to some extent. And because however much one has advanced he feels the goad of the flesh, he adds: “the hair of my flesh stood up.” The hairs are any superfluities of human corruption, the thoughts of the old life; if we shut these out of the mind we cut the hairs from the flesh, so that we are not wearied by pain. Whence Moses: “let the Levites shave all the hairs of their flesh.” But we see these more subtly in ourselves when we penetrate high things; whence it is rightly said now: “when a spirit passed, the hair of my flesh stood up.” For when the mind sees true things it torments itself more harshly over superfluous ones. So when the spirit passes the hairs are terrified, because before the force of compunction superfluous thoughts flee; because the inward vision kindles the soul against itself, and when it strictly cuts away unlawful things, the mind clings more broadly to contemplation, and almost fixes the spirit that was passing; yet even this lingering of contemplation does not fully lay open the power of the Godhead. Whence he adds: “There stood one whose countenance I knew not.” ‘One’ is said only of him whom we either will not or cannot express; and so here he explains: “whose countenance I knew not”; because man, who by obeying was to become spiritual even in the flesh, by sinning was made fleshly even in mind, so that he thinks only what he draws into the mind through images of the body; but hardly, by striving, with bodily form held down, does he know himself; and so a way is made for him to think of the eternal substance, and, all imaginings cast off, he beholds it to some extent; and even if he does not grasp what it is, he certainly knows what it is not. He seems to stand, since all things pass except those he keeps in himself, as the good. Hence when he says “when a spirit passed” he rightly adds “there stood one,” as if: him whom I felt in passing I found does not pass. He passes, because he cannot be held when known; he stands, because he is known to be unchangeable. But because whoever grasps anything of him beholds it through his coeternal image, he adds: “an image before my eyes.” The image of the Father is the Son, who says: “No man cometh to the Father, but by me.” “And I heard the voice as it were of a gentle wind.” The voice of the wind is the knowledge of the Holy Spirit, who is said to be both gentle and vehement upon the apostles; because he tempers his knowledge to us so that he can be known in some fashion, and not as he is, but slips faintly in, as to the bleary-eyed; vehement, because he who touches gently shakes our poverty mightily. So because the mind of man, however much it stretches itself, hardly ever sees anything of him, it is rightly said: “and the voice as it were of a wind”; but because even a little of divine knowledge teaches us perfectly, he adds what he learned from this hearing:
4.17:
**“Shall man be justified in comparison of God”** — Shall man be justified in comparison of God? This he knew in contemplation, that human justice compared with divine is injustice; as a lamp that shines in darkness is dark in the sun; which he could know, because he who sees the light knows what to think of darkness.
**“or shall a man be more pure than his maker?”** — Or shall a man be more pure than his maker? This he thinks who murmurs against him who scourges. But he ought to know that he who made wonderful things out of nothing does not scourge wickedly, and the founder of nature is not an unjust judge of fault. Although this man rebukes Job unjustly, yet he rightly describes the measure of the creature in comparison with the Creator. So a man thinks himself purer than his maker if he prepares a complaint against the scourge; and without doubt he puts him below himself when he reproves his judgment concerning his own affliction.
4.18:
**“Behold they that serve him”**
• the angels
• Behold they that serve him: although an angel remains unchangeable in his state, yet inasmuch as he is a creature he has the alternation of changeableness, and so he is not steadfast. For if this nature were not changeable, since it was well made, it would have fallen in none. But it had from free will to fall or to stand; and in those that stood it was merit to have fixed the motion of their changeableness by the zeal of their will. The proof of this changeableness is what he adds of the apostate.
**“are not steadfast”** — of themselves, without changeableness
**“and in his angels”** — the apostates
**“he found wickedness:”** — these things can be said generally of all, because even the good are not without swelling; or it is understood only of those who pursue the foulest pleasures of this muddy life, whom he here notes to differ from himself
**“and in his angels he found wickedness”** — And in his angels he found wickedness: by comparison with whom human weakness is gathered.
4.19:
**“How much more shall they that dwell in houses of clay,”** — earthly bodies
**“How much more shall they that dwell in houses of clay”** — How much more shall they that dwell in houses of clay: the same, earthly bodies. The earthly foundation, too, is the substance of the flesh. The moth comes from the garment and by coming corrupts it. The garment of the soul is the flesh, from which fleshly temptation is born, by which it comes to destruction, and so it is. If the angels are not unchangeable of themselves, how is man thought to remain in good, who has in himself that by which he grows old from newness? Or the angels are the holy teachers, because not without fault on this journey do they dwell in houses of clay who exult in an alluring life. The moth does damage but makes no sound; so the minds of the wicked, because they neglect to consider their losses, lose innocence; for they lose innocence from the heart, truth from the mouth, continence from the flesh, and, as time comes on, life from their age. But they do not see that they are losing these, being occupied with the cares of the world. Whence he adds:
**“who have an earthly foundation,”** — they subsist in body and soul on earthly food
4.20:
**“From morning till evening they shall be cut down:”** — spiritually; or their whole life is a cutting down
**“and because no one understandeth,”**
• thinks again what is good
• that he is being cut down
**“they shall perish for ever.”** — From morning till evening they shall be cut down, etc. That is, from the beginning of their life to its end they are wounded by committing iniquity, and, cut down, they fall into the depth. Or morning is prosperity, evening adversity; but through both they perish, because through prosperity they grow wanton, through adversity, impatient, they rise up to madness. “And because no one” of them, namely of those from morning to evening, “understandeth” what is kept here for the afflicted good, what is to come for themselves, who think these things good. But because not all are so forsaken, he adds: “And they that shall be left,” that is, the despised of the world, whom the world has left as unworthy; as the Egyptian boy, that is, the lover of the world, black with sins, is often despised and left by the world, so that he does not run with it but lies numb, broken by adversity. But David, that is, Christ, finds him and turns him to his love, and feeds him with the food of the word, and makes him guide of the way, that is, his preacher; by whose guidance he destroys the feasters, that is, the gladness of the world, which scorned to have him for a companion.
4.21:
**“And they that shall be left”** — the good, the vile, the cast-off
**“shall be taken away from them:”** — from the wicked, who lose this life and do not gain the eternal, as the wise do, etc.
**“shall be taken away from them”** — Shall be taken away from them: because God has chosen them for himself.
**“they shall die, and not in wisdom.”** — in sin
**“they shall die, and not in wisdom”** — They shall die, and not in wisdom: having put in the lot of the just, he returns to the destruction of those who do not understand. The reprobate despise the just because by their death they seek invisible things, or by death seek invisible life. But they themselves, who flee both death and wisdom, wholly forsake wisdom, not willing to die for the truth; yet they do not escape death.

5.1:
**“Call now”**
• because they are consumed so, and you are one of them
