• Since he has brought this forward truly against the wicked, though covertly setting Job among their number, puffed up with the pride of wisdom he adds open mockery against Job: “Call now,” that is, if in your affliction you cry out, God does not answer, that is, does not grant the effect, because you despised him in your quiet; “and to some of the saints,” that is, you have no saints as helpers in your affliction, because you had none as companions in your cheerfulness.
**“if there be any that will answer thee”** — because you are not even worthy of an answer
5.2:
**“Anger indeed killeth the foolish”**
• it troubles the wise but does not kill him
• Anger, etc. After the mockery he adds a sentence which is true, but wrongly applied to Job: “Anger killeth the foolish.” Meekness keeps in us the image of God, who is always calm; but anger scatters it, depriving us of many virtues, because while it takes quiet from the mind, the Holy Spirit does not rest there. But one anger is that which impatience makes, another that which zeal makes. The first comes from vice, the second from virtue, which Phinees had; with this we ought to be angry at the errors of our neighbours as at our own; it is “better than laughter, because by the sadness of the countenance” the neighbour “is corrected.” But it must not rule the mind, but be subject to reason as a handmaid; let it not be immoderate, but in avenging sin consider time and measure, first conquering itself by patience. This anger troubles the wise; but anger through vice slaughters the foolish.
**“and … the little one”** — the lower; or the one who loves eternal things
**“and envy slayeth the little one”** — And envy slayeth the little one: that is, while he envies one he thinks greater, as the devil envied man, Cain his brother, whose sacrifice he grieved to see preferred, and Esau too his brother. So the little one is slain by envy, because unless he were lower he would not grieve at another’s good. Or the little one is he who loves earthly things, the great one he who loves eternal things. So the little one is slain by envy, because no one dies of this plague except him who craves these earthly things, which do not come whole to many. Hence, if we desire anything, we envy him who receives it wholly, or who, by having a part, narrows the amount for us.
5.3:
**“I have seen a fool”** — as perhaps you were
**“with a strong root,”**
• fixed in the earth
• I have seen a fool with a strong root. Morally. Because he is made solid with all his desires in earthly love. Hence Cain first built a city on earth. The stranger to heaven lives more happily here.
**“and I cursed”**
• I rejected
• And I cursed: because when, at the sight of the prosperity of the wicked, the feet of the weak stagger, the strong, seeing what punishment follows on their glory, at once reject their prosperity. The weak man changes with the state of things: while he sees prosperity he praises it; when it changes he judges it to be nothing. But the firm man considers, along with the glory itself, the punishment that follows, and at once condemns it. But because those who prosper in the world draw many with them, he adds: “His children shall be far,” that is, his followers.
**“his beauty”** — that is, of earthly glory
**“immediately”** — without waiting for the change
5.4:
**“His children shall be far”** — imitators
**“from safety, and shall be destroyed in the gate,”** — in the day of judgment
**“in the gate”** — The gate of the kingdom is the day of judgment, in which the elect enter into glory; before it the children of this world are fools, but then they will be destroyed.
**“and there shall be none to deliver them”**
• of old, judges sat in the gates of cities, taking care that no one should enter unjustly or be driven out from there
• And there shall be none to deliver them: because there the truth delivers those whom here it presses down by discipline.
5.5:
**“Whose”** — the fool’s
**“harvest”** — goods
**“Whose harvest”** — Whose harvest: each one has a house of understanding, by which he understands and speaks right things. But because he neither loves nor does them, he fasts from the harvest he has; but he who hungers for justice, hearing right things from him, refreshes himself; whence: “What they say, do.”
**“the hungry shall eat,”** — the one longing for God
**“and … him”** — the fool
**“the armed man shall take … by violence,”**
• the devil
• with the weapons of pestilent persuasion
• the devil is armed when he bends the wise to himself, deceiving not openly but secretly
**“and the armed man shall take him by violence”** — And the armed man shall take him by violence: the devil is beaten as one unarmed when, suggesting open evils, he tries to take away all good things at once. But he comes armed when he passes by some good things untouched and secretly corrupts others.
**“and the thirsty shall drink up”** — And the thirsty shall drink up: the fool often has riches, a gift of understanding and the sacred words, but does not drink, because he does not exercise himself in them. But another, who has no such gift, has thirst, and by loving and studying attains what the gifted man does not know. This is “the stellio,” as Solomon says, which “supporteth itself on hands, and dwelleth in kings’ houses.” For he helps his understanding with his hands, and leaning on his hands holds the building of the kingdom, like the stellio, a creature that has no wings for flight. But sometimes birds that have wings, that is, the gifted, sit in the brambles. But because it would be asked why the gift is given to the negligent and the studious man is held back by slowness, he answers:
5.6:
**“Nothing upon earth is done without a cause”**
• the slothful man receives the gift so that he may be punished more justly for his negligence
• Nothing upon earth is done without a cause: because thereby the one is more justly punished for negligence, the other crowned for his study. But because we are taught to understand right things not only by study but also by persecutions, he adds:
**“and sorrow doth not spring out of the ground”** — And sorrow doth not spring out of the ground: the ground, that is, the elements of the world, are turned into the punishment of offenders. Whence it is said: “the whole world shall fight with him,” that is, for the Lord, “against the unwise.” But sorrow will not spring only from them, because punishment is not born of the things that strike, but of those who by sinning forced out the blows. But the more the outward punishment chastises, the more the mind is raised to things above; whence he adds:
5.7:
**“Man”** — the flesh
**“is born to labour”** — because the body is scourged so that the mind may fly to God
**“and the bird”** — the soul
**“to fly”** — or: for flying
**“Man is born to labour and the bird to fly”** — Man is born to labour and the bird to fly: because it is impossible to be without labour on this pilgrimage; but in that the flesh is afflicted, the mind is raised to seek high things. Or man, that is, the fleshly man, feels the evils of the world because he greedily craves its goods. But he whose mind passes beyond these, raised like a bird to the heights on the wing of hope, feels no evil, since he rejoices even in scourges. But because no one is able for these things by his own strength, he adds:
5.8:
**“Wherefore I will pray”** — that you too may fly to the labour
**“to the Lord,”** — by whom I know this is granted
**“and address my speech to God:”** — that he may hear me
**“Wherefore I will pray to the Lord, and address my speech to God”** — That is, I ask him by whom I know these things are granted.
5.9:
**“Who doth great things and unsearchable”** — Who doth great things and unsearchable: which no one is able to search out, which are wonderful even if they have grown cheap by use. It would be of less greatness to do great things if anyone could search them out, and again of less greatness to do unsearchable things if they were few; and so he adds:
**“and wonderful things without number:”** — these things can be understood of the elect, where the humble with lofty mind pass beyond all temporal things, and the afflicted are set upright by health, not by madness
**“wonderful things without number”** — Wonderful things without number: because the greatness of the divine works can neither be discussed as to their quality nor numbered as to their quantity.
**“I have seen a fool”** — I have seen a fool. Mystically. The fool is the people of the Jews, who scorned the wisdom of God in the flesh. “With a strong root,” because it overcame the elect by killing them; but the heretics too reprove its unbelief. This is what Eliphaz despises by cursing. The children are those it begets in unbelief. “Far from safety,” because even if happy here, they will afterwards be punished more heavily. “In the gate,” that is, in Christ, in whose presence the Jews fell who had flourished in the Law before his coming; whom no one delivers, because by killing the Redeemer they lost the deliverance offered them. “Whose harvest”: the harvest is the words of God, which, because the fool had them but did not eat, the hungry Gentile eats by understanding them; the harvest lost, he himself also perishes. “The armed man,” that is, the devil, carries him off by killing the life of faith in him. “The thirsty”: the Gentiles are watered by the streams of the sacred word. The same words are both harvest, because they refresh the fasting mind, and riches, because they order behaviour with great beauty.
**“Nothing upon earth is done without a cause”** — Nothing upon earth is done without a cause: he puts this because some thought that all scourges come by natural causes, according to the nature of the elements, and not from the fault of the one struck.
5.10:
**“Who giveth rain upon the face of the earth, and watereth all things with waters:”**
• with spiritual gifts
• Who giveth rain. Allegorically. These words are mystical, because Job’s friends had been taught by his company. He gives rain to the earth when he pours the grace of preaching into the dry hearts of the Gentiles.
• Watereth all things with waters, when he fills man with the Spirit to bear fruit. Man is called all things because he has something in common with all things. Or all things, that is, rich and poor and all the differences of men, because reward follows a good work. He adds:
5.11:
**“Who setteth up the humble on high”**
• those who despise temporal things he raises to heavenly ones
• Who setteth up the humble on high, so that those now despised may judge with the Lord.
**“those that mourn”** — Those that mourn: because the more they are troubled now by adversity, and chastise themselves by lamenting, the loftier the health they will have, even in this life. These things can be understood of the elect, where the humble with lofty mind pass beyond all temporal things, and the afflicted are set upright by health, not by madness, like those who rejoice when they have done evil. But these grow cheerful from the certainty of eternal salvation.
5.12: **“Who bringeth to nought the designs of the malignant”** — Who bringeth to nought the designs of the malignant: when the reprobate devise evil, God sometimes, lest they prevail against the good, takes away their strength so that they lack the effect of the deed, and are guilty before God in conscience.
5.13: **“Who catcheth the wise in their craftiness, and disappointeth the counsel of the wicked”** — Who catcheth the wise in their craftiness, and disappointeth the counsel of the wicked: because human deeds serve God’s counsels fittingly even when they resist them; as in the selling of Joseph, so that he should not be worshipped; in Saul’s demand for foreskins, so that David should be destroyed; in the death of the Lord, so that not all should believe in him. God grants some things in mercy, permits others in anger, which he then turns to the use of his own counsel; so that the things which fight against his counsel serve his counsel, and what is done without his will is not contrary to his will. Whence: “Whatsoever the Lord pleased he hath done.”
5.14:
**“in the day”** — that is, Christ
**“They shall meet with darkness”** — the wicked
**“They shall meet with darkness in the day”** — They shall meet with darkness in the day. Mystically. Because in the very presence of the truth they were blinded by the error of unbelief, seeing the miracles of Christ and doubting his Godhead.
**“and grope … as in the night”** — that is, they will try
**“as in the night”** — As in the night: by groping we seek what “we do not see with our eyes.” The Jews had seen miracles and still, as though groping, asked: “If thou be the Christ, tell us plainly.” But Christ could not be held long in their hands. Whence he adds:
5.15:
**“But he shall save”** — God
**“from the sword of … mouth”** — from detraction
**“But he shall save … from the sword of their mouth”** — But he shall save … from the sword of their mouth: the sword of the mouth is the accusation of the Jews. The hand of the violent: the Gentiles who crucified him. But Christ overcame these by rising again, in whom, the needy, that is, the humble people of the faithful, the hope of the life to come is made solid. But the iniquity which now opens its mouth wide in insult to Christ will shut it through punishment; or, converted, it ceases from its injuries.
*Morally:* The same things of the wicked in general. “They shall meet with darkness in the day.” The mind of the envious man, when it is pained at another’s good, is darkened by the ray of the sun. “And grope at noonday as in the night.” The day of good work shines outwardly in the neighbour, but they grope as in the night, because, blind with spite, they busy themselves to find something to blame. Behold Lot, that is, the just man, with the wicked opposing him, is shut within the house and protected, that is, he returns to his mind and stays within. The blind Sodomites go round about, that is, the envious search out his deeds and words, and do not find the door, that is, an opening for blame, but grope at the wall, because everywhere the praiseworthy action of the just man meets them. “They shall grope.” But the poor in spirit, that is, he who is not lifted up in himself, is saved “from the sword of their mouth,” that is, from wicked persuasion. “And the poor from the hand of the violent,” that is, from hostile power, so that he is neither drawn away by the flatteries of persuasion nor broken by the pain of torments. The poor man is not drawn away, because his hope, fixed in eternal things, is made solid against these. When the poor man comes to the fruit of this hope, the proud man falls dumb and draws in his mouth, because torments bind the tongue that spoke against the just in detraction. But that the elect may escape punishment and reach the reward, he must be purged here by scourges. Whence he adds: “Blessed is the man whom God correcteth.”
**“their”** — of the wicked
**“and the poor from the hand of the violent.”** — the humble
5.16: **“And to the needy there shall be hope, but iniquity shall draw in”** — will shut
5.17:
**“Blessed is the man whom God correcteth:”** — or: by the Lord
**“refuse not therefore the chastising of the Lord:”**
• God sometimes lets the soul be wounded by the longing of its desire, so that it may rise stronger and be healed
• And because he is blessed: “refuse not therefore the chastising of the Lord.” He refuses it who complains that he suffers unjustly. So Eliphaz, thinking that Job is struck for cleansing, not for the proving of his fortitude, because Job speaks freely, asking the causes of his striking, thinks he refuses the chastising of the Lord. So heretics turn to evil what is rightly done by the Church.
5.18:
**“For he woundeth”**
• the flesh
• For he woundeth: in two ways God wounds those whom he brings back to salvation. Sometimes he strikes in the body to heal the mind; sometimes, without outward scourges, he strikes the hardness of the mind with longing for himself, and so heals it, which lay dead and secure in the world. But while the mind pants after God and despises all worldly things, at once all things are turned into temptation for it and afflict it; but while it is worn by passing labour it is freed from lasting labour. And so he adds:
**“and cureth”** — divinely
5.19:
**“In six troubles he shall deliver thee,”** — by six he understands all the evils of the present world, which runs its course in the six days assigned to work
**“and in the seventh”** — troubled
**“In six troubles he shall deliver thee, and in the seventh”** — In six troubles he shall deliver thee, and in the seventh: the number six, which the seventh follows, signifies the work and course of the present life, because on the sixth day God, completing all things, made man, “and on the seventh he rested,” which has no evening, that is, no end. So he delivers in the seventh trouble, so that in the seventh evil may not touch; because here he wears down in fatherly teaching, but on the day of judgment hides from the lash.
5.20:
**“In famine he shall deliver thee from death:”** — even then he breathes into his faithful, without sound, what is to be done
**“In famine”** — In famine: he counts up the evils of the present life and the helps of God. The famine of the mind is the silence of the word of God; when this is withdrawn, the temptation of the flesh, which is the battle, grows strong. But God, even in famine, snatches the soul from death, because he refreshes it with his word.
**“and in battle”**
• in the temptation of the flesh
• And in battle: he makes them strong against the temptations of the flesh. But one so made sometimes fears detraction. Whence he adds:
5.21:
**“from the scourge of the tongue”**
• from the word of detraction or insult
• From the scourge of the tongue: that is, from the reproach of insult, for which a man, mocked, ceases from good. Whence David: “and from the sharp word.” From this the holy man is hidden, because while he does not seek praise here, neither does he feel insults. But because after these someone fears the tortures of the body, it follows:
**“Thou shalt be hidden”** — thou shalt be set free
**“and thou shalt not fear calamity”** — And thou shalt not fear calamity, of persecution. But because such a man prepares for himself security in the terror of the judgment to come, he adds:
5.22:
**“In destruction”** — of the body
**“and famine”** — of the soul
**“In destruction and famine”** — In destruction and famine: the destruction is hell, which torments without; the famine is hunger, because they will be separated from the sight of the eternal bread. As they sinned within and without, so they will be punished within and without. Or “from the scourge of the tongue,” that is, from the sentence of eternal damnation, which is: “Depart, you cursed, into everlasting fire.” And the just man will be hidden from the calamity that comes, because in that strictness he will be comforted with the gentle voice: “I was hungry, and you gave me to eat”; and he will laugh, cheerful from glory, no longer suffering with the damned, clinging to divine justice by sight; and it would be a lessening of beatitude if he wished anything he could not fulfil. But because here he tastes the beginnings of the security to come, so that he may not fear the old enemy, so that he may not shudder at his assault in the moment of death, he adds:
**“of the beasts of the earth”** — the devil and his accomplices
**“thou shalt not be afraid”** — at the going out of the present life
**“and the beasts of the earth”** — And the beasts of the earth, which at the time of death are let loose to snatch souls; but he who did not follow them when they flattered does not fear them when they rage; and the beginning of reward is security of mind at death. But when one lives well, he must take care not to glory in being singular, despising others, but to think again of the common good. Whence he adds:
5.23:
**“But … with the stones”** — with the elect of the Church
**“of the lands”** — namely: it will be
**“thou shalt have a covenant”** — your fellowship
**“But thou shalt have a covenant with the stones of the lands”** — But thou shalt have a covenant with the stones of the lands: the lands are, as it were, the divided nations of the Church, differing in customs and language. The stones are the elect, who are set in the building. So he who lives rightly joins himself to the stones by a covenant, because in forsaking the world he binds himself to the saints by imitation; whence the attack grows, by which, however, worn down, he is more humbly subject to God. Whence he adds:
**“and the beasts of the earth”**
• evil spirits will not attack you
• And the beasts of the earth: not ‘at peace’ but ‘peacemaking,’ because they do not have peace but make peace; because the more fiercely a man is attacked by the devil, the more he is driven to love, and a firmer peace is made with God. Or the beasts are the motions of the flesh, which, pressed down by continence as in a cage, even if they roar in tempting, yet do not break out into the deed, as into the frenzy of biting; in this they are peacemaking. Or, because they disturb, that place where one lives with no contradiction is loved the more, and so they drive to the love of inmost quiet.
5.24:
**“And thou shalt know that thy tabernacle is in peace”** — And thou shalt know that thy tabernacle is in peace, etc. Peace is either begun, which is conceived here from the longing for God, or full, which will be in the future from the sight of God. So when the mind is subjected to God, or the flesh to the mind, the tabernacle of the just man, that is, the body which the mind inhabits, has peace, the motions of the desires being reined in under justice. But this chastity of the flesh is nothing if gentleness of mind in the love of neighbour is not present. Whence he adds:
**“and visiting thy beauty thou shalt not sin”** — And visiting thy beauty thou shalt not sin: our beauty is our neighbour, in whom we see what we are; he visits him who goes to him with the steps of love, and, having looked at himself, comes down to him. And this is the tree that brings forth seed after its kind, that is, the mind which considers another from itself and brings forth the shoot of right work. Behold Paul, who comes near to all, coming down to them indeed but not falling. And he fully conquers sin who weighs from himself how he may be widened in love of his neighbour. But when the flesh is restrained and the mind exercised in virtues, it remains that he teach by speaking the life he keeps in his conduct, because from the seed of good work he gathers rich fruits of preaching. Whence he adds:
5.25:
**“Thou shalt know also that thy seed shall be multiplied”** — Thou shalt know also that thy seed shall be multiplied: for he receives the gift of speaking well who lives well, and his conscience does not hinder him as he speaks. Hence it is that the Egyptians, made slaves, receive corn for seed, who, while free before, had received it for eating; because when we are fully subject to God we are filled with the word of preaching. Before, as free men, we are fed with the sacred word, and yet are taken up with some things we seek in the world. From preaching follows a great offspring of the faithful. And this is:
**“and thy offspring like the grass of the earth.”** — the word of preaching
**“and thy offspring like the grass of the earth”** — And thy offspring like the grass of the earth: that is, countless. Or it is compared to grass because, forsaking the withering glory of the world, it grows green with inward hope. But it is not enough for the just man to do these great things outwardly unless he also penetrates to eternal things by contemplation. Whence he adds:
5.26:
**“Thou shalt enter into the grave in abundance”** — Thou shalt enter into the grave in abundance: the grave is contemplation, which hides in its inmost places those dead to the world; and the active life in a way buries, covering those dead to wicked ways. But contemplation buries more perfectly in abundance, because it has first gathered the works of the active life. He is not a perfect preacher who puts works after contemplation, or contemplation after works. Whence Christ, the pattern of life, works miracles in the cities by day and prays through the night on the mountains. Those who contemplate, fixed in the love of God, drink in what they pour out for the good of their neighbours.
**“as a heap of wheat is brought”** — As a heap of wheat is brought: because the time of action comes first, of contemplation last. And the perfect man must first exercise his mind in virtues, and afterwards store it in the barn of quiet. Or the grave is eternal rest, in which one rests the more truly the more perfectly the life of corruption is put to death. He enters it in abundance who, after gathering the works of this life, wholly dead to this changeableness, is hidden in the secret place of the true light, like wheat. Because the just feel persecutions in a time not their own, but in their own they go in like grain into the barn.
5.27:
**“Behold, this is even so, as we have searched out:”** — as if: I have not lied
**“as we have searched out”** — As we have searched out: by this he notes that he spoke above of the grave, the beasts, the stones, the tabernacle and suchlike not according to the surface, but sought the inner things in them.
**“which thou having heard, consider it thoroughly in thy mind.”** — to attend to
**“which thou having heard”** — Which thou having heard: words of boasting. Even if he taught well, it is unskilful to want to teach a better man; whence the sayings of the friends, even if right, are reproved as not rightly said.

6.2:
**“O that my sins, whereby I have deserved wrath, and the calamity”**
• the punishment of sin
• O that my sins, etc. Allegorically. Touched by scourges, he is provoked by words, so that, roused to defend himself, he might fall into obstinacy; but as, struck, he gave thanks in silence, so, provoked, he answered rightly: “O that my sins were weighed.”
**“that I suffer, were weighed in a balance”** — as if: O that the balance would come, that is, Christ, who has two scales, mercy and justice; mercy is light in forgiving, justice of greater weight in correcting and punishing
6.3:
**“As the sand of the sea this”** — the balance
**“a balance”** — A balance: Christ, holding in the Father’s hand the scale of mercy and of justice, shows sin to be light by loosing it through mercy, and calamity to be of heavy weight by dying. He also gives this grace, that the calamity itself may be known. For blind man rejoiced in exile as if in his homeland; but God, appearing outwardly, calls man back within, so that, having seen what he lost, he may grieve heavily at what he bears. So he says: “O that … were weighed,” that is, the evil of our damnation is believed light, but O that he would come who, showing the homeland, might teach that the exile is heavy. Calamity is compared to the sand which is driven out by the surge of the waves, because sinning man, moved by the waves of temptations, went out from the inmost things to the outward. It is called heavier because the punishment is shown to have been hard, while the fault is lightened through mercy. But he who through the grace of Christ has a foretaste of the homeland groans amid present things, where the ignorant laugh, weighing the judgments of God by which he is afflicted. And this is:
6.4:
**“For”** — namely: therefore
**“the arrows of the Lord”** — the blows of the Lord
**“therefore my words are full of sorrow: For the arrows of the Lord”** — Therefore my words are full of sorrow: For the arrows of the Lord: that is, the stroke of God’s punishment, which does not leave me uncorrected as it leaves many, but drinks up my spirit, that is, checks my pride, so that I say: “My spirit hath fainted away.” And I not only groan at what I suffer, but fear what you threaten. And this is:
**“are in me, … whereof”** — when they are
**“the rage”** — vengeance
**“drinketh up my spirit”** — pride
**“the terrors of the Lord war”** — The terrors of the Lord war: lest eternal death follow after this. But because he longs for the coming of the balance, he adds with what ardour the Gentiles and Judea thirst for it.
6.5:
**“Will the wild ass bray when he hath grass? or will the ox low when he standeth before a full manger?”** — as if: no
**“Will the wild ass bray”** — Will the wild ass bray, that is, the ass of the field. The ass is the Gentile people, which, as nature brought it forth outside the stalls of discipline, so remained wandering in the field of pleasures. The ox: the Jew, who, set under the yoke of God, gathering proselytes, drew the name of the Law through the hearts he could. Of both peoples many, like Job and Simeon, awaited the coming of Christ. Their grass and hay is the Incarnation, with which they are filled: “for all flesh is grass.” Refreshed by its grace, the wild ass no longer groans, and the ox does not have the manger of the Law empty, since it has received him whom the Law itself foretold. Hence, when born, he is laid in a manger, that he might refresh with the hay of flesh the animals fasting in the Law. But because before the coming of Christ the Law was held not spiritually but carnally, he adds:
6.6:
**“Or can an unsavoury thing be eaten,”**
• the unsavoury thing can be understood either as the Law without spiritual understanding, or as the philosophy of the Gentiles concerning the incarnation of the Word of God
• Or can an unsavoury thing be eaten: the same. MORALLY. He longs for the balance; we already live by faith in it, but yet for our cleansing we suffer its arrows, and fear with the terror of what is to come. But because we are sons, we ought not to fear him as Lord, but love him as Father and pant after him, where we may be fed with food, that is, his eternity, for which we now bray. Whence: “Will the wild ass bray?” The wild ass is the people which in the field of faith is bound by the thongs of no office. The ox: prelates, pressed by the yoke of offices. The food of both is the eternal refreshment, which, fasting in exile, they ardently desire. But the wicked oppose this intention by their words and ways, which are unsavoury things offered to the good, that they may let them into the belly of delight; among which words, pressed on the ears importunately, beget temptation in the heart; and although reason rejects them and the tongue condemns them, yet what is judged outwardly is hardly conquered within. So, when the saints, raised up to eternal life, drive unsavoury things from the heart, they also separate themselves from such words; and this is: “Or can an unsavoury thing be eaten?” But those already set on high, apart from fools, often, while they take care only to bear their own hard things, are not girded up for the love of truth. Whence he adds:
**“Or can an unsavoury thing be eaten”** — Or can an unsavoury thing be eaten: salt is the virtue of hidden understanding, without which the Gentiles would not be subject to the Law commanding hard things, nor taste that which, tasted carnally, brings death; because it binds offences with hard punishment, and because it teaches guilt but does not blot it out. But when they recognized the truth in it, they eat, pressed by their desires, what before they would not touch, seeking amid those carnal things him whom they love ardently. But these things fit Judea too, which through the Law had salt from the knowledge of the one God, and scorned to receive the unsavoury Gentiles; because the divine sentence, with death set before it, had forbidden Judea to make a covenant with foreigners and defile its life. Hence he says: “Or can a man taste that which when tasted bringeth death?” But, according to the elect converted to Christ, when its own people rejected the word of God it turns to the Gentiles, and those whom it did not even touch in fellowship it now receives, hungering to convert them, suffering the straits of preaching, which is despised among its own.
**“or can a man taste”** — Or can a man taste: it is hard to seek what tortures, what drives away life; but often, when one is on high, he bends down to bear the evils of fools, so as to draw them. For with his desire for heavenly things increased he is pressed hard, and for the sweetness of those things he does not fear the bitter things of the world. Whence, after the impossible taste of death, he adds:
6.7:
**“The things which before my soul would not touch, now, through anguish”** — for longing
**“The things which before my soul would not touch”** — The things which before my soul would not touch: that is, the evils of the world are now sweet foods for love of heaven. And since these are sweet: “Who will grant that my request may come?” namely:
6.8: **“Who will grant that my request may come?”** — here it is plain that he did not refuse the chastising of the Lord; because some refuse it, the Lord in anger draws back his hand from correction, even when it has begun
6.9:
**“And that he that hath begun may destroy me,”** — namely to destroy me
**“that he that hath begun may destroy me”** — That he that hath begun may destroy me: the adversary destroys, and man falls away from virtue. God destroys, and, broken from vices, he is made solid in virtue. So he who longs to draw near to God through scourges says: “that he that hath begun may destroy me”; because sometimes God begins the destruction of vices, and man, advanced in that very beginning, is lifted up; and so the enemy, shut out, creeps back more heavily, taking other spirits with him, and destroys the virtues.
**“that he may let loose”** — that is, stretch out
**“that he may let loose his hand”** — That he may let loose his hand: that is, exercise its effect. For while, against one puffed up by long prosperity, he does not exercise his love through scourges, he holds his hand bound, as it were, from striking vices; whence he says to the sinning people: “I will be angry with thee no more,” and: “my jealousy hath departed from thee.” “And cut me off”: for when pain or temptation strikes us, the pride of the mind is cut down and falls, so that it now seeks the hand of one who lifts it up.
6.10:
**“And that this may be my comfort, that afflicting me”** — And that this may be my comfort, that afflicting me: as if: some he spares here so as to strike them for ever; but let him strike me here, not sparing, which is my comfort. For the saints fear being spared here. That he said this not with a swollen but a humble mind he shows in these words:
**“nor I contradict”** — that is, I will not murmur at his examinations
**“the words of the Holy One.”** — that is, of God
**“nor I contradict the words”** — Nor I contradict the words: the words of God to us are not only things said but also things done, as here the striking of Job, which he does not contradict by murmuring; for he even calls holy him whom he endures striking him.
6.11:
**“For what is my strength”** — For what is my strength: the strength of the good is one thing, of the wicked another; for theirs is to conquer the allurements of the flesh and the world, to endure evils here for eternal things. The strength of the wicked is always to love present things and to hold out unfeelingly against the scourges of God, not to rest from craving temporal things even in adversity, to put hope in themselves. Of both Isaias says: “They that hope in the Lord shall change their strength.” For in saying not ‘shall take’ but ‘shall change,’ he made it plainly known that the strength which is laid aside is one, that which is begun another. The wicked man bears evils and dangers for the world; the just man is weak to suffer these for the world; he sees the end, how short this life is, and refuses to suffer for what he does not love. So he says:
**“For what is my strength … or what is my end”** — For what is my strength … or what is my end: that is, I cannot bear evils for the world, because I am not strong in desiring it; because when I consider the end of this life, why should I suffer for that which I scorn? For I am not like the hardness of the wicked, who are unfeeling as stone and brass. Stones when struck give no clear sound, which brass does; but because a stone lacks life, it has no feeling in its sound. So some are so hard that even when struck they give no sound of humble confession. Others give it, but not from the heart; and so they do not feel the good things they speak, and, not fulfilling them, cry out without life. But Job is neither so hardened as to be silent from confession when struck, nor ignorant of the meaning of his voice. By denying that he is strong through madness he shows that he is strong through a state of health. But lest he claim this for himself, he puts whence he has it, and, so to speak, the weak man has strength; whence he adds:
6.13:
**“Behold there is no help”** — Behold there is no help: also, for the merit of greater strength, he adds how he is forsaken by those near him:
**“and my familiar friends also”** — And my familiar friends also: if he is despised outwardly, within he presides on the throne of judgment. For he breaks out into sentences.
6.14: **“He that taketh away mercy from his friend”** — He that taketh away mercy from his friend: a friend is any neighbour; when we do him good, he helps us to life. From love of God love of neighbour is born, because he who neglects God does not know how to love his neighbour. Hence, about to say: “Thou shalt love thy neighbour,” etc., he first said: “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God.” And through love of neighbour the love of God grows strong; whence: “he that loveth not his brother whom he seeth, how can he love God whom he seeth not?” Yet this love of God is born through fear, but by growing is changed into affection. And God, so that it may be seen how near or far each one is from charity, strikes some; in which he both teaches them and betrays false friends, and gives those not struck an occasion of good work. So he who takes away mercy from the stricken forsakes the fear of God, because he openly shows that he did not love him, and wickedly sets himself up against God, whom he acknowledges neither as merciful in himself nor as just in the stricken. In Job is signified the life of the whole elect people, of which he is a member. The reprobate are joined with the good in faith and sacraments but not in charity; whence they are also called brethren. And he compares those who pass by to a torrent which passes from the mountains into the valleys, which, gathered by winter rains, dries up in summer. For those who forsake things above for the world seek the depths from the mountains. In the winter of this life many, to be dried up in the summer of judgment, pass swiftly, that is, without obstacle or difficulty, because the ascent is in labour and the descent in pleasure. A rock is pushed upward with labour, easily it slides back to the bottom; things grow with labour that quickly fall. Or they pass suddenly into the valleys, that is, to the lowest places of punishment, they from whom the days of life are snatched daily. But there are some who wish to act rightly, but some things in the present stand against them in their weakness, and while they fear to suffer these, they offend God. These are they who fear the hoary frost, which freezes below; and the snow, which falls from above, that is, eternal punishment, falls upon them; and those who fear things to be trodden underfoot from below suffer things to be feared from on high. These, if they are glorious now, at the time when they are scattered will perish outwardly too, having lost all these things, they who long ago perished inwardly by neglecting eternal things; of whom it is rightly said:
6.17: **“and after it groweth hot”** — And after it groweth hot: that is, when through knowledge of punishment they begin to burn, they will be separated from the delight of the flesh which they held with desire. The wicked do not understand eternal things except when they are already punished for earthly ones; then the mind boils, and kindles itself with the fire of a late repentance; then its hardness is melted through punishment. Hence the prophet: “vexation alone shall make you understand what you hear.” This they are to suffer then; meanwhile they are entangled in these things.
6.18:
**“are entangled”** — Are entangled: everything entangled is folded back upon itself; so the wicked, sometimes wishing for good things, stretched as it were outside themselves, are folded back, when tempted, to their accustomed evils. Or they are entangled who, even if sometimes, one wickedness overcome, they lift a foot, another reigning entangles them back even into that which they had conquered; as he who has scorned avarice is still lustful, and for the price of lust returns to avarice; so the vices hold their runaway by taking turns, and bind his steps as with snares. Whence often, weary, they return to their pleasures and do not care for the things that last. Whence he adds:
**“they shall walk in vain, and shall perish”** — They shall walk in vain, and shall perish: because they carry nothing with them of the fruit of their labour. But the just man does not appear empty in the sight of the Lord; for he carries the sheaves of justice. And he frightens men from imitating those by their end.
6.19:
**“Consider the paths”** — Consider the paths: Thema means the south wind, Saba a net. The south wind, which loosens the limbs with warmth, is here the slack looseness of living. The net is the bond of action; and man is entangled in loose acts while he does not perfectly forsake the world, while he goes not with strict zeal but with loosened steps, like one held back from the things of God by fleshly love of parents. He says “Consider,” because we love perverse things when doing them, but when we see them in others we judge them; whence, returning to ourselves, we blush for such things.
**“wait a little while”** — Wait a little while: because whatever ends is little; but he who thinks this long does not care for eternal things. Having spoken of the shortness of life, he rises against the wicked with the voice of the just.
6.20:
**“They are confounded, because I have hoped:”** — the wicked come to the good to accuse them, and when they cannot, they blush
**“They are confounded”** — They are confounded: because, namely, the wicked try to draw the good back from hope through harsh things; if they succeed, they exult; if not, they blush to have been cruel in vain. Whence he adds also what happens in the requital:
**“they are come also”** — They are come also: at the judgment the wicked come to the just, because they will see their glory, so that they may grieve more heavily seeing what they have lost. Then shame covers them, when conscience burns them as a witness. The same spiritually. Job’s friends are confounded, because while they cannot bend me to despair they are confounded; they are come, when they now recognize the steadfastness of my mind within, and they blush. He shows them to be of the number of those who do not fear God unless terrified by their own or others’ adversity.
6.21:
**“Now you are come”** — Now you are come: as if: I feared God even before adversity; you, who do not fear God out of love, are afraid only because of the blow.
**“Did I say: Bring to me”** — something
**“Did I say: Bring”** — Did I say: Bring: the Church does not need the substance of heretics, of whom Job’s friends are a figure, that is, fleshly wisdom; and it refuses to hear from them even the right things which they sometimes say against the devil about conversion, because by these they draw men to unbelief. The hand of the enemy is the strength of Satan. The mighty are the evil spirits.
6.23:
**“Or deliver me from the hand of the enemy,”** — of Satan
**“and … out of the hand of the mighty”** — of the evil spirits
**“rescue me”** — as if: no
6.24:
**“Teach me”**
• but you cannot
• Teach me: this is either joined to what goes before, or said by itself as a rebuke.
*Morally:* Did I say: Bring? Against the rich of the world, the poor man of God; against the powerful, the oppressed; against the wise, the fool, answered three things: because the poor man does not seek their substance, nor the oppressed help against the mighty, that is, the evil spirits, nor the fool the teaching of fleshly wisdom. For the good, with mind fixed on high, despise all these things as though far below; whence also, humble within, they contradict the powerful of the world freely, where love sharpens their words; they are neither free from pride nor submissive from fear, but uprightness makes them free, and their weakness humble; and what they despise in themselves they despise in others also.
**“and I will hold my peace: and if I have been ignorant in any thing, instruct me.”** — this too
6.25: **“Why have you detracted the words of truth, whereas there is none of you that can reprove me?”** — Why have you detracted, etc. He who corrects others ought to be clean; for how does an eye weighed down by dust see a spot in another? Or how does a hand that holds mud wipe away filth? Hence it is said figuratively to David: “Thou shalt not build me a temple, because thou art a man of blood”; because he who is given to fleshly acts must needs blush to instruct the minds of others spiritually. So he said: “Why have you detracted,” that is, with what rashness do you blame things heard, you who, not knowing the causes of my striking, bring forward blameworthy things to rebuke me? Two kinds of speech are harmful: that which praises perverse things, and that which even reviles right things; in the one is favour, in the other anger; for this he reproves Job’s friends. One arrives at this vice from idle words. Whence he adds:
6.26:
**“You dress up speeches only to rebuke, and … to the wind”** — in vain
**“and you utter words to the wind”** — And you utter words to the wind: to utter words to the wind is to say idle things, by which the harmful tongue is let loose, and to speak of others as is usual; afterwards it leaps forth into detraction of them too, from which come quarrels and hatreds, and peace perishes. Hence Solomon: “He that letteth out water,” that is, lets the tongue loose into a flood of talking, “is the head of quarrels”; because he who does not rein in his tongue scatters concord. Hence Ecclesiastes: “He that putteth silence on a fool appeaseth wrath.”
**“you utter words”** — You utter words: those who slip away through harmful words fall from every state of uprightness; because the mind, like water, when hemmed in returns to the heights whence it came, and when let loose runs away through the depths. Likewise, by the restraint of silence it returns to the knowledge of itself; but by superfluous words it is scattered out of itself and laid wholly open to the enemy. Whence it is said: “As a city that lieth open and is not compassed with walls, so is a man that cannot refrain his own spirit in speaking.” Silence is the wall of the mind, within which, however, it is sometimes pressed too tight; and when it is restrained from speech immoderately, it boils within with thoughts, and despises others who speak the more freely because the more secretly; and when it suffers some injustice, the pain boils more within, because it does not flow out through a calm tongue. Also, when it sees the evils of others, it denies them the use of medicine. Whence the prophet: “Woe is me, because I have held my peace.” So let the tongue have a door, which is now shut, now opened.
6.27:
**“upon the fatherless”**
• that is, the humble
• Upon the fatherless: see how great a weakness he weighs himself to be; and though he complains that they wish to overthrow him, yet he testifies that he is a friend, because charity, even when hurt, does not cease. The Church does the same against heretics. And the good, being strong, do not fear to suffer adversity; whence he adds: “However finish what you have begun.” Nor, being kind, do they cease to preach the truth to their very persecutors; whence he says: “give ear,” etc. For they are not well armed with the shield of patience against what is inflicted, by which they may be safe, without the sword of the word by which they may conquer. This is what the Apostle says: “Charity is patient, is kind.” If one is lacking, it is not charity: namely if one bears with those he does not love, or does not bear with those he loves.
6.28:
**“However … what you have begun”** — that is, the troubles
**“finish …, give ear,”** — because I do not tremble
**“and see whether I lie.”** — as if he said openly: though you are ungrateful for correction, yet I do not hide my inner things from you
**“see whether I lie”** — See whether I lie: because the humble man does not command what he says by authority but persuades by reason; but because opponents, given the occasion of reasoning, break loose into contention, he adds:
6.29:
**“Answer, I beseech you, without contention”** — Answer, I beseech you, without contention: because heretics, in their questionings, do not aim to reach the truth, but to seem victors.
**“and speaking that which is just, judge ye”** — And speaking that which is just, judge ye: because he who speaks is subject to the judgment of the hearer. Between his heart and his tongue let there be a fair judge, so that nothing goes forth hastily from the heart through the tongue, but he examines it before he speaks. And because they first judge rightly of their own words, he adds about others’ words:
6.30: **“And you shall not find iniquity in my tongue”** — And you shall not find iniquity in my tongue: because folly does not sound to you in me if it does not proceed from your own conscience. So the Church first destroys the falsehoods of its enemies, afterwards opens the truths, for which there is no room while false things are held for true. By the tongue is meant open speech; by the jaws, hidden pondering; because what the Church preaches outwardly it keeps by living.

7.1:
**“The life of man … is a warfare”** — The life of man … is a warfare: he expresses what he rightly thinks. Warfare, or temptation according to another translation, which comes to the same thing, because temptation is a warfare, that is, a fight against demons. And it is not said that life is tempted, but that it is temptation itself, because, being now corrupt, it begets troubles for itself out of itself; and though now among good things, yet out of weakness it always brings forth what virtue must kill, and it feels evils springing up within the very goods, as sloth in the leisure of contemplation, vainglory in abstinence. But by the name of warfare something more is hinted: that it is both a fight and daily tends to its end; whence the course of a soldier’s service is also expressed.
**“and his days are like the days of a hireling”** — And his days are like the days of a hireling, who wishes the days to pass quickly so that he may come to the reward of his labour. So is every just man; and as the hireling sweats at others’ labours but prepares his own reward, so the just man is subject among worldly and evil things so that he may lay hold of heavenly things. Take care that the day does not go empty of work and the reward be lessened. He suffers hard things that he may be crowned the more; though the wage is already in his heart, yet the heat is felt the more heavily in the body, so that afterwards there may be refreshment in rest. And this is:
7.2:
**“As a servant longeth for the shade”** — rest
**“As a servant”** — As a servant: every elect man is well called a servant so long as he is under the yoke of this corruption, before he comes into the liberty of glory.
**“as the hireling”** — As the hireling: who would grow weary from the heaviness of his work if he were not relieved by the hope of the end; but when he has seen it he thinks nothing of what he feels.
7.3:
**“So I also have had empty months”** — without reward
**“empty months”** — Empty months: empty of the things of the world, because the good do not seek them by their acts; and they endure the wearisome nights of adversity when they are already in the torment of the body. Or empty months, because now there is labour but not yet reward.
**“and … wearisome nights”** — the darkness of adversities
**“wearisome nights”** — Wearisome nights: he counts those who heap up for themselves the adversities of the present time by exercising themselves in virtues. The Church has empty months in the weak, who do earthly things without the reward of life; wearisome nights in the strong, who bear manifold things. And it is well said not days but months, because they feel not in the actions themselves but at the end that they have acted in vain. Or by night ignorance is meant; he who returns from it to the light washes with weeping what he did emptily. So he, as a servant longs for the shade, has empty months, because the more he seeks the eternal refreshment, the more he sees how emptily he laboured for this life. And as the hireling waits for the end, he counts wearisome nights, because the more he sees the reward from the end of the work, the more he groans that he long did not know what he seeks and that he laboured in vain.
7.4:
**“If I lie down to sleep, I shall say: When shall I arise?”**
• when shall I come to the day
• If I lie down to sleep, etc. According to the history, the mind of one in pain is expressed, which, driven by grief, wanders through various desires: in the night it longs for the day, in the day for the evening; because pain does not let what is present please, and, having found this heavy, it awaits something else with consoling desire; but not even so does the pain end. Whence:
**“and again”** — namely, in the day I say
**“I shall look for the evening, and shall be filled with sorrows even till darkness.”** — And shall be filled with sorrows. And this is the cause of the sorrow:
7.5:
**“My flesh is clothed with rottenness and the filth of dust,”** — because he sat on the dunghill
**“is clothed”** — Is clothed. The same more subtly in the Church. By sleep, the torpor of idleness; the evening, which suits sleep, figures the desire for idleness. By rising, the exercise of action. So the mind of man, because it would not stand when it could, now cannot stand even when it will, but is always changed by desires, so that at rest it longs for action, busy it longs for rest. Or to sleep is to lie in sins, from which the just man tries to rise; but when he has risen he feels himself lifted up by the very virtues. Hence he also seeks to be tempted by adversities, by which he may be better kept, saying: “prove me and try me.” Or the evening is the temptation to sin, and it provokes the more just man more sharply. Whence Moses too says that one is led from morning to evening, when the shadow of temptation follows the light; which yet in the elect is not night but evening, because it darkens the light but does not put it out; and it is not even feared, but awaited as something that will profit them. But however much they strive, they have no whole health here; whence he adds: “and shall be filled with sorrows even till darkness,” because he does not find security until he wholly leaves the time of temptation. And he adds the cause of the sorrow.
**“My flesh is clothed”** — My flesh is clothed: that is, the fleshly life which I lead is either defiled by evil working, or, though restrained from that, is darkened in memory by the images of sins, which rise like dust before the eyes. The Church in some feels the rottenness of the lust of the flesh; in some, given to earthly acts, it is sprinkled with dust. Of both he adds:
**“my skin is withered and drawn together.”** — the outer part of the body, which, when it draws no moisture from the inner parts, withers and is drawn together
**“my skin”** — My skin: the skin in the Church are those who give themselves only to outward cares, whose hearts despair dries up; and so they are drawn together, not stretched out through long-suffering toward eternal life. They cling to present things; which happens because they do not attend to how fleeting this life is. But the Church does the opposite.
7.6:
**“My days have passed more swiftly than the web is cut by the weaver,”** — therefore the things that flow in do not please me
**“My days … more swiftly”** — My days … more swiftly: as the web grows thread by thread, so life grows day by day; but the more it grows the more it tends to the cutting. But the swiftness of life, which is always failing, passes even the haste of the web. And so the elect do not fix their heart on it. Whence he says:
**“and are consumed without any hope.”**
• without meditation
• whence
• And are consumed, etc. That is, I place no trust in these things; what the reprobate do, I do not.
7.7:
**“Remember”** — therefore forgive me my sins
**“that my life is but wind,”** — short
**“that … is but wind”** — That … is but wind: eternal life is solid; this life is judged neither solid nor lasting. And so: “Remember,” that is, look kindly on one passing swiftly; because the consideration of human brevity is an offering pleasing to God. And because after life passes there is no place to deserve pardon, he adds:
**“and my eyes shall not return to see good things.”** — so as to do right works
**“and … shall not return”** — And … shall not return: that is, after death the mind, seeing its requital, is not called back to show good works; whence the rich man, despairing of himself, which is an increase of punishment, prays for his brethren. Behold, life passes; what follows remains.
7.8:
**“Nor shall … behold me”** — will console
**“the sight of man”** — the mercy of the Redeemer
**“thy eyes are upon me”** — without judgment
**“and I shall be no more.”** — Afterwards too: “Nor shall the sight of man behold me.” That is, the mercy of the Redeemer, which softens the hardness of sinners, as when he looked upon Peter. He does not free after death him whom grace does not reform before. Not the sight of man, but “thy eyes”: that is, as strict judge you will see in order to strike; and I, who here, awaited for repentance, stood, will now be no more. This fits the just man, who fears everything he does and knows beforehand that, mercy removed, he would perish; and he does not stand before the eyes, because life is hardly enough if justice presses on him: “Nor are the stars,” that is, those who shine with holiness, “pure in his sight.” The guilt and punishment of the human race are briefly added:
7.9:
**“As a cloud is consumed, and passeth away:”** — vanishes
**“As a cloud is consumed”** — As a cloud is consumed: a cloud, made thick, is raised to the heights, is driven by the wind so that it runs, is dissolved by heat so that it vanishes. So the heart of man shines forth by its talent, is driven by the breath of demons through evil desires, but at the regard of the judge fails as by the heat of the sun; and after it is handed over to the places of punishment it does not return to that to which it clung by love, which is the house of the mind. Or hell is despair, into which one dead in sins falls, and afterwards there is no way of return. The despairing man is compared to clouds, because he is darkened by gloom and made thick by many sins, but is scattered by the brightness of judgment. Such a man does not return to his house, that is, to the heart, of which it is said to the man who was healed: “Go into thy house.”
**“so he that shall go down to hell”** — because he raised himself to the heights, driven by the wind of temptations
**“shall not come up”** — to this life
7.10: **“neither shall his place know him any more”** — Neither shall his place know him any more: man’s place is God, who created him to abide in him; man deserted him by sinning. But God sought the runaway through the Incarnation. But afterwards he does not know the one condemned who now acts more wickedly, saying: “I know you not.” Fearing this, the just man repents anxiously, and does not spare his mouth, but confesses his sins. The affliction of the spirit, which is the fear of foreseen judgment, opens the mouth. The reprobate also confess their sins, but not with a contrite spirit so as to weep for their evils. But this bitterness of mind makes him speak against himself and quarrel, and now attends to other things which, secure, he passed by, and he puts before himself the good things he received from God and the evils he gave back. But, repenting thus, spurning pleasures for eternal things, he still feels opposition from the corruption of the flesh.
7.11:
**“Wherefore I”** — Job
**“will not spare my mouth,”** — but will confess
**“I will speak in the affliction”** — in confession
**“of my spirit:”** — or: in the pain of heart
**“I will talk with the bitterness”** — that is, I will spur myself to compunction
**“of my soul.”** — of life
7.12:
**“Am I a sea,”**
• he speaks as if I must be bound fast
• Whence he adds: “Am I a sea?” The prison is the flesh, which hinders from high things. The sea: the hearts of the fleshly. The whale: the devil, who swims through slippery thoughts. He, then, with his fleshly ones, is rightly ploughed by the prison of his punishment, so that they may not do whatever evil they wish. But I, who am already in heaven in heart, why am I pressed by the prison of the flesh? This is said not proudly but out of love of the truth. But God puts it off for our good. Kept back from true rest, he returns to the heart as to rest against the strife of the flesh. And this secret place of the heart is called a bed or couch, where, weary from outside, he turns over the hidden words of his thoughts. But there too there is strife; because while the flesh, like the wall of the house, is shaken, the bed too is disturbed; and the more he thinks, the more he sees how strict the judge is, what shame it is to be confounded before the angels and all the saints, what punishment then follows; and so he is frightened as by sleep and vision, because he imagines it somehow, but does not see the thing as it is. But literally too the devil thrusts prosperity on the covetous and adversity on the timid through dreams, so as to affect them more; and the saints too, whom he is less able to tempt awake, he tempts more heavily asleep; which God kindly permits, so that not even sleep may be empty of the reward of suffering. Hence God is said to do what the evil spirit does. He has set out how many stumbling-blocks there are on every side; now he adds counsel against them.
7.13:
**“If I say: … shall comfort me”** — against this, that he is delicate in the flesh
**“My bed”** — the mind, in which I rest
**“and I shall be relieved speaking with myself on my couch:”** — in the secret place of the heart
7.14:
**“Thou wilt frighten me”** — afterwards, while I await the just judge
**“with dreams”** — through imaginings
**“and … with visions”** — of the night
**“terrify”** — with terror
7.15:
**“So that … rather chooseth hanging”** — of longing for high things
**“So that … rather chooseth”** — So that … rather chooseth: the soul is the intention of the mind, the bones the strength of the flesh. What is hung is lifted from the bottom. So the soul is hung up toward eternal things, so that the bones may die; because for love of eternal life it kills in itself all the strength of the outward life, so that it despairs, that is, wholly forsakes the goods of the present life, lest it put hope in them; and further it uses them lawfully, but the perfect man fails in them. And because I despair of these:
**“my soul …, and my bones death.”** — namely, that I may come to eternal life
7.16:
**“I have done with hope”** — of earthly things
**“I shall now live no longer:”** — I have no consolation in earthly things
**“spare me, O Lord,”** — that I may be consoled with eternal things
**“spare me, O Lord”** — Spare me, O Lord: that you may give eternal things, because by contempt of those these are better hoped for. While he asks to be spared he proves that he did not despair of God. That “he chose hanging” is “I have done with hope”; from the same he brought in “spare me”; that “the bones choose death” is “I shall live no longer,” this the third time.
**“my days are nothing”** — My days are nothing: he who considers eternal things, returning to himself, rightly calls these days nothing, and dreads to be strictly judged. Whence he adds:
7.17:
**“What is a man that thou shouldst magnify him?”** — by the gift of reason, the pouring in of grace
**“What is a man”** — What is a man: God magnifies man with many a spiritual gift, and sets his heart upon him, because he judges more strictly for what he has given. But what is man? as if: even though magnified beyond himself by your gifts, yet because he is flesh, if he is judged without mercy he cannot bear it. Whence he adds further:
7.18:
**“Thou visitest”** — you raise up
**“him early in the morning”** — with the brightness of virtues
**“Thou visitest him early in the morning”** — Thou visitest him early in the morning: it is early morning when man comes from the night of vices and ignorance to the light; in which he is also at once proved; for lest he glory that he has good things from himself, he is allowed to be shaken by temptation, so that the height of God and his own weakness may be seen; as Solomon after wisdom is tempted by harlots. Man suffers this in the whole of this mortality. Whence: “How long wilt thou not spare me?”
**“and thou provest him suddenly”** — you humble
7.19:
**“How long wilt thou not spare me, nor suffer me”** — how long do you allow me to be struck by temptations
**“my spittle”** — My spittle: spittle slips from the head into the mouth, and is swallowed from the mouth into the belly. The head is God, from whom we take our beginning. The belly: the mind, which takes the food of understanding and rules all the members of actions. The spittle: the savour of inmost contemplation; in this way it passes to the mouth but not into the belly, because our understanding is now steeped in it, but the mind is not fully satisfied. It is in the taste, not in the fullness. Christ mixed this with the clay of human thought, and, man in the world, the man born blind is enlightened. But God will spare man fully when he lets him swallow the spittle, when he admits him to the perfection of his contemplation. He who wishes to deserve this confesses the evil he has done.
7.20:
**“I have sinned: what shall I do to thee,”** — that I may be washed from my faults
**“I have sinned: what shall I do to thee”** — I have sinned: what shall I do to thee? as if: I find nothing to offer you in recompense, because all the virtue of man is weak for washing away guilt. Or “what shall I do to thee?” as if: all good things profit not you but us.
**“O keeper of men?”** — O keeper of men: because he has so forsaken us that we cannot keep ourselves, and if we attempt anything we are weighed down by sins. Whence:
**“why hast thou set me opposite”** — an enemy
**“why hast thou set me opposite to thee”**
• Why hast thou set me opposite to thee: when man believed the serpent he became God’s enemy, and scorned to seek him. And God set him opposite himself, counting him an enemy for his pride. But this opposition of guilt is to man a weight of punishment, and he carries himself as a heavy weight while he bears so many things in the flesh, so many in the soul. So he had to be put under who proudly raised himself up; this is what is said: “a heavy yoke is upon the children of Adam.” Job says this with a groan; that things are so, he does not blame justice, but seeks mercy.
• Why hast thou set me opposite to thee: because, made lower, he is now opposed to the higher, that is, to God; and so our lower part, sensuality, has been made opposed to the higher, that is, to the spirit, so that they always fight.
7.21:
**“Why dost thou not remove my sin?”**
• of fleshly concupiscence
• Whence he adds: “Why dost thou not remove?” Behold the longing for the Mediator, “who taketh away the sins of the world.” Or sin will be fully taken away when man is changed into incorruption. So he longs for the Redeemer or for the resurrection; whence he joins both the punishment he deserved from his origin and the judgment he fears from his own action. Behold now it was said to sinning man: “Dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return.”
**“and why dost thou not take away my iniquity? Behold now I shall sleep in the dust:”** — or: I shall sleep
**“in the morning”** — In the morning: that is, at the coming of the judge, when all things are open. God’s seeking is to judge strictly, before whom not even the just man stands; but this is the comfort of deliverance, that the humble man says he cannot suffice. So he bewails the death which is now, and fears the judgment which threatens.

8.1: **“Then Baldad the Suhite answered, and said:”** — he sets upon him about hypocrites
8.2:
**“How long”** — that is, always
**“wilt thou speak these things, and how long shall the words of thy mouth be like a strong wind?”** — Then Baldad the Suhite answered, and said: How long, etc. It must be known first of all that, as Eliphaz chiefly charged the most holy Job with pride, though he also touched briefly on hypocrisy, so this man means chiefly to charge him with hypocrisy. But before he does so he puts something first, from which it is weighed how burdensome Job’s words were to him, namely words of edification. As though, then, he could no longer bear him speaking well, he broke out indignantly into these words, saying: “How long wilt thou speak these things?”, as if to say: why do you speak useless things? “And the words of thy mouth like a strong wind?”
**“How long wilt thou speak these things”** — How long wilt thou speak these things: because words of edification are heavy to the wicked man, as though he cannot bear them; and because he does not wish to be corrected, he accuses what is well said.
**“like a strong wind”** — Like a strong wind: while he attributes manifoldness to his speech, he blames the poverty of his understanding. And note that there are four kinds of speaking. Some are full both in mouth and in sense, who are to be praised; some narrow in both, who are to be pitied; some full in sense but unable to speak it out, who are to be helped; some poor in sense but torrents in tongue, who are to be despised; which this man twists into a charge against Job.
8.3:
**“Doth God pervert”**
• that is, cast down
• Doth God pervert: Job had neither denied nor been ignorant of these things; but it is the way of the wicked, lest they seem ignorant, to speak boastfully of good things known to all as though unknown. So Baldad, as though Job had grieved over the snatching away of his goods, praises the justice of God, but in the manner of false men, who praise God in prosperity, thinking these things owed to them as to just men, and say that others are scourged as for guilt; but if any adversity touches them, they blame God’s examination. So heretics, when they see the Church corrected by God, swell with perverse preaching, saying that they prosper by their merits and that she is worthily afflicted; and so they seek an opening to creep in. Reproaching also the deaths of others, as though they perished justly, they strike others.
**“judgment”** — judges unjustly
8.4:
**“Although thy children have sinned against him,”** — against him
**“and he hath left”** — forsook
**“them in the hand of their iniquity:”** — in the destruction of death
8.5: **“Yet if thou wilt arise early to God, and wilt beseech the Almighty:”** — Whence he adds: “Although thy children have sinned.” “If thou wilt arise early”: as if: let them be in the light, the Church in the night, which they call to rise through the knowledge of God and to wash away the past through the prayer of repentance, if clean in thought, upright in work.
8.6:
**“If thou wilt walk clean”** — namely, in thought
**“and upright”** — namely, in working
**“he will presently awake unto thee”** — He will presently awake unto thee, who now sleeps as to helping you, since you are straying.
**“and will make … peaceable”** — that is, he restores to you the security of tranquillity
**“and will make the dwelling of thy justice peaceable”** — And will make the dwelling of thy justice peaceable: that is, he will restore the tranquillity of the present life, which alone they reckon to be God’s reward.
8.7: **“that … thy former things”** — That … thy former things: because they promise both that lost things will be recovered and still greater rewards of the present life, or the dwelling of justice. They call the counsel of the mind that which is made peaceable, because if they draw men to their side, they fall silent from contention. They also promise riches of understanding, saying: “Insomuch that thy former things.” But because their words are not easily believed, they bend the sayings of the fathers into an argument for their error.
8.8: **“For inquire of the former generation, and search diligently into the memory of the fathers:”** — Whence it is added: “For inquire of the former generation,” etc. They warn not to look but to search, because they do not wish to be seen what is clearly plain to all.
8.9: **“we are but of yesterday”** — We are but of yesterday: sometimes they teach morally that present things are guessed from the past, namely from their passing, that these things are nothing. Whence he adds: “we are but of yesterday,” because if the former generation is recalled, this life is known to pass quickly like a shadow.
8.10:
**“And they shall teach thee:”** — as if: in the fathers you will learn that God does well to the good, but the hope of the hypocrite will perish
**“they shall teach”** — They shall teach: they praise the fathers with us, so that they may attack us the more from that.
**“out of their hearts”** — Out of their hearts: as if: you have simplicity of spirit in your mouth, not in your heart; they the opposite. Often the wicked, not attending to themselves, tear at the good, and either bring forward good things which they learned not by seeing but by hearing, or thrust on others the evils they themselves do; and so they excuse themselves in deeds and judge in words. So Baldad, a pretender to justice, says wonderful things against hypocrites, and presumes to teach the just man about things that would suit the wicked. A fool, who, while his gardens thirst, pours water into the river.
8.11:
**“Can the rush be green without moisture?”** — For he says: “Can the rush be green?” He compares the hypocrite to a rush or sedge, which grows green with the warmth of holiness, without the fruit of work; yet not without water, because he receives graces, to prophesy, to cast out demons, etc., but green in colour; while he seeks praises outwardly, proud, he grows on high, but is empty of fruit. The rush in flower is the hypocrite in praise. The sedge is not plucked by hand, because rising with sharp edges it cuts the hand; so the hypocrite, if plucked by the hand of correction, is angered for his wounded reputation and cuts at the life of the one correcting him, so as to show himself innocent not by his own acts but by others’ crimes.
**“or a sedge-bush grow without”** — or: without
8.12:
**“When it is yet”** — the rush
**“in flower, and is not”** — the sedge
**“plucked up with the hand, it withereth before all herbs.”** — loses its greenness
**“before all herbs”** — Before all herbs: the just too are herbs according to the flesh, because “all flesh is grass”; who wither, because their works fail with the life of the flesh. But the hypocrites’ wither before, because they soon forsake good things once they have obtained the things for which they pretended. “These are the grass upon the tops of houses, which withereth before it be plucked up.”
8.13:
**“Even so are the ways of all that forget God, and the hope of the hypocrite shall perish:”** — namely, in the day of requital
**“Even so are the ways of all”** — Even so are the ways of all: see to whom he compares the rush or sedge. The hope of the hypocrite is glory and suchlike worldly things, which perish; eternal things remain.
8.14:
**“shall not please him”** — which, even if it pleases now, will yet displease
**“His folly”** — when a great thing is sold for a cheap price
**“His folly shall not please him”** — His folly shall not please him: folly is to sell a great thing for a cheap price, that is, to do laborious good things for favour. In this he now delights, but in punishment it will displease him, and then he will know that all the things that passed away were nothing.
**“and his trust shall be like the spider’s web.”** — Whence: “And his trust shall be like the spider’s web.” The spider’s web is woven with care and scattered by a puff of wind. So whatever the hypocrite sweats out, the breeze of favour carries away.
8.15:
**“He shall lean”** — he will bend himself
**“upon his house, and it shall not stand:”** — it
**“He shall lean upon his house”** — He shall lean upon his house: the house of the mind is any thing which the soul inhabits through love. So the house of the hypocrite is favour. Or the house is confidence in his holiness, which will stand before men but not before God.
**“he shall prop it up”** — He shall prop it up: what cannot stand by itself is propped so that it may stand. So the hypocrite, when he sees his life falling in the judgment, props it with a count of his works, saying: “Lord, have not we prophesied in thy name, and cast out devils?” But the house of praise so propped does not rise, because in all he did he never lifted his mind from the earth; and so he is not raised to the reward of requital; so he will be rejected in the judgment. But before, he is held to be such by men.
8.16:
**“to have moisture”** — green
**“He seemeth”** — to himself
**“He seemeth to have moisture”** — He seemeth to have moisture: the rush, the hypocrite, seems moist in the night, that is, appears to men steeped in the grace of holiness, but before the sun, in the day of judgment, he will wither.
**“before the sun cometh”** — but the present reward will not stand, because
**“and at his rising his blossom”**
• of the hypocrite
• And at his rising his blossom: every plant is first brought forth from the earth, is touched by breeze and heat, nourished by rains, and at last brings forth the shoot of its seed. But the rush is born with its flower and brings forth the shoot of its seed along with itself. So the saints here grow by doing good, feel the heat, and at last at the end seek requital. But the hypocrite, as soon as he begins something good, receives the reward of praise, forgetting even what he was before; and the good things that become known before their time perish the more quickly, namely while the mind is not yet strengthened by humility; as new plants wither at a touch, a new wall falls easily which, when dried, does not yield even to the ram. Hence Moses: “Thou shalt not plough with the firstling of a bullock.” The hypocrite, even when he acts rightly, wishes to be seen by many. And so he adds about the rush:
8.17:
**“upon a heap of stones”** — he who carries treasure on the road wishes to be robbed
**“His roots”** — namely, of the rush
**“His roots … upon a heap of stones”** — His roots … upon a heap of stones: from the root are the thoughts. Stones, because ‘men’ is not added; and men are both good and bad.
