So the hypocrite, who abides among stones, multiplies his thoughts in seeking the admiration of men; for through all that he does he seeks praise with hidden thought, having openly what enemies may plunder. Like Ezechias, who, after many benefits done to him, showed all his goods to the messengers of the king of Babylon; whence he soon hears that all will be carried away to Babylon; so, while praise is sought, virtue and beauty are handed into the hands of the enemy. Whence Job says:
**“shall be thick …, and among the stones”** — men, whose favour he seeks and among whom he dwells. He says ‘stones’ because he cannot bear fruit among them
**“he shall abide.”** — he will separate
**“and among the stones he shall abide”** — And among the stones he shall abide: because he stands where he makes solid the intention of his mind; and, even if he is full of good things, “if one swallow him up,” that is, if God takes him by death “out of his place,” that is, from the favours of this life, he will say: “I know thee not,” as is also said to the foolish virgins. And deservedly, because it is not enough for him unless he makes others like himself too; and this is what he says: “For this is the joy of his way,” etc., so that he may be punished for their guilt too. But
8.18:
**“If one swallow him up”** — death
**“out of his place, he shall deny him,”** — that is, from the favours of this life
**“and shall say:”** — namely, the inward judge
8.19:
**“For this is the joy of his way,”** — of his intention
**“that … again out of the earth”** — by earthly love
**“others may spring”** — hypocrites like himself
8.20:
**“God will not cast away”** — because he rejoices to have harvests
**“the simple,”** — the innocent
**“God will not cast away the simple”** — God will not cast away the simple, whose simplicity is now called foolishness by the cunning of the double-minded.
**“nor reach out”** — in the present or in the future
**“his hand to the evildoer”** — that is, help, so that they may be raised again
**“nor reach out his hand”** — Nor reach out his hand, to lift them up from the depth in which they seek glory. The evildoers are hypocrites, who do not even do good things well. Or because outwardly they show themselves pure and simple to their neighbour, within they hide their doubleness; against whom Moses says: “Thou shalt not wear a garment woven of wool and linen.”
8.21:
**“Until … be filled”** — Until … be filled: not that he will do so after, which is certain, but not before, which may seem doubtful to men; as if: neither before the judgment does he forsake the simple, nor does he cease to strike the wicked.
**“thy mouth be filled with laughter”** — Thy mouth be filled with laughter: that is, the mind with the joy of eternal security; whence: “and thy lips with rejoicing.” Jubilation is when such gladness is conceived in the heart that speech cannot unfold it, yet the mouth sounds it.
8.22:
**“They that”** — this is said of Job on behalf of all the good
**“They that hate thee”** — They that hate thee: confusion will clothe the enemies of the just in the judgment, because then, when the judge is seen, all their evils are turned over before the eyes of the mind, and the guilt that weighs them down clothes them on every side. They come to this because here they loved only passing things.
**“shall be clothed with confusion”** — as if he said: you who will be good after repentance
**“and the dwelling of the wicked shall not stand.”**
• the world, in which they pitched their tent, will perish; what then for them?
• Whence he adds: “And the dwelling.” That is, the building of eternal happiness, which they multiply only for it to fall on top of them, so as to defend themselves here from needs as from heat and rain; in which the mind dwells that the good traveller despises.

9.1: **“And Job answered, and said”** — And Job answered, and said: the perverse, to whom the person speaking is displeasing, attack everything he says, whether wicked or right; but Job, to whom not the person but the fault is displeasing, seeing that Baldad had said right things, “Doth God pervert judgment?”, and had brought forward true things against hypocrites, approves what he heard. Truly I know that the humble man, set under God, receives justice; the man who sets himself beside him loses it, because he who compares himself to him, claiming for himself what is God’s, deprives himself of the good he received. And he considers too that every merit of our virtue, if strictly judged, is a fault.
9.2:
**“Indeed I know it is so,”** — that is, that God does not overthrow or pervert judgment
**“and that man cannot be justified”** — what is just
9.3:
**“If he will contend with him,”** — He adds: “If he will contend with him,” by presuming on his own merits and claiming the glory of his virtue not for God but for himself.
**“he cannot answer him one for a thousand”** — He cannot answer him one for a thousand: that is, he cannot lift himself up against him, even about the very beginning of a good life, which is signified by one. A thousand is put for the whole, as: “the word which he commanded to a thousand generations.” The unit is multiplied into ten, ten into a thousand; so because we begin from one so as to come to a thousand, by one the beginning of a good life, by a thousand the perfection of life is understood. So he who receives the highest goods, if he is lifted up by them, shows that he does not have even the beginning. And lest the weak man contend, let the sight of God’s power frighten him.
9.4:
**“He is wise”** — that is, God
**“He is wise in heart”** — He is wise in heart: do not think your hidden things lie concealed, because he is wise; once known, you will not escape, because he is strong, and he who resists him brings himself to confusion.
**“who hath resisted him, and hath had peace?”** — Who hath resisted him, and hath had peace? He who creates orders created things so that they agree with him, and in this is their peace; and he who tries to fight against his ordering loses peace; as the angel, lifted up by his own restlessness, and man, who is vexed by the trouble of the flesh, because they would not be subject to their maker, both lost peace.
9.5:
**“Who hath removed”** — from unbelief
**“mountains”**
• that is, the saints
• Who hath removed mountains, etc. Having spoken generally of the confusion of pride, he shows by the ruin of Israel what punishment awaits the proud.
**“Who hath removed mountains”** — Who hath removed mountains: the holy preachers, from the Jews to the Gentiles; which the Jews did not know, who were overthrown in this, thinking it a joy to themselves that they lost the light when the mountains were removed.
**“and … knew it not”** — namely this
9.6:
**“Who shaketh the earth”** — that is, the Jews
**“out of her place,”** — He shaketh the earth out of her place, because he drew the Jews out of their borders through the Romans.
**“and the pillars thereof”** — the priests
**“the pillars”** — The pillars: the priests, princes and doctors of the Law were shaken, because they themselves were not allowed to live for themselves, since they drove out the apostles; moreover they were forsaken in the darkness of their error.
9.7:
**“Who commandeth the sun”**
• that is, the brightness of the preachers
• Who commandeth the sun: the sun shines by day, the stars by night; because the preachers both open the contemplation of the true light and instruct rightly about earthly things; “under a seal.” We shut something under a seal so that we may bring it out when the time comes; so Judea is now deprived of light, but at the end will be visited. So Elias and Enoch are now hidden, afterwards they will appear. The glory of the preachers, driven back by the Jews, is spread through all nations.
9.8: **“Who alone spreadeth out the heavens, and walketh upon the waves of the sea.”** — Whence: “Who … spreadeth out the heavens,” that is, makes the apostles, driven out by the Jews, honoured everywhere. “Alone,” who wonderfully dispensed this, even when the bitterness of the world raged in the killing of the good. “And walketh upon the waves,” that is, treads them down while he calms them by wonder at signs. Jeremias: “I have set the sand a bound for the sea,” that is, to break the glory of the world he chose the cast-off and the poor; while the sea rages before it, the Church advances.
9.9: **“Who maketh Arcturus, and Orion, and Hyades, and the inner parts of the south.”** — And this is: “Who maketh Arcturus.” He uses the names of the philosophers so as to express those things by their usual name, as God too takes up the words of men: “It repenteth me,” and suchlike. Arcturus shines with seven stars at the axis of the sky; it always turns and never sets. This is the Church universal, which is signified by the seven churches and the seven candlesticks in the Apocalypse, having the gifts of sevenfold grace; it shines from the axis of truth; it is always troubled, but does not fail till the end of the world; rather, like Arcturus, it turns and is raised up. Whence he soon adds: “Orion,” stars which rise in winter time, and at their rising stir up storms and trouble sea and lands. These are the martyrs, whom, while heaven, that is, the Church, brought them forth, winter, that is, the frailty of the wicked, exercised in storm; and it roused not only the turbulent but the calm too to kill them. “Hyades”: they rise in the forehead of the Bull in spring, when the warmer sun lengthens the days. These are the doctors of the Church, who, after the martyrs were taken away, came to the knowledge of the world at a time when, winter held back, faith shines and burns more brightly. ‘Hyetos’ in Greek is ‘rain’ in Latin; hence the Hyades are named from the rains which they bring when they rise, from which the crops grow more richly; then a new sun shines more brightly in the minds of men. After these it remains that the Church should come to see the inner things of the homeland above. Whence he adds: “and the inner parts of the south.” The south wind is the fervour of the Holy Spirit. Its inner parts are the hidden orders of angels and the secret recesses of that homeland, which the warmth of the Spirit fills, where the souls of the saints, and afterwards the risen, are hidden like stars in hidden places, where the sun is seen at noon. These stars are the eyes of the bride; the inner parts of the south are what lies hidden within. Job, wondering at the things said outwardly, tries to tell of the inner things, all that is done outwardly or inwardly. But because this cannot be unfolded, he grasps it better by failing, saying:
9.10: **“Who doth things great”** — Who doth things great: he fulfils it better who confesses that he cannot fulfil it, and he speaks more eloquently who is silent in amazement. Great in power, incomprehensible in reason, numberless in multitude. But why should we wonder at things outside us, when we do not know even what is done toward us?
9.11: **“If he come to me, I shall not see him: if he depart I shall not understand.”** — Whence he says: “If he come to me.” He comes when he gives gifts; he goes away when man is provoked by temptations of the flesh; but his coming and going are not known, since the end of things cannot be foreseen; because sometimes one lifted up by virtues falls, and what was thought grace was anger; and one weakened rises humble, and it is grace which seems anger; and yet man, blind as he is, will render an account of his acts to God.
9.12:
**“If he examine on a sudden, who shall answer him?”** — Whence he adds: “If he examine on a sudden.” He examines suddenly when he calls the unsuspecting to judgment; but no one is able to answer, because even the life of the just gives way if mercy is lacking. Or he examines when he knocks with hard things, so that man may know what he is; but he cannot answer, because, being dust, he says nothing against the divine judgments; which is shown more plainly when he adds:
**“or who can say: Why dost thou so?”** — Who can say: Why dost thou so? We ought to revere the deeds of God, because they cannot be unjust; and not to discuss them, because to seek the reason of his counsel is to be proud against it. But he who looks at himself as weak, though he does not see God’s counsel, has its reason; and the humble man appeases the anger which the proud man kindles unquenchably.
9.13: **“God, whose wrath no man can resist, and under whom they stoop that bear up the world.”** — Whence he says: “God, whose wrath no man can resist.” Moses and Phinees and other saints often resisted the wrath of God; but God himself so raised them up to resist him that, in the things men justly suffered, their piety, which is so great before God, might prevail. But in the things defined before God no one resists, when he himself does not breathe into them to pray; so that even Moses himself did not enter the land of promise. No one resists the wrath of God, as is plain in the Jews, whom he forsakes, taking up the Gentiles; and he bends to himself those who bear up the world, that is, who bear the cares of the world, the princes of the earth, called basileis in Greek; laos is ‘people.’ Basileus, that is, the base of the people which he supports. So those who bear up the world are the powers of the nations, or the angelic virtues, by whose ministry the world is ruled. Who then opposes him to whose power even the angels bow? Or one who is bent does not see above himself; so the angels too are bent, because they do not grasp the height of God. Turning from these to himself, he humbly holds himself cheap before the power of God, saying:
9.14: **“What am I then”** — What am I then: that is, if an angel is not able to consider him, with what mind do I dispute about his judgments, I who am pressed down by the flesh? Our words to God are works; but with these man cannot speak with God, because in them there is no confidence before the fine judgment of God.
9.15: **“I, who although I should have any just thing, would not answer, but would make supplication to my judge.”** — Whence he adds: “I, who although I should have,” etc. “Would make supplication.” After justice he needs prayer to God, so that what is too little in itself may avail through the mercy of the judge, even if justice is full in the more perfect. “Any just thing” is said because the mind of man hardly carries out what it grasps, and what it grasps is little. And prayer, because it is shaken by many thoughts, fears to be rejected even if it is heard.
9.16: **“And if he should hear me when I call, I should not believe that he had heard my voice.”** — Whence he adds: “And if he should hear me when I call.” For since, as David says, now “they mount up to the heavens,” when they reach the heights, now “they go down to the depths” through foul temptations, they have no certainty of being heard. See how finely he judges himself and lays open his weakness. “What am I?” He does not trust in justice but flees to prayer; he who said “although I should have any just thing” says fearfully of prayer too: “if he should hear me when I call.” Job looks round so, because he sees that he cannot bear the force of the judgment.
9.17: **“For he shall crush me in a whirlwind, and multiply my wounds even without cause.”** — Of which he says: “For he shall crush me in a whirlwind.” He who despised him when awaited in calm will be crushed in a whirlwind. “In a whirlwind,” because he fears that works will be strictly required there in the commotion of the elements, since he sees that some are condemned without works for original guilt; in whose voice he says: “and multiply my wounds without cause,” because they themselves did nothing. Whence it is said: “None is clean in his sight, not even the infant of one day.” “Without cause”: by the reckoning of human sense; but with God it is just that the tree should keep in its branches the bitterness it drew from the root. These things are said spiritually too of Job, who foresaw the scourges of God in the whirlwind, fearing, and, having foreseen, bore them. Whence he says: “and multiply my wounds without cause,” because he was struck not for guilt. Whence above: “that I should afflict him without cause.” He adds the continuance of these wounds:
9.18: **“He alloweth not”** — He alloweth not: a full proving; torments tear without, temptations chasten within; whence he says he is filled with bitterness. But the equity and power of the one striking soften the force of the pain.
9.19: **“If strength be demanded, he is most strong: if equity of judgment, no man dare bear witness for me.”** — And this is: “If strength be demanded.” As if: no one dares, because he examines merits who does not search them out by another’s testimony, but, a silent observer, waits long. No one else can be a witness for me, because I cannot even be one for myself.
9.20: **“If I would justify myself, my own mouth shall condemn me: if I would shew myself innocent, he shall prove me wicked.”** — And this is: “If I would justify myself.” I am not able to be a witness to my innocence, nor do I know that I have it. And this is: “Although I should be simple.” He who knows the good he does, is he not proud in some way? Again, he who does not know the good in himself, how does he guard it? Against both it is needful to value right things, that they may be guarded, and as least things, lest we be lifted up. But there are some things that cannot easily be known; for sometimes what virtue begins, fault finishes. Hence Moses: “Thou shalt follow justly after that which is just,” so that one defends justice for love of it, not of reward. And because he cannot fully examine himself, he bears this exile of blindness with distress.
9.21: **“Although I should be simple, even this my soul shall be ignorant of, and I shall be weary of my life.”** — Whence he adds: “and I shall be weary of my life.” But there is comfort in this darkness when the just power of God is brought back to mind, which both punishes the wicked and passes beyond the just.
9.22: **“One thing there is that I have spoken, both the innocent and the wicked he consumeth.”** — And this is: “One thing there is.” Either the innocent man is consumed, because from the consideration of inmost purity he seems to be nothing; the wicked, because, being known, he is condemned; and this word of thought I have brought forth within me. Or he consumes the innocent and the wicked, because by the merit of the first fault they are drawn alike to the destruction of the flesh. Against these losses of the human race he seeks the grace of the Redeemer, who by the single death of the flesh might destroy our double death, of flesh and soul.
9.23: **“If he scourge, let him kill at once, and not laugh at the pains of the innocent.”** — And this is: “If he scourge, let him kill at once.” For God to laugh is to be unwilling to pity affliction; whence he says to the reprobate: “I also will laugh in your destruction.” Every desire is a punishment while it is put off; whence Solomon says: “Hope that is deferred afflicteth the soul.” This was the punishment of all the elect before the coming, at whose prayers God laughed while he put them off. Or the laughter of God is gladness, because he rejoices when he is sought more ardently by us. So he gives him joy from punishment who, through holy desires, chastens himself for love of him. He reveals that he alone bore the death of the flesh.
9.24: **“The earth is given”** — The earth is given: the earth is the flesh; the wicked one, the devil. His hand: the killers of Christ, against whose mind the devil could do nothing, so he killed the flesh through his henchmen. The judges of this earth were the priests and Pilate, whose face, that is, hearts, the wicked one covered, so that they should not know God. Because the devil with his followers is one person, Scripture often speaks of him so as to pass suddenly to his body. The persecuting people is well understood by the name of the wicked one, when he says: “and if it be not he,” that is, if that people is not wicked, who is ever to be thought wicked? Turning his eyes from the unbelief of the Jews to himself, he grieves that he goes out of the world before Christ comes.
9.25: **“My days have been swifter than a post: they have fled away and have not seen good.”** — And this is: “My days have been swifter than a post.” It is a runner’s task to announce what is to follow; so all the elect before the coming, announcing Christ, were runners; but because they die before, they grieve that they pass more swiftly than a runner, so as not to see present him who alone is called good. Of whom he also adds:
9.26: **“as ships”** — As ships: he who carries fruit enjoys the smell, but brings food for others; so the ancients were fed by the smell of the one to come, but by prophesying brought the fruit itself to us. Fruit is usually mixed with chaff so that it may be carried unharmed to land; so in the sayings of the fathers the chaff of history keeps the spiritual things. They often turn from the height of the Godhead to the Incarnation, like the eagle, which fixes its eyes on the sun, yet bends them to a carcass when it needs food; and the carcass is Christ in his death, by which we are fed. But because the people of Israel, once full of the spirit of prophecy, did not remain in the faith which it foretold, it lost prophecy; the speech turns, in compassion, to their hardness.
9.27:
**“If I say: I will not speak so: I change my face, and am tormented with sorrow.”** — So: “If I say: I will not speak so.” Israel would not speak as before, when it denied him whom it foretold; in which its inner face is changed by the filth of unbelief, so that it is not known by God; whence it remains for it to be tormented with eternal sorrows.
*Morally:* “My days have passed more swiftly.” The first man was so made that his life could be stretched out through time, not run out; but because he sinned he suffered the running down which man always endures and yet desires while he longs to live. He groans at the losses of this running down in the voice of the human race. “They have fled away”: because man would not stand toward the light, by fleeing he lost his sight, so that he cannot see the good which is, for which he was made. “As ships carrying fruits”: the fruit of the land through the waves. Man’s land is paradise, in which he would have remained innocent, but through guilt he came to the waves of changeableness. The fruits of the land: the speech of the cleansed; the power of work; the understanding of God, which, because man would not eat it in the land of rest, he carries over the sea, and tries to keep amid so many temptations, not without wood, that is, the cross by which we are remade. Or a ship that carries fruit has a sweet smell but has no heavy weight; so man too, driven out, when he raises himself to seek again things above, perceives the smell of heavenly things by remembrance, but, not having the weight of life, is driven lightly here and there; and like the eagle, which flies on high but by the craving of the belly seeks the earth, so man, made on high, fell to earth for the taste of forbidden food, where he feeds on the flesh of pleasure. But when we treat of these things a question presses: why did God make one he foresaw would perish? Why did the good and almighty not make such a one as could not perish? Lest this thought break out into pride, he humbly checks himself, saying: “I will not speak so,” but, weak, I will be restrained from such an inquiry. In which the face of the mind is changed, because, seeing itself weak, the mind which sought high things reveres what it does not know. In which there is sorrow, because he is greatly afflicted who is blind to understanding the things that concern himself. To these common evils he fears to join his own.
9.28: **“I feared all my works, knowing that thou didst not spare the offender.”** — Whence he adds: “I feared all my works,” etc. They were good indeed, but even these are to be feared by those who truly wish to please God. For two things are to be feared in good works: sloth and fraud. Lesser love of God makes sloth; love of self makes fraud, when for good deeds the silent gratitude of the human heart, or the breeze of favour, or any outward thing is desired. But blessed is he who shakes his hands from every gift: the hands of heart and of mouth. Against these, fear must be had, which strengthens us in the knowledge that he will not spare the offender; for even if he calls sinners to repentance, yet he never passes over sin without punishment: either man punishes it or God; whence even after baptism we die for original sin. But while he trembles more than is right, he is weary of living, as if he would not come to life even through labours.
9.29:
**“But if so also I am wicked, why have I laboured in vain?”**
• after fear he comes to tears of despair, so that the humility of entreaty may carry good work up to its reward; but neither life nor tears make perfectly clean while this corruption holds; whence he adds: “If I be washed,” etc.
• Whence: “But if so also I am wicked.” He does not regret having laboured, but grieves that amid his labours he is uncertain of the reward. The just man is uncertain in such a way as to trust, and trusts in such a way as not to grow sluggish in security.
9.30: **“If I be washed as it were with snow waters, and my hands shall shine ever so clean:”** — “In vain,” I say, because: “If I be washed.” He who crushes himself so as to be afflicted with lamentation washes himself with waters, but not of snow unless humility is present, which shines white before God, while it neither despises another nor murmurs against God. Or snow water comes from the air, while other waters spring from outside. So he who weeps for eternal things is drenched with snow water; he who is pricked in prayer for earthly things, with water of the earth. The hands are the works, “ever so clean,” as though not truly clean under this corruption.
9.31:
**“thou shalt plunge me”** — Thou shalt plunge me: that is, you will show me plunged, because the nearer we come to him, the more we recognize our filth from his cleanness.
**“my garments”** — My garments: the garment of the soul is the body, which Solomon bids “at all times be white”; and if it is mixed with blood, that is, with fleshly desires, Isaias says it is to be burned.
**“and my garments shall abhor me,”** — Shall abhor, that is, will make abhorrent; as it is said of Judas: “he hath possessed a field of the reward of iniquity,” that is, caused it to be possessed. In the abhorrence of the garment there is this heavier thing, that it does not know the mind of the one who reproves it.
9.32: **“For I shall not answer a man that is like myself: nor one that may be heard with me equally in judgment.”** — Whence he says: “For I shall not answer a man.” Among men we both hear objections and answer them and are heard; but in the judgment of God he hears us, because he sees all we do, but we do not hear him, because we do not fully understand what displeases him. He cannot be heard on equal terms, nor is there anyone who can reprove both, that is, God and me. He reproves who goes against one by the authority of reason. So he who does right now contradicts the anger of the judge not with the groan of prayer but with the confidence of authority. Job sees how perversely man did, how strictly God is angry, and that there is no human justice to contradict; and so he longs, namely, for the Mediator to come after, who would both reprove man so that he should not offend, and by suffering stand against God so that he should not strike him. And he put his hand between both, because he both gave man an example of action and showed God in himself works by which he might be appeased, which no one before him could. He also did this more wonderfully, that he corrected the hearts of offenders by meekness rather than by terror.
9.33: **“There is none that may be able to reprove both”** — as Isaias says: “Cease to do perversely, learn to do well … and then come, and accuse me”
9.34: **“Let him take his rod away from me, and let not his fear terrify me.”** — Whence he adds: “Let him take his rod away from me”: the rod of the Law, by which he punishes; but Christ took it away and showed the ways of life by meekness. He willed to be feared as God but loved as Father.
9.35:
**“I will speak, and will not fear him: for I cannot answer while I am in fear.”** — Whence he adds: “I will speak, and will not fear him.” Now he has not fear but affection as toward a father. Behold, the staff, that is, the fear of the Law, when sent, does not raise the boy; but Eliseus himself, fitting himself to the boy and breathing seven times, that is, through the love of the Spirit.
**“answer”** — Answer: that is, to repay with deeds worthy of him; but no one fearing like a slave has answered God’s benefits. Only he who does not fear, through the confidence of love, has rendered him worthy service. He is not pure who would do evil if it were allowed.

10.1: **“My soul is weary of my life,”** — My soul is weary of my life: to one who loves, this life, which was sweet before, is wearisome; even grieving, he bears it. And this is: “My soul is weary of my life.” But when this life grows cheap for love of the heavenly, he who used to defend his faults now accuses them. And this is: “I will let go my speech,” which I used in my defence, now “against myself,” because by confessing I accuse myself; not as one who still blushes to confess, since he does not forsake evils with so great a desire; but because sometimes one who confesses openly does not groan, but speaks rejoicing of things to be mourned, he adds: “I will speak in the bitterness,” so that bitterness may punish what the tongue accuses. From repentance security is born, and more confidently he asks how he is being dealt with. And this is: “I will say to God: Do not condemn me,” because my punishment puts out your torments.
10.2:
**“I will say to God: Do not condemn me: tell me why thou judgest me so.”** — that is, by the present affliction; whether for future security, or for what fault in particular, spiritually; because even if just, he still has some evils
**“why thou judgest me so”** — Why thou judgest me so: in two ways he judges here. Either he sends a punishment which drags the unchanged to the eternal one; or by this punishment he puts out the future one. So he is troubled by the uncertainty of this judgment, and he who is in doubt about his life asks in thought. But when the virtue of his life is looked at, a comfort is answered as it were by the judge, because he does not strike to destroy one whom even in striking he keeps in innocence. So he says: “tell me why” you scourge, whether for security or for what fault in particular; because even if he is just, he still has some evils; and so he asks that God judge him to himself, so that what God punishes in him he too may punish by weeping. Therefore I seek the cause, for I know it is not unjust.
10.3:
**“Doth it seem good to thee that thou shouldst calumniate me”**
• I ask why, but I know that it is justly and not to destroy me
• And this is: “Doth it seem good?” This question requires a denial, as if he said: I know that you, who are supremely good, do not think it good to oppress a poor man by calumny; and so I know that what I suffer is not unjust; and so I grieve the more that I do not know the cause. He does not say “oppress the innocent,” because he does not dare to speak of his justice, but “the poor man,” because he considers his weakness.
**“and oppress me”** — or ‘the poor man’ in another reading
**“the work of thy own hands”** — The work of thy own hands: as if: you do not wickedly destroy one whom you made freely.
**“of the wicked”** — Of the wicked: that is, of the evil spirits, who, since they cannot return to life, seek companions for death; whose counsel was to break by adversity Job, upright in prosperity; but God does not allow him to be tempted beyond his strength.
10.4: **“Hast thou eyes of flesh”** — Hast thou eyes of flesh? The eyes of the flesh recognize only things done in time, because they are also closed with time; and human sight follows any work; it does not run ahead.
10.5: **“thy days”** — Thy days: also, the years of man differ from the eternal one, to whom nothing is past, nothing future, but who sees all things as present.
10.6: **“That thou shouldst inquire after my iniquity”** — That thou shouldst inquire after my iniquity, and so know that I have done nothing wicked: as if he humbly asked why you prove by scourges in time one whom you knew perfectly with you before all time.
10.7: **“And shouldst know that I have done no wicked thing, whereas there is no man that can deliver out of thy hand.”** — Whereas there is no man, etc. As if: what remains for you but to spare, since no one can oppose you? For the more that no one can hold back your vengeance, the more easily mercy ought to spare. But that he may be appeased, since we cannot offer our own work, let us offer him his own work.
10.8:
**“Thy hands, O Lord”** — Thy hands, O Lord: as if: weigh it mercifully, lest what you made should perish.
**“have made me”** — Have made me: as to the soul.
**“wholly round about”**
• as if: because there is no one who can deliver, then do you deliver me, because you made me
• Wholly round about: as to the body; not the race of darkness. That the condition of man may be shown worthier than the rest, he is said to have been made by hands, with counsel going before: “Let us make man to our image and likeness,” whereas of the rest he said only: “Be made.”
**“and dost thou thus … on a sudden”** — And dost thou thus … on a sudden: as if: one whom you set before others with such dignity, why do you despise with such vileness? But along with this dignity, which is through the spirit, there is weakness through the flesh, which may move a merciful judge.
10.9: **“Remember, I beseech thee, that thou hast made me as the clay, and thou wilt bring me into dust again.”** — Whence he says: “Remember, I beseech thee, that thou hast made me as the clay.” Hence the fault is pardonable, while it is unforgivable in the angel, who was strong. Clay is when water soaks earth. So is man, when the soul waters the flesh, whose death he openly adds: “and thou wilt bring me into dust again.” As if: look at the matter and the punishment, and spare the fault. Because he has brought forward the nature of man as made, he adds the order of his begetting.
10.10: **“Hast thou not milked me as milk, and curdled me like cheese?”** — Whence he says: “Hast thou not milked me as milk?” etc. Man was made as clay, but, begotten, he is milked like milk from the woman, is curdled like cheese in the flesh, is clothed with flesh and skin, is made firm with bones and sinews. After the creation of the body, which is the lesser thing, he adds the wonderful breathing in of life.
10.12:
**“life and mercy”** — Life and mercy: but he gave these goods in vain unless he himself keeps them.
**“and thy visitation hath preserved my spirit.”** — Whence he adds: “and thy visitation,” etc. The same of the inner man. The inner man is clay, because the grace of the Spirit is poured into the earthly mind and waters it so that it may be raised to God. But lest it grow proud by continual use, the Spirit forsakes it for a time, and, brought back to dust, it dries up, so that it is now driven by the wind of temptation, so that man may know himself; for when man is left and shaken, he thinks more finely of the gifts of God. “Hast thou not milked me as milk?” When the mind is drawn by the Spirit of God from its old state, it is milked like milk, because it is formed in a kind of beginning. It is curdled like cheese when, growing rich in thoughts, it is pressed together, so that it no longer flows away in desires but is made solid in one love. But against these first beginnings the flesh murmurs from its old habit. “With skin and flesh,” that is, the mind is hemmed in by the siege of fleshly motions; but he who outwardly lets them loose for wars, inwardly strengthens it with the bones of virtues, so that it may be humble and strong. And God grants the uprightness of right living because he spares past offences. “Life and mercy”: life is given when kindness is breathed into evil minds; but this is not given unless mercy first washes away the evils done before. Or mercy follows the life given, to keep it, because he visits mercifully, either by pricking to love or by scourging to fear, so that the human spirit may be kept. After he has spoken of the gifts of mercy to himself, he adds generally: “I know that thou rememberest all things,” as if: why do I tremble for myself, who know that all nations are to be gathered? “Although thou conceal these things in thy heart,” because you do not yet judge with open speech. Those certain of pardon are wont to be touched by the memory of their former wickedness and to be knocked at, against their will, by unlawful thought.
10.13: **“Although thou conceal these things in thy heart,”** — as to me, so also to all
10.14:
**“If I have sinned”**
• but not wholly clean
• Whence he adds: “If I have sinned,” etc. God spares for an hour when he soon washes away guilt by the gift of tears. But he does not allow us to be clean, because even unwilling we bear the memory of evil with delight, which is for scars to fester. This is “the man who,” as Moses says, “is defiled by a dream in the night,” that is, by hidden temptation, who “is commanded to go forth out of the camp,” that is, to despise himself in comparison with the continent; “in the evening he is washed with water,” that is, seeing his failing he washes himself with tears; “after sunset he returns into the camp,” when the flame of thought cools, he takes up the confidence of the fellowship of the good. But when the mind is shaken by the memory of evil, it is sometimes dragged to commit it more heavily than before, and the man becomes wicked, to whom, even if he is raised up, there will be the woe of eternal damnation. But if the just man tries to resist, yet, pressed by labour and lasting affliction, he is not allowed to lift his head; but so he will be freed. God keeps these assaults for his own, so that they may not grow proud in security, but, knocked about, may fix their hope more firmly in God’s help alone.
**“and thou hast spared me for an hour: why dost thou not suffer me to be clean from my iniquity?”** — if he took away the guilt by pardon, why does he not wipe it from the memory too?
10.15: **“And if I be wicked, woe unto me:”** — and since I am not clean, I shall be either wicked or wretched in the labours of the struggle
10.16:
**“And for pride thou wilt take me as a lioness,”**
• man was taken, because he is now held in prison by that very thing by which he boldly transgressed
• and this happens so that I may not grow proud
• And this is: “For pride … as a lioness.” The lioness, while greedily seeking food for her cubs, falls into a pit. For it is said that in her path a narrow, deep pit is made, in which a beast is placed, so that the lioness is provoked to throw herself in, from which she cannot get out by leaping. Joined to it is another pit, in which there is a cage, so that when the lioness is pressed from above, wishing to hide herself, she enters the cage; shut in it she is no longer feared, but, fenced round with bars, she is lifted out. So the mind of man, made in freedom, while it wished to feed the desires of the flesh, fell into the pit of deception for the forbidden food, where it endured the cage, that is, the prison of corruption; but, called back to pardon by grace, it is always held tight by the prison, lest it wander through desires. So man, free, fell of his own will; but brought back under discipline he lives better shut in. So too daily, when someone presumes on his virtues, a wonderful dispensation prepares something for him in which, delighted, he falls; from which he does not get out by himself, but, his weakness known, God leads him out as one bound. For the pride by which he lifted himself up for his virtues, he is bound in humility when he has fallen. God turns away from the proud, and the compunction of highest love departs, for he does not even feel his losses; but let God return and strike through grace, because the man visited, advancing, weeps, who perished glad. “Wonderfully,” not penally, because through weeping the mind is raised to the heights and rejoices to be so afflicted, because it advances. But if we grow sluggish in holy desire, he sets before us the examples of those who watch well.
**“and returning thou tormentest me wonderfully.”** — because you depart from the proud
10.17:
**“Thou renewest”** — but if for an hour I am slothful
**“thy witnesses against me”**
• when the good of the witnesses is seen, anger is feared; whence also, displeased in comparison with them, I punish my evils
• And this is: “Thou renewest thy witnesses.” The witnesses of God are those who bear witness by works to the rewards that will follow. These are against us when their life convicts our wickedness and proves that what they did can be done by us. Seeing the good of the witnesses, we, being unlike them, fear the more to be condemned.
**“and multipliest thy wrath upon me, and pains war against me.”** — And this is: “Thou multipliest thy wrath,” that is, you show it manifold; because if he scourges even the good, what will happen to the wicked? So, the manifold wrath foreseen, man returns to himself and punishes his wickedness. And this is: “and pains war against me.”
10.18:
**“Why”** — then
**“didst thou bring me forth out of the womb?”** — the same as above in other words
**“Why … out of the womb”** — Why … out of the womb: the same as above: “Why did I not die in the womb?”
10.19: **“I should have been as if I had not been, carried from the womb to the grave”** — I should have been as if I had not been, carried from the womb to the grave: the same as was said there: “As a hidden untimely birth,” etc., “or as they that being conceived have not seen the light.”
10.20:
**“Shall not”** — because
**“Shall not the fewness”** — Shall not the fewness: let the delight of the present life not capture me, because it passes quickly.
**“suffer me”** — Suffer me: that is, temper the scourges, so that I may weigh the evils I suffer, and weep; because the excess of pains sometimes weighs down the soul so that it cannot do this, and there is grief without grieving. Or often man does not know how great the burden of his sin is; or, if he knows and condemns it, hindered by the desire of the flesh and the habit of evil, he cannot weep worthily, unless God lets him go and, freed, rouses him to tears; which the foresight of hell does most of all.
10.21:
**“Before I go, and return no more, to a land that is dark and covered with the mist of death:”**
• eternal, so that they may never see the light of God
• Whence he says: “Before I go.” Hell is called a land because captives are held there. “Before I go”: not that he who mourns goes, but that he goes who does not mourn; as if I said to a debtor: pay before I bind you. “And return no more,” because mercy no longer frees the damned.
10.22:
**“of misery and darkness”** — Of misery and darkness: because pain torments without those whom blindness of mind darkens within. Or there no one returns to the light any more, as in this land, where, even if there is misery, it is allowed to return to the light by conversion.
**“the shadow of death”** — The shadow of death: death is separation from God; the shadow, its darkness; because the fire of punishment has burning and not light, so that those who sinned in both may be punished in both.
**“no order”** — No order: not that God does not order the torments according to the merits of each; because, even if hell is one, not all will feel it in one way, as now men do not feel the heat of the sun alike. But in the mind of the damned, through the shadow of blindness spoken of before, there will be great confusion, which will torment them within as the flame without. Or there will be no order, because in the punishments the proper nature of things is not kept. Whence he adds: “but everlasting horror dwelleth.” Here fear is of evil to come; when one already suffers it, fear has gone. There fear torments even in the torments themselves. Here the flame that burns gives light; there it burns and darkens. See how heavy the torment, where the torments are at odds with their own natures, as the living were at odds with the will of God. And fear remains there with the punishments because no end of punishments will be hoped for in the future. But the fire, which does not give light for comfort, sometimes gives light for punishment; because by its light they will see in punishment, that they may grieve the more, their followers, for love of whom they offended. That they will grieve at the torment of their friends is proved by the rich man, who, mindful of his brethren, asked that they might not come to the torments; he who saw Lazarus would see them in punishment.

11.1: **“Sophar”** — Sophar: they follow one another in turn, as the very situation is against a strong athlete.
11.2:
**“Shall not he that”** — Shall not he that: he begins with insults. It is the way of the wicked not to agree with things rightly said, but to answer against them; to whom even few words seem many, because they are against the views of those who think nothing right except what they themselves think.
**“or shall a man full of talk be justified?”** — as if: ought we not also to speak to you? It is a punishment to the wicked man to keep silent, and he who neglects to be corrected does not listen patiently
**“or shall a man full of talk”** — Or shall a man full of talk: a true sentence, for it is read: “the work of justice shall be … silence”; but not said in its place. He who cannot bear right things, neglecting to be corrected, girds himself to answer.
11.3:
**“Shall men hold their peace to thee only? and when thou hast mocked others, shall no man confute thee?”** — for you can be confuted
**“Shall men hold their peace to thee only? and when thou hast mocked others”** — Shall men hold their peace to thee only? and when thou hast mocked others: he whom conscience bites thinks all right things a mockery of himself, and takes things said generally to be said of him. Hence he is also kindled to speak against them, so as to cover his shame even so, as though he were not guilty if he accused others. Whence, lying, he adds:
11.4: **“For thou hast said: My word is pure”** — For thou hast said: My word is pure: Job had not said this; but it is a comfort to wrongdoing if the life of the one who rebukes is stained, even falsely.
11.5:
**“And I wish that God would speak with thee,”**
• but God would prove you wicked
• And I wish, etc. The perverse wish good things in words, so as to seem kind, and so that the evils of the present may be shown. Hence this man too says: “I wish that God would speak with thee,” as if he said: you now speak to yourself; you think of God carnally; you are empty of the spirit of truth; as if: I pity your ignorance rather than your punishment.
**“and would open his lips to thee,”** — as if: as to me
**“his lips”** — His lips: that is, the judgments by which, as by opened lips, he shows men his will, which lies hidden in his secret dispositions. With opened lips this teaching is done, so that he may show the secrets of wisdom. The public works of the wisdom of God are that he kindly orders those whom he made freely, breathes good things into them, perfects and keeps them, which is plain to all. His secret works are what he does on the contrary in the wicked, whom he forsakes; which few can search into, but none can find out. Yet he sees it in some way, and finds by not finding, who understands that they are incomprehensible, so that he may humbly fear and say: “Who art thou that repliest against God?” This man, skilled through the study of knowledge, ignorant through the boldness of pride, wishes for a better man what he has. The law of God is charity, through which the precepts of life are in the mind, which is called the fullness of the law. Manifold, because it spreads out to all the deeds of virtues and draws back from every evil; and he who attends to it carefully recognizes how much he sins against God daily; and if he recognizes his sins, he bears scourges patiently.
11.6:
**“That he might shew thee the secrets of wisdom”** — he would show wisdom
**“and that his law is manifold,”** — of God
**“and thou mightest understand that he exacteth much less of thee, than thy iniquity deserveth.”** — And this is: “And thou mightest understand that he exacteth much less of thee, than thy iniquity deserveth.” Unjustly he charges the just man with iniquity; but this insult comes from zeal for God and is pardonable. Not knowing the merits of the just man, he adds mockery out of ignorance:
11.7:
**“Peradventure”** — this I wish for you, but
**“thou wilt comprehend the steps of God, and wilt find out the Almighty perfectly?”** — as if: you will not find him, but
**“Peradventure thou wilt comprehend the steps of God”** — Peradventure thou wilt comprehend the steps of God: the kindness of visitation, which shows us the way, so that we may follow one not yet seen, until we come to contemplation. These cannot be comprehended, because we do not know whence, where, or in what ways the gifts of his Spirit come; whence: “and thou knowest not whence it cometh, and whither it goeth.” In the future the Almighty will be found by sight, but not perfectly, because his essence will be fully seen by no one.
11.8:
**“He is higher than heaven”** — He is higher than heaven: because by the uncircumscribed nature of his Spirit he transcends all things.
**“he is deeper than hell”** — He is deeper than hell: because in transcending he bears up from beneath.
11.9: **“longer than the earth”** — Longer than the earth: because he exceeds the measure of the creature by the lastingness of eternity. “Broader than the sea,” because he so possesses times as to narrow them under the presence of his power. Or the heavens are called the angels, hell the demons, the earth just men, the sea sinners. So neither do the angels reach his height, and he judges the cunning of the demons far more finely, and his patience surpasses the long-suffering of the just, and his presence fills the deeds of sinners everywhere. Or man is heaven by contemplation, hell by the darkness of temptations, earth while he bears fruit, sea while he is driven by changeableness. But man’s contemplation fails in God. And if he examines himself in temptations, he fears God’s finer judgments, and his requital at the end surpasses his works. And however much the mind wavers in searching out the strictness to come, it does not know it; whence: “Who knoweth the power of thy anger?” Or, according to the Apostle: the breadth of God is love, which gathers in even persecutors; the length, by which, bearing long, he leads to the kingdom; the height, because he transcends even the understanding of the glorified; the depth, because he incomprehensibly carries out judgment on the damned in hell. He shows the same things now too: breadth by loving, length by bearing, height by surpassing understanding and prayers, depth by judging the unlawful motions of thoughts. But how unsearchable the height and depth are, no one knows except him who by contemplation is carried to the highest things, or who, resisting hidden motions, is troubled by temptations. Hence it is said to Job, despised: “He is higher,” etc., as if: when are you able to know his height and depth, you who neither know how to be carried to the highest things by virtue nor how to reprove yourself in temptations?
11.10:
**“If he shall overturn”**
• and since it is so
• If he shall overturn: he overturns heaven when he destroys man’s contemplation; hell, when he lets one fearful in temptations fall into worse; the earth, when he cuts off the fruit of good work through adversity; the sea, when he confounds our wavering by the terror of judgment. Heaven and hell are pressed together at once when contemplation lifts up and temptation darkens the same mind; whence: “I see another law in my members, fighting against the law of my mind.” Earth and sea at once, when sure faith in eternal things strengthens the same mind, and from some little changeableness the breeze of doubt turns it, as in him who said: “I do believe, Lord: help my unbelief.” This happens by a hidden dispensation, so that when the mind is raised it is attacked by the remnants of wickedness, so that it is either exercised by resisting or broken by being led astray.
**“all things, or shall press them together, who shall contradict him?”** — Whence he rightly says: “Who shall contradict him?” or “Who can say to him: Why dost thou so?” Because no one can withstand the judgment of God, or penetrate it by searching. Why he overturns or presses together, he adds: “For he knoweth.” When the mind is lifted up by pride because things go well, God forsakes it even in its virtues, so that man may find what he is. And because God, by bearing with them, sees vices grow up, by judging he confounds good things. Iniquity is put after vanity; all things that pass are vain; if they bind us, iniquity begins. Or vanity is called the lighter guilt, iniquity the heavier. And from lighter things, use making everything light, man is led to heavier. Hence Solomon: “He that contemneth small things shall fall by little and little.” Vanity is said to be known and iniquity to be considered, as it were more carefully, because God leaves not even lesser things unpunished, and girds himself more intently to strike greater ones. Where vanity with iniquity drags one, namely to swelling, he adds: “A vain man is lifted up into pride.” The vain man is made bold by guilt; forgetting himself, he loses humility; and, serving his desires, he shakes himself free of the yoke of divine love, so as now to go freely through pleasures. By the wild ass’s colt he notes every kind of wild beast, which, let loose to the motions of nature, is not held by the reins of masters; so he who is not held by discipline runs boldly, a wanderer, through his desires in unbridled freedom.
11.12:
**“A vain man is lifted up into pride, and … like a wild ass’s colt”** — a rebuke
**“thinketh himself born free”** — so is every vain man, but you are the worst among such
11.13:
**“But thou hast hardened thy heart”**
• you do not grow soft with the fear of God, so that your heart is as if of stone
• But thou hast hardened thy heart: the heart is said here to be hardened not through virtue but through unfeelingness. And he says to spread the hands to God, that is, to be proud of the virtue of one’s works against the grace of the giver. So the reprobate, when they cannot convict the elect of weakness of action, accuse them of the crime of pride. But he who until now has rebuked the just man now adds as though teaching: “If thou wilt put away from thee the iniquity that is in thy hand,” etc. Iniquity in the hand is guilt in work; injustice in the tabernacle is iniquity in the mind. For the mind is called a tabernacle, in which we are hidden within ourselves when we are not seen outwardly in work. To lift up the face is to raise the soul to God through the efforts of prayer; this face a stain defiles if the conscience of its guilt accuses it.
**“and hast spread”** — he who, speaking before God, attributes to himself the good things he does, stretches out his hands to God in pride
**“thy hands to him.”**
• works
• but
11.14:
**“If … the iniquity that is in thy hand”**
• these things are true, if they were rightly said
• every sin is done either by thought alone, or by thought and deed
**“thou wilt put away from thee”** — so that as the work is pure the thought may be pure
**“and let not injustice remain in thy tabernacle”** — in the heart
11.15:
**“Then mayst thou lift up thy face”** — the mind, in which we are recognized, so that we may be loved by God
**“without spot”**
• which would make one distrust one’s prayers
• he rises to God without spot who neither commits sin in himself nor lets it pass in others
**“and thou shalt be steadfast”** — And thou shalt be steadfast: because the more solidly he stands in good acts, the less he trembles at the judgment.
11.16:
**“misery”** — present
**“Thou shalt also forget”** — when eternal things are seen
**“Thou shalt also forget misery”** — Thou shalt also forget misery: the soul feels the evils of the present life the more harshly the more it neglects to weigh the good that follows. But if it fixes the eye of the heart on the things that last, it sees that whatever tends to an end is nothing.
**“and remember it only as waters that are passed away”** — And remember it only as waters that are passed away: because the miseries that pass do not shake with force, but pour in a touch of sorrow; while he grieves outwardly at the blow, inwardly he grows cold from temptation, against which the divine light is kindled the more. Whence it is added: “And brightness like that of the noonday shall arise to thee at evening.” The noonday brightness at evening is the renewal of virtue in temptation.
11.17:
**“And brightness like that of the noonday, shall arise to thee at evening:”**
• so that charity may burn the more, the more it was feared to have set
• for often so many temptations besiege us that they bend us to the fall of despair; but the Creator looks on our darkness and pours back the rays of the light withdrawn
**“and when thou shalt think thyself consumed”** — but you will not be
**“thou shalt rise as the day star”**
• because the life of the just foretells what the brightness of the world to come will be, that is, of Christ, who does not yet appear
• And when thou shalt think thyself consumed, etc. Because falling outwardly he is renewed inwardly, and the harder the things he bears, the more surely he hopes for the rewards.
**“and when thou shalt think thyself consumed, thou shalt rise”** — At evening: when the just man has begun to sink through outward evils, then his brightness begins; on the contrary the light of the wicked is in the day of this life, darkness in the evening.
11.18:
**“And thou shalt have confidence, hope being set before thee, and being buried thou shalt sleep secure.”**
• Solomon: “Whatever shall befall the just man, it shall not make him sad.” Again: “the just, bold as a lion, shall be without dread”
• And this is: “And thou shalt have confidence,” etc. “And being buried thou shalt sleep secure.” The buried sleep securely, because while they watchfully penetrate their inmost things, they hide themselves from the laborious burdens of this world under the leisure of quiet.
• Or buried, that is, dead, you will be secure of the crown.
• Or buried is he who searches out all the hiding places of the soul, and, finding nothing to bite him, sleeps secure within himself, hidden from the acts of the world.
11.19:
**“Thou shalt rest”** — also
**“Thou shalt rest, and there shall be none to make thee afraid”** — Thou shalt rest, and there shall be none to make thee afraid: for he who is fixed in the longing for eternity, since there is nothing in the world that he craves, there is nothing in the world that he fears.
**“and many shall entreat thy face.”** — while he preaches right things he breaks out into what he silently covets; and while he lives as if innocently, he wishes to be seen as an intercessor for men
**“and many shall entreat thy face”** — And many shall entreat thy face: the wicked, when they preach right things, promise others as a great thing what they themselves covet. But lest by promising long it become plain what they are, they quickly return to words of uprightness.
11.20:
**“the eyes”** — for you, so
**“But … of the wicked shall decay”**
• because in that day all their thoughts shall perish
• Whence it is added: “But the eyes of the wicked shall decay.” By the name of eyes the intention is expressed. So the eyes of the wicked decay, for when death takes the wicked away, their desires surely end with their life. From them every way of escape also perishes, because their malice finds no place where it may hide itself from the punishment of the strict judge.
**“and the way to escape shall fail them”** — here they avoid in some way what displeases them; not there
**“and their hope the abomination of the soul”** — that is, earthly things, in which the flesh rests but the spirit fails
**“and their hope the abomination”** — And their hope the abomination: because the spirit perishes for ever from the very thing by which the flesh lives sweetly for a time.

12.2:
**“Are you then men alone, and shall wisdom die with you?”** — Sophar said this truly but without discretion, because he pours liquid over a better man’s full vessel, not to teach but to make himself known. He is bold against a better man because he thinks all are beneath him. So too all heretics. But the Church calls the proud back from their own esteem to equality. Whence Job adds: “Are you then men alone?” He who thinks he goes before all in reason exults that he alone is a man.
**“Are you then men alone”** — Are you then men alone: for he who reckons that he alone is wise, what else does he think but that this same wisdom dies with him?
12.3:
**“I also have a heart as well as you, nor am I inferior to you.”** — but
**“I also have a heart as well as you”** — I also have a heart as well as you: to correct their pride he denies that he is inferior; and, so as not to pass the limit of his humility, he is silent about being superior. See how discreetly he shows in this what they ought to think of themselves.
**“for who is ignorant of these things, which you know?”**
• whence he returns to himself, having nothing outside, and, afflicted, pours himself out in prayer
• after he has called them back from fear to equality by rebuking them, he begins to teach
**“for who is ignorant of these things, which you know”** — For who is ignorant of these things, which you know? As if he said: since the things you say are known to all, why do you swell singularly over the knowledge of what is said?
12.4:
**“He that is mocked by his friends as I,”** — because he who is mocked for guilt is not worthy to be heard
**“He that is mocked by his friends as I”** — He that is mocked by his friends as I: because human mockery makes him near to God whom innocence of life keeps a stranger to human wickedness.
**“shall call upon God”** — the inward witness
**“and he will hear him: for the simplicity of the just man is laughed to scorn.”** — by the double-minded, as foolishness
12.5:
**“The lamp”** — he who is freed from the devil is thought dead by the fleshly, but Christ lives
**“despised”**
• which is
• because they do not have what they themselves love
**“in the thoughts of the rich”** — not the thing is in fault, but the swelling
**“The lamp despised in the thoughts of the rich”** — The lamp despised in the thoughts of the rich: the name of the rich signifies the pride of the proud. The simplicity of the just is called both a lamp and despised: a lamp because it shines within; despised because it is reckoned cast-off in the minds of the fleshly.
**“is ready for the time appointed.”** — but they will shine, because they will judge with Christ
**“is ready for the time appointed”** — Is ready for the time appointed: the appointed time of the despised lamp is the predestined day of the last judgment, in which it is shown with how great power each just man who is now despised shines.
12.6:
**“The tabernacles … abound”**
• but these things are not to be cared for, in which even the reprobate abound
• he who does not have riches easily despises them; he who has them hardly reckons them cheap; which Job does, saying that they abound for the reprobate
**“of robbers”** — because they are not grateful for good things, but worse
**“The tabernacles of robbers abound”** — The tabernacles of robbers abound: he shows that the riches of the present life are nothing, saying that they abound for the reprobate, who boldly provoke God; who very often are the prouder against God the more they are enriched by his bounty, and beyond their merit. Those can be called robbers who, while they say what they do not do, take away in speaking the words of the just. As robbers they took by violence what he himself gives. But God gives one thing in mercy, lets another be held in anger. And what robbers do perversely God permits justly, so that their guilt may be increased and he who suffers may be struck for former things; and what he forbids to be done he justly permits to be done. But he also fills some with gifts of teaching who, growing proud from them, provoke him; who, robbers in themselves, perversely usurp the words of the just, and yet have received from God the good things they have.
**“and they provoke God boldly; whereas it is he that hath given all into their hands”** — or: ‘to the hands’
12.7:
**“But”** — truly he himself
**“ask now the beasts”** — as if: even if these do not think in agreement about the power of God, yet the creatures themselves show the Creator in themselves
**“But ask now the beasts, and they shall teach thee”** — But ask now the beasts, and they shall teach thee: the beasts are the duller in sense; the birds of the air, the lofty wise.
12.8:
**“Speak to the earth”** — those given to earthly action
**“and it shall answer thee: and the fishes of the sea shall tell.”** — the searchers of the world
**“the fishes”** — The fishes: the curious are understood. And the sense is: if you ask these, they confess God the Creator of all. It can also be understood according to the letter.
12.9:
**“Who is ignorant”** — he adds what these things, when asked, teach
**“that the hand of the Lord hath made all these things?”** — he who made all things disposes how they ought to be governed
12.10:
**“In whose hand”** — power
**“is the soul of every living thing”**
• the life which gives sense to animals
• or ‘soul’ is taken for the bodily life of man too; ‘spirit’ is put here not for the soul but for the spiritual effect
**“In whose hand is the soul of every living thing”** — In whose hand is the soul of every living thing: in this place the soul of every living thing signifies the very life of the body. The spirit of all flesh, that is, the effect of spiritual understanding in man, which are in God’s power. By the soul of every living thing the life of beasts can also be signified.
**“and the spirit of all flesh of man.”** — of man, who tends to spiritual understanding
12.11: **“Doth not the ear discern words”** — Doth not the ear discern words? From these bodily things he shows how diverse things the same Spirit works, so that one receives the gift of wisdom, another of knowledge, another of tongues; or “the ear discerns words and the palate of him that eateth the taste,” as if he said openly: the words of teaching which reach you only as far as the ear touch my palate too by the inmost savour of understanding. There is one sense, of the brain, but in the ear and the mouth and the other different instruments it discerns as though diverse in a diverse way, so that it does not see in the ear nor hear in the eye; so wisdom is one, but it gives to some more, to some less, to one knowledge, to another kinds of tongues, and so on. Or: what the reprobate hear, as you do, I taste; and what you know savours to me to the marrow through inmost love.
12.12: **“In the ancient is wisdom”** — In the ancient is wisdom: for those sayings are made solid in the root of wisdom which grow strong through the practice of living, even by the experience of deeds. And he shows on whose gift they depend.
12.13:
**“With him is wisdom and strength,”** — in the first coming wisdom goes before; strength in the second coming
**“With him is wisdom”** — With him is wisdom: for with God: “In the beginning … the Word was God,” who is both the power of God and the wisdom of God. He has counsel because he disposes his own; understanding, because he knows ours.
**“he hath counsel and understanding.”** — by counsel can be noted the delay of hidden judgment, by which he bears with sinners for repentance; as if: he understands all things; he is not ignorant, but acts by counsel
12.14:
**“If he pull down, there is no man that can build up”** — If he pull down, there is no man that can build up: the Almighty pulls down the human race when he forsakes it; he builds up when he fills it; and unless this is done, it is admonished outwardly by the preacher in vain.
**“if he shut up a man,”** — by rejecting
**“if he shut up”** — If he shut up: every man, through what he does wrongly, what else does he make for himself but a prison, so that the guilt of his soul presses on him, even if no one accuses him outwardly? But for God to shut up is not to open to those shut in, and not to soften the reprobate heart through grace.
**“there is none that can open.”** — as Isaac did not for his firstborn Esau
12.15:
**“If he withhold the waters, all things shall be dried up”** — If he withhold the waters, all things shall be dried up: because if the knowledge of preachers is withdrawn, the hearts of those who could have grown green in eternal hope dry up. Or because by the name of water the grace of the Holy Spirit is signified. If the grace of the Holy Spirit is withdrawn from the mind of the hearer, the understanding at once dries up. And that he says ‘waters’ in the plural he referred to the sevenfold grace.
**“and if he send them out, they shall overturn the earth.”**
• so as to do the opposite of the former
• but because to many a longer life is given and not wisdom, he adds on whose judgment the gifts depend: “With him”
**“and if he send them out, they shall overturn the earth”** — And if he send them out, they shall overturn the earth: for if the grace of the Holy Spirit is poured in, at once the earth is overturned, because the hardness of the sinful mind is changed from the obstinacy of its immovability.
12.16:
**“With him”** — also
**“is strength”** — in the second coming
**“With him is strength”** — With him is strength: in the earlier words, in which he says: “With him is wisdom and strength,” he plainly shows that what he taught meekly, how it was to be believed, he shows terribly in the power of judgment. But in the following words, in which he says: “With him is strength and wisdom,” he shows more clearly than light that first in the judgment he will destroy the reprobate by power, and, the reprobate driven off, will show the elect in the kingdom what the wisdom of the Father is.
**“he knoweth both the deceiver, and him that is deceived.”** — but because even before the last judgment he judges secretly, he adds: “he knoweth”; knowing, he judges one whom he ‘knows not,’ that is, does not approve
**“he knoweth both the deceiver, and him that is deceived”** — He knoweth both the deceiver, and him that is deceived: he knows the deceiver, because very often he sees his earlier evils, and by just judgment lets him fall into other sins too. He knows him that is deceived; for since men often commit evils which they know, they are allowed to be deceived, so that they fall into evils which they do not know; which is wont to happen sometimes for cleansing, sometimes as the beginning of vengeance.
12.17:
**“He bringeth counsellors to a foolish end”** — He bringeth counsellors to a foolish end: he calls counsellors the preachers who give their hearers the counsel of life. When they preach for temporal things they are led to a foolish end, because they tend there by labour from where, by uprightness of mind, they ought to flee.
**“and judges to insensibility”** — And judges to insensibility: those who are set over others to examine their conduct are rightly called judges; but when they do not discuss them carefully, nor know how to correct them, they are brought to insensibility.
12.18:
**“He looseth the belt of kings, and girdeth their loins with a cord.”** — with sin, whose delight rules the members, so that he may show in public how detestable are those whom pride defiles within
**“He looseth the belt of kings”** — He looseth the belt of kings: for in those who seemed to rule their members well, he destroys the girdle of chastity for the fault of pride. And because the delight of the flesh is in the loins, he girds their loins with the cord of sin and delight.
12.19:
**“He leadeth away priests without glory”**
• whose glory is the uprightness of those under them
• before God, to whom they bring no fruit
• He leadeth away priests without glory: because before the judge they will not find the glory which they do not now seek, by zeal in preaching, in the conduct of those under them.
**“and overthroweth nobles.”** — while they rejoice in temporal rule instead of eternal, and fall into pleasures
**“and overthroweth nobles”** — And overthroweth nobles: because when by just judgment he forsakes the mind of rulers, they neglect heavenly things and fall here into their pleasures.
12.20:
**“He changeth the speech of the true speakers”**
• because speech is withdrawn from one who does not act, so that he who does not work may not dare to speak; and by just judgment it comes about that he who refuses a good life has no tongue
• He changeth the speech of the true speakers: because often those who were truthful in preaching heavenly things, when they love temporal things, fall to speaking earthly things; the speech of the true speakers is changed. Or it can be understood of the Jews, who before, truthful, announced that Christ would come, but denied him when present.
**“and taketh away the doctrine of the aged.”**
• because they do not follow the precepts of their forebears
• Elias will turn back the hearts of the children to their fathers when he makes them understand concerning Christ what the fathers foretold
**“and taketh away the doctrine of the aged”** — And taketh away the doctrine of the aged: the doctrine of the aged was taken away because the Jews by no means followed, by believing, the things which they remembered their fathers had foretold.
12.21:
**“He poureth contempt”** — lest anyone glory in good or despair of evil
**“upon princes,”** — upon those who lord it over the conquered, if they are proud of it
**“and … them that were oppressed”** — by vices
**“relieveth”** — through repentance
**“He poureth contempt upon princes”** — He poureth contempt upon princes: the Jews, remaining in the commandments of the Law, seemed to be princes through faith; the Gentiles lay hidden, pressed down in the depth through unbelief. But when Judea denied the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation, the Gentiles believed. So: “He discovereth deep things out of darkness,” when the allegorical senses are mystically recognized in the hidden words of the prophets.
12.22:
**“He discovereth deep things out of darkness”** — and while those fall, these are revealed; an open sentence is brought forth from the hidden counsel of God, so as to show what he thinks of each one
**“and bringeth up to light the shadow of death.”** — it is wicked working, which comes forth from the devil as from a body; which lies hidden from those who do it, but God brings it to light when he makes the cause known so that it can be destroyed
**“and bringeth up to light the shadow of death”** — And bringeth up to light the shadow of death: he calls the shadow of death the hardness of the Law, which inflicted death of the flesh, which is the shadow of the death of the soul. And the shadow of death is brought to light when, the death of the spirit being understood, which Christ commanded us to fear, the fleshly punishment removed, the death of the flesh is not feared at all.
12.23:
**“He multiplieth nations, and destroyeth them”** — according to the letter, because daily they are born and die, but in the resurrection he restores them
**“He multiplieth nations, and destroyeth”** — He multiplieth nations, and destroyeth: because he both spreads the nations by fruitfulness of offspring and yet leaves them in their own unbelief; and those whom he had left in the fall of unbelief he at length brought back at the end; and when they are so restored, what follows comes about.
12.24: **“He changeth the heart of the princes”** — He changeth the heart of the princes: the heart of the princes of the earth was changed when the chief priests and elders of the people tried to withstand him whom before they preached; and, deceived by their malice, they tried in vain to walk where there is no way; because for their cruelty, seeking to put out his name, there could be no open way against the author of all things.
12.25:
**“They shall grope as in the dark, and not in the light, and he shall make them stagger like men that are drunk.”** — while he shows himself to them as one who could both work divine things and suffer human things
**“They shall grope as in the dark”** — They shall grope as in the dark: for he gropes as in the dark who does not see what he touches; so these too, amid so many miracles, asked: “What sign dost thou shew, that we may believe thee?” And they staggered like drunken men. Everyone who strays is led now here, now there; so these sometimes said: “Unless this man were of God, he could not do any thing,” sometimes: “Is not this the carpenter’s son?”

13.1:
**“Behold … all these things”**
• already are
• Behold … all these things: for all these things were made present to blessed Job by the spirit of prophecy. For he saw things to come as present in him to whom future things do not come nor past things go away; but of the very things that were to come he saw some to be in works, others in words.
**“my eye hath seen,”** — as present
**“and my ear hath heard them, and I have understood them all.”**
• as a prophet
• There follows: “my eye hath seen, and my ear hath heard,” etc. But because things said have no use if they lack understanding, there follows: “and I have understood them all.” For when something is shown or heard, if understanding is not given, it is not prophecy at all. Of which understanding he shows that he is not lifted up when he says: “According to your knowledge.” By these words he made known how great his humility was, who denies he is inferior to those whose life he had far surpassed by living holily, and affirms that he knows according to their knowledge, he who, knowing heavenly things, passed beyond their earthly thoughts by the spirit of prophecy.
13.2:
**“According to your knowledge I also know: neither am I inferior”** — in life
**“to you”** — or: to you
13.3:
**“But yet I will speak to the Almighty,”**
• in prayer
• Or he reasons with God who, obeying him here, will afterwards judge the peoples with him; who even meanwhile does not cease to judge the wicked.
**“But yet I will speak to the Almighty”** — But yet I will speak to the Almighty: we speak with the Almighty when we pray for his mercy. We reason with him when, joining ourselves to his justice, we discuss our deeds with fine searching.
**“and … to reason”** — about his own things
**“I desire … with God.”** — in judgment
13.4:
**“Having first shewn that you are forgers of lies, and maintainers of perverse opinions.”** — truth arises not from fabrication but from nature
**“Having first shewn that you are forgers”** — So the Church speaks of heretics. “Having first shewn that you are forgers.” For as a building is put together with stones, so a lie is put together with words.
13.5:
