**“And I wish you would hold your peace”** — And I wish you would hold your peace: seeing them wish to appear what they were not, he warned them to be silent, so that they might not appear what they were. For a fool, if he holds his peace, will be counted wise, if he is not betrayed by other signs.
**“And I wish you would hold your peace, that you might be thought to be wise men.”** — Because the fool, by speaking against him, is not able to weigh the words of the wise man, after silence he adds: “Hear.” Because the heretics cannot defend from the truth the things they understand wrongly of God, they seek falsehoods by which to lead weak minds astray.
13.6: **“Hear ye therefore my reproof”** — Hear ye therefore my reproof: so he rightly brought in reproof first and judgment after; because unless the swelling of the fool is first pressed down by reproof, the judgment of the just man is by no means known through understanding.
13.7: **“Hath God any need of your lie”** — truth does not need to be propped up by falsehood
13.8:
**“Do you accept his person”**
• to accept God’s person is to take up his authority in judgment
• Do you accept his person? The just, when they rebuke, are always aware of their own weakness and suffer with others inwardly; because it belongs to him alone to discuss the sins of men without compassion who, from the almighty power of his nature, does not know how to sin. They were accepting his person who had rebuked Job as though they had nothing blameworthy in themselves. And he strives to judge for God who, when he blames another, is not made weak within himself through compassion.
**“and do you endeavour to judge for God?”** — forgetting yourselves
13.9:
**“Or shall it please him”** — anyone
**“from whom nothing can be concealed?”** — because he judges in him what he feels within, not what he seems to serve outwardly
**“or shall he be deceived as a man, with your deceitful dealings?”** — no
**“shall he be deceived as a man, with your deceitful dealings”** — Shall he be deceived as a man, with your deceitful dealings? Heretics offer deceit to God, because they assert things which do not please him for whom they speak, and while they try to defend him they offend him.
13.10:
**“He”** — but
**“He shall reprove you, because … his”** — He shall reprove you, because … his: there are those who perceive the truth of God in the heart and attack it outwardly so as not to seem conquered; these accept his person in secret. Or there are those who, when they return to their mind, contemplate the justice of God and tremble, but afterwards return to iniquity. These, in secret within themselves, accept the face of God as of one who sees bodily; because when they become present to him they flatter him with tears, and when they withdraw as it were from his sight they disparage him by their conduct. And they are to be struck the more, the more they know the right judgments of God in the hidden place of thought.
13.11:
**“As soon as he shall move himself, he shall trouble you”** — As soon as he shall move himself, etc. In human speech the very strictness of his uprightness is called God’s movement, which will trouble through vengeance the reprobate who will not be troubled here through repentance.
**“and his dread shall fall upon you.”** — which you do not foresee, as the just do who take precautions
**“and his dread”** — And his dread: because to the reprobate fear does not bring forth rest, but punishment brings forth fear; whence the prophet: “Vexation alone shall make you understand what you hear,” because when they are punished for the commandments of God which they despised, then they understand what they heard.
13.12:
**“Your remembrance”** — which you laboured to spread
**“shall be compared to ashes, and … shall be brought to clay”** — because it is put where the breeze snatches it away, that is, in earthly things; but the just man is in eternal memory, who entrusts his deeds to the eyes of God
**“Your remembrance shall be compared”** — Your remembrance shall be compared: however much one labours for the memory of his name, he has put his memory as it were as ashes, because the wind of mortality quickly snatches it away; “and … shall be brought to clay.” The neck is brought to clay when each proud man is humbled into death and the lifted-up flesh wastes in rottenness.
**“your necks”** — pride, which now is lifted up in so many things, not knowing what follows
13.13:
**“Hold your peace a little while, that I may speak whatsoever my mind shall suggest to me.”** — I speak not carnally but spiritually; whence he turns the rebuke to mystical words: “Why do I tear?”
**“Hold your peace a little while, that I may speak”** — Hold your peace a little while, that I may speak: he shows that they spoke from the sense of the flesh, whom he therefore holds back to silence, so that he may speak what his mind suggests to him. As if he said: I speak not carnally but spiritually, because I hear by the sense of the spirit what I bring forth by the service of the body.
13.14:
**“Why do I tear my flesh with my teeth, and carry my soul in my hands?”**
• even if the just man does not profit others, yet he never ceases to give good examples; whence Job shows the virtue of patience still to his friends; whence he adds: “Although he should kill me”
• And carry my soul in my hands, etc. To carry the soul in the hands is to show the intention of the heart in working, which is done for the edification of the neighbour. And the sense is: why do I either judge myself strictly before men, or show what I seek in my work, if I profit my neighbours neither by pointing out evils nor by showing good things?
**“Why do I tear my flesh with my teeth”** — Why do I tear my flesh with my teeth? The teeth in this place are the inner senses, which chew and break up as it were each thing they think, and pass it to the belly of memory. With these teeth the saints, if they find anything fleshly in themselves, pursue it fiercely in themselves, so that they may be found blameless, and the wicked, seeing this, may be amended. And the sense is: why do I discuss with my inner senses the fleshly things done in me, if I cannot profit my onlookers, that is, you?
**“with my teeth”** — With my teeth: the teeth are the inner senses, which search into each thing. Hence Jeremias: “He hath broken my teeth one by one,” because blindness is begotten in the senses according to the measure of sins. Hence it is also said: “He that eateth the sour grape, his teeth shall be set on edge.” The sour grape is fruit before its time, which he eats who feeds on the delight of this life; whence the inner sense is bound so that it cannot chew spiritual things.
13.15:
**“Although he should kill me, I will trust in him:”** — another man hopes when God does him good
**“Although he should kill me”** — Although he should kill me: he is truly patient who is both worn down by adversity and yet is not bent from the uprightness of hope. “But yet my ways.” For the Lord is then found as Saviour if now, for the fear of the Lord, your sin is reproved by yourselves.
**“but yet … my ways in his sight”** — he who brings the power of God back to mind and judges himself stands in the sight of God. Whence Elias: “As the Lord liveth, in whose sight I stand”
**“I will reprove”** — whence this profit may come
13.16:
**“And he shall be my saviour: for no hypocrite shall come before his presence.”** — because he does not put the strictness of God before his eyes while he desires to please in human eyes; but
**“for … shall not come”** — For … shall not come: he will come indeed before the judgment seat of the judge; but because he now pretends not to consider his faults, pouring himself out wholly, he believes the words of his neighbours in his praise and rejoices, and refuses to come into the sight of the Lord by bringing his sins back to memory.
13.17: **“Hear ye my speech, and receive with your ears hidden truths.”** — Hear ye my speech, etc. By naming hidden truths he shows that he has figurative speeches. Whence he adds in the voice of the faithful people: “If I shall be judged.” This does not disagree with his own person either, of whom the Lord said even greater things: “that there is none like him.” He says more humbly that he is just, not more than others. What is it that he said above: “I will reprove my ways in his sight,” and below: “thou wilt consume me for the sins of my youth,” and now says: “If I shall be judged, I know that I shall be found just”? But, attributing iniquity to himself and his cleansing to God, he both knows himself a sinner of himself and is not ignorant that he has been made just by gift.
13.18:
**“If I shall be judged”** — in the last judgment, before which I am now scourged, though good
**“I know that … just”** — he knew himself just, and does not deny that he was justly scourged; he is scourged out of abundant grace, so that his merits may be increased, not so that his sins may be wiped away
**“I shall be found”** — and when just
13.19:
**“Who is he that will plead against me? let him come:”**
• and would that I might be blameless within too, toward which the just man labours in every way
• but
• Who is he that will plead against me? Because in outward acts he has nothing for which he may be blamed, he freely looks for an accuser; but because the hearts of the just too blame themselves for foolish thought, it is added: “why am I consumed holding my peace?” As if he said: as I have lived so as to fear no accuser outwardly, would that I had lived so as not to fear an accusing conscience within me. For he is consumed holding his peace who finds within himself that by which he is burned.
13.20:
**“Two things only do not to me, and then from thy face I shall not be hid:”** — when you have removed these two things
**“Two things only do not”** — Two things only do not: and here he calls the face of God the punishment by which, when he looks on sins, he punishes; from which no one is hidden unless the two things he asks for are removed; of which there follows: “Withdraw thy hand far from me.” By the hand which he asks to be withdrawn he signifies the Law, which held the people under the stroke of vengeance and under which men served in fear. In these words he seeks the time of grace and redemption. And the sense is: remove from me the hardness of the stroke, take away the weight of dread, pour in the spirit of security; because he cannot be just in your sight who serves you not through love but through dread.
13.21:
**“thy hand”** — the stroke of the Law, which punishes
**“Withdraw … far from me”** — he wishes punishment and fear to pass, so that he may come to love
**“and … thy dread”** — by which one served under the Law
13.22:
**“Call me, and I will answer thee”** — be present bodily; and, present, he laid open to men the sins which they did and did not know. Whence he adds: “How many are my iniquities?”
**“Call”** — Call: he seeks the presence of Christ, so that through it he may both hear what he does not know and hear in the things he knows. Or God calls by choosing, man answers by obeying; man speaks by desiring, God answers by appearing. But so, panting, he examines himself more finely: “How many are my,” etc. “Call me, and I will answer thee.” God’s calling is to look upon us by loving and choosing. Our answering is to obey his love with good works.
**“or else I will speak”** — Or else I will speak: we speak when we ask for his face through desire. He answers those who speak when he appears to us who love him.
13.23:
**“How many are my iniquities and sins?”** — every man confesses himself a sinner, but is ashamed to be called wicked
**“How many are my iniquities and sins”** — How many are my iniquities and sins? The labour of the just is to find themselves, and, finding, to bring themselves to better things by weeping and correcting. Iniquity seems heavier than sin, crime than offence.
13.24:
**“Why hidest thou thy face”** — Why hidest thou thy face? Man had the contemplation of God in paradise, but through guilt he fell into darkness. And roused by punishment he returns to love and says:
**“and thinkest me thy enemy”** — And thinkest me thy enemy: because if you looked on me as a friend you would not deprive me of the light of your vision.
13.25:
**“Against a leaf, that is carried away with the wind”**
• who fell from the tree in paradise
• how cheap man is
• Against a leaf, that is carried away with the wind: man is called a leaf, who is carried away by the wind of temptation and moved by the breaths of desires. He is also called straw, for because through the flesh he was near the earth, even when he seemed to stand he is recorded as straw. But because he lost the greenness of inmost love, he is now dry straw. And the sense is: why do you press with such uprightness one whom you know to be so weak?
**“thou shewest thy power,”** — how great is the strictness of God
13.26:
**“For thou writest bitter things against me”** — For thou writest bitter things against me: because what we speak passes, what we write remains, God is said not to speak but to write bitter things when his scourges last long upon us; for once for all he fixed the sentence on the mortality of the flesh, which cannot be changed until the last.
**“and wilt consume me for the sins of my youth.”** — And wilt consume me, etc. It is plain that the sins of the young and the old are heavy, if the just so fear what they offended in a weak age.
13.27:
**“Thou hast put my feet in the stocks”** — Thou hast put my feet in the stocks: God put man’s foot in the stocks because he bound his wickedness with the strong sentence of his strictness.
**“and hast observed all my paths”**
• because he judges each of his things finely
• And hast observed all my paths: a path is narrower than a way; and because we take ways as actions, we rightly take the paths of actions as thoughts.
**“and hast considered the steps of my feet:”** — he examines intentions, or the wicked deeds by which there is stumbling to others
**“and hast considered the steps of my feet”** — And hast considered the steps of my feet: he called the intentions of works steps; or wicked works, which, when we do them, we give a bad example to the brethren who watch, and, as it were with foot bent out of the way, leave crooked footprints for those who follow.
13.28:
**“Who … as rottenness”**
• that is, who am bound by weak flesh
• Who … as rottenness: as a garment is eaten by the moth born from itself, so man has in himself the rottenness by which he is consumed. Or he is tempted from the corruption of his flesh, as a garment is consumed by the moth born from it.
**“How many are my iniquities”** — How many are my iniquities: as if: man, for the blindness of exile, does not know what befalls him, because he hides himself from the face of God; which, warned now by the punishment itself, he grieves over.
**“Against a leaf”** — Against a leaf: man was a tree in his making, but, dried up in temptation, a leaf; straw in his casting down.
**“and wilt consume me for the sins of my youth”** — And wilt consume me for the sins of my youth: because he finds that he sinned in youth, he fears the deeds of his youth. But there are ages in the mind too. First, infancy, when one is innocent and cannot speak what he is. Then childhood, in which he says what he wishes. After, youth, which is first in working. Then young manhood, fit for strength. Then old age, fitting for maturity. So the just, when they have advanced higher, in the discernment of maturity fear the more about their beginnings, as though they were then without discernment.
**“am to be consumed”** — to be worn away by the corruption of the flesh
**“and as a garment that is moth-eaten.”** — because temptation comes out of the flesh, which consumes and bores through without sound, that is, so that sometimes the mind does not feel it

14.1:
**“Man born of a woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries.”** — because all things here are misery
**“Man born of a woman”** — Man born of a woman: here by the name of woman weakness is signified. And the sense is: what strength has he in himself who is born of weakness? Who is both narrowed for life and widened for misery?
14.2:
**“Who cometh forth like a flower, and is destroyed”** — men born in the world are flowers in the field; life in the flesh is a flower in the hay
**“Who cometh forth like a flower”** — Who cometh forth like a flower: because he shines in the flesh, but is destroyed, because he is brought back to dust and rottenness.
**“and fleeth”** — daily, moment by moment
**“as a shadow”** — the life of man is compared not to the sun but to a shadow, because, having lost the love of God, he lost the warmth of heart and remained in the cold of iniquity
**“and fleeth as a shadow”** — And fleeth as a shadow: he compared man not to the sun fleeing but to a shadow. For he who has not the warmth of heart in the love of God, and yet does not hold the life he loves, flees as a shadow.
**“and never continueth in the same state.”** — but passes from infancy into childhood, so through the other ages to death; so too he is changed according to the mind
**“and never continueth in the same state”** — And never continueth in the same state: for he always fails by the very thing by which he believes he advances in the span of life.
14.3:
**“And dost thou think it meet”** — and since he is such, and you so great
**“And dost thou think it meet to open thy eyes upon such an one”** — And dost thou think it meet to open thy eyes upon such an one? For God to open his eyes is to exercise judgments and to see whom he is to strike.
**“and to bring him into judgment with thee?”** — having considered God as judge, he again considers his own weakness; as if: you ought not to judge but to cleanse
14.4:
**“Who can make him clean that is conceived of unclean seed?”**
• whence: “I was conceived in iniquities”
• Who can make him clean that is conceived of, etc. For he who alone is clean of himself is able to cleanse unclean things. For our very conception, because of the pleasures of the flesh, is uncleanness. Or he means Christ alone, who was not born of unclean seed.
**“is it not thou who only art?”** — clean through yourself
14.5:
**“The days of man are short,”**
• but
• by the consideration of the eternal the shortness of time is more plain
**“The days of man are short”** — The days of man are short: because with God even passing things stand, he declares that the number of the months is with him. Or by days the shortness of time, by months the multiplied spaces of days are signified; so the days of man are short. But because our life is stretched out afterwards, the number of our months is recorded to be with God.
**“and the number of his months is with thee: thou hast appointed”**
• short, and you
• he decreed from eternity prosperity, adversity, death and all things; or in spiritual things God sets each one a bound and measure, because no one grasps as much as he desires, lest he lift himself up in the things he has; as also happened to Paul
**“his bounds which cannot be passed.”**
• or: to pass
• but
**“thou hast appointed his bounds which cannot be passed”** — Thou hast appointed his bounds which cannot be passed: for none of the things that happen to men in this world happen without the hidden judgment of God.
14.6:
**“Depart a little from him, that he may rest,”**
• that is, remove the force of the scourge; another kind of departing does not let him rest
• Depart a little from him, etc. Depart, that is, now take away the scourges of the present life and show the goods of eternal rest.
**“until his wished for day come”**
• by the showing of future rest, until, namely, it comes itself
• Until his wished for day come, when he receives eternal rest in recompense for his labour.
14.7:
**“A tree”** — do so, because man is more despised than a tree
**“hath hope:”** — this one
**“A tree hath hope: if it be cut”** — A tree hath hope: if it be cut: he hints how despised the human race is, and how much even senseless things seem to go before it. Or according to the mystical sense the tree is preferred to man; for here every fleshly man is understood as man, the just man as the tree, who, when he is struck by suffering in death, is restored by the greenness of eternal life.
**“and the boughs thereof sprout”** — And the boughs thereof sprout: because from the suffering of the just man the faithful receive the greenness of spiritual life.
14.8: **“If its root be old in the earth, and its stock be dead in the dust:”** — If its root be old in the earth, etc. The root of the just man is holy preaching, because from it he springs and in it he subsists; which in the hearts of the earthly is believed to be spent in all its strength. And the stock dies in the dust, because his body is put to death in the hands of the persecutors.
14.9:
**“At the scent of water, it shall spring”** — At the scent of water, it shall spring: because through the breath of the Spirit he makes the green blade of virtue in the hearts of the elect by the example of his work.
**“and bring forth leaves, as when it was first planted”** — And bring forth leaves, as when it was first planted: to bring forth leaves when the stock is cut down is, when the just man is put to death bodily, to rouse the hearts of many to grow green by the example of his suffering; “as when it was first planted,” that is, he shows in the effect of work the greenness which he had before in the foreknowledge of the Creator. Or the root of the just man is human nature itself, which grows old in the earth when it returns to dust. The stock dies when the body is scattered from its form. At the scent of water it springs, because it rises again through the coming of the Holy Spirit. And it brings forth leaves as when it was first planted, because it returns to that form for receiving which it had been created in paradise, if it had not sinned.
14.10:
**“Man”** — the sinner
**“But … when he shall be dead”** — by guilt
**“and stripped”** — of justice
**“and consumed,”** — by punishment
**“I pray you where is he?”** — who is neither in the homeland nor can be long in exile
**“But man when he shall be dead”** — But man when he shall be dead: man dies by the very loss of justice; he is stripped of the garment of innocence granted in paradise; he is consumed by the destruction of the flesh that follows. Where then is he who is not in his love, where true being is?
14.11: **“As if the waters should depart out of the sea”** — As if the waters should depart out of the sea: the sea is the mind of man; the thoughts of the mind are like the waves of the sea. So when man dies the waters depart, because in that day all their thoughts shall perish. And the river, made empty, dries up, because when the soul is withdrawn the body remains empty, like an empty river-bed. The present life is compared to the sea and the river, because now it is touched with the bitterness of adversity, now we are filled with the sweetness of prosperity.
14.12:
**“So man when he is fallen asleep”** — above, in the comparison of the tree, man was called dead from the life of justice; here the death of the flesh is called sleep, from which one quickly rises
**“shall not rise again;”** — he does not deny that he rises at all, but “till … be broken”
**“till the heavens be broken, he shall not awake”** — Till the heavens be broken, he shall not awake: because when the end of this world comes, the human race will awake from sleep. Or Christ is the tree which, cut down by the Passion, grows green by the Resurrection, through which the boughs, that is, the faithful, grew. The root, that is, his preaching, grew cheap among the unbelieving in the dust, that is, he was despised in the hearts of the persecutors, because he could be killed in the flesh. “At the scent of water,” because by the power of God the flesh returned to life. He brought forth leaves, because the apostles, who had withered, rushed to faith as before; in comparison with whom man is dust. Whence: “But man when he shall be dead.”
14.13:
**“Who will grant me this, that thou mayst protect me in hell,”** — but at least protect me in hell, so that you hide me not in the places of punishment but in the higher ones
**“Who will grant me this, that thou mayst protect me in hell”** — Who will grant me this, that thou mayst protect me in hell: knowing that before the coming of the Mediator he would go down to hell, he asks there for the protection of the Creator.
**“and hide me”** — from torments
**“till thy wrath pass,”**
• by which you punish sins
• And hide me till thy wrath pass, etc. The wrath of the Lord, as regards the souls of the elect, passed at the coming of our Redeemer, because he led them back from the bars of hell to the joys of paradise.
**“and appoint me a time when thou wilt remember me?”**
• whence: “But when the fulness of the time was come, God sent his Son,” etc.
• but
**“appoint me a time when thou wilt remember me”** — Appoint me a time when thou wilt remember me: he asks for the coming of the Redeemer to the underworld.
14.14:
**“Shall man that is dead, thinkest thou,”** — he comes down to the weak
**“live again?”**
• he will truly live
• Shall man that is dead, thinkest thou, etc. He takes up the words of weakness so as to strengthen them more strongly afterwards.
**“Shall man that is dead, thinkest thou, live again”** — Shall man that is dead, thinkest thou, live again? Just men are wont, in a matter they hold certain and solid, to take on themselves the words of the weak, but again to contradict the doubt by a strong sentence. Whence there follows: “All the days.”
**“all the days”** — he strengthens them
**“in which I am now in warfare,”** — because this life always tends to its end
**“I expect until my change come.”** — in which change this will happen
**“all the days in which I am now in warfare”** — All the days in which I am now in warfare: he who awaits his change with such desire hints how certain he is of the resurrection.
14.15:
**“Thou shalt call me”** — now, while corruption lasts, we do not answer the incorruptible one, because we are not like him but far away
**“Thou shalt call me, and I will answer thee”** — Thou shalt call me, and I will answer thee: we truly answer God when he calls, when at the command of the supreme incorruption we rise again incorruptible.
**“to the work of thy hands thou shalt reach out thy right hand.”** — because
**“to the work of thy hands thou shalt reach out thy right hand”** — To the work of thy hands thou shalt reach out thy right hand: as if he said: therefore the corruptible creature will be able to stand fast unto incorruption, because it will be raised by the hand of your power. Or the right hand is called the Son, who, incarnate, was sent to raise man up.
14.16:
**“Thou indeed hast numbered my steps, but spare my sins.”** — as if: in this too there is wonderful mercy, because you weigh the evils and yet mercifully forgive them
**“Thou indeed hast numbered my steps, but spare”** — Thou indeed hast numbered my steps, but spare: he numbers the steps and spares the sins, because he considers our acts finely, and only here forgives the penitent mercifully.
**“hast numbered …, but spare”** — Hast numbered …, but spare: he numbers while he turns us to weep for each thing we have done; he spares, because he does not punish what we have punished. Whence he adds further: “Thou hast sealed up.”
14.17:
**“Thou hast sealed up”** — you will spare, because even if you sealed up, you cured
**“my offences as it were in a bag”**
• Thou hast sealed up as it were in a bag, etc. In secret, so that at some time they might come out in public. He seals and cures, because he neither leaves them unpunished nor will punish them in the judgment. Or the heart of man is God’s bag, in which evils are sealed while they are looked at carefully; and if man acknowledges them, God forgives.
• Or: “Thou hast sealed up as it were in a bag,” etc. He seals up offences in a bag because he attends to them in the secret of his judgments, so as to strike.
**“but hast cured”** — through scourges
**“hast cured”** — Hast cured: because here, through scourges, he forgives utterly.
**“my iniquity.”**
• sins and iniquity, I say
• because
14.18:
**“A mountain falling cometh to nought, and a rock is removed out of its place.”** — this often happens, that when cliffs fall a rock is carried to other places, and waters hollow out stones
**“A mountain falling cometh to nought, and a rock”** — A mountain falling cometh to nought, and a rock: there are two kinds of temptations: one which is brought about by a sudden event, another which comes into the mind little by little and stains the soul by light suggestions. And the sense is: as here senseless things now fall swiftly, now, steeped by the softness of waters, are consumed little by little, so too him whom you made rational, and who is set on high like a mountain, you either cast down by sudden temptation, like David, or allow to be consumed by long and slow temptation, like Solomon.
14.19:
**“wear away the stones”**
• by constancy
• The rock, that is, the mind of the just man, is carried; “out of its place,” that is, from justice to guilt by too great a push. The stones, that is, the strength; the waters, constant allurements. The ground, that which bears fruit.
**“Waters …, and with inundation the ground by little and little is washed away: so in like manner thou shalt destroy man.”**
• as the mountain falls and the stone is consumed
• and yet
14.20:
**“Thou hast strengthened him for a little while, that he may pass away for ever:”** — another reading: ‘pass through’
**“Thou hast strengthened him for a little while, that … for ever”** — Thou hast strengthened him for a little while, that … for ever: man was strengthened for a little while, because here he received the strength of living for a short time; but in this shortness, where he was strengthened, he gathers that by which he may find himself in eternity, either to rejoice always or not to escape punishment.
**“thou shalt change his face”** — and because you strengthened him that he might pass
**“thou shalt change his face, and shalt send him away”** — Thou shalt change his face, and shalt send him away: man’s face is changed when his form is worn away by death. And he is sent away, because from the things which he held willingly he is forced unwillingly to pass to eternal things.
14.21:
**“Whether … come to honour”** — after he is sent away
**“his children … or dishonour, he shall not understand.”** — the children for whom he strove here with such love; the souls not of the just, who see the brightness of God (for there is nothing outside that they do not know), but of the wicked, which, examined, do not know whether their works are approved or rejected
14.22:
**“But yet his flesh, while he shall live, shall have pain”** — But yet his flesh, while he shall live, shall have pain: for they suffer tribulation of the flesh here even because they live spiritually.
**“and his soul shall mourn over him”** — And his soul shall mourn over him: for it is fitting that man should always find sorrows in himself, who, leaving the Creator, sought joy in himself.

15.2:
**“Will a wise man answer as if he were speaking in the wind, and fill his stomach with burning heat?”** — truly into the wind and into heat, because you accuse
**“Will a wise man answer”** — Will a wise man answer? All things that are perceived in the saints displease the wicked as though brought out into the wind; nor do they think the words of the good are things said by reason, but goads of fury. Whence it is added: “and fill … with burning heat”; they even try to cloak, by defending the Lord, the things they think insultingly. Whence he adds: “Thou reprovest him by words.” And they think no one has the fear of the Lord except him whom they have drawn to the folly of their profession.
15.4: **“As much as is in thee, thou hast made void fear, and hast taken away prayers from before God.”** — Whence he adds: “As much as is in thee,” etc. “Hast taken away” is said, that is, removed. As if he said: presuming on your own justice, you scorn to pray for the grace of your Creator. When heretics find no true evils against the good, they invent things to reprove, so that they may seem just.
15.5:
**“For thy iniquity hath taught thy mouth”**
• from a perverse life you have taught yourself to speak perverse things
• For thy iniquity hath taught thy mouth: iniquity teaches the mouth when from an evil life is conceived what is said worse.
**“thou imitatest the tongue of blasphemers”** — Thou imitatest the tongue of blasphemers: heretics, as though revering God, deny lowly things such as his flesh and death, and say that the Church which confesses these things blasphemes; and if anything adverse befalls her, they say it happens for this injury.
15.6:
**“Thy own mouth shall condemn thee, and not I: and thy own lips shall answer thee.”**
• Whence he says: “Thy own mouth shall condemn thee,” etc. Sometimes they wish to crush as though by reasoning. Whence: “Art thou the first man?” This defence of God is taken up by them so that they may seem learned; and while they seem to defend the divine glory, they make their own knowledge known to men. Hence he who began to speak of the wisdom of God at once fell into his own pride, saying: “What … we,” etc.
• Or: “shall condemn.” They assert that his own lips answer him, so that the fault of his speech is the cause of the scourge.
15.7:
**“Art thou the first man that was born, or wast thou made before the hills?”** — so that you can speak of the eternal
**“Art thou the first”** — Art thou the first? As if he said: you who speak of the eternal, weigh that you are temporal; you who dispute about his wisdom, weigh that you do not know his counsel.
15.8: **“Hast thou heard God’s counsel, and shall his wisdom be inferior to thee?”** — so that you dispute about his counsel
15.9:
**“What knowest thou that we are ignorant of?”**
• as if: with another teaching you
• What knowest thou that we are ignorant of? These words plainly show from what pride of mind comes all that sounds as if in defence of the Lord.
**“what dost thou understand”** — by yourself
15.10: **“There are with us also aged and ancient men, much elder than thy fathers.”** — There are with us also aged and ancient men, etc. Heretics, because they cannot establish their views by reason, try to defend them before fools by the authority of the ancients; and they say that the doctors of the Church were their masters, and they say that adversities befall the Church for its wicked confession. And this is: “Is it a great matter?”
15.11:
**“Is it a great matter”** — as if: even since you are such, your evils come to you from your guilt
**“that God should comfort thee?”** — because if you corrected yourself by the profession of faith, you would have comfort from the scourges
15.12: **“Why doth thy heart elevate thee”** — Why doth thy heart elevate thee? Often the mind of the just is lifted up to contemplate higher things, so that outwardly their face seems to be struck still. But the reprobate think this force of contemplation comes about through hypocrisy; for what is in themselves they think is in others.
15.13:
**“Why”** — then
**“Why doth thy spirit swell against God”** — Why doth thy spirit swell against God? Very often the just, afflicted by some necessities, are forced to tell of their works, as blessed Job had done, which is thought pride; but things brought forth with a humble heart are not proud in the ears of God; and as it is a heavy fault to claim for oneself what is not, so very often there is no fault if one humbly speaks of good that is.
**“such words”** — Such words, about your good deeds. Yet Job in these did not swell against God, but humbly said what he had truly done. Often the just and the unjust have the same words, and those please by the very thing by which these offend; as the Pharisee, who justifies himself in deed, and Ezechias, who justifies himself in thought.
15.14:
**“What is man”** — but you ought not to swell
**“What is a man”** — What is man? By the very fact that he is called homo, he is described as earthly and weak; for he is named from humus, the ground.
**“that he should be without spot”** — among wicked reproofs he mixes true things, but does not say good things well
**“and he that is born of a woman that he should appear just?”**
• of corruption
• And he that is born, etc., that he should appear just: for how should he appear just who is born of her who was the cupbearer of injustice? For the woman first poured injustice for the man in paradise.
15.15:
**“Behold among his saints none is unchangeable”** — by nature; but by clinging to unchangeable truth he becomes unchangeable by grace
**“and the heavens are not pure”** — by themselves
**“in his sight.”** — Behold among his saints, etc. And the heavens, etc. By the name of the heavens he repeated what he signified by the name of the saints, who before the strict judgment of God cannot themselves be perfectly clean.
15.16:
**“How much more”** — because not even the heavens are clean
**“is … abominable”** — in evil things
**“man …, and unprofitable”** — in good things, which are destroyed by evil ones so that they do not please
**“who drinketh iniquity like water?”** — who does unlawful things without fear, as though swallowing the drink of injustice without hindrance
**“How much more is man abominable”** — How much more is man abominable: any perverse man is abominable for the uncleanness of his stain, unprofitable for want of the justice of a perfect life; he is said to drink iniquity because what is drunk has no delay in swallowing. So because guilt is committed by the unjust man without any second thought, iniquity is drunk like water.
15.17:
**“I will shew thee, hear me:”**
• and
• I will shew thee: as if he said: since it is established that Job is not clean, he promises to set out sentences against him; things that ought indeed to be said, but not to this man; which he fortifies with the authority of the fathers.
**“I will shew thee”** — I will shew thee: because he who speaks things heard teaches with less authority than he who speaks things he has seen, Eliphaz, to claim greater authority for himself, says: “I will tell thee what I have seen.” It is the mark of the arrogant that when he has perceived something right, or a little, he is lifted up by it, and as the more learned demands reverence from better men.
**“and I will tell thee what I have seen”** — because
15.18:
**“Wise men”** — as I
**“Wise men confess”** — Wise men confess: see the boldness of heretics, who are confounded by their condemned fathers, and yet bring out sentences with authority, and even leap forth in their praise, and boast of them as the only ones who profited the Church, saying that to them alone was the earth given, that is, the Church to rule, and that no stranger, that is, the devil, passed through their hearts. Behold the sentences: “All his days.” The elect too are wont to be proud in some acts, but before they end their life they change their hearts from pride. But the wicked man is proud all his days, and so ends his life that he does not depart from pride at all.
15.19: **“To whom alone the earth was given, and no stranger hath passed”** — or: has passed
15.20:
**“all his days”** — as if: you are not clean but proud
**“The wicked man is proud”** — trusting in present things, not knowing how uncertain his happiness is
**“and the number of the years of his tyranny is uncertain.”**
• he is a tyrant within, even if he does not afflict his neighbours outwardly, because God looks not at what he can do but at what he wills
• And the number of the years, etc. Properly a tyrant is one who rules in the common state not by right. But every proud man too exercises tyranny in his own measure. For what one does in the state, another in a province, another in a city, another in his own house, another does through hidden wickedness within himself in thought, even if he cannot in deed. And the sense is: “The wicked man is proud all his days,” etc.; but why is he lifted up as if about something certain, whose life is held in uncertainty?
15.21:
**“The sound of dread is always in his ears”**
• an uncertain life is a punishment to him even here, because he is struck by the very thing he does, always fearful and suspicious lest he suffer from others what he did to others; but the innocent man is secure
• The sound of dread is always, etc. A wicked mind is always in labours, as a good one is always calm; because either it contrives evils to inflict, or fears lest they be inflicted on it here by others.
15.22:
**“He believeth not that he may return”** — from sins to justice, since so many things press on every side
**“from darkness to light”** — as one wrapped in darkness despairs of light; whence the wicked man, when he comes into the depth, despises
**“looking round about for the sword on every side.”** — He believeth not that, etc. Because, believing he is struck by snares on every side, despairing of salvation he always grows in wickedness.
15.23:
**“When he moveth himself to seek bread”**
• this too is a punishment to him
• this too is a cause of doing evil
• When he moveth himself, etc. Bread here is the pay of the present life. The day of darkness is understood as the time of vengeance. So in his very act this perverse man weighs the anger of the judge as present, but is not turned from evil.
• Or: “When he moveth himself,” etc. Even if he sometimes fears, seeing the judgments of God coming on him, yet while he seeks present things, overcome by avarice, he despises them.
**“he knoweth that … is ready at his hand”** — in act
**“the day of darkness”** — within himself a witness of his damnation, and yet he does not rest; outwardly he rejoices, inwardly he fears; within is the accuser
15.24:
**“Tribulation shall terrify him, and distress shall surround him, as a king that is prepared for the battle.”** — well is he called a king, because, even if he trembles, he raises himself by boldness; he chooses to suffer anything so long as he does what pleases him
**“Tribulation shall terrify him”** — Tribulation shall terrify him: in everything the wicked man does he is surrounded by tribulation and distress, because his heart is confounded with anxiety and suspicion; if he wishes secretly to steal or to lie, he fears to be caught, and labours how it may be covered. The way of truth is level; the road of lying is heavy. He is compared to a king prepared for battle, because a king who is prepared for battle is so suspicious of the enemy that he fears that the army he leads may give way, lest by the desertion of his soldiers he lie open to the darts of the enemy. So the wicked man, doing false things and speaking false things, dreads lest he lose his soldiers, that is, the arguments of falsehood, and lie open to the darts of truth, if perhaps he lacks something to set against it out of deceit.
15.25:
**“For he hath stretched out”** — therefore all these things
**“his hand against God,”** — this is plainly of Antichrist and all his members
**“For he hath stretched out … against God”** — For he hath stretched out … against God: to stretch out the hands against God is to persevere in wicked working, despising his judgments. And he is strengthened against the Almighty, because he is allowed to prosper in his evil action, who runs against him with neck raised up, while he boldly commits the things that displease the Creator.
**“and hath strengthened himself against the Almighty.”** — he who perversely craves against God is allowed by just judgment to fulfil it, nor, the power being denied him, does he return to himself to repent
15.26:
**“He hath run against him with his neck raised up”**
• abounding in earthly things, he is raised up against God
• He hath run, that is, in evil work he had no obstacle from adversity.
**“and is armed with a fat neck”** — And is armed with a fat neck: the fat neck is pride grown rich, propped up, as it were by much flesh, by abundant things.
15.27:
**“Fatness hath covered his face”**
• because the care of earthly things occupies and blinds
• Fatness hath covered his face: fatness covers the face because the desired abundance of earthly things weighs down the eyes of the mind.
**“and the fat hangeth down on his sides.”**
• it is not enough for them of themselves, unless their followers too glory from them
• And … on his sides, etc. The sides of the rich are those who cling to them. The fat hangs down from his sides, because whoever clings to a powerful and wicked man himself also swells with his power as with fatness.
15.28:
**“He hath dwelt”** — such a one
**“in desolate cities, and in desert houses that are reduced into heaps.”** — cities and houses, buildings, make heaps when they fall
**“He hath dwelt in … cities”** — He hath dwelt in … cities: because a city is named from the dealings of those living together. The desolate cities are the very throngs of the perverse who serve him, by whom he is praised. The desert houses are the wicked thoughts which this wicked man inhabits, because through everything he does he seeks to please the thoughts of wicked men. They are called desolate and desert because they are forsaken by the Almighty. They are reduced into heaps, because while all the wicked, by their confused actions, join one another to perverse works, they show beyond doubt that they have fallen from the building of life.
15.29:
**“He shall not be enriched,”**
• also
• or: shall not be inhabited, which is the same; because the proud thought will not be inhabited by the grace of its author, and so he whose mind God does not inhabit is not enriched with virtues
**“He shall not be enriched”** — He shall not be enriched: because the thought of the proud will not be inhabited by the grace of its author.
**“neither shall his substance continue”** — Neither shall his substance continue: as if he said: what he seems to have outwardly passes, and that which could not pass he does not have inwardly.
**“neither shall he push his root in the earth.”** — as a tree that has no root in the earth falls even at a light breath, so he who is strengthened against God stands without a root, and is quickly torn up by the sentence of God
**“neither shall he push his root in the earth”** — Neither shall he push his root in the earth: because his life is torn up at the movement of a hidden sentence as at a light breath. Or he will not push his root in the earth, because he never plants the thought of his heart in the longing for eternal life.
15.30:
**“He shall not depart out of darkness”** — He shall not depart out of darkness: for because he does not seek the light of justice, he does not depart from darkness.
**“the flame shall dry up his branches”**
• by whose example those who cling to him are burned with desires
• The flame shall dry up his branches, etc. Because those too who are joined to him burn with earthly desires, so that they do not bear the fruit of good work, because through wickedness they pant to crave weak things.
**“and he shall be taken away by the breath of his own mouth.”** — the more the proud man prevails here, the more his tongue is let loose against men and against God
**“and he shall be taken away by the breath of his own mouth”** — And he shall be taken away by the breath of his own mouth: because he will receive the sentence of the blow for not restraining the breath of his mouth with the fear of God.
15.31:
**“He shall not believe, being vainly deceived by error,”**
• and justly
• He shall not believe, vainly, etc. Because almsgiving cannot redeem him, which the robbery of the poor he has committed does not allow to rise before the eyes of God. Or he cannot obtain by almsgiving the lengthening of temporal life so as to escape the end that is due.
**“that he may be redeemed with any price.”** — almsgiving after guilt is a price by which one may be redeemed, but it avails nothing to him who remains in evil
15.32:
**“Before his days be full he shall perish”**
• because his wickedness too cuts life off
• Before his days be full he shall perish: because he sets long days before his mind while he cannot reach the time he waits for; as it were he perishes before his days are fulfilled. Or “Before his days be full,” because if he has perhaps begun something good, before it grows strong in him through length of time, he slips back to outward things.
**“Before his days be full”** — Before his days be full: the days of the foreknown can be neither increased nor lessened, unless it happens that they are so foreknown as to be either longer with very good works or shorter with very bad ones; as Ezechias earned an increase by tears, and it is said of the perverse: “death meeteth the undisciplined.”
**“his hands shall wither away”** — His hands shall wither away: they are dried up from all good working.
15.33:
**“He shall be blasted”** — even if he does good things, yet not with a right intention
**“as a vine when its grapes are in the first flower,”**
• namely the work
• He shall be blasted as a vine, etc. If excessive cold or heat touches a flowering vine, the flower is shaken off and the grape wastes away. So some who, after perverse journeys, desire to follow holy ways, before good desires grow strong in them the prosperity of the world, which entangles them outwardly, draws them back from the warmth of inmost love, and as by cold puts out whatever seemed to appear in them of the flower of virtues. And heat befalls in flower those whom the craving for human praise, though fervent in holy zeal, makes strangers to fruit. Whence he adds: “and as an olive tree that casteth its flower.” The olive, when it is in flower, if it is touched by excessive mist, is emptied of fruit. So those beginning good things, if they begin to delight in praises, lose the fruit of their work, as by the mist of favour, by which a darkness of understanding comes about, so that they cannot discern with what intention they do anything.
• Or: “in the first flower.” The weak man ought not to rule, nor to do lower things, because he grows cold in earthly acts. Or when he sees that what he does pleases, he does the same good things more ardently, and as it were burns in holy zeal; whence he perishes by heat.
**“and as an olive tree that casteth its flower.”** — the olive casts the flower it put forth, because it does not bring the beginnings of good work to perfection
15.34:
**“the congregation”**
• he shall be blasted, because
• for this happens to those who do not follow God with a pure heart
**“For … of the hypocrite is barren,”**
• if the intention is not good, even the good work that is seen perishes
• For the congregation of the hypocrite, etc. Hypocrites gather good works, but their very gathering is barren, because by what they do they do not seek to receive fruit in the eternal requital.
**“and fire shall devour their tabernacles”**
• because with the heat of avarice they show greater good deeds
• And fire shall devour their tabernacles, etc. He calls tabernacles the bodies in which their souls dwell, which here the desire for praise, and afterwards the fire of hell, will burn up.
**“their tabernacles”** — Their tabernacles: thought is the tabernacle in which the mind dwells, which the heat of avarice lays waste. Or he calls the heart the tabernacle, which the burning for praise consumes. Or the body is the tabernacle of the soul, and those who burn here in mind will burn in the flesh in the fires of hell.
**“who love to take bribes”**
• of praise
• earthly ones; because they seek greater gifts from all, fire will devour their tabernacles
15.35:
**“He hath conceived”**
• by envying
• He hath conceived: the mind of the hypocrite too is never free from evil, because he envies others the things he craves, so that he may be brighter by despising them. Hence he also prepares deceits, so that he alone may take the esteem.
**“sorrow, and hath brought forth”** — by disparaging
**“He hath conceived sorrow”** — He hath conceived sorrow: when he thinks perverse things; he brings forth iniquity when he begins to carry them out.
**“his womb prepareth deceits”** — His womb prepareth deceits, that is, the mind in which thoughts are begotten conceives greater malice against neighbours the more it seeks to be seen as more innocent than all. He said this because he thought Job was struck for hypocrisy.

16.2:
**“I have often heard such things as these:”** — namely, the things which the wicked throw at the good who oppose them, before they are accused of them themselves; and the good have a reward from their patience, even if not from the others’ conversion
**“I have often heard such things as these”** — I have often heard such things as these: the elect often hear others’ evils as if their own, and the crime is fastened on them by those who commit the crimes they fasten on. “You are all troublesome comforters.” The wicked, when they see the good labouring in adversity, try to persuade them to evil in the very act of seeking to comfort them.
**“you are all troublesome comforters.”** — in this you are troublesome, because you seem to comfort, because among sweet things you bring in poison; yet the good, not broken by it, defend right things. Whence Job: “Shall,” etc.
**“troublesome comforters”** — Troublesome comforters: care must be taken that rebuke is not given in the time of mourning, because even if some ought rightly to be rebuked, yet in affliction he who ought to soothe the pain should not increase it.
16.3:
**“Shall windy words have no end?”** — therefore they have no end
**“Shall windy words have no end”** — Shall windy words have no end? The wicked bring out windy words. For their sayings, even if sometimes sound in sense, are yet puffed up through pride.
**“or is it any trouble to thee to speak?”**
• that is, will trouble come to you from your speaking? Not because the sufferer does not pay you back; but if you did this to a wicked man, he would pay you back with trouble, and you would be silent sooner
• as if: no trouble comes to you; but I could
**“or is it any trouble to thee to speak”** — Or is it any trouble to thee to speak? As if he said: you speak the more, the less you hear anything troublesome from me about your own conduct.
16.4:
**“I also could speak like you: and would God”** — and since you are not corrected by words, would that you felt what I feel; a loving prayer, by which he wishes them the scourges of God, not for punishment but for correction
**“I also could speak like you”** — I also could speak like you: he tells what he could have done; but lest he forsake justice, he turns aside from what he could have done.
**“your soul were for my soul.”** — not mine for yours, lest I be like the wicked
**“and would God your soul were for my soul”** — And would God your soul were for my soul: in these words it is shown that he intends this: that his friends, who did not know how to suffer with him through charity, might learn by experience how they ought to have pitied another’s affliction; whom, tamed by pains, he would comfort, by showing that through the outward suffering inward health was growing strong in them. He would also wag his head, because he would bend his mind to compassion, and strengthen them among the scourges, softening the force of their pain with gentle words. And he would move his lips as sparing them, because he would rebuke their evils with measured reproach.
**“I would comfort”**
• then
• saying that scourges profit
**“you also with words,”** — so you ought now to have done to me
16.5:
**“I would strengthen you with my mouth, and would move my lips, as sparing you.”** — not wholly, because even if I brought in vices too intemperately
**“as sparing”** — As sparing: note ‘as,’ because the Church, mixing the rigour of discipline with meekness, spares the well-disposed subject by not sparing him, because she rebukes freely but frees from guilt. But the forward man, who would be made worse by correction, she does not spare by sparing, because she seeks a time when, speaking to all in common, she inveighs against that kind of fault; so that he, hidden under cover, is struck more temperately and healed. This is said of the hidden faults of the forward powerful. For if the preacher is silent about open ones, he seems to approve them, and they grow into an example.
16.6:
**“But what shall I do?”** — but because nothing tames you
**“If I speak, my pain will not rest:”**
• because the perverse are happy here
• But what shall I do? If I speak, etc. Though this fits the person of blessed Job, yet it fits the Church as the things above do; whose pain does not rest when she speaks, when she sees that the perverse are not corrected by her speech; and when she is silent the pain does not depart, because even if, turned away, she falls silent, she groans the more at the very fact that she is silent, because she sees that while she is silent the faults of the perverse grow.
16.7:
**“But now my sorrow hath oppressed me”**
• but evils from outside, from outsiders
• under his own person he shows the persecution of the Church in the last times, namely of Antichrist
• But now my sorrow hath oppressed me; and all are brought to nothing. The Church is pressed with sorrow when she sees the perverse grow in malice. And her members are brought to nothing when the weak, by imitating the wicked, are weakened worse, and are as it were brought to nothing, because while, loving passing things, they forsake the abiding essence of God, they tend as it were to not-being. “But now” is said because the time of the Church’s sorrow is now; joy follows afterwards. But it often happens that the holy Church not only bears unbelievers and adversaries set outside, but hardly bears the snares and hostility of those she has within. Whence fittingly in the voice of the blessed man it is soon added: “My wrinkles bear witness.” The wrinkles of the Church are all who live double in her, who proclaim the faith in words and deny it in works. These, in time of peace, because they see that this same faith is held in honour by the powers of this world, falsely say they are faithful. But when sudden adversity troubles the Church, they at once show what they contrive in their faithless mind. And the sense is: those rebuke me by pursuing me who, set in my body, do not amend the malice of their doubleness.
**“and all … are brought to nothing”** — while the wicked grow, the weak are moved by it toward earthly things
**“my limbs”** — as the strong through the bones, so the weak through the limbs
16.8:
**“My wrinkles”** — evils within, from those of the household
**“bear witness against me, and”** — now
**“a false speaker riseth up”** — this at the end, under Antichrist
**“and a false speaker riseth up against my face”** — And a false speaker riseth up against my face: while they do not presume to contradict her preaching openly, the Church suffers the false speaker as it were behind her back. But when the time of malice breaks out, he who now disparages in fear comes before her face to contradict, because he withstands the words of the true faith with open voices. And since this is done through the evil spirit, he turns his words to describing him.
16.9:
**“He hath gathered together his fury against me, and threatening me he hath gnashed”** — in the powerful
**“He hath gathered together his fury”** — He hath gathered together his fury: the devil, the prince of false speaking, has fury against the Church now, but it is scattered, because he stirs hidden temptations through individuals. But when, having received licence, he rages openly against her, he gathers his fury against her, because he draws himself together with his whole intention to afflict her. He gnashes his teeth against her and looks on her with terrible eyes, because through some he carries out cruel things against her, and through others he plans what to carry out.
**“with his teeth upon me”** — with his persecutors, who tear
**“my enemy … with terrible eyes”** — with the foolish of the world
16.10:
**“They have opened their mouths upon me,”** — who plan, and inflame with counsels of persecution
**“and reproaching me”** — They have opened their mouths upon me, and reproaching, etc. Because the reprobate open their mouths in reproach when they both do not fear to preach error and mock the preaching of the right faith.
**“they have struck me on the cheek”** — They have struck me on the cheek: the cheek of the Church is the holy preachers, who convert the life of the fleshly by the word of correction. These the reprobate persecute above all; and when they even kill them, they are filled with that punishment which above all torments or chastens the mind of the Church.
**“my cheek”** — My cheek: Peter is the jaw, who kills and eats. Samson holds the jawbone of an ass and kills his enemies; that is, Christ holds simple heralds in the hand of his power and kills the fleshly from their vices. The jawbone, thrown on the ground, poured out waters, because the bodies of the heralds, given over to death, show great miracles.
**“they are filled”** — another reading: ‘satisfied’
16.11:
**“God hath shut me up with the unjust man, and hath delivered me into the hands of the wicked.”**
• and since this is so
• God hath shut me up, etc. The people of the elect is shut up with the unjust man when its flesh is given over for a time to the persecutors of the old enemy. It is delivered not in spirit but into the hands of the enemies, because the less they can take it in mind, the more cruelly they burn against its flesh.
16.12:
**“I that was formerly so wealthy”** — the Church in time of peace fed her own with the wealth of preaching
**“am all on a sudden broken to pieces:”**
• because the mind of the weaker falls when unprepared
• I that was formerly so wealthy, am all on a sudden broken, etc. He signifies the mind of the weak, because, while they do not know how to foresee adversity, it is the heavier to them the more unexpectedly they bear it. Or the Church suffers these things in some of her own who slip back, who after the wealth of doctrine are sometimes turned by sudden vices.
**“he hath taken me by my neck, he hath broken me,”** — He hath taken me by my neck, etc. The neck here signifies the upright bearing of freedom, which the enemy holds in time of persecution. He constrains it when the weak do not dare to preach freely the true things they think. Or he calls his neck those in the Church who, under pretext of defending uprightness, serve the vice of pride; this the enemy bends by the strictness of his persecution.
**“and hath set me up to be his mark”** — And hath set me up to be his mark: a mark is set up so that it may be struck by the shooting of arrows. So the faithful people is set up as a mark for its enemy, because he always attacks it with his acts when he afflicts it with his persecutions. Whence the Apostle: “For yourselves know that we are appointed thereunto.” As if he said openly: why do you wonder at our wounds in this time, who, if we seek eternal joys, have come to this, to be struck?
16.13:
**“He hath compassed me round about with his lances”** — He hath compassed me round about with his lances: the Church is surrounded by lances from her enemy when in her members she is attacked on every side by the cunning assailant with the darts of temptations.
**“he hath wounded my loins”**
• in you who consent
• He hath wounded my loins: when the enemy draws the faithful people to lust, he strikes it in the loins. And he is said to wound together with us, because what he suggests wickedly to us we, following, fulfil of our own will, and as it were wound ourselves together with him.
**“he hath not spared, and hath poured out my bowels on the earth.”** — this is not literally of Job; and by this note that all these things are said mystically
**“he hath not spared, and hath poured out my bowels on the earth”** — He hath not spared, and hath poured out my bowels on the earth: he calls the bowels of the Church the minds of those who hold her mysteries in themselves; when the old enemy drags them to worldly business, he pours her bowels on the earth. “He hath not spared,” that is, he has not left off.
16.14:
**“He hath torn me with wound upon wound,”**
• and so
• He hath torn me with wound, etc. In her weak ones the Church is torn with wound upon wound when sin is added to sin, so that guilt is piled up more heavily.
**“he hath rushed in upon me”** — whom, grown used to him, one cannot even wrestle against
**“like a giant.”** — for this
**“he hath rushed in upon me like a giant”** — He hath rushed in upon me like a giant: because truly the evil spirit fights like a giant against the soul overcome by evil habit; because the more often the soul subjects itself to him, the more unbearable it makes him to itself. But because very often it returns to repentance, there follows: “I have sowed sackcloth upon my skin.” By sackcloth and ashes repentance is understood; by skin and flesh, the sin of the flesh. So sackcloth is sewn as it were over the skin and the flesh is covered with ash, because the guilt of the flesh is covered by repentance, lest it be seen for vengeance at the examination of the strict judge.
16.15: **“I have sowed sackcloth upon my skin, and have covered”** — he says all these things in the person of Christ, of whom he is a figure
16.16:
**“My face is swollen with weeping”**
• the strong man mourns for what he did not do in the weak one, whom he helps to pardon, as though he had done it
• My face is swollen with weeping: the face of the Church is those who, set in government, appear first, so that from their appearance there may be honour to the faithful people. These mourn the faults of the weak. But when they see some return to pardon and others persist in iniquity, they stand amazed at the hidden judgments of God, which they do not understand. Whence it is added: “and my eyelids are dim.” Those are called eyelids who keep watch to foresee the journeys of the people; but when not even the watching prelates understand the hidden judgments of God, the eyelids of the holy Church grow dim.
16.17:
**“These things have I suffered without the iniquity of my hand, when I offered pure prayers to God.”**
• he alone had pure prayers to God before all, who even in his Passion prayed for his enemies
• and therefore
**“These things have I suffered without the iniquity”** — These things have I suffered without the iniquity: he turns from the words of the body to the words of the head; because he suffered without the iniquity of his hand, “who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth.” The earth did not cover his blood, because the holy Church has now preached the mystery of her redemption in all parts of the world.
16.18:
**“O earth, cover not thou my blood,”** — the sinner, receiving the price of redemption, confesses and praises
**“neither let my cry find a hiding place in thee.”** — lest the sacrament of the Passion be idle, we ought to imitate what we receive, and to preach it so that it may become known to others
**“neither let my cry find a hiding place in thee”** — Neither let my cry find a hiding place in thee: the cry of our Redeemer is the blood of redemption, which is received by the faithful; which, as the Apostle says, “speaketh better than that of Abel”; because the blood of Abel asked for the death of the fratricide; the blood of the Lord obtained life for the persecutors. This cry finds a hiding place in us if the tongue is silent about what the mind believes.
16.19:
**“For behold … in heaven”** — let it not be hidden, because even if they denied, because God did not appear in the Passion, there is a witness in heaven
**“my witness”**
• because: “No one knoweth the Son, but the Father”
• For behold … in heaven, etc. The witness of the Son is the Father. As in the Gospel: “And the Father himself who hath sent me hath given testimony of me.”
**“and he that knoweth my conscience is on high”** — And he that knoweth my conscience is on high: because the Father works with the Son by one will, one counsel. These things can also be referred to the body. For the Church suffers these evils for eternal things; and lest she tremble about her resurrection, she already has as witness in heaven him who rose from the dead. He is also called one who knows her conscience, because he knows our nature not only by creating it but also by taking it up. This voice can also fit each of us along with Job himself. For everyone who seeks earthly praise for what he does seeks a witness on earth; but he who hastens to please the Almighty in his acts considers that he has a witness in heaven. But such a man ought not to fear the reproofs of men.
16.20:
**“are full of words”** — indeed they are
**“My friends …: my eye poureth out tears to God.”**
• he who has a witness in heaven, if he is blamed by men, should not care
• Whence it is added: “My friends are full of words: my eye poureth out tears to God.” When friends are full of words, that is, when those too who are joined with us in faith disparage us, the eye must needs pour out tears to God, so that our whole intention may flow down in the compunction of inmost love, and may raise itself to inner things the more, the more it is forced to return within by outward insults.
16.21:
**“And O that a man might so be judged with God, as the son of man is judged with his companion!”**
• would that I knew why this is so for me; that, as I am heard by God, so I might hear what God says of me
• And O that a man might so be judged with God, as the son of man is judged with his companion! We indeed always know that we are sinners; but yet, set under the scourge, we do not know for what sin more than others we are scourged, and we examine ourselves so as, if in any way we can, to find the cause of the striking. And the sense is: as he who comes to judgment with his companion both says what he thinks and recognizes what is said against him, so I would hear everything that is said of me to you. But because this cannot be done in the present, he groans indeed at the blindness of the present life, but yet comforts himself with its shortness.
16.22:
**“For behold”** — therefore I say ‘would that,’ of a thing which is not, because
**“For behold short years pass away”** — For behold short years pass away: everything that passes is short; and we walk in the path of death, by which we do not return; not that we are not brought back to life by rising again, but because we do not come again to the labours of this mortal life, or to acquiring rewards by labours.

17.1:
**“My spirit shall be wasted, my days shall be shortened,”**
• he who considers what he will be like in death is always fearful in working; whence: “In all thy works remember thy last end, and thou shalt never sin.” Whence this man too says: “I have not sinned”
• My spirit shall be wasted: the spirit of the elect is wasted by fear of the judge, and if they find any fleshly thoughts in themselves they consume them by the ardour of repentance. But the spirit of the wicked grows thick through the swelling of pride.
**“and only the grave remaineth for me”** — And only the grave remaineth for me: he considers himself almost dead because he is not at all unaware that he is going to die.
17.2:
**“I have not sinned”** — I did no fault and received scourges; not that he was wholly without sin, but he did not deserve these
**“and my eye abideth in bitterness.”** — Whence there follows: “I have not sinned.” He did not sin so much as to deserve these scourges, because he was struck not to correct guilt but to increase grace. Or the head says this, who without guilt took on the punishment of guilt, that is, the bitterness of the Passion; in whose voice he adds: “Deliver me,” through remission.
17.3: **“set me”** — Set me beside thee, by the Ascension; afterwards, because Judea was stirred against the disciples, he adds: “and let any man’s hand,” etc., because now they act in vain against him who sits in heaven; of whom he adds further: “their heart far.” For if they had known the keeping of discipline, they would by no means despise the precepts of the Redeemer.
17.4:
**“Thou hast set their heart far”** — you allowed it to be far, as it was
**“from understanding,”** — discipline is in all the things which God brought on for sin, from which their heart is far, even if the body is under it
**“therefore they shall not be exalted”** — Therefore they shall not be exalted: for those who do not at all try to keep their life through discipline always lie in the depths through their desires, and do not raise their mind to the hope of the heavenly homeland.
17.5:
**“He promiseth a prey”** — He promiseth a prey: he turns the sentence to the head of the wicked, namely the devil, whose companions are the apostate angels who fell with him. His children are the perverse men who are begotten into malice by his wicked persuasion. So he promises a prey to his companions, because he promises the evil spirits that the souls of the wicked will be seized at the end.
**“and the eyes of his children shall fail.”** — the devil and all the wicked are so much one body that the body is reckoned by the name of the head, and the other way round; and so here he returns from the many to the one
**“the eyes of his children shall fail”** — The eyes of his children shall fail: because he rouses the intentions of men to hope only for earthly things; but the intention of a wicked love does not last, since what it loves is known to fail swiftly. Or he calls his companions the cruellest men, his children those whose wickedness is still increasing.
17.6: **“He hath made me”** — He hath made me: everyone who is struck by a scourge is made as it were a byword of the people, and an example; because every fool, when he wishes to curse anyone, takes the curse from the likeness of him whom he sees struck in time.
17.7:
**“is dim”** — because it does not penetrate the secret of God
**“through”** — another reading: ‘to’
**“indignation”** — or: to indignation
**“is dim through indignation”** — Is dim through indignation: the eye grows dim through indignation when those in the Church who have the light of truth see the perverse prevail against the innocent, because they are troubled by wonder at the hidden judgment. But when the just grow dim to indignation, the weak very often fall even to unbelief.
**“and my limbs”** — of weakness
**“are brought as it were to nothing.”** — Whence there follows: “And my limbs as it were to nothing.” By the name of limbs is expressed the tenderness of the weak, who, when they see the perverse flourish and the just tormented, repent that they have begun good things.
17.8:
**“The just shall be astonished at this”**
• he opens more plainly what he said: “is dim to indignation”
• The just shall be astonished at this: this is what he had said: “My eye … through indignation.”
**“and the innocent shall be raised up against the hypocrite”**
• he who does no harm to others too, cannot do perfect things, and envies the glory of the pretender, because he does not yet despise all things perfectly
• And the innocent shall be raised up against the hypocrite: the perfect innocent is raised up against the hypocrite when he despises him with his flower, and, preaching right things, declares to others that he is to be despised.
17.9:
**“And the just man shall hold on his way,”** — And the just man shall hold on his way, etc. Because while he sees him obtain worldly things from a perverse will, he himself is bound more strongly to the love of heavenly things.
**“and he that hath clean hands”** — And he that hath clean hands: because, seeing the earthly glory of the perverse, he despises temporal things the more, the more he sees that even the wicked have them.
17.10:
**“Wherefore be you all converted”** — by faith, or from evil
**“and come”**
• by work, or by doing well
• Wherefore be you all converted, etc. After he has brought in the outward advances of the wicked and the inward ones of the good, he exhorts the elect to be converted by forsaking evil and to come by doing good.
**“and I shall not find”** — would that
**“among you any wise man.”** — And I shall not find among you, etc. Longing for their conversion, he wishes that he may not find any wise man among them; as if he said: learn to be fools in your own eyes, so that you may be truly wise in God.
17.11:
**“My days have passed away,”** — after the leisure of quiet persecution returns; and when happiness passes, the care of earthly management, which in some way draws back from eternal things, ceases in the elect
**“my thoughts are dissipated, tormenting my heart.”** — he who seeks heavenly things says he is tormented while he is forced to deal with low things; whence he reckons adversity as gladness for the quiet of the heart; and this is: “They have turned night into day”
**“My days have passed away”** — My days have passed away: he calls the days prosperity; the thoughts tormenting the heart, the care of earthly happiness; which, the more heavily it presses on the elect, the more finely they think that account will be required of them by the judge; these thoughts are scattered together with the earthly happiness itself.
17.12:
**“They have turned night into day”** — They have turned night into day: the scattered thoughts turn night into day, because sometimes it pleases the just more to suffer evils from adversity than to be wearied by the care of earthly management from prosperity.
**“and after darkness I hope for light again.”** — because prosperity and adversity alternate in turn
**“and after darkness … again”** — And after darkness … again: light is hoped for after darkness, because after the night of the present life the eternal light is looked for.
17.13:
**“If”** — but also
**“I wait hell is my house,”** — because he who leads out has not yet come
**“and I have made my bed in darkness.”** — because he does not yet see there the face of the Creator
**“If I wait”** — If I wait: the earlier saints could endure adversity, and yet, led out of their bodies, they could not be freed from the places of hell. Then indeed man made his bed in darkness, when by consenting to the persuader he forsook the light of justice. And because the just were held in hell, and yet did not have torment from their own acts, to have made one’s bed as it were in darkness is to have prepared rest for oneself in hell.
17.14:
**“I have said to rottenness:”** — but because this comes from the punishment of weakness, he adds the weakness itself
**“I have said to rottenness”** — I have said to rottenness: he calls rottenness his father, because every man comes down from an origin already corrupted. The worms are mother and sister as regards the matter of corruptible flesh, because we both came from rottenness and came with the rottenness we carry. Or nature is called mother and habit sister, because from the one we are with the other; and these, namely mother and sister, are worms, because from corruptible nature and perverse habit we are forced to be wearied in mind by restless thoughts as by worms.
17.15:
**“Where is now then my expectation”**
• in these sicknesses or pains
• Where is now then my expectation? The expectation of the just was Christ, whom they knew would come at some time, but sought to come sooner.
**“and who considereth my patience?”**
• he expresses burning desire
