• Whence ‘now’ is added here: “And who considereth my patience?” God considers the patience of the just, but is said as it were not to consider it in appearing less quickly to the wish of desire, and putting off the grace of his dispensation to longer times.
17.16:
therefore the elect, so as to waste the spirit, suspect that their departure is near, considering the shortness of life
**“shall go down into the deepest pit”**
• he adds the losses of the delay; what he had said, he repeats in the voice of pain
• Shall go down into the deepest pit: before the coming of the Mediator Job was to go down to hell; but how into the deepest? Or does he call the upper places of the underworld the deepest hell? For as regards the height of heaven, this air is hell; as regards the height of the same air, the earth, which lies below, can be understood both as hell and as the deep; but as regards the height of the earth, those places of hell which are higher than the other receptacles of hell he calls in this place the deepest hell. And he says that all his things go down there, where his soul alone was to go down, because what he leaves of himself on earth he feels not to be himself until it returns to incorruption. Or all things go down into hell because the requital of all labours was still awaited to be received only in the rest of hell.
**“All that I have”**
• all, that is, the soul, because one is wholly there where he can feel what he receives; or all the labours, all that he did, from which the reward there; whence he adds
• but
**“thinkest thou that there at least I shall have”**
• he says this not so much for himself as to make us fear
• without the judgment of mind which you have
**“rest?”**
• he shows that he desires this, and is in doubt
• Thinkest thou that there at least, etc. It must be weighed which of us is secure of rest, if even he trembles about it whose praises of virtue the very judge who strikes him proclaims.

18.2:
**“How long will you throw out words?”** — he accuses him first of boasting, afterwards of impiety
**“How long will you throw out words”** — How long will you throw out words? He asserts that blessed Job has broken out into pride, whom he declares to throw out words.
**“understand first”**
• what you say
• Understand first: he signifies with how great pride he had swollen, who thought Job spoke what he did not understand.
**“and so let us speak.”** — then
18.3:
**“Why”** — for
**“are we reputed”** — by you
**“Why are we reputed”** — Why are we reputed? It is proper to the human mind to suspect that what it does is done to itself. For he who is used to despising the good reckons that he is despised, and from the suspicion of contempt he leaps forth to indignation and heaps on insults.
**“as beasts”** — without the judgment of mind which you have
18.4:
**“Thou that destroyest thy soul in thy fury,”** — as if whatever is against him is fury
**“Thou that destroyest thy soul”** — Thou that destroyest thy soul: the reprobate reckon the zeal for uprightness, or the spiritual grace of holy preaching, to be the madness of fury, by which they reckon that the souls of the faithful perish.
**“shall the earth be forsaken for thee”** — by God
**“shall … be forsaken for thee”** — Shall … be forsaken for thee? The Church says that God is truly worshipped only in her, and that there alone is salvation. But against this the heretics: if this is true, all the earth which we, many as we are, inhabit everywhere is forsaken by God. As if: outside you we have God and salvation. Or: “shall … be forsaken for thee,” that is, so that whoever is outside you is not saved at all?
**“and shall rocks be removed out of their place?”**
• as if: will our teachers leave their own views for yours? Not because the evils you suffer prove you wicked
• And shall rocks be removed, etc. The heretics call rocks those whom they reckon to excel in lofty senses, whom they deny are moved from their own place at the voice of the Church, because such men refuse to agree with the humble. The reprobate, seeing the adversities of the Church, are lifted up into an arrogance of justice, as though the just suffer for guilt. Hence this man mocks the scourges of Job.
18.5:
**“Shall not the light of the wicked be extinguished,”**
• if he says this of the present life he is mistaken; if of the end of the wicked man, it is made true
• Whence he adds: “Shall not the light of the wicked be extinguished?” This could rightly be said of the wicked man; it ought not to have been said against the saint. He calls light the prosperity of the present life. But the light of the wicked man is put out, because the prosperity of a fleeting life ends with it.
**“and the flame of his fire not shine”** — And the flame of his fire not shine: he calls fire the heat of temporal desires, whose flame is the outward beauty or power which proceeds from its inner burning; but it will not shine, because on the day of departure all outward beauty is taken away.
18.6:
**“The light shall be dark in his tabernacle”** — The light shall be dark in his tabernacle: sometimes we take darkness as sadness, light as joy. So the light in the tabernacle of the wicked man grows dark, because in his conscience the joy he had from temporal things fails.
**“and the lamp that is over him, shall be put out.”** — and then
**“and the lamp that is over him, shall be put out”** — And the lamp that is over him, shall be put out: a lamp is light in an earthen vessel; so the light in the vessel is joy in the flesh. So the lamp that is over him is put out, because when the requital of his evils follows the wicked man, fleshly joy is scattered in his mind. And it is well said not ‘which is with him’ but ‘which is over him,’ because earthly joys possess the mind of the wicked.
18.7:
**“The step of his strength shall be straitened”**
• even here, lest they return to good things
• The step of his strength shall be straitened, etc. Because punishment will afterwards bind the strength of his malice which he now exercises.
**“and his own counsel shall cast him down headlong”** — And his own counsel shall cast him down headlong, etc. The wicked man now has a counsel: to crave present things, to forsake eternal ones; but he is cast down headlong by his own counsel, because by it he is plunged into the darkness of eternal punishment.
18.8:
**“For he hath thrust his feet into a net”** — For he hath thrust his feet into a net, etc. He who puts his feet into a net does not draw them out when he will. So he who casts himself into sins does not rise at once when he will.
**“and walketh in its meshes”** — And walketh in its meshes: he who walks in the meshes of a net entangles his steps by walking, and when he tries to free himself to walk, he is bound so as not to walk.
18.9:
**“The sole of his foot shall be held in a snare”**
• he carries out the binding, that is, his life is bound in guilt to the end; whence, despairing, he is kindled to worse things
• The sole of his foot shall be held, etc. Because, namely, his end will be bound fast in sin.
**“and thirst shall burn against him.”**
• for the wicked man to thirst is to covet the goods of this world
• while the devil binds him with sins, he thirsts for the death of the sinner
• And thirst shall burn against him: because the more he weighs that he is bound by evils, the more he despairs of his return, and by that very despair he burns more fiercely for the lusts of this world. In his soul thirst burns against him, because he who acted perversely is kindled to act more perversely.
18.10:
**“A gin is hidden for him in the earth”** — A gin is hidden for him in the earth: a gin is hidden in the earth when guilt is concealed under earthly advantages, so that man sees what he can covet, and yet by no means sees in what snare of guilt he sets his foot.
**“and his trap”**
• while the bait, that is, what pleases, is sought, a hidden snare holds; because what he does to others he fears from others. He adds: “Fears shall terrify him on every side”; he thinks all are such as he is to all
• ‘trap,’ that is, a gin
**“upon the path.”**
• in the action he craves
• And his trap, etc. For the enemy looks at the habits of each, to what vice they are near, and puts before their face those things to which he knows the mind is more easily bent: lust to cheerful and merry characters, anger and pride to harsh minds. So he sets the trap where he sees the path of the mind is, because he puts the danger of deception there where he has found the way of a thought near at hand.
18.11:
**“Fears shall terrify him on every side”** — and what these do follows: “shall entangle”
**“and shall entangle his feet.”**
• so that his steps are not free to do well
• but would that
• Fears shall terrify him on every side: because often each man fears to be good for this reason, lest he suffer from the wicked what he remembers he did to the good; and while he fears to suffer what he did, terrified on every side, suspicious on every side, he loses his footing in good work.
18.12:
**“Let his strength be wasted with famine,”** — he wishes it not in the spirit of one cursing but of one foretelling
**“Let … be wasted with famine”** — Let … be wasted with famine: our flesh is weakness; the strength is the rational soul, which can resist through reason in fighting down vices. It is wasted by famine when it is fed by no refreshment of inner food.
**“and let hunger invade his ribs.”** — and
**“and let hunger invade his ribs”** — And let hunger invade his ribs: the ribs are the senses of the soul, which, hidden, protect the thoughts like bowels. Let hunger invade the ribs of the wicked man, because inner hunger thins the senses of the mind, so that they by no means rule their thoughts within, but wander to the outward things they seek.
18.13:
**“Let it devour the beauty of his skin,”** — the things outside, as in the skin
**“Let it devour the beauty”** — Let it devour the beauty: the beauty of the skin is outward temporal glory; by the arms works are signified. He calls death the sin which kills the soul. So the firstborn death is pride, “the beginning of all sin.” So the firstborn death devours the beauty of his skin and his arms, because pride overthrows the glory or the working of the wicked man. For he could have been glorious even in this life if he had not been proud.
**“let the firstborn death consume his arms.”** — and he could have been commended to God by his works, if there had not been pride
18.14:
**“Let … be rooted out”**
• also
• the rich man could have glory and wealth without guilt if he had them in humility; but if he trusts in them, God roots him out
**“of his tabernacle”**
• from the earth
• Let … be rooted out of his tabernacle, etc. His confidence is rooted out of his tabernacle when the perverse man, who had prepared many things in this life, is scattered by sudden death.
**“his confidence …, and let … tread”**
• while he is pressed down here by vices, or by punishment at the end
• And let … tread, etc. Because here he is either pressed down by the vices which drag him to destruction, or at the time of death he is subjected to the power of the demons.
**“upon him like a king”** — who is not resisted
**“destruction”**
• the devil, or sin
• therefore destruction rules over them, because even if the occasion of sinning is lacking, yet desire is not lacking in their hearts
18.15:
**“Let the companions of him that is not, dwell in his tabernacle”** — Let the companions of him that is not, dwell in his tabernacle: that is, let the apostate angels live in his mind through most wicked thoughts, his companions, namely; who for this reason now ‘is not,’ because he has already gone away from the highest essence.
**“let brimstone be sprinkled in his tent.”**
• by which the eternal fire is kindled
• Let brimstone be sprinkled, etc. Brimstone is sprinkled in the tabernacle of the wicked man whenever the delight of the flesh rules in his mind. For by brimstone the stench of the flesh is understood. And because such a one remains in evil, whence he cannot bear the fruit of good either, he adds: “Let his roots be dried up beneath.” By roots we understand the thoughts which lie hidden and produce visible works; by the harvest, open working. So every perverse man, while he sets his thoughts on the lowest things and does not crave the joys of heavenly greenness, lets his roots be dried up beneath; his harvest above is worn away, because all his working is reckoned as nothing by the judgment above.
18.16: **“Let his roots be dried up beneath,”** — whatever it may seem to men
18.17:
**“the memory of him”** — also
**“Let the memory of him perish”** — Let the memory of him perish: the wicked man tries to establish his memory on earth when he strives to spread the glory of his praise. And he rejoices that his name is renowned in the streets when he spreads the working of his iniquity far and wide.
18.18:
**“He shall drive him out of light”** — He shall drive him out of light: he is led from light to darkness when he is condemned from the honour of the present life to eternal torments. He speaks of each wicked man so as to turn to the head, that is, the devil, who in Antichrist will spread the name which the wicked now imitate.
**“and … out of the world”** — in which he glories
**“shall remove him”**
• because at the end he will be condemned with all his followers
• because his iniquity ends with the world, and his people will be punished with him
• And … out of the world shall remove him, etc. When the judge from above appears he is removed from this world to punishments; all which can also be understood of the head of the wicked, Antichrist.
18.19:
**“His seed shall not subsist,”** — persuasion
**“nor his offspring”** — action
**“among his people, nor any remnants in his country.”** — Whence there also follows: “His seed shall not subsist,” etc. Because all the wicked who were born into wicked actions by his persuasion will be struck together with their head. That these things are to be understood of Antichrist he opens in this, when he says: “They shall be astonished at his day”; because he will then show such great signs and do such cruel and hard things that he will bring to amazement those whom he finds at the end of the world; and the former fathers, Elias and Enoch, who are kept for his overthrow, he will pierce with the fear and pain of fleshly death; because even if the elect cannot be conquered by torments, yet because they are men they fear the torments which they conquer.
18.20:
**“They that come after him shall be astonished at his day”** — the elect
**“and horror shall fall upon them that went before”** — And horror shall fall upon them that went before: that is, the hearts of the elect will be struck with dread; whence it is written: “insomuch as to deceive, if possible, even the elect”; not that they will fall, but that they will tremble from the flesh.
18.21:
**“These”** — because he has said many things of the wicked and of their head, he concludes generally
**“men are the tabernacles of the wicked,”** — in which he remains
**“and this the place of him that knoweth not God.”** — who before held another’s place in the praise of men
**“These men are the tabernacles”** — These men are the tabernacles: he referred to this what he had said: “He shall drive him out of light into darkness, and shall remove him out of the world.” And the sense is: he who is now lifted up by not knowing God then comes to his own tabernacles, when he is plunged into torments. Or: “These then are the tabernacles,” as if: in his day the saints will be astonished; so these things foretold, and darkness, etc., will be his tabernacles, and there he will dwell. See that in the conclusions of their speeches they show plainly enough that they believed holy Job was struck for iniquity.

19.2:
**“How long do you afflict my soul”**
• because these things, even if just, are unjustly said against Job, he says he is afflicted
• How long do you afflict my soul? The good are worn down by the speeches of the wicked when those swell against them in words who lie either in perverse faith or in wicked ways.
19.3:
**“Behold, these ten times you confound me”** — Behold, these ten times you confound me: because he had heard rebukes from them five times and answered five times, he declares that he has been confounded ten times; because both in being heavily rebuked and in speaking words of teaching to those who do not listen he suffered confusion: in his own rebukes, because he does not profit them; in their rebukes, because he grieves at the wickedness he hears.
**“Behold, these ten times”** — Behold, these ten times. Mystically. The Church keeps the Decalogue, to which the wicked cause confusion as often as they withstand the divine words in their acts.
**“and are not ashamed to oppress me.”**
• out of fear of men the wicked sometimes return to themselves, fearing more to displease God; but sometimes, having despised God, they reverence man less
• because
**“and are not ashamed to oppress”** — And are not ashamed to oppress: there are some whom a wickedness suddenly arising invites to commit wickedness, but yet human shame calls them back.
19.4:
**“For”** — as if: which you ought not
**“For if I have been ignorant”** — For if I have been ignorant: the knowledge of heretics is not with them, because it is against them while it puffs up; but the ignorance of the Church, in that she cannot penetrate secrets, is with her, because it is for her while it humbles. And because what heretics seek to know is pride, so that they may seem learned against the good, he adds: “you,” on the contrary, from my being struck, ought to be raised against yourselves, fearing worse things for yourselves. For the good man is raised first against himself, afterwards against others.
19.5:
**“But”** — or: and
**“you”** — forgetting yourselves
**“have set yourselves up against me,”** — And this is: “But you have set yourselves up against me.” That is, you leave yourselves, who ought to be reproved, and rebuke me with strict sentences.
**“and reprove me with my reproaches.”**
• the proud think temporal evils to be reproaches
• And reprove me with my reproaches: because those who had known him as just before the scourges now judged him unjust from his very striking.
19.6:
**“At least now understand,”** — At least now understand, etc. The Lord had said of him: “thou hast moved me against him, that I should afflict him without cause”; which he asserts of himself, that he was not afflicted by the Lord with an equal judgment. For if his life and his scourges are weighed, he seems afflicted with no equal judgment; but because God heaped up his merits from the scourge, he did not afflict Job with an unjust judgment.
**“that God hath not … with an equal judgment”**
• as regards the life he led
• And this is what he says: “that God hath not … with an equal judgment.” It must be established, then, both that God dealt rightly with Job and that he does not lie who says it was not done equally; otherwise the devil, whom God praised, would have won in what he had promised about the blessed man’s guilt. Not pride but pain wrung this out. If a good man, with a humble mind, when cause or pain demands it, says good things of himself, he does not sin.
**“and compassed me with his scourges”** — And compassed me with his scourges: when so great an affliction presses us down that the soul cannot breathe again with the comfort of anything, we are no longer only struck by scourges but also girded with them, because we are surrounded on every side by the lash of tribulations.
19.7:
**“Behold I cry”** — with reproaches
**“Behold I cry suffering violence”** — Behold I cry suffering violence: God, knowing what will profit us, pretends not to hear the voice of those who grieve or mourn, so that he may increase the profit and life may be cleansed through punishment. But some of the faithful do not know this grace of dispensation; in whose person it is now said.
**“and no one will hear: I shall cry aloud, and there is none to judge.”** — because
**“Behold I cry suffering violence … and there is none to judge”** — Behold I cry suffering violence … and there is none to judge: it is said when God pretends not to judge the cause against the adversary; because judgment is put off so that the merits of the holy man and the punishment of the adversary may grow.
19.8:
**“He hath hedged in my path round about”** — he adds more about his suffering
**“and I cannot pass, and in my way he hath set darkness.”** — because he both sees himself struck and does not find a life deserving the striking
**“Behold I cry”** — “He hath hedged in my path.” From the figure of the Church, in which the weak think themselves in despair because they are heard more slowly; in some of whom the way is hedged so that they cannot pass, who see what is to be done but cannot fulfil it; to others there is darkness in the way, who cannot even discern what is to be done. “He hath hedged in my path,” etc. He saw his path hedged round with lashes when, wishing to pass to security, he could not escape the scourges; and he found as it were in the way of the heart the darkness of ignorance, he who could not penetrate why he was so scourged.
19.9: **“He hath stripped me of my glory, and hath taken the crown from my head.”** — He hath stripped me of my glory, etc. Plainly these things fit Job. But mystically each one’s glory is justice, which covers and protects from death; which is taken from the weak through adversity, because it clung like a garment outwardly. The crown is the reward of victory which is on the head; the heavenly reward in the mind; but those lose this who do not hold out in the struggle. Or the head is the priests and leaders of the Church; but these too forsake the heavenly rewards, and when they fall the army falls more widely.
19.10: **“He hath destroyed me on every side, and I am lost, and he hath taken away my hope, as from a tree that is plucked up.”** — Whence he adds: “He hath destroyed me on every side, and I am lost, and as from a tree that is plucked up.” A tree is driven by the wind so that it falls; so the weak man is dragged by threats to injustice and leaves the eternal things he hoped for; and because sometimes he who, terrified by punishments, forsakes justice yet does not escape punishments.
19.11: **“His wrath is kindled against me, and he hath counted me as his enemy.”** — He adds: “His wrath is kindled against me.” For him who is so struck that his strength is overcome God strikes not as a son through discipline but as an enemy through anger; whence the prophet too: “I have wounded thee with the wound of an enemy, with a cruel chastisement.” And because the evil spirits often suggest many things to the hearts of the afflicted, and steal whatever good there is, he adds: “His troops have come together,” that is, the evil spirits, who are busy searching out the ways of men; who make themselves a way in the hearts of the afflicted when, amid the adversities that are borne outwardly, they do not cease to send in wicked thoughts also.
19.12:
**“together”** — he tells his own things so as to open the mysteries of himself and of the Church
**“His troops have come …, and have made”** — permitted by God
**“and have besieged … round about”** — And have besieged … round about: they besiege the tabernacle round about when they surround the mind with temptations on every side. Or these things fit blessed Job according to the history too, who judged himself struck not as a son to be corrected but as an enemy, while he gathered before his eyes the evils he endured. Through him the robbers made a way, because the evil spirits received licence to strike him. They besieged his tabernacle round about, because, his goods and children taken away, they wore down his whole body with sores.
19.14: **“He hath put my brethren far”** — He hath put my brethren far: now he uses the voice of the Redeemer. The brethren were put far from him, and the acquaintances departed, who, holding the Law, knew how to prophesy him, and did not at all recognize him present. For the Jews, near by the flesh and acquainted by the teaching of the Law, as though forgetful, denied him incarnate with the words of unbelief, whom they had faithfully prophesied with the words of the Law.
19.15:
**“They that dwelt in my house”**
• whose task is to serve constantly in the house
• They that dwelt in my house: that is, the priests, whose origin, assigned to the service of God, was now held by their office in that condition. The maidservants are the souls of the Levites, serving more familiarly at the secrets of the tabernacle, as at the inner parts of a chamber.
**“and my maidservants have counted me a stranger”** — They did not revere him incarnate.
**“and I have been like an alien in their eyes.”**
• while he was not recognized in his own house, he was as an alien
• And I have been like an alien, because he was not known by the Synagogue; whence the prophet too: “Why wilt thou be as a stranger in the land, and as a wayfaring man turning in to lodge?” For he who was not heard as lord is believed not the possessor of the field but a tenant. He turned in like a wayfarer to lodge, because he took away few from Judea and, going on to the calling of the Gentiles, finished the journey he had begun.
19.16:
**“I called my servant”** — I called my servant: the servant was the Jewish people, obeying out of fear, whom he determined to draw to himself by bestowing gifts, as by sending out words; but it did not answer, because it scorned to render works worthy of his gifts.
**“I entreated him with my own mouth”** — I entreated him with my own mouth: I who had commanded him so many precepts by the mouth of the prophets entreated with my own mouth; because, shown in the flesh, while he humbly spoke the commandments of life, he asked the proud servant, as it were, to come.
19.17:
**“My wife hath abhorred my breath”** — My wife hath abhorred my breath: the wife of the Lord is the Synagogue, subject to him in the covenant of the Law with fleshly understanding; which abhorred his breath when it understood the flesh of the Lord carnally, and dreaded to believe God him whom it saw as man. For the breath is from the flesh.
**“and I entreated the children of my womb”** — And I entreated the children of my womb: by the womb of God we ought to understand his counsel, in which we were conceived before the ages through predestination, so that, created, we might be brought forth through the ages. So he entreated the children of his womb, because, incarnate, he humbly asked those whom he had made.
19.18:
**“Even fools despise me”**
• the peoples, as the Pharisees and doctors
• Even fools despise, etc. Because while those skilled in the Law despised God, the crowd of the people followed their unbelief. Leaving the wise, he had come to seek the poor and the foolish; whence with an increase of pain he says: “Even fools,” for whom I took on folly, “the Word made flesh,” despised me.
**“and when I was gone from them”** — And when I was gone from them: the Lord as it were came near to the heart of the peoples when he showed them miracles, and as it were went away when he showed no signs; and they would not give faith to him when he rested from miracles.
19.19:
**“have abhorred me”** — and what wonder about the people
**“They that were sometime my counsellors”** — those who counsel him in his own affairs, whom he loves the more the more they win for him
**“My counsellors have abhorred me”** — My counsellors have abhorred me: the scribes and doctors of the Law, who used to teach the people for life, had been the counsellors of the Redeemer to come in his members. As in his members God says he is fed and clothed, so also that he receives counsel.
**“and he whom I love most is turned against me”** — And he whom I love most is turned against me: the order of doctors, which before, serving in preaching, was loved most; whom the crowd followed not only to not believing but even to persecuting God.
19.20:
**“The flesh being consumed … to my skin”** — And then what follows was done: “The flesh being consumed, to my skin.” In the bones the strength, in the flesh the weakness of the body is signified. So by the bone Christ, by the flesh the disciples, who in the time of the Passion savoured weak things. By the skin, which is outside the flesh, the holy women are figured, who served the Lord with outward ministries. So as if the flesh were consumed, the bone of the Lord clung to his skin, because his strength, while the disciples fled in the time of the Passion, found the women beside him.
**“My bone hath cleaved”** — The flesh, which had clung to the bone while the disciples, though weak, preached the faith of truth to the peoples. And while the holy women prepared the outward supports needed by the body, they remained in the body as skin outside.
**“and nothing but lips are left”** — speech
**“and … are left”** — And … are left: the teeth are the apostles. Only the lips were left about the teeth when the two walking after his death knew indeed how to talk about him, but now dreaded to preach him or to bite the vices of unbelievers. But now he returns to Job’s own words. “Nothing but” lips; even for the happy there is nothing else about the teeth than lips; and so it is plain that these things are said mystically.
**“about my teeth.”**
• the apostles, who bite the fleshly by correction and break the hardness of the obstinate
• and since these things are so
19.21:
**“Have pity on me, have pity on me, at least you my friends,”** — even if they afflict him with insults, yet he calls them friends, because to good minds even the things that seem adverse become prosperous
**“Have pity on me”** — Have pity on me: it is the mark of the devout, when they suffer from adversaries, to be moved not so much to anger as to prayer. And he says he was touched by the hand of the Lord, as Satan himself had said: “put forth thy hand, and touch his bone.”
**“because the hand of the Lord”** — not of Satan
19.22:
**“Why”** — for
**“Why do you persecute me”** — Why do you persecute me? The more justly God strikes the vices of others, the less he has any vice in himself. And the sense is: you so afflict me for my weaknesses as if you yourselves, like God, had nothing of weakness.
**“as God”** — As God: they do the same as God, because they do what almighty God permits to be done. But they do not will the same, because while almighty God, by loving, brings about cleansing, the wickedness of the unjust, by raging, exercises malice. Or: as though not weak themselves, who ought not to rebuke when God strikes, lest they add pain to pain, but to comfort. But when the hand of the Lord ceases, then rebuke can be given to those who deserve it.
**“and glut yourselves with my flesh?”** — And glut yourselves with my flesh? Those whose mind hungers for the punishments of their neighbours seek to be glutted with others’ flesh. Or those who feed on the disparagement of another’s life are glutted with others’ flesh.
19.23:
**“Who will grant me that my words may be written?”**
• as if: I desire these things to be written so that they may become known to others too as an example
• Who will grant me, etc. He does not want the hard things he bears to be covered by silence, but to be drawn into knowledge by example, so that others may be built up to patience.
• Who will grant me: these things fit the Church too, which, keeping the two testaments, asks a second time that her words be written, saying: “Who will grant me that my words may be written? Who will grant me that they may be marked down in a book?” etc. And because she speaks with strong sentence now to those heavy with the weight of avarice, now to hard hearts, she writes with an iron pen on a plate of lead, or with a chisel in flint. Note also that by the book she understands the hearts of both, but afterwards divides the book itself into the plate of lead and the flint.
**“Who will grant me”** — Who will grant me: by the iron pen the strong sentence of the fathers; by the lead the people of Judea, heavy with sin; by the flint the Gentiles are figured. So all that he endured, taught by the strong sentence of the fathers, both the people of Judea and the Gentiles came to know. What is written in lead is quickly blotted out; in flint it is carved with difficulty, but remains. So Judea received the words of God quickly and quickly forsook them; the Gentiles hardly received them, but having received them kept them strongly.
19.24:
**“With an iron pen”** — with strong sentence
**“and in a plate of lead”** — or let them be marked in a plate of lead
**“or else”** — or: with a chisel
**“be graven with an instrument in flint stone.”** — therefore I wish these things to be written
19.25:
**“For I know that my Redeemer liveth,”** — whom others think dead
**“For I know that my Redeemer”** — For I know that my Redeemer: he does not say ‘Creator’ but ‘Redeemer,’ plainly announcing him who, after he created all things, redeemed us from captivity by his Passion. And he lives who fell in the hands of the wicked.
**“and in the last day”** — And in the last day: because the resurrection which he showed in himself he will at some time bring about in us too; for the resurrection which he showed in himself he promised to us, because the members follow the glory of their head. For by example he showed what he promised in reward, so that as the faithful knew that he had risen, so they might hope for the rewards of resurrection in themselves at the end of the world. And this is what he says: “And in the last day … out of the earth,” etc. As if: through his resurrection I hope for the like for myself, but at the end; because our bodies are still put off from the glory of the resurrection until the end of the world; as the other rods remained dry, but only the rod of Aaron, that is, the body of our priest, burst forth into the flower of resurrection; by which flower he is shown to be the priest who intercedes for us.
19.26:
**“And I shall be clothed again with my skin”** — he sets out the effect of the resurrection, namely lest they think it another
**“and in … flesh”** — not in an airy or other body, but in the same flesh
**“my”**
• I shall be
• when
**“I will see my God.”** — in the spirit
19.27:
**“Whom I myself shall see”** — Whom I myself shall see, etc. Our flesh after the resurrection will be the same and different: the same by nature, different by glory. And it will be spiritual, because incorruptible; and palpable, because it will not lose the essence of its true nature.
**“and my eyes shall behold”**
• not only of the heart but also of the body
• I myself, and my eyes, etc. He expressly shows the truth of the resurrection; for it is not one who dies and another who rises, as those say who say the body to come will be invisible and impalpable, as Eutychius said, but the very same.
**“and not another: this my hope is laid up in my bosom.”** — this is most certain to me
**“is laid up”** — Is laid up: we believe we have nothing more certainly than what we hold in our bosom. So he held hope laid up in his bosom, because he was confident with true certainty in the hope of resurrection. But because he made known the day of resurrection to come, now already, whether in his own voice or in the type of the holy universal Church, he reproves the deeds of the wicked and foretells the judgment which follows on the day of resurrection. As if: and because the resurrection is to come, fear the judgment that will then be, and cease from evil.
19.28:
**“Why then do you say now: Let us persecute him,”**
• he reproves deeds
• Whence he at once adds: “Why then do you say now?” The perverse, because they wish to find an accusation in the tongue of the just man, seek the root of a word, from which they may take the beginning of speaking and spread the branches of talkativeness. But yet the holy man, in pity, shows them the evils they should flee, saying: “Flee then.” To flee the face of the sword is to appease the sentence of strict punishment before it appears.
**“and … occasion”** — by the wicked
19.29:
**“Flee then”** — he judges the punishment
**“and know ye that there is judgment.”** — which, if by not fearing you do not know
**“and know ye that there is judgment”** — And know ye that there is judgment: everyone who acts perversely, by the very fact that he despises this, does not know that there is a judgment of God.

20.2:
**“Therefore various thoughts”** — Therefore various thoughts: as if he said: because I consider the terror of the last judgment, therefore I am confounded in fear by the tumults of my thoughts.
**“and my mind is hurried away to different things.”**
• as if: I act so, but
• as if: you are not seen to be just, who are already punished
**“and my mind is hurried away to different things”** — And my mind is hurried away to different things: when, with anxious dread, it weighs now the evils it has done, now the good it neglected to do, now the blameworthy things it is in, now the right things it sees are still lacking to it. These men, from the company of Job, knew indeed how to live rightly; but, not knowing how to weigh the judgments of God finely, they believe that the just cannot be struck here. And so they suspected him to be wicked, and slip into rebuke; to which yet they come down with a certain reverence.
20.3: **“The doctrine with which thou reprovest me, I will hear, and the spirit of my understanding shall answer for me.”** — Whence this man adds: “The doctrine with which thou reprovest me,” etc. Having put these things first with moderation, he reproaches him openly, saying: “The doctrine with which thou reprovest me, I will hear.” Those who sift the words of the speaker take his teaching not as a help but as an occasion of contest, so that they may judge what they hear rather than follow it. And this is: “The doctrine with which thou reprovest me.” As if he said openly: I hear your words indeed, but whether they are rightly spoken I discern by the spirit of my understanding. And this I find: that the praise of the wicked, etc.
20.4:
**“This I know”** — puffed up with the spirit of his own knowledge, he turns back on Job things which fit the wicked
**“from the beginning, since man was placed upon the earth,”** — Therefore he adds: “This I know from the beginning.” For if we lead the eyes of the mind from the very rise of the human race up to this time, we see how short everything was that could be ended.
20.5:
**“That the praise of the wicked is short”** — which is in the favours of tongues
**“and the joy”** — in these honours
**“of the hypocrite but for a moment.”**
• on account of the punishments he sees, he thinks the good things he had once seen were hypocrisy
• But for a moment: because the gladness passes, the punishment remains; it appears for a moment, it disappears for ever.
**“and the joy of the hypocrite”** — And the joy of the hypocrite: the joy of the hypocrite is like a point. For as the pen, when it is set on the point, is lifted, so the hypocrite, while he touches the praise of the present life, loses it.
20.6: **“If his pride mount up even to heaven, and his head touch the clouds:”** — let his understanding be equal to the saints
20.7:
**“In the end he shall be destroyed like a dunghill”** — for his vices he will be trodden down in death, who was glorious here
**“If … mount up”** — If … mount up: that is, even if he pretends to lead a heavenly life, even if he shows off his understanding as like that of true preachers, yet in the end he will be destroyed like a dunghill, because his mind will be condemned for the stench of his vices.
**“and they that had seen him shall say: Where is he?”** — know this
**“and they that had seen him”** — And they that had seen him: those who saw him lifted up will say, when he is put out, ‘Where is he?’ Because he appears neither in this world where he had been lifted up, nor in the rest of eternity, where he was thought to belong.
20.8:
**“As a dream that fleeth away he shall not be found, he shall pass as a vision of the night:”**
• because it is not a thing but a vision
• As a dream that fleeth away, etc. The life of the hypocrite is a kind of vision of a phantom, which shows in image what it does not have in truth. It is compared to sleep, because all praise and glory is lost by him while it is held. And he will pass as a vision of the night, because what he sees himself rich in for a moment by men’s esteem is from the showing of a phantom, not from the solidity of virtue; and when his mind awakes in death, he knows that he saw the favours of men while sleeping.
20.9:
**“The eyes that had seen him”** — The eyes that had seen him: the place of the hypocrite is the heart of flatterers; for there he rests where he finds favours. So the eye that had seen him will not see him, because in death he is hidden from his lovers, who were used to look on him with admiration.
**“neither shall his place any more behold him.”**
• or: his own
• Neither shall … any more behold him, etc. Because the tongues of flatterers do not follow him with favours to the judgment.
20.10:
**“His children shall be oppressed”** — His children shall be oppressed: because those who are born into hypocrisy by imitating him, since they do not hold the solidity of truth, fail in poverty of heart.
**“and his hands shall render him”** — as a debt
**“and his hands”** — And his hands: because they will seize a just damnation from their wicked working. Meanwhile what follows comes about.
**“his sorrow.”** — because he shows himself such here, habit strengthens what he began badly; or he will lose the good things he has for those he pretended
20.11:
**“His bones shall be filled with the vices of his youth”**
• it is a proverb: “a young man according to his way, even when he is old he will not depart from it”
• His bones shall be filled with the vices of his youth: the youth of the hypocrite is the beginning of wickedness; the hard bones in him are the habit of wickedness. So his bones are filled with the vices of his youth, because the hard habits of wickedness in him were taken from the vice of a very evil beginning; and these bones will sleep with him in the dust. To sleep in the dust is not to cease from iniquity until dust, that is, until death. Otherwise, he calls bones something strong and sound which the hypocrite sometimes has in his working; whose bones will be filled with the vices of his youth, because, while, fickle and light, he does many things childishly, even in the things he has done strongly he grows soft in vice; and for his bones to sleep in the dust is for even whatever was done well, along with his wicked actions, to be emptied of all solidity and to perish.
**“and they shall sleep with him in the dust.”** — all pretence is dust, in which even the bone perishes
20.12:
**“For when evil shall be sweet in his mouth, he will hide it under his tongue.”** — which sounds well
**“For when … shall be sweet”** — For when … shall be sweet: iniquity is sweet in the mouth of the heart, which he covers under the covering of smooth speech. For the evil would be on the tongue and not under the tongue if the hypocrite, speaking, laid open his malice.
20.13: **“He will spare it, and not”** — He will spare it, and not: he spares the evil he loves who does not pursue it by repenting, and does not leave it but hides it in his throat, because he so keeps it in thought that he never brings it out in speech.
20.14: **“His bread in his belly”** — His bread in his belly: very often the hypocrite is eager to be taught with the bread of the sacred word, not to live by it but to appear learned; but while he understands wickedly the word of teaching which he seeks badly, he also slips into heresies. It happens to him that he dies of the bread as of the gall of asps. But because, even if he understands God’s words rightly, he does not keep them in work at all, he loses them in the present life, so that he does not know what he wished to do.
20.15: **“The riches which he hath swallowed, he shall vomit up, and God shall draw them out of his belly.”** — And this is: “The riches” of the sacred Law, which he swallowed by reading, he will vomit up by forgetting; which God by just judgment tears out of his memory.
20.16:
**“He shall suck the head of asps”** — the asp is small; it is the hidden temptation of the demons, whose head, that is, beginning, is first born in the heart; captured by it, one is afterwards dragged violently; as in paradise too the devil first persuaded man smoothly, and after consent now drags him even when he resists
**“the head of asps”** — The head of asps: the asp is a small serpent; the viper has a longer body, and is so born that it comes out violently. So he will suck the head of asps and the viper’s tongue will kill him, because when he gladly takes in the beginning of a suggestion secretly, he will afterwards hand himself over, conquered, to violent temptations. Or because the asp kills quickly with its poison, the viper more slowly: by the asp violent and sudden temptation, by the viper gentle and long-lasting temptation is signified. Hence his death is said to be in the sucking of the head, and in the tongue of the viper, because sudden temptation often kills as it rises; the long one, because it suggests wicked things by persuading for a long time, kills as the viper from its tongue.
**“and the viper’s tongue shall kill him”** — as if ‘vi pariens,’ bringing forth by force; by which violent temptation is signified
20.17:
**“Let him not see the streams of the river, the brooks”** — another reading: ‘of the brook’
**“of honey and of butter”** — the hypocrite, pierced by the poison of the demons as of serpents, does not see the gifts of the Holy Spirit, intent on favours outside; whence: “He shall be punished for all that,” etc.
**“Let him not see the streams of the river”** — Let him not see the streams of the river: the streams of the river are the gifts of the Holy Spirit: faith, hope, charity; which the hypocrite does not truly consider, because he attends only to visible things. And the river is the brook, the overflowing flood of the Spirit, which is gathered in the soul of the contemplative. This Spirit fills us with honey and butter alike, because whom he fills he gladdens both with the sweetness of Christ’s Godhead and with faith in his Incarnation. For honey, falling from above, that is, from the air, signifies the sweetness of the Godhead; butter, which is from flesh, the mystery of Christ’s Incarnation.
20.18:
**“He shall be punished for all that he did,”** — another reading: ‘he shall pay for all that he does’
**“and yet shall not be consumed:”** — he whose life was dead in guilt, his death will live in punishment
**“He shall be punished for all that he did”** — He shall be punished for all that he did: for he will pay in torment for the unlawful desires he kept here; nor will he be consumed in death, but he is forced to live without end so as to be tormented without end; so that he whose life here was dead in guilt, his death there may live in punishment. Let him say then: “He shall be punished for all that he did, and yet shall not be consumed,” because he is tormented and not put out; he dies and lives; he fails and subsists; he is always being ended and is without end.
**“according to the multitude of his devices so also shall he suffer.”** — those practised in evil invent more than they learned from the habits of others; whence there will be new torments for them
**“according to the multitude”** — According to the multitude: for although the pain of all the damned is infinite, yet those receive heavier torments who found out many things by their own iniquities and desires.
20.19:
**“Because he broke in and stripped the poor:”** — he puts the guilt under the punishment, that is, covetousness, which is “the root of all evils”
**“he hath violently taken away a house which he did not build.”** — as if: he ought to have built, and on top of that he robs; he did not give of his own, whence damnation; but he took another’s, whence heavier
**“Because he broke in and stripped the poor: … a house”** — Because he broke in and stripped the poor: … a house: he breaks and strips the house of the poor man, because him whom he crushes by power he does not blush to plunder by avarice. And it is well added: “And yet his belly was not filled.” For the belly of the wicked man is avarice, and in it is gathered whatever is swallowed with perverse desire. And it is plain that avarice is not put out by the things desired but increased. For like a fire, when it has received wood to consume, it grows; and the very thing by which the flame seems for a moment to be held down is seen a little after to spread.
20.20:
**“And yet his belly was not filled:”** — avarice
**“and when he hath the things he coveted”**
• the more quickly an evil wish is allowed to be fulfilled, the more quickly it is punished
• And when he hath the things he coveted: it is a sign of greater anger when what is wrongly desired is granted, because sudden vengeance follows from it; because he has obtained this too, which he coveted while God was angry.
20.21:
**“There was nothing left of his meat”** — There was nothing left of his meat: when the hypocrite is struck nothing is left of his food, because when he is led to torments he is made a stranger to all that he had possessed.
**“and therefore nothing”** — at all
**“shall continue”** — or: shall remain
**“of his goods:”**
• that is, in the things he craves; and because he will be stripped even of the things by which he is fed, nothing will be good for him
• Therefore nothing, etc. Because, taken from this life, he goes naked to the judge.
20.22:
**“When he shall be filled, he shall be straitened,”**
• that is, not even here will he be free from punishment
• that is, when he has heaped up many things, he becomes anxious from the very heaping, in which he thought there was rest
**“When he shall be filled, he shall be straitened”** — When he shall be filled, he shall be straitened: when he has heaped up many things he is straitened, for he is anxious how to keep what he has acquired.
**“he shall burn, and every sorrow shall fall upon him.”**
• and
• He shall burn, and every sorrow, etc. On this side and that he fears those who lie in wait; he dreads the more powerful, lest he suffer him as a man of violence; he sees a poor man and suspects a thief. He also takes great care of the things heaped up, lest they be consumed through negligence by the failing of their own nature; afterwards he is given over to eternal torments. But because the perverse man, the more quickly he arrives at his desire, the more easily he is snatched to torment.
20.23:
**“May his belly be filled,”**
• since riches bring so many evils
• There follows: “May his belly be filled.” For God to rain war is to strike with the darts of his judgments, as with thickening drops of rain; so that when the wicked man is already snatched to judgment, now he remembers that he coveted wrongly and gathered what he coveted worse; now he grieves that he leaves what he gathered; and at last he feels the fire of vengeance which he scorned to foresee so as to live well.
20.24:
**“He shall flee from weapons of iron, and shall fall upon a bow of brass.”**
• because while he foolishly guards against temporal evils, he will fall into eternal ones
• He shall flee from weapons, etc. The avaricious man sometimes steals others’ goods through pride, because he seeks to be over others; sometimes he robs from fear of want, when he suspects that his own goods cannot suffice him. Hence it is that he says: “He shall flee from weapons of iron.” The weapons of iron are the necessities of the present life, which press hard and pursue the life of the needy. So passing necessity is compared to iron, because rust consumes iron. By brass, which is usually harder to consume, the eternal sentence is figured; which, because it is not attended to by the wicked man, is justly compared to a bow, because it strikes from ambush. So he will flee from weapons of iron and fall upon a bow of brass, for while, fearing present necessities, he robs many things through avarice, he sets himself in the way of the blows of eternal judgment. Meanwhile: “The sword is drawn out, and cometh forth from its,” etc. The wicked man, while he contrives wicked things in thought, is like a sword in its scabbard. It comes out of the scabbard when it is laid open through the iniquity of evil working. Drawn out, by the seducer; coming forth, by his own will.
20.25:
**“The sword is drawn out”** — by the enemy who persuades
**“and cometh forth from its scabbard”** — by his own choice, by which he consented
**“and glittereth in his bitterness:”** — because vices follow vices; and if they are not all done at once, they are all at once in the mind; even if he does not show them all, he craves to do them all
**“and glittereth in his bitterness”** — And glittereth in his bitterness: by the name of lightning brightness with striking is expressed. So he who, set in power, harms others is called glittering, because by that by which he is lifted up against the good as by the light of glory, the life of the good is tormented.
**“the terrible ones shall go and come upon him.”**
• demons
• The terrible ones shall go and come, etc. The evil spirits are terrible to good minds, to be dreaded and fled; they each serve certain vices; they go and come over the mind of the perverse man; and even if some evils leave him, others take hold of him. For often he is stirred with the fury of anger, and when the fury has gone, lust lays waste his mind. When lust is set aside for a time, pride in his continence is put in its place.
20.26:
**“All darkness is hid in his secret places:”** — because sometimes good things are on the surface
**“All darkness is hid”** — All darkness is hid: for he who does not carry out all things in effect at once, silently holds all harmful things in his mind.
**“a fire that is not kindled shall devour him,”**
• the fire of hell is properly expressed, which, being bodily, burns the wicked bodily, and is not kindled by the effort of man, like this fire of ours, nor fed with wood, but, created once, remains always
• And therefore: “A fire that is not kindled shall devour him.” The fire of hell, which is not kindled by human effort, but was created by God from the beginning of the world.
**“he shall be afflicted when left”**
• he will be punished in soul and body, because he sins in both
• He shall be afflicted when left, etc. The tabernacle of the wicked man is the flesh, because he dwells in it gladly; with it his spirit will be tormented. The good do not set their joy in the flesh but in heaven.
• Left by the flesh, from which he is drawn away; which he loved here and did not wish to leave; then, because of the torments, he will wish to leave it but will not be able.
**“in his tabernacle.”** — his body
20.27:
**“The heavens shall reveal”**
• the perfect, who will judge him with God
• The heavens shall reveal: because here he spared neither the good nor the wicked, at the dreadful examination the life of the just and of sinners alike will accuse him.
**“his iniquity,”** — even if it is hidden now
**“and the earth shall rise up”** — the earthly, who are now redeemed by tears and alms
**“against him.”**
• to accuse
• then
20.28:
**“shall be exposed”**
• now the offspring of the hypocrite is hidden, because even if the working is plain, the intention lies hidden; then the thought will be uncovered
• Shall be exposed: when all the evil that was born in his conscience is shown at the coming of the judge.
**“The offspring … shall be”** — intention
**“he shall be pulled down in the day of God’s wrath.”** — He shall be pulled down in the day, because in the time of vengeance, snatched to torments, he is separated from the face of the eternal judge.
20.29:
**“This is the portion of a wicked man from God, and the inheritance of his doings from the Lord.”** — because not even wicked words will be without punishment
**“This is the portion of a wicked man”** — This is the portion of a wicked man: for when the justice of God exacts punishment from the reprobate for their perverse acts, it repays them evils even to the requital of words.

21.2:
**“Hear, I beseech you, my words”** — against the proud man’s sayings he humbly adds: “Hear, I beseech you”
**“and do penance.”** — he humbly asks so as to lead them to salvation, in which he may profit himself and his hearers
21.3:
**“Suffer me, and I will speak,”** — the saints are ready to tolerate perverse things as they are to teach rightly, and do not fear to be mocked
**“and after, … my”** — in which he may profit himself, if he cannot the hearer
**“if you please”** — good to you
**“Hear, I beseech you, my words, and do penance”** — Suffer me, and, etc. It must be noted that when he was going to add: “do penance,” he first said: “Hear.” But when he was going to add: “after, if you please, laugh at my words,” he first said: “Suffer me.” For hearing belongs to one who is willing, suffering to one who is unwilling. For the good, when they speak, attend to two things in their speaking: namely, to profit either themselves and their hearers, or themselves alone if they cannot profit their hearers. For when the good things they say are heard well, they profit both themselves and their hearers together. But when they are mocked by their hearers, beyond doubt they have profited themselves, whom they have made free from the fault of silence. So blessed Job, to profit himself and his hearers, says: “Hear, I beseech you, my words, and do penance.” And that he may pay what he owes even if he cannot profit his hearers, he adds: “Suffer me, and I will speak,” etc.
21.4: **“Is my debate against man”** — Is my debate against man? If blessed Job, pleasing God, displeased men, he would have no causes of sadness. But because he believed from the present scourges that he had displeased God, made doubtful about his past life, he now called his soul to sadness; who, if the scourges were absent, and he were debating with man about the merits of his life, ought by no means to have been saddened. “Is my debate against man?” As if: not being a hypocrite, if I were dealing with men about my life I would not fear, and if I displeased them I would not care; but because I am rightly worn down along with God. “But you, hearken,” as if: I fear God, but not you.
21.5:
**“Hearken to me”** — Hearken to me: that is, consider what I have done, and wonder at what I suffer.
**“and lay your finger on your mouth.”** — that is, restrain yourselves from the fault of words; or the finger is called discretion, that is, let the tongue be reined in by discretion, so that you may see to whom the right things you say against the hypocrite are to be said
**“and lay your finger”** — And lay your finger: that is, join the virtue of discretion to your speech.
21.6: **“As for me, when I remember, I am afraid, and trembling taketh hold on my flesh.”** — As for me, when I remember: because he had not forgotten his acts, it is plain that he says this in mockery. And the sense is: if I remember that I had anything of the hypocrite, I at once tremble in the weeping of repentance. And he declares that his flesh, if he remembers, is shaken with fear, that is, his weakness is wearied by dread of vengeance. But because Sophar asserted many things about the sudden damnation of the wicked, in which he bit at Job, he adds against his sayings: “Why then do the wicked live?” They are raised up with honours, strengthened with goods, because the divine patience bears with them.
21.7:
**“Why then”** — even if I am struck for guilt
**“do the wicked live”** — this life, except because God permits it
**“are they advanced,”** — with honours
**“and strengthened”** — And strengthened: so that it lasts long in them; but because there are those for whom to have these things is a punishment, because they have no heirs to whom to leave them.
21.8:
**“Their seed continueth”** — He adds: “Their seed continueth,” etc. As proof of happiness, heirs are given with the inheritance.
**“before them”** — Before them: lest any necessity withdraw even from their eyes the things in which the soul exults. But lest in them, being barren, the race be put out, he adds: “a multitude of kinsmen.” See, life, honours, riches, children, grandchildren are said to be theirs; but if care at home burned within, this happiness would not be glad.
21.9:
**“Their houses are secure and peaceable, and the rod”** — discipline
**“of God is not upon them.”** — Whence he adds: “Their houses are secure.” For what would the happiness spoken of above be if it were not glad? If within, prosperity in the fields too.
21.10: **“Their cattle have conceived, and failed not: their cow has calved, and is not deprived of her fruit.”** — Their cattle have conceived, etc. To the owners of flocks the first happiness is if the flock, having no barrenness, conceives; the second, if what is conceived comes to birth; the third, if what is born is brought on to growth by feeding. But this is less if the flocks grow and the keepers of the flocks do not increase; whence the fruitfulness of the household is added: “Their little ones go out like a flock,” etc., so that as greater things have been granted to be had, so many may spring up to keep them.
21.11:
**“and their children”** — of the keepers
**“dance and play.”** — And their children dance, etc. But lest we should believe that play cheap, he says: “They take the timbrel and the harp”; as if: while the masters swell with honours and goods, those under them rejoice in playful acts.
21.13:
**“They spend their days in wealth,”**
• in these and other ways
• They spend their days in wealth: because every length of the present life is known to be a point when it is ended by its end. For whatever could pass was sudden.
**“and in a moment they go down to hell”** — And in a moment they go down to hell: but the end is very bad; see where he was heading, that the prosperity of the present life is no witness of innocence, because both those who enjoy it perish and those who are scourged are freed; which is against Job’s friends.
21.14:
**“Who have said to God: Depart from us,”** — if not in words, in conduct
**“Who have said to God: Depart from us”** — Who have said to God: Depart from us: they say to God: Depart from us, who refuse to give him entrance to themselves and attack him with wicked acts.
**“we desire not the knowledge of thy ways.”** — these are not ignorant, but unwilling to know
**“the knowledge of thy ways”** — The knowledge of thy ways: the way of God is peace, humility, patience; those who despise these say: “we desire not the knowledge of thy ways.”
21.15:
**“Who is the Almighty”** — and further they said
**“that we should serve him?”**
• for, given to outward things, they suspect that the invisible one does not exist; or, if they believe he exists, yet since they seek only earthly things from him, if they see these lacking to those who serve him, they despise him, saying: “What doth it profit us,” etc.
• Who is the Almighty, etc. “For the fool hath said in his heart: There is no God.”
**“and what doth it profit us if we pray to him”** — And what doth it profit us if we pray to him? The wicked, who seek not God but outward gifts, when they see that these are lacking to those who serve him, scorn to serve him themselves.
21.16:
**“Yet because their good things are not in their hand”** — the good, if they have earthly things, have them under their power
**“Yet because … are not”** — Yet because … are not: he has good things in his hand who, by despising temporal things, holds them down under the rule of his mind. But whoever loves them sets himself under them rather than them under himself.
**“the counsel of the wicked”** — namely of the wicked
**“may the counsel of the wicked be far”** — May the counsel of the wicked be far: the counsel of the wicked is to seek earthly glory and neglect eternal. But because in this life they do not prosper continually, there follows: “How often shall the lamp of the wicked be put out?” Often the wicked man reckons the life of his children to be his lamp; but when a son who is loved too much is taken away, the lamp of the wicked man that was seen is put out; so it is with works and honours too.
21.17:
**“and a deluge come upon them,”** — because God often strikes what he sees preferred to himself
**“and … come upon them”** — And … come upon them: a deluge comes upon the wicked when they suffer waves of pain from some adversity.
**“and he shall distribute the sorrows”** — And he shall distribute the sorrows: he who keeps eternal sorrows for the wicked man sometimes pierces his mind here too with temporal sorrow; for because he strikes both here and there, he distributes the sorrows of his wrath over the wicked man, so that he may be crushed by a double crushing.
21.18:
**“They shall be as chaff before the face of the wind,”**
• light, who here are rooted and heavy to their neighbours and immovable
• They shall be as chaff: because by the breath of God’s anger they are suddenly lifted and carried off to the fire.
**“and as ashes”** — because even if he seems green, he is now seen consumed in the judgment of God
**“which the whirlwind scattereth.”**
• whence: “a mighty tempest shall be round about him”; and again: “God shall come manifestly: our God shall come, and shall not keep silence”
• And as ashes which the whirlwind scattereth: because the whirlwind, snatching them, carries them off to eternal torments.
21.19:
**“God shall lay up … for his children”**
• to the third and fourth generation, because the children can see the life of their parents, which they imitate, up to the third and fourth generation; vengeance extends to those who saw what they wrongly followed
• God shall lay up for his children: because he who imitates his parent’s iniquity is bound by his offence too.
**“the sorrow of the father”** — the sin and the punishment
**“and when he shall repay, then shall he know.”**
• guilt closes the eyes, punishment opens them
• And when he shall repay, etc. For the wicked man does not know the evils he has done except when he begins to be punished.
21.20:
**“His eyes shall see”**
• see, knowledge comes late to them
• because before he did not see the guilt
**“his own destruction, and he shall drink of the wrath of the Almighty.”**
• therefore, because he is so hard that he neither fears things to come nor dreads to be struck in the things he loves
• His eyes shall see his own destruction, etc. Because he had grown so hard in iniquity that he did not fear to be struck even in the things he loved, so long as he fulfilled what he had perversely thought; of which hardness it is added: “For what is it to him?” Not that in hell he does not think of his kin, as the rich man did; but here he does not abstain from pleasure either for his friends or for his own life. It is a heavy fault not to yield even to the fear of torment.
21.21:
**“For what is it to him what befalleth his house after him:”**
• as if he said: while he lived
• Or: “For what is it to him?” His house is struck for his guilt; but what is it to him what befalls his house after him? See, in vengeance for his wicked work the length of life which there could have been is shortened. But what is it to him if the number of his days is halved? And in this, then, the sinner raises himself against God, where almighty God breaks his raising. And not even the blow inflicted humbles the mind which obstinacy against the Lord hardens in its resolve. And it must be noted how heavy the guilt of the fault is, both to set the punishment for guilt before the mind and yet not, even for fear of torment, to bend the neck of the heart under the yoke of the Creator. But why God allows the human mind to fall into such blindness, let no one presume to discuss.
**“and if”** — what is it to him
**“the number of his months”** — which he would have by nature
**“be diminished by one half?”** — through his own guilt
21.22:
**“Shall any one teach God knowledge”** — through certain things the things we doubt in ourselves are resolved: if he judged the angels justly, nothing remains to complain of concerning men
**“who … those that are high”** — the angels
**“judgeth”**
• these are the things we seek
• There follows: “Shall any one teach God knowledge?” That is, he does nothing unjustly with us who justly judged even the angelic nature, finer than ours; whence nothing remains to complain of.
21.23: **“One man dieth”** — One man dieth: see, he sets out those things in which who would discuss the secret of the Almighty, by asking why he allows these things to be so? The surface of the letter is plain enough by itself. But that he says: “His bowels are full of fat.” Allegorically. For fat comes from abundant food; so from abundance of goods comes pride, with which the mind swells. The bones for these men are the strength of their dignities, in which is the marrow of their household riches, without which outward power is as it were dry. Or the bones are hard habits; the marrow, the wicked desires which moisten them, that is, keep them in pleasure. Others there are who have nothing here but long to have; and because they cannot, they are afflicted; these die in bitterness without works. See, the rich man rejoices emptily, the poor man is afflicted more emptily. Of both he adds: “And yet they shall sleep together in the dust.” What care is there about a different life, prosperous or adverse, when the end in the dust is alike? That life is to be thought on where with the resurrection one comes to an unlike end, where the happy man passes to punishment, the afflicted to rest.
21.26:
**“And yet they shall sleep together in the dust”** — the life of the elect and of the reprobate is unlike; the corruption of the flesh in death is alike: so let neither riches lift up nor want trouble
**“And yet … together in the dust”** — And yet … together in the dust: allegorically. That is, they will close the eyes of the mind in earthly desires.
**“and worms shall cover them.”** — And worms, which come from the flesh, that is, fleshly cares press on them; which is not so in Job, who neither swelled with what he had nor was anxious over what he lost; but they think so; therefore he adds: “Surely I know your thoughts.” For him whom they saw struck they believed to have been wicked. They believed him wicked whom they see forsaken by glad things; which none think except those who still cling to the present and do not pass perfectly to eternal things.
21.27:
**“Surely I know your thoughts”** — as if: since it is so, you are to be reproved, who despise one struck
**“and your … judgments”** — from their judgments he knew their thoughts
21.28: **“For you say: Where is the house of the prince? and where are the dwelling places of the wicked?”** — but
21.29:
**“Ask any one of them that go by the way”**
• to whom these things seem nothing
• Whence he adds: “Ask any one of them that go by the way.” He is called a wayfarer who attends to the present life as his way and not his homeland; who scorns to trust in the love of the passing world, but seeks eternal things.
**“these”** — which I
**“and you shall perceive that he knoweth … same things,”** — and therefore he is allowed to prosper here
21.30: **“Because the wicked man is reserved to the day of destruction, and he shall be brought to the day of wrath.”** — but
21.31:
**“Who shall reprove his way to his face?”** — as if: now many reprove in his absence, but not so in his presence
**“and who shall repay him what he hath done?”**
• that is, who will punish him for his deeds
• Or: “Who shall reprove?” etc. It is plain that the ways of the wicked man are frequently reproved here, especially when his prosperity goes away, which often happens; but here he looks to Antichrist: who but God? Because neither Elias nor Enoch will do it by their own strength, but by God’s.
**“Who shall reprove his way to his face”** — Who shall reprove his way to his face? While he was speaking of the body of all the wicked, he suddenly turned his words to the head of the wicked, Antichrist. Which of men would dare to rebuke him to his face, whose sight he dreads to bear? Or to reprove his way is to disturb his prosperity by eternal punishment coming between; which the Lord alone will do, of whom it is written: “whom the Lord Jesus shall kill with the spirit of his mouth.”
21.32:
**“He shall be brought to the graves”** — He shall be brought to the graves, etc. This in life, because graves cover the dead. By graves the reprobate are signified, in whom souls put out from the life of beatitude lie hidden as in graves. So this man will be brought to the graves, because he will be received only in the hearts of the wicked.
**“and … in the heap”** — the multitude
**“shall watch … of the dead.”**
• he will exercise his cunning
• And shall watch in the heap of the dead, etc. Because in the gathering of sinners he puts forth the snares of his cunning; and since the wicked are many, they are rightly called a heap.
21.33:
**“He hath been acceptable to the gravel of Cocytus”** — He hath been acceptable to the gravel of Cocytus: Cocytus is called the mourning of the weak. The gravel is the pebbles of rivers, which the flowing water drags along. So the gravel of Cocytus are those who will not resist pleasures strongly, and by their daily falls tend to mourning. So Antichrist, who is bitter and despised by the elect, is sweet to the reprobate through gifts and miracles. Cocytus in Greek is ‘mourning,’ which is understood of women or of any weak ones who are not strong in the Lord. Hence the philosophers say that the river Cocytus runs in the underworld, signifying that there is wicked mourning there.
**“and he shall draw every man after him”** — And he shall draw every man after him: here man is understood as one who savours human things. He draws every man after him, because he snatches all whom he finds fleshly under the yoke of his rule; and even now, before he appears, he draws innumerable ones, even if not all, because many are drawn back from fleshliness.
21.34:
**“How then do ye comfort me in vain,”** — the wicked man prospers in the world; I, though innocent, am struck. Hence he reproves his friends
**“How then do ye comfort me in vain”** — How then do ye comfort me in vain? Because if the wicked man is allowed to prosper in this life, which has been shown of Antichrist, it is necessary that the elect man should be held back under the rein of the scourge.
**“whereas … answer”** — or: answers
**“your … is shewn to be repugnant”** — or: are
**“to truth?”** — Whereas your answer, etc. For they could not comfort him, in whom they went against the truth by their speeches. For when they called him a hypocrite, since they committed a fault by lying, they increased the punishment of the afflicted just man; because the fault of another’s falsehood tortures one who loves the truth.

22.2:
**“Can man be compared with God, even though he were of perfect knowledge?”**
• because man’s knowledge is nothing compared with God’s knowledge
• Can man be compared with God? Those who fail against the words of truth repeat even well-known things, lest by keeping silent they seem beaten. So Eliphaz, pressed by blessed Job’s speeches, says what no one is ignorant of; for he says: “Can man be compared with God?” etc. For in comparison with God our knowledge is ignorance. For we are wise by sharing in God, not by comparison with him. What wonder then that he says, as if teaching, what could have been known even if it were left unsaid? He then adds, as if defending God’s power: “What doth it profit God if thou be just?” For in all that we do well we help ourselves, not the Lord. So it is said to him by the Psalmist: “I have said to the Lord, thou art my God, for thou hast no need of my goods.” For he does not need the goodness of his servant, but bestows the goodness he receives, so that the goodness offered profits not him but first those who receive it and afterwards give it back. Eliphaz further adds what no one is ignorant of.
22.3: **“What doth it profit God if thou be just?”** — you help yourself, not him; whence: “for thou hast no need of my goods”
22.4:
**“Shall he reprove thee for fear,”** — neither does your justice profit him, nor does he reprove you from fear, but for your wickedness
**“Shall he reprove … for fear”** — Shall he reprove for fear? Who, even out of his wits, would think that God reproves us from fear and sets his judgment against us out of dread?
**“Shall he reprove thee for fear”** — Shall he reprove thee for fear? Those who do not know how to measure their words slip into idle sayings.
22.5: **“And not for thy manifold wickedness”** — And not for thy manifold wickedness: he who did not restrain himself from idle words flared up into insulting ones. See, from a sluggish heart he came to idle words, and from idle words, through the crime of falsehood, he flared up into insults. For these are the falls of growing fault, that the tongue, when it is not restrained, by no means lies where it has fallen but always goes down to worse.
22.6:
**“For thou hast taken away the pledge of thy brethren without cause,”** — For there follows: “For thou hast taken away,” and the rest that follows. These things are plain according to the letter, even if they are made up about Job. But mystically heretics are figured by them, and the Church, as we have said, by Job. The pledge, then, is the gift of the Spirit, by which we are made sure of the promises. Or the confession of sin; whence Moses: “When thy brother oweth thee any thing,” that is, when he has sinned against you, “and thou take a pledge from him,” that is, when you now hold the confession of his sin, “thou shalt restore the pledge before the going down of the sun,” that is, give back pardon for the confession before the sun of justice sets for you through grief of heart. So because the Church urges those returning from the heretics to confess the fault of their error, the heretic says: “Thou hast taken away the pledge,” etc., that is: you uselessly demand confession; or: those who come to you lose spiritual gifts.
**“and stripped the naked”** — And stripped the naked: he is naked who enjoys purity of heart, without the veil of doubleness; and such a one sometimes receives the doctrines of heretics, which they call clothing; but because such a one easily returns to the Church, the heretics call him naked and stripped of their garment by the Church. He is called weary who is worn out under the burden of the world; to him, they say, the Church (which they mock for its lack of skill) has not given the water of doctrine, as they who are talkative to everyone do; and they think they have not withdrawn bread while they answer boldly about things that cannot be grasped. And they believe themselves learned above all when they more unhappily presume to speak of unknown things; whereas the Church either modestly keeps silent even about things known to one whom they could not profit, or humbly confesses that she does not know unknown things and calls the curious back to the sense of ordered humility, when she says to them through her preacher: “Not to be more wise than it behoveth to be wise, but to be wise unto sobriety.” And again: “Be not highminded, but fear.” And again: “Seek not the things that are too high for thee, and search not into things above thy ability.” And again: “Thou hast found honey, eat what is sufficient for thee, lest being glutted therewith thou vomit it up.”
