Whence it is said to Peter: “Kill and eat.” So the Church passed into Judea but did not pass through it, because she snatched a few from it to the faith, yet did not utterly put out the unbelieving people from its faithlessness. But, driven back by the Jews, what did she do? “He hath stretched forth his hand to the flint,” because she sent the arm of her preaching to the hardness of the gentiles.
28.9:
**“to the flint”** — the gentiles
**“He hath stretched forth his hand”** — the strength of preaching
**“he hath overturned mountains from the roots.”** — because those whom he drains of earthly things he waters with heavenly
**“he hath overturned mountains from the roots”** — He hath overturned mountains from the roots: the roots are the inmost thoughts of the proud. The mountains were overturned from the roots, because the powers of the world fell from their inmost thought to worship God.
28.10:
**“In the rocks he hath cut out rivers,”** — from hard things the rivers of preaching flow out
**“In the rocks he hath cut out rivers”** — In the rocks he hath cut out rivers: that is, in the hard hearts of the gentiles he opened up rivers of preaching.
**“and … every precious thing”** — he who is despised by himself is great to God
**“hath seen”** — chose
**“and his eye hath seen every precious thing”** — And his eye hath seen every precious thing: God saw a precious thing when he looked on human nature, cast down in its own eyes, with the illumination of his wisdom’s grace.
28.11:
**“The depths also of rivers”** — the Jew sees the surface
**“he hath searched”** — makes them be searched
**“The depths also of rivers he hath searched”** — The depths also of rivers he hath searched: the Lord searches the depths of rivers and brings hidden things into the light, because by his gift spiritual exposition now lights up the dark sayings of the ancients. But because the sayings of God are not pierced without his wisdom, he adds, about searching out those same words: “But where is wisdom to be found?” He set out two things and added two in reply, not solving but increasing what he puts forward. He sets out two things, about the place and about the price. It is plain that not even man’s wisdom can be held by a place or bought with things. Yet he speaks mystically not of created but of creating Wisdom. Otherwise how could he say lower down, after gold, which is dearer, that crystal cannot equal it, as if for immense praise? So he speaks not solving but increasing what he had put forward. And he says Wisdom: “Christ, the power of God, and the wisdom of God.” Man does not know its price, because he finds no worthy merit of work by which to obtain it. For we have been redeemed by grace, and by no merit of ours did the Wisdom of God come to us.
28.12: **“But where is wisdom to be found, and where is the place of understanding?”** — for the mind which understands these things speaks justly
28.13:
**“Man knoweth not the price thereof”** — it is not said that there is a price and it is not known, but that it is not known because there is none
**“neither is it found in the land of them that live in delights.”** — for if they were truly wise, they would rather mourn in this exile
**“neither is it found in the land of them that live in delights”** — Neither is it found in the land of them that live in delights: he calls the human soul land. This wisdom cannot be found in the land of those who live in delights, because whoever is still fed by the pleasures of this life is separated from the understanding of eternal wisdom.
28.14:
**“The depth saith:”**
• he looks back to what he said above: “But where is wisdom,” etc.
• he does not say where wisdom is, but where it is not
**“The depth saith: It is not in me”** — The depth saith: It is not in me: he calls the depth the hearts of men, which are both fluid through falling and dark through the mist of doubleness. Which depth surely confesses that this wisdom is not in it, because the wicked mind, while it longs to be wise in a fleshly way, shows itself foolish toward spiritual things.
**“The depth”** — The depth: the wisdom of the world, which is foolishness with God. “Saith” by its very works.
**“the sea”** — The sea: the minds of the restless. Israel has the sabbath, Egypt the flies, that is, restlessness. And the sea says: “It is not.” For no one fully receives it except one who strives to draw himself away from all the tossing of fleshly actions. And the troubled minds of worldly men cry out by that very fact that they are far from true wisdom, in that they are not at rest; because this Wisdom of God was to be made flesh, so that to redeem the human race he would send neither holy angels nor holy men, but would come through himself.
28.15:
**“The finest gold shall not purchase it,”**
• he looks back to what he said: “Man knoweth not the price,” etc.
• he does not say what its price is, but what it is not
• There follows: “The finest gold shall not purchase it.” The holy angels are called the finest gold, who, continuing in the innocence in which they were created, both shine with the brightness of justice and are stained by no filth of fault. But none of them was sent for our redemption.
**“The finest gold shall not purchase it”** — The finest gold shall not purchase it: men can be gold, but not the finest, because they shine, but not without the infection of fault.
**“neither shall silver be weighed in exchange for it.”**
• nor is Moses the author of salvation, who judges evils but does not heal them
• Neither shall silver be weighed in exchange for it: because the life of just men preaching, or writing the words of God, however strong in the light of holiness, does not convey to us by its presence the coming of the Wisdom from above.
28.16:
**“It shall not be compared with the dyed colours of India,”** — but neither does uprightness of life from the philosophers suffice
**“It shall not be compared with the dyed colours of India”** — It shall not be compared with the dyed colours of India: by India this world is taken here, in which the life of men is begotten dark through fault. The dyed colours of India are the wise men of this world, who, at first foul through unbelief and mostly through action, are darkened before human eyes with the colour of an uprightness laid over them; and since they lack the virtue of things, they pretend by the arrangement of their words, as by colours laid over, to be other than they are; from these the Wisdom of God stands far off. The commandments of God please without eloquence, like a garment without dye.
**“or with the most precious stone sardonyx, or the sapphire.”** — nor are these the most precious stones, but he chose these to signify something else mystically
**“or with the most precious stone sardonyx, or the sapphire”** — Or with the most precious stone sardonyx, or the sapphire: the sardonyx has the likeness of red earth, the sapphire an airy look. So by the sardonyx are taken men, or the fathers of the Old Testament, following certain earthly things; by the sapphire the preachers of the New Testament, seeking heavenly things alone; or the angels.
28.17:
**“cannot equal”** — that is, shining in themselves
**“Gold or crystal … it,”** — open to one another
**“Gold or crystal cannot equal it”** — Gold or crystal cannot equal it: after it has been said that gold is not compared to this wisdom, it is further added, as if rising, that not even crystal can equal it; which does not hold according to the letter. In crystal any liquid is shown outside such as it is held within. By gold and crystal we take the fellowship of the saints in the homeland above, who will shine with the brightness of blessedness, and the bulk of the members will not hide the mind of each from the eyes of another. Who, even if they will be like him because they will become blessed, yet are not equal because they are creatures.
**“neither shall any vessels … be changed for it”** — Neither shall any vessels be changed for it: a high vessel of gold: Elias and John and Jeremias. But whoever believed any of them to be the Christ exchanged a high and eminent vessel of gold for Wisdom; because the Church believes Christ not one of the prophets but the Lord of the prophets.
28.18:
**“High and eminent things shall not be mentioned in comparison of it:”** — because those are of themselves, these of him
**“shall not be mentioned in comparison of it”** — Shall not be mentioned in comparison of it: for what are men compared with God? Nothing.
**“but wisdom is drawn out of secret places.”** — because: “thou knowest not whence he cometh, and whither he goeth”
**“but wisdom is drawn out of secret places”** — But wisdom is drawn out of secret places: because, since it is invisible, it is found only invisibly. It is said to be drawn because, as we draw breath that the body may live, so the spirit of wisdom is drawn from inmost places that the soul may stand in life. And rightly “out of secret places,” because this wisdom is poured hiddenly into hearts, as it is said of the Spirit: “and thou knowest not whence he cometh, and whither he goeth.”
28.19:
**“shall not be equal to it”** — who is from heaven
**“The topaz of Ethiopia”**
• man converted from the blackness of sins
• And see that whereas before he had set it above the angels, the ancient fathers, the holy philosophers, the glorified prophets, now in this place he rebukes specially the heretics, who make men converted from sins equal to the God-man, since these are sons by grace, he by nature; which he shows when he adds: “neither shall it be compared to the cleanest dyeing.” They are the cleanest dyeing who humbly keep the grace of the virtues that has come upon them. For they would not be dyed if they had had holiness by nature.
**“The topaz … shall not be equal to it”** — The topaz shall not be equal to it: because it gleams with every colour, the topaz is called as it were “topandion.” And the sense is: none of the saints, though full of every virtue, yet gathered from this blackness of the world, can be equal to it.
**“neither”** — above he called the colours of India not clean
**“to the cleanest dyeing”** — baptism is called a dyeing, where the foul are made comely
28.20:
**“Whence then cometh wisdom?”** — it comes from him from whom it sprang
**“Whence then cometh wisdom”** — Whence then cometh wisdom? Because it is born of the invisible Father, its way is hidden. Whence the prophet: “Who shall declare his generation?” And the place of its understanding is the human mind. So because he from whom it came forth is invisible, and it is uncertain to us in whose mind, being understood, it rests, it is rightly said: “Whence then cometh wisdom? and where is the place of understanding?”
28.21:
**“It is hid from the eyes of all living.”** — “For man shall not see me and live,” because no one sees spiritually and lives fleshly, but dies to the flesh
**“It is hid from the eyes of all living”** — It is hid from the eyes of all living: because so long as one lives here, God cannot be seen in the form of his nature; but through images he was seen by Moses and Jacob and others.
**“the fowls”** — the angels
**“and the fowls of the air know it not”** — And the fowls of the air know it not: because, set in this corruptible flesh, they too do not pierce the power of his nature by seeing, though they now fly by the merit of holy contemplation. In sacred Scripture birds are sometimes given to be understood in a bad sense, sometimes in a good. For by birds sometimes the powers of the air are designated, opposed to the efforts of the good. Whence it is said by the voice of Truth: “Because the seed which fell by the way side, the fowls came and ate it up”; because surely the malignant spirits, besieging human minds, while they thrust in harmful thoughts, tear the word of life out of the memory. And again: “The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air nests,” etc. By the name of foxes, the deceitful and fraudulent; but by the name of birds these same proud demons are designated. But on the other hand birds are usually put in a good sense; as in the Gospel the Lord, when he announced the likeness of the kingdom of heaven from a grain of mustard seed, said: “It is like to a grain of mustard seed, which a man took and cast into his garden, and it grew and became a great tree, and the birds of the air lodged in the branches thereof.” For Christ is the grain of mustard seed, who, planted in the burial of death, rose up a great tree. For he was a grain when he died, a tree when he rose again: a grain through the humility of the flesh, a tree through the power of majesty. The branches of this tree are the holy preachers, of whom: “Their sound hath gone forth into all the earth,” etc. In these branches the birds rest, because holy souls lift themselves from earthly thought on certain wings of virtues, and in their sayings and consolations breathe again from the weariness of this life.
28.22:
**“Destruction and death have said: With our ears we have heard the fame thereof.”**
• that is, the finders of death and destruction, namely the malignant spirits, have said: “With our ears we have heard”
• Destruction and death have said: With our ears we have heard the fame thereof: because to see God is the same as to have him; so the wicked do not see this wisdom, because, driven back through pride, they could by no means have it. And to have heard its fame is to have known its power from its might.
28.23:
**“God”** — the Father
**“understandeth the way of it”** — the way is through the passage of the humanity, the place through the seat of the Godhead; or its way is that it comes to the heart of man, the place the heart in which it abides
**“God understandeth the way of it”** — God understandeth the way of it: as if he said: it is known to God either when Wisdom comes to men through the flesh, or how it remains invisible with the Father even when it has appeared outside. For the place, not a local one, of Wisdom is the Father, according to that saying: “I am in the Father.” Or God understands its way, because to discern it belongs to the divine sight alone. Or by what means the understanding of wisdom comes to the heart of man. Or whose mind does not lose the understanding of life it has received. But because this Wisdom, made manifest through the flesh, was to fill the hearts of the elect in all parts of the world:
28.24: **“For he beholdeth the ends of the world: and looketh on all things that are under heaven.”** — There follows: “For he beholdeth the ends of the world.” For God to look on is to re-form to grace what was lost.
28.25:
**“Who made a weight for the winds”** — Who made a weight for the winds: in Scripture souls are usually signified by the swiftness and height of the winds; which, when grace from above fills them, it makes heavy with ripeness put in or usual, so that they do not leap away from attention to God with light movement. Or to make a weight for the winds is to temper the glory from virtues granted to the elect here with weakness mixed in.
**“and weighed the waters”** — in this his power appears
**“by measure.”** — unless this be a guard, from his own weakness
**“and weighed the waters by measure”** — And weighed the waters by measure: he calls waters the minds filled with the Holy Spirit, which he weighs by measure, because the saints, who are caught up to the highest things by the Spirit lifting them, are held down by certain temptations lest they grow proud with any haughtiness. He lifts them indeed, but with measure: they do not advance as much as they wish, lest they be lifted up. Elias did wonderful things, but fled from a woman, struck with fear.
28.26:
**“When he gave a law for the rain, and a way for the sounding storms.”** — because the Spirit and Word of the Father, which if it can be known, he told man what he can take from it
**“When he gave a law for the rain”** — When he gave a law for the rain: the rain is the sayings of the preachers, which persuade gently. A law is set for the preacher, that by living he may fulfil what he persuades. He calls the sounding storms terrible words about the judgment to come. And he set a way for the storms when he made an entrance for his preachers to hearts struck with terror of the judgment. But the law is set first so that afterwards the way may be opened, because that voice pierces the hearer’s heart which keeps in work what it has sounded.
28.27:
**“Then he saw it, and declared”** — Then he saw it, and declared: he saw this Wisdom made flesh, that is, made it be seen and declared by the preachers, and made it be prepared and searched by the hearers. For whoever has taken care, by living well, to have it favourable on the day of judgment prepares it for himself.
**“he saw it, and declared, and prepared, and searched it”** — He saw it, and declared, and prepared, and searched it: he saw, because it is form; declared, because it is the Word; prepared, because it is the remedy; searched, because it is hidden. It must be noted that these four aforesaid fit God the Son of God himself.
28.28:
**“And he said to man: Behold the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom:”**
• “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom”
• And he said to man: Behold the fear, etc. Because we cannot pierce the nature of wisdom, what it is in itself, by God’s condescension we have heard what it becomes in us. For it is certain that he has it of whom it is not uncertain that he fears God.
**“Behold the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom”** — Behold the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom: as if he said: if you fear God, it is plain that you are full of wisdom, which among men is called the fear of the Lord. But because he truly understands the force of divine fear who guards himself from all wicked works, he adds: “and to depart from evil, is understanding.”

29.1:
**“Job also added, taking up his parable, and said:”** — he hints that he speaks mysteries in figures
**“Job also added, taking up his parable”** — Job also added, taking up his parable: in this last speech he designates the last time of the Church, when she is forced to bear being mocked by her adversaries, that is, the fleshly and the heretics or the gentiles, whom she now strives to hold down by the authority of wisdom, lifted up with unbridled boasting. And blessed Job, holding the figure of the Church, which will then be in straits and yet will remember our quiet, both tells her past things and announces to others the things to come. For the Church will be pressed by such evils that she will long with a sigh for these wretched times of ours.
29.2:
**“Who will grant me, that I might be according to the months past,”**
• the Church will be pressed by such evils that she will long with a sigh for these wretched times of ours
• Whence he says: “Who will grant me, that I might be according to?” A set number of days is called months. And by the name of months he signifies gatherings of souls. So the Church remembers how great gains she brought back from the souls gathered by her preaching.
• Fittingly the last speech treats of the last times, when the error which is now hidden will be open.
**“the months past”** — The months past: days, while they are gathered into months, are taken away, because the Church, while she gathers shining souls, hides them in inner places. Or the month is put for the perfection which will be theirs in rest, for whom it is now in working; which the Church now remembers.
**“according to the days in which God kept me?”**
• he recounts what she was like in those months; now the weak are kept in the bosom of peace, but then they will fall
• According to the days in which God kept me: because then, in those who fail through persecution, she will reckon that same keeping which she now sees in these.
29.3:
**“When his lamp shined over my head,”** — When his lamp shined over, etc. The light of sacred Scripture is called a lamp. So now the lamp shines over the head of the Church, because the sacred words light up the darkness of our mind.
**“and I walked by his light in darkness”** — And I walked by his light in darkness: the Church, even if she does not pierce the hidden things of another’s thought, because she does not, as it were, know the face of God in the night, yet sets the steps of good work guided by the light of the speech from above.
29.4:
**“As I was in the days of my youth”** — in these words the pretence of religion too is not undeservedly lamented, because some even now do not desire to be Christians but to seem so; to whom, namely, God is in public, not in secret
**“As … in the days of my youth”** — As in the days of my youth: the Church was grown up when, filled with the Spirit, she was fruitful in conceiving sons through the ministry of preaching. The little Church had no breasts, since before she advanced she cherished none by preaching; grown up, when joined to the Word of God, she begets sons by preaching; but then she will be barren with old age.
**“when God was secretly in my tabernacle?”**
• that I might advance secretly within
• and I kept it outside too
**“when God was secretly in my tabernacle”** — When God was secretly in my tabernacle: he calls the dwelling of the mind a tabernacle. Whoever thinks silently on God’s commandments, God is secretly in his tabernacle. For to show how much he advanced within, he declared that God had been secretly in his tabernacle; and to show also how much he kept the works of uprightness outwardly, he adds: “When the Almighty was with me.”
29.5: **“When the Almighty was with me: and my servants round about me?”** — There follows: “and my servants round about me.” Those are called servants who serve the heavenly commandments, who are now round about her, because they are found in almost all nations.
29.6:
**“When I washed my feet with butter”** — When I washed my feet with butter: the feet of the Church are the ministers of lower works, who, while they carry on outward things for necessary uses, cling to the earth like feet by their lowest ministry. But those who preside ought to minister to such men the pouring of fatness by the voice of frequent admonition, which Job did for his own. For feet are usually torn by the roughness of the road. The feet of God are the preachers, who are not without fault but are washed with butter, because by the fatness of good work the dust gathered, or the glory of preaching, is poured over and cleansed. Or the feet, as it were weary, are anointed with butter when the preachers are cherished by the good works of those who minister to them, that is, by the fruit rather than the gift; so it is from the voice of the head. From the voice of the body, the feet are those who minister outward things.
**“and the rock poured me out rivers”** — Christ, at whose teaching rivers flowed everywhere
**“of oil?”**
• the preachings of inward anointing
• because they run and anoint
• And the rock poured me out rivers of oil: because in her the preachings of Christ of inward anointing flow out. From this rock the rivers of oil came forth, the books of the evangelists. Or he calls the gifts of the Spirit rivers of oil.
29.7:
**“When I went out to the gate of the city”** — When I went out to the gate of the city: by the gate of the city every good action is designated, by which the soul enters the assembly of the heavenly kingdom. So now the Church goes out to the gate of the city, because, to obtain entrance to the heavenly kingdom, she puts herself forth in holy actions. It was the custom of the ancients that the elders should sit in the gate and judge the cases of those coming in, so that the people of the city might be peaceable, into which the quarrelsome might not enter; which Job too did.
**“and in the street they prepared me a chair?”** — And in the street they prepared me a chair: because in the breadth of great authority she shows the freedom of her teaching. For she who preaches with public voice the right things she perceives sits as it were in the street on a chair, when she fears nothing over her preaching and, pressed by no one’s errors, hides herself under silence.
29.8:
**“saw”** — then
**“The young men … me, and hid themselves:”** — because they fear to be caught in their hidden things
**“The young men saw me, and hid themselves”** — The young men saw me, and hid themselves: he says young men because they are supported by no weight of counsel; old men, those ripe with the long age of character. And the sense is: the unripe dread the vigour and uprightness of the Church; those of long age glorify it.
**“and the old men rose up and stood.”** — the light flee; the perfect, by rising up, revere the merits of life
29.9:
**“The princes ceased to speak”** — The princes ceased to speak: he calls princes or rulers the authors of heretical wickedness. And the sense is: when I was allowed to preach with public voice, everyone who was not subject to the truth dreaded me.
**“the finger”** — The finger: they lay it on the mouth when they show, by false complaints, that they are held back not by the reason of speech but by the hand of power.
29.10:
**“The rulers held their peace”**
• who draw the erring after them
• The rulers held their peace: surely those who try to draw erring peoples after them are now curbed, so as not to dare to speak perverse things, both by the weight of authority and by the force of reason. Their tongue cleaves to their throat, because even if they do not dare to speak perverse words aloud, yet within themselves they hide all the false things they plan to put forward against the true faith.
**“and their tongue cleaved to their throat.”**
• because even if they do not dare to speak perverse things freely, yet they hide them within themselves
• And their tongue cleaved to their throat: against this Jeremias says of the last times: “The lamias have drawn out the breast,” that is, the heretics, who have a human face but through ungodliness beastly hearts. Then they will preach their error freely. For at that time, when holy Church is pressed by adversity, freedom of speech is given to all the wicked preachers. Then they suckle their whelps, because, as wicked followers, while they slip perverse things into the souls of little ones, they strengthen them by nourishing them toward ungodliness.
29.11:
**“The ear that heard me blessed me, and the eye that saw me gave witness to me:”** — he says that he was held in reverence by those who heard and saw, against the rebukes of his friends
**“The ear that heard … blessed”** — The ear that heard blessed: there he said what he showed by teaching, here what by mercy; there he brings forth and fills with words, here he defends from evils.
**“The ear that heard me blessed me”** — The ear that heard me blessed me: what he was like in speech, what in work, is shown. He blesses the words of the Church who completes in work what he has heard. He bears witness to her who answers the examples of her life by living well.
29.12:
**“Because I had delivered the poor man that cried out;”** — the witness is about this
**“Because I had delivered the poor man that cried out”** — Because I had delivered the poor man that cried out: the Church delivers the poor man crying out when she looses the faults he has committed for the sinner who begs pardon.
**“and the fatherless that had no helper”** — And the fatherless that had no helper: she delivers the fatherless when each one, the old father the devil being dead to him, runs to the bosom of holy Church and finds in her the help of exhortation.
**“and the fatherless that had no helper.”** — And the fatherless that had no helper: these are the works of great mercy: to deliver the poor, to snatch away the fatherless about to perish, to console the widow. These the Church shows both bodily and spiritually.
29.13:
**“The blessing of him that was ready to perish came upon me”** — see how gentle is he who above was stern, when he said: “The young men saw me, and hid themselves,” etc. Rulers must hold both: namely, that the vigour of discipline should rule gentleness, and gentleness adorn vigour; and so each be commended by the other, so that vigour be not stiff nor gentleness slack
**“The blessing of him that was ready to perish”** — The blessing of him that was ready to perish: the blessing of him that was ready to perish comes upon her when she forestalls the destruction of the sinner and leads him back from the pit of fault by holy exhortations.
**“and”** — or: because
**“the heart of the widow”** — not of the young man or young men
**“and I comforted the heart of the widow”** — And I comforted the heart of the widow: the heart of the widow receives great comfort when the faithful soul learns in the words of the Church something about the coming of him to whom she is spiritually joined.
29.14:
**“I was clad with justice: and I clothed myself”** — with justice
**“I was clad with justice”** — I was clad with justice: he is clad with justice as with a garment who protects himself on every side with good work and leaves no part of his action naked. For that Pharisee who went up to the temple to pray opened the city of his heart to the enemies lying in wait through haughtiness, which he had closed in vain by fasting and alms. The other places are fortified to no purpose when one place, by which an entrance lies open to the enemy, is not fortified. Eleazar, killing the elephant, fell beneath it; so he who overcomes vices, if he is proud, falls beneath them. He dies under the enemy he killed who is lifted up over the fault he overcomes.
**“as with a robe”** — on every side, so that there is nowhere an entrance for the enemy; otherwise it avails nothing
**“and a diadem”** — because the judgments of the just, through the glory of great work, lead to the crown of reward
**“with my judgment”**
• the good man always judges within himself what he owes to God, what to his neighbour, and cleanses himself of vices
• With my judgment: I was clothed with judgment, which is compared to a crown, which is placed on top, because he seeks to be crowned in heaven, not on earth. He opens his good things so that his friends may be raised up, not rebuking, but may imitate them in silence. The memory of former things also avails against despair, in place of rebukes.
**“and a diadem … with my judgment”** — And a diadem … with my judgment: the judgment of the just is called a diadem, because by it they long to be rewarded not in earthly and lowest things, but above.
29.15:
**“an eye”** — see what bowels of mercy
**“I was”** — I myself
**“to the blind, and a foot to the lame.”** — I was an eye to the blind, and a foot to the lame, etc. For blessed Job had both given his hand to the one himself, and upheld the other by carrying him himself, because he knows that the mind is weighed by God more than the deed. The Church is an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame. For she enlightens the blind by preaching, and upholds the lame by helping. For he is blind who does not yet see where he should go; and he is lame who cannot go where he sees. Or the gentile people is called blind, and the Jewish people lame; because the one did not have eyes, that is, the law, because, not having received the law, it did not see where it ought to have gone; the other, on the contrary, held the law indeed by knowing it, but did not stretch out in it the step of right work.
**“I was an eye to the blind”** — I was an eye to the blind: after justice, mercy; because he does well the things that are merciful who first keeps the just things, so that mercy may be drawn from the fountain of justice. For how is he merciful to another who is unmerciful to himself and does not yet love himself? To whom is he good who is wicked to himself?
29.16:
**“I was the father of the poor:”**
• what he bestowed he gave from affection, not from fear of judgment
• because the force of mercy had imitated nature in him, so that he looked on them as sons through love, over whom he presided as father through protection
**“I was the father of the poor”** — I was the father of the poor: for the poor in spirit are begotten by her preaching.
**“and the cause which I knew not,”** — by working
**“and the cause which I knew not”** — And the cause which I knew not: the Church, when through the elect she judges the evils of the fleshly, searches out what she does not know, because she searches out by working the evils she does not know, correcting them through judgment.
**“the cause which I knew not”** — The cause which I knew not: just in his own actions, merciful in the weakness of his neighbours, he is also energetic in the business of the poor, so that he who seeks eternal things may stretch out to all merits. Whence Solomon: “He that feareth God, neglecteth nothing.” Yet lesser things are to be left for greater.
**“I searched out most diligently.”** — whence let no one be hasty in sentence
29.17:
**“I broke the jaws of the wicked man”**
• by laying bare his snares
• I broke the jaws of the wicked man: the wicked man is the devil. By the jaws his hidden snares; by the teeth the committing of open fault is shown. So it is first necessary to bring to light the hidden contrivances of his counsels, so that we may be able to call back our hearer’s soul from open falling.
**“and out of his teeth I took away the prey.”** — the soul which he had already bitten by breaking it with sin, by turning it to the salvation of life
29.18:
**“And I said: I shall die in my nest,”** — in the calm of peace
**“And I said: I shall die in my nest”** — And I said: I shall die in my nest: by the name of nest the calm rest of faith is expressed, by which each weak one is nourished. So the voice of those who will then be is anticipated by the voice of blessed Job, who believed that in the time of peace they would pass to the things above, that is, fly from the nest.
**“and as a palm tree”**
• that is, growing little by little; or at last there will be prosperity and strength
• And as a palm tree: it advances slowly but stays long in its greenness; and at the bottom it is slenderer, at the top it thickens near the fruit (unlike other trees); and below it is rough, above it is fair to touch and sight. So she believed she would multiply her days like a palm, who promised herself the leisure of peace for a length of many days, and thought that the minds of the faithful would rise stronger right to the end; which is now not so. The Church believed she would multiply her days like a palm, who, a danger suddenly arising, grieves that the grace of her peace, both slowly won by the faithful, has been cut off more swiftly by the unfaithful. The Church is like a palm, despised below and girded with rough things, fair above; and whereas others are strong in earthly things and weak in heavenly, for which they will do or suffer little, she is weak toward the earth, strong above; nor does she, like some, do more at the beginning and less at the completion.
**“shall multiply my days.”** — I said
29.19:
**“My root”**
• because with spiritual mind she always attends to knowledge
• My root: by the name of root hidden thought is designated. The root is opened beside the waters when the thought of the mind is hiddenly opened to receive the streams of truth.
**“root”** — Root: of the Church, Christ made flesh, who, invisible in Godhead, was opened through the flesh and known to the peoples.
**“is opened beside the waters, and dew”** — which comes from above
**“shall continue in my harvest.”**
• which is gathered below
• And dew shall continue in my harvest, etc. Understand: “I said.” The harvest of the Church is taken to be when perfect souls, drawn away from their bodies, pass like ripe crops cut from the earth to the heavenly barns. Dew will continue in the harvest, because grace coming from above makes us worthy to be gathered from lower things.
29.20:
**“My glory”** — I said
**“My glory shall always be renewed”** — My glory shall always be renewed: she bewails as it were lost glory, because she knows that those whom she believed were serving as soldiers of a new life are serving old desires.
**“and my bow in my hand shall be repaired.”**
• by working
• And my bow in my hand shall be repaired, etc. Scripture is the bow, from which terrifying sentences come to the hearts of men like striking arrows. The bow is repaired in the hand when whatever is known of the sacred word is fulfilled by living; which at the end will fail in many, and which is so even now.
29.21:
**“They that heard me”** — these things are true of Job, but in the figure of the Church
**“waited for my sentence,”** — not like these erring men who now run ahead as if teaching
**“They that heard me, waited”** — They that heard me, waited: she remembers past times, in which everything said by her was heard by the faithful with fear; and she bewails the impudence of her adversaries.
**“and being attentive held their peace”** — And being attentive held their peace: they hold their peace at her counsel who do not dare to attack her words, but believe them.
29.22:
**“To my words they durst add nothing”**
• see the reverence of the hearers
• To my words they durst add nothing: the heretics presume to add something to her sayings when they try as it were to amend the uprightness of her preaching.
**“and my speech dropped upon them.”**
• see the dispensing of the teachers
• And my speech dropped upon them, etc. In this dropping of speech is taken the measure of preaching according to the capacity of the hearers.
29.23:
**“They waited for me as for rain”** — They waited for me as for rain: we wait for the words of holy preaching as for rain when with true humility we acknowledge the dryness of our heart, so as to be watered by the drink of holy preaching.
**“and they opened their mouth as for a latter shower.”**
• Christ himself is late, at the end of the world
• Christ at the end of the world gave himself for us as an evening sacrifice
• whence: “I will give you the early and the latter rain”
• And they opened their mouth as for a shower: because while we receive the words of holy preaching in the last part of the age, we open the mouth of the heart as for a latter shower.
29.24:
**“If at any time I laughed on them, they believed not”** — If at any time I laughed on them, they believed not: the Church says this from the voice of the head. For God to laugh is to prosper the way of the saints by following favour; but we do not believe our Redeemer when he laughs, when we receive the grace of his favour, many gifts of his already bearing witness, and yet still waver under his judgment over our weakness. Job showed himself such to those under him that even laughing he could be feared; so a prelate ought to be feared when laughing and loved when angry, lest too much freedom make him cheap or immoderate severity make him hateful.
**“and the light of my countenance fell not on earth.”** — the eyes of the wise man are in his head, that is, Christ, whose works he sees are to be imitated; but “the eyes of fools are in the ends of the earth”
**“and the light of my countenance fell not”** — And the light of my countenance fell not: the light of blessed Job’s countenance does not fall on the earth, because he did not look on earthly things with desire. The light of the Lord’s countenance too does not fall on the earth, because the brightness of his vision does not appear to sinners. The Church too does not preach bright mysteries to earthly men.
29.25:
**“If I had a mind to go to them, I sat first,”** — because the good care first for eternal things, then for earthly; in them the Lord sits first, in others last
**“If I had a mind to go to”** — If I had a mind to go to: the Lord both comes when he wills and, when he comes, sits first; because both his coming into our heart is free, and the longing of desire for him in our thought is not equal to other desires.
**“and when I sat as a king”** — And when I sat as a king: the Lord sits as a king in the heart, because he rules in thought the motions of minds that clamour round, which stand round him like an army. Or he sits as a king with his army standing about, because a crowd of virtues stood round him presiding over the minds of the elect. He is also the comforter of mourners, by the promise in which he says: “I will see you again, and your heart shall rejoice.” If we refer it to the Church, in her the order of teachers presides as a king, which the crowd of the faithful stands round; which comforts the hearts of mourners, while it gladdens minds afflicted by the hardship of the present pilgrimage with the promise of the eternal homeland. To sit is the rod of rule; to console, the ministry of devotion.
**“and when I sat as a king, with his army standing about him, yet I was a comforter of them that mourned.”**
• A comforter of them that mourned, etc. He who has heard of God’s justice so as to fear, let him hear of his mercy too so as to trust, so that there may be fear and hope together.
• In the ark with the tables there are both the rod and the manna; that is, with knowledge of sacred Scripture, in the breast of the ruler there is the rod of strictness and the manna of sweetness.

30.1:
**“But now”** — from here on he shows, in the last time, things contrary to those said before; because they began from the Church, not the Church from them
**“But now the younger in time scorn me”** — But now the younger in time scorn me: those younger in time mock the Church when those who have gone out from her despise the words of her teaching.
**“whose fathers I would not have set with the dogs of my flock:”**
• even if they seemed to have some right things, yet because they did not think rightly about the Lord, she does not set them with the dogs of her flock, that is, does not count them among the right preachers
• Whose fathers I would not have set, etc. The flock of the Church, then, is the multitude of the faithful. The dogs of the flock are the holy teachers, who have stood forth as teachers of the faithful. So the Church disdains to set the fathers of the heretics with the dogs of her flock, because, judging between them, she spits out the inventors of errors and scorns to number them among the true fathers.
30.2:
**“The strength of whose hands was to me as nothing”**
• because without charity, without the look of holiness
• The strength of whose hands was to me as nothing: the strength of the hands is greatness in working; but the strength of the hands of heretics is said to be as nothing to holy Church, because she sees that whatever they do, true faith being lost, is of no merit.
**“The strength of whose hands”** — The strength of whose hands: the more they err, the more they show themselves great in works; and sometimes they do miracles, yet are not holy for that. For the proof of holiness is not to do signs, but to love each one as oneself, and to think true things of God and better things of one’s neighbour than of oneself.
**“and they were thought unworthy of life itself.”** — that is, of the miracles they do, because they are not humble; or of the Christian name, which they attack
30.3:
**“Barren with want and hunger”** — Barren with want and hunger: for by immoderate daring, the more they long for knowledge of the knowledge from above, the more they lose it.
**“Barren with want and hunger,”** — And hunger: because they long to know whence to be learned and talkative, not to be ordered in character; whence they scarcely grasp outward things, who think they have pierced secret ones.
**“who gnawed in the wilderness,”** — And this is: “who gnawed in the wilderness,” etc. The heretics, who are separated from the fellowship of the universal Church, are said to gnaw in the wilderness. That is gnawed which cannot be eaten; because those who strive to understand Scripture by their own power, not helped by grace from above, cannot eat it, but gnaw it as with certain bites, while they do not reach its inner parts. Or the covetous gnaw with the tooth, taking others’ things by force; but those lick who take them by the flattery of the tongue.
**“disfigured with calamity and misery”**
• Disfigured with calamity and misery: they are said to be squalid with calamity and misery, because they are despised both for the ruin of their character and for the perversity of their senses.
• Disfigured with calamity and misery: calamity is as it were sickness; misery is the neglect of it, by which it becomes heavier. No one would be squalid if he did not add the misery of pleasure to his necessities.
30.4:
**“And they ate grass, and barks of trees,”**
• And they ate grass, etc. To eat grass is to understand the plainer sayings of Scripture or to keep the least precepts. But they eat the bark of trees who in the sacred volumes revere only the surface of the letter. Or surely to eat grass is to imitate certain light and tender things of the ancient fathers; but to eat the bark of trees is to do their works on the surface, but not to keep a right intention in those same works.
• For what is designated by grass but the tender life, close to the earth, of those who begin well? And what by the bark of trees but the outward works of those who already long for lofty things? So to eat grass and the bark of trees is to scatter, by pestilent persuasions as by certain teeth of their malice, either the efforts of those who begin well or the workings of some who already, like trees, stretch toward higher things. The reprobate eat grass when they consume the beginnings of the weak by mocking them. They eat the bark of trees too when by the hand of perverse counsel they strip the covering of good works from the life of those growing rightly. These in certain acts they strip like trees, but those like grass, because, despising them, they drag them along and as it were eat what they tread on. The strength of some, already rising on high, they partly pull down; but the tenderness of others, still placed below, they utterly crush. Or grass is earthly consolation, bark the outward glory which God sometimes gives to his elect, when he lifts them up with outward honours and makes them honourable above others. But the wicked sometimes despise their life indeed, but long to obtain their happiness in this world. So because they seek here the flatteries of passing consolation, they eat grass. And because in their thoughts they meditate on their outward glory, they eat the bark of trees. And since in all these things they serve avarice alone, they are filled with the root of the juniper.
**“and the root of junipers was their food.”**
• because in errors they seek earthly gains
• avarice lies hidden in the heart, but brings forth openly in work the prickings of all sins
• And this is: “and the root of junipers was,” etc. Junipers have as it were thorns instead of leaves. And a thorn is every sin, because while it draws to delight it tears the mind as by pricking. So by the root of the juniper avarice is designated, which is “the root of all evils,” as it were of thorns; which is the food of the heretics, because mostly they pursue only outward gains in their words.
30.5:
**“Who snatched up these things out of the valleys, and when they had found any of them, they ran to them with a cry.”**
• all the present life, compared with the things above, is at the bottom; in which, when they find even a little gain, they run with a cry, quarrelling over it and breaking the look of holiness laid over them
• All these things are about the heretics, or about other fleshly men who press on her within.
**“Who snatched up these things out of the valleys”** — Who snatched up these things out of the valleys: they snatch them out of the valleys because with a proud spirit they gather these things from the humble sayings of the fathers. And while they boast that they have found them for their own fathers, they run to them with cries, because everything they perceive they try, from longing for praise, to spread abroad to the ears of men.
30.6:
**“They dwelt in the desert places of torrents”**
• whence stolen waters are sweeter
• They dwelt in the desert places of torrents: he calls the inventors of perverse doctrines torrents, which, cold from the heat of charity, swell as in the numbness of winter time, but are dried up by the arguments of Catholics as by the heats of the sun. So those who follow their errors dwell in the desert places of torrents. The inventors indeed have been put out by the truth, but their disciples still defend what they taught. Or the torrents are the holy heralds, whose desert places are the earthly things the wicked love.
**“and in caves of earth, or upon the gravel.”**
• wavering minds
• Or upon the gravel: we call gravel the tiniest stones, which river water drags along. The heretics dwell upon the gravel, because they drag along those minds of men which are made firm by no weight of stability.
**“and in caves of earth”** — And in caves of earth: for heretics meet in secret little gatherings, so as to give their error by hiding the reverence they cannot give it by reason; whence stolen waters are sweeter. Or caves are evil thoughts where hypocrites lie hidden. The gravel is the present life, which is always being driven along; the foot of one who clings to it is set on the surface of the gravel, but slips to the bottom; so he who, for love of the world, does even lawful things goes down even to evil ones.
30.7:
**“They that”** — even
**“among these kind of things”** — over which they ought to weep
**“They pleased themselves”** — ignorant of true joy
**“They pleased themselves among these kind of things”** — They pleased themselves among these kind of things: by the name of briers he signifies the prickings of sins. Perverse minds rejoice in the iniquities they ought to weep over. Whence Solomon: “Who are glad when they have done evil, and rejoice in most wicked things”; because surely they attend to the passing things they receive and neglect to look on the abiding goods they lose.
**“and counted it delightful to be under the briers.”**
• because they boast with gladness of that by which, in ruining others, they carry thorns, as if leaders to justice; or the wicked delight in things by which yet they are pricked with adversities, which they had learned from fools; or there is no one who does not disagree with the condition of his fortune
• Whence it is openly added: “and counted it delightful to be under the briers.” They rejoice in temporal things indeed, but yet, since they cannot manage them without tribulation, the wretches are pricked by the care by which they are pressed. And this is what Jeremias says: “He hath inebriated me with wormwood”; because the human race, even if it receives many bitter things, yet like a drunkard does not understand what it suffers, but rejoices as if in good things, gaping so after earthly things. Whence Osee: “Ephraim is a heifer taught to love to tread out the corn”; because even when she could freely be free from the labours of the world, yet from habit she returns, even uncompelled, to the same habit of labour, so that, used to weariness, it does not please her to cease from the yoke of worldly servitude even when she may.
30.8:
**“The children of foolish”** — for ignorance
**“and base men”** — infamous for wicked works
**“The children of foolish and base men”** — The children of foolish and base men: the children of those who were the masters of errors; who, by teaching perverse things, are foolish through ignorance; by living wickedly, base through action; who have been made exiles from the land of the living.
**“and not appearing at all upon the earth.”**
• even if they long to be seen; or in the Church, for the vileness of their works, they do not appear to God
• and who before were as it were revered while they were in the Church in appearance
30.9:
**“Now I am turned into their song”** — Now I am turned into their song, etc. The time of the Church is expressed in which she is publicly mocked by the reprobate.
**“and am become their byword”** — And am become their byword: she will be made a byword by the wicked, because when they see the good die by torments they take from them a likeness for cursing, saying: “Pardon to you as to that butchered one.”
30.10: **“They abhor me, and”** — They abhor me, and: the wicked flee far from the Church, not by steps of the feet but by qualities of character. And to spit in her face is to confound the just even in their presence, and to send loose words against them in insult like dribbling spittle. But because holy Church knows to attribute her good things to the mercy of the Redeemer, she knows to attribute her evils to the justice of the judge.
30.11:
**“For he hath opened his quiver”**
• this happens because God
• There follows: “For he hath opened his quiver,” etc. By the quiver the hidden judgment of God is designated. So when the Lord sees sins and yet does not move his hand to vengeance, he holds as it were a closed quiver; but by striking he shows how much he was displeased by what he long saw and bore with in us.
• The quiver is the hidden counsel from which he sends forth the arrow, that is, the open sentence. We see that man is scourged, but not for what cause; but in the chastening the force of the counsel is opened.
**“and hath afflicted me, and hath put a bridle into my mouth.”**
• but we grieve the more at what we suffer from those in whom we trusted
• She spares the wicked by keeping silent, yet urges her life on them by patience.
**“and hath put a bridle into my mouth”** — And hath put a bridle into my mouth: for the holy teachers, when they see the hearts of those who resist forsaken by God, fall silent, afflicted and groaning, lest they speak to the unworthy, who would become worse as well.
30.12:
**“At the right hand of my rising, my calamities”** — At the right hand of my rising, my calamities: our Redeemer is called the rising (the East). For because light rises from the east, he is rightly called the rising by whose light of justice the night of our injustice is lit up. So at the right hand of the rising calamities arise, because those too leap forth to persecution who were believed to be elect, to be at the right hand. And he rightly asserts that they arise forthwith, because, since those who persecute were not strangers, evils come from them suddenly and forthwith. But if the faithful are truly called the right hand, calamities arise at the right hand of the rising, because when persecution breaks out the just suffer the onslaughts of the wicked.
**“they have overthrown my feet”** — They have overthrown my feet: by the feet of the Church her lowest members are signified, which, while they serve earthly works, can be deceived the more quickly the less they understand lofty things.
**“and have overwhelmed me with their paths as with waves”** — And have overwhelmed me with their paths as with waves: the path of the adversaries is compared to waves, because the life of the wicked, troublesome with insolent restlessness, falls like a tempest to sink, so to speak, the ship of the heart.
30.13:
**“They have destroyed my ways”** — They have destroyed my ways: let blessed Job say this of the malignant spirits; let the Church say it of the persecutors, who destroy her ways when they trouble the way of truth in the minds of some weak ones by foul persuasion.
**“they have lain in wait against me, and they have prevailed”** — They have lain in wait against me, and they have prevailed: those lying in wait prevail when they pervert, by pretending good things, those whom they cannot openly drag into evil.
**“and there was none to help.”** — as if God had forsaken for a time in order to test
**“and there was none to help”** — And there was none to help: mostly the just, caught in tribulation, reckon that the hand of the helper is slow, when the savagery of the persecutors straitens them a little longer; and the remedies of the deliverer are swift indeed, but seem slow to pain.
30.14:
**“as when a wall is broken”**
• or the wall is the fortification of discipline
• As when a wall is broken: the Redeemer is a wall to us, who forbids the course of the malignant spirits to reach our hearts; but the wall is as it were broken when by the persuasions of the wicked the faith which is in our Redeemer is scattered in the hearts of some; whatever happens, because power is given by God to the enemies.
**“and a gate opened, they have rushed in upon me”** — And a gate opened, they have rushed in upon me: when power is given to the perverse in this life, what else is opened but the gate of error? As if a wall were broken and a gate opened, the wicked rush in upon the good when the perverse, having received temporal power, try also to destroy the defences of faith in the hearts of some.
**“and have rolled themselves down to my miseries”** — And have rolled themselves down to my miseries: the reprobate roll themselves down through their own miseries to ours too, when they drag even some united with us into the evils in which they themselves are entangled.
30.15:
**“I am brought to nothing”** — I am brought to nothing: in the reckoning of the wicked we are brought to nothing when we do not hold the temporal goods which they love as the highest.
**“I am brought to nothing:”**
• I am brought to nothing: allegorically. To such men whatever they see of the virtues of the good is nothing; even if at times they think of eternal things, passing delight takes it away.
• All these things that are said allegorically are also to be taken according to the history, which is plain.
**“as a wind thou hast taken away my desire”** — As a wind thou hast taken away my desire: the faithful people declares that it suffers what it grieves that those it loves suffer. So the wind takes away desire when any passing thing destroys the longing for eternity.
**“and my prosperity hath passed away like a cloud.”** — And my prosperity hath passed away like a cloud, etc. A cloud stands out on high, but the breath drives it on its course. So prosperity passed like a cloud, because the glory of the perverse, the higher it is, the less it is fixed. Having completed the desires and acts of the weak, he returns to the voice of the elect.
30.16:
**“And now my soul fadeth within myself”** — in the future it will grow green again, passing beyond itself
**“And now … within myself”** — And now … within myself: now our soul fades and is weakened within ourselves, but is restored in God; and it becomes so much the farther from the greenness of joy as, still driven back from the light of its maker, it retreats into itself. Because in the time of the last persecution many will fall and few will stand, here he says few things of the good and more of the perverse. Whence he soon returns to those who fall.
**“and the days of affliction possess me.”** — afterwards there will be days of gladness
30.17:
**“In the night my bone is pierced with sorrows”** — In the night my bone is pierced with sorrows: he speaks of his own things so that they fit the falling too; because a multitude of worms swarming through the hollows of his ulcers tore the holy man’s body. But the bone of the Church is pierced with sorrows in the night, because the saints, pressed by the darkness of tribulation, are bored through by affliction, so that even those who had the vigour of strength in her now have as it were a certain hole of fear.
**“and they that feed upon me, do not sleep.”** — And they that feed upon me, because the malignant spirits, who consume the fleshly members of the Church, know so much the less how to rest from temptation as they are weighed down by no weight of flesh.
30.18:
**“With the multitude of them”** — they are heavy and many
**“my garment is consumed,”** — With the multitude of them my garment is consumed, etc. What else is taken as Job’s garment but his body? But the garment of the Church is the souls of individuals, which surround her by believing and faithfully clinging to her. So he says: while those who torture are many, very many are destroyed who clung to her by the bond of love.
**“as with the collar of my coat”** — As with the collar of my coat: the collar of the coat goes round the neck. But if the neck is squeezed, the use of the voice and the breath of life are killed. And the reprobate squeeze the Church at the neck, that is, in the preachers, as with the collar of a coat, because by their persecutions they try to put out in her the life of faith and the voice of preaching.
30.19:
**“I am compared to dirt”**
• if any prefer to die rather than keep silent, they are held cheap
• I am compared to dirt: in the judgment of the reprobate the Church of the elect is compared to dirt, because, trodden under for a time, she is despised. She is likened to embers and ashes, because they reckon that she has come only to the evils which they see shown in her bodily.
30.20:
**“I cry to thee, and thou hearest me not: I stand up, and thou dost not regard me.”**
• therefore I wish to be changed; but because God delays, therefore I groan
• Grief urges the patience of the saints into speech, and, delayed so as to advance, they fear lest they fail.
**“I cry to thee”** — I cry to thee: the Church in the time of her persecution stands by faith, cries by desires, but grieves as if she were not regarded, while she sees her wishes put off in tribulations; which happens so that the merits of the sufferers may grow.
30.21:
**“Thou art changed to be cruel toward me”**
• striking strictly and not sparing fault
• Neither cruelty nor changeableness comes into God; but he added “to me,” so that the cruelty and change may be not in the quality of the judge but in the mind of the sufferer.
• Thou art changed to be cruel toward me: it is said of God after our manner, so that by things near to us we may sometimes climb to the highest. But nothing worthy can be said of him.
**“and in the hardness of thy hand”** — And in the hardness of thy hand: the hand of God is said to be contrary to our will when by striking it pursues what displeases him in us.
30.22:
**“Thou hast lifted me up”** — the lifting up of temporal and fleeting happiness happens only so that it may dash one down the worse, suddenly, into the lowest things; in Job it seemed to be so in others’ eyes, in the weak it truly is
**“and set me as it were upon the wind, and thou hast mightily dashed me.”** — Thou hast lifted me up, and set me as it were upon the wind: because the glory of the present life is seen as on high, but is made firm by no stability; he who rejoices in passing prosperity is set, as it were lifted up, upon the wind. These words, which fit the person of Job, he adds not as to what he was but as to what he seemed to be. For he did not suffer this fall in mind, because no adversity cast down him whom no prosperity had corrupted. In the Church too the weak, who rejoice in passing successes, seem lifted up upon the wind; but in the time of persecution, when the breeze of prosperity has passed, their lifting up at once collapses.
30.23:
**“I know that thou wilt deliver me to death, where a house is appointed for every one that liveth.”**
• eternally
• Hell was the house of all before the coming of Christ; no one escapes the death of the flesh; and these things fit Job himself. Mystically, the weak, who, living fleshly, come to the house of death. But because some fall into pleasures who return through penance, for whom stripes are instruction, not destruction, he adds: “But yet thou stretchest not forth thy hand to their consumption.” The Lord does not stretch out his hand to the consumption of sinners when by striking he rebukes them from sins and saves those who fall, while he wounds in bodily health those falling into fault, so that, laid low outwardly, they may rise inwardly.
**“I know that thou wilt deliver me to death”** — I know that thou wilt deliver me to death: for no one comes here who does not go on by the steps of his corruption toward the death of the flesh.
30.24: **“But yet thou stretchest not forth thy hand to their consumption: and if they shall fall down thou wilt save.”** — since he adds this not of himself but of others, he shows that he signifies in himself the persons of many
30.25:
**“I wept”** — it is more to give of oneself than of one’s goods
**“heretofore”** — once
**“I wept heretofore for him that was afflicted”** — I wept heretofore for him that was afflicted: compassion is more than a gift, because often even one who does not have compassion gives something. But one who truly has compassion never refuses what he sees is necessary to his neighbour. The Church, when she sees the afflicted in the laments of penance, joins her weeping to them in continual prayer.
**“for him that was afflicted, and my soul had compassion on the poor.”** — In the time of the last persecution the Church brings back to memory the good things she did in the time of peace; longing for eternal joys, but, while they are put off, pressed by evils.
30.26:
**“I expected good things”** — to have them as soon as possible
**“and evils are come upon me:”** — He adds: “I expected good things, and evils are come upon me.” The faithful people expects good things but receives evils.
**“I waited for light”** — eternal brightness
**“and darkness broke out.”** — of persecutions
**“I waited for light, and darkness broke out”** — I waited for light, and darkness broke out: she waits for light and runs into darkness, because she hopes, by the grace of reward, to be present now at the joys of the angels, and yet, put off longer here, she bears the hands of persecutors, like Tobias.
30.27:
**“My inner parts have boiled without any rest,”**
• who, knowing her secrets, the better they know where she is most pained, the worse they do not rest at all from afflicting her
• My inner parts have boiled without any rest: she would grieve less at these evils if they were done by an adversary; but they torture more heavily when done by those from whom good things were hoped; and this is her inner parts.
**“My inner parts have boiled without any rest”** — My inner parts have boiled without any rest: for the inner parts of holy Church to boil is to bear in the cruelty of persecution even those whom she had carried before like her bowels through the love of faith.
**“the days of affliction have prevented me.”** — but these I bore heavily even before
**“the days of affliction have prevented me”** — The days of affliction have prevented me: for the Church of the elect knows that she will suffer many evils in the last persecution. But the days of her affliction forestall it, because even in the time of peace she bears heavily the life of the wicked among her, who already show in their wicked ways what is to come.
30.28:
**“I went mourning”**
• even if lifted up, as he says above: “Thou hast lifted me up,” etc.
• I went mourning, etc. The holy man, lifted up with goods and honours, went mourning, because even if the glory of power showed him set over men, yet within by his mourning he offered to the Lord the sacrifice of a contrite heart. The Church too goes mourning through prosperity, because she reckons nothing truly prosperous until she grasps the good which she singularly seeks.
• Or: even if he abounded in so much, mourning held him within under discipline, and from the licence of power he did not break out into impatience. Whence: “without indignation, I rose up.” Impatience is almost always the friend of power.
• Calves to be slaughtered are left in free pastures; the one to be kept is pressed by the yoke. Those come through pleasant meadows to the pit; this one through a rough road to the homeland.
**“without indignation; I rose up, and cried in the crowd”** — Without indignation; I rose up, and cried in the crowd: often the tumults of seditious men provoke the minds of those set over them; who, if they are good, have a cry against the tumults of the insolent but have no fury, since they do not cease to teach those whom they bear with mercifully.
30.29:
**“I was the brother of dragons”** — in time of peace the Church suffers within her the wicked and the feigned; so too Job was good among the wicked, which is the perfection of goodness
**“I was the brother of dragons, and companion”** — I was the brother of dragons, and companion: by the name of dragons the malicious; by ostriches, which have wings and do not have flight, pretenders are designated, who have only the look of holiness.
30.30:
**“skin”** — in whom the Church was fair, now she is foul
**“My … is become black upon me”** — because power is given to them too against the Church; but Job says he suffered outside and within
**“and my bones”** — as Paul burned with the dryness of weariness at some falling, when he said: “Who is scandalized, and I am not on fire?”
**“My skin is become black”** — My skin is become black: by the name of skin the weak of the Church are signified, who serve outward usefulness. By the bones the strong, who care for heavenly things, in whom is the framework of the body. So the skin is blackened and the bones dry up with heat, because while the weak leap forth to iniquity, and, often having taken a place of honour among the reprobate, serve against the Church, the strong who are in her are tortured with zeal for the faith.
30.31:
**“My harp is turned to mourning, and my organ into the voice of those that weep.”**
• when preaching is silent, the elect man grieves
• Or: the harp sounds through strings, the organ through pipes. The string of the harp is the intention of those who work rightly, which is stretched through affliction of the flesh toward another life, the flesh dried, so that the string may have a fitting sound. If the string is stretched too little it does not sound, but if too much it sounds hoarse; because abstinence avails nothing unless the body is well tamed, or if it is worn down too much; because vices are to be put out, not the flesh.
**“My harp is turned to mourning”** — My harp is turned to mourning: as if he said: in the time of my peace I preached through some, who also tame the flesh, small things after the manner of a harp, through others great and sounding things after the manner of an organ. But now the harp and the organ are turned to mourning, because when I see myself despised I bewail those who do not hear the song of preaching.

31.1:
**“I made a covenant with my eyes, that I would not so much as think upon a virgin.”**
• with consent of delight
• Up to here he has listed the evils he suffered; now he begins to tell the good things he did. Because death enters through the windows of the senses, he guards them outside, lest through them the soul desire outward things. They ought not to look at what is not lawful to be desired.
**“I made a covenant with my eyes”** — I made a covenant with my eyes: now he lists his own virtues in order, so weaving the history of his life as to put in among them very rarely something that can be understood mystically. “I made a covenant with my eyes.” For so that he could keep the thoughts of his heart chaste, he made a covenant with his eyes, lest he first look carelessly on what he would afterwards love unwillingly. It is said to the serpent by God: “Upon thy breast and belly shalt thou go.” On the belly when he works lust in deed through human members; on the breast when he defiles in thought; but because one comes to the deed through thought, which is placed in the breast, therefore Job, because he fortified his thought, overcame breast and belly with one guard, saying: “that I would not so much as think,” etc. Which he added because he put out not only the act of lust but the thought, which is abundant justice.
31.2:
**“For what part should God … have”** — as if: if I were not clean
**“in me from above”** — seeing
**“For what part should … have in me”** — For what part should he have in me: as if he said: the maker of the heights refuses to have me as his possession if my mind wastes away before his sight with weak desires. For no good things please God without cleanness of mind.
**“and what inheritance the Almighty”** — because other good things do not please without cleanness
**“from on high?”**
• seeing me
• I would not be the part of God, because
31.3:
**“Is not destruction to the wicked, and aversion to them that work iniquity?”**
• elsewhere: injustice
• I must act carefully, because
• Is not destruction to the wicked? Then there will be aversion to the reprobate, when they see themselves made anathema from the inheritance of the strict judge.
31.4:
**“Doth not he consider my ways, and number all my steps?”** — because no good or evil things are without retribution
**“Doth not he consider my ways”** — Doth not he consider my ways? By the name of ways he declares actions; by the term steps, the motions of minds or the advances of merits. And if the Lord considers the ways of each one, he so numbers the steps that not even the tiniest thoughts, and the slightest words which have grown cheap with us by use, remain unexamined in his judgment.
31.5:
**“If I have walked”** — and since God sees all, I wish to be perfected in the example of Christ
**“in vanity, and my foot hath made haste to deceit:”**
• vanity belongs to lightness, deceit to malice. So he uses the right order, because through light things one comes to malicious ones
• If I have walked, etc. Knowing he is seen, he takes care; yet he is not secure and perfect, because among the ancients he weighs, in the precepts of the Christ to come, how much he lacks of perfection. So he says: “If I have walked.”
31.6:
**“Let him weigh me in a just balance”** — he is weighed in this, that he is called to the example of his life
**“Let him weigh”** — Let him weigh: as if he said: as far as the measure of human life goes, I do not see evils in me. But unless the Mediator appears, who surpasses all, I do not know how far I stand from true simplicity.
**“in a just balance”** — In a just balance: by the name of balance “the mediator of God and men” is designated, in whom our merits are weighed equally, and in whose precepts we recognize what we lack in our life. And the sense is: if I have ever done anything lightly, anything ruinously, let the Mediator appear, that in his life I may recognize whether I was truly simple. For he who had surpassed the powers of his times was seeking the Mediator of God and men, so that, weighing himself in him, he might recognize whether he had truly kept a simple life.
**“and let God know”**
• God is said to know when he makes us know
• that is, let him make me know
**“my simplicity.”** — but
31.7:
**“If my step hath turned out of the way,”**
• through consent, not through what one suffers unwillingly
• If my step hath turned, etc. The step turns out of the way as often as our thought leaves the road of uprightness through consent to error.
**“and if my heart hath followed my eyes”** — if sight serves evil thought, work soon follows
**“and if … hath followed my eyes”** — And if … hath followed my eyes: for as temptation is drawn in through the eyes, so sometimes, conceived within, it forces the eyes to serve it outside.
**“and if a spot hath cleaved to my hands”** — And if a spot hath cleaved to my hands: as if he said: I neither wished to see what I might desire, nor by seeing followed what I desired. Nor did a spot cleave to my hands, that is, fault to my actions; because if he ever thought anything unlawful, he did not let it reach as far as works.
31.8:
**“Then let me sow and let another eat”** — Then let me sow and let another eat: to sow is to preach the words of life; to eat is to be filled with good works. And the sense is: let not me but another do what my mouth speaks. For a woman suckles her son when awake and kills him when asleep; so a master awake in knowledge and asleep in life, if he nourishes the hearer by watchings and preaching, kills him by the sleep of the body.
**“and let my offspring”** — those whom I begot by the word
**“be rooted out.”**
• by example
• and
**“and let my offspring be rooted out”** — And let my offspring be rooted out: whoever does not live according to what he speaks tears up by his work those whom he begot by the word from the stability of uprightness.
31.9:
**“If my heart hath been deceived upon a woman”** — If my heart hath been deceived upon a woman: by this the holy man is shown not even to have thought about the stain of fornication.
**“and if I have laid wait at my friend’s door”** — And if I have laid wait at my friend’s door: by this he plainly shows that he was free from the guilt of adultery. It is a great thing that Job gave examples of cleanness, who did not receive it at that time when, grace not yet revealed, the rule had not come forth which would check the wantonness not only of the body but of the heart. Now, even after the Lord’s prohibition, the contrary is done; according to what he says: “If my heart hath been deceived,” etc.
31.10: **“Let my wife be the harlot of another, and let other men lie with her.”** — if I have done this, let the same fault be turned into punishment for me
31.11:
**“For this is a heinous crime”**
• a crime
• For this is a heinous crime: in this, sin and crime differ, because every crime is a sin, yet not every sin is a crime. And in this life many are without crime, but no one can be without sins. So, defining the crime of lust well, he says: “It is a fire that devoureth even to destruction,” because the stain devours not only to defilement but to destruction.
**“and a most grievous iniquity.”** — no one is without sin, many without crime. Sin defiles the soul of the good, crime puts it out
31.12:
**“It is a fire that devoureth even to destruction, and rooteth up all things that spring.”** — elsewhere: offspring
**“and rooteth up all things that spring”** — And rooteth up all things that spring: the things that spring in the soul are good works; because if the evil of lust is not resisted, those things too which seemed good perish. But in such great cleanness of chastity he shows how humble he was when he adds: “If I have despised to abide judgment with my manservant.” He who did not refuse to be judged with his menservants and maidservants clearly shows that he had been swollen against no neighbour. And among these things it is good to look at how much discretion the holy man’s life was guarded with in all things. For not far above he said: “The young men saw me, and hid themselves: and the old men rose up and stood. The princes ceased to speak,” etc. But now he says: “If I have despised to abide judgment with my manservant,” etc. Who can worthily consider such lofty tempering of virtues in this man? In whom there is such authority of rule that leaders are held to silence, such humility of heart that maidservants are allowed to come to judgment on equal terms. See, it appears in a wonderful way: in power mightier than princes, in dispute equal to servants; in the assembly of princes mindful of rule, in dispute with servants mindful of his condition; for he sees himself a servant under the true Lord. So he does not lift himself above his servants in height of heart. Whence he adds at once: “For what shall I do?”
31.13:
**“If I have despised to abide judgment with my manservant”** — or: menservants
**“or my maidservant”** — or: maidservant
**“my”** — or: my
**“when they had any controversy against me:”** — an ellipsis, as if: I did not do these things
31.14: **“For what shall I do”** — a great check on the swelling that comes from power
31.15:
**“Did not he that made me in the womb”** — the humble man does not consider that he presides, but the common nature; he does not rejoice to preside but to profit
