**“Did not he … in the womb make”** — Did not he … in the womb make: to mighty men the virtue of humility is great; having considered the equality of their condition, he now turns to the works of liberality.
31.16:
**“If I have denied to the poor what they desired”** — the humble
**“If I have denied”** — If I have denied: after chastity and humility he adds about liberality. By this it is shown that he served the poor not only in their need but also in their desire.
**“and have made the eyes of the widow wait:”** — the light of giving is not darkened by slowness
**“and have made the eyes of the widow wait”** — And have made the eyes of the widow wait: what is sought with true humility, that is, what is asked not from desire but from necessity, must be given without delay, so that the merits of good works may be increased not only by the gift but also by the swiftness of the gift.
31.17:
**“If I have eaten my morsel alone, and the fatherless hath not eaten”** — an ellipsis everywhere
**“If I have eaten my morsel alone”** — If I have eaten my morsel alone: I not only gave outwardly but had the needy with me. Nor is company to be kept with just anyone, but with those from whom merits may grow; whence he declares that he had the fatherless as a companion. For some are used to bestow much, but shrink from having the poor as companions in their household life, not having the grace of a common life. But he would reckon he did wrong to devotion if he ate alone what the Lord had created for all in common. Nor does he attribute this devotion to himself but to the grace of God; he says: “For from my infancy mercy grew up with me.” He makes known that he obtained these bowels of devotion by his maker’s grace; because, as he was not formed in the womb by his own work, so neither was he devout from the womb by his own power. For mercy, even if it was of his choice that it should advance with him, yet it was not of his choice that it should come out of the womb with him. The virtues are companions: let not humility, when it reveres a neighbour, forsake liberality, nor liberality swell up toward the needy. Neither through ungodliness fail to cover one who shares your nature, nor through pride cease to revere him whom you cover; as it is said: “That they may receive you into everlasting dwellings,” where it is shown that we offer gifts to patrons rather than give gifts to the needy.
**“thereof:”** — nor is this devotion from me, but from the grace of God
31.18:
**“For from my infancy mercy grew up with me: and it came out with me from my mother’s womb:”**
• it is plain that this cannot be except from God
• here note his humility
31.19:
**“If I have despised him that was perishing for want of clothing,”** — because some give more for acquaintance than for nature
**“If I have despised him that was perishing”** — If I have despised him that was perishing: that he did not despise the poor man showed the virtue of humility; that he covered him, that of devotion. And he shows that he had pity on an unknown neighbour, whom he calls one passing by, because with a devout mind nature counts for more than acquaintance, as in Job.
**“and”** — if I have despised
31.20: **“If … have not blessed me”** — here devotion is noted
31.21:
**“If I have lifted up”** — here patience is noted
**“If I have lifted up my hand against the fatherless”** — If I have lifted up my hand against the fatherless: as if he plainly said: not even then did I wish to raise power against the fatherless for the business of my own advantage, when I saw myself superior in judgment, even by justice. For here by the name of the gate he signifies the judgment that was held in the gate.
**“even when I saw myself superior in the gate:”** — in judgment
31.22:
**“Let my shoulder … from its joint”** — unity
**“fall”** — let it fall from the body, which I would not use for usefulness; or let unity be broken
**“Let my shoulder fall from its joint”** — Let my shoulder fall from its joint: if I refused to do the good things I uttered with my mouth, let me lose that very member of the body which was given me for working. Or by the shoulder, to which the arm is joined, the bond of social life is designated; by the arm, working. In saying: “If I have lifted up,” etc., he asserts that he kept patience; and he who does not, his shoulder falls from its joint when, not able to bear anything adverse, he leaves brotherly concord. And his arm is broken with its bones, because all his working, with whatever virtues it seems to be joined, will be loosed unless patience is kept by the bond of charity. And because some virtues without others are either nothing at all or imperfect, to show that they were joined in him he lists them one by one; having spoken of the rest, then, he tells with what mind he possessed riches.
**“and let my arm”**
• good working
• he loses his own good works who refuses to bear others’ evils
• concord and unity are never kept without patience; but when unity is broken the arm is broken
**“with its bones be broken.”** — elsewhere: be shattered
31.23:
**“For I have always feared God as waves swelling over me,”** — He adds: “For I have always feared God as waves swelling over me.” When swelling waves hang over from above, and threaten the death they bring, then no care for temporal things, no delight of the flesh, comes back to the mind of the sailors; they even throw out of the ship the things for which they undertook long voyages. All things come into contempt of mind through love of living. So he fears God as swelling waves over him who, while he longs for true life, despises all he carries here as possessor. Or he calls swelling waves the last power, when, all the elements stirred up, the judge from above, coming, brings the end of all things; which the saints dread daily.
**“and his weight I was not able to bear”** — And his weight I was not able to bear: since he who considers with attentive mind the coming of the last judgment surely sees that so great a dread hangs over that he fears not only to see it then but even to foresee it now.
31.24:
**“If I have thought gold my strength, and … to fine gold”** — fine gold is the raw mass of gold; for, fixing his hope and delight on the grace of God, he sins neither from the quantity of gold nor from hope
**“If I have thought gold my strength”** — If I have thought gold my strength: for he would have despaired of the Creator if he had put his hope in the creature. For he who leans on what is falling must fall with what falls.
**“have said: My confidence:”** — namely: thou art
31.25:
**“If I have rejoiced over my great riches”** — he sets his foundation in flowing waters who trusts in temporal things, and is snatched away with them
**“and because my hand had gotten much.”** — If I have rejoiced over my great riches, etc. For nothing apart from God suffices for the mind which truly seeks God.
*Mystically:* Mystically: gold is the talent of bright understanding; fine gold the mind, which, while it is cooked by the fire of love, always keeps its brightness. And the sense is: I did not attribute it to my talent if I understood anything truly, nor to my mind if I did any good things. Great riches are the abundant sharpness of counsels which the hand of the seeker finds, that is, which the thought of the one handling them brings forth. So he finds great riches who, by searching the sacred words, obtains abundant understanding. And it is not a secure gladness to know them, but to keep them; because of him to whom much is committed more is required, and while it is given out at interest it is lost unless it is paid out carefully. Understanding either grows numb with idleness or vanishes with haughtiness; and so he says: “If I have rejoiced.” But when he carries out what he understands, from the fact that it is shown outside he often slips; but blessed Job, as he did not extol the gold of understanding, so neither the light of working. And after such great things as he said above, what great thing is it not to have worshipped created things? He says that he did not even see them, that is, that he did not look with desire at the beauty of the present light; so that he delighted neither in gold nor in bodily light; like him who says: “I have not desired the day of man”; in which he cannot rejoice because he did not see them through desire. For the outward light, if it is loved carelessly, blinds the heart, gaping outward, to the invisible light.
31.26:
**“If I beheld the sun when it shined”**
• the sun and moon, appointed for human uses, are called the host of heaven; in the worship of which many fell
• And the sense is: “If I beheld the sun.” Almost only the good do not see their own good things, which they give others to see; nor the moon, that is, the fame of good work, which shines for those walking in darkness. Job did not extol these either, which were more to be feared. For then, like a tall tree, one is shaken more by the blasts; that which through understanding was in the seed, through working in the garden. And from praises he was made arrogant not only not in words but not even in silent thought. When the wicked wonder at good things, a lamp burns in the night; but when the good wonder at the best things, the sun shines in the day. When good shines in the body’s action it is a lamp, that is, light in an earthen vessel; when in the mind’s contemplation, the sun from heaven.
**“and the moon going in brightness”** — And the moon going in brightness: he calls the moon fame, which, shining in the night of this life, takes strength from good work. “And my heart in secret hath rejoiced”: for there are those who are lifted up within themselves by their own praises and rejoice.
31.27: **“And my heart in secret hath rejoiced,”** — And this is: “And my heart in secret hath rejoiced.” And because the unconsidering mind, drawn by favours, sometimes praises what it has done, he adds: “and I have kissed my hand with my mouth.” By the mouth speech is designated; so he kisses his hand with his mouth who praises what he does.
31.28: **“Which is a very great iniquity, and a denial against the most high God.”** — Which is a very great iniquity, and a denial, etc. Because whoever attributes to himself what he does is convicted of denying the grace of his maker. “Very great”: every sin which comes from weakness does not lose hope, because it seeks pardon from God. But presumption, the farther it is from humility, the more heavily it is in despair; and while it attributes strength to itself, it does not seek it from God.
31.29:
**“If I have been glad at the downfall of him that hated me”**
• true love, which loves both friends in God and enemies for God
• If I have been glad at the downfall: because, loving even his enemy, while he grieved with his adversary as he fell, by the other’s evils he himself grew toward good.
**“and have rejoiced that evil had found him.”** — he who rejoices at his enemy’s evil grieves at his good
31.30:
**“For I have not given my mouth to sin”**
• for I was a stranger to the fault of cursing
• he who calls down evils he cannot bring shows what he would do if he could
**“For I have not given”** — For I have not given: for some strike with cursing those whom they reckon adversaries, because they can by no means strike them by power.
**“by wishing”** — or: by waiting for
31.31:
**“If the men of my tabernacle have not said”** — If the men of my tabernacle have not said: for he bore with adversaries living with him, because he did not yield to wrongdoers by keeping silent, but went against them by uprightness.
**“Who will give us of his flesh that we may be filled?”** — if I loved those set over me and bore with adversaries living with me
**“Who will give us of his flesh”** — Who will give us of his flesh? This mystically of Christ, with whose flesh they desired to be filled: either the Jews of his household, wishing as it were to put out his body by consuming it, or the believing gentiles, who are refreshed daily from his body.
31.32:
**“The stranger did not stay without”**
• in the foregoing, charity is patient; in these, kind
• The stranger did not stay without: about to tell of his liberality in the grace of hospitality, he first set out what he was like within himself, because outward gifts are seasoned by the inward cleanness of the heart.
**“my door was open to the traveller.”** — and while so lofty in work, while so humble in mind
31.33:
**“If as a man I have hid my sin, and have concealed my iniquity in my bosom.”** — truly humble: what he says of himself of his own accord he does not deny when another accuses
**“If as a man I have hid my sin”** — If as a man I have hid my sin: he sees that it is the property of man, because it comes down by imitation of the old parent. For Adam wished to excuse his sin through the woman, the woman through the serpent.
**“If I have hid”** — If I have hid: he who knows his many good things are preached everywhere covers any evils he has, and believes himself holy; but the truly humble man knows his evils and opens the voice of confession. And to conceal iniquity in the bosom is to hide it in the hiding places of conscience and not uncover it by confession. In these he openly shows that he said true things of his good things, who did not keep silent about his evils. He is truly just who avoids evils, and does not hide from men those he cannot avoid. There, justice; here, the guarding of justice. But because from true humility a secure authority is born, so that he who does not pant after high things within fears nothing outside, he speaks with confession expressed.
31.34:
**“If I have been afraid at a very great multitude”**
• as if he said more openly: while others were stirred up against me outside, I myself remained undisturbed within
• He adds: “If I have been afraid at a very great multitude.” To covet nothing of the world is great security, so that, clinging to the unchangeable, one is not disturbed in mind when all things below are disturbed, even if at times one is outwardly, through weakness of the flesh.
**“and the contempt of kinsmen hath terrified me:”** — he who does not fear to be despised does not leap out through the tongue
**“and the contempt”** — And the contempt: the good, even when despised, do not open their own things when they do not profit others, because it would be showing oneself without profiting; as Jesus kept silent to Herod, who was not seeking profit, and so suffered himself to be mocked.
**“and the contempt of kinsmen hath terrified me”** — And the contempt of kinsmen hath terrified me: there are those who fear to be despised; these are forced to go out of the door, because, beaten by insults, while they open about themselves things that were not known, they go out as it were through the door of the mouth.
**“and I have not rather held my peace, and not gone out of the door.”**
• with which we open secrets
• but
**“and I have not rather held my peace”** — And I have not rather held my peace: he rightly puts first “I held my peace,” because he who, impatient, does not know how to keep silent goes out of the house of conscience. This mystically of Christ, who did not fear the many persecuting and despising him, who both kept silent and did not go out and avenge himself by power.
31.35:
**“Who would grant me a hearer”** — Who would grant me a hearer: he seeks the Mediator, knowing that the prayers of human desire for the rest of eternal deliverance cannot be heard except through their advocate, of whom it is added:
**“that the Almighty may hear my desire;”**
• through him
• “In his excess” man is truthful above himself, and recognizes about the quality of man that “every man is a liar,” even that same man himself
**“and that he himself that judgeth would write a book”** — And that he himself that judgeth would write a book: “The Father judgeth no man, but hath given all judgment to the Son.” He, coming for our redemption, established a new testament for us, and will at some time be the author of judgment, who is now the maker of the book: then he will strictly demand what now he gently commands. But why does blessed Job ask for a book to be written by the judge, who could not reach the times of the New Testament? But he uses the voices of the elect and asks in their meaning, because he provided for them in all things for the future. For he himself by the Spirit had long held this book with him, which by the grace of inspiration he had received both to know by seeing and to announce by foreseeing. But why, blessed Job, do you desire a book to be written?
31.36: **“That I may carry it on my shoulder”** — That I may carry it on my shoulder: to carry the book on the shoulder is to fulfil sacred Scripture by working. And it is described first as carried on the shoulder and afterwards as put about like a crown, because the commandments of the sacred word, if they are now well carried in work, afterwards show us the crown of victory in reward.
31.37:
**“At every step of mine I would pronounce it”** — but because no one is made at once on the highest steps
**“At every step of mine”** — At every step of mine: he calls the increases of the virtues steps, since by them one climbs so as to come to obtain heavenly things; and he pronounces the book as it were at each of his steps who shows that he has received its sentence not by words only but also by works.
**“and offer it as to a prince”** — And offer it as to a prince: what we offer we hold in the hand. So to offer the book to him coming to judgment is to have held the words of his precepts in action.
31.38:
**“If my land cry against me”**
• the uncultivated only cry out and do not grieve; the cultivated weep through compassion, grieving at their neighbours’ evils as their own
• If my land cry against me: for a greater showing of his progress, at the last he sets an imprecating condition. Because this cannot hold according to the letter, it must be understood mystically. Everyone who holds the rights of rule over the faithful committed to him, what else does he hold but land to be cultivated? But the land cries against its possessor when either a private household or holy Church murmurs against him who presides over something just; which, as regards the rude and those cultivated by no works, is called land.
**“and with it the furrows thereof mourn:”** — and are silent
**“and with it the furrows thereof mourn”** — And with it the furrows thereof mourn: those are called furrows who, intent on hearing and keeping holy preachings, cut from their former hardness of mind as by a ploughshare of the tongue, receive the seeds of exhortation; who, worn by the ploughshare of reading, when they see the innocent weighed down in the least things, are turned to laments through compassion. So if he who presides acts perversely toward those under him, both the rude cry out against him and the perfect mourn.
31.39:
**“If I have eaten the fruits thereof without money,”** — if he who presides acts perversely toward those under him, the rude cry out against him and the perfect mourn
**“If I have eaten the fruits thereof without”** — If I have eaten the fruits thereof without: he who presides and he who is under are servants to each other, if this one obeys and that one provides carefully. “And have eaten the fruits thereof without money”: to eat the fruits without money is to receive provision from the Church but not to give that same Church the price of preaching. Job did not eat the fruits of the land without money, because he gave back the word of admonition to those under him, from whom he received the fruits of bodily service.
**“and have afflicted the soul of the tillers thereof:”** — for greater goods
**“have afflicted the soul of the tillers thereof”** — Have afflicted the soul of the tillers thereof: the ruler of the Church afflicts the souls of the tillers if, envy biting him, he contradicts others who preach rightly. “And have afflicted the soul of the tillers thereof”: sometimes the ruler of the Church, while he claims power for himself alone, contradicts others who preach rightly through envy; but the devout pastor, who does not seek his own glory, wishes to be helped by all. If, I say, I did this or that, then instead of wheat, that is, greater goods, thistles, the least evils; instead of barley, that is, the least goods, thorns, greater evils. For the thistle is softer than the thorn, which is harder for pricking. And it is, to say it briefly: if I did this or that, instead of the goods that refresh for ever let evils that prick be paid back to me. Or in wheat the spiritual work that refreshes the mind; in barley the dispensing of earthly things is figured, in which we prepare food as for fleshly beasts, which also has some chaff mixed in. And here even that ruler against whom the land cries sometimes sows wheat and barley; but the subjects who are weighed down in many things do not think those few good things good which are in some way defiled. So he says: if I did not do the great things I ought, let me receive the prickings of murmuring from those under me, even for the good I did. So prelates must take care not to give an example of evil, and subjects not to judge the deeds of prelates easily, contradicting the order of God who gave them power, as it is written: “All power is from the Lord God.” And of these it is written: “Obey your prelates,” lest it be said of you: “And they murmured, and perished by the serpents.” Of those, then: “The glory thereof as the flower of the grass.”
31.40:
**“Let thistles grow up to me instead of wheat”**
• the least evils
• Let thistles grow up to me instead of wheat: for the thistle springs up instead of wheat and the thorn instead of barley when, in the last reward, in which the payment of labour is sought, the pricking of pain is found.
**“and instead of barley”** — instead of the least goods
**“thorns.”** — greater evils

32.1:
**“So these three men ceased to answer Job, because he seemed just to himself.”**
• to the three, not to himself, Job seemed as it were swollen
• So these three, etc. At last we have set out blessed Job’s sentences, full of mystic power, in which he answered against the words of his friends; now it remains for us to come to the words of Eliu, which must be weighed with so much the more serious circumspection as they are also uttered with a more fervent spirit through the boldness of youth. Blessed Job, known to God alone and to himself, was to be brought to our knowledge in his calm; he was touched by the scourge, so that he might spread the scent of his strengths the wider, as, like spices, he gave off a better fragrance from being burned. He knew how to rule those under him devoutly in good times and to guard himself strictly from evils. He knew how to use well the things he had, but we did not know whether he would remain patient when they were taken away. He knew how to pay daily sacrifices to God for his children while they were safe, but it was uncertain whether he would offer him the sacrifice of thanksgiving even when bereaved. So, lest prosperity cover any vices, it was fitting that pain should lay this open. So licence to tempt was given to the cunning enemy against the holy man. He, while he longed to destroy his good things, known in many ways, showed also the good of patience which lay hidden. For he burned the flocks, put out the households, crushed the heirs, struck the health of the body, and, to hurl the dart of a heavier temptation, kept back the wife’s tongue, so that grief through the losses of things might lay low the holy man’s strong and solid breast, and cursing through the words of his wife might pierce it. But as many wounds as he raging inflicted, so many victories he unknowingly supplied to the holy man. His friends, who inveigh against him as if while advising, express the figure of the heretics, who under the appearance of advising carry on the business of leading astray; whence also, while they make speeches to blessed Job on the Lord’s behalf, they are rebuked by the Lord, because all heretics, while they strive to defend God, offend him. Whence it is aptly said to them by Job: “I desire to reason with God, first shewing you to be forgers of lies, and maintainers of perverse doctrines.” So it is plain that they bear the figure of the heretics, whom the holy man refutes as serving the maintaining of perverse doctrines. So in the three names of Job’s friends three falls of ruin in the heretics are expressed. For unless they despised God they would never think perverse things of him; and unless they drew themselves into oldness, they would not err in the understanding of the new life; and unless they destroyed the contemplation of the good, the judgments from above would never reprove them with such strict examination for the fault of their words. So by despising God they keep themselves in oldness; and by keeping themselves in oldness they harm the contemplation of the upright with their wicked speeches.
32.2:
**“was angry and was moved to indignation”** — Was angry and was moved to indignation: Eliu is interpreted ‘this is my God’ or ‘God the Lord’; by him the faith of the arrogant placed within the Church is rightly designated, because they confess God the Lord. Barachel, ‘blessing of the Lord.’ Buzite, ‘contemptible’; because it fits arrogant preachers that in the eloquence of preaching they receive the blessing of divine grace, but in their haughty ways they show it to be contemptible. Ram, ‘lofty.’ For the people of the faithful is lofty, which here despises the lowest and cast-off things of life. So Eliu is said to be of the kindred of Ram, because every arrogant preacher placed within the Church is joined to the holy peoples by the truth of faith, though he is separated from their life by the wickedness of haughtiness.
**“now he was angry against Job”** — Now he was angry against Job: for the followers of vainglory, when they set themselves above men, rebuke some for foolish senses, others for unworthy merits; that is, they reckon some know nothing, others do not live well; even while they justly accuse all placed outside the Church of thinking wicked things. They also despise those within for the contempt of their life; and those outside they press by the truth of what is said, those inside they press by the manner of saying, that is, by the vice of haughtiness.
32.4:
**“So Eliu waited while Job was speaking,”** — by this deed he showed what he had done before
**“So Eliu waited while Job was speaking”** — When it is said that Eliu waited while Job was speaking, because they were his elders that were speaking, it is openly shown that he kept honour not out of reverence for blessed Job but for his friends; because the arrogant placed within the Church despise the Church they defend. And mostly they revere the talents of those who are wrongly wise more than the simple life of the innocent. And though the Church is older than the heretics, because they went out from her, yet Eliu is described as younger, because after the wars of the heretics had been waged, men fervent in talent came forth to the contests against the enemies, and from that they began to be arrogant. After these too the younger Eliu is joined in reproaching blessed Job, from whose person the kind of certain teachers who are faithful, yet arrogant, is designated. His words we do not easily understand unless we weigh them from the Lord’s rebuke that follows. For the Lord says of them: “Who is this that wrappeth up sentences in unskilful words?” And when he says sentences but does not add at once what kind, he surely wants good ones to be understood. For when sentences are named, unless they are also called bad, they cannot be taken badly. For we take sentences in a good sense when they are put without an added rebuke, as it is written: “The sluggard is wiser in his own conceit than seven men that speak sentences.”
32.5:
**“But when he saw that the three”** — the heretics
**“were not able to answer”** — to the Catholics
**“he was exceedingly angry.”** — as he disagrees with those by the truth of his senses, so with these by the wickedness of his ways
32.6: **“Then Eliu the son of Barachel the Buzite answered and said: I am younger in days, and you are more ancient; therefore hanging down my head, I was afraid to shew you my opinion.”** — Then Eliu the son of, etc. Because these things lack the solidity of weight, they do not need subtlety of exposition; because while he kept silent out of regard for his age he was wiser, but when, setting himself first, he despised long age in others, he became childishly foolish. For against his sentence greater age speaks, and wisdom is taught by a multitude of years. Because even if age does not give sense, yet it powerfully exercises experience.
32.7: **“For I hoped that greater age would speak, and that a multitude of years would teach wisdom.”** — or: knowledge
32.8:
**“But, as I see, there is a spirit in men, and the inspiration of the Almighty giveth understanding.”** — he would say this rightly if he did not claim that understanding for himself
**“But, as I see, there is a spirit in men”** — But, as I see, there is a spirit in men: it is no small condemnation to glory privately in a good which is given in common; to know where the good began and not to know how to use the good one has received. For there are four kinds of swelling: when a man reckons he has good from himself; or, if he believes it is given from above, yet thinks he has received it for his own merits; or when he boasts of having what he does not have; or when, despising others, he wishes to appear singular. This fourth kind comes nearer to the devil, who wished to be above the angels; because into this kind every human mind frequently slips, so as to glory in having singularly what it has. For whoever rejoices to have good singularly, whoever seeks to seem loftier than others, imitates him who, despising the good of the fellowship of the angels, setting his seat in the north and proudly longing for likeness to the Most High, tried through wicked desire to break out as it were to a certain summit of singularity. From this the Lord checked the disciples returning from preaching, lest they rejoice in the singularity of miracles, saying: “I saw Satan like lightning falling from heaven”; who was singularly lifted up, so that in his ruin they might learn what to fear from haughtiness.
32.10: **“Therefore I will speak: Hearken to me, I also will shew you my wisdom.”** — or: opinion
32.11:
**“For I have waited for your words,”** — he shows proudly that he kept silent
**“For I have waited for your words”** — When he says: “For I have waited,” etc., he declares that he kept silent at the words of the old men from the zeal of a judge rather than the wish of a speaker. Though these things better signify the life of the arrogant, who, sometimes placed within the Church, when they see the adversaries of that same Church, are used to weigh in them not their years of time but the intention of their words. For however much older the heretics are than these arrogant men, yet they boldly try to crush those in whose words they rebuke perverse doctrines.
**“I have given ear to your wisdom, as long as you were disputing”** — elsewhere: you were disputing
32.12:
**“And as long as I thought you said some thing, I considered:”** — he weighs not years but the intention of the words
**“but, as I see, there is none”** — Often the heretics, because they are usually despicable even to men, when they see the Church revered by all who rule, try to tear her reputation with whatever slanders they can, saying: “all temporal things are supplied to her for this reason, that the rewards of eternal gifts are taken away from her.” Eliu opposes their voice, saying: “Lest you should say.” As if: you say in vain that God has cast her down, and that she is revered as man; because she now glories in such a way that the heavenly may follow more abundantly. As if the arrogant faithful said against the heretics: because you see the Church flourishing for a time in the honour of men, do not believe she has been cast down by the Lord; but it is nothing. For God gives comforts on this journey and keeps eternal rewards for her when she arrives.
32.13: **“Lest you should say: We have found wisdom, God hath cast him down, not man.”** — it is a prohibition, as if: do not say this, that Job has been cast down by God as incorrigible, who does not yield to your sentences and authorities
32.14:
**“He hath spoken nothing to me”** — He hath spoken nothing to me: Eliu had heard blessed Job publicly, but he says: “He hath spoken nothing to me,” because surely all the arrogant hear the voices of the Church but pretend that they are not said to them, because they scorn to amend the vice of haughtiness. Nor do they reckon that they are refuted about pride, because they think themselves humble, who even despise being refuted, since they reckon themselves wiser than those who refute them.
**“and I will not answer him according to your words.”**
• but I speak, because whatever he said is nothing to me; he who thinks himself humble, and wiser than the one who accuses him, does not reckon that he is accused of pride
• And as to his saying: “and I will not answer him according to your words”: he rightly says that he will not answer blessed Job according to their words, because the arrogant answer against the Church, but not like heretics placed outside. For they do not contradict her by preaching wicked things, but by living perversely; because they do not think unworthy things of God like heretics, but suspect themselves of being worthy more than they need.
32.15: **“They were afraid, and answered no more”** — They were afraid, and answered no more: Job’s friends are rightly related to have been afraid at Eliu’s words, because sometimes the arrogant defenders of the Church, though they do not keep the order of speaking, yet disturb their adversaries by the force of what they say.
32.16:
**“Therefore because I have waited,”** — open display
**“and they have not spoken: they stood, and answered no more:”**
• because he thinks nothing of what they have if it is hidden
• Therefore because I have waited, etc. The end of speech for the wise is usually to speak until they impose silence on their adversaries; for they do not desire to show themselves, but to check those who teach wicked things. But after it has been said of Job’s friends: “They were afraid, and answered no more,” or: “they left off speaking,” Eliu adds and says: “I have waited, and they have not spoken: they stood, and answered no more.” And Eliu multiplies words when they are now silent, because the arrogant man hastens not to overcome the sayings of his adversaries but to display his own wisdom.
32.17: **“I also will answer my part, and will shew my knowledge.”** — So there follows: “I also will answer my part,” etc. Every arrogant man reckons this his part, if he not so much has knowledge as displays it; because surely all the haughty do not long to have knowledge but to show it. Therefore it is rightly said by Moses: “The vessel that hath no cover, nor binding over it, shall be unclean,” etc. But holy preachers reckon it their part if within they themselves rejoice in wisdom, and outside they check others from error. Nor do they so go out of themselves in speaking as to put the joy of the mind in the display of discerning speech; but they meditate on the good of knowledge in the secret of the heart, and rejoice there where they perceive it, not where, among so many snares of temptations, they are forced to become known.
32.18:
**“For I am full of matter to speak of, and the spirit of my bowels straiteneth me.”** — because the proud see the saints speak great things and be honoured for it, and they follow these things only so as to be held famous
**“I am full of matter to speak of”** — I am full of matter to speak of: it often happens that wise men, when they consider that they are not heard, impose silence on their mouth. But when they see that crimes grow while they keep silent, they bear a certain force of their spirit so as to break out into speech of open rebuke. Whence Jeremias, when he had imposed silence on himself, saying: “I will not make mention of him, nor speak any more in his name,” at once added: “And there came in my heart as a burning fire, shut up in my bones, and I was wearied, not being able to bear it.” But often, in like manner, the anxiety of vainglory, by no means containing itself within silence, inflames the mind of the arrogant to the urge of speaking as if with the zeal of charity, and drives it to unbridled speech; whence Eliu, stretched by the spirit of haughtiness and not containing himself within the bars of silence, says: “I am full of matter to speak of,” etc. By the belly the bosom of the heart is taken, by the new wine the fervour of the Holy Spirit. For Eliu is shown in the puffing up of haughtiness as if he were kindled by the ardour of the Holy Spirit; he compared the spirit of his sense, in that he kept silent, to new wine without a vent.
32.19: **“Behold, my belly is as new wine which wanteth vent, which bursteth the new vessels.”** — And he rightly says: “which bursteth the new vessels,” because the fervour of the Holy Spirit is scarcely contained not only by the old but even by the new life; so the new wine bursts the new vessels, because the power of his fervour goes beyond even spiritual hearts. He calls weak consciences, or the earthly vessels of bodies, vessels.
32.20: **“I will speak and take breath”** — I will speak and take breath: he rightly says: “take breath,” because as it is the toil of the just to see wicked things and not correct them, so it is a heavy toil for the arrogant if they do not show what they know. For they can scarcely bear the force boiling within if they make known a little too late all that they perceive. So it is necessary that when a good thing is done, their haughtiness be first overcome in the heart, lest, if it comes forth from the root of wretched haughtiness, it bring forth the wretched fruits of wickedness.
32.21:
**“I will not accept the person of man, and I will not level God with man.”** — because as it is the toil of the just to see evils and not correct them, so it is a toil for accusers if they do not show what they know
**“I will not accept the person of man”** — I will not accept the person of man: he rightly does not level God with man, because he does not know how long he will remain here or when he will be taken to God’s judgment; and he rightly says: “after a while,” because however long the time of the present life has been, it is by that very fact the shorter in that it does not last. For it is not fitting that whatever is bounded by an end be judged long-lasting. But among these sentences, which he utters solid from the truth, he breaks out again into words of haughtiness, saying: “Hear,” etc.

33.1:
**“Hear therefore, O Job, my speeches, and hearken to all my words.”** — among true sentences he again breaks out into words of haughtiness
**“Hear therefore, O Job, my speeches”** — Hear therefore, O Job, my speeches: it must be weighed from how great haughtiness it comes down, that he warns blessed Job to hear him, that he declares he has opened his mouth, and promises that his tongue will speak within his jaws. For it is the property of the arrogant not to be able to minister rightly the right things they know, nor to bring in humbly the things they teach.
33.2:
**“Behold now I have opened my mouth, let my tongue speak within my jaws.”** — what I perceive against you, I tell prudently and quietly
**“let my tongue speak within my jaws”** — Let my tongue speak within my jaws: to speak within the jaws is to speak quietly and not to shout with cries. The arrogant within the Church are said to speak as it were within the jaws when they do not cry out against adversaries living outside, but rebuke those placed within the Church. And often the arrogant pretend to flee arrogance, and speak privately to individuals as if secretly, so that they may glory both in their sense and in their contempt of arrogance. Sometimes they are so shameless that, while others keep silent, they praise what they say.
33.3:
**“My words are from my upright heart, and … a … sentence”**
• which is nothing but true
• So he adds: “My words are from my upright heart.” Simplicity of speech is the praise of great virtue; which, because the arrogant do not have it, they assert they have, so as to be heard more securely. And they announce that they will speak purely, because men of this kind fear their doubleness will be caught, and they mix true things with false so as to be believed the more quickly. So because Eliu both declared that he would speak purely and, by calling his sayings sentences, ran ahead with favour, he now adds that same sentence he promised, saying: “The spirit of God made me.” He tells that he was made by the spirit and given life by the breath. For of Adam’s making it is written: “He breathed into his face the breath of life.” And note that he uttered a true sentence when he said he was made by the Spirit of God, but uselessly and not in its place. Whence Moses: “The man that hath an issue of seed shall be unclean.” The seed is speech, which makes the hearers fruitful; but if it flows out unseasonably it defiles the one who emits it, so that even what he has thought rightly is fouled, and he is not believed and loses the power of begetting. But let us hear whether these things which he rightly asserts are rightly followed through.
33.4: **“The spirit of God made me”** — see, the sentence
33.5: **“If thou canst”** — If thou canst: again he breaks out into the arrogance of proud haughtiness while he tells the order of the true condition. And he repeats the same thing in other words, saying: “Behold God hath made me as well as thee.” The arrogant remember that they were made equal with men, but set themselves above them by the swelling of knowledge; and in that they are no longer equal, they bring back to a marvel the fact that they were equal by birth.
33.7: **“But yet … my wonder”** — But yet … my wonder: Paul humbly calls his high things “the word of consolation,” speaking to the Hebrews; this man calls his least things a wonder and eloquence; because it is the property of the arrogant that before they speak they reckon they are saying wonderful things, and forestall their speech with admiration; which the haughtiness of the mind does.
33.8: **“Now thou has said in my hearing”** — Now thou has said in my hearing: he adds what he said.
33.9: **“I am clean, and without sin”** — I am clean, and without sin: against these words, which he relates blessed Job said, he brings forth his sentence, saying: “Now this is,” etc. For surely blessed Job had said truly that he had been scourged without fault. For he said this of himself which the Lord said of him to the devil: “Thou hast moved me against him, that I should afflict him without cause.”
33.12:
**“Now this is the thing in which thou art not justified”** — Now this is the thing in which thou art not justified: for he did not know that by his scourges vice is not wiped out but merit increased; and because he had said he was without sin, he rebukes him, scourged, with this sentence. But it must be noted that blessed Job said his foot had been put in the stocks, but he by no means said in this way what is charged against him, that he had been clean and without sin, or unspotted and without iniquity. But Eliu, while he strove to rebuke with severity the things that were said, adds lyingly things that were not said, so as to seem to accuse learnedly. And this because the arrogant long to accuse more than to console, and believe that evils befall men only for iniquities.
**“I will answer thee”**
• after so many words of haughtiness he opens his knowledge
• I will answer thee: this is said so that the scourged man, considering that God is greater than he, may in all that he suffers set himself below his judgment, than which he does not doubt he is less, and may believe what he suffers from the better one to be just, even if he does not know the causes of that justice.
33.13:
**“Dost thou strive against him”**
• but you
• Dost thou strive against him: it is the property of an afflicted heart that in all it longs for (and yet feels the order of things to be contrary) it would wish, if it could be, to be answered by divine voices why it is so or not so, so as to consult God about every dispute of things, and rest once the reason of his answer is known.
33.14:
**“God speaketh once, and repeateth not the selfsame thing the second time.”** — but God does not answer individuals with a private voice, because he has established a word by which he satisfies all
**“God speaketh once”** — God speaketh once: but Eliu, foreseeing that the Lord established sacred Scripture, and in it answered the public or hidden questions of all, says: “Dost thou strive against him, because he hath not answered thee to all words? God speaketh once,” etc. As if he said: God does not answer the hearts of individuals with private voices, but builds such a word as satisfies the questions of all. For in the word of his Scripture each of us finds our cases if we seek them. For there we are all answered in common in what we suffer particularly; there the life of those who went before becomes the pattern of those who follow. For to bring forward one out of many: see, when we are affected by some suffering or trouble of the flesh, we perhaps wish to know the hidden causes of that suffering or trouble, so as to be consoled in what we suffer by the very knowledge of things. But because we are by no means answered individually about our particular temptations, we run back to sacred Scripture, where we find that when Paul had been tempted by weakness of the flesh he heard: “My grace is sufficient for thee; for power is made perfect in infirmity.” This was said to him in his own weakness for this reason, that it might not be said to each of us one by one. So in sacred Scripture we have heard the voice of God, to Paul when he was afflicted, lest when perhaps we are afflicted we seek individually to hear it with private consolation. For God’s speaking is to beget the Word, because besides the Only-begotten he begot no other word; and for us to wonder at this is in some way to see, as a closed eye perceives light. But because this wonder is not easy for those busied on earth, he shows how God’s speech comes to us through a dream.
33.15:
**“By a dream in a vision by night,”** — with the mind at rest from the business of the world, as Moses on the mountain receives the law
**“By a dream in a vision by night”** — By a dream in a vision by night: in sleep the outward senses sleep and inward things are seen. So if we wish to contemplate inward things, let us sleep from outward entanglement. In daylight we see more surely; but in a vision by night we see through images; and the saints, so long as they are in this life, look on the secrets of the divine nature as under a certain imagining, because they do not yet contemplate them more openly as they are.
**“when deep sleep falleth upon”** — elsewhere: upon
**“men, and they are sleeping in their beds:”** — that is, when one ceases from outward action, whence there is rest in the mind
**“and they are sleeping in their beds”** — And they are sleeping in their beds: because then we come to know the secrets of the Godhead, when we withdraw from the tumultuous lust of this world into the chambers of our mind.
33.16:
**“Then he openeth the ears of men”** — Then he openeth the ears of men: for when they are lulled from outward actions, with open ear they hear the causes of the inward examination.
**“and teaching”** — by opening
**“instructeth them in what they are to learn.”** — And teaching instructeth them, etc. Because while they consider subtly either the public scourges or the hidden judgments, they do not cease to afflict themselves by weeping. And it is rightly said: “And teaching instructeth them,” etc., because to the mind that considers and tears itself through penance, the laments of compunction are as it were certain wounds of suffering. For there are four qualities by which the soul of the just man is strongly affected in compunction. Either when it remembers its evils, considering where it has been; of which Paul: “I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because,” etc. Or when, fearing the sentence of God’s judgments and searching with itself, it thinks where it will be; of which: “I chastise my body, and bring it into subjection: lest perhaps,” etc. Or when, carefully attending to the evils of the present life, it considers mourning where it is; whence: “while we are in the body, we are absent from the Lord.” Or when it contemplates the good things of the homeland above, which, because it does not yet obtain them, it looks on mourning where it is not. Whence the Apostle: “We see now through a glass in a dark manner,” etc.
33.17:
**“That he may withdraw a man from the things he is doing, and may deliver him from pride.”** — he who is turned from the things he has done is delivered from pride, because: “Pride is the beginning of all sin”
**“That he may withdraw a man”** — That he may withdraw a man: what has man made of himself but sin? And he longs to avoid what he has made, and returns humbly to the order of his condition; while he flees his own works, he loves himself such as he was made by God. And to be proud against the maker is to overstep his precepts by sinning, because he shakes off as it were from himself the yoke of his lordship, to which he scorns to be subject through disobedience.
33.18: **“Rescuing his soul from corruption: and his life from passing to the sword.”** — Rescuing his soul from corruption: to pass to the sword is to pass from this corruption of vices to the sword of punishments. But surely he snatches his life there from the vengeance of torment, whose mind he here draws away from the delight of sin.
33.19:
**“He rebuketh also by sorrow in the bed,”** — we are pricked within, lest there be haughtiness
**“He rebuketh also by sorrow in the bed”** — He rebuketh also by sorrow in the bed: the bed is taken as temporal rest. So he rebukes by sorrow in the bed, that is, in the rest of the present life he troubles him either by the goads of temptation or by the affliction of the scourge. For he makes the road of this world rough for the elect, lest, while anyone is fed by the rest of the present life as by the pleasantness of life, it delight him more to journey long than to arrive quickly.
**“and he maketh all his bones to wither.”** — because they were as it were thrust in as companions of the good
**“and he maketh all his bones to wither”** — And he maketh all his bones to wither: we take the bones as virtues; and he makes the bones wither, because when in that rest which we prepare for ourselves from this world we are affected by the scourge of temptation, we who could have been puffed up by our virtues are thinned by weariness at the weakness we have come to know; and all that fat and green rejoicing in our strengths will suddenly be dried up by the grief of anxiety.
33.20:
**“becometh abominable to him”** — so that he may prove what is from himself, what from God’s gift
**“abominable”** — Abominable: he calls the delight of the present life bread. For each one, when the prosperity of living well smiles on him, grows cheerful; and that very cheerfulness refreshes the mind like desirable food. But when he is struck by temptation, all joy is rejected by his mind, which before rejoiced as if filled with that same joy.
**“Bread … in his life, and to his soul the meat which before he desired.”** — that is, to the afflicted mind whatever before satisfied it pleasantly is turned to bitterness
33.21:
**“His flesh shall be consumed away, and his bones that were covered shall be made bare.”** — because through adversities the merits of virtues are laid open
**“shall be consumed away”** — Shall be consumed away: as we are tempted by vices lest we be lifted up within, so outside we are worn by scourges lest, the world flattering us, we be led astray to seek anything outside.
**“His flesh shall be consumed away”** — His flesh shall be consumed away: by the name of flesh the delight of the flesh is taken. So it is consumed away and the bones are laid bare, because when fleshly delight is thinned by the reproving scourges, the strong things of the virtues which lay hidden as it were under the flesh are laid open. For no one knows how much he has advanced except amid adversities.
33.22:
**“hath drawn near”** — elsewhere: will draw near
**“His soul … to corruption, and his life to the destroyers.”**
• in adversities not only the vigour of strength is uncovered but also the weakness of humanity
• His soul hath drawn near to corruption, etc. The soul of the tempted just man is said to draw near to corruption, because he is not ignorant that, from his own strengths, he is close to ruin, so that he attributes it not to himself but to the Lord that he is far from ruin. So he draws near to the destroyers, because through weakness of the flesh he sees himself close to the death-bringing sins, from which by the divine gift he is made so much the farther as he finds himself close to them by his own merits. Yet God’s protection is believed less necessary if it is always had; it is usefully withdrawn sometimes, so that it may be shown that without it man is nothing.
33.23:
**“If there shall be an angel speaking for him, one”**
• elsewhere: one
• having shown the general plague in one, he brings in the general remedy
**“If there shall be an angel … for him”** — If there shall be an angel for him: this angel is taken as Christ. He speaks for us to the Father, one of those like us. For while in all his workings he surpasses us by immense power, in one thing only, that is, in the truth of the form, he does not differ from us; who speaks to the Father for us by this, that he shows himself like us. For his speaking is to show himself man for us; apart from whom no just one would be found to intercede without sin for sinners.
**“among thousands,”**
• or: thousands
• One among those like him: because truly man, but not born as others, not dead as others. For he rises of necessity, by himself, and on the third day.
**“to declare man’s uprightness,”** — To declare man’s uprightness: the angel declared man’s uprightness. For, interceding for sinners, he showed himself a just man who would merit pardon for others.
33.24:
**“He shall have mercy on him”** — He shall have mercy on him: the Mediator has mercy on man in this, that he took the form of man.
**“and shall say: Deliver him”** — And shall say: Deliver him: his saying is to deliver man by taking on the nature of man and to show it free. For from that flesh which he took he showed this too to be free, which he redeemed.
**“that he may not go down”** — That he may not go down: of whom above: “His soul hath drawn near to corruption”; that is, because by knowing himself he is not ignorant that he is close to corruption, therefore let him not go down into corruption.
**“I have found wherein I may be merciful to him”** — I have found wherein I may be merciful to him: as if he openly said: because there was no man who could appear as a just intercessor before God for men, I made myself man to be merciful to men; and while I showed myself man, I found in what just man I might be merciful to men.
33.25:
**“His flesh is consumed with punishment, let him return to the days of his youth.”** — by a wonderful dispensation God turns this into punishment for us, by which we committed fault
**“His flesh is consumed”** — His flesh is consumed: for in numbers the human race was pressed by the torments of vices and punishments; but when the Redeemer came, it returns to the days of its youth, that is, is renewed in the wholeness of its former life, so that it does not remain in that into which it fell, but, redeemed, returns to that for the receiving of which it was made.
33.26:
**“He shall pray to God, and he will be gracious to him:”**
• even man himself after the angel; otherwise man would never raise himself to seek eternal things
• He shall pray to God: because while our Redeemer intercedes with the Father for us, we too, the numbness of our former life shaken off, are kindled to the state of prayer; so it is aptly said: “He shall pray to God, and he will be gracious to him.” For he says first that the angel asks and afterwards man; who, unless the Lord himself first, interceding with the Father through his incarnation, asked for our life, our insensibility would never rouse itself to ask for the things that are eternal; but the prayer of his incarnation went before so that the awakening of our numbness might follow.
**“and he shall see his face with joy”** — this rightly after bitternesses, so that, sad at himself from terror of the judgment, and so with cleansed eyes, he may see the good things he seeks
**“and he shall see his face”** — And he shall see his face: for after the contests of toils, after the waves of temptations, the soul is suspended in ecstasy, so as to contemplate the knowledge of the divine presence. And joy (jubilation) is called the unspeakable joy of the mind, which can neither be hidden nor opened in words; and yet it is betrayed by certain motions, though it is expressed by no proper terms.
**“and he will render to man his justice.”**
• from the grace of contemplation follows the justice of working
• the justice of God is in giving, man’s in receiving
**“and he will render to man his justice”** — And he will render to man his justice: not what he had from himself, but what he received when he was made, that he might have it; so that it may please him to cling to God, so that he may dread his threatening sentence.
33.27:
**“He shall look upon men, and shall say: I have sinned, and indeed I have offended,”** — he would not know himself a sinner unless he had justice
**“He shall look upon men, and shall say: I have sinned”** — He shall look upon men, and shall say: I have sinned: Scripture never calls those men except those whom it distinguishes from the beasts by reason, that is, whom it shows not worn down by the beastly motion of passions. And the sense is: he looks on the examples of holy men, and weighing himself by their working together, he grasps that he is wicked.
**“and I have not received what I have deserved.”**
• punishment questions whether man truly knows himself
• I have sinned, and indeed I have offended, and … what I have deserved, etc. He who considers the examples of the wicked recognizes that he has been struck less than he deserved, because in their justice he sees how grave a fault it was that he erred.
**“I have sinned, and indeed I have offended”** — I have sinned, and indeed I have offended: indeed, not like one who confesses himself a sinner in words, and yet defends himself if he is accused; such a one wishes to seem humble, not to be.
33.28:
**“He hath delivered his soul from going into destruction, that it may live and see the light.”**
• for the life of the good is a living reading, looking at which he will say
• He hath delivered his soul from going into, because when divine grace goes before in good working, our free choice follows; we are said to deliver ourselves, who consent to the Lord delivering us.
**“that it may live and see the light”** — That it may live and see the light: namely the light of truth, which one dead in heart cannot see; or he then, living, looks on the light who attends with the free eyes of the heart to the Lord in the form of Godhead at the judgment.
33.29: **“Behold, all these things God worketh”** — Behold, all these things God worketh: of the tempted and scourged man it was said above: “Bread becometh abominable to him in his life,” etc. And below is joined: “He shall pray to God, and he will be gracious to him,” etc. In these sentences both above the grief of bitterness and below the gladness of security is set. And soon is added: “all these things God worketh three times within.” As if he said: what I have said of one is done three times in each one; that is, we find grief and gladness alternating in the mind of each elect man in three ways: in conversion, in testing, in death. In conversion there is heavy grief, when he wishes to throw off the heavy burden of temporal desires and carry the light yoke of the Lord in free service; but that familiar fleshly delight of his meets him. And what anxiety of heart is then in him, when on this side the spirit calls, on that the flesh calls back, so that it can be said of him: “Bread becometh abominable to him in his life,” etc. But because divine grace does not let him be long affected by this difficulty, it breaks the chains of sins and, consoling him, leads him to the freedom of a new way of life, and the following gladness refreshes the preceding sadness; because in the beginning God provided pleasant things, which no one should think the perfection; so that it can be said of him: “He shall pray to God, and he will be gracious to him,” etc. But after the first voice of grief and gladness, which each one comes to know through the effort of conversion, a second springs up, lest he be loosened by the negligence of security; as the enemies met them in the desert after the Egyptians were drowned: immediately bitter things, so as to test in the end the highest. For it often happens that vices rising up torture one already converted more than at the beginning, and now, now bend the mind of one resisting toward the fall of despair; so that it ought to be said of him: “Bread becometh abominable to him in his life,” etc. But because merciful God allows us to be tested by temptations, not reproved, consolation quickly comes, and calms the attacking motions of thoughts with inward peace, so that it ought to be said of this tempted and delivered man: “he shall see his face with joy.” After the infections of striking and after the hardship of testing, as he approaches the loosing of the flesh, sometimes even the just soul is troubled by terror of strict vengeance, fearing more the evils it does not understand; and even if it could taste anything calm in this life, it is shaken at the coming of the moment of death, so that it ought rightly to be said: “Bread becometh abominable to him in his life.” But because the souls of the just are often purged from any foreign infections by the very dread of death, they receive eternal reward. And often by a certain contemplation of the inward reward they grow cheerful before they are stripped of the flesh, and it is rightly said: “he shall see his face with joy,” etc. But because the mind of each elect one is worn either by the toil of conversion, or by the temptation of testing, or by dread of the loosing, and, purged by that very wearing, is set free:
33.30: **“That he may withdraw their souls from corruption, and enlighten them with the light of the living.”** — There follows: “That he may withdraw their souls from corruption.” The light of the dying is that which we see with bodily eyes. And they are enlightened with the light of the living who, despising the temporal light, run back to the splendour of the inward brightness, so as to live there where they see the true light, where light is not one thing and life another.
33.31:
**“Attend, Job, and hearken to me: and hold thy peace, whilst I speak.”** — it is the property of the arrogant man to mix proud things with true
**“Attend, Job, and hearken to me”** — Attend, Job, and hearken to me: Eliu, after he has set out many deep things of wisdom, shows by this speech what he is like within himself. For it is immense pride to demand reverence for oneself from an elder and to command silence on a better man.
33.32:
**“But if thou hast any thing to say, answer me”** — But if thou hast any thing to say, answer me: just preachers, while they rebuke, out of the grace of humility inquire whether perhaps they are mistaken in what they rebuke, and give leave to those rebuked to confess if they feel anything more just for themselves. The arrogant long to imitate this. For, putting haughtiness aside for a little in their words, they seek justice in those they rebuke, as if they might perhaps find it, not because they think so, but because they long to be adorned with the appearance of humility, lest they seem swollen, as they are.
**“for I would have thee to appear just.”**
• he did not say this from the heart, since, not waiting, he at once adds
• For I would have thee to appear just: because he did not utter this from the heart, he did not wait to hear what he had asked. For at once he added: “And if thou have not, hear me.” Eliu did not allow what he had asked to be said, but soon broke out with what he was carrying within.

34.1:
**“And Eliu continued his discourse, and said:”**
• as if these things were poured down from heaven upon the unworthy
• And Eliu continued his discourse, and said: what is shown by the word of this pronouncing but the puffing up of haughtiness, so that words which came from the high root of pride might come forth with a certain loftiness, as it were, and strictness?
34.2:
**“Hear ye, wise men, my words, and ye learned, hearken to me:”** — he fears too much who thinks his words are not fittingly heard except by the wise
**“Hear ye, wise men, my words”** — Hear ye, wise men, my words: as if he said: as the ear does not know foods nor the throat words, so no fool understands the sentence of the wise. So you wise men, understand what I say, you who can know the things that have been said. But because no one would admit the preaching of the arrogant if they did not mix in something with the image of humility, he again comes down as it were to a certain concord of equality.
34.3: **“For the ear trieth words, and the mouth discerneth meats by the taste.”** — the ear: he does not seek to make men wise, but to show himself to the wise, so that, learned, he may be heard by the learned
34.4: **“judgment”** — Judgment: whether he sought this judgment out of humility is weighed from what follows.
34.5:
**“For Job hath said: I am just, and God hath overthrown my judgment.”**
• let us judge about this
• For Job hath said: I am just, etc. That he said this not at all, the words of the sacred text, when searched, bear witness.
34.6: **“For in judging me there is a lie: my arrow is violent without any sin.”** — see, he who sought judgment has brought forth judgment, from the fault which he invented, so that no sentence from Job might afterwards be waited for
34.7:
**“What man is there like Job, who drinketh up scorning like water?”** — the arrogant man seeks more to scold than to cherish, so as to seem superior
**“What man is there like Job”** — What man is there like Job: so that one understands: none. See, him whom the Lord told the devil was just beyond comparison, Eliu asserts a sinner beyond comparison; of whom he adds: “who drinketh up scorning like water,” etc. When water is drunk it is taken in so fluidly that it is not held back from being swallowed by any thickness of its own. And to drink up scorning like water is to mock God without any obstacle of thought.
34.8: **“Who goeth in company with them that work iniquity, and walketh with wicked men?”** — from the company of the reprobate he judged him worthy of damnation
34.9:
**“For he hath said: Man shall not please God, although he run with him.”**
• because the proud man is a stranger to truth, he who exalts himself soon broke out into false things; what he rebukes in another he wickedly invents
• For he hath said: Man shall not please, etc. That he did not say this at all, anyone who reads blessed Job’s words recognizes.
34.10:
**“Therefore, ye men of understanding, hear me:”** — Therefore, ye men of understanding, hear me, etc. Again with the arrogance of pride he seeks those who, as worthy, may be able to understand him.
**“far from God be wickedness”**
• it is not as Job says
• Far from God be wickedness: he said well, because there is no iniquity or wickedness in almighty God.
34.11:
**“For he will render to a man his work,”** — which yet is not here, as he thinks
**“and according to the ways of every one he will reward them.”** — For he will render to a man his work, etc. In this life this is by no means done. For he both freely forestalls many committing unlawful things and turns them to holy works, and chastens some devoted to right acts by the scourge coming between.
34.12:
**“For in very deed God will not condemn without cause,”** — at the last, even if here he afflicts without cause
**“For in very deed God will not condemn without cause”** — For in very deed God will not condemn without cause: he cannot condemn without cause by that condemnation by which at the last he punishes all that each one has wickedly committed here; nor does the Almighty overthrow judgment, because even if the things we suffer seem less than right, yet they are decreed right in the hidden examination.
34.13:
**“whom”** — for
**“What other hath he appointed over the earth”** — What other hath he appointed over the earth? For he rules the world through no one else who made it through himself, and he does not need helps for ruling who did not need them for making. But he says this so as to show that if almighty God does not neglect to rule by himself what he created, he certainly rules well what he created well, because what he made devoutly he did not dispose undevoutly.
34.14:
**“If”** — therefore
**“he turn his heart to him, he shall draw his spirit and breath unto himself.”** — and then
**“If he turn … to him”** — If he turn … to him: his heart is crooked when it longs for the lowest things; it is made straight when it is lifted to the things above. He puts spirit for inward thoughts, and breath, which is drawn through the body, for outward actions. So for God to draw the spirit and breath of man to himself is, for the conversion of his desire, to change both our inward and our outward things, so that all that man is may both glow inwardly by desiring toward God, from whom he is, and outwardly restrain himself by taming himself.
34.15: **“All flesh shall perish together”** — All flesh shall perish together: all flesh perishes together when no one any longer serves its motions. Man returns into ashes when he is touched by the spirit of humility and remembers that he is nothing but ashes.
34.16:
**“If then thou hast understanding, hear what is said,”** — he has swollen from the things he perceived sharply, and despises others; and so, by seeing more, he is blind, because he does not see himself
**“If then thou hast understanding, hear what is said”** — If then thou hast understanding, hear what is said: these are the daily failings which take place in the hearts of the reprobate, so that they always go on to worse. Above he doubted whether blessed Job could utter what is just; but now he discusses whether he could at least hear what is said.
**“and hearken to the voice of my words.”** — and you need this
34.17:
**“Can he … that loveth not judgment”** — like you
**“be healed?”** — and this is true, but he does not say it truly
**“and how dost thou so far condemn him that is just?”** — namely the Lord, whose justice he adds: “Who saith to the king”
**“Can he be healed that loveth not judgment”** — Can he be healed that loveth not judgment? He loves judgment who examines his ways minutely and, entering the inner chamber of the mind, weighs what the Lord gives him and what he owes the Lord. Which Job had done, who in the expiation of his sons offered even for thoughts; nor had he condemned him who is just, but, set in pain, he asked with humility why he had been struck without sin. So because Eliu said that he who does not love judgment cannot be healed, accusing blessed Job of not loving judgment and of having condemned him who is just, he at once adds the justice of that same Just One, that is, the Lord, saying: “Who saith to the king: Thou art an apostate,” etc. A proud ruler slips into the fault of apostasy as often as he delights to preside over men and rejoices in the singularity of his honour, as if he were not one of those who preside, and not under the Lord; which is only from imitation of him who, despising the fellowship of the angels, said: “I will ascend above the height of the clouds, I will be like the most High.”
34.18:
**“Who saith to the king: Thou art an apostate: who calleth rulers ungodly?”** — because they drag their followers into evil
**“who calleth rulers ungodly”** — Who calleth rulers ungodly: because while they preside by dominating, they drag those under them into ungodliness by the example of their pride. Power is only well ruled when it is held not by loving but by fearing it; and for it to be ministered rightly, it is first necessary that not desire but necessity lay it on. Precepts ought neither to be forsaken from dread nor embraced from lust, lest either someone become worse proud, as if from humility, if he despises the order of the divine dispensation by fleeing it, or cast off the yoke of the ruler above by the very fact that private rule over others delights him.
34.19:
**“Who accepteth not the persons of princes:”** — because God judges man by what he himself is as man, not by things lying around him, as we do
**“Who accepteth not the persons”** — Who accepteth not the persons: he does not know the tyrant contending against the poor man, because he will declare at the judgment that he does not know all the proud who press down the life of the humble.
**“nor hath regarded the tyrant, when he contended against the poor man:”** — by the prince and the tyrant any proud man can be taken, by the poor man the humble
**“for all are the work of his hands.”** — or: all things
**“for … the work”** — For … the work: as if he said: he destroys powerfully when he wills, as he powerfully created when he willed.
34.20:
**“They shall suddenly die,”**
• by the judge’s sentence
• who here were willing to be humbled
**“They shall suddenly die”** — They shall suddenly die: however late the wicked are taken from this life, they are taken suddenly and abruptly, because they do not know how to foresee their end by thinking.
**“and the people shall be troubled at midnight”** — And the people shall be troubled at midnight: he calls the darkness of the heart night. And they pass through bowed at midnight who, humbled at the negligence of their darkness, pass through to death; who pass indeed while they live, but pass through when they die.
**“and take away”** — those whose task it is to gather
**“the violent”** — who was violent with his hand
**“without”** — he does not see who snatches him, but is snatched
**“hand.”**
• invisibly
• And take away the violent, etc. Understand: the divine judgments; because, a sudden end pressing on, he who visibly snatched is invisibly snatched away.
34.21:
**“For his eyes are upon the ways of men,”** — the wicked man, long waited for, did not believe he was seen
**“For his eyes are upon the ways of men”** — For his eyes are upon the ways of men: the wicked man who has long been waited for is suddenly taken away for this reason, that the eyes of the Lord are upon the ways of men.
**“and he considereth all their steps.”** — that is, the things he long looks on with dread he at some time does not leave unavenged
**“and he considereth all their steps”** — And he considereth all their steps: he calls steps the several workings, or the alternating motions of thought, by which, as by paces, we either go away from God or draw near to him.
34.22:
**“There is no darkness”** — so that he should not know their thoughts
**“and there is no shadow of death”** — he does not forget what has been done, but sees what is done and does not forget what he sees
**“There is no darkness, and there is no shadow of death”** — There is no darkness, and there is no shadow of death: by darkness he designates ignorance, by the shadow of death forgetfulness. Forgetfulness is called the shadow of death, which it imitates, because it takes a thing from the sense as death takes it from life. Or any change is an imitation of death; which is not in God, with whom “there is no change, nor shadow of alteration.” And as he is unchangeable, so he sees piercingly; nor does he forget who is not changed.
**“where they may be hid who work iniquity.”** — they can neither be hidden nor then be amended
34.23:
**“For it is no longer in the power of man”** — For it is no longer in the power of man: he speaks of judgment, not that by which he punishes through eternal retribution, but that which, conceived in the mind, he washes away through conversion. In this judgment of the mind we are absolved the more quickly the more strictly we hold ourselves guilty; nor are the times in which there is leisure for doing this to be let slip, because after the times of this life there is no leisure for doing it.
**“to enter … with God”** — To enter … with God: here the reprobate were allowed to come to God in judgment, which they will not then be, even if they desired it. This judgment is that by which we judge ourselves here; for they would not desire the judgment of damnation.
34.24:
**“He shall break in pieces many and innumerable”**
• so then; but now by hidden judgment he will break many; so now each must take care not to wander outside himself
• He shall break in pieces many and innumerable: this is done daily. Some slip from the state of justice, and others obtain the place of life as they fall. That he said innumerable: either he wished to express the multitude of the reprobate, or wished to show that those who perish are not held within the number of the elect.
34.25:
**“For he knoweth”** — that justly
**“For he knoweth their works”** — For he knoweth their works: it must be known that the wicked man is broken in the night in two ways: either when he is struck by the tribulation of outward punishment, whence it is said “into the exterior darkness”; or when he is blinded within by hidden knowledge. And the Lord is said to bring on night when he has not willed to free from blindness.
34.26:
**“He hath struck them, as being wicked, in open sight.”**
• even if they do not seem ungodly to men. For he who does evil loses faith while he thinks he sins unpunished
• the ungodly man is properly called the unbeliever; the Church is the place of those who see, where the light, that is, God, is seen
**“He hath struck them, as being wicked”** — He hath struck them, as being wicked: this is said of those whom divine vengeance finds within the Church persisting in iniquities. For they stood there where they seemed to see God. There they loved darkness where the light of truth is looked on. These show themselves devout in the Church; but because divine judgments cannot be hidden, they are struck as ungodly.
34.27:
**“Who as it were on purpose have revolted from him,”**
• the examples of humility
• Who as it were on purpose have revolted, etc. From weakness it is usual to love good but not be able to fulfil it. But to sin from zeal is neither to do good nor to love it. One sins either by ignorance, like Paul the persecutor, which is lighter; or by weakness, like Peter who denies, which is heavier; or by zeal, which is worst.
**“and … all his ways”** — the way is whatever Wisdom made flesh did in time
**“would not understand”** — the wicked saw the reproaches of Christ, but did not understand where they lead
