**“and would not understand all his ways”** — And would not understand all his ways: not to know is ignorance; to have refused to know is pride. For the proud despise the deeds of the Lord’s humility.
34.28: **“So that they caused the cry of the needy to come to him”** — So that they caused the cry of the needy to come to him: for when these are proud, those who are oppressed by the proud cry to God; or because when these fall the poor, that is, the humble in spirit, are put in their place; which they are said to do because it happens by their fall; or when they sin the cry of the poor is heard, because while the Jews were proud against the Lord the prayers of the gentiles reached God. Or because these things can be taken of rulers: when they forsake the office of preaching for the cares of the world, they drive those under them to a cry, who murmur why a pretender holds the place. But because rulers have their own judge, it is a great caution for subjects not to judge rashly the life of those who rule. For not in vain did the Lord himself pour out the money of the changers and overturn the chairs of those who sold doves; surely signifying that through the masters he judges the life of the peoples, but through himself examines the deeds of the masters; though even the vices of subjects which are now either overlooked or cannot be judged by the masters are yet without doubt reserved for his judgment. Or by the swelling of the mighty the pride of the Jews, by the cry of the needy the desires of the gentiles, are figured. So while the Jews were proud, the prayers of the gentiles reached God; whose judgments he does not dare to discuss but reveres with wonder.
34.29:
**“For when he granteth peace, who is there that can condemn? When he hideth his countenance,”** — “Yea, Father; for so hath it seemed good in thy sight”: what pleases God cannot be unjust
**“For when he granteth peace”** — For when he granteth peace: if you wonder that the gentiles were taken up: “when he granteth peace, who is there that can condemn?” If you are astonished that Judea was lost: “when he hideth his countenance, who is there that can behold him?” And because God judges the least things as the greatest, each as all, he adds: “whether it regard nations.” As if he openly warned: understand this judgment, which is described over one nation, as over all too, so that one is driven back, another chosen, hiddenly but none unjustly. So what we see done in the greatest things, let us fear warily in each of us too. He exercises this subtle judgment, that one is driven back, another chosen, both over the nations and over all men; because the Lord so attends to each as if he had leisure from all, and so attends to all at once as if he had leisure from each. And because he passed from the kind to the class, now from the class he turns to the kind and shows what Judea properly deserves.
34.30:
**“Who maketh a man that is a hypocrite to reign for the sins of the people?”**
• Antichrist, whom even those who despise him in word already follow by living
• Who maketh a man that is a hypocrite to reign, etc. He designates Antichrist, the head of all hypocrites, whom Judea will receive as her merits demand, because she would not have the true king reign over her. As it is said in the Gospel: “I am come in the name of my Father, and you receive me not: if another shall come in his own name, him you will receive.”
34.31:
**“Seeing then I have spoken of God, I will not hinder thee in thy turn.”** — the arrogant man, because he defends evils, doubts humbly in good things, because he seeks favour; but he is truly humble in good things who is not a defender in evils
**“Seeing then I have spoken of God, I will not … thee”** — Seeing then I have spoken of God, I will not … thee: the arrogant usually have this as their property, that they ask their hearers whether they have perhaps said anything out of order at the moment when they know they have said something praiseworthy. And they do this not because they doubt their sayings, but because they seek favours from the judgment of the hearers. But they cannot stay long in that very image of humility which they take on in appearance; for if the hearer considers their sayings silently for a little, they soon uncover themselves. Whence Eliu suddenly leapt out from the appearance of humility to words of swollen accusation.
34.32:
**“If I have erred, teach thou me:”** — he would not ask if he knew he had erred
**“if I have spoken iniquity, I will add no more.”**
• but
• Saying: “Seeing then I have spoken. If I have erred, teach thou me,” etc. For as it often happens that the wicked too speak good things, so Eliu remembers that a little above he said many strong things, and so, as a follow-up, asked whether perhaps he had erred. For he would not ask if he believed he had erred. For it is, as has been said, the proper fraud of the arrogant to be eager to ask about error at the moment when they know they have not erred; who in turn scorn to ask, or to be accused, whenever they truly know they have erred. For the arrogant man desires not to be humble but to seem so; and this feigned humility, since it is as it were a burden to the haughty man, he soon shakes off.
34.33:
**“Doth God require it of thee, because it hath displeased thee?”**
• as if: I am innocent, who answer being struck
• Saying: “Doth God require it of thee?” I am to render account to the Lord. Why is my iniquity now rebuked by you, which it is plain will not be required of you at the judgment? The just, when they are unjustly attacked by men, seek God as their witness; whence it is the custom of the wicked, when they are accused, to seek the judgment of God rather than of men; and they do not fear God but blush before men, lest anyone now accuse what not he but God will judge.
**“for thou begannest to speak, and not I”** — For thou begannest to speak, and not I: he says this because those who begin to speak in contention are usually more blameworthy than those who answer; yet this man answered wicked things to one who began rightly.
**“but if thou know any thing better, speak.”** — it is not your concern; but yet again he cloaks it
**“but if thou know any thing better, speak”** — But if thou know any thing better, speak: by granting a place for speaking, he showed that he displayed humility; though, when he says: “if thou know any thing better, speak,” this very thing is excessive pride, to have doubted the knowledge of the better man.
34.34:
**“Let men of understanding speak to me,”** — it is not your concern; his haughtiness appears
**“Let men of understanding speak to me”** — Let men of understanding speak to me: as if he said: this man is not justly allowed to speak, because he does not deserve even to hear the words of the wise.
34.35: **“But Job hath spoken foolishly”** — But Job hath spoken foolishly: he believed Job spoke without discipline because he spoke of himself as just in his works. Eliu would perhaps say true if the author of discipline himself had not reckoned of him these same things that Job said of himself. For he declared that he had been struck without cause.
34.36:
**“My father”** — because the harshness of the proud extends even to cursing, he prays God against Job
**“let Job be tried even to the end:”**
• he does not wish him testing out of goodwill, he who already accuses him of a fall amid the scourges; but, cruel, he does not know how to have compassion on pain, nor, lofty, on the humble, but rather afflicts him
• My father, let Job be tried even to, etc. He asks that he be struck still further with words of cursing, whom he accuses of having already sinned under the hand of the one striking. And because he believed him struck for fault, therefore he did not reckon that the bowels of devotion should be shown him even amid so many pains.
**“cease not from the man of iniquity”** — Cease not from the man of iniquity: he calls him a man of iniquity whom God by his own testimony declares just above all.
34.37:
**“Because he addeth … upon his sins”** — Because he addeth … upon his sins: he accuses him both of having deserved scourges for sins and of having sinned after the scourges.
**“let him be tied fast in the mean time amongst us”** — Let him be tied fast in the mean time amongst us: as if he said: let him learn from our assertion that he is by no means equal to the divine examination.
**“and then”** — as if he will not be able to

35.1: **“Moreover Eliu spoke these words:”** — Moreover Eliu spoke these words: this is rightly put often of him who strives to say not only unfitting things but many things more perversely, ending some and beginning others, so that immense talkativeness may go on. For the arrogant both speak many unfitting things and are always eager to be beginning in their speech, so as to make their hearers hang on that very speech, whereby they may wait to hear something as it were new.
35.2:
**“Doth thy thought seem right to thee”** — Doth thy thought seem right to thee? He had not said he was more just than God, but: “Let him propose equity against me, and let my judgment come to victory.”
**“that thou shouldst say: I am more just than God”** — That thou shouldst say: I am more just than God: so it seemed to him from Job’s words, but not so to God; because men weigh the heart from the words, God the words from the heart.
35.3:
**“For thou saidst: That which is right doth not please thee:”**
• or: good
• strong sentences follow, but they do not fit the person of Job
**“For thou saidst: That which is right doth not please thee”** — For thou saidst: That which is right doth not please thee: he had said none of these things; but the arrogant, when they cannot answer justly the things that are, rebuke by lying things that are not.
35.4: **“Therefore I will answer thy words”** — Therefore I will answer thy words: in the foregoing sayings he related as it were blameworthy words of blessed Job, and set them before himself as matter for speaking; and he discusses with strong sharpness what he deceitfully invented for himself as matter for speech.
35.5:
**“Look up to heaven and see, and behold the sky, that it is higher than thee.”** — in the creatures we recognize how far we stand from the Creator
**“Look up to heaven and see”** — Look up to heaven and see: saying this, he surely gathers that he ought to consider how much less he can either profit or harm God by his action, who cannot profit or harm the height of heaven and the sky; though in heaven and the sky we may take the powers above, so that when we see that the angelic spirits still stand far off from us, we may recognize how far we stand from the very Creator and Lord of spirits.
35.8:
**“Thy wickedness may hurt a man that is like thee:”** — which is not so with the spirits above, who cannot be changed
**“and thy justice may help the son of man.”**
• but even the evils of men profit the good
• A man that is like thee, etc. Human wickedness harms him whom it defiles by perverting him; and in turn our justice helps him whom it changes from wicked actions. But because the wickedness of the reprobate, after the manner of threshing, presses the life of the elect, as if separating grains from chaff, so as to purge it. And when Moses called, Pharao, by pressing them hard, even forced them to go out; so the evils which press us here compel us to go to God; whence the toils of the elect under the oppressions of the wicked.
35.9:
**“By reason of the multitude of oppressions they shall cry out:”**
• because these abound in the world
• So he adds: “By reason of the multitude of oppressors they shall cry out.” We can call all the wicked oppressors (slanderers): not only those who snatch outward goods, but also those who, by their evil ways and the examples of a reprobate life, strive to scatter our inward goods; because what they cannot urge by words they sometimes try to wrest by unbridled force.
**“and”** — that is
**“and shall wail for the violence of the arm”** — And shall wail for the violence of the arm: when we are forced by violence to sin, we already bear a tyrant. But because the weak, if anything adverse befalls them, grow faint at what is thrown at them, Eliu, having set out first the things by which the strong advance, soon pursues the faintheartedness of the weak in the oppressions of the wicked, thrusting on Job the reproaches of faintheartedness.
35.10:
**“And he hath not said: Where is God, who made me,”** — the weak man, like Job, thinks he is forsaken
**“And he hath not said: Where is God, who made me”** — And he hath not said: Where is God, who made me? It is the custom of sacred Scripture to pass suddenly from the singular number to the plural and the reverse. Whoever is already broken by the tribulation of adversities by no means contemplates by whom he was made. For he who made one who was not does not forsake what he made without governing it.
**“who hath given songs in the night?”** — that is, gladness in tribulation
**“who hath given songs in the night”** — Who hath given songs in the night: a song in the night is gladness in tribulation; because even if we are afflicted by the pressures of time, yet we rejoice in hope of eternity. And the sense is: the weak man, when he is pressed, is wearied by too much faintheartedness from the hope of joy, and does not say: “Where is God, who made me, who hath given songs in the night?” For if he said this, he would temper the violence he suffers.
35.11:
**“Who teacheth us”** — the weak man does not say this
**“more than the beasts of the earth”**
• who slip through the flesh
• Who teacheth us more than the beasts of the earth: as if the weak man is not strong in adversity because in prosperity he does not refrain from the gluttony of beasts nor from the flight of birds. The beasts of the earth are those who long for the lowest things by the habit of a fleshly life. The fowls of the air are those who pry into lofty things with the zeal of proud curiosity. So God teaches us more than the beasts of the earth and the fowls of the air, because while we recognize what we are, we neither sink beneath the lowest things by flowing down, nor are inflamed by lofty things through pride. Or by the beasts earthly men, by the birds the demons are designated. And it is understood: “this too he did not say.” Or the creeping things, which cling to the earth with their whole body, are those wholly earthly in thought; the animals which are lifted from the earth by the belly but are bent toward the earth are good things which are done for earthly ends.
**“and … more than the fowls of the air”** — who are lifted up in mind
35.12:
**“There shall they cry, and he will not hear”** — as God sometimes delivers his own for the sake of enemies, that they may be converted, so sometimes he does not hear his own for the damnation of the persecutors
**“There shall they cry, and he will not hear, because of the pride of evil men”** — There shall they cry, and he will not hear, because of the pride of evil men: there, namely in tribulation. As if he said: the guilt of the oppressors forbids the voices of the oppressed to be heard; and the just are not visibly delivered because the unjust do not deserve to be invisibly saved; and while these are worn down in tribulation, the wickedness of those is filled up. And so he does not quickly hear the one crying, and yet knows what he suffers. So it is plain that it is put off for good; whence: “thou wilt not hear, and it is not for folly to me.” But because many are broken by the slowness of help, he adds: “Yea when thou shalt say.”
35.13: **“God therefore will not hear in vain”** — God therefore will not hear in vain: he says two things: that he does not hear the one crying in vain, and yet that he looks on what he suffers. He hears and pretends not to, because what we ask to be fulfilled quickly is better prospered by that very slowness.
35.14:
**“Yea when thou shalt say: He considereth not: be judged before him,”** — if despair steals upon you, attend to all the things he has given you, and you will no longer mistrust
**“and expect him.”** — you need this
**“Yea when thou shalt say: He considereth not”** — Yea when thou shalt say: He considereth not: as if he said: when God is believed not to consider for this reason, that he has mercy slowly, enter the inner chamber of your thought. And there, before his eyes, receive the judgment of your cause. And discern what you have brought by living, or what he has brought mercifully. And then you return to the confidence of hope, when you blush at the good things of such great kindness, so that among adversities you may confidently wait for him whom you remember to have been gracious even after your sins. But while we are long afflicted, the wicked are not, because without the stroke they rush to worse.
35.15:
**“For he doth not now bring on his fury,”** — Whence: “For he doth not now bring on his fury.” He long bears with the wicked because he damns them for ever.
**“neither doth he revenge wickedness exceedingly”** — Neither doth he revenge wickedness exceedingly: for there are few things he scourges in this life. “Not exceedingly,” because if he punishes some things here he reserves more; and sometimes he begins to strike what eternal damnation completes. Some things he punishes lest he seem not to care for human affairs; some he reserves, so that we may perceive that a judgment remains.
35.16:
**“Therefore Job openeth his mouth in vain,”** — the true things he said he twisted to the despising of the just man; whence virtue is greater in the humble
**“Therefore Job openeth his mouth in vain”** — Therefore Job openeth his mouth in vain: he asserts that blessed Job both said many things and knew nothing of all the things he himself spoke.
**“and … without knowledge”** — And … without knowledge: it is the property of the arrogant man to think the many things he says few, and the few things he hears many. And though Job kept silent toward him, he accuses him over his words to his friends, so as to win more silence from him for himself.

36.1:
**“Eliu also proceeded, and said:”**
• as if he had said nothing yet, he begins long things
• Eliu also proceeded, etc. He had already said many things, and hopes to be borne with a little longer, because the arrogant judge they suffer a heavy loss if they confine their knowledge in brevity of speech. For they believe they show themselves the more learned the more they can open themselves out with multiplied talkativeness.
36.2:
**“Suffer me a little, and I will shew thee: for I have yet somewhat to speak in God’s behalf.”** — under pretext of God he seeks reverence for himself
**“for I have yet”** — For I have yet: the arrogant, because they often perceive that the reverence of silence is not given them, when they demand silence for themselves, which they do not deserve, put God forward in appearance.
36.3:
**“I will repeat my knowledge”** — I will repeat my knowledge: holy teachers often repeat if they say anything rather obscurely, so as to pour it into the hearts of the hearers by the voice of repetition; which the arrogant long to imitate, not so as to profit the hearers, but because they wish to seem eloquent in their judgment.
**“and I will prove my Maker just”** — And I will prove my Maker just: lest swelling be plain under the name of knowledge, he cloaks it, adding something about God’s justice. He says this so that, while he speaks as it were of God’s justice, whatever flows out arrogantly may be excused before human judgments.
36.4:
**“For indeed my words are without a lie, and perfect knowledge shall be proved to thee.”** — in what is to be said
**“For indeed my words are without a lie”** — For indeed my words are without a lie: he could not keep silent what he reckoned loftily of himself, and ran ahead by praising the right thing he perceived. For the just sometimes praise what they say, not for their own praise but to make their hearers attentive; whence the proud too praise their own things, but with another heart.
36.5:
**“God doth not cast away the mighty, whereas he himself also is mighty.”** — as if he said: power is not evil in its nature, but the wickedness and pride which come forth from it
**“God doth not cast away the mighty”** — God doth not cast away the mighty: namely those who administer the height of power intent on others’ advantages and not lifted up by their own praises; who long to profit, not to preside. Whence in the Book of Kings: “An evil spirit from the Lord troubled Saul.” If from the Lord, why evil? If evil, why from the Lord? Evil by the will which it has from itself; from the Lord by the power and creature, whence it is just, because “all power is from the Lord God.” And because by no means just power but wicked action is condemned.
36.6:
**“But he saveth not the wicked, and he giveth judgment to the poor.”**
• the law is not consulted about an enemy but about a citizen who sins; so in the judgment the ungodly will not be judged but the sinner
• There follows: “But he saveth not.” That is, he destroys the haughty, but makes the humble free through judgment. Or he gives judgment to the poor, because those who are now wickedly oppressed will then come themselves to judge over their oppressors. Note that some things are harmful of themselves, like sins; some from things adjoining, as marriage from the care of the world, power from haughtiness, by which one is like the devil. But he presides well who rules over vices rather than over brothers; because he is set over for vices, not for nature.
36.7:
**“He will not take away his eyes from the just,”**
• but then he looks more when he lets them be troubled
• He will not take away his eyes from the just, etc. He is believed to have taken his eyes from the just because they are torn here by the unjust without vengeance; of whom there follows: “and he placeth kings on the throne.” They are kings because they know how, not by consenting to the motions of their temptations to give way, but by ruling them to be over them. These are placed on the throne of the kingdom for ever, and there receive worthily to judge others by the very fact that here they do not know how to spare themselves wickedly. And by adding “for ever” he openly suggests that he is not speaking of an earthly throne.
**“and he placeth kings on the throne for ever”** — from this kingdom he places them in the eternal
36.8: **“And if they shall be in chains”** — And if they shall be in chains: the chains are the bonds of this pilgrimage, still kept. Bound with these chains Paul said: “Having a desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ”; and he saw himself bound with the cords of poverty when, looking at the true riches, he said: “That you may know what the hope is of his calling, and what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints.” Or by chains and cords temporal punishment is taken, so that punishments may draw those whom rewards do not invite.
36.9: **“He shall shew them their works, and their wicked deeds, because they have been violent.”** — And he rightly adds: “He shall shew them their works.” For when we come to know the glory above more by loving it, we perceive that they were heavier.
36.10:
**“shall open”** — or: opened
**“He also shall open their ear”** — He also shall open their ear: to open the ear is to open the understanding of thought. And when the ear is opened each one is corrected, when within he receives the desires of eternal goods and recognizes what evils he has done outside.
36.11: **“If they shall hear and observe, they shall accomplish their days in good”** — If they shall hear and observe, they shall accomplish their days in good: by good, right action; by glory, the reward above is signified. Those who are eager to obey the heavenly precepts accomplish their days in good, their years in glory, because they complete both the course of the present time in good work and their consummation in happy reward.
36.12:
**“But if they hear not, they shall pass by the sword,”** — they are both struck here and do not escape the torments afterwards
**“and shall be consumed in folly.”**
• because by scourges they heap up sins
• But if they hear not, they shall pass by the sword: because both vengeance strikes them in tribulation and the end shuts them in folly. For it is folly that iniquity so binds them that not even punishment holds them back from fault.
36.13:
**“Dissemblers”** — worse, hypocrites
**“Dissemblers and crafty men prove the wrath of God”** — Dissemblers and crafty men prove the wrath of God: when he said dissemblers he aptly added “and crafty,” because unless they are skilled in wit they cannot fittingly pretend what they long to seem. So before the judge they can have no excuse of ignorance, because while they display every manner of holiness before the eyes of men, they are themselves a testimony that they are not ignorant of living well.
**“neither shall they cry when they are bound.”** — confession is a strong cry to God
**“neither shall they cry when they are bound”** — Neither shall they cry when they are bound: the dissembler is as it were bound when he is tied by the scourge of striking; and yet, when he is so struck, he shrinks from showing himself wicked, because he is used to seeming holy. Or they are led bound and will not cry, because, overcome by the importunity of human praise, they think they are called holy even when they die in sins. The wicked man who does not long to seem holy does not blush in the scourge to confess what he is; which the hypocrite does not, but, about to die by the last stroke, wishes to remain in the judgment of men such as he was seen to be. Or he does not confess even then for this reason, that, deceived within, he thinks he is what he is called by the judgment of God, who deceived others outside.
36.14:
**“shall die in a storm”** — which rises unforeseen
**“Their soul … and their life among the effeminate.”** — he does not live manfully whom praise corrupts
**“Their soul shall die in a storm”** — Their soul shall die in a storm: for they seemed to live as it were calmly when they took care to rejoice in the praise of holiness. But a sudden whirlwind of inward striking casts down those whom the arrogance of outward favour lifts up. Because it has been said of the damnation of the reprobate and of the deliverance of the humble, there follows: “He shall deliver the poor out of his distress.” The poor man is delivered out of his distress when each is set free from affliction.
36.15:
**“He shall deliver the poor out of his distress”** — which he suffers here so as to seek eternal things; whence he adds: “and shall open”
**“and shall open his ear in affliction.”** — which prosperity closes
**“and shall open his ear in affliction”** — And shall open his ear in affliction: to open the ear in affliction is to open the hearing of the heart by the wounds of stripes.
36.16:
**“Therefore he shall set thee at large out of the narrow mouth”**
• because of the scourges he thinks he is weighed down by heavy iniquity, whose depth he adds: “which hath no foundation”
• Therefore he shall set thee at large out of the narrow mouth: everyone who, deserting the way of life, throws himself into the darkness of sins plunges himself as it were into a well or a pit. And if he is pressed down by daily committing and by the habit of iniquity, so that he cannot rise to higher things, he is straitened as it were by the narrow mouth of the well. And he is set very much at large out of the narrow mouth who, after the yoke of iniquities, is led back by repenting to the freedom of good work, so as to be straitened by no difficulties in doing good things.
**“which hath no foundation”** — Which hath no foundation: sin has no foundation, because it does not subsist from its own nature but grows in the good of nature. Or he put foundation for depth, wishing to signify the abyss of hell, whose mouth is sin, through which one goes on to hell. Or sin has no bottom, in which the fallen soul is daily cast down to worse things, as in the well into which it has fallen it finds no bottom on which to fix itself.
**“and the rest of thy table shall be full of fatness.”** — he wishes to console Job’s words with the reward of eternal things, as if he promised of himself freely what was due to him by right
**“and the rest of thy table”** — And the rest of thy table: the rest of the table is the refreshment of inward fullness, which is said to be full of fatness, because it is prepared by the delight of inward pleasure.
36.17:
**“Thy cause hath been judged as that of the wicked, cause and judgment thou shalt recover.”**
• the just will then judge all things the more powerfully, the more they have been judged here
• But they recover cause and judgment, because from that justice by which they now live, they will then shine forth at the height of judicial power. And Eliu promises these things as if new, which is the custom of the arrogant man; who, because he thinks he becomes cheap when he comes down to gentle things, soon rebukes so as to be feared.
**“Thy cause hath been judged as that of the wicked”** — Thy cause hath been judged as that of the wicked: the cause of the good is justice; their cause is judged as that of the ungodly, because their justice is wearied here by the fatherly scourge.
36.18:
**“Therefore let not anger overcome thee”**
• if anger overcomes correction, it oppresses before it corrects, and under the look of zeal for justice it is fury
• Therefore let not anger overcome thee: the arrogant, who wish to appear kind for the praise of men, reckon as a motion of anger whatever is done by the censure of discipline; and while for the praise of men they wish to appear kind, they reckon that those are oppressed by good rulers whom they see restrained from vices against their will.
**“to oppress any man: neither let multitude of gifts”** — or: of places, which is in the older books; that is, because you are revered everywhere; if you read “of gifts,” it needs no exposition
**“turn thee aside.”** — Neither let multitude of gifts turn thee aside: because you are revered everywhere, beware lest you be lifted up by the haughtiness of that same reverence. And he said “turn aside” (bend) because everyone who is lifted up in time is bent by the very fact that he is lifted up. These words fit the arrogant within the Church. As if it were said to holy Church: beware lest, if you are lifted up by the veneration of the whole world, you fall from inward intention.
36.19:
**“Lay down thy greatness”** — Lay down thy greatness: the arrogant, the martyrs having been taken away to the things above, mock the Church as if consoling her, saying: by no means trust that you have greatness, because, the former fathers having been taken away, you no longer have any in whose life you may glory.
**“and all the mighty of strength”** — And all the mighty of strength: as if it were said: those clung to you as truly mighty who held in you by living what they spoke by teaching. But now those who preside over you are mighty in look, not in strength. For the greatness of the Church is in the mighty, who fought for the truth even to death; when these are taken away, the proud, who set themselves first as if they alone were left to the Church, mock the Church as if consoling her: as if you no longer have true mighty men who may be troubled, and in whom you may glory, but those who preside over you now are weak. For they do not know that when the strong are taken away, the weak are strengthened by God in their place. But those they once knew as weak they believe never grow strong. And because they see certain prelates propped up by earthly power, which is weakness, they despise all according to their reckoning of these, and scorn that these are put in the place of the ancient fathers.
36.20:
**“Prolong not the night that people may come up for them.”**
• but
• There is added: “Prolong not the night.” Peoples, as being numerous, are these weak ones who live everywhere at their pleasure. He says this truly but not humbly, and he strikes more by rebuking than he consoles. Whence he also adds: “Prolong not the night.” As if he said: do not act in the darkness of your ignorance so as to put the weak in the place of the strong. For to prolong the night so that peoples may come up in place of the mighty is if it is brought about through negligence that the unlearned and weak obtain the places of strong teachers.
• Morally, in individuals.
• Whence he says: “Lay down thy greatness.” For, struck by vice, it perceives what it is and ceases to be great, and lays down all the mighty fears of the mind without tribulation; because when humility advances through temptation, adversity itself is prosperous; yet this is not done without adversity, which makes for the mind a night of sadness. But this night ought not to be prolonged but quickly ended by consolation, because in it peoples come up in place of the mighty, that is, unworthy and manifold thoughts. For, troubled, now it thinks it has lost all, now what it had been, now what it is now, now whether it can rise again, now whether, conquered, it can remain. Eliu says such things rightly, if he knew to whom. For this does not fit Job, to whose insult too he adds: “Beware thou turn not aside to iniquity.” He follows iniquity after misery who, after the evils he bears through correction, inflames himself with a burning heart by the torches of impatience. Which Eliu believed blessed Job had done, because he heard him, set amid the scourges, speak out with free voices; not knowing that all he said he uttered not from the iniquity of impatience but from the virtue of truth, because by the sentence of the inward judge he did not err even when he justified himself.
**“let not anger overcome thee”** — Let not anger overcome thee: let him who corrects others’ things first see that he is not overcome by anger, which would exceed the measure of punishment and oppress. And for anger to overcome the mind, the cause is the multitude of places, that is, of idle thoughts, in which the mind rests. For the mind, poured out over so many things and bent, does not give itself to justice. The mind of the just man strives always to cling to one thing; the wicked man’s varies, because apart from God nothing suffices, and so what he just now asked for he soon loathes. But when the mind is gathered, it adds: let it know that what it does is great, for otherwise it would not do it. For that very knowledge is the entrance of haughtiness; whence God allows it to be tempted, so that, weak, it may be humbled.
36.21:
**“Beware thou turn not aside to iniquity”** — Beware thou turn not aside to iniquity: the proud call this the misery of the Church, that they are condemned while God waits.
**“for this thou hast begun to follow after”** — elsewhere: to follow
**“for this thou hast begun”** — For this thou hast begun: he condemns uncertain and unknown things as certain and known. For he does not know whether Job said the things he heard from him from impatience or from virtue.
36.22:
**“Behold, God is high in his strength, and none is like him”**
• even if some say he is John, Elias or Jeremias
• Behold, God is high, etc. Eliu, who above brought in many things morally, now lifts himself to the secrets of prophecy. Nor is it a wonder how an arrogant man could be filled with the prophetic spirit, since even Saul was in the number of the prophets, and an ass received reasonable words. So Eliu beholds the humble coming of the Redeemer, saying: “Behold, God is high,” etc. As if he said: he who will be seen humble in weakness remains high in strength.
**“among the lawgivers.”** — Moses, Josue, the prophets are lawgivers
**“none is like him among the lawgivers”** — None is like him among the lawgivers: we can call lawgivers those whom we know admonished the people to right things from the law; but none of these is like him who alone is without sin, the Son without adoption.
36.23:
**“Who can search out his ways?”** — his judgments: that he chooses this one, rejects that one; Judea is rejected, the gentiles chosen
**“or who can say to him: Thou has wrought iniquity?”** — Who can search out his ways? etc. As if he said: he whose action cannot be searched, how can he be rebuked? For no one judges well what he does not know. Whence he adds: “Remember that thou knowest not his work.” Men have sung of the Lord, because his power is made known to us either by the spirits above or by all perfect teachers; and even those who preach him revere his judgments as unpierced. And the sense is: he of whom all the strong have spoken, his judgments are hidden from the eyes of your mind.
36.24:
**“Remember that thou knowest not his work”** — his judgments
**“concerning which”** — of whose power
36.25:
**“All men see him”**
• it is seen that he is God, but not his judgments
• All men see him: every man, by the very fact that he was made rational, ought to gather from reason that he who made him is God. And to behold him afar off is not yet to see him by sight, but still to weigh him only from wonder at his works.
**“every one beholdeth afar off.”** — even the just man in this life; the wicked man even in the other
36.26:
**“Behold, God is great, exceeding our knowledge:”** — then we know something as it were in part, when we perceive that we cannot know him worthily
**“Behold, God is great, exceeding our knowledge”** — Behold, God is great, exceeding our knowledge: because God is present everywhere, when “behold” is said of him he is spoken of as present even to those who do not see; of the brightness of whose greatness whatever we know is beneath him.
**“the number of his years”** — it signifies that it is long, but incomprehensible
**“is inestimable.”** — because man cannot measure eternity
**“the number of his years is inestimable”** — The number of his years is inestimable: he wished to speak of eternity somehow, and called that very length of eternity years. For when we wish to stretch out the shortness of time, we extend moments through hours, hours through days, days through months, and months through years. So because he wished to say something vast, but found nothing wider to say, he multiplied years without reckoning of number, saying: “the number of his years is inestimable”; so that, while it multiplies the things that are long with itself, human weakness may recognize that it cannot measure the length of eternity.
36.27:
**“He lifteth up the drops of rain”** — lest they appear to the world
**“and poureth out showers like”** — more abundantly
**“floods”**
• even if abundant water stands in you, yet it fell drop by drop from the cloud; lest you set yourself before it
• He lifteth up the drops (stars) of rain, etc. The stars of rain are those who so shine by the merits of life that they also rain the word of preaching. Such were the prophets, in whose stead, when the Lord took them away, he sent the apostles. After the outward sacraments fell silent, there were those who rained like floods; or, the apostles having been led back to the things above, the Lord opened up divine knowledge with a larger outpouring through the tongues of the expositors who followed. Or the Lord withdrew the stars of rain and poured out showers like floods, because when he took the preaching apostles away from Judea, he watered the world with the grace of new teaching. “Stars of rain”: those are stars and not rain who live well but do not teach, as there are stars in the sky which rain does not follow. But others are rainy stars; and these are the two kinds of the just.
36.28:
**“Which flow from the clouds”** — Which flow from the clouds: because if the teaching of understanding did not begin from the holy apostles, it would by no means flow more largely through the mouths of the saints.
**“that cover all above”** — That cover all above: when clouds cover the air, if we lift our eyes to heaven, we look not at heaven but at them; so our understanding is not allowed to pass to divine things unless it is first formed by the examples of the saints who went before, the prophets and apostles.
36.29:
**“If he will spread out clouds as his tent,”**
• see what he does in the world through the clouds
• clouds: men are a tent for God, who rests in them on the way, hidden
**“If he will spread out clouds”** — If he will spread out clouds: the Lord spreads out the clouds when, opening the way of preaching to his ministers, he spreads them abroad on every side over the breadth of the world. These clouds are called his tent, which is usually set up on a journey, because, coming to us through grace, he is covered within the minds of his preachers.
36.30:
**“And lighten with his light from above,”** — words do not suffice for believing without miracles
**“And lighten with his light from above”** — And lighten with his light from above: through these clouds he lightens with his light, because through his preachers he lights up the darkness of our insensibility even with miracles.
**“he shall cover also the ends of the sea”** — He shall cover also the ends of the sea: for when these clouds rain with words, and when they open by miracles the force of flashing preaching, they turn even the farthest bounds of the world to divine love.
36.31:
**“For by these he judgeth people”** — For by these he judgeth people: by the words of the preachers, that is, the drops of the clouds; by these lightnings of miracles God judges peoples, because he calls their hearts, terrified, to penance. If anyone says: what if God sees that some will act wickedly after baptism, and therefore, forestalled by death, they are not brought to baptism? If it is so, then the sins of some are punished before they are committed; which God does not do, who sets free even from those committed; but the judgments are hidden.
**“and giveth food to many mortals.”** — that is, to the wicked and the tyrants
**“and giveth food to many mortals”** — And giveth food to many mortals: through the same clouds through which terror is struck, food is also given, because the dispensing belongs to the preachers, so that they know how to afflict minds in such a way that they also know how to nourish the afflicted with consolation. And he does not say to all but to many, for not all have faith.
36.32:
**“In his hands he hideth the light,”**
• or: in his hands
• Whence it is openly added: “From the savage he hideth the light.” The savage are those who lift themselves up with haughty thoughts; to whom the knowledge of truth is denied.
**“and commandeth it to come again”** — And commandeth it to come again: because the light of truth which is hidden from haughty and busied minds is revealed to the afflicted and humbled. Or the light was hidden from the savage, that is, the Jews, who dared to contradict the Redeemer for this reason, that among themselves they stood out as savage. But those who are to be received to faith at the end of the world, he commands it to come again to them; the wicked are blinded in their works; to which yet it is commanded to come again, because when they know themselves sinners they receive the light of grace.
36.33:
**“He sheweth his friend concerning it”**
• lest you doubt about it
• He sheweth his friend concerning it: he who strives to keep God’s will in his precepts is called his friend. So of this light of the eternal homeland God shows his friend that it is his possession, so that he may by no means despair through the frailty of his weakness, but may be strengthened by the example of the head to overcome, so that he may come up to it. So whose heart does not tremble at being lifted to so great a consideration?
**“that it is his possession, and that he may come up to it.”**
• or: approach
• Christ alone ascends, because he is one with the body

37.1: **“At this my heart trembleth, and is moved out of its place.”** — So there follows: “At this my heart trembleth.” Fear is put here for ecstasy, because as in ecstasy, so in fear the mind is taken out of itself. And the place of the human heart is the delight of the present life. So the sluggish heart, long given to earthly thoughts, when it is suddenly lifted through ecstasy to the highest things, has changed the place of its low thinking. But how this is done follows: “Hear ye attentively the terror of his voice.” Because the sinner, while he carries his heart weighed down in low thoughts, if he is touched by the breathing of divine grace, understands that all he does is punished by the strict judge’s punishment. It turns over in his mind how terribly the sentence will come from the judge’s mouth: “Depart from me.” So because the proud heart is first shaken by terror, so that, shaken, it may be made firm in love, it is rightly said: “he shall hear the hearing of his voice in terror.”
37.2: **“and the sound that cometh out of his mouth”** — And the sound that cometh out of his mouth: by the mouth of God the Only-begotten is designated; because as he is called his arm, since through him the Father works all things, so he is also called his mouth, through whom he speaks to us. And by the sound of the mouth the Spirit of the Lord can be designated, of whom it is written: “And suddenly there came a sound from heaven,” etc. By the terror of the voice too the force of dread can be understood, and by the sound of the mouth the sweetness of consolation; because the Spirit first terrifies those he fills away from earthly action, and afterwards consoles them with the hope of heavenly things.
37.3:
**“under”** — or: beneath
**“He beholdeth … all the heavens”**
• as if after the high he looks also on the lower; for the Church is now thought to be forsaken because she does not do miracles as the apostles did
• He beholdeth under all the heavens, etc. As if he said: he who rules the highest does not forsake the farthest. Because what is done spiritually is not seen by the fleshly. For there are those who reckon that God does not care for human affairs and that they happen by chance; whence he adds: “all the heavens.” Or he calls the preachers heavens. So the heavens having been lifted up, the Lord looks on the lower things, because even when the highest preachers have been taken away he ceaselessly cares for our weakness too.
**“and his light is upon the ends of the earth”** — And his light is upon the ends of the earth: because after the lofty life of those who went before, he takes in even the ways of sinners with the illumination of his grace, or gathers the nations to faith. Or the ends of the earth are the ends of sinful men. For often, looked on by grace from above, they return to God at their last.
37.4:
**“After it a noise shall roar,”** — So there follows: “After it a noise shall roar.” For him whom the Lord has filled by enlightening he turns his life into lament; and after it a noise will roar, because when he enters the mind it is plain that the groaning of penance follows.
**“he shall thunder with the voice of his majesty”** — He shall thunder with the voice of his majesty: God thunders with the voice of his majesty when he makes known to us, already prepared through laments, how great he is in the things above. Set on earth, we hear the sound even from the higher things, when, thinking earthly things, we suddenly dread the sentence of terror from above.
**“and shall not be found out, when his voice shall be heard.”** — whence you hear his voice when you are pricked to compunction, “but thou knowest not whence he cometh, and whither he goeth”
**“and shall not be found out, when … shall be heard”** — And shall not be found out, when … shall be heard: the voice of the Lord is heard when the breathing of his grace is conceived in the mind. But this voice of the Spirit coming upon it, which works itself into the ear of the heart, not even the mind enlightened by it searches out. For it cannot weigh by what passages the invisible power flows into it, in what ways it comes to it, in what it goes away.
37.5:
**“God shall thunder wonderfully with his voice”** — God shall thunder wonderfully with his voice: God thunders wonderfully with his voice because he pierces incomprehensibly into our hidden hearts; and the excess of that same driving takes place in the mind, while nothing sounds in the voice; and so, by the oldness of life, habit is changed.
**“he that doth great and unsearchable things.”**
• the completion of the work appears outside, but the manner of the working lies hidden within
• So it is added: “he that doth great and unsearchable things.” So that man, given to earthly uses, weighed down by wicked desires, suddenly glows toward new things and grows cold toward his accustomed ones.
37.6:
**“He commandeth the snow to go down upon the earth”** — How this is done follows: “He commandeth the snow to go down.” Waters drawn up on high are packed together so as to become snow. But when that snow comes to the earth it is turned again into the liquid of waters. So the waters are the minds of preachers, which, while they raise themselves to contemplate things above, are made solid with higher understanding. So snows come from the heavens to earth when the lofty hearts of the saints, which are now fed by solid contemplation, come down for brotherly charity to the humble words of preaching. For water is drawn up from below, so as afterwards to be given back to the earth from above. So he who has been raised up from the earth looks back on what he was and comes down to the rest.
**“and the winter rain,”** — So there follows: “and the winter rain, and the shower of his strength.” Winter is the present life, in which the cold numbness of our mortality binds us. This winter has rains, surely the preachings of rulers, which will cease in the eternal summer.
**“and the shower of his strength”** — And the shower of his strength: the shower of God’s strength is the preaching of the Godhead; for the shower of weakness is the preaching of the incarnation. And because, having heard the power of God, we soon return to ourselves, weighing what we have done ill or well, he adds: “He sealeth up the hand of all men.” For men scorn to weigh the evils they do; but, struck by preaching, they will wake up and recognize the weight of their wicked works. Or the Creator made man rational, so that he could not be ignorant of what he has done, and is compelled by the law of nature to know whether what he does is wicked or right. Because above he brought in the virtues of God’s clouds, he now brings it about that the attack of the adversary too against the life of the good may be made known. Or, after the wicked members, he adds about their head.
37.7: **“He sealeth up the hand of all men”** — “The firstling of an ass thou shalt change for a sheep,” that is, turn the beginnings of an unclean life to innocence
37.8:
**“Then the beast shall go into his covert”** — lying in wait for those who go by
**“and shall abide in his den.”** — For there follows: “Then the beast shall go into his covert.” This is that beast which the dying Lamb cast out of the hearts of many, which enters the hearts of the reprobate. And so the beast is taken as the ancient enemy, who first savagely attacked man and tore the wholeness of his life by evil persuasion. When, after the thunder of the clouds, at the end of the world he invades Antichrist, what else does he do but go into his covert, so as to abide in his own den? The hearts of the persecuting Jews too were before the den of this beast, who handed over to the gentiles to be struck him whom they could not lawfully kill themselves.
37.9:
**“Out of the inner parts shall a tempest come, and cold out of the north.”**
• that is, from the Lesser Bear
• So it is added: “Out of the inner parts shall a tempest come.” Scripture, when it mentions the inner parts over against Arcturus, designates the southern region opposite to the parts of the north. So by the name of the inner parts the Jewish people is expressed. For those who knew God were held in the warmth of faith, glowing as it were under the noonday sun. But the gentiles, because they had reached no knowledge of the understanding from above, remained cold, as without sun, under the north. So out of the inner parts a tempest comes and cold out of Arcturus, as if he said: from the Jews malice arises persecuting, from the gentiles power pressing down; while what Judea sought out of envy, the gentile judge carried out by Roman authority.
37.10:
**“When God bloweth there cometh frost,”** — So against this envy there is added: “When God bloweth there cometh frost.” Because the more the Holy Spirit breathed on the hearts of the faithful, the greater the miracles of virtues he bestowed, the more the numbness of heavier envy grew in the minds of the unbelieving. So water had been turned to frost while, the world going after the Lord, the envy of the Jews remained sluggish. But because the Lord loosed the hardness even of so great unbelief:
**“and again the waters are poured out abundantly.”** — There follows: “and again the waters are poured out abundantly.” Because after the Lord bore the savagery of the Jews even to death, he melted their hearts from the hardness of unbelief, and from hard persecutors they became great preachers, so that a so much richer harvest of the elect might rise up.
37.11:
**“Corn desireth clouds”** — So there follows: “Corn desireth clouds.” The elect are God’s corn, to be stored in the heavenly barns, who now in the threshing of the floor bear with the chaff; but this corn waits for the streams of the clouds so as to grow.
**“and the clouds spread their light”** — And the clouds spread their light: for the clouds to spread their light is for the holy preachers to spread wide the examples of life both by speaking and by doing.
37.12:
**“Which go round about, whithersoever the will of him that governeth them shall lead them,”** — as if: wherever he leads, and to what? Because as they cannot go where they will, so neither can they act as they will
**“Which go round about”** — Which go round about: God’s clouds go round about everything, because by the light of preaching they light up the ends of the world; but because, subject to the divine nods, they cannot fulfil what they will, they cannot go except where the will of him that governs them leads them.
**“to whatsoever he shall command them upon the face of the whole earth:”** — or: of the earth
**“to whatsoever he shall command them upon the face of the whole earth”** — To whatsoever he shall command them upon the face of the whole earth: for often they long to act one way and are disposed another. For mostly they strive to correct gently, and yet their speech is led into harshness; mostly they long to cut some off harshly, and yet their vigour is reined in by the spirit of gentleness.
37.13: **“Whether in one tribe, or in his own land”** — Whether in one tribe, or in his own land: by one tribe Juda is understood, which in Scripture is mentioned as famous and many above the rest. And the whole of Juda together is called God’s land, which then brought forth to him the fruit of faith when the whole world strayed under the worship of idols. And the place of mercy is the gentiles themselves, who received reconciliation from mercy alone. So the Lord spoke of his clouds, whether in his land or in one tribe or in whatever place of his mercy, because he gave the preachers of the Old and New Testament sometimes to the tribe of Juda alone, and rejected almost the whole of Israel for the wicked government of its kings; sometimes he willed the clouds to shine in the place of his mercy, because he showed holy preachers to the gentiles too.
37.14:
**“Hearken to these things, Job: Stand, and consider the wondrous works of God.”** — as if weary of the weights of lofty things, he adds through boasting: “Hearken,” as if he said: you who are less than I
**“Hearken to these things, Job: Stand, and consider the wondrous works of God”** — Hearken to these things, Job: Stand, and consider the wondrous works of God: he saw him as it were lying down in comparison with himself, whom he warned by the words of such great preaching to stand. For there are those who consider God’s wonders lying down, because they wonder at the power of his working without following it.
37.15:
**“Dost thou know when God commanded the rains, to shew the light of his clouds?”** — through words the light of the clouds appears; unless the rain falls, it is not known what is in the clouds
**“Dost thou know when God commanded the rains”** — Dost thou know when God commanded the rains? Eliu examines blessed Job about things to come and humbles him as it were for ignorance. And he calls the words of preachers the rains of the clouds, and the sense is: if you already see the preachers who are to come into the world, do you grasp when the Lord drives them to preach by the filling of the Spirit, or in what ways he makes the brightness of their life known to the world?
37.16:
**“Knowest thou the … paths of the clouds”** — Knowest thou the … paths of the clouds? For these clouds have very fine paths, namely the ways of holy preaching. So they bind those by paths who do not go out from the track of their intention by wandering through the broad desires of the world. Which paths are great, because the narrower they are in the present life for the very guarding of life, the more they are widened in the eternal reward.
**“and the perfect knowledges?”** — which is done only by the gift of the Holy Spirit
**“and the perfect knowledges”** — And the perfect knowledges: perfect knowledge is both to do all things carefully and to know that of one’s own merits there is nothing.
37.17:
**“Are not thy garments hot, when the south wind blows upon the earth?”** — they are not humble within themselves
**“Are not thy garments hot”** — Are not thy garments hot? This is said generally of the Church and specially of Job. By garments clinging to a living body the life of disciples joined to masters who live well is signified. For garments cannot be warm of themselves; but joined to the body of the living, while they cover the breathing pores of the limbs, they give out the warmth flowing from within; and from them the warmth returns to the body while the teachers are kindled the more for the good of those under them. And the sense is: in vain do you attribute to yourself those whom you see advance in virtues, reckoning that they grew warm through you; because unless the favour of the Holy Spirit touched them, they would remain cold in their insensibility. After he has said these things strongly, he adds through arrogance:
37.18:
**“Thou perhaps”** — it is mockery
**“hast made the heavens with him, which are most strong, as if they were of molten brass.”** — which is not easily consumed by rust
**“Thou perhaps hast made the heavens with him”** — Thou perhaps hast made the heavens with him: by the heavens the angelic spirits who were created in the heavenly places can be designated. The minds of the elect clinging to heavenly things are most strong, as if of molten brass, because they are consumed by no rust of changeableness away from the wholeness of the strength they began.
37.19: **“shew us what we may say to him: for we are wrapped up in darkness.”** — Again he adds mockingly: “shew us what we may say to him.” You, who already enjoy the great light of understanding, ought to teach us, who are wrapped in the darkness of ignorance.
37.20:
**“Who shall tell him the things I speak?”** — Who shall tell him the things I speak? He says this despising him, as if he openly said: the things I, perceiving them sharply, speak unheard of his praises, who can tell them, or after he has heard them?
**“even if a man shall speak, he shall be swallowed up.”** — he who swelled arrogantly now adds by way of teaching: “even if a man shall speak”
**“even if a man shall speak, he shall be swallowed up”** — Even if a man shall speak, he shall be swallowed up: everything that devours something, drawing it inward, hides it from sight, and snatches into the depth a thing that could be seen on the surface. So man, when he keeps silent about God, seems to be something by the reason in which he was made. But if he begins to speak of God, at once it is shown that he is nothing, because he is swallowed up by the immensity of his greatness. But he truly became known to men when he showed himself to them, having taken up humanity; which, because it had not yet been revealed:
37.21:
**“But now they see not”** — men
**“the light:”** — There follows: “But now they see not the light.” But how this same light is seen by men he suggests when he says: “the air on a sudden shall be thickened into clouds.” By the air the minds of worldly men are designated, which, given to the countless desires of this life, are scattered hither and thither, fluid like the air. But the air is thickened into clouds when loose minds are strengthened by the grace of the regard from above with firmness of virtue. For clouds are the firmer the denser they are. And all the apostles had been air; but suddenly the air was thickened into clouds, because through the regard of grace from above the loose hearts of fishermen were turned into the solidity of preachers; who, since, their ministry carried out, they run back to the secrets of heaven:
**“and the wind shall pass and drive them away.”**
• but because they run with rain even to death, he adds what comes of it
• There follows: “and the wind shall pass and drive them away.” The passing wind is the present life; the passing wind drives the clouds away, because the course of temporal life takes the apostles away from the flesh, and hides them from the surface of the earth in secret rest, as in the pole of heaven. But what is done in holy Church from their labours he adds: “Gold out of the north.” By the north the gentiles, bound by the cold of sin, are signified; by the name of gold the souls of the faithful. So gold is said to come out of the north, because from the gentiles, long cold with the numbness of faithlessness, the life of the faithful, precious to God, is multiplied within holy Church.
37.22:
**“and to God praise with fear.”**
• not glad only, because he fears for himself
• And to God praise with fear, etc. “To God” is said as if it were said by those who are on God’s side. So when gold came out of the north, a fearful praise came forth to God, because when the gentiles brought the brightness of their faith, the multitude of the Hebrews already faithful praised the divine judgments with dread; because surely Judea was justly driven back while the gentiles were devoutly called; and she feared the losses of her rejection when she saw the gains of another’s calling.
37.23:
**“We cannot find him worthily:”** — even if we find him, not worthily
**“We cannot find him worthily”** — We cannot find him worthily: because whatever we perceive in him is from faith, not yet from sight. Yet he adds what he considers he has now found.
**“he is great in strength, and in judgment, and in justice, and he is ineffable.”** — he cannot be perceived worthily, how much less spoken
**“he is great in strength, and in judgment, and in justice”** — He is great in strength, and in judgment, and in justice: great in strength, because he overcomes the strong adversary. Great in judgment, because even if here he presses down his elect through adversities, at some time he lifts them up in the glory of eternal prosperity. Great in justice, because even if here he bears long with the reprobate, yet at some time he damns them without end.
37.24:
**“Therefore men shall fear him,”** — he says right things which yet he does not do, as a crooked bow shoots at itself
**“Therefore men shall fear him”** — Therefore men shall fear him: he calls men those who are strong for understanding.
**“and all that seem to themselves to be wise, shall not dare to behold him.”**
• he who wishes to see the wisdom of God in passing, let him climb the sycamore tree, that is, humbly choose the foolishness of the world
• And all that seem to themselves to be wise shall not dare to behold him, etc. By these words he suggests the skilled indeed but arrogant, in which he touched himself. For those who seem wise to themselves cannot contemplate the wisdom of God, because they are as far from its light as they are not humble within themselves.

38.1:
**“Then the Lord answered”** — sometimes God speaks gently, so as to be loved; sometimes terribly, so as to be feared
**“Then the Lord answered Job out of a whirlwind, and said”** — Because he speaks to one who is scourged, he is said to have spoken out of a whirlwind. But whether he spoke to him through himself or through an angel is doubtful. For the stirrings of the air could have been made through an angel, and these words that follow conveyed through him. And again an angel could have shaken the air outwardly into a whirlwind, and yet the Lord inwardly, through himself, have sounded the force of the sentence into his heart without words.
38.2:
**“Who is this”** — as if: what he says I know, but who says it I know not
**“that wrappeth up sentences in unskillful words?”** — because by strictness he presses him down so that he may not be lifted up
**“Who is this that wrappeth up sentences in unskillful words”** — The first reproach is such a question: “Who is this?” And we do not say this except of one we do not know. And for God not to know is to reprove; he surely does not know the arrogant, that is, does not approve their life. And in saying “sentences” and not adding what kind, we take good ones, which the unskilled man put forth wrapped in words, because they had been uttered with words of boasting. For the fault of unskilfulness is to understand the right not rightly, that is, to bend the heavenly gift to the appetite for earthly praise. So, this being despised, the words are turned to teaching Job.
38.3:
**“Gird up thy loins like a man”** — Gird up thy loins like a man: to gird the loins is to rein in lust either in deed or in thought. But since we know that Job was endowed with chastity, why is it said to him: “Gird up thy loins like a strong man,” that is, restrain lust, unless because there is one lust of the flesh and another of the heart, by which we glory in our chastity and virtues? So it is said to him that he who had first overcome the lust of corruption should now restrain the lust of pride.
**“I will ask thee, and answer thou me.”** — while I stir you to lofty things which you cannot grasp, answer, that is, see yourself humble
**“I will ask thee, and answer thou me”** — I will ask thee, and answer thou me: our Creator is wont to question us in three ways. Either when he strikes us with the strictness of the scourge, and shows how much patience is in us or lacking to us. Or he commands certain things we do not want, and lays open to us our obedience or disobedience. Or he opens some hidden things to us and hides others, and makes known to us the measure of our humility. So blessed Job, after the questioning of the blows, is examined by the questioning of speech, so that he may consider what the things above are, and, while he hardly grasps them, may return to himself, so as to know how near to nothing he is in comparison with things above. For he who, laid low with sores, stood so firm in virtues had to be humbled. So he sends a medicine ahead of one who is to overcome and to be restored to prosperity. “Where wast thou when I laid up the foundations of the earth?” In Scripture we take foundations to be the preachers, whom the Lord set first in the whole Church, and on them the structure of the building that followed rose up. So lest Job be lifted up in mastery over the power of his virtues, in the first part of the speech he is examined by the remembrance of the holy preachers, so that the more wonderful he saw them come, the more cheaply he might value himself in comparison with them. And the sense is: consider the virtue of the strong, and weigh me, their author before the ages; and when you look up to them whom I made in time as wonderful, weigh how much you ought to be subject to me, whom you know to be the author of wonders without time.
38.4: **“Where wast thou when I laid up the foundations of the earth?”** — even if this was future in deed, it was already done in predestination
38.5:
**“Who hath laid the measures thereof, if thou knowest?”** — among which are all the elect
**“or who hath stretched the line upon it?”**
• of hidden judgment
• Or who hath stretched the line upon it? No one is ignorant that God stretches these lines, but this is said to Job so that he may recall what he could know and pass over, weighing more sharply that the ordering of man is not in human strength but in the hand of God. Lines of measurement are stretched in the dividing of lands. And the Lord, coming to the Church in the flesh, measured the measures of the earth with lines, because he marked off the bounds of the Church with the fineness of hidden judgment. The hidden lines or measures of this earth were stretched when the preachers, by the working of the Holy Spirit, were called into some parts of the world to go, and kept back from others so as not to approach them.
38.6:
**“Upon what”** — if not upon me
**“are its bases grounded?”** — teachers or prophets
**“Upon what are its bases grounded”** — We take the bases of this earth to be the teachers of holy Church, who bear up the whole weight of the Church by the fixed seriousness of their ways.
**“or who laid the corner stone thereof”**
• because he joined both the two peoples to each other and both the corners
• He adds: “who laid the corner stone thereof?” Morally. The corner stone is a twofold understanding: that in God’s precepts we do outward things, or by contemplating perceive inward ones. To which our mind would never rise unless the Creator had taken up our nature, who showed in himself the examples of both lives. And so he is the corner: in the cities he teaches and heals; on the mountains he prays; so that neither contemplation be forsaken for care of neighbours, nor care of them for contemplation. The mystery of whose incarnation even the angels wonder at. “Or who laid the corner stone thereof?” Him who, receiving in himself here the Jewish people, there the gentile people, joins as it were two walls in the one building of the Church. Since this can be said not of the founding of the world but of the Church, it is plain that what goes before too ought not to be said of the origin of the world. And when he had said much of the building of the Church, he added how even hostile nations were joined to it.
**“Where wast thou when I laid up the foundations of the earth”** — Morally. As the mind of the wicked is dust, so that of the just is earth, whose foundation is faith. So “Where wast thou,” that is, you, a sinner justified by me: call to mind where I found you, and you will be humble. And because man is proud even of good things, God sets a measure on those who advance, so that through what is lacking what is present may be kept humbly. Whence he adds: “tell me if thou hast understanding: who hath laid the measures?” Who but God, who gave this to one and that to another, so that out of many there may be one body. The line is stretched over the soul of the just man when the examples of the fathers are shown to it, so that it may keep its measure and go neither short nor beyond; upon which are the bases, that is, the soul’s intentions, on which the whole rests; whence: “If thy eye be evil.” These are grounded on the foundation, that is, Christ, because we are made firm on the foundation more strongly when we follow the words of God from the inner precepts and weigh them by understanding in the inmost sense.
38.7:
**“When the morning stars praised me together”**
• with the evening stars, that is, elect men
• When the morning stars praised me together, etc. For even the elect angels wondered at the mystery of Christ’s incarnation; who, because they were created first in time, are not unfittingly called morning stars. Or because, often sent to exhort men, while they announce the coming morning they chase the darkness of the present life from human hearts. These morning stars praise the Redeemer’s power along with the evening ones, because together with the men redeemed at the end of the world they glorify the bounty of grace from above.
**“and all the sons of God made a joyful melody”** — And all the sons of God made a joyful melody: it is called jubilation when the gladness of the heart is not fulfilled by the power of the mouth. So the angels praise, who already see the breadth of such great brightness on high. But men make jubilee, who still bear the narrowness of their mouth below. And because the Lord knew these things as future, he tells them as done. But because when the good make jubilee, envy inflames the wicked, whom yet God moderates:
38.8:
**“Who shut up the sea with doors,”** — what God did to the sea he adds
**“when it broke forth as issuing out of the womb:”** — Of whom there is at once added: “Who shut up the sea with doors,” etc. The sea is the world; and by the name of the womb is designated the hidden and malicious thinking of the fleshly. Through this womb the wicked conceive, when they think evil. Through it they bring forth, when they carry out the evil they have thought. So the sea broke forth as issuing out of the womb when the waves of worldly threats, conceived from the wickedness of fleshly thinking, raged for the ruin of holy Church. But by God’s doing this sea was shut up with doors, because holy men were set against the swellings of the persecutors as a kind of doors, so that by their miracles the wrath of the persecutors might be broken and the Church stand.
**“Who shut up the sea with doors”** — Who shut up the sea with doors: morally. The sea is our heart, troubled with fury, bitter with quarrels, swollen with pride. “When it broke forth as issuing out of the womb.” The womb of wicked thinking is youth, of which it is said: “The imagination and thought of man’s heart are prone to evil from his youth.” And the Lord alone shuts up the sea with doors, because he sets the bars of inspired fear against the wicked movements of the heart.
38.9:
**“When I made a cloud the garment thereof”**
• so that it might not see what it does
• Of which sea there follows: “When I made a cloud the garment thereof.” The raging sea is clothed with a cloud, because the cruelty of persecutors is clothed with the veil of its own folly, and is not able to see the light of truth. And because it is held in by the ordering from above, lest it be let loose against the saints as far as it wills, there follows: “and wrapped it in a mist as in swaddling bands.” By swaddling bands the feet and arms are bound, lest they be tossed hither and thither with loosened freedom; because the persecutors of the Church, by the unsteadiness of a restless heart, indeed think childish things, but, held in by hidden ordering, do not stretch out their arms where they will; and even if they lightly desire to commit every evil, they are by no means allowed to carry it out.
• When I made a cloud the garment thereof: our heart, tumultuous with thoughts, is clothed with a cloud, because it is darkened by the confusion of its restlessness so as not to behold eternal rest purely. “And wrapped it in a mist as in swaddling bands,” because it is still bound back from contemplating the highest things by the tender senses of its weakness. “I set my bounds around it.” The Lord sets his bounds around this sea, because he humbles our heart, still troubled by the vexation and care of its corruption, under a measure of contemplation, so that though it longs for more, it yet does not climb beyond what is granted it. Or because he looks on the unlawful movements of the heart, and in some he forbids them consent, in some he holds them back even from delight. Surely he sets bounds on the raging sea, so that it by no means goes out into deed, but the wave dashes itself, murmuring, within the bosom of the mind in temptations. “He made it bars and doors.” By the doors we take the virtues, by the bar the strength of charity. For the raging sea scatters these doors, namely the virtues, unless charity, set against it from the hidden part of the mind, binds them fast. “Hitherto thou shalt come, and shalt go no further,” because while each of the elect is both tempted by vices and yet strives against doing what is wickedly suggested, the sea is as it were held shut. Which, even if within it presses the mind with the tumultuous waves of thoughts, yet does not pass the shores of good living that have been set.
38.10:
**“I set my bounds around it,”** — raging against it
**“I set my bounds around it”** — Because he moderates the wrath of the persecutors by the ordering of his judgments.
**“and made it bars and doors”**
• the glory of Christ and the reverence of the preachers
• And made it bars and doors: the holy teachers, open by preaching to those who follow, shut by their authority to those who resist, are called doors, because they both open the entrance to the faithful and again set themselves against the faithless lest they enter. And by the bar, by whose setting the doors are made firm, the incarnate Lord is designated, because he set these doors the stronger against the onrush of the raging sea the more he strengthened them by his keeping.
**“and doors”** — And doors: he repeated “doors” for confirmation. But if you take the sea generally as the world, the Lord set doors against the world, reining it in first by the law, afterwards by the Gospel; and this “out of the womb,” that is, when the world was growing up near its origin. And then he clothed it with a cloud, because then not openly the light …; he set bounds around its immoderate wanderings, that is, the limit of the precepts. And because he checked the movements of men by sending the Mediator, he adds: “I made it bars”: Christ, who made firm the doors, that is, the precepts, by doing them, and the sea goes no further. Whence he adds: “The sea saw and fled.”
38.11: **“and here thou shalt break”** — And here thou shalt break: a broken wave sinks back into itself when wickedness, overcome, is accused by the very one who did it. “Hitherto thou shalt come, and shalt go no further.” Because surely there is a hidden measure of judgment both of when the storm of persecution leaps forth and when it rests, lest either, not stirred up, it should not exercise the elect, or, unmoderated, should sink them in the deep. “And here thou shalt break thy swelling waves.” When the knowledge of the faith is stretched even to the persecutors, the swelling of the troubled sea is calmed, and there the sea breaks its waves, because coming to the knowledge of the truth it blushes at all it did wickedly. But because this is said to blessed Job so that the glory of his heart from so many virtues might be pressed down, let these things also be discussed morally.
38.12:
**“Shall not”** — you too
**“since thy birth command the morning,”** — through the incarnation he enlightens the elect
**“Didst thou since thy birth command the morning”** — Didst thou since thy birth command the morning? Allegorically. Understand: as I did. The rising of Christ’s Godhead has no before and after, but the rising of his humanity has. Through this rising the dawn knew its place, because the morning knew him. Or the dawn is turned from darkness into the light of morning. Or by the name of the dawn the Church is designated.
