**“who hath spoken inconsiderately”** — As if he said: I would defend my speech if I had uttered it with the weight of reason. Or, after the tongue is convicted of having used lightness, what remains but that it be reined in by silence?
**“answer”** — Answer: he is reproved for silence as before for speech; if he does not know why he was struck, let him yet in silence revere it, because it is from a just one.
**“What can I answer …? I will lay my hand upon my mouth.”**
• work will cover speech; this he says of himself, and in figure of the Church, which covers with the merits of life the faults of the tongue, which no one can tame
• I will lay my hand upon my mouth, etc. That is, that in which I see that I have displeased the strict judge by my speech, I hide before his eyes under the veil of right work.
40.5:
**“One thing I have spoken”**
• that I believed myself just
• One thing I have spoken: for us to speak to men is to open a hidden meaning. But for us to speak to the divine ears is to show the movement of the mind even by the expression of action. And blessed Job confesses that by his speaking he had sinned twice. For to speak one thing unlawfully is to do things worthy of the scourge. And to speak another is even to murmur about the scourge. And the sense is: I believed myself right among men, but now that you speak, I have found myself wicked both before the scourges and stiff after the scourges.
**“which I wish I had not said:”** — because, with you teaching, I have learned that man has no justice
**“and another, to which I will add no more.”** — that I doubted about the scourges, as if less patient
**“to which I will add no more”** — To which I will add no more: because now, the more finely I understand while you speak, the more humbly I search into myself. For a man nearer the light feels what he was before, and loves the more what he now tastes, and judges what lies beneath, and the worthier he is, the more unworthy he seems to himself, and the nearer he is, the farther away.
40.7: **“Gird up thy loins like a man: I will ask thee, and do thou tell me.”** — And the Lord answering Job, etc. What it is for the Lord to answer out of the whirlwind, what for blessed Job to gird his loins, what is God’s asking and what is man’s telling, has already been treated in the Lord’s first speech.
40.8:
**“Wilt thou make void my judgment:”** — while you dispute from your merits against my scourges
**“Wilt thou make void my judgment”** — Wilt thou make void my judgment? Whoever strives to defend himself against the scourges tries to escape the judgment of the one who scourges, like Saul.
**“that thou mayst be justified”** — That thou mayst be justified: because he knows that he is struck without guilt, he is rebuked lest he grow insolent, and is called back to hidden judgments, so that he may believe that what is done by God is just, even if he does not see the cause.
40.9:
**“And hast thou an arm like God?”** — because Job surpasses men, God challenges him to consider his majesty, so that he may think nothing of himself
**“hast thou an arm”** — Hast thou an arm? For God to have an arm is to beget the Son who works.
**“canst thou thunder with a voice like him”** — Canst thou thunder with a voice like him? To thunder with the voice is to show the Son, consubstantial with himself, terribly to the world.
40.10:
**“Clothe thyself with beauty, and set thyself up on high and be glorious, and put on goodly garments.”**
• he who is the same in judgment, but according to each one’s conscience he will be tempered to him, angry or appeased
• Clothe thyself, etc. Understand: as I do. For he clothes himself, of whom it is written: “The Lord hath reigned, he is clothed with beauty.” He is set up on high with us when he is shown to our minds to be impenetrable in his nature. He is glorious who, while he enjoys himself, has no need of praise coming to him. He puts on goodly garments, because the choirs of holy angels whom he created he took up for the use of his beauty, and he shows himself the Church as a kind of glorious garment, “not having spot or wrinkle.” But because by the name of goodly garments he suggests how he joins the just to himself, he shows also how he separates the unjust from himself, saying: “Scatter the proud.” Understand: as I do; because I bear with them even in the time of quiet, united against me, and at some time, coming strict, I scatter them in my fury.
40.11: **“and behold every arrogant man, and humble him”** — And behold every arrogant man, and humble him: as if he said: as I do. For the sinner is looked on by the Lord in two ways: either when he is converted from sin, or when he is punished for sin. And in both ways the arrogant man is laid low in humility.
40.12: **“Look on all that are proud”** — Look on all that are proud: understand: as I do. For the proud are confounded by the Lord’s looking on them, either here condemning their crimes, or there feeling punishments from justice. And the place of the wicked is pride, because it is written: “Pride is the beginning of all sin.” Where ungodliness springs from, there it is contained; so the wicked man is crushed in his place when he is pressed down by the very pride by which he lifts himself up.
40.13:
**“Hide them in the dust together,”**
• whence he will say: “I know you not”
• Hide them, etc. As if he said: as I do. For the Lord by just judgment hides the proud and wicked in the dust, because he allows their hearts to be pressed down by the very earthly business which they choose, having despised the love of the Creator. But with what intention he set all these things first, he shows, saying:
**“and … their faces”** — the intentions of the heart
**“plunge … into the pit.”** — the higher they are lifted up in earthly glory, which is at the bottom, the deeper they are sunk into the abyss
40.14: **“Then I will confess”** — Then I will confess: as if he said: if you can do terrible things, these which I have put forth, then credit to yourself and not to me all the good things you have done. But if you cannot destroy others who sin, it is plain that you are not able by your own strength to free yourself from the guilt of wickedness. And because in the words that went before the Lord brought in the power of his greatness, now in what follows he shows the wickedness of the ancient enemy, so that the good servant, having first heard the virtues of the Lord, might know how much he should love, and, having afterwards known the craft of the devil, might learn how much he should fear. For in the words that follow the Lord makes known to his faithful servant all the enemy’s schemes: all that he seizes by oppressing, all that he flies round by lying in wait, all that he terrifies by threatening, all that he coaxes by persuading, all that he breaks by bringing to despair, all that he deceives by promising. So he begins all the contests of his shiftiness, saying:
40.15:
**“Behold behemoth”**
• or: Vehemoth
• rescue is loved less if the greatness of the danger is not known
**“whom I made with thee, he eateth grass like an ox.”**
• the fleshly
• but those who obey the world, of filth; for it is held for very little
• Behold behemoth which, etc. Under the name behemoth he suggests the ancient enemy; and it is interpreted “animal”; who was made with man not by oneness of time but by the knowledge of reason. So because in the whole nature of things there is no rational animal except the angel and man, whatever cannot use reason was not made with man. So let it be said: “Behold behemoth whom I made with thee,” so that, while man considers that he who was made with him in reason has perished, he may dread the fall of pride near to himself from the very perdition of his neighbour. But because it has been said with whom behemoth was made, let us hear what, lost, he does.
• He eateth grass like an ox, etc. Oxen feed only on clean hay. So he desires to eat grass like an ox, because he seeks to crush with the tooth of his suggestion the clean life of the spiritual; which indeed prevails in those who lead a clean life by effort, but do not seek to please God by it; these are elect in human judgments, but grass in God’s fine examination. So because the Almighty makes known what our enemy does, he now makes known since he prevails, so that the wickedness of his craft, the more openly it is known, the more easily it may be overcome.
**“Behold behemoth whom I made with thee”** — Behold behemoth whom I made with thee: all things are said to have been made together, because when he first made heaven and earth, the things that have their origin from them were made together in substance, but they do not have it in form, which were shown afterwards on the following days: the sun and moon from heaven, shrubs and the like from the earth. Not so man and behemoth, because one is not from the other. If “together” because in the action of God, which is without time, the same would be said of all things; but “together” through the image of wisdom.
40.16:
**“His strength”** — this first after the eating of grass, because after he has taken the spirit he soon stretches himself out to the corruption of the flesh
**“is in his loins”**
• on the day of birth, that is, of conversion, the navel is not cut, that is, lust is not cut away
• There follows: “His strength is in his loins,” etc. The seed-plot of intercourse is said to be in the loins in men, in the navel in women; so because both sexes are laid under the power of the devil chiefly through the weakness of lust, both his strength is said to be in the loins against males, and his force in the navel against females. And it is well said that the strength is in his loins or navel, not in theirs, because surely they become his own body, who, deceived by the coaxing of foul suggestions, succumb to him through the loose ways of lust.
40.17:
**“He setteth up his tail like a cedar,”**
• because then with power, miracles
• He setteth up his tail, etc. By the name of cedar the proud power of the wicked is designated. And the tail of behemoth is said to be that last end of the ancient enemy, when he enters his own vessel, that lost man who is specially called Antichrist. Whom, because he is allowed to lift him up into the swelling of power, now by the honours of the world, now by signs and wonders of feigned holiness, rightly by the Lord’s voice his tail is compared to a cedar. For as the cedar leaves the shrubs behind by its growing, so then Antichrist, gaining the glory of the world for a time, will surpass the measures of men both in the height of honour and in the power of signs. And he is well said to set up (draw tight) his tail, because his whole strength is gathered and packed together in that one damned man, so that he does strong and wonderful things through him the more, the more he drives him on with gathered forces. This he also does through himself, without that man: his first suggestion is soft, which can easily be crushed, but once received it is strengthened by use. The head is grass, the tail a cedar; he wounds with the tooth of delight, with the tail he draws tight and binds; for by consent and use it so hardens and grows that even one willing cannot easily be loosed. On those too whom he has taken, when they are already near death, he heaps heavier faults. So he draws tight his tail when through small vices he makes men worse at the end. Sometimes the grace of God drives out what was received; but when he is driven out he rages more sharply and goes out tearing, for then he rends the mind with pains when he is compelled to go out; and in this he is said to draw tight his tail. But because he has said what the head of the unjust is like, there follows of his members:
**“the sinews of his testicles are wrapped together.”**
• evilly entangled and covered, they cannot be loosed
• because the weak man falls more wickedly
• The sinews of his testicles, etc. He has as many testicles as he possesses preachers of his iniquity. The sinews of his testicles are wrapped together, because the arguments of his preachers are knotted with deceitful assertions, so that the perverse things they urge seem right and cannot be untied. Or his testicles are those who corrupt the hearts of the innocent by the example of their action, and by their example supply other offspring of error; whose sinews are wrapped together and evilly entangled, while they can by no means be loosed by correction. Or the testicles are the wicked thoughts and suggestions by which the defiled soul begets a wicked work. Their sinews, that is, crafty arguments, are so wrapped together that if anyone wishes to flee sins, he cannot without some snare of sin, nor can he be loosed from one without being bound by another. As if someone swears to another, and afterwards a grave crime of his is found which he wishes to do: he fears to betray it lest he be a perjurer, to keep silent lest he be an accomplice. Or one leaving the world, if he is sometimes incautiously commanded by a superior to do the things of the world and leave the things of God: if he obeys, he forsakes God; if he does not obey, he has despised God in his superior, and already returns to his own pleasures. Or one who has risen to church government for a price, beaten by tribulation, attends to the fact that he entered wrongly; but wishing to give it up, he fears the guilt of the flock’s desertion; wishing to keep it, he fears lest the guilt be heavier, to possess what he bought; for he sees neither without the guilt of crime. But if there is no way of escape without sin, let the lesser be chosen, and the entanglement of behemoth is loosed, when one is drawn to the greatest virtues through lesser things committed.
40.18:
**“His bones are like pipes of brass, his gristle”** — the weaker act more wickedly
**“His bones are like pipes of brass”** — His bones are like pipes of brass: the bones are counsels, in which is the whole strength of him who kills not by force but by craft. Through the testicles, that is, suggestions, he puts in things openly harmful; through the bones he counsels as if from good; whence they are compared to pipes of brass, which soothe the ears with sweetness of song and soften the heart; so his deceitful counsels give back a coaxing sound from outward things, which a man can both have and be good; and so they draw the heart to pleasures, so that by praising how well he has done of himself, so that he ought not to be subject to others, he aims at pride. But he tempts more hardly when, under the appearance of virtue, the snare is hidden as if weak. Whence “his gristle is like plates of iron.” Gristle has the appearance of bone but not its firmness; that is, certain vices have the appearance of right but not the virtue: as under the appearance of zeal lies anger, and under gentleness slackness. So through this he makes rewards be hoped for from which punishments follow. But that is more easily corrected at which one blushes; but what is thought virtue, with more difficulty; whence they are compared to plates of iron. This beast has flesh, has bones; but we take his bones to be those in his body who are stronger, in whom, when iniquity has hardened greatly, the whole frame of the body stands through them. Who, because they seek to be seen admirable in power, and yet sometimes show their hearers the sweetness of the tongue, are compared to pipes of brass, because, in the manner of unfeeling metal, they have the sound of speaking well but not the sense of living well.
**“like plates”** — so that it may seem what it is not
**“of iron.”** — by iron the other metals are cut
**“his gristle”** — His gristle: gristle has the appearance of bone, but has not the strength of bone. So his gristle is said to be like iron, because those in his body who are not able to show virtues are kindled more sharply against the voice of the faithful. For when they consider that they cannot do signs and wonders, they prove themselves faithful to him through cruelty. Who are rightly compared to plates of iron, because while they seek to spread themselves round about in cruelty, they stretch themselves out as it were into plates of iron. But this behemoth, who in the last time through his members, or through himself always, exercises himself with such art of iniquity against God’s elect, of what nature, of what condition he is, as if giving the causes of such craft and such strength, he added:
40.19:
**“He is the beginning of the ways of God,”** — so if God did not spare this proud one, what will become of proud man?
**“He is the beginning of the ways”** — He is the beginning of the ways: whence the prophet: “Thou wast the seal of resemblance” [of God]; what does he not have, in whom is the likeness by way of image, which in him is sealed as being one in essence? Again: “Every [tree] of paradise was not like him,” etc. The hosts, even if they are lofty, are not set above or made equal. Again: “Every precious stone was thy covering,” because he had as his adornment all the angels, whom he surpassed; yet this highest one dust, that is, the man Christ, overcame, whose heir too is whoever overcomes. For we take the ways of God as his actions. So behemoth is called the beginning of God’s actions, because surely when he created all things, he first made this one, whom he made more eminent than the other angels. Having heard so many virtues of the ancient enemy, having known such greatness of his condition, who would not sink under the blow of despair? But because he checks our pride by showing the enemy’s power, he also cherishes our weakness, adding:
**“who made him”** — he can do much by his condition, but he is checked by his author
**“he will apply his sword.”**
• everything that is applied is brought back into itself
• Who made him, etc. The sword of behemoth is his very malice in harming; but by him by whom he was made good by nature his sword is applied, because his malice is restrained by divine ordering, lest he be allowed to strike the minds of men as much as he desires.
40.20:
**“To him the mountains bring forth grass:”** — from the success of this world proceed pride and many desires and cares, like grass, by which the devil’s hunger is fed
**“To him the mountains bring forth grass”** — What is the grass of the mountains but the loose pleasure that is begotten from the heart of the proud? For the lofty of the world bring forth grass to this behemoth, because they offer him their loose and slippery pleasures, and refresh him with what they do wickedly.
**“all the beasts of the field”** — because the heart of the proud is laid under every vice
**“shall play”** — or: shall play
**“there all the beasts of the field shall play”** — There all the beasts of the field shall play: the beasts are the unclean spirits, the field the world. And the beasts of the field play in the grass of the mountains, because the demons, cast down from on high into this world, delight in the wicked works of the proud. But because we have heard what this behemoth eats, now let us hear where meanwhile he rests through wicked desire.
40.21:
**“He sleepeth under the shadow”**
• where nothing moves him
• when the sun’s heat withdraws, shadow is made, that is, the numbness and coldness of sin, the rest of the devil
**“in the covert of the reed,”**
• where there is an appearance, like the bark of a tree, but not solidity
• He sleepeth under the shadow, in the covert, etc. In this place by the name of the reed the minds of worldly men given to temporal glory are designated. Who are the emptier within themselves, the higher and sleeker they are shown outwardly; because while they reach out over the surface toward outward glory, they flow away, made firm by no strength within. So he is said to sleep in the covert of the reed, because he holds as if at rest the hearts of those whose pursuits he stirs to the craving for temporal sleekness and height. For he cannot sleep in the hearts of the saints, because even if at any time he settles in them for a brief moment, the heat of heavenly desires wearies him, and he is pricked to withdraw as often as they sigh with inmost love for eternal things.
**“and in moist places.”** — where they press footprints well, where the foot slips
**“in moist places”** — In moist places: the moist places are the minds of earthly men, which the moisture of fleshly lust, because it fills them, makes fluid. The moist places are also voluptuous works or the genital members. If this is so, what else is designated by moist places but lust? So that by the reed the pride of glory, and by the moist places the lust of the body, is designated. These two rule very much in man: the one is of the spirit, the other of the flesh.
40.22:
**“The shades cover his shadow,”** — if the just rebuke these evils, some come to meet them, lest others be corrected
**“The shades cover his shadow”** — The shades cover his shadow: the shades are the devil’s. All the wicked, while they serve the imitation of his iniquity, draw as it were the appearance of an image from his body. And as the reprobate in the plural are his shades, so in the singular each sinner is his shadow. But the shades of this behemoth cover his shadow, when sinners defend another who sins in the same thing in which they are conscious of evil in themselves.
**“shall compass him about”** — Shall compass him about: by the barrenness of willows the life of sinners, who grow green with words without fruit, is signified. By the brook the course of this mortal life is expressed. So the willows of the brook compass behemoth about, because the lovers of mortal life, strangers to good acts as to fruits, cling to him the more tightly, the more largely the delight of passing pleasure soaks them; for he waters them as at the roots of the brook, while the love of fleshly life makes them drunk in their thoughts. But because we have heard what is paid to him by his clients, now let us hear also what he does in them.
40.23:
**“he will drink up a river”** — He will drink up a river: by the name of the river the downward flow of the human race is signified. By the name of the Jordan, those who are already steeped in the sacrament of baptism, because in this river the sacrament of baptism happened to be begun. So because the human race, flowing down to the depths, drew into itself as it were a river up to the times of the Redeemer, it is well now added: “and not wonder.” For the devil did not hold it a great thing that he carried off unbelievers. But because after the coming of the Mediator he seizes even some of the faithful who neglect to live rightly, there is rightly added:
**“and he trusteth”** — And he trusteth: or those who have known the faith of the truth but neglect to live faithfully can be called a river, because they flow downward; the Jordan is called their going down. There are also some who, longing for the ways of truth, cast themselves down and come down from the pride of their old life. And the sense is: he will drink up a river, because he does not think it great when he devours those who run downward through the very pursuits of their life; but he strives greatly to seize those whom he sees, having despised earthly pursuits, now joined to heavenly things. But against him he gives the help of consolation, of whom it is added:
40.24:
**“In his eyes as with a hook he shall take him,”** — with sharp words he bore the probing of the devil, who scented the Godhead through the miracles, saying: “Not in bread alone doth man live,” etc.
**“In his eyes”** — In his eyes: when he had shown the snares of behemoth and his unbridled strength, by which he terrifies, he commends the coming of his Son, by which he cherishes, and suggests in what order this behemoth is to perish; who made of himself a hook for the death of the devil. For he took a body, so that in it behemoth might seek the death of the flesh as his food; but there was the Godhead, which would pierce the jaw of the robber. And he was caught by the hook in his eyes, because he both knew and bit; and having first confessed by knowing, by confessing he trembled, and at last afterwards did not fear, when he hungered in him for the death of the flesh as his own food. So because it has been said what our head did by himself, now there follows what he does through his members.
**“and … with stakes”** — And with stakes: through the nostrils a scent is drawn, and by the breath drawn in it comes about that even a thing placed far off is known. So by the nostrils of behemoth his crafty snares are designated, through which he strives most shrewdly to know the hidden good things of our heart, and to scatter them by most wicked persuasion. So our Lord bores through his nostrils with stakes, because, piercing his crafty snares with the sharp senses of the saints, he unnerves them. But because behemoth is spread out through various devices of fraud, he is further marked by another name joined to it.

41.1:
**“Canst thou draw out the leviathan with a hook,”**
• from the waters of the human race
• as I, who send my Son
• For there follows: “Canst thou draw out?” Leviathan is called “their addition,” namely of men, on whom he once brought the guilt of transgression and daily stretches it, by most wicked suggestions, even to eternal death. He can also be called Leviathan in mockery; for to the first man he declared that he would add godhead, but he took away immortality. So he can be called in mockery “the addition” of men, to whom, while he promised to add what they were not, he took away by deceiving even what they were. But he was caught by a hook, because, while in our Redeemer he bit the bait of the body through his attendants, the barb of the Godhead pierced him. The line of this hook is that lineage of the fathers recorded in the Gospel, by which this hook was wonderfully let down into these depths of the waters, where the whale, with open mouth, was devouring almost all. At the end of the line the hook is Christ.
**“or canst thou tie his tongue with a cord?”** — but if he is no longer openly powerful, he bites by snares; the Lord puts a ring in his nose
**“or canst thou tie … with a cord”** — Or canst thou tie … with a cord? Because by a cord sins are signified, it is said by the prophet: “Woe to you that draw iniquity with cords of vanity.” Iniquity is drawn with cords when guilt is drawn out by increase. Again, by a cord faith is expressed, as Solomon bears witness: “A threefold cord is not easily broken,” because the faith which is woven from the mouth of the preachers out of the knowledge of the Trinity, remaining strong in the elect, is broken up only in the heart of the reprobate. So here nothing hinders the name of cord from being understood either as sin or as faith. For the Lord made flesh tied Leviathan’s tongue with a cord, because, appearing in the likeness of sinful flesh, of sin he condemned sin, and condemned all the preachings of his errors. Or Leviathan’s tongue is bound with a cord, because when faith became known in the world through the holy preachers, the teaching of the world ceased to break forth.
41.2:
**“Canst thou put a ring in his nose,”** — the power of judgment hems in his snares
**“Canst thou put a ring”** — Canst thou put a ring? By the nostrils the snares, by the ring the omnipotence of divine power is signified. So a ring is put in his nostrils when his shrewdness is held back, surrounded by the strength of protection from above, lest he prevail against the weaknesses of men as much as he explores with hidden devices of betrayal. By the name of ring the help of hidden judgment can also be designated. Whence the power of judgment is called a ring, because it binds on every side like a sickle, because it gathers within itself and can by no means be avoided.
**“and”** — or: or
**“or bore through his jaw with a buckle”** — Or bore through his jaw with a buckle: the buckle does not differ from the understanding of the ring, because it too binds where it is put by going round. So the Lord bores through Leviathan’s jaw with a buckle, because by the power of his mercy he so meets the malice of the ancient enemy that sometimes he loses even those he has already taken, and they fall as it were from his mouth, because after faults committed they return to innocence. Or he has in his mouth not him who sins but him whom he tempts; but his jaw is bored through, because by that by which he crushes the just he loses them, because thus they are humbled in good things, like Paul.
41.3:
**“Will he make many supplications to thee, or speak soft words to thee?”**
• namely as to me
• There follows: “Will he make many supplications to thee?” Understand: as to me. If these things are referred to the person of the Son incarnate, he also spoke soft words when he said: “We know that thou art the Son of God,” and “If thou cast us out, send us into the herd of swine.” Or he makes many supplications to the Lord when on the last day of judgment the wicked, who are his body, beg to be spared.
41.4:
**“Will he make … with thee”** — as with me
**“Will he make a covenant with thee”** — Will he make a covenant with thee? Understand: as with me. In a covenant the will of disagreeing parties is fulfilled, so that each comes to its wish and ends the quarrels with the desired end. So the ancient enemy, by his malice, disagrees with God’s innocence, but even in disagreeing does not depart from his judgment. For he always seeks to tempt the just with ill will; yet the Lord permits this to happen either mercifully or justly. So this licence of tempting is called a covenant, in which both the desire of the tempter is carried out, and yet through it the will of the just Redeemer is wonderfully fulfilled.
**“and wilt thou take him”** — And wilt thou take him? Understand: as I do. By the covenant which he is said to make with the Lord, he is declared to be taken as a servant, because he obeys the nods of divine power by that by which he exercises the wrath of his most wicked will. So he is a servant by covenant, because while he is allowed to fulfil his will, he is bound by the will of the counsel from above, so that, willing, he tempts God’s elect, and by tempting, unknowing, proves them. And it is to be noted that he is said to be taken by the Lord not only as a servant but as a servant for ever. For Leviathan, after the end of the present life, will be handed over with his body to the flames; and when the just behold these torments they grow in the praises of God, because they see in themselves the gift with which they have been rewarded, and look in those on the punishment they have escaped. So if both here the temptation of this Leviathan and there his damnation profit the just, he is a servant for ever, while unknowing he serves the praises of God: for there is just punishment there and unjust will here.
41.5:
**“Shalt thou play with him as with a bird,”** — he is an animal when he tempts through lust, a serpent when through malice, a bird when through pride
**“Shalt thou play with him”** — Shalt thou play with him? Our adversary is first called behemoth, afterwards Leviathan, now is compared to a bird in the mockery of his perdition. Behemoth, which is interpreted “beast,” because he no longer lifts himself up with any breath toward the beauty of heavenly things, is a beast by brute sense, a dragon by the malice of harming; a bird because he is proudly lifted up by the subtlety of his nature. With him, as with a bird, the Lord played, when in the passion of his Only-begotten he showed him the bait but hid the snare. He saw what he would take in his mouth, but did not see what would hold his throat; and, mocked in the manner of a bird, he bore the snare of his Godhead while he bit the bait of his humanity.
**“or tie him up for thy handmaids?”** — in himself, whose pestilence is hemmed in; or in his members, who are restrained by terror
**“or tie him up”** — Or tie him up: understand: as I do. In menservants, even if their condition is despised, manhood is strong. But in handmaids, both condition and sex lie low together. And he well declares that he ties up Leviathan not for menservants but for handmaids, because, sending his preachers for our redemption against the pride of the world, he left the wise and chose the foolish, left the strong and chose the weak, left the rich and chose the poor. But because he suggests whom the Lord sends against him, now he adds also what those who are sent do.
41.6: **“Shall friends cut him in pieces”** — Shall friends cut him in pieces? Leviathan is cut in pieces as often as his members are separated from him by the sword of the divine word. And he names friends those whom above he calls handmaids; he also calls them merchants. For the holy preachers are first handmaids through fear, afterwards friends through faith. At last merchants, when they pay out preaching and bring back faith to the apostles.
41.7:
**“Wilt thou fill nets with … skin”** — with the foolish
**“Wilt thou fill nets”** — Wilt thou fill nets? By the nets or cabins of fishes the churches of the faithful, which make up the one Catholic Church, are designated, which gather out of every kind of fish, because they catch the wicked with the good, the proud with the humble, the wrathful with the gentle, the foolish with the wise. And in the skin of this Leviathan, which is on the outside, are the subjects serving these last things. And by the head the rulers are designated. So he says: “Wilt thou fill nets with his skin, and the cabins of fishes with his head?” Understand: as I do. Who first gather within the Church of the faithful the last and lowest, as the devil’s skin; after a little, his head, that is, the prudent adversaries, I subject to myself. For first he gathered the unlearned, afterwards the philosophers.
**“and the cabins of fishes with … head”** — with the prudent
41.8:
**“Lay thy hand upon him”** — That is: as I do. Who, checking him with strong power, he is not allowed to rage more than is expedient. Or to lay the hand upon him is to overcome him by the might of virtue, so that the sense is: do you check him by your own virtue?
**“remember the battle,”** — if you attend well to the devil’s strength, in how many ways he harms, you do not murmur at what you suffer, because these things profit and free from him
**“and speak no more.”** — Whence there is added: “remember the battle, and speak no more.” As if it were said: if you consider the battle of the hidden enemy against you, you do not accuse whatever you suffer from me. For it is done by the medicine of divine ordering, that the inward wound is closed by outward pains, and by the cuttings of the scourges the inner rottenness of vices, which could have taken hold of the mind, is driven back. But because Leviathan flatters himself with a false promise about the divine mercy:
41.9:
**“Behold his hope shall fail him,”** — There follows: “Behold his hope shall fail him,” etc. Which must be so understood of him that it can also be referred to his body, because the wicked, who do not fear the strictness of divine justice, flatter themselves in vain about mercy; and at once, for our consolation, he announces his future destruction.
**“and in the sight of all he shall be cast down.”** — And in the sight, etc. He shall be cast down in the sight of all, because when the eternal judge appears terribly, with the legions of angels standing by and all the elect brought to this spectacle, this cruel beast is led captive into the midst, and now with his body, that is, with all the reprobate, will be handed over to eternal fires. And it is well that he shall be cast down in the sight of all, because his death, seen, will then give joy, whose life is now borne with. But lest we should complain, saying: “Lord, who art not ignorant that this Leviathan is of such strength, why dost thou rouse him in the contest of our weakness?” he added:
41.10:
**“I will not stir him up, like one that is cruel”** — And as if the reason were at once asked of us: how do you not stir up like one that is cruel him whom we know, since you allow him to invade and devour so many?
**“for who can resist my countenance?”**
• those whom I choose I can snatch away
• He adds: “for who can resist,” etc. As if he said: I do not stir him up like one that is cruel, because I mightily snatch my elect out of his strength. For on account of this power it is said: “for who can resist my countenance?” And again, I damn the proud not unjustly but with reason. For to this it refers:
41.11:
**“Who hath given me before”** — Who hath given me before: as if he said: I am compelled by no reason to spare the reprobate, because I am not held their debtor by their action.
**“All things that are under heaven are mine.”** — All things that are under heaven, etc. It is plain that both the things that are under heaven and those that are above the heavens serve his will. But because he is speaking of Leviathan, who is no longer held in the seat of the ethereal heaven, he declares that all things that are under heaven are his, so as to teach that he too who fell from heaven serves his power. As if he said: this Leviathan lost my blessedness indeed, but did not escape his Lord.
41.12: **“I will not spare him, nor his mighty words, and framed to make supplication.”** — I will not spare him, etc. Here it is understood of his body, that is, all the wicked. For there are some within the Church who have long prayers to God but do not have the life of those who pray. And by the fact that mighty words framed to make supplication are mentioned, the plain emptiness of the prayer is understood and shown. For to pray truly is to sound forth bitter groans in prayer or groans in compunction, and not framed words.
41.13:
**“Who can discover”** — the more he is broken, the more subtly he tempts; but the Lord uncovers it
**“the face of his garment?”** — Who can discover, etc. Understand: but I? Leviathan tempts the religious in one way, those given to this world in another. For to the wicked he openly puts forward the evils they desire; but lying in wait secretly for the good, he deceives them under the appearance of holiness; and in that the work of iniquity is softened, it is often clothed with the appearance of holiness. And the garments of his pretence cannot be uncovered except through the grace of God, who breathes into the minds of his servants the grace of most subtle discernment, so that, his malice being uncovered, they may see bare his face, which he hides covered under the habit of holiness.
**“or who can go into the midst of his mouth?”** — Or who can go into the midst of his mouth? etc. Understand: but I? Who through the discerning minds of the elect examine the words of his suggestions, and show that they are not as they sounded. For they seem to promise good, but draw to a lost end. So to go into the midst of his mouth is to pierce the words of his craft, so that one weighs not what they sound but what they aim at. Adam would have gone into the midst of his mouth had he not neglected to weigh carefully the intention of his persuasion.
41.14:
**“the doors”** — through which one enters to see him as in his power
**“of his face”** — The doors of his face, etc. The doors of his face are the wicked teachers, through whom the way of perdition is opened; which the Lord opens, because he makes the minds of hypocrites understandable to his elect. And because Antichrist, coming, will gain even the highest powers of this world, he will try to draw the hearts of men to himself by preachers sent to them and to bend them by the powers stirred up.
**“Who can open …? his teeth are terrible round about.”** — There follows: “his teeth are terrible round about.” He calls these teeth too, whom above he called doors. For the perverse preachers are his doors, because they open the entrance of perdition. They are his teeth, because those whom they catch in error they break off from the solidity of the truth; whose preaching could easily be despised, but the terror of worldly powers joined to it exalts it. So round about his teeth there is terror. As if it were said openly: these perverse preachers crush some by persuading, because there are others round about them who afflict the minds of the weak by terrifying them.
41.15:
**“His body is like molten shields,”**
• hard against darts, but fragile by their own falling
• His body, etc. Every vessel that is molten is hard indeed, but when it falls is wont to be fragile. So the body of Leviathan, that is, all the wicked, who are hard through obstinacy but fragile through their life, are compared to molten shields, who, lest the words of those who rebuke them reach them, prepare as it were shields of defence against the darts of their opponents.
**“shut close up with scales pressing upon one another.”** — Shut close up with scales, etc. The devil’s body, that is, the reprobate, when it is rebuked for its iniquity, tries to excuse itself with whatever evasions it can, and puts up as it were certain scales of defence so that it cannot be pierced by the arrow of truth.
41.16:
**“One is joined to another,”** — because he fears for himself when they are rebuked together
**“and not so much as any air can come between them:”** — One is joined to another, etc. These scales of sinners are both hardened and joined together, lest they be pierced by any breath of life from the mouth of preachers. For those whom like guilt joins in agreeing stubbornness, perverse defence also packs together, so that they protect one another with mutual defence about their crimes; and while they shield their iniquities with proud defence, they by no means let the breaths of holy exhortation enter into them.
41.17: **“They stick one to another and they hold one another fast, and shall not be separated.”** — They stick one to another, etc. For those who could have been corrected if divided endure united in the stubbornness of their iniquities, and holding one another they cannot be separated, because they are bound to one another’s defence by this, that they remember they are like each other in all things. Having described the body, the speech is brought back to the head, to what it will do in the last time.
41.18:
**“His sneezing”** — the last stirring, through Antichrist
**“is like the shining of fire,”**
• shining with miracles
• His sneezing, etc. In sneezing a puffing rises from the chest, which, when it finds no open pores to flow out, touches the brain, and going out packed through the nostrils at once shakes the whole head. So in this body of Leviathan, that is, in the evil spirits or in reprobate men, a puffing rises from the chest when pride lifts itself up from the power of the world; which as it were finds no pores to flow out, because in that in which it is lifted up against the just it is prevented, by God’s ordering, from prevailing as much as it desires. And rising up it touches the brain and shakes it, because Satan’s gathered pride troubles the head, when it rouses the very author of the evil spirits, through Antichrist, to the persecution of the faithful. Then his packed puffing goes out through the nostrils, because the whole iniquity of his pride is shown by the open blasts of malice. And because the wise of the world cling to his tyranny:
**“and his eyes”** — whose counsellors are the wise of the world
**“like the eyelids of the morning.”**
• promising better things, like the serpent in paradise
• There follows: “his eyes,” etc. By the eyes, which, clinging to the head, serve the use of seeing, his counsellors are not unfittingly designated, who, while by perverse schemes they foresee how things are to be done, offer as it were a road shown to the feet of his evil workers; who are compared to the eyelids of the morning. We take the eyelids of the morning as the last hours of the night, in which night as it were opens its eyes, while it already shows the beginnings of the coming light. So the prudent of the world, clinging to the malice of Antichrist with perverse counsels, are as the eyelids of the morning, because the faith which they find in Christ they declare to be as it were the error of night, and promise that the veneration of Antichrist is the true morning. They pledge themselves to drive back the darkness and to announce the light of truth by shining signs.
41.19:
**“Out of his mouth go forth lamps”** — Therefore there follows: “Out of his mouth,” etc. Those who foresee are called eyes; those who preach, the mouth. But out of this mouth go forth lamps, because they kindle the minds of the hearers to the love of faithlessness; and where they seem to shine through wisdom, there they burn up through wickedness.
**“like torches of lighted fire”** — Like torches of lighted fire: a torch, when it is kindled, has indeed a sweet smell, but a dark light; so the preachers of Antichrist, because they claim for themselves the appearance of holiness, practise the works of iniquity; because even if what they give off smells pleasant, yet what they shine with is black. They smell sweet through the pretence of justice, but burn darkly through the committing of wickedness.
41.20:
**“Out of his nostrils”** — on account of these, the surer sight grows dim in the elect
**“goeth smoke,”**
• which troubles even the eyes of the elect but does not blind them
• Out of his nostrils goeth, etc. For the sharpness of the eyes is wounded by smoke. So smoke is said to go out of his nostrils, because from the snares of his miracles a darkening doubt is begotten even in the heart of the elect. And well in this darkness of smoke the very fervour of souls is also expressed, when there is added:
**“like that of a pot heated and boiling.”** — Like that of a pot, etc. Each soul is then like a boiling pot, bearing the onrush of its thoughts like the foam of burning waves, which both the fire of zeal stirs and temporal oppression itself holds shut within, in the manner of a pot. Or smoke is declared to go out of his nostrils, by whose harmful breathings wicked thought is born in human hearts, by which the sharpness of the mind is dulled; the force of which smoke he expresses when he adds: “like that of a pot heated and boiling.” For the pot is heated when the human mind is driven on by the persuasions of the malignant enemy. And the pot boils when it is now kindled, by consent too, in the desires of wicked persuasion, and throws off as many waves as it were by boiling, through which it stretches its wickednesses even to inward works; which he follows out still more openly.
41.21:
**“His breath kindleth coals”** — His breath kindleth coals, etc. What does he call coals but the minds of the reprobate, kindled in earthly lusts, setting others aflame for unlawful things? So he blows on the coals with as much breath as, by the effort of hidden suggestion, he sets human minds aflame for unlawful things.
**“and a flame cometh forth out of his mouth.”** — And a flame, etc. The flame of his mouth is the very urging of his hidden speech.
41.22:
**“In his neck strength shall dwell,”** — In his neck, etc. By the neck of Leviathan the stretching-out of pride is designated, because, lifting himself up against God with the pretence of holiness, he is also raised up by the swelling of power. And strength is said to dwell in his neck, because power, joined to it, also supports his pride. For whatever is then proudly lifted up is also carried out with the force of worldly power. And because he who becomes known to his friendship through perverse ways first loses the riches of the mind:
**“and want goeth before his face.”**
• first he takes away the good things, lessens the strength, and then pours in the knowledge of his iniquity
• There follows: “and want goeth before his face,” etc. By the face knowledge is wont to be designated. So want goes before the face of Leviathan, because by tempting he strips minds of virtues through negligence before he who is tempted recognizes his snares. So by what is said, “In his neck strength shall dwell,” the force of violence is shown; and by what is added, “and want goeth before his face,” the subtlety of fraud is designated. Or it goes before his face, because after he appears in that damned man whom he will take up, the riches of miracles are taken away from holy Church. For when prophecy is hidden, the grace of healings will be taken away.
41.23:
**“The members of his flesh”** — The members of his flesh, etc. The flesh of Leviathan is all the reprobate, who do not rise by desire to the understanding of the spiritual fatherland. And the members of his flesh are those who are joined to the same who act perversely and go before them into iniquity; and so the unity of the reprobate presses the life of the good the more hardly, the harder it sets itself against it by those gathered together. But what the divine mercy at last does against him he adds.
**“cleave one to another”** — Cleave one to another: but if they were divided like the sea, Israel would pass over to the land of promise; so that as it is harmful if unity is lacking to the good, so it is more harmful if it is not lacking to the wicked.
**“he shall send lightnings against him,”** — but lest we be frightened by this, he adds
**“and they shall not be carried to another place.”** — He shall send lightnings against him, etc. By the name of lightnings the dreadful sentences of the last judgment are designated, because those they strike they burn for ever. Which shall not be carried to another place, because by their fire they burn not the grain but the chaff. But because punishment does not correct this Leviathan, there follows:
41.24:
**“His heart shall be as hard”** — His heart shall be as hard: the heart of the ancient enemy shall be hardened like a stone, because it will never be softened by any penitence of conversion. Who, because he will be fitted only for the blows of eternal vengeance, it is fittingly added:
**“and as firm as”** — And as firm as: an anvil is set up for this, that it may be struck with frequent blows. So Leviathan shall be made firm like a smith’s anvil, because he will be hemmed in by the bonds of hell, so as to be beaten by the continual striking of eternal punishment. On the anvil other vessels are formed, but it itself is not changed into another vessel by so many blows.
41.25:
**“When he shall raise him up, the angels shall fear,”**
• it appeared to the angels, that is, the preachers, what is commanded from what follows; for he adds: it was preached to the gentiles
• When he shall raise him up, etc. He has put the future for the past. For when Leviathan fell from the citadel of blessedness, even the elect angels were terrified at his ruin, so that, when the fall of pride cast him out, fear itself might make them firm to stand more strongly; and they were purified, because, he going out with the reprobate legions, the elect alone remained. Or if it is read as future, he calls the preachers angels, who will fear when he is raised up, because when he is snatched away by the whirlwind of judgment, those who can be found in their bodies, shaken with immense terror, tremble, though they are messengers of the fatherland above. And because by this dread whatever rust of light vices could have been in them is burnt out of them, he fittingly added:
**“and being affrighted shall purify themselves”** — And being affrighted shall purify themselves: those who are in the flesh cannot but be shaken with such terror by the strict judge, when all the elements are shaken; but yet the hope of the kingdom near at hand gladdens their minds. And meanwhile what he does follows:
41.26:
**“When … shall lay at him”** — When … shall lay at him: in this place by the name of sword anger is signified. And he who is swept away through the steep places of fury is said not to lay hold of the sword but to be laid hold of by the sword. So Leviathan, because through the reprobate man he has taken up he is unbridled in the anger of every kind of cruelty, is said to be laid hold of by the sword. “Nor a spear, nor a breastplate,” because the devil, coming into Antichrist, will appear of such strength that, if help from above were lacking, he would both blunt the sharpness of the preachers and destroy the long-suffering of the patient.
**“a sword”** — A sword: that is, that lost man will have taken up the devil, or anger itself. He who takes up anger for the use of justice holds the sword; he by whom anger is condemned is both swept away through steep places and laid hold of by it.
41.27: **“For he shall esteem … as”** — For he shall esteem … as: what above he called the spear he has here below repeated with the name of iron, and what above the breastplate, here brass. For iron is sharpened so that the adversary may be wounded, while brass is consumed by almost no rust. So by iron the darts of preaching, and by brass the constancy of long-suffering, is designated. So iron as straw and brass as rotten wood, because, unless divine grace protects, he consumes both the strength of the preachers like chaff by the fire of his wickedness, and reduces the constancy of the patient to dust like rotten wood. But the more he is lifted up, the more the saints gird themselves against him. That the arrow of truth then does not profit in the reprobate, he adds; but the saints themselves are despised. And this is: “like stubble.” But what wonder if he despises the strength of men, who also scorns the torments of the judgment from above? And this is: “As stubble.”
41.28:
**“The archer shall not put him to flight,”** — The archer shall not put him to flight, etc. He takes arrows as the words of the preachers. And the sense is: the preacher’s arrow does not shake him out of the hearts of the reprobate, because whoever is laid hold of by him now scorns to hear the words of the preachers.
**“are to him like stubble”** — Are to him like stubble: by the sling the Church is figured. For as, when the sling is whirled round, stones come out of it by which the breasts of adversaries are struck, so when the Church is turned by the rolling of the times through the round of tribulations, strong men come forth from her, by whom, as by the blows of a stone, the hearts of the wicked are beaten. So because Leviathan, having taken up that damned man, despises any strong men of the Church as weak, the stones of the sling are turned to stubble for him.
41.29:
**“As stubble will he esteem”** — As stubble will he esteem: because by the hammer coming from above the weight of the heavenly blow is expressed, what is it that Leviathan despises the hammer, but that he scorns to dread the stroke of punishment from above? And “as stubble,” because he prepares himself against the weights of just wrath as against the lightest terrors.
**“and he will laugh him to scorn who shaketh”** — And he will laugh him to scorn who shaketh: to shake the spear is to prepare eternal death for him from strict punishment. But he laughs to scorn him who shakes the spear, because whatever is heavy, whatever horrible, he foresees, he does not fear to suffer. But the more he sees that he cannot escape eternal torments, the harder he rises up in practising wickedness. Whence comes what follows:
41.30:
**“The beams of the sun shall be under him,”** — which also profits the good
**“shall be under him”** — Shall be under him: by the sun’s beams he shows the sharpness of the wise. And the sense is: those who within the Church seemed by the sharpness of wisdom to sprinkle as it were rays of light, and by the authority of uprightness to shine from above, bend themselves to the power of Leviathan both by the perversity of their work and by the coaxing of flattery, while they subject themselves to earthly powers acting wickedly. So he lays the light of heaven under his feet when the wise, by immoderate sharpness, think wicked things in the Scriptures, or are in some way made subject to him.
**“and he shall strew gold under him”** — now in mystery, and then openly
**“like mire.”** — it was not virtue before God, even if before men
**“he shall strew gold under him like”** — He shall strew gold under him like: in this place gold is taken as the brightness of holiness. Mire is either the avarice of earthly things, or the contagion of wicked teachings, or the filth of fleshly pleasures. For many who within the Church seemed to shine with the brightness of justice he subjects to himself either by the lust for earthly things, or by the contagion of erring teaching, or by fleshly pleasures; and so he strews gold under himself like mire. But if this is done against those whom some virtue shows bright, what will he do with those who are openly wicked?
41.31:
**“He shall make the deep sea to boil like a pot,”** — There follows: “He shall make … to boil.” By the sea the life of worldly men, by the deep their high and hidden thoughts are expressed. This deep sea Leviathan makes to boil like a pot, because in the time of the last persecution he strives to stir the minds of the reprobate against the life of the elect by the flame of cruelty; because, persuaded by pestilent error, they so serve Antichrist in these things that they think they are then rather offering service to Christ.
**“and shall make it as when ointments boil.”** — There follows: “and shall make it as …” Ointments, when they boil, give off the fragrance of sweetness. So because Leviathan so seduces the hearts of the reprobate that whatever they do from the iniquity of faithlessness they suppose they do for the truth of right faith, what they practise out of zeal for religion smells good to them as it were.
**“and shall make it”** — And shall make it: they are the more savage, the better they seem to themselves to act. Whence, to increase the delusion, signs follow them.
41.32:
**“A path shall shine after him,”** — where he passes, he leaves wonder from his miracles
**“shall shine after him”** — A path shines after Leviathan, because the works of those whose hearts he pierces he makes bright with wonders. Whence in the Gospel: “There shall arise false Christs and false prophets, and shall shew great signs and wonders.”
**“he shall esteem the deep as growing old.”** — those whom he does not take in this way he invades otherwise, so that they do not hesitate to cling to pleasures, because the punishments have an end
**“he shall esteem the deep”** — He shall esteem the deep: the deep is put for judgment, old age for the nearness of the end. So Leviathan shall esteem the deep as growing old, because he so makes foolish the hearts of the reprobate as to pour into them the suspicion that the judgment to come will as it were be ended. For he esteems the deep to grow old who thinks that the punishment from above will at some time end in its torments.
41.33:
**“There is no power upon earth”** — There is no power upon earth: after his force and frauds he briefly adds the hugeness of his strength. His power is declared to be more eminent than all upon earth, because even if by the desert of his action he fell below men, yet he surpasses the whole human race by the condition of the angelic nature; even if he lost blessedness, he did not lose the greatness of his nature, because he surpasses all human things; even if he lies beneath the merits of the saints. So the higher the devil’s nature is, the greater is man’s glory in overcoming.
**“who was made”**
• free and unbridled by his own vice
• Who was made, etc. He was indeed so made by nature that he ought to have feared his Creator chastely; but by his perversity he was made such that he feared no one. For he scorned to be subject to him by whom he had been made; whose pride is still described.
**“to fear no one.”** — neither God nor what he will suffer
41.34:
**“He beholdeth every high thing”** — He beholdeth every high thing: that is, he looks down as from on high on all, as placed beneath him; because by his intention he strives against his author, he disdains to think anyone like himself. For he turns his craving for loftiness into stiffness of mind, so that he is now unfeeling; and it is a remedy for the proud man to despise what he cannot surpass. Which also fits his members, because all who are lifted up by the swelling of the heart despise with the haughtiness of pride all whom they see.
**“he is king over”** — He is king over: after many things he shows whence all things come. This is the devil’s title, as humility is Christ’s, by whose sign each army is told apart. The Lord therefore put pride at the end of his speech, so that, when after all the evils they speak of the pride of this Leviathan, he might show what was worse than all evils; and by its being placed at the bottom it is shown to be the root of vices. For as the root is covered below, but the branches spread out from it outwardly, so pride hides itself within, and from it open evils come.

42.1: **“Then Job answered”** — Then Job answered: after the Lord had shown his faithful servant how strong and how crafty Leviathan his enemy is, while he laid open his strength and his frauds, blessed Job answered to both, saying:
42.2: **“I know that thou canst do all things”** — I know that thou canst do all things: for against his strength he says: “I know that thou canst do all things.” And against his hidden schemes he added: “and no thought is hid from thee.” Whence he reproaches the same Leviathan, saying:
42.3:
**“Who is this”** — as I
**“that hideth counsel without knowledge?”** — Who is this? etc. Leviathan hides counsel without knowledge, because although he hides himself with many frauds against our weakness, yet he is uncovered to us by the holy inspiration of our protector. So, having heard the strength and craft of the devil, and the power of the Creator, which both strongly holds him in and mercifully covers us, blessed Job lays open what he thinks of himself, saying:
**“Therefore I have spoken unwisely, and things that above measure exceeded my knowledge.”** — Therefore I have spoken unwisely, etc. What he had said he would believe he had said wisely, if he did not hear the words of the higher wisdom, in comparison with which all that is wise in us is foolish. And the more he advances in contemplating the knowledges of God, the more he knows himself to be nothing. And he believes that his knowledge went beyond measure, because in the words of God he recognized more of the secrets of his wisdom than he had reckoned. So Moses too, from the time he heard the Lord, says he has become more impeded and slower of tongue.
42.4:
**“Hear”** — therefore
**“and I will speak:”** — if you hear
**“Hear, and I will speak”** — Hear, and I will speak: for God to hear is to perceive our desires; for us to speak to the Lord is to gape toward him with eager desires. And because each one asks since he does not know, for man to ask the Lord is to know himself ignorant in his sight. And for God to answer is to teach by hidden inspirations him who has humbly known himself ignorant. And the sense is: “Hear, and I will speak”: mercifully perceive my desires, so that, while your mercy, perceiving them, helps them, they may rise to you more manifold.
**“I will ask thee”** — I will ask thee: that is, I know myself ignorant from the contemplation of your knowledge. “Answer”: teach one who humbly knows his own folly. For what he would ask, out of the desire of humility, and that he sought God to answer him out of the teaching of inspiration, is made plain; for he declared that he would ask, but asking nothing he adds:
42.5:
**“With the hearing of the ear, I have heard thee, but now my eye seeth thee.”**
• let him acknowledge great things of mercy
• With the hearing of the ear I have heard, etc. By these words he shows that as much as sight is higher than hearing, so much does what he was before differ from what he afterwards gained through the scourges. And because with the inward eye he had beheld the light of truth more, judging the darkness of his humanity he saw more.
42.6:
**“Therefore I reprehend myself”**
• behold the haircloth by which he is pricked in grief
• Whence there follows: “Therefore I reprehend myself,” etc. The less each one sees himself, the less he displeases himself. And the greater the light of grace he perceives, the more he knows himself to be blameworthy. But because there is no knowledge of blame unless the laments of penance also follow:
**“and do penance in dust and ashes.”**
• I am proud of no gift of God, because, taken from dust, I know that by the sentence of death brought upon me I am brought back to dust
• There follows: “and do penance,” etc. To do penance in dust and ashes is, having contemplated the divine essence, to know oneself to be nothing but dust and ashes.
42.7:
**“And after the Lord had spoken these words to Job,”** — And after the Lord had spoken, etc. Because we would be in doubt, God judges about the words of Job, who rehearsed the deeds of his virtue, and of his friends, who defended the glory of God’s justice against him.
**“he said to Eliphaz the Themanite: My wrath is kindled”**
• first he cuts the wound
• He said to, etc. Job was praised to the enemy; he is preferred to these; and yet, because man cannot be without blame before the eyes of God, he is praised in comparison with others, and yet has, from being a man, something to be judged. For he believed he was scourged for guilt, not for grace, and in this he is rebuked, and yet preferred to his friends.
**“against thee, and against thy two friends, because you have not spoken the thing that is right before me,”** — within, where many displease who please outwardly
**“as my servant Job hath.”**
• because he said nothing proudly but humbly
• Right before me, etc. For as far as human judgments go, Job’s friends would be believed to have said many things in their words more rightly than he; but because God is just and merciful, he both strictly refutes his friends through justice and kindly converts them through mercy.
42.8:
**“Take unto you therefore”** — he shows the remedy
**“seven oxen, and seven rams, and go to my servant Job, and offer for yourselves a holocaust:”**
• because they have no pardon of guilt unless, by the Spirit of sevenfold grace, they are gathered to the universal peace from which they had been cut off
• For there follows: “Take unto you therefore,” etc. The inward physician first made known the rottenness of the wound, and afterwards showed the remedies for obtaining health. And because Job’s friends bear the figure of heretics, they are commanded to offer through Job, because they cannot appease the Lord’s wrath by sacrifice unless they are converted to the Catholic faith, which Job signifies; so that they may obtain salvation by the prayers of him whose faith they attacked with perverse assertions. And by the bulls the neck of pride, by the rams the leadership which is exercised by heretics over the deceived peoples, is expressed. So to offer bulls and rams in sacrifice is to slay proud leadership by the humility of conversion, so that, the neck of pride being tamed, those who long tried to go before by teaching may learn to follow by obeying. And they are atoned for by seven sacrifices, because, returning to the Church through the victim of humility, they receive the gifts of the Spirit of sevenfold grace.
**“and my servant Job shall pray for you: his face I will accept,”**
• the proper mirror of the elect is to think of themselves as below those above whom they are
• And my servant Job, etc. So the Church prays for heretics. Those contained in the ark are saved; outside, the water kills all. In one house, that is, the Church, the lamb is commanded to be eaten, and none of its flesh to be carried outside; “give not that which is holy to dogs.”
**“that folly be not imputed to you: for you have not spoken right things before me, as my servant Job hath.”** — For you have not, etc. The sentence which he had spoken once in judging he confirms by repeating it again; and so that the justice of blessed Job and the injustice of his friends may be shown more plainly, his praise and their blame are brought out with a repeated voice, so that, repeated, they may appear outwardly as fixed as they are held within. Whence Pharaoh’s dream too is doubled.
42.9: **“So Eliphaz the Themanite, and Baldad the Suhite, and Sophar the Naamathite went, and did as the Lord had spoken to them, and the Lord accepted the face of Job.”** — by praying for others, he profited himself
42.10:
**“The Lord also was turned at the penance of Job, when he prayed for his friends.”**
• see then the order: correction follows the excess, penance the correction, pardon the penance, gifts the pardon
• Samuel: “Obedience is better than sacrifices,” because by sacrifices another’s flesh, by obedience one’s own will is slain; so, the pride of his own choice being held down, man appeases God more quickly. The virtue of obedience is shown from its opposite, because to refuse to obey is as the sin of witchcraft and as it were the crime of idolatry. So obedience alone is what possesses the merit of faith, without which each one is convicted as faithless. Solomon: “An obedient man shall speak of victory,” because while we are humbly subject to another’s voice, we overcome ourselves in the heart. It is to be known that evil is never to be done through obedience, but sometimes, through obedience, a good that is being done ought to be broken off. For the tree in paradise which God forbade man to touch was not evil; but so that man, made well, might grow through the better merit of obedience, it was fitting that he should forbid him even something good, so that what he did might be the more truly virtue, the more, ceasing even from good, he showed himself more humbly subject to his author. But it is to be noted that it is said: “Of every tree of paradise thou shalt eat: but of the tree of knowledge of good and evil, thou shalt not eat.” For he who forbids his subjects any good must grant many things, lest the mind of the obedient perish utterly, if, driven back from all good things, it fasts entirely. Sometimes the prosperous things of this world are commanded, sometimes the adverse. So if anyone pants after prosperous things from his own desire, when they are commanded him he empties himself of the virtue of obedience. If he undergoes adverse things unwilling and against his will, he lessens for himself the merit of obedience. So let us serve in prosperous things from the command alone, in adverse things from devotion alone; as Moses has nothing of his own, because he is let off by prayers so as not to be set over Israel; Paul is led into adversity even of his own will.
**“The Lord also was turned”** — The Lord also was turned: it is plainly shown that, repenting for himself, he deserved to be heard the more quickly the more devoutly he interceded for others; which each one then heaps up more truly if he spends it even for his adversaries. It was shown before that he was heard for his friends; here it is said of himself, that he obtained this by praying for others.
**“And the Lord gave Job twice as much as he had before.”**
• by praying even for others they profit themselves
• And the Lord gave, etc. Because by the kindness of the gracious judge the supports of consolation overcome the loss of our temptation, the testing tempts him less than the reward consoles him.
42.11:
**“And all his brethren came to him, and all his sisters,”** — And there came, etc. So then brothers and sisters come to Christ, when out of that people which is joined to him by kinship, either those who will be strong, as brothers, or the weak, as sisters, run together to him through the knowledge of faith with devout rejoicing. Then they ate bread in his house, when, the keeping of the letter being set aside, they are fed in the Church on the mystical word as on the marrow of the grain.
**“and all that knew him before,”** — And all that, etc. For no one who fully learned the law was ignorant that Christ was to be born. Whence too they answer Herod: “In Bethlehem of Juda.”
**“and they ate bread with him in his house:”** — They ate with him, etc. In the eating of bread charity, in the moving of the head wonder is designated.
**“and bemoaned him”** — And bemoaned him (literally, moved the head over him): in this place to move the head is to shake off the insensibility of the mind, and to draw near to the knowledge of faith with steps of cruelty …
**“and comforted him”** — And comforted him: to comfort one struck with grief is to rejoice with him over his pardon after the blow. For the more anyone is seen to grow cheerful over the restored health of his neighbour, the more he shows that he grieved over its taking away. Those comfort Christ, comfort the Church, who come to their senses from unbelief and forsake the wickedness by which they had fought against him. But in the scourge they would not comfort, because at the time of his passion the Hebrews scorned to believe in God. Whence the Psalm: “I looked for one that would comfort me, and I found none.” So at the end the believing Hebrews gather together and pay the vows of their offerings to the Redeemer in the power of the Godhead, as to Job made whole.
**“And every man gave him one ewe, and one earring of gold.”**
• by these gifts we are compelled to seek a mystery allegorically
• And gave him, etc. By the ewe innocence, by the earring obedience, that is, the hearing adorned with the grace of humility, is expressed. And though these things were truly said according to the history, yet they were done in figure of holy Church. Who, even if she now loses many through the blow of temptation, yet at the end receives double, when, the gentiles having been taken up, Judea too consents to the faith. And it is to be noted that in this place the ewe is offered with the earring and the earring with the ewe, because the adornment of obedience is joined to innocent minds, as the Lord bears witness: “My sheep hear my voice.” So no one offered blessed Job an earring without a ewe, and no one a ewe without an earring, because he does not obey our Redeemer who is not innocent, and he cannot be innocent who scorns to obey. And because obedience itself is to be kept not from fear but from charity, they are said to have offered a golden earring, so that in the obedience which is shown charity may shine, which surpasses all virtues as gold the other metals. But because no true obedience, no innocence can be in the divisions of heretics, they offer a ewe, but one; that is, coming to holy Church with innocence and obedience, let them bring a mind which the schisms of sects do not divide. And because at the end the Jews, at the call of Elias, will come more abundantly to this banquet with gifts, there is added:
42.12:
**“And the Lord blessed the latter end of Job”** — And the Lord blessed, etc. Job is blessed more in his latter end than in his beginning, because, as regards the taking up of the people of Israel, as the end of the world presses on, the Lord consoles the grief of holy Church with a manifold gathering of souls.
**“more than his beginning.”** — More than his beginning, etc. “They shall still increase in a fruitful old age,” because when life is put off, strength is drawn out for the better, and by the increase of the times the struggles of merits grow.
**“And he had”** — of these it was said more fully at the beginning
**“fourteen thousand sheep”** — Fourteen thousand sheep: these are plainly seen to be double, but the sons are said to have been given back as many as were lost, so that those who had been killed may be shown to live; and so these too are double, because God restored ten to him in the flesh, and kept the ten who had been lost in the hidden life of souls.
42.14:
**“And he called the names of one Dies,”** — that is, light
**“And he called the names of one Dies”** — And he called the names of one Dies: everyone who is chosen by the mercy of the Redeemer is designated by these names, because in creating the human race he made it Dies (Day), in redeeming it Cassia (for “we are the good odour of Christ unto God”), and in taking it up Cornustibii. For we who were created light, and are now Cassia, redeemed, shall one day be Cornustibii, taken up in the exultation of eternal praise. And Cornustibii is compounded of cornu (horn) and tibia (pipe). So by Cornustibii the song of those who rejoice is expressed. First too man shone as with day by his creation; afterwards, redeemed, he is filled with the fragrance of virtues, by which what he lost is restored; thirdly, in the resurrection of the flesh, he will be taken up into the harmony of eternal praise; but before the wedding he prepares the bride so as to fill her.
**“and the name of the second Cassia,”** — the fragrance of virtues
**“and the name of the third Cornustibii.”** — the song of those who rejoice
42.15:
**“And there were not found in all the earth women so beautiful as the daughters of Job:”** — Whence: “And there were not found … women so beautiful,” etc. For the souls of the elect surpass, in the grace of their beauty, the whole human race that lives on earth after the manner of man; and the more they despise themselves by afflicting themselves outwardly, the more truly they are set in order within.
**“and their father gave them inheritance among their brethren.”** — but because among the perfect there are also the weak, to these too the father kindly gives inheritance with the brothers
**“and their father gave them inheritance”** — And their father gave them inheritance: so they are recalled as beautiful, from the number of the perfect. They also, as from the figure of the imperfect, as weak women, receive inheritance among their brothers. So the sisters are admitted with the strong to heavenly things. For by the custom of the old life women do not have inheritance among males, because the severity of the law, choosing the strong and scorning the weak, strove to ordain strict things rather than kind ones. But when the merciful Redeemer came, the weak too is taken up with the perfect into the kingdom.
42.16:
**“And Job lived after these things, a hundred and forty years, and he saw his children, and his children's children, unto the fourth generation, and he died an old man, and full of days.”** — And Job lived after these things, etc. He is empty of days who, however long he has lived, wastes the times of his age in vanity. But on the contrary he is called full of days whose days by no means pass away by perishing, but from the daily reward of good work are kept with the just judge even after they have passed. In figure of the Church: if we multiply fourteen by ten, we come to the number one hundred and forty. And the Church is rightly reckoned by ten and four multiplied, because, keeping both Testaments, and living both according to the decalogue of the law and according to the four books of the Gospel, she stretches up to the height of perfection. And Job is well said to live after the scourges, because the Church is first struck by the scourge of discipline and afterwards made strong by perfection of life. Who also sees her children and her children’s children unto the fourth generation, because in this age, which turns through the four seasons of the year, she beholds offspring being born to her through the mouths of the preachers to the end of the world. She sees her children’s children when from the same faithful she begets others to faith and recognizes others. Who dies an old man and full of days, because, as the light follows, from the reward of daily works, laying down the weight of corruption, she is changed to the incorruption of the spiritual fatherland.
